### Series title page

**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, ENTIRE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIMES OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION WHICH HAVE SURVIVED THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, CAREFULLY CORRECTED BY COLLATION WITH THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS COMPLETED DURING THE THREE MOST RECENT CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH SPECIAL ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING THE INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ARRANGED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY SET WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND ALSO WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER BELOW; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DUBIOUS AND APOCRYPHAL WHICH YET POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDEXES: the first, an index of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers wrote upon any theme may be seen at a glance; the second, an index of Holy Scripture, by which the reader may readily ascertain which Fathers commented upon individual scriptural passages from each book, and in what places in their works. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if one weighs: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the completeness of the correction, both the variety and the number of works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently uniform throughout the course of the whole work, the low price, and, especially, this one methodical and chronological collection of six hundred fragments and shorter works hitherto scattered here and there, now for the first time gathered together in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

# In the Year of the Lord 1136: Honorius of Autun

## Prolegomena

[Col. 0009]

# Historical-Literary Notices Concerning the Life and Writings of Honorius

## I

(Dom Roger Wilmans, Preface to the fragments of Honorius’s *Summary of the Whole* and *Image of the World*, published in vol. X of the distinguished Pertz’s *Writers of Germany*)

A remarkable fate indeed befell Honorius, priest of Autun: though he was the author of many books and held a distinguished place among the learned writers of his age, learned men in more recent times have tried to deprive him both of his name and of his country.

> [Note: [Col. 0009] Honorius himself supplies, at the end of his work *On the Lights of the Church, or On Ecclesiastical Writers* (*Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons, XX, p. 1038), a catalogue of books whose subjects are for the most part irrelevant to our purpose. Nearly all the titles of the books, with the author’s name omitted, occur in the catalogue of books which Brother Henry bestowed upon this church, namely Göttweig; Pez published this document, written in the twelfth century, in *Novus Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, II, p. VIII. Compare also Trithemius, ed. Fabricius, p. 90, and *Magna Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris, 1654, IX, 1135.]

They deprived him of his name without justification. For what the distinguished F. C. Lebret argued on this subject in our *Annals*—namely, that the true name of our writer was Luitold—cannot stand at all.

> [Note: [Col. 0009] *Archiv*, V, 528.]

For when we examine the passage in the supplement to the *Chronicle of Mondsee* (Munich, 1749, quarto) upon which Lebret’s conjecture rests, we readily understand that Luitold was not the author’s name, but the name of the copyist of the Mondsee manuscript.

> [Note: [Col. 0009] In the cited work, p. 392, the following is listed among the books of the monastery of Mondsee: “Honorius Christianus, addressed to a solitary, *On the Image of the World*. Its first book describes the globe of the whole world, its second the times of the world, its third the kingdoms of the world from Adam to Philip, king of the Romans, brother [son] of Frederick; copied by the hand of Luitold, professed monk of Mondsee. Parchment, quarto, twelfth century.” These facts plainly show that it is the same manuscript as the Viennese one examined by Pertz (*Archiv*, II, 537; X, 497). Moreover, it is established that all the manuscript books of the library of Mondsee [Col. 0010] were brought to Vienna after the suppression of the monastery.]

Much more important, however, are the arguments advanced by Lebeuf concerning Honorius’s native country.

> [Note: [Col. 0010] *Recueil de divers écrits*, Paris, 1738, I, 254.]

From the character of the third book of *On the Image of the World*, from which we too shall give a few passages concerning German affairs, Lebeuf wishes to infer that the writer was German by nationality and could by no means have been born in the Burgundian town of Autun.

> [Note: [Col. 0010] For in Honorius there is mention of no kings or cities except those of Germany. Whether the statements Lebeuf makes on p. 266 concerning the pallium of the bishop of Autun are correct, others may judge.]

Yet one consideration seems to stand in the way of the learned man’s opinion—an opinion otherwise highly meritorious in the field of medieval antiquities: namely, that Honorius calls himself “of Autun” at the end of the aforementioned book *On the Lights of the Church*.

> [Note: [Col. 0010] In *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons, XX, p. 1038, he speaks of himself as follows: “Honorius, priest and scholastic of the Church of Autun, published works not to be despised, etc., etc. This little book on the lights of the Church follows Jerome and Gennadius. He flourished under Henry V. Posterity will see who shall write after him.”]

Nothing certain is known of Honorius’s life, and only a few things are established concerning his age.

> [Note: [Col. 0010] Honorius dedicated his commentary on the Song of Songs to Abbot Simon, and his commentary on the book of David to the latter’s predecessor Cono; see *Archiv*, X, 613. Nothing further has hitherto been ascertainable concerning these abbots.]

That he flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century may be inferred from his own works. For in the second book of *On the Image of the World*, while discussing the method of finding the year of the Lord, he plainly indicates that he wrote after 1112 and before 1137.

> [Note: [Col. 0010] II, ch. 93 (*Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum Lugdunensis*, vol. XX). Following Wattenbach’s conjecture, we give the passage in this corrected form: “To find the year of the Lord,” etc. (See *Image of the World*, book III, ch. 93.)]

If you compare this passage with the conclusion of *On the Lights of the Church* quoted above, where he declares that he himself flourished during the reign of Henry V, you will not doubt that he had already completed between 1122 and 1125 those works which he himself lists there, including the *Summary* and *On the Image of the World*, but that later he repeatedly issued both books enlarged by continuations.

The first edition of *On the Image of the World*, which ends with the eighteenth year of Henry V, that is, the year 1123,

[Col. 0011]

was unknown to everyone until the present day, when it was discovered by Pertz and put to our use. It survives in the Cotton manuscript collection, Cleopatra B. IV, parchment, twelfth century.

Honorius’s other historical work, which he himself calls, in the catalogue of books published by him, the *Summary of the Whole Concerning Universal History*,

> [Note: [Col. 0011] In the catalogue of books at Göttweig cited above, the same book occurs under this title: “Summary of the Whole, containing a chronicle from the beginning of the world down to our times.” Trithemius, ed. Fabricius, p. 90, calls it the *Summary History*.]

had long been known to Arnold Wion,

> [Note: [Col. 0011] Compare his *Tree of Life*, II, ch. 69, vol. I, p. 426: “A *Summary of Histories or Chronicles*, a great work; formerly in the possession of Lazius, but now a manuscript in the imperial library at Vienna.”]

but had not yet seen the light of day, so that Pez himself wondered whether it might still be found.

> [Note: [Col. 0011] *Novus Thesaurus*, II, p. VI.]

It survives in two Viennese manuscripts, of which:

1. The first, Imperial Library 382, *Historia profana* 81, formerly 48, written on parchment folio, passed, according to Arnold Wion’s testimony, from the books of Lazius into the Imperial Library. It is now defective, since the final quire is lacking, in which was contained the history of events from the reign of Constantius IV onward.

2. The second, 3415, *Historia profana* 451, paper folio, fifteenth century, bequeathed in 1540 by Bishop Johann Faber to the College of Saint Nicholas, is of excellent quality. Wattenbach transcribed it from the year 726 onward, and it supplied the basis for our edition. Since it ends in the twelfth year of the Emperor Lothair, 1135–1136, it is clear that it presents to us the text of the second or third edition.

> [Note: [Col. 0011] It nevertheless carries events only as far as the year 1133.]

Honorius himself indicates in his preface the purpose that led him to compose this compendium: “For there are many,” he says, “who plead, as though they were legitimate causes of their ignorance, that they lack an accumulation of books. Mercifully providing for these, I have gathered this compendium from the whole of Scripture; in it I have considered a sufficient provision to be made for those hastening toward the homeland of life.”

But if you ask what sources he used in constructing the work, it is impossible to resolve the matter so as to leave no doubt. For he certainly drew more than once upon Einhard’s *Annals of Fulda*

> [Note: [Col. 0011] Years 807, 822, 824, 825.]

and Sigebert,

> [Note: [Col. 0011] Years 825, 874, 877.]

and many passages of the *Chronicle of Würzburg* (*Scriptores*, VI, 17, 32) prove that Honorius also made use of that chronicle: passages borrowed verbatim from our author precisely where the Würzburg chronicler adds something of his own

> [Note: [Col. 0011] Years 726–800, 824, 841, 877, 888–1067.]

or proceeds independently.

> [Note: [Col. 0011] For example, *Scriptores*, VI, p. 26, lines 44, 45, 63; p. 28, line 47; p. 30, lines 31, 59.]  
> [Note: [Col. 0012] Cited work, p. 31, from line 23 onward.]

A similar relationship exists between Honorius and the Annalist of Würzburg (*Scriptores*, II, 328 ff.); to the latter he plainly owes the years 1067–1087.

Apart from these, however, some matters remain whose origin it has either been impossible to discover altogether or permissible only to conjecture. Such are the accounts by Honorius of the foundations of the cities of Bremen, Bamberg, and Speyer, and of the conversion of pagan peoples; these occur in almost the same words in the *Salzburg Chronicle* (*Scriptores*, IX). Since in that chronicle these matters are assigned to definite years, everyone sees that they cannot have flowed from Honorius. We must therefore conclude that both Honorius and the Salzburg chronicler drew from a source now hidden from us. There are certain considerations which seem to prove that this source was the book excerpted from Hermann of Reichenau, enlarged by a monk of St Gall with notices taken from elsewhere, and then copied at Göttweig.

> [Note: [Col. 0012] Compare Pertz, *Scriptores*, V, 73.]

For Pertz, who inspected this manuscript, states that it was also used by the Salzburg monk. A second argument, no less weighty, is added. For, again according to Pertz,

> [Note: [Col. 0012] Cited work, p. 74.]

that Göttweig book contains a notice concerning Kempten in the year 774. This notice is absent from the *Salzburg Chronicle*, the *Würzburg Chronicle*, and Hermann himself, but is found in our author.

Honorius reduced this *Summary* again to an epitome when, in the third book of the *Image of the World*, in setting forth the arrangement of the globe, he proposed to give an outline history of events from Adam down to his own times. The Munich manuscripts, diligently collated by the distinguished Foringer, keeper of the Royal Library at Munich, who kindly communicated their variant readings to us, show that at least five editions of this book were published by Honorius himself. Among these editions:

The first edition of 1123, mentioned by Honorius himself, survives in one London manuscript (see above); we designate it 1 A.

The second, composed in 1132 or 1133, survives in the Kaisheim manuscript (Munich Library 74), which is the basis of our edition; the Aldersbach manuscript (ibid. 81), written in the twelfth century; the London manuscript (Arundel no. 270),

> [Note: [Col. 0012] Compare *Scriptores*, VII, A. 2.]

and the Fulda manuscript of the late twelfth century.

> [Note: [Col. 0012] Formerly Weingarten, shelfmark G. 11. The same hand which wrote all the works in this most excellent manuscript—the Weingarten Chronographer, Honorius of Autun, and the fables of Fulgentius—added a very brief continuation extending to the death of Henry VI, which we shall print below. A hand nearly contemporary with it, using paler ink, appended another, more explicit continuation, embracing events from the death of Henry VI to 1208. Gerard Hess published this from this very manuscript of ours, *Monumenta Guelfica*, p. 71. “Whose descendant—down to p. 76—held the kingdom.”]

The first two agree completely with one another and we designate them 1; the London manuscript 1 B; and finally the Fulda manuscript 1 C. They end in the eighth year of Lothair.

The third, written in 1139, in the second year of Conrad III, indiction II, is found in the manuscripts:

- Latin Munich 536, twelfth century (siglum 2);
- St Emmeram DLXXIII, thirteenth century (siglum 3);
- Schäftlarn, following Otto of Freising’s *Chronicle*, parchment manuscript Munich 1003, twelfth century (siglum 4);
- St Emmeram FLXXVII, paper, fifteenth century (siglum 4*).

The fourth, written after 1139 and before 1152, survives in the manuscripts:

- Tegernsee 368, paper, fourteenth century (siglum 5);
- St Emmeram CLII, paper, fifteenth century (siglum 6);
- Colmar, parchment, octavo, thirteenth century, collated by Pertz (siglum 6a);
- Melk D. 23, folio, parchment, twelfth century, collated by Pertz (siglum 6b);
- Zwettl 172, described by Wattenbach, parchment, twelfth century (siglum 6c); and
- Herold’s Basel edition of 1544 (siglum 11).

The fifth, published after 1152, survives in the manuscripts:

- St Emmeram G. CXV, twelfth century (siglum 7);
- Indersdorf 393, twelfth or thirteenth century (siglum 8);
- Polling 36, twelfth or thirteenth century (siglum 9);

[Col. 0013]

- Oberalteich 211, fifteenth century (siglum 9a); and in the first editions (siglum 10),

> [Note: [Col. 0013] A monk of Hamersteben used a similar exemplar; Waitz examined his excerpts, Wolfenbüttel, Augustan collection 76, 30, paper, sixteenth century.]

as well as the Speyer edition of 1583 (siglum 12).

Honorius appears to have died not long after 1152. This may readily be inferred concerning a writer who expressly affirms that between 1122 and 1125 he had already flourished and published the greater part of his books.

So far as I know, Honorius is cited by only one medieval writer, Engelhus,

> [Note: [Col. 0013] In Leibniz, *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium*, II, 1110.]

who seems to have used a continuation of the *Image of the World* enlarged with additional material. The *Summary*, however, was frequently copied by the monks of Admont in the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries; from this book they drew certain notes added in the margin to Otto of Freising’s *Chronicle*.

> [Note: [Col. 0013] Admont manuscript 164, folio, parchment, late twelfth century. These notes occur at the end of V, 31, 33; VI, 27; VII, 15.]

We shall print the entire *Summary* from the year 726 onward, a portion of the first book of the *Image of the World* concerning Germany, and the end of the third book. To these we shall append the continuations of the *Image of the World* which the Munich manuscripts contain, together with those transcribed by Pertz from manuscript 1 B, and by Wattenbach from manuscript 6c and the Vienna and Admont manuscripts.

**Roger Wilmans**

## II

(*Literary History of France*, by Benedictine Religious, vol. XII, p. 165.)

### § I. — History of the Life of Honorius

[lacuna] the title of this article

> [Note: [Col. 0013] “Honorius, priest and scholastic of the Church of Autun, [Col. 0014] later a solitary.”]

states almost everything that we certainly know about the person of Honorius. If Arnoul Wion is to be believed,

> [Note: [Col. 0014] *Lignum vitae*, book II, p. 69.]

the designation “Solitary” borne by him ought to be understood as “Monk”; from this Wion concludes that he was a Benedictine. This is a conjecture which nothing compels us either to accept or reject.

The stories of other modern historians are different.

> [Note: [Col. 0014] Vigner, *Bibliothèque historique*, under the year 1120; Munier, *Recherches sur Autun*, p. 41; Saulnier, *Autun chrétien*, p. 96.]

Some place Honorius in the episcopal see of Autun; others relate that, when that see was offered to him, he refused it in order to follow King Louis the Younger on crusade. These anecdotes, visibly begotten by imagination, do not merit the trouble of a critical refutation.

M. Le Beuf’s singular opinion concerning Honorius’s homeland, though no truer, demands rather more consideration. In one of his dissertations,

> [Note: [Col. 0014] *Dissertations*, vol. I, p. 254 ff.]

this scholar undertakes to take the writer not only from the Church of Autun but from France itself, in order to give Germany the credit of his birth. These are the reasons by which he supports this historical paradox.

First, he maintains that the surname *Augustodunensis*, by which the Honorius with whom we are concerned is distinguished from others of the same name, has misled people in two respects.

1. He says that nobody before Trithemius styled him thus. Yet he admits that this designation occurs at the end of a work by Honorius himself: his treatise *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, whose final article reads: “Honorius, priest of the Church of Autun, published works not to be despised.” But this passage does not trouble the dissertation writer, because he regards it as an addition made by a foreign hand. Proof of this assertion, which he merely advances, would not have been superfluous. Let us nevertheless suppose the addition genuine: at least it must be admitted that it precedes Trithemius’s age by a considerable time, since all the manuscripts upon which the different editions of this treatise were made contained it.

There is more. Honorius bears this same surname in several manuscripts at the head of works from his pen. We shall mention especially manuscript no. 999 of the King’s Library, whose writing belongs to the thirteenth century. There his treatise *On the Jewel of the Soul* occurs with this contemporaneous title: *The Jewel of the Soul of Honorius of Autun*.

2. M. Le Beuf maintains that, even if the disputed designation is accepted, it ought not to be understood of the city of Autun, but either of Augst near Basel or of Augsburg, capital of Swabia. It is true that he has found no monument in which the term *Augustodunensis* is employed to designate a citizen of the latter city; but he found that in the eighth century a bishop of Augst styled himself “Bishop of the Church of Augustodunum.” This discovery inclines him to locate Honorius in that city rather than in either of the other two.

Unfortunately, there is here a minor inconvenience which this critic did not perceive: long before the twelfth century, the town of Augst had been destroyed and its bishopric united to that of Basel. On this point we refer to the learned Schöpflin’s *Alsatia illustrata*.

> [Note: [Col. 0014] P. 677.]

M. Le Beuf next accumulates passages from Honorius through which, according to this critic, Honorius proclaims his German origin. We answer that this proves nothing except that the books from which these passages are extracted were composed in Germany. Indeed, the emphasis with which Honorius speaks of details of that country gives every reason to believe that he lived there for some time. Yet, in order to reconcile all the facts, one must also admit that this was only after he had left the Church and the scholastic office of Autun in order to embrace retirement.

The choice of a foreign land by a man wishing to devote himself to the solitary life contains nothing surprising. Examples of migrations occasioned by such a motive are too common. If we are asked when this change of country occurred, we think it should be placed during the reign of Henry V, about the year 1120. As for the place Honorius chose for his home in Germany, it can be determined only by saying, on his own authority, that it was situated in the lands of the Duke of Austria. We have no more information concerning the date of his death. He was still alive under the pontificate of Innocent II. That is all we are permitted to affirm.

### § II. — His Printed Works

Honorius of Autun was one of the most prolific writers of his century. Although the enumeration of his writings found at the end of his treatise *On Ecclesiastical Writers* is considerable, it is nevertheless far from complete. Many others, later in date than that list, have been discovered. Some of these are in the hands of the public; the rest were described by Dom Bernard Pez with the precision for which that critic is known.

[Col. 0015]

> [Note: [Col. 0015] *Anecdota*, vol. II; introductory dissertation, pp. V–VII. Pez’s dissertation is printed below.]

Obliged to give an account of this entire literary output, we shall begin with the works which Honorius himself attributes to himself—on the understanding, however, that only those which have been published will be mentioned here; the remainder is reserved for the following paragraph.

1. A treatise entitled *Elucidarium*.

> [Note: [Col. 0015] Anselm, works, new edition, pp. 457–488.]

Critics were long divided concerning its true author. On the authority of certain manuscripts, some attributed it to Saint Anselm, under whose name it was printed at Paris in 1560 by Morelet, in one octavo volume, through the care of Claude d’Espence; it was reprinted at Liège in the same format in 1586, and afterwards inserted among the authentic works of the holy doctor in all his editions, except the latest, in which it is relegated to the Appendix.

Others, by a far less plausible conjecture, ascribed it to Saint Augustine. Several gave credit for it to Abelard, some to Guibert of Nogent; and finally there were those who gave it to William of Coventry, a fourteenth-century Carmelite. Dom Rivet,

> [Note: [Col. 0015] *Literary History*, vol. IX, p. 443.]

in his discussion of Saint Anselm, demonstrated very well the falsity of all these attributions.

But the doubt he raises concerning the identity of the *Elucidarium* which we possess and that of Honorius disappears when one consults the account our author gives of his own work in the cited list of writings. For he says that he divided it into three books: the first concerns Jesus Christ, the second the Church, and the third the future life. Now this is precisely the division of the work in the hands of the public.

It is true that some slight difference of principles may be observed between this work and the others which came from Honorius’s pen. But one should note that this is the first attempt of a schoolboy who, pressed by fellow pupils admiring his progress, ventured to commit to writing the result of what he had learned. The preface says: “Having often been asked by my fellow pupils to resolve certain little questions, I was unable to resist their insistence by refusing.” The work indeed reveals a novice hand, but one capable of producing excellent work later. The whole of theology is treated briefly in questions and answers.

There are errors, but not as many as Nicholas Eymerich, the fourteenth-century Dominican, charged against it in the work he wrote in opposition, entitled *The Elucidarium of the Elucidarium*. Despite these blemishes, these first fruits of Honorius’s labor were warmly received for several centuries. The *Elucidarium* was translated twice into French and once into German. None of these translations has yet been printed. Of the two French versions, one in prose, the work of Geoffrey of Waterford, an Irish Dominican of the thirteenth century, belongs to the manuscripts of M. Baluze transferred to the King’s Library. The other, in verse, is found among the manuscripts of the King of England.

> [Note: [Col. 0015] Royal Library of England, p. 292, no. 11.]

We cannot state either its age or its author, because the catalogue that makes it known to us says nothing of either. As for the German translation, Dom Pez assures us that it bears the date 1314.

2. The work entitled *The Seal of Mary*, which must be joined to an *Explanation of the Song of Songs*, of which it is, as it were, a continuation. In the former, the author applies to Jesus Christ and the Holy Virgin what the sacred text which he comments upon in the latter says about the love of Bridegroom and Bride.

The exceptional esteem in which Martin Delrio, a Jesuit, held these two shorter works led him to insert a large part of the second and something of the first in his *Commentary on the Same Book*, printed at Paris in 1604. In his preface he says that Honorius of Autun briefly, learnedly, and ingeniously unveiled the four senses of the Song of Songs; that his work, though very little read, deserves to be read extensively; and that, having found two manuscript copies, he extracted from them everything which seemed to him most noteworthy for the edification of the public.

He then gives a summary of this work, which may be checked against the octavo edition printed at Cologne in 1540 and against the editions found in the great Libraries of the Fathers.

3. A dialogue between master and disciple entitled *The Inevitable*.

> [Note: [Col. 0015] *History of Predestination.*]

Honorius’s purpose in it is to explain the mystery of predestination and reconcile it with free will. This work would be excellent but for two or three passages that give off an odor of Semi-Pelagianism. Yet our author has been accused of falling into the opposite extreme.

It is true that the work presents gross contradictions in the edition published by George Cassander at Basel in 1528 and repeated at Cologne by Sylvius in 1552. This led Father Duchesne, a Jesuit, to say that all the texts do not come from the same pen, or that the author had no common sense.

> [Note: [Col. 0015] In 1528 *The Inevitable* was published after Faustus of Riez’s treatise *On Free Will*, and in 1552  
> [Col. 0016] after several short works of Saint Prosper and Hilary, disciple of Saint Augustine; both editions were octavos, as was Conen’s edition. The work is also reprinted in the collection of Cassander’s works, pp. 623–639.]

The alternative is valid; but one must add that John Conen, a Premonstratensian of Tongeren, more faithful and more sensible than Cassander and guided by better manuscripts, removed these contradictions in a new edition of *The Inevitable* which he published at Antwerp in 1620 and 1624. This edition subsequently entered the three great Libraries of the Fathers.

4. *The Mirror of the Church*, a collection of sermons on various subjects. John Dietemberg published it at Cologne in one octavo volume in 1531, together with the sermons of Saint Caesarius of Arles, whom he mistakenly calls Felicarius. Olearius,

> [Note: [Col. 0016] *Scriptors*, vol. I, book II.]

who knew nothing of this edition, announces as the first and only edition that printed at Basel in 1544.

5. *The Jewel of the Soul* (*Gemma animae*). This is a liturgical compendium divided into four books. The first treats of the Mass, its ceremonies and prayers; of the church, its parts and ornaments; and of the ministers of the altar and their vestments. The second concerns the canonical hours of day and night. The third deals with the principal feasts of the year. The fourth explains how to reconcile the divine office of the entire year with the various days and seasons in which it is celebrated. M. Dupin [Note: [Col. 0016] Twelfth Century, p. 518.] gives a very sound judgment on this work when he says that it is full of mystical reasons and explanations having no basis other than the author’s imagination. Nevertheless, in its literal portions one observes valuable traces of twelfth-century liturgy and other ecclesiastical usages.

Thus, for example, it shows that when the bishop proceeded to the altar, he was accompanied by two priests and preceded by seven deacons, seven subdeacons, and an equal number of acolytes, each carrying a candlestick (bk. I, ch. 4); that after making his confession he gave the kiss to the two priests (ch. 7); that the first deacon and the first subdeacon kissed the altar with him when he had ascended it (ch. 3); that the hosts [Col. 0017] were made in the shape of a denarius, *in modum denarii*—“in the form of a denarius” [Note: [Col. 0017] This practice of making the breads to be consecrated so small had been introduced as early as the preceding century; and Bertinold, a priest of Constance who was writing at that time, complained in his *Exposition of the Roman Order* that the bread offered had been reduced to a form so small and so [Col. 0018] thin that it had scarcely any longer the appearance of bread. In mockery he called these offerings *minutias nummulariarum oblatarum*, “the trifling bits of coin-like offerings.” [[Col. 0017] Georg. Cassander, *Liturg.*, Cologne edition, ch. 21, pp. 66–77.]], and did not exceed it in size (ch. 35); that an image of the Savior, together with the letters of his name, was impressed upon them, just as the image and name of the ruler were impressed upon coinage; that the singers wore caps upon their heads and carried staffs in their hands (ch. 228); that two of them presented at the altar, one the bread upon a cloth and the other the wine; that the archdeacon’s duty was to pour the wine into the chalice (ch. 38); that the episcopal staff was of wood, its curved portion of ivory, with a golden or crystal knob joining the two parts together (ch. 219); that abbots’ croziers differed from bishops’ by having a black curved part (ch. 238); and that, after anointing the baptized person’s head with oil, the priests covered it with a mitre, which he kept for eight days (bk. III, chs. 111, 113).

Speaking of the ceremonies of Easter, Honorius says that at Rome, on that day, when the pope enters the church, tow is kindled above his head; its sparks are caught by the ministers or fall to the ground. This ceremony, he adds, was instituted to warn him that all things are reduced to ashes and that he himself must return to them.

His precision in speaking of the Eucharist earns him a distinguished place among witnesses to the tradition concerning the doctrine of the real presence. With reference to this mystery he says (bk. I, ch. 105) that “as the world was made from nothing by the word of God, so likewise, by the word of Jesus Christ his Son, the nature of these things”—the bread and wine offered in the sacrifice—“is truly changed into the body and blood of Our Lord.” And below (ch. 106): “The term mystery,” he says, “is used when one sees one thing and understands another: thus one sees the species of bread and wine, but believes them to be the body and blood of Jesus Christ.” Had Thomas Walden attended to these words, he would have been more equitable toward our author; and, instead of placing him, as he did [Note: [Col. 0018] Vol. II, ch. 90.], among Berengar’s adherents, he would have counted him among his most declared opponents.

This work is one of our author’s productions that has been most frequently reprinted. The first edition appeared at Leipzig in quarto in 1514. The second, issued at Cologne in 1549, forms part of a folio volume containing Amalarius’s and Walafrid Strabo’s treatises *On Ecclesiastical Rites*, together with the Liturgy of Saint Basil and the Life of Saint Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz; the whole was collected through the care of Johann Cochlaeus. The third, published in the same city in 1568, contains in a folio volume several other treatises by various authors on the same subject. The fourth came from the Venetian presses in 1572, together with several analogous writings gathered in an octavo volume under the common title *Mirror of the Church*. The fifth, produced at Rome in 1590, and the sixth, at Paris in 1610, are merely repetitions of the third. Finally, the work was reprinted in the three great *Libraries of the Fathers*.

6. *The Sacramentary*, or treatise on the causes and mystical meaning of rites. There is only one edition of this work, for which the public is indebted to the care of Dom Bernard Pez. Its subject is the same as that of the preceding four books, treated in the same manner, but more briefly and with somewhat greater order and method.

7. *The Hexaemeron*, or treatise on the work of the six days. Honorius addresses it to his pupils, for whose use and at whose request he says he composed it. He advises those who are pleased with it to place it at the head of his *Elucidarium*. The reason is not very evident. This writing is merely a mystical and highly labored explanation of the first chapter of Genesis. The author counts 4,184 years from the creation of the world to the Incarnation. He assigns the Blessed Virgin only twelve years when she gave birth to the Savior, who, he maintains, suffered at the age of thirty-four. These are the sole remarkable features of this commentary, which Dom Pez likewise brought out of obscurity. This editor maintains that the preface and the final chapter are not by Honorius. His proof is that both pieces are absent from the Melk copy, which is five hundred years old.

8. *The Eucharistion*: this is how it must be read according to all the manuscripts, and not *Eucharisticon*, as it is described in all editions of Honorius’s treatise *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. The work, divided into twelve chapters, contains a very faithful exposition of the Church’s belief regarding the sacrament of the Eucharist. Yet, according to Dom Pez, a fifteenth-century hand had written in the margin of the Melk manuscript from which he drew it the following note: “It seems that this book ought not to be read publicly, because of certain points in which the author appears either to have erred, or at least to have expressed himself in such a way that he cannot be understood without great application.” But the learned editor rightly observes that this note is by an ignorant scholastic who wished to judge the expressions of the ancients according to the petty questions debated in his own day. He then proves that Honorius expressed himself very correctly concerning the doctrine of the real presence and transubstantiation.

9. *Knowledge of Life*, or *Treatise on God and Eternal Life*. This book, to which the author gave the form of a conversation between a master and his disciples—or, according to the Melk manuscript, between a solitary and his hearers—bears the name of Saint Augustine in a manuscript in the King’s library [Note: [Col. 0018] St Augustine, *Works*, vol. VI, appendix, pp. 169–183.]. It was from a similar copy that the Greeks, having learned of this work, translated a considerable fragment of it into their language under the following title, which we render in French as: *Opinions of Saint Augustine on the Trinity, drawn from his book Knowledge of the True Life, in which, in dialogue form, the brethren ask questions and the master answers.*

This fragment, comprising chapter 11 and those following through chapter 18, except chapter 15, which was omitted, is found in a collection of Latin Fathers translated into Greek, printed at Basel in 1578 through the care of Leunclavius. But the latest editors of Saint Augustine have proved very well that one cannot fail to recognize Honorius as the author of this treatise, which they inserted in full among the spurious works of that holy Doctor.

In the preface our author indicates that he was the target of envy’s darts, and that he did not receive them with indifference. He exhorts his adversaries to lay aside the poison that consumes them, to adopt charitable dispositions, and to follow him peacefully into the vast forest of Scripture, which he is ready to enter—not to introduce new material there, as they accuse him of doing, but to gather there the fruit of life. He then sets out his purpose, which is to treat the principal truths of Christian philosophy.

[Col. 0019] Entering upon his subject, he proves that our coarse understanding, accustomed to judge everything by the senses, cannot, without the help of faith, know what concerns God and created spirits. He divides the latter into two kinds: angels and human souls. He shows what they have in common and what distinguishes them. As for the supreme Being, he says, since he is incomprehensible by nature, we cannot determine precisely what he is. Nevertheless, he adds, since the intellectual substance desires in some fashion to know him, let us try to define him, at least imperfectly and enigmatically. Having given the definition commonly used in the schools, he sets himself to prove that God exists. From this he proceeds to the means by which one may attain to see and contemplate him in his glory.

His disciples, satisfied with what he has told them on this point, ask that, after demonstrating to them the unity of the divine essence, he teach them how there is in that same essence a trinity of persons. This is the subject of their conversation from the tenth chapter to the nineteenth. Honorius answers all their questions according to the principles of Saint Augustine and Saint Anselm, frequently employing their words without naming them. The following twenty-eight chapters concern God’s mercy, justice, wisdom, immensity, and immutability; the profundity of his judgments in the unequal distribution of his gifts; the origin of evil; human misery, its cause and its remedy; the necessity and characteristics of faith; the state of souls released from bodies; the manner in which the saints hear our prayers; the resurrection of the dead; and the blessedness of eternal life.

Such is the outline of this treatise, in which one observes a sound and lucid metaphysics drawn from Scripture and tradition. Of all Honorius’s works, it appears to us the most polished, both in the selection and accuracy of its thoughts and in its method and expression.

10. *The Image of the World*, in three books. This work is preceded by two letters: one from a certain Christian, who describes the author as a man endowed with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; the other from Honorius in reply to Christian’s letter. The final sentence of the latter, beginning with the words *ad instructionem*—“for instruction”—is used in certain manuscripts as the beginning of the first book; whereas in all printed editions that book begins *Mundus dicitur*—“The world is called.” This difference misled Dom Rivet [Note: [Col. 0019] *Literary History*, vol. IX, p. 451.] into believing that Honorius’s *Image of the World* was not the same work as that which appeared under this title. It is one of those mistakes that, in a lengthy undertaking full of thorny disputes, escape even the most attentive mind.

We shall give a very brief account of these three books. The first is an abridgment of cosmography such as might have been produced in an age when geography and astronomy were still in their infancy. The author compares the world to an egg and recognizes only three habitable parts of the earth. The second treats of time and its divisions: namely, hours, days, months, years, Olympiads, the various cycles, regulars, concurrents, epacts, the Paschal term, movable feasts, and embolism or intercalation. The third is a brief universal chronology, ending in the earliest editions with Emperor Lothair II and in later editions with Frederick Barbarossa. Perhaps in the autograph it ended with Emperor Henry V. This is all the more probable because the work is earlier than that *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, in which Honorius, speaking of himself, says that he flourished under the empire of that prince.

As many as seven editions of the *Image of the World* are counted [Note: [Col. 0019] Fabricius, bk. VIII, p. 818.]. The first, without indication of place or year, belongs to the beginnings of printing. The second was issued at Nuremberg in 1491 by Caspar Hochfeder. Illyricus produced the third at Basel in 1497, in quarto, attributing the work to Saint Anselm. The fourth—in which Honorius’s name occurs for the first time [Note: [Col. 0020] Library of Saint Allyre of Clermont.]—was again issued at Basel in 1544, together with six other writings by the same author, through the care of Johann Herold, by the heirs of Cratander, in an octavo volume. The fifth, in the same format, dates from Speyer in 1583, printed by Bernhard Albin. The sixth forms part of the twelfth volume of the *Library of the Fathers*, printed at Cologne. The seventh appears in the twentieth volume of the same collection, published at Lyons.

This book was also honored with an Italian translation under the title: *Il libro de Imagine mundi composito da Honorio filosofo solitario, per loquale se potra intendere molte gentilissime e digne cose*—“The book *On the Image of the World*, composed by Honorius, solitary philosopher, through which many very noble and worthy things may be understood.” This translation survives in manuscript in the King’s library [Note: [Col. 0020] Royal manuscript library, no. 7239.].

11. The treatise *On the Pope and the Emperor*, entitled *Summa de Apostolico et Augusto*—“Compendium on the Apostolic [Pope] and the Augustus [Emperor].” The author’s purpose is to establish two propositions: the preeminence of the priesthood over the empire, and the incapacity of secular princes to confer ecclesiastical dignities. On the first point, Dom Pez, the editor of this book, very judiciously observes that if Honorius had confined himself within proper limits, by merely preferring one order to the other, he would have encountered few opponents in his own time or ours. For the essential point in dispute was not which of the two orders ought to prevail, but what consequences followed from the preeminence rather generally conceded to the first. It was these consequences that were disputed: some exaggerated them without measure, while others restricted them with equal indiscretion.

Honorius, siding with the former, goes so far as to maintain that it belongs to the pope to elect the emperor with the consent of the princes, as likewise to consecrate and crown him. On the second point he reasons as follows, and this is not the worst reasoning in his book: “I ask whether ecclesiastical dignities are spiritual or secular. Every sensible person will doubtless answer me that they are of the former kind. I ask again what is the nature of royal power. I shall be told that it is secular. Therefore,” I shall reply, “it does not belong to that power to confer a spiritual dignity.”

He then investigates the origin of the contrary practice and believes that he finds it in an alleged privilege granted by Pope Leo III to Emperor Charlemagne, to establish in his name and as his vicar bishoprics in Gaul and Germany. But as soon as the Church saw, he says, that men without morals and without reverence for her, having seized the empire without the pope’s consent, were taking it upon themselves to sell bishoprics and other ecclesiastical dignities for money, then, struck by the abuse and profanation they made of sacred things, she wisely withdrew her rights from the hands of strangers, in order to dispense them herself according to the laws of propriety and equity.

12. *The Ladder of Heaven*, a mystical work divided into two parts that bear little relation to one another: the great and the little ladder. Before Dom Pez, who brought out its edition, it was taken as certain, on the authority of Antoine Hierat, that the *Ladder of Heaven* was the same work as the treatise *On the Affections of the Sun*, of which we shall speak below. But now that both writings are available, it is evident that they differ from each other as much as morality, the subject of the first, differs from physics, with which the second is concerned.

[Col. 0021] 13. *Explanation of the Psalter*. This commentary, like that on the *Song of Songs* and the treatise *Image of the World*, is dedicated to Abbot Conon, probably the same man who passed from the abbey of Siegburg to the archbishopric of Regensburg in 1126. In the preface Honorius says that he adopted as his text the Gallican Psalter rather than the Roman, because the former was in use in the churches of the country where he was. Now, he adds, the Gallican Psalter is that translated from the Septuagint, whereas the Roman was made from Symmachus, or from I know not what other interpreter.

He then explains what the Psalter is and why it is so called. Next he treats the subject, object, arrangement, and author of the Psalter. This preface, in which some good things occur among many useless statements and falsehoods, was published by Dom Pez together with a small number of the psalms commented upon by Honorius: namely Psalms I, V, L, LI, C, CI, and CL. The editor states that complete copies of this work exist not only among the manuscripts of Melk Abbey, but also in other German libraries, which he identifies. He adds that at the end of these manuscripts there is a commentary by the same author on the canticles sung at Lauds and Vespers, and on the Apostles’ Creed.

14. The catalogue or treatise *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, entitled *De luminaribus Ecclesiae*—“On the Luminaries of the Church.” Of its four books, the first is drawn from Saint Jerome; the second from Gennadius, whose judgment on Cassian and Saint Prosper the author adopts, deciding in favor of the former in the disputes they had concerning grace. The third is only an abridgment of Saint Isidore. The fourth, borrowed for the greater part from Bede and other bibliographers, contains only seventeen authors, Rupert being the next to last and Honorius himself the last. Of both it is said that they flourished during the reign of Emperor Henry V, which shows that this work was composed during Rupert’s lifetime; Rupert died under Lothair II.

It has already been observed that M. Le Beuf regards the article on Honorius as an addition made by a foreign hand. Before him Fabricius had entertained the same thought because the following praise of our author occurs there, in connection with his commentary on the *Song of Songs*: *Miro modo Cantica canticorum exposuit, ita ut prius exposita non videantur*—“He expounded the *Song of Songs* in a wonderful fashion, so that it seems not to have been expounded previously.” But might it not be answered that Honorius, acting as historian, spoke of his work as the public spoke of it at that time? What is certain is that this article occurs in all editions and all extant manuscripts, and that it appeared in one of the oldest manuscripts, from which the fifteenth-century Melk manuscript was copied.

Besides the three great *Libraries of the Fathers*, in which this catalogue found a place, we have four other editions. The first forms part of the seven writings by our author printed, as already stated, at Basel in 1544. The second appeared at Cologne in octavo in 1580, printed by Maternus, among analogous works by Saint Jerome, Gennadius, Saint Isidore, Sigebert, and Henry of Ghent, through the care of Suffridus Petrus. The third was published by Aubert le Mire in his collection of the same bibliographers, issued at Antwerp in 1639 in a folio volume; this edition was renewed by M. Fabricius at Hamburg in 1718, with notes throwing great light on the text.

Such are the printed works of our author listed in the catalogue or treatise of which we have just given an account.

Among those not named there, but possessed by the public, the most considerable is the treatise *On the Philosophy of the World*, divided into four books. It appears at the head of the seven writings by Honorius published at Basel in 1544. It subsequently entered the great *Libraries of the Fathers* at Cologne and Lyons.

In the first book our author speaks of God, the soul of the world, angels, and the human soul. Having proved God’s existence from the necessity of admitting Providence, he investigates why the Father is called power, the Son wisdom, and the Holy Spirit will; and why creation is attributed to the Father, the incarnation to the Son, and the remission of sins to the Holy Spirit. Concerning the soul of the world, he proposes various opinions and refers the reader, to learn his own, to his glosses on Plato, which are no longer extant [Note: [Col. 0021] “Fragments of Honorius on Plato were recently published by Dom Cousin in the appendix to Abelard’s book *Sic et non* [*Yes and No*].” [Col. 0022] EDITOR.].

He distinguishes two kinds of angels: the good and the evil. Of the former he makes three classes. The first, according to him, inhabits the firmament in order to regulate the course of the stars; the second resides in the heaven of the planets; the third is dispersed over the earth to care for humankind. He says almost nothing of the human soul because, he says, he is to treat it thoroughly in the final book. From there he proceeds to the principles of physics and concludes with arguments concerning the manner in which creation was carried out.

The subject of the second book is the arrangement of heaven.

The third concerns water, air, fire, the five zones, rains, and other meteorological phenomena.

The fourth treats of the earth and its inhabitants. But what principally occupies Honorius is man, of whom he provides a fairly extensive but nevertheless very superficial anatomical description. What he says concerning the soul does not answer to what he had promised.

In the prefaces prefixed to each of these books, he inveighs vehemently against his envious detractors, whom he flatters himself that he will confound by his successes. This work was scarcely suited to stop their mouths.

The second writing is an abridgment of practical astronomy, entitled *De solis affectibus*—“On the Affections of the Sun.” It is the fourth of the seven books in the Basel edition already mentioned. The manuscript from which it was published in that collection, as well as in the great *Libraries of the Fathers*, was very defective; or else those who printed it were poor readers, for it contains gross computational errors and others producing nonsensical meanings.

The third is the book *On Heresies*, in which Honorius briefly surveys the ancient heresies or sects of Jews, pagans, and Christians. He counts eight among the Jews, nine among the pagans, and sixty-seven among the Christians, ending with the Agnoetae. This small work, inserted into the great *Libraries of the Fathers*, was first printed at Helmstedt in 1612, together with Constantine Hermenopoulos’s *Catalogue of Heretics*, in a quarto volume.

The fourth, likewise printed in the great Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, is a chronological list of popes ending with Innocent II. In a manuscript of the King’s library it is followed by a similar list of Western emperors; both lists are merely a continuation of the fourth book *On the Philosophy of the World*, which immediately precedes them in the same manuscript. The final words of that book demonstrate this clearly: *Non arbitror infructuosum seriem temporum huic operi inserere, quo lector cuncta transacti mundi tempora queat uno intuitu agnoscere*—“I do not judge it unprofitable to insert into this work a sequence of times, so that the reader may recognize in a single glance all the periods of the world that has passed.”

The fifth contains questions and answers on Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. We observe, following Cornelius à Lapide [Note: [Col. 0022] Commentary on Ecclesiastes, p. 6.], that these two kinds of commentary are drawn word for word from those [Col. 0023] of Salonius, a fifth-century writer, except that our author has transposed one passage of this interpreter and partly omitted or altered another. For what Salonius says about Solomon’s three names at the head of Ecclesiastes, Honorius employs in the preface to his explanations of Proverbs; and at the end of those same explanations, he abridges or suppresses what the other had included in his own. This plagiarism does no honor to our author’s memory, assuming that he intended to pass off Salonius’s work as his own. However that may be, after these questions and answers were published at Cologne in 1554 under the name of Honorius of Autun, together with other writings in an octavo volume, they were subsequently inserted in the *Libraries of the Fathers* at Cologne and Lyons.

The following works were brought out of obscurity by Dom Pez.

1. A book entitled *Summa duodecim quaestionum*—“Compendium of Twelve Questions.” This was its occasion. Two men, Honorius says, one a canon and the other a monk, met while traveling and asked each other what they were and whence they came. “I belong to Saint Peter,” said the canon; “and I,” said the monk, “to Saint Michael.” The former maintains that his patron is more worthy, as prince of the Church and gatekeeper of heaven. The other maintains, on the contrary, that his own is more worthy, being not only an angel but provost of the heavenly court. As the dispute had grown very heated without anything being decided, certain persons, says our author, asked for my judgment on the matter. I first replied orally; then, at their request, I set my reply down in writing.

To resolve so futile a question, Honorius undertakes to establish twelve metaphysical points, at the end of which one is almost as far advanced as before. This work is dedicated to a certain Thomas, “all radiant with the splendor of wisdom,” in the author’s expression.

2. A dialogue between master and disciple on eight theological questions, which the latter proposes and the former resolves. The two most important are:

1. Would Jesus Christ have become incarnate if man had not sinned? The master replies affirmatively, on the grounds that, in his view, the principal motive of the Incarnation was not the repair of sin but the deification of human nature.

2. What is the destiny of children who die without baptism? Reprobation and eternal fire, replies the master.

3. A treatise *On the Exile and Homeland of the Soul*. This Thomas, to whom the author had dedicated his *Compendium of Twelve Questions*, is again the Maecenas whom he celebrates at the head of this book. But he had increased in dignity in the interval between these two writings, since Honorius here credits him not only with every gift of wisdom but also with apostolic grace, which seems to mean that he had been promoted to the episcopate. The subject our author discusses with him concerns human and divine sciences. He says that our exile consists in ignorance and our homeland in possession of true wisdom, which he undertakes to unfold. There is nothing here that deserves notice.

4. A treatise *On Free Will*, addressed to an abbot named Gottschalk. Its purpose is the same as that of *The Inevitable*, but executed more briefly. There are only six chapters by Honorius; the remainder consists of passages from several Fathers.

5. A short discourse *On the Life of the Cloister*, containing a mysticism little suited to the capacity of ordinary readers.

## § III.—His Unprinted or Lost Writings

As we have already indicated, Dom Bernard Pez will serve as our guide in enumerating our author’s unprinted or lost writings.

1. A treatise *On the Incontinence of Priests*. It was included in the list of books that a monk named Henry had presented to the abbey of Göttweig in the twelfth century. But it is no longer found among the manuscripts of that house, and it cannot be said where it exists.

2. A large work entitled *Summa totius de omnimoda historia*—“Compendium of the Whole of Universal History.” It is included in the donation of the monk Henry and listed under Honorius’s name. Dom Pez says that he saw and examined in the library of Göttweig an anonymous chronicle bearing this title, in which important matters for the history of Germany occur. But what makes him doubt that it is the same as Honorius’s work is that it extends only to 1058 and that the author calls Adalbert, Margrave of Austria, his lord.

Nevertheless, it seems easy to answer this doubt. First, since the manuscript is from the twelfth century, as Dom Pez admits, is it not natural to identify it with that which came from the monk Henry? That this chronicle ends in the middle of the eleventh century proves absolutely nothing against Honorius, since either the manuscript may be mutilated or the author may not have had leisure to carry his work further. As to the fact that the author indicates that he lived under the authority of the Margrave of Austria, we have already recognized that Honorius, wishing to devote himself to retirement, transferred his residence from France to Germany.

We might add something more definite if we had seen the copy of Honorius’s *Chronicle* which, according to Arnoul Wion, passed from the hands of Lazius into the emperor’s library in the sixteenth century. However that may be, Bellarmine was mistaken in naming an edition of this chronicle published at Basel in 1544. The work is still in obscurity [Note: [Col. 0023] “The *Summa totius*, though not complete, was recently published in the *Monuments of Germany* of the most illustrious Pertz.” [Col. 0024] See below. EDITOR.].

3. Extracts from Saint Augustine on the nature and properties of the soul, arranged in dialogue form. Dom Pez discovered them at Melk Abbey only after publishing his second volume of *Anecdotes*, in which he had included Honorius’s works. He expresses regret for this omission and promises to repair it later; but he did not keep his word.

4. A book of theological questions, treating of limbo, hell, heaven, and so forth, likewise drawn from Saint Augustine and other Fathers. Dom Pez also intended to publish it, but left the matter there.

5. *The Key of Physics* (*Clavis physicae*). “Some,” says our guide, “take this work of Honorius to be his books *On the Philosophy of the World*. But,” he adds, “the manuscript of the monastery of Zwettl teaches us otherwise. For it expressly states that the *Key of Physics* was an abridgment of the five books of a certain Chrysostomius. This work, therefore, has not yet appeared; but we hope one day to give it to the public.” This too was a promise never fulfilled.

6. A collection entitled *Pabulum vitae*—“Nourishment of Life.” It is listed in Henry’s donation, but the Göttweig copy is lost, and no other is known.

7. Another collection of sermons, entitled *Refectio mentium de festis Domini et sanctorum*—“Refreshment of Minds on the Feasts of the Lord and the Saints.” It likewise formed part of Henry’s books and still existed in Trithemius’s time; but today it is not known what became of it.

[Col. 0025] 8. *Historia solemnis*—“Solemn History.” Thierry of Engelhusen names this work in the list of authors whom he says he used in composing his *Chronicle of Chronicles*. But is it distinct from, or identical with, the *Summa totius* discussed above? This we cannot decide.

9. Homilies on the Gospels not expounded by Saint Gregory. This too is a work whose existence cannot be guaranteed.

10. A very short tract on the ten plagues of Egypt. A copy, written in the fourteenth century, is preserved in the Charterhouse of Gemnic in Germany.

11. Our author had composed, as we have already observed on his own testimony, glosses on Plato: a work lost or deeply buried. [Note: [Col. 0025] See note 46.]

12. A volume of Letters, known only from the testimony of Trithemius.

13. A work entitled: *Suum quid de virtutibus et vitiis* [“Something of One’s Own concerning Virtues and Vices”]. D. Pez, speaking of this production, says: “What sort of monstrosity this may be, we have not yet discovered.” Whatever the work may ultimately have been, it is certainly thus listed among Honorius’s minor works in the donation of the monk Henry.

14. Doublet [Note: [Col. 0025] *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, p. 128.] further attributes to our author a commentary on the *Hierarchy* of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite; but it is unknown from what source this historian drew this anecdote, and neither is any bibliographer known who assigns such a work to him, nor any library in which it is found.

It is unnecessary to refute the error into which Polycarp Leyser fell [Note: [Col. 0026] *Historia poetarum medii aevi*, under “Honorius”] by attributing to our author certain elegiac verses published by D. Mabillon in the first volume of his *Analecta* under the name Honorius Scholasticus. The editor’s note, which places in the sixth century the death of Jordan, bishop of Ravenna, to whom these verses are addressed, sufficiently shows that Leyser confused two writers of the same name.

§ IV.—His genius, learning, doctrine, and manner of writing.

Although posterity has derived no great assistance from the writings of Honorius, it would nevertheless be unjust to say that they were useless to his own age. Certainly, as in the writings of almost all his contemporaries, one finds in them no new discovery and no trace of that inventive genius which knows how to perfect and enlarge the knowledge it has received; yet they may be regarded as a repository of tradition in several branches of learning. Our author indeed possessed and transmitted nearly all that was then known of mathematics, cosmography, geometry, and metaphysics. He was even distinguished in the latter field, as his treatise *On the Knowledge of God and Eternal Life* shows—a work genuinely worthy of the two great names under which it appears in certain manuscripts.

Without being a profound theologian, he was far from a novice in theology, notwithstanding certain errors or misunderstandings visible in some of his writings. His *Elucidarium*, which has given the greatest occasion for criticism, would have found favour with critics had they observed that it was the fruit of his earliest theological studies. His treatise *The Inevitable* displays greater maturity. It is regrettable, as has been said, that two or three blemishes appear in it, disfiguring it and preventing it from ranking with the best writings of the period on the same subject.

The gift our author possessed for interpreting the sacred books appears in his Commentary on the Song of Songs. If he was not equally successful with the Psalms, few interpreters of that age succeeded better. The mystagogical notions prevailing in the twelfth century scarcely permitted one to grasp the true spirit of a text whose literal sense is the basis of all the others. These same notions led him astray and made him advance many absurdities concerning ecclesiastical rites. Thus sound minds are corrupted when they allow themselves to be carried away by the prejudices and bad taste established by unsound minds.

As for his manner of writing, it seems defective to us in more than one respect. In almost all his writings, the different pieces composing them are neither arranged methodically nor brought together intelligently. He is an author who ordinarily gives birth as soon as he conceives, without much concern for what precedes or what is to follow. Hence comes the negligence also noticeable in his style. He might have corrected his faults had he worked over his writings with greater leisure and reflection, as indeed he guarded against them in some works.

III.

(D. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum novissimus*, “Introductory Dissertation” to vol. II, p. IV.)

Honorius, priest and scholastic of the church of Augustodunum in Burgundy, flourished with no small reputation as a writer from about the year 1090 until the year 1120. It is rendered highly probable that before the end of his life he assumed the monastic habit by numerous manuscripts, close in date to Honorius’s lifetime, which most expressly bear the name “Solitarius” [Solitary]. That the terms “solitary” and “monk” are identical is clear from the *Rule of Solitaries* of the priest Grimlaicus, whose first chapter begins in these words:

“First, therefore, one must investigate why he is called either monk or solitary; and then, with the aid of divine mercy, let us duly proceed to explain the remaining matters. For he is called a monk by Greek derivation because he is single. For *monas* in Greek is called ‘singleness’ in Latin. Therefore ‘solitary’ is the interpretation of the term ‘monk.’ Accordingly, whether he is called monk or solitary, it is one and the same thing,” etc.

We have excerpted these words at greater length for the purpose of making plain to all the reason why Honorius seemed to us to be classed among Benedictine monks. Arnold Wion, in *Lignum Vitae*, book II, chapter 69, on the authority of Nicholas Aurificus and Melchior Hittorp, calls Honorius not merely a monk but also an abbot; he adds, however, that they do not explain in what place Honorius exercised that office. But for us it will suffice to have called him a monk, since in all the ancient codices we have examined there is no trace of the title of abbot, nor anywhere any ancient testimony on that point.

A catalogue of works published by Honorius is found here and there among writers who have treated of ecclesiastical authors. Before them all, however, Honorius himself took the lead, concluding the fourth book *On the Lights, or Writers, of the Church* with a careful catalogue of his own minor works. Moreover, that Honorius wrote several other works after the books just mentioned, *On the Lights of the Church*, [Col. 0027] the Gemnic manuscripts do not permit us to doubt. From these, by the kindness of the venerable Fathers Leopold Wydemann and Sebastian Treger, Carthusians of Gemnic—whom we have commended elsewhere—we now for the first time bring to light not a few hitherto unpublished works bearing Honorius’s name.

Since, moreover, in surveying libraries we encountered certain unexpected materials by which even the published books of Honorius may receive illumination, it is useful to review somewhat more carefully his minor works—not only those published here by us, but also those already printed elsewhere—following the order kept by Honorius himself, while omitting, however, works already commonly known. He wrote, therefore:

1. The *Elucidarium*, in three little books: he divided the first concerning Christ, the second concerning the Church, and the third concerning the future life. A manuscript exists in the library of Klosterneuburg, in a parchment folio codex of the twelfth century, where it begins: “The *Elucidarium*, as it is called, of Anselm. M[aster], having often been asked,” etc., as in the printed editions. In a parchment manuscript at Gemnic, four hundred years old, the following is prefixed: “Gregory: It is superfluous to inquire about the author when the Holy Spirit is believed to be [the author].” A German translation of the same work is found in two manuscripts in the library of Melk, of which the first is from the fifteenth century and the other ends in the year 1414; nor is the dialect of the translation older.

2. The little book *On Holy Mary*, entitled *The Seal of Holy Mary*. It is printed in various editions of the *Libraries of the Fathers*.

3. One work *On Free Will*, called *The Inevitable*. In a parchment folio manuscript at Melk, marked b, no. 64, are excerpts from the little book called *The Inevitable*, published by the Solitary, unknown in origin and name. This manuscript is five hundred years old.

4. One little book of Sermons, called *The Mirror of the Church*. Olearius, in the *Bibliotheca Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum*, vol. I, under H, reports on the authority of Daumius that this *Mirror of the Church* was printed at Basel in 1544. But we have seen, both in the library of Göttweig and in that of St Mary the Virgin of the Scots, a printed octavo copy of this *Mirror*, published at Cologne in the house of Quentel in 1531—thus thirteen years earlier than the Basel edition. In this Cologne edition, an *Admonition* and sermons of Feliciarius, bishop of Arles, are appended to Honorius’s *Mirror*. Yet no one of that name is found in the catalogue of the archbishops of Arles in Denis de Sainte-Marthe’s *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I.

5. *On the Incontinence of Priests*, called *The Stumbling-Block*. We have nowhere yet found this book. At Göttweig there is a parchment folio codex, six hundred years old, containing a list of books which Brother Henry donated to this church. Several little works of Honorius are listed there, among them a well-corrected *Elucidarium* and the *Stumbling-Block on the Incontinence of Priests*. But today these codices are missing from Göttweig, as are almost all the books included in Henry’s donation.

6. *The Sum of All Things concerning Universal History*. This work is listed thus in the donation of Henry just mentioned: “A sacramentary concerning mysteries; the *Sum of All Things*, containing a chronicle from the beginning of the world down to our times.” We did indeed inspect in the library of Göttweig a chronicle of that sort, from the creation of the world, in a parchment folio manuscript written in a hand of about the twelfth century, which contains much excellent material pertaining to German affairs. But because that work extends only to the year 1058 and its author calls Adalbert, margrave of Austria, “my [lord],” we believe it to differ from Honorius’s *Sum of All Things*.

Arnold Wion, book II of *Lignum Vitae*, chapter 69, states that this great work was once in the possession of Lazius, but was then, about the year 1595, a manuscript in the imperial library at Vienna. If this is true, Gotthard Olearius is mistaken when, in the passage cited, he writes that Honorius’s work *On Universal History*, together with many others, undoubtedly perished. Indeed, Possevino, in the *Apparatus*, p. 767, states that it was published at Basel in 1544. But this author commits so many errors concerning Honorius that he deserves no credence.

7. *The Jewel of the Soul concerning the Divine Offices*. This work has often gone to press. John Mabillon, in his *Italian Journey*, no. 27, judged it a slight matter indeed, but nevertheless not to be passed over in silence, that a book on ecclesiastical rites entitled *The Jewel of the Soul*, by Honorius of Augustodunum, bears the name Honorius Solitarius in a five-hundred-year-old Ambrosian manuscript.

8. *Sacramentary concerning the Sacraments*. As Honorius himself writes in the prologue, he collected this little book from the writings of the saints so that those lacking an abundance of books might have their want relieved through this compendium. Honorius further wishes there that the work be called *Sacramentary*, because through it every sacrament of the divine office is disclosed to the uninstructed. It now appears for the first time from a fourteenth-century Gemnic manuscript, through the work and care of the learned Father Leopold Wydemann. Henry’s donation proves that another manuscript copy of the same work once existed at Göttweig, where there are mentioned “Honorius’s *Jewel of the Soul concerning the Divine Sacraments*, a *Sacramentary concerning Mysteries*,” etc. But that manuscript has perished.

9. *Neocosmus concerning the First Six Days*. This work is listed among the other minor works of Honorius in Henry’s donation just mentioned, though the manuscript is now reckoned among those lost at Göttweig. Two handwritten copies still exist at Benediktbeuern: one in a parchment quarto manuscript, five hundred years old, where it is entitled “Hexaemeron of Honorius of Augustodunum”; the other in a parchment folio manuscript, six hundred years old, where it bears the title *Neocosmus*. It is also found in parchment folio manuscript B. 64 in the library of Melk, under this title: “A little work of a certain solitary concerning the works which God made in the first six days.” This Melk manuscript is five hundred years old.

We publish it from a four-hundred-year-old manuscript of the Carthusian house at Gemnic, assisted by the often praised—and deserving praise—Father Leopold Wydemann. Moreover, that short preface prefixed in our edition to chapter 1, since it is absent from the Benediktbeuern and Melk manuscripts, does not seem genuine or derived from Honorius himself. Nevertheless, we did not wish to remove it from the said place because the Gemnic manuscript contained it. The same is our judgment concerning the final chapter of this little work, which is likewise absent from the Melk manuscript.

We therefore judge its genuine beginning to be chapter 1: “Because many [have written] many things concerning the first six days,” etc.; and its ending to be contained in chapter 5 in these words: “through whom even now every bodily creature is transformed into a better state,” although in the Melk manuscript the work ends somewhat earlier, as follows: “but in these temporal things he made all temporal and bodily things really through species and forms.” Finally, one may wonder why Honorius, in his catalogue of his writings, entitles this little work *Neocosmus concerning the First Six Days*, whereas in chapter 1—which, as we have observed, contains Honorius’s genuine preface—he himself seems to desire that *Hexaemeron* be prefixed as the title of this elucidation of his. But the title of a book, being left to the author’s discretion, need not be closely examined so long as the subject and work are established.

10. *Eucharistion concerning the Body of the Lord*. The editions of Honorius’s *On the Lights of the Church* wrongly read *Eucharisticon*. For that one must read *Eucharistion*, not *Eucharisticon*, is taught by all the manuscripts we have seen in which this book *On the Body of the Lord* occurs, specifically the parchment quarto manuscript of Holy Cross, five hundred [Col. 0029] years old; the often-cited donation of the monk Henry of Göttweig; the Dorothean manuscript, no. 54, four hundred years old; and finally the Melk manuscript from which we first publish the book, a paper folio marked L. 52, which Wolfgang of Emerstorf copied faithfully from old exemplars, as he himself noted at the end in these words:

“Brother Wolfgang Frischman of Emerstorf, a monk of the monastery of Melk, wrote out this volume in simple and not very elegant characters, but nonetheless from ancient exemplars. Deign, most excellent reader, whoever you may be that profit from it, to remember him for God’s love. The work itself was also completed on the day after the feast of the virgin Margaret, in the year of the Lord 1451.”

Moreover, in this manuscript *Eucharistion* begins, which means “good grace.” Finally, Honorius’s work *On the Lights of the Church*, in the same volume written by Wolfgang, expressly has *Eucharistion*, not *Eucharisticon*.

A hand of the fifteenth century, in the cited Melk manuscript, noted concerning Honorius’s book *On the Body of the Lord* that this treatise should not be read publicly because of certain points contained in it in which the author appears to err, or at least to require much discriminating consideration. This observation is undoubtedly that of a scholastic man, one who measured the sayings of the ancients by the subtle little questions of his own age. For nothing occurs in Honorius that departs from the common doctrine or language of the ancient doctors.

Chapter 5 alone will show how Catholicly he thought concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist, which takes place by transubstantiation. “Christ,” he says, “was the Word of the Father, through whom he created all things. The same Word changed the nature of bread and wine into the substance of his flesh and blood, as [he changed] water into wine; and he gave his own substantial body, born of the Virgin, and no other, to his followers to eat; and on the next day offered that same body, and no other, to God the Father on the altar of the cross for the life of the world. The Church likewise today, through the hands of priests, makes the same thing, and no other, which Mary gave birth to. The faithful people likewise today receive the same thing, and no other, though made from another bread, which Christ delivered with his own hands. And although individual priests offer individual hosts, they do not make individual bodies: all make one [body], though at different times. And although they divide the offerings into very many fragments, [they do not divide] parts [of Christ], but each receives the whole. Otherwise, if Christ, once divided, were eaten by the people, there would be nothing to give one hungry again, or there would be as many bodies of Christ as there are sacrifices of priests. But now the one body of Christ is eaten by all the people, and wholly by each person; and yet it is most truly believed to remain whole and entire at the right hand of the Father. What human reason cannot prove, Catholic faith allows no one to doubt. But whoever does not believe will not share in this body, because he has proved worse than an unbeliever.”

And in chapter 8, where he asks why the Eucharist is called a sacrament, or whether it is to be believed as reality or figure, he responds with complete clarity:

“In Christ two substances are proclaimed: visible humanity and invisible divinity. Thus two things are considered in this sacrament. Since the appearance and taste of bread and wine are seen outwardly, whereas inwardly the body and blood of Christ are understood, it is therefore called a sacrament. Every sacrament shows one thing outwardly and indicates another to be understood inwardly, just as letters do: their shapes and characters are seen outwardly, but their force and meanings are understood inwardly. Hence, although the flesh and blood of Christ are believed in reality, it is nevertheless not inappropriate for it to be called sacrament or figure,” etc.—than which nothing could have been written more Catholicly.

11. *Knowledge of Life concerning God and Eternal Life*. It occurs in an octavo manuscript of Melk, p. 40, written in a twelfth-century hand, under the name of blessed Augustine; yet this name itself has been added in a later hand. Another fifteenth-century hand notes in the same place that it appears to be Honorius’s by its style and by his own statement in *On the Lights of the Church*. In another parchment folio manuscript at Melk, B. 64, five hundred years old, this little work is entitled: “Knowledge of Life, published dialogically by a certain Solitary.” There again another hand—scarcely later than the fourteenth century—notes in the margin that the work is attributed to Honorius.

Nor is this unworthy of observation in the latter manuscript: in the dialogue, not a master speaks to disciples or brothers, but a solitary speaks to hearers. This notably confirms the opinion of our Benedictine Fathers, who in the recent edition of Augustine, vol.
