VI, first vindicated for Honorius of Augustodunum this little work, which had for some time been falsely attributed to Saint Augustine.

12. *Image of the World concerning the Arrangement of the Universe*. We have seen three old editions of this work. The first is a Nuremberg folio edition prepared by Caspar Hochfeder in 1491, in which the author is called Honorius Inclusus [the Recluse]. The second is a Basel quarto edition issued by Master John Amerbach in 1497; in it the work is attributed not to Honorius but to Saint Anselm, whose minor works both editions chiefly concern and present. The third edition, finally, is in smaller folio, and gives neither place nor time at which or when it was produced. A copy is held by the library of Melk in a manuscript-and-printed composite volume marked E, no. 55.

Although this edition was produced with rather crude type, it is nevertheless far more genuine and correct than that inserted in their *Library of the Fathers* by Andrew Schott, S.J., and Antony Hierat, theologians of Cologne. We therefore readily believe that it is the oldest of the editions mentioned by us. The title of Honorius’s three books in this edition reads: “Christian to a certain Solitary concerning the Image of the World. To Honorius: ‘By the sevenfold Spirit,’ etc.” Then follows the Prologue to the *Image of the World*: “Honorius to the foster-child of Wisdom,” etc. This work is preserved in manuscript in several Austrian libraries.

13. *The Highest Glory concerning the Apostolic [See] and the Emperor*. In this book Honorius treats of the pre-eminence of the priesthood over kingship, a matter over which a great conflict arose in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Some maintained that kingship was in no way subject to the priesthood; others defended the contrary view with loud cries. Honorius attacks the former rather sharply in more than one place, declaring that they cannot equate kingship with the priesthood unless they wish to be called either flatterers of princes, ignorant of affairs, or downright stupid men.

“Let us now,” he says in chapter 8, “make inquiry in familiar terms of those for whose sake we undertook this little work—those who, for love of money, for the favour of praise, and in order to obtain from princes themselves the honour of some dignity, themselves most ignorant, preach to the unlearned that all dignities everywhere hang in the hand of kings. Those who say these things: are they laymen, monks, or clerics? If they are laymen, they must then be mocked as foolish, or rather corrected by the wise as ignorant. But if they are monks, then they are mad: either, ignorant of truth, they err; or, knowing the error for the sake of avarice, though wise, they pretend not to know the truth. But if they are clerics, they are out of their minds, for they take away from the ecclesiastical order the right bestowed upon it by the Lord himself and confer it upon lay power; indeed, they strip themselves of their own liberty and, with Cain, subject themselves to the servile ordering of laymen. Therefore the foolish assertions of all these people must be refuted by sensible persons—indeed, rejected by all who use reason—since kingship is rightly subject to priesthood, and the people to the clergy; and as the sun surpasses the moon, spirit the soul, and the contemplative life the active, so the priesthood surpasses kingship.”

Such are Honorius’s words. Had he kept within the just limits of comparison and contented himself with placing one class above another, he would have found no one who differed vehemently from him, either in his own time or ours. The dispute and controversy was aflame not so much concerning the pre-eminence of these two classes as concerning the necessary consequences flowing from the pre-eminence of one over the other. Thus, while some restricted those consequences and others enlarged them, our Honorius, siding with the latter, proceeded so far in chapter 4 as to think that the Roman emperor ought to be [Col. 0031] elected by the Apostolic [See] with the consent of the princes, constituted head of the people by the acclamation of the populace, and consecrated and crowned by the pope.

“But here perhaps,” writes Honorius, “the contentious and unskilled in knowledge will break forth and assert that the emperor is to be elected not by the Apostolic [See] but by the princes. I ask them whether a king is to be constituted by subjects or by prelates. ‘By prelates,’ they say. ‘By which [prelates]?’ ‘By dukes and counts.’ But dukes and counts are subject to bishops as, so to speak, their lords, because they hold benefices and estates of churches from them. Therefore the king must be constituted by Christ’s priests, who are the true princes of the Church; nevertheless, the consent of laymen must be sought. Therefore, because the priesthood rightly constitutes the kingdom, the kingdom will rightly be subject to the priesthood.”

How coherently such reasonings and conclusions hold together, insofar as they concern the election of emperors and kings, has long ago been shown by other most learned men.

Moreover, the book of Honorius that Antony Hierat wrongly confounds in the Cologne *Library of the Fathers* with Honorius’s *Series of Roman Pontiffs* was brought forth from a three-hundred-year-old Gemnic manuscript by Father Leopold Wydemann. To him we also owe the following little work of Honorius. The *Highest Glory* also exists in the library of the canonry of Tirnstein, in a fifteenth-century paper quarto manuscript, and in the parchment manuscripts of Melk E. 85 and L. 24, the former four hundred and the latter three hundred years old.

14. *The Ladder of Heaven concerning the Degrees of Vision*. Antony Hierat, or Andrew Schott, wrongly thought this little book to be the same as Honorius’s work *On the Affections of the Sun*; the editors of the Cologne *Library of the Fathers*, which we use, adopted their edition. For *The Ladder of Heaven* is not philosophical in subject, like the book *On the Affections of the Sun*, but theological or ascetical. Honorius constructed it for the sake of those who, as he says in the prologue, strive to ascend to spiritual things but, ignorant of the order of the steps, throw themselves down precipices; and, because they do not climb step by step but rush heedlessly headlong, find neither this nor that support of rectitude on which to make their step firm. Hanging by their own weight and oppressed by what they see, they abandon the vain path and wander back into the opinions of profound fable and the darkness of ignorance.

“Moved in piety by the poverty of their minds, I equipped for them a ship, richly supplied, from exile to their homeland; and I raised a ladder, regularly set out with suitable steps, from mire to heaven. If they strive to climb it rightly, they will see the King of Glory in his beauty. Therefore, if it seems good, let this little book be called *The Ladder of Heaven*.”

We have already informed the reader that this little work must be credited to the venerable Leopold, who extracted it from the manuscript of his Carthusian house cited above, a manuscript certainly very difficult to read. It is likewise listed in the donation of the monk Henry of Göttweig in these words: “*Neocosmus concerning the first six days; Ladder of Heaven concerning the three heavens; Jewel of the Soul*,” etc. But nothing of these remains any longer in the library of Göttweig.

15. Certain passages *On the Soul and God*, excerpted from Saint Augustine and composed in dialogue form. This Dialogue survives in a parchment manuscript at Melk marked P. 40 and compiled about the twelfth century; we deeply regret that we discovered this only after the second volume had been printed. But it will have its proper place in subsequent volumes, in which there will also appear a large book of theological Questions concerning the limbo of the Fathers, hell, heaven, etc., drawn from the same source. We do not doubt this to be by the same Honorius, both because of similarity of style and because of agreement in opinions.

Meanwhile, take the order and beginning of the Dialogue *On the Soul and God*. First, several opinions of the ancients concerning the nature of the soul are set forth, excerpted from Cassiodorus, as the scribe notes in the margin, and from others. The first begins: “The soul is properly said of a human being, but not also of cattle, because their life is known to be established in the blood,” etc. Then follows Honorius’s brief preface: “What I have excerpted from the work of blessed Augustine, I have taken care to commit to writing for students who lack books.” Finally, the dialogue begins as follows:

D[isciple]: “As I have often thought about the soul, and am wholly ignorant whence it is, what it is, of what kind it is, and how great it is, I ask you to disclose, to one who asks, what you think on these matters by God’s inspiration.”

M[aster] replies: “I shall not be unprepared for this task, because I am occupied with it by frequent meditation,” etc.

All of this will be made clearer to the reader in the edition itself.

16. “An exposition of the whole Psalter with the Canticles in a remarkable manner.” For the Melk manuscript L. 52 teaches that this passage must be punctuated thus, and not: “An exposition of the whole Psalter with the Canticles. He expounded the Song of Songs in a remarkable manner,” etc., as the latest Fabrician edition has it. This very extensive Exposition of Honorius exists in two paper folio volumes of the library of Mondsee, or Lake of the Moon, where “the work of Honorius Solitarius, a religious man,” ends in the year 1438; and in a parchment manuscript of Klosterneuburg written in a thirteenth-century hand, where it begins: “The prologue of Honorius Solitarius, a religious man, begins. To Father Christian,” etc.

It also exists in three parchment folio volumes, transcribed in the same period, in the library of Melk; the first is marked h. 54, the second J. 45, and the last J. 14. From a four-hundred-year-old Gemnic manuscript you have a specimen of this Honorian Commentary: namely, the Preface and the Exposition of Psalms I, L, LI, C, CI, and CL. If these do not displease learned men, perhaps someone will not be lacking to undertake an edition of the entire work. Other matters worthy of observation in the Melk manuscripts are noted there.

17. *The Song of Songs, so that the preceding exposition may not be seen.* [Note: [Col. 0031] Edition: “so that it was previously expounded.”] The Exposition of the Song of Songs was long ago printed, but without the prologue, which the distinguished Father Edmund Martene eventually published from a Signy manuscript in vol. I of the *New Treasury of Anecdotes*, col. 363. From it, moreover, the authority of the Melk manuscripts is confirmed, in which Honorius dedicates and addresses his Exposition of the Psalms to Abbot Chuno; and, conversely, those manuscripts indicate whom the “C.” in the prologue to the Song of Songs denotes. But the monastery of which that Chuno was abbot remains unknown.

The prologue to the Canticles published by Martene also occurs in a three-hundred-year-old paper folio manuscript of the canonry of Dorothea, and in manuscripts at Zwettl and Aspach.

18. The Gospels which Blessed Gregory did not expound. We have yet seen this work in no library.

19. *The Key of Physics concerning the Natures of Things*. Some think this work of Honorius to be altogether identical with his published four books *On the Philosophy of the World*. But a manuscript of the monastery of Zwettl teaches us otherwise, in which the following is noted: “This book is said to have been excerpted by Honorius Solitarius from five books of a certain Chrysostomius.” Then: “The prologue to the *Key of Physics* begins: ‘When I behold many [persons] in my mind,’” etc. The manuscript is five hundred years old and marked no. 261.

Therefore Honorius’s *Key of Physics* is still unpublished, but is at last to be brought to light by us in subsequent volumes. [Note: [Col. 0031] He did not keep this promise.] This would already have been done had not the opinion of learned men hindered us. See the Cologne *Library of the Holy Fathers*, vol. XII, part I, p. 929.

20. *Refreshment of Minds concerning the Feasts of the Lord and the Saints*. The work is still hidden. It once existed in the monastery of Göttweig, as is clear from the donation of the monk Henry, where, among other little works of Honorius, is placed *Refreshment of Minds*, containing sermons to the brethren in chapter. Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 357, wrongly calls this little work *Refreshment of Months*, unless perhaps this is a mere typographical error, retained nevertheless by more recent editions.

21. *Food of Life concerning the Principal Feasts*. We have not yet encountered it anywhere. In Henry’s donation, together with other [Col. 0033] books of Honorius, the monastery of Göttweig receives *Food of Life*, containing sermons for feast days. But the Göttweig copy has perished.

22. The little book *On the Lights of the Church*. It has been printed more than once, although all rightly demand a more correct and carefully revised edition. Excellent is the Melk folio manuscript L. 52, copied by Wolfgang of Emerstorf, as he says, from an old exemplar. Another manuscript of the same monastery of Melk is K. 24, in quarto, of the same age—that is, the fifteenth century.

Let these observations suffice concerning the catalogue of works compiled by Honorius himself. But since, as we wrote above, after the work *On the Lights of the Church* he brought several other little works to light, we shall append a list of these also, so far as it is possible.

23. *On the Ten Plagues of Egypt, Spiritually Understood*. This very brief little work appears under Honorius’s name in a parchment manuscript at Gemnic, which, as the venerable Father Leopold testifies, was very elegantly written in the fourteenth century.

24. *The Lesser Ladder of Heaven*. Honorius’s name is absent from a three-hundred-year-old paper folio manuscript at Gemnic. Nor does Father Leopold attribute the little work to Honorius except conjecturally. To us it appears to be nothing other than a sermon.

25. *The Book of Twelve Questions*. The chief of these questions is: “Does the holy archangel Michael precede the blessed apostle Peter, or Peter Michael?” Honorius assigns the first place to blessed Peter in chapter 6, where one may read these words of his:

“Therefore, as much as the order of seraphim surpasses in dignity the order of archangels, so much does Peter, prince of the apostles, surpass Michael, one of the order of archangels. Hence Rome, the head of the world, bestowed the primacy of government upon the apostle Peter, not upon the archangel Michael; and the whole Church throughout the world conferred an episcopal see upon Peter not only in private places but also in principal cities.”

Thus Honorius. The little work is now brought before the public from a four-hundred-year-old Gemnic manuscript.

26. *Eight Questions concerning the Angel and the Human Being*. These have been extracted from the cited manuscript of the same Carthusian house. These questions are by no means trivial, but some touch on matters still controversial among the most weighty authorities today, such as this: “Why does God leave in misery some innocent persons—namely infants whom the water of baptism has not regenerated?” Honorius says that this can no more be investigated by us than one can inquire why he did not make angels archangels, or the latter thrones; why he did not make women men, or beasts birds; or why he gave the peacock such beauty of plumage above other birds, and many similar things. “For he has made and makes all things whatsoever he willed.” Thus Honorius, certainly prudently and soberly.

27. *On the Soul’s Exile and Homeland*, otherwise *On the Arts*. The same Gemnic manuscript in the library supplied this little book to us, through the care of Father Leopold, by whose kindness and diligence we have also obtained everything that follows. Honorius dedicated it to a certain Thomas, to whom he also addressed the book of Twelve Questions listed under no. 25. Its entire subject is ascetical, as one may grasp merely by examining the chapter summaries into which we have divided it.

28. *On Free Will*. This little book is wholly different from Honorius’s other little work *On Free Will*, called *The Inevitable*, although the doctrine contained in both is nearly the same. Honorius dedicates it to a certain Gottschalk, “labouring in faith and works in a holy purpose, set over Christ’s flock by word and example”; this seems to indicate that Gottschalk exercised the office of abbot somewhere. In the four-hundred-year-old Gemnic manuscript, the little work is followed by authorities from the Fathers Ambrose, Augustine, Fulgentius, etc.; from these, unless we are mistaken, it is manifest that Honorius wished to think or teach nothing concerning the doctrine of free will except what he had received from his predecessors.

29. On the Cloistered Life. This little work appears under Honorius’s name, together with other writings most certainly by him, in the Gemnicensis manuscript in octavo, copied by the venerable Bartholomew, Carthusian of Gemnicum and, in 1459, prior of the Charterhouse of Eysbach.

30. On the Philosophy of the World, four books. It exists in the Libraries of the Fathers.

31. On Affections Alone, or Dispositions, one book. That this has wrongly been confused with *The Ladder of Heaven, on the Degrees of Visions*, is clear from what we noted under number—or rather work—14.

32. A Succession of the Roman Pontiffs. It exists in the Libraries of the Fathers.

33. On Heresies, one book. It is found there. A manuscript, much more correct, exists in the Melk manuscript of Wolfgang of Emerstorf, marked L. 52, copied from ancient exemplars.

34. Questions and Answers to Them on Solomon’s Two Books, Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. See the Libraries of the Fathers.

35. On the Soul, one book. Thus Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 357. But there can be no doubt that this great man was misled by a defective manuscript. Thus Honorius’s book *On the Soul* is by no means distinct from his little work *On the Soul and on God from St. Augustine*, which, composed in dialogue form, we said above under no. 15 is preserved in the library of Melk.

36. A Dialogue from Augustine’s Short Works, one book. Thus again Trithemius, whom the things just said demonstrate to be mistaken. That is, Trithemius fashioned three works out of one and the same work of Honorius.

37. A Book of Letters to Various Persons, according to the same Trithemius. But as yet we see nothing of them.

38. *To Each Virtue Its Due*, on Virtues and Vices. What kind of monstrosity this is, we have not yet discovered. Whatever work it may have been, however, it is certainly listed among Honorius’s little works, as we think, in the donation of the monk Henry, in the following terms. Since this donation has been of remarkable use to us in elucidating Honorius’s writings, and contains other things capable of casting light upon ancient little works, we shall not hesitate to present it here in full.

These are the books which Brother Henry bestowed upon this church (of Göttweig).

A Psalter notably expounded. The Song of Songs wonderfully expounded. Matthew glossed. The Apocalypse expounded. Likewise, the Song of Songs with glosses. *The Key of Physics*, namely an extract from the book *Periphyseon*. *The Mirror of the Church*, containing most delightful sermons for the people. *Refreshment of Minds* [Note: [Col. 0033] The manuscript seems to read “of mourners” (*moerentium*).], containing sermons for the brethren in chapter. *The Nourishment of Life*, containing sermons for feast days. A well-corrected *Elucidarium*. *The Stumbling-Block*, on the incontinence of priests. *Eucharistion*, on the body of the Lord. *Neocosmus*, on the first six days. *The Ladder of Heaven*, on the three heavens. *The Gem of the Soul*, on the divine sacraments. *Sacramentary*, on mysteries. *The Sum of All*, containing a chronicle from the beginning of the world down to our own times. *Image of the World*, in which the whole world is described. *The Sum of Glory*, on the Apostolic See and the Emperor. *To Each Virtue Its Due*, on virtues and vices. *The Seal of Saint Mary*, in which the Song of Songs is expounded in reference to Saint Mary. *Knowledge of Life*. *The Inevitable*, in which free choice, predestination, and God’s grace are discussed. Anselm, *On Free Choice*. Eucherius, *On Hebrew Names*. Isidore, briefly [Col. 0035] on the whole Bible. Likewise Isidore’s Sentences on both Testaments. Plato’s *Timaeus*. Virgil’s *Eclogues*. Theodulus. Odo’s *Music*. Serenus, *On the Medical Art*, containing Bede’s extracts from Galen and Hippocrates. Gerland’s *Abacus*. An abridged Priscian. Abbo, *On Rules*. Phocas, *On the Art of Grammar*. Likewise a little book *On Penultimate Syllables*. A book of verses. Aleran’s *Rhetoric*. Extracts from Martianus. Priscian on constructions, containing also a model of metres. A book of prayers. A book *On the Lights of the Church*, that is, on ecclesiastical writers. A book containing sacred songs. Extracts from the books of St. Augustine *On God and the Soul*. Various questions. Various glosses. Dionysius’s computation in Greek, containing an abacus and a map of the world. A martyrology, containing various pages on computation. A wheel-diagram, in which the seven liberal arts are depicted. Likewise a wheel-diagram, in which the Trojan War is depicted. Likewise a wheel-diagram containing various pictures. Likewise a defeated quire [reading uncertain: *Quaternio devictus*]. Thus far the Donation of Henry, in a parchment folio manuscript at Göttweig, written in a twelfth-century hand.

IV

FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latinitatis*, vol. III, p. 277.

Honorius, a Frenchman, of Autun, priest and teacher in Burgundy, about the year 1130, is also called “the Solitary” in an old Ambrosian manuscript of the *Gem of the Soul*, examined by Mabillon, p. 14 of his *Italian Journey*; likewise in the Gotha manuscript of the commentary on the Song of Songs, concerning which Salomon Ernst Cyprian writes in the *Catalogue of Gotha Manuscripts*, p. 101; and also, as Bernard Pez testifies, in a Zwettl manuscript of the *Key of Physics, on the Natures of Things*, and in another Melk manuscript, both books five hundred years old, to which Honorius gave the title *The Inevitable*. Indeed, is he not called “the Recluse” in the Nuremberg edition of the *Image of the World* of 1491? His portrait appears in an old manuscript of the four books *On the Philosophy of the World*, prefixed to the German theological journal *Unschuldige Nachrichten von Alten und Neuen Theologischen Sachen* for 1718. A catalogue of his writings was either composed by himself or, as I rather believe, appended by a friend to the fourth book of *On the Lights of the Church*, in its final chapter. I shall append it with my observations, having also compared what the aforementioned Pez learnedly observed in his introductory dissertation to volume II of the *Anecdota*.

1. He divided the *Elucidarium* into three little books: the first on Christ, the second on the Church, the third on the future life. This *Promptuary*, or *Elucidarium*, appeared under Anselm’s name at Paris in 1560, octavo, and among the works of Anselm of Canterbury. Some have wished Guibert of Nogent, others William of Coventry the Carmelite, others Augustine himself, to be its author. [Note: [Col. 0035] *Italian Journal of Scholars*, vol. XX, p. 39.] In 1393 Nicholas Eymericus set his *Elucidarium of the Elucidarium* against this *Elucidarium*. See Jacques Quétif, vol. I, p. 711 ff. Pez saw a German translation of the *Elucidarium*, written in 1414, in the library at Melk.

2. The little book *On Saint Mary*, entitled *The Seal of Saint Mary*, an allegorical exposition of the Song of Songs, is in the Cologne *Libraries of the Fathers*, vol. XII, and the Lyons edition, vol. XX, p. 1217, from the Cologne edition of 1540, octavo.

3. *On Predestination and Free Choice*, called *The Inevitable*. George Cassander published this dialogue at Cologne in 1552, octavo; it was reprinted thence in Cassander’s works, pp. 623–639; then, from the edition of John Conen, hostile to Cassander’s memory, Antwerp, 1620–1624, octavo, in the Libraries of the Fathers: Paris, vol. IX; Cologne, vol. XII and its supplement of 1622; and Lyons, vol. XX, p. 1128.

4. A little book of sermons, called *The Mirror of the Church*. It appeared through John Dietenberg at Cologne in 1531, octavo, with the sermons of Feliciarius—an erroneous form for Caesarius.

5. *On the Incontinence of Priests*, called *The Stumbling-Block*. It does not survive.

6. *The Sum of All*, concerning universal history. It may be seen to differ from the brief *Chronicle on the Ages of the World*, held by Possevino to be the same work, from the creation of the world to the author’s own time. That chronicle occupies the place of the fifth book among the seven books of Honorius published at Basel in 1544, octavo; and, together with the book *On Times* (below, no. XII), forms the third book in the *Image of the World*, published at Speyer in 1583, octavo. These seem to be the same works which Lambecius attests exist in the Imperial Library, II, pp. 3 and 70: the three books of Honorius *On the World and the Succession of Times and Events*, down to Conrad III, or the year of Christ 1137. Certainly the *Sum of Histories, or Chronicles*, a great work, listed among Honorius’s writings by Arnold Wion in vol. I of the *Tree of Life*, p. 426, has not hitherto been published. It was formerly in the possession of Lazius, but now is in the Emperor’s library at Vienna in manuscript. This is the distinguished chronicle cited by Theodoric Engelhus, ending with Lucius III, that is, in 1181.

7. *The Gem of the Soul*, on divine offices, the office of the Mass, ministers of the Church, canonical hours, and the solemnities and ceremonies of the whole year. Leipzig, 1514, quarto; reprinted in the *Mirror of Ancient Devotion*, Cologne, 1549, folio, published by John Cochlaeus with Amalarius, Walahfrid Strabo, Basil’s Liturgy from an old translation, an Exposition of the Mass, and the writer of the Life of St. Boniface the Martyr and of the catalogue of bishops and archbishops of the see of Mainz. Afterwards it appeared among writers on the same subject: Cologne, 1568; Rome, 1590; Paris, 1610, folio; and in the Venetian *Mirror of the Mass*; and in the Libraries of the Fathers, Cologne, vol. XII, Lyons, vol. XX. It is cited by Theodoric Engelhus.

8. *Sacramentary*, on the sacraments, or on the causes and mystical meaning of the rites of the divine office in the Church. Honorius declares that he compiled it from the writings of the saints, so that those who lack an abundance of books may have their poverty relieved by this compendium of them. The most celebrated Bernard Pez first published it, vol. II of the *Anecdota*, pp. 249–545.

9. *Neocosmus*, on the first six days. This is the *Hexaemeron* which we have published by the same Pez, vol. II of the *Anecdota*, pp. 71–88.

10. *Eucharisticon*, on the body and blood of the Lord, or *Eucharistion*, which means “good grace”; the same Pez published it, vol. II of the *Anecdota*, pp. 349–362.

11. *Knowledge of Life*, on God and eternal life. It appears in the appendix to the works of St. Augustine, Benedictine edition, vol. VI, Amsterdam edition, p. 649. Under Augustine’s name, a fragment from this book, *On the Holy Trinity, from the book* Περὶ τῆς γνώσεως ἀληθοῦς ζωῆς, “On the Knowledge of True Life,” occurs in Greek with a Latin translation, published at Basel in 1678, octavo, by John Leunclavius after Manuel Comnenus’s Embassy to the Armenians, pp. 584–599.

12. *Image of the World*, on the arrangement of the universe. It appeared divided into two books: the first on the globe of the whole world, and the second on [Col. 0037] times—mathematics, or instruction. The first is among the seven books published at Basel in 1544, octavo; but already, at the beginning of printing, it appeared together with the second book, *On the Difference of Times*, and the third, *On the Succession of Events* down to the year of Christ 1137, without place or year, in folio; [Note: [Col. 0037] See the index of books printed in the fifteenth century owned by the distinguished Christian Gottlieb Schwartzius, Nuremberg, 1727, octavo, pp. 68 ff.] and at Nuremberg in 1491, folio; Basel, 1497, quarto; and Speyer, 1583, octavo; also under Anselm’s name at Basel, 1497, quarto; and in the Libraries of the Fathers, Cologne, vol. XII, and Lyons, vol. XX, p. 964.

13. *The Sum of Glory, on the Apostolic See and the Emperor*, or on the pre-eminence of priesthood over kingship, in Bernard Pez, vol. II of the *Anecdota*, pp. 179–198.

14. *The Ladder of Heaven*, on the degrees of visions. The Greater Ladder: a dialogue on the order of knowing God in creatures through a threefold degree—bodily, spiritual, and intellectual—in Bernard Pez’s *Anecdota*, vol. II, pp. 157–170; and the Lesser Ladder, on the degrees or virtues of charity, pp. 173–176.

15. Certain extracts from Augustine *On the Soul and God*, composed in dialogue form. Having found this later in a Melk manuscript, Pez promised to publish it thereafter; he notes that from this one writing Trithemius, in chapter 357, made two works: one *On the Soul*, and the other a *Dialogue from Augustine’s Short Works*.

16. An exposition of the whole Psalter with the Canticles, in a remarkable manner [Note: [Col. 0037] This does not seem to have been written by Honorius about himself, but by one of his friends.], addressed to Abbot Cuno. From this Pez published the preface together with expositions of Psalms 10, 51, 51, 100, 100, and 150, vol. II of the *Anecdota*, pp. 97–154. There he notes that, after finishing the Psalter, Honorius also expounded the canticles said daily in Lauds, as well as the canticles *Benedictus*, *Magnificat*, and *Nunc dimittis*, the Lord’s Prayer, and the Apostles’ Creed. In the preface Honorius says that he will explain the Gallican Psalter rather than the Roman, because “we chant it in our churches.” The Gallican Psalter is that which was translated by the Seventy Interpreters [Note: [Col. 0038] Understand “by the Seventy Interpreters” as though it read “from the Seventy Interpreters.” Thus immediately below, “by Symmachus,” for “translated from Symmachus into Latin.”]; but the Roman is that which was interpreted by Symmachus, or by I know not whom else.

17. He expounded the Song of Songs in such a way that earlier expositions seem not to exist. Andrew Schott first published this commentary in the *Library of the Fathers*, Cologne, 1618; it was reprinted in other editions, such as Lyons, vol. XX, pp. 1153–1217. A short prologue was published by Edmond Martène, vol. I of the *Anecdota*, pp. 363 ff.

18. The Gospels which Blessed Gregory did not expound. It exists nowhere.

19. *The Key of Physics*, on the natures of things, extracted from five books by a certain Chrysostomius. It begins: “Since I behold many things in my mind.” This work is distinct from the four books *On the Philosophy of the World*; the eminent Pez promised to publish it.

20. *Refreshment of Minds* [Note: [Col. 0038] Trithemius, chapter 357, incorrectly prints “of months” (*mensium*).], on the feasts of the Lord and the saints. It does not survive.

21. *The Nourishment of Life*, on the principal feasts. It does not survive.

22. *A Book on the Lights of the Church*, divided into four little books. Honorius abridged the first from Jerome, the second from Gennadius, and the third from Isidore; he either added the fourth himself or compiled it from Bede and others. This is the sixth among the seven books published at Basel in 1544, octavo. Afterwards it appeared with Jerome, Gennadius, Isidore, Sigebert, and Henry of Ghent, edited by Suffridus Petrus, Cologne, 1580, octavo; and in Aubert Miraeus’s *Ecclesiastical Library*, Antwerp, 1639, which I had reprinted with a supplement at Hamburg, 1718, folio. Finally, it appeared in the Libraries of the Fathers.

Besides these works mentioned by Honorius himself, or by his friend, it is fitting to list also the following published works:

The four books *On the Philosophy of the World*, which occupy the place of the third among the seven books of Honorius published at Basel in 1544, octavo, and were also reprinted in the Libraries of the Fathers.

*On Affections Alone*, the fourth among the same seven books, p. 277, Basel, 1544, octavo, in the Libraries of the Fathers.

The book *On Heresies*, the seventh in the same Basel collection, and in the Libraries of the Fathers; also at Helmstedt, 1611, quarto, with the *Catalogue of Heresies* and the *Profession of Faith* of Harmenopulus, a Greek writer, in Latin.

*On the Ten Plagues of Egypt*, spiritually interpreted. Bernard Pez published it, vol. II of the *Anecdota*, pp. 91–94.

The book of Twelve Questions to Thomas. There, pp. 201–212, where, among other things, in chapter 6, p. 208, one may read these words: “By as much as the order of seraphim surpasses in dignity the order of archangels, by so much Peter, prince of the apostles, surpasses one from the order of archangels.”

The book of Eight Questions on Angel and Man. There, pp. 215–224.

The little book *On the Exile and Homeland of the Soul*, under the other title *On the Arts*, which it describes under the image of ten cities: grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, arithmetic, music, geometry, astronomy, physics, mechanics, and household management. There, pp. 227–234.

The little book *On Free Choice*, to Gottschalk—very different from the other work on the same subject mentioned above under no. 3. There, pp. 237–246. Passages are cited from Ambrose, Anselm, Augustine, Fulgentius, Gregory the Great, John Chrysostom, Isidore, and Peter Damiani.

Questions and Answers to Them on Solomon’s Two Books, Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. Cologne, 1540, octavo, and in the Libraries of the Fathers.

A succession of Roman pontiffs, more than thirty of whom were crowned with martyrdom. It occurs in the same Libraries of the Fathers, for example Lyons, vol. XX, pp. 1026–1027.

Nowhere survive the book of letters to various persons, which Trithemius mentions, nor *To Each Virtue Its Due*, on virtues and vices, which Pez names among the books of Honorius formerly bestowed upon the church of Göttweig by Brother Henry, but which the injuries of time have taken away.

Honorius seems to indicate some work of his own before the prologue to the *Gem of the Soul*, writing as follows (*Library of the Fathers*, Lyons, vol. XX, p. 1046): “After, with Christ’s favor, I had traversed with prosperous course the sea of Scripture in the *Sum of All*, and had, with much sweat, brought my shipwreck-prone little vessel through shoals and pirates, scarcely reaching the desired shore, you inhabitants of Zion again thrust me into the waves of thought,” etc.

He refers the reader to his *Little Glosses on Plato* in book I of *On the Philosophy of the World*, chapter 15. Ibid., p. 999.

Honorius of Autun. A little book entitled *On the Gem of the Soul* exists in my possession in an old parchment manuscript and differs from the printed editions by many variant readings. I therefore believe that the person who reprinted this little work after collating it with old manuscript copies would not expend labor in vain. It is especially worth noting that in that manuscript the work is entitled not, as in the printed editions, *Gem of the Soul*, but *Gem of the Church*. Moreover, in the very first chapter of the work certain additions occur which are not to be despised. For after the word “to profit” (*prodesse*), our manuscript adds: “so that it may continually be permitted to the memory of you to share in the prayers of all,” etc. MANSI.

V.

(*Library of the Ancient Fathers*, Lyons edition, vol. XXI, p. 963.)

[Col. 0039]

Antonius Hierat greets the pious reader.

Behold, reader, we give you in one bundle, for the sake of the public good, all the extant works of Honorius of Autun, now at last revised by Father Schott of the Society of Jesus, our singular friend, although he lacked here ancient parchment manuscripts written with the pen. Yet the man who first brought part of them to light from Cratander’s press at Basel professes that he had obtained four very ancient manuscripts of the *Image of the World* and compared them with one another. The second edition, following forty years later, in the eighty-fourth year of that century after 1500, at Speyer of the Nemetes, from the press of Bernard Albinus, was much more correct and richer by one book. I see that this work was also attributed to Hugh of Saint Victor by John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim; some ascribe it to Anselm of Canterbury—perhaps because, treating the same matters, they gave the same title to their cosmography. Moreover, some give him the surname “the Recluse,” others “the Solitary”; most call him a priest, and I myself think them one and the same person. Finally, as a third step, there has been added to our edition Honorius’s *Gem of the Soul*, or four books *On Divine Offices and the Rite of the Sacrifice of the Mass*, which also treat the canonical hours. In the final book of *On the Lights of the Church*, or *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, the author Honorius, enumerating his labors, acknowledges these books as his own; and Trithemius, as usual, mentions their beginning as authentic. This work formerly appeared at Leipzig in the fourteenth year after 1500, and lately at Paris in the *Liturgical Works*, not at all more accurately, together with the third edition of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*. We have brought together, as you see, works published separately (*σποράδην*) and made them somewhat better than before—indeed, richer. For commentaries on Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, and on the Song of Songs, have been added.

HONORIUS OF AUTUN: PART ONE OF THE WORKS, DIDACTIC AND HISTORICAL.

[Col. 0039]

FOUR BOOKS ON THE PHILOSOPHY OF THE WORLD.

(*Library of the Ancient Fathers*, Lyons edition, vol. XXI, p. 995.) (G)*

THE CHAPTER HEADINGS BEGIN.

BOOK ONE.

[Col. 0039A] CHAP. I. What philosophy is. CHAPS. II–III. Things which exist and are not seen, and things which are seen. CHAP. IV. What it is to know something perfectly. CHAP. V. By what arguments God’s existence is proved. CHAPS. VI–VII. Why the Father is called power and the Son wisdom. CHAP. VIII. On the begetting of the Son. CHAP. IX. Why the Holy Spirit is called will. CHAP. X. Why he proceeds from the Father and the Son. CHAP. XI. On their co-eternity. CHAP. XII. Why certain things are attributed to one person, although he does nothing without another. CHAP. XIII. Why is the Incarnation attributed to the Son? CHAP. XIV. Why is the forgiveness of sins attributed to the Holy Spirit? CHAP. XV. What is the soul of the world? CHAP. XVI. What is a celestial and ethereal living being? [Col. 0040A] CHAP. XVII. What is an aerial being? CHAP. XVIII. What is a moist being? CHAP. XIX. Are angels bodies or spirits? CHAP. XX. On demons. CHAP. XXI. Much concerning the elements. CHAP. XXII. On the creation of fish and birds. CHAP. XXIII. On the creation of the other animals and of man, and at what time the creation of the world occurred.

BOOK TWO.

CHAP. I. What ether is and its adornment. CHAP. II. That frozen waters are not above the ether. CHAP. III. What this means: “He divided the waters which are under the firmament.” CHAP. IV. That nothing is seen above the ether. CHAP. V. In how many ways authority speaks concerning the higher regions. [Col. 0041A] CHAP. VI. On the firmament and the stars. CHAP. VII. Whether the fixed stars move. CHAP. VIII. How many circles are said to exist in the firmament. CHAP. IX. Which are visible. CHAP. X. Where the Milky Way begins. CHAP. XI. On the zodiac and the origin of its name. CHAP. XII. On the arrangement of the signs. CHAP. XIII. On the invisible circles. CHAP. XIV. On the two colures. CHAP. XV. On the horizon and the meridian circle. CHAP. XVI. On the motion of the firmament and the poles. CHAP. XVII. On Saturn, why a star is called cold, and in how many ways names of qualities are attributed to things. CHAP. XVIII. On Jupiter. CHAP. XIX. On Mars. CHAP. XX. On Venus. CHAP. XXI. How the same star is both Lucifer and Hesperus. [Col. 0041B] CHAP. XXII. On Mercury. CHAP. XXIII. On the station and retrogradation of the aforesaid stars; that the sun is beneath Mercury and Venus; and on their circles. CHAP. XXIV. When the circles of Venus and Mercury appear more freely. CHAP. XXV. Whether the planets move with the firmament or against it. CHAP. XXVI. Why the sun moves obliquely, and on winter and spring. CHAP. XXVII. Why the sun moves higher in spring and autumn, and on the four seasons of the year. CHAP. XXVIII. What a natural and an ordinary day are. CHAP. XXIX. The source of the inequality and equality of days. CHAP. XXX. The cause of eclipses, and why they do not occur every month. CHAP. XXXI. Why the moon has neither brightness nor heat, and on the new and full moon. [Col. 0041C] CHAP. XXXII. On lunar eclipses, why they do not occur every month, and on the shapes of shadows.

BOOK THREE. ON METEOROLOGICAL MATTERS.

CHAP. I. On air. CHAP. II. How the five zones exist in the air. CHAP. III. What differences arise on earth from the air. CHAP. IV. The source of rains. CHAP. V. Why the rays and heat of the sun tend toward the earth. CHAP. VI. Why the sun heats the earth and the higher fire does not. CHAP. VII. That drops of blood will fall before the end of the world, or why it is said to rain blood. CHAP. VIII. The source of hail and snow. CHAP. IX. Why snow never occurs in summer, although hail occurs then. CHAP. X. On thunder and lightning. [Col. 0041D] CHAP. XI. Why lightning occurs only in summer. CHAP. XII. BOOK ONE.

[Col. 0041]

PREFACE.

[Col. 0041D]

Since, as Tully says in the prologue of his *Rhetoric*, “eloquence without wisdom harms; but wisdom without eloquence, though only slightly, nevertheless benefits; while wisdom with eloquence benefits most greatly,” those err who, setting aside what benefits and does not harm, cling to what harms and does not benefit. For this is to dissolve the marriage of Mercury and Philology [Note: [Col. 0041D] In Martianus Capella.], sought with such care by Virtue and Apollo and approved by the assembled gods. It is also to sharpen a sword constantly, but never strike in battle. Yet we know that many who arrogate to themselves the name of teacher do not merely do this, but even swear that others ought to act thus. Knowing nothing whatever of philosophy, ashamed to confess that they do not know something, and seeking consolation for their ignorance, they proclaim as useful to the less cautious things which they do not know to be of no use. But since, as Terence says, “It is no wonder if a prostitute acts shamelessly” [Note: [Col. 0043D]

“But it is remarkable if a woman behaves shamelessly!” (TERENCE, *Andria*, IV.iv.16)], setting aside their shamelessness, we have resolved to say something about philosophy, in order that we may advance its devotees according to our ability and stir those who do not love it to love it. Beginning, therefore, from “God, the first cause of things,” we shall continue our treatise down to man, saying much about man himself; but we make this the principle of our discourse: if anything in this work appears imperfect, let it be attributed to human imperfection, and let what will be useful in it not therefore be blamed. For good things are not to be censured because of one badly spoken thing, just as evil things are not to be praised because of one well-spoken thing. For sometimes Thersites is awake and Ulysses sleeps,

> And in a long work it is permissible for sleep to steal in.  
> [Note: [Col. 0044D] “Yet in a long work it is permissible for sleep to steal in.” (HORACE, *Art of Poetry*, v. 361.)]

Therefore, beginning to treat philosophy, let us say what philosophy is.

### CHAPTER I.—What philosophy is.

Philosophy is true comprehension of things which exist and are not seen, and of things which exist and are seen.

### CHAPTER II.—Things which exist and are not seen.

[Col. 0043C] Incorporeal things exist and are not seen; for sense can do nothing outside underlying matter.

### CHAPTER III.—Things which exist and appear to exist.

Corporeal things exist and appear to exist, whether they have a divine or a perishable body. For bodies are subject to spirit. Since philosophy consists in knowledge of both kinds, let us discuss both, beginning with those which exist and are not seen. These are: the Creator, the soul of the world, demons, and human souls.

### CHAPTER IV.—What it is to know something perfectly.

But since the Creator is prior to all things—for all have existence from him, while he has it from no one—let us begin with him. Yet because the saints say that God cannot be perfectly known in this life, let us show what it is to know something perfectly, so that it may be understood why the Creator cannot be perfectly known in this life. Eleven questions are asked concerning each thing: whether it is; what it is; how great it is; in relation to what it is; what kind it is; what it does; what is done to it; where it is; how it is situated in a place; when it is; and what it has. To know something perfectly, then, is to know these eleven things concerning it.

But although we know that God exists, we do not perfectly comprehend what he is. The magnitude of him who fills all things exceeds the narrowness of our understanding. Human wisdom fails in explaining his relation. We do not comprehend his qualities; infinite tongues would not suffice to recount his actions. What is done to him is not an acting agent’s power but a willing one’s permission. Where is he? Above all things, beneath all things, wholly and undivided? How is he in a place, when he is not spatial? What can be said of the time of him who is before all time? What he has—he who holds all things in the palm of his hand—no one can perfectly explain. Thus we do not wholly fail to know him, whose existence we know; nor do we know perfectly him concerning whom we are ignorant of the things stated above.

### CHAPTER V.—By what arguments it may be proved that God exists.

And since we have said that God’s existence can be known in this life, let us set forth the arguments by which this may be proved even to unbelievers: namely, from the creation of the world and its daily ordering.

For since the world consists of contrary elements—hot and cold, moist and dry—those elements were joined in the composition of the world either by nature at work, by chance, or by some craftsman. But it is nature’s property always to flee its contrary and seek what is like itself. Therefore nature did not join contrary elements. Nor were they joined by chance. For if chance had made the world, why would it not make a house or something of that kind, which is easier? Again, if chance had made the world, certain causes would have preceded the world, whose concurrence would have produced it. For chance is the unforeseen occurrence of an event from converging causes. Since, therefore, nothing preceded the world except the Creator, the world was not made by chance, but by some craftsman. That craftsman was not a human being, for the world was made before humanity; nor indeed an angel, since angels were created with the world. Therefore God is the one who made the world.

The same is proved from its daily ordering. Things that are ordered are ordered wisely. Therefore there is some wisdom, for nothing is wisely ordered without wisdom. That wisdom is either divine, angelic, or human. But it is not human wisdom, which causes things to live and speak. For if human wisdom fashions the form of a human being or another animal, it cannot confer motion and life upon it. How, moreover, could angelic wisdom order the angels themselves? Therefore it is divine wisdom which has done this. But every wisdom is someone’s wisdom. Therefore there is one whose wisdom it is; and he is neither angel nor human being: therefore God. Thus, through daily reasoning one arrives at divine wisdom, and through wisdom at the divine substance. Hence divine wisdom is called the seal and image of divinity.

The philosophers said that in this divinity, the creator and governor of all things, there are power to act, wisdom, and will. For if he could act but did not know, how did he make things so beautiful? If, again, he made them but did not will to do so, he made them either ignorantly or under compulsion. But what could he not know, who knows even the thoughts of human beings? Who could compel him who is able to do all things? Therefore in divinity there are power, wisdom, and will. The saints call these three persons, transferring to them names from ordinary usage because of a certain affinity: they call divine power Father, wisdom Son, and will Holy Spirit.

### CHAPTER VI.—Why power is called Father.

Power is called Father because it creates all things and orders them with fatherly affection.

### CHAPTER VII.—Why wisdom is called Son.

Wisdom is called Son, begotten by the Father before the ages and yet co-eternal with him, because, as a son is temporally from a father, so wisdom is eternally and substantially from power.

### CHAPTER VIII.—On the begetting of the Son.

And since we have said that the Son was begotten by the Father and yet is co-eternal with him, let us say something about that begetting. First let us pray that, should one find the statement, “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. 53:8), it may not be thought to hinder us. For this was said not because it is impossible, but because it is difficult.

The Father, then, begot the Son; that is, divine power begot wisdom when it foresaw how it would create things and order those which had been created. Since it foresaw this before the ages, it begot wisdom—that is, the Son—before the ages. And it begot him from itself, not from another, because it possessed this knowledge neither by anyone’s teaching nor by the experience of use, but by its own nature. From the time when it was before—if it is permissible to say it—eternally, from the time when it knew this, it was not without knowledge of these things. Thus he is eternal because wisdom is eternal. Therefore the Father begot the Son, co-eternal and consubstantial with himself.

### CHAPTER IX.—Why will is the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0045C] Divine will is called the Holy Spirit. Properly speaking, *spiritus* means breath. But because a person’s will is often discerned in breath and breathing—for one breathes differently when glad and differently when angry—they metaphorically called divinity “spirit,” but, by antonomasia (*ἀντονομαστικῶς*), “holy.”

### CHAPTER X.—Why he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

This Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son because divine will and goodness are shown in effect from the fact that God is so powerful and wise. For the Holy Spirit’s proceeding from the Father and the Son means nothing other than that the divine will extends from power and wisdom to the creation and governance of things.

### Chapter XI. On Their Coeternity

This goodness and will are coeternal with the Father and the Son. For He was not powerful and wise in such a way as not also to be good and willing to create; because for God, to be, to be good, and to will before time what He did are the same. For there is no mutability in Him. Therefore the divine will and goodness are coeternal with those aforementioned. But this Trinity of persons is unity of essence. For the divine substance, power, wisdom, and goodness are one.

### Chapter XII. Why Certain Things Are Attributed to One of the Persons, Though None Acts Without the Others

Although these cooperate in all things—for divine power never does anything without wisdom and will, nor wisdom without power and will, nor will without power and wisdom—nevertheless certain works [Col. 0046A] are referred to power, and thus to the Father; certain works to wisdom, and thus to the Son; and certain works to will, and therefore to the Holy Spirit. The sending of the Son is attributed to power, that is, to the Father, though wisdom and will also effected it.

### Chapter XIII. Why the Incarnation Is Attributed to the Son

The Incarnation is attributed to wisdom, that is, to the Son, though power and will also effected it; and it is rightly ascribed to wisdom. For although He was so powerful that He could have delivered the human race from the devil’s power by will alone, He nevertheless preferred to join divinity to humanity, so that He who was to reconcile God and man might possess in himself what belongs to man and what belongs to God.

For if he were God only, the devil would never lay hands upon him. How, indeed, would a servant [Col. 0046B] lay hands upon the recognized Son of a mighty Lord? Hence it is written: “Had they known, they would never have crucified the Son of God” (1 Cor. II.8). But if he were man only, how would a captive man free a captive? For all have sinned and need the grace of God (Rom. III.23). Therefore our Redeemer was God and man, and still is, so that by divinity he might be able to save, and by humanity might remain hidden from the devil; so that, when the devil attacked the innocent one beyond right and law, he might justly lose the authority entrusted to him.

### Chapter XIV. Why the Remission of Sins Is Attributed to the Holy Spirit

The remission of sins is attributed to the divine will and goodness, because through will and goodness He pardons what, through power and wisdom, He could punish as soon as it had been done [Col. 0046C]. But because, while speaking of the Divinity, we have gone beyond the narrow limits of our knowledge, let us for the present pass on from it in silence to the remaining matters, praying this: that if anything be found here which is not written elsewhere, it may not be judged heresy. For it is not heresy merely because it is not written; it is heresy if it is contrary to faith.

In the preceding division, concerning things which are and are not seen, we first set forth God the Creator, the soul of the world. Therefore, having completed the discussion of the Creator, let us say something concerning the soul of the world.

### Chapter XV. On the Soul of the World

According to some, the soul of the world is the Holy Spirit. For by divine goodness and will—which, as we said above, are the Holy Spirit—all things live which live in the world. Others say that the soul of the world [Col. 0046D] is a natural vigor implanted by God in things, by which some merely live, while others live, sense, and discriminate. There is nothing that lives, senses, and discriminates in which that natural vigor is not present.

A third group says that the soul of the world is a certain incorporeal substance which is wholly present in individual bodies, although, because of the sluggishness of certain bodies, it does not exercise or operate in all in the same way. Wishing to indicate this, Virgil says:

> To the extent that harmful bodies do not impede the seeds.  
> (Aeneid VI.731)

Thus in a human being there is that individual soul. If someone concludes, “Then there are two souls in a human being,” we say: no; because we do not call the soul of the world a “soul,” just as we do not call the head of the world a “head.” Plato says that this was devised from divisible and indivisible substance, and from the same and different nature. Whoever seeks an exposition of this will find it in our *Glosses on Plato* [Col. 0047A].

We said that the third kind among things which are and are not seen is demons. Beginning to treat of them, let us say how many orders of them there are and why they are called demons.

### Chapter XVI. What a Heavenly and Ethereal Animal Is

Plato wished there to be three orders of demons, from the highest down to the lowest, affirming that nothing exists without a rational creature. For he says that in the firmament there is a certain rational animal, which he defines thus: “A rational, immortal, heavenly, impassible animal”—namely, the stars in the firmament [Col. 0047B], of which we shall speak in their proper place, for they belong among things which are and are seen.

Next, he said that in the ether there is a kind of invisible animal—from the firmament down to the moon—the first order of demons, defined thus: “A rational, immortal, impassible, ethereal animal.” Its office is to devote itself solely to divine contemplation and to live from that contemplation.

### Chapter XVII. What an Aerial Animal Is

In a lower region, namely around the upper part of the air or near the moon, he says that there is another kind, defined thus: “An aerial, rational, immortal, passible animal, imparting care to human beings.” According to him, its office is to carry human prayers to God and God’s will to human beings [Col. 0047C], whether through dreams, signs, inward inspiration, or vocal admonition. It is called passible because, loving the good, it rejoices with their prosperity and sympathizes with their adversity.

### Chapter XVIII. What a Moist Animal Is

The third order is in this moist part of the air, defined thus: “A moist, rational, immortal, passible animal.” Its office is to envy humankind and, out of envy, to plot against it, because man ascends by humility from the place from which it descended by pride. It is so lustful that it even has intercourse with women and sometimes begets offspring. Hence those demons which copulate in this manner are called incubi.

They differ from the other demons in this: the first two orders are called καλοδαίμονες (*kalodaimones*), that is, “knowers of good”; for καλός means “good,” and δαίμων, “knowing.” These, however, are called κακοδαίμονες (*kakodaimones*), that is, “knowers of evil,” for κακός means “evil.” Do not be troubled by the shared name, since both those and these are called demons, as though “knowers”; for both are also called angels, whence “evil angel” and “good angel.” The lower part of the world, that is, the earth, is inhabited by a rational, mortal animal—namely, man—of whom we shall speak in his proper place (Book IV) [Col. 0047D].

### Chapter XIX. Whether They Are Bodies or Spirits

Concerning the aforesaid demons, it is asked whether they have bodies, since they are animals and every animal is said to be a body, or whether they are spirits, as the prophet says: “Who makes his angels spirits” (Ps. CIII.4).

Some therefore say that they are bodies, but so subtle that they cannot be perceived by the senses [Col. 0048A]. In comparison with our bodies, which are dense and gross, they are called spirits, just as air, although a body, is called spirit because of its subtlety. This is supported by the authority of blessed Gregory, who, speaking of angels in the *Moralia*, says: “In comparison indeed with our bodies angels are called spirits; but in comparison with that supreme and uncircumscribed Spirit, they must be called bodies.”

The authority of blessed Augustine likewise supports this, for in a certain *Enchiridion* he gives a chapter with the title, “What sort of bodies angels have” (*Epistle* 115, to Nebridius). Others say that they are not bodies but spirits; but because they are not everywhere and move from place to place, in comparison with the supreme Spirit, who is wholly and entirely everywhere, they were called bodies by blessed Gregory. It does not follow from this [Col. 0048B] that they are bodies. Thus: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. I.20), not because God considers the wisdom of this world to be foolishness, but because in comparison with God’s wisdom it is foolishness; and it does not therefore follow that it is foolishness.

Regarding that chapter of blessed Augustine, “What sort of bodies angels have” (*In the Enchiridion*), they say that Augustine is there speaking of the bodies which angels assume when they appear to human beings—whether these are true bodies or not; yet he does not say that angels themselves are bodies. We, however, incline more to the view of those who say that they are spirits.

### Chapter XX. On Demons

Let no one think it unsuitable that Plato says there are two kinds of *kalodaimones*, since Scripture also says that there are nine orders of angels [Col. 0048C]. Plato divided them according to places, but Holy Scripture according to offices. Thus the nine orders of angels are contained in those two kinds, and conversely.

After the discussion of the Creator, the soul of the world, and demons, it remains to treat of the soul of man. But since we are going to speak of man, let us defer speaking of his soul until that place, so that there may be one continuous treatment of man and his soul.

Thus far our discourse has dealt with those things which are and are not seen. Let the pen now turn to those which are and are seen. But before we begin to speak, we ask that, if while discussing visible things we say something probable but not necessary, or necessary but not probable [Col. 0048D], we may not be blamed for it. For, as philosophers, we set down what is necessary even if it is not probable; but as natural philosophers, we add what is probable even if it is not necessary. Yet let it be considered whether any among the moderns have treated these matters more plausibly.

Therefore, since we are to discuss things which are and are seen, and since they are bodies, and all bodies consist of elements, let us begin with the elements and show what an element is; why there are four elements and not fewer; what the chaos of the elements was; and how it was resolved.

### Chapter XXI. On the Elements

An element, then, as Constantine says in the *Pantechne* (Παντεχνή), is a simple and smallest part of some body: simple with respect to quality, smallest with respect to quantity. Its explanation is as follows: an element is a simple part, one which has no contrary qualities. But since bones and similar things might seem to possess this character, to exclude them he adds “smallest”: that is, a part of something which is not itself a part of any other of those same things [Col. 0049A].

Thus letters are called elements by analogy, because they are parts of a syllable in such a way that no part of them exists. This Constantine wished the four humors to consist of elements, and bodily parts condensed from humors: both ὁμοιομερῆ (*homoiomerē*), that is, similar or uniform parts, such as flesh and bones; and organic, that is, instrumental parts, such as hands, feet, and the like. From both kinds of parts the human body consists.

Therefore, according to him, none of the four visible things which some have regarded as elements is an element: neither earth, nor water, nor air, nor fire. For none of them is simple in quality and smallest in quantity. In earth there is something hot, something cold, something dry, and something moist; and since this is evident even to the bleary-eyed and barbers, let us omit its proof. For things plainly true or plainly false need not be proved, but only those concerning which there is some doubt. Earth is not simple in quality and smallest in quantity, and therefore is not an element. The same can be shown concerning water, fire, and air.

An element, therefore, consists of simple and smallest particles from which these four visible things are constituted; and they are understood as elements not because they are seen, but by rational division. For, figuratively speaking, the human body is divided into organic parts, namely hands and the rest. Organic parts are divided into ὁμοιομέρειαι (*homoiomereiai*), that is, similar parts [Col. 0049B]—particles of flesh, bone, and the rest. The *homoiomereiai* are divided into the humors of melancholy; and humors into elements, that is, simple and smallest particles.

This division can occur partly in actuality, but only through reason and conceptual distinction. For the human body can actually be divided into limbs and into *homoiomereiai*; but only the intellect divides *homoiomereiai* into humors and humors into elements. For, as Boethius says in his commentary on Porphyry: “The power of the mind’s understanding is to separate things joined and to join things separated.”

But someone will ask, “Where are the elements?” We say: in the composition of the human body and of other things, just as a letter is in the composition of a syllable, even though it is not by itself. Yet there are some who, like rustics, do not know that something exists unless they can grasp it by sense: “The merely natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit” (1 Cor. II.4). Yet for the wise, insensible things ought to be investigated more than sensible things.

Since, therefore, those simple and smallest particles are elements: that which is cold and dry is earth; that which is cold and moist is water; that which is hot and moist is air; and that which is hot and dry is fire. Since, then, the four visible things are composed of these, that in which cold and dry particles predominate is called earth, after that element; that in which cold and moist particles predominate, water; that in which hot and moist particles predominate, air; and that in which hot and dry particles predominate, fire [Col. 0049D]. Therefore, if we wish to give them suitable names, let us call the aforesaid particles “elements,” and these four visible things “elemented things.”

There are some who have never read the writings of Constantine or of any other natural philosopher, who think themselves too proud to learn from anyone, and who, through arrogance, invent what they do not know lest they seem to have nothing to say. They say that elements are the properties or qualities of the visible things, namely dryness, coldness, moisture, and heat. Plato cries out against them, in the *Timaeus*, calling elements materials, whereas no qualities can be the material of anything. For matter is that which, on receiving form, passes into another thing.

Joannicius likewise cries out against them in his *Isagoge*, saying that elements are one thing and their mixtures another—the mixtures being hot and dry, and so with the rest. Again Macrobius cries out against them, saying (*Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, I.6): “Since in the individual elements there were diverse qualities, he gave to each such a quality that in that to which it adheres it might find one kindred and like it: thus water finds coldness with earth, air moisture with water, and fire heat with air.” Hence he says that elements are not qualities, but qualities are in elements [Col. 0050B]. If, then, what is in something differs from that in which it is, qualities are not elements.

Others say that the visible things are elements, supporting this with the authority of Juvenal, who, speaking of gluttons, says:

> Meanwhile their tastes seek elements through every region,  
> (*Satires* XI.14)

that is, game on earth, fish in water, birds in air. Since this opinion is true and not contrary to Constantine’s authority, let us explain how it can stand together with that opinion. Constantine, then, as a natural philosopher treating the natures of bodies, called their simple and smallest particles “elements,” as it were first principles. Philosophers, however, treating the creation of the world rather than the natures of individual bodies, called these four visible things “elements of the world,” because the world consists of them and because they were first created—or are created—as will be shown below [Col. 0050C]. Therefore there is no contradiction between them.

But someone objects: “None of these is an element, since there is none of them that is not made from these four elements.” They prove this as follows. There is something of water in earth, because we see something moist issuing from it. In the same earth there is something of air, as is proved by smoke evaporating from it; and something of heat, as we perceive by touch. The same is proved of the others. They also support this by Plato’s authority in the *Timaeus*, where he says: “Since this passes into water and water into earth, why is it called earth rather than water?”

We reply that in each of these there is indeed something of the others, but they are not thereby made out of them, because these are present accidentally, not substantially. Since earth is porous and surrounded by waters, some moisture and some air enter into it. Since it is in the middle of the world and fire is equally distant from it on every side, what wonder if it receives some heat from that source? But because we pursue brevity in this work, let us leave to the ingenuity of others the investigation of what is in the remaining things and how it happens to them. For the beginning should come from the teacher, but completion from one’s own intelligence.

They again say [Col. 0051A] that Plato asked why earth is called earth rather than water when it is thus dissolved. We understand him there not to be speaking of the element, but of a part of the element which is thus dissolved; for the whole element is never dissolved. Therefore he calls what is dissolved not “earth” but “earthly,” that is, a part of earth; but what remains and retains the property of earth they call earth and an element. But, God willing, we shall speak sufficiently about this.

The aforesaid particles, then, are the elements of bodies, as Constantine says. But the visible elements of the world require a discussion of this sort: why each was made, and why there are four and not fewer. Yet because the opinion that relies upon the authority of a wise man is weaker, let us show what Plato thought on the matter. “The rationale,” he says, “is of divine kind or beauty, that he should determine to create such a world as would admit sight and touch.” As if to say: since God, through goodness alone and not need, determined to create the world—being perfectly good—he willed it to be such that it could both be seen and touched, so that man, perceiving even with his eyes the creation of things and, through their governance, the divine power, wisdom, and goodness, might fear the power, venerate the wisdom, and imitate the goodness.

He then adds: “Nothing could be seen without the benefit of fire, nor touched without solidity, nor could anything solid exist without earth.” When we speak of the bodily senses, we shall show how sight cannot exist without fire, nor what is tangible without earth. He adds afterward: “Therefore God laid fire and earth as a kind of foundation.” But because there are contrarieties in them—earth is massive, blunt, and immobile, whereas fire is subtle, mobile, and sharp—God saw that they could not be joined without a middle term; and therefore he created a middle between them.

Since we have mentioned their joining, let us say what mixture is and what the conjunction of contraries is. A mixture of contraries occurs when two become one in such a way that neither remains what it was before: thus, if what is hottest is mixed with what is coldest, something tepid results, neither the hottest nor the coldest remaining. The conjunction of contraries occurs when two become one in such a way that each remains what it was before. In contraries having active qualities, this cannot exist without a middle term. The active qualities are heat and cold; we shall discuss this when speaking [Col. 0051D] of man (Book IV).

For if one is set against the other, they resist; one dissolves the other. Therefore, if they are to subsist, a middle must exist. If it is of such a kind that it belongs more to one than to the other, it gradually passes into the other to which it belongs more, and the conjunction is undone. Thus, if between the hottest and coldest something is placed which belongs more to the hot, the cold will perish and that conjunction will be dissolved. But if the middle is such that it belongs equally to the two extremes, passing into the matter of neither more than of the other, it will preserve their conjunction.

Therefore, wishing that the two elements mentioned should not be mixed but joined, so that each might remain what it is, God created between them not one middle only [Col. 0052A], but two: namely water and air. For if he had placed water alone between them, since it belongs more to earth than to fire—it shares with earth massiveness and bluntness, and with fire mobility—that conjunction would not endure. The same is true if he had placed air alone: for it shares subtlety and mobility with fire, and bluntness with earth.

But someone will say: “Even if one of these would not suffice, God could have made it sufficient.” We reply that we do not set a limit upon divine power, but say that, among things which exist, none could suffice, nor could there, according to the nature of things, be anything that would suffice. Since we have already shown why one of these would not suffice, let us make clear why nothing could exist that would suffice.

When between two things there are two contrary qualities, because the number two can be divided into two equal parts, there can be something which, retaining the property of each, suffices as a middle. Thus, since earth and air possess two contrary qualities—earth being cold and dry, air hot and moist—water, which shares all coldness with earth and moisture with air, itself cold and moist, suffices between them.

But if the contrariety of certain things consists in three qualities, then, just as three cannot be divided into two equal parts, no middle that relates equally to both can be found. For it must receive one quality from one and two from the other; thus, and not otherwise, three can be wholly divided. But a quality cannot be divided in half; therefore there cannot be a middle except one sharing one quality and two qualities [Col. 0052C].

Someone will again say: “Even if according to this pairing of qualities—συζυγία (*syzygia*)—there can be one middle, namely that which is made from two qualities, they could have had this. For if between fire and water, which have contrary qualities, there is air, which shares one quality with one and another with the other, why could there not be one middle between fire and earth, which in the pairing of two qualities do not have their qualities wholly contrary, unless it received one quality from each?” Fire is hot; earth is cold and dry.

We reply: according to this arrangement a middle was neither necessary, since they agree in one quality, namely dryness, nor could it exist. For there could be no such middle as received something from each: either it would receive heat from fire and dryness from earth, and thus be the same as earth; or it would receive heat from fire and coldness from earth. Apart from this, I think, nothing can be imagined; but it is impossible for anything to be hot and cold.

Since there are four elements and four qualities belonging to them, six combinations arise, four possible and two impossible. The four possible are hot and dry, hot and moist, cold and moist, and cold and dry. The two impossible are hot and cold, and moist and dry. Therefore the Creator placed two elements in the middle, because for the reasons given one could not suffice as a middle.

The disposition of the elements is this: earth occupies the lowest place, then water, then air, while fire is highest. For if anything were below earth, earth, being naturally heavy, would tend toward it; for heavy things naturally tend downward. But if anything were above fire, fire would tend toward it by its lightness and seek to be separated from the others. Water is placed beside earth because, although water is naturally heavy, it is not so heavy as earth and therefore should occupy the second place. Then air, heavier than fire and lighter than water, is rightly placed between the two [Col. 0053A].

And since we have taught what an element is, how many there are, why there are not more, and have indicated the cause of their ordering, let us speak of chaos—that is, the confusion of the elements—which existed in the beginning. We shall first set forth the common opinion, then refute it, and finally confirm our refutation.

Nearly all say that in the first creation the elements did not occupy fixed places, but were mixed into one mass, and for that reason at one time all ascended together and at another all descended together (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I; Hesiod). They add as the reason that the Creator wished thereby to show how great the confusion of things would be if he did not order them by his power, wisdom, and goodness. They then support this by Plato’s authority, who says in the *Timaeus* that God brought the elements from disordered motion into order.

We, however, say that the opinion they advance is false, that the reason they give is unsuitable, and that the authority they cite is not rightly understood. Let us first prove their opinion false, then their reason unsuitable, and finally the authority wrongly understood.

Tell us, then, whoever asserts this: were the elements at that time bodies or not? If they were not bodies, they were spirits, or properties of spirits or bodies. If they were neither spirits nor any property of a spirit, they could be matter; and therefore not elements. The elements, then, were bodies and occupied places; for every body is in some place. If they were in a place, they were either where they now are or elsewhere; but outside the elements there is no place. Therefore the elements were where they now are. Even if they were arranged as they are now, they were in these four places. At some time, then, the elements occupied the lowest place, at another time the highest place, and the two middle places.

Therefore, if—as you assert—they all descended together, some would descend, but there would be no place into which they could descend. Likewise, if they all ascended together, some would ascend, but there would be no place into which they could ascend [Col. 0053D]. Therefore they did not all ascend together or all descend together; their opinion is false.

The reason they give is unsuitable: namely, that God did this in order to show how great the confusion of things would be unless his goodness ordered them. To whom would he show it? To an angel? But an angel knows the divine will by nature and grace. To man? But man did not yet exist, unless these things were preserved until man’s creation; yet they were ordered before man was created.

Their reason is unsuitable, and Plato’s authority is not rightly understood by them. For when Plato says that God brought the elements from disordered motion into order, he does not say that they were ever moved disorderly. What place could there be for disorder when God disposed all things? Rather, if they were not ordered by God in the way in which they are, they would be disorderly. Since it is natural to earth to tend downward and to fire upward, unless earth occupied the lowest place and fire the highest, earth would always seek a lower place and fire a higher; and there would thus be disordered motion. The Creator brought this into order by assigning earth the lowest place and fire the highest, so that fire has nowhere to descend and earth nowhere to ascend.
