Therefore God brought the elements into order from disordered motion—not motion which existed, but which could have existed. It is as when, by the warning of one of our friends, we escape something that would happen if he were not there: we say that he delivered us from this evil, not because the evil first existed and he afterward rescued us from it, but because it would happen to us if he were not there [Col. 0054B].

At the first creation the elements were where they now are. Earth, however, was covered with waters; water was denser; air likewise was denser and darker than it now is, since neither sun, moon, nor other stars existed to illuminate them. Fire was denser than it now is. That earth was covered by water, not illuminated by any light, not distinguished by buildings, not filled with its animals, and adorned by no grass; that water and air were both dense and dark; and that stars did not appear above—this they called χάος (*chaos*), that is, “confusion of the elements.”

Hence Moses says: “The earth was empty and void, and the earth was upon the face of the abyss” (Gen. I.2). This explains those words. When water was raised as far as the greater part of the air, and the air was dense, and fire likewise dense, some earth and water lay beneath it; these, congealed and hardened by the heat and dryness of fire, created the visible and luminous bodies of the stars.

That there is something of the lower and upper elements in the composition of the stars can be proved by the following reasoning: they are visible, bright, and mobile. Since they are visible, they derive this from what is visible; they have visibility from visible and invisible sources, but nothing visible can come from what is invisible, as Lucretius says (*On the Nature of Things* II):

> Do not believe that what is perceptible can be produced from imperceptible things.

Macrobius says: “Every doubled quality increases; it never produces its contrary.” Blessed Paul says to the Hebrews: “By faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that visible things might be made from invisible things” (Heb. II.3) [Col. 0054D]. Therefore they do not derive their visibility from fire and air. Their visibility derives from the visible, that is, from earth and water together. Since they are bright and mobile, they do not derive this from what is dark and immobile; therefore not from air and fire, which are bright and mobile.

The stars were therefore made from the four elements, but among the lower elements water predominates in them, and among the upper elements fire. This can be proved from their activity: they give heat to the earths and draw moisture to nourish themselves, for like things rejoice in like things.

Someone will object: since air contains more moisture than fire and also heat, though not as much, why were the bodies of the stars not made in the air? We reply: although air is hot, it is also moist [Col. 0055A]; therefore it could not condense by drying and so create something luminous and visible. Thus, if dense water is placed beneath fire, it often condenses and turns into a stony substance; but if it is placed beneath something hot and moist, such as boiling water, so that it receives heat from that alone, it does not condense.

Or, according to Constantine: since there are four elements and each has two qualities, each has one quality intrinsically and another from another. Fire is hot in itself and dry from earth; air is moist in itself and hot from fire; water is moist from air but cold in itself; earth is dry in itself but cold from water. What is in each thing from itself prevails more than what is from another. Since in air moisture is from itself and heat is from another, namely fire, moisture prevails in it, and it could not by drying create stellar bodies.

Again, of greater importance was the Creator’s will that the stars should be in the air. Since the air is near the earth, if stars were in it, they would burn the earth by their proximity, and nothing could live upon it.

### Chapter XXII. On the Creation of Fish and Birds

After the bodies of the stars were created, because they are of a fiery nature, they began to move; and by their motion they heated the air beneath them. But through the mediation of air, the water was heated. From heated water various kinds of animals were created. Those which possessed more of the upper elements are birds. Therefore birds sometimes remain in the air through the lightness of the upper elements, and sometimes descend to earth through the heaviness of the lower elements. But those which possessed more water are fish. They can live in this element alone [Col. 0055C], and not in another.

Thus fish and birds were made. Hence it is written (in Ambrose’s hymn, Thursday at Vespers):

> God of mighty power,  
> who from the waters bring forth a race,  
> sending part back to the deep  
> and raising part into the air.

### Chapter XXIII. On the Creation of the Remaining Animals and of Man, and at What Time the Creation of the World Took Place
With these things thus created from the effect of the higher bodies, where the water was thinner, it was dried by heat and by the creation of the aforesaid things only to such an extent that there appeared in it, as it were, certain patches in which human beings and other animals dwell. But since the earth, beneath the water lying over it, was muddy and boiling from heat, it produced from itself diverse kinds of animals. [Col. 0055D] And if fire was more abundant in any part, choleric animals were born, such as the lion; if earth, melancholic animals, such as the ox and ass; but if water, phlegmatic animals, such as pigs. Yet from a certain portion in which equal elements meet in equal measure, the human body was made. This is what the divine text says: that God made man from the mud of the earth (Gen. II, 7). For one must not believe that the soul, being spirit, light, and pure, was made from mud; rather, it was bestowed upon the human being by God. Hence Scripture says: “God formed man from the mud of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. II, 7).

Therefore, although diverse melancholic animals, and countless phlegmatic and choleric ones, were created, only one human being was created, because, as Boethius says in the *Arithmetic*: “Every equality is scant and finite; inequality is numerous and manifold.” But, just as that which first approaches equality, though less so, is nevertheless somewhat tempered, it is plausible that the woman’s body was created from nearby mud; and therefore it is neither wholly unlike what man is, nor wholly different from man, nor as well tempered as man, because the hottest woman is colder than the coldest man. And this is what the divine text says: that God made woman from Adam’s side (Gen. II, 21). For it must not be believed literally that the first man was constituted in that manner.

But someone will say: by the same reasoning, might not several men and women have been created, and might they still be? We say that this is true if the divine will so wills it, because, for anything to exist through nature’s operation, the divine will must first precede it. Again, someone will say that it detracts from divine power to say that man was made in this way. We answer, on the contrary, that it confers something upon God, because we attribute to him both the giving of such a nature to things and the creation, through nature operating in this way, of the human body. For in what respect are we contrary to divine Scripture if we explain how what it says was made, was made? If the wise Julius told me that something had been made and did not explain how, while another said the same thing and expounded it, what contradiction is there in this?

But because they themselves do not know the powers of nature, they do not want others to inquire into anything, so that all may share their ignorance; rather, they want us to believe like peasants and not seek a reason, so that the prophecy may now be fulfilled: “The priest shall be as the people” (Isa. XXIV, 2; Hos. IV, 9). [Col. 0056C] We, however, say that reason must be sought in all things; but if it fails anyone, what the divine text affirms must be entrusted to the Holy Spirit and to faith. Hence Moses says: “If the lamb cannot be eaten, let it not immediately be burned with fire; but first let him summon a neighbor joined to his household; and if even thus they are not sufficient for eating the lamb, then at last let it be burned with fire” (Exod. XII, 4). For when we inquire into something concerning divinity, if we are not sufficient to comprehend it, let us summon a neighbor joined to our household—that is, let us inquire of one who remains in the same Catholic faith. But if neither we nor he are sufficient to comprehend it, then let us burn it in the fire of faith.

But these men, though they have many neighbors joined to their household, through pride refuse to summon anyone. [Col. 0056D] They prefer ignorance to asking another; and if they know someone to be inquiring, they cry out that he is a heretic, presuming more upon their own hood than trusting in their wisdom. But I beg you: do not trust the clothing. For what the satirist said has now been fulfilled:

> There is no trust in a brow. For what street does not abound  
> in gloomy obscenities?  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* II.8)

And again:

> Rare is speech among them, and great their desire for silence.  
> (*Ibid.* v. 14)

And since we have mentioned the first creation, which they say was made at different times on different grounds, let us explain who says what time it occurred, and for what reasons. [Col. 0057A] The Hebrews, then, and the Latins say that the beginning of the world was in spring. Hence Virgil, speaking of the days of spring, says:

> I should not believe that other days shone forth  
> at the first origin of the growing world,  
> or that they had a different course.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* II.338)

He then adds:

> . . . . . It was spring then; great spring was driving  
> the world . . . . .

Their reasoning is this: whatever comes into being is created from a proportion of qualities; but no season except this is temperate. Therefore the creation of things took place in spring, not at another season of the year. The Egyptians, however, say that creation took place in July. Following them, Macrobius says that on the birthday of the world the Moon occupied Cancer and the Sun Leo (*Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, I.21). Their reasoning is this: at the first creation there was so much moisture that the earth was covered by waters, and so great a quantity of moisture could not have been tempered without the greatest heat. Therefore the creation of the world took place in the season in which there is the greatest heat, that is, in summer.

# BOOK II

[Col. 0057]

# PREFACE

[Col. 0057B]

In the preceding section we have briefly touched upon, in proportion to the smallness of our ability, those things which exist and are not seen, and the elements which certain persons have taught to be visible. Now let us endeavor to speak of each one and of its adornment. But although we recognize that many seek ornament of language and few know the truth, glorying not in the multitude but in the integrity of the few, we shall labor for truth alone. For we preferred to promise naked truth rather than falsehood clothed in a covering.

Yet if anyone is displeased by the dryness of our discourse, if he knew the occupations of our mind, he would not merely refrain from seeking ornament of speech, but would marvel at what we undertake. For what room at all can remain for verbal ornament when one must consider what and how [Col. 0057C] we should read; then expound what has been read; declaim in disputations against falsehood; judge the discoveries of others; sharpen the tongue against the attacks of the envious? Thus there is now fulfilled in us that saying concerning the children of Israel, who, while rebuilding the Temple, held a sword in one hand and a stone in the other (II Esdr. IV, 17). But enough of this. Let us now begin to speak of the individual elements and the adornment of each, beginning with the highest, that is, with fire.

## CHAPTER I.—What the ether is and what its adornment is

Fire, then, is the region from the moon upward; it is also called ether. Its adornment is whatever is seen above the moon, namely, both fixed and wandering stars.

## CHAPTER II.—That there are no frozen waters above the ether

[Col. 0057D]

But perhaps someone will ask whether there are frozen waters there, above which other waters are situated. For some say that above the ether there are frozen waters which, stretched out like a skin, meet our eyes, and above which waters are held fast, on the authority of the divine text, which says: “He placed the firmament in the midst of the waters,” and again: “He divided the waters which are under the firmament from those which are above the firmament” (Gen. I). But since this is contrary to reason, let us show why it cannot be so, and in what manner divine Scripture is to be understood in the passages just cited.

If there are frozen waters there, then is there something weighty and heavy? But the first place of weighty and heavy things [Col. 0058B] is earth. Again, if frozen waters are there, are they joined to fire or not? If they are joined to fire, since fire is hot and dry, while frozen water is cold and moist, a contrary is joined to its contrary without an intermediate: therefore there could never be harmony there, but only the conflict of contraries. Further: if frozen water is joined to fire, it will either be dissolved by the fire or extinguish it. Since, then, fire and the firmament remain, where are the frozen waters joined to fire? If they are not joined, is there something between them and the fire? But what? An element? Yet no visible element was made above fire. Why, then, is it not seen? It remains, therefore, that there are no frozen waters there.

## CHAPTER III.—How the statement “He divided the waters which are under the firmament” is to be understood

[Col. 0058C]

But I know what they will say: “We do not know how this is so; we know that God can do it.” Wretches! What is more wretched than to say this? For they say that God can do it, yet neither see that it is so, nor have a reason why it is so, nor can show the use for which it is so. For God does not do everything that he can do. To use the words of a rustic: God can make a calf from a log; has he ever done so? Therefore let them either show the reason, or the use for which it is so, or cease to declare that it is so.

Therefore, if there are no frozen waters there, neither are other waters above them. But when the divine text says, “He divided the waters which are below the firmament from those which are above the firmament” (Gen. I, 7), it calls air the firmament, because it strengthens and moderates earthly things. Above this are waters suspended vaporously [Col. 0058D] in clouds, as will be shown in what follows; these are divided from the waters beneath the air. Likewise, “He placed the firmament in the midst of the waters” should be expounded in this way, although we believe that this was said more allegorically than literally.

## CHAPTER IV.—That nothing is seen above the ether

Again they will say: “What then is that dense thing of watery color which we see there? It is not fire. For if air cannot be seen because of its excessive subtlety, much less can fire, which is more subtle. Further, such a color is not fiery.” To this we say: nothing is seen there; rather, sight fails there, and out of that failure of sight it fabricates there something dense. For when that inner ray which performs vision is directed toward the heights, and there is no obstacle there from which it may be reflected, [Col. 0059A] it fails, and in failing grows dense. But because it passes through the eye, in which there is a watery and crystalline humor—as we shall show when speaking of the composition of the eye—and because, when it fails, no other color meets it there, it fabricates for itself such a color, namely a watery one.

They will object: “If nothing is seen there, how is it said that heaven covers all things? And when we say that the stars are in the firmament, that there are twelve circles in the same firmament, in one of which are the twelve signs [below, chs. 5 and 6], do we mean that these are a failure of our sight?” Since this, then, seems to rest on authority, let us answer these objections from that authority itself.

## CHAPTER V.—That authority speaks of the upper regions in different modes

Authority, then, speaks of the upper regions in three modes: mythically, astrologically, and astronomically. Nemrod, Hyginus, and Aratus speak mythically when they say that that bull was transferred and changed into a constellation, and likewise concerning the others. This mode of treatment is especially necessary, for by it we know in what part of heaven each sign is situated.

To treat them astrologically is to say what appears in the upper regions, whether it is so or not. For many things seem to be there which are not there, because sight is deceived, as Marcianus Hyspaicus [perhaps *Hispanus*, or possibly Capella?] treats the matter. To treat them astronomically is to speak of what is there, whether it appears so or not; this is how Julius Firmicus and Ptolemy treat them. Therefore, when it is said that heaven covers all things, this is an astrological statement, because it appears so; or ether is called heaven because it is inlaid with diverse stars.

## CHAPTER VI.—On the firmament and the stars

[Col. 0059C]

It is called the firmament because by its heat and by the influence of the stars it strengthens and moderates what lies beneath. Heaven, then, covers all things because all things are contained beneath or within the ether. The fixed stars are said to be set in the ether like a gem in gold, because, remaining in it, they are always seen in the same part of it. Others are called wandering because they are seen now in this, now in that part of heaven. And since we have mentioned the fixed stars, let us ask whether they move or are altogether without motion, and, if they move, how they move.

## CHAPTER VII.—Whether the fixed stars move

Some maintain that they do not move, but are carried to rising and setting by the firmament, as though fixed in it. Others say that they too move by their own motion, because they are fiery in nature and nothing in ether or air can be sustained without motion; but they always move in the same place and around themselves. A third group says that they move from place to place, yet none of these motions is perceived by our eyes, because they consume so vast a space in traversing their circles that human life, which is short, does not suffice to apprehend so slow an advance within so brief a point of time.

Although we agree with this opinion that they move from place to place, we offer another reason why their motion is not perceived. It is this: every motion is distinguished either through something immovable or through something less mobile. When something moves, if we see something mobile or less mobile, [Col. 0060A] we perceive motion when we see the moving thing pass it or approach it. But if something moves outside itself and we see neither anything immovable nor anything less mobile, its motion is not perceived. This may be demonstrated by a ship moving across the sea.

The motion of the stars, then, is perceived through something immovable or less mobile placed above them, but never through something beneath them. Thus we distinguish the motion of the planets by the signs, because they are seen now under one sign, now under another. But above the stars just mentioned there is nothing visible, and therefore there is nothing by which their motion may be distinguished. Therefore they move, but they are called fixed because their motion is not perceived for the reason stated.

## CHAPTER VIII.—How many circles are said to be in the firmament

[Col. 0060B]

In the same firmament philosophers said that there are twelve circles, two visible and the others invisible. Let us discuss the visible ones.

## CHAPTER IX.—Which are visible

There are, then, two visible circles: γαλαξίας, that is, the Milky Circle—for γάλαξ means “milk,” and ἀγός, “circle”—and the zodiacal circle.

## CHAPTER X.—Where the *galaxias* begins

The *galaxias* begins near the north, on the eastern side, and at some point passes through Cancer and Capricorn, returning to its starting-point. It is so called because of its remarkable brightness. If anyone wishes to know why that remarkable brightness is in that part, let him read Macrobius (*Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, Book I).

## CHAPTER XI.—On the zodiac and why it is so called

[Col. 0060C]

The zodiac rises from Capricorn through Aries to Cancer, and descends from Cancer through Libra to Capricorn. Understand “descent” and “ascent” according to our own position. This circle, as Macrobius relates, was divided by the flow of water into twelve equal parts, each of which is called a sign, because by them we mark in what part of heaven the sun and the other planets are, from which part they have departed, and to which they are to pass. But because these parts bear the names of animals—Aries, Taurus, and the rest—the circle that contains them is called the zodiac; for ζῷον means “animal.” If anyone seeks the causes of the names, let him read Helpericus.

## CHAPTER XII.—On the arrangement of the signs

[Col. 0060D]

The arrangement of the signs is as follows. Nearest to us is Cancer, namely at the boundary of our habitable zone and the torrid zone; then Leo descends obliquely, followed by Virgo, then Libra, lying in the middle of the torrid zone; beyond it is Scorpio, then Sagittarius, and after that Capricorn, farthest from us. Then, rising obliquely, come Aquarius, then Pisces, then Aries; opposite Libra in the middle of the torrid zone above is Taurus, then Gemini, and then Cancer. We shall explain, when speaking of the sun, which sign belongs to which month and why.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On the invisible circles

There are nine other invisible circles, five of which are parallels. One is called the equinoctial; it passes through the middle of the torrid zone [Col. 0061A] and through Aries and Libra, dividing heaven into two hemispheres. It is called equinoctial because, when the sun reaches it, it makes day equal to night; we shall speak of it below. Another of the parallels is called the conjunction of our habitable zone and the torrid zone. The third is the conjunction of the same zone and the frigid zone. The fourth, on the other side, is the conjunction of the torrid zone and the other habitable zone. The fifth is the conjunction of that same zone and the other frigid zone, as appears in the later diagram.

But because authority declares that there are zones in heaven, whether they are in ether or air we shall discuss when treating of air. Those five circles are called parallels, that is, equally distant, because they are equally distant from the middle circle, the equinoctial. For the junction of our habitable zone and the torrid zone is as far from it as is the corresponding junction of the other zone. Likewise, the junction of [Col. 0061B] our habitable and frigid zones is as far from it as the corresponding junction of the other zones.

## CHAPTER XIV.—On the two colures

After these are the two colures, whose origin is in the middle of the north; but one descends through Cancer and rises through Capricorn, returning to the same starting-point. The other goes through the east and Aries, returning through the west to its starting-point. Thus they intersect at the summit of the north and divide heaven into four quadrants. They are called *coluri*, as if *colon uri*, “the limb of a wild ox,” so called because of incompleteness—not because they themselves are incomplete, but because that portion of the other pole which they intersect is never seen.

## CHAPTER XV.—On the horizon and the meridian circle

The two remaining circles of the number already mentioned are the meridian [Col. 0061C] and the horizon. The meridian is the line marking that part of heaven in which the sun, when situated there, is equally distant from rising and setting. The horizon is where heaven appears to be joined with earth; it is called *horizon* as though “a boundary.” These two are drawn last on the sphere, because they vary according to the different observers or inhabitants.

## CHAPTER XVI.—On the movement of the firmament and the poles

The movement of ether, or fire—which for the reasons already given is called heaven and firmament—is as follows. Since fire is by nature always in motion, and there was nothing above it to which it could rise, as we have shown, and it could not descend because that would be contrary to its nature, while all lower places were occupied by the lower elements; and since it was also useless for it to descend, for in descending it would burn the earth and nothing could live upon it: therefore it has movement where it can, and it moves in a circle. It moves in a circle not by occupying different places, but by having its parts differently and differently situated in the same place. Thus, turning itself in a circle from east through west, it carries the stars with it, both wandering and fixed.

Yet, although it revolves around the earth, it does so not directly but obliquely around our habitable region, as can be seen from the poles alone. A pole is an immovable star, one at this end and another at the other. The axis is an intelligible line drawn from pole to pole through the middle of the earth, about which the firmament revolves. Therefore, if the firmament revolved directly, one pole would be directly above the earth and the other below the earth, or at its sides. But because one is raised midway in the heaven on our side, and likewise the other on the opposite side, the line called the axis is oblique, and the firmament revolves obliquely around it.

And since we have sufficiently refuted the false opinion of certain persons about the firmament, established and proved our own, and have not been silent concerning the fixed stars in it, its circles, and its movement, let us begin to speak of the planets. Let us therefore take our beginning from the highest of the planets.

## CHAPTER XVII.—On Saturn, why a star is called cold, and in how many ways names of qualities are attributed to things

Saturn, then, is called the highest of the planets, taking thirty years to traverse the zodiac. Hence in myths he is called an old man. This star is said to be cold and harmful. Let us first discuss its coldness, then its harmfulness.

The ancient astrologers demonstrated that this star is cold and dry when, knowing that the sun was in Cancer, they observed that in some year it scorched the lands less than usual. Knowing that this did not occur through the nature of the sun, they investigated which planet was in the same sign as the sun; and, having found it, they said that the cause of the coldness came from it. But someone will say: since every stellar body is fiery in nature—as its motion and brightness prove—how can one star be called cold and another hot? Nor do we prove this by the argument of those who say that Saturn is cold because of its proximity to frozen waters, just as the moon is cold because of its proximity to earth and water. For we have shown above that frozen waters cannot exist in the upper regions (above, Book II, ch. 2).

Some say that there are several qualities of fire, joined together in some bodies and separate in others. Thus, just as there is something fiery and hot yet not bright, so there is something bright yet not hot. They say that fiery things are not hot unless they are joined to some dense and moist nature, which they transform into their own substance. Hence, if a fiery thing lacks the proximity of dense moisture, heat fails in it. They prove this by the sun: in mountain valleys, where the air is denser, it exerts great heat; in the upper regions, because of the subtlety of the air, it does not exert heat. Perpetual snows are evidence of this. But we shall say enough about this when speaking of the position of the earth. These same persons also maintain that, above the moon, no heat is felt because of the ether’s excessive subtlety.

We, however, say that names of qualities are attributed to things in three ways: by their effect—thus wine is called hot because it produces heat, though it feels cold; by sensation—thus we call boiling water hot, although it is naturally cold; or by a sign—thus we say that a healthy person sleeps well and breathes without difficulty. Therefore, when a star is called cold, the name is assigned by its effect. Although it is hot in itself, if it produces cold, it is called cold. Thus, because Saturn joined with the sun lessens heat, it is called cold by reason of its effect, though it is hot in itself.

But perhaps someone will ask: if stellar bodies are fiery, how does it happen that some produce cold? For a reason can be found in all things; but in some matters recourse must be had to creation. Yet we can give this explanation: different fiery bodies, because of nearness and distance, heat more or less. Thus Saturn, being farther from us, does not heat the earth; but the sun, being nearer to the earth, burns it more. Or let us say that although some star is hot, it has other qualities unknown to us, through which its heat cannot descend. But since we have posed the question in the middle of our discussion, “Not all of us can do everything,” let it be for each person’s ingenuity to inquire what may be discovered for resolving this question.

The same star is called harmful because of its coldness, especially when it is retrograde; hence in myths it is said to carry a sickle. For one carrying a sickle harms more while retreating than while approaching.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On Jupiter

After Saturn comes Jupiter, taking twelve years to traverse the zodiac. This star is beneficent, since its qualities are so well tempered, as has been proved from its conjunction with the sun. But when it lies between Saturn and Mars, whether it is in the upper apogee of its circle or the lower, their harmfulness is moderated by its beneficence. Hence myths say that Jupiter drove his father Saturn from his kingdom: because, having become nearer to Saturn, he removes Saturn’s natural harmfulness. He is also said to have fathered diverse offspring through adultery, because by joining himself to the aforesaid bodies he produces diverse effects in earthly things.

## CHAPTER XIX.—On Mars

The third star is Mars, hot and dry, and therefore harmful, traversing the zodiac in two years. But, placed between Jupiter and Venus, which are beneficent stars, its proximity lessens both its own harmfulness and their beneficence. It is said to rule in battles because it imparts heat and dryness, from which spiritedness arises. For hot and dry persons are spirited.

## CHAPTER XX.—On Venus

Fourth, according to the Platonists, is Venus, a hot and moist star, and therefore beneficent, traversing the zodiac in nearly a year. She is said to commit adultery with Mars because, when she is in the upper apogee of her circle and has become close to Mars, she is less beneficent. She is called the goddess of lust because she imparts heat and moisture, and lust thrives in those who are hot and moist.

For, to say briefly regarding Venus what we shall explain more fully when speaking of man: those who are hot and dry strongly desire sexual indulgence because of heat, but through dryness cannot endure its effect; and if they engage in it, it is especially harmful to them. Those who are cold and moist, on the contrary, desire it poorly, but endure it. But those who are cold and dry neither desire it nor experience its effect; its effect is especially beneficial to their bodies.

## CHAPTER XXI.—How the same star is called Lucifer and Hesperus

It is called Lucifer when it is seen before the sun, Hesperus when it is seen after it in the evening. Hence there is a question: can it be Lucifer and Hesperus at the same time of year? Some say that this is impossible. Since it is of equal speed with the sun and completes its course in nearly the same space, how could it follow the sun in the evening and precede it in the morning of one and the same night? Therefore at one time of year it precedes the sun, and then it is Lucifer; at another it follows, and then it is Hesperus.

Others say that at one and the same time of year it is seen before sunrise and after sunset, though it does not precede and follow the sun, since this would be impossible. They say that this star is higher than the sun; thus it is visible longer in the evening even though it does not follow the sun, and earlier in the morning even though it does not go before it. It is called Lucifer and Hesperus at the same time of year, not because it precedes and follows, but because, owing to its height, it is seen before and after.

A third group says that Venus and Mercury are nearly of the same color and size and always accompany the sun. When they accompany it in such a way that one precedes and the other follows, the one preceding in the evening is not seen because of the sun’s brightness, while the one following appears after its setting. Conversely, in the morning the preceding one is seen, while the following one is hidden by the brightness of day. But because they are of one color and size, they were regarded as one and the same star.

## CHAPTER XXII.—On Mercury

Mercury is fifth, likewise completing its course in nearly a year. Venus is said to have committed adultery with it because, when it is in the lower apogee of its circle, Venus mingles her qualities with its own.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—On the station and retrogradation of the aforesaid stars; that it is true that the sun is below Mercury and Venus; and on their circles

The sun is sixth. But let us first explain the station and retrogradation of the aforesaid stars, and then why the Chaldeans and their followers said that the sun is in the middle of the planets, above Venus and Mercury. The Egyptians, whom Plato followed, said that it was sixth and placed above Mercury and Venus.

Some say that there is a certain part in the circle of each star at which, when it reaches it, the sun makes it stand still or move backward; but they do not say why. [Col. 0064D] We say that they are never seen to stand still, because, being fiery in nature, they must always be in motion; yet they sometimes appear to stand still, through ἄρσις and θέσις, that is, elevation and depression. For all astrologers agree that each of the planets is at times farther than usual from the earth, and then it is elevated; at times it descends more toward the earth, which we call being depressed. Therefore, when they are elevated or depressed, if this occurs in a direct manner, they are seen beneath the same part of a sign and are believed to stand still. But if they bend backward obliquely, they appear to move backward.

The cause of this elevation or depression is the sun. Since it is the source of all heat, it sometimes dries out the higher and lower regions more than usual. Hence the dried stellar bodies, being lighter than usual, rise. If, again, it draws more moisture than usual for its nourishment, they descend as heavy bodies. Thus, their supposed station is an astrological statement, because it appears so.

Next we must say why the Chaldeans call the sun fourth, while the Egyptians and Plato call it sixth. It is true that the sun is below Mercury and Venus, near the moon. Since the moon is cold and moist, the sun, which is hot and dry, had to be near it, so that the moon’s coldness might be tempered by the sun’s heat and its moisture by the sun’s dryness, lest, being near the earth, it render the earth ill-tempered. Again, since the moon lacks light of its own, as we have shown, and receives it from the sun, it is reasonable that it should be placed immediately below the source of its light, without an intervening body.

Yet although this is true, the Chaldeans saw the matter differently for the reason we shall state. The sun, Mercury, and Venus are so conjoined that they complete their courses in nearly the same span of time—namely, a year, more or less. Therefore their circles are nearly equal; but according to the size of their circles, the planets take a shorter or longer time in traversing the zodiac. Since, then, they are nearly equal, one cannot wholly contain another. Therefore they intersect each other: the circle of Venus, with the lower part of its circle, intersects the upper parts of the circles of Mercury and the sun, and contains more of the Mercurial than of the solar circle. The circle of Mercury, in its upper part, intersects the Venusian circle, namely the lower part of the solar circle. But the solar circle, in its upper part, intersects both the Mercurial and Venusian circles—more of the Mercurial, less of the Venusian. But because a description placed before the eyes enters the mind more easily, let us show that intersection by a diagram.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—When the circles of Venus and Mercury appear more freely

Since the circle of the sun is surrounded by their lower parts, it is rightly called inferior to them. What lies below the sun does not obscure it as much as what lies above it. Therefore the sun was considered superior to them. But let us now turn the discussion to the sun and the other planets. Since the remaining planets move as the sun does, let us speak of the sun’s movement, so that similar points may be understood concerning the others.

## CHAPTER XXV.—Whether the planets move with the firmament or against it

The general opinion of all philosophers is that the firmament revolves from east to west, but that the sun and the other planets move with a contrary motion, from west to east. This is shown to the eyes by the arrangement of the signs. [Col. 0066A] [Col. 0066B] For Aries is so situated that, when it is in the middle of the sky, Taurus lies between it and the east, then Gemini, then Cancer; between the same Aries and the west lie Pisces, then Aquarius, then Capricorn, as appears in this diagram. Therefore, if the sun tended toward the west, it would pass from Aries into the sign situated toward the west, namely Pisces, and then into the rest. But since it passes to the signs situated toward the east, from Aries into Taurus and then the others, it unquestionably moves contrary to the firmament.

They also add a reason why it had to be so. Since the firmament revolves from east to west, if the planets moved similarly, the force would be so great that nothing could stand or live upon earth. Therefore, in order that their rays might oppose that motion and moderate its force, they were turned to a contrary motion. Yet, although they are carried contrary to the firmament, the firmament nevertheless carries them with itself toward the west and thence toward the east. It is as if someone on a ship moved in the direction opposite to that in which the ship runs; nevertheless the ship carries him with it wherever it goes, and he is not for that reason at rest in respect to the contrary motion. Thus their gradual movement toward the east is their natural course; their movement toward west and east results from the force of another.

Helpericus says that this cannot be so. Since the sun is not among the stars fixed in the firmament, how can it be carried by it? If someone is outside a ship, how can he be carried by it? Regarding the fact that the sun goes toward the signs placed to the east, he says that it appears so but is not truly so. For, he says, when the firmament and sun tend by natural motion from east to west, whatever is beneath the first part of Aries—because the firmament sometimes passes more swiftly than the sun—when the sun is in the twentieth part of one sign, then truly the sun comes toward the east; but not that part of the sign which was formerly seen above the sun is now seen above it, rather the following part. Thus, as this happens day after day, it appears that the sun goes toward the later signs when it does not. Anyone can prove this by the moon. For since it is certain that the moon does not run toward the north, if clouds run before it, when they pass the moon it appears that the moon runs toward the later regions.

But because the most learned of all philosophers agrees with the first opinion, and it is true, we agree with it. Against this, he said that the sun could not be carried by the firmament because it is not in it. Although they may say that this is weak according to our opinion, in which we say that the ether is called the firmament [the printed text has *firmum*, perhaps for *firmamentum*], we nevertheless say that, even if it is not in the firmament, it can still be carried by it. To persist in the same example of a ship: if something light is beside a ship, it is carried along by the ship’s force as though it were in it. Therefore, since the sun is light and fiery in nature, it can be carried by the firmament even if it is not in it.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—Why the sun moves obliquely, and on winter and spring
The sun and the other planets therefore move from west to east, not in a straight course but obliquely: that is, descending and ascending toward the east, in accordance with the disposition of the signs mentioned above. But [Col. 0067B] someone will ask: What necessity was there for the sun to move obliquely rather than straight? The answer is: a great necessity, as we shall show. But first let us set forth the changes produced by its oblique course, beginning from the more remote point, that is, Capricorn.

When, therefore, the sun enters Capricorn—which occurs in mid-December—it enters the sign for one month and leaves it in mid-January; and the season is assigned to the sign into which it enters, because then, being farthest from our inhabited region, it binds that region in cold. For earth and water are naturally cold unless warmed by the sun. Likewise, since there is nothing by which it may dry out, the air thickens into clouds, which dissolve into rain. Thus arises a certain division of the year called winter. Winter is wet and cold, and extends until the sun has passed through Aquarius and Pisces, [Col. 0067C] entering the first in mid-January and the second in mid-February. Winter therefore consists of three months and is one of the four seasons of the year.

“In it the pores of the earth’s surface are constricted by cold, and heat cannot evaporate; remaining within, it nourishes the roots of herbs and trees and performs the office of a pregnant mother.”

Yet it does not bring growth, because neither heat nor moisture, from which all growth comes, can rise on account of the cold of this constriction. But we shall explain in the treatise on air whence frost, snow, hail, rain, thunder, and lightning arise.

Water, phlegm, and decrepit old age resemble this season, for these are cold and wet. In it choleric persons fare better, phlegmatic persons worse; young people better, the decrepit worse. The worst illness is that arising from phlegm, namely the quotidian fever; less bad is that arising from choler, such as the tertian. During this season it is beneficial to increase one’s food. For the pores of the human body are constricted by cold; hence the heat remaining inside consumes more. Therefore, against inner depletion, it is fitting to supply outward nourishment. Hence among the ancients the god of winter was depicted with a fat belly and was called *Spurius*, from the filth of a marsh. In this season it is good to use hot and dry things.

But when the sun, ascending, reaches Aries, which it enters in mid-March, it is neither more remote nor more near, being situated, as it were, in the middle [Col. 0068A] of the torrid zone. Hence the air of our inhabited region is neither hotter nor colder, neither drier nor wetter, but is tempered between the four qualities. From this tempering the pores of the earth open, and moist vapor evaporates; rising through the roots of trees and herbs, it gives them growth and vitality (Macrobius). Hence a month of this season is called April, because then the earth opens into flowers. The distinctive trait of this season is its instability: at one time rainy, because of the nearness of winter; at another dry, because of the nearness of summer; likewise, for the same reason, at one time hot and at another cold. Thus people often fall ill in March, because human bodies are opened by warmth and immediately damaged by sudden cold. But if someone preserves himself during [Col. 0068B] this season, he will fall ill later in it than at another time.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—Why the sick die more often in spring and autumn; and concerning the four seasons of the year

Here someone asks: Why is it, then, that if someone falls ill, he does not die as often in winter as in spring? Since illnesses arise from harmful humors spreading through the limbs, in the cold of winter the humors are constricted and cannot flow out.

But in the warmth of spring they are likewise dissolved; and, flowing through the limbs, they overcome a person and he dies. This temperate period, beginning with Aries, extends while the sun is in Taurus and Gemini, entering the first [Col. 0068C] in mid-April and the second in mid-May. Air, blood, and childhood resemble this season because they are hot and wet. In it melancholic persons fare better, sanguine persons worse; old people better, children worse. The worst illness is that arising from blood; less bad is that arising from melancholy, such as quartan fever. In this season it is appropriate to use cold and dry things.

But when the sun ascends as far as Cancer, by its nearness it burns and dries the earth. Hence summer is hot and dry. Beginning in mid-June, when the sun enters Cancer, it continues while it is in Leo, which it enters in mid-July, and while it is in Virgo, which it enters in mid-August. It is characteristic of this season to dry up the roots of herbs and trees. It resembles [Col. 0068D] fire, choler, and youth, for these are hot and dry. In it phlegmatic persons fare better, choleric persons worse; the decrepit better, young people worse. The worst illness is that arising from choler; less bad is that arising from phlegm. In this season it is useful to employ cold and wet things. Drink should be increased and food reduced. For, since the pores of the body are opened by heat, natural heat evaporates, and food is consequently not digested so well. But because drink quickly passes into the blood, it should be increased.

Here a question arises. Since these variations in the aforesaid seasons occur through the nearness and remoteness of the sun, and since the sun, when in Leo, is as far from our inhabited region as when it is in Gemini; when in Virgo, as when in Taurus; and when in Libra, as when in Aries—[Col. 0069A] why does it produce heat and moisture in those three signs, but heat and dryness in these two? The answer is this: when it is in the three spring signs, it produces heat because it is near, and moisture because of the nearness of the preceding winter. But when the sun is in Leo and Virgo, it produces heat through its nearness. Yet, because moisture has already been dried up by the heat of spring and summer, there is nothing to temper the heat and no source from which moisture may arise. Hence the weather is hot.

But when it is in Libra, because moisture has now been entirely dried up and heat extinguished, autumn arises, cold and dry. In it fruits containing moisture within them, such as clusters of grapes and the rest, are gathered ripe through the double dryness of summer and autumn. Autumn begins [Col. 0069B] in mid-September, with the sun entering Libra, and lasts while the sun is in Scorpio and Sagittarius, entering the first in mid-October and the second in mid-November. Earth, melancholy, and old age resemble this season because they are cold and dry. In it sanguine persons fare better, melancholic persons worse; children better, old people worse. The worst illness is that arising from melancholy; less bad is that arising from blood.

To speak generally: in every season of the year, the worst illness is that produced by a humor similar in temperament to the season, for the matter of the disease is increased by the qualities of the season. Less bad is an illness produced by a humor contrary to the season, for the matter of the disease is diminished by the season’s quality. In this season it is beneficial to use hot and wet things. This season is uneven because of the nearness of the preceding summer and the following winter; consequently, people are indiscriminately endangered by the juices of fruits.

Here arises a question similar to the preceding one. Since the sun in Scorpio is as far from us as it is in Pisces, and in Sagittarius as far as it is in Aquarius, why does it produce one set of qualities in the former and another in the latter? The solution is easy. In the former signs, namely Scorpio and Sagittarius, because moisture has been dried up in summer and the sun has now passed the middle of the torrid zone, there are cold and dryness. In the latter signs, since the sun is likewise remote, there is coldness; but because the heat which dries the air has long since failed, the air gradually thickens into clouds, and the weather becomes wet. Although, as we have said, winter is cold and wet, at its beginning [Col. 0069D] it is colder and less wet; at its end wetter and less cold; and in its middle equal in both. Spring, at its beginning, is wetter and less hot; at its end hotter and less wet; and in its middle equal in both. Summer, at its beginning, is hotter and less dry; at its end drier and less hot; and in its middle equal in both. Autumn, at its beginning, is drier and less cold; at its end colder and less dry; and in its middle equal in both.

It should be noted, however, that although these are the four seasons’ properties, they nevertheless vary accidentally. Thus, if a hot planet, such as Mars, hot and dry by nature, is present with the winter signs; likewise, if a cold and wet planet is present in summer, the season is more wet and dry [Col. 0070A] than usual [as printed; perhaps “wet and cold” is intended]. Therefore the prudent physician must always observe which signs the sun occupies and which planet is [Col. 0070B] with it in the same sign, so that he may know what the coming summer and the other seasons will be like and may have a remedy ready against the quality to come.

Since, then, the sun produces these variations by ascending and descending obliquely, let us see what harm would follow if it always revolved in a straight course. No one doubts that if it always moved as near to us as in summer, we should always have heat.

[Col. 0070C] Nor could anything grow. Likewise, if it were always as remote as in winter, there would always be bitter cold, and no fruits or herbs would grow. But someone will say: “If it moved thus, there would be spring in Aries, where it would be equally distant, and it would always produce for us the equal temperateness of spring; no harm would result.” We say, on the contrary, that the worst harm would result. For the earth would never conceive within itself, as it does in winter; nor would any fruits that might grow tend toward ripeness. Without these, the multitude of living creatures could not survive.

And since we have spoken of the sun’s natural motion, let us now speak of what it does when carried back [Col. 0070D] by the firmament. Since the sun strives by its natural motion from west to east against the firmament, it is daily carried back by the firmament toward the west. While it is above the earth, it produces brightness, which is called day; while it is beneath the earth, darkness is in the upper region, and this is called night. It should be observed that one day is natural and another customary. Let us discuss the natural first, then the customary.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—What the natural and customary day are, and their divisions

The natural day contains a period of twenty-four hours, namely, the customary day and night. Thus we say that there are thirty days in a month, although [Col. 0071A] it contains both days and nights. Physicians divide this into four parts: from the ninth hour of the night to the third hour of the customary day, it is said to be hot and wet; from the third hour of the customary day to the ninth, hot and dry; from the ninth hour of that day to the third hour of the night, cold and wet. Thus certain illnesses fare worse or better in different parts of the same day according to the aforesaid account of the seasons.

The customary day is the period during which the sun is carried from rising to setting. They divide it, like the natural day, in four ways. In its first part the sun is red; then it shines; afterward it is hot; finally it descends and is warm. Hence in fables four horses are assigned to Phoebus, their names corresponding to the foregoing accounts. The first is called *Eous* [printed *exactus*], that is, “red”; [Col. 0071B] the second *Lacteus*, that is, “shining”; the third *Lampas*, that is, “burning”; the fourth *Philogeus*, that is, “earth-loving.” In these customary days, three variations occur in the course of the year: sometimes they are equal to the nights, sometimes longer, sometimes shorter.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—The cause of the equality and inequality of days

This is the cause of these variations. When the sun is in the winter signs, the swelling of the earth, which is in the middle of the torrid zone and lies between us and it, prevents us from seeing it quickly and is the reason why it is removed from our sight. Hence its brightness above the earth is shorter for us, and so the day has a long shadow—and therefore night. But when it is in Cancer and [Col. 0071C] the other summer signs, because it rises on this side of the earth’s swelling, it is seen early in the morning and is removed late from our sight. Its brightness above the earth is consequently longer, and the shadow shorter. But when it is in Aries or Libra, because it is equally distant from us, it is equally above and beneath the earth; hence there is equal brightness and equal darkness.

## CHAPTER XXX.—The cause of a solar eclipse, and why it does not occur every month

Having listed the effects of the sun, both from its natural and accidental motion, let us discuss its eclipse: why and at what time it occurs. The sun is [Col. 0072A] in the middle of the zodiac, a place called the ecliptic. The moon is placed beneath it in such a manner that, if a line were drawn, it would pass through the middle of the sun, moon, and earthly body. Then the moon causes its rays to be blocked, and they cannot descend to the earth because of the covering of the lunar body. Hence this never occurs except at the thirtieth moon, because on another day it is not placed directly beneath the sun.

Yet it does not occur at every thirtieth moon. But whenever it does occur, it occurs then. For if, on the thirtieth day of the moon, it is so opposed to the sun that one is somewhat toward Cancer and the other toward Capricorn, the moon cannot deprive us of the sight of the sun or of the descent of its rays. But since we have discussed the sun according to our ability, let us next discuss the moon.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—Why the moon has neither brightness nor heat of its own; and concerning the new moon and full moon

[Col. 0072B]

Because of its nearness to water and earth, the moon has a denser body than the other stars; hence it has no brightness or heat of its own, but is kindled by the sun. For if it had heat of its own, since it is near the earth, it would bring upon the earth every month the heat of summer and the cold of winter; and nothing could live amid such continuous variations. Therefore it lacks brightness and heat, though it is illuminated by the sun placed above it—not always equally, however, but now after the new moon, now at the full moon, now at the dark of the moon.

Some say that when it is placed beneath [Col. 0072C] the sun in the same sign, it is obscured by excessive brightness and cannot appear; but when it moves away from the sun, brightness begins to appear in it. Hence, the farther it is removed from the sun, the greater brightness appears in it. But because it first appears on the side of the sun, their view seems false.

It seems to us that every luminous body, when something dark is placed beneath it, makes shadow on the side opposite itself and brightness on its own side. Therefore, when the moon—which, as we said, is naturally dark—is placed beneath the sun, it puts brightness upon that side of itself which is above, toward the sun, and makes shadow on the opposite side, toward the earth; hence the moon is not seen by us. But when it moves away from the sun, brightness begins to appear like a slender horn, and it is called *μονοειδής* (*monoeidēs*), “single-formed” or crescent-shaped. The farther it moves away, the more brightly it descends, so that on the seventh day it is called *διχότομος* (*dichotomos*), “divided through the middle.” It should be noted that as brightness descends, shadow rises, and conversely. After the seventh day until the thirteenth it is *ἀμφίκυρτος* (*amphikyrtos*), “less than full” and greater than half; on the fourteenth day, because it is removed from the sun by a diameter [it is] *πανσέλητος* (*pansēlētos*), “full moon.” This may be proved from the fact that it rises as the sun sets: all the shadow has now risen and all the brightness descended.

Thereafter it begins to approach the sun, and shadow descends while brightness rises. Hence brightness fails on our side, and it becomes first, [Col. 0073A] [Col. 0073B] in its descent, *ἀμφίκυρτος* (*amphikyrtos*), then *διχότομος* (*dichotomos*), and afterward *μονοειδής* (*monoeidēs*). All these things will be clearer to the eye from the figure set forth above.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—The eclipse of the moon, why it does not occur every month, and the forms of shadows

A lunar eclipse occurs when the sun and moon are arranged on the aforesaid ecliptic line so that the sun is in the lower hemisphere, the moon in the upper, and the earth in the middle; thus, if a line descended from the middle of the lunar body, it would pass through the middle of the earthly and solar bodies. Then the higher-interposed swelling of the earth directs its shadow as far as that line; therefore the sun’s rays cannot kindle the moon. It suffers eclipse until, by moving, it has passed the swelling and brightness begins to appear in it. Hence it is never eclipsed except at the fifteenth moon, because it is then opposite the sun. Yet this does not happen at every fifteenth moon; but whenever it does happen, it occurs because of the shape of the earth’s shadow.

Let us first explain the forms of shadows made by a round body placed opposite a source of light. Every shadow of such a body is either cylindrical or conical. A cylinder is a long, round figure, increasing equally and not converging into lines at its summit. Therefore a shadow of such a shape is called cylindrical. It occurs whenever the luminous body and the dark body are of the same size, in this manner.

[Col. 0073D]

[Col. 0074A] Since the bodies of the sun and earth are not equal—for the sun is eight times larger than the earth—the earth’s shadow cannot be a *κύλινδρος* (*kylindros*), a cylinder. A basket (*calathus*), however, is a figure rising from a point into a broad upper part. Hence a shadow of this figure is called *καλαθοειδής* (*kalathoeidēs*), basket-shaped. This occurs when the luminous body is smaller than the dark body, in this manner. But the earth’s shadow cannot be basket-shaped, because, as Macrobius proves, the sun is greater than the earth. A conical shadow is so called because it proceeds from a broad base to a point; it occurs if the luminous body is greater than the dark body, as is shown in the following diagram.

[Col. 0074B]

Therefore, because the solar body is greater than the earth, the earth’s shadow is conical. When the sun and moon are, as we have said, so placed that the cone of the earth’s shadow points directly at the moon, it darkens it; nor does it receive rays from the sun until it has passed beyond the cone of shadow. But if at the fifteenth moon they are not so arranged, but one is somewhat toward the north and the other toward the south, the cone of shadow is not directed straight toward the moon and does not darken it, but passes beside it, in this manner.

[Col. 0074D]

[Col. 0075A] Having seen why the lunar eclipse occurs and why it does not occur every month, let us say what we think concerning the shadow that is always seen in its middle. [Col. 0076A] Since the moon is cold and wet, although it is illuminated by the sun, it retains some part of itself in which a certain natural darkness always appears.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0075]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0075A]

Although, occupied with the work of teaching, we have little time for writing, yet we discern that many have departed from philosophy after tearing away its garments and snatching up little scraps, believing that the whole of it has passed over to them. Stirred by philosophy herself crying out lest she remain naked, we have sewn the torn fragments together with the pen of our small ability. We are not ignorant that we are exposed to the bites of envy; [Col. 0075B] and today it is dangerous for us to know and to possess anything. But since, as someone says:

> Nothing is more just than envy, which immediately gnaws  
> At its very author, tormenting his mind;

and Horace says (*Epistles* I.ii.57):

> The envious man grows lean at another’s prosperity.  
> The Sicilian tyrants devised  
> No greater torment than envy.

Certain of their torments, though not doubting the many bites of venomous men, and, like Catos pursuing ferocity through the heat of Libya, armed with various arguments against the faint-hearted, let us proceed to what follows.

## CHAPTER I.—On air

Since we have taught, in a manner suitable to our purpose, what seemed proper to us concerning the ether and its adornment, [Col. 0075C] let us teach concerning the air joined to and subject to it, showing what happens in it and from what causes. Air, then, extends from the moon down to the earth. The nearer it is to the earth, the wetter and denser it is; the farther away, the drier and brighter. Since it lies beneath the sun, it receives heat and moisture from it. But because the sun never passes beyond the limits of the torrid zone, it kindles the part of the air near it and leaves the remote part devoid of its heat.

## CHAPTER II.—How there are five zones in the air

There are therefore five distinct regions in the air, called zones by the ancients—not, as some suppose, above the moon. For there all things are immutable, since there is no contrariety there. Since ether, which is called fire, and the bodies of the stars are fiery, [Col. 0075D] whence could cold exist in any part there? But I know that these people have erred through the words of philosophers who declare that there are five zones in heaven. Against this we have a twofold defense. First, air is often called heaven; hence birds are called birds of heaven. Second, five parts of ether are superimposed on the five parts of air, and the part of ether is called by the name of the air beneath it. Thus the part superimposed on the cold zone is called cold, though there is no cold in it; and the part superimposed on the torrid zone, torrid—not because there is any burning heat in ether.

## CHAPTER III.—What differences arise on earth from the air

The upper fire is so subtle that it cannot kindle [Col. 0076A] anything until it is mixed with what is wet and dense. The same differences occur in the earth from the air above it. For the quality of the air affects the earth beneath it. Thus there are five zones in the air and five on earth. Let us therefore discuss the air over our inhabited region, showing what occurs in it and why; and let us begin with the varieties of rain, because rain is common to every season.

## CHAPTER IV.—The causes of rain

[Col. 0076B]

Rain has different causes. Sometimes dense and wet vapor evaporates; as it rises, exceedingly small drops gather around one another, and, becoming larger and heavier, fall, and rain results. At other times the air is thickened by the coldness of earth and water and passes into a watery substance; dried by the heat of the sun, as ice by fire, it falls in very tiny particles. Sometimes the sun draws moisture to nourish its color, and that which is more liquid in it passes into a fiery substance. But that which is heavier falls downward; thus, after the most intense heat, we see a flooding of rain occur. But this presents a question.

## CHAPTER V.—Why the sun’s rays and heat tend toward the earth

[Col. 0076C]

Since it is characteristic of fire to tend upward, why do the sun’s rays and heat tend toward the earth? To this we say that the sun is of a fiery nature not because it consists of fire alone, but because fire predominates in it. For we have already taught that the bodies of the stars are made from the four elements, although fire predominates. Since the sun consists of the four elements, though with fire predominant, that which it contains from earth and water tends toward its like—that is, toward earth and water. But because it proceeds from the source of heat, it carries with it some heat, by which earth and water are warmed. And because it is the nature of heat to ascend, the heat which descends in the aforesaid way raises again with itself some moisture, which, by boiling, it transfers [Col. 0076D] into its own substance.

## CHAPTER VI.—Why the sun warms the earth but the upper fire does not

If, then, we may speak properly, let us say that the sun raises moisture upward, rather than attracts it. Thus it is called a source of heat because it warms what lies below it in this manner; but the upper fire does not. Since it is an element not made from elements, it contains nothing that descends to lower things. Hence the part of air and earth subject to the sun is hot, but the remote part is cold, even though it is subject to ether.

But someone will say: “Is not fire, wherever it is, hot?” We answer: “No, unless it is joined to what is wet and dense.” Therefore, although there is fire above the moon, there is no burning heat there, because the wet and dense matter by which fire may be kindled is lacking; nor is there cold or darkness, but one continuous brightness and no change. But someone will object that Aristotle says: “It is impossible for fire not to be hot.” We answer that Aristotle there spoke of lower fire, which, always mixed with some dense matter, never ceases to be hot. We say that fire is hot not actually, but naturally.

The fourth cause of rain is wind lifting moisture from ponds, rivers, and lakes. Hence frogs and fish have often been seen by many people falling from the air. For, as we have said, when water is lifted by the wind, frogs and fish may be carried up with it; when they descend by their natural heaviness, the ignorant are astonished. Therefore no season of the year is free from rain. For in every season either wet vapor evaporates, the air thickens from cold, or moisture is raised by heat or wind.

## CHAPTER VII.—That drops of blood will fall before the end of the world, or why blood is said to rain

[Col. 0077B]

This rain, sometimes thickened more than usual and kindled by excessive heat, becomes red and dense like blood. Those who see it and do not know the cause of things say that blood is raining. Hence it is plausible that it was said that drops of blood will fall before the end of this world. And since the world is to end by burning, as Scripture testifies when it says in Psalm 49:

> Our God shall come openly;  
> our God shall not be silent.  
> Fire shall blaze before him  
> (Ps. XLIX [49]:3).

And elsewhere: “He who will come to judge the living and the dead, and the world through fire.” Waters spread out in the clouds by heat will be thickened by burning heat; once kindled and made red, they will fall in the likeness of blood.

At times, in rainy weather, a multicolored bow appears in the clouds. Let us say whence it arises and why so many colors appear in it. Since, as we said above, the sun’s heat raises moisture or wet vapor evaporates, the waters in a cloud are as though in a glass vessel: where it is thinner and hotter, it displays a red color; where denser, purple or black. Hence that bow never shines except on the side opposite the sun. For the air is so irradiated by the sun’s brightness that diverse colors appear in it.

## CHAPTER VIII.—The causes of hail and snow

[Col. 0077D]

Having considered the causes of rain and of the heavenly bow, let us discuss hail. When moisture is raised in the aforesaid way, a cold and dry wind often arises in the upper regions; by freezing drops of water with its coldness, it changes them into a stony substance. And because drops are round—as may be proved from the round holes which they make in stone by falling repeatedly—hail descends round. Hence the verse:

> A drop hollows out a stone, not by force but by frequent falling.

Snow, however, consists of the aforesaid drops, frozen after they have thickened but before they become large.

## CHAPTER IX.—Why snow never occurs in summer, although hail occurs then

[Col. 0078A]

Here they will ask: Since hail often occurs in summer, why does snow never occur then in the lower regions near mountains? We answer thus: in summer moisture is raised by some heat, and, as it rises, drops gather together; becoming larger and then frozen by cold, they produce hail. In winter, however, because cold is near the earth, drops of water are constricted by the coldness of the season before they become large, and are changed into snow. But in summer, because cold is not near the earth, they do not freeze until they have been raised high and have become large and dense. Therefore snow never occurs in summer, although hail does. Let us discuss the causes and manner of thunder and lightning.

## CHAPTER X.—On thunder and lightning

As vapor, therefore, tends upward, as we have said, when it reaches the top of the air, the uppermost part of the air is moved by the preponderance of moisture. Its particles, meeting one another like waves of water, make a crash. The air, warmed by this motion, passes into a fiery substance, and lightning results. Although it occurs with a crash, it reaches us sooner because sight is swifter than hearing.

Therefore, when they are generated here and there from condensed wet vapor, as we said, if the force rises upward, it is thunder without lightning. But if that force tends downward, yet is not so great as to reach an obstacle, it is not yet a lightning bolt. But when it reaches an obstacle, it splits what stands in its way.

Yet because it is the nature of the motion of air to tend upward, if no material prevents its exit, it returns and gathers together scattered fires. If, however, there is much moisture in this lower part of the air, the air in that violent motion cannot be ignited, and there is lightning that splits but does not burn. But if there is no moisture there, it catches fire from motion and dryness, and there is lightning that burns. A lightning bolt is a part of the air reaching an obstacle with violence as a result of some collision. Thunder is the sound of parts of air meeting one another. Lightning-flash is a part of the air ignited and shining through violent motion.

Therefore a lightning bolt is not a stony substance, as some maintain. For if it were a stony substance, it would not dart hither and thither or return upward; nor, when it struck flesh, would it crush bones. Lightning therefore more often strikes down high places because, descending obliquely from on high, it returns more quickly to high places. But since some maintain that a certain kind of lightning is a stony substance, lest we seem through ignorance or envy either to have censured it or passed it over in silence, let us briefly set it forth or explain it.

They say that when wet vapor rises upward—for it is characteristic of wet vapor to be raised upward, as we have often explained—some earthly substance rises with it. By the sun’s heat this thickens into a stony substance and remains enclosed in the hollow of a cloud until [Col. 0079A] the cloud is split by some violent force; then that stone, driven forth, strikes some high object.

## CHAPTER XI.—Why lightning occurs only in summer

Here someone will ask: Since wet vapor, as we have said, rises in every season of the year, why do lightning and thunder not occur in every season? We answer: although they derive their being from rising wet vapor, they do not occur until it reaches the top of the air. This may be demonstrated by comparison with the sea. When the sea is stirred at its bottom by rising vapor, it cannot be driven here or there because of its density. But when that disturbance reaches its top, the waves are driven here and there, and a storm results.

That a storm begins at the bottom may be proved from the fact that before a storm we see seals stirring the waves. Hence Pliny says that they are called *nautae dormitoriae* (“sleeping sailors” [as printed; perhaps corrupt]) and sleep at the bottom of the sea. Yet when vapor, as we have said, stirs the bottom of the sea, they are awakened and rise to the top. Sailors, seeing this and certain from experience though uncertain of natural philosophy, predict that a storm is coming, because the storm has already begun at the bottom.

The same is true of the air. While vapor occupies the lower parts of the air, it cannot drive the air here or there because of its density. But when it reaches the top, it drives it here and there because of its mobility, and thunder and lightning occur. In winter, although the air is dense, the heat is not great enough to raise dense vapor to the summit of the air. Remaining therefore in the lower part of the air, it produces winds and rains. In summer, whose heat is greatest and by which it is raised, various collisions of the parts of the air occur; hence lightning and thunder result. In autumn, which is cold and dry, there is neither moisture to be raised nor heat by which it may be raised.

## CHAPTER XII.—On the fact that stars sometimes seem to fall

In this same air no star is seen to fall, although something falls. Since stars are fiery by nature and their proper place is ether, they never descend to earth. Moreover, since they are very large, even though they appear small because of their remoteness, if one fell it would occupy the whole earth or the greater part of it. They do not, therefore, fall, but seem to fall.

For often there is wind and disturbance in the upper parts of the air, though not in the lower; from that disturbance air becomes ignited [Col. 0079D] and shining and moves through the air. When it begins to shine outside some star, it removes that star from our sight by its own brightness, and the star seems to have fallen. But someone will ask: “Why, then, do we not see that star?” To this we answer that the star may be seen, but that it is not known to be that star. For, as we have said, the ignited air moves onward; denser air, and therefore at times slower, follows it. Being placed between us and that star, it removes the star from our sight. But before it passes and the star appears, the firmament, revolving toward the west, has carried that star farther on with it. When it appears, because it is seen in another place than before, it is thought to be another star.

## CHAPTER XIII.—That a comet is not a star

[Col. 0080A]

Concerning the comet that appears at a change of empire, we hold that it is not a star, because it is neither one of the fixed stars nor a planet. That it is not one of the fixed stars appears from the fact that its motion is perceived. Nor is it a planet, since it is often seen outside the zodiac and does not follow the motion of the planets. Moreover, if it were a star, it would be in some hemisphere. When, therefore, the stars of that hemisphere appear, why does this one, which seems greater, not appear? It is not, then, a star, but a fire kindled by the will of the Creator to signify something.

## CHAPTER XIV.—On the refluxes of Ocean
Since we have rapidly passed over the air and the things that occur in it, in the interests of the brevity we have sought, let us begin to speak of water and its position.

[Col. 0080B]

Divine Wisdom, foreknowing that nothing can live without heat and moisture, and that earth and water are cold, placed above the middle of the earth the source of all heat—that is, the sun—so that it might warm the earth equally on either side. But since nothing could live by heat alone, beneath the middle of that same source of heat it placed a source of moisture, so that the earth might be moderated on both sides by these two.

There is, then, a source of moisture in the middle of the torrid zone, in the middle of the equinoctial circle, surrounding the earth. Many do not believe it exists because, owing to the excessive heat, it cannot be reached. Yet natural philosophers believe that it must exist by the necessity already stated, and call it the True Sea, or Ocean. When this sea reaches the West, it makes two refluxes there,

[Col. 0080C]

one turning southward, the other northward, following the sides of the earth. Likewise, in the East it makes two refluxes, turning toward the aforesaid sides. When the western reflux and the eastern one, both turning toward those sides, meet each other, the sea is forced back by the impact and is swallowed up backward. Thus occurs the celebrated rising and falling of the sea, called the waves [or, the sea-tide in the sense of its flow] of the sea. Likewise the other two meet one another at their extremity.

There are others who say that mountains lying beneath the sea are the cause of the sea’s waves. When the sea likewise reaches them, it falls back and is swallowed up; the channel behind is filled, but that in front is first emptied. If the front is emptied first, it in turn returns backward, and the rear is emptied, while the aforesaid western reflux, turning northward, is filled in front.

[Col. 0080D]

When it reaches the end of Africa, touching the sides of the earth, between Calpe and Atlas, as far as the region near Jerusalem, it is called the Mediterranean, receiving different names from different lands. Anyone wishing to know how it rises and falls, and what names it receives from the regions from which they are taken, should consult a map of the world. But since a description set before the eyes enters the mind more readily, let us place before the eyes what we have said. In the following diagram, the western reflux, turning northward, is called the Atlantic Sea from the adjacent Mount Atlas; beneath it are England and the neighbouring islands. From the eastern reflux, turning northward, arises the Indian Sea. Likewise, from the other refluxes turning southward, we must suppose that various seas arise.

[Col. 0081A]

But this should not be described on our authority, because their position remains unknown to us owing to the intervening torrid zone.
