## CHAPTER XV.—On the origin of the winds

[Col. 0081B]

Since it is our view that winds arise from those refluxes, let us discuss their origin, both the cardinal winds and the intermediate ones. Since, as we said, in the West two refluxes divide from that source of all moisture, one toward the south and the other toward the north, the air is set in motion at that division. If the impetus is so great that it reaches us, it produces the wind called Zephyrus.

The two eastern refluxes, by their division, produce the wind called Eurus. When the eastern and western refluxes,

[Col. 0081C]

turning northward, meet one another in the middle, the air is moved and the northern wind arises, called Boreas. It is cold because it originates in the cold zone; dry because it drives the clouds from this quarter of the earth toward the middle; and rainy near the borders of the torrid zone. When it crosses the torrid zone, it becomes warm; although it is cold to us, there it is warm.

Likewise, when the two refluxes turning southward meet one another in the middle, Auster is produced. Although beyond the torrid zone it is dry and cold, like Boreas among us, since it arises in the cold zone, yet because it passes through the torrid zone it is warmed and reaches us warm. Driving the clouds before it as far as the quarter of the earth in which we live, it produces

[Col. 0081D]

rain for us. Thus it is warm and moist for us accidentally, although cold and dry at its origin.

Having seen whence the cardinal winds arise, let us also see whence the four intermediate winds arise. If, among the two refluxes turning northward and producing Boreas in the manner stated, it happens that the eastern one is more rapid through some accident, it meets the western one beyond the middle toward the north, and an intermediate wind arises between Boreas and Zephyrus. But if the western reflux meets the eastern beyond the northern middle, an intermediate wind arises between Boreas and Eurus. Likewise, if the other two refluxes meet each other beyond the middle, now on this side, now on that, they produce two intermediate winds: one between Eurus and Auster, the other between Auster and Zephyrus.

But by setting a figure before the eyes we shall lessen the labour.

[Col. 0082A]

Let us make one like the preceding, in which the refluxes do not meet each other in the middle: in the first, let the cardinal winds be understood from it; in this, the intermediate winds.

But since in one figure we can show no more than two, let the others be understood by analogy with these. The question is asked: if winds arise from the causes stated,

[Col. 0082B]

when the refluxes divide and meet one another every day—as the daily tides attest—why do winds not occur every day? We answer that, although they do occur every day, they do not make an impetus that reaches us. It often happens that what we do not think is wind passes through other regions or the higher parts of the air, and is nevertheless not felt by us.

Some say that caverns of the earth are the causes of winds. For when portions of air enter them, because of their fluidity, as one portion enters and another seeks to leave, a conflict arises; the air, being disturbed thereby, produces wind. Hence Aeolia, because it is cavernous, is called the region of winds. Others say that moist vapour rising upward, by its weight, moves the air and produces wind.

[Col. 0082C]

We, however, have taught that the first, second, and third are causes of winds.

## CHAPTER XVI.—Whence some water is fresh and some salt

Let us explain whence salt water arises. The natural taste of water is tasteless; hence phlegm is naturally tasteless, though it becomes salty by accident. The reason is this: since the sea, as we have said, lies beneath the torrid zone, it is thickened by heat and becomes salty. For it is certain that through boiling water turns into salt.

But someone may say: since all waters arise from this salty origin and return to the same place—as Solomon testifies when he says, “To the places from which the waters go forth, they return” (Eccles. I)—for one must not believe that waters are annihilated, but that they return in a cycle—

[Col. 0082D]

why are some waters fresh and others salty?

## CHAPTER XVII.—That strained and attenuated water produces fresh springs

The solution is this: since the earth is cavernous, water enters it by reason of its fluidity. Passing through subterranean channels, it is strained and attenuated, loses its salty taste, and, breaking forth at the earth’s surface, produces springs and various streams of fresh taste.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—Whence wells have moisture

There is disagreement about whence wells obtain their moisture. For if springs had their source from subterranean channels, would they not fill up and flow away? Against this we say: although they have their source from subterranean channels, they do not nevertheless fill up. It happens that the channel does not end there,

[Col. 0083A]

but extends on either side. Thus the water of the well passes onward and does not bubble upward. But where a spring is, the channel ends. There, because of the density of the earth, the water cannot flow farther downward and is compelled to bubble upward.

Others say that the source of a well is not subterranean channels but the sweat of the earth. Since the earth contains some moisture, if it is perforated, drops of water descend like the sweat of a human being, and from this comes the water of a well. We think that both are causes. That wells arise from subterranean channels is proved by the fact that well-water is immediately found beside rivers, and that it often happens that, when a second well is made, water is taken away from the first. That they arise from the earth’s sweat is proved by the fact that well-water is found in dry and arid places.

## CHAPTER XIX.—Why the water of wells and springs is cold in summer and warm in winter

[Col. 0083B]

That the water of wells and springs is warm in winter happens thus: since winter is naturally cold, and the pores of the earth are constricted by cold, heat cannot evaporate; remaining within, it warms the earth and the water. In summer, however, when the pores at the earth’s surface have been opened by heat, vapour evaporates and the heat is diminished. Hence water breaking forth from within emerges cold. Thus well-water is very cold in summer; spring-water, because it is nearer the warm air, is less cold; river-water still less so; and rain-water less cold still.

Thus fresh water is made by straining through the earth’s subterranean channels. But those waters from whose moisture springs arise across the surface

[Col. 0083C]

of the earth, rather than through subterranean channels, are thick and salty, and are called seas.

## CHAPTER XX.—Whence conflagration or flood arises

Since it is the common opinion of philosophers that earthly things come to an end sometimes by flood and sometimes by conflagration, let us see whence each occurs. Since water, as we said, lies beneath the source of heat, it happens that moisture gradually increases and overcomes heat, until it reaches such a point that, restrained by no shores, it spreads across the lands and submerges earthly things.

[Col. 0084A]

When this moisture has been dried by the heat of the sun and the dryness of the earth, it happens that heat gradually increases and overcomes moisture, until it grows to such an extent that, spread through the earth, it burns the lands.

Some say that this happens through the common elevation or depression of the planets. For if all the planets are elevated at once and moved farther than usual from the earth, they take up less moisture. Therefore moisture increases, spreads through the earth, and produces a flood. But if one, two, or three are elevated without the others, it does not nevertheless increase. What increases through their elevation is dried by the proximity of the others. In the same way, when all are near, they burn the lands and conflagration occurs, because what those near at hand do more greatly by their proximity, the others at a distance do less greatly.

It should be noted that one flood is universal,

[Col. 0084B]

another particular. A universal flood cannot be continuous, but a particular one can. Thus mortal things perish alternately. Therefore, since there was a destruction of the world by flood in the time of Noah (Gen. I), the world will end by conflagration.

## CHAPTER XXI.—Why during the lunar month moisture sometimes increases and sometimes decreases

Since at the end of this volume the condition of the sea has been discussed, let us see why its tide decreases during the first seven days of the lunar month and increases during the next seven. When there is conjunction of the moon with the sun, the whole brilliance of the sun that kindles the moon cannot attenuate the air beneath it or dry up moisture. Then the tide is full.

But when the descending brilliance begins to kindle the moon, the moon dries the air

[Col. 0084C]

and diminishes the moisture. The farther the brilliance descends, the more the moisture is dried, until the seventh day. On the seventh day, because half of the moon is wholly illuminated, it warms the moisture through the intervening air. The moisture, boiling, rises upward, and so the tide increases until the fourteenth day. But in the third week, because the heat that raises it decreases, the sea’s tide remains still. In the fourth, because heat fails as the illuminating brilliance diminishes, the air becomes thick and the moisture increases; consequently it surges until the new moon.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0083]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0083D]

The sequence of the preceding books, beginning from the first cause of things, has descended as far as the earth. It does not indulge the itching of ears, but serves the profit of its readers; and for that reason it does not please the minds of fools. For now this has been fulfilled: “There will be a time when they will not endure sound teaching, but according to their own desires will heap up teachers for themselves, with itching ears” (II Tim. IV:3).

What freedom of study can still be hoped for when we know teachers to be flatterers of their pupils, pupils to be judges of their teachers, and both to impose a law of speaking and silence? For in a few cases teachers,

[Col. 0084D]

if they perceive the voice and countenance of a flatterer, will put on a bold face; and if anyone follows a teacher’s severity, he is driven from the schools, like a mad schoolmaster from prostitutes, and is called cruel and inhuman. Thus he may now use the words of Umbricius:

> … and therefore I go forth as nobody’s companion,
>
> Like a cripple, a body useless through a disabled right hand.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* III.47; citation incomplete in the source.)

Therefore teachers are driven away where they ought to be loved, according to that saying of Ovid:

> By the very means through which you seek us, you often drive away our resources.

But since it belongs to the upright person not to bend the mind toward worse things,

[Col. 0085A]

but to conform it to better ones, let us turn our minds away from worse things and, having conformed them to better, proceed to the rest. And since we have spoken of the other elements, their adornment, and the concise accounts that follow them, let us begin to speak of the earth and its adornment.

## CHAPTER I.—On the earth and the world

The earth, then, is an element situated in the middle of the world and is therefore the lowest. The world is arranged in the likeness of an egg. For the earth is in the middle, as the yolk is in an egg. Around it is water, as the white is around the yolk. Around the water is air, like the membrane containing the white. Outside, enclosing all things, is fire, in the manner of an eggshell.

## CHAPTER II.—On the different qualities of the earth

[Col. 0085B]

This earth, thus placed in the middle of the world and receiving all weights upon itself, is naturally cold and dry; yet in its various regions it has different qualities by accident. The part of it beneath the torrid zone, subject to that region of air, is torrid and uninhabitable because of the sun’s heat. But its two extremities, subject to cold regions of air, are cold and uninhabitable. The part subject to the temperate region of air is temperate and inhabitable.

But since, as we have said, two of its regions are intemperate, there are two temperate regions below, capable of habitation: one outside the torrid zone, the other beyond it. Yet although habitable, we believe that only one is inhabited by anyone, and not even all of it. But because philosophers speak of the inhabitants of both, not because they are there but because they can be there, let us say something about those whom we do not believe exist, for the sake of understanding philosophical reading.

[Col. 0085C]

## CHAPTER III.—On its inhabitants

The habitable part of the zone in which we are is divided into two. Since the temperature of the air is all around the earth, some part is temperate and habitable. But because the refluxes of Ocean encircle the sides of the earth according to the character of the horizon, they divide it into two. We inhabit its upper part; our Antipodes inhabit the lower. Yet none of us can reach them, nor any of them us. From the north, cold and the refluxes prevent passage; from east and west, the sun and the refluxes do so.

Likewise the other habitable region is divided into two: the upper part is occupied by our *antioi* (ἀντίοι, “those opposite”), and the lower by their *antipodes* (ἀντίποδοι, “those with feet opposite”). Thus in the two habitable regions there are four kinds of inhabitants. Some agree with others at certain times and differ at others.

Therefore we and our antipodes have summer, winter, and the other seasons at the same time; but when we have day, they have night, and conversely. For if summer arises from the sun’s proximity and winter from its remoteness, while spring and autumn arise from a moderate distance, and if the signs of the zodiac are equally distant from us and from them—since they preserve the earth and occupy their natural place—then in whatever sign the sun is, it will be equally related to us and them and will have the same effects. Rightly, then, we have similar variations, though not day and night at the same time.

[Col. 0086A]

For day arises from brightness, while night results from the earth’s shadow. The shadow is always in the part opposite the sun’s brightness: when daylight shines on the upper part of the earth, the shadow of night lies upon the lower part, and conversely. Thus there is no hour in which it is not day in some region and night in another.

But the question is asked: if we and they have summer and winter at the same time, but when we have day they have night, then in summer we have very long days and short nights; will they therefore have short days and long nights during their summer—which is not natural to summer? To this we reply: although when we have day they have night, there is nevertheless a period in which day is common to us and them, though for one it is evening and for the other morning.

[Col. 0086B]

For when the sun is rising for us, it is still setting for them; we have morning and they evening, so that around the first hour it is not yet night for them. Likewise, at sunset, from the moment when the sun begins to descend for us, it begins to appear for them; then it is morning for them and evening for us. Accordingly, we and they have days and nights equal in length, though not at the same time. The same applies in winter. Let the ingenuity of readers investigate how this is so.

We and the *antioi* (ἀντίοι, “opposite dwellers”) have similar day and night, but when we have summer they have winter, and conversely. For in the same hemisphere we and they have brightness together and shadow together; but when the sun is near us, it is far from them: when we have summer, they have winter. But here arises a question similar to the preceding one; anyone approaching it equipped by the earlier discussion will easily find its solution.

[Col. 0086C]

We and the antipodes of the *antioi* have neither summer nor winter, day nor night at the same time. The *antidikoi* (ἀντίδικοι, “opponents”)” and their antipodes stand in the same relation as we and our *anteci*; our antipodes and theirs as we and their *anteci*. Since we have sufficiently taught about the three habitations and their inhabitants, let us begin to speak of our own.

Our habitation extends from east to west and from south to north. Although called temperate, it is not equally temperate in all its regions. The part nearer the torrid zone, such as Libya and Ethiopia, is hot and dry; the part near the cold zone is cold and moist. The western portion is cold and dry; the eastern hot

[Col. 0086D]

and moist. What is equally distant is equally temperate.

## CHAPTER IV.—On the boundaries of Asia, Africa, and Europe

This region likewise has three principal parts: Asia, Africa, and Europe. Asia begins in the east and extends laterally from the north as far as the torrid zone; it is bounded by the Tanais and the Nile and occupies the middle part of the habitable region. Europe and Africa occupy the other two.

The boundaries of Africa are: the Nile on the east; the torrid zone on the south; the Mediterranean Sea on the north; and the reflux of the Mediterranean on the west. The boundaries of Europe are: the Tanais on the east, extending to the Mediterranean Sea; the reflux on the west;

[Col. 0087A]

and the cold zone on the north, as follows:

## CHAPTER V.—Why some mountains have perpetual snows

There are also mountains in this region whose summits have perpetual snow,

[Col. 0087B]

although there is very great heat in their valleys. But the question is asked: since heat comes from the sun and from above, and mountains are nearer the sun than their valleys, why is there snow on their heights and not in their valleys?

We answer, as we have briefly touched on above, that although heat comes from the sun, which is itself of a hot nature, it can heat nothing unless it is mixed with moisture, which it transforms into its own nature. Therefore, on the mountains mentioned, because the air is thin owing to its great distance from the earth, it cannot be kindled by the sun; but driven here and there by its lightness, it becomes cold. In the valleys, however, because the air is dense and therefore almost motionless, it is quickly kindled and becomes warm.

This may be proved by the following comparison: if the air is motionless,

[Col. 0087C]

it is kindled and warm; but if a wind comes and moves it, cold is felt. Another question arises: if the air on the heights of those mountains is so thin, whence does it become thickened into clouds and snow? We say that this air does not become thickened; rather, moist vapour rising from the valleys is condensed by the cold of the heights into clouds and snow.

## CHAPTER VI.—What qualities the earth acquires from different winds

This same habitable region, being exposed to different winds, acquires different qualities. If any part of it is enclosed by mountains on the east, north, and west, while being open to the south, it is hot and dry, good for habitation in winter and very bad in summer. If the reverse is the case, it is bad in winter and good in summer.

A region exposed to the east and similarly enclosed on the other sides is hot and moist, good in spring; conversely, it is cold and dry, bad in autumn but good in spring. What we have said about parts of the earth may be proved by the windows of a house: southern windows are bad in summer and good in winter;

[Col. 0087D]

northern windows the reverse. Hence the ancients made southern and northern dining rooms, so that they might recline in the southern one in winter and in the northern in summer (Vitruvius bears witness to this).

## CHAPTER VII.—On grafted trees

Since we have sufficiently discussed this element and its parts, it follows that we should speak of the earth’s fruits and trees. But since Macer and Dioscorides teach all this plainly, let us be silent about them.

[Col. 0088A]

We shall set down only one question and its solution:

Since trunk and grafted shoot are of different natures, what causes their growth? The cause of growth is vapour coming from the earth through the roots and trunk. As it descends, piercing the roots, it draws with it some substance of earth and water, thereby supplying the cause of life, growth, and bearing fruit. This rises through the trunk; and the trunk retains what suits its own nature and, digesting it by natural heat, transforms it into pith, trunk, and bark. What rises to the grafted shoot, the shoot likewise directs into its own nature insofar as suits it.

Since this question and solution from the aforesaid authors seem to us more than sufficient, it remains to say something about the terrestrial animal.

[Col. 0088B]

Although every terrestrial animal is mortal, some are rational. But because irrational animals are innumerable and greatly relevant to the study of philosophers, we shall postpone discussion of their natures, and of why some ruminate while others do not, in order to discuss what is more worthy: the rational and mortal animal, namely the human being. Since the human being consists of two things, soul and body, we shall first teach about the human body, which comes within our knowledge, and then about the powers of the soul.

But since in the first book we have taught about the composition of the first human, male and female alike, and how and in what manner the human was made from mud, let us speak of the human being’s daily creation, formation, birth, ages, limbs, and the functions and uses of the limbs.

## CHAPTER VIII.—What semen is

[Col. 0088C]

Since human conception occurs from semen, let us say something about it. Semen is the useful [perhaps: male] seed, composed, as is supposed, of the substance of all the limbs. That it is composed from the substance of all the limbs appears from the fact that all the limbs are created from it, and it is natural that like things should be born from like things. There is another argument for this: if the father has an incurable infirmity in any limb, the son will have the same infirmity in the same limb.

## CHAPTER IX.—Why intercourse does not occur in childhood

The time for intercourse begins from the fourteenth year. But the question is asked: since semen derives its cause from heat and moisture, and childhood is hot and moist, why does intercourse not occur in it? We answer that at that age the passages serving this purpose are constricted; consequently semen cannot issue forth.

[Col. 0088D]

In other ages they are open and suited for intercourse. In old age and senescence, however, intercourse scarcely occurs because of coldness. This activity is troublesome after eating and before sleep, for the natural heat which ought to digest food is diminished. After sleep, however, because the food has been digested and turned into blood, is the proper time for it. What bodily complexion is suited to this activity should be sought in the second part.

## CHAPTER X.—On the womb

The womb is the recipient of this seed, shaggy within so as to receive semen better; it possesses seven chambers, stamped with the human figure as a coin is. Hence a woman can give birth to seven, but never more, in a single birth. And since sterility sometimes arises from the womb, let us say something about it.

[Col. 0089A]

## CHAPTER XI.—What is the cause of sterility

The cause of sterility, then, is excessive dryness, excessive moisture, excessive heat, or excessive cold. For since semen consists of the temperate substance—that is, blood—it requires the same condition if something similar is to arise from it. Sometimes excessive fatness is the reason why nothing is conceived: from it the mouth of the uterine sac is blocked, so that semen cannot enter. Hence Virgil says in the *Georgics* (III.136) that mares should be made lean at the time of intercourse. He then adds the physical explanation:

> Lest too much fatness block up the sluggish furrows.  
>
> [Note: Col. 0089. Virgil reads otherwise:
>
> > … lest, through excessive indulgence, the use become too dull  
> > in the field of generation and block up the sluggish furrows.]

Again, frequent intercourse is a cause of this condition: the womb becomes smooth within like oiled marble

[Col. 0089B]

and cannot retain anything. But if there is no cause of sterility in a woman, and semen suited for generation enters the womb, it is immediately closed so tightly, Hippocrates says, that not even a needle can be inserted, and conception has taken place. We said “suited for generation” because if it is too hot or too dry, it is not fit for generation.

## CHAPTER XII.—Whether a woman can conceive unwillingly

But the question is asked whether male semen alone, without female semen, is sufficient for generation. Some say that it alone suffices. Their proof is this: a man has often had intercourse with a woman against her will and while she was weeping, and she sometimes conceives, when no semen of the woman can be present; for emission of semen does not occur without pleasure.

[Col. 0089C]

We say that female semen too is present in conception, since this may be proved from the infirmity which a child acquires in a corresponding limb from its mother. As for the claim that a child is conceived by a woman unwilling to it, we say that, although it displeases her at the beginning, at the end it nevertheless pleases her through the frailty of concupiscent flesh.

But because the menses usually cease in conception, let us explain how this happens and why they then cease.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On superfluities

Since every woman is naturally cold—for even the hottest woman is colder than the coldest man—she cannot digest food well; and there remains a superfluity that is purged every month and is called the menses. Once conception has taken place, however, heat is doubled by

[Col. 0089D]

the fetus; food is therefore digested better, and superfluities as great as before do not arise. Likewise, because the fetus is nourished from the blood of the womb, purification is not needed.

## CHAPTER XIV.—Why a human being does not walk when born

This is why other animals walk as soon as they are born, whereas a human being does not: a human being is nourished in the womb from menstrual blood. But why are women more ardent in desire after conception, whereas brute animals cease from it altogether? Because women are colder than men, they are more lustful than men. Why, after intercourse, a woman with leprosy is not harmed, whereas a man who approaches her becomes leprous,

[Col. 0090A]

we shall postpone discussing, lest we offend the hearts of religious persons, should they happen to take this work into their hands, by speaking long about such a matter.

## CHAPTER XV.—On the formation of the human being in the womb

Once semen has been placed in the womb and its mouth has closed, if it remains on the right side, because the liver lies near the right side of the womb, the fetus is nourished with better and warmer blood and becomes male. If, however, it is on the left side, which is distant from the source of heat—that is, the liver—it will be female. If it is not properly on the right but somewhat toward the left, though more toward the right, the result is an effeminate man. If it is on the left, yet somewhat toward the right, the result is a masculine woman.

When the seed has been placed in one of the four parts mentioned, the digestive power begins to act,

[Col. 0090B]

thickening it by warming it with the mother’s heat. But through dryness it creates a sac enclosing the conception within itself, lest superfluities joining it should corrupt it. This sac grows and arises with the child.

On the seventh day after conception, as Macrobius relates (*Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, I.6), drops of blood begin to appear on the surface of the sac. In the third week they sink into the very fluid of conception; in the fourth they coagulate into a kind of liquid solidity, as it were between flesh and blood. In the fifth week, if the child is to be born in the seventh month—or otherwise in the seventh week, if it is to be born in the ninth—the formative power begins, whose office is to provide the human shape.

This is followed by the assimilative power, whose office is to change what is cold and dry into cold and dry, as bones are; what is cold and moist into phlegmatic matter, as the lung is; what is hot and dry into choleric matter, as the heart is; and what is hot and moist into sanguine matter, as the liver is.

[Col. 0090C]

Then follows the hollowing power. Its office is to hollow out the hands, perforate the nostrils, and perform the remaining such operations. Once the limbs have been formed, assimilated, and hollowed, moist vapour begins to course through the veins and arteries, imparting movement and life. This movement begins on the seventieth day from conception if the child is to be born in the seventh month; otherwise, if in the eighth, on the nineteenth [day; the reading is materially uncertain]. But since all things that live in time require some food, the nutritive power follows, extending until death.

## CHAPTER XVI.—Whence a child is nourished in the womb

[Col. 0090D]

But the question is asked how and in what manner a child is nourished in the womb. We say that it is joined to the womb by certain sinews in the navel, through which it is nourished and grows by pure blood descending from the mother’s liver. Hence, because it receives what has already been digested, it does not require evacuation of superfluity.

## CHAPTER XVII.—On birth, and why those born in the seventh month live

Birth follows these powers already mentioned, and it has two terms: the seventh month and the ninth. But this involves a question. Why, if a child is born before the seventh month, can it not live; why does one born in the seventh live, but one born in the eighth not?

[Col. 0091A]

Natural philosophers say that before the seventh month there is not enough movement in the child for it to be able to live if born. In the seventh there is movement sufficient for life; therefore the child, moving itself and breaking the weak sinews by which it is joined to the womb, is born fit for life. In the eighth month, weakened by the movement of the seventh, it cannot live, until, restored during that month and part of the ninth, it begins to move again, breaks the sinews, and is born fit for life.

Since, when born, it has been nourished in heat and moisture and comes forth into something unlike these, it feels the opposition and gives forth a cry of distress [the transmitted *aemulationis*, “of rivalry,” should apparently be read *ejulationis*, “of wailing”]. Therefore the first human voice is a voice of pain.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On infancy and sensation

[Col. 0091B]

From birth until the fifth year is infancy, because during one part of it the child cannot speak, while during the other, if it speaks, it speaks imperfectly. At this age it can have sensation, but not reason or understanding. Let us therefore say something about sensation. As for why reason and understanding cannot exist at such an age, since they are powers of the soul, we shall say enough on this when speaking of the soul.

Since sensation takes its beginning from the animal power, and the natural and spiritual powers precede it, let us touch upon these powers, beginning with the natural one, which comes first. Since the human being consists of four elements, heat and moisture produce a warm, moist vapour. Diffused through the limbs, it moves them

[Col. 0091C]

and performs the threefold digestion; it is called the natural power. Since mention has been made of the three digestions, let us inquire what digestion is, where it occurs, and how it is performed.

## CHAPTER XIX.—On digestions and the urinary stone
Digestion, then, is a change produced in some thing by boiling. The first digestion takes place in the stomach, the second in the liver, the third in all the members; therefore let us speak first of the first. Since the human body requires growth at a certain age, and restoration at every age (since it is wasted by internal and external heat and cold), it was necessary that food and drink should enter, from which alteration and growth might arise. But if food is coarse, it was necessary that, before it entered the stomach, it should be made fine and dry.

[Col. 0091D]

For this purpose the teeth are prepared—born from phlegm descending through the gums, and from cold condensed and hardened—that they may grind the food. The tongue, like the hand of a miller, turns it and returns it beneath the teeth; it is spongy for this purpose, so that, receiving the juice of the food, it may distinguish its taste. Thus a certain preparation for the first digestion takes place in the mouth. Food so prepared with drink descends through the *ussophagus* [Greek: ὐσσόφαγον], that is, by the gateway into the stomach, whose entrance is wider; there it is cooked and changed into the appearance of barley-gruel (*typsana*), and this is the first digestion.

There is, however, a question whether the stomach is hot by nature. Some say that it is hot by nature; otherwise food could not be cooked. Therefore, since it cooks and transforms food, it is hot.

We, however, say that the stomach is naturally cold and accidentally hot. It is also of a sinewy nature, so that when a person eats more than usual it may expand, and when less, contract. Again, it needed to be sinewy, lest it be injured when it received anything hard and unchewed. Since everything sinewy is of a cold nature, the stomach too is cold. Yet, so that it may retain food better until it cooks it, it is shaggy or villous inside. Although naturally cold, it is warmed accidentally. For it lies upon the liver, in such a way that it is almost wholly enclosed by it. On its right side is the gall-bladder, and on its left the heart; these are hot and dry. Thus the stomach is hot, like a pot set upon a fire.

If we wish to speak properly, we say that food is cooked in the stomach.

[Col. 0092A]

Food, then, having been changed into the form of barley-gruel, leaves through the *ussophagus*, an opening called the gateway, and enters the intestine called the duodenum, so named because in each person it has the measure of twelve fingers of that same person. Leaving behind what is suitable for its nourishment, it passes into another intestine called the jejunum, because it retains nothing from it. Certain veins coming from the liver join this jejunum; through them the more fluid part passes into the lower regions of the liver, namely the meseraic veins, so called because they change the juice. But what is cold and feculent descends into the long intestine and into evacuation; and this is the superfluity of the first digestion.

The fluid part which passes into the lower regions of the liver is digested by the liver’s heat.

[Col. 0092B]

Whatever there is in it that is hot and dry passes into yellow bile; through certain veins it is conveyed to the gall-bladder, which is the seat of bile. From there a certain part passes into the stomach to strengthen it. What is cold and dry passes into melancholy and goes to the spleen, the seat of melancholy. But a certain part descends to the stomach, in order to strengthen its retentive power. What is cold and moist is changed into phlegm and passes to the lungs, the seat of phlegm; a certain part is conveyed to the stomach because of the expulsive power. But if it is hot and moist, it is changed into blood and remains in the liver, which is the seat of blood.

Thus four humours are generated in the liver, having their proper seats: bile, phlegm, melancholy—that is, black bile—and blood. Blood has the liver; phlegm, the lungs, although some say that phlegm has no proper seat but remains with the blood, so that it may move more readily through the members. This is the second digestion.

[Col. 0092C]

What is superfluous there passes through the *lirin*, or *hylē* [Greek: λίριν, or ὕλην], or “quilim” vein, which lies near the spleen and descends to the kidneys. The kidneys retain what is fluid there for their own nourishment, and send the rest through the urinary pores to the bladder. What leaves through the male member is called urine, and this is the superfluity of the second digestion.

But because children have narrow urinary pores, what remains there in a thick state is changed into a stony substance. At other ages, however, because the pores are open, a stone is not generated there but around the kidneys. Therefore in children stone arises in the neck of the bladder; in old people, around the kidneys.

Blood generated in the liver in the manner described passes through the veins to all the members; when digested by their heat, it is transformed into their likeness. Its superfluity leaves through sweat. Another part returns to the liver and, having been cooked there, descends and leaves with the urine; it is called sediment. But if it is at the bottom of the urine, it is called *hypostasis* [Greek: ὑπόστασις], that is, subsisting nature or substance; if in the middle, *eniemenon*, or *eniēmi* [Greek: ἐνιέμενον, ἐνίημι], “pouring down into the belly below”; if at the top, *nephile*, *nephi*, that is, purification.

[Col. 0092D]

What its presence in different places signifies; what it means when it is continuous or divided; and what proceeds from its substance and heat—this is not ours to say. Whoever wishes to know this should read Theophilus, *On Urines*.

## CHAPTER XX.—That Man Is Naturally Hot and Moist; and Whence He Is Tall or Short, Slender or Stout

[Col. 0093A]

Another function of this natural power is to produce growth, which results from moisture and heat. For that something rises belongs to heat; but that it thickens belongs to moisture. Yet it will be said: if growth comes from heat and moisture, whence do choleric and melancholic persons grow, of whom the former are cold and dry, the latter hot and dry?

We say that no human being is not hot and moist, though some are so more and some less. For example, a human being is naturally hot and moist, and balanced among the four qualities; but because nature becomes corrupted, it happens that these qualities are intensified or diminished in someone. If heat is intensified in someone and moisture diminished, he is called choleric, that is, hot and dry—yet he is not without moisture. If moisture is intensified and heat diminished, he is called phlegmatic. If dryness is intensified and heat diminished, he is melancholic. If they are equally present, he is called sanguine.

All human beings, therefore, are naturally hot and moist; but because qualities are intensified or diminished, they receive the name of the intensified quality and of its opposite, that is, the diminished one. In every complexion a person can grow, though more in one and less in another; in one toward length, in another toward breadth. Choleric persons are tall and slender: tall because of heat, slender because of dryness. Sanguine persons are tall because of heat and fat because of moisture.

[Col. 0093B]

Phlegmatic persons are short because of coldness and stout because of moisture. Melancholic persons are slender because of dryness and short because of coldness. These natural properties are often altered accidentally: choleric and melancholic persons become fat through idleness or eating, while sanguine and phlegmatic persons become slender through abstinence or labour. That sanguine, phlegmatic, and other persons alike are short results from the smallness of the womb or of the semen.

This natural power has certain principal members, certain serving and assisting members, certain members serving one another, and certain serving neither. But because Johnitius has sufficiently discussed this in the *Isagoge*, setting that aside let us pass to sleep, which pertains to the natural power.

## CHAPTER XXI.—On Sleep

Sleep, then, is the repose of the animal powers together with the intensification of the natural powers. It occurs when moist vapour rises upward and fills the nerves through which the animal power is accustomed to descend. The animal therefore ceases to see and hear, and so forth, until that vapour has been dried by natural heat; then the animal spirit begins to rise and to awaken some animal sense.

## CHAPTER XXII.—Whence Dreams Arise; and on the Animal and Spiritual Powers

Dreams arise from the remnants of thoughts, from food and drink, from temperature and complexion, and from one’s manner of lying down; and this signifies nothing.

[Col. 0094A]

Others arise through the ministry of angels; others from a cause in the world; others from the power and freedom of the soul. We have ready proofs of all these things. But since this does not greatly concern our purpose, and we are moving toward the end of the volume, let us omit it and pass to the spiritual power.

The aforesaid vapour, becoming refined as it passes through various openings and arriving at the heart, dilates it so that it may draw in air and temper the inner heat; it constricts it in order to expel superfluities. It is then called the spiritual power, which the arteries serve.

But let us come to the animal power. The aforesaid vapour, ascending through the nerves and being filtered, becomes so subtle that, when it reaches the brain, it is called spirit. Descending through various instruments, it performs various animal powers, as we shall show. Since these proceed from the brain, let us first speak of the brain itself, then of how the senses proceed from it; and since it is contained in the head, let us begin there.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—On the Head

The head is a spherical substance, as though compressed by two fingers before and behind. It is round so that the brain may move in it more easily, and so that superfluities, remaining in corners if there were any, might not corrupt it. It is compressed before and behind because of the nerves proceeding from it: the anterior nerves perform sensation, the posterior voluntary movement of the body.

[Col. 0094B]

On its outer part is the skull, to whose membrane hairs adhere. These are born from vapour ascending and leaving through the pores. For the vapour which leaves, being dry, is constricted by the coldness of the air and changed into a bodily substance; when another vapour leaves, it drives upward what has hardened, and thus the hairs grow. But because it is natural for a heavy thing to descend, they curve downward. Hence, since superfluities are lacking at no age, growth of hair is lacking to no one.

The same is true of nails, which are formed from superfluities of the heart issuing through the tips of the fingers and hardened by cold. Other hairs, of the beard and chest, are absent at a certain age. Beards are absent from the female sex. For a beard arises in a man from heat, on account of the double heat of the heart and testicles; in a woman it cannot arise on account of coldness, unless she is unnaturally hot. For the same reason eunuchs have no beard. In childhood it cannot arise because the pores are constricted. Since hair is formed from rising vapour, it takes its colours according to the qualities of each person’s complexion. Enough is said about these matters in natural philosophy; let us pass to the rest.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—On the Brain

[Col. 0094C]

Under the skull are two membranes, called meninges. The outer one is harder and is called the *dura mater*; the one nearer the brain, lest it injure it, is thinner and is called the *pia mater*. Under these is the brain, of which Constantine gives this definition: “The brain is a white and fluid substance, without blood.”

The question is asked whether it is cold or hot. We say that it is naturally cold, lest it be dried out by continual motion. There are three chambers in the head: one at the prow, and one at the stern in the posterior region. The first chamber is hot and dry and is called the phantastic, that is, visual or imaginative, because in it is the power of seeing and understanding. It is hot and dry so that it may draw in the forms and colours of things.

The middle chamber is called the *logistikon* [Greek: λογιστικὸν], that is, rational, because in it is the power of discrimination. What the phantastic chamber draws in passes to this chamber, and there the soul discriminates it. It is hot and moist, so that in discriminating it may conform itself more readily to the properties of things.

[Col. 0094D]

The third is called memorial, because in it is the power of retaining something in memory. What has been distinguished in the logistic chamber passes to the memorial chamber through a certain opening, which a little membrane closes until it is opened when we wish to communicate something or recall it to memory. This chamber is cold and dry so that it may retain better, for it belongs to the cold and dry to constrict.

But someone will say: how could this have been proved in anyone? We say: through wounds received in these parts. When someone had good understanding, reason, and memory, physicians observe that, when he receives a wound in one of these chambers, he loses that power while retaining the powers of the others. Thus Solinus in the *Polyhistor* (cf. Pliny, book VII) tells of someone who, after receiving a wound in the back of the head, fell into such ignorance that he did not know that he had had a name. Therefore the ancients rightly said that the seat of wisdom is in the head. For the things that make a person wise have their seat in the head: namely understanding, reason, and memory.

From this brain nerves proceed to the eyes, through which the animal spirit, issuing forth, produces sight, as we shall show. But first let us say something about the substance of the eyes.

## CHAPTER XXV.—On the Eyes

[Col. 0095A]

The eye, then, is a certain round and bright substance, somewhat flat on its surface, consisting of three humours and seven coats. It is round so that it can turn this way and that; flat on the surface so that it may receive more readily the forms and colours of things; shining and gleaming because of its humours, so that it may be penetrated by the visual spirit; and composed of coats so that superfluities may be expelled and not injure it. Whoever wishes to know the names and arrangement of the humours and coats should read Panthenius.

Nature established two eyes so that, if one were injured, the other might remain. Let us now speak of sight.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—How Sight Takes Place

When the natural spirit, passing through nerves proceeding from the brain, has reached the eyes, and upon issuing finds some brightness, whether of the sun or another source, it extends as far as the object before it. For, presenting itself, it diffuses itself through that brightness and, informed by the forms and colours of the object, passes through the eyes and through the phantastic chamber; thus sight is produced. Hence we distinguish by sight the shapes and colours of things.

[Col. 0095B]

The Stoics, however, say that the visual spirit does not reach as far as the object, but that the eye receives the shapes and colours of things into itself; the ray reaches it, is similarly informed, and produces sight. Others say that the spirit reaches the object with forms and colours, but does not inform the eye; the ray reaches the eye, and, being informed, returns and produces sight.

We prefer the opinion that the visual spirit reaches as far as the thing. The proof is that we often acquire the same infirmity from looking at someone with sore eyes. Whence could this be, unless the visual spirit, reaching the corruption of the eyes, is corrupted and, returning, corrupts the eye?

An easy proof of the same thing is as follows. Since persons have contrary complexions—some are hot, others cold, some moist, others dry—the visual spirit issuing from someone carries that person’s qualities with it; spreading over the face of another person of contrary quality, it corrupts that person. Contraries are harmed by contraries. Hence old women lick the face and spit, and by this cure it: they spit out what is harmful there.

[Col. 0095C]

Thus, for sight to occur, three things are necessary: an inner ray, an external brightness, and an object presented to it. When these concur, sight occurs; when any one of them is absent, sight fails.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—On Direct Viewing, Looking Into, and Looking Downward

There are three species of sight: *contuitio*, *intuitio*, and *detuitio*. *Contuitio* is when we see something with no image encountered in it; but, in showing how sight occurs, we have said enough about it. *Intuitio* is when we see something on whose surface some image appears. *Detuitio* is when something appears not on the surface but in the depth, as in water; it is called *detuitio*, as though “looking downward.”

It remains, therefore, to speak of looking. Since the same reasoning applies to them, let us discuss *detuitio* also, so that what we establish concerning it may be understood concerning *intuitio*. When the visual spirit is directed toward seeing something, it is driven here and there by its mobility; informed by the forms of surrounding things, if it reaches something dark, it cannot be seen because of its own subtlety. But if it reaches something radiant, it appears because of that thing’s brightness.

[Col. 0095D]

Aristotle, however, said that no image appears to him there, but that a person sees himself and what is behind him in this way: when the aforesaid spirit presents something radiant, that thing’s ray, struck back, is reflected and returns to the face of the observer, perceiving that face and the things behind it. But because this takes place through the mediation of a mirror, this is thought to appear in the mirror. Some say that the air between the person and the mirror is marked with various forms and colours; hence, if something is set before it, it appears shining, but if the contrary occurs, it does not.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—On Hearing

Hearing occurs as follows. When air, struck by the natural instruments, has received the form of the voice, it goes forth and informs the first part of air it encounters with a similar form, and that part informs another, until it reaches the ears. The ears are dry and hollow, like a drum. When they resound, the animal spirit is stirred; descending to the ears through certain nerves, it takes on a similar form, and thus formed returns to the logistic chamber and produces hearing.

[Col. 0096A]

The other senses take place similarly, the same animal spirit descending from the brain through nerves to their instruments. And since the soul judges what is perceived by them, it is time to discuss the soul and its powers.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—What the Soul Is

The soul is a certain spirit joined to the body, conferring a capacity fit for distinguishing and understanding. That distinguishing and understanding come from the soul is proved thus: as concern for the body increases, those powers diminish; as bodily concern decreases and concern for the soul increases, they increase. For if they came from the body’s nature, they would increase as concern for the body increased; when a cause is increased, its effect is increased.

Again, since every creature is either body or spirit, it was fitting that a human being should consist of spirit and body, so that he might have some affinity with both. Thus he has in common with lifeless bodies merely to exist; with herbs and trees, to live; with brute animals, to sense; and with spirits, to discriminate. Hence in Holy Scripture man is called “every creature.”

## CHAPTER XXX.—Which Actions Belong to the Soul and Which to the Body

[Col. 0096B]

Since a human being consists of soul and body, with the soul ruling—for in it he is like the Creator—it would be unfitting if the body had its own actions and the soul had none. But someone will say: how am I to distinguish which actions in a person should be judged to belong to the soul and which to the body?

We say: all actions that human beings share with brute animals or with lifeless bodies, even if the soul performs them in human beings, ought not to be called actions of the soul but of the body. But actions found in human beings which cannot exist in any other body belong to the soul. To discriminate and understand belongs to the soul; to sense and similar things belong to the body.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—How Bodily Motions Occur

But someone will say: if these are not actions of the soul, they ought not to be called either virtues or vices of the soul; why, then, are they condemned or forgiven? We say that, although they are not its actions, they can be its vices. For the soul was given to a human being in order to correct the unlawful motions of the body; these motions occur through its ignorance or negligence.

[Col. 0096C]

Just as, if a pupil or servant sins through the negligence of a teacher or master, the teacher or master is not free from fault, so neither is the soul when these things occur. Therefore it is not free from fault, even though they are not its actions.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—How the Soul Is in a Human Being

Since a human being consists of soul and body, the question is asked whether the soul is attached, concreted, mixed, or joined to the body. For everything that is in a composition is so in one of these ways.

It is not attached, for then the soul would be outside the body and would not move it equally. Everything attached is outside that to which it is attached, and things exert greater force when near, as when fire is placed near something. It is not concreted. A concreted thing passes from its own substance into another’s substance, as water through boiling becomes salt. Since the soul does not pass into the substance of the body but always remains spirit, it is not concreted with it.

[Col. 0096D]

Nothing mixed retains its own being; body and soul, therefore, are not mixed. They are joined, then, but in such a way that the soul, retaining its own being, is whole and entire in every part of the body.

Here someone objects: if it is whole in every part, then when one part of the body is cut off, is the whole soul cut off from the body? We say that the soul is not in any part of the body except while it is joined to a body fit for life. Therefore, when a part of the body is separated, the soul remains in the other parts, in which it had previously been whole.

Again, it is asked whether soul and body are from the same source or different sources. We say that the soul has no determinate source except the Creator alone, who gives being to all things. Hence Plato, the most learned of all philosophers, says that the Creator God, having himself created the stars, entrusted to spirits the task of forming the human being, while he himself made the soul and delivered it to them; for human bodies come into being and grow through the ministry of spirits and the influence of stars, while the soul comes into being by the will of the Creator.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—On the Time of Its Union with the Body

[Col. 0097A]

Again, it is asked whether the human soul exists before the body and when it is joined to it. We say that it does not subsist beforehand. This can be proved by reason and authority: for if it existed beforehand, it would be either in misery or blessedness without preceding merit. This is proved on Augustine’s authority, who says that God creates new souls daily.

No one determines the time of its union with the body; but to us it seems to be after the operation of the formative and hollowing powers. For then the natural power begins to run through the members, without which there can be neither life nor soul in the body.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—On the Powers

The powers of this soul are various: understanding, reason, and memory. Understanding is the power of the soul by which a person perceives incorporeal things, together with certain reason why they are so. Reason is the power of the soul by which a person perceives what a thing is, wherein things agree with others, and wherein they differ. Memory is the power by which a person firmly retains what has been previously known.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—Why an Infant Does Not Discriminate or Understand

[Col. 0097B]

But it is asked: since these are properties of the soul, why does an infant, in whom there is also a soul, not discriminate or understand, and so forth? To this we say that the human soul, having its origin from the Creator, is from its beginning perfect in its kind. Hence whatever the soul knows from its beginning could equally be known by a human being, were it not for the heaviness of the flesh. This can be proved from the first human being, who, before the corruption of humanity, possessed perfect human knowledge from the moment he existed.

But once humanity has been corrupted, it is corrupted from the moment it is joined to the body; nor can it exercise its properties until, through practice, experience, and some instructed teaching [the text reads *exsecrata*, probably *exercita*, “practised”], it begins to discriminate. It is as if someone with very keen eyesight were thrown into a dark prison: he could not see unless he became accustomed to the darkness or a light were kindled.

Hence Virgil:

> … How greatly do harmful bodies retard us?  
> (*Aeneid*, VI.731)

In the first age, however, neither practice nor experience has preceded, nor is the time suitable for instruction. For since that age is hot and moist, it immediately digests and desires food; consequently it requires frequent intake and outflow, and a thick vapour is generated. Rising, this vapour disturbs the brain, in which lies the power of discriminating and understanding.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—On Youth, Old Age, and Decrepitude

[Col. 0097C]

Youth follows this age; it is hot and dry. The natural moisture which a person contracts in the mother’s womb has been dried; hence a vapour not so thick is generated, nor is the brain so disturbed. This is an age suitable for discriminating, and so forth—especially if the lamp of diligent instruction is kindled.

Old age follows, cold and dry. Natural heat has been extinguished; hence memory flourishes at this age, though bodily strength fails. Memory comes from coldness and dryness, whose function is to constrict; bodily strength comes from heat, whose function is to make an onset.

Decrepitude follows, cold phlegm; hence memory fails at that stage and people become childish. For phlegm has an expulsive power. The dissolution of soul and body follows it. A person cannot live long after natural heat has been extinguished.

[Col. 0097D]

Since we have taught enough about the human being, let us speak of teaching and being taught: what kind of persons should be sought as teachers; what kind should be chosen as pupils; what complexion is suitable for learning; at what age it should begin and when it should end; and what is the order of discrimination.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—What Kind of Teacher Should Be Sought

A teacher should be sought who teaches neither for praise nor in hope of temporal profit, but solely for love of wisdom. For if he loves his own praise, he will never wish his pupil to attain his own perfection. He therefore withholds instruction, lest he be equalled or surpassed in what he loves more. If he teaches even when motivated by the hope of temporal gain, he will not care what he says, provided he can extract money. Trifles often please more than useful things.

But if he comes to teaching from love of knowledge, he will neither withhold instruction from envy nor evade known truth in order to extract something; nor, if the number of companions diminishes, will he cease, but he will be watchful and diligent for his own instruction and that of others.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—What Kind of Pupil

[Col. 0098A]

For instruction, a person should be chosen who does not argue against teaching and is not proud, lest he seem to be something when he is nothing; one who loves his teacher as a father, or even more than a father. For we ought to love more those from whom we receive greater and more worthy things. From a father we receive our state as untaught; from a teacher, our being wise, which is greater and more worthy. Good teachers, therefore, should be loved more than parents.

It is not only just that teachers be loved more; it is useful, so that their opinions may please us and so may the words of one whom we love. For the words of one whom we do not love often displease us also, and we avoid them while endeavouring not to imitate those whom we do not love.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—What Complexion Is Suitable for Learning

Although the sanguine complexion is suited to learning, anyone in any complexion can become accomplished through labour, since labour conquers all things.

## CHAPTER XL.—What Age and What Limit for Learning

[Col. 0098B]

Adolescence is suitable for beginning instruction, because, as Plato says, the age of a human being is like wax: if it is too soft, it does not receive a shape—or does not retain it; likewise if it is hard. Therefore neither an age too tender nor one too hardened is suitable for learning.

The limit of learning is death. Thus a certain wise man (Theophrastus, cited in Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, IV), when asked, “Where is the limit of learning?”, replied, “Where the limit of life is.” A certain philosopher, when he was dying at the age of ninety, was asked by one of his pupils whether he grieved at death. He replied, “Yes.” When asked why, he said: “Because I have only now begun to learn” (Valerius Maximus, book VIII, chapter 7, on Solon).

## CHAPTER XLI.—What Is the Order of Learning

The order of learning is as follows. Since all learning is through eloquence, one must first be instructed in eloquence. It has three parts: writing correctly and correctly pronouncing what is written, which grammar provides; proving what must be proved, which dialectic teaches; and adorning words and thoughts, which rhetoric hands down.

[Col. 0098C]

Therefore we must be initiated into grammar, then dialectic, and afterward rhetoric. Equipped with these as with weapons, we ought to approach the study of philosophy. Its order is this: first the quadrivium—first arithmetic itself, second music, third geometry, fourth astronomy—then Holy Scripture. For we arrive at knowledge of the Creator through knowledge of creation.

Since grammar precedes in every discipline, we have proposed to speak of it. Although Priscian says enough, he gives obscure definitions and does not expound their causes and origins; nor does he omit the different parts and different accents in each. The ancient glossators, moreover, have connected the text adequately, and for the most part truly; they have also extracted the rules well, but they erred in expounding the accents.

What these writers have said inadequately, therefore, we have proposed to say—though obscurely—in our work, so that one may seek there certain causes of the origins mentioned above and expositions of Priscian’s definitions.

[Col. 0098D]

From the ancient glosses, however, let him seek the continuation and exposition of Priscian’s text, and the expositions of the rules, almost everywhere and for the most part. But since, following abbreviations, we have spoken above of the subjects proposed—namely of things which exist and are not seen—so that the reader’s mind may approach the remaining subjects to be learned more eagerly, let us here bring the length of the fourth part to an end.

[Col. 0101]
