## CHAPTER I.—On the Hemisphere

No one sees a hemisphere, because if sight is directed over the earth and in a straight line toward the firmament, one does not see half the sky. We reply:

[Col. 0102A]

although the earth is flat, nevertheless a line extended along the earth, even if it is straight, is not inclined; rather, there is a swelling, and where the earth fails, sight still descends along the same line as far as the sky, since sight can never be crooked. Therefore, if the earth were flat, as some think, one would see both poles; whereas now it is round.

## CHAPTER II.—On the Rising and Setting of the Sun

Why the sun in summer seems to rise and set in the north, while at noon it is in the south, reason as follows. For anyone above whose crown the pole hung, the sun would go around the earth as though about his feet. Yet, on moving away toward the south, so far that the summer tropic is partly hidden behind, we nevertheless see it at an angle toward the north, like the extremities of its parallel, which is equally distant from the pole on every side. Therefore the sun, being on that parallel, cannot be nearer to the pole on one side than on the other. For if the sun had to proceed from east to its rising along the line that appears, then at noon it would be nearer to the pole—which cannot be.

[Col. 0102B]

Hence the following question is resolved: how the diameter is ascertained at sunrise, since the sun appears to rise in a straight line and the shadow of the rising sun ought there to be the same as at the horizon on which it rests. But it must be noted that it rises obliquely, as if along an arc.

## CHAPTER III.—On Artificial Hours
Every day except at the equinox there are artificial hours, always twenty-four equal to one another, in this way: divide the whole interval equally into twelve equal parts, whether it be short or long. Natural hours exist only at the equinox.

### CHAPTER IV.—The altitude of the sun and of a climate.

There is one altitude of the climate and another of the sun. The altitude of the sun [Col. 0103B] is observed daily—that is, how much the sun rises each day at noon. The altitude of a climate, however, is called the distance from the head of each person to the sun at noon on the equinox. It is rightly called the altitude of the climate: for, since in each person’s climate the highest point for him is that which is above his head, in our climate there are forty-seven degrees from the sun at noon on the equinox to that point; therefore it is so high. Our climate is such that, if sixty-eight degrees were added to the sun, it would reach above our zenith; and thus at noon on the equinox the sun rises sixty-two degrees above the horizon: add sixty-eight, and there will be ninety degrees up to our zenith.

### CHAPTER V.—The earth and the size of the sun.

[Col. 0103C] When philosophers assert that the earth is a centre, they speak truly. For just as a point within a circle has no customary proportion to it, so neither has the earth to the higher bodies. Therefore, when Macrobius says that the earth is a point in relation to the sun’s circle, while the sun is eight times larger than the earth, it is evident what relation the earth bears to the sun’s circle. Yet, because this relation is not a customary one, the earth is called the centre of that circle, being, as it were, far smaller in comparison with it than the sun.

### CHAPTER VI.—The swelling of water.

The question is raised whether water has a convexity. This seems impossible, since it is fluid and descends to a level surface. But one must see that this is not so: its nature is always to descend into a convex form, as may be seen in a drop; and wherever there is water, [Col. 0103D] place your eye on one shore, and, because of the swelling in the middle, you will no longer see the other shore.

### CHAPTER VII.—The sun’s proximity.

The nearer the sun is, the longer the days it makes—true; but it is nearer in its rays than I should wish—true; therefore does it make longer days than ours? False. Determine it thus: its proximity makes a longer day for the Rhodians than they formerly had, but not a longer day in relation to others, only in relation to itself.

### CHAPTER VIII.—That nothing which rises with the sun sets before the sun.

Likewise, concerning what we say about more than a hemisphere at the rising of the direct signs, an objection is made: the sun rises with some part, but no part which rises [Col. 0104A] with the sun sets before the sun. Yet we say that in the evening a hemisphere, and no more, is above us. Therefore only a hemisphere rises. To this we reply that among the parts which rise with the sun’s degree, and those which emerge after it, some of those parts, I say, roll into the lower hemisphere before the sun’s setting.

### CHAPTER IX.—How an eclipse occurs.

Why is the whole sun subject to eclipse? To this we say that sight itself will judge. An eclipse, they say, occurs thus: even if there were no human being in the world, nevertheless the moon must be below the sun when it is at the sun’s centre; thus, when it is at the earth’s centre—that is, on the equinoctial circle, that is, in Aries or Libra—then by its opposition it brings darkness upon the whole world.

[Col. 0104B] But it seems otherwise to me; for I do not believe an eclipse can occur in this way. Since we are placed in this northern light [perhaps “place” or “region”], and the moon lies below the sun as we look upon it, the moon does not rise in the south, nor does anything obstruct there; therefore no eclipse occurs there. When darkness is thus produced, stars are seen in the daytime during an eclipse. Nor can it occur on that side of the zodiac, but only on this side, because only when the moon wanders to the limit of the zodiac’s latitude does it stand opposed to our sight.

The moon is larger than the earth. For if the whole earth were one mass of fire, and someone were where the moon now is, the earth would not appear to him from there as large as the moon appears to us from here—that is, from the earth. But an objection is made: wherever the moon may be, can it make an eclipse over the whole earth, since it is so large that it covers the entire earth? [Col. 0104C] We answer: a large and broad thing, when near, deprives someone of his whole view; when distant, it does so less.

It seems to me that, if the sun suffers an eclipse, it must suffer it on the ecliptic line, even if the moon does not. But if the moon suffers one, it must be in eclipse even if the sun is not; and this is according to our reasoning, not according to the common view.

### CHAPTER X.—The moon’s leap.

The moon’s leap is nothing other than the subtraction of one day from the nineteen-year cycle. For what ought to be gathered in each lunation is reserved; and because too much is reckoned in each, one day is consequently removed in one instance. This may be seen by the converse. In a leap year there are 366 days; this does not arise from an increase proper to that year alone, since all years [Col. 0104D] are equal, but what had previously been omitted in individual years is corrected in the fourth. In the same way, the last embolismic year has one day fewer than the other embolismic years. This is not a loss belonging to that year alone, but a correction there of what had previously been reckoned too much in individual lunations. Therefore, when the author says that the moon is kindled after twenty-nine days and before the twelfth hour is completed, he speaks correctly, so that from these small portions one day may be gathered.

Climates are marked from east to west.

### CHAPTER XI.—The east and other directions.

It seems reasonable that those who have the same east should also have the same west, and that those who have the same noon should also have the same east; but both propositions [Col. 0105A] are false, as will presently be clear. Let us place one man in the first climate, another in the fourth, and another in the seventh, in a straight line from north to south. Then for the more northerly man the sun will rise earlier, since he has longer days. Again, place a man to the east, at the side of the southern man, so that he sees the sun rise at the same time as the northern man. Behold: they have the same east, but not the same west.

### CHAPTER XII.—Noon.

In the same arrangement of persons, you will also see that those who have one and the same noon do not have the same east. For, placed on the line from north to south, the first two whom I mentioned will both have noon when the sun comes to that line; yet they have not had one and the same [Col. 0105B] east. The more northerly man sees the sun rise earlier, since he is to have longer days.

### CHAPTER XIII.—Cancer and Capricorn.

Cancer is said to be nearer to us than Capricorn; some attempt to deny this as follows: the earth is a centre, but a line drawn from the centre to any part of a circle will be equal; therefore the line drawn from the earth to Capricorn is like that drawn to Cancer. The whole earth is the centre, not every individual part of its upper surface.

### CHAPTER XIV.—The horizon.

There is one horizon of the earth and another of heaven. A short and a tall man have different horizons; Macrobius too hints at this when he says: “Human sight extends beyond one hundred and eighty stadia from there, because beneath that point it can vary.” But the horizon of heaven is altered neither by a person’s height nor by any change of place. For if one person stood in the highest tower and another at its base, both using an astrolabe at the same time, and the sun’s ray passed through the aperture of one and at the same time through the aperture of the other, then the earth’s horizon varies with every movement, but the horizon of heaven does not.

### CHAPTER XV.—The equinox.

Some assert that those have an equinox above whose heads the summer parallel lies. Thus every circle drawn in the manner of a colure appears half-visible to the person over whose head it is drawn; therefore, the person over whose head the summer tropic is drawn sees only its half and thus has an equinox. [Col. 0105D] Some truly affirm this to be so, but it is not so. For, because of our position, it seems in some manner to rise at the extremities and bend toward the south in the middle; and it is joined to the circle drawn straight from east to west above someone’s head. But he says: “Above whose head some part of that circle lies, the whole circle revolves above him,” which he can prove: turn a globe as you please, hold something above the parallel, and turn it; the circle will always stand opposite that which is above it.

There is also another difficulty, namely when one sees more of the parallel. But they say that the nature of that place is such that one degree here produces more effect than three there, because of the sun’s proximity. [Col. 0106A]

### CHAPTER XVI.—Day and night.

Day is the sun shining upon the earth, or illuminated air. But at the equinox, before sunrise and after sunset, the air is illuminated; therefore night is not equal to day. Yet it must be observed that in such statements the nature of the thing expressed is not considered through its cause. Those who study the gnomonic art count only as day the time from the shadow at sunrise to the shadow resting upon the horizon; and it is true that there is day when the air is illuminated. But although the air is in light before day exists, the counting begins through the division of the hours.

Again, when a natural day of twenty-four hours is discussed, we call “day” the interval [Col. 0106B] from sunrise to sunrise, which is the revolution of the firmament. But if anyone says that meanwhile the sun has traversed one degree, and that thus in a natural day more than the firmament is revolved, this is true, but is not reckoned, because in so great a whole this is almost nothing. Thus, on account of that daily degree, there are in a year more revolutions of heaven than days—that is, 365 days and 366 revolutions. For example, today the sun rises with the first degree of Aries, tomorrow with the second; and thus in one day the whole firmament and one degree are revolved. On the second day, the same amount. Thus in two days the firmament revolves twice, and two degrees also.

### CHAPTER XVII.—The parallels.

Perhaps someone may ask—and the question seems worthy of asking—whether a person who, while in the middle of the torrid zone, saw all the parallels half-visible, would, upon departing thence, have the parallels changed by the change of place: namely, whether he would gain more of some and lose as much of others. If this is so, then he either gains more or loses something even of the equinoctial parallel; and if that happens, an equinox cannot occur for him. But it must be observed that almost all parallels change, except the equinoctial. This is effected by its nature as a half-circle. [Col. 0106C]

### CHAPTER XVIII.—The diversity of clocks.

It is not useless to know the varieties of clocks. In a concave clock standing in the ground, in the form of a foot, as it seems to me, the variation [Col. 0106D] of the risings will follow the variation of the days; and, I think, the shadow travels there along the upper rim. But in one suspended above the ground, I judge that only true noon can be observed, while the shadow travels below.

### CHAPTER XIX.—Finding an interval on a clock.

To find the thirteenth interval on a clock, divided according to the measures of things, proceed as follows: divide the gnomon into eight, and divide these parts on the clock by an equal measure. At one, therefore, the measure will be eight times the gnomon; at two, four times; at three, twice and one third; at four, twice; and so on [to] eight equal parts. Then the shadow exceeds the gnomon; therefore, with one measure added to the shadow, the shadow will be one and an eighth times the gnomon; with two, one and a quarter times; with three, one and three-eighths times; and so on indefinitely. [Col. 0107A] Likewise, if any interval is divided into two equal parts, it is a gnomon, but one and a half times the first, and so forth.

### CHAPTER XX.—Why the sun is called middle in number.

When the sun is said to be in the middle numerically, not spatially, it seems that it ought rightly to be spatially in the middle. Hence Ovid says of Phaethon:

> “So that heaven and earth may endure equal heats,  
> keep beneath the earth: in the middle you will travel safest.”  
> *Metamorphoses* XI.134.

But, since it is nearer to the earth, it does not bring equal heat to the upper and lower regions. I reply: it is the nature of heat to rise; and although it is farther from the upper regions, this is compensated by the nature of ascent, so that here proximity has effect, there the nature of ascent.

### CHAPTER XXI.—The light of the stars.

If all stars receive their light from the sun and do not lose that same light by day or by night, why are they not seen by day as by night, or obscured at night as by day? I reply: daytime brightness prevents it; but at night they are seen because they are in a bright region through the dark air. [Col. 0107B]

### CHAPTER XXII.—Distinct spheres.

That the spheres are distinct, and that the eclipse is distinct in such a way that there is a space between one sphere and another, is nothing. For how would the planets be drawn by the sphere of the firmament, which is outermost? Therefore all that ether is one continuous whole and moves by a natural motion, namely circular motion, drawing the planets with it. Since it must move, but can move neither upward nor in another straight line, it is carried round in a circle. [Col. 0107C]

### CHAPTER XXIII.—Why the earth is cold.

Although the words of authority say that the temperate region is tempered by neighboring heat and cold, this must nevertheless be understood thus: know that our whole region is naturally cold. But in the cold zone, because the sun has withdrawn far away, it permits much to its natural condition; and that which possesses much cold seems to moderate heat, whereas rather the immoderate heat diminishes the earth’s naturally cold condition, making it less cold.

When the sun illuminates eight degrees of sixty in the torrid zone and is in the summer tropic, it produces heat for those under the winter tropic, though not as violent as before. Therefore it appears that it ought to cast equal heat through the same number of degrees of sixty toward the north; and, if that is so, no region is now cold. The solution is this: the air of the torrid zone is so inflamed by the presence of the solar body that it soon becomes hot through the sun’s daily presence. But when the sun is placed in Capricorn, since it is thirteen degrees of sixty distant from the cold zone, the solar body’s absence permits the air’s natural, terrestrial coldness to consolidate and grow cold. Thus, even though the sun sometimes approaches it more closely, it nevertheless has less dominion over it than over the more distant region, because presence kindles it. Proximity does not contribute as much as duration and frequency of kindling, as we see with the sun: in Leo, though more distant, it is hotter than in nearer Cancer. [Col. 0107D]

### CHAPTER XXIV.—The line of the zodiac.

They say that the line of the zodiac, because it is oblique, is longer [Col. 0108A] than the equinoctial; this is not so. For every line, however it may be drawn, provided it passes through the centre, is equal to the others. Its apparent obliquity arises from the diverse cutting of the parallels; in its own nature the ecliptic line is as straight as the equinoctial.

### CHAPTER XXV.—Where the zodiac is drawn.

Since the zodiac is drawn obliquely through the torrid zone, the question arises whether the sun girds each part of the torrid zone, since the zodiac never leaves it. The solution: the sun unquestionably traverses the earth’s torrid zone, not the heaven’s torrid zone. If anyone attempts to show otherwise thus—“The sun is far beneath the firmament and is carried by it contrary to all parts of heaven’s torrid zone”—this is false. Since heaven’s torrid zone itself, being carried round, draws the sun, the sun cannot be carried contrary to its parts. This would be true, however, if the sun, once carried round, stood still while heaven’s torrid zone likewise continued moving. [Col. 0108B]

### CHAPTER XXVI.—Where the planets go.

Either opinion may be opposed: whether the planets move contrary to the firmament or with the firmament. They do not move contrary to the firmament, because no thing, while being carried by another, can outstrip it by its own motion and speed; nor would it outstrip it by an oblique but by a straight line. Thus the sun would be somewhere outside the zodiac. Because all stars are of fiery nature, they must move; for fire is always in motion.

### CHAPTER XXVII.—The equinoctial line.

Those who were in the torrid zone would always have an equinox. Nor do I say merely that their day is equal to their night, but that days are equal to days and nights to nights. For although the equinoctial line is greater than the others, the day upon it does not become longer, because it is carried round more quickly there. Likewise, even if the revolution in Cancer were higher than that under Libra, it would nevertheless not be rolled round more quickly or slowly on either line. [Col. 0108C]

### CHAPTER XXVIII.—The solstice in Cancer.

If the solstice is in the first degree of Cancer, that degree has no counterpart. On either side, however, the twenty-nine degrees of Cancer and the twenty-nine degrees of Gemini correspond to one another; likewise the first degree of Gemini corresponds to the first degree of Leo, and so through the rest. Yet these signs are not opposite one another; they are equally distant from the solstitial point.

### CHAPTER XXIX.—Why sight is reflected.

[Col. 0108D]

It is proper and natural that sight should be reflected from a polished surface back upon the observer; this is certain. But an objection is made from a staff: I touch someone’s shadow in water, yet do not touch him. The solution: indeed, at the place where I seem to touch the image, sight is obstructed from falling into the depth.

Establish this argument in some such way, that sight rebounds from a polished surface: a face placed in light is seen because sight rebounds from a mirror. Again, turn the face away from the light, so that the face is in darkness; even if the mirror is in light, you will not see your own face, because, when sight rebounds into the darkness of the face, it does not see the face, being hindered by darkness. Plato therefore also treats the nature of mirrors in order to prove his doctrine concerning [Col. 0109A] sight, for he says that fire issues through the eyes because it appears in mirrors.

### CHAPTER XXX.—The twelve signs obscuring the sun.

Establish thus that the twelve signs obscure the sun: place some object at the navel of the world in the upper hemisphere, and one man opposite it likewise at the navel of the lower hemisphere. Then, when the sun’s middle body has risen above the horizon, its brightness immediately obscures the six upper signs, and likewise the six lower signs; thus twelve. To this one must reply that it happens that the sun takes them away from both the one man and the other, yet no fewer than six are seen. For the sun always illuminates the whole sphere of heaven, since in it is the light of all; but at that time it also illuminates the half of the earthly body which is situated in shadow, because they see through shadow: they see six signs, and thus someone has part of our hemisphere above his own horizon. “And because of the illuminated air I see no sign?” The other man sees the signs of the same hemisphere, but through shadow; for it is one thing to see through brightness beyond shadow, another to see through shadow toward brightness. [Col. 0109B]

### CHAPTER XXXI.—That the planets are not always equally swift.

When the planets are said to be equally swift, this cannot be so. For if they move contrary to the firmament, those which are higher are impeded more than the lower; and thus the higher and lower cannot complete an equal space in the same time. Therefore, if you say: “They are equally swift with respect to their own motion, where each labors only as much as another,” they are not equally moved. For if a planet is carried along while moving contrary to the firmament, it must be impeded; nor can anything be drawn along without being slowed. [Col. 0109C]

### CHAPTER XXXII.—The ascending sun and what it effects.

It must be observed that, when the sun rises toward heaven, as in Gemini it spends two days beyond thirty, it compensates while descending, so that it divides the opposite signs between them whatever was beyond thirty. For since each sign is divided into thirty parts and the sun is said to spend thirty days in each according to an equal division, whatever more than thirty it spends in Gemini is given to Sagittarius; and thus there will be sixty days from the two, as with the other opposing signs.

Likewise it must be observed that the equinoctial circle divides the zodiac equally, but it does not divide the planetary apogees into two equal parts. Therefore the solar apogee is shorter from Libra to Aries than from Aries to Libra. Thus the sun spends more days in the right hemisphere than in the left. [Col. 0109D]

### CHAPTER XXXIII.—In Aries the sun increases the days.

Likewise, from Aries through three signs it spends two more days than in the remaining three. For, with sixteen hours diminished in Cancer, Cancer corresponds to Taurus in number of days and hours, and thus those two days remain over in Gemini. Degrees equally distant immediately before and immediately after the solstice correspond, if the sun is not in them. [Col. 0110A] For from Aries to Cancer there are ninety-four days; from Cancer to Libra, ninety-four. Therefore it cannot be said that the sun customarily descends as it rises, because then it would spend as many days here as there. Nor can it be said that we omit two days there before the equinox, because then the equinoctial circle would have to incline toward the sun.

Rather, this must be said: the ascending sun, because of its excessive ascent, passes through little of a degree’s space; but while descending it passes through more of a degree’s space. That is, the extremities of this sphere are farther apart than those of the sphere which it makes while ascending. Thus the day immediately after the solstice is not altogether like that which occurs before the solstice; nevertheless, little is lacking for the space which the sun completed while ascending through two days to be divided then among all the degrees. [Col. 0110B] That it spends more days in the right hemisphere does not harm the equinox, for the force lies not in the fewness or multitude of days but in their half. At the boundary of Gemini and Cancer there may be both altitude toward heaven and altitude of proximity to us. Yet altitude toward heaven is assigned to Gemini, because there it ends; altitude toward us is assigned to Cancer, because there descent begins.

### CHAPTER XXXIV.—The line tending through the centre.

[Col. 0110C] For making objections and questions, first lay down and know this: sight is admitted upon a plane such as the earth, and, where it does not adhere to the earth, it continues to fall, according to its descent from the eye, even to the firmament. This is why a hemisphere is seen. Likewise, it must be known that a line is drawn through the earth’s centre, from pole to pole, and likewise from east to west through the earth’s centre to the firmament.

Now let one person be in the middle of the torrid zone and another in the lower hemisphere opposite him. Their sight, with lines thus drawn through the earth’s centre in the shape of a cross, will not meet except at the ends of the lines—that is, where they meet the firmament. Therefore, when the sun comes to the line drawn through the earth’s centre, it is not yet seen; but when it comes to the line of sight, it then first rises. Therefore the space through which it is not seen is longer than that through which it is seen. Therefore those who are in the torrid zone cannot have an equinox.

There is yet another difficulty: a degree rises before the planet. [Col. 0110D] The solution of these objections is as follows. No philosopher ever doubted that there are two horizons, one upon a plane and another at a height. The measurement of the horizon on the plane is made known by Macrobius; the measurement of that which is at a height does not fall within comprehension. It must be known, however, that the hemisphere of the earth cannot be seen because the earth’s convexity intervenes, whereas the hemisphere of the firmament is seen by sight directed upward.

As for the lines understood to intersect at the earth’s centre and to be extended through the earth from pole to pole and from rising to setting, understand this: you do not see the place where they are understood to emerge, nor anything of the line itself, except where their ends are joined to the degrees on the firmament itself, as the present diagram shows. But [Col. 0111A] you will say: “Then the sun’s degree is seen before the sun itself?” We answer thus: we do not deny it, nor is it incongruous to one who understands correctly if a part of its degree is seen before the sun. The magnitude of a degree surpasses the magnitude of the sun by an infinite and incomprehensible quantity; even if the sun were fixed to that degree, this would often occur.

But I do not grant that, where the whole degree emerges earlier, you should understand in the same way in the west that a part of the degree still appears when the sun has already been withdrawn from sight. Why, then, will you call the natural day not from sunrise to sunrise, but from the rising of a degree to the rising of that same degree?

### CHAPTER XXXV.—Whether the sun is longer beneath the earth than above it at the equinox.

What they say—that the sun is longer beneath the earth [Col. 0111B] than above it at the equinox—is false. They are deceived in this: they do not think that the sun is above the earth unless it meets their sight. But it is not so. For when it rises above the aforesaid line, namely that which passes over the earth, it begins then to be in our hemisphere, although we do not see it and it has not reached the point to which sight is directed.

This can be proved by the following comparison. If someone were in the lower hemisphere opposite the person whom we have placed in the upper hemisphere, he would not see the sun any more than the upper person, because their lines of sight do not meet in the region of the sun but in the firmamental degree itself, from which they are far distant. And the farther any star descends from the firmament, the greater is the interval between the upper and lower sun [i.e. solar position; the Latin is elliptical].

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—The morning star and the evening star.

[Col. 0111C]

By necessary reasoning it is therefore proved that, if Venus is above the sun, it is on the same day both morning star and evening star at once. Nor do we incur any inconvenience from this except that we have two morning stars and two evening stars. For sometimes on one day we have them nearer to the earth, namely when both wander above the sun; and we have two morning stars and one evening star when one is above the sun and the other in front of it; at other times, two evening stars and one morning star, when one is above the sun and the other behind it.

If the firmament had withdrawn farther from the earth, we would not see a hemisphere. If we saw the sun on the eastern line, we would see more than a hemisphere, because sight would have to be directed through [Col. 0111D] the sun toward heaven lower down than it is now, where it meets the eastern line in heaven. When the sun comes to the eastern line, it is not immediately seen; likewise, before it sets, so far as sight is concerned, it passes beneath the western line. According to what, then, shall we say that there is an equinox? It cannot be said to be according to the sun, because for a longer time it is not seen than it is seen.

I reply: the equinox is said to be according to the sun because, while it still seems almost to rest upon the eastern line, its edge reaches its rising. Nor can it be ascertained by water or by a clock that it remains hidden for a longer interval than it is seen; for since the sun is larger than the earth, so large a thing within so small a difference does not immediately produce a noticeable distinction. The region of the degree, however, is seen before sunrise, while its stars are dimmed. Venus, although rarely, is nevertheless sometimes above the sun and comes to the line of sight before the solar body; although Venus is smaller than the sun, it is not smaller by as much as the earth is. A more acute investigation of this will not be useless. [Col. 0112A]

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—That the clock has no parts in the first and last hour.

[Col. 0112B] On the clock the first and last hour have no parts, because in the first hour its beginning is not considered but only its end, and in the last hour its end is not considered but only its beginning. But how does the sun revolve nine times in an hour, when something belongs to the first hour? I mean in its passage from the eastern line, which rises, though the east is not seen.

Or how can the celestial circle and the astrolabe, or the clock which has a gnomon, correspond to one another, when the sun is not seen to rise upon the said line? The answer is that the sun is of such magnitude that in a small matter it makes no difference. When the alidade rests upon the eastern line, the ray passes through both apertures; for the sun is large and remote from the earth. Thus, although its edge itself is not seen on the eastern line, it does not hinder the instruments, because the principles are given according to how things are observed in the instrument. Therefore the equinox is rightly said to be according to the sun as well: in the instrument it traverses half the circle during as much time as it is not seen. Hence the reasoning seems to have one result, the thing another; but let us follow the observed operation [Col. 0112C] as it has been ascertained.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.—Why the sun is said to be the two-hundred-and-sixteenth part of its circle.

When the sun is said to be the two-hundred-and-sixteenth part of its circle, this seems untrue, because if as many suns were placed from east to west and beneath, they would not fill the entire circle. The answer is that the circle of which it is the two-hundred-and-sixteenth part is different; and our sight deceives us, because it cannot fall upon the circle in which the sun revolves in the ether, but falls upon the firmament itself. The sun is not a part of the firmament’s circle, but of its own circle in which it is carried, which is near the earth.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—The plane and the height.

[Col. 0112D] Does there occur at a height, by equal removal, the change which occurs on a plane? The answer: if one person stood upon the highest point of the earth and another at its lowest, there would arise between them the difference which on a plane is the change of noon or shadow. For it is one thing for sight to meet the sun at its rising, another for someone to stand opposite the sun when it is elevated high up. The sun is so great that no one easily escapes its centre; and thus, when one person has noon, another far removed from him also has noon. This is no wonder, since, when the sun is elevated high up, its centre is the same for both.

### CHAPTER XL.—Degrees and climates.

Once one degree on earth has been observed by means of a shadow, it is evident that all 340 are to be investigated. Likewise climates are found by the variation of the shadow. [Col. 0113A] Therefore it seems that one degree contains one climate; but our inhabited world sometimes has divisions of sixty, each containing seven degrees. Thus not every change of shadow makes a climate; rather, in each climate there is a noticeable variation of shadow at the beginning, middle, and end. Why, then, are there said to be twelve at the seventh climate rather than at the fortieth? This must be investigated.

All planets are said to be of the same speed, which does not seem possible, because the higher they are, the more they are impeded by the firmament. The reply: the higher are indeed impeded more than the lower; yet all have equal speed, because the higher they are, the lighter, and the lighter they are, the swifter. But the firmament impedes the higher more; this is no wonder, because by nature they are swifter, and thus they are moderated to the lower. [Col. 0113B]

### CHAPTER XLI.—The winter sun.

When the sun has our parallel, it is eight degrees of sixty distant from the winter one and five from the northern. Therefore, ought those in the cold zone to have more heat than some who are in the torrid zone? The solution: there is no part of the torrid zone above which the sun does not pass twice in the year. But it comes to these parts only once. Therefore not proximity but constancy produces heat.

### CHAPTER XLII.—Rising times may be equal; setting times not likewise.

Not all who can have the same rising can have the same setting. Proof: those in the climate of the Rhodians have a longest day of sixteen hours. If someone were now to go from Syene so far east that the sun rose for him two hours earlier than for the person in Syene, he would have sunrise together with those in the Rhodian climate, but would not have sunset with them. [Col. 0113C]

### CHAPTER XLIII.—That noons and settings are not equal.

Not all who have the same noon have the same setting. Proof: we say that those beneath the line extended from pole to pole have the same noon, but not the same setting. For when the sun is in Cancer, it sets more quickly for the Rhodians [Col. 0113D] than for us, and rises later than for us.

### CHAPTER XLIV.—That the sun administers ethereal light.

The question is raised: since the sun is the administrator of all ethereal light, why was it not placed in the middle? The answer: the sun ought to illuminate both higher and lower regions by light and heat; but since it is the nature of all heat always to rise and never to descend, it had necessarily to be nearer the lower than the higher regions.

### CHAPTER XLV.—The solar body.

When half the solar body comes above our horizon, it obscures six signs in our hemisphere and likewise six in the lower hemisphere—therefore twelve? [Col. 0114A] The solution: this is true, and yet it obscures only six, because those in the West see six; and the reason why they see them is that shadow is still before their eyes.

### CHAPTER XLVI.—Those in the middle of the torrid zone.

The question is raised concerning those in the middle of the torrid zone: do they always have an equinox? The answer: they do, because they always see half of the parallels. Again, the question is raised: when the sun has the equinoctial parallel, is day and night then longer than when it has the tropics? The answer: no, because the smallest circle in the sphere does not revolve more swiftly than the longest. You may prove this concerning the equinox in the following way: if someone were placed in the middle of the torrid zone, he would see all the parallels half-visible, [Col. 0114B] each of which completes its whole revolution in twenty-four hours and its half in twelve. Whichever of them the sun follows in rising and setting, it completes its revolution for him in the same interval as the sun.

The planets called *anōmaloi* (ἀνώμαλοι) are those which do not proceed in the following year as in the preceding, as Mars does especially. *Anomale* means “without rule.”

### CHAPTER XLVII.—Morning and evening rising
Let it be noted that one rising is morning, another evening. Morning rising occurs when a star precedes the rising sun, after midnight. Evening rising occurs when a star appears after the sun’s setting. Moreover, one rising is cosmical, another heliacal, another achronychal. A cosmical rising occurs when any star emerges from the lower [Col. 0114C] hemisphere into the upper hemisphere. A heliacal rising occurs when the sun, moving away from a star, allows it to be seen. An achronychal rising occurs when, as the sun sets, any of the wandering stars that is positioned opposite the sun along a diameter comes forth. For ἀχρόνικος means “untimely” or “without a time.” One setting is cosmical, another heliacal. A cosmical setting occurs when any star descends from the upper hemisphere into the lower. A heliacal setting occurs when the sun, approaching a star, causes it not to be visible.

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—What Morning and Evening Station Are

One station is morning, another evening. Morning station occurs when, before sunrise, the sun is in station at its proper limit. Evening station occurs when, as the sun sets, some planet appears in station. Of the planets themselves, [Col. 0114D] some are hypolitic, that is, transitory; some stationary; some retrograde; and some anomalous. Hypolitic or transitory planets are those which proceed from an earlier sign toward a later one; and although all do this, the sun and moon do so especially. For these two proceed from earlier to later signs in such a way that they never stop and never move retrograde. If someone objects that the sun stops, because it moves more slowly in Gemini than in Sagittarius, say that it never stops. For it is equally swift everywhere; but because it has a greater space to complete there, it is said to stop there, as is apparent at the extremity.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—Whence the Stars Were Created

That the stars were materially made from waters can be proved by this argument. For since [Col. 0115A] it is manifest that the two upper elements, fire and air, by their nature are without any density, nothing of these can by its nature—except accidentally—be accessible to sight. Therefore, when certain unlearned people say that they see the sky when the air is clear, although they imagine themselves to see something, it is utterly false that they perceive it. For where sight fails, there is error: the sense produces an imagination of seeing what it does not see. Just as someone with closed eyes seems to himself to see darkness. For although sight takes its origin from the light of the eyes, it is nevertheless of no use unless it is reflected from the obstacle of some dense body. [Col. 0116A] But if this lower air, which is between us and a wall, or some material object, or anything of that kind, cannot impede sight so as to be perceived, much less can that which is higher and purer. Hence air is properly called *caelum* (“sky”), because it is hidden from our sight. It is therefore established that every visible body has some density, which arises from the thickness of water or earth. For clouds, condensed from the vapour of waters, appear visible; likewise flames which arise in cloudy air, or in some material that is being burned, arise from vapours,

# EPISTLE OF CHRISTIANUS TO HONORIUS THE SOLITARY CONCERNING *THE IMAGE OF THE WORLD*

[Col. 0119]

May CHRISTIANUS, enlightened by the sevenfold Spirit in the threefold faith, and cleansed by the seven banks of threefold philosophy, after the week of this life be crowned with the seven beatitudes, and in the eighth contemplate the Trinity in unity.

Because, being ignorant among the ignorant, I am wrapped in the darkness of ignorance, I seem to lead a sad and mournful life as a blind man. Therefore, because I know that you are surrounded by the immeasurable light of wisdom, I ask, together with many others, that you may impart to us some little spark of your flame-emitting knowledge, while it is not diminished in you: that you may set forth for us, as if on a little tablet, an exposition of the world. For it seems miserable to behold daily the things made for our sake, and, together with senseless beasts, to remain wholly ignorant of what they are.

# EPISTLE OF HONORIUS TO CHRISTIANUS, ON THE SAME SUBJECT

To the foster-child of wisdom, diligently searching out hidden things, flourishing now in the depth of knowledge unto the salvation of man, and hereafter in Zion seeing face to face the Lord, in whom all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.

Since you devote yourself continually and zealously to reading, and thirstily draw out the marrow of all Scripture, you ask me, dearest friend, to depict for you the form of the entire world—as the common saying has it, “the sheep asked the goat for wool”—so that you may refresh the eye of the body therein just as you are accustomed to nourish the sight of the heart upon the structure of the universe. You yourself know better how laborious and how dangerous this undertaking is. It is laborious for one occupied with other matters; dangerous because of the envious, who never cease to malign everything which they cannot imitate, and do not fail to tear with venomous tooth, like a bristly goat, what they cannot attain. What they openly criticize they read attentively in secret, and from our labour they arrogate knowledge to themselves, which they trample underfoot like swine trampling pearls. Yet since I owe you not only my labour but my very self—especially since I understand that I was born not for myself alone but for the whole world—setting aside those wasting away with envy, who with spiteful hearts gnaw not me but themselves, I undertake this difficult work. For relentless labour—indeed, charity—conquers all things. Thus, for the instruction of many who lack an abundance of books, this little book is published and is called *The Image of the World*, because the arrangement of the entire world may be seen in it as in a mirror; and in it too a pledge of our friendship may be left to posterity. But I put into it nothing except what the tradition of the elders commends.

# BOOK I

[Col. 0121]

## CHAPTER I.—On the Form of the World.—Etymology of “World.” What the World’s Shape Is Like

[Col. 0121A]

The world (*mundus*) is called as though “moved on every side,” for it is in perpetual motion. Its shape is round, like a ball; but it is distinguished by elements after the likeness of an egg. For an egg is surrounded outwardly on every side by a shell; within the shell is the white, within the white the yolk, and within the yolk a drop of fat. Thus the world is surrounded on every side by heaven, as by a shell; within heaven is the pure ether, as the white; within the ether the turbid air, as the yolk; and within the air the earth, as a drop of fat.

## CHAPTER II.—On the Creation of the World.—Five Modes of the World’s Creation

The creation of the world is described in five modes. First, before temporal ages, the immensity of the world is conceived in the divine [Col. 0121B] mind; this conception is called the archetypal world, as it is written: “What was made in him was life” (John 1). Secondly, this perceptible world is created in matter according to the pattern of the archetype. As one reads: “He who remains for ever created all things together.” Thirdly, this world is formed through kinds and forms in six days, as it is written: “In six days the Lord made his works, very good” (Gen. 1). Fourthly, one thing is born from another: for example, a human from a human, livestock from livestock, a tree from a tree, each thing from the seed of its own kind, as is said: “My Father works until now.” Fifthly, the world will yet be renewed, as it is written: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21).

## CHAPTER III.—On the Four Elements.—Why They Are Called Elements; How Many Elements There Are; How They Are Mixed with One Another; Their Position

[Col. 0121C]

The elements are called, as it were, *hyle*, “bindings”; but ὕλη means “matter.” They are the things of which all things consist: namely fire, air, water, and earth. These revolve into one another in a circle, while fire is changed into air, air into water, and water into earth; and again earth is changed into water, water into air, and air into fire. Each holds the others by its own qualities, as by certain arms, and they in turn blend their mutually discordant natures in a harmonious covenant. For dry and cold earth is joined to cold water; cold and moist water is bound to moist air; moist and warm air is associated with warm fire; and [Col. 0121D] warm and dry fire is joined to dry earth. Of these, earth, as the heaviest, occupies the lowest place; fire, as the lightest, the highest; and the other two occupy the middle, as a kind of bond of solidity. Of these, the heavier water takes the place nearest earth, while lighter air holds the place nearest fire. To earth are assigned walking creatures, such as humans and beasts; to water, swimming creatures, such as fishes; to air, flying creatures, such as birds; and to fire, shining bodies, such as the sun and stars.

## CHAPTER IV.—On the Seven Names of Earth.—*Terra*, *tellus*, *humus*, *arida*, *sicca*, *solum*, *ops*

The lowest element is denoted by seven names, [Col. 0122A] because it is called *terra*, *tellus*, *humus*, *arida*, *sicca*, *solum*, and *ops*. *Terra* is said to derive from *terere*, “to wear down,” and signifies the entire element. *Tellus* is so called as though “bearing up fruits”; it is land suited to crops or planted with vines and fruit-bearing trees. *Humus* comes from *humor*, “moisture”: it is marshy and untilled land. *Arida* is waterless land, which is always parched by the heat of the sun, such as Libya. *Sicca* is land which, after being rained upon at some time, quickly dries out, such as Judaea. *Solum* derives from solidity, as mountainous places do. *Ops* derives from riches, where wealth—namely gold and gems—is abundant, as in India.

## CHAPTER V.—On the Form of the Earth.—The Earth Is Round; Its Circumference; the Earth as the Centre of the World; the Earth Is Supported by No Props; Ocean Surrounds the Earth; Veins of Waters and Springs

The earth’s shape is round, whence it is called *orbis*, “sphere.” [Col. 0122B] For if someone placed in the air were to look down upon it from above, the whole vastness of mountains and hollowness of valleys would appear less upon it than a finger would upon a very large ball held in one’s hand. The circumference of the earth is measured at one hundred and eighty thousand stadia, reckoned as twelve thousand and fifty-two miles. This earth is situated as the centre in the middle of the world, like a point in the middle of a circle, and is supported not by any props but by divine power, as one reads: “Do you not fear me, says the Lord, who hung the earth upon nothing? For it is founded upon its own stability” (Ps. 103); like another element, it occupies the boundary set by its own quality. It is encircled by Ocean as by a rim, as it is written: “The deep is its garment” [Col. 0122C] (ibid.). Within, it is penetrated by channels of waters as a body is by veins of blood, through which its dryness is watered everywhere. Hence, wherever the earth is dug, water is found.

## CHAPTER VI.—On the Five Zones.—The Uninhabitable Circles or Zones; Three Zones; Two Habitable Zones; It Is Shown by an Example Why Only the Two Middle Zones Are Habitable; Five Circles

The earth is divided into five zones, that is, circles. The two outermost are uninhabitable because of cold; the middle one is uninhabitable because of heat, since the sun never withdraws from it and never approaches the former. The two intermediate zones are habitable, tempered here by heat and there by cold. For example, if a fire is lit outdoors in winter, [Col. 0122D] it produces five lines: one hot in the middle, two cold around it, and two temperate between these. If it moved about like the sun, it would certainly produce five circles. Of these circles, the first is called northern, the second solstitial, the third equinoctial, the fourth wintry, and the fifth southern; but only the solstitial one is known to be inhabited by us.

## CHAPTER VII.—On the Three Parts of the Habitable World.—The Three Habitable Parts of the Earth

The habitable zone in which we dwell is divided by the Mediterranean Sea into three parts. One of these [Col. 0123A] is called Asia, another Europe, and the third Africa. Asia extends from the north through the east to the south; Europe from the west to the north; Africa from the south to the west.

## CHAPTER VIII.—On Asia.—Paradise

Asia is named from a queen of that name. Its first region in the East is Paradise: a place indeed distinguished by every delight, inaccessible to human beings, surrounded by a fiery wall reaching to heaven.

## CHAPTER IX.—On Paradise.—The Fountain of Paradise

In it is the tree of life, namely, a tree from whose fruit whoever eats will remain immortal forever in one and the same condition. In it also rises a fountain which divides into four rivers. These rivers are concealed in the earth beneath Paradise, [Col. 0123B] but pour forth in far-distant regions elsewhere.

## CHAPTER X.—On the Four Rivers.—Phison or Ganges; Geo or Nile; Tigris; Euphrates

For Phison, which is also the Ganges, rises in India from Mount Orcobares and, flowing eastward, is received by Ocean. Geon, which is also the Nile, rises near Mount Atlas, is immediately swallowed by the earth, and, flowing through it by a hidden channel, issues forth again on the shore of the Red Sea. It circles Ethiopia, flows through Egypt, and, divided into seven mouths, enters the great sea near Alexandria. The Tigris and Euphrates rise in Armenia from Mount Barchoatro and, turning southward, join the Mediterranean [Col. 0123C] Sea. Beyond Paradise there are many desert and impassable places, because of various kinds of serpents and wild beasts.

## CHAPTER XI.—On India.—Why India Is So Called; Mount Caucasus; India’s Boundaries; the Indian Ocean; an Island Having Two Summers and Two Winters in One Year and Remaining Green at Every Season; Mount Caspius; the Caspian Sea; Gog, Magog, Garmani, Orestae, Coatrae, Pygmies; White Pepper; Macrobians, Agroctae, Bragmans; Those Who Slaughter Their Parents; Those Who Eat Raw Fish

Next comes India, named from the river Indus. It rises from Mount Caucasus in the north, directs its course southward, and is received by the Red Sea. India is bounded on the west by this river, and the Indian Ocean is named from it. In this ocean is also situated [Col. 0123D] the island of Taprobane, famed for ten cities. It has two summers and two winters in one year, and is green in every season. In it are also the islands of Chrysa and Argare, fertile in gold and silver and always blooming. There also are golden mountains which cannot be approached because of dragons and griffins. In India is Mount Caspius, from which the Caspian Sea receives its name. Between it and the sea, Gog and Magog, most savage peoples, are said to have been enclosed by Alexander the Great. They feed on human flesh and raw beasts. India has forty-four regions and many peoples: the Garmani, Orestae, and Coatrae, whose forests touch the sky. In its mountains are Pygmies, men two cubits tall, who wage war against cranes, bear children in their third year, and grow old in their eighth. Among them [Col. 0124A] pepper grows white in colour; but when the serpents that abound there are driven away with flame, it takes on a black colour from the burning. There are likewise Macrobians twelve cubits tall, who fight against griffins, which have the bodies of lions and the wings and talons of eagles. There are likewise Agroctae and Bragmans, who voluntarily throw themselves into fire from love of another life. There are others who slaughter their parents, already worn out by old age, and prepare their flesh for feasting; and one who refuses to do this is judged impious. There are others who eat fish entirely raw and drink the salt sea.

## CHAPTER XII.—On Monsters.—Those Who Give Birth Only Once; Arimaspians, Cyclopes, Sciapods; Headless Men; Those Living on the Scent of an Apple Alone

There are certain monsters there, some classed with humans [Col. 0124B] and some with beasts. Such are those who have backward-facing soles and eight toes on each foot—sixteen altogether; and others who have dogs’ heads and hooked claws, whose clothing is the skins of livestock and whose speech is the barking of dogs. There too certain mothers give birth once only and eat their grey-haired offspring, who become black-haired in old age and exceed the long span of our lifetime. Others give birth at five years old, but their offspring do not exceed their eighth year. There are also one-eyed people, Arimaspians, and Cyclopes. There are also Sciapods, who, supported by one foot alone, outrun the wind in their course, and, when they lie on the ground, make themselves shade by raising the sole of their foot. There are others without heads, whose eyes are in their shoulders; instead of nose and mouth they have two openings in their chest; and they have bristles like beasts. There are [Col. 0124C] others near the source of the river Ganges who live on the scent alone of a certain apple. If they go farther away, they carry an apple with them, for they die if they inhale a harmful smell.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On Beasts.—Ceucocroca; Eale; Untamed Bulls; Manticore; Three-Horned Oxen; Unicorn; Huge Tortoises; Magnet; Diamond

There are serpents there so enormous that they devour stags and even swim across Ocean itself. There is there the beast Ceucocroca, whose body is that of an ass, haunches of a stag, breast and legs of a lion, feet of a horse, an immense divided horn, and a great gape of the mouth reaching to the ears. In place of teeth it has solid bone; its voice is almost human. There is another beast there, the Eale, whose body is that of a horse, jaws of a boar, tail of an elephant, and cubit-long horns. One of these it bends back over its spine while fighting with the other. When that one is blunted, it brandishes the other for combat. It is bristlingly black in colour, and is equally strong in water and on land. There are tawny bulls there, dreadful with their reversed bristles; they have a large head, and the opening of their mouth reaches from ear to ear. These too alternately project or lower their horns for battle. They repel every missile with their hard backs. If captured, they can be tamed by no art. There is also there the beast Manticore: its face is human, it has a triple row of teeth, the body of a lion, the tail of a scorpion, blue-grey eyes, and a blood-red colour; its voice is the hissing of serpents. Fleeing dangers, it flies, swifter in running than a bird in flight, and it consumes human flesh. There are also three-horned oxen having horses’ feet. There is likewise the unicorn, whose body is that of a horse, head of a stag, feet of an elephant, and tail of a pig; [Col. 0125A] it is armed with a single horn in the middle of its forehead, four feet long, shining and wonderfully sharp. This beast is exceedingly fierce and gives terrible bellows. It pierces through with its horn whatever stands in its way. When captured it can be killed, but it cannot be tamed.

In the Ganges too are eels three hundred feet long. There are also certain worms there which, like a crab, have two arms six cubits long; with these they seize elephants and plunge them beneath the waves.

The Indian sea also produces tortoises from whose shells humans make themselves spacious dwellings.

India also produces the magnet-stone, which draws iron, and the diamond, which can be broken only by goats’ blood.

## CHAPTER XIV.—On Parthia.—Why Parthia Is So Called; Arachosia; Assyria, Media, Persia; Persepolis; the Origin of Magic; Pyrrhites; Synelites

[Col. 0125B]

From the river Indus to the Tigris lies Parthia, divided into thirty-three regions. Parthia is named from the Parthians, who came from Scythia. In it is the region of Arachosia, named from the town of Arachosia. In it also is Assyria, named from Assur, son of Shem, who first inhabited it. There is also Media in it, named from King Medus, who, building a city, called it Media; from this city the region too changed its name. There is also Persia in it, named from King Perseus, who built the city of Persepolis, from which the region [Col. 0125C] took its name. The art of magic first arose there. Persia produces the stone pyrrhites, which burns the hand of the person squeezing it, and synelites, whose brightness waxes and wanes with the moon.

## CHAPTER XV.—On Mesopotamia.—Nineveh; Babylonia; Babylon; Chaldaea, Where Astronomy Was First Invented; Arabia; Saba; Mount Sinai; Midian

From the river Tigris to the Euphrates is Mesopotamia, so called in Greek from its two rivers because it is situated in the middle of two rivers. In it is the city of Nineveh, a journey of three days in extent, built and named by King Ninus. In it too is the region of Babylonia, named from the city Babylon. The giant Nimrod founded it, but Queen Semiramis restored it. Its [Col. 0125D] wall is fifty cubits broad and two hundred cubits high; the circuit of the city is four hundred and eighty stadia; it is secured by a hundred bronze gates and watered by the river Euphrates, which runs through its middle. Its citadel, Babel, is written to be four thousand paces high.

There also is Chaldaea, in which astronomy was first invented. There too is Arabia, also called Saba, from Saba son of Cush. Frankincense is gathered there. There is Mount Sinai, also called Horeb, upon which the law given to Moses was written down; near it was the city Midian, in which Jethro served as priest. In it are many peoples: Moabites, Ammonites, Idumaeans, Saracens, Midianites, and many others.

## CHAPTER XVI.—On Syria.—Damascus; Reblata; the Province of Commagene; Phoenicia; Tyre; Sortyx; Sidon; Mount Lebanon; the Source of the Jordan; Palestine; Ascalon; Jerusalem; Canaan

[Col. 0126A]

From the Euphrates to the Mediterranean Sea is Syria, named from a certain King Syrus. In it is Damascus, built and named by Damascus, Abraham’s freedman; formerly it was called Reblata. In it is the province of Commagene. There is also Phoenicia, named either from the phoenix bird, which is found only in this land, or from King Phoenix, son of Agenor. In it are situated the cities Tyre, also called Sortyx, and Sidon. In it also is Mount Lebanon, at whose foot the river Jordan rises. There is also Palestine in it, named from the city of Palestine, now called Ascalon. There is Judaea in it as well, named from Judah son of Jacob, from whose tribe kings came. In it [Col. 0126B] is also Canaan, named from Canaan son of Ham. In it is Jerusalem, which Shem, son of Noah, built and named Salem. But Jebus, son of Canaan, also inhabited it; hence King David gave it the name Jerusalem, as though *Jebusalem*, from Jebus and Salem. His son Solomon adorned it with gold and gems and called it Jerosolymia, as though *Jerusalemonia*. When it had been overthrown by the Babylonians, Zerubbabel rebuilt it; but later the Roman army utterly destroyed it. Afterwards the Emperor Aelius Hadrian restored it and named it Aelia.

## CHAPTER XVII.—On Palestine.—Samaria; Sebastia; Sichisma; Galilee; Nazareth; Pentapolis; Sodom; Gomorrah; the Dead Sea; Saracens; Hagarenes; Ishmaelites; Nabataeans

[Col. 0126C] In Palestine also is the region of Samaria, named from the city Samaria, which is now called Sebastia and was formerly Sichima, named from Shechem. In it too is Galilee, in which lies the city Nazareth, situated near Mount Tabor. In it also is the region Pentapolis, named from five cities. In it once stood Sodom and Gomorrah. In it is the Dead Sea, into which the streams of the Jordan are swallowed. In it also are Saracens, said to be named from Sarah, who are also Hagarenes, from Hagar. Likewise they are called Ishmaelites from Ishmael. In it also are the Nabataeans, named from Nebaioth son of Ishmael, whose peoples are twelve.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On Egypt.—Euxia, Later Called Egypt; the Thebaid; Thebes; Monks; Babylon in Egypt; Alexandria

The regions named above, beginning from the east, [Col. 0126D] extend in a straight line to the Mediterranean Sea. Egypt is joined to them as far as the south, and is said to contain twenty-four peoples. It rises in the east at the Red Sea and fixes its boundary westward in Libya. It was first called both Good Abundance and Euxia; later it was called Egypt from King Aegyptus, brother of Danaus. Surrounded on every side by the river Nile, it is shaped like the letter Delta and is famous for one hundred thousand villages. Clouds do not darken it, rains do not water it; rather, the overflowing Nile makes it fruitful. In it is the province of the Thebaid, named from the city Thebes, which Cadmus, son of Agenor, coming into Egypt, built and named Thebes after the Thebes which he had built in Boeotia. Mauritius ruled there, and the Thebans are named from it. [Col. 0127A] A vast wilderness borders upon it, in which a multitude of monks formerly lived. King Cambyses, after conquering Egypt, founded a city to which he gave the name Babylon; it is now the capital of that kingdom. There too the victorious Alexander built a city, which he named Alexandria after himself.

## CHAPTER XIX.—On Caucasus and the Regions of the East.—Amazons; Massagetae; Colchians; Sarmatians; Seres; Bactra; Hyrcania; Hirnia; Scythia; the Hyperborean Mountains; Albania; Armenia; Mount Arath; Iberia; Cappadocia

The following regions are joined to those written above as far as the North. Mount Caucasus rises from the Caspian Sea in the East and, bending through the North, stretches almost as far as Europe. The Amazons lived on it, women indeed who fought like men. [Col. 0127B] With them dwell the Massagetae, Colchians, and Sarmatians. Seres is a city of the East from which the region Serica, its cloth, and its people are named. After it is Bactra, named from the river Bactrus. Hyrcania joins it, named from the Hyrcanian forest, in which are birds whose feathers shine through the night. Scythia and Hirnia join it; their peoples number forty-four. There are the Hyperborean Mountains. Albania follows, named from the whiteness of its people, because people are born there with white hair. Armenia is joined to it; in Armenia is Mount Arath, upon which Noah’s ark came to rest after the flood, and its timbers are seen there even to this day. Iberia is joined to it. Cappadocia joins that land, named from a city of the same name; there mares conceive by the wind, but their offspring live no more than three years.

## CHAPTER XX.—On Asia Minor.—Ephesus; the Body of John the Evangelist Rests at Ephesus; the City of Nicaea; Bithynia; Nicomedia

[Col. 0127C]

Asia Minor lies next beyond this; it is almost everywhere surrounded by sea. In it is the city of Ephesus, built by the Amazons, where the body of John the Evangelist rests; and also the city of Nicaea, where the great synod was held. The first province of Asia Minor is Bithynia, formerly Berica, then Mygdonia, and afterwards called Bithynia from King Bithynus. In it is a city of the same name. There is also the city of Nicomedia, built and named by King Nicomedes.

## CHAPTER XXI.—On the regions of Asia.—Smyrna; Galatia; Phrygia; Troy; Lycaonia; Caria; the river Hirnus; Lydia; Thyatira; Isauria; Cilicia; Mount Amana, also called Taurus; Tarsus; Lycia; Pisidia; Pamphylia; the Euxine Pontus.

[Col. 0127D]

Bithynia is also called Greater Phrygia; in it is the city of Smyrna, built by King Theseus. Galatia adjoins it, so called from the Gauls, whom King Bithynus summoned as allies and, after his victory, allotted land to them. Phrygia follows, thus named after Phrygia, daughter of Europa. It is also called Dardania after Dardanus, son of Jupiter. In it is a city of the same name, built by him. There is also the city of Troy, built and named by King Tros. It is likewise called Ilium after King Ilus; its walls are called Pergama.

Lycaonia and Caria lie beside it; in the latter flows the river Hirnus, renowned for its golden sands. From there comes Lydia, called after King Lydus, brother of Tyrrhenus. In it is also Thyatira. Then comes Isauria, so called from the breeze (*aura*) which blows through it on every side. After this is Cilicia, named from the city of the same name, which Cilix, son of Agenor, built; from it the region received its name. In it is Mount Amana, also called Taurus. There is also the city of Tarsus, built by Perseus and made glorious by the residence of the Apostle Paul. Then come Lycia, Pisidia, and Pamphylia. The Euxine Pontus is a region of many peoples, from which the Pontic Sea likewise takes its name. Ovid, and later Clement, were banished into exile there.

Having passed through Asia, let us cross over to Europe.

## CHAPTER XXII.—On Europe.—The Riphaean Mountains; the river Tanais; the Maeotian Marshes; Theodosia.

Europe is named from King Europus and from Europa, daughter of Agenor. First, towards the north, are the Riphaean Mountains, the river Tanais—so called after King Tanaus—and the Maeotian Marshes, adjoining the Great Sea near the city of Theodosia, which divide [the regions].

## CHAPTER XXIII.—On Scythia.

From the river Tanais begins Lower Scythia, extending southward as far as the Danube. In it are these provinces: Alania, Dacia, and Gothia.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—On Upper Germany.—The origin of the name Germany; the boundaries and limits of Upper Germany; Swabia; Raetia; Bavaria; Regensburg; Eastern Francia; Thuringia.

From the Danube to the Alps is Upper Germany, said to be named from the begetting (*germinando*) of peoples. To the west it is bounded by the Rhine, and to the north by the river Elbe. In it is the region of Swabia, named from Mount Suevus. It is also called Alemania, after Lake Leman. It is likewise called Raetia.

[Col. 0128C]

In it the Danube rises; it is enlarged by sixty principal rivers and, divided like the Nile into seven mouths, enters the Pontic Sea. In it is Noricum, also called Bavaria, in which is the city of Regensburg. Then there is Eastern Francia, adjoining Thuringia, which Saxony follows.

## CHAPTER XXV.—On Lower Germany.—Denmark, that is, Norway; Moesia; Lower Pannonia; Bulgaria.

From the river Elbe begins Lower Germany, which towards the north is met by the Ocean. In it are Denmark and Norway. From the Danube—or rather, around the Danube eastward—as far as the Mediterranean Sea is Moesia, named from the yield of crops (*Messium proventu*); then Lower Pannonia and Bulgaria.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—On Thrace.

[Col. 0128D]

Then comes Thrace, called after Thras, son of Japheth. It has the river Hebrus and a city, Hebron, built and named there.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—On Greece.—Cethim; Illyricum; Dalmatia; Epirus; a spring in Epirus; Chaonia; Molossia; Helladia; Attica; Athens; Boeotia; the distinction between Thebans and Thebaeans; Aonia; the Peloponnese; Thessaly; Macedonia; Emathia; Mount Olympus; Thessalonica; Achaea; Arcadia; the Arbaston stone; Upper Pannonia; Mount Pennine; Histria.

From the Mediterranean Sea is Greece, named after King Graecus, formerly called the land of Cethim; towards the south it is bounded by the Great Sea. It is also called Illyricum, and in it is the province of Dalmatia, called after the city of Dalmi. There is also Epirus, so called after Pyrrhus, son of Achilles.

[Col. 0129A]

In Epirus is a spring in which lit torches are extinguished, and extinguished torches are lit again. There is also Chaonia, named from a city of the same name, which Helenus, brother of Hector, built and named Chaonia out of love for his brother Chaon. It is likewise called Molossia, after the city of Molossia, which Molossus, son of Pyrrhus, built and called Molossia after his own name.

There also is Helladia, named after King Hellas, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha. This is also Attica, named after King Attis. It is Greece proper. In it is the city of Athens, built by King Cecrops. There is also Boeotia, named from an ox, because Cadmus, son of Agenor, arriving there found an ox; after sacrificing it to the gods, he built Thebes. He named the province Boeotia. From this Thebans are so called; from the other [Thebes], Thebaeans.

The same province is called Aonia, after the spring Aon, consecrated to the Muses. There also is the Peloponnese, named after King Pelops and the city of the same name. There also is Thessaly, named after King Thessalus; and Macedonia, called after King Macedon. This is also Emathia, named after King Emathus. In it is Mount Olympus, which rises above the clouds. In it also is Thessalonica, built by King Thessalus, son of Graecus. There is Achaea, named after King Achaeus and the city of the same name. There is also Arcadia, likewise called Sicyonia after King Sicyon. Arcadia produces the Arbaston stone, which, once set alight, cannot be extinguished.

Then comes Upper Pannonia as far as Mount Pennine. To its north is Histria, named after the river Hister, which is also the Danube.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—On Italy.—The various names of Italy; Rome; forms of cities according to beasts; Rome has the form of a lion; Brundisium that of a stag; Carthage that of an ox; Troy that of a horse; Tuscany; Campania; Apulia; Umbria; Etruria; Lombardy; the Po and Eridanus; Venice; the origin of the name Gaul; the source of the Rhine.

[Col. 0129C]

Italy was formerly called Great Greece; later it was called Saturnia after Saturn. Then it was called Latium because Saturn, driven out by Jupiter, hid there. Afterwards it was called Ausonia after King Auson. Finally it was named Italy after Italus, king of the Sicels. It rises from the Alps and fixes its boundary in the Great Sea. In it is the city of Rome, built and named by Romulus.

The ancients shaped cities in the forms of the principal beasts, for symbolic significance. Hence Rome has the form of a lion, which presides over the other beasts as their king. Its head is the city built by Romulus; its brick buildings are arranged on both sides, whence they are called the Laterans. Brundisium had the form of a stag, Carthage of an ox, and Troy the figure of a horse.

[Col. 0129D]

In Italy is the province of Tuscany, named from incense and sacrifices. There is also Campania, named after the city of Capua, built by King Capys. There is also Apulia. There is also Umbria, so called because it survived the rains at the time of the Flood. There is also Etruria, named after King Etruscus; and Lombardy, named from long beards.

The Po, also called the Eridanus, a river of Italy, rises in the Apennine Mountains and flows into the sea. Venice, named after King Benecus, was first called Benetia and afterwards Venetia. Gaul is said to be named from the whiteness of its people, for *gala* means “milk” in Greek. The Rhine rises in the Alps and, turning northward, is received into a bay of the Ocean.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—On Gaul.—Belgic Gaul; Francia; King Francus; Lugdunensian Gaul; Comata; Togata; Narbonensian Gaul; Aquitaine.

[Col. 0130A]

From the river Rhine is Belgic Gaul, named from the city of Belgis. It rises at Mount Jove and reaches the British Ocean towards the north. It is also called Francia after King Francus, who, coming from Troy with Aeneas, founded Troy beside the Rhine and named the land Francia.

To its west lies Lugdunensian Gaul, also called Comata because of its long hair, and Togata because of its long garments. To the south it has Narbonensian Gaul, named from the city of Narbonne; to the west, Aquitaine, named after the waters of the Rhône and Loire.

## CHAPTER XXX.—On Spain.—The river Iberus; the six provinces of Spain.

[Col. 0130B]

Next is Spain, named after King Hispanus; it was formerly called Iberia after the river Iberus, and Hesperia after King Hesperus. Towards the west it is bounded by the Ocean. It has six provinces: Tarraconensis, Carthage, Lusitania, Galicia, Baetica, and Tingitana, named after their principal cities.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—On Britain.—Britain; England; Ireland; the soil of Thanatos, which kills serpents; islands; Orkneys; Scotland; Chile; the frozen sea.

Opposite Spain, westward in the Ocean, are these islands: Britain, England, Ireland, Thanatos, whose soil, carried to any land whatever, kills serpents; the island in which the solstice occurs; the thirty-three Orkneys; Scotland; and Chile, whose trees never shed their leaves and in which there are six months of continuous day—namely, in summer—and six months of continuous night in winter.

[Col. 0130C]

Beyond it, towards the north, is the frozen sea and perpetual cold. We have traversed Europe. Let us pass over to Africa.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—On Africa.—Libya; the city of Paratonium; the Catabachmonian Mountains; the Altars of the Philaeni; Cyrenaica; Cyrene; Pentapolis; Tripolis; Byzacium; Heusis; Carthage; a description of Carthage; Gaetulia; Numidia; Hippo; Mauritania; Stiffia; Caesarea; Tingitana.

Africa is named after Apher, one of the descendants of Abraham. It begins east of the river Indus and, turning southward, stretches westward. Its first province is Libya, named after a queen of the same name. It begins at the city of Paratonium and the Catabachmonian Mountains, and ends at the Altars of the Philaeni.

[Col. 0130D]

The Libyan Sea is named from it. Next is Cyrenaica, named after the city of Cyrene, itself built and named after a queen of that name. It is also called Pentapolis after five cities: namely Berenice, Arsinoë, Ptolemais, Apollonia, and Cyrene, thus named after their respective founders. Next is Tripolis, named after three cities: Occasa, Berete, and Great Leptis. After this is Byzacium, named after two cities, namely Adrumetus and Byzantium.

Then comes Heusis, in which is great Carthage, built by Dido, also called Elissa, and named Carthada after the town of Cartha. But, having been destroyed by the Romans and rebuilt, it was called Carthage. Its wall was seventeen cubits wide. After it is Gaetulia. Then Numidia, in which Jugurtha reigned. In it is the city of Hippo, where Augustine was bishop.

[Col. 0131A]

Next is Mauritania, named from blackness. In it is the province of Stiffensis, named after the town of Stiffi; another, Caesariensis, named after the city of Caesarea; and a third, Tingitana, named after the city of Tingis.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—On Ethiopia.—Saba; the Garamantes; a spring among the Garamantes; the Troglodytes; Gades; the Gaditanian Sea; the Atlantic Sea; where astronomy was set down.

To the south lies Ethiopia, named after Ethan: one Ethiopia is in the East, in which is the city of Saba, whence came that queen who visited Solomon; the other is in the West. Between them are the Garamantes, named after the city of Garama. Among them is a spring so cold by day that it cannot be drunk, and so hot by night that it cannot be touched. To their east dwell the Troglodytes,

[Col. 0131B]

who catch wild beasts by swift running. Within Ethiopia are vast desert places because of the heat of the sun, and serpents of diverse kinds unknown to humankind. Then comes the greatest Ocean, said to boil like a cauldron from the heat of the sun.

At Africa’s farthest western bounds is the city of Gades, built by the Phoenicians, from which the Gaditanian Sea takes its name. In the Ocean itself is the very high Mount Atlas, from which the Atlantic Sea is named. Atlas was a king of Africa, brother of Prometheus. The mountain took its name from him because, sitting upon it, he set down astronomy; hence he is said to support the heavens. Having traversed the bounds of Africa, let us approach the islands of the sea.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—On the islands, and on the “new world,” as they say.—Cyprus; Paphos; Crete; the Adriatic Sea; Abydos; the Hellespont; Cos; the Cyclades; Rhodes; the brazen Colossus, seventy cubits high; Tenedos; Carpathos; the Carpathian Sea; Cythera; Delos; where quails were first seen; Icaria; Naxos; Melos; Paros; Parian marble; the Sardian stone; Cydon; Samos; where earthenware vessels were discovered.

[Col. 0131C]

Islands are so called as though “placed in the salt sea” (*in salo sitae*). In the Mediterranean Sea is the island of Cyprus, opposite Syria, named after the city of Cyprus. It is also called Paphos after a city of the same name. Crete is named after King Cretus; it is also called Centapolis, after its hundred cities. It lies opposite the Libyan Sea, which is also called the Adriatic after the city of Adria.

Abydos is an island in the Hellespont, in Europe. The Hellespont is named after the city of Helle. Cos is an island of Atrica (the reading is uncertain). The Cyclades are so called because they are arranged in a circle; for *kyklos* means “circle.” There are fifty-four of them, situated opposite Asia.

[Col. 0131D]

The first of these is Rhodes, named after the city of the same name and situated in the east. In it formerly stood the brazen Colossus, seventy cubits high. Tenedos lies to its north, named after the city of Tene and its founder of the same name. Carpathos lies to its south, opposite Egypt; hence the Carpathian Sea and Carpathian ships. Cythera lies to the west, named after Mount Cithera. It is also called Porphyris.

Delos lies in the middle of the Cyclades and is named after a city of the same name. It first appeared at the time of the Ogygian Flood, and therefore took the name Delos, since *dēlos* means “manifest.” It is also called Ortygia, after the *ortygometes*, that is, quails,

[Col. 0132A]
