which were first seen there. Icaria is named after a shipwrecked Cretan boy; the Icarian Sea is named from it. Naxos is the island of Dionysus, also called Bacchus. Melos, also called Storia, is a round island. Paros is named after the city of the same name, built by Paros, grandson of Jason. It produces very white marble, called Parian, and the Sardian stone. Cydon is an island; mastic grows there. Samos, named after the city of Samos, lies in the Aegean Sea. From it came the Sibyl and Pythagoras. Earthenware vessels were discovered there.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—On Sicily.—Called Trinacria from its three mountains; Mount Etna; Scylla; Charybdis; where comedy was invented; the Vulcanian Islands; the Stoechades.

Sicily is named after King Siculus. [It is] called Italy. Formerly it was called Sicania after King Sicanus, and lies opposite Italy.

[Col. 0132B]

It is also called Trinacria after its three mountains. In it is Mount Etna, whose sulphurous fires boil up. In its strait are Scylla and Charybdis. The Cyclopes formerly lived there. Comedy was invented there. The Aeolian Islands, named after King Aeolus, lie near Sicily. They are also called the Vulcanian Islands because they are full of fire. There are nine Stoechades Islands situated opposite Massilia.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—On Sardinia.—Hot springs that inflict blindness on thieves; Corsica; Cyrene; Ebusus; Colubria; the Balearic Islands; where slings were invented; the Gorgons’ Islands; the Hesperides; golden apples; the congealed sea; Meroë; Syene; the Lost Island.

Sardinia, named after Sardus, son of Hercules, lies opposite Numidia. Neither serpents nor wolves are produced there.

[Col. 0132C]

There is there a “sun-fleeing” creature (*solifuga*), like a spider, which kills people by its bite. There is also an herb resembling parsley, which contracts the mouths of those who eat it and kills them as though laughing. There are hot springs which bring healing to the sick but blindness to thieves.

Corsica, named after a woman named Corsa, lies opposite Liguria. She first came there seeking her bull; reporting the fertility of the place, she caused it to begin to be inhabited by Ligurians. It is also called Cyrene after Cyrinus, son of Hercules, because he inhabited it. Ebusus is an island opposite Spain; serpents flee from it. There is also Colubria, full of serpents. There too are the Balearic Islands, where slings were invented.

The Gorgons’ Islands are in the Ocean near Atlas. The Gorgons formerly dwelt in them.

[Col. 0132D]

Near them are the Hesperides, named after the city of Hesperia. In them sheep with white fleeces abounded, excellent for making purple dye. Hence they are said in fable to have possessed golden apples; for *mēlon* means “sheep” in Greek. Among them was that great island which, Plato writes, was submerged with its people; in size it surpassed Africa and Europe, and where it was is now the Congealed Sea.

Meroë is an island in the river Nile, at the head of Ethiopia, where one’s shadow vanishes in summer. In it is ebony wood. Near it is the city of Syene, where there is a well made by philosophers, sixty cubits deep; at its bottom the sun shines with a direct ray in June. There is an island in the Ocean called the Lost Island, surpassing all lands by far in the pleasantness and fertility of every kind of thing, unknown to humankind.

[Col. 0133A]

Having once been discovered by chance, it was afterwards sought but not found, and is therefore called the Lost Island. Brendan is said to have come there.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—On hell.—We have gone around the islands; now let us seek the lower regions also. On the names of hell.—Acheron; Styx; Phlegethon.

Hell is called *infernus* because it is situated below. For just as the earth is in the middle of the air, so hell is in the middle of the earth. Hence it is also called the lowest part of the earth. It is a place dreadful with fire and sulphur, broad below and narrow above. It is called the lake or land of death because souls descending there truly die. It is also called the lake of fire because souls are submerged in it as a stone in the sea. It is called the land of darkness because it is obscured by smoke and a cloud of stench.

[Col. 0133B]

It is called the land of forgetfulness because, just as they themselves forgot God, so God forgets to show them mercy. It is called Tartarus from horror and trembling, because there are weeping and gnashing of teeth there (Matt. 8). It is also called Gehenna, that is, “land of fire.” For *gē* means “earth,” and our fire is said to be a shadow of its fire. Its depth and recess is called Erebus, full of dragons and fiery worms. It is called the gaping mouth and the abyss, as if a black chasm. Its places exhaling stench are called Acheronta, that is, vents emitting unclean spirits. There is Styx, which in Greek means “sadness.” It is also called Phlegethon, the infernal river, dreadful in stench and heat because of the nearness of fire and sulphur.

There are many other places as well, whether punitive places in islands, fiercely cold with frost and wind, or continually boiling with fire and sulphur.

[Col. 0133C]

We have examined the fiery places of hell; let us flee to the refreshment of waters.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—On water.

Water, placed as the second element, is named from equality, whence also *aequor*, “a level expanse.” It is gathered in the sea, distributed into rivers, divided into springs, joined through streams, scattered over lands, and thinned through the air. It surrounds the whole earth and separates all regions and provinces. Its immeasurable depth is called the abyss, as though it has no bottom; yet it has a bottom, although an exceedingly deep one.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—On the Ocean.

[Col. 0133D]

Ocean is called as though “swifter than the years” (*ocior annis*), or as though the border of the zones. For it surrounds the five zones of the world like a border.

## CHAPTER XL.—On the sea’s tide.

The Ocean’s tide—that is, its advance and retreat—follows the moon: by the moon’s drawing it is pulled back, and by its impulse it is poured forth again. It appears to flow in and return twice every day. It rises when the moon waxes and falls when it wanes. When the moon is at the equinox, greater waves of the Ocean arise because of the moon’s nearness; when it is at the solstice, smaller waves arise because of its distance. In nineteen years it returns, like the moon, to the beginnings of its motion and to equal increases.

## CHAPTER XLI.—On the whirlpool.—How a whirlpool occurs.

[Col. 0134A]

The *ampotis*, that is, a whirlpool, likewise in the Ocean at the rising of the moon, with a greater tide, rolls up and spews back the waves. This whirlpool, which swallows and disgorges whole waters and ships, arises thus: there is in the earth a very deep abyss, of which it is written, “All the fountains of the great deep were broken up” (Gen. 7). Beside it are hollow places and widely open caverns. In these, winds are conceived from the exhalation of the waters, and they are called the spirits of storms. By their breath they draw the sea’s waters through the open caverns of the earth into the abysses, and, when overflowing, drive them back again with great force.

## CHAPTER XLII.—On earthquakes.—How earthquakes occur.

[Col. 0134B]

Earthquakes also arise from these winds. For when winds enclosed in hollow places strive to burst out, they shake the earth with dreadful roaring and make it tremble.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—On fissures.—The cause of fissures in the earth; what an earthquake is and what a fissure is; why Sicily vomits flames and casts forth sand and stones; the origin of the barking of Scylla’s dogs.

Fissures in the earth also arise from this cause: hollow places, chilled by continual waters, are broken apart by confined winds and, falling inward, open into a chasm. We read that many cities have been swallowed by such fissures. What thunder is in a cloud, earthquake is in the earth; what lightning is there, a fissure is here. Floods of the sea occur with earthquakes, when the same breath has been poured in or received into a receding hollow.

[Col. 0134C]

Thus the land of Sicily, because it is cavernous and layered with sulphur and bitumen, lies almost wholly open to winds and fires. As the breath within contends with fire, it often belches forth smoke, vapours, or flames in many places; or, when the wind presses more fiercely, it ejects masses of sand or stones. Thus, after the example of Mount Etna, the fire of Gehenna endures so long a burning, said to be nourished by the waters of the Aeolian Islands: the rush of waters drags the breath down with it to the lowest depth and smothers it until, spreading through the veins of the earth, it kindles the fuel of fire. Scylla’s dogs are fabled to bark when sailors at a distance are terrified by the roaring of waves, which the tide dashes together as the whirlpool swallows them.

[Col. 0134D]

For a similar reason fire also rises in other lands and foreshadows Gehenna.

## CHAPTER XLIV.—On cold.—Why the outer parts of the Ocean are bleak with perpetual cold.

As heat arises from fire, so cold arises from water. Hence the outer parts of the Ocean are bleak with hard frost and perpetual cold because they lack the sun’s heat. But that part of the Ocean which divides the middle of the world continually boils with heat because the sun is constantly above it.

## CHAPTER XLV.—On fresh and salt waters.

The Ocean is not increased by the meeting of rivers, because fresh streams are partly consumed by the salt shallows or carried away by winds or the sun’s vapour; partly they return through hidden channels to their own rivers. Therefore, although watered by so many rivers and rains, it remains salt, because, when the sun has drawn off the sweet, thin liquid—which the force of fire more readily attracts—all the harsher and thicker substance remains.

[Col. 0135A]

Therefore the surface wave of the sea is fresher, and its depths more bitter. The moon’s nourishment is in fresh waters, but the sun’s is in bitter waters.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—On the Red Sea.—The origin of the name sea.

The Red Sea flows out of the Ocean, but draws its rosy colour from the land, which is altogether red with a blood-like colour and stains the nearby shores. A sea (*mare*) is so called because it is bitter (*amarum*). It runs through the veins of the earth by a hidden channel, deposits bitterness in the earth, and bursts forth sweet in springs. Finally it flows back into itself, as it is written: “To the place from which the rivers come, they return, that they may flow again. All rivers enter the sea.”

## CHAPTER XLVII.—On the twofold nature of water.—Why the sea does not overflow; why springs are cold in summer but warm in winter.

Water is nevertheless said to be twofold in nature, namely salt and fresh. The salt water of the sea is heavier; the fresh water of springs and rivers is lighter. Since it is read that the Lord brought forth a spring in Paradise and, dividing it into four rivers, commanded it to water the whole earth in the four quarters of the world, it is said that the outflow of all springs and rivers of fresh water proceeds from that spring or those rivers and flows back to the mother abyss of the same spring.

[Col. 0135B]

Although all this water enters the sea, it does not mix with the bitter waters. Rather, being light, it glides over the heavy waters and returns to its hidden course. This is why the sea does not overflow though all rivers enter it. Thus the uppermost wave of the sea is not as bitter as that which lies in its depth.

The reason springs are warm in winter and cold in summer is this: in summer the heat of the air drives cold into the earth, and thus water becomes cold; in winter the cold of the air drives heat into the earth, and thus water becomes warm.

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—On hot water.

Since all water is either fresh or salt, we must consider how some water bursts forth hot or foul-smelling. There are certain subterranean caverns naturally full of sulphur. When wind is generated in them, its blast sets the sulphur alight; certain places also belch forth this fire, as happens in Sicily.

[Col. 0135D]

When water runs through these fiery places, it draws heat and stench from them. If it bursts forth near that place, it boils, vomiting flame; but if it has travelled farther away, it is scarcely warm, and then becomes wholly cold.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—On deadly waters.

There are other places full of serpents, which infect their surroundings with poison. When this rises from the earth, it kills those who drink it, as the spring Styx does.

## CHAPTER L.—On the Dead Sea.—The nature of bitumen.

That the water of the Dead Sea is not moved by winds and permits nothing living in itself results from springs of bitumen, by which the tower of Babel was built. The nature of bitumen resists water and cannot be divided except by menstrual blood.

## CHAPTER LI.—On animals of the waters.—Why birds fly in the air; amphibious creatures.

[Col. 0136A]

Fish and birds dwell in waters because we read that they were made from them. Birds fly in the air and live on land because air is moist like water, and earth is mixed with water. Certain animals created from earth, however, can dwell in waters—such as crocodiles and hippopotamuses—because water is greatly mixed with earth.

## CHAPTER LII.—On predictive signs at sea.

When, during a night voyage, the oars sparkle, there will be a storm. And when dolphins leap more frequently from the waves, the wind will rise from the direction in which they are travelling, and clouds shaken from the waves will open the sky in that direction.

Let us rise from the depths of the waters and suspend the pen of writing in the air.

## CHAPTER LIII.—On air.—Demons dwell in the air.

Air is everything resembling emptiness which is seen from the earth up to the moon, from which the breath of life is drawn. Because it is moist, birds fly in it as fish swim in water. Demons dwell in it, awaiting with torment the day of judgment. From it they take bodies for themselves when they appear to human beings.

## CHAPTER LIV.—On winds.—What is wind?

Winds are generated from it. A wind is air set in motion and stirred. It is nothing other than a wave of air, divided into twelve, each receiving its own name; of these, four are cardinal and the others adjacent to them.

## CHAPTER LV.—On the cardinal winds.—North; east wind; south wind; why southern winds produce greater storms; breeze; Altanus.

[Col. 0136C]

The first cardinal wind is the North, also called Aparctias, producing cold and clouds. On its right is Circius, also called Thracius, producing snow and hail. On its left is Aquilo, also called Boreas, binding the clouds.

The second cardinal wind is the East Wind, also called Apeliotes, temperate. On its right is Vulturnus, also called Calcias, drying everything. On its left is Eurus, producing clouds.

The third cardinal wind is the South, also called Notus, producing moisture, heat, and lightning. On its right is Euroauster, warm; on its left, Euronotus, temperate. Southern winds make greater storms,

[Col. 0136D]

because they blow from low places over the sea.

The fourth cardinal wind is Zephyrus, also called Favonius, loosening winter and bringing forth flowers. On its right is Africus, also called Lybs, producing storms, thunder, and lightning. On its left is Corus, also called Argestes, producing cloudy weather in the east and clear weather in India.

Besides these are two winds: Aura, on land, and Altanus, at sea.

## CHAPTER LVI.—On clouds.—How clouds arise; the origin of the name clouds.

Winds by their breath draw waters into the air; gathered together, they condense into clouds. Clouds (*nubes*) are so called as though “ships of storms” (*nimborum naves*). When winds shut within them strive to burst out, they crash with a great roar,

[Col. 0137A]

and, when the clouds collide, strike out terrible fire.

## CHAPTER LVII.—On thunder and lightning.

Thus thunder is the sound of clouds and winds. The fire struck out from them is lightning; and this fire penetrates whatever it touches because it is subtler than our fire and is driven by the great force of winds. Lightning from the North and thunder from the East portend a storm; a blast from the South portends heat.

## CHAPTER LVIII.—On the rainbow.—How the rainbow occurs.

A four-coloured bow is formed in the air from sun and clouds when a ray of sunlight, admitted into a hollow cloud, is reflected back and refracted toward the sun. It is as when the sun shines into a vessel full of water and its brightness is cast upon the ceiling. From heaven it draws a fiery colour; from water, purple; from air, hyacinth-blue; and from earth, a grass-green colour.

## CHAPTER LIX.—On rain.—How rain occurs; rain and cloudburst.

Rain falls from clouds. When small drops gather into larger drops, and the nature of the air can no longer bear them—while wind does not drive them and the sun does not dissolve them—they fall to earth.

[Col. 0137B]

A slow and continuous falling is called rain (*pluvia*); a sudden and headlong descent from clouds is called a cloudburst (*nimbus*). Although it has been drawn from the bitter waters of the sea, it is made fresh by being boiled in the air by the sun’s fire, just as sea water poured upon soil acquires a sweet taste.

## CHAPTER LX.—On hail.—The formation of hail.

[Col. 0137C]

Drops of rain frozen in the air by winds and cold congeal and are changed into little stones of hail.

## CHAPTER LXI.—On snow.—How snow occurs.

Snow is formed from the vapour of water not yet condensed into drops, when frost intervenes first. It does not fall on the high sea.

## CHAPTER LXII.—On dew.—The source of dew; hoarfrost.

Dew comes from the air when, weighted with water, it drips under the coldness of night and the moon’s brightness. If the night’s cold is more severe, dew whitens into hoarfrost.

## CHAPTER LXIII.—On mist.—How mist occurs.

Mist arises when moist exhalations are drawn vaporously into the air or driven down to earth by the rays of the sun.

## CHAPTER LXIV.—On smoke.—What dissolution of wood occurs in fire; why smoke is bitter.

[Col. 0137D]

Smoke also rises from water. Every body consists of four elements. Wood is a body which, thrown into fire, burns through the fiery material contained within it. Its earthy material is burned into ash. Its airy and watery material vanishes into the air through smoke.

It is bitter either because water’s nature is salt or because it is mixed with earth.

## CHAPTER LXV.—On sparks.

What are seen at night as falling stars are not stars, but sparks drawn by the blowing winds from the ether into the air and immediately extinguished in the moist air.

## CHAPTER LXVI.—On pestilence.—How and where pestilence of the air arises; the origin of the name fire.

[Col. 0138A]

Pestilence arises when air is corrupted by dryness, heat, or storm; taken in through breathing or eating, it produces disease and death. All that I have described occurs below the moon in the air; above, it is always clear.

## CHAPTER LXVII.—On fire.—The bodies of angels are fiery.

Fire is written as the fourth element, as though it were called “not begetting” (*non gignis*). It extends from the moon to the firmament. It is as much subtler than air as air is thinner than water, and water more rarefied than earth. It is also called ether, as though “pure air,” and rejoices in perpetual brightness. From it angels take bodies when they come

[Col. 0138B]

sent to human beings.

## CHAPTER LXVIII.—On the planets.—Why they are called planets; the irregular motion of the planets.

In it seven stars are carried in separate circles contrary to the world; because of their wandering course, they are called planets—that is, “wandering stars.” By the immense speed of the firmament they are swept from east to west; yet finally they are shown to travel by their natural course contrary to the world, just as a fly, if carried round in a mill-wheel, would nevertheless seem by its own motion to move against its revolution. Wandering neither lower nor higher because of the obliquity of the zodiac, and impeded by the rays of the sun, they become irregular, retrograde, or stationary.

## CHAPTER LXIX.—On the moon.—Why the moon has no light of its own; the origin of the cloudlet in the moon; the moon’s proper motion; predictive weather signs in the moon.

[Col. 0138C]

The Moon is the first of the planets and the smallest of the stars. Yet it appears larger than the rest because it is carried nearest to the earth, in the first circle. Its body is spherical, fiery by nature, but mingled with water; hence it has no light of its own. Rather, like a mirror, it is illuminated by the sun. And therefore it is called *luna*, as though *lucina*, that is, “born from light.” What appears in it like a little cloud is believed to arise from the nature of water. For it is said that, if water were not mingled with it, it would illuminate the earth like the sun—indeed, owing to its proximity, it would lay it waste with the greatest heat. For its globe is much larger than the earth, although, because of the height of its circle, it can scarcely be seen as larger than the bottom of a measure. The moon shines on that side which faces the sun; [Col. 0138D] it is dark on the side turned away from the sun. Although, when farther removed from the sun, it is wholly [illuminated], nevertheless it waxes and does not wane; rather, by the interposition of the earth, it is deprived of the light which it receives from the sun. Although it is daily carried from east to west by the force of the firmament, yet, striving against the world, it traverses all the signs of the zodiac in twenty-seven days. It is said to complete its own circuit in nineteen years. If the moon on its fourth day is red like gold, it will indicate winds; if blackened by spots on the upper horn, a rainy beginning of the month; if in the middle, a clear full moon.

## CHAPTER LXX.—On Mercury.—Its motion.

The second planet is Mercury, also called Stilbon: spherical in shape, fiery in nature; surpassing the moon in size, receiving light from the sun, and traversing the zodiac in three hundred and thirty-nine days. [Col. 0139A]

## CHAPTER LXXI.—On Venus.—Its motion.

The third planet is Venus, son of Aurora and Zephalus; it is also called Hesperus, Lucifer, and Vesper. It is round, fiery, and, striving against the world, like Mercury traverses the zodiac in three hundred and forty-eight days.

## CHAPTER LXXII.—On the sun.—Why the sun is so called. The size and motion of the sun. Why days are longer in summer and shorter in winter.

The fourth planet is the sun, or Phoebus, so called either because it alone shines while the other stars are darkened, or because it is shining above all things. It is spherical in shape, fiery in nature, eight times greater than the earth in size, and supplies light to all the stars. It is carried from east to west [Col. 0139B] by the force of the firmament; but striving against the world, it moves through the entire zodiac in three hundred and sixty-five days. It is believed to complete its own circuit in twenty-eight years. Its presence produces day, and its absence night. For just as it shines above the earth throughout the day, so throughout the night it shines beneath the earth. Traversing the northern region of heaven, it makes our days long and brings summer; traversing the southern region, it brings us short days and winter.

## CHAPTER LXXIII.—On prognostic signs from the sun.

If the sun is spotted at its rising, or hidden beneath a cloud, it foretells a rainy day; if pale, a stormy one; if it seems hollow, so that, shining in the middle, it sends out rays to south and north, [it foretells] wet and windy weather; if it sets pale into black clouds, a north wind.

## CHAPTER LXXIV.—On Mars.—Its motion.

The fifth planet is Mars, also called Pyrois: spherical and glowing with fire. It traverses the zodiac in two years. [Col. 0139C]

## CHAPTER LXXV.—On Jupiter.

The sixth planet is Jupiter: round, temperate, traversing the zodiac in twelve years.

## CHAPTER LXXVI.—On Saturn.—Its motion.

The seventh planet is Saturn, also called Phaethon, son of the Sun. At its rising, after thirty years, whoever has cast an image from bronze will prove it to speak like a real human being. Spherical and cold, it moves against the higher world and traverses the zodiac in thirty years. [Col. 0139D] All of them, however, complete their circuits after five hundred and thirty-two years and repeat the same [courses] as before.

## CHAPTER LXXVII.—On the apsides of the planets.

From the centre of the earth, the apsides [ἀψίδες], that is, the circles of the planets, are at their highest: Saturn in Scorpio, Jupiter in Virgo, Mars in Leo, the sun in Gemini, Venus in Sagittarius, Mercury in Capricorn, and the moon in Aries; [they are] at the middle points of all their courses, and conversely at their lowest and nearest to the centre of the earth.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII.—On the colours of the planets.

Each has its own colour: Saturn white; Jupiter bright; Mars fiery; Lucifer glowing white; Vesper gleaming; Mercury radiant; the moon gentle; the sun burning. They change colour, however, because of neighbouring circles: [Col. 0140A] the colder into paleness, the hotter into redness, the windy into a dreadful aspect, and [those distant] from the earth into darkness.

## CHAPTER LXXIX.—On the path of the planets.

The zodiac, that is, the circle of the twelve signs, is divided throughout into twelve parts; beneath these the seven planets are borne. The sun [moves] only beneath the middle two; the moon through its entire breadth; Venus exceeding it by two parts; Mercury through eight parts—two in the middle, four above, two below; Mars through four in the middle; Jupiter beneath the middle [part] and two above it; Saturn beneath the two middle [parts], like the sun.

## CHAPTER LXXX.—On the sound of the planets.—Why the sound of the planets is not heard by us. Music.

These seven spheres revolve with sweet-sounding harmony, and their revolution produces most pleasing concords. [Col. 0140B] This sound does not reach our ears because it occurs beyond the air, and its magnitude exceeds our narrow hearing. For no sound is perceived by us except that which is produced in this air. From the earth to the firmament heavenly music is measured, after whose example our own music is said to have been invented.

## CHAPTER LXXXI.—On celestial music.—The proportions of the planets. Why philosophers invented the nine Muses.

For if, on earth, A is placed at the moon, B at Mercury, C at Venus, D at the sun, E at Mars, F at Jupiter, and G at Saturn, the measure of music is certainly found; whence from the earth to the firmament seven tones are discovered. From the earth to the moon is one tone; from the moon to Mercury, a semitone; from Mercury to Venus, a semitone; thence to the sun, [Col. 0140C] three semitones. From the sun to Mars, one tone; thence to Jupiter, a semitone; thence to Saturn, a semitone; thence to the zodiac, three semitones. Taken together, these make seven tones. A tone contains fifteen thousand six hundred and twenty-five miles. A semitone, however, contains seven thousand eight hundred and twelve and a half miles. Hence philosophers invented nine Muses, because from earth to heaven they discern nine consonances, which they found naturally implanted in human beings.

## CHAPTER LXXXII.—On the human being as microcosm.

For just as this world is distinguished by seven tones, and our music by seven notes, so the fabric of our body is joined together in seven ways, since the body is coupled with four elements and the soul with three powers; these are naturally harmonized by the art of music. Hence the human being is called *μικρόκοσμος* (*microcosmos*), that is, “the lesser world,” since he is known to correspond, in such a harmonious number, to celestial music. [Col. 0140D]

## CHAPTER LXXXIII.—On measure, or the distances of the planets.

From the earth to the moon are twelve thousand six hundred stadia, which are fifteen thousand six hundred and twenty-five miles. From the moon to Mercury are seven thousand eight hundred and twelve and a half miles; thence to Venus, the same distance. Thence to the sun are twenty-three thousand four hundred and thirty-seven and a half miles. From the sun to Mars are fifteen thousand six hundred and thirty miles. To Jupiter are seven [Col. 0141A] thousand eight hundred and twelve and a half miles. Thence to Saturn, the same distance. Thence to the firmament are twenty-three thousand four hundred and thirty-seven and a half miles.

Thus from earth to heaven there are one hundred and nine thousand three hundred and seventy-five miles.

We have passed beyond fire through the spheres of the planets; now let us penetrate the heavenly things.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV.—On heaven.—Why heaven is so called. Prognostics of weather from the appearance of heaven.

Heaven is called, as though *casa ilios* [κάσας ἡλίου], that is, “house of the sun”; or like an engraved vessel, because it is marked with stars. Heaven is of a subtle and fiery nature, round, and set everywhere at equal distances from the centre of the earth. [Col. 0141B] Hence it is seen as convex and central on every side, and is whirled about daily with indescribable speed.

If heaven is red in the evening, [it signifies] a clear day.

If in the morning, it signifies stormy weather.

There are two gates of heaven: the east, through which the sun comes out;

the west, through which the sun enters.

## CHAPTER LXXXV.—On climates.

Climates, that is, regions of heaven, are four:

the eastern, from sunrise;

the solstitial, to the winter [point];

the southern, thence to the winter sunset;

the western, from there to the solstitial [point];

the northern, from the solstitial sunset to the corresponding sunrise.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI.—On the quarters.—Adam’s name is composed from the four quarters of the world: ΑΔΑΜ.

[Col. 0141C]

The east is named from the rising of the sun;

the west from its setting;

the south is called, as it were, *medidies*, “middle day.”

But the north is named from seven stars. A bull is called *trion*, as though *terion*; hence *septentriones*, as though “seven *teriones*,” that is, oxen. These quarters are called in Greek ἀνατολή, δύσις, ἄρκτος, μεσημβρία: “rising,” “setting,” “north,” and “midday.” From them is formed the name Adam, who is the lesser world.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII.—On the firmament.

The upper heaven is called the firmament because it is a firmament between the waters. It too is spherical in form, watery in nature, and adorned on every side with stars. [Col. 0141D] It is formed from waters, solidified like ice in the manner of crystal; hence it is called the firmament.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII.—On the axis.

In it are two poles, so called from polishing: one northern, because it is always visible to us; the other southern, which is never seen by us, because, set on the slope of the globe, we are obstructed by the swelling of the earth. Upon these heaven revolves like a wheel on an axle.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX.—On the stars.—Why stars do not appear in daytime. Why they are called stars. The distinction between *stella*, *sidus*, and *astrum*.

Heaven is everywhere starred; but they do not appear during the day because, overcome by the brilliance of the sun, they lie hidden, just as the sun, covered by a cloud, does not shine. A *stella* is, as it were, a standing moon. [Col. 0142A] For the stars stand fixed in the firmament and do not fall, though it runs with wonderful speed. One is called a *stella*; many together, an *astrum* or *sidus*.

## CHAPTER XC.—On constellations.—Why *sidus* is so called.

Constellations are called *sidera* from observation, because sailors and travellers observe them.

All stars are round and fiery; their arrangement is known to God alone, who numbers the stars and alone knows their names, signs, powers, courses, places, and times. But the wise people of the world assigned them names of animals or human beings, so that they might be recognized by people.

## CHAPTER XCI.—On the zodiac.—Why it is so called.

In the middle of the firmament are twelve signs arranged crosswise and equally marked out around the circuit. [Col. 0142B] Their arrangement is called in Greek *zodiacus*, in Latin *signifer*, because it bears signs having the names of animals. For ζῷον means “animal.”

## CHAPTER XCII.—On Aries.—Why a ram is used as a sign.

The first sign of the zodiac is Aries, consisting of several stars. According to the story, it was the ram that carried Phrixus and Helle across the sea to Colchis on its golden fleece, and for this reason was transferred among the constellations. It is used as a sign because, just as a ram lies throughout summer on its right side and throughout winter on its left, so the sun, moving beneath that sign, traverses the right-hand part of heaven.

## CHAPTER XCIII.—On Taurus.

The second sign is Taurus, because Jupiter, in the rape of Europa, changed himself into a bull and was transferred among the constellations. [Col. 0142C] Its significance is that the sun, placed beneath that sign, thrusts forth its rays more forcefully like horns and makes the earth fit for ploughing.

## CHAPTER XCIV.—On Gemini.

The third are the Twins, namely Castor and Pollux, sons of Jupiter, transferred among the constellations after their return from Troy. They are used as a sign because the sun remains beneath this sign for two days longer than beneath the others.

## CHAPTER XCV.—On Cancer.

The fourth is Cancer, which struck the mighty Hercules while he was killing the Nereid Hydra [read: the Lernaean Hydra], and therefore earned a place among the constellations. It signifies that, just as a crab moves backward, so the sun, on coming to this sign, bends its course back.

## CHAPTER XCVI.—On Leo.

[Col. 0142D] The fifth is Leo, the mighty lion slain by Hercules and transferred among the constellations. It indicates that, just as a lion is of hot nature in its forepart and cold in its hind part, so the sun in that sign makes the month of August hot at first and cold at its end.

## CHAPTER XCVII.—On Virgo.

The sixth is Virgo, namely Erigone, daughter of Icarius the priest, snatched up among the stars. It is used as a sign because, just as a virgin does not bear children, so September, the month of that sign, produces nothing.

## CHAPTER XCVIII.—On Libra.

The seventh is the balance held by Virgo, namely Blance, or Justice, daughter of King Astraeus, called Justice because of her fairness and transferred among the constellations. [Col. 0143A] She weighs the merits of human beings and presents them to Jupiter in the balance. She is placed above the preceding Virgin. It signifies that the sun produces the equinox when it passes beneath that sign.

## CHAPTER XCIX.—On Scorpio.

The eighth is Scorpio, which struck the mighty Orion while he was killing the beasts of the earth, and, by favour of the earth, earned the stars. It is used as a sign of hail because in that month, namely November, hail occurs more frequently in certain lands.

## CHAPTER C.—On Sagittarius.

The ninth is Sagittarius, also the Archer, namely Aleon of Crete, who shot the scorpion that had carried off his son and did not strike his son; for this reason he earned the stars. It indicates the frequent strokes of lightning that [Col. 0143B] occur in December in certain places. Its lack of lower limbs signifies that then the sun seeks the lower regions.

## CHAPTER CI.—On Capricorn.

The tenth is Capricorn: a she-goat secretly nourished the infant Jupiter, cast out by his father; Jupiter later transferred her among the constellations. Its meaning is that, just as a goat seeks the heights, so at that season the sun climbs to the heights of heaven. The fact that its extremity ends in a fish indicates that the end of that month is rainy.

## CHAPTER CII.—On Aquarius.

The eleventh is Aquarius, namely Ganymede, son of King Troilus, Jupiter’s beloved, placed by him among the stars and made cupbearer of the gods. It signifies that, [Col. 0143C] when the snows have melted, that season is watery.

## CHAPTER CIII.—On Pisces.

The twelfth are the Fishes. When the gods fled the giant Typhoeus into Egypt, Venus and her son Cupid, changed into fishes, hid in the waters. Since people for a long time avoided fish lest perhaps they should devour the gods, those two were transferred among the constellations. It signifies, indeed, that the season is rainy.

## CHAPTER CIV.—Hyades.

The Hyades are called rainy ones. For ὕα in Greek means “rain”; hence in Latin they are called *suculae*, “little sows,” from *sucus*. They are seven stars in the forehead of Taurus.

## CHAPTER CV.—Pleiades.

The Pleiades are so called as though “the many.” For *plion* means “more.” [Col. 0143D] They are seven stars in the knee of Taurus. They were the daughters of King Atlas and Plaia. Thus from their father [they are called] Atlantides; from their mother, Pleiades, as though Plaeades; from the island, Hesperides. They are also called Vergiliae because they rise in the springtime. One of them was Maia, mother of Mercury.

## CHAPTER CVI.—Arctos.

To the right of the zodiac, toward the north, are these signs: next to the axis, Arctos, namely the Wain, which constellation is also called the Septentrion and Helice. Its stars are said to be larger than the sun. Callisto, daughter of King Lycaon, was violated by Jupiter, but changed by Juno into a bear. Then Jupiter carried her away again among the stars.

## CHAPTER CVII.—Bootes.

[Col. 0144A]

There follows the constellation Boötes, that is, “guardian of the Wain,” also called Arctophylax. He was the son of Callisto and was placed among the stars by Jupiter.

## CHAPTER CVIII.—Arcturus.

Then is Arcturus, namely the Wain, also called Cynosura. She too was violated by Jupiter, changed by Juno into a bear, and transferred by Jupiter among the stars.

## CHAPTER CIX.—Python.

Between the two Wains is the enormous serpent Python, sent against Latona by Juno, which Apollo slew after the Flood; because of his outstanding bravery, he transferred it among the stars.

## CHAPTER CX.—Corona.

[Col. 0144B] Nearby is the crown, made by Vulcan, given by Bacchus to Ariadne, daughter of Minos and Pasiphaë, and placed among the stars.

## CHAPTER CXI.—Hercules.

Next is the constellation Hercules. When the giants fought against the gods and the gods came together into one part of heaven, heaven threatened to fall. But Hercules supported it with Atlas; therefore he earned heaven.

## CHAPTER CXII.—Lyra.

Near this is the lyre, invented by Mercury.

## CHAPTER CXIII.—Cygnus.

Near it is the swan: Jupiter, for love of Queen Leda, changed into a swan and was carried among the stars.

## CHAPTER CXIV.—Cepheus.

Joined to this are King Cepheus and his wife Cassiopeia. [Col. 0144C]

## CHAPTER CXV.—Perseus.

Associated with him is Perseus, son of Jupiter and Danaë, having beside him the constellation of his wife Andromeda, daughter of King Cepheus.

## CHAPTER CXVI.—Deltoton.

Among them is Deltoton, also called the Triangle, namely in the shape of Egypt, because it saved the gods from the face of Typhoeus.

## CHAPTER CXVII.—Serpentarius.

Near it is placed Serpentarius, namely Erichthonius, also called the Charioteer, who first yoked a four-horse chariot because he had serpentine feet. Hence he is also called in Greek Ophiuchus: ὄφις means “serpent.”

## CHAPTER CXVIII.—Pegasus.

[Col. 0144D]

Near this is placed Pegasus, namely the winged and horned horse, having fiery breath and iron feet, created from the blood of the Gorgon.

## CHAPTER CXIX.—Delphinus.

Joined to it is Delphinus, which brought Amphitrite to Neptune in marriage and for that reason earned the stars.

## CHAPTER CXX.—Aquila.

Then is Aquila: Jupiter, changed into an eagle, carried off Ganymede, whom he transferred among the stars.

## CHAPTER CXXI.—Sagitta.

Below this is the arrow, given by Hercules to Philoctetes, by means of which Troy was conquered.

[Col. 0145A] To the left of the zodiac, toward the south, are these signs.

## CHAPTER CXXII.—Hydra.

Hydra, which had fifty heads, slain by Hercules and transferred among the stars because of its distinction.

## CHAPTER CXXIII.—Crater.

Above it is the bowl, in which Tagaton—that is, the highest God—mixed the food from which he made souls, and from which souls still drink the cup of Lethe when bodies perish.

## CHAPTER CXXIV.—Corvus.

Above it is the raven, beloved by Apollo and carried among the stars.

## CHAPTER CXXV.—Orion.

Next is Orion, who was born from urine and transferred among the stars. [Col. 0145B] If his stars shine, the weather will be clear; if they grow dim, there will be a storm.

## CHAPTER CXXVI.—Procyon.

Near him is Procyon Anicani, also called Anticanis, said to be Orion’s dog and placed among the stars because of its distinguished death.

## CHAPTER CXXVII.—Canicula.

Connected with this is Canicula, also called Sirius; from it the dog days take their name. It was the dog of Erigone, daughter of Icarius the priest. Grieving for her murdered father, she hanged herself with a noose when, led by the dog, she found him. Both were carried among the stars.

## CHAPTER CXXVIII.—Lepus.

Then is the hare, chased by Ganymede and transferred among the stars by Jupiter.

## CHAPTER CXXIX.—Eridanus.

[Col. 0145C]

There follows the river Eridanus, also called the Po. Phaethon, son of Phoebus, unable to guide his father’s chariot, set the world on fire and therefore perished in this river by Jupiter’s thunderbolt. He was changed into the Eridanus and transferred among the stars.

## CHAPTER CXXX.—Cetus.

Associated with it is Cetus, which Perseus slew when it wished to devour Andromeda; Jupiter placed it among the stars because of the deed of his son.

## CHAPTER CXXXI.—Centaurus.

Near this is the Centaur, namely Achilles’ teacher, placed in heaven because of his extraordinary courage.

## CHAPTER CXXXII.—Ara.

[Col. 0146A]

Also the sanctuary, that is, the altar on which the gods swore when Saturn and Jupiter fought one another.

## CHAPTER CXXXIII.—Argo.

Next is Argo, namely the first ship, made by Typhoeus at the city of Argos and carried up into heaven.

## CHAPTER CXXXIV.—Pistrix.

Finally is Pistrix, or Chimaera, the beast that was lion in head, goat in middle, and dragon in tail; slain by Bellerophon and transferred among the stars.

## CHAPTER CXXXV.—Canopus.

There is also Canopus, the famous star of Egypt, which is not seen at all by us, just as the North is not seen by the Troglodytes near Egypt.

Of these signs, one half is always above the earth [Col. 0146B] and one half beneath it; and the part of heaven which appears above the earth is called a hemisphere, that is, half the heaven.

## CHAPTER CXXXVI.—The Milky Zone.—Why it is white.

The Milky Zone is white because all the stars pour their lights into it.

## CHAPTER CXXXVII.—On the comet.

Comets are stars hairy with flames, appearing in the Milky Zone toward the north, foretelling a change of kingdom, or pestilence, or wars, or winds, heat, or drought. They are seen for seven days; if longer, for eighty.

We have surveyed the constellations wrapped—indeed polluted—in fables. Climbing higher, let us behold the morning stars and the Sun of suns.

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII.—The watery heaven.

[Col. 0146C]

Above the firmament are waters suspended like a mist, which are said to surround heaven in a circle; hence it is called the watery heaven.

## CHAPTER CXXXIX.—The spiritual heaven.

Above it is the spiritual heaven, unknown to human beings, where is the dwelling of angels arranged in nine orders. In it is the paradise of paradises, into which the souls of the saints are received: that is, the heaven which is read in the beginning to have been created with the earth.

## CHAPTER CXL.—The heaven of heavens.

Far above this is said to rise the heaven of heavens, in which the King of angels dwells.

## BOOK TWO

In the preceding little book we set before the eyes of the body the globe of the whole world; in the following one, let us now set before them the time in which it revolves.

[Col. 0145]

## CHAPTER I.—On the age.—What the age is.

[Col. 0145D]

The age is before the world, with the world, and after the world. This belongs to God alone, who was not and will not be, but always is.

## CHAPTER II.—On eternal times.—That angels began before the world.

Eternal times are beneath the age, and these pertain to the archetypal world and to the angels, who began to exist before the world, are with the world, and will be after the world.

## CHAPTER III.—On the times of the world.—A comparison concerning the end of time. Why time is so called and what it is. The parts of time.

[Col. 0146D]

The time of the world is the shadow of the age. It began with the world and will end with the world. It is as though a rope were stretched from east to west and, being gathered up daily by folding, were finally altogether used up. Through it the ages are extended; beneath it all things placed in this world run their course. By it the life of each person [Col. 0147A] is measured. By it the succession of days and years is bounded.

Time is named from *temperamentum*, “a tempering,” and is nothing other than the alternation of things.

It is divided into atoms, omens (*ostenta*), moments, parts, minutes, points, hours, quarters, days, weeks, months, seasons, years, cycles, ages, and centuries.

## CHAPTER IV.—On atoms.

An atom is called “indivisible.” It is smaller than that which flies in the sunlight. It is the least interval of time, like the movement of an eyelid, which is also called a blink of the eye; and it is the three-hundred-and-seventy-sixth part of an omen (*ostentum*).

## CHAPTER V.—On omens (*ostenta*).

[Col. 0147B] An omen (*ostentum*) is that which shows something to those looking. It is the sixtieth part of one hour and contains three hundred and seventy-six atoms.

## CHAPTER VI.—On moments.

A moment is the movement of the stars, whence it takes its name. It is the fortieth part of an hour, containing an omen (*ostentum*) and a half.

## CHAPTER VII.—On parts.

Parts are so called from the division of the zodiac, which is divided into thirty days for each month. A part is the fifteenth part of an hour, containing two moments and two parts of a moment.

## CHAPTER VIII.—On minutes.

A minute is a smaller interval on a clock. It is a tenth, sometimes a fifth, of an hour, having [Col. 0147C] two minutes and half an hour. [The wording and numerical relation are corrupt or uncertain.]

## CHAPTER XIX.—On points.

A point is a small passage of the point on a clock. It is a fourth part in the sun. [The chapter number and wording are transmitted as printed.]

## CHAPTER X.—On hours.

An hour is the limit of each thing. An hour is the time for which standing water is moved by the throwing of a stone; it is the twelfth part of a day, consisting of four points, ten minutes, fifteen parts, forty moments, sixty omens (*ostenta*), and twenty-two thousand five hundred and sixty atoms. It is called from the clock, that is, the definite boundary of time in clocks.

## CHAPTER XI.—On the quarter.

A quarter is the fourth part of a day, having three hours; of a natural day, however, six hours.

## CHAPTER XII.—On the day.—Why the day is so called. Another definition of the day.

[Col. 0147D]

A day is the seventh part of the ordinary week, containing twelve hours; a natural day, however, [contains] twenty-four. A day is called from distinguishing, because it distinguishes light from darkness. A day is air illuminated by the sun: when the sun is above the earth, it is day here; when it is beneath the earth, it is day there.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On long and shorter days.

When the sun traverses the northern part of heaven, to us who are placed on the slope of the earth it rises earlier and sets later, and therefore makes longer days. But when it traverses the southern part, it seems to us to rise later and set sooner, because the swelling of the middle of the round earth [Col. 0148A] is set before our sight; then indeed it makes days shorter for us, but very long days for that other region.

## CHAPTER XIV.—On the signs of the zodiac and the sun’s parallels.

The zodiac, consisting of twelve signs and stretched from north to south, girds heaven in a winding course. Passing beneath it, the sun divides the world into eight parallels, that is, circles, each of which produces a different day. The length of the zodiac is divided into three hundred and sixty parts and its breadth into twelve. The division into parts is nothing other than the sun’s progress in one day. Each sign, therefore, rises during two hours and sets during two, and the sun remains in each for thirty days. As it runs beneath the signs of the oblique zodiac in the winding path of a serpent, it distinguishes the world into eight circles.

## CHAPTER XV.—On the first circle.

[Col. 0148B]

The first circle extends from India southward, through the Red Sea and Africa, to the Pillars of Hercules. For Hercules, traversing the world, set up pillars there where he thought the end of the world to be. In this circle, at the equinox, the gnomon—that is, the pointer of a sundial—at midday, being seven feet high, casts a shadow four feet long; the longest day has fourteen equinoctial hours.

## CHAPTER XVI.—On the second circle.

The second goes from western India through the Medes and Persians, Arabia, Syria, Cyprus, Crete, Mount Lilybaeum in Sicily, and reaches the northern parts of Africa. At the equinox the gnomon of thirty-five feet [Col. 0148C] casts a shadow of only twenty feet. The longest day is fourteen hours and a fifth of an hour.

## CHAPTER XVII.—On the third circle.

The third rises from the Indians nearest to Imaus and extends through the Caspian Gates, Taurus, Pamphylia, Rhodes, the Cyclades, Syracuse, Catana, and Gades. All the gnomons cast shadows of thirty-eight inches. The longest day is fourteen hours, one half, and one thirtieth of an hour.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On the fourth circle.

The fourth, from the other side of Imaus, extends through the Ephesian Sea, the Cyclades, northern Sicily, the eastern regions of Narbonensian Gaul, and eastern Africa, to the west. [Col. 0148D] A gnomon of thirty-five feet casts a shadow of twenty feet. The longest day has fourteen hours and two thirds of an hour.

## CHAPTER XIX.—On the fifth circle.

Within the fifth circle, from the entrance of the Caspian Sea, lie Bactria, Armenia, Macedonia, Tarentum, the Tuscan Sea, the Balearic Islands, Spain, and Media. A gnomon of seven feet casts a shadow of six feet. The longest day is fifteen hours.

## CHAPTER XX.—On the sixth circle.

The sixth encompasses the Caspian peoples, the Caucasus, Samothrace, Illyria, Campania, Etruria, Massilia, Spain, Tarraconensian [Spain], Media, and thence passes through Lusitania. A gnomon of nine feet casts a shadow [Col. 0149A] of eight feet. The longest day is fifteen hours and one ninth of an hour.

## CHAPTER XXI.—On the seventh circle.

The seventh begins from the other shore of the Caspian Sea and passes through Thrace toward Venice, Cremona, Ravenna Transalpina, Gaul, the Pyrenees, and Celtiberia. A gnomon of thirty-five feet [casts] a shadow of thirty-six. The longest day is fifteen hours and three fifths of an hour.

## CHAPTER XXII.—On the eighth circle.

The eighth goes from the Tanais through Lake Maeotis and the Sarmatians, Dacians, and a part of Germany, into Gaul. The gnomon is as above. The longest day is sixteen hours.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—On the four circles of the sun.

[Col. 0149B] Beyond these, the sun makes four circles: two in the south and two in the north. One in the south runs through the island of Meroë and Ptolemais, a city of the Red Sea, where the longest day is twelve hours and half an hour longer. Another runs through Syene in Egypt, where [the longest day] is thirteen hours. One in the north runs through the Hyperborean mountains and Britain, [where it is] seventeen hours. The other is Scythian, from the Rhipaean ranges to Thule, where it is day for six months and night for the other six.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—On the varying shadow of days.—The well at Syene. The Fiscii peoples.

In still other places on earth the sun varies the shadow. For the shadow of the pointer, which is called the gnomon, in Egypt, at midday on the equinoctial day, is a little more than half the measure of the gnomon. In Rome the shadow lacks one ninth of the gnomon. [Col. 0149C] In Ancona it exceeds [the gnomon] by one thirty-fifth. In Venice, at the same hours, the shadow equals the gnomon. At Syene, at midday on the solstitial day, no shadow is made; and there a well, made by philosophers for this very purpose, is entirely illuminated within. In the south are peoples called Fiscii, who cast their shadow on both sides. In India, above the river Hypanis, the shadow disappears on the solstitial day. Among the Troglodytes, forty-five days before the solstice and as many afterwards, the shadow wholly disappears. During these ninety days the shadow falls to the south. On Meroë, an island of the Nile, the shadow disappears twice yearly, when the sun is in the twelfth degree of Taurus and the fourteenth degree of Leo. In India are places called Ascia, where there are no shadows and [Col. 0149D] where the north is not visible.

## CHAPTER XXV.—On the horizon.

The horizon is the extent which each person’s sight marks out in a circle, where heaven is thought to hang over the earth on every side. This can be perceived more clearly on the open sea, where no obstacle presents itself. The horizon extends through a length of three hundred and nine stadia. For the visual ray does not extend beyond one hundred and eighty stadia directly before the observer. But when sight reaches this distance, failing, it bends back into a curve. This number doubled makes the horizon before and behind.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—On the division of the day.—Why morning, midday, and late afternoon are so called.

The ordinary day has three divisions: morning, midday, and late afternoon. [Col. 0150A] Morning, from sunrise to the fourth hour, is called from *mane*, “good,” since nothing is better than light; or from the Manes, that is, the gods of the underworld, who in the morning release the day that they have enclosed throughout the night. Midday is from the middle of the day and is called, as it were, the “pure and clear day.” Late afternoon is from the ninth hour to sunset and is so called because it checks the course of the sun.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—On the beginning and end of days.

The Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Persians, beginning the day in the morning, end it in the morning; the Egyptians, from sunset to sunset; the Romans, from midnight to midnight; the Umbrians and Athenians, from midday to midday; Christians, from evening to evening.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—On the names of days.—Why the order of the planets is not retained in naming the days of the week. How Christians name the days.

[Col. 0150B]

The Hebrews name the days thus: First [day] of the Sabbath, or of Sabbaths, or first Sabbath; second Sabbath; third Sabbath; fourth Sabbath; fifth Sabbath; sixth Sabbath; Sabbath.

The pagans, however, [name them] thus: Day of the Sun, Day of the Moon, Day of Mars, Day of Mercury, Day of Jupiter, Day of Venus, Day of Saturn. But since these names derive from the planets, one must consider why they do not keep the same order. The reason is this: the natural day is divided into twenty-four hours, and if one hour is assigned in rotation three times to each planet, then, when all have been spent, the planet to which the first hour again falls has the name of the day assigned to it. Christians, however, name the days thus: [Col. 0150C] the Lord’s Day, second feria, third feria, fourth feria, fifth feria, sixth feria, Sabbath.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—On the night.

Night is called from harming, because it harms the eyes. Night is the absence of the sun, the shadow of the earth. Shadow is made by a body and light. For when the sunlight is beneath the earth, the body of the earth produces a shadow above, which reaches as far as the moon.

## CHAPTER XXX.—On shadow.

Shadow is called, as it were, “against the ray,” namely of the sun. Where light is equal to the body, there the shadow too is equal; where light is greater than the body, there the shadow diminishes; where light is weaker than the body, there the shadow increases without limit. When the sun surveys the southern quarter of heaven, it lengthens night for us; but when the northern, it shortens it for us.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—On eclipse.—How it happens.

[Col. 0150D]

When the moon enters the shadow of night, it fails of light, and this failure is called an eclipse. The sun, however, suffers eclipse through the interposition of the moon, when, that is, the moon passes under the sun on the same line.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—On the seven periods of the night.

Night has seven periods: namely twilight, evening, the time of silence, the untimely time, cockcrow, the morning time, and dawn.

1. Twilight is uncertain light. For *creperum* means “uncertain.” It is between darkness and light.

2. Evening [is named] from the star called Vesper.

3. The time of silence is when all things fall silent—that is, are quiet.

[Col. 0151A] 4. The untimely time is midnight, when it is not time to work.

5. Cock-crow, when the cocks sing.

6. Morning, when dawn approaches in the early day.

### Chapter XXXIII.—On the Week

A week (*hebdomada*) is called the fourth part of a lunar month; in Greek it is named from the number seven: for ἑπτά means “seven.” In Latin it is called *septimana*, as though “seven mornings,” that is, days.

It has seven kinds.

The first is the divine week, in which God created all things in six days and rested on the seventh.

The second is that in which this world revolves, in which we work for six days after God’s example.

The third is the seven weeks together before Pentecost is celebrated [Col. 0151B]. In it the Law is given to the Jews, the Holy Spirit to Christians.

The fourth is that of seven months, during which the three feasts of Tabernacles were observed.

The fifth is that of seven years, during which the year of remission was kept, in which the people were commanded to abstain from work.

The sixth is that of seven times seven years, after which the Jubilee year was observed as a festival.

The seventh is that of seventy times seven years, after which Christ was promised to be born by Daniel—or rather by the angel.

### Chapter XXXIV.—On Months. The Lunar Month; the Solar Month

A month is the twelfth part of the year. It is called from *mensura*, “measure,” or from *Mene*, which is “moon” [Col. 0151C].

The lunar month is completed in twenty-nine days and twelve hours.

The solar month, however, is completed in thirty days and ten and a half hours. A lunar month runs from new moon to new moon. The moon traverses the zodiac in twenty-nine days and twelve hours: twice twelve makes twenty-four, which is a complete day. Since this cannot be divided, it is assigned to one month. Hence one month has a thirtieth moon-day, another a twenty-ninth.

A solar month is the passage through one sign. The sun remains in each sign for thirty days and a half, because a half in two signs makes a complete day. Since this cannot be divided into two, it is assigned to one month [Col. 0151D]; and therefore one month has thirty-one days, another thirty.

### Chapter XXXV.—On the Names of the Months

The Hebrews, following Moses as their authority, name the months thus, beginning with April, in which they celebrate Passover:

| Nisan | April |
|---|---|
| Liar | May |
| Sinan | June |
| Thamus | July |
| Ab | August |
| Elul | September |
| Thirsi | October |
| Marhesvan | November |
| Casleu | December |
| Tebet | January |
| Sebat | February |
| Adar | March |

The Egyptians, following Abraham as their authority, reckon the months from September. Thus they call them:

| Θώθ (*Thōth*) | September |
|---|---|
| Φαωφί (*Phaōphi*) | October |
| Ἀθύρ (*Athyr*) | November |
| Χοιάκ (*Choiak*) | December |
| Τυβί (*Tybi*) | January |
| Μεχειρ (*Mecheir*) | February |
| Φαμενώθ (*Phamenōth*) | March |
| Φαρμουθί (*Pharmouthi*) | April |
| Παχών (*Pachōn*) | May |
| Παυνί (*Pauni*) | June |
| Επιφί (*Epiphi*) | July |
| Μεσορή (*Mesore*) | August |

The Greeks, following Phoroneus as their authority, begin the months from December, calling them thus:

| Ἀπιλλαῖος (*Apillaios*) | December |
|---|---|
| Αὐδυναῖος (*Aydynaios*) | January |
| Περίπιος (*Peripios*) | February |
| Δύστρος (*Dystros*) | March |
| Ξαντικός (*Xantikos*) | April |
| Αρτεμίσιος (*Artemisios*) | May |
| Δεύτιος and Δαίσιος (*Deutios* and *Daisios*) | June |
| Πάνεμος (*Panemos*) | July |
| Λώοος (*Lōoos*) | August |
| Τορπιαῖος (*Torpiaios*) | September |
| Ὑπερβερίταιος (*Hyperberitaios*) | October |
| Δῖος (*Dios*) | November |

### Chapter XXXVI.—On the Months of the Romans

Romulus assigned ten months to the Romans. He named the first March, from Mars, who was born in Phrygia in this month and whose son he falsely proclaimed himself to be.

He called the tenth December.

But Numa Pompilius added two, namely January and February.

The months of the Romans are named from idols, kings, and numbers.

### Chapter XXXVII.—On January

The first, January, is called from the idol Janus, the god of beginnings, because this month is the beginning of the year. It is also called from *janua*, “door,” because through it the year enters.

### Chapter XXXVIII.—On February

[Col. 0152D]

The second, February, is named from Februus, that is, from the idol Pluto, god of the underworld, to whom they sacrificed in this month while they purified the city with lights in his honor. It is called from *febris*, that is, cold, because that season is cold.

### Chapter XXXIX.—On March

The third, March, is named from the idol Mars, god of war, father of Romulus, founder of the Roman people; soldiers sacrificed to Mars in this month. It is also called from males, because all living creatures desire males at this time.

### Chapter XL.—On April

The fourth, April, is named from Aphrodisius or Afrili, that is, from the idol Venus, goddess of love, to whom this month was consecrated [Col. 0153A]. It is also called, as it were, *aperilis*, because it opens the earth into flowers.

### Chapter XLI.—On May

The fifth, May, is named from Maia and Jupiter, as though from majesty, or from Maia, mother of Mercury, to whom merchants sacrificed in this month. It is also named from the elders, namely the Roman leaders, who sacrificed to Jupiter in this month.

### Chapter XLII.—On June

The sixth, June, is named from Juno, goddess of sovereignty, to whom it was consecrated. It is also named from the younger men, who defended Rome by arms and sought from Juno the summit of royal power.

### Chapter XLIII.—On July. Why It Was Called Quintilis

The seventh, July, is named from Julius Caesar, who was made emperor in this month and in this month was enrolled among the gods [Col. 0153B]. It was formerly called Quintilis, because it was the fifth from March, which Romulus had established as the first.

### Chapter XLIV.—On August. Why It Was Called Sextilis

The eighth, August, is named from Augustus Caesar, who was victorious in this month and enlarged the Roman empire. For this reason he deserved divinity. It was formerly called Sextilis, because it was the sixth from the first month, March.

### Chapter XLV.—On September

The ninth, September, as it were “the seventh rain.”

### Chapter XLVI.—On October

The tenth, October, as it were “the eighth rain.”

### Chapter XLVII.—On November

[Col. 0153C]

The eleventh, November, as it were “the ninth rain.”

### Chapter XLVIII.—On December

The twelfth, December, as it were “the tenth rain.” For these are rainy months, and therefore take their names from number and rains.

### Chapter XLIX.—On the Kalends

The Kalends are called from the verb καλέω (*kaleō*), “I summon.” For the pontiff was bound to announce the new moon to the king; after his sacrifice, he cried “Kalo” five or six times, and by this sign summoned the people to the assembly-house, called for this reason the *Calabria*, for sacrifice. From this verb καλέω it was decided to call the first day of the month the Kalends.

### Chapter L.—On the Nones

Then, for nine days, the common people were summoned from the countryside to gather in the city [Col. 0153D], and there received from the king or pontiff the ordinances for observing the feast days; hence they are called the Nones. They are also named from market-days and the merchandise which they either brought to the city or bought there.

### Chapter LI.—On the Ides

The Ides are the days that divide the months, from *iduare*, “to divide.” They are also called from *idaea*, “form,” because the moon displays the fullness of its form in the middle of the month.

The Hebrews, Egyptians, and Greeks observe neither Kalends, Nones, nor Ides, but reckon only the days from new moon to new moon.

### Chapter LII.—On the Alternations of the Year

The succession of the year is divided into four seasons, and each is distinguished by three months [Col. 0154A]. It is called an alternation because it changes turns in the year: namely, into spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

### Chapter LIII.—On Spring

Spring is a fourth part of the year, consisting of three months. It is called from flourishing, because then the meadows grow green and the woods put forth leaves. It is moist and warm, and the equinox occurs in it.

### Chapter LIV.—On Summer

Summer is a fourth part of the year, consisting of three months, and is called from *aestus*, “heat.” It is hot and dry. It is also called harvest, and the solstice is observed in it.

### Chapter LV.—On Autumn

Autumn is a fourth part of the year consisting of three months [Col. 0154B]. It is called from *autumo*, “I gather,” namely the fruits of the earth. It is dry and cold. It is also called the vintage, and in it the equinox of the balance is equalized.

### Chapter LVI.—On Winter

Winter is a fourth part of the year; it is completed by three months and is named from harsh cold. It is cold and moist, and the solstitial day occurs in it.

### Chapter LVII.—On the Unequal Character of the Seasons

This succession, however, takes place only in our regions. In India, where the risings of the stars are different, there are two summers and two harvests in the year; in the middle is a mild winter. In Egypt also, in the very middle of winter, nature clothes the plain with grasses and flowers and the woods with foliage; at times it loads the trees with fruit.

### Chapter LVIII.—On the Elements

[Col. 0154C]

The four elements are also joined to the qualities of the four seasons. Earth, dry and cold, is connected with autumn; water, cold and moist, with winter; air, moist and warm, with spring; fire, hot and dry, with summer.

### Chapter LIX.—On Man as a Microcosm

The human body is tempered by these same qualities; hence it is called a microcosm, that is, a lesser world. Blood, which increases in spring, is moist and warm, and predominates in children. Red bile, increasing in summer, is hot and dry, and abounds in young people. Melancholy arises from black bile and increases in autumn among those more advanced in age. Phlegms dominate in winter among the old.

[Col. 0154D]

Those in whom blood prevails are cheerful, compassionate, laughing, and talkative.

Those in whom red bile prevails are lean, greedy, swift, bold, irascible, and agile.

Those in whom black bile prevails are steadfast, serious, restrained in character, and deceitful.

Those in whom phlegms prevail are slow, sleepy, and forgetful.

### Chapter LX.—On the Year

A year is called from renewing, because it renews all things that pass away.

It is also called *annus*, as though *annulus*, “a ring,” because it turns back upon itself like a circle.

The term “year” is understood in many ways.

### Chapter LXI.—On the Lunar Year

[Col. 0155A]

The lunar year is named in five ways.

The first lunar year is when the moon traverses all the signs of the zodiac; it consists of twenty-seven days and eight hours.

The second, two days and four hours longer, is the period after the moon is rekindled by the sun; this is properly called a month.

The third is called the common year; it is completed by twelve such months in three hundred and fifty-four days.

The fourth is the embolismic year, that is, the added increase; it is completed by thirteen months in three hundred and eighty-four days. Both of these begin and end among the Hebrews with the Paschal month. Among the Romans, however, they begin with the moon of January [Col. 0155B] and end there.

The fifth is the lunar, or nineteen-year, year, when after nineteen years the moon returns to the same phases.

### Chapter LXII.—On the Solar Year

The solar year is when the sun traverses all the signs of the zodiac; it consists of three hundred and sixty-five days and six hours.

### Chapter LXIII.—On the Leap Year

A leap year occurs when, in the fourth year, the bissextile day is inserted, and it is recognized as one day longer than the preceding year. There is also another solar year, when after twenty-eight years the sun completes the cycle of concurrents.

### Chapter LXIV.—On Mercury’s Year

Mercury completes its cycle in three hundred and thirty-nine days [Col. 0155C].

### Chapter LXV.—Venus’s Year

Venus’s year is completed in three hundred and forty-eight days.

### Chapter LXVI.—Mars’s Year

Mars’s year consists of two solar years.

### Chapter LXVII.—Jupiter

Jupiter’s year extends over twelve years.

### Chapter LXVIII.—Saturn

Saturn’s year is completed in thirty years.

### Chapter LXIX.—The Great Year

The great year revolves in five hundred and thirty-two years.

Besides these, there are two legal years: one called the year of remission, comprising a cycle of seven years [Col. 0155D]; the other, the Jubilee, of fifty years.

### Chapter LXX.—On the Civil Year. Why Plato Posits So Many Thousands of Years

The Hebrews begin the civil, that is solar, year in spring from the equinox; the Greeks from the solstice; the Egyptians from autumn; the Romans from midwinter. Among the Indians one month is a year; among the Egyptians in former times a year consisted of four months; among the Acarnanians, of six months; among the Lavinians, of thirteen months; among some peoples, each season of the year—spring and the rest—is reckoned as a year. Hence Plato posits nine thousand years, while Tully posits fifteen thousand years.

### Chapter LXXI.—On the Bissextile Day. Why the Intercalary Day Is Placed in February

The solar year, as has been ascertained by observation of the horoscope-clock, is completed in three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter [Col. 0156A]. A quarter is a fourth part of a day, namely six hours. In four years, four quarters make twenty-four hours, which is a complete day. This day is therefore intercalated in the fourth year on the sixth day before the Kalends of March and is called bissextile. Julius Caesar inserted it and by it corrected the error of the entire computation. The Egyptians and Greeks place it at the end of the year; the Romans insert it in February because that month is shorter than the others. For formerly an entire month was intercalated there. It is not placed before the sixth day before the Kalends of March because on the seventh day before the Kalends of March they purified the city with great solemnity, and they were not permitted to begin anything before the festival had passed.

[Col. 0156B]

The bissextile cycle is completed in four years.

The indictional cycle, beginning in October, is completed in fifteen years.

The nineteen-year cycle, beginning with the Paschal moon, is completed in nineteen years.

The solar cycle, beginning in March, is completed in twenty-seven years.

The great cycle is completed in five hundred and thirty-two years.

### Chapter LXXII.—On Olympiads

An Olympiad is four years. At Elis, a city of Greece, it was instituted that every four years people should gather at Mount Olympus and hold athletic games there; hence they are called Olympiads.

### Chapter LXXIII.—On Lustra

[Col. 0156C]

A *lustrum* is five years. For tribute was paid to the Romans by all peoples: bronze for five years, silver for five years, gold for five years. They always came to Rome every five-year period and purified the city; hence each five-year period is called a *lustrum*.

### Chapter LXXIV.—On Indictions

All indictions together are called from proclamation (*indicendo*), because after every fifteen years they always returned to the first assessment, that is, bronze.

### Chapter LXXV.—On Age. The Six Ages of Man; the Six Ages of the World

An age or generation is the life of each individual person, or one hundred years. An age also occurs when no one survives who is now living [Col. 0156D]. There are likewise six ages of man.

The first, infancy, lasts to seven years; the second, childhood, to fourteen years; the third, adolescence, to twenty-one years; the fourth, youth, to the fiftieth year; the fifth, old age, to the seventieth year; the sixth, decrepitude, to one hundred years or until death.

There are no less six ages of the world.

The first is from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the Babylonian captivity; the fifth thence to Christ; the sixth to the end of the world.

### Chapter LXXVI.—On the Age

[Col. 0157A]

An age (*saeculum*) is a thousand years; it is called *saeculum* because it follows itself, “unto age of age.”

*Saeculum*: time, in Greek.

*Saeculum*: the time of the Law.

*Ages of ages.*

*Ages*: the times of Christians.

*Ages*: the times of Jews and pagans.

There is also “the age of age,” the kingdom of heaven, which follows this age, as it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord, unto age of age” (Psalm 83:5).

### Chapter LXXVII.—On the Nineteen-Year Cycle

The nineteen-year cycle is so called, as though “a circle of nineteen years.” For during so many years the moon completes its course [Col. 0157B], striving against the firmament.

It is divided into two:

Into twelve common and seven embolismic years.

They are called common when two equal periods, namely twelve lunar months from one Passover to another, coincide.

The embolismic year, called the additional year, is that which has thirteen months—that is, thirteen new moons—from one Passover to another. All this occurs because Passover may not be celebrated before the equinox and before the fourteenth moon of April, which is called the first month among the Hebrews.

### Chapter LXXVIII.—On the Ogdoad

It is further divided into two: into an octad and a hendecad [Col. 0157C]. An octad is eight years; a hendecad, eleven. For two common years always precede an embolismic year. But in the eighth position one common year precedes the embolismic year, and this number is called the octad. Then again, two common years always precede the third embolismic year. But in the eleventh position only one precedes the embolismic year. This number is called the hendecad.

### Chapter LXXIX.—On the Solar Cycle

The solar cycle is completed in twenty-eight years, because of the seven leap years. For the leap day must touch each day of the week and thus return through the same days. Seven times four makes twenty-eight, since the bissextile day is inserted only in every fourth year.

### Chapter LXXX.—On Counting on the Finger-Joints

[Col. 0157D]

You will calculate the lunar course on the joints together with the nails as follows. Begin at the base of the thumb of the left hand, count through each joint and nail, and at the end of the little finger you will have nineteen years.

Calculate the solar course on the joints of both hands, without the nails, as follows. Begin with the little finger of the left hand and count across the four fingers. In every fourth position mark the bissextile year. Do likewise on the other hand, and you will have twenty-four years. Then count two years on each thumb; joined to the preceding years, these make twenty-eight years.

The solar course is twofold. One course follows the firmament daily from east to west [Col. 0158A]; the other, striving against the firmament, proceeds in twenty-eight years.

### Chapter LXXXI.—On the Great Year

The great year is made up of these two cycles. For twenty-eight times nineteen, or nineteen times twenty-eight, make five hundred and thirty-two years, after which all the planets and all the stars return to the first point from which they set out and return as before along the same paths. The moon traverses each sign of the zodiac in two days, six hours, and two-thirds of an hour. It traverses all the signs in twenty-seven days and eight hours.

### Chapter LXXXII.—On the Cycles

Mercury traverses each sign in twenty-eight days and six hours, and the whole zodiac in three hundred and thirty-nine days [Col. 0158B].

Venus traverses each sign in twenty-nine days and five hours, and circles the whole zodiac in three hundred and forty-eight days.

The sun traverses each sign in thirty days, ten hours, and a half; it passes through the entire circuit of the zodiac in three hundred and sixty-five days and six hours.

Mars traverses each sign in sixty days and twenty-one hours, and all the signs in two years.

Jupiter’s star remains one year in each sign; it travels through them all in twelve years.

Saturn remains in each sign for two years, one hundred and eighty days, and fifteen hours—that is, half a year [Col. 0158C]; and, because of its very great height in relation to heaven, it traverses the entire zodiacal circle in thirty years, moving, like the others, against the heaven.

### Chapter LXXXIII.—On the Authors of the Cycle

Eusebius of Caesarea first compiled the cycle. Afterwards Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, set it out more clearly at the request of Pope Leo; then the abbot Dionysius issued it in writing at Rome, as it is held today.

### Chapter LXXXIV.—On the Equinox and the Solstice

The four signs of the zodiac, situated at equal distances in the shape of a cross, produce the equinoxes and solstices. For the sign of Aries, in which the sun is placed, is situated in the east and produces the vernal equinox. Libra [Col. 0158D], in which the moon was established, is in the west, opposite to it, and produces the autumnal equinox. Cancer occupies the heaven toward the north, where it is highest, and produces the summer solstice; Capricorn presses upon the heaven toward the south, where it is lowest, and produces the winter solstice.

“Equinox” is called from “equal” and “night”; in Greek it is *isemeria* (ἰσημερία), from “equal” and “day,” as though “equal day.”

The Law and the Gospel proclaim, and inspection of the horoscope-clock plainly proves, that the vernal equinox is to be reckoned not on the eighth but on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. For according to the Law it was not permitted to celebrate Passover before the equinox. Whoever reads the Gospel carefully will see that the Lord suffered not on the eighth but on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.
