If, therefore, the equinox falls on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [Col. 0159A], then the Lord celebrated Passover before the equinox, contrary to the Law—he who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. The Jews also acted contrary to their ancestral custom by keeping Passover at an unsuitable time. But since neither of these things occurred, after the equinox on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April had passed, the Lord celebrated Passover with the Jews according to the customary practice on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April; on the Paschal day, which was the tenth day before the Kalends, he redeemed us by his blood. He rose on the eighth day before the Kalends.

The horoscope-clock likewise shows that the autumnal equinox is to be reckoned not on the eighth but on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.

A solstice is so called because the sun stands still: that is, it can rise no higher in the sky but turns its step backward [Col. 0159B].

The horoscope of the clock declares that the summer solstice is to be reckoned not on the eighth but on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July. It makes the night shortest and the day longest, when the sun ascends the sign of Cancer.

For the same reason, the winter solstice is proved to be reckoned not on the eighth but on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, when the sun, situated in Capricorn, is known to make the day shortest and the night longest.

### Chapter LXXXV.—On the Lunar Leap

The moon, departing from the sun, follows it again after twenty-nine days and twelve hours; but before the twelfth hour is completed, it is rekindled by the sun. For from the hour there remain in each month four moments, one single unit of a moment, and one atom [Col. 0159C]. These, accumulated every year, make a complete day after nineteen years. This day is subtracted from the lunar count, when the first day is reckoned as the thirtieth. It is called the lunar leap. The lunar leap occurs in the nineteenth year and in July because Egypt, the mother of astronomy, did this also.

### Chapter LXXXVI.—On Small Fractions

Since small fractions are frequently used here, and perhaps are less known to many, it should be known that an *uncia* is a twelfth part of anything; a *bes* (*bissa*) is two parts of a thing divided into three, with the third removed. Any such part is called a *triens* of a thing divided into four parts. The fourth part is called a *quadrans* [Col. 0159D]; the remaining three, a *dodrans*.

### Chapter LXXXVII.—On the Weekday Regulars

The weekday regulars and concurrents begin with March, from which the Romans formerly reckoned the beginning of the year. For they were invented by the Romans. They are called “regulars” because they guide calculators; “concurrents” because they coincide with the regulars. The regulars have the following beginning. The solar year consists of three hundred and sixty-five days. The sun remains thirty days in each of the twelve signs. Thus twelve times thirty, or thirty times twelve, makes three hundred and sixty. Five remain. These are the regulars of March. In the remaining months they arise as follows: divide the days of the preceding month together with its regulars into seven equal parts; assign what remains to the following month [Col. 0160A] as its regulars. For example, March has thirty-one days and five regulars, which are five times seven, with one remaining. This will be the regular of April. So in the rest.

Alternatively: whatever weekday the Kalends of the months had in the first year, so many will be the monthly regulars. For example, at the Kalends of March there are five; therefore five are the regulars of the Kalends of April: one weekday and one regular. So in the rest.

### Chapter LXXXVIII.—On the Concurrents

The concurrents have the following beginning. The solar year has fifty-two weeks and one day. This one will be the concurrent in the first year of the solar cycle, because it regularly coincides in finding the first weekday at the Kalends of the months. Add one in each year up to the seventh. In the fourth year the bissextile day is counted among the concurrents. In that one year one concurrent is skipped; in the bissextile year use the bissextile for the concurrent in January and February; in the remaining months, use the concurrent.

The first year at the creation of the world had no concurrents. Wednesday fell on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, or the sixth day before the Kalends of March. There were that many concurrents in that year [Col. 0160B].

Add the concurrents to the regulars. If the result is less than seven, that will be the weekday on the Kalends of each month. If it exceeds seven, subtract seven: what remains will be the weekday. For these regulars and concurrents do not exceed the number seven.

### Chapter LXXXIX.—On Regulars and Epacts

[Col. 0160C]

The regulars and epacts begin with September, which the Egyptians place at the beginning of the year. For they were invented by them. These regulars have the same beginning as the preceding ones; therefore September has five.

In the remaining months they are found as follows: take the days of the preceding month with its regular; if it has a thirtieth moon, subtract twenty-five; assign what remains to the following month as its regular.

Alternatively: in the first year the fourth moon fell on the Kalends. Subtract eleven; however many remain, that many will be the lunar regulars. For example, at the Kalends of September the moon will be the sixteenth; subtract eleven, and five remain [Col. 0160D]: five will be the regular. So in the rest.

The epacts arise as follows. The solar year has three hundred and sixty-five days, the lunar year three hundred and fifty-four; the former exceeds the latter by eleven days. These eleven are called epacts, that is, additions, because they are added each year to the regulars of the months to find the moon. Therefore add eleven every year. If the number is below thirty, these will be the epacts of the present year. If it is above thirty, subtract thirty: however many remain will be the entire moon. In the nineteenth year, namely, there are eighteen epacts. Add to these the eleven days of the lunar leap, and there will be thirty epacts in the first year. Therefore the first year of the nineteen-year cycle has thirty epacts. But it is said to have none, because thirty are rejected in each month [Col. 0161A], and the moon is found by the solar regulars. Whatever the moon is on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, such will be the epacts of that year.

### Chapter XC.—For How Many Hours the Moon Shines

The first moon shines for four points, the second for eight, the third for twelve; and so, until the full moon, four points are added each day. In its waning, likewise, four are taken away each day. At the full moon it shines the whole night; when it is the thirtieth, it shines not at all.

In lunar computation, five points make one hour. Therefore, by taking four points for each day and assigning five to each hour, you will readily see for how many hours the moon shines in the night.

It should be noted that timber cut during the waning moon, or after the months of July and August, will remain unharmed by worms and decay [Col. 0161B].

### Chapter XCI.—By How Many Parts the Moon Is Distant from the Sun

Multiply whatever age of the moon by four, multiply this number by three, and however many you find in the sum, by so many parts of the zodiac you will know the moon to be distant from the sun; and after the same number of days the sun will come to the same place.

### Chapter XCII.—In Which Sign the Moon Is

The sun remains thirty days in each sign. See, therefore, in which sign it is, and how many days it still has to remain in it; assign that number from the sum mentioned above to that sign. Distribute the remainder of the same sum among the following signs, thirty to each; and you will know the moon to be in the sign that falls short of thirty.

### Chapter XCIII.—On the Years of the Lord

[Col. 0161C]

To find the year of the Lord, multiply by fifteen the indiction cycles since his Incarnation, which are seventy, adding twelve because three indictions preceded the year of Christ’s Nativity, and the result is one thousand and twenty.

> **Note:** [Col. 0161D] Observe in what year of the Lord’s Incarnation the author wrote this little book.—D. Roger Wilmans advises that this passage should be restored as follows (*Prooemium to Honorius*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica* X, 125, note 9): “To find the year of the Lord, multiply by fifteen the indiction cycles since his Incarnation, which are LXXIV [LX in the first edition; LXX in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* and in the twelfth-century Admont manuscript], adding XII, because three indictions preceded the year of Christ’s Nativity, and the result is 1122 [1120 in the first edition and the *Bibliotheca Patrum*]. For 74 × 15 = 1110 + 12 = 1122.”

Add to these the indiction of the present year, and you will have the year of the Lord.

### Chapter XCIV.—On Finding the Indiction

To find the indiction, divide the elapsed years of the Lord, together with the three indictions that preceded his Nativity, by fifteen. Whatever remains is the indiction. If nothing remains, it is the fifteenth.

### Chapter XCV.—On Finding the Epacts

[Col. 0161D]

To find the epacts, divide the years of the Lord by nineteen, and multiply the remainder by eleven. If it is below thirty, it will be the epact of that year. If above, subtract thirty, and however many remain you will have as epacts. When the Lord was born, there were eleven epacts.

### Chapter XCVI.—How the Solar Year Is Found

[Col. 0162A]

To find the solar year, add nine to the years of the Lord, because so many years of the solar cycle preceded his Nativity. Divide this sum by twenty-eight; however many remain, that is the year. If nothing remains, it is the twenty-eighth.

### Chapter XCVII.—How the Concurrents Are Found

To find the concurrents, take the years of the Lord and add to them a fourth part of the whole number on account of the bissextile calculation. Add four regulars, because that many concurrents preceded Christ’s Nativity. Divide this entire number by seven; whatever remains will be the concurrents of that year. If nothing remains, they are seven.

### Chapter XCVIII.—On Finding the Bissextile Year

To find the bissextile year, divide the years of the Lord by four [Col. 0162B]. However many remain, that is the number of years since the bissextile year. If nothing remains, it will be bissextile.

Likewise, subtract one from the solar cycle and divide by four; the remainder is the year since the bissextile year.

### Chapter XCIX.—On Finding the Lunar Cycle

To find the lunar cycle, subtract two from the years of the Lord, which remained in that cycle when he was born—for seventeen had preceded—and divide the rest by nineteen. Whatever remains will be the year of the lunar cycle. If nothing remains, it will be the nineteenth. This is properly the Roman cycle, as the nineteen-year cycle is the Hebrew one. And as Passover is known by this one, so the moon’s ascent is known by that one.

To find the year of the nineteen-year cycle, always add one to the years of the Lord, because the Lord was born in its second year [Col. 0162C], and divide by nineteen. The remainder will be the current year; if nothing remains, it will be the nineteenth year.

### Chapter C.—On Years and Cycles

Change the years from the beginning of the world on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, because that is the first day of the age; change the year of the Lord on the eighth day before the Kalends of January; the lunar cycle on the Kalends of January; the solar cycle likewise; the nineteen-year cycle on the new moon of April; the concurrents on the Kalends of March; the epacts on the Kalends of September; and the indictions on the Kalends of October.

### Chapter CI.—On Finding the Keys of the Terms

To find the keys of the terms, take the years of the nineteen-year cycle and the seven days of the week; joined together they make twenty-six, and this is the first key. In the second year, join the nineteen-year number to the first key, and they make forty-five. Subtract thirty; fifteen remain, and this is the second key. Do this for each year through the nineteenth. In the nineteenth year add eighteen because of the lunar leap, and thus you will find the first key [Col. 0163A]. Remember here that, whenever the aforesaid number exceeds forty, after thirty is removed the remainder again is the key.

### Chapter CII.—On the Paschal Term

The Paschal term is the fourteenth moon of April, and the Passover of the Hebrews. Therefore, wherever the fourteenth moon falls after the vernal equinox, there without doubt is the Paschal term, and our Passover will fall on the following Sunday. If the term falls on the Lord’s Day, Passover must be celebrated on the following Sunday. You may most easily find this term by the verses for the Nones of April and by the weekdays.

Alternatively.—The terms are to be sought from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April to the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May. You may find them thus. Place the term of the preceding year on the first joint of the thumb of the left hand, and calculate the days of the terms through the individual joints and nails of the fingers of the same hand. Whatever term falls on the first joint will be the term.

Alternatively.—Begin from the term of each year and count backward to the twelfth letter; you will have the term of the following year if it is a common year. But if there is an embolismic year, count to the twentieth letter, and you will have the term. For example, count backward from the term of the first year, which is the Nones of April; at the twelfth letter, which is the eighth day before the Kalends of April, you will have the term of the second year, which is common. From this point count to the twentieth letter, upon which the Ides of April fall [Col. 0163C], and you will have the term of the third year, which is embolismic.

Otherwise.—Begin at the base of the thumb, and count backward through the individual joints of the three fingers; on the fourth finger you will have the limit. For example: in the first year on the day of the Nones of April, in the second on the Nones, in the third on the Nones, in the fourth on the Nones. The limit falls on the first Kalends of April, the second Kalends, the third Kalends, the fourth Kalends, the fifth Kalends, the sixth Kalends, the seventh Kalends, the eighth Kalends.

You will find the regular numbers of the same limit thus: assign the Kalends of April to the first weekday, and so count the days up to the limit of that same year. Whichever weekday the limit is, so many will be the regular number. For example: assign Sunday to the Kalends of April, and on the Nones of April five weekdays will occur [Col. 0163D]. Therefore the regular number will be five. So likewise in the rest. Moreover, if the limit is before the weekday, count backward. If it is after the Kalends, count backward in the antiphon as follows: Sunday, Saturday, Friday, and so in order. But in the antiphon, thus: Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday; and so in order.

## Chapter CIII.—On the Limit of Septuagesima

After the seventh day before the Ides of January, wherever the tenth moon occurs, there will be the limit of Septuagesima. You will find it thus: by however many days the Paschal limit is distant from the Kalends of April, whether backward or forward, by that many days the limit of Septuagesima will be distant from the fifth day before the Kalends of February, either forward or backward.

## Chapter CIV.—On the Lenten Limit

After the eighth day before the Ides of March, wherever the second moon occurs, there will be the limit of Lent; you will find it to be distant from the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, after the manner of the Paschal limit. In a leap year, seek Septuagesima from the fourth day before the Kalends of February, and Lent from the eleventh day before the Kalends of March.

Septuagesima indeed in every leap year.

Lent, however, only when the limit has occurred before the leap day.

## Chapter CV.—On the Rogations

The limit of the Rogations is the twentieth moon of May. [Col. 0164B] Seek it from the Nones of May, as above.

## Chapter CVI.—On Pentecost

The limit of Pentecost is the fourth moon of June. Seek this in every respect from the thirteenth day before the Kalends, as above. To find the weekday, add the concurrent numbers of the present year to the regular numbers; if the total is below seven, that will be the weekday; if above, subtract seven, and the remainder will be the weekday.

## Chapter CVII.—On Advent

From the fifth day before the Kalends of December until the third day before the Nones of the same month, wherever Sunday occurs, there will be the Advent of the Lord.

## Chapter CVIII.—On the Embolism

The first embolism is on the fourth day before the Nones of December, the first moon, in the second year of the nineteen-year cycle; [Col. 0164C] the second is on the fourth day before the Nones of September, in the fifth year; the third on the second day before the Nones of March, in the eighth year.

In that same year, on the Kalends of May the moon will be twenty-seven days old, and on the Kalends of July twenty-nine epacts will intervene, unless it is a leap year.

The fourth embolism is on the fourth day before the Nones of January, in the eleventh year.

In that same year the moon will be twenty-eight days old on the Kalends of March, with epacts intervening, unless it is a leap year.

The fifth will be on the fourth day before the Nones of November, in the thirteenth year.

The sixth will be on the fourth day before the Nones of August, in the sixteenth year.

The seventh will be on the third day before the Nones of March, in the nineteenth year.

[Col. 0164D] In that same year the moon will be twenty-eight days old on the Kalends of May and on the Kalends of August, contrary to the epacts, a lunar leap having been made in July. But if the lunar month of the embolism on the third day before the Nones of March is neglected, in the nineteenth year the Paschal limit will not fall in that year on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

## Chapter CIX.—On Egyptian Days

The days are called Egyptian because they were discovered by the Egyptians. And because Egypt is said to mean “darkness,” they themselves are called dark from this, since they are said to bring the unwary to the darkness of death.

# Book Three

[Col. 0165]

## Exhortation

[Col. 0165A]

Through the described revolving course of time, the revolving world itself thus revolves. But let us now set aside time’s mutability and direct our minds toward the stability of eternity.

I do not think it fruitless to insert into this work the succession of times, so that the reader may profitably come to know all the periods of the world now past.

Sathael, the first archangel, the seal of God’s likeness, created full of wisdom and perfect in beauty amid the delights of the heavenly paradise, did not remain even one full hour; and through pride he incurred eternal exile together with all who agreed with him.

Adam, the first man, formed in Hebron in God’s image, dwelt in paradise with Eve for seven hours; [Col. 0165B] through transgression of the command, he underwent the exile of this world. In it he begot thirty sons and as many daughters, apart from Abel and Cain.

He himself died in Jerusalem after nine hundred and thirty years. Buried at the place of Calvary, he rested there for some time. Then, transferred to Hebron, he returned to the earth from which he had been taken.

Abel, Adam’s son, was killed at Damascus by his brother Cain at the age of thirty.

Seth, Abel’s brother, lived nine hundred and twelve years.

Malaleel lived eight hundred and ninety-five years.

Jareth lived nine hundred and sixty-two years.

[Col. 0165C] Enoch lived three hundred and sixty-five years and was transferred into paradise.

He discovered letters and wrote certain books.

Adam died in his time.

Methuselah lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years.

Lamech lived seven hundred and seventy-seven years.

Giants arose, whose height was fifteen or thirty cubits.

### Kingdom of Cain

Cain was the first to found the city of Enoch, in which he himself first reigned.

After him his son Enoch succeeded.

[Col. 0165D] His son Gaidat succeeded him.

Then Maevia, his daughter, succeeded him.

Her son Mathusael succeeded her.

Then Lamech succeeded him.

He perished in the flood. He also killed Cain.

Jabal, son of Lamech, discovered the use of tents. His brother Jubal discovered music.

Their brother Tubal discovered the craft of working iron and bronze.

Their sister Noema discovered the art of varied weaving.

[Col. 0166A] Noah, the tenth from Adam, lived nine hundred and fifty years. The flood occurred in his time.

Also in his time the rainbow and rain were first seen, and the use of meat was granted to humankind.

## The First Age

This first age contains, according to the Hebrew truth, one thousand six hundred and forty-two years.

According to the Seventy Interpreters, two thousand two hundred and sixty-two.

Ten generations.

## The Second Age

Shem, Noah’s son, is the same person as Melchizedek; he lived six hundred and two years. In his time the human race was divided into three classes: free persons, soldiers, and slaves. The free descended from Shem, the soldiers from Japheth, the slaves [Col. 0166B] from Ham.

Arphaxad, son of Shem, lived three hundred and thirty-eight years; according to the Seventy Interpreters, five hundred and sixty-five.

Cainan lived four hundred and thirty-eight years.

Salem lived four hundred and thirty-three years; he founded Salem.

From him came the Samaritans and Indians.

Heber, from whom the Hebrews derive, lived four hundred and sixty-four years.

Babel was built in his time.

Peleg lived two hundred and thirty-nine years. In his time languages were divided into seventy-two.

Idolatry also arose in his time.

Reu lived two hundred and thirty-nine years. In his [Col. 0166C] time the kingdoms of the Scythians and Egyptians arose.

Serug lived two hundred and thirty years. In his time the kingdoms of the Assyrians and Sicyonians began.

Nahor lived one hundred and forty-eight years.

Terah lived two hundred and five years.

Babylon was founded.

This second age contains, from the flood to Abraham, according to the Hebrew truth, two hundred and ninety-two years and ten generations. According to the Seventy Interpreters, nine hundred and fifty-five; or, with the addition of Cainan, whom the Seventy and Luke include, one thousand and seventy-two, and eleven generations. From Adam to Ninus there are three thousand one hundred and eighty-four years, which have been [Col. 0166D] either omitted or unknown to all historians.

Under Serug, in the second age, Nimrod was the first to reign at Babel, a giant thirty cubits high. His son Assur, from whom the Assyrians derive, succeeded him.

### Kingdom of the Assyrians

His son Belus reigned sixty-five years.

Sacrifices were first offered to Belus.

His son Ninus reigned fifty-two years.

[Col. 0167A] He founded Nineveh.

In his time the magical art was discovered by Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, whom Ninus himself conquered and killed in war; he also subdued Syrophanes, the first Egyptian idolater.

Abraham was born in the time of Ninus.

After Ninus, Semiramis, his wife, reigned for forty-two years under Abraham.

She founded great Babylon and subdued India and Ethiopia.

Her son Ninias succeeded her.

Under Isaac, Arrius, also called Erioch, succeeded Ninias.

Xerxes succeeded him.

After him Beloch reigned.

Then Armamitres.

[Col. 0167B] After him Baal, also called Balaeus.

Then Mamitos.

Next Saporus.

After him Agatides.

Under Caleb, Amyntas.

After him Lamperes.

After him Oeneus.

Then Eutropis.

Next, under Azariah, also called Uzziah, Sardanapalus.

Under him the kingdom of the Assyrians failed, having stood for one thousand one hundred and sixty-four years.

After the division of languages under Reu, the kingdom of the Scythians arose sixty years before that of the Assyrians; Tanaus first reigned there, and from him the river Tanais takes its name.

[Col. 0167C]

### Kingdom of the Egyptians under Kings

In Egypt the first of the kings was Pharaoh; after him the city of Pharos was named, as were the later kings.

Then Zoes.

The seventeenth from him was Amasis, under whom Joseph came into Egypt.

Hebron reigned after him.

Then Amenopolis.

Next Mespres, under whom Joseph died.

Then Nuffar reigned.

After him Muthusis.

Then Thyomosis.

Likewise Amenophis, Horus, Hencres, and Achoris. Likewise Cencres, who was drowned in the Red Sea.

[Col. 0167D]

### Kingdom of the Arcadians

Among the Sicyonians, that is, the Arcadians, the first to reign under Serug was:

Aegialeus, also called Aegelasus.

Archas succeeded him, and Arcadia takes its name from him.

Then Tantalus.

After him, under Abraham, Europs, who subdued Europe, whence it is called Europe; in whose time Efron, also called Enac, a giant, founded Ebroe, eight years after which Tanais was founded in Egypt by Tanaus, under Isaac.

Then the Europeans arose.

Telsion succeeded Europs.

Then Tiriacus, to whom sacrifices were offered.

After him Leucappus.

[Col. 0168A] Then Mesappus, also called Zephysus.

After him Eratho.

Then Ptolemy.

Next Orthopolis.

After him, under Moses, Marathos.

Then Corax.

Then Hercules.

Next Menalion.

After him Parthenopaeus.

After him Phineus.

Then Phallax.

Next Dodanus.

Then Polyphidus.

After him Pelasgus.

After him Zeuxippus, whom Alethes, king [Col. 0168B] of the Corinthians, killed.

And then the kingdom of the Sicyonians, which had stood for nine hundred years, came to an end.

Thereafter priests ruled the people.

## The Third Age

Abraham, the twelfth from Noah.

Abraham lived one hundred and seventy years.

To him Christ was first promised, and circumcision was first given to him. He discovered Hebrew letters. He also taught astronomy to the Chaldeans and geometry to the Egyptians.

In his time five cities—Sodom and Gomorrah with the others—were submerged.

Isaac lived one hundred and twenty years.

[Col. 0168C] In his time the kingdom of the Argives arose.

Jacob lived one hundred and forty-seven years.

In his time there was a flood lasting nine months in Achaea, under Ogygius king of the Thebans, in which Cerambus is said to have flown.

At this time Minerva flourished in Africa.

Shem, who was Melchizedek, died in Jacob’s time.

In the six hundred and second year Memphis was founded in Egypt.

Joseph lived one hundred and ten years.

At this time there was famine for seven years.

Kohath, son of Levi, Joseph’s brother, lived one hundred and thirty-three years.

Amram, his son, lived one hundred and thirty-seven years.

[Col. 0168D] In their time the children of Israel were oppressed in Egypt, and Cecrops founded Athens.

Moses, his son, lived one hundred and twenty years.

In his time Egypt was struck by ten plagues.

He led the children of Israel out of Egypt, and he was the first to write down the law for the people.

In his time there was a flood under Deucalion in Thessaly.

Also in Moses’ time the city of Lacedaemon and the Delphic temple were founded by Cecrops.

### Times of the Judges

Joshua, also called Jesus, lived one hundred and ten years.

In his time the Jordan was dried up for God’s people, and the sun stood still for the space of two days.

[Col. 0169A] Caleb succeeded Joshua; at Joshua’s death he was one hundred years old.

Fables were invented in his time.

At this time Orpheus flourished in music on Lesbos.

At this time Saturn and Jupiter also lived, as Solinus and Varro write.

The first, Persian Sibyl flourished.

Othniel, son of Caleb, judged the people for forty years.

In his time Catherinus founded Thebes. Aioth judged Israel for eighty years.

The first civil war.

In his time there was war between the people of Israel and Benjamin on account of the Levite’s wife, violated at Gibeah; [Col. 0169B] forty thousand men of Israel and thirty-five thousand one hundred men of Benjamin were killed.

Troy was built.

Amphion the musician flourished.

Shamgar ruled the Jewish people for ten years. At this time the kingdom of the Laurentians arose.

Barak with Deborah judged Israel for forty years.

In his time there was the second, Libyan Sibyl.

Picus was king in Italy.

Gideon judged Israel for forty years. Hercules lived in his time.

Orpheus the musician flourished.

Abimelech, son of Gideon, reigned over the children of Israel for three years.

[Col. 0169C] Theseus lived in this time.

Tola judged Israel for twenty-three years. In his time there was the third, Delphic Sibyl.

Priam was in Troy.

Jair judged Israel for twenty-two years.

At this time there was the Theban war.

The nymph Carmentis.

Jephthah judged Israel for six years.

In his time lived the Amazons and Theseus.

Abessan judged Israel for seven years.

At this time Boaz took Ruth.

At this time also the fourth Sibyl flourished, the Erythraean or Babylonian.

Achialon judged Israel for ten years.

In his time Troy was besieged.

[Col. 0169D] Labdon judged Israel for eight years.

In his time Troy was taken.

On the Greek side, eight hundred and seventy-seven thousand were killed.

On the Trojan side, six hundred and eighty-six thousand.

Aeneas fought with Turnus in Italy.

Blind Samson judged for twenty years. At this time the kingdom of the Albans arose.

Ascanius founded Alba.

Eli the priest judged Israel for forty years.

[Col. 0170A] At this time the fifth, Cumaean Sibyl flourished, to whom Aeneas came.

Samuel judged Israel for twelve years. In his time lived Orestes and Pylades; the kingdom of the Lacedaemonians then arose.

Saul, the first king of the Hebrews, reigned twenty years, or forty, as the Acts of the Apostles testify.

In his time David killed Goliath the giant.

This third age of the world contains, according to either authority, fourteen generations from Abraham to David, and nine hundred and forty years.

From the flood to David there are two thousand one hundred and seventeen years.  
[Note: [Col. 0169D] From a comparison of these numbers it would follow that the flood was only seven years distant from the creation of the world—an absurdity obvious to everyone. We have therefore corrected them from the most excellent work entitled *Art de vérifier les dates* [*The Art of Verifying Dates*], [Col. 0170D] so that the former number becomes one thousand two hundred and sixty-three years, and the latter two thousand nine hundred and nineteen. EDITORS.]

From the beginning of the world to David, two thousand one hundred [Col. 0170B] and twenty-four years.  
[Note: [Col. 0169D] From a comparison of these numbers it would follow that the flood was only seven years distant from the creation of the world—an absurdity obvious to everyone. We have therefore corrected them from the most excellent work entitled *Art de vérifier les dates* [*The Art of Verifying Dates*], [Col. 0170D] so that the former number becomes one thousand two hundred and sixty-three years, and the latter two thousand nine hundred and nineteen. EDITORS.]

### Kingdom of the Idumaeans

In the third age the first king of the Idumaeans was Balak, son of Beor.

After him Jobab, also called Job, reigned.

Then Husan.

Next five other kings.

Then chiefs.

Job, however, was the fifth from Abraham.

Abraham begot Isaac.

Isaac begot Esau, also called Edom, from whom come the Idumaeans. Esau begot Zara.

He begot Job under Moses.

Balak’s son Sefer was king of Moab and Midian; he hired the diviner Balaam, who is read of as Elihu in the Book of Job [Col. 0170C].

Job was tested at eighty-nine years of age. After his affliction he became king and lived one hundred and forty years.

### Kingdom of the Argives

At Argos, Inachus first reigned under Isaac for fifty years.

His daughter Io sailed from Greece to Ethiopia and, coming into Egypt, there discovered letters and taught laws. She ruled justly, whence she was called the goddess Isis. Her husband Osiris lived under Jacob.

Phoroneus succeeded Inachus.

Apis, also called Epaphus, succeeded him; later, reigning in Egypt, he was called Serapis.

After him Argus reigned under Joseph; from him came the city Argos and the Argives.

[Col. 0170D] Then Honoreus, who first yoked oxen to the plough.

Eriasus succeeded him.

Phorbalus succeeded him under Moses.

Then Tophas.

Then Jasius, Dardanus’ brother.

Then Stelenus.

Then Danaus, under Adar, who had fifty daughters. His brother Aegystus had as many sons, all of whom, save one, were killed by the daughters.

[Col. 0171A] Egypt was named after this Aegystus.

After Danaus, Abas reigned.

His son Acrisius succeeded him.

Then Euristeus.

Then Euchippus.

Then Adrassus (under Jephthah), through whom Theseus destroyed Argos, and thus the kingdom of the Argives failed.

Also in the third age, under Moses, Prometheus, king of the Caucasus, first taught philosophy in the East. Atlas, his brother and king of Africa, taught astrology. Hesperus, their brother, reigned in Italy and called it Hesperia.

### Kingdom of the Athenians

Under Moses Cecrops, who first reigned there, founded Athens and subdued Egypt when Pharaoh was drowned in the Red Sea.

[Col. 0171B] Menander reigned after him.

Then, under Caleb, Amphitryon, father of Hercules. Next, under Othniel, Erichthonius, inventor of the chariot.

After him Pandion, father of Progne and Philomela.

Then Aegeus.

Next Theseus.

After him Demophoon.

After him Mnesteus.

Then Melanto.

Next Codrus, under Samuel, who surrendered himself to the enemy for his people.

After him a magistrate presided over the people.

### Kingdom of the Amazons

In this age the Amazons reigned in Asia.

First Marpesia and Lampeto, who founded Ephesus [Col. 0171C].

Then Synope.

Next, under Tola, Antiope and Hippolyte.

After her Oretria.

After her Penthesilea.

Pyrrhus killed her at Troy.

### Kingdom of the Trojans under Othniel

In this age also Dardanus reigned in Phrygia.

His son Erichthonius succeeded him under Aioth.

His son Trous succeeded him, and Troy takes its name from him.

His son was Ilus, from whom came Ilium.

His son in turn was Laomedon.

His son Priam, father of Hector and Paris, succeeded him under Jephthah.

Then the Greeks destroyed the kingdom of the Phrygians, [Col. 0171D] which had stood for eight hundred and two years.

### Kingdom of the Thebans

Cadmus founded Thebes, first reigned there, and discovered Greek letters.

Pentheus succeeded him.

Laus succeeded him under Gideon.

Oedipus succeeded him.

Eteocles and Polynices succeeded him.

Creon succeeded him [read: them].

After him, under Jephthah, Theseus destroyed Thebes.

In Crete Saturn reigned under Joshua.

Jupiter reigned after him.

Then, under Aioth, Minos.

[Col. 0172A] Next Idomenus, who, with others, besieged Troy under Aioth.

Liber reigned in India under Barak.

Perseus reigned in Persia and killed Liber.

### Kingdom of the Mycenaeans

At Mycenae Tantalus reigned.

Then his son Pelops.

Next his son Atreus.

After him, under Jephthah, Agamemnon and Menelaus, his sons.

After them Orestes, son of Agamemnon.

### Kingdom of the Italians under Moses

In Italy reigned:

First Hesperus, from whom Hesperia.

Oenotrius, son of Lycaon, under Caleb.

Dardanus.

Italus, from whom Italy.

[Col. 0172B] Sabinus, from whom the Sabines.

Janus Saturnus, from whom Saturnia.

Latius Picus, who discovered augury.

Faunus.

Evander, whose mother Carmentis discovered Latin letters, under Samson.

Latinus, from whom the Latins are named.

After him the kingdom of the Laurentians failed.

## [The Fourth Age]

### Kingdom of Jerusalem, or Judah

In the fourth age David, the fourteenth king from Abraham, reigned in Jerusalem for forty years.

At this time Homer flourished and Carthage was founded.

The prophets Nathan and Gad.

[Col. 0172C] Solomon, son of David, reigned forty years.

He made the first temple in Jerusalem.

Rehoboam, son of Solomon, reigned seventeen years.

In his time the kingdom of Israel arose.

Smyrna was founded by the Amazons.

Abia reigned three years.

Samos was founded.

Asa reigned forty-one years.

Jehoshaphat reigned twenty-five years.

Elijah the prophet flourished.

At this time it did not rain for three years.

He was the first to raise a dead person.

Joram reigned eight years.

Elisha the prophet flourished.

[Col. 0172D] Elijah was translated.

Azariah reigned one year.

Athaliah, his mother, reigned seven years.

Joash, son of Azariah, reigned forty years.

Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, was stoned.

Amaziah reigned twenty-nine years.

Uzziah reigned fifty-two years.

The prophets Isaiah, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, and Micah flourished.

In his time the sixth Sibyl flourished.

The kingdom of the Assyrians was transferred to the Medes; it had stood for three hundred and fifty-five years.

The kingdom of the Macedonians arose.

Jotham reigned sixteen years.

[Col. 0173A] In his time the Olympiad was instituted by the Greeks at the city of Elis.

Ahaz reigned sixteen years.

Rome was founded.

The Roman kingdom arose.

Israel was deported.

Hezekiah reigned twenty-eight years.

Romulus established the senate and the year.

Manasseh reigned fifty-five years.

Numa added two months. He was killed by slaves.

Amon reigned two years.

Arion the cithara-player flourished.

Josiah reigned thirty-one years; he was killed by the king of Egypt.

In his time Nineveh was destroyed by King Cyaxares, [Col. 0173B] after having stood one thousand four hundred and seventy years from Ninus.

The Samian Sibyl and the prophet Jeremiah flourished.

Joachaz, son of Josiah, reigned three months.

Eliachim, son of Josiah, reigned eleven years.

Jechonias, also called Joachim, son of Joachim, reigned three months.

Zedekiah, son of Josiah, reigned eleven years. In his time Jerusalem was destroyed by the Babylonians. After him the kingdom of Judah failed, having then stood for five hundred and forty-nine years.

This fourth age of the world, from David to the Babylonian deportation, contains, according to the Hebrew truth, four hundred and seventy-five years; according to the Seventy Translators, twelve more; [Col. 0173C] fourteen generations. From the beginning of the world, four thousand six hundred and ten years.

### Kingdom of Israel

In this age Jeroboam reigned in Israel for twenty-two years.

King Abia defeated him, and he died.

His son Nabath reigned two years.

Baasa killed him.

Baasa reigned twenty-two years. He died of illness.

His son Sela reigned two years.

His servant Zamri killed him.

Zamri reigned seven days.

Amri, commander of the army, killed him.

Amri reigned twelve years in Samaria. He [Col. 0173D] died of illness.

His son Ahab reigned two years. He fell through a lattice and died.

Joram, brother of Ochozias, reigned twelve years.

Jehu, Ahab’s servant, killed him.

Jehu reigned twenty-eight years. He died of illness.

His son Joachaz reigned seventeen years. He died of illness.

His son Joash likewise reigned seventeen years.

His son Jeroboam reigned forty-one years.

His son Zacharias reigned six months. Sellum killed him.

Sellum reigned one month.

[Col. 0174A] Manahen killed him.

Manahen reigned ten years. He died of illness.

His son Phaceia reigned two years.

Phaceia, his general, killed him.

Phaceia reigned twenty years.

Osee killed him.

Osee reigned nine years.

King Salmanasser transferred him together with all the people among the Assyrians, and thus the kingdom of Israel failed, having stood for three hundred and fifty years.

Tobias lived during this captivity.

### Kingdom of the Macedonians under Uzziah

In Macedonia Karanus first reigned twenty-eight years.

Perdiccas succeeded him.

[Col. 0174B] Alexander succeeded him.

Then Archelaus, son of Perdiccas.

Then Amyntas.

Then Philip.

Then, under Darius, Alexander the Great.

Then Philip, Alexander’s brother.

Then Cassander.

And the kingdom of the Greeks stood for seven hundred years, until the time of Ptolemy Philometor, when it failed.

### Kingdom of the Albans under Samson

At Alba Aeneas reigned three years.

He founded Lavinium and perished by lightning under Eli.

Ascanius, also called Julius, son of Aeneas, from whom came the Julian family.

Sylvius Posthumus, brother of Ascanius, reigned [Col. 0174C] thirty-nine years. From him all the kings of Alba were called Sylvii.

Aeneas Sylvius reigned thirty-one years, under David.

Latinus Sylvius reigned fifty years.

His son Alba reigned thirty-nine years. From him came the Alban kings.

Aegyptus, or Epyrus, or Atis Sylvius, reigned twenty-four years, under Asa.

Capys Sylvius reigned twenty-eight years. He founded Capua.

Carpentus Sylvius reigned thirteen years.

Tiberinus Sylvius reigned nine years.

The river is called the Tiber after him because he was [Col. 0174D] drowned in it; previously it was called the Albula.

Agrippa Sylvius reigned forty years.

Aremulus Sylvius reigned nineteen years. He perished by lightning.

Aventinus Sylvius reigned thirty-seven years. Mount Aventine takes its name from him.

Procas Sylvius reigned twenty-three years, under Uzziah.

Amulius Sylvius reigned forty-three years. His brother was Numitor; Numitor’s daughter Rhea bore Remus and Romulus, who killed Amulius and restored Numitor to the kingdom. Under him the kingdom of the Albans failed, having then stood for four hundred and fifty years.

### Kingdom of the Romans

Romulus founded Rome and first reigned thirty-seven years.

[Col. 0175A] He perished by lightning.

Numa Pompilius reigned forty-one years.

He discovered necromancy and first instituted sacred rites. He died of illness.

Tullus Hostilius reigned thirty-two years. He too perished by lightning under Josiah.

Ancus Martius reigned twenty-three years. He founded Ostia. He died of illness.

Tarquinius Priscus reigned thirty-seven years. He instituted the circus and games at Rome. Ancus’ son killed him.

Servilius Tullus reigned thirty-four years. Tarquinius killed him, under Cyrus.

Tarquinius Superbus reigned twenty-five years. [Col. 0175B] He was expelled from the kingdom, and consuls were created; and the kings had ruled for two hundred and forty-three years.

## The Fifth Age

### Kingdom of the Babylonians

In the fifth age Nebuchadnezzar reigned at Babylon for forty-four years.

The eighth, Cumaean Sibyl flourished.

The prophet Ezekiel flourished.

His son Evilmerodach reigned eighteen years.

Daniel and the three youths flourished.

Egesar, his son, reigned forty years. The seven sages flourished.

Labosordach reigned nine months.

The prophet Habakkuk flourished.

[Col. 0175C] Baltazar reigned seventeen years. Cyrus killed him and destroyed Babylon.

### Kingdom of the Persians

Cyrus first of the Persians reigned with Darius for twenty-five years.

He released the captivity.

The queen of the Amazons killed him.

The ninth Sibyl flourished.

Cambyses, also called Nebuchadnezzar, son of Cyrus, reigned eight years.

Judith lived in his time.

He founded Babylon in Egypt.

The Magus Smerdes reigned seven months.

Pythagoras the philosopher flourished.

[Col. 0175D] Darius reigned thirty-six years.

Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi flourished.

His son Xerxes reigned twenty years.

The tenth, Phrygian Sibyl flourished.

Artabanus reigned seven months. Herodotus flourished.

Artaxerxes reigned forty years.

Hippocrates the physician flourished, and Ezra.

His son Xerxes reigned two months.

Socrates flourished.

Sogdianus reigned eight months.

Democritus flourished.

Darius, son of Artaxerxes, reigned nineteen years.

Plato flourished.

[Col. 0176A] Artaxerxes Ahasuerus, son of Darius, reigned forty years.

Esther flourished.

The eleventh, Tiburtine Sibyl flourished.

Artaxerxes, also called Ochus, reigned twenty-six years.

Aristotle flourished.

Arses, also called Xerxes, reigned four years.

Zeno the Stoic flourished.

Darius, the last of the Persians, reigned six years.

Alexander killed him. Under him the Persian kingdom failed, having stood for two hundred and thirty-eight years.

### Kingdom of Alexandria

Alexander the Great founded Alexandria. He [Col. 0176B] died by poison and reigned twelve years. He destroyed Tyre.

Ptolemy, also called Soter or Lagides, son of Lagus, reigned in Alexandria forty years. He died of illness, and from him the other kings were called Ptolemies or Lagidae.

Ptolemy Philadelphus, son of the former, reigned thirty-eight years. He died of illness.

The Seventy Interpreters flourished.

He founded Philadelphia.

Ptolemy Euergetes, Philadelphus’ brother, reigned twenty-six years; he likewise died. Under him the son of Sirach flourished.

Ptolemy Philopator, Euergetes’ brother, reigned seventeen years. He died of illness.

[Col. 0176C] Ptolemy Epiphanes reigned twenty-four years. He died of illness.

Philometor reigned thirty-five years.

Ptolemy Euergetes, brother of the preceding, reigned twenty-nine years. He died in the same manner.

Ptolemy Physcon, also called Soter, reigned seventeen years. He was driven from the kingdom because he killed his brother’s son.

Ptolemy Alexander, brother of Soter, reigned ten years; he too was expelled from the kingdom because he killed his mother.

Ptolemy Physcon, the same as above, reigned a second time, eight years. He died of illness.

Ptolemy Dionysius reigned thirty years; he [Col. 0176D] had Cleopatra as his sister.

He killed Pompey. He himself perished in a shipwreck.

Cleopatra, Ptolemy’s sister and wife, reigned twenty-two years. She died by a serpent, and thus the kingdom of the Ptolemies and Lagidae failed, having stood for two hundred and ninety-five years.

### Kingdom of Syria

Seleucus reigned in Syria after Alexander the Great. He founded Seleucia.

Ptolemy Lagides killed him under Philadelphus.

His son Antiochus, also called Soter, reigned after him. He founded Antioch. He died of illness.

Antiochus Theos, son of the latter, reigned after him. He likewise died.

[Col. 0177A] Seleucus Callinicus, together with his brother Antiochus, son of the preceding ruler, reigned after him.

Ptolemy Euergetes killed him.

Antiochus the Great, together with his brother Seleucus Ceraunus, son of Seleucus, then reigned.

He had a daughter, and both perished by lightning.

Seleucus Eupator, son of Antiochus the Great, reigned after his father. Two men killed him by poison under Philometor.

Antiochus Illustris, hostage at Rome.

Epiphanes, Seleucus’ brother, reigned after him. Under him were the wars of the Maccabees.

He died in great torment of pain.

Antiochus Eupator, son of Antiochus, reigned after his father. Demetrius, son of Seleucus, killed him.

[Col. 0177B] Demetrius, son of Seleucus, then reigned. Alexander, son of Antiochus, killed him.

Alexander Nobilis, son of Antiochus, reigned after him. Ptolemy Philometor killed him.

Demetrius, son of Demetrius, reigned after him. King Mithridates killed him.

Antiochus, son of Alexander, reigned after him. Tryphon killed him.

Alexander, son of Antiochus, reigned after him. The general Diodotus killed him.

Antiochus the First, son of Demetrius, reigned after him. He was killed in Parthia.

Antiochus Spondius, son of Antiochus, reigned after him. He fled from the kingdom.

Demetrius Mario, brother of Antiochus, reigned after him. [Col. 0177C] King Alexander of the Jews killed him under Pompey.

Antiochus, also called Dionysius, brother of King Demetrius, reigned. The king of the Arabs killed him.

After him the kingdom of Syria failed, having stood for two hundred and seventy years.

## On the Consuls and Dictators of Rome

After the kings, the Romans had consuls, of whom we shall note the principal ones here.

In the 244th year from the founding of the City: the first consuls, Brutus and Tarquinius. They waged war against King Porsenna.

In the 248th year from the founding of the City: Valerius and Posthumius, consuls, defeated the Sabines and Aurunci.

In the 251st year of the City: Laertius was created [Col. 0177D] dictator and commander.

He presided over the consuls.

The consuls were Posthumius and Comminius.

In the 253rd year of the City: Posthumius, dictator; Brutus and Venusius, consuls. They fought with Tarquinius Superbus.

In the 258th year of the City: Valerius, dictator; Appius and Servilius, consuls. They fought with the Volscians and the equites.

In the 262nd year of the City: Cincinnatus, taken from the plough, was made dictator.

Minutius and Sempronius, consuls. They freed the City from its enemies.

In the 265th year of the City: Cassius and Proculus, consuls.

[Col. 0178A] A serious uprising between [the text reads *contra*, corrected to *inter*: “between”] the senators and the plebs.

In the 271st year of the City: Fabius and Manilius, consuls. They fought with the Veientes.

In the 283rd year of the City: Aemilius and Quintius, consuls. They instituted the lustrum.

In the 292nd year of the City: Volumius and Publicola, consuls. They waged a great war against exiles and slaves.

In the 302nd year of the City: the decemvirs were created as proconsuls.

In the 312th year of the City: military tribunes were created as proconsuls.

In the 316th year of the City: Mamertus was again made dictator, and Gorgonius and Sergius consuls.

They waged a very great war against the Falisci and [Col. 0178B] the Fidenates.

In the 322nd year of the City: Aurelius, dictator; Julius and Mento, consuls. They waged a great war against the Volscians and the equites.

In the 327th year of the City: Aemilius, dictator, and four military tribunes were appointed as proconsuls. By them the Veientes were defeated seven times, under Alexander.

In the Year of the City 336. Cornelius, dictator. Fabius and Cossus, consuls. They fought with the Volscians and the cavalry.

In the Year of the City 348. Camillus, taken from his farm, dictator; military tribunes with consular power. They defeated the Etruscans, under Ptolemy.

In the Year of the City 362. The three Fabii were made military tribunes with consular power. They fought with the Gauls. But the Romans were defeated. [Col. 0178C]

In the Year of the City 398. Sulpicius, dictator. Popilius and Manlius, consuls. They defeated the Gauls.

In the Year of the City 409. Valerius and Cornelius, consuls. They defeated the Samnites in a severe war.

In the Year of the City 412. Torquatus and Decius, consuls. They fought with Alexander, king of Epirus, and killed him.

In the Year of the City 467. Fabricius and Curtius, consuls (under Philadelphus). They fought with Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, and killed him.

In the 475th year from the founding of the City. Genutius, consul, defeated the Africans and the Tarentines.

In the year 477. Sempronius, consul, defeated the Picentes.

In the year 483. Claudius and Fabius, consuls. They defeated the Sicilians and the Carthaginians, under Philadelphus. [Col. 0178D]

Cornelius and Duillius, consuls, fought with Hannibal the Elder, commander of the Carthaginians, and killed him.

Regulus and Manlius, consuls, fought with Hamilcar, commander of the Carthaginians, and killed him.

Paulus and Fulvius fought a naval battle with the Carthaginians and were victorious.

Metellus and Furius, consuls, fought with Hasdrubal, commander of the Carthaginians, and killed him.

Atilius and Manlius, consuls, were defeated by Hannibal, son of Hamilcar, the commander.

Scipio and Sempronius were defeated by the same man.

[Col. 0179A] Aemilius and Varro, consuls, were killed with their whole army by the same man.

Scipio, afterwards called Africanus, defeated and captured Mago, Hannibal’s brother and commander.

Laevinus, the other consul, captured Hanno, commander of the Africans.

Scaevola, consul.

Gracchus, praetor, was killed.

Marcellus, consul, defeated Hannibal in battle. Caro Censorinus, consul, conquered Spain.

Fabius, consul, destroyed Carthalo, Hannibal’s commander, with his entire army.

Drusus and Flaminius, consuls, killed Hasdrubal, Hannibal’s brother, with his entire army.

Laelius, consul, defeated King Syphax.

[Col. 0179B] The other Scipio, consul, defeated Hannibal and the entire people of Carthage, and brought in Terentius.

Licinius and Cassius, consuls, defeated the Macedonians in a very great battle.

Censorinus and Manlius, consuls, together with Scipio destroyed Carthage, killing all its people; it had stood for seven hundred years.

Metellus and Marius, consuls, defeated King Jugurtha in various battles.

Manilius and Scipio, consuls, defeated the Cimbri and Teutones in a very great battle, under Tuisco.

Sulla, consul, defeated King Mithridates in many battles.

Cinna, consul, killed the senate, and was himself killed.

Tullius and Antonius, consuls, destroyed Catiline and his followers.

[Col. 0179C] Pompey, dictator and consul, fought in the East with twenty-two kings and conquered them.

Crassus, dictator and consul, conquered Parthia and was killed there, under Dionysius.

Julius Caesar, dictator and consul, conquered Gaul and defeated Pompey, the consul, together with all the peoples of the East. He was the first monarch and reigned for five years.

He composed the leap-year—indeed, the great cycle.

He was killed by the senate.

From him rulers were called Caesars.

Lepidus, dictator and consul, conquered Africa and Sicily.

[Col. 0179D] Antony, dictator and consul, conquered Egypt and Judaea.

Octavian, dictator and consul, afterwards called Augustus, defeated Antony and Cleopatra in a very great battle and brought peace to the whole world.

After him the consuls ceased, having existed for four hundred and seventy-four years. Augusti, or Caesars, succeeded them.

## CONCERNING THE PRIESTS

These priests presided over the people of God under the Law until Christ, forty-seven in number.

Aaron, Eleazar, Phinehas, Abishua, Bukki, Uzzi, Zerahiah, Meraioth, Amariah, Ahitub, Zadok, Ahimaaz, Azariah, Johanan, Azariah, Amariah, Ahitub, Zadok, Shallum, Hilkiah, Azariah, Zerahiah; at the Babylonian deportation, [Col. 0180A] Jozadak. After the return: John, Joiakim, Eliashib, Joiada, Jonathan; under Alexander the Great, Jaddua, Onias, Simon, Eleazar, Manasseh, Onias, Simon, Jason, Menelaus, Lysimachus, Judas Maccabaeus, Jonathan, Simon son of John, Simon, Aristobulus, Alexander, Hyrcanus, Aristobulus under Herod, Antigonus. He was killed by Antony, the Roman consul; Herod the Idumaean was appointed king, and reigned for thirty-six years.

Thus the priests descended from Aaron came to an end. They had presided from Aaron until Christ for one thousand six hundred and seven years.

The fifth age, from the Babylonian captivity until Christ, contains fourteen generations and [Col. 0180B] five hundred and eighty-seven years.

From the beginning of the world until Christ, according to the Hebrew truth, there are 4,763 years; according to the Seventy Interpreters, 5,228.

## THE SIXTH AGE: CONCERNING THE ROMAN AUGUSTI AND CAESARS UNTIL FREDERICK I

In the sixth age Augustus Caesar reigned fifty-six years and six months.

In his time Christ was born.

He died by poison.

John the Baptist was renowned, as were the poets Virgil, Horace, and Ovid.

Cologne was founded by King Agrippa.

Augsburg was founded by King Drusus, Augustus’s stepson.

[Col. 0180C] Tiberius, Augustus’s stepson, reigned thirty-three years; he perished by poison.

In this time John was beheaded.

Christ was crucified.

Gaius Caligula reigned three years and ten months. He was killed by his own people.

Matthew wrote the Gospel.

Philo was renowned.

Claudius reigned thirteen years and eight months. Mark wrote the Gospel. He too perished by poison.

The first persecution of Christians.

Nero reigned thirteen years and nine months; he killed himself.

Luke wrote the Gospel.

James the apostle was stoned by the Jews.

[Col. 0180D] Peter was crucified.

Paul was beheaded.

Lucan and Josephus were renowned.

Galba and Piso reigned seven months. Otho killed them.

Otho, three months. He killed himself.

Vitellius, eight months. Vespasian killed him.

Vespasian, nine years; he died of a flux of the belly.

Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans; it had stood for 1,089 years.

The second persecution.

Titus, two years and two months. He died of illness.

Domitian, Titus’s brother, fifteen years and five months. Statius was renowned.

[Col. 0181A] He was stabbed by his own people.

Nerva, one year and four months. He died of illness.

John wrote the Gospel.

The third persecution.

Trajan, nineteen years and six and a half months. He died of a flux of the belly.

John the apostle died.

Aelius Hadrian, twenty-one years. He died of illness. He rebuilt Jerusalem and named it Aelia.

Aquila the translator was renowned.

The fourth persecution.

Antoninus Pius, with his sons Aurelius and Lucius, twenty-two years and three months.

[Col. 0181B] Marcus Antoninus Verus, with his brother Lucius Aurelius Commodus, nineteen years and one month.

Under these emperors Agapitus, a boy of fifteen, was crowned with martyrdom.

Lucius Antoninus Commodus, son of Antoninus, thirteen years.

Theodotion the translator was renowned.

Aelius Pertinax, six months. He was killed in the palace by the soldier Julianus.

Theophilus wrote the Paschal Cycle.

The fifth persecution.

Julianus reigned seven years. He was killed by a servant.

Severus Pertinax, seventeen years; the emperor Albinus killed him.

Narcissus the bishop was renowned.

[Col. 0181C] Antoninus Caracalla, seven years; killed by enemies.

The fifth edition was discovered.

Macrinus, one year; killed by soldiers.

The sixth edition was discovered.

Aurelius Alexander, thirteen years; killed by a soldier.

Origen was renowned.

The sixth persecution.

Maximian, three years. He was killed by Pupienus, who himself, having usurped the empire, was also killed.

Gordian, seven years; killed by his own people.

Philip, with his son Philip, seven years. He became a Christian through Origen. Decius [Col. 0181D] killed them both.

The seventh persecution.

Decius, one year and eight months; killed by the devil.

Antony was renowned.

Gallus, with his son Volusianus, two years and four months. He was killed by Aemilius.

Aemilius, reigning three months, was killed.

The eighth persecution.

Valerian, with his son Gallienus, fifteen years. One was captured and blinded by the Parthians; the other was killed by soldiers.

Under this emperor, namely Gallienus, six tyrants ruled.

The first, Genus, was killed at Mursa.

[Col. 0182A] The second, Posthumus, reigned ten years in Gaul; he was killed.

The third, Aemilianus, was killed at Mainz.

The fourth, Marius, was killed in the same place.

The fifth, Victorinus, was created by the Gauls and killed.

The sixth, Tetricus, was killed by soldiers.

The ninth persecution.

Claudius, one year and nine months. He died of illness.

Quintilius, his brother, reigned seventeen days and was killed.

Aurelian, five years and six months; killed by his own people.

Tacitus, six months. He was killed near Pontus.

Florianus reigned two and a half months and was killed at [Col. 0182B] Tarsus.

Probus, six years and four months. He was killed by soldiers.

He himself killed three tyrants: Saturninus, Proculus, and Bonosus.

Carus, with his sons Carinus and Numerian, reigned two years. Carus died by lightning. Carinus was killed by his companions.

The tenth persecution.

Diocletian, with Herculius Maximian, twenty years. One was expelled from power; the other was killed.

Constantius, with Galerius Maximian, sixteen years. He died in Britain, killing himself.

Carausius reigned seven years. He was killed by Allectus.

[Col. 0182C] Allectus reigned three months. His prefect killed him.

Achilleus, emperor, was killed in Egypt.

Maximius Severus, four years. He perished by treachery at Tarsus.

Constantine, son of Constantius by his concubine Helena, thirty years and ten months. He was baptized by Sylvester, and for this purpose the Council of Nicaea was assembled.

Constantinople was founded.

Maxentius and Licinius, ten years: both were killed by Constantine.

Crispus, son of Constantine son of Constantius, and Licinius, son of Licinius, Caesars, were killed by Constantine.

[Col. 0182D] The emperor Dalmatius was killed by soldiers. Constantius, with his brothers Constantine and Constans, twenty-four years, five and a half months. Constantius died of illness. Constantine was killed by his brother; Constans was killed in Spain.

Under Constantius there were these seven tyrants:

1. Magnentius, who killed himself.

2. Decentius, his brother, who ended his life by the noose.

3. Gallus, whom Constantius himself killed.

4. Silvanus, whom he also killed.

5. Vetranio, who laid down the imperial power.

6. Nepotianus, whom Magnentius’s commanders killed.

7. Julian, who afterwards became Augustus. He reigned two years and eight months.

[Col. 0183A] He became an idolater and was killed by the martyr Mercurius.

Jovian, eight months; he died of illness.

Athanasius was renowned.

Valentinian, with Valens, eleven years. Valentinian died of a hemorrhage.

The tyrant Procopius was killed.

Valens, with Gratian and Valentinian, his brother’s sons, four years.

The tyrant Firmus was killed.

Martin, Ambrose, and Jerome were renowned.

Gratian, with his brother Valentinian, six years; Gratian was burned by fire.

Valentinian was killed by the Goths; or, as others maintain, Gratian was killed by the tyrant Maximus, and Valentinian was [Col. 0183B] expelled from power.

Theodosius and the Valentinian mentioned above, eleven years. He was hanged by a noose.

Maximus and Victor, his son, emperors, were killed.

The tyrant Eugenius was killed.

Arcadius, son of Theodosius, thirteen years; he died.

Chrysostom and Augustine were renowned.

Honorius, brother of Arcadius, with Theodosius, his brother’s son, fifteen years; he died.

King Alaric devastated Rome, which had stood for 1,064 years.

Under Honorius there were seven tyrants:

1. Eucherius, whom Honorius killed.

2. Constantine, whom Count Constantius killed.

[Col. 0183C] 3. Constans, son of Constantine, whom Count Gerontius killed.

4. Maximinus; he went into exile.

5. Jovian, who was soon killed.

6. Attalus, whose hands were cut off by Honorius.

7. Heraclianus; he was killed by soldiers.

Theodosius, son of Arcadius, the Younger, twenty-six years.

Augustine died then.

The tyrant Gildo was killed.

Valentinian, son of Count Constantius, twelve years.

Attila, king of the Huns.

Martian and Valentinian, seven years, were killed [Col. 0183D] by Attila.

The Angles invaded Britain.

Leo the Great, seventeen years; he died.

Victorius wrote the Paschal Cycle.

Zeno, seventeen years; he died.

Theodoric, king of the Goths.

[Col. 0184A] Anastasius, twenty-eight years, a heretic, perished by lightning.

Fulgentius the bishop was renowned.

Justin the Elder, eight years. He died.

Benedict the abbot and Boethius were renowned.

Justinian, nephew of Justinian [sic], thirty-eight years.

Dionysius the abbot wrote the Paschal Cycle.

Justin the Younger, eleven years; he died.

King Totila was killed.

Tiberius Constantine, eight years; he died.

The Lombards invaded Italy.

Maurice, twenty-one years; killed.

Pope Gregory was renowned.

The tyrant Phocas, eight years, was killed. England was converted.

[Col. 0184B] Heraclius, twenty-six years, died of dropsy.

The Cross was exalted.

Constantine, son of Heraclius, six months, perished by poison.

Heraclonas, two years; his nose was cut off.

Isidore the bishop was renowned.

Constantine, son of the preceding emperor, twenty-eight years; he was killed.

Constantine, his son, twenty-seven years; he died.

The Sixth Council of Constantinople.

Justinian, son of Constantine, ten years; his nose and tongue were cut off.

He was expelled from power.

[Col. 0184C] Leontius, three years. Justinian killed him.

Cuthbert the bishop was renowned.

Tiberius, seven years. Justin destroyed him in custody.

Bede was renowned in England.

Justinian, for a second time, with his son Tiberius, six years; he was killed by philosophers. The other was beheaded.

Pippin, king of the Franks.

Philippicus, one year and six months.

He was blinded by Anastasius.

Anastasius, six years.

He was captured by Theodosius and ordained a priest.

Theodosius, one year. He was Catholic and died.

Leo, eight years, a heretic.

Constantine, son of Leo, thirty-five years, [Col. 0184D] a heretic.

Leo, son of Constantine, five years.

Constantine, son of Leo, with his mother.

## CONTINUATION I

> [Note: [Col. 0185] Added in 6 c by another hand.]

[Col. 0186B] Emperor Frederick died by drowning on the Jerusalem expedition. His son Henry succeeded him. Having captured many nobles of that land and afflicted them with various punishments, he subjugated Apulia to himself. At length, after many victories, while fortune smiled on him and he was embracing the summit of the honours of the whole world, he died—to the disturbance of many, alas for sorrow. [Col. 0187A] After his death, very many disturbances arose everywhere in the lands.

## CONTINUATION II

> [Note: [Col. 0187] Extant in 1 C.]

Conrad reigned 15 years. Frederick reigned 38 years. In his time Saladin occupied Jerusalem.

In the year 1187, his son Henry reigned 7 years. Sicily and Apulia were subject to him.

## CONTINUATION III

> [Note: [Col. 0187] From codex Lun. in quarto 81, now Vienna 818, described by Wattenbach.]

Frederick, 38. Henry, his son, 8. King Philip, his brother, 11. He was treacherously killed at Bamberg by Otto the Count Palatine.

## CONTINUATION IV

> [Note: [Col. 0187] From Admont codex 400, quarto, twelfth century. We owe this also to Wattenbach.]

After him Frederick was elected [Note: [Col. 0187] “But who after him” erased. What follows was added in another hand.]. His son, Emperor Henry, succeeded him and died in Apulia on the third day before the Kalends of September. King Philip was killed by Otto the Count Palatine. Otto obtained the empire, but soon lost it through the princes of the whole land; Frederick, king of Apulia, was elected. But who [Note: [Col. 0187] “But who … will see” added by a third hand.] is to obtain the kingdom after him, posterity will see.

## CONTINUATION V

> [Note: [Col. 0187] Added to codex 8 by a later hand of the mid-thirteenth century, indeed by the former owner of this codex, Nicholas Staglinus, as is clear from the autograph note to be read at the foot of the page. Foringer.]

Emperor Frederick reigned 35 years. He threw down the walls and towers of the Milanese. After this he undertook the Jerusalem expedition: passing through Hungary, he subdued Greece, defeated the sultan of Iconium and many nations of pagans by fire and sword. On the eve of the Apostle Barnabas, in the river Saleph, when he wished to refresh his body in a bath, he ended his final day. Henry, son of Emperor Frederick, reigned 10 years. He subjected Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily to the [Col. 0187C] empire. In his time Christendom had peace and justice. With his aid and counsel, the princes of Germany, out of love for the Crucified One, besieged Tours; and while they were besieging it, he paid Adam’s debt in Apulia.

Frederick II, son of Henry V the emperor, king of Sicily, elected against Otto in the year of the Lord 1221, [Col. 0188A] reigned 33 years. He was deposed by Pope Innocent IV. Returning from Parma to Apulia, he was killed by poison and buried at Foggia. But who is to obtain the kingdom after him, posterity will see.

Conrad is elected king.

In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1146, Conrad and Louis, kings, go to Jerusalem.

1152. Conrad died and Frederick succeeded him.

1156. Frederick was appointed king. In 1158 he powerfully subdued Milan; in 1162 he utterly destroyed it.

Pope Alexander came to Venice and held a synod, and the persecution was brought to peace.

**Here ends the book of Honorius Inclusus, *On the Image of the World*.** [Note: [Col. 0187] What follows was written in another but contemporary hand.]

[Col. 0188B] A.D. 1189. Emperor Frederick, clothed with the sign of the cross, set out for Jerusalem to conquer the enemies of the cross. But before he reached the borders of the land of Jerusalem, he ended his life [Note: [Col. 0187] In the margin: “He was drowned in the river Saleph between the two mountains Corium and Cornitem.”]. He died in 1190; his son King Henry succeeded him and, having been ordained at Rome in the year 1191, assumed the reins of imperial dignity.

In 1197 Emperor Henry died.

In the year of the Lord [1347] . . . . Emperor Louis died. In the same year there was a great earthquake before the Conversion of Saint Paul.

## CONTINUATION VII

> [Note: [Col. 0187] Added to the Kaisersheim codex by later hands of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.]

Conrad. Frederick. Henry. Philip. Otto. Frederick. Henry. Conrad, his brother. Conrad, his son, reigned two years. Rudolf [Col. 0188C] the count reigned 18 years. Adolf the count reigned 6 years and two months. Albert, duke of Austria, son of King Rudolf, reigned 10 years. Henry, count of Luxembourg, reigned 6 years. After him Louis of Bavaria reigned 25 years. While he was still alive, Charles, king of Bohemia, began to reign; he is emperor today.

[Col. 0187]

# SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE HISTORY, IN EVERY RESPECT, FROM THE YEAR 726

*(Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores, vol. X, p. 128.)*

[Col. 0187D] Standing in the vineyard of the Lord, I observed many people zealously engaged in pious work like a swarm of bees, but very many more still languishing in sluggish idleness. I rejoiced with the former, who by living deeds build the eternal Jerusalem and, through virtues, fit themselves as [Col. 0188D] living stones; but I pitied the latter, who, deprived through sloth of the denarius, alienate themselves from the walls of this splendid building. Yet, when I realized that they lacked tools, I was concerned to assist their [Col. 0189A] need. Therefore, lest they should lose the denarius set before them, I have supplied each person with whatever is necessary for the work. For there are very many who advance ostensibly valid excuses for their ignorance, saying that they lack an accumulation of books. Compassionately providing for them, I have gathered this compendium from the whole of Scripture, in which I judged that those hastening toward the homeland of life have sufficient provision. And therefore I have thought it right to call it *The Summary of the Whole*, since in it the sequence of all Scripture seems to be noted in summary.

The whole scriptural record of sacred authority is called one book, etc.

A.D. 726. [Note: [Col. 0189] “Bede dies,” in the margin.] [Chronicle of Würzburg, *SS.* VII, 26.] Charles, son of Pippin (son [Note: [Col. 0189] written above the line.] of Ansegisel, son of Arnulf, bishop of Metz), held the leadership of the mayors of the palace for 27 years. [Col. 0189B] He fought against the Saracens, devastated Frisia, and invaded Gascony. Pope Gregory III sent to Charles the keys of Saint Peter’s tomb and the chains of the same saint, with great gifts, so that he might withdraw from the party of Emperor Constantine, who had succeeded Leo; but Charles received the envoys with honour, bestowed gifts on them, and sent them back to Rome with his own envoys. Then he fought the Saracens in Gothia, entered Saxony, and died. Pope Zacharias succeeded Gregory III.

A.D. 742. [Note: [Col. 0189] “Fulda is built. Bishop Burchard was renowned. Audogarius, abbot of Kempten,” in the margin.] Pippin, son of Charles, with his brother Carloman, was mayor of the palace for 11 years. Carloman received Austria, Alemannia, and Thuringia; Pippin, Burgundy, Neustria, and Provence. Carloman devastated Gascony and Alemannia, made peace with the [Col. 0189C] Saxons, then went to Rome, was made a cleric by Pope Zacharias, built the monastery of Saint Silvester on Mount Soracte, and became a monk there; afterwards he went to the monastery of Saint Benedict. In the same period Radagaisus, king of the Lombards, did likewise. Pope Zacharias found the head of the martyr George enclosed in a casket, with a Greek-written label, and transferred it to the city of Rome. He also translated the dialogue of blessed Gregory into Greek. At the embassy of Bishop Burchard and Abbot Fulrad, Pope Zacharias commanded that Pippin be made king.

A.D. 743. [Note: [Col. 0189] “Boniface suffered martyrdom,” in the margin.] Pippin, by the authority of Pope Stephen, who succeeded Zacharias, was called king of the Franks; anointed with oil by Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, [Col. 0189D] and raised in the city of Soissons to the throne of the kingdom, he reigned 16 years. King Childeric, his head shaven, was sent to a monastery. Pippin attacked Lombardy in war, pressed Saxony in war, and invaded Gascony. Abbot Othmar was exiled to an island in the Rhine. There was an eclipse of the sun. The head of John the Baptist was found. The body of Saint Nazarius was brought [Col. 0190A] to Lorsch. King Pippin died.

A.D. 768. [Note: [Col. 0189] “The bodies of Gordian and Epimachus are brought into Alemannia,” in the margin.] Charles the Great, son of Pippin, with his brother Carloman for 3 years, afterwards alone for 44. Charles attacked Saxony. He subdued the Lombards together with Italy and came to Rome in triumph. Then in Italy he killed Rotgaud, captured Spain, and repeatedly restrained rebellious Saxony by arms. He came again to Rome, and his son Pippin was baptized by Pope Adrian. Famine and mortality devastated Francia. The bishopric of Bremen was built by King Charles [Note: [Col. 0189] “was established,” Admont codex.], and Willihad was made its first bishop. [Chronicle of Würzburg.] He killed the rebellious Saxons in a great slaughter and made them Christians. There was an eclipse of the sun. Charles went to Rome, and crosses appeared on his garments. Then he defeated the Slavs and Huns in war. Duke Gerold, standard-bearer, was killed in [Col. 0190B] battle. In the time of the great Charles, Emperor Constantine was blinded by the Greeks; likewise Pope Leo was blinded by the Romans, though not completely, and his tongue was cut out. He came to Charles in Saxony and sought assistance. On his account Charles set out for Rome with an army, restored the pope, and killed or exiled his accusers. By divine action the pope recovered his sight [cf. Chronicle of Bernold]. Charles was acclaimed Augustus of the Romans and crowned on Christmas Day by Pope Leo; the Greeks made peace with him. [Einhard, *Annals of Fulda*, 807.] Aaron, king of the Persians, sent Charles a fine-linen tent, precious silken cloths, balsam, an elephant, and also a clock of brass, wonderfully constructed by mechanical art: the course of the twelve hours turned by a water-clock, [Col. 0190C] with the same number of bronze balls, which fell when an hour had been completed and by their fall caused the bell set beneath them to ring; twelve horsemen were added, who came out through twelve windows as the hours were completed, and by the force of their emergence closed the same number of windows which had previously stood open. A fleet of 200 ships of Northmen and Danes came, devastated Frisia and all the adjacent islands, defeated the Frisians in three battles, and imposed upon them a tribute of one hundred pounds of silver. An earthquake occurred, followed by mortality. There was an eclipse of the sun, and Charles died.

A.D. 814. [Note: [Col. 0189] Bishop Ansgar converted the Danes and the Swedes. An eclipse of the sun occurred in Gemini in A.D. 1518, and immediately afterward, at the beginning of 1519, the most merciful Emperor Maximilian died, in a sixteenth-century marginal hand.] Louis, son of Charles, 27 years. He was made emperor by Pope Stephen, who succeeded Leo. On Stephen’s death Paschal became pope. [Col. 0190D] [Chronicle of Würzburg.] King Bernard rebelled against Louis and soon afterward died. Heavy snow persisted for a long time. Wetti, a monk at Reichenau, saw a marvelous vision. In the time of Louis, son of Charles, in Thuringia a turf-bank fifty feet long, fourteen feet wide [Note: [Col. 0189] high, Admunt manuscript], six feet high [Note: [Col. 0189] “feet high” lacking in the Admunt manuscript], was cut away and lifted from the earth without human hands, and was cast a distance of twenty-five feet to another place. Likewise, in Saxony a certain place swelled up in the manner of an embankment, [Col. 0191A] and during a single night raised itself like a rampart for a distance of one league [Note: [Col. 0191] *leuge*, Admunt manuscript] [Note: [Col. 0191] *subvexit*, “lifted itself,” Admunt manuscript, for *subrexit*, “rose”]. An eclipse of the sun occurred, and Louis died.

A.D. 831. Lothar, son of Louis, 17 years. He was crowned by Pope Paschal. In his time [EINHARD, loc. cit., 824, 825; SIGEBERT, A.D. 825], during a sudden storm, a huge mass of ice with hail fell from heaven: it was fifteen feet long, seven wide, and two feet thick. At the same time, a girl of twelve, after receiving communion at Easter, abstained from all food and drink for three years; afterward she began to live like other people. The abbot of Saint-Denis brought the bones of Saint Sebastian the martyr from Rome to the city of Soissons and placed them in the basilica of Saint Medard. While they still lay unburied, [Col. 0191B] such signs and miracles shone forth there that no mortal could comprehend the number of miracles or recount their variety. Emperor Lothar, by judgment of the bishops, laid down his arms because he had abandoned his wife, and was shut up to perform penance; afterward he was absolved, died at Ingelheim, and was buried at Metz.

A.D. 841. Louis, son of Lothar, together with his brothers Lothar, Charles, and Pippin, 36 years. [Annals of Würzburg, SS II, p. 238 f.] War flared up among the brothers over the division of the kingdom; a great battle was fought, and there was such slaughter on both sides that the present age had never remembered so great a carnage among the Frankish people. Then they divided the kingdom among themselves: Louis obtained Germany, Charles Gaul, [Col. 0191C] and Lothar Italy. In the time of this Lothar, Northmen and Danes, coming by ship as far as Paris, devastated Charles’s kingdom; in Frisia they fought three battles and won. King Pippin of Aquitaine was seized by his own men and handed over, together with the kingdom, to King Charles; he was made a cleric and thrust into a monastery. A man struck by lightning was wholly consumed, while his clothing remained unharmed. Lothar became a monk in the monastery of Prüm, where he also died; in his place his son Lothar became emperor. Lothar dismissed his lawful wife and took another, with the consent of Theutgaud, archbishop of Trier, and Gunther, archbishop of Cologne. For this reason they were deposed by Pope Nicholas, while the king was summoned to a synod. He came and, together with seventy princes, underwent judgment by the Body of the Lord concerning the accusation laid against him; [Col. 0191D] then he and them all perished by sudden death. In the time of Louis, Lothar’s brother, one night a cloud rose from the north and another came from the east and south; they hurled fiery darts at one another, then, joining together like armies in battle, clashed in confusion. At this time a woman baked white loaves for sale on the feast of Saint Lawrence and took them from the oven blacker than ink [SIGEBERT, 874].
