At a certain time, as harvest approached, some worms, like locusts, flying with four wings and having six feet, came into Germany from the east and covered the entire surface of the earth [Col. 0192A] like snow, devastating everything in the meadows. They had broad mouths and long bodies, and two teeth harder than stone, with which they could gnaw the hard bark of trees. Their length and thickness were like a man’s thumb; they were so numerous that in one hour of daylight they consumed a hundred *iugera* of crops near the city of Mainz. When they flew, they covered the entire air for the space of one mile so completely that those on the ground could scarcely see the sun’s brightness. Some killed in different places were found to contain entire ears of grain, with kernels and awns, within themselves. When some had gone westward, others arrived; and for nearly two months, almost every day, their flight presented a dreadful spectacle to onlookers. Then it is reported that in Italy, for three [Col. 0192B] days and three nights, blood rained from heaven. There was an earthquake, and a comet was seen. King Lothar, brother of Emperor Louis, died, and Charles, king of the Gauls, seized his kingdom. Soon war was begun at Tribur between Emperor Louis and Charles. Louis, king of Germany, died and was buried at Milan. After him Charles, king of Gaul, was crowned emperor, but was attacked by Carloman.

A.D. 877. [Chronicle of Würzburg.] Charles, son of Louis, with his brothers Carloman and Louis, 11 years. Carloman and Louis died, and Charles gave up the kingdom. After Charles’s death, Carloman seized the Roman Empire. A great cattle plague occurred. [SIGEBERT, 877.] While dogs were tearing up and eating corpses, one day they all gathered in a single place and departed from it, so that not one of them, alive or dead, could be found.

A.D. 888. [Chronicle of Würzburg.] Arnulf, son of Carloman, 12 years. Emperor Charles died. Arnulf utterly destroyed the army of the Northmen, subjected Italy and Burgundy to his kingdom, came to Rome, and became emperor. A great famine persuaded people to eat one another. The Hungarians ravaged Italy, and Arnulf died.

A.D. 900. Louis, son of Arnulf, still a very young boy, 12 years. The Hungarians entered Bavaria, and more than a thousand of them were killed. They invaded Carinthia; battle was joined, and very many were killed on both sides, [Col. 0192D] but the Hungarians more grievously. Then they devastated Saxony and Thuringia. War of the Franks with the Hungarians. King Louis died.

A.D. 912. [Note: [Col. 0191] Bishop Heriger flourished, in the margin.] Conrad, son of that Conrad whom Adalbert of Bamberg killed, was raised to the kingdom and reigned seven years. The Hungarians were killed by the Alemanni and Bavarians near the river Inn. Comets were seen. The Hungarians devastated Alemannia with sword and fire and invaded Alsace. King Conrad died.

A.D. 919. Count Henry became king and reigned 18 years. The Hungarians devastated all Francia, Gaul, Alsace, [Col. 0193A] and Alemannia with sword and fire; Henry killed them in Swabia. Duke Burchard was killed. Alemannia was entrusted to Hermann, and Henry died.

A.D. 937. Otto the Great, son of Henry, 38 years. The Hungarians, devastating Francia, Alemannia, Gaul as far as the ocean, and Burgundy, returned through Italy. The monasteries of Saint Gall and Saint Boniface were burned. There was a severe winter and a mortality among animals. The Hungarians fought the Bavarians and were defeated. Otto subjected Italy to himself and expelled King Berengar. A fiery stone, like a mass of glowing iron, came rolling from the west, and a dragon was seen. The Hungarians attacked Noricum, Francia, and Italy and devastated all Bavaria; near Augsburg, a city of Alemannia, [Col. 0193B] they were defeated in battle by King Otto and slaughtered in immense carnage. Crosses appeared on garments. Otto came to Rome and became emperor. In Saxony he founded the city of Parthenopolis. A sign appeared in the sun; then there was an eclipse of the sun. A certain fiery-colored sign appeared in the sky, and Otto died. Saint Ulrich died in the fiftieth year of his episcopate.

A.D. 975. Otto II, son of Otto the Great, 9 years. In Calabria, after his army had been killed by the Greeks, he leapt from a ship and escaped by swimming. Then he died and was buried at Rome.

A.D. 984. Otto III, son of Otto II, still a very young boy, 18 years. There was a great famine. Duke Wenceslas suffered martyrdom. Bishop Adalbert, from the city of Prague, was crowned with martyrdom by the Prussians. The monk Notker was held in high renown. [Col. 0193C] Otto died and was buried at Aachen.

A.D. 1002. Duke Henry of Bavaria became king and reigned 23 years and 5 months. He subdued Italy, Bohemia, and Duke Bolesław together with the whole Slavonic people. Pope Benedict crowned him. He founded Bamberg, whose church Pope Benedict dedicated. The Rus’, Poles, and Hungarians [Note: [Col. 0193] “The Lusatians also, and the Poles,” Admunt manuscript] became Christians. A great famine arose, and there was an earthquake. Henry died and was buried at Bamberg.

A.D. 1025. Conrad reigned nearly 15 years. Great dissension arose in the kingdom against him, but he made his son Henry king; he himself went to Rome and became emperor. With an army he attacked Pannonia, but King Stephen made peace with him. King Rudolf of Burgundy, when dying, sent his diadem to Emperor Conrad. [Col. 0193D] Conrad attacked eastern Francia against Otto; then he ravaged Burgundy, subdued Slavonia, and the Slavs called Liutici became his tributaries. Pilgrim, bishop of Cologne, died, and Hermann succeeded him. Queen Cunigunde and Duke Hermann died. Stephen, king of the Hungarians, converted with all his people to faith in Christ. An eclipse of the sun occurred, and Conrad died and was buried at Speyer, which he himself founded.

A.D. 1040. The pious King Henry, son of Conrad [Note: [Col. 0193] omitted in the manuscript], 17 years. Entering Bohemia, he devastated everything with fire and plunder, [Col. 0194A] and by an oath subjected its rebellious duke to himself. Then he entered Hungary with an army, put the defeated tyrant Ovo to flight, restored to the kingdom King Peter, who had been expelled by the Hungarians, and, having subjected the Hungarian kingdom to himself, returned with the highest honor. He married Agnes, daughter of William, prince of Poitou. He secured the greatest peace throughout the whole kingdom. There was a great pestilence among cattle and a harsh winter. Henry entered Italy and was peacefully received by the Romans; he synodically deposed three popes who had not been duly appointed, made Suidger, bishop of Bamberg, pope, and named him Clement. By him he himself was consecrated emperor and augustus; leading his army through Apulia and many provinces in victorious success, he returned with great honor and brought the body [Col. 0194B] of Saint Wicdo from Italy to Speyer. Pope Suidger died and Poppo succeeded him; after him Bruno, also bishop of Toul, was appointed pope. A synod was assembled at Mainz, over which Bruno the Apostolic and Emperor Henry presided. Archbishop Bardo died, as did Hermann the Cripple. Gebhard, also called Victor, succeeded Pope Leo. Famine afflicted many provinces; want and scarcity prevailed everywhere, and Henry ended his life.

A.D. 1067. Henry, son of Emperor Henry, began to reign while still a very young boy and reigned 49 years. His mother Agnes assumed the duchy of Bavaria. Pope Victor died, and Frederick, also called Stephen, was appointed; [Col. 0194C] after him Alexander was ordained. [Annals of Würzburg.] A comet was seen, and England was subjected to the Northmen. Duke Otto of Bavaria rebelled against the king. Soon the princes too conspired against him. The Saxons destroyed Harzburg, violated the tomb of Henry’s son, and scattered his bones. Pope Alexander died, and Hildebrand, also called Gregory, succeeded him. A battle was fought near the Unstrut. Duke Rudolf was chosen king. Würzburg was besieged. A battle was fought near Strowi and another near Fladecheim. Another battle occurred near the Elster, in which King Rudolf was killed. Henry besieged Rome and installed Wibert as pope. Hermann was raised as king, and war was waged between the Swabians and Bavarians near Hostetin. Rome was [Col. 0194D] taken, and a great pestilence occurred. King Hermann invaded eastern Francia in hostile fashion. Henry, returning from Italy, besieged and captured Augsburg, then ravaged Saxony. A battle was fought near Bleichfeld. King Hermann was killed. Another battle took place near the town of Gleichen between King Henry and Margrave Ekbert. An eclipse of the sun occurred. Conrad, Henry’s son, was made king and rebelled against his father. A most severe pestilence occurred. After Pope Gregory’s death, Otto, bishop of Ostia, also called Urban, was ordained supreme pontiff. At this time fiery globes flashed in the sky and then disappeared again into another part of the heavens. Soon peoples and nations, tribes and tongues, of every sex and age, set out from the western parts [Col. 0195A] of Spain and Gaul and journeyed eastward; they visited the Lord’s tomb at Jerusalem amid much bloodshed. Pope Urban died and Paschal was appointed. Henry, son of Henry, was chosen king; rebelling against his father, he captured him and stripped him of the royal insignia. A comet was seen for a long time. The younger Henry besieged Cologne; meanwhile his father died and was buried at Speyer. [Note: [Col. 0195] Bishop Anselm flourished in England, in the margin.]

A.D. 1106. Henry, son of Henry, 23 years [cf. Annals of Saxony, 1107]. When he had held an assembly at the town of Goslar [Note: [Col. 0195] “of the princes” added by the Admunt manuscript] [Note: [Col. 0195] *haberet*, “was holding,” Admunt manuscript, for *habuisset*, “had held”], and had arranged the affairs of the kingdom as he wished, suddenly [Note: [Col. 0195] “and had arranged … suddenly” omitted in the Admunt manuscript] an immense storm arose, terrible with lightning-flashes, sheet lightning, and thunder [Note: [Col. 0195] “and sheet lightning and thunder” omitted in the Admunt manuscript], and terrified the king and all the people. Immediately the pommel of the king’s sword, when touched, vanished like melting wax [Col. 0195B], and the design on his shield was erased. Then the king entered Flanders with a strong force, devastated everything with sword and fire, and subjected Count Robert together with all his people. After this he attacked Pannonia with an army, but nothing worthy of remembrance occurred there. He also entered Poland with a multitude; after ravaging it with plunder and fire, he returned. Then, with all his resources, he entered Italy, devastating towns, castles, and municipalities with sword and fire. At Rome he was consecrated emperor by Pope Paschal; but he himself seized the pope and dispersed clergy and people by terror. He returned after stripping the City, and cruelly persecuted the priests of the Lord and the princes. On this account the princes swore against him and drove him by arms from the kingdom. A battle was fought against him near Welfesholz, in which he was defeated [Col. 0195C] and expelled from his homeland. There was an earthquake, and many walls collapsed. Pope Paschal died and Gelasius was appointed in his place. Henry expelled him from Rome and appointed as pope Gregory, also called Burdinus. On Gelasius’s death Calixtus succeeded him; by him Henry and his pope were excommunicated. Burdinus was captured by Calixtus and shut up in the monastery called Cava. After this Henry granted to the Church that, by ecclesiastical right, it should appoint bishops and abbots through the election of clergy and people; that the person elected should receive the regalian rights from the king; and the king himself was absolved from the ban by Pope Calixtus, and peace was restored to the Church. Calixtus died and Honorius succeeded him. Then there was a famine, followed by a dreadful storm lasting many days, [Col. 0195D] with thunder, lightning, and hail, and an eclipse of the sun for one hour. Henry died and was buried at Speyer. Duke Lothar of Saxony was chosen king.

A.D. 1125. Lothar, duke of Saxony, reigned 11 years. Duke Frederick of the Swabians, [Col. 0196A] son of Emperor Henry’s sister, rebelled against him. Three suns were seen in the sky at the ninth hour. Bishop Norbert was held in renown for preaching and religious life. Lothar attacked Bohemia with an army, but was defeated and returned after many of his men had been killed. Conrad, brother of Duke Frederick, was raised as king by the Swabians. Speyer was besieged by Lothar against Frederick, but was not taken. [Cf. ANSELM OF GEMBLOUX, 1128.] At that time the sky was seen to burn during the first hour of the night. Then at midnight fire was again seen in the sky. Again and again the same thing was seen by many persons. One night an excessive brightness, like fire, was seen by many to fall from heaven; it is also reported that in some places great hail, like goose eggs, fell, among which very large ice fell. Certain villages, contrary to the direction of the wind, [Col. 0196B] were wholly consumed by fire, and many conflagrations occurred, among them the burning of Utrecht, the church of Paderborn, and many monasteries of saints. [Cf. ANSELM, 1131.] Lothar again besieged Speyer and took it victoriously. Pestilence followed, among both humans and animals. Pope Honorius died, and two popes were appointed: namely, Anacletus, also called Leo, whom Rome accepted, and Innocent, whom the Church received. Likewise, in the first hour of the night, the northern part of the sky appeared as if drenched in blood. Pope Innocent came into Gaul, to the city of Liège, where King Lothar met him with all the bishops of Germany; they chose Innocent as pope, rejected Anacletus, and swore to undertake an expedition into Italy in order to bring the pope to Rome. Meanwhile Lothar [Col. 0196C] entered Denmark with an army, received into submission King Niels of the Danes and his son Magnus, together with hostages, and returned victorious. Then, having assembled an army, he set out for Italy and proceeded to Rome with Pope Innocent to be crowned. On the way he encountered, as is said, the ambushes of Duke Frederick; angered by this, he burned the city of Augsburg, killed many citizens, and lost very many of his own men. In Italy he lost the greater part of his forces. After many hardships he entered Rome, was honorably received by the Roman senate and people, and was crowned emperor with the queen by Pope Innocent; he returned in peace (A.D. 1133). An eclipse of the sun occurred on 2 August, at midday, for nearly an hour, such as had not been seen for a thousand years. Finally [Col. 0196D] the entire sky was darkened like night, and stars were visible throughout almost the whole sky. At last the sun emerged from the darkness appearing like a star, then like a new moon, and finally resumed its proper form [cf. Continuation of Marianus Scotus, SS V, p. 562].

[Col. 0197]

## Four Little Books on the Lights of the Church, or on Ecclesiastical Writers

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica*, Hamburg, 1718, folio, p. 73.)

## Little Book I, Extracted from Jerome

[Col. 0197A] I ask you, reader—if indeed you can listen notwithstanding the gift of envy—not to disparage the labor of this little work. For I kept watch so that you might sleep; I labored so that you might rest. Your only labor will be to be filled with understanding by reading it through, and, thus endowed, to be accounted distinguished by all. But if, which I fear more, with a sickly heart and clouded countenance you press an envious tooth upon these little flowers artfully woven together, and with venomous tongue pluck apart the dewy garland joined with pure white lilies, envy will indeed envelop you, its nearest servant, in the darkness of ignorance; but good will shall lead me, through the light of knowledge, to glory and honor. In this little book I have set down by name all ecclesiastical writers from the time of Christ to our own times whom I have been able to learn from Jerome, Gennadius, Isidore, Bede, and [Col. 0197B] others.

### Chapter I

Simon Peter, son of John, from the village of Bethsaida in the province of Galilee, brother of the apostle Andrew and chief of the apostles, wrote two letters called canonical. The Gospel of Mark is also said to be his. But the books of which one is entitled *His Acts*, another *Gospel*, a third *Preaching*, a fourth *Apocalypse*, and a fifth *Judgment*, are rejected among apocryphal writings. After his episcopate of the church of Antioch, he went to Rome to overthrow Simon Magus; there he held the episcopal chair for twenty years, until the fourteenth year of Nero, by whom he was crucified and buried at Rome (Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 1).

### Chapter II

[Col. 0197C] James, brother of the Lord, surnamed the Just, son, as some think, of Joseph by another wife, but, as others hold, of Mary, sister of the Lord’s mother, wrote one of the seven Catholic Epistles. After the Lord’s Passion he was ordained bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles, governed the Church for thirty years, and was buried beside the temple of the Lord, where he had been thrown down (Jerome, ch. 2).

### Chapter III

Matthew, also called Levi, from a tax collector became an apostle; he was the first in Judaea to compose the Gospel of Christ in Hebrew letters for the Hebrews (Jerome, ch. 3).

### Chapter IV

Jude, brother of James, left one of the seven Catholic Epistles (Jerome, ch. 4).

### Chapter V

[Col. 0198A] The Apostle Paul, formerly Saul, outside the number of the twelve apostles, of the tribe of Benjamin and from the Judaean town of Gischala, wrote ten letters to churches: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, and one to the Hebrews. In addition, he wrote four to his disciples: two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon; and one to the Laodiceans, which is indeed read but rejected by everyone. In the fourteenth year of Nero, on the same day as Peter, he was beheaded at Rome for Christ and buried on the Ostian Way, in the thirty-seventh year after the Lord’s Passion (Jerome, ch. 5).

### Chapter VI

Barnabas, a Cypriot also called Joseph, a Levite [Col. 0198B] ordained with Paul as apostle to the gentiles, composed one letter for the edification of the Church, which is read among apocryphal writings (Jerome, ch. 6).

### Chapter VII

Luke, a physician of Antioch and follower of the Apostle Paul, wrote the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles at Rome. He died in Bithynia in his eighty-fourth year and was later transferred to Constantinople (Jerome, ch. 7).

### Chapter VIII

Mark, Peter’s disciple and interpreter, wrote the Gospel for the Romans. He suffered martyrdom in the eighth year of Nero and was buried at Alexandria (Jerome, ch. 8).

### Chapter IX

[Col. 0198C] The Apostle John, son of Zebedee and brother of James, wrote the Gospel for the bishops of Asia, the Apocalypse, and three Catholic Epistles. He died under Trajan in the sixty-eighth year after the Lord’s Passion and was buried at Ephesus (Jerome, ch. 9).

### Chapter X

Hermas, whom the Apostle Paul mentions in his letter to the Romans, wrote the book called *The Shepherd* (Jerome, ch. 10).

### Chapter XI

Philo the Jew, an Alexandrian by nation and of priestly lineage, wrote one book *On the Life of Our People Living under Mark*. His outstanding and innumerable works survive: on the five books of Moses; one book *On the Confusion of Tongues*; one *On Nature and Invention*; one *On the Things We Pray for and Attest by Sense*; one *On Education*; one *On the Heir of Divine Things*; one *On the Division of Equal and Contrary Things*; one *On the Three Virtues*; one *Why the Names of Some Persons Have Been Changed in the Scriptures*; two books *On Covenants*; one *On the Life of the Wise Man*; one *On the Three Virtues*; five books *That Dreams Are Sent by God*; five books of *Questions and Solutions on Exodus*; four books *On the Tabernacle and the Decalogue*; *On Sacrifices and Promises*; *On Curses*; *On Providence*; *On the Jews*; *On the Manner of Life of Alexander*; *That Dumb Animals Have Reason of Their Own*; *That Every Fool Is a Slave*; *On the Apostolic Men*, which he entitled *On the Contemplative Life*; two books *On Agriculture*; and two [Col. 0199B] *On Drunkenness*. He wrote the Second Book of Maccabees. [Note: [Col. 0199D] See Jerome, ch. 11, and Bellarmine in the *Catalogue*, where he treats of Philo and the author of the books of Maccabees.]

### Chapter XII

Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Corduba, pupil of the Stoic Photinus and uncle of the poet Lucan, wrote certain letters to the Apostle Paul, and the Apostle wrote some replies (Jerome, ch. 12).

### Chapter XIII

Josephus, son of Matthias, a priest from Jerusalem, captured by Vespasian, wrote at Rome seven books on the Jewish captivity, another twenty-four books of *Antiquities*, from the beginning of the world to the fourteenth year of Emperor Domitian, two works of controversy against Apion, the Alexandrian grammarian, and one entitled *On Power*, in which the martyrdoms of the Maccabees are arranged (Jerome, ch. 13).

### Chapter XIV

[Col. 0199C] Justus of Tiberias, from the province of Galilee, wrote a history of Jewish affairs and certain brief commentaries on the Scriptures (Jerome, ch. 14).

### Chapter XV

Clement, whom the Apostle mentions in the letter to the Philippians, fourth bishop of Rome after the Apostle Peter—for Linus was second and Anacletus third—wrote a very useful letter to the Church of Corinth, *The Itinerary of Peter*, *The Disputation of Peter and Apion*, and many other works counted among the apocrypha (Jerome, ch. 15).

### Chapter XVI

Dionysius the Areopagite, a philosopher converted by the Apostle Paul and ordained bishop at Athens, wrote a book *On Hierarchy* and many [Col. 0199D] other works. [Note: [Col. 0199D] Concerning Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, the following is read in the old Roman Martyrology, published by Heribert Rosweyde at the Plantin Press in 1613: “On the fifth day before the Nones (3rd) of October, at Athens, Dionysius the Areopagite, who under Hadrian suffered various torments, as Aristides is witness in the work which he composed on the Christian religion. This work is held among the Athenians as most famous among records of antiquity.” Concerning Saint Dionysius, bishop of Paris, the same Martyrology reads as follows: [Col. 0200D] “On the seventh day before the Ides (9th) of October, at Paris, Bishop Dionysius, with his companions, was put to the sword by Fescenninus.” Thus the old Roman Martyrology posits two Dionysii: one the Areopagite, disciple of Saint Paul the Apostle; the other bishop of Paris, struck with the sword by order of Fescenninus when Decius and Gratius were consuls—that is, in the year 250 of Christ—as Gregory of Tours recounts in Book I of the *History of the Franks*. I have thought it proper to mention this briefly; I leave the rest to each person’s judgment.]

### Chapter XVII

Ignatius, third bishop of the church of Antioch after the Apostle Peter, wrote a letter to the church of the Ephesians, another to the Magnesians, a third to the Trallians, a fourth to the Romans, then letters [Col. 0200A] to the Philadelphians and Smyrnaeans. He suffered martyrdom under Trajan (Jerome, ch. 16).

### Chapter XVIII

Polycarp, disciple of the Apostle John and ordained by him bishop at Smyrna, wrote a very useful letter to the Philippians and certain things concerning the day of Easter. Under Commodus he was delivered to the fire for Christ (Jerome, ch. 17).

### Chapter XIX

Papias, hearer of John and bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, wrote five volumes, entitled *Explanation of the Sayings of the Lord* (Jerome, ch. 18).

### Chapter XX

Quadratus, disciple of the apostles and bishop of Athens, wrote a book on behalf of the Christian religion, very useful and worthy of apostolic teaching (Jerome, ch. 19).

### Chapter XXI

[Col. 0200B] Aristides, a most eloquent Athenian philosopher, wrote a volume containing an exposition of our doctrine (Jerome, ch. 20).

### Chapter XXII

Agrippa, surnamed Castor, a very learned man, argued most forcefully against the twenty-four books which the heretic Basilides had composed on the Gospel (Jerome, ch. 21).

### Chapter XXIII

Hegesippus, near in time to the apostolic age, composed five books, weaving a history of all ecclesiastical events from the Lord’s Passion down to his own time (Jerome, ch. 22).

### Chapter XXIV

Justinus, philosopher from the Palestinian city of Neapolis, son of Priscus Bacchius, wrote four books on behalf of Christ’s religion against the gentiles; one *On the Monarchy of God*; one entitled *Psaltes*; [Col. 0200C] one *On the Soul*; a dialogue against the Jews; distinguished volumes against Marcion; and a book against all heresies. Finally he shed his blood for Christ (Jerome, ch. 23).

### Chapter XXV

Melito, an Asian and bishop of Sardis, composed a book on behalf of Christian doctrine. He also wrote two books *On Easter*; one *On the Life of the Prophets*; one *On the Elders*; one *On Body and Soul*; one *On Baptism*; one *On Truth*; one *On the Generation of Christ*; one *On His Own Prophecy*; one *On Hospitality*; another book entitled *The Key*; one *On the Devil*; one *On the Apocalypse of John*; and six books of excerpts (Jerome, ch. 24).

### Chapter XXVI

[Col. 0200D] Theophilus, sixth bishop of the church of Antioch, composed a book against Marcion; three volumes addressed to Autolycus; one book against the heresy of Hermogenes; and other treatises (Jerome, ch. 25).

### Chapter XXVII

[Col. 0201A] Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, published an eminent volume on behalf of the faith of Christians, five books against the gentiles, three *On Truth*, and two against the Cataphrygians (Jerome, ch. 26).

### Chapter XXVIII

Dionysius, bishop of the church of Corinth, wrote many letters to churches: one to the Laodiceans [Note: [Col. 0201D] Read “the Lacedaemonians.”], another to the Athenians, a third to the Nicomedians, a fourth to the Cretans, a fifth to the churches of Pontus, a sixth to the Ignosians [Note: [Col. 0201D] Read “the Cnossians.”], a seventh to the Romans, and an eighth to Chrysophora, a holy woman. He flourished under Marcus Antoninus (Jerome, ch. 27).

### Chapter XXIX

Pinytus, a Cretan and bishop of the city of Knossos, wrote a very [Col. 0201B] elegant letter to Bishop Dionysius (Jerome, ch. 28).

### Chapter XXX

Tatian, heresiarch, wrote innumerable volumes. He was a disciple of the philosopher Justin, flourished especially in rhetoric, and founded a new heresy. [Note: [Col. 0201D] The *Harmony of the Four Gospels* found in volume VII of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers* is not Tatian’s but Ammonius of Alexandria’s; Jerome discusses him in chapter [Col. 0202D] 55 of the *Catalogue*. In the same volume there is a book, *Diatessaron of the Gospels*, whose author was this Tatian the Syrian, leader of the Encratites. See Jerome, chapters 29 and 55.]

### Chapter XXXI

Philip, a Cretan and bishop of the city of Gortyna, published an excellent book against Marcion (Jerome, ch. 30).

### Chapter XXXII

Musanus, a writer of no mean distinction, composed a book against certain persons who had inclined toward the heresy of Tatian (Jerome, ch. 31).

### Chapter XXXIII

Modestus wrote a book against Marcion and certain other works (Jerome, ch. 32).

### Chapter XXXIV

Bardesanes, renowned in Mesopotamia, [Col. 0201C] wrote innumerable volumes against almost all heretics. He was exceedingly eloquent and founded a new heresy (Jerome, ch. 33).

### Chapter XXXV

Victor, thirteenth bishop of the city of Rome, wrote volumes concerning Easter and certain other matters (Jerome, ch. 34).

### Chapter XXXVI

Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons in Gaul, wrote five books *Against Heresies*; a short volume *Against the Gentiles*; another *On Discipline*; for his brother Martianus, *On Apostolic Preaching*, a book of various treatises; for Blastus, *On Schism*; for Florinus, *On Monarchy*; an excellent exposition *On the Ogdoad*; and certain works for Pope Victor concerning Easter (Jerome, ch. 35).

### Chapter XXXVII

Pantaenus, a disciple of the Stoic school, [Col. 0201D] learned in both Holy Scripture and secular literature, composed many commentaries on Holy Scripture at Alexandria. Sent to India, where Bartholomew had taught, he found the Gospel of Matthew there and brought it back with him (Jerome, ch. 36).

### Chapter XXXVIII

Rhodon, an Asiatic by birth, instructed at Rome in the Scriptures by Tatian, published very many writings, especially a work against Marcion. He also composed elegant treatises on the Hexaemeron and an eminent volume [Col. 0202A] against the Cataphrygians. He flourished under Commodus (Jerome, ch. 37).

### Chapter XXXIX

Clement, presbyter of the church of Alexandria, pupil of Pantaenus and holder after him of the ecclesiastical school, wrote eminent volumes full of learning and eloquence, both on the divine Scriptures and on the equipment of secular literature. Among these are eight books of *Stromata* and *Outlines*; one *On the Instructor*; one *On Easter*; one *On Fasting*; one *On Discussion*; another entitled *What Rich Man Shall Be Saved?*; one book *On Detraction*; and one *On Ecclesiastical Canons*. Origen was his disciple (Jerome, ch. 38).

### Chapter XL

Miltiades wrote an outstanding volume [Col. 0202B] against Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, and other books against gentiles and Jews (Jerome, ch. 39).

### Chapter XLI

Apollonius, a most eloquent man, wrote an eminent and extensive volume against Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla. Tertullian wrote against him. He flourished under Severus (Jerome, ch. 40).

### Chapter XLII

Serapion, bishop of Antioch, wrote a letter to Caricus and Ponticus concerning the heresy of Montanus. He also composed a book for Domninus, one *On the Gospel*, and other short letters (Jerome, ch. 41).

### Chapter XLIII

Apollonius, senator of the city of Rome, composed an eminent volume on behalf of our faith. By decree of the senate he was beheaded for Christ (Jerome, [Col. 0202C] ch. 42).

### Chapter XLIV

Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, formerly called the Tower of Straton, composed a synodical and very useful letter concerning Easter (Jerome, ch. 43).

### Chapter XLV

Bacchylus, bishop of the Corinthians, composed an elegant book concerning Easter (Jerome, ch. 44).

### Chapter XLVI

Polycrates, bishop of the Ephesians, wrote a synodical letter to Victor, bishop of Rome (Jerome, ch. 45).

### Chapter XLVII

Heraclius composed commentaries on the Apostle (Jerome, ch. 46).

### Chapter XLVIII

Maximinus discussed in an eminent volume the celebrated question: Whence comes evil, and whether matter was made by God (Jerome, ch. 47).

### Chapter XLIX

Candidus published most beautiful treatises on the Hexaemeron [the Six Days] (Jerome, ch. 48).

### Chapter L

Appion likewise composed treatises on the Hexaemeron (Jerome, ch. 49).

### Chapter LI

Sextus, under Severus, wrote a book *On the Resurrection* (Jerome, ch. 50).

### Chapter LII

Brabianus published certain short works pertaining to Christian doctrine (Jerome, ch. 51).

[Col. 0203A] ### Chapter LIII

Judas discussed most fully the seventy weeks in Daniel, and carried his *Chronicle* down to Severus (Jerome, ch. 52).

### Chapter LIV

Tertullian, a presbyter of the African province and of the city of Carthage, son of a proconsular centurion, a man of keen and vehement intellect, wrote many volumes. In particular, however, he composed works against the Church: *On Modesty*, *On Persecution*, *On Fasts*, *On Monogamy*, five books *On Ecstasy*, a sixth against Apollonius, and many other volumes which do not survive (Jerome, ch. 53).

### Chapter LV

Origen, also called Adamantius, whose father was Leonides and whose mother was . . . . . , was established at Alexandria by Demetrius, bishop of that same city, in the place of Clement the presbyter. Such was his zeal for the Scriptures that, contrary to the disposition of his age and nation, he learned the Hebrew [Col. 0203B] language; and, besides the Seventy Interpreters, he assembled other versions also into one work—namely those of Aquila, a Pontic proselyte, of Theodotion the Ebionite, and of Symmachus, of the same doctrine. He also wrote commentaries on the Gospel according to Matthew. Moreover, he collated the fifth, sixth, and seventh editions with the others. He also learned dialectic, geometry, arithmetic, astronomy, music, grammar, rhetoric, and all the schools of philosophy so thoroughly that he even had as followers students of secular literature, and remarkable crowds came to him. He wrote six thousand books. He flourished under Severus (Jerome, ch. 54).

### Chapter LVI

Ammonius, an eloquent and very learned man, renowned [Col. 0203C] in philosophy, composed at Alexandria, among many splendid monuments of his genius, an elegant work on the harmony of Moses and Jesus, and devised the Gospel Canons subsequently followed by Eusebius of Caesarea (Jerome, ch. 55).

### Chapter LVII

Ambrose, first a Marcionite and afterwards corrected by Origen, a deacon of the Church of Alexandria, wrote many letters to Origen. Origen dictated innumerable volumes for him (Jerome, ch. 56).

### Chapter LVIII

Trypho, a pupil of Origen, highly learned in the Scriptures, produced many short works, especially the book which he composed *On the Red Heifer* in Deuteronomy, and *On Abraham’s Dividing of the Dove and the Turtledove* [Col. 0203D] (Jerome, ch. 57).

### Chapter LIX

Minucius Felix, a distinguished advocate at Rome, wrote a dialogue of disputation between a Christian and a heretic, and a book *On Fate* against astrologers (Jerome, ch. 58).

### Chapter LX

Gaius held a very notable disputation against Proclus, a follower of Montanus (Jerome, ch. 59).

### Chapter LXI

Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, having fallen into a certain heresy and been corrected by Origen, wrote various short works, especially letters. There is also extant a dialogue of Origen and Beryllus (Jerome, ch. 60).

### Chapter LXII

Hippolytus, bishop of a certain city, wrote on Easter and the times, and several commentaries on the Scriptures: on the Hexaemeron; on Exodus; [Col. 0204A] on the Song of Songs; on Genesis; on Zechariah; on the Psalms; on Isaiah; on Daniel; on the Apocalypse; on Proverbs; on Ecclesiastes; on Saul and the Pythoness; *On Antichrist*; *On the Resurrection*; against Marcion; *On Easter*; an account against all heresies; and *On the Praise of the Saviour* (Jerome, ch. 61).

### Chapter LXIII

Alexander, bishop of Cappadocia, wrote a letter to the Antiochenes, another to Origen, another to Demetrius, and other letters to various persons. He was crowned with martyrdom under Decius (Jerome, ch. 62).

### Chapter LXIV

Julius Africanus wrote five volumes *On the Times*. Under the emperor Aurelius he undertook an embassy for the restoration of the city of Emmaus, afterwards called Nicopolis (Jerome, ch. [Col. 0204B] 63).

### Chapter LXV

Geminus, a presbyter of the Church of Antioch, composed certain monuments of his intellect (Jerome, ch. 64).

### Chapter LXVI

Theodore, afterwards called Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus and a pupil of Origen, wrote a paraphrase of Ecclesiastes, brief indeed but very useful, and other letters on faith (Jerome, ch. 65).

### Chapter LXVII

Cornelius, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote a letter to Fabius, bishop of the Church of Antioch, concerning the Roman and Italian synod; another concerning Novatian and those who had fallen; a third concerning the proceedings of the synod; and a fourth, very lengthy letter to the same Novatus and Fabius (Jerome, ch. 66).

[Col. 0204C] ### Chapter LXVIII

Caecilius Cyprian, an African and bishop of Carthage, composed many works brighter than the sun. He suffered under Valerian, as Cornelius did at Rome (Jerome, ch. 67).

### Chapter LXIX

Pontius, Cyprian’s deacon, left an excellent volume, *The Life and Passion of Cyprian* (Jerome, ch. 68).

### Chapter LXX

Dionysius, bishop of the city of Alexandria and a most distinguished pupil of Origen, wrote four books to Dionysius, bishop of Rome; *On Repentance* to the Laodiceans; likewise a *Canon on Repentance*; *On Martyrdom* to Origen; *On Repentance and the Order of Offences* to the Armenians; *On Nature* to Timothy; *On Temptations* to Euphanor; [Col. 0204D] and also many letters to Basilides (Jerome, ch. 69).

### Chapter LXXI

Novatian, a presbyter of the city of Rome, who seized the episcopal chair against Cornelius and refused to receive the lapsed, wrote *On Easter*, *On the Sabbath*, *On Prayer*, *On Jewish Foods*, *On Attalus*, many other works, and a great volume *On the Trinity*, which very many consider Cyprian’s (Jerome, ch. 70).

### Chapter LXXII

Malchion, a most eloquent presbyter of the Church of Antioch, conducted a dialogue against Paul of Samosata (Jerome, ch. 71).

### Chapter LXXIII

Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia, composed a book against Mani (Jerome, ch. 72).

### Chapter LXXIV

Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea [Col. 0205A] in Syria, composed a volume *On Easter*; and ten books on arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic (Jerome, ch. 73).

### Chapter LXXV

Victorinus, bishop of Poetovio, wrote commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Habakkuk, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, and the Apocalypse of John; against all heresies; and many other works. Finally, he was crowned with martyrdom (Jerome, ch. 74).

### Chapter LXXVI

Pamphilus the presbyter, the close friend of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, burned with so great a love for the divine library that he copied with his own hand the greater part of Origen’s volumes, and twenty-five volumes of Origen’s *Questions on the Twelve Prophets* [Col. 0205B]. Under Maximinus he suffered martyrdom for Christ (Jerome, ch. 75).

### Chapter LXXVII

Pierius, a presbyter of the Church of Alexandria, wrote a very long treatise on the prophet Hosea and other various treatises, with such elegance of style that he was called the younger Origen (Jerome, ch. 76).

### Chapter LXXVIII

Lucian, a most eloquent man and presbyter of the Church of Antioch, later bishop of Nicomedia, laboured with great devotion to the Scriptures and wrote a book *On Faith* and letters to several persons. He suffered under Maximinus and was buried at Helenopolis (Jerome, ch. 77, where he is not called bishop).

### Chapter LXXIX

Phileas, of the Egyptian city called [Col. 0205C] Thmuis, noble in birth and rich in possessions, composed a most elegant book *In Praise of the Martyrs*. He was beheaded for Christ (Jerome, ch. 78).

### Chapter LXXX

Arnobius the rhetor wrote two volumes against the Gentiles (Jerome, ch. 79).

### Chapter LXXXI

Firmianus, also called Lactantius, a pupil of Arnobius, wrote at the schools of Africa an *Itinerary* in hexameter verse; another book entitled *The Grammarian*; another, most beautiful book *On the Wrath of God*; seven books of *Divine Institutions against the Gentiles*; two to Asclepiades; seven books of letters to Demetrius, his pupil; one book *On Persecution*; four books of letters to Probus; [Col. 0205D] two books of letters to Severus; and one book to Demetrias, *On the Workmanship of God, or the Formation of Man*. He was tutor to Caesar Crispus, son of Constantine (Jerome, ch. 80).

### Chapter LXXXII

Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, most diligent in the divine Scriptures and, with Pamphilus the Martyr, a most careful investigator of the divine library, published innumerable volumes, including these: twenty books of *Gospel Exposition*; fifteen books of *Gospel Questions*; five books of *Theophany*; ten books of *Ecclesiastical History*; a universal history and its epitome; *On the Discrepancy of the Gospels*; ten books on Isaiah; thirty books against Porphyry, who at the same time was writing in Sicily, as some suppose; one book of *Topics* [Col. 0206A]; six books in defence of Origen; three books *On the Life of Pamphilus the Martyr*; *On the Martyrs*; other short works; very learned commentaries on the one hundred and fifty Psalms; and many other works. He flourished especially under Constantine, and, because of his friendship with Pamphilus the Martyr, received from him the surname Eusebius Pamphili (Jerome, ch. 81).

### Chapter LXXXIII

Reticius, bishop of Autun, wrote commentaries on the Song of Songs and another large volume against Novatian (Jerome, ch. 82).

### Chapter LXXXIV

Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia and afterwards of Tyre, composed books against Porphyry in polished and carefully ordered language; *The Symposium of the Ten Virgins*; an excellent work *On the Resurrection*; [Col. 0206B] works against Origen, and against that same author *On the Pythoness*; *On the Departure of the Soul*; commentaries on Genesis and the Song of Songs; and many other works. He was crowned with martyrdom under Decius and Valerian (Jerome, ch. 83).

### Chapter LXXXV

Juvencus, a Spanish presbyter of most noble lineage, rendered the four Gospels in hexameter verse in four books, and wrote some other works in the same metre pertaining to the order of the sacraments. He flourished under Constantine (Jerome, ch. 84).

### Chapter LXXXVI

Eustathius, a Pamphylian by origin, first bishop of Beroea in Syria and then of Antioch, composed many works against Arian doctrines, volumes *On the Soul*, works against Origen, and innumerable [Col. 0206C] letters (Jerome, ch. 85).

### Chapter LXXXVII

Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra, wrote many volumes of diverse exposition under Constantine and Constantius, especially against the Arians (Jerome, ch. 86).

### Chapter LXXXVIII

Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, wrote under Constans two books against the Gentiles; one book against Valens and Ursacius; one book *On Virginity*; several works *On the Persecutions of the Arians*; *On the Titles of the Psalms*; *The History of the Monk Antony*; and many other works (Jerome, ch. 87).

### Chapter LXXXIX

Antony the monk, whose life Athanasius recorded in a distinguished volume, sent [Col. 0206D] seven letters to various monasteries, apostolic alike in thought and expression (Jerome, ch. 88).

### Chapter XC

Basil, bishop of Ancyra and of the fortress of Mechaea, wrote under Constantius against Marcellus, a book *On Virginity*, and some other works (Jerome, ch. 89).

### Chapter XCI

Theodore, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, published under Constantius commentaries on Matthew, John, and the Apostle, in an elegant and clear style (Jerome, ch. 90).

### Chapter XCII

Eusebius, bishop of Emesa, possessed of an elegant and rhetorical genius, produced innumerable books. Chief among them are works against Jews and Gentiles, works addressed to the Novatians, ten books on the Epistle to the Galatians [Col. 0207A], and very many, though brief, homilies on the Gospels. He flourished under Constantius (Jerome, ch. 91).

### Chapter XCIII

Triphyllius, bishop of Ledra in Cyprus [Note: [Col. 0207D] Λεδριῦν, “of Ledra,” in Cyprus.] or of *leuteōntos* [λευτεῶντος; reading uncertain], a most eloquent man, wrote under Constantius commentaries on the Song of Songs and many other works (Jerome, ch. 92).

### Chapter XCIV

Donatus, from whom the Donatists throughout Africa took their name, wrote many short works under Constantius pertaining to his heresy, and a book *On the Holy Spirit* consonant with Arian doctrine (Jerome, ch. 93).

### Chapter XCV

Asterius, philosopher of the Arian party, wrote under Constantius commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans, the Gospels, and the Psalms, besides many other works (Jerome, ch. 94).

### Chapter XCVI

Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, wrote books against [Col. 0207B] the emperor Constantius (Jerome, ch. 95).

### Chapter XCVII

Eusebius, a Sardinian by nation, formerly lector of the city of Rome and bishop of Vercelli, was banished by the emperor Constantius to Scythopolis and then to Cappadocia because of his confession of the faith. Having returned under the emperor Julian, he published the commentaries of Eusebius of Caesarea on the Psalms (Jerome, ch. 96).

### Chapter XCVIII

Fortunatius [Note: [Col. 0207D] Fortunatianus.], an African by nation and bishop of Aquileia, wrote under Constantine commentaries on the Gospels, arranged by headings (Jerome, ch. 97).

### Chapter XCIX

Achatius [Note: [Col. 0208D] Arcadius.], bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, produced eighteen volumes on Ecclesiastes and six concerning the doctrine of the peoples. Besides these, he composed many varied treatises. He became so prominent [Col. 0207C] under the emperor Constantius that he installed Felix, an Arian bishop, in place of Bishop Liberius (Jerome, ch. 98).

### Chapter C

Serapion, bishop of Themuis [Note: [Col. 0208D] Thmuis.], who received the surname Scholasticus because of the elegance of his intellect, a friend of the monk Antony, published an excellent book against Mani; one *On the Titles of the Psalms*; and useful letters to various persons. He flourished under Constantius (Jerome, ch. 99).

### Chapter CI

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, was banished to Phrygia from the Synod of Béziers through the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles. Under Valentinian he composed twelve books against the Arians and another book *On Synods*, which he wrote to the bishops of Gaul; commentaries on the Psalms—namely, on the first [Col. 0207D] and second, from the fifty-first through the sixty-second, and from the one hundred and eighth to the end. In this work, following Origen, he also added some things of his own. He wrote two books to Constantius; one against Valens and Ursacius, containing the history of the Synods of Rimini and Seleucia; a work to the prefect Sallustius, or against Dioscorus; a book of hymns; another, *On Mysteries*; a commentary on Matthew; treatises on Job; an elegant book against Auxentius; several letters to various persons; [Col. 0208A] and a book on the Song of Songs (Jerome, ch. 100).

### Chapter CII

Victorinus, an African by nation, teaching rhetoric at Rome under Constantius, wrote very obscure books in dialectical fashion against Arius, and consequently they are not understood even by learned persons; he also wrote commentaries on the Apostle (Jerome, ch. 101; Gennadius, ch. 60).

### Chapter CIII

Titus, bishop of Bostra, wrote vigorous books against the Manichaeans under Julian, along with several other volumes (Jerome, ch. 102).

### Chapter CIV

Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, published many brief works in heroic metre under Theodosius (Jerome, ch. 103).

### Chapter CV

Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea in Syria and son of a presbyter, composed innumerable works on the holy Scriptures under Theodosius, and thirty books against Porphyry [Col. 0208B] (Jerome, ch. 104).

### Chapter CVI

Gregory Baeticus, bishop of Elvira, composed various treatises and an elegant book *On Faith* (Jerome, ch. 105; Gennadius, ch. 16).

### Chapter CVII

Pacian, bishop of Barcelona in the Pyrenean region, renowned alike for his life and his discourse, wrote various short works against the Novatians under Theodosius (Jerome, ch. 106).

### Chapter CVIII

Photinus, a disciple of Marcellus, was ordained bishop of Sirmium. Having fallen into the heresy of Ebion, he wrote several volumes, especially works against the Gentiles and a book to Valentinian (Jerome, ch. 107).

### Chapter CIX

Phoebadius, bishop of Agen in Gaul, [Col. 0208C] published a book against the Arians and many other works (Jerome, ch. 108).

### Chapter CX

Didymus of Alexandria, blind from an early age and therefore wholly ignorant even of the alphabet, presented so great a miracle of himself to all that he learned dialectic and geometry—disciplines especially requiring sight—perfectly. He wrote many numerous and distinguished works: commentaries on the Psalms; commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew and John; a work *On Doctrines*; two books against the Arians; one book *On the Holy Spirit*; eighteen volumes on Isaiah; three books on Hosea; five on Zechariah; commentaries on Job; and many other works (Jerome, ch. 109).

### Chapter CXI

Optatus, an African and bishop of Milevis, [Col. 0208D] wrote six books under Valens against the calumny of the Donatist party (Jerome, ch. 110).

### Chapter CXII

Aquil(l)ius Severus, a Spaniard, composed under Valentinian a volume, as it were an *Itinerary*, containing the course of his whole life in both prose and verse; he called it *Catastrophe* (Jerome, ch. 111).

### Chapter CXIII

Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, repeatedly expelled from and restored to the Church, wrote certain volumes under Theodosius (Jerome, ch. 112).

### Chapter CXIV

Euzoius the bishop composed various and numerous [Col. 0209A] treatises (Jerome, ch. 113).

### Chapter CXV

Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, wrote books against all heresies and many other works (Jerome, ch. 114).

### Chapter CXVI

Ephraem, deacon of the Church of Edessa, composed many short works, including one *On the Holy Spirit* (Jerome, ch. 115).

### Chapter CXVII

Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, formerly called Mazaca, produced excellent books against Eunomius, a volume *On the Holy Spirit*, nine homilies on the Hexaemeron, and various treatises. He flourished under Gratian (Jerome, ch. 116).

### Chapter CXVIII

Gregory Nazianzen, a most eloquent man, composed all his works to a total of thirty thousand verses [Col. 0209B]. These include: *On the Death of His Brother Caesarius*; praises of the Maccabees, Cyprian, Athanasius, and Maximus the philosopher and later bishop; a book in hexameter verse, *Virginity and Marriage*, debating against one another; two books against Eunomius; one book *On the Holy Spirit*; and one against the emperor Julian. He flourished under Theodosius (Jerome, ch. 117).

### Chapter CXIX

Lucius, bishop of Alexandria and of the Arian party, composed formal Easter letters and not a few small books of various expositions (Jerome, ch. 118).

### Chapter CXX

Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus, wrote commentaries on the Apostle and many other works (see [Col. 0209C] Jerome, ch. 119, and Suidas in the *Lexicon*).

### Chapter CXXI

Eunomius, bishop of Cyzicus and of the Arian party, wrote much against the Church. Apollinaris, Didymus, Basil of Caesarea, Gregory Nazianzen, and Gregory of Nyssa answered him (Jerome, ch. 120).

### Chapter CXXII

Priscillian, bishop of Ávila, who through the faction of Idacius and Ithacius was put to death at Trier by Maximus, published many short works (Jerome, ch. 121).

### Chapter CXXIII

Latronianus, of the province of Spain, a very learned man comparable with the ancients in metrical composition, was likewise put to death at Trier with Priscillian. He published many works in different metres [Col. 0210A] (Jerome, ch. 122).

### Chapter CXXIV

Tiberianus, a Baetican, wrote an *Apology* in a swollen and elaborate style (Jerome, ch. 123).

### Chapter CXXV

Ambrose, bishop of Milan, wrote the *Hexaemeron*, *On Duties*, *On the Sacraments*, and many other excellent works (Jerome, ch. 124).

### Chapter CXXVI

Evagrius, bishop of Antioch, of keen and ardent intellect, published treatises of diverse exposition and translated the *Life of the Blessed Antony* from Greek into Latin (Jerome, ch. 125).

### Chapter CXXVII

Ambrose of Alexandria, a pupil of Didymus, wrote against Apollinaris a dogmatic volume of many [Col. 0210B] verses and commentaries on Job (Jerome, ch. 126).

### Chapter CXXVIII

Maximus the philosopher, born at Alexandria, was ordained bishop at Constantinople and expelled. He wrote a notable book *On Faith against the Arians*, which he presented to the emperor Gratian (Jerome, ch. 127).

### Chapter CXXIX

Gregory, bishop of Nyssa and brother of Basil of Caesarea, read to Jerome and Gregory Nazianzen his books against Eunomius; he also wrote many other works (Jerome, ch. 128).

### Chapter CXXX

John [Note: [Col. 0209C] St John, bishop of the city of Constantinople, was called Chrysostom—“Golden Mouth”—because of the golden excellence of his speech. An Antiochene by birth and formerly presbyter of the Church of Antioch, he was born of noble parents. In rhetoric he was a pupil of the sophist Libanius; in philosophy, of Andragathius; and in the sacred Scriptures, of Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus. He was joined in the closest friendship with Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen. He published very many volumes on the sacred writings, both commentaries and homilies, issued in Greek and Latin at Paris in nine volumes, and in Latin at Antwerp in 1619, in six volumes. His life was written at greatest length by Palladius, his pupil and bishop of the Church of Helenopolis, in the dialogue which he held with Theodore, deacon of the Church of Rome. Cassiodorus wove together the same account from the *Tripartite History* of Socrates, Theodoret, and Sozomen. George, patriarch of Alexandria, likewise gave a very full account, drawing both upon Palladius’s aforementioned dialogue and upon other writings, of all that could be desired concerning Chrysostom’s life. Also relevant is the oration of Emperor Leo, surnamed the Peaceful, [Col. 0210C] on Chrysostom. Suidas, or whoever it was who enlarged Suidas’s *Lexicon* after him, surveyed, though briefly, the principal points in Chrysostom with great elegance [Col. 0210D]. Whoever wishes for more should consult Metaphrastes, likewise Nicephorus in Books XI, XII, XIII, and XIV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, and Baronius in the *Annals*. Chrysostom died in exile at Comana on the Black Sea, on 24 September, in the year 407. He lived fifty-two years and eight months, and occupied the see for nine years, six months, and twenty days. He was therefore born in the year 355, about March, as Sozomen records, Book I, ch. 26. Moreover, in his books *On the Priesthood*, Chrysostom introduces as speaker not Basil the Great, as Sixtus of Siena supposed, but Basil of Seleucia, as Andreas Schottus noted from his manuscript Suidas. Cicero called Aristotle “a golden river of speech”; Greece attributed a similar encomium to Chrysostom.], a presbyter of the Church of Antioch, follower of Eusebius of Emesa and Diodorus [or Theodore], composed many short works (Jerome, ch. 129).

[Col. 0210C] ### Chapter CXXXI

Gelasius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, after Bishop Eunomius [Note: [Col. 0210D] Euzoius.], wrote certain chapters in a careful and polished style (Jerome, ch. 130).

### Chapter CXXXII

Theotimus, bishop of Tomis in Scythia, published brief treatises in the form of dialogues and in the manner of ancient eloquence, divided into short clauses (Jerome, ch. 131).

### Chapter CXXXIII

Dexter, son of Pacian, distinguished in secular life and devoted to the faith of Christ, composed a universal history (Jerome, ch. 132).

### Chapter CXXXIV

Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, [Col. 0211A] published a book *On the Holy Spirit* (Jerome, ch. 133).

### Chapter CXXXV

Sophronius, a man exceedingly learned, composed while still a boy praises of Bethlehem and a notable book *On the Overthrow of Serapis*, and translated Jerome’s works into Greek (Jerome, ch. 134).

### Chapter CXXXVI

Jerome, born to Eusebius as father in the town of Stridon on the borders of Pannonia, wrote under Theodosius the *Life of the Monk Paul*; one book of letters to various persons; an exhortation to Heliodorus; the *Disputation of a Luciferian and an Orthodox Believer*; a *Chronicle of Universal History*; translated twenty-six homilies of Origen on Jeremiah and Ezekiel; works *On the Seraphim*, *On Hosanna*, and *On the Frugal and the Prodigal Son*; three homilies *On Three Questions of the Old Law*; [Col. 0211B] two homilies on the Song of Songs; one letter against Helvidius concerning the holy Mary; one to Eustochium [Col. 0212A] *On Preserving Virginity*; one book of letters to Marcella; one consolatory letter to Paula on the death of her daughter; four books of commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians; likewise three books on the Epistle to the Ephesians, one book on the Epistle to Titus, and one on the Epistle to Philemon; commentaries on Ecclesiastes; one book of *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*; one book *On Places*; one book *On the Holy Spirit*; thirty-eight homilies on Luke; seven treatises on the Psalms, from the tenth through the sixteenth; *On the Captive Monk*; the *Life of Blessed Hilarion*; and the *Life of Paula*. He translated the New Testament from Greek and the Old Testament from Hebrew into Latin; expounded the Twelve Prophets; and composed innumerable letters and countless other works [Col. 0212B] (Jerome, ch. 135).

## Book II, Selected from Gennadius

[Col. 0211]

[Col. 0211B] ### Chapter I

James, surnamed the Wise, bishop of the noble Persian city of Nisibis, a confessor under Maximian, wrote twenty-six books: *On Faith against All Heresies*; *On General Charity*; *On Fasting*; *On Prayer*; *On Love for One’s Neighbour in Particular*; *On the Resurrection*; *On Life after Death*; *On Humility*; *On Patience*; *On Repentance*; *On Satisfaction*; *On Virginity*; *On the Perception of the Soul*; *On Circumcision*; *On the Blessed Unleavened Bread in Isaiah*; *On Christ, That He Is the Son of God and Consubstantial with the Father*; *On Chastity against the Gentiles*; *On the Construction of the Tabernacle*; *On the Conduct of the Gentiles*; *On the Persian Kingdom*; and *On the Persecution of Christians*. He also wrote a *Chronicle*. He died under Constantius (Gennadius, [Col. 0211C] ch. 1).

### Chapter II

Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote one letter to a certain Dionysius *On the Incarnation of the Lord* (Gennadius, ch. 2).

### Chapter III

Paulonas, a presbyter and disciple of blessed Ephraem, a man of very keen intellect and learned in the divine Scriptures, separated himself from the Church and wrote many things contrary to the faith (Gennadius, ch. 3).

### Chapter IV

Vitellius, an African, defending the Donatist schism, wrote against the Gentiles and against us, as though we had been betrayers of the divine Scriptures in the persecution; and he discussed many matters pertaining to ecclesiastical rule. He flourished under Constans (Gennadius, ch. 4).

### Chapter V

Macrobius, a presbyter and likewise a Donatist, later secretly bishop in the city of Rome, [Col. 0211D] wrote one book to confessors and virgins, moral in character but containing very necessary teaching (Gennadius, ch. 5).

### Chapter VI

Heliodorus the presbyter wrote a book *On the Natures of Primeval Things* (Gennadius, ch. 6).

### Chapter VII

Pachomius the monk, founder of the Egyptian cenobitic communities, wrote a Rule suitable for both kinds of monks, which he had received at an angel’s dictation. [Col. 0212B] He also wrote letters to the associates in his superiorship, in which he enclosed an alphabet veiled in mystical mysteries, or an intelligence exceeding ordinary human usage, revealed, I believe, only to those of their own class or merit. He also wrote on Easter (Gennadius, ch. 7).

### Chapter VIII

Theodore the presbyter, Pachomius’s successor, wrote letters to other monasteries, arranged in the language of the holy Scriptures (Gennadius, ch. 8).

### Chapter IX

Orsiesius the monk, colleague of both the aforementioned men, a man perfectly trained in the Scriptures, composed a book seasoned with divine salt and constructed out of the instruments of the whole monastic discipline; in it almost the whole Old and New Testament is [Col. 0212C] concisely set forth (Gennadius, ch. 9).

### Chapter X

That Macarius of Egypt, renowned for signs and miracles, wrote only one letter to the younger members of his profession (Gennadius, ch. 10).

### Chapter XI

Evagrius the monk, the close disciple of the aforementioned Macarius, distinguished in divine and human literature, wrote many things necessary for monks: namely, *Lives of the Fathers*, and eight books against the promptings of the eight principal vices, drawn from testimonies of the sacred Scriptures. He also composed instruction for cenobites and synodites suited to communal life, and one booklet for virgins consecrated to God, appropriate to their religious vocation and sex. He published also a few very obscure sayings, knowable, as he himself says, only to the hearts of monks (Gennadius, ch. 11).

[Col. 0212D] ### Chapter XII

Theodore, a presbyter of the Church of Antioch, a man prudent in learning and eloquent in speech, wrote fifteen books *On the Incarnation of the Lord* against the Apollinarians and Eunomians, amounting to fifteen thousand verses (Gennadius, ch. 12).

### Chapter XIII

Prudentius, a man educated in secular literature, composed the *Dittochaeum*, drawing selected persons from the whole Old Testament. He also composed, in the manner of the Greeks, a *Hexaemeron* on [Col. 0213A] the making of the world. He also composed small books which he titled in Greek: *Apotheōsis* (Ἀποθέωσις, “Deification”), *Psychomachia* (Ψυχομαχία, “Battle of the Soul”), and *Hamartigenia* (Ἁμαρτιγένεια, “Origin of Sins”); that is, *On Divinity*, *On the Conflict of the Soul*, and *On the Origin of Sins*. He also made one book in praise of the martyrs and another against Symmachus (Gennadius, ch. 13).

### Chapter XIV

Audentius, a Spanish bishop, wrote against the Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians, especially against the Photinians (Gennadius, ch. 14).

### Chapter XV

A certain Commodianus wrote a book against the pagans (Gennadius, ch. 15).

### Chapter XVI

Faustinus the presbyter wrote seven books, addressed in the person of Queen Flaccilla, against Arians and Macedonians, and one book to the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius (Gennadius, ch. 16).

[Col. 0213B] ### Chapter XVII

Rufinus, presbyter of the Church of Aquileia, no small part of the Church’s teachers, possessing an elegant talent for translating from Greek into Latin, made available to Latin readers the greater part of the Greek library: namely, works of Basil, bishop of Caesarea; of Gregory Nazianzen, a most eloquent man; the books of Clement of Rome’s *Recognitions*; nine books of the history of Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine, to which he added two; the sayings of the philosopher Sextus; and [Pamphilus,] *Against the Astrologers*. He did not translate all of Origen, because Jerome too translated certain portions. He expounded the Creed in such a way that, by comparison with his exposition, others scarcely seem to have expounded it at all. He also discussed Jacob’s Blessing over the patriarchs in a threefold sense: historical, moral, and mystical. He wrote many letters [Col. 0213C] exhorting readers to the fear of God. He answered his detractor in two volumes (Gennadius, ch. 17).

### Chapter XVIII

Tichonius, an African by nation, learned in divine literature, not ignorant of secular literature, and zealous in ecclesiastical affairs, wrote three books *On Civil War* and *Expositions of Various Questions*. He also composed eight rules for discovering the meaning of the Scriptures, which he included in one volume. He also expounded the Apocalypse of John in its entirety, finding nothing carnal in it but understanding everything spiritually. He flourished under Theodosius (Gennadius, ch. 18).

### Chapter XIX

Severus the presbyter, surnamed Sulpicius, of the province of Aquitaine, a man noble in birth and learning, [Col. 0213D] wrote the *Life of Martin, Bishop of Tours*, and that of Paulinus of Nola [Note: [Col. 0213D] Here Honorius is mistaken, as elsewhere, when he writes that the life of St Paulinus, bishop of Nola, was committed to writing by Severus Sulpicius. See Gennadius, chs. 19 and 48.]; and many letters to his sister, exhorting her to love of God and contempt for the world. He also wrote two to Paulinus and others to other persons. He flourished under Arcadius (Gennadius, ch. 19).

### Chapter XX

Antiochus wrote one long volume against avarice [Col. 0214A] and a homily on the man born blind. He died under Arcadius (Gennadius, ch. 20).

### Chapter XXI

Severianus, bishop of the Church of Gabala [Note: [Col. 0213D] Gabalensis, “of Gabala.”], learned in the divine Scriptures and a marvellous declaimer in homilies, was frequently summoned to Constantinople by Bishop John and by the emperor Arcadius to preach. He wrote an exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians and a very pleasing little book *On Baptism and the Solemnity of Epiphany* (Gennadius, ch. 21).

### Chapter XXII

Nicetas, bishop of the city of Remesiana, composed in simple and polished language six brief instructions for those preparing for baptism. The first is on candidates for baptism; the second on the errors of paganism; the third on faith in the one [Col. 0214B] majesty; the fourth against astrology [Note: [Col. 0213D] *Genethliology*, i.e. natal astrology.]; the fifth on the Creed; and the sixth on the sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb. He also wrote a booklet to a fallen virgin, an incentive to amendment for almost all who fall (Gennadius, ch. 22).

### Chapter XXIII

Olympius, a Spanish bishop, wrote a book *On Faith* against those who attribute guilt to nature rather than free choice (Gennadius, ch. 23).

### Chapter XXIV

Bachiarius, a man polished and lucid in Christian philosophy, published pleasing short works *On Faith* (Gennadius, ch. 24).

### Chapter XXV

Sabbatius, bishop of the Gallican Church, at the request of a chaste virgin dedicated to God named Secunda, composed a book *On Faith* against [Col. 0214C] Marcion and Valentinus, his originator, and against Eunomius and his teacher Aetius (Gennadius, ch. 25).

### Chapter XXVI

Isaac wrote a book *On the Three Persons of the Holy Trinity and the Incarnation of the Lord*, a discussion of the utmost obscurity and an involved style (Gennadius, ch. 26).

### Chapter XXVII

Ursinus the monk wrote against those who decree that heretics must be rebaptized (Gennadius, ch. 27).

### Chapter XXVIII

Another Macarius, a monk, wrote at Rome a book against astrologers (Gennadius, ch. 28).

### Chapter XXIX

Another Heliodorus, a presbyter at Antioch, [Col. 0214D] published an excellent volume on virginity, furnished with the holy Scriptures (Gennadius, ch. 29).

### Chapter XXX

John, [Note: [Col. 0213D] John Nepos Silvanus, forty-fourth bishop of Jerusalem, died in A.D. 416 after occupying the see for thirty years. Praylius succeeded him; letters from Praylius to the bishop of Rome, sent in the following year, survive. Thus Baronius states in the *Annals*, on the authority of Theodoret, Book V, chapter 37 [Col. 0214D]. But Idatius says in his *Chronicle* that John, bishop of Jerusalem, survived until A.D. 418 or 419. John Wastelius of Aalst, a Douai doctor of theology of the Carmelite order, has ready for publication three books of *Vindications for John of Jerusalem*. In them he attempts to assign to John of Jerusalem various works falsely attributed to John Chrysostom, Origen, and others. In the first book he investigates the author of the work, or incomplete commentary, on Matthew, and concludes in favour of John of Jerusalem. To him he also attributes [Col. 0215D] various homilies, as well as extracts and fragments of commentaries on Mark and Luke published under Chrysostom’s name. In the second book he attempts to defend the book published under the name of John of Jerusalem, *On the Institution of the First Monks, Who Began under the Old Law and Persevered under the New*, addressed to the monk Caprasius. In the third book he argues on behalf of St Augustine, who praises the same John of Jerusalem. We leave all these matters, and others relating to them, to be examined by more discerning critics when they have appeared.], bishop of Jerusalem, wrote a book against the detractors of his studies, saying that he had followed Origen’s intellect, not his faith (Gennadius, ch. 30).

[Col. 0215A] ### Chapter XXXI

Bishop Paul wrote a short work on repentance (Gennadius, ch. 31).

### Chapter XXXII

Helvidius, disciple of Auxentius and imitator of Symmachus, wrote a book about St Mary full of error. Jerome answered him with a short work full of doctrine (Gennadius, ch. 32).

### Chapter XXXIII

Theophilus, bishop of the city of Alexandria, wrote a large volume against Origen and another against the Anthropomorphite heretics, who believe that God consists of a human form and limbs; he also issued a Paschal Cycle and three books *On Faith* (Gennadius, ch. 33).

### Chapter XXXIV

Eusebius wrote *On the Mystery of the Lord’s Cross and the Constancy of the Apostles* (Gennadius, ch. 34).

### Chapter XXXV

Vigilantius, a presbyter by nation a Gaul, [Col. 0215B] holding a church in the parish of Barcelona in Spain, wrote certain works full of heresy; Jerome answered him (Gennadius, ch. 35).

### Chapter XXXVI

Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, urged Augustine, while still a presbyter, in many letters to exercise his intellect, so that he might appear as a new Ambrose, an impeller of Origen’s work (Gennadius, ch. 36).

### Chapter XXXVII

Bishop Vigilius wrote, to Simplicianus, five books in praise of the martyrs (Gennadius, ch. 37).

### Chapter XXXVIII

Augustine, an African and bishop of the town of Hippo, a man renowned throughout the world for divine and human learning, sound in faith and pure in life, wrote works so many that they cannot even be found: fifteen books *On the Trinity*; [Col. 0215C] twenty-two *On the City of God*; and innumerable others (Gennadius, ch. 38).

### Chapter XXXIX

The presbyter Orosius, [Note: [Col. 0216D] It is commonly believed that the *Apology against Pelagius* mentioned at Gennadius, chapter 39, was written by Paulus Orosius. But Peter Wastelius, Book III of his *Vindications for John, Forty-Fourth Bishop of Jerusalem*, contends that this *Apology* was written by some impostor favourable to the errors of Pelagius and Nestorius, although in wording, or in a slightly different sense, it seems to condemn Pelagius. We entrust examination of this matter to ecclesiastical critics.], Spanish by origin, an eloquent man and knowledgeable in history, wrote seven books in which he described history from the origin of the world down to his own time. Augustine sent him to Jerome to learn the nature of the soul. He flourished under Honorius (Gennadius, ch. 39).

### Chapter XL

Maximus, bishop of the Church of Turin, a man sufficiently devoted to the divine Scriptures, composed treatises in praise of the apostles and of John the Baptist, and a general homily on all the martyrs. He also expounded many passages of the Gospels and Acts of the Apostles wisely. He produced two treatises on [Col. 0215D] the life of St Eusebius, bishop and confessor of Vercelli; a work *On St Stephen*; a book *On the Grace of Baptism*; works *On Avarice*, *On Hospitality*, *On the Eclipse of the Moon*, *On Almsgiving*, *On the Passion of the Lord*, *On the General Fast of the Servants of God*, *On the Special Fast of Lent*, and *On the Kalends of January*; [Col. 0216A] many homilies *On the Nativity of the Lord*, *On Epiphany*, *On Easter*, and *On Pentecost*; and very many other works. He flourished under Theodosius (Gennadius, ch. 40).

### Chapter XLI

Petronius, bishop of the Church of Bologna, a man of holy life, trained from youth in monastic pursuits, wrote *Lives of the Egyptian Monastic Fathers*. He flourished under Theodosius (Gennadius, ch. 41).

### Chapter XLII

Pelagius, the heresiarch, wrote three books on faith in the Trinity and a book on the active life, in support of his heresy. Augustine answered him (Gennadius, ch. 42).

### Chapter XLIII

Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote the decree of the Western and Eastern Churches against the Pelagians, which his successor Pope Zosimus later promulgated more widely [Col. 0216B] (Gennadius, ch. 43).

### Chapter XLIV

Caelestius wrote three moral letters to his parents from the monastery, in the form of short books (Gennadius, ch. 44).

### Chapter XLV

Julian, bishop of Capua, a man of sharp intellect, learned in the divine Scriptures and schooled in Greek and Latin, fell into the heresy of Pelagius. He wrote four books against Augustine, and then another seven books. There is also a book of disputation between the two, defending their respective positions (Gennadius, ch. 45).

### Chapter XLVI

Lucian, a holy presbyter, wrote the revelation of St Stephen in Greek. Avitus, a presbyter Spanish by origin, translated it into Latin [Col. 0216C] (Gennadius, ch. 46).

### Chapter XLVII

Paulinus, bishop of Nola in Campania, composed brief but numerous works: a consolatory short work addressed to a certain Celsus, in place of an epitaph, upon the death of a Christian and baptized infant; several letters to Severus; and a panegyric to the Emperor Theodosius concerning the victory over tyrants. He also produced a Sacramentary and a Hymnal; many letters to his sister on contempt for the world; various treatises on various subjects; a book on repentance; and one *In Praise of the Martyrs*. He flourished under Honorius (Gennadius, ch. 48).

### Chapter XLVIII

The presbyter Eutropius wrote two consolatory letters, in the form of books, to two sisters, servants of Christ, in elegant and clear language [Col. 0216D] (Gennadius, ch. 49).

### Chapter XLIX

Another Evagrius wrote the disputation of Simon the Jew and Theophilus the Christian, which is known to almost everyone (Gennadius, ch. 50).

### Chapter L

The deacon Vigilius composed, from the tradition of the Fathers, a Rule for monks, in concise and clear language, containing the entire discipline of the monastic profession [Col. 0217A] (Gennadius, ch. 51).

### Chapter LI

Atticus, [Note: [Col. 0217D] Concerning Atticus, bishop of Constantinople and successor of Arsacius, Suidas says in his *Lexicon*: “Atticus, bishop of Constantinople after Arsacius, who had the administration of ecclesiastical affairs after Chrysostom, was by origin from Sebaste, a city of Armenia. From boyhood he was educated in philosophy by a monk of the Macedonian sect. Those who then excelled in philosophy at Sebaste had come forth from the school of Eustathius, whom we knew as bishop and leader of the monks in that place. After Atticus had been liberally educated, [Col. 0218D] he became cautious and prudent. He laboured in reading ancient writers, spending nights in turning their pages. Afterwards, having said a long farewell to writing, he devoted himself to a manner of life given to rhetorical exercises.” From these words of Suidas it seems possible to infer the age of Suidas himself [ [Col. 0217D] Or rather, of the writer whose words Suidas adduces.]; for he says that he knew Eustathius, bishop of Sebaste and teacher of Atticus. Atticus died about A.D. 425 and had Sisinnius as his successor in the see of Constantinople.], bishop of Constantinople, wrote for the empresses, the daughters of the Emperor Arcadius, a most excellent book *On Faith and Virginity* (Gennadius, ch. 52).

### Chapter LII

Nestorius, the heresiarch, presbyter of the Church of Antioch and an outstanding declaimer in speech, composed innumerable treatises on various subjects (*hypotheseis*, ὑποθέσεις). Afterwards, as bishop of the Church of Constantinople, he wrote a book *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, full of heresy (Gennadius, ch. 53).

### Chapter LIII

Caelestine, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote a volume against Nestorius. Sixtus, Caelestine’s successor, likewise wrote against Nestorius (Gennadius, ch. 54).

[Col. 0217B] ### Chapter LIV

Theodore, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, wrote against Nestorius a book composed with dialectical skill (Gennadius, ch. 55).

### Chapter LV

Fastidius, bishop of the Britons, wrote one book *On the Christian Life* to a certain Fatalis, and another, *On the Preservation of Widowhood*, containing sound doctrine worthy of God (Gennadius, ch. 56).

### Chapter LVI

Cyril, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, published treatises on various subjects (*hypotheseis*, ὑποθέσεις). He also composed very many homilies, books *On the Decline of the Synagogue* and *On Faith against Heretics*, and a book specifically against Nestorius (Gennadius, ch. 57).

### Chapter LVII

Bishop Timothy composed a book *On the Nativity of the Lord according to the Flesh*, which he believed had occurred at Epiphany (Gennadius, ch. 58).

[Col. 0217C] ### Chapter LVIII

Leporius, still a monk and afterwards a presbyter, followed Pelagian doctrine but was corrected by Augustine; he wrote a book describing his amendment (Gennadius, ch. 59).

### Chapter LIX

Victorinus, a rhetorician of Marseilles, published books on Genesis (Gennadius, ch. 60).

### Chapter LX

Cassian, an African by origin, was ordained deacon at Constantinople by Bishop John the Great. At Marseilles, as a presbyter, he founded two monasteries, one for men and one for women, which survive to this day. Taught by experience, he wrote in learned language; or, to speak more plainly, he found words adequate to his thoughts and gave his language force through action. He wrote on matters necessary for the profession of all monks: namely, three books *On the Monk’s Habit*, and on the canonical order of prayers and [Col. 0217D] psalms observed day and night in Egyptian monasteries; one book of *Instructions*; eight books *On the Origin, Character, and Remedies of the Principal Vices*, treating each vice separately [Col. 0218A]. He also arranged the *Conferences* held with the Egyptian Fathers: on the monk’s purpose and end; discernment; the three callings to serve God; the struggle of flesh against spirit and spirit against flesh; the nature of all vices; the death of the saints; the mutability of the soul; the eight principal vices; the quality of prayer; the perfect; chastity; God’s protection; spiritual knowledge; divine gifts; friendship; defining and not defining; the three ancient kinds of monks and a fourth recently arisen; the faith of the cenobite and the hermit; satisfaction in repentance; the relaxation of Pentecost; nocturnal illusions; the Apostle’s saying, “For I do not do the good that I wish”; [Col. 0218B] and mortification. Finally, at the request of Leo the archdeacon, afterwards bishop of the city of Rome, he wrote seven books *On the Incarnation of the Lord* against Nestorius. In these he ended both his writing at Marseilles and his life, under Theodosius (Gennadius, ch. 61).

### Chapter LXI

Philip, a presbyter and pupil of Jerome, published a book on Job and several letters (Gennadius, ch. 62).

### Chapter LXII

Eucherius, presbyter of the Church of Lyons, explained every obscure passage of the holy Scriptures to the bishops Salonius and Veranus. He also compressed into brief form Cassian’s writings, which had been extended at length. He flourished under Valentinian (Gennadius, ch. 63).

### Chapter LXIII

Vincent, a Gaul by origin and presbyter at the monastery on the island of Lérins, [Col. 0218C] a man learned in the holy Scriptures, wrote a very powerful disputation. Concealing his name, he entitled it *The Pilgrim against Heretics*. He flourished under Theodosius (Gennadius, ch. 64).

### Chapter LXIV

Syagrius wrote *On Faith against Heretics* (Gennadius, ch. 65).

### Chapter LXV
