Isaac, presbyter of the Church of Antioch, wrote much against the Nestorians and Eutychians. He also lamented the destruction of Antioch in a long poem, instructing his hearers with that melody by which the deacon Ephraem had lamented the fall of Nicomedia. He died under Leo (Gennadius, ch. 66).

### Chapter LXVI

Salvian, presbyter of the Church of Marseilles, learned in humane and divine letters, and [Col. 0218D]—to speak without envy—a teacher of bishops, wrote many works in scholarly and clear language: three books *On the Good of Virginity* to the presbyter Marcellus; four books against avarice; [Col. 0219A] five books *On the Present Judgment*; one book to Bishop Salonius; one Hexaemeron on Genesis; many homilies delivered to bishops; and several works on the sacraments (Gennadius, ch. 67).

### Chapter LXVII

Paulinus composed treatises *On the Beginning of Lent*, *On Easter Sunday*, *On Obedience*, *On Repentance*, and *On the Newly Baptized* (Gennadius, ch. 68).

### Chapter LXVIII

Hilary, bishop of Arles, learned in the holy Scriptures, carried out the work of preaching with correction for all, without respect of persons. He flourished under Valentinian (Gennadius, ch. 69).

### Chapter LXIX

Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote a letter against the presbyter Eutyches to Flavian, bishop of the Church of Constantinople. He flourished under Leo [Col. 0219B] (Gennadius, ch. 70).

### Chapter LXX

Mochimus, a Mesopotamian presbyter at Antioch, wrote an excellent short work against Eutyches (Gennadius, ch. 71).

### Chapter LXXI

Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, wrote a highly persuasive book to Emperor Leo (Gennadius, ch. 72).

### Chapter LXXII

Asclepius, an African and bishop in the territory of Bagae [or Vagae], wrote against the Arians (Gennadius, ch. 73).

### Chapter LXXIII

Peter, presbyter of the Church of Edessa and an outstanding declaimer, wrote treatises on various subjects; and, after the manner of St Ephraem the deacon, composed psalms in metre (Gennadius, ch. 74).

### Chapter LXXIV

Peter, [Note: [Col. 0219D] In Gennadius, chapter 75: Paul.], a Pannonian by origin, [Col. 0219C] presbyter, wrote two books on virginity and contempt for the world.

### Chapter LXXV

Bishop Pastor composed a small short work in the form of a Creed (Gennadius, ch. 76).

### Chapter LXXVI

Victor, bishop of the city of Cartenna in Mauretania, wrote one book against the Arians, one *On Repentance*, and a consolatory book to a certain Basil on the death of his son. He also composed many homilies (Gennadius, ch. 77).

### Chapter LXXVII

Buconius, bishop of the Mauretanian town of Castellum, wrote against the enemies of the Church—the Jews, Arians, and other heretics. He also composed an excellent volume on the sacraments (Gennadius, ch. 78).

[Col. 0219D] ### Chapter LXXVIII

Musaeus, presbyter of the Church of Marseilles and learned in the divine Scriptures, selected from the holy Scriptures readings suited to the feast-days of the entire year, responsories and psalm-verses appropriate to the seasons and readings, an excellent volume on the sacraments, and certain homilies (Gennadius, ch. 79).

### Chapter LXXIX

Vincent, a presbyter by nationality a Gaul and trained in the divine Scriptures, produced a commentary on the Psalms (Gennadius, ch. 80).

### Chapter LXXX

Syrus, [Note: [Col. 0219D] In Gennadius, chapter 81: Cyrus.], Alexandrian by origin, a physician by profession, from philosopher become monk, [Col. 0220A] and a man skilled in speaking, wrote elegantly and forcefully against Nestorius.

### Chapter LXXXI

Samuel, presbyter of the Church of Edessa, composed many works against the heretical enemies of the Church (Gennadius, ch. 82).

### Chapter LXXXII

Claudianus, presbyter of the Church of Vienne, a man skilled in speech and subtle in disputation, composed three, as it were, books *On the State or Substance of the Soul* (Gennadius, ch. 83).

### Chapter LXXXIII

Prosper, bishop of the Aquitanian region, scholarly in language and vigorous in argument, composed many works: a *Chronicle* from the creation of the first human being to the capture of Rome by Genseric, king of the Vandals. He also wrote a book against Cassian’s short works, which the Church of God approves as beneficial but which he denounces as harmful [Col. 0220B]. Indeed, Cassian’s and Prosper’s opinions concerning God’s grace and free will are found to be opposed to one another. Pope Leo’s letters *On the Incarnation of Christ against Eutyches* were also dictated by him (Gennadius, ch. 84).

### Chapter LXXXIV

Faustus, formerly abbot of the monastery of Lérins and afterwards made bishop at Riez in Gaul, a man sufficiently devoted to the divine Scriptures, composed a book *On the Holy Spirit*, an outstanding work *On the Grace of God by Which We Are Saved*, and other works (Gennadius, ch. 85).

### Chapter LXXXV

Caesarius, bishop of the city of Arles, celebrated for holiness and virtues, wrote excellent and pleasing short works very necessary for monks, including works *On Grace* and *On Free Will*. He flourished under Anastasius (Gennadius, ch. 86).

[Col. 0220C] ### Chapter LXXXVI

Bishop Servus Dei wrote against those who say that Christ, while living in this life, did not see the Father with his bodily eyes, but only after his resurrection from the dead and ascent into heaven, when he was transferred into the Father’s glory—this being given to him as recompense for martyrdom. From the Scriptures he showed that the Lord Jesus always saw both the Father and the Holy Spirit with bodily eyes (Gennadius, ch. 87).

### Chapter LXXXVII

Victorius, an Aquitanian by origin and a most diligent calculator, composed a Paschal cycle after the four earlier computists: Hippolytus, Eusebius, Theophilus, and Prosper (Gennadius, ch. 88).

### Chapter LXXXVIII

Theodoret, bishop of the city of Cyrrhus, [Col. 0220D] founded by Cyrus, king of the Persians, wrote *On the Incarnation of the Lord* against the presbyter Eutyches and Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, who deny that Christ possessed human flesh. He also wrote ten books of ecclesiastical history. He flourished under Leo (Gennadius, ch. 89).

### Chapter LXXXIX

Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, refined in language and keen in intellect, wrote a complete commentary on Daniel and many homilies (Gennadius, ch. 90).

### Chapter XC

Theodore, [Note: [Col. 0220D] In Gennadius, chapter 91: Theodulus.], a presbyter in Coele-Syria, composed a book against heretics *On the Harmony [Col. 0221A] of the Old and New Testaments*. He flourished under Zeno.

### Chapter XCI

Sidonius, bishop of the Arverni, wrote various pleasing short works to different persons, in various metres or prose, and an outstanding volume of letters. He flourished under Zeno (Gennadius, ch. 92).

### Chapter XCII

John, formerly a grammarian and then presbyter of the Antiochene diocese, wrote certain works against heretics, *On the Person of God and Man* (Gennadius, ch. 93).

### Chapter XCIII

Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote a large and distinguished volume against Eutyches and Nestorius, treatises on various writings and sacraments in polished language, and letters against Peter and Acacius. He also composed hymns in the manner of Ambrose. He flourished under Anastasius (Gennadius, ch. 94).

[Col. 0222A] ### Chapter XCIV

Honoratus, bishop of the African city of Constantine, wrote an exhortatory letter to a certain Arcadius (Gennadius, ch. 95).

### Chapter XCV

Bishop Cerealis, an African by origin, published a short work *On the Catholic Faith* (Gennadius, ch. 96).

### Chapter XCVI

Eusebius, [Note: [Col. 0221D] In Gennadius, chapter 97: Eugenius.], bishop of the African city of Carthage and a public confessor, wrote an exposition of the faith and the disputations which he held with the Arian bishops.

### Chapter XCVII

Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles, wrote eight books against all heresies, six against Nestorius, eleven against Eutyches, and three against Pelagius; treatises *On the Thousand Years* and on the Apocalypse; and a letter on faith (Gennadius, ch. 100).

## Third Book Supplemented from Isidore

[Col. 0221B] ### Chapter I

Osius, bishop of the city of Corduba, wrote to his sister a letter *In Praise of Virginity*, adorned with beautiful and eloquent expression. At the Council of Sardica he himself also issued very many decisions. In old age, terrified by Constantius, he assented to Arian impiety. When, seated with the arrogance, as it were, of royal power, he attempted to pronounce sentence against Gregory, bishop of Elvira, his mouth turned aside, his neck was likewise twisted, he was thrown from his seat to the ground, and immediately expired (Isidore, ch. 1).

### Chapter II

Idatius, bishop in the Spanish provinces, surnamed Clarus and renowned for his eloquence, wrote a book against Priscillian’s doctrine and his magical practices. Having, together with Bishop Ursacius, been deprived of communion with the Church because of the killing of that same Ursacius, of whose death they had been the accusers, he was condemned to exile [Col. 0221C] (Isidore, ch. 2).

### Chapter III

Siricius, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote decretal works (Isidore, ch. 3).

### Chapter IV

The presbyter Paulinus published a short work *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, according to a threefold interpretation. At Augustine’s request, he wrote the *Life of Ambrose* (Isidore, ch. 4).

### Chapter V

Proba, wife of the proconsul Adelphus, composed a cento concerning Christ, fitted together from Virgilian verses; it is counted among the apocryphal writings (Isidore, ch. 5).

### Chapter VI

John, bishop of the see of Constantinople, surnamed Chrysostom, wrote many distinguished short works and various treatises. Very many streams of his eloquence [Col. 0221D] have been translated from Greek into Latin. Overwhelmed by the hostility of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, innocently condemned by the Emperor Arcadius, and expelled from his bishopric, he died after being banished to Pontus (Isidore, ch. 6).

[Col. 0222B] ### Chapter VII

The presbyter Sedulius published three books composed in heroic metre. The first most powerfully recounts the signs and mighty deeds of the Old Testament; the others proclaim the sacred events or miracles of Christ’s deeds (Isidore, ch. 7).

### Chapter VIII

Possidonius, [Note: [Col. 0222D] In Isidore, chapter 8: Possidius.], bishop in the province of Africa, wrote the *Life of St Augustine*, in which he enumerates more than four hundred of Augustine’s books.

### Chapter IX

Primasius, an African bishop, composed in scholarly language three books *On Heresies*, addressed to Bishop Fortunatus (Isidore, ch. 9).

### Chapter X

Proterius, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, wrote letters to Leo, bishop of the Roman see, concerning the feast of Easter (Isidore, ch. 10).

### Chapter XI

Paschasinus, bishop of Sicily, published [Col. 0222C] one Paschal letter to the aforesaid Pope Leo (Isidore, ch. 11).

### Chapter XII

John Scotus, or Chrysostom, exceptionally learned in the Scriptures, wrote in elegant style a book, *Peri physeōn* (Περὶ φύσεων), that is, *On the Nature of All Things*.

### Chapter XIII

Theodulus, an Italian by origin, wrote one eclogue woven from the Old Testament and pagan fables, in which he established the truth of faith and destroyed the falsehood of unbelief.

### Chapter XIV

Julian, surnamed Pomerius, a Moor by origin and ordained presbyter in Gaul, wrote eight books *On the Nature of the Soul*, in dialogue form. The first contains what the soul is and how it is believed to have been made in God’s image. In the second he discusses whether the soul is bodily or incorporeal. In the [Col. 0222D] third he discusses from what source the first human’s soul was made. In the fourth, whether a new soul is made without sin and whether it derives, by original propagation, the first human’s sin from him. In the fifth he describes what faculty the soul possesses. In the sixth he discusses the source of that conflict by which spirit opposes flesh, or flesh spirit. In the seventh [Col. 0223A] he writes about the difference between lives and deaths, the resurrection of flesh and soul, the death of the flesh, and its resurrection. In the eighth he discusses those things which will occur at the end of the world; questions customarily raised concerning the resurrection; and the ends of the good and the evil. He also composed one short work *On the Training of Virgins*; three further prognostic works *On the Contemplation of the Future Life, or on Active Conduct*; and likewise works *On Vices and Virtues* (Isidore, ch. 12).

### Chapter XV

Abbot Eugippius composed the *Life of St Severinus the Monk* and a Rule for monks (Isidore, ch. 13).

### Chapter XVI

Fulgentius, an African and bishop of the Church of Ruspe, distinguished in confession of the faith, most abundantly learned in the Scriptures, sweet in speech and subtle in teaching and disputation, wrote much. Among his works are: *On the Grace of God and Free Will*; seven books of answers against heretics; one book *On the Holy Trinity*; a book *The Rule of the True Faith*; another *On the Sacrament of Christ’s Incarnation*; two books *On the Truth of Predestination*; a book *On Questions*; a book of disputation; very many treatises and sermons. He flourished under Anastasius [Col. 0223B] (Isidore, ch. 14).

[Col. 0224A] ### Chapter XVII

Bishop Eucherius, elegant in his thoughts and ornate in expression, published one short work *In Praise of the Desert*, composed in sweet language (Isidore, ch. 15).

### Chapter XVIII

Hilary, bishop of Arles, wrote the *Life* of his predecessor, Bishop Honoratus, [Note: [Col. 0223B] “Honorius” in the text; “Honoratus” in the note.], in charming and distinguished language (Isidore, ch. 16).

### Chapter XIX

Aprigius, bishop of the Church of Pax Julia in Spain, learned in eloquence and knowledge, expounded the Apocalypse of John the Apostle with subtle understanding and brilliant language—plainly better than the earlier ecclesiastical writers had expounded it. He also wrote several other works (Isidore, ch. 17).

### Chapter XX

The Emperor Justinian published certain books *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, which he also sent through various [Col. 0224B] provinces. He also composed a rescript against the Illyrian synod (Isidore, ch. 18).

### Chapter XXI

Cassiodorus, [Note: [Col. 0223B] The author of the *Variae* was called by all his names Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator, a man most renowned for his writings and offices; yet, through an inveterate error, if one may say so, we call him “Cassiodorus.” For we should not listen to those who think that he was called *Senator* pre-eminently (κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν), as though Cassiodorus had been his proper name. [Col. 0223C] His true and proper name was *Senator*: he placed it at the head of all his letters in Books XI and XII of the *Variae*, and he gave that name alone in his own *Fasti* in the year 513, when he dealt with his consulship. But the error born from the opinion already mentioned prevailed: because *Senator* was thought to be an epithet rather than a name, he is commonly called Cassiodorus as though that were his personal name, whereas it was in fact a cognomen derived from his father’s name. For Senator’s father was named Cassiodorus; from him the son was called Cassiodorus Senator, and, as stated, by all his names Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator. Thus our Senator had a father named Cassiodorus, to whom Theodoric, king of the Goths, granted the patriciate after the prefecture of the praetorium. The author of the *Variae* himself tells much about this man, his grandfather, and his father in Book I, letters 3 and 4, and Book III, letter 28 was also written to him. To Senator the son, of whom Honorius speaks in this chapter, not Theodoric but King Athalaric, his grandson, granted the prefecture [Col. 0223D] and then the patriciate, as is clear from Book IX, letters 24 and 25, in which he is rightly called Senator: “We have heaped our benefits upon the most noble Senator, abundant in virtues, rich in character, and filled with great honours.” He wrote twelve books of the *Variae Epistles*; also the most devout book *On the Soul*; two books *On the Instruction of the Divine Scriptures, or Readings*; *On the Figures and Tropes of Sacred Scripture*, from Bede [ [Col. 0223D] Bede lived after Cassiodorus.]; *On Orthography*; *On the Seven Disciplines*; *On Friendship*; *On the Paschal Computation*; and a short *Chronicle* from the beginning of the world to the times of Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths in Italy—that is, to A.D. 519. He also wrote twelve books of a *History of the Goths*, as he himself affirms in the preface to his letters. Jordanes, or Jornandes, bishop of Ravenna, who lived in A.D. 530, produced an abridgement of this history [Col. 0224B]. William Fornerius, a jurist of Orléans, arranged for all these works to be published at Paris in 1600 after collation with manuscript codices and with explanatory notes. Cassiodorus further wrote commentaries on the Psalms, drawn almost wholly from Augustine and printed at Basel in 1491; and, on the *Song of Songs*, printed with Aponius at Freiburg in 1538 [Col. 0224C]. Finally, he compiled the *Tripartite History* from three Greek authors—Socrates, Theodoret, and Sozomen—translated into Latin by Epiphanius Scholasticus. John Cochlaeus first published his *Chronicle* and dedicated it to Thomas More. Jacobus Pamelius arranged for the publication by Plantin of the *Institution of Divine Letters*. After holding every office in the Roman commonwealth and at the court of King Theodoric, Cassiodorus finally took leave of the world and became a monk. He founded the monastery of Vivarium near Rhegium in Calabria, presided over it as abbot, established there a school of sacred literature, and died an old man about A.D. 560.], a prefect at Ravenna from the senatorial order, a philosopher by learning and a monk by profession, translated the *Tripartite History* from Greek, expounded the Psalter magnificently, and wrote many other works.

## Chapter XXII. Boethius

[Note: **[Col. 0224C]** Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, philosopher and orator, distinguished by wisdom, eloquence, piety, and martyrdom, was highly praised by Ennodius, Cassiodorus, Procopius, and others. In the year of Christ 510 **[Col. 0224D]** he was ordinary consul without a colleague. Ordered to be executed by Theoderic, king of the Ostrogoths in Italy, together with his father-in-law Symmachus in 526, he died gloriously at Pavia.

Onuphrius Panvinius is mistaken in thinking that Boethius was again consul in 522 together with his father-in-law Symmachus. For in that year Boethius’s two sons, Symmachus and Boethius, were ordinary consuls. He gave one the name of his father-in-law, their grandfather, and the other his own name. Concerning their joint consulship Boethius himself writes in Book II of *The Consolation*: “When you saw your two sons, both consuls together, being conducted from your house amid the throng of the Fathers and the rejoicing of the people. And what need is there to speak of your sons as consuls, when, even while still boys at that age, the image of their father’s or grandfather’s talent already shone forth?”

I know that Julius Martianus Rota, author of **[Col. 0225A]** the *Life of Boethius*, held another view, making his sons Patricius and Hypatius, who jointly held the consulship in the year 500. But this is certainly an excessive **[Col. 0225B]** error. Apart from the fact that he ought to have remembered that those were Greek and Eastern consuls and had nothing to do with Boethius’s family, the words of Boethius just cited could have disproved it. They make clear that these sons of his were boys of consular rank when he wrote his *Consolation* in exile. This plainly could not be said if they had been consuls twenty years, or indeed more, earlier.

Some write *Boetium*, others *Boethium*; the latter would be more correct if the Greek origin of the word were considered. But usage has prevailed, so that we more commonly say *Boetius*. Besides his philosophical works, he wrote a book *On the Holy Trinity*, addressed to Symmachus, his father-in-law; a book *On the Unity of the Trinity*; a book *On the Two Natures of Christ*, against Eutyches; a book *On the Faith*; and five books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, or of his exile. After Rudolph Agricola and John Murmellius, John Bernartius elucidated these with a commentary, and the Plantin press published them in 1607. **[Col. 0225C]** His works were jointly printed at Venice in 1491 and at Basel in 1546.

As Boethius excelled in verse and prose, so he embraced both Greek and Latin learning. All his works testify to this, as do Ennodius, Book VIII of the *Letters*, and Cassiodorus, Book I of the *Variae*, Letter 45. The people of Pavia annually celebrate his birthday on 23 October; he was buried there in the church of St Peter in Ciel d’Oro, where St Augustine also rests, as Philip Ferrari relates in his *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*. Some have observed that ancient Roman eloquence ended with Boethius.

After Martianus Rota, Francis Moncada, Marquis of Aitona, most learned in Greek and Latin—whose untimely removal in 1635 the Low Countries mourned—wrote his *Life* in Spanish. Would that someone would bring it to light. As for Symmachus, Boethius’s father-in-law, **[Col. 0225D]** Ennodius’s twenty-fifth letter in Book VII is addressed to him. Boethius adorns him with this praise in Book II of the *Consolation*: “Symmachus my father-in-law is still safe and vigorous, that most precious glory of the human race, a man made wholly of wisdom and virtues.” Ennodius declares that eloquence and nobility were hereditary in the family of the Symmachi—and rightly so, since nearly all were learned and distinguished by the highest offices.

It will not be out of place here to distinguish by individual notes the Symmachi who lived in Boethius’s age and in the preceding century, beginning with the branch of Symmachus the orator.

I. L. Aurelius Avianus Symmachus was prefect of the City in 364. An account of his merits and a testimony to his eloquence are contained in the inscription of a statue which the emperors ordered to be erected for him in duplicate, at Rome and Constantinople. Marcellinus, Book XXVII, calls him a learned man. Only one letter **[Col. 0226A]** to his son Symmachus remains, with a few epigrams surviving from those which he had written on eighty eminent men of his age.

II. Q. Aurelius Symmachus, son of Lucius, the orator. His are nine books of *Letters*, and a tenth book of *Relations*, which he wrote while prefect of the City. Among them is read the famous relation concerning the Altar of Victory, to which St Ambrose and Prudentius replied. He was proconsul of Africa in 370, prefect of the City in 384, and finally ordinary consul with Tatianus in 391. His wife was Rusticiana, daughter of Orfitus; his mother was the full sister of Acyndinus the consul, whom he therefore calls his maternal uncle. He is the man who debates in Macrobius’s *Saturnalia*, to whom Ausonius sends his *Griphus*, and of whom St Augustine speaks when he writes, in *Confessions*, Book V, chapter 13, that Symmachus, a *vir perfectissimus*, sent him to Milan for the profession of rhetoric. Prosper, Book III of *On the Promises*, chapter 38; Sidonius, Letter 1 and elsewhere; Socrates, Book V, chapter 14; and Cassiodorus, Book XI, also treat of him.

III. Q. Flavianus Memmius Symmachus, the orator’s only son, by whom his father’s letters were arranged and published after his **[Col. 0226C]** death. He too was proconsul of Africa in 415 and prefect of the City in 420. His are the *Relations* concerning the dispute of Eulalius against Pope Boniface, written to the Emperor Honorius and inserted by Baronius in his *Annals*. He had also been candidate quaestor and praetor in early life. For Symmachus frequently mentions in his letters both offices held by his son, and Olympiodorus of Thebes, quoted by Photius, records the expense of his praetorship while ranking the Symmachi among the wealthiest men of Rome.

IV. Q. Aurelius Symmachus—for so he is called in Valentinian’s Novel 4—was ordinary consul with Aetius, consul for the third time, in 446. He was, I think, the grandfather of the widow Galla mentioned in Fulgentius’s letter, in which Fulgentius addresses Galla, daughter of the patrician Symmachus: “And although long ago you had been illustrious among secular persons through a grandfather, father, father-in-law, and husband who were consuls.”

V. Q. Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, patrician and Boethius’s father-in-law, to whom Boethius dedicates several of his little works, was **[Col. 0226D]** ordinary consul without a colleague under Odoacer in 485. King Theoderic selected him, together with others, as judge in the case of Basilius and Praetextatus, who were accused of magical arts; see Cassiodorus, Book II, Letter 22. Cassiodorus also preserves other letters of Theoderic himself to Symmachus. Pope Hormisdas mentions him in Letters 28 and 66. Finally, Theoderic, stirred up by the impious accusations of informers, cruelly put him to death together with Boethius, his son-in-law, as Procopius relates in Book I of the *Gothic War*. Two daughters of his are mentioned: Rusticiana, Boethius’s wife, and Galla, of whom, besides Fulgentius, Gregory the Great treats in *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 14. He left no son.

For the following VI. Symmachus, Boethius’s colleague in the consulship of 522, was not the son of this patrician Symmachus but his grandson, born of his daughter Rusticiana and Severinus Boethius. So, in substance, Sirmond maintains in his notes on Ennodius.]

Boethius, patrician or consul, wrote a book *On the Holy Trinity* and another *On Consolation*; **[Col. 0225A]** he translated from Greek the *Quadrivium*, that is, arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy; and he expounded dialectic. He was killed at Milan by Theoderic, king of the Goths.

## Chapter XXIII. Facundus

Facundus, bishop of the Church of Hermiane, published twelve books *On the Profession of the Catholic Church* (Isidore, chapter 19).

## Chapter XXIV. Justinianus

Justinianus, bishop of the Church of Valencia, one of four brothers, all bishops and born of the same mother, wrote a book of *Answers* to a certain Rusticus concerning questions that had been asked. The first answer concerns the Holy Spirit; the second is against the Bonosians, who call Christ **[Col. 0226A]** an adopted Son and not a proper Son; the third concerns Christ’s baptism, which may not be repeated; the fourth, the distinction between John’s baptism and Christ’s; the fifth, that the Son, like the Father, is invisible (Isidore, chapter 20).

## Chapter XXV. Justus

Justus, bishop of the Church of Urgell and brother of the aforesaid Justinianus, published a small work expounding the *Song of Songs*. His brothers Nebridius and Elpidius also wrote certain works (Isidore, chapter 21).

## Chapter XXVI. Martinus

Martinus, most holy bishop of the monastery of Dumium, sailed from the regions of the East to Gaul. There, after the peoples of the Suevi had been converted from Arian impiety **[Col. 0227A]** to the Catholic faith, he established a rule of faith and sound religion, organized churches, founded monasteries, and composed abundant precepts for pious instruction. He also wrote a book *On the Distinctions of the Four Virtues*—prudence, courage, justice, and temperance—and another volume of letters, full of the cultivation of every virtue (Isidore, chapter 22).

## Chapter XXVII. Avitus

Bishop Avitus, learned in the knowledge of the sacred writings, published five small works composed in heroic metre: the first, *On the Origin of the World*; the second, *On Original Sin*; the third, *On the Judgment of God*; the fourth, *On the Flood of the World*; the fifth, *On the Passage of the Red Sea*. He also wrote for his sister Fulcina one book *On the Praise of Virginity*, composed in most beautiful verse and fitted with an elegant epigram **[Col. 0227B]** (Isidore, chapter 23).

## Chapter XXVIII. Dracontius

Dracontius composed in heroic verse a hexameron on the creation of the world (Isidore, chapter 24).

## Chapter XXIX. Victor

Victor, bishop of the African Church of Tunis, wrote a distinguished *History* from the beginning of the world down to the time of Justin (Isidore, chapter 25).

## Chapter XXX. Benedict

[Note: **[Col. 0227D]** Benedict, an Italian by nation and a native of Nursia, standard-bearer and chief of monks in the West, founder of the monastery of Monte Cassino, fell asleep in the Lord there in the year of salvation 539. Pope St Gregory I recounts his deeds at length in Book II of the *Dialogues*. The people of Ingolstadt published Gregory’s book in Greek and Latin in recent years. I have discussed the various ascetic Rules and Constitutions at length in our *Code of Rules*, published at Antwerp in 1638.]

Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Cassino, wrote the Rule of monks, promulgated throughout the world; this book is said to be full of the spirit of all the righteous.

## Chapter XXXI. John

John, bishop of Constantinople and a Cappadocian by nation, published for Bishop Alexander a book *On the Sacrament of Baptism* (Isidore, chapter 26).

## Chapter XXXII. Gregory

Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome, instrument of the Holy Spirit, incomparable with all **[Col. 0227C]** his predecessors, wrote many things more splendid than the sun and more precious than refined gold: *Pastoral Care*, addressed to the aforementioned John; a book on Job, addressed to Bishop Leander, expounded in thirty-five volumes from the abundant spring of his eloquence; and a *Dialogue on the Miracles of the Saints*, addressed to Peter the archdeacon. He is said to have expounded for the people, in sermons, forty Gospel oracles—indeed the entire text of the four Gospels; **[Col. 0228A]** twenty homilies on Ezekiel; and innumerable letters, the collection of which is called the *Register*. He flourished under Maurice (Isidore, chapter 27).

## Chapter XXXIII. Gregory

[Note: **[Col. 0227D]** Georgius Florentius Gregorius succeeded the deceased St Euphronius, bishop of Tours, in the episcopal see in the twelfth year of Sigebert, king of Austrasia, in the one hundred and seventy-third year after the departure, or death, of St Martin—that is, in the year of Christ 573—as may be inferred from Gregory himself, Book I, chapter 1, of the *Miracles of St Martin*.

He wrote one book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, two books *On the Glory of the Confessors* **[Col. 0228D]**, one book *On the Miracles of St Julian*, and four books *On the Miracles of St Martin*. He also wrote ten books of the *History of the Franks*, which he completed in the twenty-first year of his ordination, 594. After various editions, Andreas Duchesne carefully corrected them with the help of five manuscript codices and published them at Paris in 1636, in Volume I of the *Writers of the History of France*.

In the same volume he appended the *Chronicle* of Fredegar Scholasticus, which Fredegar wrote at the command of Count Childebrand, uncle of Pepin, king of the Franks. It carries the account from the end of Gregory of Tours’s *History* to Pepin’s own consecration, and had hitherto been published as an Appendix to Gregory. In Duchesne you will also find the *Chronicle* of Marius, bishop of Avenches.]

Gregory, bishop of Tours, wrote a book of history.

## Chapter XXXIV. Leander

Leander, formerly a monk and then bishop of the Church of Seville in the province of Baetica, a man gentle in speech, eminent in ability, and illustrious in life and learning, composed two books against the doctrine of heretics; one for his sister Florentina, *On the Instruction of Virgins*; one against the Arians; one *On Contempt for the World*; and many letters to Pope Gregory and to other fellow bishops. He also composed, in sweet-sounding style, prayers on the entire Psalter and many pieces in praise of the sacrifice. He flourished under Phocas (Isidore, chapter 28).

## Chapter XXXV. Licinianus

**[Col. 0228B]** Licinianus, bishop of Carthago Spartaria, learned in the Scriptures, wrote a letter *On the Sacrament of Baptism* and many other letters on various matters. He flourished under Maurice (Isidore, chapter 29).

## Chapter XXXVI. Severus

Severus, bishop of the see of Málaga, wrote a small work against Vincentius, an Arian bishop, and one *On Virginity*, called *The Ring*. He flourished under Maurice (Isidore, chapter 30).

## Chapter XXXVII. John

John, bishop of the Church of Girona and a Goth by nation, wrote a Rule necessary for monks and for all who fear God (Isidore, chapter 31).

## Chapter XXXVIII. Eutropius

Eutropius, bishop of the Church of Valencia, wrote a letter *On the Anointing of Chrism* and another *On the Distinction of Monks* (Isidore, chapter 32).

## Chapter XXXIX. Maximus

Maximus, bishop of the city of Saragossa **[Col. 0228C]**, composed many works in verse and prose, and a certain history of the Goths (Isidore, chapter 33).

## Chapter XL. Isidore

Isidore, bishop of Seville, wrote innumerable small works, including: twenty-two books of *Etymologies*; a book of *Glosses*; a book of *Sentences*; *Synonyms*; and a book *On Difference*. He expounded the whole Old Testament in two ways, historically and allegorically, and wrote many other works. He flourished under Heraclius.

# Fourth Book: A Collection on Various Writers

## Chapter I. Bede

[Note: **[Col. 0228D]** St Bede, an Anglo-Saxon by origin, died in 734, as the continuator of his English history and Matthew of Westminster report. The people of Cologne published in 1612, in eight volumes, all his works that could be found; but would that some Briton might undertake the task of reviewing them against the authority of manuscript codices. These volumes contain not a few works falsely attributed to Bede; consult Bellarmine in his *Catalogue*, Possevino in his *Sacred Apparatus*, and Baronius in his *Annals* concerning them.

Certainly, the *Life of St Vedast* was written not by Bede but by Alcuin; the *Life of St Patrick*, by Probus; and the *Life of St Columban*, by the monk Jonas. Paul the Deacon wrote the *Life of St Arnulf of Metz*. Baronius, in his account of the year 562, attributes the commentaries on the Epistles of St Paul not to Bede but to Peter, abbot of Tripoli, praised by Cassian; but Bellarmine argues for Bede in the book cited. Bede lived and died in his monastery by the River Tyne, in the diocese of Durham.]

Bede, monk and priest of the English province, wrote innumerable works, including these: four books *On Genesis*; four books *On the Tabernacle and Its Vessels and the Garments of the Priests*; two books *On the Building of the Temple* **[Col. 0228D]**; one book of thirty questions on the Book of Kings; three books on Solomon’s *Proverbs*; seven books on the *Song of Songs*; three books on Isaiah, Daniel, the Twelve Prophets, part of **[Col. 0229A]** Jeremiah, Ezra, and Nehemiah; two books on Tobit; one book on the Canticle of Habakkuk; also many chapters on the Books of Kings and Chronicles, Job, the Pentateuch of Moses, Joshua, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Isaiah, and Ezra; four books on the Gospel of Mark; six on Luke; two books of Gospel homilies; many chapters on the Apostle; two books on the Acts of the Apostles; seven books on the Catholic Epistles; three on the Apocalypse; chapters on the whole New Testament; a book of letters to various persons; one book on the six ages; nine books on the resting-places of the children of Israel; one on Isaiah; one on the calculation of leap year; nine on the equinox; and works on the histories of the saints.

He translated the book of the life and passion of St Felix the Confessor **[Col. 0229B]** from verse into prose; corrected from Greek into Latin the life and passion of St Anastasius; composed the life of St Cuthbert, monk and bishop, in verse and prose; wrote a history of the English in five books; a martyrology concerning the feasts of saints; a book of hymns in diverse metres or rhythms; a book of epigrams in elegiac metre; one book each *On the Nature of Things* and *On Times*, and another, larger book *On Times*; a book *On the Orthography of the Alphabet*; a book *On the Art of Metre*; and *On Schemes and Tropes*, that is, on the figures and modes of expression in Holy Scripture. **[Col. 0230A]** He flourished under Leo, died at Rome, and was buried there.

## Chapter II. Alcuin

[Note: **[Col. 0229C]** Flaccus Alcuin, a Briton by birth, Bede’s pupil, summoned into Gaul by Charlemagne and made abbot of the monastery of St Martin near Tours, ceased to live in the year 804. Andreas Duchesne arranged for all his works that could be found to be published at Paris in 1617, with a prefixed life of Alcuin arranged chronologically.]

Alcuin, an Englishman by nation, deacon of the city of York, a schoolman by office, an abbot by rank, and master of Emperor Charles, wrote a brief account of all the liberal arts for the aforesaid emperor, and many other outstanding works.

## Chapter III. Amalarius

[Note: **[Col. 0229D]** Amalarius, deacon of the Church of Metz, composed four books *On the Divine Offices* at the command of Louis the Pious. Printers have hitherto wrongly attributed these books to Amalarius Fortunatus, bishop of Trier.

Amalarius of Metz, as I have said, was a deacon—the person whom Honorius incorrectly calls bishop of Metz in this chapter—and was a man of far-reaching learning, contemporary with Amalarius, bishop of Trier. From Amalarius of Metz, after access had been granted to the books in the palace at Aachen, the *Form of Instruction for Canons and Canonesses Living Canonically* was compiled from various opinions of the ancient Fathers and doctors, and was approved by the judgment and authority of the Council of Aachen in 816. Sirmond observed this from the *Chronicle of Ademar of Angoulême*. I arranged for this *Form of Canonical Instruction*, illustrated with notes by me, to be published at Antwerp in 1638 with the *Code of Clerical Rules and Constitutions* **[Col. 0230B]**.

As to Amalarius Fortunatus, bishop of Trier, he was sent by Charlemagne to Constantinople to Emperor Michael Balbus together with Peter, abbot of Nonantola in the diocese of Modena **[Col. 0230C]**. He had as his successor in the see Hetto, whose letter to Frotarius, bishop of Toul, Sirmond cites in his notes on Volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*.]

Amalarius, bishop of Metz, wrote four books on the divine sacraments under Louis.

## Chapter IV. Rabanus

[Note: **[Col. 0230C]** Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda in Hesse or eastern Francia, was a pupil not of Bede but of Alcuin. In 847 he was ordained archbishop of Mainz in place of Otgar, and he died in 856, as the Annals of Pithou and Lambert of Aschaffenburg testify. All his works that could be found by Jacob Pamelius and George Colvenerius were published at Cologne in three volumes in 1627.]

Rabanus, from abbot of the monastery of Fulda made bishop of Mainz, wrote the remarkable book *On the Mystery of the Holy Cross* and expounded the entire Old and New Testament. He flourished under Louis.

## Chapter V. Paterius

[Note: **[Col. 0230C]** Paterius, disciple of Pope Gregory I and *secundicerius* of the Holy Roman Church—whom Bede mentions in his Commentary on the Song of Songs—collected from the works of the same St Gregory three books of explanations on various books of both Testaments, printed at Rome in folio in 1553. He flourished in the year of Christ 600. So Molanus in his manuscript *Sacred Library*.]

A certain Paterius compiled into a book the testimonies of Scripture which blessed Gregory expounded while introducing them.

## Chapter VI. Smaragdus

[Note: **[Col. 0230D]** Smaragdus, abbot of the Benedictine monastery of St Michael in Saxony, wrote among other things the *Diadem of Monks*, printed at Antwerp in 1540; a Commentary on the Rule of St Benedict, Cologne, 1575; and Collections on the Epistles and Gospels for the whole year, printed in folio at Strasbourg in 1536. He flourished in 980.]

**[Col. 0230B]** Smaragdus, abbot of the monastery of St Michael, expounded the lessons and Gospels to be read in the divine offices throughout the yearly cycle; composed a book suitable for the monastic profession, which he called *The Diadem of Monks*; and explained a more extensive grammar by expounding Donatus.

## Chapter VII. Haymo

[Note: **[Col. 0230D]** Haymo, monk of Fulda and pupil of Rabanus Maurus, later third bishop of Halberstadt in Saxony, wrote seven books on the Apocalypse; six books *On Love for the Heavenly Homeland*; an epitome of sacred history; commentaries on the Twelve Prophets, the Song of Songs, the Psalms, and all the Epistles of St Paul; and homilies on the Gospels. Some of these were printed at Cologne, others at Antwerp, Paris, and elsewhere. Baronius thinks he died in 853; others date his death to 834.]

A certain Haymo wrote homilies on the solemn Gospels. He also composed a book on the pleasure of the world.

## Chapter VIII. Henry

A certain Henry wrote homilies on the Gospels.

## Chapter IX. Notger

[Note: **[Col. 0231B]** Notger, abbot of the monastery of St Gall among the Swiss, is regarded as the inventor of the *Sequences*, as they are called, which Pope Nicholas permitted to be sung in Masses. Others ascribe this invention to Notger, bishop of Liège, who died in 1007. Some suspect that the two were one and the same Notger, first abbot of St Gall in Switzerland and afterwards bishop of Liège; but this is not proved by the writers on the history of Liège.]

**[Col. 0231A]** Notger, abbot of the monastery of St Gall, composed sequences, troped verses, and many other works. He flourished under Otto.

## Chapter X. Paschasius

[Note: **[Col. 0231B]** Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corbie in Picardy, a province of the kingdom of France, flourished in the reign of Emperor Louis the Pious. He was the first to write seriously and extensively *On the Truth of the Lord’s Body and Blood in the Eucharist* against Bertram the priest. After Nicolas Mameranus and John Ulimmerius, Jacob Sirmond reviewed **[Col. 0231C]** his works against the authority of manuscript codices and arranged for them to be published together at Paris.]

Paschasius composed a book *On the Body of the Lord*.

## Chapter XI. Peter

[Note: **[Col. 0231C]** Peter Damiani—so called from the name of his brother Damian—cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Ostia, was first a monk in the wilderness of Fonte Avellana. Thereafter he founded various monasteries in the dioceses of Camerino, Perugia, Faenza, Rimini, and others; finally, at Faenza, in a monastery of his own foundation, he fell asleep in the Lord in the year 1080. His deeds were written by the monk John, his disciple; John Antony Flaminius; Augustine Fortunius, a Camaldolese monk; and Jerome Rubeus in his *History of Ravenna*. Constantinus Caetanus collected all his works into three volumes and published them at Rome in recent years.]

Peter, surnamed Damiani, became a bishop from being a monk and hermit. He wrote a book against those who considered Simoniacs to be reordained, and many other works. He flourished under Henry the Pious.

## Chapter XII. Hermannus

[Note: **[Col. 0231C]** Hermannus Contractus, descended from the family of the counts of Veringen in Swabia and a monk of Reichenau, wrote a *Chronicle* from Christ’s birth to the year 1054, **[Col. 0231D]** in which year he also died. Christian Urstisius had appended to the commonly published edition of Hermannus another, fuller version, set opposite it; but Henry Canisius published a third edition in 1601, in Volume I of *Ancient Readings*, much enlarged and corrected from a manuscript codex of the Augsburg monastery of Saints Afra and Ulrich.

To investigate the cause of this diversity: some think that, in writing the *Chronicle*, Hermann experienced what many writers have experienced in the past and do today, who continually shape, vary, and enlarge their offspring by revising it. Others ascribe this variation to copyists: one added certain things, another cut them out, each according to his own judgment. For I observe that this was mostly done in antiquity in books which monks copied for private or public use.]

Hermannus, a monk surnamed Contractus, wrote certain works and composed sweet-sounding chant. He flourished under the same Henry.

## Chapter XIII. Bernoldus

[Note: **[Col. 0231D]** Bernoldus, also called Bernaldus and Bertoldus, priest of Constance, is, unless I am mistaken, the same man who **[Col. 0232B]** carried the *Chronicle* from the year 1054, where Hermannus Contractus ends, down to the year 1000 [an apparent textual error or uncertainty]; and who wrote various small works for Pope Gregory VII against the schismatics. Some were published by Gretser in his *Apology for the Same Pontiff*, and some by Sebastian Tengnagel at Ingolstadt in 1612.]

Bernoldus, priest of the Church of Constance, composed the Roman Order under Henry IV **[Col. 0231B]**.

## Chapter XIV. Lanfranc

[Note: **[Col. 0232B]** Lanfranc, a native of Pavia, became archbishop of Canterbury after being abbot of Caen. He attended the Roman council convened against Berengar and wrote a book *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist* against him. The people of Louvain and others printed it after John Ulimmerius had corrected it against the authority of manuscript codices. Clement Reyner arranged for the statutes which he prescribed to Benedictine monks in England to be published at Douai **[Col. 0232C]**.]

Lanfranc, bishop of Canterbury after being an abbot, wrote a book *On the Body of the Lord* **[Col. 0232A]** against the heretic Berengar. He flourished under the same Henry.

## Chapter XV. Anselm

[Note: **[Col. 0232C]** St Anselm, born at Aosta among the Rhaetians, pupil of Lanfranc, bishop of Canterbury, and himself bishop of Canterbury after being abbot of Bec, passed to the better life in 1109. The people of Cologne published his collected works in three volumes in 1573; later, the people of Lyons published fuller editions. See Bellarmine’s judgment on them in his *Catalogue*. John Picard published his three books of *Letters* separately at Paris. Many other letters of his survive in the library of John Cotton in England and elsewhere. His life was written by Eadmer or Edmer—corruptly, Edinerus—a monk of Canterbury, who also committed to writing chiefly the events in England from 1066 to 1122. Anselm of Laon, the schoolmaster, was another man.]

Anselm, pupil of this same Lanfranc, bishop of the Church of Canterbury in the English province after being its abbot, wrote many memorable works, including: the book called *Why God Became Man*; one book of the *Monologion*, namely on the Holy Trinity; one *On the Incarnation of the Word*; one *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*; one *On the Fall of the Devil*; one *On Free Will*; *On the Grace of God*; *On Predestination*; and many other works worthy of God.

## Chapter XVI. Rupert

[Note: **[Col. 0232C]** Rupert, abbot of Tuitiensis—the Benedictine monastery on the Rhine, situated on the German bank opposite Cologne—died on 4 March 1135. **[Col. 0232D]** He wrote many works, printed in three volumes at Cologne in 1577 and previously at Antwerp and Louvain. He himself lists his works in his letter to Cuno, bishop of Regensburg, to whom he dedicates his books *On the Divine Offices*.

He errs when he writes that, when the Eucharist is consecrated, the bread is not changed into Christ’s body but assumed by the divine Word, just as humanity was assumed. Bellarmine refutes this error in his *Catalogue* and in Book III, chapters 11 and 15, of *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, as do others in many places.]

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Tuitiensis, enlightened by a vision from the Holy Spirit, expounded almost the whole of Scripture in an excellent style. He flourished under Henry V.

## Chapter XVII. Honorius

[Note: **[Col. 0232D]** Among the various works of Honorius of Autun survive: commentaries on the books of Solomon, Cologne, 1540; the *Dialogue on Predestination and Free Will*, 1552; and other small works of his, printed there in 1531; the *Jewel of the Soul*; *On the Office of Mass and Its Ceremonies*, Leipzig, 1514; three books *On the Image of the World*, Speyer, 1583; and other works printed elsewhere.

His work *On the Luminaries of the Church*, or *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, which we now present, seemed best divided into four books, because the first three are drawn almost entirely from Jerome, **[Col. 0233A]** Gennadius, and Isidore, and therefore contain something like an epitome. Yet Honorius wove into or appended to this work quite a few writers absent from those three ancient cataloguers. He also occasionally inserted in this very recapitulation matters that provide much light. **[Col. 0234B]** He lived at Autun in Burgundy, during the reign of Henry V, about the year of salvation 1120.]

**[Col. 0232B]** Honorius, priest and schoolmaster of the Church of Autun, published works not to be despised: the *Elucidarium*, in three books, the first **[Col. 0233A]** distinguished as concerning Christ, the second concerning the Church, the third concerning the future life; a little book *On Holy Mary*, entitled *The Seal of Holy Mary*; one *On Free Will*, called *The Inevitable*; a small book of sermons called *The Mirror of the Church*; *On the Incontinence of Priests*, called *The Stumbling-Block*; *The Sum of All Things*, concerning universal history; *The Jewel of the Soul*, concerning divine offices; the *Sacramentary*, concerning sacraments; *The New World*, concerning the first six days; *Eucharistion*, concerning the Body of the Lord; *Knowledge of Life*, concerning God and eternal life; *The Image of the World*, concerning the arrangement of the universe; *The Supreme Glory*, concerning the Apostolic See and the Emperor **[Col. 0234A]**; *The Ladder of Heaven*; *On the Degrees of Visions*; certain extracts from Augustine *On the Soul and God*, written in dialogue form; an exposition of the entire Psalter with the Canticles, in a remarkable manner; an exposition of the Song of Songs such that earlier expositions seem not to have existed; the Gospels which blessed Gregory did not expound; *The Key of Physics*, concerning the natures of things; *The Refreshment of Minds*; *On the Feasts of the Lord and the Saints*; *The Food of Life*, concerning the principal feasts; and this little book *On the Luminaries of the Church*. He flourished under Henry V. Posterity will see who shall write after him.

# Book on Heresies

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, XX, 1038.)

## Preface

**[Col. 0233D]**

Having briefly noted those who illuminated the Church with the bright light of Catholic teaching, it remains briefly to note those who obscured it, as it were, with the dark smoke of heretical doctrine. A heresy, therefore, is called a “choice” (*electio*). Hence a heretic is called a “chooser” (*elector*), because each person chooses the sect which **[Col. 0234D]** he follows. A person becomes a heretic through error and contention, when he obstinately defends his error and despises the sayings or writings of the wise. Such a person indeed contradicts the Church and is alien to its faith. But a person who understands Scripture differently from its true meaning is not to be judged a heretic, provided that he corrects himself when he hears instruction from a teacher.

## On the Heretics of the Jews

**[Col. 0235A]**

Among the Jews there were these eight heresies.

The Pharisees were the clerics of the Jews, and their name means “separated.” Their heresy consisted in preferring their own traditions to God’s commandments.

The Sadducees were the monks of the Jews, and their name means “righteous.” Their heresy consisted in denying the resurrection of bodies and declaring that the soul perishes with the body. They received the Law of Moses but rejected the writings of the prophets.

The Essenes were certain Jewish heretics who said that he is the Christ who taught them every kind of abstinence.

The Marbonites were other heretics who say that he is the Christ who taught them to observe the Sabbath in every matter.

**[Col. 0235B]** The Genistae were heretics who gloried in being of Abraham’s seed. For in Babylon certain Jews had intermarried with pagan women, while others had intermarried with Israelites; on returning to Jerusalem, they separated themselves from all the people and took this name for themselves as a boast.

The Meristae were heretics who accepted some prophets and did not accept others.

The Samaritan heretics observe the Law alone and reject the prophets.

The Emerobaptists are heretics who wash their garments and bodies daily.

## ON THE HERETICS OF THE PAGANS

The philosophers were the patriarchs of heretics; among them there were many heresies.

The Platonists, so called from Plato, said that God created souls, and angels [Col. 0235C] bodies; that after many ages souls return into different bodies; and that all things return to their former condition.

The Stoics were so called from a place. For the Stoa was a portico at Athens in which the deeds of wise and brave men were displayed. In it the philosopher Zeno instructed his disciples. They say that every sin is equal: that stealing a grain of wheat is as grave as stealing gold. They maintained that blessedness consists in the soul alone, and that the soul perishes with the body.

The Academics were so called from Plato’s estate, the Academy. They hold all things to be uncertain. The discoverer of this sect was Arcesilaus, and its follower Democritus, who said that truth lies hidden as water does in a deep [Col. 0235D] bottomless well.

The Peripatetics were so called from walking about, because their founder Aristotle disputed while walking. They say that the soul is in part eternal and in part mortal; they maintain that things are done by chance.

The Cynics were so called from their filthiness. Like dogs, they had intercourse with their wives in lanes and public streets, saying that marriage is just and therefore honourable, and that it ought rightly to be performed in public.

The Epicureans, so called from the philosopher Epicurus, place the highest good in bodily pleasure; they say that the soul is nothing other than a body, and that the world is governed not by God but proceeds from atoms.

The Gymnosophists philosophize naked by day in deserts, [Col. 0236A] covering only their private parts. They throw themselves into fire out of love for another life.

Some philosophers said that this world is God, as Dionysius did; some said that mind is God, as Thales of Miletus did; some, that God is the soul abiding in human beings and luminous, as Pythagoras did; some, that he is changeless and outside time, as Plato did; some, that he is unbound mind, as Cicero says in the first *Tusculan Disputation*; some, that he is spirit and mind, as Virgil says in *Aeneid*, book VI, verses 726–727.

Likewise, other philosophers differ: the Platonists declare the world incorporeal; the Stoics, corporeal; Epicurus, composed of atoms; Pythagoras, of numbers; Heraclitus, of fire. In the Christian Church there were these heretics.

The Simoniacs were so called from Simon Magus, who attempted to purchase from the apostles, with money, [Col. 0236B] the gift of the Holy Spirit. They say that creation was made not by God but by a certain higher power. All who buy spiritual things are Simoniacs, to be condemned with Simon Magus; but those who sell them are Gehazians, to be reproved with Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, who sold the healing which Elisha had given freely; and therefore Naaman’s leprosy clung to him.

The Menandrians were so called from Menander, Simon’s disciple. They maintain that the world was made not by God but by angels. They deny that Christ suffered. They hold wives in common.

The Nicolaitans were so called from Nicholas the deacon, Stephen’s companion, who made his wives common property.

The Gnostics were so called from the excellence of their knowledge. They say that the soul [Col. 0236C] is of God’s nature; they invent a good God and an evil one.

The Carpocratians were so called from a certain Carpocrates. They say that Christ was merely a human being born from both sexes.

The Cerinthians were so called from a certain Cerinthus. They observed circumcision and proclaimed that, after the resurrection, a thousand years of bodily pleasure would follow.

The Nazaraeans were so called from the village of Nazareth. They confess that Christ is the Son of God, yet observe all things of the old Law.

*Ophis* means “serpent.” Hence the Ophites are heretics because they worship the serpent, on the ground that in Paradise it introduced the knowledge of virtue.

[Col. 0236D] The Valentinians were so called from a certain Valentinus. They introduce certain ages or aeons into the origin of God the Creator; they say that Christ assumed nothing bodily from the Virgin, but passed through her as water through a pipe.

The Apellites were so called from a certain Apelles. They say that Christ appeared not truly as God, but as a human being in appearance.

The Aconthians were so called from “rulers.” They say that all God’s works are works of angels.

The Adamites were so called because they imitate Adam’s nakedness. They pray naked and have intercourse naked.

The Caini are so called because they hated Cain.

The Sethians were so called from Seth, Adam’s son, whom they say is Christ himself.

[Col. 0237A] The Melchizedekians were so called because they proclaim Melchizedek not as God’s priest but as God’s power.

The Angelics are so called because they worship angels.

The Apostolics are so called because, possessing nothing of their own, they do not admit those who make use of anything in this world.

The Cerdonians were so called from a certain Cerdo. They assert two contrary principles.

The Marcionists were so called from a certain Marcion. They assert one God as good and another as just, as though there were two principles of the Creator.

The Artotyrites were so called from their offering. They offer bread and cheese, saying that from the first human beings an offering was celebrated from the fruits of the earth and from sheep.

The Aquarians are so called because they offer water alone in the cup [Col. 0237B] of the Sacrament.

The Severians arose from Severus. They do not drink wine; they do not receive the Old Testament or the resurrection.

The Tatianists were so called from a certain Tatian, and are also called Creatians. They abominate meat.

The Alogi are so called as being “without the Word.” They do not believe God to be the Word and do not receive the Gospel of John or the Apocalypse.

The Cataphrygians were so called from the province of Phrygia, from which Montanus came. They maintain that the Holy Spirit was transmitted not to the apostles but to themselves.

The Cathari were so called from purity. They deny forgiveness of sins to penitents; if widows remarry, they condemn them as adulteresses; they proclaim themselves purer than others.

[Col. 0237C] The Pauliani arose from Paul of Samosata, a bishop. They say that Christ did not always exist, but took his beginning from Mary.

The Hermogenians were called from a certain Hermogenes. They make the matter of the world equal to God.

The Manichaeans were so called from a certain Persian, Manes. They introduce two natures and substances, that is, a good and an evil one; they maintain that souls flow forth from God as though from some fountain. They reject the Old Testament and receive the New only in part.

The Anomians live without law.

The Anthropomorphites were so called from “man”; for *anthrōpos* means “man.” They maintain that God has human limbs and a human form, although God is [Col. 0237D] spirit and incorporeal.

The Heraclites arose from a certain Heraclius. They admit monks only, reject marriage, and do not believe that infants possess the kingdom of heaven.

The Novatians were so called from Novatus, a presbyter of the city of Rome. They do not admit the lapsed to penance, and they rebaptized those already baptized.

The Montanists were so called from mountains. In time of persecution they hid in mountains and separated themselves from the body of the Church.

The Ebionites were so called from Ebion or from poverty [perhaps from Greek *penia*, “poverty”]. They regard Christ as merely a perfect and righteous man. They are semi-Jews: they retain the Gospel and observe the Law carnally.

[Col. 0238A] The Photinians were so called from Photinus, bishop of Smyrna. They proclaim that Christ was conceived from Mary by Joseph in marital intercourse.

The Aerians were so called from a certain Aerius. They despise offering sacrifice for the dead.

Likewise the Aetians were named from Aetius.

The Eunomians were so called from Eunomius, a certain dialectician and disciple of Aetius. They assert that the Son is like the Father, and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son; they also say that no sin is imputed to those who remain in the faith.

The Origenists were so called from Origen. They say that the Son cannot see the Father, nor can the Holy Spirit. They also say that souls sinned at the beginning of the world and, falling from heaven in accordance with the diversity of their sins, entered different bodies on earth as into fetters; and that for this reason [Col. 0238B] the world was made.

The Noetians were so called from a certain Noetus. They say that Christ is himself both Father and Holy Spirit. They understand the Trinity in names of offices, not in persons; hence they are called Patripassians, because they say that the Father suffered.

The Sabellians were so called from Sabellius, Noetus’s disciple. They maintain a single person of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The Arians arose from Arius, presbyter of Alexandria. They posit different substances in the Trinity.

The Macedonians were so called from Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople. They deny that the Holy Spirit is God.

The Apollinarists were named from Apollinaris. They say [Col. 0238C] that Christ assumed a body only, without a soul, and had his divinity in place of a soul.

The Antidicomarianites contradict Mary’s virginity, saying that after Christ’s birth she had intercourse with a man.

The Metangosites [perhaps Metangiotae] are so called from a vessel. For *angios* means “vessel.” They say that the substance of human flesh was fashioned by the devil.

The Colicians were named from a certain Colicus. They say that God does not make evils, contrary to the saying: “I am the Lord creating evils.”

The Florians were so called from a certain Florinus. They say that God created evils, contrary to the saying: “The Lord made all things good.”

The Donatists were named from a certain African Donatus. They assert [Col. 0238D] that the Son is less than the Father and that the Holy Spirit is greater than the Son, and they rebaptized Catholics.

The Bonosiacs arose from a certain bishop Bonosus. They maintain that Christ, the Son of God, is adoptive rather than proper.

The Circumcellions, that is, country-dwellers, are the same as the Coropites, following the heresy of those above. Out of love for martyrdom they kill themselves, that they may be called martyrs.

The Priscillianists were named from Priscillian, a bishop. In Spain he composed a mixed doctrine from the heresies of the Gnostics and Manichaeans.

The Luciferians arose from Lucifer, bishop of Smyrna [Cagliari]. They refuse to receive those who fell into heresy and afterwards returned to the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0239A] The Jovinianists were so called from a certain monk Jovinian. They maintain that there is no difference between married people and virgins, or between those who abstain and those who feast.

The Helvidians were named from a certain presbyter Helvidius. They say that Mary bore other children to Joseph after Christ’s birth.

The Paterniani arose from a certain Paternus. They say that the lower parts of the body were made by the devil.

The Arabici were so called from the province of Arabia. They maintain that the soul dies with the body, and that both rise again at the last day.

The Tertullianists were so called from Tertullian, presbyter of Carthage in the African province. They proclaim that the soul is not immortal but bodily; they affirm that, after death, the souls of sinners are changed into demons.

[Col. 0239B] The Tessarescaedecadites were so called from “fourteen”: for *tessera* means four and *deca* ten. They celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth moon.

The Nyctages were named from sleep or night. They reject night vigils, saying that night was given for rest.

The Pelagians arose from a certain monk Pelagius. They place free choice before God’s grace, saying that the will suffices for fulfilling divine commands.

The Nestorians were named from Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople. They proclaim holy Mary not as Mother of God but merely mother of a human being. Positing one person for the flesh and another for the divinity, they affirm not one Christ in Word and flesh, but one Son of God and another son of man.

[Col. 0240A] The Eutychians were so named from Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople. They deny that there are two natures in Christ; rather, after the assumption of flesh, they proclaim that his sole nature is divine—namely, that the flesh was changed into divinity.

The Acephali are so called “without a head”; for *a* means “without,” and *cephalē* means “head.” They have no founder; they deny two substances in Christ and proclaim one nature in his person.

The Theodosians and Gaianites arose from Theodosian and Gaian, bishops of Alexandria. They assert one nature in Christ out of two.

The Gnoites were so called from ignorance. They say that Christ’s divinity is ignorant of future things concerning the last day.

The Tritheites were so called from “three.” Just as they assert three persons [Col. 0240D] in the Trinity, so they assert that there are three gods.

There are also other heresies without names: some of them think that God has a threefold form; some say that Christ’s divinity is passible; some give Christ’s birth from the Father a beginning; some proclaim one operation and one will in Christ, of divinity and humanity; some deny that human beings were delivered in hell by Christ’s descent; some do not think that God has an image.

Likewise, others differ concerning the state of the world: some imagine innumerable worlds; some make water coeternal with God; some walk barefoot; some do not eat with other people; some doubt concerning Christ’s body—all of whom the whole Catholic Church condemns.

[Col. 0239]

## COMMENTARY ON PLATO’S *TIMAEUS*, WHOSE AUTHOR APPEARS TO BE HONORIUS OF AUTUN

(Victor Cousin, *Ouvrages inédits d’Abailard*, appendix, p. 646.)

It is known that Plato’s *Timaeus* was known through the Commentary of Chalcidius at least from the eighth and ninth centuries, since it is found in manuscripts dating from that period. It is also known that the doctrines expounded there had become, in the twelfth century, a subject of study and controversy. The influence of Platonic theories is visible in Bernard of Chartres. Yet it remains uncertain whether Bernard knew Plato otherwise than through Macrobius. Abelard never cites anyone but Macrobius; and only one twelfth-century author is positively known to have commented on Plato: that author is Honorius of Autun. Not only does he deal, in the first book of the *Image of the World* (chapters 81 and 83), with an explanation of the famous numbers of the *Timaeus*; but in the first book of his *Philosophy of the World* (book I, chapter 15), after reporting several opinions current in his own day concerning the soul of the world, he refers, for an explanation of Platonic doctrine on that point, to glosses which he had written on Plato: “Plato says that it was conceived from divisible and indivisible substance, and from the same and different nature; whoever seeks an exposition of this will find it in our little glosses on Plato.” It would therefore be possible that the commentary contained in the Saint-Germain manuscript, 1195, was Honorius’s. Indeed, the author (folio 60 verso, column 1) tells us that he had composed a book on physics which he calls “our *Philosophy*,” in which he had demonstrated that no bodies can be situated in a region higher than that of fire: “Therefore, by natural aspiration, nothing ought to be higher than fire. What they say, namely that frozen waters are there, is so absurd that we disdain to refute it. We have sufficiently said the same in our *Philosophy*.” Now this idea recurs in several places in the *Philosophy of the World* (book III, chapters 5, 6, etc.). Finally, the authors mentioned in the commentary before us are precisely those whom Honorius of Autun ordinarily cites in his writings on physics: Boethius, Macrobius, and Constantine the African. Here are some extracts from the Commentary on the *Timaeus*:

> “Those beginning Plato’s *Timaeus* must inquire what was the reason for that composition; what it treats; how it treats it; and to what part of philosophy it belongs; and also its title. The reason for composing this work was as follows. Since it is certain among all who philosophize rightly that justice holds the chief place in the preservation of the commonwealth, their greatest effort was directed toward its investigation. Thrasymachus the orator defined it thus: ‘Justice is what most benefits him [we have supplied *him*] who has the most power,’ observing that, for the preservation of justice, the governance of the commonwealth is transferred to him who has the greatest power. When this definition was recounted in the schools, Socrates said: ‘No; rather, justice is what most benefits him who has the least power.’ For the person who has the greatest power preserves himself and his possessions without any justice at all; but the one who has the least power does so least of all. And because he had given so perfect a judgment concerning it, his disciples asked him to compose a treatise about it. Satisfying their wish, he dealt with one part of justice itself, namely positive justice. For justice is of one kind positive and of another natural. Positive justice is that invented by human beings, such as the hanging of a robber; natural justice is that not invented by human beings, such as love of parents and the like. But because positive justice appears most of all in the institutions of the commonwealth, in his treatise on it he turned to the commonwealth, in order to show justice in connection with it. Yet because in no commonwealth could he find perfect justice which he might set forth as an example, he invented a new one after the pattern of the ancient Athenians.
>
> “Then Plato, his disciple, having composed ten volumes on the commonwealth, wished to complete what his master had omitted and composed this work on natural justice. But because it appears especially in the creation of the world, he turns to that creation. Hence we may say that the subject of this book is natural justice, or the creation of the world; for he treats creation because of natural justice. He deals with such a subject in this manner: by showing the efficient, formal, final, and material cause of the world; then the cause of the conception of the soul, its mode, its union with the body, and the powers it exercises in it; afterward, the creation of heavenly, aerial, aquatic, and creeping animals. Then he treats the ages of humankind, the function and usefulness of its members, and finally primordial matter. He treats such material to this end, and in such a manner, that, seeing divine power, wisdom, and goodness in the creation of things, we may fear one so powerful, reverence one so wise, and love one so gracious.
>
> “It is not subordinate to only one part of philosophy, but contains something from several. That this may be understood more clearly, let us set forth the divisions of philosophy. Philosophy, then, is a true comprehension of things that are and are not seen, and of things that are and are seen. It has two kinds: practical and theoretical. There are three practical kinds: ethics, concerning instruction in morals—for *ethos* means ‘custom’; economica [thus], concerned with administration—for *economus* means ‘administrator’; and politics, or civic science—for *polis* means ‘city’; this teaches how a commonwealth should be managed. Likewise there are three kinds of theoretical philosophy: theology, mathematics, and physics. Theology concerns divine things; for *theos* means ‘God’ and *logos*, ‘reason.’ Mathematics contains the quadrivium and is called mathematics, that is, doctrinal science. *Mathesis* with aspiration means ‘teaching’; without it, ‘vanity.’ It is called doctrinal in the preeminent sense because instruction in the quadrivium is more perfect than in the other arts. In the others, instruction is conveyed by voice alone; in this one it is conveyed both by voice [Col. 0247] and by the eyes. For, when a rule is spoken by the mouth, it is displayed before the eyes in a figure. Mathematics has four species: arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy. Physics concerns the natures and mixtures of bodies; for *physis* means ‘nature.’ Music has three species: instrumental, cosmic, and human. Instrumental music has three: melic, metric, and rhythmic. Melic has three: diatonic, enharmonic, and chromatic.
>
> “Therefore this work contains something from every art: from practical philosophy, in the recapitulation of positive justice; from theology, where it speaks of the efficient, formal, and final cause of the world and of the soul of the world; from mathematics, where it speaks of numbers and proportions; and from physics, where it speaks of the four elements, the creation of animals, and primordial matter. Its title is: ‘Here begins Plato’s *Timaeus*, named after a certain disciple of his.’ For Plato’s custom was to entitle volumes from the names of his disciples, in order to confer honour on the disciple, avoid arrogance, and remove from rivals an opportunity for criticism. Or it is called *Timaeus* as though ‘flower’; for *thimio* [thus] means ‘I flower,’ because it contains the flower of philosophy.
>
> “Isocrates, etc. Plato’s *Timaeus* was long considered difficult, not because so perfect an author had said anything obscurely, but because readers did not know the arts which he necessarily mentions. For, when dealing with the creation of the world, he had to make mention of the various arts, introducing demonstrations in accordance with the properties of each. It was therefore unknown to the Latins until the time of Pope Hosius. Knowing that it contained many useful things not contrary to the faith, Hosius asked his archdeacon Chalcidius, skilled in both languages, to translate it from Greek into Latin. Obeying his authority, Chalcidius translated its first parts. But, because he did not know whether they would please him or not, he sent them to him for judgment, so that, if they pleased, he might undertake the remainder with greater confidence. And since they were difficult to understand, he made a commentary upon them; and with the translated portion and the commentary he sent this letter, whose content is as follows. At the beginning he excuses himself for ignorance; afterwards he seeks Hosius’s goodwill; then he explains why he did not translate the whole work and why he wrote a commentary upon the translated part.
>
> “The literal exposition is as follows. It was difficult to translate Plato’s book from Greek into Latin; but your virtue and friendship made it easy for me. Yet someone might say to this: ‘Can virtue do this?’ He proves it indeed [lacuna] by the authority of Isocrates, saying as follows: ‘Isocrates’—that rhetorician Isocrates of whom one reads in rhetoric—in his *Exhortations*, that is, in the book so named, praising virtue, said that virtue is a disposition of the soul in accordance with the mode of nature and reason, and that ‘the cause of all prosperity lies in it [virtue].’ For every prosperity comes from virtue, because, as Boethius proves, all things which happen to the good are good, while those which happen to the wicked are evil; and virtue is the cause of all good things, that is, temporal and eternal. [Thus.] And when he had said these things, he added that virtue alone brings matters to practicable ease; that is, it makes impossible things easy—not by nature, but by practice. And lest anyone think he was speaking falsely, he adds *praeclare*, that is, openly and truly: ‘For what indeed?’ He proves that a difficult thing is easy for virtue by removing from virtue those things which produce difficulty. These are reluctant beginning and impatience of labour; and this is what he says: ‘What can weary noble greatness of soul,’ that is, virtue—and this is a periphrasis—‘when it undertakes,’ that is, begins, as though he said, ‘nothing honourable.’ Or, ‘What undertaking, that is, what thing begun, can weary it?’ Nothing, certainly. For before beginning, virtue considers whether it has sufficient strength to finish, so that it may spare itself labour.
>
> “But because what lacks alternating rest is not lasting, he adds: ‘as though overcome by difficulties.’ To interpose labours is a necessity of nature; to be conquered is frailty. The point is the same. Having proved that virtue makes a difficult matter easy, he says the same of friendship, which is a certain virtue: ‘the force of friendship is the same as that of virtue.’ Friendship is goodwill toward another for the sake of the person loved, together with that person’s equal goodwill. He explains how its force is the same: it is an equal disentangling, that is, an unravelling, of almost impossible things, that is, difficult things. *Tricae* are the meshes of a net; hence *intricare* means ‘to entangle’ and *extricare*, ‘to disentangle.’ ‘When one…’ He adds how friendship makes a difficult matter easy: when one of the friends—for friendship in actuality exists between at least two—commands devoutly, that is, commands things due, honourable, and possible; and when they assist the accomplishment of a pleasing work, that is, the completion of a work pleasing to both; the other by a resolve to obey, that is, obeying from resolve and willing intention. To obey from resolve is to obey without hope of reward, without the compulsion of fear, and without a tie of blood.
>
> “‘You had conceived,’ etc. Up to this point he excused himself from the charge of arrogance; now he seeks the goodwill of the same Hosius through the fact that Hosius foresaw a useful undertaking. ‘You had conceived in your mind,’ that is, had foreseen. But before he explains what this was, lest the conception seem bad, he commends Hosius thus: ‘With every pursuit of humane learning flourishing.’ Study is an intense application of the mind to doing something, with great willingness. Yet some studies concern humane learning, such as the practical disciplines; others concern divinity, such as the theoretical disciplines. Although this man flourished in all of them, he flourished especially in the pursuits of humane learning, because he was a human being. Or, human studies are called all those things which can be known by human beings, and in all of them he flourished. But because study without natural ability is insufficient, according to that saying of Horace:”
