“Neither diligence without a rich vein, nor raw talent, I see, can accomplish anything”; he also adds talent. Talent is the natural power of quickly understanding something; hence *ingenium* [talent] is so called as though “born within.” But since some talents are supreme, others slight, others middling, to crown the praise he adds “excellent.” Then, having commended him, he shows that he had conceived a worthy hope of the work’s outcome—that is, of Plato’s work being brought from Greek into Latin. But lest this translation seem superfluous, he adds “unattempted,” for no one had yet translated it. “And although.” In another way he seeks his goodwill, namely by removing arrogance from it. At once: what you enjoined upon me, you could have done better than I. And although you yourself—that is, you could have made this translation—could have done it more easily, because you are a teacher, and more suitably, because you have greater authority, yet you preferred to impose it upon him—that is, upon me—whom you judged to be another yourself, that is, whom you loved as yourself. This is taken from Tully, who says in his book *On Friendship*: “My friend is another self.” But lest he seem to have imposed it either through ignorance or indignation, he says: “I believe, because of your admirable modesty.” For one kind of modesty is good, another bad. Bad modesty is when we are ashamed, though lukewarm in doing good, to confess or abandon the evil we have done; good modesty is that by which we are ashamed to commit evil, and judge ourselves unequal to the knowledge or virtue that is in us.

“Could I?” Someone might indeed say to this: even if he had commanded it, still you began out of arrogance when you could have excused yourself. He proves that he could not, and this is the point: “I ask you,” O someone—or O Osius—could I excuse myself from the task, that is, this duty imposed upon me by you, although the matter—that is, the translation of that work—was arduous, I of whom you had so thought (*senseras*, “you had thought,” thus the manuscript; the edition has *censeres*, “you judged”), whom you considered another yourself? As though he said: No. “And who never”: he proves that he could not, by an argument from the lesser; for he had never contradicted that man’s will even in some small matter, much less in this one. This is the point: “And would I contradict one so great?” To indicate the magnitude, since many great things are insignificant, he adds: “and so honorable a desire,” which never … that is, a duty belonging to you. A duty is a fitting act which, according to the customs and institutions of the state, or by law or by nature, we ought to perform. “Not even in solemn matters,” that is, common matters; for *solon* [as printed] means “common,” whence *solemnia* [solemn observances] are so called as common festivals. “Usual matters,” that is, daily matters, in which friend often contradicts friend as if in trifles, but never in serious things.

“In which.” Someone might say: even if you could not excuse yourself thus, you would say that you did not know. The answer: I did not wish it to be thought a crafty pretence of ignorance. For some, in denying in this way, cunningly feign ignorance. This is the point: “in which,” that is, in which request, a refusal—that is, avoidance—of this splendid task by the excuse of ignorance, that is, by excusing oneself through ignorance and saying that I did not know, would have been, that is, could have been considered, a crafty pretence of knowledge.

“And so forth.” The excuse was not suitable; I obeyed, especially because I knew that, God willing, you commanded this. This is the point: I was certain that this task, that is, the duty of this translation, was not imposed upon me by you without divine prompting, that is, divine will. Therefore, because there was no ground for excuse and because you did not command without divine prompting, I undertook the first parts of Plato’s *Timaeus*, with a more eager mind in beginning, strengthened by hope in completing; and I not only translated them but also made a commentary on that translated part itself.

As Priscian says concerning boys’ exercises: “to devise” (*comminisci*) is to gather into one many things retained in the mind through study or instruction. Thus a *commentum* [commentary] can be called a gathering into one of many things retained in the mind through study or instruction. Although under this definition any book could be called a *commentum*, today we call a *commentum* only an exposition of another book; and this differs from a gloss. For a commentary follows only the sense and deals with nothing concerning the continuity or exposition of the wording. A gloss, however, pursues all those things; whence it is called *glossa*, as it were “tongue.” For it ought to expound so plainly that the teacher’s tongue itself seems to be teaching.

“Thinking,” etc. Up to this point he excused himself from arrogance and made Osius kindly disposed by praising him; then he made him receptive by showing that he had translated Plato’s *Timaeus*. Now he shows why he made a commentary on those parts: namely, because they were difficult to understand by themselves; and thus he renders him attentive, saying: I made a commentary, and superfluously, namely, “thinking,” etc. Plato’s book in Greek is the exemplar or concealed thing, while its Latin version is its image. But the image is more obscure than the exemplar itself, because the translation of any book is more obscure than its composition in its original language. He then shows why he divided the book and did not translate it all at once: the length of the work and uncertainty whether it would please or not; and this is the “cause,” etc.

One might believe from this beginning that our commentary will merely be a paraphrase of Chalcidius’s commentary. But this is not so. Chalcidius proposed only to provide the interpretation of passages in the *Timaeus* which presuppose knowledge of sciences such as arithmetic, geometry, music, and so forth. Here, by contrast, we have a regular commentary which follows the text step by step and omits nothing.

> “One, two, three. Plato, intending to treat natural justice, recapitulates what he had said concerning positive justice, so that the treatment of justice may be one and continuous. He does this in the following way, introducing four persons—Socrates, Timaeus, Hermocrates, and Critias—under the following fiction. Since it was the custom of the Athenians to gather on Pallas’s feast day in the house of some philosopher, in order to be instructed by him in some subject, he imagines that Timaeus, Hermocrates, Critias, and a fourth man, whose name he here suppresses, assembled on Pallas’s feast day in Socrates’ house; that they were instructed by him concerning positive justice; and that, when the discussion had ended and mutual inquiry had been made by them—that is, inquiry concerning justice—and a promise given, the next day arrived. But, not finding the fourth of his companions, he began thus to speak: ‘One, two, three.’

> But it is asked why Plato, who is known to have done nothing without a reason, began his book with numbers; and, if it was to begin with numbers, why with these numbers rather than others [we have supplied *rather*], why he set down three numbers and no more, and why he named them with cardinal rather than ordinal numbers. First, then, as a Pythagorean, knowing that the greatest perfection exists in numbers, since indeed no creature can exist without number whereas number can exist without any particular thing, he began with perfect numbers in order to show the perfection of his work. He chose these numbers because they are parts of the perfect number, namely six. A number is perfect when its parts added together yield an equal sum. Now the second part of six is three, its third part two, and its sixth part one; added together, these give the same sum, namely six. Therefore, because of perfection, he began with the parts of the perfect number.

> Moreover, among these numbers are found proportions that produce musical consonances. Between two and one is a double ratio; from this arises the octave (*diapason*). Between three and one is a ratio of five to four (*sesquiquarta*); from this arises the fifth (*diapente*). Between four and three is the ratio of four to three; from this arises the fourth (*diatessaron*). Therefore, because he had decided to treat the creation of things, which was made harmoniously and proportionally, he rightly began with numbers possessing ratios.

> He sets down only three numbers because, according to Boethius’s authority, he treats three things in a simple way: divine matters intellectually, mathematical matters doctrinally, and physical matters naturally. To treat divine matters intellectually is, all opinion removed, to establish by certain reason whatever is said concerning divine things. To deal doctrinally with mathematical matters is to treat subjects belonging to the quadrivium so that what is stated by rule is displayed before the eyes in a figure, as is done in the quadrivium. To treat physical matters naturally is to discuss the natures of bodies using physical reasoning. He calls them by cardinal, not ordinal, names, lest he seem to prefer one to another. These are Socrates’ words when he comes the following day and does not find all his companions: ‘One, two, three: O Timaeus, I seek the fourth of your number.’ That fourth was Plato, who in a sense withdrew himself from the work when he attributed it not to himself but to Timaeus, for the reasons stated above. ‘Who yesterday,’ etc.”

The author continues at length to comment on the preamble to the *Timaeus*. It is unnecessary to follow his developments on Deucalion’s flood, based on bad physics and entirely devoid of interest. His explanations of the origin of Athens and the tale of Erichthonius are of no greater value.

The commentary on Timaeus’s actual speech begins two-thirds of the way down the first column of the said folio 56 verso. Its beginning is as follows:

> “Thus the *Timaeus*, a treatise on natural justice, turns chiefly toward the creation of the world. ‘In order that it might belong to eternity …’ He shows its four causes—namely, efficient, formal, final, and material—in order to make clear that something perpetual can be created from such causes. The efficient cause is the divine essence, the formal cause divine wisdom, the final cause divine goodness, and the material cause the four elements. In order that these may be better understood, he sets forth a two-membered division. In one member are contained the efficient, formal, and final causes of the world; in the other, the material cause and effect. The division is this: whatever is either lacks generation and always is, or has generation and does not always exist.

> That we may understand this better, let us say what generation is; what it is to have generation; what it is to lack generation; what it is always to exist; and what it is not always to exist. Generation, then, as Boethius says in his fifth book on the *Categories*, is entrance into substance, that is, the beginning of existence; to lack generation is to lack a beginning of existence. Always to exist is to exist without past and future; not always to exist is to pass through temporal successions. Therefore that which never began to exist and has neither anything past nor anything future lacks generation and always is. This belongs to the divine essence: for it has neither a beginning of existence nor changes of time. This is the efficient cause of the world, since it is the creator of all things.

> The same belongs to divine wisdom. For if God lacks a beginning, he could not have existed without wisdom; for to be and to be wise are the same for him. Therefore his wisdom also lacks a beginning. It always exists because for him there is nothing past and nothing future, but all things are present. This is called the formal cause of the world’s creation because he formed the world in accordance with it. For just as a craftsman, wishing to make something, first arranges it in his mind and then, having procured material, works in accordance with his mind, so the Creator, before creating anything, held it in his mind and then fulfilled it in act. Plato calls this same thing the archetypal world: a world because it contains all things that are in the world; archetypal, that is, the principal form. For *archos* [as printed] means ruler, and *typos* [as printed] form or figure.

> The same belongs to divine goodness, for it lacks a beginning and is always present. That is the final cause of the world, because, as will appear below, he created all things by goodness alone. Thus under this member are contained the efficient, formal, and final causes of the world; under the other, however, the material cause and effect, and the two elements; and whatever has its beginning from them has an essence and varies through temporal successions,” etc.

We do not think it necessary to carry these extracts further. We shall give only one more passage, of particular interest because it concerns ideas. It concerns this sentence of Plato: “The sensible world, in which are contained all the kinds and, as it were, certain sources of intelligible living beings.”

> “And here is a periphrasis of the archetypal world, that is, divine wisdom, in which intelligible living beings are contained. Plato’s custom was to call divine knowledge concerning a thing by the name of that thing itself, while also adding the distinction ‘intelligible.’ Thus he calls divine knowledge concerning a human being ‘an intelligible human being,’ concerning a stone ‘an intelligible stone’; and these same things he calls *ideas*, that is, forms. For just as he knew things, so he formed them. Therefore, in the divine mind, which is the archetypal world, are contained the kinds of intelligible living beings, that is, cognitions concerning the different kinds of animals. ‘And as it were certain sources.’ For as a stream comes from a spring, so all things that exist come from those things which are in the divine mind, since they are truly contained in it.”

The commentary in our manuscript extends no farther than folio 60 verso, at the end of which it is suddenly interrupted. Thus we possess of Honorius of Autun’s work only a fragment comprising scarcely half of the first part of the *Timaeus*. Here are its final lines:

> “Nor indeed were hands necessary for him, ‘since nothing,’ etc.; nor feet, because no motion for which feet are necessary belongs to him. That this may be easier, let us say that one kind of motion is local and another non-local. Local motion occurs when the whole thing is found now in one place, now in another. There are seven kinds of local motion: forward, backward, upward, downward, rightward, leftward, and circular. Feet are necessary for this. But none of these can belong to the world, outside which there is no place. Non-local motion, also called rational motion, is either spiritual or bodily. Bodily rational motion in one place means having its parts differently while remaining in the same place; this belongs to the firmament, because one part of it is now in the East, now in the West. Spiritual motion belongs to the soul, for souls move in order to understand, etc. Thus rational motion belongs to the soul and the firmament, spiritual motion to the soul; and this is the point: ‘nor did he deem feet necessary for it,’ because no kind of local motion belonged to it, as has been explained, but rational motion—that is, motion in the same place—which is called rational.”

## Second Part of the Works of Honorius of Autun: Exegetical Works

[Col. 0253]

# Hexaemeron

(From a manuscript of the renowned Charterhouse of Gaming in Austria, extracted by the venerable Dom Leopold Wydemann, priest and librarian of that house; edited by R. P. Bernard Pez in vol. II, part I, p. 69 of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*.)

## Preface

[Col. 0253A]

“This temple was forty-six years in building.” Mary was twelve years old when she bore Christ; Christ, however, at the age of thirty-four, gave up his life in the Passion and died. Now twelve, thirty, and four make forty-six, the years in which the temple of Christ’s body was being built and was destroyed by the Jews. The number forty-six is also found in the name Adam: among the Greeks, A signifies one, D four, and A again one, making six; M, however, signifies forty. Therefore the temple is built in forty-six years while Christ is generated from Adam.

## Chapter I. On the New World

[Col. 0253B] Because many have discoursed much concerning the first six days and, holding differing views, have made them more obscure to the simple, your assembly asks that it be set forth in writing what should chiefly be thought about them. Therefore, following the authority of the Fathers, I lay open to you the obscurity of this text. Whoever approves this should inscribe *Hexaemeron* at the beginning of our *Elucidarium*.

First it is asked why Moses wrote of the fall of man but kept silent concerning the fall of the angel. But one should know that authors of books attend chiefly to coherence in their writings, so that intention may uniformly accord with subject matter. Moses’ intention, indeed, is figuratively to recount the restoration of the human race through Christ; and he strives in every way to adapt his subject matter to that intention. For he asserts that all things were created “in the beginning,” that is, in Christ, and afterward maintains that all things were restored in him. Throughout the entire text of his narrative, moreover, nothing is set down except what figuratively accords with Christ or the Church. Hence he carries his narrative as far as the deliverance of the people from Pharaoh and the beginning of Joshua, who leads the people into the land of promise, signifying, of course, the true Jesus, who delivered the people of believers from the devil. To him the Father gave dominion over heavenly and earthly things, and at the end of time he will lead the Church into the land of the living. [Col. 0254A] Therefore, because the Son of God, through whom are all things, mercifully redeemed man from destruction but justly abandoned the angel in guilt, Moses describes the fall of the redeemed but suppresses in silence the fall of the abandoned.

His subject matter here is the sensible world, into which man was driven after the Fall, and the coming into this world of God’s only-begotten Son, maker of the world and liberator of humankind. Moses prefigures him in diverse mystical senses and foreshadows him in things themselves: when he frees the people from Egypt through the Paschal lamb and calls them back to their lost homeland; when he marks in advance the whole condition of the Church through the wonderful tabernacle; and when he foretells all its sacraments through legal sacrifices. Hence the New Testament is so joined to the Old [Col. 0254B] that whatever the Old sets forth, the New seems to unfold. For this reason both begin from the beginning: the one begins, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”; the other, “In the beginning was the Word.” John’s Gospel, indeed, is placed first in the canon.

It should be noted that Moses the prophet calls the Son the beginning and recalls that all things were created in him; John the apostle, however, proclaims the Father as the beginning, and the Son as always existing in him, equal to him, and all things as made through him. For they harmoniously declare to us the one substance of both. Thus it is said (Gen. 1): “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”; that is, God the Father created in the Son both heavenly and earthly things, visible and invisible. “And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters,” or cherished the waters; that is, he enlivened all things that were to be produced from the waters. Note the Trinity: the creation of the world is ascribed to God the Father, the ordering of things to the Son, and the vivification or adornment of all things to the Holy Spirit.

Simply, however, the literal exposition is this: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” that is, in a moment God made all bodily and incorporeal things. By the name “heavens” are understood incorporeal things, such as angels, and all spiritual things that are not seen by us. By the term “earth” are indicated bodily things, such as this heaven and earth [Col. 0254C] and all things seen by us. Alternatively: “In the beginning,” that is, first, God made heaven and earth, then the rest. The earth was “formless,” namely, as to fruits, and “void,” namely, as to animals. This is not written of heaven because the highest heaven, called the heaven of heaven, is found immediately upon its creation full of its praisers, that is, angels. For they were the morning stars that praised God in the creation of the world; and, on seeing God’s wonderful work suddenly proceed from nothing, all the sons of God shouted aloud with joy. The evening stars proceeded to praise the Creator when the elect human beings were afterward created; in death they set, like stars, and for this purpose, at the rising of the eternal day, they shall shine forth through resurrection to rejoice together.

[Col. 0255B] “And darkness was upon the face of the deep”; that is, the earth was immersed in the abyss, that is, covered by the depth of waters. This water was dark because it had not yet been illuminated by any light. But no creature existed that was called darkness, since darkness is proved to be nothing other than the absence of light. This gloomy image of things is called chaos or unformed matter. The form of the elements at that time was as follows: the earth was bounded by the same limits as now, but was entirely covered by waters; and its appearance was such as it still has beneath the depth of the sea. Fire lay hidden in stones and iron; air adhered mixed with earth and water. Water covered the entire surface of the earth and filled the whole space up to heaven, joining itself to the upper waters that are still above the heavens. Yet it was not thickened as it is now, but spread abroad like a thin mist.

## Chapter II

“And God said: Let there be light.” When “he said” is written of God, it is said according to our manner and expresses the efficacy of one commanding. God’s speaking is nothing other than creating all things through his Word. Through this Word he brought forth this bodily light from the element of fire and introduced it into this world. That light then displayed such brightness as now appears before the rising of the sun, and illuminated the thin waters as it now illuminates the air. For twelve hours it remained above the earth as the sun does now; for twelve it illuminated the lower regions [Col. 0255D] of the world.

“And God saw the light, that it was good.” That is, he gave rational creatures understanding of how good are all things which they see by light. “And he divided the light and darkness”: namely, so that light might shine twelve hours above the earth and twelve beneath it; and darkness, driven away by light, might lie hidden twelve hours beneath the earth and as many above it. The zone which glows with fire in the middle of the world also enjoys through it the equinox.

“And he called the light day, and the darkness night”: that is, he caused them to be called so. We similarly say that someone “made a house” when he ordered it to be made. “And evening and morning came to be, one day.” Evening is the end of day, while morning is the end of night; joined together, these make twenty-four hours and constitute one day. It is called not “first” but “one” day because the same day is always repeated, as it is written: “By your ordinance the day endures” (Ps. 118 [119]:91). During those first three days, night remained entirely dark because neither moon nor stars illuminated it. It should be noted, moreover, that the day begins in light and ends in light, because all God’s works begin from Christ, who is the true light, and all are completed in him.

“And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters.” That is: the firmament placed in the midst of the waters and called heaven is affirmed to have been hardened from those waters after the manner of crystal; for which reason Josephus calls it the crystalline heaven. The waters which remained above this heaven [Col. 0256B] retained the former water’s rarefied condition. Those which occupied the lower space were gathered into the density they possess today. Hence follows: “Let the waters under heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.” At God’s command the waters, previously spread thinly like a mist, were suddenly gathered by thickening into one place. That place is called the ocean; and the earth, formerly muddy, dried out and was made fit for germination.

After the middle spaces between heaven and earth had appeared empty, fire and air, which had previously lain hidden in the earth pressed beneath the waters, freely occupied their fitting places. Fire naturally filled the higher parts of the world and air the lower; and then all things deserved to be illuminated more clearly by the light newly created. It should be known that all springs and rivers flow from the ocean and flow back into it. They leave behind their natural bitterness in the earth through which they run by hidden channels. Likewise, water is lifted into clouds by the force of winds’ breath and again deposited on the earth through rain. Most rivers which now divide regions burst forth in the Flood. It is asked: since all rivers enter the sea, why does the sea not overflow? But it is handed down that by its natural attraction the sun drinks up in a day all that flows into the sea during the entire night from fresh waters, and again sends it down to the lands through rains.

“And God called the dry land earth, and called the gatherings of waters seas”: that is, he caused them to be so called, as has already been said.

[Col. 0256D] “And God saw that it was good”: that is, he implanted in the mind of rational creatures knowledge of how good are all things created by God. “And he said: Let the earth bring forth green grass and fruit-bearing trees.” As soon as water withdrew from the lands, the earth at once, by God’s command, produced every kind of herb and tree, and even their already ripe fruits. It should be noted that this occurred in the spring season; and therefore the year itself is accustomed to observe this same thing at that time.

“And God said: Let great lights be made in the firmament of heaven”: that is, beneath the firmament of heaven. The sun is said to be placed in the middle of the world, the moon situated in this air, and the planets fixed in their circles; the stars alone are said to be impressed on the firmament. It should be noted that in creation all things are completed in groups of three days, because all things are perfected through the Trinity. In three days the elements, and in three days the things beneath them, are completed. For in the beginning heaven and earth are created from nothing as material; fire and air lay covered in the earth by waters. Then on the first day light is made clear from fire; on the second, heaven is solidified from water like crystal; on the third, the earth is founded, water separated from it, and the earth itself adorned with flowers and groves. On the fourth, the upper heaven and air are illuminated by the sun, moon, and stars produced from fire. On the fifth, the lower air is made fruitful with birds and the water with fish. On the sixth, the earth is burdened with animals produced from itself.

The first three days, which passed before the rising of the sun, passed according to the equinoctial rule, that is, with equal spans of day and night. The fourth, too, which produced the lamps of sun and moon, was distinguished by the equinox. It is asked what became of the newly created light after the splendor of the sun shone forth. It is reported that just as the thinness of the waters was first reduced into the thickness of the ocean, so the tenuity of light was condensed into the substance of the sun and thickened into the globes of the moon and stars; and its bright glory was further adorned by these brilliant jewels.

## Chapter III

“And he made two great lights: the greater to rule the day, and the lesser to rule the night.” They are called great lights because they appear great to us. Yet the moon is said to be the least of the stars; the northern stars are written to be larger than the sun. It is asked what dark feature is seen in the moon’s body. It is said that the globe of the moon is formed of fire and water. For if it were wholly fiery, the earth would be scorched and burned by its proximity. But now its heat is moderated by the element of water, and the dark feature is therefore seen in it. Hence it comes about that the moon lacks its own light and shines only when illuminated by the sun; night dew also flows from it, and it shines upon the earth. Sometimes they shine over the earth; sometimes, when clouds are opposed, they do not shine; but they always fill with radiance the places in which they remain fixed.

“And let them be for signs and seasons.” They serve as signs because Easter must be celebrated by us at a fixed time; sometimes they also indicate storm or fair weather, sometimes even something future. They are also signs for sailors and for travellers through sandy regions. They serve for seasons because, by fixed measurement, they produce the equinoxes and solstices of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. They serve for days because by their rising and setting they make days now longer and now shorter. They serve for years because the moon completes its common year in 354 days, while the sun completes its year in 365 days; the planet Mars completes its course in two years, Jupiter in twelve, and Saturn in thirty.

“And God said: Let the waters bring forth creeping things and flying things.” Here Scripture reveals why the Spirit of God cherished the waters: because he intended first to produce living creatures from this element and to make all things fruitful by its admixture. He permitted kinds of fish and creeping things to swim in the waters, but commanded birds to fly in the air. For the nature of air is said to be nothing other than water, and it is reported to give vital breath to all living creatures. Therefore storms are said to arise in the air as in the sea. Water condenses into clouds and is again dispersed by winds into rain. From the collision of clouds themselves thunder crashes, and lightning flashes from the striking forth of fire. Winds are produced from storms; rain becomes hail through them; and through the harshness of cold rain is changed into snow. This turbulence occurs only in the air. [Col. 0258B] But the spaces between heaven and air are believed to be full of perpetual light and tranquility. This air, moreover, is darkened only at night, which is produced by the earth’s shadow. The higher ether rejoices in unbroken day. The stars that seem to fall by night are not stars, but little fires drawn from the ether into the air by the breath of winds.

“And God said: Let the earth bring forth cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth.” It should be noted that two kinds are produced from waters, namely swimming and flying creatures; but three are formed from earth, namely walking, crawling, and slithering creatures.

Therefore, when everything necessary for human use had been created, man himself was also brought forth from earth and placed as lord over all other things. He is said to have been created in the image [Col. 0258C] and likeness of God so that he may be understood as a heavenly animal, being separated from other living creatures by reason and intellect. Because the Lord at some time intended to unite himself with him, he gave him participation with every creature: namely, discernment with angels, sensation with animals, growth with herbs and trees, and being with stones. He composed his body from the four elements, filled his soul with knowledge, and placed him over every bodily creature. It is also reported that he was about thirty years old when he was created, and that he possessed Solomon’s wisdom, Samson’s strength, and Absalom’s beauty.

“And God said: Behold, I have given you power over all things.” Before sin, man had all things subject to him; after sin, he himself became subject to all things. Before human guilt, the earth produced nothing harmful, no poisonous herb, no barren tree; afterward, as punishment for man, it put poison in herbs and took fruit from trees. Birds did not live by seizing other birds, nor did wild beasts tear little animals for food; rather, all alike took nourishment from the herbs of the earth. Hence follows:

“And they shall be for food to you and to them.” Later, however, not only do birds lay snares for birds and wild beasts for animals, but even domestic animals violently attack man himself. “And God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good.” Everything God made, considered separately, is good; considered in the totality, it is very good, [Col. 0259A] because although one thing seems contrary to another, each is nevertheless proved necessary.

Hence it is asked: since the devil was created among God’s good creatures, how can he be called good, when he is evil beyond all expression? Likewise, the question is raised concerning serpents and other animals that are harmful and are therefore thought evil. But one should know that the devil was created good by God, but changed himself into evil. Yet in a certain way he is called good because he is proved necessary in God’s commonwealth, while he justly punishes God’s adversaries like a most cruel executioner. Serpents and other similar animals are likewise proved good because they exact just punishments from human beings or are useful for various medicines.

[Col. 0259B] “And God rested on the seventh day and sanctified it” (Gen. 2). God the Father established the seventh day for the old people to celebrate; God the Son made the eighth day, which is also the first, to be observed by the new people. Each is pregnant with a great sacrament. For just as God is written to have completed the works of this world on the seventh day, so this world is said to extend through seven thousand years. And just as God is read to have rested from his work on the seventh day, so the bodies of the righteous are believed to rest in graves after their labor, while their souls rest in joy. The seventh day also signifies the day of judgment, on which every work of the Church will be completed and eternal rest will be rendered to it as recompense.

But the Lord’s Day, which is designated both first and eighth, prefigures eternity: when, labor having ended after seven thousand years, an eighth age begins, in which is hoped for one day better than thousands, granted through the Son alone to all believers. Therefore, by the rest of the seventh day is indicated the rest of souls in the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; by the rest of the eighth day is expressed eternal rest in the eight beatitudes.

Six days likewise signify the six ages of the world. On the first day light is created, and in the first age man is placed in paradise to enjoy eternal light. This day is closed by evening when the human race is overwhelmed in the Flood. On the second day the firmament is made solid amid the waters, and in the second age the human race is preserved from the waters in the Ark. This day ends in evening, [Col. 0259D] when the Pentapolis, with all its inhabitants, is consumed by fire. On the third day the earth is separated from the waters, and in the third age the faithful people are set apart from the unbelieving: when Abraham and his descendants are separated from the nations by circumcision, and afterwards the children of Israel by the Law. This day is brought to its evening when that same people are devastated on every side by the nations. The fourth day is illumined by sun and moon, and the fourth age is adorned by David’s kingdom and Solomon’s Temple. This day concludes in evening when, the Temple having been destroyed, the people are led captive into Babylon. On the fifth day birds are brought forth from the waters, while fish are left in them; and in the fifth age many are released from captivity, while very many are held in it. This day ended in evening when Judaea deserved to be made subject to a Gentile king. On the sixth day man [Col. 0260A] is formed from clean earth, and in the sixth age Christ is begotten from the Virgin. On that day also God made the animals; and in the sixth age he called the faithful—his animals—to the pastures of life, and refreshed them with the food of his body. This day will be completed in evening when this world is destroyed by the final fire. On the seventh day God rested from all his works, and in the seventh age he will rest in all the saints after the works of the six days, when God will be all in all. This day is not bounded by evening, because that rest is confined by no end.

## CHAPTER IV

What blessed Augustine thinks concerning these days we shall state as briefly as possible for students. Yet we recast his views in our own style, to prevent the reader’s weariness. For if I set out his own words, [Col. 0260B] neither does the page contain the length of his argument nor does a weak intellect bear the weight of his reasoning.

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” That is, God the Father created all things at once, both spiritual and bodily, in his Son—that is, in his Wisdom—as it is written: “He who remains for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18:1). And again: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made; in him was life” (John 1:3–4). This means that everything afterwards made materially and capable of being formed was always present causally and predestinarily in the Word of God. Hence it is written: “who made the things that are to come.”

By the name of heaven and earth every creature universally is comprehended. Yet it must not be thought that any insensible thing was created by God before the angels, [Col. 0260C] for every sensible thing is declared more worthy than an insensible one. Thus the angelic nature, which is intellectual, is created first, where God is said to have created heaven in the beginning. Thus it is written of the first angel: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40:14). It is called heaven because God dwells in it and the divine mysteries are hidden in it; and it is called the heaven of heaven.

“But the earth was empty and void”: that is, bodily creation, not yet formed, but causally placed in the Word of God. “And darkness was upon the face of the deep”: that is, all things to be created from the waters were not yet distinguished into forms for that purpose. “And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters”: that is, the Spirit of the Lord distinguished into forms all things which he determined should come to be from water or through a mixture of water. [Col. 0260D] Yet one must know that God did not first make matter and then form; rather, he brought forth all things formed at once, just as song proceeds together with the voice. Moreover, the reading that he made this or that thing on this or that day is expressed in our manner; it is not to be understood from this that he did not make all things together, as Scripture says.

I think no human being can know how much time elapsed between the creation of the angels and that of this world, unless God revealed it to him—especially since time did not yet exist, but began with this world, and time is nothing other than the alternation of day and night, or of the year—for example, spring, summer, autumn, and winter—or the change of things from past to present and from present to future. All things that God created are believed to remain for ever, [Col. 0261A] although some are changed into others. And since this world was formed scarcely six thousand years ago, it seems frivolous to suppose that angelic nature began together with it. Therefore the angels are held to have existed long before this bodily world in blessed and eternal life; whence they are also written to have praised God with a loud voice at this world’s creation. For God the Creator says to Job: “When I laid the foundations of the earth and the pivots of the world, the morning stars praised me, and all the sons of God rejoiced.”

“And God said: Let there be light; and he called the light day.” It is asked whether God made some spiritual or bodily light by whose sight the angels might rejoice, or formed some day by whose presence they might delight. But this is excluded by reason, [Col. 0261B] since the intelligible is known to be better than the sensible. Therefore God himself is understood as the light—the one written to be the true light—by whose vision angelic nature is illuminated as this bodily day is lit by the sun.

Thus it is said: “God said: Let there be light.” That is, through his Word God poured the light of his wisdom into angelic nature, and then gave it knowledge of all things still to be created. “And there was light.” For the true and eternal light, God’s wisdom, made bright wisdom—that is, rational understanding—and bestowed it upon angelic spirits, so that they might distinguish creature from creature; as it is written: “Wisdom was created before all things.” Thus God said, “Let there be light,” when he illumined the angels with the light of wisdom. For she is “the brightness of eternal light.” Light came to be when they knew [Col. 0261C] that God had already made in wisdom all things which were still to come; in which wisdom they already beheld all the causes and reasons of things. “And God saw that it was good”: namely, that they distinguished the Creator from the creature and, despising the creature, loved the Creator whom they praised. “And he divided the light from the darkness”: that is, he distinguished the formed, intelligible creature from the unformed one, when he gave it knowledge of what was still to be created.

“And he called the light day, and the darkness night.” Here it is asked whether, before this world, there had been day or night which were called by these names and succeeded each other in alternation. But since it is proved that before this sensible world time did not exist, and since day and night are undoubtedly time, we are necessarily instructed to understand here not a temporal but an eternal day. For angelic nature is the eternal day which the Lord has made, in which we shall rejoice and be glad when, after the resurrection, we are equal to the angels and see God face to face as he is. Thus God called light day when he himself—the true light, dwelling in inaccessible light, and the everlasting day—like the eternal Sun, illumined with his brightness the angels shining with the light of wisdom, as this bodily sun illumines this day. [Col. 0261D] He likewise called darkness night because he separated, by the greatest distance, bodily creation still hidden in unformed matter from spiritual creation. For every bodily creature, compared with a spiritual one, is rightly called darkness.

“And there was evening and morning, one day.” It should be noted that it is called not “the first day,” but “one day,” because angelic nature, called day, begins from the eternal day, God, in such a way that it is bounded by no end. This is that “one day better in the courts of God than thousands,” because indeed a portion of angelic life is proved better than many thousands of years spent here in affliction.

It is asked: since bodily light is said not to exist in heaven, what sort of radiance is believed to shine upon the angels? And should that homeland be thought dark, with angels imagined to lie hidden in darkness? But it must be understood that there are countless angels, each of whom surpasses this sun sevenfold in brilliance and receives inexpressible radiance from the Eternal One. For that city has no need of sun or moon, but almighty God is its light; [Col. 0262B] sun and moon marvel at his beauty, and the angels are proclaimed to desire to gaze into him. If this world were illumined by as many suns as there are days in the yearly cycle, with what glory, do you think, would it be adorned? And truly, if that were so, all that light, compared with the heavenly light, would be darkness. Therefore no light or day other than the brightness of God and the splendor of angels and saints is believed to exist there; these surpass beyond expression every visible radiance.

It is also asked what the kingdom of heaven is, or what reward is bestowed there upon blessed spirits: whether pleasant places or shining walls are to be imagined there, or costly garments and varied delights are to be expected. But since the kingdom of heaven is read to be nothing other than peace and joy, no attractiveness of places or buildings, nor possession of most precious bodily or incorporeal things, is shown to exist there. Rather, the vision of almighty God alone is declared; in contemplating him the blessed perpetually enjoy eternal peace, full joy, and every abundance of all goods, and in enjoying are ever satisfied without satiety and without end.

Hence evening and morning are named here, but night is not mentioned in these six days. For that eternal day declines as if into evening when angelic nature considers creation in itself. It rises as if into morning when it bursts forth in praise of the Creator for the wondrous creation. And the day shines, as it were, when it beholds creation subsisting eternally in the Word of God through Truth itself; [Col. 0262D] but night is not introduced because their knowledge is covered by no ignorance.

Holy Scripture accommodates itself to human understanding, like a mother to the ways of infants, or like wax receiving again the impressions of seals. With a motherly gait it walks with the slow; with the capable it flies to the heights; by its height it mocks the proud; by its depth it terrifies the attentive; by its truth it feeds the great; by its accessibility it nourishes the little.

Thus Scripture tells the wise that God created all things together in one day; it tells the slower that God completed his works in six days. For the capable scarcely understand that God is said to have created all things at once in one day—indeed, in a single glance of the eye. But the slower easily grasp, just as fruit that is broken is eaten by little children, that all creation was completed in six days. Therefore, by the one day in which it indicates that all things were created, it suggests the luminous nature of angelic substance, which the eternal Sun of righteousness irradiates with his splendor. On that day he made all things, when he granted the angels foreknowledge in his Word of all things still to be created.

But by the six days in which it says that the Lord perfected his works, it suggests such perfection of God’s creation as is expressed through the number six. This number is called most perfect among numbers because it is completed in every respect by its parts. For it is resolved into one, two, and three, and is restored entire from those same numbers: one, two, and three make six. The most expert of philosophers, Plato, [Col. 0263B] did not fail to know this rule; because of the perfection of that number he began his book thus: “one, two, three.”

By unity, then, is understood God himself, the fountain and beginning of all things, who alone is truly said to be one. From him arises two, when spiritual creation is brought forth by him; and from him also is born three, when the bodily world is created. This number is doubled when it is made manifest to intelligible nature that all things subsist from the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit. The number six, therefore, is completed when a threefold creation—namely, spiritual, sensible, and insensible—is seen to be contained by a threefold Maker, that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Hence also God is described as resting from his works on the seventh day, because after perfection God is known to rest from his creature in himself, [Col. 0263C] and that creature to have rest only in him.

## CHAPTER V

God also said: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters.” And it was so; and God made the firmament and called it heaven.

All this is repeated in the following sense: “God said: Let there be a firmament,” that is, in his Word he eternally established that it should be made. “And it was so,” namely, in the knowledge of the angels, who beheld already subsisting in God’s Word that which was still to come into existence. “And God made the firmament,” afterwards, namely, in the form in which it is seen today. “And he called it heaven,” that is, he taught humankind to call it so. [Col. 0263D] “And there was evening,” when the angelic fellowship, called light or day, considered the creature of the firmament in its own nature; and “there was morning,” when it praised the Creator for it. Thus the second day came to be when angelic spirits are illumined from God’s eternal day by the light of wisdom. By him they are named day or light, and through him things still to be created are revealed to them.

God further said: “Let the waters that are under heaven be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear.” And it was so. And the water was gathered into one place, and God called the dry land earth. This is interpreted in the same way as above. “God said: Let the waters be gathered,” that is, in his Word he eternally ordained that they should be gathered. “And it was so,” namely, angelic nature knew in God’s Word that it was to be done in this manner. [Col. 0264A] “And the water was gathered, and dry land appeared,” afterwards, namely, in the form in which each creature now brings forth plants or animals. “And there was evening,” when the creatures of water and earth are considered in themselves by the angels, called days; and “there was morning,” when the Creator is praised for them. The third day comes to be when intelligible nature itself is illumined by the Trinity and the several things to be created are shown to it beforehand.

The same is to be understood of the other days. Yet it should be noted that morning, not evening, is assigned to the seventh day, and on that day God is said to have rested. For certainly every creature had morning through its beginning from the eternal day, God; but it will have no evening of any end, and through the sevenfold Spirit it rests eternally in its Maker.

Holy Scripture declares that God created all things together, and yet announces that he completed his works in six days. That he created all things together is to be understood in truth. But the division among the six days signifies nothing other than a certain distinction or ordering of things: namely, when each creature is distinguished from another or from the Creator in the understanding of angelic reason. Hence evening and morning are introduced: evening when a creature is seen by angels in its own nature, and morning when the Creator is exalted in praise for it. The days are so called because by them all things are contemplated in the Word of God.

First, then, light is placed in order, also called day, and angelic substance is indicated; it is illuminated by the light of eternal wisdom. Second, [Col. 0264C] the firmament is set in place, from which this bodily world begins. Third, the forms of sea and land are placed, in which the nature of herbs and trees is formed not actually but potentially. Fourth, sun and moon with the stars are placed, potentially indeed, in the fiery element. Fifth, birds from moist air and swimming creatures from water are again brought forth potentially. Sixth, animals from the earth, together with man, are likewise produced potentially. Because this order is distinguished in God’s Word by the number six through angelic nature, called day, the same day is rightly described as repeated six times. The Lord blesses this same day and rests in it, because he sanctifies angelic nature by filling it with the sevenfold Spirit and grants it rest in himself.

The following Scripture makes clear that all these things are to be understood in this way:

“This,” it says, “is the book of the generation of heaven and earth in the day when God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it sprang up in the earth.” This surely is said of that one eternal day on which God is written to have created all things together. Therefore, just as man is made in God’s likeness, so too these temporal days are said to be created in the likeness of those six—or rather seven—days eternally abiding in the Word of God; and all things also formed in this world are not unreasonably said to be created in the likeness of the forms existing in God.

From this point the sequence of bodily creation is set forth, where it is asserted that a spring bursting forth from the earth watered the whole earth; [Col. 0265A] that God formed man and planted paradise; and it is read that he brought forth animals and trees from the earth.

But on what day of the week, and in what order—whether in one day or several—he formed all things into species is unknown. Yet it is thought that, after the structure of the world had first been made with its lights, he then made man first within this world, as it were the lord of the world, and his dwelling, namely paradise; then, for man’s subjection, brought forth the creatures of birds, fish, and beasts, and their food, namely herbs and trees. All these are read to have been created at once and brought to man; after these woman also was formed, and all things are reported as made subject to him. Whether man remained in paradise for a long time is uncertain, although many maintain that he dwelt there for a considerable period.

Therefore, in those eternal six days God created all things causally and rested from every work on the seventh. But in these temporal days he made all temporal and bodily things actually, through species and forms; he gave them the law of growing, enduring, and producing others from themselves. And the Son continues to work all these things with the Father even now, through whom every bodily creature is still transformed into a better state.

## CHAPTER VI. On Christ’s Incarnation

The Wisdom of God entered, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March], the womb of the Blessed Virgin Mary, in the four thousand one hundred and eighty-fourth year from the origin of the world; the five hundred and thirteenth year of the eighth great Paschal cycle; the forty-second of Octavian [Col. 0265C] Augustus; the eighth of the solar cycle; the eighteenth of the nineteen-year cycle; the fifteenth of the lunar cycle; the second indiction; with . . . seven epacts concurrent; on Friday; on the tenth day of the moon; and in the twelfth year of the age of that Virgin herself.

In that womb he built his body over nine months and six days, that is, over forty-six sixes, namely two hundred [Col. 0266A] and seventy-six days. For this interval is calculated from the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when he was conceived, to the eighth day before the Kalends of January [25 December], when Christ was born. Therefore he was born on the seventh day before the Kalends of January [26 December], in the third indiction, on or within Sunday, at night. From that birth, he was circumcised on the eighth day and presented in the Temple on the fortieth day. In that Temple he is found as a twelve-year-old youth questioning the wise; and in the twenty-eighth year [Note: [Col. 0265C] An error.], and on the third day of Christ’s thirtieth year, he is baptized by John; and in the thirty-third year and a half, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the day on which he had been conceived, he is seized by the Jews. By their tongue he is first crucified at the third hour, and at the sixth hour is raised upon the cross by soldiers. On that cross he remained for three hours, namely the sixth, seventh, and eighth; [Col. 0266B] and at the ninth hour he expired. From that hour to the dawn of the resurrection are forty hours, counting the ninth hour itself. During these hours Christ’s lifeless body lay, having been placed in the tomb in the evening; in it he rested for thirty-six hours. Rising at dawn, on the first day of the Sabbath, he remained on earth for forty days wherever and however he wished. But on the fortieth day, in the sight of his apostles, he entered heaven and sat at the right hand of his Father. Therefore, on the tenth day from the Ascension, he sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles.

On the day when the first man was made, the second man was conceived. For on the sixth day both the old man was made in paradise and the new man was conceived in the Virgin’s womb. And at the hour when the earthly man took the fruit, [Col. 0266C] thereby to destroy the human race, at that same hour the heavenly man endured the cross and death’s bitterness, thereby to redeem the whole world. Therefore, as it seems, on the same day the obedient man returns to paradise with the thief, and the disobedient man is compelled with the woman to enter the exile of his condemnation.

[Col. 0265]

## ON THE TEN PLAGUES OF EGYPT, SPIRITUALLY UNDERSTOOD

(From a manuscript of the renowned Gemnic Carthusian monastery in Austria, communicated by the venerable Father Leopold Wydemann, librarian of that same monastery. Edited by Dom Bernard Pezius in *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part I, p. 89.)

[Col. 0265D] The first plague of Egypt was water changed into blood, in which they slew the infants of the Hebrews and its fish died. The second was frogs brought forth from streams and marshes, filling the surface of that land. The third was gnats—that is, goat-flies—exceedingly troublesome to humans and beasts with fiery stings, produced from the dust of the earth. The fourth was the dog-fly (*cynomyia*), or rather the common fly (*coenomyia*), that is, every [Col. 0266D] kind of fly filling earth and air. For *coenos* means “common,” whence *coenobium* is called “common life.” The fifth plague was a pestilence of animals. The sixth: blisters, pustules, and sores made from the ash of the furnace. The seventh: thunder, lightning, and hail striking down everything. The eighth: locusts and *bruchi* [caterpillars], which devastated in herbs and trees what the hail had left. The ninth: darkness that could be felt, for [Col. 0267A] three days, in which dreadful images appeared to them as though they were dreaming, terrifying them. But where the children of Israel were, there was light, and these plagues did not touch them. The tenth plague was that Egypt’s firstborn—that is, all its heirs—were slain, and their gods crushed.

According to Cornelius and Orosius, these plagues occurred over five years, namely two each year. For after each plague a time for repentance was given; but when the king hardened himself, a plague was inflicted again. Yet since, as the Apostle writes, all these things happened to them as figures, and since he also asserts that the Law is spiritual, we must see what they signify spiritually.

Pharaoh, whose name means “stripping” or “scattering,” is the devil, who stripped humanity of the glory of immortality [Col. 0267B] and scattered it among various errors. His kingdom is Egypt, which means darkness or tribulation; and it consists of those made dark by ignorance, unbelief, and sins, who afflict those devoted to good works. Moreover, Pharaoh is not a man’s name but a title of rank, just as among us rulers are called kings or Augusti while bearing their proper names. That Pharaoh who was drowned in the sea was called Ceucris. The plagues of the Egyptians are the blows inflicted upon sinners.

Egypt’s water is the wisdom of this world; fish wandering in the waves are philosophers curious about worldly matters. This water is changed into blood and its fish die when secular wisdom binds souls in sins and kills its followers; for blood signifies sins, as it is written: “Deliver me from bloods” (Psalm 50), that is, from sins. The infants of the Hebrews were killed by the Egyptians in the water, that is, those simple in faith were led astray by the erroneous books of the Gentiles.

The frogs, croaking in marshes, are poets who proclaim the foul deeds of their predecessors, made sordid in the mire of luxury. Egypt is struck by this plague when the teaching of such persons overturns the heart of worldly people.

The stinging gnats with fiery goads are the restless, driven by varied desires. Those gnats are begotten from the dust of the earth because the restless are devoted only to earthly desires. They cling especially to goats because these people especially sit upon the stench of lust. By this third plague are struck those who do not have the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0267D] who is written as the third Person in the Trinity.

The dog-fly, however, is the heretic, who indiscriminately barks against Catholics in the manner of dogs; and, like flies driven away, returns in flight through importunate disputations. The many kinds of flies are the many kinds of heresies, which trouble Catholics in many ways, and, when driven away by sound teachings, attack them again.

The pestilence of animals is the reprobate life of carnal people, who, living beastially and decaying in their carnal life, perish as though by pestilence.

The bursting blisters, boiling pustules, and burning sores formed from furnace ash are the envious, wrathful, and hate-filled, who strike through anger and hatred and incur sores through murders of souls.

[Col. 0268A] Thunder is the threats of the powerful; lightning, the terrors of persecutors; hail, the robberies of brigands. Each of these strikes the Egyptians when they afflict worldly people through adversities.

Locusts and *bruchi*, which gnaw the fresh green of flowers, are the double-tongued and the slanderers; by evil conversation they corrupt the good morals of those beginning well.

The palpable darkness is the unbelievers, who lead many away from the light of truth into the darkness of error. In this darkness dreadful images appear that terrify them, because they imagine certain monstrous things about future punishments, and those who believe such things are rightly frightened by them. But light shines where the children of Israel are, because the joys of eternal brightness stand open to the children of light.

Egypt’s firstborn, which are its heirs, [Col. 0268B] are lovers of the world, who inherit Egypt, as it were, because they love this world alone. But Egypt’s firstborn are struck when lovers of the world are removed from this life by death and handed over to eternal punishments. Their gods too are condemned when their prelates are assigned eternal penalties with them. This is also understood within us. Spirit and soul are our parents; virtues are their children. Among these the firstborn is faith, which shall be heir of Christ’s kingdom. The striking angel kills it when heresy, invented through the devil, extinguishes faith in the soul, lest it be able to be heir of the Father’s kingdom.

The remedy for these ten plagues is the Ten Commandments written on two tablets of stone. On one tablet were the three that concern love of God; [Col. 0268C] on the other, the seven that concern love of neighbour.

The first commandment is: “Worship one God,” which pertains to the Father.

The second: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain,” that is, “you shall not swear falsely,” which pertains to the Son.

The third: “Keep holy the Sabbath day,” that is: “On one day of the week rest from bodily works and give yourself to God,” which pertains to the Holy Spirit.

The fourth: “Honour your father and mother.”

The fifth: “You shall not kill”—understand: neither by hand, nor tongue, nor heart.

The sixth: “You shall not commit adultery”—understand: neither in deed, nor counsel, nor will.

[Col. 0268D] The seventh: “You shall not commit theft.”

The eighth: “You shall not bear false witness.”

The ninth: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s property.”

The tenth: “You shall not desire another’s wife, nor anything that is his.”

These are contained in the number ten because it is the limit of all numbers; and therefore the denarius will be given as the wage to those labouring in the vineyard—that is, in the Law of the Lord—which is the end of our works. The number three and the number seven comprise this ten: because three signifies faith in the Trinity, while seven signifies action. Both are fulfilled in the twofold love through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit in these seven days. The stone tablets of the Law signify hard hearts that refused to receive love. [Col. 0269A] The Law is given in fire because transgressors of the Law are handed over to fire; but the lawgiver’s face appeared radiant because observers of the Law shall shine like the sun. Amen.

[Col. 0269]

# EXPOSITION OF SELECTED PSALMS

Excerpted from his unpublished, extensive Commentary on the Psalms.

(From a manuscript of the renowned Gemnic Carthusian monastery in Austria, made public by the venerable Dom Father Leopold Wydemann, librarian there. Edited by Dom Bernard Pezius, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part I, p. 95.)

## THE AUTHOR’S DEDICATION

[Note: [Col. 0269C] The rubric of the Melk manuscript, written in the thirteenth century by Otto of Veldsberg, prior of Melk, is as follows: “Here begins the book of Honorius to Abbot Chuno [Col. 0270C] on the first fifty psalms of the Psalter: ‘Blessed is the man. To Christian, reflecting the Father’s Word and example,’ etc.”]

To Christian, a Father reflecting the Father’s Word and example like a mirror, leading the flock entrusted to him by the narrow path to the pastures of life: Honorius, the devoted servant of those who serve Christ, offers the affection of devout prayer, that, when the Prince of shepherds appears, he may be set over all the good things of the Lord in the dwellings of the righteous.

Your zeal, venerable Father, burning ardently in the Scriptures, has powerfully stirred my mind to undertake the work you command, and drives the little boat of my talent into an unnavigable sea, though one which may nevertheless at some time be crossed by the breath of the Holy Spirit and the oars of your prayers. For with the strong impulse of charity you urge me to take up the splendid burden of service to the brethren: namely, to unlock with the pen the abundance of heavenly sweetness enclosed in the Psalms, and to offer from a grimy vessel the sweet draught of the Holy Spirit to those who thirst for righteousness. Thus those who continually ruminate upon the psalms may taste upon the inward palate the surpassing sweetness of heavenly nectar, lest heavenly words perhaps flow from their mouths like tasteless water, or, like pipes in instruments, produce an empty sound.

When I weigh the greatness of this difficult work, I tremble; but when I consider in it the fullness of grace, I rejoice in the charge laid upon me, trusting that I shall be supported by the prayers of all who may be helped in the Scriptures by my labour. Therefore let this work be dedicated to the name of your dignity and, through you, published for the benefit of the faithful.

We shall explain the Gallican Psalter, not the Roman, because we chant the former in our churches. The Gallican Psalter is that translated by the seventy interpreters; the Roman is that interpreted by Symmachus, or by I know not whom else. For six translations are received by the Church: those of the Seventy, Theodotion, Symmachus, Aquila, the fifth edition whose author is unknown, and Saint Jerome. We shall treat the translation of the Seventy interpreters, drawing upon the others where necessary.

# EXPOSITION ON THE PSALMS

## What the Psalter is and whence it is so called

[Col. 0269B]

Much must be said to the unlearned about the Psalter; but to the learned, a few points must be briefly set down. The Psalter is a musical instrument stretched with ten strings, triangular and fashioned in the shape of the letter delta. In Hebrew it is called *nabla*, and in Latin *organum*: broad below and hollow above; struck below, it gives forth sound above. From this instrument this book is called the Psalter, and the hymns sung upon the instrument are called psalms. What rhythms are among us—that is, songs composed with a fixed number of syllables and fitted to the strings of the lyre—psalms are among the Hebrews: compositions in varied metre fitted to the strings of the Psalter. The modulation of song signifies contemplation, while the psalms themselves signify good action. The mysteries of this book are veiled in coverings and riddles lest, being open to everyone, they become cheap.

## How it pertains to logic

[Col. 0270B]

Philosophy is love of wisdom: for *philo* means love, and *sophia* means wisdom. It is divided into three parts: physics, ethics, and logic—that is, natural, moral, and rational science. For *physis* means nature, *ethys* custom, and *loys* reason. Genesis pertains to physics because it speaks of natures; Paul’s Epistles pertain to ethics because they treat morals; the Psalter pertains to logic, also called theoretical science, because it speaks of the rationale of divine knowledge.

It is handed down that David composed the Psalter in five days and extended it into five books: it was redeemed through five thousand years and through Christ’s five wounds.

## On the title, intention, subject matter, and author

[Col. 0270C]

The title of this book is “Book of Hymns.” A hymn is praise of God composed in metre. For all [Col. 0271A] the psalms run in the Hebrew language in a fixed metre, but translators took no care to preserve this for the sake of the simple. A title is so called from *Titan*, that is, from the sun: for just as the rising sun illumines the world, so the following title illumines the whole work. It is also called “The Book of Soliloquies concerning Christ,” because it speaks without a personage concerning the whole Christ, namely head and body.

The intention of the entire book is to urge us to be conformed to Christ through imitation, so that through him we may return to the highest glory, from which, lost through Adam, we came into the deepest misery.

Its subject matter is Christ and the Church; it falls under theoretical—that is, divine—knowledge. Its usefulness is to know how to avoid vices and do good; its final cause is the attainment of eternal life.

David, king and prophet, inspired by the Holy Spirit, composed all the psalms concerning Christ and the Church and added titles as certain keys: for as a door is opened with a key, so the psalm’s meaning is unlocked by its title. Some psalms are titled under the names of Asaph, Idithun, Ethan, or others, not because they composed them, but in order that the interpretation of those names may be indicated. Some are inscribed with the names of Haggai and Zechariah, who lived long after David; this declares the manifest inspiration of the Holy Spirit, to whom all future things are present.

Who also foretold the name of King Josiah long beforehand, and described in the psalms the future mysteries of Christ as they later came to pass [Col. 0271C]. Moreover, three hundred men were appointed to perform this work with music before the ark of the Lord, over whom four precentors presided: Asaph, Jeduthun, Ethan, and Heman. Hence certain psalms are entitled with their names.

## On the arrangement of the psalms

The psalms were composed by David not in order, but separately and scattered about. After the Law had been burned by the Chaldeans, however, Ezra the prophet invented new letters, renewed the Law, gathered the psalms into one volume, assigned them an order for definite reasons, and attached titles like keys for unlocking hidden mysteries. For it is handed down that David first composed “Blessed be the Lord my God”; but Ezra, because of the mystery, placed “Blessed is the man” first [Col. 0271D], and then the rest in their ensuing order.

## On the form or figure of the psaltery

The psaltery, which sings of Christ and the Church, expresses in its shape Christ’s body. For when it is struck below, it resounds above; and when Christ’s body is suspended upon the wood of the cross, his divinity resounds through miracles. Delta, after whose shape the psaltery is made, is marked as the fourth letter in the alphabetical order; and Christ’s body is composed of four elements; or, the Church, which is his body, is built up by the four Gospels.

The psaltery also represents the figure of a human being, who consists of an upper and a lower part, namely body and soul. Such a person ought to strike the lower part—that is, afflict his body [Col. 0272A] with fasts and prayers—so that he may thus render sweet melody to God from above, according to the saying: “They mortify the flesh; they strengthen the spirit.” This is accomplished in the triangular psaltery, that is, in confession of the Trinity; and on ten strings, that is, in the ten commandments of the Law. A string is dried, twisted, and stretched; so too a person ought to be dried from fleshly desires, twisted by virtues, and stretched by charity, because no action is of value without charity; as in the saying: “If I distribute all my possessions,” etc.

The ten strings stretched upon the psaltery are the ten commandments of the Law, conveyed through Christ. Ten is divided into five and five, and the five senses are found doubled in Christ’s body; through these the ten strings sound sweetly [Col. 0272B] while they represent the ten commandments by deeds. Therefore, although the Psalter is counted as one volume, it is nevertheless distinguished by five divisions, as though by five books. These are doubled when understood of Christ’s divinity and humanity, or of Christ and the Church, or of the active and contemplative persons.

## On the number of psalms

One hundred and fifty psalms are written in the Psalter, because, just as in former times the crime of the world was washed away by the flood over one hundred and fifty days, so the sin of the penitent Church is washed away by the waters of tears in one hundred and fifty psalms. Therefore the fiftieth psalm is set for penitence, the hundredth for judgment, and the hundred and fiftieth for praise [Col. 0272C]; because surely one who repents here will escape judgment and, through Christ, attain everlasting praise.

## On the mystery of the psalms

This book writes of the head, the body, and each individual member: that is, of Christ, the Church, and each of the elect. Thus at times the head of Christ speaks, that is, his divinity; at times the head of the Church, that is, his humanity; at times the body of Christ, that is, the whole Church; at times the Church journeying here on earth; at times the Church reigning with Christ in heaven; at times a healthy member, that is, the righteous person; and at times a sick member, that is, the sinner. This is why the persons in the psalms vary in this way.

[Col. 0272D] The Holy Spirit speaks of the head, as in: “Blessed is the man,” that is, Christ, “who has not gone” (Ps. 1), etc. The head speaks of itself, as in: “But I have been established king by him” (Ps. 2), etc. The Holy Spirit speaks of the body, as in: “The queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. 44), etc. The body speaks of itself, as in: “I speak my works to the king” (ibid.), etc. The healthy member speaks, as in: “Guard my soul, for I am holy” (Ps. 85), etc.; the sick member, as in: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak” (Ps. 6).

Therefore psalms sung by the faithful benefit both the living and the dead, just as food taken by the mouth benefits all the members. For through the words of the Holy Spirit, both the dead and the living will be written in the book of life [Col. 0273A] when they are counted in Christ’s body through unity of faith. For just as infants profess their faith through their godparents at baptism, so the unlearned or the dead entreat God through the mouths of those singing psalms. A soul also placed in torments cries out, like an afflicted member, through the mouth of the Church: “Out of the depths I cried” (Ps. 129), etc.

This book is the key of heaven and the gate of paradise: through it heaven is opened, and through it eternal life is entered. Therefore all who are to be taught through books should begin their learning with this one. This book begins with blessedness and ends in the jubilation of praise, because blessedness is given through Christ, who is the blessed man, where there is perpetual praise and the sweet multitude of jubilation. This book is figuratively called the Psaltery; properly, David; and specially, because of its excellence, the Prophet. Hence one sometimes reads, “as in the Psalter,” sometimes “as in David,” and sometimes “as it is written in the Prophet”: all of this is said of this book.

The Scripture of the Old Testament is written with the Holy Spirit as its author and is divided into three parts: history, prophecy, and hagiography. History narrates past events; prophecy announces future events; hagiography exults in the joys of eternal life. This book holds a place among hagiography because it shines more fully with praises of the eternal homeland [Col. 0273B].

## Note

[Col. 0273C] Sacred Scripture is understood in five ways. Sometimes according to history alone, when it relates past events, as there: “God formed man from the clay and placed him in paradise” (Gen. 2). Sometimes according to history and allegory, as there: “Jacob took Leah and Rachel as wives”; this happened in fact, but it foreshadowed that the active and contemplative life must be joined to Christ. Sometimes according to prophecy alone, when it foretells future events, as there: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7). Sometimes according to the letter alone, when it commands something, as there: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Deut. 5). Sometimes according to allegory alone, as in the Song of Songs. All these modes are found in this book. History: “In the beginning, you, O Lord, founded the earth” (Heb. 1). History and allegory: “He struck [Col. 0273D] the rock, and waters flowed” (Ps. 77); which happened both in Christ and in the wilderness. Prophecy: “Blessed is he who is to come in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117). The letter alone: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36). Allegory alone: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way” (Ps. 109).

This book is known to be arranged after the form of the world, which is divided into three periods: one before the Law, another under the Law, and a third under grace. Thus this book is divided into three fifties of psalms, in which the whole company of saints is found. The first fifty psalms set forth all the righteous who lived before the Law, from Abel to Moses; through penitence they came to the jubilee, that is, the fiftieth year of remission—namely, Christ [Col. 0274A], the acceptable year of the Lord. The second fifty psalms present all the righteous who lived under the Law, from Moses to Christ, who obtained Christ through mercy and judgment.
