The third fifty psalms sing of all the saints who will arise under grace, from Christ’s time until the end of the world; through charity, described in “Blessed are the undefiled,” and through the ascents of virtues found in the fifteen gradual psalms, they are led to the praises of eternal jubilation.

The Psalter speaks not to the outward but to the inward person. For the Holy Spirit speaks in it, not to the flesh but to the spirit, and therefore it is understood wholly spiritually. Thus, just as the manna of old contained every delight [Col. 0274B] and every flavor of sweetness, so the song of this book contains every spiritual delight and can be applied to every sense according to whatever one’s intention may be.

When it is sung in choir, its words are those of the Church praising God; when sung by a righteous person, they are words of thanksgiving; when recited by a sinner, they are words begging pardon; when sung for the dead, they are words of a soul crying to God from punishment. Wherever the intention of the singer turns, the sense of this Scripture immediately conforms itself to the singer’s affection. With one who curses it curses; with one who blesses it blesses. It curses the members of the devil, as there: “Cursed are those who turn aside [Col. 0274C] from your commandments” (Ps. 118); it blesses Christ’s members, as there: “Blessed are you by the Lord” (Ps. 113).

Having usefully set forth these preliminary matters, let us proceed directly to the text. It follows:

## THE FIRST PSALM: ON CHRIST’S INCARNATION

**VERSE 1.—“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly.”** The first psalm has no title because it properly concerns Christ, who has no beginning. It is also the title of all the psalms, because all are opened through it, since all are understood of Christ. It is likewise called the monad, that is, unity, because it describes him who alone is properly worshipped as unity. And just as all numbers proceed from unity, so all the psalms take the beginning of their numbering from this one [Col. 0274D]. It is also called the head of the book because it is recorded as written concerning Christ, the head of the Church, as the Lord himself says: “In the head of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will” (Ps. 39). This psalm has two parts: the first, “Blessed is the man,” in which Christ’s incarnation and his body, the Church, are indicated; the second, “Not so the ungodly,” in which the devil’s body is shown.

The subject of this psalm is Christ with his body, that is, the Church of the faithful; the devil’s body, that is, the multitude of the wicked; the final judgment; the kingdom of the righteous; and the punishment of the evil. Its purpose is to call people back from evils, invite them to goods, and show that the human race, having fallen through Adam into misery, is restored through Christ to glory. Its author [Col. 0275A] is the Holy Spirit; its writer, David, king and prophet.

The words of this psalm are taken from the first age of the world, from Adam to the time of the flood. Certain things understood before the psalm’s opening are taken from Adam. “Blessed is the man,” from Abel; “but in the Law of the Lord,” from Enoch; “and he shall be like a tree,” from the tree of life in paradise; “not so the ungodly,” from the giants; “therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment,” from the flood; “for the Lord knows the way of the righteous,” from those who were in the ark; and “the way of the ungodly shall perish,” from those who perished in the flood, appear to be taken. They signify that Christ with all the elect will pass through the final judgment to blessedness, and the devil with the reprobate will undergo eternal punishment. This psalm [Col. 0275B] is understood in three ways: of Christ, of the Church, and of each individual elect person. Let us first consider it, then, concerning Christ, and take the beginning of our treatment from him who is the beginning.

Adam, the earthly and old man, was wretched: he went from righteousness to unrighteousness, from blessedness to misery, from paradise to exile, from life to death, in the counsel of the ungodly—that is, demons giving him evil counsel. He stood in the way of sinners because he remained fixed in error; and he sat in the seat of pestilence when he taught wickedness to posterity by his perverse example. Here three deaths are expressed, in which all Adam’s descendants are entangled: they arise from consent, act, and habit. For, when the devil persuaded him, man consented when he desired what God had forbidden. And because he departed from the state of uprightness [Col. 0275C] when he wished to be like God, he lost blessedness and underwent the death of the soul. This is “in the counsel of the ungodly,” namely demons, whose counsel is to abandon righteousness and apostatize from God; and this is the first death.

“He stood in the way of sinners” when, carrying desire into action, he ate the forbidden fruit. The way of sinners is transgression of the commandments; and because man entered this way, he was also brought low by the death of the flesh. This is the second death.

“He sat in the seat of pestilence” when, through a perverse habit, he set an evil example for others. For the seat of pestilence is the teaching of wickedness. Through this a third death was brought upon man, namely just condemnation. In this manner the first man went away and perished with his followers [Col. 0275D].

But Christ is the second Adam, the heavenly and new man: the blessed man, who bestowed blessedness upon humanity, when, though always existing as God, he chose to become man. He “has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly,” because he did not depart from righteousness amid the temptation of demons giving him perverse counsel. He “has not stood in the way of sinners,” because he committed no sin; and he “has not sat in the seat of pestilence,” because he taught no evil either by word or example.

The devil attacked him by three modes of temptation, by which he had conquered the first human being and victoriously subjected him to three deaths. He urged gluttony upon Christ when he wished stones to be changed into bread; he urged vain glory [Col. 0276A] when he told him to cast himself down from the Temple; he urged avarice or pride when he offered all the kingdoms of the world. But because Christ proved victorious, in that he did not go into desire, stand in vain glory, or sit in avarice, he redeemed the human race from the three deaths of thought, speech, and deed.

Sitting belongs to rulers or teachers; pestilence is the desire to rule, which so tickles everyone that it leaves not even monks untouched. He sits in the seat of pestilence who holds a prelate’s office through an appetite for dominion. Lest he give anyone an example of this ambition, Christ, the Lord’s man, refused the kingdom offered to him by the crowds in the wilderness. Christ indeed did not do the things stated above; but what did he do?

[Col. 0276B] **VERSE 2.—“His will is in the Law of the Lord.”** The Law of the Lord is to avoid evil and do good; this is righteousness and love. For righteousness is avoiding evil, and love is doing good. Christ’s will was in the Law of the Lord, which is righteousness, when, holding righteousness without turning aside, he was obedient to the Father unto death. Likewise, his will was in the Law of the Lord, which is love, when, loving his own to the end, he laid down his life for them. Hence it follows:

“And in his Law he shall meditate day and night.” That is, in prosperity and adversity. In the day he meditated on the law of righteousness when he fled from the crowds wishing to make him king; in the night he meditated on the law of love when he freely went to meet the Jews who wished to seize him, or were seeking him for his Passion [Col. 0276C]. Yet in chronological time, the former happened by day, and the latter by night.

**VERSE 3.—“And therefore he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters.”** That is: he will be comparable to the tree of life planted in paradise, concerning which it is said: “To the conqueror I will give to eat of the tree of life which is in paradise” (Rev. 2). Paradise is called the garden of delights and signifies the Church, in which are the delights of Scripture. The place of pleasure is the Father’s majesty, the eternal delight of the blessed; the fountain flowing from it is Christ, proceeding from the Father’s breast; the streams watering paradise are the gifts of the Holy Spirit that make the Church fruitful. The tree of life is wisdom, the life of souls. This tree, namely Christ [Col. 0276D], is planted beside streams of waters: that is, he was incarnate in the virgin’s womb according to the descent of the Holy Spirit, whose gifts flow everywhere like streams. It gave fruit in its time when, after the Ascension, at the time appointed by the Father, he sent the Holy Spirit to the apostles.

Or, the streams of waters are the fall of peoples, beside whose downward course—not in its current—that tree was planted, when Christ appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, not in sinful flesh. This tree gave its fruit in its time when he gave his body to the faithful as food. Of this time it is written: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4). Alternatively, the streams of waters are human mortality, beside which this tree was planted when Christ became mortal [Col. 0277A]. Hastening toward the current of death, he said: “If they do this in the green tree,” that is, in this fruitful tree, “what shall be done in the dry,” that is, in the barren? This tree gave fruit in its time when, in his Passion, it brought forth the restoration of humankind. It says “its fruit” because no one else, however holy, could give it. Or the tree of life is the cross bearing Christ, the fruit of life. Or Christ is compared to a tree because, as a tree protects by shade and refreshes by fruit, so Christ in this life protects his own from the heat of vices by the shade of his love and in the life to come will refresh them with the sweetness of his contemplation. This is signified by the tree of life planted in paradise beside streams of waters springing from the place of pleasure; whoever eats its fruit shall not die forever.

[Col. 0277B] The tree of the cross is the tree of life planted in paradise, that is, in the Church, beside streams of waters, that is, alongside the currents of Scripture, because the Passion of the cross was fulfilled in accordance with the proclamations of the prophets. The fruit of this tree is Christ hanging upon it; whoever eats of his body shall not die forever. It is said further of this tree that it “shall give its fruit in its time.” The tree of the cross gave fruit in its time when, at the time of the Passion, it bore Christ for the salvation of human redemption. Christ too gave his fruit in his time when, on the day of the Resurrection, he brought the faithful the joy of eternal exultation; he gave fruit in his time when, on the day of the Ascension, he gave heaven to humanity. The cross [Col. 0277C] will give fruit in its time when, appearing at the judgment, it will show Christ as having suffered for humankind. Christ will give his fruit in his time when, after the judgment, he will render to God and the Father the Church purchased with his blood and reveal himself to him as equal to the Father. Concerning this tree it further follows:

“And its leaf shall not fall.” The leaf of the tree is teaching concerning the cross of Christ’s Passion. For as fruit is covered by leaves, so a deed is clothed in the word of teaching. Therefore, just as the leaf of the palm, indeed of the tree of life, shall not fall, so the promise of Christ’s teaching remains firm in respect of deeds. Hence it is expressly added:

“And whatever he does shall prosper.” Just as the things done by Adam at the tree of transgression [Col. 0277D] turned to human adversity, so all things done by Christ on the tree of Passion resulted in human prosperity. His teaching, signs, and everything that he did in Passion, Resurrection, or Ascension all turned to the prosperity of human salvation. What he will yet do at the judgment will prosper, when his enemies are justly condemned by him and the righteous worthily crowned. The Holy Spirit set forth such a man as an example for humankind, as though saying: “Imitate this good man, who did not go, stand, or sit in evil—you who through the first man came down from the highest glory to the lowest misery—so that in this life he may shade you from the heat of vices and in the life to come restore you to the glory you lost.”

[Col. 0278A] Thus far concerning the head; now let us consider the body, which is the Church.

The multitude of the faithful, from the beginning of the world to its end, is written to have one heart and one soul; and therefore, because of unity of faith and unity of love, it is called one man. This is the blessed man who by faith and action is fitted for blessedness; he is called a man because through the strength of virtues he is robust against vices. This blessed man did not go in the counsel of the ungodly when the faithful people before Christ’s coming did not turn away from the worship of God to idolatry through fear of tyrants or the teaching of philosophers. The blessed man likewise did not go in the counsel of the ungodly when, after Christ’s coming, the Christian people did not turn from the Catholic faith to unbelief through fear of persecutors or the persuasion of heretics [Col. 0278B]. “And he has not stood in the way of sinners,” because he did not remain long in error, but quickly passed through it. “And he has not sat in the seat of pestilence,” because he did not teach idolatry or heresy.

Here three virtues are indicated—faith, hope, and charity—through which the believing people strives to return to its homeland. Since it believed in the true and one God, it did not go into idolatry or heresy; since it hoped for future goods, it did not stand in error—for to stand in the way of sinners is to persist in error; and since it loved God’s Law, it did not sit in the teaching of wickedness. But “his will is in the Law of the Lord”—understand, in fulfilling it.

The Law of the Lord was written by Moses for the old people; the Gospels too are the Law of the Lord, entrusted to the new people [Col. 0278C]. Before Christ’s coming, the will of the faithful people was in the Law of the Lord when it strove to fulfil the commands of the Law; the will of the Christian people was in the Law of the Lord when it strove to fulfil the precepts of the Gospel. “And in his Law he shall meditate day and night”: that is, he shall be occupied in love at every time. In the day he meditates on God’s Law when in peace he loves friends in God; in the night he meditates on it when, in persecution, he loves enemies for God’s sake.

“And therefore he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters.” A tree sends its root downward and its trunk upward; branches issue from the trunk, leaves from the branches, fruit hangs beneath the leaves, and seeds lie hidden in the fruit. Love is compared to this tree [Col. 0278D], by which the multitude of the faithful strives to climb to the heights. The root fixed in the earth is the love by which one loves one’s neighbor on earth. The trunk rising on high is love loving God. The tree’s branches are the various virtues of charity; its leaves are good words; its flowers, good will; its fruit, good works; and its seed, sound teaching. This tree is planted beside streams of waters because the tree of charity is founded upon the currents of Scripture.

Water does three things: it washes away dirt, quenches thirst, and gives back an image. So the fountain of wisdom flowing from the place of pleasure—that is, Christ proceeding from the Father’s breast—through charity washes away the filth of sins, quenches the thirst of ignorance, and restores God’s image to the soul. This tree will give its fruit in its time because charity [Col. 0279A] sometimes devotes itself to contemplation and sometimes labors in action. The leaf of this tree shall not fall, because no word spoken by a good person remains without reward.

“And whatever he does shall prosper,” because, whether things are favorable or adverse, all are changed into prosperity for the saints, for whom all things, whether good or evil, work together for good.

Observe the order: first we are taught to turn away from evil; then to do good; finally, to eat from the fruit of the tree of life. The Church keeps this order with those being baptized: first it teaches them to renounce the devil, his works, and his pomps; then to believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; after this, to eat of Christ’s body.

[Col. 0279B] These things have been said concerning the body; now a few things must be said concerning the members.

## Application of the first psalm to any believer

Every faithful person is a member of the Church, Christ’s body, and will be made blessed by Christ the head if that person remains in the wholeness of the body, that is, in the unity of the Church. *Beatus* (“blessed”) is said to mean either “well increased” or “well fitted”: increased in glory, or fitted for blessedness. A person is blessed when nothing is lacking that he wishes for and he wishes for nothing harmful. A man (*vir*) is so called from strength (*vires*), being strong rather than weak against vices.

Therefore every believer who is stable in faith and action is the blessed man who has not gone in the sight of the ungodly—that is, who has not apostatized from God into any unbelief through the counsel of demons [Col. 0279C] or wicked people.

Here a syllogism may be formed. A syllogism is an argument that establishes certainty regarding a doubtful matter. Syllogisms lie hidden in Sacred Scripture as fish in deep water; and, just as fish are drawn from the water for human use, so a syllogism is drawn from Scripture for usefulness. It consists of three members: proposition, assumption, and conclusion, in this manner: “Blessed is the man whose will is in the Law of the Lord; no one whose will is in the Law of the Lord has gone in the counsel of the ungodly; therefore no blessed man has gone in the counsel of the ungodly.” This is called a categorical syllogism. In this way, throughout this whole book, you will call them categorical syllogisms.

“And he has not stood in the way of sinners”: that is, he has not remained in any vice, which is a way leading to death, although [Col. 0279D] through human error he may have walked in it for a time. For we commonly say, “I stayed in that city for so many years,” meaning, “I remained.” “For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death” (Matt. 7). “And he has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” A seat is the place of teachers, while pestilence is contagion among animals. The seat of pestilence is the teaching of wickedness; or the seat of pestilence is heresy, which, like contagion among flocks of sheep, has spread far and wide through the minds of the faithful. In the Hebrew it is written, “in the seat of scoffers or mockers,” and this is understood of Pharisees or heretics who mock the Lord or the Church. Therefore he has not sat in the seat of pestilence who has not taught evil by perverse example unto the end.

[Col. 0280A] The ungodly person is one who sins against God or parents; the sinner, one who sins against himself; the pestilent person, one who lays waste his neighbors. Here three falls of the soul are indicated: thought, speech, and act. The blessed man has not gone in the council of the ungodly when he does not consent in will to a thought introduced by demons; he does not walk in the way of sinners when he does not speak evil; he does not sit in the seat of pestilence when, by doing evil, he does not teach it. These are figured by the three dead persons whom the Lord raised: the girl raised in the house; the young man raised outside the gate; and Lazarus summoned from the tomb. The girl dead in the house is the soul dead in thought through delight; the young man borne outside the gate is the mind dead through consent to an act; the old man stinking in the tomb [Col. 0280B] is the human being buried in a perverse habit. It follows:

“But his will is in the Law of the Lord,” by turning away from evil, “and in his Law he shall meditate day and night,” by doing good. Law (*lex*) is said to derive from binding (*ligare*), because a person is bound to God’s commandments by the cords of obedience. “And he shall be like a tree planted [beside] streams of waters”: that is, such a person shall flourish like a palm in faith and bear fruit like an olive in action. The tree planted beside streams of waters—that is, the fruitful tree itself—is watered by the fountain springing up into eternal life; and it “shall give its fruit in its time,” that is, in the time of tribulation it shall bring back the fruit of patience. The time of the evil is to fulfil here the desires of the flesh; the time of the good is to mourn here over the evils of the world. The evil, in [Col. 0280C] their time, bring forth thorns and thistles of sins; the good, in their time, put forth flowers of virtues and fruits of good works. But in the time of tribulation the evil, like dry wood, will burn in fire; the good, like the sun, will shine in God’s kingdom. “And its leaf shall not fall”: that is, when set amid hardship, like Job, he will not utter an evil word. “And therefore whatever he does shall prosper,” because every adversity and sorrow will be changed into his joy.

After the members of Christ have been described, the ungodly follow, who are the devil’s members.

## Application of the second part of the psalm to the ungodly

The good are those who turn away from evil and do good. **(VERSE 4.) “Not so the ungodly”**—understand, they are not so in will [Col. 0280D], nor so in action. But what are they like? Like dust: dry in wickedness, moistened by no dew of charity, “which the wind casts away from the face of the earth.” The wind is temptation; dust, those who are light in character; the face of the earth, Christ’s flesh, who took the form of earth when he appeared like us in flesh. Therefore, just as a whirlwind lifts dust from the earth and whirls it around, so the wind of temptation raises the unstable from faith in Christ, turns them in the circle of fleshly desires, and scatters them from the land of the living.

Alternatively: “Not so the ungodly”—not as those who, by imitating the blessed man, will advance into likeness to the tree of life, so that by beholding his blessedness and eternity they themselves may be blessed and eternal, according to the saying: “The days of my people shall be according to the days of a tree” (Isa. 65) [Col. 0281A]. Rather, being fruitless like dry wood, fit for fire, they will be cast out through desires by the north wind, that is, the devil, from the face of the earth, that is, from the stability of the Church, so that they may become dust and food for the serpent.

**VERSE 5.—“Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the counsel of the righteous.”** The ungodly are those sinning against God and parents; sinners are those persisting in evils. Or the ungodly are pagans and Jews; sinners are heretics and false Christians. There are two judgments: one of confession here, the other of final examination. In this judgment the priest is judge; the human being is the accused and accuser; conscience is witness; penitence is the judge’s sentence. Moreover, the counsel of the righteous is the conversion of sinners. Therefore the ungodly do not rise in this judgment because they do not recognize their profound fall into shameful acts [Col. 0281B], and so refuse to confess and repent of their crimes. Nor do sinners rise in the counsel of the righteous—understand, because they are unwilling to turn from wickedness to goodness. Or they do not rise in the sight of the righteous, that is, they refuse to be in harmony with those whom they also hate.

But in the final judgment all, both reprobate and elect, will rise in the flesh, and all will stand before Christ’s tribunal to render an account of their own deeds. But the ungodly will not rise in judgment, that is, so as to judge the righteous there as they did here; rather, they will rise to be judged by the righteous and justly condemned for their deeds. Nor will sinners rise there in the counsel, that is, in the assembly, of the righteous, because here they were unwilling to rise to righteousness in the counsel of the righteous; and therefore they will not share in their blessedness.

[Col. 0281C] 

## On the four orders

There will be four orders at the judgment: two of the elect and two of the reprobate. One order of the elect comprises the perfect, who do not come into judgment but will be judges with the Lord. The other order of the elect comprises those who will not fear evil report, but, called by the judge’s sweet voice, “Come, blessed ones” (Matt. 25), will enter into the joy of their Lord. The third order is that of unbelieving reprobates, because they are already judged and condemned; and because these sinned without the Law, they will perish without the Law. The fourth order is that of believing reprobates, who confessed God with words but denied him in deeds; and because they sinned against the Law of God, they will be judged through the Law, when the Judge says to them terribly: “Depart from me [Col. 0281D], accursed ones” (ibid.), etc.

All this happens because **(VERSE 6)** “the Lord knows the way of the righteous”: that is, he approves their life and, praising it, rewards their deeds when they go with him into eternal life. But he does not know the way of the wicked, that is, he will reject their life; and therefore “the way of the ungodly shall perish”: that is, the affections of the evil, in which they ran about as on paths, will then perish utterly when they enter eternal punishment with the devil.

## Conclusion

This psalm begins at the origin of the world and closes at the end of the age, because the world, beginning in Christ, who is the beginning and the end, also ends in him [Col. 0282A]. This psalm is sung on the Lord’s night because Christ rose on it, of whom it is written in this psalm; and on this day the Church, Christ’s body, will also rise, to which this psalm is suited. It is likewise sung on the feast of any saint because every faithful person is reckoned a member of the Church, whose structure is contained in the description of this psalm.

## PROLOGUE TO THE FIFTIETH PSALM

This psalm is written as the fourth of the penitential psalms because through the four virtues—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—a person is made perfect. The seven penitential psalms are set forth because sins are remitted through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The first is assigned to the spirit of fear; the second, to the spirit of piety; the third, to the spirit of knowledge; this fourth, to the spirit of fortitude [Col. 0282B], which is counted as one of the four principal virtues. In this psalm humility and prayer are especially indicated, through which sins are most fully forgiven.

It is placed fiftieth, the same number as the days of Pentecost, and signifies the joy which the penitent obtains through pardon. This was expressed through the fiftieth year, called the jubilee—that is, full of jubilation—in which the people recovered its lost inheritance, and the person who had been sold returned to lost freedom. Thus through penitence the lost inheritance of paradise is recovered, and one returns to former freedom. For a person conquered by desire is sold under sin, since everyone who commits sin becomes a slave of sin. In the number fifty, ten is multiplied five times [Col. 0282C], because after the five ages of the world Christ, the salvation of humankind and the tenfold number of life, is born; through him the Holy Spirit, who is the remission of sins, is given.

## On the title, history, and figure
The title of this psalm is: (VV. 1, 2) “For the end. A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.” The history is well known. Uriah, one of David’s commanders, had a beautiful wife; the king, seeing her bathing, desired her, ordered her brought to him, and lay with her. Meanwhile her husband was stationed with the army at the siege of a certain city, but through David’s counsel he perished by being killed. After this was done, the Lord sent Nathan the prophet to David [Col. 0282D], who set before him a parable concerning a sheep and a guest; by this he charged him with the sin he had committed. David, however, acknowledging his committed crime and terrified by the Lord’s dreadful threat, performed heartfelt penitence, composed this psalm as satisfaction, and obtained again his former grace from the Lord.

This psalm, therefore, is attributed to David, king and prophet, who looked toward the end, that is, toward Christ, through whom he saw that his sin would be forgiven: “when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.” That is, when Nathan the prophet rebuked him for the adultery committed with Bathsheba and for the murder of Uriah.

Nathan, who admonished David concerning penitence, is said to mean “he gave,” [Col. 0283A] and signifies the order of teachers who give the faithful people counsel concerning penitence. He proposed the parable concerning the sheep, because the good shepherd laid down his life for the sheep. In the literal sense, moreover, the man who had many sheep was David, who had many wives; the poor man who had one sheep was Uriah, who had only one wife.

The guest for whom the poor man’s sheep is killed is unlawful love, which is nourished by intercourse with the wife. Note that lust was a guest in David’s house, but held a kingdom in Solomon’s.

The falls of saints are written down so that the power of the physician may be commended for the healing of the despairing sick person, and that those who have fallen may be encouraged by their example to hope for pardon. [Col. 0283B] But fools take from the saints a pattern for sinning and flee from the pattern for repentance.

Since sin was imputed by God to David as to other human beings, and was also severely punished in him, the question arises why he is presented as a figure. But it must be understood that God chose the Israelite people out of the whole human race as a figure; that people was a shadow of the Christian people. For whatever it did, even unknowingly, foreshadowed something that would one day come to pass. Yet more particularly, whatever the Holy Spirit wished to be written through the prophets concerning them or all peoples of former times was a figure of what was to come. Hence it is written: “All things happened to them in a figure” (1 Cor. 10). Thus David bore the figure of Christ, Bathsheba that of the Church, and Uriah the image of the devil. And just as she, while bathing in the spring of Cedron [Col. 0283C], stripped of her garments, pleased David and was judged worthy to come to the king’s embraces, while her husband too was slain by royal command; so also the Church—that is, the assembly of the faithful—cleansed from the filth of sins by the washing of sacred baptism, is known to be joined to Christ the Lord, and the devil was annihilated as the apostles attacked him. The names themselves indicate this. For David means “desirable”; Bathsheba, “well of the covenant”; Uriah is called “the glory of my God,” and denotes the devil, who appropriated to himself the glory of his God, saying: “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). He is also called “My light is God,” signifying him who transforms himself into an angel of light.

Just as Bathsheba did not endure intercourse with her former husband after she was joined to David, so the Church [Col. 0283D] is not joined to the devil after she has come to Christ the Desirable One, who was the expectation of the nations. She was the well of the covenant, because the abyss of the old Law lay hidden in her. Uriah fell through David’s counsel, and through Christ’s counsel the devil lost the Gentile world. Nor should you be surprised that Christ is figured by an adulterer, the Church denoted by an adulteress, and the devil represented by a chaste man: for nothing contributes to shamefulness if it is indicated in golden letters, nor does anything detract from honesty if it is denoted in letters of ink.

### On the subject, purpose, and usefulness of this psalm

The subject of this psalm is the prayer of the penitent David; its purpose is to instruct us by David’s example in penitence and prayer. Great benefit is conferred upon the faithful in this [Col. 0284A] prayer: so that the righteous person may not trust in his own righteousness when he sees that the most righteous David fell, and the sinner may not despair when he hears that so great a sinner obtained pardon. The words are taken from David’s own repentance and are suitable for every faithful person who, after falling, has recourse to the Lord with satisfaction and prayer.

“For if thou hadst desired it” is drawn from the history in which God rejected Cain’s sacrifice because he did not offer righteousness. Or it is taken from the history in which the Lord despised Saul’s sacrifice, because he neglected to render obedience. It signifies that God rejects the offering of one who disdains to offer charity and humility. “Deal kindly” is drawn from the future history in which Jerusalem is destroyed by the Babylonians [Col. 0284B], but is built again by Zerubbabel and Jesus the priest, and an acceptable sacrifice is offered to God; or from the history in which Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans but rebuilt anew by the emperor Hadrian, in which Christians now offer sacrifices acceptable to God. It signifies, however, that Zion—that is, the Church—is here destroyed by pagans and heretics, but is rebuilt in the heavenly Jerusalem from living stones through Jesus, the supreme Priest and King, Christ.

### On the division of this psalm

This psalm is divided into five parts, because penitence is performed on account of the guilt of the five senses. The first is: “Have mercy on me, O God,” in which is the penitent’s satisfaction. The second: “Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop,” [Col. 0284C] in which is confidence in mercy. The third: “Turn thy face away,” in which is the veneration of the Trinity. The fourth: “I shall teach the wicked,” in which is the penitent’s future preaching. The fifth: “Deal kindly,” in which the acceptance of penitence is indicated.

In the preceding psalm a terrible judgment is described, and the gentle admonition of the king is added. Therefore the sinner, frightened when Jesus said: “Why dost thou declare my righteousness?” (Ps. 49), runs to the judge with the sacrifice of penitence, saying:

### Explanation of the psalm

**V. 3.**—“Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy.” God’s mercy is so great that it brought down the Creator of the world from heaven, clothed him in an earthly body, made him equal to us in mortality though equal to the Father in eternity, and imposed upon the Lord of the world the form of a servant; so that the living bread itself might hunger, the fountain of life thirst, strength become weak, and almighty life die. Great mercy it was: for the Creator to be created for our sake, the Ruler to serve, the Redeemer to be sold, the Exalter to be humbled, the Giver of life to be killed. According to the measure of this great mercy, have mercy on me. Christ is the fountain of mercy in which David, Peter, Zacchaeus, Paul, Mary, the thief, and countless others were washed; concerning him there follows:

“And according to the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my iniquity.” The multitude of God’s mercies is greater than the multitude of all sins. [Col. 0285A] Because thy mercy is manifold and my misery is great, according to the measure of thy abundant mercies blot out the greatness of my iniquity. The comparison is drawn from wax, on which an ugly image has been impressed: when that image has been erased, the wax is reshaped to receive a beautiful image. For only the person whose every iniquity is blotted out shall be written in the book of life.

**V. 4.**—“Wash me yet more from my iniquity.” Thou didst first wash me in the fountain of baptism; now wash me yet more in the fountain of tears. “And cleanse me from my sin.” Thou didst wash me in baptism from original sin; cleanse me now from actual sin.

**V. 5.**—“For I acknowledge my iniquity.” Therefore forgive thou, because I am punished by tears; therefore spare me mercifully. “And my sin is always before me”: that is, like a horrible image it stands before me, which I continually behold with open and closed eyes, and which I desire to annihilate by praying and weeping. Above it is said: “I shall rebuke thee and set thy sins before thy face” (Ps. 49). The penitent forestalls this: he places his sin always before himself, beholding and mourning it. True penitence is both to mourn sins committed and not to commit sins that ought to be mourned.

Therefore I pray to thee, because (**V. 6**) “against thee only have I sinned and done evil before thee”: thou who alone art without sin and alone art good. Note: he addresses Christ himself, the Father of mercy; all human beings are held bound by the chains of sins, but thou [Col. 0285C] alone art true and righteous. “That thou mayest be justified in thy words,” when thou sayest: “Which of you shall convict me of sin?” (John 8); and when the prophet says of thee, “He committed no sin”; and: “The prince of this world shall come to thee and shall find nothing of his own” (John 14). “And mayest overcome” all human beings in righteousness when thou art judged by the unrighteous, who say: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26), and: “If he were not an evildoer, we would not have delivered him to thee” (John 18).

Otherwise: “Against thee only,” thou who art King of kings, “have I sinned and done evil before thee,” thou who beholdest all things and who promised that thou wouldst be born from my stock. But now the whole people says: “Christ will not be born from David, who committed such a sin”; and thus thy promise becomes void in human opinion. Therefore forgive [Col. 0285D] my sin, that thou mayest be justified in thy words by fulfilling thy promise, lest thou appear deceitful rather than true; and that thou mayest overcome when judged by worldly people who judge that, because of my many sins, thou ought not to render the things promised. Make it manifest that the words concerning the promise made to me are to be fulfilled not from my merits but by thy righteousness alone. Thou alone art righteous in thyself; others are righteous through thee.

**V. 7.**—“For behold, I was conceived in iniquities.” That is, in original sin, because all sinned in Adam. “And in sins my mother conceived me.” David was not born of adultery, but of Jesse, a righteous man, and his wife; nor is marital intercourse sin. Yet because a mortal person is propagated from mortal parents, he is rightly said to be conceived in sins. [Col. 0286A] Death is the punishment of sin, possessed from parents as though by inheritance, though administered through the concupiscence of the flesh. Christ, however, conceived without concupiscence, was born without sin; he was mortal not by nature but by will, and therefore conquered all things.

**V. 8.**—“For behold, thou hast loved truth.” That is, confession. Behold, it is clear that thou didst first love to produce truth in me—that is, knowledge of sin and penitence—because thou didst first will it for me. “The uncertain and hidden things of thy wisdom thou hast made manifest to me”; that is, thou didst reveal to me the mysteries of thy Son, which thou indeed revealedst to many, but showedst to me with certainty: first, that I might acknowledge thee to have a Son; then, that I might know that he would come from my seed, so that I foretold his passion and [Col. 0286B] resurrection as though seen. Therefore:

**V. 9.**—“Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.” That is, thou shalt cleanse me through the blood of the Son of God. The history is touched upon: the blood was sprinkled with a bunch of hyssop over the leper, and he became clean. This blood signified the blood of the Son of God, by which lepers in body and soul are cleansed. Hyssop, a small herb that checks swelling of the lungs, signifies Christ’s humility, by which he offered himself to God. Hyssop is said to penetrate a rock with its root; that rock is Christ. “Thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow”; that is, thou shalt purify me through the washing of baptism, and I shall be whiter than snow. The soul has its own brightness, just as the body has its own; and among all visible creatures nothing is whiter than snow, beyond which is the brightness of the soul in the body. [Col. 0286C] And after thou hast done this:

**V. 10.**—“Thou shalt give joy and gladness to my hearing.” Above thou didst say: “Hear, my people, and I shall speak” (Ps. 49). Behold, I hear obediently what thou commandest and do not resist; and to this hearing of mine thou shalt give joy and gladness. Joy pertains to absolution from sin; gladness, to the reception of everlasting life. He shall give joy and gladness to hearing when he says: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25), etc. Having heard this voice, “the humbled bones” shall rejoice, namely the supports of the soul weakened in penitence. By bones, reason and free choice are also understood, bent down in sins; these shall rejoice when thou restorest the power of reason and the capacity of free choice. For while a person delights in sins, reason [Col. 0286D] is blinded and free choice weakened. “That thou mayest give joy and gladness to my hearing”:

**V. 11.**—“Turn thy face away from my sins.” For God to look upon or remember our sins is to will to punish them; to turn his face away from sins or forget them is to will not to punish. Otherwise, God always sees the acts and thoughts of all people and never forgets, for with him all things past and future are present. “And blot out all my iniquities”: blot out original and actual sins—that is, forgive them—because our committed offense is, as it were, written upon certain tablets, while it is contained in divine knowledge. And do not merely forgive sins, but also:

**V. 12.**—“Create in me a clean heart, O God.” Thou who [Col. 0287A] canst do this, cleanse the soul from the darkness of ignorance, so that I may behold and understand thee purely. “Create” is used here for “restore.” Create a clean heart: that is, give a clean understanding. The heart is put for understanding because in it the source of thoughts is said to be. “From the heart,” the Lord says, “thoughts proceed” (Matt. 15). Thus the heart is also conoid, having the form of fire, so that it is fittingly fashioned in such a position from which counsel can come to us. The natural philosophers also teach that the heart is the first thing formed in a human being. “And renew a right spirit within me”: give wisdom anew—that is, give thy Son to my understanding—so that I may be able to act well, because he is the rule of every right action. It is not the Spirit but the human being who is renewed when re-formed from the oldness of sin.

[Col. 0287B] **V. 13.**—“Cast me not away from thy face.” One is cast away from God’s face when he is disdained as beyond healing. Renew me thus, that thou mayest no longer cast me away from conformity to him, which is thy face through which thou art known, and do not allow me further to exceed thy line. “And take not thy Holy Spirit from me,” namely, the spirit of prophecy or of love.

**V. 14.**—“Restore to me the joy of thy salvation.” That is, cause me to have joy in the salvation of thy Son. He knows that he has lost the grace of the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit flees sinners and does not dwell in a body subject to sins. “And strengthen me with a principal spirit,” so that I may not sin again or depart from thee through instability of mind. Here the Trinity is expressly set forth: in the principal spirit, the Father; in the right spirit, the Son; [Col. 0287C] in the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit himself is understood. The principal spirit is not so called because he is earlier in time or greater, but because both the Son and the Holy Spirit are said to be from him, while he is not said to be from them. If thou shalt do this and give me the things I have asked:

**V. 15.**—“I shall teach the wicked thy ways.” That is, I shall instruct other sinners by word and example in thy mercy and righteousness, and through me the ungodly shall turn to thee from error.

**V. 16.**—“Deliver me from bloods, O God, O God of my salvation.” In the singular number, *blood* is understood as a part of the body, or as the human being himself, or as offspring. As a part: “Blood came forth from the Lord’s side” (John 19); as the human being: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to thee” [Col. 0287D] (Matt. 16); as offspring: “He was born of high blood,” that is, of noble stock. But *bloods* in the plural signifies sins or deaths. The God of salvation is Christ, through whom salvation is given to believers. O God of all, who art the God of my salvation, deliver me from deaths. He therefore uses *bloods* for deaths because death comes through the shedding of blood. He had many deaths: one by which he killed himself through sinning; another by which he killed Bathsheba in soul; a third by which he deceitfully killed Uriah. “And my tongue shall rejoice in thy righteousness”: that is, if thou shalt do this, then my tongue shall joyfully proclaim to others thy righteousness, by which thou forgivest sins and advance people in good works. Above it is said: “Why dost thou declare my righteousness and take my covenant in thy mouth?” (Ps. 49). [Col. 0288A] Now, absolved from guilt, he joyfully declares the righteousness of God. Hence it follows:

**V. 17.**—“O Lord, thou shalt open my lips,” which guilt had closed: thou shalt make them fit and clean to proclaim thy righteousness; “and then my mouth shall declare thy praise,” that is, the praises of thy righteousness. Sinners do not dare speak lest they be rebuked and their sins reproached to them. Their lips are opened for speech when, turning back from sins, they are justified; then, enlivened by God’s Spirit, they despise human glory, hold human praise and reproach in equal contempt, and freely rebuke sinners, as Paul did. Their mouths declare God’s praise when they confess their sins before people, so that others may take from their salvation an example of conversion. I offer the praise [Col. 0288B] of God as sacrifice, not the sacrifice of animals:

**V. 18.**—“For if thou hadst desired sacrifice, I would have given it.” But I understand that thou dost not desire sacrifice from sinners, because thou didst say above: “I will not accept calves from thy house, nor goats from thy flocks” (Ps. 49). Certainly thou shalt not delight in holocausts, namely those offered from animals. But since such things were offered as figures, which thou now refusest to receive for sins, I know what sacrifice thou dost receive.

**V. 19.**—“A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God.” That is, a spirit sorrowful for sins will be a pleasing sacrifice; “a contrite heart,” that is, afflicted by penitence, “and humbled,” that is, devoted by pious confession, thou, O God, wilt not despise as thou dost the sacrifices of the Law. I foresee that such a sacrifice will be made to thee by Zion, and therefore:

[Col. 0288C] **V. 20.**—“Deal kindly, O Lord, in thy good will with Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.” By Zion knowledge of God is denoted; by Jerusalem, charity. Jerusalem is one city composed of angels and human beings; its portion had been destroyed in Adam, and for it he prays: deal kindly—that is, deal generously—by giving faith and every good life to those who are to be Zion; and do this in thy good will, that is, by thy grace, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built through chosen human beings, who were destroyed among the apostate angels. Or: deal kindly with Zion, that is, with the primitive Church from the Jews; and let the walls of Jerusalem be built—that is, through it establish the Church from the Gentiles. Or let the walls of Jerusalem be built from Jews and Gentiles through faith and love, [Col. 0288D] to whom deal kindly by giving perseverance and reward. Zion, which means “watching,” is the present Church; Jerusalem, which conveys “vision of peace,” is the Church reigning in heaven, built from living stones. Therefore deal kindly with Zion—that is, with the present Church—by giving sinners pardon and confession, so that through them the walls of Jerusalem may be built: that is, through such stones the number of the elect in heavenly Jerusalem may be restored. The walls of Jerusalem are angels and human beings.

**V. 21.**—“Then [thou shalt accept] the sacrifice of righteousness.” That is, then the sacrifice of a contrite spirit and a broken heart will be supremely acceptable to thee. “Then thou shalt accept oblations and holocausts,” namely, faithful people offering their whole selves to thee and distributing their possessions to the poor. Or [Col. 0289A] the sacrifice of righteousness is the Lord’s body, sacrificed for us as a lamb; oblations are confessors or any faithful persons offering themselves to Christ through faith and action; holocausts are martyrs consumed by the fire of suffering, or by any torture of the body. “Then the wicked [shall offer] calves upon thy altar,” namely the priests of the Church. God’s altar is Christ; calves are Christians, new in faith and renewed in baptism. And, like cloven-hoofed calves, they discern between good and evil; they are ruminants, that is, they recall God’s precepts and words to memory; and they are armed with horns, that is, strengthened by the powerful examples of the saints. These calves are placed upon the altar when, through the priests of the Church, they are offered to God through Christ; and thus through them the walls of Jerusalem are restored.

[Col. 0289B] Otherwise: now, in the present age, thou acceptest as a sacrifice for iniquity a contrite spirit; in the future, thou shalt accept the sacrifice of righteousness, of praise alone, where those dwelling in thy house for ages of ages shall praise thee. For this is the sacrifice of righteousness. Then the righteous shall be an oblation and holocaust, when divine fire shall wholly consume them, their souls shall be clothed with wisdom and their bodies with immortality, and death shall be swallowed up in victory. Calves shall be all the elect, released from the bonds of the Law and misery, made young by a new age, and placed upon Christ the altar, in whom they shall rest without end.

### Conclusion

This psalm is therefore frequently used by penitents, so that through its power, like David, they may be built into the walls of heavenly Jerusalem. Note that the penitent [Col. 0289C] first laments his own sins, then proclaims God’s mercy to others, and finally prays for those in error. It is sung at Lauds in Lent because through penitence one comes to eternal praise. It is sung at Lauds on weekdays because those who escape the darkness of sins come to true light and eternal gladness. For this reason it is frequently repeated at the Hours, so that every faithful person, a living stone like David, may be placed in the heavenly building.

## Prologue to the Second Fifty-Psalm Collection

It is read that, when David the prophet had grown old, he chose four thousand young men from Israel to sound the psalms with great delight on organs, harps, lyres, timbrels, cymbals, trumpets, and with their own voices—the psalms which he himself produced by the Lord’s inspiration. This sweet union of song, divided into three parts, consisted of the rational, belonging to the human voice; the irrational, belonging to musical instruments; and the common, belonging to both parts. For the singers sang together with the instruments. That sweet and pleasant music foretold the Catholic Church in such an act: gathered from diverse languages and varied harmony, it was to hand down concord in one faith by the Lord’s gift, and, assembled from the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—it resounds Christ’s praises with the same psalms.

The psalms are divided into twelve parts: in the first part, Christ’s bodily life; in the second, the nature of his divinity; in the third, the conspiracy of the ungodly against him; in the fourth, the Church’s admonition against them; [Col. 0290A] in the fifth, Christ’s prayer in persecution; in the sixth, the supplication of penitents; in the seventh, Christ’s petition to the Father according to his assumed humanity; in the eighth, parabolic and tropological allusions pertaining to Christ; in the ninth, manifold praises, now pertaining to his humanity, now to his divinity; in the tenth, the gradual psalms; in the eleventh, the works of the Trinity; and in the twelfth, praises with *alleluia* are written.

## Prologue to Psalm Fifty-One

The five decades now written signify the five ages of the world, in which the body of the Church, arranged in its members, has through the labor of the five senses been gathered into the walls of heavenly Jerusalem. For before Christ’s advent the faithful prepared themselves under the five [Col. 0290B] books of Moses for the heavenly building; now, under grace, the five prudent virgins, who are all the faithful of the Church, prepare themselves under those same books, spiritually understood, for the same structure.

Now, with the sixth decade, the Holy Spirit begins with the body of the wicked, which in the sixth age of the world began to persecute Christ and the Church. And as the first set of fifty begins with Christ, who is the head of the body of those to be saved, the blessed man who rewards his own with eternal blessedness; so this set of fifty begins with Antichrist, who is the head of the body of those to be damned, the son of perdition who drags all those agreeing with him into eternal destruction.

[Col. 0290C] This psalm occupies the fifty-first place, a number arising from three and ascending through seven to ten. For three times seven and three times ten are fifty-one; this number signifies that those who suffer persecution in the three parts of the world for faith in the Trinity are brought through the sevenfold Spirit to the ten of eternal life.

The title of this psalm is (VV. 1, 2): “For the end; an understanding of David, when Doeg the Edomite came and announced to Saul and said to him: David has come into the house of Abimelech.” The history is well known. Saul wished to kill David, who fled and came to Abimelech the priest, receiving from him holy bread and the sword of Goliath. [Col. 0290D] Doeg, Saul’s keeper of mules, saw this and reported it to Saul. Saul therefore, enraged, killed all the priests of the Lord. By this is signified the persecution of Antichrist in God’s Church. Doeg means “moved,” and Edomite means “earthly”; he denotes Antichrist, who will move the whole earth to worship himself. Saul signifies death; David, the life of Christ; Abimelech, the Church; the sword signifies royal power, and the loaves of presentation signify the glory of the priesthood. Through David Christ is expressed as king; through Abimelech, as priest. This is the understanding of David the prophet, extending toward the end of the world and denoting in this psalm the things that shall take place in the last times: when Antichrist comes into the world and calls upon death to punish Abimelech—that is, begins to kill in the Church all the righteous, [Col. 0291A] because they receive Christ’s faith and are his house.

Otherwise: Saul means “petition” and signifies death, which God did not make, but which man desires by sinning. Thus in the title of the fourteenth psalm it is written, “On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul,” because death, the last enemy, shall be destroyed. David means “the desirable one,” the life desired by all the blessed. Abimelech, interpreted “the kingdom of my Father,” is the Church, the heavenly kingdom which groans as a stranger among the citizens of the earthly kingdom. Doeg the Edomite, meaning “earthly motion,” is the Babylonian people, always wandering in the motion of earthly things and never at rest. He is keeper of mules—that is, of the barren, [Col. 0291B] who are barren in good works while bearing the burdens of sins.

Christ, the king of life, came into the Church, which is the kingdom of his Father. But Saul—that is, the devil, king of death—and Doeg—that is, lovers of the world, who are the kingdom of Babylon—persecute both Christ and the Church. And because this shall happen especially in the times of Antichrist, this psalm is attributed to him.

The subject of this psalm is the Holy Spirit’s invective against Antichrist, because he persecutes the Church without cause. Its purpose is to make us cautious concerning Antichrist’s persecution by foretelling the persecution itself and his damnation, and by showing the faith and constancy of the righteous who shall then exist. The words are taken from the history in which Doeg gloried in the expulsion of King David [Col. 0291C] and in the killing of Abimelech the priest. This signifies that the Jewish people gloried because they killed Christ the king and priest, just as Antichrist shall glory that he will eradicate royalty and priesthood from the Church. This psalm is divided into four parts: the first division is, “Why dost thou glory?” in which is the Holy Spirit’s invective against Antichrist; the second, “Therefore God,” in which is Antichrist’s destruction; the third, “The righteous shall see,” in which is his damnation; the fourth, “But I,” in which the praise of the faithful is set forth. The psalm is divided by a *diapsalma*, because the faithful people are distinguished from the unfaithful by the Holy Spirit. The following voice is that of the Holy Spirit, who in the person of the faithful people inveighs against Antichrist, whose cruel persecution is here shown.

[Col. 0291D] ### Explanation of Psalm LI

**V. 3.**—“Why dost thou glory in malice, thou who art powerful in iniquity?” Malice is not only doing evil but also teaching it and compelling others to evil. Antichrist glories in this malice when the whole world is turned from the worship of the true God to reverence for himself. He is powerful in iniquity because, by immense riches and astonishing signs, he is able powerfully to accomplish every iniquity. O son of perdition, why dost thou glory in malice, which shall bring thee so great a ruin? Thou seemest powerful in iniquity, but thou shalt suffer torments powerfully.

**V. 4.**—“All day,” that is, at every time, “thy tongue has devised injustice”: that is, thy mind has meditated injustice—how thy tongue might [Col. 0292A] speak the malice which thou wouldst accomplish in deed. “Like a sharp razor thou hast wrought deceit.” A razor was a shaving instrument. Antichrist shall be the devil’s razor: for as a sharp razor shaves hairs from flesh, so he draws away from the righteous their outward goods by deceit. And as a razor renews the face when the hairs have been shaved, so he renews in holiness Christians cleansed from sins through deceit. And as a razor sometimes harms the flesh by wounding it, so he wounds some by torments and harms others in soul by deceiving them with miracles. Thou hast made deceit sharp when thou pretendest to teach well in order to lead people into error.

**V. 5.**—“Thou hast loved malice more than kindness.” Reason teaches thee kindness, but thou lovest malice more, because thou punishest the good and raisest the evil above them; [Col. 0292B] and thou not only doest evil but also drawest others away from good. For, he says, “thou hast loved iniquity more than to speak equity,” when thou shalt condemn the righteous because of righteousness and exalt the wicked. But malice and iniquity shall plunge thee into the abyss; kindness and equity shall raise the righteous into heaven.

**V. 6.**—“Thou hast loved all words of precipitation, O deceitful tongue”: that is, thou hast loved to speak every deceitful word that leads to a precipice. A deceitful tongue is the servant of fraud, in those who hold one thing in their heart and utter another with their mouth. Once Antichrist’s wickedness has been described, his destruction follows.

And because thou rejectest good and lovest evil:

**V. 7.**—“Therefore God shall destroy thee for ever.” Christ, who is true God, shall destroy thee and thy power by the brightness of his coming, and this “for the end,” that is, eternally. And because he shall pluck thee from thy exaltation, that is, kill thee; and shall remove thee from the tabernacle of the body or of this world to everlasting punishment; and, understand, shall pluck up thy root from the land of the living. His root is desire for human glory, which one fixes in the power of a kingdom; he is plucked from the land of the living because he is not permitted to reign in it. It is handed down literally that, when many Christians flee from Antichrist’s presence into Egypt and he determines to pursue them, he will pitch his tent on the Mount of Olives; there the Spirit of the Lord, whom some understand to be Michael, will kill him, and from this tent he shall depart to hell, where the Lord ascended into heaven.

[Col. 0292D] **V. 8.**—“The righteous shall see his condemnation and fear God”; or, some shall fear because they consented to him, and some because they doubted on account of his signs. Others shall laugh over him, rejoicing that they escaped his cruelty. They shall judge his deed worthy of derision and say:

**V. 9.**—“Behold the man who did not make God his helper”: that is, behold, it is clear that he was a man who made himself God and disdained to have the true God as his helper. This was prefigured in Simon Magus, who pretended to be God, but in falling was shown to be a deceiver. He does not trust in God’s help, but “hoped in the multitude of his riches”: that is, he placed his hope not in God but in many riches—in gold and silver, [Col. 0293A] eloquence and knowledge—through which he thought to save himself. “And he prevailed in his vanity”: that is, he shall think himself to prevail over and rule all evil and good people in the vanity by which he teaches himself to be God. For it is the greatest vanity that, despising God, he commands that he himself be worshipped as God. In this he prevailed over those to whom he persuaded that he was God; he himself shall perish because he was a barren tree.

**V. 10.**—“But I,” the Christian people whom he persecuted, “am like a fruitful olive tree”; therefore I shall be saved for ages. Oil means mercy; the fruit of the olive is works of mercy. The Gentile people, like a wild olive, was grafted into the good olive tree—that is, the primitive Church—anointed with holy oil in baptism and joined to it through faith and action. “In the house of God,” that is, in the Catholic Church, I have therefore hoped in the mercy [Col. 0293B] of God “for ever and ever,” that is, here and in the future, not in riches as did Antichrist, my persecutor.

**V. 11.**—“I shall confess to thee for ever and ever, because thou hast done [it].” That is, I shall praise thee in heart, mouth, and deed as long as I live, because thou hast made me such, and hast rendered just judgment concerning Antichrist. “And I shall wait for thy name,” that is, Christ thy Son, who shall come for judgment and render to me the reward of life for my labor, “because it is good in the sight of thy saints”: because then the saints receive the supreme good when they behold Christ in the glory of the Father. Otherwise: I shall not hasten to attain thy name, which is God, as Antichrist did; but by living well I shall wait to receive thy name, so that I may be co-heir with thy Son, who, being Son, is consequently also God. [Col. 0293C] For the saints see this to be good, those who shall be in this supreme good for eternity.

This whole passage can be referred to the body of the devil, namely all the wicked, who are members of Antichrist. Doeg the Edomite is the Jewish people stirred up for earthly things; Saul is death or the devil; David is Christ; the house of Abimelech is Jerusalem in Judaea, the kingdom of Christ’s Father. David came into the house of Abimelech when Christ came into the temple at Jerusalem, the house of his Father. Doeg reported this to Saul when the Jewish people handed Christ over to death. He gloried in wickedness, by which he killed the prophets and the righteous. He was mighty in iniquity, by which he delivered the Lord himself to death [Col. 0293D]. All day, that is, at every time, he devised injustice against Christ and the apostles, whom he shaved away from the land of the Jews with deceit, as with a sharp razor. He loved words of casting down when he forbade them to preach Christ, by which he cast himself down from the kingdom into death, as the devil from heaven and Adam from paradise.

Therefore God destroyed him from the Law, plucked him from the city, removed him from his land among the nations, and removed his root—that is, his offspring—from the land of the living, that is, from the Church.

God will also finally destroy the whole body of the devil, which now glories in malice and mightily oppresses the righteous: at the end of the world he will destroy all the ungodly; he will pluck that body from the fellowship of the righteous when, winnowing it, he removes the chaff from the wheat. From the tabernacle—that is [Col. 0294A], from the Church, which is now God’s tabernacle—he will remove it when he casts it into the lake of fire and sulphur. He will pluck up its root from the land of the living when he utterly uproots the seed of the ungodly from the kingdom of heaven and casts it into the land of death. For the servant, Doeg, shall not remain in the house for ever, but the son—the faithful people—remains for ever.

The righteous will see God’s terrible judgment upon the ungodly people and will fear; but they will be purified by this fear. And they will laugh over him, that is, they will rejoice in God’s just judgment, because they have escaped the persecution of the wicked and present condemnation. And they will say: “Behold the man”—Antichrist—“who has fallen into punishment with his whole body; who did not make God his helper, but placed his hope in many riches,” [Col. 0294B] all of which he has lost. “But I shall be in the house of God, in the heavenly Jerusalem, flourishing in joy like an olive tree; I did not hope in riches, but in his mercy; and I shall praise his name for ever, because I behold the highest good eternally.”

## Prologue to Psalm 100

The fiftieth psalm sings of repentance, but this hundredth psalm of mercy; for in the judgment those who have brought forth the hundredfold fruit of repentance in patience will receive the reward of life. This psalm is fittingly placed after the preceding one, in which the Church’s thanksgiving for the conversion of the Jews is written; because the final judgment immediately follows the faith of the Jews. Therefore it is reckoned in the hundredth place, because in the judgment the hundredth sheep is joined to the heavenly flock through the mercy of the loving shepherd [Col. 0294C].

### On the title, subject matter, intention, and division of the psalm

The title of the psalm is: “A Psalm of David himself”; that is, this praise of good action is attributed to Christ himself, the victorious judge, delightful in appearance. Its subject is the merits of the Church, to be rewarded in judgment. Its intention is to exhort us to do good and turn away from evil, so that we may receive mercy in judgment. Its words are drawn from the government of David, who governed the kingdom of Israel well, hated the wicked, and loved the good; and it signifies the government of Christ, who governs the Church well, hates the wicked, and loves the good.

It has two sections, because the Church’s action has two divisions: namely, avoiding evil and doing good. One part begins, “Mercy and judgment,” in which seven things to be avoided are noted; the other, “My eyes,” in which six things to be practised are considered. It is the voice of the Church [Col. 0294D].

## Exposition of Psalm 100

**Verse 1.—“I will sing of mercy and judgment to thee, O Lord.”** Mercy is sung of the present, judgment of the future. O Lord Trinity, I shall joyfully proclaim to others the mercy to be ascribed to you, which you show here to penitents, and the judgment which you show in the future to those remaining in hardness of heart; for to the former you give joys, to the latter punishments.

**Verse 2.—“I will sing psalms and understand in the blameless way.”** That is: because you are a just judge, I shall do good by abstaining from evils. Singing belongs to contemplation [Col. 0295A]; psalm-singing to action. The blameless way is innocence. True innocence is that which harms neither itself nor another; for “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10), and no one sins first against another rather than against himself. In this way I shall sing psalms by doing good, and I shall understand when you come to me—that is, when you reward me.

Alternatively: I shall sing psalms and shall be innocent, and shall understand that you will render rewards for this innocence. O Bridegroom, when will you come to me, to lead me, your bride, out of Babylon and bring me into Jerusalem, your city? He now explains the blameless way: “I walked in the innocence of my heart”; that is, I abstained not only from perverse action but also from evil thought in the heart; and this “in the midst of my house,” that is, in the common fellowship of all who dwell in the house of the Church.

[Col. 0295B]

### On the seven vices to be avoided

From this point he enumerates his merits, for which he hopes for heavenly things: first he sets forth seven things to be avoided by all, then six things to be done by all. The things to be avoided are: imitation of an unjust deed, transgression of the Law, murmuring, malice, detraction, pride, and greed. This is what he says:

**Verse 3.—“I did not set an unjust thing before my eyes.”** That is: I did not set before the eyes of my heart the intention of doing evil, nor did I imitate those doing it, nor consent to those who did it. “I hated those committing transgressions”: I hated parents, relatives, and friends who transgressed your law—yet not the persons, but the errors of persons.

**Verse 4.—“A perverse heart did not cleave to me.”** That is [Col. 0295C], the evil will of one who murmurs, or the perverse counsel of another, did not find me agreeing with it. Murmurers and those devising evil by perverse counsel were not my companions. “I did not acknowledge one departing from me who was malicious”: that is, I avoided one dissenting from my purpose as though I did not know him; or, I so abhorred a heretic departing from me by perverse doctrine and acting maliciously that I regarded him as unknown.

**Verse 5.—“The one who secretly slandered his neighbour, him I pursued.”** That is, whoever disparaged his brother in secret and sowed discord, I attacked as an enemy. The slanderer sins more grievously than the fornicator: the latter kills only himself, but the former both himself and his neighbour. The wicked are not only to be avoided so that they may be ashamed, but also pursued so that they may be corrected [Col. 0295D]. In the Hebrew it is written: “I killed him,” because slanderers are slain by the sword of their own tongue.

“With the proud eye and the insatiable heart I did not eat”: that is, I did not eat with the proud and the covetous. Every proud or covetous person is envious; because, while desiring to appear alone powerful or rich, he is distressed by others’ goods and delighted by others’ evils. I did not enter into the banquet of envy with such people; indeed, I so abominated them that I did not permit them at my table. Hence Scripture also commands us not even to take food with such a person (1 Cor. 5).

Pride is especially marked in the eyes: the proud, thinking themselves worthier than others, disdain even to look at others. Greed is assigned to the heart, because the heart empty of God is not satisfied by perishable things [Col. 0296A]. These two vices are especially notable above others because they are worse than all: “pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10), and “greed is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6). By the former an angel fell from heaven; by the latter man fell from paradise. From these two, as from the devil’s fountains, all evils flow and draw the wretched down to Tartarus. All these things which have been mentioned are not only to be avoided, but also hated and pursued.

### On the six virtues to be practised

**Verse 6.—** There follow six things to be done: faithfulness, chastity, humility, preaching, holy conduct, and the opposition of the wicked. Concerning these it is added: “My eyes are upon the faithful of the land, that they may sit with me.” That is: my concern was not for the nobles and rich of this world, that I should place them over your people [Col. 0296B], but for the faithful of the Church, that I should appoint them prelates and rulers, who might sit with me in judgment and judge your people justly. “He who walks in the blameless way ministered to me”: that is, I ordained as ministers of the altar not the unchaste, but the chaste and innocent.

**Verse 7.—“He who practises pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house.”** That is, those sinning publicly and defending it proudly did not remain openly with me in communion, because I excluded them from the sacraments and from the house of the Church; but the humble and obedient were my fellow-citizens. “He who speaks iniquity did not direct himself before the sight of my eyes”: that is, a flatterer, desiring to please by wicked words, did not direct himself toward what pleased me; or, idle talkers did not please my eyes [Col. 0296C], so as to be my messengers, but rather preachers and those persuading people toward good.

**Verse 8.—“In the morning I killed all sinners of the land.”** That is, in good action, which is a kind of morning of the eternal day, I killed all the sins of my earthliness. And by my example I brought to nothing all who sinned and desired only earthly things. “That I might destroy from the city of the Lord all workers of iniquity”: that is, by words and deeds I opposed the wicked, in order either to turn them from iniquity to righteousness or to separate them altogether from the Church.

### Application to Christ

These things also suit Christ the judge: “My eyes are upon the faithful of the land, that they may sit with me”; that is, I chose peoples and other faithful persons from the earth, that they might sit with me as judges in the judgment [Col. 0296D]. “He who walks in the blameless way ministered to me”: that is, my blameless ministers shall be where I am. Those who stain themselves with impurity do not minister to Christ; and those who seek what is their own do not serve Christ, and therefore shall not be with Christ.

“He who practises pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house.” No one who does evil works, which descend from pride, shall dwell in my house, the heavenly Jerusalem. “He who speaks iniquity did not direct himself before the sight of my eyes”: that is, not only those acting wickedly but also those speaking wickedly shall not be before my sight; that is, they shall not see my face. “In the morning I killed all sinners of the land.” The present life is like night; eternal life is like day, whose morning is the day of judgment [Col. 0297A]. On that morning the Lord will kill with the sword of his mouth all sinners of the land—that is, those desiring earthly things—saying: “Depart from me, all workers of iniquity” (Luke 13). “That I might destroy from the city of the Lord all workers of iniquity.” Then he will separate the kids from the lambs, the tares from the wheat, and the chaff from the grain; and from the city of heavenly Jerusalem and the fellowship of the saints he will cast them down with the devil and his angels into eternal fire.

## Prologue to the Third Fifty

There are four kinds of prophecy. For it is sometimes made through deeds, sometimes through words; sometimes through revelation, sometimes through the hidden revelation of the Holy Spirit. Prophecy occurs through deeds, as in the passage of the Hebrews through the Red Sea to the promised land, which [Col. 0297B] foretold our passage from the darkness of ignorance through baptism to the heavenly Jerusalem. It occurs through words when angels communicate future events to prophets by speech. It occurs through revelation when future things are signified by certain images to those placed in ecstasy, as to Daniel and Ezekiel. It occurs through hidden inspiration, as with David, to whom the Holy Spirit inwardly showed future things concerning Christ.

Sometimes prophecy concerns the past, as: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). Sometimes it concerns the present, as: “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1). But sometimes it concerns the future, as: “Behold, the Lord will come to judgment, and all his saints with him.”

The first Fifty took its beginning from Christ and his body; the second began with Antichrist and his body [Col. 0297C]; this third begins with the misery of the whole human race and the building of Zion, and is completed in praise of inward glory.

## Prologue to Psalm 101

The labourers in the Lord’s vineyard have now been set forth in ten decades: those who laboured according to the Decalogue of the Law for the denarius of life. The Holy Spirit now enters the eleventh decade, in which the transgressors of God’s Law are especially marked: those who either refused to enter the Lord’s vineyard, as Jews and pagans did; or, having entered, were idle in it, as false Christians were; or entered and departed with scandal, as heretics did.

This psalm is one of the seven penitential psalms, in which remission through the sevenfold Spirit is indicated. It is placed fifth [Col. 0297D] because Christ’s Passion is described in it: through his five wounds humanity is redeemed from sins. The first penitential psalm is assigned to the spirit of fear; the second to the spirit of piety; the third to the spirit of knowledge; the fourth to the spirit of fortitude; this fifth to the spirit of counsel, because through Christ, the Angel of Great Counsel, the human race is delivered from death, as is narrated in this psalm.

It is fittingly placed after the psalm in which judgment is described, because through repentance a human being escapes the sentence of judgment. It fittingly concerns penitents because it declares that ashes are to be eaten as bread and drink mingled with weeping. This is the hundred and first psalm, which is ten times ten and one; and it signifies [Col. 0298A] that, to those fulfilling the ten commandments of the Law, the denarius of life is promised, which is the one God.

### On the title, subject matter, intention, and division of the psalm
