**Verse 1.—** The title of the psalm is: “A prayer of the poor man, when he has been distressed and has poured out his petition before the Lord.” That is: this is the prayer of the Lord Jesus, who, though rich in the glory of the Father, became poor for us, mortal and capable of suffering. The prayer was made when he was distressed—that is, when he grieved over the destruction of the human race—and poured out his prayer before the Lord on the Mount of Olives; when, saddened unto death, he entered agony, prayed at greater length, and his sweat ran down to the ground like blood (Luke 22).

The subject matter of the psalm is the misery of the human race and Christ’s prayer or Passion for it. Its intention is to show [Col. 0298B] that man is saved by Christ’s grace alone, and to exhort us to prayer and repentance. The words are taken from Adam, whose bone clung to flesh when God built his rib into a woman and replaced flesh for it; and they signify that the power of God, namely the Word, became flesh and clung to flesh when he built the Church from his own body.

This psalm is divided into three parts, because in it three kinds of human beings are indicated under the figure of three birds. The first part begins, “Lord, hear,” in which the prayer of the penitent is set forth. The second, “I am smitten like grass,” in which the misery of the human race is lamented. The third, “But thou, O Lord,” in which humanity’s restoration through Christ is explained. It is the voice of the human race in Christ; the misery of the entire human race is lamented here so that the judge may be moved to mercy; and the building of the heavenly Zion from living stones is sung. Since Christ is one among human beings, he speaks on behalf of all human beings. He is both judge and advocate; both mediator and reconciler of the world [Col. 0298C].

## Exposition of Psalm 101

**Verse 2.—** The human race, distressed through Christ on the Mount of Olives, prayed; through Christ on the cross it cried: “O Lord Father, hear my prayer, which I, as man, pour forth for the human race because it is distressed in misery; and let my cry come to you, that it may be delivered from misery.” Prayer is petition with a lesser degree of attention, whereas a cry has great intention of heart; hence Moses is told, “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14), although he is recorded as having said nothing. Christ prayed [Col. 0298D] for human beings on the Mount; on the cross he cried out for them.

**Verse 3.—“Do not turn your face from me.”** From me, your Son praying, as you turned it from Adam when he sinned. God’s face is knowledge of him; in paradise man in some measure saw God’s face, because he possessed a very great knowledge of him. When he sinned, God turned his face from him, because he withdrew from him the knowledge of himself. Therefore he now prays that God may restore this knowledge to those who believe in him. “In whatever day I am afflicted, incline your ear to me”: the human race prays this in Christ. From the time man fell from paradise, he has been in tribulation on all days; therefore he must call upon God in tribulation on every day, so that God may incline the ear of mercy toward him [Col. 0299A]. The comparison is with a physician bending down toward a sick person who cannot raise his voice. God inclined his ear to humanity when Christ humbled himself on the cross, unto death (Phil. 2). “In whatever day I call upon you, hear me speedily.” On the day of his Passion Christ called upon the Father for the salvation of human beings; the Father heard him speedily when he restored humanity through him. Hear me.

**Verse 4.—“For my days have failed like smoke.”** This is the voice of the human race in Christ. The days of man in paradise were eternal; in this world they became unstable like smoke. For as smoke rises high and vanishes, so human time grows from childhood into youth, then into old age, and then, turning toward death, fails. “And my bones have [Col. 0299B] dried up like *cremium*.” The bones of the soul are rationality and free choice, which were so weakened in man after sin as is *cremium*, losing its strength when its juice has been extracted in a frying-pan. Hence another reading or translation has: “They have been crushed as in a frying-pan.” Rationality dried up because it lost the perceptiveness it had before. Free choice dried up because it does not possess the facility it had before. Literally, too, bones deprived of marrow dry in the grave, just as *cremium*, stripped of its fat, dries in a frying-pan. This is so because—

**Verse 5.—“I was smitten like grass, and my heart dried up.”** “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40), whence Christ took human flesh; and therefore he was smitten like grass, that is, with sufferings as another human being. As grass is green for a time but, cut by the sickle, soon dries, so man flourishes for a short while, languishes when struck by illness, and, cut down by death, his heart dries because he loses spirit and understanding [Col. 0299C]. Why will this happen? “Because I forgot to eat my bread.” The bread of the soul is the commandment of life. God gave bread to man to eat when he set before him the commandment of life to keep. For when he said, “Observe this, lest you die” (Lev. 8), it was equivalent to saying: “Eat this bread, that you may live.” Man forgot to eat his bread when he was not solicitous to keep the Lord’s commandment. Forgetting the commandment, he touched what was forbidden; forgetting to eat bread, he drank poison. Therefore his heart was struck and dried up like grass. Christ put on this grass, turned it into bread, and restored the man smitten by the serpent and dried up by death.

[Col. 0299D]

**Verse 6.—“At the sound of my groaning, my bone clung to my flesh.”** The voice of man’s groaning was the voice of the devil, who said: “Eat, and you shall be like gods” (Gen. 3). Because he heard this voice, he incurred the groaning of pain and death. “Bone” denotes masculine strength; “flesh,” feminine weakness. At the sound of groaning, bone clung to flesh when, by the devil’s persuasion, the man consented to the woman. For Eve was made from Adam’s bone, and flesh was replaced for her. This bone clung to flesh when, expelled from paradise, he united himself with woman through concupiscence. For if they had remained in paradise, they would have begotten children without concupiscence, pain, or defilement. But because they heard the devil’s voice, they unite through concupiscence in a bestial manner [Col. 0300A]; in pain and groaning they give birth; they nourish the born with milk, as beasts nourish their young; and in pain and groaning, dying, they return to earth.

This is also the voice of Christ: “At the sound of my groaning, my bone clung to my flesh.” Christ’s bone was his divinity, which clung to flesh when the Word put on flesh because of the cry of groaning from the human race, calling to God in misery. The bone also clung to flesh when Christ joined himself to the Church.

**Verse 7.—“I became like the pelican of the wilderness.”** The pelican is a large Egyptian bird, as large as a stork, naturally always wasted by leanness, and there are two kinds of it. One always dwells in pools and feeds on fish; in Latin it is called *onocrotalus*. The other always dwells in the wilderness, and its food is poisonous animals, namely serpents, crocodiles, and lizards [Col. 0300B]. This bird is said to kill its young and mourn them for three days; on the third day it wounds itself and, by the sprinkling of its blood, restores its chicks to life. It is called the pelican “of the wilderness” to distinguish it from the one that dwells in pools.

Christ was made like this bird because he alone was born from a virgin; he ate, as it were, poisonous animals when he took sinners into his body; and he revived, as it were, slain offspring by the sprinkling of blood when he gave life through the shedding of his own blood to human beings dead in sins.

“I became like a *nycticorax* in a dwelling-place.” *Nycte* means “night,” *corax*, “raven”; *nycticorax* means “night-raven.” Some call it a toad, others an owl; it loves only darkness. Christ was made like this bird: darkened by sufferings as though a sinner, loving darkness—that is, sinners—not that they might remain darkness, but that they might become light, that is, righteous persons. A dwelling-place is where, after a house is destroyed, only the walls remain. Hence in the Hebrew it is written, “among ruins,” in which the night-raven dwells. The dwelling-place was the Jewish people, inwardly destroyed by the crowd of demons. In this dwelling-place Christ became like a *nycticorax*, because in the hearts of the Jews he was reckoned as a sinner. The *nycticorax* flies only by night, and Christ delivers sinners only through death. Or: “I became like a *nycticorax* in a dwelling-place” when I slept, troubled, in the tomb [Col. 0300C].

**Verse 8.—** Then: “I watched,” because I rose from death; “and I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof.” The sparrow separates itself from other birds and dwells on the roof of a house, or in high and secure places. The house is the world; the roof is heaven. Christ became like a solitary sparrow on the roof because he alone, God and man, dwells in heaven. In the Hebrew it is, “like a solitary bird.” Christ was the pelican of the wilderness, alone born of the Virgin and alone living without sin; the *nycticorax* in the dwelling-place, dead in the tomb; the solitary sparrow on the roof, alone God and man in heaven.

By the three kinds of birds three kinds of human beings are also signified. The pelican of the wilderness is the believing people from the Gentiles; Gentile life was like a wilderness because it was inhabited by no saint. The *nycticorax* is the people converted from the Jews, who were a dwelling-place of demons. The sparrow is the people who, from among Christians, having turned to the contemplative life, fly in mind to the roof of heaven [Col. 0301A], where, separated from worldly actions, they dwell alone.

**Verse 9.—** Before I poured out blood, like the pelican for its children, “my enemies reproached me all day”; that is, throughout the whole time of my life the Jews reproached me, calling me a carpenter’s son, demon-possessed, and a friend of tax-collectors. Or: throughout the entire day of the Passion my enemies reproached me when they mocked me all day with blows and spittle and taunted me on the cross. And those who previously praised me, saying, “We know that you are truthful” (Matt. 22; Mark 12), “swore against me” when, their council gathered, they condemned me to death. And this was because—

**Verse 10.—“I ate ashes as bread.”** That is [Col. 0301B], I incorporated sinners into myself as though they were righteous. “And I mingled my drink with weeping”: that is, I mingled good persons with those for whom there was cause to weep, and I drank sinners as though they were righteous. Therefore those reproaching him said: “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 22). The comparison is drawn from places where wine is perhaps mixed with water.

By ashes are understood sinners repenting in ashes and sackcloth. For the sinful man was told: “You are ashes, and to dust you shall go” (Gen. 3). Bread denotes those hungering for righteousness; the cup, those thirsting for life; weeping, those grieving over their sins. Christ ate ashes as bread when he joined penitents to those hungering for righteousness. He mixed his drink with weeping when he joined those grieving over sins to those thirsting for life.

Alternatively [Col. 0301C], drink is taken within and weeping comes forth without. Christ mixed his cup with weeping in his Passion when he drew the Gentiles into himself as a sweet drink and expelled the Jews outside as weeping. Literally too, he mixed his drink with weeping when the impious offered him, as he thirsted, vinegar mixed with gall.

**Verse 11.—** This happened “because of the face of your wrath and indignation,” that is, because of the presence of your vengeance and the grievous punishment which I suffered on account of Adam. Capacity for suffering and mortality, which are punishments of sin, are called the wrath and indignation of God. This wrath of God remains upon one who does not believe in Christ; through Christ God’s wrath will be removed and the immortality of the kingdom given. Because of your wrath I have suffered many punishments in the pit of misery, “because, lifting me up, you dashed me down”: that is, by free choice you raised me up; by the judgment of justice you dashed me down.

This again is the voice of the human race in Christ. God raised man above all living creatures by reason and understanding; but because, “set in honour, he did not understand,” he dashed him down into misery. For just as none of those creatures has such honour, so none has this misery. Only man, after many miseries of this life, is thrust after death into avenging punishments. Therefore the preceding words also suit the penitent, whose bones dried up like *cremium*, because through guilt he forgot to eat his bread and, at the sound of groaning, his bone clings to his flesh. That is, because through fasts and weeping his bones may be seen through his flesh, and thus through excessive thinness he has become like a pelican; through black and dirty garments signifying the blackness of sins, like a night-raven [Col. 0302A]; and through wandering alone, like a sparrow. To him, all day, enemies—that is, the unrepentant or demons—reproach him because he eats ashes as bread and mingles his drink with weeping. For he fears God’s wrath and indignation: God raised him up when he created him in his own image, but because of guilt dashed him down when he subjected him to all punishments. There follows the voice of Christ: “For this, my Father, you raised me up upon the cross and dashed me down in death.”

**Verse 12.—“My days declined like a shadow.”** That is, they became transient and unstable like a shadow. This is Christ’s own voice concerning himself and those following him; above it was the voice concerning himself and his descendants: “My days failed like smoke, and I was smitten like grass, and my heart dried up.” Days are like shadow or smoke because I lived for a short time; and I, whom you, the God of life, assumed, dried up like grass because, consumed by sufferings, I withered in death on account of the human being whom I grieved to see dry up in death like grass [Col. 0302B].

**Verse 13.—“But you, O Lord, remain for ever.”** That is, your days are always enduring, and you are able to lead us to them. “And thus your memorial shall be from generation to generation”: that is, your mercy, by which you remember them, shall be in this life and in the other—namely, in Zion and among the Gentiles. Or: your memorial shall be in the generation of the Jews and in the generation of the Gentiles.

**Verse 14.—“You, rising up, will have mercy on Zion.”** God lay, as it were, when the people of Zion worshipped idols; then he rose, as it were, when he sent them his Son, the true God. Then he had mercy on Zion when he chose the primitive Church from the Jewish people and bestowed faith and virtues upon it. In me you will rise and have mercy on Zion, because it is time to have mercy on her, because the time of grace has come in which you will have mercy on her. Of this time it is written: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4)—for what purpose? That he might redeem Zion, that is, those who were under the Law.

**Verse 15.—** Zion will be built as an inhabitable city, “because her stones were pleasing to your servants”: that is, the prophets, living stones built into Zion, were pleasing to your servant-builders, the apostles, who understood that they had foretold this building [Col. 0302D]. Through these stones preaching was promised; from them the instruction of the Gospel proceeded; through their proclamation Christ, the cornerstone, was known. “And they will have pity on her earth”: namely, the builders, who made heaven from earth. From that earth came one wall: so many thousands of believers laying the price of their possessions at the apostles’ feet. Another wall coming from the Gentiles follows.

**Verse 16.—“And the nations will fear your name, O Lord.”** You are the cornerstone, joining in yourself two walls coming from opposite directions. The nations will fear—that is, reverence—your name, which is “Lord.” Or: they will revere me, your Son, who am your name. “And all kings of the earth will fear your glory”: that is, all rulers will venerate you in your glory [Col. 0303A] and, like walls, will converge upon the cornerstone.

**Verse 17.—“For the Lord has built Zion in her powers.”** Come, living stones, see: Zion is built for construction, not for ruin; the ark is built—beware the flood. But, when Zion has been built, he who was formerly seen in his weakness will be seen in his glory. Another translation has “in his majesty,” that is, in the power of divinity. And for what reason did he build this house?

**Verse 18.—“Because he looked upon the prayer of the humble.”** Patriarchs, prophets, and ancient fathers humbly asked God to rebuild in the world the house built in paradise and destroyed by the devil, and to restore in heaven the fallen city ruined through him. God therefore looked upon the prayer of the humble when he sent his Son into the world, who joined the faithful people together in one Church [Col. 0303B]. “And he did not despise their prayer,” because he fulfilled their desire by promising human beings equality with angels.

**Verse 19.—“Let these things be written for another generation.”** Namely, let these benefits—prayer, Passion, remission, building, and hearing—be kept in memory in the other generation; this generation, made another when it was formerly lost, and built into the house of God, should always have these things before its eyes. “And the people who shall be created will praise the Lord”: that is, the Christian people, dead in sins and newly created in virtues, changed from idolatry into another worship, will praise the Lord for the benefits mentioned above.

**Verse 20.—“For he looked down from his holy height.”** That is [Col. 0303C], through me, holy in body and lofty in divinity, he looked upon the misery of humankind. “The Lord looked from heaven upon the earth”: that is, through me, heaven looked mercifully upon earthly persons.

**Verse 21.—“That he might hear the groaning of those in fetters.”** That is, that he might free those who groan from the bonds of sins; “that he might loose the sons of those who have been slain from sins,” that is, the Gentiles, imitators of the slain—namely Adam and Eve—who were the destroyers of the whole human race. The groaning fettered people were the Jews; the children of those who had been slain were the pagans. In the Hebrew it is written, “sons of death,” that he might loose the sons of the devil from sins.

**Verse 22.—“That they may declare the name of the Lord in Zion,”** that is, in the Church, “and his praise” at last in the heavenly Jerusalem.

[Col. 0303D]

**Verse 23.—“When the peoples and kings are gathered together as one.”** That is, they declare this name of the Lord in Zion so that peoples and kings may come together into the unity of faith, in order to serve the Lord.

**Verse 24.—“He answered him in the way of his strength.”** That is, the gathering of peoples and kings in Zion answers the Lord Father in the way of his strength, namely by the imitation of his Son, who is the way of his strength. The Word, the power of God, entered to human beings through Jesus Christ and, by this way, brought those who had strayed back to life.

Alternatively: Jerusalem, or her praise—that is, the Church, called from the whole world—answered Christ in the way of his strength, because, like Christ, she too walked in virtues. Her voice follows here: “Make known to me the shortness of my days.” That is: the Church, established in the way of strength [Col. 0304A], answered, saying: “Show me when these few days will end, when the consummation of the age will come, and when the eternal years will arrive.” And it is said to her: “The Gospel will be preached among all nations, and then the end will come” (Matt. 24).

Literally, too, the Lord answered Jerusalem in the way of strength when he approached his Passion and the people received him with palms; when he heard the people’s song in it, he answered them and declared to her the shortness of her days, saying: “The day will come when your enemies will surround you, cast you and your children who are in you to the ground, and will not leave in you one stone upon another” (Luke 19).

What follows to the end of the psalm is the speech of the other generation and of the newly created people, freed from fetters, who gathers in Zion and sings praise concerning eternity.

**VERSE 25.**—“Do not call me back in the middle of my days,” that is, do not withdraw me from your years, I who am set in the middle of my days. Two parts taken together are each one half, although one is greater and the other smaller: thus, if one day were compared with a hundred years, the eternal years are one half, and the days of this life are the other half. In one half—that is, the temporal half—man is; in the other—that is, the eternal half—God is. Therefore it follows: “Your years are from generation to generation,” that is, from the present age into the future one.

Alternatively: From my temporal half—that is, from the fewness of my days—do not call me back as I stretch toward your half, falling back through abandonment [Col. 0304C] into error; rather, draw me as I strive toward eternity with your help.

Alternatively: When half my course has been completed, do not call me out of the world uncorrected and imperfect; but allow me to live out the entire time that you have appointed, as you did for Hezekiah, so that, corrected from my former state and made perfect in good actions, I may attain, as a perfect man, to your years, which are eternal.

**VERSE 26.**—“In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.” This is drawn from the new creation of the world, where it is written: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). The Beginning is Christ, in whom God made heaven, earth, and all things; as it is written: “All things were made through him” (John 1). And just as there was then a beginning of the world, so here there was a beginning of the new creation—that is, of the Church. In this beginning, you, God the Father, founded the earth when you established the Church in Christ. “And the heavens are the works of your hands,” that is, the apostles formed through the working of the Holy Spirit.

**VERSE 27.**—“They themselves shall perish,” because they will die according to the body; the visible heavens also shall perish, because “heaven and earth shall pass away” (Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 21). But you remain always in one state. Since it is said here, “The heavens shall perish,” it is asked how that Scripture can say, “The earth stands forever” (Eccles. 1), and again, “Every creature of God remains forever.” One should know that the form of things will perish, while their substance itself will remain forever. “And all shall grow old like a garment”: the heavens are like the garment [Col. 0305A] of the world; they age and fail through oldness in the form in which they now are.

**VERSE 28.**—“And like a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed.” Heaven is the covering of the earth; it is rolled up like a tent. But once judgment has been completed, the heavens will be changed into another form, because the Lord will then make a new heaven and a new earth; and the moon will have the glory of the sun, and the sun the light of seven days.

The bodies of the saints are the garments of the soul. Therefore all the saints “shall grow old like a garment,” that is, all bodies will first fail through old age and finally through dissolution, being compared to a garment worn away until it is reduced to nothing. Bodies are likewise the covering of souls, in which souls, being covered, are not seen. Afterwards you will change them from this dissolution [Col. 0305B] like a covering: namely, bodies that had formerly belonged to souls, into the glory of the sun, and souls into equality with angels. Thus the heavens—that is, the saints—will be changed.

But you are the very same as you were when you made the world from nothing; you have not grown old; you are first before all things and last after all things, because you are ever new. “And your years shall not fail,” that is, your eternity remains forever. You are unchangeable and invariable because eternal; and those whom you made heavens out of earth, you will make eternal.

**VERSE 29.**—“The children of your servants shall dwell,” that is, Christians, the children of the apostles whom they begot through the Gospel, shall possess those unfailing years of yours, dwelling in the everlasting kingdom, where there is eternal joy [Col. 0305C] and security that will never end. “And their seed shall be directed for ever,” that is, other Christians, begotten from them, shall be directed into eternity.

Alternatively: Your years are eternal, and in those years “the children of your servants shall dwell”; that is, your servants shall possess those years through children—that is, through good works—and “their seed shall be directed for ever,” that is, the tears they sow beforehand they shall reap in joy.

See what the Son of God accomplished by praying, when he led the human race to eternity!

## PROLOGUE TO PSALM 150

The subject matter of this final psalm is the marriage-feast of the Lamb. For after the King has held judgment with his people, he will bring his bride, coming to him from Babylon, into the new Jerusalem [Col. 0305D] with the whole multitude of angels and saints. In this procession trumpets resound; at the wedding organs ring out. This psalm treats of this. Its purpose is to urge us to hasten to that feast.

Its words refer to the aforesaid prophets, who exhorted the people returned from captivity to celebrate the feast in the rebuilt Temple of Jerusalem. It likewise exhorts us, returned from the captivity of the devil and vices, to praise God with renewed life, so that, when our final captivity has been loosed, we may celebrate that feast with the saints in the new Jerusalem. Its title is *Alleluia*, that is, “Praise the Lord,” you who have also come to the Bridegroom’s banquet. This psalm is the one hundred fiftieth: by one hundred perfection is expressed, by fifty the exultation of jubilee. This number signifies [Col. 0306A] that those perfected in holiness shall be in eternal jubilation. This psalm is uniform, because unity of mind, language, and praise will always be among the saints. It is the voice of the Holy Spirit.

## Exposition of Psalm 150

**VERSE 1.**—O you elect, who have gone out to meet the bridegroom and bride with lamps alight, “praise the Lord in his saints”: that is, praise him in consideration of how he sanctified you and made you equal to the holy angels. “Praise him in the firmament of his power”: the firmament of power is the confirmation of the saints after the resurrection, when the saints will be so established in power that they will no longer wish to sin, just as the confirmed angels did not wish to fall. For this reason praise the Lord, because you have now been so established in power by him that, like [Col. 0306B] angels, you no longer desire to sin.

**VERSE 2.**—“Praise him in his powers,” that is, praise him for the diverse powers bestowed on you by him, through which you have now come to heavenly things. Another translation has: “Praise him in his dominions,” that is, praise him because he has made you powers, together with the angelic Virtues and Powers, all enemies having been placed beneath your feet. “Praise him according to the multitude of his greatness,” that is, praise him in view of the multitude of his greatness, by which he has magnified you in heaven and crowned many thousands of thousands, on account of their many riches, with glory and honor.

“Praise him with the sound of the trumpet”: the trumpet signifies victory, because when war is ended and enemies put to flight, victors customarily [Col. 0306C] sound the trumpet. Therefore praise him for the victory by which you conquered the devil and, having subdued the enemies of soul and body, entered the heavenly citadel as victors. The sound of the trumpet is also the most excellent charity of praise which they will sound with the angels. The trumpet likewise signifies preaching. Thus in the Apocalypse seven angels are said to have sounded the trumpet (Rev. 8), signifying that saints have preached in the world at every time. Or the trumpet suggests a royal reception; hence we read that angels sound the trumpet when they announce the coming of the eternal King. Praise the Lord—you who were “in the sound of the trumpet,” that is, in preaching—because you preached the Lord in the world and foretold the advent of the supreme King.

“Praise him with psaltery and [Col. 0306D] harp.” The psaltery, which sounds from above, signifies the soul; the harp, which sounds from below, signifies the body. Praise the Lord because he has glorified you in soul and body. The psaltery also expresses the contemplative life, and the harp the active life. Praise the Lord because you lived in the contemplative and active life, for which you have received eternal rewards. Or by the psaltery heavenly things, and by the harp earthly things, are understood: that is, praise God in contemplation of the higher and lower creation.

**VERSE 4.**—“Praise him with drum and choir.” A drum is made from dried and stretched skin, signifying flesh made unchangeable and strengthened against every corruption. Praise God for this: that he has changed your flesh, formerly fragile, with such firmness [Col. 0307A] that it will henceforth be subject to no corruption. A choir is the harmonious concord of singers and signifies the fellowship of angels and human beings praising God in united rejoicing. Praise the Lord because you have entered this choir and have been joined to these singers.

“Praise him with strings and organ.” Strings are animal entrails, dried and thinned, that sound sweetly; they signify the inward thoughts of the righteous, dried by vigils and fasts, refined by holy meditation, and sounding the sweetest melody of a pure conscience. The organ, having various pipes sounding together in harmonious modulation, signifies the diverse deeds of saints, not discordant through their united love. Praise the Lord with strings, that is, for holy thoughts that, like strings, sound sweetly. [Col. 0307B] Praise the Lord with the organ, that is, for good deeds that, like organs, ring out pleasantly.

**VERSE 5.**—“Praise him with well-sounding cymbals.” Cymbals shine and sound after they have been cast in fire. They signify the bodies of saints which, after passing through the fire of tribulation, will shine like the sun and sound forth God’s eternal praise. In these cymbals—that is, in these glorified bodies of saints—praise the Lord; and with cymbals of jubilation, that is, in justified souls. For jubilation is the inexpressible praise of God uttered only by the soul. And what more need I say?

**VERSE 6.**—“Let every spirit praise the Lord.” That is: all angels who are spirits, and all human beings made spiritual, praise the Lord, because [Col. 0307C] he has prepared such a banquet for you. Or: Let every spirit be for you material for praising God: the spirit of angels, whom he has established in charity; the spirit of human beings, whom in glory he has made equal to angels; the spirit of demons, whom he has subjected to the saints; the spirit of the wicked, whom he has justly consigned to punishments. Likewise, at this time let the spirit of living creatures be material for praising the Lord, creatures to whom he has given life in so many diverse bodies—of birds, fish, and beasts.

It should be noted that music is made in three ways: by voice, breath, and striking. By voice, through the throat and windpipe of the singing person; by breath, through pipes; by striking, through harps. These three kinds resound at this marriage-feast: voice in the choir, breath in the trumpet, and striking in the harp. They signify mind, spirit, [Col. 0307D] and body, which celebrate the Trinity forever in praise.

Moreover, through the different musical instruments are expressed the diverse orders of those praising God in the Church. The saints are priests living chastely, who offer the body and blood of Christ in sacrifice. The Power of God are those through whom he works miracles, such as Martin and Benedict. His Dominions are those through whom he restrains demons and vices, such as prelates. His multitude are the faithful, such as subjects. The trumpets are preachers; the psaltery, those who perform spiritual works, such as monks; the harp, those who discipline themselves, such as hermits and recluses. The drum is those dead to vices, such as martyrs; the choir, those living harmoniously in common life, such as regular canons. The strings are those worn down by fasts, such as penitents; the organ, those harmonious in preaching and [Col. 0308A] action, such as confessors. The cymbals are those leaping for joy because of mercy and love, such as the remaining faithful. With these musical vessels every spirit—that is, every spiritual person—praises the Lord. Such instruments shall resound the eternal *Alleluia* at the marriage-feast of the Lamb. Therefore we regularly use these three psalms at daily Lauds, so that we may be able to sing praises with the angels in the new Jerusalem.

## Epilogue of the Psalter

For the benefit of all readers, let us conclude the sum of the whole work in a brief epilogue. God is the Father of Christ; the body of Christ is the Church; the nourisher of the Church is the Holy Spirit, whose nourishment is sacred Scripture. Through it the Church grows in its members into a perfect man, until it comes to the bridal chamber of its bridegroom. [Col. 0308B] The Psalter, moreover, is like a cellar from which diverse dishes and many kinds of drink are brought forth for the bride’s banquet.

In the first decade, the infancy of the Church is nourished as though with milk, while it is restrained from the way of sinners and taught to meditate on the law of the Lord. In return for this obedience, the blessedness lost through Adam is promised to be restored through Christ. This blessed Man, appointed King by the Father, slept in death for our sake and rose again; he established in peace, in one and the same place, the children of men drawn forth from the lower world. There those who labored in groaning shall rejoice forever. Having ascended on high, crowned as Judge with glory and honor, he shall reign forever in his holy temple.

In the second decade, the utterances of the Lord, tested in the fire of the Holy Spirit, form the childhood of the Church in truth. Truth enlightens the eyes of its heart, so that it may know the Lord to be among the righteous generation; that those entering his tabernacle without blemish are fulfilled with joy at the sight of the Lord and satisfied with good things when his glory appears; and that it may love the Lord who bowed down the heavens and descended, cleansing it from the gravest sin and becoming helper and redeemer to the wretched. The Lord remembered this sacrifice when he placed a crown of precious stone upon his head.

In the third decade, the adolescence of the Church is instructed by Christ’s example in patience, because he became the reproach of human beings, though his kingdom shall rule over the nations. In a place of pasture, where nothing shall be lacking, he will set the one who is innocent in hands and clean in heart. His soul shall abide in good things who does not disdain to wash his hands among the innocent. He shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, when his flesh blooms anew in the resurrection, when the Lord blesses his people in peace, when he changes mourning into joy in the great abundance of his sweetness which he has accomplished for those who fear him.

In the fourth decade, the youth of the Church is constrained to repentance by bit and bridle, so that its soul may be rescued from death, because the death of sinners is most evil; the Angel of the Lord, pursuing them, will confine them in Tartarus. Those who work iniquity are expelled by God, and the unrighteous shall perish. But he will rescue the afflicted and humbled from all iniquities, and the Lord will put [Col. 0309A] a new song into its mouth; in the evil day he will deliver it and make it blessed in the land of the living.

In the fifth decade, the youth of the Church, instructed by scourges and victorious through constancy against adversities, longs for God, the fountain of life, who makes its youth glad. For his sake it is put to death all day long, like a sheep for slaughter, so that it may be brought with joy and exultation into the temple of the King, where it may be free from occupation and behold God. There the princes of the peoples are gathered in the city of the Lord of hosts. Then the righteous shall rule in the morning over the wicked, and God’s salvation shall be shown to them, when the walls of Jerusalem, fallen in the angels, are rebuilt through human beings.

In the sixth decade, the manhood of the Church is now fed with solid [Col. 0309B] bread, while it is strengthened for battle against vices. Hence, soon fervent in good pursuits, it becomes like a fruitful olive tree and becomes intelligent, or one seeking God, who helps it against evils. It sacrifices willingly to him, takes wings like a dove and flies to rest, so that it may please God in the light of the living, who will rescue its soul from the midst of the lion cubs when the Lord breaks the jaws of the lions. Therefore it will sing of God’s strength in the morning, when, leading it out of tribulation into a fortified city, he gives an inheritance to those who fear his name.

In the seventh decade, manhood, refreshed by solid food, is admonished to despise the world. Therefore its children do not wish to covet plunder or set their hearts on abounding riches, but wish to bless God in [Col. 0309C] their life. They proclaim the works of God and desire to be filled with the good things of his house. They pass through fire and water into refreshment. They ask that the Lord may cause his face to shine upon them, so that they may feast with the righteous in God’s presence, when he becomes wonderful in his saints, when he saves Zion, in which those who love his name shall dwell; when all who seek and love him rejoice and are glad in God; when their mouth is filled with praise, so that they may sing a hymn to God throughout all eternity.

In the eighth decade, the mature age of the Church is made drunk with the drink of knowledge, so that it may serve the Son of the King, who alone performs great wonders and to whom alone it is good to cling. He has worked salvation in the midst of the earth. Breaking the horns [Col. 0309D] of sinners, he will exalt the horns of the righteous in peace, in which his place has been made. He led his people by the hand of Moses and Aaron; he fed them with the bread of angels. He avenged the blood of his own, repaying their neighbors sevenfold. He planted a vineyard from his chosen ones, fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock, etc.

In the ninth decade, the same mature age of the Church is gladdened by the cup of wisdom, when human beings are called gods and sons of the Most High by God, and by them he alone is preached as Most High over all the earth. To reach him, the blessed arrange ascents in their hearts from the valley of tears, so that glory may dwell in their land. He rescues their souls from the lowest hell and establishes them in the glorious city in which is the dwelling of all who rejoice [Col. 0310A]—the city in which that man who was free among the dead, wounded, sleeping in the tomb, placed in the lower pit, is great and terrible above all who are around him; where, filled in the morning with God’s mercy, they shall rejoice and delight throughout all the days—those whom he rescued from tribulation, glorified, filled with length of days, and to whom he showed his salvation face to face.

In the tenth decade, the old age of the Church, intoxicated, pours forth teaching for others. In fruitful old age it flourishes in virtues like a palm tree and multiplies in works like a cedar of Lebanon. It is the seat of God, prepared against sea and rivers, trained in knowledge and taught from the law of God. Therefore it invites the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand to rejoice to him in psalms and sing [Col. 0310B] a new song to him, because he delivered them from the hand of the sinner and revealed his righteousness to the nations. For he is great above all peoples; he will lead those serving him in gladness into exultation, and in judgment he will destroy from his city all workers of iniquity.

In the eleventh decade, the same age of the Church is urged to prayer, so that its seed may be directed forever, its youth renewed like that of an eagle, and itself restored through the Spirit of God sent forth; so that it may always seek the face of the Lord, do judgment and justice at every time, understand the mercies of the Lord, have a heart prepared for his commandments, and praise him in the midst of many. He is the Beginning, begotten from the Father, sent forth amid the splendors of the saints, the redemption [Col. 0310C] of peoples through the New Testament.

In the twelfth decade, the old age of the Church is taught by the fear of the saints, followed by glory and riches in everlasting remembrance. The Lord, having once made it barren, has made it dwell in his house as a joyful mother of children; he blessed its children, little and great alike. It shall please the Lord in the land of the living; it shall sacrifice an offering of praise in the midst of Jerusalem, where all nations and all peoples praise God. Entering through the gates of righteousness, they walk blamelessly in the way of the law of the Lord, so that they may come from their sojourning in the world and from the inhabitants of Kedar to the mountains, where, by God’s help, they may be guarded from every evil.

In the thirteenth decade, the same age of the Church is taught to ascend from the tumult of the world by the steps of virtues to [Col. 0310D] the peace of Jerusalem. It is built as a city by tribes and thrones. There servants and maidservants lift their eyes to the Lord dwelling in heaven, so that by his help they may cross intolerable water and come to those who dwell in Jerusalem, where there is peace upon Israel, filled with joy and exultation. There, after the sleep of death, the inheritance of the Lord is given to the chosen children: the reward, the fruit of Mary’s womb. There they shall see the good things of Jerusalem throughout all the days of eternal life, and the blessing of the Lord shall be upon those whom he redeemed from all iniquities, and for whom God himself will be the recompense in their soul.

In the fourteenth decade, the decrepit age of the Church is gently drawn to meekness. He has chosen it for his dwelling and rest, and there brothers dwelling [Col. 0311A] together bless God in the nights: he dwells in Jerusalem, his mercy is forever, and those returning from Babylon sing to him a hymn from the songs of Zion in the presence of angels, their days established in the eternal way, where the upright shall dwell with the face of God, having become an evening sacrifice.

In the fifteenth decade, the same age of the Church is persuaded to persevere in confession. The righteous await it until the Lord repays them, when he brings its soul out of tribulation. After war it will sing a new song. The saints will bless him as exceedingly praiseworthy when he gives judgment to those suffering injury, when he completes Jerusalem by building it and, blessing its children, satisfies them with the fat of wheat. In that new Jerusalem there will be a hymn for all saints [Col. 0311B] when they rejoice in their dwellings, when, judgment completed, the King-bridegroom brings the queen-bride into the new Jerusalem. Angels shall sound trumpets as for a king, [Col. 0312A] and all saints shall forever rejoice with organs and cymbals as for a Bridegroom.

Because we have reached the long-desired harbor with a favorable course, it is time, having lowered the sail, to give thanks to our helmsman, the giver of all good things.

*Here ends.*

Having completed the Psalter, the same Honorius also expounded the Canticles sung every day at Lauds, namely the canticles *Benedictus*, *Magnificat*, and *Nunc dimittis*, the Lord’s Prayer, and the Apostles’ Creed. He concludes this entire work at last with these words:

> The work which we undertook concerning the Psalter or the Canticles we have brought, by God’s help, to the finishing touch. But I ask all children of the Church who are to read this work to give thanks with me to Christ for this labor and to pour out prayers to the merciful Forgiver for [Col. 0312B] my failings. And let them know that in this work nothing is mine except the labor alone; the opinions are those of the saints.

[Col. 0311]

# QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS ON THE TWO BOOKS OF SOLOMON: PROVERBS AND ECCLESIASTES

(*Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, Lyons edition, XX, 1140.) (C, G)*

## PREFACE

By how many names was Solomon called? By three, as the Holy Scriptures most plainly teach: Solomon, Jedidiah, and Ecclesiastes.

Why was he called by these three names? He was called Solomon, that is, “peaceful,” because there was peace in his kingdom. He was called Jedidiah, that is, “beloved of the Lord,” because the Lord loved him.

In what language is the name *Ecclesiastes* spoken? In Greek, for in Hebrew he is called *celeth* [*coheleth*, or *coeleth*].

What do *Qoheleth* and *Ecclesiastes* mean in Latin? Ecclesiastes is called the one who gathers together the assembly of the Church. Hence in Latin he is rightly called a *concionator*, a public speaker, because he addresses an assembly—that is, speaks to the people—and his discourse is directed not particularly to one person but generally to all. Therefore in the holy Church the public speaker may rightly be called a preacher.

How many books did Solomon produce? Only three, corresponding to the number of his names: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs.

What does Solomon say in Proverbs? Or what does he teach in Ecclesiastes or in the Song of Songs? In Proverbs he teaches the little child and instructs him, as though a son, through varied sayings. In Ecclesiastes, however, he instructs a man now of mature age, so that he may understand that in the things of this world nothing is lasting, nothing glorious or great, but that all things we see are brief, perishable, and vain. In the Song of Songs he joins the man now made perfect and adorned with every various virtue to the embraces of the bridegroom, our Lord Jesus.

Whom, in particular, do this Solomon, Jedidiah, and Ecclesiastes signify? Our Lord Jesus Christ, who is our Solomon—that is, the one making all things peaceful through his blood—who “made both one” (Eph. 2:14): that is, from two peoples he constructed one Church. Hence the Apostle says: “Christ is our peace, who made both one” (ibid.). He is Jedidiah, that is, the beloved Son of the Father, of whom the Father himself says to his disciples: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). He is likewise Ecclesiastes, that is, our preacher, who gathered together the assembly—that is, the holy Church from the whole world—to which he speaks, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). He is the son of David, to whom the blind men cried in the Gospel, saying: “Have mercy on us, son of David” (Matt. 9:27). He is also our king—not of the earthly Jerusalem, but of that heavenly Jerusalem which is the mother of us all.

# ON PROVERBS

[Col. 0313]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0313A]

What does Solomon mean when he says (v. 17): “The net is spread in vain before the eyes of the winged”? Are birds not often caught in nets? Certainly they are. Who, then, are these winged ones?

They are the saints and elect of God, who have the wings of faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues. They also have spiritual eyes, by which they both guard against the snares of the ancient enemy and foresee sins. Therefore the net is spread in vain—that is, to no purpose—before the eyes of the winged: the snare of the devil’s wiles is set before holy and elect persons, because those whose manner of life is in heaven can easily overcome the devil’s snares on earth.

What is the wisdom of which Solomon says [Col. 0313B] (v. 20): “Wisdom preaches outside; in the streets she gives her voice”?

It is Christ Jesus, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 1:24). How, then, did this wisdom preach outside? Before his passion, he preached inside—that is, in secret—because he showed the mysteries of his divinity to few people, namely, to the disciples alone. But after his resurrection he preached outside, because, after the Holy Spirit had been sent from above, he openly proclaimed through the apostles to the world that he was the Son of God.

How did he give his voice in the streets? He who had formerly preached in secrecy, in hiddenness, and among the one people of the Jews, afterwards preached openly through the apostles in the broad expanse of peoples and among crowds of nations, according to what he commanded them, saying: “What I say to you in darkness,” that is, in secret, “say in the light,” that is, openly; “and what you have heard in the ear,” that is, in private, “preach upon the housetops” [Col. 0313C] (Matt. 10:27), that is, openly and before people.

How should one understand what he says (v. 21): “At the doors of the gates of the city she utters her words”?

The city signifies the holy Church, gathered from both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles. The doors of this city’s gates were the holy teachers, who introduced believers into it by preaching the word of the Gospel. Therefore Wisdom preached her word at the doors of the gates when Christ was speaking in his apostles.

## CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0313D]

What does he mean when he says (v. 2): “Incline your heart to know prudence”? How can a person incline his heart?

He inclines his heart to know prudence who humbles himself and corrects his soul from [Col. 0314A] sins, so that he may become worthy to receive the mysteries of divinity.

## CHAPTER THREE

What does this mean (v. 5): “Do not lean upon your own wisdom”? For who leans upon his own wisdom?

The person who trusts that by his own wisdom or his own powers he can fulfill the divine commandments.

Again he says (v. 7): “Do not be wise in your own sight.” Who is wise in his own sight?

Certainly the person who exalts himself above others as though more learned and boasts of what he has been able rightly to know and understand from the sayings of the Fathers.

What is true wisdom?

To fear the Lord and depart from evil.

How do you know that this is true human wisdom?

[Col. 0314B] Because it is written in the book of Job: “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil, understanding” (Job 28:28).

Who is the man of whom Solomon says (v. 13): “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom”?

He who receives the teaching of truth—that is, of the Gospel—with the ear both of body and heart, and seeks in the sacred Scriptures to know the will of the Lord.

When does prudence abound (ibid.)?

When one hears the divine commandments with great love and delight of heart, and endeavors to fulfill them in deed.

What does he mean when he says (v. 17): “Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths peaceful”? What are these paths or these ways of hers?

The ways of wisdom are the actions of the Lord which he performed in the flesh, or his teachings contained in the books of the Gospels. These ways are beautiful because they are divine. The paths of wisdom are the Lord’s commands and precepts; these paths are rightly called peaceful because all the Lord’s precepts lead to eternal peace.

Of what law or counsel does Solomon speak when he says (v. 21): “Keep my law and my counsel”?

He speaks of the law and counsel of the wisdom of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is the law of wisdom, which says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments,” that is, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal” (Matt. 19: [Col. 0314D] 17), etc.

What does he mean when he says (v. 32): “Every mocker is an abomination to the Lord”? Who is a mocker?

The person who despises to fulfill the words of God which he knows. A heretic is a mocker, corrupting the words of God by understanding and teaching them perversely. Also a mocker is one who despises the great promises of God as though they were small, and scorns the punishment of eternal condemnation as though it were tolerable. Again, a mocker is one who contemptuously insults his simple and poor neighbors. The Lord abominates all such people, and “his speech is with the simple” (v. 32), because heavenly wisdom enlightens by grace those who have no duplicity within themselves.

## CHAPTER FOUR

Why does Solomon say (v. 3): “I too was my father’s tender son, and only-begotten before my mother”? How was he only-begotten before his mother, since a brother born of the same mother preceded him, as the Scripture of the Book of Kings testifies?

It is true that his brother preceded him; but that brother, as soon as [Col. 0315B] he was born, departed this life without a name, as though he had never existed. Therefore Solomon calls himself only-begotten.

## CHAPTER FIVE

What does he mean when he says (v. 9): “Do not give your honor to strangers, nor your years to the cruel one”? Of what honor does he speak, and whom does he call strangers?

Of this: “Man was made in the image of God” (Gen. 1:27). He calls demons strangers, and the meaning is: Do not, by living badly, subject your honor—that you were created in God’s image—to unclean spirits.

Whom does he call cruel, and of what years does he speak?

He calls the spans of life “years,” and the devil “the cruel one.” The meaning is: Do not, by living badly, hand over to the devil the span of life which God gave you.

Of what cistern does Solomon speak, or of what flowing waters from a well, when he says (v. 15): “Drink water from your own cistern and streams from your well”?

He calls the Catholic teaching—that is, the teaching of the Old and New Testaments—the cistern; the well, the depth and height of that same Catholic teaching; water, knowledge; and streams, the abundance and plenty of knowledge, the various meanings of sacred Scripture. By these words he teaches us to beware the teaching of heretics and to attend to the reading of sacred Scripture. The meaning is: “Drink water from your own cistern”: keep and fulfill in deed the teaching that you preach to others; and let the streams of your well—that is, the abundance of your discourse or knowledge—flow forth richly [Col. 0315D] in you in good works.

Why does Solomon say, “Let your fountains be poured forth abroad, and divide your waters in the streets” (v. 16), when he immediately adds, “Have them for yourself alone, and let no strangers share them” (v. 17)? If we pour our fountains abroad and divide our waters in the streets, how can we possess them alone?

Although there seems to be a contradiction in the words, there is none, because these statements can be understood only spiritually. We pour forth our fountains when we pour into others the force of preaching, when we proclaim the words of sacred Scripture. We divide waters in the streets when we preach to peoples. For *platea*, “street,” is named from breadth, and it is a Greek word. Therefore we divide waters in the streets when, among a multitude [Col. 0316A] of hearers, we spread abroad words of knowledge and distribute the divine utterances according to each person’s capacity. If we ought to divide waters in the streets, how, then, ought we to have alone the waters that we distribute in the streets? When we preach divine words to others, we nevertheless possess the waters alone because we seek no human praise from that preaching.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

What does Solomon mean when he says of his law (v. 3): “Bind it on your fingers; write it on the tablets of your heart”? Who can bind the law on his fingers? Or, if he did so, what use would it be?

“On the fingers” means in actions. Whoever fulfills and adorns the law by good works binds it on his fingers; “on the tablets of the heart” means in the breadth of thought. Therefore the person who receives the law with joy and commits it to memory writes it on the tablets of his heart.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

What does Wisdom mean when she says (v. 30): “I delighted day by day, playing before him”—that is, before the almighty Father—“at all times, playing in the world”? Did Wisdom—that is, the Son of God—play childishly before the Father?

By no means! But what does he mean when he says, “playing”? That is, rejoicing. For he played every day, that is, he rejoiced that he was one, namely of one substance with the Father from the beginning, from the days of eternity.

How did he play at all times in the inhabited world?

Because when the time of the world and its creatures began to exist, [Col. 0316C] the Son himself rejoiced, because he remained what he had always been in the Father.

## CHAPTER IX

What does he mean when he says (v. 1), “Wisdom built herself a house”?

Because Wisdom built herself a house. Wisdom—that is, the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ—built herself a house because he himself created in the Virgin’s womb the man whom he assumed into the unity of his person.

How did she “hew out seven pillars” (ibid.)?

She hewed out seven pillars because, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, she raised up Churches throughout the world; like pillars, they uphold and preserve [Col. 0316D] the remembrance of his name, that is, the mystery of his incarnation. It can also be understood otherwise: the house of Wisdom is Christ’s Church, while the pillars of this house are the holy teachers. These pillars are rightly said to be seven, because the holy teachers are filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. How, then, did Wisdom hew out these pillars? She hewed out the pillars because she separated the minds of preachers from love of the present age and raised them up to bear the structure of that same Church.

Of what maidservants does Solomon speak when he says (v. 3), “She sent out her maidservants to summon people to the citadel and to the city’s walls”?

By maidservants he means the holy apostles. Why does he call them maidservants? Because of their lack of learning, weakness, and poverty: [Col. 0317A] he chose as apostles unlearned, weak, poor, and despised men, whom he sent into the world to preach, so that they might call the faithful peoples to the citadel of eternal blessedness and to the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER X

Who is the wise son (v. 1) who gladdens his father? Or who is the foolish son who is grief to his mother?

The person who properly keeps the mysteries of faith and baptism that he has received, and fulfils them in deed, is a wise son; such a one undoubtedly gladdens God the Father. But the one who corrupts the mysteries of faith and baptism he has received by evil works or heretical perversity is a foolish son; he is indeed grief to his mother, namely the holy [Col. 0317B] Church, because he causes her sorrow.

What does Solomon mean when he says (v. 10), “The fool will be beaten with lips”? How can a foolish person be beaten with lips?

“Beating” here signifies condemnation. Therefore the fool will be beaten with lips because he will be condemned for the wicked and evil words he has spoken. Hence it is also said elsewhere: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21), because each person will either be justified by his words or condemned by his words (Matt. 12:37). Why is the tongue said to have hands, when it cannot have hands? This is said metaphorically, that is, by transference, just as winds are said to have wings. For the hands of the tongue are the words themselves, by which, in speaking well, it merits [Col. 0317C] life, or, in speaking badly, merits death. Alternatively: in Holy Scripture hands often signify works, as in: “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands” (Ps. 127:2). He says, “in the hands of the tongue,” that is, in its works. For the works of the tongue are good or evil conversations, from which death or life is born.

Who is this sluggard of whom Solomon says (v. 26), “As vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who sent him”?

The sluggard is the Catholic who lives badly, who neither labours nor works so as to deserve to attain eternal blessedness. By vinegar and smoke is signified the faithlessness of heretics; by eyes and teeth, the preachers [Col. 0317D] of the holy Church. They are rightly called eyes because they foresee the right paths; and fittingly also teeth, because they are accustomed to provide spiritual food to the faithful. Therefore, as vinegar is to teeth and smoke to eyes—that is, as the faithlessness of heretics is opposed to good teachers, because it grieves them and produces trouble and tears—so the sluggard, that is, the bad Catholic, is burdensome to those same good teachers who sent him, that is, who commanded him to fulfil his faith by works. He is burdensome because he destroys faith by depraved works.

## CHAPTER XI

What does he mean when he says (v. 21), “Hand in hand, the wicked will not be innocent”? How can an evil person be hand in hand, and therefore not be innocent?

[Col. 0318A] One who joins hand to hand does nothing. Therefore, so long as the wicked are hand in hand, they will not be innocent; for even if for a time they withdraw their hands from evil work, nevertheless, as long as they remain wicked, they cannot possess innocence of heart. Hence it has already been said: “A perverse heart is an abomination to the Lord” (Prov. 11:20).

How should one understand what he says (v. 22): “A gold ring in its snout: a beautiful and foolish woman”?

That is: if you fasten a gold ring in a pig’s snout, then, while it goes about turning and digging the earth with its nose, it plunges the gold ring into a wallow of mud; and then the gold ring loses the beauty it had. Likewise, therefore, a foolish woman, if she possesses beauty of face or receives ornaments of earrings, necklaces, [Col. 0318B] and garments, defiles the beauty of her face and loses her adornment if she loves to contaminate herself with the mire of lust and to be corrupted by adulteries.

But how is this saying to be understood spiritually? Whoever meditates attentively on the Holy Scriptures and constantly searches the divine utterances receives the adornment of knowledge. If he corrupts this by living badly and destroys what he understands, he has a gold ring in his snout; but, like a pig, by digging in the earth he defiles it and plunges it into mud, because he has sullied by unclean action the adornment through which he received knowledge of the Scriptures. Such a soul is a beautiful and foolish woman: beautiful indeed through knowledge, but, given over to carnal pleasures, foolish in action.

What does he mean when he says (v. 25), “The soul that blesses [Col. 0318C] will be made fat; and she [quae; variant qui, ‘he’] who makes drunk will herself [ipsa; variant ipse, ‘himself’] also be made drunk”?

There are many who make others drunk but are not themselves made drunk. He does not speak here of bodily drunkenness, but of spiritual drunkenness. Therefore, the soul that blesses will be made fat, because whoever blesses outwardly by preaching receives spiritual richness—that is, he is enlarged and increased by spiritual grace. Likewise, the person who strives by sacred speech to make the minds of his subjects drunk will himself be made drunk, because he is filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Why did he not say “the person,” but “the soul that blesses will be made fat”?

In the divine Scriptures a part is often used for [Col. 0318D] the whole, that is, “soul” for the whole person. Conversely, the whole is also used for a part, as in: “They have taken my Lord” (John 20:13). “Lord” is said in place of the Lord’s body.

Who is the one of whom he says (v. 26), “Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples”? Is someone to be cursed merely because he does not disclose all his grain to everyone?

The grain is the words of holy preaching. Therefore, whoever hides this grain—that is, keeps within himself the words of holy preaching and refuses to announce the divine utterances to others—is cursed among the peoples, because he will be condemned for the fault of silence. He could have benefited many; but because he refused, he will rightly be punished for the punishment of many.

[Col. 0319A] Who are those who sell grain, of whom it immediately adds (ibid.), “But blessing is upon the head of those who sell it”?

Those sell grain who proclaim to their own people the words of life and holy preaching. What price do they receive from them? The price of faith and holy confession. How will blessing come upon their heads? Because the Lord will say to each of them: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into joy” (Matt. 25:26).

What does he mean when he says (v. 29), “Whoever troubles his own house will possess the winds”? How can anyone possess winds?

Here he calls the mind a house—that is, the place in which each person dwells, as it were, by his thoughts—and he calls unclean spirits winds. Therefore, whoever does not fear [Col. 0319B] to disturb his house, that is, his mind, with evil and harmful thoughts, will indeed possess winds, because through evil thoughts he makes a way for demons to enter and dwell within him.

## CHAPTER XII

How is one to understand (v. 4), “A diligent woman is a crown to her husband; but she who does things worthy of disgrace is decay in his bones”?

A good and chaste woman brings honour to her husband in all things; because she loves him and governs him and his household well, she is a crown to him, because she adds grace to his virtues, by which he may be crowned by the Lord. But an adulterous woman, although she may seem beautiful, is nevertheless decay in his bones, because inwardly she defiles her limbs with the stench [Col. 0319C] of lust.

How should one understand what he says (v. 9), “Better is a poor man who is sufficient for himself than one who is glorious and in need of bread”?

Truly better is the unlearned and simple person who does the good things he knows, and thereby merits eternal life in heaven, than the glorious one—that is, the person distinguished by learning and scriptural instruction, or invested with a teacher’s office—who lacks the bread of love because he loves neither God nor neighbour; or rather, he lacks bread because he does not do what he understands or teaches.

Who is the shrewd person (v. 23) who conceals knowledge?

“Shrewd” is used here in a good sense, [Col. 0319D] that is, wise and prudent. Thus a shrewd person, wise and prudent, sometimes deliberately conceals knowledge for two reasons. First, because he cannot speak to weak hearers as to spiritual people but only as to carnal people; that is, he does not dare disclose to them the great mysteries of Holy Scripture that he knows, lest perhaps they be scandalized. Second, because he does not wish to give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine (Matt. 7:6).

## CHAPTER XIII

What does he mean when he says (v. 4), “The sluggard wills and does not will”? If he wills, how does he not will?

By the sluggard is signified the person who does not wish to exert himself in good works. Thus the sluggard wishes to reign, but does not wish to labour for God; he wishes to attain blessedness, [Col. 0320A] but does not wish to fulfil Christ’s commands in order to merit obtaining blessedness. Of such a person James says: “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jas. 1:8).

Who is the messenger of the wicked, of whom he says (v. 17), “The messenger of the wicked will fall into evil”?

The messenger of the wicked—that is, an angel of the devil—was Arius and Sabellius, together with the other heretics; or also the whisperers, who are indeed angels of Satan. These certainly fell into evil, that is, into the torment of eternal Gehenna.

Who, then, is the faithful envoy of whom it follows (ibid.), “But a faithful envoy is health”?

A faithful envoy is every Catholic preacher and teacher who obtains eternal health [Col. 0320B] and salvation for himself and his hearers.

## CHAPTER XIV

Why does he say (v. 19), “The evil will lie before the good, and the wicked before the gates of the righteous,” when in this life the good more often lie before the evil, and the righteous before the gates of the wicked?

At the last judgment, when the righteous have been crowned, the evil and wicked who afflicted them in the present life will be condemned. Therefore he says: “The evil will lie before the good, and the wicked before the gates of the righteous.” Yet what he says does not concern nearness of places, since the good and evil will not then be near one another; rather, it concerns the sight of the good, since the good will always see the torments of the evil, so that without end they may render greater thanks to God their deliverer.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0320C]

What does he mean when he says (v. 11), “Weight and balance are the Lord’s judgments”?

Because, as he himself willed, he gave each person a measure and grace of faith (Rom. 12:3).

Whom does he call (ibid.) “the stones of the age [or: of the bag]”?

The righteous and strong in faith. Therefore all the stones of the age—that is, God’s holy and chosen ones—are the work of the Lord, because no one is chosen by the Lord through his own strength or merit to be fitted for the heavenly building, but only through God’s mercy.

## CHAPTER XVII

What does he mean when he says (v. 6), “The crown of old men is the sons [Col. 0320D] of sons, and the glory of sons is their fathers”? If the sons of sons are evil, how are they the glory of their fathers? And if the fathers are evil, how are they the glory of their sons?

By old men he means here the patriarchs and prophets, whose sons are the apostles, and whose sons’ sons are the successors of the apostles, namely the holy preachers. All these are the crown of the old men—that is, of the patriarchs and prophets—because they celebrate with worthy praise those through whose examples and prophecies they came to the kinship of grace. How are the fathers the glory of their sons? For it is indeed a great glory for the preachers of the New Testament that they have merited to be sons of the ancients, that is, of the patriarchs.

What does he mean when he says (v. 14), “Whoever lets loose water [Col. 0321A] is the beginning of quarrels”? Does one who lets enclosed water flow down provoke quarrels? Or is it not rather wine than water that commonly provokes quarrels?

This is said figuratively. For by water is signified a frivolous, flowing, and unrestrained tongue, unstable like water. Therefore whoever lets loose water—that is, freely and immoderately releases his tongue—is the beginning of quarrels, because one who does not restrain his tongue provokes disputes and contentions and destroys concord.

## CHAPTER XVIII

What does he mean when he says (v. 16), “A person’s gift broadens his way and makes room for him before rulers”? What is this gift that broadens a person’s way and makes room for him before rulers?

[Col. 0321B] This gift is the gift of charity, or of the other virtues which the faithful receive from the Lord. This gift broadens his way, that is, his activity, because the more each faithful person is inwardly filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, the more he broadens his way outwardly—that is, multiplies his progress in good works—and daily grows and increases in holy desires and good works. How does this gift make room for a person before rulers? Because among the great rulers of the Church, in the future, it bestows upon him the summit of honour and the glory of eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER XIX

Why does he say (v. 24), “The sluggard hides his hand under his armpit and will not even bring it to his mouth”? Who is so lazy that, in eating or drinking, he does not bring his hand to [Col. 0321C] his mouth?

Whoever hides his hand under his armpit clearly does not wish to extend it to any task or labour. Therefore by the sluggard is signified every sluggish and idle preacher who does not wish to fulfil in deed what he teaches. For the person who strives to fulfil it in deed stretches his hand to his mouth.

## CHAPTER XX

Who is that sluggard of whom he says (v. 4), “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plough; therefore he will beg in summer, and it will not be given to him”? What if the sluggard refuses to plough in cold weather? In summer, will he not be able to find someone to give him something?

For sluggards often find faithful people who give them alms both in cold and in summer. But [Col. 0321D] the sluggard here signifies the one who, because of idleness and the adversity of this world, which is signified by cold, neglects to labour in God’s service. Therefore, on the day of judgment he will beg because he will have no good works by which he may merit to receive eternal blessedness; for “whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Gal. 6:8). Why, then, is the day of judgment compared to summer and to God’s kingdom? Because then every cloud of our sadness will pass away, and the days of that life will shine with the brightness of the eternal sun.

What does he mean when he says (v. 10), “Weight and weight, measure and measure: both are an abomination before God”?

By “weight and weight, measure and measure,” he means [Col. 0322A] differing weights and differing measures. Thus, according to the letter, whoever keeps varying weights and measures in his house does so in order to weigh and measure one way for himself and another way for his neighbour; this is an abomination to the Lord. Hence the Lord commands in the law of Moses: “Let there be for you an equitable measure and a just sextarius” (Lev. 19:36). But how should this be understood spiritually? The person who has differing weight and differing measure in his own house is the one who always seeks in his own actions some reason for himself to be praised, while in the actions of others he searches for grounds on which they may be blamed. Such a person too is abominable to the Lord, because to the extent that he desires to please himself, he displeases God, who searches all the hidden things of hearts.

[Col. 0322B] How should one understand what he says (v. 14), “‘It is bad,’ says every buyer; and when he has gone away, then he will boast”?

According to the letter, a buyer commonly disparages what he wishes to buy and says, “It is bad, it is bad.” Yet if he has bought well, when he has gone away he will boast. But how is it understood spiritually? He is truly a buyer who wishes to acquire eternal rewards for himself in heaven. He strives to purchase heavenly things with earthly things, enduring things with perishable things, eternal things with temporal things. Therefore, whatever such a buyer suffers in the present, he calls bad because he understands it to be so. Yet because he patiently endures every adversity for God, when he has departed from the world he will boast, because he will attain blessedness.

[Col. 0322C] Again, how should one understand what he says a little later (v. 21), “An inheritance hastily acquired in the beginning will lack blessing in the end”?

This inheritance may be understood as the acquisition of avarice. Therefore, whoever wishes to multiply riches in this life through the wickedness of avarice must lose the blessing of the eternal inheritance in the future. Alternatively: whoever wishes to seek good works for human praise hastens at the beginning as though toward an inheritance. Therefore at the end they will lack blessing, because they receive no reward from God. Of such people it is written: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2).

What does he mean when he says (v. 25), “It is the ruin of a person to devote the holy and afterward reconsider vows”?

[Col. 0322D] To “devote the holy” means to bind oneself by a vow. But the impious devote the holy because they bind themselves by a vow to persecute holy persons and kill them, just as the seventy [or: more than forty] men, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, bound themselves by a vow not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul (Acts 23:21); and pagans, as we often read, devoted the blood of Christians to their gods. What does “afterward reconsider vows” mean? To reconsider promises after vows is to persecute holy persons, speak evil of them, and despise them as though they were worthless slaves. How, then, is it a person’s ruin to devote the holy and afterward reconsider vows? For if it is sin when someone persecutes, offends, or injures God’s holy persons, it is therefore ruin to him, because [Col. 0323A] in persecuting the saints he prepares for himself the destruction of eternal condemnation.

## CHAPTER XXI

How should one understand what he says (v. 1), “Like divisions of waters, so is the heart of the king in God’s hand”—only the king’s heart, and not that of all people—when elsewhere it is written, “In his hand are all the ends of the earth” (Ps. 94:4)? If all the ends of the earth are in his hand, that is, in God’s power, are not the hearts of all people also in his hand?

Here we should not understand by “king” only one who is king in name and rules others temporally, but every holy, faithful, and devout Christian man, whose soldiers are the sacred virtues and who knows how to overcome vices within himself. [Col. 0323B] Therefore, just as the Lord fills the farthest reaches of earth and air through manifold divisions of waters, so he turns the heart of the king wherever he wills; for just as he gives divisions of graces to angels and people according to his will, so he fills the hearts of kings—that is, of saints—with various teachings and adorns them with diverse virtues.

Who is the person (v. 16) “who has strayed from the way of instruction and will dwell in the assembly of giants”?

By giants he means unclean spirits, that is, demons, of whom blessed Job also says: “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters, and those who dwell with them” (Job 26:5)—that is, demons and all whom they deceive and who consented to them—are tortured under punishments. Why are demons called giants? Because [Col. 0323C] demons are proud, arrogant, and wickedly strong, as the giants once were. Therefore all who have strayed from the way of instruction—that is, from the way of truth—will dwell in the assembly of these giants, that is, demons, because they are tortured together with demons.
