What is the city of the strong? Or who is the wise one of whom he says (v. 22), “The wise one ascended the city of the strong and destroyed the might of its confidence”?

By city he means the world; by the strong, demons. This world was once the city of the strong because, given over to the worship of idols, it served demons and placed its confidence for life in their worship; yet they are not gods, but works of human hands. Who is this wise one who ascended this city? The Virgin’s Son, [Col. 0323D] the Lord Jesus Christ, God’s power and God’s wisdom. He ascended this city when, born in the flesh, he appeared visibly to the world. He indeed destroyed the might of its confidence because he overthrew and removed from the world the worship of the gods in whom the Gentiles trusted.

## CHAPTER XXII

What does he mean when he says (v. 14), “The mouth of the strange woman is a deep pit”? Who is the strange woman whose mouth is a great pit?

By the mouth of the strange woman he means the mouth of a prostitute. Therefore whoever willingly listens to the words of a prostitute and willingly receives her kisses, as it were knocks at the door of the deep pit, that is, hell. Unless he quickly withdraws himself from her conversation or kiss, God abandoning him, he will immediately sink into the depth [Col. 0324A] of death. This is what he adds (ibid.): “He with whom the Lord is angry will fall into it.”

What does he mean when he says (v. 17), “Apply your heart to my instruction,” and shortly afterward adds (v. 20), “Behold, I have written it threefold, in thoughts and knowledge, in order to show you certainty and words of truth”? How did he set down instruction and knowledge threefold? Or what is it to apply the heart to instruction?

To apply the heart is to understand holy and righteous teaching. He set down his teaching threefold because he commanded everyone to strive to fulfil it in thought, speech, and deed.

Of what boundaries does he speak when he says (v. 27), “Do not cross the ancient boundaries which your fathers [Col. 0324B] set”?

By ancient boundaries he means the boundaries of truth and faith which Catholic teachers held from the beginning. He therefore commands that no one receive the truth of sacred faith and evangelical teaching otherwise than it has been handed down by the holy Fathers; or he commands that no one interpret the utterances of Holy Scripture otherwise than in accordance with the truth and intention of the Holy Spirit in each holy writer or teacher.

## CHAPTER XXIII

What are those riches of which he says (v. 5), “Do not raise your eyes to riches which you cannot possess, because they will make wings for themselves like eagles and fly into heaven”? What riches—that is, wealth or abundance—can make wings for themselves?

[Col. 0324C] These riches are the hidden things of divinity and the secrets of heavenly mysteries. The sense is: Do not raise the eyes of your mind to investigate the hidden things of divinity and the secrets of heavenly mysteries, which you cannot penetrate or understand, because they are open only to eagles—that is, manifest only to the citizens above.

## CHAPTER XXIV

What does he mean when he says (v. 16), “For the righteous person will fall seven times and rise again”? If he is righteous, how is he said to sin?

Here Solomon speaks of slight and daily sins, without which none of the righteous could be or can be in this life. For in this present [Col. 0324D] life no one is [adeo, “so”] righteous that, whether compelled or willing, he does not sin frequently on individual days through ignorance, forgetfulness, thought, speech, necessity, or the frailty of the flesh. Nevertheless, because he is righteous, aided by divine grace, he rises again through repentance, fasting, prayer, and almsgiving. Why is he said to fall seven times, neither fewer nor more? For the number seven is customarily used for universality or generally, as in: “Seven times in a day I have given praise to you” (Ps. 118:164), that is, at every time; and again, “I will bless the Lord at every time” (Ps. 33:1). Seven also sometimes signifies often or frequently. This may most fittingly be understood thus: the righteous falls seven times—that is, often—and often rises again; [Col. 0325A] or certainly, at every time he falls and rises, by divine grace, as was said above.

How should one understand what Solomon says (v. 27), “Prepare your work outside, and diligently cultivate your field, so that afterward you may build your house”? What is this work that we must prepare outside?

By work he means good action; therefore he added “your,” that is, useful and necessary to you. We prepare our work outside when we order our conduct well outwardly and arrange it so as to please God. How do we cultivate our field diligently? If we cleanse our body from the thorns of vices. How do we build our house after cultivating the field? [Col. 0325B] If we first order our outward actions well, then we build ourselves a house when we preserve purity of life and cleanness even in thought, and adorn the dwelling-place of our mind with devout thoughts.

## CHAPTER XXV

Who is the Lord, or who are the kings of whom he says (v. 2), “The glory of the Lord is to conceal a word, and the glory of kings to investigate a saying”?

This Lord must be understood as the Son of God, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, whose glory it was to conceal the Word—that is, to conceal that he was the Son. For when he appeared in the flesh, he chose rather to profess himself the Son of Man than the Son of God, so that the devil would not recognize him and thus, by his passion, he might redeem the human race. For if the devil had recognized that he was the Son of God, he would certainly not have crucified him. Thus it was the Lord’s glory to conceal the Word—that is, in the form of a human being to conceal the power of his divinity—so that, while he displayed the weakness of flesh, the devil would hasten to hand him over to the Passion, and so Christ, through the devil’s ignorance of the Passion, might attain the glory of the Resurrection. Who then are the kings whose glory is to investigate the saying? These kings were the holy apostles, who diligently strove to investigate the Lord’s saying by which he indicated that he was God. For wherever he did not openly show himself to be God, but meant his saying to be understood mystically, they searched it with the utmost diligence; such is the saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10: [Col. 0325D] 30). For when he concealed the divinity of the Word and showed the weakness of the flesh, he asked these kings, saying: “Whom do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16:13). To him the most eminent of the kings, namely the blessed apostle Peter, investigating his saying which he had often heard before, immediately answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 16).

What does that which immediately follows mean: “Heaven above, earth below, and the heart of kings unsearchable”? Who are these kings whose heart is called unsearchable?

By kings he means prophets and apostles, who, through revelation of the Spirit, merited to know the hidden things of divinity. By the heart of kings is signified the knowledge of apostles and prophets. How should one understand what he says: “Heaven above, earth below, and the heart [Col. 0326A] of kings unsearchable”? Just as human beings cannot comprehend the height of heaven and the depth of earth, so the capacity of our frailty cannot comprehend or penetrate the height of the knowledge and understanding of prophets and apostles.

## CHAPTER XXVI

How do these statements agree with one another, or how can they be consistent: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him” (v. 4), and “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself” (v. 5)?

These statements indeed seem very contrary to one another. Yet they agree well if we consider them carefully. By saying, “Do not answer a fool according to his folly,” he warns us [Col. 0326B] that, because a fool does not receive wisdom, we should not imitate his conduct, but rather despise and reject it; and whenever we speak, we should speak not shamefully, not furiously, not proudly, but honourably, patiently, and humbly—that is, wisely—lest we become like them. By what follows, “Answer a fool according to his folly,” we are warned to rebuke and reprove him wisely, and openly to show how great his folly is, lest, if perhaps he does not recognize his own folly, he think himself wise.

Who is the whisperer of whom he says (v. 22), “The words of a whisperer are as though simple, and they reach the innermost parts of the belly”?

By whisperer he means an instigator of strife and a double-tongued person, who feigns praise with flattering words. Therefore his words seem simple, but they reach the innermost parts of the belly, because the whisperer always seeks to hear something from which he may sow quarrels, by which the stomach is vexed and all the inward parts disturbed.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Who is that hidden love of which he says (v. 5), “Open rebuke is better than hidden love”?

Because it is much better openly to correct someone by rebuking him than secretly to love him through a pretense that indulges his sin.

What does he mean when he says (v. 7), “A sated soul will trample [Col. 0326D] the honeycomb; a hungry soul will take even bitter things as sweet”? How does a sated soul trample a honeycomb?

According to the letter, a sated soul tramples the honeycomb because whoever is filled with food despises and rejects sweet food; but one who is hungry, even if he receives some bitterness in food, makes light of it. Spiritually, however, it is understood thus: the sated soul is the soul of the rich, who have their consolation in the present life because they abound in the resources of temporal things; hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who are full, because you will hunger” (Luke 6:26). Therefore the soul of the rich tramples the honeycomb because, for earthly goods, it despises the sweetness of the kingdom of heaven. But the hungry soul takes bitter things as sweet because whoever hungers and thirsts for righteousness receives every bitterness as sweetness, [Col. 0327A] because for love of eternal blessedness or sweetness he patiently endures every adversity of the present life.

What does Solomon mean when he says (v. 23), “Diligently know the condition of your livestock, and consider your flocks”? Does he teach shepherds to inspect wool-bearing flocks?

No. For he speaks to the shepherd of the Church, and the sense is: Pay careful attention to those over whom you are set, and know the dispositions and actions of each one; if you find in them any defilement of vices, strive quickly to correct and amend it.

What does Solomon mean when he says (v. 25), “The meadows are laid open, green plants have appeared, and hay has been gathered from the mountains”? Who is ignorant of what he says [Col. 0327B] here?

Truly no one, if we take these words according to the letter. How, then, should they be understood? Spiritually, however. What do the meadows signify? By meadows are signified heavenly mysteries, which are called meadows because they are the pasture of the faithful. These meadows—that is, the divine mysteries—were long shut up under the signs and figures of the law. How and when were these meadows opened? The meadows were opened because, through the grace of the Lord and Saviour, the heavenly sacraments were revealed, when he opened the understanding of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45). Then green plants also appeared, that is, the new teachings of evangelical truth and grace. What is signified by hay gathered from the mountains? By mountains [Col. 0327C] are signified the holy Fathers, teachers of the Old Testament; by hay, their writings. Thus hay was gathered from the mountains. The holy Fathers are signified by mountains because the writings of the holy Fathers of old were gathered for the feeding and refreshment of the Lord’s sheep—that is, faithful souls.

## CHAPTER XXIX

What does he mean when he says (v. 13), “The poor person and the creditor have met one another; God is the illuminator of both”? Who are this poor person and creditor who have met one another?

The poor person is the humble hearer of God’s word; the creditor is the one who, by preaching, entrusts to the poor person—that is, the humble hearer—the money of God’s word. When do the poor person and the creditor meet one another? When hearer and preacher together come to one and the same [Col. 0327D] grace of divine mercy; hence it follows, “God is the illuminator of both,” because without the grace of divine mercy neither could the one preach nor the other believe.

What does he mean when he says (v. 18), “When prophecy fails, the people will be scattered”? What is this prophecy, whose failure scatters the people?

Prophecy is priestly instruction and teaching. Therefore when the teaching and instruction of priests fails, the people will be scattered; for when priests’ admonition and rebuke are lacking, the people are left to their own will and judgment and immediately become corrupted by various sins and vices.

## CHAPTER XXX

How is every word of God a fiery shield, [Col. 0328A] as Solomon says (v. 5), “Every word of God is a fiery shield to all who hope in him”?

Every word of divine authority is called a fiery shield because it both illuminates with the fire of charity the hearts of the elect who place their hope in God, consumes and purges the filth of vices that it finds in them, and defends them from the snares of enemies and every adversity.

What is the leech, of which he says that it has two daughters? For he says (v. 15): “The leech has two daughters, who say, ‘Bring, bring,’ and are never satisfied.”

The leech is the devil, who always thirsts for blood—that is, he desires to draw human beings into sins and continually kindles the thirst for sinning. What are those two daughters of the leech, who say, “Bring, bring,” and are never satisfied [Col. 0328B]? Luxury and avarice. For the more anyone indulges in luxury, the more he delights in it; likewise, the more anyone heaps up riches for himself, the more he continually desires to increase them.

Why did Solomon introduce the example of the stellio, when he says (v. 28): “The stellio supports itself with its hands and dwells in kings’ houses”?

It was in order to stir up the lazy and slow-witted to learning and good works. What kind of animal is the stellio? It is a kind of very sluggish lizard, but of variegated colour; hence it received the name *stellio*, because it is marked and mottled with spots like stars. What, then, does it signify? It signifies those who are slow of intellect and yet, by daily effort and diligence, ascend to the court of the eternal King: that is, although with great [Col. 0328C] labour, they attain knowledge of the holy Scriptures and are able to penetrate the secrets of heavenly mysteries. Of such persons it is written in the Gospel: “To him who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound” (Matt. XIII.12), because to one who has the zeal to read will be given the ability to understand.

What are those three of which Solomon says (vv. 29–31): “There are three things that go well, and a fourth that proceeds prosperously: a lion, strongest of beasts, which fears no encounter; a cock girded about the loins; and a ram; nor is there a king who can resist him”? Are these the things that go well? Whom does that lion signify?

It signifies him of whom it is written: “The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” [Col. 0328D] (Rev. V.5), namely, the Lord Jesus Christ. He is called the strongest of beasts because “what is weak in God is stronger than men.” What is that weakness of God? God’s weakness was to assume the flesh of our mortality. But this is stronger than human beings, because the very man who was born of the Virgin was perfect God. Why does this lion fear no encounter with anyone? Because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. II.22); hence he himself says: “Behold, the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John XIV.30). What does the cock girded about the loins signify? Holy preachers. Why are preachers called cocks? Because amid the darknesses of the present life—that is, sins—they urge and teach people to destroy these darknesses, and by preaching announce the true light, namely, the glory [Col. 0329A] of eternal blessedness. Why are these cocks said to be girded about the loins? Because these preachers restrain within their members luxury, avarice, and lust. What does the ram signify, against whom no king can stand? By the ram are denoted holy confessors and priests, who, like rams, go before the flock because by their examples they lead the faithful people as they walk. If these rams live spiritually and rightly, no king can resist them, because no persecutor, however savage, can hinder their purpose; for even if evils are inflicted upon them, they endure everything patiently for Christ’s sake.

What is that fourth thing (vv. 29, 32) “which proceeds prosperously”?—“There is one who appeared foolish after he was raised on high.” Who is this?

[Col. 0329B] It is Antichrist, who will be exalted on high—that is, to a lofty position—because, although he will be a most wicked man, he will disdain to call himself the Son of God and will falsely claim that he is God. Once raised on high, how will he appear foolish? Because in that very exaltation and pride he will suddenly be struck down by the divine sword and perish. Why does he say of the preceding three, “There are three things that go well,” but of this one, “a fourth which proceeds prosperously”? Why did he not similarly say of this one that it “goes well,” but says “prosperously”? Because everything that proceeds prosperously does not always proceed well, nor does everything that proceeds well always proceed prosperously. What, then, are the things that proceed well or prosperously? Those things proceed well which walk in holiness and righteousness. Those proceed prosperously which possess prosperity in this life. The lion, the cock, and the ram go well [Col. 0329C] but not prosperously, because Christ too fulfilled the will of God the Father in all things, yet endured many adversities, and finally even death. Likewise holy preachers and confessors strive to fulfil the divine will, but endure many persecutions in this life. Antichrist, however, does not proceed well, because in his pride he will do everything contrary to God’s will; yet he proceeds prosperously because, though only for a short time, he will enjoy great glory and prosperity.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Who was King Lamuel, of whom he says (v. 1): “The words of King Lamuel, the vision with which his mother instructed him”?

Lamuel is a Hebrew name; in Latin, “in whom God is.” He is indeed Solomon, king of Israel, in whom [Col. 0329D] God was; for unless God had dwelt in him, he could neither have understood nor written so many and such great divine mysteries. Who was his mother, who instructed him and taught him the vision? According to the literal sense, it may be understood as his bodily mother, namely Queen Bathsheba, who wisely instructed him. But in this place nothing is better understood as the mother than spiritual and divine grace, which invisibly instructed him in his heart and taught him the understanding of wisdom that he proclaimed and wrote outwardly for humankind.

Who is that strong woman of whom he says (v. 10): “Who shall find a strong woman? Her price is far off and from the uttermost bounds.”

The strong woman is called the Catholic Church, which [Col. 0330A] is called a woman because she gives birth to spiritual children from water and the Holy Spirit. She is called strong because, for faith in and love of her Creator and Redeemer, she despises and rejects all the adversities and prosperities of this age. Why did Solomon say, “Who shall find a strong woman?” Because through the Holy Spirit he knew that none of the patriarchs or prophets, nor indeed any of the elect at all, would suffice for the redemption of the human race, except the sole mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. II.5). Therefore he says, “Who shall find a strong woman?” because, through the Spirit, “no one” is understood. Why did he immediately add, “Her price is far off and from the uttermost bounds”? To show that Christ was to come not in his own time but long after him, and unlike him: namely, a pure man, free from the filth [Col. 0330B] of sin. Yet at the end of the ages the Son of God would descend from heaven, and, born of a virgin, would be perfect God and man. This is what he means by “far off,” that is, long afterward. It signifies the time from Solomon’s days until the Virgin’s childbirth. He says “from the uttermost bounds” because “his going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. XVIII.6). What price did the Lord give for this woman? Himself, as the Apostle says: “He loved us and gave himself up for us as an offering and sacrifice, a sweet-smelling savour” (Eph. V.2).

How did the strong woman become like a merchant’s ship? For Solomon says (v. 14): “She became like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from afar.”

A merchant is so called because he is always [Col. 0330C] intent on acquiring and multiplying wares and his profits. A merchant’s ship, laden with diverse merchandise more abundant in its own country, travels from place to foreign place, so that, having sold there everything it brought, it may carry home more valuable goods. Thus the strong woman—that is, the holy Church—always desires to be adorned with the riches of virtues and to abound in good works, sailing through the sea of this age, so that by means of it she may gain through her virtue—that is, acquire—greater gifts of divine grace. Who is that merchant of the ship? The Lord Jesus Christ, who gave the price of his blood and redeemed the Church. Therefore, following the example of the merchant, that is, of her Lord and Redeemer, the holy Church always strives to increase for herself the profits of virtues and good works [Col. 0330D], that through them she may deserve to acquire greater rewards, namely those of eternal blessedness. This is what is meant by “bringing her bread from afar”: in all the good which she does in time, she desires only the satisfaction of the living bread, because she awaits only eternal recompense.

What is meant by his saying (v. 22): “She made herself a variegated garment; fine linen and purple are her clothing”? What is a variegated garment?

It is one customarily made very strong by varied weaving. What, then, is signified by the variegated garment? The strong works of the holy Church and the diverse adornments of virtues, of which the Prophet says: “The queen stood at your right hand in a golden garment, surrounded by variety” (Ps. XLIV.10). How are fine linen and purple the clothing [Col. 0331A] of the woman, that is, of the holy Church? Fine linen is a kind of very white flax; thus bodily chastity and purity of holy conduct are fittingly denoted by fine linen. By purple, however, the shedding of blood is denoted. Therefore the strong woman—that is, the holy Church—clothes herself in fine linen when she preserves bodily chastity and shines with the brightness of holy conduct. She clothes herself in purple when holy martyrs within her shed their blood for Christ’s name.

If fine linen and purple are the clothing of the holy Church, why then does he say later (v. 25): “Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she shall laugh on the last day”?

There is no contradiction, because strength and beauty are the clothing of the holy Church: strength, because for Christ’s faith [Col. 0331B] and righteousness she patiently endures the wickedness and persecution of evil people; and beauty, because she works righteousness and adorns herself with the grace of virtues.

Why, then, does he say, “She shall laugh on the last day,” when the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke VI.25)?

In the sacred Scriptures laughter commonly signifies joy. Hence the Lord says: “Blessed are you who now weep, for you shall laugh” (Luke VI.21), that is, you shall rejoice. Blessed Job likewise says: “The mouth of the truthful shall be filled with laughter,” that is, with joy [otherwise in the Vulgate: “Until your mouth is filled with laughter”] (Job VIII.21). Therefore the strong woman—that is, the holy Church—will laugh on the last day: that is, she will rejoice in the recompense of the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0331C] Who are the woman’s children, who proclaimed her most blessed (v. 28)? Or who is her husband (ibid.), who praised her?

The children of this woman—that is, of the holy Church—are [Col. 0332A] all the elect. Her husband is the Lord Jesus Christ. For the Church’s children, namely all the elect, will rise from the dust of the earth on the last day of judgment and, adorned with the glory of immortality, will proclaim their mother most blessed: that is, they will praise the holy Church which gave them birth from water and the Holy Spirit. Her husband also will rise and praise her, the Lord Jesus Christ, when on the day of judgment he appears manifest in the power of his divinity and praises her, saying at the judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. “For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat” (Matt. XXV.34), etc.

Why, then, did Solomon use the past tense, saying (v. 28), “They rose”? He ought to have said, “They will rise.”

What Solomon knew to be future he held to be most certain, and therefore, in prophetic fashion, used the past for the future [Col. 0332B].

Of whom does he say what follows (v. 29): “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all”?

By “many daughters” he means the churches of heretics and the crowds of evil Catholics, who are called Christ’s daughters or churches. Why are they called Christ’s daughters or churches? Because of faith, the sacrament of baptism, and the adoption as children which they received in baptism. What riches did these daughters gather? Prayers, fasts, alms, bodily chastity, restraint of the tongue, meditation on the Scriptures, and the other riches of good works. These are true riches if they are performed with a spiritual intention, namely for the recompense of the heavenly kingdom; otherwise they profit those who do them nothing [Col. 0332C]. Thus those daughters—the churches of heretics or the crowds of evil Catholics—gathered riches in vain, because they either erred in faith or performed such good things for vain glory.

## ON ECCLESIASTES

[Col. 0331]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0331C]

What does Ecclesiastes mean when he says (v. 2): “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” when it is written in the book of Genesis: “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. I.31)? If all things made by God [Col. 0331D] are very good, how is everything vanity—and not only vanity, but vanity of vanities?

Heaven and earth, seas and all things contained within this circuit are indeed good in themselves, since they were created by the good God; but compared with God, they are certainly to be reckoned, or ought to be reckoned, as nothing, because God will always remain what he is, whereas all those things will pass away. For “the things which are seen are temporal and passing; but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. IV.18).

Why did he repeat his statement twice, saying: “Vanity of vanities, Ecclesiastes said, and all is vanity”?

To emphasize the magnitude of vanities, he repeated his statement, thereby showing that [Col. 0332C] all worldly glory will wither like the flower of grass and pass away like smoke.

Of what generation does he say (v. 4): “A generation passes away, and a generation comes”?

He speaks of the generation of the Jews and of the Gentiles. For the first generation, that of the Jews, departs because it perished through unbelief; and it is succeeded by the generation gathered from the Gentiles, namely the holy Church of the faithful, which is saved through faith in Christ. It can also be understood in this way: a generation comes and a generation goes—that is, as some die, others are born; those whom you previously saw you no longer see, and you begin to see those who were not there before [Col. 0332D].

Why does Solomon say (ibid.), “The earth stands for ever,” when the Lord says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth shall pass away” (Luke XXI.33)?

They will indeed pass away, according to God’s declaration, through being made better, but not through annihilation; for, purified in the fire of judgment, they will be improved, since they will be renewed but not utterly destroyed. For heaven above and earth below will burn only to the extent to which they could be polluted by the wickedness of human beings and demons together. [Col. 0333A] Therefore, according to Solomon’s declaration, the earth will stand for ever, because it will never be destroyed but will be improved and renewed.

What did Solomon intend to signify when he said (v. 5): “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; and there, being reborn, it turns through the south and bends toward the north”? For who does not know that the sun rises and sets, and returns by paths unknown to us to the place whence it rose, in order to rise again?

Solomon said this in order to show that the sun itself, given to humanity for the light of day, by its mutability—that is, by its rising and setting—daily displays the destruction of this age. For by these changes of seasons [Col. 0333B], and by the rising and setting of the stars, Solomon teaches that human life daily does not cease to perish and fail. What does this sun, which rises and sets daily, spiritually signify here? It signifies that true sun, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the sun of righteousness, of whom the prophet says: “For you who fear the Lord, the sun of righteousness shall arise” (Mal. II.2). This sun of righteousness rises daily for those who fear him—that is, for his faithful people, namely holy and devout persons. It also sets at noon for false prophets—that is, heretics and evil Catholics—because on account of their sins they lose the light of his grace. It also sets for unbelievers, because they do not deserve to be illumined by the light of faith.

What does he mean by saying (v. 7): “All rivers enter [Col. 0333C] into the sea, and the sea does not overflow; to the place from which they issue, the rivers return, that they may flow again”? For who knows that they return to their place in order to flow again?

That Ecclesiastes, namely Solomon, knows it through the grace of the Holy Spirit; but this our Ecclesiastes, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is himself the creator of the waters by the power of his divinity, because he is equal to God the Father, knows it most fully: rivers that enter the sea flow down into the abyss, return through hidden channels to the heads of springs, and begin again to bubble up from the womb of the abyss. But spiritually, what do these rivers signify? By these rivers are denoted holy preachers, who, as they shine with virtues and flash with teaching, truly flow as rivers, because by their holy preaching and action together [Col. 0333D] they irrigate the dry earth of carnal hearts, so that these may bear the fruits of good works. How, then, do these rivers return to the place from which they issue, in order to flow again? Because in every teaching and work they perform, holy preachers return to the praise of their Creator, so that they may offer praises and thanks to the Lord, their author, through whom they received both the capacity to do such things and every good that they are. For they always return to the fountain of true light, lest perhaps they dry up and wither, so that from it they may receive the water of wisdom and the grace of virtues in order to flow again—that is, to fill themselves with good works and pour the streams of spiritual teaching into others’ hearts. All faithful holy persons also are rivers [Col. 0334A]; and these rivers return to the place from which they issue, because through holy desires they return to the love of their Creator and offer him praise and thanks for all good things, from whom they received them.

What does Solomon mean when he says (v. 18) that “in much wisdom there is much indignation; and he who adds knowledge adds sorrow”? How is there much indignation in much wisdom?

There is much indignation in much wisdom, and he who adds knowledge adds sorrow, because the greater the wisdom a person receives, the more he is indignant with himself and grieves to be subject to vices and sins and not to possess virtues. For the more anyone advances in wisdom, the more he is angry with himself for the evil deeds he has done, and is saddened and grieves [Col. 0334B] under his sins. Therefore he who adds knowledge adds sorrow; and the more he knows heavenly and earthly things, the more he labours in grieving and weeping so that he may escape the snares of errors and be freed from the misery of this age.

## CHAPTER II

Why does he say (v. 2): “I considered laughter an error, and said to joy, ‘Why are you vainly deceived?’” when laughter is natural to human beings and the Lord says in the Gospel: “Rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. V.12)?

Solomon does not condemn natural laughter, that is, modest and decent laughter. Hence elsewhere he says: “A wise man will scarcely laugh quietly” (Ecclus. XXI.23); rather, he calls dissolute, immoderate, and boisterous [Col. 0334C] laughter an error. Such laughter is called *cachinnus*, “loud guffawing.” Likewise, he calls not spiritual joy but temporal joy a deception. Those who do not mourn their past evils or understand the ruin wrought by their sins guffaw and rejoice in temporal goods, because they consider vain and brief things to be everlasting goods; and therefore, deceived by the pleasantness of the present life, they are daily harassed by the error of this age.

Why does Solomon say (v. 14): “The eyes of the wise man are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness”? Surely the fool’s eyes are also in his head?

The eyes here are not bodily but spiritual eyes: namely, the eyes of the mind, that is, the senses and intentions of the soul. By the head, however, Christ is denoted; hence the Apostle says: “Christ is the head of man” [Col. 0334D] (1 Cor. II.3). The wise man’s eyes are in his head because he directs and places all his intention in Christ, and always lifts up the eyes of his mind to imitate heavenly things. But the fool walks in darkness because he is blinded by the darkness of both his folly and his sins, and through love of this world is cast away from heavenly things. For he hates heavenly things and loves earthly ones; he despises what is eternal and loves what is temporal. Therefore he cannot lift his eyes to heaven like the wise man, because he thinks not of the things that are God’s but of those of this age.

(V. 13.) What is the difference between the wise man and the fool? The difference is that the former is enlightened and adorned by the brightness of wisdom, whereas the latter is darkened and disfigured by the error of his folly [Col. 0335A]. Indeed, the distance between the wise and the foolish is as great as that between day and night, light and darkness. How, then, is there finally a difference between the wise man and the fool when the destruction of both is one and the same? (V. 16.) For thus it is said (ibid.): the learned dies as does the unlearned, the wise as the unwise. Although the wise and the foolish have one end and a similar death, and the wise is often more afflicted than the foolish in this life, their remembrance will not be alike in the future, nor will they receive an equal crown or recompense. For on the day of judgment the wise will be raised to the glory of the heavenly kingdom, while the foolish will be plunged into the torments of eternal condemnation. Who is that wise man, as far removed from the fool as light is from darkness? Is it the man who possesses only an abundance of philosophical learning [Col. 0335B] or shines with the eloquence of the liberal arts? Certainly not, because worldly wisdom is hostile to God (Rom. VIII.7), and carnal wisdom, though adorned with the flowers of eloquence, nevertheless contains within itself no spiritual fruit and no fruit of everlasting blessedness. But he is truly wise who loves God, keeps his commandments, and, insofar as human frailty allows, strives to fulfil his will in all things. Of him it is said (v. 26): “God gave the good man wisdom before him, and knowledge and joy.”

Why does Solomon say (ibid.): “But to the sinner he gave affliction and superfluous care”? For if God gave sinful man anxiety and superfluous care, how does he himself sin if he afflicts himself with superfluous cares [Col. 0335C] and concern for temporal things?

The cause of superfluous care and evil anxiety is not in God, but in the one who first sinned voluntarily; for, as his sins required, he deserved to have superfluous care and anxiety. Therefore the statement, “But to the sinner he gave superfluous care and anxiety,” is to be understood as follows: because his own deserts required it, God permitted these things to be given to him—namely, because he was a sinner.

## CHAPTER III

What does Solomon wish to demonstrate by saying (v. 1): “All things have a time”? If all things have a time, then does the substance of divinity also have a time [Col. 0335D]?

Far be it! That ineffable and eternal essence of the divine majesty, which created all things from nothing, is not enclosed by place, constrained by time, or bounded by any space. Therefore, to show what things he meant, Solomon immediately added, saying (ibid.): “And all things under heaven pass through their own intervals.” For he wishes to show that all things in the world are mutually contrary, and that none of all things under heaven and contained within time is everlasting.

Of what planting or uprooting does Solomon speak when he says (v. 2): “A time to plant, and a time to uproot what has been planted”? Does he speak of the planting or uprooting [Col. 0336A] of trees or herbs?

No. He says this of the birth and death of human beings. For what he says above, “a time to be born,” is what follows: “a time to plant”; “to plant” means “to be born.” And what he says above, “a time to die” (ibid.), is what follows: “a time to uproot what has been planted” (ibid.); for “to uproot” means “to die.” The rising and setting of human beings—that is, the time of birth and the time of death, the time of planting and the time of uprooting—is known to God alone. For he himself appointed both the time in which each person should be born and planted for life, and the time in which each should die and be uprooted from this life—that is, eradicated by the sentence of death.

[Col. 0336B] What does he mean when he likewise says (v. 3): “A time to kill, and a time to heal”? No one doubts that a time for healing is granted by God. But did God establish a time for killing others? Or can a human being ever heal one whom he has once killed?

Certainly not. But the time to kill and the time to heal belong to him alone who speaks through Moses, saying: “I shall kill and make alive; I shall strike, and I shall heal” (Deut. XXXII.29). He indeed appointed both the time in which sinners are killed and the time in which the sick—that is, those weakened by sins—are healed. For he kills when he afflicts sinners either with bodily infirmity or with some adversity of this world, so that they may be corrected [Col. 0336C], die to sins, and live to God. God often chastises the wicked in order to kill and heal them—that is, that they may cease to be what they are and begin to be what they are not. There is therefore also a time for healing, when almighty God mercifully afflicts those whom he kills—that is, by adversities—and pierces them by a hidden inspiration and calls them to repentance.

Of what destruction and building does he speak when he says (v. 3): “A time to destroy, and a time to build”? Does he speak of the building or destruction of houses? What good would there be in saying this? For who does not know that some destroy and others build houses?

Solomon does not speak here of the destruction of houses [Col. 0336D], but of destroying evils and building goods, because it is necessary first to destroy evils and then to build goods, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI.27). Thus he says that there is a time to destroy evils and a time to build goods, because God has granted us in the present life to destroy evils and build goods: that is, first to erase sins in ourselves through repentance, and afterwards to construct the building of virtues through holy desires.

Why does Solomon say (v. 4): “A time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn and a time to dance”? Who does not know that we weep at one time and laugh at another? Or what was the point of saying, “a time [Col. 0337A] to mourn and a time to dance”? Did he perhaps wish to show that we ought to practise the frivolities of dancing?

Far be it! For we ought not to behave in a buffoonish manner. Rather, the present life is the time for weeping, and the future life is the time for laughing. Whoever strives in the present life to cleanse his sins by daily weeping and tears will laugh in the future life—that is, will rejoice. Likewise, the present life is the time for mourning, and the blessed life the time for dancing. For in the movement of dancing a person manifests the joy of the mind and the exultation of the soul. Whoever therefore strives in the present life to remove sins by mourning will dance in the future life—that is, he will rejoice and exult in the glory of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0337B] What does he mean when he says (v. 5): “A time to scatter stones, and a time to gather them”? What benefit is there in scattering stones? Or what benefit is there in gathering them, unless perhaps someone wishes to build a house?

Solomon does not speak for this reason, but of the scattering and gathering of the Gentiles. For by stones the Gentiles are denoted. Hence blessed John the Baptist says: “God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham” (Matt. III.9; Luke III.8). The time to scatter stones was before the Lord’s coming, because the Gentiles did not remain in the unity of faith but, departing from God, were scattered, since they worshipped various gods and revered diverse places [perhaps: idols]. The time to gather stones, however, was after the Lord’s coming because, as the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” [Col. 0337C] (Gal. IV.4). Then indeed he began to gather stones, because, when the mystery of his Passion had been accomplished, he sent the apostles throughout the whole world, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII.19). Then, when the mystery of his Ascension into heaven had been celebrated on the fortieth day, as soon as the report of his name had been spread abroad by the apostles, stones—that is, the Gentiles, scattered far and wide throughout the world by varied worship of idols—were gathered, because, rejecting and abominating idols, they rested in unity of faith.

Why does he again say (v. 8): “A time for love [Col. 0337D] and a time for hatred,” when John says in his Epistle: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III.15)?

There is indeed a time for love when, after God, we ought to love father and mother, wife and children, and other relatives. But there is a time for hatred because, for confession of Christ, we must at once despise and hate father and mother and all relatives if they oppose us in the way of God, as holy martyrs are often recorded to have done.

What does he again mean by saying (v. 8): “A time of war and a time of peace”? How is there a time of war when the Lord says in the Gospel: “Agree with your adversary quickly while you are with him on the way” (Matt. V [Col. 0338A].25); and again: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also; and to one who wishes to take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well” (Matt. V.39; Luke VI.29)?

Truly, for us there is always a time of war and struggle as long as we remain in this present age, because we must always fight against the snares of the ancient enemy—that is, defeat the powers of evil spirits. But the time of peace will come when we have departed from the present age; for if we have fought well in this age, we shall be crowned in the future and rest secure in eternal peace in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Why does Solomon say (v. 12): “God made all things good in their time,” when above he said that all things are vanity [Col. 0338B] (Eccles. I.2)? If all things are vain, how then are they good?

All things are vain because they are transitory; nevertheless all things are good because they were created by the good God. They are indeed good, but not always good—rather, good in their proper time. For it is good to keep watch, and good also to sleep; yet to keep watch always, or to sleep always, is certainly not good.

Why does Solomon speak doubtfully, saying (v. 21): “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of Adam ascends upward, and the spirit of beasts descends downward?” For who does not know that the spirit of beasts descends—that is, that of all sinful people and brute animals alike is dissolved with the body—but that, as soon as it departs from the body, it is either led to glory or plunged [Col. 0338C] into punishment?

A little earlier Solomon showed that, as regards the body’s lowliness, there is no difference between beast and human being: as a human being dies, so does a beast, and as a beast is reduced to dust, so too is a human being. But in order to show that, according to the dignity of the soul, human beings differ greatly from beasts and cattle, he added: “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of Adam ascends upward, and the spirit of beasts descends downward?” He shows that this alone is the difference between human beings and beasts: the human spirit ascends to heaven, whereas the spirit of beasts or cattle descends to earth, because it dies and is dissolved together with the flesh. Therefore when Solomon says, [Col. 0338D] “Who knows?” as though no one could know this, he says “Who knows?” to signify difficulty or rarity, as in the saying, “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII.3), that is, no one, or very few. For what is impossible cannot happen at all; but what is difficult can happen, though with great labour. Spiritually, however, what do those children or those beasts signify? The children of Adam signify holy or elect persons, who are deservedly called human beings because they live rationally, holy, and spiritually. By beasts, however, carnal persons are denoted, who are called beasts because they live bestially and carnally, like beasts and cattle. Thus the prophet David says: “You will save human beings and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. XXXV.7). [Col. 0339A] It often happens that those who seem righteous human beings sin, turn away from their righteousness, and commit iniquity; conversely, that those who are evil and ungodly turn from their iniquity and practise equity and righteousness. Therefore Solomon says: “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of Adam ascends upward, and the spirit of beasts descends downward?” because the condition of this life is so uncertain that even a sinner, called a beast, may rise through conversion in repentance and ascend to heaven, while a righteous person who turns from his righteousness may fall into sin and be plunged into hell.

## CHAPTER IV

What does he mean when he says (v. 5): “The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh”? For who is so foolish as to eat his own flesh?

[Col. 0339B] This fool is to be understood as the sluggard of whom Proverbs says: “The sluggard hides his hand under his armpit” (Prov. 19:24). This fool and sluggard folds his hands and eats his own flesh, because he prefers to live in idleness and lethargy and to have a fistful of meal rather than to acquire by labor that by which he may be fed. “He eats his own flesh” is said hyperbolically. What is meant by “hyperbolically”? A hyperbole, so called in Greek, is when something incredible is stated. How, then, is “he eats his own flesh” said hyperbolically? Because it is incredible that anyone should eat his own flesh; but, in order to heighten this fool’s sloth, he says, “he eats his own flesh,” in order to show that the fool would rather have his flesh waste away through hunger and fail in the misery of starvation than be sustained by the labor of his hands.

Who is that one of whom Solomon says (v. 8): “There is one, and he has no second, neither son nor brother nor any kinsman; and yet he does not cease from labor,” that is, from gathering riches; nor are his eyes satisfied with riches; and it is therefore the greatest vanity that he has gathered riches and does not know for whom he gathers them, or to whom he will leave them? Spiritually, whom does that one who has no second signify?

Our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone is by nature the Son of God, and who alone descended as God from heaven to redeem the human race. How does he have neither son nor brother, when in holy baptism all Christians are made sons of God and brothers of our Lord Jesus Christ? He alone is Son in the proper sense and by nature; all the rest are adopted sons, and therefore his brothers not by nature but by grace. How, then, does this one not cease from labor? Because he patiently bears our sins, mercifully waits for repentance, and daily intercedes for us with God the Father. How are his eyes not satisfied with riches? Because he always desires our salvation.

Who is that threefold cord of which Solomon says (v. 11): “A threefold cord is not easily broken”?

This is the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: in divinity they are three persons, but one nature. Why then does he say, “not easily broken”? For what is difficult can be done, although with great labor. Can this cord, then, be broken? Truly, never; because the nature of the holy Trinity is indivisible. But “difficult” here must be understood as “impossible,” because it cannot happen that the nature of the Trinity should be divided.

[Col. 0340A] Who is that poor and wise child (v. 13), who is better than an old and foolish king?

Our Lord Jesus Christ, who is called a child because of his innocence and simplicity, since he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth. Though rich, this child became poor for our salvation. He is truly wise, because “in him dwells bodily all the fullness of divinity” (Col. 2:9). Who is that old and foolish king? The devil,

[Col. 0340B] who has reigned in the human race almost from the world’s beginning, and is therefore called old; and he is truly a foolish king, because the more people he deceives, the more punishment he accumulates for himself. For in the kingdom of this old and foolish king—that is, of the devil—was born the most excellent child, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, who became “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 17:14; 19:16).

What does he mean when he says (v. 17), “Guard your foot when entering the house of God”? Does he instruct us to guard our foot against stumbling on stones when we enter the house of God, that is, the church of God?

Although we should always enter God’s house decently, with fear and silence, he nevertheless teaches that not the bodily foot but the foot of the soul must be guarded,

[Col. 0340C] that is, the entrance of the body, so that we may pour out pure prayers in God’s sight. And this is the sense: When you enter the house of God, namely the church, guard your foot—that is, the approach of your mind—lest you stumble in evil thoughts, so that your prayer may be directed purely to God.

## Chapter V

What does he mean when he says (v. 5), “Do not give your mouth so as to cause your flesh to sin”?

When one speaks vanities and lustful words by which the flesh is incited to sin, this means: do not say, “I do not sin, but it is the sin dwelling in me,” that is, the frailty of my flesh. If you say this, you provoke God to anger, as though he himself were the author

[Col. 0340D] of your wickedness and sin.

## Chapter VI

What does he mean when he says (v. 7), “All human labor is for his mouth, but his soul will not be filled”? How can everything for which a person labors be in his mouth?

A wise ecclesiastical man has all his labor in his mouth, because he daily meditates upon, preaches, and teaches everything that he learns in the Scriptures. And his soul will not be filled, because what he has learned does not suffice him; rather, he always desires and strives to learn more and more.

What does he mean when he says (v. 9), “It is better to see what you desire than to desire what you do not know”? How does one crave, or desire, what one does not know?

[Col. 0341A] He who discerns with the eye of the mind between good and evil sees the good that he should desire and the evil that he should reject. But one who follows the desires and lusts of his heart often desires what he does not know, because he wants to grasp what he cannot.

Of whom does Solomon say (v. 10), “The name of him who is to be has already been called, and it is known that he is man”?

Of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose name was called beforehand in the holy Scriptures before he himself took flesh from the Virgin; and it was known to the prophets and saints of God that a true man was to come.

If this was said of our Lord Jesus Christ, what does the following mean (v. 10): “And he cannot

[Col. 0341B] contend in judgment against one stronger than himself”? Who is that stronger one against whom our Lord Jesus Christ cannot contend in judgment?

The Lord Father, who is stronger, because the Son, according to his humanity, is less than the Father.

## Chapter VII

What does he mean when he says (v. 4), “Anger is better than laughter,” since laughter is a natural thing?

Anger is not always a vice; sometimes it is even a virtue, when we are angry with ourselves or with others who sin. This anger, then, is better than laughter, because laughter dissipates the mind and joy corrupts a person’s spirit. This anger corrects and reforms the sinner.

What does he mean when he says (v. 8), “Slander troubles the wise man and destroys the strength of his heart”? For one who is

[Col. 0341C] truly wise is troubled by no oppression and cast down by no adversity.

The wise person meant here is not one who is perfect and consummate in wisdom, but one who has already begun to possess wisdom and yet is not perfect. Such wisdom is easily troubled by human slander or some adversity, and loses the vigor and strength of its soul because, when it does not bear adversities patiently, it is tormented by impatience.

What does Solomon mean when he says (v. 11), “Do not say in your heart: What do you suppose is the reason that former times were better than the present?” It is evil to say this because, as he himself says there, such a question is foolish. Why foolish? Because there is one God, the creator of all times and days. Were there not

[Col. 0341D] good and bad times?

Indeed there were; but virtues make times good for us, while vices and sins make them bad. Therefore we ought always to live so well that the present days may be better for us than the past.

What does Solomon mean when he says (v. 17), “Do not be excessively righteous, nor be wiser than is necessary”? What evil is there if a person is very righteous? Or who can be wiser than is necessary?

That person is excessively and unduly righteous whose righteousness is harsh and cruel, and who provokes others to complaint and murmuring. For example, someone who sees his brother sin and would rather condemn and punish him than correct and reform him through repentance is certainly excessively and unduly righteous.

[Col. 0342A] How does a person become wiser than is necessary? When he thinks proudly, concerning which the Apostle warns: “Do not think lofty thoughts, but fear” (Rom. 11:20; 12:16). He also thinks more wisely than is necessary who wishes to understand things that he cannot comprehend or penetrate.

Why does Solomon say (v. 19), “He who fears God neglects nothing,” when the Apostle James says, “We all stumble in many things” (Jas. 3:2)? Did James or the other apostles not fear God, though they confessed that they stumbled in many things?

They certainly feared him, and stumbled in many things, because there is no one upon earth who does good and does not sin. How, then, is it true that he who fears

[Col. 0342B] God neglects nothing? Whoever possesses holy and chaste fear neglects nothing, because he is neither exalted by prosperity nor cast down by adversity; whatever happens to him does not make him sorrowful. Who is the person who has the holy and chaste fear of God? One who wishes to offend God in nothing and, so far as God deigns to assist him, wishes and strives in all things to fulfill his commandments.

What does he mean when he says (v. 20), “Wisdom will strengthen the wise man above ten princes of the city”? What is this wisdom, and who are these princes?

Wisdom here signifies our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God the Father. The ten princes of the city—that is, of the heavenly Jerusalem—are the rulers of the Church, because they govern her daily. Why, then, are they called ten? Because there were ten orders of angels, but one fell through pride; and therefore the good angels always labor so that their number may be completed from human beings and they may attain the perfect number—that is, ten. How then does wisdom

[Col. 0342C] strengthen the wise man above the ten princes of the city? Because the help of wisdom—that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ—is greater than that of the angels.

What does Solomon mean when he says (v. 20), “I found one man out of a thousand; but among all women I found none”? Were there not many holy women, virgins and widows alike, who pleased God by modesty, chastity, and good works, and of whom very many

[Col. 0342D] were crowned by martyrdom?

Indeed there were, and even now there are very many virgins and widows acceptable to God. But Solomon says this because in his own time he could scarcely find a good man among many men. Among women, however, he found none, because all had abandoned themselves to lust. Can this statement be understood spiritually? Indeed it can. By the man is signified a good thought of the mind, while by the woman a carnal and dissolute thought. Thus among a thousand men scarcely one pure and clean thought is found that is not disturbed and outwardly defiled by perverse thought. But among women none is found pleasing to God, because carnal and perverse thought is not acceptable to God.

## Chapter VIII

[Col. 0343A]

What does he mean when he says (v. 5), “He who keeps God’s commandment will experience no evil”? How will he experience no evil, when holy men who kept God’s commandments suffered many evils in this age?

It is true because one who keeps God’s commandments—that is, everything that God commanded and enjoined—will experience no evil in the future; that is, he will suffer and endure no evil on the day of judgment. Although he may suffer some evils in this life, they are slight and transitory. For in the future life he will suffer no evil, because he will attain the reward and glory of eternal blessedness.

## Chapter IX

[Col. 0343B] What does he mean when he says (v. 4), “A living dog is better than a dead lion”? What does Solomon mean by a living dog or a dead lion?

The living dog signifies the Gentiles; the dead lion, the people of the Jews abandoned by God. Therefore this living dog is better before God than the dead lion, because we who believe from among the Gentiles, living through faith, know God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But the Jews, dead through unbelief, know nothing. Alternatively: the dog is a sinner who confesses himself dead through sins and, rising through repentance, begins to live through righteousness. The dead lion is the righteous person who trusts in his own righteousness and glories in his own merits and, being thereby exalted in pride, is dead before God. Therefore the humble sinner

[Col. 0343C] corrected through repentance is better than the proud righteous person: for the latter is abominable, while the former is acceptable to God.

What does he mean when he says (v. 8), “Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not fail from your head”? Can anyone always have white garments? And even if someone were so rich that he could always have white garments, since that is altogether difficult, how can it happen that oil should never fail from his head? Who could ever bear always to have his head anointed with oil?

This statement must be understood not historically but spiritually. For garments signify virtues by which the soul is clothed and adorned.

[Col. 0343D] Oil signifies a work of mercy, that is, almsgiving, or certainly spiritual joy. And this is the sense: “Let your garments be white at all times”; that is, whatever good things you do, let them be clean and pure, so that they may be acceptable to God; never fail in good works, and always strive to have spiritual joy.

## Chapter X

What are the flies of which Solomon says (v. 1), “Dying flies destroy the sweetness of ointment”?

Literally, if flies die in precious ointment, they destroy its sweetness. Yet Solomon intends spiritual flies here. What then are spiritual flies?

[Col. 0344A] Demons, vices, and sins: all these destroy the sweetness of the ointment, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit.

What does he mean when he says (v. 21), “The heart of the wise man is at his right hand, and the heart of the fool at his left”? For who has his physical heart in his right or left hand?

Truly no one; and therefore this statement must be understood spiritually. How? By the heart is signified intention or thought; by the right hand, a good work; by the left hand, an evil work. Therefore the wise person’s heart is at his right hand, because the thought and intention of a wise man tend and labor toward this end: that he may always do good, so that on the day of judgment he may deserve to stand at the Lord’s right hand—that is, among the lot of the righteous—and to glory with them in eternal blessedness. But the fool’s heart is at his left

[Col. 0344B] hand, because he adds evil deeds to the evils he thinks, on account of which he will be placed at the left—that is, among the lot of the reprobate—on the day of judgment, and will be punished with them forever.

Who is that spirit of whom he says (v. 4), “If the spirit of one having authority rises over you, do not leave your place”? Who is the one having authority, whose spirit, if it rises over us, means that we must not leave our place?

The devil, prince of this world; his spirit is evil suggestion. How does the devil’s spirit rise over us? By persuasion he causes us to think evil thoughts. Therefore, if through the devil’s suggestion an evil impulse rises in our heart, we must not give it a place, but must fight strongly against it,

[Col. 0344C] lest perhaps we carry the evil thought into action. It can also be understood thus: If you possess humility of life, purity, chastity, patience, and charity, and the devil suggests to you pride, lust, impurity, or hatred, do not leave your place—that is, humility—lest you become proud; and the same is to be understood concerning the rest.

What does Solomon mean when he says (v. 16), “Woe to you, O land, whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning”? Was not the land of Israel blessed, which had David as its young king, when he was twenty years old at the time he assumed the kingdom? Was not Josiah a good king, though he began to reign in youth?

David and Josiah were indeed good kings; but truly woe to the land whose king is young—that is, one in whom wisdom and prudence are slight, weak, and carnal. He who follows youthful desires hates righteousness, truth, and judgment. How do princes eat in the morning? When princes live luxuriously, they eat in the morning; and therefore woe

[Col. 0344D] to the land whose princes eat in the morning, because they love the pleasure of this age and the delight of the flesh more than the welfare of the people, and thus, through luxurious living, come to judgment.

How is it that (v. 17), “Blessed is the land whose king is noble and whose princes eat at their proper time”?

If a king is noble—handsome in wisdom, splendid in justice, adorned with good character and deeds—the land over which he presides is truly blessed, because he rules it in judgment and equity and exalts justice. Who are those princes who eat at their proper time? Those who do not live luxuriously, who do not love the pleasure of this age, who do not live in feasting and drunkenness, but seek food only for bodily sustenance. Therefore blessed is the land that has such princes, because, since they love justice and equity, they do not pervert justice.

[Col. 0345A]

## Chapter XI

What does he mean when he says (v. 2), “Give portions to seven, and also to eight”? What are these portions of seven and eight?

By the number seven the Old Testament is signified, on account of the Sabbath, which is the seventh day sanctified in the Law. By the number eight the New Testament is signified, on account of the Lord’s Day, which is the eighth day consecrated by the Lord’s resurrection. How, then, should what he says be understood: “Give portions to seven, and also to eight”? In this way: receive both Testaments, the Old and the New, with equal reverence, and diligently fulfill their commandments.

What does he mean when he says (v. 3), “If a tree falls to the south or to the north, in whatever place it falls, there it will be”? Will a tree that falls toward the north or south remain there? Does it not often get moved to other parts of the world?

[Col. 0345B] No one doubts this. But this statement must be understood spiritually. By the tree a human being is signified,

[Col. 0345C] because each person is like a tree in the forest of the human race. By the north, which is a cold wind, the punishment of hell is signified. And this is the sense: Wherever a person has prepared a place and future dwelling for himself, there he will be when he dies. That is, if by living well he has prepared for himself a place in the south, when he falls—that is, when he dies—he will remain forever in the rest of paradise and the glory of the heavenly kingdom. But if by living badly he has prepared for himself a place in the north, he will suffer the punishments of hell for ages of ages.

What does he mean when he says (v. 4), “He who observes the wind does not sow, and he who considers the clouds never reaps”? Who is so foolish as always to observe

[Col. 0345D] the wind so as not to sow, and to consider the clouds so as never to reap?

This statement must be understood spiritually. For storms are often produced by wind and clouds. By the wind the devil is signified; by the clouds, the adversities of the present age. Whoever fears the persecution of the devil or the adversities of the world does not sow—that is, he does not preach the word of God or do the good that he can. Nor will he ever reap, because even if he begins some good works, he does not bring them to perfection. What, then, must be done? Without regard for the clouds and without fear of the winds, we must sow amid storms—that is, amid every adversity we must preach God’s word and always do the good works that we are able to do.

[Col. 0346A] What does Solomon mean when he says (v. 6), “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening let not your hand cease”? For who can always sow morning and evening, especially when no one dares sow in freezing weather?

The seed here is not to be understood as wheat or anything else of that kind, but as the seed of a good work, from which grows the fruit of righteousness and the reward of eternal recompense. What, then, does he teach by saying, “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening let not your hand cease”? That at no time and at no age should we cease from good works; that evening may find our morning righteousness, and the rising sun in turn may increase our evening mercy. In youth and old age alike, may an abundance of virtues always commend us to God.

[Col. 0346B] “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening let not your hand cease”—that is, always exercise yourself in good works.

## Chapter XII

What does he mean when he says (v. 5), “The almond tree will blossom, the locust will grow fat, and the caper plant will be scattered”? What benefit was there in saying this, since no one is ignorant that the almond tree usually blossoms, the locust grows fat, and the caper plant is scattered?

This statement must be understood spiritually and contains a great mystery. By the almond tree our Lord Jesus Christ is signified, because just as the almond nut consists of shell, stone, and kernel, so by the almond stone divinity is signified; by the locust, the Gentile people; by the caper plant, the

[Col. 0346C] Jewish people. How should this statement be understood? “The almond tree will blossom,” that is, Christ will be born and shine forth with miracles. “The locust will grow fat,” that is, the Gentile people will believe and be filled with spiritual goods. “The caper plant will be scattered,” that is, the Jewish people will perish because of unbelief.

Why are the words of the wise compared with goads and nails? For Solomon says thus (v. 11): “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven in deeply.”

The words of the wise are most fittingly compared to goads and nails, because they do not know how to stroke the faults of sinners but to prick them. Those who are truly wise undoubtedly have words that are nails and goads:

[Col. 0346D] they do not cherish sinners with flattery, but rebuke them with harsh reproof and, as though pricking their secret consciences, stir them to lamentation and labor so that they may be corrected.

What does he mean when he says there, “Which were given by the counsel of teachers from one shepherd”? Who are those teachers by whose counsel the words of the wise were given? Or who is the one shepherd from whom they were given?

The teachers are the holy prophets and apostles. The one shepherd is God, from whom all the words of the wise were given, because he himself taught the teachers—that is, the prophets and apostles—and instructed their counsel, since he gave words in their hearts and mouths.

What does Ecclesiastes mean when, at the end of his book, he says

[Col. 0347A] (v. 13), “Fear God and keep his commandments. This is the whole human being”? How can this alone be the whole human being—that is, fearing God and keeping his commandments? For the portion of people who neither fear him nor keep his commandments is much greater than that of those who fear and keep them.

Indeed the number of the wicked is greater than that of the good, because, as the Lord says, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16), and the multitude of unbelievers is incomparably greater than that of believers. What, then, does Solomon wish to show here? In these words he shows that one who does not fear God and keep his commandments is not a human being. Why is he not a human being? Because he does not preserve the measure and rational order

[Col. 0347B] of his nature. What is the rational order and measure of human nature? To live rationally. For among all animals, only the human being was created a rational animal, since among all living creatures only the human being received reason and understanding from God, so that he might recognize his Creator, love and fear him,

[Col. 0348A] and praise him with mouth and heart alike. What is it to fear God? To fulfill his will and do the good works that ought to be done. Therefore one who does not fear God and keep his commandments is not a human being. What, then, is he? A beast. How is he called a beast? If he is cruel to his household, subjects, or neighbors, he is a lion, not a human being. If he is a robber, he is a tiger or wolf. If he is an adulterer, fornicator, or unclean person, he is a dog or pig; if he is foolish, he is compared with an ass. A deceitful and hypocritical person is fittingly likened to a little fox. The same is to be understood of the rest. Who is truly human? Only the one who fears God and keeps his commandments is human.

## Peroration

[Col. 0348B] We have humbly set down these things concerning Solomon’s Proverbs, lest, believing nothing other than what we find written according to the outward form of visible things in figurative expressions, we should rather, when instructed by figures, ascend to knowledge of the things that are true.

## [On the Song of Songs]

[Col. 0347]

# Exposition on the Song of Songs

(*Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*, XX, 1153.)

## Here Begins the Letter of Honorius, Outstanding Teacher, on the Song of Songs

[Col. 0347C]

Honorius, to one seeking the gift of wisdom with Solomon: may you obtain from the true Peacemaker what you ask.

Because I expounded, however inadequately, the book of David for your predecessor, the venerable Abbot C[onon] of blessed memory, you, his successor, ask—indeed, by commanding, demand—that I expound the book of Solomon for you. You maintain that it is just that, as I offered to the father of the father a work produced with great sweat, so I ought to offer to you, as the son of the son, a work elucidated by my pen. Therefore I did what you commanded and set forth plainly the book of Solomon entitled *Song of Songs*, celebrated in the mouths of many but unlocked in the understanding of few. By the illumination of the Holy Spirit, I made clear for all diligent readers a work obscure to the idle,

[Col. 0347D] claiming for myself nothing but the labor alone, while assigning the interpretations to their authorities [variant: “to the authority of the saints”].

## Here Begins the Prologue to the Book of Solomon Called the Song of Songs

At the beginnings of books, three things are sought: namely, author, subject matter, and intention. The author, so that you may know the writer’s name—whether he was pagan or faithful, Catholic or heretic. The subject matter, so that you may know whether he treats of wars, weddings, or what other matters. The intention, so that you may learn whether he recommends or discourages the matter of which he treats, or what usefulness the book, when read, confers.

The author of this book is the Holy Spirit, speaking

[Col. 0348C] through the vessel of wisdom, Solomon, the writer of this book, who was a most wise king and an outstanding prophet. Therefore one does not read “a reading from the book of Solomon,” but “a reading from the book of Wisdom.” Solomon composed three works in heroic meter, and distributed them also among the three branches of philosophy: ethics, physics, and logic. He assigned Proverbs to ethics, in which he taught good morals, as there: “Hear, my son, the instruction of your father, and do not forsake the law of your mother” (Prov. 1:8). He assigned Ecclesiastes to physics, in which he discussed the natures of things, as there: “All rivers enter the sea; to the place from which the waters flow, they return in order to flow again” (Eccl. 1:7). He assigned the Song of Songs to logic, in which he willed, or taught, that the rational soul should be joined to God through love, as there: “Love is strong

[Col. 0348D] as death. Many waters could not quench charity” (Song 8:6–7).

“Author” is an equivocal term. An equivocal term is one which is one in spelling but diverse in meaning, as “lion.” For there is the lion as a heavenly constellation in heaven, the terrestrial lion as a beast on earth, and the aquatic lion as a fish in water. There is also Leo as a human name, namely that of an apostolic ruler or an emperor; and there is a lion as a painting or sculpture. So too “author” is equivocal. There is the author of a city—that is, its founder—as Romulus of Rome; there is the author of a crime—that is, its leader or standard-bearer—as Judas of Christ’s death; and there is the author of a book—that is, its composer—as David of the Psalter and Plato of the *Timaeus*. “Author” is also a common noun, said to derive from *augere*, “to increase.”

[Col. 0349A] The subject matter of the book is bridegroom and bride, that is, Christ and the Church, as is read in the Gospel: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29); and likewise: “Ten virgins went out to meet the bridegroom and bride” (Matt. 25:1). Christ is called bridegroom by analogy, because as a bridegroom is carnally joined to his bride and becomes one with her, so Christ, through the flesh he assumed, is united with the Church, and she, through eating his body, is incorporated into him. Hence she is written to be his body, of which he is read to be the head, and all the elect, joined to him through faith and love, are his members: these are its subject matter.

This book treats of marriages which take place in four modes: historically, allegorically, tropologically, and anagogically. According to history, marriages occur in two ways: either by carnal intercourse

[Col. 0349B] or by betrothal alone. By betrothal alone, as with Mary and Joseph. By carnal intercourse, as with Solomon and Pharaoh’s daughter, whom he joined to himself by the right of marriage, and for whom he built a house adorned with gold and gems.

According to allegory likewise, marriages occur in two ways. The first is that in which the Word of God joined flesh to himself—that is, in which God assumed human nature, which, exalted at the Father’s right hand, he placed upon the throne of glory. The second is that in which Christ, God and man, joined to himself the universal Church—that is, the entire multitude of believers—through participation in his body. He betrothed her with his blood, washed her in the laver of baptism, and endowed her with the various gifts of the Holy Spirit.

According to tropology too, marriages occur in two ways: first, that in which the soul is joined to Christ through love;

[Col. 0349C] second, that in which the soul, which is the lower power of the inner person, is united through consent to the divine law with the spirit, which is its superior husband. From this marriage spiritual offspring is born, that is, good work.

According to anagogy likewise, marriages occur in two ways: first, that in which Christ, rising from death as the new man, ascended into heaven and joined the multitude of angels to himself; second, that in which, still after the resurrection, he united the whole Church to himself in the vision of the glory of his divinity.

Three marriages are read of in the Gospel. The first is there: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding for his son” (Matt. 22:2). The second is there: “Be like people awaiting their master, when he returns from the wedding” (Luke 12:36). The third

[Col. 0349D] is there: “And those who were ready entered with him into the wedding” (Matt. 25:10).
