The first wedding was when the King of heaven joined human nature to his Son, Christ. There the bridal chamber was the Virgin’s womb, from which he “came forth as a bridegroom from his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18:6). To this wedding he invited all the patriarchs before the Law and all the prophets under the Law. The second wedding was when Christ, the new man, ascended to heaven and joined the multitude of angels to himself. To this wedding he summoned all nations through the apostles. The third wedding will be after the judgment, when through the angels he transfers the Church to the heavenly Jerusalem and joins her to himself in the bridal chamber of glory through the vision of his very divinity. To this wedding, through the prelates of the Church, he draws many willing persons and compels many unwilling persons to enter. The subject matter of this

[Col. 0350A] book is woven from these weddings; therefore it is also called an *epithalamium*, that is, a wedding song.

Its intention is to join the Church, or any soul that is Christ’s bride, to Christ the bridegroom through love. This love is divided in two, namely love of God and love of neighbor. Love of neighbor has two forms: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16); and “What you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. 7:12). Love of God has one form: that we keep his commandments, as is written: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14:23).

For the title of this book is *Song of Songs*, that is, “praise of praises.” For just as in the Law some things are called holy and others holy of holies, more sacred than these, so it is called *Song of Songs* because it is set above all songs. For some songs are songs of victory, as: “Let us sing to the Lord” (Exod. 15:1); some are songs of thanksgiving, as: “My heart has exulted in the Lord” (1 Sam. 2:1).

[Col. 0350B] But these songs sing of the marriage of Christ and the Church, and therefore surpass all songs. The difference between a *canticum* and a *carmen* is that a *carmen* is scanned according to a fixed metrical rule, while a *canticum* is sung with melody. A *canticum*, moreover, is the mind’s delight in eternal things, and it signifies the good life through which the joy of eternal exultation is acquired.

And it should be known that these words, “Let him kiss me” (Song 1:1), are not themselves a song, but speak about the song, [Col. 0350C] because they sing of the good life of the righteous, which consists in love. For the song is the life of the righteous; the Song of Songs is the life of the perfect.

“Book” (*liber*) is an equivocal term. For *Liber* is Bacchus, the god of wine; *liber* is also a free-born person; likewise *liber* is the inner bark drawn from a tree, upon which the ancients were accustomed to write, whence copyists were also called *librarii*. A *liber* is thus that in which one reads.

This book is one of the seven books of the Hagiographa. Holy Scripture, therefore, is divided into two parts: the Old and the New Testament. The writers of the Old Testament were prophets, while the writers of the New Testament were apostles; but the author of both is the Holy Spirit. Of the Old Testament, as is read or written: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” [Col. 0350D] (Ps. 84:9). Of the New, as is read: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

The Old Testament is divided into three parts: history, prophecy, and hagiography. History narrates past events, as Genesis does. Prophecy foretells future things, as Isaiah does. Hagiography treats eternal things, as David does. There are seven books of the Hagiographa, corresponding to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: namely, Job, David, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Songs, the Book of Wisdom, and Ecclesiasticus. Of these, Job is assigned to the spirit of wisdom; David to the spirit of understanding; Proverbs to the spirit of counsel; Ecclesiastes to the spirit of fortitude; the Songs to the spirit of knowledge; the Book of Wisdom to the spirit of piety; and the book of Jesus son of Sirach to the spirit of fear. These [Col. 0351A] are the seven pillars by which the great house of Wisdom is supported.

And it should be noted that the Songs are assigned to the spirit of wisdom, because knowledge of the whole of Scripture is contained within the Songs.

Moreover, it should be noted that the Songs occupy the fifth place among the Hagiographa, because there are, indeed, five degrees of love: sight and conversation, touch and kisses, and consummation. First, a maiden pleasing in appearance is chosen; then the lover speaks to the chosen one; third, he embraces her with gentle touch; fourth, he kisses her; fifth, the matter is consummated by deed. Thus God predestined and chose the primitive Church in the patriarchs by sight, when he said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18).

[Col. 0351B] In Moses and the prophets he addressed her, saying: “If you do what I command you, I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exod. 23:22). He touched her by the presence of his assumed flesh, saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). He gave her a kiss when, victorious over death and rising again, he restored to her the peace she had lost, saying: “Peace be with you” (John 20:19). The consummation still remains; it will occur when, after judgment has been completed, he brings her also into the joy of her Lord, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

Every book of Holy Scripture has its own divisions and its own numerical meanings. For example, the Psalter is divided into three parts and sets forth the three ages [Col. 0351C] of the world: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. In these all the righteous fought against vices and sins, and the psalms sing their victories. Those psalms are divided into fifteen decades, which are fitted, as it were, as so many steps into a ladder raised toward heaven, by which the victorious may climb from the valley of tears to the kingdoms of heaven.

This book, however, is divided into four parts, because the Church, Christ’s bride, of whom it sings, is gathered from the four regions of the world, through the four Gospels, into the bridegroom’s chamber. He himself says: “They shall come and recline from west and east, from south and north, with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8:11).

The bride was brought from the east when the multitude [Col. 0351D] of the elect before the Law was chosen into the faith of the patriarchs, who believed this promise: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18), that is, in Christ. The bride was brought from the south when the multitude of peoples under the Law was gathered into the faith of the prophets, who believed this prophecy: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel, that is, God with us” (Isa. 7:14): this was Christ, God and man. The bride was brought from the west when the multitude of the Gentiles under grace was drawn to the faith of Christ through the apostles. The bride is brought from the north when, under Antichrist, the multitude of unbelievers is converted to the faith.

Alternatively, the east signifies childhood, the south youth, the west old age, and the north decrepitude. From [Col. 0352A] these a great multitude is daily gathered through faith and love into the embrace of the bridegroom.

This division is represented in the book itself by four persons, to each of whom one part is assigned: the daughter of Pharaoh, the daughter of the king of Babylon, the Shunammite, and the mandrake. Two of these exist in reality and two in signification. For Pharaoh’s daughter was in fact joined and united to Solomon in marriage. And the queen of the south, who is figuratively called the daughter of the king of Babylon, in fact came to the temple of the Lord adorned with gold, silver, and gems. But the Shunammite and the mandrake—that is, a headless maiden—are introduced solely for their signification.

Pharaoh’s daughter was brought from the east in a chariot. The queen of the south was brought from the south on camels. The Shunammite was brought from the west in Aminadab’s four-horse chariot. The mandrake was gathered from fields in the north [Col. 0352B] and carried in hands.

Pharaoh’s daughter was the Hebrew people, which was born and grew up under Pharaoh’s rule. Solomon joined her to himself when the Lord transferred the vine from Egypt and planted it in Judaea. She is brought to the bridegroom in a chariot because under the Law she is led to the worship of the true God. But she deserted God’s chariot and mounted Pharaoh’s chariots when the Hebrew people, abandoning God’s Law, took up idolatry at the command of their rulers. For the kings and priests of Israel were Pharaoh’s chariots when they introduced Egyptian idolatry among God’s people through the golden calves at Bethel.

Indeed, Pharaoh means “stripping” or “scattering,” and he is the devil, who stripped them of divine worship and scattered them by various errors. Moreover, this bride came from the east because she was first in the world to receive the worship of God, and she herself brought forth according to the flesh the sun of righteousness.

The daughter of the king of Babylon—that is, of the devil—is the Gentile world. Babylon, indeed, means “confusion,” and it is this world, in which the human race has been confounded by many sins. Its king is the devil, who rules all those confounded in sins. His daughter is the Gentile world, born in the confusion of idolatry. But, made queen of the south, she came to Solomon because, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, whom the south wind signifies, she came to the true peace-making Christ, to reign in heaven. He brought her into the temple of the Lord, because Christ made her the temple of the living God.

She brought gold and gems for the adornment of the temple, [Col. 0352D] because by wisdom and the ornament of virtues she adorned the house of God—that is, herself. She came borne upon camels because she had been instructed by philosophers, who were fit for teaching useful arts as camels are fit for bearing burdens, though they were twisted and deformed by sins. She came to the bridegroom as though from the south, because she transferred herself from the heat of worldly glory to the worship of Christ.

But the Shunammite came from the west in Aminadab’s chariot. Shunem is the city from which came that Shunammite whose son Elisha raised from death. For he first sent a servant with a staff, but the servant could not raise the dead boy. Elisha came, conformed himself to the dead one, and he immediately arose. This dead man signifies the human race. The servant who laid the staff upon the dead man was Moses, who laid the staff of the Law upon those dead in sins; it oppressed them more, rather than raising them. [Col. 0353A] Elisha, whose name means “my God is salvation,” is Christ: salvation given to us by God. Made mortal in the likeness of human beings, he raised the dead human race.

Moreover, the Shunammite means “captive,” and she is the Synagogue, still held captive in unbelief by the devil. She is brought to the bridegroom from the west because at the end of the world she will be converted to faith in Christ. And this is in Aminadab’s chariot. Aminadab was the priest in whose chariot the ark, formerly captured by the Philistines, was brought back to Jerusalem. The ark came from Judaea to the Gentiles when Christ transferred himself from the Synagogue to the Church. The ark will be returned to Jerusalem when, under Elijah and Enoch, Christ returns to Judaea now converted. Aminadab, whose name means “my willing people,” is Christ, who offered himself in a voluntary death for his people.

[Col. 0353B] His chariot is the Gospel, in which he travelled through the world. The wheels of this chariot are the four evangelists. Its horses are the apostles, who drew this chariot when they preached Christ’s Gospel throughout the world. Hence it is written: “You shall ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3:8). Upon this chariot the Shunammite is brought to the bridegroom when the Synagogue is received into fellowship with Christ through the Gospel.

But the mandrake—that is, the headless maiden—comes from the north. The mandrake is a plant having a human form but lacking a head. It signifies the multitude of unbelievers after Antichrist, when the mandrake’s head is cut off—that is, when Antichrist is killed, who is written to be the head of all evils. Then she returns to the true head from the north, that is, from unbelief, and is subjected to him in holiness. She is gathered from the field because this multitude is assembled from the whole world. She will be brought in hands because she will be joined to the Church through visible works. The subject matter of this book is treated under these four figures. The sequence of the whole book’s composition is as follows.

## ANOTHER PROLOGUE OF HONORIUS, THE MOST EMINENT DOCTOR, ON THE SONG OF SONGS BEGINS

The emperor of the heavenly commonwealth, wishing to have an heir, begot for himself a coequal Son, whom “he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages” (Heb. 1:2). In order that he might have children as co-heirs of the kingdom, the Father betrothed to him a queen and a concubine—that is, angelic and human nature.

Meanwhile, a certain prince seized tyranny and wished to be like the Most High. The queen consented to his tyranny, deserted the emperor, and attached herself to the tyrant. Defiled by adultery with him, she was deprived of the royal throne and condemned with that same tyrant to eternal exile. The concubine was immediately preferred in dignity and designated for the crown of the kingdom.

The crown was deferred at that time because she was not yet perfectly adorned. The highest adornment of human nature is obedience to the divine command. Therefore the king’s son placed the chosen woman, to be adorned for the royal crown, in paradise as though in a bedchamber. He gave the commandment as the material for her adornment, commanding her to adorn herself with obedience and promising that, once adorned, he would receive her into the royal hall and fellowship of the kingdom.

Her rival, seeing this and envying it, was inwardly wounded with grief of heart that one lower than herself in dignity should be preferred, while she herself was deprived of glory and honour. She craftily deceived the unwary woman, declaring that the adornment of obedience would not benefit her but rather harm her. Alas, she received the adornment from the deceived woman when she persuaded her to obey herself rather than God!

Therefore the bridegroom, offended because she had cast aside the adornment he had given her—indeed, had given it to his rival, whom he had rejected—expelled her from the chamber of paradise. He withheld his favour until she should recover the lost adornment from her rival; then she might hope for the bridegroom’s favour and the crown of the kingdom. This was to be accomplished by resisting vices and lusts and by obeying God’s commands even unto death.

Human nature received this adornment of obedience when Christ was obedient to the Father unto death: that is, made man, he maintained the obedience owed to God so firmly that, not even conquered by death, [Col. 0354B] he abandoned it. Once recovered in this way, the bride thereafter retained this adornment so firmly that it could not be torn away from her even by a thousand deaths.

Thus, expelled from paradise, she wandered in the world to recover the adornment, because she still had neither Law nor teacher. Giants, sent by her rival as though they were robbers, led her further astray and defiled her with many stains of vices. Moved by compassion for her miseries, the bridegroom destroyed her enemies by the flood. But he entrusted her to Noah, as though to a tutor, to be guarded. Noah enclosed her in the ark as though in a school to be instructed, where she lay hidden in small number among clean and unclean animals.

There she was taught that Noah prefigured the Christ to come; that the ark bore the type of the future Church; that the clean animals were those lawfully using marriage; and that the unclean animals were those unlawfully defiling themselves. The flood signified baptism, which would be the destruction of sins and the salvation of the righteous. The raven which went forth from the ark and did not return signified future heretics, departing from the Church and never to return. But the dove returning with an olive branch signified either the grace of the Holy Spirit sent into the Church, or the simple fallen who return in repentance.

Then, at the prompting of her rival, enemies built a tower from which they publicly attacked her and turned her from love of the bridegroom to the embrace of the adulterer—that is, from the worship of God to the worship of an idol. But when she was in distress, the bridegroom came to her aid: he divided and confounded the languages of her enemies, and committed her to Abraham, his friend, under the guardianship of Sarah. Abraham led her from Mesopotamia into the promised land, [Col. 0354D] where she deserved to hear: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). And again: “Your seed shall possess the gates of its enemies” (ibid., 17). There he begot Isaac, heir of the world.

Here it says that Abraham, whose name means “father of many nations,” prefigured Christ, the future Father of all believing nations. Sarah, whose name means “princess,” expressed the Church, which would obtain in heaven the supremacy of her rival. Abraham’s seed was to be Christ, her bridegroom, in whom all nations were to be blessed. The gates of the enemies were the places of the fallen angels, in which she was to be placed. Isaac, whose name means “joy,” signified the eternal joy which she would receive as her inheritance. Mesopotamia, whose name means “between rivers,” signified the fleeting riches of the age [Col. 0355A] and the passing honours of the world, from which Christ led the Church forth and introduced her into the promised land—that is, paradise.

Hence Abraham’s steward brought that same woman, in Rebekah, from Mesopotamia to Isaac; Isaac took her in marriage and begot two sons: one blessed by his father, the other rejected. To this Rebekah the Lord also says: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your womb; one people shall overcome another people, and the elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23).

That steward bore the figure of the teachers who led Rebekah—whose name means “patience,” that is, the Church destined to suffer much for Christ—from Mesopotamia, that is, from the fleeting things of the world, to Isaac, whose name is “joy,” that is, to Christ the true joy. The two sons are the two orders of the Church: the clerical order, blessed for divine offices, and the lay order, excluded from this office. The two peoples are the spiritual and the carnal within the Church. Of these, the carnal, greater in number, serves the spiritual, fewer in number.

Then Jacob is set forth in Leah and Rachel. One was fruitful, the other long barren; at last the latter bore him who saved Egypt from the danger of famine, and for this reason was called the Saviour of the world. Jacob, whose name means “wrestler” or “one who sees God,” is Christ, who entered into conflict with the devil for the bride and conquered, and who always beholds God the Father. The two sisters are the two lives in the Church, namely the active and the contemplative. The active life is fruitful in carnal persons; the contemplative is barren in spiritual persons, yet she shall have a son who will save the world from [Col. 0355C] famine of the word of God, the true Saviour of the world.

After these things, suffering famine, she enters Egypt and is subjected to slavery by Pharaoh. When she cries out, Moses is sent as teacher and leader to help her. By the blood of the lamb he redeems her from Egypt, leads her out through the Red Sea with the spoils of Egypt, drowns the pursuing enemies, instructs her in the wilderness with the divine Law, makes the tabernacle from Egyptian spoils, and refreshes her with bread from heaven and water produced from the rock. Joshua son of Nun receives her, brings her into the promised land, defeats the enemies, and apportions their land to her as a possession.

Through these things she is taught that, though enduring the word of God, she would be enveloped in the obscure teaching of the Pharisees and thus subjected to the devil by many errors, until the true teacher, Christ, should come. He would redeem her from error and from the devil’s power by his own blood, as by that of an immaculate lamb. Coming, he washed her in baptism, overwhelmed sins as enemies in the sea, instructed her with evangelical teaching, refreshed her with his body and blood, and transformed worldly wisdom, as though Egyptian spoils, into weapons of righteousness when he taught her to fight heresies by means of it. The true Jesus—that is, Saviour—will yet bring her into the promised land, that is, paradise; and, when her enemies, namely demons and persecutors, have been condemned, he will distribute the dwellings of the heavenly kingdom to each according to merits.

For this bride Samson is shut up in Gaza and besieged by enemies; but, having broken the gates and terrified the enemies, he goes forth victorious and reaches the mountain summit. Samson, whose name means “sun,” is Christ, the sun [Col. 0356A] of righteousness. For the bride, the Church, he is shut up in the tomb or hell and besieged by guards; but, wrenching apart the gates of hell, he terrified the demons, rose from the tomb, put the soldiers to flight, and victoriously penetrated the summit of heaven.

Likewise David, walking upon the roof, saw her naked, grieved that she was joined to Uriah, and, after Uriah was slain, joined her to himself. From her David begot the vessel of wisdom. David, whose name means “beloved,” is Christ, wholly desirable; remaining upon the roof of heaven in the Father’s glory, he saw the Gentile world stripped of virtues and the robe of immortality, and grieved that she was joined to the devil. Uriah also means “the light of my God,” and signifies the devil, who transforms himself into an angel of light. Christ killed him in idolatry with the sword of preaching, joining the Church to himself; from her he begot children who love wisdom.

This David sang beforehand in the ten-stringed Psalter all the mysteries of Christ the bridegroom and the Church the bride. And Christ opened the Church’s understanding so that she might understand all that had been written concerning him in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.

After David, Solomon joined her to himself in Pharaoh’s daughter, and, receiving her in the queen of the south in the temple of the Lord, enriched her with many gifts. He built that temple from three materials: cut stones, cedar wood, and pure gold. He taught her ethics in Proverbs, natural philosophy in Ecclesiastes, and theology in the Songs.

Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” is Christ, true peace, reconciling all things in heaven and on earth (Col. 1:20). He joined to himself in faith the primitive Church coming out of Egypt, as though she were Pharaoh’s daughter. Receiving the Church coming from the Gentiles, as though the queen of the south, he joined her to his faith and endowed her with various gifts of grace. He will also receive her into the temple of heaven, which he will construct from three materials, namely from three orders of saints: married persons, continent persons, and virgins.

For married persons in the Church are like cut stones, perfected in the six works of mercy. Continent persons are like cedar wood, whose works are incorruptible. Virgins are like pure gold, shining with pure chastity and true charity. He spoke many things to her in parables, as it is written: “Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables” (Matt. 13:34). He discoursed to her at length concerning natures; he expounded theology throughout when he taught heavenly things.

Then the bride is taken captive to Babylon, but is released from captivity by King Cyrus, surnamed Christ, and is recalled to Jerusalem by Jesus the priest. By this it is taught that the Church, in her members, is carried captive into many heresies and various vices, in which she is confounded before God and angels. But, repenting, she is freed by Christ Jesus, the true priest, and returns to Jerusalem—that is, to the Church, or to the heavenly Jerusalem.

For this bride the Maccabees fought even to death, and martyrs shed their blood for the Church. After so many and such great evils, after so many and such great labours, after so many and such great miseries, the bridegroom himself visited his bride in peril. He restored to her the lost adornment through his obedience, washed her from filth by baptism, and clothed her with teachings, signs, and examples. He permitted the fatted calf—that is, himself—to be killed for her banquet; he adorned her with his blood and sealed her with the sign of the cross. He entrusted her to the *paranymphi*, that is, the apostles, and himself went to heaven to prepare the wedding.

Moreover, the *paranymphi* adorned her, once received, with signs and teachings even unto death; the martyrs, their successors, made her radiant with their blood; and teachers adorned her with many writings. When she has been perfectly adorned, a multitude of angels will bring her to the bridegroom’s heavenly court to be crowned. Having seated her upon the throne of glory, he will make her co-heir of his kingdom.

And this must be particularly noted: how often the tyrant and her rival tested her with many evils; by how many methods, stratagems, snares, and arts they strove to turn her from the bridegroom’s love, and yet could not prevail. To recount a few out of many: at first they enviously struck down Abel, her standard-bearer; through the giants they inflicted many wicked deeds upon her; and they afflicted the patriarchs in various ways. They sold Joseph, her foster-child, through his brothers, falsely confined him in prison, afflicted her while she lived as a stranger in Egypt through Pharaoh and his people with various torments, and cruelly killed her children.

As she was departing Egypt, they attacked her with the counsels and arms of the impious. Once established in the promised land, they harassed her under the judges and kings with many wars. They killed her prophets by various punishments, cruelly tore apart the Maccabees, and under the apostles and their successors they dismembered all the Church’s members with refined and unheard-of punishments at the hands of Jews and Gentiles, killing them by a thousand deaths. Finally, through heretics with false doctrine and through false Christians with hypocrisy, they harassed her everywhere. Yet in all these things they did not prevail against her.

Even now under Antichrist they will assail her by every kind of temptation in order to turn her from love of the bridegroom [Col. 0358A] and cause her to lose the promised crown; but they will by no means prevail, because she will receive eternal glory for her patience, whereas they will suffer eternal punishment for their envy.

While she was still little, before the Law, the patriarchs instructed her through figures concerning Christ. Under the Law, the prophets formed her in uprightness through Scriptures. When she was marriageable, under grace, the apostles adorned her with signs, teachings, and examples. Still to come, the choir of angels will lead her in joy and exultation into the temple of the King; the King of glory will crown her with glory and honour, unite her in joys within the bridal chamber, when he reveals himself to her as he is, coequal with the Father.

Her growth through six ages is distinguished by the different times of the world. Her infancy was from Adam to Noah; her childhood, from Noah to Abraham; her adolescence, from Abraham to David; her [Col. 0358B] youth, from David to the Babylonian captivity; her old age, from the Babylonian captivity to Christ; and her decrepitude, from Christ to the end of the world. From these acts, these ages, and these times, the book of this Scripture concerning such a bride is woven.

Nor should this be passed over: Pharaoh’s daughter has in her company the patriarchs, the prophets, and all the righteous from Abel to the thief. But the daughter of the king of Babylon has in her company the apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and all the elect from the centurion who said in the Gospel, “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. 27:54), to Elijah and Enoch. The Shunammite has in her company all who, under the preaching of Elijah and Enoch and under the persecution of Antichrist, shed their blood for Christ or died in faith in Christ. But the mandrake has in her company all who, after the death of Antichrist, shall have been converted to repentance throughout the world.

Having thus set these things forth beforehand, let us approach the literal sense itself; and the approach is as follows.

## FIRST TREATISE

[Col. 0357]

[Col. 0357C] The son of the king of Jerusalem betrothed to himself the daughter of the king of Babylon through four messengers. She replied to them: “Who is your lord?” But they said: “Our lord is King of kings and Lord of lords, King of glory and Prince of peace.” And she said: “Is he beautiful?” They replied: “Sun and moon marvel at his beauty, because he is fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44:3), “and wholly desirable,” upon whom angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1:12). And she said: “Is he powerful?” They replied: “His power is from sea to sea” (Zech. 9:10). And she said: “Is he rich?” They replied: “Glory and riches are in his house, and he shall make them drink from the torrent of his delight” (Pss. 3:3; 35:39). And she said: “Is he honoured with gifts?” They replied: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabs and of Sabadona shall bring them” (Ps. 71:10). And she said: “What is his service?” They replied: “All nations serve him” (ibid., 11). And she said: “What is his praise?” They replied: “All nations magnify him” (ibid., 17).

Having heard these things, she replied: “May your lord himself come and kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1), and tell me what pleases him, and I shall do [Col. 0358C] his will.

The heavenly Jerusalem’s king is God, whose son is Christ. The king of Babylon, of this world, is the devil, as it is written: “The prince of this world has been judged” (John 16:11). His daughter was human nature, made so through imitation of sin.

For “father” is spoken of in Scripture in four ways: in two ways by generation and in two ways by imitation. By generation, Adam is called the father of this race, and Abraham the father of Isaac. By imitation, God is called the Father of the righteous, as in: “Be perfect, that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:48); and again: “One is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23:19). Likewise by imitation, the devil is called the father of the wicked, as in: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:41). By imitating him in evil, human nature became his daughter.

The Son of God betrothed this human nature when he made known to the patriarchs that he intended to assume human nature into himself. He sent messengers when he wished the prophets to announce this to the human race. They became, as it were, heralds when they proclaimed in the world the glory of his kingdom, his power, and his other insignia.

But the bride of Christ is understood in two ways: namely, the human flesh which he assumed, and the Church which he incorporated into himself. Human nature married him when he assumed flesh into divinity. The Church will yet marry him when he receives her into fellowship in the kingdom. This bride is divided, as it were, into two persons: the Synagogue and the Gentile world. To the latter the prophets were messengers; to the former the apostles were sent. Yet from these two there is one bride, namely the catholic Church, brought to Christ through messengers and married to him through human nature. This bride, therefore, desiring the bridegroom’s coming, says:

## CHAPTER ONE

**VERSE 1.**—“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” As though she said to the messengers: “He who has so often greeted me through you, who has communicated so many secrets to me through you, let him himself come and greet me with his kiss, and reveal his will to me with his own mouth.”

Holy Scripture is understood in four ways: historically, allegorically, tropologically, and anagogically. This is expressed by the table of the bread of the Presence in the tabernacle, which is supported by four feet. The tabernacle is the Church, in which service is rendered to Christ. The table is Holy Scripture, upon which is the setting forth of the loaves, that is, the refreshment of souls. The four feet are the four senses: history, when an event is narrated as it occurred; allegory, when the matter is expounded concerning Christ and the Church; tropology, which is applied to soul and spirit; and anagogy, when it is understood concerning the life above.

[Col. 0359C] In the vision of God, by which Ezekiel foresaw the entire future condition of the Church, he saw, among other things, a wheel within a wheel (Ezek. 1). It had four faces, and the spirit of life was in the wheels (ibid., 20). This wheel is Holy Scripture. The wheel within the wheel is the new Law hidden in the old. The four faces are the four senses: historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical. The spirit of life is in the wheels because the teaching of eternal life lies hidden in the Scriptures.

In history the event is marked according as it occurred. In allegory the interpretation of names is considered. In tropology a comparison of the events that occurred is investigated. In anagogy the likeness of things is weighed.

For example, the historical sense is that Solomon is called peaceful and built the temple in Jerusalem in seven years. The allegorical sense is that Solomon is called peaceful and is Christ; Jerusalem is “vision of peace” and is the Church, which Christ made into a temple for himself out of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The tropological sense is that, just as Solomon built the temple from wood and stones, so every believer makes within his own soul a temple for God from good works and the examples of the saints. The anagogical sense is that, just as Solomon made the temple in Jerusalem from precious stones, so Christ established in the heavenly Jerusalem a temple from living stones, that is, from all the elect.

Thus the historical sense is this: Pharaoh’s daughter, who was to be joined to Solomon, overcome by love replied to his messengers: “I no longer wish to be greeted through you messengers; let Solomon himself kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” The allegorical sense is this: Solomon is Christ; Pharaoh’s daughter is the Church, who answered the messengers—that is, the prophets—saying: “He who long ago kissed me through your mouth by consoling me and promising peace, let him himself at last kiss me with the kiss of his mouth: that is, he who was so often promised through the prophets, let him at last be incarnate and kiss me by his presence, and with his own mouth declare to me that the peace once lost has been restored.”

A kiss is so called as though it were “a drink of the mouth” (*oris poculum*). By the kiss peace is understood; by the mouth, the Word of the Father, that is, the Son. God kissed the bride as though with another’s mouth when long ago he spoke to the fathers in many portions and in many ways through the prophets (Heb. 1:1). He kissed her as though with his own mouth when, in these last days, he spoke in the Son (ibid., 2), saying: “Peace be with you” (John 20:19). That is to say: Know that the peace and grace which you lost in paradise through the devil have now been restored to you through my Son.

The first man also, expelled from paradise because of disobedience, lost for the human race peace and God’s grace. Therefore the primitive Church—namely Abel and the other righteous up to Abraham, then the patriarchs up to Moses, and from him the prophets up to John the Baptist—foreseeing in the Spirit that this peace would be restored through Christ, desired that he should be incarnate more swiftly. Accordingly, immediately after he was born the angels announced that peace had been restored, saying: “Peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Therefore the bride says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” As though she openly said: “May my bridegroom, who in anger expelled me from paradise because of the lost adornment and withheld his grace from me, now unite himself to me through assumed flesh; and through him may my adornment and the kiss of peace be restored to me.” For in the kiss flesh is joined to flesh and spirit is joined to spirit. Thus Christ is joined to the Church through flesh, and the Church is joined to his divinity through the Spirit. Further, by the touch of flesh love of neighbour is expressed, while by the touch of spirit love of God is expressed; through these Christ is joined to the Church.

Alternatively, human nature, designated as the bride and desiring to be deified in relation to angelic nature, says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” As though she said: “Let the Son of God, my promised bridegroom, come; by kissing me, let him join human nature to himself, and let him teach the way of salvation with his own mouth.” Out of excessive desire she speaks to one absent, addressing him as present and kissing her, saying: [Col. 0360D] “Your breasts are better than wine.” That is, your teachings, which are like milk, nourishment for children, are sweeter than other doctrines, which do not nourish but kill the simple and destroy children.

The tropological sense is this. The faithful soul, Christ’s bride, reflecting where she has been, where she will be, where she is, and where she is not—namely, that she has been in original and actual sin, that she will be at God’s dreadful judgment, that she is amid the vanities of the world, and that she is not in eternal blessedness—groaning and trembling says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” As though she said: “Let him who, in my flesh, sits at the right hand of the Father—my advocate and righteous judge—visit and kiss me as I grieve over my sins and tremble at his judgment; and with the sign of peace, the pledge of friendship which he promised penitents with his own mouth, [Col. 0361A] let him kiss me.”

Anagogically, however, it is thus: the Church, a pilgrim here below and longing for that homeland, says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” As though she said: “He who speaks to me daily in the Scriptures and promises eternal joys—let him at last appear in person at the judgment and, with his own mouth, grant the joys of peace, saying: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world’” (Matt. 25:34).

She speaks to one absent, so that greater affection may be expressed. The writing of this book is called a drama—that is, a love-song, sung by lovers without characters. Hence that song also is called dramatic in which different persons are introduced but nevertheless not named. [Col. 0361B] Thus in this book praises are sung by different persons without names. The song of the bride has preceded.

The song of the bridegroom follows.

**VERSE 1:2.**—“For your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments.” Historically this is understood thus: Solomon, receiving Pharaoh’s daughter when she came to him with a kiss, said: “You desired my kiss, and I kiss you, delighting in your breasts; for your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments.” That is to say: “I would rather enjoy your breasts than be intoxicated with wine or delighted by the finest ointments.”

Allegorically it is expounded thus: Christ, [Col. 0361C] coming in the flesh, says to his bride: “You asked to be kissed by me, and by my presence I kiss you; that is, I shall touch you with my sweetness and restore to you the peace you lost. I shall unite myself to you in faith and love, and you shall bear me children, co-heirs of the Father’s kingdom, whom you will nurse at your breasts; for your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments.”

This book is spiritual and speaks spiritually to spirits placed in bodies through bodily comparisons. The whole Church is like one body, whose head is Christ (Eph. 5:23), while the head of Christ is God (1 Cor. 11:3). The members of this body are the various orders in the Church: for example, the eyes are teachers, such as the apostles; the ears, obedient persons, such as monks; the nostrils, discerning persons, such as masters; the mouth, those who speak good things, such as presbyters; the hands, those defending others, [Col. 0361D] such as soldiers; the feet, those sustaining others by feeding them, such as peasants. As the Apostle says: “He himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as pastors, others as teachers, for the building up of the body of Christ” (Eph. 4:12), that is, of the Church. Its breasts are the two Testaments, from which unformed souls receive the milk of teaching, just as little children suck milk from their mothers’ breasts.

Wine, which puffs up and intoxicates its drinkers, is worldly wisdom, which makes those who embrace it foolish and inflated, as does dialectic. For secular knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up (1 Cor. 8), that is, spiritual knowledge. Therefore he says: “Your breasts are better than wine,” that is, the teaching drawn forth from your two Testaments—namely, from their works—by which you nurse and nourish your children who are little in faith, is better. This is to say: “It pleases me [Col. 0362A] more than the teaching of the Pharisees, although they teach one God.” By saying “better,” he shows that those other things too are good, because useful. For the liberal arts are useful, since they are instruments of Holy Scripture, as hammers are for a smith and weapons against heretics. Yet the testimonies of Holy Scripture, uttered with authority, are better, “fragrant with the finest ointments,” that is, redolent of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

A good ointment, in the literal sense, is one made from wild herbs and heals external wounds; a better ointment, made from finer ingredients, cures an illness beneath the skin; the best ointment, composed of precious spices such as nard, drives away inward pains or preserves the body from decay—like that ointment of Mary in the Gospel which she poured over Christ’s head.

[Col. 0362B] In the spiritual sense, a good ointment is the oil for the sick, with which the sick are anointed in the Church; a better ointment is holy oil, with which kings and priests are anointed; the best ointment is chrism, by which Christians are anointed into Christ’s kingship and priesthood.

Tropologically, a good ointment is the natural law: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another,” through which Abel, Enoch, and others pleased God. A better ointment is the written law, as: “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13), and so forth. The best ointment is under grace, as: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live” (Ezek. 33:11).

Allegorically, a good ointment is remission of sins in baptism through the Holy Spirit; a better ointment is good life after baptism through [Col. 0362C] the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that we may live soberly, devoutly, and justly; the best ointment is the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: namely, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and fear of the Lord. With the fragrance of such teaching the breasts of Mother Church are perfumed.

Anagogically it is understood of the soul thus: to the soul fearing judgment and seeking peace from the judge, the Bridegroom, who is also judge, says: “Because in repenting you seek from me the kiss of peace, I shall kiss you by forgiving your sins and granting you the peace of blessed life; for your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments.”

Two human beings are spoken of: the outer and the inner. The outer consists of three things: body, life, and external sense. [Col. 0362D] The inner likewise consists of three: internal sense, reason, and understanding. The body consists of the four elements—that is, earth, water, air, and fire—and in this we have something in common with stones. Life is the power of the soul that gives life to the body, and this we share with herbs and trees. Sense is the power of the soul that endows the body with sensation, and this we share with beasts and all living creatures. This sense is fivefold: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. By sight we distinguish colors; by hearing, sounds; by smell, odors; by taste, flavors; by touch, hard and soft things.

Internal sense is the power of the soul by which we imagine things past, present, and future. Reason is the power of the soul by which we distinguish the genera and species of images. Understanding is [Col. 0363A] the power of the soul by which we understand incorporeal things, such as love and wisdom. In these three consists the inner human being, in whom we have nothing in common with beasts. In this the image of God is expressed, and to this the Holy Spirit speaks in the Scriptures.

The difference between image and likeness is this: image belongs to the essence of nature, whereas likeness belongs to imitation of good or evil. We possess the image of God otherwise by nature; we lost likeness by sinning. Therefore, just as the outer human being has members suited to itself, so the inner human being has members suitable to it. Its words, then, are wisdom and knowledge, by which it so satisfies the unlearned as a mother nurses children at her breasts.

The wine that overturns the mind is external concern, by which she is anxious to minister to brothers and to honor and [Col. 0363B] adorn the churches of God. But her breasts are better than wine, because teaching by which she forms the unlearned in virtues pleases God more than concern by which she adorns churches liable to fall. These breasts are fragrant with the finest ointments because wisdom and knowledge, which nurse the unlearned, abound in the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

It is also expounded anagogically thus. Christ, the Father of the age to come, says to the Church longing for the heavenly homeland: “Because you so greatly desire the face of my presence and so earnestly seek from me the kiss of true peace, I shall kiss you; that is, I shall give you eternal peace with the angels and reveal myself to you as true peace. For your breasts are better than wine.”

The Church’s two breasts are the two commandments of charity, by which she forms her children in active and contemplative life, [Col. 0363C] so that they may render good, not evil, to anyone for evil. Wine, however, is the severity of the law, which commands that eye be returned for eye, tooth for tooth, and the killer be killed. But the Church’s breasts are better than wine, because the clemency of charity pleases God more than legal severity. These breasts are fragrant with the finest ointments because the commandments of charity are redolent, full of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

**VERSE 2.**—“Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens have loved you.” The bridegroom came to the bride, sent by the Father and anointed, so that he might also anoint the bride.

According to the historical sense, Pharaoh’s daughter, kissing Solomon, is understood to have perceived the fragrance of oil from his royal anointing and to have said: “Your name is oil poured out.” [Col. 0363D] That is: “As your head is fragrant with the oil of poured-out anointing, so the fame of your royal name, or of your peace, shines everywhere. Therefore young women love you.” Even if this did not occur in fact, though it could have occurred thus, it certainly occurred in signification.

According to the allegory, after the bridegroom by his kiss filled the bride’s breasts with ointment for nourishing children—that is, after Christ by his incarnation poured out the gifts of the Holy Spirit for teaching his children—she rejoicing said: “Your name is oil poured out.” Oil, while hidden in a vessel, does not give off fragrance; but poured out, it does. So Christ, while hidden in the Father’s bosom, seemed to give no fragrance; but when poured out and appearing in flesh, his name—that is, knowledge of him—became known to the whole world.

His name is Christ, meaning “Anointed One,” [Col. 0364A] which formerly lay hidden in the synagogue, where only kings and priests were anointed with oil and God was known only in Judaea. Now in the Church it has been poured out over every race of humankind, who are anointed with oil and chrism into Christ’s kingship and priesthood. Hence they are called Christians from Christ, and this name is now praiseworthy from the rising of the sun to its setting.

His name also is Jesus, meaning “Savior.” This name lay hidden in Joseph, who was called savior of the world because he saved Egypt from famine. It lay hidden in Joshua, leader of God’s people, who led the redeemed people into the land of promise. It also lay hidden in Jesus the priest, who brought the people back from captivity to Jerusalem. But this name was poured out when it became evident to all nations that he was the true Savior [Col. 0364B] who saved the world from the danger of famine of God’s word, who will lead the redeemed people into the land of promise—that is, into paradise—and who, as true king and priest, will lead the people from the captivity of the devil to the heavenly Jerusalem.

The name of Jesus is proclaimed throughout the whole earth, because through it everyone is marked with the oil of baptism; and the once-famous name of Moses is now scarcely heard from anyone, because the killing law is now abolished. Therefore he says: “Your name is oil poured out.” As though he said: “Just as poured-out oil gives a pleasant fragrance, so the fame of Christ’s name, made incarnate, shines everywhere.”

[Col. 0364C] Again, oil has six distinguishing qualities. Oil is called mercy; oil is a sign of peace; oil warms the weak; it heals wounds; it provides light for lamps; and it rises above all liquids. This signifies Christ, who is our mercy and our peace, who warmed us when weak by preaching, healed the wounds of sins through his wounds, supplied light by signs and miracles, and surpasses all saints.

While the bride enjoys the bridegroom’s kisses, a choir of young maidens enters and a hymn is sung by them. Thus, when the Church received Christ, a multitude of the faithful hastened together everywhere and sings praises to its receiver. Therefore it adds: “Therefore the young maidens have loved you,” that is, the souls of the faithful serve you in faith and love.

According to the tropological sense, a faithful soul [Col. 0364D] pours out its name like oil when it diffuses among its neighbors, by example, the fame of good action as a pleasant fragrance. This oil lies hidden in a vessel when no good work shines before one’s neighbors.

To such persons it is commanded: “Let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). The young maidens love this soul because faithful souls imitate it in goodness.

According to anagoge, however, the name of the Church walking toward heaven is poured out like oil when, because of the fragrance and light of good works, she is received into heaven like Christ. Saints and angels love her because they will rejoice with her forever in the oil of gladness—that is, in Christ and the Holy Spirit. This name now lies hidden like oil in a vessel, as long as she remains a pilgrim in this world.

The bride’s voice is added further.

**VERSE 3.**—“Draw me after you.” [Col. 0365A] Here it is understood that, after Solomon had received Pharaoh’s daughter with a kiss, he went up into the house he had built for himself, and she, wishing to accompany him, said: “Draw me after you.” The young maidens, that is, her girls, add: “We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” That is: “We shall run after you wherever we perceive the fragrance of your ointments.” He speaks according to the custom of that land, where noblewomen commonly used ointments so that, through their fragrance, they might better please their husbands, as is read concerning Esther and Judith.

Allegorically: after Christ [Col. 0365B] poured out the name of Christianity over every kind of humankind and drew the young maidens—that is, faithful souls—to love of himself by the fragrance of the oil of the Holy Spirit, he returned to heaven by a hard way to prepare for the bride a banquet of eternal sweetness. She wishes to follow him by the same way but cannot, and cries: “Draw me after you.” That is to say: “Give me strength to follow your footsteps on this way by which you went before to glory.”

The way of the Lord is not to desire the world’s prosperity and patiently to suffer its hardships for his sake. By this way he entered into glory. When the Jews wished to make him king, he fled; when they wished to crucify him, he willingly offered himself. He commands those following him to go by this way, saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. [Col. 0365C] 16:24), that is, imitate me. No one walks by this way unless drawn, as it is written: “No one comes to me unless the Father has drawn him” (John 6:44).

God draws us to himself in two ways and drives us in two ways. He draws us by promises of the sweetness of the heavenly homeland; he drives us by threats of the fire of Gehenna. He also draws us by diverse gifts and drives us by various scourges. Thus Moses drew the people by promising the riches of kings and drove Pharaoh by blows.

God draws some unwilling persons when his grace comes before them, inspiring them to will the good. He follows those who are willing by helping them, so that they may be able to do good. Therefore grace is when we are anticipated so that we may will; freedom, when we follow willingly; captivity, when we refuse to follow; frailty, when [Col. 0365D] we fall back while following; merit, when we do not fail in following—and we attribute this not to ourselves but to grace; eternal reward, the joy of the whole Church throughout the whole world, which constitutes one catholic Church.

The young maidens are as though newly made, because they have been renewed through baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Church says to the bridegroom, that is, Christ: “Draw me after you.” The young maidens—namely, her daughters, the churches—say that through grace he is to be imitated: “We too shall run in faith and love, in the fragrance of your ointments,” that is, in consideration of your miracles, or in the fame of your works, or in faith in eternal goods.

Tropologically, the faithful soul, willing what is good but unable by itself, cries to Christ: “Draw me after you.” [Col. 0366A] That is, “Give grace, so that I may come to you, who are the way, truth, and life, following your footsteps.” For no person turns to repentance unless drawn by grace.

Anagogically, the pilgrim Church, desiring heavenly things and unable to attain them by itself, cries: “Draw me after you—from this world to heavenly glory—so that I may see you there face to face; for no one can reach it by himself unless the grace and right hand of God draw him.”

**VERSE 3.**—“We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” The Church, perfect in faith and work, is called the bride, worthy to be crowned and placed in the bridal chamber of glory. Those still imperfect in faith, however, are called young maidens. All these say to the bride, namely, to the perfect in the Church: “We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” [Col. 0366B] That is: “Go before us by doing and teaching the way of the Lord, and we shall follow the fragrance of your ointments”—that is, imitate the examples of your works. For the Church’s ointments, as we said above, are the various gifts of the Holy Spirit; the fragrance of the ointments is the fame of good works.

By saying “we shall run,” he suggests that we must hasten toward life while we have time, as it is written: “Run while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12:35). The bride enters joined to the bridegroom’s side; after her the maidservants enter, because the perfect go before by their examples and others follow by imitation. This is applied tropologically thus: when those who have fallen see someone perfectly converted, they say: “We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments,” that is, “We shall imitate your example.”

[Col. 0366C] Anagogically, however, those fervent in love of the heavenly homeland say to the Church hastening toward things above: “We shall run after you from virtue to virtue, into the fragrance of spiritual joys.”

**VERSE 3.**—“The king brought me into his storerooms.” The bride, having entered the bridegroom’s inner chambers, returns to the young women and announces to them that they should run, so that they too may be brought in. The Hebrews relate that Solomon composed this book in honor of Pharaoh’s daughter, for whom he also built an incomparable house. According to the historical account, after bringing her into it, he showed her his treasure and offered various cups from the storerooms.

For a storeroom is so called as concealing wine. The young maidens, drunk from it, sing: “We shall exult and [Col. 0366D] rejoice in you.” That is: “We rejoice together in your honor, mindful of your breasts above wine,” that is, remembering the king’s saying: “Your breasts are better than wine,” namely, “They please me more than wine.” And because you please the king, the upright love you—that is, all good people rejoice with you, while the evil envy you.

According to allegory, the Church, drawn by Christ through grace into Holy Scripture, says: “The king brought me into his storerooms.” The storerooms, in which various drinks are kept, are the books of Holy Scripture, from which various teachings are offered to those thirsting for righteousness. When the reading about Joseph is read, it is as though a cup against adultery is offered; when the Scripture concerning Judith is recited, it is as though chastity is offered to drink. Christ brought the bride into these storerooms [Col. 0367A] when he opened her understanding so that she understood the Scriptures.

Christ is properly called king according to the flesh, by which he is set by the Father over the human race, as it is written: “But I have been appointed king by him” (Ps. 2:6). And again, to Pilate: “You say that I am a king” (John 18:37). Again: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18). And again: “He is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead” (Acts 10:42). He alone can introduce into Scripture, who alone could open the seven seals of the book: his incarnation, birth, passion, despoiling of hell, resurrection, ascension, and future judgment.

The young maidens say to the bride: “By giving us drink you have made us exult and rejoice; therefore we shall exult and rejoice [Col. 0367B] in you.” We shall exult in the body, namely by doing bodily works: vigils, fasts, almsgiving. And we shall rejoice in the mind, namely by doing spiritual works: reading, praying, preaching—and this in you. These works have no value unless they are in the catholic Church, “mindful of your breasts,” that is, holding in remembrance both laws, which are your breasts, from which we have sucked, so that we may serve the Lord in holiness and righteousness. And this is “above wine,” that is, above worldly wisdom, which teaches us to seek human praise and gather earthly riches. Therefore the upright love you, because those who think rightly concerning Christ love your teaching.

[Col. 0367C] According to the moral sense, when someone comes from secular life into spiritual observance, he says exultantly: “The king brought me into his storerooms.” Monastic enclosures are like certain storerooms, in which there are cups of manifold consolation. For when the lives of saints are read to converts, it is as though certain cups are set forth for those thirsting for righteousness. The cloistered then say: “We shall exult and rejoice in you,” that is, “We rejoice in body and soul over your conversion, mindful of your breasts”—that is, mindful of the pursuit of wisdom and knowledge—“above worldly concern.” Therefore the upright love you, that is, all penitents imitate you.

According to the higher sense, however: the Church, already received into heaven, says in rejoicing: “The king brought me into his storerooms.” That is, into the joys of every kind of glory, [Col. 0367D] where those who hunger and thirst for righteousness shall be filled, shall be made drunk from the abundance of God’s house, and he shall give them drink from the torrent of his delight. The saints rejoicing with her in glory sing: “We shall exult and rejoice in you,” that is, “In all things we shall rejoice together in your glory, mindful of your breasts”—namely, the twofold love by which you instructed your children—“above wine,” that is, above legal observance, from which you forbade them. Therefore the upright, that is, the holy angels, love you.

**VERSE 4.**—“I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” Literally, it is to be understood that noble women in Jerusalem came to the queen with gifts and, seeing that she was dark-complexioned, despised her. To them she said: “O daughters of Jerusalem, though I am black, yet [Col. 0368A] I am beautiful: black as the tents of Kedar, beautiful as the skin of Solomon. Do not consider the fact that I am dark, because the sun discolored me on the journey; fear also darkened me, because the sons of my mother fought against me—that is, my brothers fought against enemies before my eyes—and meanwhile they made me keeper in the vineyards, where I was darkened by the sun. Through fear I did not guard my vineyard,” that is, I did not protect myself from the sun. Whether this occurred thus in fact matters little, since a mystical meaning is understood here.

In the spiritual understanding, the Church, brought by Christ into the storerooms of Holy Scripture, proclaimed to others what she drank there; whence she immediately incurred the persecution of unbelievers. Those imperfect in faith, seeing [Col. 0368B] the good proscribed, exiled, and tortured by various punishments, despised her as if abandoned by God, and considered her life madness and her end dishonored (Wis. 5:4). She teaches that she suffers such things for Christ and that through them she is adorned in the inner human being for glory, saying: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skin of Solomon.”

Jerusalem, meaning “vision of peace,” signifies the heavenly homeland, where Christ’s eternal peace shall be seen. Its daughters are faithful souls destined to reign in the heavenly Jerusalem. She is called *formosa* (“beautiful”), as though *forma osa*, “hateful on account of form.” For *formum* is iron glowing in fire; hence things are called *formosi*, namely roses red in color and lilies shining with milky whiteness. Therefore the Church is called beautiful, because [Col. 0368C] refined in the fire of tribulation, she is red in her martyrs and white in her virgins.

[Col. 0368C] Kedar was a son of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, so hated by his fellow citizens that he was safe nowhere but continually moved his tents, which were very black from sun and weather. That people of Kedar too is said still to have black tents, namely covered outside with black skins and spread within with white linen. Kedar, meaning darkness or blackness, signifies sinners black in sins and tending toward eternal darkness. Their black tents signify evil actions, in which, as in tents, they dwell never secure and hateful to all.

[Col. 0368D] While Solomon built the temple, he covered the ark of the Lord outside with reddened skins, darkened by sun and weather, but adorned within with gold and gems. Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” is Christ. His skin—that is, his flesh—was reddened with his own blood and darkened by spittle, scourges, and the cross; inwardly it was adorned with gold and gems, that is, with wisdom and signs. The ark was covered by this skin because Christ’s divinity was veiled by flesh.

This skin signifies the Church, outwardly reddened by the blood of suffering and blackened by the adversities of the world, but inwardly adorned with the gems of virtues. Therefore the perfect Church says to the imperfect: “I am indeed black, because in the sight of this world I am despised on account of the sufferings that I endure, like the tents of Kedar”—that is, as though I belonged to thieves and robbers black in sins—“but I am beautiful like the skin of Solomon, because I am adorned with virtues after Christ’s example.”

[Col. 0369A] Indeed, the Church was once so hated by her fellow tribesmen that no place was safe for her to remain; she constantly fled and moved from city to city. Hence many were scandalized, judging Christians more miserable than all people. To them she said: “Do not consider me because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me.” What does this mean? “Do not attend to the punishment for which I am despised by the world; rather, consider the cause for which I endure punishment. I suffer these things not for theft or any crime, but for Christ, who is the sun of righteousness. That sun discolored me—that is, the love of whose burning heat made me dark to the world.”

By “sun” Christ is sometimes understood, sometimes persecution: Christ because of brightness, persecution because of heat. When the sun of righteousness illumined me, then the sun of persecution darkened me, because the sons of my mother fought against me.

[Col. 0369B] Note that Pharaoh’s daughter speaks this—that is, the Church brought out of Egypt and gathered under the apostles to Christ. Her mother was the Synagogue, and her sons the Jews, who attacked the Church in many ways. They killed Christ, stoned Stephen, killed both Jameses, scourged some, and persecuted others. They made me keeper in the vineyards because, having driven me from their own territories, they made me overseer of all the churches. I say “made me overseer,” because they were the cause of my being placed over them. “I did not guard my vineyard.” That is: I was not permitted to preserve the primitive Church in Judaea.

The Church is called a vineyard by comparison, because, as a vineyard is dry outside, so the Church is dry in external things but flowering within. In it Christ is the true vine; the apostles are the branches bearing the drink of life; all the elect are the workers.

[Col. 0369C] In the moral sense, when a faithful soul in holy observance adopts unadorned dress and a humble habit, it is despised by fleshly friends and relatives. To them it is said: “You, my friends, who wish to be daughters of Jerusalem—that is, of the Church—I appear black to you, that is, despised because of contempt for worldly things, and you regard me as the tents of Kedar, that is, as hypocrites who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7:15). They are dwellings of darkness, namely of demons. “But I am beautiful in the Lord’s sight, like the skin of Solomon,” namely like Christ’s flesh, outwardly worn down by vigils and fasts, inwardly adorned with virtues.

[Col. 0369D] For as skin is that of a dead animal, so I have been put to death with respect to vices and therefore am a dwelling of Christ, the true Peaceful One. Accordingly, you carnal persons, do not consider me black because of a mean habit; rather, consider that I undertook this condition for the cause of Christ, the true sun. Though he was rich, he became poor for my sake, that he might make me rich. He discolored me when he changed me from the color of worldly adornment to this habit.

Nor is it surprising that I appear black to you—that is, despised—because not Jews or pagans but the very Christian sons of my mother, namely the Church, fought against me: by slandering me, envying the quiet of spiritual life, [Col. 0370A] and drawing me back to secular affairs. And when they could not do otherwise, they made me keeper in the vineyards; that is, for the sake of gain they placed me over secular people. Thus I did not guard my vineyard; that is, under the pretext of love of neighbor I neglected spiritual life.

The lives of individual persons are called vineyards by comparison. As a vineyard is enclosed by a wall, so the soul is surrounded by the body. And as a vineyard has branches bearing fruit, so the soul has thoughts producing deeds. Secular persons set a spiritual man as keeper in these vineyards when, for gain’s sake, they choose him for the office of prelate. But he does not guard his own vineyard when he neglects spiritual life and undertakes the care of secular business.

The higher understanding is as follows: the Church, longing for the heavenly [Col. 0370B] homeland and hastening to draw others with her through preaching, says: “You lovers of the world, daughters of Jerusalem in name but not in reality, I appear black to you in active life, that is, in secular affairs, like the tents of Kedar—that is, like sinners—but I am beautiful in contemplative life, that is, in spiritual things, like the skin of Solomon, adorned with virtues. Therefore do not consider me dark in secular things, because inwardly I shine, illumined by the eternal sun in spiritual things.

“And rightly I am dark, because the sons of my mother fought against me: namely, heretics and false Christians, children of the Church in faith but not in deed, attacked me with false teachings and corrupt conduct. They made me keeper in the vineyards; that is, because of them I undertook concern in secular matters, and [Col. 0370C] did not guard my vineyard, because because of them I interrupted contemplation of heavenly things.”

**VERSE 6.**—“Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.”

In the literal sense, she speaks in the manner of a powerful woman seeking her husband on the hunt and afraid of falling upon a soldier’s guard. But because she directs her words to a shepherd, she shows what she intends allegorically. The Church, black in persecution—that is, despised—and placed as keeper in the vineyards, sees clusters together with grapes, that is, evil people mixed with good in the vineyards. Since they cannot be distinguished even by the very press of suffering, she asks from the shepherd himself a sign of discernment—he who separates sheep from goats—saying: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.”

Christ is called a shepherd by comparison because he feeds the flock of believers in the pastures of Holy Scripture and leads the lost sheep back to the green meadows of paradise. The faithful are called sheep because they are simple and innocent. Noon, when the sun’s heat is intense, is the time of persecution. Then Christ lies down in the hearts of believers who hold faith and love to the end, and feeds by wisdom the mouths of those confessing him, avoiding the vicious heat of those who deny him.

To wander is to err. Moreover, the flocks of companions are gatherings of heretics. Many among them suffered, but could not be martyrs because they lacked charity, without which not even suffering itself avails, as the Apostle says: “If I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. [Col. 0371A] 13:3).

Therefore the Church, set between persecutors and heretics, between true and false martyrs, says: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves,” and so forth. As though she said: “Tell me, O Christ, whom I love above my soul—that is, above my life—and for whom I endure every suffering. Give me a sign by which I may know the place of your dwelling in the time of persecution, lest, while seeking to venerate you in the choir of martyrs, I unknowingly worship the devil for your sake in a gathering of heretics.”

For as the Church of believers is the temple of the living God, so the church of evildoers is the temple of the devil. And as Christ is worshiped in the temple of the faithful, so the devil is honored in the temple of those who err. If anyone honors a heretic, a rich man, an adulterer, or a plunderer for the sake of gain, that person plainly worships in him the devil whose temple he is.

Companions are called, as it were, “those who eat together,” who receive Christ’s sacraments with us, read the Scriptures, pray with us, preach Christ, and yet are not of Christ’s sheep because they seek not the things of Jesus Christ but only their own things, that is, gain and human praise; and, contrary to the command and example of the shepherd, they do not love their brethren. The sign for recognizing such people is this: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). Therefore Christ’s dwelling is in those in whom the mark of love is found.

Tropologically, however, the faithful soul, set among true and false brethren, says: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you rest at noon.” [Col. 0371C] Noon, when the sun burns with heat, is temptation, which inflames the flesh with lust or the soul with the heat of anger. A shady place, however, is a chaste mind. And just as a shepherd turns aside in the heat of noon to a sheltered place, so Christ rests amid the heat of temptation in the chaste, whom he also feeds with his teaching or divine contemplation. Yet many are chaste in body, not in mind—compelled by fear, not by love of Christ. They have the will to sin but lack the opportunity to carry it out. Christ has no dwelling in such persons, because “the spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wisdom 1:5). The companions, however, are false brethren, who receive Christ’s sacraments together with the true, outwardly display holiness by their garb, but are ravening wolves in sheep’s clothing, because they do not love the true brethren. [Col. 0371D] Their sign is this: “By their fruits you shall know them” (Matt. 7:20). For when trees blossom, they all appear alike; and those bitter in fruit are often more beautiful in blossom, and are distinguished only by their fruit. So false brethren fast, keep vigils, sing, and receive communion together with the true sons of God, but are distinguished only by fraternal hatred, through which they are recognized as the temple of the devil. Concerning such people the anxious faithful soul says: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves.” For the soul to speak to Christ is to seek knowledge of Christ with all its longing; and for Christ to speak to the soul is to disclose to it the hidden things of truth. That she says “whom [my soul] loves” in the third person expresses great desire for one who is absent. “Soul” is used for “life,” as in: “He who hates his soul,” that is, his life, preserves [Col. 0372A] it (John 12:25). Therefore she says: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you rest at noon”—as though she said: “O Christ, true life, whom I love above my soul, that is, above my life, make known to me by inward inspiration those in whom you rest in the heat of temptation and whom you feed with the nourishment of your love, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions; that is, lest, while I seek to honor you among true brethren, I be found, with a wandering mind, to worship the devil among false brethren.” For where charity, which is God, does not dwell, falsehood, which is the devil, reigns.

Anagogically, however, the Church, disdaining present things and desiring those to come, says: “Tell me, you whom,” etc. Noon is called, as it were, *medidies*, that is, the middle day, or *mera*, that is, the pure day, when the sun shines brightly in the center of heaven. [Col. 0372B] It signifies the splendor of eternal brightness, in which Christ, the sun of righteousness, shines in the midst of the Father and the Holy Spirit. The flocks of the companions are the orders of angels, who are companions because they are fellow-partakers of the eternal banquet. Therefore the Church says to Christ: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves,” etc.—as though she said: “O sun of righteousness, who have made me dark when you changed me from love of the world to love of yourself, make known to me the glory in which you shine, equal in the brightness of divinity to the Father and the Holy Spirit, and in which you feed angels by your vision, lest I begin to wander after the flock of your companions; that is, lest with a doubtful mind I imagine that you are placed in the ranks of angels as one like ourselves.”

**VERSE 7.**—“If you do not know yourself, O beautiful one among women.” Literally, he seems to point out the place to the beloved seeking him [Col. 0372C] saying: “If you do not know the place in which I dwell, follow the tracks of the flocks, and you will find me in the shepherds’ tents.” Allegorically, however, he shows the bride who asks about the place where the bridegroom dwells the very place of his habitation, saying: “O beautiful one”—understand, beautiful in faith—“among women,” that is, among heresies: “you are my place, and in you is the place of my rest, and apart from you I have no place to remain. But if you do not know that you are the place of my dwelling, come out of this ignorance, and go after the tracks of the flocks; that is, imitate the examples of the Jews, who had only one place in Jerusalem where they sacrificed to God, in which there was a tabernacle or temple, the place of the ark of the Lord. And there [Col. 0372D] pasture your kids; that is, teach those who are carnally minded beside the shepherds’ tents, that is, according to the writings of the prophets.” “Beautiful” is said as though “lacking dust,” and signifies the Church of the perfect, lacking the dust of sins. “Woman” is said as though *mollier* (“softer”), and signifies the multitude of heretics or of the imperfect, who are soft—that is, prone to sin. The flocks signify the Jews, who are gathered by the staff of the Law for the worship of God.

Kids are the carnally minded, wanton in their lustfulness, who are to be placed at the Judge’s left hand. The shepherds are the prophets, whose tents are their writings. For just as soldiers dwell in tents, so those who fight against vices exercise themselves in the Scriptures.
