This may also be understood another way: if, through doubt, you do not know that you are my place among the perfect, [Col. 0373A] come out of this doubt and go—not by bodily steps, but by the affections of the heart—after the tracks of the flocks, that is, after the faith of the peoples who have gone before; and pasture your kids, that is, instruct the carnal, beside the shepherds’ tents, that is, according to the teaching of the apostles. Otherwise: if you do not know that you have been redeemed by my blood and that my seat has been established in you, go out from my fellowship and go after the tracks of the flocks, that is, follow the examples of those who err; and pasture your kids, that is, teach the carnal, beside the shepherds’ tents, that is, according to the teaching of heretics.

Tropologically, the bridegroom says to the soul seeking Christ’s place: “O beautiful one in your manner of life among women,” that is, among false brethren, “in you is the place of my dwelling,” [Col. 0373B] in which the seat of love has been established, as it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” And if, in the contemplative life, you do not know that you are my place, go out into the active life and go, by working, after the tracks of the flocks—that is, after the deeds of those living in communities—and pasture your kids beside, etc.; that is, instruct your carnal thoughts according to the life of penitents, in whose life, work, and teaching I have established my place.

Anagogically, Christ says to the Church desiring heavenly things: “O beautiful one in love for eternal beauty among women,” that is, among spiritual churches bearing children for me: “if in this life you do not know what you will be in that glory, depart from the body [Col. 0373C] and go after the tracks of the flocks, that is, imitate the examples of the martyrs; and pasture your kids, that is, refresh peoples with the sacraments at festivals beside the shepherds’ tents—that is, after the likeness of the bodies of the apostles or of those successors of theirs who were shepherds of peoples. Their bodies are called tents, as the Apostle says: ‘The putting off of my tent is swift’ (2 Pet. 1:4), that is, the dissolution of my body. If, stripped of the body, you rest with their bodies, you will also reign in heaven in spirit with their spirits.”

**VERSE 8.**—“I have likened you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.” The literal sense seems to be as though Solomon had said to Pharaoh’s daughter: “You are not worthy to wander after flocks, you who were brought in Pharaoh’s royal chariot with a procession.” [Col. 0373D] Moreover, the history touched on here is that in which the people of God, afflicted in Egypt, are freed through the blood of the lamb, led through the Red Sea, and brought by heavenly food into the promised land; Pharaoh pursued them with chariots and horsemen and was overwhelmed by the waves of the sea.

Its allegory is as follows. Egypt means “tribulation,” and this world is full of tribulation. Egypt also means “darkness,” and signifies hell, dreadful with darkness. The people were afflicted in Egypt; the Christian people are oppressed in this world. Moses, who freed the people from Egypt through the blood of the lamb, is Christ, the true Lamb, who redeemed the people by his own blood from the tribulation of the world and from the darkness of hell. The Red Sea is baptism reddened by Christ’s martyrdom; [Col. 0374A] the promised land is the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom. Pharaoh, whose name means “one who crushes,” is the devil, who crushed the human race in sins. He will be overwhelmed by the waves of the sea with chariots and horsemen when he is cast into the lake of fire and sulphur with heretics and persecutors. Therefore the bridegroom says, consoling the bride: “O my beloved,” that is, “my confidante, to whom I have made known all that I heard from my Father: because you have suffered such things from persecutors and heretics as my people once suffered in Egypt, and have not followed the flocks of heretics but fled into the shepherds’ tents, therefore I have likened you to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.” That is: I have regarded you as like my army afflicted in Egypt, when Pharaoh pursued it [Col. 0374B] in chariots. And as I freed it then, so I shall free you from the flocks of heretics and from persecutors, who are Pharaoh’s chariots—that is, the devil’s—and I shall bring you with the shepherds, who are my chariots, into the land of the living.

Tropologically, my beloved bride is among Pharaoh’s chariots when the faithful soul is set among false brethren, who are the devil’s chariots. He will liken her to his cavalry because he will associate her with the preachers of the Gospel. These are his riders because they fight his warfare. They are also horses because they draw the chariot of the Gospel through the world. Of them it is written: “Riding upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3:8).

Anagogically, the Church fleeing Egypt, this world, [Col. 0374C] and tending toward the true homeland, is among Pharaoh’s chariots as long as she is mingled here with the wicked. She will be likened to Christ’s army when she is associated with the angelic ranks.

**VERSES 9–10.**—“Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove; your neck like necklaces. We will make for you golden earrings, variegated with silver.” In the historical sense, he speaks in the manner of a lover praising his beloved and promising her gifts. For she found in the shepherds’ tents the one whom she had sought at noon, and heard from him this praise and these promises. In the allegorical sense, however, the Church, in persecution, seeing both heretics and Catholics suffering as though for Christ, and fearing to be deceived by doubtful error, sought the bridegroom [Col. 0374D] among the flocks of the companions—that is, the heretics—and did not find him; she sought him in the shepherds’ tents—that is, among Catholics—and found him there. He received her with praise and promised gifts, saying: “Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove,” etc. When bodily members are used in Scripture, only their functions are signified; but when ears are introduced, their colors or natures are assigned. The whole Church is one body, whose head is Christ and whose members are the orders of the elect.

In the cheeks modesty is signified. The cheeks of the Church, therefore, are that order of righteous persons who are ashamed to sin secretly before God and openly before human beings, such as monks and hermits. These cheeks are beautiful because they are ashamed of having sinned or of sinning. The turtledove is sky-colored, [Col. 0375A] and instead of singing it moans. It lacks gall, but rejoices in one mate. This bird bears the figure of Christ, who had a sky-like color when he taught the heavenly life. Instead of singing, he moans when, looking up to heaven, he groans because he finds the human race deaf and mute in God’s praises. He lacked gall because he had no deceit. He rejoices in one mate, that is, in the fellowship of the one Catholic Church. Therefore the bride’s cheeks are like the cheeks of a turtledove because that order in the Church which is ashamed to sin imitates Christ—that is, imitates the apostles—who have a sky-like color because their conversation is in heaven. Instead of worldly joy, they groan with unutterable groanings. They lack the gall of malice and rejoice in one mate, Christ.

“Your neck like necklaces.” The neck joins head and body and conveys food received from the head [Col. 0375B] into the body. The neck of the Church is the order of prelates, who by word and example join the Church’s body to Christ the head, and by preaching convey into the Church’s body the food of sacred Scripture received from Christ the head. A necklace, which adorns and protects the breast, is the sign of a betrothed virgin, so that an adulterer may not put his hand into another’s bosom. Therefore the Church’s neck is like a necklace because the order of prelates adorns by right living and protects the breast of the virgin Church betrothed to Christ by right preaching, lest the adulterous heretic thrust the hand of perverse doctrine into the bosom of Catholic faith. It should be noted that these two orders are set before the others because they are known to be more necessary in the Church: one by preaching to the unlearned, the other by praying for them. Therefore the bridegroom says: “O beloved, [Col. 0375C] black in the tents of Kedar, beautiful in the shepherds’ tents, your cheeks are beautiful and your neck like a necklace.” These are my riders, your shepherds, because they are like the turtledove—simple in life—and like a necklace, adorning you with the Scriptures. By them you may be protected against the flocks of heretics, by whom you feared to be corrupted. And that you may be protected with such an adornment, I and the Father and the Holy Spirit—or I and my craftsmen, your adorners—will make for you golden earrings, namely the sacred Scriptures bright with wisdom, variegated with silver, that is, diversified with eloquence. The God who once said, “Let us make man” (Gen. 1:26), now says to humanity: “We will make earrings for you,” that is, for your honor. For sacred Scripture was made by the holy Trinity, [Col. 0375D] written by holy men, and, when preserved, is an honor to the soul.

The moray is a fish which, remaining in its hole, is coiled and gathered into a ball; it does not eat, but draws out moisture and juice by sucking. In its likeness are made *murenulae*, that is, earrings, which adorn women and signify the sacred Scriptures, which teach obedience, the ornament of souls. By sweet exhortation these Scriptures, like the moray, draw the moisture of sin out of the simple and humble. Gold, which surpasses all metals, signifies wisdom, which transcends all things. The earrings are golden because sacred Scriptures shine with wisdom, tested in the fire of the Holy Spirit as gold is. Silver, which shines and sounds, expresses eloquence, which glitters with tropes and figures and sounds sweetly with rhetorical [Col. 0376A] ornaments. The Scriptures are variegated with silver, that is, distinguished by eloquence and diversified with maxims.

To variegate is to diversify, to twist in a winding manner like a worm. With these necklaces the bride is adorned by the bridegroom’s craftsmen. Tropologically, just as the outer person has limbs, so the inner person has them. The soul’s cheeks, therefore, are modesty, by which it is ashamed to have done what ought not to have been done or to have neglected what ought to have been done. The soul’s neck is understanding, which joins soul and spirit as head and body. For the soul has two powers: the higher, called spirit, by which we deal with spiritual things; [Col. 0376B] and the lower, called soul, by which we arrange bodily matters. Understanding, like a neck, joins these two by recognizing spirit and soul to be one substance. It conveys food received from the head into the body when it stores in the belly of memory the spiritual things that it understands. Its necklace is inward perception, marked by various maxims and precious stones; its earring is obedience, adorned with the gold of wisdom and the silver of knowledge. In the anagogical sense, however, the Church sighing for the heavenly homeland assumes the manner of the turtledove, which laments that it is a pilgrim in this world and asks one thing of the Lord: that it may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of its life (Ps. 22:6). The ornament of this necklace is the earring, that is, Christ shining in the glory of the Father. Another translation has: “We will fashion for you likenesses of gold, with distinctions of silver, until the king is at his table.” [Col. 0376C] This means: “Gold—that is, my face—you cannot see in the present life; but through the illumination of the Scriptures you will see the likeness of heavenly brightness as in a mirror, in an enigma, until that which now lies hidden in divinity appears to all.”

**VERSE 11.**—“While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” Literally, it may be understood that the beloved found the beloved whom she sought lying in the shepherds’ tents; he adorned her with necklaces made from gold and gems, while she offered him perfumes prepared from nard, myrrh, and clusters.

Allegorically, however, the primitive Church, before Christ’s advent, sought God in many of her children in the books of the Gentiles [Col. 0376D] and so wandered among the flocks of the companions. But she found him reclining in the shepherds’ tents, that is, lying in the books of the prophets. He gave her necklaces marked with gold and gems because he entrusted to her the legal commandments, full of precious promises; and she gave him precious perfumes when she offered herself to be saved through his incarnation, passion, and resurrection. And this was meanwhile, while the king was at his table—that is, while Christ, the King of glory, lay hidden in the bosom of the Father. To recline is to remain in secret. By nard Christ’s incarnation is signified; by myrrh, his passion; and by the cluster, his resurrection. For species of trees or herbs are used in Scripture for symbolic meaning. Nard is a small, thorny, fragrant aromatic shrub, [Col. 0377A] from which excellent perfumes are made, such as that which Mary used from nard in the Gospel. Nard, therefore, is used for humility and for the ointment by which the sick are healed. Christ was nard, an ointment-bearing tree, when he became the medicine of the human race. He was small, that is, humble, because, though he was in the form of God, he humbled himself to the form of a servant. Thorny, because born from sinners. Fragrant, because full of virtues; he became the ointment of our health when the power of his divinity healed every sickness and every infirmity. Therefore it is said: “While the king was at his table”—namely Christ, the King of glory, while he was in human flesh—“my nard,” namely his power, which became my medicine, “gave forth its fragrance,” that is, spread knowledge of itself among the peoples [Col. 0377B] when he gave sight to the blind, raised the dead, and healed all the sick. Or: “While the king was at his table,” namely Christ after the Ascension in the glory of the Father, “my nard,” that is, my activity, gave forth its fragrance, namely fragrant service. Then the bride found in the shepherds’ tents—that is, in the teaching of the apostles—the beloved whom she had sought so long. He gave her necklaces, that is, the various charisms of the Holy Spirit, and she offered perfumes, namely the works of saving faith. Otherwise: “While the king was at his table,” namely in the bosom of the Father or in the womb of the Virgin, “my nard,” that is, my humility, gave forth the fragrance of good works. Nard also signifies the Church’s humility, through which the health of good example arises for others. Or the voice here is understood as that of the Church awaiting redemption [Col. 0377C] in hell and saying: “While the king was at his table,” that is, Christ on the cross, “my nard gave forth its fragrance,” that is, humility experienced salvation, because “my beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh”; that is, Christ endured bitter death for me, by which he redeemed me from death. Myrrh is an Arabian shrub five cubits high, like the thorn called acanthus; its gum is green and bitter, whence it received the name *myrrha*. Its spontaneously flowing gum is more precious; that drawn out through a wound in the bark is less valuable. It is healthful for healing infirmities and useful for embalming dead bodies, so that they are not consumed by worms and decay. Myrrh signifies the bitter death of Christ, who brought a remedy for our infirmities [Col. 0377D] and drove from us the decay of sins. Hence he received myrrhed wine on the cross, and Joseph embalmed his body with myrrh. By “bundle” is meant the gathering of sufferings. Christ became a bundle of myrrh when, taken down from the cross, he was anointed with myrrh and aloes. Therefore the bride says: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh,” as though she said: “My beloved, whom I love above all, who was nard to me in the incarnation, has become myrrh to me in the passion, enduring bitter death for me and teaching me to suffer bitter things of the world for his sake; and therefore—

**VERSE 12.**—“He will dwell between my breasts.” That is, he will be preached by the fathers of both Testaments, who are my breasts. Or: the death of my beloved, which he underwent for my salvation, will always be in my memory [Col. 0378A]; and he who was myrrh to me in death has become a cluster to me, that is, joy in the resurrection. Hence follows:

**VERSE 13.**—“My beloved is to me a cluster of cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi.” Cyprus is said to be an island which produces clusters of remarkable size beyond all lands; or *cyprus* is an Egyptian tree like a willow, having marvelously fragrant flowers and clusters. A cluster is used for joy; *cyprus* means “conversion” or “flowering,” and signifies Christ’s resurrection, in which his dead flesh flowered anew and bestowed eternal joy upon those converted. Christ was the cluster of this cyprus, pressed in the winepress of the cross; from it came the wine which gives those converted fullness of joy. This is the cluster which two men carried on a pole to the children of Israel—namely Christ hanging on the cross—which the prophetic and apostolic order [Col. 0378B] preached to the peoples who were to see God. Therefore he who was a bundle of myrrh in the bitterness of the passion became a cluster of cyprus in the sweetness of the resurrection. For myrrh makes sorrowful, wine makes joyful. Therefore the bride says: “My beloved is to me a cluster of cyprus,” as though she said: “He who hung on the cross for me like a cluster upon a pole has become for me a drink of joy; and therefore he is my beloved, because I love him above all.” And this is in the vineyards of Engaddi, that is, in all Churches. Engaddi is a spring near Jerusalem in which priests washed the kids that they were to sacrifice; and hence it is called “the spring of the kid.” It signifies the font of baptism, in which kids—that is, sinners—are washed from vices. The vineyards are Churches washed in the font of baptism and producing for others the wine of life. Otherwise, Engaddi is a place [Col. 0378C] where balsam trees grow, cultivated after the manner of vineyards; for this reason he calls them vineyards. Chrism is made from balsam and oil, with which Christians are consecrated. Therefore the cluster of cyprus is in the vineyards of Engaddi because Christ, the drink of joy, is in Churches anointed with holy chrism: he was nard in being born, myrrh in dying, and a cluster in rising again.

Morally, the king is at his table when Christ rests in the soul of the righteous. For the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom. The nard of this soul gives fragrance when its humility spreads the reputation of good works. The beloved becomes for it a bundle of myrrh when it gathers in its mind all the bitter things of Christ’s passion and resolves to suffer bitter things from neighbors for his sake. He dwells between its breasts because he abides in its heart [Col. 0378D]—which is between the breasts—through love. The cluster of cyprus, whose name means conversion, becomes its own in the vineyards of Engaddi when it rejoices over those who have been converted, baptized, and perform penance.

Anagogically, while the king is at his table, the bride’s nard spreads fragrance, because while Christ lies hidden in the glory of the Father, the Church everywhere spreads the renown of good works. She gathers the beloved like a bundle of myrrh between her breasts when, through love for him, all things which the world honors or loves seem bitter to her. She contemplates the cluster of cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi, the place of balsam, when she desires to see Christ, the drink of life, in heaven among those anointed with chrism.

**VERSE 14.**—“Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are those of doves.” In the historical sense, [Col. 0379A] the king highly praises the queen adorned with necklaces. In the allegorical sense, Christ celebrates with praise the Church adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. By the plural “of doves,” or by the twice-repeated “beautiful,” two Churches are signified: one before Christ’s advent under the prophets, the other after Christ’s advent under the apostles. Yet they are one beloved, because both are joined to Christ in one faith. What the former believes will happen, the latter believes has happened. Let no one be troubled that we call them two or more Churches, although one Catholic Church is preached. For although it is one, still, because of different conditions, times, and places, it is not unjustly called many, just as many lands are written of although the earth is one. The Church is compared to a dove because she is enlightened by the seven [Col. 0379B] gifts of the Holy Spirit, just as the dove is adorned with seven characteristics. For the dove nests in the rock, nourishes other birds’ young, chooses pure grains, lacks gall, does no harm with its beak, dwells beside streams, and flies in flocks. So the Church nests in the rock—that is, in Christ—by faith and works. By word and example she nourishes those alien to the kingdom of God. She chooses pure maxims from the books of Gentiles or heretics. She lacks the malice of envy. She harms no one by detraction. She dwells beside the streams of Scripture so that she may escape the seizure of hawks, that is, demons. She labors to draw many with her to joys. The eyes of the one dove—that is, of the Church before Christ’s advent—were the prophets, who foresaw for her Christ, the eternal light, and were therefore called seers. The eyes of the other dove, namely the Church after Christ’s advent, were the apostles from the same people, who led her to Christ, the true light. Therefore the bridegroom says: “O my beloved, to whom I have made all my secrets known, because I have healed you by the nard of my flesh, [Col. 0379C] redeemed you by the myrrh of my death, and made you drunk by the cluster of my resurrection: behold, in my presence you are beautiful in faith; behold, before human beings you are beautiful in action, because your eyes—that is, your overseers—are simple like doves’ eyes, namely the prophets and apostles, teachers of the Churches. For as eyes guide a person lest he strike against a stone, so teachers guide the Church to life lest she strike against God’s Law written on stone.”

Tropologically, the soul is Christ’s beloved: [Col. 0379D] beautiful when washed from original sin, and itself beautiful when free from actual offense. Its eyes are reason, by which it distinguishes true things from false, and intention, by which it foresees the face of God. These eyes are doves’ eyes if it does good things with a good intention; but they are ravens’ eyes if it does good things with an evil intention—for example, if it preaches or gives alms for the sake of gain or praise.

Anagogically, the pilgrim Church is beautiful in love of God in the contemplative life, and itself beautiful in love of neighbor in the active life; and therefore she is God’s beloved, sighing for heavenly secrets. Her eyes, leading her to life, are bishops and other teachers; they are the eyes of doves, illuminated by Christ and the Holy Spirit. For Christ is compared to the dove, [Col. 0380A] which has seven characteristics, because he is preached as full of the sevenfold Spirit; hence a dove was offered in sacrifice for him. The dove also bears the figure of the Holy Spirit, who subsists substantially in seven gifts; hence it appeared as a dove over Christ, and the dove brought an olive branch back to the ark. Those eyes lead her to behold these, so that in light she may see light: namely, the Son in the Father, and the Spirit in both.

**VERSES 15–16.**—“Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and lovely; our bed is flowering; the beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings cypress.” In the historical sense, the beloved sought and found the lover occupied in hunting at noon; adorned and praised by him with necklaces, she returns with him [Col. 0380B] to the royal court. Resting with the beloved in bed, she praises the bridegroom, the bed, and the house. In the allegorical sense, however, the Church sought Christ, occupied in capturing souls, through the various torments of persecution at noon; she found him through patience, and he adorns her with virtues and praises her for perseverance. She calls him back, as it were, from field to palace, while he places her, restored from persecution to peace, in the bed of rest and security. For this repose of peace she sings joyfully in praise: “O my beloved above all others, I, who was ugly and foul through myself, have been made beautiful through you, because you are naturally beautiful in the virtues of divinity and lovely in the holiness of humanity, making people beautiful in faith and lovely in action. For Christ, according to divinity, is beauty itself, [Col. 0380C] from whom all things that are beautiful are beautiful; the sun and moon marvel at his beauty, and angels desire to look upon him. According to humanity, however, [Col. 0380C] he himself is more beautiful than the children of men, because by nature he was always such as he appeared on the mountain when he shone like the sun. But because mortal sight could not behold the brightness of his face, he lay hidden under a mask, as it is written: ‘Behold, we see him having neither form nor beauty’ (Isa. 53:2). Thus Moses’ face became so beautiful through conversation with God that the people of Israel could not look upon him, and therefore he had a veil before it. Hence it is written that Moses’ face was horned, because it emitted rays like the sun.

“Our bed is flowering.” According to the Church’s different conditions, divine discourse speaks of it in different ways. [Col. 0380D] It called the time of persecution “noon,” when the sun’s heat burns. But it calls the time of peace a “bed,” in which there is the repose of security. Thus persecution was called noon, in which the Church was scorched; thus the peace of the Church is called a bed, in which she rests secure in contemplation of her bridegroom. It is called *lectulus*, a little bed, because the peace enjoyed by the Church is brief. This bed is flowering because in the time of peace the people of the faithful are intent upon good deeds, whereas in persecution they were almost dried up from good endeavor. Or the bed is the Lord’s man, in whom God the bridegroom rested together with his bride, human nature. For “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). It is called our little bed because through Christ’s flesh the Church is [Col. 0381A] joined to God. This bed is flowering because he is immortal with eternal youth, though he had previously been, as it were, dry—that is, mortal. And because you are beautiful, begotten of a beautiful Father, and our bed is beautiful, brought forth from a chaste mother, therefore our houses too are beautiful, built by our craftsmen from cedars and cypresses: “the beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings are cypress.” Beams are the upper boards of a house, that is, the roof; ceilings are the lower panels, fitted for painted decoration. Cedar is an incorruptible, fragrant wood, whose resin surpasses others because it heals weak limbs, kills the worms of ulcers, and by its odor drives away serpents and flies. Cypress is a wood next to cedar in virtue, suitable for temple beams; with impenetrable solidity it never yields to a burden, and once cut never rots. God’s house is the Church, in which Christ dwells as a householder in a house. The many houses are the many Churches [Col. 0381B] according to the different conditions of lands, such as the Roman, Jerusalemite, Constantinopolitan, and other Churches. The beams of these houses, which repel rain and storms, are bishops and other prelates of the Churches, who defend God’s house—the Church—from heretics by writings and teachings. These beams are cedar because their works are incorruptible and fragrant through reputation. Their teaching, like resin, heals sins and drives away vices or demons. The painted ceilings of these houses are the Church’s subjects, namely the continent and the married, adorned with alms and good works. They are cypress and fitted for God’s temple [Col. 0381C] because they do not return, like a dog, to the vomit of sin.

Tropologically, the faithful soul is a bed in which Christ dwells through love. This bed flowers when the soul exercises itself in prayer and reading. The bed of the soul is also a good conscience, in which the soul rests securely as in a bed. This bed flowers when it gives others an example of good life. The soul itself is also God’s house, in which Christ dwells as a bridegroom in a bridal chamber. Its beams are the principal virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. Its ceilings are examples of obedience, compared with cedar or cypress because, as these trees multiply in branches, so they multiply in good works. Or the house of the soul is the body; its beams are the five senses, and its ceilings the bodily members, which are cedar and cypress when they serve at the spirit’s command.

Anagogically, [Col. 0381D] the bed of Christ and the Church is the contemplative life, in which it rests from worldly tumults. This bed flowers when the multitude of believers exercises itself in the arts and in the Scriptures. The houses built by craftsmen with cedar and cypress wood are cloisters constructed by holy Fathers through rules and honorable institutions.

Cedar beams are superiors and abbots fragrant with holiness, who strengthen others by word and example and extinguish by mortification the worms of sins. Cypress ceilings are monks and all religious, whose examples of holiness adorn God’s temple and bear others’ burdens through prayer. And [Col. 0382A] just as a cut cypress does not grow green again—and was therefore customarily carried before the bier of the dead—so they never return to the secular things they have renounced. They always behold death as though present, and in purpose and conduct desire to be built together into God’s dwelling.

## CHAPTER II
**Verse 1.**—“I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters.”

In the literal sense, it is to be understood that the beloved’s bed was surrounded by flowers, whose fragrance and beauty delighted her when she said, “Our bed is flowering”; and he, caressing her, spoke these words to her.

Allegorically, the Church of the perfect, which is Christ’s bed, is surrounded by flowers when it is encompassed by those who are merely flowering in faith, that is, the imperfect. For in a flower there is not [Col. 0382B] yet fruit, though fruit is hoped for. Thus the imperfect possess faith but not works. Their flower is Christ—that is, he is adorned through their faith—who says: “I am the flower of the field.” This means: “The fact that our bed is flowering among believers comes from me, because I am the flower of the field, that is, the adornment of the Christian people.” A flower is said to derive its name from *fluere*, “to flow,” because it quickly passes away.

A field is uncultivated pastureland, spontaneously producing flowers. The field is the whole Church in incorrupt faith, in which are the pastures of life, and which produces various flowers—that is, diverse orders of the righteous: the roses of martyrs, the lilies of virgins, the violets of confessors, and other flowers of the continent and of those lawfully married. The flower of this field, that is, its beauty, is Christ, the adornment of all believers. The flower of the field properly [Col. 0382C] is a small, very reddish flower; and it is Christ, made humble and reddened by his own blood. The field, that is, uncultivated ground, is the inviolate Virgin, whose flower is Christ, because he was born from the Virgin.

He himself is the lily of the valleys, because he is the honor of his humble parents. Five features are considered in a lily: it is white, it has a projecting golden color, it is fragrant, spreading, and always bent down. So Christ is white in his humanity, golden in his divinity, fragrant in preaching, spreading in receiving penitents, and bent down in condescending to sinners and raising them up. He is the lily of the valleys, that is, the ornament of believers. For as valleys lie between two mountains, so believers [Col. 0382D] stand between two laws, or between two peoples—namely, Jews and Gentiles.

“As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters,” as though he said: “As I am the lily of the valleys, that is, the ornament of the humble, so you, my beloved, shall be a lily among thorns, that is, the glory of the Gentiles. And as I was a lily among thorns, namely among the Jews who pricked and tore me, so you, Church, my beloved, shall be among the Gentiles, daughters of Babylon—that is, of confusion—who will prick you with many thorns of sufferings and tear you with many punishments.” Three things are noted in the thorn: it quickly flowers, quickly withers, and pricks with its points. So the wicked quickly flourish in riches and quickly wither in virtues; therefore they are fit for fire. By evil habits they prick the good.

Alternatively, as a lily among thorns—that is, as a lily [Col. 0383A] is the adornment of thorns—so you shall be the glory of daughters whom, resting on the flowering bed, you will bring forth. Or you will be an adornment through faith and doctrine amid heresies which wish to be your daughters, though they are thorns and daughters of Babylon, that is, of confusion.

Morally, Christ is the flower of the field, the honor and fragrance of his bed, namely the faithful soul whole in faith, whom he makes flourish in holy study. This soul is the lily of the valleys, that is, the beauty of humble souls; they are valleys because, among the proud and rich, they are cast down by poverty, as though situated between mountains. And as Christ was a lily among thorns, namely among Pharisees and hypocrites, so the faithful soul is among the daughters of Babylon, namely false brethren who are hypocrites.

[Col. 0383B] According to the anagogical sense: the field, namely uncultivated ground, is the order of virgins in the Church, whose flower is Christ, because he is their delight, crown, and reward. The valley, however, is the order of married persons, situated as though between two mountains, between virgins and the continent; Christ is their lily, namely their brightness and joy. And as a lily is among thorns in beauty and fragrance, so the Church of the perfect is among the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, among the perfect—in the beauty of life and the fragrance of doctrine. Those are called perfect who have left all things of the world, as the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor” (Matt. 19:21). Those are called imperfect who still make use of the world, concerning whom it is further written: “Your eyes saw my imperfect substance, and all shall be written in your book” (Ps. [Col. 0383C] 138:16).

It should be noted that a lily, when touched, loses its fragrance; likewise virginity, once touched, loses its good reputation.

**Verse 3.**—“As an apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons. Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat.”

In the literal sense: the queen, rising from the bed to walk about, came under the shade of a tree, ate its fruit, and there spoke these words.

Allegorically, the Church had been darkened by the sun of persecution, scorched at noon by the heat of temptation, torn by executioners as a lily by thorns, and finally wearied by the weight of afflictions. It sought the shade of the tree of life and desired the bed of rest. Resting in that shade, it sings: “As an apple tree among the trees [Col. 0383D] of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons. Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat.”

*Malus* is an equivocal word. There is *malus*, “evil,” and *malus*, an apple tree. There is also *malus*, the mast of a ship—that is, the tree supporting its sail. Of a man we say *malus*; of the tree, *haec malus*; but of the apple, *hoc malum*. The apple tree has three things in itself: cooling shade, refreshing fruit, and pleasing fragrance. This apple tree is Christ, who overshadowed the human race when he stretched out his arms upon the branches of the cross; and he refreshed those believing in him with his body and filled them with the sweetness of his delight.

The forest is the Synagogue; the trees of the forest are the Jews, fit for nothing except fire. The beloved among the sons—understand, sons of the devil—is Christ [Col. 0384A] among Gentiles, idolaters, and sinners, overshadowing and refreshing them.

Alternatively, the apple tree is Christ; the trees are the apostles, from whom the house, namely the Church, was built; the forest is the Church, consisting of diverse trees—that is, the elect and saints. The beloved among the sons of God is Christ among prophets, apostles, and martyrs, who are sons of God and fellow heirs of Christ. “For as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1:12).

“Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat.” The comparison is with someone carrying a burden in the heat and hurrying toward the shade of a tree. The human race, which through eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil had lost Paradise, bore the heavy burden of sins in the heat of vices; this burden drew it downward into the precipice of torments. Therefore it hastened to the tree [Col. 0384B] of life and sought the refreshment of souls. For shade signifies refreshment. Shade is produced from light and a body; it refreshes travelers from heat and protects them from storm.

The tree of life is the holy cross; its fruit is Christ; its shade is the protection or refreshment of the human race, consisting of the light of divinity and the body of humanity. Of this shade it is written: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). Under this shade, for which it had long desired, the Church sat when it rested in faith in Christ’s cross. Through Moses it desired this shade, saying: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send” (Exod. 4:13); through David: “Lord, bow your heavens and come down” (Ps. 163:5); and through Isaiah: “Would that you would rend the heavens and come down!” (Isa. 64:1).

[Col. 0384C] Therefore, as the apple tree surpasses all the trees of the forest in shade, fruit, and fragrance, so Christ surpasses all saints in the shade of protection, the fruit of doctrine, and the fragrance of life. And as this tree draws travelers to itself in the heat by shade, fruit, and fragrance, so Christ by his sweetness draws to himself the human race traveling through the heat of temptations; he refreshes it by his body or teaching, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).

Refreshed by its fruit, the Church rejoices, saying: “His fruit is sweet to my throat.” The fruit of this tree is evangelical teaching. The Church’s throat is the order of teachers in the Church. The throat’s function is to receive food and emit sound; so teachers in the Church receive the food of spiritual doctrine by reading [Col. 0384D] and emit their voice by teaching others. Therefore the fruit of the tree of life is sweet to the Church’s throat when the Church’s teachers sweetly drink in spiritual teaching for themselves and pleasantly pour it forth for others.

Tropologically, the beloved is among the sons as an apple tree among the trees of the woods when Christ, through love, is among the cloistered sons of the Church, overshadowing them against vices and refreshing them with his body or teaching. Under his shade the faithful soul sits when, turning aside from the heat of worldly life, it desires to be refreshed in the rest of spiritual life. Its fruit is sweet to that soul’s throat when either the cloistered religious life pleases it or the Lord’s body tastes sweet to it upon the palate of the heart, through which it understands itself to be saved.

[Col. 0385A] Anagogically, the Church reigning in heaven, contemplating Christ commanding the angels, says: “As an apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons.” That is: “As Christ, beloved of the Father and of me, was in the world more delightful than all saints, so in heaven the Son of God is delight among all angels. Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat”: that is, through him I found the rest of souls which I always desired. “And his fruit was sweet to my throat”: that is, joy won through the cross brings sweetness to my life. Rejoicing in that sweetness, it says:

**Verses 4–7.**—“The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he ordered love within me.”

In the literal sense, the queen who ate beneath the tree drank in [Col. 0385B] the wine-cellar, and rejoicing, told this outside to the young women: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar,” where, intoxicated and inflamed with the king’s love, she fell into languor. Therefore she says to her companions: “Support me with flowers; surround me with apples, because I languish with love.” These words suggest that they took branches and flowers from the place where they had sat, with which she, faint with love, asks to be supported as with staffs lest she fall. As she is about to fall, the king embraces and consoles her; and, so that she may rejoice, he says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” The king places her upon the bed and adjures the companions: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not stir up or awaken my beloved until she herself wishes.”

Allegorically, the Church which ate from the fruit of the tree [Col. 0385C] of life—that is, Christ’s body from the cross—drinks cups of wisdom in the cellar of sacred Scripture. Hence it joyfully sings: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar.” Above it said: “The king brought me into his cellars” (Song 1:3); but here it says: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar.” There human nature, the bride of the Word, spoke; here the Church from the Gentiles, bride of Christ, speaks. For God’s Word united human nature to himself by a kiss when he assumed human flesh, as it is written: “The Word was made flesh” (John 1:14). He anointed it as queen with the oil of his name when he willed the assumed man to be God and to command angels. He drew it after himself when, victorious over death, ascending into heaven, he took our flesh with him. Hence, rejoicing, it sings: “The king brought me into his cellars”: that is, the King of glory brought me through human nature into heavenly joys.

But here the Church, redeemed through the cross and introduced through the apostles into the divine mysteries, says: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar”—that is, Christ, King of kings, whom all kings worship, brought me through faith into the primitive Church, which is the wine-cellar because within it are diverse cups of wisdom and various charisms of the Holy Spirit.

The primitive Church is that Church which, under Christ and the apostles, was converted from the Jews, when “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and they had all things in common” (Acts 4:32). Into it the Church from the Gentiles was introduced when Cornelius and [Col. 0386A] his household, and Gentile Samaritans, were joined to the faithful through baptism and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Within it he ordered love when, united in love, he distributed them into diverse ranks, making some apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, others pastors, and others teachers.

Alternatively, the wine-cellar is sacred Scripture. Christ brought the Church into it when he gave it spiritual understanding, as it is written: “He opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45). He ordered love within it when, through the Scriptures, he arranged three degrees of love: first, that one should love God above all; then one’s neighbor as oneself; and finally even one’s enemy for God’s sake. We also establish ranks in love when, after God, we love our parents, then spouses and children, [Col. 0386B] then brothers and relatives, then household members and fellow citizens, and finally enemies—namely Jews and pagans.

The bride relates this as she goes out to the young women awaiting her: that is, the perfect Church speaks to other Churches, its daughters, saying: “Support me with flowers; surround me with apples.” By flowers are understood boys and those simple persons flourishing in faith; by *mali*, that is, trees, are understood young men fruitful in works. The perfect Church seems to say to the imperfect: “Since I have been intoxicated with the wine of Scripture and love has been ordered within me through diverse degrees, support me with flowers; that is, through your preaching place beneath me boys flourishing in faith. Surround me with apple trees; that is, through your examples multiply within me young men fruitful in good works, so that I may give them to drink what I have drunk and order love [Col. 0386C] within them.”

The comparison is with a house already collapsing from age, which is supported by props lest it fall. Thus the Church, deprived of honorable elders, is in some way supported by boys flourishing in faith lest it collapse.

Another comparison is with shoots newly sprouting, which surround their mother, that is, the tree; or with soldiers who surround their lord with weapons lest an enemy assault him. So the faithful surround mother Church, as though standing in their midst, with good deeds: some labor in almsgiving, others in reading, others in prayer; and they surround her with the weapons of Scripture, lest the hostile devil or heretic assault her. “You Churches, my daughters, support me with flowers,” that is, with good sons, “lest I fail; but meanwhile may I rest in your [Col. 0386D] works, because I languish with love”—with love for my beloved, whom I am not yet able to see, and with love for the heavenly homeland which I do not yet possess.

“For this reason, his left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” By the left hand he signifies the glory of the present life; by the right hand, the glory or blessedness of eternal life, as it is written: “Length of days is in her right hand; in her left are riches and glory” (Prov. 3:16). Christ is the head of the Church. Therefore it says: “His left hand is under my head”: that is, I place under my head—namely Christ, whom I love above all riches—the glory of the present life. “And his right hand will embrace me”: that is, eternal blessedness will receive me. Or the order of the righteous, who will be at Christ’s right hand, loves me.

Alternatively, “his left hand is under my head,” [Col. 0387A] that is, the old Law, because I despise its carnal ordinances; “and his right hand,” that is, Christ’s Gospel, “will embrace me,” drawing me to obey it. Or: his left hand, that is, the active life, is under my head, that is, under Christ, in which I serve him; and his right hand, that is, the contemplative life, will embrace me, in which, resting, I please him. And lest anyone disturb me in this rest, the bridegroom forbids it, saying: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and stags of the fields, do not stir up or awaken my beloved until she herself wishes.”

By the roes, which seek high places and see the hunter from afar, are signified the prophets, who, lifted into lofty contemplation, foresaw Christ and the mysteries of the Church from afar. By the stags, which leap over thorn thickets and overcome poison, are signified the apostles, [Col. 0387B] who, leaping over the thorns of sins, suffering the thorns of punishments, overcame the world’s malice.

The fields are the two Churches: one before Christ’s coming, under the prophets; the other after his coming, under the apostles. In these fields are diverse flowers, namely all believers. Or the fields are the two Testaments, in which are flowers, namely beautiful sayings. In one field the roes, namely the prophets, ran, when they foretold to the old people that Christ was to come. In the other field the apostles ran as stags when they made Christ known to the Christian people.

The daughters of Jerusalem are all Catholic Churches, called Churches of Jerusalem because they are to behold eternal peace in heaven. For Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” To them the bridegroom says: “O Churches, daughters of the heavenly Jerusalem, I, your [Col. 0387C] God, adjure you”—that is, “I bind you by the sacrament of my incarnation and of your baptism”—commanding you, by the roes and stags of the fields, that is, the prophets and apostles, teachers of peoples, not by force or reward to stir up my beloved, or disturb her while she sleeps apart from the world’s tumult through love of me; nor awaken her from the sleep of contemplation by forcing her into secular affairs, until she herself wishes—that is, until she herself willingly wishes, through compassion for her neighbors, to undertake the burden of governing.

There are many powerful people who compel spiritual men to governing offices for the sake of gain, so that they may receive benefits from them. Such persons awaken the beloved from the sleep of rest, and Christ forbids through prophets and apostles that this be done. But when spiritual persons themselves perceive that it is expedient for them to preside over brethren, they rise voluntarily from rest; though unwilling, they accept the burden of rule [Col. 0387D] and assist their afflicted neighbors.

Morally, the bridegroom is brought by the bride into the wine-cellar when someone, Christ drawing him, enters a cloister, where he drinks the wine that gladdens the human heart when he draws from the Scriptures promises of joy. In this place love is ordered when God is loved first, then the superior, then the elders, and then the other brethren according to the merits by which they are loved. Flowers support him, and apples—that is, trees—or apples, that is, fruits (for both readings are possible), surround him when boys and young men surround him in holy studies. He languishes with love when he sees that not all brethren love Christ.

[Col. 0388A] The left hand—that is, present life—is beneath his head, that is, beneath his mind; and the right hand—that is, eternal life—embraces him, because he pursues this alone. For the mind is the head of the soul: as the head rules all members, so the mind orders thoughts. Alternatively, the left hand is the virtues necessary in this life, while the right hand is the incorruptibility to be given in the future. The left hand is under the head when virtues are under the mind; the right hand will embrace him when incorruptibility is given to him in the future. Because such a person is here compared to a roe and stag, Christ threatens that no one should disturb him in this rest.

A roe has four natures: it seeks high places, distinguishes good herbs from bad, chews the cud, and heals its wounds with dittany. So the spiritual person ascends to the heights of virtues, separates good [Col. 0388B] judgments from bad, ruminates in preaching upon the spiritual food which he ate in reading, and heals the wounds of sins with the medicine of repentance.

A stag likewise has four natures. When they seek islands far away, they swim across the sea in herds, and each carries another’s head upon its haunches. When pursued by dogs, they leap over thorns. When growing old, they draw a serpent from its cave with their nostrils and eat it. They run to a spring to drink. In order to renew their horns and hair, they cast them off. So the righteous, when hastening toward the homeland of Paradise across the sea of the world, bear one another’s burdens when the wicked persecute them. They leave behind temporal goods which, like thorn thickets, are impediments to life. They draw the serpent from its cave with their nostrils because by the breath of exhortation they remove the devil or sin [Col. 0388C] from the hearts of brethren. Having swallowed poison, they run to the spring because they wash committed sins in the spring of tears. They cast off horns and hair because they reject riches, which are superfluities, and, renewed in virtues, grow young.

According to the anagogical, that is, higher sense, the Church already received into heaven says: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar”: namely, Christ, King of glory, brought me into the heavenly homeland, where those thirsting for righteousness “shall be intoxicated with the abundance of the Lord’s house, and he shall give them drink from the torrent of his delight” (Ps. 35:3).

It should be noted that where bringing in is mentioned, Christ is called King, because the Church whom he brings in [Col. 0388D] is his kingdom, over which he himself will reign as King. Within her he will order love, because he will assign virgins living in love to their dwellings, widows to theirs, and married persons to theirs. Flowers surround her, apples encompass her, when the elect, found in faith and works, surround her in glory. She languishes with love because she is not satisfied by being satisfied with the sight of her beloved. The bridegroom’s left hand is under her head: that is, the Church left in this life is under his protection; and his right hand will embrace her because the multitude of angels rejoices in her fellowship. There the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, all faithful souls; and the roes, namely prophets or other saints who ascended to the heights of heaven through virtues; and the stags, namely apostles or other elect who leaped over the thorn thickets of sins, rejoice with her in glory.

[Col. 0389A] **Verses 8–10.**—“The voice of my beloved: Arise, hasten, my beloved.”

**History.** While the bride slept, and no one dared awaken her, the bridegroom himself awakens her and commands her, upon rising, to direct her young women to their tasks. At the bridegroom’s voice she rises and sends her companions to cultivate the vineyards and catch the little foxes.

**Allegory.** The bride, as it were, slept when the Church, gathered under the apostles after the Lord’s ascension, remained in Jerusalem for twelve years without preaching. The bridegroom awakened her and advised her to send the young women to work when Christ, through the sheet let down from heaven to Peter, in which were all kinds of animals, instructed that the Gospel should be preached to all peoples (Acts 10:19). The bride sent companions to cultivate the vineyards and catch foxes when the Church sent apostles and their [Col. 0389B] disciples to convert Gentiles and suppress Jewish or prophetic heresies.

Note that she sent young women, as elsewhere it is written that Wisdom sent her maidservants to invite peoples to the table. That is, Christ, the Wisdom of God, sent rustic and despised men to invite peoples to the banquet of eternal life. The bride, awakened by the bridegroom, addresses the young women: “This voice which I heard—‘Arise, hasten, my beloved’—is the voice of my beloved. Therefore we must arise and obey him in the work to which he calls me. For he said: ‘Go, teach all nations’” (Matt. 28:19). And elsewhere: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have appointed them” (Acts 13:2), namely to preach to the Gentiles.

Likewise, when the Macedonian appeared to Paul, saying: “Cross [Col. 0389C] into Macedonia; help us” (Acts 16:9). For when the shepherd’s beloved slept, the sheep wandered through byways; but the good Shepherd caused his beloved to wake and gather together onto the way the scattered flock which he had gathered by himself, so that there might be one shepherd and one fold.

And note that above he adjured the young women not to awaken the bride, whereas now he himself awakens her, because all times have their proper time. Spiritual persons ought in a time of peace to rest in contemplation, but in a time of persecution or heresy they ought to fight against God’s enemies by preaching and writing. The young women say: “Have you seen him whose voice you heard?” And she says: “Behold, I now see him present, because he who was formerly promised comes, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills.” The comparison is with stags, which run leaping on [Col. 0389D] mountains. Hence follows:

**Verse 9.**—“My beloved is like a roe or a young stag.”

The mountains, which rise high above the plains of the earth, are prophets, who surpass the common life of human beings by the height of virtues. The hills are Pharisees, who stood out among God’s people by knowledge of the Law. The bridegroom therefore comes leaping upon the mountains because Christ came into the world by certain leaps, as was foretold by the prophets. He made a leap from heaven into the Virgin’s womb; from the womb into the manger; from the manger to the cross; from the cross to the tomb; from the tomb to heaven. He skipped over the hills when he passed by the proud Pharisees and chose the humble apostles.

[Col. 0390A] Alternatively: he came leaping upon the mountains because he willed that his leaps should be preached through minds, that is, through virtuous men. He skipped over the hills when he willed that one still imperfect in preaching should refrain. For it is necessary that people first learn and act, and afterward teach, as it is written of the Lord: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1).

Alternatively, one who leaps is now upward, now downward; so Christ was above in divinity and below in humanity. The rising sun first appears on mountains and afterward on hills. The mountains were the apostles. Christ leaped upon them when, through his name, they raised the dead and performed other miracles and signs. He skipped over the hills when the followers of the apostles also performed signs.

He is like a roe because he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, when he was born from sinners. [Col. 0390B] For as the righteous are signified by sheep, so sinners are signified by roes. Or he is said to be like a roe because, just as the roe runs swiftly and selects good herbs from harmful ones, so Christ swiftly fulfilled obedience to the Father and will separate the good from the evil in judgment. He is also like a young stag in the variety of virtues and miracles. A young stag is of variegated color; in blazing sun it seeks a shady place in which to rest from the heat. So Christ rests in chaste minds from the heat of vices. By stags, which run and leap swiftly, are figured the prophets and patriarchs, who swiftly ran in the Lord’s commandments without complaint and leaped from virtue to virtue.

[Col. 0390C] The young stag of stags is Christ, son of patriarchs and prophets. A young stag is said to derive its name from *innuo*, “I give a sign,” for it hides itself from hunters when its mother signals to it. Christ is like a young stag of stags because, as the son of patriarchs, he was sold like Joseph and offered by his Father like Isaac. And as a young stag runs more swiftly than stags, so Christ, who committed no sin, outruns all saints in swiftness. Christ is therefore compared with these animals which delight in leaps because, running through the aforesaid leaps, he is exalted above all the righteous.

The young women say: “Where is he now?” The bride says: “Behold, he is behind the wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices.” The comparison is with a person unable to enter his beloved’s chamber and speaking to her through the window. The wall is a partition separating house from house; it signifies original sin or mortality, which came from sin and separates us from God. Adam began to build this wall, and all his posterity labors to complete it. The Jews built it by many sins and therefore rejected Christ, the precious, chosen cornerstone, who restrained them from sins; unbelieving, they stumbled against him and fell. But this stone grew into a great mountain, upon which Zion, the city of the great King, began to be built. It receives within itself as citizens all who believe in it; it says: “In my God I shall pass over a wall” (Ps. 17:30), because he committed no sin. Christ stood behind this wall in order to push it down, because [Col. 0391A] he was made mortal in order to destroy original sin.

He who stands labors, and Christ labored so greatly in destroying this wall that he even sweated blood. The windows, which send light into a house, are the apostles, who poured into the Church, God’s house, the light of the knowledge of God. The lattices—that is, small openings in a wall through which the sun sends forth its rays—are the prophets, through whom the Sun of righteousness sent the rays of his knowledge into the world. Lattices are also the projecting portions at the front of a house. Hence *cancellarii*, that is, the king’s spokesmen, are so called: they declare to the people the king’s edicts from the lattices. Such also were the prophets, who in the front part of the house, namely the Synagogue—which was the shadow of the house of the Church—announced God’s commandments to the people.

[Col. 0391B] Lattices are also places in the choir in which chanters are arranged; they enclose all who are set in diverse ranks. Therefore the bridegroom looked upon the bride through the window when Christ poured into the Church the light of his knowledge through the apostles. He looked upon her through the lattices when through prophets or other teachers he sent her the rays of his knowledge. One who looks through a window is partly seen and partly not seen; so Christ, remaining in flesh, was partly seen as God in miracles and partly not seen in the weakness of his Passion. Because he stood behind the wall, he could not be joined to the bride; and therefore through the window he gave kisses and words, because so long as mortality stood between, he could not be perfectly united to the Church. [Col. 0391C] Nevertheless, through the window of his body he offered kisses of teaching.

When the wall is destroyed, he is joined to the bride, because, when mortality has been removed, he will be revealed to the Church as he is. The Church says: “My beloved, whom I love above all, who came to me leaping and, standing, struck the wall—he, looking through the windows and lattices, awakens me and speaks to me, saying: ‘Arise, hasten, my beloved.’” That is: he who came into the world according to the Scriptures and destroyed our death commands me through prophets and apostles to preach this to others, saying: “O primitive Church, which have long ceased from preaching, arise from your rest—that is, prepare yourself for labor, for preaching to the Gentiles. Hasten, because the time is short. And, if you do this, you will be my beloved, making friends for me through faith from those who are enemies through unbelief. And you will be my dove, enlightened by the sevenfold Spirit; like a dove adorned with seven natures, making them simple. And you will be my beautiful one, making those deformed by vices beautiful in virtues, and, accompanied by them, you will come to me to receive your reward.”

It should be noted that these words and what follows are the bride’s representation of the bridegroom’s words. You have an opportune time for preaching. For now (v. 11) winter—that is, unbelief—has passed; the rain—that is, persecution—has gone and withdrawn. Winter, which binds the earth with frost so that it cannot bear fruit, is unbelief, which binds human hearts with the coldness of malice so that they cannot bring forth the fruit of faith. This winter lasted until Christ; but [Col. 0392A] when he, the Sun of righteousness, rose, winter passed, and spring, by the warmth of the faith of the Holy Spirit, thawed the earth and produced the flowers of virtues.

Rain is a shower that comes violently and quickly passes away. So persecution came violently, but, because Christ conquered in his own, it quickly passed away. Yet while the apostles and their successors preached, persecution did not go away but increased greatly. It is nevertheless said in the past tense, “it has gone,” because it withdrew quickly like rain. To go away is one thing; to withdraw is another. One goes away who wishes to return; one withdraws who does not wish to return. Under the kings of the Gentiles persecution at times went away and returned again; but in Constantine’s time it withdrew, not to return.

Persecution had to be aroused so that those proved might be crowned. Rain also signifies the storm of wars. Before Christ’s advent, [Col. 0392B] the greatest storm of wars raged throughout the whole world, so that no one could migrate from one land to another without being regarded as a spy; but after Christ, true peace, came, the rain of wars withdrew.

**Verses 12–14.**—“Then flowers appeared in our land”: namely, persons flowering in faith appeared in Judea, formerly possessed by the tyrant devil but reclaimed by me through the victory of the cross. Therefore now in our land the time of pruning has come, so that barren branches may be cut away and flowers may spring forth more abundantly, bearing plentiful fruit: namely, that vices may be cut off and virtues planted. The voice of the turtledove, that is, Christ’s preaching, was also heard in our land, namely in Judea, now through our faith; or it is the voice of preachers who by their song announce the departure [Col. 0392C] of winter and the arrival of spring; who in place of song render a humble moan; who are lovers of chastity; who flee human intercourse; and who always remain in the wandering mountains or on their summits, because, though placed in the world only in body, their manner of life is in heaven, mindful of their sojourn and of their promised homeland. Or it is the voice of penitents groaning over their sins that was heard.

“The fig tree also put forth its grossi”: namely, the Synagogue, like a fig tree having leaves—that is, luxuriant foliage—but no works, and therefore cursed by the Lord, cast away the carnal senses of the Law. For *grossi* are unripe fruits of the fig tree, which fall when shaken by a light touch.

For as the voice of Christ the dove sounded in the land, the fig tree of the Synagogue, shaken, cast off its unripe figs—that is, the bitter senses of the Law—and produced sweet figs, that is, the apostles, who might minister sweet food allegorically to believers. And because the fig tree of the Synagogue produced the apostles, the flowering vines gave forth fragrance: that is, the Churches converted from the Jews, flourishing in faith, gave the reputation of good works. The pressed flower of the vine makes a kind of drink, beneficial to health and pleasant for consumption. The flower of the vine is faith in Christ; the cup made from it is the holy Gospel, which bestows eternal salvation and the delight of life.

Note that the bride who is sent to cultivate the vineyard is called by three names: beloved, dove, beautiful. For the cultivation of the vineyard—that is, preaching—is entrusted only to those in whom right faith, pure love, and simple conduct are found, so that, by doing what they teach, they may be God’s friends rather than working for gain; that they may be dovelike; and that they may be beautiful in love. These seven things are set forth by the Holy Spirit, because Christ’s vineyard is cultivated in seven ways through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: through preaching the winter of unbelief is dissolved, the rain of wars is calmed, the flowers—the beginnings of good things—are produced, the branches of vices are cut away, the voice of the dove, that is, of simple preaching, is gladly heard in cultivated ground, namely, in the now-believing heart. The fig tree bears fruit—that is, each believer bears a good work—and thus the cultivated vineyards, namely Churches flowering in faith, give off the fragrance of virtues.

Now Pharaoh’s daughter is sent for Babylon’s daughter, and with her the king’s envoys are sent for the queen of the south. To her the bridegroom says: “Arise, my beloved.” Above he said, “Arise,” and he repeats, “Arise,” because we arise in two ways: when we raise the mind either to acting or to teaching. Therefore it is said, “Arise,” that is, raise your mind to act rightly and provide an example. Again it is said, “Arise,” that is, raise your mind to teach others.

For to arise is to lift oneself upward. He arises who does and teaches the good that he has learned. “O my beloved, to whom I have made known all the secrets of my Father, arise, and bring Babylon’s royal daughter to me, that she too may become my beloved. You who formerly, dwelling among the inhabitants of Kedar, were dark, now beautiful through my gifts: teach her, now ugly in vices, to be beautiful in virtues; and, adorned with that charity, come to the wedding. You, my dove, filled through me with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, teach her simplicity, that she may receive the sevenfold Spirit, nesting in the clefts of the rock and in the caverns of the wall”: that is, placing hope of salvation in Christ’s wounds and in the promises of Holy Scripture.

For the rock is Christ, upon which rock the Church, the house of the Lord, is built. From this rock flowed water that satisfied the children of Israel, because blood and water streamed from Christ’s side, redeeming and washing this dove. The clefts of this rock are Christ’s wounds, which are defenses for the dove, that is, the Church, against hawks, that is, demons. The wall is Christ’s side; the cavern of the side is the wound made by the soldier’s lance. In it this dove has placed the nest of hope. Or the wall is a wall built around vineyards without mortar. It signifies Scripture, which encircles the Churches, held together without heresy. For as mortar is the binding of stone, so heresy is the binding of souls.

The caverns of this wall are the profound meanings of Scripture, in which these doves hide themselves from vices.

It should be noted that he exalts by three names those whom he sends to preach, because the order of teachers must know the Lord’s secrets as friends, so as to know what they are to teach; be beautiful through purity, so that their life may shine before their hearers; and, like a dove, shine in the sevenfold natures through the seven virtues mentioned above. To her it is said:

[Col. 0394A] **VERSE 14.**—“Show me your face.” A person is known by the face; therefore the face of the Church is good action, by which she is known. She shows this face when she teaches others publicly to do what she does secretly. One’s face is shown to the Lord when, for God’s sake, a good work is offered to one’s neighbors as an example. “Let your voice sound in my ears”: namely, what you promised on the day of your betrothal, in baptism—that you would preserve yourself for me—teach others also to preserve. For your voice will be sweet, understand, to your hearers, if you live as you teach; and your face will be fair—that is, your action will be pleasing to me. *Decorous* is said as though from *decus oris*, “the beauty of the mouth.” For it is fitting to speak and act in such a way that God delights in it. The bride still rehearses the bridegroom’s words. He spoke the preceding words to the bride; now he turns to the maidens, saying:

**VERSE 15.**—“Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyard, for our vineyard has blossomed.” As though he said: “Our vineyard has blossomed, which my beloved has cultivated with great labor; but behold, foxes break in and seize its fruit. You maidens, catch them and drive them from the vineyard.” Foxes hide themselves in burrows and never walk on a straight path. When hungry, foxes also feign themselves dead with open mouths; in this way they deceive and devour birds.

By these are signified heretics, who argue in secret, never keep the straight path of faith, and pretend to be Catholic and humble in order to deceive the simple. Preachers catch them when they conquer and rebuke them by reason and authority. They are called little for this reason: because they pretend to be humble. Or they are called little because, just as little ones are overcome by great ones, so they are defeated and fail before Catholics. They destroy vineyards—that is, undermine them—when they divide Churches through heresies and schisms. But the one vineyard, namely the Catholic Church, flowers in right faith and bears the fruit of action everywhere. Rejoicing, she says:

**VERSES 16–17.**—“My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies.” My beloved has said these things to me, and I, understand, shall obey him, who feeds among the lilies; that is, he delights in the works of those who are bright in virtues, who are an ornament to others, as the lily among thorns. And he feeds among them for so long, and I shall obey him by teaching others for so long, until the day breathes—that is, until the knowledge of eternal brightness comes, where all see the true light—and until the shadows decline, that is, until the ignorance of this present life passes away.

Day is the presence of the sun, whereas night is the earth’s shadow. When the sun rises, day comes with a gentle breath; then the shadow of the earth, which is night bent beneath the earth, vanishes. So, when Christ, the Sun of righteousness, has shone forth, and the day of eternity has breathed with the refreshment of the righteous, the ignorance, persecution, and shadow of this life will vanish.

The comparison is with one wearied by excessive heat, who is refreshed by wind and a sweet breeze. Thus the Church, wearied by the heat of tribulations, is refreshed when Christ comes. Pharaoh’s daughter, sent on behalf of Babylon’s daughter, prays her bridegroom that by his help he may bring her, saying: “O my beloved, return by grace to Babylon’s daughter, from whom you withdrew because of idolatry. Be in her like a doe, which seeks high places and chooses wholesome herbs over harmful ones, so that you may separate those to be saved from the mass of perdition and cause them to seek the heights of heaven. Or be in her like a young stag, which runs swiftly and seeks a shady place, so that you may make her run swiftly to faith and baptism, and seek the shade of virtues from the heat of vices—you who stand over the preachers, giving them your word to speak with boldness” (Acts 4:31). They are mountains by contemplation in God’s house, which is the Church, just as these animals dwell upon the mountains of Bethel because of pasture.

Bethel means “the house arising,” or “the house of vigils,” or “the house of God.” It is the Church that rises to heavenly things, in which there are vigils of praise against demons and vices, and in which God dwells through faith. Its mountains are teachers lofty in virtues, over whom Christ is the doe and young stag when through them he separates good persons from evil and makes them run through the examples of the saints. Does and young stags dwell on the mountains of Bethel when individual believers, through the teaching of the saints, hasten toward the heights of heaven.

In the tropological sense, the beloved awakens the bride from sleep when Christ, through inward inspiration, calls a spiritual man from cloistered quiet to the governance of the Church. He leaps upon the mountains when he leads him from virtue to virtue through the examples of the Fathers. He will be like a doe and a young stag when he chooses good interpretations, seeks the heights of virtues for the prize of life through the example of the saints, and pushes against the wall when he wisely overturns the counsel of evildoers. He looks through lattices and windows when he diligently attends to apostolic and prophetic Scriptures.

The beloved speaks to him through lattices and windows so that he may arise, when Christ teaches him through prophets and apostles to exhort his neighbors to live well.

He himself arises when he obeys him in all things. He hastens when he preaches in season and out of season; and so he becomes God’s friend when he makes others God’s friends. He is a dove when he lives simply; beautiful when he forms others toward good things; he comes when he fulfils God’s commands. Hence winter passes when the harsh conduct of the people entrusted to him, hardened in wickedness, is melted by the warmth of divine love and passes into the spring of holy conduct. The rain withdraws when the temptation of persecutors ceases. For when he restrains wicked persons from wickedness, he immediately suffers persecution from them, because “all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12). When the rain departs, flowers appear, because when persecution by the wicked ceases, beginnings of good things spring forth. He cuts off branches when he separates rebels from the Church. The voice of the dove is heard in the land when penitents return to the Church through lamentation. The fig tree produces unripe figs when a good tree—that is, a good person—produces a good work. Flowering vineyards give fragrance when Churches or cloisters under him send forth the reputation of good works. He arises when he resists heretics.

[Col. 0396A] He becomes God’s friend when he persecutes God’s enemies. He is beautiful when he restores the erring to God’s likeness. He comes when he causes the negligent to come to the wedding of the Lamb. He is a dove that nourishes alien young when he makes children of perdition, children of Gehenna, and children of wrath into children of the kingdom and children of God. He nests in the clefts of the rock when he commands them to trust in Christ’s wounds. He dwells in the cavern of the wall when he proclaims that they should hope in the teaching of Holy Scripture. He shows his face to God when, through the good he does, he looks to God’s recompense. For one whom conscience accuses hides his face and is ashamed to speak. He shows his face who fulfils in work what he teaches in word. His voice sounds in God’s ears when he lives and preaches. He catches little foxes when he corrects false brothers according to the rule of righteousness, or drives the incorrigible from the assembly of the brethren, lest they undermine vineyards—that is, overthrow congregations of the righteous through pretense. The beloved is pleasing to her in his promises, and she is pleasing to him in obeying his commands. He feeds among lilies because he is refreshed by the life of saints, white with virtues. “Until the day breathes,” that is, until the light of truth appears to all and the shadow passes away. For as the Synagogue was a shadow, and whatever that people did was a shadow of the thing which we now do, so the sacraments and festivals of the Church are shadows of future glory. Likewise all evils of the present life are shadows of the evils of the future life. Therefore, when the light of eternal glory has shone, the shadow of sacraments vanishes and present tribulation withdraws. The beloved returns to this man when, hypocrites having been expelled, the number of the perfect increases.
