[Col. 0396C] The beloved will be a doe to him when through him he separates the good from the evil. He will be a young stag when he causes any persons to run toward conversion. And this is upon the mountains of Bethel: that is, he does this through the prelates of God’s house.

In the anagogical sense, the beloved awakens the bride from sleep when Christ calls the pilgrim Church to heavenly things. She sees him leaping on mountains and hills when she beholds him reigning at the right hand of the Father above the orders of angels and saints. She sees him like a doe and a young stag because she will behold, born of the patriarchs, the Judge of the living and the dead. He stands behind our wall, looking through windows and lattices, because he will show her the flesh taken from us—mortal, but in the Father’s glory immortal—as he had promised through prophets and apostles. She herself arises because she meets the caller for joys; she hastens where, as the beloved, she sees heavenly secrets; where she will be a dove full of the sevenfold Spirit, beautiful because without spot. There the winter of every adversity passes; the rain—that is, the numbness and cruelty of this present life—withdraws, because when she is led out of the body to contemplate God, she is led in her own substance.

Drops of words are no longer necessary, so that the rain of preaching must be poured out, because what she was able to hear less fully here, she will see more fully; nor is temptation necessary, by which anyone must be tested. Then flowers appear in the land, because when the soul begins to taste certain first beginnings of sweetness from the life of eternal blessedness, it seems, while going forth, already to smell in flowers what, after it has gone forth, it will possess more abundantly in fruit. Then the time of pruning comes, because, with every vice cut away, it will lack death and punishment.

Then immediately, in the land of the living, it will hear Christ’s voice as a dove: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:23). And the fig tree produces its unripe figs when it receives the fruit of its labor, the reward of eternal life. Flowering vineyards give their fragrance because the Churches that flowered here in virtues, there emitting the fragrance of sweetness, provide eternal delight. The beloved will be joined in glory with these friends: beautiful in the embrace of the Holy Spirit; a dove in the cleft of the rock, that is, in Christ’s secrets; and in the cavern of the wall, that is, in the dwelling places of the heavenly city. There Christ shows her his face, when she sees him face to face in his majesty (1 Cor. 13:12).

[Col. 0397B] His voice will sound in her ears when she hears him say: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34). This voice is sweet, and that face is fair, into which angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1:12). The little foxes that destroy vineyards are caught because, through the angels, all scandals will be gathered and thrown into the furnace of fire (Matt. 13:41). Afterwards the vineyard will always flower, because the Church will rejoice with Christ forever. The beloved is joined to her, and she to him who feeds among lilies, because he reigns among the companies of saints, white in virtues. Or he now feeds among lilies because he is refreshed by the progress of the saints until the end of the age. “Until the day breathes and the shadows decline.”

The wild animals from which the comparison is drawn feed throughout the whole night; when dawn comes, they seek safe places for themselves. Thus Christ, while the world, which is night, endures, feeds during that night upon the virtues of the saints. When the day of eternity breathes and Christ, the Sun of righteousness, has risen, he will no longer labor among the faithful, but “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28). Then, returning from judgment, he will be like a doe, which chooses good herbs and seeks high places, because, having chosen the good to himself, he will reign in the high glory of the Father. And he will be like a young stag, which rests in a shady place, because in the refreshment of the saints he himself will rest as their refreshment, upon the mountains of Bethel—that is, above all the angelic orders of the heavenly Jerusalem, which is God’s house.

## SECOND TREATISE

[Col. 0397]

[Col. 0397B] The preceding treatise concerned Pharaoh’s daughter; the following one will concern Babylon’s daughter. Now the king’s envoys, sent for the queen of the south, arrive and bring the bride upon camels with a great retinue. Pharaoh’s daughter, coming out from the vineyard with her companions, received her with great rejoicing and, amid the loud applause of the attendants, led her into the king’s temple. The king endowed her with royal generosity and brought her into the prepared banquet. That is, the apostles, sent for the Church of the Gentiles, convert her to faith in Christ by signs and preaching. The multitude of believers from Judaea joins itself to her in thanksgiving. It leads her by word and example into the Lord’s temple, that is, into the primitive Church. And the King of glory, Christ, enriches her with many gifts of wisdom and knowledge and calls her to the banquet of his body, or of Holy Scripture. For it is read that Paul and Barnabas and others, having been sent to preach to the Gentiles, returned to Jerusalem and reported to the brethren how much God had done among the Gentiles through them, with what eagerness the Gentiles had received the faith, and how the Church established in Judaea had rejoiced over their conversion (Acts 21:19). Therefore Babylon’s daughter, formerly wretched in idolatry—the Gentile world, daughter of confusion—now queen of the south because converted to the true King Christ, speaks to Pharaoh’s daughter, namely the Church from the Jews, recounting to her the miseries she suffered in her former life, saying:

## CHAPTER III

**VERSE 1.**—“Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves.” The comparison is with a woman who anxiously seeks her beloved in the night, grieves because she has not found him, and continues searching and wandering until she finds him and joyfully clings to him. The bed is unbelief, in which the Gentile world rested securely. Night is understood as secular philosophy, obscure through its intricate propositions. Therefore she says: “Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves,” as though saying: “I, the fullness of the Gentiles, lying sick as though in a bed in my unbelief, sought through the night—that is, the obscure books of philosophers—by reading and questioning, the knowledge of him whom my soul, now knowing him, truly loves. That is, I love him above my life: him who first loved me and has now received me through faith. I sought him many times in the writings of the Gentiles and did not find there one equal to the Father, born of a virgin for the human race.” For many Gentiles searched earnestly for the way of salvation by which they might come to the highest good, where true blessedness might be found; but they did not find it, because they did not believe in Christ, who is the way, truth, and life. And when I did not find truth among them, I said:

**VERSES 2–3.**—“I will arise and go about the city; through the lanes and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves.” “I will rise from the bed of unbelief and go about”—that is, examine—the Church, the city of God, and question its citizens. “Through the lanes,” that is, through the examples of martyrs, “and through the squares,” that is, through the teachings of confessors, “I will seek him whom my soul loves,” that is, whom natural reason loves. A city is so called as though from the unity of citizens, and it signifies the Church. Those who dwell in it ought to have one heart and one soul in love. A lane is a narrow way, signifying those who proceed by the strait way to joys. The narrow way is to fast, keep vigil, discipline the body, abstain from women, and love enemies.

A square is a broad way, signifying those who tend toward heavenly things by the wide and spacious way: those lawfully married, occupied as necessity requires in secular affairs, and yet devoted to almsgiving.

“I will abandon the uncertain doctrine of philosophers and turn to the certain teaching of Christians. From those who live the contemplative life and those who live the active life, I will learn what chiefly pleases him whom my soul—that is, natural reason—loves above all. For I sought him long ago in the schools of secular people and did not find among them the certain way of truth. At last, while I was thus diligently seeking truth and desiring the blessed life, the watchmen found me: that is, the apostles, preachers ready to teach, as Peter found Cornelius, Philip the Eunuch, and Paul found Dionysius. By word and example they diligently guard the city, namely the Church, lest enemy demons or heretics secretly break in and destroy in soul some unwary citizen.” I questioned them, saying:

“Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” As though she said to the king’s envoys sent for her: “I sought among my fellow-citizens, the philosophers, and did not find him; but you proclaim to me the Savior of the world, whom you saw living among human beings. Have you also seen with the eyes of the heart the glory of his majesty?” They say, “A little.” “For we saw him giving sight to the blind, raising the dead, and shining on the mountain with the glory of divinity like the sun.” But when I had passed beyond them—that is, when through their teaching I had passed in mind from earthly to heavenly things—I found my bridegroom equal to the Father, the Word through whom all things were made, whom my soul loves because he himself is love and life. I held him, found in faith, and will not let him go in action because of any tribulation, until by my preaching I bring him into my mother’s house—that is, into the Gentile nation—and into the chamber of her who bore me, that is, the homeland of the Gentiles, so that all may believe in him.

Or the mother is the Synagogue, which gave birth through faith to the Church of the Gentiles. Her house is Judaea, in which the Synagogue will be gathered at the end of the world under Antichrist. The Church brings the beloved through faith into this mother’s house so that all Israel may be saved. For they will turn at evening—that is, at the end of the world—and will suffer hunger for God’s word like dogs (Ps. 58:7), and will go about the city, that is, the Church, to hear from Christians the word of salvation. The birth-mother is the nurse, and signifies the Law, which nourishes the children of the Church with its milk; its chamber is Jerusalem or the hearts of believers. The beloved is brought into the chamber of the birth-mother when Christ is preached through the Law in Jerusalem and believed as true God in the heart. After the king had brought the queen of the south into Pharaoh’s daughter’s house for the banquet, he also made her rest in her chamber, as one wearied from a journey, and forbade anyone to disturb her, saying:

**VERSE 5.**—“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the does and stags of the field, do not awaken or rouse the beloved until she herself wills.” This is to be understood of the Church from the Gentiles as it was first understood of the Church from the Jews. Christ, the King of glory, brought the Church from the Gentiles, led in by the apostles, into Pharaoh’s daughter’s house—that is, into the faith of the primitive Church—and taught her to rest from the tumult of the age in its chamber, namely in the contemplative life. Through prophetic and apostolic writings he forbids anyone to disturb her from this quiet for the sake of gain by calling her to secular business. Behold, the good shepherd has led the wandering flock to his sheepfold and made one flock under one shepherd. The little verse, “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,” is repeated in the song of love in order to show that the Lord does not take less care of the Church gathered from the Gentiles than of that gathered from the Jews, but bears equal concern for the peace of both. For this queen of the south is seized by love of the bridegroom no less than the first beloved woman from the Jews.

The Church sleeps when it devotes itself peacefully to contemplation; it wakes when it preaches eternal life to others by word and example, so that its light may shine before human beings and, seeing its works, they may glorify the Father in heaven (Matt. 5:16). The faithful soul sleeps when it withdraws itself from carnal desires; it wakes when it hastens by good works toward the vision of the Creator. The pilgrim Church sleeps when it rests in tombs with its body dead, as it is written: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 126:2). It wakes when it rises on the day of judgment and receives the kingdom prepared for it from the beginning.

According to the moral sense, the bed is carnal pleasure, in which one rests who lives amid the delights of the age. Night is death, as the Lord says: “Night comes, when no one can work” (John 9:4). Therefore, one seeks God upon the bed during night when, living carnally and with death approaching, one asks the Lord for a reprieve of life. But one does not find what one seeks, because one asks for the reprieve not in order to make satisfaction to the Lord for sins, but to abound longer in accustomed pleasures. Such a person must rise from the bed of carnal life and traverse the city—that is, Holy Scripture—with full attention, seeking salvation of soul through lanes and squares, that is, through spiritual and secular persons. He does not find it because he has not washed away in repentance the stains of his former life. But the watchmen who guard the city find him, because learned men who keep watch over the Scriptures train him in repentance and satisfaction.

He asks them about the salvation of his soul; and when he has passed beyond them—that is, when he has performed true repentance through their teaching—he finds the salvation he sought. Having found it, he must hold it by good action and not let it go through any temptation, until he brings Christ the beloved into his mother’s house—that is, into the soul, which is the house of grace and has begotten him for God—and into the chamber of his birth-mother, that is, into the heart, which is the chamber of wisdom, his nurse. Otherwise, the bed is the secret place of the spiritual life, and night the disturbance of the world. In this bed, when a faithful soul lives in holy conduct and suffers disturbance from its brethren, it seeks by reading and prayer him alone whom it loves, in whom it may have peace and rest.

But it does not find here the one it seeks, because, so long as it lives in the world, it is away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6), who is peace, rest, and blessedness. Therefore it arises and goes about the city because it lifts itself with all its strength to search Holy Scripture. It seeks the beloved through lanes and squares because it surveys the lives of spiritual and secular people living in contemplative and active life, to see whether it may find anything to imitate through which, pleasing the beloved, it may attain him. But it does not find him here because, so long as it does not enjoy his vision, it does not rest.

The watchmen of the city find it because expounders of Holy Scripture, wakeful in doctrine, seek such a soul that they may bring it to Christ by their teaching. Questioning them, it passes a little beyond them and finds the beloved, because, reading their writings, it quickly finds by true sight the God it sought. It passes through them because it sees in them the image of him it seeks; yet it passes beyond them because it begins to imitate and behold God, who is beyond. It holds him by love and does not let him go through any disturbance, until it brings him by examples into the cloister, the house of its mother’s congregation, which begot him through exhortation, and into the chamber of its birth-mother, that is, the understanding of Holy Scripture, which nourished it with the milk of knowledge, so that others too may understand him as God.

According to the higher sense, the bed is the body, in which the soul lies as though sick; night is this world, covered in the darkness of ignorance. The Church, a pilgrim here, seeks the beloved during night upon the bed when, placed in the body that weighs down the soul and covered in the darkness of ignorance, it longs to see Christ, the eternal light. When it finds him, it rises, goes about the city, and seeks through lanes and squares him whom it loves. For it despises all earthly things for love of him and raises itself to search heavenly things; it surveys in mind the orders of angels and saints, perhaps through them it may see the true light. The guardians of the city find it because angels, who always see the face of the Father (Matt. 18:10), meet it and show it the beloved’s glory through contemplation. When it passes a little beyond them, it finds the beloved, because, when it has transcended in mind the choirs of angels, it will see Christ reigning at the right hand of the Father. It holds him by contemplation and will not let him go by pursuing earthly things, until he himself brings it into the heavenly Jerusalem, which is our mother and the house of the angelic multitude, and into the chamber of his birth-mother—that is, into the paradise of exultation, which is the chamber of the Church, its nurse.

A sinful human being with his followers was expelled from the paradise of delight. A repentant thief with his followers was received into the paradise of exultation. The queen of the south, awakened from repose by the king himself, comes forth from the chamber adorned with jewels. The daughters of Jerusalem receive her with song: “Who is this?” (v. 6). They honorably lead her to Solomon’s bed; there the mighty men of Israel meet her armed, and they bring her (v. 9) with great display into Solomon’s litter, that is, into the banquet-house. Namely, the Church of the Gentiles, instructed by the apostles in the contemplative life and adorned by Christ with many gifts of the Holy Spirit, came forth from the secrecy of intimate contemplation at the bridegroom’s prompting into the public sphere of good action and preaching, while in many torments at various times it offered its neighbors examples of patience. Believers from the Jews, admiring its change and its strength of endurance for Christ, extol it with great praises and proclaim that Christ, expelled from the Synagogue, rested in it as in a bed.

Indeed, the Church is Christ’s bed, because one rests in its faith and love as a weary person rests in a bed. It is also the banquet-house, because Christ is refreshed by its works, or is fed as hungry in the poor. In it also the fattened calf is killed for the prodigal son (Luke 15:27), when the Gentile people are refreshed by Christ’s body and blood, and those hungering and thirsting for righteousness are satisfied with various dishes of Scripture. Therefore Pharaoh’s daughter—that is, the Church from the Jews—wonders that Babylon’s daughter, that is, the Church from the Gentiles, is made equal to her in all things, and joyfully cries:

**VERSE 6.**—“Who is this who comes up through the wilderness?” The comparison is with the people led by Moses from Egypt through the Red Sea, who ascended by a difficult road through the wilderness toward their homeland. Amalek made war upon them on the way; Joshua, who is also Jesus, defeated him and led the victorious people, nourished with manna, into the land of promise. Thus the Church of the Gentiles, freed by Christ from Egypt, this world, and from the power of Pharaoh, that is, the devil, was led out through baptism reddened by Christ’s blood. It ascends through the wilderness of the world by a hard road toward the homeland of heaven, because it must enter the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations. Amalek—that is, the devil—wages war against it on the path of righteousness through persecutors, heretics, and false Christians. But it conquers all these things through its leader, the true Jesus, who feeds it with his body and blood and brings it into the land of the living, namely paradise. Therefore it says: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” This is said in wonder, not as a question. The Synagogue was God’s land, cultivated by the plow of the Law and fruitful through prophets and other righteous persons. The Gentile world, however, was a wilderness, fruitful in no harvest of virtues and instructed in God’s worship by no prophet or angel.

A rod is the correction of children through fear of punishment; the rod signifies fear of the Lord, through which the Church ascends to wisdom, as it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10). Smoke is holy desire, produced by the fire of divine love. Spices are a mixture of aromatic substances and signify a multitude of virtues. Myrrh is the mortification of martyrs; frankincense, the sacrifice of confessors; every powder of the perfumer, the devotion of all Christ’s faithful. For a perfumer is a physician who prepares spices, that is, various medicines; and he signifies Christ, who made Scripture a medicine for diverse diseases of vices.

[Col. 0403A] Here six stages of ascent to perfection are described, or six orders of the elect in the Church are expressed. From the rod of fear one ascends to the smoke of compunction; from there to the spices of virtues; then to the myrrh of mortification; then to the frankincense of confession, so as to become a living sacrifice to God; finally to every powder of the perfumer, that is, to imitating all the examples of Christ’s followers. Or, by the rod, which is straight, are understood the upright in heart; by smoke, penitents; by spices, cloistered persons; by myrrh, martyrs; by frankincense, confessors; and by every powder of the perfumer, married persons and other faithful people. Thus it is said, “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness?” as though saying: “She who was once despaired of and abandoned by God, now converted to faith—how glorious she is, and how worthy of praise and admiration, she who ascends by the stages of virtues through the wilderness of the world to the heights of heaven, like a column of smoke: a column rising from earth to heaven, and smoke which leaves the depths and seeks the heights; smoke, I say, from spices—that is, from the fragrance of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer, that is, from all medicinal substances.” Smoke, born from fire and rising on high, gradually withdraws from human sight. Thus the Church, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit into love of God, does not cease to ascend until, withdrawn from earthly things, it is caught up to heaven’s invisible realities. At the same time smoke partly rises and partly disappears in higher places; thus the Church is newly born in some of its members, while in others it is gathered above into heavenly things.

By myrrh is understood mortification of the flesh; by frankincense, the sweetness of prayer; and by powder, every kind of virtue, through which the Church ascends to the highest things in each order of the elect.
of the peoples.

Tropologically, the Bride ascends through the wilderness when the soul rises from the pleasures of the flesh to the heights of the virtues, through the wilderness—that is, through the seclusion of the cloistered life—where it is separated from the enticements of the world and devoted to heavenly commands; like a rod and smoke, abandoning earthly things and seeking heavenly ones, gathering the spices of the virtues, and, in the manner of spices, emitting from itself the fragrance of a good reputation, smelling of the myrrh of mortification and the incense of prayer, and furnishing its brethren, by example, with the powder of all virtues [Col. 0403D].

But anagogically the Bride ascends through the wilderness when the Church, here a pilgrim through the world, climbs toward heaven, like a little rod of smoke: that is, like those who were upright as a rod and, through smoke—that is, through a troubled heart—weep for their sins; and who, like spices, gave forth the fragrance of virtues; who mortified themselves for Christ; who offered themselves to God as incense through a holy life; and who gave good examples to others. When the daughters of Jerusalem marvel and ask whither the queen has ascended through the wilderness, she says to them: “To Solomon’s bed.” To the faithful from Judaea, who marvel at the sudden grace of God in the Church of the Gentiles, namely that through torments themselves it was ascending to heavenly things, she says: “Do not marvel that I ascend by difficult paths, but [Col. 0404A] rather imitate me, following Christ’s footsteps through hardships; for I hasten to Solomon’s bed, that is, to eternal blessedness, which is the bed of Christ, the true Peacemaker, in which all the saints rest with him; and I hasten that I may here become his bed through faith, so that he may rest in me through grace, and that there I may rest in his bed. I shall show you this bed, so that you too may ascend to it and rest in it.”

**VERS. 7, 8.**—“Behold, Solomon’s little bed: sixty valiant men surround it, from among Israel’s mightiest; all holding swords, and most skilled for battles.”

As though she said: “I, the Church, am the little bed of Christ, the true Peacemaker, in which the saints delight in his embrace, when the tumults of vices have been lulled to sleep. Sixty valiant men with swords surround me: that is, all who are perfect in the Law and the Gospel protect me from heretics by their writings. Therefore come, and rest securely in me.” The diminutive “little bed” is used because the saints’ rest here is brief. Literally, this is understood to mean that Solomon, richest of kings, possessed a bed adorned with gold and gems, guarded by the watches of many soldiers.

But allegorically Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” is Christ, the true Peacemaker, who made all things peaceful in heaven and on earth. His bed is the Church, in which he rests through faith, having been driven out of the Synagogue. This bed is adorned with gold and gems—that is, decorated with wisdom and virtues. Sixty valiant men with arms surround it because all the perfect defend the Church by writings and examples. It should be known [Col. 0404C] that numbers are set down in Holy Scripture for a great mystery. Every number is either perfect or imperfect. A perfect number signifies the perfect in the Church; an imperfect number signifies the imperfect within it. A perfect number is one completed by its parts; an imperfect number is one which does not attain its total from its parts, or exceeds it.

Six is a perfect number because it consists of its parts. Its parts are one, two, and three: for six times one, or twice three, or three times two, makes six. This is not so with the number eight, whose parts are one, two, and four; for eight times one, or twice four, or four times two, makes eight. Yet these parts collected together do not make eight [Col. 0404D] but seven; for one, two, and four make seven.

The number twelve, however, exceeds its own total. Its parts are one, two, three, four, and six. For twelve times one, or twice six, or three times four, or four times three, or six times two, makes twelve. Yet these parts gathered into one—namely one, two, three, four, and six—make sixteen. All numbers are contained in four series. The first is called simple: one, two, three, up to ten. In this series only six is perfect; all the others are imperfect. The second series is called multiple: ten, twenty, thirty, and so on up to one hundred. In it only sixty is found perfect, its parts being ten, [Col. 0405A] twenty, and thirty. For ten stands for one, twenty for two, and thirty for three. Thus six times ten, or twice thirty, or three times twenty, makes sixty—which no other number below a hundred does.

The third series is likewise multiple: one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, and so on up to one thousand. In it only six hundred is perfect, for six times one hundred, or twice three hundred, or three times two hundred, makes six hundred. There one hundred stands for one, two hundred for two, and three hundred for three. The fourth series runs from one thousand up to a thousand thousands, or a thousand times a thousand thousands; those following are called myriads. In this series, whatever holds the sixth place is always perfect: namely six thousand, sixty thousand, or six hundred thousand.

The number sixty, therefore, consists of six and ten: for six times ten, or ten times six, makes sixty. By ten is understood the old Law on account of the Decalogue, where it is written, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX), etc.; but by six, the new Law on account of the six works of mercy: “I was hungry and you gave me to eat” (Matt. XXV), etc. By the sixty, then, are understood all the perfect under the Old and New Testaments, such as prophets and apostles: furnished with spiritual arms, strong against vices, steadfast in good works. They surround Solomon’s bed because they fortify the Church, Christ’s bed, by prayer, preaching, example, and writing. They are from among Israel’s mightiest because they are chosen from the Christian people, who will see God. For Israel is a name of blessing and means “a man seeing God,” and signifies the people of the faithful [Col. 0405C] who shall see God. From these are chosen those most valiant men, unconquerable in virtues and strengthening others toward good: all holding ready, in faith and deed, the swords of the preaching of the New and Old Testaments, and most skilled in spiritual battles, knowing the thousand arts of demons and the natures of vices. For they do not fight against human beings but against spiritual wickednesses, and by their writings against heresies.

**VERS. 8.**—“Each man’s sword is upon his thigh, because of the terrors of the night.”

That is: each person’s work must correspond to his preaching. For he fights by work and sword; by preaching he begets, as it were, by the thigh, fearing that, while his life is despised, the word of his preaching may be held in contempt. The word of preaching is called, by likeness, a sword or [Col. 0405D] blade; for as a sword separates soul from body, so the word of God separates the soul from vices, or the evil from the good. By the thigh generation is denoted. The two thighs are the two Laws, through which teachers beget spiritual children. The terrors of the night are the devil’s snares, which lead the unwary to the eternal darkness of hell.

Therefore, as a sword cutting the body is placed upon the thigh, so the word of God, cutting away vices, has mastery over each person’s preaching drawn from the Old and New Testaments, in order to cut off thoughts from the soul and evil works from the body; to beget children of the Church, heirs of God’s kingdom; and to repel the terrors of the night—namely, the snares of the devil and the wiles of heretics, enemies of the Church.

It should be noted that God completed all [Col. 0406A] his works in the number six, which consists of three, two, and one. By three, the Trinity is signified; by two, love of God and neighbor; and by one, the unity of the Church is expressed, in which all the perfect are guardians of Christ’s bed.

Tropologically, Solomon’s little bed is spiritual conduct or the soul of a righteous person, in which God rests, as it is written: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon one who is humble and quiet and trembles at my words?” (Isa. XLII, 2). Sixty men from Israel surround this bed: that is, all spiritual persons contemplating God in their minds surround it by word and example, holding the swords of discernment and cutting off false brethren from true ones; taught by virtues for battles with vices. For each man’s sword is upon his thigh: that is, the severity of life rules each person’s carnality [Col. 0406B] while they mortify the flesh and reduce the body to servitude, because of the terrors of the night—namely, the snares of the devil’s fraud, by which they draw the unwatchful into the night of eternal damnation.

But according to anagogy Solomon’s little bed is eternal blessedness, in which the Church, now departed from this world’s exile, rests. Sixty valiant men from Israel surround it, because all the saints of the Old and New Testaments, seeing God, encircle it, holding swords—that is, showing it the rewards which they have now received because, in life, they fought against vices with the sword of the saving word, when they were trained—that is, exercised—for spiritual battles. Each man’s sword is upon his thigh because each person’s reward will appear, which he received because [Col. 0406C] with the sword of discernment he cut off fleshly lust, lest he be a companion of demons in the night of eternal death.

When the queen has entered the banqueting-house, attended by many daughters of Jerusalem who marvel at her ascent to Solomon’s bed, she urges them to enter the banquet with her, praising the beauty of the house and saying:

**VERS. 9, 10.**—“King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon; he made its columns of silver, its reclining-place of gold, its ascent of purple; he paved its midst with love for the daughters of Jerusalem.”

“And therefore enter with me, and in so renowned a house attend a renowned banquet.” That is, the Church of the Gentiles, made Christ’s bed and a banqueting-house, invites all, whether from Jews or Gentiles, to come into herself through faith, rest through love, and enter upon the feasts of eternal sweetness through action. *Ferculum* is equivocal: it means a dining-room, a bed, a table, a dish, and food; the word is derived from *ferre*, “to carry.” It is handed down that the great furnished upper room in which Christ reclined with the apostles when he gave them his body (Mark XIV, 15) stood in the same place where Solomon had formerly made this *ferculum*, into which he brought the queen.

It should be known, however, that literally King Solomon, abounding in many luxuries, made such a council-hall or dining-room as is written here, in which he had a bed and a table adorned with gold and gems. A *consistorium* is a house of judgment; a dining-room is a house of banquet.

[Col. 0407A] But allegorically Christ made a house of judgment, in which he judges the good unto glory and the evil unto punishment. He also made a banqueting-house, in which he refreshes with his body and his Gospel all who believe in him, saying: “Come to me, in faith and love, all who labor amid the tribulations of the world and are burdened with sins or afflictions, and I will refresh you with eternal refreshment” (Matt. XI, 28).

In this house he placed a bed and a table—that is, cloistered rest and Holy Scripture—so that those weary in the labors of the age may rest in the bed, and those suffering hunger for the word of God may receive food from the table. For Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” is Christ, who dissolves enmities between God and man and makes all things peaceful in heaven and on earth; he [Col. 0407B] is the King of glory, ruling the individual orders of the Church. He made for himself a *ferculum*, that is, a banqueting-house, from the woods of Lebanon: namely, the Church, from all the elect, for his own honor.

Lebanon is a mountain in the promised land, at whose foot the Jordan rises. Its woods are cedars, surpassing all trees in beauty and height, incorruptible, fragrant, and unharmed by worms. Whenever names of mountains, cities, or places occur in Holy Scripture, then either the interpretation of the names, the site of the places, or the significance of deeds done there is denoted. And although the whole part of Scripture called the Hagiographa is full of similitudes, this book especially is woven together through similitudes.

Christ is called, by similitude, a mountain, because two things are marked in a mountain: firmness and height. So Christ is firm in power and lofty in virtue. According to Daniel, this mountain filled the whole world, because Christ’s preaching filled the whole globe. [Col. 0407C] According to Isaiah, all nations ascend this mountain, because all nations believe in Christ. According to David, the city of God is built upon this mountain (Ps. XLVII, 3), because the Church is founded upon Christ’s firm faith and his arduous commands.

Lebanon means “whitening,” and Christ is white because he was born of a chaste Virgin without the stain of sin. From this mountain the Jordan arises because baptism arose from Christ. The woods of this Lebanon are all the elect: beautiful in faith, lofty in hope, fragrant in love. From them the Church, the banqueting-house, has been made. The silver columns supporting this house are the apostles and their episcopal successors: upright in preaching, polished in eloquence and life, sustaining the house of the Lord by word and example.

Within it is a golden reclining-place: the common life of those in cloisters, in which Christ inclines himself to rest, and they rest from worldly labor in order to contemplate God. It is golden because pure in wisdom and brilliant in love. Within it is a purple ascent: the choir of martyrs, made purple by its own blood. Purple is made from the blood of a fish. The fish is Christ, who lay hidden in the human race as a fish in the waves, but was caught by the hook of our mortality. With his blood [Col. 0408A] the purple has been dyed—namely, the Church, which, following Christ’s footsteps, has been made purple by its own blood. By this ascent those climb to Christ who pour out their blood for Christ after the example of the martyrs.

The middle parts are paved with love. Literally, the pavement between the two walls was wonderfully laid with marble and glass inlays, marked out with every kind of history pertaining to love. For various forms of images were impressed upon that work. But it signifies, in the Lord’s house, the crowd of faithful persons toiling in agriculture, who show images of love impressed upon themselves while they assist their neighbors in need from their own resources. Solomon made this adornment for the daughters of Jerusalem because Christ arranged the Church, his house, so that [Col. 0408B] some in it might be columns, some a reclining-place, some an ascent, and some, through works of love, daughters of Jerusalem, of eternal peace.

Tropologically it is understood thus: “King Solomon made himself a *ferculum* from the woods of Lebanon”—that is, a cedar bed. He made its columns—that is, the sides of the bed—of silver; its reclining-place, where the head rests, of gold; its ascent, namely its footstool, of purple; and paved the middle with love—that is, its bed-coverings were woven with things expressing love. The bed made of the woods of Lebanon is the holy soul, made Christ’s resting-place by the examples of the saints. Its columns are the four principal virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. These are silver—that is, brilliant—because they make brilliant the souls [Col. 0408C] which they support.

Its golden reclining-place is a good conscience, pure as gold and refined in the furnace of tribulation, upon which Wisdom reclines. Its ascent is the desire for heavenly things, because in a certain way it ascends while it despises earthly things and desires heavenly ones. This ascent is purple, because whoever labors through the difficult steps of the virtues immediately suffers persecution from evils and becomes a martyr even without the shedding of blood. Its middle parts are paved with love because, between the golden reclining-place and the purple ascent, there are vigils, almsgiving, and fasts: when seasoned with love, these will be acceptable; without love they will be of no use. Such a bed is made for the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, so that faithful souls, the daughters of the Church, [Col. 0408D] may rest in it, and Christ the Bridegroom may rest in them.

But anagogically it is expressed thus: “King Solomon made himself a *ferculum* from the woods of Lebanon”—that is, a cedar table. He made its columns—that is, the legs of the table—of silver; its reclining-place of gold, upon which the ancients used to rest their heads after a meal; and its ascent of purple steps. He paved its midst with love—that is, he varied the tablecloth with figures representing love. The table is Holy Scripture, in which are various dishes of delights. *Ferculum* is also a dish, so called from *ferre*, “to carry”; this again is Holy Scripture, carrying the dishes of life.

This table was made from the woods of Lebanon because Holy Scripture was made from the prophets and apostles of the Jewish people, whitened in the worship of the one God and afterward made white in Christ’s baptism. For both “whitening” and “making white” are meanings of Lebanon. [Col. 0409A] These woods are incorruptible because their deeds are enduring before God. The columns of this table—that is, its legs—are the four senses: history, allegory, tropology, and anagogy. These columns are silver because the Scriptures shine in eloquence. Its golden reclining-place is the Lord’s body, pure and without the stain of sin.

Refined in the fire of the Passion and shining with the brightness of immortality, it is that upon which God reclined when he visited the human race. Its ascent is purple: namely, the sacred cross made purple by the blood of Christ the Fish, through which Christ ascended to the glory of the Father, and through which the pilgrim Church, following him, climbs to joys. Its middle parts are paved with love because all [Col. 0409B] Christ’s works, from the Incarnation to the Passion or Ascension, are full of love. Or the table of Holy Scripture is full of cups of love. This love is placed in the middle—that is, in common—so that through it all may become daughters of the heavenly Jerusalem, and may rest in the bed of eternal quiet and in the golden reclining-place, that is, in the splendor of eternal brightness; they approach the table of the eternal banquet and celebrate the wedding-feast of the Lamb with the angels.

After the adorned queen arrives, the crowned king proceeds to the banquet; and through the city’s streets the herald calls out to the daughters of Zion to see King Solomon crowned with a diadem, and, inviting them, says:

**VERS. 11.**—“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother [Col. 0409C] crowned him, on the day of his betrothal and on the day of his heart’s joy.”

This is the voice of Christ’s preacher-heralds, inviting the daughters of Zion—that is, all the Churches throughout the world—to behold the crowned Christ. Zion is a mountain in Jerusalem, upon which stands the citadel in Jerusalem called David’s tower, and it means “watchtower.” Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” Zion, therefore, figures the present Church, which still beholds future glory “through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. XIII, 12). Jerusalem designates the Church reigning in heaven, which already enjoys the vision of eternal peace. The daughters of Zion are all the Churches spread throughout the world, daughters of the universal Church.

To them the preachers—that is, the heralds of the eternal King—say: “Go out from [Col. 0409D] Babylon, daughters of Zion, and see the crowned King of Jerusalem.” One is, as it were, sitting at home in Babylon when one lies hidden in the confusion of unbelief; one goes out from Babylon, as it were, when one is converted from unbelief to faith in Christ.

The daughters of Zion go out to see King Solomon in the diadem when the Churches throughout the world, having gone out from their former life through faith, contemplate with wonder Christ, the King of glory, the true Peacemaker, in his crown of thorns. His mother, the Synagogue, crowned him with it on the day of Preparation, which was the day of his betrothal, when he betrothed her with his blood; and on the day of his heart’s joy—that is, on the day of Passover, when she rejoiced that she had crucified him as an evildoer with thieves. For it was the Jews’ solemn day of Passover [Col. 0410A] when they crucified Christ; hence another translation has: “On the day of solemnity and joy.”

Or they see the King in a diadem when they perceive Christ in human flesh, because his mother Mary surrounded him on the day of his betrothal—that is, on the day of the Incarnation, when he made human nature his bride—and on the day of his heart’s joy, namely, on the day of the Resurrection, when the assumed human nature, now made immortal, was translated into eternal joy. Or the Virgin Mother rejoiced greatly in her Son’s immortality.

Literally also, the daughters of Zion went out to see Christ in the crown of thorns when the multitude of people and weeping women followed him to the cross, to whom he said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not [Col. 0410B] weep over me, but over yourselves” (Luke XXIII, 28), etc.

According to the moral sense, the daughters of Zion go out to see the crowned King when the souls of the faithful are converted from ignorance to knowledge, or from an evil conscience to confession, or from evil conduct to good conduct, so that they may follow in their hearts Christ’s Passion, which he endured on that day when Judaea, his mother, placed the crown of thorns upon him; and may contemplate in their minds the glory that the Father gave him on the day of solemnity and joy—that is, on the day of the Resurrection, when he crowned him with glory and honor and set him over all his works (Ps. VIII, 67).

According to the higher sense, the daughters of Zion go forth to see the crowned King when souls leave their bodies and enter the palace of heaven, to see the King [Col. 0410C] of glory in his beauty. His mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, crowned him when she received God-made-man, the victor over the devil, crowned by God with triumph, on the day of solemnity and joy—namely, the day of the Ascension—when he bestowed eternal joy upon the Church.

As the herald calls through the city and invites the people to the banquet, the daughters of Zion fly out in companies from their houses and hasten to see the crowned king and the queen adorned with gems. The king embraces her, praises her member by member, and gives her many gifts after praising her. That is, while the apostolic trumpet resounds throughout the world and invites the peoples of the nations to the eternal feast, all nations rushed out from the houses of idolatry and hastened to see the glory of the eternal King, Christ, and of the Church. Christ received the Church coming to him [Col. 0410D] in a sweet embrace and bestowed many gifts of grace upon her. He praises her member by member when he approves the works of faith in the individual orders of the Church. For the whole Church is one body, whose head is Christ, and the head of Christ is God (1 Cor. XI, 3). The members of this body are the different orders of the elect, here distinguished in seven divisions because they are ordered by the sevenfold Spirit. To her he says:

## CHAPTER IV

**VERS. 1.**—“How beautiful you are, my beloved; how beautiful and fair you are!”

As though he said: “O Church, when you were formerly an enemy in Babylon, now converted to me as my beloved, now knowing my secrets: how beautiful you are in the adornment of virtues—very beautiful inwardly in faith, beautiful outwardly in deed, and fair, that is, very dear, in preaching, because you do what you teach and show by example what you exhort.”

“Your eyes are doves’ eyes.” When members of the body occur in Scripture, their offices are denoted; when birds or animals occur, their natures or colors are denoted. The office of the eyes is to shine from the head and provide guidance to the body. Doves are simple and do not harm other birds. The Church’s eyes, therefore, are its bishops and other prelates, its overseers, shining from Christ the Head. Before human beings they shine in word and deed and lead the Church, Christ’s body, to life through examples and writings. These eyes are like the eyes of doves—that is, like fitting guides of Churches, who are [Col. 0411B] doves because they possess seven virtues, as the dove has seven characteristics.

Or your very eyes are doves because they are simple and seek to harm no one. Apart from that which lies hidden within—namely, apart from love, which appears in my eyes alone—you are beautiful in word and example, by which you appear outwardly to human beings; but you are more beautiful before me in what you hide inwardly, in love and virtues. Or you are beautiful in preaching, in your prelate-eyes, apart from hypocrisy and heresy, which lie hidden inwardly in hypocrites and heretics.

“Your hair is like flocks of goats.” Hair adorns and protects the head; goats climb to high places. The Church’s hair is the common people, who adorn her with faith, as farmers do, or protect her with arms, as soldiers do. The flocks [Col. 0411C] of goats are the multitudes of the faithful who, under the apostles, ascended from virtue to virtue unto martyrdom.

After their example, innumerable lay persons in the Church became martyrs like hairs. They ascended from Mount Gilead, which is called “heap of testimony” and is understood as Christ’s army of martyrs, who bear witness to Christ while they shed blood for him. Christ himself is Mount Gilead from which they ascended, because he went before by his example, and they followed him in suffering. He will bear witness to them when he confesses them before the Father, since they confessed him here before human beings (Matt. X, 32).

[Col. 0411D] The story is as follows. Jacob, blessed by his father, went as a sojourner to Laban in Mesopotamia, where he took two wives, begot twelve sons, and returned to his father. Laban pursued and caught up with him, and made a covenant with him. As a memorial of this covenant they gathered a heap of stones, which they called Gilead—that is, “heap of testimony”—so that neither of them might cross it in order to harm the other.

Jacob is Christ; Laban is the devil. Jacob, blessed by his father, is sent into Mesopotamia, and Christ, blessed by the Father, is sent into the world, where he sojourns with Laban, the prince of this world. Jacob took two wives and begot twelve apostles; he returns to his father and Laban persecutes him. So Christ returns to the Father in heaven, and the devil [Col. 0412A] persecutes him in his members. The heap of stones is the multitude of martyrs gathered to Christ. Laban is not permitted to cross this heap, because the devil is not permitted to harm any of those who believe in Christ.

**VERS. 2, 3.**—“Your teeth are like flocks of shorn”—supply, “sheep.”

Teeth bite, grind food, and send it into the body. Sheep, however, nourish others with milk and clothe them with wool. The Church’s teeth, therefore, are the interpreters of Holy Scripture, such as confessors, who bite back at biting heretics, break down the hard letter of Scripture by exposition, and transfer it, as it were, into the Church’s memory, like a stomach. They are like flocks of shorn sheep: that is, like those who under the apostles abandoned all things and, like shorn sheep, lived naked, innocent, and in common. [Col. 0412B] They feed their neighbors with the milk of teaching and clothe the poor with their goods as with wool. And as dead sheep nourish with their flesh and clothe with their skins, so these, dead to the flesh, feed the Church with their writings and clothe it with their examples.

These sheep ascended from the washing-place: that is, they ascend from virtue to virtue, as those washed in baptism promised. All these sheep bear twin offspring, because all those despisers of the world are full of the twofold love, and make those whom they beget for Christ by teaching learned in the twofold love. “And none among them is barren”—supply, “sheep”—but is cast out, because none among religious persons is idle in good work, and the useless person is excluded from them.

“Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon.” Lips disclose the secrets of the heart, while a ribbon binds the hair lest it hang loose. The Church’s lips are teachers, who in teaching disclose to others the things which the teeth—that is, the interpreters—have expounded. They are like a scarlet ribbon: that is, like those who in the primitive Church taught Christ’s Passion and restrained those who were erring from sins. Scarlet is red in color and sets forth the value of Christ’s blood, by which the Church was redeemed. These teachers recount this to their neighbors and bind them back from unlawful things by word and example, like a ribbon. “And your speech is sweet.” The speech of teaching is sweet when someone fulfills in deed what he teaches in word, because when a person’s life is despised, that person’s speech also is held in contempt.

[Col. 0412D] **VERS. 3.**—“Your cheeks are like a fragment of a pomegranate.”

In the cheeks is modesty. Pomegranates are red. Punic is the land of Africa, so called from the fruits—that is, Phoenician fruits—which arrive there, where pomegranates grow: fruits full of seeds and exceedingly red. It signifies Christ’s Passion, or martyrdom in the Church. The Church’s cheeks are those ashamed to sin, such as monks and hermits. They are like a fragment of a pomegranate: that is, like those who suffered under the apostles after Christ’s example and were chaste. For as a fragment of pomegranate is red outwardly and white inwardly, so they are outwardly red in suffering and inwardly white in chastity. They are full of seeds—that is, good examples—apart from that which lies hidden within: namely, apart from [Col. 0413A] the love hidden in the heart, or apart from the tinder of sin hidden in the members.

**VERS. 4.**—“Your neck is like David’s tower.”

When proper names occur in Scripture, then either the interpretation of the name, the person’s office, or the significance of a deed performed by that person is denoted. Thus in Melchizedek three things are considered: the interpretation of his name, “king of righteousness”; his royal and priestly office; and the sacrifice of bread and wine which he offered. He prefigured Christ, who is the King of righteousness and the true priest, who offered bread and wine in the sacrifice of his body.

Likewise, in David three things are considered: the interpretation of his name, “beloved” or “strong of hand”; his office as king and prophet; and the deed he performed in overcoming Goliath in battle. He likewise signified Christ, who is the King of glory and, in that glory, beloved—upon whom angels desire to look (1 Pet. I, 12)—and is the true prophet because he foretold all future things; and he is strong of hand because he conquered the strong devil on the cross.

The neck joins body and head; a tower protects citizens from enemies. The Church’s neck, therefore, consists of those wise in the Scriptures, joining the Church to Christ by word and example. Like the impregnable tower of David—that is, like the primitive Church, founded as a tower by Christ, the true David, the Beloved and Strong of Hand, against persecutors and heresies and fortified with the gifts of the Holy Spirit—so these persons are strengthened by Christ through the defense of the Scriptures, to defend the buildings of faith and repel the enemy’s darts, so that they may protect [Col. 0413C] the citizens of Jerusalem, who are the simple, from the citizens of Babylon, who are heretics, Jews, pagans, and false Christians.

This tower was built with battlements: that is, that Church was fortified with the unconquerable sayings of Scripture by which it may defend itself against enemies. Or the apostles were its battlements because they fought against unbelievers for the Church with the arms of patience.

“A thousand shields hang from it.” This is because innumerable defenses drawn from reason were bestowed upon that Church, by which it might protect itself from adversaries. There hangs all the armor of the strong, because all the deeds of those who bravely conquered vices are held up before it as an example: Joseph conquered lust, Moses avarice. Thus those who are the Church’s neck and David’s tower—because they join the Church to [Col. 0413D] Christ and protect its citizens from enemies—have authoritative books as their battlements; they possess a thousand shields, innumerable defenses from Scriptures and reasons; and they possess all the armor of the strong, namely the written sufferings of all martyrs and the lives of saints set before them.

Alternatively, David’s tower is Holy Scripture, built by Christ, the true King, to defend the Church, his Bride, against enemies. It is built with battlements—that is, with authoritative books—in which the prophets and apostles, its defenders, fight before it and defend it. In this tower hang a thousand shields, which are all the teachings of the righteous from both the Old and New Testaments, and all the armor of the strong, which consists of the examples of all [Col. 0414A] the saints who make others strong against vices.

The number one thousand is multiplied from ten and one hundred. For ten times one hundred, or one hundred times ten, is one thousand; and ten repeated ten times makes one hundred, and likewise one hundred repeated ten times makes one thousand. By ten is understood the reward promised in Christ’s vineyard—that is, in the Church—to those laboring under the Decalogue of the Law. By one hundred is understood the multiplicity of virtues, which is repeated so many times through the Decalogue. By one thousand, however, is understood the fullness of joys which will be given to victors striving or fighting for righteousness.

The thousand shields, therefore, are all the teachings of the righteous who lived under the Law’s Decalogue, in the multiplicity of virtues, for the fullness of joys. With these arms those who are the Church’s neck [Col. 0414B] fortify the Church.

**VERS. 5, 6.**—“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a doe.”

Breasts provide milk for little children, while fawns run swiftly so as to be in high places. The Church’s breasts are those learned in both Laws, who pour into little ones in Christ the sweet milk of teaching from each Law. The two fawns are the active and contemplative: that is, secular and spiritual persons, still little ones in faith in Christ. They run swiftly to the milk of teaching from the two Laws, or of the twofold love, and climb from the valley of tears in order to dwell in the heights of heaven.

These are like two twin fawns of a roe deer; that is, they are like the two peoples converted to the faith from Jews and Gentiles under the primitive Church. This Church [Col. 0414C] was a roe deer, because, as the roe deer seeks the heights, so it ascended from the Law to grace. And its fawns are twins, because, as twins are nourished by the same milk, so Jews and Gentiles converted alike are nourished by the same doctrine of Christ and the same sacraments.

These fawns feed among lilies; that is, the faithful in both kinds of life delight in the virtues of those who were like lilies, white in chastity, and fragrant in holiness, until the day breathes forth—that is, until the full knowledge of God comes—and the shadows decline, that is, ignorance passes away. As long as they are here in the world, they suck the milk of both Laws from the breasts of Mother Church among the lilies—that is, among the flowers of the Scriptures—and feed upon the examples of the saints. When that day of eternal brightness has come and Christ, the sun of righteousness, has shone forth [Col. 0414D], there will no longer be a time for teaching or learning; but, once all the darkness of this life has been brought to an end, all will shine like the sun, because they will see God as he is, in equality with the Father.

Observe the seven members of the bride praised by the bridegroom, that is, the seven orders of the elect in the Church. They are: the eyes, which perceive hidden things; the hair, which, freed from vices, passes through the eye of a needle—that is, the gate of heaven; the teeth, which correct the wicked; the lips, which disclose the secrets of Scripture; the cheeks, which blush at their own sins or those of others; the neck, which by preaching dispenses the vital breath, or the food of doctrine, unto eternal joys; the two breasts, those learned in both Laws from the two peoples.

According to the moral sense, the bridegroom praises the bride’s members when Christ approves each work of the faithful soul. For it too has its own fitting members, by which it performs its duties; it is his beloved because it performs Christ’s commands. It is called beautiful twice, because it has been cleansed from original and actual stain. Its eyes are reason and intention, whose keen sight discerns the spiritual senses of Scripture and directs itself toward what must be pursued; these eyes are those of doves if it simply performs what it sees must be done. Its hair is the subtle thoughts proceeding from its head, that is, its mind; it ascends to Gilead like flocks of goats when it directs itself toward imitating the martyrs. Its teeth are its continual meditations, by which it breaks down the hard meanings of Scripture and conveys them into the belly of memory; they are like shorn sheep, because they are stripped of superfluous thoughts [Col. 0415B]. Its lips are confession, by which, confessing with the mouth unto salvation, it opens what it believes in the heart unto righteousness. These lips are a scarlet ribbon when it confesses that Christ’s blood is the price of its redemption; and by this it restrains its hair, that is, its thoughts, from sins. Its cheeks are modesty, by which it blushes to sin or to have sinned. They are like a fragment of pomegranate, because outwardly they redden with charity and inwardly grow white with chastity. Its neck is understanding, which joins spirit and soul while understanding both to be one substance. This neck is like David’s tower with battlements and a thousand shields, because the understanding of the wise soul is fortified by a thousand sayings of Scripture. Its breasts are wisdom and knowledge, by which it offers the milk of doctrine to the unlearned [Col. 0415C]; they are like fawns of a roe deer because they nourish the little ones in Christ—that is, the humble—with the milk of doctrine and advance them to the heights of virtues.

According to the anagogical sense, this is understood more profoundly of the pilgrim Church. And lest anyone be disturbed because we speak of synagogue and Church, let us distinguish them, first treating of synagogue and Church. The synagogue is the multitude of faithful under the Law. The Church is the multitude of believers under grace. “Synagogue” means a gathering, a term belonging to irrational creatures or stones, because the Jews were gathered by the rod of the Law, being hard for the worship of God. “Church,” however, means a calling together, a term belonging to human beings, because Christians were called by the word of preaching to faith in Christ.

The primitive Church is called the multitude of the righteous from Abel until Christ; but properly speaking, the primitive Church is the whole body of faithful first gathered through Christ and the apostles from Jews and Gentiles. The Church of the Gentiles is the multitude of believers brought to faith in Christ from every nation through the apostles and their successors. The universal Church is the whole of Christianity spread throughout the world. The Church of the imperfect is the people living in the active life, which uses this world as though not using it and keeps love of neighbor by supplying their necessities. The Church of the perfect is the clergy established in the contemplative life, which, having passed beyond the world, strives to fulfill love of God by reading and praying. The pilgrim Church [Col. 0416A] is the multitude that, in both kinds of life, longs for heavenly things.

The Church reigning in heaven is the throng of souls already enjoying the presence of Christ, its bridegroom. Thus the pilgrim Church has its own members, just as the primitive Church had its own. The eyes of the Church before the Law were the patriarchs, who prefigured Christ for it. The eyes of the Church under the Law were the prophets, who foresaw Christ for it in their writings. The eyes of the Church under grace were the apostles, who led it to Christ by signs and miracles. The eyes of the pilgrim Church are bishops and other prelates, who lead it to eternal life by preaching and examples; it is called Christ’s beloved because it is summoned to heavenly secrets. It is said twice [Col. 0416B] to be beautiful because it is fair in active and contemplative life, in faith and in work.

Its hair is boys or laypeople; its teeth, voluntary poor persons; its lips, clerics; its cheeks, monks; its neck, hermits; its breasts, teachers. It is a dove because it is full of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; a goat because it seeks the heights; a sheep because it is innocent; a ribbon because it is constrained by religious discipline; a pomegranate because it is full of the seeds of good works; David’s tower because it is unconquerable by heretics; a roe deer because it chooses good things out of evil. Through these virtues in its members it already reigns in heaven.

The tabernacle of Moses, carried on the journey, prefigured the pilgrim Church. Solomon’s Temple, built in the homeland, prefigured the reigning Church. In the tabernacle were the holy places, in which the people sacrificed, and the Holy of Holies, in which the priests made offerings. By the holy places is understood the active life, in which secular persons serve; by the Holy of Holies, the contemplative life, in which spiritual persons labor. Yet all the mysteries of the present Church are also expressed in the same tabernacle. The tabernacle was moved from place to place and carried by the people journeying toward their homeland. So the Church is changed from a lower to a better condition, until, when the journey of this life is complete, it is transferred to the homeland of paradise.

The Temple, however, was built in the homeland by Solomon over seven years from three materials: namely, cut stones taken from the sea, cedar wood, and the purest gold [Col. 0416D]. Thus the Church, the temple of God in the heavenly homeland, is built together by Christ the truly peaceable one, through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, into a dwelling for God, from three orders of the elect: married persons, squared amid the salt waves of worldly tribulations; the continent, fragrant in virtues; and teachers, tested like gold in adversity and shining in wisdom. Into this Temple the tabernacle was transferred, because the present Church is transferred into fellowship with that Church which already reigns. For this reason the queen of the south came from Ethiopia into that Temple, because this Church will enter heaven from the darkness of the world.

After the king had feasted with the queen, he rose from there and went to the mountain of myrrh, that is, to Lebanon. For in Lebanon grow trees from which [Col. 0417A] myrrh and frankincense are gathered. The queen followed him there with the daughters of Zion, having gone out to see the king, and was received by him with this praise.

**VERS. 7, 8. — “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no stain in you.”**

It should be understood literally that Solomon, a very wealthy king, had built at royal expense a tower in Lebanon, in which he was accustomed to live during the summer because of the temperate air there, owing to the streams of the Jordan. It must also be carefully noted that in this Song only the words of lovers are represented, while their actions are understood; for even now those singing in dances represent in their songs not the actions but the words of lovers.

The allegory is this: after the Church of the Gentiles had been received [Col. 0417B] into fellowship with Christ and refreshed at the banquet of his body, it immediately grew in part into the mountain of myrrh and in part rose to the hill of frankincense. For as soon as it recognized that Christ its king had suffered for it, the army of martyrs undertook war against tyrants and the multitude of confessors began battle against heretics.

The bodies of the dead were embalmed with myrrh, while frankincense was placed in sacrifice to God. The mountain of myrrh, therefore, is the multitude of martyrs, who rose like a mountain to the lofty virtue of patience when they were put to death for Christ amid various torments. The hill of frankincense is the multitude of confessors, who rose above the people like a hill in holiness and offered themselves to God as an odor of sweetness. Christ goes to this mountain and this hill, saying: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.” It is as though he said to the Church coming to him: “I see the ranks of my soldiers, namely the martyrs, laboring in struggle for me. Therefore I will go and bring aid to those fighting by giving patience, and I will prepare the crown of glory for those who conquer. I will come also to the battle line of the confessors, that I may assist those fighting by supplying wisdom and crown the victors with glory and honor.”

On this mountain and this hill Christ stood through faith; with eyes of mercy he saw all the formations of his army—that is, every order of the Church throughout the world striving for righteousness—and he praised the Church, that is, approved such works, saying: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved.” That is to say: “O Church, my beloved, [Col. 0417D] knowing the Father’s secrets, you are beautiful in your eyes, your hair, your teeth, and your other members: in patience, steadfastness, and wisdom. Therefore you are beautiful, and no stain of crime is in you, so that no one, defeated in battle by torments or vices, may fail, but that one fighting with the arms of righteousness may emerge victorious.”

“Therefore, after the battle, come to me in all your members, and I will crown you: ‘Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come; you shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon.’” That is, “I will place upon you a crown made from jewels taken from these mountains.”

Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, and its name means “whitening” or “making white.” By Lebanon the Jewish people are here understood, exalted in royal power and white through divine worship. By Lebanon is also understood [Col. 0418A] the Gentile people, which was exalted in empire and whitened by worldly glory. Thus it is said: “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon.” As though he said: “O my bride, by bearing spiritual children for me, come in faith with a great company from Lebanon—that is, from the Jewish people, white in divine worship. Come with a great multitude from Lebanon—that is, from the Gentile people, made white by empire and worldly glory. Come to me also with the throng of the fallen converted to repentance, and with these and for all these you shall be crowned.”

Observe that he calls the bride from Lebanon to the crown, Lebanon to which she had followed him, because Christ will crown the one who has followed him to the heights of virtue. And from where is the bride crowned? “From the summit of Amana and the peak [Col. 0418B] of Senir and Hermon.” Amana is a mountain of Cilicia, also called Taurus; Senir and Hermon are mountains of Judea, in which lions and leopards dwell. Mountains are kings and princes who exalt themselves in pride; demons dwell in them. They are lions because they are cruel, leopards because they are wicked through diverse arts. The bride is crowned from these when by her preaching she has expelled demons and converted rulers to Christ.

Amana means “restless,” “turbulent,” or “God of watchfulness”; Senir, “stench” or “night-bird”; Hermon, “anathema” or “accursedness.” The summit of Amana is the devil, the head of those who are Amana—that is, restless, turbulent, biting, and watchful in malice. He is likewise the peak of those who are Senir: those stinking with lust and unstable like birds in the night of ignorance. He is also the peak of those who are like Hermon—that is, accursed, namely excommunicated by their own iniquity. Jewels for the bride’s crown are chosen from these mountains when such persons are converted to repentance through her. She fights against these battle lines and conquers when she converts them to good.

She is also crowned “from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” A lion sometimes signifies Christ, sometimes the devil, and sometimes a proud ruler. It signifies Christ in the words, “Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered,” on account of strength, because he conquered the devil, and because a lion raises its cub on the third day: so also the Father raised Christ on the third day. A lion signifies the devil in the words: “Your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8), on account of ferocity. A lion also signifies a ruler in the words: “I was delivered from the mouth of the lion” (2 Tim. 4:17), that is, from Nero’s power, on account of eminence. For the lion is king of beasts, and beasts in Scripture are used for their natures. In this place lions signify demons. Their dens are the profane and unclean.

Leopards, however, are heretics, variegated in the doctrine of error; their mountains are the heresiarchs, namely their bishops and teachers, proud and swollen with eloquence. In such people demons dwell like beasts in caves. The members of the Church fight against such persons, and the Church is crowned for those whom it has defeated and converted.

Alternatively, Amana means “lofty,” and the Father is indicated, who is exalted above all things. Senir means “thick lamp,” and Christ is understood, who is the lamp of the Church unto life. Hermon means “consecration,” and the Holy Spirit is understood, through whom the Church is consecrated in baptism. The summit of Amana, or the peak of Senir and Hermon, is God the Father. Therefore the Church will be crowned from the summit of Amana, or the peak of Senir and Hermon, when God the Father exalts it in glory for faith in the Son and the consecration of the Holy Spirit.

Now the king urges his soldiers to battle, that they may receive the crown of life; for no one will be crowned unless one has competed lawfully (2 Tim. 2:5). To compete lawfully is to fight until night—that is, until death; namely, to resist vices and sins. For these to be crowned is to be raised to eternal glory. Therefore he says:

**VERS. 9. — “You have wounded my heart, my sister [Col. 0419B], my bride.”**

As though he said: “O Church, my sister—that is, co-heiress of the kingdom—and my bride, bearing for me children who are co-heirs of heaven, do not regard it as burdensome, for my sake, to undergo the toil of conflict; for I first underwent, for your sake, the sweat of battle, in which I was wounded even unto death.”

By “heart” love is understood, which is said to be in the heart; the container is put for what it contains. The comparison is with someone who loves another and whose heart is wounded by love. Thus Christ was wounded by love for the Church on the cross. “You first wounded my heart when, for love of you, I was scourged in order to make you my sister, namely co-heiress of the kingdom. You wounded my heart again when, hanging upon the cross for love of you, I was wounded in order to make you my bride, a participant in glory. And this was through one of your eyes and one lock of your neck.”

The comparison is with someone captivated by the beauty of a maiden’s eyes or hair, as Holofernes was by Judith. The Church’s eyes are its prelates, who lead it to heavenly things. Its locks are its subjects; its neck is the perfect, whom such hairs adorn. “One” of its eyes or locks is the unity of faith possessed by prelates and subjects. For this unity you pleased me, and I loved you, and I received these wounds; and for this unity you must fight, that you may be crowned. All this is said to the bride appointed for the kingdom, that she may receive a crown equal to that of the rival—that is, the glory of angelic nature. She is called beloved because the bridegroom disclosed to her the secrets of Scripture; sister because he made her his co-heiress; bride because she bears children for him for the kingdom.

In the tropological sense [Col. 0419D], the mountain of myrrh is the contemplative life, while the hill of frankincense is the active life. Contemplatives are myrrh because they have put to death their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5:24). Active persons are frankincense because by good actions they offer God an odor of sweetness. Christ goes to these when he aids them in tribulations and temptations. In these, the faithful soul is wholly beautiful when it is blameless in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord, or when it loves God with all its strength and its neighbor as itself. There is no stain in it when it lacks heresy and fault.

It comes by faith; it comes also by action; it comes by preaching; it comes also to Christ in thought, speech, and deed. It comes in youth, [Col. 0420A] comes in old age, comes in decrepitude; it comes to faith in baptism; it comes to rest at life’s end; it comes to glory in the resurrection. And this is from Lebanon, that is, from the brightness of virtues; thus it becomes the bride of Christ, joined to him in love.

Alternatively, there are three renunciations. The first is when one renounces the devil. The second, when one renounces the world. The third, when one renounces oneself and follows Christ. Thus the soul comes from Lebanon to Christ when it renounces the devil’s pomps in baptism; it comes from Lebanon when it renounces the delights of the world; it comes a third time when it renounces its own wills and wholly gives itself over to the obedience of its superiors.

It will be crowned because it fled from Mount Amana—that is, from those who are restless and turbulent—and because it fled from [Col. 0420B] Mount Senir and Hermon—that is, from those stinking in sins, unstable in good, and excommunicated from the good. It will be crowned because it is now the temple of the Holy Spirit, though its heart was formerly a den of lions, that is, demons; or because it separates itself from the unclean, who are dens of demons, and from the mountains of leopards, the proud false brethren.

It wounds Christ’s heart when, as it repents, he compassionately indulges it; it wounds his heart when, as it desires him, he graciously condescends to it. And this occurs “in one of its eyes,” that is, in one intention, when it asks only one thing of the Lord: that it may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of its life (Ps. 26:4), that is, throughout all the time of Christ, who is its life. And it occurs “in one lock of its neck,” that is, in one thought of understanding, by which it understands that there is one God, the highest good.

Anagogically, the mountain which the king entered is heaven, which Christ, king of glory, ascended.
