It is the mountain of myrrh and hill of frankincense—that is, there is seen the dwelling of martyrs and confessors; the beloved wholly beautiful, namely the reigning Church, glorious in all its orders. There is no stain in it, because that court receives no stain of sin; and because the angels are without sin, those who are to be made equal to them must also be without the stain of sin. It comes from Lebanon—that is, from the brightness of worldly glory in rulers; it comes also from Lebanon, that is, from the whiteness of virtues in spiritual persons; it comes from Lebanon in baptized believers. It will be crowned from the summit of the three mountains [Col. 0420D], because it will be glorified by the deity of the three Persons, as the names of the mountains suggest: Amana indeed means “lofty,” by which the Father is understood; Samur, “lamp,” by which the Son is understood; Hermon, “consecration,” by which the Holy Spirit is indicated.

Let no one be disturbed that there are different interpretations of the Hebrew mountains, because interpretations of names change according to the different sense of Scripture. For at one time they are understood in a good sense, at another in a bad sense. They are understood in a good sense when referred to Jerusalem—that is, the multitude of faithful—but in a bad sense when referred to Babylon—that is, unbelievers.

In that glory the queen will see the king of glory, her beloved, crowned in majesty, whom here she saw wounded on the cross by love for her. There [Col. 0421A] will be “one” of the eyes and locks, that is, the unity of all prelates and subjects enjoying that vision; their joy will be God of peace and the sweetness of concord among all. The queen, summoned from Lebanon to be crowned, comes with a very great company. In this company she had forty of Israel’s strongest men, most skilled in war, holding swords, and daughters of Zion. With them she undertook the battle against Amana, Senir, and Hermon for the crown; victorious, she approached the king, who here received her with praise.

**VERS. 10–15. — “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride,” through “Arise, north wind.”**

In this manifold praise he recounts her brave deeds performed in war: namely, that she armed those who were to fight with breasts, trained them for combat with udders, healed the wounded in battle with ointments, strengthened the fearful with lips, fed those weary in battle with honey and milk, sent them back to battle clothed, refreshed the victors in the garden with various herbs and a spring, and led them into paradise among diverse kinds of fruit.

Then in praise he describes ten legions, which he sent into battle against the enemy’s lines. By all these things is indicated the multitude of the Church of the Gentiles, which comes from Lebanon—that is, from the brightness of worldly glory—to Christ with a great company of believers. In that company it had as companions kings, profane princes, and persons of every class, profession, and condition. With them it undertook spiritual war against demons, the enemies of souls, and earned the crown of life from the King of glory. Concerning this battle one of its commanders said: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers” (Eph. 6:12). That is: our battle is not against human beings, but against demons. Likewise another mighty warrior says: “The life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7:1); “all the days in which I now serve, I await until my change comes” (Job 14:14). For the faithful serve in the camp of their king against the citizens of Babylon for the crown, which is the change, when the righteous will shine like the sun and be equal to angels.

Observe the artistic order. He first mentioned the crown and then introduced the battle, although battle comes first and the crown, which is the reward of battle, follows; because a crown is promised to those who fight and given to those who conquer. It should also be noted that in this praise [Col. 0421D] the historical sense fails, just as at times allegory, tropology, or anagogy does not continue throughout.

In the first six items the instruments of spiritual battle are praised: namely breasts, udders, ointments, lips, tongue, and garments. By these are denoted the six ages of combatants. Thus, by breasts infants are figured; by udders, boys; by ointments, adolescents; by lips, young men; by the heart beneath the tongue, old men; by garments, the decrepit. By six works of mercy these labor in this battle, that they may receive the crown of the number six, which is full joy.

Then three refuges of the combatants are set forth: garden, spring, and paradise. For in this war those wounded by sins are healed in the garden of the Catholic Church by the herbs of repentance and confession [Col. 0422A]; they are washed in the spring of tears; they are refreshed in the paradise of the Scriptures. Thus they are transferred into the garden of delights to Christ, the fountain of life. After this, ten legions of combatants are signified by the ten kinds of trees in paradise—namely by cypress, nard, and the rest—because those who sweat in this battle under the arms of the commandments are brought to the tenfold reward. Finally, the spring and well are included in the praise, by which the Gospel and Law are understood, because Christ refreshes his warriors with the streams of the Law and Gospel and brings the crowned to refreshment.

Therefore the king says to the queen’s nurse: “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! Your udders are better than wine.” Breasts (*mammae*) belong to girls who do not have milk but are capable of having it. Udders or breasts (*ubera*) belong to women who have milk and are so called from abundance. The breasts (*mammae*) of the Church are infants learning in schools and others still untrained in faith, sucking the milk of doctrine yet not bringing it forth by teaching others, though capable of doing so. These breasts are very beautiful, because those diligent in learning virtues—the arms against vices with which they will someday fight against God’s enemies—greatly please God.

The udders or breasts (*ubera*) of the Church are teachers learned in both Laws, who pour the milk of doctrine into children being taught and instruct their mouths for spiritual war. Wine which intoxicates and deranges is secular philosophy, which inflates human minds and raises them to boastfulness. But the Church’s breasts are better than wine, because the doctrine of teachers drawn from both Laws is more useful, because it builds up in twofold love [Col. 0422C], than philosophical doctrine, which inflates minds.

Observe that he so often repeats “sister” and “bride.” By this confidence is given to the Church: that it is Christ’s co-heiress as a sister of a brother, and sharer in the kingdom as bride of a king. “And the fragrance of your garments is above all spices.” The ointments of the Church are the virtues of spiritual persons, who, as it were with ointments, cure the wounds of sins when they train people in virtues. Spices are certain fragrant preparations made of many ingredients for embalming dead bodies; but they are superstitious preparations, which the Jews especially used. By them carnal observances are superstitiously signified.

The fragrance of ointments is the fame of virtues arising from charity in spiritual persons, or the reputation of works performed through the Holy Spirit. This fragrance is above all spices: that is, it pleases God more than all the sacrifices of the Law, which were figures of these things. These matters are introduced in the Song of Love because pagans disputed with Christians about philosophy, Jews about legal observance, while Christians trusted in divine grace alone. Philosophers maintained that human salvation consists in the pursuit of wisdom; Jews contended that it consists in the religion of legal observance; Christians contended that it consists in faith in divine grace. The bridegroom, acting as judge, approves this position and rejects their contention, saying: “Your breasts are better than wine”; that is, study in Sacred Scripture, by which grace is sought, is better than philosophy, because free choice without grace does not effect salvation. “And the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices”: that is, the teachings and virtues of spiritual persons please me more than all the traditions of carnal Pharisees.

**VERS. 11. — “Your lips, my bride, drip honeycomb.”**

The lips of the Church are those who tell others the doctrine which they themselves sucked from the breasts of Mother Church. These lips drip like honeycomb when they sweetly instill in hearers the sweet doctrine they have drawn from teachers. A honeycomb is honey in wax. Honey in wax is spiritual understanding hidden in the letter. But the honeycomb drips when sweet allegory flows from the letter.

Alternatively: honey lies hidden in the honeycomb, while wax is visible; so visible is the frail flesh in which wisdom lies hidden like honey in wax. “Honey and milk are under your tongue.” The tongue is the interpreter of the heart, because what the heart thinks, the tongue expresses. The heart of the Church is the wise, who conceive divine meanings through the spirit of wisdom and write them down. Its tongue is those who bring forth in interpretation what the wise, as its heart, conceived. Honey is the sweet doctrine of allegory, fitting for the learned; milk is the simple doctrine of history, suitable for little ones, that is, the unlearned. Honey and milk are said to be under the Church’s tongue when both allegorical and historical doctrine, conceived in the heart, is expressed with a sweetness of words as great as the sweetness experienced in honey and milk.

“And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.” With a garment naked and foul things are covered. The Church’s garments are good works, by which the ugliness of previous sins is covered. The fragrance [Col. 0423C] of garments, therefore, is the example of good works. Those who are about to fight against vices are clothed with these as with a breastplate, by which they can “extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one” (Eph. 6:16). This fragrance is like frankincense because the practice of good action pleases God just as the incense of prayer does. For the fragrance of frankincense signifies the incense of prayer, as it is written: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. 140:2).

**VERS. 12. — “A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed.”**

In those who are breasts (*mammae*), that is, the imperfect, you are an enclosed garden and sister; in those who are udders (*ubera*), that is, the perfect, you are an enclosed garden and sister-bride. Again, in those who are the fragrance of your ointments, that is, contemplatives, you are an enclosed garden; in those who are the fragrance of garments, that is, active persons, you are an enclosed garden. Likewise, in those who are lips you are an enclosed garden; in those who are tongue you are an enclosed garden.

In a garden medicinal herbs and diverse flowers grow. The garden is the Church, in which are many virtues of the saints, like diverse kinds of herbs medicinal for diverse wounds of sin. In this garden are various flowers, the diverse orders of the elect: martyrs like roses, confessors like violets, virgins like lilies, and other faithful like other flowers. The gardener of this garden is Christ, who is also its bridegroom; he plants it by grace and waters it by doctrine. This garden is enclosed among contemplatives, namely fortified against demons by the protection of angels. It is also enclosed [Col. 0424A] among active persons, because it is surrounded by the defense of teachers against heretics. In this garden, the herbs and flowers are all the faithful flourishing in faith and works.

The comparison is with the garden of paradise, which is said to be enclosed everywhere by a wall of fire and fortified by angelic guardianship, so that fire keeps human beings out of it and angels drive demons from it. Thus the Church is God’s garden, surrounded by divine protection and a wall of fire, fortified by angelic guardianship, so that neither demons nor evil people can prevail to harm it. This is said so that their assaults may not be feared in spiritual battle when such great defenses protect it.

In this garden is a fountain that waters it, namely Sacred Scripture, by whose streams the Church is watered. This fountain is sealed because the understanding of Sacred Scripture is sealed within the letter, like writing under a seal, lest what secret the bride possesses be laid open to the unworthy. In this garden there is also the fountain of baptism, in which the wounds of sins are washed. It is sealed, namely consecrated by the holy cross or the word of God; sealed against pagans, opened to catechumens.

Alternatively, a fountain washes away dirt, quenches thirst, and restores an image. This fountain is Christ, the fountain of life, from whom flow rivers of living water—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—with which he waters the garden of the Church, so that it may bring forth the fragrances of the flowers of life. He washes away the filth of sins, quenches the thirst of those thirsting for righteousness by the fullness of his vision, and restores to souls the lost image of God. He was sealed because he was veiled by flesh as by a seal. Now he is sealed because he is hidden from us in the glory of the Father [Col. 0424C].

This fountain is also written to be David’s fountain standing open, because Christ’s mercy lies open to all repentant persons, that they may wash themselves with tears, just as David washed in it the wounds of his guilt. But the Church itself is also a fountain, because it overflows with spiritual grace and wisdom; from it flow abundant streams of doctrine, by which it waters the plantings of its garden so that they may put forth very many shoots. “Shoots” are little branches springing from trees or herbs. Concerning these, the text continues.

### Verses 13–14

**Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of orchard-trees.**

The garden of the Church, watered from the fountain of Scripture, has put forth so many shoots that from them a paradise has grown. A garden is a place where herbs or vegetables grow; a paradise is a place where trees grow. Literally, the paradise of delight is a place in the eastern regions, full of every bodily pleasure, where the first parents were; because of the fault of disobedience they were expelled from it. In it is the fountain from which paradise is watered, and which is divided into four rivers. There is also in it the tree of life—that is, such a tree that, if a human being had eaten from it, he could never bodily die. Hence after the transgression it is written: “See lest perhaps he take from the tree of life and live for ever” (Gen. 3:22). There was also there the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, from which, if they ate, they would know good and evil.

Before eating the fruit of this tree Adam knew good and evil: good by experience, evil only by knowledge; just as a physician knows the pain of a wound by knowledge, not by experience. But after sin he knew evil—that is, hunger, thirst, and other discomforts—by experience, and good only by knowledge. This did not lie in the nature of the tree, but in human disobedience. The inhabitants of the regions around paradise say that flowers and fruits are sent out to them from paradise by the rivers which flow from it, and that people live from these.

Allegorically, the Church is paradise, full of every spiritual delight. For paradise means “garden of delights,” and in the Church are the manifold delights of the Scriptures, of diverse arts, and of many virtues. In this paradise is a fountain, namely baptism or Christ, by whose streams—that is, spiritual charisms—such a paradise is watered. The four rivers of this fountain are the four Gospels. The tree of life is the holy cross, whose fruit is Christ’s body; whoever worthily eats of it shall not die eternally in soul. Fruit-bearing trees are the saints; the fruit of the holy trees is their works; the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is free choice.

In this spiritual paradise grow diverse kinds of trees—that is, diverse orders of the elect. There grow pomegranates, namely African trees which produce pomegranates, or red fruits called *malogranata*, “full of grains.” These are martyrs, red with blood and full of works as of grains. That garden, watered by the fountain, put forth these trees when the holy Church, drenched in baptism, produced martyrs with the fruits of orchard-trees—that is, with examples of good works.

There too grows *cyprus*, an aromatic tree in Egypt, having a seed like coriander. It has a white, translucent, fragrant manna-like substance, cooked in oil; from this a juice is pressed which is called *cyprus*, from which royal ointment is prepared—so called because the royal disease is cured by it. The aromatic *cyprus* tree, abundant in Egypt, is the conduct of spiritual people, which first flourished in Egypt, that is, in the darkness of this world, which “Egypt” signifies. Its seed is like manna, which had every delight and every flavour of sweetness, because the life of the righteous possesses every spiritual delight and every taste of holiness. The seed is white, bright, and fragrant, because their conduct is white in chastity, bright in activity, and fragrant in charity. Its juice is cooked with oil and turned into royal ointment, because their life is tested by the flames of temptations as gold; for the royal disease—that is, the leprosy of the soul—is healed by this ointment.

Mary offered this ointment to the Lord in the house of Simon the leper, because the Church, by her example, offers to the Lord heretics whom she heals from the leprosy of the soul—that is, from heresy.

There also grows nard, an aromatic tree—that is, fit for aromatics—small, very fragrant, and warm, from which the finest ointment is made. These are the humble and innocent, who make themselves small, that is, despised, before their neighbours, and anoint those wounded by sins with the fragrance and ardour of charity.

There grows also saffron, a reddish flower—that is, golden in colour. These are the wise, shining with divine wisdom.

There grows also *fistula*, a small aromatic shrub, which is cassia, stout and with purple bark, useful for curing pains of the internal organs. Because of its smallness, some reckon it among fragrant herbs. These are those who are patient for Christ and ready to lay down their lives for their brethren.

There grows also cinnamon, a short but fragrant and sweet tree, ash-coloured, twice as effective as cassia for medicinal use. These are penitents, who regard themselves as weak and, doing penance in ashes, give a sweet fragrance to the Church. The cinnamon tree has three barks: the upper is called cassia, the middle cinnamon, and the third amomum. The middle is sweeter than the rest. These, however, when separated by someone, are loosened from the tree by excessive heat: they are monks, who loose themselves from the world for Christ’s love.

These trees grow in that paradise with all the trees of Lebanon, that is, cedars and other fragrant trees. These are all the faithful, whose faith and activity are incorruptible and fragrant.

There also grow myrrh and aloe with all the finest ointments. Myrrh is a tree whose juice is stacte, preserving flesh from worms and decay. These are hermits or chaste persons, mortifying themselves against vices and preserving their flesh from the decay of lust. Aloe too is a tree of most pleasant fragrance, so that it is burned on altars in place of incense; but it has an extremely bitter juice which resists corruption. These are the continent, who restrain the wantonness of the flesh through the bitterness of life.

The finest ointments are the more precious ones, made from the first flowers of precious species, such as the costly spikenard of Mary in the Gospel. These are prelates and others filled with the chief charisms of the Holy Spirit—that is, with the foremost gifts among believers—who, burning in word and example, heal, as it were by ointment, the wounds of sick souls.

It should be noted that these kinds of trees or herbs from which ointments are prepared are introduced because they signify the orders of the elect, like companies serving in the camp of a king, whose wounds are healed by ointments. Therefore he compares the bride both to a garden, a fountain, and a paradise, as though plainly saying to her: “Do not fear to fight against the ranks of Amana, for you have such warriors in your company; secure in their steadfastness and arms, you will overcome your enemies and be crowned victorious by me. You will heal those wounded in battle with your herbs, because you are a garden of medicinal herbs; you will refresh the weary with your streams, because you are a fountain of spiritual waters; and you will satisfy the victors with your fruits, because you are a paradise—that is, a garden of fruits, of spiritual dishes.”

Literally, it should be known that Solomon enclosed such a garden with a wall in Lebanon, in which he had planted these kinds of herbs and trees. In it also the source of the Jordan sprang up, concerning which he adds:

### Verse 15

**A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon.**

It is called “of gardens” because above he set forth two gardens. Living waters are waters which flow: water which stands is as though dead; water which runs is as though alive. Notice that he says, “which flow with force from Lebanon,” because the streams of the Jordan flow with great force from Lebanon. There are two springs, Jor and Dan; where these two meet, they make the river Jordan.

The abundance of waters is therefore introduced in order that the overflowing abundance of rewards may be shown, rewards which will be given to conquerors who are brought to the fountain of life, Christ, and to the well of living waters—that is, the Holy Spirit, the well of spiritual gifts. For he has set forth ten kinds of trees of paradise, by which he expressed ten orders of the elect in the spiritual paradise. They fight against vices under the ten commandments, in order to receive the reward of the denarius, namely the crown of glory.

Such is the fruit of the garden; but its fountain, that is, its irrigation, is “a fountain of gardens and a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon.” A fountain is where a stream issues forth; a well is where water lies hidden in the depth.

Therefore the fountain of gardens is the Gospel, the irrigation of Churches living in the active and contemplative life. This fountain sprang forth from Lebanon, ran into the garden of Jerusalem, flowed from Mount Sion, and watered all the gardens of the world. That is: Gospel teaching sprang from Christ, ran into the garden of Jerusalem—that is, the primitive Church—flowed from Mount Sion through the apostles to the nations, and watered all the Churches.

The well of waters, however, is the profound law of divine meanings, which lie hidden in the letter of the Law as water in a deep well. These waters are living because they make those who understand them spiritually live. These waters flow with force from Lebanon because they come abundantly from the Jewish people. For Lebanon means “whitening,” and signifies the Jewish people whitened by divine worship. From this Lebanon the streams of Law and Prophets flowed, and through the apostles they poured with force into the Church of the nations, who expounded the Scriptures abundantly in a spiritual sense.

Alternatively, Lebanon means “whitening,” and signifies Christ born of a chaste Virgin. From this Lebanon waters flowed with force when the gifts of the Holy Spirit flooded believers like a rushing torrent and filled them with knowledge of all languages. Of these waters he himself said: “He who believes in me, from his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38), that is, charisms of the Holy Spirit, which make believers live with God.

All this is introduced here so that the bride may know that her warriors are filled with the teaching of Christ and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and will be rewarded just as the apostles, Christ’s warriors, were filled with Christ’s teaching and the gifts of the Holy Spirit and rewarded with the prize of life.

The fountain also signifies those capable of the word of God; the well signifies those who scarcely understand the mysteries. A cistern is a collection of rainwater: these are the dogmas of heretics.

Tropologically, the faithful soul is Christ’s bride, joined to him by love and bearing spiritual children—that is, good works. She is also his sister, because she is co-heir of his kingdom. For “those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:12). The soul has members appropriate to herself. Her breasts are pursuits of learning and reading, by which she draws the milk with which later to nourish little ones—that is, the unlearned. Her bosoms are wisdom and knowledge, from which she provides the milk of teaching to the unlearned. Her ointments are good exhortations, by which she heals the wounds of souls more than by the wine of worldly prudence. Her lips are confession, by which she confesses with the mouth what she believes in the heart, or reveals sins in confession. Her tongue is the interpretation of thought when she speaks, orally or in writing, the good counsel of her heart. Her garments are virtues, in which she is adorned as a body is adorned with clothes. Hence it is written: “The Lord has clothed me with the garment of salvation and the robe of joy” (Isa. 61:10).

The soul is also a garden because she resembles a garden: full of good thoughts as a garden is full of herbs, full of virtues as a garden is full of flowers. This garden is enclosed, that is, protected from demons by good works. She is also a fountain, because heavenly teaching flows from her and waters other gardens, namely faithful souls; this fountain is sealed by the seal of holy faith.

Likewise the holy soul is paradise, full of spiritual delights. The fountain of this paradise is charity, which waters this paradise so that it may bring forth precious fruit. The four rivers of paradise are the four principal virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. The tree of life is wisdom; its fruit, immortality. Fruitful trees are useful disciplines; the fruit of the trees, the habits of the godly. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the observance of the commandment. Ointment-bearing signs—nard, saffron, and the rest—are virtues: chastity, goodness, humility, and other ointments for sick souls. The fountain and well within her are Gospel and legal teaching, or knowledge.

Anagogically, the paradise of exultation is the dwelling of the saints in heaven, full of every delight. Paul was caught up into this paradise, and into it the Lord brought the thief. In this paradise, the fountain which flows from the place of delight is Christ, the fountain of life flowing from the Father’s heart, from whom the life of all things proceeds. The tree of life is God’s wisdom, or the Holy Spirit, inspiring eternal life in all. The fountain and well of living waters is the fullness of all joys. In the remainder of this chapter the anagogical sense fails.

There are therefore four paradises: the earthly paradise of delight; the heavenly paradise of exultation; the paradise of religion, namely the Churches; and the paradise of virtue, namely souls.

After Amana, defeated in battle with his followers, fell vanquished, behold, Aquilo, another enemy, brought grave war against the queen. But, defeated, he fled into the garden and lay hidden there in ambush like a thief. While the queen refreshed her victorious army there, the king came, found the hidden enemy, expelled him shamefully from the garden, and invited Auster, the gardener of the garden, saying:

### Verse 16

**Arise, Aquilo, and come, Auster; blow upon my garden.**

That is, after the persecution of tyrants had ceased and the patience of the saints had been crowned, the madness of heretics immediately arose in the Church and brought against the Church a war more cruel than that which she had previously endured from pagans. For the enemy stationed within the walls and attacking the citizens is more destructive than the enemy excluded outside and assaulting the walls.

Therefore, while Christ’s soldiers, after the sweat of persecution, enjoyed the rest of peace in the garden of the Church, behold, the twisting dragon, conquered by the martyrs, lifted his head from the den of malice, poured the poison of unbelief through Christ’s ranks, sprang unexpectedly from ambush like a thief, and everywhere struck down unwary soldiers with the darts of error. Through wicked persons he infused into the minds of believers an unheard-of heresy, by which he corrupted the whole garden of the Church as with a kind of leprosy.

But Christ, the King of glory, gave help to his own when he destroyed every heresy through the wise and drove it from his garden with the scourges of anathema. Once Aquilo had been expelled, Auster entered, because when heresy had been cast out of the Church, Auster—that is, the Holy Spirit—blew upon the garden by inspiring true faith in its teachers. And immediately the garden’s aromatics flowed when the holy Fathers brought forth the doctrines of true faith.

Therefore the King, when he comes, says: “O Aquilo, malignant enemy, rise from your hiding places and depart from my garden. But you, Auster, cultivator of the garden, come and blow upon my garden, so that its aromatics may flow, sufficient for the victors.”

Aromatics are fragrant substances, namely the fruits of the aforesaid trees—nard, cinnamon, and the other trees of Lebanon. He says “flow” because aromatics flow from trees by the heat of the Spirit, as resin from cedar or fir.

Aquilo is a harsh, cold wind, which stiffens and kills flowers. Auster is a warm, gentle wind, which loosens the earth and brings forth flowers. Aquilo is the devil, who brought harsh persecution upon the Church, made the faithful like hardened earth and prevented them from producing good works, and killed those flowering in faith by various tortures. He lay hidden in the garden like a thief when, defeated in persecution, he vomited the hidden poison of heretical perversity upon the faithful like a dragon.

Auster, however, is the Holy Spirit, who blew upon the garden with his grace when he inspired right faith in the Church, thawed the earth—that is, hearts overturned by the frost of unbelief—and brought forth the flowers of faith. When he blew, the garden’s aromatics flowed, because the teachings of faith immediately overflowed in the writings of the Fathers.

The Church is called a garden by comparison. As in a garden there are lilies, roses, other flowers, healthful herbs, and likewise thistles, nettles, and other harmful and useless plants, so in the Church there are martyrs, confessors, virgins, and other faithful persons. There are also heretics, schismatics, and false brethren. In the latter Aquilo lies hidden; in the former Auster blows, and from them flow the aromatics of virtues.

Alternatively, Aquilo signifies the hardships of the world, and Auster its prosperities. They are told to rise and blow upon the garden permissively, not commandingly, in order to test it, so that its aromatics may flow—that is, so that they may bring tribulations upon the faithful, and that the sweet fragrance of their patience and steadfastness, as in Job, may spread abroad to many. Prosperities test the mind more often than adversities, because adversities withdraw the mind from the enticements of the flesh, while prosperities entice it into wantonness.

Tropologically, the garden is the cloister; its flowers and healthful herbs are brethren united in faith and love; its nettles and useless plants are hypocrites and false brethren. Aquilo rises in the garden to test it when the devil disturbs the concord of brethren through false brethren. But Auster comes and blows upon the garden when the Holy Spirit strengthens the community of brethren in patience and concord. Aromatics flow when virtues previously hidden, tested by temptations, come to the knowledge of neighbours.

Anagogically, Aquilo will arise in the garden when Antichrist still attacks the Church; but Auster will blow upon the garden when the grace of the Holy Spirit inspires the faithful with constancy of faith against him. Then the garden’s aromatics will flow because martyrdoms for faith in Christ will abound.

Alternatively, Aquilo will arise in order to depart from the garden when, after Antichrist has been killed, persecution withdraws from the Church. Auster will blow upon the garden when the multitude of the fallen returns to repentance through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Then the garden’s aromatics will flow because the examples of the saints’ patience and steadfastness under Antichrist will abound in the Church.

Alternatively, Aquilo will depart from the garden when, at the final judgment, the devil departs from the Church condemned. Auster will blow upon the garden when Christ comes and renews the Church with the consolation of the Holy Spirit. Then the garden’s aromatics will flow, when the righteous receive eternal rewards for their merits.

When Aquilo departs and Auster enters the garden, the queen gathers aromatics with which she refreshes the victors, and invites the king, standing outside, to the banquet of the victors, saying:

## Chapter V

### Verses 1–2

**Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his orchard-trees.**

That is, once persecution had been annihilated through Christ and heresy condemned everywhere, the Church, now living in peace and concord of faith and enduring many trials, gathered the writings of the Fathers as aromatics and established, from the example of their spiritual virtues, a kind of banquet. She desires Christ to be present so that her work may be acceptable, saying: “He who promised to remain with me until the consummation of the age, let him now come by grace into me, his garden, so that he who kept me unharmed among persecutors and heretics may now keep me, living in peace, unshaken by the trials of adversity and prosperity; and may he produce from me such shoots, the fruit of whose orchard-trees he himself may eat—that is, may he cause such spiritual persons to spring up from me as he may wish to incorporate into himself as sweet food.”

For the orchard-trees of the garden are the elect in the Church. The fruit of orchard-trees is good works. The beloved will eat the fruit of his orchard-trees when Christ incorporates the elect into himself through good works, so that they may be one with God, as food is transformed into the body of the eater.

Alternatively, the Church, grieving that the Synagogue has for so long been separated from faith in Christ, prays that it may be joined to her, saying: “My beloved, who by faith expelled Aquilo, the devil, from me, his garden, introduced Auster, the Holy Spirit, by grace, and multiplied in me the aromatics of charisms—may he also come by grace into Judaea, his garden, in order to eat the fruits of his orchard-trees; that is, through faith may he incorporate into himself the multitude of those who are to be converted.”

Morally, the beloved comes into the garden and eats the fruit of his orchard-trees when Christ multiplies his gifts in the assembly of spiritual persons and refreshes himself with their works as with sweet food. According to the higher sense, the beloved eats the garden’s fruit when Christ takes the elect from this world into his glory.

The King, entering the queen’s banquet, says:

**I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my aromatics. I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.**

By myrrh, martyrs are understood; by aromatics, confessors. A honeycomb is honey in wax, and signifies souls in bodies; honey outside wax signifies souls outside bodies. The honeycomb denotes those who rose bodily with the Lord and ascended bodily with him. Honey denotes the souls of the saints delivered from hell by Christ. Wine signifies those who in the primitive Church intoxicated others with teaching; milk, those nourished with the milk of teaching.

He has set forth six orders of the elect whom he has led to the glory of the perfect. For the number six, being perfect, signifies perfection, as if he said: “O Church, my sister in inheritance, my bride in spiritual generation: I have already come by the incarnation into my garden, Judaea; and I have already gathered myrrh with aromatics, because I have gathered to myself in heaven the harvest of martyrs together with confessors fragrant in faith and work. I have eaten honeycomb with honey, because I have already taken into glory those whom I raised bodily together with the souls whom I delivered from hell. I have drunk wine with milk, because I have already joined teachers with hearers to the angels in heaven,” saying: “O angels, my friends, eat; and you, archangels, my beloved, drink and be intoxicated.” That is to say: “Those whom I have brought triumphantly from the earth, incorporate into your fellowship as sweet food, and receive into your joy as a sweet drink. And as diners rejoice to be satisfied by various dishes and drinks, so rejoice that these are counted among your fellowship.”

He repeats all this in order, as it were, to say to the Church of the nations: “As I have already glorified those of my primitive Church by my incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension, so I will glorify those Jews still to be converted. Likewise I will join to the angels in glory those born from you and perfected in faith.”

Alternatively: “O sister and bride, you pray that I may come into you, my garden, bringing you help against the trials of the world; but I came into the garden in the time of persecution, bringing help to the martyrs, whom I have already crowned for their sufferings. I came also to help confessors fighting against heretics, whom I have already glorified in heaven. Thus I will help you as you fight against the trials of the world, and crown you when you conquer.

“I have already gathered in my garden my myrrh—that is, martyrs who suffered bitter things for me in the Church—and gathered them to myself in glory with my aromatics, that is, with all who are distinguished by the renown of good works, such as confessors. Notice that he says ‘my’: for heretics too have their own martyrs and confessors, who are not Christ’s but the devil’s myrrh.

“You invite me to a banquet. I have already eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have already drunk my wine with my milk. Honeycomb are those who seek the sweetness of spiritual understanding in the Scriptures and make it clear to others. Honey are those who gladly taste the feasts of the divine word set before them and desire insatiably to feed upon them. Wine are strong teachers of heavenly things, intoxicating others with wisdom. Milk are hearers still weak, nourished by the milk of teaching toward good conduct. All these I incorporated into myself as sweet food, and poured them into myself as sweet drink, because I have taken them all into glory.”

Now the King addresses the victors feasting in the garden—that is, all those in the Church triumphing over vices:

**Eat, friends; drink, and be intoxicated, beloved ones.**

That is: “You warriors of the Church, my friends, who do what I commanded by my example, eat honeycomb with honey; that is, join to yourselves such men as may refresh you, hungry for righteousness, with sweet teaching. And by my example drink wine with milk; that is, gather to yourselves such teachers as may intoxicate you, thirsty for righteousness, with the wine of wisdom and nourish you with the milk of teaching. Be intoxicated with wisdom from such persons, and, filled with charity, you will be most beloved to me. You will be food and drink to me as they are; I will incorporate you into myself as I incorporated them, and place you with me in glory.”

Morally, the bridegroom gathers myrrh in the garden when Christ cuts off with the sickle of death from the assembly of spiritual persons those mortifying their members and crucifying themselves to vices and lusts, and leads them into the storehouses of blessedness. He gathers aromatics when he gathers to life those fragrant in virtues. He eats honeycomb with honey when he receives those sweet in conduct and works. He drinks wine with milk when he chooses the wise together with the simple for glory.

According to the anagogical sense, Christ gathers myrrh and aromatics from the garden when he gathers into the garden of blessedness some elect persons in the Church embittered by tribulations and others fragrant in virtues. He eats honeycomb with honey when he places teachers of sweetness in the sweetness of eternal rest. He drinks wine with milk when he intoxicates from the torrent of his delight those subjects who have drunk the draught of teaching, saying to the angels: “Eat, friends; drink and be intoxicated, beloved ones”—that is, “Rejoice in the fellowship of these as diners rejoice in being satisfied with diverse food and drink.”

Some ask whether humanity would have been created if an angel had not fallen. They think the fall of angels was the cause of the creation of human beings; but they are mistaken. For reason teaches, and sacred authority agrees, that even if the entire multitude of angels had remained in heaven, a multitude of human beings would nevertheless have been created on earth. As the angel has his place in the universe, so humanity has its place in the universe. Indeed, all Scripture proclaims that this world was made for humanity; if humanity had not been created, consequently this world too would not have been made. This is most absurd.

Foreseeing this error, the Holy Spirit guards against it through Scripture by declaring that heaven was created before angel or human being, crying: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). Heaven and earth are the world. Why did he make heaven? That it might be the dwelling of angels. Why earth? That it might be the dwelling of human beings. The Lord himself testifies that angel and human being were made together, saying to Job: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you” (Job 40:10), that is: “When I made the angel, I made the human being too.” Sacred Scripture also proclaims that all things were made together, saying: “He who remains for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18). Therefore the human being was made not for the angel, but for himself; the world was made for the human being. The fall of angels was repaired through humanity, because God the Creator became human, and consequently the human being became God.

[Col. 0433B] Again it is asked whether the Son of God would have been incarnate if humanity had not fallen. They think that the human fall was the cause of Christ’s incarnation; but they are not mistaken. For reason plainly declares, and the authority of sacred Scripture accords, that because the human being sinned in paradise, God therefore assumed human nature. From eternity it was predestined with God that humanity should be deified. For as God is immutable, so his predestination is immutable. If God were not incarnate, humanity would not be deified; and thus God’s predestination would be changed, which was impossible. Therefore God had to become incarnate in order that humanity might be deified.

Authority appears to support this reasoning. Before Adam sinned, God through Adam foretold that Christ would be incarnate from Adam’s flesh and that the Church would be joined to him, saying: “The two shall be in one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). The Apostle expounds it thus: “This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32). Behold, the incarnation of God was foretold before human sin; therefore, because humanity sinned, Christ, who was immortal, became mortal. If he had been born in the state of immortality, he would never have died, and humanity would have been deified without the intervention of his death. This could not occur. Therefore, because Christ was born in a state in which he could die, he willed to die. But because he rose to life, he took death away from humanity and restored the life which had been lost. As all die in that state of death, so in this state of life all will be made alive in Christ and, according to God’s immutable predestination, will be deified.

Hence the Apostle says: “He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world” (1 Pet. 1:20). It is as though he said: “Before the world existed, God determined that his Son should become incarnate and that we human beings should be deified in him.” When the apostate angel fled this one reigning in heaven in the Father’s glory, he found him hidden in the womb of his mother on earth, one day to judge him.

It is further asked: if humanity had remained in paradise, would evil persons have been born from it? But reason teaches that if humanity had not sinned, it would have been righteous and immortal, and all born in that state would have been righteous and immortal. Only such persons would therefore have been born. But after humanity sinned, it was unjust and mortal, as were all born in that state. The unjust and mortal existed only on account of Christ . . .

But Christ is God and human. Therefore from among all the unjust, some are justified through Christ in order that they may be deified in him. But why the rest are not deified or justified—is it not he who chooses whom he wills and rejects whom he wills? Up to this point the fullness of the Gentiles entered. From here up to the entrance of the Synagogue, a time of peace for the Church is indicated.

When, therefore, the banquet of the victors was ended, the queen went to sleep, saying to the watchmen of her chamber: “If the King seeks me, say: ‘I sleep, but my heart is awake,’ that it may receive him.” The Church held, as it were, a great banquet with the victors when she held a great council with many confessors in the city of Nicaea. Its various dishes were the diverse chapters of the Scriptures. When it ended, she went to sleep, because, all heresy having been condemned there, persecution ceased, the rest of peace returned, and the Church withdrew herself from worldly cares, established divine offices, and devoted herself to divine contemplation.

She now says to the imperfect, still craving earthly things: “Following my example, put aside the reins; seek heavenly things. As I sleep—that is, rest from the business and cares of the world—so my heart keeps watch in meditation on the Scriptures and contemplation of eternal life, that it may receive enduring goods.”

While the queen slept, dissension arose among the soldiers, born not from enemies but from idleness. As it increased, the King awakened the queen and urged her to rise and calm the soldiers’ tumult. Thus, while the Church rested in contemplation, many vices arose among the faithful: namely new heresies, disagreements, sects, schisms, and many other things. Therefore Christ warned her through Scripture to interrupt the rest of contemplation and still the tumult of vices by exhortation and correction.

Notice that first a crown is set before the bride for combat against Amana—that is, for resistance to the cruelty of persecutors; then for labour against Aquilo—that is, for the harassment of heretics. Third, a reward is promised her for vigilance against the drops of night—that is, for exhorting and correcting the fallen. Therefore the bride repeats the words of the bridegroom awakening her, saying:

### Verse 23

The voice of my beloved, knocking at the door of my chamber, was this: “Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my spotless one, that I may enter to you, for my head is full of dew and my locks full of the drops of the night,” having stood all night beneath the open sky and heard the tumult of the soldiers. To him I replied: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again, so as to rise and open to you? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them, walking where you command?”

These words show Christ’s concern for the negligent and erring: that spiritual persons may be corrected, and that the Church may be roused to the fervour of contemplation and to distaste for secular administration. The voice of Christ, beloved of the Father and of the Church, knocking—that is, admonishing—at the door of the hearts of spiritual persons in the Scriptures, is this: “O Church, my sister, because through me you are a co-heiress of the kingdom; my friend, because through me you are made privy to heavenly mysteries; [Col. 0435A] my dove, because through me you are filled with the Holy Spirit; my spotless one, because through me you are cleansed from sins: open for me, by exhortation, the door of the hearts of those who have shut it with the bolt of evil deeds and have become drops of the night, that is, members of demons. And you shall be my sister if, through grace, you make those whom wickedness has disinherited my co-heirs; you shall be my friend if you make friends, through steadfastness in faith, of those who are enemies through unbelief; you shall be a dove if you make simple those who are double-hearted; and you shall be spotless if you make those stained with vices spotless through virtues. For my head is full of dew: that is, faith in my divinity is filled with error. And my locks are full of drops of the night: that is, my faithful are filled with the sins of demons.”

For the head of Christ is God; by the head is understood faith in the divinity, [Col. 0435B] while by dew—which falls at night and departs under the heat of the sun—is understood the error of unbelief, which comes from the night of ignorance but departs at the light of truth. The locks, that is, the hairs, are the faithful, adhering through faith to Christ their head. The drops of the night are those fallen from among the faithful, as drops fall from hairs, into the opinions of heretics; or they are those consenting to demons in sins, demons which are nights leading to eternal darkness. Thus by the head and the dew of night are understood those erring in faith in the divinity; by the locks and drops of night, those consenting with demons in sins.

“Open for me the door of their hearts by teaching, so that I may enter through grace, dwell in their hearts through faith, and make my dwelling in their minds through good works.”

The voice of the Church replying to Christ, as though refusing the care of secular affairs and therefore fleeing governance, is: “I have taken off my tunic.” That is: “I have put off secular concern; how shall I put it on again?”—that is, how shall I take it up again? She says this not in disobedience, but in flight from secular honour. For one who is set over secular matters is cast down in spiritual matters; for as the body is clothed with a tunic, so the mind is entangled with the care of worldly affairs. Spiritual persons do not wish to put this garment on again after taking it off, but to devote themselves in spiritual matters to God alone. Yet those called by God set aside their own will and unwillingly take up the burden of governance for their neighbours’ sake. Therefore they say with groaning: “I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” The feet of the soul are the affections by which it is carried toward its various desires, as the body walks upon its feet; [Col. 0435D] these are desire, fear, joy, and sorrow. It desires earthly things, fears that it may fail to obtain what it desires, rejoices in what it has gained, and grieves for what it has lost. It has washed these feet when it has cleansed earthly affections with the tears of repentance. It fears to soil them again because one placed in secular government can scarcely, or not at all, avoid the filth of sins.

But when the bride delays to open to the knocking bridegroom, he touches her now not by voice but by hand. Terrified by this touch, she rises to open to him. So, when the Church in its spiritual persons refuses to undertake care for its neighbours, Christ sets before it the work of his obedience; terrified by this, it does for its neighbours what Christ did for his enemies. Hence it continues:

### Verses 4–5

“My beloved put his hand through the opening, [Col. 0436A] and my belly trembled at his touch.”

The comparison is with one who knocks at the door of his beloved’s chamber and, when she does not open to him, touches her through the window with his hand; she then rises and opens to him. The hand of the beloved is Christ’s work of obedience. For by the hand is expressed the work done through the hand. The opening of the beloved’s chamber is the bodily ear, while the body is the chamber of the soul.

Therefore the beloved put his hand through the opening when, through the bodily ear, he sent into the soul’s memory the work of his obedience: when he left the glory of the heavenly kingdom, undertook the toil of this exile, and preached repentance, the remission of sins, and the kingdom of heaven to his enemies, so that, following his example, she might endure the world’s labour and come to the aid of a neighbour placed in danger of soul. [Col. 0436B]

But the belly of the Church trembled at Christ’s touch because, when each spiritual person considered his own frailty, he was afraid at Christ’s deed: lest he should be inadequate for the office imposed on him after Christ’s example, and, becoming disobedient, should perish apart from Christ. By the belly, a soft member, are understood the frail in the Church, from whom nevertheless spiritual children are begotten.

“Touched by the bridegroom’s hand and trembling, I rose to open to my beloved.” I was touched by his example concerning my disobedience. Trembling, I rose from the place where I slept, because I interrupted the repose of contemplation, in order to open to my beloved hearts hardened in wickedness and closed against goodness.

Observe that she does not open to the beloved knocking by voice, but immediately opens to him when he touches by hand, because the door of the heart is opened more by the example of a work than by the voice of preaching, so that Christ may be brought in through faith. [Col. 0436C] But once he has undertaken government, when a spiritual man begins to do good works before his neighbours and to exhort them to act well, the wicked immediately begin to oppose him, and sometimes, after being rebuked by him, even threaten him with death. Hence it continues:

### Verses 5–6

“My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers with the finest myrrh.”

By hands is indicated action; by myrrh, persecution; by fingers, endeavours; and by the finest myrrh, the utmost tribulation. Finest myrrh is the best myrrh, elsewhere called chosen myrrh, and it signifies Christ’s death. Therefore the queen who gathered spices when the south wind blew bore myrrh in her hands; hence she now says: “My hands dripped with myrrh.” That is: “My works, which were examples of mortification, brought upon me the bitterness of persecution. My fingers were full of the finest myrrh”: that is, “My endeavours, which imitated Christ’s patience, brought upon me the tribulation of death, resembling Christ’s death, which he suffered from those whom he taught the way of salvation.” [Col. 0436D]

Observe that three were crucified: Christ, the confessing thief, and the blaspheming thief. Whoever innocently suffers evils or death is crucified with Christ. Whoever is guilty but confesses sins is saved with the confessing thief. Whoever is guilty and suffers without confessing is condemned with the blaspheming thief.

“I rose at the bridegroom’s touch in order to open to him; and by dripping myrrh”—that is, “by the abundant bitterness which I suffered following Christ’s example”—“I opened [Col. 0437A] the bolt of my door to my beloved.” The Church is the city, house, or temple of God, whose door is faith, through which one enters to Christ, the master of the household. The bolt of the door is unbelief or hardness of heart, through which the door of faith is barred, lest Christ enter the house of the soul. But the bolt of the door is opened when unbelief is destroyed by reason or hardness of heart softened by gentle speech. Thus the knocking bridegroom is received into the chamber of the heart.

Therefore it is written: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I will enter to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3:20). Christ stands at the door and knocks when heavenly grace visits a heart shut by wickedness. But that person opens this door who receives the offered grace through repentance. Christ will enter and dine with him when he has filled the soul of the penitent with wisdom and satisfied it with the consolation of the Scriptures.

But where the knocking one is not admitted, he turns aside and passes to one who opens for him the door of the heart. Therefore it fittingly continues: “But he had turned aside and passed on.” For he turns aside from those who bar their hearts to him with the bolt of hardness; but he passes to those who open to him through repentance. The comparison is with someone who knocks for a long time at the door of his beloved, is not admitted, and goes away in indignation. The beloved also turns aside and passes on when his divinity exceeds the mind’s thought. But because, wherever the divine word is received, a heart hardened in wickedness is immediately softened to repentance, it rightly adds:

### Verse 6

“My soul melted when my beloved spoke, saying: ‘Open to me, my sister.’”

The bride, having opened the door and not found her beloved, comes to the choir of the daughters of Jerusalem, who had come with her. In a plaintive voice she tells them that she did not open to her knocking beloved; that afterwards, when she sought him, she did not find him; that when she called, he did not answer; that the watchmen of the city struck and wounded her and took away her veil. Anxiously she asks that, if they find him, they should tell him what she has suffered for love of him. The comparison is with a loving woman who anxiously seeks her beloved at night, heedlessly encounters the watchmen, loses her clothes, receives blows, and afterwards sorrowfully relates these things to her companions.

By the bride in this passage is understood the Church of penitents, seeking through repentance and confession the beloved lost through sin; and she speaks thus in a grieving voice to the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, to spiritual and religious persons in confession: [Col. 0437D] “My soul, which was hardened in wickedness when the north wind blew, melted when the south wind blew, when my beloved said these words: ‘Open to me, my sister, whom I made my co-heiress by my blood.’ At this voice my soul was pierced and melted, like wax, so as to express the bridegroom’s image.”

Further, the spirit—that is, the higher power of the soul—speaks here: “I sought, by reflection, the riches of his patience, by which he endured me so long while I was sinning and stubbornly provoking him; yet I did not find the boundless mercy that spares sinners. I called with the cry of my heart, wishing to know his hidden judgments: why he bears with the wicked for so long, punishes the good, sometimes chooses the wicked through repentance, rejects the good through sin, converts one of two alike in sin and leaves the other; [Col. 0438A] and he did not answer me—that is, he did not disclose it to me through the Scriptures—so that I might place confidence not in my own works but in his mercy.

“He himself sought me when he left the choirs of angels in heaven and sought me in the world as a wandering sheep. He called when he said: ‘Return to me, you returning children, and I will restore you’ (Jer. 3:14). I despised this voice. Therefore the Lord does not hear me when I cry in tribulation.

“The watchmen who go about the city found me thus seeking and calling: namely, the prelates of the Church, guardians of God’s law by word and example, who go about the city—that is, who fortify the Church with the Scriptures. [Col. 0438B] They found me full of sins and abominations; they struck me with fear of judgment and of sins, and wounded me with compunction and repentance. They took away my cloak, namely, the multitude of sins with which I was surrounded, by means of the penance imposed upon me—the watchmen of the walls, that is, the teachers of the books by which the Church, God’s city, is enclosed as by a wall. Or, they removed my cloak, that is, the veil of ignorance, when they explained God’s hidden judgments to me.”

Therefore, to the watchmen of the city, or the watchmen of the walls, who found me such and treated me in this manner, I said with great groaning:

### Verse 8

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love.”

As though she said: “You spiritual souls of heavenly Jerusalem, daughters through the sacrament of faith, I bind you: if you find my beloved in the Scriptures—that is, if by reading you understand the deeds of my beloved (for the person who knows another’s character and life finds him)—then tell him through me; that is, teach me to make him known by giving thanks and preaching to others. For one announces him who teaches another to announce him. [Col. 0438C] For I languish with love: that is, because of love for him I languish over earthly things and desire heavenly things alone.

“And these are the deeds of the beloved: namely, that the Most High hates sinners and has mercy upon penitents; and that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). Mercy toward penitents; truth toward sinners. “You shall make this known through me: that he is to be loved, because he mercifully spares those who open to him the door of their heart through repentance, and justly punishes those who bar the door of their heart to him by evil living.”

Observe that the author sets forth six features of the grieving soul, because in the six ages or six days it performs six works of mercy, through which it comes to the perfection of the number six: namely, that at the Lord’s voice the soul melts in compunction; that it seeks him in anxious conduct; that it invokes him with laments; that through desire for him it is scourged by adversities all day—that is, at every time—wounded with sufferings, and stripped of necessary possessions. This lament is included in the song of love because the faithful soul, Christ’s bride, is joined to him through repentance: “There shall be joy among the angels in heaven over one sinner doing repentance” (Luke 15:10).

This lament belongs more to tropology than to allegory, because here the Church exhorts penitents to good conduct. Therefore allegory ends here. But according to anagogy, the pilgrim Church sleeps while its heart watches when it becomes insensible to earthly and perishable things and longs only for heavenly things. The voice of the beloved knocks upon it when he calls it to the heavenly homeland through bodily affliction or approaching death. It immediately opens to him because it gladly accepts his call. For as a sister it is introduced into the Lord’s inheritance; as a friend it is admitted into heavenly secrets; as a dove it is illuminated by the Holy Spirit; as spotless it is placed in the bridegroom’s chamber. It puts off its tunic when it lays aside the body; it washes its feet when, through final repentance, it cleanses even the slightest dust of thoughts. The beloved [Col. 0439B] puts forth his hand when he touches it with the pain of death. But its belly trembles at his touch because, for the least sins committed through bodily frailty, it deserves the Judge’s sentence. Yet it rises to open to him, because it longs for the vision of him who is above. Its hands drip with myrrh because it presents the works by which it has here been mortified for Christ, so as to receive eternal rewards for them. In what follows, anagogy ceases.

To the bride anxiously seeking her absent beloved and inquiring about him of the daughters of Jerusalem, the choir of the daughters of Jerusalem replies:

### Verse 9

“What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest of women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have thus adjured us?”

The daughters of Jerusalem are the Churches which above were called daughters of Zion. They went out to see the crowned king, entered the battle against Haman with [Col. 0439C] the queen, and were refreshed by her in the gardens. They are understood as the Churches converted from Judaea, in which Jerusalem or Zion is situated, to faith in Christ; together with the Church of the Gentiles, they undertook the spiritual battle against the devil and were refreshed by spiritual banquets, namely, the Scriptures or Christ’s body.

Sometimes in this book the daughters of Zion are Churches converted from the Jews, while the daughters of Jerusalem are Churches called from the Gentiles. For, literally, Zion is smaller in its walls and in the number of its inhabitants, while Jerusalem is greater both in buildings and in the number of its citizens. Thus Churches from the Jews are fewer in number of faithful, while Churches from the Gentiles are greater in number of believers.

In this place the daughters of Jerusalem are Churches or souls of the imperfect, wishing to learn Christ’s mysteries from the mother Church, which belongs to the perfect. Observe that in this dramatic Song there is a change of speakers, as in the comedies of the pagans. Earlier the voice of the Church of penitents was introduced; now the voice of the Church of imperfect persons wishing to learn is introduced; and immediately afterwards follows the voice of the Church of perfect persons teaching others. All this is because of the unity of the catholic Church, which in all its members is one bride of Christ, who is one person in two natures. Because of this union, he sometimes says: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), and at other times: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Therefore the daughters of Jerusalem say to the mother Church—that is, the imperfect to the [Col. 0440A] spiritual: “What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest of women?” This means: “O Church, mother of believers, fairest of women—that is, most whole among all those producing spiritual offspring in faith, works, and preaching—teach us how great in divinity is your beloved, Christ, born from the beloved God the Father. And teach us what your beloved is as born from the beloved: that is, how glorious he is in miracles in his humanity, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary his mother, since you have thus adjured us, or thus taught us the sacraments of faith, that we should believe Christ to be God born of God the Father and man made from his mother.”

He is called the Lordly man, conceived of the Holy Spirit, because he was assumed into divinity not through any preceding merits but by God’s gift alone.

The Church of spiritual persons replied, teaching the mysteries of Christ to the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, to the Churches or souls of imperfect, worldly persons. It distinguishes this doctrine, as it were, into ten members of the body, because the whole teaching of sacred Scripture exists in the Decalogue of the law. This mystical teaching is inserted in this chapter because the subject is the Church’s peace: the depths of wisdom are to be learned in peace and put into practice in persecution. It should also be observed that this chapter departs from history and anagogy. Allegory and tropology, however, shine forth because it concerns Christ alone and his members.

### Verses 10–16

“My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands.”

By whiteness is marked the splendour of holiness; by redness, the ardour of the Passion. The beloved of the Church is Christ, whom it loved above life and above all earthly things, when, in persecution, for love of him it despised honours, dignities, and worldly friendships, and underwent death itself through various bodily torments. In his humanity he is white, because born of a Virgin and clean from the stain of sin. He is ruddy in martyrdom, because he washed sinners in his blood. He was chosen by God the Father from among the thousands of apostles and companies of saints, that the world might be reconciled through him. The number thousand signifies perfection. Christ was chosen from among thousands—that is, from among all perfect persons—to redeem the human race, which no other could do.

Observe that, all other virtues being passed over, the beloved is praised only by two: purity of life and martyrdom, because through these the faithful are formed in chastity and patience, through which they are especially saved, as it is written: “Without holiness no one shall see God” (Heb. 12:14); and again: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

But according to his divinity, “his head is finest gold.” Christ’s head is divinity, because as the head contains the body, so divinity contains humanity. This head is finest gold—that is, most pure—for as gold surpasses all metals in brilliance and dignity, so Divinity surpasses all things in honour and majesty. This gold is finest because Divinity is the highest good, from which every good flows as from a fountain, just as the vigour of all the senses descends from the head. [Col. 0441A]

“His hair is like uplifted palms.” That is, the angelic powers, clinging especially to God as hair to a head, always gaze upon his beauty. Or his hair consists of divine dispensations, because they are straight like uplifted palms, but black like a raven because contemptible to fools.

“His eyes are like doves beside streams of water.” That is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit which he gives do not permit those who love him to wallow in mud like pigs, but render them clear and transparent in the likeness of water, possessing nothing dark. Therefore they are compared to streams and clear waters, not to troubled pools, because they see God and are filled with the light of divine charisms. And because these charisms are given by grace alone, it continues: “which are washed with milk,” because as a mother gives milk to her children by natural affection alone, so God gives the gifts of charisms to his children by grace alone. “Which sit beside abundant streams,” because the more clearly they see of God, the more they strive to know higher things.

“His cheeks are like beds of spices.” That is, the modesty and piety which shone uniquely in Christ delighted those present with the sweetness of his teachings and drew those absent, just as beds of spices delight those who behold them by grace of fragrance and appearance. These beds are planted by spice-dealers—that is, physicians, namely the apostles and prophets, physicians of souls—who, with a concordant voice, described not only Christ’s sayings but also his conduct in sacred pages, as it were in beds.

“His lips drip the choicest myrrh.” That is, the words of his teaching which promise the brightness of the heavenly kingdom to those enduring grievous things drip choicest myrrh: that is, they preach contempt of the world and its pleasures. “His hands are rounded”: that is, his works are polished and perfect like work turned on a lathe. What he taught in word he fulfilled in deed, so that he might confirm his teaching by works to those who marvelled. These hands are golden because the glory of divinity perfected the virtues which he exercised as man; they stir us to hope and love of heavenly things. “Full of hyacinths.” The hyacinth is a plant with a purple flower, driving away fevers with the sweetness of its fragrance; this is Christ’s Passion, which drives away the disease of unbelief. His hands were full of hyacinths because, pierced with nails on the cross, they were sprinkled, as it were, with the purple colour of blood’s redness.

“His belly is ivory.” That is, the frailty of his humanity shines with the whiteness of chastity and is free from every sin. [Col. 0441D] This belly is “set with sapphires,” a stone resembling a clear sky and signifying the loftiness of heavenly things, because partly human frailty is understood by hunger, temptation, weariness, and death; partly divine exaltation, by miracles, resurrection, and ascension.

“His legs are marble columns.” That is, the courses of his incarnation are upright and firm, because whatever was accomplished through him was disposed by God before the ages. These columns are “founded on golden bases,” that is, upon prophets shining with wisdom, because he appeared in the flesh as he had been foretold by them in the divine dispensation.

“His appearance is like Lebanon.” That is, his beauty is the adornment of all saints, as Lebanon is the adornment of all mountains. [Col. 0442A] “Chosen as cedars.” That is, as cedars surpass all other trees, so Christ is pre-eminent above all saints. For as Lebanon is distinguished by height and breadth, so Christ surpasses all who have sprung from earth. And as that mountain bears noble trees in abundance, so he raises and preserves all saints rooted in himself. And as the cedar surpasses all the beauty of woods in loveliness, strength, height, and fragrance, so the beloved is “fairer in form than the children of men,” because he did not receive God by measure, but received God wholly, while we all have received from his fullness.

“His throat is most sweet.” That is, the inward savour and sweetness of his words, tasted by few, is most sweet; and those who taste it hunger for more. The throat is also the hidden ordering of his goodness, by which it came about that he should speak outwardly to us. “And he is altogether desirable”: that is, God and man, because not only according to divinity but also according to humanity, from the very beginning of his conception to the triumph of his Passion, resurrection, and ascension, he is altogether desirable.

### Verse 16

“Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.”

As though she said: “O Churches, or faithful souls, daughters of Jerusalem, if you wish to love Christ and be loved by him, you must understand him to be such as I have described.” This allegory applies particularly to Christ; the tropology which follows applies more to his members.

Christ is the head of the Church, because as all members are directed by the head, so all the elect are directed by Christ. [Col. 0442C] This head is finest gold, that is, refined gold (*obrizum*), because as other metals gilded with that gold take on gold’s brilliance, so all who are called Christians from Christ’s name will shine like the sun in his kingdom.

“His hair is like uplifted palms.” The palm signifies victory. It is a tree narrow below and broad above, and signifies the life of the righteous, who walk through the narrow and constricted way—that is, through fastings, vigils, and other bodily hardships—into the breadth of charity, so that they may attain victory in the contest. The “uplifted parts of palms” are the same as *spatulae*, that is, longer branches always stretching upward. They never lose their greenness while they remain on the palm, but when cut off they immediately wither. Therefore his hair consists of the faithful who, through the victory of virtues, stretch toward heavenly things and never lose the greenness of faith while they proceed by the narrow way to life; if they depart from it, they immediately wither from life.

Some say that the uplifted palms are a kind of aromatic tree, which the Latins call fir or *spata*. For in Greek fir is called *elatēs* (ἐλάτης), and it signifies saints stretching toward higher things. This hair is black like a raven: that is, the righteous are despised in the world, as Christ was. The raven signifies sinners. Christ is called a raven because he was reckoned among sinners by those who said: “We know that this man is a sinner” (John 9:24); and again: “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18:30). His hair is black like this raven because the faithful are as despised by the ungodly as Christ was by the Jews, to whom it was said: “These are evildoers and deceivers.” The raven also does not feed chicks unlike itself, and Christ rejects Christians unlike himself.

“His eyes are like doves beside streams of water.” These are the wise who behold him in their hearts, and through whom others behold him. They are simple as doves, resting upon the Scriptures and flowing with the divine Spirit. These doves are “washed with milk”: that is, cleansed from earthly things by sweet teaching; and they “sit beside abundant streams”: that is, they dwell beside the most abundant gifts of the Holy Spirit. The streams are the Scriptures of the Old Testament; the abundant streams are the rich and overflowing teaching of the Gospel. Doves commonly sit beside streams so that they may see the flight of birds in the water by their shadows and thus avoid their talons. In the same way, saints perceive the deceits of demons in the Scriptures; from the deception they observe, as from a shadow, they recognize the enemy and flee. These streams are called abundant because, whatever counsel is sought in the Scriptures, it is found there in full.

“His cheeks are like beds of spices.” These are modest prelates, ashamed to hear shameful things, much less to do them. They have within themselves the shoots of many virtues. These beds are planted by spice-dealers: that is, the pages concerning virtues were written by the apostles or any preceding fathers.

“His lips are lilies dripping choicest myrrh.” Choicest myrrh is the best myrrh and signifies Christ’s death, which is best because it is the redemption of the whole world. Christ’s lips are those who disclose his will and are like lilies, white in virtues. These lilies drip choicest myrrh: that is, they teach by word and example the bitterness of Christ’s death.

“His hands are rounded and golden.” That is, those doing good works are blameless before human beings, shining like gold. These hands are full of hyacinths because they labour only in hope for and desire of heavenly things. The hyacinth is a stone of sky-blue or green colour, changing with the air; the saints flourish in virtues, desire heavenly things, and adapt their conduct to the times.

“His belly is ivory, set with sapphires.” Christ’s belly consists of those who have wives as though they had none, maintaining toward their spouses the fidelity of chastity. For the elephant, from whose bone comes ivory, is a chaste animal and of such cold nature that, if a thin linen cloth is placed upon its bone—that is, upon ivory—and a live coal is placed upon the cloth, the coal is extinguished without injury to the cloth. Its unbroken bone encloses its body; hence it is called invulnerable. It signifies saints who are chaste and invulnerable to the devil’s darts. A sapphire is a stone having the appearance of a clear sky. Therefore Christ’s belly is set with sapphires when married persons are content with heavenly disciplines.
