“His legs are marble columns.” These are those who support religious persons from their own resources. Like marble columns, they are upright in knowledge and unbreakable by vices. They are founded on golden bases: that is, on faith in the patriarchs and apostles, shining through works of chastity.

“His appearance is like Lebanon.” These are virgins, white in purity of life, bright in chastity, and fragrant like cedars in their works. “His throat is most sweet”: that is, those who utter words of teaching are most sweet. “And he is altogether desirable”: namely, lovable in himself and in all his members. Such, as I have said, is my beloved in himself and in his members; and he is my friend because I love him alone, and love comes from him. You too, daughters of Jerusalem—that is, Churches destined to behold peace in heaven—love him.

Observe that, just as the ten orders of the elect are described through ten members of the body—namely, the head, hair, and the rest—so their virtues are expressed through ten things—namely, gold, palms, and the rest—which shall be rewarded with the denarius of life. The denarius of life is also assigned to the anagogical sense.

The first order is that of prelates, signified by the head, whose works shine like gold because they shine in wisdom and charity. [Col. 0444B] This gold is finest because charity and wisdom surpass all virtues.

The second order is that of subjects, that is, the obedient, expressed by the hair, whose action is likened to the palm or raven: for by zeal in good action it is green like a palm, and in tribulation it is dark like a raven.

The third order is that of teachers, represented by the eyes, whose works are compared to doves or streams because they live simply and flow in teaching.

The fourth is that of religious persons, shown by the cheeks, whose actions are like spices because they are fragrant in life and reputation.

The fifth order is that of masters, signified by the lips, who are likened to lilies or myrrh because they excel in purity of heart and mortification of flesh.

The sixth order is that of soldiers defending the Church by arms, shown by the hands, whose works are assigned to gold and hyacinth because in time of peace they are adorned with purity, and in time of war with discernment. [Col. 0444C]

The seventh order is that of married persons, understood by the belly, which is described as like ivory or sapphire because it is distinguished by modesty and heavenly desire.

The eighth order is that of farmers, denoted by the legs, which are compared to columns or the sea, because they are upheld by human uprightness and stability.

The ninth order is that of virgins, expressed by the appearance, that is, beauty, which is likened to Lebanon or cedar because it is adorned both by the whiteness of chastity and the fragrance of action.

The tenth order is that of the continent or of those who pray, expressed by the throat and likened to sweetness because a pure life and holy prayer are approved as sweetness to God.

Let no one be troubled that the same sense of Scripture is now assigned to some and now to others, because in this the unity of the Church is especially commended, when it is transferred now from prelates to subjects and now from subjects to prelates. Therefore observe that above, in praise of the Church fighting amid persecution, seven orders of the elect were described through seven members of the body. But to this Church living in peace the ten orders set out above are assigned, because that Church fought against persecutors armed with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, while this one, armed with the ten commandments of the law, fights against vices for the denarius of life.

After the bride had explained to the daughters of Jerusalem the character of the beloved, the choir of the daughters of Jerusalem replied:

[Col. 0445A] **VERSE 17.**—“Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women?” The comparison is drawn from companions who diligently seek a beloved with their friend. The daughters of Jerusalem are churches or souls of the imperfect; Jerusalem itself is the Church of the perfect. The churches are called women because they give birth to spiritual children. She is beautiful who is free from the stain of heresy; more beautiful who flourishes in zeal for good action; most beautiful who shines in the urgency of preaching. Therefore the imperfect say to the perfect, the carnal to the spiritual, the active to the contemplative, subjects to prelates, the unlearned to the learned: “Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women?” O Church of spiritual persons, most pleasing to God among the churches that bring forth spiritual offspring through faith and works, teach [Col. 0445B] us how you seek as though absent him whom you preach as present everywhere; and, if he is present, how he is to be seen; and, if absent, how he is to be found. And we shall seek him with you in faith and devotion.

To go away is one thing, to turn aside another. He goes away who travels into the distance; he turns aside who, avoiding the heat, withdraws to a nearby place in the shade. Christ went away bodily when, with his disciples looking on, he ascended into heaven; but spiritually he turned aside when by grace he came from the Synagogue into the Church. He is to be seen here by believing, sought by praying, found by living well, since it is written: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24).

It is asked how God may be said to go away or to come near. It must be known [Col. 0445C] that there are three kinds of motion. One is local and temporal, properly belonging to a body, which moves from place to place through time. Another is temporal but not local, properly belonging to a spirit, which moves through time but not place when it thinks of past or future things. The third is neither local nor temporal, but eternal, properly belonging to God, when he moves by willing to do what he eternally decreed should be done. Thus God is said to go away when he withdraws grace from the unworthy; he is said to come near when he grants his grace to those whom he has made worthy of it. Yet there is no change of place or time there.

Again, it is asked: since God is wholly everywhere, how is he said to be wholly somewhere? For whatever is wholly somewhere has no part elsewhere. Everything contained [Col. 0445D] in a place is extended through space in three dimensions—length, breadth, and height—and is bounded by six surroundings: above and below, right and left, before and behind. But every dimension and circumscription is far removed from God, who is written to be spirit.

It should be known that a thing is said to exist in three ways. Everything that exists is either locally in a place, non-locally in a place, or non-locally outside place. A body is locally in a place: it occupies the place by its bulk and does not allow another thing to be there at the same time where it is. For example, wine in a wineskin occupies all the interior space, and vinegar cannot be poured in unless the wine is poured out. But a soul is non-locally in a body: it occupies no place there, but [Col. 0446A] non-locally gives it life and sensation, and need not withdraw to make room for food or drink to enter. God, however, is non-locally outside place, simply containing all places equally in himself and encompassing all times by his presence. Therefore he is wholly everywhere, because he is the substance, reason, cause, place, space, and limit of all things.

The bride—that is, the order of teachers in the Church—answers the order of learners, the daughters of Jerusalem:

## CHAPTER VI

**VERSES 1–2.**—“My beloved descended from the Synagogue by grace into me, the Church, his garden. Watered by the streams of the Gospel, I bring forth the shoots of virtues. And he came to the bed of spices,” that is, to the assembly of spiritual persons, where there is a gathering of good works, [Col. 0446B] “that he may feed in the gardens”: that is, delight in good works in churches fruitful in faith and works, or in cloisters fragrant with the flowers of virtues; “and gather lilies,” that is, gather the works of the chaste into the unity of faith, and join those white in virtues to the angels.

Therefore he is not to be sought outside me, his garden, and especially in the beds of spices and in the gardens—that is, in cloisters, in the assembly of spiritual persons—for I prepare, understand, a place in myself for my beloved to dwell through humility and chastity; and my beloved prepares for me with himself a place of reception. He who feeds among lilies—that is, delights amid the holy desires of chaste minds—is to be found there.

The Church is Christ’s garden by analogy: just as a garden produces diverse flowers of shoots, so the Church produces diverse followers of virtues. The beloved descends into this garden when Christ mercifully condescends to the faithful in the Church, whether by bestowing the gifts of the Holy Spirit, remitting sins, or granting requests.

A bed is a plot of ground in a garden laid out with equal sides on either hand, repeatedly turned over by a diligent digger, and cleared of superfluous weeds. It signifies the cloistered life, cleansed from vices by confession and penance, adapted through regular disciplines to the seed of God’s word and to virtues; in it grow the spices of virtues, whose fragrance delights Christ. A bed also signifies the faithful soul, cleansed by penance and levelled by religious devotion; from it the spices of good works give off fragrance, on which the bridegroom feeds.

The bride, together with the daughters of Jerusalem, finds the beloved long sought, gathering spices and lilies in the garden, because the Church finds Christ—sought with great longing in the Scriptures—approving the pursuits of the chaste in the assembly of spiritual persons. He receives her with this praise:

**VERSE 3.**—“You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and comely, like Jerusalem; terrible as an army arrayed for battle.” *Acies* is equivocal. The *acies* of the eyes is the pupil of the eye; the *acies* of weapons is the edge of a sword; the *acies* of camps is a battle-line of soldiers. This means: O my friend, desiring to know my secrets, you are beautiful in the will and desire with which you seek me; sweet in the voice with which you stir others through mutual conversations to seek me; and comely because you provide examples [Col. 0447A] of good works—like Jerusalem, that is, like the primitive Church existing under the apostles in Jerusalem, or like the Church now existing in the heavenly Jerusalem. You are terrible to demons and heretics, or false brethren, in conduct and disputation, like a battle-line arrayed in camps against enemies with an equipment of weapons.

The Church is divided into three orders: teachers, the continent, and the married, prefigured by Noah, Daniel, and Job. Noah governed the ark amid the waters; Daniel was continent in the king’s court; Job governed the care of a wife. They are also indicated in the Gospel, where it is written: two in the field, who are teachers; two in the bed, who are the continent; two at the mill, who are married. In each of these there are battle-lines of virtues, equipped with weapons, arrayed in [Col. 0447B] the camps of the Lord—that is, in churches or cloisters—against the ranks of vices. Teachers attack heretics or demons by disputation; the continent, living soberly, fight against the unchaste; married persons, through marital fidelity and almsgiving, avoid the darts of lust. These battle-lines, thus equipped, are terrible because the lives of the righteous appear dreadful to those who live wickedly. They are burdensome to them in practice, and they dread even to hear their counsels.

The comparison is drawn from soldiers who are always ready in camp to resist their enemies. The camps of the Romans were terrible because they oppressed the whole world, but they were not sweet because they did not possess true peace. In the Church, however, terror does not remove sweetness, nor sweetness terror: she lives a heavenly life upon earth and strives to draw the barbarous minds of diverse nations into her own rite.

By the bridegroom’s saying, “You are beautiful, my friend,” it is indicated that the queen has come to the king in royal adornment; by his saying, “terrible as an army arrayed for battle,” it is understood that she has come attended by an armed multitude. For she who entered battle with Amana and the north has not yet laid down her weapons, being still to fight against the drops of the night. This signifies that the Church, which defeated persecutors through patience and overcame heresies through wisdom, has put on the adornment of virtues in peace, but nonetheless continually keeps watch with spiritual weapons, by which she may resist false brethren.

But while the bride, insatiably gazing on the beauty of her beloved now found, marvelled in astonishment at the splendour [Col. 0447D] of his comeliness, the bridegroom said to her:

**VERSE 4.**—“Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away.” As if he said: Do not gaze upon me so intently amid the crowd, for I shall go into the palace, and there I shall offer you my whole countenance to enjoy. That is, when the Church with all attention seeks the beloved in the Scriptures and likewise finds him in created things, she marvels at his wondrous wisdom in the genera and species of things and strives with great longing to know it perfectly. But she is told: “Turn your eyes away from me,” that is, turn away from my divinity the intelligence and intention, the eyes of the heart, “for they have made me fly away”: that is, the very eyes of your heart see how far I surpass every human and angelic intellect.

As if he said: Let it suffice you that [Col. 0448A] you see me by experience in Scripture and in visible creation. Do not seek to see me wholly in this life, which you cannot do because of your frailty; nor seek to attain on the journey what will be given you in the homeland. Afterwards you shall see me wholly when you arrive with me in the palace.

The comparison is drawn from an eagle, which is scarcely seen when high in the air, but is not seen when it flies still higher. So, when God is seen to some extent in contemplation, he is suddenly snatched from the eyes of the heart, and is perceived to transcend every intellect far beyond measure. He fixes the eyes of his heart upon God who seeks perfectly to know the Trinity in persons and unity and equality in the essence of the Godhead; but God himself flies away from the eyes of the beholder while the beholder perceives that what he desires to see is incomprehensible to him. Thus he turns his eyes away from God and bends them toward creation, striving to contemplate in created works him whom he could not see in his own essence.

Not only must you not turn your eyes away from me, but you must also restrain your hair from me.

Hair signifies subtle thoughts, which rise in multitude as a flock of goats climbs up to the rocks; and this is from Gilead, that is, from Christ, who is “a heap of witness” or “the strength of martyrs.” For they think about Christ: how he could be conceived without sin from the sinful mass; how he could be born without a man from the Virgin alone; how one incapable of suffering could suffer; and how the immortal one could die. From there their thoughts rise to the Godhead, when they consider how Christ is the image of the invisible God, equal to the Father; how he is God’s wisdom and God’s power; how all things were made through [Col. 0448C] him; and how he sustains all things by the word of his power. Bind up these thoughts like hair, and do not seek things higher than yourself, because you cannot know them fully.

**VERSE 5.**—“Hide also your teeth from me, which are like flocks of sheep coming up from the washing.” Teeth are keen understandings which, by expounding, break up the foods of Scripture. Flocks of sheep coming up from the washing are the faithful emerging from baptism, who refresh others with the milk of doctrine or clothe them with good examples. Shorn sheep, indeed, are those who have left everything for Christ. Those have put forth teeth who sharpen their understandings in expounding the Scriptures, wishing to know how those are placed in glory who, baptized innocently, [Col. 0448D] lived here as sheep or left everything for Christ. But they hide their teeth when they withdraw their understandings from this inquiry and perceive that these things are ineffable in this life.

**VERSE 6.**—“Turn also your cheeks away from me, which are like the rind of a pomegranate.” Cheeks compared with pomegranates are teachings concerning martyrs, full of redness, which carefully investigate how martyrs fare in that life. They turn these cheeks away when every judgment about such matters fails, because all these things are unknowable to a human being in this life. These words are addressed to those who inquire with excessive desire into the state of the blessed life but, overwhelmed by its immensity, fail in their attempt.

But although these things are said anagogically, they must also be said allegorically. [Col. 0449A] Anagogy looks to the whole Church; allegory pertains to the orders of the Church. By hair, teeth, and cheeks, therefore, are signified the three orders in the Church, as three battle-lines arrayed against enemies. By goats, sheep, and pomegranates their virtues are expressed. Thus the King praised the queen and praised her ranks, because Christ approves the virtues of the Church and approves the works of her members, saying (v. 4): “Your hair is like a flock of goats that have come up from Gilead.”

The hair of the Church is the married, who cling to her by faith as hair to a head. Like a flock of goats they ascend from Gilead when through works of mercy they strive toward Christ. For Gilead means “heap of witness” and signifies Christ, into whom his witnesses or martyrs are gathered. Goats appear on this mountain when the faithful, by Christ’s example, undertake the rough things of the world, through which, like goats, they climb to the heights of heaven.

“Your teeth are like flocks of sheep which have come up from the washing.” The teeth of the Church are teachers, who grind the food of sacred Scripture and send it into the body of the Church. They are like flocks of sheep because they live innocently, nourish their neighbours with the milk of doctrine, and clothe them with good examples. Those sheep came up from the washing to be shorn; so these men, washed from sins by baptism, rise to virtues and leave earthly things in order to follow Christ naked. All these sheep bear twins, because teachers are full of the works of twofold love. And none among those sheep is barren, because none among teachers is empty of good works.

“Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate.” The cheeks of the Church are the continent, who blush at sin; they are exceedingly red like the rind of a pomegranate, because they blush chastely not only for their own sins but also for the sins of others. Thus you appear outwardly before human beings apart from your eyes—that is, apart from the charity hidden inwardly before me.

After the King praised the armed battle-lines, he burst forth in praise of the queen, saying:

**VERSES 7, 8, 9.**—“There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number. One is my dove, my perfect one; she is one to her mother, chosen for her who bore her.” Solomon, wisest and richest king, was a most ardent lover of women. [Col. 0449D] He had three hundred queens and three hundred concubines. Among the queens, as is believed, there were sixty nobler and worthier than the others; by comparison with the others he calls these alone queens, and introduces them here for the sake of the mystery. Likewise, among the concubines there were eighty more distinguished than the rest by birth and favour; he sets these alone here for the sake of their signification.

Moreover, among the queens there was one surpassing the others both in nobility and dignity, called the queen of queens. She is not inappropriately thought to have been Pharaoh’s daughter, whom he is also believed to praise here in the literal sense. As she came forth crowned, queens, concubines, and daughters praised her, saying: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed for battle?” [Col. 0450A] This indicates that she came forth with a multitude of armed attendants; for it is read that, with golden shields, they always went before the king and queen, and above it is written that sixty armed mighty men guarded Solomon’s bed.

Leaving these matters aside, let the allegory be brought forward. David, who was always engaged in wars, represented Christ fighting here for the Church. Solomon, however, who was always in the tranquillity of peace, bore the figure of Christ reigning in heaven. He made the temple in which he received the queen of the south, because Christ prepares a dwelling in heaven in which to receive the Church. Solomon, whose name means “Peaceful,” is Christ, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace, and “of his peace there shall be no end.”

Solomon was a lover of many women, and Christ is a lover of many souls. He has sixty queens and eighty concubines: that is, all souls of the perfect in the contemplative life and all souls of the imperfect in the active life. These two numbers are set in this Song for a mystery: one is perfect, the other imperfect, and they signify the perfect and imperfect in the Church. Sixty is perfect because it consists of its own parts, as was said above, and it signifies the perfect. Eighty, however, is imperfect because it is not completed by its own parts, and therefore signifies the imperfect.

Sixty is also produced by multiplying six and ten: six times ten, or ten times six, makes sixty. This number signifies all who are perfect in the six works of the Gospel and the ten commandments of the Law. Their souls are called queens because they love Christ the bridegroom for heavenly things and are coheirs of the eternal kingdom. But eighty is produced by multiplying eight and ten: eight times ten, or ten times eight, makes eighty. This number signifies carnal persons who keep the Decalogue of the Law for worldly rank and the riches of the age, who are contained within the four regions of the world and the four elements.

Therefore their souls are called concubines, because they do not love the bridegroom for the kingdom but serve him for temporal things. Maidens are souls reborn in Christ throughout the world, still unformed in faith [Col. 0450D] and in need of the doctrine of milk. Their number is not known among human beings, as is that of queens and concubines, because the number of the elect to be placed in heavenly blessedness is known to God alone. Or the maidens are without number because those not renewed by the bridegroom’s sacraments are not counted in the number of queens and concubines.

He calls them maidens whom above he named daughters of Zion or Jerusalem: they have now come with the queen to the king and have welcomed her with the king’s praises. Concerning her it follows: “One is my dove, my perfect one.” This is to say: The orders of the elect are indeed diverse: some are called queens, some concubines, and some maidens. Yet though there are so many queens among spiritual persons, so many concubines among carnal persons, [Col. 0451A] and so many maidens among little ones, from all these there is one catholic Church, which is queen of queens: “my dove,” because through me she is filled with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; “my perfect one,” because through me she is filled in all her orders with every virtue and every charism. Therefore she is one, understand, heiress of her mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, and one chosen for her mother, grace, which chose her from the world and joined her to the citizens of heaven.

“The daughters saw her and called her most blessed.” Those called maidens above because they were reborn in Christ are now called daughters because they will be heirs of Mother Church. They saw the queen because they regarded the Church as filled in all her orders with Christ’s gifts and adorned with virtues; and therefore they called her most blessed because they heard that, after so many gifts of grace, she was summoned to eternal blessedness. The Church was blessed when she was called from idolatry to faith in Christ; more blessed when she was enriched with diverse gifts of the Holy Spirit; she will be most blessed when, joined to the angels in supreme blessedness, she sees God.

The queens and concubines also—that is, spiritual and carnal persons—marvelling at and proclaiming the mighty works of God, praised her, saying:

**VERSE 9.**—“Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn?” That is: How glorious is she, glorified with so many virtues and gifts, who comes forth toward Christ from every part of the world in faith, works, and preaching, like dawn rising under the apostles. For as dawn rising drives away the darkness of night and brings the sun into the world, so the Church at her birth drove away the darkness of ignorance and introduced the sun into the world by words and examples.

“Beautiful as the moon” under persecutors, because, illumined by the true sun, she flooded the night of the world with Gospel light; “chosen as the sun” in peace under religious persons, because she represents in herself the image of the true Sun, walking in all righteousness, holiness, and truth. And in all these things she is “terrible as an army arrayed for battle,” because in all her orders and all times she was fortified with spiritual arms, so that no adversity could prevent her from displaying in herself the beauty of the moon in the night of laborious action and the image of the sun in the hope of recompense.

Alternatively, the Church was dawn before the Law, moon under the Law, sun under the Gospel, and an army’s battle-line under Antichrist. She was dawn in the prophets, moon in worldly dignities, and sun in the wise. Likewise, she is dawn in married persons, moon in the continent, sun in teachers, and an ordered battle-line in all. So too she is dawn in children, moon in young persons, sun in the aged, and a battle-line in each against demons and false brethren.

It is asked why camps of fighters are so often introduced in this Song of lovers. This is because, just as soldiers take brides after their military service is completed, so faithful souls, after the warfare of this life, enter the embrace of their bridegroom, Christ. Human nature, expelled from paradise, labours throughout the whole time of this life by fighting, in order to receive its adornment, by which it may obtain the promised crown of the kingdom. For after the sweat [Col. 0452A] of combat, the crown of praise shall be given.

And this must be especially noted: twelve times battle has been waged by the bridegroom or the bride—six times before Christ’s coming, and again six times after Christ’s coming.

The first war was in the palace between the tyrant and the emperor, and between the princes and powers of each, when the tyrant seized the empire and wished to be like the Most High. In this war the queen—that is, angelic nature—consented to the tyrant, the devil, and underwent eternal exile with him. For, defeated by God the King, he fell with all his followers from the court of heaven and underwent the punishment of the prison of hell.

The second war was under the giants, between the sons of God and the daughters of human beings—that is, between the descendants of Abel and Cain’s offspring. It began with Abel and Cain and ended in the Flood. [Col. 0452B] In this war Abel, the bride’s standard-bearer, fell, yet gained the victor’s crown.

The third war was under the builders of the tower, between free persons and slaves. It began with Shem and Ham and ended in the division of languages.

The fourth war was under the patriarchs, between the circumcised. It began with Abraham and Pharaoh and ended in the overthrow of Pharaoh’s army in the Red Sea. In this war Ishmael persecuted Isaac, Laban Jacob, Joseph’s brothers Joseph, and the Egyptians Israel.

The fifth war was under the Law when it had been given, between worshippers of God and Gentiles. It began with Joshua and Amalek and ended under Solomon’s peaceful reign.

The sixth war was under kings and prophets, between Jews and Israelites, or between Babylonians and Jews. It began with Rehoboam and Jeroboam and ended under Augustus in a time of peace. [Col. 0452C] In this war all the leaders of the primitive Church—that is, the prophets—fell, and nevertheless received the palms of victory.

Under grace, however, the first war was between the bridegroom and the adulterer—that is, between Christ and the devil. It began with Herod and the children, and ended in the destruction of idolatry and the calling of the Gentiles. In this war the bridegroom entered into single combat with the adulterer when, on the day of battle—that is, on the Preparation—he pierced him with the spear of the cross. Immediately he sent the commanders of his army to recover, with their peoples, the cities unjustly occupied by the tyrant: that is, he sent the apostles throughout the world to recall to faith in the true King, Christ, villages, towns, and cities besieged by the devil through idolatry.

The second war was under persecutors, [Col. 0452D] between Christians and pagans. It began with Peter and Nero, or Simon Magus, and ended under Constantine. In this war Stephen, the queen’s standard-bearer, fell; all her commanders—that is, the apostles—fell; and likewise the whole army of martyrs was overcome and gained the crown of life.

The third war was under confessors, between heretics and catholics. It began with Arius and Bishop Alexander and ended in the Council of Constantinople. In this war Athanasius, Jerome, Augustine, and many others were illustrious, equipping Christ’s soldiers with splendid arms.

The fourth war is now being waged under religious persons, between true and false brethren. It indeed began with Judas and [Col. 0453A] Peter, but gained its greatest strength when cloistered religious life began to be established. It will end under Antichrist, or rather at the end of the world.

The fifth war will be under Antichrist. It will begin with the preaching of Elijah and Enoch and end in Antichrist’s death. In this war the queen’s leaders, Elijah and Enoch, will fall, along with the whole army of martyrs and Antichrist himself, the leader and head of evils. Then the Shunammite will be allied with the queen of the south, and Mandrake will be joined to them.

[Col. 0454A] The sixth war will be between the King of Glory and the king of pride, between angels and human beings. In this war King Christ, arriving with the whole army of angels, will burn this Babylon, the devil’s city; he will cast the enemy himself with all his followers into the lake of fire and sulphur; and, once the war has been completed, will crown his bride with glory and honour, place her in the bridal chamber of glory, and unite her to himself, because he will reveal himself to her as he is, equal to the Father.

## THIRD TREATISE

[Col. 0453]

[Col. 0453B] The preceding exposition related that the queen of the south waged three wars for the crown: one against Amana, another against the north, and a third against the drops of the night; that she came as victor to be crowned by the king; that in her retinue she had sixty queens, eighty concubines, and innumerable maidens; and that she was favourably received by the king. She brought forth ordered battle-lines from the camps and displayed the insignia of war: dawn, moon, and sun. She herself went forth in triumph with all her retinue.

Moreover, the standard of dawn, crimson in colour, went before the battle-line of martyrs, which entered into combat against the rank of persecutors, whose leader was Amana. The standard of the moon, bright with white splendour, went before the battle-line of confessors, which had armed itself against the rank of heretics, [Col. 0453C] whose chief was the north wind. But the standard of the sun, flaming in brightness, preceded the battle-line of the wise, which took up arms against the rank of false brethren, who are the drops of the night.

The following exposition, however, relates that a new bride came from the west and was magnificently received by the king. For while the queen of the south triumphs with her company and rejoices with the king, behold, the bridegrooms’ friends, Elijah and Enoch, bring the Shunammite in Aminadab’s four-horse chariot with many thousands. Queens and concubines, and likewise maidens, together with the queen of all, receive her with the greatest applause and lead her with great joy to the garden of nuts, to the king. The king rejoices at her coming and sings this song to her:

**VERSES 10–11.**—“I descended into the garden of nuts [Col. 0453D] to see the fruits of the valleys.” For after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered into faith in Christ at the end of the world, the Synagogue too will then receive faith in Christ through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch; and he will receive her with this praise: “I descended into the garden of nuts,” that is, I took the form of a servant and came into the world “to see the fruits of the valleys,” that is, to reward the works of the humble.

As if he said to the Synagogue coming to faith: Rightly do you come to me, for I first came to you when I descended from heaven into Judea, which was a garden of nuts—that is, a dwelling-place of the faithful—who outwardly endure the bitterness of tribulation but inwardly possess sweetness through hope of reward. In a nut three things are noted: [Col. 0454B] the outer rind, which is bitter; the inner shell, which is hard; and the kernel, which is sweet. The rind signifies those for whom vices are bitter; the shell, those who break their bodies with vigils and fasts; the kernel, spiritual persons.

For this reason I descended into the garden of nuts—that is, into Judea—“to see the fruits of the valleys,” that is, the works of the people dwelling in Jerusalem, which is called a valley because it was placed among the kingdoms of the Gentiles as among mountains; “and to see whether the vine had flourished,” that is, whether the Synagogue, called the Lord’s vineyard—which he himself transferred from Egypt and planted in Judea—was bringing forth persons flourishing in faith; “and to see whether the pomegranates had budded,” that is, whether any, through faith, desired to be sprinkled with their own blood. And if I did not find such things there, I would teach them to do them; [Col. 0454C] but they rejected me and, after subjecting me to insults, killed me.

Disturbed by these words, the Synagogue answered: “I did not know,” understand, these things; “therefore I did such things.” When I saw you living among human beings as a human being, I did not know that you were God; when I saw you hanging among thieves, I did not know that you were the Saviour. For if I had known you to be the Lord of glory, I would never have crucified you. But you blinded me in order to accomplish through me the salvation of the human race; and therefore I did not know what I was doing. For “my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab,” that is, my animal nature made me distrust because of Gospel teaching, which prohibited me from circumcision given by God and legal ceremonies, and taught baptism and other new institutions.

There are three things in a human being: flesh, animal nature, and spirit. Flesh is weight and burden; animal nature is the desire of the flesh, according to which we live and savour nothing true; spirit is that which justifies. The Azotites fought against the children of Israel and, after defeating them, seized the ark of God. Therefore, struck in their rear parts by divine vengeance, they received from consulted gods the answer that they could not be freed from that infirmity unless they returned the ark. The ark was then placed upon chariots and brought back to the house of the priest Aminadab. Christ’s four-horse chariot is the Gospel; its four wheels are the four Evangelists, who will run throughout the whole world near the end of the world. The ark is Christ’s humanity; the manna in the ark is Christ’s divinity.

[Col. 0455A] The ark was taken among the *Allephylos* [Philistines], and Christ was brought to the Gentiles through the apostles. The ark was returned upon chariots into Judea, and Christ will be returned into the Synagogue at the end of the world through the Gospels. It was brought from the house of Aminadab by David into Jerusalem. Aminadab means “the willing one of my people,” and signifies Christ, willingly offered for the sins of the people. His house was Jerusalem, from which the Father transferred him to the heavenly Jerusalem. The chariot of this Aminadab, as has been said, is the four Gospels. Because of these the soul of the Synagogue was troubled, since her animal understanding began to be greatly disturbed when she heard Christ’s Gospel preached throughout the world. Yet she will ride in this chariot when she is led through Gospel teaching to faith in Christ.

Thus the new bride could not endure the king’s presence—she who, after many insults, had condemned him to a most shameful death—and therefore began to withdraw from his face. But the chorus of queens and daughters of Jerusalem calls her back, saying:

**VERSE 12.**—“Return, return, Shunammite; return, return, that we may look upon you.” That is, after the Synagogue killed Christ the King, she was ashamed to be under his rule. But the voice of preachers calls her back, saying: “Return, return, Shunammite.” Shunem is the city in which Elisha raised the dead, and it signifies the world in which Christ raised the human race. Shunem means “captivity”; hence the Shunammite is called captive, and signifies the Synagogue held captive by the devil in unbelief. The Shunammite is also called scarlet, redeemed by Christ’s blood.

To her the preachers of the Gospel say [Col. 0455C] four times, “Return”: namely, from the four regions of the world. Turn from the error of unbelief to faith in Christ; or return to your Redeemer, who calls you and wishes to receive you: return to him by believing in him; return to him by loving him; return to him by performing his commandments; return to him by hoping for the life promised by him—“that we may look upon you,” that is, imitate you. Or return through the four Gospels; return through the four virtues, so that, beholding your conduct, we may praise the Lord. For the Jews converted at the end of the world will be of such conduct that the Church will marvel and follow their example. Through Elijah and Enoch they will be converted at the evening of the world; they will suffer hunger for God’s word like dogs and go around the Church, the city of God, to hear the word of the Lord from Christians; and they will live by the same institutions as the Church once did under the apostles.

At this summons the Shunammite returned to the king and was received into favour by him. She immediately established, in praise of him, choruses of singers and camps of fighters against enemies. For the converted Synagogue will at once praise Christ in every place and fight everywhere against vices. Therefore the king says to the Shunammite queen, as she beholds and marvels at his adornment:

## CHAPTER VII
### Chapter VII

**Verse 1.**—“What do you see in the Shulammite but the choirs of camps?” He says “choirs of camps” on account of choirs of singers. The choirs of camps are bands of soldiers singing for victory, and they signify companies of believers [Col. 0456A] fighting against vices and rejoicing in victory.

Now *chorus* is equivocal. A *chorus* is a measure of thirty modii, concerning which the Gospel says, “a hundred measures of wheat” (Luke 16:7). A *chorus* is also a wind. A *chorus* is a musical instrument. A *chorus* is likewise a place for those who sing psalms. A *chorus* is also a multitude of singers.

As though he were saying: “O Church, you will see nothing else in the Synagogue converted to me but choirs singing praise to me and camps fighting for the truth.” For there will then be such a time as has not existed from the beginning of the world: a time of persecution, tribulation, and error. For pseudo-prophets will then arise and perform such great signs and wonders that even the most learned will be led into error. Moreover, the leader and head of all [Col. 0456B] evils, Antichrist—the man of sin, the son of perdition, who exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped—will display himself with every kind of sign and lying wonder, that is, wonders of no saving value, as though he were God. By these he will test the elect, and he will torment with every punishment those who do not consent.

Finally, as Daniel and the Apocalypse testify, he will attack the Church with ten kings. Against him this Shulammite, undertaking war, will arrange ten orders of righteous persons, as it were ten legions in camps; armed with spiritual weapons, they will enter upon battle with him. The king enumerates these orders when he praises the ten members of the Shulammite, because he approves for reward the deeds of those who praise him and fight for righteousness, saying:

[Col. 0456C] “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince”—understand, of David, whose daughter the Synagogue was. Christ is the prince of the Church, and the Shulammite is his daughter through faith and regeneration. Her steps are good affections, by which one advances from virtue to virtue; they are beautiful through good action, and this “in sandals,” that is, in the examples of the Apostles.

For sandals are made from the skins of dead animals, and they are the examples of the righteous dead in Christ. The Church is Christ’s body, whose members are the orders of the righteous; the likenesses of the bodily things signify their virtues. Therefore by the steps—that is, by the feet—of the converted Synagogue, the first order of the righteous is indicated. In it are farmers, who, like feet, bear the body while they sustain the Church with necessary things [Col. 0456D]. These walk in sandals while they live according to the examples of the righteous; and they resist Antichrist in the first battle-line, when, despising him, they lose both life and possessions for Christ.

The second order of the righteous consists of married people, signified by the joining of the thighs. Hence it continues: “The joining of your thighs is like necklaces, fashioned by the hand of a craftsman.” *Femur*, “thigh,” belongs to men; *femen*, “thigh,” to women. By the joining of the thighs is understood the fruitfulness of offspring; by necklaces, adornment and protection; by the craftsman’s hand, the excellence of the work. For the work of the craftsman himself is more worthy than that of a pupil learning.

The joining of the thighs of the Synagogue is like necklaces, because the married persons [Col. 0457A] joined in thigh within her, together with the children whom they beget, adorn the Church in faith and action, as the hand of the craftsman made—that is, as Christ’s operation taught. Or the joining of the thighs is the concord of the two peoples, Jewish and Gentile, in the one faith of Christ. Christian sacraments unite them, and they beget spiritual children. This joining is like necklaces, because their concord agrees as the two Testaments agree, both of which foretold this union.

These necklaces were fashioned by the hand of the craftsman, because the two Testaments, which adorn the Church like necklaces through the examples of the saints and protect it against heretics by their sayings, were composed by God the Father, the craftsman of all things, through the Son, who is his hand, through whom he made all things; and in this work the Holy Spirit was fire. Thus their union—that is, their hearts—adorns the Synagogue and protects it against the cruelty of Antichrist. This union was made by the hand of the craftsman: that is, the joining of these peoples was ordered by the counsel of Christ, who alone knows why he will have stirred up the Jews until that time.

The third order consists of the delicate and soft, signified by the navel, concerning whom it continues:

**Verse 2.**—“Your navel is a rounded bowl, never lacking cups.” The navel is a soft member and the middle part of a human being, who has six parts above it—head, eyes, nose, mouth, neck, breast—and the navel is the seventh. Below it there are six—foot, shin, loin, hip, thigh, belly—and the navel is the seventh. It signifies those who [Col. 0457C] aspire through the seven works of mercy to the sevenfold rest which will be given through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. These are like a rounded bowl, never lacking cups: that is, always full of cups. They are shaped by charity, planted through the exercise of virtues, and always full of the cups of teaching, so that those thirsting for righteousness may be abundantly made drunk. This is said so that, if the soft—that is, the imperfect—will be such in the Synagogue, what manner of persons ought the perfect there to be believed to be?

The fourth order consists of the married, or of those who use this world as though they did not use it. They are represented by the belly, concerning whom it immediately adds: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies.” By the belly spiritual generation is expressed; by the heap of wheat, the distribution [Col. 0457D] of alms. He has used wheat for every kind of grain, that is, the species for the genus.

The belly of the Synagogue is like a heap of wheat because those who possess worldly goods within it bring forth spiritual offspring by the liberal giving of alms; and while they heap up good works, they collect or pile up wheat, as it were, into one heap. This heap is surrounded by lilies, that is, fortified by virtues. Stakes are called *valli*, by which a surrounded heap stands lest it fall. Therefore a heap of wheat is surrounded by lilies when the distribution of alms is encompassed by the whiteness of virtues. Such giving is easily scattered by the wind of human praise unless it is supported by other virtues.

Note that above he mentioned a cup, but here wheat, because those persons make the thirsty for righteousness drunk, whereas these satisfy those hungry for righteousness while distributing to others the wheat of God’s word [Col. 0458A]. But those act well who give both food and drink bodily to the needy. And note that the heap is wider at the bottom and narrower at the top, because many give alms, but few abandon their possessions.

The fifth order consists of teachers, signified by the breasts, concerning whom it says:

**Verse 3.**—“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle.” As though he were saying: those nursed by the milk of your breasts, or instructed in the teaching of the teachers of both laws, are like the two peoples, converted from Jews and Gentiles under the Apostles. They were fawns because they ascended toward the pursuits of religion; twins because they burned with twofold love; offspring of the gazelle because they chose good herbs from harmful ones—that is, because they distinguished evil people from good within the Church [Col. 0458B].

When a gazelle is pursued by dogs, it throws itself from a rock and sends its horns ahead, lest its body be injured. Thus the converted Synagogue, pursued by persecutors, despises earthly things and gives its body to punishment lest the soul be harmed.

Her children, nursed at her breasts, will be fawns: reborn in Christ, twins in faith and charity, fleeing the heat of vices and running to martyrdom for Christ.

The sixth order consists of religious persons, represented by the neck, concerning whom it continues:

**Verse 4.**—“Your neck is like an ivory tower.” These are spiritual persons, who join the Shulammite to Christ by word and example. Since, like a neck, they unite head and body, they are like an ivory tower: that is [Col. 0458C], like the elephant, unconquerable in virtues. Elephants are accustomed to carry towers from which men fight, as is read in the book of Maccabees. Thus spiritual men bear Holy Scripture as a firm tower, from which they fight against the enemies of God’s kingdom. Ivory also signifies their chastity, since that animal is reported to be of a chaste nature.

The seventh order consists of those called prelates, indicated by the eyes, concerning whom it follows: “Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of multitude.” Heshbon is a city having only one gate, in which there is a single spring that makes many pools. Those leaving the city wash themselves and the things needing washing in them, and nobody can enter the city except through them.

Heshbon means “girdle of sorrow” and signifies the Church, which girds those coming to it with the sorrow of repentance. Nor can they enter through it except by the gate of faith and the font of baptism; although it fills many places, baptism is nevertheless one. The eyes of the Synagogue are like pools in Heshbon: that is, its overseers, its presbyters, are like the prelates of the Church, full of the streams of teaching. By preaching they lead unbelievers through the gate of faith and the font of baptism into the Church, in which is the sorrow of repentance, and they give them to drink from the water of wisdom. These pools are at the gate of the daughter of multitude: that is, at the entrance of the Synagogue to Christ, which is the daughter of the multitude of Gentiles, because the multiplicity of the Gentiles will beget [Col. 0459A] the Synagogue through the Gospel as though a daughter, and the pools of sacred understanding will pour over her.

The eighth order consists of the discerning, indicated by the nose, concerning which it is written: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.” Solomon, the wisest king, made in Lebanon a very high tower for pleasure, from which he might look out toward Damascus, the capital of Syria, whose inhabitants attacked that tower. There too, it is said, Abel was slain; and therefore it is called “having” or “thirsting for blood,” because there the earth first opened its mouth and drank human blood.

Lebanon means “whitening” and signifies Christ, who makes those believing in him white in baptism or in virtues. The tower placed upon this mountain is the Church, fortified by teachers [Col. 0459B] and Scriptures. It looks toward Damascus—that is, toward the devil thirsting for human blood—so that it may foresee his snares and fortify its citizens through caution.

The nose of the Synagogue is like the tower of Lebanon: that is, the discerning persons within it are like the wise in Christ’s Church. As the nose distinguishes odors and stenches, so they separate true from false Christians. They are firm and fortified against the devil’s snares, and with the watchful sight of the heart they look toward Damascus—that is, the devil—so as to avoid the enemies sent by him, namely vices.

The ninth order consists of the highest priests, represented by the head, concerning whom it continues:

**Verse 5.**—“Your head is like Carmel.” Carmel is the mountain upon which Elisha lived, and where he saw [Col. 0459C] fiery chariots and horsemen—the angelic army sent to help him. Its name means “knowledge of circumcision” or “thirsting for circumcision.” It signifies the lofty contemplative life in the Church, in which the true Elisha, Christ, dwells; Elisha means “the Lord’s salvation.” In it are angelic armies to bring him aid against his enemies; and it has knowledge of spiritual circumcision, so that it may circumcise itself from vices and thirst for the circumcision of sins, rejecting the circumcision of the Jews.

Therefore the head of the Synagogue is like Carmel: that is, its high priests are like the high priests of the Church, possessing the knowledge of circumcision in order to cut away vices, not to mutilate the flesh like the Jews.

[Col. 0459D] The tenth order consists of the princes defending it, represented by the hair of the head, concerning whom it immediately continues: “The hair of your head is like the purple of a king, joined to channels.” The peoples of Tyre and Sidon bind wool, from which they are to make purple—that is, royal clothing—in channels; they pour the blood of shellfish over it and dye it. For marine shellfish, cut around with iron, shed tears of purple blood. When these are collected, a dye of purple color is made, with which wool is dyed to make a king’s garment.

Hair adorns and protects the head, while purple is the clothing of kings. Here hair signifies the princes in the Church, who adorn the priesthood as a head and protect it with righteousness as with arms.

[Col. 0460A] Purple made from the blood of a fish is Christ’s passion: Christ, like a fish roasted in the fire of the cross, caught in the salt sea of the world with the hook of our death. The channel is the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, or the heart, or the conscience. Therefore the hair of the Synagogue’s head—that is, its princes adhering to the priesthood—are like the princes of the Church, who adorn and protect it. They are like the purple of a king because, by the example of Christ’s passion, they pour out their own fervor for Christ, in order to become the garment of Christ the King. This purple is joined to channels because Christ’s passion is fixed in their hearts through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; or it is joined to channels, that is, placed beside the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore the bridegroom praises each member of the bride because Christ approves for reward each order of the converted Synagogue in faith and deed.

And note that the bridegroom’s praise began from the head and descended to the legs, whereas the bride’s praise began from the feet and ascended to the hair of the head. For Christ descended downward to the earth, while the Church will ascend from earth to heaven.

But note also this: there the higher and more worthy members are praised, while here the lower and weaker are praised, because all the perfect rise to the heights of virtue through Christ’s examples, but the weak and imperfect make progress in good through the Church’s teaching.

Moreover, note that just as the Church produces ten orders of righteous persons, as though so many battle-lines against Haman—that is, the devil, prince of persecutors—so the Synagogue will produce ten orders of righteous persons, as though so many [Col. 0460C] battle-lines against Antichrist, prince of evils. For each fights with the weapons of the Decalogue for the denarius of reward.

For by the denarius are signified the ten states of the Church, five before Christ’s coming and five after his coming.

The first state was under the given but unwritten law in Paradise, which said: “Do not eat, lest you die.” If she had kept it, she would never have yielded to the law of death; but, having become a transgressor of this law, she became mortal.

The second state was under the natural law, which said: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another.” This state extended from Adam to Abraham, and in it she used one language and one divine worship.

[Col. 0460D] The third was under circumcision, from Abraham to Moses. In that state diversity of languages and idolatrous worship arose, and under it she was instructed in religion through the figures of the patriarchs.

The fourth was under the written law, from Moses to David or Solomon. Under this state she was instructed for future things through the tabernacle and mystical sacrifices.

The fifth was under the writings of the prophets, from David to John the Baptist, in which the law and prophets ceased. Under this state she was formed toward better things through prophetic teaching.

The sixth was under the Gospel, in which she was invited to the wedding of the Lamb by Christ himself, the bridegroom, and by the Apostles, his attendants; and through the gift of the Holy Spirit she enjoyed knowledge of all languages.

[Col. 0461A] The seventh was under the martyrs, in which she was attacked by persecutors and daily crowned for endurance.

The eighth was under the confessors, in which she was variously harassed by heretics and schismatics, but was imbued with right faith by the writings of the wise.

The ninth is now under religious persons, in which she is more grievously troubled by false brethren and hypocrites than by public enemies—pagans or Jews—but is especially adorned by the multitude of those in cloisters.

The tenth will be under Antichrist, in which she will be tested outwardly by bodily torture and inwardly by the deceit of signs. In this state also the Shulammite and the Mandrake come to the queen of the south and together welcome the bridegroom who is coming.

These things have been said concerning the Synagogue, as it were historically. Now they must be said allegorically concerning the Church, to which the bridegroom says:

“I went down into the garden of nuts.” As though he were saying: “That you are beautiful as the moon and chosen as the sun does not come from yourself but from me. For I am the Sun of righteousness, who illumines the eternal day of the angels. I descended to you, the moon, and illumined you, so that you might illumine the night—that is, the ignorance of unbelievers—that they might be light in the Lord. I placed camps in you and ordered them against vices; and I made you a garden of nuts, that is, a guard of the battle-lines of the faithful. Into this garden I descended through grace, when I abandoned my vineyard, namely Judaea, on account of unbelief.”

In the nut three things are considered: bitter *amurca*, the hard shell, and the sweet kernel.

By these three orders in the Church are indicated: by the *amurca*, married persons embittered in the tribulations of the world; by the shell, continent persons hard against vices; by the kernel, virgins sweet in virtues.

Note that the Church found the bridegroom in a garden of spices, gathering lilies. The Synagogue found him in a garden of nuts, gathering pomegranates. For in the peace of the Church he gathers into his kingdom the chaste, fragrant in good pursuits; in persecution, he gathers martyrs reddened by their own blood. And why did he descend into the garden? To see the fruits of the valleys: that is, to make the valleys, namely the humble, bring forth good works, and to make others see them as an example. For what we show to others, that we ourselves carefully look upon and test by seeing.

[Col. 0461D] A valley is a place set between two mountains, and it signifies the humble placed between the two laws. Therefore he descended to see whether the vineyards had flowered: that is, to make the Churches, which are the vineyards of Christ the vine, flourish in faith, and to make others look upon this as an example; and to see whether the pomegranates had budded: that is, to make martyrs arise, and to make others behold and imitate their endurance.

Alternatively, the converted Synagogue will be a garden of nuts—that is, a protection of converts—who will be outwardly bitter in tribulations and inwardly sweet in virtues. Christ descends into this garden through grace to see the fruits of the valleys, flowering vineyards, and pomegranates: that is, to reward the works of the humble, the faith of believers, and the endurance of martyrs.

[Col. 0462A] The rest that follows is to be understood of the Synagogue as explained above. But concerning the Church the allegory already begun must be continued, which says:

“I did not know; my soul troubled me.” As though she were saying: “I did not know the true God, and therefore followed a foreign one. After I came to know him, my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Amminadab. That is, my animal life troubles me because of the four Gospels of Christ, who was voluntarily crucified for me, in which Christ says: ‘Unless you repent, you will perish and go into eternal fire.’”

Then the Apostles or their disciples, who drew this chariot through the world, said to me:

“Return, return, Shulammite; return, return, that we may look upon you.” The Shulammite, whose name means “captive,” was Gentile humanity, held captive by the tyrant in idolatry. She returned from the error of unbelief to Christ, the true king, through faith; she returned from the filth of idolatry through baptism; she returned from an evil life through repentance; she returned from Gentile observance through good works. The daughters of Zion—that is, the Churches converted from the Jews—beheld her burning with zeal for holy conduct and imitated her.

Thus the primitive Church, hearing that the king had compared the Church of the Gentiles to dawn in married persons, to the moon in continent persons, to the sun in teachers, and to camps in martyrs, beholds her beauty and wonders at her sudden transformation. The king addresses her, saying: “What will you see in the Shulammite [Col. 0462C] except the choirs of camps?” As though he were saying: “O primitive Church, in the Shulammite—that is, in Gentile humanity, formerly captive to the tyrant but now made free by me—you once saw only the discord of wars. But you will see no longer anything but choirs of camps: choirs singing to God, and camps fighting against demons and vices.”

He immediately enumerates these choirs and camps in praise, because he approves their works for reward.

“How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince!” That is to say: “O Church, formerly daughter of the prince of this world, the devil, but now daughter of the Prince of peace, Christ: before me in faith and before human beings in deed, those are exceedingly beautiful who bear you toward good pursuits by their exhortations, as by certain [Col. 0462D] steps; and this in sandals, that is, in the examples of the saints, in whose footprints they walk and urge you to follow.”

“Also the joining of your thighs is like necklaces, fashioned by the hand of a craftsman.” That is, those who join the two laws, which are your thighs, by spiritual understanding, so that they may bear spiritual offspring, adorn you like a necklace by their teaching. This understanding was made through Christ, who is the hand of God the Father, the craftsman of all things, when he opened their understanding that they might understand the Scriptures.

“Likewise your navel is a rounded bowl, never lacking cups.” That is, those who are still fragile and weak within you are fashioned, as it were, by the lathe of good action; and like a bowl full of cups, they offer their neighbors cups of charity.

[Col. 0463A] “Your belly also is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies.” That is, those who beget spiritual children now sow by alms, which later they will reap as heaps of wheat—that is, as rewards for works—surrounded by lilies, that is, crowded about by virtues. For Christ is the wheat, from whose bread we are daily refreshed; his heap is the multitude of believers.

“Your two breasts also are like two twin fawns of a gazelle.” That is, those who draw nourishment from the two Testaments, which are your breasts, are as zealous in divine worship as the two ancient peoples, Judah and Israel, who were twins, namely equal in God’s law, sons of the gazelle, that is, of the Synagogue. He has put breasts for those who suck the breasts, the producer for the product. Or the two breasts are the two commandments of charity; the two fawns are the active and contemplative persons, twins in love and children of the gazelle, namely the Church.

[Col. 0463B] “Your neck indeed is like an ivory tower.” That is, those who join you, the body, to me, the head, by word and example, are firm in virtues like a tower and chaste in conduct like the elephant, whose mouth is ivory.

“Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon.” That is, those who foresee good things to come for you and lead you by their teaching to them are full of the waters of wisdom, like pools in Heshbon: that is, like the prophets and Apostles, who taught the sorrow of repentance for the joy of future glory. These pools—that is, apostolic or prophetic teachings—are at the gate of the daughter of multitude: that is [Col. 0463C], in the faith of the Church, the multitude of believers, which is called a daughter because she is believed to be heir of the kingdom.

“Your nose also is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.” That is, those within you who are discerning, who distinguish vices from virtues, are strong like a tower, and this by being established in Lebanon, that is, in Christ. The fearful flee to them, because they look toward Damascus, that is, toward the devil thirsting for human blood, and watchfully forestall his snares.

“Your head also is like Carmel.” That is, your prelates, who rule you in spiritual matters as the head rules the members, who preside over you at the summit of Christ your head, are lofty in virtues and circumcise you from vices and sins by spiritual circumcision.

[Col. 0463D] “The hair of your head is like the purple of a king, joined to channels.” That is, your princes, adhering in faith and devotion to Christ the head, or to the priesthood, are made purple by the blood of passion, like the flesh of Christ the eternal King. This purple is joined to channels: namely, Christ’s passion is fixed in their hearts; or, joined to channels means that Christ’s passion is joined to the gifts of the Holy Spirit. In all these things you are beautiful and praiseworthy because you are imitable by all peoples.

In the tropological sense, the garden of nuts is any cloister or place of spiritual persons, who are like nuts: outwardly bitter in the affliction of the flesh, inwardly sweet in virtues. Christ descends into this garden when he bestows upon them the various gifts or charisms of the Holy Spirit: [Col. 0464A] upon one wisdom, upon another knowledge, upon another chastity, upon another humility. There he sees the fruits of the valleys when he rewards the works of the humble; or he sees them through others when they imitate what he commands, saying: “Let your light shine before human beings, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

There he also sees flowering vineyards: that is, cells fervent in different disciplines of the arts. He approves their studies and shows them to others for imitation. There too he sees pomegranates: that is, those who patiently mortify themselves by the example of martyrs. He looks upon them when he presents them to others as an example. For his “seeing” is to approve, to show to others, or to reward.

In this garden the soul of every person converted from the world [Col. 0464B] troubles him, when his former animal life troubles him; and this is because of the chariots of Amminadab, that is, because of the threat of God’s Gospels, which say: “The wicked shall go into eternal fire.”

Christ’s chariot, moreover, is the soul of the righteous. Seeing it, the convert is troubled when he is ashamed of his carnal way of life. To him either the Gospel or a righteous person says:

“Return, return, Shulammite; return, return, that we may look upon you.” The Shulammite, whose name means “captive,” is the soul captured by the devil in sins and vices. It returns from that captivity to Christ in four ways: through repentance, confession, good action, and good exhortation.

[Col. 0464C] For the sinner must first bewail sins in repentance; then flee to priests in confession; then make satisfaction by doing good; and finally draw others to conversion through exhortation. Or the soul returns in four ways when it embraces the four cardinal virtues.

Others behold such a person for imitation when a worldly person, abandoning the world, enters a cloister in order to die to the world.

When anyone worldly marvels at this person’s sudden conversion, it is said to him through spiritual persons: “What will you see in the Shulammite except the choirs of camps?” That is, in the soul formerly captive to vices but now converted to virtues, you will see no longer anything but the praises of God and battle against the snares of the devil.

[Col. 0464D] For converts continually praise God for their salvation and constantly fight against vices. There are also true choirs of camps in cloisters, because in choirs they rejoice before God, and in cloisters, as in camps, they fight against demons. Since the soul has members suited to itself, each is praised through its proper office.

“How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince!” The soul was the daughter of the prince, the devil, when it was his captive; now through conversion it has become the daughter of Christ the Prince.

Her steps are four affections: desire, fear, joy, and sorrow. These bear her toward works as feet bear the body toward places. They are [Col. 0465A] beautiful in sandals when, according to the examples of the Fathers, she desires virtues or eternal life, fears sin or hell, rejoices in good things, and grieves over evil things.

Or the soul’s steps are its thoughts, by which it advances toward readings.

“The joining of your thighs is like necklaces.” The soul’s thighs are fear and love, through which it bears good work, which is spiritual; and it will be an heir of the kingdom. By fear it turns aside from evil; by love it does good. Their joining is faith, because it believes in the punishment it fears and in the joy it loves. This joining is like necklaces because, as a necklace adorns and protects the breast, so faith adorns and protects the soul. It was made by the hand of the craftsman because faith [Col. 0465B] was given through Christ.

“Your navel is a rounded bowl, never lacking cups.” The soul’s navel is temperance, because, as the navel is midway between the upper and lower members, so temperance lies between virtues and vices.

It is like a rounded bowl full of cups because it is rounded by circumspection and fruitful in wisdom. And as drink moderates thirst and gladdens the heart, so temperance restrains the heat of vices and checks immoderate ardor by the fruitfulness of virtues.

“Your belly is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies.” The soul’s belly is memory, in which it stores the food of Sacred Scripture. It is like a heap of wheat because, as grains are accumulated in a heap, so many [Col. 0465C] sayings and images are gathered together in memory. They are surrounded by lilies because they are crowded about by pure thoughts.

“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle.” The soul’s two breasts are wisdom and knowledge, with which it nourishes the foolish and ignorant. They are like fawns of a gazelle, which always seek high places, because they train those nourished by them to climb to the heights of virtues. The two are twins when, in twofold love, they seek heavenly things. He said “fawns of a gazelle” to distinguish them from fawns of stags, which run swiftly; this one, however, seeks high places.

“Your neck is like an ivory tower.” The soul’s neck is understanding, which joins soul and spirit as the neck joins head and body. This neck is like [Col. 0465D] an ivory tower because its tower is unconquerable by heresies.

“Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon.” The soul’s eyes are intention and reason, by which it sees virtues and vices. They are like pools in Heshbon: that is, full of the waters of thoughts and always surrounded by the girdle of sorrow, which is what Heshbon signifies.

For the soul continually grieves when it considers the punishments of hell and the joys of the heavenly kingdom. These pools are at the gate of the daughter of multitude: that is, these thoughts are always set in meditation upon death. Death is the gate of multitude because all human beings go out through it.

“Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.” The soul’s nose is discernment between virtues [Col. 0466A] and vices. It is like the tower of Lebanon because no hypocrisy can deceive it through Christ’s power. And it looks toward Damascus because it is always watchful against the devil, so as to flee his stench and retain Christ’s fragrance.

“Your head is like Carmel.” The soul’s head is the mind, because, as the members of the body are ruled by the head, so the soul’s thoughts are ordered by the mind. It is like Carmel, which means “knowing circumcision,” because it knows how to circumcise itself from superfluous thoughts.

“The hair of your head is like the purple of a king, joined to channels.” The hairs of the soul’s head are thoughts. They are like the purple of a king because they always meditate upon the nature of the passion of Christ, the eternal King. This purple [Col. 0466B] is joined to channels because Christ’s passion is fixed in the consciences of souls.

According to the anagogical sense, the garden was the perpetual Virgin, into whom Christ descended when he clothed himself with humanity in her. In this garden the dry rod flowered, which brought forth the gentle Christ.

There are three things in a nut: *amurca*, shell, and kernel. Thus there are three things in Christ: flesh, bones, and soul. The partition dividing the nut in the form of a cross is the holy cross, which divided Christ’s soul from his body.

The nut is also Sacred Scripture, whose bark or shell is the letter, and whose kernel is spiritual understanding. In the remaining matters the anagogy fails.

Let us return to the Synagogue, which we proclaim [Col. 0466C] as returned to Christ.

After the king has praised each member of the Shulammite, because he has approved the works of every order for reward, he extols her herself with special praise, saying:

“How beautiful you are, and how lovely, dearest one in delights.” As though he were saying: “Because you count as great delights the beauty of your members—that is, the virtues of your orders of righteous persons—you are exceedingly beautiful outwardly in works and lovely inwardly in virtues in these delights, and therefore most dear to me.”

“Your stature is likened to a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters.” The stature of the Church is perseverance in struggle. This stature began to grow in Abel and will endure to the last elect person.

[Col. 0466D] Or, stature began to grow in the Apostles and will be completed in the conversion of the Synagogue.

The palm is rough below and beautiful above; it signifies victory and is understood as Christ’s life, which here on earth was harsh in the suffering of the passion and, after the victory of the cross, was beautiful in heaven.

Therefore the bride’s stature is likened to the palm tree because the Church’s perseverance in suffering is likened to Christ’s endurance. This Church was harsh here amid afflictions, but, having gained victory over vices, shines beautifully in heaven. The palm also preserves its leaves, and the Church retains the same mysteries of faith amid the changing condition of the world.

The Church’s breasts are the two Testaments, from which preachers draw the milk of mystical understanding. These preachers are called breasts because they provide [Col. 0467A] the milk of teaching to beginners. They are likened to clusters because, as clusters are full of wine, so they are full of knowledge. And as pressed clusters intoxicate, so they, pressed in the world, offer the milk of teaching.

It should be noted, however, that each Law contains three things within itself: commandments, examples, and promises. The commandments of the Old Law are: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:13–14), and so forth. The examples are that David did not kill Saul, his enemy, in the cave when he could easily have done so; and that Joseph did not commit adultery when his mistress pressed him with a seductive embrace. The promises are: “If you do these things, I shall give you milk and honey.” The commandments of the New Law are: “Love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you” (Matt. 5:44). The examples are that Christ prayed for those who crucified him, [Col. 0467B] and Stephen for those who stoned him. The promises are: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, the things which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

And it should be noted that each Law was given in fire, which has two natures, heat and brightness, because each burns the transgressors of the Law and illumines its observers. Therefore the face of the giver of each Law shone like the sun, because each taught the way to the brightness of eternal light. Thus Moses’ face shone so brightly that the children of Israel could not look upon his countenance because of the brightness of his face. But the face of Christ, giver of the New Law, shone like the sun upon the mountain, when Elijah appeared with him, and Moses, giver of the Old Law; and his promises also are [Col. 0467C] that “the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” It follows:

“I said, I will climb the palm tree, that I may seize its fruits.” As though he said to the Shunammite: Your stature of perseverance has been likened to the palm—that is, to my victory—because I climbed the palm and drew you after me to victory: namely, when I was lifted up on the cross, I drew all things to myself, you among them.

For “I said” means: I firmly ordained with the Father before the ages that I would climb the palm—that is, the cross, upon which I should conquer the tyrant—and then seize its fruits: namely, all who are to be saved, among whom the final Jews are a part; and, once the tyrant is conquered, I shall draw the fugitives [Col. 0467D] to myself. The comparison is with one who climbs a tree and draws down its hanging fruit. So Christ climbed the tree of the cross and gathered to himself the elect scattered amid many errors. The fruits of the palm of the cross are the resurrection, ascension, coming of the Holy Spirit, and salvation of the world. Christ seized these fruits when he raised to life in himself the human race dead in Adam, gave human beings through the Holy Spirit knowledge of all languages, and saved all through baptism into his death. He recalls the palm of the cross to the converted Synagogue so that she may remember herself redeemed through the cross and love her Redeemer.

“And through this palm your breasts shall be like a cluster of the vine, and your fragrance like that of apple trees.” He specifies the cluster of the vine, which is sweet, [Col. 0468A] in contrast to the cluster of the forest, which is bitter. The breasts of the Shunammite are the preachers, who offer the milk of doctrine to beginners. The vine is the Church; the cluster is Christ pressed in the winepress of the cross, from whom the drink of life flowed. Thus the teachers of the Synagogue are pressed in the persecutions of Antichrist, and from them cups of life flow to the faithful. The fragrances of the Shunammite are the renown and reputation of good works and preaching; they are like the fragrances of apple trees—that is, like the preachings of the apostles. For the apostles were like apple trees, in which there is fragrance and fruit: they scattered the fragrance of a good life and refreshed others with the sweet fruit of doctrine.
