And note that the preachers of the Synagogue are likened to Christ in the pressures of suffering; [Col. 0468B] their preachings, however, are likened to those of the apostles, because they will be of such perfection that no torments can bend them away from Christ. “And through this palm your throat shall be like the finest wine.” The throat of the Shunammite consists of those who utter the word of doctrine. They are like the finest wine because they so sweetly intoxicate those thirsting for righteousness; just as the best wine does not puff one up, but checks the injury of thirst.

It should certainly be noted that in the Gospel the Church is compared to five virgins, and is instructed in love for the bridegroom by five books; and in this Song of Love the beauty of her members is praised five times. As it were, five Churches are described here: the primitive Church; the Church of the Gentiles; the Church of the perfect, toiling in persecution; that of the imperfect, warring [Col. 0468C] in peace; and the Church of the Synagogue converted to faith. For in the number five faith and action are denoted; in the number three, faith in the Trinity; in the number two, the action of twofold love.

The first praise is that of the primitive Church, where it is written: “Behold, you are fair, my friend” (Song 1:14). In it three members—the cheeks, neck, and eyes—are praised, and three orders of the righteous are represented: the apostles, despisers of the world, and penitents.

By the eyes, indeed, her apostolic guides are signified, who led her from the darkness of ignorance to the praise of truth.

By the neck are denoted religious persons who, despising the world, led a common life; they received spiritual [Col. 0468D] food of doctrine from Christ the head, and conveyed it into the body of the Church by living and teaching.

By the cheeks are indicated penitents who blushed because they had sinned. This praise is contained in the number three because the Trinity was first made known to this Church.

The second praise is that of the Church of the Gentiles, where it is written: “How fair you are, my friend!” (Song 4:1). In it seven members are praised because she is compared to seven mystical things; in the members the orders of the Church are understood, and in the things their virtues. These orders are distributed through the sevenfold Spirit, while some are said to be filled with the spirit of wisdom, others with the spirit of understanding, others with the spirit of counsel, others with the spirit of fortitude, others with the spirit of knowledge, others with the spirit of piety, and others with the spirit of the fear of the Lord. Through the number seven eternal rest is also understood, [Col. 0469A] which after the seven days of this age will be given to all the righteous.

The third praise is that of the Church sweating under persecution, where it is written: “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister!” (Song 4:10). The number six marks this praise, and signifies perfection, because those who in the six ages perform the six works of mercy shall possess perfect joy.

The fourth praise is that of the Church living in peace, where it is written: “You are fair, my friend” (Song 6:3). In it three members are praised, and three orders of the elect are indicated: married persons, widows, and virgins, who are adorned by faith in the Trinity.

The fifth praise is that of the Synagogue converted to faith, where it is written: “How fair and beautiful you are” (Song 7:6). The number six belongs to this praise because this Church [Col. 0469B] shines in perfection; and this praise is preceded by the praise of ten members, signifying the corresponding ten orders of the elect who, through the Decalogue of the Law, are to receive the denarius of life.

It should be noted, however, that the praise of the members precedes the praise of the primitive Church and the praise of the Synagogue; but in the case of the Church of the Gentiles and the others, the praise of the Church both precedes and follows the praise of the members. For many orders of righteous persons preceded the primitive Church and the converted Synagogue, and scarcely converted each by deeds, writings, and sayings.

But the Church of the Gentiles came to Christ at the first calling of the apostles, and established orders for herself; therefore her praise comes first.

[Col. 0469C] According to the tropological sense, the delights of the faithful soul are the sacred Scriptures. Amid these delights the soul is beautiful when it lacks heresy and shines with right faith; amid them it is comely if it glitters with good works, and thus is most dear to Christ. Its stature is the perfection of virtues, which began with the first rudiments of faith and grows through perfection into a perfect man—that is, into perfection of virtues. This stature is likened to a palm tree, which narrows below and widens above, because the pursuit of virtues is at first narrow through action, but afterwards broad through contemplation. The soul’s breasts are wisdom and knowledge, by which it nurses the unlearned as though they were little children; they are likened to clusters because they are full of teachings. Or the soul’s breasts are the two commandments of charity, from which it offers the milk of doctrine [Col. 0469D] of both Laws; they are compared to clusters because of the world’s pressure and the abundance of doctrine. The soul climbs the palm when it believes itself saved through the victory of the cross; it seizes the fruits of the palm when it worthily eats the body of Christ which hung upon the tree of the cross. Or it seizes its fruits when it receives the reward of life set forth through the cross. After faith in the cross, the soul’s breasts shall be like a cluster of the vine, not of the forest, because its preachings are full of sweetness. For the signification of things changes according to the diversity of senses. In this place, indeed, the soul’s breasts are its teachings, full of the wine of preaching, like clusters of the vine. Its fragrances are like those of apple trees—that is, the reputation of its virtues is like that of the saints; or its prayers are like the fragrance of incense. [Col. 0470A] “Your throat” is the voice of its praise or confession; it is like the finest wine, which does not puff up by intoxication but gladdens the heart by refreshment.

According to the anagogical sense, however, the delights of the Church reigning with Christ are the joys of the exultant paradise. Amid these delights she herself is beautiful and comely, because there she shines like the sun and moon, and is most dear to angels and Christ. Her stature is equality with the angels, and is likened to the palm because she was straitened on earth but is enlarged in heaven. Her breasts are compared to clusters because the apostles and other teachers are full of cups of eternal sweetness. She climbs the palm because through the victory of the cross she reaches the tree of life, concerning which it is written: “To the victor I shall give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. [Col. 0470B] 2:7). She already grasps its fruit, of which whoever eats shall not die for eternity.

Her breasts are like a cluster of the vine, because the joys with which she is intoxicated in return for the pressures of the world are like the joys of Christ pressed on the cross. For he himself is the cluster of the vine, the Church’s drink, the fountain of life. From him she shall be made drunk when it is said to her: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21). Then her fragrances shall be like those of apple trees—that is, her delights shall be like those of angels. And her throat shall be like the finest wine—that is, her praise shall be like the praise of those at a banquet. While the bridegroom praised the throat of the Shunammite—that is, while Christ compared those uttering the word of preaching in the Synagogue to the finest wine—she seized from the speaker’s mouth the word through which salvation is given to the world, [Col. 0470C] saying:

“Worthy for my beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew over.”

As though she said: My pure preaching has been compared through you to the finest wine because it does not puff up preachers but edifies hearers. It is worthy for my beloved to drink—that is, it makes worthy those whom he himself may drink, whom he may pour like sweet wine into his body, the Church. And it is worthy to be chewed over by his lips and teeth—that is, to be committed to memory by his teachers. Christ’s teeth are interpreters of Scripture; his lips are those who utter what has been interpreted. They chew over the finest wine when they lay up sweet doctrine in the belly of memory and draw it out again for teaching, just as cattle, when ruminating, draw already-eaten food from the belly back into the mouth and chew it, [Col. 0470D] then store it again in the belly.

And note that the bridegroom drinks the wine, while the lips and teeth ruminate, because teachers expound the Scriptures with great labour and scarcely convert hearers; but he himself, by the easy motion of inspiration, converts the predestined and pours them into the body of the Church like a drink without difficulty. After seizing the word from the bridegroom’s mouth, the bride opens her throat and belches forth the word of salvation like the finest wine, offering it to the still-unbelieving Gentiles, saying: “You unbelieving Gentiles, turn to Christ, and he will receive you as he received me. For I have been converted to my beloved, and his turning has been toward me.” As though she said: I, the Shunammite, long captive to the devil; I, the Synagogue, long turned away from Christ, have now been converted to him; and he has turned [Col. 0471A] toward me by grace, who was long turned away from me because of unbelief.

This can also be understood of the Church of the Gentiles, which says to the young women: “I belong to my beloved, and his turning is toward me.” As though she said: I, formerly an exile from God, have been converted to him from every error, as a citizen and member of his household; and he, formerly angry with humankind, has turned toward me, clothed in the nature of our mortality. Therefore you also turn from evil conduct to the former way, and he will turn toward you in forgiveness.

[Col. 0472A] Tropologically, the faithful soul turns to the beloved when it turns from an evil life to repentance, or from a secular life to a spiritual one; and the beloved turns toward it when he bestows his grace upon it, which he previously withdrew when, because of fault, he turned himself away from it. Anagogically, the Church longing for things above turns itself toward the beloved when it passes from the world to heaven; and he turns himself toward it when he receives it into the fellowship of angels. Thus far the Synagogue has entered; now Mandragora will enter in what follows.

## FOURTH TREATISE

[Col. 0471]

[Col. 0471A] After the entire retinue of the Shunammite had been received into the king’s hall and admitted to the royal wedding, behold, [Col. 0471B] from the north a new bride approaches with great ceremony: Mandragora, headless, is brought to the bridegroom. He places upon her a golden head crowned with a diadem, and receives her at the wedding. For the Shunammite, returning from the royal city, found Mandragora, a royal maiden without a head, lying in a field. Moved by the greatest pity for her, she returned to the king and earnestly begged him to go with her and help the wretched woman. Therefore the king came with the Shunammite into the field; finding the wretched woman miserably naked, he raised her up, clothed her, placed a golden head upon her, and led her into the wedding.

Mandragora is a herb having the shape of a human body without a head, and signifies the multitude of unbelievers then to come, whose head will be Antichrist, the head of all evils. But Mandragora’s head will be cut off when [Col. 0471C] Antichrist is killed. After his death, the Synagogue, seeing the conversion of the unbelievers, now without Antichrist as their head and also lacking Christ as their head, desires that they be joined to her in faith in Christ and exalted by Christ as their head. Therefore she says to the bridegroom:

**Verses 11–12.—“Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field; let us remain in the villages.”** This is to say: O my beloved, whom I love above all, who came to me through grace and visited me by the presence of gifts, come now also through grace to the multitude of unbelievers; visit it through repentance, gifts of grace, and preachers. Let us go out into the field of the world and scatter among the peoples the seed of God’s word—you by breathing inspiration, I by preaching, working, and teaching. Let us remain long in the villages, that is, in the gatherings of pagans; [Col. 0471D] let us rise early for the vineyards, that is, let us promptly establish Churches. The field is the Christian people, cultivated by the plough of the Gospel; but the villages are pagans, uncultivated in unbelief and vices.

The beloved sits as it were in concealment when Christ does not warn the perverse to conversion through manifest scourges, or call unbelievers to faith through preachers. He goes out publicly into the field when he visibly chastises the wicked so that they may correct themselves, or summons unbelievers to faith through teachers. The Church likewise lies hidden as it were in concealment when it devotes itself to contemplation and does not preach to neighbours who are straying; it comes out of concealment into the field when it girds itself for public preaching. Therefore after the death of Antichrist, bridegroom and bride meet in the field [Col. 0472A] when Christ and the Church, through prelates, take counsel how they may call Christians who had fallen into unbelief through fear of Antichrist [Col. 0472B] back to repentance, or turn those still unbelieving to faith through preachers. They remain in the villages when they linger especially in preaching among gatherings of pagans.

The comparison is with those who go strolling in a field and gather in villages for a spectacle. The night was the time of Antichrist’s persecution; the morning, the time of peace after Antichrist’s death. Thus bridegroom and bride rise in the morning for the vineyards, having slept as it were during the night, when after Antichrist’s death they rouse themselves to establish Churches, or restore and renew those destroyed under him, or gather together those scattered which they saw destroyed under him but, as though sleeping, did not resist. It follows:

**Verses 12–13.—“Let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the blossoms [Col. 0472C] bear fruit, whether the pomegranates have flowered.”** That is: through preachers let us make them see whether the vine, namely the Synagogue, has flowered in faith, so that they may imitate it in faith; whether those flowering in faith carry out works of faith, so that they may imitate them; whether imitators of martyrs flower in patience, so that they may imitate them. “There I shall give you my breasts”: that is, in that field I shall set forth, to your honour, all the doctrine of both Laws, which are my breasts, so that beginners in faith may suck from them the milk of doctrine.

“And after I expressed my breasts, the mandrakes gave fragrance at our gates.” Mandragora, as has been said, is a herb having the shape of a human body but lacking a head, useful for many medicines; it signifies the Gentile world, which possessed human reason [Col. 0472D] but did not possess Christ, the head of the faithful, and had many useful maxims. The bridegroom placed a golden head upon it when he set before it in faith his divinity, which surpasses all things as gold surpasses all metals; he will crown it with glory and honour and unite it to himself in the brightness of his vision. Thus the headless mandrakes are pagans without Christ as their head, after Antichrist, their own head, has been taken away. They gave fragrance at the gates—that is, an example of good works in the virtues through which one enters heaven to the reward of blessedness. Or the gates of the Church and of Christ are the prophets and apostles; at these gates the mandrakes gave fragrance when pagans converted to Christ spread in apostolic teachings, and against heretics, the reputation of good opinion.

“Not only shall I give you breasts, but I have kept for you, my beloved, all new and old fruits.” That is: I shall not only set forth to those then being converted the doctrine of both Laws, but I have also kept for you all the works of the apostles of the New Law and all the works of the prophets of the Old Law—that is, I shall expound them for you to those people; and not only their works, but I shall also relate to them in order your deeds, which I wish I had seen with my own eyes as they saw them. They wish the following to be understood thus:

## CHAPTER VIII

**Verses 1–2.—“Who will give you to me as my brother?”** That is: which holy patriarch or prophet can grant me that I may find you outside—that is, see you living in the flesh among human beings, teaching from the Scriptures and performing miracles, as those saw you long ago [Col. 0473B] whose eyes were blessed—and kiss you as Simeon, Anna, and many others did, and hear from your mouth words of peace restored to human beings through you? Then let none of the unbelievers despise me, as they have done hitherto, calling me blinded and rejected.

You, Christ, King of glory, I call my brother: you who were born from my lineage, who sucked the breasts of my mother, and questioned the teachers concerning the Law and the Prophets—these being the breasts of my mother, the Synagogue—when you, the Wisdom of the Father, sat among the teachers, hearing and questioning them; or when on Sabbaths you read from the Law and the Prophets in synagogues and expounded them to others.

Note that she speaks as though to one present and walking with her in the field, by which the excessive ardour [Col. 0473C] of love or sorrow is expressed. This is, as it were, a lament of the faithful Synagogue, grieving deeply that her mother, the Synagogue, crucified the Lord of glory whom she saw perform so many miracles. It is as though she said: If only it were possible for me to see Christ, promised to me through the Law and Prophets, now sent to our fathers, having come forth in human flesh from the bosom of the Father, born from my lineage and made my brother, spiritually expounding the Law and Prophets and performing many signs, just as they could see him; then I would embrace him with my whole heart and no longer be despised by any Christian as though banished from the kingdom of God.

The comparison is with a woman inflamed by excessive love, who carefully watches to see whether she may find her beloved outside [Col. 0473D] and speak with him and enjoy his company. But because I cannot see you in the flesh as they did, at least I shall grasp you by faith as you flee from me into the sublimity of divinity; and by preaching I shall lead you into the house of my mother—that is, into Judaea, which is the house of my mother, the Synagogue—and into the chamber of my mother who bore me—that is, into Jerusalem, which is the chamber of the Law, my mother who bore me.

Or I shall grasp you by prayer as you flee from the Jews still unbelieving, that is, as you withdraw your knowledge from them; and by teaching and offering an example I shall lead you into the house of my mother, that is, into the multitude of the Synagogue, my mother; and I shall lead you into the chamber of my mother who bore me—that is, into the spiritual understanding of the Law, my nurse—so that through the Law and Prophets they may understand that you are the true God. There [Col. 0474A] you will teach me—that is, in that faith you will make your knowledge known to me more fully than through the Prophets and the Law.

“And I shall give you a cup of spiced wine”: that is, through the understanding of faith I shall make for you a cup composed of many virtues, to be poured into your body, the Church, like sweet wine flavoured with many spices. “And must of my pomegranates”—understand, “I shall give you”: that is, I shall render to you divine service from imitators of martyrs. Pomegranates are the same as Punic apples; they are red and full of seeds, and their juice has the flavour of must. They signify patient imitators of martyrs, full of good works as of seeds and sweet with doctrine as must. By wine, therefore, teachers of the Old Law are understood; by must, teachers of the New Law, whose [Col. 0474B] labour I shall offer you in honour.

The king, then, having received wine and must from the bride, embraced her; therefore, rejoicing, she sings:

**Verse 3.—“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.”** As though she said: I set the riches and glory of the world after love for him, and love only the rewards of eternal blessedness promised by him. For Christ is the head of the Church; his left hand is the glory of the life of repentance, while his right hand is eternal blessedness, as it is written: “Length of days is in his right hand; in his left are riches and glory” (Prov. 3:16). Thus the bridegroom’s left hand is beneath the bride’s head when she prefers love for Christ to the riches of the world; and his right hand shall embrace her when the choir of saints, established in eternal blessedness, loves her on that account. This verse is assigned above to the primitive Church; here it is repeated again at the conversion of the Synagogue, because the same perfection of faith and action is found in this Church as in that one.

Beneath the bridegroom’s embrace, the bride, as if wearied by love and sorrow, falls asleep; and lest anyone disturb her in this rest, the bridegroom commands:

**Verse 4.—“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not awaken or rouse my beloved until she herself wills it.”** Namely, the Synagogue, converted to faith, despising earthly things and desiring heavenly things alone, sleeps as it were when she withdraws herself from all earthly business and devotes herself wholly to the contemplation of heavenly things. The daughters of Jerusalem—that is, the daughters of the universal Church—awaken her from this sleep when they urge spiritual persons to preach [Col. 0474D] to carnal persons. The bridegroom forbids this lest it be done for gain or human favour, saying: O daughters of the universal Church, who shall behold eternal peace in the heavenly Jerusalem, I adjure you—that is, I bind you by the sacrament of faith—not to rouse my beloved Synagogue, newly converted to me, from the rest in which she rests from worldly affairs; nor make her awaken from the sleep of contemplation until she herself wishes, for God’s sake alone, to gird herself for the labour of preaching.

This verse is now repeated for the third time: first it is assigned to the primitive Church, second to the Church of the Gentiles, third to the converted Synagogue; and in every case harmony in the one faith of the Trinity is signified. This, said as it were historically of the Synagogue, is also understood allegorically of the Church of the Gentiles.

[Col. 0475A] The bridegroom goes out into the field with the bride when Christ, through the Church’s preachers, scatters the seed of God’s word in the world ploughed by the Gospel’s plough. He remains with her in villages when, through preaching, he dwells among peoples inhabiting cities and villages. He rises with her in the morning for the vineyards when he hastens to establish many Churches. Night was from Adam until Christ’s resurrection; thereafter came the morning in which the light of truth shone forth. In it Christ and the Church rose for the vineyards because after the resurrection they established many Churches. He saw with her the vine flowering, the flowers bearing fruit, and the pomegranates flowering when he set before the churches, as examples for the weak, some flowering in faith, others producing fruits of faith, and others who had suffered martyrdom.

[Col. 0475B] There he gave her his breasts because for such persons the Church set forth, for Christ’s sake, the doctrines of both Testaments. After these things the mandrakes gave fragrance at the gates, because the Jews, without Christ as their head, spread among the peoples the form of holy conduct, being established in faith and the gates of the love of life.

> **[Note: Col. 0475D] Something appears to be lacking.**

The bride kept all new and old fruits for her beloved because the Church expounded to the Jews, in honour of Christ, all the works of the New and Old Laws. The comparison is with one for whom a friend preserves fruit during a long absence and joyfully offers it on his return. So the Church preserved for the Jewish people, long wandering from faith, the mysteries of both Laws, which she opened to them through Christ when they came to faith.

Christ was the Church’s brother because he made God, his natural Father, the Church’s Father by grace; and he made the Church his sister, namely co-heir of the heavenly kingdom. He sucked the breasts of his mother, namely the primitive Church, when he expounded to her the Law and Prophets spiritually. The Church found her beloved outside when she believed that the Word had become flesh; the Word had, as it were, lain hidden within when it remained in the beginning. She received his kiss when she heard that peace had been restored to her through him. Afterwards no one despised her, because, when persecution was calmed through Christ, every order of kings and princes honoured her. She grasped her beloved as it were by the hand and led him into the house of her mother when, by working and preaching, she brought Christ into the body of the Synagogue itself; and she led him into her mother’s chamber when she brought him into the understanding of the Jewish people. [Col. 0475D] That people was her mother and nurse, because from it were born the apostles, who begot the Church through the Gospel and nourished it by the doctrine of the Law.

There the Church is taught that she herself was called through Christ’s grace, while the Synagogue was blinded because of false righteousness, but is now again illumined through grace. This Church gives Christ a cup of spiced wine when it offers in honour of Christ a good work that intoxicates neighbours with wisdom, charity, and eloquence; or when it offers in sacrifice the blood of Christ consecrated from wine. It gives Christ the must of pomegranates when it presents divine service from persons filled with virtues, or when it puts forth examples of virtues in the saints. The beloved’s left hand [Col. 0476A] is beneath the Church’s head because the mystery of the incarnation and the gifts he gives in the present life are beneath her head—that is, beneath her mind—because, supported by them in the present against worldly disturbances, she rests and in a sense sleeps with him. His right hand, that is, future goods and the full vision of himself, shall embrace her because it will surround her on every side so that no storm of misery can intervene. Worldly persons awaken her from sleep when they try to draw her away from the rest of contemplation to outward affairs; but Christ, through the Scriptures, adjures them not to do this for gain.

Tropologically, the faithful soul goes out into the field and remains in villages when it imitates peasants or villagers in good morals; or when any spiritual person, laying aside the study of reading and prayer, labours with his hands [Col. 0476B] so that he may have something to give to one suffering need (Eph. 4:28). It rises in the morning for the vineyards when it raises itself wholly to imitate the lives of those in cloisters; for cloisters are spiritual vineyards in which are cups of life. Every faithful person sees the vine’s flowers, the fruits of flowers, and the flowers of pomegranates when he strives to imitate the Church’s faith, the works of the faithful, and the patience of martyrs. There he gives breasts to his neighbours when he sets forth the doctrine of twofold charity.

Then the mandrakes shall give fragrance at the gates because secular persons now converted, who were without a head because they had wished to have no prelate, spread the reputation of good works in the virtues which are the gates of life. He keeps all new and old fruits when, after conversion, he gathers for imitation all the works of the ancient and modern Fathers. Christ makes such a person his brother when he chooses him as co-heir of the kingdom. Christ sucks the breasts of the mother—the faithful soul—when he spiritually expounds the two Testaments of the Church, mother of faithful brethren dwelling together as one. Or the mother of a convert is the congregation of spiritual persons, whose breasts are regular observances; Christ sucks them when he instructs every convert in monastic disciplines. He finds Christ outside who performs works of love in the needs of neighbours. He finds him within who conquers the desires of the flesh through Christ. He kisses Christ who is united to him by inward love. No one despises such a person, because he will please both angels and human beings.

[Col. 0476D] He grasps Christ as it were by the hand and leads him into the house of his mother when he brings good works into the cloister, the house of the congregation that is mother of converts. He leads him into the chamber of his mother who bore him—that is, into the understanding of the rule of his cloister, his nurse—when he teaches that Christ is understood in it. There, namely in the cloister, he is taught what is promised in heaven to converts. There will be given to him a cup of spiced wine, that is, doctrine composed from the Scriptures of the wise, and must of pomegranates, that is, examples of the righteous. Christ’s left hand is beneath his head—that is, the goods of a repentant life are in his mind, which is the head of the soul; and Christ’s right hand shall embrace him—that is, virtues and good works in body and soul: works in the body, virtues in the soul. Beneath this right hand he falls asleep when he forgets earthly things and contemplates heavenly things; and lest anyone draw him from this rest into the tumult of the age, Christ adjures them through the Scriptures.

[Col. 0477A] Anagogically, the Church, a pilgrim here, goes out with Christ into a field full of flowers when, departing from this world, it enters with Christ the paradise of delight. It remains in villages when it is received into dwellings prepared for it by God. It rises in the morning for the vineyards when on the day of judgment it raises itself to the heavenly Churches. For the whole time of this age is like night in comparison with the age to come. But the day of judgment is a kind of morning of the eternal day, which is better than thousands of years.

Each person’s life is like a night; the future life, however, is morning. [Col. 0477B] In that morning every believer rises to the vineyards when, after death, he reaches the heavenly Churches. There he sees the flowers of the vineyard and the fruits of the flowers, and the blossoms of pomegranates: that is, the rewards of the faithful, the denarius to be given to those who work well, and the recompense to be repaid to the martyrs. There the Church will give Christ her breasts, because she will present in eternal glory the teachers of both Laws. There the mandrakes at the gates will give forth fragrance, because in death, which is the gate of life, they will give the living a reputation for their life, while they shine with miracles on earth, though their souls live in heaven. These mandrakes once were such when they cast off the devil, the head of all evils, and put on Christ, the head of all the righteous; and now, like mandrakes, they are remedies for many [Col. 0477C] illnesses. There the bride has kept for her beloved all fruits, new and old, because the heavenly Church will present to Christ for recompense all the works of the saints of the Old Law and all the works of the saints of the New Law. There she will see Christ, her brother—that is, the man born from the human race—in God, he who made her his sister, namely a co-heiress of the kingdom. This brother sucks the breasts of the Church, because the Lord’s manhood possesses, and imparts to his own, the joys of the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, the fullness of the angels. The Church finds within, in the Father’s glory, him whom she saw here outside in the flesh. She kisses him, long desired, when she is joined to his sweetness in eternal peace. No one will henceforth despise her, because she will be equal to the angels, [Col. 0477D] though here she was the reproach of men and an object of contempt to the proud.

There she grasps in eternal love her beloved, long sought and scarcely at last found; and she will bring him into the house of her mother—that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the house of her mother, the angelic Church—when she enters into it with him for eternal nuptials, and into the chamber of her mother, that is, into the secret of the glory of Christ’s humanity, which she will behold in his Father’s glory. There Christ will teach her what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what things God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). There he will give her a cup of spiced wine and must of pomegranates: that is, the full joy both of angels and of human beings, which will be like wine and must, the delight of those at a feast. Or [Col. 0478A] the bride will give the beloved wine and must, because she brings forth the saints of the Old and New Laws, to whom full joy will be given. There the bridegroom’s left hand will be under her head, because she will see all the glory of the world beneath the power of Christ, who is her head. And his right hand will embrace her, because the fellowship of angels and the unanimity of the saints, who will be at Christ’s right hand in judgment, will associate her with themselves. In that right hand she will rest from every disturbance; and no one will awaken her from this repose, because no one will take her joy from her.

While the Shunammite sleeps in the bridegroom’s arm, behold Mandragora, adorned with a golden head, is brought to the bridegroom with a great retinue; and the choir of the daughters of Jerusalem receives her with this praise.

**VERSE 5.—“Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, [Col. 0478B] abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?”**

That is, while the faithful Synagogue rests in peace after the persecution of Antichrist, the multitude of unbelievers—after Antichrist, their head, has been removed and Christ, the true head, received—is led to the Church to be joined to Christ through preachers; and all the faithful receive it with this exultant praise: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness?” That is: how glorious and worthy of praise is she who comes up from the wilderness of unbelief by the steps of the virtues to Christ—formerly abounding in the various pleasures of the world, but now abounding in the spiritual delights of Scripture or in the works of the righteous—not trusting in herself, but leaning upon her beloved; that is, placing all her hope in him from whom alone comes all salvation, as it is written: [Col. 0478C] “There is no other name given under heaven in which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

The comparison is with that people which, having been led out of Egypt, ascended from the wilderness to the promised land through Joshua son of Nun, abounding in the delights of legal observances and the mysteries of the tabernacle, and leaning upon Moses, its beloved. It signifies the people which ascends through Jesus Christ from unbelief to the Church and from the world to eternal glory, abounding in the delights of the Scriptures and trusting in Christ alone, its leader.

The ninth bride, entering before the king, was received by him with these words. It follows:

“Under the apple tree I awakened you.” As though he said: “You have indeed done well to come to me, because I raised you when you were dead and made myself your head.” But when [Col. 0478D] he says, “Under the apple tree I awakened you,” he looks to the whole human race, which died under the tree of transgression and was raised under the tree of the cross through Christ. There, under the tree of the curse, your mother was corrupted; there your mother was violated. The mother of the human race is human nature, which before sin was incorruptible, incapable of suffering, and immortal; but, corrupted through the devil’s deceit, it became subject to suffering and death.

Moreover, her mother was Eve, mother of all, who before sin was undefiled, since she was polluted neither by concupiscence nor by defilements. Violated by the serpent’s persuasion, she was at once made subject to concupiscence, defilements, and pains. But Christ restored incorruption to the corrupted mother when, rising from death, he made human nature incorruptible in [Col. 0479A] his own person. He restored the violated mother when he preserved inviolate the Virgin, his own mother. Therefore he says, “Under the apple tree I awakened you,” as though he were saying to the entire human race: “Under the tree of the cross I raised you by my death from perpetual death, you who had died under the tree of the curse, where your mother, human nature, was corrupted by the devil, when she cast away her adornment—that is, obedience—by eating of the forbidden fruit. Thus she was condemned, because she immediately lost the honor of incorruption and immortality. And there your mother Eve was violated by the serpent, when, expelled from paradise, she lost the blessedness of conceiving and found the pain of giving birth. And because I raised you from death to life…”

**[Col. 0479B] VERSES 6–7.—“Set me as a seal upon your heart.”**

That is: impress the image of me, your friend, upon your memory as a seal is impressed upon wax, so that its image may be stamped out; love me as I loved you, I who laid down my life for you. “And set me as a seal upon your arm.” That is: set my example upon your activity, so that you may act as I did, I who loved my enemies and died for the ungodly. For by the seal is understood the image, by the heart memory, and by the arm activity. The ancients wore engraved stones in rings or bracelets, with which they sealed letters sent to friends; from this the comparison is drawn. An image is engraved upon a signet, and it produces that image when impressed on wax.

The signet is Christ’s humanity, upon which the image of Christ’s divinity is engraved; the wax, however, is the human soul, formed in God’s image. [Col. 0479C] For Christ, as it is written, “is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1:15), because he is equal to the Father. God impressed this image upon man when he created the inner man in the image and likeness of God. In the image the Trinity is indicated; in the likeness, equality. The one who forms Christ’s image in his heart is one who thinks of him as equal to the Father. He impresses Christ’s image upon this person who believes that human nature is united to deity. He places Christ’s seal upon his arm who sets before himself Christ’s example of action for imitation, and who, by living in holiness and righteousness, fashions himself into God’s likeness.

And what are Christ’s works which the bride must imitate? Namely, that he loved his enemies so greatly [Col. 0479D] that he died for the ungodly. And this is why love is strong as death and zeal hard as hell. That is to say: just as death conquers all strong things and is therefore stronger than all, so love is stronger than all, for it conquered me, the strongest, and compelled me to death for your sake. And just as hell is harder than all hard things and is therefore unbreakable, so zeal—that is, my jealousy—is unconquerable: I was jealous of the devil because he possessed you, my bride, and afflicted you with a cruel death, since I loved you so greatly that I redeemed you by my death. Therefore it is just that you should love me so greatly that, by imitating me, you undergo death for me. And if you have love, you will be able to undergo death for me, because its lamps are lamps [Col. 0480A] of fire and flame.

Lamps are vessels of light, and they signify the spiritual vessels of charity: within they burn with love; without they shine by action. They are lamps of fire because they burn for themselves, and lamps of flame because they shine for their neighbors. Such persons despise torments and bodily death because they love eternal life. “Many waters could not quench charity, nor could rivers overwhelm it.” That is, neither flatteries nor threats, persecutions nor terrors, overcome one who loves, so that he fails to fulfill my will. For the one who loves me will keep my word—that is, my commandment that you “love one another as I have loved you” (John 15:12). The comparison is with a great conflagration which neither rains nor rivers can extinguish. By waters are understood flatteries; by rivers, [Col. 0480B] temptations, which cannot turn spiritual persons from good to evil. Love is more precious than all things, because:

**VERSE 7.—“If a man gives all the substance of his house for love, he will despise it as though it were nothing.”**

That is: if anyone, using reason, gives all his substance for food for the poor and delivers himself to martyrdom without love, so that he may deserve to possess God, who is love, he has given as though nothing; for he will despise all that he has given unless he has love itself. All this is said so that, if the bride wishes to be joined to the bridegroom, she may imitate him in love as fully as possible; for “he who loves remains in God” (1 John 4:16), and “he who does not love remains in death” (1 John 3:14).

[Col. 0480C] These things are written, as it were, historically concerning Mandragora; they may also be adapted allegorically to the converted Synagogue. After the Shunammite awoke from sleep, she came to the king in royal attire, with many persons joined to her. Leaning upon him, she ascended to the throne of the kingdom; and the choir of the daughters of Jerusalem received her with this praise:

“Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” That is, the Churches of the Gentiles, marveling that the Synagogue, newly converted, has ascended to such a height of virtue and draws unbelievers to herself from every side by preaching and acting, burst forth in her praise, saying: “Who is this?” That is, how praiseworthy is she who ascends from virtue to virtue to Christ, from a people in the blindness of unbelief, from the wilderness, abounding in the delights of Scriptures and virtues, leaning upon [Col. 0480D] her beloved—that is, established upon Christ, now her beloved. Or, “upon my beloved”: though she herself was blinded, he has now also become her beloved, after she was illumined by him as the moon is illumined by the sun.

It should be noted that this praise, “Who is this?” is now given for the third time. First, it is placed in praise of the Church of the Gentiles. Second, it is assigned to the praise of the Church of penitents. Third, it is assigned to the Church to be converted from Jews and Gentiles, because all are praised together in the same faith of the Trinity.

Alternatively, because the entire multitude of the faithful, from the first Abel to the last elect person, is called one Church, which is gathered into faith in the Trinity in three periods of the world: before the Law under the patriarchs, in [Col. 0481A] the Law under the prophets, and in the Gospel under the apostles. These three praises may likewise be referred to the Church’s three divisions. The first concerns that which, under the patriarchs, ascended to faith in the Trinity; the second, that which, under the prophets, ascended to faith in the Trinity; the third, that which, under the apostles and their successors until the end of the world, ascends to faith in the Trinity.

The king addresses the Shunammite, seated on the royal throne, saying:

“Under the apple tree I awakened you.” By this it is understood that she slept under the tree and that he awakened her there. Three things are indicated in an apple: fruit, fragrance, and shade. The apple tree is Christ’s cross, whose fruit is Christ, who is the fragrance of sweetness and refreshment from the heat of vices for travelers toward life. [Col. 0481B] The Shunammite slept under the tree when the Synagogue lay dead from the tree of transgression. Christ raised her to life beneath the apple tree when he underwent death for her on the cross, which was the tree of life. Therefore he says: “Under the apple tree I awakened you,” as though saying to the converted Synagogue: “You ought rightly to love me, because I first loved you and redeemed you by my death on the cross. There your mother was corrupted,” that is, beneath the cross the Synagogue was condemned in hell, she who cried: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). “There your mother was violated”: namely, your nurse, the Law, was transgressed, which says, “Do not put to death the innocent and righteous” (Dan. 13:53). Or the mother was violated when the Law was changed from letter [Col. 0481C] to spirit. Or the mother, namely the Jewish nation, was violated when, in vengeance for the cross, it was taken captive by Titus and Vespasian. And because I delivered you from this evil and took you as my bride: “Set me as a seal upon your heart”—that is, impress my image upon your memory as a signet upon wax, so that you may love me as I loved you. “And set me as a seal upon your arm”—that is, impress the model of my action upon your own action, so that, as I died through many torments for love of you, so you may die through various torments for love of me. This the Church did in the martyrs during the time of persecution.

“For love is strong as death”: that is, as death conquers all things, so love conquers all things; it compelled me to death for your sake. [Col. 0481D] “Zeal is hard as hell.” Zeal is understood both in a good and in a bad sense. It means either imitation or indignation—that is, envy. For to emulate is to imitate the good, to be indignant at evils, or to envy one’s betters. The Apostle speaks of the good: “Emulate,” that is, imitate, “the better gifts” (1 Cor. 12:31). But of evil: “They emulate you not well” (Gal. 4:17). And of Joseph it is written: “His brothers emulated him” (Gen. 37:11), that is, envied him. Therefore the Church’s zeal was hard as hell, because, as hell is unbreakable, so the Church’s imitation—by which it imitated Christ’s love or action—was unconquerable. This is so because “its lamps are lamps of fire and flame”: that is, possessing charity within, they burned as fire; outwardly, they shone by action as flames. [Col. 0482A] By fire is understood burning ardor; by flames, brightness. Lawrence, Stephen, and others like them were lamps—that is, vessels of charity—in whom the fire of the Holy Spirit burned and the flame of action shone outwardly. Many waters—that is, worldly flatteries and pleasures—could not extinguish charity in them; nor could rivers—that is, threats and tribulations—overwhelm it so as to turn them from the truth, because neither death nor life nor any creature could separate them from Christ’s love (Rom. 8:39).

“If a man gives all the substance of his house for love, he will despise it as though it were nothing.” That is, love cannot be compared with all the substance of the world, because “God is charity” (1 John 4:16), and it alone must be purchased by death and held without end.

[Col. 0482B] A faithful soul comes up from the wilderness when it abandons an evil life and ascends by the steps of virtue to spiritual conduct. It abounds in delights when it is delightfully fed with the dishes of the Scriptures. It leans upon its beloved because it cleaves to Christ’s love alone. Christ awakened it beneath the apple tree when he made it alive by faith in the cross, though dead in sins. There its mother was corrupted—that is, in the sin of concupiscence human nature became mortal—and there its mother was violated, namely, Eve’s flesh became subject to suffering because of sin. Christ will yet raise it and make it incorruptible and incapable of suffering. Therefore it places Christ upon its heart as a seal, because it so forms his teaching and life in its heart [Col. 0482C] as though it always saw him present. It places him upon its arm as a seal when it continually considers the example of Christ’s works and desires to imitate them.

In such a person love is strong as death, because, just as death kills the body and renders it insensible, so true love kills the soul’s worldly concupiscences and makes it insensible to all earthly desires. And in it zeal is hard as hell, because, just as hell holds firmly those whom it has swallowed, so the soul firmly retains the imitation of virtues which it has begun and does not abandon it because of any hard things in the world. This soul is a lamp of charity, in which the fire of divine love burns and the flame of good work shines outwardly. In this soul many waters—that is, the manifold pleasures of the flesh—cannot extinguish charity; [Col. 0482D] nor can rivers—that is, temptations—overwhelm it, so that it does not always burn and shine. Such is this love: “If a man gives all the substance of his house for love, he will despise it as though it were nothing.” That is, if he abandons everything in the world, it profits him nothing unless he possesses charity itself, which is God.

We should consider what love is. Love, then, is a great desire for enjoying some thing which someone wishes to possess. It is divided into two kinds: love of God and love of neighbor. Love of God is to despise all advantages and disadvantages for the sake of enjoying God. It is fulfilled by three expressions: that we love God with all the soul, all the mind, and all the strength—that is, with feeling, reason, and understanding. [Col. 0483A] Love of neighbor is to set aside private advantages for the sake of enjoying one’s friend. It is fulfilled by two commandments: “Do not do to another what you do not wish to be done to you” (Tob. 4:16); and, “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. 7:11). No one wishes to suffer loss; let him inflict it on no one. Everyone wishes to be helped in necessity; let him help others in necessity. All this is fulfilled by the saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27). Not to inflict loss upon one’s neighbor is to turn away from evil; to aid one’s neighbor in need is to do good. Therefore the Law was written upon two tablets, because it contains within itself the two commandments of charity.

Fear is the author of charity. Fear is the anxiety of being endangered. It is divided into two kinds: servile fear and filial fear. [Col. 0483B] Servile fear is avoiding evil lest one pay the penalty. Filial fear is doing good lest one incur the Father’s offense. Servile fear pierces the soul as sharp iron pierces leather. Filial fear introduces love into the soul, binding the soul to God, as a bristle draws a linen thread through so as to bind leather together. Iron is hard: it is servile fear. The bristle is less hard: it is filial fear. Linen is soft: it is love. The iron and bristle come out, but the linen remains within; so charity drives out fears and itself remains within.

Again, fear is divided into two kinds: there is fear of God and fear of the world. Of the fear of God it is written: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. 18:10). But of worldly fear it is said: “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). [Col. 0483C] The fear of God is reverence for him, and it has two forms: when one who loves God fears either that he has neglected something of God’s commandments or that he has not fulfilled everything according to God’s pleasure.

The fear of the world has four forms: fear of low esteem, fear of weakness, worldly fear, and servile or Jewish fear. Fear of low esteem occurs when someone commits evil lest he appear contemptible to others—for example, when someone commits murder or adultery lest he appear contemptible to murderers or adulterers. Fear of weakness occurs when someone commits evil—namely murders, robberies, or arsons—lest he lose temporal benefits from his lords.

Worldly fear occurs when someone avoids evil lest he pay the penalty; for example, when someone avoids theft [Col. 0483D] because he fears hanging, or avoids sacrilege because he fears having his legs broken. Servile or Jewish fear occurs when someone observes the commandments of the Law lest he be condemned by the Law. The first two forms drive one toward evil; the following two draw one back from evil. Charity casts them all out, since it alone does good out of love for righteousness.

According to the anagogical sense, the bride will come up gloriously from the wilderness when the Church, now a pilgrim here, migrates from the wilderness of the world to the joys of heaven to be glorified. The choir of the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, the harmony of angels—will receive her with this praise: “Who is this?” That is, how blessed is she who comes up from the world to heaven; and it will bring her into its fellowship, where she will abound in the delights of paradise because she will rejoice in the Lord’s good things, when she sees face to face God himself, whom angels desire to behold; [Col. 0484A] where she will hear the harmony of angels and the instruments of the saints, and will perceive the fragrance of sweetness itself; where she will be made drunk from the abundance of the Lord’s house and will be satisfied when the Lord’s glory appears. There she will lean upon her beloved, because she will always be established in the Lord’s joy.

Christ will awaken her beneath the apple tree because, after this life, he will make the whole human race alive unto life through the victory of the cross, which suffered death through the tree of transgression. Then the Church will be received into that glory where her mother was corrupted through pride—namely, angelic dignity—and where her mother was violated—namely, the number of the elect was diminished. The Church herself will restore it when she possesses incorruption and completes the number of the elect. Then she will place Christ as a seal [Col. 0484B] upon her heart, because she will see in herself, as an image impressed on wax, him who is the image of God. She will place him as a seal upon her arm because she will receive him himself as the reward for the labor of her works. There love is strong as death, because, as death has drawn all the reprobate to destruction, so God’s love will draw all the elect to joy. There zeal is hard as hell, because, as hell swallows all emulators—that is, all imitators of the devil—so the court of heaven will receive all emulators—that is, imitators of Christ. There all the elect will be lamps of charity, when, with lamps lit, they go forth to meet the bridegroom and bride. They will always burn like fire in the love of God, when they shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father; and, as here waters of delights [Col. 0484C] and rivers of persecutions did not extinguish the charity of the saints, so the rewards of charity will have no end.

The house of men is this world. If all the substance of this world were given, it could not be compared with the reward of charity that will be given to Christ’s lovers, for Christ is charity. After the bridegroom had commended to Mandragora, coming to him, the dignity of love, he turns to the Shunammite and says:

**VERSE 8.—“Our sister is little and has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken for?”**

That is, when she is to be married. The comparison is with a little girl who, though promised to a man, does not yet have breasts—that is, breasts fully developed—and is not marriageable. It signifies the Church which will believe in [Col. 0484D] Christ after Antichrist: it will be small in the number of believers and will not have breasts, namely sufficient teachers, by whom it must inwardly be prepared, not yet to be brought into the bridal chamber.

It is as though he said: “The love which I commended is great; but Mandragora, newly converted and made our sister because she is co-heiress of the kingdom, is little in faith—that is, untrained and tender in religion—and therefore too weak for such great love as to undergo death for my love. This is especially so because she lacks breasts—that is, preachers—to imbue her sufficiently with this love. What, then, shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken for?” That is, what will become of her on the day of judgment, when she must be judged for her works or rewarded, if she has not love? For one who has love has God, [Col. 0485A] because God is love; but one who does not have it has no inheritance in the kingdom of God.

Alternatively: our sister, Mandragora, is little in the number of believers and has no breasts—that is, teachers who, by providing the milk of doctrine, may increase her number. What, then, will happen on the day of judgment, when she is to be associated with the angels, if the number of the elect is not completed? The Shunammite replies:

**VERSE 9.—“If she is a wall, let us build silver battlements upon her.”**

That is to say: if she is small, let us make her great; namely, let us send craftsmen to gather precious stones and make her into a wall, and let us build silver battlements upon her. That is, let us send preachers—you by inspiring, I by acting—who will gather living stones, that is, elect [Col. 0485B] people, into one faith through teaching and make them a dwelling place for God. Let us place over them such prelates as shine like silver through eloquence and defend their subjects from vices and heretics with the weapons of virtues.

“And if she is a door, let us fasten it with cedar boards.” That is to say: if she has no breasts—that is, teachers—let us fasten together cedar wood; that is, let us gather many examples of saints, whose works are incorruptible and drive away worms, that is, demons. From these let us make a door—that is, a certain entrance of faith—through which many may enter into her and the number of believers in her may be multiplied.

Alternatively: if some perfect person is a wall, namely fortified in natural ability and strong in virtues, let us build silver battlements upon her; [Col. 0485C] that is, let us make him her defender, shining in eloquence. Or, “let us build silver battlements upon her”: that is, invincible judgments, luminous with divine speech, with which he may instruct and defend her from enemies. And if anyone imperfect is a door, opening for others by teaching the entrance of salvation, let us fasten him with cedar boards: that is, let us set before him the unfading examples of devout men, by which he may draw many to conversion and bring them through the door of faith into God’s house, that is, into the Church.

Three things are indicated in a wall: it is made of many stones, fortifies citizens within, and repels enemies from without. Thus the Church consists of many faithful, whom it binds together with the cement of charity; it fortifies by the faith of the cross those dwelling within it; and it separates enemies, namely pagans and heretics, from itself by communion. [Col. 0485D] Three things are also indicated in a door: entrance, exit, and the way between. Entrance is faith, by which one enters the Church; exit is perseverance, by which one goes out to life; the way between is works done in love.

When the wall has been made and the door fastened together, the bride sings exultantly:

**VERSE 10.—“I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower.”**

As though she said: “I who was little in number have become many in firm believers, as a wall is made of stones; and therefore I am worthy that silver battlements should be built upon me—that is, that such prelates should be set over me as will teach me, by the brilliance of their eloquence, the charity commended to me by the bridegroom, and defend me from heretics with the weapons of Scripture. And I who had no breasts—that is, teachers—now have such teachers, lofty and firm in virtues as a tower, through whom there can be entrance to the way of salvation; and therefore I am worthy to be fastened with cedar boards—that is, to be strengthened by the examples of saints, through which they may instruct me in works of charity.”

[Col. 0486A] By boards is understood a picture, by cedar incorruptibility, and by fastening together concord. Painted boards are spread out before people when the examples of saints are set before them; these are incorruptible before God like cedar and drive away serpents—that is, demons. Teachers and elect persons fasten them together by the concord of imitation.

Alternatively, every perfect person says: “I am a wall,” namely strong against vices and therefore to be placed in the building of the Church, so that silver battlements [Col. 0486B] may be built upon me—namely, sacred Scriptures brilliant with the word of God—by which I may be a defense and ornament to the Church. “And my breasts are like a tower”: that is, my doctrine is firm, and it makes hearers rise, in the manner of towers, to the height of virtues.

Note that the perfect person is compared with a wall, while his breasts—that is, his doctrine—are likened to a tower, because his life is fortified against the vices of the world, while his doctrine is lofty in virtues. He says to the imperfect: “I am the door” (John 10:9), because by teaching I open to the less learned an entrance into life, and therefore I ought to be fastened with cedar boards—that is, confirmed by the examples of saints. I, the bride, began to be such when—understand, from the time when—I became before him as one finding peace. That is, from the time when the persecution of Antichrist ceased and Christ’s peace [Col. 0486C] was restored to me, I began to be built by his craftsmen into a wall of living stones, and my breasts began to rise in virtues.

For after the death of Antichrist there will be the greatest peace in the world, but only for a short time, as it is written: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thess. 5:3)—that is, the day of judgment. In that peace the Church will be gathered for worship of the one God. Of this the bride adds:

**VERSE 11.—“The Peaceful One had a vineyard in that which has peoples; he gave it to keepers.”**

That is to say: when Antichrist, the author of discord, has been killed, Christ, the true Peaceful One, will make peace in the world; and in that peace he will make for himself a vineyard, namely the universal Church, which [Col. 0486D] produces branches abundant in wine—that is, teachers pouring out the drink of life. This vineyard will be in that peace which has peoples, that is, all nations, unlike the peace which existed under Solomon among one nation of the Jews. He will entrust this vineyard to keepers—that is, to prelates—to guard and govern.

This is said because there is doubt whether the Church at that time will be governed by any prelates, since the day of judgment is believed to be near. But one should know that in those days the Church will be in its offices and orders as it is today. The Lord says that, as in the days of Noah people planted, ploughed, and performed other works until the flood came, so it will be in the days of the Son of Man (Luke 17:26): that is, before the day of judgment they will plough, plant, and do other works until the fire comes. [Col. 0487A] Therefore the past tense “was” and “he gave” is used for the future, in order to show the certainty that this is arranged by God, as though it had already occurred. He next adds what fruit that vineyard will yield:

“A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.” That is, each person will leave all that he possesses in this world and give it to the poor, that he may receive the reward promised to those laboring in this vineyard. For everyone who labors in this vineyard until night—that is, until the end of life—will have as his reward the denarius, that is, Christ, who is the highest good. The fruit of this vineyard is the heavenly kingdom. By the number one thousand, moreover, perfection is understood. Those are called perfect who leave all things of the world, as the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that [Col. 0487B] you have and give to the poor” (Matt. 19:21). By silver, which is precious, is understood worldly substance, which seems precious to people. Therefore one brings a thousand silver pieces for the vineyard’s fruit who leaves all that is in the world and gives it to those in need for the sake of the heavenly kingdom.

Alternatively, “a man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit”: namely, Christ, God from the Father and made man for us, brings full joy as the reward for this vineyard’s labor. By one thousand is understood fullness of joy; by silver, the reward of work. A thousand silver pieces are four pounds, and all the elect are comprehended in this number. For all the elect who are called from the four regions of the world, through the four Gospels, to the work of this vineyard, and labor in it to the end, receive fullness of joy as their reward.

[Col. 0487C] The workers of this vineyard, wearied by the weight of the day and heat, and harassed by many evils from adversaries, say to the householder: “He has released his vineyard from his own keeping, which he entrusted to keepers; therefore he does not rescue us from tribulation, though he sees us laboring so greatly for his sake.” The householder replies:

**VERSE 12.—“My vineyard is before me.”**

That is, it is in my keeping. I see those working. I see those keeping watch. I see those causing tribulation. I see those who are idle. And I render to each his reward according to his labor. “But your thousand, O Peaceful One, and two hundred for those who guard its fruit.” That is, a thousand silver pieces will be given to the workers and two hundred to the keepers. O vineyard, a thousand silver pieces will be for your peacemakers—that is, those who obtain peace for you before God—and two hundred silver pieces will be for the peacemakers of those who guard its fruit; that is, [Col. 0487D] they will obtain peace for the vineyard’s keepers.

Twelve hundred make one thousand two hundred. This number indicates that those who left all things after the example of the twelve apostles and labored in this vineyard according to their teaching receive a hundredfold here and, in the future, a thousand silver pieces—that is, full joy. The keepers of the vineyard, that is, the prelates of the Church, will receive two hundred silver pieces—that is, a twofold reward in body and soul—when the lesser shine as stars, the greater as the moon, and the learned as the brightness of the firmament, that is, as the sun.

It should be noted that throughout this nuptial Song, from the beginning of the book to the end, vineyards and clusters are introduced, [Col. 0488A] and signify the universal Church and the elect within her. Christ is her vine; the apostles and all the elect are the branches; their wine is doctrine, which gladdens the hearts of the faithful. What has been said concerning the mandrake may also be understood of the Shunammite, concerning whom the queen of the south, Pharaoh’s daughter—that is, the Church of the Gentiles—complains through the teachers of the primitive Church, saying:

“Our sister, the Shunammite”—that is, the Synagogue newly converted—“is little”; under Elijah and Enoch she is small in the number of converts, and she has no breasts—that is, no sufficient teachers, nor breasts of the Law and the Prophets spiritually interpreting these things for her. “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?” That is: what shall become of her in the time of Antichrist’s persecution, [Col. 0488B] when she must be tested concerning the faith? What answer will she make to adversaries who question her concerning the faith? The primitive Church answers through the Scriptures, namely the Epistles of Peter, Paul, and the others: “If she is a wall, let us build upon her silver battlements.” That is, if she wishes to be firm in faith and constant in suffering, like a wall against enemies in a siege, let us compose for her such writings as will enable her to defend herself against adversaries, answer their captious questions abundantly, and resist heretics courageously.

“But if she is a door, let us fasten her with boards of cedar.” That is, if she wishes by word and example to be an entrance for others into life, let us set before her many examples of the saints of old, by which she may adequately instruct those who are to be brought into the faith. Therefore the Synagogue, built up by the Scriptures [Col. 0488C] and joined together by the examples of the righteous, cries out joyfully: “I am a wall,” that is, firm in faith and strong in suffering; “and my breasts are like a tower,” that is, my teachers are lofty in virtues and terrible to enemies. Or: my doctrine is impregnable. “From the time when I became, before him, like one finding peace”: that is, from the time when I received the faith of Christ and obtained his grace.

Judea had no peace with Christ or with humankind after she unhappily cried: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). For she is dispersed throughout the whole world, serves all nations under tribute, and every people demands Christ’s blood from her hand. But after she has been converted to Christ, [Col. 0488D] she will have peace with all nations. She found peace, as it were, before him when she obtained communion with the Church; and she will then possess that communion fully, when, united with the angels, she rejoices with the Prince of Peace. Of this Synagogue it is added:

“A vineyard belonged to the peaceful one in it, which has peoples; he entrusted it to keepers. A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.” Judea, namely, enjoyed the greatest peace under Solomon and held many peoples under tribute. Like a fruitful vineyard transferred from Egypt and planted in the land of promise, she put forth shoots for us—namely, the prophets—from whom the drink of the Scriptures flowed as from grapes. The king entrusted this vineyard to keepers when he assigned it to princes to govern. For its fruit a man brought a thousand silver pieces, [Col. 0489A] when Ptolemy, king of Egypt, devoted to the Scriptures, sent abundant money to the high priest of the Jews because he had sent him the sacred Scripture through the seventy translators.

Afterward this vineyard was turned to bitterness: it bore not grapes but wild grapes, when, contrary to the Law, it killed the just and innocent Christ, the true vine of life, and expelled from itself his branches, the apostles, who bore the fruit of life. Therefore all who passed along the way harvested it, when the Romans and all the surrounding nations devastated it.

This vineyard, cultivated anew by the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, will truly be a vineyard for the Peaceful One, namely Christ, in that peace—or in that vineyard—which has peoples, that is, in the catholic Church, which contains all peoples. He [Col. 0489B] will entrust it to keepers, namely teachers of the faith, under whose guardianship it will produce precious fruit: the glorious blood of the martyrs. For this fruit the man brings a thousand silver pieces: Christ, having become a man from her, will give her for her labor the reward of eternal life, signified by the thousandfold number. Therefore it continues:

“My vineyard is before me.” That is, the Synagogue, formerly not mine because of unbelief but alienated from the kingdom of God, is now mine because of faith; she is before me, doing good works and teaching others, so that I may reward those laboring in her and guarding her, and punish those devastating her. He now turns to the vineyard, saying: “A thousand are yours, O peaceful one, and two hundred for those who guard its fruits.” As though he said: O Synagogue converted to me, do not fear; [Col. 0489C] for you have now found peace before me, because a thousand will be your peacemakers—that is, all the perfect pray that Christ’s peace may be brought about—and two hundred peacemakers, that is, all the perfect of the Old and New Law, pray for peace for those who guard its fruits. Since he first said, “A thousand are yours, O peaceful one,” one asks why he subsequently said “its fruits,” and not “your fruits.” This is because he directs his words to those outside the vineyard, so that they may hasten to enter it through faith and labor in it through love, and thus deserve to be rewarded for such fruit.

In the moral sense, all this is understood of the faithful soul converted from the world to a particular religious life. The voice of prelates says of her:

“Our sister is little and has no breasts. [Col. 0489D] What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?”

As though they said: the soul of our brother newly converted, who is our sister, is little in religious profession—that is, inexperienced and unskilled in conduct—and has no breasts, that is, she does not adequately possess the teaching of the queen. What, then, will become of her on the day of temptation, when she must be tested by her former vices—that is, by demons? For the devil tests those converted to religious life far more sharply than those immersed in the waves of the world. The soul is little before it grows through the increase of virtues, and therefore does not have breasts of preaching to offer weak hearers. But it is mature when, joined to the word of God and filled with the Holy Spirit, it becomes fruitful in the conception of children through the ministry of preaching: children whom it brings forth by exhorting and bears by converting. [Col. 0490A]

The voice of those filled with a like spirit answers: “If that soul is a wall,” that is, if she wishes to remain steadfast in the congregation, “let us build upon her silver battlements”; that is, let us instruct her with sayings bright in eloquence, by which she may fortify herself against temptations and teach others to abstain from vices. “And if she is a door,” an entrance for others to conversion by word and example, “let us fasten it with boards of cedar”; that is, let us adorn it with many examples of the Fathers, so that through it an entrance into life may stand open to many.

The soul, built up by the teachings of prelates as by the stones of craftsmen and adorned by the examples of the Fathers, cries to those living in the world: You who labor in worldly affairs, enter by my example, as through a door, into the rest of spiritual life. For I, formerly like you, unstable in sins, have become [Col. 0490B] like a wall, steadfast in spiritual things; and my breasts—that is, the teaching of my life—are like an impregnable tower. “From the time when I became before him like one finding peace”: that is, from the time when I passed from the tumult of the world into cloistered quiet. For one toils, as it were, amid the clamor of wars who labors among the adversities of the world and the enticements of the flesh; but one finds peace before God, as it were, while resting in spiritual life. This peace will be possessed fully when, feeling no conflict between flesh and spirit, one rejoices in eternal peace.

What follows—“a vineyard belonged to the peaceful one”—means any congregation of the righteous, in which the branches are spiritual men and the wine is sweet doctrine. It has peoples, namely many converted to religious life. The true Peaceful One, Christ, entrusted it to keepers [Col. 0490C] to cultivate, namely spiritual prelates such as Augustine and Benedict, for instruction. “For its fruit a man brings a thousand silver pieces,” when anyone leaves all that belongs to the world and enters the cloister in order to receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life. Or, “for its fruit a man brings a thousand silver pieces,” when Christ gives eternal life to one who has persevered in good until the end. Hence it continues: “My vineyard is before me”; that is, the cloistered life undertaken for my sake is in my presence, so that I may reward all who labor in it for me and condemn those who live wrongly in it.

And you, O soul, who found peace before me when you were converted from the world to me, will yet have full peace when you see me in eternal peace. For “a thousand [Col. 0490D] will be your peacemakers,” that is, all the perfect will make me at peace with you; “and two hundred peacemakers will be for those who guard the fruits of its vineyard,” that is, all the perfect in active and contemplative life will reconcile with me those who observe the ordinances of spiritual life. For as a thousand, so a hundred signifies perfection or fullness of reward; and two hundred, as it were, two thousands.

In the anagogical sense, this is the voice of the Church already reigning in heaven, lamenting to the angelic host over the pilgrim Church:

“Our sister is little”: that is, the Church still on pilgrimage, our future co-heiress, is still imperfect in the number of the elect; “and she has no breasts,” that is, no sufficient number of teachers to instruct her toward perfection. “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?” [Col. 0491A] That is: what will become of the imperfect on the day of judgment, when they are to be justly judged by the Judge? Many there are who have not only failed to leave everything as the perfect have done, but have not even redeemed their sins through alms to the poor; therefore they will be condemned.

The angelic voice answers: “If she is built by craftsmen as a wall of living stones, let us build good works upon her by exhortation, so that these may be for them on the day of judgment battlements shining like silver,” when those on the left will be told: “Depart, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Luke 13:27). “And if she is open through preaching, like a door, so that through her there may be an entrance into life for the faithful, let us fasten her with boards of cedar”; that is, by exhortation let us throng her with spiritual children, that they may fill up the number of the elect and rejoice with us in our fellowship.

Therefore the Church, seeing herself built as a wall of living stones [Col. 0491B] into a dwelling place for God and seeing the angelic tower of the heavenly Jerusalem restored through herself, sings exultantly:

“I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower.” As though she said: I have been built by the craftsman Christ from elect human beings, like a wall of stones around the heavenly Jerusalem, like a wall around a city. And my breasts—that is, the teachers who give me the milk of doctrine—have been raised up like a tower in Jerusalem in place of the angels who fell. Thus I began to be built as a city through learned craftsmen, the apostles and their successors, from the time when I became before him like one finding peace. The human race had no peace with God and the angels after it transgressed God’s command in Paradise through the first parent.
