[Col. 0491C] But it found peace with God, as it were, when it believed in Christ, who is true peace.

The angelic choir sang this peace to human beings of good will when Christ, the Prince of Peace, came from the palace of heaven into the prison of the world. As he was departing from here, he left this peace to his own, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). Having conquered death and destroyed the devil, the author of wars, he brought this peace to the children of peace—that is, to the peacemakers—saying: “Peace be with you” (John 20:19). By this peace the Church desired to be reconciled to God over the churches of the Gentiles, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”: that is, through Christ let him restore to me the peace which I lost. She now possesses this peace in hope; afterward she will possess it in reality, when she sees Peace itself face to face and possesses all the bounds [Col. 0491D] of Jerusalem in peace.

This Church was a vineyard for the true Peaceful One, Christ, in that peace which has peoples—understand, Christians—or which has little ones, that is, the humble. In it he himself was the true vine, and the wine was evangelical doctrine. He entrusted it to keepers, namely the apostles and other prelates, to propagate and extend; under them it produced noble fruit, namely martyrs, confessors, virgins, and other faithful persons. For this fruit Christ the man brings a thousand silver pieces, namely the denarius of reward, which is full joy, to all the laborers of this vineyard. Therefore it continues: “My vineyard is before me,” namely my Church in this life, a vineyard planted by me, the householder, and propagated throughout the world through the apostles, will always be before me in heaven, seeing my glory and the presence of the Father and [Col. 0492A] the Holy Spirit. And there, O vineyard, a thousand will be your peacemakers: that is, all angels and saints, O Church, will through me have peace with you. “And two hundred for those who guard its fruits”: that is, all who have governed this vineyard well will eternally possess peace of body and soul.

Up to this point the king remained in the garden of nuts with the queen of the south and Pharaoh’s daughter, where he received the Shunammite and the Mandrake into favor. She now says to the supreme queen:

**VERSE 13.**—“You who dwell in the gardens, the friends are listening; make me hear your voice.” As though she said: O Queen of queens, you who dwell with the queens and daughters of Jerusalem, here with me in the gardens I have now adorned you with royal attire and gathered all nations under your dominion. Make me now hear your voice—that is, your petition. What further do you ask? The friends, that is, my princes, are listening to learn what more you wish and what you require of me.

The queen answers: This is my petition: that you depart from here and take me with you. She says this in equivalent terms:

**VERSE 14.**—“Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.” That is to say: Depart from this place and return to Lebanon, the mountain of spices, where the royal palace is; take me there with you. And as a gazelle chooses wholesome herbs from harmful ones, so separate me from my enemies; and gather to me all my elect and friends at the wedding prepared for me. And as a young stag swiftly runs from heat to shade, so bring me swiftly into the royal hall.

That is, the Church, gathered from all nations to Christ and adorned by him with every virtue, prays that he may someday lead her from the valley of tears to the mountain of heaven, to the heavenly palace, where, separated from her enemies, she may rejoice with her friends in everlasting glory. [Col. 0492C]

It should be noted that four gardens are set forth in this book: the enclosed garden, the garden of fruits, the garden of spices, and the garden of nuts. The enclosed garden was the Virgin Mary, incorrupt Mother of God, into whose garden Christ the Bridegroom descended when he entered the enclosed womb of the Virgin. The garden of fruits was the Jewish people, which produced sweet fruits when it brought forth a multitude of believers in the primitive Church, who were of one heart and one soul. In that garden he harvested myrrh when he endured the bitterness of [Col. 0492D] the Passion in Judea. The garden of spices was the Church of the Gentiles, in which was gathered an assembly of saints; the Bridegroom descended into it when, through the preaching of the apostles, he came among the Gentiles. The garden of nuts is the Synagogue still to be converted, in which many endure outwardly the bitterness of the flesh but inwardly possess the sweetness of virtues; the Bridegroom will descend into it when, through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, he visits the Synagogue. In these gardens the Church dwells, because at different times she changes her various states.

Another translation reads “in the gates,” and these are understood as virtues or apostolic Scriptures, which are the gates of life; the Church dwells in them while adorning herself with virtues through the apostolic Scriptures. Therefore the Bridegroom says to the Church:

[Col. 0493A] “You who dwell in the gardens, make me hear your voice.” As though Christ says to the Church of the perfect: You who dwell through religious observances in churches, in which you bring forth shoots of virtues and flowers of saints, make me hear your voice; that is, make your preaching among the perfect such that it is worthy for me to hear, because the friends—that is, the angels made by me, your friends and your peacemakers—listen, in order to bring it to me to be rewarded. Or: make me hear your voice, that is, your petition, because your angelic friends listen in order to bring it to me for fulfillment. Or: make me hear your voice, that is, your petition, because the angels, etc. The comparison is drawn from the case in which the bridegroom’s friends listen to what the bride requests, so that her petition may obtain its answer from the bridegroom.

One makes God hear one’s voice who [Col. 0493B] preaches to one’s neighbors about eternal life not for gain but solely for God. Or one makes God hear one’s voice who asks of God not earthly but eternal things. Now the entire preaching or prayer of the Church is that a separation be made between good and evil, so that the good may enjoy the peace they love, while the wicked may either be converted to them or separated from them. Hence it follows:

“Flee, my beloved.” That is, pass away from the chaff and withdraw me from my enemies, as one who flees and hides himself from them. “And be like a gazelle,” discerning the good from the evil, as the gazelle distinguishes wholesome herbs from harmful ones; “and be like a young stag,” distinguishing the unchaste and resting among the chaste, as the young stag, avoiding heat, rests in shade. You, I say, who are the young stag of the deer—that is, the son of the patriarchs, who leapt over the [Col. 0493C] thorn-bushes of sins—be among the grains, namely among us, who are mountains of spices, lofty in virtues and fragrant through good works. Or, you who are a young stag of deer, in human flesh assumed from the patriarchs, be upon the mountains of spices, namely above the choirs of angels, associating with them a multitude of human beings. “Young stag of deer” is used to distinguish it from the young of a gazelle: the latter seeks the heights, while the former runs swiftly.

The whole company of the kingdom of heaven is contained in this verse. By the beloved is understood Christ; by flight, passage from the world to life; by the gazelle, the Church; by the young stag of deer, the people of the saints; and by the mountains of spices, the orders of angels. All these will be gathered at the marriage of the Lamb, [Col. 0493D] when the Church is separated from the wicked and, crowned with glory and honor in the heavenly Jerusalem, is placed as queen upon the throne of the kingdom in place of her rival, namely the condemned angelic nature; and she will also be joined in glory to her Bridegroom, the Word of God united to her in the flesh.

In the moral sense every faithful soul dwells in gardens when it is filled with the greenness of hope and good works. The hope of this world is dry, for all that is loved here quickly withers. Therefore she who dwells in gardens must make the Bridegroom hear her voice—that is, she must exercise the gift of preaching in the measure in which she delights in him whom she desires—for the friends, namely all the elect, listen, desiring to hear words of life so that they may return to their heavenly homeland. For her the Beloved flees, because [Col. 0494A] he who became comprehensible in the flesh surpasses the understanding of our mind in his divinity. Those who ascend the mountains of spices are likened to the gazelle and the young stag, because through grace he ascends into and rests in those who are always fragrant with virtues.

In the anagogical sense the beloved woman dwells in gardens when the Church rejoices in Paradise. Or she dwells in gates when through the apostles, who are gates of life, she judges the nations. The day of judgment itself is also called a gate, as in: “He shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” (Ps. 126:5). That is, on the day of judgment the Church will not be put to shame when she speaks to her enemies—the pagans, Jews, and heretics—taunting them because they put her to shame here and therefore are now put to shame. That day is the gate of life, because through it the righteous will enter eternal life; it is also the gate of death, because through it the wicked will go into [Col. 0494B] eternal punishment.

At that gate the Church makes the Bridegroom hear her voice, saying: “Lord, if I have found grace in your sight, show me yourself, that I may see your face, into which angels desire to look.” Then she herself will hear the Bridegroom’s voice when he sets her over all his goods, saying: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21). There follows the bride’s voice, which the Bridegroom wishes to hear: “Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.” The Beloved flees from the wicked when he leads his bride from the miseries of the world to the joys of heaven. He will be like a gazelle when he chooses the elect from the reprobate as grain from chaff. He will be like a young stag when he rests among the saints as a young stag rests in shade. He will then be upon the mountains of spices when he reigns [Col. 0494C] over the heights of angels and human beings, in whom the fragrance of virtues is sweet. Or the gazelle itself with the young stag will be upon the mountains of spices when the Church with the people of the faithful possesses the gates of her enemies, namely when she inherits the places of the apostate angels. See to what end this song has been brought: it has led the fallen human race before God’s presence.

This book is therefore read on the feast of St. Mary, because she herself bore the figure of the Church, which is virgin and mother: virgin, because uncorrupted by every heresy; mother, because she continually bears spiritual children through grace. Therefore all that has been said of the Church can also be understood of the Virgin herself, bride and mother of the Bridegroom. There is a little book [Col. 0494D] published by us entitled *The Seal of St. Mary*, in which the whole Song of Songs is specially applied to her person.

That our labor may be profitable to all, let us briefly recapitulate everything in an epilogue.

This book begins where the human race received peace, that is, the grace of God. By “Let him kiss me,” Christ’s Incarnation is signified; it brought to humanity the peace it lost in the first parent, a peace always desired by the Church. For Christ, the Word of God and bridegroom of human nature, is true peace, to whom our nature is united. When God became man, then surely man became God. The peace which the conqueror of death brought, he restored to believers by his resurrection, saying: “Peace be with you” (John 20:19). This was the kiss [Col. 0495A] of God’s mouth: peace restored through the Word of God, because then our nature in Christ became impassible and immortal, as it had been created in the beginning.

By “breasts” is understood evangelical doctrine; by “ointments,” the charisms of the Holy Spirit; by “a name like oil poured out,” the new name of Christianity, conferred upon believers through holy oil in baptism. By “Draw me,” Christ’s Ascension is signified, after which the Church desires to be drawn into heaven. Therefore follows “the fragrance of the ointments,” namely the sweetness of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. “The king brought me in” expresses the conversion of the primitive Church, which occurred after the Holy Spirit was given. “I am black” signifies the tribulation endured by the primitive Church from unbelieving Jews. “Tell me” expresses the distress brought upon her by the perversity of heretics. “If you do not know yourself” indicates the protection of the apostles [Col. 0495B], which was for her like the tents of shepherds.

By nard, the bundle of myrrh, and the cluster of cypress, Christ’s Passion is set before her, that she may imitate it through patience. For by nard is understood Christ’s Incarnation; by myrrh, his Passion; and by the cluster of cypress, his Resurrection. By “Behold, you are fair, my friend,” and the remaining words which follow down to “upon my bed,” are expressed Christ’s praise of the faith and labor of the primitive Church, the Church’s thanksgiving for the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and her preaching to the nations. By the words “upon my bed” down to “I will go to the mountain of myrrh,” is signified the introduction of the Church of the Gentiles, which through the apostles was led from the desert of unbelief to Solomon’s bed and to the litter for the banquet; she was received by the daughters of Zion [Col. 0495C] and magnificently praised by the peaceful king.

By the words “I will go to the mountain of myrrh” down to “an enclosed garden,” is signified the Church’s conflict, in which she fought with the arms of faith and patience against Amana, Sanir, and Hermon—that is, against the rulers of the Gentiles, [Col. 0496A] who were leopards and lions, namely savage persecutors. By the words “an enclosed garden” down to “Arise, north wind,” the various classes of aromatic plants signify the various orders of the righteous, like different legions of martyrs fighting for Christ. By “Arise, north wind” down to “I sleep,” is expressed the Church’s affliction, by which she was troubled under heretics for the faith. By “I sleep” is understood the Church’s peace and security. By “I rose to open” is signified her preaching. By “My soul melted” is understood the Church of penitents. By “What is your beloved?” down to “I went down to the garden of nuts,” the Church of the imperfect is taught the mysteries of Christ by the Church of the perfect. By “I went down to the garden of nuts” down to “Come, my beloved,” are described the conversion of the Synagogue, [Col. 0496B] its conflict under Antichrist, and the praise of its members, that is, its orders. From there to the end of the book are expressed the calling of unbelievers after Antichrist, the rewarding of the faithful, and the separation of good and evil at the final judgment. After this the universal Church, Christ’s bride, united in the flesh to the Word of God, will be crowned with glory and honor for her conflict and joined to her Bridegroom in the chamber of glory—that is, in the manifest vision of God.

As, with the help of God the Father, we expounded David the father, so, with the help of God the Son, we have elucidated Solomon the son. Therefore let us all render thanks to the Holy Spirit, composer and expositor of both works. [Col. 0496C]

Songs worthy of the marriage-bed of chastely burning love  
Have together been fittingly written by my ministry.  
A praise worthy of God the King is fittingly ended in the marriage-song.

Here ends Honorius’s exposition on the Song of Songs.

[Col. 0495]

# THE SEAL OF BLESSED MARY, IN WHICH THE SONG OF SONGS IS EXPOUNDED

The disciples to the master.

[Col. 0495D]

To the excellent master, register of books, the multitude of disciples wishes to see in Zion the God of gods. The whole assembly of brethren gives thanks to your diligence because, through your labor in the *Elucidarium*, the Spirit of Wisdom has unfolded for them so many coverings. Therefore, with one voice, we all ask you again to undertake a new labor and, for the sake of charity, explain to us why the Gospel, “Jesus entered into a certain castle” (Luke 10:38), and the Song of Songs are read concerning St. Mary, when they seem to have absolutely nothing to do with her.

## The Master’s Answer

Because I have resolved to bear the burden of the day and the heat in the Lord’s vineyard for a denarius, I do not wish, like a barren fig tree, to occupy the ground in vain, but, like a fruitful olive tree, to bring some adornment [Col. 0496D] to God’s house, that I may sometime deserve to receive a dwelling in it. Therefore, since your company graciously received the little book which I sent, I shall endeavor, by the key of David, to unlock for you the matters about which you seem to be uncertain.

Accordingly, let this little book be published to the glory of the Son of God and the honor of his Mother, and let the name *The Seal of St. Mary* be given to it. May he himself grant understanding, whose wisdom surpasses all understanding.

# The Seal of St. Mary

You say that you wonder why the Gospel, “Jesus entered,” and the Song of Songs are recited on the feast of St. Mary, since the simple suppose that neither seems to speak, as it were, of her at all. First, then, you should know concerning the Gospel that nothing could be found in the whole sequence of Scripture [Col. 0497A] more suitable, more fitting, or more worthy to be read on her holy solemnity.

Thus it is said: “Jesus entered into a certain castle” (Luke 10:38). In a castle there is a high tower, in which are battlements against enemies; outside there is a wall, which gives protection to those within. This castle was that sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, namely the glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, who was fortified on every side by the continual guardianship of angels. In her was a high tower, namely humility, reaching to the heights of heaven; hence it is said: “The Lord has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48). Her exterior wall was chastity, which furnished inward protection to the other virtues. The Lord entered this castle when, in the Virgin’s womb, he united human nature to himself.

“And a certain woman named Martha [Col. 0497B] received him into her house, and she had a sister named Mary.” Martha signifies the active life; Mary, the contemplative life. The perpetual Virgin Mary is proclaimed to have cultivated both most excellently in Christ. For she rendered him all the services of the active life. From childhood she received into the lodging of her womb—resplendent with the jewels of virtues—him who for our sake was an exile and a stranger in this world. She fed him when hungry with her own breasts; she comforted him when weeping upon her knees. She warmed him when weak with baths, wrapped him naked in cloths, bound him crying with swaddling bands, and pressed sweet kisses upon him when he smiled. She was exceedingly careful in her frequent service: fleeing from Herod’s face into Egypt and, returning again, finding Archelaus. [Col. 0497C] She was greatly troubled about many things, everywhere seeking safe hiding places by which to conceal and keep him hidden.

That she is said to complain concerning her sister because she had left her alone in the labor means this: when Mary saw Christ seized by the ungodly, cruelly dragged away, bound, struck, beaten, mocked, condemned with criminals, and bitterly tortured upon the gibbet of the cross, she would gladly, if it had been possible, have given her own life for his deliverance.

And although she knew that divinity dwelt bodily in him, she anxiously complained in her mind, as it were, that it did not help him, but had left as though guilty one whom it exposed to so many evils as though he were rejected. Sitting at the Lord’s feet, she thirsted with heart and ear for his words; she also preserved them in her heart, reflecting upon them through the office of the contemplative life. Always [Col. 0497D] meditating on spiritual things, she desired heavenly things. For the fountain of wisdom himself had made his dwelling in her; therefore all treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden in her. Now that Martha’s labor has been removed, the true Mary enjoys in that life, not figuratively but in reality, that one thing necessary: clinging to her Son’s embraces, she is eternally satisfied with the sight of his divinity together with the angels.

Today the glorious Virgin passed into that glory, in which her Son exalted her as Queen of Heaven above all the orders of angels. The best part which she chose here, she received twofold today from the Lord’s hand; it shall never be taken away from her, but, when full joy is given to the saints, shall be increased a hundredfold.

## On the Epistle
Why, then, is the praise of Wisdom read on her day? [Col. 0498A] A sufficiently plausible reason is made clear. Christ is the Wisdom of God, whose person speaks here: “In all things”—that is, among all nations—“I sought rest,” but only “in the inheritance of the Lord,” that is, in the Church, “I found a place to dwell.” Rejoicing, she adds: “He who created me rested in my tabernacle.” The tabernacle of the Church—or of God—is the blessed ever-virgin Mary, as it is said: “He set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII [19]:6). In her the Son of God, coming as man, rested; and from her he came forth “as a bridegroom from his chamber” (ibid.). “Dwell in Jacob, and inherit in Israel; and send down roots among my elect.” The apostolic order is Jacob, that is, supplanter of vices; it is likewise Israel, namely, the man who sees God. In this Jacob the Virgin of God dwelt, and with this Israel she inherited the kingdom of God [Col. 0498B] and among them she sent down the chosen roots of her chastity and humility.

“Thus I was established in Zion.” Zion is called a watchtower, and it is the Church, in which the Mother of God is established as a pillar by writings and preachings; upon her praiseworthy life the whole Church leans and is upheld. “And likewise I rested in the sanctified city.” The sanctified city is the heavenly country, illumined by eternal brightness. There the perpetual Virgin now rests with angels and saints, yet shines crowned with glory and honor above them all. Hence she says: “My power is in Jerusalem.” Zion signifies the present Church; Jerusalem, however, the heavenly country. Mary is called Queen of Heaven; therefore, not undeservedly, Jerusalem is proclaimed her dominion. And because here she took root among an honored people, that is, among the people of believers, by the example of her holiness, therefore her inheritance will be in the portion of her God, that is, in the divinity of her Son. And this will be “in the fullness of the saints,” that is, when the number of the elect has been completed: she will have praise and glory from all.

“I was exalted like a cedar in Lebanon.” Lebanon is a mountain in the land of promise, where cedars grow and from whose root the Jordan flows. Lebanon means “whiteness,” and is the Jewish people, made white by the worship of God and Holy Scripture. In it the glorious Virgin was exalted like a cedar, that is, surpassing the merits of all by the fragrance and beauty of holiness. From her womb flowed forth, as the Jordan from the mountain, he who consecrated the font of baptism for the world. “Like a cypress on Mount Zion.” A cut cypress does not grow green again; therefore in ancient times it was carried before the funerals of the dead. Thus the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, was a cypress on Mount Zion, that is, in the true watchtower—the Church—whose mind, once dried up like the fig tree, never grew green again with worldly joys. Therefore she is set forth in preaching before all those who are to be mortified for Christ. “Like a palm tree I was exalted in Kadesh.” The palm is given to victors, and this in Kadesh, that is, among the sanctified, for whom the gracious Virgin is a palm of sanctification, since through her noble offspring they obtain victory and sanctification. “Like a planting of roses in Jericho.” Jericho means “moon,” that is, the Church; in it the rose signifies martyrs, all of whom the holy Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*, Mother of God) surpasses by the eminence of her suffering, as the rose excels other flowers in redness.

For when she saw the Son of God, born from herself, so innocently tormented on the cross, she endured in her soul a torment greater than that of all martyrs. Hence she was more than a martyr: others suffered in body, but she in soul, as it is said: “A sword shall pierce your own soul” (Luke 2:35).—“Like a beautiful olive tree in the fields.” Oil signifies mercy; the field is unploughed land and signifies virgins, who have not been furrowed by the ploughshares of a man’s embrace. Among them the chaste Χριστοτόκος (*Christotokos*, Christ-bearer) is very beautiful, like a fair olive tree in the fields. From her flowed the oil of joy and mercy, which, healing us from infirmity, anoints us for the kingdom of heavenly glory. “Like a plane tree I was exalted beside waters in the streets.” The waters are peoples walking through the streets, that is, in secular life—namely, flourishing in marriage—among whom the illustrious Virgin shone like a plane tree when she fruitfully bore noble offspring.

“Like cinnamon.” Cinnamon is called “of the immaculate,” and signifies the innocent, for whom this rod was cinnamon, when from an immaculate womb she brought forth the giver of innocence. It is, moreover, an aromatic tree of ash-gray color, and signifies penitents, for whom this glorious woman was again cinnamon when she poured forth to them Jesus, the remedy of life. “Like balsam giving forth fragrance, I gave an odor.” Balsam smells sweetly; with it the foreheads of Christians are signed; with it also priests and temples of God are consecrated. Like precious balsam this Virgin gave an odor, when she bore for the world Christ, the sweet fragrance of souls, who signs us with chrism for his kingdom and, making us his temples, himself as king and priest consecrates us in the King.

“Like choice myrrh.” The bodies of the dead were embalmed with myrrh. For all who renounce the world and die with Christ, the Virgin already so often named—and to be named still more often—Mary was not merely myrrh, but choice myrrh, when she crucified her flesh to the allurements of the world and afflicted herself with fasts and vigils. She breathed forth the fragrance of sweetness when she bore Christ, the fragrance of angels, who above all offered himself as choice myrrh to death for us, to God the Father, as a sweet-smelling offering, that he might make us, dead to vices, partakers of his divinity. Now, with the help of her of whom we speak, and with the joint assistance of your prayers, let us turn our pen to the Song of Songs and explain why these things are read concerning her. [Col. 0499D]

## Song of Songs

The glorious Virgin Mary bears the type of the Church, which is virgin and mother. It is also proclaimed a mother because, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, children are daily begotten to God through it in baptism. It is called virgin because, preserving the integrity of faith inviolate, it is not corrupted by heretical perversity. Thus Mary was mother in giving birth to Christ, and virgin in remaining closed after childbirth. Therefore all that is written concerning the Church is read of her also quite fittingly. It is therefore said:

## CHAPTER I

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Him whom kings and prophets did not deserve to see or hear, the Virgin deserved not only to bear in her womb, but also to give frequent kisses when he was born, and to receive many things from his holy mouth. “For your breasts are better than wine.” He who feeds angels in the bosom of the Father here sucked the breasts of his Virgin Mother. “Fragrant with the best ointments,” that is, filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit—although it is not inappropriate to understand literally that the Virgin often anointed her most beloved Son with the finest ointments. “Your name is oil poured out.” Oil poured into other liquids floats above them and also heals the sick. The Virgin’s name is Mary, which means “star of the sea.” Those who invoke her help in tribulation float above every adversity through her, as oil does: like the Jewish boy whom she protected from the flame in the furnace, and whom his father threw in there because, among Christian boys, he had received the body of the Lord. Those weakened by sins who trust in her receive health more swiftly through Christ, the oil: thus Theophilus, who repudiated Christ in writing and handed himself over into the devil’s hands, received his written bond back from the devil through her and obtained forgiveness of his guilt. Likewise, Mary, enveloped in many stains, through her had not merely forgiveness of her crimes but also shone by glorious miracles.

Those who sail on the sea of this age, and in imitating her humility and chastity look upon her as a star, safely enter through her into the harbor of life. Thus it is related of a certain man that, whenever he passed before the Virgin’s altar, he would bow and say, “Hail, Mary.” When at the point of death demons, confident of him, gathered to lead him into the abyss, the merciful Virgin suddenly came, professed him to be her chaplain, rescued him when the wicked had already despaired of him, and thus he escaped safely, head unharmed, through her. Therefore “the young women loved you,” that is, virgins imitate you. “Draw me after you,” she says to the Son, namely, to the exercises of virtues. Mary did not learn from her Son to create the heavens, but to take root in humility and meekness, as he said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). Therefore she was drawn after Christ into heaven. “We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments,” that is, believers hastening to joys imitate the examples of her life. “The King brought me into his chamber,” that is, the King of glory took her into eternal life. “We shall exult and rejoice in you,” that is, believers rejoice in her intercession. “Mindful of your breasts.” [Col. 0500D] Mary’s breasts were chastity and humility; in these the company of the righteous delights. “More than wine,” that is, more than human glory, “the upright love you,” that is, angels honor you.

“I am black,” that is, born of the poor; “like the tents of Kedar,” that is, like one among sinners; “beautiful like Solomon’s curtain,” that is, I am the covering of the true Peacemaker, who covered the ark, that is, Christ; and therefore a daughter of Jerusalem, that is, a sharer in the vision of true peace. “Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me”: that is, though I sprang from the lowly, the Sun of righteousness chose me, lowly as I was, for his mother. Therefore “the sons of my mother fought against me,” that is, the prophets, sons of the Synagogue, preached concerning me. Or the apostles, sons of the mother of grace, fought against me, that is, preached for me against heretics [Col. 0501A] who said that she bore not God but a phantom, or that she had borne a child by a man. “They made me keeper of vineyards,” that is, an example of virginity in all churches. “My vineyard,” that is, my virginity, “I did not keep,” but the Holy Spirit did.

“Tell me, you whom my soul loves.” Mary’s soul loved Christ; therefore he made known to her all the secrets of the Father. “Where you pasture, where you lie down at midday.” The most chaste Virgin Mary was midday, shining and burning with the Holy Spirit, into whom Christ came down from the heat of the lustful. He lay down in her humility; he suffered in her chastity. “Lest I begin to wander among the flocks of your companions”: that is, make known to all that you rested in me, lest heretics tear me apart, saying: “If a virgin gave birth, it was a phantom.” By their sacraments your companions are made manifest; therefore I wander among their flocks, because in their sects and assemblies I am their psalm. “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women.” Mary did not know the stain of defilement, and therefore is beautiful, that is, blessed among all women. She went forth from feminine frivolity and advanced from virtue to virtue. “After the tracks of the flocks,” that is, through the examples of the saints, “and she fed the kids,” that is, carnal people, with holy works, “beside the tents of the shepherds,” that is, according to the teaching of the apostles.

“I have compared you, my friend, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots.” As the people of God were delivered from Pharaoh through Moses’ rod, so the Church was delivered from the devil through the rod of Jesse, Mary, and her flower, that is, Christ. “Your cheeks are beautiful.” The cheeks of this Virgin are her manner of life in the active and contemplative life; they are modest, ashamed to sin, like those of the turtledove, that is, mourning earthly things and sighing for the joys of the heavenly kingdom. “Your neck,” that is, the faith which joined her to God the head, “is like necklaces,” that is, an ornament in the whole Church. “We shall make for you little chains of gold, inlaid with silver”: that is, the apostles and their followers compose from all these things, in your honor, Scripture adorned with wisdom and eloquence. “While the king was at his table,” that is, Christ in the bosom of the Father, “my nard gave forth its fragrance,” that is, through humility he entered the Virgin’s womb. For nard signifies humility; fragrance signifies Christ’s incarnation. “He shall dwell between my breasts,” that is, incarnate, he shall be borne in my womb. “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh.” This was when he hung on the cross before her. “My beloved is to me a cluster of henna,” that is, he was joy to her in the resurrection, “in the vineyards of Engaddi,” that is, in the churches of the faithful.

“Behold, you are beautiful, my friend.” Mary is called friend because she bore the Father’s secrets. Behold, you are beautiful before God in humility; behold, you are beautiful before human beings in chastity. Beautiful in virginity, beautiful in fruitfulness, beautiful in virtues, beautiful in works; beautiful here in the praise of men, beautiful in heaven in the praise of angels. She is called beautiful twice because she is declared without inward or outward blemish. “Your eyes,” that is, the intentions of your works, “are like doves,” that is, sincere and simple. Or your eyes—that is, the examples which lead others as eyes do—are full of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and fair.” Christ is beautiful from the chaste Virgin, fair from the Father. “Our bed is flowering.” Mary was Christ’s bed, in whom he rested as in a bed. He says “our,” because the Father and Holy Spirit were always with him. Flowering, namely, in virtues. She is also the house of God in which he dwelt. Its beams are her chief virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. Its ceiling is her good works. She herself is also a field, namely, unploughed land, untouched by a man, or humble.

## CHAPTER II

“I am the flower of the field.” Her flower is her Son; she herself is “the lily of the valleys,” that is, the adornment of humble parents. “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among daughters”: that is, as the lily surpasses thistles and nettles in beauty and sweetness, so Mary surpasses all churches in the beauty of chastity and the sweetness of holiness. “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest,” so was Christ among all the prophets and apostles, shading her with the Holy Spirit from every carnal delight. “I sat under his shadow whom I desired”: that is, I have now come into rest, to the vision of him, where sun and moon marvel at his beauty. “His fruit is sweet to my throat,” that is, his glory is sweet to my soul. For I now behold this, because the King of glory brought me into the wine chamber, that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem. There he ordered love within me, so that him whom formerly I loved as a son I now love as God.

“Support me with flowers; surround me with apples.” By flowers are understood the innocent; by apples, that is, domestic trees, other saints. She who is innocent is exalted by the innocent; she who is holier is glorified by the saints. She languishes with love because she desires continually to gaze upon God. “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.” That is, heavenly and earthly things magnify her. “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,” that is, I bind you by the sacrament of my incarnation, O souls of the faithful—speaking through the gazelles and stags of the fields, that is, through the prophets and apostles, teachers of peoples—“do not awaken my beloved,” that is, do not disturb my mother by any perverse doctrine, until she herself wills it: namely, as the prophets and apostles taught, that the Virgin bore God and man. “The voice of my beloved,” namely, my Son, commanded these things which I have said—he who leaped from the bosom of the Father into his mother’s womb. “Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills.” He who leaps is now above, now below. Christ came to the Virgin as if leaping, because in divinity he surpasses the mountains, that is, the angels in heaven; in humanity, he surpasses the hills, that is, the apostles on earth. From heaven he leaped into the Virgin’s womb, thence into the world, then into hell, and again into heaven.

“My beloved Son is like a gazelle,” which chooses good herbs from bad; so he chooses the good from the perverse; “and like a young stag,” which rests in the shade; so he rested in the chaste Virgin. “Behold, he stands behind our wall.” The wall is our mortality. Christ stood behind the wall when he took mortal flesh from the Virgin. [Col. 0503A] We lay crushed beneath the wall because we were naturally mortal.

But he stood not beneath, but behind the wall, because he was mortal by will, not by nature. He stood in order to thrust down the wall, that is, to destroy mortality. “Looking through the windows”: born of the Virgin, he looked upon the world when he was made known to men through the apostles. He also looked through the lattices, because he was revealed through the writings of the prophets.

The blessed Virgin herself was also the window of heaven through which the Sun of righteousness shone into the house of the world. My beloved, namely my Son, speaks to me: “Arise from mortal life; hasten to immortality, my friend,” that is, my confidante, “fair in chastity, and come to the joys of heaven. For now the winter of your anguish on my account has passed; the rain of your tribulations has gone; all pain has wholly departed. The flowers,” that is, your rewards, “have appeared in our land,” that is, shine in the land of the living. “The time of pruning,” of every evil from you, “and of your recompense, has come. The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land,” that is, the voice of exultation and joy is continually heard in the dwellings of the righteous. “The fig tree,” since you were fruitful, “has produced its first figs,” that is, good works, for which you will be rewarded. “The vines,” that is, churches flourishing in virtues by your examples, “have given forth the fragrance” of good works, for which you too will be crowned. “Arise from temporal misery, my friend,” in humility; “my beautiful one,” in chastity; “and come to eternal rewards, my dove,” that is, simply trusting “in the openings of the rock,” that is, in my wounds which I endured for your deliverance; “in the hollow of the wall,” that is, believing the sentence of Holy Scripture, which says: “God himself will come and save us” (Isa. 35:4); and again: “By whose bruise we are healed” (Isa. 53:5). For as a wall protects a vineyard, so Holy Scripture fortifies the Church. This Virgin recalled when she saw him pierced by nails.

“Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears.” By face is understood the beauty of her glory; by the sound of her voice, her praise by angels. “For your voice is sweet,” that is, your praise among angels is very great; “and your face is beautiful,” that is, your glory is supreme. “Catch for us the little foxes.” Little foxes are heretics, who destroy vineyards, that is, poison the churches of the simple with their venom, saying: [Col. 0503D] “If a virgin gave birth, it was a phantom.” They are caught as in a net when they are concluded by this syllogism: God can do all that he wills; he willed to be born of a Virgin; therefore that which the Virgin bore was God and man. “For our vineyard has flowered,” that is, Mary bore Christ. My beloved Son spoke to me thus, as I have said, and I give thanks to him who feeds among lilies, that is, delights among the ranks of armies, until the day of eternity breathes and the shadows of this temporality decline.

### The Virgin’s prayer for converts

O my beloved, whom I bore, who fled the incestuous: now return to penitents and be like a gazelle, separating the chaste from the incestuous. Or make yourself like a swiftly running young stag, swiftly receiving the vows and prayers of those converted from perversity; and establish them upon mountains, that is, lofty in virtues, in the house of the Lord, namely, the Church. The Mother of God herself is also Bethel, that is, the house of God, in which the Son of God dwelt. Her mountains are the prophets who foretold her. They are also the apostles who preached concerning her. What she herself thinks through the Spirit concerning Christ she declares in these words:

## CHAPTER III

“On my bed,” that is, in the repose of my contemplation, “by night,” that is, in this life, “I sought”—understand, the divinity of Christ—“him whom my soul loves.” I sought to know him in his Godhead and did not find him, that is, I could not reach his height. And I said: “I will arise,” in heart to heavenly things, “and in mind I will go around the city,” that is, the hosts of angels, “through streets and squares,” that is, through angels and archangels; “I shall seek Christ whom my soul loves.” I sought him among the orders of angels and found none of them like him. “The watchmen found me,” that is, the angels who guard the city, that is, the Church. There is no doubt that angels frequently held conversation with the sacred Virgin. And I asked them: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” that is, tell me whether at least you understand Christ’s divinity. They said, “A little.” Although angels understand much concerning God, yet in comparison with Truth himself it seems little. For no angel understands God as he knows himself. For: “No one knows the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27), which he is believed to have done for his Mother.

“When I had passed beyond them,” that is, when I had surpassed their nature in contemplation, “I found him whom my soul loves,” far surpassing all the understanding of angels. I held him by believing him equal to the Father, and I shall not let him go by loving him, until I introduce him by word and example into the house, that is, the Church, of my mother, that is, grace, and into the chamber of my mother who bore me, that is, into the assembly of the Synagogue. That is to say: What I have learned concerning Christ through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, I proclaim to Jews and Gentiles.

### [The body (?) concerning the Virgin, addressed to the teachers]

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, not to awaken my beloved,” as was said above. This is repeated here: let nothing frivolous be preached concerning her by teaching anything against her. There follows the praise of the angels when they came to meet her, seeking the heavenly kingdoms: “Who”—that is, how glorious—“is this who ascends to the palaces of heaven through the desert,” that is, leaving the dangerous world? She is “a little rod,” that is, a straight rule, “of smoke from spices,” namely, contrition and diverse virtues: myrrh, that is, martyrs; frankincense, that is, confessors; and every powder of the perfumer, that is, all Christ’s faithful. For he himself is the true perfumer, that is, physician of souls. The congregation of the righteous is the collection of his herbs. To all these the Virgin was the seasoning of virtues, like precious aromatic powder.

What follows seems to be words of the Church concerning the assumption of Mary’s body. “Behold Solomon’s bed; sixty mighty men surround it.” The body of the Blessed Virgin is the bed of the true Peacemaker, namely Christ. Sixty mighty men, that is, many thousands from the strongest of Israel—that is, the highest angels who truly see God—surround it and bring it to the heavens. All hold swords, that is, safeguards against the devil; and are most skilled for battle, namely most powerful against the powers of the air. Each one’s sword, that is, protection, is upon his thigh, that is, around the body whose thigh bore Christ, because of nocturnal terrors, that is, lest demons strike her with terrors.

There follow the words of teachers teaching concerning her. “King Solomon made for himself a litter.” Christ, the true King of peace, made for himself a litter, that is, a couch for a banquet, “from the wood of Lebanon,” that is, he chose the Virgin from patriarchs and kings; in her he reclined as upon a couch, himself set for the banquet, because believers feast on the flesh which he took from the Virgin. “Its pillars he made of silver.” The pillars supporting the Virgin’s life are the four Gospels written concerning her, silver in truth, namely bright and resonant in preaching. “Its back was of gold.” This was the Lord’s body taken from her, upon which divinity reclined. It was golden, namely adorned with wisdom and love. The Virgin herself was also the back, into whose womb Christ reclined; golden, shining with the splendor of chastity. “Its ascent was purple.” This was the holy cross, on which by his passion her Son made for us an ascent to heaven. “Its midst he paved with love,” that is, he filled their common life with the sweetness of love, for the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, for believers to imitate. Therefore, daughters of Zion, that is, souls who are daughters of the Church, go forth from your carnal way of life and see with the eyes of the heart King Solomon, that is, Christ the true Peacemaker, “in the diadem with which his mother crowned him,” that is, in the mortal flesh with which his mother, Mary, clothed him, “on the day of his marriage,” namely the day of his birth, when he espoused the Church; or on the day of his passion, when he laid down his life for her; “and on the day of the joy of his heart,” that is, on the day of his resurrection. Then the same Virgin and the apostles were made as joyful as they had previously been sorrowful over his death.

## CHAPTER IV

### The Son’s praise of his Mother

O my friend, to whom I made known the secrets of the Father: how beautiful you are in humility and chastity! How beautiful you are in faith and action, and therefore fair in heavenly glory! Your eyes are simple like those of doves, which, looking upon other birds, do not desire to tear them apart; so you, seeing young men, did not desire to join yourself to them in obscene embraces—apart from that which lies hidden within, namely love. The eyes of the Virgin are the prophets who foresaw her long beforehand and foretold many things concerning her. Her eyes are the apostles, who displayed her great deeds and her Son’s miracles to the people. They were doves because, full of the Holy Spirit, they lived simply. The blessed Virgin herself is also the eye of the dove, because she is the guiding leader of the Church, apart from that sweet affection which lies hidden within, in the sight of God alone.

Your hair was not curled so that the minds of young men might be enticed by it. The Virgin’s hair is chaste persons, because they adhere to her religion as hair to the head. These are like flocks of goats which climb to the heights. So they ascend from virtue to virtue to Gilead, namely to Christ, the mountain of our testimony. Your teeth were not devourers of delicate food. The Virgin’s teeth are those who bring forth subtle explanations concerning her. They are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing, because they have been washed in baptism and stripped themselves of worldly goods for Christ. “All with twin births,” that is, full of a twofold love, “and none barren among them,” that is, no one empty of good action.

Your lips were not deceitful, but drawn tight by the mortification of the flesh from vanity, like a scarlet ribbon; and your speech is sweet, because it is wholly about God and the future rest. The Virgin’s lips are also those who disclose to others God’s secrets concerning her; her speech is their preaching. Your cheeks were ashamed before men, avoiding their company, apart from that modesty which lies hidden within the heart. As a fragment of pomegranate is red outside and white within, so you were red in suffering and white in chastity. Her cheeks are also virgins who are ashamed to sin. Your neck was not stretched out in pride; therefore David, namely Christ, made you a tower, that is, the defense of the Church. The Virgin’s neck also consists of those writing concerning her, who, as a neck swallows food, swallow the food of God’s word and transmit it to others as to the body. These are like David’s tower, impregnable to heretics, built with battlements, that is, furnished with many sayings. A thousand shields hang from it, namely the defense of Holy Scripture—every weapon of the mighty for overthrowing the perversity of heretics attacking the holy Virgin.

Your breasts were not touched by the hand of that man; therefore the young stag who feeds among lilies, namely Christ, who delights in the chaste, sucked them. The Virgin’s two breasts are the two laws which are written in praises concerning her and her Son. “Two young twins of a gazelle” are the two peoples of the Church, eagerly drawing from Holy Scripture the milk of sayings concerning holy Mary. They feed among lilies, that is, delight in the Scriptures, until the day breathes—that is, until Christ comes—when they see the glory of the Mother of God, and the shadows decline, that is, when the things they now behold in a riddle pass away.

By the following words Christ calls his Mother to heavenly things: “I shall go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.” That is to say: I shall come with a multitude of angels to summon the Queen of Heaven, who is a mountain of myrrh—that is, of martyrs, who are myrrh, that is, height—and a hill of frankincense—that is, of confessors, who are frankincense, that is, loftiness. And I shall speak to her these words: “My friend, who bore the Father’s secrets, you are wholly beautiful, because in each of your senses, as I have said, you are gracious through virtues. And because there is no stain of sin in you, come from Lebanon,” that is, from the whiteness of chastity, “to the joys of heaven. You are my bride because I am one with the Father, whose Son you bore while remaining closed. Come from Lebanon,” namely from the brightness of holy life, “to be greatly exalted in the banquet-hall of the heavenly citizens. Come to spiritual joys. You shall be crowned from Mount Amana”: that is, you shall receive the crown which you merited in triumph over the devil, who is Mount Amana, which is a nocturnal bird—that is, he is “king over all the children of pride” (Job 41:25), leading the erring to the night of death. “You shall be crowned also from the summit of Senir and Hermon”: namely, because the rulers of the world were humbled through the fruit of your womb; they had been the dens of lions, that is, the dwelling place of demons, and mountains of leopards, that is, strongholds of heretics.

“You wounded my heart”: that is, for love of you I endured on the cross the torment of wounds. “My sister,” because you are co-heir in the kingdom of the Father; “my bride,” because you bore me for God the Father. “You wounded my heart”: that is, I was inwardly touched by pain when, hanging on the cross, I saw you grieving. “With one of your eyes,” that is, with one maternal affection—eyes, that is, good examples—“and with one hair of your neck,” that is, with one ornament of humility by which you clung to me as the neck to the head.

There follows the Son’s praise offered to his Mother as she arrives at the house of his Father.

“How beautiful are your breasts,” namely humility and chastity, from which the sobriety of virgins sucked the milk of holiness. Therefore, sister, that is, co-heir in the kingdom, and bride, because by your example you bore virgins to me. “Your breasts are more beautiful than wine.” The Virgin’s breasts were examples in the active and contemplative life, by which, as with milk, she fed little ones in faith. These were more beautiful than wine, that is, worthier than legal teaching. “And the fragrance of your garments above all spices”: that is, the sweetness of your breasts is more acceptable than the sacrifice of carnal observances.

### The Father’s praise of the Virgin

“Your lips, O bride, drip honeycomb.” He called her bride because she bore the Son for him. Her lips are those who disclose God’s secrets concerning her; they drip like honeycomb because all their words concerning her overflow with sweetness. “Honey and milk are under your tongue.” The Virgin’s tongue denotes those who proclaim her praises, from whom honey and milk flow because their teaching satisfies the wise and the unlearned. “And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.” The fragrance of her garments consists in those converted through the renown of her examples, who are frankincense to God: that is, their prayer rises like incense.

### Again, Christ concerning his Mother

“A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride.” She was a garden of herbs or trees, that is, full of virtues; enclosed in childbirth, namely by the seal of the Holy Spirit. “A garden enclosed” again, because after childbirth the seal of virginity was not opened. “A sealed fountain.” She too was a fountain, that is, the first example of virginity. This fountain was sealed, that is, consecrated by Christ’s passion. “Your streams” [Col. 0508A]—that is, your imitators—“are a paradise of diverse trees.” Some are pomegranates, namely martyrs; some fruit trees, namely confessors; some cypress, healing others by the ointment of their examples; some nard, that is, the humble; others saffron, red with love; others reed, mortifying vices; others cinnamon, penitents; and all the trees of Lebanon, that is, all Christ’s faithful. “From you flowed the fountain of gardens,” that is, through you came the baptism of believers; “and a well of living waters,” that is, Christ, who is the wisdom of the Holy Scriptures. And these flow from Lebanon with great force, because they overflowed from the brightness of your holiness with the abundance of the Holy Spirit. Whence comes all this? Because God the Father commanded such things, saying: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden”: that is, let the north wind—the Devil—have no place to tempt you; but let the south wind—the Holy Spirit—possess you, my garden. “And let its spices flow,” that is, let my Only-begotten be incarnate through you.

## CHAPTER V

There follow the words of the Virgin, desiring Christ to come into her.

“Let my beloved,” that is, Christ, “come into me, his garden, and eat the fruit of his fruits,” that is, incorporate into himself the service of my works.

Words of Christ applauding his Mother: “O my sister,” co-heir in the Father’s glory, “spouse” of the Father, because you bore me. “I came into you, my garden,” by assuming flesh. “I gathered my myrrh,” gathering martyrs by my passion, “with my spices,” that is, with confessors. “I ate my honeycomb with my honey.” By the honeycomb Christ’s body is understood; by the honey, his soul. For he ate the honeycomb with honey when, rising again, he joined to his soul—never thereafter to die—the body taken from the Virgin. “I drank my wine with my milk.” By milk, human beings are understood; by wine, angels. He drank wine with milk when, ascending in the human flesh born of the Virgin, he joined human beings to angels. To them he immediately says in rejoicing: “Eat, friends, and be intoxicated, beloved ones”; that is to say: As diners delight in various dishes and rejoice at the presence of friends, so you, my angelic friends, rejoice and exult, because I have increased your joy by a numerous multitude of human beings. Moreover, I have bestowed new festivals, when I brought my mother—your queen indeed—into your joys.

By what follows, the Virgin consoles the Church, still labouring here: “I sleep,” that is, I rest in glory, “and my heart watches,” praying for you. “The voice of my beloved,” namely, my Son, “is knocking,” that is, admonishing me thus: “Open to me,” that is, obtain from me by your prayers a just ground for showing mercy to all: “my sister,” now in the Father’s glory; “my friend,” bearing divine mysteries; “my dove,” filled with the Holy Spirit; “my undefiled one,” separated from every stain of sin; “because my head is full of dew, and my locks,” that is, my elect, “are mingled with the perverse.” Just as drops falling upon the head run down from the hair, so the reprobate, coming to faith but acting wickedly, are drawn back through “the night,” that is, the devil.

The Virgin continues: If you do not wish my prayers to be rendered vain, you ought to imitate me in these things. “I have put off my garment,” that is, I have left worldly things behind; and I said, “How shall I put it on?” that is, I shall never return to them. “I have washed my feet,” that is, I have purified my affections; and I said, “How shall I defile them?” that is, I shall not return to the vomit by entertaining fleshly enticements. Therefore my beloved, namely God, whom I chose before all others, “put forth his hand,” that is, sent his Son into the world, “through the opening,” namely through me, who became for him the opening through which he came to human beings—narrow indeed by humility, but bright by chastity, and therefore passable for him alone. “And my belly trembled at his touch,” that is, it was astonished at his entrance.

“I arose,” that is, I raised my mind upward, in order to open to my beloved by prayers, so that I might appease him on behalf of humankind; and I joined works to prayer. “My hands dripped with myrrh,” that is, my deeds abounded in the mortification of the flesh. “And my fingers were full of the finest myrrh,” that is, my efforts were proved by various tribulations. In this way I opened to my beloved, namely my Son, “the bolt of my door.” Here the grammar is intransitive in my signification. For the holy Virgin was the door through which Christ entered the world; but the bolt was the mass of human sins, which is called hers because she too is believed to have been born in sins. She removed this from the door when, by holy living, she avoided sins. Or he enters with the beloved, because through her mercy came into the Church. Hence it follows: “And he had turned aside through me,” and had passed into the Church; daily he removes the bolt of sins by prayers, and through her the entrance of Christ’s grace lies open to us.

“My soul melted” in compunction, when the beloved spoke of the wondrous and desirable vision of the Father. “I sought him” by thought, and found his greatness of flesh weighed down by a cloud. “I called” with intense longing, and he did not answer me by showing the majesty of his divinity. “The watchmen who went around the city,” that is, who fortify God’s Church, found me while I was seeking through contemplation; they struck me with grief when they said that they themselves did not know God perfectly, and they wounded me because they kindled me more ardently toward the endeavour of seeking. “The guardians of the walls,” that is, the prophets and apostles, teachers through books, “took away my cloak,” that is, taught me to put off the life of the flesh.

“O daughters of Jerusalem,” namely faithful souls, for whom I diligently pour out prayers, “I adjure you by my example: if you find my beloved Son, equal to the Father, through contemplation, tell him,” that is, make yourselves known to him by good works, so that, as I languished with love for him, you too may endure every hardship for his love.

The Church’s praise to the Virgin concerning Christ follows.

“What is your beloved beyond a beloved?” that is, how magnificent is your Son, begotten from the Father’s womb, “most beautiful among women,” that is, blessed among every race of mothers. “What is your beloved beyond a beloved?” that is, how glorious is your Son from the Father’s bosom? Therefore we seek him by faith and works, because you have so adjured us, that is, taught us by word and example.

The Virgin’s praise of her Son.

“My beloved Son is white,” that is, born through a virgin; “ruddy” through his passion; “chosen from thousands,” namely before angels and holy beings. “His head is the finest gold”: just as gold surpasses all metals, so his divinity surpasses all things. Or Christ is the head of the Church, which he adorns as gold with his splendour. “His locks are like lofty palms,” namely crowned with thorns for our victory, “black as a raven,” that is, counted among criminals. Christ’s locks also are those adhering to him as to their head, flourishing like a palm in virtues, and black as a raven, namely darkened by tribulations after Christ’s example.

“His eyes are like doves,” shining with the fullness of the Holy Spirit. For by the dove the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is understood, which is said to be active in seven natures. Hence it also appeared over the Lord in the form of a dove. Christ’s eyes also are the doctors of the Church, full of the gift of the Holy Spirit, and this “beside streams of water,” that is, in the knowledge of the Scriptures; “washed with milk,” that is, whose souls are cleansed by the brightness of virtues; “and seated beside most abundant waters,” that is, conversing through the most plentiful gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“His cheeks are like beds of spices,” because he was pleasing to the eyes of all who looked upon him. His cheeks likewise are the modest, who are like beds of spices, that is, planted with a collection of virtues and cultivated by perfumers, that is, adorned with apostolic teachings. “His lips are like sayings,” delightful as lilies, comely with the whiteness of chastity, “dripping the first myrrh,” that is, teaching mortification through love. His lips are those who disclose his will, and who drip the first myrrh because they preach the chief works of charity.

“His hands are rounded,” or “turned,” “of gold,” that is, his works are complete in their perfection and shine with every grace, “full of hyacinths,” that is, virtues. His hands also are those doing good, who are rounded and golden, that is, perfect in character and conspicuous in goodness, full of hyacinths, that is, almsgiving.

“His belly is ivory,” that is, the frailty of his humanity is chaste because he was born of a virgin; and therefore it is like ivory taken from the elephant, which is said to be a most chaste animal; “adorned with sapphires,” that is, varied by heavenly signs. Christ’s belly also consists of the weak in the Church, who are ivory, that is, chaste, adorned with sapphires, that is, varied by a pure conscience.

“His legs are marble columns,” that is, his beautiful firmness in the resurrection, which is the unbreakable support of the Church; “founded upon bases of gold,” that is, upon faith and charity. His legs also are those strong in righteousness and supporting others by example; they are marble columns, that is, upright and unbending before vices, founded upon golden bases, that is, steadfast in evangelical and apostolic teaching.

“His appearance is like Lebanon,” that is, he is the beauty of all saints, just as Lebanon is the ornament of all mountains; and as cedars excel all trees, so he is chosen before all holy angels. “His throat,” that is, his teaching or promise, is most sweet; and he is altogether desirable in humanity and divinity. Hence even angelic sublimity is insatiable in the sight of him. Such, as I have said, is my beloved Son, and he is now my friend in the Father’s glory, O daughters of Jerusalem, namely the Church of the faithful.

The Church to the Virgin.

“Where has your beloved gone,” who is wholly everywhere, “O most beautiful among women?” that is, holier than all mothers. “Where has your beloved turned aside,” whom no place contains? Tell us whether he comes more familiarly to any, and, imitating you in faith and works, we shall seek him with you.

## CHAPTER VI

The Virgin’s response follows.

“My beloved,” whom the whole world cannot contain with the Father, taking flesh from me, descended from the Father’s bosom “to his garden,” that is, the Church, to gather virtues; “to feed in the gardens,” that is, to delight in the fruitful; “and to gather lilies,” that is, the chaste into eternal granaries. I pleased my beloved for this work, and my beloved pleases me before all others. He “feeds among the lilies,” that is, delights among the companies of the chaste, and thus spoke gently to me: “You are beautiful” in chastity, and therefore “my friend,” sweet through pious examples; and therefore beautiful in heavenly glory like Jerusalem, that is, like the angels who see the Father’s face and enjoy the Lord’s peace; terrible against vices like an army drawn up against heretics and demons.

“Turn away your eyes from me, because they have made me turn away”; that is to say: Delight in my humanity, for you cannot approach my divinity perfectly; the more subtly you behold it with the eyes of your mind, the more you will see it to be remote from your condition. “Your hair was not braided with gold,” and therefore it is now encircled with the angels’ diadem. Her hair also is the virgins who adhere to her in imitation; they are like a flock of goats ascending to the heights of virtues, “which appeared from Gilead,” that is, who do this as a witness for Christ.

“Your teeth were not accustomed to voracity,” and therefore they now delight in God’s sweetness. Her teeth also are those who explain subtle matters concerning her; they are like flocks of sheep shorn of sins, as though they had come up from the washing of baptism. All have twin offspring, that is, are full of twofold love; none among them is barren, that is, idle in good work. As the rind of a pomegranate is red, so are your cheeks, that is, your outward modesty shines in chastity, apart from your hidden things, namely the charity concealed within.

“There are sixty queens,” that is, many souls who rule their own minds in the active life through the six works of mercy; “and eighty concubines,” that is, many labour in the contemplative life to bind themselves in the embraces of the bridegroom, so that they may attain the eight beatitudes; “and maidens without number,” that is, the people of the faithful living beneath them. You alone surpassed the merits of all, and therefore alone are chosen before all. “My dove,” into whom I poured the charisms of the Holy Spirit; “my perfect one,” whom I made perfect by the gifts of virtues. She is the one imitable by her mother, namely the present Church; chosen by her parent, namely the multitude of angels.

The daughters of Zion, that is, of the Church, saw her with the eyes of the heart and declared her most blessed, as it is said: “All generations shall call me blessed” (Luke 1:48). And the queens and concubines, that is, the active and contemplative, praised her, saying: “Who is this?” that is, what manner of woman is this who comes forth from the sinful mass, like dawn rising out of darkness, from whom proceeds the Sun of righteousness to illumine those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death? In the present life she is beautiful as the moon in the night; in the heavenly homeland she is chosen as the sun among the stars; formidable by her examples against vices, like an army drawn up against demons.

Because the Virgin said that the beloved had descended into the garden, the Son adds in confirmation: “I descended from the Father’s bosom into you, the garden of nuts, through the material of flesh.” Nuts are all the faithful: outwardly bitter through the affliction of the flesh, inwardly sweet in the soul. Through the Virgin’s childbirth, this became a fruitful garden, in which Christ, the tree of life, sprang forth when he bore the fruit of eternity in its season. I did this “to see the fruits of the valleys,” that is, to reward the works of the humble who live after your example; “and to see whether the vines had blossomed,” that is, to make the vineyards, namely the churches, behold your life and blossom in good deeds after your example; “and whether the pomegranates had budded,” that is, so that through the example of your patience they might desire to undergo suffering for me.

The words of the penitent Church, at some time to be converted from the Jews, follow.

She grieves that she so long erred concerning the Virgin and her offspring, and makes satisfaction for her error in these words: “I did not know,” glorious Virgin, that you were full of grace and that the fountain of grace flowed from you. “My soul troubled me,” that is, the zeal for the Law which I held to be my soul taught me to do this; and this happened because of “the chariots of Amminadab,” that is, because Christ’s Gospels, rejected—or rather driven away—by me, rushed through the regions of the world. “Return, return, O Shulammite,” long captive to the devil: return through faith to Christ’s mysteries; return through hope; return through love of God and neighbour; return through action, so that those who are now in Christ may behold you by imitating your words and deeds.

## CHAPTER VII

Christ speaks to his Mother concerning the Church to be converted.

“What will you see in the Shulammite but the dances of camps?” That is to say: In the Church to be converted from the Jews, nothing will be seen but a chorus praising God and an army fighting against vices.

Praise of the Church to be converted concerning the Virgin.

“How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince.” Prince David the king is understood, who is read to have been a prince among God’s people; and because the Virgin descends from his seed, she is called his daughter. Her steps are her affections, which will be beautiful in sandals, that is, in the examples of the saints. “The joints of your thighs are like necklaces”; that is to say, your thighs are blessed, from which came forth the precious pearl, namely Christ, the priceless necklace, who is the garden of the whole creation, “made by the hand of an artificer.” The artificer is God the Father; his hand is the Son, through whom he made all things and through whom the incarnation too was ordained.

“Your navel”—understand, blessed—in which the Son of God hung. For as a shield hangs on a slope, so the infant hangs upon the breasts. This Son is “a rounded bowl never lacking drink,” that is, he offers abundant draughts of inward taste to all who thirst. Your womb also is blessed, in which lies hidden the incarnate only-begotten Son of God; he was wheat, from which the bread of the faithful is made. He is also a heap, because in him the people of believers are gathered together; “surrounded by lilies,” that is, encircled by choirs of virgins.

“Your two breasts”—understand, blessed—because God’s wisdom sucked them. The roe is the Church. The two fawns are the two peoples of the faithful, from circumcision and uncircumcision; they sucked milk, humility and chastity, by imitating the breasts of the blessed Virgin. Your neck is blessed, often encircled by the arm of the Son of God embracing you; and therefore it is like a tower of ivory, because it is firmly fortified by chastity against pride. Your eyes are blessed, because they saw what kings and prophets did not deserve to see.

Or the Virgin’s eyes are the words of her teaching, which are like pools in Heshbon, that is, leading to the sorrow of repentance, as she said: “His mercy is from generation to generation upon those who fear him” (Luke 1:50), namely the penitent. And these are “at the gate of the daughter of the multitude.” The gate is the perpetual Virgin, through whom, while she remained closed, the King of heaven entered the world to us. And she belongs to the daughter of the multitude, because through her the multitude of the faithful will enter the palace of heaven.

Your nose is blessed, because it perceived Christ, the fragrance of eternal life. Or her nose was her foreknowledge, because by the Spirit she discerned the sayings of the prophets to be fulfilled in herself. “The tower of Lebanon,” that is, she was Christ’s defence, “which looks toward Damascus,” that is, stands erect against the devil. Your head is blessed, which you so often bent in order to kiss the Son of God, “like Carmel,” that is, circumspect in virtues. The locks of your head are blessed, which Christ as an infant wished to touch with his divine hands. And they are like royal purple, because you tore them in grief at the time of his passion. And all these things are “joined to channels,” that is, fixed in the hearts of believers.

When Christ praised his mother, he began from her head; but the Church’s praise began from her foot, because Christ came from the heights to the depths in order to raise his mother to the heights, while the Church climbs to what is high through the Virgin’s merits.

The Son’s praise follows.

O dearest Mother, how beautiful you are in chastity, and therefore lovely in heavenly glory! And because you are dearest to me because of these things, you therefore enjoy heavenly desire. “Your stature is likened to a palm tree.” Christ was a palm upon the cross, because through him the palm of victory is obtained. Her stature, that is, Mary’s lofty glory, is likened to it, because as he is King of heaven, so she is Queen of angels. “And your breasts to clusters,” that is, your merits are likened to martyrs, who were pressed like clusters in their sufferings.

And therefore it came to pass because I said, that is, because I ordained this with the Father: “I shall assume flesh from a Virgin. I shall ascend the palm,” that is, the cross; “I shall seize its fruits; I shall draw all things to myself.” “Then your breasts shall be like a cluster of the vine,” that is, your merits will be imitable by all, like my Gospels; for I am the cluster of the vine, namely the drink of the Church. This is the cluster which the children of Israel bore upon a pole (Num. 13:25). The pole was the cross; the cluster was Christ; the bearers were the apostles and prophets.

The vine from which the cluster was borne was the flowering body of the Virgin; this cluster was pressed in the winepress of the cross, and from it flowed the drink of the faithful. “Your fragrances are like apples,” that is, your examples are to be imitated like those of the apostles. “Your throat is like the best wine.” Good wine is legal instruction; better is evangelical learning; best is the infusion of the Holy Spirit. The Virgin’s throat is her teaching, inspired by the Holy Spirit, which is like wine to drink, that is, pleasing to imitate. For she said: “He scattered the proud; he exalted the humble” (Luke 1:51–52).

He applauds her praise, saying: It is fitting for my beloved to do this, namely, “to spare the subject and subdue the proud.” “To be chewed by his lips and teeth.” God’s lips are those who disclose his will; his teeth are those who crush vices. By these the Virgin’s teaching is to be chewed over, that is, committed to memory: namely, that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (1 Pet. 5:5).

In what follows, the Virgin recounts the words which she addressed to the Son for the Church to be converted from the Jews. “I poured out prayers to my beloved for you, and his conversion is toward me,” that is, through me he willed to turn toward you in mercy. Thus indeed I said: “Come, my beloved, to the Synagogue in mercy, because you fled from her because of the guilt of unbelief. Let us go out through faith into the field,” namely into the whole world; “let us remain through action in the villages,” that is, among all nations. “Let us rise early for the vineyards,” that is, for the synagogues of the Jews; let us make that last imminent dawn shine in their hearts. “Let us see whether the vines have blossomed,” that is, let us make them see in mind how the Church has flowered in faith. “Whether the flowers bear fruit,” that is, let us make them see how they have shone through martyrdoms. “There I shall give you my breasts,” that is, in honour of you they will imitate my examples.

It should be noted that *if* is said three times; that is, if they see these things, they will imitate them in thought, speech, and action. “The mandrakes,” that is, the Gentiles, who like headless mandrakes were without God, “gave the fragrance of good works at our gates,” that is, in virtues. And because now the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, it is now time for eternal Israel to be saved; “for you, my beloved, I have kept all fruits, new and old.” That is to say: When they are converted, they will keep all the commandments of the New and Old Testaments in honour of you.

## CHAPTER VIII

“Who will give you to me as my brother,” born from the Jewish people, “sucking the breasts of my mother,” that is, nurtured under the Law in the Synagogue, “so that I may find you outside,” that is, so that I may see you worshipped by the Jews who are still outside the faith, “and kiss you,” that is, behold you loved by them; “and no one may now despise me,” namely no Jew who does not believe that I remained a virgin. “I shall take hold of you,” that is, I shall prove that you took flesh from me without a man’s seed; “and lead you through faith into the house of my mother,” that is, into the body of the Synagogue itself, “and into the chamber of my parent,” that is, into the understanding of the Jewish Law. “There you will teach me” to be worshipped by them and to keep the Lord’s commandments. “And I shall give you a cup,” that is, good work will be offered to you by those imitating me, “of spiced wine,” namely wisdom and charity making others drunk, “and new wine of my pomegranates,” that is, divine service filled with virtues. “His left hand is beneath my head,” that is, they will despise temporal things for Christ, who is my head; “and his right hand will embrace me,” that is, prompted by him, they will seek heavenly things alone.
