The Son, on behalf of his Mother, addresses the Church newly converted from the Jews.

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not awaken my beloved,” that is, do not think anything sinister concerning my mother the Virgin. This is repeated a third time to teach how great a veneration the Mother of God deserves.

Praise of the Church converted from the Jews, admiring the Virgin’s glory, follows.

“Who is this?” that is, how great or how worthy is she who, virtuous, ascends from the desert of the world, abounding in heaven’s delights, “leaning upon her beloved,” that is, exalted so greatly above the choirs of angels?

The Son recounts to his mother the perversity of the Jews and indicates the manner of life of those who will one day be converted. “Under the apple tree I raised you up,” that is, redeeming you on the cross, I exalted you above the heavens. “There your mother,” namely the Synagogue, “was corrupted,” cursing me with her own mouth as she crucified me, when she said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). “There your parent was violated,” that is, the Law was transgressed by them, which says: “Do not put the righteous man to death” (Dan. 13:53).

But now, because they turn to me with their whole heart: “Set me as a seal upon your heart,” that is, imprint my image upon their hearts through love; “as a seal upon your arm,” that is, imprint the example of me through action; “for love is strong as death,” that is, just as they formerly deserved death through unbelief, so now through love may they find life. “Jealousy is hard as hell,” that is, just as they formerly fell into hell because of hardness, so now through the correction of vices they will enter heaven. “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flames,” that is, those among them who possess charity will burn with the fire of the Holy Spirit and shine with good works.

I tell you that “many waters,” that is, worldly pleasures or riches, could not extinguish their love; nor did “rivers,” that is, every kind of tribulation, overwhelm it. “If a man gives all the substance of his house for love, he will despise it as nothing”; that is, if anyone offers them all the glory of the world, he will not be able to separate them from Christ’s charity.

The Virgin’s concern for the Church from the Jews follows.

“Our sister, the Synagogue,” to be joined with us by faith in the Father’s inheritance, to be counted among our fellow citizens, “is little and has no breasts,” that is, no preaching from which she may draw an example of life. “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken with?” That is, what will become of the Synagogue at the time when Enoch and Elijah shall preach to her?

Christ’s consolation to the Virgin.

“If she is a wall, let us build upon her”; that is, I shall build her up in virtues as a wall, fortified on every side against vices. And this through “bulwarks of silver,” that is, Scriptures shining with eloquence. “If she is a door,” that is, I shall make her a door of example to others, so that through her they may enter into life. “Let us fasten it with cedar boards,” that is, I shall adorn her with spiritual children.

The Virgin’s promise.

“I shall be a wall to them”: if they imitate my life, they will be unconquerable by vices; “and your breasts a tower,” that is, through my examples they will be safe in good things. “From the time when I became before him like one finding peace,” that is, from the time when I appeased him for them by prayers and obtained for them his peace and grace, this came to pass because “I was a vineyard to the peaceful one,” namely Christ, because the true vine, the offspring of the blessed, willed to spring up in me. “In that which has peoples,” that is, in my race, which bore the humble, namely the apostles. “He gave it to keepers,” that is, he entrusted this people to the apostles, saying: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, but go to the sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 10:5).

Or he gave me, his vineyard, to guardians when, hanging upon the cross, he said: “Behold your mother” (John 19:27), because the other apostles too supplied her necessities. “A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit”: that is, each faithful person gives all that he has in order to gain Christ, the fruit of this vineyard.

Christ to the faithful.

“My vineyard is before me,” that is, my mother is in my glory. “Your thousand, O peaceful one,” that is, many branches from me the vine will sprout through faith and imitate you in chastity; and therefore they will inherit life, rejoicing in peace. “And two hundred silver pieces to those who keep its fruit,” that is, those who preserve me, the fruit of life, by good works will receive a double reward. “You who dwell in the gardens,” that is, now, O Mother, you are honoured by both; “the friends listen”: all the elect, imitating you, obey me. “Make me hear your voice now,” that is, make known what more you desire.

The Virgin’s supplication for the separation of the righteous from the reprobate follows.

You who in this life lay hidden among good and evil, now flee from the wicked, my beloved, and make yourself like the roe which distinguishes good herbs from bad: so in your judgment separate the reprobate from the elect. And make yourself like the fawn of stags, which is accustomed to rest in the shade. So, passing beyond the chaff, rest among the grains. And do this “upon the mountains of spices,” that is, upon the height of angels, among those who are mountains and spices, because you are in all things all things to these: lofty in merit and fragrant in reward.

Let these things be said concerning the Song of Songs.

Now a few further things ought to be added in honour of the Virgin. But since it is written, “Beautiful praise is not in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9), I do not presume with polluted lips to praise the Mother of the Creator. Finally, the sanctifier and lover of holiness himself proved how worthy she is of praise, judging her worthy of his own garment. Since he chose rather to be born from a Virgin, the reason has now become clear to all: because, just as death entered through a virgin woman, so life ought to enter through a virgin woman. And there was another reason.

God makes human beings in four ways: from earth, as Adam; from a man alone, as Eve; from man and woman, as us; and Christ from woman alone—a privilege reserved for himself. But why, when ascending into heaven, he did not take her with him, but left her here on earth for two years as an example to the faithful, is for this reason: that by the sorrow of his absence she might be tested like gold in fire; that afterward she might be set above the angels in greater excellence; and that heaven too might be gladdened with a new joy when the heavenly citizens festively went forth to meet their queen, the Mother of God.

Her Nativity was not formerly celebrated, but when divinely revealed, it is said to have been celebrated in the following manner. There was a solitary man of holy life who each year heard harmony in heaven on the night of her Nativity. When he wondered why he did not hear this at another time, he began to ask God what it signified. Angels of the Lord appeared to him and related these things: “The perpetual Virgin who bore God was born on this night. Although this is unknown to human beings, it is celebrated by angels in heaven.” When this revelation had been made public, the celebration of her Nativity was established by the Church.

Why the custom arose that flowers and herbs are consecrated on her feast is shown to be for two reasons. One is that her feast is adorned with flowers, because on that day it is sung of her: “Flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys surrounded her.” By roses we understand martyrs; by lilies, virgins; by other flowers or herbs, all saints who are fragrant in goodness. The blessed Virgin Mother of God was both virgin and martyr. Although, therefore, she is greatly glorified by all saints, she is believed to be glorified especially by virgins and martyrs.

The other reason is that, since by right all new fruits ought to be blessed before they are tasted—and this is scarcely observed even in monasteries—the Church decreed that on her feast the first fruits of the crops should be blessed by priests. Why a procession is made on that day is indicated by two reasons. One is that her most holy body—or she herself—was borne for burial with a procession of apostles and other disciples of Christ. The other is that her most blessed spirit was borne heavenward by angels proceeding with the Son of God. Her body afterward, having been raised again, is believed to have been placed in heavenly glory.

That the Church is accustomed to carry candles in its hands on her feast it adopted from the rite of the Gentiles. The Roman Empire had subjected the whole world to itself, and tribute was consequently paid to the Romans by all peoples. When they came, they went around the city with lights in honour of their gods—or rather, demons—because, as they supposed, these had subjected the world to them.

Why they did this in February, when the sign of Aquarius is present, was for this reason. The sign of Aquarius is opposed to the sign of Leo. For six signs are opposed to six others. The philosophers said that souls had been created from eternity and placed in corresponding stars. When, looking down from on high, they saw little bodies being generated in mothers, they desired to become embodied and, through this desire, to fall from the heavenly places. Again the philosophers taught that there were two gates of heaven: one in the sign of Cancer, through which souls went out; the other in the sign of Capricorn, through which they returned. When souls, going out from Cancer, arrived at Leo, there they would begin to descend toward Aquarius, and thus would fall through all the planets and in this manner become embodied. Then, having put off the body through the realm of Pluto, namely the dark realm—Pluto too being worshipped in that same month—they ought to return; and thus, reaching Aquarius, they would regain their former dignity and enter Capricorn, the corresponding star. They therefore carried lights with the intention that afterward a bright passage through dark places might be granted them. These things, indeed, they did while deceived by error.

But we carry them spiritually, by divine ordinance. The whole world is subjected to Christ’s rule; consequently the tribute of divine service is rendered by all. Three things are considered in a candle: light, wax, and wick. The light shines, the wax melts, and the wick vanishes in burning; these signify Christ. The light is his divinity, as he himself said: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). The wax is his humanity, as he likewise said: “I became like melting wax” (Ps. 21:15 [Vulgate]). The wick is his mortality, consumed by the fire of the passion. Because Simeon understood this concerning Christ, he therefore rejoiced while carrying him in his hands and said: “A light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel” (Luke 2:32).

For this signification the Church carries a light in its hands on that day, so that, with the five virgins, having kindled the lamps of virtues through the five senses, after the death of the flesh it may deserve to escape the realms of darkness and, through the most brilliant star, Mary the Mother of God, see in the light of the Father the light who is Christ. Therefore celebrate the Queen of heaven with votive praises, that she may continually intercede for you with her Son, the King of angels, so that after this wretched pilgrimage you may reign with her for ages. Amen.

## APPENDIX TO HONORIUS’ COMMENTARY

### [Col. 0519]

### AN EXPOSITION OF THE SONG OF SONGS BY AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR

### THE PROLOGUE OF THE FOLLOWING WORK BEGINS

### [Col. 0519A]

This is why books of sacred authority have been written not plainly, but as if under a covering. When a bridegroom sends his bride a ring or some little gift, he wraps it in cloth and afterward seals it. He who seals it sees it only in part; the bearer is not permitted to see it. But when she has received it, she unwraps it, unseals it, and sees what has been sent. Christ the bridegroom sent his bride, the Church, a ring—that is, Sacred Scripture—and wrapped it in cloth, that is, in carnal observances. The prophets, in writing, sealed the letter, since they saw future things only in part through the Spirit; but the Jews, its bearers, did not see them at all.

The bride, that is, the Church, receiving it through the key of David—that is, Christ—unsealed it and removed the carnal observances as though they were the cloth.

He saw the hidden gold, that is, spiritual understanding. The Lord showed Moses, when he was placed with Him on the mountain, that Christ would be incarnate, and the future state of the Church [Col. 0519B], and that it itself would be divided into two groups: contemplatives and actives. And He commanded, under this figure, that an ark be made of wood and gold, and a tabernacle fashioned of gold, silver, bronze, hyacinth, purple, scarlet, fine linen, and goats’ hair. The ark made of gold and wood is Christ, existing from divinity and humanity.

The tabernacle is the Church: gold signifies the wise, such as the apostles; silver, the eloquent, such as interpreters; bronze, teachers; hyacinth, those who contemplate heavenly things; purple, martyrs; scarlet, those burning in the love of God; fine linen, confessors or virgins; goats’ hair, penitents.

In the tabernacle there was what is called the holy place, in which the priests ministered; and there was what was called the Holy of Holies, into which the ark was placed. What is called the holy place signifies the active persons, among whom teachers labor; but the Holy of Holies signifies the contemplatives, among whom Christ dwells.

[Col. 0519C] The tabernacle is changed into a house when the Church, taken up from this prison, is placed in the heavenly palace. Foreseeing the future condition of this house, Solomon built the house of the Lord in Jerusalem in seven years, from squared stones, cedar wood, and the purest gold. In its construction neither hammer nor axe was heard.

Solomon is Christ. The temple in Jerusalem is the gathering of the righteous; its building on high is their placement in heaven.

There are three orders in the Church: Noah, Job, and Daniel. Noah signifies teachers; Job, married persons; Daniel, contemplatives.

Therefore squared stones are married persons, squared by the four virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. Prudence is to be skilled and provident in divine and human matters. Fortitude is not to be bent from good to evil either by threats or rewards. Justice is to render to God what is His and to human beings what is theirs. Temperance is not to exceed the proper measure in all these things and to restrain the impulses of the flesh. Cedar woods are teachers, whose works are incorruptible and fragrant [Col. 0520A] in virtues. Gold signifies contemplatives, who shine before God with a pure heart. With these living stones the house in heaven is built in seven years, that is, through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. No hammer is heard there, because there will be neither pain nor death there.

Solomon, therefore, taking material from the tabernacle of the covenant—that is, from the Church’s present condition—and from the temple of the Lord—that is, from its future condition—wrote this book, entitled *Song of Songs*, that is, surpassing all songs. In it he described the betrothal of the Church through Christ’s incarnation; its protection, by which here in Babylon it is guarded by groomsmen; and its final union, by which it is assumed into heaven.

The author of this book is the Holy Spirit; its writer, however, is Solomon. Its subject is the bridegroom and the bride, that is, Christ and the Church, which he divides into friends and female friends, that is, contemplatives and actives. Its intention is to unite to God the soul which has already been made perfect by the love of God. Its final cause and usefulness are that, after reading the book, one may know how to love God and neighbor. The narrative around which the style proceeds is as follows: the son of the king of Jerusalem betrothed to himself the daughter of the king of Babylon through messengers. At last, wearied by these deputations, she replied: “Let your Lord Himself come and tell me what pleases Him.” Coming, he gave her a pledge, commended her to friends and female friends, and went away to prepare the wedding. Returning again with a great army, he led the bride from Babylon into Jerusalem, his own city. Those who treated her badly he thrust into prison; those who treated her honorably he invited with himself to the wedding and made heirs of the kingdom. Jerusalem is the kingdom of heaven; the king of this city is God; His son is Christ; the messengers are the prophets; Babylon is this world; the king of this city is the devil; his daughter is Gentile paganism; the bridegroom’s coming is Christ’s incarnation; the pledge is His blood; spiritual female friends are, for example, bishops; secular female friends, kings and princes. The bridegroom’s departure is Christ’s ascension. His return is the day of judgment; the army, the orders of angels; [Col. 0520C] those treating her badly, heretics and evil Catholics; the prison, hell. Those treating her honorably are good Catholics; the wedding is the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom without end.

Here ends the prologue.

Solomon was called by three names, and according to each one he produced a single volume: namely, *Proverbs* according to the name *Ydida*, that is, “Beloved”; in that work he instructs the untrained and foolish, and thus first comes to be loved by them. *Ecclesiastes*, however, according to the name *Ecclesiastes*, that is, “Preacher,” by which he preached to those whom he had taught in *Proverbs* to possess good morals, so that, knowing worldly things to be transitory, they might despise them. According to the name Solomon, that is, “Peaceful,” he produced the *Song of Songs*, which in Greek is called Ἄσμα ἄσματων, “Song of Songs”; in Hebrew *Sir hasirim* [*Shir ha-Shirim*], “Song of Songs”; and in Latin *Cantica canticorum*, “Song of Songs.” By it he shows those already instructed how to desire God in word and deed. Therefore in *Proverbs* he is called ethical, that is, treating of morals; in *Ecclesiastes*, physical, that is, treating of the nature of things; and in the *Songs*, theological, that is, speaking [Col. 0521A] of divine things—because we assign these matters literally to the former, but spiritually to Solomon himself. For He Himself spoke in *Proverbs* to the untrained; He is especially the Beloved, of whom it was said: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). He likewise is the Preacher, who taught them to despise transient things and strive toward heavenly things. He is the Peaceful One, who, having destroyed the dividing wall, made both one.

IN *PROVERBS* HE IS ENTITLED: “THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON, SON OF DAVID, KING OF ISRAEL, BEGIN.” Likewise, note.

Since he was speaking to many who chose not wisdom but the person, it was necessary to demonstrate his authority. In the *Songs*, however, he prefixed none, because he does not preach, but merely displays the desire of the perfect soul.

The title also fittingly applies to Christ, who is Solomon, son of David—that is, “strong of hand.” For who is strong of hand except He of whom it was said: “He shattered the bronze gates” (Ps. 106:16)?

[Col. 0521B] “King of Israel,” that is, of those who see God; likewise king of the heavenly Jerusalem. For believers first acknowledge God and thus speak in Jerusalem.

Historically, he was first anointed in Hebron, whence he was called king of Israel in that part of the kingdom; afterward throughout all Judea, which was the head of the kingdom. This Solomon, foreseeing in the Holy Spirit the state of the Church both in his own time and in the future, prefixed titles in this way according to the intention of his writing.

“The Song of Songs begins,” that is, here begins a collection of expressive utterances, which signify *songs*, that is, good deeds, that is, good words, which are called the *Song of Songs*. As though he said more plainly: here are indicated deeds and words that surpass in perfection all those by which the Church praises God. Thus the perfect Church begins.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0521C] VERSES 1–3.—“Let him kiss me.” As though she said: “May He who preached to me in *Proverbs*, He who preached to me in *Ecclesiastes*, where He says, ‘Hear, O daughter, and see’ (Ps. 44:11), and so forth, He who rescued me from adultery, join me to Himself.” We understand this union by “let him kiss,” because this book is called nuptial, in which four persons are introduced: namely, bridegroom, bride, male friends, and female friends. For the bridegroom first kisses the bride and joins her to himself by the kiss of his mouth. And because some are joined to Christ only for a time, as Judas was, she says “by a kiss,” by that union which is commanded in the Old Testament through the prophets and in the New Testament through the apostles; these are His mouth, because He spoke through them.

“For your breasts are better than wine.” Christ, hearing the faithful soul’s desire, answers her: “Because I see you are worthy, I shall fulfill what you seek—namely, because you will nourish good children for Me.” “Whence is this a sign to Me? Because your breasts,” that is, preachers who nourish hearers like children, “are better than wine,” that is, secular learning, which puffs a person up like wine, as it is said: “It adds horns to the poor man” (HORACE, *Odes*, III, to XXI, 18). For this still applies to heretics, who in a certain way teach better than secular persons. He adds: “Fragrance,” that is, sweet odor, “of the finest ointments,” that is, of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. He used “finest” to distinguish them from carnal ones, as if to say: “What your preachers bless does not arise from evil thought but from divine inspiration.” Yet one must consider goodness not only in speech, but also in deed and thought. For the faithful soul’s deeds themselves, crying out to God, say, “Let him kiss me,” while she thinks: “Do I act so that I may be worthy to be joined to Christ?” Nor should Christ be understood as speaking to the Church otherwise than in the sense that she herself thinks: “If I do this, I shall be such a person.”

The Church, hearing herself praised by the Bridegroom and knowing that every perfect gift is from above (Jas. 1:17), says: “Lord, the fact that I teach well must not be credited to me, but to Your name, because Your name,” that is, the renown of Your name, “is poured-out oil.” [Col. 0522A] When oil is contained in a vessel, it does not give off much fragrance; but once poured out, it yields the greatest scent. Applied also to a wound, it penetrates inward and heals wounds. Thus, while the Son of God was contained in the Father’s bosom, He did not give forth fragrance; but after He descended from heaven and was incarnate, His name was preached everywhere and received on earth; and, rightly understood, it healed the wounds of sins. And because, O Christ, Your preaching healed us, therefore maidens loved You—that is, they will love You, and, newly converted, will walk not in the manner of the old Adam but of the new. Therefore, if they love You because of the oil of Your name, how much more do I! And because I am such, and this is through You:

VERSE 3.—“Draw me after You,” that is, go before me so that I may follow You. And if the flesh resists, still draw me to You. The female friends, hearing the bride desire to be joined to her bridegroom and the bridegroom assent to her, say: “Lady, You are being drawn; we too shall run in faith and work. [Col. 0522B] We shall run to enter with You into that rest. We too, placed in the fragrance,” that is, in the good reputation, “of Your ointments,” that is, of works proceeding for You from the gifts of the Holy Spirit, “after You,” that is, in imitation of the Bridegroom.

To them the bride replies: “You say that you run after me, and you do well, because I have a place in which to reward you. For the king has brought me into his storerooms,” that is, into the fullness of his blessedness; there he will reward me. This is said by comparison, because if a king is to marry a queen, he first displays his riches. The female friends, hearing that she has been brought in and hoping to become sharers in her blessedness, turn toward Christ and say: “O Christ, because You have brought in the bride, therefore, that we too may be brought in with her, we shall exult,” that is, we shall do good works. For when someone works well, the whole body moves. “Thus we shall also exult and rejoice”—but in mind—as though to say: “We shall both work well and think upon that which shall be our joy in You,” namely, striving toward You, that is, in hope of You. And because this might be only temporary, she says: “Mindful,” that is, imitatively remembering, “of Your breasts,” that is, Your commandments, “more than wine,” that is, better than secular learning; that is, we shall never forget Your commandments, which say: “Not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered, shall be saved” (Matt. 24:13). And this is deservedly so, because our teachers, who love You, do so; therefore we, their imitators, ought to love You. The bride, understanding that they follow her—or derive from her—and fearing that they may fail when evils press upon them, foretells what threatens her, so that afterward she may exhort them to perseverance.

VERSES 4–5.—“I am black, but beautiful.” As though she said: “If you wish to imitate me, you must suffer many tribulations, as I too have suffered.” She states the effect for the cause: “I am black in body because of tribulations, but beautiful inwardly.” “I say this to you, who strive to be daughters instructed by doctrine, who are already enrolled in the higher heavenly Jerusalem. And I am black like the tent of Kedar,” who was deservedly black. For Kedar means “darkness,” the son of Ishmael, who because of his wickedness was so hated by all that he never dared remain in a fixed dwelling, but always lived in tents. Of him it is written: “His hand against all, and the hand of all against him” (Gen. 16:12). We should not, however, understand the tents to be black, but him in the tents. Thus I am undeservedly black, as Kedar is deservedly a tent-dweller; but inwardly beautiful like Solomon’s skin, taken from dead animals, cleansed of hairs, which protected the ark of God. Every faithful person is Solomon’s skin: for Christ’s sake such a person mortifies the flesh, cleanses it from the hairs of superfluities, and protects the Lord’s gold, that is, the Church, in which the Holy of Holies is contained, from the rain of demonic assault.

“Do not look upon me because I am dark,” that is, although I suffer tribulations and am thereby black, do not nevertheless be frightened when you see that I am dark, “because the sun has discolored me”—that is, because I have suffered tribulations for Jerusalem’s sake. [Col. 0523A] “The sons of my mother,” that is, because I suffered for Him, those who are already sons—that is, instructed by the preaching of those to whom I belong—have fought against me, that is, imitating me, they have fought against vices. “Against me” is said after the manner of those who, wishing to imitate someone, place themselves before that person so that they may fully observe that person’s bearing. And because “they made me a keeper in the vineyards,” that is, they proposed to guard themselves by my example—“in the vineyards,” that is, in themselves, made vineyards by my example, who are inwardly green through virtues and outwardly dry through tribulations and fasts like a vineyard—“but I gave myself only to guarding them, so that I did not guard my own vineyard,” that is, my own life, by which I might acquire another vineyard—that is, other good persons—for whom I would be a guardian; that is, I did not guard myself or attend to my own care.

VERSES 6–8.—“Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday.” The voice of the female friends, as though she said: “Since they have now progressed so far through imitation of me that they are called not your sons but the sons of your mother—that is, your brothers and fathers—I too wish to imitate you. But when I see you darkened in torments, I see others no less so; therefore, since I cannot distinguish you from them, O Christ, whom my soul loves, tell me,” that is, give me the discernment to know, “where you pasture,” that is, in whom Your pastures are, that is, in whom You delight; “where you lie down,” that is, where You frequently rest, “at midday,” that is, in the fervor of charity, “lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions,” that is, in imitation of heretics, who are flocks—that is, living beastially, not clinging to heavenly things but fulfilling lust—because they exalt themselves so highly as to call themselves Your companions, that is, equals of Yours, or chief friends.

“If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women.” As though Christ said: “You do well to wish to distinguish those among whom I pasture. For if you do not know yourself,” that is, your own people whom you ought to imitate, “O most beautiful among women”—that is, how you surpass other sects in virtues—“you will become foul among women.” We understand “women” as sects because, as women bear and nourish children, so does every sect. “You shall go out,” that is, if you do not know, go out—that is, you shall go out from the fellowship of the good. And “where?” that is, you will withdraw entirely: you will not merely err yourself, but will lead others astray. You, going after the footprints—that is, imitating the words and works—of the flocks, that is, of heretics: this is what He says, “Feed,” that is, you will nourish your kids, that is, your subjects rotten in word and deed, “beside the shepherds’ tents.” Heretics always associate themselves with the faithful, but never enter the dwelling-place of the Christian religion; they remain beside it because they imitate the faithful. Therefore the greatest care must be taken lest, thinking heretics faithful, we wander after them. He calls them shepherds’ tents because all faithful persons who keep watch to guard the flock suffer, while in this world, as though under continual hindrance.

“To my cavalry.” As though He said: “I said, ‘If you do not know, you shall go out,’ but neither shall you remain ignorant nor shall you go out. [Col. 0523D] For I shall lead you away from seducers, just as I led the children of Israel away from Pharaoh’s pride.” This is what He means by “to my cavalry,” that is, to my army which served me, namely, being in chariots, that is, in pride. For pride sat in Pharaoh’s chariots; Pharaoh means the devil. As though He said: “I likened you to those who were in Pharaoh’s time, so that just as I led them out of Egypt and brought them through the Red Sea into the land of the wilderness, so I brought you from Egypt—that is, from the darkness of this world—through the Red Sea, that is, baptism, into the promised land, that is, your mother Jerusalem, Pharaoh and his pomp having been drowned in the sea of baptism, so that you might remain my female friend.”

VERSES 9–12.—“Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove.” As though He said: “I shall lead you out, and I shall do this through your cheeks and your neck. And who are your cheeks and your neck? Let this be a sign to you: they are beautiful with the beauty of virtues, namely, having a life like that of the turtledove, which ordinarily gives forth a groan instead of song and is content with one mate.” We understand preachers by the cheeks because two things are noted in cheeks: teeth, by which food is broken up, and the sign of modesty. These are found in faithful preachers, in whom there is always shame at sinning, and whose teeth destroy vices. They are deservedly compared to the turtledove, since their whole life is groaning and sorrow for their own and others’ sins, and they are content with one husband, namely Christ.

By another comparison we understand the same persons through the neck, because through the neck the lower members are joined to the head and all things pass through it to the lower parts. Thus the commandments of our head, namely Christ, are transmitted through preachers to the lower members of the Church; through them, as through columns, we are joined to Christ. They are well compared to necklaces because they adorn the Church with wisdom and teaching, and nourish the bosom of virtues, lest the adulterer, the devil, lay on it the hand of violence.

The male friends, that is, the perfect in the Church, hearing themselves called cheeks and neck by the bridegroom and promised that they will become leaders of the Church, willingly offer themselves for leadership. “We shall make for you little ornaments,” that is, earrings, because a little lamprey, when caught, curls itself into a ring like an earring. By earrings, which hang at the ear, we signify preaching, which tends toward the ear; by the roundness of the earrings, the perfection of preaching. “Of gold.” What among metals is more precious than gold? By gold we signify charity, which appears greatest among virtues because it is refined with great labor. Therefore by it we signify wisdom, because it is acquired with great labor. “We shall make them for you,” that is, for your benefit we shall make your preaching with wisdom and charity. “Inlaid with silver,” divided like little worms, with silver—that is, with divine speech, shining like silver through the art of composition. And deservedly, because your bridegroom has done things beyond telling. This is what He says: “While the king was at his table,” that is, needing no one, in the repose of His divinity, [Col. 0524C] He made me abound in virtues. This is what He says: “My nard,” that is, my humility, “gave forth its fragrance,” that is, the pattern of good work.

Although above He said “we shall make” in the plural, here he uses the singular because, though there are many in the Church, they are one in the unity of faith. And He not only made me fragrant, but also was incarnate and died for me. Therefore “my beloved is a bundle,” that is, a burden, “of myrrh,” that is, of sorrow received from His death, because myrrh was customarily placed in the tombs of the dead. Hence the Magi brought myrrh to the Lord’s crying cradle, signifying His death, for my honor; for many employ it not merely to honor but rather to dishonor, whereas remembrance of the Lord’s Passion is the highest honor. “He shall remain between my breasts,” that is, in my preaching: whatever I shall preach will be seasoned by remembrance of Him. Or “within my breasts,” that is, in the heart, which is situated within the breasts. “He was to me a cluster of Cyprus,” that is, an intoxicating cup. A cluster is a bunch of grapes; Cyprus is an island abounding in excellent vineyards. Hence he says:

VERSES 13–16.—“A cluster of Cyprus,” that is, remembrance of His Passion intoxicated me so that, in preaching for my own people, I do not hesitate to undergo death. Or one who is intoxicated by Cypriot wine forgets oneself. “In the vineyards,” that is, among those made inwardly green and outwardly dry. Through me I shall be intoxicated among my own, about to suffer death for Him. But because some appear to be vineyards and are not, he added “Engaddi,” that is, “cleansed.” Engaddi is a mountain and means “spring of the kid,” that is, of baptism, to which kids—that is, those rotten with vices—come, and from which lambs—that is, those cleansed—depart.

Or thus: because He made me fragrant, the burden of sorrow will remain in my heart. “My beloved to me,” that is, continually remembering His Passion, I shall grieve greatly; and He will be “in the vineyards of Engaddi,” that is, among us, “a cluster of Cyprus,” that is, the joy of His resurrection, so that by wine we signify joy. Christ, hearing the compunction of the preachers [Col. 0525A] and the kindness they show toward the lesser members, says to her who above said, “Tell me,” and so forth: “Behold, you whom I said would go out and become foul if you did not know yourself—since they themselves gladly assent to you, whom I have given as leaders to guide you in faith—you are beautiful in faith by imitating them, and you are my female friend,” that is, thus you have become a sharer in my secrets. “Behold, you are beautiful in works,” and deservedly, because “your eyes,” that is, your overseers, whom above I called cheeks and neck, “are like doves.” It is said in the transition: “Your eyes are like doves.”

In the dove we observe seven characteristics, which are also attributed to the virtues of the faithful, through which we signify the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. It lacks gall and harms no one; so the faithful person, lacking all gall of wickedness, deceives no one by fraud. It nourishes the young of others; so the faithful person incorporates the children of iniquity into himself and nourishes them with spiritual teaching. It selects attractive grains; so the faithful person, reading the Holy Scriptures, chooses wholesome sayings. It nests in holes of rock in order to avoid the attacks of serpents; so the faithful person places his dwelling in the openings of Christ’s side and thus drives away the devil, because he has such hope in Him who died for him that the devil cannot enter at all. It lingers over streams of water so that, seeing in the water the shadow of the hawk, it may keenly avoid its approach and carry drink from there to its young; so the faithful person, studying the Scriptures, avoids the coming of the enemy and gathers sayings with which to give drink to his young. It has groaning instead of song; so the faithful person groans for his own and others’ offenses.

She, hearing herself praised by the Bridegroom, says: “O Lord, You say that I am beautiful, but behold, You alone are beautiful by nature, my Beloved, in divinity, and fair in humanity. I, however, am so through You and Yours. And because I am beautiful and You are beautiful, deservedly our bed,” that is, knowledge, “in which You and I rest, is flowery with virtues.” And because it could happen that, when the wind of temptation blows, it loses the brightness of virtues, he says, “like the flower of the field when the north wind blows.” “The beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings are cypress.” Beams are the upper part of a house, repelling rain; by them [Col. 0525C] we understand preachers, who protect the Church from demonic rain. By different houses we understand Churches according to their successive renewals, in which diverse faithful persons are gathered together as different walls in a house. Their wall, roof, and foundation are cedar—incorruptible, that is, unfailing—whose fragrant works drive away the serpent, that is, the devil. Cedar is an incorruptible tree whose odor drives away serpents. “Our ceilings,” that is, those who are beneath preachers, such as hermits, like ceilings—that is, the carved upper part of a house under the beams—are cypress, that is, incorruptible. As though it were said: “Even if they do not drive out demons by preaching, still they are unfailing in faith and work.” Cypress is an incorruptible tree.

The Bridegroom replies: “You rightly call Me beautiful, and therefore our little bed flowery, because I am the honor of the field,” that is, the honor of the Church. We understand the Church by the field because, just as different flowers grow in a field, so different faithful persons exist in the Church. Or [Col. 0525D] the field is level and open; so is the faith of the saints.

## CHAPTER II

VERSES 1–6.—“I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys,” that is, the honor of the humble, who are watered by the water of preaching dripping from both mountains, that is, the Old and New Testaments. And as I am a lily among thorns, that is, piercing torments, and do not lose my fragrance, so you, my female friend, are among daughters, that is, various sects, which pierce you as thorns do; yet you retain the brightness of virtues.

Or thus: “I am the flower of birth,” because, as a flower is produced without union, so Christ was begotten without seed—that is, in an untilled field—from the undefiled Virgin; “and the lily of the valleys,” that is, the glory and beauty of humble parents. For just as I am a lily among thorns, that is, protectors, so you, my female friend, ought to be among piercing daughters. And if I suffer more, I shall flee to You, refreshed by Your fruit, shade, and fragrance.

Or thus: It is no wonder that I retain honor among thorns, because You sustain me. “As [Col. 0526A] an apple tree among the thorny trees is more lovely, so is my friend among the sons,” that is, the faithful in the Church. In the apple tree we observe three things: fruit, shade, and fragrance. Therefore travelers, exhausted by the sun’s heat and the labor of the journey, desire no tree more than one whose shade refreshes them from the burning heat and whose fruit and fragrance restore them. So faithful people, exhausted in the heat of this torment and on the journey, flee to Christ and are refreshed in the shade of His confession; they are sustained by His fruit, that is, the Eucharist; and by the fragrance of His goodness the stench of vices is expelled. Therefore, because He is such, “I desired Him and sat down,” that is, I rested, avoiding the heat of torments and secular labors. “I sat beneath the shade of Him whom I desired”: that is, the fruit, that is, the Eucharist, “was sweet to my throat,” because just as the throat tastes bodily things, so the heart tastes spiritual things.

But if some are so withdrawn that they have already fled human sight, like many hermits, and do not partake bodily of the Eucharist, they nevertheless partake spiritually, by faith and hope. “The king brought me into the storerooms.” As though she said: “Because I fled to Him, He brought me into the chamber,” that is, into wine-like blessedness, that is, forgetfulness: He bestowed upon me such blessedness that I entirely forgot past things, like one drunk. “He ordered charity in me,” that is, He placed in me every order of charity: namely, that I should love neighbor and God, and the enemy for God’s sake, so that I would not hesitate to undergo the gallows of death for the salvation of my children.

“Support me with flowers.” As though she said: “Because He made me possess charity, therefore I love you; and because I love you, support me,” that is, fill me into the number of the perfect, “with flowers,” that is, with virtues. As though it were said: “Abound in virtues that may sustain you, so that you may be worthy to share in the gifts of God in the Church; and work in such a manner that she herself may clothe you against the cold of iniquity.” Yet I say this to you not for earthly advantage, but because “I languish from love,” that is, I love intolerably Him who ordered charity in me, because He commanded us even to love enemies, and I strive to join you to Him. And because I love Him so greatly, “His left hand is beneath my head,” that is, [Col. 0526C] beneath my mind, which is the head of thoughts. As though it were said: “All earthly things which are in creatures, weaker things of God just as the left side in a human being is weaker in comparison with the right, shall be beneath my mind,” that is, my mind shall despise them. “And His right hand,” that is, heavenly things, “shall embrace me,” that is, whatever I do in this world will be done with regard to heavenly things. As though it were said: “Not only do I urge this upon you; He Himself says it to you.”

VERSE 7.—“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,” that is, I bind you, “by the roes and hinds of the fields,” that is, by the faithful living in the Church, “do not awaken or disturb” from rest of mind—that is, be obedient to your teachers. For while He preaches to faithful persons who are not rebellious, He rests as though in a bed. Or if you repel Him for a time, you will nevertheless not cause “my beloved,” that is, my bride, to wake—that is, you will not wholly disturb her—until she herself wishes, namely, to correct you, that is, until what has long displeased her in you becomes worthy of correction. By the words “I adjure,” we observe that those to whom He preaches are persons whom He wishes to convert to the faith of the saints. For an adjuration by God’s saints would have no power over unbelievers, just as if a pagan adjured someone by Jupiter.

“O daughters of Jerusalem,” namely, future daughters. In the roe four things are noted that also belong to the faithful: sharp sight for choosing wholesome herbs, and likewise the faithful person chooses divine sayings; they climb from mountain to mountain, and likewise the faithful ascend from virtue to virtue; they chew again food that has been eaten, and likewise the faithful bring divine sayings they have understood back to memory; if wounded, they eat the herb called dittany, and likewise, if struck by the devil’s arrow, the faithful flee to Christ and are healed.

In hinds three things are noted. They swallow serpents and afterward run to a spring; having tasted it, they are cleansed of poison and renew their coats. Likewise the faithful, after tasting the devil’s poison, run to the spring, Christ, and are stripped of the coats of vices. When chased by dogs, with their antlers laid over their backs, they make their way through thorns so as to avoid the dogs’ assault there. So the faithful, setting the antlers of virtues above the frailty of the flesh, avoid the threats of tyrants. They change pastures; gathered together, they make a single troop, and thus each one going before supports the head of the one following, lest they fail under the burden of their antlers. So, if a faithful person sees a neighbor lacking necessities, he supports that neighbor by providing food, as Saint Nicholas did for the man who had intended his daughters for prostitution. If he sees that neighbor weighed down by penitence for sins, he lightens him by taking a share upon himself.

VERSES 8–9.—“The voice of my beloved.” As though she said: “This voice which I have just spoken is not mine but my Beloved’s. For He adjured us, and the whole human race, when for our redemption He deigned to assume flesh and undergo death. For who is so hard, so stony, while possessing reason, that, if he knows that God suffered so much for servants, he does not think himself admonished to return to the homeland from which he originated?”

As though Christ Himself had spoken in His own voice: “Behold, He will come.” As though it were said: “Truly He spoke in this manner. For He Himself came to be incarnate, and His coming is powerful.” As though He had said: “If you possess reason, [Col. 0527B] leaping,” that is, He came to display His leaps: namely, from heaven into the womb, thence to the cross, and the rest; “upon the mountains,” that is, upon the apostles, “leaping over the hills,” that is, over us lesser persons, because through the smallness of our understanding we do not fully know His leaps as did the apostles, to whom heavenly secrets were revealed.

“My beloved is like…” He is of such appearance as He was shown to come in the preceding verse, through those ancients who fully knew His coming and could fully bear testimony to it. Now, because He is wise and swift in abandoning sins and working miracles, by the roe we understand discernment of who should be chosen and who should not; by the young hart, swiftness—for it is swifter than its parents among hinds; by the patriarchs, whose progeny included the apostles and Christ Himself according to the flesh. Truly He was swifter: for neither the Levite nor the priest healed from wounds the man half-dead who had gone down from Jerusalem to Jericho, until the Samaritan placed him on his beast and entrusted him to the innkeeper.

“Behold, He stands.” As though it were said: “Since He Himself adjures you, you ought rightly to obey both His own people and Him, because He stands behind the wall”: He remains to destroy our vices, which are like a wall between us and Him. This is said by comparison with a ruler who, wishing to enter someone’s city, stands beside the walls until he appeals to them, looking through a window. “Whose favor has had pity upon us through the windows,” that is, through present miracles, because, as windows illuminate a house, so Christ’s miracles illuminate human hearts. Yet in saying “present” we have no authority from the word itself; rather, from what follows we understand past miracles. And He rightly looked, because He not only preached but worked miracles, so that those unwilling to believe us might at least yield to miracles. For His concern to redeem us was so great “through the lattices,” that is, through the fathers of old—namely Moses and Aaron and the rest—who promised us many miracles and were the beginning of the Church, like the lattices of a temple.

VERS. 10–17.—“Behold, my beloved speaks to me,” that is, in those things previously mentioned he speaks to you, meaning to me, so that I may lead you to faith. “Arise,” that is, hasten, setting earthly things aside; hasten without delay, “my friend, my dove” in faith, “my beautiful one” in conduct, “and come,” that is, cause others to come—which you are able fittingly to do. For now “winter,” that is, the coldness of iniquity, has passed; “the rain,” that is, the persecution of tyranny, has gone and wholly withdrawn; “the flowers,” that is, the beginnings of virtues, have appeared—that is, people begin to act well, which is a sign of virtue in our land, though still to come, for whoever cultivates himself with the ploughshare of correction in hope of eternal recompense. It is “the time of pruning,” that is, that superfluities, if any remain in them, may be cut away by preaching. “The voice of the turtle-dove has been heard in our land.” As though it were said: Truly it is the time [Col. 0528A], for it has heard my preaching. Christ compares himself to a turtle-dove because of chastity and the mournful sound of its voice. “The fig tree,” that is, Judaea, hitherto barren, “has put forth its green figs,” that is, good works. “The vines,” that is, the nations, vines that will flourish in action, “have yielded their fragrance,” that is, the renown of good conduct. “Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove”: because of the intervening words he returns to what was said above. “In the clefts of the rock,” that is, in the wounds of Christ. Whatever you preach concerning Christ’s wounds, do not depart from speaking of him; for those who are hostile to you are, as it were, serpents, while the dove is in the cleft of the rock. “In the hollow places of the wall,” that is, in the protection of the Fathers, because many prophets tend toward one point, as many stones toward the building of a wall. “Show me your face,” that is, your mind; for as a man looks at the face, so God looks into the heart. As though it were said: Let your mind be so pure that it is worthy in my sight. “Let your voice sound,” that is, let your preaching sound in my ears; let it be such as is worthy to be heard by me. Truly, if you preach, you will be heard by me, and I shall see your face. “For your voice is sweet” [Col. 0528B] “and your face beautiful.” “Catch for us the little foxes which destroy the vineyards.” As though he said: You indeed will preach, but care must be taken lest heretics deceive you by their preaching. This is what he says: “Catch,” that is, intercept their opinions, lest they have anything to mingle in opposition. “Foxes,” that is, heretics, because of their cunning; “little,” because they pretend humility. “Which destroy,” that is, gnaw with the tooth of deception, “the vineyards,” that is, the churches; and one must beware. For “our vineyard,” namely the one to come, “has blossomed,” that is, has already begun to act well; “and my beloved speaks to me,” and therefore I shall obey him “until the day breathes,” that is, until the day of judgment cools us from the labour of the world, “and the shadows incline,” that is, pass away—namely, earthly things.

And that I may be able to obey you, so that it may attain its effect, let him breathe again—that is, let him appear to me as present in assistance. But because he said, “Return,” it should be noted that certain preachings have not been heard. For God then seems absent when hardened hearers do not consent [Col. 0528C]. “Be like a roe,” having keen sight, “or a young stag,” performing miracles more swiftly, redeeming the human race from the enemy; that is, come in such a way as swiftly to choose those who are to be chosen. “Upon the mountains of Bethel,” that is, protect us who are mountains of God—that is, preachers in the house of God. For Beth is interpreted “house,” or “God.” Lord, you must return, so that your preaching may be fulfilled through me; for unless someone preaches to them, they cannot be converted any more than I was able to be. But because preachers found me, I was converted. And this is what she relates.

## CHAPTER III

VERS. 1–5.—“Upon my bed,” that is, I was upon a bed—that is, amid earthly riches, in which I slept away from the good in sins. “By night,” that is, through pagan authors, who lead to the night of hell, “I sought,” that is, by imitating their examples, “him whom my soul loves,” that is, my intention: I wished to be joined to God, from whom I had heard God’s name, but not the way that leads to him. [Col. 0528D] “I sought him.” As though it were said: Often, in excessive distress, I sought him, “and did not find him,” that is, I could not have knowledge of his kiss upon them. Therefore I resolved within myself, saying: “I will arise” from the bed of vices, “and go about the city,” that is, I shall strive to imitate the sayings and deeds of those who are in the city—that is, in the Church. For as a city is surrounded by walls and is more cultivated in civic life, so the faithful are cultivated in virtues by which they are protected. “Through the streets and squares which go around the city,” that is, I shall go around the city, that I may seek him whom my soul loves “through the streets,” that is, among the martyrs, who lead a more austere life; “through the squares,” that is, among confessors and other good people, who have a broader way—namely, by imitating them. “I sought him,” namely through the night, “and did not find him.” The cause stated above is repeated. I imitate these, therefore, since I did not succeed through hearers—that is, the books of the pagans—because “the watchmen found me,” that is, they preached to me: the watchmen are preachers who keep watch to guard the city. To them I said: “Have you [Col. 0529A] seen him whom my soul loves?” As though it were said: Before I believed them, I investigated whether such men had seen—that is, had knowledge of—the living God in word and deed. “A little while after I had passed by them”: having, as it were, examined them, I learned through them to cast off my error; and after I had passed a little way beyond my error through them—that is, through their preaching. This is said as though she meant: I made a passage from place to place. “I found him whom my soul loves”: I acquired a greater ardour for acting well, or greater knowledge. Since I found him, and watched with my desire and my beholding, “I held him,” that is, he never afterwards departed from my memory; “nor will I let him go until I bring him,” that is, make him manifest by my preaching, “into the house,” that is, into the nation of the Gentiles, which is my mother according to the flesh. Nor shall I bring him only into the nation, but also “into the chamber of my mother that bore me,” that is, into the hearts of certain persons among the Gentiles, who are Gentiles according to the flesh. By “bedchamber” the heart is understood, because, just as limbs move about in a bed, so thoughts move about in the heart.

[Col. 0529B] VERS. 5–9.—“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.” Christ, hearing of the effect among the Gentiles in the conversion of Judaea, adjures those who are to be converted not to be rebellious. Or she herself, as the Gentile Church, adjures that she may use no compulsion upon those to whom she preaches. “Who is this who comes up,” from virtue to virtue, but hitherto “through the wilderness,” that is, through Gentile life, hitherto deserted by the Law and by divine miracles, “like a column of smoke,” that is, upright in virtues; of smoke, that is, of good works; “from aromatic spices,” that is, of confessors; “myrrh,” that is, of martyrs; “frankincense,” that is, of confessors; “and every powder,” that is, of all good persons who are ground down by fasts and persecutions, like powder; “of the perfumer,” that is, of Christ, who compounds virtues as a perfumer compounds spices. This means: She is a column, tending uprightly toward the heights; this uprightness possesses the renown of good action, and this in every part—namely, martyrs, confessors, and certain good persons. From all these Christ compounds the rest as though they were aromatic spices. “Behold the bed”: the Gentile Church replies, saying, It is no wonder that I am such. “Behold Solomon’s bed,” that is, mine, where the true Solomon lays down his head. “Sixty,” that is, those who keep the six works of mercy—visiting the sick, clothing the naked, giving drink to the thirsty, feeding the hungry, and the other things read in the Gospel—and who observe the Decalogue of commandments, that is, the perfect; and “mighty,” that is, persevering, “of the mightiest of Israel”: they are so persevering as to be most steadfast, seeing God in all things. “They surround” [Col. 0529C] it, that is, they keep watch night and day, in order to guard the bed—that is, themselves and others. “All holding swords”: this explains “they surround.” “Swords,” that is, the word of preaching, because they slay people in what ought to be slain in them. And because some, though knowledgeable, are nevertheless not capable, he says, “most learned for the battles of vices.” And because it remains that, if a person’s life is despised, his preaching also is despised, he adds: “the sword of each one,” that is, watchful guarding, “upon his thigh,” that is, upon the concupiscence of the flesh, since lust arises in the thigh. And this is “because of terrors in the night,” that is, the hidden snares of the devil which lead to night. He then shows how someone may attain that bed—that is, may himself become the bed. “A litter,” that is, a table at which we ought to be refreshed, so that afterwards we may rest in the bed, namely Scripture, “for himself,” that is, for his own honour, “King Solomon,” that is, Christ, made “of the woods,” that is, of the frankincense, “of Lebanon,” that is, of the white ones. Lebanon is interpreted “whitening.” This means: The Scriptures were made for Christ’s honour from the lives of the Fathers, so that by imitating them we may ascend to the bed.

VERS. 10, 11.—“He made its pillars of silver,” that is, he made the Old and New Testaments the light and brilliance of heavenly speech, upon which the Scripture concerning the Fathers might rest. For unless the deeds of the Fathers were established as not differing from the precept of the New and Old Testament, they could not stand. “Its reclining-place of gold”: he made golden—that is, loving and wise—those who expound both the lives of the Fathers and the New and Old Testament; such, indeed, are those upon whom the Son of Man lays his head. “Its ascent of purple,” that is, the cross of Christ, by whose example people are made purple—that is, martyrs; through the redness of purple we signify the blood by which they ascend to Jerusalem. “Its midst he paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem,” that is, he ordered the bed through love in its midst, so that others besides martyrs might ascend; and this is for the daughters of Jerusalem, not for the sons—that is, for the weak, who cannot endure martyrdom. Here is signified God’s mercy: he does not command all to become martyrs, but commands even those who are his bed to possess love in the midst—that is, a love held in common by martyrs and others. “Go forth.” As though it were said: Since Solomon is such, go forth from your error and see—that is, acknowledge Solomon to be the King of kings and Lord of lords. You daughters of Jerusalem, if you acknowledge your King, you will be his citizens; you who are set “in the diadem,” that is, in his remembrance—he who was the cause of his own crown when the enemy had been conquered and the spoil brought back. That is, the diadem [Col. 0530B] with which “his mother crowned him,” namely holy Mary, “on the day” of his espousals: that is, hold in remembrance the day of his death, by which he espoused the Church to himself; “and on the day of the joy of his heart,” that is, hold the day of his resurrection, which was the joy of his heart—that is, of the apostles and the rest of the good. Or thus: “In the diadem,” that is, remember the Passion, when a crown of thorns was placed upon him, “with which his mother crowned him,” namely Judaea; “and on the day of his espousals,” that is, of his nativity, because when he assumed flesh he espoused the Church to himself. What follows is as written:

## CHAPTER IV

VERS. 1–3.—“How beautiful you are, my friend!” Christ, hearing her very great affection, praises her in each particular. “How beautiful you are,” namely in work—that is, in virtues—“my friend, to whom I have declared whatever I heard from the Father”; “how beautiful you are,” namely in work. “Your eyes,” that is, your overseers, “are doves” [Col. 0530C], that is, they are doves through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, apart from that which is hidden within, although the virtues appear outwardly. “Your hair,” that is, the weaker persons who cling to the head as hairs do, is “like flocks of goats,” that is, ascending from virtue to virtue; through a flock we signify concord. “Which have come up from Mount Gilead”: inasmuch as they are mountains, namely Gilead, “the heap of testimony,” that is, all martyrs. For a martyr is a witness. Gilead is the mountain upon which Jacob and Laban piled up a heap of stones, that is, a witness of the covenant. “Your teeth,” that is, preachers who grind down vices, are “like flocks of shorn sheep,” that is, themselves shorn of superfluities, as sheep are stripped of the weight of wool and dirt. “Which have come up from the washing,” that is, baptism: by being baptized, they have ascended the mountain of virtues. All yours, namely, bear twin offspring—that is, love of God and neighbour—and none among them is barren, that is, none fails to perform a good work. “Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon,” that is, your preachers, in the Old and New Testament, are harmonious in word and deed; they are a ribbon, namely harmonious, binding the faithful by preaching to Christ their head. They are also scarlet, that is, red with the blood of martyrdom: they both teach others and endure martyrdom in themselves. This proves that they are ribbons, because their speech is sweet: for you do not demand eye for eye, but command love for an enemy. “Your cheeks are like a fragment of a pomegranate.” And because they devour vices while outwardly enduring martyrdom, they are white in their multitude of virtues. For pomegranates in Africa are reddish outwardly, but when broken open within they are white; and by the pomegranate seeds we signify the multitude of virtues. “Apart from that which is hidden within” was expounded above.

VERS. 4–7.—“Your neck is like the tower of David,” that is, your preachers, by whom lesser persons are joined to Christ, and through whom the words of preaching are conveyed into Christ’s members. “Like the tower of David,” that is, the impregnable defence of him who is strong of hand, because his soldiers put the enemy, the devil, to flight. “Built with bulwarks,” that is, with firm judgments by which the enemy may be attacked and repelled. “A thousand shields,” that is, countless good works, which protect the faithful like shields, “hang from it,” that is, are visible within. “All the armour of the mighty,” that is, all good works and all such judgments by which the strong may fight and defend themselves. “Your two breasts,” that is, teachers who disclose the spiritual meaning of the two writings, the Old and the New, “are like two twin fawns of a roe,” that is, in each alike swift in fulfilling. “Of a roe,” that is, of the Fathers, who were described as choosing good and rejecting evil, and as ascending from virtue to virtue. “Twins,” that is, harmonious, “feeding among the lilies,” among bright virtues, “until the day breathes and the shadows incline. I will go to the mountain of myrrh.” As though he said: Since you are such as I have said, I shall go to the mountain—that is, I shall show myself through miracles to be in you, who are the mountain of myrrh [Col. 0531B], that is, of martyrdom. For bodies of the dead were anointed with myrrh so that they might be preserved from corruption; likewise martyrdom preserves the faithful uncorrupted from temptations. “And to the hills of frankincense,” that is, to confessors: though they are not as lofty as martyrs, their life nevertheless gives fragrance like frankincense. As though he said: I shall display miracles in martyrs and confessors; and not merely because you are martyr and confessor, but because you are beautiful, my friend, even in your lesser members, “and there is no spot in you,” that is, no interruption of good work. For whether a believer sleeps, he sleeps for the Lord; whether he eats, he eats for the Lord. This is said by comparison with a coat of mail, where the openings between the rings are called spots, through which even the smallest iron may penetrate; but the works of believers are so continual that they cannot in any way be penetrated.

VERS. 8–11.—“Come from Lebanon.” As though he said: Since I love you so greatly, come—that is, persevere—so that, by cultivating yourself and others, when the course has been completed and the faith kept, you may at last be received into eternal blessedness. “From Lebanon,” that is, from the brightness of virtues. “My bride,” because you will nourish children for me. His saying “come” three times should be noted, as though he said: Come in childhood, like John the Baptist and Nicholas; come in youth, like Martin; come in old age, like John the Evangelist. Come willingly, and compelled by weakness, and from the places of purgation. “You shall be crowned,” that is, come in such a way as to be worthy of the crown of glory. “From the summit of Amana,” that is, by your preaching those will be converted who are heads among the members of the devil. Amana is a mountain and is interpreted “night-bird,” that is, the devil, who while watching places hidden snares for people everywhere, as in the night—that is, in obscurity. “From the peak of Sanir,” that is, from those who wish inwardly to appear superior and exalted, because Sanir is interpreted “God of watchings,” that is, the devil, who watches in order to devour whomever he can. “And Hermon,” that is, those who anathematize their sins by doing penance. Hermon is interpreted “anathematizing.” “From the dens,” that is, from those in whom the lion rests—that is, the devil because of his cruelty. “From the mountains” [Col. 0531D], that is, from those who are mountains among leopards—that is, heretics, who boast in their sect as leopards do in their variety of colour. “You have wounded me.” As though he said: I ask you to come, because I love you exceedingly. This is spoken by analogy with lovers wounded by the arrow of love. “My sister,” that is, my co-heiress; “my bride,” because of the rearing of children. “You have wounded my heart”: a repetition of love. “With one,” that is, with unity of faith, “of your eyes,” that is, of your overseers; “and with one,” that is, with unity, “lock,” that is, of your locks—for many form one—“of your neck,” that is, of your preachers. This means: because of the unity of your preachers and the unity of your hearers, who surround the preachers to hear preaching as hairs surround the neck. And therefore your breasts are beautiful—that is, those who do not yet labour at preaching, and in whom there is only hope, just as in breasts there is hope of giving milk. “My sister, my bride, your breasts are more beautiful than wine,” that is, your perfect preachers are better than wine, that is, worldly learning. “And the fragrance of your ointments” [Col. 0532A], that is, the renown of your works, by which the wounds of the devil are healed, is above all carnal spices. “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb,” that is, your preachers are mutually harmonious in the New and Old writings, as are your lips. “A dripping honeycomb,” that is, flowing; such is their preaching. “Honey,” that is, strong preaching, “and milk,” that is, gentle preaching; for honey is not given to infants, but milk. “Under your tongue,” that is, in your heart. “And the fragrance,” that is, the renown, “of your garments,” that is, of good works, which clothe you before God, is like the fragrance of frankincense, which drives away every stench.

VERS. 12.—“A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride.” As though he said: Therefore I shall go to you, because I shall be able to delight in you, who are a garden—that is, filled with many virtues—enclosed on every side by the key of virtues, so that no good thing may go out and no evil thing enter: a garden enclosed by virtues and works. “A fountain”: as a fountain waters the whole garden, so the fountain of baptism waters the whole Church. “A fountain,” that is, in that Church [Col. 0532B] is baptism sealed with the sign of the cross. “Your shoots.” As though he said: You are such; but those converted by preaching will be like shoots, that is, little branches springing at the root of great trees. They will be a paradise, that is, the delight of pomegranates—that is, of martyrs—and your shoots will be with the fruits of fruit trees, that is, confessors: those whom they themselves convert. That is, they will be such persons in whom their teachers, namely both martyrs and confessors, delight. We understand confessors throughout, because he first says pomegranates and afterwards fruit. He says absolutely: “Those shoots will be Cyprus with nard.” Cyprus is a tree in Egypt whose fruit is boiled with oil and made into royal ointment. Thus a believer, emerging from the darkness of this world, produces fruit cooked by the gifts of the Holy Spirit; with it Christ, who is King of kings, is anointed. Nard is a very lowly but fragrant tree: thus believers are humble, yet give off the fragrance of good conduct. “Nard with saffron,” that is, humble people enduring martyrdom. For saffron is a red-coloured herb signifying martyrdom. “Reed and cinnamon.” Reed is a tree with hard bark which, when crushed, is drunk and heals the internal organs. Thus believers suffer crushing in the flesh, which heals in the soul. Cinnamon is a root of ash-colour and is interpreted “spotless”; it signifies those who become spotless through repentance and make themselves lowly in reputation like ashes. “With all the woods of Lebanon”: all made white and strong through the brilliance of virtues. As though he said: All who can be signified by Cyprus, nard, and so forth will be converted through you—that is, good persons besides those mentioned. “Myrrh and aloes.” By myrrh we signify the suffering of martyrdom; by aloes, which are extremely bitter in taste but, when taken inwardly, heal bodily affliction, we signify fasting, vigils, and the rest—things which, when they are done, seem harsh and intolerable, yet inwardly heal the soul. “With all spices,” that is, with all the gifts of the Holy Spirit. And the joining of trees with ointments is fitting, because [Col. 0532D] when we restrain the flesh from wantonness, it follows that we receive greater gifts of the Holy Spirit.

VERS. 15, 16.—“And a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow swiftly from Lebanon.” He has described the shoots that will come; now he describes the source from which they are watered, namely the fountain of baptism, which is the fountain of the gardens of the Church, by which the whole Church is watered. “A well of living waters”: by the well, the depths which it contains—that is, mysteries; by the living waters, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which never fail. This means: the fountain of baptism contains the mysteries of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which flow “from Lebanon,” that is, from men made bright and from preachers, with force—that is, without any vice standing in their way. Thus the Holy Spirit works so fully through preachers in hearers that no vice can resist. “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind.” As though he said: Since my garden is such, and such shoots will come, therefore arise, north wind—that is, Satan, who chills the minds of people from the ardour of love—arise, that is, prepare yourself to attack my people; and come, that is, inflict torments on them in your members. “South wind, blow upon my garden,” that is, you, Holy Spirit, blow upon my garden; inspire my people, lest they fail in tribulations, “and its spices will flow”: if they persevere in suffering, then their good works will be made known. Or thus: As though he said, Your shoots will be such that this may happen: “Arise,” that is, depart, north wind, who lie in wait for my garden; “and come, south wind,” Holy Spirit, blow upon my garden—that is, inflame those who will be my garden—and then the spices will flow.

## CHAPTER V

VERS. 1, 2.—“Let my beloved come into his garden.” Hearing herself praised by her beloved, the bride thus desires his coming: Since my shoots are such, and this cannot be accomplished through me, let my beloved therefore come into me, his garden—that is, show through miracles that he is present with me in preaching—“that he may eat” [Col. 0533B], that is, delight in the fruits of his trees, that is, in us, who are his fruits, and seek such persons as may become his garden. Christ promises his coming to the bride, saying: You ask me to come, and I shall come. Let this be a sign to you: because I formerly came into my garden, that is, into the primitive Church, so I shall come into you, since you are my sister and bride. “I gathered my myrrh.” As though he said: In these I shall display miracles, and at last I gathered, that is, as it were gathered sheaves in the garden, my myrrh—that is, my martyrs—with spices, that is, the other elect. “I ate my honeycomb with my honey.” As though he said: Not without reason did I receive them, because both their lesser and their greater preaching delighted me; this is what he says: I ate the honeycomb, that is, the preachers, with honey, that is, strong preaching about me. “I drank”—the same as “I ate”—“my wine,” that is, preaching. This means: I came to them, displaying miracles through them; that is, I found them in the blessedness of eternal life because their life and preaching pleased me. Thus I shall receive you also into eternal blessedness, if you have fought lawfully. “Eat, friends, and drink.” As though he said: I shall come to you; but you, friends—that is, preachers, to whom I have revealed all things—preach in such a way that you may eat them, that is, delight in those to whom you preach. “And drink”: this is the same as “eat,” but applies to lesser persons, because infants do not eat. “And be intoxicated, beloved.” Be so intent upon the word of preaching that, as far as you are concerned, you forget your labour and suffering. “I sleep.” Hearing the bridegroom’s exhortation, the bride replies: My bridegroom exhorts me to preach, but I sleep—that is, I rest from every care. And lest this be understood as bodily sleep, she says: “My heart watches,” that is, I sleep from earthly things in such a way that I meditate upon the law of God day and night. “The voice of my beloved knocking”: that is why I watch for preaching, because this is the voice of my beloved knocking, that is, admonishing, because the bridegroom himself exhorts me, saying [Col. 0533D], “Open to me,” that is, remove for me the veils of sins from the hearts of unbelievers. “Sister,” that is, co-heiress; “friend,” to whom I have entrusted my secrets; “dove,” filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit; “undefiled,” without interruption of good works. Open, I say, because “my head,” that is, my divinity, is full, that is, surrounded by “dew,” that is, persecutors, whose opinions are nocturnal like dew: they say that they believe in God, but are darkened by demonic opinions. “And my locks,” that is, those who are to be mine, so devoted in love as locks—that is, curled hairs of my head—which will cling to me, “are full of drops of the night,” that is, nocturnal opinions: those who are now thought to be members of Christ, and also those who, when they were converted, were holding evil opinions of destruction.

VERS. 3.—“I have taken off my tunic,” that is, I reject every worldly care, that I may hasten to preaching. “How shall I put it on again?” that is, how shall I entangle myself again in worldly matters, abandoning preaching, when he himself says, “Open to me, my sister”? “I have washed my feet,” that is, with a better intention in their works, abandoning them not merely in word but by an example of goodness in deed.

VERS. 4, 5.—“My beloved put in his hand.” As though she said: I shall be able to preach well, because my beloved has put—that is, will put—his hand into helping me. “Through the opening,” that is, through the ears of the hearers; he himself will make them listen willingly through the opening, namely of his sides: when they hear that I suffered for the redemption of the human race, they will be pierced with compunction. “And my belly,” that is, my weaker members, will tremble, grieving for their sins, “at his touch,” namely at his help. Therefore “I arose,” that is, I shall arise, to open the hearts of the faithful to my beloved. “My hands,” that is, I shall be able to preach well because the bridegroom’s help is present, and because my life is not to be despised. This is what he says: “My hands,” that is, my works [Col. 0534B], “dripped myrrh,” that is, by what they give forth they show that myrrh may be perceived in my work: if necessary, I shall not refuse to suffer death. “My fingers,” that is, the discernment of my preaching, were full of myrrh—that is, charity. For myrrh is an ointment, by which we signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit; but he adds “most excellent,” from which we understand charity, because it is the most excellent of the other virtues. Yet because it is used in tombs, we may understand her to say that she has such great charity together with discernment in preaching that she does not hesitate to undergo death for the salvation of those subject to her.

VERS. 6, 7.—By “the bolt of my door” he means the universal Church. As though she said: He commands that it be opened; what shall I do?
