A sign to me is that formerly I opened the bolt, that is, the closure of my door—that is, the minds of those who are now mine. “But he had turned aside”: that is, I opened to my beloved, but not without his help, because he had turned aside—that is, had descended from heaven into me—and passed on. As though it were said: He cannot yet be wholly understood or comprehended by me. This is what “he had passed on” means: because no one in this life is granted a full visitation of God, he is said to pass on; that is, he shows himself more fully in the future by being seen. “My soul melted.” As though she said: Because he had turned aside into me, my soul—that is, that of my wretched people—melted from the hardness of iniquity through the heat of the Holy Spirit; that is, after I preached to them, they consented more readily. This is what she means by “when he spoke.” After I preached, with my beloved helping me, “I sought him and did not find him.” Above I said that he had passed on; and because the bride said that he had passed on—that is, she did not possess full knowledge of the Divinity—I sought through the holy Scriptures, striving to reach perfection, but “did not find him,” that is, I fell short. “I called,” that is, I persevered in seeking, “and he did not answer me,” that is, I could never search so much as to see him fully. This is spoken by analogy: when a person who answers at a spring is sought, he is found. “The watchmen found me.” One may ask how she, while hidden and subject to idols, had opened the hearts of others. Christ answers: “The watchmen found me,” namely in preaching; the watchmen are preachers who guard the city—that is, the Church—from the enemy. “They struck me,” that is, caused me to experience compunction; “and wounded me,” which is more, that is, imposed upon me penance for sins. Or thus: they struck me when they said generally, “Whoever sins and does not do penance will be damned”; they wounded me when, in a spiritual sense, they censured each person’s crime individually. When the preaching had been delivered, “they took away”—that is, caused me to lay aside—“my cloak,” namely the earthly things by which I was covered. “The keepers of the walls,” that is, of the holy Scriptures, which guard the Church as walls guard a city. Or the walls are virtues, which protect each person.

VERS. 8–10.—“I adjure you, daughters.” As though she said: Since I have despised all vain things for love of him, I ask you to see that you act in such a way that it may become known in your works that I preached to you, so that the greatness of my love for you on Christ’s account may appear. This is what she says: “I adjure,” that is, bind you, daughters of the Jerusalem to come, if it helps that you have found him—that is, since through me you have already come to know the beloved—“that you may tell him,” that is, show him your good works, “that I am sick with love.” For they do not act well unless preaching is done to them, nor is preaching done unless they are directed. “What is your beloved more than another beloved?” Judaea, hearing her serve her beloved with such ardour, says in wonder: What is your beloved above a beloved? As though it were said: He is great, as I see from your love—that is, from your affection for him—that he is great. Since you are “the most beautiful among women,” that is, among sects, and I recognize that you love him greatly because you adjured us. The repetition, “What is your beloved?” comes from excessive longing, because Judaea too desires to love him. “My beloved is white,” that is, appearing in the flesh without vices, “and ruddy,” through the blood of martyrdom; “chosen from among thousands.” The number one thousand is perfect and signifies universality; thus it is said: This one alone was chosen by God the Father, among all patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and the rest, to redeem the human race.

VERS. 11–13.—His head, that is, the divinity which is the head of the divine man, is finest gold: that is, his divinity is precious above all things, as gold among the other metals. His locks. Thus far he has been described in himself, both according to humanity and divinity; now, however, in his members, namely in the faithful. The locks, that is, the faithful, who, although they are soft among the rest, are as hairs among the members of the head. Like raised ears, or ears held together in the palms, through which we mark strength as it were through a troop of the faithful. By “raised” we understand their intentness toward heaven, as if he said: Your faithful possess many virtues because of heavenly rewards. Black as a raven. Raven chicks, while they are unfledged, are white; and because they do not resemble their parents, they are not fed by them. But, forced by hunger, they emit a certain stench, [Col. 0535C] so that flies, attracted by it, swarm about their beaks; and, when many have gathered, they swallow them. But after they become black, they are loved and fed by their parents. Thus, while we, young members of the Church and of Christ—that is, of our parents—refuse to follow in their footsteps within God’s sect, we are not fed by them; but, emitting the stench of vices, we feed on flies, that is, the opinions of the devil. Yet when we begin to be blackened by the judgments—that is, by the tribulation—of sufferings, enduring them in imitation of our parents, namely the Church and Christ, we are loved and fed by them. Hence it is said, “black as a raven”: that is, enduring the blackness of sufferings, so that they may be loved by Christ and the Church as a raven is by its parents, once it has become black in their likeness.

His eyes, that is, the overseers through whom he provides for the welfare of his Church, are like doves—that is, filled with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit—over streams of water: that is, dwelling upon the judgments of the Scriptures, they guard themselves against the coming of the ancient hawk; [Col. 0535D] washed with milk, that is, first cleansed from defilements by the teaching given to infants. And they sit beside very full streams: that is, first washed—namely, given to drink—with milk, and afterward they attained the fullness of the Spirit’s gifts.

His cheeks, that is, preachers, chaste devourers of vices, are beds of spices: that is, seats of virtues, planted—that is, ordered—by perfumers, namely Christ’s apostles, who plant virtues in the faithful as a perfumer plants herbs with which he sows aromatic plants in a bed. His lips, that is, preachers in the Old and New Testaments, agree in word and deed. Lilies, that is, gleaming in whiteness, dripping, that is, displaying, the first myrrh: namely, charity compelling one toward martyrdom; that is, such great charity in words and deeds that it does not hesitate to suffer martyrdom.

VERS. 14, 15.—And his hands are rounded gold. By hands good works are denoted; by “rounded,” the constancy of good work, tending toward the same end as a turning lathe; by “golden,” charity together with wisdom. And this is to say: [Col. 0536A] His workers never cease from good work, acting with charity and wisdom. Full of hyacinth: that is, whatever they do is done through the gift of the Holy Spirit, because hyacinth is fiery in color.

His belly, that is, the gentler members in the Church, is ivory: that is, gleaming with chastity. For ivory is white, and the animal is most chaste. Set with sapphires: particular virtues look toward heavenly things. Sapphire is the color of air. Or, “set with sapphires,” because human frailty is understood partly through hunger, weariness, thought, and death; and divine exaltation partly through miracles and the glory of resurrection. For in this interpretation we understand human frailty in the Lord’s manhood through the belly.

His legs, that is, his bearers, his preachers, are marble columns: that is, they steadfastly preserve uprightness; by the column, uprightness; by marble, solidity. Founded—that is, established—upon the foundation of the Trinity, which is golden above all things, like a column upon bases. His appearance is like Lebanon: that is, as Lebanon surpasses other mountains in the height and grace of its trees, so Christ surpasses all saints in the height of his merits. Chosen as cedars: that is, as the cedar, an incorruptible tree which drives away serpents, is chosen in constructing buildings, so the only Son of God was chosen to redeem the human race.

VERS. 16, 17.—His throat is most sweet: that is, his preaching is most sweet, because it heals the inward parts. And he is altogether desirable, because he is wholly God and wholly man, into whom angels desire to look. God in the majesty of the Father; man in the virginity of the mother; in the former, Creator; in the latter, Savior. Such as I have described is my beloved; and, O you who ought to be daughters of Jerusalem, this is my friend. For the more devotedly anyone loves God, the more intimately he has God as his friend. As if she said: You must understand him to be such, if you wish to have him as your friend.

Where has your beloved gone? The Church from among the Jews, hearing that he is such, desires to become his bride and says: O fairest among women, where has your beloved gone? As if she said: [Col. 0536C] We thought that he was with us, but I see that he has departed. Show, therefore, to whom he has gone away from us; where has he turned? That is, to whom has he descended, so as to remain in those who love him? If you show us who are his seats, by imitating them we shall gain knowledge of him; then we, with you—that is, placed in your sect—shall seek him in word and deed. The Church from the Gentiles, hearing the desire of Judaism, shows it whom it ought to imitate, as follows:

## CHAPTER VI

VERS. 1.—My beloved has descended: that is, I make it manifest in the wondrous experience of the thing, into his garden, that is, into the Church. And because in the Church there are both grains and chaff, he says to what part he has descended, namely to the perfect, so that through them he may join others to himself—not that he is not also among the lesser members. And, so that it may appear clearly that he is there, he has descended to a bed of spices: that is, to the more perfect, in whom virtues are ordered as spices in beds. To feed in the gardens: that is, he descends to the more perfect [Col. 0536D] so that through them he may acquire virtues, who may become for him a garden in which he delights. And that he may gather lilies: that is, adorn in them the multitude of virtues.

VERS. 2–5.—I am my beloved’s: that is, because he descended to the bed so that through me he might acquire faithful people for himself, I obey my beloved, and my beloved, namely, helps me. He feeds—that is, delights—among lilies: that is, amid the whiteness of virtues. Fair: as though it were said, “Since I see in you this will, that you should make others sharers in me, you are therefore fair,” that is, without envy, my friend; sweet, that is, without the harshness of envy in thought; and lovely in deed, like Jerusalem, that is, like those who are now the vision of peace. Terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps. And because you are so fair to me, you are so terrible to the enemy as a battle-line of camps: that is, as soldiers when they are arranged for battle, where no place is left without defense; for thus we are all the more terrible to malignant spirits.

Turn away, turn away: as though he said, “And although I am [Col. 0537A] so fair that you seem able thereby to possess the fullness of my knowledge, nevertheless turn the eyes of your mind away from me”: that is, do not labor to possess complete knowledge of divinity. And because they have made me fly away—that is, withdraw—from your knowledge: that is, the more you investigate the nature of divinity, the less you seem to yourself to know. Therefore no one ought to labor to know more than is fitting, until we come into our homeland, where that which is partial shall be done away and we shall see as it were face to face.

Truly you are fair, because your hairs, that is, your faithful people, are like a flock ascending from virtue to virtue. By the flock we understand harmony of faith. Which appeared—namely, the head of Gilead: that is, through me, who am the head of Gilead, that is, the heap of testimony, to whom all martyrs are gathered. All with twin offspring: that is, all yours are in the love of God and Christ. By “barren” is meant that no good work is absent from them.

VERS. 6–8.—Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate. [Col. 0537B] The rind of a pomegranate is reddish, through which we denote sufferings; but within it is full of grains and white, whence we understand purity and the multitude of virtues. This is to say: Your cheeks, that is, your chaste preachers who destroy vices, are outwardly reddened by sufferings, inwardly cleansed in soul from vices and radiant in virtues. Apart from your hidden things: that is, you lack those things which ought to be hidden, namely heresy.

There are sixty queens. As if one asked: “Who are those daughters, queens, and concubines who will praise the bride’s beauty?” He replies: sixty, that is, those who observe the six works of mercy and the ten commandments of the Law. These, I say, are such queens as, through love and the contemplation of the heavenly Spirit, by the preaching of faith and truth and the font of sacred baptism, bear spiritual offspring for the eternal King. Eighty: that is, those who preach for earthly things. By the number eighty we denote the four regions of heaven and the same number on earth, and thus the whole world. As if it were said: Those who preach for the sake of any earthly things are [Col. 0537C] concubines—that is, teaching by preaching and baptizing Christ solely for carnal ends. And young women are without number. The young women are Churches, whom above he called daughters of Zion: that is, newly reborn in baptism. He says they are without number—neither eighty nor sixty—because, owing to the newness of faith, it cannot be fully perceived whether they are sixty or eighty.

My dove is one. As if he said: Although I praise my bride in each respect, she is nevertheless one both in faith and in the other virtues; my dove, that is, abounding in the gifts of the Holy Spirit; my perfect one, in every goodness; one, namely inwardly and outwardly, to her mother, that is, to the preachers who nourished her in faith; chosen for her mother, who bore her in faith. As if he said: One in faith and chosen among all sects, and in likeness to those who convert them from error to faith and those who afterward nourish them with the food of saving doctrine. And because she is such, the daughters [Col. 0537D] of Zion—that is, those newly converted to contemplation of the Lord—will see her; also the queens, that is, the perfect who rule themselves and do not ascend to Solomon’s bed for earthly gain but out of love for their husband; and the concubines, that is, earthly preachers, who preach not for love or honor of Christ but for earthly gain, will praise her. For although they preach indeed for the price of earthly things, nevertheless they bless the Church in praising it. The Church from among the Jews, hearing the Gentile Church so greatly praised by the bridegroom, marvels thus at its preaching.

VERS. 9.—Who is this who advances from virtue to virtue, and is fair as the dawn, because now the light of truth has risen in her, the darkness of ignorance having passed away? For dawn rises in the elect when the darkness of former perversity is driven away and it turns itself toward the splendor of new light. Therefore, in that light which is denoted by the coming of the strict Judge, the body of the condemned enemy does not see the rising of the dawn, because when the strict Judge comes for the judgment of recompense, each person, oppressed by the darkness of his dead, does not know with what brightness the light of the inner heart rises. [Col. 0538A] Then indeed my chosen one is carried up to the heights, that she may be illumined by the rays of divinity; and the more she is poured out by his regard, the more, with grace flashing forth, she is lifted above herself. The day is denoted, which, seeing a fuller light through the restoration of its bodies, is brought to completion. Thus the dawning of the dawn is the voice of the Lord making the Church bright; the reprobate do not know how to see him, because, oppressed by their evils, they are dragged into darkness from the sight of the strict Judge.

Fair as the moon: we denote a greater light in the moon, but perfect light through the sun. The moon receives light from the sun, as the Church does from Christ. And as the moon illumines the night, so the Church illumines the night of the world. As the sun alone shines and drives away every darkness, so the Church of the faithful alone shines in the world and drives away all the darkness of heretics, because it bears the image of its Creator in all righteousness and holiness. Terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps. Although the bride is so fair, she is nevertheless terrible to the powers of the air in unity, charity, faith, and hope.

VERS. 10–12.—I descended into the garden of nuts. Christ and his Church resume the words which they had addressed to Judaism. As if he said: Because the bride is such that queens, concubines, and daughters deservedly praise her, I descended—that is, in effect, through miracles I shall make myself appear to have descended—to the garden of nuts, that is, to the more perfect. And although Christ is in all his members, he is nevertheless more perfectly in Peter than in Cornelius, in Martin than in Brictius. In the nut three things are denoted: bitterness outwardly in the husk, beneath which is the shell. [lacuna] of the flesh, while from the soul of the Creator comes the sweetness of virtues. That I might see: that is, through greater miraculous virtues I shall show; that I may make the fruits appear, namely the fruits of those who are valleys—that is, the humble—watered from both Testaments. And that I might inspect: that is, that I might make it be inspected whether they had flowered, namely whether those who are to become the vineyard—that is, the perfect—already had the beginnings of virtues; and whether they had begun to put forth [Col. 0538C] the beginnings of virtues, namely those who are to become pomegranates, that is, martyrs.

I did not know; my soul troubled me. The Synagogue, seeing Christ descend to his bride, grieves that it delayed so long; and thus it gives the reason why it had not previously come to faith. I did not know that the gifts of the Holy Spirit were given to human beings, nor that the Son of God had become incarnate, because my soul—that is, the perverse understanding which I possessed in my Law—troubled me: that is, did not allow me to turn to the knowledge of truth. Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, that we may behold you. Do not be troubled, but return to the knowledge of your Redeemer, who was promised to you especially in the Law and the Prophets. Return in purity of faith and perfection of works. O Shulammite, that is, captive now in the bond of unbelief, return to your Redeemer, that you may be saved.

## CHAPTER VII

VERS. 1.—What will you see in the Shulammite except the choirs of camps? You grieve for the hardened Synagogue; near [Col. 0538D] is the time when you will see in it choirs fighting against malignant spirits and praising God. How fair are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince! Now the praises of the Church are uttered by the bridegroom himself; and first in it are praised the steadfastness of works and the mortification of pleasures. He calls her also daughter of the prince, that is, of Christ, because of the grace of baptism and the nobility of virtues. The joint of your thighs is like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artisan. In the joint of the thighs is denoted the harmony of the two peoples, fruitful with spiritual offspring; this, like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artisan, is strengthened by the ineffable bounty of our Creator. Good works are expressed by necklaces.

VERS. 2–4.—Your navel, that is, the frailty of our weakness, becomes a rounded bowl when, warned by the awareness of our mortality and weakness, we zealously endeavor with ready mind to offer our neighbors the cup of the saving word. Your belly is like a heap of wheat surrounded [Col. 0539A] by lilies. A heap of wheat surrounded by lilies is an abundance of good work, which alone is gathered into the belly of everlasting memory. In wheat is expressed the multiplication of good work; in lilies, chastity.

Your two breasts. This verse has been discussed above. Your two breasts are the teachers of each people, twin fawns because of their one harmony. Your neck is like a tower. Again, teachers are denoted in the neck; they are compared to an ivory tower because of their firmness and beauty, and bestow upon the city of God both strength and splendor. Your eyes, that is, your overseers, are like pools in Heshbon, that is, abundant in wisdom. Heshbon is a city whose name means “girdle of sorrow.” As pools water the whole city, so preachers water the minds of faithful people, who are girt with sorrow—that is, with fasting and other labors—who are at the gate, namely at the entrance, of the daughter of the multitude: that is, of the faithful tending toward the great, namely God. Again, the eyes of the Church are teachers because of their providence, as the neck is because of nourishment. And they are rightly compared to pools, because they never cease [Col. 0539B] to provide the streams of doctrine to their hearers.

Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon. Again, in the nose are denoted the dispensers of God’s word, on account of discernment. A tower, because it holds a most eminent place in the Church and faces Damascus, that is, the bloodthirsty and impious; for Damascus is interpreted “drinking blood.”

VERS. 5–9.—Your head is like Carmel, and the locks of your head like royal purple bound to channels. In the head the mind is denoted; in the locks, cognitions. And as the members are governed by the head, so thoughts are governed by the mind, so that they may be occupied in Carmel—that is, in lofty things—and in the passion of Christ, expressed by the name “purple.” The channels are the hearts of the saints, in which such thoughts are occupied. How fair you are, that is, in spiritual virtues! Your stature, that is, the uprightness of good action, always tends toward victory. The breasts are compared to teachers because of the milk of first instruction; and they are equated with clusters because of the mysteries of sweetest eternity. [Col. 0539C] I said: I shall climb the palm tree. For the most victorious cross is openly compared to the palm, upon which Christ, ascending, grasped the fruit: that is, the gifts which he bestowed upon the holy Church. Therefore from that time the cluster of the vine sprouted: that is, holy teachers, who abounded in greater knowledge and grace after the cross and resurrection of the Savior. And the fragrance of your mouth is like apples; your throat like the finest wine. In the throat the voice of present teaching is denoted; in fragrance, the renown of one absent: that is, he gave to the apostles and greatest preachers power to heal, and not to another, upon whom he expended the whole care of service and love.

VERS. 10–13.—I am subject to my beloved, and his turning is toward me: he alone loves and helps me, lest I fail on the way. Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field; let us remain in the villages. For the Church is utterly unable to proceed by going out to do good works, or to remain by persevering in the exercise of good works, [Col. 0539D] or even to rise to the purpose of acting well, or to discern how far the minds of its hearers have advanced, unless by the grace of God, who said: “Behold, I am with you,” etc. (Matt. XXVIII, 20.) Again, by fields Christians are denoted; by villages, pagans; by vineyards, Churches; by flowers, faith; by fruits, virtues; by pomegranates, martyrs. There I shall give you my breasts: that is, the instructors of my little ones, because in all these things holy teachers make progress.

The mandrakes gave fragrance at our gates. Mandrakes are compared to the virtues of saints because of their many kinds of medicines. The gates of the Church are holy teachers. At gates such as these, mandrakes give fragrance when each of the chief persons brings forth from himself the palm of virtues. All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you. New and old fruits are the commands or promises of the New and Old Testaments, all of which the Church refers to his grace.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0540A]

VERS. 1–3.—Who will grant me that you be my brother? This is the voice of the saints of old who hoped for Christ’s advent in the flesh. Sucking the breasts of my mother: that is, being born and nourished in the Synagogue, according to the nature of the human condition. That I may find you outside. The beloved was within when “the Word was in the beginning” (John I, 1); outside when “the Word became flesh” (ibid., 14). And I shall kiss him: that is, I shall see him face to face and speak mouth to mouth. And now no one will despise me. Before Christ’s advent the Church was confined only within the narrow bounds of Judaea; after his ascension, it is throughout the whole world.

I shall take hold of you and lead you into my mother’s house, welcoming you in devotion when you come; and, when the dispensation of the flesh has been accomplished, welcoming you as you return into my mother’s house, where our mother is the heavenly Jerusalem. There you will teach me. You will make me hope for greater things than I had in the Law. And I shall give you a cup of spiced wine: that is, fervent love adorned with the varied spices of virtues. And the must of [Col. 0540B] my pomegranates: that is, the triumphant glory of martyrs, who do not hesitate to pass through sword and flames to you. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me. The left hand denotes the gifts of the Incarnation, and the right hand expresses the future joys of the saints with Christ.

VERS. 4, 5.—I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem. Who is this who ascends from the wilderness, abounding in delights? This is the voice of the Synagogue marveling how the Church had ascended from the wilderness of Gentile life into the bridegroom’s embrace, abounding in delights—that is, in the beauty of every gift—leaning upon her beloved: that is, referring all that she possesses to the grace of her beloved, in whom I set before myself alone the pattern to imitate. Under the apple tree I raised you up. The bridegroom himself answers the Synagogue on behalf of his bride. Under the tree of the cross I recalled you from everlasting death. There your mother was corrupted; there your parent was violated: that is, the greater part of the people, by denying Christ and choosing Barabbas, was rejected at the cross.

VERS. 6–8.—Set me as a seal upon [Col. 0540C] your heart, as a seal upon your arm. We bind signs upon arm or finger in remembrance of some matter. By the heart thought is denoted, and by the arm action. For love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as hell. My love for you, O Synagogue, is strong even unto death, but your jealousy against me was hard as hell. Yet turn jealousy into love, and you will be bride, sister, and friend to me. Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame. The lamps of love are the hearts of the faithful: fire because of the fervor of the heart, flames because of the efficacy of action. Many waters could not extinguish charity, nor shall rivers overwhelm it. By many waters and rivers he means the onrushes of temptations. If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he would despise it as though it were nothing. The saints, indeed, despised all their substance as though it were nothing because of the greatness of love.

Our little sister has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken for? [Col. 0540D] This denotes the first times of the Church arising from the Gentiles, when it was still small and less fit to preach the word. As though the bridegroom had said to the Synagogue about her: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken for?” As if he said openly: The Church of the Gentiles is indeed small in number and not yet sufficient to undertake the mystery of the word.

VERS. 9.—If she is a wall, let us build silver battlements upon her. As if he said: If she has within herself some persons who are strong, brilliant in intellect, or trained in philosophy, we shall add to them silver battlements: that is, knowledge of the divine Scriptures. If she is a door, let us enclose it with boards of cedar. If there are simple people who nevertheless eagerly desire instruction, let us set before them examples of the righteous of old. Cedars denote the virtues of saints, and boards the breadth of charity. To these words she herself replies:

VERS. 10.—I am a wall. I am built of living stones. My breasts are like a tower, since I became before him as though in peace: that is, having teachers most strong as a tower, and able to nourish little ones. A vineyard belonged to the Peaceful One in her who has peoples. The vineyard, that is, the catholic Church abounding in the fruit of faith, belonged to the Peaceful One, namely Christ, who made all things peaceful, in the place that has peoples. He entrusted it to guardians: prophets, apostles, or angelic ranks. A man brings for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver: that is, in the eternal recompense of this vineyard he brings a thousand pieces of silver; that is, for the gaining of the heavenly kingdom he leaves behind all things of the world.

VERS. 11–12.—My vineyard is before me. Voice of the bridegroom. Yet although I commend you to other guardians, I always hold you in my presence, seeing and rewarding your devoted labor in all things. Your thousand, O Peaceful One. “Thousand,” with “pieces of silver” understood, as though he had said: Let those who leave all their possessions for love of me keep them reserved in peace—signifying the simpler people in the Church, who lose for God’s charity all their substance, denoted by the thousandfold number. And two hundred for those who guard its fruits, namely pieces of silver, [Col. 0541B] for those who guard its fruits, who are holy teachers: they leave all worldly things and never cease to labor in the word of preaching; they are rewarded with a double recompense, denoted by the hundredfold number.

Because our discourse must end, hear from me this final farewell. Always dwell in the garden of virtues, and know that your friends—that is, angelic spirits and the souls of saints—always behold you and rejoice in your progress.

VERS. 13, 14.—Make me hear your voice: that is, may the voice of your preaching, insofar as you are able, always be heard by me. To this the bride replies: Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag upon mountains of spices. As if she said openly: Since, appearing in the flesh, you bring me the commands and gifts of life, now that these have been accomplished, return to the bosom of the Father. O my beloved, be like a gazelle or a young stag upon mountains of spices. And let this be my consolation: because I cannot behold you in continual vision, at least remember to console me by frequent visitation.

Here ends the exposition of the Song of Songs.

Solomon sang this book with wondrous sweetness,

which contains the noble songs of bridegroom and bride,

and recounts their companions and faithful female companions of the bridal chamber.

[Col. 0542B] I pray you, young man, remember to commit these to your mind.

They sing to you the true precepts of everlasting life,

by which that man will make your vain trifles sound false and evil.

Singing here and there the praises of the Church and of Christ:

these songs are better than the false Maro’s great songs.  
*[The printed reading is corrupt: “minui [magni] falsi … Maronis.”]*

# THIRD LITURGICAL PART OF THE WORKS OF HONORIUS OF AUGUSTODUNUM

[Col. 0541]

# THE JEWEL OF THE SOUL, OR, On the Divine Offices and the Ancient Rite of Masses, and on the Canonical Hours and Solemnities of the Whole Year

*(Library of the Fathers, XX, p. 1046, from the edition issued in 1514 by Melchior Lotter, printer of the city of Leipzig.)*

## THE BRETHREN TO HONORIUS THE SOLITARY

[Col. 0541] The host keeping watch in the camps of the eternal King, toiling under the onslaught of vices attacking from every side, desires to be equipped by a suitable instructor in arms for triumph over vices and to know the sacraments of the divine offices. But, partly through lack of books and partly through the manifold occupation of affairs, we are quite unable to do so. We ask you, therefore, that, as in many other matters, so also in this undertaking you may be willing to assist us by your pen.

> **[Note: [Col. 0541] John Trithemius, praising this opening, confirms the author; and the style, corresponding to his other little works, also indicates it.]**

## HONORIUS’S RESPONSE

[Col. 0541] After, with Christ’s favor, I had traversed the sea of Scripture in a favorable course to its utmost extent, and had scarcely brought my shipwreck-prone little vessel, borne with much toil through shoals and pirates, to the desired shore, you inhabitants of Zion thrust me again into the waves of thought and allow me neither to recover my strength nor to repair the ship’s equipment. For you say that now is the time for labor and afterward for rest; now the time for sowing, later for receiving fruit. Compelled by this hope, I have undertaken a burden exceeding my powers. Sustain me with your prayers as I set out on my voyage, so that, having laid aside the weight of sins, I may be permitted to reach with fixed anchor the desired harbor of rest. Therefore, at your command, I loose the ropes of words from the harbor of leisure, drive the battered little boat of my pen into the storms of meditations, [Col. 0543] spread the sails of meanings to the wind, and commit the hope of seed to it. May he grant a favorable course, who by his nod calms both sea and winds.

## Honorius’s Preface to *The Jewel of the Soul*

[Col. 0543] It grieves me to consider in mind the many who are seized by madness, who are not ashamed to investigate with the utmost effort the abominable fictions of poets and the deceptive arguments of philosophers—things which ordinarily bind the mind, thereby drawn away, in the inextricable knots of vices—while they utterly ignore the religion of Christian profession, through which the soul may reign forever with God. For it is the height of folly to wish to know the laws of a tyrant and not to know the decrees of the supreme emperor, and not to understand those things which one must necessarily do every day.

What, indeed, does Hector’s battle, Plato’s disputation, Maro’s songs, or Naso’s dirges profit the soul? Those poets now shriek with their like in the prison of infernal Babylon under Pluto’s cruel rule. But God’s wisdom heaps the greatest glory upon one who continually chews over, by investigating, the deeds and writings of prophets and apostles; no one doubts that they now rejoice in the palace of heavenly Jerusalem with the King of glory. For, in the judgment of the wise, the difference between one who understands and one who does not understand is as great as that between one who sees and one who is blind. For one who does not understand what he does is like a blind man who does not know where he is going, and like Tantalus perishes of thirst amid waters. And although the simplicity of the faithful pleases our God, he approves the understanding of the wise as much as light before darkness. For this reason, as you commanded, I have produced a little book *On the Divine Offices*, to which I gave the title *The Jewel of the Soul*. For as gold is adorned by a jewel, so the soul is adorned by divine office.

# BOOK ONE: ON THE SACRIFICE OF THE MASS AND THE MINISTERS OF THE CHURCH

[Col. 0543]

## CHAPTER I.—Outline of the matters to be treated in four books

[Col. 0543A]

First, then, let us consider the Mass, through which life is restored to us; the Church, in which it is performed; and the ministers of the Church, through whom it is celebrated. Next, let us discuss the (remaining) Hours, which are the due of our service. Third, let us speak of the solemnities of the year. Fourth, let us duly add a discussion of the harmony of the offices.

## CHAPTER II.—On the Mass

The Mass received its name for four reasons: two from embassy, and two from dismissal. For *missa* is called an embassy: first, because in its office Christ’s embassy is represented to us, by which he exercised an embassy from the Father for the human race. Second, *missa* is called an embassy because in it the priest performs an embassy to the Lord on behalf of the Church. It is called *missa* from dismissal: first, because the people, who assemble as though for judgment, are dismissed by the judge when the case has been completed. Second, it is called from dismissal because the gathering of the people, which is bound, as it were, by law to attend Vespers and Matins, is dismissed once the sacrifice has been celebrated.

## CHAPTER III.—On the first office

The Mass is divided into seven offices. In the first of these Christ’s embassy is performed, which Moses is known to have prefigured: he is read as god of the Gentiles, pope of priests, and king of peoples. For he is established by God as god to Pharaoh, prophet to Aaron the priest, and leader of the people. He exercises God’s embassy in Egypt; is received by the elders and the people; gathers the scattered people; subdues Egypt by signs; frees those oppressed by the tyrant from harsh servitude; leads them out of Egypt; and brings them into the land of promise. Thus Christ, God of gods, priest of priests, [Col. 0544A] king of kings, exercises the Father’s embassy in the world; he is received by angels and shepherds, who bear the figure of the Church. He gathers into one faith the children of God who were scattered; he subjugates the world by diverse signs; freeing those oppressed by the devil, he leads them out of hell and brings them into the homeland of paradise. The bishop’s procession, which bears Christ’s figure, represents all this to us.

## CHAPTER IV.—On the bishop’s procession

After the bells have sounded, the pontiff proceeds vested; seven acolytes with lights go before him, after whom walk seven subdeacons with complete books. Again, after these come seven deacons, followed by twelve elders. After them go three acolytes with censers carrying incense. [Col. 0544B] After them the Gospel is borne before the bishop; he follows it, walking between two persons, and the leading men with the people accompany him. When he enters the choir, the singers receive him with the verse, “Glory be to the Father”; he gives them peace, then goes to the altar. When the chant has ended, he says the prayer and then proceeds to sit down. Some of the ministers sit with him; others stand beside him. This presents Christ’s presence to us, as it were.

## CHAPTER V.—The significance of bells
The bells are the prophets. The bells rang because the prophets foretold Christ’s coming. The pontiff enters the church, and Christ enters this world—that is, the Church. The bishop comes forth vested from the sacristy, and Christ came forth from the Virgin’s womb, clothed in beauty, like a bridegroom from his chamber [Col. 0544C]. The deacons, subdeacons, and acolytes who precede the bishop signify the prophets, the wise men [Col. 0545A], and the scribes, who announced to the world Christ’s coming in the flesh. The deacons signify the prophets, who preach to the people that Christ has already come and is yet to come, and who proclaim from the Gospel the life to come. The subdeacons with their plenaries represent the wise, who declared that in Christ the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily. “Wisdom,” that is, the subdeacons, goes “in the midst of maidens playing tambourines,” so as to teach whom the tambourine-players ought to praise. The tambourine-players are the singers resounding with praises. The maidens are the new churches praising God, their flesh subdued. The acolytes with lights bear the type of the Scribes, who, by expounding the Scriptures, ministered the light of knowledge to the faithful. Each group is accordingly assigned seven, because through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit the mysteries [Col. 0545B] of the Mass are accomplished. The elders, with the chaplains who follow them, are understood to be the twelve apostles. The three acolytes who carry censers with incense are the three Magi, who offered gifts to Christ at his birth. The Gospel is carried before the bishop because through Christ’s teaching a way to life is prepared for us. The bishop is escorted by two, and Christ is borne into the world by the two Testaments through prophets and apostles. The crowd of people accompanies the bishop because the people of the faithful strive to follow Christ to heavenly things. While the present office is being performed in the Church, no one sits, because those called to the worship of God are assigned to Christ’s labor.

## CHAPTER VI.—On the Chariot of God

[Col. 0545C] Meanwhile, while the choir sings, the bishop proceeds to the solemnity as though borne in a chariot, because God’s chariot is read to be manifold, with tens of thousands, and the bishop’s retinue is distinguished by ten orders: the first order is the doorkeepers; the second, readers; the third, exorcists; the fourth, acolytes; the fifth, subdeacons; the sixth, deacons; the seventh, presbyters; the eighth, singers; the ninth, laymen; the tenth, women. Thus Christ entered the world while the chorus of prophets sang, borne in the chariot of Scripture and accompanied by the orders of saints. The singers receive the approaching bishop with *Gloria Patri* (“Glory be to the Father”), and the angels received Christ as he came with *Gloria in excelsis* (“Glory in the highest”). Two choirs sing praises together because the two peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles, met Christ as he came with praises.

[Col. 0545D] By the singing of the Introit is understood the praise of the Church from the Jews; by the *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”), the praise of the Church from the Gentiles. By the *Gloria in excelsis*, moreover, is understood the harmonious praise of both in faith in the Trinity, for the attainment of equality with angelic dignity. By the Introit, too, the order of the patriarchs is represented to us, through whom the Christ who was to come was prefigured. By the prophetic verse the order of the prophets is indicated, through whom Christ’s birth was foretold. By the *Gloria Patri* the apostolic order is recalled, through whom Christ is preached as having already come, and by whom the Trinity is also made known to the Church. By the Introit repeated a second time the order of doctors is denoted, through whom Christ is declared still to be coming for judgment. Further, by the *Kyrie eleison* are signified peoples of diverse languages, by [Col. 0546A] whom Christ is praised together with the angels in the *Gloria in excelsis*.

## CHAPTER VII.—What the Bishop’s Entrance Signifies

As he enters, the bishop extends peace to the clergy, because Christ, entering the world, brought peace to humankind, which it had lost in the first parent. Then he enters the sanctuary, bows before the altar, prays, and makes confession. He implores forgiveness because Christ entered Jerusalem to suffer; he bowed himself to death in order to wash us; at the supper he prayed to the Father for the Church; and afterward he granted perfect forgiveness to Peter, penitent and confessing, or to the thief, and then to all the people.

After this he kisses two priests, because through Christ, the cornerstone, two walls are joined in one faith. Then he gives peace to the other ministers at the right [Col. 0546B], because Christ preached peace to those far away and to those near, and, coming from East and West, joined them in the bond of peace. He kisses the altar and the Gospel because through Christ’s passion human beings and angels are joined in peace. For by the altar the Jews are denoted; by the Gospel, the Gentiles.

After this, taking the censer, he censes the altar in the figure of the angel who in the Apocalypse stood at the altar with a golden censer, from which the smoke of aromatic offerings rose before the Lord. For Christ, the angel of great counsel, offered himself for us upon the altar of the cross; his body was the censer of the Church. From it God the Father received the sweetness of fragrance and became merciful to the world. The smoke of the aromatic offerings is the prayers of the saints, which rise to God above Christ the altar through the burning of charity, or through coals kindled by the illumination [Col. 0546C] of the Holy Spirit.

Then he kisses the altar because Christ was sacrificed on the altar of the cross for our peace. Then the *Gloria in excelsis* begins and the choir sings together, because through his death Christ restored to human beings the glory of angels, in which the joyful people of the saints loudly resound with praise. Then, turning toward the people, he says, *Pax vobis* (“Peace be with you”), because Christ, rising from the dead, restored peace to the Church and said to his own, “Peace be with you.” Then he says the prayer on the right-hand side because Christ has now passed from death to life and has brought us from exile into our homeland. The prayer signifies that blessing with which, as he was about to ascend to heaven, he blessed his own. When these things have been done, the bishop proceeds [Col. 0546D] to sit; and Christ, when all things had been duly accomplished, ascended into heaven and rests seated at the Father’s right hand. Some sit with the bishop, while others stand in attendance upon him, because some of the elect now rest with Christ, while very many still serve him here in labor.

## CHAPTER VIII.—What the Candle-stands Signify

When the bishop ascends to his seat, the candle-stands are moved from their places in a single line, except for the first, as far as the altar. By the candle-stands the various gifts of the Holy Spirit are expressed; by the one line is denoted the unity of the Holy Spirit in the individual gifts. It begins from the first because the Holy Spirit proceeds from Christ and reaches as far as the altar—that is, to the hearts of the elect.

## CHAPTER IX.—What the Ministers Signify

[Col. 0547A]

The deacons who precede the bishop and kiss the altar signify the righteous who suffered for truth before Christ’s coming. Then they stand upright behind the bishop, because many, following Christ’s footsteps, underwent death for him. Some stand at the right and others at the left, because the right signifies the contemplative life and the left the active life. Those standing at the right are serving Christ in the contemplative life; those standing at the left are serving Christ in the active life.

Two deacons go in turn, one after the other, to kiss the sides of the altar, because Christ sent his disciples two by two before his face into every town. Their kiss signifies their words as they entered: “Peace to this house”; the altar signifies the hearts of the elect. [Col. 0547B] Afterwards they return to the bishop, and the disciples returned to Christ, reporting the works of miracles. There ought to be as many subdeacons and acolytes as deacons. There are seven deacons because the apostles chose seven deacons for ministry. And because the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit accomplish the mysteries of the Mass, seven deacons also minister, because seven disciples labored at fishing after the resurrection, and he invited them to breakfast.

By the seven subdeacons are understood the seven pillars of Wisdom’s house. By the seven acolytes are understood the seven lamps of the tabernacle, or the seven lampstands in the Apocalypse. If five deacons minister, they signify the five who were with the Lord at the raising of the girl (Mark 5). Five [Col. 0547C] subdeacons serve because five parts of Scripture taught these mysteries. For the Old Testament is divided into the Law and the Prophets; the New is divided into the Acts of the Apostles, their Epistles, and the prophecy of the Apocalypse. There are five acolytes because the five books of Moses testified to these mysteries.

If three deacons minister, they signify the three apostles who were with the Lord on the mountain at the Transfiguration. There are three subdeacons because the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets foretold these mysteries. Three acolytes serve because faith, hope, and charity accomplish these mysteries. If one deacon ministers, he signifies that young man who remained with the Lord in his passion, namely John, when, having cast off the linen cloth, [Col. 0547D] he fled naked (Mark 14); by one deacon Stephen is also signified, who alone attained Christ through his death.

## CHAPTER X.—What the Subdeacon Signifies

One subdeacon serves because the whole of Scripture taught this mystery. One acolyte serves because this mystery is accomplished only in the unity of the Church.

## CHAPTER XI.—What the Acolytes Signify

The acolytes hold lights as far as the *Kyrie eleison*, because doctors, the illuminators of the Church, ought to provide the faithful with light by word and example, until they themselves begin to invoke the Lord according to his ways and recognize Christ, the true light, as enlightening every soul. The seven candles are the seven gifts of the Holy [Col. 0548A] Spirit. The candle standing in the middle is Christ. Then the lights are arranged in order toward the bishop because the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are distributed to the Church through Christ. The acolyte who carries the censer signifies Joseph, who carried Christ about everywhere; he also signifies the apostle Paul, who by preaching carried Christ’s fragrance throughout the whole world. It is not permitted for six, four, or two to minister, because an even number can be divided and the Church ought not to be divided; therefore God delights in an odd number (Virgil, *Eclogues* VIII.75).

## CHAPTER XII.—On the Censer

The censer signifies the Lord’s body; the incense, his divinity; the fire, the Holy Spirit. If it is golden, it signifies his divinity [Col. 0548B] surpassing all things; if silver, it displays his humanity shining with all holiness; if bronze, it declares his flesh, fragile for our sake; if iron, it indicates his flesh, having died, overcoming death in the resurrection. If the censer has four lines, it signifies that the Lord’s body consists of four elements and was full of four virtues—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. The fifth line, which separates the censer from itself [i.e. its parts from one another], signifies Christ’s soul, which by death had separated itself from the body. But if it is held together by three lines, it signifies that human flesh, a rational soul, and the divinity of the Word make one person of Christ; the fourth, which divides the parts, is the power that laid down the soul in death for the sheep. If, however, it is supported by only [Col. 0548C] one line, it signifies that he alone was begotten of a virgin without defilement and is proclaimed as “free among the dead” (Psalm 87 [Vulgate numbering]). The circle to which all these things are attached is the divinity by which all these things are contained, whose majesty is enclosed by no boundary.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On the Church and the Second Office

In the preceding office the subject was Christ, our head; in the following one it is his body, the Church. Mary, Moses’ sister, prefigured it: when the people had been delivered, she led the singing and the crowd answered with song. Thus, while Christ is seated, the reader recites the Epistle from the pulpit and the choir resounds with song; because, while Christ is seated in heaven, the order of doctors sounded Scripture forth to the world [Col. 0548D], and every people everywhere sounded praise to Christ. A higher place is assigned to the bishop so that he may watch over and, as it were, guard the people, just as a place is provided for the vinedresser to guard the vineyard. Thus the Lord, seated high in heaven, guards his chariot—that is, his city, namely the Church.

## CHAPTER XIV.—On the Subdeacon

While the subdeacon reads, we customarily sit. The reading is preaching; the sitting and response of the hearers are the confession of believers. Readers and singers are the Lord’s merchants. While the subdeacon reads the Epistle, the candles are arranged in reverse order, from east to west, because the light of teaching was spread from East to West—that is, through the whole world—by the apostles. By the Gradual is understood the conversion of the Church from the Jews; [Col. 0549A] by the Verse is understood conversion from the Gentiles. By the *Alleluia* is expressed the joy of both in faith. The Sequence signifies the song of victory by which the souls of the righteous exult in the living God for their deliverance, just as the children of Israel sang a song of victory for their rescue. Hence some make a long *pneuma* [melismatic vocalization] with instruments in jubilation, which is called a *jubilus*, because they imitate the applause of rejoicing victors.

## CHAPTER XV.—On the Bishop

The bishop, seated at the right of the altar, observes with his face turned toward the choir as they labor, because Christ, seated at the right hand of God, looks with his face turned toward the Church into the heart of each person and promises to reward those laboring for him. Thus, when Stephen labored for him (Acts 7), he rose to aid him.

## CHAPTER XVI.—On the Singers

[Col. 0549B]

The singers who direct the choirs are the apostles who instructed the churches in God’s praises. Those who sing the Gradual signify those who serve Christ in the active life. They stand singing on the steps because the righteous will go from virtue to virtue on the ladder of charity. Those who sing the *Alleluia* signify those who praise Christ in the contemplative life. These stand higher while singing because such persons ascend into heavenly things by contemplation upon the height of virtues. The choirs shall sing the Sequence in alternation because the multitudes of angels and human beings in the house of God shall praise the Lord for ever and ever.

## CHAPTER XVII.—On the Ploughing Servant

It is read in the Gospel concerning the ploughing servant that, when the work in the field has been completed [Col. 0549C], he returns home and, after rendering service to his master, reclines at the banquet (Luke 17). God’s field is the hearts of the faithful; the ploughing servant is the order of preachers. By the reader of the Epistle are expressed the doctors who cultivated God’s field by preaching; by the response, the faithful who, responding through good works, brought forth the fruit of righteousness. The plough is our service. The oxen drawing from either side are those singing to the Lord with all their strength on both sides. The precentor, who encourages the singers by hand and voice, is the servant who, threatening the oxen with a goad, cheers the oxen with a sweet voice.

The reader gives the Lord’s law to hearers who have recently been called through the offices of the singers in God’s school to the wedding feast. “School” means a calling, in [Col. 0549D] which, if anyone still lies numb with the deaf ears of the heart, the singer sounds with a lofty trumpet the sweetness of melody in his ear, that he may be awakened. The singers who respond to the first singer are the voice of hearers as though awakening and praising the Lord. The Verse is the ploughing servant, who by the sweetness of modulation ploughs the hearts of the carnal, which open like a furrow in confession by voice and tears. They plough who cleave hearts with the plough of compunction; in the reading the hearer is fed, as it were, like an ox. The ox is fed for this purpose: that the work of agriculture may be performed by it. The ox is the preacher; the singer is, in a manner, the oxherd, who cheers the oxen so that they may draw the plough more gladly—that is, he urges the singers to sing more joyfully. The earth is cleft when the hearts of the hearers are pierced with compunction. Such [Col. 0550A] laborers, when they return from the field of this world, enter the eternal banquet with their Lord.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On Another Figure

The bishop sits during three portions of the Mass: namely, while the Epistle is read and while the Gradual and *Alleluia* are sung, because Christ is said to have sat for three days among the doctors in the temple. The subdeacon who reads the Epistle signifies John the Baptist, who preached before Christ. For by the Epistle John’s preaching is understood; by the Gospel, Christ’s preaching is indicated. Therefore the Epistle precedes the Gospel because John’s preaching came first. And, just as John is remembered as Christ’s forerunner, so the Epistle comes before the Gospel, which is Christ’s. The Gospel is proclaimed in a higher place than the Epistle is read because Christ’s preaching [Col. 0550B] is acknowledged to be more worthy than John’s. Nevertheless, the subdeacon reads in the same pulpit as the deacon because all the people supposed John to be Christ. The Gradual signifies the calling of the apostles, by which they turned to Christ; the *Alleluia*, their joy at Christ’s presence and his miracles; and the Sequence, the jubilation of their souls, by which they exulted in the promised hope. Here the bishop ordains the ministers of the Church because Moses ordained Aaron and the Levites for the ministry of the tabernacle, and Christ ordained the seventy-two whom he sent out to preach.

## CHAPTER XIX.—On the Third Office

In the third office the subject returns to the head, and Christ’s preaching is recalled to our memory. Moses prefigured this office when he ascended the mountain to the Lord and received from him the tablets of the covenant. The Lord set forth the commandments while all the people listened; Moses expounded the statutes of the law; and the people answered that they would keep them all (Exodus 19). Thus the deacon goes to the bishop, receives the book from the altar, and reads before the people the Gospel, in which the divine commandments are contained. The bishop, preaching to the people, expounds these things; and the people, through *Kyrie eleison*, while the clergy through *Credo in unum Deum* (“I believe in one God”), pledge themselves to observe all of them. But how this was performed through Christ and the apostles must be stated briefly.

## CHAPTER XX.—On the Deacon

By the bishop Christ is represented to us; by [Col. 0550D] the deacon, the apostolic order. The deacon who reads is Peter, who answers for all. The bishop blesses the deacon who is about to read because Christ, having summoned the apostles, filled them with blessing when he gave them power over all demons and sent them to preach the kingdom of God (Luke 9). The deacon receives the Gospel from the altar and proceeds to read it because “from Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2). In this place, indeed, the altar signifies Jerusalem, where the apostles received from the Lord the word of preaching and, going forth, preached throughout the whole earth.

The deacon carries the book on his left arm because the left signifies the present life. In this life alone, moreover, the Gospel ought to be preached, because in the life to come no one requires instruction: for all, from the least to the greatest, [Col. 0551A] shall know the Lord. He ascends the ambo from the southern side because Christ came to Jerusalem from Bethlehem, which is to the south; hence it is said: “God shall come from the south” (Habakkuk 3).

## CHAPTER XXI.—What the Two Candles Signify

Two candles precede the Gospel because the Law and the Prophets preceded it and foretold the Gospel. The two lampstands carried before it are the two commandments of charity taught through the Gospel. The two acolytes carrying them are Moses and Elijah, among whom the Lord shone like the sun on the mountain (Matthew 17; Mark 9; Luke 9). While the Gospel is read, the candles are set upon the floor because the shadows of the Law and the enigmas of the prophets are understood by the lowly through the light of the Gospel. After the Gospel has been read, [Col. 0551B] the candles are extinguished, when those things spiritually set forth are understood through the light of the Gospel. The censer is carried before the Gospel because Christ, an odor of sweetness, sacrificed for us in the fire of his passion, is preached.

## CHAPTER XXII.—What Is Signified by the Gospel Being Read from the Ambo

The Gospel is read in a high place because Christ is said to have preached on a mountain. It is also read on high because the evangelical precepts are lofty, and by them the height of heaven is climbed. A light burns before the Gospel because evangelical teaching illuminates the Church, and because the Word of God provides us a light unto life. According to the order, the deacon turns southward while reading the Gospel because men customarily stand in this part, to whom spiritual things ought to be preached. For men signify spiritual persons, and the south signifies the Holy Spirit.

But now, according to the customary practice, he turns northward, where women stand, who signify carnal persons, because the Gospel calls carnal persons to spiritual things. The north also signifies the devil, who is assailed through the Gospel. For by the north is denoted the unbelieving people [Col. 0551C] to whom the Gospel is preached, that it may be converted to Christ.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—On the Deacon’s Signs and Greeting

When the deacon has ascended the lectern, he first greets the people with *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), because whenever the apostles entered a house to preach, they first greeted their hearers with *Pax huic domui* (“Peace to this house”). When he says, *Sequentia sancti Evangelii* (“The continuation of the holy Gospel”), he makes the sign of the holy cross upon his forehead, in which is the seat of shame. By this he indicates that he is not ashamed of the Lord’s words. For whoever is ashamed of the Lord’s sayings, the Son will be ashamed of that person before the Father and the angels at judgment (Luke 9). Indeed, the cross and the Gospel were for unbelievers a reproach of great shame.

Then he signs his mouth because he declares that he confesses God’s words with his mouth, since confession with the mouth is made unto salvation (Romans 10). Next he signs his heart, so that he may exclude from himself the spirit of pride and make known unto righteousness those things which he confesses with his mouth. Thus, by signing the heart is understood faith in the word; by signing the mouth, confession of Christ; by signing the forehead, the practice of the Gospel. [Col. 0552A] Then clergy and people sign themselves and cry out, *Gloria tibi, Domine* (“Glory to you, O Lord”), because they declare that they worship Christ crucified and will obey his words. Thus, when the apostles preached the words of God, the peoples praised the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—On the Staves

While the Gospel is read, the staves are laid down, because when the Gospel was preached, legal observances were laid aside by the people. For by a precept of the Law, those who ate the Paschal lamb while journeying toward their homeland held staves in their hands. According to this custom, the singers are known to hold staves during the office of the Mass while the true Paschal Lamb is blessed, signifying that those who desire to hasten to the eternal homeland and to the feast of angels ought to defend themselves by eating the heavenly Lamb [Col. 0552B] and by staves against enemies—that is, by the sentences of Scripture against demons. They lay them down during the Gospel because, when they come to Christ, whom the Gospel signifies, they will need no supports from the Scriptures.

By the staves priests also are denoted, by whose teaching those weak in faith are supported. These staves are laid down in the Gospel because the teachings of all priests are set after Christ’s Gospel. Then the head-coverings also are removed because, when Christ preached the Gospel, the veils of the Law were removed. We too uncover our heads because with unveiled face, not in an enigma, we see the Lord in the Gospel (2 Corinthians 3). After the Gospel has been read, the deacon returns to the bishop and offers him the book to kiss; he immediately replaces it in its place because [Col. 0552C] the apostles, after accomplishing their preaching, returned to Christ. They also reported that demons had been subjected in his name, as though they restored the book to its place when they attributed everything not to themselves but to the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXV.—On the Sermon

Then the bishop preaches to the people because, after Christ had become known to the people through the apostles, he himself began to preach to all. The bishop instructs the people concerning repentance, faith, and confession because Christ taught repentance, faith in God, and remission of sins through confession and baptism. After this the people sing *Kyrie eleison* and the clergy *Credo in unum Deum*, because they affirm that they believe what the deacon [Col. 0552D] read and what the bishop preached. Thus, after Christ and the apostles taught the people, praises resounded to God when faith had been received. Meanwhile the Gospel, with incense, is carried through the choir and offered to each person to kiss, because the apostles carried Christ—the odor of life—through the world and, by his word, offered eternal peace to all nations.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—On the Fourth Office and the Church

In the fourth office the signification returns to Christ’s body, that is, the Church, and sets forth its action to us. The people of Israel formerly bore its figure when they offered various gifts to Moses as he came down from the mountain, in order to make the tabernacle, in which an altar was made upon which the priest [Col. 0553A] sacrificed the people’s offerings. Thus, when the bishop comes down from the pulpit, the people offer various offerings, for which the priest and ministers will sacrifice upon the altar with singing. Thus, when Christ, about to suffer in Jerusalem, came down from the Mount of Olives, the crowd met him and offered palms and flowers with a song of praise; for these he offered himself as a sacrifice upon the altar of the cross. The pontiff represents Christ; the ministers, the crowd of disciples. The people making offerings are those meeting him with palms; the singers singing are those resounding *Hosanna*.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—On Sacrifice

Some of the people sacrifice gold, some silver, some other substance. The priest and ministers offer bread and wine with water. Those who offer gold [Col. 0553B] signify the Magi, who offered gold to the Lord. Those who offer silver signify those who put money into the treasury. Those who sacrifice from other things are those who sent the Lord necessities, which Judas carried. They also signify those who, through the apostles Paul and Barnabas, sent offerings to the apostles at Jerusalem. Those who offer bread are those who devote their spirit to the Lord as a sacrifice of praise. Those who offer wine are those who lay down their souls for their brethren. Those who offer water are those who surrender their bodies to punishment for Christ.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—On the Three Sacrifices

First men offer, signifying those strong in Christ, [Col. 0553C] because in the primitive Church the righteous, having endured harsh things under persecutors, fell as Christ’s victims. Then women sacrifice, signifying those more frail, because in times of peace the faithful sacrifice to the Lord not themselves but an offering of praise. Last of all priests and ministers offer, who are the teachers and leaders of the people, because under Antichrist the faithful will offer themselves to Christ as a wine-sacrifice through diverse torments.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—On the Seven Legal Sacrifices

The ancients offered seven sacrifices according to the Law, which Christians still imitate. For the rite of the Synagogue has passed into the religion of the Church, and the sacrifices of the carnal people have been transformed into [Col. 0553D] spiritual observance. They are these: the legal sacrifice, the voluntary sacrifice, the sacrifice for sin, the sacrifice of thanksgiving, gifts, vows, and whole burnt offerings. The person who offered tithes or firstfruits, or things prescribed by the Law, offered a legal sacrifice. The person who freely offered something of his goods to God offered a voluntary sacrifice. The person who, after transgressing a commandment of the Law, offered a goat, offered a sacrifice for sin. The person who offered a gift to God for victory offered a sacrifice of thanksgiving. The person who contributed something for the adornment of the temple offered gifts. The person who, placed in the peril of war, vowed something to God and afterward paid it, offered vows. The person who, offering a lamb, burned it all upon the altar offered whole burnt offerings. For a *holocaust* is so called because it is wholly burned.

## CHAPTER XXX.—On the Sacrifice of Christians

[Col. 0554A]

Thus Christians offer legal sacrifice when they give God tithes of their possessions. They offer voluntary sacrifice when they contribute something of their possessions to those serving God. They offer for sin when, for penance imposed, they give something to priests, religious persons, or the needy. They offer in thanksgiving when they offer something to God for rank or for some grace bestowed. They offer gifts when they contribute something toward church buildings or their adornment. They offer vows when, placed in war, shipwreck, or some danger, they vow something which, once delivered, they offer to God and the saints. Those offer whole burnt offerings who leave the world and distribute all their possessions either to the needy or contribute them to monasteries. The people offer these sacrifices. [Col. 0554B] But priests and ministers, as Christ instituted, offer bread and wine.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—On the Sacrifice of Bread

This sacrifice is made from bread because Christ declared himself the living bread (John 6), whom Scripture foretold as the bread of angels (Psalm 77 [Vulgate numbering]). This bread is made without leaven because Christ was without sin. But bread is made from leaven because Christ declared himself a grain of wheat. The grain, however, is threshed out from its husk, dried by insults and reproaches, ground by Jews and Gentiles like two millstones, sifted, sprinkled, and kneaded together, when, separated from his own, drenched with his own blood, he was fastened to the cross. There, like bread [Col. 0554C] baked in the fire of passion, he was changed into immortality.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—On the Church and Its Signification

Christ’s body is therefore made from bread, which is made from many grains, because the Church, Christ’s body, is nourished by it, and the Church is gathered from many elect persons. These grains—that is, the elect—are threshed out from the husk of their former life by the flail of preaching; dried by penitence, they are ground as if by two millstones, while they are instructed little by little through examination in the two laws. Sifted, sprinkled, and kneaded together, they are separated from unbelievers, reborn through the water of baptism, and joined in faith through the bond of charity by the Holy Spirit. Like loaves baked in an oven, they are changed to whiteness when, tested in the furnace of tribulation, they are refashioned into God’s image. [Col. 0554D] Made into bread in this way, they are nourished by Christ’s bread, and they shall not die eternally.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—On the Sacrifice of Wine

This sacrament is made from wine because Christ called himself the vine, and Scripture declares him the wine of joy. A grape, pressed in a winepress by two pieces of wood, is liquefied into wine; and Christ, pressed by the two beams of the cross, had his blood poured forth as drink for the faithful. Christ’s blood is therefore made from wine, which is pressed from many grapes, because by it the Church, Christ’s body, is refreshed, and the Church is gathered from many righteous persons. It is trodden by the pressures of the world as in a winepress and incorporated into Christ through sufferings.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—On Water

[Col. 0555A]

This sacrifice is made from water because water came forth from Christ’s side, and the angel explained to John that the waters are peoples. Water is therefore mixed with wine because the people, redeemed by Christ’s blood and washed in the water of baptism, are made participants in Christ by the food of this bread and the drink of this wine. This bread is changed into flesh because Christ, the Paschal Lamb, is slain for us and our flesh is redeemed from death. The wine passes into blood because Christ, pouring out his blood, laid down his soul for us and cleansed from sins our soul, which dwells in the blood. This sacrament is not accomplished without water because this mystery is performed for the people alone, who are also daily nourished by it.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—On the Form of the Bread

[Col. 0555B]

The bread is formed in the shape of a denarius because Christ, the bread of life, was betrayed for the number of denarii, and because he is the true denarius to be given as a reward to those laboring in the vineyard. The image of the Lord with letters is therefore impressed upon this bread because the image and name of the emperor are inscribed upon a denarius; through this bread God’s image in us is restored, and our name is recorded in the book of life.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—Why Mass Is Sung Daily

Although Christ redeemed believers by his death once for all, the Church nevertheless necessarily repeats this sacrament every day for three reasons. One reason is that those laboring in the vineyard may daily be nourished by it; another, that those who are daily joined to the number of the faithful may by it be incorporated into Christ; the third, that the memory of Christ’s passion may daily be impressed upon faithful minds for imitation. It is offered in the following order.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—On the Subdeacon

The subdeacon carries the chalice in his left hand, the paten in his right, and the corporal above them, because in this place the subdeacon signifies Christ; the chalice, his passion; the left hand, the present life; the paten, the cross; the right hand, eternal life; and the corporal, the Church. Christ drank the chalice of passion in the present life, which he first asked the Father to take away from him. Through the cross he entered into the Father’s glory, and the Church never ceases to imitate his passion. The corporal is whitened with much labor, and the Church is conformed to Christ through many tribulations. [Col. 0555D] Our subdeacon, Christ, carried, as it were, the paten with the chalice when he bore the cross to his passion.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—On the Singers
One cantor offers the oblation with a cloth, and the wine with the cruet; another provides the water to be mixed with the wine. He who offers the wine signifies the Church from the Jews, which changed the rite of the Law into Christ’s sacrifice. He who offers the water signifies the Church from the Gentiles, which offered the Gentile people to Christ. These two also prefigure Enoch and Elijah, who will offer the Jewish people to Christ as a sacrifice. They offer the oblation not with bare hands but with cloths whitened through much labour, because Christ’s body is worthily received only by those who crucify their flesh with its vices and desires. [Col. 0556A] The cruet in which the wine is offered signifies our devotion, which is carried in the vessels of our hearts. Finally, the archdeacon, pouring water into the chalice, offers it to the bishop, because Christ, whom the deacon here signifies, joined the Church to himself in his Passion, offered her to the Father on the cross, and at the end will unite the body to its head, when he has delivered the kingdom to God the Father.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—On the priest’s prayer.

After receiving the sacrifice, the bishop, bowing before the altar, says the prayer *Receive, holy Trinity*, because Christ, having bowed down at the disciples’ feet after handing over the sacrifice at supper, stood before the table and prayed to the Father. Then he says, “Pray,” because Christ instructed the apostles to pray. [Col. 0556B] Thereupon he says the prayer over the offering secretly, because Christ prayed more fully in secret on the Mount of Olives, when an angel appeared strengthening him. The interval of silence after the Offertory signifies the time when Christ hid himself in Jerusalem before the Passion, like the paschal lamb, which the Jews kept enclosed on the tenth day of the moon and sacrificed on the fourteenth.

### CHAPTER XL.—On the Secret.

When the sacrifice has been arranged, the priest recites the prayer in silence, because this same sacrifice lay hidden in the sacrifices of the Fathers. For it was concealed in Abel’s lamb; in Abraham’s ram it had hidden itself in place of Isaac. It had concealed itself in the paschal lamb, the red heifer, and the scapegoat (Lev. XVI). Then the pontiff offers sacrifice for the people, because Christ offered himself for the Church. [Col. 0556C] Then the sacrifice is incensed, because Christ, an odour of sweetness, offered for us, is accepted by God.

### CHAPTER XLI.—On the Preface.

In the Preface there follows the sacrifice of the angels, who are believed to be present at this sacrifice. For they stand before the supreme Emperor as soldiers, and sing praises to their Emperor; distinguished by the thrice-repeated threefold cry, they honour the Trinity with a sacrifice of praise and continually offer, in imitation, a victim of jubilation. Therefore the priest also sings this aloud, because he represents the sacrifice of the angels, which is praise.

### CHAPTER XLII.—On the sacrifice of the angels.

The angels and archangels therefore praise God’s majesty; [Col. 0556D] the dominions adore it. Powers and principalities tremble in wonder. The heavens—that is, the thrones—and the virtues rejoice. Cherubim and seraphim celebrate together sweetly. David and Solomon imitated this sacrifice, the harmony of the angels: they ordained that hymns should resound at the Lord’s sacrifice through organs and other musical instruments, and that the people should cry out praises. Hence we still customarily make the organs resound in the office of sacrifice, while the clergy sing and the people cry aloud. The angels therefore offer the sacrifice of praise while the Holy Spirit sounds in harmony. “Holy” is repeated three times because the Trinity is praised together; “Lord God” is said once because the Unity is revered.
