Joined to the angels’ sacrifice is the sacrifice of the spirits of the righteous, who adore Christ’s humanity; and for the redemption of the human race there is sung: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” [Col. 0557A] This hymn is sung partly by angels and partly by human beings, because through Christ who is offered in sacrifice the human race is joined to the angels. For the praise of the angels is: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth. Heaven and earth are full of thy glory. Hosanna in the highest.” But the praise of humankind is: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest.” During this chant they make the sign of the cross, because they signify their reception of the sign of Christ, against whom there is contradiction.

### CHAPTER XLIII.—On the four orders.

It should be noted that males make their offerings first, because in the first age the patriarchs bore forward this sacrifice in their own sacrifices. Women offer second, because in the second age the Jews prefigured this [Col. 0557B] sacrifice through legal sacrifices. Priests offer third, because ministers offer: for in the third age the apostles received this very sacrifice and taught it to the faithful, who daily offer the seven sacrifices written above, because after this life angels with blessed human beings will praise the Lord for ever and ever.

### CHAPTER XLIV.—On the fifth office and Christ’s battle.

The fifth office is veiled by the wings of the cherubim. In it are represented the victim of the high priest and the battle of the King of glory. Moses prefigured this when he prayed on the mountain with arms outstretched, while Joshua—also called Jesus—was fighting Amalek, devastating the kingdom of the defeated enemy and bringing back the people with the joy of victory (Exod. XVII). Thus Christ, on the mount of the cross, prayed with arms outstretched for the unbelieving and contradicting people; [Col. 0557C] and, though conquered, as leader fought Amalek—that is, the devil—with the banner of the holy cross, devastated the kingdom of the defeated foe, despoiled hell after overcoming the malignant enemy, and recalled to heaven, with the glory of victory, the people rescued from darkness.

### CHAPTER XLV.—Mystery.

The bishop represents all this and seeks, as it were, to express it through dramatic vestments. For he represents Christ fixed on the cross when he recites the Canon with outstretched hands, as though fighting against Amalek (Exod. XVII), while he imitates Christ’s Passion against the devil by signs of crosses. The ministers, meanwhile, are arranged on either side like ranks of combatants: the deacons behind the bishop, the subdeacons behind the altar. [Col. 0557D] The army returns in triumph, because, having received communion, it returns joyfully to its own place.

### CHAPTER XLVI.—On Christ’s Passion.

In this office Christ’s Passion is enacted upon the cross of chrism: the altar is understood as the cross, upon which the corporal is spread out in the form of Christ’s body. The corporal is made from the pure linen of the earth and, through much labour, is turned white; Christ’s body is born from the pure Virgin and, through many sufferings, is restored to the brightness of the resurrection. When the corporal is folded, neither its beginning nor its end appears, because Christ’s divinity lacks a beginning and has no end. The oblation is placed upon it because flesh assumed by divinity is fixed to the cross. The chalice with wine and water is placed on the right, [Col. 0558A] because blood with water is proclaimed to have flowed from Christ’s side. When the priest says, “This oblation therefore,” he bows down toward the altar, because there the Passion begins: Christ had bowed himself obedient to the Father, for us, down to the altar of the cross (Phil. II). Then the oblation or chalice is raised in the priest’s hand, because Christ is lifted onto the cross for our salvation and his blood is sacrificed for our redemption.

Meanwhile, the deacons standing behind the bishop bear the figure of the apostles, who all fled when they abandoned him during the Lord’s Passion. But the subdeacons standing behind the altar, opposite the bishop, represent the women and acquaintances who, standing at a distance, saw Jesus’ Passion. The priest bows before the altar when he says, “Humbly we beseech thee,” because there Christ’s Passion ends and Christ, bowing his head, gave up the spirit. [Col. 0558B] Within the Canon the deacon washes his hands, because Pilate washed his hands during the Lord’s Passion, declaring himself as clean of Christ’s blood as his hands were clean of dirt. The priest raises his voice when he says, “To us also sinners,” signifying that the Church, already formed from Christ’s side, broke forth in confession of the Redeemer, when through the voice of the centurion she cried thus: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. XXVII).

### CHAPTER XLVII.—On Joseph.

When the priest says, “Through all ages of ages,” the deacon comes, raises the chalice before him, covers part of it with a cloth, places it on the altar, and covers it with the corporal. In this he represents Joseph of Arimathea, who took down Christ’s body, covered his face with a sudarium, [Col. 0558C] laid him in the tomb, and covered it with a stone. Here the oblation and chalice are covered with the corporal, signifying the clean linen cloth in which Joseph wrapped Christ’s body. The chalice here signifies the tomb; the paten, the stone that had closed the tomb. The three sections—namely, “Let us pray,” the commandments, the Lord’s Prayer, and “Deliver us, Lord”—signify the three days during which Christ rested in the tomb.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.—On the acolyte who holds the paten, and how he figures Nicodemus.

Within the Canon the acolyte holds the wrapped paten, which here the subdeacon carries down. The subdeacon gives it to the archdeacon, who, having kissed it, hands it to one of the deacons to hold and to break the Lord’s body upon it. [Col. 0558D] The acolyte who held the paten bears the likeness of Nicodemus, who brought myrrh and aloes for the Lord’s burial (John XIX). Moreover, the subdeacon and archdeacon, together with the other deacon holding the paten, represent the three Marys, who came to the tomb with spices. While the seven petitions are said in the Lord’s Prayer, the deacons stand bowed, waiting to be strengthened by communion, because the apostles waited seven weeks after Christ’s death to be strengthened by the Holy Spirit. The subdeacons meanwhile rest, because the women were silent on the Sabbath, which is the seventh day.

### CHAPTER XLIX.—On the cross.

[Col. 0559A] This sacrament is performed solely through the cross, because Christ hung as the Father’s sacrifice on the cross and redeemed the fourfold world on the cross. Six orders of crosses are made because the world was completed in six days and Christ’s body is restored by the number six. It is blessed by an odd number, which cannot be divided into two equal parts, because Christ’s enduring body is not divided. Either we make three crosses and express faith in the Trinity, or we sign with five and denote Christ’s fivefold Passion. Through the six orders we comprehend all the ages of the world, which we express as united to Christ through the cross.

### CHAPTER L.—On the first order and the three crosses.

In the first order, we make three crosses where we say, “These gifts,” and indicate the first age before the Law. We distinguish it by three intervals: one from Adam to Noah, another from Noah to Abraham, and the third from Abraham to Moses. [Col. 0559B] In these intervals the righteous, in faith in the Trinity, greeted Christ from afar through their sacrifices and suffered many torments in this faith. In the first age Abel offered Christ in the lamb and suffered the torment of death for him. In the second, Melchizedek offered Christ’s flesh and blood in bread and wine, and suffered the sufferings of wars inflicted by the kings of the nations in faith in Christ. In the third, Abraham sacrificed Christ in Isaac and slew him in the ram, enduring varied sufferings in this faith.

### CHAPTER LI.—On the second order and the five crosses.

In the second order, we make five crosses where [Col. 0559C] we say, “Blessed, inscribed,” and express the age of the Law, in which the righteous represented Christ through the sacrifices of the five books of the Law and suffered many torments for faith in him. For five is divided into two parts, namely three and two; and that age is divided into two intervals. One was from Moses to David, the other from David to Christ. By the number three are denoted the judges from Joshua to David, the kings from David to the Babylonian captivity, and the princes from Zerubbabel to Christ. By the number two, however, are signified priests and prophets. From these, Moses sacrificed Christ in the paschal lamb; as the Apostle testifies, he endured many adversities for faith in Christ, whom he preached through the Law (Heb. XI). Samuel anointed Christ in David; [Col. 0559D] both of them represented Christ in sacrifices and endured, in the figure of Christ, persecution from the faithless king Saul. Elijah and the other prophets prefigured Christ by sacrifices, utterances, and writings, and suffered various punishments for faith in him.

### CHAPTER LII.—On the third order.

In the third order we take the bread into the hand and bless it, making known the age of grace, in which Simeon received Christ, now born, the living bread, into his hands and blessed him with joy. Then we raise and bless the chalice, expressing the time of the supper, when Christ raised the bread and chalice in his hands and blessed them, and thereafter gave his body and blood to the apostles. Hence even now, when the Lord’s words are recited in order, [Col. 0560A] bread and wine are changed into the Lord’s body and blood.

### CHAPTER LIII.—On the fourth order and the five crosses.

In the fourth order, we make five crosses where we say, “A pure victim.” We call to mind the time when Christ received five wounds on the cross and redeemed five ages.

### CHAPTER LIV.—On the fifth order and the three crosses.

In the fifth order, we make three crosses where we say, “Thou dost create all good things, sanctify them,” and indicate Christ’s body—that is, the primitive Church—which received faith in the Trinity and endured many torments for Christ.

### CHAPTER LV.—On the sixth order and the five crosses.

[Col. 0560B] In the sixth order we make five crosses where we say, “Through him,” and again express Christ’s body, namely the Church from the Gentiles, which reverently received Christ’s fivefold Passion and, by imitating it, patiently endured diverse torments.

### CHAPTER LVI.—On the five orders of crosses.

Likewise, through the five orders of crosses are signified the five ages of the world, which are saved through the cross and Christ’s body. Hence also, in the Canon, “Through Christ our Lord” is said five times, because the world is redeemed through Christ’s five wounds. In the sixth order the chalice is touched with the oblation, because it is indicated that, at a definite age, Christ drank the chalice of suffering on the cross for all. When we say, “Through him,” we make four [Col. 0560C] crosses over the chalice with the oblation, and impress the fifth on the side of the chalice, because we make known that Christ received four wounds in hands and feet and the fifth in his side.

When Christ’s body has thus been made, we touch the rim of the chalice and thereby signify that, when the first human being’s body was formed, God breathed the breath of life into his face and gave life to the woman from him (Gen. II). So God—through whom, with whom, and in whom are all things—breathed the Holy Spirit into the face of the dead human race and, through his body, gave life from it to the Church. The chalice is touched at four points because the human race, scattered into the four regions of the world and given life through the four arms of the cross, will at the end of the world be raised to life through Christ.

### CHAPTER LVII.—On the number of signs.

[Col. 0560D]

It should be noted that throughout the Canon twenty-three signs are made, because the righteous in the Old Testament under the Decalogue of the Law, and the righteous in the New Testament through the Decalogue of the Law and in faith in the Trinity, are participants in this sacrament. We make the signs with three fingers because we express the Trinity. If you multiply twenty-three by three, you will have sixty-nine. But when we say, “The peace of the Lord,” we make three signs over the chalice not with the fingers but with a particle of the oblation; if you add these to the preceding signs, you will have seventy-two signs. This certainly signifies that the seventy-two languages scattered by pride have been gathered into one through Christ’s humility, redeemed through the cross and Passion, and made participants in him through his body and blood. [Col. 0561A]

### CHAPTER LVIII.—On the seven sacrifices.

In the Canon is commemorated the action of seven sacrifices, by which the Church, Christ’s body, is joined to Christ its head. First is the sacrifice of the innocent; second, that of apostles and martyrs; third, that of confessors; fourth, that of religious and continent persons; fifth, that of married persons; sixth, that of those who have died in Christ; seventh, that of those dead in soul, namely penitents.

From “Thee therefore” to “Communicating,” the sacrifice of the innocent is denoted: they offered themselves into Christ’s sacrifice when they were sacrificed for him. From “Communicating” to “This oblation therefore,” the sacrifice of the apostles and martyrs is represented. There are recited the names of those [Col. 0561B] who offered themselves to God as a living sacrifice when they shed their blood for him. From “This oblation therefore” to “Which oblation, thou, O God,” the sacrifice of confessors is commemorated: they suffered many dangers at the hands of heretics and continually offered Christ a sacrifice of praise. From “Which oblation, thou, O God” to “Humbly we beseech thee,” the sacrifice of religious persons is shown: they crucified their flesh with its vices and desires and thus became Christ’s sacrifice. From “Humbly we beseech thee” to “Remember, O Lord,” the sacrifice of married persons is declared: through faith and almsgiving they become participants in Christ’s body. From “Remember, O Lord,” the sacrifice of the dead is shown: they departed in confession of Christ and have been joined to the faithful.

The priest represents Christ’s death [Col. 0561C] when he bows at “Humbly we beseech thee”; fittingly, after his death comes commemoration of the departed, since he is believed to have died for them. From “To us also sinners” to the end of the Canon, the sacrifice of penitents is expressed: they immolate themselves as a sacrifice to Christ through tears and the pains of penitence, grieving that they have slain their souls by sins, so that they may receive life in him who is proclaimed to have died for the ungodly. Therefore the priest raises his voice there, because penitents are known frequently to roar in groaning of voice and heart as they utter bitter sobs. The Lord represented these when he called Lazarus from the tomb with a loud voice (John XI). In this section the names of martyrs are also recited, because penitents are worn down by varied torments. Through these seven sacrifices the Church, Christ’s body, is made and joined to Christ its head. [Col. 0561D] This is expressed through the Lord’s Prayer, which follows these sacrifices with seven petitions, because through prayer and this unique sacrifice the Church participates in Christ.

### CHAPTER LIX.—On the five prayers.

The prayer of the Canon is divided into five for this reason: the prayer of the faithful is heard only through Christ’s fivefold Passion. In three places we pray for prelates and subjects, because we distinguish the Church into teachers, continent persons, and married persons. In the fourth place we offer for the departed. In the fifth we petition for penitents.

First we offer for prelates where we say: “First of all, which we offer to thee for thy Church”; and then we name the pope, the bishop, and the king. We pray for subjects where we recite, “Remember, O Lord, thy servants and handmaids,” and there we may name whomsoever we wish. Second, we petition for prelates when we say, “This oblation therefore of our service.” We add for subjects when we say, “And of all thy household.” Third, we entreat for prelates when we recite, “Wherefore, O Lord, we thy servants, mindful,” and petition for subjects when we add, “And also thy people.” We sacrifice for the departed when we say, “Remember also, O Lord,” where we may also recite their names. We offer for penitents where we say, “To us also sinners.” All these things are commemorated in the Canon because all things are reconciled in the death of the Redeemer.

### CHAPTER LX.—On the sixth office and the bishop’s blessing.

[Col. 0562B]

The sixth office, in which the pontiff blesses the people, expresses Christ’s descent into hell. Moses bore the figure of this when, at his death, he blessed the children of Israel and commanded that those brought out of Egypt should be led into their homeland by Jesus, who is also Joshua (Deut. XXXI). Jacob, dying, also expressed this when he blessed his sons and foretold much to them about their future inheritance (Gen. XLIX). Christ fulfilled both blessings when, dying, he descended to hell, blessed by his visitation the people sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, and led those brought forth from prison into the heavenly homeland. The bishop shows this when he blesses the people and immediately refreshes them with spiritual food.

It should be noted [Col. 0562C] that he always blesses with three clauses and confirms them all by a fourth—namely, “May he deign to grant this”—and by a fifth concludes the rest through the blessing of God the Father. This is because God blessed this world three times, confirmed the remainder a fourth time, and by the fifth blessing will grant it to possess the inheritance. First, he blessed the first human beings when he commanded them to increase and multiply. Second, he blessed human beings when, after the world had been destroyed by the flood, he commanded Noah and his descendants to increase and multiply (Gen. IX). Third, through Abraham God blessed the world when, in his blessing, he promised Christ to him (Gen. XVIII). Fourth, he blessed the world when he sent us his Son, blessing us; when about to ascend into heaven, he blessed his own and through the Holy Spirit strengthened the rest (Luke XXIV). [Col. 0562D] Fifth, he will bless the world when he completes the final blessing of those entering their homeland thus: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you” (Matt. XXV).

### CHAPTER LXI.—On the seventh office and the Lord’s Resurrection.

The seventh office indicates the Lord’s Resurrection, when, after overcoming death and despoiling hell, he gave peace to the whole world, because he had now made all things in heaven and on earth peaceful; and he ate with his disciples and gave them the remains. Thus the pontiff, after overcoming the devil by spiritual warfare, gives peace to those present when he says, “Peace be with you,” and distributes the heavenly bread. Jesus, who is also Joshua, prefigured this when, after bringing in the people, he distributed the land by lot among the conquered enemies (Josh. XXXII). [Col. 0563A] The pontiff puts a portion of the oblation into the chalice, signifying that Christ’s soul returned to his body.

### CHAPTER LXII.—On the peace of the Lord.

Then “Peace be with you” is said because Christ, appearing to his own, said, “Peace be with you” (John XX). He gives peace because, in rising, Christ restored to the human race the peace it had lost. The kiss of peace is given for three reasons. For one reason, clergy and people kiss one another because human beings rejoice that through Christ, who is our peace, they have merited their Lord’s grace and friendship with the angels. A second reason is that, through the kiss of peace, brothers in Christ show themselves to the ministers of the Church as sons of God the Father through Christ’s reconciliation, and desire to be refreshed in concord and love by the one bread of Christ, who is the God of peace. [Col. 0563B] The third reason is that, just as in a kiss flesh is joined to flesh and spirit to spirit, so every person is commanded to love his neighbour in need of the flesh through neighbourly love, and God in need of the spirit through love of God. Those who eat Christ’s body without being bound by such a kiss of peace, like Judas, take judgment upon themselves through false peace.

### CHAPTER LXIII.—On the breaking of the oblation.

The oblation is broken because the bread of angels is broken for us on the cross, so that the breaking of our sins may be restored through eating it. The pope does not break the oblation, but bites a portion from it and puts the remainder into the chalice, because Christ bit hell and sent into paradise those taken from it. [Col. 0563C] The deacon holds the chalice while the pope receives the blood, signifying the angel who, when Christ rose, removed the stone from the tomb. Once the priest has communicated, the chalice is immediately removed from the altar, because Christ, having risen, dies no more and his body is not found in the tomb. The deacon distributes the blood because the angel made known the Lord’s Resurrection. The subdeacon receives the Lord’s body from the deacon and carries it to the presbyters to be broken for the people, signifying that the women received from the angel the words concerning Christ’s Resurrection, brought them to the apostles, and that they in turn distributed them to all the people by preaching. When the Apostolic One descends from the altar, he gives communion to the peoples, because, as he descends from the altar of the cross [Col. 0563D] and rises from death with Christ, the people partake of eternal glory. The bishop breaks the oblation because the Lord broke bread for the disciples at Emmaus (Luke XXIV). He divides the oblation into three parts: retaining one for himself, he gives two to the deacon and subdeacon, because the Lord, having broken bread, divided one part to himself and two to Cleophas and Luke.

### CHAPTER LXIV.—On the three parts of the oblation.

The oblation is not consumed whole, but divided into three: one part is put into the chalice, another is consumed by the priest, and the third is placed in a pyx as viaticum for the dying. This is because the Lord’s body is threefold: that which was taken from Mary, rose from death, and entered heaven; that which still labours on earth in the elect; and that which already rests in the tombs. The portion [Col. 0564A] put into the chalice is the Lord’s body already assumed into glory; the portion eaten by the priest as by an apostle is Christ’s body—that is, the Church—still labouring on earth; the portion left on the altar is the Lord’s body resting in tombs—that is, the Church dead in Christ, which will rise through union with Christ’s body.

### CHAPTER LXV.—On the three communions.

First the bishop receives communion, because Christ ate before the apostles a portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb, and gave them the remains (Luke XXIV). Then the ministers receive communion, because the Lord ate breakfast with the disciples at the Sea of Tiberias. After this the people receive communion, because the Lord, about to ascend, ate with the multitude of disciples. The corporal is folded because the folded sudarium is found. The *Agnus Dei* and the chant at communion signify the faithful’s joy at Christ’s Resurrection. The prayer which the bishop subsequently says is the blessing with which the Lord, about to ascend, blessed the faithful. [Col. 0564B] The deacon turns to the people and says, “Go, the dismissal is made,” signifying the angels who, speaking to the apostles, commanded them to depart and foretold that Christ would return for judgment. The clergy answer, “Thanks be to God,” and the people depart, because believers, having seen Christ’s Ascension, gave thanks. They went to Jerusalem and daily blessed the Lord in the temple. The blessing which the pope or priest gives over the people after Mass is the spiritual blessing which the Holy Spirit brought to the faithful on the day of Pentecost, when he filled believers with every spiritual blessing. It also represents that final blessing [Col. 0564C] by which the Church will enter the bridal chamber of her bridegroom. When these things have been performed, the bishop returns to his own place because Christ too, his embassy completed, returns to the Father’s glory. Thus the Church also, after all things still to be done have been duly completed, will be rescued from this exile through Christ and led into the heavenly Jerusalem. The corporal remains on the altar because the purity of chastity ought to remain in priests. The altar likewise signifies Christ, the corporal the Church, which is affirmed to remain eternally in Christ hereafter.

### CHAPTER LXVI.—On the Lord’s bread.

It is reported that formerly priests received flour from each house or family—something the Greeks [Col. 0564D] still preserve—and from it made the Lord’s bread, which they offered for the people and distributed to them when consecrated. For all who offered flour attended the Mass, and for them the Canon said: “Of all those standing around, who offer to thee this sacrifice of praise.” But after the Church had indeed increased in number while declining in holiness because of fleshly people, it was decreed that those able to do so should communicate every Sunday, or every third Sunday, or on the greatest feasts, or three times a year, lest before confession and penance for some crime they should incur judgment upon themselves. And because, when the people did not communicate, there was no need for so large a bread to be made, it was decreed that it should be formed or made in the likeness of a denarius, and that the people should offer denarii instead of flour for the oblation, [Col. 0565A] so that they might recognize the Lord who was betrayed for denarii. Those coins, however, were to go to the use of the poor, who are Christ’s members, or to something belonging to this sacrifice.

### CHAPTER LXVII.—On the prayer over the people.

It was decreed that bread should be blessed after Mass and distributed to the people in place of the blessing of communion; this was also called *eulogia* (“blessing”). But because this was not permitted in Lent, the Church instituted that the prayer over the people should be said, so that through it the Church might be a participant in communion.

### CHAPTER LXVIII.—On the procession.

Now, that we may pour some sweetness into the minds of readers or hearers, let us say something about the procession. In the Mass Christ’s embassy into the world for us was enacted; in the procession our return to our homeland is enacted. Therefore, for the solemnity of the procession, the Church imitates the joy of God’s people as they departed from Egypt. Delivered by signs and wonders, they came to Mount Sinai. There, having received the Law and made the tabernacle, they made their way, as in a kind of procession, toward the promised land. [Col. 0565B] The armed people advanced in companies, bearing signs and banners in front; the Levites carried the tabernacle, and the priests sounded trumpets. The ark of the covenant was carried by the priests, while Aaron the high priest, adorned, and Moses, leader of the people, carrying his rod, followed. On the way Amalek met them with his army and wished to bar their passage by arms (Exod. XVII). [Col. 0565C] Jesus, fighting against him, emerged victorious and opened the people’s way to their homeland. This Jesus gave us the pattern of procession when he marched around Jericho with the ark and all the people, the priestly order sounded trumpets, and the people resounded with shouting. Jericho fell, and the victorious people gained the kingdom.

### CHAPTER LXIX.—The meaning of processions.

The people rescued from Pharaoh through Moses are the Christian people redeemed from the devil through Christ. The tablets of the Testament were received from the mountain, and the books of the Gospel are taken from the altar to be carried. That people went armed, and the Christian people goes marked with faith and baptism. Standards were borne before their companies; crosses and banners are carried before us. [Col. 0565D] A pillar of fire went before them, and the light of candles goes before us. That people was sprinkled with blood; this people is sprinkled with holy water. The Levites carried the tabernacle of the covenant; here the deacons and subdeacons carry plenaries (*plenaria*, books containing the full readings) and caskets. The ark of the testament was carried by priests; the shrine or bier containing relics is carried by fathers. Aaron, the adorned high priest, follows; among us the bishop, namely the high priest, follows wearing his mitre. If the king is present, the ruler of the people with a sceptre signifies Moses, the leader of the people with his rod. If the king is absent, then the pontiff represents both: Moses, by carrying a staff; Aaron, by covering his head with a mitre. The sounding of trumpets is represented by the sound of bells.

### CHAPTER LXX.—What a procession to another church signifies concerning the homeland.

[Col. 0566A]

When we make a procession to another church, we make our way as though to the promised land. When we enter the church singing, we arrive rejoicing as though at our homeland. When we carry the shrine or relic-bier around the monastery with chant and bell-ringing, we go around as though with the ark around Jericho, with trumpet-sound and the people’s shout. Jericho falls before us when worldly desire has withered in our hearts. For this reason we follow the cross that goes before us: we are commanded to follow Christ crucified in all things, and no one can reach him unless that person has crucified himself to the world, its vices, and its desires.

### CHAPTER LXXI.—On the ark.

[Col. 0566B]

David and Solomon also instructed us concerning procession. They brought forth the ark of God with hymns and songs; David placed it in the tabernacle, and Solomon in the temple beneath the wings of the cherubim. When we enter a church with the shrine, we carry the ark into the temple with joy, as it were, and proclaim that we shall enter the heavenly court with Christ and the Church—both of which the ark signifies. The ark is placed under the wings of the cherubim and praise is sung by the people, because Christ’s humanity will be placed among the highest angelic orders, the cherubim and seraphim, and will be adored in everlasting jubilation by the company of angels and human beings.

### CHAPTER LXXII.—On Christians’ spiritual battle.

The Mass also imitates the conflict of a certain battle [Col. 0566C] and its victorious triumph, in which our enemy Amalek is cast down and the way to our homeland is opened to us through Jesus. For Jesus, our emperor, fought with the devil and restored to human beings the heavenly commonwealth, destroyed by enemies. Although he could have brought forth twelve legions of angels (Matt. XXVI), or seventy-two thousand soldiers, he drew up only the small force of twelve apostles and conquered the seventy-two kinds of languages. The procession of the pontiff, clergy, and people is like the advance of an emperor and an army to battle. When they are clothed beneath in albs and above in copes or other solemn vestments, they are like soldiers about to fight, protected beneath by cuirasses and above by shields. [Col. 0566D] When they leave the choir, they proceed as though from the royal court. The imperial standard and banners are borne in front by standard-bearers, as the cross and banners are carried before us. Two armies, as it were, follow when they proceed on either side in ordered ranks while singing. Between them walk the masters and precentors, like leaders of cohorts and inciters to battle. The senior members follow, like commanders of armies and arrangers of battle-lines.

### CHAPTER LXXIII.—That the bishop spiritually performs the role of an emperor.

The bishop proceeds with a staff, like an emperor with a sceptre. Holy things are carried before the bishop, just as imperial insignia are borne before a king. A cross is carried before an archbishop, as it is borne before an emperor; he is adorned with the pallium, as a king is embellished with a crown. A crowd of people accompanies him [Col. 0567A], like an infantry army. When they proceed from the basilica, companies rush forth as if from a royal city. When we proceed to another church, we go as though to storm a fortress; when we enter it with song, we receive it as though at its dedication and summon helpers thence to our aid; but when we return to the monastery, we make for the place of conflict. We carry a shrine with relics against demons, as the children of Israel carried the ark of God against the Philistine enemies. When we enter the church, we arrive, as it were, at the station. When bells sound, soldiers are urged to battle as though by martial trumpets. Battle-lines are, as it were, drawn up for combat when they are arranged on either side in the choir. He who holds the cross with the banner before the archbishop is the standard-bearer, who [Col. 0567B] carries the standard before the emperor in battle.

### CHAPTER LXXIV.—That the singer is a standard-bearer and trumpeter.

The singer who begins the chant is the trumpeter who gives the signal for battle. The precentors, who direct the choir on either side, are commanders who marshal the ranks for battle. Singers cover their heads with small caps and carry staffs or tablets in their hands, because combatants cover their heads with helmets and protect themselves with weapons of war.

### CHAPTER LXXV.—On spiritual warfare.

War is joined with the blare of trumpets and the shouting of crowds; and our spiritual war begins with the ringing of bells and the singing of the clergy. For the struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against [Col. 0567C] spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. VI). Thus they fight like valiant soldiers when they sing from either side with all their strength. The most wicked enemies shoot the fiery darts of desire; strong men vigorously repel them with the shield of faith, and strike down with the sword of God’s word the enemies of vices that press fiercely upon them.

### CHAPTER LXXVI.—That singers perform the office of commanders.

Singers urge others to harmony by hand and voice, because commanders also impel others toward combat by leading with their hands in battle and exhorting with their voices. Meanwhile the bishop stands at the altar and recites a prayer for those engaged in struggle, just as Moses prayed on the mountain for those fighting (Exod. 17).

### CHAPTER LXXVII.—On the singer: that he performs the office of herald.

[Col. 0567D]

The reader who recites the Epistle is a herald who proclaims the emperor’s edicts through the camp. The better voices are chosen to sing the Gradual or Alleluia, and those stronger in hand are brought forward for single combat. When some fail in singing, others come to their assistance; likewise, when some are greatly fatigued in battle, others steadfast in heart assist them. Then they rejoice over the sequence with voice and instruments, because they celebrate victory with applause and song. The deacon who recites the Gospel on high is the herald who, once the battle is over, summons the dispersed ranks with a trumpet. The bishop’s address exhorting the people signifies the emperor’s address praising the victors [Col. 0568A]. The offering of oblations at that point signifies the distribution of spoils before the emperor to the victors. The Offertory chant is the praise offered to the emperor.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII.—On David compared with Christ, and Goliath with the devil.

Accordingly, after the manifold enemy had been overcome by Jesus—who is also Joshua—and the victorious people, because of an abundance of peace, had relaxed into negligence, the Philistines again gather against Israel, and cruel war is proclaimed. From among them Goliath comes forth and demands single combat. David meets him with a shepherd’s bag, sling, and stone; when he has thrown him down, he pierces him with his own sword. But the people, delivered, offer a victim to God for victory and joyfully sing praises in thanksgiving. When David comes to Jerusalem [Col. 0568B], a crowd of peoples rushes to meet him and receives the saviour of the people with hymns.

So too, after vices have been overcome by the Christian people, they rise up anew and a sharper war is brought against the negligent soul. From among them comes the giant Goliath, namely the devil, demanding single combat when he entices any Christian person toward individual vices. A strong mind meets him, like David, with sacred Scripture, with a sling and with a vessel of milk [Note: [Col. 0567] That is, with an ephah of gruel and ten loaves (1 Sam. XVII, 17).], and throws him down: it conquers him through Christ’s humanity, which was a rock for the thirsty people and a cornerstone for believing peoples; and it cuts down the prostrate foe with his own sword when it overcomes the malignant enemy in frail flesh.

### CHAPTER LXXIX.—Mystery.

Therefore, when the sacrifice is prepared by the subdeacon and others, [Col. 0568C] David is, as it were, armed by Saul and the people (1 Sam. XVII). When the offerings are laid upon the altar, David’s arms are, as it were, laid aside. Then, when the bishop comes to the altar, David proceeds, as it were, against the Philistine. By the chalice the milk-vessel is understood; by the corporal, the sling; by the offering, the rock. The Preface that is sung was the cry by which the giant champion was challenged to single combat; through the petition of the Canon, we understand the prayer of the people. The priest’s bowing is the whirling of the sling after the stone has been placed in it. The elevation of the bread is the casting of the stone. Where he bows again, it signifies that the enemy is struck down. But where the deacon comes to the priest and, raising the chalice with him, sets it down, it signifies that David ran to the fallen man [Col. 0568D] and, drawing his sword, cut off his head. Then, peace having been given, the people communicate, because, peace having been won through David, the people share in sacrifice offered to God. The chant at Communion is the people’s praise in exultation for victory. The prayer and blessing that follow are the trophy with which David, coming to Jerusalem, was received by the people. When these things have been performed, the people return home, because then, after victory, the people went back to their homes with joy.

### CHAPTER LXXX.—Again, on the Mass and judgment.

For the Mass imitates a kind of judicial proceeding, whence the Canon is also called an *actio* (“action” or “case”). An *actio* is a cause conducted in a public assembly before judges, because in [Col. 0569A] the Mass the case of the people is conducted with God as judge. When the bell sounds, the people are summoned to the hearing, as it were, by a herald. Indeed, the oratory is like a praetorium, in which God the judge is believed to sit upon his tribunal and before which the people stand as defendants. The devil is the accuser; the priest, the defender. Therefore, since the judge is offended by the devil’s accusation and by the people’s guilt, the priest who has undertaken the people’s case is compelled to undergo single combat, so that the informer’s deceit may be refuted, the people’s innocence proved, and the judge’s wrath appeased. At once he puts on spiritual arms, engages the adversary, and rescues the anxious people.

### CHAPTER LXXXI.—On the battle with the Philistine.

This had already occurred, as was said, in figure, when David, having fought with Goliath, delivered the people from [Col. 0569B] his tyranny (1 Sam. XVII), because Christ too underwent single combat with the devil and delivered the people oppressed by him. For the Philistines attacked Israel, and the host of demons harassed the human race; the enemies directed their battle-line against God’s people, and demons stirred tyrants against the righteous; the enemies fortified themselves with a rampart, and demons strengthened errors through philosophers and poets. Goliath reproached God’s ranks, and the devil insulted God’s worshippers through idolatry. David is sent by his father to battle, and Christ is sent by the Father into the world for combat. David tended sheep, and Christ gathered the innocent into the pastures of life. David overcame a bear or a lion, and Christ overcame the devil tempting him. David, leaving the sheep, heads for the place of conflict [Col. 0569C], and Christ, abandoned by his disciples, comes to the assemblies of his enemies. At David’s arrival, a cry arises in the camp; and when Christ comes among the Jews, a cry arises: “He is guilty of death.” David is clothed by the soldiers in Saul’s armour and immediately removes it (1 Sam. XVII); Christ is clothed by the soldiers in Pilate’s garments, namely purple and a scarlet cloak, and immediately stripped of them. David carried a staff against the Philistine, and Christ bore the cross against the devil. David received a milk-vessel, and Christ received a vessel full of vinegar. The enemy is thrown down by sling and stone, and the devil is conquered by Christ’s flesh. For by the sling Christ’s flesh is understood; by the stone, his soul; by David, his divinity. Thus the rock shot from the sling penetrates the forehead of the proud one [Col. 0569D], because Christ’s soul, shot forth from the flesh by torments, penetrates the tyrant’s realm and plunders hell. He slays the conquered foe with his own sword, because through death he conquered the author of death. When David returns, the people rejoice; and when Christ returns from hell, the people of the faithful rejoice with him. David coming to Jerusalem is received by crowds with singing; and Christ, about to ascend from Jerusalem into heaven, is received by hymn-singing angels with praises.

### CHAPTER LXXXII.—On the priest’s arms.

Therefore the priest, our champion about to engage the people’s enemy, is equipped with spiritual weapons, because he is to fight against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. VI, 12). Thus he puts on sandals in place of greaves, covers his head with the amice in place of a helmet, and clothes his whole body with an alb in place of a breastplate. When he puts the stole around his neck, [Col. 0570A] he brandishes a spear for resistance. He girds himself with a cincture in place of a bow and hangs the subcingulum from it in place of a quiver. He is protected by the chasuble in place of a shield and uses the maniple as a spiked club for a boxer. Further, he is armed with the book, in which is the word of God, in place of a sword; by confession the devil is renounced to the Lord, and thus the enemy is challenged to single combat. For he fights, as it were, with all his strength when he recites chant, prayers, and the rest against the devil. When, for the Gospel, he throws the chasuble over his shoulder, he takes up the sword, as it were. While the Gospel is read, he attacks the devil as though with a sword.

### CHAPTER LXXXIII.—On tragedies.

It should be known that those who recited tragedies in theatres represented to the people, by gestures, the actions of combatants. So our tragic actor represents to the Christian people, in the theatre of the Church, by his gestures the battle of Christ [Col. 0570B], and impresses upon them the victory of their redemption. Accordingly, when the priest says “Let us pray,” he represents Christ placed in agony for us, when he instructed the apostles to pray. By the secret silence he signifies Christ led to sacrifice like a voiceless lamb. By the extension of his hands he denotes Christ’s stretching out upon the cross. By the chant of the Preface he represents Christ’s cry while hanging on the cross. For he sang ten psalms, namely from “My God, look upon me” to “Into your hands I commend my spirit,” and so expired. By the silence of the Canon he intimates the silence of the Sabbath. By peace and communion he signifies the peace given after Christ’s resurrection and the sharing of joy. Once the sacrament has been completed, peace and communion [Col. 0570C] are given to the people by the priest, because, our accuser having been thrown down in single combat by our contest-president, peace is announced by the judge to the people, who are invited to the banquet. Then, through “Go, the dismissal is made,” they are commanded to return home with joy; each gives thanks to God with rejoicing and returns home gladly.

### CHAPTER LXXXIV.—Again, on the Mass, the seven “The Lord be with you,” the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the mystery of the Mass.

The Mass is called an embassy. The whole time from Christ’s entering the world until the Church enters heaven is a time of embassy; and Christ’s embassy will end when Christ’s bride is led from this Babylon into the heavenly Jerusalem. That this time is divided by seven intervals signifies that the embassy [Col. 0570D] is accomplished through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Hence, at Mass, “The Lord be with you” is said seven times, because the mystery of the Mass is performed through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

First, after the Introit, “The Lord be with you” is said. The Introit signifies Christ’s entrance into this world, by which he saved the human race through his incarnation. The Introit chant is the joy both of angels and of human beings which they had at his birth. The first gift of the Holy Spirit is wisdom, when God’s Wisdom came incarnate. The prayer following signifies our reconciliation through him; the Lesson, however, signifies the teaching or example which he gave in baptism. The Gradual signifies his fasting or temptation; the Alleluia, the ministry of angels who ministered to him.

Second, [Col. 0571A] “The Lord be with you” is said before the Gospel, by which he saved the world through his preaching; for the Gospel signifies the time of Christ’s preaching. The second gift is the spirit of understanding, because then he taught people to understand spiritual things.

Third, “The Lord be with you” is said before the Offertory: this is the time when he went to Jerusalem to suffer and saved the crowd coming to meet him with palms. The Offertory chant signifies the praise of that people. Hence, in the same signification, the people still customarily offer sacrifice at the Offertory. The third gift is the spirit of counsel, because then he disclosed God’s plan for which he came, namely to redeem human beings by his passion. The silence that follows is the time when Christ remained in Jerusalem until the Passion, which came immediately on the sixth day, as though a Paschal lamb kept enclosed.

Fourth, [Col. 0571B] “The Lord be with you” is said in the Preface, with hands extended: it signifies the time when Christ hung extended upon the cross. The fourth gift is the spirit of fortitude, because then he defeated the devil. That the Preface is said aloud signifies the ten psalms which he himself cried upon the cross, namely from “God, my God, look upon me” to “Into your hands I commend my spirit”; or it signifies the tumult that occurred around the cross while things heavenly and earthly were disturbed. The ensuing silence of the Canon was the time after his death when his followers lay hidden in fear and trembling.

Fifth, “Peace be with you” is said instead of “The Lord be with you.” It is the time when Christ rose and greeted his followers with these words. The fifth gift is the spirit [Col. 0571C] of knowledge, because then he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures. The chant that follows is the joy they had until his ascension.

Sixth, “The Lord be with you” is said after Communion: it is the time when Christ, leaving human beings and ascending, greeted the angels coming to meet him. The sixth gift is the spirit of piety, because it was the greatest act of piety that he bore human nature above the stars. The prayer that follows is his present intercession with the Father for us.

The seventh “The Lord be with you” is said at the end of Mass. It signifies the time when Christ, coming at the end of the world, will greet the saints coming to meet him for judgment. The seventh gift is the spirit of fear, because then the angels will tremble. [Col. 0571D] “Go, the dismissal is made” follows; that is, to those on the left: “Go, you wicked, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). But the blessing that follows is to those on the right: “Come, blessed of my Father” (ibid.).

### CHAPTER LXXXV.—Rabanus Maurus on the Mass.

Those things celebrated in the office of the Mass before the Gospel is read relate to the Lord’s first coming, up to the time when he hastened to Jerusalem to suffer. The Introit, however, relates to the choir of prophets, when, as Augustine says: “Moses was a minister of the Old Testament; the prophets, of the New.” *Kyrie eleison* relates to those prophets who lived around the Lord’s coming. *Gloria in excelsis* relates to the company of angels, because the joy of Christ’s birth is announced to the shepherds. The first [Col. 0572A] Collect relates to what the Lord did at about his twelfth year, when he sat in the midst of the teachers, hearing them and asking them questions (Luke II). The Epistle pertains to John’s preaching. The Responsory pertains to the goodwill of the apostles, who, called by the Lord, followed him in his preaching up to the aforesaid time.

Thereafter, what is done in the office of the Mass relates to the period from the Sunday when the children came to meet him until his Ascension, or Pentecost. The prayer which the priest says from the Secret to *Nobis quoque* signifies the prayer which Jesus made on the Mount of Olives. What follows signifies the time when the Lord lay in the tomb. When bread is put into wine, it shows the Lord’s soul returning to the body. [Col. 0572B] What is afterward celebrated signifies those greetings Christ gave his disciples. The breaking of the offerings signifies the breaking which the Lord performed for the two at Emmaus (Luke XXIV).

### CHAPTER LXXXVI.—Now it must be said whence the Mass took its beginning and who enlarged it; again, on the Mass.

In the first place, the Lord Jesus, priest according to the order of Melchizedek, instituted the Mass when he made his body and blood from bread and wine and commanded his own followers to celebrate these things in memory of him. The apostles enlarged it when they said over bread and wine the words which the Lord spoke, together with the Lord’s Prayer (Acts II, 9). Then their successors decreed that the Epistles and Gospels should be read; some added chant [Col. 0572C], and others other things—those who loved the beauty of the Lord’s house (Ps. XXV).

### CHAPTER LXXXVII.—On the Introit and the other parts of the Mass: by whom they were first instituted.

Accordingly, Pope Celestine instituted the singing of psalms at the Introit of the Mass. Pope Gregory later composed, setting them to melody, the antiphons for the Introit of the Mass. Hence the first verse of the same psalm is still sung at the Introit, whereas formerly the whole psalm was sung at the Introit. The Nicene synod composed *Gloria Patri*, but Pope Damasus instituted its singing at Mass. The angelic choir first sang *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, but Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, composed it from “We praise thee” to the end; Pope Telesphorus established that it should be sung at Mass. [Col. 0572D] Pope Symmachus decreed that it should be sung only on feasts. “The Lord be with you” is taken from the Old Testament, namely the book of Ruth. “Peace be with you” is taken from the New, that is, from the Gospel. “And with your spirit” is from Paul’s Epistles, and “Amen” from the Apocalypse. The apostolic order taught that these should be said, the Lord being their teacher; and Pope Clement or Pope Anacletus decreed that they should be said at Mass. Bishop Ambrose instituted the prayers. But Pope Gelasius enlarged them and instituted their use at Mass.

### CHAPTER LXXXVIII.—On the Epistle and Gospel.

Pope Alexander decreed that the Epistle and Gospel should be read at Mass. Jerome the priest compiled the Lectionary and Gospel-book as the Church has them today [Col. 0573A]; but Pope Damasus ordered that they be read in the manner now customary. Ambrose composed the Gradual and Alleluia, but Pope Gregory instituted their singing at Mass. He also decreed that on feast days the neume, called the jubilus, should be sung jubilantly. But Abbot Notker of Saint Gall composed sequences for the neumes, which Pope Nicholas permitted to be sung at Mass. Pope Anastasius decreed that no one should sit while the Gospel is read. The Constantinopolitan synod composed *Credo in unum Deum*, but Pope Damasus instituted its singing at Mass. Pope Gregory composed the Offertory and decreed that it should be sung at Mass.

### CHAPTER LXXXIX.—On vestments and chalices.

The apostles and their successors celebrated Masses in ordinary clothing and with wooden chalices. [Col. 0573B] But Clement, following the tradition of the apostle Peter, took the use of sacred vestments from the Law; and Pope Stephen decreed that Masses should be celebrated in sacred vestments. Pope Zephyrinus instituted the use of glass chalices; Pope Urban, pope and martyr, instituted offerings in gold or silver chalices and patens. Pope Alexander decreed that bread and wine alone should be offered, as the Lord himself instituted, and ruled that water should be mixed in, as apostolic tradition also teaches. Pope Sylvester decreed that the offering should be made on a linen corporal, just as Joseph wrapped the Lord’s body in a clean linen cloth (Matt. XXVII; Luke XXIII). Pope Leo decreed that “Pray for me, a sinner” should be said. He also composed the Prefaces. “Lift up your hearts” is from Jeremiah; “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God” is taken from the Apostle. Dionysius the Areopagite is thought to have [Col. 0573C] composed the Prefaces, but Pope Gelasius instituted their singing at Mass. “Holy, holy, holy”: Pope Sixtus composed one half from Isaiah and one half from the Gospel, and instituted its singing at Mass.

### CHAPTER XC.—On the Canon.

Pope Gelasius composed the Canon. But Pope Gregory inserted the clause “and dispose our days.” Pope Leo added “a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim.” The Lord indeed taught the *Pater noster*; but Matthew composed it; Pope Gregory decreed that it be sung at Mass, as apostolic teaching handed down. He also added the preceding clause, “Let us pray, instructed by saving precepts,” and the following, “Deliver us, Lord.” Bishop Martialis, disciple of the apostles, handed down the episcopal blessing, through the teaching [Col. 0573D] of the apostles, whose special concern increased the service of God. Ambrose began to say it, and from him its use grew strong even to the present. The Apostolic [i.e. the pope], however, says only this after Mass is completed: “The peace of the Lord be always with you.” Pope Innocent decreed that it be said and that the peace be given. Pope Sergius composed *Agnus Dei* and instituted its singing at Mass. Pope Julius prohibited dipping the Lord’s body into the blood, and Pope Gelasius excommunicated one who received the Lord’s body but did not receive the blood. Pope Gregory composed the Communion and instituted its singing at Mass. “Go, the dismissal is made” is taken from the Old Testament: namely, where Pharaoh ordered the people to go out of Egypt, or where Cyrus [Col. 0574A] commanded the people to depart from Babylon. It should be known that the Mass took its name from this “Go, the dismissal is made.” “Let us bless the Lord” is taken from the Psalter; “Thanks be to God” from the Apostle; but Pope Leo decreed that these be said. From all these things Pope Gregory is handed down as having ordered the Mass as it is handed down through the Church today.

### CHAPTER XCI.—On the names of the offices of the Mass.

To these must be added the reason for each name. *Officium* is called, as it were, *officium* (“duty”). *Missa* is called, as it were, a sending-away, because in this office catechumens, excommunicated persons, and penitents are sent outside the Church. The Introit is named from the priest’s entrance, because, as the priest approaches the altar, it is sung by the choir. We sing the Introit because we signify that we receive Christ in the priest. We sing *Gloria Patri* because [Col. 0574B] we make known that we adore the Trinity.

### CHAPTER XCII.—On *Kyrie eleison*.

*Kyrie eleison* means, “Lord, have mercy”; *Christe eleison* means, “Christ, have mercy”; *ymas* means “us.” This is sung in Greek because the Mass is commanded to be sung in three languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—as the title written at the Lord’s Passion is also said to have been. *Alleluia*, *Osanna*, and *Amen* are Hebrew; *Kyrie eleison* and *Christe eleison* are Greek; the remainder of the office is Latin. *Kyrie eleison* is said three times because the Trinity is adored, which was venerated by the ancients before the Flood, by the patriarchs before the Law, and by the prophets under the Law. *Christe eleison* is sung three times because Christ is adored in the Father and the Holy Spirit, who, by the Father’s will and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, accomplishes [Col. 0574C] our salvation. Again, *Kyrie eleison* is repeated three times because Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are worshipped by angels, by the spirits of the righteous, and by human beings. Thus *Kyrie eleison* is sung so that the priest’s following prayer may be heard.

### CHAPTER XCIII.—What *Gloria in excelsis* is.

The priest alone begins *Gloria in excelsis*, and the choir sings it together, because one angel alone began it and the host of the heavenly army sang it together. When he begins it, he turns toward the East, because the angelic choir sang these words toward the east, at Bethlehem by the tower of Adiezer. Through “Peace be with you” or “The Lord be with you,” he greets the people, as the Lord greeted the world by his coming. The priest greets the people with the salutation of the Old Testament, and the bishop with the salutation [Col. 0574D] of the New Testament, because the New Testament is worthier than the Old. The people pray that the Lord may be with his spirit, so that he may be reminded to pray with spirit and mind. He prays with the mouth who merely utters the words. He prays with mouth and spirit who distinguishes by interpretation the words that he utters with his mouth. He prays with spirit and mind who directs to the Lord and to heavenly things the words that he says. He says not “I pray” but “Let us pray,” because he expresses the voice of the whole Church.

### CHAPTER XCIV.—On prayer.

Prayer is called from praying, because in it present and future goods of body and soul are sought for the people. It is called a Collect because under it the people are gathered into one. This is the difference between a prayer [Col. 0575A] and a Collect: it is called a prayer when it is said at Mass, but a Collect when it is said over the people at a station during a procession. It is also called a *missa*, because in it the people’s prayer is sent through the priest to the Lord. We say it at the right side of the altar because we pray to be set among those at the right in judgment. We direct all prayers to God the Father and conclude through our Lord Jesus Christ in the Holy Spirit, because we believe that all rightly requested things are given by the Father through the Son in the unity of the Holy Spirit. We say “through him who is to come” only in exorcisms, in which we adjure the devil by the coming judgment.

### CHAPTER XCV.—On the direction of prayer. For three reasons we turn toward the East when we pray.

[Col. 0575B]

One reason is that our homeland, namely Paradise, is in the East, from which we grieve that we have been expelled. Therefore, when praying, we turn toward Paradise because we seek to return there. Another is that in the East the body of heaven and the light of day rise. Therefore we turn toward the East because we signify that we adore Christ, who is the East and the true light, and that we ought to be his heaven, so that his light may choose to rise within us. A third is that the sun rises in the East, and through it Christ, the sun of righteousness, is represented. From him we have the promise that in the resurrection we shall shine like the sun. Therefore, in prayer we turn toward the sunrise, so that we may understand that we adore the sun of the angels and may be recalled to remembrance of the glory of our resurrection, when we see the sun—which we observed as though dying in the West—rising in the East with such great glory [Col. 0575C].

### CHAPTER XCVI.—What the Epistle is.

A Lesson is called from reading. An Epistle is called, as it were, something sent. *Epistello* and *stello* mean “I send,” because, just as prophecies were sent after the Law, so epistles were sent after the Gospel. We read it because through it we make our way to Christ. The Gradual is named from the steps, because it is sung on the steps. It is also called the Responsory, because while the choir sings, one person answers with a verse, and while that person sings the verse, the choir answers. It is called a verse because it returns to the beginning. *Alleluia* means “Praise the Lord.” In *Alleluia*, “praise,” among the ten names of God, is placed as one which is called “Lord.” The verse of this chant is so called because it returns again to the *Alleluia*. [Col. 0575D] The Sequence is so called because it follows the neume of the jubilus. The Tract is named from drawing, because it is sung in a drawn-out manner, that is, continuously. We sing the Gradual because we ought to go step by step from strength to strength. We sing *Alleluia* because we make for the joy of the angels. We rejoice over the Sequence because we shall see the Lord’s face in jubilation. We sing the Tract because through labour we shall arrive there. We read the Gospel because through its teaching we shall receive joys.

### CHAPTER XCVII.—On the Gospel.

The Gospel is called “good news.” *Eu* means “good”; *angelon* means “message.” For it announces life after death, rest after labour, and a kingdom after service. [Col. 0576A] The Sequence is so called because the things announced before it follow. It is also called the beginning of the Gospel because the Gospel-book begins there. Where “Let us pray” is said after the Gospel, among the Greeks a prayer follows. The Offertory is called, as it were, the chant of those offering. We sing it because we ought to offer ourselves to God as a sacrifice. Priests wash their hands, that is, their works, through tears of compunction. Here the book is placed at the left side so that the priest may be freer to receive the sacrifice. And because sorrow is signified by the left side, which then represents Christ’s Passion.

### CHAPTER XCVIII.—On sacrifice.

Sacrifice is called, as it were, something made sacred. *Immolatio* is so called because it was ground on the altar’s *mola* (“mill”). A *hostia* is so called because it was offered before the door for battle. A *victima* is so called because it was sacrificed for victory. A holocaust is called wholly burnt: for all of it was burned on the altar. A sacrament is called, as it were, a sacred oath. It is called a Secret because it is said secretly. When the sacrifice is placed on the altar-cross, made by the bishop with the *schismate* [uncertain term], Christ’s body is, as it were, fastened to the cross.

### CHAPTER XCIX.—On the sacrifice of bread and wine.

*Pan* means “all.” Therefore it is offered here because every salvation of soul and body is received in it. Wine is called, as it were, that which is born from the vine. It is offered so that, as branches are joined to the vine, so we may be grafted into Christ. Water is called from equality; it is mixed with the sacrifice so that, reborn from water, we may be satisfied from the fountain of life and made equal with angels. “Through all ages of ages” is said because ages follow one another: when some pass away, others succeed. [Col. 0576C] *Amen* means “truly”; through it the whole sacrament is confirmed, because through it the world also is created. For it means “Let it be,” the word God used in the creation of the world when he said, “Let there be light,” and so forth. The Son of God himself is also surnamed *Amen*, as is said in the Apocalypse: “Thus says the Amen, the faithful witness” (Rev. III). We say “The Lord be with you” here because we make known to the people that the King of heaven is present. We say “Lift up your hearts” because we do not doubt that the host of angels is drawing near. For they are present at this sacrifice and, receiving our vows, carry them to the Lord. We say “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God” because we render him thanks for all benefits. Nothing in this sacrament occurs without a rational [Col. 0576D] signification.

### CHAPTER C.—On alpha and omega, and its cross: α + ω.

Therefore the form of these letters, T and X, is not made without a great mystery. For it signifies the two substances in Christ. On one side it is covered, on the other it is concealed; Ω is attached: this is Christ’s humanity, which begins from the mother’s side and is joined to divinity through O, which is enclosed on every side by a circular circumference: this is Christ’s divinity, which is neither disclosed by a beginning nor bounded by an end. The top of the letter is also joined in the form of a cross +: this is the holy cross, through which human things are joined to divine.

### CHAPTER CI.—On the Preface.

The Preface is called a preliminary utterance, namely, of the Canon that follows. [Col. 0577A] It is also called preparation because it prepares our minds for Christ’s mystery. In it we commemorate the orders of angels because we show that a multitude of heavenly citizens is present. *Majestas* (“majesty”) is called, as it were, greater power. *Coelum* (“heaven”—read this carefully) is called, as it were, *casa elios*, “house of the sun.” *Seraphin* with *n* denotes several angels; *seraphim* with *m*, one.

### CHAPTER CII.—Why it is called *Sanctus*.

We sing *Sanctus* with the angels because by this sacrifice we proclaim that earthly things are joined to heavenly. *Sanctus* is called [Note: [Col. 0577D] Rather, from *sancire*, as though *sancitus*.] “touched” or “increased” by blood. *Dominus* means “giving less.” *Deus* means “removing guilt.” *Sabaoth* means “of armies,” namely, king of the host of angels. *Osanna* means “saving,” that is, “Save us, you who dwell in [Col. 0577B] the heights.”

### CHAPTER CIII.—On the Canon.

The Canon is called a rule because by it the consecration of the sacraments is performed according to rule. It is also called an *actio* because in it the people’s case is conducted with God. It is said silently for three reasons. One is that we speak with God, to whom we are commanded to cry not with the mouth but with the heart. Yet we say the words so that we may know what we ought to direct our intention toward or ask for. The second is lest the people, wearied [rather, afflicted by boredom] by such a lengthy recitation, depart, or the priest’s voice fail through so prolonged a cry. The third is lest words so holy, belonging to so great a mystery, become cheapened when the common people, knowing them through daily use, say them in unsuitable places.

Hence it is reported that, when the Canon was originally recited publicly [Col. 0577C] every day, everyone knew it through use; and when shepherds in a field said it over bread and wine, they suddenly found flesh and blood before them and, struck down by divine power, perished. Therefore, by synodal decree and under anathema, it was commanded that no one should say the Canon except from a book, in sacred vestments, over an altar and over the sacrifice; and that no one should offer this sacrifice except in gold or silver vessels. Since not everyone can possess these, those do nothing improper who depict the Crucified One here in books, because through it Christ’s Passion is impressed upon the eyes of the heart.

“Thee, therefore,” he says, because he beholds the Lord as though present. It begins with the letter T because this represents the form of the cross. *Clemens* (“merciful”) is so called as though from *clara mens*, “a clear mind”: when a person fears, the mind is troubled; when one senses the Lord to be gracious, the mind becomes clear. These + gifts, with respect to the bread, in which are water and flour. These + offerings, with respect to the wine, in which are water and wine. These holy + sacrifices, with respect to both: undefiled, that is, without stain. For the paschal lamb had to be without blemish, and Christ was without the stain of sin. The Church is called a convocation, because it is summoned into one faith not by fear but by the love of the Holy Spirit. It is called catholic, “universal,” because this religion is observed throughout the whole world. The pope is called “father of fathers.” Orthodox is called “rightly glorifying” [Note: [Col. 0578D] Rather, rightly believing in the faith.], namely, [Col. 0578A] existing in the right faith. “Remember, O Lord, thy servants”: here we may name whomsoever we wish. The offering is made only for the faithful, as is said: “Whose faith is known to thee.”

## CHAPTER CIV.—On the Twelve Apostles and Holy Mary

“Communicating with.” Therefore the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, is named here because this sacrifice is brought forth to the world from her. The twelve apostles are named because these sacraments are confirmed by their teaching and blood. For in testimony to this sacrifice Peter, Andrew, and Philip were crucified; Paul and James, Matthew and Bartholomew, were beheaded; James, Simon, and Thaddaeus were slain; John was tortured by poison and exile; Thomas was [Col. 0578B] pierced through.

## CHAPTER CV.—On the Twelve Names of the Martyrs

Then the names of twelve martyrs are recited, by whose suffering this sacrifice is commended. Some of these were high priests, some bishops, some deacons, and some laymen, because every rank and every order bore witness to this sacrament. Linus, Cletus, Clement, Sixtus, and Cornelius were Roman pontiffs; Cyprian was archbishop of Carthage; Lawrence was archdeacon; Chrysogonus, John, and Paul were soldiers; Cosmas and Damian were physicians. All these shed their blood for the sacrifice of our Christ.

“This offering, O God, we beseech thee, in all things make Bene + dictam [blessed]”: that is, by blessing with the Holy Spirit, fill this earthly material—as Adam was formed from earth—[Col. 0578C]. Make it A + scriptam [inscribed]: that is, assign it to the divinity, marked with the form of thy Son. Make it Ra + tam [ratified]: that is, make it firm in truth in our faith. Make it reasonable and, in accordance with our devotion, acceptable.

“On the day before,” that is, on the preceding day. “This is my body.” As the world was made from nothing by the Word of the Lord, so by the words of the Lord these outward forms of things are truly changed into the Lord’s body.

## CHAPTER CVI.—On the Chalice

“This most excellent chalice.” The chalice is the same in mystery as that which Christ held in his hands, although it is another in its metallic material. “Of the eternal testament.” A testament is called that document by which the inheritance of one who has died is confirmed to the living. The new and eternal testament has been written for us in Christ’s blood, by whose death the heavenly kingdom has been secured as an inheritance. It is called a mystery where one thing is seen and another understood. The appearance of bread and wine is perceived; the body and blood of Christ are believed. A + pure victim, with respect to the body; a + holy victim, with respect to the blood; a + spotless victim applies to both.

Alternatively: a + pure victim, namely one set apart from other victims; a + holy victim, that is, one sanctifying us; a + spotless victim, that is, one cleansing from stains. The + holy bread of eternal life, namely that by which, fed, we are made eternal; and the chalice of [Col. 0579A] everlasting salvation, namely, by whose taste we attain eternal salvation.

“Righteous Abel.” Abel is mentioned here because he offered this sacrifice in his lamb, and he himself, innocent like Christ, died (Gen. IV). For he was killed at thirty years of age, just as Christ was crucified at thirty years of age. “The sacrifice of Abraham our patriarch.” Patriarch means “highest father.” He bore the figure of God, who offered his Son for us, as Abraham offered Isaac (Gen. XXII). The ram is sacrificed and Isaac escapes; so the flesh of Christ is sacrificed for us, while his divinity remains unharmed. “Thy high priest Melchizedek,” whose name means “king of righteousness.” He, without father and without mother, is likened to the Son of God (Gen. XIV; Heb. VII), who in heaven had no mother and on earth lacked a father. He is king of righteousness because he will reward the righteous [Col. 0579B] and justly condemn the unrighteous. Melchizedek expressed Christ’s sacrifice by bread and wine, which Christ transferred into the sacrament of his body and blood. Therefore the sacrifices of these persons are recited at this point, because immediately afterward, by the priest’s bowing, Christ’s death is commemorated, which was prefigured by them.

“Command these things to be carried by the hands of thy holy angel to thy altar on high.” Angel means “messenger.” Christ was the Angel of great counsel when, by the counsel of the Father, he announced through the Son that this world would be redeemed. The exalted altar in the sight of God is Christ at God’s right hand. Upon this altar the Church offers spiritual victims, and upon it God receives the vows of the faithful and the sacrifice of righteousness. This angel carries these sacraments to the exalted altar when, interceding for us, he appears before the face of God [Col. 0579C] (Apoc. VIII). Those who partake of this altar, namely Christ, will be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace.

## CHAPTER CVII.—On the Names

“Remember, O Lord, thy servants.” Here you may name anyone, but not on the Lord’s Day. The names of the living were written in a book and recited at the altar within the canon; this was called the book of the living. Likewise, the names of the dead were recited here from a book; but this was omitted on Sundays, because some believed that souls had rest on account of the Lord’s resurrection.

“With the apostles and martyrs, with John.” Some wish John the Baptist to be understood; others, Mark, who is also read as being called John [Col. 0579D]; the latter is more likely meant here. Eight martyrs and seven virgins are placed here, by whose blood this sacrament is approved, because through this sacrifice one comes, in the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, to the eight beatitudes.

## CHAPTER CVIII.—On the Orders

Different ranks and sexes are introduced here because this sacrament is confirmed through every rank and sex: among the evangelists, John, also called Mark, who was bishop and martyr at Alexandria; among deacons, Stephen, who was the first martyr after Christ; among apostles, Matthias, who died for Christ; among the seventy-two disciples, Barnabas, who offered himself for Christ; among patriarchs, Ignatius, bishop of Antioch; among popes, [Col. 0580A] Alexander, Roman pontiff; among presbyters, Marcellinus; among exorcists, Peter; among married persons, Felicity and Perpetua; among virgins, Agatha and the rest. All of these confirmed this sacrifice with their blood and deserved to be numbered in Christ’s body.

“Through whom thou dost always create all these good things”: thou makest us a new creation in Christ. Thou san + ctificas [sanctifiest] us through baptism in him; thou vi + vificas [givest life] through the Holy Spirit in the soul; thou Bene + dicis [blessest] us by a special blessing, or the final blessing: “Come, ye blessed” (Matt. XXV)—and grant us, namely, eternal life after death. Through + him thou createst us; with + him thou createst us; in + him thou raisest us to life. It should be known that no one may say or add anything in the canon except what has been established by apostolic men. If anyone [Col. 0580B] presumes to do so, it is ascribed not to devotion but to presumption. Therefore the Lord’s Prayer is sung aloud, so that those about to communicate may be reconciled in peace by forgiving one another their offences.

## CHAPTER CIX.—On the Lord’s Prayer

“Our Father.” God wished to be Lord of the Jews, as of servants, but Father of Christians, as of sons. Therefore he cast those out of the house as useless servants and granted these an inheritance as sons; and even now he feeds them with the bread of angels and the flesh of the fatted calf. “Who art in heaven,” that is, in the saints. “Hallowed be thy name.” God’s name is hallowed when we, united to his Son, are received as co-heirs in the kingdom of the Father. Then his kingdom comes when his kingdom, the Church, reaches heavenly things. “Thy will be done, as in heaven so also on [Col. 0580C] earth,” when earth—that is, flesh—puts on a heavenly body, and people desire nothing evil but are equal to angels. He gives daily bread today when, in this exile, he refreshes us with his body. He forgives our debts if he grants that we can forgive others. He does not lead us into temptation if he frees us from temptation. He will deliver us from evil if he rescues us from sin and hell.

The name of holy Mary is commemorated here so that through her we may be delivered from present, past, and future evils, through whose childbirth we are made children of God. The three apostles are named because every word is affirmed to stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses (Matt. XVIII), and three orders bear witness to this sacrament: teachers, the continent, and married persons. [Col. 0580D] Here you may name whichever saints you wish, because every member of the Church shares in Christ’s sacraments.

## CHAPTER CX.—On Peace

When the priest kisses the paten and signs himself, he declares that through the cross and this sacrifice all things in heaven and on earth have been reconciled. Peace is called from *pactum*, “a covenant,” because God made a covenant with human beings: that he would be gracious to them through his Son.

## CHAPTER CXI.—On the *Agnus Dei*

Christ is called a lamb because he is the one who, according to the law, was sacrificed at Passover, through whom the people will be freed from bondage.
