John called him the Lamb of God who would take away the sins of the world (John I). Therefore, at the breaking, we sing *Agnus Dei*, that we may worthily receive the flesh [Col. 0581A] of this Lamb. Although this Lamb is wholly received by all the people and wholly by each individual, he nevertheless undoubtedly remains whole and entire in heaven. For the sacrament received by the mouth is reduced to nourishment for the body; but by the power of the sacrament, through which the inward person is satisfied, eternal life is attained.

The people intending to communicate ought to abstain from their wives for three days beforehand and thereafter remain apart from them for three days. For the people of God abstained for so many days when they received the law. The *Agnus Dei* is sung three times because a threefold body is understood: that which remains in heaven; that which walks on earth; and that which rests in tombs. Eucharist is called “good grace”; *eulogia*, “good blessing”; communion, “participation.” We sing this so that we may share in God’s grace with the righteous. [Col. 0581B] It is called “the completion” because by it the Mass is completed.

“Ite, missa est”: permission to depart. “Deo gratias”: an exclamation of thanksgiving. When these things have been performed, the people give thanks to God and return to their own homes, just as the people of Israel departed Egypt by Pharaoh’s permission; and gave thanks to God when, by Cyrus’s command, they returned from Babylon to Jerusalem, and then gave thanks to God. So, after receiving the final blessing, we shall go to our heavenly homeland and shall remain always in thanksgiving. Therefore after Mass we shall sing the hymn of the three children, namely *Benedicite* (“Bless, all ye works”), because we bless the Lord for all his benefits, whom afterward we shall praise for ever and ever. The Council of Toledo instituted its singing and subjected those who neglected it to anathema [Col. 0581C].

## CHAPTER CXII.—On the Four Kinds of the Mass

The Mass is divided into four kinds according to entreaties, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings. From the beginning of Mass to the offertory are entreaties; from the secret prayer to the Lord’s Prayer are prayers; thereafter to communion are petitions; from then to the end are thanksgivings.

## CHAPTER CXIII.—On the Three Hours of the Mass

It is permitted to sing Mass at three hours: the third, sixth, and ninth. On feast days, at the third; on ordinary days, at the sixth; in Lent or on fasting days, at the ninth hour. Mass is sung at the third hour because at the third hour Christ was judged for his passion, when [Col. 0581D] the Jews cried, “Crucify, crucify” (Luke XXIII), and the soldiers scourged him. Mass is celebrated at the sixth hour because at the sixth hour Christ was sacrificed for us on the cross. Mass is sung at the ninth hour because Christ is said to have undergone death at the ninth hour.

## CHAPTER CXIV.—That One Mass Should Be Celebrated

Mass should be celebrated once in a day by one priest, just as Christ willed to be sacrificed once. But if necessity compels—that is, if two feasts occur together—two or three may be celebrated, because the Romans also do this on the day of the Lord’s Nativity; and Christ’s passion is threefold: he suffered through the tongues of those insulting him, the hands of those striking him, and the nails of those crucifying him. For he was sacrificed in figure by the patriarchs; sacrificed by the prophets; and likewise [Col. 0582A] sacrificed for us by the Father and by himself. Yet it is read of Pope Leo that he often celebrated seven Masses in one day, sometimes nine.

No one ought to celebrate Mass without priestly vestments, each of these having been consecrated, and without a consecrated altar. No one except an ordained person may read the epistle or Gospel, just as no one except an ordained person may sing the Mass. After receiving washing, no one may celebrate Mass or communicate; if anyone does so, that person will be liable to severe penance.

## CHAPTER CXV.—On *Gloria in excelsis Deo*

“Glory in the highest” is never sung except at the third hour, at which the Holy Spirit is read to have descended upon believers and filled them with glory and rejoicing. On the two Sabbaths of Easter and Pentecost it is sung at the ninth [Col. 0582B] hour because lost glory is restored to those baptized.

## CHAPTER CXVI.—On One or Several Prayers in the Mass

As a rule, one prayer is said, just as one epistle or one Gospel is read. But if a feast occurs on the Lord’s Day, two may be said, because Roman authority also does this at the second Mass on the day of the Lord’s Nativity. Sometimes we say three because we read that the Lord prayed three times before his passion. At times we say five because in this office we enact the Lord’s fivefold passion. Occasionally we employ seven because of the seven petitions in the Lord’s Prayer, which we have learned that the apostles alone said concerning this sacrament. Whoever exceeds this number will wander as a blind person.

## CHAPTER CXVII.—On Kneeling in Lent

[Col. 0582C]

In Lent we say, “Let us bend the knee” at Mass because we signify that we humble body and soul in penitence. We fall to the ground for three reasons. The first is that we worship Christ in the flesh, remembering in reverence that he descended to earth and put on flesh from the earth in order to wash us. The second is that we recall that we, who stood in paradise with angels, now lie among brute animals, and we groan that our soul is pressed down to earth by the bodily mass. The third reason is this: one who stands is made equal to other human beings; one who lies on the ground is likened to beasts. And while we stood in righteousness, we were like rational beings. But after we fell into desires of the flesh, [Col. 0582D] we are found in the mire with beasts, as though irrational. Therefore, because we see ourselves unlike other human beings in our deeds, we are ashamed to be made equal to them even by the posture of the body. And we cry out penitently over our soul’s fall into vices when we fall bodily to the ground. We make our belly cling to the earth and our soul to the pavement, so that through Christ, made earth for us, we may be able to rise from earthly desires.

This rite took its beginning from Abraham, when, prostrate upon the earth, he worshipped the Lord (Gen. XXIV); the prophets imitated him, falling to the earth and worshipping the Lord. But the bending of knees was taken from the Gentiles, who rendered this honour to kings whom they worshipped prostrate or with bent knee. But we, with the Apostle, [Col. 0583A] say to God: “I bend my knees to the Lord” (Eph. III).

## CHAPTER CXVIII.—On Light at Mass

Light signifies the Holy Spirit. Therefore Mass is celebrated with light because this sacrament is consecrated through the Holy Spirit, and those who receive it worthily are illumined by the Holy Spirit. Light signifies joy because this sacrament of the Mass bestows eternal joy. In the *Credo in unum Deum*, when we say “and was made man,” we bend the knee because we worship Christ made man and crucified for us.

## CHAPTER CXIX.—On When the *Credo in unum Deum* Is to Be Sung

“I believe in one God” is sung on every Sunday and on feasts [Col. 0583B] of the Lord and of the holy cross, on feasts of holy Mary, on the natal days of the apostles, on the feast of All Saints, and at the dedication of a church, because something concerning these seems to resound in it. The book of the Gospel is kissed during the *Credo in unum* because the peace restored through Christ is declared.

## CHAPTER CXX.—On the Prefaces

Pope Pelagius established that nine prefaces should be sung, namely: “Because through the incarnate …,” for the Nativity; “Because when thine only-begotten …,” for Epiphany; “Who by bodily fasting …,” for Lent; “Who didst accomplish the salvation of the human race …,” for the Lord’s passion or the holy cross; “Thee indeed, O Lord, at all times …,” for Easter; “Who after the Resurrection …,” for the Ascension; “Who, ascending above all heavens …,” for Pentecost; “Who with thine only-begotten Son …,” for the Trinity; “To beseech thee, O Lord, humbly …,” for Peter and Paul, which is also said for several apostles.

Pope Gregory added a tenth, “Who thy Church …,” for Saint Andrew, which is customarily said everywhere for any individual apostle. More recently, Pope Urban II is known to have added an eleventh for holy Mary, which is widely used everywhere. Pope Zacharias decreed that no priest should enter the altar with a staff or stand at the altar with his head covered.

## CHAPTER CXXI.—Why *Gloria Patri* and *Alleluia* Are Not Sung for the Dead

At the Mass for the dead, *Gloria Patri* and *Alleluia*, which signifies joy, are not sung because it imitates mourning, and we are warned by this that we came into this world for sorrow and leave it through mourning [Col. 0583D]. The bodies of the dead ought not to be present at the Mass of the living because they do not respond with us or communicate with the living. This signifies that those who are dead in sins and do not receive Christ’s sacraments will not be able to participate in the communion of the living with Christ. Thus far concerning the sacrifice of the Mass.

# HERE BEGINS ON THE CHURCH

We have spoken briefly concerning the Mass; now let us examine a few matters concerning the church in which it is performed.

## CHAPTER CXXII.—On the Altar

Noah is read to have first constructed an altar for the Lord; then Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob built altars, which are understood as nothing other than upright stones [Col. 0584A] upon which they slaughtered sacrifices, burning them with fire placed underneath. At times fire came down from heaven and consumed the offered sacrifice. Thus Cain killed his brother because heavenly fire consumed Abel’s sacrifice while his own remained untouched (Gen. IV).

The difference between *altare* and *ara* is that an altar is called, as it were, a “high thing” or a “high ara,” upon which priests burned incense. An *ara*, however, is called as it were from *area*, that is, “a level place,” or from burning, because sacrifices burned upon it. For *ara* is Greek for what is called “imprecation” in Latin.

## CHAPTER CXXIII.—On the Tabernacle of Moses

When the Lord led his people out of Egypt, he showed Moses a particular tabernacle on Mount Sinai (Exod. XXVI), after whose pattern he commanded a material one [Col. 0584B] to be made. He also ordered precious vessels and sacred vestments to be made; established an altar for sacrifices, priests and Levites for ministries; and decreed that silver or bronze trumpets be made for calling the people together. Moses completed all these things in marvellous workmanship according to the pattern shown him, and dedicated the tabernacle with the people’s joy.

After this had been worn out by age, the Lord commanded a temple to be made for himself and sent King David, through a prophet, a document describing how the temple ought to be built. Solomon built a wonderful temple renowned throughout the whole world, as the Lord commanded in the document (III Kings V). He also made a golden altar, most precious vessels, and sacred vestments; he assigned priests, singers, and Levites to the services of the temple [Col. 0584C] as the Lord commanded in summary. When all had been duly done, he dedicated the temple with the greatest solemnity and placed the ark in it. Since both prefigured the Church, the Christian people formed churches in accordance with the pattern of each.

## CHAPTER CXXIV.—On the Tabernacle of the People

The tabernacle which the people had on their journey bore the form of the world and represented the Church, which on the journey of this world has no lasting city but seeks the city to come (Heb. XIII). The tabernacle was fashioned according to the world, and the elements and everything in the world were prefigured in it, because this whole world has now become God’s temple, dedicated by Christ’s blood (Heb. IX). Within it the universal Church, existing as God’s tabernacle [Col. 0584D], continually celebrates the living and true Lord with praises and desires that from a tabernacle it may become a temple.

One part of this tabernacle was called the Holy Place, in which the people sacrificed; it is the active life, in which the people labour in love of neighbour. The other part was called the Holy of Holies, in which priests and Levites ministered; it is the contemplative life, in which the purity of religious persons, in love of God, longs for heavenly things. Christians therefore make churches according to the form of the tabernacle. The front part of the building, where the people stand, is made after the Holy Place. The sanctuary, where the clergy stand, is made after the Holy of Holies. The Church borrowed the ministry of Levites and priests for the order of Christ’s ministers. It converted vessels, vestments, and the rite [Col. 0585A] of sacrifices into the custom of ecclesiastical observances. It transferred the blast of trumpets into the sound of bells.

## CHAPTER CCXV.—On the Temple

But the temple which the people possessed in their homeland in peace prefigures the temple of glory, built of living stones in the heavenly Jerusalem, in which the Church rejoices in everlasting peace. This is divided into two because the temple of the heavenly court is distinguished by the difference between angels and human beings. In it the golden altar is Christ, the glory of the saints. In this temple all the elect will be priests and singers; they themselves, precious vessels tested in the furnace of tribulation, will shine like the sun in the garment of salvation and gleam in the clothing of righteousness.

## CHAPTER CXXVI.—On the Church’s Seven Names

[Col. 0585B]

Therefore our church received its pattern from the temple made by Solomon. The Church is distinguished by seven names because the Church of Christ is supported by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, as the house of wisdom by seven columns (Prov. IX). *Ecclesia* is called a convocation because in it the people of the faithful are summoned to hear God’s judgments and to Christ’s banquet. The synagogue was called a gathering because it was gathered, like a flock of irrational cattle, by the rod of the law. The Church, however, is rightly called a convocation because it is summoned into one faith by the love of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER CXXVII.—On the Basilica and the Other Names of a Church

[Col. 0585C]

This building is called a basilica, that is, a royal place, because in it service is rendered to the King of kings. *Basileus*, indeed, means king, as though from *basis laos*, that is, “pillar of the people,” because the people are supported by his rule. This building is also called κυριακή (*kyriakē*), “belonging to the Lord,” because in it the Lord of lords is served. For *Kyrios* means “lord.” This building is also called the house of God because the Lord is worshipped in it; a house of prayer because the people of the faithful gather there for prayer; and the hall of God because the banquet of the eternal king is celebrated there. It is also called an oratory because it is a place for the faithful to pray. It is called a temple, as though an “ample roof,” because the gathering of the people is united beneath one roof within it. [Col. 0585D] A monastery is called the dwelling of monks; for *monos* means “alone,” and *steron* means “dwelling.” Larger churches are called temples; smaller ones are called *sacella*, and, from goatskins, also chapels.

## CHAPTER CXXVIII.—On Chapels

For ancient nobles had small churches made of goatskins while travelling; from this they called them chapels, and their custodians chaplains. Chaplains are also named from the cape of Saint Martin, which the kings of the Franks always had in battle, and those carrying it were called chaplains. *Gapenum* means a house to which the poor flock to seek alms. From it comes the diminutive *capella*, in which Christians poor in spirit assemble to seek alms for the soul.

## CHAPTER CXXIX.—On the Orientation of a Church

[Col. 0586A]

Churches are turned toward the East, where the sun rises, because in them the Sun of righteousness is worshipped, and paradise, our homeland, is proclaimed to be in the East. Therefore by the church is figured the Church which is assembled within it for God’s service. This building is set upon a rock, and the Church is founded upon Christ, the firm rock. It rises on high with four walls, and the Church rises in virtues through the four Gospels. This building is constructed from hard stones, and the Church is gathered from those strong in faith and works. The stones are joined with mortar, and the faithful are bound together by the bond of love. The sanctuary is the first-fruits of the Church gathered from the Jews; the front part of the building is those serving God in the active life.

## CHAPTER CXXX.—On the Windows of a Church

[Col. 0586B]

The transparent windows, which exclude the storm and admit light, are teachers who resist the whirlwind of heresies and pour the light of teaching into the Church. The glass in the windows, through which the ray of light is cast, is the mind of teachers, which contemplates heavenly things as though through a mirror in an enigma.

## CHAPTER CXXXI.—On the Columns of a Church

The columns which support the building are bishops, who uphold the structure of the Church on high by uprightness of life. The beams which join the building are secular rulers, who fortify the Church by sustaining it. The roof-tiles which repel rain from the building are soldiers, who protect the Church from pagans and enemies.

## CHAPTER CXXXII.—On Painting

[Col. 0586C]

Paintings on the ceiling are examples of the righteous, which display the ornament of morals to the Church. Painting is made for three reasons: first, because it is the literature of the laity; second, so that the building may be adorned with such beauty; third, so that the lives of those who came before may be recalled to memory.

## CHAPTER CXXXIII.—On the Halo in a Church

The lights painted around the heads of saints in churches in the shape of a circle indicate that they enjoy being crowned with the light of eternal splendour. They are painted in the shape of a round shield because they are now defended, as with a shield, by divine protection. Hence they sing in rejoicing: “O Lord, thou hast crowned us with the shield of thy good will” (Ps. V). The custom [Col. 0586D] of carving figures began with the Law, where Moses, by the Lord’s command, made two cherubim of gold (III Kings VI). The custom of painting churches began with Solomon, who instituted the making of various carvings in the Lord’s temple. The use of the candlestick and censer began with the Law.

## CHAPTER CXXXIV.—On the Pavement

The pavement, trodden by feet, is the common people, by whose labour the Church is supported. Crypts constructed beneath the earth are those who cultivate a more hidden life. The altar upon which sacrifice is made is Christ, upon whom the Church’s sacrifice is accepted. Therefore Christ’s body is consecrated upon the altar, because the people believing in him are nourished from him: they become one with Christ, as many stones become one altar. Relics are placed in the altar [Col. 0587A] because in Christ all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. II). Chests are placed upon the altar: these are the apostles and martyrs, who are read to have suffered for Christ. The cloths and vestments with which the altar is adorned are confessors and virgins, by whose works Christ is adorned.

## CHAPTER CXXXV.—On the Cross

The cross is raised above the altar for three reasons: first, because the sign of our King is set in the house of God as in a royal city, that it may be worshipped by soldiers. Second, that Christ’s passion may always be represented to the Church. Third, that the Christian people, crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. V), may imitate Christ. Banners are raised so that the Church may continually remember Christ’s trophy.

## CHAPTER CXXXVI.—On the Mercy-Seat

[Col. 0587B]

The mercy-seat, which is placed above the altar, is Christ’s divinity, which is propitious to the human race. The steps by which one ascends to the altar are virtues, through which one reaches Christ. The washing-place by which hands are washed beside the altar is mercy flowing from Christ, through which people are cleansed from defilements in baptism or penitence.

## CHAPTER CXXXVII.—On Hangings

The hangings suspended in the Church are Christ’s miracles, which are read in the Church. The pulpit which is raised high and from which the Gospel is read is the life of the perfect, to which one comes through evangelical teaching when, leaving all things, one follows Christ. The Church is continually illumined by the light of a lamp [Col. 0587C], and Christ’s Church is always illumined by the light of the Holy Spirit. Baptism is celebrated in the Church because the catholic Church is the mother from whom a new offspring is begotten for Christ.

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII.—On the Door

A door is so called from obstructing or showing. The door which obstructs enemies and shows friends the way to enter is Christ, who, opposing the unbelieving by righteousness, keeps them from his house and, showing the entrance, brings the faithful in through faith.

## CHAPTER CXXXIX.—On the Choir

The choir of psalm-singers took its origin from the dancing company of singers, which antiquity established there for idols, so that those deceived might praise their gods with voice and serve them with their whole body. By dances they wished to signify the circling [Col. 0587D] revolution of the firmament; by the joining of hands, the connection of the elements; by the sound of singers, the harmony of the sounding planets; by bodily gestures, the movement of the constellations; by clapping hands or stamping feet, the crackling of thunder. The faithful imitated this and converted it to the service of the true God. For it is read that the people, having gone forth from the Red Sea, led a dance, and Mary sang before them with a timbrel (Exod. XV); that David danced with all his might before the ark and sang psalms with the lyre (II Kings VI); and that Solomon established singers around the altar, who are read to have resounded songs with voice, trumpets, organs, cymbals, and lyres. Hence even now [Col. 0588A] they endeavour to use musical instruments in choirs, because the celestial spheres are said to be borne about with sweet melody.

## CHAPTER CXL.—On the Harmony of the Choir

A choir is so called from the harmony of those singing, or from the crown of those standing around. For formerly singers stood around altars in the manner of a crown; but the bishops Flavian and Diodorus instituted choirs singing psalms antiphonally. Two choirs of psalm-singers signify angels and the spirits of the righteous, praising the Lord, as it were, in responding voices. The chancel rails in which they stand signify the many dwelling-places in the Father’s house (John XIV). When they sometimes go in procession from the choir to an altar and sing there at the station, this signifies that souls departing this life come to Christ and sing to God in the fellowship of angels.

## CHAPTER CXLI.—On the Crown

[Col. 0588B]

A crown is suspended in the church for three reasons: one, because the church is adorned by it when illumined by its lights; another, because its sight reminds us that those who here serve God devoutly receive the crown of life and the light of joy; the third, that the heavenly Jerusalem may be recalled to our minds, after whose pattern it seems to have been made.

It consists of gold, silver, bronze, and iron. Gold represents those resplendent in wisdom; silver, those shining in eloquence; bronze, those sweetly sounding in heavenly teaching; iron, those mastering vices. The towers of the crown are those who fortify the Church with writings; its lamps are those who shine in good works. Gold represents martyrs; silver, virgins; bronze, the continent; iron, those serving in marriage. The gems glittering in the crown [Col. 0588C] are those also radiant in virtues. Metals refined in fire are taken for the crown’s ornament, and the elect, tested in the furnace of tribulation, are chosen for the adornment of the heavenly Jerusalem. The chain by which the crown is held aloft is hope, by which the Church is suspended from earthly things toward heavenly. The highest circle to which it is attached is God, by whom all things are held together.

## CHAPTER CXLII.—On Bells

The signals now given by bells were formerly given by trumpets. These vessels were first discovered at Nola in Campania. Hence they are so called: the larger vessels are called *campanae*, from the region of Campania; the smaller, *nolae*, from the city of Nola in Campania. Thus they signify preachers who summon the people to church. Their ringing is the preaching of those whose [Col. 0588D] sound has gone out into all the earth and whose words unto the ends of the world (Ps. XVIII). They are cast from bronze, which is hard and resonant, because their preaching is hard against vices and resonant concerning virtues. They are made in the shape of vessels because preachers are called vessels of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER CXLIII.—On Towers
Towers, in which the bells hang and ring, are the two laws, by which preachers, suspended from earthly things toward heavenly things, preach the kingdom of God. The clapper is made of iron, which subdues all hard things: it is the tongue of those who overcome every adversity. The fastening by which it is bound is moderation, by which their tongue is tempered. The rope,

[Col. 0589A]

by which the bells are moved to sound is Holy Scripture, woven from many sayings, by which preachers are moved to preach. The rope descends from the wood, and Holy Scripture descends from the wood of the cross and the Lord’s Passion. The wood is held from above, because the cross and Passion of Christ were preached beforehand by the prophets, and the Gospel is joined to the Law, and apostolic teaching is woven together with prophecy. The priest grasps the rope when, taught by Scripture, he performs good works. The rope draws him upward when Scripture holds him suspended in contemplation; he himself draws the rope downward when he descends from contemplation to the active life. From the pulling of the rope the bell rings, because from good action it resounds.

### CHAPTER CXLIV.—On the bell-tower

[Col. 0589B]

The bell-tower, which is set on high, is lofty preaching, which speaks of heavenly things. Nor is a cock placed upon the bell-tower without reason. For the cock wakes those who sleep [Note: [Col. 0589D] Pliny, *Natural History*, book X, chapter 21.], and by this the presbyter, the cock of God, is admonished to awaken sleepers by the bell for Matins.

### CHAPTER CXLV.—On stationing

In church, men stand on the southern side, signifying that those stronger in faith and fervent with the ardour of the Holy Spirit ought to become leaders, since they must endure the heat of the world’s temptations. Women, however, stand on the northern side, showing that the more fragile ought to be subject, since they cannot bear the heat of temptations and temper the heat of the flesh by the remedy of marriage.

### CHAPTER CXLVI.—On women

[Col. 0589C]

Women also, after childbirth (Lev. XV), do not enter the church, because they signify that the unclean are excluded from the heavenly temple. Otherwise, if their weakness permitted it, they would be allowed to enter churches on the very day on which they gave birth, in order to give thanks to God. For this signification, in many places menstruating women who have had intercourse with men customarily stand outside the church; and for this reason penitents ought not to enter the church. Pope Linus, by the command of the blessed Peter and Paul, decreed that women should be veiled in church.

This is done for three reasons. The first is that, since they are the devil’s snare, the minds of young men may not be entangled by their loosened hair. The second is that some women may not be lifted up in pride because of the beauty of their hair, while others may not be disfigured because of its ugliness.

[Col. 0589D]

The third is that the guilt of original sin, which came through woman, may be recalled to our memory. For Christ is the judge of evils, and the priest is his vicar. Before the priest, therefore, a woman ought to veil herself as one accused and, conscious of so great an evil, hide herself before the judge. Hence the Apostle says that a woman should be veiled “because of the angels” (I Cor. XI), that is, the priests. For in churches they are not permitted to speak (II Cor. LVI), that is, to address the people. Nor are we permitted to speak in church except in hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs, and in prayer, so that we may be joined to heavenly things.

### CHAPTER CXLVII.—On the cemetery

[Col. 0590A]

The cemetery, which is called the sleeping-place of the dead, is the bosom of the Church; for just as it gave birth to Christ, from the womb of baptism, to those dead to the world, so afterward, cherishing in its bosom those dead in the flesh, it restores them to eternal life.

Churches built in the form of a cross show that the people of the Church ought to be crucified to the world. Those made round, in the form of a circle, show that the Church is built through the circle of the world into the circle of the crown of eternity by love.

### CHAPTER CXLVIII.—On the cloister

The cloistered structure beside the monastery is derived from Solomon’s portico, built beside the Temple. In it all the apostles remained unanimously,

[Col. 0590B]

and gathered in the Temple for prayer; the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and held all things in common (Acts IV). In accordance with this pattern, religious live unanimously in the cloister and assemble day and night in the monastery for God’s service. Believers, too, leave secular affairs behind and lead a common life in the cloister.

### CHAPTER CXLIX.—That the cloister is paradise

Moreover, the cloister represents Paradise (Gen. IV), while the monastery represents Eden, the more secure place of Paradise. The spring in this place of delight is, in the monastery, the font of baptism; the tree of life in Paradise is the body of the Lord in the monastery. The various fruit-bearing trees are the various books of Holy Scripture. For the enclosure of the cloister bears the figure of heaven, in which the righteous are separated from sinners just as professed religious are secluded from secular persons in the cloister.

[Col. 0590C]

Moreover, monasteries represent the heavenly Paradise. The spring and the tree of life signify Christ, who is the fountain of life and the food of the blessed who live eternally. In the monastery two choirs sing praises to God; and in the heavenly Paradise angels and saints will praise the Lord with sweet harmony for ever and ever. The community of those living in the cloister has one heart and one soul in religious life and possesses all things in common; likewise, in the heavenly homeland all the elect will have one heart and one soul in love, and all will possess all things in common, because whatever each lacks there he will possess in others, where God will be all in all. In the cloister individuals hold individual places according to order,

[Col. 0590D]

and in Paradise individuals will receive individual dwelling-places according to their merits.

### CHAPTER CL.—On the dedication of a church

The dedication of a church is the nuptial union of the Church and Christ. The bishop who consecrates it is Christ, who has espoused the Church. The bishop blesses the font in the atrium and sprinkles around it, because Christ consecrated the font of baptism in Judaea and commanded all nations throughout the world to be washed in it.

### CHAPTER CLI.—On an unconsecrated building

An unconsecrated building is the pagan world, ignorant of God

[Col. 0591A]

and shut in by the barriers of unbelief. Twelve candles kindled around the building illuminate it; and the twelve apostles illumined paganism throughout the world with the light of teaching. The candle shines and burns; the apostles shone in speech and burned in charity. The bishop strikes three times with his staff above the lintel of the door and says: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates” (Ps. XXIII). By the bishop Christ is understood; by the staff, the sceptre of power. The threefold striking signifies threefold power in heaven, on earth, and in hell.

Thus the Lord, as it were, struck the door three times with his staff when he granted the Church the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, and granted that the gates of hell should not prevail against it (Matt. XVI). He also commands the princes of darkness

[Col. 0591B]

to remove the gates of death from the Church, while the everlasting—that is, heavenly—gates are lifted up, and the righteous enter into life.

### CHAPTER CLII.—On the gates

The gates of death are vices and sins; the gates of life are faith, baptism, and good action. By him who answers from within, the devil is understood, who is driven out of the house of the Church. For he, like a strong man armed, guarded his own courtyard when he possessed this world as if by right. But one stronger came, drove him out, and distributed his spoils (Matt. XII; Luke XI), when Christ conquered him by his Passion and rescued the Church from his dominion.

Then the door is opened and the bishop enters, because the Church opened to Christ the door of faith and devoutly received him within herself. The bishop entering says,

[Col. 0591C]

“Peace to this house,” because Christ, entering the world, bestowed upon humankind the peace which, risen from the dead, he offered to his own: “Peace,” he says, “be with you” (John XX). He cries “Peace to this house” three times, because this indicates the reconciliation of the Church accomplished through the Trinity, or because there is one God, one faith, one baptism (Eph. IV).

Then the bishop prostrates himself and prays to the Lord for the consecration of the building; and Christ, before his Passion, prostrated himself on the mountain and prayed to the Father for the sanctification of the Church. Rising, the bishop does not greet the people with “The Lord be with you,” but invites them to prayer with “Let us bend the knee,” because unbelievers and the impious are not to be greeted but urged to conversion and penitence.

### CHAPTER CLIII.—On the alphabet

[Col. 0591D]

After this he writes the alphabet on the pavement with his staff, beginning at the left eastern corner and ending at the right western corner. Then he begins another alphabet at the right eastern corner and completes it, writing, at the left western corner. These two alphabets meet in the middle of the church in the form of a cross, and openly indicate what they symbolize for us.

### CHAPTER CLIV.—On the four corners of the church

The four corners of the church are the four regions of the world. The writing inscribed upon the ground is simple teaching impressed upon earthly hearts. The bishop begins to write from the left corner because Christ began to teach from Judaea. It is compared to the left corner because, on account of unbelief, it is reckoned among those on the left.

[Col. 0592A]

It is called the eastern corner because Christ, who is the East, arises there according to the flesh. The bishop leads the writing to the right corner because Christ’s teaching reached as far as the Church. For it is likened to the right corner because it is counted with those on the right. It is the western corner because unbelief fell there, and Christ, the Sun of righteousness, set in death for it.

### CHAPTER CLV.—On the right corner

Again, the bishop begins the writing at the right eastern corner and completes it at the left western corner, because by his teaching Christ began the Church in its firstfruits and will complete it at the end of the world among the people of Israel. The Church of the firstfruits is called the right

[Col. 0592B]

corner because it is the queen who is written to stand at God’s right hand. It is called the eastern corner because “light rises for the upright” in it (Ps. III). The people of Israel, however, are called the left corner because they are still not ashamed to persist in unbelief. They are called the western corner because, when the world has already set, after the fullness of the Gentiles Israel will be converted to Christ.

The two alphabets, which meet in the form of a cross from different corners, are the two peoples who, from differing observances, came together through Christ into the one faith of the cross. For they are the two Testaments, which, joined together, set forth the cross of Christ’s Passion. One, however, is written in Greek, the other in Latin, because the Greek language is recognized as pre-eminent over others because of wisdom, and Latin because of imperial power;

[Col. 0592C]

both are converted to faith in the cross. Both, moreover, are written with the staff because all these things are accomplished through preachers. Up to this point, all that preceded was, as it were, the preface to the consecration. From here the dedication of the church begins; and therefore, by what now follows, Christ’s Passion and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit are indicated, through which the Catholic Church is consecrated.

### CHAPTER CLVI.—On “God, come to my assistance”

After this, the bishop, standing before the altar, invokes divine help through the verse, “God, attend to my assistance,” so that he may be able worthily to consecrate the building to God’s name. He adds “Glory to the Father,” without *alleluia*, because he makes known that glory is to be sung to the Trinity in that building;

[Col. 0592D]

he does not add *alleluia* because it has not yet been consecrated for the voice of exultation. After the consecration, however, *alleluia* will be sung, because, once every illusion of demons has been excluded, God will be praised in it.

So Christ, the true bishop, approaching the altar of the cross, invoked the Father’s help by which he might sanctify the Church; he sang, as it were, “Glory to the Father” when he underwent death for the Church to the glory of the Trinity. He did not add *alleluia* when the whole world was disturbed at his Passion. But after the Resurrection, as after the consecration, *alleluia* was sung, because heaven and earth rejoiced at his Resurrection.

### CHAPTER CLVII.—On salt and ash

Then water is blessed; wine is mixed in, and salt

[Col. 0593A]

and ash are also mingled with it. By salt, through which all foods are made savoury, Christ, the Wisdom of God, is signified—the Wisdom through which all received the power to know and understand. Then Elisha put salt into the water and the waters were healed (IV Kings II), because God sent Wisdom, that is, his Son, among humankind, and they were healed.

In the Law a red heifer was commanded to be burned in fire and the people to be purified with its ashes (Num. XIX). The red heifer was burned into ash for the people’s purification; Christ, reddened with blood and reduced to ash by the fire of Passion, is that by which the company of the faithful has been purified. This ash is mingled with salt when humanity is resumed by divinity in the Resurrection. Ash is also mingled with salt when we Christians, who are ash and are called the Church, are associated with Christ’s divinity.

### CHAPTER CLVIII.—On wine and water

[Col. 0593B]

Likewise, divinity is understood through wine, humanity through water. These two are mingled when our humanity is joined to divinity through Christ’s blood. A cross is made three times over the water with salt and ash, because through the cross Christ impressed upon humankind faith in the Trinity. Moreover, through each of these things the Church’s sacrifice, offered in this dedicated building, is expressed: through salt and ash, Christ’s body in divinity is prefigured; through wine and water, Christ’s blood, which is consecrated with water, is prefigured.

### CHAPTER CLIX.—On the temple

It should be noted that all this is referred to the human being, who is called God’s temple. First the bishop opens the door;

[Col. 0593C]

then he pours forth prayers; after this he writes the alphabet; then he blesses water with salt and ash, mixes in wine, and then anoints. Thus, for anyone converted to the Lord, the door of faith is opened; then prayer is offered for that person; then Scripture is inscribed upon the mind when the catechumen is instructed by exorcisms; thereafter, through faith, the catechumen is taught Christ’s divinity and humanity; then purified by the font of baptism; finally anointed with chrism, and thus made the temple of God.

### CHAPTER CLX.—On the altar and cross

After this the priest dips his finger and makes a cross at the four horns of the altar. Here the altar represents the primitive Church in Jerusalem. Christ the bishop, as it were, made the cross over the altar when he underwent the cross in

[Col. 0593D]

Jerusalem for the Church. He marked the four horns of the altar when he saved the four parts of the world by the cross. Then he sprinkles seven times toward the altar, because after the Resurrection Christ commanded the Church to be baptized in the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Water is sprinkled with hyssop, a bitter herb said to penetrate the hardness of stones; it signifies Christ’s flesh embittered in the Passion, through whom baptism is given and the hardness of the Gentiles is softened unto faith. Then he goes around the altar while sprinkling, because the Lord sustains his angel around those who fear him. The altar is sprinkled three times because the Church is cleansed from the three deadly sins: of deed, speech, and thought. Then he proceeds through the whole church and sprinkles the walls on both sides,

[Col. 0594A]

because Christ commanded the people to be baptized throughout all Judaea. Meanwhile the psalm is sung: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered,” because when Christ rose, the demons and the Jews, his enemies, were scattered. And when Christ’s Resurrection and baptism were preached throughout the world, God’s enemies were scattered from the Church.

### CHAPTER CLXI.—On the ministers

The bishop sends ministers to go round the church singing, because Christ sent the apostles to preach baptism throughout the whole world. Walking through the middle of the church, the bishop sings the antiphon, “My house”; and Christ, visiting through teachers, made it his house. But, beginning the antiphon “I shall enter,” he then goes singing to the altar and

[Col. 0594B]

pours what remains of the water at the base of the altar, because Christ poured out the streams of teaching in Jerusalem, and from there the font of baptism sprang forth.

After this the altar is wiped with a linen cloth, by which the Lord’s Passion is understood. For linen rises from the earth and, through labour, is changed to whiteness; and Christ is born of the Virgin and, through the great labour of Passion, returned to the brightness of the Resurrection. The altar is wiped with this cloth when the tribulation of the Church is soothed by the example of Christ’s Passion. Then incense is offered: that is, the prayers of the righteous, who offer themselves to God as a fragrance when they afflict their bodies for him.

### CHAPTER CLXII.—On oil and the altar

Afterward the bishop pours oil upon the altar, making a cross in its middle and upon its four horns,

[Col. 0594C]

because Christ poured out the Holy Spirit upon the primitive Church in Jerusalem, where he also underwent the cross; afterward he bestowed these gifts upon the faithful throughout the four parts of the world. Then the antiphon is sung: “Jacob set up a stone as a pillar”; the stone was anointed. Christ was anointed by the Father with the Holy Spirit, namely with the oil of gladness; he was made the head of the corner (Ps. XLIV; CXVII), when both peoples were joined in him.

The altar is anointed three times—twice with oil, the third time with chrism—because the Church is marked with faith, hope, and charity. When the oil has been poured out, the antiphon is sung: “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field.” By the field is understood the breadth of the world, through which the Church is spread everywhere. This field blooms with flowers when the Church shines with virtues. The scent of flowers is the fragrance of good works. The roses are

[Col. 0594D]

martyrs; the lilies, virgins; the violets, those who despise the world; the green herbs, the wise; those in flower, the proficient; the souls full of fruits, the perfect.

### CHAPTER CLXIII.—On chrism

Finally, with his thumb he makes crosses of chrism upon the walls of the church, beginning at the right side and continuing to the left, because the anointing of chrism, beginning from the primitive Church, reached the Church of the Gentiles. Meanwhile the antiphon is sung, “The Lord has sanctified his tabernacle.” The Church is now God’s tabernacle in the journey of this world; afterward it will be a temple in anticipation. Then comes the antiphon, “Precious stones.” Precious stones are those who composed the Holy Scriptures. The walls and towers of Jerusalem are the defences of the Scriptures,

[Col. 0595A]

by which Jews, heretics, and pagans are kept off. The gems are sacred sayings.

### CHAPTER CLXIV.—On incense

Then the bishop makes a cross of incense upon the altar and bows himself to prayer. Christ also, the bishop of bishops, places the incense of the cross upon the altar because he intercedes for us with the Father. For to make a cross of incense is to show the Father his Passion for the Church and to intercede for us. Hence the bishop begins the antiphon: “Strengthen, O God, what you have accomplished in us,” with “Glory to the Father,” because Christ prays to the Father for the Church, that he may establish in it the redemption which he himself accomplished and subject all the earth to it.

He adds the source from which this grace proceeded: “from your holy temple, which

[Col. 0595B]

is in Jerusalem” (Ps. LXVII). For in Jerusalem the salvation of the human race began and from there flowed into the whole world. Jerusalem is the Church, in which is Christ’s temple, in whom the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily; yet, poured out through the Holy Spirit, it flowed forth abundantly to humankind. “Glory to the Father” is added because the Trinity accomplishes this salvation, and therefore praise and glory are sung to the Trinity.

### CHAPTER CLXV.—On vessels and ornaments

After this the subdeacons or acolytes present to the bishop, for blessing, the vessels, linens, and all ornaments. These are those chosen for the adornment of the Church and consecrated by the bishop for the Church’s service; they are called God’s vessels. When these things have been done, the bishop goes to the place

[Col. 0595C]

where the relics of the Powers were during the night with vigils, and lifts them up, carrying them to the place prepared. Thus Christ, the true bishop, after preparing a place for us, takes up from their places the righteous who in the night of this present life guard themselves from evil with watchful minds, and leads them into his Father’s house.

Hence the antiphon is sung: “Walk, saints of God; enter the city of God,” that is, the heavenly Jerusalem. The words which follow, “A new Church has been built for us,” mean the new Jerusalem, which “is built as a city” (Ps. CXXI). Various antiphons are sung: they imitate the rejoicing and exultations of the angelic powers, which accompany souls departing from the body until they receive the dwelling-places due to their merits.

[Col. 0595D]

Coming before the altar, where the relics are enclosed, the bishop stretches a veil between himself and the people, because the places of souls are hidden from the sight of mortals.

### CHAPTER CLXVI.—On the relics of saints

The relics are sealed in the altar because souls are placed in heaven. The antiphon is sung: “The saints shall exult in glory,” because souls rejoice in the angelic court.

### CHAPTER CLXVII.—On the garment of souls

After this the altar is clothed, because at the Resurrection souls are clothed with bodies. The altar was bare while souls had been placed in heaven without bodies. The altar is clothed when the soul is clothed in a mortal and incorruptible body.

### CHAPTER CLXXVIII.—On the day of judgment

[Col. 0596A]

After this the bishop blesses the altar, and Christ blesses the Church with these words: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV). The bishop returns to the sacristy with his orders and clothes himself in other vestments; and Christ returns to the world for judgment with the angelic orders. He is clothed in other garments because he will show a servile form to the impious, when they see him whom they crucified; while the righteous will see the King of glory in his beauty.

Then the church is adorned and lights are kindled, because then the works of the righteous will shine, and, adorned on their account, they will shine perpetually like the sun. Then the singer begins, “Terrible is this place.” For what is more terrible than that day, when angels will fear and the impious will go into eternal punishment?

[Col. 0596B]

Then the bishop proceeds solemnly, and the office is performed with all joy, because, once judgment has been accomplished, God will be seen face to face in his glory; God will be all in all (I Cor. XIII), and as light is to the eyes, so joy will be to souls.

### CHAPTER CLXIX.—On a definite place and sacrifice

Therefore, just as Mass is properly celebrated in a dedicated church, so sacrifice is lawfully offered in the Catholic Church, and outside it no sacrifice is accepted by God. Although God can and ought justly to be blessed and invoked everywhere—in field, wilderness, sea, or every place of his dominion, as, for instance, in the temple of the whole world—nevertheless, at a fitting time the faithful rightly hasten to church so that God may be invoked and worshipped there. For there he promises to grant every thing which two ask in agreement,

[Col. 0596C]

and he is said to be present wherever two or three gather in his name (Matt. XVIII).

It is right that the Christian people should gather in the oratory as if at a tribunal, hear the judgments and commands of the eternal King, and receive from the banquet of the fatted calf. Therefore, when the people gather in church, a temple is, as it were, built for God to inhabit. The Church within the church is the Christian people in the dedicated hall. The temple within the temple is any baptized person within the consecrated building.

### CHAPTER CLXX.—On a violated church

If a church is violated by homicide or adultery, it is dedicated again. Likewise, if a human being—the temple of the Holy Spirit, dedicated in baptism—is violated by a criminal sin, that person must be renewed again by the font of tears. If the seal of the altar is removed, it is commanded that it be consecrated again. Likewise, if the seal of faith is removed from the altar of the heart by some heresy, it must be reconciled again through penitence.

[Col. 0596D]

If the principal altar is moved, it is decreed that the church be consecrated again. Likewise, if the bishop, the head of the Church, changes from faith to heresy, the whole people subject to him are defiled; and therefore it is fitting that, together with him, they be received again into the Catholic faith through penitence and sanctification.

A church which has been violated and not consecrated again will be unclean and open to dogs. Likewise, if a person violates God’s temple—that is, himself—by a mortal crime and does not cleanse it again through penitence, it will be a dwelling-place for demons.

[Col. 0597A]

Those who have been killed are not carried into church, lest the pavement be stained with blood. For this reason some think that women who die in childbirth should not be carried into church, though this may lawfully be done.

### CHAPTER CLXXI.—On the construction of a church

It is good, therefore, to build churches and to adorn those already built with vessels, vestments, and other ornaments. But it is far better to expend those same resources for the needs of the poor and, through the hands of the poor, to send one’s wealth beforehand into heavenly treasures (Matt. VI), preparing there a house not made by hands but eternal in heaven (II Cor. V), in which one may dwell eternally with angels.

It should be known, however, that holy places do not save those whom wicked works separate from the Church, nor, conversely, do terrible places harm those who live piously. Nadab and Abihu, priests, were consumed by fire in God’s tabernacle (Lev. X); Korah, Dathan, and Abiram were swallowed by the earth before the tabernacle (Num. XVI).

[Col. 0597B]

Eli, the high priest, perished in a holy place with his neck broken (I Kings IV). Uzzah died when struck down beside the ark (II Kings VI). Joab was killed beside the altar (III Kings II). King Uzziah was covered with leprosy in the Temple (II Chron. XXVI). Finally, the violated Temple was destroyed, and the people who transgressed the Law were led captive from it (IV Kings XXV).

Conversely, Joseph did not perish in the cistern or in prison (Gen. XXXVII); Moses did not undergo death in the river (Exod. I); Job did not perish on the dunghill, nor Jeremiah in the mud (Job II; Jer. XXXVIII); Daniel was not harmed in the lions’ den, nor the three youths in the fiery furnace (Dan. III, VI); Peter did not perish in prison, nor Paul at sea (Acts XII; II Cor. XI). Indeed, the devil fell from heaven and man fell from Paradise (Gen. III; Isa. XIV). But the righteous are visited by God on earth and raised from hell to heavenly things.

[Col. 0597C]

### CHAPTER CLXXII.—On the ministers of the Church

We have now spoken of the Church as God gave it; it remains for us to speak of the Church’s ministers. The Church, therefore, received the use of priests and ministers from the Synagogue. Moses first appointed them by the Lord’s command for service in the tabernacle (Exod. XXVI). Then David and Solomon likewise, by the Lord’s command, appointed singers and Levites in the Temple; following them, the apostles arranged ministers of the Church in the Christian

[Col. 0597D]

religion (Acts VI).

### CHAPTER CLXXIII.—On Christians

Christians are so called from Christ, and their mode of life is divided into laity, monks, and clerics. *Laos* means “people”; hence *laici*, that is, persons of the people. *Monas* means “singleness”; hence monks, that is, those living singly.

### CHAPTER CLXXIV.—On clerics

*Cleros* means “lot” or “inheritance.” Hence clerics: that is, those allotted to the Lord’s inheritance. For they receive the tithe and sacrifice, which are called God’s portion or inheritance because they are offered, by God’s command, for God’s service. Clerics are called from “lot” because priests under the Law were chosen by lot;

[Col. 0598A]

and among the Gentiles, anyone who had several children chose one by lot for the clergy. All ministers of the Church are called clerics. But they are arranged in seven ranks because they are consecrated by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. These are: doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, and presbyters.

### CHAPTER CLXXV.—On doorkeepers

Those who in the Synagogue were called gatekeepers or temple servants are called doorkeepers in the Church. Their office under the Law was to open and close the Temple, as Samuel did, and to exclude from God’s house those Jews who were defiled and those Gentiles who were unclean—that is, uncircumcised. In the Church, however, their office is to bring catechumens who are to be baptized into church, receive at the door penitents reconciled through the bishop, and bring them back into God’s house.

When they are ordained, the keys of the church are handed to them by the bishop, so that they may open the church doors to believers and close them to unbelievers, and may open God’s temple—which they themselves are—to virtues and close it to vices.

[Col. 0598B]

### CHAPTER CLXXVI.—On readers

Those who were singers in the Temple are readers among us. Their office was to make resound in the Temple the hymns composed by David or the songs composed by Solomon, as Asaph and Jeduthun did, and to rejoice before God with organs or cymbals. In the Church their office is to recite Holy Scripture and to sing responsories, graduals, and *alleluia* alone before the people, to God’s praise.

When they are ordained, a book is handed to them

[Col. 0598C]

by the bishop, so that they may fulfil in deeds what they proclaim to the people from books. The precentor is one who sings first; the succentor, one who follows the chant; the *centor* or cantor, one who sings in harmony; the psalmist, one who recites psalms; the *symmysta*, that is, secretary or confidant of secrets, one who explains Christ’s mysteries.

### CHAPTER CLXXVII.—On exorcists

An exorcist is called an adjurer. Taught by Solomon, they adjured demons and expelled them from possessed persons, as the seven sons of Sceva the priest did. In the Church their office is to exorcize infants who are to be catechized and, through the words of God, to forbid demons access to the bodies of those to be baptized; likewise, by exorcisms to drive demons away from energumens—that is, possessed bodies.

When they are ordained, a book is handed to them by the bishop

[Col. 0598D]

so that they may fulfil the admonitions of the books and thus be able to expel demons from others.

### CHAPTER CLXXVIII.—On acolytes

Those who under the Law were called arrangers of lights are among us called acolytes—that is, *cerarii*, from wax. They lit or extinguished lights in the Temple, replenishing them with oil and tending the lamps; Nadab and Abihu were among them (Exod. XXIV). In the Church their office is to carry a light or censer before the priest at Mass or at the Gospel, and to serve in adorning the altar with cloths or coverings. When they are ordained, a candlestick and a pitcher or flask are handed to them by the bishop, so that they may be admonished

[Col. 0599A]

to have the lamp of good works shining in their hands and the oil of a good conscience in the vessels of their heart.

### CHAPTER CLXXIX.—On subdeacons

Those who among the Hebrews are written as *Nachumei*, that is, “serving in humility,” are called among us subdeacons, that is, subordinate ministers. Their office under the Law was to receive from the people the sacrifices offered and to carry water or whatever necessities were required for the Temple’s service; Nathanael is said to have been among them (John I). In the Church, however, their office is to read the Epistle and to present at the altar to the deacon the chalice and paten with the corporal cloth. Hence they are also called hypodeacons, that is, servants of the deacon.

When they are ordained, the sacred vessels—that is, the chalice and paten—and a hand-towel

[Col. 0599B]

are given to them by the bishop, so that they may know themselves to be God’s vessels and present themselves clean for this ministry.

### CHAPTER CLXXX.—On deacons

The Levites are called *assumpti*, “those taken up,” from Levi, the son of Jacob; through them all sacrifices were administered under the priests. Eleazar and Ithamar are named among them. The Church calls these deacons, that is, ministers, because they serve the priests. Their office in the Church is to read the Gospel, arrange the sacrifice upon the altar, distribute the Lord’s blood, give the people leave to depart, and, if necessary, preach and baptize. When they are ordained, the bishop gives them a stole so that they may know themselves bound by God’s law and may in every way devote themselves to chastity in God’s service. An archdeacon is called the chief deacon, as Stephen

[Col. 0599C]

or Lawrence was.

### CHAPTER CLXXXI.—On presbyters

A presbyter is called an elder, not in age but in understanding. For “the grey hairs of humanity are understanding” (Wis. IV). Under the Law these were called princes of the people, such as Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, or magistrates of the Temple, such as Nicodemus and Gamaliel; through them the people’s sacrifices were offered. A presbyter is called one “providing a way” [from Greek **πρεσβύτερος**, “elder”], namely, for the people from the exile of this world to the homeland of the heavenly kingdom.

Their office is to celebrate Masses, offer sacrifice for the people, distribute the Lord’s body, preach, baptize, absolve penitents, anoint the sick, bury the dead, lead the people to Mass, weddings, warfare, satchels, staffs, judgments, and bless water, candles, palms, ashes,

[Col. 0599D]

or any things pertaining to food. At their ordination, the bishop lays hands on them and grants the power of binding and loosing, so that they may live in such a manner as to be able to bind and loose others. He lays upon them the sweet yoke of the Lord when he encircles their neck with the stole, so that they may obey God’s law in such a manner as to be able to govern others. He anoints their hands with chrism, so that all that they bless may be blessed, and so that they may refrain from every unclean work, in order worthily to be able to consecrate Christ’s body.

### CHAPTER CLXXXII.—On priests again
A priest (*sacerdos*) is so called as though “giving sacred things” (*sacrum dans*). For he gives the Lord’s body, or the other sacraments, to the people. A priest is also called a “holy leader” (*sacer dux*) [or rather, “one giving sacred things”], [Col. 0600A] because by word and example he offers leadership toward life to the people. Both bishop and presbyter are called priest, because through each the sacrament is given. An archpresbyter is called the chief presbyter. A dean is one set over ten presbyters. A provost is one set over others. A chorepiscopus is one set over the choir of priests as the bishop’s vicar. A vice-bishop is one who performs the bishop’s office. These are represented by the seventy men who, receiving Moses’ spirit, were set over the people (Num. XI).

## CHAPTER CLXXXIII.—On Bishops

The order of bishops is divided into three: bishops, archbishops, and patriarchs. A bishop is said to be one intent upon a *scopos* [rather, from Greek ἐπισκοπέω, “I watch”]; hence a bishop is called a superintendent, as one who looks down from on high [Col. 0600B] upon the conduct and life of those subject to him. For just as the keeper of a vineyard, sitting aloft, looks about in every direction, so the bishop, keeper of Christ’s vineyard—that is, of the Church—sitting as though on high, looks upon and instructs the people placed under him. Hence he is also called a watchman, because, just as a watchman is placed in a high tower so that he may observe approaching enemies and urge the citizens to resist, so the bishop is stationed, as it were, in a watchtower, that he may strive to arm the people against the enemies, demons and heresies.

He is likewise named *praesul*, because he is thought to preside for counsel. He is also called *antistes*, as though “standing before,” because he appears to stand above the people. For *anti* means “against.” Thus he is called *antistes*, as though “one standing against,” because the shepherd is seen to stand against heretics as against wolves and to protect the sheep. He is also [Col. 0600C] called pontiff, as though “a bridge made.” For the bishop’s life ought to be a bridge for the people over the sea of this age to the homeland of paradise. Or rather, he is called pontiff as “making a bridge,” because he makes, as it were, a bridge for the people when by sound doctrine he leads them over the marshes of heresies to the courts of life.

## CHAPTER CLXXXIV.—On the High Priest

In the old law Aaron was called high priest, because he ruled over the other priests and Levites (Exod. XXXI). He bore the tetragrammaton, the name of God, and once a year made an offering for the people. Under the law Aaron was the first anointed with oil as high priest. But in the Gospel James the apostle was the first to be ordained bishop at Jerusalem by the apostles. Hence, when a bishop is ordained, it is commanded that he be consecrated by twelve bishops [Col. 0600D] or, if necessity compels, at least by three, just as Paul was ordained by Peter, James, and John. His anointing with oil is received from the law, in which king, priest, and prophet were anointed with oil.

## CHAPTER CLXXXV.—On the Laying On of Hands

That blessing is given by the laying on of hands is believed to have arisen from Isaac’s laying hands on Jacob when he blessed him (Gen. XXVII). Moses likewise laid hands on Joshua when he set him over the people as their leader (Deut. XXXI). And the Lord in the Gospel laid hands on the apostles when he appointed them rulers and priests of the Church (Matt. XIX). The apostles themselves also laid hands on others when they gave the Holy [Col. 0601A] Spirit.

The bishop’s office is to ordain presbyters and the other ministers of the Church; to veil virgins; to confirm the baptized; to consecrate chrism and oil; to dedicate churches; to sanctify by blessing the vessels and vestments of the church; to excommunicate rebels; to reconcile penitents; and, in a synod of clergy or an assembly of the people, to disallow ecclesiastical rights. When the government of the Church is entrusted to him, he receives a staff as a shepherd, and a ring as an *apocrisiarius*, that is, a sealer of secrets, so that with the staff of doctrine he may drive Christ’s flock to the pastures of life, and with the ring of faith may seal for Christ’s bride the mysteries of the Scriptures.

## CHAPTER CLXXXVI.—On Archbishops

An archbishop is called the chief bishop, or prince of bishops; for *archos* means chief or [Col. 0601B] prince. He is also called metropolitan. A metropolis is called the mother of cities, and therefore bishops of principal cities are called metropolitans. Their office is to consecrate bishops, summon councils, and restore rights that have fallen away. Moses held this office when he consecrated Aaron the pontiff with oil (Exod. XL). A cross is carried before them, and they are adorned with the pallium in the form of a cross, because, if they imitate Christ crucified, they are rewarded with the collar of victory.

## CHAPTER CLXXXVII.—On Patriarchs

A patriarch is called the chief of fathers, or prince of fathers. For a patriarch is called the father of the ark, namely, the Church. Only three of them are recorded, whose figure Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are read to have borne. Of these, [Col. 0601C] one held primacy in Asia, being preeminent in the episcopate at Antioch. Another held primacy in Africa, holding the pontificate at Alexandria. The third ruled in Europe, adorned with the mitre of the Roman summit.

The Church established these three sees as principal because the prince of the apostles consecrated them by his own sitting there: he presided over two of them, while Mark the Evangelist assigned the third to his name. But after the Nicene synod bestowed this privilege on the Roman pontiff—that, just as Augustus ranked above kings, so he should be held above all bishops and called pope—the right of the patriarchate was transferred to the city of Constantinople, that is, second Rome.

The reason why the other sees were moved is believed to be this. When Christians, abandoning God’s law, imitated pagans in their foul works, they were delivered by God’s judgment into the hands of those who, after destroying the Christians, possessed their places. Thus the patriarchate of Antioch was transferred to Jerusalem. Moreover, the Alexandrian patriarchate was placed at Aquileia, because Mark the Evangelist, who presided at Alexandria, first presided over that city. Yet some maintain that the bishop of Carthage enjoys this translation. Their office is to consecrate archbishops and to restore the decrees of the canons.

## CHAPTER CLXXXVIII.—On the Pope

The pope is called Father of fathers, or guardian of fathers. He is called universal because he rules the whole Church. He is also called apostolic [Col. 0602A] because he performs the office of the prince of the apostles. He is further called supreme pontiff because he is seen to be the head of all bishops. His name is changed at his ordination because Peter’s name was changed by Christ when he was set over the Church. To him are given the keys, as the Lord gave Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that he may know himself to be the gatekeeper of heaven, into which heaven he ought to introduce the Church.

Melchizedek prefigured him in his office, for Melchizedek’s priesthood was incomparable to the others. The pope’s office is to order masses and the divine offices, to alter canons according to the needs of the time for the Church’s benefit, to consecrate the Augustus, to give pallia to archbishops and privileges to bishops or other religious persons, and to govern the whole Church as Christ does. Thus the pope rules the Church in Christ’s stead; [Col. 0602B] bishops preside over it in the place of the apostles. Presbyters represent the seventy-two disciples. The remaining ministers represent the deacons appointed by the apostles (Acts VI).

## CHAPTER CLXXXIX.—On the Consecration of the Pope

The pope, Christ’s vicar, and all bishops, the vicars of the apostles, ought to be ordained on the Lord’s Day, at the third hour, when the apostles were consecrated with the invisible oil of the Holy Spirit. Oil supplies lamps with light and heals wounds. So the Holy Spirit supplied the apostles with the light of knowledge and healed the wounds of sins. Bishops are therefore anointed with oil, that they may be taught that they have received the Holy Spirit given to the apostles, and that their life and teaching may shine before humankind and that they may strive to cure them of vices. They are consecrated on the Lord’s Day because on that day too the apostles were ordained by the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0602C] and so that they may be reminded that they have risen with Christ and should walk in newness of life.

## CHAPTER CXC.—On the Order of Ministers

The ministers of the Church or altar are ordained on the Sabbath, which means “rest,” because they are commanded to rest from every servile work and to devote themselves to God’s service.

## CHAPTER CXCI.—On Presbyters

Presbyters, however, are consecrated toward evening, which belongs more particularly to the Lord’s Day, because they are incorporated into Christ, whose body they make. Orders are given at the four seasons because the four ranks of those who bless the Lord are understood: acolytes, subdeacons, [Col. 0602D] deacons, and presbyters. Under the guardianship of the four Gospels, they are chosen for the ministries of the Church spread through the four quarters of the world.

## CHAPTER CXCII.—On Virgins

Virgins are veiled on the feast days of the apostles because, through apostolic men as through bridegrooms’ attendants, they are consecrated as brides to Christ; and because the apostles first handed down to the Church the practice of virginity to be observed, having received it from Mary, the perpetual Virgin.

## CHAPTER CXCIII.—On the Tonsure of Clerics

The tonsure of clerics took its beginning from the practice of the Nazarenes. At the law’s command, they shaved their hair and burned it in sacrifice to the Lord. Nazarenes are called holy; hence, after their example, the apostles taught ministers of the Church to cut their hair as a sign, by which they might remember that they ought to serve the Lord in holiness. Christ made us priests and kings to himself, being himself king and priest. The shaved portion of the head is a priestly sign; the portion covered with hair, a royal sign. For the priests of the law wore upon their heads a tiara, that is, a little cap of fine linen, round in the shape of a half-sphere; kings wore golden crowns. Thus the shaved part of the head represents the tiara, and the circle of hair the crown.

## CHAPTER CXCIV.—On Christ as King and Priest

The priest under the law also shaved his head and beard when he offered sacrifice for the people. The king wore a crown when he came forth to greet the people. Thus Christ our king bore a crown of thorns [Col. 0603B] when, humble and mighty, he came forth to fight a duel for the soldiers and defeated the king of pride. The same Christ, the supreme priest, laid aside his hair on Calvary when he offered himself as an acceptable sacrifice on the altar of the cross. Therefore, by the circle of hair we represent the crown of thorns; by the bareness of the shaving we express Christ’s baldness.

Among the ancients, it was customary to make bald those captives whom they intended to crucify; hence it is written: “From the captivity, [from] the bared head of enemies” (Deut. XXXII). Therefore the place in which they were made bald was called Calvary, where the Lord is thought to have been made bald.

## CHAPTER CXCV.—That the Apostle Peter First Invented the Tonsure of Clerics

The apostle Peter was captured by pagans and handed over [Col. 0603C] for the mockery of Christians, with his beard shaved and his head made bald. He subsequently ordered this to be done sacramentally, understanding that unbelievers, though unwittingly, had nevertheless, by God’s permission, performed it as a figure; just as the cross was formerly an object of derision but is now the Church’s glory (Gal. V; 1 Cor. I).

By the head, the principal part of the soul—that is, the mind—is denoted; and it is adorned with thoughts just as the head is adorned with hair. It ought to be shaved by the razor of the fear of God of superfluous thoughts, so that it may be able, with the face of the heart laid bare, to contemplate heavenly things. The roundness of hair that remains is the adornment of virtues. The hairs are made equal in a circle because all virtues are perfected in the harmony of charity. And because we shave the beard, [Col. 0603D] we resemble beardless boys. If we imitate them in humility, we shall be made equal to the angels, who always flourish in youthful age.

## CHAPTER CXCVI.—On the Tonsure of Magicians

It should be known that Simon Magus and his followers shaved the head in such a way that, from ear to ear across the middle of the head, they made something like a street—whence it is still commonly called a *platta*—and by the head they wished heaven to be understood, and by the path of tonsure the zodiac, because they claimed to be heavenly beings.

## CHAPTER CXCVII.—On the Clerical Crown

Our tonsure, however, is represented in the law, when it is commanded that a little crown four fingers wide be made upon the table before the altar, and above it a smaller golden crown. By the table on which the bread of the presence was set [Col. 0604A] (Exod. XXXIX), our altar is understood, upon which Christ’s bread is daily placed. The crown four fingers wide is represented by the circle of our hair; the upper little crown is figured by the *platta* [“it joins the plait of the little crown”].

## CHAPTER CXCVIII.—On Sacred Vestments

Let this brief account of the ministers of the Church suffice; now a few remarks about sacred vestments must be added. Sacred vestments were taken from the old law. Ministers of Christ or of the Church serve in white garments because the angels, ministers of the eternal King, appeared in white. Thus white vestments remind them to imitate God’s angelic ministers in Christ’s service through the purity of chastity. The garments by which the outer body is adorned are the virtues by which the inner [Col. 0604B] person is adorned. Seven garments are assigned to priests, who are also known to be distinguished by seven orders, so that through the sevenfold Spirit they may shine with seven virtues, adorned with which they may go forth with the angels for Christ’s ministry.

## CHAPTER CXCIX.—On the Priest’s Preparation

Therefore a priest intending to celebrate Mass—that is, to fight a spiritual battle for the Church—must be clothed in spiritual arms, by which he may be guarded on every side against the enemies who incite vices. First he puts off his everyday clothes and puts on clean garments, because one who is to handle or receive Christ’s body ought to put off the old person with its deeds—that is, vices or sins—and put on the new person, created according to God—that is, virtues and [Col. 0604C] good works (Eph. IV). Then he combs the hair of his head because the priest ought to order the dispositions of his mind. Water washes his hands because he ought to wash away carnal deeds with tears. Then he wipes them clean of dirt because it is fitting that he wipe away the past deeds of the flesh through penitence.

## CHAPTER CC.—On Washing the Hands

The priests of the law, when about to sacrifice, washed themselves in a basin made from the mirrors of women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle. The basin made from women’s mirrors signifies sacred Scripture, which is written from the transparent life of holy souls. These women watched at the entrance of the tabernacle because they continually fixed their attention on God’s eternal tabernacle. In this basin [Col. 0604D] priests who are about to sacrifice ought to wash themselves: that is, they should carefully examine their life in sacred Scripture, cleanse themselves of stains by the examples of the saints, and so enter upon the Lord’s sacrifice.

## CHAPTER CCI.—On the Amice

Then he puts on the shoulder-garment, which in the law is the *ephod* (Exod. XXX), but among us is called the amice. With it he covers his head, neck, and shoulders—whence it is also called a shoulder-garment—and, fastened at the breast, girds it by two bands at the nipples. By the amice, which is placed on the head, hope of heavenly things is understood. We cover the head with the amice when we serve God for the hope of heaven. We surround the neck, through which speech is uttered, with it when, for the hope of life, we set a guard upon our mouth, so that we utter from our mouth nothing except what sounds forth God’s praise. [Col. 0605A] We cover with it the shoulders, by which burdens are borne, when we patiently bear the Lord’s light burden. We do this if, for the hope of future things, we undertake the labor of the active life and assist our neighbors in their need.

By the borders of the amice faith and action are understood, joined on either side to hope. These are fastened together before the breast: one appears and the other is concealed, because faith and action are joined into one; faith indeed is hidden in the heart, while action is outwardly displayed for the edification of neighbors. One border lies hidden and the other appears, because our action shines before our neighbors, whereas our intention lies hidden within before God. The breast is girded by the shoulder-garment because, through hope of the heavenly homeland, evil thought is restrained from the priest’s breast. The two bands that gird the amice at the nipples [Col. 0605B] are fear of punishment and desire for life, which the spirit of heavenly things impresses on our breast.
