This garment is white because all these things are splendid before the Lord.

## CHAPTER CCII.—On the Alb

Next the alb is put on. In the law it is called the linen tunic or the garment reaching to the heels; among the Greeks, *podis*. By it chastity is signified, with which the whole life of a priest is adorned. It descends to the ankles because the priest ought to persevere in chastity until the end of life. The hood through which the alb is put on is the profession by which the observance of chastity is promised. The tongue-piece, now fastened and now unfastened in the hood, is the power of the priestly tongue, which now binds sinners and now looses penitents. This garment is narrowed in the middle and widened at the extremity, and multiplied by many seams, [Col. 0605C] because chastity is indeed constricted by the pressures of the world, but widened in charity and multiplied by many virtues. This garment gleams with whiteness because holiness shines before God among the angels.

## CHAPTER CCIII.—On the Girdle

After this he is girded with the girdle, which in the law is called the belt and among the Greeks *zōnē*. By the girdle—which is bound about the loins, constraining the alb so that it does not hang loose and impede the step—is understood the guarding or conscience of the mind, by which lust is restrained and chastity kept in check, lest it slip away toward fleshly things, lest the course of good works be impeded, and lest desire itself drive one from life to ruin.

## CHAPTER CCIV.—On the Stole

[Col. 0605D]

Then he surrounds his neck with the stole, which is also called the garment of prayers, and by which obedience to the Gospel is understood. For the Gospel is the Lord’s sweet yoke, while obedience is a strap. Thus the priest is bound by straps to Christ’s yoke when his neck is encircled by the stole. At first it is laid upon the left shoulder and drawn across the heart to the right side, because obedience to the Gospel is first undertaken in the active life. Then, through love, it is extended to the right in the contemplative life; then it is brought around by the neck to the right shoulder and is not lifted from the left, because afterward obedience is raised through the love of God into contemplation and is not torn away from one’s neighbors in the active life through love of neighbor.

## CHAPTER CCV.—On Innocence

[Col. 0606A]

By the stole innocence also is expressed, which, lost in the first human being, is received again through the slain fatted calf. Blessed are those who preserve this stole from the stain of crimes, or wash it when stained with tears, because theirs is power over the tree of life—that is, in Christ they will possess the glory they had lost. The patriarchs before the law used this garment and were called firstborn. It was a priestly garment, which the elders, with their father’s blessing—as Jacob received it from Isaac—put on, and in which they offered victims to God as pontiffs. Hence it is said: “Sell me your birthright” (Gen. XXV); and again, “Esau’s stole.” A stole is called a “sent garment” (*missa*). For it was a white garment reaching to the feet; but after the alb began to be worn, it was altered into the stole [Col. 0606B] seen today.

## CHAPTER CCVI.—On the Subgirdle

After this, the subgirdle, called a *perizoma* or subcinctorium, hangs doubled around the private parts. By it is understood the practice of almsgiving, by which the shame of sins is covered. It is doubled because each person is commanded first to show mercy to his own soul by avoiding sins, and then to supply necessities to a neighbor.

## CHAPTER CCVII.—On the Chasuble

Then the chasuble is placed over all the garments, and by it charity is understood, which is believed to surpass all virtues. The chasuble is called, as it were, a little house (*parva casa*), because, just as a whole person is covered by a house, [Col. 0606C] so charity embraces the whole body of virtues. This garment is also called *planeta*, which denotes wandering, because its wandering border is lifted on either side over the arms. It is doubled in two places, namely at the breast and between the shoulders; in two places, that is, on each arm, it is tripled. It is doubled at the breast because through charity holy thought and good delight are produced. It is doubled between the shoulders because through it adversities from neighbors and adversaries are borne. The garment is raised to the arms when charity performs good works. It is tripled on the right arm when, in the love of God, service is rendered to monks, clerics, laypeople, and Christians. It is tripled on the left when, through love of neighbor, bodily necessities are supplied to evil Catholics, Jews, or pagans. [Col. 0606D] The chasuble is raised over the right arm so that friends may be loved in God; it is folded over the left so that enemies may be loved for the Lord’s sake. On its upper part the shoulder-garment is attached externally, because hope always embraces charity.

## CHAPTER CCVIII.—On the Maniple

Finally, the priest places the *favonem* on his left arm; it is also called a maniple and a handkerchief, by which sweat and nasal filth were formerly wiped away. By it penitence is understood, because the stain of daily transgressions is wiped away. It is worn on the left arm because only in the present time is our life cleansed by penitence. Adorned with these vestments, the priest proceeds and makes confession, because, even though he shines with these virtues, it is fitting that he call himself an unprofitable servant, accusing himself of past deeds so that he may judge himself guilty [Col. 0607A] and find grace before God.

## CHAPTER CCIX.—On the Seven Vestments of the Bishop

The bishop is clothed in the same seven vestments and is further adorned with another seven: sandals, dalmatic, rational, mitre, gloves, ring, and staff. Sandals are called from the *sandica* plant or from *sandarac*, with which they are said to be painted. They are believed to have been received from the Lord himself or from the apostles, in which they are said to have preached. They are a kind of cut shoe, in which the foot is partly covered and partly seen bare. Gospel preaching is thereby understood, for it is partly opened and partly closed to hearers.

## CHAPTER CCX.—On Sandals

Sandals are made from the skins of dead animals, [Col. 0607B] because the apostles and doctors fortified their preaching by the writings of the prophets, namely God’s living creatures. The sole of this shoe covers the foot underneath against the ground, while the upper part is bare, because Gospel preaching ought to be covered through the letter for carnal persons but uncovered through allegory for spiritual persons. A tongue rises beneath the heel from white leather, because the preacher ought to separate himself from earthly business and be innocent and without deceit of tongue. The tongue rising from and separate from the leather is their speech, because good testimony is borne to the bishop. The upper tongue is the speech of spiritual persons, who choose him for the works of preaching. The sandals are surrounded with white leather within because the preacher’s conscience ought to be white with purity before God. But black appears outside because [Col. 0607C] his life should be humbled before human beings. The upper part through which the foot enters is sewn with many threads because he must pour heavenly preaching into minds through many sayings. The tongue above the foot is the preacher’s tongue to the people. The line descending from the tongue to the end is evangelical perfection, which tends toward God. The lines proceeding from either side are law and prophecy, which bear witness to the Gospel. The fastening is the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, which is loosed by the hand of preaching. He treads upon the carpets spread beneath his feet, that he may learn to despise earthly things and love heavenly ones. The priests of the law had breeches by which they covered shamefulness; priests of the Church wear sandals because [Col. 0607D] they preach purity also to others.

## CHAPTER CCXI.—On the Dalmatic

The dalmatic is named from the province of Dalmatia, where it was first invented. It was derived from the Lord’s seamless tunic and the apostles’ *colobium*. The *colobium* was a hooded garment without sleeves, such as we still see in monks’ cowls or sailors’ tunics. Saint Sylvester is said to have transformed the *colobium* into the dalmatic and, after sleeves had been added, instituted its wearing beneath the sacrifice. The pontiff wears it at Mass, where Christ’s Passion is celebrated, because it is formed in the shape of a cross. This garment is white because Christ’s flesh was born of a chaste virgin, and the pontiff’s life ought to shine with chastity. It has the form of a cross because Christ underwent [Col. 0608A] the punishment of the cross for us, and the pontiff ought to crucify himself to vices and desires.

The sleeves of this garment are the wings of our hen. By every saying, she brooded over the first human beings in paradise as a hen broods over eggs in a nest; she gathered the Church’s chicks beneath the wings of grace and mercy. So the pontiff ought, by preaching, to gather the faithful beneath the wings of the Old and New Law, spread himself over them in examples, and protect them by prayer from the birds of heaven—that is, demons. It ought to be seamless like the Lord’s tunic, because integrity of faith ought to be undivided.

## CHAPTER CCXII.—On the Dalmatic and What It Signifies

By the dalmatic holy and undefiled religion is also signified, because the visitation of orphans and widows and the preservation of an unstained life are commanded. The dalmatic [Col. 0608B] has two scarlet lines before and behind, because the Old and New Law shine with love of God and neighbor, with which the pontiff ought to be adorned. The same purple bands signify Christ’s blood, shed for the two peoples. Undefilement belongs to love of God, and visitation of brethren to love of neighbor. By the scarlet color is understood a work of mercy, rendered to widows and orphans because of the twofold love. The fringes extending from the dalmatic are the words and examples of the preacher, which proceed from religion. The fringes hang before and behind because the commandments of love remain in the Law and the Gospel.

There are fifteen fringes on either side of each pair of lines, arranged before and behind, because in the Old Testament fifteen psalms, like fifteen steps, proceed from the way of charity, and in the New likewise fifteen branches grow from the tree of love. These branches are: “Charity is patient, is kind; it does not envy; it does not act improperly; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not seek its own interests; it is not provoked; it thinks no evil; it does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices together in truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; charity never fails” (1 Cor. XIII).

The left side has fringes, signifying the troubles of labor, because the active life is anxious and troubled about many things. The right side has none, because the contemplative life remains at rest, and the queen standing at the right hand has nothing left-handed in herself. The fullness of the sleeves is the cheerfulness of the giver.

## CHAPTER CCXIII.—On the Rational

[Col. 0608D]

The rational was taken from the law. It was made of gold, hyacinth, and purple, measuring one span (Exod. XXVIII). Doctrine and truth, twelve precious stones, and the engraved names of the sons of Israel were attached to it; and the pontiff wore it on his breast in remembrance of the people. In our vestments it is represented by the ornament fastened with gold and precious stones to the upper chasubles at the breast. It admonishes the pontiff to abound in reason, to strive toward Christ—who measures heaven with a span—through the gold of wisdom, the hyacinth of spiritual understanding, and the purple of patience; to shine with doctrine and truth, to gleam with the gems of virtues, to imitate the twelve apostles in holiness, and to remember the whole people in sacrifice.

## CHAPTER CCXIV.—On the Pontifical Mitre

[Col. 0609A]

The pontifical mitre too was taken from the usage of the law. It is made from fine linen, and the tiara, the *Ydaros* fillet, is called a cap. The mitre, which covers the head wherein the senses are situated, is the guarding of the senses against the enticements of the world through the Lord’s commandments, for the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him.

The mitre is also the Church, while the head is Christ, whose figure the bishop bears. Thus the mitre, made from fine linen brought to whiteness by much labor, surrounds the pontiff’s head when the Church, cleansed by baptism and made white through the labor of good works, longs to see her head, Christ, in glory and does not hesitate to imitate him in various sufferings for the crown of glory. The pontiff’s head is also adorned by the mitre when the Church, enlightened by his teaching, [Col. 0609B] rejoices in his dignity as the company of clergy and people accompanies him.

## CHAPTER CCXV.—On Gloves

The use of gloves was handed down from the apostles [perhaps “bishops”]. By hands, works are understood; by gloves, the concealment of works. For just as hands are sometimes covered by gloves and sometimes laid bare when the gloves have been removed, so good works are sometimes concealed to avoid arrogance and sometimes displayed for the edification of neighbors. Gloves are put on when this is fulfilled: “Beware of doing your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them” (Matt. VI). Conversely, they are removed when this is fulfilled: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify [Col. 0609C] your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V). Gloves are seamless because the pontiff’s actions ought to accord with right faith.

## CHAPTER CCXVI.—On the Ring

The use of the ring is believed to have been received from the Gospel, where the guest of the fatted calf is clothed in the first robe and adorned with a ring (Luke XV). Long ago kings used to seal letters with a ring, and nobles also customarily used it to pledge their brides. It is reported that a certain wise Prometheus first made an iron ring as a token of love and set a diamond in it, because, just as iron subdues all things, so love conquers all things; and just as diamond is unbreakable, so love is unconquerable. [Note: [Col. 0609D] Pliny, preface to book XXIII; Coelius Rhodiginus, book VI, *Antiquarian Readings*, ch. 19.] He ordained that it be worn on that finger in which he discovered a vein leading to the heart; hence it also received the name “ring finger.” [Note: [Col. 0610D] Aulus Gellius, book X, *Attic Nights*, ch. 10. See Pliny, book XXXIII, *Natural History*, ch. 1.]

Later golden rings were instituted in place of iron ones, and gems in place of diamond, because, just as gold surpasses all metals, so love surpasses all good things; and just as gold is adorned by a gem, so love is adorned by affection. Therefore the pontiff wears a ring so that he may recognize himself as the Church’s bridegroom and, if necessary, lay down his life for her, as Christ did; so that he may seal the mysteries of Scripture against the faithless and unseal the secrets of the Church.

## CHAPTER CCXVII.—On the Episcopal Staff

The staff is taken from the authority of the Law and the Gospel. [Col. 0610A] It is also called a pastoral rod, *capuita* [uncertain reading], a ferule, and a crook (*pedum*). When Moses tended sheep, he carried a rod in his hand. At the Lord’s command, when he went to Egypt, he took it with him; by signs performed through it he terrified the enemy, who like wolves were devouring the Lord’s sheep. With this rod he led the Lord’s flock out of Egypt through the Red Sea; with it he brought forth food from heaven and drink from the rock; with it, as to pasture, he led them to the land flowing with milk and honey. Yet this rod was nothing other than a pastoral staff, with which he drove the flock as a shepherd. Among writers this staff is called a *pedum*, because the feet of animals are held back by it. It is a curved stick by which shepherds draw back the feet of their flocks.

## CHAPTER CCXVIII.—Again, on the Bishop’s Rod and Staff

[Col. 0610B] In the Gospel too, the Lord commanded the apostles to take nothing for preaching except a rod (Mark VI; Luke IX). And because bishops are shepherds of the Lord’s flock, as Moses and the apostles were, they therefore bear a staff as an emblem of guardianship. By the staff, with which the weak are supported, the authority of doctrine is signified. By the rod, by which evildoers are chastened, the power of governance is figured. Pontiffs therefore carry a staff so that they may raise up the weak in faith through doctrine; they bear a rod so that through authority they may correct the unruly. The rod or staff is curved, so that by teaching it may draw back to penitence those wandering from the flock; it is sharp at the end, so that by excommunicating it may drive back rebels and by authority frighten heretics, like wolves, away from Christ’s sheepfold.

## CHAPTER CCXIX.—On the Kind of Staff

[Col. 0610C]

This staff is made from bone and wood; a crystal or gilded sphere is attached; it is ornamented at the upper head and sharpened with iron at the end. By the staff, as has been said, is understood the authority of doctrine, by which the Lord’s flock is nourished by the shepherd and compelled toward the pastures of life. By the hard bone is indicated the harshness of the Law; by the wood, the gentleness of the Gospel; by the jewel of the sphere, Christ’s divinity. By the upper head is denoted the kingdom of heaven; by the iron at the end, the last judgment. Thus the staff is carved from bone when the hardness of sinners is repressed by the harsh Law. It is turned from wood when doctrine is formed from Christ, the wood of life, and the people are strengthened [Col. 0610D] in virtues. Bone is joined to wood through the jewel because the old law is interwoven with the new through Christ’s divinity.

## CHAPTER CCXX.—On the Sphere
By the little sphere, then, love is understood, by which the bishop’s severity or gentleness is embraced. For the bishop’s teaching ought to be so joined by love from both laws that he strives through charity to unite the Church to Christ. All these things are polished by the art of smoothing, because they are adorned with every holiness. The mouth is bent back so that the erring people may be drawn back to the Lord through teaching. The head is placed at the top, while eternal life is set before those who have been converted. At the end the staff is hardened with iron, while every preaching is concluded by the Last Judgment. On the curve is written: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Habakkuk 3; Tobit 3), lest anger on account of the flock’s fault so overcome the pastor’s mind; rather, by word and example he should recall sinners to the mercy of the Redeemer. On the little sphere is written: “Man, insofar as he is a man, should remember himself to be a man,” lest he be puffed up by the power bestowed upon him. Near the iron is written: “Spare,” so that he may spare those subject to him in discipline, in order that he himself may find grace from the highest Shepherd; therefore the iron too ought to be blunted, because the priest’s judgment should be tempered with clemency.

## CHAPTER CCXXI.—On the archbishop’s adornment.

With these insignia the archbishop shines; moreover, he has authority through the pallium, so that he may show himself to set Christ’s Passion before the people. For on the two bands of the pallium, before and behind, is the purple sign of the holy cross, because the bishop ought to bring forth from both laws testimony to Christ’s Passion. The two hanging bands are the two laws setting forth Christ’s Passion.

## CHAPTER CCXXII.—On the archbishop’s pallium.

The pins by which the pallium is fastened are the nails by which Christ’s body is fixed to the cross. The circle by which the bishop is encircled around the neck is the golden necklace given as a reward to those who contend lawfully. Thus the pallium admonishes the bishop to bear the mortification of vices; the crosses of the pallium, to imitate Christ’s Passion in mind and body; the two bands, to be instructed in all things by the two laws; the pins, to be crucified to the world through fear of God; the circle, to strive so to preside that he may receive the necklace of the crown of life. And because so great mysteries lie hidden in the pallium, it is worn during Christ’s sacrifices. Therefore a cross is also carried before the archbishop, that he may be reminded to follow Christ crucified, so as to attain the crown of glory. The pallium, moreover, was instituted in place of the golden plate on which the high priest, under the Law of God, wore inscribed upon his forehead the name *tetragrammaton*, that is, four letters. For the four letters of that name foreshadowed the four arms of the cross, just as the pallium now represents the form of the cross. And because this golden plate in the form of a cross was borne on the bishop’s forehead, the precious cross, impressed with chrism, is borne upon the foreheads of Christians. The pallium, however, is bestowed by the Apostolic See alone, because this dignity is rightfully received from the Roman pontiff. Those whom the apostles set over provinces were called archbishops; those whom they placed over pagans were called bishops; and the successor of the apostles was called the Apostolic One (above, ch. 188). To him was granted by the Church the power to appoint archbishops throughout the provinces, a power received through the bestowal of the pallium.

## CHAPTER CCXXIII.—On the garments of the patriarch and of the Apostolic One.

Patriarchs also, and the Apostolic One, use the pallium, since they are known to possess the same office. Moreover, when the Apostolic One proceeds at Easter, a torch of tow is suspended above him; set alight, it is allowed to fall upon him, but is caught by the ministers or by the ground. By this he is reminded that he himself will be reduced to ashes and that the glory of his adornment will be turned into cinders.

## CHAPTER CCXXIV.—On the crown of the emperor and Augustus.

The emperor’s crown is a circle of the globe. Augustus therefore wears a crown because he declares that he rules the monarchy of the world. A crown is also called victory; hence victors were crowned, and the Augusti were called conquerors of the world. An arch is curved above the crown because Ocean is said to divide the world. The rod of the sceptre is the power of kingship. Imperial garments are the powers subject to him. The purple garments admonish the emperor to possess the principal virtues; the sceptre, to love judgment and justice, so that he may possess the throne of glory with the princes of heaven; the crown, to live in such a way that he may receive from the King of kings the crown of life. It is said that, after Augustus has been crowned by the Apostolic One and adorned with royal vestments, a beggar’s bag is placed upon him from above, so that by this he may be reminded that, just as he has ascended to the summit of kingship, so he may descend to the beggary of the bag—as Diocletian, who was first Augustus but afterwards became a gardener. A cross is carried before Augustus so that in all things he may follow Christ the King.

## CHAPTER CCXXV.—On the diadem of kings.

The diadem of kings signifies the extent of their kingdom, and all who contended in the contest received a diadem. The diadem therefore intimates to kings that, if they contend for justice, they shall reign crowned with the King of all. These royal insignia are said to have been first invented by Ninus.

## CHAPTER CCXXVI.—On the garments of ministers of the lower rank.

[Col. 0612C]

To ministers of the lower order—namely, doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, and acolytes—three sacred garments are granted, because they will indeed be joined to the radiant angels who minister. For here they are clothed for the ministry of the Trinity in faith, hope, and charity. They wear the shoulder-cloth, by which the shoulders that bear burdens are covered, so that they may learn to bear one another’s burdens and to minister necessities to Christ in His members. They wear the ankle-length tunic, that is, the alb, so that they may put on humility and serve Christ in it to the end. They are commanded to gird their loins with a belt, that is, a girdle, so that they may know how to restrain carnal desires through continence.

## CHAPTER CCXXVII.—On the cappa.

[Col. 0612D]

The cappa is the proper garment of singers and appears to have been borrowed from the hyacinth-blue tunic of the Law; hence, just as that was distinguished by bells, so this is marked by fringes. By this garment holy conduct is foreshadowed. Therefore it is worn by each order. At its upper part it has a hood, which signifies heavenly joy. For if the conduct of Christ’s ministers now stands in heaven, when their ministry is completed they will enter into the joy of the Lord. It reaches to the feet because one ought to persevere in holy conduct to the end. By the fringes labour is denoted, through which the service of God is completed. This garment remains open in front because eternal life lies open to Christ’s ministers who live holy lives. Moreover, in the tunic the sound of bells (Ecclus. 45) is the voice of singers chanting to God. They are written to have been seventy-two, because praises are sung to God from the seventy-two books; and the same number of pomegranates is reported as interspersed among them, because from those same books the deeds of the righteous are set before us as an example.

## CHAPTER CCXXVIII.—On caps.

For singers adorn their heads with caps because they proclaim that they desire the Lord in three ways, so that they may praise God, who is the head of all, for ever and ever. They carry staffs in their hands so that they may strive to invite others with them whither they themselves hasten.

## CHAPTER CCXXIX.—On the garment of subdeacons.

The garments mentioned above are granted to the subdeacon. In addition, two others are added: the fitted tunic and the towel. He wears the fitted tunic, also called the close-fitting tunic, so that he may clothe himself with justice as with a breastplate and serve God in holiness and righteousness. He carries the towel, with which dirt is wiped from vessels, so that by repentance he may wipe from himself the past evils of defilement. It should be noted, however, that the towel is fashioned more prominently for the subdeacon than for the others, because where a fanon is now carried, formerly a small napkin (*mappula*) was carried.

## CHAPTER CCXXX.—On the garment of deacons.

The use of the dalmatic is granted to the deacon. It is fashioned in the form of a cross because through him the sacrifice upon the altar is placed as Christ’s body upon the cross. By this he is admonished continually to carry in his body the mortification of the cross, like Luke; to serve, like Stephen, in holy religion by visiting widows and orphans; and to serve, like the same Stephen, in the aforesaid degrees of charity. The hood of the dalmatic is narrowed because imitation of the holy cross constricts every worldly occupation. The stole is placed upon his left shoulder and drawn across the back to his right side, so that he may subject the active life to the yoke of the Lord and, through the exercise of pious labour, advance to the contemplative life.

## CHAPTER CCXXXI.—On the deacon’s chasuble.

When the deacon wears the chasuble, he then signifies preachers who with their whole desire yearn for the contemplative life and, fervent in love, preach heavenly things to others. At times they take off the chasuble and gird themselves with it, because they demonstrate by examples of good works what they preach by mouth. Therefore the deacon leaves the choir, takes off the chasuble, places it folded upon his shoulder, and girds it at his right side, because preachers ought sometimes to interrupt the work of preaching, prayer, or reading and come to the aid of neighbours in need. He places the chasuble, as though folded double, upon his shoulders when, on account of twofold love, he undertakes labour for the brethren. He girds it on the right if by this he seeks eternal things alone. The bared side also signifies Christ wounded for us. The deacon returns to the choir and reads the Gospel, because after the preacher has ministered to Christ in His members, he ought to return to the work of preaching which he left. When the ministry is completed, the deacon puts on the chasuble, because the preacher who first ministered with Martha ought afterwards to hear the word of God with Mary. The subdeacon also wears the chasuble because he imitates the deacon whom he serves.

## CHAPTER CCXXXII.—On the garments of clerics.

[Col. 0614A]

The garments of clerics have been received from the ancients. Singers, indeed, used them in the Temple, as David and Solomon established (2 Chronicles 20). Senators also used garments of this kind, from whom they passed into ecclesiastical use. These white garments signify purity of life, because it is right that clerics should serve God in holiness and righteousness. This garment is loose because clerical life ought to be generous in almsgiving and good works. It is ankle-length because it teaches perseverance in good works to the end. The tongue of this garment is the cleric’s tongue, which ought both to praise the Lord and to urge the people to the praise of God.

## CHAPTER CCXXXIII.—On clerics’ tunics.

[Col. 0614B]

During the days of Lent, or at another suitable time, they use woollen tunics because ministers of the Church are commanded to serve Christ the King in humility. For if they follow Christ’s gentleness and humility, they are brought to Christ into fellowship with the angels. On the clerical garment a tongue is fashioned because the Lord’s seamless tunic is handed down as fashioned thus: the wings are the seraphim; upon the head, faith and hope; upon the arms, twofold love; upon the body, penitence and action.

## CHAPTER CCXXXIV.—On clerics’ shirts.

The shirt of priests is fashioned with two tongues because a twofold power is entrusted to them. With one tongue they bind sinners; with the other they loose penitents. The cappa appears to be derived from the chasuble. By it clerics are admonished to walk in charity and to demonstrate charity to others by word and example; charity is accustomed to adorn all virtues.

## CHAPTER CCXXXV.—Clerics ought not to bear arms.

Clerics ought not to bear arms because they must fight not against men but against demons by means of virtues, just as Moses did not bear arms, but fought with prayers while Joshua fought Amalek (Exodus 17; Deuteronomy 25). Thus the apostles and their followers fought not with weapons but with prayers, and taught us not to resist but rather to suffer injuries.

## CHAPTER CCXXXVI.—Laypeople may bear arms.

Laypeople, however, ought to bear arms in order to protect the Church from pagans and to free clerics for the service of God. Hence their garments too are close-fitting, so that they may be made ready for battle. But just as laypeople may not usurp clerical office, so they ought not to wear clerical dress; and just as clerics may not bear arms even against pagans, so they ought not to wear lay garments.

## CHAPTER CCXXXVII.—What the cowl signifies.

The monks’ cowl is derived from the apostles’ *colobium*. Their tunic, however, is fashioned like a dalmatic. These two garments bear the form of a cross because monks crucify themselves to vices and desires; through them the six wings of the seraphim are represented, because those angels are described as nearest to God. The two parts at the head by which they cover the head are the two wings which signify faith and hope. The two sleeves are the two wings by which they fly, signifying twofold love; while the two parts of the cowl, before and behind, are the two wings by which they cover the body, signifying penitence and action. If they imitate these beings by praising God, they will be joined to them in joy. The blackness of this garment is contempt for the world. The garment’s length is perseverance in good works.

## CHAPTER CCXXXVIII.—A staff is granted to the abbot.

The pastoral staff is granted to the abbot because the care of the Lord’s flock is entrusted to him. He ought certainly to support it with the staff of teaching and drive it toward the pastures of life with the rod of instruction. For by the staff teaching is understood; by the rod, discipline. Hence it is said: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Psalm 22). The curve of this staff ought not to be white but black, because in the care entrusted to him he ought not to seek worldly glory. The summit of the curve ought to be spherical because all his discipline ought to be divine.

## CHAPTER CCXXXIX.—The beginning of the religious life of nuns.

The dress and religious life of holy women took their beginning from Saint Mary. The blackness of the garment is contempt for a man’s embrace. The veil is a sign of modesty and of future honour. For at weddings they veil their head and face so that they may appear forbidden to all men, and may know that for this reason the crown of life is laid up for them.

## CHAPTER CCXL.—On the clothing of nuns.

That certain virgins use white garments appears to have been derived from Saint Cecilia, who shone outwardly in splendid clothing and inwardly in chastity; yet worldly desire was foul in her heart. For the white garment displays the vow of virginity.

## CHAPTER CCXLI.—On widows.

The first widow before the Law was Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, from whom the practice of widowhood began. Under the Law Judith and many others imitated her; under grace Anna and very many others followed, who despised second marriages. Their dress too is contempt for the world.

## CHAPTER CCXLII.—On converts.

Female converts, who wear the same habit, took their model from Mary Magdalene.

## CHAPTER CCXLIII.—The baptized wear white garments.

The baptized wear white garments because they signify that they have recovered lost innocence. Their mitre represents the crown of kingship; the alb, the stole of priesthood. For they have now been made kings and priests, and co-heirs of Christ, King and Priest.

# BOOK TWO: ON THE CANONICAL HOURS

[Col. 0165]

[Col. 0615C] In the preceding book we set forth, as the Lord deigned to grant, the Mass and the Church, together with its ministers. Now, as we promised, let us speak of the remaining hours, which the Lord may again inspire, beginning with the Lord’s night, on which we were redeemed from slavery to freedom and transferred from death to life.

## CHAPTER I.—On the office of nocturns.

The nocturnal office represents for us the watch of the citizens above. For the heavenly Jerusalem, which is “built as a city,” is preserved through angelic watchfulness. They divide their turns as though into three watches, distinguish each by three hours, and guard each by three orders, while they continually sing praises to the Trinity amid earthly companies in sweet-sounding harmony. And because the present Church is proclaimed as destined to enter this city and the fellowship of these citizens, it too is called Jerusalem and therefore imitates the watches of that city in its own watches. But because it bears its members here, it performs this office by night. It does so on the Lord’s night because on this night it merited fellowship with the angels.

This city is represented by the basilica, in which clergy and people are gathered as an army for military service. Signals are given to soldiers by trumpets; to Christians, signals are given by bells. Like soldiers assembling, they salute their emperor when, through the verse, “Lord, open my lips,” they begin the praises of Christ. For when they go to sleep at night, they fortify themselves with the sign of the cross as with a seal; by that same sign they now open themselves, unloosing mouths closed during the night for God’s praise. But because they watch in vain unless the Lord guards the city (Psalm 126), they invoke divine help through the verse, “O God, come to my assistance.”

The singer who begins the invitatory is the herald who calls the watchmen to their watch by a trumpet. After the psalm “Come,” all sing the hymn, like soldiers who, gathering in camp, exalt their king with praises. Then they divide the watches among themselves by chanting three nocturns. Each watch is distinguished by three hours, and each nocturn is marked out by three psalms. Angelic watches are kept by three orders, and in our watches the orders of psalms, lessons, and responsories are signified, because the heavenly watch is celebrated by the nine orders of angels. Thus the three nocturns remind us of the entire soldiery of the Church, which serves in the camp of the Lord during three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace.

## CHAPTER II.—On the first watch.

The first watch is understood as the time before the Law; it is assigned, as it were, three hours because it is distinguished by three intervals.

### What the first watch signifies.

The first hour of this watch was from Adam to Noah. In it Abel, Enos, Enoch, and Lamech kept watch for this city, as the first psalms indicate. “Blessed is the man” (Psalm 1) expresses Abel, whose name is interpreted “like a tree”; he produced the fruit of righteousness when he was struck down by the people of this city. “Why have the nations raged?” (Psalm 2) proclaims Enos, who served the Lord in fear and whom Scripture recalls as the first to call upon the Lord’s name (Genesis 4). “Lord, how they have multiplied” (Psalm 3) suggests Enoch, whom the Lord took up when He transferred him from earthly things (Genesis 5). “Lord, do not in Your anger” (Psalm 6) sets forth Lamech, whose prayer the Lord heard when He gave him such a son as preserved the human race from the Lord’s wrath in the Ark (Genesis 6:9). These psalms are sung under one *Gloria Patri* because the righteous of that time are believed to have worshipped the Trinity. Four are sung because they are known to have shone in the four virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. The antiphon by which they are set to melody signifies their praise of God.

## CHAPTER III.—On the second hour.

The second hour of this watch was from Noah to Abraham. Noah, Shem, Heber, and Terah kept watch in it, as the following psalms suggest. “Lord my God” (Psalm 7) expresses Noah, whom the Lord found righteous in his generation and therefore saved from the pursuing waters (Genesis 6). “O Lord, our Lord” (Psalm 8) corresponds to Shem, whom the Lord crowned with glory and honour when He exalted him above his brothers by his father’s blessing. “I will confess” (Psalm 9) suggests Heber, who recounted all God’s wonders when he destroyed the city of the giants. “In the Lord I trust” (Psalm 10) sets forth Terah, who trusted in the Lord when an impious people compelled him to worship fire, whose portion of the cup was fire and sulphur. These sets of four psalms too are sung under one *Gloria Patri*, because those fathers also, radiant in the four virtues, are known to have worshipped the Trinity. The antiphon of the melody displays the devotion of their praise.

## CHAPTER IV.—On the third hour.

[Col. 0617D]

The third hour of the watch was from Abraham to Moses. In it Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph kept their turns of watching, as the psalms that follow proclaim.

“Save me” (Psalm 11) expresses Abraham, when the holy man failed—namely, when he almost alone worshipped God and the whole world was given over to idolatry.

“How long, Lord, will You forget?” (Psalm 12) suggests Isaac, to whom the Lord granted blessings when he presented the figure of Christ in all things.

“The fool has said” (Psalm 13) shows Jacob, whom the foolish Laban devoured as food when he repeatedly defrauded him. Yet because the Lord was his hope, He turned evil away from him; therefore Jacob rejoiced and Israel was glad.

“Lord, who shall dwell?” (Psalm 14) displays Joseph. He entered without blemish when he refused fornication, and worked righteousness when he freed the people from the danger of famine. These groups of four also conclude under one *Gloria Patri*, because these watchmen, shining in the four virtues, are read to have worshipped the Trinity. The melody of the antiphon is the praise rendered by them to the divine majesty. These antiphons are also certain songs of the watchmen.

## CHAPTER V.—The versicle.

The following verse is called from “turning,” because the choir turns from the psalms toward the East, and because it turns from the psalms toward love. By the Lord’s Prayer, which is said secretly, the king’s secret counsel is understood. After the *Pater noster*, the priest says the verse aloud, like a king giving a command to envoys. The successive readers are the succession of envoys. He who says, “Bid, lord, give the blessing,” asks, as it were, permission to depart. The priest’s blessing is the emperor’s permission. The lesson itself is the performance of the commissioned embassy. “But You, O Lord,” expresses the envoy’s return when he returns the entrusted command.

## CHAPTER VI.—On the lessons.

The lessons likewise represent the preaching of those fathers; the responsories, their lives, by which they responded to their preaching. Lessons are read after Abraham’s watch because letters are said first to have been handed down after the Flood through him; he was the first to teach astronomy to the Chaldeans and to instruct the Egyptians in mathematics. Lessons are also read after the first watch because, when the first period had passed, the books of the Law were issued by Moses for the instruction of the people.

## CHAPTER VII.—On the second watch and second nocturn.

The second watch is understood as the time of the Law. It too is distinguished as though by hours, since it is divided into three intervals: the first from Moses to David, the second from David to Babylon, and the third from Babylon to Christ—or, respectively, priests, judges, and kings—as the text of the psalms declares.

## CHAPTER VIII.—On the first hour.

For “Preserve me, O Lord” (Psalm 15) expresses the priests, whose portion of inheritance and cup was the Lord. They kept the watches in the first hour of this watch, when Aaron and others after him taught the people the Law of the Lord. “Hear, O Lord, my righteousness” (Psalm 16) suggests the judges, whose judgment went forth from the Lord’s countenance.

## CHAPTER IX.—On the second hour.

These undertook the care of watching in the second hour, when Gideon and others judged the people according to God’s law. “I will love You, O Lord” (Psalm 17) shows the kings, whom the Lord made head of the nations. They kept the watches of the third hour, when David and others governed the people in justice.

## CHAPTER X.—On the *Gloria Patri* and the third nocturn.

Each psalm is sung with the *Gloria Patri* because each of the aforesaid orders is written to have worshipped the Trinity; therefore three psalms also are sung. The three antiphons by which the psalms are sung are the praises rendered by those righteous persons to the Trinity. The following lessons are the preaching of those watchmen, while the responsories are their actions, by which God’s ordinances were here made song. Lessons are read after the watch of the kings because books of the prophets were written in that time; and they, in the time of the Law—like the second watch—instructed the people and sounded forth the song of good works.

## CHAPTER XI.—On the third watch and third nocturn.

The third watch is the time of grace, which endures until the end of the world. It is divided as though into three hours, being distinguished as the time of apostolic preaching, the time of persecution, and the time of peace.

### On the first hour.

In the first hour of this watch the apostles kept watch; Psalm 18, “The heavens declare,” displays them. Every speech and utterance heard their voices, while their sound went forth into all the earth.

### On the second hour.

In the second hour the martyrs undertook the duty of watching; Psalm 19, “May the Lord hear you,” proclaims them. God’s name protected them in tribulations, and He remembered all their sacrifice.

### On the third hour.

Constantine, leader of peace, with the faithful undertook the watch of the third hour; Psalm 20, “The king shall rejoice in Your strength, O Lord,” suggests him. For that king rejoiced in Christ’s strength when Taurus was raised to life in the name of Christ by Silvester in an assembly of the whole world. He rejoiced exceedingly in God’s salvation when he assembled the great synod at Nicaea; therefore the Church placed a crown of glory upon his head and gave him great splendour. The faithful people still keep the guard of this watch; their king trusts in the Lord. The final verses of the psalm touch upon the times of Antichrist. The Lord will make him a furnace of fire, in which He will test His vessels. At the time of His countenance, that is, on the day of judgment, the Lord will trouble him with all the wicked in His wrath, when fire devours them. But then the Lord will exalt the watchful Church in His strength, and it shall sing His mighty deeds for ever. These psalms each end with the *Gloria Patri* because the Trinity is venerated by all these persons. They are three because they flourished in faith, hope, and charity. The antiphonal melodies are the Church’s thanksgivings and certain songs of the watchmen.

## CHAPTER XII.—That Paul was a watchman.

Paul, a watchman, sang a sweet song in the first hour when he rejoiced thus over the calling of the Gentiles: “To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen” (1 Timothy 1).

## CHAPTER XIII.—Lawrence the watchman.

Lawrence, a watchman, made sweet melody in the second hour when he gave thanks thus upon the gridiron: “I give You thanks, Lord, because I have deserved to enter Your gates.”

## CHAPTER XIV.—Gregory the watchman.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] Ἀπὸ τοῦ Γρηγορέω, “from *grēgoréō*, ‘I keep watch.’”]

Gregory, a watchman, sounded a delightful harmony in the third hour when he taught that the divine office should be performed by the art of music. By the lessons that are recited, the instruction of the faithful is signified. The responsories that are sung are their examples, by which others are formed; hence the name “responsory”: life responds to teaching through song. By the chant of penitents is understood the conversion of one who turns from evil to good. For just as one who sings the verse alone labours, so the penitent undertakes labour when making satisfaction for his fault. After the verse, however, the beginning of the chant is the common rejoicing of all over the convert. All assist such a person through prayers, just as they assist the singer, because the angels also rejoice in heaven over one sinner doing penance (Luke 15). By this singers imitate soldiers on watch: if one of their companions strays among enemies, they are grieved; but if, escaping danger, he returns, they rejoice with him. Glory to the Father is always joined to the third responsory because everything present, past, and future is subject to the Trinity. The Gospel is recited at the third watch because it was then preached in the third period. Likewise, in the third nocturn *alleluia* is often sung in the antiphons because in that period the praise and joy of eternal life were foretold. All these things are performed on the Lord’s night because all the aforesaid persons are saved through faith in Christ’s resurrection. Moreover, “We praise You, O God” represents joy and gladness to us because the Church, delivered on the day of judgment, rejoices. Perhaps someone may wonder why we posit only three watches, although four watches of the night are handed down. Let such a person know that, when the meaning is referred to the night of the age, only three watches are posited on account of the three periods, for which also three nocturns are sung. But when it is referred to the night of time, four watches are written and sung through four lauds. And it should be known that when *nocturnus* is said, a chant is meant; but when *nocturna* is said, an hour is understood.

## CHAPTER XV.—On midnight.

We perform the nocturnal office at midnight because the Lord is read to have struck the sleeping Egyptians and liberated the wakeful Hebrews at midnight. It is performed at midnight because the Lord is read to have been born at midnight in Bethlehem, and immediately praises were sung to Him by angels; they also appeared with light to shepherds keeping the watches of the night. And thus it is at midnight and on the Lord’s night because the Lord at midnight and on the Lord’s night despoiled hell and delivered His wakeful people at midnight. It is likewise at midnight because the Lord at midnight and on the Lord’s night will come for judgment; He will scatter from His city those sleeping away from good works, but will bring those watchful in good works to the place of rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XVI.—On the authority of the saints.

[Col. 0621A]

We have authority from the saints to rise at night and sing praises to our Creator. For David (Psalm 118) and the prophets rose at midnight to confess the Lord’s name; the Lord spent the night in prayer; and Paul and Silas sang psalms in prison at midnight (Acts 16), when a great light shone there by divine power. Those who imitate them also share in their rewards.

## CHAPTER XVII.—Jerome’s arrangement.

Jerome first arranged in Bethlehem, where the Lord chose to be born, the nocturnal office and the remaining hours as the Church sings them today. Pope Damasus next established that they should be celebrated in the same rite throughout all churches. *Anti* means “against,” while φωνή (*phōnē*) means “sound”; hence *antiphon* takes its name from sounding around a sound, because when the antiphon is begun, the psalm is sung according to its tone. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, first heard an angelic choir in heaven singing alternately, and taught his Church to sing according to this form; from him it passed to all churches. A responsory is called from “responding,” because, while the choir sings, a verse is answered by one person, and the choir in turn answers it again by beginning the chant. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, first composed this chant, and from him the whole Church received its form. For he composed hymns which the Church still sings in praise of Christ.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On the Lord’s vineyard.

[Col. 0621C]

The nocturnal office is also an imitation of those labouring in the vineyard (Matthew 20). When we sing at night in the Church for God’s service, we gather as though to work in the vineyard. For the present life is compared to night, darkened by the shadows of ignorance. When we begin God’s praise with “Lord, open my lips,” we begin, as it were, the work of the vineyard. Immediately we invoke divine help with “O God, attend to my help,” in order to complete the work we have begun; by “Come,” moreover, we urge one another to God’s service, as workers do. Then we sing a hymn to God because we have overcome nocturnal illusions, and thereby imitate those who sing while they work. Then, when we chant psalms alternately, we labour at the work as though competing with one another; when we read lessons, we instruct ourselves for the work; when we sing responsories, we give thanks as though the work were completed. For reading refreshes the mind; therefore, when we read lessons, we refresh souls wearied in the divine work as though they were vineyard labourers. When we sing responsories, we render praises as though after refreshment. Thus, when we chant psalms again, we rise refreshed for labour. The different nocturns are the various hours at which labourers entered the Lord’s vineyard. In order that the labour of this vineyard may be lightened for us, the example of those who first bore in this vineyard the burden and heat of the day is set before us through psalms and lessons.

## CHAPTER XIX.—On the priest.

The priest who begins therefore bears the figure of the householder who hires labourers to cultivate the vineyard (Matthew 20). The singer who chants “Come, let us rejoice” represents the steward inviting them to cultivate the vineyard. The hymn, moreover, represents the song they eagerly begin after the work is completed. The psalms indicate to us the deeds of different saints who laboured in this life. Thus the first groups of four psalms show the morning, namely from Adam to Noah. The second groups of four indicate the third hour, namely from Noah to Abraham. The third groups of four proclaim the sixth hour, namely from Abraham to Moses.

## CHAPTER XX.—Abel in the morning.

Thus Abel was the first, at morning, to undergo the labor of this vineyard; the first psalm, *Blessed is the man*, represents him, teaching us [Col. 0622B] to meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, as though to labor in a vineyard. For he himself, the first martyr, first offered the fruit of martyrdom, like a fruitful tree. After him Enos cultivated this vineyard; Psalm II, *Why have the nations raged?*, signifies him. It establishes us in serving the Lord in this vineyard with fear, when the nations descended from Ham raged wickedly and devised vain things against the Lord. Then Enoch became a cultivator of this vineyard; *Lord, how many are they* (Ps. III) sets him forth, admonishing us to rise from sleep and cry to the Lord with our voice. Because a multitude of wicked people surrounded him, the Lord received him. Lamech too entered upon the labor; *Lord, rebuke me not in thy anger* (Ps. VI) makes him known. It instructs us to wash our bed with tears each night [Col. 0622C], lest we perish with those whom the Lord rebukes in his anger.

## CHAPTER XXI.—The third hour: Noah

*O Lord my God, in thee have I hoped* (Ps. VII) shows Noah, who cultivated this vineyard as at the third hour and first taught us to plant vines. Because he hoped in the Lord, the Lord delivered him amid the waters. *O Lord, our Lord* (Ps. VIII) proclaims Shem, who after the Flood announced throughout all the earth the wonderful name of the Lord in this vineyard: he who will crown with glory and honor all who praise him, and who perfected praise from the mouths of infants and sucklings. *I will confess to thee, O Lord* (Ps. IX) indicates Heber as a cultivator of this vineyard, admonishing us to sing psalms to the Lord who dwells in Zion. *In the Lord I trust* (Ps. X) indicates Terah, who [Col. 0622D] trusted in the Lord as a cultivator of this vineyard and admonished us to serve the Lord in his holy temple.

## CHAPTER XXII.—The sixth hour: Abraham

At the sixth hour Abraham entered this vineyard, as the portion *Save me, O Lord* (Ps. XI) declares, when the world worshipped idols. *How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me?* (Ps. XII) represents Isaac laboring in this vineyard; the Lord did not forget him when he supplied a ram to be slain in his place. Isaac admonished us to sing to the Lord and make psalmody to his name, who bestows every good thing upon us. *The fool hath said* (Ps. XIII) signifies Jacob, who bore the burden and heat of the day with the foolish Laban, and taught us to call upon the Lord. *Lord, who shall dwell?* (Ps. XIV) sets forth Joseph, who labored without stain in this vineyard [Col. 0623A] and admonished us to glorify the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—On the verse

That a verse is said after the psalmody has been interrupted signifies that, after labor has ceased, the multitude is released for refreshment. The readings that are read are diverse dishes by which the workers are refreshed in turn. The blessings that precede them represent the blessings of religious persons, by which he blesses the food. The responsories sung after the reading are the praises rendered after food has been taken.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—The ninth hour: Moses

The second nocturn is the ninth hour. At it Moses and Aaron, and the other priests of the Law, cultivated the vineyard of the Lord. In Psalm XV, *Preserve me, O Lord*, they called the Lord their Father and their cup [Col. 0623B], and taught us to bless the Lord who grants understanding. At this hour the judges labored; Psalm XVI, *Hear, O Lord, my righteousness*, denotes them. They prayed that their judgment might proceed from the countenance of the Lord, and admonished us to cry to the Lord by night. At this hour kings too labored, who declare themselves appointed head over the nations in Psalm XVII, *I will love thee, O Lord*; they instructed us to invoke the Lord in praise. The modulation of the verse is a separation from labor; the readings are the refreshment of the workers; the responsories are their praises.

## CHAPTER XXV.—The eleventh hour: the apostles

In the third nocturn the eleventh hour is represented. At it the apostles set their shoulders to the burden; Psalm XVIII, *The heavens declare*, sings of them, for they taught us the righteousnesses of the Lord. At this hour the martyrs bore a heavy burden as in great heat; Psalm XIX, *May the Lord hear thee*, speaks of them, for they admonished us to invoke the Lord in the day of tribulation. At this hour the confessors are workers, represented in Psalm XX, *Lord, in thy strength* [Col. 0623C]; they were not deprived of the desire of their lips and persuaded us to sing and make psalmody of the powers of the Lord. By the following verse and the Gospel that is read is understood the conversion of the Gentiles, who sing as though in a responsory that they were hired into the Lord’s vineyard through the Gospel, having stood idle throughout the whole day in the marketplace of unbelief. By the *Te Deum laudamus* is understood their joy, to whom, when the work is done, the denarius is given in the evening—that is, eternal life at the consummation of the age [Col. 0623D]. We imitate them in the nocturnal office so that we may deserve with them the denarius, Christ, who is life. Because all these things are hoped for through Christ’s resurrection, this manner of chant is therefore used on the night of the Lord’s resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—On the verses

The ancient fathers invoked God in every work; indeed, even the Gentiles thought that God ought to be invoked in the smallest matters. Therefore we begin every Hour with the verse, “O God, come to my assistance,” so that we may invoke divine help in every action.

The verse “I remembered in the night” signifies the time before the Law, when the patriarchs remembered the Lord’s name in the night of ignorance [Col. 0624A]. It also represents the Lord, who prayed for us on the cross, that the Church might remember his name in the night.

The verse “At midnight I arose” denotes the time of the Law, when the prophets arose from the night of ignorance to the light of knowledge. It also shows the Lord, who rose from the dead at midnight, so that the Church too might rise at midnight to confess his name.

By the verse “Be exalted, O Lord,” the time of grace is signified, because the Lord is exalted in his strength—that is, at the right hand of the Father. If the Church sings his mighty works in the night, he too will exalt her in joy.

“Hear, O Lord, the prayers of thy servants,” taken from the book of Paralipomenon (II Par. VI), pertains to the patriarchs represented by the first nocturn. “Show us, O Lord,” or whatever else is taken for the season from the Psalter or another prophecy [Col. 0624B], pertains to the prophets signified by the second nocturn. “Through the prayers and merits of blessed Mary and of all the saints” pertains to St Mary and the apostles, whom the third nocturn celebrates. “Command, Lord, a blessing” is addressed to the Lord, to which “But thou, O Lord” is joined; the latter is taken from the psalm *Blessed is he that understandeth*. The priest, however, who holds the place of the Lord, gives the blessing.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—On the feast of saints

On saints’ feasts we perform the nocturnal office as on the night of the Lord’s resurrection, because we believe that they obtained their joys through Christ’s resurrection. We celebrate with nine psalms and an equal number of readings and responsories because we proclaim that they are in the fellowship of the nine [Col. 0624C] orders of angels.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—On the monks’ Matins

Moreover, the divine office ordered by blessed Benedict signifies almost the same things, especially since it tends to the same end: namely, the praise of God and the proclamation of the righteous. It was received by the Church because it was set forth by one filled with the spirit of all the righteous, and confirmed by the authority of the apostolic pontiff Gregory.

For it is clear that this same man, full of God, had in view those laboring in the vineyard and keeping watch in vigils when he distributed the psalms in this manner and divided the Lord’s night into three vigils by means of three nocturns. Yet he assigned the psalms according to the number six and the readings according to the number four [Col. 0624D], because the action of the active life is signified by six, on account of the six works of the Gospel by which one labors, as in a vineyard, during these six days; while the perfection of the contemplative life is represented by four, on account of the four Gospels by which continual watch is kept against the enemies of souls, namely vices and demons. Thus, by six psalms those laboring in the Lord’s vineyard are declared; by four readings those keeping watch in the Lord’s camp are shown; by the responsories the cheerfulness of those laboring is indicated.

It should be noted that this organizer of divine service began with the psalm *Lord, in thy strength* (Ps. XX), which concerns the peace of the Church, and concluded the office with the remaining psalms that sound forth Christ’s Passion. For on the cross the Lord began with “My God, my God, look upon me,” and thus, singing ten psalms [Col. 0625A], ended in the verse, “Into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Ps. XXI). He instituted this on the night of the Lord’s resurrection because Christ undoubtedly reached the peace of resurrection through the Passion and bestowed peace upon the Church through his Passion. If we, dwelling in peace, imitate Christ’s Passion in vigils by crucifying ourselves, we shall be enriched through Christ with peace in the resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—On the third nocturn

This same man of God assigned three canticles to the third nocturn because he wished the Trinity to be praised in faith, hope, and charity. Accordingly, he instituted that these canticles be sung with *Alleluia*, because he taught that those who praise the Trinity should be called to the song of heavenly joy. Then he commanded four Gospel readings, admonishing Christ’s watchers to be armed through the teaching of the four Gospels with four virtues: that they may be prudent in divine and human matters; strong in adversity and prosperity; temperate in all their acts in rendering God’s service and obeying their superiors; and that they may add these four things also, if they perform all these things cheerfully [Col. 0625B].

After these things he established the singing, beloved of God, of *Te Deum laudamus*, so that they might ascribe nothing to themselves in all these things, but attribute everything to divine praise and call themselves unprofitable servants. By *Te Deum laudamus* is also understood the song which the workers sing for joy after their work has been accomplished. Then the Gospel is ordered to be read, by which eternal life is promised; this is understood as the denarius to be given to the workers after their labor. By the hymn *Te decet laus*, sung at the end [Col. 0625C], is understood that final rejoicing when, having received the denarius of life, they exult in the Lord because they are permitted to go from labor to rest, from the vineyard to their homeland.

## CHAPTER XXX.—On bows

When, entering a church, we bow toward the altar, we adore the king as soldiers do. For we are soldiers of the eternal King, always present in readiness for a special military service. When we bow to east and west, we show that we adore God as present everywhere. We ought to follow him with such rational motion from the rising of our birth to the setting of death as we see the heaven carried from east to west by its natural revolution. Monks signify this more expressly, as they turn their whole body [Col. 0625D] from east to west.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—Note the dignity found in the Matin Lauds

Among the Gentiles the infernal gods were called *Manes*, because they were thought to send the day forth to the earth in the morning, after holding it enclosed, as it were, throughout the night. [Note: [Col. 0625D] See M. Varro, *De lingua Latina*, and Festus.] From *Manes*, therefore, comes *mane*, “morning,” that is, “good,” because nothing seems better than light. From *mane* comes *matutina*, as it were, praise offered to God for the light bestowed.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—First reason

We sing this Hour for the reason that we believe the world was created at this hour. At this hour the morning stars shone joyfully and praised God, who made them, in sweet harmony; that is, the angels were created at that hour. They are also called sons of God, and immediately, at the creation of the world, joyfully acclaimed their Creator with a great voice and sweet concord. We imitate them by singing at this hour, we who are called evening stars, so that, if we follow with praise the Sun, Christ, setting for us, we may through him be brought to the rising of light—that is, in the resurrection—to the morning stars.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—Second reason

At this hour the Lord led his people through the Red Sea and drowned their enemies, as it is written: “It came to pass in the morning watch that the Lord looked through the cloud and slew the Egyptians” (Exod. XIV). At the hour when the former were baptized in the sea and the cloud [Col. 0626B], the latter were cast into the waves.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—Third reason

At this hour Christ rose victorious from death, brought the day back to us from the underworld, led back from the tyrant’s kingdom the people redeemed by his blood, and plunged their enemies into the abyss.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—Fourth reason

At this hour, at the end of the world, the righteous will awake from the sleep of death, when they pass from the night of this world to the light of eternal brightness. The time of night that precedes the nocturn therefore represents the time of death that preceded the Law. The nocturn represents the time when the people worshipped the Lord under the Law. The Matin Hour, when [Col. 0626C] light approaches, shows the time from Christ’s resurrection until the end of the world, when the Church sings a song to her beloved. The psalms sung here seek to express both the time of the Law, which preceded like a shadow, and the time of grace, which afterward shone forth like light in visitation.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—“The Lord hath reigned”: First Sunday Laud Psalm

The first psalm, therefore, *The Lord hath reigned*, signifies that time of the Law when, after liberating his people, the Lord reigned over that same people and, like a king, established for them a law to be kept. He clothed himself in splendor when he wished to be worshipped in the wondrous tabernacle. It also expresses the time of grace, when, after redeeming his people from death and rising again, the Lord reigned throughout the world and clothed himself in the splendor of immortality [Col. 0626D].

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—“Make a joyful noise”

The second psalm, *Make a joyful noise*, shows the time of shadow when the Lord’s people, the sheep of his pasture, entered his gates—that is, the land of promise—in confession; when that whole land rejoiced in him and served him with gladness. It also sets forth the time of grace, when the Church received Christ’s faith, all the earth rejoiced at the apostles’ preaching, and served the Lord with gladness.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—“God, my God”

[Col. 0627A]

The third psalm, “God, my God, I watch unto thee from the dawn,” indicates the time of shadow when, after enemies were defeated under Solomon, the people rejoiced in peace; when they exulted within the veil of the temple and the king and all the people, swearing by God, praised him.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—“May God have mercy on us”

Another psalm, namely, “May God have mercy on us,” is joined to this psalm under one *Glory be to the Father*, because the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Israel are joined in one Law. It also expresses the time of grace, when, after persecution had been calmed, the Church received peace. Therefore it watches unto the Lord from the dawn and meditates upon him at Matins, because he had been its helper. King Constantine rejoices in God [Col. 0627B], through whom the whole Church, swearing in Christ, rejoices in peace, while the mouths of heretics speaking iniquity are stopped. Another psalm, “May God have mercy on us,” is joined to this one under one *Glory be to the Father*, because the Jewish people will yet be united with the Church in one faith.

## CHAPTER XL.—“Bless all works of the Lord, the Lord”

The canticle *Benedicite*, which claims the fifth place for itself, signifies the time of shadow when, in the fifth age, Nebuchadnezzar cast the three youths into the fiery furnace, where an angel, releasing them, sang that same hymn with them. It also represents the time when Antichrist is said to be about to cast the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe, descended from Noah’s three sons—into the furnace of tribulation. Hence it is sung without the *Glory be to the Father*, because then every praise of the Church will be silenced [Col. 0627C].

## CHAPTER XLI.—“Praise the Lord from the heavens,” “Sing,” and “Praise,” under one “Glory be to the Father”

*Praise the Lord from the heavens* declares the time of shadow when the people returning from Babylon rebuilt the temple for the Lord. It also shows the time when, Antichrist having been slain, the Church will praise the Lord and, through fear, restore by repentance those who have fallen into the house of God. These three psalms are sung under one *Glory be to the Father* because then Christians, Jews, and Gentiles are known to praise the Lord in one religion.

## CHAPTER XLII.—On the hymn

The hymn expresses the time of shadow when Judas Maccabaeus, after the temple had been dedicated, sang a hymn to the Lord with the people for victory; it also signifies the time when the Church will sing a hymn to the Lord for victory over Antichrist.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—On the chapter

The chapter read by the priest is the angel’s message by which the forerunner of Christ is promised to Zacharias. It also declares the final hour, when the angel’s last trumpet will awaken the dead to life. The following verse, “The Lord hath reigned,” declares that, as Christ reigned in the Church after the resurrection, so after the general resurrection he will reign in all the elect. Some say the verse “O Lord” at Matins [Col. 0628A], and the resurrection of the Church is thereby expressed.

## CHAPTER XLIV.—On the canticle “Blessed be God”

By the canticle *Benedictus*, sung at the dawning of day, is signified the coming into this world of Christ, the true light. Zacharias sang it to greet him when he visited his people in this world and illumined those sitting in the darkness and shadow of the death of hell. It also represents the time when, at the last things, Christ—the splendor of eternal glory and sun of righteousness—will illuminate the world by the rising of his coming, and the Church, caught up to meet him, joyfully acclaims his praises. Her bridegroom visits her and illumines with his brightness her who has long sat in the darkness of this world.

## CHAPTER XLV.—On the prayer and suffrages

[Col. 0628B] By the prayer that follows is understood that final blessing: “Come, ye blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV). The suffrages of the saints sung afterward are the many mansions in the Father’s house, into which each person is introduced according to merits. These Lauds are sung on Sunday because, through faith in Christ’s resurrection, these joys will be given to the righteous in the resurrection. They are also frequently used during Easter because they represent the time of Christ’s resurrection and of our own. They are sung on saints’ feasts because the saints now rejoice in the joy which they will receive doubly in the resurrection. Blessed Benedict expressed this same meaning in the ordering of his office, changing only this: he ordered *May God have mercy* to be sung first in honor of the holy [Col. 0628C] Trinity.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—On private nights

On the Lord’s night we celebrated our liberation and equality with the angels; on private nights we commemorate the bondage of our exile. For whoever is overcome by someone is called that person’s servant. The devil conquered the human race in the first parent and subjected it to harsh bondage. Therefore, that we may be made [free] from this bondage, let us labor at divine service in the night Hours, so that we may come from the night of this life to eternal light. Yet because we lament that our bondage has been extended through the six ages of the world, we celebrate this office on the six nights of the week.

## CHAPTER XLVII.—On the twelve Hours

Because we assign twelve Hours to the night, we sing twelve psalms, so that we who are held in bondage through the twelve months of the year may be granted freedom through the teaching of the twelve apostles.

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—On the six antiphons over the nocturn

We sing six antiphons so that through the six works of the Gospel we may pass from the night of death to the light, Christ. These six works are: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, receiving the stranger, visiting the sick, and redeeming the imprisoned.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—Twenty-four Hours

The sun likewise illumines the whole world above and below, through day and night, in twenty-four Hours. By its light it obscures the stars that are present in the day, and illuminates those absent in the night. It prefigures Christ, the Sun [Col. 0629A] of righteousness, who illumined this world above as in the day while, by his presence, he enlightened it through teachings and miracles. Below, however, he shone upon it as in the night when, by his death, he visited those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. He veils the stars present in the day when he hides the saints, in the glory of his presence, from the darkness of the world. Thus, absent, he illuminates the stars in the night, because he illumines the righteous in the night of this life.

## CHAPTER L.—On the twelve psalms

Therefore we sing twelve psalms at night and the same number by day, corresponding to the Hours in which we have said that the stars are illuminated on every side by the sun. Thus may we Christians, made stars in baptism, be illumined by the eternal Sun in every Hour, if we reverently bless the Lord at every time [Col. 0629B].

Because, conquered by sin, we have been assigned to servitude and must eat bread in the sweat of our brow (Gen. III), we are accustomed to perform necessary work by day. At night, however, when no one can work, we keep watch in vigils, so that when he returns from the wedding we may return with him to the rights of freedom. We also read three lessons because the Lord established three watches: “If,” he says, “he comes in the first, in the second, or in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants” (Luke XII). These three watches signify the three ages of a human being: childhood, youth, and old age, in which all of us are commanded to await the Lord with continual watchfulness in good works. Thus we read three lessons, while in faith in the Trinity we instruct one another in divine work during the three ages. We sing three responsories [Col. 0629C] while glorifying the Trinity by faith, hope, and charity. The psalms are rendered, as it were, for the first watch; the readings for the second; the responsories for the third; and the Matin Lauds for the fourth watch of the night, as a due payment. Blessed Benedict likewise instituted twelve psalms and three readings on private nights with this same meaning, changing only this: he inserted the readings among the psalms, because he wished these things to be done at midnight.

## CHAPTER LI.—On private nights and the Lauds when we sing “Have mercy on me, O God”

The night that preceded represents our life in sins; the nocturnal office represents the service of our exile. In the Matin Lauds we now tend toward freedom through repentance when we sing, “Have mercy on me, O God.” Because through repentance one passes from the darkness of death to the light of life, the following is sung in the second psalm every weekday morning: in *My words*, “In the morning I will stand before thee, and in the morning thou wilt hear my voice” (Ps. V); in *Judge me, O God*, “Send forth thy light” (Ps. XLII); in *To thee is praise due, O God*, “Thou shalt delight the goings forth of morning and evening” (Ps. LXIV); in *Lord, thou hast been our refuge*, “May it flourish in the morning,” and, “In the morning we are filled with thy mercy” (Ps. LXXXIX); in *Lord, hear*, “Make me hear thy mercy in the morning” (Ps. CXLII); and in *It is good to confess*, “And to declare thy mercy in the morning” (Ps. LXXXXI) [Col. 0629D].

## CHAPTER LII.—“God, my God”

Because forgiveness of sins is granted through charity [Col. 0630A], the third psalm is sung concerning the love of God, for whom our soul thirsts and whose right hand has received us when repentant.

## CHAPTER LIII.—“May God have mercy on us”

In the following psalm, *May God have mercy on us*, love of neighbor is added, in which it is asked that the countenance of God may shine upon us and that God’s salvation may be known among all nations. These two psalms are sung under one *Glory be to the Father* because the commandments of twofold love are fulfilled in one Christian profession.

Moreover, in the psalm *God, my God*, Christ’s divinity is expressed, whose mercy is better than lives; in *May God have mercy*, his humanity is expressed, through which our frailty is enlightened. Since these two substances are worshipped in the one person of Christ, these two psalms are sung under one *Glory be to the Father*. Since penitents are saved in faith in this name, these two psalms also signify faith and action, through which converts obtain the freedom of pardon. And since servants obtain the freedom of the spirit through the six works of mercy, six canticles of victory are sung over six days.

### “I will confess”

In the first canticle, *I will confess*, we exult with Isaiah (Isa. XII), because, as he overcame an unbelieving people, so we have overcome sins; and the Lord, who was angry with us on account of sins, is reconciled to us on account of repentance.

### “I said in the midst of my days”
