In the second, *I said*, we rejoice with Hezekiah [Col. 0630C] (Ezek. XXXVIII), because, as he escaped bodily death, so we have escaped the death of the soul. Therefore we sing in gladness: “The living shall confess thee, as I do this day.”

### “My heart hath rejoiced”

In the third, *My heart hath rejoiced*, we rejoice with Anna (I Kings II), because, as she conquered her rival, so we have conquered the flesh that opposes us. Therefore we say joyfully: “My heart hath rejoiced in the Lord,” who mortifies the flesh in its vices and gives life to the soul in virtues.

### “Let us sing”

In the fourth, *Let us sing to the Lord*, we rejoice with the people of Israel (Exod. XV), because, as they escaped Pharaoh and the Egyptians through Moses, so we escape the devil and demons through Christ. Therefore we joyfully echo: “Let us sing gloriously to the Lord.”

### “O Lord, I heard”

In the fifth, *O Lord, I heard*, we rejoice with Habakkuk (Hab. III), because, as he and the people escaped Babylon, so we have escaped the confusion of sins; and we exult that the devil has been defeated by the horns of the cross—that is, its arms—who went forth before the Lord’s feet [Col. 0630D].

### “Hear, O heavens”

In the sixth, *Hear, O heavens*, we rejoice with Moses (Deut. XXXII), because, as he received the promised land when the enemies had been conquered, so we have received the promised forgiveness when vices and sins have been conquered. We sing a song to the Lord, who repays vengeance upon enemies and will be merciful to the land of his people.

[Col. 0631A]

### “Bless”

Then in the seventh, *Bless, all things*, we triumph with the three youths (Dan. III), because, as they escaped Nebuchadnezzar and the fiery furnace, so we have escaped the devil and the fire of hell. Therefore we bless with every creature of the Lord, because in the resurrection we shall overcome everlasting flames.

### “Praise the Lord from the heavens”

Next we sing *Praise the Lord* (Ps. CXLVIII), because we have deserved a triumph over vices; we express that triumph through the hymn.

### The chapter

The chapter consoles us, when the priest, in the person of the Lord, exhorts us to watch and stand firm in faith.

[Col. 0631B]

### On the verse

We applaud because of this consolation when we say the verse, “In the morning we are filled with thy mercy” (Ps. LXXXIX). Having now received freedom, we burst forth into joy because we give thanks to our Deliverer, saying thus:

### “Blessed”

“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel” (Luke I), because he visited us in sins, effected redemption through repentance, freed us from the hand of our enemies, gave through the bowels of mercy the knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of sins, and directed us, enlightened from death, into the way of peace.

### On the prayer

The prayer said by the priest is the pardon which [Col. 0631C] the Lord grants to those who have returned to him.

### On Saint Benedict

Saint Benedict likewise taught that servants of sins attain freedom and the joy of victory through repentance. He instituted almost the same psalms, but the same number of them, and the same canticles on the same weekdays, with the same meaning.

### On the seven canticles

Seven canticles are sung in the week because the world is saved through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

### Sunday

On Sunday *Bless all ye works* (Dan. III) is sung, because God created all things in the first age, and on the same day all things were renewed through Christ’s resurrection.

[Col. 0631D]

### First weekday

On the first day God created light, and on this day all things are summoned to praise God because all things have been illumined by light.

### Second weekday

In the second age the Flood occurred, which signifies baptism. On the second weekday the canticle concerning baptism is sung, as “You shall draw waters” (Isa. XII); and Christ is said to have been baptized on the second weekday. On the second day God made the heaven and separated the waters from the waters, just as through baptism he separates unbelievers from the faithful.

### Third weekday

In the third age Isaac was delivered from death, because the true Isaac—that is, Christ—delivered his people from death through faith in the holy Trinity. On the third day God separated land from sea, that is, the Church from the Synagogue [Col. 0632A].

### Fourth weekday

In the fourth age Anna was bitter and her rival was rejected. Therefore her canticle is sung on the fourth weekday, because through the four Gospels the Church was chosen and the Synagogue cast off. On the fourth day the sun, moon, and stars were made. Christ is the sun, the Church the moon, and the saints are the stars.

### Fifth weekday

In the fifth age the Lord delivered his people from Babylon. Therefore on the fifth weekday is recited the canticle sung by the children of Israel when they were freed from Pharaoh in the Red Sea after the Paschal lamb. On the fifth weekday [Col. 0632B] the Lord delivered his body, by which he liberated his people from the devil. On the fifth day God made birds and fish from the waters: he lifted birds into the air and left fish in the waters, because through his five wounds he raises the righteous to the heights and condemns the wicked to the depths.

### Sixth weekday

On the sixth day God created man; in the sixth age Christ was crucified. Therefore on the sixth weekday the canticle of the Passion is sung, where it is said, “Horns are in his hands” (Hab. III), that is, the arms of the cross, because the Lord suffered on that same day.

### Saturday

On the Sabbath God rested from all his works. Therefore on Saturday the canticle *Hear, O heavens* (Deut. XXXII) is sung; it was given to the children of Israel after the labor of their journey, when they were already entering the promised land. Thus, in the seventh age, after the labor of this world, the Lord will give rest to the saints [Col. 0632C].

### On the Benedictus

As light draws near, the *Benedictus* is sung at Lauds (Luke I), because by that canticle our light is announced to us.

### On the Magnificat

At Vespers, namely at the end of the day, the *Magnificat* is sung, because at the end of the world God will scatter the proud and exalt the humble.

### On Simeon’s canticle “Now dismiss”

At Compline, *Nunc dimittis* (Luke II) is sung because after judgment the saints will be brought into peace.

[Col. 0632D]

### On the Hours and times

We sing the seven canonical Hours in the day as a duty for the seven degrees which we have received from the sevenfold Spirit. We have the model from the apostles and other saints, that we may praise our Creator seven times in the day, so that we may be able to praise him with the angels in his house for ever and ever. Each day represents for us the whole time of this age, during which we labor in the Lord’s vineyard at diverse Hours.

### On the time of Matins

Matins recalls for us the time when the first parents praised God in paradise.

[Col. 0633A]

### On Prime

Prime indicates the time when Abel, Enoch, and the other righteous rendered praise to God.

### On Terce

Terce signifies the time when Noah and the others, having gone forth from the ark, blessed God.

### On Sext

Sext declares the time when Abraham and the other patriarchs glorified God.

### On None

None shows the time when the prophets under the Law magnified God.

### On Vespers

Vespers recalls the time when the apostles and their followers sang hymns to God.

[Col. 0633B]

### On Compline

Compline admonishes us of the time when, at the end, under Antichrist, the righteous will give thanks to God.

## CHAPTER LIV.—On the Hours and ages

The day also represents for us the life of each person, in which one is taught at diverse ages, as at diverse Hours, to labor in the Lord’s vineyard according to the Law of the Lord (Matt. XX). Thus by Matins we commemorate infancy, in which we were born, as it were, from night into day when we came from our mothers into this world. We rightly praise God at this Hour, when we rejoice that in baptism we have been reborn from the night of error into the light of truth.

By Prime we recall childhood, the age at which we began to learn books. We rightly render praises to God at this Hour, when we were instructed in his service [Col. 0633C]. By Terce we recollect adolescence, the age at which we received Orders. We rightly glorify God at this Hour, when we were joined to his ministers. By Sext we indicate youth, the age at which we were promoted to the rank of deacon or priest. We therefore fittingly bless God at this Hour, when we were chosen as leaders and teachers of peoples. By None we mark old age, when many of us from the clergy undertake ecclesiastical dignities, like the heavier burdens of the vineyard. It is fitting, therefore, that we magnify God at this Hour, when he chose to exalt us over his people.

At Vespers we call to mind decrepitude, when many of us first came to the conversion of a better life, having stood idle, as it were, in the marketplace throughout the whole day (Matt. XX), while we lived our whole life in vanity [Col. 0633D]. At this Hour it is fitting that we exalt God in praise, because he deigned to join us to his praisers. By Compline we consider again the end of our life, when we hope to be saved through confession and repentance.

## CHAPTER LV.—The same concerning the Hours of the day

By the day and night offices, the Church also celebrates the mysteries of Christ. Christ was seized for us at night; therefore we sing the nocturn at night. He was mocked in the morning; therefore we sing Matins. At the first Hour he was handed over to the Gentiles; therefore we sing Prime. At the third Hour he was scourged; therefore we sing Terce. At the sixth Hour he was crucified; therefore we sing Sext. At the ninth Hour he died [Col. 0634A]; therefore we sing None. At evening he was taken down from the cross; therefore we sing Vespers. At the end of the day he was buried; therefore we sing Compline.

## CHAPTER LVI.—On the nocturnal Hours

At the nocturnal Hour the Lord despoiled hell; at the Matin Hour he returned victorious from death. At Prime he appeared to Mary. At Terce he met the two women going from the tomb. At Sext he appeared to James; at None, to Peter; at Vespers he revealed himself to the two walking to Emmaus; at Compline he ate with the apostles.

### Chapter LVII.—On the Hours of Day and Night

Moreover, at night Peter wept over his denial; afterwards he laboured all night at fishing. In the morning Christ stood on the shore and filled the net with fish. At the first hour he ate with the seven and entrusted his sheep to Peter. [Col. 0634B] At the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the believers. At the sixth the Lord reclined with the eleven. At the ninth he ascended into heaven while they looked on. At Vespers, before the Passion, he supped with them and delivered his body. At Compline he prayed to the Father for them.

### Chapter LVIII.—On Prime on Sundays

On the Lord’s Day we sing nine psalms at Prime, so that with the nine orders of angels we may praise the Trinity in the joy of the Resurrection. In the first five psalms we sing of Christ’s Passion, because we signify that Christ reached the glory of the Resurrection through a fivefold Passion. If we now wish to imitate him, we shall reign with him in the Resurrection. Then we add four, [Col. 0634C] because we proclaim that the Church praises God in the four quarters of the world through the four Gospels. Through *God, in your name* we express the abandonment of error; through *Give thanks* the confession of praise; through *Blessed are the undefiled* the practice of God’s law; through *Reward* the quickening of the soul; through *Whoever wishes* we set forth our faith, in which we include all the rest, and through which we believe that we are joined to the angels.

### Chapter LIX.—On the Faith Published at Four Times

The Catholic Church receives the Catholic faith as set forth—or rather, confirmed—at four times, and preserves it inviolate in the four regions of the world. First, it lays as its foundation the Apostles’ Creed, namely, “I believe in God,” since it sings this daily at the beginning of the day and at the beginning of the hours, namely at Prime; through it it brings its works to completion, since it recites it at Compline. Next comes the faith, “I believe in God the Father,” which is read in synods and which the Nicene Synod produced. Third, at Mass, in the assembly of the people, it chants the faith, “I believe in one [God],” which was promulgated by the Council of Constantinople. Fourth, it repeats daily at Prime the faith, “Whoever wishes,” which Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, produced at the request of the Emperor Theodosius; through the remaining hours the Holy Trinity is worshipped.

### Chapter LX.—On Prime on Ordinary Days

On ordinary days, in the daytime office, we imitate labourers working in the vineyard and entering at different hours to cultivate the vineyard (Matt. 20). Moreover, [Col. 0635A] the priest who begins imitates a shepherd, who in the morning drives out into the pastures sheep that have been shut in all day. The flock of sheep is the Christian people; the pastures are the Lord’s commandments. Beasts hostile to God’s flock lie in wait upon the paths. On one side the roaring lion goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5); on another, the plotting dragon kills with poison those who stray and greedily swallows up those who wander. Here the rushing wolf seizes and scatters the sheep; there the attacking bear tears the flock and disperses it. Therefore the shepherd cries, “O God, come to my assistance,” so that the sheepfold may escape these dangers. The sheep of the Lord’s pasture invoke the supreme shepherd in the hymn, that he may protect them from harmful things in their daily actions.

### Chapter LXI.—“God, in Your Name”

Then through the psalm *God, in your name* they set out upon the way, [Col. 0635B] and ask the Lord to deliver them from danger by his strength, since strangers have risen against them and the mighty have sought their souls; they ask that God in his strength may scatter those enemies and rescue them from every tribulation.

#### “Blessed Are the Undefiled in the Way”

Through *Blessed are the undefiled* (Ps. 118 [119]) they enter the vineyard, which is the Christian religion, and feed in the pastures of life, namely in the law of the Lord. There they work diligently while searching out God’s testimonies.

#### “Reward”

There they labour stoutly when, in *Reward*, they contemplate the wonders of God’s law. They cultivate it with utmost care when they expound their faith in *Whoever wishes*. [Col. 0635C] By the law of the Lord—that is, love—we return to our homeland; through the psalm *God, in your name* we are girded for the journey; in the psalm *Blessed are the undefiled* the love of God is received, and in *Reward* the love of one’s neighbour.

#### On “Whoever Wishes to Be Saved”

Likewise, the faith *Whoever wishes* expresses our course; for we walk by faith so that we may come to sight.

#### On the Chapter

In the chapter the master of the household consoles the labourers, because everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. Therefore, joyfully, they repeat the faith in the responsory and, with Peter, call upon Christ, the Son of the living God. In the verse, “Arise, O Lord” (Matt. 16), they ask him to aid them [Col. 0635D] in the work they have begun.

#### On “Kyrie Eleison”

*Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) and *Christe eleison* (“Christ, have mercy”), which follows, are said for three reasons: first, so that an excessive thought which has crept upon those singing may be dismissed; second, so that the following prayer of the priest may be heard; third, so that the Lord’s Prayer, adorned as it were with a brief preface, may be said more attentively. It is said silently because in it we speak to God, who looks not at words but at the heart. Its final part is said aloud so that it may be affirmed by all. By the two verses, namely, “The soul shall live” and “I have gone astray like a sheep,” penitents are understood, who are led back to the flock by the shepherd like wandering sheep. They immediately recite the Creed, [Col. 0636A] because by faith they purify hearts which evil works had stained.

#### On “I Believe in God”

“I believe in God” is said secretly because hidden penance is enjoined upon those who have sinned secretly.

#### On the Prayers and Confession

For this reason prayers, confession, and prayer follow: because through such fruits penitents are received into communion. For the same reason the seven penitential psalms and the litanies are sung.

#### On the Chapter “Precious in the Sight”

Shepherds are accustomed to change places and drive their flocks to other pastures. Religious persons imitate this when, following their superior [Col. 0636B] from the church, they gather in chapter; there salt is given to God’s animals to lick when the passion or life of the saints is announced to them in the Martyrology. The shepherd sets before them, as it were, fodder when by the verse “Precious in the sight” he proposes the patience of the saints. Then he invokes divine help three times through “O God, come to my assistance,” that God’s flock may escape the danger to souls. Then he blesses, as it were, the sheepfold when he asks that they may be guided and sanctified in the law of God. After this they are refreshed by a reading, and then each is sent to work, like cultivators of a vineyard.

#### On Terce

While Terce is sung, it is as though new labourers are working in the vineyard.

#### On Sext

[Col. 0636C] While Sext is sung, it is as though the labour is undertaken by others.

#### On None

While None is sung and psalmed, it is as though the burden is again undertaken by others. At Vespers the denarius is received. Terce, Sext, and None are celebrated with three psalms because in these three hours the Trinity is worshipped. But it is asked: since Prime is said, why does Terce, rather than Second, follow? Again, since Terce is placed, why is Sext then said rather than Fourth or Fifth? And why does None follow Sext, rather than Seventh or Eighth? One should know that the day is divided into twelve hours, and for each hour one section of the psalm *Blessed are the undefiled* is sung. [Col. 0636D] For the first hour, *Blessed are the undefiled*; for the second, *Reward*; for Terce, *Set forth the law*; for the fourth, *Remember*; for the fifth, *Goodness*; for Sext, *My soul has failed*; for the seventh, *How I have loved*; for the eighth, *I have hated the unjust*; for None, *Wonderful*; for the tenth, *I cried out*; for the eleventh, *Princes*. Through this psalm God’s law—that is, charity—is proclaimed to us; in it the labourers work daily for eternal life. Hence in each section something concerning the law is mentioned, because through this alone, as by a royal road, one enters the heavenly homeland.

#### On “Blessed Are the Undefiled”

In *Blessed are the undefiled* it is said, “who walks in the law”; in *Reward*, “I considered the wonders of your law,” and “Have mercy on me according to your law.” In *Set forth the law*, [Col. 0637A] “I shall search out your law.” In *Remember*, “I have not departed from your law,” and “I have said that I would keep your law.” In *Goodness*, “The law of your mouth is good to me.” In *My soul has failed*, “Not as your law.” In *How I have loved*, “I have loved your law.” In *I have hated the unjust*, “I have loved your law.” In *Wonderful*, “They have not kept your law.” In *I cried out*, “I have not forgotten your law.” In *Princes*, “But I have loved your law,” and “Your law is my meditation.” The office is always concluded at the third hour, because the Trinity is worshipped in all things.

### Chapter LXII.—On Vespers

The Church solemnly celebrates Vespers because Abraham and the other patriarchs before the Law, and priests and prophets under the Law, offered sacrifices at evening; [Col. 0637B] and because the Lord, supping at evening, delivered his body to his disciples. The five psalms of this hour signify the five wounds of Christ, who at the evening of the world sacrificed himself for us. The verse also indicates this: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands [is] an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140 [141]). At the twelfth hour the day is closed, and, once their work has been performed, the labourers are given the denarius (Matt. 20). The end of each person is understood when each receives recompense for the life that has passed.

#### On the Five Psalms at Vespers

Therefore five psalms are sung, because people will be rewarded for the labour of the five senses. The hymn which follows is understood as praise for victory; for just as those persons rejoice after labour when they have gained their reward, so these rejoice after conquering the world for the sake of eternal glory. The chapter rouses them [Col. 0637C] to rise and meet the coming Lord; through the following verse they knock, as it were, at the door and ask that it may be opened to them. With the lamps of good works lit, they enter into the joy of their Lord with the five virgins (Matt. 25).

#### On the Canticle “Magnificat”

Therefore, with the canticle of Saint Mary, their soul magnifies the Lord and their spirit rejoices in the Lord, who has done great things for them, whose mercy is for ever.

#### On the Prayer

The following prayer is a blessing by which each person is blessed by the Lord. When Vespers is sung for the preceding day, the time of the present life is indicated: because from the beginning of the world day came first and night followed, signifying that the joy of Paradise came first, but death—alas!—followed humankind. When, however, it is celebrated for the following day, then the joy of the life to come is signified, because from Christ’s Resurrection night comes first and day follows, signifying that after the death of the flesh the day of life will be granted to believers.

### Chapter LXIII.—On the Office of Saint Mary

We sing the office of Saint Mary or of all the saints, bound by no law but from devotion, so that, since as unprofitable servants we negligently render the service we owe, we may offer gifts to the friends of our Lord, in order through them to make our service acceptable [Col. 0638A] and obtain the grace of our Lord.

#### On the Blessing of Food and Reading

The custom of blessing food, or of giving thanks after food, began with the Lord himself, who blessed the five loaves and said a hymn after supper. Saint Augustine, moreover, insisted upon reading at table, for he wished minds to be refreshed with bodies, because man lives not by bread alone but by the word of God (Matt. 4).

#### On the Collation

Religious persons received the practice of gathering for collation from the holy fathers, who used to come together at evening and discuss the Scriptures together; and what they then mutually shared was called “collations.” These and similar things are read at collation.

### Chapter LXIV.—On Compline and Confession in the Evening and Morning

At Compline we make confession in order to wash away whatever we have committed during the day. At Prime we do so in order to punish whatever we have sinned during the night. It is called Compline because by it our daytime service is completed. And because at night our body is deprived of human senses, it is for this reason more earnestly commended to God in this hour. Four psalms are sung because we subsist from four elements.

#### On the Hymn “Te Lucis”

Through the hymn we ask victory over nocturnal illusions; [Col. 0638C] through the verse we seal ourselves, as the pupil of the eye, with the sign of divine protection.

#### On “Nunc Dimittis”

Through *Now dismiss* we desire God’s peace and light.

#### On “Our Father”

Through the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed of faith we fortify ourselves against enemies.

#### On “I Believe”

At Prime we say “Our Father” and “I believe in God” because we begin all our works through Christ, in whom we believe. At Compline we say the same because we conclude in him the actions of the day. For through Compline, which is sung when night receives the day, there is brought back to our memory [Col. 0638D] that time when our life is taken over by death. Therefore we begin with “Turn us,” that we may be turned from evils and God’s anger may be turned away from us. And because we despair of our merits, through the verse “O God, attend to my help” we call upon God.

#### On Compline: “When I Called”

Then we sing the psalm *When I called* (Ps. 4), which is sung concerning the Lord’s death on Holy Saturday, so that, sleeping in death, we may rest in the peace which is Christ. Next we sing *In you, O Lord* (Ps. 30 [31]), which the Lord sang upon the cross when, already expiring, he commended his spirit into his Father’s hands, so that he may then be willing to receive our spirit. Then we add *He who dwells* (Ps. 90 [91]), which we sing concerning the Lord’s temptation or Passion, so that [Col. 0639A] in the time of night the Lord may rescue us from the temptation of the asp and basilisk, and deliver us from the attack of the lion and dragon. Then we sing *Behold now* (Ps. 133 [134]), so that we may be blessed in the house of the Lord. In the hymn, chapter, and verse we seek victory, that we may triumph in Christ, who conquered the world. In the canticle of Simeon we ask for peace, that, just as Simeon (Luke 2), after seeing Christ the light, entered into the peace of life, so we, after the light of faith, may enter the peace of rest.

### Chapter LXV.—On the Office of Monks

It is asked why Saint Benedict ordered the hours for monks differently from the custom of the Church, or why Gregory, foremost among apostolic men, approved this by his authority. But one should know that this was provided, I think, by the most wise arrangement of a man full of the spirit [Col. 0639B] of all the righteous: namely, that the contemplative life, as by its habit, so also by its office, might be distinguished from the active life, and that the religious observance of monastic discipline might be commended by this privilege. Hence blessed Gregory, endowed with every wisdom, perceiving that the man full of God had arranged all things under the aforesaid signification, is rightly read to have strengthened them by his authority. For although he changed the psalms, he nevertheless assigned everything the same signification. Indeed, because for six days in this life, as through six ages, labour is performed in the vineyard, so that, just as there is rest on the Lord’s Day, the denarius of life may be received in the seventh age. Therefore he is seen to have instituted for Prime on six days psalms concerning those righteous persons who are remembered to have laboured in the Lord’s vineyard through six ages, as at different hours. [Col. 0639C] (Matt. 20).

### Chapter LXVI.—Sunday Prime

On the first day, then, he instituted *Blessed is the man* (Ps. 1) with the rest, because they signify Abel and the other righteous who, in the first age, entered the Lord’s vineyard as it were in the morning.

#### Monday

On the second day he decreed that *O Lord, my God* (Ps. 7) should be sung with the others; these represent Noah and those holy persons who, in the second age, laboured in the vineyard as it were at the third hour.

#### Tuesday

On the third day *Arise, O Lord, let not man prevail* (Ps. 9) is sung, in which Nimrod is understood, he who first instituted idolatry; through him [Col. 0639D] Antichrist is expressed, who exalts himself above everything that is called God. *In the Lord I trust* (Ps. 10 [11]) is also sung, which signifies Terah; and *Save me* (Ps. 11 [12]), which signifies Abraham, because in the third age they toiled in this vineyard.

#### Wednesday

On the fourth day he instituted *How long, O Lord* (Ps. 12 [13]) with the rest, which suggests Joseph and the children of Israel living as strangers in Egypt; in the fourth age they bore the burden and heat of the day as it were at the sixth hour.

#### Thursday

On the fifth day he wished *Preserve me, O Lord* (Ps. 15 [16]) to be sung with the others; it expresses priests, judges, and kings, [Col. 0640A] who, in the fifth age, as it were at the ninth hour, began to work in this vineyard under the Law.

#### Friday

On the sixth day *With the holy you will be holy* (Ps. 17 [18]) is sung, in which John the Baptist is understood; and *The heavens declare* (Ps. 18 [19]), which signifies the apostles; and *May he hear you* (Ps. 19 [20]), which signifies the martyrs, who cultivated this vineyard in the sixth age, as it were at the ninth hour.

#### On the Hours

At the three hours, namely Terce, Sext, and None, [Saint Benedict] established that psalms of the fifteen steps should be sung, because through the fifteen steps of charity he taught that the Trinity is approached. He decreed that Vespers should be celebrated with four psalms because through the four Gospels he instructed people to attain the denarius. [Col. 0640B] He judged that Compline should end with three psalms because he wished all things to be completed in faith, hope, and charity. He is said to have received this ordering of the psalms from blessed Ambrose. On the Lord’s Day, moreover, he instituted the hours from that psalm which indicates God’s law, namely charity, because at the Resurrection God, who is charity, will be reward and rest to all who labour piously here in the law through charity. At Prime, moreover, four sections are sung, but at the remaining hours nine sections, because through the four virtues those who labour here in Christ are led to the nine ranks of angels.

### Chapter LXVII.—On the Nocturns

Just as in former times days were dedicated by pagans to idols, so now each is dedicated by Christians to Christ God. [Col. 0640C] On Sunday, indeed, he was conceived. Therefore on that day we sing at the nocturn *Blessed is the man* (Ps. 1), because he entered the Virgin’s womb by the counsel of the Father and went forth as a bridegroom from his chamber. At the nocturn is sung: “You are my Son; this day I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). At Vespers: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109 [110]).

On Monday he was baptized; therefore on that day we sing at the nocturn *The Lord is my light* (Ps. 26 [27]), in which it is said, “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters” (Ps. 28 [29]), while the Father by voice, the Son by touch, and the Holy Spirit by appearance sanctified them. At Vespers the Son says, “I shall be pleasing to the Lord” (Ps. 114 [116]); and the Father sounded forth, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3).

On Tuesday he was born; therefore on Tuesday we sing at the nocturn *I said, I will guard my ways* [Col. 0640D] (Ps. 38 [39]), in which it is said, “You did not require a holocaust for sin. Therefore, behold, I come” (Ps. 39 [40]); and the Father says, “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44 [45]). At Vespers: “Let peace be in your strength” (Ps. 121 [122]), because there was great peace in the world when Christ, our peace, came, who made true peace for us.

On Wednesday he was betrayed by Judas. Therefore on Wednesday we sing at the nocturn *The fool has said* (Ps. 13 [14]), because foolish Judas said, “There is no God” (ibid.), but [he was] great. Concerning him Christ himself says in the same nocturn: “But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance, who took sweet food with me” (Ps. 54 [55]). Concerning the Jews also: “They sharpened their tongues like a sword; they stretched the bow, a bitter thing, so that they might shoot [Col. 0641A] the blameless in secret” (Ps. 63 [64]); and at Vespers: “They have often fought against me. Sinners have built upon my back” (Ps. 128 [129]).

On Thursday he began the new law and gave his body; therefore on Thursday we sing at the nocturn *Save me* (Ps. 11 [12]), in which we sing, “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77 [78]). That night he was also seized; therefore we sing, “God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him” (Ps. 70 [71]). At Vespers he gave his eyes no sleep until he found a tabernacle for God, namely the Church, through the cross.

On Friday he was crucified; therefore on Friday we sing at the nocturn *Rejoice in God* (Ps. 80 [81]), in which it is said that his enemies made a noise (Ps. 82 [83]), that they put him in the lowest pit (Ps. [Col. 0641B] 87 [88]) when he was delivered up, and that he was like a man without help, reckoned among the dead (ibid.). At Vespers: “They sharpened their tongues like serpents; all day they prepared battles in the day of war” (Ps. 139 [140]).

On the seventh day he lay buried; therefore on Saturday we sing at the nocturn *Sing to the Lord* (Ps. 97 [98]), in which it is said that, struck down, he withered like grass (Ps. 101 [102]), and that he languished like a pelican killed by its parent. At Vespers: “Man has become like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow” (Ps. 143 [144]).

On the eighth day he rose; therefore on Sunday we sing: “I slept and rose again, and the Lord received me” (Ps. 3); “he did not abandon my soul in hell” (Ps. 15 [16]); and “he set me as head of the nations” (Ps. 17 [18]). At Vespers: “He shall drink [Col. 0641C] from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. 109 [110]), because the Lord raised up the needy from the dust.

### Chapter LXVIII.—Sunday

The same matters are noted in the office of Saint Benedict. On Sunday, the Conception: as there, “Lift up your gates, O princes, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23 [24]). At Vespers: “He makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children” (Ps. 112 [113]).

#### Monday

On Monday, Baptism: as there, “By the word of the Lord [Col. 0642A] the heavens were established” (Ps. 32 [33]), and “the waters of the sea [were gathered] as in a wineskin” (ibid.). At Vespers: “The Jordan was turned back” (Ps. 113 [114]).

#### Tuesday

On Tuesday, the Nativity: as there, “The Lord of hosts is with us” (Ps. 45 [46]); and, “As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord” (Ps. 47 [48]); and again, “We have received your mercy, O God” (ibid.). At Vespers: “From the fruit of your womb” (Ps. 131 [132]).

#### Wednesday

On Wednesday, the betrayal: “They planned to reject my price” (Ps. 61 [62]); and, “Those who sat in the gate spoke against me” (Ps. 68 [69]). At Vespers: “Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who [Col. 0642B] will repay” (Ps. 136 [137]); and, “The Lord will repay for me” (Ps. 137 [138]).

#### Thursday

On Thursday, the eating of his body: “He gave them bread from heaven” (Ps. 77 [78]). At Vespers: “Let my prayer be directed as incense” (Ps. 140 [141]).

#### Friday

On Friday, the Passion: “O God, the wicked have risen against me, and they have not set you before their sight” (Ps. 85 [86]); and, “You did not help him in battle” (Ps. 88 [89]). At Vespers: “I looked to the right and saw, and there was no one who knew me” (Ps. 141 [142]).

#### Saturday

[Col. 0642C] On Saturday, the burial: “The sun knew its setting” (Ps. 103 [104]). At Vespers: “His spirit shall go forth” (Ps. 145 [146]).

#### Sunday

On Sunday, the Resurrection: “My soul shall live for him” (Ps. 21 [22]). At Vespers: “Light has risen” (Ps. 111 [112]). The insertion of *Glory to the Father* among certain psalms was done in accordance with the Hebrews, who insert *diapsalma* among certain psalms where they understand a loftier meaning.

## Book Three. On the Solemnities of the Whole Year

[Col. 0641]

### Chapter I.—On the Advent of the Lord

[Col. 0641D]

We have said these few things, however inadequately, concerning the hours; now it remains that we briefly touch upon the solemnities.

We celebrate the Advent of the Lord for three reasons. First, because we recall the time in which we know that he was foretold by the saints of old. Second, because we anticipate his face with praises, since we are not ignorant that he will come to each of us at the end of life. Third, because we commemorate that time in which we still hope that he will be present as judge. In the Lectionary and Gospel Book five weeks are marked for the Advent [Col. 0642D] of the Lord, because through the five ages of the world his Advent was foretold from ancient times. In the Antiphonary and the Gradual Book four weeks are assigned to it, because Christ’s Advent was proclaimed through the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, and the books of the Gentiles. At this time, *Glory in the highest* and *We praise you, O God* are not sung, because the righteous before Christ’s Advent were held in the sadness of hell. At this time also the dalmatic and the *subtile* are not worn, because the garments of innocence and immortality were restored to us through Christ. All these things are omitted also so that they may be [Col. 0643A] embraced more festively at the Nativity of the Lord, and so that the grace of the New Testament may be known to surpass that of the Old.

#### On the Responsory “Looking from Afar”

The responsory *Looking from afar* is sung in the person of John the Baptist, who, looking from afar—that is, from earth to heaven—proclaims the power of God, namely divinity coming in flesh; and [he proclaims] the cloud covering the whole earth, namely unbelief enveloping all Judaea. He said, “Go out to meet him,” when he prepared the way of the Lord. Three verses are sung for this responsory because all this was foretold through the Law, prophecy, and psalmody. For three times are understood: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace, in each of which this future event was proclaimed. Hence in the third verse is sung, “Lift up your gates, O princes, and he who is to reign shall enter.” [Col. 0643B] Three verses are sung also because the Trinity is worshipped in this matter; therefore *Glory to the Father* is added. The responsory is repeated because Christ’s Advent is again expected by the faithful.

As Christ’s divinity is honoured in *looking*, so his humanity is honoured in *I was looking*. Hence it is sung: “Behold, the Son of Man comes in the clouds of heaven.” The third responsory shows how divinity was incarnate: “The angel Gabriel was sent, who said to the virgin, ‘Hail, Mary, full of grace.’” This is confirmed by the Apostle: “We await the Saviour”; it is also strengthened through the prophet, who said: “Hear the word of the Lord. Behold, a virgin shall receive [in the Vulgate, ‘shall conceive’]” (Isa. 7); it is likewise [Col. 0643C] confirmed through the Law, as Moses says: “I beseech you, O Lord”; and because he has now come, “let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult.”

#### On Lauds

Morning Lauds express both advents of Christ: the first, on that day when the mountains—the apostles—proclaimed sweetness, and the hills—the teachers—flowed with the milk and honey of teaching. Then the daughter of Zion, that is, the Church from the Jews, rejoiced; then the daughter of Jerusalem, that is, the Church from the Gentiles, exulted. His second advent is expressed by the antiphon, “Behold, the Lord will come.” The first by the antiphon, “All you who thirst,” when the faithful came to the water of baptism. The second by “Behold, the great prophet will come,” when Jerusalem will be renewed. The antiphons “The Holy Spirit” [Col. 0643D] and “Do not fear, Mary,” express his first advent. The weekday antiphons are various prophecies.

### Chapter II.—On the Second Sunday in Advent

The second Sunday denotes the preaching of the prophets concerning Christ’s Advent to Jerusalem, where is sung, “Jerusalem, he will come quickly,” and “City of Jerusalem,” and “Jerusalem, arise.”

### Chapter III.—On the Third Sunday

On the third Sunday Christ’s second Advent is foretold, where is sung, “Behold, the Lord will appear,” and “with him thousands of saints.”

### Chapter IV.—On the Fourth Sunday

On the fourth Sunday the calling of the Gentiles through Christ’s Advent is declared; there, in the person of the apostles, is sung, [Col. 0644A] “Sound the trumpet in Zion; call the nations,” and “see how great is he who enters to save the nations.” And, “The root of Jesse, who shall arise to rule: in him the nations shall hope.”

#### On the Week Before the Nativity of the Lord

The following week, which is called the Preparation before the Nativity of the Lord, has in it the history *Cry aloud in strength*, sung with six morning Lauds, because through the six ages of the world the people were prepared for his Advent, and we are prepared for his Advent through the six works of mercy.

### Chapter V.—On the O Antiphons

The seven O’s are sung more in admiration than in calling, and in them are marked the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, through which this Incarnation is administered and through [Col. 0644B] which Christ is invited by the Church. For he is Wisdom, in whom the Father made all things, who came in the spirit of wisdom to teach us the way of prudence. He is Adonai, the name revealed to Moses, to whom he gave the law on Sinai, who came through the spirit of understanding to redeem us. He is the Root of Jesse, who stood as a sign to the peoples when he willed to be worshipped everywhere through the sign of the cross; he came to deliver us in the spirit of counsel. He is the Key of David, who opened heaven to the righteous, closed hell, and came through the spirit of fortitude to lead the bound out of the prison-house. He is the Dayspring and Sun of righteousness, who came to enlighten us through the spirit of knowledge. He is the King of the nations and the cornerstone, who came to save humankind through the spirit of piety. He is Emmanuel, coming to us through Israel, who came to save us through the spirit [Col. 0644C] of fear, giving to all the gifts of love. If twelve O’s are sung, then the twelve prophets are represented, who are read to have preached Christ’s Advent.

### Chapter VI.—On the Vigils of Saints

Vigils began with the shepherds, who kept watch over their flocks when Christ was born (Luke 2). According to ancient custom two nocturnal offices were performed on major feasts: one at the beginning of the night by the bishop with his chaplains, without *Come*; the other at midnight by the clergy, as is still solemnly celebrated. The people who had gathered for the feast used to keep vigil all night in praises. But after revellers turned this good into mockery [Col. 0644D] and devoted themselves to shameful songs and dances, drinking and fornication, vigils were forbidden and days of fasting were appointed, though they retained the name “vigils.” Therefore, according to the ancient custom, two offices are assigned to the night of Christ’s Nativity. In one are sung the antiphons “The Lord said to me,” “He placed [his tabernacle] in the sun,” “Be lifted up,” and the responsory “Behold the Lamb of God,” with the rest. In the other are sung the antiphons “The Lord said,” “Like a bridegroom,” “Grace is poured forth,” and the responsory “Today unto us,” with the others.

### Chapter VII.—On the Nativity of the Lord

A festival is called, as it were, a “divinity of the calendar,” that is, an annual right or the right of divinity, because on that day the right due to divinity is paid annually. A celebration is called, as it were, the rite of celibates—that is, of the chaste—because on it the rite of heavenly beings [Col. 0645A] is performed by the chaste. *Socan* [reading uncertain] means “frequent”; hence it is called a solemnity because on it the Church is frequented by the assembly of the people.

The Nativity of the Lord is so called because on it Christ is believed to have been born in flesh. The Church celebrates this Nativity because in former times not only kings, but all persons, celebrated their birthday. Therefore we too celebrate his temporal birth because through him we are reborn to eternity. Christ willed to be born at the end of the year because he came into the world at the end of the age. He was pleased to be born at night because he came hidden, that is, concealed beneath flesh. After his birth the daylight is prolonged because those who believe in him are called to the light of eternity.

The invitatory “Christ is born for us” is sung in the person of the angels, by whom the shepherds—or rather the whole people—[Col. 0645B] are invited to pray to Christ. To him we joyfully sing three psalms; in the readings we rejoice through the oracles of the prophets; in the responsories we sing with the angels. These responsories represent all things in heaven and earth restored through this Nativity, and the infernal regions condemned. In the first responsory, in which “The host of angels rejoices” is sung, the restoration of heavenly things is sung. In the second, in which “True peace has descended” is sung, the restoration of earthly things is sung. In the third, in which “He entered into our region” is sung, the liberation of those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death is recalled. Since it is not doubted that the Trinity accomplished all these things, *Glory to the Father* is sung also with each responsory.

### Chapter VIII.—On the Neuma of the Creation of the World, and Why It Is Sung Rather on A Than on Another Vowel

[Col. 0645C]

The jubilation of the neumas signifies these things: that the fabric of the world was ineffably created through the Word of God. Therefore the neuma is jubilated at the creation of the world. It is sung on *a* because *a* is declared to be the first sound of a human being at birth; and at the first creation of the world the morning stars praised the Lord, and all the sons of God, namely the angels, jubilated with a loud voice. We imitate their first jubilation by *a*. And because he is sung to have gone forth ineffably from the Virgin as a bridegroom from his chamber, the neuma is as it were modulated on *a*. Because he is proclaimed ineffably coequal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the neuma is jubilated in *Glory to the Father*. And because he himself is commemorated as Alpha and Omega, namely beginning and end, [Col. 0645D] the neuma is modulated on *a* and *ω*.

### Chapter IX.—On the Second and Third Nocturn

In the second Nocturn we recall the devotion of the shepherds, whom we read to have hastened to Bethlehem and found Christ in the manger; we express this especially through the responsory “Whom did you see?” and “O great mystery.” In the third time joy and gladness came into the world; therefore in the third Nocturn the Church sings Alleluia more frequently in the antiphons. Through the Gospels the narrative of the shepherds is set forth, through whom Christ’s Nativity is made known. Women are accustomed to visit a woman in childbirth and bring her gifts of hospitality; the Church [Col. 0646A] imitates them in the responsories, when we greet now Christ and now Saint Mary, offering as it were gifts suitable to the Son and fitting also to the mother.

### Chapter X.—On the Neuma and Truth, and Why [It Is Sung] on E
The neuma is therefore jubilated on *veritate* (“truth”), because we join in praising the Word who ineffably became flesh. For the first cry of a woman giving birth is said to be *e*, and the Word that was born is flesh, a noun expressed in the feminine gender. Then *Te Deum laudamus* represents for us the hour at which Christ was born, whom we praise with the angels. Therefore we immediately add the Mass, in which we sing *Gloria in excelsis* with the angels and offer the sacrifice born for us. After Mass, the Gospel *The Book of the Generation* is read, in which, as it were, a line is woven onto a hook by which Leviathan is drawn out from the human race [Col. 0646B]. Here some sing *Te Deum laudamus*, because they rejoice that they have been drawn out of Leviathan’s jaws.

## CHAPTER XI.—On the Morning Praises

Then the Church, as though leading a dance, sings songs to her Bridegroom and Liberator in the morning praises. In the Mass that follows, the praise of the shepherds is celebrated, by which the Lord, found by them, is praised. In the third Mass, which is sung at the third hour, his birth from the Father is solemnized. Hence the Gospel *In the beginning* is recited for it.

## CHAPTER XII.—On Saint Stephen

In the nocturnal office for Saint Stephen, the wrestling-ground is imitated, in which one contends for a crown. In the office of the day, this contest-president is, as it were, crowned for victory. Hence Stephen is suitably called *stephanus*, that is, “crown” [Col. 0646C]. The order of Levites keeps his day solemn because Stephen was the first deacon.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On Saint John

The falling asleep of Saint John the Evangelist belongs to the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; but because it could not be observed there on account of the celebrated office, the Church instituted the observance of his feast here, when he returned from exile, or when his own church was dedicated. In the chant for Saint John we imitate lovers, who endeavor to extol their friends with songs. Some jubilate the neuma on *intellectus* (“understanding”), because Saint John had written of the ineffable Word of God through the spirit of understanding. The priestly order keeps this day as a feast because he especially exalted the priesthood by word and example, when he even appointed a certain robber to the priesthood [Col. 0646D].

> [Note: [Col. 0645D] Concerning this young man, see Cardinal Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. I, under the year of Christ 98, from Eusebius, book III, [Col. 0646D] chapter 17; Clement of Alexandria; and Chrysostom, *To Theodore after His Fall*.]

## CHAPTER XIV.—On the Innocents

Because we do not sing *Te Deum laudamus*, *Gloria in excelsis*, or *Alleluia* for the Innocents, we imitate their mothers, whom we do not doubt to have been in sorrow. For this reason chants of joy are likewise not sung, and neither dalmatic nor tunic is worn, because that same choir of infants is remembered to have descended to the lower regions. If their feast falls on a Sunday, we perform everything for them as we do for other saints, because we believe that in the Lord’s resurrection they were joined to the saints. On their octave likewise we sing *Alleluia* and other chants [Col. 0647A], because we know that, after Christ’s resurrection, they were received into joy. Children solemnize their feast because they were the first to go before Christ into their reward. *Gloria Patri* is sung according to the order for the Innocents, which is never omitted except in the Lord’s Passion.

## CHAPTER XV.—On the Octave of the Lord

On the octave of the Lord we perform the whole office for Saint Mary, because on the day of her childbirth we could not do so on account of the solemnity of her Son. This signifies that, if we serve Christ devoutly in this life, in the octave—that is, the future life—we may rejoice in the glorification of the Church, which Mary prefigured. Christ wished to be born from Mary and not from another because she was the first in the world to know virginity.

## CHAPTER XVI.—On the Sunday “While Deep Silence”

[Col. 0647B]

The Sunday occurring between the Nativity of the Lord and Epiphany signifies that time in which the Lord was in Egypt; hence at Communion the chant is sung: “Take the child and his mother” (Matt. 2).

## CHAPTER XVII.—On Saints and Their Octaves

The birthdays of saints are celebrated because through death they were born out of this world into eternal life. Their octaves, however, are observed because in the octave—that is, in the resurrection—their glory will be doubled through Christ.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On Epiphany

The eighth day before the Ides of January was once celebrated on account of the threefold triumph of Augustus Caesar [Col. 0647C]. We celebrate this same day, which we call the Lord’s Epiphany, for three reasons: because on that day the Lord was revealed to the Gentiles under the guidance of a star; because, thirty years later, on the same day he was baptized in the Jordan; and because, when the year had come round, on that very day God was manifested at a wedding through the conversion of water into wine. It is therefore called Epiphany or Theophany, because it means “appearance,” “manifestation,” or “showing forth.” For it is handed down that on this day the Lord satisfied five thousand persons with five loaves. Thus, in the first nocturn comes the appearance of the star; in the second nocturn, the visit of the Magi; in the third, the Lord’s baptism. In the rites of the Mass are treated the conversion of water into wine, or the feeding of the people with loaves.

## CHAPTER XIX.—On the Magi

[Col. 0647D]

Zoroaster, the first king, invented magic; Balaam arose from his seed, and he foretold this concerning Christ: “A star shall arise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise up from Israel” (Num. 24). From his lineage came these Magi, who came to the Lord with gifts. The Magi are so called as though they were mathematicians—that is, persons skilled in the stars. The Lord wished to be sought by them because he wished to have testimony from the wise persons of the world, through whom also the people of the Gentiles believed. He wished to be found by three because he wished to be worshipped from the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe. He wished this to happen through a star because he wished the people to be converted through sacred Scripture. He wished it to happen on the twelfth day after his birth [Col. 0648A] because he wished to draw the world through the twelve apostles.

The Lord wished to be baptized for three reasons: first, to fulfil all righteousness; second, to confirm John’s baptism; third, to sanctify the waters for us. He wished to be baptized after thirty years and then to preach because he wished us, having attained knowledge in mature age, to teach the people. He wished to be baptized by John and not another because he wished to have testimony from him before the people, since the Jewish people believed him to be a prophet.

## CHAPTER XX.—On Matins

On this night we do not sing the invitatory, because with the Magi we avoid Herod’s deceitful invitation; yet in the sixth place we sing the psalm, “Come, let us rejoice” (Ps. 94), because we rejoice that in the sixth age of the world the Gentiles came to faith [Col. 0648B]. In the third nocturn we sing the antiphon “The rush of the river” (Ps. 45) and the psalm “God is our refuge” (ibid.), because we know that in the third time the river of baptism made glad the city of God, namely the Church. Therefore in the third nocturn we frequently use *Alleluia*, because we proclaim that joy came through baptism in the third time.

## CHAPTER XXI.—On the Octave of Epiphany

On the octave of Epiphany the baptism of the Church is celebrated, as in the antiphons *Veterem hominem* (“The old man”) and *Te qui in spiritu* (“You who in the Spirit”). It is baptized in water because this element is proved to be contrary to fire. From the tinder of sin the fire of punishments is kindled [Col. 0648C], but through the water of baptism it is extinguished. Therefore we read that the Holy Spirit brooded over this at the beginning. Water washes away filth, quenches thirst, and restores an image; thus through baptism we are washed from the stains of our sins, given drink from the fountain of life, and renewed in the image of God.

## CHAPTER XXII.—The Sunday after the Feast of Epiphany

On the Sunday after the feast of Epiphany, or after twelve days, the Gospel is read: “When Jesus had become twelve years old” (Luke 2), because, just as after twelve days, so now after twelve years we commemorate the event. On the Sunday following the octave, the Gospel “A wedding took place” (John 2) is read because, just as after a week, so then it is handed down as having occurred after a year [Col. 0648D].

Three weddings are read of in the Gospel. Of the first it is written: “A certain king made a wedding for his son” (Matt. 22). We celebrate these weddings at the Nativity of the Lord, in which God was joined to human nature; its bridal chamber was the womb, from which he “fairer in form than the sons of men” (Ps. 44) came forth “like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18).

Of the second it is said: “Be like men waiting for their master when he returns from the wedding” (Luke 12). We celebrate these at the Lord’s Ascension, when the victor ascended to heaven and the new man united angelic nature to himself.

Of the third it is read: “Ten virgins went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride”; and shortly afterward: “Those who were ready entered [Col. 0649A] with him to the wedding” (Matt. 25). We celebrate these at the Lord’s resurrection, when the bridegroom rose again; for these weddings will take place in the future resurrection, when Christ will bring his bride, the Church, out of the Babylon of this world into the heavenly Jerusalem. Of these it is written: “Blessed are those called to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Rev. 19). At Pentecost we celebrate that the bride was endowed with the various gifts of the Holy Spirit, when “to one was given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge” (1 Cor. 12).

## CHAPTER XXIII.—On the Octave of Saint Agnes

On the octave of Saint Agnes, her birth is written of, because she is said to have been born on that day.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—On the Purification of Saint Mary

*Hypapantē* means “meeting,” because on this day Simeon [Col. 0649B] and Anna met Christ when Mary and his parents brought him to the Temple (Luke 1). He was circumcised on the eighth day and presented in the Temple after forty days because we, who are his body, if we are circumcised from vices in this life, shall, after fulfilling the Decalogue of the law through the four Gospels, be brought into the heavenly Temple. When we hold a procession on this day, we meet the Lord, as it were, with Simeon and Anna.

Our present procession with lights derives from the custom of the Gentiles, whom we know to have purified the city with lights in this month. By the wax of the candle Christ’s humanity is expressed; by its lamp, his mortality; by the light, his very divinity. For Christ is the light of the saints and a burning fire for the impious. Therefore, holding candles in our hands as a figure of Christ [Col. 0649C], we cry: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple.” We do this on Saint Mary’s feast so that, with the five prudent virgins and lamps of good works alight, we may meet Christ the bridegroom (Matt. 25), and through Saint Mary enter the heavenly city for the wedding. In this, women imitate Saint Mary: after childbirth, once forty days have passed, they enter the church; for those who do not imitate the Blessed Virgin in the present life, understood through forty days, do not deserve to enter the heavenly Temple.

## CHAPTER XXV.—On Saint Blaise

That the faithful people, on the feast of Saint Blaise, light lamps for houses or animals, or give alms, arose from an institution of the martyr himself [Col. 0649D].

> [Note: [Col. 0649D] 3 February. February is so called from *februando*, “purifying.” See Cardinal Baronius, *Roman Martyrology* [Col. 0650D], commentary.]

When that blessed bishop, tortured with every punishment for Christ, lay in prison, a certain woman brought him food together with a light. He taught her that, after he had been killed, she should make a light in his memory, distribute alms, and that necessities would never fail her. After he passed through martyrdom to Christ, the woman did as she had learned from him; she quickly prospered in every good thing, and from her this custom spread throughout all the churches [Col. 0650D].

## CHAPTER XXVI.—On the Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle

The Chair of Saint Peter is celebrated because on that day he was raised to be bishop of the Church at Antioch [Col. 0650A]. We annually commemorate his see with festivity so that through him a seat may be prepared for us in heaven.

> [Note: [Col. 0650D] 22 February.]

## CHAPTER XXVII.—On the Consecration of Salt and Water

The sprinkling of salt and water began with the prophet Elisha: he mixed salt into water and drove away barrenness (4 Kings 2). Hence Pope and martyr Alexander ordained that salt and water be blessed and the people sprinkled, so that every phantom of demons might be driven away from them through the word of God. Likewise their dwellings are sprinkled and demons are kept away from them. We do this on Sundays according to the canons because we have been sprinkled with Christ’s blood, just as we read that the Jewish people, according to the law, were sprinkled with the blood of a lamb.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—Why Isaiah Is Read in Advent, and Paul after the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0650B]

During the Lord’s Advent, Isaiah and the other prophets are read because the prophets, and Isaiah especially, foretold that Christ would be born. After the Lord’s Nativity, however, Paul’s Epistles are read because the apostles, and Paul most particularly, proclaimed Christ as already born.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—On the History “Lord, Do Not in Your Wrath”

At the Nativity of the Lord we ought to rejoice with the angels because we have deserved to receive Christ in the flesh. But because we have fallen into worldly joy, we have indulged in banquets and excesses. Therefore we sing the history “Lord, do not in your wrath” (Ps. 37) for repentance, and read the Epistle of Paul which instructs in repentance [Col. 0650C].

## CHAPTER XXX.—On the Period from the Nativity of the Lord to Septuagesima

It is established that there are two lives of the Church: one which labors here in exile, the other which rejoices in the heavenly homeland. Thus the period from the Nativity of the Lord until Septuagesima signifies the time in which every faithful person, after regeneration, toils for Christ in the present life. Therefore *Alleluia* is sung in that season, because in this life one struggles in hope of eternal joy.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—On the Saturday When Alleluia Is Laid Aside

The Saturday on which *Alleluia* is dismissed signifies that time in which every blessed person is led from this life to rest [Col. 0650D] and the joy of heavenly gladness; for *Sabbatum* means “rest.” It is laid aside at Vespers—that is, at the end of the day—because at the end of life, after labor, every person is borne into rest with the song of angels. But if it is laid aside in the nocturnal office, this signifies that the Church, in each faithful person, is led out from the night of this laborious life with a song of joy and brought to that life in which there is splendor, perpetual light, and joy without end.

This is done on Sunday night because through Christ’s resurrection joy is now given to souls, a joy which will be perfected in the future resurrection. All this is represented in the responsory when it is sung thus: “While she is present”—that is, while the Church imitates, in the active life, that life in the contemplative state which they desire, as they pant toward it with all their effort. “While she has withdrawn herself”—that is, from this life—she triumphs forever crowned before the Lord in the blessed life.

And in that responsory, “May the angel of the Lord accompany you; return to your treasures,” because just as Tobias is led by an angel and brought back with joy (Tob. 5–12), so the faithful soul, taken from the flesh, is led by angels with joy into the heavenly treasures. By the words that follow, “May you return to us with joy,” the Paschal season is expressed, in which the resurrection is understood, when joy and gladness return to the Church and she herself is joined to the rejoicing angels [Col. 0651A]. This is also observed in the other responsories.

That *Alleluia* is more frequently sung in “Praise the Lord from the heavens” (Ps. 148) signifies that the choir of angels and saints meets the faithful soul departing from here with a song of joy. It also signifies that on the day of judgment all the saints and angels will come together as one and will jubilate to God for ever and ever [Col. 0651B].

## CHAPTER XXXII.—On Septuagesima, Easter, and Pentecost

During the period from Septuagesima until Easter, *Alleluia* is omitted; this represents us, who are left here in labor and sorrow. Easter, however, when *Alleluia* is sung, signifies the time when each person, departing from this labor, is joined to those who rejoice. The time from Easter until Pentecost [Col. 0651C], during which *Alleluia* is sung to the Lord, signifies that after the resurrection all the elect will be glorified eternally in body and soul.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—On Easter: Why It Is Celebrated According to the Course of the Moon, after the Jewish Manner

The question is asked why Easter is not celebrated annually, as is the Lord’s Nativity or the feast of saints, but is observed according to the course of the moon after the Jewish manner—especially since the legal Passover was the shadow of the true one, in which Christ, the true Lamb, “our Passover,” was sacrificed, and since the Church, having recognized the truth and tending toward spiritual things, rejects all legal observances. But it must be known that just as the Hebrew people prefigured the festival of the Christian people, so the Church, through her feasts, foreshadows the solemnities of the age to come. Therefore she celebrates them according to the heavenly bodies, the stars [Col. 0651D].

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—On the Sun, That It Bears the Type of Christ

The sun, which appears unchanging to our sight, bears the type of Christ, who is the sun of righteousness, the unchanging splendor of divinity. And because the Lord’s Nativity is celebrated according to its course, it consequently does not change from year to year.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—On the Stars, That They Signify the Saints

The stars likewise, which appear unchanging, signify the saints, who now reign unchangeably with Christ; therefore their birthdays are celebrated annually. And because some stars are brighter than others, we keep some feasts more solemnly than others [Col. 0652A]. And because stars rise at different hours of the night, the solemnities of saints are held at different times of the year.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—On the Moon, That It Signifies the Church

The moon, which is continually seen to wax or wane, figures the present Church, which still lives in exile amid the decline of this life. This Church figuratively celebrates three festivals according to the course of the moon, by which she urges herself toward future feasts: Septuagesima, in which she recalls her pilgrimage in this world; Lent, in which she commemorates her return; and Easter, or Pentecost, in which she calls to mind her reception into the homeland.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—On Septuagesima

[Col. 0652B]

Septuagesima is so called from seventy because seventy days are counted from this Sunday to the Saturday of Easter week. By these seventy days we represent the seventy years in which we know the people of God to have been captive in Babylon; through those seventy hundreds of years—that is, seven thousand years—we remember that we lament our captivity in the exile of this world.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—On the History of Nebuchadnezzar

Nebuchadnezzar is the devil; Babylon is this world or hell; Jerusalem is paradise. Nebuchadnezzar led the people captive from Jerusalem into Babylon when the devil seduced the human race from paradise into this world [Col. 0652C]. The people were oppressed in Babylon by harsh servitude for seventy years, and the human race was afflicted for seventy times a hundred years in the world or in hell. The people had ceased from musical arts and songs of joy, afflicted themselves with grief and fasts; and the human race had lost joy and gladness and fallen into sorrow and misery. Because we now recall this, we omit *Gloria in excelsis* and *Alleluia*, which is a song of joy. And because they wore mourning garments, we do not wear dalmatics and subdeacon’s vestments, which are ceremonial garments.

By the chant of the Tract we express the groaning of harsh servitude. It should be noted that two Tracts sound sorrow, but the third joy, because under the two periods before the law and under the law [Col. 0652D] we were in sorrow, whereas in the third time, with Christ’s coming, we are in joy. *Out of the depths* and *You have shaken* sound tribulation; *Jubilate* sounds the exultation of joy. Likewise, *He who dwells* and *To you I have lifted up* sound mourning; *Those who trust* sets forth a song of joy. Similarly, *They have often assailed me* and *God, my God* sound sorrow, but *Praise* sings joy; because if here we afflict ourselves by confession and repentance, in the resurrection we shall have joy with the saints.

After sixty years Cyrus, the king who ruled Babylon, subjected the kingdom to himself and released the people from captivity; and Christ reigned in the world in the sixth age, overcame hell, subjected the world to himself, and released captives from hell. One part returned to its homeland with Zerubbabel, or with Jesus the priest [Col. 0653A], and another part remained in captivity, because one part of the faithful returned to the heavenly homeland with the true king and priest Jesus, while another part remained here in labor. The people returned to Jerusalem with joy, yet they were not free from anxiety concerning wives, children, and companions. This we express when in Easter week we sing one *Alleluia* and still do not omit the Gradual.

But after the completion of the seventieth year, Darius or Ahasuerus completely released the captivity, and all the people, with women and children, returned to their homeland under Ezra, whose name means “helper,” or Nehemiah, whose name means “comforter”; then they had a double joy. This we signify when we sing two *Alleluias*, namely *This Is the Day* and *Praise*. So also, when a faithful soul departs from this exile, it rejoices with Christ in its soul; this one *Alleluia* at Easter suggests it. Yet, as it were, the faithful soul does not yet omit the Gradual, while it retains anxiety concerning the body and works. *Alleluia* is begun on one Saturday and doubled on another Saturday; and Saturday is called “rest,” because now souls alone glory in rest, but in the resurrection their glory is doubled [Col. 0653B].

For when the seven thousand years have ended, the captivity of the human race will be completely ended, and the whole people of the faithful will return to their homeland with Christ, the true protector, and the true comforter, that is, the Holy Spirit. Their bodies and works, like wives and children, will return to their souls; then they will rejoice forever in double joy. We recall this when, the Gradual having been set aside, we frequently sing *Alleluia* at Pentecost [Col. 0653C].

It should be noted that Septuagesima begins on Sunday and ends on Saturday because our captivity began with the dwelling-place of paradise and will continue in this way until the future rest. It extends through ten weeks because through the Decalogue of the law one reaches everlasting joy. Therefore, because at Septuagesima we recall our captivity, we then read Genesis, in which the expulsion of the human race from paradise is read, and it is sung in the responsories, as there: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread.” At Lauds we sing *Have mercy on me, O God* and *Give thanks*, one of which concerns repentance, the other praise, because through repentance one comes to joy. In the antiphon *Have mercy on me, O God*, and in the Mass, *The groans of death surrounded me* [Col. 0653D], the human race groans because it has lost joy and gladness and found tribulation and pain.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—On Sexagesima

Sexagesima is known to fall within Septuagesima and to be named from sixty; it signifies the time of the Church’s widowhood, during which she journeys here in the world away from her bridegroom. It ends also on the Wednesday of Easter week. Sexagesima extends through six times ten, and the six works of the Gospel and ten commandments of the law are expressed. These are the works of the Gospel: “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was naked, and you clothed me; I was a stranger, and you received me; I was sick and in prison, and you visited me” [Col. 0654A].

The commandments of the law are these: “You shall not worship strange gods; you shall not swear falsely; sanctify the Sabbath day”—which we do on Sunday; “Honor your father and mother; you shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property; nor his wife and all that is his.” For the servant who has done these things will hear: “Come, my blessed ones.” Therefore on Wednesday, which is the end of Sexagesima, this office is sung: *Come, my blessed ones*. In the nocturnal office and in the Mass, by “Rise up, why do you sleep?” the Church laments her exile and asks the Lord for her deliverance.

## CHAPTER XL.—On Quinquagesima

Quinquagesima likewise is contained within Septuagesima and ends on Easter Day; through it repentance is expressed [Col. 0654B]. Hence the fiftieth psalm is appointed for repentance. Therefore on this day the Flood is read and sung, because it extends through three times fifty days: repentance is undertaken through faith in the Trinity, for words, deeds, and thoughts. It should be noted that first the Flood is sung of, then Abraham’s obedience, and then the healing of the blind man is added, because one who has washed himself from the stains of sins by repentance, and then obeyed God’s commands, will rejoice in being enlightened by Christ.

Five times ten make fifty because the works of the five senses are washed away through penitence by the Decalogue of the law, and one reaches Christ’s resurrection, on which day the joyful words are sung: “I have risen, and I am still with you.” On this day, in the antiphon *According to the multitude* and in the Mass *Be to me a God* [Col. 0654C], the Church calls upon divine help and asks to be delivered from exile. In Septuagesima, in the Gospel, we cultivate the vineyard; in Sexagesima, the soil. In the Tract *You have shaken*, we break it up; in the Gospel, we scatter the seed of the word. In Quinquagesima, we gather the fruit of light in the blind man who has been enlightened.

## CHAPTER XLI.—On the Beginning of the Fast

Those who returned from captivity built a temple for the Lord. And we, who have been freed from diabolical captivity, ought in these days to build ourselves into the temple of God. We make its foundation on Wednesday because Solomon is read to have built a temple to God in the fourth age. But the temple of Christ’s body was built in forty-six years, by which number the Church is incorporated into Christ [Col. 0654D]. Mary was twelve years old when she bore Christ; Christ was thirty-four years old when, released by death, he fell. These years, added together, make forty-six, and so many days are there from the beginning of the fast until Easter, the day on which Christ restored the temple of his body which the assault of the Jews had previously destroyed. Therefore, so that the Church may be built together into the temple of his body, she is known to devote herself to fasting and prayer for forty-six days—the number of days in which an infant is said to be formed in the womb.

## CHAPTER XLII.—On the Name Adam

The name Adam also consists of four letters, from which the same number is made. These letters are taken from the four regions, which in Greek are called *Anatolē*, *Dysis*, *Arktos*, and *Mesembria*—East, West, North, and South. In Greek numerical values, alpha (*a*) signifies one; delta (*d*), four; again alpha, one; and mu (*m*), forty: added together, they make forty-six [Col. 0655A]. Adam, therefore, is divided through his race and scattered like seed into the four parts of the world; but through Christ he is gathered into one, when the Church is united in the body of Christ taken from Adam.

Therefore, because the Church is gathered into Christ by the four Gospels, she is shown to fast for these four days before Lent. She also afflicts herself for four days because the Gospel read at the beginning of Lent predicts four orders that will exist at the judgment: one of those judging, such as the perfect; another of those saved through judgment, such as married persons; a third of those condemned, such as unbelievers lacking good works; and a fourth of those who perish without judgment, such as the unbelieving. She abstains for four days also because she laments four causes: namely, that she mourns herself cast out of paradise because of food; that she grieves at needing bestial food in this exile; that she fears being led to Tartarus after this life; and that she does not rejoice with the elect in the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0655B].

She moreover mortifies herself for four days, so that, by following the four virtues—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—as though four pillars, she may support her fast; so that the soul, which had committed itself to four deaths—of thought, speech, action, and impenitence—may rise again through observance of the four Gospels.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—On Wednesday at the Beginning of the Fast

[Col. 0655C]

By the day on which we put ashes upon the head, we recall the day of our expulsion from paradise, on which it was said: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return.” Therefore, so that we may be able to return, we perform repentance in ashes and sackcloth. And because we strive to return to our homeland and know that enemies oppose us on the way, we take up our weapons—humiliation, prayer, and affliction—so that we may fight against spiritual wickedness. Therefore, when we hold a procession on this day, we go, as though armed, to meet the enemy for battle. For this reason we begin the fast on Wednesday.

## CHAPTER XLIV.—On Lent

Lent is so called from forty because forty days are counted from that Sunday until the Lord’s Supper [Col. 0655D]. Through these forty days we represent the forty years in which we know that the people of God returned from Egypt to their homeland; but we recall our own return, by which we tend from this world toward the heavenly homeland. For the children of Israel served for a long time under Pharaoh in Egypt; but freed through Moses, they crossed the wilderness for forty years, had food from heaven and drink from the earth, and thus came to the land flowing with milk and honey.

So also we served under the devil in this world for a long time, but have been freed through Christ. Therefore, through the ten commandments of the law and the four Gospels, which multiplied together make forty, we ought to return to paradise, so that, fed with Christ’s body and given drink with his blood, we may reach the land flowing with milk and honey—that is, the region of the living [Col. 0656A]. They entered the promised land after forty-two stopping-places and immediately celebrated Passover; and we shall celebrate Easter after forty-two days and rejoice in our deliverance. That all Christians ought to fast in Lent, we have authority from the Gospel and from the law (Matt. 4; Exod. 34), as I shall now say.

## CHAPTER XLV.—On the Lord’s Fast, and Why We Do Not Fast at the Time When the Lord Fasted

From the Gospel, because the Lord himself fasted forty days without any food; from the law, because Moses twice abstained from all food for forty days.
