Likewise Elijah remained fasting for forty days (3 Kings 19) [Col. 0656B]. Daniel also went without food for three weeks (Dan. 1). But the question is asked: since the Lord fasted after Epiphany, immediately after his baptism, why did the Church institute the fast before Easter? She did this for three reasons.

First, because before Easter Christ’s Passion is celebrated, so that she may suffer with him through bodily affliction and may deserve to reign with him. Second, because, since all things in spring are stirred by natural motion toward lust, they may be restrained from the onrush of sensuality through fasting. Third, because at that time the children of Israel entered the promised land, or those people returned from Babylon, and both immediately celebrated Passover; so that we also, after our labor is accomplished, celebrating Easter, may rise with Christ and reign with him eternally after this life [Col. 0656C].

Thus by singing the Tract we signify the weariness of the journey. So that we may humble ourselves under the mighty hand of the Lord, we say, “Let us bend the knee.” And because we have the command to pray for kings, all those in high places, and all who are under distress, we say the Prayers on these days. Since we read of the tongues of angels and human beings, we express the language of angels through Hebrew and make known that of human beings through Latin. Therefore, because we do not praise the Lord among the angels, we do not sing the Hebrew *Alleluia*, as though it were the voice of angels. But because we labor with human beings on earth, we sound the Latin *Laus tibi, Domine, rex aeternae gloriae*—“Praise to you, Lord, King of eternal glory”—as though it were the voice of human beings [Col. 0656D].

On these days the deacon wears the chasuble folded back over his shoulders, because in the present time every preacher bears the burdens of neighbors. On these days too the prayer over the people is said, because whoever is blessed here by good actions will afterward be enrolled in eternal blessing. On these days *Ite, missa est* (“Go, the dismissal is made”) is not said, because it is signified that, although this is true at every time, especially in this season every Christian ought to be occupied in God’s service.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—On the Veil Suspended in Lent
Because during these days we hang the veil, we have received this from the Law, by whose command a veil woven with marvelous workmanship and beautiful variety was hung in the tabernacle between the holy place and the Holy of Holies, by which the ark was veiled from the people [Col. 0657A]. This veil is heaven, adorned with marvelous variety and distinguished by gleaming gems; it is hung for us as a veil between bodily and spiritual things, by which Christ and that heavenly homeland are now hidden from us. Afterwards heaven, like a book, will be rolled up, and like a tent will be folded together; and then the face of the Lord will be revealed to us, and heavenly glory will be laid bare.

Also, from converse with God, Moses’ face was radiant like the sun. He hung a covering before it, so that the people might be able to look upon him (Exod. 34). The glorified face is Sacred Scripture. The covering that concealed the face is carnal observance, which veiled the understanding of the Law. This covering still lies upon the hearts of the Jews, and therefore they cannot see the splendid meaning of the Law. And because the mystery of Scripture [Col. 0657B] is veiled from us during this season, a veil is spread before our eyes on these days. The priest and a few others enter behind the veil, because the mysteries of Scripture are disclosed only to a few teachers. At Easter the veil is removed, and the adornment of the altar is seen by all the people, because at the resurrection all things will be naked and open, where the blessed will see the King of glory in his beauty. Thus also, at Christ’s Passion, the veil of the Temple was torn, because through his death heaven is opened to us, as is the book closed with seven seals (Apoc. 2). For in rising he removed the covering, when he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, and opened heaven to believers.

## CHAPTER XLVII.—On the Seven Weeks

The seven weeks of abstinence, namely from Quinquagesima [Col. 0657C] until Easter, are appointed because sins are remitted in seven ways: first through baptism; second through martyrdom; third through almsgiving; fourth through forgiveness of a debt; fifth through preaching; sixth through charity; seventh through repentance.

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—On the Six Weeks

We fast for six weeks because we sin in the six ages, and therefore now hasten to make satisfaction through the six works of the Gospel. And because we are Christ’s members, we must begin with ourselves: namely, refresh ourselves, hungry for the bread of life, with the food of charity; give drink from the flowing Scripture to ourselves, thirsty for righteousness; clothe with virtues those naked in holiness; receive into the lodging of holy conduct those wandering in vices and error [Col. 0657D]; visit through confession those sick with the disease of iniquity; redeem through repentance those shut up in the prison of evil custom; and then bestow these things bodily also upon others first.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—On Lent

The year revolves through four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—and is completed through three hundred and fifty-six days. Therefore, just as we give tithes from other things, so we give a tithe of our days when we fast forty days, so that whatever we have done in the four seasons against the ten commandments of God, we may correct in these four sets of ten days. There is also another meaning: man consists of four elements; the Law consists of ten commandments [Col. 0658A]. Therefore, because we have transgressed God’s commandments through four qualities, we appease the Lord by abstaining for four times ten days.

The four days before Lent seem to have been instituted on account of the Sundays, but this is not so. For by the four days the four Gospels are understood, and by the following forty the ten commandments, because the authority for Lent has been derived from the Gospel and from the Law; therefore forty-four days have been dedicated to abstinence. But it is asked to which part of Lent the Sunday days belong, and why they are not fasted; and no one of the wise doubts that this is done with very great reason.  
[Note: And thus it has been defined in the councils [Col. 0657D].]

## CHAPTER L.—On the Six Sundays of Lent

The whole time of this life, from beginning to end [Col. 0658B], is understood through Lent, because it is a time of affliction, just as the Easter season signifies the future time of rejoicing. But the weeks are the six ages of the world.

### On the First Sunday: “He called upon me”

The first Sunday is the time of the first age, when human beings were in Paradise in joy.

### On the Second Sunday of Lent: “Remember”

The second Sunday is the time of the second age, when they were in the ark, rejoicing in their deliverance.

### On the Third Sunday of Lent: “My eyes”

The third Sunday is the time of the second age, when under Joseph they rejoiced in their salvation while others were perishing from hunger.

### On the Fourth Sunday of Lent: “Rejoice, Jerusalem”

[Col. 0658C] The fourth Sunday is the time of the fourth age, when under Solomon they enjoyed the greatest peace.

### On the Fifth Sunday, of the Passion: “Judge me”

The fifth Sunday is the time of the fifth age, when, freed from Babylon, they returned to Jerusalem.

### On the Sixth Sunday, of Palms

The sixth Sunday was the time of the sixth age, from the Lord’s resurrection until his ascension, when they rejoiced in the presence of the bridegroom. There is also another Lenten season: that is, the life of each individual person, which is afflicted here by the sorrow of tribulation. The six weeks are the ages of man: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, old age, and decrepit old age. The fortieth day is the Old and New Testament. For by four [Col. 0658D] the four Gospels are understood, while by ten the ten commandments are understood; and four times ten is forty. The six Sundays are the six chief works of the Gospel, namely (Matt. 25): “I was hungry, and you fed me. I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; in prison, and you redeemed me.”

## CHAPTER LI.—The Fifth Sunday from Septuagesima

The fifth Sunday before Septuagesima indicates the fifth age, in which the people were returning from captivity. Therefore on this Sunday the responsory “Father, I have sinned” (Luke 15) is sung, and the Gospel concerning the prodigal son is recited on Saturday, because, just as he returned to his father, so the people [Col. 0659A] then returned to their homeland. This Sunday is also called the second Sunday of Lent, because the Gentile people, through the teaching of the Law and Gospel, and the Christian people through repentance, through faith and works, or through the two commandments of charity, return to the Lord Father as the prodigal does.

## CHAPTER LII.—On Mid-Lent, the Sunday “Rejoice”

Mid-Lent indicates the time when Cyrus permitted the people to depart. For this is known as the seventh Sunday from Septuagesima, because after seventy years the people return from captivity to Jerusalem. Hence the office concerning Jerusalem is fittingly sung on that day. The nocturnal office, however, treats of the liberation of that same people from Egypt and signifies our liberation, by which in the seventh age we shall be delivered [Col. 0659B] from this world. There are likewise six ages of the world, in which people live here; the seventh is that in which the dead shall rest in their graves.

## CHAPTER LIII.—On the Scrutiny

That the scrutiny is conducted in this week seems to have the following reason. Those placed in captivity mingled their seed with the nations, but when they returned they had unjust priests. Therefore Ezra and the prophets carefully examined the genealogies, separating Jews from Gentiles and priests from Jews. So we too, in this week, separate believers from unbelievers and assign them to our religion. *Scrutiny* is so called from *scrutinizing*, that is, from inquiring or examining, because the faith of those to be baptized is inquired into or examined. [Col. 0659C] A catechumen is called one who hears or is instructed: before baptism he hears the faith and Christian religion by which the priest instructs him concerning how he may live after baptism. Those seeking baptism are called *competentes*; little children, or those mute, deaf, or foolish, are catechized and baptized through the petition of believers, and are saved through their faith. Catechization is called instruction; exorcization, adjuration.

## CHAPTER LIV.—On Wednesday

The scrutiny is held on Wednesday for three reasons. First, because on Wednesday the stars were created and placed in heaven with the sun and moon: so on this fourth day believers are added to Christ the sun and the Church the moon, and as stars are enrolled in heaven. Second, because in the fourth age the Temple of the Lord was built: so now on Wednesday a temple is prepared for God [Col. 0659D] in those to be baptized. Third, because on Wednesday Christ was betrayed by Judas to the Jews for the Church: so they themselves are assigned on Wednesday to rise into Christ’s body.

## CHAPTER LV.—On Infants

First the infants are brought to the door of the church, with males placed on the right and females on the left. Their names are written down by the acolyte, because faith is the door by which one enters the Church, and the name of every believer is named in heaven. Those who act manfully will stand at God’s right hand in judgment; but those who live effeminately will be placed on the left.

## CHAPTER LVI.—On Renunciation

Then the exorcist, whose proper office this is, [Col. 0660A] asks whether they renounce the devil, so that through this renunciation they may enter under Christ’s dominion. For every human being, because born in original sin, is by right assigned to the devil’s dominion. Believers escape his right when they submit themselves to Christ’s yoke.

## CHAPTER LVII.—On Works

They also renounce the works of the devil: some of these the spirit, some the flesh, performs at his prompting. Works of the spirit are pride, vain glory, anger, and such things; works of the flesh are fornication, drunkenness, and the like.

## CHAPTER LVIII.—On Pomp

They also renounce the pomp of the devil: spectacles, games, dances, adornment of clothing or other things, and every kind of excess.

## CHAPTER LIX.—On Faith

[Col. 0660B]

They are then questioned concerning faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, without which no one is recorded as pleasing God. After this confession the devil is blown out, so that a dwelling-place for the Holy Spirit may be established in them.

## CHAPTER LX.—On the Cross

Then, with a cross impressed on their foreheads as though with a seal, they are marked against demons, and God’s house is fortified against enemies. We use no other sign against the devil than the sign of the cross because, trembling as one conquered by this sign, he immediately takes flight. The cross is impressed upon the forehead, where the seat of shame is, because they confess that they are not ashamed of Christ crucified.

## CHAPTER LXI.—On Salt

[Col. 0660C]

Then through prayers they are received into the unity of the Church. Through the taste of salt they are seasoned with teaching and wisdom. Then the devil is exorcized, that he may depart from those who oppose him. Males are exorcized separately and females separately, because it is fitting that those who understand history less should be instructed separately in allegory from those who understand more. Hence also “Therefore, accursed one” is found three times, because it is made known that the devil is resisted through faith in the Trinity.

## CHAPTER LXII.—On the Creed

When he says the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer over their heads, he fortifies God’s temple against demons, as it were.

## CHAPTER LXIII.—On Saliva

When their ears and nostrils are touched with saliva, this signifies [Col. 0660D] that the teaching which, flowing from his mouth, entered through their ears may also emit a sweet fragrance as long as they draw breath through their nostrils.

## CHAPTER LXIV.—On Light

After this, catechumens are enlightened by the acolyte, who is the kindler of lights, so that the darkness of sins and blindness of error, expelled, may be illumined by the light of understanding. Then the Gospel is read over them by the deacon, because Gospel teaching is set before them.

## CHAPTER LXV.—On Entrance

After this they are introduced in order by the doorkeeper, because, once the Gospel has been completed, they are brought by the doorkeeper, the Holy Spirit, through Christ the door, into the hall of heaven. This scrutiny is conducted seven times before Easter because [Col. 0661A] it is rightly accomplished through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER LXVI.—On the Station

After the catechumens have been brought in, the males are to be stationed in the south and the females in the north, because the stronger are evidently to be placed against the heat of storms, while the weaker are to be instructed under teaching. Then four lessons are read, through which they are instructed in the precepts of the four Gospels. Hence at once the four beginnings of the Gospels are recited, by which they are summoned from the four quarters of the world to heaven’s palaces. Then two infants, one of the males and the other of the females, are borne by acolytes into the sanctuary, because persons of both sexes, or from both peoples, are converted to evangelical faith.

## CHAPTER LXVII.—On “I Believe in One God”

[Col. 0661B] “I believe in one God” is sung in Greek over the males and in Latin over the females, because every language is denoted by these two. For the Greeks surpassed all peoples in philosophy, while the Romans ruled all peoples. Thus the wise are understood through the Greek language, and rulers through the Latin. Faith is accordingly sung in Greek and Latin because every tongue shall confess to the Lord. When these rites have been accomplished, they leave the church, because those who are not yet under Christ’s reign cannot take part in Christ’s mysteries or be counted among God’s children.

## CHAPTER LXVIII.—On the Two Lessons

Two lessons are read at Mass, through which catechumens are instructed in the teaching of both Testaments, or in the practice of twofold charity. [Col. 0661C] For the two lessons suit both those to be baptized and those already baptized: those to be baptized, that they may hasten as swiftly as possible to cultivate the Lord’s vineyard; those baptized, that they may complete the work begun, so that with the man born blind they may receive eternal light. Yet “Let us bend the knee” is said only once, so that they may be gathered into the unity of faith.

## CHAPTER LXIX.—On Saturday

On Saturday likewise two lessons are read for the same reason, and so that they may strive to hasten into rest—which is called *sabbath*—because the scrutiny is held also on this Saturday.

## CHAPTER LXX.—On the Passion of the Lord

From Passion Sunday until Easter, “Glory be to the Father” is omitted from the chant because the Son, who is the third person, is commemorated as dishonored by sufferings [Col. 0661D] for us. At Easter, however, it is sung, when Christ is glorified through the resurrection. At this season the prophet Jeremiah is read, who is known especially both to have foretold Christ’s Passion and to have represented it in himself. We celebrate Christ’s Passion for two weeks because we proclaim that he suffered for two peoples and at the hands of two peoples. For by the two weeks we signify the Old and New Testament, because we know that the old announces him as about to suffer, while the new announces him as already having suffered. Two times are also denoted: one before the Law, the other under the Law, in which Christ was foretold as about to suffer by figures from the patriarchs and by Scriptures from the prophets. Therefore in this season we observe Christ’s Passion with the affliction of fasting, because at this season we know that the people of God were afflicted by the Egyptians [Col. 0662A], that a lamb signifying Christ was sacrificed for them, and that Pharaoh was crushed by plagues.

## CHAPTER LXXI.—On the Saturday before Palm Day

The Saturday of this week is free from the office because on this day the Apostolic See celebrates the *mandatum*, since on the Lord’s Supper it cannot do this because of the magnitude of the office. This day is not given an office so that the Church may imitate her head in this ministry. For on this day Jesus came to Bethany, reclined in Simon’s house, and Martha ministered. Mary filled the house with ointment. Simon means “obedient.” Jesus reclined in Simon’s house when he rests in the Church that obeys him. We minister to him with Martha [Col. 0662B] when, following the example of the high priest, we serve his members—that is, the poor or the brethren. With Mary we fill the house with the fragrance of ointment when we strive through the pursuit of virtues to fill the Church.

## CHAPTER LXXII.—Palm Sunday

Palm Sunday is so called because on this day the crowds went out to meet the Lord with palms and received him triumphantly with praises. It signifies that through abstinence we have now conquered vices, and now receive Christ coming to us with the palm of victory. When we make a procession on this day, we go out as it were to meet Christ with the children. The Passion is read on this day because the paschal lamb, to be sacrificed for us, was enclosed on this day. On this day the children of Israel crossed the Jordan on dry feet [Col. 0662C] and entered the promised land in triumph. This week is called greater because it is held notable on account of its most important offices. It is also called the week of pardon because penitents are absolved in it.

## CHAPTER LXXIII.—On Monday and Tuesday

On Monday and Tuesday two lessons are read, as at Mass on the Nativity of the Lord, because Christ’s Passion is foretold by the Law and the prophets.

## CHAPTER LXXIV.—On Wednesday

On Wednesday Christ is betrayed for two peoples. Therefore two lessons are read on this day; “Let us bend the knee” is said at each, because Christ is worshiped by both peoples, in whose name heavenly and earthly knees are said to bend. The tract has five verses because Christ had five wounds. On this day the veil is taken down because at Christ’s Passion the veil is torn and the enmity between God and human beings is dissolved.

## CHAPTER LXXV.—On Thursday

Thursday is celebrated for four reasons. On this day criminals expelled from the Church are received; on this day chrism and oil are made; on this day the Lord performed the *mandatum*; on this day, dining with his disciples, he delivered his body. This day is called pardon because today pardon is given to penitents by the pastors of the Church, and criminals, their penance completed, are introduced into the Church today.

## CHAPTERS LXXVI AND LXXVII.—On Penitents

[Col. 0663A]

That the Church excludes criminals from the Church has its pattern from the Lord, who immediately expelled Adam when he sinned from Paradise and subjected him to penance. Hence even now seven years are given to penitents for satisfaction, because the human race is condemned to this exile for seven thousand years. Adam performed penance for a long time in exile; then he descended into the prison of hell, until Christ the true High Priest absolved him by his Passion and restored him to Paradise. That penitents wander through churches imitates Cain, who, after killing his brother, was a wanderer and fugitive on the earth (Gen. 3). That penance is performed in woolen garments or haircloth is taken from Job, who performed penance in [Col. 0663B] dust and ashes and covered himself with sackcloth (Job 16, 30, 42). Similarly, the Ninevites prostrated themselves in ashes and covered themselves with haircloths (Jonah 3). That they grow their hair and beards they received from Joseph or David. That they prostrate themselves upon the ground signifies that sinners, with the goats on the left, are delivered in judgment to hell. The staff signifies pilgrimage, because they alienate themselves from God’s kingdom. It also signifies correction, by which one returns to communion with the Church. Today they are introduced into the church by the bishop because the repentant thief is introduced into Paradise by Christ. That, once received, they cut their hair and put on clean clothing signifies that they have laid aside the multitude of sins and have now put on garments of virtues. This too was received from Joseph, who, when brought out [Col. 0663C] of prison, was shaven, washed, and adorned with garments of joy.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII.—On the Excommunicated

That the Church casts sinners out from the Church, receives penitents, excommunicates the proud and rebellious, and declares the unrepentant unworthy of burial, again has its pattern from the Lord, who expelled sinful humanity from Paradise but opened heaven to the penitent; yet excommunicated the devil when proud and rebellious, separating him from heaven and the heavenly Church; and because he is not bent by repentance, he is never received. Therefore penitents are saved through grace; proud excommunicated persons are incorporated into the devil.

## CHAPTER LXXIX.—On Penitents

[Col. 0663D] That penitents are received on Thursday seems to have this reason. On Thursday God created fish and birds from the sea; he left fish in the waves but raised the remaining birds into the air. By fish are understood the avaricious, the curious, and lovers of the world; by birds are understood those who desire heavenly things. Thus the former are left below like fish, the latter are taken up to heavenly things like birds. At the end of the fifth age John the Baptist also came, taught repentance, and taught sinners to seize the kingdom of heaven by force. Therefore the Church performs these things on Thursday.

## CHAPTER LXXX.—On Chrism

Today chrism also, which is called anointing, is consecrated. Through it believers are named Christians from Christ—that is, anointed persons [Col. 0664A]—and are assigned as co-heirs of his kingdom. It took its beginning from the Law, in which the Lord commanded Moses to compose it from the purest oil and balsam. By this likewise the ark of the covenant and the tabernacle were dedicated, and Aaron the high priest or the king was consecrated.

## CHAPTER LXXXI.—On Holy Oil

A second ointment was made according to the Law, which was called holy, with which only kings and priests were anointed; in place of it holy oil is consecrated today. And because Christ came into the world as king and priest and willed believers to be his members, we are therefore anointed as kings and priests with this oil alone; with chrism we are dedicated to God in the temple, and with this on our foreheads we are assigned to his kingdom. Balsam smells sweet, while oil [Col. 0664B] gives light. Anointed with these, we ought to give forth a fragrance through faith and shine through good works. And because we are members of Christ the king and priest, we ought to govern our conduct and sacrifice ourselves to God.

## CHAPTER LXXXII.—On the Oil of the Sick

The oil of the sick is also blessed today, a practice received from the Gospel. For the Lord taught the apostles to anoint the sick with oil, and the apostle James commanded in writing that this be done (James 5). These anointings are made from no liquid other than oil because oil is called mercy, and Christ is represented, whose mercy has saved us, he who himself bore our infirmities. Chrism is therefore made in the place where peace is given, because through Christ all things in heaven and on earth are reconciled.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII.—On the Ampulla

[Col. 0664C]

When the ampulla containing chrismal oil is borne to the altar, it is covered with a white linen cloth; a light is carried before it; two priests precede—one with incense, the other with a cross—while the deacon walks in the middle with the book of the Gospel; others carry a pallium above them; two persons lead them with chant. By this they imitate the procession of God’s people, who journeyed through the wilderness as a figure of Christ and the Church. He who carries the light represents the angel who bore the pillar of fire before the people. The priest with incense is Aaron with the priestly censer. The deacon with the Gospel is Moses with the book of the Law. The priest with the cross is Jesus, that is, Joshua with the writing. The clean linen cloth [Col. 0664D] is the ark. The ampulla of chrism is the jar with manna. The pallium carried above them is the tabernacle or the covering shade of the cloud. All this was a shadow and prefigured the truth.

He who carries the light before is John the Baptist, who was a shining and burning lamp before Christ. The deacon, walking between the two, is Christ, who appeared in the midst of Moses and Elijah. The pallium that covers them is the bright cloud which overshadowed them. The oil of chrism in the ampulla is divinity in human flesh. The clean linen cloth is holy conduct. The ampulla is covered before it is carried to the altar; when offered at the altar it is uncovered, because before his Passion Christ was hidden in the flesh; upon the altar of the cross the weakness of his flesh appeared, as it were, naked; after his death his divinity shone forth manifestly. Then [Col. 0665A] the ampulla is partly covered and partly uncovered, and is saluted, because Thomas touched Christ’s naked side, while his hidden majesty is adored. Then the whole ampulla is covered so that it may be seen no longer, yet it is saluted while covered, because Christ is assumed into glory and yet, though unseen by all the people, is venerated.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV.—On Christ’s Supper

This day is also called the Lord’s Supper because the Lord is handed down as having dined today with his disciples. Then he ate the legal lamb, he himself the true Lamb of God, and thus imposed an end upon the Law. He delivered his body, and thus began the new Law and incorporated us into himself through it. He is believed to have done this because today the lamb is read as having been sacrificed at evening by the children of Israel in Egypt. Today he also washed the disciples’ feet [Col. 0665B], signifying that he washes us, who are his lowest members, from the filth of sins. When we perform the *mandatum* today after his example, we call to mind that we are his members and ought to live in charity.

## CHAPTER LXXXV.—Why “Glory in the Highest” Is Sung at the Chrism

Today “Glory in the highest” is sung at the chrism because the angelic choir rejoices in the reconciliation of penitents and the anointing of believers. At the third *Agnus Dei*, not “Grant us peace” but “Have mercy upon us” is sung, and peace is not given, because Judas betrayed with a kiss of peace him who was our true peace. Solemn garments—that is, the dalmatic and *subtile*—are worn today because penitents are restored to the garments of holiness for the Masses [Col. 0665C], and chrism and oil are prepared today for those to be baptized as though they were heavenly garments.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI.—On the Stripping of the Altars

Today the altar is stripped, and on the third day it is covered. The altar is Christ; its vestments are the apostles. Because they fled today, leaving Christ behind, they left the altar as if bare.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII.—On the Extinguishing of Lights and Their Number

On these three days we celebrate the Lord’s burial. We count three days and nights as seventy-two hours. Therefore we extinguish the same number of lights, because on these days we mourn the extinguishing of the true light; and we represent the grief of the seventy-two disciples at the setting [Col. 0665D] of the eternal day and Sun of righteousness, whose hours they were. For three hours, namely from the sixth hour until the ninth, darkness existed while Christ hung upon the cross. We represent these three hours by three nights, which we darken by the extinguishing of lights. By day, because it is illumined by the sun, Christ is understood; by night, which is illumined by the moon, the present Church; by the twelve hours of day or night, the twelve apostles, who serve both Christ the day and the Church the night. Therefore, because day and night amount to twenty-four hours, and because during festal nights twenty-four “Glory be to the Father” are sung, twenty-four lights are lit on these nights and extinguished one by one with each chant, because, in the manner of the apostles, we fall into sorrow [Col. 0666A] at the setting of the true Sun.

“For the crown of our head has fallen; our dance has been turned into mourning.” First, “Glory be to the Father” is sung at the verse “O God, come to my assistance”; second, at the psalm “Come”; third, at the hymn; nine times at the psalms; three times at the responsories; and the *Gloria* sounds in “We praise thee, O God.” Again it occurs in the verse “O God, come to my assistance”; then five times in the psalms; and again in the hymn and at the *Benedictus*. These, when counted, make twenty-four hours; on account of this chant of joy we bewail the extinguished Sun of righteousness.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII.—Why the Invitatory Is Not Sung

The invitatory is not sung, so that we may be admonished to avoid the assembly of the wicked, because the Jews assembled together against Christ in one place and plotted against the Lord of glory. “Command, Lord, a blessing” [Col. 0666B] and “But thou, O Lord” are not said, and no blessing is given, because our shepherd, who gave blessing, has departed. The rams of God’s flock, who were to become shepherds of the Church, were also scattered by wolves. For by “Command, Lord” are understood those going out to preach; by “But thou, O Lord,” those returning from preaching. Because on these days they were neither sent by Christ to preach nor returned to him, neither is said. The lessons are recited not by reading but by lamenting, because, like King Josiah and Jeremiah, Christ our king is mourned by the Church as slain. The bells do not sound, through which preachers are signified, because on these days they not only kept silent but also denied the truth. A signal is made by the sound of the board, through which terror is understood [Col. 0666C], because great fear was instilled in the disciples by the Jews. The sound at the *Benedictus* is the signal of Judas, by which he betrayed the Lord, saying: “Hail, Rabbi” (Matt. 26). The clamor of those singing *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—is the tumult of those seizing Jesus. What follows in silence and darkness signifies that the disciples trembled in secret.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX.—On Parasceve

*Parasceve* is Greek; in Latin it means “preparation.” The Jews who were scattered among the Greeks prepared on this day those things necessary for the Sabbath; therefore the Greeks called every Friday *parasceve*. On this day, then, occurred the solemn day of the Jewish Passover, on which they customarily sacrificed the lamb. On this same day they killed Christ, the Lamb of God the Father [Col. 0666D], and celebrated the Paschal feast with this victim. On this day they were brought out of Egypt, and on this same day they were redeemed from hell. For on the sixth day God created man; in the sixth age, on the sixth weekday, at the sixth hour, he redeemed him. Therefore Mass is not celebrated on this day in the usual manner, because Christ, the true priest and victim, is sacrificed today for the Church. The office today begins with a lesson because formerly every Mass began with a lesson. This is observed today because Christ’s Passion, which the Mass signifies, is commemorated today. The title, which is the heading of the lesson, is not pronounced because the head of the Church is cut off today. Two lessons are read because Christ dies for two peoples. What is foretold by the Law and the prophets [Col. 0667A] is thereby indicated; accordingly, one lesson is read from the Law and the other from prophecy.

## CHAPTER XC.—On the Tract “Lord, I Have Heard,” and Why It Has Only Four Verses

The tract “Lord, I have heard” is distinguished by four verses because the four elements are cleansed by Christ’s Passion and the four regions of the world are saved by the four horns of the cross. He is suspended between heaven and earth because through his Passion heaven and earth are joined, and the whole world is dedicated as a temple to God by his blood.

## CHAPTER XCI.—On the Tract “Deliver Me, O Lord”

The tract “Deliver me” properly expresses the contest of Christ’s Passion, where he says, “Shade my head in the day of battle.” In its place, formerly, “He who dwells” was sung on account of the verse: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and shall trample the lion and dragon” [Col. 0667B] (Ps. 90). For the devil, who tempted him as a dragon after the fast, openly attacked him today as a lion.

## CHAPTER XCII.—On the Passion of the Lord

After Christ’s Passion, the crucified one is represented before our eyes, whom the Church exhorts us to imitate. During the Passion a cloth is torn, because Christ’s garments were divided by the soldiers.

## CHAPTER XCIII.—On the Lord’s Garment

The seamless garment, however, is not torn, but a lot is cast for it. This signified that heretics and schismatics strove to tear the Church through heresies, but the unity of the Catholic faith did not suffer a tearing.

## CHAPTER XCIV.—On Fire

[Col. 0667C]

In the Roman Church at the sixth hour fire is extinguished, and at the ninth rekindled, because at the sixth hour the sun hid its light from the world, which it restored at the ninth hour.

## CHAPTER XCV.—On the Prayers for All Orders

When the Passion has been read through, prayers are said for all orders, because Christ is crucified for all ranks and peoples. “The Lord be with you,” which is the priest’s office, is omitted because our priest is killed today. At each prayer we bend the knee, because we show that all nations bend the knee to Christ. We do not bend the knee for the Jews because we signify that they bent their knees to the Lord in mockery today, and thus indicate that believers must avoid this. Then the cross is brought forward for veneration and is sung in three [Col. 0667D] ways because, when Christ was crucified, the inscription was written in the three languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. Thus “My people” is sung in Hebrew; *agios*, “holy,” in Greek; *sanctus*, “holy,” in Latin; because Hebrew is proclaimed the mother of all languages, Greek the teacher of all languages, and Latin the ruler of all languages, and Christ’s Passion is praised by them all.

## CHAPTER XCVI.—On the Cross of the Lord

Then the cross is uncovered and venerated because, just as Christ was then mocked on the cross by unbelievers, so now he is humbly adored by believers. No wise person adores the cross, but Christ crucified; nevertheless, in venerating the cross, he salutes it. Over the Lord’s body three formulas are said: “Let us pray”; “Admonished by saving commands: Our Father”; and “Deliver us, we beseech thee, O Lord,” because Christ lies hidden in burial for three days, and in such a manner Mass was formerly celebrated by the apostles.

## CHAPTER XCVII.—On the Two Nights

Christ was buried for two nights and one day. The two nights signify our two deaths, namely those of soul and body. The day signifies his death, which was the light of our deaths; it interposed itself among our deaths as day among nights, and, conquering both, drove them away.

## CHAPTER XCVIII.—On the Forty Hours

He was dead for forty hours in order to restore to life the four regions of the world, dead in the Decalogue of the Law. Therefore on these nights three nocturns with nine lessons [Col. 0668B] and responsories are sung, because three kinds of people dying before the Law, under the Law, and under his own time are redeemed by him and joined to the nine orders of angels.

## CHAPTER XCIX.—On Holy Saturday

*Sabbath* means rest; therefore this Sabbath is called holy because, just as God rested on the seventh day from all work, so Christ is read to have rested in the tomb on the Sabbath after the labor of his Passion.

## CHAPTER C.—On the New Fire
Today all fire is extinguished, and a new fire is kindled again from crystal or flint, because in Christ’s death the whole observance of the Law is put to sleep, and in Christ’s resurrection the light of the new Law is revealed. The new fire is Christ’s new teaching. The transparent crystal is Christ’s [Col. 0668C] flesh, made radiant in the resurrection. The fire struck from crystal or flint is the Spirit poured forth from Christ upon the faithful.

### CHAPTER CI.—On the Paschal candle.

Today the candle is blessed, and from the beginning of the consecration it is lighted from the new and blessed fire. The candle lighted from the beginning is Christ, full of God from the beginning of his conception. The two candles during the consecration are illuminated from the fire of the blessed candle, signifying that prophets and apostles are enlightened by Christ’s Spirit. There are two because Christ’s teachers burn with twofold love and shine by word and example.

### CHAPTER CII.—On the years of the Lord’s incarnation written on the candle.

The year of the Lord is written on the candle, because Christ is the acceptable year of the Lord: whose twelve months are the [Col. 0668D] apostles, all the days the elect, and the hours baptized children. The candle also represents the pillar of fire which went before the people of God as they departed from Egypt. The deacon who consecrates it is the angel who bore it. The candle is carried before the neophytes to baptism, because the pillar of fire was borne before the people to the Red Sea, which prefigured baptism, as it is written: “All were baptized in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10). Pope Zosimus instituted the blessing of the candle, but Bishop Ambrose composed the blessing. [Likewise Prudentius and Ennodius, bishop of Pavia.] The candle is distributed to the people on the octave of Easter, because Christ will be bestowed upon the faithful as their reward in the final resurrection.

### CHAPTER CIII.—On the Lessons.

[Col. 0669A]

There are two orders in the Church: the wise and the foolish. By the Lessons read at Mass in the daytime, the wise are instructed. By those read at Matins in the night, the foolish are taught; hence they are also expounded. Therefore today the Lessons are read in the nocturnal tone, because this suits the foolish—that is, catechumens still placed in ignorance. We do not announce the title of the Lessons, because we mark the neophytes, who are not yet signed upon their foreheads for the kingdom of God. Titles are recited with readings so that the authors of heavenly teaching and citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem may be known. But because the neophytes do not yet know the citizens of that city, the readers by no means pronounce the title.

### CHAPTER CIV.—On the four Lessons.

[Col. 0669B]

Four Lessons are read through the four sacraments of this day; and because four kinds of faithful—namely, the simple, the understanding, the advanced, and the wise—are instructed by four modes, namely through history, allegory, tropology, and anagogy.

### CHAPTER CV.—On the first Lesson.

The first Lesson expresses Christ’s rest in the tomb and restores to us eternal rest through baptism, just as Noah gave rest to humankind in the first age through the Flood. For as God rested from every work on the seventh day, and Christ rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, so the Church in the seventh age will cease, like Christ, from every labor.

#### On the second Lesson.

[Col. 0669C]

The second Lesson indicates the regeneration of the Church, narrating the people’s passage through the Red Sea.

#### On the third Lesson.

The third indicates the union of Christ and the Church, saying that seven women seized hold of one man. For the Church, filled with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, is joined to the one man, Christ.

#### On the fourth Lesson.

The fourth proclaims the heavenly kingdom, which the Church hopes Christ will give her. For it says: “This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord.”

### CHAPTER CVI.—On the table of the tabernacle.

The table in God’s tabernacle was supported by four feet; by it sacred Scripture is signified, instructed in the four aforesaid [Col. 0669D] modes (chapter 104). This table is set before the neophytes today while the four Lessons are taught: the first foot is history; the second, allegory; the third, tropology; the fourth, anagogy. History is that which narrates events done; allegory, that which indicates another thing through an event done; tropology, that which instructs morals; anagogy, that which leads the sense upward.

### CHAPTER CVII.—On the first Lesson.

The first Lesson, “In the beginning God created heaven” (Gen. 1), instructs the simple through history, declaring humanity’s first creation. Therefore the priest asks in the prayer that God may restore in the catechumens his image, which he created in the first human beings.

#### On the second Lesson.

[Col. 0670A]

The second Lesson, “It came to pass in the morning watch” (Exod. 14), teaches those of understanding through allegory. It says that the Egyptians were drowned in the sea and the Hebrews saved, signifying that sins and demons are drowned, while the faithful are saved in baptism. Hence the song of victory, “Let us sing to the Lord,” immediately follows, because the people rejoice when the enemy has been overcome and they are delivered. In the prayer the priest prays that, as those people were freed from the Egyptians, so these may be freed from demons.

#### On the third Lesson.

The third Lesson, “Seven women shall take hold” (Isa. 4), instructs the advanced in morals through tropology, exhorting them through Christ to become wise, understanding, prudent, knowing, devout, and fearing God. “The Lord will wash away the filth of the daughters of [Col. 0670B] Zion with the spirit of judgment, and the blood of Jerusalem with the spirit of burning” (Isa. 4), because what is light is washed away by tears, while what is grave is burned away by the fire of harsh penitence. A Canticle likewise follows this, because eternal joy follows good morals. The priest prays that after present things they may receive eternal goods.

#### On the fourth Lesson.

The fourth Lesson, “This is the inheritance of the servants of God” (Isa. 54), leads the wise through anagogy to contemplate heavenly things, since it declares heaven to be the inheritance of God’s servants. Two canticles follow it, because in that inheritance they will rejoice with body and soul.

#### Again on the first Lesson.

[Col. 0670C]

In the first Lesson catechumens hear that they were made for the joys of paradise, but sold voluntarily under sin. Therefore no chant follows this Lesson, because humanity is handed over from joy to mourning.

#### On the second Lesson.

In the second Lesson they are taught that, as God formerly delivered the people from Pharaoh’s slavery through the Red Sea, so he delivers them from the dominion of the devil through baptism. Therefore a chant follows, because joy is restored to them.

#### On the third Lesson.

In the third Lesson they are instructed in the sacraments of Christ and the Church, because in baptism, through the sevenfold Spirit, both filth is washed away and sins of blood are purged.

#### On the fourth Lesson.

[Col. 0670D]

In the fourth Lesson the heavenly inheritance is promised them, and this is confirmed by the canticle “Give ear, O heaven” (Deut. 32). The priest prays that this promise may be made firm. The catechumens, moreover, sing for joy. They resound with “As the hart” (Ps. 41), and the priest asks that they may thirst for the fountain of life.

#### On the canticle.

Canticles are sung because in baptism they themselves are to belong to the company of the one hundred and forty-four thousand who sing the new song, which no one can utter except those who desire the fountain of life (Apoc. 7, 14, 21).

### CHAPTER CVIII.—On the twelve Lessons according to the Romans.

[Col. 0671A]

According to Roman practice, twelve Lessons are read today, because those to be baptized are instructed by the teaching of the twelve apostles; for they are illuminated by the new grace of Christ’s Spirit, just as candles are kindled from the new fire and the blessed candle. These Lessons concern the sacraments of Christ and the Church, and clearly disclose the mysteries of this holy feast.

#### First Lesson.

The first, “In the beginning” (Gen. 1), says that humanity was created in God’s image, an image lost but received again today in baptism; and it narrates God’s rest after the works of six days, which the Church hopes for after six ages.

#### Second Lesson.

[Col. 0671B]

The second, “When Noah was just” (Gen. 6; Ecclus. 44), narrates that sinners perished in the Flood and the just were saved in the ark, indicating that sins perish in baptism and souls are saved.

#### Third Lesson.

The third, “God tested Abraham” (Gen. 22), indicates that Isaac was offered by his father, but that a ram was slaughtered in his place; it proclaims that Christ was given to us by the Father and that his body was sacrificed for the world. Therefore all nations receive blessing through him.

#### Fourth Lesson.

The fourth, “It came to pass in the morning watch” (Exod. 14), says that the Egyptians were drowned in the Red Sea and the Hebrews delivered. It then signifies that sinners are submerged in baptism [Col. 0671C] and children of God emerge. For by the priest we signify Moses; by baptism, the Red Sea; by the candle, the pillar of fire; by the catechumens, the Egyptians; and by those already baptized, the Hebrews. Hence we immediately sing the song of victory in their voice.

#### Fifth Lesson.

The fifth, “This is the inheritance” (Isa. 54), proclaims baptism, where it cries: “All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55).

#### Sixth Lesson.

The sixth, “Hear, O Israel” (Baruch 3), declares Christ’s resurrection, where it says: “After these things he was seen on earth and conversed with human beings.”

#### Seventh Lesson.

The seventh, “The hand of the Lord came upon me” (Ezek. [Col. 0671D] 37), indicates our resurrection, where it narrates that dry bones came to life.

#### Eighth Lesson.

The eighth, “Seven women shall take hold” (Isa. 4), expresses Christ’s union with the Church and baptism, where it says that the Lord washes away the filth of the daughters of Zion. Hence the Church sings a canticle to her beloved, who had made her a vineyard of Sorech.

#### Ninth Lesson.

The ninth, “The Lord said to Moses” (Exod. 12), preaches that Christ was slain for the deliverance of the Church, where it recalls the sacrifice of the paschal lamb.

#### Tenth Lesson.

The tenth, “The word of the Lord came to Jonah” (Jonah [Col. 0672A] 1), mentions Christ’s passion, three-day burial, and resurrection. It says that Jonah was cast into the sea, swallowed by a whale, and vomited forth after three days.

#### Eleventh Lesson.

The eleventh, “Moses wrote,” sets the law of God before those reborn and, in the canticle “Give ear, O heaven” (above, chapter 107, Lesson 4), promises heavenly life.

#### Twelfth Lesson.

The twelfth, “King Nebuchadnezzar” (Dan. 3), expresses baptism, in which the Holy Spirit extinguishes sin just as the angel extinguished the flame of the furnace. Hence the catechumens sing “As the hart” (Ps. 41), sounding forth with joy because they desire the fountain of life.

### CHAPTER CIX.—Likewise, another Roman order of Lessons.

[Col. 0672B]

The Romans read twenty-four Lessons today for this reason: they possess two translations, one of the Seventy Interpreters and the other of Jerome. Thus today they read twelve Lessons in Greek from the old translation, and the same Lessons in Latin from the new translation, signifying that the twelve prophets in the Old Testament and the twelve apostles in the New instruct the Church by faith and works.

### CHAPTER CX.—On the litanies before and after baptism.

Litanies are sung before baptism because the saints are understood to pray for those who are to be baptized. They are sung after baptism because the baptized are declared to be joined to the saints. For there was a rainbow around the throne and the glassy sea. The throne [Col. 0672C] is the Church; the glassy sea, baptism; the rainbow, the saints’ propitiation or intercession. For the rainbow is given to human beings after the Flood, and propitiation will be given to those reborn after baptism.

### CHAPTER CXI.—On baptism.

Baptism is called *tinctio*, “dipping” or “immersion.” Noah prefigured this in the Flood, and Moses in the Red Sea. John the Baptist first demonstrated it; the Lord himself consecrated it by entering it. By prayer the priest invokes God; by the touch of his hand he shows the water sweetened by wood through Moses (Exod. 15; Judith 5; Ecclus. 38), but the water of baptism purified by the wood of the cross. By breathing upon it he signifies the sending of the Holy Spirit and the expulsion of unclean spirits. [Col. 0672D] By immersion of the candle he shows the coming of the Holy Spirit; by mixing in chrism, the union of Christ and the Church. As in the Lord’s baptism, so in ours the Trinity is present: the Father, where “through the true God” is said; the Son, where “through Jesus Christ” is said; the Holy Spirit, where “the power of your Spirit” is said. The change of voice is the coming [or invocation, *advocatio*] of the Holy Spirit and the departure of vices.

Then the priest questions the catechumens, as before, concerning renunciation and faith, so that confession of the mouth may be unto salvation for them. Next they are anointed with holy oil on the breast and between the shoulders, so that they may be strengthened for faith and action. For by the breast faith of the heart is denoted, and by the shoulders the burden of action, because through these two a human being is saved. Then they are baptized in the name of the Trinity, [Col. 0673A] that God’s image may be renewed in them. For God consists in Trinity—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and the soul lives through three powers: memory, understanding, and will. By being immersed in the form of a cross, it is crucified with Christ to this world. What is covered beneath the waters is, as it were, buried beneath the earth. It is immersed three times because the soul dies in three ways, namely in thought, speech, and deed, and is delivered from these three deaths through faith in the Trinity. It is also immersed three times because every sin is committed in three ways, namely by suggestion, delight, and consent. It is moreover immersed three times so that a person may be freed from transgression of the natural law, the written law, and the Gospel. Because it is drawn out of the font the third time, it is seen, as it were, to rise with Christ on the third day. Because it is anointed on the head [Col. 0673B] with chrism, by this the soul betrothed to Christ is made a participant in him. Then a mitre is placed on its head and it is clothed in a white garment, because it is taken up into a kingdom and priesthood. By the mitre the crown of kingship is expressed; by the white garment, priestly dignity; for it is made a member of Christ the king and priest. By the white garment innocence is also signified, because it now receives through Christ in baptism that innocence which it lost in the first parent.

### CHAPTER CXII.—On the seven steps in baptism.

There are seven steps in baptism: three in descending, on account of the three renunciations; three in ascending, on account of the faith in the Trinity which we profess; and the seventh, by which one is assigned to the kingdom of God and enrolled as God’s son and co-heir. The candles of the neophytes are not lighted before [Col. 0673C] the “Lamb of God” is sung in the litany, that they may know that the Lamb of God took away their sins and himself enlightened them with the Holy Spirit. Although some are accustomed to give the light immediately to those raised from the font, that they may meet the bridegroom as he comes with lamps of splendid works. Finally, they are confirmed with Christ’s body and so incorporated into Christ. Baptism is performed at the ninth hour because Christ is remembered to have expired at the ninth hour, and baptism imitates his death. It is celebrated on the day of Christ’s burial because those who believe in him are buried with him in baptism. Baptism is performed once because Christ died once.

### CHAPTER CXIII.—On confirmation.

On the eighth day the baptized put off their mitres, and are signed on the forehead by the bishop with chrism; by this [Col. 0673D] they are confirmed for God’s kingdom through the sevenfold Spirit. The anointing of confirmation is a wedding garment. They preserve this anointing again for eight days while wearing white garments, and wash it on the eighth day. Some think this should be done on the third day. They put off the white garments because in the future life they will put off the shadow and put on true glory.

### CHAPTER CXIV.—On the double anointing.

Those baptized are anointed twice with chrism: once by the priest at baptism and upon the head; a second time by the bishop at confirmation and upon the forehead. This is because the Holy Spirit is given twice to the Church: once on earth and a second time in heaven. By the priest’s anointing souls are betrothed to Christ; by the bishop’s confirmation they are endowed for Christ’s kingdom. Christians [Col. 0674A] are signed with oil because the Holy Spirit is signified by oil. For burning oil gives light; as a medicine it heals; poured into waters it makes them transparent; and it floats above them. So the Holy Spirit illumines souls with the flame of love and the brightness of wisdom; by the medicine of mercy he heals wounds through forgiveness of sins; and by the admixture of his power he clarifies the waters of baptism, the darkness of sins having been driven out. Long ago the apostles performed this confirmation by laying on hands alone; their successors, however, on their transmission, by consecration of chrism.

### CHAPTER CXV.—On godparents.

The priest lifts all infants from baptism and therefore remains the father, debtor, and guarantor of faith for them all. But because he cannot adequately [Col. 0674B] discharge this duty to each individual, he entrusts them to godparents, so that they may teach them the Catholic faith and the Lord’s Prayer. Every godparent—indeed every Christian—ought to know these two things, whether in the vernacular or in Latin. For one ignorant of this is proved not yet to be a Christian and is therefore by no means admitted to receive one who has been baptized. No more than one man or one woman may come forward to lift an infant, and each should know that he or she is that child’s guarantor, in order to restore the child as he or she received it. If the godparent neglects to teach the child Christianity, he or she will undergo punishment for the child. One who has received an infant from baptism may also hold the same child at confirmation.

### CHAPTER CXVI.—That baptism is canonically celebrated only twice yearly.

Baptism is canonically administered twice a year, at Easter and Pentecost, [Col. 0674C] because at Easter Christ dies, and one is baptized into his death; at Pentecost the Holy Spirit is given, through whom forgiveness of sins is bestowed. It is administered on the Sabbath, which is called rest, because eternal rest is given through baptism. But because little children, if they are not regenerated, are excluded from the kingdom of God, in an emergency of illness, persecution, siege, or shipwreck, they are baptized at any time; and if no priest or member of the clergy is present, they should be baptized by a believing layperson in the name of the Trinity in plain water. If they survive, they are to be catechized by a priest, anointed with oil, and chrismated; they are not to be baptized again, but confirmed by the bishop. It should be known that the apostles and their disciples baptized in rivers, pools, or springs. But Clement, under Peter’s instruction, [Col. 0674D] added chrism or oil. Leo, Damasus, and Ambrose added exorcisms and blessings.

### CHAPTER CXVII.—On the day of Christ’s burial.

The day lying between Christ’s death and resurrection signifies the rest of souls from every labor after death, through which one passes to the resurrection of the flesh.

### CHAPTER CXVIII.—On the office of the Mass.

The office begins with *Kyrie eleison*, which signifies joy, because the great joy of those reborn is made manifest. *Gloria in excelsis* is sung because the peace announced by angels at Christ’s birth is given today to the baptized. The ministers wear solemn garments because those reborn, now washed, have received the first robe. In the Epistle [Col. 0675A] their joy is increased, which promises that they will be with Christ in glory. The fact that Alleluia is sung first and the tract follows signifies that humanity was at first amid the joys of paradise, then underwent the sorrow of this world; so those baptized have now received in baptism the joy of remission, but undergo again the sorrow of labor. At the Gospel no light is carried, because Christ, the true light, was still hidden among the dead. Incense is carried because through it he was visited by the women. At the Offertory the singers are silent because the women, according to the commandment, kept silence on the Sabbath. *Sanctus, sanctus*, the angels’ chant, is sung because the angels did not keep silence concerning his praise, but announced his resurrection to the women. *Agnus Dei* is not sung because the terrified women [Col. 0675B] were silent, and the apostles, hidden in the upper room, did not believe that he takes away sins or believe in his resurrection. Vespers are not sung in the customary manner; rather, only “Praise the Lord, all nations,” and the *Magnificat* with Alleluia, are joyfully sung, because that day in no way ends in evening, where God is praised without end.

### CHAPTER CXIX.—On the great mystery, the first day of the world, and Palm Sunday.

Observe the ineffable mysteries of God. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends [of April], the sun is written as entering Aries, and this is the first day of the world. Aries is the first sign of the year. When the sun enters it, the earth becomes green with flowers and the forests with leaves, because on this day God created the world; that day was then a Sunday. On this same day and on the same [Col. 0675C] Kalends, the people of God in Egypt enclosed the lamb which they were to sacrifice on the fourteenth moon. On this same day they afterward entered the promised land. On this same day, with the same Kalends and the same moon, namely the tenth, the Lord—the true Lamb—entered Jerusalem, and there remained as though enclosed until his own sacrifice.

### CHAPTER CXX.—On the equinox, the sun and moon, and the fourth weekday.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends [of April] is the equinox, because on that day, which was then the fourth weekday, God made sun, moon, and stars. On this same day and the same Kalends the people gathered in the Egyptian city of Ramesses and deliberated concerning sacrifice of the lamb. For on this day and these Kalends the Jews gathered in [Col. 0675D] Jerusalem and deliberated concerning the killing of Christ, the true Lamb; and through their counsel the eternal Sun set for the moon, the Church, and the stars, that is, the saints.

### CHAPTER CXXI.—On the eleventh day before the Kalends of April and the fifth weekday.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends of April God brought forth fish and birds from the sea, which was then the fifth weekday. On this same day and the same Kalends, namely the fourteenth moon, the people sacrificed the lamb in Egypt, through whom they passed out of Egypt as from the waves of the sea. On this very day, with these same Kalends and the same moon [Col. 0676A], the Lord gave up his body, through which he led the faithful out from the whirlpool of death.

### CHAPTER CXXII.—On the tenth day before the Kalends of April and the sixth weekday.

On the tenth day before the Kalends of April God created humanity, which was then the sixth weekday. On this same day and the same Kalends the people of God held their first Passover and departed from Egypt. On this very day, with these same Kalends and that same fifteenth moon, as Theophilus writes [Note: [Col. 0675D] Theophilus, *On the Paschal Cycle*.], Christ redeemed humanity from death by his passion; that same day was the Jewish Passover. On the Sabbath God rested from the works of the world; on that same day Christ rested in the tomb.

### CHAPTER CXXIII.—On the eighth day before the Kalends of April and Sunday.

[Col. 0676B]

On the eighth day before the Kalends of April, as Augustine writes, God created this visible world, as is written: “This is the book of the generation of heaven and earth, on the day when God created heaven and earth and every shrub.” On this same day, which was then a Sunday, the people crossed the Red Sea; on this very day, with these same Kalends, the Virgin conceived Christ, who on this same day delivered his people from hell and on this very day rose victorious from death. On this same day and with the same Kalends the Church will rise and enter the joy of the Lord, her bridegroom. Abbot Dionysius and certain others affirm that Christ suffered on the eighth day before the Kalends of April and returned from the dead on the sixth day before the Kalends of April. But the Law and the Gospel seem to speak otherwise, recalling that he was sacrificed for us on the fifteenth [Col. 0676C] moon, which was then the tenth day before the Kalends of April. During this week we are clothed in copes and other solemn vestments, because in the future resurrection we shall be clothed in every glory, when bodies are clothed with the garment of salvation and souls with the clothing of righteousness. The baptized also indicate this, because in baptism they put on white garments. We wear white, therefore, because we signify that angels in white announced the resurrection.

### CHAPTER CXXIV.—On Passover.

*Phase* in Hebrew and *pascha* in Greek are called *transitus*, “passage,” in Latin, because on that night the angel striking Egypt passed over (Exod. 14), and on that day the people of God passed out of Egypt; on the third day they crossed the Red Sea; and on that night the faithful people passed from the confines of hell to the joys of paradise, while the host of those to be baptized passes from unbelief to the light of faith. We celebrate this in the first month of the new year because in this month we were made new in Christ, and in this month—namely *apostoli* [perhaps *Aprili*, “April”]—which is the first among the Hebrews, we know that the beginning of the whole Christian religion was undertaken.

There are two kinds of year: common and embolismic. The common has twelve lunations; the embolismic has thirteen. Passover is distinguished through these two years because through two lives—namely, the contemplative and the active—one passes to the future feast. Therefore Passover is celebrated after twelve lunations because contemplatives attain the future resurrection through the ten [Col. 0677A] commandments of the Law and the two commandments of love. It is celebrated after thirteen lunations because those active in life attain the same feast through fulfillment of the Decalogue and the working of faith in the Trinity. It is celebrated in the first month because in Christ, who is the beginning, all is brought to completion; after the equinox, when the daylight is lengthened, because at this feast the people, the Church, began to seek the heights of heaven. It is celebrated in the third week of the new moon because Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed in the third age. It is celebrated on no day but Sunday because, as Sunday excels all the days of the week, so this feast excels all feasts. Hence it is called the Solemnity of solemnities, and is therefore repeated through every Sunday.

### CHAPTER CXXV.—On the shadow of Passover.

[Col. 0677B]

The reason why the Passion or Resurrection of the Lord is not celebrated on the calendar day is that Christ’s passion recalls to us the Church’s future suffering under Antichrist, and his resurrection our future resurrection. Thus, as the Jewish Passover was a figure of ours, ours is celebrated as a sign of what is to come. Therefore Alleluia, which signifies joy, is sung at this feast, because at this solemnity the eternal joy restored to the Christian people is recalled.

### CHAPTER CXXVI.—On the procession on Easter Day.

The procession held on Easter Day expresses that procession by which the King of glory proceeded from hell to [Col. 0677C] heavenly places with the host of the redeemed. At Mass the harmony of angels is represented, with the human race joined to them. Vespers begin with *Kyrie eleison*, because that feast is celebrated without evening.

### CHAPTER CXXVII.—On the three psalms at Matins during Easter Week.

At the nocturnal office three psalms are sung because the three times of this world are marked by Christ’s resurrection. Three antiphons are sung because the patriarchs before the Law, the prophets under the Law, and the apostles under Christ’s grace are glorified by Christ’s resurrection. Three Lessons are read because Christ’s resurrection is proclaimed by the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets. Three responsories are sung because the three orders of the Church—namely, the married, the continent, and teachers—will be saved through Christ’s resurrection. [Col. 0677D] After each responsory *Gloria Patri* is added because in all things the Trinity is praised together. By *Te Deum laudamus* the hour at which the Lord rose is expressed. The psalms sung at Matins Lauds properly express the time of the Sunday resurrection, as explained above. But the nocturnal *Beatus vir* is divided throughout the whole week because this week is counted as one day. Hence at Prime the psalm *Confitemini Domino* is repeated daily, on account of the verse, “This is the day which the Lord has made.”

### CHAPTER CXXVIII.—Note why “Whosoever” is not sung during this week.

“Whosoever wishes” is not sung because in the future [Col. 0678A] life, which this week signifies, all that is now believed and hoped for is rightly possessed. At all the Hours the gradual “This is the day” and Alleluia are often repeated because in that life all rejoice continually. We do not repeat the verse “God, come to my assistance” as often, because in that life we do not need help as we do here.

### CHAPTER CXXIX.—On Vespers.

Three psalms are sung at Vespers with “This is the day” and Alleluia, because through faith in the Trinity one comes to eternal joy. These three psalms also suit Christ’s resurrection, which occurred on the third day: “With you is dominion in the day of your power” (Ps. 109); “The Lord has sent redemption to his people” (Ps. 110); and “Light has risen in darkness for the upright” [Col. 0678B] (Ps. 111). Two are sung at the font because through twofold love one reaches the fountain of life. These psalms also suit both the baptized and baptism: the baptized, in “Praise, O servants” (Ps. 112); baptism, in “What is it with you, O sea, that you fled, and you, O Jordan, that you turned back?” (Ps. 113). When we go in procession to the font, we signify that the people of God passed in ordered ranks through the Red Sea or through the Jordan. The same psalms are repeated daily because this week is counted as one day.

### CHAPTER CXXX.—On the first week of the world.

For this week recalls to us that week in which God ineffably created the material of this world; and because in it all [Col. 0678C] the sons of God, newly created, rejoiced with a loud voice, therefore those newly reborn sing Alleluia in it with joyful harmony.

### CHAPTER CXXXI.—On the baptized.

Eight offices are sung concerning the neophytes because through baptism they are prepared for the eight beatitudes, which are bestowed in the eighth age of this life.

### CHAPTER CXXXII.—On the Sabbath.

On the first Sabbath two chants are sung: namely, Alleluia, *Confitemini*, and the tract *Laudate*. But on the octave, which is another Sabbath, they sing Alleluia, namely *Laudate, pueri*, and “This is the day.” On the earlier Sabbath one Alleluia is sung because the first life is not everlasting. Therefore the tract follows, because it is still a pilgrim [Col. 0678D] here. Therefore the baptized sing Alleluia because they have washed their robe in the blood of the Lamb. Therefore they sing the tract of praise because the Lord’s statutes are songs to them in the place of their pilgrimage (Ps. 118).

### CHAPTER CXXXIII.—On the intervening six days.

On the intervening six days the gradual and Alleluia are sung because during this time between baptism and the final resurrection, one labors through the six ages of humanity in active and contemplative life. But because this labor is turned into joy, the gradual is followed by Alleluia, because this psalm is sung concerning eternal joy. On the other Sabbath, which is the octave of the first, two Alleluias are sung because in the future life they will have two robes, when they will rejoice eternally [Col. 0679A] in body and soul. The following week is called *In Albis* (“in white”) because those who had formerly been confirmed customarily wore on these days the white garments received in baptism.

### CHAPTER CXXXIV.—On the great mystery of Palm Sunday and the whole week.

All these things which occurred beforehand in Christ the head will also occur in his body, the Church. Palm Sunday, when the Lord came to Jerusalem and the crowd met him with palms, is that time in which the last emperor of the Romans will go to Jerusalem and hand over the kingdom to God the Father, as the Sibyl writes. The three days before Easter are the three years during which Antichrist will reign. Throughout all kingdoms during these days, penitents are brought into the church by bishops. [Col. 0679B] Chrism is made, by which Christians are signed, and then the Jews are assigned to God’s kingdom. Feet, which are the final members, are washed, and in the final time the greatest perfection is stirred up in the Church. Lights are covered, and then all signs will be removed from the Church. Bells do not ring, and teachers then do not preach. The board is struck, and great terror is instilled into the faithful. The Lessons lament, because then all the Church’s joy is changed into mourning. The altars are stripped, and then all holy things are trampled underfoot. The loud sound of wood made at the *Benedictus* is the greatest terror that will assail the adversaries when Antichrist is slain. During these days a new fire is blessed, and at that time the fire of the Holy Spirit is rekindled in the Church. Catechumens are baptized, [Col. 0679C] and then, after Antichrist’s death, a very great multitude will be baptized. The rekindled candle is Christ’s advent. Then Christ’s resurrection is celebrated, because the Church’s resurrection follows then. This time is rightly called Passover, that is, “passage,” because then the Church is proclaimed to pass from pilgrimage to homeland, and Christ will pass from judgment and minister to his own. This is celebrated at the full moon because the resurrection takes place that day when the number of the Church, signified by the moon, is complete. The offices of Easter week represent for us the joys of the final feast.

### CHAPTER CXXXV.—On the office of the Day of Resurrection.

On the Lord’s Day, the Church, rising again, says joyfully to her Bridegroom: “I have risen, and I am still with you” [Col. 0679D] (Ps. 138:18). Then let the whole company of the elect cry out: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad” (Ps. 117:24). By the Alleluia they joyfully praise the Paschal victim, because then they celebrate the true Passover. The Offertory, “The earth trembled” (Ps. 75:9), expresses the terror of judgment upon the reprobate.

In the office of the second day the Holy Spirit comforts the elect, saying: “The Lord has brought us in.” Likewise, in another office: “He gave them to drink of the water of wisdom.” In the fourth office the very words pronounced at the judgment are sung: “Come, blessed of the Father” (Matt. 25:34). Then their praise is added: “They alike praised your victorious hand” (Wisdom 10:20), because, just as those people praised God after crossing the Red Sea, so these, after [Col. 0680A] crossing the river of fire, will praise God for ever and ever.

The sixth office signifies their escape and the condemnation of their enemies: for just as the sea covered those, so hell swallowed these. The seventh office declares their joy, in which they exult thus: “The Lord brought forth his people in exultation, and his chosen ones in gladness” (Ps. 104:43).

By the Gradual, which is sung for six days, the work of the saints in heaven is expressed; for work is understood through the number six. Their work, however, is to exult and praise God. Hence the Gradual, “This is the day,” sounds forth gladness, because it represents eternal gladness. On this day and thereafter Alleluias are sung, because then they rejoice eternally in body and soul. For the two Alleluias are the joys of angels and human beings.

That on the preceding Saturday only one Alleluia is sung signifies that the soul, released from the body, rejoices alone with the saints. That the Gradual is still sung throughout the week signifies that the soul is, in a manner, concerned for the body. Since, of course, that concern is free from fear, the Gradual therefore sounds forth gladness. On the following Saturday the Gradual is set aside and two Alleluias are sung, because at the final resurrection bodies and souls are united in joy.

## CHAPTER CXXXVI.—On the Paschal Fifty Days

The period between Easter and Pentecost is called the Fifty Days, because from the Saturday on which the two Alleluias begin until the second Saturday of Pentecost fifty days are counted, during which Alleluia [Col. 0680C] is frequently used in singing. This represents that life hoped for after the resurrection, when Alleluia will be sung everywhere throughout all the streets of Jerusalem by all people.

Moreover, Alleluia, which is Hebrew, is now sung because in that language there was at first harmony among all nations, and in that life there will be harmony among all minds, with no discord of languages. This was signified by the fiftieth year, which was called Jubilee, that is, “full of jubilation.” The Jews observed it in gladness and abstained from every work. Seven times seven years were counted up to it; and in these days seven times seven days are numbered. By this the complete joy of body and soul is declared, because the body consists of four elements and the soul of three powers, which then [Col. 0680D] rejoices unceasingly in the vision of the Trinity.

During this time we do not bend the knee, but pray standing, because then we shall stand eternally in joy with Christ.

## CHAPTER CXXXVII.—On the Anniversary Easter

It is called *Pascha annotinum*, as though “the yearly Passover.” Formerly those who had been baptized at the preceding Easter solemnly observed the day of their regeneration in the following year.

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII.—On the Greater Litany

A litany is called a prayer or supplication. It is called the Greater Litany because it is said to derive from apostolic institution. It is called Roman because it is observed by the Romans. Gregory instituted it because of the plague [Col. 0681A] that at that time cruelly ravaged the people.

Among the Romans it is performed in seven orders: first clerics; second, monks; third, nuns; fourth, boys; fifth, laypeople; sixth, widows; seventh, married women. The Church celebrates it annually so that God may turn plague away from people and animals.

## CHAPTER CXXXIX.—On the Three-Day Litany before the Ascension of the Lord

Claudianus Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, instituted the three-day litanies because of a calamity that was then consuming the people. For they were repeatedly overthrown by earthquakes and storms, and devastated by various attacks of wild beasts. This fast recalls for us the three-day fast of the Ninevites (Jonah 3).

The Church [Col. 0681B] celebrates this before the Ascension of the Lord so that, just as God delivered the Ninevites from the danger of death, so he may rescue us from calamity, wars, and enemies; preserve for us the fruits of the earth, waters, and animals; and grant us to ascend into heaven. This is indicated in the Gospel (Luke 11), where three things are set forth: bread, fish, and egg. By bread is signified the fruit of the earth, then either in grass or in ear; by fish, the fruits of the waters; by egg, the offspring of animals.

## CHAPTER CXL.—On the Feast of the Apostles Philip and James
