On the Kalends of May is written the feast of Philip and James and of all the apostles. For formerly, during Eastertide, the office was performed not for any one person individually but jointly for all, because in the heavenly homeland, which that time signifies, the joy of all is [Col. 0681C] the joy of each, and the joy of each is that of all.

Moreover, the apostles appointed this James, surnamed the Just, in Christ’s place over the multitude of believers. He became bishop and father at Jerusalem for thirty years. He began the life of monks—or rather, the common life of religious persons—so that they should possess nothing as their own but hold all things in common.

## CHAPTER CXLI.—Why the Law and Prophets Are Read before Christ’s Resurrection, and the Writings of the Apostles after the Resurrection

Before Christ’s Resurrection the Law and Prophets are read; after the Resurrection the writings of the apostles are recited, because the Law and Prophets foretold Christ’s passion and [Col. 0681D] resurrection, while the apostles announced it as already accomplished.

## CHAPTER CXLII.—The Apocalypse Is Read for Three Weeks

For three weeks during Eastertide the Apocalypse is read, in which the vision of Christ and the discourse of angels are recalled, because in that life, which the Paschal season signifies, souls rejoice in the vision of the Trinity and the fellowship of angels. Hence also the Responsories in the history, “You are worthy, O Lord” (Rev. 5:9), are sung full of joy.

## CHAPTER CXLIII.—On the Canonical Epistles of the Apostles for Two Weeks

Then for two weeks the Epistles of the apostles are read, and the Responsory, “If I have forgotten” (Ps. 136 [Col. 0682A]:5), from the writings of the prophets, namely the Psalms, is read, because eternal life is announced harmoniously through prophets and apostles—a life in which, after the resurrection, soul and body together rejoice eternally.

The Responsory “You are worthy, O Lord” signifies the entry of the apostles into the Church gathered from the Jews to the faith of the New Testament. The Responsory “I bore fruit like a vine” (Ecclus. 24:23) represents the part of the Jewish people converted to the unity of faith. In the first Responsories the gathering of hearers and the professed religious into one faith is narrated. In those that follow, the mystery of Bridegroom and bride is shown in the Church now gathered, from whom she herself was begotten: the bride herself is Jerusalem. Hence the Responsory: “I saw Jerusalem descending” (Rev. 21:2).

In the remaining material [Col. 0682B] the beauty of Jerusalem’s construction is narrated, as in the Responsory “This is Jerusalem” and “Your streets, Jerusalem.” All these must be understood mystically of spiritual buildings and the heavenly Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER CXLIV.—On the Office of the Mass

In accordance with the tenor of the offices that contain the person of the primitive Church—such as “Like newborn infants” (1 Pet. 2:2), “The mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 32:5), and “Make a joyful noise” (Ps. 99:2)—these Responsories are to be sung for three weeks.

The Responsory “If I have forgotten” is from the psalm “By the rivers of Babylon” (Ps. 136); it signifies the gentile people, who once dwelt in Babylon—that is, in the confusion of this world—and desire to be recalled through preaching and instruction to Jerusalem, that is, to the Church.

All the other Responsories concerning deliverance from the Babylon of unbelief, arrival in Jerusalem, and praise offered in Jerusalem—such as the Responsory “O God, a new song” (Ps. 143:9), “Let them now say” (Ps. 106:2), and “Bless in the churches” (Ps. 67:27)—are taken from the Psalter, which is of ten strings, in which is love of one’s neighbor for God’s sake. Through the Responsories of the Psalter the offspring indicates that it loves the Bridegroom of its mother, and that its mother plainly corresponds to the city of Jerusalem, which dwells in heaven.

The three offices, “Sing to God” (Ps. 5), “The voice of joy” (Ps. 65:8), and “Hear, O Lord” (Ps. 139:7), recall the same periods as does the Responsory. Hence those who sing them for three weeks until Pentecost do not err.

The Responsories concerning the Ascension of the Lord now comfort the bride in the person of the Bridegroom, as in the Responsory “Let not your heart be troubled” (John 14:1), and “It is time” (John 16:7); now she herself speaks to the Bridegroom, as in the Responsory “Exalt God” (Ps. 82:2); now she desires to be received to him above the stars.

At Pentecost the Romans sing nine Lessons, as on other Sundays. We, however, because those receiving baptism are baptized in three persons, praise the Trinity with three psalms until the octave. The Responsories proclaim that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete—that is, the Comforter—promised by the Bridegroom, has come to the bride, and the gifts brought to her through him: faith, works, miracles, and the other charisms.

## CHAPTER CXLV.—On the Ascension of the Lord

[Col. 0683A]

We do not celebrate the Ascension of the Lord on a fixed calendar date, because through it we commemorate the exaltation of the Church from this world to the heavenly homeland. By the procession which we hold at the Ascension of the Lord, we signify that the Lord proceeded with his disciples from Jerusalem to the Mount of Olives.

## CHAPTER CXLVI.—On the Vigil of Pentecost

On the Vigil of Pentecost four Lessons are read, for the four reasons stated concerning the Vigil of Easter. At that Vigil was read: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). At this one is read: “God tested Abraham” (Gen. 22:1). These two Lessons recall to us two fathers, [Col. 0683B] one carnal and the other spiritual. From Adam we received the beginning of every carnal generation; from Abraham, however, the origin of spiritual generation. The former, by disobeying, lost us all; the latter, by obeying God, heard: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18).

No Canticle follows that Lesson, because through Adam we are all born to mourning; a Canticle follows this one, because through Abraham’s faith all of us are reborn in Christ unto joy. Hence the Prayer also accords with it: “O God, who in Abraham’s obedience.” The Lesson “God tested [Abraham]” (Gen. 22) conveys history. The other, “Moses wrote a song” (Deut. 32), sets forth the new law, which the Holy Spirit wrote in the hearts of believers on the day of penitence, just as Moses received that law on the day of penitence. [Col. 0683C] Hence an allegorical canticle follows, in which eternal joy is promised to us.

The third Lesson declares the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit because of the seven women who cry out that they will seize one man, that is, Christ (Isa. 4:1). Through this tropology is indicated that moral dispositions are given to believers through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. A Canticle follows it, because joys follow good moral dispositions.

The fourth Lesson, “Hear, Israel” (Baruch 3:9), conveys anagogy, where it says: “Learn where wisdom is, where strength is, where prudence is, where light and peace are” (Isa. 14). A Canticle follows this, because in that life the song of joy will be sung without end.

The titles are not announced because the authors of Scripture are still [Col. 0683D] unknown to the catechumens. Some on this Vigil read three Lessons and sing four Canticles, because Law, psalmody, and prophecy teach the faith of the Trinity, and the four Gospels lead to the joy of eternal life.

The Romans read nine Lessons at Pentecost, as on other Sundays. On this day, at baptism—or at Vespers on all the highest feasts—“Praise ye” is sung; this is done because in these psalms the praises of God are shown to resound more fully.

## CHAPTER CXLVII.—On Pentecost

The ancient people celebrated Pentecost because on that day they received the Law through Moses. The Church celebrates this festival because on this day it received the new Law through the Holy Spirit. Pentecost is called, in Greek, the fiftieth day [Col. 0684A] because fifty days are counted from the day of the Resurrection until this day.

The Hebrew people counted Pentecost from the day of the sacrifice of the lamb; the Church, however, counts from the Sunday of the Resurrection, on which day it received harmony of languages through the Holy Spirit. Seven weeks are counted from Easter to this feast because the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are given at this feast.

This was formerly prefigured by the seventh year, which the Law called the year of remission (Deut. 15:1), which the people observed with gladness. They abstained from servile work; they released from service Hebrews sold because of poverty. Thus, when seven thousand years have been completed, the faithful people will obtain full remission through the sevenfold Spirit, will be freed from servitude, and clothed in liberty.

Therefore [Col. 0684B] this feast also is celebrated for seven days, because through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit full joys are bestowed upon souls and bodies in the life to come. For this reason too the final seven psalms bear the title Alleluia, by which everlasting joys to be given through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit are proclaimed.

This feast is celebrated not on a fixed calendar date, but on the fiftieth day after Christ’s resurrection and on Sunday, because through it we commemorate that rest in which we shall rest in the Holy Spirit in perpetual joy.

Note: Pentecost is one thing and the Fifty Days another. Pentecost extends from the day of Christ’s resurrection until the coming of the Holy Spirit; the Fifty Days begin on the Saturday on which two Alleluias are sung and end on Blessed Sunday, but both express the joy of body and soul [Col. 0684C].

## CHAPTER CXLVIII.—On the Paschal Fifty Days

The Paschal season extends for fifty days because, just as liberty and a lost inheritance were restored to God’s people in the fiftieth year, or Jubilee, so in the future lost liberty and the inheritance of paradise will be restored to us through Jesus in the Holy Spirit.

For five times ten make fifty: that is, a denarius for the labor of the five senses will be given in the future to those who have labored here in the Lord’s vineyard during the Forty Days, that is, in this life, under the ten commandments. For there are seven weeks and one day. Seven times seven together with one day make fifty: that is, whoever during the seven days of this life [Col. 0684D] has fulfilled the ten commandments with his five senses through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, will in the future receive him as its reward, in whom alone the joy of all is found, and who alone is that joy.

## CHAPTER CXLIX.—On the Seven Days of Pentecost

Pentecost is observed for seven days because of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, during which fasting is also observed, because as soon as they received the Holy Spirit, the faithful immediately abstained from the enticements of this world.

## CHAPTER CL.—On the Fast of the Ember Days

The fast of the Ember Days is taken from the Law. It is observed at four times because the four seasons of the year are reckoned: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. In each [Col. 0685A] there are three days, which together make twelve, because there are twelve months in a year. Therefore, so that the human being, who consists of four elements, may be reconciled to God, who is worshiped in three persons, abstinence for three days at four seasons is commanded.

## CHAPTER CLI.—On Lent

We fast the Forty Days because we render to our Creator a tenth of our days. But because we do this with the body, we afflict ourselves with abstinence for twelve days, corresponding to the twelve months, as satisfaction; and we fast these days at four seasons, three days at each, because we assign the same Ember Days to three months each.

We also know that the qualities of the elements—heat, cold, dryness, and moisture—are present in the four seasons, from [Col. 0685B] which we draw the world’s pleasures. In order to overcome this, we offer God the sacrifice of affliction at four seasons.

There is another reason. In spring we sow seeds; in summer we reap them; in autumn we gather wine and oil and likewise scatter seeds; in winter we work in gardens and on buildings. So that these may be preserved for our use, we submit ourselves to God by fasts at those same seasons.

These Ember Days are marked by the conception and birth of Christ and of Saint John the Baptist, because Christ was conceived in spring and John in autumn; Christ was born in winter and John in summer. Where we observe three days, we know that religious persons observe a Forty Days’ fast. For just as the whole Church fasts the Forty Days in spring before Easter, [Col. 0685C] so a great many observe the Forty Days in summer before the feast of Saint John the Baptist, likewise in autumn before the commemoration of Saint Michael, and also in winter before the Nativity of the Lord.

## CHAPTER CLII.—On Wednesday

On Wednesday two Lessons are read, because these fasts are instituted by the Old and New Testaments. The ancient people celebrated Passover in spring and then, afflicting themselves, ate unleavened bread; in summer they solemnized Pentecost and then, afflicting themselves, offered first-fruits; in autumn they kept the Scenopegia, that is, the feast of Tabernacles; in winter they observed the Encaenia, that is, the dedication of the Temple; and at both feasts they afflicted themselves with fasts.

For this reason two Lessons [Col. 0685D] are read on Wednesday: because in the fourth age of the world the observance of law and prophecy was handed down, and those to be ordained are commanded to be instructed in both laws. We bend the knee once at the first Collect, which is said without a greeting, because in the one Christian religion we worship one God.

## CHAPTER CLIII.—On Friday

On Friday one Lesson is recited because in the sixth age of the world law and prophecy are recapitulated in one Gospel. At it “Let us bend the knee” is said, because Christ the lawgiver is adored.

## CHAPTER CLIV.—On Saturday with Twelve Lessons

Saturday is entitled “Twelve Lessons,” not because of twelve Lessons, but because of twelve readers: for formerly at Rome six Lessons that were [Col. 0686A] read in Latin were also read in Greek, and two reasons were expressed. One was that Greeks were present who did not know Latin, and Latins were present who did not know Greek. The other was that through the teaching of the twelve apostles both peoples are united in faith.

By four Lessons are expressed the four orders that bless God, described through the Holy Spirit: “House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord” (Ps. 134:19–20). By the house of Israel are understood the people; by the house of Aaron, prelates; by the house of Levi, ministers; and by those who fear the Lord, religious persons. Thus also the ministers of the altar are distributed into acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, and priests. Endowed, as it were, with the four virtues—prudence, courage, justice, and temperance—they can bless the Lord together with the aforesaid orders of the Fathers.

“Let us bend the knee” is said five times, because prayer is made for these four orders and for the people. The four Lessons suit both the season and those to be ordained; the Graduals, moreover, suit the Lessons. The fifth Lesson is read because, just as those boys were tested in the furnace of fire, so those to be ordained are tested in the furnace of tribulation. Hence blessings are sung in their voice, because after testing they are crowned. At this Lesson we do not say “Let us bend the knee,” because we indicate that we do not worship Nebuchadnezzar’s statue with the unbelievers, but the Lord with the boys. The Tract, “Praise the Lord” (Ps. 134:3), expresses the praise [Col. 0686C] which the king rendered to the Lord after the boys’ deliverance.

## CHAPTER CLV.—Why Ordinations Take Place at the Ember Days

Ministers of the Church are ordained at the Ember Days so that they may be admonished to serve Christ and the Church under the four Gospels. They are ordained in Lent so that they may wither away from vices; in spring, so that they may flower in virtues; in the week of the Holy Spirit and in summer, so that they may be “fervent in spirit, serving the Lord” (Rom. 12:11); in autumn and at the feast of Tabernacles, so that they may gather the fruits of good works and themselves become God’s tabernacle; in winter and before the Nativity, so that they may die to the world and [Col. 0686D] be reborn with Christ in virtues.

Ordinations occur on Saturday because God sanctified the Sabbath, on which he rested; and they too ought to be holy and free for the service of God. Saturday is also the seventh day, and they are distributed through the seven grades by the sevenfold Spirit.

## CHAPTER CLVI.—On the Sunday after the Octave of Pentecost

The following Sunday is free from office because formerly the Romans performed ordinations on Sunday, though they began on Saturday evening. Therefore during Lent the Prayer over the People was not said, at which they bent not their heads but their knees, something not at all permitted on Sunday. Priests are rightly ordained on Sunday, through whom the Lord’s sacraments are consecrated.

## CHAPTER CLVII.—What the Time between Easter and Pentecost Signifies

[Col. 0687A]

The period from Easter until after Pentecost recalls for us the time in which the faithful people long preserve innocence after baptism. The period from Pentecost until Lent indicates the time in which they mortify themselves by hidden penitence for their errors. The season of Lent, however, indicates the time in which those expelled from the Church discipline themselves by making satisfaction in public penitence.

## CHAPTER CLVIII.—On January

Through the month of January, in which the year is renewed, is represented for us the time before the Flood, in which the new world began.

### On February

[Col. 0687B]

Through February, in which Alleluia is set aside, is indicated the time after the Flood, in which the whole diversity of languages was confused.

### On March

Through March, in which Lent is observed, is shown the time in which the people of God were afflicted in Egypt.

### On April

Through April, in which Easter is celebrated, is shown the time in which the same people were freed from Pharaoh and advanced joyfully to their homeland.

### On May

Through May, in which Pentecost is frequently solemnized, is shown the time in which the people flourished and rejoiced in the promised land.

### [Col. 0687C] On June and July

Through June and July, in which the history of Kings is recited, the kingdom of Saul and David is indicated.

### On August

Through August, in which the history from the books of Wisdom is sung, the priesthood of Solomon, or the whole kingdom of the Jewish people, is commemorated.

### On the Four Remaining Months

Through the remaining four months four principal kingdoms are chiefly denoted, arranged in the form of a cross: the Babylonian in the east, the Persian in the south, the Greek in the north, and the Roman in the west.

## CHAPTER CLIX.—On the History of Job

[Col. 0687D]

The history of Job, which is read in this month, represents the kingdom of the East, where it says: “That man was great among all the people of the East” (Job 1:3). Hence this history is read for two weeks, because the Babylonian kingdom is said to have lasted two weeks. Seven hundred years are reckoned in one week, and fourteen hundred in two. For that number is found from the time of Ninus, when the kingdom of the East began, until Cyrus king of the Persians, when it failed.

The remaining part of the month indicates the kingdom of the South, which flourished in Persia or Media for one week, namely seven hundred years. Hence different [Col. 0688A] histories are read then, because kings are now taken from the Persians, now from the Medes.

### On October

The following month, namely October, represents the kingdom of the Greeks, which likewise flourished for one week, namely seven hundred years, in the North. Hence the history of the Maccabees is read in this month, because the Maccabees themselves were afflicted under those same kings.

### On November

November denotes the Roman kingdom, which endured gloriously in the West for two weeks, that is, twice seven hundred years. Destroyed by the Goths, it never deserved its former condition. Hence Christ, the King of kings, is born in this kingdom.

### On December

[Col. 0688B]

December, in which the Advent or Nativity of Christ is celebrated, is assigned to the kingdom of Christians. And just as Christ’s birth is at the end of the year, so the kingdom of Christians came at the end of the world; the coming King of kings will renew it and reign eternally in his own.

## CHAPTER CLX.—On the Feast of John “before the Latin Gate,” on the Sixth Day of May

The Mass inscribed “John before the Latin Gate” is for the day on which John the apostle was cast by the Emperor Domitian before that gate into a vessel of boiling oil, but was divinely delivered.

## CHAPTER CLXI.—On the Feast of Mary at the Martyrs

The Mass inscribed “Mary at the Martyrs” is for the day on which the Roman temple, the Pantheon, was consecrated in honor of Mary, Mother of God, and of All Martyrs [Note: [Col. 0687D] First by Boniface, supreme pontiff. Below, ch. 168.] [Col. 0688C], because the solemnity of the Confessors was not yet at all celebrated. For this Mass, “Terrible” is appropriately written (Gen. 28:17).

## CHAPTER CLXII.—On the Feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, 29 June

When the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul had long lain buried together and were, after many years, to be placed in separate churches, it was unknown whose bones were which. But while people fasted and prayed, it was revealed that the smaller bones were those of the Fisherman and the larger those of the Teacher; and thus they were divided.

## CHAPTER CLXIII.—On Saint James, 25 July

The apostle James was beheaded at Easter, but was translated here.

## CHAPTER CLXIV.—On the Kalends of August and “Saint Peter in Chains”

[Col. 0688D]

The day of the Kalends of August was formerly celebrated because of Augustus’ victory on this day. Afterwards Saint Peter’s chains were placed at Rome in a church built in his honor. The day itself was made celebrated in honor of the prince of the apostles, as it had previously been in veneration of the prince of the world. This Mass, or rather this church, is called “Saint Peter in Chains,” because the church built by Queen Eudoxia in honor of the prince of the apostles was dedicated on that day, and the chains of the apostle himself were placed there.

## CHAPTER CLXV.—On the Beheading of John the Baptist, 29 August

[Col. 0689A]

John the Baptist was beheaded on the Annunciation [Note: [Col. 0689B] That is, 25 March.] of Holy Mary, but today the discovery of his head is divinely glorified.

## CHAPTER CLXVI.—On the Nativity of the Holy Virgin Mary, 8 September

The day of the Nativity of Holy Mary was established as solemn in this manner. A certain solitary leading a most holy life heard every year on the day of the Nativity of Saint Mary, Mother of God, the harmony and music of angels in heaven. As he wondered what this was, and prayed earnestly that divine mercy might deign to reveal it to him, an angel told him that Holy Mary had been born on that day. Though her birth [Col. 0689B] is unknown to human beings on earth, the angels reverently observe it in heaven. When he reported this to the [Col. 0690A] Church, it was established that her Nativity should be solemnly celebrated.

## CHAPTER CLXVII.—On the Feast of Saint Michael, 8 May: His Appearance

The Mass of Saint Michael is for the day on which the Christian people fought with pagans and obtained victory through Saint Michael the archangel.

## CHAPTER CLXVIII.—On the Feast of All Saints, the Kalends of November

Pope Gregory the Younger instituted the feast of All Saints, which Pope Boniface had earlier judged should be observed in honor of Holy Mary and All Martyrs.

## CHAPTER CLXIX.—On the Dedication of a Church

[Col. 0690B]

The dedication of a church is taken from the tabernacle or Temple, established by the Lord’s command.

# BOOK FOUR: ON THE HARMONY OF THE OFFICES

[Col. 0689]

## CHAPTER ONE.—On the Harmony of the Offices

[Col. 0689C]

Having briefly dealt with these matters concerning solemnities, we now turn our hand to the harmony of the offices. Formerly the divine office was performed in the Church as seemed good to each person. But after the unity of the Church began to be torn apart in many ways by heretics and divided by schisms into various separate assemblies, the Emperor Theodosius of blessed memory convened the Synod of Constantinople; he condemned all heresies and requested that the divine office be ordered by the synod.

Pope Damasus judged it best to entrust this task to Jerome, then most learned in the divine Scriptures. Jerome therefore, in Bethlehem, where the Lord chose to be born, distributed the psalms among Nocturns and the remaining hours, as the Church today chants them. For the office of the Mass, however, he collected Lessons and Gospels from the Old and New Testaments as he saw fit for the season and station. The Roman Church makes Stations at various places of saints, imploring the saints’ intercessions.

After the pope had received the arrangement of the divine office published by Jerome, he assembled a council and ordered it to be sung thus everywhere. Afterwards Popes Gelasius and Gregory added prayers and chant corresponding to the Lessons and Gospels; and thus it is sung today, and they instituted the celebration of the divine office.

## CHAPTER II.—On Septuagesima

Since in Septuagesima we commemorate the beginning of the world, let us also begin with Septuagesima. One pilgrimage of God’s people into Egypt is read, and one captivity of the same people from Jerusalem into Babylon; by both is signified our pilgrimage and our captivity from paradise into this world.

Two returns of God’s people are also read: one from Pharaoh through the Red Sea and the desert to the promised land; the other from Babylon to Jerusalem. By these our returns are signified. One is that by which we return from Pharaoh—that is, from the devil—through the Red Sea, that is, through baptism, or through the desert, that is, penitence, to the land of promise, that is, to the Church. The other is that by which we return from Babylon to Jerusalem, that is, from this world to heaven.

The pilgrimage indeed extends through seven thousand years; the captivity, however, is prolonged for seventy years. All these matters are signified through the seven [Col. 0690D] offices of the seven weeks, namely from Septuagesima until the Passion of the Lord. In the nocturnal office the pilgrimage is expressed; in the morning office the captivity is made known; in the Mass office the returns are recounted.

## CHAPTER III.—On Septuagesima Sunday, “They Surrounded Me”

On the first Sunday Genesis is read, in which the pilgrimage of the human race from paradise into the world is recalled. At Lauds the antiphon “Have mercy on me, O God” (Ps. 50) is sung, through which the voice of those grieving in captivity is expressed. At Mass is the voice of those groaning in pilgrimage or captivity: “The sorrows of death surrounded me” (Ps. 17:5).

In the Epistle is the return from Babylon to Jerusalem, that is, from the world [Col. 0691A] to heaven, where it says: “So run that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9:24). In the Gradual is the voice of those returning: “A helper in times of need” (Ps. 9:10). In the Gospel is the return to the Church, where it says: “Go into my vineyard” (Matt. 20:4), that is, into the Church; and this occurs through confession, whence in the office: “It is good to confess” (Ps. 91:1).

## CHAPTER IV.—On the Sunday “Arise” in Sexagesima

On the second Sunday the nocturnal and morning office is repeated, because the first age ends with two thousand years. At Mass is the voice of those returning: “Arise, why do you sleep?” (Ps. 43:23). In the Epistle are the labors of those returning to the Church, where it says: “Perils of rivers, perils of robbers” (2 Cor. [Col. 0691B] 11:26). Rivers are temptations; robbers are demons.

In the Gospel is the return to heaven: “The sower went out” (Luke 8:5), because those who sow these good works in tears shall reap eternal life in joy, as in the Offertory: “Perfect my steps in your paths” (Ps. 16:5).

## CHAPTER V.—On the Sunday “Be unto Me,” in Quinquagesima

On the third Sunday, the evil that befell humanity in pilgrimage is recalled in the nocturnal office, when people are read to have been drowned in the Flood. At Matins, through the antiphon “According to the multitude of your mercies” (Ps. 50:3), the voice of captives is indicated. At Mass is the voice of those returning: “Be unto me [Col. 0691C] a God who protects” (Ps. 30:3).

In the Epistle is the manner of return to the Church, where it says: “Love is patient, is kind” (1 Cor. 13:4). In the Gospel is the return to heaven, where it says that Jesus went up to Jerusalem (Luke 18); and in the verses of the Offertory are both returns: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way” (Ps. 118); another: “In the way of testimonies” (ibid.); and there: “I have run in the way of your commandments” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER VI.—On the First Sunday of Lent, “He Shall Call upon Me”

On the fourth Sunday, in the nocturnal office, our affliction in servitude is expressed almost in each of the Responsories, because through the four Ember seasons of the year the human race is afflicted in the four quarters of the world. At Lauds, through the antiphon, “Create a clean heart” (Ps. 50:12), [Col. 0691D] the voice of captives is suggested. At Mass, there is a return to the Church, where the Epistle says, “in watchings, in many fasts” (2 Cor. 6:5). Hence the guardianship of angels is promised in the Gradual: “He hath given his angels charge” (Ps. 90:11). The return to heaven is in the Gospel, where Christ is described as tempted by the devil (Matt. 4:1). There is no doubt that this will happen to every person at his end.

## CHAPTER VII.—On the Second Sunday of Lent, “Reminiscere.”

On the fifth Sunday our pilgrimage is recalled in the nocturnal office, where Jacob is reported to have gone into exile. At Lauds is the voice of captives, in the antiphon, “Lord, open thou my lips” (Ps. 50:17). At Mass is the voice of those returning: “Remember thy tender mercies” (Ps. [Col. 0692A] 24:6). The return to the Church is in the Epistle, where it says: “God hath called us unto sanctification” (1 Thess. 4:7). The return to heaven is in the Gospel, where the Canaanite woman comes to Christ (Matt. 17): that is, the Church comes to God in heaven.

## CHAPTER VIII.—On the Third Sunday of Lent, “Oculi.”

On the sixth Sunday our pilgrimage is recounted in the nocturnal office, when Joseph is read to have been sold into Egypt. At Lauds, captivity and the rebuilding of the Temple are expressed through the antiphon, “Deal favourably,” where it says, “Let the walls of Jerusalem be built up” (Ps. 50). At Mass, those returning say: “Mine eyes are ever toward the Lord” (Ps. 24:15). The return to the Church is in the Epistle, where it says: “Let not covetousness and all uncleanness even be named [Col. 0692B] among you” (Eph. 5:3). In the Gradual: “Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail” (Ps. 9:20); and in the Tract: “Unto thee have I lifted up” (Ps. 24:1). In the Gospel is the return to heaven, where it says, “Blessed are they that hear the word of God” (Luke 11:28). In the Communion: “The sparrow hath found herself a house” (Ps. 83:4), and at the end: “Blessed are they that dwell in thy house” (Ps. [lacuna]

## CHAPTER IX.—On the Fourth Sunday of Lent, “Laetare.”

On the seventh Sunday the fullness of our pilgrimage is expressed in the nocturnal office, where the affliction of God’s people in Egypt and their deliverance are related. In the morning Lauds the sacrifice of deliverance from captivity is set forth, where the antiphon says: “Then shalt thou [Col. 0692C] accept sacrifice” (Ps. 50:20). At Mass there is the full return to heaven, when “Rejoice, Jerusalem” is sung (Zech. 2:18), and in the Epistle: “That Jerusalem which is above is our mother” (Gal. 4:28). In the Gradual: “We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121:1). In the Gospel, five thousand are said to have been fed (John 6:10); these signify five kinds of persons—that is, contemplatives, actives, married persons, widows, and virgins—who will be satisfied there. Hence in the Communion: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. 121:3).

## CHAPTER X.—On the Two Following Sundays.

The reason why this return occurs is expressed in the following two Sundays: namely, through Christ’s Passion. They are two because there are two returns, as has been said, or two passions of Christ: one [Col. 0692D] which he suffers in himself, the other which he suffers in his body, that is, the Church.

## CHAPTER XI.—On Easter Sunday, “Resurrexi.”

Immediately follows the Sunday “I have risen,” because in the resurrection this return will be completed; and Alleluia is sung because those returning will receive complete joy.

## CHAPTER XII.—On the Two Days.

There are two days: the day of temporality and the day of eternity. The day of temporality lasts as long as a human being lives, as it is said: “Today, if ye will hear his voice” (Ps. 94:8), that is, in this time during which you live. The day of eternity has no evening, as it is said: “One day in thy courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11). Christ brought this day. This day began for the elect [Col. 0693A] with Christ’s resurrection, and in the future resurrection it will be given perfectly. Hence now it is given to some in the soul, but then it will be given to all in body and soul. Therefore it is said, “Today the Lord rose,” when Easter falls among the calendars of May, although he rose in March—indeed, many years before. Likewise it is said, “Today he was born,” or “today he appeared”: that is, on the day of grace.

## CHAPTER XIII.—Why Are Days Called “Evil” by the Apostle?

Why does the Apostle call days evil, saying, “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:16), when all things are good? I answer: so far as time itself is concerned, all days are certainly equally good. But certain days are called evil because [Col. 0693B] people are afflicted in them more than usual. For it sometimes happens that on one and the same day one person is hanged while another obtains a royal sceptre; and that day, which is called evil for the former, is called good for the latter. Thus we are accustomed to call stormy days, days of war, or days on which some misfortune occurs, evil; but calm days, days of feasting, festive days, or days on which something joyful happens, good. Moreover, when we call certain hours of days evil according to the course of the moon, we say this not with reference to time, but with reference to the natural increase or decrease of our blood.

**Question.**

Since all days belong to the Lord, why is the Day of Judgment specifically [Col. 0693C] called the day of the Lord?

**Answer.**

These days in which we live are called not the Lord’s but ours, because in them we do what we wish. But the Day of Judgment is called not ours but the Lord’s, because then he judges justly all things which he now patiently endures, and rewards each person according to what he has done.

## CHAPTER XIV.—On the Office of Lent.

In Lent certain offices concerning penitence have been instituted, such as “Thou hast mercy upon all, O Lord, overlooking the sins of men” (Wis. 11:24), and “Remember thy tender mercies” (Ps. 24:6); some concerning fasting, such as: “When ye fast” (Matt. 6:16); [Col. 0693D] some concerning one who prays, such as: “When ye pray” (ibid., v. 5); some concerning almsgiving, such as: “When thou doest alms” (ibid., v. 2), and “Break thy bread to the hungry” (Isa. 58:7), and again, “That [done] unto one of the least of mine” (Matt. 25:40); some concerning work, such as that concerning the labourers in the vineyard (Matt. 20); some concerning the station, such as that on the Saturday before the middle of Lent, where the reading concerning Susanna is read, because at that time the station is held at Saint Susanna, virgin and martyr.

Thus, on Sexagesima the reading concerning the labours of Saint Paul the Apostle is read (2 Cor. 11), and in the Prayer it is said, “May we be fortified against all adversities by the protection of the Doctor of the Gentiles,” because on that day the station is held at Saint Paul’s. The other matters which learned men, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, have composed in the divine offices are to be considered in the same way. For whatever happened before Christ’s Advent, or afterward in the Church, at this or that time of year, Jerome established in the divine office according to this, or according to what he saw to be fitting for the station.

On the Wednesday of the first week of Lent, two verses concerning necessities are sung for the Gradual because a double fast is observed. Thursdays in Lent lack an office proper to themselves, but are furnished with offices from summer Sundays. Hence their Gospels, namely those concerning the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16), and the widow’s son restored to life (Luke 7), are recited on them. For in former times they did not fast on these Thursdays; but, Pope Silvester having instituted it, they kept them as festal days like Sundays, because of many mysteries. Later they were joined to Lent, and were furnished with offices by Pope Gregory the Younger.

## CHAPTER XV.—On the Easter Office, “Resurrexi.”

[Col. 0694B]

On Easter Day the Introit is sung in the person of Christ, who, rising again and presenting himself in the Church to the Father, addresses him thus: “I have risen, and am still with thee.” The Prayer is recited in the person of the Church, which rejoices that the entrance to eternity has been opened to her through Christ. The Epistle, in the person of the angels, exhorts her to joy. This joy we echo in the Gradual, “This is the day,” and in Alleluia, because “Christ our Passover hath been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7).

The Gospel according to Mark, who is depicted in the form of a lion, is read on this day because a lion, when born, is said to sleep as though dead for three days, but on the third day is awakened by the voice of its father. So Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, slept troubled for three days, [Col. 0694C] but on the third day was raised by the Father.

The office, “The Lord brought us in,” is taken from the legal Passover which went before as a figure. For in the night they ate the lamb, and on the following day, namely Easter Day, they were led out of Egypt; and Moses addresses them in these words: “The Lord brought us in” (Exod. 13:5). The Offertory also, “And this day shall be unto us,” is taken from the same day; all the rest concerns the newly baptized.

## CHAPTER XVI.—These Matters Also Must Be Noted.

Four things must be noted concerning Easter: it is to be celebrated in the third week of the April moon, which is the first month among the Hebrews; after the equinox, when the day is lengthened; after the fourteenth moon, when the moon has begun to seek the higher parts of heaven; and on the Lord’s Day.

The three weeks signify the three ages of the world: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. Passover began to be celebrated in the first age, before the Law, when the lamb was sacrificed in Egypt and people were delivered through its blood. In the second age, under the Law, Passover began to be observed when it was annually commemorated by the command of the Law. In the third age, under grace, Christ, the true Passover, was sacrificed for us; therefore it is observed in the third week.

That it is after the equinox, when days lengthen, signifies that after Christ’s resurrection the darkness of unbelief and death began to diminish, and the light of faith and life began to increase. That it is after the fourteenth moon, when the moon seeks the heights, signifies that then the Church began to seek the heights of virtues and heavenly things. [Col. 0695A] That it is on the Lord’s Day is because the world was created on that day. On that day, moreover, the Lord rained manna; on that day he also rose.

The office “Resurrexi” signifies Christ’s resurrection, because, rising from death, he presents himself to his bride, the Church, saying: “I have risen, and am still with thee” (Ps. 138:18). She, applauding, joyfully answers: “Thou hast laid thy hand upon me” (Ps. 72:24). In the Gradual, “This is the day,” and in the other chants and the rest, the singing of angels and the joy of human beings are expressed, as they glory in Christ’s resurrection. From Adam to Christ it was as though night, while all the people wandered in the darkness of sins; but when Christ rose from the underworld, a clear day dawned which led believers to eternal light. Hence all [Col. 0695B] this period is counted as one day. Therefore Vespers does not begin with “O God, come to my assistance,” but is joined to the celebration of Mass by “Kyrie eleison,” because that day is proclaimed to lack an evening.

## CHAPTER XVII.—Again on Easter Day.

The seven offices of this week likewise suit the baptized, who have received the sevenfold Spirit and who, through faith, have died to the world, been buried with Christ in baptism, and now have risen from vices to virtues and from death to life. Thus the human race, which fell in Adam, rising through Christ says: “I have risen, and am still with thee.” It prays in the Prayer, addressed by the spirit of wisdom, that through devout vows it may be worthy to attain the entrance to eternity opened through Christ.

In the Epistle it is admonished by the Spirit to meditate on Christ [Col. 0695C] sacrificed for it, to live without malice and wickedness, in sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5), and so it may enter eternity. Rejoicing in this promise, it says: “This is the day which the Lord hath made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. 117). Then, exhorting all the faithful to Christ’s praise, it adds: “Give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever” (ibid.). It exults in the Alleluia because of the promise of equality with angels: “Christ our Passover hath been sacrificed; let us feast in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5:7–8).

In the Sequence, however, the rejoicing of angels is denoted, who rejoiced in the salvation of human beings; hence at the end it is sung: “Let the stars, the earth, and the sea rejoice, and let all spiritual choirs in heaven rejoice in the Trinity.” In the Gospel [Col. 0695D] Christ’s resurrection is proclaimed, by which the human race is shown to have returned to life (Mark 16). All cry that they believe in him, when they together sing, “I believe in one.” The Offertory, “The earth trembled” (Ps. 75:9), brings to our recollection the earthquake which occurred at Christ’s resurrection, as it is written: “And behold, there was a great earthquake” (Matt. 28:2). That earthquake foreshadows the one which Scripture proclaims will occur in our resurrection: “Yet once more,” it says, “I will shake not the earth only, but also heaven” (Hag. 2:7; Heb. 12:26). Moreover, in the Preface that Paschal Lamb is praised together with the angels, by whose sacrifice the faithful people are freed from Egyptian servitude in order that they may return free [Col. 0696A] to the homeland of paradise. In the Communion, it gives thanks for its salvation.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On the Office, “Introduxit nos Dominus.”

On Monday the baptized are admonished by the spirit of understanding how great are the gifts that Christ has bestowed upon them. “The Lord,” it says, “brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey”: that is, into the Church, now flowing with the milk of teaching and, in the future, with the honey of eternal glory. In the Prayer they ask that they may obtain liberty and eternal life. The Reading immediately teaches them that through the name of the risen Christ they can obtain forgiveness of sins and life. Rejoicing in this hope, they celebrate the Gradual, “This is the day,” and Alleluia in Christ’s praise. Then Christ’s resurrection is narrated to them in the Gospel (Luke 24), lest they forget that they have been saved by his resurrection. Likewise in the Offertory and Communion, they are urged to render thanks for their deliverance.

## CHAPTER XIX.—On the Office, “Aqua sapientiae.”

On Tuesday the spirit of counsel teaches the baptized how great a grace Christ has bestowed upon them. “He gave them,” it says, “the water of wisdom to drink” (Ecclus. 15:3): that is, the water of baptism cleansed them, evangelical teaching healed them, and raised them to heavenly things. In the Prayer they ask that, by living accordingly, they may obtain these things. The Reading teaches them that Christ underwent death for them and, by rising, overcame death; if they wish to imitate him, they will reign with him. Therefore, rejoicing, they sing the Gradual, “This is the day,” and exalt Christ through Alleluia.

In the Gospel, Christ’s resurrection is recited to them [Col. 0696C] (Luke 24), through which the peace of reconciliation is given to them. In the Offertory, the appearing of the fountains of waters is recalled—namely, those of Baptism and Penitence. In the Communion, they are exhorted to seek the things above, so that they may be worthy to reach that place where Christ sits at God’s right hand.

## CHAPTER XX.—On the Office, “Come, ye blessed of my Father,” Wednesday.

On Wednesday the spirit of fortitude teaches those reborn in Christ with what sweet voice Christ will call them at the last into the kingdom they had lost. “Come,” he says, “ye blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34). In the Prayer they ask that they may receive eternal joys. In the Reading Christ’s Passion and resurrection are recited to them, through whom sins are wiped away for penitents and eternal life is given. They dance for joy through the Gradual, “This is the day,” and shout Alleluia to Christ.

Then the Gospel tells them that after his resurrection Christ ate with seven disciples (John 21), by which they are prefigured as, filled with the sevenfold Spirit, destined to feast with Christ after the final resurrection. Hence in the Offertory it is declared that man ate the bread of angels. In the Communion, those who worthily eat this bread are taught that they will no longer die, but will live with Christ.

## CHAPTER XXI.—On the Office, “The Victorious Hand,” Thursday after Easter.

On Thursday the spirit of knowledge admonishes the baptized to praise Christ, as the people freed from Egypt did after the Red [Col. 0697A] Sea: “They praised together thy victorious hand, O Lord”—that is, Christ (Wis. 10:20). In the Prayer they beseech that they may fulfill faith by works. In the Epistle Reading they are taught that, as the Ethiopian coming to Jerusalem is baptized (Acts 8), so those coming from the blackness of sins to the Church are saved through Christ’s Passion. In the Gradual, “This is the day,” the joy of converts is expressed; in Alleluia, Christ’s praise is set forth. In the Gospel his resurrection is recalled to them, in which they are called Christ’s brothers (John 20:17). In the Offertory the day of eternal solemnity is proclaimed to them, in which they are promised entrance into the land flowing with milk and honey, that is, paradise. Therefore in the Communion they are exhorted to praise God, through whom they are called out of darkness into marvellous light [Col. 0697B] (1 Pet. 2:9).

## CHAPTER XXII.—On the Office, “The Lord Led Them Forth.”

On Friday the spirit of piety makes known to those reborn in Christ that they have thus been delivered by Christ from the devil’s oppression, as the children of Israel were once delivered from Pharaoh. In the Prayer they ask that they may imitate the Christian profession in works, so that through Christ’s resurrection they may come to the right hand of God. Through the Gradual, “This is the day,” they express their joy; through the Verse, “The stone which the builders rejected” (Ps. 117:22), they sing of Christ’s Passion; and through Alleluia they extol his resurrection. In the Gospel Christ’s appearance to them after his resurrection is read (Matt. 28). All who are baptized in his name are taught, when he promises to be with them [Col. 0697C] until the end of the world. Hence in the Offertory “This is the day,” that is, Friday, is enjoined upon them as a memorial, on which they know that they were rescued from the enemy by Christ’s death. In the Communion those baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are taught and admonished to keep his commandments, that they may be worthy to see him after the resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—On the Office, “The Lord Led Forth His People,” Saturday in Albis.

On Saturday the spirit of the fear of the Lord recalls to the baptized the grace of Christ the Redeemer, who redeemed them from death and will bring them back into paradise. “The Lord,” it says, “led forth his people in exultation, and his chosen in joy” (Ps. 104:43). In the Prayer they entreat that they may be worthy of eternal joys. The Reading teaches them that Christ, the cornerstone, has joined them as living stones to himself in the heavenly building—indeed, has chosen them as kings and priests (1 Pet. 2). Therefore they exult with immeasurable joy, and sing two Alleluias in Christ’s praise.

In the Gospel Christ’s resurrection is proclaimed to them (John 21), through which the Gentile and Jewish peoples, saved, are prefigured by John and Peter. Their voice also resounds in the Offertory, by which they greet Christ as having come for their redemption: “Blessed is he that cometh” (Matt. 21:9). In the Communion, those joined to Christ through baptism are taught that they ought to strive by virtues toward his kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—Sunday in Albis, “Quasimodo geniti infantes.”

In the office of the octave of Easter, the baptized are admonished [Col. 0698A] to remember that they are “as newborn infants” (*quasimodo geniti infantes*) in Christ, and to desire the milk of Holy Scripture, so that they may grow in his body unto salvation. In the Prayer they ask that they may retain the Paschal sacrament in conduct and life. The Reading declares that they have been born of God, that the world is to be overcome by them through faith, and teaches that they will triumph with Christ in the resurrection (1 John 5). Therefore, since then they will obtain joy and gladness in body and soul together, they sing two Alleluias.

Then in the Gospel they hear Christ’s resurrection, through whom they have received the Holy Spirit and remission of sins (John 20). This resurrection is confirmed in the Offertory and Communion, so that their future resurrection may be believed. It should be noted that throughout the offices of this week Alleluia is sung four times at the Introit [Col. 0698B] and three times elsewhere, because the Holy Trinity is praised from the four quarters of the world on account of Christ’s resurrection and humanity’s salvation.

## CHAPTER XXV.—Second Sunday after Easter, “Misericordia Domini.”

On the second Sunday the baptized proclaim to the world the grace of Christ and joyfully cry out: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 32:5). Here they proclaim the Trinity: in “the mercy of the Lord” they declare the Holy Spirit; in “the word,” the Son; and in “God,” the Father. They sing first of the person of the Holy Spirit because they have been sanctified in him. Second, they set forth the person of the Son, through whom they have been redeemed. Third, they declare the person of the Father, to whom they have been reconciled. And because they praise the Trinity, they cry Alleluia three times.

In the Prayer they wish perpetual gladness to the faithful and ask for everlasting joys. In the Epistle the voice of preachers is understood, through whom Christ is proposed to the peoples as an example (1 Pet. 2). Through one Alleluia is understood the joy of converts, through the other the joy of preachers. In the Gospel two flocks, one from the Jews and the other from the Gentiles, are shown converted to one true shepherd, and made into one fold [John 10]. In the Offertory, “God, my God,” they are shown to invoke one shepherd. In the Communion he himself answers them that he is the shepherd, knows them, and is known by them.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—Third Sunday after Easter, “Jubilate Deo, omnis terra.”

[Col. 0698D]

On the third Sunday those reborn in Christ summon the whole world to Christ’s praise, and leap for joy in thanksgiving: “Make a joyful noise unto God, all the earth” (Ps. 67:4). Here they proclaim the Trinity, denoting the Father in “God,” the Son in “his name,” and the Holy Spirit in “his praise.” Since they rejoice that through the two commandments of love they will be saved in faith in the Trinity, they sing Alleluia twice, and then a third time.

In the Prayer they ask that, turned from error, they may fulfill the Christian life. In the Epistle they are instructed in the contemplative life, when they are exhorted to abstain from carnal desires (1 Pet. 2). They are also taught the active life, when they are commanded to be subject to every human creature [Col. 0699A] (1 Pet. 2). In one Alleluia contemplatives, fervent in love of God, rejoice; in the other actives, serving in love of neighbour, exult. In the Gospel they are promised the vision of God and a joy which shall never be taken from them (John 16). Therefore, filled with great joy, they break forth in Christ’s praise in the Offertory: “Praise the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. 145:2). He himself again promises them in the Communion his vision and an ascension to the Father together with his whole body, that is, the Church.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—Fourth Sunday after Easter, “Cantate Domino.”

On the fourth Sunday they exhort converts to be baptized and to praise Christ, and themselves joyfully lead the singing: “Sing unto the Lord a new song” (Ps. [Col. 0699B] 97). Here they commemorate the Trinity, denoting the Father in “the Lord, who hath done wondrous things” (ibid.); the Son in “he hath revealed his righteousness among the nations” (ibid., v. 2); and suggesting the Holy Spirit. Since they have received the faith of the Holy Trinity in the four quarters of the world, they sing the Trinity through four Alleluias. In the Prayer they pray that they may attain true joys.

The Epistle instructs converts to remember that, generated through God’s word, they are the beginning of God’s new creation (Jas. 1). And if, by hearing God’s word, they abhor vices, their souls will be saved. They sing Alleluia twice because they exult both that they have escaped death and that they have been deemed worthy to possess life in hope. In the Gospel the Holy Spirit is promised to them, who, it is declared, will teach them all truth (John 16). Hence in the [Col. 0699C] Offertory they invite the whole world to God’s praise and joyfully cry together: “Make a joyful noise unto God, all the earth” (Ps. 97:4). In the Communion the threefold judgment of the Holy Spirit is proclaimed, by which the world is reproved concerning the unbelief of the reprobate, the righteousness of the saints, and God’s hidden yet just judgment.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—On the Fifth Sunday, “Vocem jucunditatis.”

On the fifth Sunday, the baptized, as if in the fifth age, liberated from Babylon, proclaim their liberator to all peoples. In the office, “The voice of joy,” they joyfully cry that he has delivered his people, and therefore commemorate the Trinity through three Alleluias. In the Prayer they ask that they may think and do what is right. In the Epistle they are taught to visit orphans and widows and to keep themselves unspotted from the world, so that they may thus reign with God (Jas. 1). Through the two Alleluias two resurrections are indicated: one of souls now, the other of bodies hereafter. In the Gospel they are exhorted to full joy, which will be given in the future resurrection (John 16). Hence in the Offertory all the faithful are admonished to praise God, through whom they will receive such joy: “Bless,” they say, “our God, O ye nations” (Ps. 65:8). In the Communion all are again exhorted to resound Christ’s praises, through whom such great gifts are given to humankind: “Sing unto the Lord” (Ps. 95).

## CHAPTER XXIX.—On the Rogations, and the Office “Exaudivit.”

As the earnestness [Col. 0700A] of preachers is understood through the office “The voice of joy,” so the concern of those turning from error is expressed through the office “He heard.” In the Prayer they ask that they may be protected from every adversity. In the Epistle they are admonished to confession; in the Gospel, to prayer (Luke 5). In the Offertory, “I will confess,” is their confession. In the Communion, “Ask, and ye shall receive” (Luke 11), their prayer is understood.

## CHAPTER XXX.—On the Vigil of the Ascension and the Office “Omnes gentes.”

In the office “All nations” they clap their hands because they have abandoned error. In the Prayer they ask that they may be transferred to that place which they believe their head has reached. In the Reading their conversion is suggested, when the multitude is recalled to have had one heart and one soul. In [Col. 0700B] Alleluia they rejoice in God, who had bestowed such great grace upon them. In the Gospel he prays the Father for the members (John 17), that they may become one with him. In the Offertory the ascension of the head is expressed, and the members are promised that they will follow him. In the Communion, having become one with him, they pray their head that the Father may keep them from evil.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—On the Ascension and the Office “Viri Galilaei.”

In the office, “Men of Galilee” (Acts 1), the angels announce to the faithful Christ’s ascension and his return for judgment, so that, joyfully awaiting him, they may not despair of ascending to God. In the Prayer they ask that they may be able to dwell in heavenly places; the Reading and Gospel recount to them how Christ [Col. 0700C] ascended to heaven (Acts 1; Mark 16). In one Alleluia Christ’s ascension is praised; in another the Church rejoices in her own ascension. In each Alleluia the praise of angels is expressed; in the other, the joy of human beings rejoicing at Christ’s ascension. The Sequence represents the singing of angels, by which it exults in Christ’s triumph. In the Offertory and Communion likewise the faithful pursue their head with praises, that they may deserve truly to follow him.

The Rogations of the Ninevites are observed for three days because the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—or the three orders of the Church, married persons, continent persons, and teachers, are afflicted in penitence. They are observed for three days because the Church’s three parts [Col. 0700D] of the world, or the same three orders, will be grievously oppressed under Antichrist for three years. The day of the Ascension represents the Day of Judgment, on which day the Church is proclaimed as destined to ascend to heaven. Therefore it is sung: “As ye have seen him ascending into heaven, so shall he come” (Acts 1:11).

## CHAPTER XXXII.—Sunday within the Octave of the Ascension, “Exaudi, Domine.”

The Sunday following the third day signifies eternal rest, which after the three ages of the world—namely, before the Law, under the Law, and under grace—is bestowed upon the three orders mentioned above. Hence the Church rejoices: “I have sought thy face; thy face, O Lord, will I seek.” In the Prayer it asks that it may serve his majesty with a sincere heart. In the Epistle the goods are enumerated [Col. 0701A] for which the righteous will then be rewarded (1 Pet. 4). In the Gospel it is said that because they are now made outside the Synagogue, they will then enter God’s court (John 15); through this consolation the Gentiles rejoice in the Alleluia, Offertory, and Communion.

After this Pentecost is celebrated six days later, when the Spirit was distributed to believers, because after the six ages of the world the faithful will be disposed through the grace of the Holy Spirit in diverse dwelling places. It is celebrated after six days because for the six evangelical works which they performed during the six days of the week, they will then be rewarded in joy. That it occurs ten days after the Ascension is because they will be enriched with the denarius of life for the ten commandments of the Law.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—On the Vigil of Pentecost.

[Col. 0701B] In the office of the Vigil of Pentecost, those to be baptized are instructed how through faith and works they may merit heavenly things; Mother Church rejoices at their salvation as “Kyrie eleison” and “Glory be to God on high” resound. In the Prayer she asks for them that the gift of the Holy Spirit received may be confirmed in them. In the Reading, the twelve apostles are recalled to have received the Holy Spirit (Acts 19:1), through whom the entire body of believers in the four quarters of the world is signified. In Alleluia and in the Tract, “Praise the Lord,” they praise God because they have escaped the error of unbelief. In the Gospel they are promised the consolation of the Holy Spirit and the manifestation of his divinity (John 14:18). In the Offertory they ask that he send them the Holy Spirit. In the Communion the outpouring of the Holy Spirit is sung, by [Col. 0701C] which the whole body of believers is made fruitful.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—On Holy Pentecost Day and the Office “Spiritus Domini.”

The seven offices of this week correspond to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, whom the baptized have received. In the office “The Spirit of the Lord” (Wis. 1), the spirit of wisdom is glorified, through whom knowledge of the voice is given to believers; and because this gift is poured into the four quarters of the world, Alleluia is sung four times. In the Prayer they ask that they may rejoice in the consolation of the Holy Spirit.

The Reading suggests to the baptized how the primitive Church received kinds of tongues through the Holy Spirit (Acts 2), of which they have been deemed worthy to be children and have received the same Holy Spirit. Out of joy they sing two Alleluias, [Col. 0701D] because they have received the Holy Spirit twice: once when they are baptized, a second time when they are confirmed, just as the Spirit was once given on earth and a second time from heaven. Moreover, the Sequence represents the kinds of tongues, by which the Church resounds Christ’s praises in all languages.

In the Gospel, before a dwelling-place is promised to Christ’s lovers through the Father’s and Son’s love, the coming of the Holy Spirit is promised, who will teach them all things (John 14). In the Offertory they pray that this may be confirmed in them; in the Preface they praise the Holy Spirit with the angels, into whom angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1:3). His outpouring is sung in the Communion, when he is believed already to descend into those who desire him.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—On the Office “Cibavit eos Dominus,” Monday.

[Col. 0702A]

In the office, “He fed them” (Ps. 80:17), the spirit of understanding is denoted, who is called “the fat of wheat” and “honey from the rock,” that is, Christ; for Christ is called both a grain of wheat and a rock. The faithful have been fed with his fatness and filled with his honey when they have been filled with the sweetness of the Holy Spirit. And because this grace is spread through the four regions of the world, Alleluia is sung four times. In the Prayer they ask that he grant them peace together with faith.

The Reading teaches them how the grace of the Holy Spirit was given to the Gentiles (Acts 10). Therefore they joyfully sing Alleluia twice, because Jews and Gentiles had received the Holy Spirit. The Gospel says that God gave his Son for them, so that if they believe in him [Col. 0702B] they may have eternal life (John 3). In the Offertory they hear that the Holy Spirit thundered from heaven and opened to humankind the font of baptism. In the Communion it is sung that all things are taught by the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—On the Office of Tuesday, “Accipite jucunditatem.”

In the office “Receive joy” (2 Esdr. 4), the Church honours the spirit of counsel, who gives her the joy of eternal glory and calls her to heavenly kingdoms. And because through twofold love, in faith in the Trinity, they will obtain this grace, they sing Alleluia five times. In the Prayer they ask to be cleansed by the Spirit and protected from every adversity. In the Reading they are taught [Col. 0702C] that the gifts of the Holy Spirit are given through prayer (Acts 8). Therefore they sing Alleluia twice, because they sing with spirit and mind, and will pray with spirit and mind. The Gospel makes known to them that the Holy Spirit, the doorkeeper, will lead them through Christ the door to the Father, who is life. In the Offertory it is recalled to them that they are refreshed with the bread of angels. In the Communion, made one with Christ, they are to be glorified by the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—On the Office of Wednesday, “Deus, dum egredereris.”

In the Office *God, when you went forth* (Ps. 67), the Spirit of fortitude is magnified. Just as, in delivering the children of Israel from Egypt, he went before them in fire, so, in rescuing the faithful from this world, he goes before them in the fire of love [Col. 0702D], making for them a way through the commandments and dwelling within them through graces. And because they are summoned from the four quarters of the world to the heavenly homeland, *Alleluia* is sung four times. In the Prayer they ask that through the Holy Spirit they may be brought to the truth of Christ. Two readings are read, because the two peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles, are gathered by the Holy Spirit into the faith. In one, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit is recited; in the other, miracles wrought through him are commemorated. In one *Alleluia* the joy of Jews who have been converted is expressed; in the other, the exultation of Gentiles who have been baptized is received. Two readings are likewise read because those to be ordained are commanded to be taught in the Old and New Testaments. To both groups, namely the baptized and those being ordained, the living bread is preached in the Gospel [Col. 0703A] (John 6), so that, refreshed by it, they may never die. In the Offertory they ask that the Holy Spirit be sent to them. In the Communion they hear that peace is given to them.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.—On Thursday.

In the Thursday office, *The Spirit of the Lord* (Wisdom 1), the Spirit of knowledge is exalted, through whom knowledge of spiritual things is given to the faithful. In the Reading and the Gospel, those fallen into sins are consoled when signs wrought through the Holy Spirit are recalled.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—On the Friday office, “May my mouth be filled.”

In the office *May my mouth be filled with praise* (Ps. 70), the Spirit of piety is glorified, through whom the Trinity is praised together. And because he is exalted with praises in the four regions of the world, *Alleluia* is sung four times. In the Prayer [Col. 0703B] the Church asks not to be disturbed by enemies. In the Reading the delight of the face of God is promised to her (Joel 2). In the Gospel forgiveness of sins and healing of the soul are foretold (Luke 5). Hence in the Offertory she praises God, and in the Communion proclaims the gratuitous gifts of the Holy Spirit.

### CHAPTER XL.—On the office “The Love of God” on Saturday.

In the office *The Love of God* (Rom. 5), praise is sung to the Spirit of fear, through whom love is introduced into the soul. And because the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—receive the Holy Spirit in faith in the Trinity, they sing *Alleluia* three times. In the Prayer they ask the Lord to pour out the Holy Spirit upon them. [Col. 0703C] Six readings and the Gospel (Luke 4), the seventh, are read because the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are recalled. Seven are therefore read because on this day the ministries of the Church are advanced through seven grades by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. By the first reading the doorkeepers are instructed; by the second, the exorcists; by the third, the readers; by the fourth, the acolytes; by the fifth, the subdeacons; by the sixth, the deacons; and by the Gospel, the priests. By each individual *Alleluia* the praises of the several grades are expressed. In the Offertory, moreover, the prayers and offerings of the priests for the Church are understood. In the Communion Christ’s coming and eternal joy are promised to his ministers.

### CHAPTER XLI.—Sunday of the Holy Trinity, “Blessed.”

[Col. 0703D] The Sunday which follows concerns the Holy Trinity, because a greater baptism received and a greater gift of the Spirit ought to lead them to exercise faith in the Trinity through good works. Let us now consider the remaining matters.

### CHAPTER XLII.—On the course from Septuagesima until after Pentecost.

Thus, by Septuagesima is understood that time when the people of God were oppressed by Pharaoh in Egypt; and it signifies the time when the human race, before Christ’s coming, was oppressed by the devil in this world. By Easter, however, is understood the time when the children of Israel were delivered from Pharaoh through the lamb; and it signifies the time when the faithful were redeemed from the devil through Christ. By the forty days from Easter to the Ascension of the Lord are understood [Col. 0704A] the forty years in which the children of Israel returned to their homeland with joy and gladness; and they signify the time in which the faithful rejoiced in Christ’s resurrection. By the Rogation Days, when crosses are carried through various places, is understood that time when the children of Israel entered the land of promise, carried the ark of the Lord through various places, and overthrew many cities; it signifies the time when the faithful gathered to the ascending Lord and went up to Jerusalem. By Pentecost, when the gifts of the Holy Spirit are celebrated, is understood that time when the children of Israel, having conquered their enemies, divided the land among themselves; and it signifies the time when the faithful received the various gifts of the Holy Spirit. By the following week is indicated that time when [Col. 0704B] judges ruled the people of God; and it signifies the time when the apostles, judges of the world, governed the people of God by their presence. Further, the Sunday *Lord, in your mercy*, when the history *God of all* is sung, displays that time when the kings of Israel were harassed by enemies in many battles; and it signifies the time when martyrs were subjected to different tortures by persecutors.

### CHAPTER XLIII.—The first Sunday from Pentecost until the Advent of the Lord.

King David, then, afflicted by Saul and his servants, driven from his homeland and compelled to go among the nations, distrusting his own strength but relying upon God’s help, says: “Lord, I have hoped in your mercy” (Ps. 12). [Col. 0704C] The Prayer *O God, strength of those who hope in you* suits him, since it calls God strength and asks for his aid. In the Epistle, which testifies that God sent his Son to save the world, is displayed the consolation of the prophets, who foretold that David would be saved from his enemies and promised him the kingdom of Israel. In the Gradual, “I said: Lord” (Ps. 40:5), David attributes his persecution to his sins. In the *Alleluia*, “Lord my God, in you I have hoped” (Ps. 7:2), he asks to be delivered from his enemies. In the Gospel the person of each is represented (Luke 16), since Saul is understood in the rich man, David in Lazarus. Saul, proud like the rich man, clothed himself in purple and feasted splendidly every day. David, like ulcer-covered Lazarus, was cast out by men and wandered needy through the woods, like a leper. [Col. 0704D] Lazarus’s sores were licked by dogs, while Gentiles who received David comforted him. Saul died and, like the rich man, was plunged into hell; David obtained the royal sceptre, and after death Lazarus was joined to Abraham in rest. In the Offertory, “Attend to the voice of my prayer” (Ps. 5:3), David asks for his deliverance. In the Communion, “I shall recount all your wonders” (Ps. 9:2), he gives thanks for benefits bestowed.

### CHAPTER XLIV.—Under grace.

Thus, when the Christian people are oppressed by unbelievers, heretics, or evil Catholics, and driven from city to city, they are known to cry to the Lord: “Lord, in your mercy” (Ps. 12). In the Prayer they invoke divine help, that they may please him both in will and in action. In the Epistle they are consoled [Col. 0705A] when it is affirmed that God sent his Son for their salvation. In the Prayer they implore God’s mercy. In the *Alleluia* they ask to be delivered from their persecutors. The Gospel represents the unbelieving people by the rich man and makes the Christian people known by poor Lazarus. For the unbelieving Jewish people clothed themselves in purple when they gloried in nobility of the flesh. They feasted splendidly when they were instructed in ceremonies through the sacred Scriptures. The Gentile people, however, clothed themselves in purple when they exalted themselves above other nations because of the monarchy of their empire. They feasted splendidly when they were celebrated by philosophical and poetic writings. The flock of heretics, too, clothed itself as it were in purple when, puffed up by worldly pomp, it despised the humble. It feasted splendidly while it was fed by the continuous discourses [Col. 0705B] of secular eloquence. Evil Catholics likewise clothe themselves as it were in purple when they are proud of the adornment of costly garments. They feast splendidly while they strive to devote themselves only to pleasures and desires of the flesh. But the humble Christian people, confessing their sins, despising earthly things, and seeking heavenly things alone, are cast out like ulcer-covered Lazarus when they are despised by Jews, Gentiles, heretics, and evil Catholics. Yet when the rich man dies, he is cast into hell, because unbelievers and the perverse, who spend their days here amid good things, descend in a moment to hell; but when Lazarus dies, he is borne into Abraham’s bosom, because the Christian people, afflicted here, will afterwards enjoy joy and rest. Hence in the Offertory [Col. 0705C] they invoke God as King; in the Communion they recount his mighty works.

### CHAPTER XLV.—The second Sunday after Pentecost: “He became,” under the Law.

The following Sunday seems to represent David’s kingdom. For after Saul had been slain, David was summoned by the Gentiles and exalted upon the royal throne. Rejoicing, he says: “The Lord became my protector” (Ps. 17). The Prayer *Of your holy Name* suits this, saying that God’s beloved are never deprived of his governance. The Epistle also agrees, saying that he was translated from death to life (1 John 3). For, delivered from the danger of death, he was transferred into the kingdom. Hence also in the Gradual, “To the Lord, when I was troubled” (Ps. 119:1), he rejoices that he has been heard; in the *Alleluia*, [Col. 0705D] “God is judge” (Ps. 7:12), he exalts the just judgment of God with praise, since God cast down proud Saul and set humble David over the people. Thus the Gospel accords, recounting that someone made a great supper, invited many, and that very many did not come (Luke 14). For there is no doubt that David, having gained the kingdom, prepared a great banquet for the people. Those unwilling to come were of Saul’s family. In the Offertory, “Lord, turn” (Ps. 89:13), he prays to be delivered from enemies on every side. In the Communion, “I shall sing to the Lord” (Ps. 103:33), he gives thanks to him who bestowed so many good things upon him.

### CHAPTER XLVI.—Under grace.

All this is understood of the Christian people, who, oppressed by persecutors in the martyrs, are summoned to the heavenly kingdom. [Col. 0706A] Rejoicing in their deliverance, they say: “The Lord became my protector.” In the Prayer it is made known that they came through fear to love. The Reading says that the world hated them, but that they have now passed from death to life (1 John 3). In the Offertory they pray for their souls, which they do not doubt are still joined to their bodies. In the Communion they render praises to the Lord, from whom they received good things. This office is appropriately sung around the feast of St John, who, sent by the Lord at the hour of supper, is said to have invited God’s peoples to the banquet. At other times it is sung around the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, who are read to have summoned the Gentile people from the streets and hedges of error to God’s banquet. Moreover, in the chant is expressed the voice of those preaching and praising God [Col. 0706B], who was their protector, delivered them from tribulation, and bestowed every good thing upon them. The voice of those converted from error is also understood: the Lord led them out into the breadth of love, delivered their souls, and bestowed heavenly goods.

### CHAPTER XLVII.—On Saint John the Baptist.

The responsories for Saint John the Baptist are taken from the prophets and from the Gospel, because he was the end of prophecy and the beginning of the Gospel. At the feast of the Apostles, in the third nocturn and at Lauds, antiphons with *Alleluia* are sung; at this feast they are not sung, because the glory of the New Testament is greater than that of the Law. John’s Nativity occurs before the Lord’s resurrection; but the Nativity of the Apostles is in heaven after the Church’s glorification by the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0706C] Therefore these antiphons are adorned, while those are not.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.—On the Vigil of Saint John the Baptist and its office.

At the feast of Saint John the Baptist, and at the principal feasts, two offices are celebrated. One is at night, performed at the beginning of the night without the *Gloria*, and is called the vigil; hence the preceding day is also called a vigil. The other is around midnight and ends in daytime; in its third nocturn it has *Alleluia* in the antiphons. Through one office the legal custom and the Sabbaths celebrated as figures of future things are recalled; through the other, the resurrection of the Lord and our future feast. It is therefore performed with *Alleluia*, because it passes into fellowship with the angels. At the vigil of saints, however, [Col. 0706D] “Let us bend the knee” is not said, because the Mass appears to belong to the night of the following day; but *Alleluia* is omitted because of the fast.

### CHAPTER XLIX.—The third Sunday after Pentecost: “Look upon me,” under the Law.

The following Sunday seems instituted concerning David’s repentance. After his adultery with Bathsheba and the killing of Uriah, when the prophet rebuked him, he repented from the heart.
