Groaning, he says: “Look upon me and have mercy on me” (Ps. 24:16). The Prayer *Our supplication* is not said for this Sunday, since it is assigned to the octave of Pentecost. The Gregorian Prayer, however, *Protector of those who hope in you*, accords with repentant David, who begs that God’s mercy may be multiplied over him lest he lose eternal goods. [Col. 0707A] The Epistle, “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God” (1 Pet. 5), likewise sets forth the prophet’s admonition by which he urged the king to repentance. In the Gradual, “Cast your thought upon the Lord” (Ps. 54:23), is marked the consolation of the same prophet, by which he consoles the now-penitent king. In the *Alleluia*, “I will love you, Lord” (Ps. 17:2), David praises God, whom he calls the refuge of the wretched. The Gospel therefore agrees, proclaiming that there is joy among the angels over one repentant sinner (Luke 1:5). In the Offertory, “Let all hope in you” (Ps. 9:11), David applauds God from hope of pardon, because he has not abandoned those seeking him. In the Communion, “I cried out” (Ps. 16:6), he gives thanks because, his sin forgiven, he has merited the communion of the faithful.

### CHAPTER L.—Under grace.

[Col. 0707B]

By repentant David is understood the people of the faithful, who, after idolatry—as after adultery with Bathsheba—and the killing of the righteous—as after Uriah’s murder—turn to repentance. In the Prayer they do not cease to ask that God’s mercy be multiplied over them. The Epistle warns them to humble themselves under God’s hand through repentance and to resist the devil, who seeks to devour them like a lion. The Gradual counsels this people, now made anxious, to cast their thought upon the Lord; in the *Alleluia* they speak praises to God, who is a refuge to the afflicted. The Gospel strengthens them toward pardon when it recalls the angels’ joy over one sinner. In the Offertory they praise the giver of pardon, who saves those hoping in him. [Col. 0707C] In the Communion they give thanks because they have received communion in Christ’s body. This office is also sung around the feast of Saint John the Baptist or of the Apostles, who are read to have called the people to repentance.

### CHAPTER LI.—The fourth Sunday after Pentecost: “The Lord is my illumination,” under the Law.

The Sunday nearest to this suggests David’s affliction, by which his son Absalom, through God’s judgment after the sin involving Uriah, afflicted him. Expelled from the kingdom, David trusts in the Lord, saying: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” (Ps. 26:1). Concerning victory, moreover: “Those enemies who trouble me themselves were weakened and fell. Though camps should stand against [Col. 0707D] me, my heart will not fear” (ibid. 2–3). The Prayer “Grant, we beseech you, Lord” accords with him, since he asks that the course of the world be peacefully directed for him. The Epistle agrees well with this matter, declaring that the suffering of this time is not comparable with future glory (Rom. 8). Further, in the Gradual, “Be merciful, Lord” (Deut. 21:8), and in the verse, “Help us, O God our saviour” (Ps. 78:9), is understood the voice of those fighting against Absalom. In the *Alleluia*, “Lord, in your strength the king shall rejoice” (Ps. 20:2), is understood the voice of the same persons rejoicing in victory. The Gospel does not differ from this matter, since it states that the same measure will be measured back [Col. 0708A]. For David paid for what he committed wickedly, and Absalom justly received what he had deserved impiously. In the Offertory, “Enlighten my eyes” (Ps. 12:4), David’s prayer is expressed while the war is being waged; he prays that he may not sleep in death, lest his enemy prevail and rejoice over him. In the Communion, “The Lord is my strength” (Ps. 17:3), he praises God for victory, calling him his strength and helper.

### CHAPTER LII.—Under grace.

David was afflicted after sin; the Christian people, after idolatry, are oppressed by unbelievers. They trample worldly adversities and rejoice in hope of the heavenly things promised, saying: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. 26). In the Prayer they ask that the Lord may peacefully direct for them the course of the world. [Col. 0708B] This order of preachers in the Epistle lightens temporal penalties, declaring that the sufferings of this time are not comparable with future glory (Rom. 8). Further, the oppressed invoke God’s help in the Gradual; in the *Alleluia* they exult over victory against evils. By “king” is meant the Christian king, who governs morals and actions by the sceptres of virtues. The Gospel promises a good measure to those whom the world afflicts with adversities for God’s sake. In the Offertory the Christian people pray that the enemy, namely the devil, may not rejoice over their death. In the Communion they applaud God, who has proved their helper.

### CHAPTER LIII.—The fifth Sunday after Pentecost: “Hear, Lord,” under the Law.

After the scourges, the people gather to David and restore him to the kingdom with great rejoicing. Moreover, the kingdom is promised by the Lord to [Col. 0708C] his son; the office of this Sunday seems established on these matters. For David prays for the stability of the kingdom in this way: “Hear, Lord, my voice” (Ps. 26:4). The Prayer, *O God, who have prepared invisible goods for those who love you*, suits him, as he seeks to obtain God’s promises, which God promised concerning the kingdom to his son. The Epistle also accords with him, because he did not return evil for evil and therefore possessed blessing as an inheritance. The Gradual, “Our protector,” is David’s prayer for the people; but the *Alleluia*, “In you, Lord, I have hoped,” represents prayers of praise for himself. The Gospel agrees with this matter, recounting that crowds pressed upon Jesus and the disciples caught a multitude of fish (Luke 7). [Note: [Col. 0707D] But this is already the Gospel of the Fourth Sunday, not the Fifth.] For crowds gathered to David, and his friends drew very many to him from every side [Col. 0708D]. In the Offertory, “I will bless the Lord,” he gives thanks for benefits granted, to him who gave him understanding. In the Communion, “One thing have I asked of the Lord” (Ps. 26), he asks for the building of the temple, which Solomon afterwards completed (3 Kings 5; 7:8).

### CHAPTER LIV.—Under grace.

The Christian people likewise, once after the affliction of persecutors, are restored to tranquillity; and the peace of eternal life is promised to them as consolation. In the Introit, “Hear, Lord, my voice” (Ps. 26:7), they pray for the Church’s present condition. In the Prayer they ask for the future promise, which surpasses every desire [Col. 0709A]. The Epistle exhorts all to unanimity in prayers, that they may deserve to inherit blessing, saying that the Lord’s eyes are upon the righteous and his ears toward their prayers (1 Pet. 3). The Gospel, which commemorates the crowds running to the Lord and the disciples catching many fish (Luke 7), indicates that crowds of Gentiles gathered to the Church and that preachers drew many from the whirlpool of error by the net of faith. In the Offertory they bless God, who has given them understanding concerning eternal things. In the Communion they ask one thing: that they may remain forever in the house of the Lord. This Sunday sometimes falls within the octave of Saint Peter, and therefore he is mentioned in the Gospel. More often, however, it occurs around the feast of Saint James, whose Gospel also mentions the fishing [Col. 0709B], since these fishers indeed drew men wandering amid the waves of error by the net of preaching and led them to the harbour of eternal life.

### CHAPTER LV.—The sixth Sunday after Pentecost: “The Lord is strength,” under the Law.

The present Sunday is instituted because Solomon was made king by David at the Lord’s command. As David drew near to death, having conquered his enemies, he gave thanks to God, calling the Lord the strength of his people. He also gave thanks for his son, calling God “the protector of the salvation of his anointed,” that is, Solomon. Then he commends the subject people to God: “Save your people, Lord, and bless your inheritance” (Ps. 27:9). The Prayer *God of hosts* agrees with this matter, in which he asks God [Col. 0709C] to preserve and nourish good things in his son. Through the Epistle is denoted the exhortation of Nathan the prophet and Zadok the high priest, by which they exhort Solomon, renewed through anointing, to walk in newness of life (Rom. 6). In the Gradual, “Turn, Lord” (Ps. 6:5), is understood their blessing upon the king and prayer over the people. In the *Alleluia*, “All nations” (Ps. 46:2), is understood the people’s applause at the king’s anointing. Through the Gospel is suggested David’s exhortation, by which, as he is dying, he addresses his son: he forbids him homicide and anger, and commands that, before he offers sacrifice, he forgive those who sin against him. Further, in the Offertory Solomon asks God to perfect his steps in his paths. In the Communion, “I shall go around and sacrifice to God” (Ps. 28:6), he vows that he will build a house [Col. 0709D] for God’s name.

### CHAPTER LVI.—Under grace.

As Solomon is made king by his father, so Constantine, the prince of peace, is set over the Christian people by the pope. Therefore the Church sings exultantly: “The Lord is the strength of his people” (Ps. 27:8). In the Prayer she supplicates the Lord to grant him an increase of religion and to nourish good things in him. The Epistle makes known to us the preaching of Pope Sylvester, which declares that the emperor was buried with Christ in baptism and asks that, reborn through the anointing of chrism, he may walk in newness of life (Rom. 6). In the Gradual his prayer over the people is expressed; through the *Alleluia* is understood the applause of the Christian people at the conversion of the king; [Col. 0710A] through the Gospel is suggested the teaching of priests. Constantine is instructed in the Christian religion, which teaches him to avoid homicide and anger and, when offering sacrifice, to forgive offences committed against him by his neighbours. In the Offertory the king himself prays that God may perfect his steps in his paths. In the Communion he vows to God what he afterwards devoutly fulfils: namely, to build a house for the Lord’s name, since it is clear that the Church of God, a house, was erected and adorned through him.

### CHAPTER LVII.—The seventh Sunday after Pentecost: “All nations,” under the Law.

In the month of August, when the history “In the beginning God created” (Gen. 1:1) is read, Solomon’s peaceful kingdom is represented to us; the present Sunday is appointed as an honour to that kingdom. For the people who laboured under David in wars, with wars everywhere quieted under Solomon, burst forth rejoicing in God’s praises with these words: “All nations, clap your hands; he has subjected peoples to us” (Ps. 46:2, 4). The Prayer, “O God, whose providence,” suits these words: God has removed all harmful things from them and granted all things advantageous. The Epistle suggests the teaching of the prophets, who persuaded the people to serve God in righteousness. The Gradual, “Come, children” (Ps. 33:12), suggests Solomon’s admonitions, by which he instructs his subjects in observance of the Law. He promises them a reward from God, saying: “Approach him and be enlightened” (ibid., verse 6). In the *Alleluia*, “Great is the Lord” (Ps. 47:2), he praises God, who made him praiseworthy in Jerusalem. Some sing the *Alleluia*, “Deliver me from my enemies” (Ps. 58:2), [Col. 0710C] which suits him well because God delivered him from all enemies. The Gospel does not differ from this matter, narrating that the Lord satisfied four thousand men with seven loaves (Matt. 14), because Solomon, who bore the type of the Lord, filled with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, fed the four parts of the world with the word of God. The Offertory, “As in holocausts of rams” (Dan. 3:40), shows Solomon’s sacrifice, which he offered to the Lord at Gibeon. The Communion, “Incline your ear” (Ps. 87:3), expresses the king’s prayer, by which he sought wisdom from God and immediately received it.

### CHAPTER LVIII.—Under grace.

Solomon is marked by the sceptre, and Constantine is crowned with the crown [Col. 0710D] of kingship. The people had peace under Solomon, and the Church flourished in peace under Constantine. Therefore she sings joyfully: “All nations, clap your hands; he has subjected peoples to us.” In the Prayer she asks that God may remove every harmful thing. Through the Epistle, the urgency of preachers urges her to strive to serve the Lord in virtues as she had formerly served demons in uncleanness (Rom. 6). The Gradual, “Come, children,” indicates to us Constantine’s words by which he invites the peoples of the world to Christian religion. In the *Alleluia*, “Great is the Lord,” she praises God, whom he had made praiseworthy in the city of the Church; or the *Alleluia*, “Deliver me, Lord, from my enemies,” suits him well because God everywhere protected him from enemies in war through the banner of the holy cross. [Col. 0711A] The Gospel recalls four thousand men filled with seven loaves, because at that time Christ abundantly filled the four parts of the world with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The Offertory expresses Constantine’s sacrifice, by which he offered himself to God and established Christ’s worship; or it suggests the Church’s sacrifice of praise, which she offered to God for the religious prince. For Azariah with his companions recited those same words in the furnace, and the angel of the Lord delivered them from the fire. Thus Constantine was delivering from distress the Church which persecution had recently afflicted. The Communion makes known to us Constantine’s prayer, by which he asks concerning the Church’s condition.

### CHAPTER LIX.—The eighth Sunday after Pentecost: “We have received,” under the Law.

[Col. 0711B] The present Sunday is appointed concerning the famous temple, built at Jerusalem by Solomon in a third order. He adorned it with gold and jewels and established in it the worship of God as splendid through the ministries of priests. Their praise is represented here when the Lord is sung to in this manner: “We have received, O God, your mercy” (Ps. 47:10). The Prayer, “Grant, we beseech you, Lord,” agrees with them, in which they pray to think and do what is right. The Epistle suits them, in which those led by the Spirit of God are called children of God and heirs of his kingdom (Rom. 8). The Gradual, “Be for me a God” (Ps. 30:3), calls that place a house of refuge. The *Alleluia*, “To you praise is due, O God” (Ps. 64:2), expressly and plainly declares that a hymn is rendered to God in Zion and a vow in Jerusalem. [Col. 0711C] And in the verse “We shall be filled” (ibid., 5), it calls the temple of God holy. It should be noted that almost wherever “Jerusalem” is written, a long neume is placed, because by this jubilation in the heavenly Jerusalem is expressed; but wherever the *Alleluia* is accompanied by a verse, a twofold joy is denoted. The Gospel also agrees, saying that not all who call upon God in the temple merely by name will enter the kingdom of heaven. The Offertory promises that the humble people will be saved (Ps. 17:28); the Communion, “Taste” (Ps. 33:9), indicates the communion of priests which, under the Law, they received from the loaves of the Presence.

### CHAPTER LX.—Under grace.

Solomon first made a temple for the Lord at Jerusalem, and Constantine, first of the emperors, built a church at Rome in honour of the Apostles Peter and Paul; and his mother Helena established a temple for the Lord at Jerusalem. The same ruler built very many churches, which he endowed with great resources and great gifts and adorned with the ministry of clergy. A house is also founded for the Lord by Constantine when, at his command, the celebrated Council of Nicaea is gathered, in which the Church, the house of God, is magnificently built up when heresies are destroyed and the faith strengthened. The house is divided into three parts, because the Church is divided, in the faith of the Trinity, into teachers, the continent, and the married; it is adorned with gold and gems when it is illuminated by sacred Scripture and holy men. After Constantine had therefore established peace in the Church at this council, the holy synod joyfully [Col. 0712A] exclaims: “We have received, O God, your mercy” (Ps. 47:10). In the Prayer they ask for the Spirit by whom they may think and do what is right. In the Epistle this synod teaches that those led by the Spirit of God are known to be children of God and heirs of his kingdom (Rom. 8). In the Gradual it invokes God as protector. In the *Alleluia* it joyfully sings a hymn to God for the Church’s peace. The Gospel agrees especially with this matter, naming heretics false prophets and ravening wolves (Matt. 7), whom this synod separates from Christ’s sheep. In the Offertory it declares that the humble people will be saved. In the Communion it urges the faithful to communion in Christ’s body. This office frequently occurs around the feast of Saint Mary, who was the temple of God, in which temple the Church received God’s mercy.

### CHAPTER LXI.—The ninth Sunday after Pentecost: “Behold, God,” under the Law.

[Col. 0712B]

After the seventh year Solomon’s temple is dedicated; therefore after the seventh day this Sunday is observed to be appointed for the same matter. At this dedication the king, with the people, offered gifts to God and brought the ark of the covenant into the consecrated temple with hymns and praises. Rejoicing that God had favoured his vows, he says: “Behold, God helps me” (Ps. 53:6). The Prayer, “May the ears be opened,” suits him well, since he asks that in the temple God grant to penitents the things they desire. The Epistle seems to suggest the king’s exhortation, by which he warned the people not to imitate those who proved idolaters, fornicators, and murmurers, and for that reason many [Col. 0712C] thousands of them perished by a reprobate death. As Solomon prayed, the majesty of the Lord appeared in the temple; the people worshipped and praised it. The Gradual, “O Lord, our Lord” (Ps. 8:2), expresses this praise; the *Alleluia*, “Attend, my people, to the law” (Ps. 75:1), puts forth God’s own address to the people. The Gospel agrees well, recounting that individual debtors came to the steward and wrote down their master’s debts (Luke 16), because individual professed votaries came to Solomon and offered their vows to God. In the Offertory, “The ordinances of the Lord” (Ps. 18:9), Solomon exhorts the people to the righteousness of the Law. In the Communion, “Seek first,” he promises them good things from God.

### CHAPTER LXII.—Under grace.

[Col. 0712D]

With faith strengthened by the sevenfold Spirit in the Nicene Synod, the whole Church is filled with joy; the triumphant king with the people, the world, is arrayed in a new rejoicing. Therefore the Church sings joyfully: “Behold, God helps me” (Ps. 53:6). In the Prayer she asks that she may ask God for those things which please him. The Epistle suggests to us the concern of teachers, who dissuade the people from idolatry, fornication, and murmuring (1 Cor. 10). In the Gradual is shown the praise of the peoples; in the *Alleluia*, the joyful preaching of the teachers. In the Gospel the debts of the Lord are reported as written down by the steward (Luke 16), and ecclesiastical laws are handed down through Constantine. In the Offertory she urges the humble people toward God’s righteousness; in the Communion [Col. 0713A] she asks them to seek God’s kingdom and thus affirms that all things will be given them by God.

### CHAPTER LXIII.—The tenth Sunday after Pentecost: “When I cried out,” under the Law.

The following Sunday is instituted concerning Solomon’s prayer and the Lord’s appearance. For when the temple had been dedicated, the Lord appeared to Solomon, made known that he had consecrated the temple and heard his prayers for all that he had prayed, and promised that, if Solomon and the people kept his law, he too would fortify the temple with the people against enemies. But if they rejected his law, he would also destroy this temple with the people. Therefore Solomon, rejoicing that he was heard, says: “When I cried out to the Lord” (Ps. 54). The Prayer, “O God, who make your omnipotence known,” suits this, saying that those who hasten toward the divine promises are made sharers in heavenly goods. [Col. 0713B] In Solomon’s temple he distributed divine ministries through the Levites, as God had commanded him through the prophet. This Epistle makes known divisions of ministries, describing that to some wisdom, to others knowledge, to others kinds of tongues, and to others interpretation of sayings are given (1 Cor. 12). The Gradual, “Keep me, Lord” (Ps. 16:8), suggests Solomon’s prayer, by which he prays for the temple’s protection. The *Alleluia*, “Rejoice in God” (Ps. 80:2), indicates how he urges the people or priests to rejoice in God. In the Gospel God’s promise to Solomon is expressly marked where, entering the temple, he is read to have said: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. 21). His threat, however, occurs in that place where he says: “Your enemies shall cast you to the ground [Col. 0713C] and shall not leave in you one stone upon another” (Luke 19). In the Offertory, “To you, Lord” (Ps. 24:1), Solomon commends his whole self to God. In the Communion, “You shall accept sacrifice” (Ps. 50:21), he repeats his vows.

### CHAPTER LXIV.—Under grace.

Thus, with the faith strengthened at the Council of Nicaea, the glory of the Lord appeared in the Church, while he worked many signs through his own. Therefore the Church, rejoicing for her own glorification and for the expulsion of heretics, sings: “When I cried unto the Lord” (Ps. 54:17). In the Prayer she asks that she may become a sharer in heavenly goods. In the Epistle, moreover, are distinguished those through whom wondrous deeds are recorded as having been done (1 Cor. 12).

For some were endowed with the word of wisdom, such as Flavian, bishop of Antioch, and Diodorus, bishop [Col. 0713D], who first instituted antiphonal choirs for psalmody; and very many others who resisted heretics through many books. Others became illustrious in speech, such as Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, who expounded the Catholic faith in *Whoever Wills*; Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, who wrote the *Ecclesiastical History*; Basil, bishop of Cappadocia; Gregory Nazianzen; John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople; and very many others who adorned the Church in that age by their eloquence. Others shone in faith, such as the Emperor Constantine, who then received the faith, and many others who at that time defended the faith [Col. 0714A] in writings and speech.

Others were eminent in the grace of healings, such as Antony and the other Egyptian Fathers, who performed many healings among the people. Others were resplendent in the working of miracles, such as Martin, bishop of Tours; Nicholas, bishop of Myra; Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus; and many others, who adorned the world with numerous miracles. Others possessed prophecy, as John the hermit did. Others shone in discernment of spirits, as Macarius did. Others had received kinds of tongues, such as Ephrem, Jerome, and very many others, who treated extensively of the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages. Others excelled in interpretation of utterances, such as Jerome himself, the presbyter; Ambrose, bishop of Milan; and Augustine, bishop of Hippo, who expounded the sacred Scriptures [Col. 0714B] by interpreting them.

The Church asks in the Gradual that these gifts may be preserved within her; in the Alleluia she rejoices before God for the gifts. In the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0713D] Today’s Gospel is that of the Pharisee and the Publican entering the Temple.] the Lord is said to enter the temple of the Church, cast out those buying and selling spiritual things, call his house a house of prayer (Matt. 21), and foretell with weeping that it would be destroyed (Luke 19:42). This happened in part under Julian, and in part will happen under Antichrist. Under Julian [Note: [Col. 0714D] Rather, under Titus Vespasian, according to Josephus and Hegesippus.] it was cast down to the ground and trampled by the Gentiles. Under Antichrist, one stone shall not be left upon another when the elect are scattered from one another. In the Offertory the Church commends herself wholly to God. In the Communion she offers God a sacrifice of praise. It should be noted that the Gospel is read here in which the destruction of Jerusalem [Col. 0714C] is foretold, because in this month it is recorded to have been accomplished first by Nebuchadnezzar and afterwards by the Romans, in the same month.

## CHAPTER LXV.—The Eleventh Sunday after Pentecost: “God in his place,” under the Law.

The Queen of Sheba hastens to Jerusalem, desires to see Solomon and his temple, and offers gold and gems; hence this Sunday has deserved to receive its office from this event. Having seen his temple, she burst forth in praise of God. Therefore the Church, under her figure, sings thus: “God, in his holy place” (Ps. 67:6). The Prayer, “O God, who by the abundance of thy mercy,” is suited to her, in which she asks that God may grant what prayer does not dare to ask. The Epistle agrees with her, because, having heard Solomon’s wisdom, she despises herself [Col. 0714D] and says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15).

The Gradual expresses her praise, in which it says that her heart hoped in the Lord and that she wishes to confess to him willingly. In the Alleluia, “O Lord, God of my salvation” (Ps. 37:23), she rejoices in mind before God, whom she calls salvation. The two men who entered the temple (Luke 18) were Solomon and the queen. He gloried in his works; she, humbly like the Publican, entreated God. In the Offertory, “I will exalt thee, O Lord” (Ps. 29:2), her praise is indicated, by which she rejoices that she has been received by the Lord. The Communion, “Honour the Lord from thy substance” (Prov. 3:9), alludes to the gifts [Col. 0715A] of the queen, which she offered to the Lord, and she went down to her house justified.

## CHAPTER LXVI.—Under grace.

Solomon renews Jerusalem with its gilded temple; the queen had come from the furthest regions to see it. Constantine likewise enlarged the Christian religion through the outstanding city of Constantinople, which the Church, flocking together from every side, desires to visit. The queen brought gold and gems; and the Church brought forth persons brilliant in wisdom as with gold, and shining in virtues as with gems. Therefore, rejoicing in Solomon—that is, Christ—because of his temple, she sings: “God, in his holy place” (Ps. 67:6).

The Prayer is well suited to the evangelical Publican, who asks that God may forgive what his conscience fears and add what prayer does not presume to ask. The Epistle [Col. 0715B] agrees with this, in which he calls himself the least. In the Gradual he declares that he will confess to him not under compulsion but willingly (1 Cor. 15). In the Alleluia he praises the God of his salvation. In the Pharisee of the Gospel (Luke 18) is understood the proud flock of heretics; in the Publican, the humble people of Catholics. In the Offertory the Church renders praises to God, who received her as she came to him. The Communion exhorts her to share her goods with the members of Christ, and thus, justified, to return to the fatherland of paradise. For in this Communion thanks are given to God because grain and wine are then gathered.

## CHAPTER LXVII.—The Twelfth Sunday: “O God, unto my help,” under the Law.

After Solomon’s death, the kingdom is divided; therefore the month of September also is divided in the histories. Its first part is unified in one history; the following part changes into various histories, because the kingdom of Judah was established in the one family of David, whereas the kingdom of Israel was seized by many. Therefore the history is read of those who were mingled among the Gentiles, such as Job, Tobias, Judith, and Esther; for after Solomon’s death the kings, together with the people, abandoned the worship of God and mixed themselves with the worship of the Gentiles.

The prophet Elijah forbade this, and his life gave this Sunday its office. When they sought to take his life, he fled into the wilderness and thus poured out prayers to the Lord: “O God, unto my help” (Ps. 69:2). The Prayer, “Almighty and merciful God,” suits him: it declares that God is worthily and laudably served by his people, while he shut heaven for three years and six [Col. 0715D] months by his prayers against rebels (3 Kings 8). The Epistle agrees with him, saying: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3), because the Jews sought to kill him. God, who is the life-giving Spirit, gives life.

In the Gradual he blesses the Lord: “I will bless the Lord at all times” (Ps. 33:2). In the Alleluia, “O Lord, thou hast been our refuge” (Ps. 89:1), he takes refuge in God while praising him. The Gospel agrees with him, recounting that one deaf and mute was healed by the Lord (Mark 7), because Elijah calls back the Jewish people—deaf to the law of God and mute in God’s praise—to the worship of God. The Offertory, “Moses prayed” (Num. 21:17), expresses Elijah’s prayer, by which [Col. 0716A] he removed God’s wrath from the people as Moses did. The Communion, “From the fruit of thy works,” alludes to the people’s praise, because when rain was given they rendered praise to God from the fruits of the earth.

## CHAPTER LXVIII.—Under grace.

After Constantine’s death, the Church too was torn apart and divided into parties by heretics. One part was strengthened in the Catholic faith; the other changed into many schisms. Therefore, because the crowd of heretics, abandoning the true worship of God, attacks the Catholic people, worshippers of true religion, as Jezebel attacked Elijah, it cries thus to the Lord: “O God, attend unto my help” (Ps. 69:2). In the Prayer it asks that it may run without stumbling to God’s promises, as an heir does.

The Epistle recounts its persecution, where [Col. 0716B] it says: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3); for heretics killed Catholics, whose souls God gave life. And because the Catholic people conquered in all things, therefore in the Gradual it blesses the Lord at all times. In the Alleluia it calls God its refuge. In the Gospel (Mark 7), the deaf and mute flock of heretics is understood, which is compelled by Catholics to hear the true faith and confess the Catholic religion; for it the Church prays in the Offertory that God may not be angry with it. In the Communion Catholics give thanks to God for the abundant goods flowing from those converted.

## CHAPTER LXIX.—Again concerning the same Sunday.

This office is celebrated now because in this week the death of Moses is read. The history of Job [Col. 0716C] is also now read because Job and Moses are found to have been contemporaries. [Note: [Col. 0715D] Rather, Moses is thought to have written the book of Job.] And because the people, placed among enemies, are deprived of Moses’ help, they are understood to cry thus to the Lord: “O God, unto my help.” In the Prayer they ask that they may run to God’s promises—namely, to the land of promise—without stumbling because of enemies.

The Epistle concerns Moses especially at the place: “So that the children of Israel could not look upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance” (2 Cor. 3). In place of Moses the people received Joshua as leader (Deut. 31); therefore in the Gradual it blesses the Lord. In the Alleluia it declares that God became its refuge. In the Gospel (Mark 7) the same people are described, who are said to be deaf and mute in the law of the Lord; for them Moses prays in the office that God’s wrath may be turned away from them. The Communion, “From the fruit [Col. 0716D] of thy works” (Ps. 103:13), makes known the people’s praise, which it renders from its fruits in the possessed land, where it had an abundance of bread, wine, and oil. In this Communion praise is also rendered by the Church to God, because at this season the fruits of bread, wine, and oil are gathered.

## CHAPTER LXX.—The Thirteenth Sunday: “Look down, O Lord,” under the Law.

This Sunday received its office from the prophet Elisha. For Samaria, besieged by enemies, was oppressed by famine and distress. But through the merits of Elisha the multitude of enemies was put to flight and the city was freed from danger [Col. 0717A] (4 Kings 2, 3, 4, etc.). During the siege he calls upon God thus: “Look down, O Lord, upon thy covenant” (Ps. 72:20). In the Prayer he asks that the people may love God’s commandments, so that he may deliver it from danger.

The Epistle indicates what it suffered because of transgression of the law, for it says: “The law was set down because of transgression” (Gal. 3). In the Gradual, “Look down, O Lord” (Ps. 12:4), he invokes God when the king had ordered him beheaded because a woman had eaten her own son through hunger. In the Alleluia, “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord” (Ps. 94:1), he urges them to praise God, who would give them every abundance in Christendom; they should go before his face in confession, he who would deliver them from enemies.

The Gospel recounts that a man fell among robbers and was healed by a Samaritan [Col. 0717B] (Luke 10), because the people of Israel fell among robbers when the Gentile people [Note: [Col. 0717D] Titus Vespasian, Roman emperor, concerning whom see above, chapter 64.] besieged them: from some they took spoils, while others they left wounded and half-dead. The Samaritan—that is, Elisha—healed him, when by his prayers he delivered him from danger. In the Offertory, “In thee, O Lord, have I hoped” (Ps. 30:2), he glorifies God for the people’s deliverance. In the Communion, “Bread from heaven” (John 6:31), he gives thanks for the abundance bestowed upon them.

## CHAPTER LXXI.—Under grace.

Thus the Church is attacked by Julian and afflicted by famine and scourges. It cries to God: “Look down, O Lord, upon thy covenant” (Ps. 73:20). In the Prayer it asks an increase of faith, hope, and charity, by which it may attain God’s promises. The Epistle [Col. 0717C] indicates this promise, declaring that Christ was promised to Abraham (Gal. 3). In the Gradual the Church again invokes God’s help, because Julian foretells that after the war he will inflict persecution upon it. In the Alleluia it summons the people and rejoices in praise of God, who delivered it from dangers after the tyrant’s death.

The Gospel agrees well, recounting that robbers wounded a man and that he was healed by a Samaritan (Luke 10), because the Christian people fell among robbers when they endured many cruel things from persecutors: they were stripped, wounded, and tortured in various ways. The true Samaritan brought them to the inn when Christ led them to the joys of paradise. In the Offertory it gives thanks for the tyrant’s death and for its own deliverance. [Col. 0717D] In the Communion it sings praises for benefits bestowed.

## CHAPTER LXXII.—The Fourteenth Sunday after Pentecost: “Our protector,” under the Law.

The following Sunday is instituted from King Hezekiah, who, when sick even unto death, prayed thus to the Lord: “Our protector, behold, O God.” Therefore the Prayer says, “Keep, O Lord,” because without thee human mortality slips and falls (Ps. 83:10). To him the prophet Isaiah foretold, through escape from death, the incarnation of Christ, all the mysteries of the Church, and the future rewards of the saints. This prophecy is indicated in the Epistle, as where it says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, [Col. 0718A] joy, peace” (Gal. 5), and so forth.

Having recovered his health, the king went up to the temple and gave thanks to God. The Gradual, “It is good to confess to the Lord” (Luke 17), and the Alleluia, “For God is great” (Ps. 94:3), express these praises. The Gospel agrees with him, recalling that of ten lepers cleansed one returned and gave thanks (Ps. 91:2), because although the Lord conferred many benefits upon the kings of Israel and Judah, Hezekiah alone rendered the thanks due for benefits received. The Offertory fits well, where the Lord sent his angel (Ps. 33:8), who killed more than eighty thousand of the enemy and delivered the king and people who feared God from dangers. The Communion, “The bread which I will give” (John 6:52), alludes to Isaiah’s oracle, by which he foretells that Christ would come for human salvation [Col. 0718B].

## CHAPTER LXXIII.—Under grace.

The Church sings this under the type of Theodosius the Great, who proved a defender of the Church. Through him the Lord protected the Church from heretics, as through Hezekiah he fortified Jerusalem against enemies. The Prayer represents his words: “Keep, O Lord, thy Church by perpetual propitiation.” The Epistle, which recounts vices and virtues (Gal. 5), suggests the synod gathered in his time, in which vices are rejected and the virtues to be followed are affirmed.

The Gradual and Alleluia set forth the praise of the emperor, which the Church renders for concord. The Gospel agrees well, recounting that one of the lepers gave thanks (Luke 17), because it is established that among heretical emperors he alone praised God in the Catholic faith [Col. 0718C]. Hence, as the Offertory says, “The angel of the Lord” (Ps. 33:8) encamped around him and delivered him from all evils. The Communion indicates that after the penance imposed upon him by Ambrose, he deserved the bread of Christ and the communion of the Church.

## CHAPTER LXXIV.—Again concerning the same Sunday.

This Sunday is sung now, while the history of Tobit is recited, because the Lord sent his angel, who delivered Tobit from blindness, his son from the fish, and Sarah from the demon. The Offertory also, “The angel of the Lord shall encamp” (Ps. 33:8), looks to the feast of St Michael, which occurs frequently at that time. Therefore clerics are ordained in this week, because Isaiah names beforehand the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0718D], and this Sunday receives its office from his prophecy.

Ordination takes place in September because, according to the law, the Feast of Tabernacles was celebrated in this month. For those ordained are ministers of the Church, namely, of God’s tabernacle. It takes place in the third week because it was instituted by the apostles in the third season.

## CHAPTER LXXV.—On the Four Seasons.

In the fourth age Levites are chosen by David and Solomon for the ministries of the temple of God—that is, of the Church. To the former it is commanded from the law; to the latter it is said by the Holy Spirit: “Rejoice in God, our helper” (Ps. 80:2). Two readings are read because those to be ordained are distinguished into ministers and priests, and these are commanded to know two laws and fulfil the two commandments of charity.

One reading is suited to September, saying that the ploughman will overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes the one casting seed. The other is suited to those being ordained, declaring that Ezra taught the people, who praises the Lord thus: “Who is like the Lord?” (Ps. 112; Mark 9:29). The Gospel agrees with the fast, proclaiming that this kind of demon goes out by nothing except prayer and fasting. In the Offertory the chosen clergy say: “I will meditate upon thy commandments” (Ps. 118). In the Communion, “Eat the fat things” (2 Esdras 8), they exhort the people to rejoicing.

## CHAPTER LXXVI.—On Friday.

Friday represents the penitence of those being ordained [Col. 0719B], to whom the Holy Spirit cries: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice” (Ps. 104). In the Prayer they pray that they may please God in body and mind. The reading instructs them in conduct and promises forgiveness (Hosea 14). In the Gradual they invoke God thus: “Turn, O Lord, a little” (Ps. 89). In the Gospel they are consoled, where sins are said to have been forgiven to the penitent woman (Luke 7). Filled with joy, they cry in the Offertory: “Bless the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. 112). In the Communion they ask God to remove from them the reproach of their sins.

## CHAPTER LXXVII.—On Saturday.

On Saturday those to be ordained are called to grace, to whom this cry is made: “Come, let us adore God” (Ps. [Col. 0719C] 94). Four readings are read because those to be ordained are divided into four orders: acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, and presbyters. Their doctrine is signified through the readings; their life through the Gradual.

Then the reading from Daniel concerning the three youths, who were tested in the furnace, is read (Dan. 3), because ministers of the Church are examined in the furnace of tribulation. The hymn “Blessed art thou, O Lord” (ibid.) follows because they are commanded to bless God at all times. Then the Epistle concerning the first and second tabernacle is recited (Heb. 9), because if they now serve worthily in the tabernacle of the Church, they will be priests of the Lamb in the heavenly tabernacle. For this promise they rejoice in the Tract: “Praise the Lord” (Ps. 134).

The Gospel warns them not to have doctrine that is barren like an unfruitful tree, nor a life devoted to earthly things like the bent-over woman (Luke 13). In the Offertory they implore God’s help: “O Lord, God of my salvation” (Ps. 37). In the Communion they are admonished that, in the seventh month, through the sevenfold Spirit they have been introduced in seven ranks into God’s tabernacle—that is, God’s Church [Col. 0719D]—and are taught to celebrate its feasts.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII.—The Fifteenth Sunday: “Incline,” under the Law.

This Sunday receives its office from King Josiah, to whom the prophet Jeremiah foretold Jerusalem’s destruction and the people’s captivity in Babylon. He was afraid, and, gathering the people, instituted observance of the neglected law of God. The Introit of the Mass alludes to his invocation: “Incline, O Lord, thine ear unto me; gladden the soul of thy servant” (Ps. 85). The Prayer, “Thy Church, O Lord,” agrees with this, asking God to cleanse and fortify her. The Epistle indicates to us how he commanded the law of God to be observed: “Let us not grow weary while doing good; therefore let us do good” (Gal. 5).

Likewise his activity is expressed in the Gradual, “It is good to trust in the Lord” (Ps. 117). The Alleluia, “O Lord, hear” (Ps. 16), expresses his prayer. Some sing the Alleluia, “Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name” (Ps. 104), which also agrees with him, where he invited the people to praise God. Others sing the Alleluia, “My heart is ready” (Ps. 56), which agrees well with him [Col. 0720B], who prepared his heart for God’s commandments.

The Gospel alludes to his covenant, which he made with the people concerning the observance of the law: “You cannot serve God and mammon; seek the kingdom of God” (Matt. 6). In the Offertory, “Waiting I waited for the Lord” (Ps. 39:1), he praised God when he celebrated a great Passover with the people. In the Communion, “He who eats my flesh” (John 6), is indicated God’s consolation, by which he consoled him through the prophets.

## CHAPTER LXXIX.—Under grace.

The Church celebrates this under the type of Theodosius the Younger, who had bound her together in peace and concord. Josiah restored the observance of the law neglected—indeed cast aside—by his predecessors; and [Col. 0720C] Theodosius glorified with peace and Christ’s praise the Church grievously harassed by tyrants and heretics. He invokes God for himself thus: “Incline, O Lord, thine ear unto me” (Ps. 85:1). In the Prayer he asks that God may cleanse and fortify the Church.

The Epistle indicates his exhortation by which he exhorts priests to concord: “Let us not be desirous of evils, provoking and envying one another” (Gal. 5). In the Gradual he urges them to hope in the Lord. In the Alleluia, “Give thanks,” or “ready,” he praises God. The Gospel agrees well, saying that two masters cannot be served (Matt. 6), because Theodosius forbade all to serve the devil and instituted the seeking of God’s kingdom and righteousness. In the Offertory he applauds God for the Church’s concord [Col. 0720D], who put a new song in his mouth. In the Communion he is gladdened by the Church when he is proclaimed to abide in God and God in him.

## CHAPTER LXXX.—The Sixteenth Sunday: “Have mercy on me,” under the Law.

After Josiah, Jerusalem is destroyed and the people are led captive; therefore in this month the history of the Maccabees, who were oppressed by adversaries, is read. The prophet Ezekiel consoles the captive people, and the present Sunday receives its office from him. He cries for himself thus: “Have mercy on me, O Lord” (Ps. 85:3). For his people he prays thus: “Loose, O Lord, the bonds of thy peoples,” or, in the Prayer, “Thy [mercy], O Lord,” asking that the mercy [Col. 0721A] of the Lord may go before and follow them.

The Epistle expresses his affection for the people: “I beseech you not to grow weary in my tribulations for you” (Eph. 3). In the Gradual, “The nations shall fear” (Ps. 101:16), he prophesies Jerusalem’s rebuilding, where he says: “For the Lord hath built Zion” (ibid., 17). In the Alleluia, “When Israel went out of Egypt” (Ps. 113), he foretells the people’s return: as they had formerly gone out from Egypt, so now they ought to go out from Babylon.

The Gospel agrees, recalling that one dead was being carried out of a city but was raised by the Lord (Luke 7). For the Jewish people were being carried as though dead to the tomb when they were led captive from Jerusalem to Babylon. They are raised by the Lord when recalled to their homeland [Col. 0721B]. In the Offertory the prophet or the people invokes divine help, that it may deliver them from enemies: “O Lord, hasten to help me” (Ps. 70). In the Communion, “O Lord, I will remember” (ibid.), he praises God’s righteousness.

## CHAPTER LXXXI.—Under grace.

Thus after Theodosius Rome is ravaged by the Gentiles and the Christian people are taken captive. The order of doctors, who consoled them in many ways, is represented especially by Augustine in the book entitled *The City of God*. [Note: [Col. 0721] Augustine, *City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 29; chapter 45; and elsewhere.] Therefore the order of doctors invokes God for itself thus: “Have mercy on me, O Lord” (Ps. 85:3); but for the people it prays thus: “Loose, O Lord, the bonds of thy peoples.”

In the Epistle it preaches steadfastness and patience to the people, whom it admonishes [Col. 0721C] not to fail in tribulations (Eph. 5). In the Gradual it says that the nations are said to fear God and that all kings ought to give glory to God. In the Alleluia they praise God in tribulation, who delivers them from the barbarian people and works his sanctification in them. In the Gospel the dead son of the widow is recalled as raised (Luke 7), and resurrection to life is preached in them also. That people implores divine help in the Offertory, that it may deliver them from evil. In the Communion it magnifies God’s righteousness.

## CHAPTER LXXXII.—The Seventeenth Sunday: “Thou art righteous, O Lord,” under the Law.

The following Sunday is instituted from the prophet Daniel. In captivity he interpreted dreams for the king [Col. 0721D], delivered Susanna from death (Dan. 13), and was himself delivered by God from the lions’ den. Praising God, he exalted him thus: “Thou art righteous, O Lord” (Ps. 118). In the Prayer, “Almighty everlasting God,” he entreats God that the people, who on account of their merits had fallen into God’s judgment, may experience pardon; or in the Prayer, “Grant, we beseech thee, O Lord, to thy people,” he prays that the people may follow God alone.

In the Epistle he calls himself bound and strengthens the captive people in patience (Eph. 4). In the Gradual he sings of the blessed nation (Ps. 32), which God visits by chastising it. In the Alleluia, “I have loved, because” (Ps. 114), he rejoices before God, who heard his voice. Some [Col. 0722A] sing the Alleluia, “Those who fear the Lord” (Ps. 113), which is well suited to Daniel, or to his three youthful companions, or to Susanna, who hoped in the Lord and whom he delivered from dangers.

The Gospel (Luke 14) likewise agrees, because Daniel saved and released Susanna. He reclined in the lowest place, when he grieved that he was among captives; but the king ordered him to go up higher, when he set him as ruler of the kingdom after himself (Dan. 3). The Offertory, “I, Daniel, prayed to my God” (Dan. 9), especially expresses his prayer for the oppressed people. In the Communion, “Make vows and fulfil them” (Ps. 75), he urges the people quickly to fulfil their vows to God, who took away the spirit of princes when he deemed Nebuchadnezzar fit to live among beasts and handed Belshazzar over to be slain by enemies [Col. 0722B].

## CHAPTER LXXXIII.—Under grace.

Through this office the clergy now recall what once happened in the Church under Julian. This emperor lamented the people captured or killed by the Goths and exalted God’s judgment in these words: “Thou art righteous, O Lord, and upright” (Ps. 118). In the Prayer, “Grant, we beseech thee, O Lord, to thy people,” he pleads for the people that, though handed over to the Gentiles by God’s judgment on account of its merits, it may experience pardon. The Epistle (Eph. 4) indicates the admonition of doctors by which the people are strengthened in patience.

In the Gradual he proclaims the blessed nation (Ps. 32), which the Lord chastises here. In the Alleluia, “Those who fear the Lord” (Ps. 113), he declares that God, who is a helper to those hoping in him [Col. 0722C], must be praised. In the Alleluia, however, “I have loved, because” (Ps. 114), he rejoices before God, who heard him. The Gospel suits it, where it says that the Lord made him go up higher and gave him glory before all (Luke 14). The Offertory expresses his prayers, which he poured out for the people’s liberation.

In the Communion the priests urge the people not to delay in fulfilling vows to the awesome God, who took away the spirit of princes when, depriving Alaric, Theodoric, and Totila—tyrants—of their kingdom, he consigned them to Tartarus. It should be noted that in the verse of the Offertory is sung, “Michael came to my help,” because this Sunday sometimes falls near the feast of St Michael; or because the commemoration of St Michael [Col. 0722D] was instituted under the aforesaid ruler.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV.—The Eighteenth Sunday: “Give peace,” under the Law.

In the office of this Sunday, Daniel’s prayer and the conversation of the angel Gabriel are represented. When seventy years in servitude had passed, Daniel prayed for the people’s freedom. The angel Gabriel appeared to him, signifying that Cyrus would release the people and that Christ would be born for humankind’s deliverance. The Introit therefore represents Daniel’s words, by which he cries thus for the people’s salvation: “Give peace, O Lord, to those who wait for thee, that thy prophets may be found faithful” (Ecclus. 36).

In the Prayer he asks that [Col. 0723A] God may direct their hearts. In the Epistle the angel’s prophecy is made known, proclaiming that they lack nothing in any grace (1 Cor. 1). In the Gradual the prophet rejoices at the angel’s promise because it is foretold that the people will go into the house of the Lord. In the Verse he prays that peace may be given to the people. In the Alleluia, “Praise the Lord” (Ps. 134), he urges all who are to be freed to rejoice before God. In the Gospel he exhorts the people that, in their homeland, they must not forget to fulfil the law of Moses in the two commandments of love. In the Offertory, “Moses sanctified the altar” (Exod. 24), he instructs them, upon their return, to build an altar to the Lord, as Moses commanded. In the Communion, “Bring offerings” (Ps. 95), he commands them to offer gifts to God in thanksgiving.

## CHAPTER LXXXV.—Under grace.

[Col. 0723B]

Through these things the Church recalls what gifts divine grace bestowed upon them in the time of Pope Gregory. The Romans and Lombards were at discord with one another; but through Gregory’s prayer they returned to peace and received Christianity. Therefore Gregory is recorded to have prayed thus for the peace of the Christian people: “Give peace, O Lord, to those who wait for thee” (Ecclus. 36). In the Prayer he asks that hearts may be directed by God. In the Epistle his exhortation, which he made for the bond of peace, is understood (1 Cor. 1). In the Gradual he rejoices because peace is praised by them. In the Verse he again prays that peace may be in the towers of the Church. In the Alleluia he urges the people to praise God for peace.

The Gospel indicates how he joined the people together in twofold love. [Col. 0723C] The Offertory makes known that he offered a sacrifice of praise for the people’s safety, just as Moses formerly did for the people. In the Communion he commands them to offer sacrifices of praise to God for their concord. These two Communions, namely “Make vows” (Ps. 75) and “Bring offerings” (Ps. 95), admonish the people not to delay in offering tithes to the clergy.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI.—The Nineteenth Sunday: “I am the salvation of the people,” under the Law.

The following Sunday receives its office from the reign of King Cyrus, who allowed the captive people to depart. To that people Zerubbabel and the priests announce the Lord’s words and strengthen them to return, saying: “I am the salvation of the people, says the Lord.” In the Prayer they ask that everything adverse to them may be removed. In the Epistle they urge them to put on the new man through righteousness, that under God’s guidance they may return to their homeland (Eph. 4).

As the people now proceed, they invoke the Lord in the Gradual: “Let my prayer be directed” (Ps. 160). In the Alleluia, “The right hand of God” (Ps. 117), they rejoice before God, who wrought mightily with them and redeemed them from enemies. The Gospel agrees, narrating that Jesus came into his own city (Matt. 9), because it is established that the people returned to Jerusalem with Jesus the priest. In the Offertory they give thanks to God for their return: “If I should walk in the midst of tribulations” (Ps. 137). In the Communion, “Thou hast commanded thy commandments” (Ps. 118), [Col. 0724A] they declare that they will keep the law of God and ask that they may be able to fulfil it.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII.—Under grace.

This office is suited to the reign of the great Charles, who first transferred the Roman Empire to Germany. He nobly ennobled ecclesiastical rights and governed God’s people vigorously; through him there was salvation for the people. While the Lord defended him from enemies, he directed his prayer to the Lord, whose right hand wrought mightily with him; and because he stretched out his hand over that ruler’s enemies, he kept his commandments.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII.—The Twentieth Sunday: “All that thou hast done,” under the Law.

Through this month, in which the history “I saw the Lord” [Col. 0724B] concerning the prophets is sung, there is represented for us that time in which Jerusalem was rebuilt after the return from captivity. For then, through Zechariah, Haggai, Ezra, and Malachi, Christ’s coming was foretold; from their deeds this office receives its name. When those who had returned saw the city destroyed and the temple burned, they awoke and cried: “All that thou hast done to us, O Lord” (Dan. 3).

In the Prayer they ask that divine mercy may direct their hearts. In the Epistle it says that they redeemed the time because the days were evil (Eph. 5), because they redeemed themselves from enemies—who had long forbidden them to build—both with money and by wars. In the Gradual, “The eyes of all” (Ps. 144), they invoke God to favour their work. In the Alleluia the prophets [Col. 0724C] console them, because those who trust in the Lord shall not be moved.

The Gospel agrees with them, where the king made a wedding feast (Matt. 22), because at that time King Ahasuerus held a wedding with Esther and called many; or because the Jewish people, summoned to the wedding feast, came when it returned from captivity to its homeland, and the Lord entered into union with his people through observance of the law. Therefore, in the Offertory, they rejoice at their return, saying: “Upon the rivers of Babylon” (Ps. 136). But after Ezra came and began building with them, in the Communion he prayed to God thus: “Remember thy word” (Ps. 118).

## CHAPTER LXXXIX.—Under grace.

All this is referred to the Christian people [Col. 0724D], who are ravaged by the Huns or Hungarians but are afterwards gathered together in the praise of God through faithful emperors after their enemies have been overcome.

## CHAPTER XC.—The Twenty-first Sunday: “In thy will,” under the Law.

The following Sunday is appointed from the history of Esther, through whom the people of God are delivered from imminent danger and the offspring of their enemies are exterminated. She invokes God for the people in these same words: “According to thy will, O Lord” (Ps. 72). In the Prayer she prays that God may guard his household. In the Epistle the affliction of the Jews is expressed, whose struggle then was against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world (Eph. 5). In the Gradual, “Lord, thou hast been our refuge” (Ps. 89), they flee to God through fasting [Col. 0725A] and seek his aid. In the Alleluia, “Out of the depths have I cried,” they cry out because of their tribulation, and the Lord immediately delivers them. By the royal official in the Gospel, whose son was ill (John 4), Ahasuerus is understood, whose beloved was being drawn in spirit toward death. By the Offertory, “There was a man” (Job 1), Mordecai is meant: like Job he was grievously tried, but, once proved, was likewise magnified. In the Communion, “In thy salvation” (Ps. 118), he gives thanks to God because he has passed judgment upon those who persecuted him.

### CHAPTER XCI.—Under grace.

For this Sunday appears to represent our own time, in which the community of believers is afflicted by adversaries, yet is rescued from enemies through the Church’s prayer and the labor of the wise. It should be noted that in the Offertory, “There was a man” [Col. 0725B] (Job 1), the words are not repeated, whereas in the Verses they are repeated more often, because the speech of a sick person attempting to speak is interrupted, and things begun are scarcely completed, even when often resumed. In the Verses Job in his sickness is understood. By Job, moreover, Christ is signified: he suffered for us and offered himself to the Father as a sacrifice for the world; and this is expressed by the Verses. The Offertory, however, signifies the Church, which continually offers Christ and commemorates him as offered for us.

### CHAPTER XCII.—Twenty-second Sunday, “If thou shouldst mark iniquities,” under the Law.

The present Sunday appears to have been instituted from the history of Judith. For when the people of God were besieged by Holofernes at Bethulia, they are understood to have cried to God in this way: “If thou shouldst mark iniquities” (Ps. 129). The Prayer, “Our God, our refuge,” suggests Judith’s prayer, by which she sought peace and pardon for the people. The Epistle (Phil. 1) shows the consolation of the leaders, by which they raised up the afflicted people. The Gradual, “Behold how good” (Ps. 132), expresses the people’s joy when Judith returned bringing the head of Holofernes. The Alleluia, “Praise the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. 145), intimates Judith’s own joy, by which she exults in victory and the people’s deliverance. Moreover, the Gospel (Matt. 18) accords well: it recalls that the king settled accounts with his servants—Nebuchadnezzar, who was also Cambyses, took counsel with his own when he resolved to subdue all kingdoms to himself. He who owed ten [Col. 0725D] thousand talents signifies Holofernes, who became the king’s debtor on account of the great honor conferred upon him. Going out, he cast his fellow-servant into prison, just as Holofernes, going out with an army, reduced the whole people to distress. Or, he cast his fellow-servant into prison when he exposed Achior the commander to danger. The Offertory, “Remember me” (Jer. 15), represents Judith’s prayer, by which she invokes God in danger, that her words might find favor before the ruler Holofernes. The Communion, “I say unto you” (Luke 15), appears to refer to Achior’s conversion, when, after Holofernes was slain, he was added to the people of God.

### CHAPTER XCIII.—Under grace.

Since the entire body of the faithful, from the beginning of the world [Col. 0726A] to its end, is one body of God’s Church, the divine office is sometimes established from events past and sometimes from things to come. Therefore this office is also referred to the times of Antichrist, under whom the Church will be grievously afflicted, just as this people is read to have been afflicted under Nebuchadnezzar. The Church thus cried to the Lord concerning her affliction: “If thou shouldst mark iniquities” (Ps. 123). Then she prays that God may become her refuge. Through the Epistle the preaching of Elijah and Enoch is denoted, by which they console the afflicted Church. In the Gradual and Alleluia is suggested the Church’s joy, by which she rejoices over the Jews who have been converted. The Gospel accords excellently, in which the king settles accounts with his servants (Matt. 18), because Christ, the true king, will then come to judgment and require from all an account of each person’s deeds. Antichrist [Col. 0726B] too will settle accounts with the people, because he will purpose to subject all to himself. He will cast his fellow-servant into prison, because he will cruelly afflict all the people rebellious against him. The Offertory expresses the Church’s prayer, by which she asks God to remember her. God, hearing it, will quickly deliver her, when he slays Antichrist in his own tent, just as he slew Holofernes through Judith in his tent. The Communion, moreover, makes known the joy in which the righteous will rejoice over those converted after Antichrist’s destruction.

### CHAPTER XCIV.—A Sunday left vacant.

The Sunday which lacks a sung office, in whose Gospel the Lord commands tribute to be rendered to Caesar (Matt. 22), denotes the time when all the people were in mourning under Alexander the Great. He oppressed them with diverse wars [Col. 0726C] and compelled tribute to be paid him. It expresses that time in which Antichrist will bind the entire people to his service.

### CHAPTER XCV.—A Sunday left vacant.

The Sunday which follows this one without chant, in whose Gospel the woman suffering from an issue of blood for twelve years is read to have been cured by the Lord (Matt. 9; Luke 8), suggests the time under King Seleucus, when all Asia, having first been exhausted for twelve years under Alexander by the bloodshed of wars, was set free. This Sunday is not furnished with chant because the whole earth was soon disturbed by wars. It also suggests the time that will follow Antichrist’s death, when the Church, previously harassed by him with the bloodshed of persecution, will be delivered.

### CHAPTER XCVI.—Twenty-fourth Sunday after Pentecost, “The Lord says,” under the Law.

[Col. 0726D]

The final Sunday is appointed from the history of the Maccabees. After their many toilful wars, Christ is promised to come quickly, through whom they may be delivered from their enemies. The priests therefore address them in prophetic words thus: “The Lord says: I think [thoughts of peace]” (Jer. 29). In the Prayer, “Stir up, O Lord,” they pray that their minds may be stirred up for divine work. The Lesson proclaims to them that a king will be present, who, judging them in righteousness, will rescue them from their enemies. In the Gradual they give thanks for their deliverance and the confusion of their enemies. In the Alleluia they applaud him “who heals the broken in heart” (Ps. 146). The Gospel accords well, recounting that five thousand were fed with five loaves (Luke 9), [Col. 0727A] because, after five thousand years, the bread of angels was given, by which the minds of the blessed were refreshed. In the Offertory, “Out of the depths” (Ps. 129), sinners cry to the Lord that they may be made worthy of this bread. In the Communion, “Amen, I say unto you” (Mark 11), the divine voice promises them that their prayer will be fulfilled.

### CHAPTER XCVII.—Under grace.

By this office the Church recalls the tribulation which the Christian people would suffer under Antichrist, as the Maccabees suffered under Antiochus. Christ’s near coming is foretold to this people, through whom it may be rescued from the dread of all enemies. Thus he consoles the faithful: “The Lord says: I think [thoughts of peace]” (Jer. 29). In the Prayer they ask that their minds may be stirred to repentance [Col. 0727B] so that they may receive the remedies of pardon. In the Lesson Christ’s kingdom and judgment are promised to them, and in the Gradual and Alleluia they rejoice in their deliverance. In the Gospel people are reported to have flocked to Christ and been fed by him (Luke 9), because then all nations will run together to Christ’s judgment and will be refreshed by him who is the living bread. In the Offertory they ask to be made worthy of it. In the Communion their prayer is promised fulfillment. Therefore the Gospel of the five thousand is now read, because five Sundays from this point are counted to the Nativity of the Lord, when, as it were after five ages, the faithful are satisfied with heavenly bread. This Gospel is read for the further reason that it always falls about the feast of Saint Andrew, whose mention occurs in the same Gospel. It is asked [Col. 0727C] why there are more Lessons and Gospels in summer than offices. But one should know that the offices correspond to embolismic years, while Lessons and Gospels correspond to common years.

### CHAPTER XCVIII.—The order of Sunday Alleluias among certain persons.

Some observe the following order in Sunday Alleluias, which also fits the offices or seasons well. On the first Sunday: “Lord, in thy mercy,” Alleluia, “In thee, O Lord, have I hoped.” On the second Sunday: “The Lord became a protector,” Alleluia, “I will love thee, O Lord.” On the third: “Look upon me,” Alleluia, “Come, let us exult.” On the fourth: “The Lord is my illumination,” “Give thanks to the Lord.” On the fifth: “Hear, O Lord,” “He who fears God.” On the sixth: “The Lord is strength,” “Lord, thou hast been our refuge.” On the seventh: “All nations.” On the eighth: “We have received, O God,” “For God is great.” On the ninth: “Behold God,” “who heals.” On the tenth: “When I cried,” “I rejoiced.” On the eleventh: “God is in his holy place,” “My heart is prepared.” On the twelfth: “God, unto my help,” “Exult in God.” On the thirteenth: “Look upon us, O God,” “The Lord reigns.” On the fourteenth: “Our protector,” “Praise Jerusalem.” On the fifteenth: “Incline, O God,” “Lord God.” On the sixteenth: “Have mercy on me,” “Praise the Lord, all nations.” On the seventeenth: “Thou art just, O Lord,” “God is judge.” On the eighteenth: “Give peace, O Lord,” “Who has set thy borders.” On the nineteenth: “The salvation of the people,” “I will worship toward the temple.” On the twentieth: “All that thou hast done,” “Redeemer.” On the twenty-first: “According to thy will,” [Col. 0728A] “To thee is praise due.” On the twenty-second: “If thou shouldst mark iniquities,” “Out of the depths.” On the twenty-third: “The Lord says,” “The right hand of God,” or “When Israel went out.” In this month the preaching of John the Baptist is suggested, through whom Christ’s coming in the flesh is shown. Therefore both the Advent of the Lord and his Nativity are celebrated in this month.

### CHAPTER XCIX.—First Sunday in the Advent of the Lord.

The first Sunday of the Advent of the Lord takes its office from John the Baptist, under whose person the Church sings: “To thee have I lifted up my soul” (Ps. 24). In the Prayer it asks that Christ, when he comes, may rescue the human race from sins. In the Epistle it announces that the night of unbelief has preceded and that the day is drawing near through faith. In the Gradual it addresses words to Christ himself when he comes to be baptized by John: “All they that wait on thee,” etc.; [Col. 0728B] “Show me thy ways, O Lord.” In the Alleluia it asks God to show his salvation—that is, the Son of Man. The Gospel accords well, for Mark writes at the beginning of his book concerning John: “Behold, I send my angel” (Mark 1). Others read the Gospel: “When Jesus drew near to Jerusalem” (Luke 7), which also suits the Advent of the Lord because of the Verse, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” The Offertory, “To thee, O Lord, have I lifted up” (Ps. 25), refers to John’s sacrifice, where he offered to God the souls of penitents. In the Communion it proclaims that the earth shall yield fruit—that is, that Mary shall bear Christ.

### CHAPTER C.—Second Sunday in Advent, “People of Sion.”

The second Sunday is appointed in the person of the prophets, through whom Christ’s Advent is announced to the Synagogue thus: “People of Sion, behold.” In the preceding office the calling of the Jews is noted, but in this one the calling of the Gentiles, where is sung: “Behold, the Lord shall come to save the nations.” These nations pray in the Prayer that their hearts may be prepared as a way for Christ. In the Epistle they are called by the voice of the prophets. For Moses says: “Rejoice, ye nations, with his people”; David likewise: “Praise the Lord, all nations” (Ps. 116); and Isaiah: “He who shall arise to rule the nations—in him shall the nations hope” (Isa. 11). In the Gradual the Prophet says to the preachers: “Gather together unto him his saints” (Ps. 49). In the Alleluia the nations exult, saying: “We shall go joyfully into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121). The Gospel [Col. 0728D] accords well, because our redemption draws near. Therefore this Gospel is recited on the second Sunday (Luke 21), because in it Christ’s second Advent is foretold. In the Offertory the nations offer themselves to Christ and joyfully say: “O God, returning thou shalt give us life.” In the Communion the prophetic order applauds the Church from the Gentiles, saying: “Jerusalem, arise and stand.”

### CHAPTER CI.—Third Sunday, “Rejoice in the Lord.”

The third Sunday rejoices in an office spoken in the person of the apostles, through whom each people is called to faith; in their voice it is sung thus: “Rejoice in the Lord”—understand, the faithful from among the Jews—“again I say, Rejoice” (Phil. 4), namely, the faithful from among the Gentiles. In the Prayer [Col. 0729A] they pray that the darkness of their minds may be illumined. In the Apostolic Epistle it is announced to them that Christ is coming, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness. In the Gradual and Alleluia the faithful pray that Christ may come as quickly as possible. The Gospel concerning Christ’s signs and John’s sanctity is read (John 1), because Christ’s divinity is preached through John. It is read on the third Sunday because Christ becomes known in the third age of the world through miracles. In the Offertory the faithful give thanks because the Lord has blessed them by his coming and turned his wrath from them: “Thou hast blessed thy land, O Lord” (Ps. 84). In the Communion they are consoled through the preachers, and the Lord promises to save them. The offices of Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday fit the Advent of the Lord and the Ember Days, [Col. 0729B] in which they sing most devoutly that Christ will come.

### CHAPTER CII.—Fourth Sunday, “Remember us, O Lord.”

The fourth Sunday is vacant of an office because of the orders of the preceding day, but modern writers celebrate it with the office, “Remember us, O Lord” (Ps. 105). This office is sung in the person of the teachers, through whom the second Advent of the Lord is preached. They cry out thus: “Remember us, O Lord.” In the Prayer they ask that the Lord, coming in great power, may assist them. In the Epistle the faithful are urged to rejoice because the Lord is near. In the Gradual they applaud him as near to those who call upon him. In the Alleluia they ask him to come swiftly to remit their sins. In the Gospel they are told to prepare the way for the Lord, [Col. 0729C] who will come soon. In the Offertory and Communion the Virgin is greeted, through whose childbirth the world is saved.

### CHAPTER CIII.—On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, “Today you shall know.”

The Vigil of the Lord denotes the present life, in which Christ’s coming to us is announced. Therefore it is sung in the office: “Today,” that is, in this life, “you shall know that the Lord will come; and in the morning,” that is, in the future life, “you shall see his glory” (Exod. 16). Hence in the Prayer: “May we who have joyfully received him as Redeemer also behold him coming as Judge in security.” Two Lessons are read because Christ was to be born, as preached by the prophets, and is preached as born by the apostles. Therefore one is recited from a prophet and the other from the Apostle. In the Gradual Christ’s Nativity is promised, but it is said that he will be seen at the last morning. The Alleluia is not sung at vigils or in the Ember Days because of the fast; but if the vigil falls on Sunday, it is sung on account of the Lord’s resurrection. The Gospel and Offertory sing of the imminent Nativity. The Communion, however, promises Christ’s second Advent: “The glory of the Lord shall be revealed” (Isa. 40).

### CHAPTER CIV.—At the Nativity of the Lord: the first Mass at night, “The Lord said unto me.”

On the holy day of the Lord’s Nativity Pope Telesphorus instituted the celebration of three Masses for this reason: it is established that the three ages of this world are saved by this unique Nativity. By the Mass sung at night is designated the time before the Law, which was enveloped in the darkness [Col. 0730A] of ignorance. Therefore at this Mass is read: “The people that walked in darkness” (Isa. 9). The Introit expresses the rising of the true light, when the Son of God, being born, says to the world: “The Lord said unto me” (Ps. 2). “Glory in the highest” represents the angelic choir, which then first sang this hymn. The Prayer is spoken in the person of the shepherds, who ask to enjoy in heaven that light which shone on earth. Two Lessons are read because these things are proclaimed by the Old and New Law. They are therefore recited alike because the Old and New Testaments are harmoniously joined. In the Gradual the Father commends the birth of the Son, whom he recalls having begotten before Lucifer, the morning star (Ps. 109). Before Lucifer, that is, before the first archangel, the Father begot him; before Lucifer—that is, before the star—the mother bore him at midnight. The Nativity is suggested by the voice of the one born in the Alleluia, “The Lord said unto me” (Ps. 2), which the Church joyfully sings in his praise. The Gospel sets forth how this Nativity occurred. The following “I believe in one God” signifies that the Church professes herself to believe in the one born, who is given to us as food.

### CHAPTER CV.—Mass at dawn, “A light shall shine today.”

By the Mass celebrated at the dawn of the Law, the age of the Law is understood, in which the light of faith is poured into the world through the Scriptures. Hence under this signification is sung: “A light shall shine today” (Isa. 9). In the Prayer the Church asks that, being suffused with new light, she may deserve to shine in deed as in faith. Two Lessons are read, [Col. 0730C] because Christ is born for two peoples. The Gradual is sung in the person of the shepherds, by whom Christ, once found, is thus worshipped: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us” (Ps. 117). In the Alleluia, “The Lord reigns” (Ps. 96), their praise is expressed, which the Gospel immediately recounts. In the Offertory his divinity is praised by the Church; in the Communion his incarnation is proclaimed.

### CHAPTER CVI.—The principal Mass, “A child is born unto us.”

By the third Mass, celebrated at the third hour of the day, is denoted the third age of the world, namely grace, in which the child was born through whom the world was created, when the angel of great counsel (Isa. 9) came and brought the day of eternity. In the Prayer [Col. 0730D] the human race asks him to rescue it from the yoke of sin. Two Lessons, from the Prophet and the Apostle, are recited because this grace is preached through prophets and apostles, and active and contemplative persons are saved through this Nativity. The Gradual is sung in the person of the prophets, in which Jews and Gentiles are urged to praise God because God made known his salvation—that is, his Son—to the Jews, and revealed his righteousness, namely the same Son, to the Gentiles. The Alleluia is joyfully sung in the person of the apostles, through whom the Church from the Gentiles is urged, together with the primitive Church, to worship Christ. By the melody of the Sequence, moreover, is understood the jubilation of that Church itself. In the Gospel the sublimity of his divinity is related, which all praise in the Offertory thus: [Col. 0731A] “Thine are the heavens and the earth” (Ps. 88). In the Communion it is promised that he is still to be seen by all.

### CHAPTER CVII.—Why the Gospel concerning Abel is read for Saint Stephen.

The Gospel in which Abel is mentioned is read for Saint Stephen because, just as Abel was the first martyr in the Old Testament, so Stephen was the first martyr in the New. This Gospel is read because of the Lord’s Nativity, on account of the words: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 23).

### CHAPTER CVIII.—The Sunday “While all things were in quiet silence.”

The Sunday “While all things were in quiet silence” (Wis. 18) suggests the rejoicing of the primitive Church, by which it exults in Christ’s Nativity.

### CHAPTER CIX.—On Epiphany, “Behold, he has come.”

[Col. 0731B]

The office “Behold, he has come” is sung in the person of the Church from the Gentiles, which rejoices in Christ’s incarnation. In the Prayer it asks to be brought to contemplate the countenance of God. The remaining parts suit the holy day on which the Gentiles came to worship the Lord.

### CHAPTER CX.—The Sunday “Upon a lofty throne.”

After his baptism Christ is said to have preached for three years, from which three Sunday offices appear to have been instituted. After the temptation, indeed, angels came and ministered to him. Hence in the Introit, “Upon a lofty throne,” is sung: “Whom a multitude of angels worships.” The Epistle says that if we are conformed to him through holiness, we shall become his members (Rom. 12).
