The Church blesses him in the Gradual, who alone does wonders. In [Col. 0731C] the Alleluia it rejoices in him, concerning whom the Gospel reads that he was subject to his parents (Luke 2). In the Offertory, “Let all the earth rejoice unto him” (Ps. 65), it is also admonished to serve in gladness. In the Communion his humanity and divinity are preached: in regard to his mother he is rebuked as man, and as the Father’s Son he is affirmed to be God.

### CHAPTER CXI.—On the third Sunday, “All the earth.”

The second office is instituted concerning Christ’s miracles; hence the Gospel in which he began his signs is read. This office is sung in the person of the human race, because all the earth is exhorted to worship Christ as God (Ps. 65). In the Epistle are written the gifts of grace brought about through Christ, namely prophecy, teaching, exhortation, love, and the rest. In [Col. 0731D] the Gradual the Church applauds God, who sent his Word and healed her from destruction; in the Alleluia and Offertory it rejoices in him. In the Communion, as water was changed into wine (John 2), it sings that he changes wine into his blood.

### CHAPTER CXII.—On the fourth Sunday, “Worship God.”

The third office is sung in the person of the angels (Ps. 96), by whom Christ God is worshipped and through whom their number is restored. In the Prayer the faithful ask that God may protect them with his right hand. In the Epistle they are admonished through the preachers not to return evil for evil, but to provide good things before God and human beings (Rom. 12). In the Gradual Christ is praised, through whom the nations are converted. In the Alleluia the angels [Col. 0732A] are invited to praise, because the nations are saved through Christ. In the Gospel the leper and the sick man are cured (Matt. 8), because the Jewish and Gentile peoples are healed through Christ. In the Offertory the Church sings praise to him for both peoples, whose right hand has wrought power (Ps. 117). In the Communion all who were turning to faith marvelled at his signs and words (Luke 4).

### CHAPTER CXIII.—On the same fourth Sunday.

On the fourth Sunday the Gospel is recited in which, when Christ had entered the little boat, the sea was stirred, and he, sleeping, was awakened by his own (Matt. 8). This is because in the fourth year after his baptism Christ ascended the cross; the devil, as wind, stirred up the crowd of Jews; and Christ fell asleep in the sleep of death, from which the prayer of his own quickly raised him.

### CHAPTER CXIV.—On the office of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.

Offices concerning saints are instituted so that they suit partly the season and partly the day. Thus the office for Saints Gervasius and Protasius, “The Lord gives peace,” is sung because peace between the Romans and Lombards is recorded as having been made on that day.

### CHAPTER CXV.—Why Verses are said with the antiphons at the night office of Saint Paul, and likewise for Saint Lawrence.

The nocturnal office of Saint Paul is distinguished by Verses to the antiphons because he is read to have labored more than all the apostles. Likewise, Verses to the antiphons are sung for Saint Lawrence because his passion is preferred above that of all martyrs. The same should be noted regarding the others.

### CHAPTER CXVI.—On the office of the dead.

In the office of the dead we imitate the offices of the Lord’s death or burial. Therefore the Invitatory is not sung and blessings are not given for the Lessons, because they too are omitted there, and mourning or grief is enacted in this chant. We ring bells for the dead for two reasons: that the living may pray for them, and that they may reflect that they too will die and prepare themselves to go to the kingdoms of heaven. May he who lives and reigns without end happily bring us there. Amen.

### CHAPTER CXVII.—Extract from the Roman Order.

[Col. 0732D]

Now, with Christ’s help, we have explained the offices as they appeared appropriate; we have decided to add a few matters concerning the Roman Order.

#### On the Advent of the Lord.

From the Advent of the Lord until his Nativity, *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise thee, O God”) and *Gloria in excelsis* (“Glory in the highest”) are not sung, and *Ite, missa est* (“Go, the dismissal is made”) is omitted; it is never said unless *Gloria in excelsis* is sung. Dalmatics and subdiaconal vestments are likewise not worn. If within the Advent of the Lord the feast of Saint Andrew or Saint Thomas, or the Dedication of a Church, occurs, we do not omit the aforementioned glorifications. On Friday, the office of the Holy Cross is not sung; nor is that of the Holy Trinity on Sundays [Col. 0733A]. At Sunday Lauds, “The Lord reigns” is sung with the rest.

#### On the history “Cry aloud with strength.”

The history “Cry aloud with strength” does not belong to the Ember Days but to the week immediately preceding the Lord’s Nativity, just as those responsories belong to the week before Easter. Therefore they have Lauds for each day. In this week the O-antiphons are sung, in which “Come” is written; only seven are found.

#### On the Lord’s Vigil.

On whatever weekday the Lord’s Vigil falls, it takes that weekday’s psalm and canticle with its antiphon; but the preceding Saturday shall have the canticle “Hear, O heavens,” with the antiphon “Await.” If the Lord’s Vigil falls on Sunday, it takes six responsories from the history “Sound the trumpet” and three from the vigil, with Lauds; it takes the Mass from the Vigil and the Hours from Sunday.

#### On the Nativity of the Lord.

At the Nativity of the Lord, *Te Deum laudamus* is sung after the ninth responsory, before Mass. At Mass, however, not *Ite, missa est* but *Benedicamus Domino* (“Let us bless the Lord”) is said.

#### On Saint Stephen.

On the feast of Saint Stephen we sing the entire second Vespers of Saint Stephen. We do likewise for Saint John on the following day. At the Nativity of the Innocents, *Gloria in excelsis*, *Te Deum laudamus*, Alleluia, and *Ite, missa est* are not sung; [Col. 0733C] dalmatics are not worn. *Gloria Patri* (“Glory be to the Father”) is never omitted except in the Passion of the Lord. If their feast falls on Sunday, we omit none of these things. We also sing everything on their octave, if the Nativity of the Lord or another following feast falls on Sunday. We sing the office “While all things were in quiet silence” after the Nativity of the Innocents, and repeat the same on the following Sunday. On the Lord’s octave, not “A child is born,” but “Thy countenance” is to be sung, because the whole office on that day concerns Saint Mary. Therefore the Alleluia “After childbirth” is sung, along with the Prayer, “O God, who by the fruitful virginity of blessed Mary hast bestowed upon the human race the rewards of eternal salvation.” If the Vigil of Epiphany falls on Sunday, the office “While all things were in quiet silence” is observed in full as on the preceding Sunday. If it falls on another [Col. 0733D] day, the same office is sung, but with the Lesson “We know” (*Scimus*) and the Gospel “Herod having died.” At Epiphany the Invitatory is not sung, but the office begins from the psalm “Bring unto the Lord”; and the antiphon “Of the river,” with the psalm “God is our refuge,” is reserved for the third nocturn. If Epiphany falls on Sunday, the Sunday within the octave is deferred; but if a Sunday occurs within the octave, “Upon a lofty throne” is sung in full. This too is repeated on the following Sunday if necessary. On the Sunday within the octave, Sunday psalms are to be recited with the chant of Epiphany. On private days within the octave, weekday nocturns with antiphons and responsories of Epiphany are to be sung. Morning Lauds also are to be performed for the feast. According to the Roman order, [Col. 0734A] we never omit a weekday nocturn when we say three responsories, except in Easter and Pentecost week. Every year “Upon a lofty throne” shall be sung within the octave of Epiphany, even if several weeks appear before Septuagesima. But if only one week occurs between Epiphany and Septuagesima, it will compress the two offices into itself. After the octave of Epiphany the Epistles of Paul are read, whether on Sunday or on weekdays. If two feasts with a full office fall on one day, one is to be celebrated in full; the other is to be commemorated with an antiphon and prayer, or deferred to another day, as the feast of Saint Paul is. After Mass we make no commemoration of a saint for whom we sing three responsories. On a feast of nine Lessons, *Gloria in excelsis*, [Col. 0734B] *Te Deum laudamus*, and *Ite, missa est* are sung, unless it falls within Advent of the Lord or Septuagesima. *Credo in unum Deum* (“I believe in one God”) is sung on all Sundays and on feasts of Saint Mary, the apostles, the Holy Cross, Dedication, and All Saints. Whenever *Gloria in excelsis* is sung, dalmatics and subdiaconal vestments are always worn. Pope Alexander II decreed that Alleluia should be omitted at Vespers and that the weekday sequence (*heptaticus*) should begin with responsories at Nocturn. The same history is then repeated on the following day, from this point until Easter. *Gloria in excelsis*, *Te Deum*, *Ite, missa est*, the dalmatic, and the *subtile* are omitted.

#### On the Purification of Saint Mary.

If the Purification of Saint Mary falls within Septuagesima, we omit nothing of it except Alleluia. Likewise at the Chair of Saint Peter and the Annunciation of Saint Mary, we sing *Gloria in excelsis* according to the order. But if the Annunciation of Saint Mary falls in the three days before Easter, it is anticipated on the Saturday before Palm Sunday.

#### On the office at the beginning of the Fast.

At the beginning of the Fast we sing Mass at None; Vespers follows immediately, and we do everything as in Lent. We say the Preface, “Who by bodily fasting,” daily, both on Sundays and other days, until the Passion of the Lord. On Saturday the office is “Be unto me a God”; in the following week the Ember Days of Lent are observed. On Wednesday, at the first Prayer, only “Let us bend the knee” is said; [Col. 0734D] at the second, indeed, “The Lord be with you” is said, not “Let us bend the knee.”

#### On the Passion of the Lord.

From Passion Sunday until Easter, *Gloria Patri* is not said at the Responsory, Introit, or the psalm “Come, let us exult,” where the repetition is customarily changed: that is, the invitation is repeated from the middle to the second verse, and from the beginning. The same applies on this Saturday to “Judge me, O God.”

#### On Palm Sunday and the whole week.

On Palm Sunday and on Monday and Wednesday, “The Lord be with you” is said before the Passion, but “Glory to thee, O Lord” is not added. During Palm Week the Preface of the Holy Cross is said. If we celebrate saints during [Col. 0735A] the Passion of the Lord, we do not omit *Gloria Patri*. On Monday and Tuesday two Lessons are read continuously, as at the Masses of the Nativity of the Lord; the same is done on the Saturday after Mid-Lent. On Wednesday after Palm Sunday two Lessons are read, and “Let us bend the knee” is said for each.

#### On the Lord’s Supper.

At the Lord’s Supper, on Good Friday, and on Holy Saturday, after the *Benedictus*, *Kyrie eleison*, prayers, and the collect are to be said quietly according to the order. At the Lord’s Supper *Gloria Patri* and *Gloria in excelsis* are kept silent, except where chrism is consecrated; dalmatics are nevertheless worn. On that day it is forbidden under anathema for anyone to break the Lenten fast [Col. 0735B].

#### On Good Friday.

On Good Friday one begins not with the Prayer but with the Lesson. Before the Passion, “The Lord be with you” is not said, and titles for the Lesson are not pronounced. At each Prayer, except that for the Jews, “Let us bend the knee” is said and immediately followed by “Rise.”

#### On Holy Saturday.

On Holy Saturday the great candle is to be blessed by the deacon and lit before the blessing, and on the night of Easter distributed to the people to fumigate their belongings.

#### On the Lessons before Baptism.

Before Baptism twelve Lessons are read according to the order, but the titles are not pronounced. After baptism the priests who wish to do so come forward to celebrate Mass. At Mass the Offertory, Communion, and *Agnus Dei* are not sung, and *Ite, missa est* is not said.

#### On the holy day of Easter.

At Easter the lamb is blessed not at the altar but at the table, and *Credo in unum* is sung daily until the octave. The Gradual Verse, “Blessed is he who comes,” is to be sung on Thursday; and “The stone which they rejected,” on Friday, because of Christ’s Passion. On the Saturday within the octave of Easter the antiphon “When it was evening on that day” is sung at Vespers, because that same Gospel, formerly extending as far as “Thomas alone,” was read on that Saturday. At weekday Vespers [Col. 0735D] the psalms are said with Alleluia; on Sunday night we say the Sunday nocturn and nine Lessons; and thus on each day nocturns with Alleluia, unless a feast of nine Lessons occurs. At Lauds every day we recite “The Lord reigns.” The practice, held by many from this point until after Pentecost, of singing three psalms and reading three Lessons is said to have been instituted by the Council of Mainz, but is not received by the Roman Church.

#### How singing is to be conducted between Easter and Pentecost.

From Easter until Pentecost, on a feast of three responsories we sing only one Alleluia at Mass. On a feast of nine Lessons we sing two, one concerning the Resurrection; we repeat not the first or another of the feast, but the second. We say the Easter Preface daily until the Ascension of the Lord. On the Vigil of the Lord’s Ascension, the office “The voice of joy” is sung at Mass. None is sung for the coming feast.

#### On the Vigil of Pentecost.

On the vigil of Pentecost four lessons are read before baptism without titles; at Mass “Let us bless [the Lord]” is said, not “Go, the dismissal is made.” At Pentecost “I believe in one [God]” (*Credo in unum*) is sung daily. In this seventh [week] the summer fast of the Ember Days is observed; Alleluia (“Praise the Lord”) is sung in place of the Gradual, and “Let us bend the knee” is not said. At the Mass of the fast, “Glory in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis*) is not sung, because Mass is celebrated after the sixth hour; but it is never sung except at the third hour according to the order, except at the Lord’s Supper, [Col. 0736B] on Holy Saturday, and on the Vigil of Pentecost. Hence some sing two Masses, one of the feast and the other of the fast: the festive one with *Gloria in excelsis* and *Credo in unum*, the other indirectly. This is customarily done on the feast of Saint Thomas during the winter fast, and on the feast of Saint Matthew during the autumn fast, and on the Annunciation of Saint Mary, namely in Lent: so that the first Mass answers to the feast and the second satisfies the fast.

## On the Octave of Pentecost

On the octave of Pentecost nine lessons are read, and as many responsories concerning the Holy Spirit are sung. On the following day we read and sing the books of Kings at Nocturns, and at Mass the office “Lord, in your …” (*Domine, in tua*), which, if necessary, we repeat on the following Sunday. [Col. 0736C] Some sing in this week the office of the Holy Trinity, which the Romans do not receive. For Albinus, Charlemagne’s master, at the request of Archbishop Boniface, instituted a Mass of the Holy Trinity on Sunday; of Wisdom on Monday; of the Holy Spirit on Tuesday; of Charity on Wednesday; of the Angels on Thursday; of the Holy Cross on Friday; and of Saint Mary on Saturday.

## On the Ember Days

In the third week of September and the fourth of December the Ember Days are to be celebrated; and at all the prayers on Saturday “Let us bend the knee” is said, except where the lesson from Daniel is read. On Wednesday, at the first prayer only “Let us bend the knee” is said, without the salutation; at the second, the salutation is said without kneeling. [Col. 0736D]

## CHAPTER 118.—How Reading Is to Be Done through the Year

These books are authoritative, and these are to be read in the divine offices. From Septuagesima until the Passion, let the Pentateuch be read, which Moses wrote; and the book of Joshua, which he himself wrote; and the books of Judges and Ruth, which Gideon and Samuel are said to have written. From Passion Sunday until the Lord’s Supper, let the prophet Jeremiah be read, which he himself wrote. On the three days before Easter, let his Lamentations be read. From the octave of Easter for three weeks, let the Apocalypse be read, which the apostle John wrote. Then for two weeks let the canonical Epistles be read, which the apostles James, Peter, John, [Col. 0737A] and Jude wrote. From the Ascension of the Lord until Pentecost, let the Acts of the Apostles be read, which the evangelist Luke wrote. From the octave of Pentecost until the Kalends of August, let the books of Kings be read: the first of these Samuel wrote, the second Nathan, and the third and fourth Jeremiah. Also the two books of Chronicles, which the wise men of the Synagogue wrote.

From the Kalends of August until September, let the Proverbs of Solomon, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, and the Book of Wisdom be read, all of which Solomon wrote; and Ecclesiasticus, which Jesus son of Sirach composed. From the Kalends of September for two weeks, let the book of Job be read, which he himself wrote. Then for one week, the book of Tobit, which he wrote. Then for one week let the book of Judith be read, which [Col. 0737B] she herself or Achior wrote. Then for one week, let the book of Esther be read, which Mordecai composed, though it is rather believed to have been written by Ezra; and let the book of Ezra himself be recited, which he is certainly known to have published.

From the Kalends of October until the Kalends of November, let the books of Maccabees be read. Simon the priest is said to have written the first of them, and his son [Col. 0738A] John its final part; the second is known to have been issued by Philo the Jew, learned in Greek. From the Kalends of November until the Kalends of December, let Ezekiel, Daniel, and the twelve minor prophets be read. These are said to have been written by the elders of the Synagogue, though they are more properly believed to have been issued by the prophets themselves. From the Advent of the Lord until the Nativity of the Lord, let Isaiah be read, who is beyond doubt himself the author. After the octave of Epiphany, let the Epistles of the apostle Paul be read until Septuagesima. He himself wrote them all, but the evangelist Luke translated into Greek the Epistle to the Hebrews, composed in Hebrew.

But now it is time for us to lay down the pen, and perhaps meanwhile to recover some strength for another task. But you, brothers beloved of God, at whose command [Col. 0738B] I undertook this burden and at whose prayer I now set it down, I beg that your devout prayers may obtain from God that, this very little seed having been sown, rich harvests may spring up by Christ’s increase, and that all who labour in it may reap an abundant fruit in joy.

[Col. 0737]

# SACRAMENTARY, OR A BOOK ON THE CAUSES AND MYSTICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF THE RITES OF THE DIVINE OFFICE IN THE CHURCH

(Extracted from a manuscript codex of the renowned Carthusian monastery of Gaming in Austria by the venerable Lord Father Leopold Wydemann, priest and librarian of that monastery; published by the Reverend Father Bernard PEZ in *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*, vol. II, part I, p. 247.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0737C]

I have compiled this little book *On the Sacraments* from the writings of the saints, so that those who lack an abundance of books may have their poverty relieved by this compendium of them. Let its name be written *Sacramentary*, because through it every sacrament of the divine office is disclosed to those who do not know it.

## CHAPTER I.—On Septuagesima

Septuagesima is so called because from that Sunday until the Saturday of Easter week there are seventy days. It begins on Sunday and ends on Saturday. It signifies the time of the captivity of God’s people, who, by sinning, departed from God and through his mercy returned to rest. God’s people were held captive in Babylon for seventy years; during those years they hung their instruments upon the willows, and [Col. 0737D] sat weeping beside the rivers. When that number was complete, they returned to Jerusalem.

The whole duration of the world extends through seven thousand years. [Col. 0738C] Divide these by the number one hundred and you will have seventy hundreds of years; from each hundred give one year as a tithe, and there will be seventy years. From each of these years give one day, and you will have seventy days, by which the whole duration of our pilgrimage is brought to our remembrance. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, led the people captive from Jerusalem to Babylon; the devil led the human race astray from Paradise into this pilgrimage of the world. The seventy years of captivity are the seventy hundreds of years of our pilgrimage. The Jews fasted during their seventy years in captivity; we, throughout the whole course of this life, which revolves through seven days, should chastise our body and subject it to servitude. They hung up their instruments; we, on these [Col. 0738D] days, do not sing Alleluia and *Gloria in excelsis*, songs of joy. Thus we signify that in this life we groan because we are separated from the joy of the angels. [Col. 0739A] We sing the Tract at Mass because with labour and groaning we make our way toward our homeland. Sitting beside the rivers, they wept; humbled, we sigh over the passing flow of our mortality.

On Easter Saturday one Alleluia is sung. For, once the seventy years had passed, only the men returned to Jerusalem, while the women and little children still lingered on the journey. This signifies that, after the end of this life, which is the time of our captivity, our body returns to the repose of the earth, while the spirit alone is joined to the saints in joy. For *Sabbath* means “rest.” Those men, of course, were anxious for their wives and little children; when these arrived on the eighth day, they possessed a twofold joy. And so meanwhile, during Easter week, we frequently sing the Gradual; when the eighth day of the Resurrection arrives, the Gradual having been set aside, we double the Alleluia. For the saints, though placed in joy, await the Day of Judgment—at which the angels will tremble—as though anxious for their wives, that is, their bodies, and for their children, that is, their works. When these are received in the final resurrection, they will rejoice in heaven with a double joy without end.

Septuagesima begins on the tenth moon of the second month. The condition of this world is divided into three periods: one before the Law, another under the Law, and a third under grace, that is, under the Gospel. The first month, January, in which Alleluia is sung, represents the time before the Law. Since people then lived according to their own pleasure, they sang, as it were, a song of joy—that is, Alleluia. In the tenth moon of the second month [Col. 0739C] Alleluia is set aside, because in the second period the people are restrained from the licence of sin by the ten commandments of the Law. Then they gave up Alleluia when, with sorrow, they abandoned the habit of sin. After the captivity the Temple is renewed; after the return from this exile, the heavenly Jerusalem is built through Jesus the great priest out of living stones—that is, out of us.

## CHAPTER II.—On Sexagesima

Sexagesima falls within Septuagesima. It is called Sexagesima because from that Sunday until the Wednesday of Easter week there are sixty days. There are six works of the Gospel: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, receiving strangers, visiting the sick, and redeeming prisoners. And there are ten [Col. 0739D] commandments of the Law:

1. Worship one God.
2. You shall not make for yourself a graven image.
3. You shall not commit perjury.
4. Sanctify the Sabbath day.
5. Honour your father and mother.
6. You shall not kill.
7. You shall not commit adultery.
8. You shall not steal.
9. You shall not bear false witness.
10. You shall not covet your neighbour’s possession.

Six times ten is sixty. Whoever fulfils the Decalogue through the six works of mercy will belong to the Wednesday of Easter, on which the office will be, “Come, blessed ones.” This Wednesday corresponds to the fourth age of the world, in which David and Solomon reigned. In the fourth age, that people renowned for heavenly faith, glorious through the reign of David and Solomon, and further ennobled throughout the world by the height of the most holy Temple. In our Wednesday—that is, in the [Col. 0740A] fourth period, of which the first was under the Patriarchs, the second under the judges, the third under the Kings and Prophets, and in the fourth, under the Apostles, David triumphs—that is, “strong of hand,” who conquered the lion, that is, the devil—and Solomon, the eternal, peaceful one, reigns. He builds for God the Father the most noble Temple when he says, “Come, blessed of my Father,” and it is toward this that we must run through Sexagesima. The number six belongs to labour; ten belongs to reward. Every labour is performed in six days; the denarius is given to the workers in the vineyard.

## CHAPTER III.—On Quinquagesima

Quinquagesima is so called because fifty days are counted from that Sunday to Easter Day, and they are seven weeks. There are five senses [Col. 0740B] of the body: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. There are ten commandments of the Law, as we have said; five times ten is fifty. If anyone fulfils the Decalogue of the Law through the five senses by the sevenfold Spirit, he will belong to the day of Resurrection.

In the office of Septuagesima we bring to mind the fall of the first human being, who, having come into exile, said: “The sorrows of death surrounded me,” etc. The Epistle exhorts that person to battle: “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from all things,” namely from fornication, impurity, avarice, and the other vices. Set in battle, he cries: “A helper in times of need, in tribulation,” etc., “out of the depths”; and in the Gospel a labourer is introduced to cultivate the vineyard. [Col. 0740C]

In Sexagesima we doubt whether the Lord is with us, and therefore cry: “Rise up, why do you sleep, O Lord?” etc. The Epistle strengthens us to escape captivity: “You gladly endure it if anyone brings you into slavery.” Captives who obey, we take up according to the Gradual—that is, out of tribulation—we who were troubled in Septuagesima. We ascend to seek our own Lord and say: “Let the nations know,” etc. In the Tract, “You have shaken, O Lord,” etc., the earth is shown as shaken by the conscience of sins. In the Gospel the seed is introduced: in Septuagesima we cultivate the vineyard; in Sexagesima we sow the seed. In Quinquagesima we hold our own Lord and say: “Be to me a God,” etc. The Epistle instructs those set on campaign through the fifteen steps of the ladder of charity, saying: [Col. 0740D] “Charity is patient,” etc. Then we shall say to God, the victor of our warfare: “You are God,” etc. The Tract commands us to serve God, who made us and not we ourselves. In the Gospel we gather the fruit that we sowed in Sexagesima. This fruit of light the blind man—who was prefigured by the Lord—sought and found. The Postcommunion likewise shows this: “They ate,” indicating that we have been satisfied by the body of the Lord.

The three stages belong to the three offices. The first contains the lament of captives who do not wish to remain under the dominion of vices; the second displays the desire to flee, provided their own Lord is willing to receive them and not repel them; the third considers [Col. 0741A] how one should flee, now presuming upon reception. The first Tract, “Out of the depths,” and the second, “You have shaken,” sound sorrow; but the third, “Make a joyful noise,” proclaims joy. For before the Law and under the Law we had the sorrow of perdition, but under grace came to us the joy of salvation. Likewise, “He who dwells” and “To you I have lifted up” express sorrow; “Those who trust” announces joy. Again, “They have often attacked me” and “God, my God” express sorrow; “Praise” cries out joy.

Three returns of the people of God are read of: one under Zerubbabel the leader and Jesus the great priest, numbering fifty thousand persons; a second under Ezra, who renewed the Law; and a third under Nehemiah, who rebuilt the Temple. We return from the confusion of sins through repentance and confession; then the Law of God is restored in us through good works; finally, by blessing and building up our neighbour, a Temple is built for God.

## CHAPTER IV.—On Ash Wednesday

On Wednesday we place ashes upon our heads, that we may remember the sentence spoken to the first human being: “You are dust, and to dust you shall go”; so that, though we were formerly immortal, through penitence and humility we may return to immortality. This is done on Wednesday so that, just as the sun and moon were created and the world illuminated on that day, so we may turn from the darkness of sins to Christ the sun and the Church the moon. Until this day we have been on campaign from Septuagesima onward; today we enter battle. Thus the prayer of the Mass declares, saying: “Grant us, O Lord, the defenses of Christ’s warfare.” Likewise, the lesson shows by what arms [Col. 0741C] we ought to fight, saying: “With fasting, weeping, and mourning; let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber,” etc. And the Gospel: “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face.” We celebrate Mass at the ninth hour because at the ninth hour the human being, expelled from Paradise, went into exile; and Christ, expiring on the cross at the ninth hour, called that person back to life.

From this day until Easter there are forty-six days. The Temple in Jerusalem was built in so many years. This Temple signifies the body of the Lord, of which we are members. In order that we may be joined to Christ our body, we abstain for so many days. It is said that Mary was twelve years old when she bore Christ. When Christ suffered, he was thirty-three and a half years old, which is reckoned as [Col. 0741D] a whole number; and these make forty-six years. Thus this Temple—that is, the body of Christ—was built in forty-six years. The Jews destroyed it by killing him, but it was rebuilt in three days by rising again.

Alternatively, Adam is understood as the human race, as though broken and gathered from being scattered across the whole world. Thus, in Greek, *anatolē* means “east,” *dysis* “west,” *arktos* “north,” and *mesēmbria* “south.” The initial letters of these words form ADAM. *A* signifies one; *d* signifies four; again *a* signifies one; *m* signifies forty. By this number Christ’s flesh descended from Adam. For a child is formed in its mother in forty-six days. [Col. 0742A] The number six signifies the six ages of the world, or the six days in which we labour here, or the six works of mercy mentioned above. The number forty signifies the Decalogue of the Law and the four Gospels; with these, and with our head—that is, Christ—we triumph on the day of Resurrection.

The second Adam came in the flesh so that, through repentance and baptism, the first Adam might be refashioned in his image—the Adam who is in the four parts of the world. Since Adam is scattered through the four parts of the world, let us return through that number to Adam who gathers, whom the whole world contains in its initial letters.

Thursday and Saturday after the beginning of the fast lack a proper office, because the ancients began Lent from [Col. 0742B] Septuagesima; they left Thursday free as Sunday, and did not fast on Saturday. But after Lent began from the beginning of the fast, two days of the week besides Sunday remained without offices. On Saturday there are twelve lessons. The prayer over the people is not said because “Let us bend the knee” was once said at it; and this may not be done on Sunday, to which consecration belongs, and because those who are consecrated ought to stand upright in virtues.

## CHAPTER V.—On Lent

Lent is so called because from this Sunday there are forty days until the Lord’s Supper. God’s people were oppressed in Egypt by Pharaoh, and, freed through Moses, crossed the Red Sea on dry ground; [Col. 0742C] but the enemy pursuing them in hostility perished in the waters. After this God gave the Law to the people, fed them with heavenly manna for forty years, brought water from the rock, and then led them into the land flowing with milk and honey. Egypt is this world; Pharaoh is the devil; the Hebrew people are the Christian people, whom Moses—that is, Christ—freed from the power of Pharaoh, that is, the devil. He led them through the Red Sea—that is, through baptism, made red by Christ’s blood—and drowned the enemies, that is, sins. He gives the Law because he forbids sins; he leads through the wilderness for forty years because he commands us to fulfil the four Gospels through the ten commandments of the Law. He feeds us with manna—that is, with his body; he gives the fountain from the rock—that is, blood from his side; and leads us into the land of promise—that is, [Col. 0742D] Paradise.

In Lent some part of the battle has been accomplished. This is told us by him whom we invoke as Protector in the Mass: “He called upon me,” etc.; and in the Epistle: “In an acceptable time I heard you,” etc.; and in the responsory: “May the angels of the Lord guard us.” In the Tract, we are surrounded by the shield of truth. In the Gospel we hasten to triumph, that we may say to the enemy: “Begone, Satan, to destruction.”

Moses fasted forty days, Elijah the same number, and Christ likewise. The Law is signified through Moses, prophecy through Elijah, and the Gospel through Christ. That is, the Law, the prophecies, and the Gospel exhort us to a fast of forty days, so that we may mortify the four qualities of the body through the ten commandments [Col. 0743A] of the Law, knowing that through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God.

From this Sunday there are forty-two days until baptism. The children of Israel had that many stations when they were baptized in the sea and in the cloud, when they left the land of Egypt and harsh slavery and arrived in the land of promise. There are likewise as many generations in Christ’s genealogy. Those who journey toward the heavenly homeland arrive there through forty stations, like the children of Israel; in these forty days those reach it who pass to Christ through baptism. They reach him by the same number by which Christ reached us. Christ descended from the first patriarch Abraham to the Virgin through forty-two generations; we ascend through Christ, who is the chief of the patriarchs, [Col. 0743B] to the kingdom of heaven by fulfilling the four Gospels through the Decalogue of the Law. Four times ten makes forty. This world has four regions: east, west, south, and north; the year has four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter; the human being consists of four elements: earth, water, fire, and air. Moreover, from one to four, ten are counted arithmetically. This signifies that the human being in the four parts of the world, through the four seasons of the year, was to fulfil the Decalogue of the Law and the four Gospels. Lent begins on the second moon of the third month, that is, March, because in the third period, that is, under grace, the two commandments of charity were given, by which a person might fly to heaven as though on two wings.

[Col. 0743C] From Septuagesima there are sixty days until the Wednesday before the Lord’s Supper. These sixty days bring to our remembrance the pilgrimage in which we are away from the Lord. The three days that remain signify the three-day fast of the Ninevites. In order that our sins, by which we are afflicted, may be abolished in the Lord’s resurrection, we must suffer with Christ’s death for three days, so that we may not be ensnared through the lust of the eyes and the pride of life. Through the six days that remain until Saturday, good works are recalled; on Saturday—that is, in rest—we are restored to the perfect liberty of souls.

Lent is celebrated before the Passion of the Lord because this laborious life is figured by forty, and in it we ought to fast from friendship with this world; [Col. 0743D] for if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him. Veils are hung in the churches because in this life the mysteries of heaven are concealed from us.

## CHAPTER VI.—On the Wednesday of the Fourth Week

On Wednesday the scrutiny takes place. The ears of the catechumens are touched so that they may receive the word of God with the ear of the heart and obey it. Their nostrils are touched so that they may reject the stench of vices. The beginnings of the four Gospels are read so that they may cast off four vices—folly, inconstancy, lust—and be imbued with four virtues—prudence, courage, justice, and temperance. [The source apparently omits a fourth vice.] The Lord’s Prayer and the Creed are entrusted to them so that, just as the Hebrews departed from the Egyptians, they too may depart from vices. Two lessons are read: one recalls them from error; the other [Col. 0744A] instructs their conduct, because two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, are converted to the faith. The responsory, “Come, children,” calls them to faith; “Blessed is the nation” praises those who work well. The Gospel approves those washed in Siloam—that is, baptized in Christ. That this is done on Wednesday of the fourth week of Lent signifies the following. Through Lent the whole duration of the world is signified; the six days represent the first six ages of each individual person. Wednesday and the fourth week of Lent correspond to the fourth age of the world and to the age of one person. The fourth age extends from David to the Babylonian deportation, when the period of kings began among God’s people, as in the youthful age. This age is suited to royal power. In this age the Christian empire took its beginning, the Lord having sworn to David: “From [Col. 0744B] the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne.” Therefore catechumens approach the Christian name on Wednesday of the fourth week, which was prefigured by the fourth age of the world, in which Christ’s kingdom was promised, concerning which the angel says: “The Lord God will give him the throne of his Father,” that they themselves may come to that kingdom through faith and works.

On the Saturday before the Lord’s Passion, two lessons are read by which catechumens, namely males and females, are instructed, because the scrutiny was also held on this Saturday.

## CHAPTER VII.—On the Saturday before Palm Sunday

The Saturday before Palm Sunday is free from office because the pope gives alms. On this day Jesus came [Col. 0744C] to Bethany, where Lazarus had been dead, and they made him a supper there. And Mary, taking a pound of ointment, anointed Jesus’ feet, wiped them with her hair, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment. On that day the pope does to Christ’s members what she did to his head. Christ’s feet are the poor; the pound of ointment is justice; the hair is our goods superfluous to ourselves but necessary for the poor. The fragrance in the house is a good reputation in the world.

## CHAPTER VIII.—On Palm Sunday

Palm Sunday is the day when the Lord descended from Bethany to Jerusalem and a crowd came to meet him with palm branches. In memory of that event, we customarily carry branches through our churches and cry: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” As his Passion approached, [Col. 0744D] the Lord approached the place of his Passion, because he willingly chose to die for us. On the tenth day of the first month, the Law commanded that the lamb to be sacrificed at Passover be brought into the house; and on the tenth day of that same month—that is, five days before Passover—the Lord entered the city in which he would suffer. *Palma* means “victory.” Having overcome the devil and the world, the Lord entered the city with palm branches; having conquered vices and sins, we shall enter the heavenly Jerusalem with palms of victory. This is called the Greater Week because the greater offices and passions are read in this week. On Monday and Tuesday a double lesson is read because Christ suffers for two peoples.

## CHAPTER IX.—On the Wednesday of the Greater Week

[Col. 0745A]

On Wednesday the cruel counsel of the Jews and Christ’s gentleness are brought to our memory. In the Introit, *In nomine*, the words “and every tongue confess” are omitted, because the Jews did not confess but destroyed the Lord. One human being suffered two deaths: the death of the body and the death of the soul. In the first lesson and the first responsory, the death of the soul is recalled; in the second lesson and second responsory, the death of the body. Christ died for both: the Saviour’s flesh for the salvation of bodies, and his blood was poured out for souls. One human being had one soul; therefore a single verse follows the first responsory. The second responsory has five verses, just as the human being died through the five senses. [Col. 0745B] On that day the veils are taken down because, in Christ’s Passion, all the mysteries of Scripture are opened to us. The Passion that is read causes us to recall our own death.

## CHAPTER X.—On the Day of the Lord’s Supper

On Thursday oil is consecrated in three forms. On that day the Lord’s body is reserved until the next day; it is also renewed in commemoration of the Lord’s Supper; the brothers’ feet and the pavements of the church are washed; and the altars are stripped until Holy Saturday. On that day penitents come for absolution, and *Gloria Patri* is sung in the office of the Mass. On the fifth day the Lord produced birds and fish from the waters; in the fifth age, which extended from the Babylonian deportation, the Lord came into the world and drew forth birds—that is, the wise—and fish—that is, the unwise—from the sea of error. Today [Col. 0745C] the anointing oil is prepared because in the fifth age Christ came, to anoint us for kingdom and priesthood. Visible oil is in the sign; invisible oil is in the sacrament; spiritual oil is within. The oil for the sick is consecrated in the office itself for the consecration of the Lord’s body, because Christ dies for the sick. Chrism is consecrated at the place of the peace, that those anointed, bearing the same name as Christ—that is, Christians—may enjoy his peace. Holy oil is consecrated there, by which we are anointed as kings and priests of the Lord.

On that day the Law of the Old Testament comes to an end: for, when Moses died, Joshua was appointed leader; because the Law, corrupted by Pharisaic traditions, Christ is incarnate. He, eating Passover with his disciples today, set an end to the old Law and gave a beginning to the grace [Col. 0745D] of the new, handing over to them the mystery of his body and blood. It is reserved for the following day because at the judgment he is presented wounded.

The Lord’s Supper is celebrated at the day’s end because the righteous will feast in the Lord’s presence at the end of the world. The brothers’ feet and the church pavement are washed because through Christ sins are remitted to us who are the Lord’s feet and who are the Church—that is, the assembly. Hence penitents too are absolved. In the fifth age the Lord came and dissolved the Law, which punished sins, and instituted grace, which remitted offences. The altars are stripped of their vestments. The altar is Christ; the vestments are the saints, who left him and fled. For three days—Thursday, Friday, and Saturday—[Col. 0746A] we celebrate the Lord’s Passion and burial; therefore we omit *Gloria Patri* and the ringing of bells. Today the commandment is performed which the Lord performed with his disciples. Peace is not given at Mass because Judas betrayed the Lord with a kiss. Chrism is made today because today the new Law begins in the giving of the body of the Lord. Likewise, new fire, produced from crystal, is blessed today because, once the smoke of the Law has been extinguished, the light of grace is kindled by Christ’s gift. Penitents are absolved today because today the Lord remitted sins through the new Law, saying: “My body shall be handed over for you, and my blood shall be poured out for you, for the remission of sins.” *Gloria Patri* is silent because the Son of God is killed. The lights are extinguished because the true light—that is, Christ—is extinguished.

[Col. 0746B] The Lord’s body is retained for the following day—though this is not done at Rome—so that communion may be received with the Lord’s Passion on Friday. Before it is blessed, the ampulla containing chrism is wrapped in a white silk shroud, so that half may be visible; but after blessing it is covered, so that no one may see it uncovered, and all may salute it. The ampulla containing chrism is Christ’s body received from the Virgin. The bishop breathes into the ampulla three times, thereby declaring that the Holy Spirit dwells bodily in Christ. Before he went to the altar of the cross, he was for a time covered and for a time uncovered. He was covered when he fled into Egypt and endured human necessities; he was uncovered when he worked miracles. The white shroud is his most pure way of life. Afterwards it is covered so as not to be seen, because Christ, [Col. 0746C] after ascending into heaven following the Resurrection, appeared invisible. We still salute him because we worship him daily. The station is held at the Lateran. The Lateran is so called from Lateranus, who was once beheaded by the Caesarian sword.

## CHAPTER XI.—On the Day of Parasceve

*Parasceve* means “preparation,” because on that day the Jews prepared what was necessary for the Sabbath, as they once did with manna. On the sixth day the earth was filled with animals, and the first human being was formed in God’s image; immediately from the side of the sleeping man a rib was taken and a woman formed. In the sixth age of the world Christ is incarnate, and on the sixth day he is crucified. From his side, as though sleeping upon the cross, blood and water flowed, from which he built the Church. The lesson says: [Col. 0746D] “On the tenth day of the month let each man take a lamb by families and households, and keep it until the fourteenth day of this month; and all the children of Israel shall sacrifice it at evening.” Our Lord is the lamb who entered Jerusalem on the tenth day, was handed over on the fourteenth, and was sacrificed for us on the fifteenth day. The responsory follows with four verses: when Christ assumed human nature, he assumed a body composed of four elements. He hung upon the cross like a judge seated on a tribunal; he judged the converted thief for glory, the unconverted one for punishment. He hung in the middle between two thieves; hence one verse: “In the midst of two animals you shall be known.” There are two classes [Col. 0747A] of afflicted persons: those afflicted who are corrected belong to the converted thief; those not corrected belong to Judas and to the unconverted thief.

Today the Lord’s Passion is brought to mind, for our imitation: for he suffered so that we might follow in his footsteps. Thus the lesson says: “The lamb shall be without blemish. You shall also take a kid and keep it,” etc. The lamb without blemish is Christ’s immaculate body; the kid is his body—that is, we who are sinners. Both animals are mentioned in the observance of Passover. The sacrifice of the paschal lamb is Christ’s sacrifice; the kid is our mortification. The lesson concerning our resurrection also follows, saying: “He will make us alive after two days, and on the third day he will raise [Col. 0747B] us up,” because, if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him. The Tract, “He who dwells,” according to the Romans, promises us life after many labours, where it says: “With length of days I will satisfy him, and I will show him my salvation,” that is, Christ.

Then follows the Passion: in it we see, as it were, Christ himself upon the cross. Two deacons strip the altar, removing things in the manner of thieves, because, when Christ was handed over into the hands of the wicked, the apostles fled and hid themselves like thieves. Mass is not sung on the sixth and seventh days, because for two days the apostles were in mourning, and in their sorrow fasted for those two days; therefore the sacraments are not celebrated at all for two days. Prayers are recited for all ranks, so that in adversities we may have recourse to the patience of Christ’s Passion and to prayers. [Col. 0747C] For the Jews, we do not say, “Let us bend the knee,” because they bent the knee in mockery. We omit the kiss of peace, so that we may avoid among our brethren what Judas did to the Lord.

Then the cross is saluted, but Christ is adored, because we were redeemed on the cross. The cross benefited not only us, but also the angels and all the powers in heaven, and disclosed to them a mystery which they had previously not known. We prostrate ourselves bodily before the cross, mentally before God. As God redeemed the human race through a man, though it had perished through a man, so he restored through wood him who had fallen through wood. Lost Adam had been dispersed through the four regions of the world; the salvation of Adam embraced the four regions of the world through the position of his body upon the wood. The body of the Lord is brought out with the chalice, with unconsecrated wine; [Col. 0747D] the chalice consumed on Thursday is the end of the old Law. Unconsecrated wine is sanctified through consecrated bread.

## CHAPTER XII.—On Holy Saturday

On Holy Saturday vigils are held, because the Lord rose at midnight; and at midnight he will also come, in likeness of the Egyptian time, when Passover was celebrated: the destroyer came, the Lord passed over the tents, and the doorposts of our foreheads were consecrated by the blood of the lamb.

The Romans bless wax mixed with oil and make lambs from it; on the octave they give them to the people for incense and for fumigating houses. Wax is Christ’s humanity; oil is mercy; the lamb made of wax [Col. 0748A] is Christ sacrificed at Passover. The paschal candle signifies the pillar of fire which went before the children of Israel; the deacon who blesses it signifies the angel who bore it.

After eating the lamb, they departed from Rameses on the first day, from Succoth on the second, and on the third from Etham, on which day the pillar appeared. The first day is Christ’s Passion; the second, his descent into hell; the third is Christ’s resurrection. He is a pillar of fire by night, that is, terrible to sinners; a pillar of cloud by day, that is, gentle toward the righteous. The pillar went before those baptized in the sea and cloud; the paschal candle goes before our catechumens. The light is Christ and the grace of the resurrection, by which the present night and the catechumens are illuminated. When they are baptized, by a threefold immersion they are buried with Christ, and with him they will rise [Col. 0748B] from the death of vices.

The paschal candle is blessed by the deacon according to the Roman custom, which makes the lambs. This candle goes before the bishop, who is the head of the people, during the eight days of the neophytes, because the pillar of fire went before the people as far as the promised land. The candle is lit from new fire, to signify Christ’s new teaching in the New Testament, or the new grace by which the night—namely, that of the Lord’s resurrection—was illuminated. Two smaller candles lit from it are the choir of apostles illuminated by Christ. Both go before the catechumens to baptism; both go before us to the promised land: Christ illuminates the Church directly, and also through the apostles.

That catechumens are instructed on the Wednesday after mid-Lent and on Saturday signifies [Col. 0748C] that catechumens are to be imbued with faith and works. In the Church there are two orders, namely the wise and the foolish. By the readings read at Mass in the daytime the wise are instructed; by those read at Matins in the night the foolish are imbued, and therefore they are expounded. Thus on this day the readings are read throughout the whole nocturnal office, because this is suited to the foolish, namely catechumens still placed in ignorance.

The reason they are read without titles is this: to those who are known as citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, to the wise—the authors of the books should be announced, so that, through love for the sweetness of their fellow-citizens’ names, they may drink in the readings more eagerly. But because catechumens do not yet know the citizens of Jerusalem, an unknown author is proclaimed to them to no purpose; authority would be cheapened for them [Col. 0748D] through ignorance. Four readings are read, by which catechumens are instructed.

The table of the tabernacle has four feet. The tabernacle is the Church; the table is sacred Scripture; its four feet are these: the historical sense, the allegorical, the tropological—that is, moral—and the anagogical—that is, higher—sense. History is when an event is related as it happened, as in this history: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” in which the creation of the world and the formation of man are recounted. In this reading the catechumen learns how man was formed and how he fell, lest he himself consent to the flesh as Adam did to Eve.

The second reading is, “And it came to pass in the morning watch,” etc., in which the salvation of the Hebrews and the drowning [Col. 0749A] of the Egyptians are recounted. By this historical event the catechumen is taught that he can be delivered from the hand of the devil through the water of baptism.

Allegory is when, through mystical words or events, the mysteries of Christ’s present reality and of the Church are signified; as in the third reading: “Seven women shall lay hold of one man,” that is, the seven graces of the Holy Spirit lay hold of Jesus, whom they had long desired because they could find no other in whom they might rest in that everlasting station. Likewise: “When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion with water, by the Spirit of judgment and the Spirit of burning.” That is, the priest washes filth with water; God washes sins by the Holy Spirit. Catechumens are shown in this reading what they ought to love—namely, the man whom the seven women laid hold of—and what baptism benefits them: [Col. 0749B] namely, that through the Spirit of judgment and the Spirit of burning, lesser and greater sins are cleansed.

Tropology is moral discourse, delivered in open or figurative words for instruction in morals; as in the fourth reading: “All you who thirst, come to the waters, and listen, you who hear me.” And again: “Let the wicked man abandon his way,” etc. In this reading the catechumen is taught to turn away from evil and do good. As the first two readings are concluded with a canticle on account of their historical narrative, so this discourse is extended by two canticles on account of the two things joined around it: good morals and the heavenly homeland.

Anagoge—that is, discourse whose meaning leads upward—is that which discusses, in mystical or open words, past things, future things, and the future life which is in heaven. Hence catechumens are told in the Canticle: “As the hart longs for fountains of water.” The canticle is sung because in baptism they are to belong to the company of the one hundred and forty-four thousand, who sing the new song which no one could sing except they. To sing is the prerogative of those who rejoice before the Lord beyond others in the innocence with which infants are undoubtedly clothed in baptism.

The priest touches the shoulders and breast of the catechumens with holy oil. Oil pertains to the gift of God’s grace, as it is said: “To another, faith in the same Spirit.” Oil is applied to the shoulders and breast as protection for mind and body; the devil corrupts us through evil thoughts and deeds. We are armed on the shoulders with holy oil—that is, the shield of faith—so that we may bear Christ’s burdens, [Col. 0749D] that is, good works. Upon the breast, as a defense against thoughts, the priest says: “Do you renounce Satan?” that is, the devil, whom you held in your mouth in darkness through the sacrifice of idols? [Reading uncertain.] “And all his works?” that is, the pleasures of the flesh, superfluous foods and drinks, and every luxury? “And all his pomps?” that is, all vain and superfluous honors? By renunciation the former guest, namely the devil, is cast out; by confession the second enters.

“Do you believe in God the Father almighty?” “I believe.” Behold, through faith an entrance is opened to the guest. “Do you believe in his Son?” “I believe.” Behold, an entrance for divine works. “Do you believe in the Holy Spirit?” “I believe.” Behold, the gifts of the Holy Spirit are given to those to be baptized.

[Col. 0750A] The devil rightly possesses infants through the sin of the first man, from which he is now cast out through exorcism. Little children are saved through the faith of their parents and godparents, just as the demon-possessed daughter in the Gospel was delivered through her mother’s faith. Those who are adults and can speak should utter their profession with their own mouths; godparents should answer for little children, because they cannot speak. For just as we are held guilty and liable through another’s sin, so our own sins are released through faith.

In the first prayer the dwelling-place of the guest who is to receive God is cleansed, and his coming is entreated: “Almighty everlasting God, be present, m. pietat. t. m.” Then thanks are given because so great a guest descends to so humble a lodging. Then the divinely wrought miracle concerning water is recalled, where it says: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters”; and that what was done in the preservation of the ark was likewise done as a figure of baptism. Then, after the devil has been expelled, the person is signed with the sign of the cross, so that the devil may have no place to return. Through the invocation of the holy Trinity, the Trinity is present in our baptistery after the example of baptism. The Father is signified where it is said, “I bless you through the true God”; the Son, where it is said, “I bless you through Jesus Christ”; the Holy Spirit, in the final words.

That the voice changes signifies the departure of vices at the presence of the Holy Spirit, now coming into the water, where it says: “May the power of the Holy Spirit descend into this fullness of the font.” Then the candles of the neophytes are placed in the water, because the Holy Spirit is signified by the candle. The pillar of fire went before the children of Israel by [Col. 0750C] night, and the pillar of cloud by day. The pillar of fire is Christ, by whom the apostles were illuminated; the pillar of cloud is the Holy Spirit, by whom the Church is illuminated. The candles of the neophytes are lit from the candles of the Church, because after the priest has introduced them into the fellowship of the Church, then their hearts will be illuminated. When the child is raised from the water, the priest anoints his head with chrism, on account of the occasion of crossing over through death: there he heals the wounds of death and loosens the bonds, as the Samaritan did the half-dead man.

If he dies without confirmation, he will indeed be saved, but will not attain full grace. Through the laying on of hands the bishop gives the Holy Spirit, that is, the nuptial garment. By oil upright conduct is understood; by balsam, holy doctrine. Wisdom pertains to [Col. 0750D] life; knowledge to doctrine. The chrismal anointing pertains to two gifts of the Holy Spirit, namely wisdom and knowledge. Oil pertains to wisdom; balsam, which spreads its fragrance far and wide, to knowledge. These two—that is, doctrine and practice—are among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Wisdom pertains to life; understanding to doctrine; counsel to doctrine; fortitude to life; knowledge to doctrine; piety to life; fear to both. These are the ornaments of the garment which God gives to our mind through the bishop’s laying on of hands; without them it is dangerous for anyone to be found at the king’s banquet. This is permitted to bishops alone, as it was to the apostles.

Without this sign we ought not to be presented before God: [Col. 0751A] when the destroyer sees that sign upon our foreheads, he passes over our houses, because we are not our own but belong to him whose sign we bear. The cross itself is fixed nowhere more suitably than where the high priest fixed the golden plate upon which the ineffable name of God was engraved. The cross is made with chrism, which is prepared from oil and balsam. Through oil the brightness of charity is obtained; through balsam, the fragrance of good repute.

The litanies made around baptism signify the intercessions of the saints for those being reborn. *Litany* is Greek; in Latin it is called *supplication*. Litanies are held before and after baptism because a rainbow is read of around the throne. The throne is the Church, upon which the Lord sits. The color of jasper is the judgment of water; the color [Col. 0751B] of sardius, the judgment of fire. The seven lamps are the seven Spirits of God. Baptism is the glassy sea, in which nothing other is seen outwardly than that which it bears inwardly. Crystal is changed from water into ice and into a precious stone, and thus the grace of baptism is figured. The rainbow is made when the sun shines upon a cloud; after the Flood it is the first sign of propitiation—the intercession of the saints—by which the Lord illuminates and protects the Church. The emerald, like a green stone, signifies those who protect others by prayer with unfading faith.

The threefold immersion signifies the three days of the Lord’s death, with whom we are buried; the lifting from the water, that we rise with him. They wear white garments for eight days, with lighted candles. The garments of the soul are our bodies, which ought to be clean and white from evil acts. The lighted candles are charity [Col. 0751C] in good works for eight days, that is, in the new Law. On Saturday the garments themselves are put off, because on the day of its departure the soul finds Sabbath—that is, rest—and leaves here its garments, that is, its body, to receive them again on the last day. The garments of the white-robed are to be worn by them until they are entirely worn out. The garments are twofold, because a twofold reward is promised to the saints in eternal life: the joy of the soul and the incorruptible glory of the body.

If after baptism we defile our bodies, that is, the garments of the soul, let us immediately hasten to a second baptism, namely repentance, in which we are cleansed by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. Seven pertains to the new Law; ten to the old. [Col. 0751D] If we keep the ten commandments through the sevenfold Spirit, we are joined to God by obedience, from whom we withdrew through disobedience; and we shall see the king himself, our Lord, in his beauty. Therefore that Saturday is ended thus: in the number seventy, seven is multiplied sevenfold by ten.

Septuagesima signifies that time when the children of Israel were oppressed in Egypt by famine and hard labor under Pharaoh, and called upon the Lord their God for their deliverance. The Wednesday at the beginning of the fast signifies when Moses went to deliver them. Lent signifies the time when the plagues were wrought in Egypt. Passover, when they came to the Red Sea, which signifies baptism. They passed through the wilderness under leaders; our neophytes are led for forty days under [Col. 0752A] priests and godparents. The pillar went before the Jews; the candle before the baptized. On Saturday they arrive at the promised land. The forty-two stations of the children of Israel are forty-two days, so that we, who were in the captivity of sins, may return through the examples of the patriarchs, through baptism, to the promised land. Those who baptize are the fathers of the baptized; the godparents are the representatives of those entrusted to them, so that, because priests have no leisure, they may be instructed by the godparents.

When “Lamb of God” is begun at the litany, the neophytes’ candles are begun, or lit, because they receive light through him who takes away the sins of the world. “Glory in the highest” is said because of the glory of the Lord’s resurrection, and because the Holy Spirit now dwells in those in whom the devil dwelt. This is the meaning of the prayer, “O God, who hast made this most holy night,” etc.; likewise of the reading, “If you have risen with Christ,” etc., and below: “For you are dead,” etc. The Alleluia, “The mercy of the Lord,” concerns the baptized; in the Tract his truth is proclaimed. Thus the Alleluia is placed first: mercy here, truth afterward in judgment.

Hebrew is the mother of the other languages and nobler; Latin is inferior and, as it were, a daughter. Hence *Alleluia*, which is Hebrew, is placed first here, which is not done in the other offices. The Gospel recalls Christ’s resurrection and the angels’ address to the women. Before the Gospel no light is carried, but incense, because this alone was offered by the women. That the offertory is not sung signifies [Col. 0752C] the silence of the women. The *Sanctus* is sung, which is the angels’ song, because angels announced his resurrection. The *Agnus Dei* is kept silent because he was not believed to take away the sins of the world. The priest, who is Christ’s vicar, performs the office because Christ appeared to whom he wished.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On the Paschal Season

Passover and Pentecost are most firmly established from the holy Scriptures, and the observance of the days of Lent before Passover has been strengthened by the Church’s consensus. During the eight days of Passover eight offices are held in commemoration of the neophytes. The first has two praises, namely Alleluia, “Give thanks,” and the Tract, “Praise”; the eighth has two Alleluias, “This is the day” and “Praise, O children,” [Col. 0752D] which is not done on any Saturday until Pentecost. The six middle days have Responsories and Alleluia.

The first life was not everlasting for the sinner; the final rest is everlasting for the penitent. The eighth day is the one which is first; thus the first life is restored, but as eternal life. Because Adam first possessed life, Alleluia is sung; and because it was not everlasting, the Tract follows, so that in the humbler language the humility of the later life may be recalled. The neophytes are still in pilgrimage, in which nevertheless they ought to praise God because they have been redeemed. The final rest, which is restored on the seventh day and fulfilled on the eighth, possesses everlasting blessedness. Therefore two Alleluias are sung on the seventh and eighth day: the first because life is restored, the second because it is everlasting. Alleluia is used because [Col. 0753A] Hebrew is the most glorious of all languages.

Two Alleluias are sung on the two Sundays. There are two reasons why the soul on the seventh day, that is, in rest, praises God: one for the joy received of everlasting life; the other for the resurrection yet to be received; or because at the resurrection mind and body will praise the Lord. On each day one Alleluia is celebrated, because meanwhile the soul praises God without the body. On the feasts of saints there are two Alleluias, because they already rejoice rather in the sight of the Lord than those souls which are only in the resurrection of the soul: one because they rest, the other because they see God.

The middle six days of Passover retain Responsories and Alleluia. The number seven signifies rest; six signifies works. Before the resurrection of the body, the souls of the saints are indeed [Col. 0753B] at rest, but they are not in that activity in which, once bodies have been received, they are quickened. For future bodies possess a certain ineffable tranquility of restful activity. By the Responsories is understood the activity of the saints in the body, which will be with every joy, as the Responsory says: “This is the day which the Lord has made,” etc. And because this joy culminates in glorification, Alleluia follows. And to show that this activity is nothing other than the praise of God, Alleluia is sung continuously through six days. The Responsories with verses from the psalm are “Give thanks,” which expresses praise. Yet this praise is concluded by Alleluia because of the nobler language. The verse “Blessed is he who comes” is sung on Thursday; “The stone which they rejected” on Friday, because of the Lord’s Passion, [Col. 0753C] which that same verse expresses.

## CHAPTER XIV.—On the Eight Days of the Neophytes

As the journey of the children of Israel from the Red Sea to the promised land signifies the whole course of the present life, so the eight days of the neophytes signify the course of the present life, in which we ought to live according to Christ’s resurrection. The Red Sea signifies baptism reddened by Christ’s blood; the dying enemies signify past sins. The people are led through the wilderness; the baptized are led to church daily. They receive manna, these the body of Christ, lest they fail on the way of this life. The pillar went before them; the candle goes before these, as a figure of the Holy Spirit, who illumines Christ’s members.

The stages of [Col. 0753D] our course are also signified in this manner. The first day, when they are baptized, is Saturday—that is, rest—and is the state of Adam before he sinned. Adam was so made that he lived without labor and nevertheless worked delightfully. This rest is given to the baptized on Saturday, that thereafter they may perform good works until the following Saturday, just as Adam was devoted to work without labor. The rest and innocent life which Adam had on the seventh day, when God rested from all his works, are now received by the baptized on Saturday. Then, because a journey through the wilderness remains for the baptized, after Alleluia we sing the Tract, that is, patience, through which they must await the promised land. Seven days follow, which pertain to good work, lest the empty house be invaded.

[Col. 0754A] After those six days baptism follows, which introduces them to the promised homeland, where there is everlasting rest: they do not return to any labor, but pass from the joy of the glory of souls to the joy of the incorruptible body. Accordingly, not the Tract but the Alleluia, “Praise, O children,” follows “This is the day which the Lord has made,” etc.

The six days between the two Saturdays recall both periods to us: that of Adam, when he was devoted in paradise to most desirable work; and that in which the children of Israel passed through the wilderness under leaders. During that period their garments were not worn out, and so at last they arrived at freedom in the promised land, which signifies the homeland in which holy [Col. 0754B] souls are received after the present age has passed.

## CHAPTER XV.—On the Day of Passover Itself and the Following Six Days

On the day of Passover the resurrection of the dead will occur at the hour and time at which the Lord rose. In the Introit Christ presents himself to the Father in the Church, saying: “I have risen, and I am still with you.” The prayer, “O God, who hast opened to us the entrance to eternity,” etc., shows that through the resurrection of its head the kingdom of heaven is opened to the saints of the Church. The Epistle admonishes us to separate ourselves from the vices against which we contended during the days of Lent. The Responsory shows how greatly those who are cleansed of vices ought to rejoice. Alleluia teaches wherein we should rejoice: because Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. The Gospel explains the cause of all this joy.

[Col. 0754C] Those six paschal days, on which we sing the Responsory and Alleluia, provide a pattern for all Sundays and feast days which we celebrate from the octave of Pentecost until Septuagesima. The Responsory and Alleluia signify the activity and joy, praise and thanksgiving, of those who persevere in the holiness they received in baptism. For they possess the future kingdom in hope in such a way that, by working here too, they may perseveringly attain blessedness. Alternatively, the active life is understood by the Responsory, the contemplative by Alleluia. We must perform acts here, in order that we may be able to attain what we hope for and await through patience. The Responsories which we sing through seven days, and on the following Sundays or saints’ feast days, signify such acts as [Col. 0754D] preaching, reading, almsgiving, visiting widows, orphans, and the sick. The Alleluia which follows signifies the praise of God, to whom the soul sanctified from every sin is transferred.

## CHAPTER XVI.—On the Fifty Days from the Octave of Passover to the Octave of Pentecost

Those fifty days following from the Saturday of Passover to the octave of Pentecost portray the other life, which we have not yet received. There will be no Responsory there, because no one will preach there, but all will be taught by God. Yet Alleluia will be celebrated there, that is, the joy of souls in received immortality, the reception of bodies, and thanksgiving to God forever. The number fifty signifies this same joy, [Col. 0755A] which among the Hebrews is called Jubilee, that is, full of rejoicing.

Weekdays portray those who confess their sins to a priest, so that they may be corrected by him and receive counsel for repentance. They pass these days without Alleluia, because praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.

## CHAPTER XVII.—On Sundays from Septuagesima to Passover

The Sundays from Septuagesima to Passover portray those who are beaten by the temptations without which the present life cannot be passed. Then Alleluia is not sung, but the Tract, because, although they pertain to contemplation on account of its sweetness and union, nevertheless such a person is not in as great joy as one who does not offend in speech; for such a one is perfect.

Through the days of Lent holy Church portrays those who are properly called penitents, except that they are not excommunicated and do not return to the hands of bishops for reconciliation. At the end of Lent she portrays them in fasting, abstinence, mourning, vigils, and obedience in good works, by which we are reconciled to God in repentance.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On the Season of Pentecost

The season of Pentecost begins from the first day of the resurrection and runs to the fiftieth day after Passover. For forty days after his resurrection the Lord dwelt with his disciples in this land and this life; after he ascended into heaven, [Col. 0755C] after ten days he sent the Holy Spirit to the faithful. Through forty days continence is signified; through ten, the reward of labor is received. Seven times seven are forty-nine; one is added, namely the Lord’s day, and they make fifty. Through the sevenfold Spirit rest will be given to us in Christ.

These fifty days after the Lord’s resurrection are not a figure of labor but of joy and rest. For this reason fasts are relaxed and we pray standing, which is a sign of the resurrection. This is also observed on every Sunday, and Alleluia is sung, signifying that our activity is nothing other than the praise of God, as it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord.”

## CHAPTER XIX.—On Rogation Days and Litanies

[Col. 0755D]

The Greater Litany was instituted by the Romans because of the wars then stirred up by enemies against neighboring kingdoms. The Epistle says: “The continual prayer of a righteous person avails much.” The Gospel sets forth three things: bread, fish, and egg. By bread are understood all good things which grow from the earth; by fish, those from the waters; by egg, animals which copulate together. All these are then in some stage of growth. The shoots of the harvest spring up, the fruits of trees emerge from blossom, the vine and the liquid of the olive break forth in their courses, and the young creatures graze the fields. When these things are necessary for our use, they should be sought from the Lord, that they may be preserved for spiritual purposes.

Thus by bread we may understand charity, by fish faith, by egg hope, [Col. 0756A] by which three the Godhead is worshipped by us. These are especially to be sought at that time when Christ’s resurrection is celebrated by the Church.

The litanies before the Lord’s Ascension were instituted as follows. In the Gallic city of Vienne a very great earthquake overthrew many churches and many people’s houses; many beasts—wolves, bears, and stags—entered the city and devoured a great number of people, and did this throughout the entire year. On the vigil of Passover, moreover, the royal palace in that city was set ablaze by divine fire. Then Bishop Mamertus appointed a three-day fast among God’s people, and the tribulation ceased. By this example the churches of God still everywhere solemnly observe three-day litanies.

## CHAPTER XX.—On the Vigil of Pentecost

[Col. 0756B]

On the vigil of Pentecost four readings are read and four canticles sung before the consecration of baptism, as on the vigil of Passover. There we read: “In the beginning God created,” etc.; in this vigil, “God tempted Abraham.” In the former no canticle follows; in the latter one follows. These two readings bring to mind two fathers: one according to the flesh, the other according to the Spirit. Adam, mentioned in the first reading, is the carnal father from whom we all take our origin. He sinned by not obeying God’s command; therefore no canticle of victory follows. Abraham, however, is the spiritual father: by imitating his faith we become children of God and are called God’s people. He restored by obedience what the first man offended by disobedience; [Col. 0756C] hence a canticle of victory rightly follows, because he killed the vice of disobedience. This reading pertains to victory.

The canticle follows: “The vineyard was made,” etc., namely the mystery of Christ and the Church, which pertains to allegory, because unless good morals had come to them, they would not have passed throughout the whole world. The second reading, “Moses wrote the canticle,” and the canticle, “Give ear, O heaven,” pertain to tropology, for they instruct morals. The third reading, “Seven women shall lay hold of one man,” in which the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit make one man out of the obedient, pertains to allegory. The fourth reading, “Hear, Israel,” in which it says, “Learn where long life and the light of angels and peace are,” pertains to anagoge.
