[Col. 0756D] In the first reading for Passover, Adam is formed from earth, and Eve from Adam: that is, Christ is born of the Virgin, and from him the Church. In the second the devil is slain in the Red Sea, that is, in Christ’s blood. Afterwards, through the love of the seven women, the human race is joined to Christ. Then it is directed toward good works in the reading, “This is the inheritance.” This order is observed on the vigil of Passover; on the vigil of Pentecost it is otherwise. In the latter is recalled how Abraham pleased God through obedience, and how his offspring delighted in good works; yet in the New Testament it is necessary that this offspring be joined to Christ through baptism, and so remain in him until it is led to the kingdom of heaven. Alleluia is sung in commemoration of Adam’s first innocent [Col. 0757A] life; but because that innocence was not everlasting, Alleluia is changed into the Tract.

Let the chrismal anointing administered by the bishop upon the head be observed for seven days, during which the Church celebrates the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles. When the Spirit has come in the seven women to his lodging, a banquet is prepared for each woman on each day. The guest of the Holy Spirit is the human mind; the individual days are stages in the mind’s progress; the banquets are these virtues: in faith, virtue; in virtue, knowledge; in knowledge, abstinence; in abstinence, patience; in patience, piety; in piety, brotherly love; in brotherly love, charity.

Oil is accustomed to warm the limbs of the weary, but balsam is accustomed to give fragrance. [Col. 0757B] The Holy Spirit anoints with oil when, through repentance, he releases the sins of the confessing soul; he anoints with balsam when he illumines the heart through the knowledge of doctrine. The Spirit was oil when he was given to the apostles on earth to release sins; balsam when he was given from heaven so that they might illuminate all by the word. We are anointed with oil and balsam so that we may be saved by faith and works.

## CHAPTER XXI.—On the Time for Conferring Holy Orders

The Saturday of twelve readings was called so not because of twelve readings but because of twelve readers. There are in fact six readings, which were read by the ancient Romans in Greek and Latin. At the Ember seasons, when we observe twelve readings, we customarily fast, even if they fall in the octave of Pentecost. When [Col. 0757C] the feast of the sevenfold Spirit and of the neophytes is celebrated, we ought to begin the twelve readings. From the time of the first month, ordination to holy orders is celebrated at the twelve readings; for in that consecration this is done, that a human being is joined to God.

The first apostles always administered ordinations in the month of December, in which the Lord’s Nativity is celebrated, so that they joined those ordained more closely to Christ’s body. For by three sets of ten decades, forty-two weeks are made in the year; according to Matthew, there are as many generations of Christ with him; and as many weeks are also found from the first Saturday of the first month to the fourth Saturday of the tenth [Col. 0757D] month.

The first consecration is celebrated on the first Saturday of the first month. It generates Christ, as it were, in Abraham’s place, through whom all nations are blessed. This consecration is celebrated in the springtime, which is a suitable season for creations. Abraham too belonged to the third age of this world, which is compared with adolescence, an age suitable for the begetting of children.

The second consecration is in the fourth month, on the second Saturday, which is the beginning of the second list of fourteen weeks. It is assigned to the place of David, who overthrew Goliath; that is, humility overthrows pride. Let those ordained be strong in hand through humility, so that [Col. 0758A] they may cast down pride. It is celebrated in June, which is a season suited to war.

The third consecration is celebrated in September, on the third Saturday, which is the beginning of the third list. It is assigned to the generation of Jeconiah, who is called “the preparation of the Lord”; for those ordained ought to prepare themselves for Christ’s coming. This consecration ends at Christ’s Nativity itself. Sometimes it ends in the third week and has thirteen weeks; sometimes in the fourth and has fourteen. Nor is this without reason: for if the list of the last set of ten decades is counted and Jeconiah is counted once, no more than thirteen generations are found with Christ himself. If Jeconiah is counted a second time, fourteen are found.

## CHAPTER XXII.—On the Fasts of the Four Seasons

[Col. 0758B]

The four fasts are the beginning of the Lenten season. The number ten contains our whole discipline, which is such that the creature serves the Creator. God the Creator is worshipped in three persons; he is worshipped by the soul, which loves him with all its heart, with all its soul, and with all its strength; and the body, composed of four elements—hot, dry, cold, and moist—is subjected to it for governance. If the soul rightly governs its three faculties and the body its four, making seven, man is subjected to the Creator, and they make ten.

The year turns through four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These four seasons are accustomed, through their own delights, to draw us back from love of the Creator. Therefore fasting must be observed in each season, so that our four [Col. 0758C] elements may be chastened, lest they be stolen away by love of the world. For these four elements are joined in their nature to the four seasons of the year.

Spring is hot and moist. In it we keep one fast, so that the element of moisture in us may be chastened, lest it consent to the deceptive beauty of spring. From moisture and heat the beauty of the earth is born. Summer is dry and hot; in it we keep the second fast, so that the element of heat in us may be chastened, lest it consent to carnal burning. Autumn is cold and dry; in it the third fast is observed, lest through some languor of spirit we wither, decay, and be found without the richness of oil in the eternal dwelling. For at that season we gather what we shall enjoy in the future. The fourth fast is observed in winter, which [Col. 0758D] is cold and moist, lest our members be dissolved through flux and luxury in feasting and drinking, and through this the love of God be neglected.

Since, therefore, four times of day hinder us from love of heavenly things—morning, noon, evening, and night—for through these we are daily drawn back from love of eternal things, each fast has three days, because each season has three months: for each month an individual day is consecrated to fasting. But since daily sins weigh us down, one fast for each season does not suffice; and therefore we introduce the season of Lent, in which daily sins are afflicted. The number ten, which belongs to our discipline, multiplied by four [Col. 0759A] makes forty. Within this number ten the holy Trinity of God presides and governs its creature, so that it may be alien to the deception of the first parent.

These fasts are likewise celebrated on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday: on Wednesday because on that day the Jews took counsel to kill Christ; on Friday because they killed him; on Saturday the fast is concluded according to Roman custom, because of the apostles’ sorrow.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—On Ordination

It is especially celebrated on that day of consecration because God sanctified the seventh day. Therefore, since the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the sevenfold Spirit given to us, sanctification is commemorated on the seventh day, in which rest is commended. [Col. 0759B] The consecration of a bishop is transferred to the Lord’s Day: he is the vicar of the apostles—indeed, of Christ; on that day he receives the gift of the Holy Spirit, the day on which it illumined the hearts of the apostles.

On Wednesday two readings are read. In the fourth age of the world the Law and prophecy flourished; those being consecrated should possess knowledge of the Law and the prophets. On Friday one reading is read, because the Law and the prophets are recapitulated in the one Gospel, which is read in the sixth age of the world. On Saturday, when the blessing is given, four readings are read, because there are four orders blessing the Lord: the house of Israel, the house of Jacob, the house of Levi, and those who fear the Lord. The fifth reading is from the fiery furnace, because those to be consecrated ought to be tested by the furnace—that is, by many tribulations—[Col. 0759C] before which we shall not bend the knee, lest we worship Nebuchadnezzar’s statue; so that their address may be separated from the error of the Gentiles. In the sixth reading perseverance in good works is taught; in the Tract humility is taught; in the *Benedictus* the blessing—that is, the praise—of those consecrated is maintained.

According to Jerome, *clerus* means “lot”; a cleric is called God’s lot, because he receives tithes—that is, the Lord’s portion. Tonsure began in the Law with the Nazirites, and in the Gospel with Peter. The priests of the Law wore a *cydaris* [turban], but kings a crown. Christ, king and priest, made us kings and priests: kings, that we may govern our morals; priests, that we may mortify the desire of the flesh. The bareness of the head is the *cydaris*; the hair signifies the crown. By the head the mind is understood, in which is knowledge of God; it must be shaven [Col. 0759D] of hair—that is, of superfluous thoughts. The crown which we wear on the lower part of the head is reason, by which we govern worldly matters.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—On Those to Be Ordained, and Their Dignity and Offices

Those who are ordained are incorporated into Christ. He himself was a doorkeeper, as he says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, the doorkeeper opens to him.” He acted as an exorcist when he expelled demons. He was a reader when he read Isaiah. He was an acolyte when he restored sight to the blind and said: “I am the light of the world.” He was a subdeacon when he changed water into wine; a deacon when he washed the disciples’ feet; a priest when [Col. 0760A] he gave his body; a bishop when he blessed them.

When a doorkeeper is ordained, he receives the keys of the church, and he opens the church door itself. If anyone introduces another into the Church by faith, he is a doorkeeper. A reader is so called from reading; we are readers when we instruct someone entering among the Christian people concerning conduct. An exorcist is called an adjurer; if anyone can expel the devil’s vice from a person by his prayers, he is an exorcist. An acolyte is a candle-bearer. The light carried before the Gospel or sacrifice signifies joy; its blessing pertains to prophecy. Whoever, by preaching, ministers the fire of the heavenly word, by which brothers may be illumined to knowledge and inflamed to love God, [Col. 0760B] is an acolyte.

A subdeacon is called an under-minister. He receives from the bishop the chalice and paten, vessels which the deacon carries to the altar for the body and blood of the Lord. It is not his office to read the Epistle, but the reader’s. A deacon is called a minister, namely of the priest, because they arrange the heavenly banquet at the Lord’s table. The laying on of hands is performed for him, by which the operation of the Holy Spirit is understood: in one, wisdom; in another, faith; in another, chastity. He receives the stole on the left shoulder—that is, the Lord’s light burden in the active life. He reads the Gospel, because, while Christ preached it, he made himself our minister.

A presbyter is called an elder, so that he may be grey not in head but in mind. His hands are anointed with oil, that they may be clean for offering sacrifices to God and generous for other works of mercy. [Col. 0760C] Formerly presbyter and bishop were the same; *sacerdos* [priest] is so called from sacred leadership. The work of the presbyter pertains to the gift of the Spirit of wisdom. A pontiff is so called as though “making a bridge” for the people to heaven. An *antistes* is one who stands before, or stands against—namely, against heretics. A bishop is one who watches over by word and example. He is the bridegroom of the Church. As many gather at a wedding, so here many flock, as though to the wedding of the Church, at a bishop’s consecration: that they may rejoice together over one ordained to perfection and jointly pour out prayers to God. He is Christ’s vicar; therefore he is anointed with oil on the head: Christ is the head of the Church; oil on the head is charity in the mind. In Christ’s place he governs the Church. The blessing of all the elect will be common, but [Col. 0760D] their dwellings will differ according to the quality of their works.

## CHAPTER XXV.—On the Vestments of Priests and Bishops

The vestments of priests pertain to the conduct of Christians. In divine services they put on linen garments; in daily affairs they use woollen ones. Linen garments are subtle prayers to God; woollen garments are coarse speech to the people. The *amictus* [amice] is so called because it is wrapped around, by which the neck is girded on every side. In this garment chastening of the voice is enjoined. Next comes the *poderis*, that is, the ankle-length garment called white, which restrains the whole body from wicked works and the mind from perverse thoughts. The girdle signifies chastity. Sandals cover the foot beneath and leave it bare above. Through sandals, or *cambagae*, the perfect person is invited [Col. 0761A] to preach the Gospel, which is not concealed by earthly advantages.

The chasuble, because it belongs to all clerics, also signifies works that belong to all: hunger, vigils, reading, prayer, and so forth. The chasuble is double over the shoulders and over the breast behind the back. By the shoulders works are expressed: the double garment on the shoulders is good works before one’s neighbour and before God. On the breast it should be double—that is, doctrine and truth: truth inwardly, doctrine directed toward people. By the stole is understood the Lord’s sweet yoke—that is, the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—On the Dalmatic

The dalmatic is holy and undefiled religion: to visit orphans and widows. The dalmatic has two scarlet lines at the back, and likewise at the front; [Col. 0761B] because the Old and New Testaments shine red with love of God and neighbour. To be undefiled pertains to God; to visit brothers pertains to one’s neighbour. The scarlet colour signifies works of mercy, which are performed from charity toward orphans and widows. By the whiteness of the dalmatic is indicated the purity of those who are visited. The fringes which extend from the dalmatic are words of preaching. The dalmatic has thirty fringes at the back and front, fifteen lines on either side, because charity produces fifteen branches in the Old and New Testaments. By the right and left shoulders are understood prosperity and adversity, in both of which charity benefits brothers.

The fifteen branches of charity are: “It is patient, it is kind, it is not jealous, it does not act perversely, it is not puffed up, it is not ambitious, it does not seek [Col. 0761C] its own things; it is not provoked, it does not think evil, it does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.” The line in the middle is, as it were, the trunk of charity. The lines or fringes on the right or left—namely those at the back—pertain to the commandments of the Old Testament; those at the front pertain to the New Testament. The left side has fringes because the active life is anxious and troubled about many things. The right side has none, because the contemplative life is tranquil. The fullness of the arms or sleeves is the cheerfulness of the giver.

The deacon who reads [wears?] the chasuble is girded with the pierced left side because he wishes to imitate Christ, [Col. 0761D] who was pierced in the side by a lance. The undershirt with which the pontiff is clothed after the *camisia* [alb] signifies inward virtues and the prayer of higher matters, which is not open to all but to the perfect and the greater: namely faith, hope, and charity.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—On the Archbishop’s Pallium

The pallium of archbishops is over all the garments; as the plate upon the forehead belongs to the pontiff alone, so by it the archbishop is distinguished from other bishops. The pallium signifies the collar which those lawfully competing used to receive. Its having two lines from top to bottom, back and front, signifies that the pontiff bears, in the shoulder-line, by doing and teaching, the commandments of the Old Testament from the beginning of Genesis to the end; and in the breast-line, the New Testament from the primitive [Col. 0762A] Church to the end.

The circle around the neck is the Lord’s discipline. In antiquity singers received a crown on the head and a collar on the neck. The crown on the head is charity in the mind; the collar on the neck is action in preaching, so that he fulfils in works what he teaches in words. The crown is the grace of the New Testament; the collar, the hope of the heavenly kingdom, whose outstanding splendour, after the likeness of a crown or collar, will never be enclosed by any end. A handkerchief is carried in the left hand, with which the superfluities of the eyes and nostrils are wiped away. These are pious and clean thoughts, by which we wipe away the troubles of the mind arising from bodily weakness and the present life.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—On Sandals

A bishop has a fastening on his sandals which a presbyter does not have. It belongs to the bishop to run here and there [Col. 0762B] through the parish to govern the people, and therefore they are fastened, lest they fall from his feet. These signify the strengthening of the steps of the mind, which move amid crowds of people. The presbyter, however, who offers sacrifices at home, walks more securely. The deacon also has a fastening on his sandals, because it is his duty to go with the retinue. The subdeacon’s are different, lest he be mistaken for a deacon.

Sandals signify the course of the preacher; the sole beneath signifies that the preacher should not entangle himself in earthly affairs. The tongue of white leather beneath the heel signifies that he should be innocent and without deceit. The tongue which rises from there, separated from the leather of the sandals, is the tongue of those outside, who bear good witness to the preacher. They are in the lower part and are, in some manner, separated from the conduct of spiritual persons. The upper tongue [Col. 0762C] is the tongue of spiritual persons, who introduce the preacher into the work of preaching; they seek these things in the preacher’s outward life. Inside, the sandals are surrounded with white leather: so the preacher’s intention should be bright before God and of pure conscience. Outwardly, however, it appears whole, because the preacher’s life seems despised by secular people.

The upper part of the sandals, through which the foot enters, is sewn with many threads, so that the two leathers may not come apart. At the beginning the preacher ought to apply himself to many virtues and sayings of Scripture, so that outward works may not be separated, before God, from those things which are inwardly intended. The tongue of the sandals, which is over the feet, signifies the preacher’s tongue. The seam, made by the cobbler’s work, running from the tongue of the sandal to its end, is evangelical perfection. The seams running from either side are the Law and the prophets, which are recapitulated in the Gospel. For they are folded back to the middle seam, which runs to the end. The fastening pertains to the mystery of Christ’s incarnation; the straps signify preaching at one’s own expense beyond what is required.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—On the Vestments of the Presbyter

The panther is a beast with seven colours: black, white, grey, yellow, green, sky-blue, and red. This panther eats various herbs, remains fixed upon a rock, and heals sick creatures that come to it from illness by its breath. By the panther the presbyter is understood, who has seven garments and seven virtues. The black [Col. 0763A] colour is humility; white, chastity; grey, discernment; yellow, wisdom; green, faith; sky-blue, hope; red, charity. The different herbs are the different sayings of Scripture; the rock is Christ; the sick beasts are human beings ill from sins. The priest heals them if he brings forth to them sayings from the Scriptures.

When the presbyter prepares himself, he begins, as it were, a duel with the devil for the Church. He places the shoulder-garment on his head—that is, hope as a helmet; the alb—that is, faith as a breastplate; the girdle—that is, chastity—as a belt; the under-girdle—that is, testimonies of Scripture or examples of the saints—as quiver and arrows; the stole—that is, obedience or justice—as lance or sling; the *fanon* in his hand—that is, action—as club; the chasuble—that is, charity—as shield; the book of the Gospel—that is, [Col. 0763B] the word of God—as sword; sandals—that is, preaching—as fighting footwear.

## CHAPTER XXX.—On Bells

Under the Law the people were summoned by trumpets; among us, by bells. A bell is made of bronze, a durable and resonant metal, having an iron clapper within. Bells are the mouths of New-Testament preachers, which endure longer than the trumpets of the Old Testament and resound more loudly. The mouths of preachers will endure until the end, and their sound will be heard afar, even to the ends of the earth. The iron within is their tongue; the rope is the measure of our life. This rope begins from the wood, signifying sacred Scripture of the New Testament, descending from the [Col. 0763C] wood of the Lord’s cross. That wood is held from above because the Lord’s cross is upheld by the prophets and ancient fathers. The rope passes down to the priest’s hand: that is, Scripture must pass into priests’ works.

The presbyter should move the bell, so that he may know that he himself is signified by it. When he follows the rope upward, let him consider how greatly he ought to raise himself to good works; when he pulls it downward, let him consider how greatly he still lies in wickedness. The binding by which the clapper is tied is a certain moderation, which knows how at the proper time to move the clapper of the tongue, so that the lips may strike. When the binding is drawn, the rope moves the clapper. Thus, when modesty moves the preacher’s tongue in accordance with the authority of sacred Scripture.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—On the Church

[Col. 0763D]

The Church is the people summoned through the ministers of the Church; the building itself is also called a church because it contains the Church. *Synagogue* means “gathering,” which pertains to cattle gathered for pasture; but *Church* means “calling together,” which pertains to rational beings. It is called *Kyrica*, that is, “belonging to the Lord”: *Kyrios* is Greek, “Lord” in Latin. It is also called a basilica, that is, a royal house: *basileos* means “king,” as though *basilaus*, that is, “basis of the people,” meaning “praise of the people.” People gather there to hear God’s judgments and eat the Lord’s body. Men stand on the southern side, women in the northern, so that the stronger sex may show that stronger saints are set amid the greater temptations [Col. 0764A] of this world, and the weaker sex that weaker persons are in a more suitable place.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—On Women’s Veils

Pope Linus, by the command of blessed Peter, decreed that a woman should enter church with veiled head, out of reverence for the priest; so that, as before a judge, she should appear subject before the priest, who is the Lord’s vicar, because of the origin of guilt; and lest men be incited to lust.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—On the Choir

A choir is the agreement of singers. It is called a choir because at first they stood around altars in the form of a crown and sang psalms. Singers are those who praise God and stir others to praise. The garments of singers are linen, white, and long: linen, that they may be subtle [Col. 0764B] in understanding; white, that they may be clean and chaste; long, that they may persevere in good to the end. The width of their copes is the breadth of charity; the fringes, good works.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—On the Ceremonies in a Bishop’s Mass

Formerly Mass began with the Reading and the Gospel; this custom is still retained at the vigil of both Easter and Pentecost. Pope Celestine instituted the Introit and the prayer. The bishop’s entrance into Mass, since he is Christ’s vicar, signifies Christ’s coming into the world and the gathering of the people to him, whether through his own preaching or that of his preachers. The bishop’s entrance is celebrated; at his seating, the office touches in part upon what Christ bodily performed on earth, or his disciples performed, until [Col. 0764C] he ascended to his Father’s seat. Hence the custom arose that no one sits in church while the present office is being performed, because those who are called to God’s worship are assigned to Christ’s labour.

While the heralds sing psalms, Christ mounted his chariot and came into the world; hence it is said: “The chariot of God is manifold, ten thousandfold.” The chariot of ten thousand is the multitude of saints in the orders of ecclesiastics and in their hearers. There are seven grades of those ordained: doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, and presbyters. The eighth is that of hearers; the ninth and tenth, that of male and female singers. “Thousand” is added because of perfection. When the Lord comes, he brings with him prophets, wise men, and scribes. Deacons occupy the place of prophets, who announce from the Gospel the life to come; subdeacons occupy the place of wise men, who know how to arrange vessels and bring forth things new and old. Acolytes occupy the place of scribes, who kindle believers’ hearts from sacred Scripture.

Incense precedes in the thurible, signifying Christ’s body full of sweet odour, which must first be preached among all nations. Then candlesticks are carried, so that, upon the foundation already laid, the light of preachers may shine before people. The subdeacons follow those already illumined, because wisdom ought to speak among the perfect. The Gospel is joined to them, in which perfection has been made clear. The bishop and those joined to him follow the Gospel, as it is said: “If [Col. 0765A] anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

Seven deacons minister to the bishop in the place of prophets because Scripture is divided sevenfold between the New and Old Testaments, which minister in the Gospel. The bishop and those joined to him are in the middle after the Gospel, because, as Christ’s vicar, he follows the Gospel. In the New Testament it is divided into four: the Acts of the Apostles, the seven Catholic Epistles, the fourteen Epistles of Paul, and the Apocalypse; in the Old into three: the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. If there are five deacons, they show five ministers of books serving the Gospel. The bishop in the middle, like the Gospel, has in the New Testament the first order of historical preaching, the second [Col. 0765B] of epistles, the third of prophecy, such as the Apocalypse; in the Old, one of law and another of prophecy. If there are three, they are the three ministries of three books: the Gospel, the source of all wisdom, in the middle; in the New Testament the other two are epistle and prophecy; in the Old one is the Law. For among the ancients all Scripture in the New Testament is called Law. If there is one, he shows the one commandment of love, as it is said: “The whole Law is fulfilled in one saying: You shall love your neighbour as yourself.” The prophet’s ministry is to establish evangelical truth from the books mentioned; and they should have before them the wisdom of the subdeacons, so that they may prophesy at the fitting time, and may fulfil the work of the acolytes, the light of teachers, by expounding the books.

Wisdom—that is, the subdeacons—go in the midst [Col. 0765C] of young female timbrel-players, that they may teach what those timbrel-players ought to praise. The timbrel-players are the singers; the singers’ ministry resounds with praises. The young women are the new Churches, praising God with the flesh subdued. When the bishop comes, he stands bowed and gives peace to the ministers on his right and left. Christ is presented to the Church, which previously desired: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” He gave peace both to those from the Jews and to those from the Gentiles. He also offers peace to the singers who stand behind, because he bestowed peace both upon those who were under the Law and upon those who were in the New Testament.

Then the singers, from the arrival of the subdeacons—that is, of God’s wisdom—understand the Trinity to praise God and say: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy [Col. 0765D] Spirit.” The deacons, like a choir of prophets, stand with him in humility and say: “Lord, teach us to pray,” because the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, teaches how to pray. The praisers of the Lord’s coming, or singers, announce that the time has come for the hearts of the fathers to be turned to the children. As Abraham saw three angels and worshipped one God, so now the sons of Abraham ought to believe and say: “As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, unto ages of ages.”

Two deacons go in turn, one on each side, to kiss the sides of the altar, because Christ sent the apostles two by two before his face. Their kiss signifies what they say upon entering: “Peace to this house.” The altar signifies the hearts of the elect. Afterwards they return to the bishop, as the Gospel reads: “For the apostles returned and reported [Col. 0766A] to him what they had done.” The disciples are with Christ; Christ prays alone.

Then the singers, recalling the time of the Lord’s passion, sing a verse from the psalter. The psalter is struck on its lower part and has at its upper part that in which it resounds. Thus the work of the Lord’s passion has a blow from below, and from above the sweetness of resurrection. Then the bishop ascends to the altar and kisses it and the Gospel. This is Christ’s ascent to Jerusalem for the cross at the time of his passion. The kiss of the Gospel is the peace of the two Gospels; the kiss of the altar is Christ’s peace with people who imitate his passion. The Gospel remains upon the altar until it is read; likewise evangelical teaching first sounded in Jerusalem and from there went out into public. [Col. 0766B]

Then the bishop moves to the right of the altar: Christ chose the right-hand life after his resurrection. The deacons stand behind him in order. Those who stand after Christ are strengthened to follow him unto death and to pass with him into eternal life. The greater part stands on the right, the smaller on the left: the right side is eternal things, the left temporal things. We ask God for eternal things—justice, wisdom, and charity—and also for temporal things, the fruits of the earth and peace in our land. Amid all these acolytes stand and hold candles in their hands: teachers should shine both in words and works.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—On *Kyrie eleison*

*Kyrie eleison* [Greek: “Lord, have mercy”] is sung for three reasons. First, that the priest’s mind may be made serene for attending to what he says with his mouth; second, that he may be worthy, so far as human nature permits, to speak with God; third, that if, through some bodily weariness, the spirit should pray without attention of mind, the Lord may not look upon this in his wrath but with a judgment of mercy. Therefore in all offices *Kyrie eleison* is said before the Lord’s Prayer: that is, “Lord, have mercy.” Then the acolytes lay down their candles: that is, after good works they humble themselves, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—On Candles

The candle standing in the middle signifies Christ, who said: “Where two or three are gathered in [Col. 0766D] my name, I am in their midst.” The seven candles are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. As the bishop ascends to the seat, the candle-stands are moved from their places into a single line, except for the first, as far as the altar. The candle-stands are the various gifts of the Holy Spirit; the single line is the unity of the Holy Spirit in each gift. That it begins from the first indicates Christ, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds as far as the altar—that is, the hearts of the elect. What is subsequently performed in the office of Mass signifies the time in which the apostles and their successors carry out the Lord’s affairs, which ends when the Gospel has been read.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—On *Gloria in excelsis*

Pope Telesphorus instituted the singing of *Gloria in excelsis* at Mass. Hilary, bishop of the Church of Poitiers, composed the *Gloria in excelsis*. Pope Symmachus decreed that the same hymn be sung on Sundays and on the feast-days of martyrs. When the priest begins the *Gloria in excelsis*, he turns himself toward the east, because the angels sang it in the east—that is, in Bethlehem, where Christ was born. The bishop’s passage to the altar signifies Christ’s passage, as we said concerning the passion, into eternal life. Therefore in this place the *Gloria in excelsis* is said, because ineffable glory in the heights came about when, by his passage, Christ united the souls of the saints to the fellowship of angels. The angel announced this joy at his birth. After the resurrection peace was given to human beings, when heavenly and earthly things are united under one Lord.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—On *Dominus vobiscum*

[Col. 0767B] “Peace be with you” is taken from the Gospel; “The Lord be with you” from the book of Ruth; and “And with your spirit” from the Epistle of Paul. When the priest says, “The Lord be with you,” he turns his face toward the people, because we present our face to those whom we greet. The greeting of presbyter or bishop and the people’s response signify that bishop and people ought to have one affection, as guests of one Lord.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—On the Collects

He says the prayer facing east, where heaven rises, because knowledge of God and of his essence is greater in heaven—in angels or the souls of saints—than among saints dwelling on earth. The priest’s prayer is Christ’s blessing over the disciples when he [Col. 0767C] ascended to heaven. When it has been completed, the bishop ascends to his seat and sits. Christ, having ordered his course, places presbyters in their appropriate order, deacons in theirs, subdeacons in theirs, the remaining grades in theirs, and likewise the hearers, each in his own place. He ascends into heaven to sit at the right hand of the Father; those will sit with him to whom it is said: “You shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” Some sit with him; others stand. Those who sit are members of Christ resting in peace; those who stand are set in conflict. Head and members are one body. In some Christ sits; in others he stands. The bishops’ place is set higher, that they may oversee and guard the people; and as the vine-grower has a higher place to guard his vineyard, that is, his city—the holy Church.

[Col. 0767D] A Reading is so called from reading, because it is not sung; while it is read, we customarily sit. The Reading is preaching; sitting is obedience; the Response is the confession of believers. Alternatively: through the Reading, the preaching of the Old Testament, which is lower; through the Response, the preaching of the New Testament, which is more excellent.

## CHAPTER XL.—On Anniversaries

Our body consists of four elements—hot, dry, cold, and moist—so that the sins which we committed through the body may be cleansed on the fourth day. After the third day—that is, on the seventh after someone’s death—we offer sacrifice for him. Alternatively, there are seven days in the week, so that whatever he sinned throughout all time, [Col. 0768A] which revolves in seven days, may be washed away: we observe the seventh day. Thirty days complete a month; each action is expressed through a day, but the end of actions through a month. Therefore the thirtieth day is observed, so that what he sinned against faith in the holy Trinity through the Decalogue of the Law may be cleansed. In a year the sun completes its course; Christ is signified by the sun, the Church by the moon. Therefore the anniversary day is observed, so that whatever we have sinned against Christ or against the Church may be forgiven.

Just as the anniversary day of saints is recalled to our memory in their honour for our own benefit, so that of the dead is recalled for their benefit. It is good at every time to pray for the dead, even if the day of their death is unknown through forgetfulness or ignorance. When sacrifices or alms are offered for all baptized dead, they are thanksgivings for the very good, propitiations for the not very bad; for the very bad, even if they provide no aid to the dead, they are nevertheless whatever consolations they may be to the living. But for those whom they do benefit, they benefit them in this: that remission may be complete, or at least that condemnation itself may become more tolerable. Yet they benefit no one there unless here they cooperate with good works.

## CHAPTER XLI.—On the Lenten Season

Septuagesima signifies our captivity from paradise into the world; Lent our return to the land of promise—that is, to paradise. Then the Tract, so called from drawing, is sung, because we tread the journey of this life with toil and hardship. Veils are hung because heavenly things are now hidden from us. The three days before Easter signify the three and a half years during which Antichrist will reign. He will be born in Babylon, reared at Chorazin and Bethsaida by magicians, and filled with the devil. He will subjugate the world to himself in four ways.

The powerful, by money: for every hidden treasure will be manifest to him. The common people, by terror: for he will inflict every kind of torment. The clergy, by wisdom: for he will know all Scripture perfectly and interpret it fittingly concerning himself. Monks and saints, by miracles: for he will perform every holy sign powerfully, even raising the dead. Therefore *Gloria Patri* is not sung, because then all praise of God will be silent. Bells are not rung because preaching will cease. Lights are extinguished [Col. 0768D] because all the Church’s oracles are taken away. Penitents are brought in because Jews are converted to faith in Christ. Chrism is prepared because they become Christians. Feet and church are washed because Jews are baptized. The Lord’s Passion is recalled because Christ’s body—that is, the Church—suffers a grievous passion. Altars are stripped because all holy things are trampled by the Gentiles. The cross is venerated, which will then be raised for mockery. Baptism is performed because then they are baptized in blood. The candle or new fire is consecrated because the grace or love of the Holy Spirit consoles them. The striking of the board is Antichrist’s terror; the great sound made at the *Benedictus* is the immense fear and astonishment of unbelievers at the death of unbelieving Antichrist.

## CHAPTER XLII.—On the Paschal Season

[Col. 0769A]

Easter is said to derive from the east, because just as there the sun rises and in the west as it were dies, so this Sun of righteousness, Christ, who underwent setting in death, here rose again. At the same time—namely, at Easter—and at the same hour at which Christ rose, our resurrection will take place. Easter is celebrated on the fourteenth moon, that is, in April, when it is full. The moon signifies the Church: when the number of the elect has been completed, then the Church will, as it were, be full; immediately in the fourth age there will be resurrection. One age was before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace, the fourth under eternal joy.

On the first day is the resurrection of the Church, which says to the bridegroom: “I have risen.” On the second day its consoler, the Holy Spirit, says: “[Col. 0769B] The Lord has brought you into a land flowing with milk and honey,” that is, full of every sweetness and delight. On the third day: “He gave them to drink the water of wisdom,” that is, he filled them with the fullness of knowledge. On the fourth, the bridegroom says to the bride: “Come, blessed of my Father.” He does not say, “I bless you,” but rather, “You are blessed of the Father” through faith and works. On the fifth day they praised “the victorious hand,” that is, Christ, by whose aid they conquered both the world and the devil. On the sixth day: “The Lord led them out in hope, and the sea covered their enemies”: what they had always hoped for, they now possess. Their enemies, that is, persecutors and demons, have been swallowed up in the sea and in hell. On the seventh day: “The Lord led forth his people in exultation, and his elect in joy.” Then they will obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and groaning will flee. Then [Col. 0769C] two Alleluias are sung, because soul and body rejoice eternally.

Therefore, on the eighth day there is sung: “As newborn infants,” because, just as an infant is born from its mother into the world, so they are born from death into life. The fifty days afterward signify eternal joy. The Ascension of the Lord signifies our exaltation into heaven. At Pentecost the Law of fear was given to the Hebrew people as to servants, in the fire of terror. Ten days after the Ascension—that is, after the ten commandments of God requiring submission—the Law of love was given in the fire of the Holy Spirit to the Christian people as to sons.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—On the Feast of Saint John the Baptist

At the Nativity of St John the Baptist Mass is sung in the morning, because the angel foretold joy, saying: “Many [Col. 0769D] shall rejoice at his birth.”

## CHAPTER XLIV.—On the Feast of Saint Peter in Chains

The day of the Kalends of August was formerly held famous because of the victory of Caesar Augustus. On that day the chains of St Peter were afterward brought to Rome, so that, as it had formerly been celebrated in honour of the prince of the world, it might now be celebrated in honour of the prince of the apostles.

## CHAPTER XLV.—On the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary

A certain solitary man heard, on one night each year, harmony in heaven. As he wondered at this, it was told him that holy Mary had been born on that night. Although her birth is unknown to human beings, it is reverently celebrated by angels. When he reported this to the Church, it was instituted that she should be venerated.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—On the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist

[Col. 0770A]

When the Beheading of St John the Baptist is observed, his head is then found. For he was beheaded about Easter, that is, at the Annunciation of St Mary; but here the event is commemorated. At Mass neither *Gloria Patri* nor *Gloria in excelsis* nor *Alleluia* is sung, after the manner of Christ’s Passion and because it took place before Christ’s resurrection.

## CHAPTER XLVII.—On Canonical Matins

At the beginning of Matins, “Lord, thou shalt open my lips” is said, so that those who at Compline were closed, as it were, under a seal, with the verse “Keep us, O Lord, as the apple of thine eye” and with the final blessing, may now be opened for the praise of God. Then [Col. 0770B] divine aid is invoked through the verse “O God, make speed to help me”; thereafter the holy Trinity is glorified through the *Gloria Patri*, in respect of things past, present, and future. Afterward the singer’s trumpet gives the signal through the antiphon of the invitatory, so that Christians everywhere may be awakened and gather at the school of the doctors and pastors of the Church.

Then twelve psalms are sung, by which are signified the Fathers who cultivated the Lord’s vineyard before the Law. By these, those who assemble for the nocturnal office are instructed that from the beginning of the world the Lord had preachers in his Church, who cultivated God’s people through their labours, so that they might seek a return to their own homeland after Christ’s resurrection. The first psalm, “Blessed is the man,” corresponds [Col. 0770C] in some manner to righteous Abel, whose blood was shed as a type of the blood of Jesus Christ. And the psalm “O Lord my God, in thee have I put my trust” suits Noah and his sons and wives, who were saved through water. And the psalm “Save me, O Lord, for the godly man hath ceased” befits Abraham, who alone stood firm against worshipping idols while the rest fell into it.

Thereupon follows the verse, through which the attention is turned to other things: namely, from psalmody to the reading, or to the Gospel hymn—that is, the *Magnificat* or *Benedictus*—or to the Lord’s Prayer, whose prologue is *Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison* (“Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy”); or to the prayer spoken by the priest alone. Then they turn toward the altar, because our minds ought to turn toward Christ. [Col. 0770D] The Romans, however, do not sing the Lord’s Prayer before the reading.

Then follow the readings and responsories, which signify the time of Abraham, who entered the vineyard at the sixth hour. We, however, are admonished at midnight to go forth before God, as it is said: “I prevented the dawning of the morning”; that is, at midnight. All the time before Christ is regarded as night; the memory of those dead in Christ is recalled during the night, because their passage and rest are compared to night.

By the psalms the work of the preachers is shown; by the readings, their teaching. A responsory is so called because it responds to the reading. The singer rises for the responsory so that he may arouse minds which have heard teaching in the reading, and that they may rise to good deeds in practice. The mind of the exhorter is restrained by the verse, [Col. 0771A] in which he alone labours, lest he be lifted up through arrogance. Formerly the *Gloria Patri* was not sung after the verse in the third responsory; instead, the preceding text was repeated. The modern practice, however, has been instituted that it should be sung, so that the Trinity may be praised in all things.

That nine readings are read and as many responsories sung signifies that through Christ’s resurrection we tend toward the heavenly Jerusalem and toward the nine orders of angels. They are divided in groups of three by the intervals of psalms in the three nocturns, in which are recalled the three times named in the Gospel: the first watch, the second watch, and the third watch. For in the first watch is recalled the future resurrection in Christ of those who cultivated the Lord’s vineyard before the Law; in the second, that of those who did so under the given Law until [Col. 0771B] Christ’s coming; in the third, that of Christ’s disciples. Hence *Alleluia* is also sung here.

“Preserve me, O Lord” commemorates those of Levitical stock resting in Christ; “Hear me, O Lord,” the rest of the Judges; “I will love thee, O Lord,” the palm of victory of the kings of the Old Testament; “May the Lord hear thee in the day of tribulation,” the triumph of Christ’s martyrs; “O Lord, in thy strength shall the king rejoice,” the abiding kingdom of spiritual kings.

These persons are members of that head whose kingdom is commemorated in the psalm, “The Lord reigneth; he is clothed with majesty.” The three nocturns on Sundays signify the resurrection of bodies; the three sung on saints’ feasts recall the blessedness of souls, which they receive [Col. 0771C] when they become citizens among heavenly and good spirits. Night signifies ignorance. From Adam until Christ it was as though night, because the light of knowledge was lacking. This night is divided into three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace; these periods are signified by the three nocturns, which are sung in the night.

Three psalms are sung in the first nocturn because the Patriarchs before the Law worshipped the Trinity, as is read: “He saw three, and worshipped one.” Three are sung in the second because the prophets under the Law invoked the Trinity, as it is written: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us.” In the third, three are sung because the apostles under grace preached the Trinity throughout the world; hence [Col. 0771D] the Gospel is read and *Alleluia* sung at that point.

The reading signifies teaching; the responsory, their life. By *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise thee, O God”) is shown the time when Christ was born and the angels sang glory to God, or when the world, having received faith, began to praise God. The verse said before Matins signifies Christ’s resurrection.

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—On Canonical Lauds

Morning Lauds signify the time from Christ’s resurrection until the end of the world. Then the day, as it were, began to rise, because the light of knowledge shone forth. The first psalm, “The Lord reigneth,” signifies that Christ reigned throughout the world after the resurrection. He made firm the circle of the earth, that is, the apostles, through his resurrection, ascension, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. The second psalm, “Make a joyful noise,” teaches the Church that was converted from Judaism to faith in [Col. 0772A] God. The third psalm, “O God, my God,” pertains to the Church gathered from the Gentiles; to it is joined the psalm “May God have mercy,” and the Jewish people are converted to faith in Christ through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah. Therefore they are sung under one *Gloria*, because one Church from two peoples will praise God.

In the fifth place, “Bless the Lord” is sung. In the fifth age of the world Nebuchadnezzar sent the three youths into the fiery furnace, in which they sang this hymn. Nebuchadnezzar signifies Antichrist, who at that time will cast the three sons of Noah—that is, the entire human race from the three regions of the world, Asia, Africa, and Europe—into the furnace of tribulation. Remaining steadfast in the Catholic faith, they will be patient in tribulation; and, tested through patience, they are found [Col. 0772B] blessed in hope through testing.

The three psalms which follow—“Praise the Lord from the heavens,” “Sing unto the Lord,” and “Praise the Lord in his sanctuary”—are sung under one *Gloria*. They teach that, after Antichrist’s killing, the saints will prevail in the steadfastness of faith, the blessedness of hope, and the joy of love in inseparable unanimity. The reading which follows is then spiritual food in the Church, increasing joy. The verse “The Lord reigneth” follows so that, just as the disciples, sorrowful at Christ’s death, joyfully sang after the resurrection, “The Lord reigneth,” so too those sorrowful under Antichrist will, after his killing, joyfully recount Christ’s triumph, saying, “The Lord reigneth.”

The hymn follows: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he hath visited and redeemed his people”; for as [Col. 0772C] Christ’s first coming was near when Zachariah sang this, so in the last time Christ’s second coming will be near. In it the saints shall serve God without fear, delivered from the hand of their enemies, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.

A day has twelve hours. The day is Christ; the hours are the righteous, who through good works cleave to the day, that is, to Christ. The equinoctial night likewise has twelve hours: the night is the life of sinners, and the hours are sinners. We who are called day are sustained by the night—that is, by alms offered for sins. Therefore, in private nights [Col. 0772D] we sing twelve psalms, so that we may remember that we are debtors on account of our sins and ought to intercede for those by whose offerings we are sustained.

The six antiphons are an intention toward the perfection of good works, so that, when we intercede for others, we ourselves may avoid evils.

Commanders in their army appointed three watches in the night to guard the camp while the soldiers slept; the fourth is in the morning time. The three readings and three responsories indicate the watches of the clergy: through the readings, teaching is directed to God’s people; through the responsories, the cry of the mind exhorts God’s people to keep watch—whether the Lord comes late, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning—lest he find them asleep. The first watch is childhood, the second youth, the third old age. Whoever, devoted to idleness in childhood, does not awaken to God’s work [Col. 0773A] should come to his senses in youth; if he neglects it then, at least in old age he should rise from the sleep of sloth to what is good.

Just as the faithful soul, stripped of the body, receives the seventh-day Sabbath, while the resurrection of the dead awaits the eighth day for holy bodies, so every soul that has awakened from the heavy sleep of negligence through ecclesiastical care, whether in the first watch, the second, or the third, immediately reaches the morning time in the fourth watch. Whenever the Romans see dawn advancing during any reading, they leave the nocturnal office and begin the morning office.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—On Morning and the Sun

Morning is the departure of darkness and the coming of dawn. [Col. 0773B] The sun approaches the heights, driving out darkness, and signifies the time of penitence for those who were formerly in the night, that is, in sins. To these the Sun of righteousness approaches, driving out darkness, that is, sins. Therefore the psalm “The Lord reigneth” is sung on a free night and signifies those who persevere in the course they have begun after baptism. “Have mercy upon me, O God” is sung on servile nights and signifies those who have fallen from their course after baptism and are afterward corrected through the prayers of the faithful.

## CHAPTER L.—On Man, and Why He Is Called a Lesser World

Man is called in Greek *microcosmus*, that is, a lesser world. His head is round, in the manner of the sphere of heaven, [Col. 0773C] in which two eyes shine like the sun and moon in heaven. His breast has the form of the air, in which are cough and breath, just as winds and rains are in the air. His belly is like the sea, receiving foods and drinks as the sea receives rivers. His feet resemble the earth, supporting the whole body as the earth supports all things. From earth he has flesh; from water, blood; from air, breath; from fire, soul. From earth he has coldness; from water, moisture; from air, dryness; from fire, heat.

He has the four seasons of the year: spring, childhood; summer, youth; autumn, old age; winter, decrepit age. Knowledge shines in him as day; ignorance is darkened as night. He has sight from fire, hearing from ether, smell from air, taste from water, touch from earth; bones from stones, nails from trees, [Col. 0773D] hair from plants, sweat from dew, thoughts from clouds. In his brain he has perception, and there is the seat of wisdom, ordering all things from there as from a tribunal; in his forehead, modesty, or rather shame; in his eyebrows, pride; in his temples, sleep; in his cheeks, the blush of modesty; in his heart, thoughts and will; in his liver, desire; in his lung, exaltation; in his stomach, strength; in his spleen, laughter; in his gall, anger; in his kidneys, pleasure; in his loins, sexual arousal; in his genitals, procreation.

With birds, fishes, and beasts he has the five senses, by which he is a mortal animal; with angels he has reason, by which he is immortal. From all these things man is a lesser world; therefore [Col. 0774A] the cycle of human birth is not without reason compared to the ordered cycle of the seasons.

## CHAPTER LI.—On the Night and Its Seven Periods

Night is so called because it harms human sight and activities. Ignorance of mind, arising from the darkness of sins, is compared to night. The morning hour signifies repentance; hence at Matins the penitential psalm “Have mercy upon me, O God” is sung.

After morning follows daybreak. For there are seven periods of night: evening, twilight, stillness of night, the unseasonable hour, cockcrow, morning, and daybreak, which is the beginning of a small light. The same hour is also called morning; thus all weekday psalms have something that sounds of morning.

## CHAPTER LII.—On the Psalms at Weekday Lauds

[Col. 0774B]

The first says: “In the morning thou shalt hear my voice; in the morning I shall stand before thee”; the second: “Send forth thy light”; the third: “Thou shalt make the outgoings of the morning and evening to rejoice”; the fourth: “In the morning let it pass away like grass; in the morning let it flourish and pass away”; the fifth: “Make me hear in the morning”; the sixth: “To declare in the morning.” In the first psalm evils are forbidden; in the second, good things are sought through hope. In the following two we celebrate the two commandments of charity: in “O God, my God,” love of God; in “May God have mercy,” love of neighbour. They are sung under one *Gloria*, because these commandments are not separated.

## CHAPTER LIII.—On the Canticles at Weekday Lauds

Then temptation follows, and victory follows temptation. Hence come the canticles which they sang after [Col. 0774C] they had been tempted and God granted them triumph. The first canticle says: “I will give thanks unto thee, O Lord, because thou wast angry with me.” Behold the scourge; hear the triumph: “Thine anger is turned away, and thou hast comforted me”: rejoice and praise. The second canticle was sung by Hezekiah after he had recovered from illness. The third by Hannah, after her rival was humbled and she herself exalted. The fourth, on account of which the Egyptians were overthrown and the children of Israel delivered. The fifth by the prophet Habakkuk for the deliverance of the Jews from the Chaldeans. The sixth by Moses after he had been afflicted on account of the Jews; and it concludes thus: “Praise, O nations, his people, for he will avenge the blood of his servants.”

The three psalms which follow, sung under one *Gloria*, signify [Col. 0774D] praise of the holy Trinity in one substance. These psalms are the end of the Psalter, because penitents strive toward the end of perfection, that is, the praise of God.

The chapter reading follows, because they instruct others in what they themselves do. The verse at Matins, “The Lord reigneth,” or “We are filled in the morning,” is the prayer of one converted, asking for present and future good things. Hence he ascends to the Lord, because he has visited and redeemed his people. The man converted through repentance becomes an evangelical man, who, in return for benefits bestowed upon the convert, exhorts him to praise the holy Trinity in “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” and says: “Blessed be the Lord, because he has visited human misery and redeemed it.” All the parts of night by which [Col. 0775A] the world was darkened have been driven away; therefore let us give thanks to God.

## CHAPTER LIV.—On the Day, Its Twelve Hours, and the Psalm “Blessed Are the Undefiled”

The day is Christ, who has twelve hours, that is, the faithful who after baptism or repentance run to him by the way of the Lord until evening—that is, until the end of their lives. A person beginning to walk in the Law of the Lord has a lion on one side and a dragon on the other: the lion in open persecutions, the dragon in hidden snares. So that we may avoid the devil’s persecutions and snares and remain safe in the day throughout the whole journey, we sing at Prime the psalm “O God, in thy name.”

In the first part of the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” we enter upon the Lord’s way; this [Col. 0775B] part is sung for the first hour of the day. The second part is for the second hour, in which God’s Law is again mentioned, as in: “I will consider the wonders of thy Law.” The verse “Arise, O Lord” asks that God may be the helper and deliverer of his flock throughout the course of the day’s journey. The third part of the psalm is said for the third hour, namely: “Set forth the Law.” The fourth part is for the fourth hour, where the Law is named, as in: “I said, I will keep thy Law.” The fifth part is said for the fifth hour, in which the Law is likewise recalled: “I have meditated on thy Law,” and so forth, “The Law of thy mouth is good to me.” The sixth part is for the sixth hour: “The wicked have told me idle tales, but not according to thy Law.” The seventh for the seventh hour: “How I have loved thy Law, O Lord!” The eighth for the eighth hour: “I have hated the wicked, and have loved thy Law.” The ninth [Col. 0775C] part is for the ninth hour, where it is said: “Thy righteousness is righteousness for ever, and thy Law is truth.” The tenth is for the tenth hour, where the Law is again mentioned, as in: “See my humiliation,” and so forth, “because I have not forgotten thy Law.” The eleventh is for the eleventh hour, where likewise mention is made of the Law: “I have hated iniquity,” and so forth, “but I have loved thy Law.” At the twelfth hour of the day the Lord gives his labourers the promised denarius. A reading is read at every course, because the saints are everywhere refreshed by divine conversation.

## CHAPTER LV.—On Vespers

Vespers is the twelfth hour, which is the day’s end and the end of each human being. The five psalms are the five senses of a human being. As at the world’s end the five virgins come with lamps to meet Christ, [Col. 0775D] so at life’s end a person, with good works performed through the five senses throughout the whole day, by which he has walked in the Law of God, strives hastily to meet Christ the bridegroom. This occurs through the steps of ascent in virtues; therefore fifteen steps are included in the vespertinal office.

The reading that follows is the preparation and adornment of those entering the King’s presence. The verse, “Evening prayer,” or “Let my prayer be directed, O Lord,” is the knocking at the chamber-door where the King sits. The Gospel hymn, namely the *Magnificat*, which holy Mary sang, warns the wise virgins—that is, the faithful—to strive toward the place where the Virgin of virgins has gone before: namely, into the Saviour’s presence.

## CHAPTER LVI.—On Compline

[Col. 0776A]

Compline is the completion of the other offices and belongs to the night. In it the common work ends; all members are left without human refuge, and we are entrusted to God alone, who neither sleeps nor slumbers. Sleep is an image of death. Therefore, in this office we recite certain psalms which we also sing on the Holy Sabbath of Easter, when the Lord rested in the tomb. Such is “When I called,” because of the verse: “In peace, in the selfsame, I shall sleep and rest.” And this: “In thee, O Lord, have I hoped,” which he sang on the cross; and we end where he ended: “Into thy hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit.”

After the Lord’s fast, the devil tempted him as a dragon in hidden snares; therefore the tract [Col. 0776B] “He who dwells” is then sung. On Parasceve, however, he tempted him as a lion openly persecuting him in the Passion; therefore, according to the Romans, the same tract “He who dwells” is sung then also. We sing this same psalm at Compline so that God may preserve us from the devil’s temptations and nightly delusions. We sing “Behold now,” and so forth, because of the verse: “In the nights lift up,” and so forth. By these four psalms the four elements are sought for us, or because four watches are observed in the night. With the verse “Keep us,” and so forth, we seal our members; and with the Gospel hymn “Now dismiss,” and so forth, we ask with Simeon for peace and eternal rest.

## CHAPTER LVII.—On Canonical Prime

It is the custom in the Church that after Prime and before Compline [Col. 0776C] the brethren assemble for the reading, which is refreshment of the mind. At Prime the Lord’s flock is directed on the way so that it may come to pasture. Let it first work, and afterward be filled with refreshment at the third hour; here all things are consumed.

On Sundays seven psalms are sung at Prime because of the sevenfold gifts of the Spirit. To these psalms are appended two sections from the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” because of the twofold commandments of love, through which the Law of God is fulfilled. Catholic faith is joined to these: namely, “Whoever wishes to be saved,” because through worship of the one God we shall be saved.

Alternatively, nine psalms are sung at Prime, by which are understood the nine orders of angels. By “Whoever wishes,” and so forth, is understood the Christian person, [Col. 0776D] who through Christ’s resurrection, commemorated on Sunday, will be joined to angels. Through the Law of the Lord—that is, through love—we return to our homeland; through the psalm “O God, in thy name” we gird ourselves for the journey. Through the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled” we receive love of God; through “Reward,” love of neighbour. In these two commandments the whole Law is fulfilled. “Whoever wishes,” and so forth, signifies our course: for we walk by faith, not by sight. The chapter “Precious in the sight of the Lord” signifies that there the Lord’s flock is driven out to pasture, so that it may walk in the way of the Lord.

## CHAPTER LVIII.—On the Mystery of the Hours

The Lord Jesus Christ was seized at night for our sake, so that he might deliver us from the captivity of the devil and from the eternal [Col. 0777A] night of hell; therefore we sing the nocturns at night. In the morning he was falsely accused before the high priests, so that he might make us secure from the accusation of the enemy; therefore we sing morning Lauds. At the first hour he was led bound before the governor, so that he might free us from the chains of sins; therefore we recite Prime. At the third hour he was condemned, mocked, and scourged, so that he might free us from eternal condemnation; therefore we sing Terce. At the sixth hour he was crucified, so that he might redeem us from everlasting torment; therefore we sing Sext. At the ninth hour he died, so that he might rescue us from eternal death; therefore we sing None. In the evening he was taken down from the cross, so that we might be removed from punishments; therefore we sing Vespers. At Compline he was buried, so that we might emerge from the grave of Tartarus; therefore we sing Compline.

## CHAPTER LIX.—Another Account of the Mystery of the Hours

[Col. 0777B]

At midnight the Lord rose; therefore we sing the nocturns. In the morning he appeared to his mother, as Sedulius says, or to Mary Magdalene, as the Evangelist affirms; therefore we recite morning Lauds. At Prime he appeared to the women going from the tomb; at Terce he was seen by James, as is supposed; at Sext, by Peter, as is believed; at None, by those walking to Emmaus; at Vespers, by those eating with him; at Compline, by all.

## CHAPTER LX.—Likewise on the Mystery of the Hours

In the beginning there was chaos, and all things were covered with darkness; therefore we perform the nocturnal office at night. First thing in the morning God created light; therefore morning Lauds are then sung. Nine psalms together with the *Benedictus* are sung at these Lauds, because the nine orders of angels [Col. 0777C] are thought to have been created then.

As though at the first hour, Adam entered the Lord’s vineyard when he was placed in Paradise to work it; therefore at Prime we sing three psalms praising the Trinity, which both formed humankind and restored it after the fall. In the fourth, namely “Whoever wishes to be saved,” and so forth, our faith is set forth. At the third hour Noah entered the vineyard; he was also the first to plant it, and from it he became drunk. At the sixth Abraham entered, who offered his son. At the ninth, David and the prophets. At these hours we recite three psalms, assigning a psalm to each hour, either because of the holy Trinity or because of faith in the holy Trinity. In the evening the apostles and their successors entered. At Vespers five psalms are sung because of the fivefold Passion [Col. 0777D] of the Lord, by which we have been redeemed from the deeds of the five senses. At Compline, that is, at the end of the world, the denarius is rendered, namely eternal rest; therefore four psalms are sung, so that the four parts of the world may be saved, or so that the four elements in the human being, who is a lesser world, may be indicated.

## CHAPTER LXI.—On the Seven Days of the Age and the Ages of the World

The first day of the age signifies the first age of the world, whose morning was Adam and whose evening was the Flood. The second day of the age signifies the second age: its morning was Noah, its evening the submergence of Sodom. The third day of the age was the third age: its morning was the origin of Abraham; its evening was Saul’s death. [Col. 0778A] The fourth day of the age was the fourth age: its morning was David, the splendour of kings; its evening, the Babylonian migration and its terror. The fifth day of the age was the fifth age: its morning was Israel’s return to Jerusalem; its evening, Christ’s rejection there. The sixth day was the sixth age: its morning was Christ’s coming; it endures today, and we are now near its end; its evening will be Antichrist’s coming. The seventh day of the age signifies rest—both that which souls have had since the first age after death and that which they will have after judgment. This day will have no evening, because that rest will have no end.

## CHAPTER LXII.—On the Last Judgment

Judgment will be in the valley of Jehoshaphat, that is, in this [Col. 0778B] world. Jehoshaphat means “judgment”; the valley is this world, and the mountain is heaven. Christ will appear in the air like the sun in heaven. The righteous will be caught up into the air to meet him; the wicked will remain on earth, while fire blazes fifteen cubits above all mountains.

There will be two classes of the good and two of the wicked. One class of the righteous consists of martyrs, virgins, and all who leave everything for Christ. These three are not commandments but counsels; therefore, because they have done more than was commanded, they will be judges with God. The other class of the righteous consists of true widows, good married persons, and penitents, to whom it is said: “Come, ye blessed,” and so forth. One class of the wicked consists of unbelievers, whether Gentiles or Jews, who will perish without judgment; the other class consists of evil Christians, or Jews of old, [Col. 0778C] to whom it is said: “Depart from me, ye cursed,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER LXIII.—On the Sundays in Advent

In the first responsory, “Looking from afar,” the singer introduces the sayings or deeds of John the Baptist. In his person he says, “Looking,” namely, at how far heaven is from earth. Of John it is said: “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth”; but of Christ it is read: “He who comes from heaven is above all.” “Behold, I see the power of God,” that is, divinity in the flesh; “and a cloud covering the whole earth,” that is, I see the darkness of ignorance covering the earthly hearts of the Jews, who do not recognize the God present in the man Christ. “Go out to meet him,” through faith and works; and say: “Tell us whether thou art he who is to reign over the people Israel.”

John sends his disciples to Christ, saying: [Col. 0778D] “Art thou he who is to come, or do we await another?” That is: if thou wilt die and visit hell, make it known, and reign over the faithful.

The three verses which occur in it signify the patriarchs before the Law, the prophets under the Law, and Christians under grace. Or the three verses teach that Law, prophecy, and psalmody foretold Christ’s coming. The *Gloria Patri* which follows signifies that the holy Trinity is to be worshipped in all these things. For this responsory recalls Christ’s divine nature; but in the second, namely “I beheld,” his human nature is manifested by the words: “And behold, the Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven.” In the former it is asked whether he ought to reign over the people Israel; here the answer is given: “And a kingdom was given to him.” Not Israel alone, [Col. 0779A] but every people, tribe, and language shall serve him. These responsories show that Christ, God and man, is king of all.

On Wednesday and Friday antiphons concerning the prophets are set in the Advent of the Lord, because those weekdays have from the beginning been present in the prophecy of Christ and the Church. On Wednesday the sun and moon, which are Christ and the Church, were placed in heaven. On Friday humanity was created, which was the figure of the future Adam.

The ecclesiastical choir, or prophetic speech, acts as messenger to Jerusalem, once the metropolis and city of the great King, and through Jerusalem to the chief persons of the whole congregation renowned for God. For Christ’s absence cannot be remembered without sorrow. Therefore these responsories [Col. 0779B] console God’s people concerning the coming of their king and defender: “Jerusalem, thy salvation shall soon come”; “City Jerusalem, behold, the Lord shall come.” This messenger of God speaks to the poor and to the common people, who are easily oppressed by the powerful. In the former he consoled the dignity of authority; in this he consoles the subject people.

“Behold, he shall appear” portrays at its beginning the King of kings, who is to come to deliver the poor and afflicted from the hand of secular power. The responsory says that he will come in the near time: “He is near, that he may come”; “He who is to come”; and “Egypt, do not weep.” The responsories of this Sunday and of the following week strive to gather a multitude of peoples, that they may be present and prepared to receive the Lord of lords. Therefore they contain very many instances of “Behold”: as in “Sound the trumpet: Behold God,” [Col. 0779C] and in “Cry aloud: Behold our God, whom I await,” and “Behold, now he shall come.” The responsory “Sound the trumpet” admonishes citizens to know of the king’s coming and announce it to their neighbours. “Look and see how great he is” warns citizens that this one who comes to save the nations is greater than kings. “It shall not be taken away” teaches that the king of the Jews, awaited in his time, stands at the gates.

## CHAPTER LXIV.—On the Antiphons at Lauds

The antiphons arranged through the seven morning offices and the seven weekdays signify the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, whose work is the conception and birth of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Therefore, in the same week, the reading from Isaiah is read, which enumerates the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, on Friday, when the first human being was created, [Col. 0779D] whom the second human being now comes to restore.

## CHAPTER LXV.—On the “O” Antiphons at the *Magnificat*
The antiphons which begin with O signify something wondrous, and show us that in these days something to be investigated is being celebrated, concerning which it is said: “The Lord will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive.” O is an interjection of wonder and belongs to some marvellous vision of the mind. And because this wonder came about through the conception and birth of holy Mary, these antiphons are more fitting for the hymn Magnificat than for Benedictus. The first antiphon, “O Wisdom,” corresponds to the first degree, namely the Spirit of wisdom. The second, “O Key of David, who openest and no one shuts,” is suited to the Spirit of understanding. The third, “O Emmanuel, king and lawgiver,” corresponds to the degree of the Spirit [Col. 0780A] of counsel. The fourth, “O Root of Jesse, who standest as a sign,” that is, as a cross, when the sun was darkened and the rocks were split, “over whom kings shall shut their mouths,” that is, the rulers of this world, who, with their rhetoric and dialectic, will fall silent at the coming of the preaching of the holy cross and holy Gospel—this is suited to the degree of the Spirit of fortitude. The fifth, “O Dayspring, splendour,” is assigned to the degree of the Spirit of knowledge. The sixth, “O Adonai and leader of the house of Israel,” corresponds to the degree of the Spirit of piety. The seventh, “O King of the nations and their Desired One,” is suited to the degree of the Spirit of fear. The eighth, “O Virgin of virgins,” suggests that the Church marvels at the wondrous birth: “Daughters of Jerusalem, why do you marvel at me?” This antiphon shows that the man who took flesh from Mary is alone perfect among the other human beings [Col. 0780B], because the sevenfold Spirit dwells in him alone. If twelve O antiphons are sung, they signify that the grace of the holy Trinity is desired from the four quarters of the world: for three times four makes twelve.

### Chapter LXVI.—On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord

On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, the responsory “Be sanctified today,” and the others, teach us that we ought to wash with tears and repentance the garments which we received in baptism, so that, just as the children of Israel met the Lord on Mount Sinai in a state of sanctification, namely by abstaining from women, so we may meet the Lord’s descent without offence.

### Chapter LXVII.—On the Nativity of the Lord

On the holy night of the Lord’s Nativity, the three nocturns [Col. 0780C] signify the three periods of the whole world: namely, the time of the natural law, the time of the law given through Moses, and the time of grace. The third nocturn, which recalls the grace of the New Testament, has an antiphon with Alleluia, because he himself is invoked; it is sung at the time when the Lord’s resurrection is celebrated by the faithful, that is, around the time of morning. In the first nocturn, the readings from the prophet signify the time before the Law, when the patriarchs prefigured Christ’s birth through figures. In the second, sermons are read; this is the time under the Law, when the holy Scriptures foretold that Christ would be born. In the third, the Gospels are read; this is the time of grace, when his birth was received by the Church. At the first three responsories [Col. 0780D], *Glory be to the Father* is sung, because the Trinity, foretold by the Law, the prophets, and the psalms, was made manifest to the world today.

The responsories follow the custom practised by royal and imperial household servants when they enter the king’s presence: each offers the king what he is able. They offer different gifts, yet desire equally to please the king in intention. So the responsories now give praise and thanks to Christ, now to his mother. The nine readings and responsories admonish us to bless God, who came to gather back the lost human being into the fellowship of the nine orders of angels.

Just as at the Nativity we give thanks, through nine readings, for God’s descent even to our lowliness, so through the same number, on the feasts [Col. 0781A] of the saints, we give thanks because they are worthy to ascend to the height of heaven, where the angels dwell.
