The Mass *The Lord said*, and the Gospel *The Book of the Generation*, belong to the hour when Christ was born. *Te Deum laudamus* and the morning lauds which follow are the praise of the angels, who at his birth sang *Glory to God in the highest*. A neume is called *mistus* (“mixed”); that neume, in the construction of the world, shows what cannot be expressed in words: how he who today was born of a Virgin fashioned and adorned the world, and how he is the light and glory of the whole fabric of the world. The neume in the verse “Like a bridegroom” signifies that Christ’s coming forth from the Virgin’s womb cannot be narrated in words; it is compared with a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber. This [Col. 0781B] neume is also sung in the responsory of St John the Evangelist on the word *understanding*, because of the outstanding understanding of St John. Hence it is also sung in *Glory be to the Father*, in which the Trinity is praised, which is perceived by understanding alone.

The second Vespers, *With thee is the beginning*, belongs more properly to the feast of the Lord’s Nativity than the preceding Vespers. Similarly, at all feasts of saints, the second Vespers belongs more properly to the feast-day than the first. The octaves of the Lord and of the other saints are celebrated because, on the eighth day—that is, in the resurrection—their glory is doubled through Christ.

### Chapter LXVIII.—On the Epiphany of the Lord

At the Epiphany of the Lord the invitatory is not sung, because of Herod’s deceit, since he sought the Lord craftily [Col. 0781C]. A psalm is sung in the sixth place because, in the sixth age of the world, the nations sought the Lord through faith. The six antiphons of the two nocturns recall the services rendered by the Magi at the Nativity. These same three Magi were ambassadors of the Gentile people dwelling on the mainland and islands, through their mystical gifts. Their three gifts prefigured Christ’s threefold person: King, Priest, and mortal man; and likewise the three functions of Christ’s members: wisdom, the power of prayer, and mortification of the flesh. The gifts of the Magi bore the embassy of these three functions.

From the gift of incense they speak the first antiphon, “Bring unto the Lord,” [signifying] the power of prayer, for he is the true Priest. From the gift of gold: “Sing unto our God”; that is, “O wise men, bring your wisdom to God the king.” From the gift of myrrh it is said of every mortal people, striving after better things, “Let all the earth worship thee,” that is, [Christ] made mortal for our sake through mortification of the flesh.

The first vigil mentions the nations who dwell on the mainland; the second vigil speaks of those who dwell on islands.

The first antiphon concerns the wise: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts.” Those are called kings who rule themselves, and wise men who rule others. The second antiphon concerns all people: “All nations,” etc. By the third antiphon priests exhort one another and say, “Come, let us worship.” But the third vigil recalls Christ’s baptism and the New Testament. The New Testament [Col. 0782A] is founded through baptism; therefore here all the earth sings Alleluia. And again the many islands say, “Worship God.” The antiphon “The rush of the river” is sung in the third vigil because of baptism; the psalm *Our God* is sung at this vigil because people were troubled on account of the New Testament and baptism. Yet “the rush of the river makes glad the city of God,” which city consists of inhabitants of the mainland and of the islands.

In the New Testament, the Church says to those baptized in Christ and dwelling on the mainland, through the second psalm, “Sing unto the Lord, all the earth,” and through the antiphon, “Worship the Lord in his holy court.” To those dwelling on the islands she says through the third psalm, “The Lord has reigned; let the earth rejoice; let the many islands be glad,” and through the antiphon, “Worship the Lord, [Col. 0782B] all his angels.” Three readings are read from the prophecy which foretold that gifts would be brought to the Lord from Sheba. Sheba is a province in which Midian and Ephah are located; it is interpreted as “conversion” or “captivity,” and signifies the nations which, converted from the devil’s captivity to God, offered the foretold gifts to their deliverer.

The responsory signifies that the nations answer the prophets’ words by deeds. The antiphon, “Today, to the heavenly Bridegroom,” recalls three solemnities through three miracles: those of the present day; on the octave of the Epiphany, the baptism of the Lord is recalled; and on the following Sunday, the miracle of water turned into wine.

### Chapter LXIX.—On the Time between the Epiphany and the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary

[Col. 0782C] The devil is grieved because he has been shut out; the Church rejoices because Christ has entered the world. The devil is grieved at the Church’s peace; the choir of angels sings joyfully: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” We, rejoicing in Christ’s presence during the preceding feasts, have, through the devil’s prompting and the frailty of the flesh, turned the pursuit of spiritual joy toward bodily concern and pleasure. Therefore, on this Sunday responsories are sung from psalms containing much prayer, and beginning with the first penitential psalm, “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy wrath.”

The time from the feast of Theophany to Septuagesima recalls the devotion and ministry of preachers, from the Church’s first preachers down to [Col. 0782D] the last of the New Testament. The Epistles of Paul, the supreme preacher, which are read at this same time, also suggest this to us. Prayer is fitting for preachers, so that their preaching may have an open door.

### Chapter LXX.—On the Feast of the Purification

*Hypapanti* means “meeting,” when Simeon and Anna met Christ in the Temple. We celebrate this feast with lighted candles because of Simeon’s words, when he took him in his arms and foretold in prophecy: “A light for the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel.” By the candles we signify that, through shining works and, like the wise virgins bearing burning lamps, we may meet Christ [Col. 0783A] the Bridegroom as he comes into the heavenly Jerusalem.

### Chapter LXXI.—On the Chair of St Peter

The Chair of St Peter is celebrated because he was then made bishop at Antioch, and the disciples were called Christians. Therefore it is commonly called the Day of Souls, because power was given to him to bind and loose souls.

Christ’s generation and the freedom of the holy preachers have been celebrated up to Septuagesima. From Septuagesima onward is celebrated the generation of those who desire to emerge from captivity and from the straits of the present pilgrimage, until Christ’s generation is born again from the middle of Lent around the Paschal mysteries. Christ’s generation and the freedom of his preachers have, for the most part, departed from this present world in order to reign with the angels before God. The time of such departure [Col. 0783B] is called night; therefore Alleluia is celebrated in this night. The Church now present, which is in this pilgrimage, on the night of Septuagesima recalls the glory celebrated among the citizens who have departed; but in the day [it recalls the condition] of those still held in captivity and sighing to return to freedom. Among these latter the brightness of Alleluia is not celebrated, because they are constrained by the sorrow of captivity; but among those who have departed Alleluia is celebrated, because they do not cease from God’s praise.

The responsory “Alleluia, she is present; let us imitate her” is taken from the Book of Wisdom, where it is said: “O how beautiful is the chaste generation with splendour!” While it is present, they imitate it. From the Nativity until the night of Septuagesima this generation seemed present; [Col. 0783C] therefore it was frequently celebrated in many offices with Alleluia. The second responsory, “Alleluia, a good name,” [signifies] that name which will be written in heaven, whose memory will be permanently formed among angels and holy human beings. This is the beautiful and chaste generation; when it has gone away, those who remain in the present world, not sons and daughters [of it], desire it. The third responsory, “You alone hold the primacy”; *this is said by the mother who has been left here in the world, to complete the body fitting for me: that I may turn toward our offspring which has been placed in straits, and celebrate praise for it in Latin, sympathetically sharing its tribulation* [Note: [Col. 0783D] The passage is corrupt.]. “You, praise of wisdom, return to your treasures,” that is, to the company of our offspring with the Hebrew [Col. 0783D] language, which triumphs before God: for there the angels will bless you. The fourth and fifth responsories ask, on behalf of what remains of their body, that Alleluia may return again to the Church now present. When the Bridegroom has risen from the dead, may the generation also, bright, chaste, and beautiful, return to us with joy through the baptismal mysteries, and may Alleluia be heard from our mouths in all the churches.

### Chapter LXXII.—On Septuagesima

“In the beginning God made,” and what follows, are appropriate to Septuagesima and to the beginning of the year. In them are suggested the wretched condition of humanity, the captivity it deserved, and the beginnings of created things are sung. The spring season is the beginning of the year: in it [Col. 0784A] are sung responsories from the histories of the first fathers, through whom holy religion was restored in the earliest times after the condemnation of the first mass.

The responsories “While the Lord was walking” and “In the sweat of thy face” remind us of humanity’s miserable change from light to darkness, from happiness to misery.

### Chapter LXXIII.—On Sexagesima

Sexagesima descends from Septuagesima. It is reckoned from six and ten. There are seven days between Septuagesima and Sexagesima, which is not without reason, although there ought to be ten. For within the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit lies the apprehension of the ten commandments of the Law. Septuagesima is completed on Saturday, when Easter is concluded; Quinquagesima [is completed] on the Wednesday of mid-Easter, from which weekday there are three days to Saturday, [Col. 0784B] and these signify that anyone who worthily seeks remission of sins at the beginning of conversion will attain contemplation of the holy Trinity.

For seventy years our fathers were in captivity; about the end of the reckoning of Septuagesima they deserved to be recalled from captivity. That captivity prefigured the captivity of the Christian people, which it suffers under the devil and his ministers. It is lamented in the psalm “Have mercy upon me, O God,” which is numbered fiftieth; that number proceeds from five, and by the five senses our sin is gathered. The psalm “Give thanks unto the Lord” is numbered one hundred and seventeenth; through this number the everlasting kingdom of God is designated. Whoever has made satisfaction through repentance in the psalm “Have mercy upon me, O God,” and has publicly confessed sins [Col. 0784C] in a foreign land, deserves to be recalled and restored to Christ’s kingdom through the psalm “Give thanks unto the Lord.” The antiphon from the psalm “Have mercy upon me, O God” recalls the satisfaction of the penitent. For we sin in two ways: either when we omit what we ought to have done, or when we do what we ought not to have done. For the sin of transgression the first antiphon cries, “Have mercy upon me, O God”; after the words of this antiphon the beginning of return from captivity is taken up. For there follows, “Give thanks unto the Lord,” etc. The beginnings of these psalms accord with one another, since both recall God’s benefits. At the beginning of “Have mercy upon me, O God” is confession of sins for washing away crimes; at the end of “Give thanks” is joyful confession and thanksgiving for benefits received [Col. 0784D].

### Chapter LXXIV.—On Quinquagesima

Quinquagesima, descending from Septuagesima, stands at the third degree, and Abraham appeared in the third age of the world. Quinquagesima receives its name from the number five; five is suited to the outward person, who is animated by the five senses, whether toward good or toward evil. The fiftieth psalm has the voice of a penitent, and the fiftieth year is the jubilee. Quinquagesima ends at the Lord’s Easter; Quinquagesima prays for sin, and joy follows at the Lord’s Easter. Here forty days are sung, because every guilt of sins is committed through the four parts of the world against the ten commandments of the Law. [Col. 0785A] For ten times four makes forty. Guilt belonging to days, from the prosperity of things, and guilt belonging to nights, from adversity, is washed away by the sacrament of heavenly baptism.

Those who are to be restored through baptism must touch upon the numbers forty and six. Through baptism the scattered first man, Adam, is gathered back from the four parts of the world into the one body of Christ, which was fashioned in forty-six years. From Wednesday of this week there are forty-six days until public baptism; therefore on this Sunday the responsory “Forty days and nights” is sung. Responsories concerning Abraham, who offered his son to God, follow, because good works follow baptism. In the antiphon “According to the [Col. 0785B] multitude” forgiveness is sought for having failed to do what we ought to have done; in this [antiphon] we pray concerning what we have done that we ought not to have done. In the antiphon “Thou art my God,” thanksgiving is offered, as though the mind believed itself to have obtained what it prayed for.

### Chapter LXXV.—On Lent

Lent receives its name from four and stands in the fourth place from Septuagesima; it is completed at the Lord’s Supper and may be understood as belonging to the cultivation of purity. The responsories of Lent are keys and titles concerning the conduct and state of the whole Lent. For in these days we must, more than at other times of the year, correct our habits, fast, weep, pray, keep vigil, be patient, repent, and give alms. By this catalogue human impurity is cleansed, and a person is washed from every [Col. 0785C] defilement.

The antiphon “A clean heart” asks for a right understanding of abstinence; the antiphon “O Lord, save me” prays that they may persevere to the end in the abstinence which they began at this time. The antiphon “Thus will I bless thee” asks that one may be strengthened by good works. The antiphon “In a spirit of humility” asks that the Lord may receive a spirit of humility and a contrite heart in these offerings and burnt sacrifices [the reading *militem*, “a soldier,” is uncertain]. The antiphon “Praise the Lord” exhorts [us] to praise God for having heard [our prayer].

On this Sunday responsories concerning Isaac and Jacob are sung. Because the father received him safe on his return from exile, the Gospel is read in this week [Col. 0785D] concerning the prodigal son, whom his father received when he returned from the swine; for God receives penitents who turn back from vices. Septuagesima, Sexagesima, and Quinquagesima are prefaces to Lent, which extends to Easter; therefore it is not called Thirtieth, Twentieth, or Tenth.

### Chapter LXXVI.—On the Second Sunday of Lent

“Lord, [open] my lips” is the renewal of the mind for the joys of building the Temple. Under King Ahasuerus the people was afflicted and the work of the Temple was interrupted. This custom is still observed in the Church after conversation has been interrupted during the time of night. At the present verse, “Lord, my lips,” the conversation is resumed. The antiphon “The right hand of the Lord” is the rebuilding of God’s house, and “For this he was made a helper.” The people, delivered from the furnace [Col. 0786A] which Ahasuerus—or, alternatively, Nebuchadnezzar—prepared for it, sings the antiphon of the three youths, “Blessed art thou.” The adversaries could not destroy the work of God’s Temple; therefore they say the antiphon, “He established them for ever.” The Church, God’s Temple, is built through repentance; but because it is hindered by Ahasuerus, that is, the devil, through persecutions or temptations, “Lord, my lips” is said. When evils are conquered, “The right hand of the Lord” is sung; in thanksgiving, “He became a helper”; for the deliverance of the three youths, “Blessed art thou”; for the reward, “He established them for ever.”

### Chapter LXXVII.—On the Third Sunday of Lent

On this Sunday Joseph’s brothers worship him, because it was to come about that the Church would worship God. The antiphon “Deal graciously” recalls the completion of the walls [Col. 0786B] of Jerusalem, which was accomplished under Nehemiah; when he prayed, the Lord resisted the adversaries. Therefore he says the antiphon, “The Lord is my helper.” Against threatening enemies he says the antiphon, “May God have mercy.” Wrath against Nehemiah and his youths among the nations was extinguished; hence the antiphon, “The power of his might.” This antiphon is understood especially of Joseph, in whom the fire of lust was extinguished when his mistress tempted him. Therefore the antiphon “Sun and moon” follows, because he saw the sun and moon worshipping him; this is a prophecy of Christ.

When the edifice of good works has been completed under Christ, the antiphon “Deal graciously” is sung; against rivals, “The Lord is my helper”; against hidden snares, [Col. 0786C] “May God have mercy”; after victory over temptation, “The power of his might”; for the praise of God, “Sun and moon.”

### Chapter LXXVIII.—On the Fourth Sunday of Lent

On this Sunday responsories concerning Moses and Joshua are sung; they brought the people of Israel into the promised land. Both signify Christ, who will bring penitents into Paradise. The antiphon “Then shalt thou accept” signifies the times of Moses, who taught that sacrifice should be offered to God, and the times of Nehemiah, who reviews the times of the Fathers, saying: “Thou gavest them kingdoms and peoples.” The antiphon “It is good to hope in the Lord” speaks of hope in the Lord alone. God humbled the inhabitants of the land before the children of Israel; therefore he says the antiphon, “May God bless us.” He saved them from the hand of their enemies, [Col. 0786D] whence the antiphon “The Lord is mighty.” There follows a catalogue of the kings of Judah who sinned against the Lord, whence the antiphon “The kings of the earth.”

Alternatively, as applied to Nehemiah: here he offered on Sabbaths and new moons; hence the antiphon “Then shalt thou accept.” The history of Ezra relates that Nehemiah and the people relied on heavenly hope alone; hence the antiphon “It is good to hope.” Then the people blessed all the men who were willing to dwell in Jerusalem; hence the antiphon “May he bless us.” Nehemiah drove away the son-in-law of the governor, concerning whom, in fear, he says: “The Lord is mighty.” Then he established the whole order of God’s ministers; hence the antiphon “The kings of the earth.”

When vices have been conquered and the sacrifice of virtues offered, every faithful soul says, “Then shalt thou accept.” Whoever hoped in the Lord, he delivered; [therefore] it says the antiphon, “It is good [Col. 0787A] to hope.” That he may keep him in good things, let him say the antiphon, “May he bless us”; against impending temptations, the antiphon “Thou art mighty, O Lord”; for victory, the antiphon “The kings of the earth.”

The three antiphons—“Blessed art thou,” “Sing the hymn,” and [the antiphon] of the three youths—recall the three youths, that is, all the faithful, praising the holy Trinity in the furnace, that is, established in tribulation in the three parts of this world, namely Asia, Africa, and Europe. Their affliction is also signified by the antiphon “In a spirit of humility.” The antiphon “Let the earth bless the Lord, and let all things that grow sing a hymn to him,” in Septuagesima joins human praise with the praise of angels. Alleluia is the song of angels; “Let the earth bless the Lord” is the praise of people set in tribulation, because the fellowship of angels is with those who suffer for God, as appeared in the furnace with the youths, one like the Son of God.

### Chapter LXXIX.—On the Fifth and Sixth Sundays of Lent

The responsories and antiphons of the two Sundays of the Lord’s Passion sound forth the passion of the Lord and of his body, that is, the Church, for as long as it journeys in this world; therefore *Glory be to the Father* is omitted in the divine office.

### Chapter LXXX.—On the Lord’s Supper and the Following Two Days

At the Lord’s Supper the responsories recall his betrayal; on Parasceve, his crucifixion; on Saturday, his burial. The striking of the boards signifies the oppression which the Church will suffer [Col. 0787C] under Antichrist for three and a half years. The lights of the Church are extinguished for three nights; these nights, with their days, contain seventy-two hours. Christ lay in the tomb for so many hours. By this present extinguishing is signified the extinguishing of joy in the hearts of Christ’s disciples while he lay in the tomb. Or these were the hours after the Lord’s betrayal until he entered among them while the doors were shut; meanwhile the apostles were in grief. Or they are extinguished because the sun was darkened for three hours, that is, from the sixth hour until the ninth, so that it might proclaim to the world that its creator was darkened in the tomb for three days.

### Chapter LXXXI.—On the Resurrection of the Lord

[Col. 0787D] At the Lord’s Resurrection three psalms are sung, because the Law, prophecy, and psalmody foretold his resurrection. Three readings are read, because the resurrection is proclaimed before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. Three responsories are sung, because angels in heaven, people on earth, and souls in hell rejoice at Christ’s resurrection. The psalms for the nocturns are sung during the week from Sunday night because of the Sunday resurrection.

### Chapter LXXXII.—On Responsories, Singers, Readers, and So Forth

A responsory is so called because, when one person ends, another responds to it. The readers who rise for this work and the singers are those who carry on the Lord’s business, [Col. 0788A] to whom it is said: “Trade until I come.” The reader gives the Lord’s law to hearers who have recently been called, through the offices of the singers, to the wedding-feast in God’s school. *Schola* means a calling, in which, if anyone still lies numb with deaf ears, the singer sounds the sweetness of melody into that person’s ear with a lofty trumpet, so that the mind may be awakened. The singers who answer the first singer are the voice of hearers, as though awakening and praising God. The verse signifies the ploughing servant in the Gospel. By the sweetness of the melody carnal hearts are split open, and they open like furrows in the confession of voice and tears. He ploughs who splits hearts with the plough of compunction. In the reading, the hearer is fed, in a manner, like an ox. An ox is fed so that agricultural work may be performed with it. The ox is the preacher; the singer [Col. 0788B] is like the ox-driver, who sings out to the oxen so that they may draw the plough more cheerfully. The earth is split when the hearts of hearers are pierced by compunction. A responsory answers the tract; this signifies the two sacrifices of doves and turtledoves.

The tract in Septuagesima signifies tribulation, as “Out of the depths.” In Sexagesima it signifies flight, as “Let them flee from before the bow.” “Praise the Lord” signifies the joy of neophytes or of those recently ordained. The dove is accustomed to live, fly, and moan in flocks; it signifies the active life, whose abundance is the responsory. The turtledove delights in solitude; it is the contemplative life, designated by the tract.

In Alleluia the eternal joy of the elect is recalled; the verse of Alleluia signifies the Church’s joy and praise of God [Col. 0788C] without sorrow. In the responsory we have sown; in Alleluia we reap, as is said: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.” The difference between Alleluia and the tract is that Alleluia always expresses either praise of God or the saints’ joy, whereas the tract sometimes expresses tribulation and sometimes joy: tribulation, as “Out of the depths,” “Thou hast moved,” “To thee have I lifted up,” “They have often attacked,” “God, my God”; joy, as “He who dwells,” “Make a joyful noise,” “Those who trust,” “Praise.” After two tracts of tribulation comes a third of joy, because resurrection follows after the two days of burial. There are two kinds of compunction: one of fear, the other of love; the tract of tribulation signifies compunction of fear, and the tract of joy compunction of love.

[Col. 0788D] Ministers remove their chasubles when they take up the office of reader or singer, for spiritual warfare is expressed in the office of reader or singer; they fight alone in reading or in melodic singing. The chasuble signifies hunger, thirst, nakedness, vigils, psalmody, and such things as must sometimes be set aside for the needs of brothers. The tablets which the singer holds in his hand are commonly made of bone; [they signify] the steadfast perseverance of good thoughts and works, or the love of God and neighbour. They are held in the hand so that the love [or possibly *direction*] of the voice may be exercised through work. Jubilation, which is called the sequence, signifies that state in which spoken words will not be necessary; rather, by thought alone one mind will show another [Col. 0789A] what it holds within itself. To this tends the discourse of preaching, which is of itself veiled by the six wings of the seraphim. The reader and singer ascend the step because teachers ought to imitate the passion of the Lord’s cross. The deacon’s ascent to the pulpit is a lofty invitation to virtues.

### Chapter LXXXIII.—On the Gospel and Its Reading

Pope Anastasius commanded that people should not sit while the Gospel is read, but stand bent, because in the new life we ought to stand in humility. Then the bishop puts incense into the censer upon the coals, so as to raise a sweet fragrance. The censer signifies Christ’s body, in which the fire is the Holy Spirit, from whom proceeds a good fragrance, that is, a good repute concerning Christ. The deacon receives a blessing from the priest, that is, preachers receive the word from Christ. Then he goes to the [Col. 0789B] altar to take the Gospel from it. The altar is Jerusalem, from which Gospel preaching went forth, as it is said: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” The deacon carrying the Gospel is Christ’s foot; he carries the Gospel on his left arm because in this temporal life it must be preached. When the deacon greets the people, all the people turn toward him, because hearers ought eagerly to receive God’s word from preachers. Afterwards the priest and all the people turn toward the east and make the cross upon their foreheads, which the deacon made first, and worship Christ, who was born in the East. The forehead is the seat of shame; we make the sign of the cross there because we are not ashamed of Christ, whom we preach crucified. At this point staffs are laid down from the hands, so that [Col. 0789C] we may be separated from the act of the Jews, who put a reed into the Lord’s hand.

### Chapter LXXXIV.—On the Candles at the Gospel

Two candles are carried before the Gospel because the Law and prophecy preceded Gospel teaching. The censer is the repute of Christ’s good virtues: incense rises in the censer; Christ’s works preceded his teaching, as it is said: “Jesus began to do and to teach.” While the deacon reads the Gospel, he stands facing north because the Gospel is preached to those cold in faith. The Gospel is read from a higher place, while the candles stand below, because the Gospel has greater authority than the Law and prophecy. After the Gospel, the candles are extinguished, because when Gospel preaching has ended [Col. 0789D] the Law and prophecy will cease.

The Gospel lying upon the altar signifies the time in which it must be preached. The preceding office sets forth Christ’s preaching up to the hour of the Passion, and that of his preachers until the end of the world and beyond. The following [office] indicates the work of Christ’s passion, resurrection, and ascension, and likewise that of his followers: either sacrifice or mortification, and resurrection and longing for heaven, where they will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father.”

### Chapter LXXXV.—On the Oblation or Offertory

The legal offering was made at the entrance of the tabernacle. Our offerings are two: one, mortification; the other, good works, at the entrance of the tabernacle, that is, in the present [Col. 0790A] life. The Law commands sacrifices to be offered for vows, voluntary offerings, sin, the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah. We offer for vows when we fulfil what we promised in tribulation; for voluntary offerings when we give thanks for what we have received; for sin when we are pierced with compunction over what we have committed; for the kingdom when we ask upright hearts for kings; for the sanctuary when [we ask] stability for the sacred ranks; for Judah when we ask for the people’s peace and unanimity.

The office which we call the *offerenda* begins where the priest says, “The Lord be with you,” and ends where he says in a loud voice, “For ever and ever.” Christ came into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday to be sacrificed; and a praising crowd [Col. 0790B] met him, whom he graciously greeted. Therefore the priest greets the people. Afterwards he says, “Let us pray,” and the singers sing, because when Christ had filled the hearts of the crowds, they immediately sang magnificent praises in prayer. The purity of the linen cloth placed on the altar is the purity of the minds of those who sing to the Lord. Having received the offering, the priest returns to the altar to sacrifice there; Christ, after receiving the vows of those singing, entered Jerusalem to be sacrificed there.

The altar in the present signifies the common life of the righteous; the offerings upon it are good thoughts and just works. The priest’s greeting shows entry into another office; the priest says, “Let us pray,” so that they may pray for the sacrifice to be made acceptable as Abel’s was, and not despised as Cain’s. The linen cloth is the body chastised [Col. 0790C] from all natural freshness and moisture; so should the mind of those making an offering be free from every carnal desire. The corporal cloth must be linen and pure; it signifies Christ’s body taken from the Virgin. Through many sweats it comes to whiteness; so Christ through many sufferings came to the brightness of the resurrection. Whoever desires to receive Christ’s body must discipline himself through many labours and make the condition of mind and body pure and white. It must be folded so that neither beginning nor end appears, because although Christ in his humanity had a beginning in being born and an end in dying, yet in his divinity he had neither.

Bread is offered because, just as bread is made from many grains [Col. 0790D], so the body of Christ, which is the Church, is gathered into one from many chosen persons; and just as bread is baked by the heat of fire, so Christ is brought to completion through suffering. Wine is offered because, just as it is pressed out from many grapes, so from many saints the body of Christ—that is, the Church—is gathered together when pressed by sufferings. And through the press of suffering Christ gave the drink of resurrection. Water is offered because the people, through the water of baptism, are mingled with Christ and incorporated into him. Prayer is addressed to the Father alone, although the whole Trinity works, lest idolatry be imagined if three persons were invoked as though they were three gods. Yet it is concluded through the Son and the Holy Spirit, so that the effect of the petition may be shown to lie in the Trinity. At all prayers, “Through [Col. 0791A] our Lord Jesus Christ” is said, so that he who eternally lives and reigns may cause us—whether still living or already dead—to live and to reign with him in heaven. At exorcisms, however, it is said: “Through him who is to come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire,” so that the devil, hearing of the future judgment, may tremble and flee through the name of him who will be judge of the living and the dead.

Seventy-two crosses are made in the canon over the offering and the chalice, because seventy-two languages were redeemed through Christ’s passion. “The Lord be with you” is said seven times in the Mass, because through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit the offered sacrifice is accepted, and through these gifts seven sins are remitted to human beings.

[Col. 0791B] The singers, as they sing the office, signify the crowd that sang to the Lord. The people give offerings to the Lord—bread and wine—that is, devout desires hidden inwardly: we ourselves ought to be a sacrifice. The priest washes his hands through good works and tears of compunction; then he prays before the altar, lest he be struck like the Beth-shemites, who unworthily looked upon the ark of the Lord. After the prayer he censes the altar, because propitiation is made through Christ, whose body the censer signifies.

The deacon mixes water with wine, because the people are united with Christ. If anyone offers wine alone without water, the blood of Christ begins to be without us; but if water is alone, the people begin to be without Christ.

[Col. 0791C] Just as many grains, gathered into one, ground, and mixed, make one bread, so in Christ, who is the living bread, the united number of the elect will be one body.

Every person entering the church ought to offer a sacrifice: the priest and ministers bread, the people wine, the singers water. Afterwards the priest prays that they may pray for him, that he may be worthy to offer God the offering of the whole people.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. On the prayer said quietly.

The secret prayer follows, and it is called “secret” because it is said secretly. All sacrifices under the Law were secret, that is, silent, because they were shadows of things to come. The Paschal lamb lay hidden in Christ. The priest speaks to God alone [Col. 0791D]; therefore a voice is unnecessary, or a resounding one, in order that the priest may be reminded what he ought to think.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. On the Preface and the *Sanctus*.

The priest says “Through all ages” aloud, so that the prayer may be confirmed by “Amen.” Here, when he says “The Lord be with you,” he does not turn toward the people, to signify devotion in offering sacrifice; and the ploughman ought not to look back.

A hymn is said because it is filled with thanksgiving and the praises of angels. It is called a Preface because it prepares the minds of the brethren for the harmony of the holy angels who attend the consecration of Christ’s body, and for reverence toward so great a consecration; therefore it is sung in a high voice.

[Col. 0792A] The present office represents the time when Christ at supper went up into the large furnished upper room and, after some delay, offered a hymn to God the Father. Here the altar is the Lord’s table, at which he ate with his disciples. The linen corporal is the cloth with which he was girded; the cloth (*sudarium*) signifies the suffering caused by Judas the betrayer. The priest ascends into the upper room when he says, “Lift up your hearts”; then he gives thanks, as Christ did to the Father. The priest’s thanksgiving is his sacrifice; the praises of the angels, or their ministries, are sacrifice. Angels and archangels praise; dominions and principalities adore; powers tremble; the heavens—that is, thrones—virtues, cherubim, and seraphim celebrate together. The tenth order, the human order, is joined to them when we pray: “Command that our voices also may be admitted with theirs” [Col. 0792B], etc.

Pope Sixtus ordained that the *Sanctus* should be sung. The order of angels says: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; heaven and earth are full.” The order of human beings adds: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” The cloth lying on the altar signifies the toil endured by angels in ministry to humankind, or by perfect men who do not cease to pray for our frailty. The corporal signifies unfeigned intention.

At the Preface the deacon stands behind the bishop and the subdeacon before his face. Those who stand behind are the disciples who fled during Christ’s passion; those who stand before his face are the women who attended him then. At the *Sanctus*, those standing before and those [Col. 0792C] behind bow down, venerating the divine majesty and the Lord’s incarnation. The harmony of the angels introduces the divine majesty by saying, “Holy, holy, holy”; the crowd introduces the Lord’s incarnation by saying, “Blessed is he who comes.” Those standing behind remain bowed until it is said, “But deliver us from evil.” They are those to whom it is said: “You are those who remained with me in my trials”—that is, the apostles, who were in great tribulation and did not dare to raise themselves, that is, to confess themselves disciples of Christ, until through the resurrection they were delivered from the evil of fear. Those standing before signify the disciples concealed for fear of the Jews. The subdeacon’s bowing signified the sorrow of the women or of the peoples at [Col. 0792D] Christ’s passion.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. On the Canon of the Mass.

From the beginning of “Therefore, you” (*Te igitur*) to the place where it is said, “Command that we be numbered among the flock of your elect,” the sacrifice of the elect is celebrated—of those who do not have anything in the flesh opposing them. Just as there were two altars in the tabernacle of Moses or in the temple of Solomon, one for incense and the other for burnt offering, so there are two sacrifices of the holy Church: one in which all carnal impulses are stilled, which is that of incense; the other in which those same impulses must daily be slain through compunctionate tears.

“Therefore, you” is said secretly lest words so holy and pertaining to so great a mystery become cheap, while people who had almost learned them through use might chant them through streets [Col. 0793A] and squares or other places where they assembled. Thus it is related that, before this custom had become established, when shepherds chanted them in the field, they were struck down by divine power. “Therefore, you” is said secretly because the priest speaks to God alone, who knows the hidden things of the heart, as is said of Hannah: “She spoke in her heart, and her voice was not heard at all.”

The Lord prayed three times on the Mount of Olives before his passion; likewise the priest makes three prayers: for the Church, for the brethren, and for the company of priests. By the number three the sacrifice of the elect is made to the Father: “These gifts, these offerings, these holy unblemished sacrifices.” By “gifts” bread is understood, in which there is water and flour. “Offerings” means wine, in which there are wine and water. “Unblemished sacrifices” acknowledges both together. We offer these for three groups [Col. 0793B]: for the universal Church; for particular brethren whose alms or gift we have received, or who are present; and for ourselves, who share communion with holy Mary and the apostles in one Lord.

There are three sacrifices which the Lord requires: to do justice, to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with God. In this prayer the linen cloth signifies Christ’s humility, which he assumed in earthly garb. The cloth on the altar signifies his toil in prayer, as it is said: “Being in agony, he prayed more earnestly.”

When he says, “Therefore, this offering,” the priest bows toward the altar: Christ humbled himself unto suffering. Here the linen cloth is Christ’s being handed over into the hands of the wicked; the cloth is the suffering arising from the betrayer. The sacrifice [Col. 0793C] of the perfect is joined to the sacrifice of angels. Then the universal sacrifice—that is, Christ’s immolation—is celebrated before “To us also, sinners”; for Christ was immolated for sinners.

“Which offering, O God, in all things”—that is, with the whole thought, the whole life, the whole understanding—“blessed” through the Father, “enrolled” through the Son, “ratified” through the Holy Spirit. The five crosses signify Christ’s five wounds. The priest’s outstretched hands signify Christ’s extension upon the cross. When it is said, “This is my body,” the bread is first changed into flesh; when he says, “This is my blood,” the wine, by the Lord’s words, is changed into blood. The linen cloth on the altar is the cloth with which he was girded; the cloth (*sudarium*) [Col. 0793D] is the toil in the washing of feet; the altar is the Lord’s table.

Following the Lord’s example, the priest takes the offering and chalice into his hands and raises them, that they may be acceptable to God, like Abel’s sacrifice, who offered a lamb in the figure of Christ; like Abraham’s sacrifice, who offered his son; and like Melchizedek’s, who offered bread and wine.

“From your gifts and grants”: gifts belong to the eternal reality, grants to the temporal reality. “A pure victim” means bread; “a holy victim,” the chalice; “an unspotted victim,” both together. When he says, “Humbly we beseech you, almighty God,” he bows before the altar, because Christ on the cross prayed from the psalm, “My God, my God,” to “Into your hands [Col. 0794A] I commend my spirit”; and then, having bowed his head, he gave up the spirit. From the place, “Therefore, remembering,” the altar represents the cross; the linen cloth, Christ’s humility unto death; the cloth, the toil of the passion. Here the subdeacons raise themselves: the disciples who were present at his passion, after his death are in some measure comforted, raise themselves, and look upon the body beloved by them while it hangs on the cross. Here the deacons wash their hands, because the filthy deeds of their former way of life are cleansed by Christ’s passion.

Adam slept, and Eve was fashioned from the side of the sleeper; Christ dies on the cross, and the Church, his body, is fashioned from the blood and water which flowed from his side. We were redeemed by blood and washed from sins by water. The first voice of this wife was that centurion [Col. 0794B] who said: “Truly this was the Son of God.” Hence “To us also” is said more loudly.

The subdeacons standing erect and watching the priest’s action are his acquaintances and the women who stood at a distance watching these things. The deacon lifts the chalice from the altar and wraps it in the cloth: he is Joseph, who took the Lord down from the cross and placed him in the tomb. The priest who raises the offering is Nicodemus, who buried the Lord with myrrh and aloes. The priest makes two crosses beside the chalice because Christ was taken down from the cross, having been crucified for two peoples. The priest’s and deacon’s lifting of the chalice is Christ’s removal from the cross; the offering and chalice are the Lord’s body. The altar is the cloth that was over his head. The offering is round in the form of a denarius, because for thirty denarii [Col. 0794C] the Lord was sold.

The subdeacons who stood before his face now withdraw, because when the Lord was buried the women withdrew from the tomb. At the words, “To us also, sinners,” the sacrifice of penitents is recalled, who crucify their flesh with its vices and desires. The altar of burnt offering is our mortification; the raising of the voice is the cry in the penitent’s heart; the sacrifice of penitents is a contrite spirit. The altar of burnt offering is the heart of those who consume carnal impulses in the fervour of the Holy Spirit. The linen cloth is the chastening of the flesh through vigils and fasts. The cloth is the very intention by which we hasten to conquer the movements of temptation. The petition follows: “Into whose fellowship [admit us].”

The subdeacon who held the paten, when the canon is finished, [Col. 0794D] at the words “And safe from every disturbance,” etc., gives it to the deacon, and he in turn to the priest; this is the service rendered by the women at Christ’s burial. The Lord’s Prayer is said aloud because it is public and common prayer, and is for the whole people. “Saving precepts” means evangelical teaching; “divine institution,” the making of the Lord’s body and blood. Here the deacons raise themselves because in the seventh petition they are delivered from evil. In remembrance of the seventh day, when Christ rested in the tomb, the Lord’s Prayer is said, which has seven petitions; on that seventh day the apostles suffered in sorrow and fear of the Jews. These three divisions of the present prayer signify the period of the Lord’s three-day burial. Thus on Good Friday [Col. 0795A] the Lord’s Prayer is said before the Lord’s body, so that we may forgive our debtors and be delivered from evil.

The subdeacons coming with the paten to receive the Lord’s body from the altar are the women who come to the tomb after the sun has risen and find him alive. After the priest says, “Peace be with you,” the offerings are placed upon the paten. This signifies that, after Christ rose from the dead and gladdened the disciples’ hearts with his greeting, the women’s desires were fulfilled when they received the joy of the resurrection. Then the Lord’s body is put into the wine. Bodily life consists of body and blood; as long as these two are vigorous in a person, the spirit is present. Christ’s blood was poured out for our soul; Christ’s flesh died for [Col. 0795B] our flesh. These two returned to their proper substance in the resurrection, and the spirit will make the new person alive, so that he may die no more. For the cross formed over the chalice with a particle of the offering sets before our eyes the very body which was crucified for us. Therefore it touches the four sides of the chalice, because through it the human race from all four quarters of the world came to the unity of one body and to the Church’s peace. The angels promised this peace, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” Hence it is now said: “The peace of the Lord be always with you.” The people then follow it by affectionate kisses. Women do not receive the peace from men, because of lust.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. On the *Agnus Dei* and the body of Christ.

[Col. 0795C]

Pope Sergius ordained that while communion is being received, the *Agnus Dei* should be sung: so that he who took away the offence of the world may now take away ours through the offering of the holy Eucharist or through the kiss of peace. The Lord’s body is received because we ought to be one in Christ, who is the God of peace, through whom heavenly and earthly things were reconciled. The apostles received this after eating and at the end of the day, because Christ was the end of the Law and the beginning of grace. But we ought to receive it fasting, since it is food surpassing every bodily food. Priests should abstain from women for three days; Christ’s body is threefold. The first is holy [Col. 0795D] and immaculate, assumed from the Virgin Mary; the second is that which still walks on earth, namely the holy Church; the third is that which lies in tombs. By the particle of the offering put into the chalice is shown Christ’s body, already risen from the dead; by that eaten by priest or people, the body still walking upon earth; by that left upon the altar, the body lying in the tomb. The same body takes the offering with it to the tomb, and the holy Church calls it the dying person’s *viaticum*. This particle remains on the altar until the end of Mass, because until the end of the age the bodies of the saints rest in tombs. The corporal which remains on the altar signifies purity of mind, to which everyone receiving the Lord’s body ought to devote himself, but especially at the end. The following antiphon is the communion [Col. 0796A]; it is a reciprocal voice and signifies those who recognized the Lord in the breaking of bread and announced him to the others.

## CHAPTER XC. On “*Ite, missa est*.”

After this the priest blesses the people; so Christ blessed them and ascended into heaven. Then he turns back to the east, that he may commend himself to the Lord’s ascension.

The deacon says, “Go, the dismissal is made,” because Christ, the unique envoy, was sent for us to the Father, bearing with him the tokens of his passion. First, that by this token he might establish for the disciples faith in his resurrection. Then, that in pleading for us before the Father, he might always show what kind of death he endured for the life of mortals. Third, that he might continually renew for those redeemed by his death how mercifully [Col. 0796B] they have been helped, by presenting the tokens of that same death. Finally, that he might show even to the faithless at judgment the wounds by which they are justly condemned. When the deacon says, “Go, the dismissal is made,” let our mind tend toward that homeland to which our head has gone before.

The Mass is called so from the place of sacrifice to the end, because at the time of sacrifice the catechumens were sent outside; and therefore it is said, “Go, dismissal,” because the assembled people are then dismissed. In Lent, however, we are as though on campaign against the devil; hence the priest fortifies us with his blessing, while the deacon cries: “Bow your heads to God.” The priest’s blessing is given at the end according to ancient custom, as Jacob, when dying, blessed his sons.

## CHAPTER XCI. On the Advent of the Lord.

[Col. 0796C]

The human race had fallen asleep, as it were, in sins; the trumpet of the prophets rouses it to receive the Lord’s advent. Awakened, it eagerly receives the Lord’s advent, saying: “To you I have lifted up,” etc. The Old Law, through the prophets, announces the Lord’s advent to the Jewish people, saying: “People of Zion,” etc. The New Law, through the apostles, foretells to the Church the Lord’s second advent, saying: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your moderation be known to all people. The Lord is near”—understand: that he may make us rejoice in soul and body.

The office “Remember us, O Lord” is not authentic [Col. 0796D]; but whether it or “Drop down, ye heavens” (*Rorate*) is sung, it is the voice of saints longing for either the Lord’s first or second advent.

The Gospel “When he had lifted up,” concerning the five loaves, is read on the fifth Sunday before the Lord’s Nativity, because through the five ages of the world the proclamation of the coming Christ sounded forth.

The Antiphonary and the Missal have four offices because the Lord’s Nativity was celebrated through the four orders of books: the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, and the Gospels. Hence the Nativity itself is often also celebrated in the fourth week. The author of the Lectionary also teaches us how mighty is the Lord who is to come to us and enter the house of our heart in order to dwell there, a house which we defile through [Col. 0797A] the excesses of our five senses. For through enticing forms the desires of fleshly pleasures enter through the eyes; evil suspicion concerning a brother through the ears; lustful odour through the nostrils; gluttony defiles through the mouth; cruelty through touch. But our coming King does not wish to dwell amid such filth. Therefore, by the five readings of the five weeks, we are urged to circumcise our five senses from every vice and prepare a worthy dwelling for the Lord, as for the true King and Prophet.

The reading says: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch, and a king shall reign and act wisely”; and the Gospel: “This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world.” Just as through the five senses, so through the four elements a person either falls into [Col. 0797B] evil works or rises to good ones. Hence in the first week the reading says: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep,” and the awakened person says: “To you I have lifted up.” During these four weeks “Glory in the highest” and the use of the dalmatic are omitted, to signify the time of the Old Testament, which passed under four dignities foreshadowing Christ’s Nativity: namely, under the patriarchs, judges, kings, and prophets.

## CHAPTER XCII. On the Lord’s Nativity.

The Lord’s Nativity is celebrated so that through the Lord himself we may be reborn in the Spirit. On that night three Masses are celebrated because through Christ’s birth the whole course of the three periods—before the Law, under the Law, and under [Col. 0797C] grace—is signified; or because the three parts of the world, Asia, Africa, and Europe, are saved. On that night “Glory in the highest” is also sung, because it was then first sung by the angels.

Pope Telesphorus ordained that on the night of the Lord’s Nativity the first Mass should be celebrated at the first cockcrow, when the Lord was born; another at daybreak, when the child was found by the shepherds in the manger and by the teachers in the Gospel; and the last at the third hour of the day, when heaven was joined in marriage to earth.

The same Pope Telesphorus ordained that Mass should not be celebrated before the third hour on feast days, at which hour the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples. On other days, when fasting is required, it is celebrated at the sixth hour, when Christ ascended the cross. [Col. 0797D] In Lent, at the ninth hour, when he expired.

The feast of Saint Stephen is held when his finding is commemorated; for it occurred after Easter, but here it is observed because of the feast days.

The Dormition of Saint John the Evangelist falls on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; but because it cannot be celebrated there, it is observed here.

On the feast of the Innocents, “Glory in the highest,” “Alleluia,” and “Glory be to the Father” are not sung, because of the mothers’ sorrow and because they descended to the underworld.

## CHAPTER XCIII. On the Circumcision of the Lord and Epiphany.

The Lord’s Circumcision is observed so that we too may be spiritually circumcised in our five senses. The eighth day before the Ides of January was once celebrated because of Augustus’s threefold triumph.

The same day is now also celebrated by us for three reasons. Three magi—that is, three kings—offered three gifts to the triune God. Christ is baptized, the Father bears witness to the Son, and the Holy Spirit is visibly manifested. A wedding is celebrated, water is changed into wine, and Christ is believed by the disciples to be God.

## CHAPTER XCIV. On the day of the Purification.

In the month of February the city was once ritually purified in pagan fashion with lights, and sacrifice was made to the spirits of the dead—that is, infernal gods. We observe this custom, instituted by the holy Fathers for divine worship, at the purification of holy Mary: carrying [Col. 0798B] lighted candles in our hands and, like the prudent virgins, bearing lamps with oil, we receive Christ and enter with him into the wedding, clothed in a wedding garment.

## CHAPTER XCV. On the funeral rites of the dead.

The Mass for the dead is conducted as at the Lord’s death: that is, without “Glory,” “Alleluia,” or the kiss of peace, for these signify joy, while in these rites sorrow is enacted. Commemoration of the dead is made before “To us also, sinners”: there the remembrance of the Lord’s death ends and our own death begins through the confession of sins. Bodies do not take part in public offices because music is not fitting in mourning. The third and seventh days for the dead are observed for this reason: they consist of soul and body. The soul is raised up, as it were, by three columns [Col. 0798C], so that it may love God with all its heart, all its soul, and all its mind. It is also rational, irascible, and desirous. By reason we distinguish good from evil, are angry at evils, and desire goods. Because this soul neglected God’s worship in thought, life, and understanding, the third day is observed so that it may be purified from these sins.

**Note.** Here certain matters concerning the body are missing in my copy.

(Here certain things to be said about the bodies of the dead are lacking in our Gemnicensis manuscript.)

## CHAPTER XCVI. On Easter Day.

The Paschal day is celebrated through seven days as though it were one day. It signifies that time when the heart of the elect shall rejoice and no one shall take their joy from [Col. 0798D] them, nor will it be necessary for them to ask anything, as is said: “I shall see you again,” etc. On that day and at that time they will ask nothing; therefore Vespers does not begin with the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” by which divine help is invoked, because no one is then tempted, but with “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*), by which the feast of the mind is signified. For *Kyrie eleison* belongs to the Mass, and these Vespers solemnly begin with *Kyrie eleison* and are joined to Masses, because that day has no evening. Hence the responsory “This is the day” is repeated at every hour with alleluia. The same psalms are sung at each Vespers because one and the same day is being celebrated. Three psalms are sung before the hymn of holy Mary because, as was said, heavenly, earthly, [Col. 0799A] and infernal beings rejoice at Christ’s resurrection. Two follow at the font because, in faith in Christ’s resurrection, the Jewish and Gentile peoples are baptized; or because in the end contemplatives and actives will be saved through Christ. At night we say a verse because, set amid temptation in this life, we need divine help; by day we do not say one, because in that life, signified by this day, we shall be secure from every temptation.

## CHAPTER XCVII. On the Sundays after Easter.

The responsory “You are worthy, O Lord” signifies the apostles’ entrance into the Church, which was gathered from Jews to the faith of the New Testament. The responsory “I am like a vine” concerns the portion of the Jewish people brought to the unity of faith. In the first responsories the coming together of hearers and leaders into one faith is narrated; in those following [Col. 0799B] is shown the mystery of bridegroom and bride in the Church now gathered, from whom that Church itself was brought forth. That bride is Jerusalem; therefore the present bride is frequently named through Jerusalem, because she began to grow in Jerusalem. Hence the responsory “I saw Jerusalem.” In the others the beauty of Jerusalem’s structure is narrated, as in the responsory “This is Jerusalem” and “Your streets.” All these must be understood mystically of the spiritual buildings of the heavenly Jerusalem, according to the tenor of the offices, which contain within themselves the person of the primitive Church—for example, “As newborn,” etc., “The mercy of the Lord,” etc., and “Make a joyful noise,” etc. These must be sung through three weeks.

The responsory “If I forget you” is from the psalm “By the rivers”; it signifies the Gentile people which formerly dwelt in Babylon—that is, in the confusion of this world—and desired to be recalled through the apostles’ preaching and teaching to Jerusalem, that is, the Church. All the remaining responsories concern liberation from Babylonian unbelief and arrival in Jerusalem, such as “God, song,” “Let [them] now say,” etc., and “In the churches.” These are taken from the Psalter, which is of ten strings: in them are love of God and love of neighbour—love of God for three reasons, love of neighbour for seven. And the responsory “The children make themselves known” (*Insinuant se proles*) teaches the offspring to love their mother’s bridegroom and their mother, and to speak to and answer the city Jerusalem, which dwells in heaven.

[Col. 0799D] The three offices “Sing to the Lord,” etc., “The voice of joy,” etc., and “Hear,” etc., recall the same times as the responsories. Therefore those do not err who sing them through the three weeks up to Pentecost.

The responsories on the Lord’s ascension now console the bride, namely the holy Church, such as the responsories “Let it not be troubled,” etc., and “It is time,” etc. Now she herself speaks to the bridegroom, as in the responsory: “Be exalted, O Lord,” etc. Now she longs to be received by him above the stars.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. On the responsories at Pentecost.

At Pentecost the Romans sing nine lessons; but we, because of the baptismal sacraments in three persons baptized, praise the Trinity with three psalms until the octave.

[Col. 0800A] The responsories proclaim that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete—that is, the Comforter—promised by the bridegroom, has come to the bride, and proclaim the gifts brought to her through him: faith, works, miracles, and the other charisms. At Easter, the Ascension, and Pentecost, we sing an antiphon with Alleluia over the psalms in Matins praises, except at the *Benedictus*, because by this we recall God’s benefits which we have received from his resurrection, ascension, and the coming of the Holy Spirit. But at the *Benedictus* we do not sing an antiphon with alleluias because of the very great tribulation that is to come.

## CHAPTER XCIX. On the feasts of Saint John the Baptist, and likewise Saints Peter and Paul.

For Saint John the Baptist, the responsories are taken [Col. 0800B] from the Prophets and the Gospel, because he was the end of prophecy and the beginning of the Gospel. At the apostles’ feast, antiphons with Alleluia are sung in the third nocturn and at Lauds; at this feast, however, they are not sung, because the glory of the New Testament is greater than that of the Law. For John’s nativity, who bore the type of the ancient Law, occurred before the Lord’s resurrection; but the apostles’ nativity in heaven took place after the Church’s illumination by the Holy Spirit. Therefore the latter is adorned with antiphons, the former is not.

At the principal feasts of saints, the Romans perform two offices in the night. The first is performed at the beginning of the night without Alleluia and is called a vigil; hence the preceding day is also called the vigil. The second is around midnight and ends in daylight; and this has [Col. 0800C] Alleluia in the antiphon of the third nocturn. Through the one office the legal observance and the Sabbaths celebrated as figures of things to come are recalled; through the other, the Lord’s resurrection and our future feast. Therefore it is performed with alleluia, because it has passed into the fellowship of the holy angels.

On the night of Saint Peter two offices are sung: one in the first vigil without an invitatory, because there the people are not invited; the other in the second vigil with an invitatory, because then the people are invited to the vigils. On the feast of Saint Paul verses with antiphons are sung because he laboured more than all. For Saint Lawrence too verses with antiphons are read because of his renowned martyrdom.

## CHAPTER C. On the lessons at Matins after Pentecost.

[Col. 0800D]

After Pentecost, on Sundays until the Kalends of August, lessons and responsories are read from the Books of Kings, a season suited to going to war. Here the deeds of the Fathers—Samuel and David, who was warlike; Elijah and Elisha—are recalled, so that as they fought against enemies, we may fight against vices.

In August, on Sunday nights, lessons with responsories are said from the books of Wisdom, because in this season of the year crops and planted things likewise tend to bear fruit; so we too, now established in mature age, ought through the pursuit of wisdom to bear the fruit of good works.

In September illness often befalls people [Col. 0801A] because of new fruits. So that at the season when abundance of goods is usually greatest we may remember that even amid such abundance we may at some time die, and may patiently endure the illnesses of that season, responsories from Job and Tobit are sung, both of whom endured sufferings. These were not kings; therefore they do not have individual months, but are read in one month, by which the kingdom of the Assyrians is understood. The Sundays on which responsories are sung and the histories read from Judith, Ezra, and Esther signify the kingdom of the Persians and Medes. The book of Tobit and Judith are not in the canon among the Hebrews, but because it received them into the number of the Hagiographa [corr. *Agiographia*, or *Hagiographia*], we sing and read from them.

[Col. 0801B] Cambyses, king of the Persians, was called by the Hebrews the second Nebuchadnezzar; under him the history of Judith was written. Ahasuerus is called Artaxerxes by the Hebrews and the Seventy Interpreters; under him the history of Esther was written.

The responsories from the history of the Maccabees recall the times and kingdoms of the Greeks. In July and August, by singing and reading, the strength, splendour, and wisdom of kingship among the people of Israel are recalled; in September, the Assyrian kingdom; in October, the kingdom of the Persians and Medes is represented to us in the deeds of Esther and Judith; and in the same month the kingdom of the Greeks is also commemorated through the deeds of the Maccabees. Because the kingdom of the Medes and Greeks had less power than that of the Assyrians or Romans, [Col. 0801C] the Roman kingdom is signified by the month of November, through which the former kingdoms came to an end.

For in the four parts of the world were the dominions of four kingdoms: the Babylonian kingdom in the east, namely that of the Assyrians; that of the Medes in the south; the Macedonian in the north; and the Roman in the west. The Assyrian kingdom was a kind of foretoken of the kingdom of the Christian people. Between the Babylonian and Roman kingdoms, the short and intermediate reigns of the Medes and Macedonians came, as it were, in the position of an aged father and a little son, like a guardian and curator, admitted by the power of time rather than by right. In November the prophets are read, as he approaches who was promised by the prophecies of the prophets. The prophets sowed in the times of the Assyrian, Median, and Greek kingdoms what Christians gather [Col. 0801D] in the time of the Roman Empire. This is recalled in the month in which Christ’s advent is foretold. He who brought forth the prophets’ sowing has also given us power to gather it. Hence the responsories of the prophets are now sung—prophets who laboured for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

## CHAPTER CI. On the dedication of a church.

When a church is dedicated, twelve candles are lit inside. For the church to be dedicated bears the type of the people or of any person coming to baptism. When they are baptized, the apostolic teaching already shines in their minds through the preaching of faith, or in the godparents of children confessing the creed. The twelve burning candles signify the preaching of the twelve apostles [Col. 0802A]; but the sacrament of baptism washes the body outwardly and purifies the spirit inwardly. Thus the bishop, circling the church, as under a threefold immersion, simply washes it outwardly with blessed water, and afterwards inwardly purifies it through greater sacraments.

But what does the closed door signify? And what does the lintel struck three times with the rod signify? What also does the bishop’s rod itself signify? All these things are certainly to be understood figuratively. For the closed door signifies that tyrant who strongly guards his own courtyard, and who fastens the bolts of his gates in the unbaptized person. The lintel signifies the human mind, not yet initiated into any sacraments but occupied by many demons. Therefore the bishop says to them in the prophetic voice: “Lift up your gates, O princes.” That pastoral rod is the power of which the Lord said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me”; and which he himself gave to his disciples, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven.” By this power demons were subjected to them, and “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” This is the rod granted by the Lord to the disciples as they went forth to preach. Therefore, by its mighty force the lintel is struck three times, so that, at the confession of the holy Trinity, the mind and place may be emptied of demons; or, as others say, it is struck three times so that threefold authority—namely over heaven, earth, and hell—may be granted to the Church.

The door having therefore been opened and its unhappy master expelled, the bishop, now entering, says, “Peace to this house,” as the Lord commands. Likewise, when Christ entered the world by his birth, peace was announced to human beings by an angel. That the pontiff may worthily perform the office he has begun, he first invokes the Holy Spirit, saying: “Come, Holy Spirit.” Then, prostrating himself in prayer to seek the intercessions of the saints, he orders the litany to be sung. When it is finished, he rises and says the prayer, yet without greeting the people, since he represents an unformed people.

But what follows is very remarkable. Why are ashes used there? Why are two lines of ashes scattered diagonally from corner to corner? And why are they not drawn straight, but obliquely? Why also are letters written in the ashes? All these things were devised by the holy Fathers according to reason; we, however, venerate them by authority.

The ashes are the humble and penitent peoples coming to the regeneration of faith from the four corners—that is, the four regions—of the world. Those four corners signify this, as it is said through the prophet: “All nations shall come to it.” The two lines are circumcision and uncircumcision, which, though long separated from one another, at last meet in the extension of the holy cross. For those two lines seem suitably to make this cross. The two lines, as has been said, are drawn not straight but rather obliquely, because circumcision and uncircumcision, while they steadfastly followed their own paths—the one in unbelief, the other in error—could not attain salvation; but, abandoning the perversity of their paths, they were saved when they came together at the cornerstone.

Why, then, are letters written in ashes? Because the peoples represented by ashes—that is, the humble and penitent who come to faith—ought to receive ecclesiastical teaching from the bishop’s mouth. And because all ecclesiastical teaching is contained in letters, letters are therefore inscribed, so that all teaching may be imparted to the faithful according to their hearers’ capacity, being drink for some and food for others. And since the holy Church is to be instructed in its own language among every nation, it received in the apostles the gifts of diverse languages. Therefore some bishops inscribe only one alphabet. Yet because ecclesiastical teaching is contained in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin speech, for this reason especially some write these three alphabets; or, according to the scale of the church, one alphabet is written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.

But it is very fitting to ask how such actions as are performed there pertain to the dedication of a church. For first the wonderful dignity of the holy Church must be shown, so that from this one may learn how great a reverence ought to be shown to a church being dedicated. The holy Church is the mother of the faithful who come to Christ from circumcision or uncircumcision; she nurses little children and strengthens the mature with bread. She is therefore shown through the figure enacted by the bishop within the church, as by an example.

When these things have been done, the bishop at last approaches in order to begin the office of dedication. Coming to the altar in the customary manner, he says: “O God, make haste to help me”; yet he does not say *Alleluia*, because it is not yet the house of the Lord. Afterwards he begins to bless the water. In its blessing, because some great sacrifice is to be performed, many sacrificial elements from both Testaments are brought together: namely wine, water, salt, ashes, and chrism. Through the bishop’s blessing these receive the power of sanctification through the working grace of the Holy Spirit. For, as Augustine says: “The word comes to the element, and a sacrament is made.”

Wine and water are accordingly counted among the greatest sacraments of the Church, since blood and water came forth from the Lord’s wound. Wine, moreover, in the sacrament of the altar truly becomes blood. But although by this blessing they become sacraments, they appear outwardly one thing and are inwardly another, because the power of the Holy Spirit works according to the manner of sanctification. Salt was placed in every sacrifice, the Lord commanding Moses, because the virtue of discernment must be present in divine offices. This ash also is received by the command of the old law. For he commanded that a red heifer be killed and burned, and that the people be cleansed by being sprinkled with its ashes. Hence Paul says: “If the blood of goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled,” etc.

Why, however, is salt mixed with the ashes before they are put into the water? Because the salt admonishes you to understand that a sacrament lies hidden in the ash. For the red heifer is the flesh of Christ: red from the blood of the cross, roasted by the tribulation of the Passion. By its ash the Jewish people were cleansed, because by Christ’s death the Christian people are washed; as Paul testifies: “All of us who have been baptized into Christ have been baptized into his death.” Therefore ashes are placed in the water three times, and the Lord lay in the tomb for three days; and for this reason one is immersed three times in baptism. Concerning wine, however, enough has been said above. Some nevertheless understand Christ’s divinity by the wine, just as his humanity is understood by the water. And so that the sanctification may be completed, chrism is poured in as the anointing of the Holy Spirit.

After these things have been done, the pontiff approaches to dedicate, beginning with the altar. The altar is understood in many ways in the holy Scriptures; here, however, the Church is understood by the altar. The Church seems to signify both the congregation of the just and that of the unjust. For just as the ark contained clean and unclean animals, so the Church contains good and evil persons in this life. Therefore, coming forward, the bishop makes a cross with blessed water both in the middle of the altar and at its four corners. For this reason the dedication began in the middle of the altar: because the holy Church took its beginning in Judea, which is in the midst of the lands, and afterwards, through the growth of faith, occupied all the ends of the earth.

The bishop sprinkles the whole altar with water seven times, because the Church is cleansed by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Meanwhile the clergy sing the antiphon, “You shall sprinkle me, O Lord,” with the verse of the psalm, “Have mercy upon me.” Water is therefore sprinkled with hyssop, because the healing virtue of that herb seems to signify the humility of our Lord Jesus Christ. Since the Lord humbled himself for us, he communicated the grace of his Spirit to his Church, so that living waters may flow from her belly. Finally, the Church is washed with water three times in circuit, so that by the power of the holy Trinity all the enemy’s snares may be driven away; and therefore meanwhile the psalm is sung: “Let God arise.”

Then the bishop returns to the altar and sprinkles that water along the length of the church, then in its height, and afterwards in its breadth, so that the Church’s sanctification may be established by this threefold sprinkling. For the holy Church possesses a certain special solidity from three virtues, as from three dimensions: namely faith, hope, and charity. For, as Isidore says, the height of the temple refers to faith, the length to hope, and the breadth to charity. Or, as Bede holds: length to faith, height to hope, breadth to charity. These, coming together in one, compose a temple acceptable to God. Some, however, sprinkle only along the length and the height, making a cross and indicating to the people that saying of the Lord: “He who bears his cross and follows me is worthy of me.”

When the office has been completed, the bishop returns to the altar with the remaining water, singing: “I shall go in to the altar of God.” He pours the water left over at the base of the altar. For the church being dedicated, as has been said, first bears the figure of the people coming to faith. Its figurative sprinkling is a certain cleansing of an unformed populace. Since it is not within human power but God’s alone to accomplish this fully, he pours the water at the altar’s base, commending to God whatever remains. And this is what is done by command of the old law.

After this, in order to commend his prayer to the Lord, the bishop burns incense, saying: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight.” The anointing of the altar follows, and indeed the order proceeds appropriately. For just as in baptism a child is first washed in the font, then sanctified by anointing, then adorned with a garment, and finally strengthened by holy communion; so the altar is first sprinkled, then anointed, then covered with a cloth—or, according to some, with waxed fabric. Something analogous is done in the child when a candle is placed in his hand. Finally, Mass is celebrated upon it.

The altar is anointed with a double anointing, namely with oil and chrism, because the holy Church is truly anointed by the Holy Spirit with a double anointing: love of God and love of neighbour. Yet the anointing of God himself comes first, so that love of neighbour may be a kind of path leading to love of God. The altar is anointed both in the middle and at the four corners, with the same meaning by which the sprinkling of water is commended. To make known that this is prefigured in the Old Testament, the bishop begins antiphons taken from it: “Jacob, rising in the morning,” etc.; “Jacob set up,” etc.; “When he went out,” etc. Meanwhile each anointed part is fumigated with burning incense, so that it may be shown to be a place of prayer and its sanctification commended to God. The church itself, however, is anointed with a single anointing, namely with the more exalted chrism, because, since she is Christ’s bride, she ought to be joined to God alone through love.

Then the bishop returns to the altar, to complete the office of his blessing.

If relics are to be deposited, the lord pontiff will go to them or send for them. When relics are outside, they signify the pilgrimage of the saints; when they are carried into the Church, they signify their conveyance into the heavenly Jerusalem.
