And their being placed in the altar signifies that, while they lived in the body, they offered themselves to God upon the altar of the heart. Or, relics of the saints are enclosed in the altar because the souls of the saints rest in heaven beneath God’s altar; and the altar-slab laid over the relics seems rightly to signify this. The veil stretched over the altar signifies the saying: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God,” which will properly occur at the time of judgment.

When the altar has been sanctified, the levites cover it with vestments, because the Lord will clothe the saints with the garment of joy and now graciously grants the stole of immortality to the souls of the saints. It belongs to levites to attend upon divine worship and now to arrange the Lord’s table, just as formerly they arranged the ark of the covenant. Though they receive no inheritance in this world, the Lord’s prohibition in the Old Testament entitles them to possess an inheritance in the Lord in heaven. They therefore fittingly clothe the altar, since by hereditary right they are clothed by the Lord with blessed immortality.

When these things have been completed, the bishop afterwards begins Mass. But if church ornaments are to be sanctified, he should bless them before Mass.

Christ is the shepherd of the flock, that is, of the Church. He carries a staff in order to lead Christ’s sheep—that is, the faithful—to the pastures of life, that is, into paradise. By the staff the weak are supported and the undisciplined corrected. The bishop carries a staff, so that he may uphold the weak in faith by word and example, and correct the unruly by rebuke. Its upper end should be curved, so that he may draw the erring back to the Church by preaching; its lower end should be sharp with iron, so that he may drive out the rebellious by excommunication. On its bend should be written: “When you are angry, remember mercy,” so that he may always exalt mercy over judgment. This bend should be made of bone, because he ought to be patient in adversity. A round sphere should join the two parts, because love joins human beings to God; upon it should be written *homo* (“human being”), so that he may remember himself to be human and not be exalted by authority. At the end should be a circle upon which is written *parce* (“spare”), so that he may spare penitents whom the sharp iron of excommunication had expelled as rebels. The bishop is the *paranymphus*, that is, the Church’s guardian on behalf of the bridegroom; therefore he wears a ring as a pledge. He adorns his hand—that is, his preaching—with good works by means of gloves. He wears a mitre upon his head because he shall receive the crown of life for his labour.

> **[Note: Col. 0805]** Here ends the Sacramentary in the Gemnicensis manuscript.

[Col. 0807]

# MIRROR OF THE CHURCH

(From a manuscript codex of the library of the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Rheinau.

> **[Note: Col. 0807C]** Catalogue of Hoenel, no. 79: A synopsis of all the manuscripts on parchment in the library of the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Rheinau, with a brief note on the age of their script, composed in 1748 by the most illustrious Augustin Calmet. (From St Gall codex 1305.)

The most reverend abbot of this monastery communicated it to us with the greatest kindness. It is a parchment manuscript in small folio, of the twelfth century, written in large and fairly neat letters; mutilated at the end, it now consists of 358 leaves. The person who copied the book scarcely ever grasped its meaning; consequently, two words are quite often contracted into one and others divided apart. At the beginning of the volume an eighteenth-century hand wrote this note: “No. XXXIII. The *Mirror of the Church*, or Sermons, of Honorius, apparently of Autun, written about the twelfth century. Thus the most reverend Abbot Calmet judged, together with his most reverend Coadjutor.”)

## THE CHAPTERS BEGIN

[Col. 0807A] (Fol. 1) First are found the title of the work and the author’s name.

Also, a request addressed to Honorius and instructions for speaking.

**I. “Let the heavens rejoice,” on the Nativity of the Lord.** Here you will find concerning the purple circle around the sun, and how a dumb animal spoke with a human voice; and the Gospel, “A decree went out,” expounded. Concerning the fountain of oil which burst forth at Rome and ran into the Tiber. Also, what it signifies that three Masses are celebrated today. Concerning the unicorn, Saint Anastasia, and Eugenia.

A twofold exposition of the Lord’s Prayer; then the Catholic Faith, together with the Confession. It also clearly instructs how prayer ought to be offered especially for the Church and for all the orders of the Church.

[Col. 0807B] **II. “The righteous man has been delivered from distress.”** Here you will find concerning the illness of Emperor Tiberius and his healing through an image of the Lord; also concerning Veronica; concerning the discovery of the body of blessed Stephen, and when it occurred.

**III. “Who are these that fly like clouds?”** Here you will find concerning the four rivers of paradise; also concerning the four living creatures and the four regions of the world; concerning the four rings by which the ark was carried; concerning rods and exchanged jewels; concerning the widow raised up and the young man restored to life; concerning a glass vessel broken and repaired; concerning the poison which John received unharmed in the Lord’s name and by which he restored the dead to life; concerning the young man converted after brigandage and made a shepherd; and concerning the date of Saint John’s death.

**IV. “These are the saints.”** Here you will find concerning the three Chaldean kings: how Herod pursued them as far as Tarsus in Cilicia. Concerning Christ’s entry into Egypt. Concerning the Persian tree consecrated to demons, which bent down to the ground before our Saviour. Also, concerning a young man and his wife violated until death, and concerning the Gibeonites. Also, what Leah and Rachel signify; and all these things, together with many others, concerning pagan kings.

[Col. 0808A] **V. “I went down into the garden of nuts.”** Here you will find concerning the Midianites, Gideon, circumcision, and what all these things signify. Also, concerning the aging eagle and the life of Saint Basil.

**VI. “Arise, shine, Jerusalem.”** Here you will find, after much else, the Gospel “When Jesus was born” expounded. Also concerning Balaam and his prophecy, and how the she-ass spoke, with many other matters and their mysteries. Also concerning Christ’s baptism and the renewal of the stag. The Gospel “A marriage was made” is also expounded here. Also, concerning the origin of the feast. Concerning the renewal of the serpent.

[Col. 0808B] **VII. “Truth has sprung from the earth.”** Here you will find concerning the continually shut gate, Aaron’s flowering rod, the nut, and an exposition of the Gospel, “After the days were fulfilled.” Also concerning lights, and concerning the Jewish boy cast into flames and rescued.

**VIII. “The stone of darkness,” etc.** Here you will find concerning Abraham’s vision and sacrifice and their meaning. Also concerning the vision of persons sleeping in one bed, grinding, and working a field, and their mystery. Also concerning Jewish pilgrimage, captivity, and return, and their mystical interpretation. Also concerning three Sirens and their meaning. Further—

> **[Note: Col. 0808C]** Perhaps *in super*, that is, “thereupon”: an exposition on the Gospel reading for Septuagesima, or an exposition is made.

—an exposition of the Gospel reading for Septuagesima (as written). Afterwards, concerning Saint Sebastian, Saint Agnes, Saint Vincent, Saint Paul, Saint Blaise, and Saint Agatha.

[Col. 0809A] **IX. “Come, children, listen to me.”** Here you will find general admonitions to priests, judges, the rich, the poor, soldiers, merchants, farmers, and married persons; also concerning the eagle; and, besides these, many good examples.

**X. “How great is the multitude.”** Here you will find concerning the ladder of charity, divided into fifteen steps. Also concerning the twofold fear of the Lord; the two commandments—love of the Lord and of neighbour—and their appendages. Also concerning the tree planted beside streams of waters. Then, how love is perfected; the Gospel concerning the blind man healed; and the rich man who renounced the world.

**XI. “Seek the Lord while he may be found.”** Here is found discussion of the fall of the first human being, the building of Solomon’s temple in seven years, and their mysteries; and why we begin the fast on Wednesday.

[Col. 0809B] **XII. “Zion, who dwell beside the daughter of Babylon.”** Here, after much else, you will find concerning David’s fountain, open for the washing away of sins, as in Paul, Cyprian, Theophilus, Mary Magdalene, Mary of Egypt, and Thaïs. Having briefly recalled these, there follows an old man of great stature who, through God’s grace, recognized the merits of each person merely by looking. Also, concerning Jonah’s prophecy, Moses, Elijah, Daniel, John’s baptism and abstinence; and the reading, “Behold, now is the time.” Also, concerning the origin of the forty appointed days; and the Gospel, “When he shall sit.”

**XIII. “Be well-disposed.”** Here is found discussion of the little bell, the panther, Jerusalem; and the Gospel, “Jesus went out.” Also concerning the bee-eater (*merops*), the stork, Tabitha, Tobias, and Peter the toll-collector.

[Col. 0809C] **XIV. “The Lord will speak peace.”** Here you will find the Gospels: “A certain man sowed good seed in his field,” and “Jesus was casting out demons.” Also concerning the prodigal son; letter-strokes; silkworms; and the conversion of Thaïs.

**XV. “Rejoice, Jerusalem.”** Here you will find the Epistle and Gospel concerning the five ages of the world; concerning Malchus the monk; and also concerning a certain rich man who died and returned again. There follows material concerning Catherine, Saint Matthias, Saint Gregory, Saint Benedict, and the anniversary of Saint Mary, where you have the nobility of that feast; the creation of the first human being, transgression, fall, restoration; Gideon’s fleece; Jesse’s rod; the verse, “I am the flower of the field”; Ezekiel’s gate; the golden statue; Daniel cast into the lions’ den and its mystical meaning; Mary of Egypt; and Zosimas.

[Col. 0809D] **XVI. “Today, if you hear the Lord’s voice.”** Here you have concerning the two persons entering the promised land; heretics; Elisha and his staff; and the dead man whom he raised. Also concerning Abel and the lamb; Cain; Noah; the curse of Ham; four and five kings; Lot; Abraham; Melchizedek; Isaac; the goat; and the red heifer. The Gospel: “Jesus, going up into a boat.” Also concerning the sheep-pool. The Gospel: “A certain man planted a vineyard.” Concerning the sinful woman Pelagia.

**XVII. “Upon the asp and basilisk.”** Here you have concerning the asp and basilisk, lion and dragon, and their nature. Also, how the Lord raised Lazarus and how he came to the Passion. Concerning Lazarus, who afterwards was bishop for thirty years. Also the Gospels: “When they drew near to Jerusalem,” and “Jesus was going to the city of Nain,” and their mysteries. Concerning the fourfold death of humankind. Why Palm Day is so called and observed. All these things formerly [or perhaps: “Here you have”]—concerning Abraham’s servant, the marriage of Isaac and Rebecca, the Jewish people’s affliction under Pharaoh and deliverance; and material is set forth concerning the bronze serpent, the twelve scouts, and very many other matters and their mysteries.

[Col. 0810A] **XVIII. “I will return to Jerusalem with mercy.”** Here you have concerning the consecration of chrism and oil; why the day is called the day of pardon, because he washed the disciples’ feet; concerning the Lord’s body and blood, his Passion, and Judas’s thirty curses. Concerning the thieves, King Josiah, and its mystical interpretation. Concerning Jonah, the Samaritan woman, and the mysteries of all these things.

[Col. 0810B] **XIX. “This is the day which the Lord has made.”** Here you have lauds, a greeting, a sequence, and the Gospel of Mary Magdalene. Also concerning Joseph, Samson’s history and its mystical significance; the nature of the lion and phoenix. (Fol. 4.) Concerning the verse: “Who is this who comes from Edom?” Also concerning the pelican, and a certain distinguished Father who fell into a furnace [*fornum*, as written] and was restored.

**XX. “Christ, rising again.”** Here you have concerning the seven-headed dragon, the crocodile, and the water-snake (*enhydris*). Also, how often the Lord appeared on that very day. The Gospel: “He manifested himself.” Mention is also made of the Babylonian and Egyptian captivities, and of what the three days before Easter signify. Afterwards, concerning Saint Mark, the discovery of the holy cross, its mysteries, and its signs. There you will find concerning King Constantine, Saint Helena, and Pope Saint Alexander. There follows material concerning the apostles Philip and James. Then, “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous man and his seed.” Concerning the Rogation Days. Here there is a threefold impediment to prayer. Also, concerning the woman sitting in an amphora and the two winged women. Also the Gospel: “The sower went out.” Concerning the institution by Bishop Mamertus and Gregory. Concerning the Greater Litany. Also the Gospel: “Which of you shall have a friend?” Afterwards, concerning the five overthrown cities; Abraham, Lot, Moses, Samuel; a certain old man who obtained in his first prayer what he wanted; and a monk who, by praying, resisted a demon sent by Julian. Also concerning five necessities, and concerning the woman who gives birth in sorrow.

[Col. 0810D] **XXI. “The sun and moon have been lifted up.”** Here you have concerning the triumph of Roman kings; the psalm verse, “You will bless the crown of the year with your goodness”; the mystery of his Ascension; the Gospel, “As the eleven disciples reclined”; the eagle’s flight; the charadrius; and the place of the Lord’s Ascension.

**XXII. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.”** Here you have concerning the work of the holy Trinity; the seven days of its feast; the seven women who took hold of one man; the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; and the twice-seven gifts which we shall have in body and soul. Also, in how many ways these were formerly prefigured and foretold: in seven lamps, seven columns, seven eyes, seven horns, and the seven natures of the dove. Also concerning the verse: “Behold how good and how”; the reading, “When they were fulfilled”; the dove bringing an olive branch back to the ark; the finger of God; the jubilee; blasphemy against the Spirit; and the six greatest days.

[Col. 0811A] **XXIII. “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree.”** Here you have concerning the palm and cedar; in what ways and by what names Saint John is commended and honoured; accordingly, the Gospels pertaining to him; also concerning the three orders of the Church and the three perfections; and concerning the death of Saint John the Evangelist.

[Col. 0811B] **XXIV. “You shall ascend, O Lord, upon your horses.”** Here you have concerning Saints Peter and Paul and the great dignity of both; also concerning Simon Magus; Maternus raised from the dead by blessed Peter; and likewise the priest George raised by Peter’s staff; where Paul was caught up to the third heaven. That, when the year had come round, he was beheaded on the same day on which Peter was crucified; that milk together with blood flowed from his neck; and that wolves devoured Nero.

**XXV. “The righteous man shall sprout like a lily.”** These and many other splendid matters are not well related to the praise of the Father. Afterwards you have concerning the conversion of Mary Magdalene; also the verse: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk”; and the servant sold who, after the seventh year, wished to leave—how his ear should be pierced with an awl. After these, concerning the wondrous and marvellous deeds of Saint James; Saint Peter at the verse, “there he found.” Concerning Noah, Shem, and Japheth; the seven Maccabees; Saint Felix and his seven sons; Saint Symphorian and his seven sons; Saint Wisdom and her three daughters. There follows material concerning Saint Lawrence and the Assumption of Saint Mary. There you have the Gospel: “Jesus entered,” and material concerning Theophilus, Saint Bartholomew, and Saint Augustine. There you have the Gospel “A certain man went abroad” expounded, and “Let your loins be girded”; mention is also made of Hermes the martyr. Concerning the beheading of Saint John the Baptist, the finding of his head, the unbelieving cleric, and Rahab the prostitute preserving the scouts.

[Col. 0811D] **XXVI. “Go out, daughters of Jerusalem.”** Here you will find much in praise of holy Mary: concerning the cedar, the star, her parents, and the heavenly messenger through whom her name and holy life were foretold. Also concerning her infancy and Joseph’s rod; accordingly, how her birth was revealed to a certain holy old man; and concerning Saint Adrian the martyr and his wife Natalia.

**XXVII. “The root of Jesse, who stands as a sign to the peoples.”** Here you have concerning a Jew who occupied the house of a certain dead Christian, in which a representation of the holy cross was found and mocked. Also, concerning a Jew travelling to Rome who rested for the night—

> **[Note: Col. 0811D]** Supplemented from the text: “rested.”

—in an ancient temple of idols; after he had signed himself because of extreme fear, the multitude of demons could do him no harm. Also concerning Julian the Apostate, and what he was in childhood; Saint Cyprian the magician and Saint Justina; King Chosroes; Heraclius, emperor of the Romans; miracles performed at Jerusalem when the cross was recovered; the sweetest fragrance; Saints Cornelius and Cyprian; Saints Matthias and Maurice; and Saint Michael.

[Col. 0812A] The Gospel: “Which of you, having a hundred sheep?” Here you have concerning the fall of the first human being; the woman clothed with the sun; the red dragon; the seven principal vices; the three parts of the Church; the three names of angels; Saint Denis, Saint Luke, Simon and Jude; and All Saints. Here you have concerning Saint Mary, angels, patriarchs, prophets, apostles and martyrs, confessors, monks and hermits, virgins; and the verse, “Behold, the scent of my son”; also the verse, “Behold, I shall make Jerusalem a praise of peace,” and the rest. Concerning Jacob’s marriage to Leah and Rachel and its mystery. Concerning the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: “Beloved by God and human beings.” Concerning Saint Martin (fol. 6), then Saint Brice, and Saint Cecilia. Here you have two Gospels: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins”; also, “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure.” “No one lights a lamp.” Concerning Saint Clement. There is found material concerning his father and mother and his sons Nicetas and Aquila; Simon Magus; Sisinnius; and other quite marvellous things concerning Saint Andrew. Here you have concerning Job and his sons and daughters. “The righteous man shall be in everlasting remembrance.” Concerning Saint Nicholas, whose deeds, full of every piety, are followed by glorious miracles. Also concerning Saint Lucy and Saint Thomas. “Many say: Who will show us good things?”

[Col. 0812C] Here is found the rich man who was clothed in purple, and the mystical interpretation of the nine punishments of hell. Much concerning the Book of Kings. Concerning the partridge and its meaning. Concerning the venerable Bishop Saint Paulinus. “Blessed are those called to the wedding supper of the Lamb.” Here you have the Gospel: “A certain man made a great supper.” Concerning Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, and her curiosity. Concerning Saint Alexis.

> **[Note: Cols. 0811D, 0812D]** From this point onward, the numerical chapter marks are absent in the manuscript.

**XXVIII. “Master, though we have laboured all night, we have caught nothing.”** There follows the Gospel: “I have compassion upon the crowd.” Concerning the ten plagues by which the Egyptians were struck; also concerning Saint Euphrosyne.

**XXIX. “The ways of Zion mourn because there are none …”**

> **[Note: Col. 0812D]** Fie manuscript.

Here you have the Gospel: “When the Lord drew near to Jerusalem.” Concerning the heifer that bore a lamb. Concerning Titus and Vespasian; Elijah and Elisha; Saint Marina and her Life, and with what end she departed.

**XXX. “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.”** Here you have the Gospel: “Two men went up into the temple.” Also concerning the spoil with which the Egyptians are despoiled; the beautiful girl captured by men; the woman bound to a wheel; the vulture; Medusa; a certain old man who had nourished a little child in the wilderness; and three fools and their mystical actions.

**XXXI. “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly.”** Here you have the Gospels: “Blessed are the eyes that saw what …,” and “Jesus went out from the region of Tyre.” Also, concerning the man who saw a crown woven of fragrant flowers descend upon his head; and the unlearned man accustomed to say only “Glory be to the Father.” Concerning the muse mentioned by Saint Gregory in his fortieth [homily or book, uncertain].

[Col. 0813A] **XXXII. “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.”** Here you have the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding-feast for his son.” Concerning the twofold calling; the wedding-song of Solomon for these nuptials. Also the Gospel, “the fig tree …”; the bent woman; and a noblewoman who pretended to be foolish.

**XXXIII. “Blessed are those who keep judgment.”** Here you have concerning the twofold judgment and the twofold righteousness. The Gospel: “There was a certain rich man who wished to settle accounts with his servants.” Concerning David and Uriah; Cambyses and Holofernes; Judith the widow (fol. 6v); King Ahasuerus, Esther and Mordecai, Haman, and the mystery of all these things.

[Col. 0813B] **XXXIV. “Blessed are all who fear the Lord.”** Here is found what the ways of the Lord are; what the three lives are; also concerning the seventeen beatitudes; Christ’s two advents; the four Sundays; and why we omit “Glory to God in the highest.” Concerning Enoch and Elijah; Antichrist and the devil; and the glory of the saints. “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord shall find when he comes.” Here you have the Gospel: “Watch, for you do not know.” Concerning the four watches; how many angelic spirits and souls of saints are encompassed by God alone; and the four watches of the present age.

[Col. 0813C] **XXXV. “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.”** Here you have concerning the three deaths; the verse, “The life of man upon earth is warfare”; the verse, “Man born of woman”; and the verse, “It is better to go to the house of mourning.” Concerning the day of death, the seventh day, and the thirtieth day; also concerning various kinds of punishments.

> **[Note: Col. 0813C]** Read from the text: “Concerning various …”

What the resurrection of the dead will be like. Concerning the priest who used to bathe; the captured soldier whom his wife rescued by her offerings; and the captured soldier whom his brother, a priest, rescued. “Blessed are the undefiled in the way.” Here you have what paths lead into the way of charitable righteousness, and what bypaths belong to Satan. “Blessed are those who love you, Jerusalem, and who rejoice in your peace.” Here you have concerning the two cities, Jerusalem and Babylon, their inhabitants and citizens; and the various kinds and customs of monks and canons.

[Col. 0814B] **XXXVI. “King Solomon made a litter of wood.”** Here you have much concerning that man and the house which Wisdom built. Also concerning the chosen, precious cornerstone; the Gospel, “Everyone who hears my word”; and then the origin of dedication. Concerning the tabernacle made in the wilderness; the temple which Solomon built in seven years; the Queen of Sheba; Jesus the high priest; the forms and construction of the temple and their mysteries; ashes, salt, wine, water, hyssop, savin, and their mystical meaning; what dedication signifies; and the Revelation of Saint John. The Gospel “He saw over Jerusalem” and its mystical meaning. Also concerning the twelve foundations of that city; the rich man who built a church with great splendour; and the widow who gave thirty little coins.

## THE MIRROR OF THE CHURCH BEGINS

[Col. 0813]

## THE BRETHREN TO HONORIUS: GREETING
(Fol. 8) When you recently sat in our assembly and spoke the word to the brethren according to the wisdom given you by the Lord, it seemed to all who were present that not you, but an angel of God had spoken. Hence very many of the brethren, pierced to the heart by your words, are already making great progress in the fear of the Lord. Therefore we earnestly ask you to set forth in writing some things of this kind for the edification of many, so that in your last moments you may be helped by the merits and prayers of as many persons as have advanced for the better by reading or hearing your discourse.

## HONORIUS’S REPLY

The most skilled painters—Ambrose and Augustine, Jerome and Gregory, and very many others—have splendidly adorned the house of the Lord with wonderful carving and varied painting. But because these works, through the magnitude of their beauty, exceed the dullness of our understanding, or rather because, worn by daily use, they have now grown old, you command me, venerable brethren, a wretched painter, to renew the splendid painting of illustrious men, though I can scarcely contemplate the brilliance of their wonderful and varied work.

Nevertheless, because you urge that most people embrace a new work more eagerly, although the old is more precious, and that very many are more lavishly delighted by new wine, although the old is sweeter, compelled by your obedience and by the love of Christ, I have painted a new work from the old for those who wish to look upon it, and have mixed a new drink for those who desire to drink. Behold: following the earlier pattern, I have painted this brief but new little panel, so that those who have not leisure to linger long in contemplating the immensity of those excellent works may not be unwilling at least on feast days to look upon some outline of this little panel. Let this little panel be called: *The Mirror of the Church.*

Therefore let all priests set this mirror before the eyes of the Church, so that the bride of Christ may see in it what still displeases her Bridegroom in herself, and may shape her conduct and actions according to its image.

## INSTRUCTION FOR SPEAKING

[Col. 0815]

When, therefore, you wish to address the people, first impress upon your mouth and breast the sign of the cross, invoking upon yourself the grace of the Holy Spirit through the antiphon, “Come, Holy Spirit,” and through the verse of the hymn, “Come, Creator Spirit.” Then invoke the Word of God through the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word,” as far as “without him nothing was made” (John 1); and the final verse: “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (ibid.).

Having therefore received within yourself the Word of God through the grace of the Holy Spirit, begin humbly in his name as follows.

## ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0815A]

“Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult. Let the mountains rejoice in praise, because the Lord has comforted his people and will have mercy on his poor” (Isa. 49).

The heavens are rightly commanded today to rejoice, because today they have deserved to be illumined with a new light and a new joy. For today the King of heaven deigned to visit the earth by his presence and to repair through human beings the loss wrought in heaven by the fall of the angels. Hence the heavens immediately displayed to the world the gladness of their joy, when they promptly sent forth a most brilliant star in service of their King.

The earth also is rightly exhorted today to exult, because today Truth, having sprung from the earth (Ps. 84), came to free it from the curse and to unite human beings, born from the earth, with the angels in heaven. It made known its exceeding exultation to the world today when, as its God was born in its bosom, it immediately brought forth, to the astonishment of all, a fountain of oil flowing from its depths.

The mountains too are exhorted to rejoice in praise of the Lord. The mountains are the patriarchs and prophets, who surpassed the merits of human beings by holy conduct just as mountains rise above the plains of the earth by their height. Today they rejoiced in the praise of God because they exulted to see fulfilled today what the patriarchs had long foretold by figures and the prophets by the Scriptures: namely, that the people of the nations, who walked in the darkness of ignorance, today saw the great light of the eternal wisdom of God. “And upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death”—that is, of hell—“light has risen” (Isa. 9): namely, Christ was born, the splendor of the eternal Father, who would afterward descend to them, snatch them from darkness, and raise them to eternal light.

The righteous too are called heavens because God dwells in them: the sun of wisdom, the moon of eloquence, and the stars of virtues shine in them. These heavens rejoiced today because what they had long desired with many prayers—their desire—was fulfilled today in Christ’s birth, and they perceived that their reward was drawing near.

By the earth, however, sinners are understood (fol. 10), in whom the thorns and briars of sins spring up. They are exhorted today to exult because they deserve to be called to pardon. “I came not,” he says, “to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9).

The mountains, moreover, are angels, who today sweetly rejoiced in praise of the Lord when they sang with a lofty voice, “Glory to God in the highest,” to the King born upon earth. They also joyfully proclaimed peace to people of good will (Luke 2), knowing that their diminished number would be restored from among them.

The sun likewise, rejoicing, clothed itself today in new brightness when it saw the Sun of righteousness rise upon the earth which it itself illumines. For a purple circle, shining far and wide, gleamed today around the sun’s ray, clearly signifying that the Sun of righteousness, risen amid the darkness of death, had undertaken to adorn the world with the purple of his blood.

It is also reported that a dumb animal spoke today with a human voice, signifying, that the mouth of the nations, previously mute, ought to be opened in praise of the Lord. These nations, seeing the star, were astonished and prepared themselves to offer gifts to the newborn King.

Today the whole creation rose up into joy, because the Son of the King of heaven, coming today from the palace of heaven into the prison of the world for a lost servant, brought joy to the whole world. The whole world rightly put on new rejoicing today, because the Lord has comforted his people.

His people are the gentle, humble, chaste, modest, merciful, patient—those who love the Lord and their neighbour. Since they were sorrowful because they had been so long delayed from heavenly joy, today they are comforted by the Lord, since not only the gates of paradise, closed because of disobedience, but even the gates of heaven are opened for them today through Christ. This is also promised to them through the angel: “He himself,” it says, “will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1).

“And he will have mercy on his poor.” The poor are those like myself who have neglected to keep the Lord’s commandments and have clung insatiably throughout their whole life to every crime. Because they groan that they are wretched and stripped naked of righteousness, they desire with all their heart to be freed by him from the misery of sins and punishments. They are poor also because they know that they cannot be saved except by the Lord’s grace alone. Therefore the Lord has mercy upon them, since he promises them hope of pardon, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near to you” (Matt. 3).

Thus the festive joy of today’s light is shared by the righteous and sinners: for a crown is promised to the righteous if they persevere in righteousness; but pardon will be granted to sinners if they hasten from wickedness to repentance.

Dearly beloved, do not consider it burdensome if the sermon is drawn out a little longer. If someone from another nation came here and lived here as a stranger, and someone known to him arrived from his own homeland, he would attentively and without weariness lend an ear to whatever that person told him about his homeland, his friends, or his fellow citizens. You are all here in pilgrimage, and therefore [Col. 0817B] you ought to hear with great attention what is announced to you about your homeland, the heavenly Jerusalem, and what is related about your Father, your mother the Church, and your fellow citizens, the angels and saints.

Nevertheless, because you are tired today and cold constrains some of you, I wish briefly to explain to you how the human race came into this world to be freed from the devil’s power.

As the Gospel relates (Luke 2), Augustus Caesar then ruled the Roman Empire, having subjected to his dominion all the kingdoms which the encircling boundary of Ocean surrounds on every side. He issued an edict that the whole world should undergo an enrolled census. He had proclaimed such a decree that every person should return to the homeland from which he had drawn the origin of his race, and should freely recover whatever inheritance he had unjustly lost; and there each person was to recite to the judge of his province the genealogy of his family, and thus the record of the scribe was to register him for the census.

At that time there was a certain man from Bethlehem, named Joseph, who had betrothed the holy Virgin Mary, mother of the Lord, though she came from poor parents, yet descended from royal stock. Because of poverty he had moved from Judea to Galilee and stayed in a certain city, Nazareth, seeking his livelihood. Therefore, while all the people throughout the world were going to the land of their birth under pressure of the emperor’s edict, Joseph too went to register for the census with his betrothed Mary in Bethlehem, the city of King David, because both he and the Virgin descended from the noble family of David.

Since throughout the whole city no lodging was vacant because of the throng of guests streaming in from every direction, and since they belonged at that time to an impoverished family, they remained in the street when lodging was lacking. Then the fullness of time arrived in which God had decreed to look down from heaven upon the earth (Ps. 13), and on that night the blessed Virgin, without pain and without defilement, brought forth the one who holds the whole world in his fist. Wrapping him in swaddling-clothes, she laid him, according to the necessity of the time, in a manger, perhaps one which Joseph or other guests lodging in the street had enclosed for their animals.

The heavens at once revealed the birth (fol. 12) with rejoicing through a new star, and the earth with exultation, because immediately fountains of oil burst forth from the hidden places of the earth. The angels also appeared to people with immense light and, singing a joyful hymn, announced the King of heaven born upon earth. These are the solemnities of this sacred day, celebrated by angels and human beings.

Now, dearly beloved, I wish in the briefest manner to unfold for you the mysteries of these things. That this most powerful king here imposed the reins of his authority upon every people signifies that the newborn King had determined to draw the whole world under the yoke of the Gospel with the straps of faith. That the world shone in deepest peace signifies that Christ, the true peace, appeared in order to dissolve the enmities between God and human beings and to raise human nature to angelic dignity by his blood.

That all returned to their homeland signifies that all were to return through Christ to the homeland of paradise. Their taken-away inheritance is restored, because the possession of paradise, which had been lost, is restored to the faithful through Christ. Individuals are mentioned by their generations and thus enrolled in writing for the census, because the faithful who confess by faith and hope that they derived their origin from paradise deserve to be confirmed by Christ for the heavenly kingdom through the anointing of chrism.

It is read that certain persons were put to death because they did not know the record of their generation, because those perish by eternal death who do not believe in the Church’s manner of begetting. The people paid Caesar a denarius bearing his image and having the weight of ten coins, because everyone who desires to be restored to the image of the Creator ought most earnestly not to delay in fulfilling the Decalogue of the law.

That Christ wished to be born in the street signifies that, having become an exile from the homeland of heaven for our sake, he came among strangers. Although all things were his and he came into his own, this world, full of miseries, was far removed from his glory. He is born at night because he who will later come manifestly is not recognized now, coming secretly as God. He is wrapped in swaddling-clothes, and our loincloth, sewn from the leaves of sins, is undone by his death. He is laid in a manger—that is, in the food-trough of animals—because his body is given to the faithful as the food of life.

An ass and an ox are said to have stood above the manger, because the Gentile people, signified by the ass, and the Jewish people, signified by the ox, are led through faith to partake of Christ’s body. A star brighter than all the rest shone because the Holy of Holies has shone upon the world today. A fountain of oil burst forth from the earth at Rome and a copious stream ran into the River Tiber, because the pure Virgin brought forth today the fountain of mercy which flowed abundantly into the human race.

The angels showed themselves to people in the great brilliance of light and with every kind of voice of praise, because they foreshadowed that, through the King born today, people would come to eternal light and to the everlasting praise of their Creator. These are the most sacred mysteries which the holy Church venerates today, rejoicing in the Lord with the angels. That three Masses are celebrated today signifies that human beings are saved through Christ’s birth in three periods: the patriarchs before the law, the prophets under the law, and the faithful under grace.

Today the daylight begins to lengthen and the shadow of night to shorten, because the splendor of eternal light appearing today has driven the darkness of vices and sins [Col. 0820A] from the human race, illumined the world with the radiance of virtues, and called it to unfailing light.

Here end, if you wish. But if time permits, add the following.

[Col. 0819A]

This feast of a unique birth, dearly beloved, was prefigured in the first man, who came forth uniquely formed from pure earth. He also immediately foretold this birth: “A man,” he says, “shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to his wife” (Gen. 2). That is, Christ left the Father in heaven and his mother, the Synagogue, on earth, and cleaved to his wife, namely the Church.

This birth was also prefigured by the patriarchs when Isaac was foretold by an angel and born from a barren and aged woman. Isaac is Christ, who is called “joy,” and who is the fullness of joy for the faithful. All the prophets foretold this in many ways. Even beasts themselves expressed it beforehand in figures.

The unicorn is said to be a very fierce beast having only one horn. To capture it, a virgin girl is placed in a field; when it comes to her and lays itself in her lap, it is captured. Christ is represented by this beast, and his invincible strength by its horn. Laying himself in the womb of the Virgin, he was captured by hunters—that is, he was found in human form by those who loved him.

It is read, dearly beloved, that the Son of God wished to descend from heaven to us in prison and to redeem us from the captivity of the tyrant. With all your strength avoid the service of the most wicked lord, who gives those serving him nothing but eternal punishments; and devote yourselves with all your heart to the best Lord, who grants everlasting joys to those serving him.

God the Father had only one Son; and because he did not wish to have him alone as heir, he sent him into exile for a runaway servant, so that when he returned he might give him the palace of the kingdom together with the Son. Flee to him with all your eagerness; serve him with all your strength, so that one day you may celebrate these temporal feasts with the angels for ever. Amen.

## ON SAINT ANASTASIA AND EUGENIA

The blessed martyr Anastasia increases for us the vowed joys of this holy day. She was of the highest Roman nobility; but she abandoned all riches for the love of Christ and devoted herself to Christians held in prison, supplying and giving them whatever was necessary. Then, seized by pagans and subjected to many tortures, she was finally cast into flames for Christ.

Today her companion, the holy virgin and martyr Eugenia, is added. Her father Philip, sent from Rome as a patrician to Alexandria, governed all Egypt subject to him. His daughter secretly left his palace with two attendants known to her, Protus and Hyacinthus; she entered a monastery of men in male clothing and there later became abbot, shining through many miracles.

Since no one recognized that she was a woman, a certain matron solicited her to the crime of fornication. When she refused the woman’s request, she was accused before the judge—namely, her own father. After he had cast all the Christians together with her into chains, Eugenia was led to tortures on account of fornication. After many words spoken with her father for Christ’s glory, she tore the garment in which she was clothed and appeared as the governor’s daughter. He immediately converted with all his household, afterward became a bishop, and not long after was beheaded for Christ above the altar during the very celebration of Mass. The heavenly fire devoured her accuser with all her household.

After these things her mother Claudia came to Rome with her daughter Eugenia, her two sons Avitus and Sergius, and the two eunuchs Protus and Hyacinthus. Avitus and Sergius became proconsuls, and many were converted through them. Many matrons were converted through Claudia, and many virgins through Eugenia. Moreover, when many soldiers were converted through Protus and Hyacinthus, they were killed on account of Christ’s name. Eugenia herself, after many struggles and diverse punishments, is today sacrificed as Christ’s victim by the shedding of her blood.

And because Christ willed to descend to earth, he gave human beings—and even young girls—the power to ascend to heaven.

Commend yourselves to these and all the saints, that through their merits you may rejoice after this miserable life in the eternal solemnity.

## WHAT FOLLOWS YOU SHOULD SAY ONLY ON THE GREATEST FEASTS

[Col. 0819C]

Dearly beloved, you ought to make your prayers to God every day, morning and evening, and also at every time, through which you may obtain all the necessities of life and future joys. The wisdom of God came to human beings in the flesh and taught us a short prayer in which he willed us to ask for all things present and future.

This prayer is compared to a river in which a lamb can walk and an elephant can swim. It is such that any simple person can learn and understand it, yet it surpasses the intelligence of every wise person. Although you all know it well, you must now say it after me.

“Our Father”; and after this tell them the individual words through to the end; then add:

[Col. 0819D]

Dearly beloved, God himself composed this prayer and taught us to climb, by it as by a ladder, to the joys of heaven. The sides of this ladder are the contemplative and active life, and supreme wisdom placed upon it seven steps of petitions.

You stand on the first step and cry to the Lord:

“Our Father” (Matt. 6). Consider, brethren, what you say. You call God Father. God did not wish to be called “Lord” but “Father” by you, so that you may think that you are brethren in him, love one another as brethren, and through this love become heirs of his kingdom. If God is your Father, then you are brethren of Jesus Christ, who is the Son of God. And if, as children, you perform works pleasing to your Father, you will without doubt receive from God an inheritance together with Jesus.

Then you say, “who art in heaven.” Although God is everywhere, nevertheless he dwells more familiarly in the saints, who are called heavens, because he illumines them more abundantly with his grace. By these words you are exhorted to ask that you yourselves may become heavens in which God may wish to dwell.

Afterward you say:

“Hallowed be thy name.” God’s name has always been holy. You ask that the name by which your Father is called may be hallowed in you in such a way that through good works you may deserve to be called his children. You are also called Christians from Christ, and you pray that you may become one body in Christ, so that with him you may receive sanctification in the kingdom of the Father.

Therefore, placed upon the second step, you say: “Thy kingdom come.” That is, may it please God to reign in you by grace, and may he make you worthy of his kingdom.

Then you set your foot upon the third step and say:

“Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.” That is, just as he is pleased in heaven by the angels, who have never sinned, so may he likewise be pleased on earth, and make us equal to the angels, as he promised. By heaven, too, the righteous are understood, and by earth sinners. You ask God that, just as his will is good in the righteous, so he may turn you from evil to righteousness and bring about his good pleasure in you also.

These three petitions pertain to God; the four that follow pertain to the world. In the three you ask for heavenly things; in the four, temporal things. You therefore climb the fourth step and cry: “Give us this day our daily bread.” Daily bread is human sustenance. You ask God that you may daily receive from him without sin the temporal provision without which human frailty cannot endure.

Bread also signifies Christ’s body, and you pray that you may continually be worthy of his body and, if not by your own mouths, yet through the mouths of priests, may worthily receive it daily. Spiritual teaching is also understood by bread, without which the soul can no more live than the body without bodily nourishment. You ask God to bestow this on you daily, lest human frailty, journeying toward its homeland, fail on the way through hunger for the divine word.

Taking hold of the fifth step, you say: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.” If you forgive those who sin against you, God will forgive you what you sin against him. If you do not forgive, neither will God forgive you; and by these words you curse yourselves, because you ask God not to forgive you. But if you omit this, you do not say the Lord’s Prayer, and therefore God will not hear you.

Leaning upon the sixth step, you cry: “Lead us not into temptation.” God tempts no one, since he examines the hearts of all. Each person is tempted by the devil, yet no one unless God permits it. And it is good for a person to be tempted, if he is not overcome by consenting to sin. For when he conquers desire, he receives the crown of life. Therefore you ask God never to allow you to be tempted by the devil so greatly that you may be overcome through consent and delight in sin; and, if you have consented, that you may quickly come to your senses.

On the seventh step you cry: “Deliver us from evil.” That is, from hell and from all things which lead us to the abyss of destruction.

Dearly beloved, through this prayer the world is reconciled to God, and our body is united with the soul. For in it are seven petitions divided into three and four parts. By three are understood the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; by four, the world, which consists of four elements: earth, water, air, and fire. Three also pertain to the soul, four to the body.

The soul is irascible, because it is angered by evils; concupiscible, because it delights in goods; rational, because it discerns goods from evils. But the body consists of the aforesaid four elements. Therefore the human being, who is called a lesser world, is joined to God through this prayer.

You should note, dearly beloved, that beginning this prayer from the height of heaven—that is, from God the Father—you call God “our Father,” and descend to the lowest depths of hell when you conclude it with “deliver us from evil.” Because the Son of God descended for us from the height of heaven—that is, from the Father—to the lowest depths, he taught us to begin the prayer from the Father. But because we lay plunged in the depth of sins, we must climb to heaven by this ladder in the following order:

“Our Father, deliver us from evil”: that is, from this depth of hell in which we lie. “Lead us not into temptation”: that is, do not permit us to commit such a crime that we should rightly fall into hell. “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors”: that is, forgive us those things through which one goes to torments. “Give us this day our daily bread”: that is, feed us sparingly with your teaching, by which we may know and be able to do good and avoid evil.

These four pertain to the active life; the three which follow to the contemplative life. The active life consists in having love for your neighbours and serving Christ in the poor or wretched by almsgiving. From this you must pass to the contemplative life. The contemplative life consists in trampling earthly things underfoot for love of God, praying continually, often attending divine worship, and willingly hearing all things that concern God.

Established in this life, you must seek with Paul the third heaven (2 Cor. 12). By the first heaven is understood the Holy Spirit, by the second the Son, and by the third the Father. These are understood in these three short verses.

“Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth” [so the manuscript]. That is: grant that we may do your will in the Holy Spirit, so that you may wish to make us equal to the angels in heaven. “Thy kingdom come.” That is: cause us to fulfil what your Son taught, so that we may be worthy to rejoice in the kingdom of the Son.

Then, arriving at the summit of highest heaven, we cry with a great voice: “Our Father, who art in …, hallowed be thy name.” That is: you who through your Son made us heavens in the Holy Spirit, make us your children by faith and works, so that through your Son you may wish to dwell in us and we may be permitted to reign in you.

The prophet foresaw this ladder in the Holy Spirit, dearly beloved, when he foretold that Christ would descend through it to earth and that we would ascend by it to heaven. “Upon him,” he says, “shall rest the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord.”

Behold, the prophet began with wisdom because he saw that Christ would descend to us from highest heaven; he ended with fear because he foresaw that we would ascend from hell to heaven through fear. Therefore we stand upon the step of fear when through fear of Gehenna we avoid sins; we halt upon the step of piety when we become accustomed to doing good; we set our foot upon the step of knowledge when we render to God what is God’s and to human beings what is theirs; we make our footing firm upon the step of strength when neither by pleasant nor by harsh things do we turn aside from what is true; we direct our steps upon the step of counsel if we strive also to advise others to do the good which we ourselves do not hesitate to do; we attain the step of understanding if we seek heavenly and spiritual things in our mind; finally, we climb the step of wisdom if, rejecting earthly things, we savour only heavenly things and those which are God’s.

The sides of this ladder are the two commandments of love. No one can reach heaven unless he is willing to climb by this ladder.

Now, dearly beloved, you have said your prayer. You must now also say your faith after me. For just as a fish cannot live without water, so no one can be saved without faith.

## THE CATHOLIC FAITH

I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth and of every creature. And I believe in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. And I believe in the Holy Spirit.

I believe that these three persons—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are one true divinity, which has always existed without beginning and will always exist without end. I believe that this same Son of God was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of holy Mary, perpetual Virgin.

I believe that for our necessity he was seized, bound, scourged, crucified, and that he died in his humanity, not in his divinity. I believe that he was buried. I believe that he went to hell and took from there those who had done his will. I believe that on the third day he rose again, and that after his resurrection he ate and drank with his disciples to prove his true resurrection. And afterward, on the fortieth day, he ascended to heaven while his disciples looked on; there he sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty, coeternal and equal in power with him.

I believe that he will still come from there to judge the living and the dead, each according to his works and according to his own mercy. I believe in the holy catholic and apostolic Church. I believe in the communion of saints. I believe in the forgiveness of all sins for which I have done penance, made confession, and which I have not repeated. I believe that with this same body in which I appear here today I must die, must rise again, and must render God an account of everything whatsoever I have done, whether good or evil; and there I shall receive recompense according to what I am found to be at the end. I believe in eternal life. Amen.

Dearly beloved, through this faith we must all be saved. You must all know it, say it often, and teach it to the children whom you have lifted from baptism. This is your battle-sign. You wage war with the devil and the vices. When they hear this sign, they immediately tremble and flee from you in terror. When you have ascended to the summit of the ladder of which you heard before, and this sign is recognized in heaven as you cry it aloud, the entrance of heaven will immediately be opened to your companions, the angels and saints.

Brethren, I believe that you frequently make confession to your priests. You should indeed do so; but because there are many things which perhaps do not come to your memory, you should now say your confession after me, so that you may receive absolution for these matters. Now say as follows:

## CONFESSION

I renounce the devil and all his pomps and all his works; and I confess to God almighty, to holy Mary, to Saint Michael and all his angels, to Saint John the Baptist and all God’s prophets, to Saint Peter and all God’s apostles, to Saint Stephen and all God’s martyrs, to Saint Martin and all God’s priests, to Benedict and all God’s confessors, to Saint Margaret and all God’s virgins, to these saints and all the saints, to you, priest, and to all my fellow Christians who see or hear me today, all my sins which I have ever committed from the hour when I first could sin until this hour, in whatever manner I have done them: knowingly or unknowingly, willingly or under compulsion, asleep or awake, by myself or with another person; those which I can now remember or have not recalled.

I confess to God that I have never fulfilled as I rightly ought and well could the promise made for me in baptism. As soon as I reached the age at which I could sin, I turned away from God and his commandments; I denied God by evil works; and again I willingly enslaved myself to the power of the devil, whom I had previously renounced, through every impurity, and until now I have served him with all zeal.

I have not sought the holy houses of God as diligently as I should. When I did seek them, I was not there with such discipline and intention as I rightly ought to have had. Whatever I heard there about God, I either mocked, did not believe, or despised to do. I have not kept or honoured Sundays and other feast days as I rightly should. I have not received the Body of the Lord as often as I should; and when I received it, I did not observe it as worthily as I ought.

I have not paid as I ought the tenth of my life [Col. 0825A; reading uncertain] and of those things which God gave me. I have never loved or honoured my father, mother, and lord as I ought, nor have I been as subject to them as I should. I have not loved all my fellow Christians as I ought, nor have I been subject or faithful to them as I should. I have not been as obedient as I should to my bishop, my priest, and the other teachers of God when they taught me.

On holy nights, nights of fasting, and at other unlawful times, I have not restrained myself with my spouse as I should. I have made void every vow which I made to God. I have hated every good thing, and hated those who did good or spoke about it. I have both done and loved every evil thing; I have consented to all evildoers and loved them.

I have sinned in murders committed and planned. I have sinned greatly in fornications, adulteries, incests, bestial fornication, every pollution and every uncleanness by which a person can defile himself. I have defiled my body and my wretched soul, by myself and with all those who were willing to consent with me.

I have sinned in perjuries, thefts, robberies, false witness, slanders, insults, banqueting, drunkenness, sorceries, frauds, and in every sin by which a person can sin. I have sinned beyond all people in word, deed, thought, and will.

This I confess to God, to these saints, and to all the saints; and I beg the clemency of God that he may grant me time and respite, so that I may amend myself in such a way as to be able to find his grace. And I beg holy Mary and all God’s saints to deign to intercede and help for me before God’s mercy, that he may grant me forgiveness of all my sins, preserve me from sins henceforth, and after this life bring me into their fellowship.

And I wish to promise God that henceforth I desire to avoid sins insofar as I can amid my frailty, and insofar as his mercy deigns to strengthen me. And today I wish to forgive all who have sinned against me, so that he too may forgive me my innumerable sins.

Dearly beloved, according to this confession which you have made and according to this promise which you have promised to God [sic], I wish to speak the words, but I ask God to perform the work.

May the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit grant you pardon and absolution from all your sins through the intercession of all your saints [sic]; may he preserve you henceforth from sins and from all evils; and after this life may he bring you into the fellowship of all his saints. Amen.

Brothers, this confession has force only with respect to those sins which you have confessed to priests, or which you committed unknowingly. But for those who have committed grave crimes and have not done penance for them—[fol. 20v] such as homicide and adultery, for which a *carrina* has been instituted—this confession has no force.

[Note: [Col. 0825C] On the meaning of the word *Carrina*, Du Cange has the following: “1. *Carena*, a word formed from *quadragena* or *quarentena*, the fortieth part. Charter of Amadeus, count of Maurienne, 1234: ‘We grant to the same house, throughout all our land, the toll, market-dues, and *careterra* on all its goods, so that none of us may presume to exact any payment. . . .’ Perhaps the word *Caria*, among the revenues of the count of Namur in 1264, belongs here, from the sealed register *Papier velu* in the Chamber of Accounts at Lille, fol. II r.: ‘And if anyone [becomes] the *Carin* of the castle of Namur.’ Hence perhaps the name *Carinlier*, for one appointed over the collection of such a due. Letters of remission, 1384, register 126, royal charter office, no. 56: ‘Gilet Germain, tanner living at Chartres and master of the Carinliers of the said city and banlieue of Chartres.’ Unless, however, *Corniliers* or *Tarinliers* should be read there, a meaning equally unknown to me.

“2. *Carena*, *Carrina*: the Lenten fast, or public penance imposed by a bishop on clergy and laity, [Col. 0825D] or by an abbot on monks, by which a person is bound to fast for forty days. John of Genoa: ‘*Carena*, public penance, and *quadragena* are the same. Therefore, one who performs this first [penance] does not enter church for forty days and wears a woolen garment; on the aforesaid days he abstains from forbidden foods and drinks, from the marriage-bed, sword-bearing, and riding. But on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday he uses, moderately, some kind of pulse and vegetables, apples or pears, or small fish, with a little beer. All these things are proved in the Decretals, “On Homicide.”’

“Burchard, book XIX, chapter 5: ‘*Carrina* (elsewhere *Carina*) is a fast of forty continuous days on bread and water.’ A manuscript Penitential: ‘Forty days on bread and water—which in common speech is called *carina*—with penance during the following seven years.’ Council of Mainz: ‘We entirely forbid *carenas* to be relaxed at dedications and at ordination seasons, and penitents to be admitted.’ Peter Damian, book II, letter 7: ‘Besides those Lents which were instituted by the Fathers . . . he secretly observes other *carinas*.’ [Col. 0826C] The same, book IV, letter 17: ‘In accordance with the rule of a *carina*, we imposed confinement in prison custody.’ And book V, letter 8: ‘Behold,’ they say, ‘a *carina* by pilgrimage; behold a new penance . . . unheard of until now.’ Reynerus against the Waldensians, chapter 5: ‘They reject public penances, such as *carenas*, especially for women.’ Caesarius of Heisterbach, book IV, chapter 37: ‘A certain knight . . . during a certain Lenten season performed a *carena* among us.’ Book V, chapter 42: ‘When another knight, having undertaken a *carena*, proposed to go to Cîteaux at the time of the general chapter.’ Alan of Lille, in the Penitential: ‘Solemn [penance] is that imposed for greater or notorious crimes, or for crimes which one has confessed, or of which one has been convicted; it is customarily called a *carena*. And as it concerns greater matters, so it belongs to the greater prelates of the Church to impose it.’ Below: ‘But it is asked how one should understand what is said concerning the imposition of solemn penance: “Perform three years on bread [Col. 0826D] and water, and perform three forties in each year”:  should this be understood to mean that he ought to fast every day, or every other day? To this we answer thus: without prejudicing a higher interpretation, the rigor of canonical censure is shown when fasting on bread and water for three years is prescribed; some understand this so that throughout the three years bread and water are not eaten during the whole week, but only during those three fasts mentioned above,’ etc.

“Summary of Raymond of the Order of Preachers:

> Young married women can complete *carenas*  
> In their own homes, etc.

“Charter of Gottfried, count of Habsburg, in Kopp, *Origines Foederis Helvetici*, no. 7: ‘That he might be reconciled to the Church for the homicide which he had committed, he granted to the religious ladies . . . an estate of ten *jugera* . . . adding this, that the same sisters should bear one *carrina* of the penance imposed upon him.’

“Add the Synod [Col. 0827C] of Salegunstadt, chapters 17, 18, 19; Ughelli, vol. IX, p. 287; Hermann Stangefolius, *Westphalia*, book II, p. 101; Baronius, year 1093, no. 16; and Filesacus, *On Christ’s Forty Days*, chapter 3.

“[*Karena*, *Karrina*: Du Cange writes under [Col. 0827D] *Carina*, I, that the latter word means an insult in Ekkehard; but I would rather refer here the occurrence in Arnio, in Pertz, vol. II of the *Scriptores*, p. 136, note 55.]

“In the Chronicle of Alberic, in Leibniz, *Accessions to History*, p. 530: ‘The beginning of Lent is called *carena*.’ Its middle point is assigned to the fourth Sunday in letters of remission of 1376, from Register 110, royal charter office, no. 199: ‘The Saturday eve of Mid-Lent,’ etc. More plainly again in other letters of 1402, from Register 157, no. 329: ‘The Sunday on which is sung in holy church, “Laetare Jerusalem,” which is called Mid-Lent,’ etc.

“*Carena* also means the remission or indulgence of such forty days, granted by the supreme pontiff or by bishops. Inscription of 1225 in the church of Saints Vincent and Anastasius at Tre Fontane in Rome, from Panvinio, *On the Seven Churches*, p. 111: ‘Let seven years and seven *carenae* of remission of confessed crime and acquittal be granted to him.’ Lambert, monk of Trier, *On the Discovery [Col. 0828C] of the Body of St Matthias*, chapter 4, §20: ‘Pope Eugenius and Adalbero, archbishop of Trier, conferred upon the dedication of our monastery . . . eighteen *carenas*.’ No. 21: ‘He conferred one year of indulgence and four *carenas*.’

“[*Chronicle of the collegiate church of St Stephen*, [Col. 0828D] vol. II of *Rerum Moguntiacarum*, p. 545, edition of 1722: ‘These are the archiepiscopal and episcopal graces given to benefactors of the fabric of the church of St Stephen at Mainz . . . Likewise, from bishops and Roman pontiffs, two thousand days and one hundred *carenas*, during which the souls of the faithful ought to be tormented and punished in purgatory.’] Add Brower, *Antiquities of Fulda*, pp. 122, 133. [Ludewig, *Reliquiae manuscriptorum*, vol. I, p. 386.] [Also the charter of Ulric, bishop of Ratzeburg, 1280, in Westphalen, *Monumenta Cimbrica*, vol. II, cols. 49; others in Gudenus, *Codex diplomaticus*, vol. III, pp. 1116, 1118, 1129.]

“*Quadragena* is the same as *carena*: an indulgence of forty days. See the bull of Pope Urban II in Baronius, year 1193, no. 16.

“3. *Carena* for *carina*: the belly or bottom of a ship, French *carène*. It is frequently found in the Informations of the city of Marseilles concerning passage overseas, from the manuscript codex of Saint-Germain.—DU CANGE, *Glossary*, new edition, p. 178.”]

Therefore I warn you that, for sins which you have committed publicly, you should undertake public penance; [Col. 0827A] but for those which you have committed secretly, first make secret confession of them to your priests before approaching the body of the Lord. For whoever receives unworthily will be guilty of the Lord’s death together with Judas. And if we give such a body to you, we act as though someone were to hand a sword to a madman so that he might pierce his own heart with it.

Because God, beloved, has willed to gather you here today in his service, you ought not to stand here idle, but pray for yourselves and for the whole holy Church of God: that almighty God may deign to give it peace, unite it, govern it, and guard it from every evil. And when her bridegroom Christ, who betrothed her to himself with his blood, comes with all the heavenly host in order to lead his bride, the Church, from this Babylonian pilgrimage [Col. 0827B] into the city of his Father, may you all accompany her into the heavenly Jerusalem. Amen.

Then you ought to pour out prayers for the apostolic lord, who is the head of the Church and from whom all the judgments of the Church ought to proceed: that almighty God may make him such a man as can worthily preside over the Church in teaching, conduct, and life, and may he himself with her at the last attain everlasting joys. Amen.

Next you ought to beseech God for our bishop, and for all priests, and for all who are established in holy orders, who ought to be the mirror of the Church: that almighty God may send his Spirit into them, and may be pleased to inspire them so that what they preach to the people in words, they themselves may fulfill in deeds, [Col. 0827C] and on the last day receive eternal life with him. Amen.

After this, you must pray for our king, whom God has willed to have as his namesake on earth: that merciful God may grant him his aid, so that he may govern and defend the Church in such a way that after this temporal kingdom he may receive from the King of heaven the everlasting crown of the kingdom. Amen.

Then it is fitting that you ask for all dukes [Col. 0828A] and counts and all judges of the Church: since it is written, “Judgment without mercy is for him who has not shown mercy,” may almighty God grant them that disposition by which they may strive to treat the people subject to them mercifully, so that they may obtain mercy from God, the merciful judge. Amen.

Next it is fitting for you to implore God’s mercy for all who have renounced the world: for monks, nuns, recluses, solitaries, and all who have made any vow to God; that the gracious God may grant them so to fulfill their purpose that after this [fol. 22] life they may deserve to obtain the promised reward. Amen.

Afterward you ought to entreat God for travelers, whether those who have set out for Jerusalem, Rome, [Col. 0828B] Saint James, or other holy places: that God may receive their vows and restore them unharmed and in peace to their friends. Amen.

Thereafter you must beseech the mercy of God for those who sail for the need of the Church: that God may protect them from every storm, make their journey prosperous, and return them safely to their kindred and friends. Amen.

Then you ought to remember the sick who are unable today to visit churches: that they may be restored to health and soundness, and, having amended their offenses in this life, may afterward be received into eternal life. Amen.

Next I exhort you to ask God for those who are on pilgrimage, for captives, prisoners in bonds, [Col. 0828C] those confined in prison, or placed in any distress: that merciful God may help each according to his need, deliver them from evils according to his mercy, and grant them all good things. Amen.

Then you ought to persist in prayers for all the Christian people: that God may guard them from all evils and from all enemies of soul and body, and bring them to everlasting peace. Amen.

[Col. 0829A] Now, beloved, you must pray for those who most need your prayers: namely, those who are dead, who can do neither good nor evil. For as water is poured upon someone burning in fire, so they rejoice when you send prayers or alms after them. First, let each one of you pray for his father, mother, spouse, children, brothers, sisters, kindred, and friends; then for all who have left you their inheritances, or bestowed any benefit upon you, or commended themselves to your prayers; and for all whose bodies rest here, and for all the faithful departed: that almighty God, who willed his Son to die for them, may deign today through [Col. 0829B] your prayers to absolve them from every punishment and pain and place them in the eternal pleasantness of paradise. Amen.

[Col. 0830A] Brothers, because Scripture says, “He who prays for another sets himself free,” I ask you to be willing also to pray for me, a wretch, who above all people especially needs your prayers: that the Merciful One may deign today to receive the sacrifice of the Church from my hands, make me myself a sacrifice to himself, enable me to amend all my sins in this life, and after death rejoice with you in the heavenly glory. Amen.

Now, beloved, lift up your hearts and hands to God, that he may mercifully hear you concerning all these things; so that you may celebrate, after [fol. 22v], with the angels and without end, the feast which you now observe, in that glory which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which has not entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him (1 Cor. II). Come now: raise your prayers [Col. 0830B] to heaven with a loud voice, and sing in praise of God: *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy.”

If excessive winter cold, great summer heat, or some obstacle occurs, then omit what has just been said; and when the sermon is finished, preach them this faith: “I believe in God the Father,” and the rest as contained in the Psalter. Immediately afterward say this confession:

[Col. 0829B] Because I believe this, therefore I confess to the Almighty and to all God’s saints that I have sinned exceedingly in every way—in words, deeds, thought, will, and every iniquity. Therefore I ask all the saints to deign [Col. 0830B] to help me, so that I may amend all these things in this life and after this life reign with them in eternal life. Amen. “Absolution.” As above.

For every sermon, you should first pronounce the verse in the Latin language, then explain it in the vernacular. If the church is dedicated in honor of Saint Stephen, you may preach about him.

[Col. 0829B] “The righteous man has been delivered from distress, and the wicked man will be given over in his place” (Prov. XI). Blessed Stephen, beloved, whose feast we celebrate today, was delivered from the distress of this wretched life; and Paul, who was then wicked, [Col. 0829C] was given over in his place to endure afflictions.

For Christ, the good shepherd, who came down from heaven to earth to seek the lost sheep and, having found it, carry it upon his own shoulders back to the flock of the heavenly court (Luke XV), caught a wolf by means of a sheep, and set him not merely as a sheep but as shepherd over sheep. Stephen was gentle as a sheep; Paul, in his cruelty, was restless as a wolf. But when the sheep died, the shepherd gave back the wolf in his place. For Paul afterward shed his own blood for Christ’s flock, though earlier he had consented to Stephen’s killing; and he who once rejected him among the wicked now rejoices with him in the glory of the saints.

O how sweet, beloved, is the fellowship of the saints; how delightful the companionship of the blessed! There [Col. 0829D] no one seeks revenge for an injury done to himself, and no one who inflicted injury fears the shame of reproach from his companion. For now Paul is not ashamed of Stephen’s stoning, but Stephen rejoices at Paul’s salvation and companionship. Paul drove Stephen toward this glory by stoning him; Stephen drew Paul toward it by praying.

It is reported of them that both were fellow pupils in Jerusalem under Gamaliel’s instruction: [fol. 24] Stephen a native, Paul a newcomer, both exceptionally eminent in nobility and wisdom, but greatly different from one another in character. Stephen was of a gentle and patient disposition; Paul was fierce and ardent. Stephen was mild and agreeable in speech; Paul excessive and violent in bitter utterances. Stephen understood that the Law and the Prophets spoke spiritually; [Col. 0830B] Paul understood all things carnally. Hence they often raised questions from the Scriptures, which Stephen nobly resolved but Paul stubbornly resisted. Moreover, Stephen’s beauty is splendidly praised, [Col. 0830C] since his countenance is compared with that of angels.

At that time Tiberius governed the commonwealth. Afflicted by a lingering illness, he could not be cured by physicians. When he was told that in Judaea there was [read: “was” for “would be”] a physician named Jesus, who drove away every illness gently not by herbal mixtures or cutting with iron, but by the command of his word alone, he sent to Judaea a man especially bound to him in friendship and ordered him to bring this physician to cure him. The man set out for Judaea by ship at great expense; but Pilate, who then held the Roman governorship in Jerusalem, received him with the greatest honor. He immediately disclosed to him the purpose of his embassy: Caesar had commanded that Christ the physician [Col. 0830D] be brought into his presence.

Pilate was terrified at hearing this and declared that he was dead. When the envoy learned that Pilate had condemned him, he charged Pilate with treason against majesty, namely, because he had sentenced such a man to death without a decree of the senate, though he could have benefited the commonwealth so greatly. Pilate, removing the accusation from himself, implicated the Jews in the blame; he replied that he had been compelled to give them his consent in this matter.

Meanwhile, as many people recounted to the envoy many miracles of Christ, and likewise affirmed that the dead had returned to life at his command, he said that this had been not a physician but God, since it was established that he had given life to the dead. Thus he charged the Jews with having killed God; and if they could not clear themselves of this charge, he would condemn them also to various punishments. The Jews, terrified by their guilty conscience, [Col. 0831A] requested a delay so that they might repel the accusation brought against them.

Meanwhile the envoy was informed about a certain image of the Lord, through which a great multitude of healings was performed [an addition such as “a multitude,” or similar, is missing]. Veronica had caused it to be painted on a cloth for love of Christ, after he had healed her of her flow of blood by the touch of his hem (Luke VIII). [Fol. 24v] He obtained it only with great difficulty and then carried it to the emperor at Rome. As soon as he saw it, his illness left him. Immediately, summoning the Romans by edict, he ordered that he be worshiped as God, from whose image even sick persons received health. But because the Senate did not consent, he destroyed many by the sword and exile.

Accordingly, after receiving the delay, the Jews assembled and adopted this manner of reply. They said that it was impossible for God to die, but that they had punished a man who obstinately violated the precepts of their law and, by publicly confounding them, took away their honor among the common people. Since Stephen was among them, distinguished by birth and skilled in eloquence, they asked him to present this reply to the envoy and excuse them from the charge laid against them.

Stephen, however, advised that they summon learned Jews from every quarter of the world to a council, deliberate more carefully, and adopt sounder counsel. It seemed to him that the charge brought against them by the Romans was true, since manifest miracles testified that Jesus was God, especially since all things done through him had been attested by the Law and the Prophets. Though they took these words badly, they nevertheless decided that Jews should be summoned from every region of the world.

Meanwhile Peter and the apostles, hearing Stephen’s [Col. 0831C] reply, secretly summoned him, instructed him in the faith, regenerated him in the font of baptism, and entrusted to him the word of preaching.
