The Holy Spirit immediately filled him, and through him performed many signs and wonders among the people. Thus Jews assembled, many of whom disputed and contended with Stephen concerning this matter; but he powerfully convicted them all from the Scriptures, because the abundance of the Holy Spirit speaking in him prevailed.

Moved by this, they seized him and brought him before the council, saying that he had blasphemed the Law and Moses. When the high priest gave him opportunity to speak, he clearly expounded before them what the Law and the Prophets had written concerning Christ. Finally, he asked why they, rebellious against the Law and the Holy Spirit, doubted this God, [Col. 0831D] whose deeds agreed in every respect with the words of Scripture. “I,” he said, “see heaven opened and him standing at God’s right hand, calling me to heavenly things.”

At first they all marveled at the propositions of the speaker and looked upon the face of the one speaking as that of an angel. But [Col. 0832A] when they heard his conclusion concerning Christ, they gnashed their teeth at him and rushed upon him shouting. They left their garments with Paul to be kept and, having cast him outside the city, [fol. 26] stoned him.

When stones had disjointed all the structure of his limbs and his strength to stand had failed, he bent his knees and fell to the ground, pouring out prayers to the Lord for them. And as the Lord prayed on the cross for those who crucified him, so Stephen prayed for those stoning him. And just as Christ’s prayer was effective, so that those who had consented to the shedding of his blood afterward shed their own blood for love of him, so Stephen’s prayer was effective, so that Paul, who then hastened to destroy him, afterward longed to save all nations.

This Stephen is called the standard-bearer of martyrs because he was the first after the Lord—namely in that same year—to enter heaven with the palm of victory. [Col. 0832B] The Jews exposed his body, torn by stones, to be torn apart by beasts and birds; but, guarded by an angel of God, it remained untouched. Gamaliel took it away by night and buried it honorably. Afterward the Romans, in vengeance for the Lord, destroyed Jerusalem, devastated the whole region, put some Jews to death by various punishments, and sold the rest everywhere.

But when Roman rulers had submitted their necks to the yoke of faith and all nations had begun to worship Christ the Lord alone, God’s will disclosed through a vision to Christians where the body of blessed Stephen had lain hidden. God magnified the joys of its discovery by seventy-three miracles. He is believed to have suffered in the month of August; [Col. 0832C] but today his festival is commemorated more solemnly, when his sacred body is said to have been found. For in ancient times his commemoration was observed only once a year; therefore both his passion and his discovery were celebrated on this day. But later devotees decreed that his discovery should be observed on the day of his passion, because they considered it unlawful to change the Church’s general institution, and because everything which the faithful show at any time in honor of the saints is referred to God’s praise—God, whom we command you to praise in his saints and magnify by blessing him at all times.

Therefore, beloved, implore Saint Stephen to be your intercessor with God, so that we may imitate him in that by which you may be able to pray for your enemies; [Col. 0832D] and, because Stephen is called “crowned,” may you deserve to be crowned with him in that glory which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which has not entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for all who love him. Amen.

If the church is in honor of Saint John, let this be the utterance of the preacher concerning him.

[Col. 0831D] “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. LXVI). [Fol. 26v] Clouds carry rain and water the dry earth. Doves, when they look through windows, do not desire to tear other birds apart as hawks do. The holy apostles, beloved, were clouds: they generously watered dry hearts with the abundant rain of teaching; where they rejoiced [Col. 0832D] to see a great harvest springing up, from which they hoped to reap fruit a hundredfold in joy.

Like doves they looked upon worldly things through the windows of their eyes: they looked upon women not with desire, like adulterers, but with a simple and chaste gaze; and they desired none of earthly things like the avaricious.

[Col. 0833A] Among them was Saint John the Evangelist, a most abundant cloud, who flooded the four quarters of the world everywhere with his honeyed teaching. Free also from the gall of envy, like a simple dove, he was therefore established by the Lord in his temple—that is, in the Church—as a steadfast dove. His life shone especially with the purity of chastity; by teaching and miracles he enlightened all churches. Therefore, though Scripture speaks generally of all the apostles, it declares this specially of him: “The voice of your thunder, O God, is in the wheel. Your lightnings shone over all the earth” (Ps. LXXVI).

By thunder is signified the high-sounding preaching of the Gospel. By the wheel is represented this world, which constantly rolls in swift revolution like a wheel. In this wheel the voice of God’s thunder resounds, while the great-sounding peal of John’s Gospel thunders forth to the world. God’s lightnings also shone over the world when, through John, Christ’s miracles became known to the world.

It is read that in paradise a fountain rises and is divided into four heads (Gen. II). Paradise, which is called a garden of delights, signifies the Church, in which are the delights of the Scriptures and which is called to the house of God, where there are glory and riches. In such a paradise a fountain rises when Christ, the fountain of all good things, is born from the chaste Virgin. The four rivers that rise from it are understood as the four Evangelists, because by their copious doctrine they watered the whole garden of the Church.

These four spiritual rivers give the Church such flavors: one provides the nourishment of milk, another the healing application of oil, a third the flavor of wine, and the fourth [Col. 0833C] the sweetness of honey. Infants are nourished with milk. Milk flows to the Church from Matthew’s Gospel, when it proclaims that Christ became little for the good and was fed with milk. The sick are healed with oil. Oil is poured upon the Church from Luke’s Gospel, when it recounts that our infirmities were healed by Christ’s blood. Those who drink wine are gladdened. Mark’s Gospel gives the Church wine to drink when it recalls the apostles gladdened by Christ’s resurrection. Honey distils from John’s Gospel when it sweetly intimates [read: *insinuat*] to the Church the divinity which is the sweetness of angels.

Because the prophet foresaw that these things were signified in them, he describes them in the figures of four living creatures. Matthew is represented by the form of a human being, through whom Christ’s humanity is set forth in writing. Luke is denoted by the appearance of a calf, through whom Christ is preached as the fatted calf sacrificed for us. Mark is shown by the figure of a lion, by whom Christ is remembered as raised from the dead like a lion. [Col. 0833D] John is declared by the likeness of an eagle, through whom Christ is shown to have flown up into the glory of the Father.

The four regions of the world also signify this concerning them, as they figuratively suggest it to those who consider. By the north, where the sun lies hidden beneath the earth, Matthew is expressed, through whom Christ’s divinity is described as having lain hidden beneath flesh. By the west, where the sun sets, Luke is expressed, through whom Christ the sun is said to have set in dying. By the east, where the sun rises daily, Mark is understood, through whom Christ, the sun of righteousness, [Col. 0834A] is handed down as risen from the dead. By the south, where the sun burns at the center of heaven, John is indicated, through whom the eternal sun is expounded as shining in the majesty of divinity.

These are the four golden rings by which the ark of the covenant was carried. The ark is the holy Church; the rings are the four Gospels by which it is carried to eternal dwelling places. These are the chariots of Amminadab by which the ark of God was brought back from foreigners to the home of its country (1 Reg. VII; Cant. VI). The ark of God was captured by the Philistines; but it was brought back to Jerusalem in the chariots of the priest Amminadab. The ark of God is the Church, which was captured by the Philistines when it was subjected to idols. The true priest Jesus brought it back from its enemies to Jerusalem in chariots when, through the teaching [Col. 0834B] of the four Evangelists, he led it up to the heavenly homeland. Among these John was preeminent, for he flooded the whole world with his preaching.

Of this John it is read that he was the son of the Lord’s maternal aunt. While celebrating his wedding, he invited Christ with his mother; but when wine failed, Christ changed water into wine and gladdened the guests (John II). On seeing this, John abandoned his bride and, himself a virgin, clung to the Virgin’s Son. Because [fol. 28v] he despised sexual union for love of him, Christ loved him above all the apostles. For when, at the supper [read: *in cena* for the corrupt *Regina austri*], he gave his body and blood to his disciples, John reclined upon Jesus’ breast (John XXI), and then drank from that fountain of wisdom what he afterward poured forth to the world: namely, the mystery of the Word hidden in the Father, [Col. 0834C] because in Jesus’ breast are hidden all treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. II).

Finally, at the altar of the cross, when Christ offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father for the world and triumphed over the prince of death, seeing his mother standing near the cross with John, he judged it best to entrust Virgin to virgin (John XIX). But after Christ left the prison of this world, revisited the heavenly palace, and sent the Holy Spirit from the Father’s seat to his disciples, John, filled with the Holy Spirit, entered the Lord’s temple with Peter, healed a lame man in the name of Jesus Christ, and baptized many Jews who were thereby converted to faith through their words (Acts III). When the high priests [Col. 0834D] had inflicted many scourges upon him and the other apostles for this reason, they rejoiced that they had suffered such things for the name of the Lord (Acts V).

After the stoning of Stephen, when Samaria had received the word of the Lord through the preaching of Philip, Stephen’s fellow deacon, the apostles sent Peter and John to confirm those who had been baptized, as bishops still customarily do in the Church (Acts VIII). After the faithful received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of their hands, they condemned Simon Magus, who wished to purchase this grace, together with all his followers (ibid.).

After these things John went into Asia and, by word and example, signs and wonders, drew the whole region to the Lord’s grace. At that time Domitian held the monarchy. [Col. 0835A] He ordered the Apostle to be seized and taken to Rome, where before the Senate he put him into a vat of boiling oil. But, protected by God’s grace, he came out unharmed. Then he banished him into exile on the island of Patmos, where the Lord frequently visited him through his angel and revealed to him all the future mysteries of the Church.

Afterward the emperor was slaughtered by gladiators on the Senate’s advice, and the Apostle was restored with honor to God’s Church. By writing and preaching he instructed churches everywhere and destroyed all heresies in every place. Meanwhile he shone with many splendid miracles, by which he shone upon the world like the sun amid darkness. He changed wild rods into gold and shore-stones into gems, and again restored the gold to the nature of rods and the gems to the substance of stones. He raised a certain widow from death and likewise restored a dead young man [Col. 0835B] to life. He restored to its former wholeness a glass vessel which had burst into many fragments. In Christ’s name he not only drank poison unharmed, but also restored to life those killed by it.

So that none of you may despair because of the greatness of his crimes, but may be strengthened in God’s mercy and trust in the prayer of Saint John, I wish briefly to tell you one thing about him which I hope will gladden your souls.

Saint John entrusted a certain young man to a bishop for upbringing. The bishop baptized him and raised him with every care. Then little by little he began to keep him more laxly and, as old men are accustomed to do, corrected the youth in nothing. When the youth sensed [Col. 0835C] that the reins of discipline had been removed from him, he immediately cast off the Lord’s yoke and rushed headlong through the winding paths of vices. First he was enticed by gluttony and drunkenness; then he was ensnared by the allurements of prostitutes; next he associated with thieves; finally he became the leader of robbers, himself a violent robber.

After some time had passed, John was summoned to the same church and, having duly arranged all matters for which he had come, asked the bishop to present to him the young man whom he had entrusted to be educated for the heavenly kingdom. With tears the bishop declared him dead: he was living in the mountain passes with robbers, as chief of robbers. Hearing this, John groaned deeply and shed abundant tears. At once he requested that a horse and guide be given him, and hurried swiftly to the mountains.

[Col. 0835D] Immediately a band of robbers surrounded him; but he, undaunted, asked to speak with their leader. The man came, savage and armed; when from a distance he recognized John, he took flight. John pursued him at full gallop, crying out:

> “Why, my son, do you flee from an unarmed old man? Why do you dread your father? [Col. 0836A] Stop, my son, stop and wait. I shall render an account to God for your soul. Certainly I will gladly undergo death for you, as Christ underwent it for the world. Only stop; do not despair. I promise you: you will receive forgiveness of sins from God.”

On hearing this, he immediately fell from his horse and fell at John’s knees. Again he baptized himself in a stream of tears, concealing the right hand conscious of the crime. John drew it out, kissed it, encouraged his fierce spirit toward repentance with many endearments, brought him with himself to the church, continued vigils and fasts with him, and restored him, thoroughly reformed, to mother Church. Then, adding an example of divine mercy, he set over that same Church the former cruel robber as a noble shepherd.

[Col. 0836B] But blessed John, beloved, if while still remaining in frail flesh he was able to bring such help to sinners, how much more now, reigning with Christ, is he powerful to intercede for all who invoke him. The Lord now appeared to him in his old age with his disciples and invited him to the heavenly banquet. Giving thanks that Christ invited him to the angelic feast, John ordered a grave to be opened for himself before the altar. Having summoned all the people, he celebrated Mass, communicated all in the Lord’s sacraments, then descended into the grave; and suddenly an immense light shone upon him from heaven.

Afterward nothing but manna was found in that grave, from which salvation is granted even to this day to all who ask faithfully. Hence it is believed that Saint John was caught up in that light by angels to heavenly places [Col. 0836C] and, in that very rapture, paid the debt of the flesh through death, and immediately was restored to life. The Church believes that this will happen to all the righteous living in the flesh on the last day: namely, that they will be caught up to meet Christ in the air, die in that rapture, and immediately be restored to life.

His falling-asleep occurred on the feast-day of Saint John the Baptist; but the Church, enlightened by his teaching, solemnly commemorates it today, on account of the outstanding office of his namesake John the Baptist, incomparable among other saints; or because this day was made honorable by his return from exile; or because it is venerable through the dedication of this very church.

Now, dearest ones, invoke him for your aid; knock by unceasing prayers, so that, since John [Col. 0836D] means “the grace of God,” he may obtain for you and for all Christians the grace of almighty God in the heavenly homeland, so that after the end of this life you may rejoice with him for ever in that glory which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and the human heart has not been able to conceive. And the rest.

If people should gather for the feast of the Innocents, it will be permissible to speak these things concerning them.

[Col. 0835]

[Col. 0835D] “These are the saints who have not defiled their garments; they shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy” (Rev. III). Holy Scripture, dearest ones, calls bodies “garments,” because, just as the body is covered by a garment, so the soul is clothed with the body. By “white garments,” moreover, eternal joy is understood. Therefore, those who do not defile their bodies after baptism with grave sins shall walk with Christ in [Col. 0836D] everlasting joy. These saints are called the Holy Innocents, whose solemnities are celebrated today, because they never stained their bodies with any filth; rather, washing them in their own blood from original sin, they made them white, and therefore deserved to walk with the Son of the Virgin in the joy of the saints. They are also called the flowers of the martyrs, [Col. 0837A] because the harvest of martyrs followed them just as fruits follow flowers. They are likewise called first-fruits, because, just as the first fruits were offered under the Law, so they were the first in the Church to be sacrificed to God. I shall briefly recount to your charity how they were sacrificed.

When the Lord was born, a star brighter than the rest appeared, by which it was made manifest to all that the King of the stars had come into the world. On seeing it, three kings came from Chaldea to Jerusalem; following the star, they offered precious gifts to the newly born King. Hearing this, King Herod was troubled and suspected a successor to his kingdom. He asked the Magi to report to him the place where the child was, saying that he too wished to worship him—cruel and impious man, craftily planning to kill the one who came to give life to all. [Col. 0837B] But they, warned by an angel in a dream, returned to their own country by another way (Matt. II). Herod, fearing that they might bring a military force to the child in rebellion against him, pursued them as far as Tarsus of Cilicia.

Meanwhile Herod was accused before Augustus as a criminal, and by imperial command was summoned to Rome. He hastened at once to Rome, vigorously cleared himself of the charge laid against him, and found such favor with Augustus that the latter permitted him to wear a crown. Meanwhile an angel commanded Joseph to go with Mary and the child into Egypt, saying that Herod would one day wish to destroy him (ibid.). When they entered Egypt, the idols are said to have fallen at Christ’s arrival. It is also reported that, when they entered the city of Hermopolis, a tall Persian tree [Col. 0837C] consecrated to demons bent itself down to the ground before the Savior. It remained there for many years afterward and bestowed many healing benefits through its fruit, sap, bark, and leaves.

Herod returned in triumph to Jerusalem, recalled to mind the child born in the preceding year, whom he suspected, and the fact that he had been deceived by the Magi; and he sent throughout Bethlehem and all the borders of his kingdom and killed every boy born within the span of one night and two years. Then there arose among mourning mothers and friends such weeping as there had formerly been wailing at Gibeah, when the tribe of Benjamin, who was the son of Rachel, was exterminated by the children of Israel, and the cry of mourning was heard far and wide (ibid.). It will be necessary to tell you [Col. 0837D] how this happened.

A certain young man married a wife from Bethlehem; when he had brought her to his homeland, he later abandoned her. She returned to her parents. But the young man followed her to Bethlehem, where he was received by the girl’s parents, reconciled with his wife, and joined to her again. Taking her with him, he set out for his homeland and, on the journey, turned aside at Gibeah for lodging. Now the young men of Gibeah gathered by night and raped his concubine until she died. Rising in the morning, he divided the corpse into twelve pieces and sent the pieces through the twelve tribes of Israel, so that, stirred by zeal for God and the Law, they might assemble and avenge the deed—read *crime*—as swiftly as possible (Judg. XXI). Therefore, assembled from all the tribes, they sent messengers to the Gibeonites [Col. 0838A] demanding that they hand over for punishment those who had committed this crime. On hearing this, they refused; indeed, gathering at Gibeah from the whole tribe of Benjamin, they stubbornly resisted. Thus the army besieged the city, and forty thousand combatants fell on both sides. For very strong men lived at Gibeah, who fought with the left hand as with the right. Therefore the children of Israel feigned flight, laid ambushes, and cunningly drew them out of the city and killed twenty thousand. Only a few barely escaped. The victors entered the city. All the men were killed by the sword. A devouring flame consumed the city itself. The fire consumed children and women alike (Judg. XX). The entire region was laid waste. Both sexes among the people were destroyed by sword and fire. Then the greatest [Col. 0838B] weeping arose, so that wailing was heard far off in Ramah; Rachel’s sons were lamented without consolation, because scarcely a few survivors were found (Judg. XXI).

From this history the prophet Jeremiah takes a likeness and foretells that Jerusalem and the tribe of Judah, who was the son of Leah, Rachel’s sister, would suffer similar things at the hands of the Babylonians (Jer. XXXI); and this shortly afterward came to pass. For the Babylonians, attacking Jerusalem, destroyed it and consumed the tribe of Judah by sword and fire. The rest of the people were led into captivity; but Babylon was afterward destroyed by Cyrus and Darius. Because all this occurred figuratively, the evangelist says that it must be fulfilled in the Church, as I must briefly explain to you. Leah signifies the Synagogue, [Col. 0838C] from whose race Christ is born. Rachel represents the Church, to which Christ is joined. Leah’s son is taken captive by Nebuchadnezzar, and the Jewish people are subjected to the service of the devil. Rachel’s son, however, is killed by sword and flame, and the Christian people are subjected in this world to various torments. The two cities, Gibeah and Jerusalem, which are burned, signify idolatry and Jewish superstition; both are consumed by the fire of the Holy Spirit. The young man who took a wife from Bethlehem is Christ, who joined the Church to himself through the human nature which he assumed in Bethlehem. The young man abandons his wife and afterward comes to bring her to his homeland: [Col. 0838D] so Christ leaves the Church in this world for labor, and afterward comes to lead her back to the heavenly homeland.

It should be noted that this same woman is described as a concubine, because a concubine is exposed to servitude, while a lawful wife enjoys freedom. Thus the Church is now exercised in labor as a handmaid, but afterward enjoys freedom as a mistress. Gibeah here denotes this world. In it the concubine is raped, because the Church in this world is shamefully defiled by heretics with perverse doctrine. She is sent to the twelve tribes to be avenged because she is entrusted to the twelve apostles to be defended. The besiegers of Gibeah are the teachers of the holy faith, who attack heretics and lovers of this world by writings and deeds. Finally, the city is burned with its inhabitants: so this world at the end will burn with its lovers. Rachel, who is said to mean “sheep,” [Col. 0839A] signifies the Church, which feeds her children with the milk of doctrine and clothes them with the wool of good works. By her son Benjamin, whose name means “son of the right hand,” the Christian people are denoted: placed at God’s right hand in judgment, they are called to the kingdom of the Father. Her weeping over her children is not consoled here, but waits for her sorrow to be turned wholly into joy. Jerusalem is laid waste by the Babylonians because the Church is tormented by persecutors through diverse punishments. But Babylon itself is defeated by two kings, because this world is continually attacked by two laws. And because this persecution began under Herod in the children and will end under Antichrist, the evangelist therefore referred all these things to the Church.

Nebuchadnezzar, moreover, bore the figure of Antichrist, [Col. 0839B] because he took the people of God captive and threw the three youths into the furnace of fire. So too Antichrist will subject the faithful people to his service and cast the three sons of Noah—Shem, Ham, and Japheth, from whom the three parts of the earth, Asia, Africa, and Europe, were filled—into the furnace of persecution.

His type also appeared beforehand in Antiochus, who cruelly oppressed the seven Maccabees together with their mother by tortures (II Macc. VII): so Antichrist will consign to atrocious punishments the seven Churches to which Paul and John write in the Apocalypse (Rev. I), together with their mother, the universal Church. Herod held his figure when he gave the little children over to death: so Antichrist will command little children to be taken from their mothers and will torment them with harsh punishments. Moreover Rachel [Col. 0839C] weeps for her children because the Church, with great groaning, implores God’s judgment over the torment of the martyrs. Yet she does not receive consolation here, because in the future they will have eternal recompense for their patience. Infants are killed because bodily torments are not accepted for Christ except from those who, lacking envy and simple in malice, die for the Lord. Those two years old—that is, born within the period of two years—are slain because they are killed in both Testaments for the two commandments of love. Christ is led into Egypt, which means “darkness,” because he departs from the Synagogue and visited [or: visits] the Gentiles, who were darkness. [Col. 0840A] When the impious king has died, he returns to Judea because, when unbelief has been destroyed by the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, he returns to Judea through faith.

After killing the infants and murdering his own wife, Herod fell into the most grievous pain and endured diverse sufferings. Since he could not be cured by physicians, he killed himself with his own hands. He himself now gnashes his teeth in eternal punishment; but these now triumph in everlasting joy.

Today the *Gloria in excelsis* and the *Alleluia* [Note: [Col. 0839D] Codex *aevia*: the abbreviation mark omitted.], the latter a song of joy, are not sung, because the Church shares in the mourning of the mothers for their children, and because that glorious company of infants descended to Tartarus until [Col. 0840B] Christ’s blood redeemed them thence after thirty years.

Mark well, dearest ones, that Christ our champion, while still a little child, placed a host of little children in the first battle line; but when he had become a young man, he brought forth the host of martyrs into the battle-lines against the enemies. For spiritual warfare must begin against vices through humility and then be waged against unbelievers through open preaching. The King of angels declared war against the king of the children of pride (Job XLI). Humble and small, he entered the city of the tyrant—that is, Babylon of this world—and at once gathered an army of little children, because he came to raise up the humble and scatter the proud through them. But after he himself had overthrown the king of pride in battle, [Col. 0840C] he sent the whole cohort of his soldiers into the ranks of the enemy. Having overcome vices and persecutors, he will gather them in the heavenly court and crown their triumph with the laurel of eternal glory.

With all devotion, dearest ones, ask these saints to be your supporters before Christ by their devout prayer, so that after this wretched life you may possess with them the everlasting glory which eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and so forth.

On the octave of the Lord you ought more rarely to deliver a sermon, lest it become cheapened, and so that the word of God, spoken more sparingly, may become sweeter to hearers. According to the occasion, moreover, you should sometimes shorten a sermon and sometimes lengthen it.

[Col. 0839]

[Col. 0839D] “I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys” (Song VI). The Son of God, dearest ones, says that he went down into a garden of nuts and saw the fruits of the valleys. The garden is the Church; the nuts are the various companies of saints. Three things are considered in a nut, by which three orders in the Church are signified: by the outer husk, married persons; by the strength of the shell, prelates; by the sweetness of the kernel, those sweetened by contemplation. The Lord came down into this garden, to such nuts, when he came from heaven into this world in human form. Valleys are the humble; fruits are good actions. The Son of God came to see the fruits of the valleys—that is, to reward the vows and works of the humble. Those who in this garden, brothers, [Col. 0840D] will not be nuts, nor, having become valleys, bear the fruits of good works, will have no part in the kingdom of God. Indeed, if they occupy the ground unfruitfully like barren fig trees, the axe of God cuts them from this garden like dry wood and commands them to be cast into the furnace of fire—that is, into hell.

The Prophet tells us how the Lord came down into this garden: “The Lord descended like rain upon a fleece” (Ps. LXXI); and: “He has overcome the rod of the oppressor as on the day of Midian” (Isa. IX). When the people of God were formerly harshly oppressed by the Midianites because of sins, and Gideon was commanded by an angel to attack the enemies, Gideon asked God for a sign by which he might hope for triumph over the enemy. With the Lord’s assent, he laid out a fleece on the threshing-floor of a field; throughout the night dew descended from heaven upon the fleece, while the threshing-floor remained dry. Therefore, having gathered ten thousand men, the people of God met their enemies, who were encamped in a hundred and twenty thousand. But by the Lord’s command the army was led to a stream and tested in this manner: it was divided from one another; three hundred drew drink with their hands, while the rest drank with mouths bent to their knees. The three hundred were commanded to go against the enemy; the others were commanded to return home. Thus the three hundred took trumpets and jars, hid lamps within the jars, came unexpectedly into the enemy camp by night, sounded the trumpets, and broke the jars with a crash. The lights hidden within appeared, and all the terrified enemies fled. Pursuing them, they killed many; scarcely a few escaped. Returning, they all divided the spoil. [Col. 0841B] Thus Gideon, having defeated the enemies, won a trophy and freed the people of God from oppression (Judg. VI, VII).

Who has ever heard, brothers, of advancing against armed enemies with jars and lamps? But because these things happened figuratively, the prophets David and Isaiah referred them to Christ’s Incarnation. Midian signifies the devil, by whom the people of God were cruelly oppressed before Christ’s coming. Gideon, who frees the oppressed people, is Christ, who brought the human race back from the devil’s slavery. The fleece laid on the threshing-floor is the blessed Virgin, chosen from the Synagogue. Dew descended upon the fleece and the threshing-floor remained dry, because blessed Mary was moistened by God’s power and God’s wisdom, while the Synagogue dried up in unbelief. The dryness of the field is the virginity of holy Mary; [Col. 0841C] the moisture of the fleece is the fruitfulness of Christ’s mother. Therefore the Lord descended like rain upon the fleece because he brought fruitfulness to the mother without taking away virginity.

The army is led to the water to be tested because the people to be saved are washed in Christ’s baptism. The three hundred who draw water with their hands are those who receive baptism in faith in the Holy Trinity and fulfill that faith through the Decalogue of the Law; therefore they will defeat their enemies—that is, vices and demons. But those who drink with bent knees are those who, having received baptism, live like brute animals; and because they will not go against the enemy, they will perish through indolence. The three hundred disturb the enemy camp with the sound of trumpets because the apostles and other teachers of the Church drive away troops of demons with the blast [Col. 0841D] of lofty preaching. Moreover, the jar signifies Christ’s humanity, and the lamp hidden within signifies his divinity. The jar is broken and the hidden light displayed, and the enemy host, terrified, is put to flight, because Christ’s flesh was broken in the Passion and dried up like a potsherd, while the light of his divinity shone in the world through miracles, and the multitude of demons vanished from the faithful. Gideon, having won victory, returns with the pomp of spoil, and the people are freed from fear of the enemy, because Christ, having defeated hell, returns to heaven in noble triumph, and the faithful people are made free from the devil’s yoke. Then indeed he overcomes the rod of the oppressor, because by the power of the cross he tramples down the violence of the devil, who continually exacted from the human race an undeserved service.

He received circumcision today because he came to fulfill the Law which he gave. Abraham was the first to be circumcised, and Christ was also promised to him. Circumcision was performed in the genital member because after sin shame first arose there for the first parents. Therefore Christ wished to endure this in his own members because he came to cut away the shame of original sin.

And you ought to know, dearest brothers, that no one has ever been saved unless baptized in some manner. Some were baptized by the shedding of blood, as Abel; very many in a figure, as Noah by the outpouring of the flood; many in a sign, as Abraham and his descendants in [Col. 0842B] circumcision; many in the Holy Spirit; Christians by immersion in water. But since Christ has transformed for us all legal observances into spiritual sacraments, we ought not, like Jews, to mutilate one member with iron, but in this way cut away vices from each of our senses. We ought to circumcise our sight so that we do not desire to look upon women lustfully. We circumcise hearing if we stop it against evil speech. Lips and tongue are circumcised if they are restrained from lies, perjuries, and detractions. The heart is circumcised if it is not allowed to wander in vain thoughts. We circumcise our hands if we do not make them instruments for doing evil. The genitals are purified by circumcision if they are restrained from lust. The feet are circumcised if they are not permitted to run toward evil.

[Col. 0842C] And so that we may be renewed in every respect in Christ, we are taught also by birds. It is said that, when an eagle grows old, the horn of its beak bends down so far that it is even deprived of the use of eating; sensing this, it sharpens itself against a rock until that curvature breaks off, and so recovers its ability to eat and its youth is renewed again. Thus we, dearest ones, when we grow old in shameful deeds and fail from the food of life, ought through confession to run to the rock, Christ, and through penance sharpen the hardness of our malice; then that youth is renewed in us through grace which was given us in baptism through the Holy Spirit. Those who now strive to be renewed in Christ in this way will deserve one day to be crowned by Christ in heaven.

But alas! Certain wretched and exceedingly unhappy persons among the number of the faithful—something we are compelled to say with deep sorrow—on this sacred night follow the rite of the Gentiles. Enticed by curiosity, indeed deceived by demons, while they desire to learn certain novel and vain things, they fall into grave danger to the soul. They profane the Christian religion, pollute their souls with unspeakable crimes, deny the true God, and in every way enslave themselves to the devil. I mean those who, at the devil’s prompting, invoke demons through sorceries in deserted places and desire to learn unknown things from them. It is necessary that they be joined with those in damnation with whom they shared conversation. You may perceive how great this wickedness is from the Law’s saying: “You shall not suffer sorcerers and diviners to live” (Exod. XXII). Canonical censure also imposes [Col. 0843A] seven years of penance for such a crime, as upon one who has voluntarily killed a human being. For what greater homicide can a person commit than to destroy his own immortal soul by such a crime, abandon God, the life of souls, and subject himself to the devil, author of death?

But those who on this night seek information at the tombs of the dead are certainly assigned with the dead to hell. Likewise all who on this night run to a spring, tree, stone, or any unconsecrated place as though they might learn something new there; or if men put on women’s clothes, or women men’s clothes, for any sorcery; or perform on this night anything contrary to sound faith—without doubt they hand themselves over into the dominion of the devil. [Col. 0843B] But those who consent to their doing such things perish with them. Therefore, dearest ones, those who have committed such things through ignorance should do penance for them while they may, commit nothing of the sort again, and forbid others from them. If they neglect this, whether willing or unwilling, they will be companions in eternal punishment of the demons whom they followed.

But you, most beloved, whom God willed to become his children and whom he made heirs of his kingdom, shun such things with abhorrence. Gather devoutly at church; praise Christ the Son of God for all his benefits; and invoke him, the true God, in all your needs. Today begin no work of God as though for a favorable outcome, but be free from every servile work for the praise of the eternal King; and he will grant you abundantly the necessities of life, [Col. 0843C] and afterward bestow everlasting joys upon you as upon children.

The venerable solemnities of this day are increased for us by the illustrious merits of blessed Bishop Basil. Endowed with wisdom, he excellently adorned the house of God—that is, the Church—by word and writing, and gloriously embellished his own times with signs, wonders, and miracles. For in his time Julian, supported at the summit of imperial power, denied Christ and transferred himself to demonic worship; [Col. 0844A] he proscribed the goods of many Christians and condemned them to various punishments. When he led an army against enemies and said that, after overthrowing the enemy, he would destroy Basil’s city, Basil kept vigil and prayed with all the people in the chapel of Saint Mary. That same Julian, though surrounded by a guard of soldiers, was pierced by a certain martyr, Mercurius, at the command of the Mother of God; and thus Basil’s city was delivered from its imminent danger.

To a certain hermit named Ephrem it was revealed that Basil was a pillar of fire. He arose and came to him. Meanwhile, while Basil celebrated the solemnities of Mass, Ephrem saw a flame rise from his mouth and reach the heights of heaven. Immediately he cried out: “Truly Basil is a pillar of fire.” [Col. 0844B] Once Mass had been celebrated, he asked Basil to obtain for him from God knowledge of the Greek language; and, Basil praying, he deserved at once to be divinely enriched with it.

A certain young man was consumed by love for a girl who was a nun. At the devil’s prompting he denied God in writing; sealing the document with his hand, he delivered himself by his own hands, along with it, into the devil’s dominion. Basil took him away from the devil, compelled the devil to return the written document, and, as a good shepherd, restored the lost sheep to the flock.

Basil obtained by prayers that a document in which a certain woman had written down all her sins, and which she had brought sealed to him, should be divinely erased.

A certain Jewish physician foretold to him his imminent death; [Col. 0844C] but Basil by prayer delayed the hour of death and through faith added the Jew to the number of the faithful. When this had been accomplished, he entered into the joy of his Lord, whom God set over all his goods. Dearest ones, ask him to become an intercessor before God for your sins, so that after the exile of this life you may deserve, with him, to obtain in the heavenly homeland the honor of that glory which eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and so forth.

## ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0843]

[Col. 0843D] “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, because your light has come and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isa. LX). Holy Church, dearest ones, is called Jerusalem, which means “vision of peace,” because she will see eternal and true peace—namely, Christ in heaven. To her, lying in the world amid longings, it is said: “Arise,” that is, rejecting earthly things, raise yourself to desire heavenly things; and then you will deserve to be enlightened by the true light and illumined by the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“Because your light has come”: Christ, whose beauty sun and moon marvel at, and upon whom angels desiring to gaze never grow sated though they are satisfied. He is the light and joy of all angels; he himself came to enlighten every human being coming into this world (John I). He is called the light of the Church because she is illumined by him as the moon by the sun.

[Col. 0844D] “And the glory of the Lord has risen upon you.” The grace of the Lord was the splendor of Christ’s miracles and teaching, because he became known to this world as glorious and wonderful. This glory rose upon the Church because, drawn by Christ’s signs and teachings, she was brought from disgrace to glory.

“Behold, darkness shall cover the earth and gloom the peoples” (ibid.). Judea, ploughed by the ploughshare of Holy Scripture, is called earth. The darkness of sins shall cover it, and the gloom of unbelief shall cover the peoples of the Gentiles. “But the Lord rises upon you” (ibid.), because through Scripture and preaching he is made known to all the faithful.

“And his glory shall be seen in you” (ibid.): namely, where the righteous shall see God, not through a mirror in an enigma but face to face as he is; where, illumined by the brightness of his splendor, they shall shine like the sun; where, with [Col. 0845A] pain and groaning fleeing away, they shall obtain everlasting joy and gladness.

The evangelist tells us in the Gospel how this light shone upon the world. When Christ, spouse of the Church, came forth from the bridal chamber of the virginal womb, a gleaming star, at the coming of light, wiped away darkness and showed that the King of stars had come. Seeing it, three kings came from the East to Jerusalem, the royal city, and sought the newborn King with gifts. On hearing this, King Herod was troubled with all his people; he suspected a successor to his kingdom and asked teachers of the Law about Christ’s birthplace. When he heard that he ought to be born in Bethlehem, he sent the Magi to seek the child in Bethlehem, saying that he would go to worship the child who was to become king—wretched man, thinking [Col. 0845B] to take life from him who could give life to all.

But when the Magi departed from the impious king, they immediately completed their desired journey with the star as guide. When it brought them to Bethlehem, it stopped over the house in which heaven’s inhabitant was lodging. Then those three exceedingly fortunate men happily entered the house with three gifts, and found three persons happier than all human beings and angels: God’s Only-begotten Son, who bestows eternal blessedness; his Mother, who bore in her womb the blessedness of all; and Joseph, who touched with his own hands the blessedness of angels. Immediately they worshipped him as God and offered him gifts as king, because they found for our sake made mortal him whom kings and prophets had not deserved to find. Warned by an angel in a dream, [Col. 0845C] they were not permitted to return to Herod, but went back to their own region by another way (Matt. II).

I shall briefly tell your love what all this signifies. That the three Magi came to the Lord signifies that the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—were to submit their necks to faith in the Holy Trinity. That they came on the thirteenth day declares that the three parts of the world received through the Gospel the Decalogue of the Law. Three times four also makes twelve. Twelve days are counted apart from the day of the Lord’s Nativity because, through the twelve apostles, the four quarters of the world were converted to faith in the Holy Trinity. The impious king disturbed at their arrival is the devil, who lies in wait for the faithful on the way of salvation. The star which leads them to Christ [Col. 0845D] is Holy Scripture, which shows you the way to life. The house in which Christ is found is the Church, or the heavenly homeland where the Lord will be seen in his glory. The gifts which the Magi offer are the good works which the faithful render to God through faith. Gold is offered to him when he is believed to be King of all and the beginning of our redemption. Frankincense is sacrificed to him when he is preached as God above all, who offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father for us. Myrrh is sacrificed to him when it is affirmed that by his mortality the corruption of our vices was destroyed. We likewise offer God these three gifts if we believe him to reign everywhere, govern all things as God, and have become mortal for us.

The Magi return to their homeland by another path because we who came through the way of pride into the misery of this exile must surely return by the way of humility to the homeland of paradise. This star was brighter than the sun; therefore, shining even by day, it could not be obscured by the sun, because it surpassed the sun of the sun by its own splendor. It also moved in the air near the earth, not in heaven with the other stars, because it made known that the Creator of the stars had shone upon the earth.

Why, on seeing the star, the Magi thought that the Lord should be sought in Judea must be briefly explained to you. In their books they had read that their prophet Balaam had written of Christ: “A star shall rise from Jacob and a mighty man shall arise from Israel” (Num. XXIV). When God led his people out of Egypt through Moses, and they had a route through the land of Midian to [Col. 0846B] the promised land, King Balak summoned Balaam, a priest of idols, to curse them and drive them from his kingdom by a curse. Mounting a donkey, he made for the king. But an angel of the Lord with a fiery sword stood in his way. Moreover, the donkey spoke and rebuked the prophet. At last, when permitted by the angel, he came to the king; and when the king had led him to a mountain summit, looking upon the camp of the children of Israel he understood that Christ would be born from them and prophesied and foretold these things concerning him: “A star shall rise from Jacob and a man shall arise from Israel, whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros” (Num. XXIII, XXIV), “and he shall subject the whole earth to himself.”

After he received money from the king, he gave counsel against the same people: namely, that girls adorned with gold and jewels should meet the approaching people with wine and an idol, and that, when the men sought union with them, the girls should first compel them to sacrifice to the idol, so that, having offended God, they might then fall by their hands. And this happened. [Col. 0846C] For young men, made drunk with wine, burned with love for the girls and, conquered by lust, sacrificed to the idol Baal-peor; whence twelve thousand perished. Afterwards the king, with all his people and his impious counselor, was pierced by the sword, and the whole region was devastated by sword and fire (Num. XXIII–XXV). These things, dearest ones, went before in figure, but signified our times.

The people led out of Egypt by Moses to the promised land are the Christian people, led by Jesus from this world to the homeland of eternal brightness. The king [added: who] stood in the way is the devil, [Col. 0846D] who blocks for us the way of life in many ways. The priest riding upon a donkey is the order of wicked priests, ruled by the irrational impulse of their desires. He is rebuked even by the donkey because their life is condemned even by the common people. The prophet is mute and the donkey speaks, because, while the clergy are silent, God’s word is often uttered by the unlearned. Hence it is said: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. LVI). Because of consciousness of their wicked life, they are silenced concerning God’s word, and, lest they be reproved by those living perversely, they do not give forth the barking of preaching. An angel with a flaming sword stands against them because the judgment of eternal fire is preached to them in all Scripture.

Balaam, climbing the mountain, prophesies of future things, yet, corrupted by money [*peccunia*, as printed], attacks God’s people; so these men too sometimes attain the height [Col. 0847A] of knowledge, preach much to the people concerning future life, and yet contradict those things by their reprobate life. Hence it is said through the prophet: “I saw on the mountain something like a building of a city, and behold, earth shall rise over the windows” (Ezek. XL). The city built on the mountain is the Church founded in Christ. Priests are the windows through which the light of divine knowledge ought to shine upon those subject to them. But alas: earth has grown over the windows and does not allow the light to enter, because desire for earthly things blinds the sight of many priests; consequently, the light of divine knowledge shines into the Church through them not at all.

The star which rose and shone from Jacob is Christ, who shone upon the world from Israel’s race; his power was like that of a unicorn, which crushes all obstacles with its horn. Thus Christ subdued the principalities [Col. 0847B] and powers of the world by the horns of the cross, and long ago subjected all kingdoms to his rule. The adorned girls with whom the people fornicate and incline to idolatry are the splendors and enticements of the world by which the people are ensnared and subjected to demonic worship. Balaam perishes by the sword because the priestly order, a blind guide of the blind, perishes under divine judgment. Finally, the king is destroyed with his people and the country is burned, because at the end the devil will be condemned with all his members; and this world, which they loved as their homeland, will be devoured by flame.

Today also, most beloved, Christ is baptized by John in the Jordan after thirty years; heaven is opened to him; the Holy Spirit is recorded as having descended upon him in the form of a dove; and the Father’s voice declares him the beloved Son [Col. 0847C] (Matt. 3). The Lord, dearest brethren, washed not his own sins but ours, and by entering it consecrated baptism for us. Heaven is opened to him, and the descending Spirit remains upon him, because those who receive baptism in his name shall be filled with the Holy Spirit; and, if they imitate the dove’s simplicity, they shall be raised to heaven with Christ. We are also instructed by animals to put off the old life and put on the new.

It is said that, after a stag has swallowed a serpent, it runs to water so that by drinking it may expel the poison; and then it casts off its horns and hair and thus receives them anew. So we, dearest brethren, after sin, must run to the fountain of tears and expel from ourselves the poison of sins [Col. 0847D], lay aside the horns of pride and the hairs of worldly excess, and take up again the horns of strength—virtues against vices.

Likewise, when a serpent has grown old, twisting itself through a narrow opening in a rock, it puts off its old skin and again puts on a new one. By the serpent every sinner is signified, growing old in many crimes. Such a person must hasten to the rock, Christ; take up the narrow way which leads to life; strip off the old garment of vices; and be clothed with the new garment of virtues.

Today also, most beloved, the Lord, invited to a wedding a year after his baptism, gladdened the guests when, the wine failing, he changed six jars of water into wine [Col. 0848A] (John 2). He gives us also to drink of this wine when he teaches us to understand these things spiritually. For the bridegroom is Christ; the bride, the Church; the guests, all those called to life; the six jars, the six ages of the world; the water changed into wine, the deeds of former people performed as figures of spiritual realities.

In the first age Abel offered a lamb to the Lord. His brother Cain killed him; and afterwards the Lord translated Enoch to heaven (Gen. 4). From this jar of water, wine is drawn by those who know the word of God when this is mystically disclosed. Abel, who sacrificed a lamb, is Christ, who offered his body to God the Father for us. Abel is killed by his brother, and Christ is slain by the Jewish people. Enoch is taken from the earth, and Christ, after his Passion, is taken into heaven.

[Col. 0848B] In the second age Noah, planting a vineyard, becomes drunk with wine; while asleep he is uncovered, mocked by one son, and covered with a garment by two. When he awakens, he assigns the mocker to servitude (fo. 44) and blesses the others unto glory (Gen. 9). This jar of water is changed when it is understood in this manner. Noah, who planted the vineyard, is Christ, who founded the Church; he is made drunk with the cup of bitter Passion and, mocked by the faithless people, is dishonoured. But he is covered by two—that is, by Hebrews and Gentiles: among the faithful, the disgrace of his Passion is venerated. For, waking from the sleep of death, he condemns the mocking Jewish people and raises to life those who honour him.

In the third age Joseph is sold by his brothers through envy. He is accused by his mistress because of his chastity, shut away in prison, brought out from prison [Col. 0848C], and set over all Egypt (Gen. 37–61).

This jar of water refreshes us with the sweet taste of a sweeter wine. Joseph, handed over by his brothers, is Christ, delivered by a disciple to the Jews. Accused as guilty by the Synagogue, as Joseph was by his mistress, he is condemned to death and shut in the tomb. Returning from the abyss, he rules the whole world.

In the fourth age David overcomes Goliath in battle (1 Kings 17), and Solomon builds the temple at Jerusalem from gold and gems (3 Kings 6). Sweet wine is drunk from the water of this jar when it is received in this manner. Goliath is overthrown by David, and the devil is conquered on the cross. The temple at Jerusalem is built from gold and gems by Solomon, because the Church, which is God’s temple, is gathered by Christ in heaven from the perfect [Col. 0848D].

In the fifth age Jesus the priest returns with the captives from Babylon and rebuilds the ruins of the temple in Jerusalem (Hag. 2). This jar of water makes us drunk with wine when it indicates these deeds as spiritually performed. Jesus, who returns from Babylon with the captives, is Jesus Christ, the true priest, who, bringing captivity back from hell, returns to heaven. The ruins of the temple are restored by Jesus in Jerusalem, and the ruined angelic court is restored through Jesus Christ.

In the seventh age all the people come to John, and he, washing them with water, separates believers from unbelievers (Matt. 3). Christ likewise changes for us the taste of the water in this jar into the sweetness of wine. The multitude of people comes to John, and he separates them in the river, because all people shall be gathered to Christ at the end [Col. 0849A], and by him believer shall be separated from unbeliever through the river of fire. Him, dearest brethren, we must love with the whole affection of our minds: he refreshes your souls with such mysteries, invited you to his wedding feast, and will one day make you drunk with the wine of eternal sweetness.

The Gentiles of old also regarded this day as celebrated because of a threefold triumph which the Romans rendered today to Caesar Augustus, since he had conquered three kingdoms—namely Parthia, Egypt, and Media—and subjected them to Roman rule (fo. 46). Nevertheless, [Col. 0850A] for three reasons the Church judges this day solemn and rejoices with triumphal praise to the King of all: namely, because today through the three Magi he subjected the three regions of the world to the sceptre of his Lordship; washed away our sins in the Jordan; and changed today the water of the Law into the wine of grace for spiritual nuptials. Submit yourselves to his rule, dearest brethren, with your whole mind and heart. Render him the service due at all times, so that after the poverty of this miserable life you may receive from him riches and glory “which eye has not seen” (1 Cor. 2), and so forth.

## ON THE PURIFICATION OF SAINT MARY

[Col. 0849]

[Col. 0849B] “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84). Christ, dearest brethren, is called Truth because through him whatever is promised by the Father is fulfilled. This Truth sprang up from the earth when he took the beginning of his humanity from holy Mary. She is therefore compared to earth, because, just as the first Adam was formed from clean earth, so the second Adam, Christ, was begotten from a pure virgin.

Righteousness also looked down from heaven. Christ is the Father’s righteousness, because through him he will give rewards to the righteous and inflict just punishments upon the unrighteous. Holy Mary was heaven, because she bore heavenly mysteries: from her the Sun of righteousness shone upon the world; the moon, the Church, shone forth; and the multitude of stars—that is, the multitude of saints—sparkled. From this heaven Christ the Righteousness looked down [Col. 0849C] when, to visit humankind, he came forth from the Virgin’s womb as a bridegroom from his chamber (Ps. 18).

Ezekiel the prophet foretold concerning this Virgin, full of every grace. The Spirit of the Lord led this prophet onto a mountain, where there was something like the structure of a city, and there he saw a gate secured by perpetual closure. Then the Lord said to him: “This gate shall remain shut forever, and the King of kings alone shall pass through it” [the Latin has *transiverit*] (Ezek. 44). The city which the prophet saw on the mountain is the Church, secure in its foundation upon Christ. The gate never opened is the holy Mother of God, who never experienced intercourse with a man. Through her Christ, the King of kings alone, passed into the world by being born [Col. 0849D], and left her enclosed in perpetual virginity. This same Virgin is written to be the gate of heaven, ever open to all who live devoutly. Through her penitents and all who desire to approach Christ have passage to life.

This undefiled Virgin is also prefigured in the sacred history. When the people were returning to their homeland from Egypt under Moses’ leadership, and the Lord’s anger was destroying them in the wilderness because of their murmuring against Moses and Aaron, the Lord commanded that rods from each tribe be placed in the tabernacle, and that they should not doubt that God had chosen the man whose rod should bear blossoms on the next day, and that they ought to obey him. Accordingly, when twelve rods had been brought and placed in the tabernacle of the sanctuary, Aaron’s rod blossomed on the next day and produced fully ripe nuts (Num. 17).

[Col. 0850B] The people crossing out of Egypt through Moses are the Christian people, returning through Christ from this world to the homeland of paradise. The tabernacle in the wilderness is the Church in this age. Aaron’s rod, dry yet flowering with fruit, is holy Mary: dry indeed in virginity, but made fruitful by the Holy Spirit and pregnant in childbirth. This rod produced the sweet nut when the Virgin gave birth to God and man. In the nut’s outer husk the flesh of Christ is denoted; in its shell, his bones; in its kernel, his soul—or, alternatively, the outer husk denotes his humanity.

By the sweetness of the kernel his divinity is declared. A nut is split in a manner resembling a cross, and Christ’s soul is divided from his body on the cross. From this nut all the souls of the elect are refreshed [Col. 0850C]; upon it all the hosts of angels feast.

On this day the blessed Virgin Mary brought this only-begotten Son of God, her Son, to the temple, and offered for him the legal sacrifice, namely two doves. The venerable old man Simeon met her, joyfully took the child in his hands, and, carrying him into the temple, gave thanks to God because he was worthy to carry the one who carries him. He also foretold that Christ was set for the fall and rising of many, as a sign of contradiction, and that a sword would pierce the soul of his mother (Luke 2). The sword of Christ was his Passion, by which the ancient enemy, pierced through, fell defeated. It passed through Mary’s soul when she saw him hanging on the cross in great grief [Col. 0850D]; therefore she was even more than a martyr. Christ was the fall of the Jews and the rising of the Gentiles: the Jews fell through faithlessness, while the Gentiles rose from vices through faith in Christ. The sign of contradiction was the cross, which Jews and Gentiles everywhere opposed.

Dearest brethren, if we wish to receive Christ in the heavenly temple, we must now offer sacrifices in the temple of the Church with the Mother of God. Under the Law it was decreed that wealthy women requiring purification should give a lamb in sacrifice, while poor women should offer two doves or a pair of turtledoves (Lev. 12). By the lamb innocence of life is denoted; by the turtledoves, the penitence of mourners—for instead of singing they groan and utter sorrowful sighs. Therefore, since we cannot [Col. 0851A] offer God the lamb of innocence, let us offer the turtledoves of penitence. Let us offer two [the Latin has *duos*], so that we may continually lament that we have lost the joys of paradise because we omitted the things we ought to have done, or that we have deserved the punishments of Tartarus because we committed many things we ought not to have done.

And it should be observed that the Lord willed to be born not from the daughter of a king or any prince, but from the poorest parents, upon whom such want of possessions had fallen that their hands could not find a lamb to offer in sacrifice. For he came, indeed, to call humble poor people back to heavenly things and to condemn proud rich people to Tartarus.

O brethren, what an innumerable multitude of heavenly citizens assembled in solemn worship for today’s feast when the virgin mother brought forth the King of glory for humankind! With what joyful company did she proceed in ordered ranks when today the Queen of Heaven went to the temple with the King of angels! O how greatly the daughters of Zion rejoiced today in the living Lord when they saw King Solomon crowned by his mother with the diadem of flesh (Song 3)! Therefore they met him with joy and exultation and led him with gladness into the king’s temple (Ps. 44). Today let young men and virgins, old men with the younger, praise the Lord’s name (Ps. 148), because he came to exalt the kingdom of his people. Let virgins rejoice and leap for Christ in devout praises, because the Virgin Mary bore to the world the Saviour who grants heavenly gifts to chaste virgins. Let widows rejoice and clap their hands in votive praise to Christ [Col. 0851C], whom the widow Anna today brought into the temple with Simeon (Luke 2), and who brings the continent into heaven’s temple. Let married women be glad and sing Christ’s praises in harmonious voice: at the entrance of his mother, married Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied (ibid.); and he shall unite to himself in the heavenly bridal chamber those who live in lawful marriage.

Let the dear age of infancy raise voices in ringing praise of Christ, because he whom the heavens could not contain lay as an infant in a cradle. John greeted him while still an infant in his mother’s womb (Luke 1). Thousands of infants praised him by their deaths for his sake under Herod (Matt. 2). Let flourishing childhood rejoice in acclaiming Christ, who as a child sat in the midst of the teachers and gave children an example of learning [Col. 0851D] (Luke 2). Let ardent youth clap its hands in rejoicing for Christ, who, becoming a young man, illumined the world by miracles.

Honourable day! (fo. 48v.) Let old age, rejoicing, sing psalms to Christ, because today old Simeon carries in trembling arms him who governs all things by his will. Let the whole world burst forth in his praise and render him due thanks in resounding high voices, for [Col. 0852A] he paid to God the Father Adam’s debt on behalf of the whole world. Because of Adam the whole world was cursed and given over to condemnation; because of Christ the whole world is blessed by God and enrolled for everlasting glory.

The Church’s custom today of carrying lights in its hands was taken from a pagan practice. In this month the Romans would make a procession through the city with lights in honour of their gods, believing that by those gods’ favour they subjected the whole world to themselves. But because today Simeon carried in his hands the light of all angels, whom he proclaimed “a light for the Gentiles and the glory of Israel” (Luke 2), the Church instituted the carrying of lights today in honour of the highest God, who by his sovereignty subjected the whole world and called it to [Col. 0852B] inaccessible light. For in the candle is understood Christ’s humanity, and in its light his divinity. Let your charity now briefly hear how the blessed Virgin Mary customarily assists those who call upon her.

A certain Jewish boy went with Christian boys to a church in which an image of holy Mary with her Son was painted upon the wall above the altar. When Mass had been celebrated and the priest distributed communion to the people, it seemed to the Jewish boy that the priest was distributing to the people a child resembling the painted child. Approaching with the others, he received raw flesh from the priest and took it home to his father. He related in order how he had received it. His father, inflamed with excessive anger, lit a furnace with much wood [Col. 0852C] and threw the boy inside to be burned. The mother cried out, and people rushed together from every direction. They broke down the doors and rescued the boy from the flames. Astonished to find him unharmed in any respect, they asked how the fire had not touched him. He replied: “The Lady whom I saw above the altar in the church, I saw sitting in the furnace. She received me in her lap, scattered the flames away from me, threw a garment over me, and did not permit the fire to come near me.” On hearing this, they raised voices and hands to the heavens and joyfully gave thanks to Christ, the deliverer of all, and to his Mother. They asked the boy’s father whether he agreed to be washed in baptism; when he refused, they handed him over to be burned in those same flames [Col. 0852D]. But they baptized the boy (fo. 50), his mother, and all the Jews who were present.

Dearest brethren, imitate this Queen of angels in humility and chastity. Pray that she may intercede with devout prayers before her Son for your miseries, so that, when he comes to be made wonderful in his saints, you may receive the crown of unfading glory in his temple. “Which eye …”

## SUNDAY IN SEPTUAGESIMA

[Col. 0851]

[Col. 0851D] “The torrent shall divide from the pilgrim people the stone of darkness and the shadow of death” (Job 28). The stone is the hardness of Judaea; the darkness, the unbelief of the Jews. Death is [Col. 0852D] the devil; his shadow is the Gentile people. As a shadow is conformed to a body, so that people is made like the devil by imitating him. The pilgrim people are the faithful [Col. 0853A] people sighing in the exile of this life. The torrent is the river of fire which goes forth from the Lord’s presence, through which the faithful people will be separated from the unbelieving at the end. Therefore the torrent shall divide the stone of darkness and the shadow of death from the pilgrim people when the fire of the last judgment separates, as tares from wheat, the Jews hardened in unbelief and Gentiles made like the devil in wickedness from the Christian people; wrapping them in the furnace of hell, it shall burn them with unquenchable fire; and it shall receive into eternal dwellings the people now exiled in the homeland of paradise.

Abraham prefigured this division when, offering God a sacrifice of three animals, he separated their parts from one another. For the Lord commanded Abraham to sacrifice to him a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old sheep, and a three-year-old goat, and, cutting them into pieces, to separate them from one another [Col. 0853B]. Offering each of these, he divided them into parts; he also offered doves and permitted them to fly over the carcasses. At night Abraham saw a burning furnace come and pass through those divisions, consuming one portion and leaving another untouched. Then God foretold to Abraham the future sojourn of his race, which afterwards occurred when it was taken into Egypt (Gen. 15). We must see why all this was done and explain how it now signifies the times to us.

By the three sacrifices are understood the three orders in the Church: teachers, continent persons, and married persons, who alone shall be saved on the day of judgment. By the ox, with which the earth is ploughed, is indicated the order of teachers, through whom the word of God [Col. 0853C] is sown in the field of this world. It is written as a cow because through it offspring are begotten for Christ. This is divided into two parts. Some preach Christ for everlasting joy; others for temporal gain. By the sheep, which provides milk for nourishment and wool for covering, is understood the order of those living the contemplative life, who give the milk of doctrine and the wool of good examples to those seeking good things in the land of the living. This sheep is divided into two because some enter the life of holy religion for the reward of future glory, while others do so for their belly and worldly favour. By the goat, a lascivious animal, is understood the order of married persons; these also are divided in two, because some [Col. 0853D], though engaged in carnal union, devote themselves to almsgiving and good works, while others serve luxury and wickedness. Each animal was three years old because the Holy Trinity is worshipped by these three orders. By Abraham God is represented, through whom the flock of the reprobate is separated from the elect. In the night the burning furnace appears in terror and moves among those divisions because the day of judgment will come unexpectedly and separate the righteous from the wicked. The doves were allowed to fly because spiritual people are lifted to heavenly things on the wings of twofold charity. One part is consumed by flame and another left behind because the works of the righteous, tested by fire like gold, shall be rewarded, while the deeds of the wicked, consumed like hay, shall be assigned to the fire.

The Lord also foretells this separation through [Col. 0854A] the last examination: “On that day two will be in the field: one will be taken and the other left; two in a bed: one will be taken and the other left; two women grinding: one will be taken and the other left” (Luke 17). The two in the field are the two portions of teachers labouring in this world: one portion on that day shall be taken to glory because of the merit of its life, while the other shall be left to punishment because of the perversity of its life. The two in the bed are the two portions resting in the repose of the contemplative life: one shall be taken to eternal rest because of sincerity, the other left to everlasting pain because of pretence. The two women grinding are the two portions of married persons, borne about by the turning wheel of secular affairs: one portion shall be taken to reward because of works of mercy [Col. 0854B], while the other shall be left to punishment because of impiety. They are described not as two male grinders but as two women, because married persons are not raised to spiritual things as men are.

This division is also announced beforehand by the prophet, who testifies that only three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—shall be delivered on the day of judgment (Ezek. 14). By Noah, who guided the ark upon the waters, teachers are signified, because they govern the Church amid the storms of the age. By Daniel, described as abstinent, the life of continent persons is expressed. By Job (fo. 52), remembered as having pleased God in marriage, the multitude of married persons is shown. Only persons found in these orders shall be delivered on that day, when the elect return from this pilgrimage to the homeland of paradise.

This pilgrimage was foreshadowed in the children of Israel, whom Pharaoh oppressed for a long time with harsh service. For in former times the Hebrew people went down into Egypt when famine afflicted them; but Pharaoh subjected them to cruel slavery. When they cried to the Lord, he sent Moses to them, who struck Egypt with many plagues and prodigies. He led the people of God through the Red Sea into a land flowing with milk and honey (Exod. 1, etc.). By Egypt this world is signified, in which the human race is exiled from the homeland of paradise and is subjected to grievous oppression by the devil. When it cries aloud to the Lord through the righteous, Christ is sent to deliver it; through him the world is shaken by many miracles. The people are led back through [Col. 0854D] the Red Sea—that is, through baptism—to the homeland of paradise, where milk and honey overflow, that is, an abundance of every good thing overflows.

This pilgrimage was likewise prefigured while the people remained in Babylonian captivity for seventy years (Dan. 9). Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, besieging Jerusalem, destroyed it and led the people captive to Babylon. There they dwelt in sadness for seventy years and did not sound the song of joy. They hung their instruments upon willows, sat beside them, and wept. When the seventy years had ended, they returned to Jerusalem and celebrated Passover with joy; afterwards, when wives and children came, they had double joy.

[Col. 0855A] All these things, dearest brethren, concern the present day. All these things prefigured the times. Jerusalem is paradise; Nebuchadnezzar is the devil; Babylon is this world. Nebuchadnezzar led the people captive into Babylon, and the devil deceived the human race into this world, where it hung its instruments upon willows and, sitting, shed tears (Ps. 136). Willows quickly take root in earth and quickly grow green again when cut. The willows are lovers of the world, who have sent down their roots into earthly things and for whom transient goods abound as they desire. Upon these the righteous hang their instruments, because they leave worldly pleasures to them. Sitting, they weep, because the humble lament their destruction with great sorrow. By the instruments heavenly [Col. 0855B] doctrine is also understood; it is hung upon the willows when spiritual teaching is withheld from worldly people because they despise it.

By the seventy years during which the people suffered in Babylon are understood the seven thousand years through which the human race is exiled in this life. For, just as every creature was ordered in the first seven days, [Col. 0856A] so this world is believed to extend through seven thousand years.

Therefore, if you divide seven thousand years into seventy hundreds and give one year out of every hundred years as, so to speak, a tithe, you will have seventy years. Moreover, if from the seventy years you tithe a day for each year, you will calculate seventy days. These are the days during which the Church does not sing Alleluia, because it recalls the seventy years of captivity, which signify the seven thousand years of our pilgrimage. Hence Genesis is also now read, in which the fall of humanity from paradise into this world is described (Gen. 3). This season is called Septuagesima because from this day until the holy Saturday of Easter there are seventy days [Col. 0856B], during which Alleluia is sung twice. The people, returning to Jerusalem, rejoice with gladness because the souls of the faithful shall now enter into the joy of the Lord; but when the end of the world is finished, they receive their wives and children—that is, bodies and works. Then indeed they shall sing Alleluia in jubilation, because they shall rejoice together in glory with body and soul.

Interweave these matters frequently in your sermons. For by words of this kind you remove their weariness.

[Col. 0855]

[Col. 0855B] Brethren, many more things might still be said to you concerning this holy day, which I must pass over in silence lest, wearied, you wish to leave before the service is completed. For some of you have come here from far away and have a long journey home. Some perhaps have guests at home, or crying children; some of you are not idle and are bound elsewhere; illness brings weariness to some; and the shame of nakedness troubles others. For the sake of all, I wish to suppress a great deal, but to say a few more things to the healthy and unoccupied.

Since today, dearest brethren, we have laid aside the song of joy and taken up the song of sorrow, I wish briefly to recount to you from the books of the Gentiles how you ought to avoid the melody of worldly delights, so that afterwards you may be able to sound sweet harmony in heaven with the angels. Anyone who finds a jewel in mud ought to lift it from the mire and set it in royal adornment. Thus it is fitting that, if anything useful is found by us in the books of the Gentiles, it should be turned to the edification of Christ’s bride, the Church.
