The wise men of the world write [Col. 0855D] that there were three Sirens on an island in the sea (fo. 54), singing a most sweet song in different ways. One sang with her voice, another with a pipe, the third with a lyre. They had women’s faces and the claws and wings of birds. By the sweetness of their song they stopped all passing ships, tore apart sailors overcome with sleep, and sank ships in the sea. When a certain leader, Ulysses, had to sail past there, he ordered himself tied to the ship’s mast, his companions’ ears stopped with wax; and so he escaped the danger unharmed and submerged them beneath the waves.

These things, dearest brethren, are mystical, although written by enemies of Christ. By this sea is understood the age, tossed by continual storms of tribulations. The island is worldly joy, interrupted by frequent pains, just as a shore is assaulted by continual [Col. 0856B] waves. The three Sirens, who by sweet song soothe sailors into sleep, are the three pleasures which soften human hearts toward vices and lead them into the sleep of death.

She who sings with a human voice is avarice, which sings such songs to its hearers: “You must gather many possessions, so that you may spread the fame of your name everywhere, visit the Lord’s sepulchre and other places, restore churches, and help the poor and your relatives.” With such a deadly song it soothes the avaricious person’s heart until the sleep of death overcomes him. Then it tears his flesh and the waves devour his ship, because this wretched man is violently torn away from his riches by pains and plunged into eternal flame.

She who plays the pipe is vainglory, which brings forth these songs to its followers: “You are young and noble; you must show yourself illustrious before all. You must spare none of your enemies, but kill all whom you can overpower. Then they will call you a good soldier.” Another song it sings is this: “You must go to Jerusalem and give many alms. Then you will become famous and all will call you good.” But to converts it sings thus [Col. 0856D]: “You must often fast, often pray, and sing aloud. Then you will hear everyone praise you in harmonious voice as a saint.” Vainglory sounds such a tune in the heart until the abyss of death devours the wretched person, empty of good.

She who produces melody on the lyre is lust, which sings such strains beforehand to its followers: “You are young; you may play with any girls, and later amend your ways in old age. This woman shines with distinguished beauty. This one possesses great wealth. If you have her, great profit will follow; yet you will be able to save your soul.” In this manner lust softens the heart of the voluptuous person until, suddenly overtaken by death, the crowd of Cocytus swallows him.

They had women’s faces because nothing so alienates the human mind from God as love of women. They had birds’ wings [Col. 0857A] because desire for worldly things is always unstable: now people crave this or that, then they covet something else. They also had birds’ claws because those whom they draw into sins they tear with pains and carry off to the torments of hell. Ulysses is said to mean “the Wise One.” He sails past unharmed because the truly wise Christian people sail over the sea of this age in the ship of the Church. By fear of God they bind themselves to the ship’s tree, that is, to Christ’s cross; with wax, that is, with Christ’s Incarnation, they seal the hearing of their companions, so that they may turn their hearts from vices and desires and seek heavenly things alone. The Sirens are drowned because desires are overcome by them through the strength of the spirit. They themselves escape the danger unharmed because through victory they come to the joys of the saints.

[Col. 0857B] That you may obtain this victory, let the reading which you have now heard recited admonish you: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize?” (1 Cor. 9). Among the Greeks there was a custom that some prize was set before runners. Yet it was given not to all who ran together, but only to the one who arrived first. The kingdom of heaven is given—that is, set before us—as a prize, toward which sacred Scripture urges us to run with all our strength, because it is bestowed not upon all who run in faith but only upon those who persevere to the end in good works.

There was another custom among them. Naked and anointed with oil, they wrestled together, and the victors were crowned with gold and laurel. We, most beloved, have been anointed with the oil of chrism [Col. 0857C]; therefore, stripped of vices, we must wrestle with the devil, because our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the assaults of vices and demons (Eph. 6). If, therefore, we conquer lust, anger, hatred, or another vice, we shall have a crown of gold and laurel, because we shall receive the splendour of eternal brightness in verdant paradise.

Today’s Gospel instructs us how to attain the prize of this glory. For the Lord says that a certain man went out early in the morning and hired labourers for his vineyard for a denarius. At the third, sixth, and ninth hour he sent others into the vineyard; in the evening he ordered those standing idle all day to enter the same vineyard. When evening came, the master commanded that the labourers be called and that each be given [Col. 0857D] a denarius, first those who had come last. When others complained that they had borne the burden and heat of the whole day and were made equal in reward with those who had laboured little, the master said that he was permitted to give what was his to whomever pleased him. Then he said that many are called, but few chosen (Matt. 20).

[Col. 0858A] This master who hired labourers into his vineyard is almighty God, who hires the faithful into the Church. In this vineyard Christ was the true vine, whose branches, spreading widely, are the saints flourishing in virtues. The labourers sweating in the vineyard are all the elect doing good works in the Church. In this vineyard, at the first hour, Abel, Seth [printed *Seht*], Enoch, and other righteous persons entered. At the second, Noah, Shem, Heber, and others began to labour. At the sixth, Abraham, Joseph, Moses, and other patriarchs undertook the burden. At the ninth, David, Isaiah, and other prophets sweated at the work. In the evening, the apostles and other faithful, hitherto as it were idle, completed the work in the Lord’s vineyard.

At the first hour also, those enter this vineyard who begin to serve God in infancy. At the second hour those enter the vineyard who are converted to God’s service in childhood. Those are joined to the workers in the vineyard at the sixth hour who are added to those serving God in youth. At the ninth hour those undertake the burden of the vineyard who come to God’s service in old age. In the evening those are admitted into the vineyard who are received into conversion in decrepit age. The denarius is first given to the last because eternal life is more often granted to such people before it is granted to children. The denarius, bearing the image of the king, by which those working in the vineyard are rewarded late when their labour is finished, is the desired vision of the Creator. It is disclosed at the end of the world to all who labour devoutly in the Church, when he is contemplated by them face to face as he is (1 John 3).

Thus a certain brother, as he was drawing his last breath and many brothers stood beside the dying man, suddenly held out a closed hand and, rejoicing with great exultation, said [Col. 0858C]: “It is well with me, it is well with me: I have received the denarius.” With this utterance he ceased from the vineyard’s labour; receiving Christ, the true denarius, he entered everlasting rest. The Lord says that he is permitted to give good things to whom he will because he bestows eternal joys upon infants, who have laboured nothing, and upon those repenting at the end (fo. 56v.), who have laboured little, before those who laboured all their life. He says that many are called but few chosen because many receive faith and baptism, but not all will enter the kingdoms of heaven—only the very few who persevere to the end in faith and action.

[Col. 0858D] In this vineyard, dearest brethren, labour with all exertion. Persevere in this labour to the end, so that, receiving Christ the denarius in the heavenly city, you may be able joyfully to cry: “As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord” (Ps. 47): things “which eye has not seen” (1 Cor. 2), and so forth.

Concerning Saint Sebastian. When his feast occurs, this seasoning should be added to the sermon.

[Col. 0857]

[Col. 0857D] In order that, after the labour of this vineyard, you may deserve to receive Christ, the denarius, you ought by devout prayers to make Saints Fabian and Sebastian—whose feast is celebrated today—your intercessors. For they laboured vigorously in the Lord’s vineyard, and therefore have deserved now to rest with Christ. Saint Fabian long presided nobly over the Church in the apostolic see by word and deed, and today offered his neck for the flock entrusted to him. Blessed Sebastian, one of the emperor’s foremost friends, strengthened many for martyrdom and was therefore seized by the pagans and compelled to sacrifice to idols. When he refused, by the emperor’s order he was bound to a post in a field and shot with arrows by soldiers. Filled with arrows like a hedgehog, he was left half alive in the field. Later, having recovered, he publicly preached Christ; and then he was beaten with clubs until he gave up his spirit.

Today also a certain very noble Mark, with his wife Martha and his sons Audifax and Habakkuk, gained the denarius of life by their blood. Having seized them, the pagans tortured them for a long time with clubs and whips; then they hung them upon the rack, tore them with iron claws, applied fire, cut off their hands, and finally killed Martha in water, while they beheaded the others and burned their bodies. Raise hands and hearts to all these, beloved. Seek them with tears, that you may deserve to be delivered from every torment of soul and body, and with them be crowned in everlasting glory, which eye has not seen (1 Cor. II), and so forth.

If Septuagesima falls on the feast of Saint Agnes, you may preach by adding this concerning her.

[Col. 0859]

[Col. 0859A] (Folio 58.) In order that you may be able, beloved, to fulfil in deeds what I have said, implore today the aid of Christ’s bride and martyr, Saint Agnes. Beautiful in face and noble in birth, when she was sought in marriage by the son of the prefect of the City, and many splendid ornaments of gold and gems were offered her by him, she despised them all as dung, because she loved only the Author of life. Therefore the prefect ordered her to be seized and led naked to a brothel. But immediately an angel clothed her in a shining garment, and through him a great light also flashed within the brothel. The prefect’s son came with his companions and entered shamelessly; at once he was suffocated by the devil and died. As the people cried out and came running from every side, Agnes prayed to God, and the angel raised the young man. Afterwards, cast into a great fire, she was not only unharmed [an added *non*, “not”], but the fire itself was extinguished. Then, struck with a sword, she became a martyr.

Consider, dearly beloved brethren, that tender girls trampled underfoot the pleasures of the world and shed their blood to obtain the joy of eternal life. Yet we wish to arrive there by sleeping, playing, eating, and drinking; but we cannot reach it except through great labours. Therefore, beloved, you must pray to this virgin, that you may overcome your frailty and triumph with her in heavenly glory, which eye has not [seen].

If it is Saint Vincent’s day, say this concerning him at the end.

[Col. 0859]

[Col. 0859B] In order that you may hasten more fervently to fulfil these things, ask that Saint Vincent may favour you today. For he was hung upon the rack for Christ, torn by cords and claws, scorched by fire, and, after many cruel torments, strengthened by angelic consolation; at last he rested in peace in prison. Since he now rejoices with the angels in heaven, beloved, knock upon him with continual prayers, that you may deserve to come where there is splendour and everlasting light and joy without end, which eye has not seen, and so forth.

If it is Saint Paul’s day, conclude the sermon by saying this.

[Col. 0859]

[Col. 0859C] In this vineyard, beloved, Saint Paul laboured tirelessly. Formerly he attacked the Lord’s flock like a most savage wolf, but the gentlest Shepherd overcame him through a sheep. For while he was ravaging the Church everywhere, he received authority from the high priest on this day and was travelling to Damascus in order to slaughter every Christian he found. Suddenly an immeasurable light flashing from heaven shone forth (folio 58 verso), struck him blind as he lay prostrate on the ground, and a divine voice thundered, rebuking him for the savagery of persecution. In that light, it is believed, Christ’s glory was manifested to him and heavenly secrets were revealed.

Therefore he fasted and prayed for three days; on the third day he was baptized and enlightened in body and soul. At once he began nobly to gather by preaching the Lord’s sheep whom he had scattered by persecuting them. And the sun that had lain hidden beneath the cloud of error, emerging from the darkness of unbelief, brought serenity to the whole world, because it shook the darkness of faithlessness from the nations and poured the radiance of eternal light into all the churches.

Scripture foreshadowed this long ago when Joseph’s servant brought out the silver cup from Benjamin’s sack. For Joseph sent his servant after Benjamin (Gen. XLIV), when Christ sent Ananias to Paul of the tribe of Benjamin (Acts V). The servant opened the sack and brought out the cup, when Ananias, baptizing Paul, made known to the world that he was a vessel of election. The silver of this vessel shone throughout the world, when the whole Church drank sweet streams of teaching from the brightness of the eloquence of this cup. Pray to him, beloved, that, as God converted him, so he may convert us from error; and that you may thus serve the Lord in fear, so that one day you may see the King of glory in his beauty, whom eye has not seen (1 Cor. II), and so forth.

If Septuagesima falls on the Purification of Saint Mary, a sermon may be made about her. At the end explain the seventy years as written above. If it falls on the feast of Saint Blaise, it may be ended thus.

[Col. 0859]

[Col. 0859D] In order that you may obtain the denarius of life, beloved, ask Saint Blaise for yourselves today. Adorned with many jewels of virtues, he was set over the Church in the episcopal mitre. After he had illumined it by a glorious life and outstanding teaching, and had adorned it with many splendid signs, he was seized by pagans for Christ’s name, afflicted with very many whippings, hung upon the rack, torn with iron combs, long worn down in a horrible prison, and thrown in to be drowned in a lake. Finally he was beheaded with two little boys. Because seven women gathered drops of his blood, they too, tortured with many torments, gave back their spirits to the stars. Thus through the labour of blood they left the vineyard and received the denarius of life. Invoke them with your whole heart, beloved, that they may deign to help you, so that after the labour of this life (folio 60) you may receive with them the glory and honour which eye has not [seen] (1 Cor. II), and so forth.

If it is the feast of Saint Agatha, conclude thus concerning her.

[Col. 0861A]

For the cultivation of this vineyard, the prayer of Saint Agatha can greatly benefit you. Seized for Christ by a pagan judge, she was handed over to an indecent matron, who displayed before her countless ornaments of gold and garments in order to turn her mind toward the delights of the flesh. But she despised them all as dung. Then, when she refused to sacrifice to idols, the judge ordered her to be beaten for a long time with stones and then thrown into a dark prison. Taken from there, she was ordered to be hung on the rack and tortured for a long time; after prolonged torture, her breasts were cut off, and she was again committed to prison and afflicted by hunger and thirst. There the Lord’s apostle visited her with a great light and afterwards healed her breasts and wounds.

After this the judge ordered her to be rolled naked upon heated shards and live coals. Then an earthquake occurred, brought down certain buildings, and crushed some persons. The virgin was again shut up in prison; but her soul was led by angels from the prison of the flesh and conducted into the heavenly bridal chamber, there to enjoy the embraces of Christ her bridegroom. Angels visibly attended her funeral rites and placed at her head in the tomb a written tablet. Afterwards the judge, while crossing a river by boat, was thrown from the vessel by the bites and kicks of horses and perished in the river. Mount Etna also belched fire, which melted earth and rocks. Then the pagans stretched the virgin’s veil against the fire, and the flames of the conflagration immediately ceased. Seek her with heart and voice, beloved, that through her merits God may deign to snatch you from the fire of eternal punishment and make you rejoice with all the elect in the joy of his countenance, which eye has not seen (1 Cor. II), and so forth.

[Col. 0861] You ought to repeat this sermon often during the year, and often weave some portion of it into your sermons. When you preach, however, you should not stand with hand extended as though hurling words into the people’s faces, nor with eyes closed or fixed upon the ground, nor with upturned countenance; nor should you shake your head like a madman or twist your mouth in different directions. Rather, as rhetoric teaches, you should speak with fitting gesture, form your words in an orderly and humble manner, utter sorrowful matters in a sorrowful voice, joyful matters in a cheerful one, harsh matters in a keen one, and humble matters in a subdued one. So that the hearers may seem more to behold the things themselves (folio 60 verso) than to hear you, you must represent them through words.

## GENERAL SERMON

[Col. 0861]

[Col. 0861C] “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. XXXIII).

You must all, most beloved brethren, receive today’s sermon with most attentive ear, because today I shall tell you how rich or poor, lords or servants, men or women, you may attain eternal joys.

### To priests

We priests ought to be your tongue, interpreting and explaining for you everything sung or read in the divine offices. For we are called by the Lord the salt of the earth, because, as salt makes food savoury, so it befits us to make the minds of the faithful savoury with the salt of wisdom, so that they may reject transient things and relish only what endures. We ought to preach to monks concerning religious life; to converts concerning holy conduct; to clerics concerning honourable life; and to laypeople concerning the liberality of almsgiving; and in every respect we ought to offer ourselves to all as an example. What we teach in words we ought to display in deeds as a mirror.

For if we tell you what is good but do evil ourselves, we shall be like a candle which gives light to others yet, melting away, fails from its own light. The Lord says to us: “Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. III). A watchman ordinarily stands on high so that he may announce to the citizens enemies he has seen beforehand. Priests are the shepherds or watchmen of the Church, whose life ought to be placed on the height of virtues, so that the coming attack of enemies—that is, of demons or vices—may be announced beforehand to Christians.

If, therefore, we preach God’s word to you, we indeed acquit ourselves, and bind you firmly. But if we do not announce to you the salvation of your soul, and you die in your sins, your blood will be required from our hand, as though we had killed you (ibid.). Therefore, beloved, you should look more to our words than to our deeds: just as, if the emperor sent you a command, you would pay no great attention to the actions of the messenger but to the commands of the sender, so that you might preserve his favour. We are ambassadors of the supreme King of all kings and report his commands to you. If you humbly obey them, you will receive nothing from us, but eternal rewards from him. If you despise them, we suffer no loss; rather, from your Lord, as rebellious servants subjected to eternal punishment, you will bear the loss of your souls.

But if we exhort you to good and ourselves do good, then we are called by the Lord the light of the world, and are saved with you in eternal life. If, however, while preaching good we do evil, we shall be like a bell by which the people are summoned to church, while it itself is worn thin by frequent striking. Thus we call the people to joys, while we ourselves hasten toward mourning. But if, while doing good, we do not teach you, we lament that the Lord calls us dumb dogs (Isa. LVI). If we neither live well nor teach, we shall be blind leaders of the blind; indeed, like smoke in a house, we darken the minds of the faithful.

Two tongues are fashioned upon our garment, because divine authority has entrusted to us the power of binding sinners and the power of absolving penitents (Matt. XVIII). Therefore, beloved, since you are the Lord’s sheep and we are your shepherds, we ought to pour out prayers for your salvation, and you for your own salvation, so that we may be able to fulfil with you in deeds what we preach to you; and, that the minds of priests may burn to do these things, let the lamp of this example shine before them.

A certain bishop taught the people entrusted to him with ardent zeal and offered himself to them as a living example in all things. Whenever he was free from other concerns, he stood continually in prayer. One day, while he was alone in the oratory, a religious man saw heaven opened above the church; from it he saw an immeasurable light poured forth and shining, descending into the same place with the sweetest melody of singers. After a long delay [source *morem*; read *moram*], he saw that same harmony, with singing, rise from the church and penetrate heaven’s heights. Immediately the priest of Christ summoned the brethren, foretold his death, and declared that a multitude of angels had come to him and promised that they would come [*venturus*; read *venturos*] on the seventh day to lead him to heaven. The event followed the prediction: on the seventh day, amid great light and the hymn-singing rejoicing of angels, he was carried to the stars. O beloved, how blessed is the soul that deserved the fellowship of angels!

### To judges

Now I address you, O judges, whom God the just Judge has established as rulers of his people. You ought not to take the words of the eternal Judge badly, but listen with a ready heart and obey them in all things with complete eagerness. Then you will obtain both riches and glory here, and joy and gladness in the world to come.

First, it befits you to heed your very name: to render just judgment to all; never to overturn judgment for money or gifts; to spare the poor in judgment, since it is written, “Judgment without mercy [will be] for one who has not shown mercy” (Jas. II); to defend the clergy, churches and things belonging to churches, widows, orphans, and the poor; to remove thieves, robbers, and brigands from God’s people; to justify the innocent in court and free them from unjust accusation; and to subject the guilty and pestilent to just punishment, so that the rest may fear. For it is better that one should perish than that he should destroy many. You yourselves ought to turn away from every evil and, by forbidding it, call back from injustice all whom you can. If you strive to do this, you will be crowned by God, the just Judge. But if by power you wish to oppress God’s people, I fear that you will incur God’s dreadful judgment. Lest these things be carried from your memory by the wind of forgetfulness, let them remain fixed there by the bond of this example.

As a certain king was hurrying to war, a widow petitioned him to avenge her son. He replied that he would do so once the war was ended. But she said, “If you are killed, who will avenge me?” And he said, “The one who reigns after me.” She replied, “What benefit will it be to you if another does it?” He acknowledged that she had spoken truly and gave her judgment in that very place. Later, when he died, because he was a pagan, he was taken to hell. But after many years had passed, blessed Gregory, passing by that king’s house, saw his image and recalled the widow’s judgment. Deeply grieving that so just a judge was being tormented eternally in hell, he began to weep abundantly for him for three days. On the third day an angel of the Lord stood before him and reported that he had been heard by God. If a pagan judge deserved, because of a just judgment, to be relieved from punishments, how much more will Christian judges deserve through justice to be crowned forever by Christ the Judge?

### To the rich

Now I admonish you, rich people, whom the rich Lord has willed to be fathers of the poor. Remember that you came naked into this world and that you will leave it naked. Since you must leave your wealth to others, hasten now to send it ahead into heavenly treasures through the hands of the poor, so that when worms devour your flesh in the grave, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings. You ought to adorn churches with books, cloths, and other ornaments; restore those that have fallen or been destroyed (folio 64); enlarge the prebends of those who serve God, thereby purchasing their prayers; build bridges and roads, thereby preparing for yourselves a way to heaven; and provide the poor, needy, and pilgrims with lodging and the necessities of food and clothing, thereby buying eternal riches for yourselves. If you do this, beloved, you will not diminish your wealth, but will find it increased a hundredfold where it cannot be taken away or diminished.

### To the poor

Let the poor bear the burden of poverty patiently, so that with Lazarus they may receive unfailing riches (Luke XVI). Let them know that in alms they receive the sins of human beings, and therefore let them strive to return prayer on their behalf and distribute to other poor persons whatever remains to them. Lest this vanish from your hearts, let it grow firm in memory through the narration of this example.

To a certain hermit, who desired this, God revealed the end of a good [added *boni*] and an evil person. Going out, he saw a poor man lying in the street and already drawing his last breath. Behold, a multitude of angels came, received his soul joyfully from the prison of the body, and led it with hymns to the heavenly palace. Proceeding thence, he saw a crowd of noble people of both sexes gathering at the house of a rich man whom a severe illness was compelling to pay the due of his final fate. And behold, suddenly a troop of demons of horrible appearance entered the house. Seeing them, the sick man cried out: “Lord, help me!” And a voice from above said: “Now, do you remember God for the first time? Now the sun of life is darkened for you. Now he himself does not help you.” The demons cruelly wrenched out his soul and dragged it to Tartarus to be tormented.

Perhaps the poor man’s corpse was devoured by beasts, but his soul rejoiced in heaven. The rich man’s body, wrapped in silk amid candles and lamps, was committed to burial; but his miserable soul was tormented among demons in hell.

### To soldiers

You soldiers are the Church’s arm, because you ought to defend her from enemies. It is fitting for you to assist the oppressed, guard yourselves from robbery and fornication, restrain those who assail the Church by evil acts, and resist those who are rebellious against priests. By such military service you will obtain splendid benefits from the supreme King. Lest these things be erased from your hearts, let them be impressed upon your memory by the seal of this example.

Illness was forcing a soldier of a certain king to pay the debt of death. The king urged him to repentance and confession. He said that he would do this (folio 64 verso) if he could not get better, because if he did it at present and afterwards recovered, he feared that the soldiers would mock him as one afraid of death. The king condemned his words and departed. Later, visiting the sick man, he again discussed with him the salvation of his soul. But that antichrist said:

“Before your arrival, two most beautiful young men entered and put into my hands a document in which I found written in golden letters whatever good I had ever done. After them countless demons rushed in with great force. They placed before me an enormous book in which I recognized written whatever evil I had done, said, or thought from infancy onward. And when their prince said why those young men were sitting beside me when they knew that I belonged to them, they rose, went out, and left me to their power. Then, at their prince’s command, the demons rushed upon me with most sharp fiery knives; one beginning at my head and another at my feet, they began to disembowel me. And now, when they have assembled together, I die and am carried off by them to hell.”

At these words the wretch, dying miserably, was dragged to torments, having neglected while alive the remedies of repentance. I have related this to you, brethren and my lords, so that, while you are still able, you may not delay turning to good.

### To merchants

Now I exhort you who are merchants: do not covet earthly gain so greatly that you make your soul saleable and lose it through frauds, perjuries, and lies. Beware of deceiving the simple and uninstructed, selling them what is useless as useful. You are servants of all nations, since you bring them necessities amid dangers of rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers on the road, and dangers in the wilderness (2 Cor. XI). Therefore all nations are bound to repay your labour with prayers. You ought not, beloved, to lose such favour for a trivial thing. Lest these words be given to the wind, let them be made firm in your hearts by this example.

A certain solitary asked God to reveal to him with whom he ought [*debere*; read *deberet*] to be made equal in reward. A divine voice answered him that he had not yet reached the measure of a merchant then on his way to him. This man’s custom was to bring every rare thing to those serving God, and then he would come by ship to visit the brethren. Meeting him, the solitary asked why he was sailing amid waves when a secure dwelling (folio 66) had been prepared for him by God in heaven. Immediately, leaving ship and all that was in it, he dwelt with the solitary as a solitary, until, his labour completed, a choir of angels placed him in the heavenly bosom. O how happily that person trades who purchases heavenly things for himself.

### To farmers

You also, brethren and my companions, who cultivate the land, are the feet of the Church, because you support her by feeding her. Obey priests concerning dues; gladly listen when they admonish you concerning your soul’s salvation; do not overstep the boundaries of fields by ploughing or harvesting; do not cut hay or wood except within the appointed boundaries [the text reads *sucumbere* (sic)]; faithfully render to God the tithe of all your goods. Whoever withholds the tithe makes plunder from God’s possessions; and if he steals God’s portion, God will take nine from him—now by storm, now by drought, now by hail, now by blight, now by pestilence, now by the violence of judges or soldiers, now by the onset of fire, now by the pillaging of thieves or robbers. You avert all these things from yourselves, beloved, if you justly give alms to the poor and tithes to those who serve God. That this sermon may strike firm root in your minds, let the stake of this example drive it in strongly.

A certain farmer suffered from a long illness. Whenever he was somewhat relieved, he devoted himself to farm work, by which he sought to support himself, his wife, and his little children. He was so silent that he was thought mute. After his long illness, he died; and as he was dying, a tremendous storm arose. Therefore everyone shook their heads, calling him utterly wretched: life had denied him health, and death denied him burial, while his stench prevented people even from entering. On the third day, while rain still hindered them, he was cast out of the house and somehow buried in the earth.

His wife, by contrast, was exceedingly healthy in body, and so talkative that every part of her body seemed to be a tongue. Moreover, she raved with such lust that scarcely any of her neighbours escaped her debauchery. She squandered the small property she had with fornicators and allowed her children to go begging. After God was unwilling to endure this any longer, she died a sudden death; but such serenity of sky was poured over the world that the very air seemed to serve her burial.

After both had died, a very little daughter remained. The thought came into her mind whether she should imitate her father’s or her mother’s life. As she considered her father’s misfortune and her mother’s good fortune (folio 66 verso), it pleased her to set her foot upon the path of her mother’s life. While pondering this, she fell asleep; and behold, a figure of fiery aspect stood before her and asked what she was considering. Terrified by his appearance, she forgot all that she had thought and said that she had no thoughts in mind. But he seized her hand and said: “Come, and see them both—your father, that is, and your mother—and then follow the footsteps of whichever pleases you more.”

He led her into a flowering field, lovely with every delight, fragrant with marvellous sweetness, and shining with splendid light. There were many thousands rejoicing there, among whom she saw her father surrounded by every splendour. He came to meet her, called her his daughter, greeted her sweetly, embraced and kissed her. Filled with joy, she asked whether she might remain there with him. He said this could not happen then, but that if she wished to imitate him, she would come there afterwards.

Then her guide held her hand and led her to see her mother. Looking to the left, she saw a most deep valley, wholly full of horror. In it was a blazing furnace, sending forth billows of foul and putrid smoke. Her mother was submerged in it up to the neck, and fiery serpents entwined around her were sucking her innards. Foul spirits stood over her and thrust her with iron forks into the whirlpool of flame. Looking up, she recognized her daughter and cried aloud in great wailing:

“Daughter, sweetest daughter, help now your wretched mother. Remember the pain I endured when I bore you. Remember with what care I nourished you. I never treated you badly. I considered fornications and adulteries a game. Now, because of them, I have found unspeakable torments. Do not despise the tears of your miserable mother, but stretch out your hand and draw me from the lake of misery.”

Moved by her crying, the daughter dissolved in tears. Immediately she was left by her guide and found herself in the bed where she had been before. Because she could not help her mother, she lived so religiously that there is no doubt that after death she came to her father.

I know, beloved, that a long sermon wearies you, and I fear that it may produce disgust in you. Yet you ought not to take badly words concerning the homeland and the heavenly court of angels. For if a buffoon in the marketplace poured out trifles [source *venias*; perhaps *naenias*] in well-crafted words, perhaps one of you would listen with attentive ear (folio 68) to what would destroy the soul. How much more ought you to receive with careful mind the words of life, through which you can attain the joys of angels.

### To married people

Let husbands love their wives with every affection of tenderness, keep faith with them in all things, and abstain from them on holy nights, on nights of fasting, and during the time when women undergo their natural infirmity. Let them raise their children in the discipline and fear of the Lord, correcting them from every evil, especially from indecency, lest, like Eli and his sons, they fall into judgment (1 Sam. IV).

Likewise, let wives deeply love, fear, and keep faith with their husbands in sincere heart; like two eyes, let them agree with one another in every good thing. Let children obey their parents in all things, because in this they especially prolong their lives. Let servants and hired labourers serve their masters faithfully and commit no fraud against them. Let masters give servants food and clothing, and hired workers their promised wage, lest afterwards they lose eternal rewards from the just Lord.

What I am now going to say you must all observe, if you wish to reign with Christ. When you rise in the morning, you ought first to make the sign of the holy cross upon yourselves, commend your souls and bodies to God’s grace, and, before doing anything else, hurry to church. Carry alms with you, or have your servant carry them. To a poor person meeting or awaiting you, cheerfully give with your own hands: the rich person a coin, one of moderate means an obol, another bread, another an old garment—whatever it may be by which a poor person is made glad. He who will say at the judgment, “What you did for the poor, you did for me” (Matt. XXV), will repay you for this.

Then, when you have come to church, you ought first to give God thanks for all his benefits: because he created you, regenerated you in baptism, liberated you from death by the blood of his Son, and called you to the joys of angels. After this, confessing your sins, fall to the ground, pour out tears and prayers for yourselves, for all the Christian people, and for all the faithful departed; ask God that you may turn away from evil with your whole heart, love the good, and complete your life in the Christian religion. Then pray for the assistance of all the saints, that you may deserve to be delivered from the enemies of soul and body.

For just as enemies of the body desire to take your life and plunder your goods, so the enemies of the soul strive to slay your souls and requite your deeds. Pride is a savage enemy: it separates people from God and the angels, joins them to demons, pulls them down from heaven’s heights, and plunges them into the depths of hell. Lust is a cruel enemy: it defiles bodies sanctified in baptism and wraps them in sulphurous fire. Anger is a great enemy, which tears the mind; hatred and discord are enemies, which gnaw away and destroy harmony. If you are safe from these enemies, then you will prevail in every respect over the enemies of the body.

If God’s service is being celebrated in church, you ought to stand there reverently until it is completed; then, having received the blessing, provide for the needs of the body. When you come to table, you ought not approach dinner like pagans who do not know God, or like brute animals. Instead, first say the *Our Father*, or bless your food with some holy word. Then cut off an alms from what is set before each of you and distribute it immediately to the poor, because in nothing can you better redeem your sins and gain eternal riches than in the poor. For as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. Then God the Father will lessen your guilt and increase your substance.

When you go to sleep, you ought all to make the sign [of the cross], commend yourselves and all that is yours to God, and pray to be delivered from sudden and unforeseen death and to be found in good deeds.

You ought faithfully to fast during Lent, the Ember Days, and all vigils, unless a feast intervenes; distribute to the needy whatever food and drink is left over to you; duly observe Sundays and saints’ feasts by abstaining from servile work; frequent churches; attend to holy readings and the accounts of the righteous; learn and teach good, do no evil and forbid it; receive the poor and pilgrims into lodging; provide necessities to the naked and needy; visit the sick with your goods and lighten their burden by consolation; and commit homicide neither in deed nor counsel. For whoever kills a human being created in God’s image will share the lot of the devil, who was a murderer from the beginning (John VIII).

You must flee from and abhor fornications and every defilement of the body, especially adulteries, knowing that by these you are especially estranged from God (folio 70). For God will judge fornicators and adulterers. Your bodies, indeed, are temples of the Holy Spirit, dedicated in baptism. Therefore whoever violates God’s temple, God destroys and condemns that person (1 Cor. III). Even birds show what a crime sexual violation is.

An eagle suspends her chicks by the claw before the ray of the sun. The chick that fixes an unflinching gaze upon the sun’s radiance, she tends with food as her own offspring; but the one that turns its sight away from the sun, she discovers to have been conceived in adultery by another eagle [*alterio*; perhaps *alterius*], withdraws its food, and casts it from the nest as an alien. Thus Christ does not supply the food of his body, and drives from the nest of paradise, one who is defiled by the uncleanness of lust.

You must not swear falsely or bear false witness. Whoever commits perjury denies God; and Christ, denying that person before the Father and angels at the judgment, condemns him (Luke XII). Whoever gives false testimony will meet that testimony: “God will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. V). You must not plunder or steal, because neither thieves nor the rapacious will possess God’s kingdom (1 Cor. VI). You must abstain as much as possible from gluttony and excessive drinking, because drunkards cannot possess God’s kingdom (ibid.). You must not curse, because those who curse are excluded from the blessing, “Come, blessed ones” (Matt. XXV), and will be punished by the curse, “Depart from me, cursed ones” (ibid.).

You must not associate with excommunicated persons: that is, do not greet them, pray with them, or eat with them; avoid kissing them. For one who associates with an excommunicated person [Note: Col. 0869D: “excommunicates” in the manuscript.] is rejected by the Church as excommunicated. Whoever gives them help by arms, money, or counsel is to be regarded as a perpetrator of their crimes. For just as ointments and every medicine avail nothing to a limb cut off from the body, so all the Church’s sacraments and prayers do not benefit one excommunicated from the Church.

For a certain very rich man died while excommunicated. Nine years later, when his wife was dying, she asked her sons to bury her beside her husband. When they opened the grave, they found the father’s body raw and intact; moreover, the sarcophagus was boiling full of bubbling water, from which a putrid stench rose. As their minds were disturbed and bewildered by this, they were told by the clergy that he had been excommunicated. Nine years earlier he had caused a sedition in a certain city and, for this reason, had received from the priest of that place the sentence of excommunication. Grieving, his sons approached that priest and asked that their father be absolved. A marvellous thing: when the priest absolved him far away in another place, the dead man’s body dissolved into ashes.

Therefore, beloved, turn away from all the things I have said must be avoided, and take care to do all the things I have said must be done, so that, when Christ comes to render to all the rewards of their labours, you may see in Zion the God of gods (Ps. LXXXIII), where are the things which eye has not seen (1 Cor. II), and so forth.

## Sunday in Quinquagesima

[Col. 0869]

[Col. 0869C] “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30). Truly, beloved, great and immense is the abundance of divine sweetness, by enjoying which the righteous overflow with every delight. This sweetness is now indeed hidden from those who fear God, but then it is revealed to those who hope in him, when, in the joy of the Lord, they shall see face to face the King of glory in his beauty (Isa. 33), and they themselves, glorified, shall shine like the sun (Matt. 13). Then, I say, they shall enjoy that sweetness into which the angels now desire insatiably to look (1 Pet. 1), when they are satisfied with the good things of the Lord—those things which no human eyes can now see, no ear hear, nor the heart of any wise person conceive, which are prepared for those who love God [Col. 0869D] (1 Cor. 2).

Today a ladder is opened to us for attaining this glory, by which the summit of heaven is today reached by the faithful. This ladder is charity, by which the humility of the Church ascends to the heights of heaven. The sides of this ladder are the twofold loves [read: “love”], namely love of God and love of neighbour. The rungs set between these sides are the various virtues by which the commandments of charity are fulfilled; and whoever duly climbs by them shall see in joy [Col. 0870C] the face of the Lord, who is charity (Job 33).

Fifteen rungs are woven in, because heavenly things are sought through fifteen degrees of charity. Thus in the temple of the Lord one ascended to the sanctuary by fifteen steps, because one climbing upon this ladder is raised to Christ, the sanctuary of the heavenly temple. Fifteen psalms are also entitled “of the degrees,” in which these virtues are taught, by which the blessed ascend to the heavens. Fifteen is three times five, because through faith in the Holy Trinity we must fulfil works of charity with our five senses.

The first rung of this ladder is patience, in which the eternal wisdom of God teaches that souls are to be possessed. [Col. 0870D] We set our foot firmly upon this rung if we patiently endure injuries and insults for Christ’s love, since he patiently bore reproaches, scourges, and death itself for us, and grants the rewards of abiding glory to those who imitate him.

The second rung is kindness, through which the worthiness of fellowship with angels is obtained. We place our step upon this rung if we repay evil not with evil but with good, and graciously provide our neighbours, according to our ability, with what they need; for Christ also repaid his crucifiers’ evil with good—namely, eternal life—for his Passion, and grants this also to his imitators.

The third rung is piety, through which the sweet fullness [read: “fellowship”] of the citizens above is gained. A devout mind ascending on this rung rises beyond envy at another’s happiness. For “through the devil’s envy death entered into the world” (Wis. 2), and those who belong to his party imitate him.

The fourth rung is simplicity, through which one enters into the abundance of heavenly joy. We set foot upon this rung if we do not act perversely, that is, deceitfully: if we withhold nothing from the service of faith, and do good not for the favour of people but for God’s cause alone.

The fifth rung of this ladder is humility, through which angelic exaltation is attained. The ascending mind is made firm upon this rung if it is not puffed up by the knowledge it has received (1 Cor. 8), and remembers that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (1 Pet. 5).

The sixth rung is contempt for the world, through which the wealth of the heavenly kingdom is acquired. Upon this rung the glorious soul rejoices if it is not ambitious, because “the mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6). But if the Lord should be pleased to say, “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14), let it not refuse to undertake the light burden of the Lord (Matt. 11), so that it may benefit [Col. 0871C] its brethren by word and example.

The seventh rung is voluntary poverty, in exchange for which abundance of glory and riches is received in the house of the Lord (Ps. 3). A person fixes his footsteps on this rung if he seeks not what is useful only to himself, but what is useful to all and pertains to Christ’s praise. Let such a person ascend joyfully, because “God has prepared in his sweetness for the poor” (Ps. 67).

The eighth rung is peace, the torch of eternal light. The mind is strengthened upon this rung if it is provoked by no one either in word or deed; if body and soul are subjected to God’s service; and if the soul, in harmony with the spirit, continually serves the Lord God. Those set upon this rung are called blessed, because they “shall be called sons of God” [Col. 0871D] (Matt. 5).

The ninth rung is goodness, through which one enters the joy of heavenly life. A person climbs this rung if he not only does no evil, but does not even think it.

The tenth rung is spiritual joy, through which one reaches the fellowship of angels. Let a person rejoice that he has climbed this rung if he does not rejoice in iniquity (1 Cor. 13), if he does not rejoice at an enemy’s ruin or at evils happening to another, but rejoices with the truth (ibid.), that is, with all things done for the honour of Christ’s glory—Christ who is truth, the reward of life, and the full joy of all.

[Col. 0872A] The eleventh rung is endurance, through which the eminence of heavenly glory is gained. The soul undertakes to climb this rung if it bears every adversity of the world for Christ. Those established upon this rung are described as blessed if they suffer persecution for righteousness, and thus inherit the kingdom of God (Matt. 5).

The twelfth rung is called faith, which makes human beings fellow citizens with angels. A person presses his foot upon this rung if he faithfully believes everything devoutly spoken or written concerning God and eternal life, because it is impossible to please God without faith (Heb. 11).

The thirteenth rung is that [addition: “to which”] hope is joined, which does not put to shame those awaiting spiritual things. The holy [perhaps add: “soul”] raises its feet to this rung if it hopes for every good thing from the future life.

[Col. 0872B] The fourteenth is long-suffering, through which equality with angels is obtained. Whoever climbs this rung shall attain it if he bears all God’s promises with evenness of mind; if he carries God’s burden until he himself comes and shakes the yoke from his neck, making him cease from labour and recline in rest.

The fifteenth and final rung is perseverance, through which the green meadows of paradise’s delight are possessed. Let the mind seeking high things rejoice that it has reached this rung if it never falls away through despair of God’s mercy. For “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 24). Whoever rightly climbs through all these rungs, God, who is charity, brings him into [Col. 0872C] the storehouses of eternal sweetness.

This [read: “these”] ladder, beloved, is raised through fear; charity, brought through it to the summit, is itself introduced into the inheritance as a son of the Lord. But fear, like a servant, is cast out (1 John 4). There are two fears: one servile, the other filial. A servant who sins fears his lord lest he be condemned; [a] son fears his father lest he be disinherited. Through servile fear let us turn away from sins, lest we fall into the punishments of dreadful torment; through filial fear let us mourn past sins, lest we be deprived of our Father’s grace and eternal joys. Through these fears, and through hope joined to charity, let us love God and eternal life; and through charity let us do every good work, that we may possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance [Col. 0872D] (Ps. 82).

Charity surpasses all virtues; indeed, all virtues proceed from it as branches from a tree, and all tend toward it as paths toward a road. This is the royal way which alone leads people from the exile of this misery into the city of the heavenly homeland. If anyone performs good works without charity, he labours in vain. Even if he possesses every virtue without charity, he is like someone carrying dust found in the wind [perhaps: “into the wind”]. For Scripture says: “If anyone speaks all tongues, both human and angelic, and says all good things to all, but has not charity, he shall be like bronze or a cymbal sweetly sounding” (1 Cor. 13). Then it says: “If anyone is endowed with prophecy, distinguished by knowledge of all mysteries and skilled in knowledge [Col. 0873A] of all things, and upheld by such faith that he can move mountains from place to place, but lacks charity, he is accounted as nothing before God” (1 Cor. 12). Again it says: “If anyone distributes all his possessions as food for the poor and gives his very self over to the fire of martyrdom, yet charity is not in him, it profits him nothing” (ibid.).

Charity is divided into two, namely love of God and love of neighbour, as the Gospel says: “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matt. 22). These are the twin wings by which the saints are raised to heaven, as the prophet testifies: “The saints,” he says, “shall take wings like eagles and shall fly” (Prov. 23). Therefore, as a bird cannot raise itself into the air without two wings, so no one can fly to heavenly things without two [Note: [Col. 0873D] The manuscript reads: “without without two,” etc.] commandments. Thus [Col. 0873B] the ten commandments of the Law were written on two tablets. On one were three pertaining to the love of God, whom we are commanded to love with all our heart, all our mind, and all our soul (Matt. 22). These were: “God is one; you shall not make a graven image” (Exod. 20), and this pertains to the Father. Then: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain”—that is, “You shall not swear falsely” (ibid.)—and this pertains to the Son. Next: “Sanctify the Sabbath day” (ibid.), which we Christians now do on the Lord’s Day; and this pertains to the Holy Spirit, in whom we shall have eternal rest when we cease from work and see God as he is, face to face (1 John 3).

In the other tablet, however, were contained the seven commandments by which love of neighbour is fulfilled, whom we are commanded to love as ourselves [Col. 0873C] (Matt. 22).

Three and four make seven. The soul has three powers: memory, understanding, and will. The body consists of four elements. Therefore, with the same love by which soul is joined to body, it is right that we be joined to our neighbours. Thus it is written: “Honour your father and mother. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness. You shall not covet your neighbour’s property, nor his wife, nor anything that is his” (Exod. 20). Beloved, none of you wishes to suffer these things; therefore let no one do them to another, and so let him know that he fulfils the law of Christ, which is charity.

Charity is compared to a tree transplanted beside streams of water, whose leaf shall not fall, and which shall never cease to bear fruit (Ps. 1). The root [Col. 0873D] of the tree, fixed downward and made firm in the earth [Note: [Col. 0874D] The manuscript reads: “fixed earth.”], is love of neighbour, extended toward friends and enemies. What grows and rises upward, however, signifies love of God. The branches issuing from it on every side are the various virtues proceeding from charity. The leaves which adorn the tree are good will, by which the community of the faithful is adorned. This leaf shall not fall, because each person shall receive a reward from God for good will. The fruits of this tree are good works. The seed in the fruit from which another tree is born is preaching, by which the hearer is fed and a branch is grafted onto the tree of charity to bear fruit. This tree shall never cease to bear fruit, because charity never grows weary of good work. It is planted beside streams of water because through the flowing waters of the Scriptures we are taught how charity is fulfilled. Therefore all God’s commandments are fulfilled through charity alone, and nothing is of value that is done without it.

You ought, beloved, to know how to perfect love. Love does not consist merely in greeting people, giving them a kiss, or wishing them a good day. Love of neighbour is perfected in two ways: first, that you do to no one what you refuse to suffer from another (Tob. 4); second, that each of you should do for others whatever you want people to do for you (Matt. 7). None of you wishes to suffer theft, adultery, or any injury; do these things to no one. You want necessities to be supplied to you by others: provide them likewise, if you can. If anyone possesses this world’s goods and sees his brother in Christ suffering need, but closes his heart against him, how does God’s charity remain in him? [Col. 0874B] (1 John 3). Such a person is like the fig tree that had no fruit but leaves only, and therefore, cursed by the Lord, immediately withered (Matt. 21).

Because this love occupies the ground fruitlessly, the axe of God’s wrath is laid to its root, so that a tree not bearing good fruit may be cut down and cast into the fire (Matt. 3). Therefore, beloved, let this love consist in providing your needy neighbours with necessities: food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, lodging to wanderers, and the comfort of visitation to the sick, captives, widows, [Col. 0874C] and orphans. Even to enemies of your religion, Jews and pagans, if they ask you, provide necessities for God’s sake. For whatever you give to a Jew for Christ’s sake, you shall receive its reward from Christ in Peter’s place.

To instruct us in these commandments, God created in us various members; and those that lack honour are more necessary. “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12). If a thorn is driven into the foot, immediately the back bends to pull it out; the eyes look carefully; the hands hasten to remove it. We Christians are all one body, whose head is Christ (Col. 1). The eyes are teachers, showing the path to the light of eternal life; the ears are those obeying the word of life; the nostrils distinguish good from evil; the mouth teaches good things; the hands defend churches, widows, and orphans; the feet feed the poor. Therefore, since we are members of Christ and of the Church, we ought to provide one another, as for our own members, with necessities according to our ability and to grieve over their sufferings. In this way love of neighbour is proved, the love which “works no evil” [Col. 0874D] (Rom. 13).

Love of God is to hold God dearer than all the glory and riches of this world. To love God is to keep his commandments. Then we love the Lord above all things if, urged by threats or blandishments to act against God’s commandments, we first lose offices, glory, and finally all possessions, and even give our bodies over to diverse torments of death, rather than depart from the Lord’s commandments. This is what the martyrs did, and therefore they came triumphantly to God, who is charity. They too were human beings like us, capable of suffering; yet neither tribulation, distress, persecution, hunger, danger, nakedness, sword, death, life, principalities, powers, things present, things to come, strength, height, depth, nor any creature could separate them from God’s charity [Col. 0875A] (Rom. 8). Therefore they have deserved to enjoy God’s great sweetness now. One comes to this great abundance of God’s sweetness through charity, which is the fulfilment of the Law (Rom. 13).

The Gospel also relates [Col. 0875B] that when the Lord was approaching Jericho, a certain blind man sat begging by the road; he asked the Lord not for money but for light, and immediately obtained it (Luke 18). Jericho means “moon,” and signifies the waning of our mortality. The Lord approached it when he assumed the flesh of our mortality. This blind man represents the whole human race, which did not know the light of eternal life. The gracious Lord, who is the true light (John 1), illuminated it with the light of faith and knowledge, and called it from darkness into his marvellous light (1 Pet. 2).

Beloved, on Wednesday you should assemble more frequently at church, confess your sins [Col. 0876A] to the priests, receive penance from them with your whole heart, place ashes upon your heads, and thereby remember that you are ash and dust. Then, for forty days, by fasting, keeping vigils, praying, abstaining from carnal desires, and persisting in good works, mortify your body for Christ and offer yourselves as a living sacrifice to God. If you thus crucify your flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5), in the future resurrection you shall reign with Christ; for “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Rom. 8).

A certain rich man, entangled in many crimes, renounced the world and entered a monastery, becoming a monk. There he refused honours offered to him, willingly bore reproaches and every adversity for Christ, and devoted himself frequently to prayer with tears. [Col. 0876B] One night, as he lay prostrate in prayer, an immense light flashed from heaven over him, and moreover a voice sounded, declaring that his sin had been forgiven. O immense mercy of our Creator, who did not forgive this man’s sins secretly but silently, but consoled him by flashing light and sounding voice, thereby urging us to repentance! Therefore, while we can, let us all hasten with our whole heart to repentance, and while it is permitted, let us come before the Lord’s face in confession (Ps. 94), so that one day we may joyfully see him in that great sweetness which eye has not seen (1 Cor. 2), and so forth.

## At the Beginning of the Fast

[Col. 0875]

[Col. 0875C] “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55). Beloved, God must be sought in this life, and in this life he must be invoked. Those who seek him in this life by faith and works shall find him after this life in gladness and exultation. But there no one finds him who does not seek him here by holy conduct. Here indeed he is near to all who call upon him in truth. There he shall be far from all who walk here in vanity. The Lord himself teaches through prophecy how he must be sought:

“Let the wicked forsake his way,” that is, his evil life; “and the unrighteous man his thoughts,” that is, his evil desires; “and let him return to the Lord,” through confession and repentance, “and he will have mercy on him,” through forgiveness, “and to our God,” by amendment to a better life, [Col. 0875D] “because he is abundant in pardoning” (ibid.): freeing from punishments and giving the reward of eternal life. To forsake evil undertakings and do good works is to seek the Lord. To persevere in good work to the end is to find God, who is eternal life. The same Lord teaches through the same prophet how he must be invoked.

“Break your bread for the hungry,” he says. “Bring the needy into your house. Clothe the naked” (Isa. 58). Forgive one who sins against you. “Then you shall call, and the Lord shall hear; you shall cry, and he shall say, ‘Here I am’” (ibid.). [Col. 0876C] At all times, most beloved, but especially in these days, seek the Lord by living well, “and your soul shall live” (Ps. 118). Invoke him by praying without ceasing, and he shall give you eternal joys.

Scripture cries out, stirring us to future good things: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance” (Rev. 2). In paradise we were amid every delight; but alas, through the devil’s cunning we fell from there into this pit of misery. Immediately a sorrowful sentence struck us, which compelled us all, alas for grief, to undergo death and return to dust. Therefore, afflicted in penitence today, we put ashes on our heads because we mourn that we are reduced to the dust of death. And because we incurred death through tasting the forbidden food, we now afflict ourselves with fasts, so that abstinence may open for us the entrance to [Col. 0876D] the tree of life which desire for the forbidden tree had closed.

For the wretched human heart, infected with many miseries, has grown numb amid miseries, hardened, and lost the sensation of pain. Therefore the merciful and compassionate Lord, the Father of mercies, had compassion on the wretched one and provided for it through many remedies of Scripture. Among them he today soothes the numb heart with the remedy of repentance, and thus admonishes it:

“Return to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning; and return to the Lord your God, because he is gracious and merciful, patient and [Col. 0877A] very merciful, and ready to relent from evil” (Joel 2). But let us hear him himself teaching how we should return: “Sanctify a fast” (ibid.). How? In these days you ought to abstain not only from strangers but even from your own wives; be free from hatred and envy; distribute to the poor whatever is superfluous to you in food and drink; persist continually in prayer; do not avenge an injury inflicted upon you, but rather pray for your enemies; obey God’s commandments in all things, opposing none of his counsels by any wicked deed.

But whoever fasts for quarrels and disputes, and after the meal gives himself over to drunkenness and luxury, the devil, I think, claims such a person as his member—one who consumes no bodily food but feeds on malice and wickedness. As it is written in Tobit, “fasting is very powerful with almsgiving” [Col. 0877B] (Tob. 12), because through fasting the devil is expelled from the soul, while through almsgiving the soul is redeemed from death. “This kind of demons can come out by nothing except fasting and prayer” (Matt. 17). And as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin (Ecclus. 3); it delivers from death and does not permit one to go into darkness.

Therefore, beloved, fast these days with all diligence, that you may overcome the devil who urges vices and desires. Redeem sins by almsgiving; gain the rewards of eternal life by prayers. Wash the baptismal garment from the filth of sins with tears; be clean in holy works. Cease at last from acting perversely. Learn now to do good: namely, help the oppressed, judge justly for the orphan, defend the widow and stranger, rescue the needy and poor from the hand of the oppressor [Col. 0877C] (Isa. 1). Then you shall be a people to the Lord, and he shall be a Lord to you.

Because humankind, departing from paradise, fell into the pit of death, the Son of God, coming forth from the court of heaven, underwent exile for its sake; by signs and miracles he awakened us from the sleep of sloth, and at last restored us to life by his death. Hence it is written: “Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the voice of one admonishing behind your back” (Isa. 30). Christ was our teacher, who taught us the commandments of life. The blessed eyes of the apostles saw this teacher, and their ears heard the words of life, which then became known to the world through preaching and to us through writings. But we, lazy and useless servants, turn our backs upon the face of our Lord when we despise and trample his commandments. Yet he admonishes us rebels from behind, that he may call back those hurrying toward destruction; he gently entreats those unwilling to return, promises life, and kindly embraces those who return, having compassion upon them as sons. [Col. 0877D] Therefore, beloved, since he is our Father and Lord, and we are clay, let us return as servants to the most merciful Lord; let us return as sons to the most loving Father.

When we were expelled from paradise, it was said to us: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3). Therefore, that we may be able to return, today we do penance in ash and sackcloth. For we are dust and ash, and the human being is a worm, the child of corruption. Since we strive to return to our homeland, we know that enemies—that is, demons—beset the road of salvation; therefore we take up spiritual weapons, namely prayer, humiliation, and affliction, so that we may fight against spiritual wickedness [Col. 0878A] and extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked enemy (Eph. 6). When today we make a procession with crosses, we go forth armed, as though to meet enemies in battle. Thus in the litany we invoke the saints to our aid, that we may be able to fight bravely and triumph in the heavenly court.

In the fourth age of the world Solomon built the Lord’s temple in seven years; after its destruction by the Babylonians, it was rebuilt by Jesus the priest in forty-six years [Col. 0878B]. Solomon is Christ; the temple is the Church. This temple is built by Solomon in seven years because the Church is formed by Christ through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. It is destroyed by the Babylonians because it is overthrown by demons through various vices; but it is rebuilt by Jesus in forty-six years because in these forty-six days the Church is built together into God’s temple. For from the present day until Easter forty-six days are counted.

The temple of Christ’s body was likewise built in forty-six years, and the Church is incorporated into it. Mary was twelve years old when she bore Christ; Christ was thirty-three years old when he fell in death. These years together make forty-six; and there are just so many days from the beginning of the Fast until Easter, on which day Christ restored the temple [Col. 0878C] of his body, which the violence of the Jews had previously destroyed. Therefore we begin the fast on Wednesday, because we proclaim that Christ began his fast on Wednesday. We know that he was baptized on Monday, and we desire to be incorporated into him through fasting. We imitate Solomon, who in the fourth age of the world built the temple as a figure of the Church, in which we now desire to be built together by Christ.

Therefore there is fasting during these four days, because the Church is gathered from the four regions of the world into the building of God’s temple. Then there is fasting for forty days, because through the four Gospels and the ten commandments of the Law this temple is made complete in Christ, for he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it (Matt. 5). Thus the letter X, which is the first in the name of Christ, signifies ten, indicates the Decalogue of the Law, and represents the form of the cross, upon which Christ, hanging, paid all our debts to God the Father for us.

Therefore, most beloved, let us imitate Christ as dearly loved children. Let us follow his footsteps that we may see him in glory. And because Scripture says, “A person heaps up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it” (Ps. 38); because the foolish and senseless shall perish, leaving their riches to strangers, while their graves shall be their houses forever (Ps. 48); because humanity shall inherit worms, beasts, and serpents: let us despise all earthly things, seek heavenly things, and now discipline our bodies by fasts, vigils, and prayers, that in the future resurrection we may reign eternally with the Lord of glory, where “eye has not seen nor ear heard” (1 Cor. 2), and so forth.

## Sunday in Quadragesima

[Col. 0879]

[Col. 0879A] “Zion, flee, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon” (Zech. 2). Zion, which means “watchtower,” is the people of the faithful, who shall behold the King of glory in heaven. Babylon, however, whose name signifies “confusion,” is this world, set in the confusion of sins. Its daughter is the whole company of the wicked, most wretched because its own iniquity shall be repaid to it. Therefore, beloved, we are Zion, dwelling with the daughter of Babylon. The Holy Spirit exhorts us through the prophet to flee from her lest we perish utterly with her.

When Lot learned that Sodom was to be overthrown, he immediately fled from it to the mountain to be saved. After he left it, the city with all its people perished by fire and sulphur (Gen. 29). Had he remained in it, the conflagration would certainly have involved [Note: [Col. 0879D] The manuscript reads “into the conflagration.”] him in destruction with the others [Col. 0879B]. No one doubts that this world shall be dissolved by fire, and that every people clinging to it in heart and mind shall be destroyed with it in a violent tempest. For Christ, the heavenly king, shall come to Jerusalem with the whole army of angels and saints, overthrow this Babylon utterly, and cast all its lovers into the lake of fire and sulphur; but he shall rescue his bride, who is a pilgrim among the Jews, and lead her into the heavenly palace.

Therefore, beloved, just as Lot fled from Sodom to the mountain to be saved, so let us, while it is permitted, flee from this world to Christ the mountain through pure confession and true repentance, that we may escape the fires of eternal punishment and be able to attend the wedding of Christ’s bride. [Col. 0879C] Those who have this gift from God should leave the world and everything belonging to the world, offer themselves and all that they possess to God, that they may receive a hundredfold and eternal life in return (Matt. 19). But those who lack this gift should at least abandon sins and the allurements of the flesh, flee to Christ through repentance, and so become sharers in the perfect.

If there were, beloved, some market where you heard that one hundred gold coins were given for one copper coin, all of you would run there with the greatest haste; you would judge those who neglected to run to be wretched and insane, and you would assail with curses those delaying. For the most worthless and perishable things, which we unwillingly lose daily, which the deceit of thieves takes from us, the violence of robbers snatches away, a devouring flame sometimes consumes, and finally cruel death violently tears us from—for these things, I say, inestimable riches are promised to us, incomparable glory shall be given us; and yet, burdened—or rather blinded—wretches that we are, we neglect those things which, once obtained, we could never lose.

Holy Scripture urges us to run for these things: “Run,” it says, “that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9). And the Lord in the Gospel [Col. 0879D]: “Run while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12). By light life is understood; by darkness, death. Therefore while we live and are healthy, let us run to repentance and satisfaction, lest death’s darkness come upon us and we wish to do so but cannot.

Let no one say to himself: “I am still flourishing in youth and strong in health; therefore I can still enjoy the joys of the world and the pleasures of the flesh. But when I am old, or begin to grow ill, then I shall be able sufficiently to amend my life. God is merciful and ready to relent from evil (Joel 2), and as he forgives one crime, so he forgives many.” This thought, beloved, the devil sends to a person in order to bring him into the habit of sinning and thus, overtaken by sudden death, drag him with himself into hell to be tormented. Therefore Scripture says: “My son, do not delay from day to day to turn to the Lord, lest his wrath suddenly come and destroy [Col. 0880B] you” (Ecclus. 5). For mercy and wrath are from him: if a person delays, death does not delay. Again: “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the time of your affliction comes” (Eccles. 12).

Therefore, beloved, in the time of youth, while we are healthy and able to sin, let us correct sins through repentance, lest in the time of affliction—that is, old age or sickness—we wish to do so but cannot. Hence the sweet and righteous Lord, who gives the law of repentance to offenders on the way, thus gently entreats those abandoning him: “Return to me, returning children,” he says, “and I will return to you and receive you” (Jer. 3). Behold, beloved, God’s gracious clemency calls us children and calls us back from flight from him and haste toward eternal punishments, that he may give us the joyful delights of sweet life.

[Col. 0880C] Therefore, while it is permitted and we are well able, let us all come before the Lord’s face in confession (Ps. 94), because just as original sins are forgiven in baptism, so actual sins are forgiven through confession. Therefore, just as no shame restrained us from committing sin, so let none call us back from confessing our guilt. For confession is God’s judgment, through which a person is justified. There are two judgments of God: one in this age, the other in the future.

In the future judgment, God shall be judge, the human being defendant, and the devil accuser. The sentence pronounced by the judge upon the guilty is: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). But in this judgment, the priest, Christ’s vicar, is judge; the person who is guilty is also accuser; and the judge’s sentence is the penance imposed. Therefore whoever is judged in this judgment is not condemned in that one. Hence it is said: “If we judged ourselves, we certainly would not be judged” [Col. 0880D] (1 Cor. 11).

Therefore, beloved, whoever perishes, perishes through his own negligence, since the prophet says: “There shall be an open fountain for David, for washing the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13). David’s fountain is the mercy of almighty God. Everyone washed in this fountain from filth shall be saved eternally. David the king and prophet committed adultery with the wife of his faithful soldier and killed that soldier by wicked counsel; but when he washed himself in this fountain through repentance, he retained his royal dignity and did not lose the grace of prophecy. Peter, who denied the Lord with an oath (Matt. 26), when he washed himself in this fountain with tears, was not deprived by the Lord of the honour of apostleship.

Paul, who cruelly persecuted the Church (Acts 9), when he washed himself in this fountain, deserved to become a teacher of the Church.

Cyprian, who had been a magician and long committed many terrible crimes, when he cleansed himself in this fountain, became a bishop, shone as a renowned teacher in a glorious life, and underwent an illustrious martyrdom.

Theophilus, who denied God in writing and enslaved himself to the devil’s dominion [Col. 0881B], having been washed in this fountain, escaped the devil’s legal claim.

Mary Magdalene, who defiled herself with many impurities (Luke 7), after washing herself in this fountain with tears, deserved to be the first to see the risen Christ (John 20).

Mary of Egypt, who for many years had been a common prostitute for all the people, washed in this fountain, afterward shone with glorious signs.

Thaïs, notorious for her crimes and devoted to every kind of filth, when she is washed in this fountain, obtains both forgiveness of her sins and the crown of life. And why should I recount more? All who from the beginning, having fallen away, returned to repentance—if they were washed in this fountain—obtained forgiveness. It lies open to all. It receives all, cleanses all from filth, and no one’s uncleanness defiles it. Hence it is said that it is open even to menstruating women, with whom no uncleanness can be compared. By this we are taught that no sin is committed by anyone which is not removed by this fountain for one who repents.
