If this fountain were shut up, we ought to strive with all our strength that it might be opened to us. But now, since it stands open to all, why do we wretches neglect our salvation (fo. 84v) and refuse to wash away our filth in this fountain? For the merciful Lord says: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.” And lest anyone delay to turn to him, he promises through the prophet: “At whatever hour the sinner turns, all his sins shall be committed to oblivion” (Ezek. XXII). He did not say after a week, or after a month, or after a year; but in that same hour in which he groans, they are forgiven him.

Hence we read that a certain holy man had [read: had] this grace from God: that he could discern the merits of individuals by their faces. One day, therefore, while the brethren were attending church, he saw them entering with cheerful countenances and shining faces, and the angels of God joyfully accompanying them. But he saw one man with an ugly, deformed, and clouded face; demons of dreadful appearance walked beside him, breathing fire and smoke from mouth and nostrils, and each drew him with a chain, while the angel of the Lord followed far behind in sorrow. When the old man saw this, he wept with loud lamentation. When the divine office had ended, he again observed them [Col. 0882A] going out with glorious faces and the angels of God proceeding cheerfully with them; and he saw the man whom he had earlier seen entering with such a wretched countenance going out with an exceedingly radiant face, with the angel of God clinging to him in embrace, while the devil followed far behind with his chain. Seeing this, the old man rejoiced; and, summoning them all, he related everything that he had seen before and afterward. When they asked him to disclose his deeds to them, the man said: “Until now I have lived in uncleanness; but today, having entered the church, I heard the reading concerning repentance, and immediately promised God that I would never again commit the same evils.” Hearing this, they gave thanks with joy, saying: “For he is good, for his mercy is for ever” (Ps. CXVII).

Behold, dearest brethren: as soon as this man promised God an amendment of life, he found mercy from him. Therefore bear fruits worthy of repentance (Matt. III), that you may obtain the pardon of divine clemency. Let one who has sinned in thought and has looked upon a woman in order to lust after her hasten to abolish this through confession, so that God may raise up his soul as he raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, dead in the house (Mark V). But let one who has fallen in words and devised some evil wash this away through confession and prayer, so that the Lord may command him to rise from deadly sin, as he commanded the widow’s son, borne outside the gate, to rise (Luke VII) (fo. 86). And let one who has departed from God in deeds redeem this more swiftly by fasting and almsgiving, so that the Lord’s mercy may raise him up, like Lazarus stinking from the tomb of crimes (John XI). Let none of you despair of God’s mercy because of the multitude of his offenses, when he hears that pardon was granted to the Ninevites after a three-day fast.

Nineveh was a great city, having a journey of one day in breadth and a journey of three days in length; more than one hundred and twenty thousand people lived in it. All of them lived so wickedly that the Lord intended to overthrow them, together with their city, as he had Sodom. Yet he sent his prophet beforehand to foretell its imminent destruction, so that through repentance they might escape the danger. But the prophet, fearing that his words would become an object of ridicule—because he knew that, if they were converted, the Lord would not overthrow the city—entered a ship, declining God’s command. Therefore the Lord stirred the sea with winds and storms and nearly engulfed the ship in waves. When the men realized that shipwreck threatened them, [Col. 0882D] they cast lots, discovered the prophet, and threw him into the waves; immediately, when the storm ceased, calm and serenity returned. But a great fish swallowed Jonah, in whose belly he travelled for three days. After the third day, at the Lord’s command, it vomited him out upon dry land opposite Nineveh. He hastened into the city, crying in a loud voice that Nineveh would be destroyed after three days. Therefore the king and all the people were converted in terror: they cast themselves in ashes, clothed themselves in sackcloth, and afflicted themselves with fasts and vigils for three days. When the Lord saw the labor of their repentance, he changed the severity of his sentence (Jonah I–III).

Behold, dearest brethren: through a three-day fast an innumerable people escaped God’s judgment. By this the Christian people are taught that, if one person were enveloped in as many crimes as all of them together, and turned to God with his whole heart, he would obtain pardon through a three-day repentance; for “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI). For the guilty, through repentance, suspend the avenging right hand of God, and in a manner violently seize through confession the kingdom of heaven which was not due to them. Therefore these days have been instituted so that we may cleanse ourselves by prayers and endeavor by fasts to make satisfaction to our Creator for our sins; for by these two things enemies are overthrown, vices conquered, and demons expelled. Amalek, whom the people could not overcome by arms (fo. 86v), Moses overthrew by prayers (Exod. XVII). When the apostles could not cast a demon out of a certain man, the Lord cast it out and began to say to them: “This kind is cast out by nothing except fasting and prayer” (Mark IX). To instruct us in fasting, the Lord fasted forty days and overcame the devil who tempted him by means of the Scriptures, and freed us from his temptation. After this angels came and ministered to him as God (Matt. IV).

When Moses had led God’s people out of Egypt and pitched camp beside Mount Sinai, Mount Sinai burned up to heaven, and from the midst of the fire God commanded the ordinances of the law while all listened. Moses, however, went up the mountain and remained there with the Lord, fasting forty days. He received from God the law written on tablets; coming down from the mountain, he found that the people had made and worshipped an idol. Inflamed with zeal for the Lord, he threw down and broke the tablets, and commanded that as many as twenty thousand of the people be slain. He went up the mountain again, abstained from food for forty days, and merited both to receive the law and to obtain pardon for the people. Moreover, his face shone with such glory that the people could not look upon him because of its brightness (Exod. XIX–XXXV).

Jezebel the queen killed the prophets of God and sought to kill Elijah. He fled into the wilderness, received food from an angel, remained forty days without food (III Kings XIX), and after this the Lord carried him into heaven in a fiery chariot (IV Kings II).

Daniel, when he abstained for twenty days, merited visions and conversations with angels; and, cast into the lions’ den, he overcame the lions and moreover received food from a prophet at an angel’s command [Col. 0883D] (Dan. VI). John the Baptist, while he devoted himself to abstinence, merited to baptize the very Savior of the world (Matt. III). But these and very many other saints fasted for eternal life, and after fasting were all glorified. How much more ought we to fast for our sins, that we may escape the dreadful punishments of eternal death. Yet then our fast will be acceptable to our God: if, abstaining from food, we also endeavor to fast from vices and sins, and cheerfully distribute to the poor whatever food and drink is left over to us. For whoever fasts from food but not from sins imitates the devil, who, though he continually abstains from bodily food, never ceases to commit evil.

The Apostle says, as we heard today [Col. 0884A] (fo. 88): “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation: giving no offense to anyone, but in all things let us show ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience, in vigils, in many fasts, and in unfeigned charity” (II Cor. VI). Whoever neglects the acceptable time now and loses the day of salvation now will have after death no acceptable time for repentance, nor a day of salvation, but a day of condemnation.

Dearest brethren, these forty days are the Christians’ *carina* [Lenten period]. For we commit many things in the year which call for this *carina*, and therefore the Church has ordained that we should fast this forty-day period for them. It is also the tithe of our life. For, just as from other things, so also we ought to give a tithe of our days. The year consists of three hundred and sixty days; and when, in this forty-day period, excluding Sundays, we fast for thirty-six days, we pay, as it were, the tithe of our days. The law likewise is completed in ten commandments; the year turns through four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—and man is composed of four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. Therefore, if with the four qualities of our body during the four seasons of the year we have sinned against God’s ten commandments, it is just that we make satisfaction to our God during these four times ten days. We do this near the Passion of the Lord because, “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.” But I wish you to know, beloved, why the forty days were instituted.

When God delivered his people from Pharaoh’s yoke, he led them through the wilderness for forty years. He rained upon them the bread of heaven, which contained every delight. He brought forth water from the rock, which provided the taste of honey and oil; their garments were not worn away by age nor stained by filth, and there was no sick person among their tribes (Ps. CIV).

At night the angel of the Lord went before them in a pillar of fire and drove away from them the terror of night. By day he protected them in a cloud from the heat of the sun (Exod. XIII). After forty-two encampments they entered the promised land. If you reckon one day for each year of the forty years as a tithe, you will calculate forty days. These are the forty days observed by the Christian people, whom the Lord redeemed from the oppression of the devil and nourishes through observance of the ten commandments and the four Gospels—that is, with his own body. He brought forth blood from his side as water from the rock [Col. 0884D]. That rock was struck twice with a rod: that is, Christ’s flesh was fastened to the two beams of the cross (fo. 88v). This drink gives the taste of honey and oil, because with the oil of mercy he heals the wounds of our sins and with the honey of eternal sweetness he satisfies us. And if the garments which we received in baptism are not worn away by vices or defiled by sins, then in the night of this dark life he will go before us with the fire of the Holy Spirit, while on the day of judgment he will protect us by the cloud of his humanity from the heat of eternal fire. From today until holy Easter forty-two days are reckoned. If we observe them by living soberly, justly, and devoutly, we shall celebrate the Lord’s Easter with rejoicing among God’s people; and as they entered the promised land through forty-two encampments, so we shall enter the joy of eternal exultation.

Therefore we ought to cleanse ourselves from sins by confession and prayer, make satisfaction to God by tears and fasts, and redeem them by alms, as the Lord says: “This is the fast which I have chosen: break your bread for the hungry, and bring needy wanderers into your house.”

We read that in the promised land three cities were established, to which those who happened unknowingly to kill a person had to flee; in these cities the relatives of the slain person were not permitted, though pursuing them, to harm them (Deut. XIX). These three cities, dearest brethren, are confession, almsgiving, and prayer. Hence the third city is called Heliopolis, that is, “City of the Sun,” because one who prays continually speaks with God. Therefore, since knowingly and unknowingly we kill ourselves in many ways, and through evil examples give our neighbors over to death, let us flee to these cities with all our effort and escape the punishments we deserve.

As we shall read tomorrow, the Lord will come in his majesty with all the angels and will gather all nations before himself [Col. 0886A]. He will place the righteous at his right hand and set the wicked at his left like goats. Then he will say to those at his right: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; thirsty and you gave me drink; naked and you clothed me; a stranger and you received me; sick and in prison, and you visited me.” Then he will also say to those at his left: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you did not give me food; thirsty and you did not give me drink (fo. 90); naked and you did not clothe me; a stranger and you did not receive me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me.” “And these shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV). Therefore, dearest brethren, while the Judge waits, let none of you neglect his salvation. Let us all run to repentance at this time, lest we then fall into punishment with those at the left; rather, may we deserve to enter the Lord’s joy with those at the right and glory without end in his praise, which “eye has not seen” (I Cor. II), and so forth.

## SECOND SUNDAY IN LENT

[Col. 0885]

[Col. 0885B] “Be quickly reconciled with your adversary while you are with him on the way” (Matt. V). This life, dearest brethren, which we live is a certain road by which we journey toward our homeland. For as many days as we spend here, so many stages, as it were, do we travel. On this road our adversary is the divine word. For when we burn to carry out anger or hatred, it says to us: “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX). When we desire to fulfill the uncleanness of the flesh, it says: “You shall not commit adultery” (ibid.). When we covet others’ goods, it says: “You shall not steal” (ibid.). When we devise evils against our neighbors, it says: “You shall not bear false witness” (ibid.). Therefore, because it opposes us in all our desires, it accompanies us on the way like an adversary. Let us quickly agree with this adversary, lest perhaps by accusing us it hand [sic] us over to Christ the Judge, and the Judge to the officer—that is, the devil—who may cast us into prison, that is, hell; for we shall not depart from there until we have paid the last farthing (Matt. V), that is, until we receive punishments even for the least sin.

For we subsist from four qualities, and therefore we must pay God four farthings: from fire, the fervor of charity; from air, the keenness of intelligence; from water, the cleansing of baptism and tears; from earth, the devotion of due service [the repeated *debite* is deleted]. But this last farthing perverts the other senses through fleshly impulses and draws them into unlawful deeds. For from fire it produces rage; from air, pride; from water, the flow of lust; and earth yields from itself the appetite for worldly desires. We are compelled to pay this farthing in prison, when we are forced to expiate earthly works in eternal punishments.

Therefore, dearest brethren, it is fitting for you during these days to come frequently to church, to listen with attentive ear to saving admonitions, to pray for yourselves and for all the people, and to avoid everywhere—yet especially in church—fables and empty talk (fo. 91v), since “for every idle word which people speak they shall render an account to God on the day of judgment” (Matt. XII). For many attend churches—something I am compelled to say with groaning—for whom it would be much better to remain at home.

When the Lord was preaching, crowds gathered to him with differing intentions. Some came because of the teaching of heavenly life, which flowed sweetly from his mouth; some because of healing, because he cured every sickness; some because of want, because with five loaves he easily satisfied five thousand people; some because of the greatness of his signs, because he gave sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, and life to the dead; some because of envy, that they might ridicule his words and turn his works to evil. So today very many flock to church: some to hear the divine office and words of life; some to confess their sins and pour out prayers to the Lord; some to converse with friends; others to lay snares for enemies; some to be seen splendidly dressed; others to talk with little women; others to ridicule God’s words and obstruct God’s work. These come sent by the devil: because, while he is occupied elsewhere, he sends them ahead so that through them he may lay snares against God’s work. But just as Christ did not cease to proclaim heavenly things to Peter and the apostles, though he knew that these tormented Judas and the Pharisees, so we ought to speak beforehand of everlasting joys to God’s children who long for their homeland, though we know that the messengers—indeed, the children—of the devil are tortured thereby.

For it was commanded in the law that little bells [*tintinnabula*, sic] should be woven into the priestly garment, so that when he entered the tabernacle their sound might be heard and he might not die (Exod. XXXIX). A garment woven with bells is the life of priests supported by preaching. For if they proclaim to the people the kingdom of God and his righteousness, they save their own souls. But if they hide righteousness and the people die in iniquity, their blood is required from the priests’ hand, as though they had killed them (Ezek. III).

There is a beast called the panther, beautiful with various colors. It enters the forest, feeds on diverse herbs, and then, standing upon a rock, gives forth a cry; and the whole multitude of beasts runs around it. The dragon alone flees. Then it breathes out a sweet odor and heals every sickness (fo. 92). By this beast are signified priests distinguished by many virtues. They ought to enter the forest of Scripture, be filled with diverse sayings as with herbs, then stand upon the rock, Christ, by good works, summon the people from every side, and then breathe out the wholesome fragrance of Scripture, heal the sick of their diseases by the remedy of the tongue, and drive the dragon, the devil, away from them.

In these days, dearest brethren, we discontinue *alleluia*, which is a melody of joy, and sing the tract, a song of sadness, because we must be sad here for our sins, so that we may someday rejoice with the angels. For this reason veils are now hung in churches, by which the secrets of the sanctuary are hidden from the people: heavenly things are hidden from us on account of sins, but through repentance are opened to us.

We read that Jerusalem was surrounded by a triple wall, and that Nebuchadnezzar, with the aid of six kings, took it by assault; he killed some inhabitants and carried others away to Babylon. Some who fled into a tower situated in the middle of the city were saved.

Jerusalem is the people of the faithful, surrounded by a triple wall: faith, hope, and charity. Nebuchadnezzar—that is, pride, the chief vice—attacks them in battle with the other six vices: envy, hatred, vainglory, avarice, gluttony, and lust. He destroys the walls, that is, faith, hope, and charity. He kills the inhabitants when he overwhelms believers in mortal sins. He leads others into Babylon when he drags those dead in sins down to hell. But the tower of the city is the protection of confession. Therefore, let every believer whose walls of virtues have been destroyed hasten to the tower of confession, lest he perish at the hands of the Chaldeans, that is, the demons.

We also read today in the Gospel that, when the Lord withdrew to the region of Tyre, a Canaanite woman cried to him for her daughter, grievously tormented by a demon, and immediately obtained her daughter’s healing (Matt. XV). Tyre is this world, to whose regions the Lord withdrew when he put on our flesh. The woman who came out from those borders is the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Her daughter, tormented by a demon, is any soul occupied by vices. She is healed when her mother prays: that is, when the converted soul is cleansed from vices by prayer. For the merciful Lord came to seek those who had perished from the house of Israel—that is, the company of angels—and to lead those found back into their fellowship (fo. 92v). Therefore, dearest brethren, sanctify the fast, that you may deserve, as sharers in his Passion, to possess with the angels the joy of eternal banquets.

Honor your prelates and all your elders; support from your own resources your parents worn out by old age or poverty. For the examples of birds urge us to perform these things.

For we read that an eagle, when it grows old, is fed by its young until it is renewed to its former youth.

Likewise, it is said that the bee-eater (*merops*), when old, is nourished by its young. The stork also, burdened by old age and stripped of its feathers, is covered round with its young’s wings and refreshed with continual food. And if birds perform such things, how much more fitting is it that human beings should fulfill them? Redeem yourselves by alms from the danger of sins and punishments, because “almsgiving is good with fasting. It delivers from death and cleanses sins” (Tob. IV, XII); moreover, it does not permit one to go into darkness, but through it eternal life will be given [the text reads *dabit*, “will give”].

Tabitha, indeed, full of good works and alms, was restored to life while widows and orphans wept. For when they showed the garments which she had made for them, Peter immediately restored her to life (Acts IX). Behold, dearest brethren, how powerful alms are. For they not only deliver from death, but even raise one from bodily death.

Tobias likewise, who had lost the light of his eyes for four years, received it again through alms and fasts when the angel visited him (Tob. II, XI).

We read of a certain tax collector who had never given alms to any poor person. One day, while the poor were discussing among themselves [perhaps *dissererent*, “were discussing”] how many good things this man and that man had bestowed upon them, one of them asserted that he would presently receive alms from that tax collector, although the latter, though very wealthy, had never shown them any kindness. Each of them staked, according to his means, that he would receive at least some very small thing from him. The man immediately ran to the tax collector’s house and with insistent cries asked for alms. At that hour bread was being placed upon the table by the servants. When the tax collector, filled with fury, looked around to see whether perhaps a stick or stone might offer itself to his wrath, to throw in the face of the shouting man, in anger he seized a wedge-shaped piece of bread and threw it into the mouth of the crying poor man [Col. 0888D]. The poor man embraced it and returned joyfully to his companions, displaying the piece of bread which, he recalled, he had received from him (fo. 94).

Not long afterward that same tax collector was struck with a severe sickness and brought to his last extremity. Demons immediately gathered about him and, while he watched, recounted all his evil deeds. When angels were present and asked his guardian for his good deeds, he said that he had never wished to give his consent to anything good, except that one day, in anger, he had thrown a piece of bread at a poor man, which he had now brought with him. The angels received the piece of bread from him and divided it into tiny crumbs. When the demons placed the heavy weights of his sins in the balance, the angels put in a crumb which outweighed them. They did this until the crumbs outweighed the demons’ weights. But the demons cried out that an injustice had been done to them, protesting that their own servant was being forcibly taken away. The matter was referred to God’s judgment; but at the angels’ prayers he was permitted to return to life. He immediately recovered from his illness, gave thanks to God’s immense mercy, and afterward every day bestowed countless alms upon all the needy.

One day he met a poor man and immediately clothed him in the costly garment which he himself wore. But the poor man wished to sell it. When the tax collector saw the garment hanging among merchandise for sale, he became sad; returning home, he wept, and so fell asleep from sorrow. The Lord Jesus appeared to him clothed in that same garment and asked why he was weeping. He replied: “Because what is given by us unworthy persons to your servants, they deem unworthy to wear. That man preferred the garment [for sale].” “See,” he said, “the garment which you gave covers me.” When he awoke, he declared the poor blessed, among whose number the Lord affirmed that he was. Immediately he sold all his property and distributed everything to the needy. Moreover, he commanded his servant to sell him [Col. 0890A] and distribute to the poor the money received for him. He scarcely compelled the servant to do this; the servant sold him to merchants and, as he had requested, shared the money with the poor. But he, once sold, served his master faithfully and gave his daily ration to those in need. He himself was content with bread and water. At last he became renowned for glorious miracles, he who had already merited the starry kingdoms.

Therefore, dearest brethren, since almsgiving thus delivers from every evil and so powerfully raises a person to heavenly things, let all practice it according to your means; hasten to lay up your possessions as heavenly treasures (fo. 94v). Let no one say that he has nothing to give. Good will is accepted from him, since the Judge promises a reward for a cup of cold water (Matt. X). And from one who lacks material goods to give, good will is accepted. Therefore make for yourselves poor friends from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings (Luke XVI), where are joys “which eye has not seen” (I Cor. II), and the rest.

## THIRD SUNDAY

[Col. 0889]

[Col. 0889B] “The Lord will speak peace to his people and to his saints, and to those who turn to heart” (Ps. LXXXIV). Because, dearest brethren, we have drifted away through unlawful desires, we have withdrawn far from our Creator and departed far from the heart. Therefore the Lord, offended by our evils and provoked to anger, said to us in wrath: “Return to the heart, transgressors” (Isa. XLVI). And because through confession and repentance we have returned to the heart, and now desire to make satisfaction through fasts and alms, he will therefore speak peace to his people, when he promises them pardon and the reward of life. “Let your eyes cease from weeping,” he says, “and your voice from sobbing, because there shall be reward for your work” (II Ps. XV). He speaks peace over his saints when he promises that they will be crowned with glory and honor (Ps. VIII). “You,” he says, “are those who have remained with me in temptations” (Luke XXII); “I shall render to you the reward of your labors.” He is also said to speak peace over those who turn to heart because he declares that he will no longer remember their names with his lips (Ps. XV).

Their names were these: thieves, robbers, fornicators, adulterers, unclean persons, drunkards, liars, inventors of evils. God no longer wishes to remember these names; but, when they have been washed in the fountain of tears and sanctified by alms, they deserve to be called by another name by him. For those formerly called incestuous by their own merit are now called chaste by grace; those formerly proud are now humble; those formerly harsh are now merciful; those formerly filthy are now called holy. These names are written in heaven; the Lord will not erase them from the book of life.

But because Christians now wage war against vices and demons, our enemies sharpen their weapons more cruelly, rise more fiercely against those who resist them, and attack more savagely those who renounce them and their service. Now they sow discord in God’s camp; now they embitter with anger, disturb with hatred, and hasten to draw people back from the path they have entered by fleshly desires [read: *a coepto*, “from the path begun”]. But (fo. 96), when Christ’s soldiers take refuge in the weapons of prayer [Col. 0890C], they overthrow all the enemy’s devices. “Resist the devil in faith,” says the Apostle, “and he will flee from you. Draw near to God through good works, and through grace he will draw near to you” (Jas. IV).

The Lord relates that a certain man sowed good seed in his field; but at night, while people were sleeping, an enemy sowed tares over it. After the seeds had risen in the blades of grass, the tares appeared as well. Seeing this, the servants asked their master how the tares had grown, since he had scattered good seed. He answered that an enemy had done this. When they wished to uproot them, he forbade it, lest perhaps they should pull up the wheat with them; he allowed both to grow until harvest, when at harvest-time he would tell the reapers: “Gather the tares into bundles for burning, but gather the wheat into my barn” (Matt. XIII).

The man who sowed good seed in the field is the Lord, who scattered heavenly teaching and virtues in the world. The enemy who, while people were sleeping, sowed tares over it is the devil, who introduces vices away from faith and good works. The servants who wished to uproot them are the prelates of the Church, who desire to separate the evil from the good. But the Lord forbids this, lest perhaps the elect be condemned together with them. Especially since very many appear before human beings, and their works may please in the judgment of the inner Judge; and many whom human judgment chooses as good are rejected as evil by the inward scrutiny. But the Lord wishes them to be mingled here, so that the good may be exercised by the evil and deserve a more abundant reward for patience. There will never be an Abel whom Cain’s malice has not tested. There will never be one blessed with Shem who is not mocked by Ham. There will never be a Joseph loved by his father against whom the hatred of his brothers does not rage. There will never be a David who obtains the royal scepter and has suffered no persecution from Saul. But at harvest-time the reapers will gather the tares and bind them into bundles for burning, because at the judgment the angels will separate the evil from the good and join thieves with thieves, robbers with robbers, cruel persons with cruel persons, envious persons with envious persons, and unclean persons with filthy persons in the punishments due to them. But they will gather the wheat into the barn when they place the elect in the joys prepared for them [Col. 0891B].

We read today in the Gospel that a certain man possessed by a demon was also blind and mute. The Lord cast the demon out of him and restored sight and speech (Luke XI). This man signifies the human race, which demons besieged while it served idolatry; it lacked sight when it did not see the light of faith. It was deprived of voice when it was mute in the praise of God. From it the Lord expelled the demon when he destroyed idolatry. He opened its eyes when he poured the light of heavenly grace into human minds. He restored the office of the tongue when he opened mouths mute in God’s praise for heavenly songs.

But after the demon’s expulsion, terrible is what the Lord says: “When an unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it goes through dry places seeking rest; and, finding none, it says: ‘I shall return to my house from which I came out.’ And when it finds it empty, it takes with itself seven worse spirits; and, going in with them, it will possess the whole as though by its own right. And that person’s latter state will be worse than the former” (Luke XI).

When any person casts out sins through confession, the unclean spirit goes out from him. It goes through dry places because it tempts holy people, in many ways, with worldly desires. But because they do not consent to it, rest is not granted to it in them. Hence it returns to the house which it left; and when it finds it empty of devotion to good works, it takes with itself seven worse spirits—that is, the seven principal vices—and invades with all wickedness the heart empty of the Holy Spirit. Then that person’s latter state will be worse than the former, because whoever returns after confession to the habit of sins is like a dog returning to its vomit.

Therefore, beloved, guard yourselves continually from sins; listen with attentive ear to God’s words and endeavor to fulfill them with a devout mind, because blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it. Flee the bitter-sweet service of the worst master—or rather, the oppression of the most cruel tyrant—and with your whole heart take up the sweet yoke and light burden of the most merciful Lord (Matt. XI). Take refuge beneath the wings of your Father, the most kindly Lord, who not only receives those who turn to him but also grants everlasting joys. For the wandering son who squandered all his substance with prostitutes, who, driven by hunger and want, returned to his father to be made equal with hired servants, he clothed after washing with the finest robe and a ring; he refreshed him with a feast prepared from the fattened calf, and, though the elder son was unwilling to enter, he made him heir (Luke XV).

This son is the Gentile people, who expended the substance of their intelligence and perception in the worship of idols. Driven by hunger for God’s word, they returned to God the Father through the preaching of teachers. He received them kindly, washed them in the bath of baptism, clothed them with the garment of virtues and the ring of faith, and gave them the calf for a feast, because he promised to have his own Son slain for them to eat; when the Jewish people refused to enter into faith, he made the Gentiles heirs of the kingdom of heaven. In order that we may strive with all our might toward this inheritance through our own labors [Col. 0892B], we ought to take examples from tiny worms.

For the ant works with all its strength throughout the summer, so that it may have food in winter. So we, dearest brethren, while we have time, should do good to all (Gal. VI), because in its season we thereby obtain eternal life.

The bee also gathers from diverse flowers and makes nectar for a sweet drink and wax for light. So let us gather sweet words and deeds from the writings and examples of the saints, offer our neighbors the cups of preaching, and possess the light of eternal life.

Silkworms also labor with great diligence to make silk and adorn the world with surpassing beauty. So let us adorn our souls with beautiful deeds [the text reads *decoribus actibus*], that we may reign with the King of glory.

The spider likewise toils with all effort over its web, even wearing out its life in labor. So, while opportunity remains, let us weave garments of virtues through good works, so that we may appear not naked but clothed (II Cor. V) before the angels on the Lord’s day. And, dearest brethren, that the Lord’s mercy may become sweet in our minds, let us draw sweetness from the salvation of Thaïs.

### Concerning Thaïs
She was a prostitute of great beauty, and widely notorious for her crimes. Because of love for her, very many were wounded daily and many were frequently killed. When one of the Fathers, named Paphnutius, heard of her, he grieved over her destruction; changing his clothing, he came to her as though for fornication. She led him into a dark chamber. But he asked to enter a still darker room. She said: “If you are ashamed before people, no one will come in [fo. 98v] by whom you may be seen. But if you fear the face of God, there is no place where you can hide from his eyes.” Then he said: “Do you believe that God exists?” When she answered that she did believe, he asked whether she believed in the kingdom of heaven prepared for those who live chastely, or doubted that the punishments of hell awaited the unchaste. When she said that she faithfully believed all these things, he said: “If you believe all this, why were you not terrified to plunge so many souls into the abyss, for all of whom, together with your own soul, you must [Col. 0893A] render an account to God?”

Hearing this, she was frightened; trembling all over, she threw herself weeping at his feet, renouncing what was past and promising to avoid what was to come. As he departed, he marked out a place and commanded her to come there after him. Then she had all her money—gold, silver, and gems—and her various household possessions brought by the hands of her boys and girls into the middle of the street; she kindled a fire and, before everyone, threw everything into it, saying: “Come and see how I give to the flames what I have gained from you by the filth of impurity.” [Note: [Col. 0893D] Manuscript: “gained,” masculine.] After this she came in mean clothing to Paphnutius on the mountain. He shut her up in a tiny cell within the dwelling of religious women, and arranged that bread and water should be given her daily at appropriate hours.

When she asked him [Col. 0893B] how she ought to pray, he said: “Take care not to raise to the Lord hands polluted by many filthy acts. [Note: [Col. 0894D] Manuscript: “polluted,” masculine.] Do not take the name of God upon lips polluted by kisses; but, prostrate upon the ground, repeat this often in your heart: ‘You who formed me, have mercy on me.’” After she had patiently spent three years in this penitence, Paphnutius, moved with pity for her, went to the mountain of Antony and asked whether she had obtained pardon. Antony had such merit before God that whatever he asked from God he immediately received.

[Col. 0894A] Antony summoned his disciples, made Paphnutius’s request known, and instructed them to persist all night in prayers and vigils. And behold, at midnight, Paul, one of his disciples, fell into ecstasy and saw heaven opened. In it he saw a bed gleaming with gold and gems, guarded by radiant virgins. When he said that this glory could have been prepared for none but his master, he heard those virgins resounding with heavenly harmony: “This is not Antony’s glory, but that of Thais, once a prostitute, but now [fo. 100] the virgin bride of Christ the Son.”” Returning to himself, he told the brothers all that God had revealed to him concerning her. They gave thanks to God, because he saves all who hope in him.

Paphnutius then came to her, ordered her to leave the cell, and told her that her sins were forgiven. She asked to remain enclosed from then on. But after she left at his command and received the Lord’s sacrament, her face shone like the sun, and she happily sought the heavenly things. You, whole assembly of the people, hope in him who thus mercifully saves sinners and so graciously glorifies converts; pour out your hearts before him, and act here in the lake of misery and valley of weeping so as to please God in the light of the living. “What eye has not seen” (1 Cor. II), and the rest.

## SUNDAY IN MID-LENT

[Col. 0893]

[Col. 0893C] “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and keep festival, all you who love her” (Isa. LXVI). The divine office, beloved, which we sang today warns us not to hunger only after earthly and perishable things, but to direct our minds toward our heavenly mother, Jerusalem. For it says: “Rejoice, Jerusalem.”

Jerusalem, which means “vision of peace,” is the Church that shall see Christ, eternal peace, in heaven. The prophet exhorts her to rejoice, because they are to be made glad in joy with the countenance of God. All who love her are also commanded to keep festival, because at the feast of the angels they shall see the face of the Lord in jubilation (Job XXXIII). Those who until now have been sorrowful because of sins are likewise urged to rejoice in gladness, so that [Col. 0893D] they may exult in pardon and be satisfied from the breasts of her consolation (Isa. LXVI).

By the breasts of the Church are understood the two Testaments, by which her children are nourished with the milk of the letter and allegory. The Jewish people suck one; the Christian people suck the other. They suck the letter; we, allegory. Milk is given from one breast when the Law consoles us thus: “Hear, Israel, the commandments of the Lord, and write them in your heart as though in a book; and I shall give you a land flowing with milk and honey” (Deut. IV), that is, the paradise of delight overflowing with every sweetness. From the other breast milk is drawn for us when the New Law promises us thus: “When Christ appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see God as he is” [Col. 0894C] (1 John III).

The prophet promises us milk from the old breast when he makes this promise: “They shall hunger no more nor thirst any more; neither shall the sun nor heat strike them, because he who has mercy on them shall guide them and give them drink from the springs of the waters of life [fo. 100v]” (Isa. XLIX). From the new breast the evangelist draws milk for us, when he says that the Lord promises us this: “The righteous shall shine like the sun” (Matt. XIII), “and shall be equal to angels” (Luke XX). From one we suck: “They shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and groaning shall flee away.” From the other we draw: “Eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. II).

Hasten with all your strength toward these joys, beloved, so that you may abound in delights from the Church’s every glory. Her glory will then be complete when, placed in the pasture-ground [Col. 0894D] of life, she lacks nothing. This glory is expressed when it is said through the prophet: “Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace and like an overflowing torrent of glory” (Isa. LXVI). O how blessed are those toward whom the Lord turns an abundance of peace like a river, and upon whom every glory streams like an overflowing torrent!

Today we read to whom this glory is granted by grace and from whom it is withheld on account of merit. “Abraham,” he says, “had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman” (Gal. IV). But the slave woman is cast out with her son, while the free woman obtains the inheritance with her son (ibid.). Abraham signifies God the Father; Hagar, the old law; Ishmael, the carnal people; Sarah [Col. 0895A], the new law; and Isaac, the Christian people. Thus the Law, observed carnally, is deprived of the Lord’s inheritance together with the Jewish people; but the Church, established under grace, is enriched with the kingdom of God together with the Christian people.

Abraham also signifies our spirit; the slave woman, our flesh; and her son, carnal works. The free woman signifies the soul, and her son, spiritual works. Therefore, as Sarah afflicted Hagar when she despised her, and commanded Ishmael—who was driving Isaac into danger of death—to be cast out (Gen. XVI), so the soul, which is mistress, should afflict with fasts and vigils its slave woman, the flesh, when she despises it. It should cast out her son who persecutes the son—that is, the carnal work that hinders the spiritual work—and should bear the son of the mistress, that is, a good work, which may receive the joy of the Lord’s inheritance [Col. 0895B].

We read also that the Lord crossed the sea and went up a mountain, and a very great multitude came to him from every side. He distributed to the crowd five loaves and two fish received from a boy, and satisfied five thousand men, besides little children and women. He commanded that the fragments left over by those who had eaten be collected, and they filled twelve baskets; seeing this, the crowds gave thanks to God (Mark VI).

By the sea [fo. 102] is understood this age, continually battered by countless storms of adversities. The Lord crossed it, because while living here he committed no sin. He went up the mountain when he ascended into heaven at the right hand of the Father. The crowd flowed around him from every side when the preaching of the apostles drew the people from every part of the world to faith in him. They are refreshed by five loaves because they are instructed in the faith through the five books of Moses. Two fish are added when psalmody and prophecy are handed on to the faithful. The loaves are described as barley loaves because, just as barley is enclosed in husks, the books of the Law are wrapped in many mysteries. The boy who carried them and did not eat [Col. 0895C] them is the Jewish people, childish in wisdom, who did not understand the sense of the Law. But Jesus broke the loaves and distributed them to the crowds when he opened to the faithful the meaning for understanding the Scriptures. Those reclining upon the grass are satisfied because only the humble are judged worthy of the Lord’s nourishment.

By the five loaves are also understood the Scripture and examples of the Fathers who lived in the five ages, by which the faithful are daily abundantly fed. In the first age Enoch refreshes us with the bread of writing, when he writes that the Lord shall come to judgment with thousands of saints. He satisfies us with the bread of example, when Scripture records that he pleased God because of righteousness and was carried off into paradise.

In the second age bread is ministered to us through Abraham, who is said to have discovered Hebrew letters, written down events from the beginning, taught astronomy in Egypt, and obeyed God in all things. In the third age we are abundantly refreshed through Moses, when we are instructed by his writings in the Ten Commandments; he is testified to have been the meekest of all men, and is described as having shone with many signs.

In the fourth age David, Solomon, and nearly all the prophets [Col. 0896A] satisfy us with sweet bread, when they instruct us through mystical writings and deeds.

In the fifth age Ezra satisfies us with bread, when he restores the burned Law and rebuilds the destroyed Temple. These loaves are distributed to the crowds when teachers mystically expound their writings and deeds to the faithful. The two fish likewise signify two offices, namely those of king and priest, which alone in the Old Testament were anointed with holy oil. But Christ caught the faithful, hidden like fish in the salt sea of the world, through the net of faith cast by the apostolic fishers, and caused all to be anointed with the oil of chrism [fo. 102v] as kings and priests. For the white garment received in baptism signifies priesthood, and the mitre placed on the head signifies the royal diadem.

[Col. 0896B] Five thousand men are fed because those who have manfully fulfilled with their five senses faith in the Holy Trinity and the two works of charity are nourished by Christ’s body. For five is divided into three and two: through three is understood faith in the Trinity, through two the operation of twofold charity. Those whom this number consecrates, Christ refreshes at his banquet. But by the little children and women are denoted heretics, who partake with us in the Lord’s sacraments. Yet because they are excluded from this number, they are not admitted to the Lord’s inheritance. The twelve apostles filled twelve baskets with the fragments of those who ate when, in the sixth age, they expounded by their teaching the writings of the earlier ages. A basket is woven from slender wicker, and the apostolic order was chosen from humble stock. It gathers the remnants [Col. 0896C] of those who eat: it dispenses the letter to ordinary people and reserves mystical meanings for the wise.

Therefore, beloved, when the crowds have been refreshed, praise God for the benefits bestowed. Prepare yourselves for his nourishment with all purity of heart and body, because chastity alone frees people in dangers and reconciles penitents to God.

For Joseph, because he was not subdued by lust, was freed from prison and moreover raised as ruler over all Egypt. Daniel, because he loves chastity, was unharmed by the savagery of lions when twice cast into the den; indeed, royal power raised him above princes.

Susanna likewise, because from love of chastity she did not violate her husband’s bed, not only escaped the hands of wicked [Col. 0896D] judges, but also consigned those false accusers—convicted by Daniel’s just sentence—to their deserved punishment.

Judith, the holy widow, by loving chastity and despising the honor and wealth of a noble-minded ruler, rescued the people of God from the danger of imminent death. Moreover, having killed the tyrant, she rejoiced in victory and triumphs to this day, worthy of praise from every mouth.

A monk named Malchus, when he was captured by Saracens along with many others, was assigned by lot to one man together with the captured wife of another man. His master entrusted to him a flock of sheep to tend and gave the woman to him in marriage. But, even when [fo. 104] compelled by his master, he was never joined to her because of his love of chastity. After some time, he fled with that same woman [Col. 0897A], but their master pursued them with a servant and camels. Out of fear they sought a cave, in whose depths a lioness was nursing her cubs. Their pursuing master ordered the servant to drag them out of the cave to be killed, while he remained outside holding the camels with drawn sword. The servant entered with his sword bare, but was immediately seized by the lioness and torn apart before the eyes of the terrified pair. When the master, angered by his delay, followed him, he immediately met the same end. Having done this, the lioness carried out her cubs and, departing, offered the place to the trembling fugitives. They mounted the camels, went away, and made known everywhere how powerful chastity is.

A certain woman caught in adultery was brought before the Lord for judgment; but after her accusers had been confuted, she was allowed to depart unharmed (John VIII). Therefore, beloved, [Col. 0897B] serve the Lord in holiness and righteousness, and he will deliver you from all the cruelty of your enemies. I wish, most beloved, to make known to your love an event by which the sloth of the negligent may be horrified and the mind of those who serve devoutly may therefore be made glad.

A certain man, distinguished by birth and wealth, died. A large crowd of relatives and his whole mourning household attended his funeral throughout the night; but at first dawn the dead man returned to his body. All who were present, turned to astonishment and amazement, fled. He hurried to the church and remained prostrate in prayer until nearly midday. Upon returning, he divided all his property into three parts: one he gave to his wife and children, one he distributed to the poor, and one he bestowed on the brothers in the monastery in which he made himself [Col. 0897C] a monk.

When asked what he had seen, he reported this: “The one leading me was radiant in garment and face. As we went toward the north, there was on the left a valley of immense depth, excessive breadth, and boundless length. One side burned with a vast fire; the other was frozen in horrible cold. In both parts souls languished under punishments, now leaping from fire into cold, now from frost into flames. Seeing this, I began to think that this was hell, of whose unspeakable punishments I had often heard. But my guide answered my thought, saying that this was not hell.

“As we went farther on, everything before us began to grow dark [fo. 105v], and through black shadows we seemed to sink, as though descending, into deeper regions. And behold, a great pit appeared before us, which belched forth sulphurous masses from its flame-vomiting mouth, then drew them back in and swallowed them. An intolerable stench also rose from that furnace and filled everything around it. Then suddenly my guide disappeared and left me alone amid this dreadful sight. While I stood there fearful and trembling, not knowing where to turn my steps [Col. 0898A] or what end awaited me, suddenly a pitiful cry arose behind me, where a multitude of souls was being dragged along by demons: the souls were lamenting mournfully, the demons mocking cruelly and hurling them with cackling laughter into that abyss. Meanwhile, hideous spirits emerged from that abyss, breathing foul fire from mouth and nostrils, and sought to seize me with fiery pincers. But as soon as my guide arrived, they hurled themselves headlong into the same pit with dreadful bellowing.

“He immediately freed me from fear and darkness and led me into the clear light of the eastern region. There another wall rose before us, having no entrance and reaching to heaven. When we came there, there was a most delightful field, conspicuous for every loveliness, more brilliant than daylight, planted with fragrant flowers and full of sweet scent. In it bands of people clothed in white rejoiced, singing a sweet hymn. I began to think that this was the kingdom of heaven, of whose unutterable joys I had often been told. But he answered my heart that this was not the kingdom of heaven.

“As we passed beyond those places of the blessed, still more splendid things appeared before us. Behold, an immeasurable light shone before us with the greatest radiance; from it blazed the sweetness of a marvelous fragrance, and the harmony of a most sweet concert resounded. This glory was such that all which I had earlier seen seemed altogether small. When I hoped that we were about to enter it, my guide turned back and, arriving at the place of those who rejoice, said to me: ‘Do you know what the things you have seen signify?’ When I answered that I did not [Col. 0898C], he said: ‘The valley dreadful with heat and cold is the place prepared for those who defer repentance for their sins until the end of life. Because they flee to repentance at death, they escape the punishments of hell. But because they are not corrected here by satisfaction [fo. 106], they are purified in these punishments, and are then freed by Masses, almsgiving, and the prayers of the faithful, and joined to those whom you see. But those who die without repentance are immediately plunged into hell, from which they are never freed for all eternity. That flame-vomiting pit which you saw was its entrance. Those who lead their lives in good conduct come here after death; but those found perfect are immediately brought into the heavenly kingdom, whose entrance is that radiant place you saw. Now you shall return to your body. If you live well, you shall be joined to these.’”

Immediately he returned to this life, and thereafter lived so holy a life that, while his tongue was silent, his life spoke of what he had seen. Therefore, beloved, if you live here soberly, righteously, and devoutly (Titus II), you will one day come to those joys where you may exult forever and God will be pleased to dwell in you—things “which eye has not seen” (1 Cor. II).

If the Chair of St Peter falls on a Sunday, the sermon may be concluded thus:

[Col. 0897]

[Col. 0897D] Beloved, commend yourselves most earnestly to Peter, prince of the apostles, whose feast we celebrate today. Since the Lord made him head of the Church, the Church today set him before her as supreme shepherd in the episcopate. For when the Antiochenes, having expelled Simon [Col. 0898D] Magus, called Peter, and the weak received health and the dead life through his shadow, they appointed him over themselves; and the faithful, who had formerly been called his disciples, were surnamed Christians. Since he has from the Lord the power of binding and loosing [Col. 0899A] and the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XVI), knock upon him with prayers, that he may free you from the bonds of sins and, opening the gates of life, introduce us to the joys of angels [Col. 0900A], which eye has not seen, etc. (1 Cor. II).

If the feast of St Matthias occurs on a Sunday, it is fitting to say this about him:

[Col. 0899]

[Col. 0899A] The intercession of the holy apostle Matthias, whose birthday feast we observe today, can greatly assist our prayers, most beloved. When Judas, one of the Twelve, sold the Lord for thirty denarii, and the Jews bought with those denarii a field for the burial of strangers, unhappy Judas hanged himself in that same field, burst open in the middle, and, spilling out his entrails, paid for the crime of his destruction [betrayal]. In his place Matthias was chosen by the apostles through the Holy Spirit, and the number twelve, consecrated by Christ, was made complete (Acts II). Preaching in Judaea, he converted many to the faith, endured many adversities for Christ’s name, and at last [fo. 106v] fell for the Lord in a glorious death. Since he is one of those who shall judge you at the last day, [Col. 0899B] entreat him with prayers and praises, that then you may deserve to be set at the right hand and to hear the sweet voice, “Come, blessed ones” (Matt. XXV). “What eye has not seen,” etc. (1 Cor. II).

## On St Gregory, Pope

The celebration of the supreme pontiff St Gregory increases for us the joys of this holy day. He adorned his own times with signs and virtues and magnificently embellished the house of God by his words and writings. This blessed man, first a layman, born of noble senatorial rank, was endowed with immense riches. Accordingly, he built seven communities from his own revenues, in one of which he himself became a monk. There, being acceptable to God and men by his holy way of life, he was ordained archdeacon by the Apostolic See and, not long afterward, raised pope of the City. By word and example he illumined the whole Church as the sun illuminates the world by its rays. Thus he had drawn England, devoted to idolatry until that time, to faith in Christ.

Before receiving the pontificate, he used to sit alone writing. One day an angel of the Lord came in the appearance of a shipwrecked man, grieving and asking for assistance; Gregory immediately gave him six gold coins. He returned again and urgently begged for help with importunate cries; the man of God likewise gave him six coins. He returned a third time that same day, tearfully begging assistance, and the man of God gave him a silver bowl. Taking it, he embraced him joyfully and departed glad.

After Gregory had received the pontificate, he fed countless poor people from the Church’s resources not only in the City but throughout the world. He therefore wished twelve persons to be present daily at his table, whom he himself might refresh with his own food. One day thirteen were present, and the thirteenth changed himself into various forms. [Note: [Col. 0899D] Something is missing.] When the table had been cleared, he allowed the twelve to leave but retained the thirteenth with him. Taking him aside, he asked who he was. He replied: “I am that shipwrecked man whom you once comforted with twelve gold coins and a silver bowl. Know that God has appointed the papacy for you as a reward for this.”

“Whence do you know,” he said, “that God has set me over the Church’s [Col. 0900A] episcopate?”

“Because,” he said, “I am his angel, appointed by him as your guardian. Whatever you ask from God, you shall obtain through me, until you stand before the face [fo. 108] which you desire.” Having said this, he vanished from the astonished man’s eyes. Gregory gave immense thanks to almighty God and began to give boundless alms, for which he has today received a hundredfold and eternal life. Beloved, imitate him by almsgiving and good works, so that through his prayers you may deserve to enter into the joy of the Lord, which eye has not seen (1 Cor. II).

## On St Benedict

We must rejoice, most beloved, on today’s solemnity of our most holy Father Benedict. As Lucifer, the morning star, shines—the radiant glory of the stars—so shone this jewel of monks [Col. 0900B]. Born of noble stock, he was sent to Rome for the study of letters; but he despised worldly wisdom and the glory of the city of Rome, loving only the ignominy of Christ’s cross. He left the City and its schools and committed himself to a priest of the Church in God’s service. But his nurse, who clung to his love more closely, came after him alone. She carelessly set down a sieve which had been lent to her, and it fell and broke into pieces. When Benedict found his nurse weeping, he restored the broken vessel to wholeness by prayer. When she hung it before the doors of the church as a sign, Benedict secretly fled, lest he be praised by people.

Proceeding into the wilderness, he encountered the monk Romanus, who afterward became the father of many [Col. 0900C] monks. Romanus gave him the habit of religion and instructed him in the manner of holy life. Romanus’s cell was situated on a mountain, at the foot of which Benedict lay hidden in a cave. Romanus daily lowered bread to Benedict on a rope with a little bell attached. But the devil, envying them both, threw a stone and broke the bell. Benedict then lived the hermit’s life for three years, unknown to people but known to God alone. God himself therefore cared for his champion. After a certain priest had prepared a sumptuous Easter feast for himself, the Lord commanded him to carry it to Benedict. Benedict endured many temptations from the devil, all of which he overcame manfully.

One day the tempter came in the form of a bird, and the breast [Col. 0900D] of the holy man burned with such unlawful love that he almost yielded to desire and left the wilderness. At once he stripped off his clothing and rolled naked among thorns and nettles until all that carnal pleasure was extinguished [fo. 108v]. After this he was appointed abbot of a neighboring monastery. But when he imposed regular discipline upon it, his disciples offered him poison in a drink. When he made the sign of the cross, the glass vessel in the server’s hand shattered as though he had thrown a stone at it in place of the cross.

Leaving them, he returned to the wilderness. When many came flocking to him, he built there twelve monasteries in praise of God. Water failed the brothers established upon a mountain, but Benedict drew a spring from the rock by prayer; because of his merit it flows down to lower ground to this day. In one monastery, too, a brother could not remain standing at prayer because the devil, in the form of a little Ethiopian, pulled him out of the choir by his clothing. Benedict struck the devil, standing outside, with a rod; and the devil fled crying out as though he had received the blow.

While one brother was cutting brushwood with a sickle, its iron blade slipped off and fell into a lake. But when Benedict extended the handle into the lake, the iron floated like wood and of its own accord fitted itself onto the handle.

A boy drawing water also fell [Col. 0901B] into the lake, and immediately was drawn from the water to a height equal to an arrow’s flight. Benedict at once perceived this in the spirit and sent Maurus to rescue the boy. Maurus later became renowned as father of many monasteries and performer of many miracles. Wonderful thing! Sent by Benedict, Maurus ran over the water as over solid land, grasped the boy’s hair, and swiftly carried him with him to shore. Looking back, he was astonished that he had walked over the waters. The boy, however, said that he had seen Benedict’s melote, or sheepskin cloak, draw him from the waves.

As by these and many other brilliant signs he shone like a lamp in the world, and the splendor of his brightness could not be endured by the envious, a certain priest began to be greatly stirred by envy, seeing Benedict’s glorious reputation spreading farther and farther every day [Col. 0901C]. Because he wished to possess Benedict’s praise but would not imitate his life, he began to disparage him before some people and to turn away from visiting him those whom he could. But when he saw the proclamations of Benedict’s virtues increasing everywhere more and more, and many people, leaving the world, being inflamed by his example toward conversion to a better life, he arranged to send him, through his servant, bread prepared with poison—thinking, unhappy man, to extinguish the lamp of the Church by his death [fo. 110].

A raven used daily to come from the forest to Benedict’s table and, after receiving bread from him, depart. Benedict therefore received the sent bread with thanksgiving and, throwing it to the raven, commanded it to carry it into a wilderness where it could not be found by a human being. The raven, long and greatly reluctant, circled the bread with croaking; at last it lifted it and carried it into the woods. After two or [Col. 0902A] three hours it returned and ate its usual bread from Benedict.

The mad priest, seized by fury, could not take the life of him whom God guarded as the apple of his eye beneath the protection of his seal. He therefore attempted to drive the souls of Benedict’s disciples over the precipice of destruction. He commanded seven shameless girls to dance naked before the cell of the man of God, so that, on seeing them, the younger brothers might be enticed by lusts from their resolve and fall upon the slippery path of luxury. Benedict saw them and knew that this was being done because of him. Having appointed an abbot there, he left the place, humbly avoiding his rival’s envy.

But that wretched priest, minister not of Christ but of Satan, was standing on his upper floor and rejoicing at Benedict’s departure when suddenly the floor collapsed and crushed all his limbs piecemeal [Col. 0902B]. Benedict wept most bitterly over his ruin and moreover imposed penance on his disciple who rejoiced at his fall. As ravens flew before him from the forest and seemed to point out the way to their fosterling, he came to Monte Cassino, where there was an ancient temple of Apollo. Having removed every defilement from it, he dedicated a church in honor of almighty God and built a monastery, gathering many brothers to Christ’s praise. As a good shepherd, he led them by words and examples to the pastures of life. Throughout his whole life he gave himself to fasts [“but in Lent only twice,” etc.] and vigils; in Lent he refreshed his body with food only twice or once in the week [Col. 0902C], and at all times either devoted himself to reading or persisted in prayer.

After he had long illumined the unworthy world by these and such glorious deeds, today he passed from the prison-house of the flesh to the heavenly palace amid the rejoicing of angels. As he departed, heaven was opened to his disciples. Into it stretched a most beautiful road, laid out with innumerable cloths and lamps; a radiant man stood upon it and said that Benedict was seeking heaven by this road [fo. 110v]. Therefore, beloved, sanctify in your hearts the Lord Jesus, who glorifies those who glorify him. Commend your souls and bodies to him by fasts, vigils, and almsgiving, so that through Benedict’s prayers you may escape the final curse and inherit the blessing which eye has not [Col. 0902D] seen (1 Cor. II), and the rest.

## ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF SAINT MARY

[Col. 0901]

[Col. 0901D] “Let him who hears say: Come” (Rev. XXII). Scripture commands us, beloved, to make known to you what we understand concerning God and eternal life, and to invite you to hasten there with us.

This day is counted among the chief feasts because the beginning of the whole Christian religion is shown to have arisen from it. On this day the world, ruined by sins, was restored to life by Christ’s Passion. On this day John the Baptist was beheaded; on this day James, brother of John, was likewise beheaded. On this holy day Christ’s Incarnation was announced by the angel to the Virgin, as today is devoutly celebrated by the whole Church.

It is read that on the day and at the hour when the first human being was created in the paradise of delights, the Son of God was also conceived as the new human being in the Virgin’s womb. For she was the paradise of apples, the fountain of gardens, because in her the tree of life rose up and from her flowed the fountain of wisdom; she abounded in every delight, and in her were hidden all treasures of wisdom and knowledge [Col. 0903A] (Col. II). It is also handed down that at the hour when Adam ate of the forbidden tree, Christ, hanging on the tree of the cross, drank vinegar with gall; and at the hour when the Lord expelled humanity from paradise, Christ brought the thief into it. The Church teaches that all this happened today. Therefore the Blessed Virgin Mary, through whom it happened, is magnified today.

For when our first parents had abounded in the delights of Paradise, and, at the devil’s offering, had drunk the cup of death, and all the offspring of their succession had lain under the sentence of death for five thousand years, God took pity because that malignant plunderer gloried that he possessed the whole human race as though by hereditary right (fol. 112). Against the draught of death thus offered to humankind through a woman at the devil’s instigation, he prepared the antidote of life, received from the human race through a woman at an angel’s ministry; and the woman who brought death into the world drove it away and, moreover, brought life to all. God sent his angel to announce to the Virgin the mystery of eternal salvation, by which he wished to reconcile the lost world to himself, in whom it pleased him to restore all things in heaven and on earth (Col. I). Thus the archangel Gabriel reverently greeted the Virgin, whom he proclaimed would be the Mother of God and Queen of the angels: “Hail,” he said, “full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women. Behold, you shall conceive and bear a Son, and he shall be called the Son of the Most High. He shall be king in Israel, and of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke I).

At these words, immediately [Col. 0903C] she who was blessed beyond the angels, impregnated by the Holy Spirit, the sacred Virgin became pregnant by the Word of God. Then she did not hasten wantonly to licentious women, nor, in the manner of women, arrogantly multiply words among them concerning the gift bestowed upon her; but she immediately and humbly hurried to holy Elizabeth, whom the gravity of her age and the merit of her life had rendered worthy of renown. Elizabeth, now in her sixth month, had conceived—when the same angel announced it to Zachariah—him who was to prepare, for the Lord coming into the world, a way into human hearts, and for this reason had concealed herself for six months. Therefore, when Mary greeted Elizabeth, John leapt at her voice in his mother’s womb, already desiring to burst forth from his enclosure and meet his Lord as he came; already wishing to emerge, as a faithful servant and friend, to embrace the King and Bridegroom.

Then Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, said that all things spoken to the Virgin by the Lord would be fulfilled. Mary therefore remained with her for three months, until Elizabeth bore the Son greater than all the prophets, who was to go before that Son himself in the world as his forerunner and herald (ibid.). Then, having returned to Nazareth, when Joseph observed that she was pregnant, he planned to put her away secretly. An angel appeared to him in a dream, warned him that she was not to be dismissed, and made known that the conception was from the Holy Spirit (Matt. I). When the appointed time had therefore been fulfilled, the star of the sea brought forth for the world the sun of righteousness, who became the light and king of all angels and the life and salvation of all humankind.

[Col. 0904A] The Law had consigned all virgins (fol. 112v) to a curse, as it is written: “Cursed is he who does not bear fruit in Israel.” God wiped away this curse from virgins through the Virgin Mary, when he himself, the author of blessing, came forth from her undefiled womb as a bridegroom from his chamber. He freed barren women from this curse when he willed that John his Baptist should be born from a barren womb.

These things, dearest ones, were formerly prefigured in many ways; these things were variously foretold by the prophets. For Moses saw the bush burning with fire and yet not consumed by the flame (Exod. III). In it the Lord appeared when he delivered his people from Egyptian bondage. This signified beforehand the blessed Virgin, whom the fire of the Holy Spirit illumined with offspring, while the flame of concupiscence did not violate her. From her the Lord visibly appeared, visited the world, and freed the people of the faithful from diabolical bondage.

Aaron likewise, at the Lord’s command, placed a dry rod in the tabernacle; on the next day it flowered and produced nuts (Num. XVII). By this sign the faithful are commended to God, while rebels are refuted. The dry rod that produced a nut is the Virgin Mary, who brought forth to the world Christ, Lord and man. Through him the righteous shall flourish like a palm tree at the end, while the reprobate shall burn in the fire like a dry fig tree. The Lord rained manna from heaven upon the children of Israel and commanded that none of it should be kept for the following day. He wished to give them fresh manna daily; but manna that was kept produced worms. By the manna holy Mary is understood, from whom [Col. 0904C] Christ the worm was born. For he himself says: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI). For a human being is born from the union of man and woman, but Christ is begotten from the Virgin alone, as a worm is formed from the earth’s soil.

Gideon, leader of Israel, spread a fleece upon the threshing-floor, upon which dew descended from heaven, while dryness held the floor. Again, spreading out the fleece, the floor was wet with dew and the fleece lacked moisture (Judg. VI). This was a sign of the victory of the faithful and the flight of their enemies. The fleece drenched with dew is the sacred Virgin, fruitful in offspring. The dry threshing-floor is her untouched virginity. Again, the floor was wet with dew because the Church shone, fruitful in the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Through this sign—that is, through the Virgin’s childbirth—the demons, who are enemies of the human race, are conquered, and the faithful shall be crowned in heaven with triumphant glory. But the fleece lacked moisture (fol. 114), because the Synagogue dried up, barren of spiritual gifts.

The prophet foresaw all this in the Holy Spirit and spoke in these words: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. XI). Jesse was the father of King David, the root of this sacred stock. From this root David grew up like a tree, from which a noble rod sprouted, because the Virgin Mary derived her origin from his lineage. This rod produced a flower when the Virgin Mary gave birth to Christ. For he himself says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II). A field is land not ploughed, and a virgin is one not married. This field [Col. 0905A] produced a precious flower when Christ, born of the Virgin, shone upon the world. This flower was the lily of the valleys—that is, Christ, the adornment of the humble. Upon him rested the Spirit of the Lord, because the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in him (Col. II). The prophet also said: “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” that is, “God with us.”

Ezekiel likewise saw a gate always shut, through which the King of kings alone passed and left it shut (Ezek. XLIV). Holy Mary is the gate of heaven: before childbirth and in childbirth she was a virgin, and after childbirth she remained a virgin.

King Nebuchadnezzar saw a statue whose head was gold, breast and arms silver, belly bronze, [Col. 0905B] legs iron, and feet clay. But a stone cut from a mountain without hands crushed the whole statue and reduced it to dust. It itself grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth (Dan. II). The different metals of the statue signify kingdoms of different powers. The stone cut from the mountain without the hands of cutters is Christ, born of the Virgin without the hands of an embracer. He shall subject all kingdoms to his rule, and he alone shall reign forever.

This Nebuchadnezzar also made a golden statue forty cubits high and six broad, which he commanded all the people to worship. When Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael refused to bend the knee to it and worshipped God alone, the enraged king commanded the furnace to be heated seven times more than usual, and ordered these three men to be cast into it bound. But the fire, by divine power cast forth from the furnace, burned those outside, while it injured not even one hair of those within (fol. 114v); indeed, it loosed their bonds. And they sang a hymn to God amid the flames, with whom the king saw the Son of God (Dan. III). Thus the Holy Spirit, illuminating the blessed Virgin inwardly with his fire, made her fruitful, while outwardly he sheltered her from all concupiscence. Thus the Son of God revealed her also to the Gentiles.

Daniel, by the king’s permission, destroyed the idol of the Babylonians and killed the dragon which they worshipped. Therefore the Babylonians, stirred to anger, cast him into the lions’ den and shut it with a great stone for seven days. The king, however, because he loved Daniel, sealed the stone with his ring lest they kill him. But the angel of the Lord carried the prophet Habakkuk from Judaea with a meal and set him above the lions’ den. He brought food to Daniel within, yet did not remove the seal. On the seventh day the king came and, finding both the seal unbroken and Daniel unharmed, gave praise to God. He drew Daniel out of the den and ordered his enemies to be shut in to be devoured by lions (Dan. XIV). Thus Christ entered the bridal chamber of the womb without removing the seal of virginal chastity, and again, with the seal preserved, the light and glory of angels and humankind came forth from the virginal palace.

[Col. 0906A] The genealogy of this Virgin is woven by the evangelists like a line ending in a hook, at whose end her Son is attached as the hook, when Jesus Christ is said to have been born of her (Matt. I). God the Father fastened this line to the rod of the Cross, on which his Son hung as a hook. Moreover, the bait of this hook was the flesh of Christ, which had been hidden in the sacred Virgin as in a fishing vessel. God cast this hook into the sea of this age and drew Leviathan out of the hearts of the faithful. The bracelet of Christ’s love pierced its jaw, so that an exit might be opened for those whom it had heedlessly devoured. Thus an exit was opened to David through repentance, whom it had devoured through adultery and murder; to Peter through weeping, whom it held in its throat through perjury and denial of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0905D] Rubric in the margin: “On Mary of Egypt.”]; to Mary through weeping [Col. 0906B], who lay hidden in its belly through many filthy crimes.

Through this, the blessed Mother of God saved her namesake, Mary of Egypt.
