Born in Egypt, she came to Alexandria while still of tender age and for thirteen years offered herself as a public prostitute (fol. 116) to all the populace. When the people hastened by ship to Jerusalem in order to celebrate there the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, she entered the ship with the others and without restraint ensnared the souls of young men in the devil’s nets. When they arrived at Jerusalem and people had gathered from every city, she wantonly inclined all whom she could to wickedness and plunged the miserable into the filthy mire of the insatiable devil’s snare.

As the feast approached and the people ran in crowds to the church, she wished to enter the temple with the others, but divine power drove her far from its doors. Repeatedly mingling with the crowds, she tried to enter, but her attempt was frustrated, since again and again she was violently thrust back from the doors. Then, prompted by God’s nod, she recalled the multitude of her crimes, saw an image of Mary the Mother of God painted on the wall, and immediately fell before it in tears, mourning her past sins and promising to avoid them in the future. Rising from prayer, she entered the temple as freely as though she were being drawn in by all those who had formerly driven her away. Having worshipped the life-giving Cross, she went out and again cast herself weeping before the sacred image. Rising from there, she bought three loaves, crossed the Jordan, and remained in the wilderness for forty years, known to God alone.

During the first fourteen years, indeed, with three loaves and wild herbs she sustained a failing spirit rather than restored her body; she endured many hardships of weather, from heat and cold, and many temptations of the devil, especially the fires of the flesh and longings for her former life. But after she had fallen prostrate upon the ground and invoked the Mother of God, she overcame all things courageously. Thereafter, cleansed from sins, she was found worthy to be a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit. By the gift of grace he inwardly enlightened her with knowledge of the Scriptures and foreknowledge of future things, satisfied her with the bread of divine contemplation, gently mitigated outwardly the hardships of weather and the passions of the flesh, and moreover glorified her with splendid [Col. 0907A] miracles.

For a certain monk, while wandering through the wilderness in Lent, seeking whether perhaps someone serving God might be found there, was led by the Lord and encountered her. When she had received a garment from him and covered part of her body, she immediately prayed (fol. 116v), disclosed his name and office, saying that he was called Zosimas and was honored with the priesthood, as she asked his blessing. Astonished, he asked who she was. He learned from her everything: where she came from, what she had done, when she had come there, and how much she had suffered there.

When he asked her to pray for the Church, she arose, stretched her hands toward heaven, and hung suspended in the air by the Holy Spirit. Seeing this, he was terrified and thought her a phantom. But she answered his thought, denied that she was a phantom, and affirmed that she was dust and ashes, clothed in baptism. Besides this, she discussed the Scriptures with him, disclosed to him all the practice of his monastery, recited the names of each of the brothers, and made known in which matters this one or that one ought to be corrected by the abbot. Finally, she foretold that bodily sickness would befall him in the following year, but asked that, after regaining health, he should visit her and bring her the body of the Lord.

Bathed in many tears, he was scarcely torn away from her. Returning sadly to the monastery, throughout the whole year he wasted away from her absence, longing with a thirsty breast to be refreshed by her presence. When Lent arrived, however, he fell into the sickness which that holy woman had foretold. After recovering from it, at the Lord’s Supper he took Christ’s body with him and departed. But she came toward him from afar on the opposite side of the Jordan [Col. 0907C], and, making the sign of the Cross upon the waters, walked over the liquid as though over solid ground. Coming to him, she received from him the Lord’s sacraments, and with hands outstretched gave thanks to God. She asked Zosimas to visit her in the following [Col. 0908A] year.

Again making the sign of the Cross, she crossed the river dry-shod; and the journey which Zosimas had previously made in twenty days, she made in the space of one hour. In the place where he first found her, she yielded her unconquered spirit to the stars. Seeing these glorious miracles, the old man offered praises to him who alone does wonders. When a year had passed, he returned to the wilderness and found her dead. Her lifeless body had lain uncorrupted in the open air throughout that entire year. Grieved by her death, distressed that he had not asked her name, and anxiously wondering whether she wished him to bury her, behold, he saw her name (fol. 118) and the day of her departure written upon the ground, and saw written instructions that he should bury her.

While he turned this over in his mind, behold, two lions came out from the forest, dug the place of burial with their claws, placed the holy body in the grave with the old man, and, their service completed, withdrew into the depths of the woods. Zosimas hurried out to the monastery and told the brothers all that God had revealed to him. Glorifying God, they transferred her body and buried it among themselves with fitting honor.

Behold Mary, who had once, enticed by the song of sirens, long endured shipwreck, at last emerged, escaped danger through the star of the sea, and reached the harbor of salvation. All who followed this star of the sea as their guide arrived at the harbor of salvation. This, dearest ones, is the star of the sea, shining brilliantly in the highest heaven above all the choirs of angels. After her humility and chastity, let all who sail upon the [Col. 0908C] sea of this age direct the vessel of their life, so that through her they may attain the harbor of life, where they may rejoice forever with all the saints, where eye, etc.

## SUNDAY OF THE PASSION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0907]

[Col. 0907C] “Today, if you hear the voice of the Lord, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. XCIV). The divine voice, dearest ones, cries out daily through sacred Scripture; it kindly calls us back when we hasten toward destruction through evil works, and sweetly invites us to the joys of everlasting life. But until now we have hardened our hearts against this voice and refused obedience to it for our own benefit. At least today, opening the ears of our heart, let us hear it obediently; and, opening the door of our mind, let us receive the word of life into the lodging of our heart, so that God may remain in us and we in him.

For without doubt, either God or the devil dwells in a human soul. Whoever has God dwelling within him always burns with love, gladly embraces the words of God, and eagerly strives to fulfill them in works. Of such a person it is said: “He who is of God hears the words of God” (John VIII). But whoever has the devil dwelling within him is always full of envy and hatred, and is reprobate in respect of every good work. Of such people it follows: “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (ibid.). For in the hearts of those who close their ears against God’s words, demons play through uncleanness and wicked desires (fol. 118v).

What is God’s voice? “Be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. XI; 1 Pet. I), and: “I will that where I am, you also may be” (John XVII). Let us hear this voice by sanctifying ourselves from evil works: namely, by fleeing fornication and every uncleanness of the body, and by avoiding women in desire, because “whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V). Let us not kill people either by deed or counsel, nor hold hatred in our hearts. “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer.” Let us neither seize another’s property by theft or violence, nor even desire to possess it, because “covetousness is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. VI). Whatever we neglect to do of God’s commands, or rashly do against them, let us wash away by confession and penitential tears; let us redeem it by alms; let us make satisfaction by vigils and fasts. If we sanctify ourselves in this manner, we shall reign with our God in heavenly glory among the saints.

Because the children of Israel despised hearing this voice in the wilderness, they did not deserve to enter the Lord’s rest. For after their deliverance from hard servitude, after their escape from pursuing enemies, after refreshment with angelic bread and drink from water brought forth from the rock, because they provoked God by murmuring and blaspheming, offended him through fornication and by worshipping idols as God, and moreover hardened their hearts against his signs and warnings, they perished, destroyed by enemies and serpents. Some were consumed by fire; others were swallowed by a chasm in the earth. Only two of the people, with the children of the transgressors who obeyed the Lord’s voice, deserved to enter the land flowing with milk and honey (Num. XXXII).

So also today, those who, after rescue from diabolical servitude, after the remission of sins in baptism, after eating the body and blood, harden their hearts against God’s words, shall not enter the Lord’s rest; rather, enemies and serpents—that is, demons—shall destroy them from life. But those who hear God’s voice in the two commandments of love shall enter the Lord’s rest like those two. Therefore, dearest ones, while it is called “today,” that is, while we live in this life, let us with ready mind follow the voice of the Lord, the good shepherd—“we are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. XCIV)—so that we may deserve to be led by him into the pastures of everlasting life (fol. 120).

But you ought not to follow or hear the voice of strangers; rather, flee them with your whole heart. By strangers I mean those whom the supreme shepherd himself calls wolves, thieves, and robbers; sparing not the flock, they strangle Christ’s sheep, redeemed by his blood, and devour the living and the dead. They are reckoned as pastors and priests in name, but in reality are seen to be despisers of God, transgressors of his law, and provokers of his wrath upon the people. Living in filth, they are a snare and ruin to the people and defile the people through offerings and gifts. As their blind guides, they lead the wretched populace, by their evil examples, into the depths of hell. Of them it is said: “Woe to you who have taken away the key of knowledge, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men. You do not enter, and you do not permit those wishing to enter” (Matt. XXIII).

They shut the kingdom of heaven against people because they do not open to them, by preaching, the gate of life; they are wise only for evil and do not know how to do good. They do not permit those wishing to enter because they draw many back from good intention by evil examples. Of them it is written: “Death entered through our windows” (Jer. IX). Priests are called the windows of the Church because through their words human hearts are illuminated. But alas! Through these windows death enters when the people commit mortal crimes through the examples of priests. They put to death souls that do not die, and give life to souls that do not live (Ezek. XIII). For they say: “If we receive money from you, we absolve you from sins and make you secure before God. For offences are remitted not through fasting and vigils but through gifts given to us, because all people will finally be saved.”

Flee this voice and their company as poison, dearest ones, and firmly believe this truthful voice: “Turn away from evil and do good,” because neither thieves, nor robbers, nor fornicators, nor drunkards, nor revilers shall possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. VI); but those who persevere in these or similar things to the end shall go into eternal punishment, while the righteous shall go into eternal life (Matt. XXV).

In these days, dearest ones, we recall the Passion of the Lord, which delivered us from the torment of eternal death and from the devil’s power (fol. 120v), reconciled us to God the Father, and enriched us with everlasting glory. For in every respect, except sin, he wished to be made like us (Heb. IV). As it is read that a woman came up the mountain to Elisha to plead for her son, but he sent his staff through a servant and had it placed upon the dead child (4 Kings IV). But the dead child was made heavier by the staff, not raised. Elisha, however, arrived, stretched himself over the dead body’s limbs, and immediately the dead child returned to life (ibid.).

This dead child signifies the human race, for which Mother Church from the beginning cries to God. He sent the staff—that is, the Law—through his servant Moses, which pressed people down all the more, burdening them in death. But Christ, the true Elisha, arriving, conformed himself to the dead one in every respect and raised him to life. This was formerly preceded by many figures; prophetic speech expressed it in many ways. For he who said that he had been likened in the hands of all the prophets was born for the Passion. In vain indeed would he be born if he did not suffer for the salvation of the world.

At the beginning of the world, Adam, formed from clean earth, is put to sleep beneath the tree of life in Paradise, and woman is built from his side (Gen. II). So Christ, born of a pure Virgin, is put to sleep in death upon the wood of the Cross; from his side, as blood and water flow, the Church is formed, redeemed by blood, and washed by water.

Abel offered a lamb to God in sacrifice and fell, innocently slain by his brother; but his blood raised a cry from the earth (Gen. IV). So Christ offered his body to God the Father in sacrifice and fell, innocently slain for us by the Jewish people, his brother. [Col. 0910D] His blood cries from the earth because the Church, having received his blood, resounds with praises to God.

When the world perished in the flood, Noah saved his family in the ark. Ham mocked him when he was drunk, naked, and weighed down in sleep; but Noah, awakening, raised Shem and Japheth by blessing and condemned Ham by a curse (Gen. VII, IX). Thus, when the world perishes in sins, Christ saves the Church by the Cross. The Jewish people mock him when he is made drunk for us with bitterness, stripped for scourging by insults and reproaches, and weighed down by the sleep of death upon the Cross. But he, awakening from death, honors his two sons—namely, clergy and people—by blessing, and rejects the unbelieving people by cursing (fol. 122).

Four kings of the nations made war against the five kings of Pentapolis; and, having overcome the five, the four captured Lot and carried off spoil from Sodom. Abraham pursued them with three hundred and eighteen men; after the enemies were put to flight, the spoil was recovered and Lot returned unharmed. When Abraham had gained the victory, Melchizedek king of Salem met him, offered bread and wine, and Abraham gave him tithes from everything (Gen. XIV).

The four kings of the nations signify four vices: joy, fear, greed, and sorrow, which are opposed to the four virtues, prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. The five kings of Pentapolis are the five senses of our body. Lot signifies our soul; the spoil, our good pursuits; Abraham, the spirit; the three hundred, faith in the Trinity; the ten, the Decalogue of the Law; and the eight, the beatitudes of the New Law. Therefore the four kings fight with the five when the four vices disturb our five senses by desires. They capture Lot and carry away the spoil when they enslave our soul from its condition of rectitude and, drawing our pursuits toward unlawful things, alienate them from the good.

Abraham—that is, the spirit of the inward person—pursues such enemies with faith in the Trinity and the precepts of both laws; once they are conquered, Lot is rescued with the spoils, because the soul is brought back to good pursuits. For tau, T, which denotes three hundred in Greek numeration, is formed in the shape of a cross, because the enemies of vices are overcome through the trophy of the Cross. After this victory, Melchizedek, king without father and without mother, offers bread and wine to the victors (Heb. VII), because Christ, king of righteousness, without mother in heaven and without father on earth, offers his body and blood as a triumphal reward to those victorious over vices. They pay tithes to him from all things—that is, in all his commandments they obey him.

Abraham, offering his son in sacrifice at the Lord’s command, left two servants with the donkey in the city. He himself ascended the mountain with his son and, having built an altar, placed Isaac bound upon it. He took up the sword and wished to sacrifice him, but an angel cried from heaven and commanded him to spare him. Looking around, Abraham saw a ram caught by its horns among the brambles. He offered this in sacrifice and went away with his son (Gen. XXII).

Abraham, who sacrificed Isaac (fol. 122v), is God the Father, who sacrificed his Son for us. Let the whole age marvel at the figures of former things, since in them so certain a signification of later things is proved to be expressed. For in the very place where Abraham set up the altar, Solomon afterward built the Temple; in the place where the ram was caught by its horns among the brambles, there stood fixed the Cross of Christ, upon whose horns he himself was caught among the Jews as among brambles. The two servants who wait with the donkey are the two peoples, namely those from the kingdom of Israel and those from the kingdom of Judah, who still persist in folly. But the true Isaac has already been sacrificed for us and exalted at God’s right hand, while the Jewish people, still waiting with the donkey of folly, have been deprived of this saving sacrifice.

The Law also prefigured these things when it commanded a goat to be offered, upon whose head all sins were to be laid by the priest’s hands, and then to be sent into the wilderness to be devoured by wolves.

This goat is Christ, begotten from [uncertain] sinners [the text reads *a [pro?] peccatoribus pro genitus*], upon whom the sins of all were laid and through him fastened to the Cross. He is sent into the wilderness when he is handed over by the Jews to the Gentiles; he is devoured by wolves when he is torn by cruel death at the hands of both.

The Law also commanded that a red heifer should be offered and burned to ashes, and that the people should be cleansed by sprinkling with its blood and ashes (Lev. XVI).

The red heifer is Christ’s flesh, reddened by blood; it was burned to ashes when, upon the altar of the Cross, it was scorched by the fire of the Passion. The people are cleansed by sprinkling with its blood, because the people are sanctified by Christ’s blood and ashes—that is, by the body of the faithful.

[Col. 0912B] This is also shown through the New Law, in which Christ is said to have descended into a little boat. While he slept in it, a great wind stirred the sea. The disciples, terrified by fear, woke him; and when he rose, the storm and winds ceased, and serenity and calm returned (Matt. VIII).

The little boat is the banner of the holy Cross, by which, through Christ’s Passion, we are carried from the sea of this age to the calm of a safe haven. The Lord entered it when he underwent the Cross for the salvation of the world. A great agitation is stirred in the sea because Judaea, disturbed, is incited to sedition. The Lord slept in the boat when he allowed himself to be overcome by the sleep of death upon the Cross. The frightened disciples woke him [Col. 0912C] when, troubled by the Jewish people’s cruelty in his death, they implored the Lord’s aid with great prayers. When he rose (fol. 124), calm returned, because all joy came to the faithful through Christ’s resurrection.

There was also a pool at Jerusalem in which priests washed sheep intended for sacrifice; it was surrounded by five porticoes. In them lay a multitude of sick people awaiting the movement of the water. At a certain time an angel of the Lord descended into the pool and stirred the water; once the water was stirred, whoever first entered it was healed of every sickness. Among the sick, one man languished under a long illness, but the Lord commanded him to rise healed and depart with his bed (John V).

The pool surrounded by five porticoes is the Synagogue, joined to the five books of the Law. The multitude of sick persons was the number of Jews oppressed by the sickness of sins. The angel of the Lord descended at the appointed time and stirred the water when Christ, the Angel of Great Counsel, entered the world and disturbed Judaea by signs, miracles, and teachings. Once disturbed, it killed the author of life; but one sick man received health because Christ soon redeemed his people from death. The sick man lacked two years of forty, because the former people lacked twofold love; having acquired it, he cast off the sickness of the soul and put on the health of life.

The Lord himself tells of a man who had a vineyard and at the appointed time sent his servants for its fruits. [Col. 0913A] The tenants seized them, tortured and killed them with various punishments, and slew others sent afterward in the same way. Finally, he sent his son, whom the wicked crowd cast out of the vineyard and killed. But when the lord came, he destroyed the wicked evildoers and leased the vineyard to other tenants (Matt. XXI).

The man who had the vineyard is the Lord, who brought Judaea out of Egypt and, expelling the nations, planted it like a beloved vineyard. He surrounded it with a hedge—that is, fortified it with the guardianship of angels and sacred Scripture. He dug a winepress because he established offerings to be made at the altar. He built a tower because he commanded that a temple renowned throughout the whole world be built in it. He sent servants, or prophets, for the fruit of good works, but the impious nation killed them in various ways. After them he sent others, namely the apostles [Col. 0913B], but slew them as it had the former ones. Finally, it killed the Son who came and warned them to repent, casting him out of the vineyard—that is, crucifying him after leading him out of the city. Therefore the Lord destroyed such tenants when he scattered the Jews throughout the whole world; he leased the vineyard to others when he transferred sacred Scripture to the Christian people, who render to God the fruit of divine service, and God repays them with the kingdom of heaven.

Christ’s Passion had been of the greatest benefit to sinners, since he had come to call not the righteous but sinners (Matt. 9). Divine mercy showed us an example of this matter in Pelagia, whom God’s predestining grace wonderfully saved. For, as is read, a council of bishops was assembled at Antioch. While they were seated, [Col. 0913C] a girl passed by, adorned with much gold and jewels and attended by a great company of young men, who could find no satisfaction in her beauty, since she spread about herself the delights of extraordinarily precious perfumes. Her name was Pelagia; but because of her excessive adornment she was called Margaret by the whole city. When all the bishops turned away and hid their faces as though from the gravest crime, one of them, named Nonnus, looked at her for a long time. At last, bursting into tears, he said to his fellow bishops:

> “Brothers, believe me: this woman has today been brought before our eyes as an example for us. Know that at the Judgment the Lord will not set before us apostles or martyrs, but will bring forward this woman [Col. 0913D] for us. For whatever she promised to her lovers, she strove with all effort to fulfill.”

After this he rose, entered the church, prostrated himself upon the ground in tears, and earnestly prayed to God that he might not be driven from God’s sanctuary by comparison with this woman. “For whatever,” he said, “I have ever promised to you, Lord God of all, I have never been diligent to fulfill. But she has faithfully fulfilled whatever she promised to corruptible human beings.”

That same night God revealed to him the girl’s salvation. For in a dream he saw himself standing at the altar and celebrating Mass, while a black dove [Col. 0914A] flew importunately around his face. Seizing it, he threw it into a pool; from it the dove emerged whiter than snow and rose into the heights of heaven. On the next day the archbishop directed this bishop of God to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass and deliver a sermon of edification to the people. While he was preaching, the same woman was present; pierced by his words through God’s prompting, she shed a flood of tears. When Mass was finished, she hurried to the bishop’s lodging and, prostrate [fol. 126] at his feet, watered them abundantly with tears after the example of the Gospel sinner. She asked for baptism from him and received it.

While the bishop sat at table with his companions, rejoicing with the angels over the girl’s salvation, behold, the devil appeared naked above the roof of the house and cried out plaintively in a loud voice:

> “O [Col. 0914B] accursed old man, why do you oppose me? Why do you rob me of my spoils? Is it not enough that you took four thousand Saracens from me and offered them to your God through baptism, unless you now also take away my beloved vessel, through whom I acquired innumerable souls of this city? Cursed is the day on which you, my adversary, were born. For your tears beat upon my dwelling like a torrent and overthrow the foundations of my house like a storm.”

Then he turned to the girl and addressed her thus:

> “O sweetest Margaret, what harm have I done you, that you have turned away from me? I enriched you with gold and jewels; I abundantly ennobled you with high-born men. Therefore return to me and enjoy your accustomed delights.”

At the bishop’s admonition, the girl made the sign of the cross, and the devil immediately vanished. [Col. 0914C] But when he came in the night, he woke her while she slept and, promising innumerable good things, begged her to return to him. Yet she drove the malignant one away through Christ’s name and the sign of the cross.

On the eighth day she took off women’s clothing, secretly went out dressed as a man, journeyed to Jerusalem, and shut herself up on the Mount of Olives. The spiritual mother who had raised her from the font, thinking that she had relapsed into error, wept bitterly. The bishop began to console her, saying that she had chosen the better part with Mary (Luke 11). After several years the chaplain of the same Bishop Nonnus went to Jerusalem for prayer and found her enclosed on the Mount of Olives. Recognized by her, he did not recognize her [the text repeats *cognitus / cognovit*], because through excessive fasting and frequent [Col. 0914D] vigils her imperial [*imperialis*, sic] face had withered away. While he remained there, she died; when her garment was removed, she was recognized as a woman, and through him her whole story became known to all. Then bishops, monks, nuns, clergy, and people gathered together, buried her worthily, and glorified him who wills all people to be saved.

To him, dearest beloved, flee with your whole heart; crucify yourselves with him as to vices and desires, so that, filled with joy, you may prosper in his presence [fol. 126v] and may have delights at his right hand unto the end. “What eye has not seen,” and the rest (1 Cor. 2).

## PALM SUNDAY

[Col. 0913]

[Col. 0913D] “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample [Col. 0914D] the lion and the dragon” (Ps. 90 [91]).

The asp is a kind of serpent that flees the charms of one who is enchanting it. For when it is being charmed, it is said to press one ear to the ground and stop up the other with its tail, lest it hear the voice of its enchanter and obey that person’s words. It infects springs and trees with poison and thus kills those who taste from them.

This asp signifies sin, which hardens the ears of our heart with earthly desires, lest we hear the admonitions of our God and obey his words for our salvation. It infects the font of baptism and the tree of the cross when it defiles with crimes those baptized in faith in Christ’s Passion. It kills those who taste from them, because criminal sin kills those who taste the word of life and the sacraments of Christ’s body.

But the basilisk, also called the little king (*regulus*), is described as a deadly [Col. 0915B] four-footed animal: whatever takes in its breath dies. Even birds flying above, choked by its breath, fall down dying and lose their feathers as though scorched by fire. This pestilential creature, though it kills everything, wastes away in death when overcome by the weasel.

The basilisk signifies death, which by its touch separates all things from life. Birds fall from on high through its breath because even the righteous, when touched by death, are stripped of life. It walks on four feet because the human race is drawn to death in four ways: through transgression of the first commandment, violation of the natural law, transgression of the written law, and contempt for the Gospel. The weasel overcomes it because Christ’s flesh destroys death by dying.

[Col. 0915C] The lion, strongest of beasts, ranges through the woodland groves. With its tail it marks the ground, and every beast fears to cross that mark. Then, rushing forward with a roar, it bursts into the forest and, tearing apart the beasts frightened by its terror, rends them.

By the lion Antichrist is understood, whose powerful strength surpasses all kings. And just as the lion circles the forest, so he encloses the world by his power [fol. 128]. He marks the ground with his tail, which the beasts tremble to cross, because he promulgates decrees that every person fears to transgress. Roaring, he makes a charge into the forest and tears the beasts that he attacks, because through terror he subjugates all nations to himself and cruelly tears apart all who resist him.

[Col. 0915D] Scripture teaches that the dragon is the greatest serpent, which harms by breath, poison, and the blow of its tail. Lifted up by the force of its venom, it flies, as it were, through the air, and the air is disturbed by it. Lying in wait for the elephant, a most chaste animal, it binds its feet with its tail and strives to suffocate it with its breath; but it is itself crushed beneath the dying elephant. From the ground, moreover, which has been stained with its blood, a precious color is obtained.

The dragon, greatest of serpents, is the devil, king of all evils. He kills by breath, poison, and the blow of his tail because he destroys souls by thought, speech, and deed. He infects thoughts with the breath of pride, pours the poison of malice into words, and binds with his tail the commission of an evil work. The air is disturbed through him because spiritual harmony is often troubled by him. He lies in wait for the chaste [Col. 0916A] animal because he persecuted Christ, the author of chastity, born of the chaste Virgin, even unto death; but when Christ died, he was crushed and overthrown. The precious red color, moreover, is taken from the ground because the Church is adorned by Christ’s blood.

Therefore the Lord walked upon the asp and basilisk when, by destroying sin and death through his death, he subjected all harmful things to his faithful. He will trample the lion and dragon when he overcomes Antichrist through his elect and condemns the devil with all his members at the final judgment. The devil is also called dragon and lion: dragon because he lies in wait through hidden temptations; lion because he seeks to overthrow through open persecutions. He was a dragon when he secretly tempted the Lord; he was a lion [Col. 0916B] when he attacked him in open persecution. But the Lord trampled lion and dragon when he humbly endured temptation and patiently endured persecution. Hence we sing concerning his temptation, “You shall trample the dragon”; but today, concerning the Passion, “Deliver me from the mouth of the lion.”

But how, dearest beloved, the Lord worked salvation in the midst of the earth (Ps. 73 [74]), I wish briefly to relate to your love. Jerusalem is said to be situated in the midst of the earth, and there the Lord was crucified for the salvation of the world [fol. 128v]. Though he was rich, he became needy and poor for us, in order to make us sharers in the surpassing abundance of his riches. Martha and Mary frequently received him into their home and supplied him with necessities from their own resources. When their brother Lazarus fell ill, they sent [Col. 0916C] to Jesus so that the illness of his friend might be made known to him. Upon coming, he found that Lazarus had already died and had been buried for four days. A great crowd of Jews had come to Martha and Mary and sought to console them for their brother’s death. But when the Lord saw the grieving crowd lamenting tearfully, he too began to weep with them (John 11).

Before this he had opened the eyes of a man born blind by anointing them with mud. Therefore the Jews now said: “Could not he who was able to make the eyes of one born blind open also have prevented this man from dying?” (ibid.). Accordingly he went with the crowd to the tomb, which a huge stone covered, and Jesus ordered it removed. The dead man, being already four days dead, stank; and his feet and hands were bound with bands. [Col. 0916D] But Jesus, giving thanks to the Father, prayed and called Lazarus out of the tomb in a loud voice. Immediately the dead man, still bound, came out of the tomb, to the amazement of all, and filled everyone with great joy (ibid.).

When the Pharisees—namely, the clergy of the Jews—heard of this unheard-of miracle, they immediately assembled a council at Jerusalem and said to one another: “What shall we do, since we know that this man performs such great signs? If we let him go on thus, the whole world will believe in him. And if he is regarded as God, the Romans will take from us our nation and the place of our dwelling.” Their high priest, however, pronounced his judgment against him: it was expedient that one man should die for the people, lest the whole nation perish (ibid.). Therefore at that council an edict was promulgated that he should be seized and killed.

[Col. 0917A] But since “there is no wisdom, no prudence, and no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21), while it did not please him, they were wholly unable to fulfill their plan of wickedness. But when it pleased him to accomplish the work enjoined by the Father—namely, to erase with his own blood the record of debt written against us in sin—he went with his followers toward Jerusalem and turned aside at Bethany to Martha, who prepared a supper for him and his companions. Lazarus, whom he had raised from death, was one of those reclining at table. His sister Mary poured precious ointment upon the Lord’s head as he reclined [the text has *recubentibus*, presumably *recumbentis*] (John 12). But Judas was enraged. And because he was unable to sell this for three hundred denarii for his own theft (ibid.), he sold the Lord himself for thirty denarii (Matt. 26).

[Col. 0917B] Because of the Paschal feast, people had gathered in Jerusalem from every part of the world. Hearing that Lazarus had been raised from the dead, they went to Bethany in order to see Jesus who raised him and Lazarus who had been raised. Therefore the Pharisees said: “We accomplish nothing; behold, the whole world has gone after the Gospel” (John 12). They therefore decided that Lazarus should be killed; but, God disposing better concerning him, he was preserved for the benefit of the Church. For it is reported that afterward he presided for thirty years as bishop of the Church in Cyprus and, as the Lord had raised him from bodily death, so he brought many back from the death of the soul to life by words and example.

The Lord, accompanied by the crowds, came to the Mount of Olives and, sending two disciples into the city, commanded that an ass tied up and a colt with her should be brought to him. [Col. 0917C] They went and brought the ass and colt; laying their garments upon them, they made him sit upon them. Others spread garments in the road, while others cut branches from olive trees and threw them into the road. When it became widely known in the city that Jesus was coming there on an ass according to prophecy, the crowds eagerly ran out to meet him, rejoicing with palm branches. They called him King of Israel and loudly cried *Hosanna* in his praise. It was that people’s custom, at the command of the Law, to celebrate solemnities with palm branches (ibid.).

But Jesus, seeing the city, wept and foretold that it would be destroyed (Luke 19), which afterward happened. For forty years after the Passion, [Col. 0917D] the Romans besieged it at Passover and, slaughtering the people, utterly destroyed it. Therefore, as he entered the city with the crowds, a multitude of children and the whole populace rushed out to meet him with palms and received the King of glory with hymns. Surrounded by them, he entered the temple and drove from it with a whip those buying and selling doves (Matt. 21). He foretold that the temple of his body would be destroyed but rebuilt after three days (John 2). In the temple, then, he performed many signs and daily taught heavenly things to the crowds.

On the fourth weekday [Wednesday] he was betrayed by Judas; on the fifth weekday [Thursday] bread and wine are consecrated for us into his body and blood; on the sixth weekday [Friday] he is crucified for the salvation of all. On Saturday he rested in the tomb; on Sunday [fol. 130v], rising from death, he gave life and joy to all who hope in him. These are [Col. 0918A] the solemnities of this holy week, which renew past things for us and bring future joys to remembrance. I shall unfold for you a few of their mysteries.

The Lord, who will raise all the dead on the last day, restored three dead persons to life; through them he showed that we are to be made alive from three deaths of the soul. He raised the girl in the house from death as though from sleep (Luke 8); he raised the young man carried out beyond the city gate in the sight of the people (Luke 7); and he called Lazarus, four days dead, from the tomb (John 11).

Through these three dead persons are signified the three deaths of the soul, by which souls are separated from the life of God. For we depart from God either in thought, speech, or action and make ourselves liable to eternal death. [Col. 0918B] The death of thought kills the soul when it desires evil by its will. “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5). Fornication is the death of the soul. Thus, as the girl lay in the house, so the soul lies dead in its conscience. If it turns to repentance, it is raised to life by the Lord.

The soul is killed by the death of words when it speaks evil. “A lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. 1), and “slanderers shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6). Therefore the person whose evil intention is made known to others through perverse counsels is carried out dead like the young man beyond the gate. But if he has recourse to tears of repentance, he rises from death as the Lord raises him.

The soul dies by the death of the body when it strives to carry out what it has thought wickedly and deliberated still more wickedly [Col. 0918C] in the most wicked manner. It is shut in like Lazarus in the tomb when it is plunged into the depths of sins; covered by a stone when oppressed by evil habit; and its hands and feet are bound with bands when it is strengthened in evil by friends and flatterers. This dead person also stinks because his reputation harms many people. He is raised only after prayer has been offered and a loud voice sent forth, because such a person is with difficulty provoked to repentance through the constant prayers of the Church and frequent preaching.

But the Lord did not wish to raise a fourth dead person, for no one asked him to do so; indeed, he forbade one who wished to bury him: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8).

[Col. 0918D] By this dead person are represented those who rejoice when they have done evil [fol. 132] and exult in the most wicked things (Prov. 2). The dead who bury them are their accomplices, like them in evil, who exalt their wicked actions with approval. For when they praise those who commit crime as though in jest, they heap earth upon the dead person, as it were. Since these do not rise in the judgment of confession, they will lie buried in hell and burn with the rich man.

Lazarus also signifies the entire human race, which, dead in its first parent, was shut up in the tomb of evil habit but is called forth from the tomb through its Redeemer when restored from sins to life. The four days during which Lazarus lay in the tomb are the four transgressions of laws by which the human race is brought down [Col. 0919A] under death’s dominion.

The first law was set before the first human being in paradise: “Do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). If humanity had observed this, it and all its descendants would have remained immortal in soul and body. But because, at the devil’s persuasion, it transgressed by eating, it was punished with death together with all its descendants. Behold one day of death.

After humanity was driven from paradise, the natural law was imposed: “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another.” If it observed this, it would escape the death of the soul. But because it neglected to do this, it brought death into the world. Behold two days of death.

The written law was given to humanity; by observing it, humanity could escape the dangers of eternal death. Since it despised this law, it pressed humanity down into death by its own weight. [Col. 0919B] Behold three days of death.

The Gospel is preached to humanity, through which eternal life is bestowed; it too is despised, and therefore humanity is handed over to death. Behold four days of death. The Lord raised to life the human race, hitherto oppressed by this fourfold death, when he went to the Mount of Olives. The Mount of Olives is the exaltation of the faithful people, anointed with the oil of joy. The Lord came to this mount when, coming in the flesh, he gathered the faithful to faith. He sent two disciples into the city because he sent into the world teachers perfected in faith and works. He sent two because he wished the two peoples, namely Jewish and Gentile, to be taught by the two Testaments. He sent two because he instituted the active and contemplative life to observe the two commandments of love [fol. 132v].

[Col. 0919C] They brought the ass and colt because they converted circumcision and uncircumcision to faith. The ass signifies Judaea, bound under the yoke of the Law; the untamed colt signifies the Gentile people, constrained by no law. They laid garments upon them when they offered them good examples. They placed the Lord upon them when they impressed Christ upon their hearts by faith. They spread garments in the road when they set examples before them. They cut branches [Col. 0920A] from the olive trees when they taught them the deeds and sayings of the prophets. The olives signify the prophets, who were anointed with oil. They spread branches from palms when, by expounding them, they applied the kings’ battles against nations and their victories to the battle of the spirit against vices. Palms signify the victory of kings, because a palm is called a victory. The crowds who met the Lord with palms are the Gentiles who received faith and fulfilled Christ’s commands through pious actions. The children who received the Lord with palms are the martyrs who came to Christ with the palm of victory. The remaining populace that meets the Lord with palms signifies those who conquer vices and meet the Lord at the judgment with the triumph of victory.

The Lord foretold the destruction of the city because he declared [Col. 0920B] that this world would be dissolved. The crowds cry *Hosanna* when they joyfully enter the city with the Lord, because, when he brings his bride the Church from this Babylon into the city of his Father, he will command those who praise him to enter the wedding feast with him. He cast from the temple those buying and selling doves because he expels from the temple of heavenly Jerusalem all who buy or sell churches, orders, or any spiritual gift.

This is called Palm Day, which the whole Church celebrates with palms and flowers in imitation of that people. Therefore, dearest beloved, praise our Redeemer with a loud voice and entreat him with continual prayers, so that, just as the Hebrew people met him with palms and flowers [Col. 0920C] when he came to his Passion and in some manner sang beforehand of his triumph over death, so we—with the palm of victory over the world—may have sung beforehand his triumph over death [the text here repeats this phrase with an apparent grammatical corruption], so that we may be able to meet him when he comes for judgment with the palm of victory over the world and vices, and with the flowers of good works; and may deserve to enter with him into the heavenly Jerusalem for the wedding feast in triumph.

Here make an end, if you wish; but if not, add the following.

[Col. 0919]

[Col. 0919C] [Fol. 124] All these things formerly came beforehand in figures and pointed, as with a finger, to our times. Abraham compelled his servant to swear upon his circumcised member, from which he foreknew that Christ would descend in the flesh, so that he might go into Mesopotamia [Col. 0919D] and bring a wife from there for his son. Bound by the oath, he went into Chaldea, found Rebecca beside a spring, adorned with gold and jewels, and brought her to Isaac. Thus the order of teachers sent by God into the world, bound by Christ’s incarnation [reading uncertain: *Christi incarnationem constrictus*], finds the Church beside the font of baptism, adorned with the gold of charity and jewels of good works, and brings her to Christ, the true Isaac.

The people are oppressed in Egypt by Pharaoh, and Moses is sent to deliver them. When he performs many signs, the magicians resist him. This Moses commanded that a lamb without blemish be enclosed on the tenth day of the first month and sacrificed at evening on the fourteenth day; its blood was to mark the doorways of houses in the form of a cross, as it was applied at four places—namely, on the threshold, on the lintel, [Col. 0920C] and on both doorposts—and the lamb itself was to be eaten roasted in the houses. Seeing this sign, the destroying angel passed over; he struck the firstborn of the Egyptians, and the Lord led his people out with gold and silver in exultation and joy. A pillar [Col. 0920D] of fire went before them by night, and a pillar of cloud protected them by day. He divided the Red Sea, through which the people crossed on dry ground. The waves covered their pursuing enemies but rescued the people from fear of them. He brought them, rejoicing, to seventy palms and twelve springs of water, and thereafter fed them with heavenly bread. He brought forth water for them from a rock struck twice; flowing alongside them, it accompanied them as far as the promised land. Some of them, ungrateful for so many benefits, murmured and perished from fiery serpents. Therefore, when the people cried out and Moses prayed to the Lord, the Lord commanded that a bronze serpent be raised up, so that those struck by serpents might be delivered from death by looking upon it.

As they approached the land, they sent twelve scouts, [Col. 0921A] who surveyed the whole land and brought back fruit from it for the multitude as evidence that the land was excellent. For they cut down a cluster of grapes, which two men carried on a pole, and brought bread in a basket. When they came to the Jordan, the river stood still and the people crossed unharmed. At the sound of priests’ trumpets Jericho fell; and, after their enemies had been conquered through Joshua, who is also Jesus, the people possessed the land flowing with milk and honey. All this is explained to us as follows.

The people are oppressed by the devil in this world, and Christ is sent by the Father to deliver them. When he performs many signs, the malice of the Pharisees resists him. He himself was the lamb without blemish, because he committed no sin. Of him it is said: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). [Col. 0921B] Like a sheep led to slaughter, he died when the good shepherd laid down his life for his sheep. On the tenth day of the first month—that is, today—he came to Jerusalem and was enclosed by the Jews; and on the fourteenth day, that is, on the fifth weekday [Thursday], his body was given up. The fourfold doors are marked with his blood when our bodies are consecrated in the form of a cross by baptism and faith in Christ’s Passion. The roasted lamb is eaten in the house when the faithful people feed in the Catholic Church upon the flesh of the suffering Christ. Egypt’s firstborn are struck when the penalties of eternal death are destroyed by the lamb’s blood. Egypt, which means “darkness,” signifies sins that lead evil-doers into the outer darkness. The angel of great counsel struck their firstborn when he destroyed by his death the punishments which sins had produced.

[Col. 0921C] The people are led out rejoicing with gold and silver because they are rescued from the tyrant at the great price of the immaculate lamb. Those who were held imprisoned in infernal darkness are illuminated by the light of the eternal Sun; rescued from death’s prison, they are placed in the palace of life. The pillar of fire goes before the people by night because the light of Holy Scripture provides us, amid the darkness of this life, a path to our homeland. By day the pillar of cloud protects them from heat because, on the day of judgment, Christ’s humanity will defend us from the heat of eternal fire. For just as the sun is beneath a cloud, so the Sun of righteousness was hidden beneath human flesh. The Red Sea is baptism made red by Christ’s blood, in which the enemies—that is, sins—are drowned. The faithful are rescued from fear of punishments. The seventy palms are the seventy books of Holy Scripture, through which the seventy disciples [Col. 0922A] taught the people to attain the palm of victory over vices. The twelve springs are the twelve apostles [fol. 136], from whom rivers of Scripture flowed through the world. Those led out of Egypt came to these springs when, redeemed by the Lord, they submitted themselves through the apostles to the yoke of faith and began to search the Holy Scriptures. They ate the bread of angels when they deserved to feed on Christ’s body. In that bread they had every delight and every savor of sweetness (Wis. 16), because those who worthily feed on Christ’s bread will have every joy and every sweetness. Water is drawn out for them from the rock struck twice because Gospel teaching is brought forth from Christ, stretched out upon the two timbers of the cross. This water offered a honeyed and oily savor because it promises us, through Christ’s mercy, the sweetness of eternal [Col. 0922B] life in the Gospel. Those ungratefully murmuring against benefits perish through serpents because those who live perversely after receiving the divine sacraments perish through demons.

The bronze serpent raised up, at the sight of which the people were saved from the serpents’ bite, is Christ stretched out upon the cross, through faith in whom the people are freed from the wound of sins. The bronze serpent lacks poison, and so does Christ lack sin. The twelve who explored the land are the twelve apostles who preached eternal life in the world. The cluster carried on a pole is Christ, proclaimed as having hung upon the cross. Two carry it because the prophetic and apostolic orders make his Passion known to the world. They also brought bread in a basket because they announced that the bread of angels had come in the flesh [Col. 0922C] and had become food for human beings. After the river has been crossed, Jericho is destroyed at the sound of the priests’ trumpet because, when the final persecution has been overcome, this world will be dissolved at the sound of the angels’ trumpet. When God’s enemies have been conquered, the land flowing with milk and honey is apportioned through Jesus to the victorious people because, when God’s enemies have been condemned by a just judgment, the land of the living, flowing with torrents of joys, is bestowed through the true Jesus upon the people victorious over vices.

Therefore, dearest beloved, since Christ has freed you by his blood from the oppression of the devil and opened the entrance to the heavenly homeland, hasten to reach him by the way of his commandments, so that you may please him in the land of the living and the dead, where he may distribute to you joys “which eye has not seen,” and the rest.

## AT THE LORD’S SUPPER

[Col. 0921]

[Col. 0921D] “I shall return to Jerusalem with mercy, and my house shall be built in her, says the Lord” (Zech. 1). As I have often told you, dearest beloved, Jerusalem [fol. 136v] means “vision of peace” and signifies the Church that will see in heaven the Prince of Peace. In this Jerusalem we are the house that God has raised by faith, furnished with virtues, washed in baptism, and adorned with gifts of graces. In this house living stones are squared by the tools of tribulations, so that a house may be built from them in heaven, in which it is declared that the axe and hammer of adversities [Col. 0922D] will not be heard.

This house fell within us when our mind collapsed from the summit of virtues into vices, and consequently the Lord withdrew from us. But because during these forty days we gather through repentance the instruments of a spiritual building, the Lord, once more made propitious, promises again: “I shall return to Jerusalem with mercy,” forgiving sins; he builds the house by bestowing charisms.

Following this example, bishops, the builders of the house, restore today the fallen house when, bringing into the Church penitents cast out of it because of crimes, they add them to the children of the Church. Today they raise up the fallen tabernacle of David when they prepare chrism and holy oil, by which the faithful are marked for God’s kingdom and all the reborn are consecrated as kings and priests. Hence those baptized, by their white garment, and priests, by their mitre, bear before them the royal diadem. Today all the shepherds of the Church rebuild God’s house when they bring wandering sheep back to the flock. Today the cultivators of the Lord’s vineyard graft back onto Christ, the true vine, the severed shoots and the broken branches of the olive tree, when they absolve through pardon those excommunicated or excluded because of crimes. Hence this day too is called the day of pardon, because those who throughout the forty [days] were bound by priests in the bonds of repentance for sins [Col. 0923B] today, when their penance has been completed, rejoice that, freed by pardon, they have been received into the bosom of the Church.

Today Christ washed the disciples’ feet and left us an example of washing the feet of brothers and the poor. For we fulfill love of neighbor in our brothers, but love of God in the poor. Whatever is bestowed on the poor is offered to Christ, as he himself declares at the judgment: “What you did to these, you did to me” (Matt. 25). Therefore, following Christ’s example, let us wash our brother and Christ’s footsteps, and may he wash away our sins.

Today Christ handed over to the Church his body and blood in memory of himself, through which she daily receives remission of sins. Whoever receives them unworthily [Col. 0923C] will be guilty of the Lord’s death together with Judas. Now that person receives unworthily who has been defiled by fornication, adultery, or any unclean act, or who has committed any criminal deed and has neglected to make confession and do penance for it, or has been ashamed to confess shameful actions. Let such persons at least today have recourse to confession and tears of repentance, so that they may receive the Lord’s body not for judgment but as a remedy for their souls.

That night Christ supped with his disciples and, bringing the old Law to completion through the mystical lamb, began the new. And after he had foretold many future things to them and abundantly instructed them with heavenly teaching, rising after a sweet prayer he commended to God the Father those who believed in him, went up the mountain and prayed, and a sweat of blood flowed from him. [Col. 0923D] There, through Judas’s betrayal, he was seized by crowds of Jews as a robber, bound as a thief, led as an accused man before the council, and mocked as an evildoer with blows and spittle. He was deserted by his disciples and denied by Peter with an oath. On the following day he was delivered bound by the Jews to the Gentiles—namely, to Pilate the governor and his soldiers—and was moreover accused as deserving death. Pilate, knowing that he had been delivered through envy, wished to release him. It was the Jews’ custom that the governor should release for them, on the feast day, whichever prisoner they requested. Pilate therefore wished Jesus to be released; but they shouted loudly that he should be crucified, while they asked that the robber be set free, who had been placed in prison for murder. [Col. 0924A] Pilate, however, washed his hands before them all and declared himself innocent of his blood. Thus the Judge of all and Giver of life is sentenced to death, and the Lord of majesty is handed over to pagan servants to be crucified. Received by them for mockery, he is clothed as a king in purple; his right hand is furnished with a reed instead of a sceptre; his head is crowned with thorns instead of a diadem; and he is greeted with bent knees. Then he is spat upon and torn by cruel scourges; after this he is led out of the city with robbers, the innocent one is crucified among criminals, and his garment is apportioned by lot. Presently the sentence of the eternal Judge struck Judas with thirty curses: he who sold the price of the world for thirty pieces of silver and was branded, for each denarius, with the cautery of death (Matt. 26–27).

[Col. 0924B] For it is decreed that a sinner [Note: [Col. 0923D] Something is missing.] be set over him and that the devil be allowed to stand at his right hand; that he be condemned in judgment (fo. 138v), that his prayer be turned into sin, that his days be few and another take his bishopric; that his sons become orphans and his wife a widow; that his sons be driven about and become beggars, that they be cast out of their dwellings, that moneylenders search out his substance, that strangers plunder his labours; that no one help him and no one pity his fatherless children; that his offspring perish and his name be blotted out in a single generation; that the iniquity of his fathers return to God’s remembrance and that his mother’s sin not be wiped away by pardon; that it ever remain before the Lord and his memory vanish from the earth; that a curse come upon him and blessing be far [Col. 0924C] from him; that he put on cursing as a garment, that it enter his inward parts like water and his bones like oil; that he be clothed in cursing as in a garment, girded with cursing as with a belt; that he be confounded and clothed with shame, covered with confusion as with a double cloak (Ps. 108).

While he is overwhelmed with so many curses, the whole world abominates him. For heaven refused to look upon him any longer, and earth shuddered to bear him. Thus he was raised into the air to be strangled by a noose and joined to the demons dwelling in the air. But the air, recoiling from him even more than from demons, thrust him away from itself; whereupon he immediately burst asunder in the middle, and Tartarus swallowed him as he fell.

But while the Only-Begotten of the Father, hanging on the cross, repaid [Col. 0924D] what he had not seized, the Jews added to the pain of his wounds by insulting and mocking him, and moreover offered him vinegar and gall to drink; but he poured out prayers for them. Of the robbers also, one reproached them with the punishment of death, while the other sought mercy. Upon this man the fountain of compassion immediately poured out the bowels of mercy; forgiving his crimes, he promised him paradise: “Today,” he said, “you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). Through him it became known to the world that, suffering on the cross for sinners, he willed to shed his blood—he who granted life to the repentant robber at the point of death. There, hanging on the cross, our judged Judge exercised judgment, [Col. 0925A] rejecting one because of wickedness and admitting the other because of confession, thereby showing that his Passion is salvation indeed for the righteous, but condemnation for the impious.

The world, seeing its Maker so cruelly tortured, recoiled from the crime and darkened the whole earth with dreadful gloom from the sixth hour until the eighth. At the eighth hour, in order to raise from the mire (fo. 140) of death the man whom he had created from clay, the Son of God bowed himself to death. As he died, the whole earth trembled and vomited forth its dead. The veil of the Temple was torn in two; the hardness of rocks was split. The dead rose and bore testimony to their Lord. Then one of the soldiers pierced the Lord’s side with a lance, and immediately a stream of blood and water flowed forth for the redemption of the world; and at the sight of these things the centurion declared him to be the Son of God. [Col. 0925B] Joseph, a very wealthy man, asked Pilate for Jesus’ body and obtained it; taking it down from the cross, he placed it in a new tomb.

Moreover Christ, descending to the gates of hell, visited those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. Himself stronger, he overcame the strong devil; with life he slew death; and, overthrowing the tyrant’s kingdom and taking spoils, he returned in triumph as victor on the third day. All this the prophets foretold would happen; all this they prefigured by diverse figures.

For the most devout King Josiah celebrated a most renowned Passover and invited all the people of the kingdom to a feast. When he was slain by the king of Egypt, he was lamented by all the people, but especially by Jeremiah. While this prophet lamented in the plain of Megiddo, where the king fell, the vein of a spring and the greenness of a tree dried up. [Col. 0925C] This Josiah is Christ, the King of righteousness, who celebrated a famous Passover for the whole world when, on the Jewish Paschal day, he offered himself to God the Father. He invited the people to the feast because, through the eating of his body, he called all the faithful to the banquet of the eternal feast. He is slain by the king of Egypt when, by the counsel of the devil, king of darkness, he is handed over to death by the Jews. He is lamented by all the people, but chiefly by the prophet, because although Christ’s death is prefigured in various ways by all the ancient people, it is chiefly prefigured by the deeds and sayings of the prophets. Moreover, all nations shall weep over his death when they see him whom they pierced (John 19). In the plain where the king fell, spring and tree dried up, because in Judaea, where [Col. 0925D] Christ fell, the font of baptism and the tree of the cross dried up, since, by remaining in unbelief, it caused neither to benefit itself. Hence these same Lamentations are recited lamentingly in churches on these days, by which the time of Christ’s death was prefigured, while this same Passion of Christ is reverently celebrated by the faithful.

Jonah also (fo. 140v) is sent by the Lord to preach; but when he boards a ship, he is shaken by a great storm. For while storms and winds rage upon the sea, he sleeps in the ship; but, discovered by lot by the frightened sailors, he is thrown from the ship into the waves, and the sea is immediately calmed. A great fish swallows him and holds him in its belly for three days; after these, at the Lord’s command, it vomits him forth alive upon dry land. He then [Col. 0926A] entered Nineveh, preached, and saved the city from destruction (Jonah 1–4).

So Christ is sent by the Father into the world to preach to the peoples; ascending the cross, he is met by the storm of persecution. Thus, while Jews and Gentiles rage against him like winds and storms, he sleeps, weighed down by death upon the cross. He is discovered by lot because he alone is chosen for the redemption of humankind. He is cast from the ship into the sea by sailors when, taken down from the cross by his own people disturbed by the Jews’ cruelty, he is buried in the tomb. The fury of winds upon the sea is calmed because, by Christ’s death, the assault of demons against humankind is checked. Swallowed by the fish and held in its belly for three days, he is vomited forth, because Christ, received by hell, is restored to the world after three days. [Col. 0926B] He preaches to the Ninevites and frees their city from destruction, because Christ preaches to the Gentiles through the apostles and saves the world from the peril of perdition.

He also, weary from his journey, sat at the spring at the sixth hour; but a Samaritan woman came to draw water. He beneficially warned her concerning the five lawful husbands, and reproved her concerning the sixth man, whom she had unlawfully. But she left her water-jar, ran into the city, and turned all the people toward him (John 4).

Christ was making a journey when, in human flesh, he came to seek the lost sheep. He laboured, weary upon the journey. He sat at the well at the sixth hour when, in the sixth age of the world, on the fifth day he drank from the torrent of death on the way, and at the sixth hour hung upon the wood over the abyss of the mystery of the cross. [Col. 0926C] The woman came from Samaria to draw water because the Church came from the Gentiles to the spring to receive baptism and deserved to receive water springing up unto eternal life, namely evangelical teaching. She had five lawful husbands because God had given her the five senses for worshipping him (fo. 142). But she polluted herself with the unlawful man when, following error and despising the worship of God, she worshipped idols. She left the water-jar when she abandoned idolatry and strove to convert the whole people of the city of the world to faith. This is the woman whose little vessels Elisha had filled with oil, because Christ had abundantly filled the hearts of believers with the oil of the Holy Spirit.

Now, dearest ones, the mysteries of God’s works must be considered. On the sixth weekday God made man; on the sixth weekday he redeemed him. At the third hour man is said to have been formed. At the third hour Christ was condemned to death in order to remake him. At the sixth hour man transgressed God’s command by eating; at the sixth hour Christ was crucified for his transgression. At the eighth hour man was cast out from the joys of paradise; at the ninth hour Christ was subjected to death for his reconciliation.

By the wood of transgression man perished; by the wood of the cross he returned. Eating the fruit of the forbidden tree, man is punished with death; rising through the fruit of the tree of life, that is, the cross, he is restored to life. By the fourfold Law man is consigned to death; by the four-branched cross he is redeemed from death. Through Eve, whose name sounds like “life,” man is deceived; through Christ, who is the true life, he is brought back [Col. 0927A] from death to life. Through the serpent the poison of death is poured into the world; through the bronze serpent raised upon the cross the sweet draught of life is poured back for all.

Christ is seized by the impious, and captive man returns from the demons. Christ is bound, and man is unknotted from the cords of sins. Christ is abandoned by his disciples, and man is joined to the hosts of angels. Christ is denied by Peter, but man, confessed before the Father and the angels, is called by the Son of God himself. Christ is struck with blows, and the goad of Satan, striking with punishments, is driven away. Christ is spat upon, and man is defended from the spitting of the insulting wife, lest he receive the name of the sandal-less man. It was the Jews’ custom that, if anyone died childless, [Col. 0927B] the woman should be joined to his kinsman. If he refused to take her, the woman, removing his sandal, would spit in his face, and he would receive the name of the sandal-less man (Deut. 25).

This widowed woman is understood as the Law interpreted carnally: her husband, the carnal people, dies; but she is joined to another husband, namely the Christian people, when, spiritually received, she is associated with it in action. Therefore those who refuse to fulfil the Law spiritually are spat upon by it with eternal shame, because Moses accuses them before the Father (fo. 142v). It removes the sandal because it takes away from them the carnal observance. They are designated by the name of the sandal-less because, existing without the merits of righteousness, their names are erased from the book of life and written upon the earth, when they are rejected in shame by the Church [Col. 0927C] of the saints.

Christ is handed over to torturing pagans, and man, delivered to demons for torment, is set free. Christ is mocked by the Gentiles, and man is rescued from the mockery of demons. Christ is stripped of his garments and clothed in purple, while man is stripped of the rags of sins and clothed in the robe of immortality. Christ is furnished with a reed instead of a sceptre, and man is inscribed for the sceptre of God’s kingdom by the writing reed. Christ’s head is encircled with a crown of thorns, and man is crowned with glory and honour. Christ is greeted in mockery, and the angels rejoice at man’s salvation. Christ is scourged, and man is delivered from the hammers that strike him. Christ is fastened to the cross, and man is raised from eternal torment to joy. [Col. 0927D] Christ is given gall to drink, and man is fed with the bread of angels. Christ is punished by death, and dead man is restored to life. Christ, made a curse for us and hanging on the tree (Gal. 3), is taken down from the cross, and man is released from the curse. Christ is buried in the tomb, and man is placed in paradise. Christ is shut up in the prison of hell, while man is received to be crowned in the heavenly court. All these things, dearest ones, Christ’s Passion has bestowed upon us.

[Col. 0928A] During these three days we celebrate the Lord’s burial, and therefore in the divine offices we imitate the disciples’ sorrow, as we do not sound forth the *Gloria Patri* and other songs of joy, nor ring the bells for the hours, so that we may also become sharers in their joy. The lights are extinguished for three nights because, when the light of angels and men was extinguished upon the cross, three hours were enveloped in darkness.

Today chrism and oil are prepared, by which God’s servants are signed upon their foreheads, because today, through the oil of Christ’s mercy, penitents are released from the devil’s yoke. Hence it is said: “The yoke shall decay because of the oil” (Isa. 10). The yoke decayed because of the oil when Christ’s mercy rescued man from the devil’s dominion.

[Col. 0928B] Tomorrow the altar is stripped and the cross is greeted, because Christ, the true altar upon which the vows of the faithful are sacrificed to God the Father, was on that day stripped by the impious for torments; and the cross, which was mocked by them, is now reverently honoured by all.

On Saturday the people are baptized, while Christ is proclaimed to have rested in the tomb (fo. 144), because through baptism one imitates Christ’s death. For by renunciation we are crucified with Christ to the world, and through baptism we are buried with him in his death. We are crucified to vices and desires when we are immersed in baptism in the form of a cross. We are buried with the Lord for three days when, immersed three times in the waters, we are covered as though with earth. When the baptized rise from the font, they rise as though with Christ to glory. Signed with chrism, they are clothed in white, [Col. 0928C] because, endowed with immortality through Christ’s death, they shall be crowned kings and priests in the kingdom of God.

By the candle consecrated on that day is signified the pillar of fire which preceded the children of Israel from the Egyptians through the Red Sea into the land of promise. And it is Christ: as that lamb, so “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,” whose blood crushed the yoke of the cruel tyrant and carried us from his dominion through baptism. By his fire, namely the Holy Spirit, the souls of all believers are illuminated, and under his guidance they gladly journey by the way of charity to the heavenly fatherland. When their enemies had been destroyed in the Red Sea, the children of Israel went forth and sang a song to the Lord. Therefore the baptized, their sins having been wiped away in baptism, sing *Alleluia*, which is a song of joy, because they receive back the lost innocence of the first parent. [Col. 0928D] Therefore, dearest ones, since the Son of God has freed us, the slaves of sin, from harsh servitude by his own blood and restored us to true freedom, let us flee the devil’s service with all our heart, and let us serve our Deliverer in holiness and righteousness all our days, so that, when he who is our life appears, we too may appear with him in glory, “which eye has not seen,” and so forth (1 Cor. 2).

## ON THE PASCHAL DAY

[Col. 0927]

[Col. 0927D] “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. 117). All days, dearest ones, [Col. 0928D] the Lord made in his majesty; but this one above all he chose in his mercy, for joy to angels and human beings. For this sacred night put an end to the night of death and misery which, beginning with Adam’s sin, had wrapped everyone in its darkness. Today, however, began the day of happiness and joy, which no evening [no evening] shall end. All the time from Adam until Christ was called the day of death, in which every human being, dying, was led to Tartarus. But this time is called the day (fo. 144v) of life and resurrection: at its beginning Christ is proclaimed to have risen with many; at its end it is not doubted that the whole human race will rise on this same day. For on this day, namely in this time of grace, the elect, removed from the flesh, shall immediately enter into their Lord’s joy (Matt. 25); but when the final resurrection has passed, they shall possess a double portion in their land, rejoicing eternally in the Lord’s blessings with both [Col. 0929B] body and soul.

Therefore in the divine offices we now say, “Today he rose,” although we know that he rose many years ago. Because of this day’s greatness, this whole week is celebrated as one day, and hence this day is sung daily. For this reason the evening hour begins not in the customary manner but with the office of the Mass, because this sacred day is the figure of that great day which no evening ends. This is that one day better than thousands, on which ineffable joys have been bestowed upon angels and humankind through Christ. Today the Lord of hosts, having conquered death, rose from hell and brought into the court of angels, as King of glory, the people redeemed by his own blood and released from the prison of death. Today the good shepherd bore back to the flock upon his own shoulders the lost sheep, found with great labour, and joined it to the rejoicing angels in heaven. On this day let us exult with God’s creation, which today through Christ’s resurrection has been restored to the rights of eternity. On this day let us rejoice with the orders of angels, because today their number is filled up by human beings. For on this day heaven’s height rejoices in serenity because today Jerusalem is rebuilt in it as a city. [Col. 0929C] Today the citizens above rejoice because, through Christ, chosen human beings are numbered among them. Today the sun, moon, and stars display their joy by shining more brightly—those which, at Christ’s death, manifested grief by concealing their rays. And rightly so: for the moon has the brightness of the sun, while the sun is promised the brightness of seven days’ light. Today the earth rejoices above every creature, because Christ is made human from its material, is buried dead in its bosom, and it is exalted in his substance above every rank of angels. Today springs, seas, and rivers are made joyful by calmness; in blessing God, they make known that Christ has washed away the world’s crimes in their waters. Today birds leap with sweet joy as they sweetly rejoice, as it were, with responsive voices in sweet melody. Today everything created by God is flooded with joy through Christ’s resurrection: the sky with serenity, the waves with calmness, forests with leaves, meadows with flowers, fields with crops, and diverse animals with joyful offspring (fo. 146). [Col. 0929D] Hell alone groans in sorrow because the mighty Lord today broke its bronze gates and iron bars. Tartarus alone, I say, is afflicted by bitter grief, because today the stronger Lion from the tribe of Judah conquered the strong lion and, returning on high, placed in the heavenly palace the prey that insatiable hell had devoured.

This is the splendid solemnity of solemnities, which, as Lucifer among the stars or topaz among gems, stands as the glory of all feasts. It is shared by angels and human beings, because today man has been restored to the heavenly seats. This sacred feast is called Pascha, that is, “Passage,” because, just as the people of the Hebrews were delivered through the blood of the slain lamb when the angel passed through Egypt to strike it, so the people of believers are defended from the devil through the blood of Christ, the true Lamb. And just as that people, freed from [Col. 0930B] Pharaoh’s yoke, passed into the land of promise, so the Christian people, freed through Christ from the devil’s yoke, shall pass into the fatherland of paradise.

Therefore, “you who have been redeemed by the Lord, sing to him a new song; his praise is in the Church of the saints” (Ps. 149). He sings the new song who, abandoning sins, begins a new life in good works.
