Let true Israel, namely the people of believers, “rejoice in him who made him” (ibid.) and who rescued him, fleeing from exile to his fatherland, with Leah and Rachel, and restrained Laban pursuing with his companions; that is, the Lord rescued the Christian people from the exile of this life—with active and contemplative life—while it was tending toward the fatherland of paradise, and restrains the devil who obstructs it [Col. 0930C] with temptations and persecutions. Let the daughters of Zion also, that is, souls reborn in Christ, today exult in their King, who will clothe them with the garment of salvation and the robe of righteousness. Today “my soul magnifies the Lord”; I ask all brothers: magnify him with me and exalt his name together with a great voice (Ps. 33), namely in Christ. Let us recount today his praises, his powers, and his wonders which he has performed, because the Lord redeemed his despised servant, lost (fo. 346v) from the pit of misery, raised him from the mud of filth, and placed him upon the throne of glory with princes. My soul exults in the Lord, whom every spirit should praise today with rejoicing. My mouth declares the praise of the Lord, and I ask that all flesh bless his holy name (Ps. 144).

A servant is led by a tyrant from the fatherland of paradise into exile, and the king’s son is sent from the palace into prison to call him back. The hundredth sheep, straying from the flock, is carried off by the wolf; but the loving shepherd clothes himself in flesh to rescue it. Thus he through whom every creature is made from nothing becomes a little man from the frail female sex. He who encloses all things in his fist is enclosed in a maiden’s womb. He through whom the whole world is created is born from a woman. Wrapped in swaddling clothes, he is laid in a manger; he who clothes the angels in glory is upheld by the throne of majesty. He in whose sight not even the heavens are declared clean is purified by circumcision and sacrifice. He is subject to human parents, [Col. 0931A] though every highest rank of angelic dignity bows in submission to his service. He by whose holiness sin is wiped away is immersed in water by a servant. He is tempted by the enemy while hungry, though by him the love of angels is confirmed in glory; he satisfies them with his ineffable sweetness, while they always desire to look upon him. He who is the source of all good things and the relief of all labours is wearied by a journey and asks for water to quench his thirst. He is overcome by sleep, though the choirs of heaven are described as watching in praise of him. He from whom comes every blessing is cursed; he whom demons tremble before (Jas. 2) is called demon-possessed. He at whose name every knee bends, of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal (Phil. 2), bends his knee to wash his disciples’ feet. He is afflicted with sadness and grief, though through him the multitude of the blessed is filled with joy and gladness.

He who thus lived among human beings, hidden under a servant’s form, shone forth as true God through signs and miracles. For the morning stars praised him at his birth (Job 38), when immediately the heavens sent a new star in his service. All the sons of God shouted for joy over him (ibid.), when the angels cried out in loud praise, “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 1). Kings hastened to be present with gifts and, in worship, bowed their necks to the King of glory. Heaven was opened above him; the Father’s voice bore witness to the Son; the Holy Spirit, descending upon him, worked with him in all things. Angels ministered to him; unclean spirits feared his presence. The true vine turned water (fo. 148) into wine; eternal life raised the dead by a word. The light [Col. 0931C] of the world restored sight to the blind and opened the blocked ears of the deaf. The Word of God loosened the bonds of mute tongues; crowds of paralytics, healed at his command, took up their beds. He checked the flow of blood; the source of life extinguished the burning of fevers. He granted walking to the lame and cleansing to lepers; he expelled troops of demons from the possessed. The living bread satisfied four thousand people with seven loaves. Again, the bread of angels fed five thousand with five loaves. He walked over the sea’s waves with dry feet and calmed the rage of the winds. He forgave criminals their sins; in his name the disciples tread down every power of the enemy. And because sun and moon marvel at his beauty, he was transfigured as God before his own disciples. And because he was “fairer in form than the children of men” [Col. 0931D] (Ps. 44), his face shone like the sun. And because he is shown to be judge of the living and the dead, Moses, dead, and Elijah, living, spoke with him.

After the true light had shone in darkness for thirty-three years and more through these and like acts, gathering the scattered children of God into one faith—or rather, abundantly instructing fugitive servants in their return to the fatherland—the dark hearts of the Jews could not bear the immeasurable radiance of flame-bearing light. Therefore, massed together with weapons and torches, they wished to extinguish it. At first they were thrown down by his word; then, with his own consent, they accomplished the world’s salvation. Thus the good shepherd is seized by thieves and robbers, but the little flock is scattered by wolves. The Lamb is sacrificed for the sheep, and life is strangled by death. Then the cornerstone, approved by God, is rejected by the builders—the stone in which the joining of the two walls coming from East and West is united (1 Pet. 2). [Col. 0932A] For in being born he drew Gentiles with gifts from the East; in dying he drew Gentiles through confession from the West. Pilate and the Roman centurion were from the West, and they called him righteous (Matt. 27) or the Son of God (ibid.). But the Jews, the cultivators of God’s vineyard, condemned the heir—afflicted with many insults and reproaches—to a most shameful death (Wis. 2), when they lifted him up on the cross as Moses did the serpent in the wilderness (Num. 22). Then the sweet cluster of henna (*cyprus*) was borne upon a pole, and the sweet draught of life was pressed from it in the winepress of the cross.

Yet heaven, which at his birth was illuminated with new light, was darkened by horrible shadows at his death on the cross. The sun, which at his birth was crowned with a golden circle (fo. 148v), was darkened by mournful gloom at his death. The earth, which at his birth poured out honeycombs of oil, trembled as though about to collapse at his death, vomiting out the dead. Taken down from the wood, with the curse undone, he slept, troubled, in the tomb. The Jews, rolling a great stone over the tomb, sealed it and set guards lest he be stolen by the disciples. They shut in Joseph, who had buried him, under guard and fortified him with a seal and guards; but Nicodemus, who had heard him, they deposed from his rank. Meanwhile the King of glory entered the dark kingdom of the tyrant with an army of angels, snatched away its spoils, returned today with noble pomp, placed those released from the abyss in heaven, [Col. 0932C] restored by human beings the fallen angelic wall, raised his body from the tomb, never again to die, and grants eternal life to all who love him. Therefore a heavenly messenger is now sent beforehand to report this to the sorrowing disciples, so that their sadness may be turned to joy. He removed the stone from the tomb and sat upon it; his face shone like lightning and his clothing like snow. At the sight of him the guards were terrified and became as dead men.

Mary, Lazarus’s sister; Mary, mother of James, later bishop of Jerusalem; and Mary, the Lord’s mother’s sister, wife of Salome, came to the tomb with precious ointments, intending to anoint the Lord so that he might not be corrupted by worms. [Col. 0932D] But at the sight of the angel they were overwhelmed with great fear, and were gently comforted by the angel. He announced to them that the Lord had risen, death having been conquered, and indicated that he would be seen in Galilee.

Meanwhile the Lord of the resurrection appeared to Joseph in prison, shining like the sun. Joseph thought him Elijah; but he declared himself to be Jesus, whom Joseph had buried and who was now raised from death, and set Joseph, taken from the prison, in Arimathea. On that same day the Jews gathered in council and sent to the prison, commanding that Joseph be brought for judgment. Those who returned reported that they had found the prison closed and the seal sound, but that when the prison was opened they found no one there. While they hesitated over this, behold, certain of the guards came running and reported that Jesus [Col. 0933A] had truly risen and that they themselves had seen angelic visions. But when the Jews did not believe them and wickedly demanded back the body entrusted to their guard, they gave this response: “Hand over Joseph, whom you guard, and we shall hand over Jesus, whom you entrusted to be guarded. But just as you could not guard Joseph so that he did not escape by divine power, so we could not prevent this man—since he was God—from rising.” On hearing this, they gave the soldiers abundant money and persuaded them to say that he had been stolen by the disciples while they slept. After receiving the money, the soldiers reported to their master both that Jesus had risen and that they had received money from the Jews.

Therefore, when the sun that knew its setting rose and again illumined with its radiance the world darkened by sorrow at its absence, immediately our [uncertain: text appears defective], which by his death had now dissolved the enmity between God and human beings, made peace between all things in heaven and on earth, and reconciled the world to God the Father by his blood, appeared to the disciples, announced peace, and gladdened their hearts with great joy. He ate broiled fish and a honeycomb with them, thereby showing that through his Passion he will give the sweetness of eternal life to all who hope in him. [Col. 0933B] Moreover, many saints who had risen with Christ came into the city and, appearing to many, told them very much about the other life and made them glad in all things of the Lord. These are the sacred joys of this day, celebrated by angels and human beings, prefigured and foretold by patriarchs and prophets.

For Joseph is sent by his father after his brothers into the wilderness, but by them, at Judah’s counsel, is sold into Egypt. He is wantonly seized by a lustful mistress and, while the household clamours, is shut in prison after resisting her. From there he is led forth; by the king he is made ruler, and the name “Saviour of the world” is imposed upon him. He is worshipped by his brothers and all the people, and Egypt is freed from famine through him.

So Christ is sent by the Father after fugitive servants, but is sold by Judas at the counsel of the Jews. He is cruelly seized by the Synagogue, wanton in carnal matters; like Joseph surrounded by the household, he is surrounded by soldiers; slain, he is enclosed in the tomb as [Joseph] in prison. Rising from there, he is established by the King of all as ruler, God above [Col. 0933D] all things; his name, “Saviour of the world,” is loved everywhere by every people. He is worshipped by eleven sun, moon, and stars because today he is devoutly venerated by Joseph and Mary and the eleven apostles. And behold, he is worshipped by all peoples and tongues (fo. 150v), and through him the whole world is saved.

In former times God’s people were afflicted by enemies, but Samson was foretold through an angel as one who would be born to rescue them. Born a Nazarite, that is, a holy man, he lived, and the spirit of strength directed his deeds. After he had grown up, he went to the nation of his enemies and slew a lion on the road. Afterwards he took honey from its carcass, married a foreign woman, proposed at a feast the riddle concerning the honey and lion, and promised a reward to those who solved it. When, with Samson himself revealing it to his wife and she in turn telling them, [Col. 0934A] they solved it, they received the promised reward. But when he returned to his father and mother in his homeland, his wife was violated by another; returning, he avenged this with foxes and fire (Judg. 13–16).

So the people of God were oppressed in this world by demons, but the true Samson—whose name means “sun,” namely Christ—was announced by an angel to his virgin mother as one who would save them. Born a Nazarite, that is, holy, he lived blamelessly in all things, and the spirit of strength dwelling in him directed all his deeds. He goes to the nation of his enemies when he proceeds into Judaea to suffer. He crushed the lion on the road when he himself, the way to life, on the road of this mortality defeated upon the cross the devil, who “goes about as a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour.” [Col. 0934B] He ate honey taken from the lion’s carcass when, drawing from hell’s belly the sweet souls of the elect whom that greedy robber had devoured, he incorporated them into himself. He joined a foreign woman to himself because he united to himself by faith the Church from the Gentiles. He proposed a riddle at the feast because he wished believers to be instructed from Sacred Scripture concerning his incarnation, his victory, and the salvation of the righteous. Its mysteries are opened daily to the Church, his bride, by the key of David, are solved by Catholic interpreters, and thus understood by the faithful, who will be rewarded by him with the prize of eternal life. But when he returns to the heavenly fatherland, to the right hand of the Father and to his mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, his wife the Church is corrupted by heretics; this he will avenge when he returns for judgment with flame [Col. 0934C] and demons.

This Samson, bound with many cords, is handed over to his enemies by his kinsmen. But he, having broken the bonds, struck down a multitude of enemies with an ass’s jawbone and put others to flight. Having won victory, he suffers from thirst; but a spring bursting forth from the jawbone refreshes the victor.

Thus Christ, bound by his own kinsmen the Jews (fol. 152), was handed over, bound, to the Gentiles for destruction. But he, loosing the bonds of death, overcame by his humanity the bands of demons, drove them from the human race, and through the apostles conquered his adversaries. For the Jewish people, through folly, was an ass. From it Christ’s flesh is born: the jawbone that crushes the hard fodder of the Law, while disclosing to us its profound mysteries. [Col. 0934D] The spring bursting forth from the jawbone is the font of baptism flowing from Christ. Our victor thirsts for human salvation, and that thirst is quenched by baptism and by the faith of the faithful.

Here likewise Samson enters a city to a woman, but is besieged by his enemies. Yet at midnight he carried off the bars of the gates and, bearing them on his shoulders, ascended a mountain through the ranks of his enemies.

Thus Christ enters to his wife—that is, to the Church held there in hell—but is besieged by enemies in the tomb. Yet at midnight he shatters the bars of hell; having taken away the captives, he empties the dens of roaring lions and the lairs of dragons, the houses of punishments and hiding places of darkness. Rising from death, he terrifies the guards and penetrates heaven’s heights.

A harlot makes this Samson drunk and lays him in her lap [Col. 0935A] to sleep. While he sleeps she shaves the hair of his head and delivers him, bound, into the hands of his enemies. By them he is blinded and consigned to prison. From there he is brought out on the day of the feast; but when, through him, two columns are shaken, the building is brought down, and as he dies a great multitude is crushed.

This harlot is the Synagogue, which made Christ drunk with bitterness and placed him asleep in her lap, when Jerusalem, by its torments, laid him down into the sleep of death. She cut off his hair when she cut off the disciples, who clung to him as it were like hairs. She handed him over bound to his enemies, because she offered the Lord, bound, to the Gentiles. He is blinded by his enemies when, by the soldiers, he is deprived of the light of this life. He is shut in prison when he is laid in the tomb and mourned. He is brought forth on the day of the feast [Col. 0935B] when, on the day of Passover—the day of the angels’ feast—he is raised from the tomb. But when the two columns are shaken, the house is brought down and the people crushed: after Christ’s passion, when two kings are disturbed, the Temple, which was the house of the Jews’ feast, is overthrown, and the people are destroyed in vengeance for Christ’s death.

Their figure is also set forth for us in the nature of animals. For it is reported that a lion sleeps with its eyes open and erases its tracks with its tail so that it cannot be found by hunters: thus the Lord Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, slept and underwent the sleep of death in his humanity, but kept watch in his divinity. He so concealed the mystery of our restoration in the flesh that [Col. 0935C] demons or persecutors could not trace it out.

For it is said that a lioness bears her cubs dead, and that at the voice of their roaring father they rise on the third day. Thus Christ, who lay dead in the tomb for three days, rose on the third day, awakened by the Father’s voice, as Jacob, the foremost patriarch, once prophesied concerning him: “Judah shall sleep like a lion’s cub. Who shall raise him? You have gone down to the prey, my son. He shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the olive” (Gen. XLIX).

[Col. 0936A] The Lord of the tribe of Judah slept like a lion’s cub when he lay hidden in death for three days; the Father raised him on the third day. He went down to the prey when he descended to the lower regions, bound the strong one, and plundered his spoils. He washed his robe in wine when his body was drenched with blood. He washed his cloak in the blood of the olive when he sanctified the Church with the oil of chrism.

Because this was to come to pass, God had formerly foreshadowed it even through birds. For the phoenix lives more than five hundred years; then it gathers branches from fragrant trees into its nest, and, striking its wings, is set alight by the sun’s heat, is burned in its nest, and on the third day is restored in the form of its former little bird. *Phoenix* means “red,” and it is Christ, of whom it is said: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (Isa. [Col. 0936B] LXIII). Edom, which means “red,” was the name given to Esau because of the red stew with which his brother Jacob fed him. From him the kingdom of Idumaea took its name, whose capital city was Bozrah. Job ruled there; by his weakness he prefigured Christ’s passion. Christ comes from Edom when he suffers at the hands of the Gentiles and his flesh is reddened by blood. His garment is dyed in Bozrah when, in Jerusalem, which was the capital of the kingdom, his garment is sprinkled with blood. Like the phoenix, he gathered branches of fragrant trees into his nest when he fulfilled Jerusalem by the writings of the prophets. He is burned with those same branches in the nest when, according to the prophets’ sayings, he is consumed in Jerusalem by the fire of the Passion. On the third day the bird is restored, [Col. 0936C] because Christ is raised by the Father on the third day.

It is also reported that the pelican loves its young so greatly that it kills them with its claws. But on the third day, through grief, it tears itself apart, and blood from its side (fol. 154), dripping upon the young, raises them from death. The pelican signifies the Lord, who so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for it; on the third day he raised him victorious over death and exalted him above every name.

Preach faith and confession to them here; then add this:

[Col. 0935]

[Col. 0935C] Dearest brethren, since Christ today rose from the dead, we too ought to rise from the death of the soul, namely sins, so that, because Christ dies no more, we may live with him forever.

One reads of a certain eminent Father that by his deeds [Col. 0935D] and words he greatly benefited the life of the brethren. Urged by the devil, he fell into the pit of fornication. But by God’s prompting he was raised to repentance, and for a whole year afflicted himself with fasts and vigils. On the night of the Lord’s Resurrection, he set up a lamp which he had furnished with oil and wood; prostrate upon the ground and drenched with a rain of tears, he prayed to the Son of God that, if his sin had been forgiven, that lamp might be lit. And behold, he looked and saw the lamp, divinely kindled, [Col. 0936C] shining with a glittering flame, and its light illuminating his heart with joy and gladness. With all his strength he gave thanks to God’s immeasurable mercy; every day he added oil to the lamp, and when he died, it was extinguished. To this fountain of mercy today, [Col. 0936D] dearest brethren, all draw near with your prayers, and commend your soul and body to the depths of his compassion, so that, when he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father and God is all in all (1 Cor. XV), through Christ’s resurrection you may be co-heirs of God’s kingdom, when the righteous shall shine like the sun (Matt. XIII) and be equal to the angels in that glory (Matt. XXII), which no eye has seen (1 Cor. II).

This [sermon] is for the octave, or for any day within the Easter season.

[Col. 0935]

[Col. 0935D] “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI). Christ, dearest brethren, having trampled down the abyss, has now risen from the dead as victor; [Col. 0936D] and he has brought us, rescued from the exile of death, into eternal life. Therefore, though dead to sins, we ought to rise with Christ to virtues, and run by the course of good works toward the prize of life set [Col. 0937A] before us. And because Christ no longer dies for us, let us walk in his footsteps, lest we die again in soul. And because death shall no longer have dominion over Christ, seated now at the right hand of God, let us seek the things above, lest eternal death again have dominion over us (fol. 154).

The seven-headed dragon, prince of darkness, drew down with his tail a part of the stars from heaven, covered them with the cloud of sins, and wrapped them in the darkness of death. Therefore the eternal Sun covered the radiance of his brightness with the cloud of flesh. At the setting of death he set for the stars; he himself, rising from the night of death, brought those drawn from the gloom back to the clear heaven. Therefore they shone joyfully for him who made them, because with great jubilation [Col. 0937B] the souls of the elect praise God who redeemed them. Leviathan, a sea-fish, has the form of a dragon; it devours a multitude of fishes, from which many return through its open jaws.

By this sea the present age is signified, continually raised in surging waves of adversity. In it the devil swims around as Leviathan and devours a multitude of souls. But God, who presides in heaven, stretched a hook into this sea when he sent his Son into this world to catch Leviathan. The line of this hook is Christ’s genealogy, woven by the Evangelists. Its barb is Christ’s divinity, while its bait is his humanity. The rod by which the hook’s line is extended into the waves is the holy cross, on which Christ was suspended in order to deceive the devil. When this Leviathan seeks greedily to tear with the tooth of death the bait of his flesh, [Col. 0937C] it is pierced by the hidden hook, and the twisting serpent is drawn forth from the waves: that is, through faith in Christ, its worship falls away among all nations, and it is drawn every day from the hearts of the faithful, pierced by Christ’s name [the text perhaps reads *confossis*, “pierced,” rather than *confusis*, “confounded”]. Moreover, its jaw is pierced by the bracelet of God’s mercy, and, when Christ presses its neck, it is compelled to disgorge the choice food which the wicked robber greedily devoured. Thus David, whom it sweetly swallowed through lust, it vomited forth, pierced by repentance; Peter, whom it swallowed through Christ’s denial, it gave back, pierced by tears; Mary, whom it devoured through desire of the flesh, it did not delay to restore, [Col. 0937D] pierced by tears. Through Christ’s mercy, an opening stands open in its pierced jaw for all; and every unwary person devoured by it can come out through repentance. “It swallows a river and is not amazed,” because it does not greatly value the fact that it devours the streams of unbelieving Gentiles. “It has confidence that the Jordan may flow into its mouth,” because it thirsts to swallow the baptized people. “It shall eat grass like an ox” (Dan. IV), because it despises those carnally minded whom it devours. Its food is called choice because it reckons it among its greatest delights if its malign persuasion is refreshed by the fall of spiritual persons. Hence it is reported (fol. 156) in books that demons who in a city had dragged many slain in a riot and very many drowned at sea in a storm down to Tartarus in a short time were ordered to be beaten with whips, [Col. 0938A] as though they had accomplished too little in so great a time; but one who, after assailing a monk in the wilderness for forty years, had scarcely at last driven him into the abyss of fornication, was crowned as worthy of praise, because he had manfully accomplished a difficult deed. Why indeed should the devil labor over those who with their whole effort are hastening to him at every hour and are anxious with all their strength not to come alone? He labors in every way to draw back and delay those who, fleeing his jaws toward life, hasten to Christ.

There is a beast called the crocodile, twenty feet in length. By day it remains in the waters, but by night on land. It attacks, tears apart, and devours passers-by; lying in the sun, it sleeps with its mouth open. There is also another creature, called the *enydrus*, filled with spines [Col. 0938B] like a hedgehog. Covering itself in mud, it enters the crocodile’s open mouth and is immediately swallowed by it. It pierces all its innards with its spines, kills the beast, and returns alive.

By the crocodile the devil is represented, because before Christ’s advent he dwelt in the fluid hearts of the Gentiles, but now in the dry minds of the Jews. He devours those who pass by, because before Christ’s Passion he seized all who died and carried them off to Tartarus. Yet even now, with open mouth, he longs to swallow the streams of the Jordan, because in his greed he hastens to devour even the baptized. The spiny little creature is Christ’s flesh, afflicted by our miseries and sufferings. It covers itself in mud when it submitted to the reproaches of death. It enters the beast’s mouth when it is swallowed by insatiable hell. But it disembowels the beast and [Col. 0938C] comes forth victorious, because Christ despoils hell and returns victorious to the stars.

Dearest brethren, death poured out its fury upon life; but life became the death of death, because conquered death gave way to it. It became the bite of hell, because it took one part from it and left another part behind. He ate the honeycomb with honey when, rising again, he clothed in bodies the souls of the elect from the lion’s mouth—the lion shattered by Samson on the way—and, ascending with them, brought them into the glory of angels. He made his beloved ones drunk with his wine [and] milk when, appearing to his own after the resurrection, he gladdened their hearts with the draught of joy. For the stars of the sea, after he himself, the true light, shone upon the world, the sun rising from death appeared to one grieving for his death (fol. 156 verso). He also revealed himself, risen as consoler, [Col. 0938D] to Mary Magdalene, whom he cleansed from seven demons, when she wept at his tomb and believed that he had been taken away from it. Appearing also to Peter, he consoles him while his heart is troubled with sorrow because of his denial. He appeared too to James, the son of his maternal aunt, who had remained without food from Friday until that day, because he had been so certain of Christ’s resurrection that he had vowed not to eat before seeing Christ alive.

He revealed himself to two women returning from the tomb and made them rejoice in his resurrection.

He also appeared as a traveler on the road to two who were going to Emmaus, and entered with them to recline at supper. But when evening came, with the doors shut, he revealed himself to all [Col. 0939A]; by peace he greeted them, and by food he confirmed his resurrection. On the eighth day he again showed them his presence and offered Thomas his side to touch.

He revealed himself to seven disciples laboring at fishing; he commanded them to cast the net to the right, in which a multitude of fish was enclosed and yet it was not torn. They themselves drew the fish to shore and entered into a meal with the Lord.

Before his resurrection too, the disciples were fishing, and their net was torn by the multitude of fishes. This sea is the present age. Into it God’s fishers—that is, the teachers of the Church—cast the net of faith by preaching, and enclosed a multitude of people. Some of them, tearing the net, sprang back into the sea, [Col. 0939B] because heretics, having broken the net of faith, went out into worldly things, since they were not of us.

After the resurrection, however, only seven were fishing, and the net was not torn. By seven all are signified who are illumined by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. For seven is divided into three and four: by three, faith in the Trinity is expressed; by four, fulfillment of the four Gospels. Therefore those who are found, at the general resurrection, in faith in the Trinity and in evangelical practice are drawn from the waves of the world by sevenfold grace to the shore of eternal firmness. They are caught also on the right side, because the righteous, separated from the wicked by angels, are set at God’s right hand. And the number of one hundred and fifty-three is recorded for them, by which are understood three orders of those to be saved. [Col. 0939C] For by one hundred, perfection, which pertains to virgins, is demonstrated; by fifty, forgiveness, which pertains to widows, is indicated; by three, faith in the Trinity, which is fitting for the married, is made known. They enter into God’s banquet with the Lord when, after judgment has been completed, they enter with him into the wedding feast, where “the righteous rejoice and feast in the sight of God and delight in gladness” (Ps. LXVII); where they “shall be made drunk from the abundance of the Lord God and, drinking from the torrent of his delight, shall be satisfied” (Ps. XXXV).

The Church now commemorates in shadow, through the solemnity of the Easter feast, the celebration of this immeasurable joy to come. Therefore it is observed not according to the conjunction of the sun but according to the lunar cycle, at the full moon of the first month; for by the moon the Church is figured, illumined by the radiance of the eternal Sun. When her circuit is completed in the elect, she will immediately be assumed to the banquet of eternal sweetness. Thus through Septuagesima, during which, laying aside Alleluia—the song of joy—we sing the song of sorrow, we recall the seventy years of the people of God’s captivity from Jerusalem in Babylon; and we signify our own pilgrimage, by which, driven from paradise’s joys into this world’s exile, we lament that we are afflicted with toil and sorrow. Through Quadragesima we recall the forty years of the children of Israel’s return from Egypt to the promised land, and express our return from this world to the homeland of paradise through observance of the four Gospels and the Ten Commandments of the Law. Moreover, through the singing of the tracts [Col. 0940A] we represent the labor of the journey, because we proclaim that through many tribulations we shall enter the kingdom of God. By the three days before Easter, the three years of Antichrist’s time are understood to be foreshadowed, during which all things in the world will be disturbed by his savagery. Therefore penitents are admitted on these days, because at that time the Jews will be converted to the Church through repentance. Therefore on these days the Passion of Christ, which is [who is] our head, is celebrated, because at that time his body, which is the Church, is tormented by various sufferings. On these days a multitude of believers is regenerated through baptism, because at that time the whole company of the faithful is renewed to life through resurrection. But by the day of Christ’s resurrection our resurrection is prefigured, because it is proclaimed that on the very day and at the very hour [Col. 0940B] on which Christ rose, the whole human race will rise. On that day the queen, the Lamb’s bride, shall stand joyfully at his right hand in golden raiment; here, while a pilgrim in Babylon, the enemy fed her with the bread of tears. On that day too the devil, her enemy, with his entire (fol. 158 verso) body, shall be cast down into the lake of fire and sulphur in the sight of all; and she, brought by the angelic host with triumphal glory into the heavenly Jerusalem, shall be placed in the royal bridal chamber to be united with her bridegroom. Because the Church hopes that this will come to pass, she celebrates this feast with such exultation. But by the Easter season, in which Alleluia is often repeated, the solemnity of eternal joy is designated, where the saints shall rejoice in everlasting glory and sing the sweet-sounding Alleluia with the angels forever.

We also make this known in the divine offices when we sing, “The Lord brought you into a land flowing with milk and honey,” which we understand as paradise, the land of the living. Likewise we sing, “Come, blessed of the Father” (Matt. XXV), which we read that the Lord will say at judgment after our resurrection has taken place. Likewise we sing: “The Lord brought forth his people in exultation and his elect in gladness” (Ps. CIV), which we believe will be done then, when they shall obtain joy and gladness and the righteous shall shine sevenfold like the sun, equal to angels (Isa. XXX; Matt. XIII). Easter is called *pascha*, that is, “passage,” because, just as the Hebrew people passed from slavery to freedom, so the faithful people shall then pass from sorrow [Col. 0940D] to joy, from corruption to incorruption, and from mortality to immortality. Hence they saw Jesus after the resurrection in Galilee, whose name conveys a completed migration, because, passing from death to eternal life, they shall see the Lord face to face as he is (1 John III). But those who refused to rise in the first resurrection shall have no part in the second resurrection. Those who say to God, “Do not come near us,” shall be straw and the smoke of a fire in his wrath; and they shall possess the land of darkness, where no order and everlasting horror dwell (Job X). Their streams shall be turned to pitch, their smoke to sulphur, and their land to burning pitch; it shall not be quenched forever (Isa. XXXIV). Then the righteous, for the double shame [Col. 0941A] which they endured here, both in body and in possessions upon earth, shall possess their double portion, because they shall rejoice in soul and body together. We now prefigure this double joy when we sound two Alleluias at Mass. The whole world also is shown now to applaud us in this festival when it is renewed with reviving adornments, as God will then, for the glory of his children, change every creature of the world: he will create a new heaven and a new earth (Isa. LXV); heaven will shine like the sun, earth will bloom like paradise, and the moon will shine sevenfold [Col. 0942A] brighter than it does now. Former things will not be remembered because of the all-surpassing glory which they shall possess. Past evils shall not come upon the heart, but they shall rejoice and exult in gladness forever. Therefore, dearest brethren, celebrate this Easter feast with continual praises of God, and prepare yourselves by good works for the feast to come, so that, when God has made Jerusalem an exultation and her people a joy, you may rejoice forever in the new Jerusalem, and God may rejoice in you, where there is splendor, everlasting light, and joy without end—the joy which eye has not seen (1 Cor. II), and so forth.

If the people have assembled for the Major Litany, you may give the sermon “Christ Rising,” or “The Eyes of the Lord”; and add these words concerning Saint Mark:

[Col. 0941]

[Col. 0941A] Today, dearest brethren, call upon Saint Mark in your needs, who was like one of the four rivers of paradise. He bears the form of a lion because, in the wilderness of this world, the voice of his preaching sounded like a lion. Hence his Gospel is read on the Easter day, because Christ is described as having risen like a lion. He was sent with Paul by the apostles to preach, and cooperated greatly with him in the word of God. Blessed Peter baptized him and raised him from the font as his son. While he was with Peter in Rome, he put forth in writing the Gospel which afterward resounded throughout the whole world. He was sent by Saint Peter to Aquileia, and there he gained a great multitude of people for Christ. Then he returned to Rome with Hermagoras, and Hermagoras was ordained bishop by Peter in his place. But Mark departed for Egypt, and Alexandria was subjected through him to the yoke of faith. Lest he should [Col. 0942A] exercise the priesthood, he cut off his own thumb. Yet because he was whole in faith, the Church elevated him as bishop in the Alexandrian see. He nobly instructed the people entrusted to him by deeds, words, and writings, and shone gloriously, renowned for miracles. On the Easter [Col. 0942B] day he was seized by pagans and cruelly afflicted: a rope was placed about his neck, and he was dragged over stony places, his flesh torn here and there by the rocks. Then he was thrust into prison, where at midnight he was strengthened by an angel; afterward the Lord himself visited him and called him to the heavenly kingdom. On the following day, while being dragged by the impious, he was released from the suffering of the flesh and joined in heaven to the rejoicing angels. His body was later translated to Venice and greatly glorified by miracles (fol. 160 verso). You ought in every respect to imitate his teaching, so that you may share his glory—the glory which eye has not seen (1 Cor. II), and so forth.

## ON THE FINDING OF THE HOLY CROSS

[Col. 0941]

[Col. 0941C] “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. IV). The light of God’s countenance is Christ, who is the radiance of his glory and the image of his substance; he is the true light that enlightens every person (John I), a light which the horror of darkness could not comprehend. This light has been marked upon us when Christ’s name has been marked with chrism upon our foreheads by the imprint of the holy cross. This sign of salvation, consecrated by the blood of the spotless Lamb, is to be revered by angels and human beings. Through it we have been reconciled from death; through it we have been restored to life. Through it the losses of the heavenly court have been made good; through it the joys of the angelic companies have been doubled. For almighty God furnished the palace of the heavenly Jerusalem completely, for his praise, with shining orders of angels [Col. 0941D]; but the first archangel, departing from God, wickedly destroyed this order and, drawing part of the angels down from heaven, led them with himself to Tartarus. Wishing to repair the loss of this fall, God made humankind from clay and placed it in the paradise of every delight. He granted every pleasure of paradise, but forbade the fruit of a single tree, for the sake of obedience. Yet the devil, driven by envy and already deprived of every good, could not bear that [Col. 0942C] this creature of clay should attain the height of that glory from which he himself, once glorious, had been expelled. In the same manner in which he fell, he drove humankind too into ruin. He claimed for himself God’s likeness and incited humankind to desire it. What more need be said? Humankind consented to the devil and ate from the forbidden tree. Through a tree, humanity became guilty and offended God. It was driven from paradise into exile, afflicted with many miseries, and consigned to death itself (Gen. II–III). Therefore the Father’s only-begotten Son rose from the throne of glory, put on flesh, and came into prison for the deceived servant. And because the immortal one is fashioned, he became decay; the eternal creator became a worm, in order to reconcile humanity to God. He overcame the devil as he tempted him, just as he had tempted the first human; triumphing on the wood of the cross, he bound the strong one, and called redeemed humanity back from exile to its heavenly homeland. [Col. 0942D] This victorious cross was foreshadowed from the beginning in many ways; through it alone all things in heaven and on earth have been restored. Through it the chrism, baptism, and sacraments of Christ’s body are consecrated for us; through it all blessings are cleansed. Through it every device of the crafty enemy is dissolved; through it all adversities are overcome.

God in the beginning planted the paradise of delight, in [Col. 0943A] which every tree was beautiful to look upon and pleasant for food; he also caused the tree of life to spring up in the midst of it. If humanity had not eaten its fruit, remaining happily in one state, it could never have died. Paradise, which means “garden of delights,” is the Church, in which are all the delights of the Scriptures; in it diverse trees, beautiful to behold and pleasant to taste, are produced, while prophets and apostles, beautiful in works and sweet in teaching, are set before us as examples. The tree of life is understood to be the holy cross, from which the fruit of eternal life is taken. Whoever eats of it worthily shall never see death (John VIII). This is the tree planted beside waters (Ps. I), because the holy cross is preached through all the streams of Scripture. [Col. 0943B] Abel is killed by wood, and Christ is fastened to the wood of the cross. A race of living creatures is raised from the waters of the flood by wood, because the Church, aided by the wood of the cross, is raised from the perilous waves of the world to the stars.

Abraham stood beneath the tree and ministered to the Lord in three angels, whom he adored as one (Gen. XVIII), rejoicing greatly that he saw the desired day. Thus the faithful people stand under the branches of the cross through faith; they minister to the Lord in his members; they honor him in three persons and worship his majesty in unity. They worship greatly, that they may see the Lord’s day in joy.

Likewise, the ram was caught by its horns among the thorns when Abraham offered his son to God (Gen. XXII); that is, Christ is entangled among the Jews by the horns of the cross when he is slain as an offering to the Father for us. Hence the prophet says: “Horns are in his hands” (Hab. III). He had horns in his hands when, for the people who contradicted him, he spread out his hands upon the arms of the cross. There his strength was hidden; but death went before his face, driven away from the elect by the cross. He appeared to us in the burning bush, when he came down to free the people from Egyptian affliction. This bush kindled by fire is the holy cross, around which the flame of the wrath, envy, and cruelty of the Jews blazed. By the thorns of the bush we understand their sharp tongues. Thus the Lord appeared to Moses in the bush’s flame when Christ, in the fire of the Passion, hung upon the cross before (fol. 162 verso) the Synagogue [Col. 0943D]. He then came down to free the people from Egypt because he descended to hell to rescue the people from there. Understanding this, Moses said: “I beseech you, Lord, send him whom you are going to send” (Exod. IV).

Moses’ rod is changed into a dragon, and the dragons of the magicians are devoured by it. This rod is the holy cross, which by its punishment put Christ’s flesh to death, and whose death overcame our two deaths, namely those of body and soul. With this rod the sea is divided, the people redeemed, and the pursuing enemy drowned in the waters; that is, by the holy cross holy baptism is accomplished, through which the multitude of those reborn is rescued from death, and the pursuing enemy—namely original sin—is overwhelmed. With this rod the rock is struck twice [Col. 0944A] and water is brought forth, when Christ is fastened to the two pieces of wood of the cross and water of redemption is drawn from him.

When the people were passing out of Egypt and in the wilderness could not drink the water because of its bitterness, the Lord showed Moses a piece of wood; cast into the water, it changed it into sweetness (Exod. XV).

The people who return from Egypt to their homeland through Moses are the Christian people who return through Christ from this world to the homeland of paradise. He sweetened their water by means of wood because death is made gentle for them through the cross. For just as water, wrapping in its whirlpool everything it seizes, drags it behind itself, so death drew into the abyss’s whirlpool everything it seized. Hence it was bitter to the former people because it had drawn them to the bitterness of punishments. But the Lord showed wood to Moses—whose name conveys “taken from water”—when he made known to the people taken from the water of baptism the power of the holy cross. By this wood water becomes drinkable, because through love of Christ’s cross death becomes desirable to many, as they hope that, once stripped of the body, they shall be clothed in the robe of immortality. This wood is laid in the water when the cross is dipped in Christ’s death. Then he drank from the torrent of this water on the way when, hanging on the cross, he paid what he had not taken.

It is reported that this wood was brought to Jerusalem and cast into the Sheep Pool. Because of its reverence, an angel descended into the pool each year and stirred the water; and whichever sick person first descended into the water came out healed. But at the time of the Lord’s Passion the pool dried up, and that wood appeared. When the soldiers sought wood suitable for a cross, it was found to be fitting in every respect. Having taken it, therefore, they made a cross from it, laid it upon Christ’s shoulders to carry (fol. 164), and raised him upon it for the salvation of the people, as the serpent in the wilderness. Then “his dominion was upon his shoulder” (Isa. IX), because through the trophy of the cross he was made prince by the Father over heavenly and earthly things. And because he, the Angel of Great Counsel, descended to the wood—that is, the cross—into the pool—that is, Judaea—and stirred it by signs and wonders, one descending into the water is healed: namely, the Christian people, who are regenerated by descending into the wave of baptism [Col. 0944D].

This holy cross is the pole on which two men carried a cluster of grapes, because the prophets who went before and the apostles who followed bore Christ, hanging on the cross like a grape cluster on a pole, into the world by their preaching.

This is the rod of the hook sent by the Father into the deep of the age, by which Leviathan is caught and the prey it devoured is drawn from its belly. It is also called the mast of the ship of the Church, on which the sail of faith is hung, held on either side by the ropes of good works. Thus the Church, borne upon the wood and swelling under the breath of the Holy Spirit, safely crosses the billowing waves of the world and joyfully reaches the desired harbor of everlasting life.

[Col. 0945A] The cross was once a kind of punishment devised for the shameful torture of the condemned, just as today thieves and robbers, judged unworthy of another end, are strangled by hanging. Hence the Jews said: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. II). But after it began everywhere to be venerated by the faithful, and very many desired to be tortured upon it for Christ, it was decreed that condemned persons should be put to death by hanging instead of on the cross’s gallows.

Since, therefore, the cross is glory for angels and human beings, I wish to unfold for you some of its mysteries.

God from the beginning created this world divided into four regions because he surely foreordained that he would restore it, having fallen, through the cross. He also formed humankind in the shape of a cross because he foreordained that he would restore it, having been lost, through the cross. Moses foreshadowed this sign [Col. 0945B] when he marked the doorposts of the house in four places—namely the threshold, the lintel, and the two side-posts—with the blood of the lamb (Exod. XII). It was also expressed by letters, since the letter T was fashioned long ago in the shape of a cross, as Ezekiel proclaimed. For the Spirit of the Lord carried this prophet from Babylon, placed him in Jerusalem, and there the glory of the Lord appeared to him. The Lord commanded the man clothed in linen to pass through Jerusalem and mark on their foreheads, by the letter *tau*, those who mourned and groaned; he commanded others to follow and kill all those not marked, beginning at the sanctuary (Ezek. IX).

The prophet is led by the Spirit to Jerusalem from Babylon, because prophecy is transferred by the Holy Spirit from the Synagogue to the Church. (fo. 164v.) [Col. 0945C] For Babylon is called “confusion,” and the Synagogue, because of unbelief, is scattered and confounded among all nations. But Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace,” because she is proclaimed as destined to behold in heaven Christ, the true peace. In this city the glory of the Lord appeared to him, when His majesty was made manifest through the writings of the prophets. The man clothed in linen, at His command, passes through Jerusalem and inscribes upon the foreheads of those who mourn and groan the *thau*, that is, the letter T, because the priestly order, by the Lord’s command, ranges throughout the Church and imprints with chrism the sign of the holy cross upon the foreheads of penitents and of those hastening to the faith. Those who follow slay the unmarked, because demons kill in the soul those who are not fortified by the seal of the cross. They begin at the sanctuary because they first seize Judaea, [Col. 0945D] in which was God’s sanctuary. The letter X also, which stands first in the name of Christ, is written in the form of a cross. This letter X signifies ten in numerals and points to the Decalogue of the Law, which the Lord came not to abolish but to fulfil (Matt. 5), when He endured the cross.

Finally, the pattern of the whole Christian religion is contained in the shape of the cross. For by its three upper extremities the Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is denoted; by the fourth, on which the three are supported, reverence for unity is shown. The profound understanding of the Apostle Paul also discloses to us the deep mystery of this holy cross. “May God grant you,” he says, “to be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length, height and depth” [Col. 0946A] (Eph. 3). The breadth of the cross is understood as those two parts by which the hands are stretched out. By this breadth is understood the twofold love which embraces friends in God and enemies for God’s sake, on either side. The length of the cross is that part along which the body of the suspended man is extended. By this length we are taught perseverance in good unto the end, because “he who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10).

The height of the cross is that part which rises above the head, upon which Pilate fastened the title written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. By it is suggested the hope of heavenly things, through which equality with the angels is hoped for by the victory of the cross. The depth of the cross is marked by the part beneath the feet, which is hidden when fixed in the earth. [Col. 0946B] God’s hidden mercy is declared by this, through which the whole world, lying in the Evil One, is sustained lest it perish. Those who follow the Lord rightly bear this cross if, crucifying themselves to vices and desires (Gal. 5), they renounce carnal longings and desire to live in obedience to God’s commandments. They ought to stand stretched out upon this cross (fo. 166), because they ought continually to be intent upon spiritual things and never bend themselves down to vices, but always stretch themselves upward in mind to comprehend heavenly things.

If the cross is laid upon the ground, it is shown to extend toward east, south, north, and west, because the four regions of the world are marked for Christ’s kingdom by the cross. For He Himself said: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12). Finally, [Col. 0946C] when He was raised from the earth upon the cross, the fourfold world was drawn to Him by the sign of the cross. But if the cross fixed in the earth is raised upright, one part of it is seen to look toward heaven, one to penetrate the earth, and parts on either side to indicate the right and left sides of the world. One part looks to heaven, because heavenly things are restored through the triumph of the cross. One penetrates the earth, because earthly things are renewed through the standard of the cross. One also penetrates Tartarus, because infernal things are destroyed through the sign of the cross. And one part indicates the right and left sides of the world, because by the power of the cross the good on the right will be judged unto glory, and the evil on the left unto punishment. For on that day the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and the light of sun and moon will not shine, because the cross [Col. 0946D] of Christ, going before Him for judgment, will shine with such radiance that it darkens the splendour of sun and moon by its own brightness.

Since today, beloved, we celebrate the Finding of the Holy Cross, it is fitting that we recount to your charity how it was found.

After the Jews had fulfilled God’s counsel, which His hand had decreed to accomplish—namely, when they crucified the Lord of glory with thieves for the salvation of all—they dug into the earth and hid at the place of Calvary the cross worthy of adoration, the life-giving cross, together with the crosses of the thieves. Thus, after Christ, the pilot of the ship, had been slain by pirates—that is, the faithless Jews—and after the ship itself, the Church, together with the holy cross, had been sunk by Charybdis—that is, the Synagogue—in the depths of the earth, the Church was engulfed by the greatest storm of persecutions and by the tempests of sufferings. [Col. 0947A] Swimming for a long time through the wreck-strewn whirlpools of diverse torments, she was scarcely lifted into the calm of peace after escaping the vortex of persecution. For when the merciful Lord awoke, the storm of persecution was checked and subdued, the tranquillity of peace was poured out upon the world, and the ship of the Church, which had lain concealed for more than two hundred years, emerged from its hidden place and was restored to the faithful.

Constantine, a most bitter persecutor of the Church, held the monarchy at that time; divine mercy, binding him with bit and bridle, compelled him to draw near to itself (Ps. 31). For when God wished to save him in soul, He covered his whole body with leprosy. Converted to the faith by Pope Silvester (fo. 166v), he was baptized and immediately cleansed from leprosy; through him peace and joy were strengthened throughout the whole Church. Helena, the mother [Col. 0947B] of the Augustus, having received the faith, was immersed in the saving laver; a vast multitude of Jews and gentiles was imbued with faith and baptism. After these things, Constantine, about to begin war against the pagans, was anxious over the outcome; but the King of kings comforted him. For in the night a radiant man appeared to him, showed him the sign of the holy cross, and promised him victory through this sign. On waking, he told the dream to his friends; having made a cross together with a standard, he carried it before his troops. The enemy was put to flight, and he himself returned victorious through the sign of the cross, his army unharmed.

Therefore Helena, kindled by love of the holy cross, hastened to Jerusalem. Having assembled the Jews, she asked that the place of Calvary be pointed out to her; it was then covered by a dense growth of thorns and brushwood and was therefore unknown. For forty years after the Lord’s Passion, [Col. 0947C] the Romans had utterly destroyed Jerusalem; and after a long time Aelius Hadrian had built another city in another place, which he called Aelia after his own name. For it is recorded that the Lord suffered and was buried outside the gate; both places are now seen by all in what is today Jerusalem.

The queen therefore offered the Jews a reward if they showed the place of the cross, punishment if they concealed it. When they maintained that the place was unknown to them, all were ordered to be handed over to the flames of fire. Terrified, they produced a certain man named Judas and asserted that all was known to him. When he denied knowing, he was cast into a pit, where he was afflicted by the privation of hunger and thirst. After he promised to show the place, he was brought out. [Col. 0947D] The queen, with the people accompanying her, went to the place; [Col. 0948A] kneeling, she poured forth prayers. The place shook, and the smoke of incense rose from the ground. Immediately they opened the earth with mattocks and found three crosses. A dead man was brought; when laid upon Christ’s cross, he was restored to life and by his resurrection and voice bore witness to the power of the holy cross. Then they also found the shining nails with which the Jews pierced the Lord’s hands and feet, and they gave thanks to God, the giver of all good things.

Judas, believing in Christ together with all the Jews, was baptized; afterward he was elevated to be bishop of the Church of Jerusalem and is remembered to have endured a renowned martyrdom for the Church entrusted to him. When the cross was found, the devil appeared with dreadful howling and declared that all his right had been taken away from him through this wood. “Judas,” he said, “betrayed his Lord and led Him to death; now another Judas has betrayed all [Col. 0948B] (fo. 168) my secrets and brought all my arts to nothing by bringing this wood into the midst. But Julian, my familiar friend, will soon be king; from him your betrayal will receive its reward.” And this indeed afterward happened: for Julian the Apostate inflicted refined tortures upon that same Judas, then bishop under the name Cyriacus. Helena built a church at great expense, set up part of the cross in it, and carried part to Constantinople, the city of her son.

Therefore let all who have been redeemed through the cross rejoice on this day; let them sing praises to Christ the Redeemer, who, after He “trode the winepress alone” (Isa. 63), reigned as God from the wood among all nations. In that winepress “a cluster of Cyprus” (Song 1) was pressed, and through its drink the return to life lies open to us all. Finally, [Col. 0948C] with this rod the good shepherd drove the flock of martyrs to the palace of the Church.

Therefore Saint Alexander, pope, whose feast is celebrated today, driven by love of the cross, was seized by pagans together with the flock entrusted to him; he was bound in chains, wasted in prison by hunger and thirst, hung upon the rack, scraped with claws, cast into a burning furnace, and was not harmed by the fire; finally, pierced with very many thrusts throughout all his limbs, he was slain. With him two priests, Eventius and Theodolus, long worn down in prison and likewise tested in fire, were at last beheaded. Through their merits and prayers, approach today the throne of glory, that, offering triumph to God, you may be permitted with them in full joy to resound the everlasting alleluia: “What eye has not seen” (1 Cor. 2).

At the feast of Saints Philip and James, deliver the sermon “Christ Rising” and conclude with these words:

[Col. 0947]

[Col. 0947D] The holy apostles Philip and James, whose solemn feast we celebrate today, “shall neither hunger nor thirst any more, nor shall heat or sun strike them; for He who has mercy on them shall rule them and give them drink at springs of the waters of life” (Isa. 49). For they who heard from Christ that there are many dwelling places in the Father’s house have today entered, crowned more splendidly with laurels, where the fountain of life turns their sorrow into joy by showing them the Father whom they desired. Now they see light in light, because they are permitted to behold the Son in the Father. Of these, Philip converted almost all Syria to Christ by signs and preaching, endured many adversities, and at last underwent the punishment of the cross for the kingdom of life; through the triumph of the cross he attained Christ crucified. James, however, son of Mary of Cleophas—namely, the mother [sic] of the Lord—and of Alphaeus, was ordained by the apostles bishop of the Church of Jerusalem (fo. 168v). When, by writings, words, examples, and signs, he had converted a very great multitude from Judaea to the faith [the text has plural *convertissent*], and on the Paschal day had borne witness before all the people in the Temple to Christ’s divinity, he was thrown down by the Pharisees from the height [Col. 0949A] of the Temple to the ground. But he was not crushed by the fall, because “the Lord placed His hand beneath him” (Ps. 36). Yet one of the scribes struck through his head with a staff and, shattering it, injured his brain. By that wound he was freed from bodily pain and death, and today is joined in glory to the King of glory, where pain and groaning flee.

The skin upon his knees and elbows was found to have become hardened [Col. 0950A] through the frequent prayers in which he is said continually to have laboured. Since these men are to sit with Christ as judges upon twelve thrones, follow their words and deeds, and pray that you may then behold Christ in joy. “What eye has not seen” (1 Cor. 2).

## IN THE ROGATION DAYS

[Col. 0949]

[Col. 0949A] “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and His ears are attentive to their prayers” (Ps. 33). Those who turn away from evil, avoiding fornications, adulteries, perjuries, thefts, false testimonies, and similar things; and those who do good, rendering to God what is God’s and to human beings what is theirs—these are righteous, and upon them the eyes [Col. 0949B] of God’s mercy look, and His ears attend to their prayers, because before they call upon Him, He says to them: “Behold, I am present.” “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (ibid.). For what purpose? “To destroy their memory from the earth” (ibid.). Let the righteous therefore rejoice that God looks upon them and hears them, and let them advance toward what is better. But those like me—that is, reeking with crimes—should abandon their sins, flee to the defence of prayer, and know that they too may be heard.

There are three ways in which our prayers are hindered so that they are not heard by God. Whoever prays to take vengeance upon enemies is not heard, but his prayer is turned into sin. Whoever keeps hatred in his heart and does not forgive one who sins against him, God does not hear when he prays. Whoever commits grievous sins [Col. 0949C] and persists in them with delight pours forth prayers in vain, because God does not hear sinners. Thus it is said through the prophet: “God’s ears are not burdened so that He cannot hear; rather, your sins stand in the way lest He hear you” (Isa. 59). Again it says: “Because of our sins, O Lord, You have placed a cloud before Yourself, lest prayer pass through” (Lam. 4). Sin [the text: *peccatum*] is heavy as lead and therefore drags a person down into the depth of the abyss. Just as a wheel is released on a mountain and rolls over a precipice to the bottom of a valley, so a soul that voluntarily abandons God and plunges into iniquity (fo. 170) never stops at a single fall, but always rushes farther into worse things. And a sin which repentance does not quickly wash away [Col. 0949D] immediately draws another by its weight; so one falls into sin from sin, until one comes to the depth of evils, and from there plunges into the pit of eternal death (Prov. 18), over whose mouth the stone of condemnation is placed. One is not permitted to go out until one has paid the last farthing (Matt. 5).

Therefore, beloved, ask God in devout prayers that “the deep may not swallow you, nor the pit close its mouth over you” (Ps. 68). Flee the desires of the world and flesh, which are the service of demons; “seek the Lord, and your soul shall live” (ibid.). For the prophet saw a woman sitting in an ephah, floating on the sea, weighed down by a mass of lead; and behold, two winged women lifted the ephah with the woman and carried it to the land of Babylon (Zech. 5). The turbulent sea is this age, stormy with adversities. The woman floating in the ephah is our soul, which presides over the body and labours amid the perils of the age. A mass of lead weighs her down because grave iniquity burdens our soul. The two women who [Col. 0950A] lift the ephah with the woman are two vices, namely pride and lust, which soften our soul and body toward unlawful things. [Col. 0950B] For pride raises a person up into self-exaltation, whereas lust presses the flesh down into uncleanness. As soon as the spirit is lifted into pride, the flesh is immediately submerged in lust. They are described as winged because those who follow them are made unstable. They carry the ephah with the woman into the land of Babylon, which means “confusion,” because those consenting to them are clothed with a double confusion: here they are shamed bodily before people, and in the future they are punished in the soul by eternal confusion, when it is said: “They shall be covered with double confusion as with a cloak” (Ps. 108). Therefore, beloved, abhor pride and lust, and delight in [Col. 0950C] the Lord, and He will give you the petitions of your heart (Ps. 36). And because you have gathered today, you ought to listen attentively to the word of God.

Our Lord Himself says that a certain man went out to sow his seed. While he sowed, some fell beside the way and was trampled down and devoured by birds; some sprang up upon rock and withered because it had no moisture; some was entrusted to thorns and was choked by thorns; and some fell upon good ground and yielded, some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, some a hundredfold fruit (Matt. 13). He who sows the seed is the priest who preaches God’s word; the field in which the seed is scattered is your hearts (fo. 170v), into which the word of God is cast. The seed thrown upon the way, trampled by passers-by [Col. 0950D] and devoured by birds, signifies those who receive God’s word but, intent upon secular business and worldly desires, tread it down as though with their feet; demons remove it from their memory, and they yield no fruit of godliness. That which falls upon rock and withers there signifies the hard of heart who, although [the text reads *quavis*, perhaps “however”] they sometimes eagerly hear the word of God, nevertheless persist in malice; and because they lack the moisture of heavenly grace, the word of God must wither in them. What the thorns choke are those whose ears are hardened against God’s word by riches, pleasures, and the cares of life. But that which falls into good ground and bears fruit is the multitude of believers who, obeying God’s word, labour earnestly in good works. Married persons yield thirtyfold fruit when they fulfil the faith of the holy [Col. 0951A] Trinity by the Decalogue of the Law; the continent yield sixtyfold when they endeavour to fulfil these things actively and especially; but virgins yield a hundredfold when they strive to please God in body and spirit.

Now, beloved, you ought briefly to hear why it has been decreed that crosses be carried on these days. It is related that the earth was parched by drought, while people and animals wasted away through pestilence; moreover, the savagery of bears, wolves, and other beasts devastated many people. Their multitude entered cities and villages everywhere and even tore infants apart in their cradles. At that time Mamertus, bishop, governed the Church of Vienne. Having assembled the people, he urged them to fast for three days, pray, and carry crosses, so that God’s mercy—which had delivered the Ninevites from destruction through a three-day observance—might assist His people in their present affliction. [Col. 0951B] When this was done, the plague was calmed, and joy and abundance of goods were given to the afflicted.

Moreover, the day called the Major Litany is recorded to have been instituted for this reason. The Tiber overflowed beyond its usual measure, entered Rome, occupied extensive districts within it, destroyed churches, and overthrew many buildings together with their inhabitants. Through its channel a huge dragon, with a great multitude of serpents, entered the sea, where all of them were suffocated. Cast upon the shore, they corrupted the air by their putrefaction [the text has plural *corrupperunt*] and brought grievous pestilence upon humankind. For arrows were seen coming from heaven; when they struck people in the groin, they died without delay. [Col. 0951C] First Pope Pelagius died; then almost all the Roman people were consumed by sudden death (fo. 172). Gregory was then elevated bishop and urged the people to fast, carry crosses, and pray. When they devoutly did this, the plague ceased and the people rejoiced in God’s peace. Hence it was established that the same day should be observed annually in the Church with the celebration of fasts and litanies, so that God might preserve us and our animals from pestilence. And because at this time it often happens, through the harshness of the weather, that seeds already sown may perish before serving our needs, it was decreed that these days likewise be observed with the same rite, namely fasts and litanies, so that the fruits of the whole year might be preserved for us from every misfortune.

That the merciful Lord may give us confidence to obtain what we ask, [Col. 0951D] He urges us to diligence in prayer. For He says: “If someone at midnight asks loaves from a friend to set before his friend who has come from the road, even if he does not give them because of friendship, he will supply what he asks because of his persistence” (Luke 11). This friend is God, who loved us and gave His Only-Begotten for us. From Him we ask bread at midnight when we seek His help in tribulation. And if He delays in helping us because of our sins, nevertheless, if we persevere, He extends His mercy to us. Without doubt, we should know that we shall be heard if we ask with insistent prayer, seek with attentive mind, and knock with tears. For one who asks his father for bread will in no way receive a stone; one who asks his father for a fish [Col. 0952A] receives no serpent; and if one asks for an egg, he is never offered a scorpion (ibid.).

By bread, which strengthens the human heart (Ps. 103), charity is signified, through which a person is strengthened in virtues. By the fish, which is nourished amid the surge of waves, faith is understood, which is brought to increase by the storms of persecution. By the egg, from which offspring is expected, hope is indicated, by which future blessedness is hoped for. But by the stone is meant hardness [the text: *duria*]; by the serpent, a venomous animal, malice; and by the scorpion, which strikes with its tail, the punishment of sins. Whoever therefore asks God for charity, He never hardens him in evils; whoever asks Him for faith, He by no means permits to remain in malice; whoever asks Him for hope, He never inflicts punishment upon him. By bread, moreover, is understood the produce now springing up in the grass; by egg, the offspring of animals is understood [the text adds *vel intelligitur*, “or is understood”]; and by fish is signified whatever nourishes each person. For these things your charity ought to pour out prayers to the Lord, that He may preserve them from the stone of hail, the serpent of pestilence, and the scorpion [Col. 0952B] of storm.

We have many examples that “the persistent prayer of a righteous person has great power” (Jas. 5). When the people of five cities provoked God’s anger against themselves by terrible crimes, Abraham asked God to spare them if He found ten righteous persons among them. The Lord said that if He found ten righteous in those five kingdoms, He would spare all the others for their sake and would moreover not overthrow the places; but because only one righteous man was found, he alone was delivered (Gen. 18). The Pentapolis, however, was overthrown with its people by fire and sulphur; and the righteous man’s wife, who accompanied him only in body but remained in mind with Sodom, was changed into a pillar of salt (Gen. 19). From this it is understood that the dwelling among the wicked of righteous people sustains them in this life: through the prayers of the righteous the balance is held further toward the right, lest their wickedness, as it deserves, suddenly sink them into destruction. But when the righteous are removed, the impious are immediately snatched away to torments, just as Sodom perished after Lot departed from it.

When God’s people were led out of Egypt by Moses, enemies attacked them with weapons on the way. Moses, however, prayed on the mountain with hands outstretched, [Col. 0952D] and Israel overcame its enemies. But if Moses let down his hands, Amalek prevailed (Exod. 17). It is clear from this that he accomplished more by prayers than the people did by arms: he obtained by praying the victory which the people could not gain by fighting. Likewise Samuel drove away enemies by prayers whom an army could not drive away by arms (1 Sam. 7). Of old the people turned away from God’s law and worship and turned to idolatry. When Elijah could not correct them by preaching, he shut heaven against them for three years and six months by prayer. Rain being withheld from heaven, the thirsty earth languished and withered, threatening its cultivators with the dangers of famine. Thus, famine pressing them, the people were compelled to worship the living and true God; and when Elijah prayed, the earth was drenched with abundant [Col. 0953A] rain, and abundance of goods was restored to the converted people (3 Kings 17–18). Behold: by the prayer of one man heaven was shut against a whole people and, when he prayed again, opened.

At a certain time, therefore, because of human sins, fields dried up through drought and the hearts of many wasted away through fear of famine. While they fasted and carried crosses with litanies, a certain father met them and asked the cause [the text: *causa*] of their affliction. When they answered, “Drought,” he asked why they did not pray. When they maintained that they had laboured greatly in prayer and obtained little, he said that, if they asked attentively, they would surely receive what they asked. Standing before all, he stretched out his hands for prayer; at the first words of his prayer rain fell, and the earth bestowed upon the farmers the fruit long denied them [Col. 0953B] (fo. 174).

There was also a monk constant in prayer. One of the demons was sent by the Emperor Julian to obtain a certain response, but by this man’s prayers it was fixed in one place for twenty days; afterward it returned empty to the king. When the king asked it the reason for its delay, it said: “I was delayed and returned with my business unaccomplished. For my route lay through that monk, but I was hindered by his prayers. And when I waited in the hope that he might perhaps finish praying, so that I might be allowed to pass, he made no end of his prayers; and, unable to go any farther, I returned empty.” Julian threatened him with punishment, but not long afterward was killed in battle and underwent the eternal [punishment; the source phrase is incomplete]. Consider, I pray, beloved, how widely the prayer [Col. 0953C] of this man extended. Certainly the devil can fly through the air, penetrate the earth, and even cross the sea; but this man’s prayer, stretching upward to heaven, barred his passage through the air; extending downward [the text: *deorse*] to Tartarus, it prevented him from going through the earth; reaching the bounds of the world on both sides, it permitted the fugitive spirit sent by the apostate person to pass nowhere. Indeed, this man sometimes refreshed his body with food, at other times with sleep; but the whole attention of his heart rose so continually to God that every action of his was prayer. Beloved, all the righteous from the beginning of the world who have deserved the kingdoms of the blessed life obtained them by praying. For all the righteous are recorded to have devoted themselves to prayer, and therefore today enjoy in full joy that for which [Col. 0953D] they prayed. Let us therefore also apply ourselves frequently to prayer, so that we may be able to attain full joy with them.

Let us ask all things in the name of Jesus if we desire our prayers to be heard. We ask the Father in Jesus’ name if we request only those things that bring salvation to the soul and are necessary to the body. When praying, however, we must distrust our own merits and have confidence in His mercy, because He Himself said: “Amen, I say to you: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you receive it, and it shall be done for you” (Mark 11). “If two of you agree concerning any matter whatsoever that they ask, it shall be done by my Father” (Matt. 18). Therefore be all of one mind in prayer; raise your hearts with your hands to God; pray for all the living and the dead who are in any distress. For if you pray for the whole Church, [Col. 0954A] as for your mother, the whole Church prays for you, as for her children. If, however, you pray for the dead (fo. 174v), you deliver yourselves: if they are in joy, they pray that you may come to them more swiftly; but if they are in punishment, they ask that you may never go there. Finally, one who prays converses with God and therefore must obtain what he faithfully asks. And since He Himself says, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18), how much more should He be believed to be present today among the multitude gathered in His name to seek the aid of the saints.
