Therefore, since the giver of all good things is in your midst as you are gathered in His name, call upon Him with devout prayers; knock with tears and invocations, that He may grant you what body and soul need and deliver you from your necessities.

Although necessities are many, there are nevertheless five principal ones which, unless [the text has *non si*, presumably *nisi*] remedied, put people in danger of death. A person must eat, for if he does not eat he dies of hunger; he must drink, for if he does not drink he dies of thirst; he must digest, for if he does not, he dies of blockage; the body must be refreshed by sleep, for if this is neglected, it fails through weariness; one must be clothed, for if this is omitted, one perishes from cold and heat. All our labour is directed to supplying these needs. “Seek first,” He says, “the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added [Col. 0954C] to you” (Matt. 6). And do not be excessively anxious about earthly things or concerned with transitory matters, for a human being will inherit worms, beasts, and serpents. Rather ask God to deliver you from these necessities and transfer you to that place where you do not need them, where “they shall neither hunger nor thirst any more” (Rev. 7), where souls rest from their labours (Rev. 14), and where they are free and see that He is God, in whose vision the angelic choirs are refreshed.

We have been taught by Him to ask this: “Ask,” He says, “and you shall receive, that your joy may be full” (John 16). For if anyone rejoices in a beautiful wife, he is saddened when death intervenes; if he delights in beloved children, he is saddened when they are afflicted by illness or taken away by death; [Col. 0954D] if he rejoices in possessions or money, he grieves when they are lost through some misfortune. But that true and full joy is to be desired by all believers with their whole longing: there they are set in the joy of the Lord above all their goods (fo. 176), continually enjoy the brightness of the eternal vision, obtain the glory of all the angels, and receive the fellowship [the text: *conturbernio*, apparently for *contubernio*] of all the saints. And this joy shall never be taken from them for ever (ibid.). Therefore a woman now has sorrow when she gives birth; but when she has borne a child, she remembers the anguish no more because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world (ibid.). This woman is the Church, which now labours in sorrow in order to give birth to a faithful people for Christ. But when, through the resurrection to eternal life, she has brought them forth, [Col. 0955A] she remembers no more the anguish of this life because of the ineffable and full joy then to be given to all her children; for then “the righteous shall shine like the sun” (Matt. 12) and “shall be equal to angels” (Matt. 22). [Col. 0956A] Beloved, where the cross is carried before us, we follow; so let us follow the examples of Christ crucified, that through the triumph of the victorious cross we may deserve to reach those joys “which eye has not seen” (1 Cor. 2).

## ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0955]

[Col. 0955A] “The sun was lifted up,” he says, “and the moon stood in her order” (Hab. 3). Christ is the eternal sun by whom all choirs of angels are illumined; He is the true light by whom all souls are enlightened. While He lay hidden here beneath the cloud of flesh, surrounded by the darkness of our frailty, at last, having emerged from the darkness of hell, He is today gloriously raised above the stars and exalted above all [Col. 0955B] angelic ranks at the right hand of the Father as Lord of majesty. But the moon, that is, the Church illuminated by Him, stood in her order when she beheld Him ascending into heaven in the apostles. For the apostles became the order of the Church when they established for her the rule of right living and taught her how to direct her course after the sun of righteousness.

O how splendid were the horns which this rising moon lifted today, when the sun, ascending on high, poured into her the ray of eternal brightness! O with what serene countenance she stood in her order when, through the apostolic choir, which became her order, and through the Virgin Mother of God, who bore her type, she beheld her own flesh in her head—that is, in her Redeemer, her Bridegroom, her God—penetrating the heavens! O what joy arises today in heaven among the angels when the Son of God, who was sent from the palace into prison for a servant—indeed, from his homeland into exile, an exile for an exile—returns today in triumph to the kingdom of His Father! Hence this day is called God’s triumph, on which, welcomed by the senate of the heavenly court with hymn-like praises, the conqueror of death and author of life is glorified [Col. 0955C] (fo. 176v).

Among the Romans there was a custom by which a triumph was bestowed on victors in this manner. After an emperor or consul had subdued some nation to the Roman Empire by arms and returned victorious with spoil, the senate and the whole Roman people went out festively to meet him and welcomed the victor with songs and praises. He was clothed in purple; a diadem interwoven with laurel [Col. 0955D] and gold was placed upon him; and he was carried into the City in a chariot glittering with gold and gems, drawn by four snow-white horses. The noble captives went before the chariot, bound with golden chains. The common captive multitude followed the chariot with hands bound behind their backs. A procession of spoil was likewise led along as a mark of victory. Thus the victor, amid great rejoicing, was brought in crowned with laurel to the highest temple, and then the spoil was distributed to the people.

Then Roman nobility bestowed the honor of a triumph upon the greatest victors for earthly glory; but God willed that, even through enemies who were to become friends, the glory of Christ, the supreme victor, should be prefigured. For the triumph of Roman kings went before as a figure of today’s triumph: Christ, the King of [Col. 0956A] glory, as sole ruler overthrew the tyrant’s kingdom; he made captivity itself captive, having been captured by him; he subdued the world, rebellious against the heavenly commonwealth; today, victorious and with noble spoil, he returned to his homeland. The senate of archangels, with all the host of heaven, went out festively to meet him and joyfully received its victorious king with hymnic melodies.

He is adorned with purple, because for the Passion he endured he is crowned by the Father with glory and honour; he is crowned with a diadem interwoven with gold and laurel when he is surrounded by the multitude of angels and human beings. For by the brightness of gold is understood the splendour of angels, while by the greenness of laurel is understood flourishing in faith. Christ is marked out by a crown, as it were, woven from these, when through him human frailty is united in glory with angelic dignity, as the Prophet says: “With all these you shall adorn yourself as with a crown” (Ps. 20). Of this crown it is written: “You will bless the crown of your year of goodness” (Ps. 64). For Christ is the year of God’s goodness, made a participant in our mortality. The months of this year are the twelve apostles; its days, the righteous; its hours, the faithful; its nights, those still wandering in the darkness of unbelief [Col. 0956C] or sins. The crown of this year is the surrounding multitude of angels and human beings in everlasting glory.

By the chariot conspicuous with gold and gems, in which the victor triumphs, the Gospel is indicated, shining with wisdom and signs; through it, once Christ’s triumph has been made known, the world rejoices. The wheels by which the chariot turns are the evangelists through whom Christ’s triumph is proclaimed. This chariot is drawn by four snow-white horses, because Christ is carried in the chariot of the Gospel by teachers, in radiant virtues, through the four regions of the world. This chariot of God is said to be manifold in ten thousands (Ps. 67), because Christ’s triumph is proclaimed by all the writers of the Old and New Testaments. Thousands rejoicing run to this [Col. 0956D] chariot, when today many thousands of angels receive the triumphant Lord. Noble captives, bound with golden chains, go before the chariot, because those redeemed by the Lord, bound by chains of love, seek heavenly things. The common people follow with bound hands, because the people, binding themselves from evil works by fear of the Lord, are borne toward joys. The procession of spoil accompanies the chariot, because the multitude of saints rising with Christ is today exalted with him to the stars. The victor is led with song into the highest temple, because Christ, triumphing amid the harmony of angels, is today brought into the temple of the heavenly Jerusalem. Afterwards the spoils are distributed among the people, because through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit diverse charisms are granted to the faithful. Hence it is said: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; [Col. 0957A] he gave gifts to men” (Eph. 4).

For today he transferred human nature, in which he endured many adversities here both for us and from us, from earth to heaven, above angelic height, to the Father’s right hand. The victor led captive the captivity long detained in the prison of hell, and brought it into the Father’s palace. He gave gifts to human beings when, pouring out the Holy Spirit upon them, he bestowed knowledge of every language (Acts 2).

Today, dearest ones, the magnificence of the Lord has been raised above the heavens; but his bride, his body—that is, the Church—is still oppressed by many afflictions among the Babylonians. Yet, as Christ, having conquered the prince of death and subdued the world, ascends today to heaven in triumph, so the Church, having overcome Antichrist [Col. 0957B] and trampled down the world, will ascend triumphantly to heaven. Through her Bridegroom, with Goliath cast down, and herself rescued from enemies, she will then be raised, full in the whole orbit of her moon, from the valley of tears; she will be placed in the bridal chamber of the eternal Sun, to be joined to the stars of angels.

Therefore she herself applauds him as he ascends in jubilation, crying out in exultation in the Song of Songs: “Behold,” she says, “he comes, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills” (Song 2). His person is expressed in the prophet Jeduthun, whose name means “leaper-over.” For Christ came into the world as one leaping upon mountains, and returned to heaven as one skipping over them. He made a leap from heaven when he came from the Father’s seat into the Virgin’s womb; from there he leapt into the manger, then into the gibbet of the cross, from the cross into the tomb, from there into the depth of the abyss, from the abyss into the world, [Col. 0957C] and from there he skipped into heaven. “His going forth,” it says, “is from the height of heaven, and his course reaches to its height” (Ps. 18).

Today he passed over all mountains and hills, because he raised the human being assumed from us above every height of angels and saints. But the Gospel reveals to us how he ascended to heaven. Appearing today to his disciples as they reclined at table, he rebuked their unbelief as teacher; he commanded them as Lord to preach the Gospel throughout the whole world; and he gave them as God the power to perform signs in his name. Then, to prove the reality of his fleshly nature, he ate with them; and he commanded them to await the promised Holy Spirit in Jerusalem. After this he led them out to Bethany [Col. 0957D] and, lifting up his hands, blessed them. And while they watched, he was raised up and carried into heaven, received by a cloud. As they looked toward heaven after him, behold, two angels in white stood by them, who foretold that he would come for judgment in the same manner in which he had now departed.

Those who saw him ascend numbered one hundred and twenty, among whom Mary his mother was present together with the apostles. All of them returned together with joy to Jerusalem and persevered daily in prayer and praise of God until they received the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost. This was prefigured in the patriarchs and prophets, when Enoch, the seventh from Adam, was taken up into paradise (Gen. 5), and Elijah [Col. 0958A] the prophet was taken up to heaven in a fiery chariot (4 Kings 2).

The feasts of this sacred day are also expressed to us through birds. The eagle flies higher than all birds and directs the sharpness of its eyes to the very ray of the sun. When it encourages its young to fly, hovering over them and spreading its wings, it takes them upon the sweep of its wings and trains them to fly. Thus Christ penetrated the heights of heaven more sublimely than all saints, when the Father exalted him above all angels at his right hand. He spread the wings of the cross over us; he defended us from demons; taking us from hard slavery, he adopted us as sons; and upon his shoulders, like a lost sheep, he carried us back to the flock. He hovered over us and summoned us to fly when, ascending through the ether, he showed himself, our head, to us his members, that we should follow him by good works.

[Col. 0958B] Ezekiel expressed this through the four living creatures (Ezek. 1), which John later saw praising the Lamb day and night (Rev. 4). For Christ was a human being in being born, a calf in dying, a lion in rising again, and an eagle in ascending.

There is a white bird called the charadrius, by means of which it is tested whether a sick person can recover. For when it is brought to the sick person, if he is about to die it turns its face away from him; but if he is going to live, it directs and fixes its gaze intently upon him. With open mouth it drinks the illness from him, flies high toward the ray of the sun, sweats out the infirmity it has absorbed, and the sick person rejoices in restored health. The white charadrius is Christ born from the Virgin. He is brought to the sick person when he is sent by the Father to the infirm human race. He turned his face away from the Jews [Col. 0958C] and left them in death; but turning his countenance toward us, he recalled us from death. Undergoing the cross, he himself bore our infirmity, and a sweat of blood flowed from him. Then he flew into the heights of heaven with our flesh to the Father and granted everlasting salvation to all.

The very place from which he ascended still proclaims to all that no one can obstruct the way for those who desire to ascend to heaven. For the place still retains the imprint which he made in the sand as he ascended; and although earth is daily taken from it by the faithful, the imprint cannot be erased. Indeed, when a church was built over the same place, and ought to have been roofed over because it was round, the space of air through which he ascended could by no means be closed, and therefore it has remained open [Col. 0958D] to this day. Into this church, too, every year a violent storm of floodwater comes from heaven and throws to the ground all the people there, plainly showing with what terror Christ will come for judgment when he violently shakes heaven and earth. For then “the heavens will pass away with a great rush, and the elements will be dissolved by heat.”

Therefore, dearest ones, since “there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” except Christ Jesus (Acts 4), who permitted himself to be lifted up on the cross for us like the serpent; and whom the Father, after he drank from the torrent of death, today exalted as head above every name in heaven (Ps. 109), incorporating us, whom he acquired by his own blood, as co-heirs with himself: let us today give glory to his praise, and let us celebrate his proclamations [Col. 0959A] with the voice of exultation, that he may gather us, his members, to himself, where he himself rejoices in the glory of the Father. “What eye has not seen” (1 Cor. 2), and so forth.

## ON PENTECOST

[Col. 0959]

[Col. 0959A] “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32). Through the Son, who is the Word of God, not only the heavens but all things were created from nothing; and lest they again dissolve into nothing, they were established by the same Word, and all their power was adorned by the spirit of his mouth. Angels too are called heavens: when others fell, they were established in love through the Word and adorned in every power through his Spirit. Hence it is written: “The Spirit of God adorned the heavens” [Col. 0959B] (Job 26), because he adorned both these heavens with stars and angels with virtues.

For angelic spirits are created through the Son, but are made alive through the Holy Spirit; through the Son the substance of light shone forth, but through the Holy Spirit its radiance gleamed; through the Son the firmament is formed, through the Holy Spirit it is set in swift revolution; through the Son sun, moon, and stars are assigned to the seasons, but through the Holy Spirit they are polished with the brightness of light; through the Son rivers are poured forth, through the Holy Spirit they receive their shifting course; through the Son the earth is formed, through the Holy Spirit it is adorned with fruits and flowers; through the Son diverse animals are brought forth, through the Holy Spirit they are endowed with vital breath; and birds are sustained in flight, fish in swimming, beasts, creeping things, and serpents [Col. 0959C] in walking through him. Through the Son the human being is formed in God’s image, but through the Holy Spirit is made alive in the soul. The Holy Spirit inspires diverse abilities; he also grants diverse arts. Through the Holy Spirit kinds of languages were given; through him, from the hidden treasuries of wisdom, the manifold streams of Scripture were brought forth.

Through the Holy Spirit the patriarchs portrayed in figures Christ and the future Church; through him the prophets spoke and foretold these same things in writings; through him the apostles, strengthened, preached these accomplished things in the world; through him the teachers, inspired, expounded the Scriptures. Through the Son the human being, redeemed, is freed from death; through the Holy Spirit the human being is regenerated in baptism [Col. 0959D] to life. Through the Holy Spirit sins are remitted; through him souls are raised from the death of crimes. Through the Holy Spirit many, despising the world, have led a religious life; through him very many have shone with signs and wonders. Through the Holy Spirit, even today, many are converted to a better life; through him very many are snatched up in mind to heavenly things. Through the Son the world is judged; through the Holy Spirit each party is rewarded. Through the Son, God the Father will create a new heaven and a new earth, but the Holy Spirit will renew all things into a better condition.

For through him heaven will be clothed with the splendour of the sun; through him the sun [Col. 0960A] will be clothed in sevenfold light; through him the moon will shine with the sun’s brightness; through him the earth will flourish with the delightfulness of paradise. Then the Son will make those transferred from labour recline, and, passing among them, will minister to them (Luke 12), because, returning from judgment, he will make the elect rest in diverse dwelling-places according to their diverse merits, and will show them face to face the glory of his divinity. But the Holy Spirit will grant them to shine like the sun’s radiance in full joy and to know the Trinity perfectly in unity.

This feast is celebrated for seven days because the Holy Spirit is venerated in seven gifts, as the prophet foretells: “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit [of the fear] of the Lord” (Isa. 11). These are the seven women who took hold of one man (Isa. 4), because the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit possessed Christ bodily.

All who fear God will ascend to heaven by the gift of this Spirit. For through him fear is bestowed, and it is divided into two kinds: there is servile fear and filial fear. A servant fears his master lest he condemn him; a son fears his father lest he disinherit him; an adulteress fears her husband lest he come; a chaste wife fears lest he [Col. 0960C] depart. When the Holy Spirit, who is love, possesses the mind, he casts out servile fear (1 John 4); but “the holy fear of the Lord remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 18). For one will no longer fear Gehenna as a slave of sin, because one seeks to commit no sin; rather, one will cleave to God as a son through delight in virtues, and therefore will possess his inheritance.

Let us obtain by prayer from his grace that we, as servants, may fear the Lord our God by turning away from evil, lest through contempt for his commandments he someday subject us to punishments—or rather, punish us as enemies rebellious against him with eternal torments. Let us ask that we may reverence him as sons, like Israel, by doing good, so that we may be co-heirs of his Son and enjoy the face of the Father. [Col. 0960D] After fear the Holy Spirit gives piety, so that a human being may serve the Creator devoutly and bestow upon the neighbour every good that lies within one’s power.

> **Note:** [Col. 0959] In the margin this verse is read: “These are the future rewards of the labours of the righteous.”

Then he inspires knowledge, so that a human being may know what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided. After this he grants strength, so that a human being may be bent toward vices neither by hardships nor by blandishments. Then he supplies counsel to reason, so that it may choose what is useful and reject what is harmful. After this he bestows understanding, so that the soul may understand eternal things through visible things. Then he inspires wisdom, so that the rational creature may despise the wonderful creation and love its Creator, who is the unchangeable good; that it may know wisely Christ alone, the fountain of wisdom, [Col. 0961A] in the Holy Spirit.

Those who flourish in these virtues through the sevenfold Spirit will obtain through him seven gifts in the body and seven gifts in the soul, when they possess double portions in their own land: in the body they will shine like the sun (Matt. 13), and in the soul they will be equal to angels (Luke 20). For by him, whose beauty sun and moon marvel at, they will be illuminated in the body seven times more brightly than the sun. Through the Holy Spirit Christ will reform the body of our lowliness, making it conform to the body of his glory (Phil. 3); and, since it is a spiritual body, he “whose word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147; the citation reads Ps. XIV) will endow it with such speed that, as quickly as sight now reaches heaven or thought the end of the world, so swiftly then [f. *tam*] will it be carried there [f. *illuc*] by the mobility of its body. [Col. 0961B]

By him also, who is the strength of all, it will be strengthened with such might that it can easily overturn masses of mountains with its foot. By him likewise, who “was free among the dead” (Ps. 87), such a grace of freedom will be present in them that every solid creature will be penetrable to them. In the vision of him, angels overflow with great sweetness and all saints abound in the greatest delights. Through him they enjoy every abundance of pleasure when, in the joy of their Lord, they are set over all their goods (Matt. 24): there they will behold the King of glory as he is, in his beauty, into whom they desire to look (1 Pet. 1); there they see the glory of all angels and saints and behold all their own members radiant within and without; there they continually hear the instruments [Col. 0961C] of saints and the harmonies of angels resounding; there they are refreshed by the sweetest scent of cinnamon and balsam (Ecclus. 24), feast exultantly in the sight of God, delight in joy (Ps. 67), are made drunk from the abundance of God’s house, and drink from the torrent of his delight (Ps. 35).

By him, who is the health of all, they are made firm in such soundness that, just as a ray of sunlight now suffers no division, so they then will suffer no bodily affliction. By him, who is eternal life, they are established in such longevity that they will never be dissolved by death for eternity.

They will have these seven gifts in the body through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; they will have an equal number in the soul, where they will rejoice perpetually in the Lord’s goods. For he himself, the fountain of wisdom, so abundantly pours into them that he grants them knowledge of all things. They are joined in ineffable friendship, because they are loved by God as sons and by angels as brothers. Incomparable concord binds them together, because neither God nor any saint differs from their will. They are exalted with immeasurable power, because they rule the new heaven and the new earth. They are raised in unutterable honour, because they are venerated by God himself and by all angels. They possess the highest security, because no one will ever take these things from them. They will have full joy [without] end; they will rejoice forever that all their friends whom they love enjoy these same goods.

These are the gifts which Christ, ascending on high, gave to human beings: those whom he led captive from death after they had been captured by the devil, he brought in as glorious victor to the star-bearing seats [Col. 0962A] of heaven. He also granted gifts to those still on earth when, through the charisms of the Holy Spirit, he gave them to shine with signs and new languages. But those found empty of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit will be tormented by as many punishments as these others enjoy goods.

These things were formerly prefigured in the Law and foretold through the prophets. For seven lamps proceed from the legal lampstand (Exod. 25), because from Christ the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit proceed to the Church. These are the seven columns by which the house of wisdom is supported (Prov. 9), because the Church, which is the house, is distinguished by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. These are the seven eyes which the prophet saw in one stone (Zech. 4), because Christ the rock gave the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit to the faithful for the illumination [Col. 0962B] of their souls. These are the seven horns of the Lamb slain for us, by which believers crush the seven heads of the red dragon (Rev. 5, 6).

Accordingly, this same Holy Spirit is proclaimed to have descended upon the baptized Lord in the form of a dove (Matt. 3), on account of the seven natures that are said to be in the dove.

### On the Seven Natures of the Dove

The dove nests in the rock, because the Holy Spirit dwells bodily in Christ. It feeds alien young, when it brings back through repentance those wandering and alienated from the kingdom of God. It chooses clean grains, because it separates the good from the evil as grain from chaff. It lacks gall, because it empties of malice those whom it possesses. It does not wound with its beak, because it [Col. 0962C] is filled with the Holy Spirit. It does not lie in wait for its neighbour; it dwells beside streams, because the Holy Spirit dwells in the wise. It flies in a flock, because the Holy Spirit grants his gifts to those gathered in the Lord’s name.

Therefore the prophet says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity. It is like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron; which descends to the hem of his garment; like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion” (Ps. 132). Brothers dwelt together in unity and gladness when the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul. Therefore the ointment descended from the head upon Aaron’s beard, because the Holy Spirit, who is spiritual anointing, came from God, the head of all, upon the apostles. By Aaron, whose name means “mountain of strength,” Christ is understood; through him the faithful are strong against vices and ascend from strength to strength. His beard was the apostles, because they clung like a beard to him who is the mouth of the Father. The ointment flowed from the beard onto the garment when the Holy Spirit poured himself into believers through the apostles’ laying on of hands.

The dew from Hermon, which signifies “anathema,” descended onto Mount Zion, which is called “the watchtower,” when heavenly grace came from the Synagogue into the Church. Mount Hermon is situated near the Jordan, where the Lord was baptized. Therefore the dew of Hermon is the Holy Spirit, who came upon the Lord at baptism on that mountain; and who today descends upon believers onto Mount Zion, on which Jerusalem is situated. [Col. 0963A] But Scripture has related to us today how this happened:

When fifty days had passed from the Lord’s resurrection, and the disciples, as he had commanded when ascending, were sitting together in Jerusalem, suddenly there came a great sound like that of a violent wind, which filled the whole house where they were seated. Tongues of fire appeared to them; inflamed by these, they began to speak the mighty works of God in the languages of all nations. Because of the approaching feast, Jews from every nation of the whole world had gathered in Jerusalem, since each year they celebrated Pentecost on account of the Law received at that time. When they heard this, they assembled together; and each one, astonished, heard from their mouths the language in which he had been born. Peter addressed them and said that these things had been [Col. 0963B] foretold through the prophets but fulfilled through Jesus, whom they had crucified. Led by repentance, about three thousand persons were baptized, and they too were filled with the Holy Spirit like the others (Acts 2).

On another day, when Peter and John had healed a lame man through the Holy Spirit (Acts 3), five thousand were baptized (Acts 4). All were enriched with the Holy Spirit; and they drank trembling the blood of Christ which they had previously shed in fury, while very many poured out their own blood for him. Having received the Holy Spirit, the apostles remained in Jerusalem for twelve days, as he had commanded. They conferred together concerning what they were to teach in the world; around the region they taught Jews and Gentiles; and through signs and wonders they converted very many to the faith. All these received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the apostles’ hands and proclaimed the powers of God in new languages.

For through the Holy Spirit the apostles restored sight to the blind, opened the ears of the deaf, loosed the tongues of the mute, raised the lame to walk, cleansed lepers, drove demons from the possessed, and raised the dead. Moreover, through staffs or garments—and some of them even through their shadow—they restored the weak to health.

After this, the Twelve, dispersed throughout the world [corrected from *mundiffusi*], suffused with the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit, fulfilled their twelvefold office through the number seven, when they brought the four regions of the world to faith in the Holy Trinity; for three times four, which are seven, make twelve. As good fishers, they drew fish formerly predestined to life by the net of faith, through signs and miracles, [Col. 0963D] from the salt sea of this age to the shore of life; and, following Christ’s example, as guides going before, they laid down their souls for the sheep entrusted to them.

After God created all things in the beginning in six days, he sanctified the seventh, because resting on it he ceased from work (Gen. 1–2). So those who strive to work in the gifts of the Holy Spirit during the six ages of the world will through him rest from all labour in the seventh. Thus we too labour during the six days of the week and rest on the seventh, because through the sevenfold Spirit we now devote ourselves to good works, while in the future we shall happily rest from every work; there through him we shall be at leisure and shall see God as he is (1 John 3).

[Col. 0964A] In the flood, the dove bringing back an olive branch announced peace to those shut in (Gen. 8), because the Holy Spirit, through the anointing of charism, restored lost peace to souls enclosed in flesh. He is also called the finger of God’s right hand, because a hand works through its fingers. Hence the magicians, unable to withstand Moses, said that this was the finger of God (Exod. 8), because they plainly saw signs performed through the Holy Spirit. Through this finger the Law was written on two tablets (Exod. 31), because through the Holy Spirit love was set forth in two commandments. By this finger the Lord casts out demons, because the works of the Son and of the Holy Spirit are inseparable.

Formerly the human race had use of only one language, but seventy-two giants built a tower against God. Offended by this, he confused their languages so that no one understood another’s speech (Gen. 11); thus he scattered them through the world—all of whom the Holy Spirit today gathered into unity of faith through kinds of languages. The Hebrew people too, freed from Egyptian slavery on the Paschal night through the paschal lamb and carried across the Red Sea, came to Mount Sinai on the fiftieth day. Smoke and fire filled it, and from the midst of the fire the Lord gave them the written Law of fear on tablets. Thus the Christian people, rescued from diabolic oppression on the Paschal night through Christ the paschal Lamb, carried across in baptism as through the Red Sea, received on the fiftieth day—that is, today—the law of love by fire, which the Lord commanded him [perhaps “them”] to write in the heart, so that afterward they might do freely out of love for God what they had formerly done under compulsion from fear.

There was also a commandment in the Law that the fiftieth year should be called the Jubilee—that is, the year of remission—that the whole year should rest from servile labour, and that a lost inheritance should be restored to its rightful heirs (Lev. 25). By this the Holy Spirit willed this time to be prefigured, in which he taught his people to rest from servile work—that is, from sin—and restored to them the lost inheritance of paradise. The Holy Spirit is said to be given twice: once on earth and once from heaven. The Spirit is given on earth that one may love one’s neighbour; the Spirit is given from heaven that one may love God. “For whoever loves God will keep his word” (John 14). [Col. 0964D] God the Father loves that person, and the Trinity will come to that person and make its dwelling with that person (ibid.).

Therefore, dearest ones, let us love God by keeping his commandments, that he may love us by preparing a dwelling for himself in us. Let us cleanse the dung of sins from the lodging of our heart through repentance and confession; let us wash away filth with tears; let us strive to adorn it with the flowers of good works, that the Holy Spirit may deign to come and prepare a worthy dwelling for himself. He also descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove (Matt. 3), because he showed him to be free from sins. But he came upon the disciples in fire (Acts 2), because, consuming sins in them, he erased the written record of sin. Thus fire went before the children of Israel and showed them the path to their homeland, because the fire of the Holy Spirit goes before them and shows through the Scriptures the way [Col. 0965A] to the homeland of paradise.

Therefore baptism is now administered, because through the Holy Spirit original sin is forgiven. Therefore we also observe fasts on these days, because through the Holy Spirit we hope to receive pardon. Whoever blasphemes the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come (Luke 12). Through the Holy Spirit remission of sins is given. Whoever despairs of pardon blasphemes the Holy Spirit and commits an unforgivable sin.

Just as, dearest ones, the Nativity of the Lord is celebrated, so also this feast is solemn for all the faithful. For as, in that feast, God came in flesh and visited human beings, so in this feast God came in fire, purifying human beings from sins and granting him (sic) many charisms. These feasts are venerable to angels and human beings because they are celebrated in honour of God himself. Finally, at the Lord’s Nativity, the Lord of majesty rose from the throne of his glory, put on the armour of war, and entered exile in order to fight for us. Good Friday was the day of battle and victory, when the Lord, strong and mighty in battle, defeated the prince of this world, the devil, [Col. 0966A] together with his attendants, and powerfully gained the victory. The day of the Lord’s resurrection is the day on which, the battle completed, he devastated the tyrant’s kingdom and gathered to himself the captivity captured by him. The day of the Ascension is this day, on which the Lord of hosts, returning with a noble procession, triumphed; received with angelic melodies, he exalted our flesh above the ether. But today is the day on which he distributes spoils to his soldiers, granting the faithful the diverse gifts of the Holy Spirit.

One day still remains, when he will bring his bride out of this Babylon: when, on the last day, he will place the Church in the heavenly Jerusalem. Indeed, concerning these days the Holy Spirit sang beforehand through the entire Psalter. Moreover, the Law and all the prophets leapt for joy in harmonious voice over these things. Therefore, dearest ones, let us now appear in righteousness before his sight, so that when his glory appears we may be satisfied at his wedding feast: seeing the goodness of his chosen ones, rejoicing in the joy of his people, in the fullness of every good thing (Ps. 105). “What eye has not seen” (1 Cor. 2).

## ON SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

[Col. 0965]

[Col. 0965B] “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree and shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. 91). The palm tree is narrow below and broad above. So too, dearest ones, Saint John the Baptist, whose votive feast we commemorate today, chose to be constrained by poverty on earth, that in [Col. 0965C] heaven he might [perhaps: “deservedly”] be exalted above all the goods of the Lord. Because he flourished beautifully in virtues, he gloriously won the palm of victory over vices. He is also multiplied like a cedar, because in merits he is made dense above all saints. For the cedar is said to have an incorruptible nature and to drive away worms; so Saint John’s life could not be consumed by the rot of sins, and by holy preaching he drove away the worms of vices.

He was the chosen arrow which the Lord hid in his quiver. Those shooting arrows customarily reserve one beyond the others, so that at the opportune time they may strike a sure blow with it. Thus God hid Saint John in the quiver of his secret counsel and reserved him; drawing him forth at the proper time, he shot him into Judea when he commanded him to prepare for his coming a way to human beings. For he was the first to instruct human beings in repentance; he was the first to preach the kingdom of heaven in the world.

Therefore the Church celebrates the birthday of no saint except that of the Lord, of Saint Mary, and of Saint John the Baptist. For John rises like the morning star, by which the nearness of the sun is known. Mary, in being born, rose like the dawn, from whom the eternal Sun proceeded. But when Christ in being born shone upon human beings, then the splendour of the Father shone upon the world, who brought us back from the darkness of death to the light of life. Since this grace was bestowed upon us through these three persons, the Church devoutly commemorates the birthdays of these alone.

Finally, the Lord declares to us in the Gospel how worthy Saint John is [Col. 0966B] of veneration: “Among those born of women,” he says, “none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Luke 7). He is declared greater than all saints and equalled only to angels; hence he is not undeservedly called an angel. His birth is announced by the same angel [Col. 0966C] who foretells Christ’s birth; his name and merit of life are announced beforehand, as are Christ’s name, Jesus, and the dignity of his kingdom. Therefore, just as the Hebrews assign ten names to God, Christians give this man ten titles. This was formerly signified by prophecy, when one prophet declared him a voice and announced him as an angel; the transmitted phrase *vocem altam angelum nunciavit* is uncertain.

He was the voice of the Word of God, because before the incarnate Word he sounded in the wilderness of the world.

He was the herald of the Judge, because he admonished people to prepare themselves for his coming by good conduct.

He shone forth as the Baptizer of the Saviour, because he merited to immerse in the waters of the Jordan him who sanctifies all things.

He was the Forerunner of the Redeemer, because he went before him by being born into the world and by suffering into hell.

[Col. 0966D] He was more than a prophet, because while other prophets asserted by preaching that this one would come, he pointed to him with his finger and declared him present.

He is also called an angel, because through him fellowship with angels is first preached.

He was a shining and burning lamp, because he went before the brightness of the eternal light.

He is called the Friend of the Bridegroom, because he is invited by Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, to the heavenly wedding feast.

He was also the bridegroom’s attendant (*paranymphus*), when he taught the bride to adorn herself with the jewels of virtues.

Elijah too was in spirit and power, because, just as Elijah will precede the Lord’s second coming, so John preceded the first. [Col. 0967A] Hence he is also said to have prepared the way for the Lord, because it is established that he preached a path for the Lord into human hearts through the pursuit of humility. The Gospel recounts how he was sent into the world. Zacharias the high priest took a noble wife, with whom he lived childless into old age. The priests served in the temple by their appointed courses: during the period of their course they stayed near the temple, but once their duty was completed they returned home. Other priests indeed served daily in the temple, but the high priest alone once a year offered a burnt offering in the sanctuary. Therefore, while Zacharias was offering a sacrifice among the Holy of Holies for God’s people, because Herod was oppressing him with unjust rule, an angel of the Lord stood at the right hand of the altar [Col. 0967B] and fear came upon Zacharias. The angel (fol. 190v) warned him not to be afraid, made known that his prayers had been heard, and foretold that a son would be born to him; that many would have great joy at his birth; that he would be filled with the Holy Spirit in his mother’s womb; that he was to be given the name John; that he would be great before the Lord; that he would go before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah; and that he would lead a holy life and convert many to the Lord. When he doubted and pleaded that he and his wife had grown old, the angel imposed silence upon him until all that he had foretold was fulfilled. When he came out of the sanctuary, after completing the sacrifice, and gave no answer to the people, they knew that he had seen a vision.

[Col. 0967C] Therefore Elizabeth, realizing that she had conceived, was ashamed and hid herself for five months. In the sixth month the same angel announced to Mary that the King of all was to be born. She immediately hastened to Elizabeth and greeted her; but the child in Elizabeth’s womb leaped at the voice of the Mother of God, and Elizabeth, immediately filled with the Holy Spirit, declared that all things foretold to Mary would be fulfilled. After she gave birth to the child, great rejoicing arose among all the kindred. On the eighth day the relatives assembled to circumcise the infant, and they thought that he should be given the name of his father, Zacharias; but his mother objected and declared that his name would be John. When they insisted that no one in his family was called by this name, they asked the father [Col. 0967D] what name should be given to his son. Taking a tablet, he wrote down the name and declared that he was to be called John. As soon as this name was set forth in writing, the bond upon his tongue was loosed, and the whole crowd was raised up in admiration and astonishment. Zacharias, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied that God had visited His people and undertaken to redeem His nation, and that it was right for us to serve Him all our days in righteousness and holiness (Luke 1). Beloved, the sick are visited and captives redeemed. Christ visited by being born those who were sick in sins in this world; but those who were captives in the exile of hell He redeemed by dying. John, therefore, while still tender in years left his parents; fleeing people, he concealed himself in the wilderness; he wore a rough garment woven of camel’s hair [“aspersa” read as *aspera*, “rough”], [Col. 0968A] and ate scant food. Recognizing him as full of the Holy Spirit, people flocked to him from every side. He enjoined repentance upon them for their sins and immersed them in baptism in the Jordan (fol. 192r). While all thought him to be the Christ, he denied that he was, and judged himself unworthy to untie the strap of Christ’s sandal [the printed variant *solvendum* means “to be untied”]. But when he saw Christ coming to him to receive baptism from him, he cried out that He was the Lamb of God, declared to all that He takes away the sins of the world, and was granted to see Him who sanctifies all things and takes away sins immersed in the waters, and the Holy Spirit descending upon Him. Thus throughout his life he maintained celibacy and the life of a hermit, led many wanderers to the way of truth, bore testimony to Christ in all things, [Col. 0968B] and patiently offered his neck to the executioner for the truth. He said of himself: “He must decrease” (John 3); but of Christ: “He must increase” (ibid.). For John’s reputation, by which he was thought to be Christ, began to diminish among the people; whereas Christ’s began to increase, for He was recognized as Christ. John too was diminished by the cutting off of his head; but Christ increased when He was raised up on the cross. The seasons themselves also signify their proclamations. For when John is born, the days begin to shorten; when Christ is born, they begin to lengthen. “From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11), because tax collectors and sinners who repented through John’s preaching entered the kingdom of heaven, seemingly not owed to them, as though by force; and even now criminals do penance and, as though by force, snatch the kingdom of heaven. Hence John is interpreted “the grace of God,” because through him the kingdom of heaven is first preached as given to humankind. The Church is divided into three orders: the married, the continent, and virgins. These will inherit different dwelling places according to their merits, since the married will receive thirtyfold fruit, the continent sixtyfold, and virgins a hundredfold.

There are three perfections in which those found will be judges with the Lord: namely virginity, contempt for the world, and martyrdom. These are not commandments but divine counsels. Since Saint John is distinguished by these, he is therefore endowed by God with three crowns. [Col. 0968D] For virginity he is adorned with a garland breathing the eternal fragrance of lilies and roses, because he was adorned in chastity, blossoming like a lily. For contempt of the world he is crowned with a purple diadem, because, flourishing in virtues, he died to the world and to vices. For martyrdom he is wreathed with a crown radiant in gold and gems, because, following the King of glory, he spurned the favor of an incestuous king (fol. 192v). Today Saint John the Evangelist departed from the prison of this world and joyfully entered the heavenly palace amid the rejoicing choirs of saints. Since this could not be celebrated today because of the great office, the Church appointed it to be solemnly observed in the week of the Nativity of the Lord. Therefore, beloved, let us today with devout praises send these namesakes, the supreme friends of God, shining among the highest angels, in prayer [Col. 0969A] to the throne of glory, “that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help” (Hebrews 4), so that the eternal joys denied us because of our deeds may be granted through their intercessions and merits—those in whom God made wonderful all His wills (Psalm 15), and whom He has now ineffably glorified in the kingdom of glory of His Son. “Where eye and ear…” (1 Corinthians 2), and the rest.

## On Saints Peter and Paul

[Col. 0969]

[Col. 0969A] “You will ride upon your horses, O Lord, and your chariots are salvation” (Habakkuk 3). God, the supreme Craftsman, beloved, built for Himself a splendid palace in heaven; but one wall collapsed and fell when the first angel fell with the multitude agreeing with him. Therefore the Son of God mounted His horses; [Col. 0969B] traveling throughout the whole world, He gathered living stones to restore the wall, and, laden with many precious stones placed upon His chariots, returned to the Father. The wall is swiftly raised; the building of God is excellently completed. The chariots of God were the Gospels, which proved salvation to all believers. The horses of God were the apostles, who drew these chariots through the four quarters of the world. Christ is carried about in these chariots when He is preached throughout the circuit of the world through the apostles. Mounted upon these horses, the true soldiers of David—that is, Christ’s martyrs—entered the contest against persecutors and joyfully fought the battles of the God of Israel. The supreme leaders of this army were Peter and Paul, whose solemnities [Col. 0969C] we devoutly celebrate today, because today, after the war was finished, they triumphed most victoriously and entered the hall of the heavenly court as chief senators and crowned princes of the apostles. While in the flesh, they shone as lights of the world through signs and writings; one day, as judges with Christ, they will shine like the sun. The whole fabric of the Church is supported by these two firm columns, and is splendidly illuminated by their deeds and sayings as by precious gems. From a boat the Lord called one of them while he was pursuing fish (fol. 194r), gave him the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and raised him as prince of the Church. The other, while pursuing people, He chose from heaven, gave him the keys of knowledge, and appointed him teacher of the nations. This is “the change of the right hand of the Most High”: from a fisherman He made a prince, from a persecutor the teacher of the world. [Col. 0969D] Thus Paul opens with his key the doors of Scripture to believers; Peter opens with his key the gates of enduring life to those persevering in goodness. Paul softens hard hearts to repentance by sweet teaching; Peter, by the authority granted him, absolves those who weep from guilt. Paul urges people toward joys by earnest exhortation; Peter draws them by mercifully opening the doors of life.

Peter, Andrew’s brother, was from Bethsaida, was called Simon by his parents, and was a fisherman in Galilee. But, called by the Lord from fishing, he left his boat and net and clung to the Author of life with his brother. Thus the Lord wove the net of faith and made them fishers of men, because through them He wished to draw many from the whirlpool of this age to the shore of eternal rest. He clung to the Lord more intimately than all the apostles, [Col. 0970A] loved Him more fervently than all, and answered before all when the Lord questioned them. Finally, when the Lord came to Caesarea and asked His disciples what the people thought of Him, and they answered that some called Him Elijah, some John the Baptist, others Jeremiah, and others another [Col. 0970B] prophet, and He asked what they themselves thought of Him, Peter answered before all: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16). The Lord pronounced his faith blessed, saying that it had been revealed to him not by fleshly descent but by “my Father.” Therefore, He said, “I will change your name to Peter; upon the rock of your faith I will also found my Church, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail, nor can the rivers of persecutions overthrow it. I make you the doorkeeper of life, giving you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Let authority be granted you such that whatever has been bound by you on earth may remain entangled in bonds in heaven also, and whatever has been loosed by you upon earth may likewise be safe in heaven from bonds” (ibid.). O how blessed is the man to whom such authority is given by God!

[Col. 0970C] Yet assuredly, since he was to be set over the Church as its shepherd, he had to be schooled by temptations so that he might know how to sympathize and suffer with his brothers. Thus, when at one time the Lord went up alone onto a mountain to pray (fol. 194v), He commanded the disciples to cross the sea in a boat. But the sea, sensing that its Ruler was absent, battered the little boat with raging storms. Fear seized the sailors, for shipwreck already threatened them; and behold, the Lord came walking upon the sea. They thought Him a phantom and cried out in fear, but He gently consoled them, urged them to have confidence, and declared that it was He. Peter said: “If it is you, Lord, command me to come to you” (Matthew 14). When He commanded him to come, Peter got out of the boat and began [Col. 0970D] to walk over the swelling waves as though over solid ground. But as the storm grew severe, terrified, he trembled, and immediately the wave opened beneath the feet that had been treading it. When it threatened to swallow him, he implored the Lord’s help with a cry; and at once, grasped by His right hand, he was upheld in danger. He walked with the Lord over the waves to the boat, and immediately the sea, sensing that its Lord was present, calmed its raging storms. O what faith burned in his breast, he who did not fear to entrust himself to the troubled waves! On that night too, when Christ offered Himself to God the Father as a sacrifice for the salvation of the world, He said that the disciples would abandon Him. But Peter declared that he would go with Him both to prison and to death. The Lord, however, affirmed that Peter would deny Him three times before the cock crowed, [Col. 0971A] as the event proved. For when the Lord, seized by the Jews, was badly treated and led like a sheep to slaughter, Peter, asked whether he belonged to His disciples, denied it with an oath and repeatedly declared in an insolent voice that he did not know Him. But when the cock crowed, the Lord looked upon him as he denied Him; and Peter went out and, punishing his deed with bitter tears, inclined himself toward the mercy of Him who looked upon him. Therefore, beloved, divine mercy permitted the prince of the Church to commit so dreadful a sin, so that in his own fall he might learn how he ought to grieve and sympathize with weak neighbors. For this reason the Lord even today permits a grave fall among the elect, so that our weakness may raise itself through them to divine clemency; so that, [Col. 0971B] when we see them rise from grave ruin through repentance and satisfaction, and eagerly undertake the pursuit of holy conduct, we too, looking upon the patience and riches of God’s mercy, may strive to emerge from the depth of our iniquities as vessels of mercy.

While Peter remained in tears (fol. 196r) and did not dare to join the other disciples, the risen Lord appeared to him and granted him consolation and pardon. On another occasion, when Peter was fishing with the others, the Lord appeared, ate a meal with them, and asked Peter for the third time whether he loved Him more than the others. Peter for the third time confessed his heart’s love, and the threefold denial was erased. For the third time the Lord entrusted His sheep to him to feed—the sheep for whom He Himself, the good Shepherd, laid down His life. Then He foretold [Col. 0971C] that Peter too would lay down his life on a cross for the honor of God and for those same sheep. After the Lord returned to the Father’s throne, Peter restored the apostolic number through Matthias, which Judas’s hanging had diminished. When the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, came and filled them with His consolation, Peter publicly proclaimed Christ to the people. He who had formerly denied Him at the timid voice of a maidservant now steadfastly preached Him before the fearsome authority of the priests. One day he had gone up to the temple with John, and behold, a certain lame man begged him to receive alms. Peter told him that he had neither gold nor silver, but would freely give what he possessed, commanding him to rise in the name of Jesus Christ and go away healed. He immediately became whole, entered the temple [Col. 0971D] praising the Lord, and a great multitude turned to God. Peter was brought before the council of the wicked; threatening words flew from every side. But Peter, an unlearned man, overcame the teachers of the people through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and by the performance of signs proved that Jesus, whom they had crucified, was God. Then, while he preached in the temple with his fellow apostles, he was seized by the rulers, imprisoned together with all of them, and placed under military guard. But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, led out the apostles, and commanded them to proclaim words of life to the people. The next day the priests assembled in council and sent to the prison to bring out the apostles. Returning, the messengers reported that they had found [Col. 0972A] the prison locked with every precaution, but, when it was opened, had found no one inside. While they discussed this in astonishment, someone reported that they were teaching the people in the temple. They were brought in and beaten with scourges, but returned rejoicing from the council because they suffered adversity for the name of Jesus. Then Peter ordained seven deacons, among whom Stephen especially shone in signs and wonders (fol. 196v); but the faithless people of the Jews hastened to overwhelm him with stones. Philip, his companion, went down to Samaria and converted a multitude of people to the faith through signs and preaching.

At that time there was there Simon Magus, who for a long while had bewitched the people by magical arts. Baptized by Philip, he had joined the throng of believers with a false heart. [Col. 0972B] Therefore the apostles sent Peter with John to confirm the baptized; when confirmed by them and immediately receiving the Holy Spirit, they began to speak in every language. When Simon Magus saw this, he offered Peter a great sum of money so that he might be given the power that, when he laid hands on someone, that person might speak in diverse languages. Peter struck him and all his followers with this curse: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts 8). From that day Simon Magus began to disturb the Church, declaring himself to be Christ and Peter to be a deceiver. Meanwhile, when the multitude of believers lived in common and someone withheld part of the proceeds from a field he had sold, Peter rebuked him, and he immediately died with his wife. O how dreadful a teacher of the Church he was, to whom the Holy Spirit was so immediately present for vengeance! [Col. 0972C] So great was the abundance of the Holy Spirit overflowing in him that the sick placed in the streets were made well by his shadow. One day, as Peter preached in the temple and the high priest with the Pharisees rejected his teaching, Peter foretold to them the destruction of the temple, which later occurred through the army of the gentiles. There was a woman named Tabitha, who gave many alms to the needy. When she died, all mourned her; sending for Peter, the widows showed the garments Tabitha had made, and he immediately restored her alive to those who were weeping. [Read *post Petro mittentes*, “after sending for Peter,” as below.]

At that time there was a centurion at Caesarea named Cornelius, constant in almsgiving and prayers. An angel of the Lord visibly appeared to him and commanded him to send [Col. 0972D] to Joppa for Peter and obey his words. Meanwhile, while Peter lay prostrate in prayer, he was carried out of himself and saw a vessel lowered from heaven by four cords, filled with different creeping things; and a voice came from above: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10). When he replied that he had never eaten anything unclean, the voice said that all things created by God were clean. When this was seen for the third time, the vessel was taken up into heaven.

The vessel lowered by four beginnings [i.e. corners; *initiis*] (fol. 198r) is the Church received into heaven through the four Gospels; within it, the diversity of serpents and creeping creatures is the multitude serving idols or sins. Peter ought, by preaching, to kill them in their sins and, through faith and good [Col. 0973A] works, transfer them into Christ’s body, which is the Church.

Cornelius therefore sent for Peter. When Peter came to him with the brethren, Cornelius recounted the vision. While Peter made Christ known to them, the Holy Spirit fell upon those hearing him; and, as all spoke in tongues, Peter ordered them to be baptized in the name of the Lord. This Cornelius was later appointed bishop of Caesarea and governed the Church worthily, distinguished by teaching and miracles.

Afterward Peter was seized by Herod, bound with two chains, committed to prison, and entrusted to the guard of sixteen soldiers. On the night before Herod was to bring him out before the people for mockery, Peter lay sleeping [Col. 0973B] between two soldiers, bound with two chains. But the whole Church poured out offerings of prayers for him; and behold, in that very night an angel of the Lord, with a great light, awakened Peter, commanded him to rise and follow him. Immediately the chains fell from his hands, and as they went out the iron gates opened for them of their own accord. Thus the prince of the Church was freed by an angel and restored to the rejoicing Church. On the next day Herod sent to the prison and ordered Peter to be brought. The prison was found shut, with the guards present, but when opened Peter was not found. As all wondered at this, an angel of God struck Herod, and he died swarming with worms.

Peter often contended with Simon Magus and exposed all his wiles before the people. Thus the false and [Col. 0973C] deceitful man was driven out of Antioch; Peter, summoned with great honor, was raised up with the episcopal mitre. Like a good farmer, he tirelessly cultivated the vineyard of the Lord, grafted into Christ—the true vine—the branches gathered everywhere from Jews and gentiles, watered them with sayings and writings, and made them fruitful with signs and miracles. Since God had lit him as the highest lamp, He decreed to place him upon the highest lampstand so that he might shine upon all established in the house of this world. Thus, scattering the word of God throughout his circuit, he arrived at Rome; there he received from Christ the governance of the supreme pontificate over the whole Church. And as he illumined the East with signs and teachings, so he made the West radiant with virtues and miracles (fol. 198v). He also ordained very many persons of religious life as bishops [Col. 0973D] and sent them to preach in diverse provinces. Through him they shone in signs and wonders and led multitudes of gentiles to faith in Christ’s name. Indeed, he himself was so outstanding in miracles that he restored health to the sick not only by prayer or the shadow of his body, but even restored life to the dead through a staff. For he raised from death Maternus, sent by him and later bishop of Trier, who had died on the journey and lain buried for forty days, by sending his staff through Valerius and Eucharius. Maternus afterward lived for forty years, preached to the gentiles, and shone gloriously with his companions in miracles. Truly the Lord fulfilled what He promised His friends: “He who believes in me,” He said, “will also do the works that I do, and will do greater than these” (John 14). The Lord indeed restored to life a man dead four days; behold, Peter raised through his staff a man buried forty days. Likewise Fronto, sent by him as bishop of the Church of Périgueux, raised his companion, the priest George, from death during a journey by means of blessed Peter’s staff.

Paul was born at Tarsus in Cilicia of noble family and called Saul by his parents. In Jerusalem he was instructed in the law by Gamaliel [printed *Gamiele*] and was a persecutor of the Church. But called by the Lord from heaven, he abandoned cruelty and strove faithfully to serve the Lord. For, struck down by Him on the road and deprived of sight, after three days he was baptized and enlightened in body and soul. Immediately he entered the synagogue of the Jews and publicly and confidently preached Christ. [Col. 0974B] Those wishing to kill him laid snares for him. The pagans guarded him in Damascus, but the faithful let him down by the wall through a gate at night. Like a strong warrior he entered the field of battle. Therefore he came to Jerusalem; Barnabas brought him to the apostles and told them how the Lord had appeared to him on the road, how he had been baptized, how confidently he had acted in the synagogue, and how he had barely escaped their hands. Filled with joy, they gave thanks to God; and Peter, James, and John gave him the right hands of apostolic fellowship, and sent him with Barnabas and others [with *ut*, “that,” printed] to preach Christ to the gentiles. Traveling through almost the whole world (fol. 200r) [Col. 0974C] and scattering the word of God, he drew East and West, as it were, within two cords to the faith, and instructed them with the abundant eloquence of Scripture. Among the other splendid signs that he performed, he deprived a magician opposing him of sight, converted the proconsul Paul, and permanently acquired his name. For it was an ancient custom that, if a powerful person were overcome by another, the name of the defeated should be given to the victor. One night, while Paul prolonged his discourse, a young man fell asleep and fell from the third story. He was taken up dead, but was immediately raised by Paul, and Christ was praised by all. Therefore, having established everything in ecclesiastical order, he returned to the apostles and reported how great things God had done through him among the gentiles. They gave thanks to God, who predestines and “wills all people [Col. 0974D] to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” While Paul prayed in the temple, he was carried up to the third heaven, transported into the heavenly paradise, saw Jesus Christ, and beheld many secrets which it was not permitted for a human being to utter. Then, burning with the Spirit and the zeal to preach, he returned to the gentiles. In almost every city he was beaten with rods or whips, or torn with stones and thrown out half alive; in many places he was bound with chains and more often shut up in prisons. After suffering these and many other adversities for Christ, he returned to Jerusalem, was seized by pagans, carried off by Jews, and sent in chains to Rome. During the voyage his ship was broken up by a storm; Paul was enveloped by the waves and remained in the depths of the sea for three days and nights. Then, lifted up by Christ, he emerged and reached the shore unharmed. [Col. 0975A] In this he proved equal to Peter in merits: he was able to live amid shipwreck beneath the waves for three days, whereas Peter had been able to walk upon them with his feet. When Paul gathered branches for a fire on an island, a viper clung to his hand, which he shook off into the fire. The inhabitants of that place, seeing this, called him a very wicked man, saying that though he had escaped shipwreck, divine vengeance would not allow him to live. But when he did not die, they said that he was a god, and through his preaching were granted to turn to the true God. On another occasion, while he preached with Barnabas in a certain city and healed a lame man, the pagans thought that he was a god (fol. 200v) and the priests wished to sacrifice to him; but through him they came to know the true God of all.

[Col. 0975B] After the ship had again been refitted by the tribune, Paul was brought to Rome and joined to Peter, his companion and fellow apostle. And just as Elijah and Enoch, at the end time, destroying the error of unbelief and confounding Antichrist, are crowned after being killed by Antichrist himself, so these men, overcoming Simon Magus, teacher of error, and despising Nero, who bore the figure of Antichrist, were crowned after being killed by him. It was fitting that the greatest should be brought to completion by the greatest ruler in the greatest place, since they were to be placed by the highest God upon the highest summit of heaven and in the highest place of the blessed. But now it will be possible to hear how they triumphed.

When Simon Magus had deceived the Roman people by many errors, one day Peter and Simon met in the city of Rome with crowds present and exchanged words in the hearing [Col. 0975C] of the people. Behold, a certain dead man was being carried out for burial, and Simon addressed the people: “What punishment,” he said, “will you inflict upon Peter if I raise this dead man?” They answered: “We will hand him over alive to the fire.” He invoked a demon and made the body move and emit groans. The crowds extolled Simon with praises and called Peter a deceiver. Peter, after scarcely calming the people, said that if the man lived, he should rise, speak, and eat; if Simon could not do this, it was the work of the devil. The people, stirred up, compelled Simon to raise the dead man; but he, feigning anger, began to depart. Immediately the people seized him in order to burn him in the flames, but Peter begged that he be spared. Then [Col. 0975D] he invoked Christ’s name and raised the dead man as though from sleep. The man reported that he had been brought before the Judge and commanded to return through Peter’s prayers; he called Peter the true friend of God, but Simon full of diabolical deception. Thus the whole assembly cried out for the one God, loudly praised Christ the Son of God, cast out Simon with curses, and, revering Peter, devoutly submitted their hands to him. Among them was Marcellus, eminent in family and wealth, in whose house Simon had lodged. He expelled Simon from himself in disgrace, but received Peter into his lodging with great affection. Simon therefore bound a very large dog inside the doors of Marcellus’s house (fol. 202r) with a chain, thinking by its terror to keep Peter from the lodging. But Peter came, loosed the dog, [Col. 0976A] and commanded it to return to its master, forbidding it to sink its teeth into him but directing it to confound the deceiver of souls. The dog then, leaping upon Simon in the midst of the city, attacked him, violently threw him to the ground, and tore all his garments to pieces. Simon was transformed into a wolf [the printed text is uncertain: *transformavit* / perhaps *transformatus*], imitated a wolf’s howl, fled from the City, and entered the hidden places of the woods. That great dog and all the boys of the city with their dogs pursued him and sought to tear the disgraced man to pieces with the bites of dogs. Thus the wonder-working man lay hidden for two years. Afterwards he came to Nero, asserted that he was God, transformed himself into various shapes by diabolical art, and declared Peter and Paul enemies of Caesar and of the Roman people. Therefore, by Nero’s order the apostles Peter and Paul were seized and brought before the emperor. [Col. 0976B] In his presence they proved Simon to be false, and Christ to reign in the Godhead of the Father. Simon promised to ascend to heaven and summon Nero to himself from earth, if only a high tower were made for him from which he might seek heaven, because this could not be done for him among sinners. Nero therefore commanded a multitude of craftsmen to build a wooden tower, and the whole Roman people gathered for the spectacle. Simon, crowned with laurel, climbed the tower and began to fly, borne by demons and piercing the air. Peter adjured them and commanded them in Christ’s name to carry him no farther. Immediately abandoned by them, he fell and was shattered into many pieces. Nero, filled with rage, ordered the apostles to perish under punishments. They were immediately chained and wasted for nine months under prison guard.

[Col. 0976C] One day, as Peter was leaving custody, the Lord met him. Peter asked Him where He was going, and the Lord answered that He was going to Rome and wished to be crucified again. Peter immediately returned to custody. Then he was brought out by the torturers and crucified before the people after the example of Christ. At his own request his cross was turned, with his feet raised upwards and his head hanging downwards. Thus the good shepherd laid down his life for the flock entrusted to him, and the Lord set the faithful servant over all His goods. Paul, however, was released that year (fol. 202v), as he himself testifies: “I was delivered,” he says, “from the mouth of the lion” (2 Timothy 4), namely from Nero’s hands. But later, when many of the emperor’s friends had been converted to Christ through him, [Col. 0976D] he was again ordered to be seized. On the same day on which Peter was raised upon the cross for the Church, he was beheaded for Christ. Milk flowed with blood from the wound in his neck, because sweet teaching always abounded in him. Afterwards Nero was driven from his kingdom by the Roman people in disgrace; hiding in the woods, he was devoured by wolves. Thus may these triumphant men merit the heavenly places through their blood and today, crowned with laurel, be exalted in the angelic court. Since they now reap in joy what they sowed in tears, following their examples and obeying their teaching in all things, let us ask Him who is glorious and wonderful in His saints that through their merits we may obtain those joys “which eye has not seen” (1 Corinthians 2), and the rest.

If the feast of Saint Benedict falls on a Sunday, the people may be instructed about him as follows:

[Col. 0977]

[Col. 0977A] **The Translation of Saint Benedict, Abbot**

“The righteous shall spring up like a lily and shall bloom forever before the Lord” (Isaiah 35). A lily is white outwardly, shines inwardly with a golden color, and is fragrant with a sweet odor. So this most holy Father, Benedict in name and deed, whose solemnity we celebrate today, was outwardly white with the brightness of chastity, inwardly shining with the golden color of charity, and breathing the fragrance of sweetness in every virtue. Therefore he will bloom forever before the Lord in glory and rejoice perpetually with the angels in joy. After working many signs, when he came to Monte Cassino and began to build dwellings there for the brothers, the devil appeared to him in a horrible form while he lay prostrate in prayer. The devil cried out that Benedict ought rather to be called cursed than blessed (fol. 204r), and shouted in dreadful tones, asking why he persecuted him. [Col. 0977B] When Benedict made no reply, the devil said that the brothers needed help in building the wall. Going away, he struck the wall at which the brothers were then working; it collapsed, crushed one of the monks, and brought death to him and grief to the others. The monk was scarcely brought to Benedict on a cloak amid great mourning, but Benedict immediately restored him unharmed to life through prayer. He then commanded him to repair the wall with the brothers, over whose ruin the devil rejoiced.

On another occasion, when a certain stone had to be placed in a building, many men could not lift it. Benedict prayed; the devil, who was sitting upon it, was driven away; and the stone was lifted by a few men and placed in a suitable position in the building. Then, at the Father’s command, the brothers dug the ground deeper there [Col. 0977C] and found an idol. When they had thrown it into the kitchen, fire seemed to come out and consume the whole dwelling. As they eagerly threw water to put out the fire, Benedict arrived, grieving that the brothers were being deceived by the frauds of the malicious enemy. When he had prayed, the devil was driven away, and all saw that building unharmed. One day a rustic brought him his dead son, and the holy man immediately restored him to life through prayer. A young monk left the monastery without the blessed man’s permission, but on the very day he reached his parents he died. After he had been buried, he was found cast out of the ground. Buried again, the earth vomited him up and could not keep him, because he did not possess Benedict’s favor. [Col. 0977D] Therefore his parents came to Benedict weeping, received an offering from his hands, bound it to the little body, and committed it to burial; thereafter they did not find it cast out again.

Certain noblewomen lived as religious converts under him, but did not restrain themselves from idle talk. The man of God commanded them to curb their tongues, otherwise he would excommunicate them. Since they did not correct themselves, they died within a short time and, during the solemnities of the Masses, were seen every day to come out of their tombs. When Benedict gave an offering for them, they no longer left their dwelling in the tombs.

Consider, dearest brethren, of what merit before God this man was, who restored life to the dead and had power so great to bind and loose souls released from the flesh.

The miracles of this man are many, and it would take too long to recount them to you one by one; nevertheless, let us relate a few more, to the praise of him who alone performs wonders. A certain priest possessed by a demon could be freed by no one; but when brought to Benedict, he at once deserved to be cured when the demon had been expelled. A certain monk (fo. 204v) had gone out to draw water, and a demon that had entered him was grievously tormenting him; but Benedict, arriving, immediately drove the enemy away by his command. A brother had resolved to leave Benedict’s cell, but a dragon met him and wished to devour him; appearing openly, it drew back the man whom it had first secretly drawn outside. Brothers had been sent on an errand; on the way they ate without permission. On their return the man of God reproved them for their transgression; when they denied it, he specified the kinds and number of foods.
