When they asked pardon, he mercifully granted it, kindly warning them to avoid sins. A certain boy-monk, noble by birth, stood beside Benedict as he ate, holding a light. While he silently entertained in his breast, through a spirit of pride, the thought of who this man might be beside whom he himself stood as servant, Benedict ordered him to put down the light and to impress the sign of the holy cross upon his heart. To the amazement of all, he reported precisely what thoughts the boy had been considering in his heart; and all began to marvel that the thoughts of his mind had sounded in Benedict’s ears as words. Benedict rebuked a faithless king who came to him deceitfully, and foretold to him all that would happen. Asked by a certain nobleman, he sent brothers to build a monastery; appearing to them by night while they were far from him, he marked out every dwelling that was to be built in the monastery. A severe famine afflicted the region, and Benedict distributed all the goods of his monastery among the needy. The brothers therefore began to be distressed because only a few loaves remained for their sustenance. The holy Father gently comforted them and earnestly entreated God’s power; and behold, suddenly they found before the monastery doors two hundred modii of the whitest flour in sacks. They gave thanks to the God who had sent it, by whose gift it was abundantly sufficient until the new harvest.

At that time someone asked Benedict for oil. Benedict ordered that the little remaining in a glass vessel be given [Col. 0978D]; but the man who had it in custody refused to give it, thinking it better to reserve it for the sick brothers. Benedict then ordered the others to throw out the vessel with its oil, lest anything contrary to obedience seem to remain in the cell. Cast by the brothers onto a rocky place, it struck there, yet neither the vessel broke nor the oil spilled. Benedict ordered it to be lifted up (fo. 206) and given to the petitioner. Rebuking the disobedient brother, he entered the oratory with all the brethren, prostrated himself before God in prayer, and there stood a cask in which oil began to rise from bottom to top.

Thus the merciful Lord always repaid his faithful servant a hundredfold [Col. 0979A], whom afterwards he set over all his goods. A certain peasant was bound by a soldier because of his possessions and driven in chains before the soldier’s horse to Benedict’s little cell; but by the holy man’s gaze alone he was freed, for when Benedict bent his eyes toward him, he immediately stood released, his chains broken. At midnight Benedict rose to confess the Lord’s name, and, standing at the window in a tower, poured forth prayers with hymns to the Lord. Behold, the heaven opened, and an immeasurable light, brighter than the noon-day sun, shone forth and drove away all the darkness of night. In its radiance the soul of a certain bishop passed through the heavens; and a portion of this light entered through the window like a ray of the sun, at which [sic] Benedict stood praying. As his holy mind was enlarged in God, he beheld the whole world in this [Col. 0979B] ray. On another occasion, as he looked toward heaven, he saw his sister’s soul, in the form of a dove, borne by angels to the stars. After adorning his days with these and many other splendid signs, he foretold his death to his disciples. Stricken by illness [Col. 0980A], he asked to be carried into the oratory; strengthened by the holy sacraments of the Lord, he breathed out his blessed spirit amid words of prayer. As angels exalted him into the heavenly homeland, his everlasting glory was divinely revealed to disciples far and near. In the cave where he had formerly hidden, a madwoman also received health. After his departure, an army of pagans destroyed his monastery, just as he had foretold while alive; and when the place had been deserted, certain religious persons transferred his body into Gaul. As we remember today, God glorified it by many signs both on the journey and at its arrival. And as God here made him wondrous among men by glorious signs, so now among all the saints he has crowned him with surpassing glory and honor. He himself now shines among [Col. 0980B] the morning stars and rejoices, and helps all who imitate him and devoutly invoke him to attain the same joys—things which eye has not seen (1 Cor. 2), and so forth.

## ON SAINT MARY MAGDALENE

[Col. 0979]

[Col. 0979B] “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9). Truly, dearest brethren, the Lord first showed by his deeds what he preached in words. For he did not call the Pharisees and others who stubbornly asserted themselves to be righteous, but the tax collectors who humbly acknowledged themselves to be sinners. Hence tax collectors and prostitutes [Col. 0979C] entered the kingdom of God before those who called him the friend of tax collectors. Thus he rejected the Pharisee in the Temple who boasted of his good deeds, but justified the tax collector who accused himself for his evil deeds (Luke 18). He whom the angels in heaven desire to behold (1 Pet. 1) came into this world to save sinners. He had drawn many out of the pit of misery and the mire of the dregs (Ps. 39), he who came to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19); and among them, as today’s Gospel has declared to us, he set before us blessed Mary Magdalene as an example of his mercy. She is said to have been the sister of Lazarus, whom the Lord raised from the tomb after four days, and likewise the sister of Martha [Col. 0979D], who often received the Lord into her home.

This Mary was given in marriage in the town of Magdala; but fleeing from him to Jerusalem, forgetful of her family and oblivious of God’s law, she became a common prostitute. After voluntarily making herself a brothel of shame, she rightly became a shrine of demons; for seven demons entered her at once and continually tormented her with unclean desires. She was brought to Jesus by her sister, and through him the seven demons were immediately cast out; healed, she returned home joyfully with her sister. Afterwards, when the Lord, invited to dinner in the house of a Pharisee from whom he had previously expelled leprosy, reclined at table, Mary came, at her sister’s persuasion, barefoot and with her hair uncovered, carrying precious ointments that she had formerly bought for the purposes of her shame. She fell down at the Lord’s feet because she grieved that she had yielded to many lovers. Streams of water flowed from her eyes because they had not kept God’s law. With tears she washed the filth of the feet of him who washed her, and she herself deserved to be washed from the filth of her crimes. With her hair she wiped the Lord’s feet—hair which she had formerly adorned with gold (fo. 208) to entice [Col. 0980C] young men. She devoutly pressed kisses upon his footprints—kisses which she had formerly offered pleasurably to seducers. She anointed the feet of him who washed her with ointment, with which she had previously rubbed her own flesh and drawn the stench of those who shamefully loved her. Everything that she had formerly offered voluptuously for the service of the flesh, she now, conversely, turned mournfully to the Lord’s service. And because she had formerly not been ashamed, before the angels, to wallow in the filth of uncleanness like a sow, now she did not fear to be humiliated before the men at table. Thus she found there the very fountain of mercy and withdrew purified from every stain.

But the unhappy host was scandalized that the Lord did not disdain to be touched by a sinner; indeed, not only the sick woman but also the physician he condemned in his heart, though he himself, wretched man, labored severely under the fever [Col. 0980D] of false righteousness. The Lord enumerated the good things omitted by him and recounted those bestowed by her, thereby indicating to us that he exacts punishment for all our negligences but confers high rewards for our own diligent efforts. Thus, confuting the malevolent man, the merciful judge absolved the accused woman as she punished herself, and true Peace permitted her to depart in peace. She returned rejoicing to her sister and devoted the remainder of her life to chastity with the utmost zeal.

Finally, when the Lord had turned aside to her sister Martha and Martha labored greatly in his service, Mary humbly clung to his feet and drank in the words of his sweetness with a thirsting heart. She longed to travel through the country with him and his followers, and ministered to him from her small means. For women were permitted among [Col. 0981A] the Jews to travel with religious men and to serve them from their own resources in their needs. Afterwards, when the Lord, hastening to his Passion for the salvation of the world, reclined in the house of the Pharisee mentioned above, and Lazarus was one of those reclining at table, Mary poured precious ointment over his head, signifying that the Church would come to him with the fragrance of virtues, and that he would anoint her with the ointment of the Holy Spirit. Judas indeed disapproved this act, but the Lord praised it, because works of the Church that are hateful to the reprobate are acceptable to our God. When the Lord hung upon the cross for us, and the flock of disciples had been scattered, their shepherd fleeing in different directions (fo. 208v), she stood undaunted and visited him in the tomb with spices. Therefore she deserved to see an angel [Col. 0981B], and the risen Lord first of all appeared publicly to her and sent her as an apostle to his apostles, so that, as the first woman had brought death to man, now a woman might announce everlasting life to men.

It is also reported of her that, after seeing the Lord ascend to heaven with the other disciples and receiving the Holy Spirit with them, she thereafter did not wish to see any man because of her love for him. Coming into the wilderness, she lived for some years in a cave. When a wandering priest came to her and asked who she was, she replied that she was Mary the sinner and said that he had been sent to bury her body. Having said this, she departed gloriously from the world which she had long abhorred, and, while angels sang a hymn, went to the Lord whom she loved greatly [Col. 0981C], and who had forgiven her greatly; he permitted her to gather lilies in the garden of spices with the shining virgins.

Now, dearest brethren, let us return to ourselves and see what must be done concerning our sins. For the falls of the saints and their repentance were written for this purpose: that we, who have imitated the fall of their weakness by rushing into evil, may also be converted to good through repentance, abandoning evil by their example. But alas! We wretches desire to imitate them in sins, while refusing to follow their examples in good deeds. And if, dearest brethren, we have hitherto labored in evil, let us at least today endeavor, following the example of this woman, to counterbalance the past by subsequent good deeds. [Col. 0981D] For blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered (Ps. 31). Original sins are forgiven through baptism; actual sins, however, are covered through repentance. What we are ashamed to have naked, we cover with a garment laid over it. So too, dearest brethren, let us be ashamed that the foulness of our shameful life should be seen by God and the angels, and let us cover it with the laments of repentance and good works. Let us offer God, for sin and transgression, a troubled spirit and a contrite and humbled heart (Ps. 50), and let us bear worthy fruits of repentance (Matt. 3), so that we may wash away lighter sins by prayers and punish heavier ones with weeping, fasts, vigils, and almsgiving (fo. 210).

For the Law commands that a kid is not to be boiled in its mother’s milk (Exod. 23). To boil a kid in its mother’s milk is to subject to mild repentance one who, because of grave crimes, is assigned among the kids to the left hand; but we do not boil the kid in its mother’s milk if we, ruined in wicked acts, afflict ourselves with harsh and severe [Col. 0982B] punishments. For we are commanded to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. Moreover, the people of Israel, coming out of Egypt, conquered their enemies in the place where they had formerly been conquered, because we, returning from this world to our homeland, can conquer the devil in the same vice in which we were formerly conquered by him; for whoever is conquered by another becomes that other’s servant. We must beware lest the devil find us servants of sin and possess us as if by perpetual right.

Indeed, there was a command in the Law that, if anyone compelled by necessity sold himself to another, he should go free in the seventh year; but if he refused to depart from service, his master should pierce his ear with an awl, and thus possess him as a servant by perpetual right (Exod. 21). When, conquered by desires, we yield as though compelled by necessity, we sell ourselves to another by making ourselves servants of sin. For everyone who commits sin is the servant of sin (John 8); but in the seventh year we shall be able to go free, because through the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit we can be released from the devil’s dominion. But the one who refuses to be free—his master pierces him with an awl; for the person sold under sin who does not, through repentance, leave this service for God as a free person, the devil will pierce with the sting of death and, possessing him as a servant by perpetual right, will torture him in eternal punishments. Therefore, dearest brethren, imitating blessed Mary Magdalene, let us cast off from ourselves the hard yoke of diabolic servitude and receive the sweet yoke of the Lord, that true liberty; and let us serve in holiness [Col. 0982D] and righteousness him for whom to serve is to reign, so that by him we may be transferred into the liberty of the glory of God’s children—things which eye has not seen (1 Cor. 2), and so forth.

## ON SAINT JAMES THE APOSTLE

[Col. 0981]

“The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18). The apostles are called heavens, in whom divine mysteries are hidden; from them shone the sun of wisdom, the moon of eloquence gleamed, the stars of virtues sparkled (fo. 210v), the lightning flashes of miracles shone, the thunders [Col. 0982D] of preaching resounded, and the rains of the Scriptures flowed. These heavens declared God’s glory when the apostles proclaimed Christ throughout the whole world. “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (ibid.). The Church is called the firmament because through the sacrament of faith it divides the faithful from the unbelieving, as waters from waters [Col. 0983A]. It proclaims the works of his hands when it preaches God’s deeds and words to its children with worthy praises.

According to the Law, the garment of the high priest was to be adorned with twelve precious stones, upon which the twelve names of the children of Israel were to be engraved (Exod. 39). Christ was the supreme and true priest, who offered to God the Father the sacrifice of his own body for us. His garment is the Church, adorned with the twelve apostles as with as many pearls. In them the names of the twelve children of Israel were expressed, because Israel prefigured Christ the Son and the twelve apostles, and they will judge the twelve tribes together with all nations. A golden diadem encircled with gems also shone upon that priest’s head, while the apostolic company encircled Christ, our head [Col. 0983B]. These men, bright as gold through holy conduct and adorned with the gems of virtues, as they preached the heavenly life around the circuit of the world, crowned Christ’s bride like a royal diadem.

It is also read that Isaac opened a well which his father’s servants had dug, but the Philistines filled it with earth. Isaac’s servants dug another well and found living water. Isaac dug a third well, which he called “Breadth” (Gen. 26). Abraham’s servants dug a well when Moses and the other prophets, servants of God, composed [*coposuerunt*, sic] the Old Testament; but the Philistines—that is, the Jews—filled it with earth, namely with an earthly and sordid understanding. Isaac opened the well when Christ made known the depth of sacred [Col. 0983C] Scripture to the apostles. Isaac’s servants also dug a well when the apostles and evangelists wrote the New Testament through the Holy Spirit. They found living water when they conveyed evangelical teaching, springing up into eternal life, to the human race. The third well dug by Isaac signifies baptism. It is given the name “Breadth” because it is spread throughout the whole world. The servants of the true Isaac, Christ—the apostles—scattered the water of this fountain across the breadth of the world (fo. 212) when they baptized all nations in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28).

From their company blessed James, whose feast we celebrate today, the brother of John the Evangelist, is said to have preached in Spain. Returning from there to visit the Church in Judea, he found it subverted by two magicians, Hermogenes and Philetus. He destroyed their deception by signs and preaching, and led the wandering flock of the Lord, attacked by wolves, back to the true shepherd. Moreover, he converted the magicians themselves—teachers of error—with many others to Christ, and made them noble teachers of the Church. Therefore the Jews, goaded by envy and stirring up a sedition, furiously seized James, led him before the tribunal of Herod, son of Archelaus Aristobulus, and, after he had been condemned by him, dragged him away to be beheaded. On the way he healed a paralytic man and baptized the scribe who was dragging him along with a rope. That man too was beheaded with him for Christ’s name; and so the laurel-crowned friend of God was seated with his companion in the senate of the heavenly court. His [Col. 0984A] body was entrusted by Hermogenes and Philetus to his other five disciples; they placed it in a ship, that it might be hidden somewhere until, with the Lord’s permission, it could be worthily buried. Having embarked, they fell asleep, and on waking the next day found themselves in Spain, where he had preached before. Carrying out the body, they placed it upon a stone, which they immediately saw sink into the stone as into a liquid element.

At that time there was in those parts a very powerful woman, Lupa by name and deed, renowned for the chief authority of the entire province. Leaving some with the body, the others entered to the lady and asked that she give them a burial-place, so that those who had refused to receive his teaching while he lived might at least receive from God his body when dead. She had them seized and sent them to the most cruel king to be killed. [Col. 0984B] The king ordered them confined in the depths of a prison until he could devise what punishments might kill them. While he reclined at a banquet, they were led out of prison by an angel and, before the people’s eyes, left the city. When the table was removed, the king sent to the prison and ordered the prisoners brought out. Opening the prison, they found no one; returning (fo. 212v), they reported the marvel. When, by the king’s command, the men were sought everywhere, and many testified that they had seen travelers passing through the city, the pursuers swiftly followed to seize the fugitives; but the bridge they had crossed broke, and they were drowned in the flood. Therefore the king and his people, terrified with fear, recalled the men with honor and received from them faith in Christ and baptism.

Then, returning to Lupa, they asked that a burial-place be granted them. But grieved that they had not only escaped the king’s cruelty but had also gained the king with all his people for God, she devised some scheme to destroy those who were striving to rescue people from destruction. She then possessed huge wild oxen, exceedingly fierce and unbroken. She ordered these oxen to be put under a yoke, the master’s body to be placed on a cart, and carried away for burial, thinking in her unbelief that a fierce beast would tear them apart. But they made the sign of the cross, yoked the oxen like lambs, and placed their master’s body upon the cart. Then the unbroken oxen seized it and drew the apostle’s body by a straight road to Lupa’s palace, far away. She now followed it devoutly and was converted to the true God; from Lupa she became Christ’s ewe-lamb. Her palace was consecrated as a church in honor of Christ and his apostle [Col. 0984D], and there the beloved of God was buried. She bestowed all her possessions upon Saint James and offered all her ornaments as gifts to God. Hermogenes became bishop, and Philetus was appointed after him. The others were set over other places; many signs were performed through them, and all the western peoples were converted to Christ through them. This blessed apostle is remembered as having been killed around Easter; but today his feast is solemnly celebrated by the Church, when the translation of his body is glorified by heavenly signs.

In the praises of this holy apostle is joined today the blessed martyr Christopher. Filled with the Holy Spirit, he preached to the nations and gathered many thousands of believers into companies [Col. 0985A]. At last, seized by a king for Christ’s name, he was chained, worn down by prison custody, beaten with iron rods, and afflicted by the flames of a blazing furnace; but Christ saved him and delivered him from it. He was placed bound to a standard in a field, pierced on every side with arrows, and finally beheaded. The king was converted and baptized with his people; he magnificently built a church [Col. 0986A] in which many benefits are bestowed through the merits of the blessed martyr Christopher (fo. 214). Therefore, dearest brethren, since these now live like brilliant stars in the sight of the eternal Sun, where all who love his name live, ask them with devout prayers that you may be permitted to share their glory in the heavenly dwellings, where eye has not seen (1 Cor. 2).

## ON THE CHAINS OF SAINT PETER

[Col. 0985]

[Col. 0985A] “Your friends, O God, are greatly honored; their dominion is greatly strengthened” (Ps. 138). Christ called the apostles, dearest brethren, not servants but friends, because he made known to them all the secrets of the Father [Col. 0985B] (John 15). They are exceedingly honored because they are now made equal to the angels in heaven. Their authority is greatly strengthened, because their binding or loosing in heaven and on earth is confirmed by God. These are the princes of peoples who are gathered with the God of Abraham, because, taken away from the misery of this wicked age, they are now exalted in everlasting glory. These are those who were born for the Fathers of the Church and made princes over all the earth (Ps. 64). For the prophets were the Fathers of the Church, who begot her for God by their writings. In their place the apostles, the sons of the Church, are born, because by her bridegroom Christ they are made princes over all the earth (ibid.). They were also called mountains because of their exalted practice of virtues—mountains that received peace for the people (Ps. 71) [Col. 0985C]—when they preached that Christ, the true peace, had restored peace to humankind. They are the eternal mountains (Ps. 75), from which the Sun of righteousness, rising from death, wonderfully illumined the plain of the Church when all the foolish of heart were troubled (ibid.). For when the apostles testified to Christ’s resurrection, the foolish Jews were gravely disturbed. Those who ascend these mountains will be able to enter heaven, because if we desire to follow the life and teaching of the apostles, we too shall certainly be able to enter the heavenly kingdom.

Beloved, we must explain why this day is solemn. For, as some suppose, Saint Peter was not released from chains on this present day; he is read to have been led out of prison by an angel around the Paschal season (Acts 12). This day [Col. 0985D], rather, is festive on account of his chains, when they were deposited in his church at Rome by Empress Eudoxia. O how greatly Christ has glorified those who glorify him! O how greatly he has exalted them above their enemies! Truly the kingdom and power are his, his the riches and glory; and he exalts whom he will and humbles whom he will. Behold: he made the poorest rustic men (fo. 214v), namely fishermen, princes of the whole world, and subjected to them all the dignities of the age and every royal power. Behold: not only solemn days are instituted in honor of that fisherman, but even in reverence for his chains; the highest bishoprics are subscribed to his name by the highest emperors. Behold: not only is his body venerated by rulers, but his staffs, chains, garments, and anything belonging to him are adored by all the people as something divine. Behold: the whole world flows from every direction into the city of Rome [Col. 0986B] for Peter the fisherman, not for Augustus, emperor of the world. Everyone seeks the fisherman’s tomb; no one seeks the sepulcher of the ruler Nero. Moreover, every Augustus who in life rules the whole world now falls before the bones of the dead fisherman, already decayed; he sheds tears with prayers and humbly entreats the emperor that the fisherman may be favorable to him—and rightly so. For he holds the keys of life, and it is fitting that he should open to all the gates of the kingdom of heaven. Thus, yes thus, Christ makes his servants illustrious; thus the King of glory rewards his soldiers, so that they not only shine crowned among the angels, but their memory also flourishes through all generations.

This day was anciently celebrated on account of the victory of Augustus Caesar. On this day Augustus, fighting Antony [Col. 0986C], gained victory; therefore the Roman people instituted the solemn observance of the day, dedicated a temple in his honor, called the month previously named Sextilis “August,” and the superstition of this day was festively repeated each year and renewed with great rejoicing by every succeeding generation. But this custom of the Gentiles was changed in this manner into a rite of the faithful. Empress Eudoxia went to Jerusalem for prayer, and an unbelieving Jew bestowed upon her a faithful gift: he offered her the chains by which Saint Peter had been bound by Herod but loosed by an angel at Easter. Embracing them above gold and topaz, she brought them to Rome and, on the counsel of the supreme pontiff, built a church in honor of the prince of the apostles, in which on the present day [Col. 0986D] she placed the precious chains. Then, by apostolic authority and imperial power, it was ordained and decreed that, just as this day had formerly been observed in honor of the highest ruler of the world, it should thereafter be celebrated in honor of the prince of the apostles and of the Church.

Therefore, dearest brethren, since today we venerate the chains of blessed Peter, the looser of sins, let us persist in prayers that through his merits we may deserve to be freed from the chains of sins, just as he himself was freed by an angel from those bonds through the prayers of the Church. For we are entangled in the cords of sins; but before we are cast into the outer darkness with hands and feet bound, let us hasten to be loosed by the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven. For whatever [Col. 0987A] he looses on earth shall be loosed by Christ in heaven (Matt. 16). Let us remember that when Ham sinned, his son Canaan was condemned by Noah to slavery (Gen. 9), because at the final judgment Christ curses every sinner’s work. Noah was uncovered; Christ was disfigured for us in the Passion. Ham mocks him because the unbelieving people reproach Christ’s Passion with scorn. Ham’s seed is punished by the curse of slavery, while the crowd of the reprobate is made subject to the service of the elect, because in a certain way they serve them by afflicting them with adversities; and as servants, at their father’s command, correct sinful children and test God’s golden vessels in the furnace of tribulation, so that they may shine brightly at the banquet of the supreme King. Finally [Col. 0987B], those servants themselves will be servants of servants, because with the demon-servants, they who are their servants will burn in eternal torments.

Noah is covered by two sons because Christ’s Passion is venerated by two peoples of believers (ibid.). From the patriarch Shem were born those who prefigured Christ’s Passion by honoring it, as Abraham did by sacrificing his son (Gen. 22), and Moses by sacrificing the lamb (Exod. 12) or lifting up the serpent in the wilderness (Num. 21). From him were born prophets who foretold Christ’s Passion in reverence, as Isaiah says: “Like a sheep, he shall be led to slaughter” (Isa. 53); and Jeremiah says: “Christ shall be taken because of our sins.” From him also were born the apostles, who reverently made Christ’s Passion known [Col. 0987C] to the world, as Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example that we may follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2); and Paul: “We preach Christ crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling-block, but to Gentiles foolishness; but to those chosen, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1). From Japheth, however, were born popes, bishops, and a multitude of martyrs, all of whom glorified Christ’s Passion through their own passions and therefore possessed blessing as an inheritance.

This day is also sanctified by a holy woman with seven martyrs, who was offered to God with her sons for the old Law by King Antiochus. The reason why the Church commemorates solemnities only for these persons of the Old Testament [Col. 0987D] is this. Antiochus bears the type of Antichrist, who will be the head of all persecutors. All who inflicted persecution upon the faithful were his members. This mother was a figure of the Church, which died for righteousness. Her seven sons [Col. 0988A] prefigured all the saints, who, filled with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, will contend for righteousness unto death, and then, crowned with laurel, will enter the joy of the Lord with their mother, the Church. This woman was seized with her sons by Antiochus and compelled to violate God’s law; but, by no means conquered, she was consumed with her children amid dreadful punishments and brought into enduring joys. While the mother watched, the hair and scalp of each son were stripped away with iron; the extremities of hands and feet were cut off; and thus they were roasted in a frying-pan boiling with pitch and sulfur. The mother, tortured through each child, whom she herself joyfully encouraged to sufferings, was finally put to death in the same manner (2 Macc. 1).

The blessed Felicity imitated her, being sacrificed for Christ with her seven sons by different punishments. Blessed Symphorosa likewise emulated her, being tortured for Christ with her seven sons by various torments. And truly, dearest brethren, these women were more blessed—those who bore from their wombs seven martyrs and, suffering through each one, were martyrs eight times over—than those who carried two apostles, Peter and Andrew, or James and John, in their wombs.

Today, too, the blessed martyr Wisdom both in name and deed, and her three daughters Faith, Hope, and Charity—beautiful in their names, more beautiful in their works—cruelly torn, shed their blood for Christ and deserved to receive eternal joys from Christ.

[Col. 0988C] And, dearest brethren, frail women, tender boys, and delicate little girls could not be bent from good to evil by torments, and therefore, delivered from every evil and pain, they have now gained everlasting joy, crowned with gladness. By contrast, we unhappy and most wretched people cannot be recalled from evils either by threats or by rewards; indeed, crushed by various kinds of punishments, we refuse to receive the Lord’s discipline and, already stinking in filth, disdain to turn to him who calls us back. Therefore, dearest brethren, at last coming to our senses from the devil’s snares and turning ourselves to the Lord, the supreme Good, let us send blessed Peter and the other saints whose feasts we celebrate today to the throne of glory with devout prayer, that we may be able to overcome our frailty and every [Col. 0988D] torment of soul and body, and may deserve to rejoice eternally with all the saints in the light of the Lord’s countenance—things which eye has not seen (1 Cor. 2), and so forth.

## ON SAINT LAWRENCE

[Col. 0987]

[Col. 0987D] “Blessed is the man who is found without blemish, and who has not gone after gold, nor placed his hope in money and treasures” (Ecclus. XXXI). Beloved, Scripture calls blessed the one who possesses all that he has wished for. Therefore Saint Lawrence is truly proclaimed blessed, who now rejoices among the angels in the abundance of every kind of glory; from whose eyes every tear is dried by the sight of God himself, and, pain and groaning having fled, he is comforted with everlasting joy and gladness. He is called a man because he was not subjected, like a woman, to perverse counsel, whether flattering or harsh; [Col. 0989A] rather, fighting manfully, he struck down the ancient enemy with his members, and therefore triumphed gloriously in heaven. He was found without blemish when, like gold, he was tested on the gridiron. He did not go after gold, nor put his hope in money and treasures; instead, distributing the gold and treasures of the Church to the poor, he acquired heavenly riches.

Therefore let us praise him today, and glorify God, wonderful in his saints (Ps. LXVII), through whom Lawrence performed wonders in his life: he who, shrinking from the life beloved by all, cast it away for the sake of true life; embracing death, hated by all, he received it for life’s sake; he who despised as mud the gold in which people put their trust; who bestowed upon the needy the ornaments in which princes glory; who opened windows long shut in the faces of the blind [Col. 0989B] and, by the sign of the cross, driving away darkness, opened them to clear light (fol. 218v); who scorned the cruel torments of the body and offered himself through fire to God as a living sacrifice, a sweet-smelling offering (Eph. V). And because, tested by suffering, he was proved perfect through patience, he shall be crowned in eternal glory. He had treasures and could have transgressed, but he would not transgress the law of his God; he had power to do evil, but, though compelled by punishments, would not do it. Therefore his goods are established in the Lord, for which he now possesses rewards without end. And the whole Church of the saints recounts his almsgiving, since he is held in the celebrated remembrance of all, and in that life riches and glory abound for him.

This man, archdeacon of the Roman Church, was a disciple of blessed Pope Sixtus. When that blessed pontiff [Col. 0989C] was being led away to martyrdom for the flock entrusted to him, Lawrence came running in lamentation and begged to be admitted with him to the punishments. The pope, then a sacrifice of Christ, entrusted the treasures of the Church to him and, consoling him kindly, foretold that he would become a martyr after three days. But Lawrence, having received the money, did not, like a miser, hide it in the ground. Rather, going about diligently, he visited orphans and widows; as a good steward, he dispensed the entrusted money to needy fellow servants; he washed the feet of the poor and healed the sick by prayer.

When all had thus been spent, the faithful servant returned to his master; and behold, Sixtus, with the two deacons Felicissimus and Agapitus, was being led to be beheaded. Lawrence cried aloud that he had spent the treasures entrusted to him upon the poor [Col. 0989D] and begged in a mournful voice that he might be allowed to suffer with him. But the soldiers sent blessed Sixtus and his companions, their heads cut off, to be crowned in the starry realms; Lawrence, however, they seized and brought before the emperor Decius. He handed him over to the prefect Valerian, commanding him to exact from Lawrence the treasure of the Church and force him to sacrifice to idols.

Valerian entrusted him to a certain Hippolytus, who placed him in prison with many others. Among these was a certain blind man who, believing through blessed Lawrence, was baptized and deserved to receive sight. When many blind persons heard this, they came to blessed Lawrence; all of them, through the laying on of his hands, saw the light of heaven. Seeing this, Hippolytus believed with all his household and put on Christ’s garment through baptism. After this Lawrence was brought to the palace of Decius, and the treasure was demanded from him (fol. 220). He promised to show the treasure if a respite of three days were granted him. When it had been granted, he assembled a multitude of poor people, whom on the third day he brought with him to the palace.

“Behold,” he said to Caesar, “you see the treasure of the Church. The hands of these have carried into the treasury of the heavenly court the treasures which you seek.”

Hearing this, the tyrant raged. He stripped Lawrence of his garments, whom Christ clothed in the robe of immortality. Then Christ’s victim was stretched upon the rack and beaten with scorpions—that is, whips furnished with scorpion-like stings—and was again thrust into prison. Brought out from there, he was compelled to sacrifice to idols; but he was not bent by terrors. Therefore it was ordered that he be beaten for a very long time with clubs, then hung upon the rack and cruelly tortured with heated plates applied to his sides. Since Christ’s unconquered soldier was not overcome by this punishment, but rather rejoiced in his torments as at a feast, he was beaten with leaded scourges—that is, whips with lead fastened to the end of the strap—and then cruelly battered with scorpions.

Meanwhile a certain soldier, named Romanus, saw a young man of glorious countenance standing by and strengthening blessed Lawrence as he wiped away his blood. Immediately he fell at Lawrence’s feet, asked to be baptized, told publicly what he had seen, and received baptism. Straightway, at Decius’s command, he too was beaten for a long time with clubs and then beheaded. Lawrence, moreover, was ordered to be taken again into prison, so that Christ might be glorified more often in his body. At night [Col. 0990C] he was brought out: his heart was tested in the love of Christ, his flesh visited by many scourges, tested by fire; and because no iniquity was found in him, he was crowned with the crown of everlasting glory. For when he was brought before Decius, he was pressed into idolatry; but Christ’s name was all the more praised by him, and so it was commanded that his mouth be battered with stones. Again he was stripped of his clothing and horribly torn by whips. Finally, made a spectacle to both angels and men, he was chained upon a gridiron and roasted alive; thus his unconquered spirit was joined among the stars to the companies of saints, while angels sang hymns.

Immediately his half-burned body began to give forth a wondrous fragrance, bearing witness that his soul rejoiced in the presence of supreme sweetness. After Lawrence had thus passed [Col. 0990D] through fire into refreshment (fol. 220v), Hippolytus buried his body, now made the consolation of the faithful. Therefore, by Decius’s command, he was seized by soldiers, beaten with clubs, and handed over to Valerian. Valerian ordered that his entire household be beheaded in his presence, and that then Hippolytus himself be tied by the necks to untamed horses and, dragged through thistles and briars, killed.

When this had taken place, Decius and Valerian descended in their chariot to the amphitheater in order to provide Christ’s enemies with a spectacle of Christians. Immediately both were seized by a demon and grievously tormented: one cried out that Lawrence, the other that Hippolytus, was binding him in fiery chains. At once Valerian was suffocated by the demon. Decius, brought back to the palace, was tormented without ceasing by demons for three days, now crying out that he was tortured by Lawrence, now by Hippolytus; finally, on the third day, he was torn from the flesh with great torment and compelled to suffer eternal punishments without end. Then Justus the priest baptized Triphonia, Decius’s wife, his daughter Cyrilla, and forty-six soldiers who believed. But Triphonia, praying to the Lord on the following day, departed to him; King Claudius, however, slew Cyrilla and the soldiers with the sword.

Thus, beloved, the battle-line of soldiers follows Lawrence, standard-bearer in the Lord’s battle; having conquered its enemies, it rejoices to have carried off the trophy. These are they who came out of great tribulation, and because they washed their robes [Col. 0992A] in their own blood (Rev. VII), they deserved to stand with palms before the Lamb (ibid.), and they shall be co-heirs of his kingdom and see their torturers tortured without end. Since these, most beloved, conquerors of tyrants were crowned among the shining angels with ineffable glory in exchange for the momentary pain of the body, let us pray that through their merits we may be conquerors of vices and may one day flourish with them eternally in that blessedness. “What eye has not seen” (I Cor. II).

## On the Assumption of Saint Mary

[Col. 0991]

[Col. 0991B] “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song VIII). Just as the people of Israel, their adversaries confounded and their enemies overwhelmed in the Red Sea, were led out in exultation from Egypt and brought through the wilderness into the desirable land with a song of gladness, so the glorious Virgin Mary, whose solemn festival (fol. 222) we devoutly commemorate today, was led out of this world in gladness and exultation, the Jews confounded and the demons submerged in the abyss. Through the wilderness of the air, amid the harmony of angels and the jubilation of saints, she was brought into the heavenly palace as Queen of Heaven. There she now abounds in delights, because amid the assemblies of angels and the ranks of all saints the torrent of God’s pleasure overflows upon her in greater abundance.

She leans [Col. 0991C] upon her beloved because, beholding the brightness of her Son’s divinity, she is continually fastened to his love by sweet affection. Now the flowers of roses and the lilies of the valleys surround her, because the red of the martyrs and the whiteness of virgins celebrate her everlasting praise in sweet melody. And deservedly so: for God himself, passing by, had made in her a lodging, as the Gospel recounted today: “Jesus entered into a certain village” (Luke X).

In a village there is a high tower, wherein are strongholds against enemies; outwardly there is a wall, which is protection for those within. This village was that sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, namely the glorious Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, because she was fortified on every side by the unceasing guard of angels. In her was a high tower, namely humility reaching to heaven’s summit; hence it is said: “The Lord has regarded [Col. 0991D] the humility of his handmaid” (Luke I). Her outer wall was chastity, which provided inward defense for the other virtues. The Lord entered this village when in the Virgin’s womb he joined human nature to himself.

“And a certain woman named Martha received him into her house; and she had a sister, called Mary.” By Martha the active life is signified, by Mary the contemplative life; and the perpetual Virgin Mary is declared to have cultivated both more excellently in Christ. For she performed for him every service of the Gospel through the ministries of the active life. For our sake she received in the lodging of her womb—resplendent with the jewels of virtues—him who was exiled from his fatherland kingdom and a stranger in this world. With her own breasts she fed him when hungry; on her knees she comforted him when weeping. When weak, [Col. 0992B] she warmed him with baths; naked, she wrapped him in swaddling-clothes; crying, she bound him with bands; smiling, she pressed sweet kisses upon him. She was exceedingly anxious about constant service, fleeing from Herod’s presence into Egypt and returning again (fol. 222v) when she heard that Archelaus was reigning. She was much troubled about many things, everywhere seeking safe hiding-places in which to conceal and shelter him.

But the statement that she complains concerning her sister, that she has left her alone in labor, means this: when Mary saw Christ seized by the ungodly, cruelly dragged away, bound, struck, beaten, mocked, condemned with criminals, and cruelly tortured upon the gibbet of the cross, she would gladly, if it had been possible, have given her own life for his deliverance. And although she knew that divinity dwelt bodily in him, she nevertheless complained anxiously, as it were, in her heart that it did not come to his aid, but had left as though guilty one whom it had exposed to so many evils as if he were cast away.

Sitting at the Lord’s feet, she drank in his words with heart and ear; through the office of the contemplative life she pondered and preserved them in her heart, ever meditating upon spiritual things and longing for heavenly things. For the very fountain of wisdom had made his dwelling in her, and therefore all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden in her (Col. II). Now, Martha’s labor having been removed, in that life she enjoys—not a figurative Mary but the true one—that one thing necessary: the joy of eternal sweetness. Clinging to her Son’s embraces, she is forever filled with the sight of his divinity among the angels. Today she passed to that glory, in which her Son exalted her as Queen of Heaven above all the orders of angels [Col. 0992D]. The best part which she chose here, she received today twofold from the Lord’s hand; it shall never be taken from her, but, when full joy is given to the saints, it shall be increased a hundredfold.

Beloved, although very many examples demonstrate that this Queen of Heaven, of singular merit, is the singular refuge of the wretched, the salvation of Theophilus proves this especially. This Theophilus was renowned for many alms and many good works. When the bishop died, all the clergy and people chose him as bishop; but he stubbornly refused out of humility, and because of this necessity another was placed over the episcopal see. That bishop arranged the offices of his administration as seemed good to himself and his own party. Thus he deprived Theophilus, who had flourished as vicedominus, of his dignity and gave it to another.

[Col. 0993A] The envious serpent (fol. 224), the devil, enemy of souls, begrudging the man’s former pious labors, wounded his mind by instilling deadly poison and grievously stirred him with hidden grief. He began in his distress to dwell upon his loss of office and to lament that he lacked his accustomed honor and the people’s favor. Therefore he implored the aid of a Jewish magician and earnestly begged him to assist him in this matter. The treacherous man sent the lost man with a letter to the devil, promising him effective help. When Theophilus arrived, behold, the devil sat aloft like a crowned king; an army of evil spirits stood round him like a company of soldiers; and he who transforms himself into an angel of light pretended, for the deception of the wretch, that many lamps were burning about him. Receiving the letter, he promised prompt aid [Col. 0993B] if only Theophilus would deny in writing Mary and her Son Jesus.

The unhappy man delayed not at all, but by a written bond denied the Virgin of God and the Son of God born from her, and placed the sealed document in the hand of the destroyer. The deceiver of souls, having deceived him, claimed him into his own lordship with a kiss, promising that he would soon bear the primacy of the entire bishopric. On the following day the bishop changed certain appointments, restoring Theophilus to his office and exalting him in all his authority as vicedominus. And when, for some time, he gloried in the dominion he had gained and rejoiced that riches flowed abundantly to him, he began, by divine prompting, anxiously to reflect within himself that, whether today or tomorrow or at any time, when he died he would have to be tormented eternally for these things.

[Col. 0993C] Fearing the divine judgment, he entered the church secretly, and for forty days continued in fasting, vigils, and lamentations. With his whole heart he repudiated his deeds; he judged himself unworthy of the intercession of all the saints, since he had denied God himself, the giver of his goods, and his Virgin Mother, chosen above all others, and had moreover, by surrendering a written document to the devil, shut against himself the door of pardon. At length, encouraged by hope in the mercy of him “who wills all men to be saved” (I Tim. II), he knocked by continual prayers at the inexhaustible depths of divine compassion and invoked his merciful Mother with abundant tears. And the merciful and compassionate fountain of pity did not reject or despise the supplication (fol. 224v) of the poor man (Ps. XXI).

For one night, worn out by excessive weeping, he fell asleep. Behold, the blessed Mother of God, consolation of the wretched, refuge of sinners, restoration of the fallen, stood beside him in his grief and told him that Christ had heard his prayers and that, through her help, he had obtained pardon for his guilt. On waking, he was indeed filled with great joy, but was again shaken by utmost sorrow when he remembered that the devil possessed the abominable document. Therefore he again threw himself on the ground, was overwhelmed with most copious tears, and his countenance was cast down. Once more, exhausted, he was overcome by sleep.

And behold again, the salvation of the world, the gate of heaven, Lady of kings, glory of women, jewel of virgins, light of the ages, rejoicing of angels, honor of believers, stood by and comforted the sorrowful man. Placing the document upon his breast, she urged him to rejoice in God’s benefits. When he woke and found the written document upon himself, he exulted in the Lord and, in jubilation, offered an ineffable hymn for his grace. “His heart and his flesh rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. LXXXIII), whom heaven, earth, sea, and all things in them should praise forever; for he alone is God, for “his mercy endures for ever” (Ps. CXXXV). He spent the rest of his life in God’s service; and, having received Christ’s body, he was illumined as a lamp is illumined from a light [Col. 0994C], and soon, through the Mother of God, was called to the heavenly kingdoms to behold Christ, the true Light, in the light of the Father.

To her, beloved, let us all flee with our whole mind; let us offer her the vows of our prayers and sacrifices of praise, so that we may behold her reigning with her Son amid the assemblies of angels and, through her favor, obtain some share in the joy of that same kingdom. “What eye has not seen” (I Cor. II), and so forth.

If the feast of Saint Bartholomew falls on a Sunday, the following may be added to the sermon:

[Col. 0993]

[Col. 0993C] On Saint Bartholomew

Today, beloved, let our devotion entreat blessed Bartholomew, so that his intercession may reconcile us to our God. For he is one of the twelve judges of the world [Col. 0993D]; therefore let us beseech him with unceasing prayers that he may set us at his right hand in judgment and obtain for us joys with the righteous. Stirred by the Holy Spirit and armed with the banner of the holy cross, he entered India to overthrow demons; through him a great multitude of people was converted to the true God. At his entrance the gods of the nations—that is, demons—were silenced, and unbelievers were astonished by the signs and wonders wrought through him (fol. 226). He destroyed idolatry in India, established churches everywhere for the name of Jesus Christ, and brought the king of the Indians with all his people to knowledge of the eternal King. Therefore he was seized by the king’s brother, beaten with clubs, then flayed, and afterward beheaded; and so, crowned with blood, he was joined to the heavenly senate. After this all those who had supported the apostle’s death were seized by demons [Col. 0994C] and expired; all the rest believed in Christ God.

Now, beloved, let us cry to the Most High, beseeching his apostle that through his holy prayer we may receive joys at the last judgment. [Col. 0994D] “What eye has not seen,” and so forth.

## On Saint Augustine

“Many shall praise the wisdom of the righteous” (Ecclus. XXXIX).

It is not right, beloved, that today we should be silent concerning the praises of Saint Augustine, especially since he himself exalted God and all the saints with many praises, and God has now transferred him among all the saints as his worthy praiser. Many praise his wisdom, and it is not erased through the age by which the Church shall be abundantly instructed unto the end. Its memory shall not depart, because this day too is celebrated on earth and in eternal glory. His name shall be sought through all generations for edification; inscribed in heaven in the book of the living, it shall never be erased.

While still a pagan and a supporter of heretics, [Col. 0995A] he came from Africa to Rome for the study of letters, at the time when Ambrose governed the Church of Milan. The brethren of Milan sent to Rome for a rhetorician by whose art their city might flourish. The Romans sent Augustine to them, knowing him to be eminently skilled in rhetorical art. Since he frequently heard Ambrose discoursing about God and eternal life, he believed; and both, filled with the Holy Spirit, first sang the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise thee, O God.” Thus amply instructed by Ambrose in divine matters, he returned to his homeland, where he was appointed bishop over the people of God.

At that time the Church, the house of God, wavering in faith and threatening to fall, trembled; but the supreme maker set Augustine as a firm silver pillar against it before it should collapse. [Col. 0995B] The whole noble structure, leaning upon him, was strengthened, while every weapon of attacking enemies was forcefully overthrown by him. For in God’s temple he shone in eloquence like silver (fol. 226v); through holy life he supported it, firm and upright as a pillar, against vices and heretics. Like a good painter, he adorned the house of God with wondrous carving and, in a marvelous manner, distinguished it with diverse jewels, as he splendidly encircled it on every side with noble and remarkable sayings.

Finally, the heretical enemies of Christ, forerunners of Antichrist, were then attacking the Church with diverse heresies, teaching simple people to depart from the true faith and fall into the precipice of error. Against them Augustine, a strong defender, went forth with the sword of God’s word, drove the savage enemies far from the city of God, and, like a good shepherd, put to flight, rebuked and terrified, the ravenous wolves [Col. 0995C] who invaded Christ’s sheepfold and strangled God’s lambs with the staff of holy Scripture.

In the Lord’s vineyard, an untiring farmer, he toiled greatly beneath the burden and heat of the day. He took care to graft many branches into the true vine; he watered them abundantly with the great flow of the Scriptures and did not cease to bring them to the flowers of fragrance and the strength of good works. In the Lord’s harvest he reaped much, he himself an energetic laborer; he built many barns in which he gathered many sheaves with joy. For these he has now received a hundredfold from the Lord of the harvest.

The Lord relates that a certain man went abroad, entrusted his money to his servants, and committed five [Col. 0995D] talents to one, two to another, and one to another. But he to whom the weight of five talents was entrusted gained another five. The one who received two likewise gained another two. But the one entrusted with one buried it in the ground and did not allow it to be of use to anyone. After a long time, the master returned and demanded the money from his servants with profit. He who received five talents returned five gained besides, was praised by his master, and, rejoicing, was exalted into joy. He who received two returned double besides; his master set him over his goods in joy. But he to whom one had been entrusted returned it, dug from the earth without profit, saying that his master was to be feared and that he had therefore not put the talent out at interest; angered at him, the master ordered it taken away and him shut up in prison (Luke XIX).

[Col. 0996A] The Lord who went abroad is Christ, who passed from this world to heaven in our flesh. He distributes money among his servants when he bestows the charisms of graces upon believers. By the five talents are understood the five senses, through which people are commanded to gain eternal things. Through sight a person gains a talent if he delights not in beholding vanity but justice; through hearing a talent is acquired if one strives to lend the ears not to slanders or tales but to divine words; those rejoice through smell in their talent who delight in drawing in not the pleasurable fragrances of the flesh but those of virtues. The office of the mouth returns a talent if it does not corrupt good morals through evil conversation, but proclaims the Lord’s praise and edifies others in God’s word; likewise, if it does not fill the belly for lust through seductive taste, [Col. 0996B] but feeds the body only with simple food for God’s service. Touch works a talent if, turning away from evil, it strives to do good. Whoever gains thus by the five senses shall be rewarded by so many rewards in the Lord’s joy.

By the two talents are signified understanding and action, by which heavenly things are commanded to be gained. Therefore, those who strive to fulfill by good actions the good things they understand receive in the Lord’s joy a double reward for the double talent. By the one talent is expressed understanding, through which the heavenly homeland is commanded to be gained. Whoever spends a good natural ability only on earthly affairs hides this talent in the ground. A talent is entrusted to each person when knowledge or any craft is divinely given him; it is hidden by him in the ground when it is expended for no usefulness to neighbors. [Col. 0996C] Then the talent is taken from him and he himself, useless, is shut in prison, when the gift bestowed upon him by God is taken away from him through death and he is carried off to punishment among the infirm because of his wickedness.

Blessed Augustine, therefore, was a useful and faithful servant. He did not bury in the soil the talent entrusted to him, but doubled it by abundantly dispensing it to his fellow servants in love of God and neighbor; indeed, he has doubled it for every generation yet to come, since he took care to pour out his noble intellect for the whole Church in a thousand volumes. His loins were girded when he restrained his life by chastity; lamps burning in his hands shone when his splendid works glittered before [Col. 0996D] human beings. He spent the first watch in sleep when, in childhood, he drank in all secular wisdom with eager heart (fol. 228v). He did not yield to sleep in the second watch when, in youth, he diligently instructed all in philosophical learning. He remained wakeful in the third watch when, in old age, he expounded the sacred books in many ways.

He also kept the first watch when he clarified for us in writings the time before the Law. He kept the second when, by expounding, he opened the obscurities of the time of the Law and the prophets. He kept the third when he commended the time of grace in many books. And because the Lord found him watching, he set him over all his goods in his city, concerning which Augustine himself expounded many glorious things. He adorned his times with splendid signs and teachings [Col. 0997A], decorated Christ’s bride entrusted to him with diverse ornaments, and made the city of God glad with varied foods and drinks. Therefore, when Christ, judgment completed, has passed into the glory of the Father, led the Church from this Babylon into his Father’s city, and delivered the kingdom to God the Father, then he shall make Augustine recline at his banquet: that is, he shall cause him to rest with all the elect in full joy, where he himself shall minister [Col. 0998A] by showing himself as he is in the Father to all who love him.

Today also Saint Hermes, most illustrious among the Romans, by shedding his blood for Christ’s name purchased the heavenly kingdoms. Beloved, pray for this, that you may deserve to be joined with them in that blessedness. “What eye has not seen” (I Cor. II), and so forth.

## On the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist

[Col. 0997]

[Col. 0997B] “If the righteous man be overtaken by death, he shall be in refreshment” (Wis. IV). Saint John, who in this valley of tears was oppressed by great distress, when overtaken by death at Herod’s hands, was relieved from affliction in refreshment with Abraham. Three Herods are recorded: one, under whom the children were killed when the Lord was born; another, his son, by whom John was beheaded; and a third, son of Aristobulus, by whom James was beheaded. The first, who sought to kill the Lord, killed himself; the second, who mocked the Lord clothed in a white garment, perished in exile; the third, who seized Peter, was struck by an angel and perished.

Philip, son of the first Herod, had taken as wife the daughter of King Aretas; Herod, his brother, took her away from him, and John rebuked him for it. But as people flocked to John from every side, Herod feared that because of John’s words (fol. 230) he might become hated by the people and be driven from his kingdom because of the incest. So he seized John and put him bound in prison. The adulteress wished to kill him, but could not discover how she might accomplish it.

One day the adulterous king, on the occasion of his birthday, gave a great banquet for his nobles; and the harlot’s daughter danced skillfully before the guests. The king swore to the girl that whatever she asked of him, she should receive. At her mother’s urging she asked for John’s head, and the king immediately ordered it cut off and brought on a dish. The girl received it and gave it to her mother (Matt. XIV). John’s body was buried by his disciples in Samaria; but the queen buried his head more deeply in the ground in Strato’s Tower [Col. 0997D], fearing that, if it were joined to the body, he might rise again and trouble the king over his incest. His body was later dug up by the Saracens, burned in fire, and its ashes scattered over the fields.

We must consider, beloved brethren, how many great and grievous tribulations the Lord permits his elect to suffer in this life, how he brings them up from the depths of the earth, and with how great glory he receives them (Ps. LXX). Behold: the greatest among those born of women is chained, imprisoned, and beheaded because of incest; a reward is given to a dancer; his body is burned as a mockery. Peter, whom God appointed prince of the Church and keeper of heaven, is hung upside-down like a dog; Bartholomew is flayed like an ox; Lawrence is roasted like a fish. Some, their bellies cut open and filled with grain, are exposed to be devoured by pigs; the genitals of others are pierced point by point with iron combs. [Col. 0998B] But those who were thus made the sport of the ungodly here were brought by angels with jubilation from the depths of the earth and received in eternal glory amid the rejoicing of the saints.

Saint John, however, was beheaded around Passover; but he is celebrated today because his head, discovered today for the second time, is glorified by splendid miracles. For after the vengeance for the blood of God’s servants had entered before him and he remembered to require their blood, Jerusalem and the whole region were devastated by sword and fire at the hands of the nations; then, rebuilt, they were frequented by believers because of Christ’s holy places. When two monks arrived, the holy Baptist revealed to them where his head lay hidden. They dug up the designated place, found the head, and departed joyfully. On the way a certain man joined them, and they gave him the head to carry (fol. 230v). But while they slept, he fled with the head and carried the precious treasure to the city of Edessa.

He had formerly left his native country because of diverse misfortunes, but now, through the merit of Saint John, riches flowed to him from every side. Recognizing this, he hid the heavenly jewel in his house, worshiped it daily with fitting honor, and at death disclosed it only to his heir, who likewise took care to render due honor to the saint. Then gradually the head was neglected by the heirs, and the place was left vacant by its inhabitants. After some time, the blessed Baptist appeared to a certain devout man and revealed that his head was buried in that same city.

[Col. 0998D] In dreams this man saw a river, and Saint John running up to baptize the people. Those baptized came out in white garments through a most bright gate and were received by splendid men into pleasant places. When he himself approached, the saint looked upon him with a joyful face and told him how his head had come there and in what place it had been deposited. He disclosed all these things to the bishop; the bishop then proclaimed a fast and proceeded to the place with clergy and people. After prayer, they found the head in an urn, gave thanks to almighty God, and brought it to the church with hymns. Drops of blood fell from it as at the very hour when it had been cut off. When a certain member of the clergy, stretching out his hand, said that he could not believe this to be Saint John’s head, immediately his hand and arm became rigid, and the entire people, praising God, were afraid.

After the procession had been made, the cleric prostrated himself before the venerable head, confessed himself guilty with voice and tears [Col. 0999A], and, as prayer was made, his withered hand was restored to health. Again the people were raised up, rejoicing in God’s praises. By these and other splendid signs, his head, found today, is honored by all; and this day is revered by all the people in his honor, so that through him they may be joined to Christ the Head. But that his head was found by monks is commemorated on the feast of Saint Matthias.

It is read, beloved, that when Moses died, Joshua—who is also called Jesus—received leadership and led the people through the Jordan into the promised land. He sent two spies from Jericho, whom Rahab the harlot received as guests. The king of the city sought to destroy them, but Rahab sent them away unharmed. Then Jericho, with all things in it, was devastated by fire; Rahab alone, with all her household, was saved by the sign of a scarlet cord (Josh. II, VI). She was also joined in marriage to a prince of the tribe of Judah, and then the land was distributed by lot to the people as a possession.

Just as Moses, through the Law, showed sins but did not remit them, so John, baptizing the people, made them confess sins but did not take away crimes. Moses proclaimed the promised land but gave it to no one; so John taught the kingdom of heaven but could give it to no one. While John lived, Christ lay hidden—he who willed both to forgive sins and to give the kingdom of heaven. When John died, the true Joshua, our Savior, received the primacy, and [Col. 1000A] leads the people of believers through baptism into the land of the living. For after John was killed, Christ first preached publicly and illumined the world with signs.

He sends two spies to Jericho because he caused the Law and the Gospel to be preached in the world. Rahab received them because the Church from the nations received both Testaments. The king of the city wished to kill them because the devil, through his members—that is, persecutors and heretics—strove to destroy both laws and kill their observers. But because Rahab receives and sends them forth, the Church sends preachers and observers of the holy laws to Christ. Jericho is overthrown and Rahab’s house is rescued with the scarlet cord, because this world shall be dissolved by fire and the Church, with all her own, is lifted from destruction into the kingdom through the purple blood [Col. 1000B] of Christ. Rahab is joined to the prince of the tribe of Judah because the Church shall then be united as a blessed bride to Christ, the true prince of all, sprung from Judah’s tribe. Then the possession is distributed to the people because the kingdom of heaven is apportioned among the elect according to different dwelling-places.

Therefore, most beloved, let us entreat the friend of the Bridegroom with our whole heart, so that, clothed in the white garment of virtues, we may be able to enter through the most bright gate into Christ, the pleasantness of paradise and receive with all the saints a portion of the eternal inheritance. “What eye has not seen” (I Cor. II), and so forth.

## ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT MARY

[Col. 0999]

[Col. 0999C] “Go forth, daughters of Jerusalem, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of solemnity” (fol. 232v) “and gladness” (Song of Songs III). The daughters of Jerusalem are faithful souls, daughters of the Church, destined to behold true peace upon heaven’s height. They are commanded to go forth through contemplation of the mind and to see King Solomon—that is, Christ, the true Peacemaker—in the glory of the Father and of peace, brighter than the sun, in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the solemn day: namely, in the flesh in which his mother, the Virgin Mary, bore him for humankind in the time of grace.

We too ought to contemplate this king in the diadem which he wore on the solemn day, when his mother, the Synagogue, crowned him for us with a crown of thorns on the day of Passover. But the substance of the flesh [Col. 0999D] in which he chose to suffer these things he assumed from his Virgin Mother, from whom he came forth as the sun from the dawn and brought into the world the light of eternal brightness. She is she whom the Lord blessed in his power, when, choosing her from among all flesh, he appeared through her for the salvation of the world. Through her he reduced our enemies to nothing, when he subjected demons—the enemies of humankind—to the faithful. Therefore her praise does not fail from the mouths of men, among whom she is celebrated today, and among the companies of angels. She is the glory of the heavenly Jerusalem and the joy of the spiritual Israel—that is, of the people who see God.

She is compared to the cedar, which grows exceedingly abundant and from which the corruption of rot and worms is driven away. Thus this blessed Virgin [Col. 1000C] was enlarged in virtues like a multiplied cedar; she did not experience the corruption of decay, and through her the demons of eternal damnation are driven away. She is called the star of the sea because through her the human race is guided from the salt sea of this age to eternal life. But your love ought to hear how this star of the sea has today come forth at its rising, she from whom the Sun of righteousness shone upon the world.

It is related that her father Joachim was born in Jerusalem and took Anna of Bethlehem as his wife. Obedient to all the Lord’s commandments, they lived without reproach and spent many years without offspring. One day, while Joachim was offering sacrifice to God, the priest rejected his sacrifice on account of his barrenness. Ashamed at this, he stayed in solitude with shepherds. [Col. 1000D] An angel of the Lord appeared to him and declared that a daughter would be born of him and would be called Mary. Then, appearing to Anna, the angel announced the same things and gave clear signs (fol. 234). Thus they came together and told one another what each had seen.

After this Anna gave birth to a daughter; according to the angel’s word, she gave her the name Mary, and offered her, when she was to be weaned, to God in the Temple. Setting her in the house of the Lord, they ascended the steps to the altar with an offering; and behold, they saw the little girl climb after them up every step. They did not doubt that she would soon ascend to the summit of virtues. While she was reared within the enclosure of the Temple with the other girls offered to God, and some task was assigned to them, [Col. 1001A] gold or purple cloth was always allotted to Mary by lot; accordingly, the others called her queen.

She was the first among women to vow virginity to God; and therefore, alone among women, she deserved, while a virgin, the fruitfulness of the highest offspring. Thus, when the priest commanded all the girls to marry, and all obeyed with willing spirit while she alone refused union with a man, he consulted the Lord on this matter. The Lord commanded that all from the tribe of Judah should be present with rods. When Joseph was present among them, his rod blossomed, and a dove came down from heaven and settled upon the flower. At this sight God was praised by those who marvelled, and the sacred virgin was betrothed to him.

Brought to Nazareth, she was most reverently greeted by an angel; the coming of the eternal King into her was announced, and thus, at the appointed time, the Sun was born from the star. Formerly this feast of her Nativity [Col. 1001B] was not celebrated at all, but it is said to have been instituted in this manner.

One of the saints heard sweet harmony sounding in heaven every year on this night, as though choirs of angels were celebrating a feast. When he asked God in prayer why he heard this only on that single night and at no other time, he was told that on that night the Mother of God had been born into the world, and that for this reason the night was celebrated by the angels. When he made this public, it was decreed that her Nativity should likewise be solemnly observed by human beings.

The sweet benefits so often bestowed by this glorious Virgin upon the wretched bear witness to the praises with which she is to be venerated throughout all ages. For she appeared in great glory to a certain man who was dying and greatly afraid because of his deeds, and asked whether he recognized her. When he said that he did not recognize her at all, she said that she was the Mother of mercy; she comforted the afflicted man, who was immediately made joyful in the joy of the Lord. Let us pay to this Virgin (fol. 234v) every proclamation of praise, for from her mercy itself proceeded. Let every miserable person flee to her, so that through her he may be reconciled to him who is [Col. 1002A] wonderful in his saints.

Therefore, dearest brethren, let us celebrate with exultant songs the Nativity of the glorious Virgin Mother of God, and let us praise her with rejoicing mouth and heart, so that through her intercession we may one day glorify her exultantly with the angels.

The feasts of this day, dedicated to God, increase for us the merits of the blessed martyr Adrian. He was the most intimate soldier of the emperor Maximian, and afterwards the dearest martyr of Christ, the highest King. Seeing Christ’s soldiers tortured with the most severe punishments, he asked what reward they hoped would be repaid to them for these sufferings. When they said that the Lord would grant them what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (I Corinthians II), he asked the torturers to register his name with theirs. On hearing this, Maximian ordered [Col. 1002B] him to be bound and confined in prison and subjected to every punishment.

His wife Natalia, most worthy of the highest praise, after learning that Adrian had been imprisoned for Christ’s name, gave thanks to Christ with joy. Entering the prison, she encouraged him toward martyrdom with many words, supplied necessities to all who were imprisoned for Christ, kissed their chains, and begged them to pray for their lord. Other women, following her example, began to minister to the saints in prison. But when, by Maximian’s order, women were forbidden to enter among the condemned, Natalia cut off her hair, put on male clothing, and thus rendered faithful service to the saints.

After this Adrian was torn with many lashes together with many others, and with twenty martyrs was tortured to death by the breaking of his legs. Thus, delivered from the pain [Col. 1002C] of death, he was joined in triumph to the Author of life. Then Natalia was called to heaven by one of the martyrs and was immediately joined with the saints in glory. Today, dearest brethren, invoke the blessed Mother of God with these martyrs; earnestly entreat them for your needs, so that after the death of the flesh you may be permitted to live with them—where eye has not seen, etc. (ibid.).

## ON THE EXALTATION OF THE HOLY CROSS

[Col. 1001]

[Col. 1001D] “The root of Jesse shall stand as a sign for the peoples” (Isaiah XI). Jesse was the father of King David, from whose seed Christ proceeded. The root of this Jesse was Christ according to his divinity, born, according to his humanity, from the shoot springing from him. He stands as a sign for the peoples because the holy cross of Christ’s Passion is the sign of the redemption of all Christians. This is the sign contradicted by Jews and gentiles; yet through it the multitude of the faithful and every creature of the sacraments is blessed, and every adversity is driven back and overcome.

This holy cross is to be venerated by angels and adored by human beings. For through the cross the devil was captured, the world set free, hell despoiled, paradise gladdened, and every Christian people throughout the world invited to the heavenly kingdoms. The heavenly homeland exults in the triumph of the holy cross, the Church rejoices, Jewish [Col. 1002D] unbelief wastes away; death is subdued by the victory of the holy cross and stripped of its most wicked tyranny. The holy cross has become for us the key of heaven and the mighty destruction of hell.

Since it is sanctified by the body and blood of Christ, it is most worthily honoured by all the faithful. It fortifies sinners, directs saints, nourishes little ones, strengthens those worn out by old age, raises the fallen, guides the righteous, corrects the unrighteous, and extends the aids of protection to all its worshippers. After the first parent fell through a tree into the sea of this age, as though into a whirlpool of shipwreck, and the greedy Leviathan swallowed the whole human race in cruel death, it pleased our Redeemer to raise the banner of the holy cross and to bind the scaly throat of the enemy with the hook of his flesh, so that, pierced by the point of the life-giving wood, the wicked robber might vomit out those whom he had devoured through the forbidden tree.
