This holy cross is for us a lamp of eternal light amid the darkness [Col. 1003A] of this life. It leads its followers to heavenly things and rejoices to confer angelic things upon those who love it. The power of this holy cross has often been divinely manifested.

In a certain city, a Christian possessed an image of the holy cross. A certain Jew came into possession of the house of its deceased owner. He invited his fellow countrymen to a banquet, not knowing that the sign of the holy cross was in the house. During the feast, when they saw the sign of the holy cross, they rose up shouting and seized the image. “Our fathers,” they said, “are reported to have scourged Jesus, and we ought to disgrace his image with scourges.” Crying out these things in their unbelief, they struck the image with lashes (fol. 236v), and—wonderful to relate—drew drops of blood from its wounds. [Col. 1003B]

Mocking this miracle in their madness, they said that Jesus had been wounded by his predecessors and that his sign too should suffer like treatment at their hands. Then they pierced it repeatedly with lances, but streams of blood flowed to Christ’s glory. Afterwards the report spread abroad, and a crowd of faithful people ran together. They caught the dripping blood in vessels and anointed their weak limbs with it. O wondrous miracles of Jesus Christ, which he works through the signs of the holy cross! Immediately the blind rejoiced in sight, the deaf in hearing, the mute in speech, the lame exulted in walking, and all the infirm leapt for joy in restored health. The Jews proclaimed Christ’s praise with a loud voice. At once they believed, were baptized, and venerated the holy cross with the highest honour.

At one time a certain Jew was travelling to Rome. [Col. 1003C] When night came on, he rested in an ancient temple of idols beside the road. But, frightened by the terror of the place, he made upon himself the sign of the holy cross. About midnight a multitude of demons arrived, among whom one sat aloft as a king and asked the others what evil each had done. As they recounted their wicked deeds, one sprang into the middle and reported that he had drawn Andrew, a man of the highest religious devotion, into love for a certain nun; the affair had advanced so far that, when he left her late at night, he playfully gave her a slap on the buttocks.

While they all cried out in praise of him, commended his cleverness, and together encouraged him to complete the undertaking, the prince of wickedness ordered them to inquire who had dared [Col. 1003D] to hide in his house. The malicious attendants ran up, inspected the Jew carefully, and said in amazement: “Behold, a vessel empty and yet sealed.” When they heard this, the evil spirits vanished like smoke, because they could not endure the name of the holy cross.

The Jew arose at that hour and came to the bishop, relating all that he had seen. The bishop, prostrate upon the ground, praised God because He had kept the Jew from sin; he baptized the believing Jew, ordained him priest not long afterwards, and dedicated the temple in which the demons had gathered in honour of Saint Andrew the Apostle. Thus both were saved by the power of the cross, though the devil boasted that he held them in his power.

But just as those predestined [Col. 1004A] for life are restored through the cross (fol. 238), so the reprobate are strangled through it. For Julian the Apostate, while still a boy, wished to learn magic. A magician shut him in a deserted house. When he came out, he began to invoke demons; terrified by the sight of them, Julian began to make upon himself the sign of the holy cross. Seeing this, the demons fled and left the wretched, frightened boy alone.

When the magician entered, he asked whether he had seen anything. Julian said that he had seen horrible Ethiopians, but that after he made the sign of the cross they had suddenly ceased to appear. The magician asserted that they had been angered by this sign and had therefore withdrawn their presence. Hence that unhappy man began to detest the Lord’s cross with such hatred that he began with all his heart to abhor and reject the whole Christian religion. [Col. 1004B] Having become emperor, he promoted paganism throughout the world and, insofar as he could, attempted to erase the Christian name from under heaven. Behold: the cross, which was the cause of salvation for all, became for him the pit of death.

On the other hand, Cyprian was saved through it, having been predestined to life before the ages. This famous magician had driven many mad by magical arts, perpetrated many horrible crimes, caused many pregnant women to miscarry their children by spells, and sacrificed their little ones to demons. Yet by the power of the holy cross he came to the way of salvation in the following manner.

There was a certain virgin, Justina, beloved of God, whom this magician tried to incline to consent to his lust. He therefore sent against her a spirit of fornication, but she repelled it from herself by making the sign of the cross. When Cyprian [Col. 1004C] asked it why it had not brought the virgin, it said that it had seen a terrible sign and immediately fled from her. Laughing at it, he sent one stronger, who likewise fled from the sign of the cross. When Cyprian asked why it had not brought the virgin, it answered that it had been unable to do so because of a certain terrible sign.

Then he took care to send the prince of demons, who transformed himself into a woman and tempted the virgin with flattering words and fiery darts. But as soon as she made the sign of the cross, that evil one vanished like smoke and returned in confusion to the magician, reporting that he had fled from a certain dreadful sign. When Cyprian asked what that sign was which had dissolved all their strength, the devil replied that the cross of Christ weakened all [Col. 1004D] their powers and that the cross triumphed over all devilish arts (fol. 238v).

Hearing this, Cyprian rejected the devil and turned to Christ. Excelling perfectly in all Christian religion, he was appointed bishop and noble teacher of the Church; and, with that same Justina, offering himself as a living sacrifice to God amid diverse torments, he became a glorious martyr. Thus the elect bear away the trophy through the banner of the cross.

Your brotherhood ought to know what today’s feast is. Chosroes, king of the Persians, ravaged Judaea and carried the holy cross away from Jerusalem into his own land. There he constructed a bronze tower as a heaven, in which he fashioned representations of the sun, moon, and stars. By a certain contrivance the tower moved and imitated the roar [Col. 1005A] of thunder. Water also rose through hidden pipes and descended through certain openings as rain.

In this tower he had fixed the cross at his right hand as his Son; on his left he had placed a golden cock as the Holy Spirit; while he himself, sitting in the middle upon a throne, commanded that he be worshipped as God the Father. The emperor Heraclius of the Romans came against him with an army, and Chosroes’ son met him at the Danube with a strong force. It pleased the people that the two leaders should enter into single combat upon a bridge, and that all should obey the victor. This was done; Heraclius gained the victory, and the entire army obeyed him.

Having subjected Chosroes’ kingdom to himself, Heraclius ascended with a few men into Chosroes’ “heaven” and found the tyrant upon his throne. He asked whether he wished to be baptized; when he refused, he cut off his head. [Col. 1005B] He ordered his still-young son and the entire army to be baptized. He himself raised the son from the font, entrusted the kingdom to him, set him upon his father’s throne, and, having taken the cross, went joyfully to Jerusalem.

He rode from the Mount of Olives on a horse adorned with imperial insignia, but the city gate was blocked before him by a joined-up wall. And behold: the holy cross shone in heaven with exceeding brightness, while an angel of the Lord stood in the gate and held it in his hand. “When,” he said, “the King of heaven entered through these gates to suffer, he came not resplendent in purple [Col. 1006A] or diadem upon a proud horse, but mounted humbly on the back of an ass.” Having said these things, the angel was received into heaven.

The emperor laid aside his ornaments, carried the cross in his hand, and sang a hymn to the Lord with all the people in jubilation. Immediately the gate was opened to him, and the holy cross was reverently exalted in the place prepared for it (fol. 240). On that same day, through the glorious cross, a dead man received life; four paralytics attained health; ten lepers soundness; fifteen blind persons the brightness of sight; very many were freed from demons; and countless others were cured of various illnesses. Moreover, as soon as the cross was carried away from Chosroes’ shrine, a most sweet fragrance wafted from that province and filled the breasts of all in Jerusalem.

Today also Cornelius, bishop of the Romans, [Col. 1006B] and Cyprian, bishop of the Church of Carthage, poured out their blood for the sheep entrusted to them and entered, to be crowned, into the heavenly kingdoms.

Now, dearest brethren, exalt the holy cross with praises and appeal to these saints with prayers, so that he who redeemed you by the cross and made you co-heirs of the kingdom by his blood may grant you, through the banner of the holy cross, to triumph over the world and to rejoice forever with the saints in the heavenly Jerusalem—where eye has not seen, etc. (I Corinthians II).

## ON SAINT MATTHEW

[Col. 1005]

[Col. 1005C] Today, dearest brethren, the Gospel has told us how the Lord made something precious out of what was worthless, when he made Matthew the tax collector an evangelist and apostle. He called him from the tax office to the apostleship and set him as judge of the world upon twelve thrones. He was the first to publish the Gospel in writing, through which Christ’s glory became known to the whole world. “There are no speeches nor words whose voices are not heard” (Psalm XVIII). Among the evangelists, the human form represents him because, more than the others, he recounts that Christ came in human form for sinners.

In Ethiopia he scattered the word of life and gathered much fruit for God through signs and miracles. He raised the king’s son from death and baptized the king with all his people. But after that king had departed to the Lord and another succeeded to his sceptre, the latter wished [Col. 1006C] to marry to himself the king’s daughter, who had been veiled by Matthew. But he could not bend the apostle’s mind to consent to this marriage. Therefore, by his order, the apostle was beheaded while celebrating the Mass at the altar, and thus was joined in triumph to the senators of the heavenly court.

After this the king ordered the house of the king’s daughter to be surrounded with a great fire; but the redirected blaze consumed the king’s palace. The king barely escaped with his son; but the son was immediately seized by a demon and strangled to a grievous death. His father, wholly covered with leprosy, was seized with madness of mind and pierced himself with his own sword. Let us entreat this apostle of God, dearest brethren, so that we may escape the death of souls and rejoice with him without end in true life—where eye has not seen, etc. (I Corinthians II).

## ON SAINT MAURICE AND HIS COMPANIONS

[Col. 1005]

[Col. 1005D] Today, beloved brethren, Saint Maurice and the thousands of martyrs whose feasts we celebrate today can greatly aid our petitions before God, if you are diligent in commending yourselves to their merits. At that time the Roman emperors ruled the entire world and every kingdom obeyed their command. Therefore a legion with its commanders was sent from the remote regions of the East as aid to the emperor Maximian. On its journey it was imbued with faith and baptism by the bishop of Jerusalem [Col. 1006D] and instructed in the divine commandments by the Roman pontiff.

When they reached Maximian, they were compelled to persecute Christians. But, refusing to obey the wicked edict, they were all killed for Christ. Their number was six thousand six hundred and sixty-six men, whose names are written in heaven. Despising the criminal commands of rulers, all deserved, crowned by their blood, to go to the King of all kings. It is reported that throughout all the mountains on this night lights burn from heaven where the corpses of those men were carried by beasts or birds. Pray to them, dearest brethren, [Col. 1007A] so that you may be delivered from darkness and enjoy everlasting light with them.

## ON SAINT MICHAEL

[Col. 1007]

[Col. 1007A] “If a man speaks, he shall be consumed” (Job XXXVII). A human being, dearest brethren, speaking of God is so consumed by the immensity of his greatness as a little stone would be if cast into the great sea. For all that one might utter about God with the highest eloquence is as though one had drawn a drop from the immeasurable ocean. For what is a human being but a worm, and what is God but incomprehensible majesty? Whose understanding in [Col. 1007B] this life can grasp, or whose mind can comprehend, what the Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity is: that God encloses all things in his fist and yet exists wholly in every place?

But since a human being, who is rottenness, can speak nothing worthy of God, who is ineffable sweetness, let us at least, according to our measure, say something today, by the grace of God, about the angelic spirits—citizens of the heavenly homeland (fol. 242). For it is fitting that we should speak sighingly among ourselves of those with whom we hope to behold the King of glory in the heavenly Jerusalem, especially since today we celebrate the solemnities of angels. They rejoice at our progress and grieve at our failings. They present our prayers and vows to God, continually report our deeds and wills, and desire that we be joined to them in everlasting joy.

There are said to be nine orders of them, wonderfully arranged for the ministries of the supreme Trinity: angels, sent to individual human beings for protection, consolation, or aid, through whom demons are restrained from harming us as much as they wish; archangels, sent to carry out or announce the highest matters, and believed to preside over individual nations; virtues, through whom [Col. 1007C] signs and miracles are administered; powers, through whom vices and demons are restrained; principalities, which rule the companies of angels; dominions, which exercise dominion over these princes themselves; thrones, through whom God’s judgments are carried out; cherubim, through whom the knowledge of divine understanding is given; seraphim, through whom the ardour of divine love is bestowed.

The Lord indicates these in the Gospel when he recalls a woman who had ten drachmas but lost one. She lit a lamp and took care to look for it; when she found it, she called together her female friends to rejoice with her (Luke XV). The woman who had ten drachmas is God’s Wisdom, who created ten orders of the elect for the heavenly palace. But one drachma was lost when man fell from joy into exile. The woman sought it by lighting a lamp when the Divinity, illuminating the world with signs in the flesh, taught man to return. She called her friends to rejoice when she invited the angelic ranks to rejoice with the human being who had been saved.

Likewise, he says that a certain man had one hundred sheep. [Col. 1008A] After losing one, he left the ninety-nine in the wilderness, went away to seek the lost one, placed it on his shoulders when he found it, and, coming home, urged his friends to rejoice with him (ibid.). The man who had one hundred sheep is God, who arranged the heavenly homeland in a hundred choirs of the elect. But one sheep went astray when man, following the wolf, the devil, wandered from the pastures of paradise. The good shepherd Christ left the ninety-nine in the wilderness when he left the ranks of angels in heaven and sought lost man upon earth. He placed him on his shoulders when he endured for us the dreadful death [printed: “night”] upon the cross. Coming home, he commands his friends to rejoice when, returning to heaven, he bids the angelic citizens rejoice with redeemed humankind.

Today the Gospel has also told how the Creator of angels and humans commands that our neighbours not be despised by us, since their angels always behold the face of the Father (Matthew XVIII). Our neighbours are not to be despised by us in their need, but rather cherished according to our ability, since they are to be made equal to angels in heaven and to share Christ’s kingdom with us. Angels have likewise been assigned individually to them for guardianship; with these angels, if they agree with them, they will inherit [Col. 1008C] glory. Even when the angels come to us as messengers, they nevertheless always look upon the Father’s face, because they do not depart from him, but move about in him who is everywhere.

We surely offend these angels if we despise our neighbours, who are their foster-children; and if we oppose them, they too oppose our prayers. In beauty they surpass the sun sevenfold, yet they continually desire, with insatiable satisfaction, to gaze upon the Sun of righteousness. The heavenly court is to be completed from angels and human beings, and therefore as many people will ascend into heaven as angels remained there. They receive joys with different companies of angels according to their different merits, just as the angels themselves are arranged in different orders.

For angels are called messengers. Therefore, those who understand what belongs to the future life and endeavour piously to announce it to their neighbours undoubtedly move toward the order of angels. Archangels are called highest messengers; those who think lofty things about God and diligently make them known to others indeed hasten into the fellowship of archangels. Those powerful in virtues who work wonders are gathered into the companionship of virtues; and those who trample vices and command demons hasten into the fellowship of powers. Those who hold primacy of holiness here will surely be there participants in the dignity of principalities. Those who, through holiness, rule over all motions of the flesh and desires of life are exalted into the brightness (fol. 244) of dominions. Those who, from zeal for God, judge the impious and sinners by opposing them [Col. 1009A] rejoice to be numbered among the thrones, upon which God sits, ordering, rewarding, and judging all things justly. Those who, filled with knowledge, sigh that they are weighed down by earthly things and held back so long from heavenly things hasten into the order of cherubim. Those who, burning with love of God, long to kindle others into love truly pass into the height of the order of seraphim.

Moreover, as Lucifer shines among the stars, so the first angel shone among these companies. As soon as, despising them, he wished to be equal to God, he fell from the highest glory into the depths of the abyss; and all who consented to his pride were cast down from heaven. Hence John relates that he saw in heaven a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon beneath her feet and a crown woven of twelve [Col. 1009B] stars upon her head. In the pain of childbirth, as though already giving birth, she cried out. Before her stood a red dragon with seven heads, threatening at once to devour the child when born. But it was frustrated in this hope, because as soon as the child was born, he was caught up to God’s throne. The woman, however, was given two wings; flying into the wilderness with them, she was saved from the dragon.

Meanwhile war arose in heaven between Michael the archangel and the seven-headed dragon. Michael and his angels fought; the dragon and his angels fought, but were defeated. Vanquished, they were cast from heaven and sent to earth. The dragon drew a third part of the stars down from heaven with his tail and threw them, darkened, onto the earth. Then voices of praising angels resounded in heaven, because the accuser of our brethren had been cast down. But the dragon vomited from his mouth a great river after the woman, and the earth, coming to the woman’s aid, swallowed it (Revelation XII). Afterwards a terrible beast appeared on earth, to which the dragon gave his power. It trampled thousands of saints; at last the lake of fire and sulphur devoured it together with the dragon (Revelation XIII). Then the new Jerusalem is seen, arranged in marvellous variety of jewels, surrounded by the guardianship of angels, and illumined by the supreme brightness of the eternal sun (Revelation XXI). These things, dearest brethren, are indeed very wonderful to hear, but exceedingly sweet (fol. 244v) to understand.

The woman seen in heaven is the Church, which is brought by Christ into the heavenly kingdom. [Col. 1009D] She is called a woman because spiritual offspring is continually born through her. She is clothed with the sun because she is surrounded by the radiance of the Sun of righteousness. The moon is said to be beneath her feet because the changeable glory of this world is trampled by the Church. She is crowned with a crown woven from twelve stars because she is marked by teaching written by the twelve apostles. She cries out in the pain of childbirth because the Church labours with great groaning to bring forth spiritual children.

The red dragon is the devil: a dragon because he is full of the poison of wickedness; red because, a murderer from the beginning, he is bloodstained. He tries to devour the woman’s newborn child because the devil continually lies in wait for the good works of the Church. But the newborn child is caught up to God because the good work of every faithful person, guarded by God, is hidden from the devil’s wickedness [Col. 1010A] and will be rewarded by him at the last.

Two wings are given to the woman, by which she is delivered from the dragon, because the Church is given the two commandments of love. With these as with twin wings, flying upward through contemplation, she is saved from the dragon in the wilderness of this world. From this dragon arise seven heads, because from the devil as a fountain arise the seven principal vices.

The first is pride, when a person exalts his own heart and, by transgressing, tramples the commandments of the Lord his God. This is “the beginning of all sin” (Ecclesiasticus X), separating the soul from fellowship with God and joining it to the devil’s body. The second is envy, when someone begrudges another’s possessing what he himself would wish to possess alone. Through it death is said to have entered the world [Col. 1010B] (Wisdom II); through it one becomes a member of the devil.

The third is vainglory, when someone labours to flourish in the vanity of this world and does all his works for human favour. Such people will have no part in the future life, because here they have received their reward (Matthew VI). The fourth is hatred, which is spiritual murder. For whoever does not love his neighbour abides in death, and whoever hates his brother is a murderer (I John III).

The fifth is avarice, when someone gathers only earthly things and places his hope in them. It is the root of all evils, because it is the service of idols (Colossians III). The sixth is gluttony, when someone gives himself only to the enticements of the appetite and, like a pig, devotes all his care to his belly (fol. 246). Those whose hearts are burdened here by gluttony will there be tortured, parched in flame with the rich man. The seventh is lust, when someone wraps himself entirely in the filth of impurity and pollutes God’s temple with every kind of defilement. Their sweetness is called a worm, and the Lord is written to be about to give fire and worm over their flesh.

From these seven heads, as from seven fountains, all vices arise; and every sin is committed under their leadership. These seven harmful heads must be overcome through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Against these heads God also gave seven legal commandments to those in the active life, and likewise Gospel commands to those in the contemplative life.

To those in the active life: “Honour your father and your mother. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness. You shall not covet your neighbour’s property—neither his wife nor anything that is his” [Col. 1010D] (Exodus XX).

To those in the contemplative life: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, those who mourn, those who hunger for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers” (Matthew V).

With this dragon Michael fights, because through his ministry God condemns him at the final judgment. Moreover, Michael, whose name means “Who is like God?”, signifies Christ, the Angel of great counsel, who conquered the devil for the Church—something that God alone had power to do. This dragon is cast out of heaven because the devil is expelled from the Church; he is sent to earth because, on account of its unbelief, he is permitted to go into Judaea, which savours earthly things. The dragon drags a part of the stars from heaven to earth because he casts down through fleshly enticements many who shine in virtues. [Col. 1011A]

The Church has three parts: namely, the perfect, the imperfect, and hypocrites. The perfect are those who serve God voluntarily through love; the imperfect are those who are subject as though compelled, through fear; hypocrites are those who publicly feign good things and secretly perpetrate evil. These are called the third part of the stars, because they are seen to shine among the stars of life—that is, among the saints; but the dragon draws them down with his tail from heaven to earth when he causes them to burst forth from feigned holiness into open wickedness. The dragon’s tail will also be Antichrist, who will carry out the final persecution and draw very many from the Church into iniquity. The dragon is said to have drawn a third part of the stars from heaven because a third part of the angels is reported to have fallen.

The dragon sent a great river from his mouth after the woman because, by his prompting, he unleashed a cruel [fo. 246v] persecution upon the Church; the earth swallowed it because Christ’s flesh consumed the storm of persecutions. The beast that appeared, to which the dragon [*tradidit*, “handed over”] his power, is Antichrist, whom the devil will fill wholly. The beast trampled down the saints because Antichrist will destroy by savage punishments all the faithful who resist him. Afterwards it will be condemned with the dragon, when the devil, together with his whole body, will be hurled by Michael, in the sight of all, into the lake of fire and sulphur. [Col. 1011B]

After this the new Jerusalem is seen, because, once judgment has been completed, the Church is brought by Michael into the heavenly Jerusalem. The translucent gems of diverse colours of this city are souls radiant in diverse virtues. Its guardianship by angels is their sweet fellowship; the illumination of God’s light is the everlasting contemplation, face to face, of the countenance of his brightness. Then the saints will joyfully offer praise to God for the casting out of their accuser, because they will exult eternally at the separation of the devil and his body.

Some wonder why the angels are thought to have no more than three names, namely Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael. You should know that these names were given to them by human beings, since the angels have such knowledge that they have no need of names. [Col. 1012A]

Yet today we especially recall the memory of Saint Michael because he is said to be set over paradise and appointed to receive the souls of the faithful. This archangel is also said to have been prince of the Israelite people, to have gone before them out of Egypt in a pillar of fire or cloud, and that God had performed through him all the signs on the way. He came to the assistance of Joshua and the people of God when they were about to fight their enemies; he delivered the people, while Daniel prayed, from the Babylonian yoke. He is said to have appeared to the faithful on Mount Gargano and to have consecrated there for himself a cave as our consolation, for a church.

At one time barbarians declared war on the Christians, who implored the aid of the archangel Michael by a three-day fast. The same angel appeared to them, advised them to go to meet the enemy, and made known that he would bring them help. Therefore the Christians, encouraged, advanced to meet the pagans and drew up their battle line beside Mount Gargano. And behold, suddenly the mountain [fo. 248r] shook; a great darkness covered it; frequent flashes of lightning gleamed; fiery missiles flew and darted into the enemy ranks. What more need be said? The enemies, some slaughtered and some struck by lightning, were turned to flight; the Christians joyfully gained victory through the help of Saint Michael. [Col. 1012B]

Today, dearest brethren, let us sing psalms to the Lord in the sight of the angels, and let us continually serve him in fear, because the angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear God and will deliver them from every distress [Col. 1012C] (Psalm 33).

> **Note:** [Col. 1011D] Manuscript: *spallamus*, “let us sing psalms.”

Therefore at all times let us invoke Saint Michael, so that, just as the Christian people were victorious through him in that battle, so in the final battle of the archangel Michael and the seven-headed dragon we may deserve, with the woman clothed with the sun, to fly heavenward on the two wings of charity, and with the victorious archangel Michael, all the host of angels, and the whole multitude of saints, to triumph in the heavenly Jerusalem. There eye has not seen, etc. (1 Corinthians 2).

## ON SAINT DIONYSIUS AND HIS COMPANIONS

[Col. 1011]

[Col. 1011D] It is fitting, dearest brethren, that today we keep Saint Dionysius and his companions in our memory with praises, so that they may deign to remember us in eternal glory. This man, foremost among the Athenians in wisdom and rank, was converted by the apostle Paul to Christ, the true Wisdom, and was appointed by the same apostle bishop over that city. He immediately and eagerly spread Christ’s name and added a multitude of unbelievers to the number of the faithful. Then he hastened to Rome to see Peter and Paul, who had been held in chains, but found them already crowned with martyrdom. Pope Clement sent him to preach in Gaul, and he became bishop at Paris. By virtues and signs he enlightened that people; by deeds and words he subjected the people to Christ the Lord. [Col. 1012D]

Then, together with Rusticus the archpriest and Eleutherius the archdeacon, he was seized by pagans, struck with fists, spat upon, mocked, dragged while cruelly bound with thongs, and brought before the prefect [source readings: *praefectus*; *praefecto*]. Since neither threats nor rewards could bend them from the true God, they were stripped, harshly scourged, and consigned to a dark prison. Brought forth from it, they were stretched upon the rack and beaten with whips. After this Dionysius, God’s victim, was stretched upon an iron bed and burned by flames [fo. 248v]; scorched, he was thrown out to be devoured by beasts. But when he made the sign of the cross, he was not harmed; therefore he was cast into a burning oven, but, when prayer had been poured forth, the fire was extinguished. Like gold tested, he was drawn from the furnace; suspended from a gibbet, he was beaten for a very long time [Col. 1013A] and was finally ordered to be shut again in prison.

While there he celebrated Masses and strengthened the faithful with the Lord’s sacraments, suddenly an immeasurable light shone from heaven. The Lord Jesus came with a multitude of angels, consoled his athlete, gave him the holy bread, and promised that he would soon grant him the kingdom of the Father. After this the saints were led out by their executioners, subjected to many insults and diverse tortures, and beheaded. Once the shepherd was killed, the Lord’s flock was attacked by savage wolves: for on that same day a great multitude of believers fell slain for Christ after the example of their teacher, and deserved to enter with palms into the sight of the Lamb.

But so that the merciful Lord might reveal the glory of his soldiers, a surpassingly great light was poured down from above, and behold, suddenly Dionysius’s corpse rose up, carrying his severed head in its hand for some distance, with an angel indeed directing his steps and heavenly light shining around him. For the heavenly host accompanied him, and a sweet-sounding hymn was sung to God. Many who marvelled believed in Christ; unbelievers, terrified by fear, fled. Afterwards a basilica was built over the bodies of the saints, in which divine grace is to this day bestowed through their merits upon those who devoutly ask. [Col. 1014A]

Dearest brethren, pour out your hearts to those who were able, through dreadful tortures, to pour out their blood, so that God may lead you from distress into spaciousness and save you with them in his kingdom. There eye has not seen, etc. (1 Corinthians 2).

## ON SAINT LUKE, ON SUNDAY

[Col. 1013]

[Col. 1013B] Saint Luke, whose feast we celebrate today, was born in Antioch, trained in the art of medicine [*sic*], instructed in apostolic doctrine, and a faithful companion of the apostle Paul; in Achaia he wrote Christ’s Gospel. He bears the form of a calf because he recounts how Christ, the fatted calf, was offered for us. After bringing very abundant fruit to the Lord by writings and words, today, a virgin more than seventy years old and full of the Holy Spirit, he died in Bithynia and entered in glory to the King of glory. [Col. 1014B] Dearest brethren, let us follow his writings and pray for his merits, so that we may be grafted into enduring joys [fo. 250r]. Things which eye has not seen, etc. (1 Corinthians 2).

## ON THE SUNDAY OF SIMON AND JUDE

[Col. 1013]

[Col. 1013C] Simon and Jude, apostles of God, whose heavenly birthdays we observe today, dearest brethren, are said to be brothers of James, the brother of the Lord. These, with the other apostles, will judge the nations and reign eternally with God the Judge. They too, like two luminaries, enlightened the world with signs and teachings, and today have taken possession of the senate of life in triumph. After Simon had made Christ known to the peoples in Egypt and Thaddaeus [printed: *Tatheus*] in Mesopotamia, both entered Persia. There they overthrew idols and converted the king of Babylon together with all his people. After many signs and wonders, they destroyed idols in a certain temple; therefore the priests [Col. 1014C] of the temples, incited by two magicians, Zaroen and Arphaxar, rushed upon the apostles and killed them together [*cunctis*, sic]. Thus, with their robe dyed purple by blood, they entered the heavenly temples.

Immediately terrible lightning flashed, consuming the magicians with the temple. The king, however, who had believed through the apostles, destroyed the temple priests, built a basilica at great expense, and transferred the apostles’ bodies into it. To them, dearest brethren, lift up your hands and hearts; beseech them with vows and prayers, that on the day of judgment you may be with them at God’s right hand. There eye has not seen, etc. (1 Corinthians 2).

## ON ALL SAINTS

[Col. 1013]

[Col. 1013D] The heavens shall confess your wonders, O Lord, and your truth in the Church of the saints (Psalm 88). The heavens daily display God’s wonders when they illuminate the world by sun, moon, and stars. The Church of the saints confesses his truth when the congregation of the righteous rejoices that all things were made through Christ, who is truth. The heavens will confess God’s wonders when, together with the stars and all creation, they are changed into incomparable splendour. Then the Church of the saints confesses God’s truth, because at the judgment the generation of the upright will be blessed by Christ (Psalm 111). The heavens confess God’s wonders because the angels, in whom God dwells, continually rejoice in God’s mighty deeds. The Church of saints confesses his truth because the assembly of the blessed in the heavenly Jerusalem eternally resounds with Christ’s benefits. [Col. 1014D]

And because today [fo. 290v], dearest brethren, we celebrate the solemnity of all saints, let us in our assembly sing with heart and mouth, together with the angels, of Christ, God’s truth; let us extol his saints with worthy praises, so that, aided by their merits, we may rejoice eternally in the Lord’s joy.

Therefore first, with a voice of exultation and jubilation, let us magnify the supreme Lord God, who by his majesty created the whole world, whom the chorus of angels continually praises with jubilation, and whose sweet praise is in the Church of the saints (Psalm 149). The Trinity in unity must be devoutly recalled by us; unity in Trinity must be humbly adored, through which angelic dignity is exalted and human lowliness lifted to heaven. The Holy One, I say, of holy ones must today be praised in his saints: by whose holiness the people of the faithful are sanctified, rewarded with eternal life, and made blessed in everlasting glory. [Col. 1015A]

Then let the glorious Mother of God, Mary ever virgin, be extolled by us with the highest praises, through whom the lost world is restored to life; she, Queen of heaven, honourable to all angels and Lady of the world, venerable to all saints. Today let us rejoice to her in sweet harmony, through whom, since she is the gate of life, we have entrance into eternal life. After this, we must glorify the wondrous nine orders of blessed spirits, in whom the seal of God’s likeness is expressed, and who happily enjoy the brightness of supreme blessedness. They are worthy always to behold the Father’s face and, because sun and moon marvel at his beauty, continually to gaze upon him. Of them three—namely Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael—bear the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in their names; the others, three times three in number, express the holy Trinity. If, praising and venerating them by a worthy life, we do so, then indeed in true life we shall be made equal to them, joining with the saints in harmony before the Lord. [Col. 1015B]

Thereafter it is fitting that today we celebrate in hymns human beings, fellow-citizens of the angels, whom we proclaim now to be companions of the angels in heaven and to praise the supreme God with them. Among them, first let the succession of patriarchs be recalled with praise, from whose seed Christ springs—he who is the glory of all saints and the joy and gladness of angels. By figures they foreshadowed Christ and the Church, and in some manner represented the mysteries of the Church by living [fo. 252r] deeds. Adam, who was created from pure earth and from whose side a woman was formed, bears the figure of Christ, who was born of a chaste virgin and from whose side the Church is built. The other principal twelve patriarchs are a figure of the twelvefold senate of apostles. Through these—namely Seth, Enoch, Noah, Melchizedek, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Job, Samuel, and David—who are named expressly, the faithful before the Law are upheld in righteousness as by firm columns. [Col. 1015C]

After them we must remember and proclaim with great praises the prophets, who foretold as present the future mysteries of Christ and glorified Christ, who would suffer for the world, by their own sufferings. Of these Elijah and Elisha prefigure Christ: one raises the dead, the other enters heaven alive. The four chief prophets—Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel—had the figure of the four evangelists, who filled the fourfold world with abundant writings. Moreover the twelve—Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi—represented the twelve apostles, who instructed by writings and examples the people faithful under the Law toward life. Among them John the Baptist, greater than all born of women, shone supremely; like Lucifer, the morning star, he went before the true Sun and shone upon the world as messenger of the eternal day. He deserved to point with his finger to the Lamb of the Father, who would take away the sins of the world, and to baptize in water him whose future advent the choir of prophets had long sung beforehand. [Col. 1016A]

Now, dearest brethren, let us celebrate with sweet-sounding melody and utmost devotion the apostles and evangelists: preachers of the new grace, heralds of eternal life, judges of the world, and rulers of the Churches. They deserved to see with their eyes, touch with their hands, hear with their ears, and learn from Christ’s own mouth the Father’s mysteries: the Word coeternal with the Father, incarnate for us. They deserved to see God himself ascend to his Father’s throne and to receive through the Holy Spirit every kind of language. They adorned Christ’s bride, the Church, with signs and writings as with gems and necklaces; washed her in their own blood; and, as valiant [fo. 252v] sailors, carried her, placed upon the little ship of the holy cross, from the sea of this age to the harbour of life. [Col. 1016B] The four evangelists, like God’s four-horse chariot, led her by their doctrine from the four corners of the earth to the heavenly palace.

Of these, Peter was crucified for Christ in Italy; Andrew was condemned to the punishment of the cross in Achaia; John was subjected at Rome to a vat of boiling oil; James was killed with the sword in Judaea; Thomas was pierced by a lance in India; Bartholomew was flayed and beheaded in Lower India; Philip, suspended on a cross in Asia, was killed with stones; James was thrown down from the Temple at Jerusalem and killed with a club; Simon and Thaddaeus [printed: *Tatheus*] were struck down in Persia; Matthew was sent to the stars by the sword in Ethiopia, and Matthias by iron in Judaea. Paul also, who laboured more than all of them, did not hesitate to offer his neck for Christ at Rome. [Col. 1016C] These friends and supreme commanders of the highest God, glorious senators, now triumph in glory in the angelic court; by their judgment all their imitators and true praisers rejoice in the lot of the righteous.

After these, we must praise the choir of martyrs, by whose intercession the world, which lies in the Evil One (1 John 5), is to be saved. As good soldiers of the eternal King, fighting for their reward, they shed their blood; and now, having gained victory over their enemies, crowned with the flourishing garland of laurel, they have deserved to triumph in heaven. Among them the standard-bearer Stephen is stoned; Lawrence, his follower, is roasted alive; George is broken upon the wheel; Maurice is pierced through by the sword; Caesarius is today thrown into the sea. [Col. 1016D] Others, tortured by various punishments, are slaughtered with iron; others are strangled by nooses, flames, or waters; others are torn apart by beasts; others are killed by scourges, hunger, or a fall from a height. All these, made the world’s mockery in diverse ways, now clothed in white robes, deserved fellowship with the angels, palms in hand, in the sight of the Lamb. Let us pursue them with praises, so that we may one day deserve by our praise to follow the Lamb with them.

Next, let us exalt the lamps of the Church—that is, the confessors, illustrious painters of God’s house—and proclaim with worthy praise their merits. They watered the whole Church with the streams of the Scriptures and nobly adorned it with signs and good examples. Among these Martin [fo. 254r] [Col. 1017A], Nicholas, Remigius, Odalricus, and countless others shone like lights of the world by glorious miracles.

> **Note:** [Col. 1017D] Manuscript: *Vdalricus*.

Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, and countless others, pouring over God’s garden the abundance of the Scriptures like the four rivers of paradise, made glad the city of God by the rushing force of their preaching (Psalm 45). Since they awaited, ever watchful, the Lord returning from the wedding feast, they have now deserved to be set in the Lord’s joy over all his goods (Luke 12).

The company of monks and hermits is joined to their praises. They crucified their flesh with its vices and lusts (Galatians 5) and therefore, as co-heirs with Christ (Romans 8), have now received a hundredfold (Matthew 19). The world recoiled from their manner of life and, shuddering at them, vomited them out from itself as unclean refuse. Yet they shone upon the world in dress and deed and withdrew from it with their whole heart and body, fleeing the crowds of people, dwelling in solitude with beasts, and therefore deserved to enjoy the conversation and vision of angels. [Col. 1017B] Among them Benedict especially shone, like a fire-breathing ray, in brilliant signs and wonders; by excellent teaching he nobly offered himself as a guiding leader, the lamp of the way for those hastening to life. From their company too Antony, Pachomius? [printed: *Bachumius*], Hilarion, Macarius, and innumerable others shone like stars in the darkness of this world’s night by signs and examples of holy life, drawing many imitators of themselves from the shipwreck of this age to the true light. Because at one time they were held in derision and as a reproachful likeness, their life thought madness and their end destruction, behold, now they are counted among the children of God (Wisdom 5). [Col. 1017C]

Accordingly it is fitting that we adapt our melody to the pure white virgins and sound forth their praises in resonant voices. They conquered their sex together with the world, despised the flesh’s enticements and worldly pomp, scorned tyrants’ threats and rewards, and through diverse tortures came to the long-desired embraces of their Bridegroom. Therefore they now follow the Lamb wherever he goes and sing the new song, which no one else can sing (Revelation 5). Among them Thecla, given over to beasts, is tortured by fire; Agatha, after her breasts are cut off, is rolled upon burning shards; Agnes, cast into flames, is slain by the sword; Cecilia [fo. 254v], placed in a boiling bath, is killed by the sword; Margaret is torn by diverse punishments; Lucy, placed upon a pyre, is slaughtered by iron. [Col. 1017D] By a like end innumerable others, tortured, approached Christ, the Son of the Virgin; others, through devout endeavours, came to be joined with them to the Virgin Mother. Since with lamps kindled they will meet the coming Bridegroom, they will enter with him into the wedding feast (Matthew 25).

Widows are joined to their praises, women in whom marriage is not repeated for Christ’s sake. Among these Felicity offered herself to God as a living sacrifice with her seven sons; Symphorosa fell as Christ’s victim with the same number; Theodota with three sons and Sophia with three daughters deserved to be offered for Christ. [Col. 1018A] Thus very many other women, subjected to diverse kinds of punishment, obtained the heavenly kingdom. Others, diligently practising continence through devout labours, now rejoice with the prudent virgins.

Now let us set the plectrum of our tongue to married people and honour them with fitting honour, through whose procreation the age is renewed, and through whom Christ is daily served in his members. Among these Adrian endured death for Christ at his wife’s urging; Marcellianus and Mark, prompted by Sebastian, despised their wives and offered themselves to danger; Eustace with his wife and children suffered death today. Countless others attained incomparable riches through good works. [Col. 1018B]

With these let us praise penitents, striving to follow their examples: those who redeemed their sins with alms and covered former evils by the good deeds that followed. Among them, the man whom the appearance of a nun deceived recovered through Basil the document handed over to the devil; Theophilus, made an apostate through ambition, repenting recovered from the devil through the Mother of God the written agreement. In the *Lives of the Fathers*, a criminal, scourged by demons among tombs, became renowned by many signs. Mary of Egypt, Pelagia, Thaïs, and the sister of the solitary man—foul prostitutes—were made ardent lovers of Christ by repentance. Countless others, through repentance, were enriched with the reward of life.

To their praises let us add all the faithful, among whose number we ourselves should strive to be. As members they clung lavishly to the body of the Church and by their work have now reached Christ the head. Among them many soldiers [fo. 256r], in order to defend Mother Church, often shed their own blood in battle; very many farmers, in order to feed her, melt away in the sweat of labour; many women excel in the modesty of chastity; very many children flourish by showing honour to their parents. [Col. 1018C] Since the wicked insult these people as they toil in the Lord’s vineyard, they now leap for joy in rest, singing God’s praises. All of them adorned God’s garden as varied flowers and breathed the fragrance of eternal life by deeds and words.

Thus when Isaac blessed Jacob, he spoke these words: “Behold, the smell of my son is like a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27). Isaac blessed Jacob because Christ declares the people of the faithful blessed. The full field is the whole world, filled with the fragrance of saints. The diverse flowers are the diverse manners of the righteous. Among them the patriarchs flourished in faith like the narcissus flower; the prophets glitter in hope like the hyacinth; the apostles, like shoots springing from the true vine, bore the blossom of grapes in charity; the martyrs shone white in patience like the rose; confessors gleamed in wisdom like saffron; virgins glistened in chastity like the lily; monks, through humility like the violet, foreshadowed the purple of kingship; married people and the other faithful, represented by other flowers, shone in virtues. [Col. 1019A]

All these feast exultantly in God’s sight and delight in gladness (Psalm 67). They will hunger no more and thirst no more (Revelation 7), but will abound according to their desire in every delight; and they will yet have a double joy, because with body and soul together they will see the King of glory in his beauty. Then indeed they will shine like the sun and be equal to angels.

If you wish, you may end here; but if it is expedient, add the following:

[Col. 1019]

[Col. 1019A] Concerning this blessed union of angels and human beings, the Lord promises in prophetic speech: “Behold, I shall set Jerusalem in precious stones” (Isaiah 54). Jerusalem, which is called “vision of peace,” is the shared dwelling of angels and human beings, contemplating face to face in the Father Christ, the true peace. It will be set in precious stones because Jerusalem, as a city, will be built from chosen human beings in precious virtues. “I shall lay her stones in order.” Jerusalem’s stones will be laid in order when the chosen, according to their merits, are assigned among the orders of angels. “Her walls [fo. 256v] [Col. 1019B] in emeralds.” The emerald walls of Jerusalem are the nine angelic orders, which grow green through the unceasing vision of God and shine in everlasting glory. “Her foundations in sapphires.” The patriarchs were the foundations of the Church, who founded her by foreshadowing her through heavenly deeds; and therefore they shone like sapphire in an airy colour. “Her bulwarks in jaspers.” The prophets are the Church’s bulwarks, because their writings are secure defences against demons and heretics. They were green like jasper, because they flourished beautifully in faith. “Her gates in carved stones.” The apostles are the gates, through whose teaching we enter the Church and through whose judgment we are led into glory. These are built of carved stones because the good examples in the writings and deeds of the apostles are presented to the faithful as though carved. [Col. 1019C] “All her borders in desirable stones.”

All the boundaries of the Church are all peoples, all languages, all nations, every rank, every condition, every age, and every sex. They are set in desirable stones because from all these are chosen persons suitable for God’s building. “All your children taught by the Lord” [variant: *universi*, “all,” for *universos*]: all the children of the Church will be taught by the Lord when, in that life, they see all things in God. For nothing is hidden from them when they behold God, in whom all things subsist. “Great peace for your children.” There a multitude of peace will fill the Church’s children, because a torrent of peace from every kind of glory will overflow within them. “You shall be founded in righteousness.” This city will be founded in righteousness because it will be established in Christ, through whom each person’s merit will be justly rewarded. “I shall appoint peace as your visitation” (Isaiah 60). When we are visited by the Lord here, we are scourged for sins; there, however, our visitation will be an increase of peace. [Col. 1019D] “And righteousness as your rulers.” When prelates here justly require our deeds of us, they rightly subject us to punishments; there, however, righteousness is imposed upon us when Christ, righteousness itself, is given to us as reward.

“In your land iniquity shall no longer be heard,” because eternal equity will reign there. “Within your borders there shall be neither crushing nor devastation,” because sweet consolation and charity abound there. “Salvation shall occupy your walls, and praise your gates,” because among angels and saints, brought in through the apostles, there will be joyful and perpetual mutual rejoicing in salvation [fo. 258r]. [Col. 1020A] “You shall no longer have the sun for light by day, nor the moon’s brightness by night; but the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and your God your eternal glory. Your sun shall no more set, nor shall your moon wane, because the Lord shall be established for you as everlasting light. Your people, all righteous, shall inherit the land for ever,” where they will possess joy and gladness. “No longer shall the voice of weeping be heard in you, nor the voice of crying any more,” but the voice of salvation and exultation, and the voice of joyful song and thanksgiving.

For in that city the instruments of the saints continually sound; there the chorus of angels without ceasing rejoices in a sweet-sounding hymn with the most pleasing melody. This city is called “The Lord Is There,” because God will be the same in all the elect there. In this glory the angels remained through charity; to it all saints came through faith and works. Neither of these avails without the other; joined together, they convey a human being to life. “For without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11), and faith without works is said to be dead (James 2). Therefore too the Law was given to God’s people on two tablets (Exodus 31), because a human being is saved by faith and works. On one tablet were contained three commandments pertaining to God, by which faith in the Trinity was expressed; on the other seven pertaining to one’s neighbour were proclaimed, by which action was instructed. [Col. 1020C]

It is also read that Jacob had two sisters, for whom he served seven years and seven years, and that from one he begot six sons, but from the other only two (Genesis 29–30). Jacob represents the people of the faithful, who come through two lives—namely the active and the contemplative—to the inheritance of eternal life. Leah is the secular life, which begets six sons while it hastens to accomplish the six works of the Gospel: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, receiving guests, visiting the sick, and consoling prisoners and all afflicted persons (Matthew 25). For this wife Jacob serves seven years [Col. 1020D] while the devout people strive to fulfil the seven legal commandments: to honour father and mother; to kill no one by hand or tongue; not to commit adultery or steal; not to bear false witness; not to covet another’s property; and not to take away his wife or anything belonging to him (Exodus 20).

Rachel, moreover, is the beautiful spiritual life [fo. 258v], which bears two sons while it continually strives either to read or pray, or to hear God’s word or preach to others. For her too Israel serves seven years while the faithful people zealously submit themselves to the seven evangelical precepts: striving to be poor in spirit, meek, mournful, hungry for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, and peacemakers (Matthew 5). And that they may deserve to flourish in these, they are formed by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1021A] and pray to attain them by the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer (ibid.).

Through the spirit of fear they are voluntarily poor, so that they may be delivered from evils and receive the kingdom of heaven as an inheritance. Through the spirit of piety they are meek, lest they be led into temptation, and so may be judged worthy to possess the land of the living. Through the spirit of knowledge they mourn their own evils and those of their neighbours; they forgive debts to those who sin against them, so that their own debts may be forgiven and their sorrow, changed into joy, may receive consolation. Through the spirit of fortitude they suffer hunger and thirst for righteousness, and therefore will be satisfied with daily or supersubstantial bread. Through the spirit of counsel they endeavour to be merciful, so that God’s will may be done on earth with human beings as it is in heaven with angels, and so that they themselves may obtain Christ, mercy. Through the spirit of understanding they are pure in heart, so that God’s kingdom may come to them and they may see God face to face as he is (1 John 3). [Col. 1021B] Through the spirit of wisdom they are peacemakers, so that the Father’s name may be hallowed in them and they may be called children of God (ibid.). And because in each of these they suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, they receive by hereditary right the kingdom of heaven with angels in supreme blessedness. And because people reproach them, curse them, and falsely say every evil against them for the Lord’s name, they will be blessed, because in joy and exultation they will have an abundant reward (Matthew 5).

Your brotherhood should know why this holy solemnity was instituted. At Rome there was an ancient temple, the Pantheon, in honour of all gods—or rather, demons—which Pope Boniface, having removed every filth of idols, dedicated in May in honour of Mary the Mother of God and all martyrs. At first only the feast of Saint Mary and the martyrs was observed; but as time passed and the Christian religion increased, the solemnity of confessors too was instituted. Hence a certain Pope Gregory instituted that same feast to be celebrated on this [fo. 260r] present day in honour of all saints, so that whatever human frailty had neglected throughout the year in the celebrations of saints might today be forgiven through their merits. [Col. 1022A]

Therefore, dearest brethren, seek the Lord today through the merits and prayers of all saints by praying (Psalm 104); seek his face always (ibid.) by living well, and you will find rest for your souls (Matthew 11) by reigning in eternal glory. Invoke all saints with mouth and heart; commend yourselves to them with vows and praises, so that whatever you have done throughout the year against the Christian religion, Christ, the Holy One of all saints, may forgive you through their intercession; and when that same King of glory comes to be made wonderful in all his saints, and has made from angels and human beings one commonwealth, may you deserve in this union to reign with him in the most brilliant palace of his kingdom, and at the wedding feast of Bridegroom and bride to sing everlasting *alleluia* with all choirs of angels and saints. [Col. 1022B]

## ON SAINT MARTIN THE BISHOP

[Col. 1021]

[Col. 1021B] **Beloved of God and of men, whose memory is in blessing** (Ecclus. 45). Beloved, Saint Martin was beloved by God, and therefore was chosen as a glorious bishop over his people. He was beloved by men, because the people of God were protected by his patronage against the enemies of soul and body. Therefore his memory is in blessing, because throughout the world he is blessed by men, and in heaven by the blessed spirits, in everlasting glory. Today, too, the name of Jesus Christ is blessed through him by the whole Church, from whom so great a patron has been set over it. He is called the jewel of priests, because by his precious life and illustrious miracles the priestly dignity is adorned throughout the whole world. Hence his praiseworthy name is celebrated from the rising of the sun to its setting (Ps. 112), and all who labor invoke him for help. He swiftly comes to the aid of all who call upon him, and through his merits God grants to each person whatever is sought. For, besides the many signs by which he is to be glorified, through him God restored three dead persons to life.

He was born in Pannonia of Roman, though pagan, parents and was educated in Italy. At the age of twelve he desired with his whole heart the desert life; but his father, while (fo 260 vo) he was a military tribune, restrained his devout desire by threats. Finally he was put in chains and, against his will, involved in military service. The wave of baptism had not yet washed him, and yet he carefully fulfilled the Gospel’s commands: he fed those who needed nourishment, and according to his ability aided the oppressed in tribulation. Content with only one servant, he himself often served that servant in turn. One winter day, as Martin was traveling with his fellow soldiers, they encountered a poor man naked and begging mercy from passers-by. When all passed by the wretched man, Martin seized his sword, divided the cloak with which he was clothed, and gave one part to the poor man. On the following night the Lord appeared to him with a multitude of angels, displayed the portion of clothing given by Martin, and declared that he had been clothed in it by Martin, though not yet baptized.

[Col. 1022C] Encouraged by this vision and strengthened in hope of greater grace, Saint Martin, when he was eighteen years old, was immersed in Christ’s font and immediately devoted himself wholly to God’s service. Meanwhile Julian, hateful to God, was hastening to battle and distributing a military bounty to the soldiers. Martin renounced military service along with the bounty; but the tyrant ordered him taken into prison, so that he might expose him unarmed to the enemy. Yet the merciful Lord provided for the welfare of all when he removed his faithful soldier from danger, because he removed the necessity of battle.

[Col. 1023A] For on the next day the enemy sought peace and submitted themselves with all their forces to the emperor.

Thereafter Martin left behind his weapons, put on the monastic habit, and joined Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. Having remained with him for some time, he set out for his parents; but the devil met him on the road and promised to oppose him in everything. Entering a forest, he was captured by robbers, bound, led into a remote place, and entrusted to one man to be guarded. Through Martin’s words that man believed in God; releasing him, he led him to the road, abjured robbery, and faithfully accompanied Martin as companion and disciple. On reaching his parents, Martin converted his mother to the Lord, but could not convert [or: cause the conversion of] his father. From there he returned to Hilary and suffered various punishments from heretics.

[Col. 1023B] At that time a certain catechumen had attached himself to him; while Martin was absent (fo 262), he died unbaptized. But when Martin returned, he dissolved in tears; and as the Lord comforted him, his sorrow was changed into joy, and immediately the dead man was raised by him. At another time, as Martin passed by, a mournful cry was heard in a certain village. When he asked the cause of the mourning, someone told him that a man had taken his own life by hanging. Martin, taking pity on the unhappy man, sent everyone out and poured forth prayers to the merciful Compassionate One. “O how near the Lord is to all who call upon him in truth!” (Ps. 144). At once the dead man was restored to life and, to the astonishment of all, went away alive with Martin. O what merit this man had before God, who restored to life one who had not feared to kill himself! Made known to the world by these wondrous miracles, Martin was, by God’s ordering, raised to the mitred office of bishop of Tours.

[Col. 1023C] With remarkable humility and diligence he ruled the flock entrusted to him, instructing his subjects by sweet teaching and living examples. He adorned his age with signs and wonders and upheld the whole Church unwaveringly as a golden column.

As Martin approached the church, demons bellowed in the church, and through possessed persons the clergy perceived that the bishop was approaching. The evil spirits were tormented by the presence of the bishop worthy of God. As soon as he wrapped himself in haircloth and prostrated himself on ashes, the host of unclean spirits was expelled from possessed people. On a solemn day, when he was about to celebrate Mass,

[Col. 1023D] he sat down in the sacristy; and behold, a poor man asked him for clothing. At once he sent the deacon and ordered him to bring a garment to the poor man. When the deacon delayed, Martin took off his own garment and gave it to the poor man. On returning, the deacon urged the bishop to celebrate Mass, saying that the people were exhausted from waiting so long. He replied that the poor man must first be clothed and then the service of God performed. Angered, the deacon bought from a nearby tavern a short black garment for a few coins and threw it down angrily at the bishop’s feet. Martin, however, entirely unmoved, ordered the deacon to go out, secretly put on the garment brought to him, and so approached the solemnities of Mass with his arms half bare. But the Lord disclosed to the people standing by the merit of the illustrious bishop: while he was celebrating Mass, a globe of fire rose from

[Col. 1024A] his head, and as the flame grew it stretched upward into the heights of heaven. Often (fo 262 vo), too, during the solemnities of Mass, Martin’s hands were seen to shine with gems and to sparkle with gold and electrum.

On one occasion, while Martin was preaching in an open field to a pagan people, a certain boy was crushed by the pressing crowd. His mother brought him to the saint with lamentation, and immediately, before all, by Martin’s prayers she deserved to receive him alive again; believing with the whole people, she gave thanks to God. Thus the holy Trinity glorifies its chosen one before men, when through him it calls three dead persons back to life.

So many outstanding signs are recorded of this blessed man that they cannot be expounded in any discourse. Let it therefore suffice that you have heard these few, lest a more extended discourse cause you weariness.

[Col. 1024B] When a certain Postumianus had traveled through the regions of the world, visited the holy Fathers in Egypt, Judaea, and Greece, and on his return recounted to the brethren many splendid and report-worthy things, it was found that Martin surpassed all their merits and deeds in miracles and holiness, and that they all did not attain the measure of Martin alone. For he gave sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute; he restored cleanness to lepers, walking to the lame, and strength to a people afflicted by paralysis. He moderated the burning of fevers, drove the fury of demons from human beings, and not only himself performed signs, but many also worked wonders in Martin’s name. Oil blessed by Martin drove away every sickness; letters sent by him, once pain was put to flight, restored health.

[Col. 1024C] Birds, beasts, and serpents obeyed his command. Clothing touched by him, or the straw upon which he slept, drove away demons or any harmful illness and granted swift healing. His cloak was carried before the kings of the Franks as a standard when they went to war, and through it, after their enemies had been overcome, they obtained victory; even those who guarded that cloak are to this day called *cappellani*, “chaplains.” Angels often spoke with him, and all manner of saints frequently conversed with him. He always directed eyes and hands toward heaven; in mouth and heart he bore Christ. He commanded kings powerfully and overcame heretics with great authority. He patiently endured wrong inflicted upon him by the envy of bishops, and gave to all an example of holiness in every respect.

[Col. 1024D] Long (fo 264) beforehand he knew his death and foretold to the brethren the day of his departure. Therefore, when the Lord had decreed to reward the glorious merits of blessed Martin and to crown with an everlasting laurel-wreath his veteran soldier after many contests, he was seized with bodily pain; and thus he was delivered alike from pain and death. With angels and saints singing together, he joyfully entered into the joy of his Lord; but the heavenly melody was perceived by many. For Severinus, bishop of Cologne, renowned for many virtues, was at that hour walking with his deacon Ervelgisus—afterwards bishop of the same place—between monasteries for the sake of prayer, when Martin’s soul, released from the flesh, entered the temples of heaven.

[Col. 1025A] Hearing the angelic harmony, he told his deacon, who did not know what it signified, that Martin, bishop of Tours, had departed from this life and that choirs of angels had received his soul. But, he said, a crowd of demons had met it, found nothing belonging to themselves, and departed confounded; and for this reason the heavenly host had rung out a hymn of praise with such exultation. Alas, beloved, what will become of us, wretches entangled in every crime, if a host of demons met Martin, who flourished in every virtue? This blessed man, seeking heavenly things, also appeared to Severus, who had already published his Life in writing.

It was Sunday when, leaving the prison of body and world, he entered the lofty palaces of heaven. On that same day Ambrose, bishop of Milan, remembered by all the Churches for his holiness and abundant teaching,

[Col. 1025B] stood at the altar about to celebrate the solemnities of Mass. He was caught up by the Holy Spirit and carried to Tours for the burial of Martin’s body. When Martin had been buried, Ambrose returned to himself; and, to the wonder and rightful amazement of all, recounted what had happened.

Therefore, beloved, blessed Martin is to be venerated by us with solemn praise and celebrated in sweet melody with the angels: the Lord was shown to him among the angels while he was still a pagan soldier; through him, once he had become a Christian and an abbot, life was restored to the dead; he was raised to episcopal dignity and adorned with virtues and miracles; a queen served him, and when a king did not rise for him, the king’s throne was seized by flames; beaten by the king’s servants, he fixed them together with their animals at the river like statues, but allowed those who repented to cross (fo 264 vo);

[Col. 1026A] he cut down trees dedicated to demons, caught them as they fell without injury, saw the shade of a slain robber, heard its spoken words, destroyed his altar [?] and other shrines; but he halted a crowd of pagans with a funeral procession and then allowed them to depart again; he fixed a pack of dogs in place and snatched a little hare from their teeth; he healed those bitten by serpents after expelling the poison; he exposed the tricks of deceivers; he extinguished a fire around himself and opened the tongue of a three-day-old infant to speech; in whose name a dog barking importunately was made mute, and whose straw, tied by nuns upon a possessed man, expelled the demon; who ordered a serpent to cross a river and cormorants to leave the river for the desert; who foretold his death long beforehand and brought the discordant into peace. When he dies, troops of angels meet him, choirs of saints applaud with their songs, heaven opens to receive him, and all heavenly things rejoice.

It is also handed down that it was revealed to a certain solitary that, on one day of Martin’s feast, so many souls were liberated from punishments through his merits as

[Col. 1026B] [Note: [Col. 1025D] Thus the manuscript always has *pro quot*, “for as many as,” in place of *quot*, “as many as.”] people came together that day for his festival. O truly blessed bishop, worthily to be declared blessed by the whole Church, through whose blessed merits blessed joys are bestowed upon souls! Beloved, let us earnestly entreat him with devout mind, that by his aid we may reign with Christ in the heavenly homeland, where “eye has not seen” (1 Cor. 2), and so forth.

Add on Sunday, concerning Saint Brictius:

[Col. 1025C] Today, beloved, let us ask holy Brictius to favor our prayers, since we know that he has great power with God. For he learned in his own afflictions how those placed in miseries ought to be helped. Envy always accompanies virtue; this is especially demonstrated by the present example. When Saint Martin shone like the sun in signs and virtues, and his sweet fame spread far and wide among peoples, many bishops—alas!—who desired the praises of his renown but refused to be adorned by the holiness of his life, contrived by some device to depose him whom the right hand of God exalted. Meanwhile a certain woman gave birth to a son wickedly conceived, and the author of the crime remained hidden. Thus the bishops, finding an opportunity for their madness, assembled a council and, having formed a plan with the woman,

[Col. 1025D] charged Martin with the crime (fo 266). Martin ordered the infant to be brought to him. Embracing him in his arms and caressing him, he said, “My son, my son.” The child, though he had not yet completed a week, broke forth in a clear voice: “You are not my father,” he said, “but John the merchant is.” Therefore, all were astounded, fell at Martin’s knees, and begged forgiveness. The worthy priest of God graciously pardoned their injury, baptized the infant, lifted him [variant: washed him] from the font, and named him Brictius.

[Col. 1026C] When Brictius had grown up, Martin trained him in monastic disciplines and ordained him priest. Although he endured many insults from him, Martin obtained from God an episcopate for him as his reward. Thus, when Martin departed to the Lord, Brictius was made bishop; and in the thirtieth year of his episcopate, what he had sinned against his master was exacted from his own hand. For an unfortunate woman bore a child from fornication, and the entire people charged the bishop with the crime. But he, following his master’s example, ordered the boy, who had completed thirty days of age, to be brought forward. Before all the people he adjured him publicly to declare whether he himself was the father. But the boy clearly denied that he was his father. Since they attributed this to magical art and called Brictius a fornicator and magician, Brictius carried burning coals around the city in his cloak and set them down before the tomb of Saint Martin.

[Col. 1026D] His garment appeared unburned; yet the furious people did not believe and expelled him from the episcopate, because he had deserved this in Martin’s case. Lamenting, he came to Rome, where the Apostolic [pope] honorably received him. After seven years he was sent back to his see, received by all the people with great honor and joy; and, having worthily completed his office, today he is joined to the saints in glory. Let us pray with all our heart to be associated with him, where “eye has not seen,” etc. (1 Cor. 2).

## OF SAINT CECILIA. If it is her church.

[Col. 1027]

[Col. 1027A] “O how beautiful is a chaste generation with charity!” (Wis. 4). Those who flourish here in chastity, if they burn with charity, will shine before the Lord with ineffable brightness. But those who live chastely without love will go through a difficult life to destruction. Whoever fulfills the desire of every pleasure is led, as it were, by a grassy path to the rack. But one who lives in bodily restraint without possessing love is dragged, as it were, through thorns to hanging.

The Lord relates that there were ten virgins (fo 266 vo),

[Col. 1027B] five of whom received the Bridegroom with lamps lit and entered with him into the wedding-feast; but five remained outside with their lamps extinguished. The prudent virgins are those who live chastely in body and spirit; although they can marry, they do not wish to do so, but reject fleshly pleasures for love of Christ. They are written as five because works of chastity are fulfilled through the five bodily senses, through which they are rendered acceptable to God. Five is also divided into three and two: through three is expressed faith in the holy Trinity, and through two, the twofold love. Therefore those who work in faith in the holy Trinity through twofold love are rightly marked by the number five. Again, by three are understood faith, hope, and charity; by two, chastity of body and soul. Whoever has lived chastely in body and spirit in these virtues will without doubt belong to this number five.

But the foolish virgins are those who, through pride, despise married women, or seek human glory from bodily virginity. Those who are proud of virginity

[Col. 1027C] are unclean before God, because, as it is written, everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God. Those who seek praise from men through chastity will not have a reward from God, because they have received it here from the men whom they sought to please. Those who with their whole desire join themselves to men—and would gladly join themselves bodily too, if opportunity were given—will, as corrupt women, be subjected by God to punishments, unless they themselves endeavor through repentance to punish this in themselves. For just as men who look upon a woman in order to desire her commit adultery (Matt. 5), so women who desire men likewise commit adultery. Those who perform any obscene acts, even if they never join themselves to men, are justly condemned by God as prostitutes. These, too, are referred to as five,

[Col. 1027D] because they strive to fulfill the uncleanness of their heart through the five senses. Lit lamps are good actions; oil is eternal glory; vessels are hearts. Therefore the prudent virgins light their lamps because, through good works for eternal glory, they shine before men. But the foolish have lamps indeed, yet lack oil, because they perform works of continence only for human favor. The Bridegroom is Christ, and the bride is the Church. He will then lead her to the wedding-feast when, after the judgment has been completed, he brings her into the heavenly Jerusalem. But while he now delays, all the virgins fall asleep, because all undergo the sleep of death (fo 268).
