[Col. 1028A] At midnight, however, the Bridegroom is announced as coming by a cry, and the virgins are urged to go out to meet him, because at midnight the coming of the eternal Judge is proclaimed to the world by the great cry of voices and angelic trumpets, and the dead are awakened from the sleep of death to meet him. The prudent then receive him with lit lamps and enter with him into the wedding-feast, because they receive eternal rewards for good works and rejoice in everlasting glory for chastity. But then the door is shut upon the foolish, whose lamp is extinguished, because there they will lack the reward of life, having received here the praises from the men whom they loved (Matt. 25).

Meanwhile, the Lord relates that a man found a treasure hidden in a field and, having sold everything,

[Col. 1028B] bought that field (Matt. 13). The treasure is Christ, hidden in the Father. He is found lying hidden in the field when, remaining in the Father, he is discovered through contemplation to be coeternal with him. For this treasure the field is bought after all things have been sold, because, by despising every earthly thing for Christ, one will deserve to behold his face. Again he says that a man found a precious pearl and, giving all he possessed, bought it (ibid.). The beauty of the precious pearl is the sweetness of heavenly life. It is bought by giving all things when one, renouncing everything and trampling every desire of the world, is rewarded with eternal sweetness. Again he says that a net was cast into the sea and enclosed every kind of fish; when they drew it full to shore, they selected the good fish into vessels and threw the bad ones outside (ibid.).

[Col. 1028C] The net is the Catholic faith, woven from many sayings of Scripture. It is cast into the sea when it is preached by teachers throughout the whole world. Every kind of fish is enclosed in it when the human race, from every language, every people, every tribe, every rank, and every sex, clings to faith and is subjected to Christ. But the full net is drawn to shore when the end of the world brings the whole human race to its conclusion. Then the good fish are chosen into vessels, when the elect are placed by angels in different dwellings according to their merits. But the bad are thrown outside when the reprobate are shut up in the furnace of fire to be tortured forever.

Saint Cecilia was one of the prudent virgins

[Col. 1028D] who shone splendidly (fo 268 vo) with the lamp of chastity. Because she met the Bridegroom with a burning lamp, she has now entered with him into the wedding-feast of eternal banqueting. She sold everything to buy the treasure, because in order to gain Christ she surrendered herself and all that was hers to death. She bought the pearl she found by giving all things, because, despising every allurement of the flesh and the pomp of the world, she has now tasted the sweetness of heavenly life. As a good fish adhering to the Gospel net, she was chosen into a vessel, because angels carried her from this world into everlasting joy.

She was of noble Roman stock and was betrothed to a man of noble birth. When the wedding had taken place, beneath she wore haircloth, above gold. When they had come to the private chambers, she converted her bridegroom to faith in Christ through sweet conversation.

[Col. 1029A] At her persuasion he received baptism from Pope Urban; on returning, he found an angel of the Lord with Cecilia. The angel brought two garlands woven [variant: covered] from sweet-smelling flowers of Paradise, placing one on Cecilia’s head and the other on Valerian’s; he further declared that they would obtain whatever they asked from God. After this Tiburtius, Valerian’s brother, arrived; Cecilia converted him to Christ by honey-sweet words, and the pope clothed him in Christ’s garment. Thus they served Christ God devoutly every day, gave many alms, conversed daily with angels, and worked signs and wonders. Afterwards they were arrested by the prefect and compelled to sacrifice to idols; refusing, both were killed for Christ.

[Col. 1030A] A certain man named Maximus saw their souls received by angels and borne with great glory to the heavenly seats. Therefore he too believed in God and was soon beaten with leaded scourges by the prefect’s command and died for Christ. Then Cecilia was shut up in baths breathing out flame, but, sprinkled by the fountain of life, she was not burned. Struck by a third blow of the sword and washed in the stream of her own blood, she was joined pure to Christ her Bridegroom. Now she herself, a glorious martyr and virgin, accompanies him among the companies of martyrs and virgins. Let us imitate her and implore God’s mercy, so that through the intervention of her merits we may rejoice in eternal gladness—what “eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2), and so forth.

## OF SAINT CLEMENT

[Col. 1029]

[Col. 1029A] (fo. 270) “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place or under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light” (Luke 11). Beloved, Saint Clement was a lamp of the Church divinely kindled and set upon the lampstand of Roman supremacy; he bestowed the abundant light of doctrine upon all whom the house of this world held enclosed. His mother Mathidia, a noblewoman, was joined to the noble Roman Faustidianus; from them he was born as the third of their sons. Endowed with remarkable beauty, she was solicited for adultery by her husband’s brother. Avoiding his mad importunity, she set out by ship for Greece with two sons, while Clement, still very small, remained with his father. But a storm arose and the ship broke apart; while the others perished, she was carried by the waves on a plank to an island.

[Col. 1029C] Her sons Faustus and Faustinus, swimming, were seized by pirates and sold to different people in different places. When the woman was long in returning, her husband sent a servant to search for her throughout Greece. When he returned and said that he had found no trace of report concerning her, the man, struck by grief, left everything and went to seek her; not finding her, he resolved to live a hidden life in exile. Thus, with parents and brothers lost, Clement remained heir to the property left behind. While he was studying philosophy and anxiously inquiring about the immortality of the soul, Barnabas came upon him by God’s ordering and satisfied him on this matter. Leaving Rome with Barnabas, he went to Jerusalem. Having heard Peter’s teaching, he received baptism and thereafter faithfully accompanied him in all things.

[Col. 1029D] Now his brothers were then called Nicetas and Aquila. They had been deceived by Simon Magus and admitted as disciples to his instruction. But when Simon Magus had been refuted in public disputation by Peter and had fled in confusion, they left Simon, attached themselves to Peter, were baptized, and firmly embraced the true faith. As Peter traveled with them to a certain island, a woman asked him for alms.

[Col. 1030A] When he asked why a healthy woman was begging alms, she began weeping and unfolded her misfortune to him. She said that she had fallen from the greatest wealth into the greatest need; that in Rome she had left a very powerful husband (fo 270 vo) with a son, that two sons had perished in shipwreck, and that, placed in exile, she had become crippled by twisting her arm in grief and tears. When the sons heard the speaker’s words, though they did not know that they were brothers, they recognized that she was their mother and were amazed to discover themselves full brothers. She was baptized by Peter and joined to her rejoicing sons. Then they came to their father, whom after long despair they recognized and brought into the holy faith.

Meanwhile Simon Magus was overturning the people of Antioch by his deceptions. Clement’s father, being a philosopher,

[Col. 1030C] went to dispute with him. Simon altered his appearance so thoroughly by magical art that anyone looking at him thought him to be Simon himself. When his sons returned to him with their mother, they recoiled from his presence and in every respect thought that he was Simon. Following Peter’s instruction, he returned to Antioch, summoned the people, confessed that he had erred and had wickedly preached against God and Peter, and promised amendment thereafter. All who thought him Simon Magus, accepting his counsel, sent for the apostle Peter; they honorably received him and submitted their necks to the yoke of faith. Afterwards, when Simon again preached his former error and blasphemed God and his apostles, the people of Antioch seized the deceptive seducer—who dared to preach again the error he had renounced—subjected him to many whippings, and expelled him from their territory with great disgrace.

[Col. 1030D] After these things Peter came to Rome with Clement. At Simon’s instigation Nero crucified Peter, and Clement, appointed by Peter, was made bishop over the Church. After he had nobly governed the Church for some time by apostolic teaching and attached many people to the faith by signs and preaching, the wife of Sisinnius, a friend of the emperor, was converted to Christ. Her husband followed her to the church out of curiosity, but during the solemnities of Mass was made blind and deaf.

[Col. 1031A] Clement restored his sight and hearing by prayer and converted him to God. While through Sisinnius a multitude of distinguished persons was brought into subjection to Christ God, by decree of Emperor Trajan Clement was banished with many others. There he brought a spring forth from a rock, built many churches, and instructed all the surrounding people in the holy faith. Therefore the emperor sent a judge, who condemned Clement and all the Christians to various punishments. Some he killed with the sword (fo 272), some he crushed by the turning of wheels, some he cast into flames, and some he exposed to beasts; but the pope himself he plunged into the sea, with an anchor tied to his neck.

[Col. 1031B] At the prayers of the Christians, however, the sea drew back its waves into its bosom for three thousand stadia; and behold, a marble temple appeared in the midst of the sea. Entering it, the faithful found a sarcophagus and saw holy Clement within it, with an anchor tied to his neck.

[Col. 1032A] It was also revealed to them that they should not remove his body, because every year, when the sea draws back its waves, it provides a passage for those entering for seven days. Thus God chose to glorify his martyr and make the power of his name known to all nations. On one occasion, when the solemnity had been completed and the people were hastening to the shore, a certain woman forgot her infant inside. When the year had come around again, he was found sleeping and unharmed, as though only a single night had passed, and everyone gave praise to God. It is also reported that every year two persons flourishing in virginal body remain inside; after a year has passed, they possess knowledge of all Scripture and are assigned to God’s service in the place called “the Household of Saint Clement.” Their death is always revealed to them one year beforehand. Beloved, today let us invoke this glorious martyr

[Col. 1032B] and celebrate him with devout praise, so that, when the ungodly are cast into fire and will not endure in their miseries, and destruction seizes unjust men, we may give thanks to the Lord’s name with the righteous and deserve to dwell with the upright before his face, where “eye has not seen,” etc. (1 Cor. 2).

## OF SAINT ANDREW THE APOSTLE

[Col. 1031]

[Col. 1031B] Formerly the nations celebrated the birthdays of kings; today the Church celebrates the birth-feasts of martyrs, not the occasion on which, born of a mortal mother, they entered this mortal life, but that on which, born by dying from the womb of the immortal Church, they entered immortal life from death.

[Note: [Col. 1031] The manuscript’s first hand has *non quo*, corrected to *in quo*; but *non quo* should be read.]

For just as the sons of kings—though not all—coming forth from their mother and entering this world are born for an earthly kingdom, so [the sons?] who pass from this world and depart into eternal life are born for the heavenly kingdom. For good soldiers who conquered enemies by fighting bravely and shed their blood for the cause of the highest emperor and august Church have therefore, after obtaining victory, deserved to become crowned co-heirs of the kingdom.

It is read that (fo 272 vo)

[Col. 1031C] blessed Job was great among all the peoples of the East, begot seven sons and three daughters, and that the sons invited their sisters to a feast. Although these things happened thus, they were nevertheless written for their figurative meaning. For the Holy Spirit—to whom past things do not pass away and future things do not come after, but all things are always present, and who made the things that were to be—through the deeds of earlier persons wove into Scripture the future deeds of the apostles. The same Spirit who composed holy Scripture through the prophets expounded it through the apostles and their successors; for the deeds of those who came before were shadows of those who came after. Thus Job, whose name means “suffering,” was a figure of Christ, who suffered in the Passion for us. He was great among all the peoples of the East because he was more magnificent, namely as the Son of God, than all angelic ranks. He had seven sons because Christ appointed the twelve apostles as his co-heirs. For seven is divided into three

[Col. 1032B] and four, and three times four make twelve; therefore the apostles are expressed by the number seven, because through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit they brought the four parts of the world to faith in the holy Trinity.

[Col. 1032C] They invited three sisters to the feast because through faith, hope, and charity they called Asia, Africa, and Europe to the heavenly banquet.

Among them blessed Andrew was eminent, whose birth-feast we celebrate today. He was Saint Peter’s full brother and his companion both in apostleship and in suffering. For as Peter glorified Christ by the cross, so Andrew magnified God by dying on the cross. Many astonishing things are reported and many wondrous and glorious things read concerning him. Among the many things he did, it is reported that he gave light in prison to the apostle Matthew, whom pagans had blinded, and raised many dead persons. At last he went forth to contend in Achaia, and through him an innumerable people was enrolled in the heavenly kingdom. Finally, in the city of Patras he was seized by the proconsul Aegeas,

[Col. 1032D] shut in prison, brought out and subjected to many lashes, and then ordered to be raised upon a cross. Seeing the cross from afar, he greeted it with joy and desired the hanging as a banquet. Suspended on the cross, he was bound with ropes so that he might die by prolonged torment. When he had remained alive, hanging on the cross for two days, and was teaching the people standing by about the blessed life, Aegeas, compelled by fear of the people, came with many others to take him down; but no one (fo 274) could touch him with their hands. And behold, suddenly an immense light shone from heaven over the one hanging. Rejoicing in it and delivered from the pain of the flesh, he entered eternal light. His body was buried by Maximilla, Aegeas’ wife;

[Col. 1033A] manna and oil flow from his tomb. But Aegeas, seized by a demon, died, and the whole people believed in Christ the Lord. Thus Christ’s veteran soldier, after victory, accompanied by an angelic multitude, triumphs today, laureate in glory; and in the senate of life, with the twelve companions—the judges of the world—he himself, a glorious judge, exults. Beloved, let us ask him to obtain for us by his merit that God may fulfill all our petitions and fill us with every joy. Which—

## OF SAINT NICHOLAS

[Col. 1033]

[Col. 1033A] “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance; he shall not fear evil report” (Ps. 111). All things that happen in the land of forgetfulness are handed over to oblivion; and everything that occurs under the sun slips from memory, like a dead man from the heart. For in whose memory now abides the once wealthy glory of kings and tyrants? Who now remembers the magnificent cities which they built, or the renowned monuments of noble triumphs which they erected?

[Col. 1033B] Where now are the pomp or riches in which they abounded, or the punishments and tortures which they inflicted upon the saints? All have passed away like a shadow, and they themselves have inherited fire and worm. But those who worshiped God will be in everlasting remembrance; their works flourish through all generations, and their names will live for ever and ever. For one who clings to God through love is one spirit with God, and, united to him through the Spirit, remains with him forever. Among these is Saint Nicholas in everlasting remembrance, because here on earth he is celebrated by human beings, and in eternal life by angels.

[Col. 1033C] He shall not fear the evil report, namely: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25); but at the sweet utterance, “Come, blessed ones” (ibid.), they shall rejoice forever.

Here sprang from a noble Greek lineage the illustrious bishop of Myra, renowned for many miracles. Newly born, he was set in the basin to be washed, but for one hour he stood unsupported by anyone, because indeed he was to be established in the degree of virtues. Soon this man of good disposition began, through abstinence, to return to the fatherland from which the first parent had been exiled through gluttony. For on Wednesdays and Fridays he drank from the breast only once in the day; therefore the abundance of heavenly grace flowed copiously into him (fol. 274v). When he had passed the boundary of infancy, with thirsting breast he drank from the streams of Scripture the secrets of heavenly life. When grown up also, bereft of both parents, he himself was appointed heir to an immense estate.

Moreover, in the same city there lived a nobleman who had fallen from the greatest wealth into utter poverty. He resolved to prostitute his three daughters, distinguished for their beauty, so that by them he might at least earn a living. Nicholas redeemed them with gold: kindly taking poverty from the father and dishonour from the girls, while purchasing heavenly riches for himself. Meanwhile the Church of Myra was bereaved by the death of its pastor; but the devout flock asked God to set a worthy pastor over it. The good shepherd swiftly consoled the desolate sheepfold, revealing Saint Nicholas to it as appointed bishop by God. After he had been established, by the election of clergy and people, as a prudent and faithful steward over the household of the Lord, the radiance of his virtues was immediately spread everywhere.

[Col. 1034A] His sweet fame too was scattered throughout the world, and through it crowds of people from every quarter were drawn to see him. A ship, therefore, laden with people was sailing toward him, when a savage storm shook it and threatened the sailors with the peril of shipwreck. Distressed, they called upon Nicholas; he immediately appeared to them and, calming the storm-waves, stilled the sea from its rage. Then they all gave thanks to him whom winds and sea obey (Matt. 8).

This saint demolished a temple of Diana; and the devil sought to avenge this by the following device. A ship full of crowds, making its way to him, was crossing the sea, and behold, the devil brought a vessel of oil in the form of Diana, tearfully begging them to convey this liquid to his saint for trimming the lamps. He complained that many obstacles delayed his arrival to him. Having accepted the oil, they rowed out into the deep; and behold, a voice from above cried out that they should cast away the oil given by the woman and know its giver to be the devil. As soon as the oil was thrown out, the water, contrary to nature, was immediately seized by flames. But as they shouted in terror, Nicholas [Col. 1034C] appeared, and the deception at once disappeared. The people sang praise to him who had rescued them from the boiling cauldron of the sea.

At a certain time an extreme famine invaded the region and afflicted Nicholas’s people most severely. Meanwhile royal ships, laden with wheat, were passing through; from them the man of God obtained several (fol. 276) measures of wheat. He distributed it abundantly among all the people, and when the sailors reached the shore, they found their measure of wheat as though they had given away nothing. In this he imitated Him who satisfied many thousands from a few loaves and had more left over in the gathered fragments than had been set out.

At another time three young men, falsely accused before a proconsul through anger—or rather avarice—were condemned to death. Hearing this, the bishop of God hastened there as quickly as possible and saved them from their impending doom. At another time three noblemen were accused before the Emperor Constantine on account of envy and condemned by the emperor. Cast into prison, they cried out to Nicholas; and he immediately appeased Constantine in dreams, by threats and terrors, concerning their destruction. On waking, the emperor summoned his magnates, disclosed the vision, and ordered the young men released without delay. They extolled in praises the mercy of their deliverer, who had rescued them from the hand of one stronger.

Having performed these and many other glorious signs, he was joined in everlasting glory to the King of glory; but the marble of his tomb is said to sweat forth an oily liquid. [Col. 1035A] Whenever any infirm person is anointed with it, health is immediately restored when sickness has been driven away. O wonderful power of Christ! As far as east is from west, and as much as light differs from darkness, so distinct are the rewards of the righteous from those of the reprobate. For as oil is said to flow from this man’s tomb, so black and foul pitch is reported to sweat from the sarcophagus of Julian the Apostate.

At one time the bishop of that see was driven from the city through envy, and immediately the drops of the sacred liquid were stopped; but when he was restored to his own seat, the health-giving dripping was at once restored, to the people’s joy. [The reading is uncertain: *stillas acri* for *stilla sacri*.] A very powerful man summoned a goldsmith and ordered him to make a golden vessel, intended as a votive offering to Saint Nicholas. When the craftsman had wonderfully carved it and adorned it with various gems, [Col. 1035B] the man admired the remarkable work, desired it, and decided to keep it for his own use. He ordered another vessel, resembling the first, to be made and intended to offer this one to Saint Nicholas in place of it. The goldsmith, however, applied the greatest diligence but could not in any way make the second as splendid as the first.

When the work had thus made little progress, the man took the gold, embarked upon a ship with his wife, son, and many others, and intended to offer the gold in place of the vessel to Saint Nicholas (fol. 276v). Having crossed a great part of the sea, he became thirsty and wished to drink from the golden vessel that he had wrongly kept. His son took it—he alone had been permitted to touch it—and, holding it to wash and clean it, let it slip from his hand through carelessness. Trying to seize it, the young man himself was plunged into the waves of the sea. Deeply grieved by this event, they reached port and sorrowfully entered the basilica of Saint Nicholas. The master placed the gift he had brought upon the altar, but, repelled by divine power, it sprang back some distance.

As all stood amazed, he related in order how he had kept for himself the vessel promised to the saint; how for this reason he had lost his son with the vessel at sea; and how the saint had refused to accept this offering. Therefore, as everyone resounded praises to God and Saint Nicholas, while the father and mother grieved intensely in tears for their guilt and the loss of their son and multiplied vow upon vow, behold: suddenly the young man flew in, unharmed, with the vessel. To the astonishment of all, he reported that Saint Nicholas had appeared to him in the deep; had caught him as he fell into the sea; had brought him safely to shore; and had guided him to [Col. 1035D] his church. Stupefied, all again and again praised God in all things, who alone performs wonders (Ps. 135). The youth’s father therefore offered the vessel, together with precious gifts, to Saint Nicholas, and returned joyfully to his own home with his family.

A wealthy merchant also lived extravagantly and improvidently; his carelessness brought him to utter poverty. He asked a Jew to lend him money. The Jew told him that, if he provided security, he would lend the money requested. The man replied that he had no security, unless perhaps the Jew were willing to accept Nicholas as guarantor. The Jew said: “I hear that Nicholas is trustworthy; I accept him as guarantor.” He therefore gave [Col. 1036A] gold to the Christian man, retaining Nicholas as security.

After the man had prospered in wealth, the Jew demanded back the money lent. The man asked for delay, and the Jew granted it, waiting three times nevertheless. Then, when the money was again demanded, the man denied it and swore that he had repaid it. The matter was brought before judges, and it was decreed by law that he should either repay the money immediately or deny the matter under oath. The Christian therefore cunningly enclosed the gold received within a staff and handed it to the Jew to carry. With him and a great crowd of people, he went to the church of Saint Nicholas (fol. 278), intending to swear.

On arriving, he swore upon the altar that he had repaid the gold which he had received as a loan and had placed as security. Then the Jew said: “I trust that Nicholas will avenge me.” The Christian received the staff from the Jew and returned happily home with his people. But he was soon punished by divine vengeance because he gloried in injuring his neighbour. On the road, a great drowsiness overcame him, so that he thought he would breathe out his soul unless he slept a little. He therefore lay down to sleep at a crossroads, placing the staff beside him.

And behold, a laden cart came along, unable to turn aside in either direction. Since the ox-drivers could not rouse the snoring man either by shouting or by striking him, they drove over the man oppressed by deathly sleep with the vehicle, and, knocking out his soul, crushed the deceiver. When they saw the gold gleaming from the broken staff, the matter became clear to everyone—the offence for which he had died by God’s judgment. As people gathered from every side, the gold was returned to the Jew, who entered the church with [Col. 1036C] the people and resounded praises to God and Saint Nicholas. Then he bound himself by a vow: if life were restored to his adversary, he himself would immediately be washed in baptism.

O mercy of Jesus Christ! O merits of Saint Nicholas! While they sang praises, the man, broken unto death in every limb, entered alive and confessed his offence before all. At this sight the Jew, with his entire household, joined our faith; and Christ the Lord and his faithful servant Nicholas were praised by all with loud voices.

Likewise, a certain pagan tax collector possessed a little image of Saint Nicholas, to whom, when setting out one day, he entrusted his money. At night thieves came and carried off all the man’s money. [Col. 1036D] When he returned and found his money taken, he filled the house with loud wailing. Then, taking up a whip, he beat the image and demanded back his money from it. Meanwhile, as the thieves divided the plunder, Saint Nicholas appeared to them and compelled them, with threats and terrors, to bring everything back that night. The tax collector rose in the morning and, seeing his money, was filled with joy; embracing and kissing the image. Saint Nicholas appeared to him and warned him concerning the salvation of his soul. He was immediately baptized with all his household and, having built a church in honour of Saint Nicholas, served Christ the Lord in praise.

While the body of this eminent bishop was being translated from Myra to Bari—[Note: [Col. 1035D] *Uarim*, “to Bari”]—it was glorified through many glorious (fol. [Col. 1037A] 278v) miracles. Indeed, within one week, one hundred and eleven persons—blind, deaf, mute, lame, withered, possessed, and afflicted with other illnesses—were restored to health through his merits. Since God so magnified him among human beings and exalted him among the saints, let us, most dear brethren, invoke him with praises and entreat him with prayers, lest God destroy our soul with the impious and our life with bloodthirsty men; but rather that we may hear the voice of praise with the saints and be able to declare all the Lord’s wonders. What eye—

## SUNDAY. SAINT LUCY.

[Col. 1037]

“The favour of princes is deceitful, and women’s beauty is vain” (Prov. 31). Saint Lucy despised the deceitful favour of human beings and scorned the vain beauty of worldly things; therefore she deserved to possess Christ, true favour and eternal beauty. And because [Col. 1037B] she feared God, she shall be praised by angels and saints and enriched from the fruit of her hands at the gates of life.

Her mother suffered from an incurable flow of blood; therefore she went with her daughter to the tomb of Saint Agatha the martyr. As Lucy fell asleep in prayer, Saint Agatha appeared to her in a shining robe, called her sister, and asked why she requested from her what Lucy herself would soon be able to grant, especially since she had prepared a worthy dwelling for Christ in her virginity. On waking, Lucy found her mother healed. She asked her never again to mention a husband to her, and, when they had returned home, began to distribute all her property to the needy. Her betrothed therefore seized her and presented her to the judge Paschasius, who condemned her to a brothel.

Accordingly, though dragged by pimps, she could not be moved; though pushed by soldiers, [Col. 1037C] she stood firm like an immovable column. Ropes were put round her feet and [or: “and” for *vel*, “or”] hands, [Col. 1038A] and many pairs of oxen were harnessed to drag and drive her; but by the weight of the Holy Spirit abiding in her she stood fixed like an immovable mountain. Then, surrounded by flames, she was unharmed; finally a sword was plunged into her throat. Since she had now beheld true peace, [Col. 1038B] she foretold peace for the Church: Diocletian the persecutor would be expelled from power, and Maximian the tyrant slain. Meanwhile Paschasius was led in chains to Rome before her eyes and was beheaded by sentence of the senate. The bride of Christ, washed in the bath of her blood, was joined to the radiant virgins, clothed in the robe of glory.

With her the blessed virgin Odilia today sings the songs of the Lamb (fol. 280). Born blind, she was condemned to exile by her father, but baptized and enlightened by Erhard, bishop of Regensburg. Distinguished by many virtues, the virgin herself was set over virgins. Adorned by divine power with very many signs, she is today joined in the heavens, by a glorious end, to the chaste. Send these, most dear brethren, to the author of chastity, that, stripped of the stain of filth [or *sordium*, “of impurities”], you may deserve to live with them in eternal [Col. 1038C] joy. “What eye has not seen” (1 Cor. 2).

Add this concerning Saint Thomas on Sunday:

[Col. 1037]

Since the Nativity of the Lord draws near to us, let us today implore the help of Saint Thomas the apostle, so that we may receive Christ into the dwelling-places of our sinful heart in such a way that we may in turn one day be received by him into the eternal tabernacles. He touched the side of the risen Lord and testified to us, in the true faith, that he had risen. In India he spread the word of God and, by signs and miracles, assigned the people to the kingdom of God. Having received from a king an unlimited sum of money to build a palace, he distributed it among crowds of needy persons. Therefore the king seized him and shut him in prison; [Col. 1038C] but meanwhile the king’s brother died. By God’s ordering he returned to life and reported to his brother that Thomas had built an inestimable palace in heaven.

The king, together with his brother and all his people, was baptized by Thomas. The apostle himself, preaching Christ, was pierced by the spear of the pontiff of idols and so, crowned with victory, was joined to the assembly of life. Let us, most dear brethren, entreat this judge of the world, that at the coming of the eternal Judge we may be saved; so that we, who believe what we have not seen, may through his merits be blessed in the heavenly palace, where eye—

## FIRST SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 1037]

[Col. 1037D] “Many say: Who will show us good things?” (Ps. 4). Truly, most dear brethren, many desire to hear the word of God, but alas, those who speak it are few. Indeed, more grievous still, most of those who do not wish or do not know how to utter the word of life persecute in hatred those who speak or do good things. These people so abhor the truth of Christ that they disdain even to hear it spoken of; and because the word of life torments them, Christ, the Word of God, separates them from his kingdom as far as darkness is from light. And since they are excluded from the kingdom of God, it is necessary in every way that these envious persons be enclosed in the Tartarean prison with the devil, author of envy (fol. 280v).

If there were no Scripture except today’s Gospel, it would suffice believers as an example of life. For the Lord relates that a certain man abounded in great riches, daily held splendid banquets, and denied the crumb falling from his table to poor Lazarus, who was moreover covered with sores. When he died, he was consigned to hell; Lazarus, however, was placed in Abraham’s bosom. Therefore, [Col. 1039A] when the rich man saw himself cruelly tormented in flames and Lazarus rejoicing in Abraham’s embrace, he begged Abraham with loud wailing to send Lazarus to let fall the smallest drop of water from his finger and cool his burning tongue. But because here he had denied a crumb of bread to the beggar, there he himself, as a beggar, did not deserve a drop of water. After he despaired for himself, he begged for the salvation of his brothers. Abraham told him that they had the writings of Moses and the prophets, and declared that, if they did not believe them, they would not believe even the dead, should they go to them (Luke 16).

This man is indicated to have been a king, since he is described as clothed in purple, for formerly only kings wore purple. But since a king is so called from ruling, and this man, a slave of sin, was subject to vices, he is called not a king but a man, because he served only gluttony [OCR: *vociferati* for *voracitati*, “greediness”] [Col. 1039B] and lust, like an irrational animal. His name is not expressed because he is not written with the righteous in the book of the living. Poor Lazarus, however, is named because his name was found written in heaven. The rich man is read to have been buried in hell because hell is said to be under the earth; and whoever is plunged there is covered by earth, just as a body is covered by dust when buried in a tomb.

There are said to be two hells, a lower and an upper. The lower is where the souls of the reprobate were tormented; the upper is where the elect awaited Christ. Of the lower it is written: “You have rescued my soul from the lowest hell” (Ps. 85); but of the upper: “Bring my soul out of hell, that it may confess your name” (Ps. 29). In the lower hell, however, nine particular punishments are said to exist: unquenchable fire; incomparable horror of cold; immortal worms; intolerable stench; striking hammers; tangible darkness; the shame of sins; the sight of demons; the hearing of mockers; and fiery bonds for each limb. The upper hell was the lowest part of the earth, a place neighbouring hell but separated from its punishments. The righteous there could be seen by the wicked who were in the lower hell.

Some doubt whether souls recognize one another in the other life. But since the rich man recognized Abraham, [Col. 1039D] whom he had never previously seen, it is clear that the wicked recognize the good there. Since Abraham recognized the rich man there, whom he had never previously seen, it is plain that the good also recognize the wicked there. Again, it is asked whether the souls of the righteous understand anything concerning the living, or the souls of the wicked perceive anything about the living. Since Abraham says, “You received good things in your life and Lazarus evil things,” it is clear that good people observe the deeds of the living, especially since they immediately assist those who call upon them. Since the rich man prays for his brothers who are living wickedly, it is evident that the damned know some things—but not all things—about the living.

Before the judgment, the reprobate behold the elect in joy, so that they may grieve more deeply that they neglected to attain it; the elect also behold the reprobate in punishment, so that they may rejoice more fully that, aided by God’s grace, they escaped it. After the judgment, however, the good will always see the wicked, but the wicked will never see the good. Observe that the man who was burned by fire in every limb specifically asks that his tongue be cooled. This indicates that each person will suffer greater torments in the member with which he made greater use of sin. Since this man here was devoted to gluttony and continually served talkativeness, he is justly said to suffer more in the tongue which he had always loosened for empty speech.

And it should be observed that no one reads that he took anything from another, but only that he did not give what was his own. If this man, brothers, who did not give away what was his own suffers so great a punishment, what should be thought of those who are always ready to seize what belongs to others? Scripture says of idle eaters, “The furrows will cry out against them”; but of thieves and plunderers, “The earth will be turned for them into burning pitch and sulphur.” This rich man did some good for human praise and received the good recompense for it here in temporal goods; Lazarus, however, had committed certain evils, which he here paid for by bodily pain. Consider, I ask you, most dear brethren, how strict God’s judgments are (fol. 282v). Behold, he asks for a drop of water who gave no crumbs of bread; and because he denied crumbs, he did not obtain a drop (Luke 16).

Therefore, my lords, you to whom God has granted the riches of this age, beware lest riches possess you as slaves [Col. 1040C] and drag you, empty of true riches, to Tartarus. Possess your riches by distributing them to the needy, and acquire true riches by means of these deceptive ones. It is not evil to have riches, but it is very grave to turn them to evil use. David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, kings for example, and others like them, possessed many riches but acquired unfailing riches for themselves through them. Cyrus, Antiochus, and Croesus, and others like them, were men of wealth because they turned their riches to pride and luxury. Since they had their kingdom of heaven here, at death they found nothing in their hands, but will grieve with that rich man in eternal poverty. Of such persons it is said: “It is easier for a camel to pass through a needle’s eye than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 1040D] (Matt. 19).

The Lord relates that a certain man had acquired very great riches; he demolished his barns and built larger ones, gathered all his goods there, and told his soul to feast and rejoice, because he would live many years and pass happy days amid these possessions. That same night the wretch died, left his riches to strangers, and entered Tartarus carrying only his sins with him. What good were riches to one who neglected to acquire eternal riches through them?

Human beings are divided into four classes: certain rich people, such as Abraham and Job, are saved; certain rich people, such as Cheneres, Pharaoh, and Nebuchadnezzar, are damned; certain poor people, such as Lazarus and monks, [Col. 1041A] are saved; while others, such as Judas and other deceivers, are consigned to eternal miseries.

The rich man, clothed in purple and fine linen, also represents the Jewish people, who gloried in the kingdom and priesthood of the Law. Royal power is denoted by purple, priesthood by fine linen. He feasted splendidly every day when, in external observance, he was fed from the dishes of the Law and prophets. The poor man, however, prefigures the gentile people, wounded with the sores of sins. He did not receive crumbs falling from the table, because he did not hear even the smallest teaching from Holy Scripture. The dogs that came and licked his sores were the apostles, God’s dogs: they thoroughly instructed him in God’s law and closed the sores of sins with the medicine of repentance.

This man dies and is carried [Col. 1041B] into Abraham’s bosom; the rich man is buried in hell (fol. 284), because many believers will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But the children of the kingdom—that is, the faithless Jews—will be cast into outer darkness because they did not believe Moses, the prophets, or Christ risen from the dead. Even now the wars of kings and their victories are read, so that through them we may be instructed to conquer sins and become victors over vices.

It is read that a certain man had two wives, one fertile and the other barren, and that at last the barren woman bore Samuel (1 Sam. 1, etc.). He deprived Eli of the priesthood, removed Saul from the kingdom, and, anointing David with oil, exalted him to the sceptre. David struck down mighty Goliath with sling and stone and cut off his head with his own sword. He laboured through many battles and, after conquering his enemies, prepared a distinguished tabernacle for the Lord; his son Solomon established the temple, famous throughout the whole world, and peace for all nations.

The man who joined two wives to himself is God, who betrothed the Synagogue and the Church to himself. Of these the Synagogue was fertile because she bore the Jewish people to carnal ceremonies. But the Church, long barren, bore a faithful son—the Christian people—to particular observances. He rejected Eli from the priesthood and Saul from the kingdom [as printed: plural *repudiaverunt*], because he excludes the unbelieving Jewish people from Christ’s priesthood and the gentile people who persecute the faithful from the kingdom of God. But [it] worships the true David—that is, the desirable Christ—as King of all, anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above all his companions.

[Col. 1041D] This David cast down mighty Goliath with a sling when he shattered the mighty devil by his humanity. The sling was Christ’s humanity, encircled and whirled about by sufferings. The stone that penetrated Goliath’s forehead was the divinity that pierced Leviathan’s jaw. Moreover, he cut off his head with the sword when, by converting kings and philosophers—indeed, the devil’s weapons—to the faith, he weakened the devil’s powers and drove out idolatry. This David waged many wars when he instructed his soldiers, the apostles and martyrs, to combat Jews, pagans, and heretics. Having cast down the enemies, he made a tabernacle for God.

In this king’s warfare, most dear brethren, let us fight against vices with the weapons of virtues, so that, crowned with the reward of life, we may triumph in the heavenly [Col. 1042A] kingdom. “For the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7), “and his days are like those of a hired labourer.” A soldier serves for a benefice; a hired labourer works for an annual wage. Thus, most dear brethren, let us serve as soldiers for the benefice of the eternal King and labour hard for the reward of everlasting life (fol. 284v).

David prefigured Christ living here among human beings and fighting against enemies for his bride [OCR: *sponso*, “bridegroom,” for *sponsa*, “bride”], the Church. Solomon represented him now reigning in the Father’s glory and triumphing with the saints in perpetual peace. Therefore, after the enemies have been defeated as by David, he will, like Solomon who built the temple, at the last judgment—when the Church’s enemies have been condemned—gather together angels and human beings to build from them the heavenly Jerusalem as a city.

[Col. 1042B] There is a bird called the partridge which broods over eggs stolen from another bird; after the chicks emerge, they return to their mother when they hear her voice. God the Father placed the first two human beings, as two eggs, in the nest of paradise. The partridge, the devil, destroyer of souls, brooded over them after stealing them, when he taught them every wickedness after seducing them away from God. They came forth from the shell and returned to their mother when, stripping off the garment of sin [OCR: *excientes* for *exuentes*], they returned to their mother, namely God’s Wisdom, Christ.

The deeds and sayings of the saints, most dear brethren, have been set down for us as an example. The acts of Saint Paulinus teach us the return to the homeland of paradise. While this venerable bishop was feeding the flock entrusted to him with vigilant care, it happened that an army of pagans [Col. 1042C] invaded the region and carried the people away captive. When the man of God had given everything he could find in his episcopal residence for redeeming captives, a certain widow asked him for the price by which her son might be redeemed. Having nothing else, he gave himself into service for the boy, and the widow received her son.

His master, namely the king’s son-in-law, made him a gardener, often conversed with him, and recognized him as a wise man. Paulinus foretold to him that the king would soon die and that he himself would reign in his father-in-law’s place. In the night the king saw in a dream that Paulinus and others judged him and deprived him of life and kingdom. On the next day he told his son-in-law of the vision, summoned Paulinus, and asked who he had been in his own land. [Col. 1042D] When he learned that Paulinus was a bishop, he offered to give him whatever he wished to ask in compensation for the wrong done him. Paulinus asked that all captives from his bishopric be released, and he immediately obtained this. For, as soon as a royal command was sent out, all the captives were brought in from every region.

Paulinus entered ships with all his people, laden with every good thing, and was carried back to his homeland with great honour and joy. He imitated the example of the good shepherd, who gave himself into service for the captive and brought the captive people back with him to the palace of the heavenly homeland. You ought, most dear brethren, to imitate him (fol. 286) and entreat him and all God’s elect, so that, when the way of the impious perishes, the Lord may know you [as printed: *vos Dominus agnoscant*] in the way of the righteous, where eye has not seen (1 Cor. 2).

## SECOND SUNDAY.

[Col. 1043]

[Col. 1043A] “Blessed are those called to the wedding supper of the Lamb” (Rev. 19). The Gospel relates, most dear brethren, that a certain man made a great supper and invited many. When everything had been prepared, he sent his servants to call those invited, and all began to excuse themselves. One said that he had bought an estate; another, that he had purchased five yoke of oxen; another, that he had married a wife and therefore could not come. Hearing this, the master ordered his servant to go out into the streets and lanes and bring in the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame. Since there was still room, he ordered the servant to compel people from the roads and hedges to enter, swearing that none of those invited should taste his supper (Luke 14).

The man who prepared a great supper and called many is God, who became man for us and invited all nations to the feast of the eternal banquet. He sent his servant to call people to the [Col. 1043B] banquet when he sent Moses through the Law to invite the people to life; but all excuse themselves from the supper, because the Jews indeed refuse to enter God’s banquet. The first said that he had bought an estate and would go out to see it. The Jewish people bought an estate, as it were, when it obtained the promised land through carnal observances. It went out to see it when it came out of Egypt to possess it.

He also bought yokes of oxen when he received the two sets of five commandments joined by the double love, with which he ought to cultivate the Lord’s field like oxen; but he went to test them when he endeavoured to observe them only for earthly things. He also married a wife because he joined the Law to a carnal understanding and therefore withdrew himself from God’s banquet. By the man who bought the estate is also understood the order of Jewish rulers, who divided the land among the people [Col. 1043C] and afterward occupied its fortifications. By the man who bought five yokes of oxen is denoted the subject people, bound in subjection by the yoke of the Law. By the man who married a wife is signified the Levitical order, to which the Law is joined particularly as a wife. Since each of these labours over earthly business, they excuse themselves from God’s banquet.

Therefore the master of the household orders his servant to go out into the streets and lanes of the city and bring in the poor and weak. The servant now sent is understood as the order of prophets. The city signifies Jerusalem, where the Ark of the Covenant was venerated and where stood the temple in which sacrifices were offered by all. Its streets were the Israelites (fol. 286v), who had spread themselves abroad into the expanse of the twelve tribes; its lanes were the Jews, who had confined themselves within the narrowness of two tribes. Thus the prophets brought people in from the streets and lanes when, by writings and words, they corrected Israelites and Jews from error.

These were poor because they lacked virtues; weak because they languished in vices; blind because they did not see the meaning of the Law; and lame because, abandoning the worship of God, they had turned aside after idols. Though these had been brought in, there was still room, and the master ordered the servant to go out into roads and hedges and compelled people to enter. The servant who compels [or, as printed, “is compelled”] people from roads and hedges to enter is the order of apostles, who gathered many from the sects and rites of the gentiles into God’s house. Roads [Col. 1044A] are the various sects of philosophers; hedges, the various rites of pagans. They entered under compulsion when the gentiles, rejecting idolatry through the signs and wonders of the apostles, believed in the true God.

The proconsul Paul entered under compulsion when Paul the apostle blinded the magician before him. Constantine entered under compulsion when Sylvester healed him of leprosy in baptism. Thus the gentiles who were brought in will dine with the Lord, but the Jews who refused to enter will not taste the Lord’s supper.

And you, dearest beloved, are called to the banquet of God. See that, entangled in any business or hindered by anyone’s friendship, you are not excused from it. For we are servants of the supreme householder, sent by him; we invite you to the feast of eternal fullness. Therefore hasten, all of you, to enter the wedding-feast of the Lamb before the door is shut, and thereafter is never opened to those entering or desiring to enter.

The Lord says: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you; and if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter into life one-eyed, weak, or lame, than, having two eyes or two hands or two feet, to be cast into Gehenna, where the fire is not quenched and their worms do not die” (Mark 9). It should be noted that the Saviour sets forth three things—namely, eye, hand, and foot—through which wretched persons are drawn back from God’s banquet; for either prelates, relatives, or dependants delay us from the Lord’s supper, and these limbs signify them.

The eye which leads us is the priest who directs us from the darkness of the world to the light of life. [Col. 1044C] He is therefore called the right eye because he strives to lead us from the left hand to the right. If he attempts by heretical teaching to draw us away from God’s way and lead us into [folio 288] error, or to withdraw us from God’s banquet by a depraved example, he must be removed from his entrusted office as a useless limb and utterly cast out from our friendship.

The right hand through which we work is father or mother, wife, or any dearest friend, by whom we are aided in all things. If these in any way call us back from the banquet, let zeal for God cut them off from us and cast them far from our diligent concern. The foot by which we are carried is any dependant through whom we are sustained in life’s necessities. If this person in any way hinders us from God’s banquet, he must be plucked away from us and excluded far from our intimacy. For it is much better for us to be saved without them than to be assigned with them to everlasting fire. For whoever is a friend of such persons is made an enemy of God (James 4); and whoever pleases these people is rejected by God in confusion.

He who buys a farm is the person who serves only earthly gain and therefore withdraws from God’s banquet. He, however, who buys five yoke of oxen and goes away to test them is the person who turns the five bodily senses, yoked in pairs, to investigating others’ actions and turns aside from God’s banquet. Hence we read that Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, went out to see the women of that land and was violated by Shechem, prince of the land (Gen. 34).

I ask your brotherhood to consider how grave a vice curiosity is. [Col. 1045A] Behold: while the daughter of the highest patriarch pursues curiosity, she is defiled by a pagan man; the city, with all its people, is destroyed by sword and flame. Dinah, indeed, is violated when any soul, curiously examining the actions of others, is joined to the devil. The city with its people will be ravaged by fire, because the body of the curious person, together with its evil deeds, will be tortured in eternal fire.

But he who takes a wife is the person who studies only to satisfy the burning of lust; and because he defiles the wedding garment, he does not approach the Lord’s banquet at all. Because these are excused from God’s feast, the poor and weak are called from the streets and lanes. Streets are broad public ways, and signify crimes committed openly through power; lanes are narrow paths, and signify those secretly devoted to wicked deeds. The poor are those who know themselves empty of good works; the weak are those who see that they have languished in the Lord’s commandments; the blind are those who have closed the eyes of their heart to the light of truth; the lame are those who have not walked in the Lord’s ways.

Yet all these, called to God’s banquet, come when, corrected by the teaching of the righteous, they approach through repentance the feast of eternal sweetness. Moreover, very many are compelled to enter from roads and hedges (folio 288 verso), when, driven by the very hardships of the world, they are converted from various errors to piety. Let all these feast in God’s sight and delight in joy (Psalm 67), because there is greater joy among God’s angels over one sinner doing repentance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance (Luke 15).

To this feast, most beloved, let us all run with voluntary willingness and with all our strength, [Col. 1045C] where we shall never hunger or thirst, but rejoice eternally with the angels. And, that we may hasten there without stumbling, let us consider the path of Alexius who goes before us.

## On Saint Alexius

Born of most noble parents, he was joined to a high-born and beautiful bride. Leaving her in bed on the first night, he went abroad; he distributed among the needy the money he had brought with him, and himself lived for many years among the poor. Among them he was found by his father’s servants, who sought him everywhere, but he was not recognized at all. From them he received alms and gave thanks to God.

But because God’s light could not remain hidden in darkness, he became known to people through the words of a certain image. Avoiding human glory, he took flight by ship; but the ship, driven by the wind, put in at the Roman [Col. 1045D] harbour. He entered his father’s house and was recognized by no one. There again he lay hidden as a poor man for many years, conspicuous in the splendor of his great goodness.

For he cheerfully endured seeing his parents flourish in power and wealth, their dependants prosper in various adornment, while the heir was squalid in extreme poverty, mocked by his own servants, and disgraced by many injuries. [Col. 1046A] He bore mournfully and patiently his father’s grief, his mother’s sorrow, the sighs of his sweet bride, and the tearful laments of the grieving household for him. He gave the alms he received to the poor; after prolonged fasts he restored his body with scanty food; and in this manner he struggled for thirty-four years.

When, however, it pleased the gracious Lord to reward this endurance a hundredfold and raise him from misery to the feast of joy, he made his merit known to all, so that he might raise the minds of the faithful to heavenly things. For while the clergy were celebrating Masses, a voice sent from heaven resounded, commanding that the man be sought through whose intercessions the Roman Empire might prosper.

But he, as an inward pain foretold that his final day was at hand, wrote all his deeds on a sheet, which, clasping in his hand, he was brought forth from the prison of the body. And, as an angelic melody sounded, he was joyfully led into God’s banquet [Col. 1046B] (folio 290).

The pope, together with the emperor and all the people, came to the house of Euphemianus, that is, his father, and found the dead man’s face shining like an angel’s. His father wished to take up the sheet, but could not. All were astonished; they poured out praises and prayers to God. The Apostolic one—the pope—approached, took the sheet, and handed it over to be read. Euphemianus, hearing the text of the sheet, trembled with overwhelming grief and fell upon his son’s body with loud lamentation. His mother came running, tearing her garment and wailing; with a mournful voice she poured forth a flood of tears.

Moreover, the noble bride, worthy of much praise, broke her mirror and lamented her bridegroom piteously. She declared that she would imitate the turtledove, which, when it has lost its mate, chooses no other. [Col. 1046C]

Meanwhile the body was glorified by signs, while its spirit rejoiced among the angels. For the blind received sight, and demons were driven from possessed bodies. The people therefore rushed together, desiring to touch the dead body. All who touched it were healed of every sickness. Thus all raised hands and voices to the stars, glorifying God who works wonders. At last, with great labour because of the crowd, the body was brought to the church; it remained unburied for seven days amid hymns and praises. Crowds of people gathered from every direction, desiring to touch the holy body, from which they drew a wondrous fragrance of most sweet odour; and, their adverse sickness driven away, all rejoiced in the health they had received.

At last, with magnificent honour, the material of the flesh [Col. 1046D] was committed to the earth, while the soul, exulting in heaven, aids all who call upon it. Let us ask this saint, most beloved, together with all the saints, that we may be able to be God’s guests; and when his wrath has quickly kindled against those whom he will trouble in his fury, may the salvation of the Lord receive us, and may his blessing come upon his people—that blessing which eye has not seen (1 Cor. 2).

Speak the sermon, “Come, children,” although it belongs to the Lord’s Day; and if one concerning saints occurs, add the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost:

[Col. 1045]

[Col. 1045D] “Master, though we laboured all night, we caught nothing; yet at your word I will let down the net” (Luke 5). Saint Peter, labouring all night at fishing, caught nothing; but, letting down the net at the Lord’s word, he enclosed a multitude [Col. 1046D] of fish. So too, when we preach to those darkened by vices and sins, we labour fruitlessly as though in the night. And therefore we catch nothing, but pour forth words in vain, because assuredly the word of God does not—[supplied: *non*, “not”]—take hold in one who savours only earthly things. Yet, letting down [Latin *laxans*; variant *laxamus*, “we let down”] the net at this word of the Lord, we administer the word of life to a people hungry for righteousness. Then we enclose a multitude of fish, because, having caught very many in the net of preaching, we lead them from the deep of sins to the shore of repentance.

Therefore Scripture says: “Speak a word of gold to one who listens”; for the speaker’s voice resounds vainly where the hearer’s mind is turned away.

The Gospel relates that a great crowd remained with the Lord for three days, that they lacked food, and that some of them had come from far away. Therefore the Lord, moved with compassion, said that if he dismissed them fasting they would faint on the way. So he divided seven loaves and a few little fishes among them and dismissed them fully satisfied. There were four thousand who had eaten, and the disciples took up seven baskets [Col. 1047B] of fragments (Mark 8).

The crowd which remains with the Lord for three days is the people of the faithful, who retain the seal of faith in the three Persons. This people lacks food when it lacks God’s word. For as the body is fed by bread, so the soul is refreshed by God’s word. Those who came from afar are those who will return to the Lord after many wicked acts; for those come from near who live in holiness from childhood. Those coming from afar are refreshed lest they fail on the way, because penitents are fed with the consolation of Holy Scripture lest they despair.

The crowd reclines upon the ground because the people of the faithful regard themselves as dust. The Lord refreshes them with seven loaves when he distributes to them the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. He satisfies them with one loaf when, by the spirit of patience, he enlightens their heart to savour divine things. [Col. 1047C] He satisfies them with another loaf when, by the spirit of understanding, he opens to them the mysteries of Scripture. He refreshes them with the third loaf when, by the spirit of counsel, he grants them to choose what is useful and reject what is harmful. He fills them with the fourth loaf when, by the spirit of fortitude, he strengthens them in good things. He revives them with the fifth loaf when he enlightens them by the spirit of wisdom. He restores them with the sixth loaf when, by the spirit of piety, he instructs them to pursue righteousness. He strengthens their heart with the seventh loaf when, by the spirit of fear, he calls them away from evil.

A few little fishes are added when examples of the faithful are set before them. Four thousand are satisfied because the four regions of the world are called through the three Gospels—“three” is presumably an error in the text—to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Seven baskets of fragments remain over because the seven books of hagiography overflow with the seven [Col. 1047D] gifts of the Holy Spirit; from these, teachers still serve refreshment to the faithful, as though from baskets.

The crowd is also fed with fish when it feeds on Christ’s body. For he is called a fish, as the Gospel relates: when men demanded the tax from him, to whom (folio 292) the angels render devout service, he commanded Peter to cast a hook into the sea and, from the mouth of the first fish that came up, take a gold didrachm and pay the tax for him and for himself. This fish was Christ, who lay hidden in the waves of this world. He had a drachm in his mouth because he brought forth the twofold Law shining in divine deeds. He was caught by the hook of divine counsel and roasted for us as food in the fire of the Passion. The didrachm is paid as tax for Christ and Peter when the faithful fulfil both the Law and the twofold love [Col. 1048A] for the honour of Christ and the Church.

The people of God are refreshed with seven loaves and instructed by the ten commandments; but Pharaoh’s people are held captive by the dragon’s seven heads and devastated by the ten plagues (Exod. 7–12).

The first plague is water changed into blood: water is changed into blood when baptism or Holy Scripture is reckoned as sin to those who defile baptism through works of impurity and pervert Holy Scripture to uphold their own errors.

The second plague covered the earth with frogs: the talkativeness of frogs is the babbling of poets, by whose fables wretches are deceived when they follow them in their desires.

The third plague was gnats piercing bodies with fiery stings: these are heretics who ensnare simple persons with harmful arguments, [Col. 1048B] piercing their minds with faithlessness and leading them to the goads of eternal fire.

The fourth plague was the affliction of flies: these are those importunate in worldly eloquence, who tear one another’s flesh through greed and assail others inappropriately with cunning words in order to take away their goods.

The fifth plague is pestilence killing animals: this is foul lust, which kills those living irrationally, or exposes those decayed in shamefulness for demons, like dogs, to tear apart.

The sixth plague produces burning blisters and ulcers: ulcers are the deceits of malicious persons; blisters, the puffings-up of the proud. These torment the wicked and, corrupting them in character, disfigure them as with a plague.

The seventh plague is hail, fire, and thunder: thunder is the terror caused by rulers; hail and fire are the cruelty [Col. 1048C] of robbers. These destroy the impious when they violently scatter them along with their possessions.

The eighth plague is caterpillar and locust: caterpillars are the ravenous; locusts are the discordant, leaping after pleasures. By devouring and gnawing away the blossoms of trees and crops, they signify that such persons corrupt good desires through evil examples and wicked conversation.

The ninth plague was tangible darkness and a certain dreadful murmur: these are unbelievers (folio 292 verso) who do not believe future things, draw others back from the light, and consign themselves to the darkness of eternal death, where there is a terrible murmur—namely, weeping and gnashing of teeth.

The tenth plague is the death of the firstborn: Egypt’s firstborn are worldly rulers and secular dignities, whom demons destroy by wars [Col. 1048D] and various means, so that the powerful suffer powerful torments.

Most beloved, let us strive by good deeds to be freed from these ten plagues, filled with the seven loaves, rescued from the dragon’s seven heads, and instructed by the ten commandments of the Law. Let us imitate those who have gone before us and entered the joys of life through many tribulations.

## On Saint Euphrosyne

Let us follow tender maidens as those who lead us toward life. Let us direct our steps through Euphrosyne’s footprints, which lead us to the courts of life. Her most illustrious Alexandrian parents, by many alms and prayers, begged God for an heir to their immense estate. He gave them a daughter, whom, when they baptized her at seven years of age, they named Euphrosyne. Her mother passed from this life, but her father, when she was already twelve, betrothed her to an eminent man.

When she was about to be given in marriage, her father brought her into a certain monastery to receive the abbot’s blessing. Blessing her, he exhorted her to chastity. Considering the manner of life of the monks, she called blessed those who here were imitators of angels and thereafter would be their companions. Returning home, she laid aside female clothing, put on male dress, and came to the monastery, saying that she was a eunuch named Smaragdus and asking to be made a monk. Received among the men, she lived many years in every holiness.

At last her father returned and, not finding his daughter, sought her with servants and friends through all monasteries and every place in all Alexandria and all Egypt. Not finding her, he mourned inconsolably. Afterwards he came to that same monastery and gave much money to the brothers, begging them to pray to God that something about his daughter might be revealed to him. They continued vigils and fasts, praying for a week and gaining nothing; and though there were three hundred and fifty, Euphrosyne’s prayer surpassed the prayers of all, as she prayed day and night that she might not be revealed in this life.

The abbot, however, consoled Paphnutius and ordered him to be led to Smaragdus, for Smaragdus lived in a solitary cell and his whole manner of life was in heaven. Seeing her father and fearing recognition, she dissolved into tears, but was not recognized at all. Her imperial countenance had withered from many vigils, and her great beauty (folio 294) had faded through weeping and fasting. He departed from her consoled; [Col. 1050A] at her encouragement he performed many acts of almsgiving.

Smaragdus, having completed thirty-nine years in holy observance, felt that the end of life was near. She summoned her father, who was then present, begged him no longer to be anxious about his daughter, revealed that she was his daughter, and asked that no one should know this; she asked him to give his possessions to the monastery and pour forth prayers for her. Having said this, she put her eyes to sleep and closed them in death; led by angels, she departed to inaccessible light. Her father fell half-dead to the ground.

When he recovered, he fell upon the body with loud lamentation and gave vent to grief in cries and tears. Hearing this, all the brothers ran together; seeing the wonders, they burst forth in God’s praise. As they kissed the holy body, a brother who had had only one eye rejoiced at receiving the other. Again and again they proclaimed her great deeds—she who, even in the weaker sex, performed such great miracles.

The body was buried in the tomb of the fathers; its soul, tested like gold in fire and proved in the furnace of tribulation, rejoiced among the radiant virgins. Her father committed himself, together with all his property, to the monastery. Becoming a monk and ending his life in holy observance, he went up to heaven to see his daughter in glory.

Most beloved, let us implore the merit of this Virgin and the intercessions of all the saints: that God may not deliver us up together with sinners nor destroy us with those who work iniquity, but may bless us with his inheritance and exalt us for ever—where eye has not seen.

## Tenth Sunday

[Col. 1049]

[Col. 1049C] “The ways of Zion mourn because there are none who come to the solemn feast” (Lam. 1). Zion, which means “watchtower,” is the Church, which shall behold the King of glory in his beauty. Its ways are understood as the lives and teachings of the saints, through whom the faithful are led to the walls of the heavenly city. These ways mourn that few come to the feast, because the righteous grievously lament that few attend the celebration of the Lord’s sacrament. For whoever separates himself here from the Church’s feast will certainly be excluded in the future from the angels’ feast.

Hence we read today that the Lord, seeing the city of Jerusalem, wept over it and foretold that it would be besieged by enemies, surrounded by earthworks, and destroyed with all its children. This city, over which God weeps, is any soul that does not mourn its sins. [Col. 1049D] Enemies will surround it when, at approaching death, bands of demons besiege it. They dig a rampart around it when, bringing its past evils before its eyes, they lead it into the pit of despair. They press it in on every side when, by horrifying appearance and gesture, they compel it to go out to punishments. They cast it down to earth when they kill the body by death. They slaughter its children when, carrying it off to Tartarus, they torture it in punishment for evil works. They will leave not one stone upon another (Mark 13), [Col. 1050C] because they will leave no thought of the hard heart unpunished. And all this happens because it does not recognize the time of its visitation (Luke 19). A soul is visited when it is chastised by God together with human beings; but it does not recognize the visitation because it refuses to accept correction.

The Lord drives sellers and buyers out of his temple because he drives from the converted, by the scourge of repentance, persons who sell faults to the devil and purchase punishments. The overthrow of the people of Jerusalem prefigured this; it occurred in the following manner.

Jerusalem’s visitation was Christ’s Incarnation. The Dayspring from on high visited it when he preached the kingdom of heaven in its midst and made it illustrious by signs and miracles. Yet it did not know the time of its visitation [Col. 1050D] when it refused to believe that he, promised by the Law and the Prophets, was God. Moreover, fearing the loss of earthly glory, it crucified the King of glory and therefore lost heavenly glory.

He spread out the wings of the cross and wished to gather them [variant: it] under the shadow of his wings—under the wings of his mercy—as a hen protects her chicks beneath her wings from a kite. But they cast the Lord underfoot, refused to hear him calling, and turned their backs toward the face of him stretching out his hands after them.

Yet God, patient and abundant in mercy, [Col. 1051A] who transplanted a vine from Egypt (Psalm 79) and leased it to husbandmen—whose prophets, sent to them, they insulted, and whose only Son they also cast out of the vineyard and killed—gave them forty-two years for repentance, so that they might obtain pardon for their guilt. But they abused the time of grace for pride and provoked God, continually increasing their sin; therefore God’s wrath rose against them and destroyed them.

For after they had rejected the prophets, wise men, and scribes sent to them; after they had whipped some, stoned some, killed some by diverse punishments, and expelled others from their borders, the God of vengeance remembered to require their blood. Thus upon them came the blood of Christ and of all [Col. 1051B] the righteous whom they had shed from the blood of Abel onward, until they killed Christ’s apostles (Luke 19).

And because they offended Father and Son, the father Vespasian and the son Titus avenged this. The boar from the wood destroyed the vineyard of the supreme householder, which they had turned into the vineyard of Sodom and from which they had drunk the wine of Gomorrah; the solitary wild beast devoured it (Psalm 79). The wood was Gentile heathendom, from which Vespasian, the boar, led forth an army and tested the vineyard—that is, Judaea—by sword and fire. The solitary wild beast was Titus, who consumed Jerusalem by a long siege.

But before the city was overthrown, throughout that whole year a star resembling a sword was seen hanging over it. A heifer brought to sacrifice gave birth to a lamb; for forty successive nights fiery battle-lines were seen in the air; the doors of the Temple opened of themselves at midnight, while a great light shone within. Voices of this kind were heard: “Let us depart from these dwelling-places.”

Therefore, after forty-two years had passed from the Lord’s Passion, Vespasian and Titus, Roman commanders, entering Judaea with a great army, devastated the entire region by fire. The people had gathered at Jerusalem from every city for the Paschal feast; the army besieged them during the Paschal season, just as they had crucified the Lord on the Paschal day.

Accordingly, as the Lord’s words foretold, surrounded by a rampart, with their siege-engines destroyed on every side, they were vigorously assaulted by enemies, yet defended with the utmost force by the inhabitants. But because they did not have the Lord God as the shield of their protection, [Col. 1051D] they fell into the enemy’s hand.

Some were consumed by famine, some by wasting sickness; some were cruelly slaughtered by their own fellow citizens, and some were suffocated by the stench of the dead. For the worst among them went about the city like dogs, snatching food from women’s hands and even from infants’ mouths. They tortured with impious sword citizens lying in the streets and drawing their last breath from hunger; they did not wholly extinguish those who wished to die, but tormented the wretches with wounds. After they had consumed as food asses, horses, and the other animals whose flesh was forbidden there, mothers themselves slaughtered their children to eat them.

Then a great cry arose in the city, and the soldiers abandoned the fortifications; but enemies burst through the walls on every side, violently invaded the city, delivered all things to devouring (folio 296 verso) flame, destroyed all the people by diverse punishments, and razed to their foundations every tower, the Temple itself, and the surrounding wall. Once everything had been overthrown, it is reported that they drew a plough over the place where the city had stood the day before and scattered salt there as seed.

In this siege, it is recorded that eleven hundred thousand died of hunger and an equal number were killed by the sword; the same number were carried away into captivity, and three hundred were crucified in vengeance for the Lord’s death. It is also handed down that thirty of them were sold for one denarius, just as they had betrayed the Lord for thirty denarii. Thus, most beloved, the Lord repaid sevenfold into the bosom of those who [Col. 1052B] had shed the blood of the saints (Psalm 78). Thus the house was left desolate (Luke 13), which they themselves had made a den of robbers (Matt. 21); and thus the Romans took away both their place and their nation (John 11).

Behold, beloved, you have heard of the captivity of the Jews; we must beware of captivity by demons. For this was written for our correction, lest the camps of the evil enemy surround us unawares. Indeed, in order that we might be free from captivity, the Son of the supreme King was given as a pledge for our redemption. And so that this may be firmly impressed upon our memory, Christ’s bread is formed in the likeness of a denarius: for he who was betrayed into the hands of the impious for thirty denarii is surely the true denarius, given as the reward of all the righteous to those who labour in the vineyard until evening.
