[Col. 1052C] This captivity was prefigured, as Holy Scripture relates to us. When Elijah was carried to heaven in a fiery chariot, and Elisha, having divided the Jordan with Elijah’s cloak, was returning to Jericho, he went up from there to Bethel. Boys mocked him, crying, “Go up, baldhead! Go up, baldhead!” (4 Kings 2). When he cursed them, two bears came out of the wood and tore forty-two boys to pieces (ibid.).

Elisha was a figure of Christ. He went up from here to Bethel when he set out from Jerusalem toward the cross. The boys mocked him, crying, “Go up, baldhead!” when the Jews, in childish understanding, mocked the Lord—scourged for us and made bald at the place of Calvary—upon the cross. For among the ancients it was customary for those to be crucified first to be scourged and shaved bald, as may also be noted in [Col. 1052D] Holy Scripture: “The sword,” it says, “shall devour flesh from the blood of the slain and from the captivity of the stripped head of the enemies” (Deut. 32). For captives who were sold were also made bald (folio 298). This appears to be expressed by our tonsure, we who bear the figure of Christ’s *censura* (“enrolment” or “marking”).

> **Note [Col. 1051D]:** So in the text. Perhaps: *censemur*, “we are enrolled/marked.”

But Elisha curses the boys when the curse, “His blood be upon us and upon our children,” is brought upon the Jews. Thus two bears came forth from the wood and tore forty-two boys to pieces when, over forty-two years, two emperors who came forth from the Gentiles cruelly crushed the Jews by force of arms.

Therefore, beloved, let us strive to escape the hands of enemies, escape captivity of the soul, reach our true King, and obtain true freedom. That we may attain this, let us walk in the footprints of the saints. The deeds of Marina alone would suffice for us if other examples were lacking.

Her father said that he wished to save his soul, change his worldly state and dress, and appoint her heir of his possessions. But she said: “Do you wish to save your soul and destroy mine?” When her father asked what pleased her, she said that he should cut her hair, dress her in male clothing, and take her with him to the monastery as his son. Because of her words he gave praise to God; having cut her hair, he took her with him for conversion. Received by the brothers, they became monks and lived a life of complete religious observance.

After some years the father passed to the place of the wonderful tabernacle (Psalm 41), but the daughter became wonderful to all in every exercise of virtue. Her father had said that her name was Marinus; because of her extraordinary religious life, however, she was called Christianus by all. She was very beautiful, pleasing to all through seriousness of character and sweetness of speech. Therefore the father of the monastery sent her with the brothers for the monastery’s benefit.

The envious devil, the twisting dragon, who once wished to make himself equal to God, grieved to see a tender maiden tread upon his scaly neck. He poured the poison of his malice into a woman pleasing to God through a woman obedient to himself; but his slippery head was crushed by her, and she gained the palm of glorious victory.

For a certain man often received travelling brothers as guests. His daughter conceived by a soldier. Her father questioned her when her womb began to swell; [Col. 1053C] but she, at the devil’s prompting, laid the charge upon the monk Christianus. Her father, filled with rage, reported this to the abbot.

When Marinus returned to the cell, the abbot charged her with the crime of fornication. Immediately she threw herself at his feet, confessed that she had erred and had acted as a human being. The abbot inflicted many scourges upon her (folio 298 verso) and drove her from the monastery as a criminal. But she remained at the monastery gates amid every hardship with the utmost patience, performing public penance as though she were guilty of wickedness, and subsisting only on alms.

Meanwhile that unhappy woman gave birth to a little child, whom the girl’s father brought to the monastery. [Col. 1054A] The abbot ordered it to be thrown before Marinus, saying that she should nourish the son whom she had wickedly acquired. Taking up the child, she went about among shepherds and, receiving milk from them, nourished it with every care. She returned to the monastery gate, striving to please God alone, the sole knower of her secret.

After three years had passed in this manner, at the brothers’ request she was received into the monastery. She was assigned the care of washing the kitchen vessels and cleaning the brothers’ quarters; she carried this out with complete cheerfulness. She was accustomed to go first to church and leave last.

Thus, when such a lamp had long lain hidden from human beings, though it shone with great brightness before God, the Light of light raised her from darkness and made her a light for all in the house of the Church. She fell into bodily illness, through which she escaped the bitterness of death and misery [Col. 1054B] and entered the joyfulness of life and gladness.

When she was not seen in church as usual, the abbot ordered an inquiry, lest perhaps she was ill. On learning that she had died, he declared her wretched because she had not even received the full time for penance, and ordered her buried far from the brothers. But when the body was stripped for washing, a woman was seen; a cry with praises was raised to the stars.

The abbot, beside himself, ran up and fell before the holy body. With great lamentation he kept crying that he had erred, that he had sinned, until a voice resounded from heaven declaring that the guilt of his ignorance had been forgiven through the merits of Saint Marina, the bride of Christ. The people flocked together because of the astounding miracle, and among them came the girl’s father. Hearing that Christianus had died, he asked God’s pardon because he had destroyed his house. Meanwhile his daughter—the printed text reads “son” [Col. 1054C]—possessed by a demon, was brought bound in chains. From her mouth the devil confessed the author of the crime and the wrong done to Christ’s virgin.

Therefore all resounded with God’s praises, whose such great benefits abound among human beings. The girl was freed at the seventh hour at the virgin’s tomb, and again the Lord was glorified in his saints. Let us constantly entreat her together with all the Lord’s elect, that we may overcome the world’s luxury (folio 300), so that the Lord may exalt us at the gates of death, and our soul may proclaim all his praises at the gates of the daughter of Zion, where eye has not seen (1 Cor. 2).

## Eleventh Sunday

[Col. 1053]

[Col. 1053D] “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin” (Psalm 31). He who here washes away his sins with tears and redeems them by alms, to him the Lord will not impute them in the future, because by punishing them here he has condemned them himself. But he who thinks not of what he has already done, but of what he may yet do, provokes the Lord’s vengeance. For whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul (Psalm 10); and whoever hates his soul certainly hates the Lord; and whoever hates the Lord, in that person iniquity shall be found unto hatred.

There are many who are filthy in sins but consider themselves righteous and condemn others as sinners. The Lord restrains their obstinacy in today’s Gospel and raises up to pardon those despised by them. For it relates that two persons went up to the Temple at Jerusalem to pray: one a Pharisee, that is, a cleric of the Jews, and the other a tax collector. The Pharisee, approaching the altar, raised hands and eyes to heaven and gave thanks to God that he was unlike other people, who were robbers, unjust, and adulterers—like that tax collector, who stood at the back—that he fasted twice in the week and gave tithes of all his goods.

But the tax collector hid himself in a corner, did not dare lift his eyes to heaven, only beat his breast, and asked God to be merciful to him. Then the Lord says that the man confessing his sins [Col. 1055A] went down justified, while the man boasting of his deeds departed rejected: for everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted (Luke 18).

Therefore, beloved, when you gather for prayer, you ought not to boast of your good deeds or condemn others, but accuse yourselves and consider everyone else righteous. Humble your souls in the sight of God; invoke him with mouth and heart, and on the day of tribulation he will deliver you and exalt you over your enemies. Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from deceit, for by his words each person will be justified, and by his words each person will be condemned (Matt. 12). Whoever prays in the way the Lord taught, the Lord will hear; but whoever prays otherwise, that person’s prayer will become sin. Ask for the necessities of life [Col. 1055B] and for eternal joys, and the Father will give you both. Many pray and do not obtain, and their prayer will be abominable, because they turn away their ear from the cry of the poor (fol. 300v). For not everyone who says to him, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does the will of his Father will enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 7). The Father’s will is that we forgive those who sin against us and give help from our possessions to those in need. By these things the petitions of our heart will be granted; by these things we shall enter the kingdom of heaven.

By the two men who are said to have gone up to the Temple, two peoples are understood: the Jewish people and the Gentile. The Pharisee approaching the altar is the Jewish people, who possessed the sanctuary and the ark. [Col. 1055C] He rehearses his merits in the Temple because he boasts to the world of his observance of the Law. He was not like the rest of humankind, because circumcision distinguished him from the peoples of the nations. The Gentiles were robbers because they seized the Lord’s goods as though by force, when they did not render him the service owed for benefits bestowed. They were unjust because, despising the Creator, they worshipped the creature. They were adulterers because, abandoning the Lord, their true bridegroom, they defiled themselves with demons. The Jews too were robbers, since they appropriated to themselves the merits of the righteous. For it is robbery to wish to possess the praise of a righteous person while being unwilling to imitate that righteous person’s holiness. Hence it is written: “He did not consider equality with God a robbery” (Phil. 2). When the first angel wished to seize that equality, he fell from blessedness. [Col. 1055D] They were unjust because they rendered neither to God what was God’s nor to a human being what was that person’s. They were adulterers because, rejecting the noble bride, the Law, they defiled themselves with idolatry. Through the week all time revolves. He fasts twice in the week because in deed and will he avoids evil. He gives tithes of everything he possesses because he fulfils the Decalogue of the Law through the ten senses of the body: five doubled make ten—for example, two eyes, two ears, and the rest. But the Jews committed evil in act and intention; they transgressed God’s commandments with all their senses.

The tax collector who stood at a distance is the Gentile people, [Col. 1056A] who were far from the worship of God. He did not lift his eyes to heaven because he desired earthly things alone. He struck his breast while he bewailed his error through repentance. And because he humbled himself through confession, God exalted him through pardon. Therefore, beloved, let us stand at a distance, so that we may judge ourselves unworthy of the Lord’s sacraments and of the fellowship of the saints. Let us not lift our eyes to heaven, so that we may judge ourselves unworthy of heaven. Let us beat our breasts, so that we may punish by tears the sins we have committed. Let us fall down before God; let us weep before the Lord who made us (fol. 302), so that he may turn our mourning into joy and, tearing apart the sackcloth of sorrow, clothe us with gladness. Let us not be robbers, for the rapacious will not possess the kingdom of God. Let us covet no one’s property; let us not ascribe to ourselves any praise not owed to us by our merits [Note: [Col. 1055D] Manuscript: “by us.”] [Col. 1056B], for those who do this will be companions of robbers. Let us not be unjust, for the unrighteous will not obtain the kingdom of God. Let us love the Lord; let us supply our neighbours with necessities. Let us not be adulterers, for God will judge fornicators and adulterers. Let us preserve the right faith and turn aside to no heresy, because this is called spiritual fornication, and God will destroy everyone who commits fornication away from him (Ps. 72). Let us fast twice in the week, namely on the fourth and sixth weekdays, because if the Pharisee did this, we ought much more to do it. And if we do not abstain at all from food, let us restrain the heart from evil intention and the hands from wicked action. Let us give God tithes of all our possessions, because if the Jew did this, the Christian ought much more to do so.

[Col. 1056C] Not only, beloved, do the sacred writings lead us to eternal life, but Gentile literature also instructs us; from it some things should be brought forward for edification. And, lest anyone be scandalized by this, let it be illustrated by sacred authority. The children of Israel plundered the Egyptians: they took gold, silver, gems, and precious garments, which they later offered in God’s treasury for making the tabernacle. But when they themselves departed from Egypt, all the temples of idols fell. Those depart from Egypt and hasten toward the land of promise who leave this world and transfer themselves to holy conduct. Then indeed shrines are overthrown, because those who had been temples of vices are destroyed as regards their sins; for they begin already to be God’s dwelling-place, and therefore evil spirits will not be able to retain in them a place of abode [Col. 1056D] any longer. They plunder the Egyptians when they transform secular studies into spiritual exercise. They offer these things for making the tabernacle when they bring philosophical arguments to the edification of the Church. They give the gold of the Egyptians when, through secular wisdom, they adorn spiritual teaching. They offer the silver of the Egyptians when they turn secular eloquence to the Church’s usefulness. They give their gems when they relate, for the exhortation of their neighbours, sayings well uttered by philosophers. They offer their garments when they recount Gentile examples to their brothers for imitation. For [Col. 1057A] in a great house (fol. 302v), not only vessels of gold and silver but also vessels of iron and clay are necessary. The great house is the Church. The vessels of gold and silver are volumes of sacred authority. The vessels of iron and clay are secular writings necessary for external matters. For just as gold is made bright through iron, so sacred Scripture shines through secular disciplines.

It is also related that, after returning from captivity, they rebuilt God’s Temple with money acquired in Babylon. Those are held captive among the Babylonians who, departing from the Catholic faith, are held among heretics, or, apostatizing from a holy profession, are held among secular people in the captivity of demons. If, by God’s favour, they return to Jerusalem—that is, to mother Church—and [Col. 1057B] bring forward for their neighbours’ edification the useful things they have learned outside, they truly build a Temple for God out of the wealth they gained among the Babylonians. The Law also commands that, if a people besieges a city and someone sees among the enemies a beautiful girl, he is to cut her nails and hair and afterward take her as his wife. We besiege a city when we attack some heresy or error of the Gentiles by writings or disputation. We behold among them a beautiful girl when we discover some saying well uttered by them. We ought to cut off her nails and hair and so join her to ourselves, because we must reject superfluities and things set against the faith; but sayings well expressed and not contrary to our faith we should weave into our books for the instruction of the faithful.

[Col. 1057C] Thus philosophers write that a woman fastened to a wheel is continually carried round, and that her head is now lifted on high, now plunged into the depths. This turning wheel is the glory of this world, which is continually borne about. The woman joined to the wheel is fortune interwoven with glory. Her head is sometimes borne upward, sometimes downward, because many people are often exalted by power and riches and are frequently cast down by poverty and miseries. They also say that a certain man, condemned among the dead, is stretched apart upon the spokes of a wheel; this wheel is carried without interruption from the height of a mountain into the depth of a valley and, rising again to the heights, falls back anew.

They further report that another man there rolls a stone to the top of a mountain, but the weight of the stone drives its roller headlong from the mountain’s summit; again the wretch rolls the stone [Col. 1057D] upward. They also tell that a vulture there devours a certain man’s liver, which, once consumed, grows again (fol. 304).

Because wise reasoning devised these stories, your charity ought to know what they mean. The person who is cast down from a mountain into the depths in the wheel’s whirling is the person who is hurled headlong from the height of power or riches into the abyss of hell. The person who rolls a stone up a mountain, which immediately rolls back down again, is the person who attains dignities or any desired things with great difficulty and through those very things is plunged into hell’s depths. The man whose liver [*jexor*, as printed] is eaten by a vulture and is said to grow green again [Col. 1058A] is the man upon whose heart lust feeds; once desire has been satisfied, foul passion is born again. For desire is in the liver, while the vulture loves the corpses of the dead.

Concerning this plague they further say that Medusa, of exceptional beauty, stirred very many to love of herself, and turned all who looked upon her into stones [the manuscript reads: “they turned”]. Perseus protected himself from her face with a crystal shield and killed her with a curved sword. This woman is lust, which presents itself as beautiful to human hearts; but she turns those who gaze on her into stones, because through pleasure she hardens the hearts of the lustful. Perseus protects himself from her with a crystal shield because the strong man, fixing his attention on the mirror of virtues, turns the face of his heart away from looking upon her. He kills her [Col. 1058B] with a curved sword because by fear of eternal fire he cuts her off from himself.

It is then read that one of the fathers raised a little son in the desert, whom lust tempted when he became an adult. His father commanded him to withdraw into the desert and devote himself alone to fasts and prayers for forty days. When twenty days had elapsed, he saw a black and exceedingly foul-smelling naked woman rush upon him. Unable to bear her stench, he began to drive her away from himself. But she said: “Why do you recoil so greatly from me, whose love makes you burn so greatly? For I am the image of lust, who appears sweet in human hearts; and unless you had obeyed your father, you too, like others, would have been cast down by me.” But he gave thanks to God, who had delivered him from the spirit of fornication. Many other examples lead [Col. 1058C] us onto the paths of life.

[Note: [Col. 1057D] A rubric in the page margin: “Concerning the three fools.”] It is read that one of the fathers went out and saw an Ethiopian in a wood cutting logs and attempting to lift them after binding them together. When they seemed heavy, he untied them and increased the load; and when they were then more burdensome, he added to them and made them unbearable. As he strives to lift them, he is crushed by their weight. Going on (fol. 304v), the father saw where [“ubi,” as printed] a woman was pouring water into a vessel; what was poured in flowed out beneath, because the vessel had no bottom. He proceeded farther, and behold, two men were approaching a city gate carrying a beam crosswise before them; and, since neither was willing to yield to the other, both remained outside. The Ethiopian who increases the load of wood is the person who always heaps up the burden of sins; when time scarcely sufficed [Col. 1058D] to amend what had been done, the unhappy person never ceases to add newer sins, until, falling into despair, he does not obtain repentance but is crushed into death by the mass of crimes. The person who pours water into a vessel lacking a bottom is the person who performs almsgiving or some good deeds but loses them through impurity or other vices; hence it is written: “He gathered money and put it into a pierced bag.” He gathers money into a pierced bag who indeed performs good deeds but stains them by evil works. Those who carried the wood crosswise are those who bear the heavy yoke of pride; since they are unwilling to yield to one another, [Col. 1059A] they will not be able to enter the gate of the heavenly city. But those who lay the Lord’s sweet yoke upon their necks and take up his light burden will enter this gate [*porta*, as printed] of the city above. Let us sigh for this city, beloved, with our whole heart; let us hasten toward it with all our strength, so that we may escape the bottomless pit and may be able to sacrifice to the Lord a sacrifice of praise in the courts of Jerusalem [lacuna] eye.

## Thirteenth Sunday

[Col. 1059]

[Col. 1059A] “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly” (Ps. 1). Adam was an unhappy man, who departed from the homeland of paradise through the counsel of the ungodly and led all his descendants into this exile. He stood in the way of sinners because he remained fixed in sins. He sat in the seat [Col. 1059B] of pestilence because he taught others sins by evil examples. But Christ proved to be the blessed man, who by the Father’s counsel went from the court of heaven into prison after the lost servant. He did not go in the counsel of the ungodly when the devil, showing him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, persuaded him to worship himself [as printed]. He did not stand in the way of sinners because he did not commit sin. He did not sit in the seat of pestilence because he taught evil neither by word nor deed. And therefore, just as that unhappy man drew all his carnal children into death, so this blessed man (fol. 306) restored all his children to life. For, as he himself relates in the Gospel: “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho; robbers fell upon him, wounded him, stripped him, and departed. Then a priest, travelling by the same road, saw him half-dead and passed by; likewise a Levite, journeying that way, saw him and went past. But a Samaritan, making his way along the same road, had pity on the sufferer; binding his wounds, he treated them with wine and oil, placed him upon his beast, and brought him to an inn. On the next day he brought out two denarii for the innkeeper, asked him to care for the man, and promised that, if he spent anything of his own beyond this, he would repay it on his return” (Luke 10).

A man indeed goes down from Jerusalem to Jericho when the first parent came from the joys of paradise to the decline of death. For Jericho, whose name signifies “moon,” denotes the waning of our mortality. He fell among robbers because, once exiled, he was immediately surrounded by a band of demons. They stripped him because they deprived him not only of paradise’s riches but also of the garment of immortality. They inflicted wounds because they poured sins into him. They left him half-dead because they left him dead in soul but living in body through God’s mysteries. The priest went down by the same road when the order of patriarchs travelled along the path of mortality. He passed by the wounded man because he could not bring help to the human race, while he himself lamented that he too was grievously wounded by sins. The Levite likewise travelled the same road because the prophetic order also proceeded along the path of death. He passed by the wounded man because he could not bring aid to fallen humanity, while he too groaned that he had been wounded by sins. But the half-dead man is healed by [Col. 1060A] the Samaritan because humanity, deceived by the devil, is healed through Christ.

Samaria was a city, the capital of the Israelite kingdom; its inhabitants [the text reads *cujus caput*, “whose head”] had been carried captive into Nineveh for idolatry, and Gentiles were settled in it. The Jews so greatly abhorred association with them [Col. 1060B] that they applied their designation to those whom they wished to curse; thus, in cursing the Lord, they called him a Samaritan. He himself was the true Samaritan, a name which means “guardian,” because the human race is guarded by him. He made the journey when he came from heaven into this world. He saw the wounded traveller because he beheld humanity surrounded by sins and miseries. He was moved with mercy over him (fol. 306v) because he experienced every pain on his behalf. Approaching, he bound his wounds when, proclaiming eternal life, he preached that people should cease from sins. He tightened the wounds with the two parts of a bandage when he restrained sins through two kinds of fear. For servile fear [Note: [Col. 1059D] Supply: “vero” (“indeed/however”).] restrains from sins through punishments; filial fear urges the saints to good works. He drew the lower [Col. 1060C] part of the bandage when he instilled the fear of hell into human hearts: “Their worm,” he says, [Note: [Col. 1060D] Supply: “does not.”] “does not die, and the fire is not extinguished.” He drew the upper part when he taught the fear of good endeavour: “The children,” he says, “of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” He pours in wine and oil when he taught repentance and pardon. For putrid wounds are cleansed by wine and soothed wounds are healed by oil. He poured in wine when he said, “Repent”; he added oil when he said, “For the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. 3). He placed him upon a beast when he bore our sins in his body upon the wood of the cross. He brought him to an inn when he joined him to the Church above. The inn, [Col. 1060D] in which animals are gathered at night, is the present Church, in which the righteous are housed amid the darkness of this life until the Day of eternity breathes forth and the shadows of mortality decline.

On the next day he brought out two denarii. One day was the day of death; the other, the day of life. The day of death began with Adam, in whom all die. The day of life began with Christ, in whom all will be made alive. Before Christ’s resurrection all people moved toward death; after his resurrection all the faithful rose toward life. On the next day he brought out two denarii when, after his resurrection, he taught that the two Testaments are fulfilled through the two commandments of love. He gave the denarii to the innkeeper [Col. 1061A] when he entrusted to the order of teachers the teaching of the law of life. He commanded the sick person to be healed because he commanded the human race to be saved from sins. The stench drives this sick person out from the inn because the adversity of this world impels the righteous to desire heavenly things. Two denarii are also given to the innkeeper when teachers are exalted by knowledge of the Scriptures and worldly honour. If they spend anything beyond this, he will repay it when he returns [Note: [Col. 1061D] Read: “will return.”], because if they exemplify by works the good things which they preach to the peoples, when the true Samaritan returns for judgment and leads the one once wounded, now healed, from the inn into the heavenly palace (fol. 308), he will recompense the diligent stewards with everlasting rewards.

That deaf and mute man also represented the human race, [Col. 1061B] whom the Lord passed through the borders of the Decapolis in order to heal (Mark 7). The Decapolis is a region of ten cities and signifies the Law’s ten commandments. The Lord passes through the Decapolis when he willed to be born under the Law’s Decalogue. They bring the deaf and mute man to him when preachers convert the human race to faith: it was deaf because it would not hear God’s commands; it was mute because it was silent in praise of the Creator. The Lord restored hearing to it when he opened its understanding to comprehend the Scriptures. He loosed the bond of its tongue when he filled its mouth with God’s praise.

The ten lepers also represented this, who were cleansed when the Lord entered a village (Luke 17). The Lord entered a village when, about to be incarnate, [Col. 1061C] he descended into the Virgin’s womb, the fortress of the Holy Spirit. The ten leprous men were all human beings, stained by transgression of the ten commandments or by the affliction of Egypt’s ten plagues. They are sent by the Lord to the priests but cleansed on the journey, because when sinners hasten to priests to confess their offences, they immediately receive pardon for what they have done. The one who gave thanks for his healing is the Catholic people, who continually give thanks to the Lord for their salvation.

Blessed were the eyes—but not everyone’s—which saw Christ and his deeds (Luke 10), and the ears which heard his teaching (ibid.); blessed also are those who did not see and yet believed (John 20). [Col. 1061D] What kings and prophets wished to see (Luke 10), this the faithful believe the apostles saw: namely, that the Lord lived among human beings and by signs and teaching led lost humanity back to its homeland. Let us love him, beloved, with our whole heart, whole soul, all strength, and all mind, and our neighbour as ourselves (Matt. 22), so that we may see him in the kingdom of his glory. Let us bless him at all times, so that we may be able to praise him in his house for ever and ever.

It is read that a certain man continually either read or kept God’s praise in his mouth through hymns or psalms. One night he saw a crown of fragrant flowers [Col. 1062A] descend from heaven upon his head. When he later died and was buried, all the crowd standing there was filled with the sweetness of a wondrous fragrance.

It is related of another unlearned man that he continually recited the hymn, “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit” (fol. 308v), and, after his death, appeared to someone with a glorious face and shining garment. When that person asked how he fared, though he had never learned letters, he replied in these words: “The Lord rules me and nothing will be lacking to me; in a place of pasture he placed me” (Ps. 22). O how greatly the simplicity of the faithful differs from the subtle intelligence of the Gentiles! Behold, this unlearned man, through the folly of faith, attained by three little words joy and knowledge of all things. But Plato, the overflowing river of human wisdom, and Aristotle, the torrent [Col. 1062B] of acute wisdom, through worldly prudence obtained the folly of misery and eternal perdition. Thus, indeed, Christ, God’s wisdom, rewards those who love him; thus he rejects those who despise him and abuse his benefits. Already the faith of Peter the fisherman [Note: [Col. 1062D] Manuscript: “fishermen.”] has syllogized Aristotelian arguments; already Tullian eloquence, falling silent before Christ’s professors, has stopped its mouth.

It is also read that a certain woman converted to Christ flourished in many good works and continually laboured in vigils, fasts, and prayers. Struck by a grave illness, she came near her end. While the faithful stood beside her bed, suddenly at midnight an immense light was poured forth from heaven; by its excessive ray everyone’s sight was so dazed that nothing but [Col. 1062C] that brightness [as printed] could be seen. Meanwhile, the doors were heard creaking from the multitude entering; voices speaking to the sick woman were heard, but could not be seen because of the splendour of the light. Moreover, a very great fragrance spread out [*fraglantia*, as printed], filling everyone’s sense of smell with marvellous sweetness. As day approached, the light departed, but the fragrance remained there for three days. On the fourth night the cell was again illuminated by a great light, whose radiance drove away the darkness of the whole night. And behold, two choirs singing psalms were heard in the street; the voices of the sexes singing could be distinguished, for the men sang psalms and the women answered. In this brightness of light, sweetness of fragrance, and joy of melody, that holy soul was released from [Col. 1062D] the bitterness of flesh and, amid the saints’ rejoicing, was led away to enjoy the loveliness of everlasting sweetness. And the higher it was led, the less the voice of those singing hymns was heard, until light and harmony were withdrawn (fol. 310); the sweetness of fragrance remained until the body was buried. Thus the Lord regards the humble; thus he raises the poor from the dungheap (Ps. 112). For this little woman was poor and of no account among human beings. But what is despised by human beings is acceptable to our Lord, and what is exalted among human beings is abominable before God. Behold, a precious gem lying in a dunghill is lifted from the sewer of worldly stench and set in a place of honour in a royal diadem, gleaming and flashing with fiery stones [Col. 1063A]. Therefore, beloved, let us entrust our souls to all the saints and persist continually in good works, so that, for the days during which we humble ourselves, we may deserve to rejoice with them eternally [Col. 1064A], and, for the years during which we live and see evils here [Note: [Col. 1063D] Perhaps supply: “while.”], may see one day in the courts of the Lord, which is better than thousands (Ps. 83). Which…

## Twentieth Sunday

[Col. 1063]

[Col. 1063A] “Blessed are those who hear the word of the Lord and keep it” (Luke 11). Many people, beloved, do not wish even to hear God’s word with the bodily ear. Many indeed hear it with the ear, but are by no means blessed, because they do not love it in practice. But those who hear it with a watchful ear, guard it with an attentive heart, and strive to fulfil it by devoted action are blessed, because [Col. 1063B] they will rejoice eternally with the Word of God.

That same Word recounts today in the Gospel that a certain king made a wedding-feast for his son. He sent his servants to call those invited, but they would not come. Again he sent others, commanding them to tell those invited that the dinner was prepared, the oxen and fattened fowls slaughtered, and everything ready. But they, neglecting this, one went to his farm and another to his business; others seized the servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them. The king, having sent armies, destroyed them and burned their city. Then he sent to the ends of the roads and ordered that anyone whatsoever be summoned. But after the wedding-feast had been filled with diners, the king entered and saw a certain man not wearing the garment used by those at the wedding; he ordered that man, with hands and feet bound, to be cast into the outer darkness, where [Col. 1063C] there would be weeping and gnashing of teeth. And he said that many are called, but few chosen (Matt. 22).

The king who made a wedding-feast for his son is God the Father, who joined the Church as bride to his Son Jesus Christ. The bridal chamber of this wedding was the womb of the holy Virgin. The servants who called the invited persons (fol. 310v) were the prophets, who announced to the Jews—invited through the patriarchs—that Christ would be incarnate. Those unwilling to come were those who did not believe the prophets. The servants sent a second time were the apostles, who preached throughout all Judaea that Christ had been incarnate for us. The prepared dinner was the fattened calf, namely Christ’s body now offered for us. The fierce oxen were tyrants, who subdued all the kingdoms of the world. The fattened fowls were philosophers, who, by searching, flew in mind to the stars of heaven. They had been killed when God’s wisdom had trampled the necks of the proud and exalted, chosen humble and poor parents, rejected the wisdom of the prudent, and appointed unlearned and simple people to preach. Everything was ready because all things pertaining to salvation had been set forth. He had opened Scripture to all; baptism and repentance stood open to all. Yet they, neglecting salvation, would not come to the Lord’s wedding, but one went to his farm and another to his business because they desired earthly gain alone and therefore could not love heavenly things. The rest treated the king’s servants shamefully and killed them because the Pharisees and chief priests [Col. 1064A] afflicted the apostles with prison, chains, and beatings; they killed some of them and drove others out of their borders with disgrace. But the king, sending armies, destroyed those murderers and burned their city when God’s ministers—the Roman rulers—entered Judaea with armies, killed the parricidal Jews by various punishments, and set the city [Col. 1064B] of Jerusalem ablaze.

Then servants are sent to the ends of the roads and commanded to call anyone whatever, because, when the Jews refuse to come to God’s wedding, the apostles go into the way of the Gentiles and invite idolaters to God’s feast. They gathered good and bad because they drew many reprobate persons together with the elect into the faith. The wedding-feast is filled with diners when the number of the elect is completed. The king will enter to inspect the diners when he comes for judgment to distinguish all according to their merits; as it is written: “The Lord will come to judgment with every despised person.” That is, he will judge as carefully the person most despised in this world as the person surpassing all others in glory. The person not clothed in a wedding garment is cast outside because whoever lacks God’s love will not be admitted to his wedding, for he is [Col. 1064C] love. The wedding garment is love, through which eternal brightness is attained (fol. 312). There hands and feet will be bound by the ropes of sins which are here bound by wicked deeds. The limbs relaxed here for evil are there constrained for punishment. Those who now willingly endure inner darkness are cast into outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth because they will pass from snowy waters to excessive heat: from smoke and fire they suffer weeping, and from excessive cold gnashing of teeth. Many are called but few are chosen, because many are indeed called to faith, but only the elect are saved. There are two callings: one outward, the other inward. Through the outward calling many were called to faith through apostles and preachers; through the inward calling few were drawn by the Son to the Father. Through the outward calling many fish clung to the net of faith, whom the selectors cast out again; through the inward calling few remained concealed, whom they chose into vessels. Now the reprobate are mingled with the elect, as chaff with grain; but when Christ comes with the winnowing-fan, the chaff is shaken out and handed over to unquenchable fire, while the grain will be gathered into God’s barn.

And we, beloved, have been called with many to God’s wedding: let us strive by good deeds to be chosen with the few. Dinner is prepared for us daily when sacred Scripture together with Christ’s body is set before us. Oxen were slaughtered for this feast because the apostles, the oxen of the Lord’s herd, fell and died for the invitation [Col. 1065A] to these feasts. Fattened fowls also were slaughtered for this feast because all those who fly in mind toward heavenly things were struck down for these banquets. The oxen were also persecutors, who scattered the faithful with horns of unbelief, but were weakened when Christ came. The birds, however, were heretics, who in some sense flew to the heights when they set their mouth in heaven and spoke iniquity on high against the Lord; but they were conquered and driven out by Catholics. Since all these things have been subdued through Christ’s power, all is prepared for our salvation. Therefore, let us not neglect to come with all haste to God’s feast for any business whatsoever. God’s banquet is the joy of everlasting life; whoever strives to fulfil God’s commands runs toward it. Called from the ends of the roads, we now recline at the wedding, because from various errors we come together to the Lord’s sacraments. And therefore, beloved, let us shine in the wedding garment: that is, let us love [Col. 1065B] the Lord above all things and our neighbours as ourselves. Whoever the king, upon entering, does not find in this garment, he orders bound and cast out of his feast; that person will see infernal darkness. The cities of those who are destroyed are burned along with them, those by whom the sent servants are shamefully treated and slain; because they are indeed permitted to be destroyed by demons, by whom preachers are afflicted here with insults, and their bodies are finally burned with unquenchable fire.

King Solomon composed a sweet epithalamium concerning these nuptials when, through the Spirit, he sang the *Song of Songs* in praise of Bridegroom and Bride. The son of the king of Jerusalem betrothed to himself the daughter of the king of Babylon, gave her into the hand of a guardian to be taught and adorned, and himself went away to prepare the banquet. Returning again with a vast retinue and splendid magnificence, he will bring her into the starry bridal chamber, taking with him into the palace the bride’s adorners for the wedding, but handing her corrupters over to the punishment of prison.

The king of Jerusalem is God, whose Son is Christ. The king of Babylon is the devil. The Gentile people were his daughter when they were devoted to idolatry. Christ betrothed her to himself from the Father when afterward, shedding his blood, he triumphed over the devil on the cross. He entrusted her to a guardian [Col. 1065D] when he committed her to the order of teachers, to be instructed in the divine Law and adorned with gems of virtues. He himself went away to procure the feast because, indeed, he ascended into heaven to prepare for her a suitable place in his Father’s house with its many dwellings. He will return with the army of all angels, rescue her from the exile of Babylonian [Note: [Col. 1065D] Manuscript: “Babylonian” (*Babylonae*).] pilgrimage, and bring her with the greatest rejoicing into his Father’s city, glorious Jerusalem. Then the bride’s adorners will enter with her, because those who here instructed the Church by writings or speech and adorned her with good examples will then shine like the sun with her at the Lamb’s wedding. But persecutors who tore her and inflicted violence upon her, and heretics and schismatics who corrupted her, will then be cast into the lake of fire and sulphur [Col. 1066A] and burn for ever.

So that we may not be excluded from this feast, the Lord instructs us by various teachings. He also relates that a certain man had a fig tree in his vineyard and, coming for three years, found no fruit upon it; lest it occupy the ground barren any longer, he ordered it cut down (Luke 13). The barren fig tree in (fol. 314) the vineyard was the Synagogue, unfruitful under the Law. The Lord sought fruit from it for three years because before the Law he admonished it to the fruit of good works through the patriarchs, under the Law through the prophets, and under grace through the apostles. But because it dried up through unbelief and occupied the ground barren, he laid the axe of his judgment to its root when he cut it down by the Roman sword [Col. 1066B].

The barren fig tree in the vineyard is also any person in the Church without good works. From that person the fruit of three years is sought when the work of faith in the Trinity is required of him; and unless he is promptly dug around by confession and the manure of repentance applied, he will be cut down by death and cast into the fire of hell.

This too was prefigured by the woman bent over, yet mercifully healed by the Lord (Luke 13). The woman bowed down to the earth was the Synagogue, bent beneath the burden of the Law. She is raised up by the Lord when a multitude of Jews, converted, is delivered through grace from the burden of the Law. Likewise, the woman bent over for eighteen years is every soul weakened under each Law (ibid.). For the ten denotes the Old Testament because of the Decalogue of the Law, [Col. 1066C] while the eight denotes the New Testament because of the eighth day, the Lord’s resurrection. Therefore the woman is bent over for eighteen years while the soul is weighed down by transgressing both Laws; but she is lifted up by the Lord unto salvation when she is saved through his grace by repentance.

Through the poor, beloved, we ought to reach the banquet of God. For the Lord commanded that we should not invite to our meal the rich or powerful, from whom we shall receive recompense here; rather, that we should summon the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind to our feast, from whom we should expect no recompense (Luke 14). For if we do this, we shall be blessed, because they will receive us into the eternal dwellings when we fail. We must proceed to [Col. 1066D] God’s feast by the paths of the saints.

It is related of a certain noblewoman that, abandoning the world, she entered a monastery in which there were five hundred girls; and, in order to become truly wise, she pretended to be foolish. She served in the kitchen ministry; she made herself the servant of all; she never took food sitting at table with the others, but ate only the rinsings of vessels and crumbs swept from the table. She was the object of everyone’s laughter and bore everyone’s hatred most patiently; she never held conversation with anyone, but strove to please God alone. Meanwhile the Lord revealed her manner of life to a certain solitary monk. Coming to the community’s cell, he asked to be admitted (fo. 314 [Col. 1067A] v) into the congregation. When all the girls had gathered before him, and only she for whom he had come was absent, he asked that every one be summoned; and she, scarcely compelled—indeed dragged—by the others, was brought forward. Around her head she wore a very black rag, with which she often wiped pots or kettles. But as she approached from afar, the holy man saw upon her head a crown shining with gold and gems, and her garment flashing with great brilliance. At once running to meet her, he threw himself at her feet and begged to be blessed by her. She likewise threw herself at his feet, commending herself to his prayers. All the nuns were astonished; they begged him not to inflict such an indignity upon himself; they called her mad—“this madwoman,” they say (*sic*). To them he [Col. 1068A] openly related what glory he had seen in her and how God had revealed this matter to him. Then all threw themselves at her feet; some confessed that they had struck her face, others that they had filled her nostrils with mustard, and others that they had inflicted other injuries upon her. After offering prayer for them, he returned to the hermitage. But she, fearing to be honoured by people, secretly fled from the monastery, preferring to suffer in a desert place. Into what place she withdrew, or with what end she died, could come to no one’s knowledge. Yet it is certain that after the misery of this life she attained the glory of the eternal kingdom. Let us seek this glory with all the elect, that we may rejoice without end at God’s wedding feast. “Where eye …” (1 Cor. 2).

## Twenty-Second Sunday

[Col. 1067]

[Col. 1067B] “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times” (Ps. 105).

There are two judgments: one exercised here by Christ’s vicar judges; the other displayed at the last things by Christ, whom God appointed judge of the living and the dead. Judgment is to distinguish the good from the evil, and to repay good things to the good and evil things to the evil. Thus in judgment Christ will separate the good from the evil, and will render joys to the righteous and punishments to the wicked. Therefore they keep judgment who love the worshippers of God and reject the despisers of God. To observe judgment is also to inflict upon someone punishments deserved by his evil merits. For those who here afflict themselves for their sins by vigils, fasts, and other devout labours are blessed, because they will not undergo eternal judgment with the wicked.

There are also [Col. 1067C] two kinds of righteousness: one natural, namely divine; the other customary, namely human (fo. 316). Natural righteousness is to serve God and obey one’s parents; customary righteousness is to observe laws and the statutes of prelates, and to live in harmony with one’s fellow citizens. Blessed, then, are those who do righteousness at all times, because from the righteousness of the Father they receive through Christ the just rewards of life.

Today’s Gospel exhorts us to the judgment of righteousness. For it says that a certain king settled accounts with his servants. One who owed him ten thousand talents was brought before him; and because he had nothing with which to repay, the master ordered him to be sold with his wife, children, and all his possessions. Falling down, he begged for mercy; and the master, taking pity, forgave him everything. But after he went out, he encountered a debtor owing one hundred denarii; seizing him, he throttled him, violently constraining him to repay the debt. This man too fell down and begged mercy, but it availed him nothing; for he consigned the wretch to prison until he should pay the debt. When the master heard this, he recalled the wicked servant, sternly rebuked him, handed him over to the torturers, and ordered the whole debt to be exacted from him (Matt. 18). In conclusion the Lord made known what he meant by these words: “So,” he says, “will my heavenly Father do to you, if you do not forgive men from your hearts” (ibid.). Beloved, these matters are greatly to be feared and continually retained in memory.

[Col. 1068B] The king who settled accounts with his servants is Christ, who brings all people into judgment for their deeds. The debtor of ten thousand talents is every transgressor of the Ten Commandments; the debtor of ten denarii is the slanderer of neighbours. Therefore, if we wish God to forgive us grave matters, let us forgive our neighbours light matters. For all that people do to us is light, because it soon passes away; but what we do against God is very grave, because it plunges us into ruin. Therefore the heavenly teacher taught us to make an agreement with the Judge: namely, to ask that our debts be forgiven us just as we forgive our debtors. And when Peter asked how often one must forgive a sinning brother—whether up to seven times—the Lord said: “Not up to seven times, [Col. 1068C] but up to seventy times seven” (ibid.), that is, four hundred and ninety times; that is, we must forgive whatever wrongdoing is done against us.

Scripture also says: “A man harbours anger against a man and hopes for mercy from God.” Therefore, whoever does not forgive a person sinning against him is never forgiven for sinning against the Lord; indeed, in torments there is exacted from him what he believes was forgiven him through repentance. But you say: “I cannot forgive one who injures me, nor love him from whom I suffer slander.” O friend, what has the man whom you seek to kill done to you? “He killed my friend,” you say. And what is the killing of a man to you? We are all servants of one Lord, king of all, who as a just judge will avenge all human injuries. Therefore whoever kills a person sins not against you but against him whose servant he killed. And if you seek vengeance for this, you will be guilty in two ways: first, because you killed your fellow-servant; second, because you took from your Lord his judgment. Thus if you avenge a murder by deed or counsel, you will surely be condemned along with murder, because “whoever hates his brother is a murderer,” and such a person has no share in eternal life (1 John 3). Yet you, good man, wish to mutilate the limbs of one whom the Son of the supreme Emperor wishes to reign with himself.

“He took away my goods,” you say. What goods? “Gold,” you say, “or silver, or a horse, or something of that kind.” O man, did you not come naked [Col. 1069A] into this world and bring none of these things with you? Nor is there any doubt that you will likewise depart naked from this world and leave everything here. All these things came from earth and will return to earth. You possess nothing here as your own; everything belongs to another. “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 23). He granted you a portion of his goods as long as it pleased him; when he no longer wished you to possess them, he ordered another to take them away. As long as he wished, he gave his goods to Job; and when it again pleased him, taking them away, he gave them to the devil. Thus Job himself says: “The Lord gave; the Lord took away” (Job 1). He did not say, “The devil took away,” because God alone had authority over them.

Since therefore you are a worm and rottenness, do not wrong God by avenging yourself upon your neighbour. But you, dear one, why do you wish [Col. 1069B] to beat him or deprive him of his possessions? “He spoke badly of me,” you say. O senseless man! What is a word but wind? Once it has flown from the mouth, it immediately vanishes into the air. He who spoke badly harmed not you but himself, because one who says even “You fool” will be liable to the fire of Gehenna (Matt. 5). But if you live badly, what benefit will anyone’s blessing give you? And if you live well, what harm will anyone’s curse do you? It is therefore miserable to increase the misery of these wretches by vengeance, when they themselves have called God’s wrath upon themselves. For the Lord will condemn murderers, will subject plunderers to punishments, and will separate the accursed [read: “the abusive speakers”] even by eternal damnation.

Therefore everything committed against us is to be forgiven; what is committed against God is to be punished by prelates. What we ourselves sin against God, let us punish by fitting repentance. What those subject to us have sinned against the law of God, let us correct not cruelly but mercifully, that we may save their souls; for “judgment without mercy [falls] upon him who has not shown mercy” (Jas. 2). But what they have committed against us by word or deed, let us forgive, and we shall receive joy and gladness.

Now let your charity hear how justly God punishes sinners [Note: [Col. 1069D] Supplement: “punishes.”] and how mercifully he protects those who call upon him. For he is the merciful Father of the good and the powerful Lord of the wicked.

King David took the wife of Uriah the commander, and by a plot caused Uriah himself to be killed. Avenging these acts, the Lord caused the child born from the adultery to die, [Col. 1069D] and stirred against him his son Absalom, whom David especially loved. Absalom publicly violated his father’s wives and moreover deprived him of his kingdom. Yet the Lord restored David, thus chastened, to the kingdom; but delivered the parricidal son to a reprobate death. David, however, repenting, was yet more consoled when Solomon—his son by the same woman—was established in the kingdom.

It is also related that King Cambyses, wishing to reign alone, ordered Holofernes, commander of the army, to subjugate to him all kingdoms of the world. Setting out with a strong force, Holofernes destroyed every fortified city round about; finally he came to Judaea and besieged Bethulia. [Col. 1070A] But the people of the Lord, fearing that he would destroy Jerusalem as he had other cities, invoked God through fasts and prayers—God who is the protector of all who hope in him—that he might set before them the shield of his protection. The inhabitants of Bethulia had run out of food, since the army had cut off their water supply. Their rulers encouraged them as they were already failing, promising the Lord’s help.

In that city there was a devout widow named Judith. After a three-day fast she put on ornaments and went down to Holofernes’ camp. When he saw her, he was immediately captivated by her beauty and arranged nuptials with the splendid magnificence of an elaborate celebration. But at night, when all were overcome with sleep through excessive wine, Judith arose and invoked God. Drawing the sword hanging by the bed, she cut off the head of the drunken commander; [Col. 1070B] she returned with the head as quickly as possible to her people (fo. 318 v). Having summoned the entire people, she displayed the head and urged them to praise God, who had granted them both deliverance and victory. Restored in spirit, they worshipped God and joyfully burst forth in praises. On the next day, at Judith’s counsel, they came out from the city with great clamour and attacked the enemy. But when the enemy found their master beheaded, struck with overwhelming grief, all turned together to flight. Their pursuers laid many thousands low in every direction and put the rest to flight in great disgrace. Returning, they gathered immense spoil, came to Jerusalem, and offered sacrifices to God, who had redeemed his people through a woman and changed their sorrow into joy. [Col. 1070C] Thus God scattered the proud and, exalting them, protected the humble (Judith 10–16). That this widow conquered the tyrant signifies that the flesh of Christ conquered the devil.

It is also related that King Ahasuerus (*sic*) gave a great banquet to all the princes and peoples of his kingdom, and during the feast ordered Queen Vashti, crowned with a diadem, to be brought in. When she refused to enter, the king deprived her of the kingdom and exalted Esther in her place. After this, the king raised a certain Haman over the kingdom and subjected all the princes to him. When all began to bend the knee before him, Mordecai, the queen’s uncle, would not worship him. Indignant, Haman planned to deliver Mordecai and all his family to death; [Col. 1070D] with the king’s seal he decreed the extermination of all Jews throughout Ahasuerus’ kingdom, and erected a high gallows upon which he wished to hang Mordecai.

Meanwhile two men wished to kill the king; when Mordecai exposed them, the king ordered them executed. But he ordered Mordecai to be clothed in purple and a crown, led through the city upon the royal horse, while Haman with his soldiers went before him and sang his praises. After this Mordecai told the queen that Haman had condemned her and all her kin to death. She proclaimed a fast for all the people and afflicted herself with them through vigils, fasts, and prayers. When this was done, she prepared a banquet, inviting the king and ordering Haman to attend as well. During the meal she begged the king for her own life and that of her people; [Col. 1071A] she related that she and all her people had been condemned by Haman. Filled with fury, the king ordered Haman to be hanged upon the very gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. Then (fo. 320) he made Mordecai a prince in Haman’s place; Mordecai ordered all Haman’s family to perish by hanging. Thus, by God’s ordering, the innocent people are delivered and the wicked seed is justly exterminated (Esther 1–16).

This king, though a Gentile, bore a type of Christ, the true King of kings, born and arisen from the root of Jesse. He gave a banquet to the princes and peoples of his kingdom, because he gave his body and Holy Scripture as food to the apostles, princes of the world, and to the faithful peoples of the heavenly kingdom. He summoned Queen Vashti, crowned with the Law and prophets, to the banquet, because he invited the Synagogue, adorned [Col. 1071B] with Law and prophets, to the heavenly feast. Refusing to enter, she is deprived of the kingdom. Captive Esther is placed upon her throne, because unbelieving Judaea is cast out of Christ’s kingdom, while the Church from the Gentiles, captive to the devil, is brought as consort of the heavenly kingdom into the chamber of the King.

Haman, exalted by the king, is the Jewish people, exalted by God through kingdom, priesthood, and divine worship. He seeks to root out the queen’s offspring because the Jewish people seek to exterminate the people of the Church. Haman also, who erected the gallows for Mordecai, signifies the devil, who raised the cross for Christ. He is hanged on that same gallows because the devil is seized upon the gibbet of the cross. Those [Note: [Col. 1071D] Thus read: “two.”] who conspired against the king are the two unbelieving peoples, Jewish and Gentile, who counselled that Christ [Col. 1071C] the king be killed. Mordecai [Col. 1072A] accuses them because the Christian people condemn their works. They are killed by the king, and these are condemned by Christ. Mordecai is distinguished by purple and crown, and the Christian people are clothed in martyrdom and eternal glory. He is led on the royal horse through the city because the Christian people are cultivated throughout the whole world by teachers. For the order of preachers is called the horse of Christ the King, upon which he is carried through the world. Haman with his soldiers sings his praises because, willing or unwilling, the Jewish people together with the Gentiles celebrate the praises of the Christian people.

The queen summons the king to the banquet because the Church invites Christ to the solemn rites of her body. She orders Haman also to attend because, by preaching, she offers her feast to the unbelieving people. Haman likewise, who raises a gallows for Mordecai, is Antichrist, [Col. 1072B] who imposes the punishment of death upon the faithful people. He is hanged upon the same gallows because he too is put to death by the punishment of death. Mordecai is appointed prince by the king because, when judgment is completed (fo. 320 v), the faithful people are set over all the Lord’s goods. Haman’s seed is exterminated because then the generation of the wicked is condemned. But the queen’s people are delivered, and their sorrow is changed into joy, because the generation of the righteous shall be blessed and shall enjoy gladness and exultation. Now, beloved, with all our heart we implore the mercy of God, who sits upon the throne and judges righteousness, rendering judgment for all who suffer injury: may he on that day separate us from the unbelieving people and join us to the faithful in his kingdom, where eye … (1 Cor. 2).

## Twenty-Third Sunday

[Col. 1071]

[Col. 1071C] “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways” (Ps. 127).

To fear God is to turn away from evil; to walk in his ways is to do good. Therefore those who fear God by avoiding sins are blessed, because they escape punishments; and those who walk in his ways by doing good are blessed, because they will enter the Lord’s joy. The ways of the Lord are his commandments, which lead human beings to the heavenly homeland. But “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24). The ways of the Lord are mercy to all who walk in them, truth to all who turn aside from them. Therefore our God is to be feared as a lord by servants and loved as a father by children. Let us flee sins through fear of him and apply ourselves to good deeds through love for him, so that, passing from this wretched life, we may escape the sorrowful life and attain, by his help, his blessed life.

There are three lives: one blessed life above us, in which the saints live blessedly with the angels; another miserable life, in which the righteous still sigh and groan here; a third sorrowful life beneath us, in which the spirits of the damned abide with demons. Therefore, for us placed in [Col. 1072C] the middle life, two ways present themselves: one leading some upward, the other leading others downward. On the right there is the narrow and constricted path, leading those who walk by it out of this misery into the delight of blessed life; on the left there opens a broad and spacious road, leading those who walk upon it into the calamity of sorrowful life.

The narrow and constricted way is to flee the desires of the world and the lusts of the flesh; not to repay evil [Col. 1072D] for evil; to mortify the body by vigils and fasts; to labour in prayer and continual praise of God. But the broad and spacious way is to play, eat, drink, fornicate, hunt, oppress enemies (fo. 322), and overflow with fleshly pleasures. The devil taught this way and by it led the human race to destruction. Christ showed the other by deeds and words, and through it brought humanity, which had been lost, back to glory. Since the prophets foresaw that the human race would return to its homeland by this way alone, all unanimously foretold Christ, the true and certain Way, and all desired to see him.

For Jacob, dying, said: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” [Col. 1073A] (Gen. 49). Moses too said: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send” (Exod. 4). David likewise said: “O Lord, bend down your heavens and descend” (Ps. 143). Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 1073D] Thus in the manuscript]: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and descend” (Isa. 64). And rightly they languished with longing for him, since they knew beforehand that he would come. For before his coming dark death covered the world and directed all by the left-hand path into perdition. All wandered as though in darkness because they did not have Christ the light; and therefore, by the spacious way on the left, they rushed with blinded heart into death. But when Christ, sun of the sun, appeared in the world—indeed, when the life of angels showed itself to mortals—grim death fled in terror and, confounded, hid itself in the depths of Tartarus, just as, at sunrise, the darkness of night is driven away [Col. 1073B] and the world is illumined by its radiance.

Therefore, beloved, since the path of salvation is open to us through Jesus and the lamp of God’s word shines on both sides of the way, let us leave the left-hand track with all our heart and take the right-hand path with all our effort, that we may arrive at supreme blessedness. This way is charity, through which the brightness of supreme blessedness is approached.

Fifteen paths lead into this way, leading to the courts of life: namely patience, kindness, and the others enumerated by the Apostle’s subtle teaching. Moreover, supreme blessedness draws to itself those walking on this way as though by seventeen arms, because Christ taught us to enter the gates of life through the ten commandments of the Law and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit, through the prophet, expressly names these seventeen distinctions of blessedness [Col. 1073C] and subtly indicates the individual dignity of each.

First he calls blessed those who overcome vices and concupiscences with the shield of faith and meditate on the Law of the Lord day and night. “Blessed,” he says, “is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly … for the Lord knows the way of the righteous” (Ps. 1). The first human being unhappily consented to wicked counsel and dragged all his followers into death; Christ, the blessed man and way of the righteous, will bring all who walk through him back to the joys of angels. Therefore whoever does not consent to sins while pressing toward this blessed man will be in supreme blessedness, like the tree of life planted in paradise (ibid.).

Second, he calls blessed those rejoicing in hope and trusting in the Lord, [Col. 1073D] not in themselves. “Blessed,” he says, “are all who trust in him” (Ps. 2), because they will rejoice on his holy mountain, that is, in Christ. Again: “Blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Ps. 33), because he will see good days in heaven (ibid.). And again: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord” (Ps. 39), because a new song will be put into his mouth (ibid.).

Third, he calls blessed repentant persons fervent in love, because “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4), and through the Holy Spirit, who is charity, remission of sins is given. “Blessed,” he says, “are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31). They are forgiven through charity and covered through good works. Such a man will be blessed, because the Lord will not impute sin to him in judgment. Here, rejoicing in the Lord with the righteous, he will be glad; with the upright in heart he will glory (ibid.).

Fourth, he calls blessed those who worship God purely and desire to become his inheritance. “Blessed,” he says, “is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he chose as his inheritance” (Ps. 32). Let these rejoice in the Lord, because praise befits such persons (ibid.). Again: “Blessed,” he says, “is the people whose God is the Lord” (Ps. 143), because, delivered from the hand of alien children, they will rejoice and sing a new song to God (ibid.).

Fifth, he calls blessed those who practise hospitality, storing up heavenly riches for themselves through the poor. [Col. 1074B] “Blessed,” he says, “is he who understands concerning the needy and poor, because on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. 40). The evil day is when a person falls into some affliction or into the hands of enemies, from which the Lord will immediately deliver him. The evil day is also the last day, when the Lord will preserve him and not hand him over to the will of his enemies, but make him blessed in the land of the living (ibid.).

Sixth, he calls blessed those elected from the Lord’s people and received to praise him. “Blessed,” he says, “is the one whom you have chosen and received; he shall dwell in your courts” (Ps. 64). Again of these: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83).

Seventh, he calls blessed those devoted to prayer, continually invoking [Col. 1074C] the Lord’s aid. “Blessed is the man whose help is from you” (ibid.) (fo. 324); these will go from strength to strength and see the God of gods in Zion, where one day is better than thousands (ibid.). Again: “Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God” (Ps. 145), because he will reign with him for ever.

Eighth, he calls blessed those who praise God and contemplate heavenly things. “Blessed,” he says, “is the people who know jubilation” (Ps. 88), because they will walk in the light of your countenance and rejoice eternally in his name (ibid.).

Ninth, he calls blessed those instructed by the Lord and taught in his Law. “Blessed,” he says, “is the man whom you instruct, [Col. 1074D] O Lord, and teach out of your Law” (Ps. 93). The Lord’s consolations will gladden their souls (ibid.) when “those who are learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many unto righteousness like the stars” (Dan. 12).

Tenth, he sets forth as blessed those who keep just judgment and do righteousness at all times. “Blessed,” he says, “are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times” (Ps. 105). These will be separated from the nations so that they may glory in praise of God, to behold the goodness of God’s elect and rejoice in the gladness of the nation of saints (ibid.).

Eleventh, he sets forth as blessed those who fear God as children fear a father and desire to keep his [Col. 1075A] commandments. “Blessed,” he says, “is the man who fears the Lord; he delights greatly in his commandments” (Ps. 111). This holy fear remains for ever and ever, and will bring children into the presence of the eternal Father. Those running in this blessedness will be in everlasting remembrance; they will possess glory and riches in the house of the Lord (ibid.).

Twelfth, he sets forth as blessed those without the stain of sin in the Way—that is, in Christ—and walking in the Law of the Lord—that is, in charity. “Blessed,” he says, “are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the Law of the Lord” (Ps. 118). Their soul shall live for ever and praise the Lord eternally (ibid.).

Thirteenth, he sets forth as blessed those who search the Lord’s commandments in order to fulfil them, and seek the Lord with their whole heart. “Blessed,” he says, “are those who search his testimonies; with their whole heart they seek him” (ibid.). These will be blessed by the Lord, just as those who turn aside from his commandments are cursed (ibid.).

Fourteenth, he sets forth as blessed those who fulfil their desire through good things. “Blessed,” he says, “is he who has fulfilled his desire from them; he shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” (Ps. 126): conquering his enemies, the demons, through humility. The gate is the day of judgment, through which one enters the palace of heaven. At this gate such persons will not be ashamed of their sins (fo. 324 v) when they speak triumphantly against their enemies; rather, they will be the Lord’s inheritance and will have as reward Christ, the fruit of Mary’s womb (ibid.).

Fifteenth, he sets forth as blessed those who fear God as servants fear a lord [Col. 1075C] and walk in his ways. “Blessed,” he says, “are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways” (Ps. 127). This fear draws a person away from sins and brings love into the soul; but when love enters, it casts fear out, because this fear has punishment (1 John 4). Those hastening in this blessedness will see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of their life and will have the peace of Israel, Christ. For whoever shall eat the labours of his hands—that is, whoever shall make good works fruitful in the ways of the Lord—is blessed, and it shall go well with him. His wife shall be like an abundant vine; that is, his flesh, rejoicing with Christ, who is the true vine. His children shall be like young olive shoots, namely works in the blessing of holy women (ibid.).

[Col. 1075D] Sixteenth, he sets forth as blessed those repaying to the Babylonians the evils they inflict [reading: “inflict”] on us. “Blessed,” he says, “is he who repays to the daughter of Babylon the recompense which she repaid to us” (Ps. 136). The daughter of Babylon is our flesh, daughter of confusion. It repays evil to us when it entices us to sin. We repay its recompense to it when we afflict it for unlawful acts committed. Those who do this receive the beginning of joy on the day of Jerusalem (ibid.).

Seventeenth, he sets forth as blessed those who seize the little ones of the daughter of Babylon and dash them against the rock. “Blessed,” he says, “is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. 136). The little ones of the daughter of Babylon are suggestions of fleshly pleasure. Those dash them against the rock who, for Christ’s passion, reject carnal things. [Col. 1076A] When these return hence from Babylon to Jerusalem, they shall sing forever the hymn from the songs of Zion (ibid.).

Behold how many blessednesses those will inherit who walk in Christ, the Way. And because the prophets understood through the Spirit that Christ would bring so many bridal gifts to the Church, they greatly desired his coming. The Church proclaims his two comings: one in which he visited the languishing world, the other in which he will judge the fallen world.

We extend his coming over four Sundays because we read that he was foretold by four orders: namely, by patriarchs, judges, kings, and prophets. By patriarchs: where Abel offered a lamb, Melchizedek bread and wine, and Abraham (fo. 326) his son [Col. 1076B]; by judges: where Joshua, who is also Jesus, defeated enemies and divided the land among the people; where Gideon set out the fleece, upon which dew descended, and likewise defeated enemies with jars; and where Samson entered Gaza to a prostitute and ascended the mountain through his enemies; by kings: where David struck down Goliath; where Solomon built the Temple; and where Josiah celebrated Passover; by prophets: where Isaiah foretold that he would be born of a Virgin, Jeremiah that he would converse with human beings, and Daniel that the Holy of Holies would come.

We also commemorate his coming through four Sundays because before the Law he was promised to Abraham and the patriarchs; by Moses and the prophets he was written down beforehand; under grace he was shown by John and the apostles; and he is still to come [Col. 1076C] manifest to all.

Therefore we now omit “Glory in the highest,” which we shall sing at his Nativity, because by being born he brought joy to the world, which previously had sorrow. Enoch and Elijah, preceding his coming, will announce that he is to come to the world [reading: “world”], just as the prophets of old foretold that he would be born. Through their preaching the Jews will be converted to faith at the evening of the world; they will suffer hunger for the word of God and, like dogs, will go about the city—that is, the Church (Ps. 58)—and will desire to gather crumbs of God’s words from the table of Christians.

At that time Antichrist will reign, and he will disturb the whole world in diverse ways. For he will draw all princes to himself by money; with the rich he will sit in secret places, like a lion in ambush to deceive; he will deceive the clergy through worldly wisdom when he utters words against the Most High; he will seduce religious persons by signs and prodigies, when he even causes fire to descend from heaven; he will shake the common people with terror when the greatest persecution rages against Christians. He will kill Enoch and Elijah, and destroy all who resist him by cruel trial. The Lord Jesus will kill him by the spirit of his mouth, whether by his command or through the ministry of Michael the archangel; and he himself will then come for judgment. He who first came to be judged will then come to judge; he who first came hidden will then come manifest.

At his coming all people will rise and meet him in companies. Every eye will see him [Col. 1077A], even those who pierced him. Fire will go before him and consume his enemies round about. Just as formerly the waters of the flood rose fifteen cubits above all mountains (fo. 326 v), so now fire will rise fifteen cubits above all mountain peaks. Then, with the righteous placed at Christ’s right hand and the wicked at his left, all things that human beings ever committed in thought, word, or deed will be manifest to all; and each will receive a recompense fitting to his merits, as the righteous are assigned to joys and the wicked to punishments. Therefore that day is called the day of judgment (2 Macc. 6), because then the just Judge, unjustly judged, will judge all things justly—he who “will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in equity” (Ps. 97).
