This is also called the day of the Lord (Zeph. 1), because on that [Col. 1077B] day a just reward will be rendered by the Lord to each person for his work.

Then the devil will be brought bound before all, and before the eyes of everyone will be hurled into the lake of fire and sulphur (Job 40). His body, that is, the whole company of the wicked, will be cast in with him; and the earth will become for them pitch and burning sulphur (*sic*) for ever and ever (Isa. 34). Then the Church, Christ’s bride, long oppressed in Babylonian pilgrimage, will be led by her Bridegroom from Babylonian exile and brought with great angelic rejoicing into the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of her Father. Then “the righteous shall shine as the sun” (Matt. 13) and “shall be equal to angels” [Col. 1078A] (Luke 20); and when all things have been renewed, God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15).

Therefore, beloved, it is now time for us to rise from the sleep of sloth (Rom. 13), so that, watchful in good works, we may joyfully receive Christ when he comes, and so that he may conform the body of our humility to the likeness of the body of his glory (Phil. 3).

Above is sweetness; below is bitterness; in this world, which stands in the middle, there is a shadowy image of both. Therefore let the sweetness of heaven draw us upward, and the bitterness of hell impel us to dread the misery of this middle life and receive the glory of the blessed life, full of joy.

While the world flourished in glory and wealth, was strong in its cities and [Col. 1078B] resources, the righteous nevertheless despised its adornment, by which they might have shone abundantly. Now the world’s glory has withered; now every honor of the age has faded; and we miserable people embrace with all our heart its withered flower. We pursue with all desire that which flees and smiles upon us; and because, now that charity has grown cold, neither anyone’s prayer nor anyone’s merit sustains it, worn out by age and driven on by excessive iniquity, it is swiftly falling and crushing all who cling to it in mind.

Now, dearest ones, let us lift up our hearts together with our hands to God; [fol. 328] let us anticipate his face in confession, so that at the approaching feast he may visit us in his salvation and, when we meet him at his coming, may place us in the heavenly palace: Where, O . . .

## ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

[Col. 1077]

[Col. 1077C] “Blessed are those servants whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching” (Luke 12). If any one of you, dearest ones, expected his master to come to him by night, he would await his arrival with complete wakefulness; he would hasten with the utmost zeal to welcome him when he came, so as to commend himself the more to his favor. Behold, our true Lord announces that he will come to us, his unworthy little servants. He declares blessed those who await his coming vigilantly and meet him as he comes. Therefore, since we do not know the day or the hour when he will come, each one of us must strive to keep watch in good conduct, lest, coming in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning, he find us unprepared (Mark 13).

The Lord comes in the evening when he commands someone to depart this life in old age. He comes at midnight [Col. 1077D] when he calls someone in youth by an unexpected death. He arrives at cockcrow when he commands anyone to die in adolescence. He comes upon him in the morning when he takes someone away in childhood. Blessed, therefore, are those whom he finds watching in faith and action, because they shall feast with him at the eternal banquet. But exceedingly unhappy are those whom he finds given over to the sleep of sloth, because he will separate them from his elect and assign them their portion with the hypocrites—that is, with the demons (Matt. 24).

And it should be noted that the Lord [Col. 1078C] is said to be coming not in the day but in the night, because no one knows beforehand when he will come. For if the householder knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly keep watch and would by no means permit his house to be broken into and his possessions taken away (Luke 12). The house is our body; the householder is the soul; the thief is death. It comes at night when it unexpectedly oppresses a person. It finds the master asleep when it finds the soul sluggish in good works. It breaks into the house, because it immediately kills the body. But, when the master has been killed, it takes away his goods, because it tears the miserable soul away from the goods of eternal life and drags it to Tartarus to be tormented.

Night is known to have twelve hours, divided into four watches, each watch being assigned three [fol. 328v] hours. Human life is compared with night [Col. 1078D] because it is darkened by the shadows of ignorance. It is measured by twelve hours because the present life revolves through twelve months. It is divided into four watches because the year is measured by four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Three hours are assigned to each watch because three months are allotted to each season. The four watches are also understood as the four ages, in which those who keep good watch shall be rewarded with a heavenly prize. Of these watches the Lord says: “If he comes in the second watch, and if in the third watch, blessed are those whom he finds watching” (Luke 12).

The first watch is childhood. Those keep good watch in it who preserve innocence. These immediately open to the Lord when he knocks, when they receive death without fear, because they know that they will soon reign with Christ.

The second watch is adolescence. Those keep vigilant guard in it who do not defile themselves with the enticements of the flesh. These likewise joyfully open the door to the Lord when he comes, because they hope that after death they will receive joys.

The third watch is youth. In it those vigilantly await the Lord who are not overcome by worldly desires but are exercised in the divine commandments. These too eagerly run to the Lord [Note: [Col. 1079D] Read: “meet him.”], because they soon reap in joy what they sowed in tears (Ps. [Col. 1079B] 125).

The fourth watch is old age. In it those await the Lord by watching who persevere in good action to the end. These receive the long-desired Lord with rejoicing, because they immediately receive from him the denarius of life for their labor.

For, as we are now about to celebrate, the heavenly King comes into the Babylon of this world to receive for himself his bride, the Church. He entrusted her to his servants to guard, while he himself went up to heaven to prepare the banquet. He commanded his servants to keep watch, so that at whatever hour he should arrive they might be ready to meet him with lamps. He promised, moreover, that he would come with great splendor and lead his bride into the city prepared for her. O exceedingly blessed are those who are ready then to meet him! For they shall enter with him into the joy [Col. 1079C] of their Lord, to the wedding feast, and, set over all his goods, shall rejoice in heaven. Alas! How exceedingly miserable are those then found asleep in sins, because, now that the door is shut, they are excluded from the eternal feast (Matt. 25).

Therefore, dearest ones, since we do not know the hour of Christ’s coming—that is, the day of our death [fol. 330]—let us all alike, young men and virgins, old men with younger ones, keep watch in good works. Let us anticipate the face of the Lord in confession, so that at his Nativity we may worthily receive the sacrament of his body, and so that, when he comes a second time, we may appear with him in glory.

Moreover, the whole duration of this age is compared with night, upon which the clear day of the age to come rises, illumined by the Sun of righteousness. [Col. 1079D] For just as the time of night, compared with the light of day, is darkened with grim gloom, so the light of all the days of this age, compared with the light of the days of the age to come, is reckoned utterly dense darkness. O what splendor, and what glory, is proclaimed of the light of that day, which is illumined by the very Sun of angels, whose beauty this sun and moon here admire! O what grace belongs to that day, which all angels and all saints shall illuminate, each of whom will shine sevenfold more than this sun!

And if this world, illumined by only one sun, is proclaimed so beautiful, what must be thought of that life which is illumined by so many suns? But perhaps someone says: “This [Col. 1080A] sun gives forth great light because it shines with a great body; but what light can souls give forth, however serene they may be, when they are altogether small?” Certainly this sun is bounded by our eyes; its ray is not permitted to penetrate [Note: [Col. 1079D] Read: “to penetrate.”] any body placed in its way; it is covered by clouds and wholly hidden from us at night. But angelic spirits and the souls of saints are comprehended by no bodily place; they are believed to be bounded only by God, who is incomprehensible and unbounded, and are known to penetrate by the light of their brightness all things standing in their way. Each, illumined by the eternal Sun, shares its immeasurable radiance with that day, and they delight one another with reciprocal brightness. The proclamations of all the prophets sang of the incomparable glory of this day, because this [Col. 1080B] day is better than thousands of years.

Thus the night of this period is divided, as it were, into four watches, because this world is distinguished by four intervals.

The first watch was from Adam to Noah. In it a few, keeping wakeful watch in goodness, escaped danger; but the flood submerged those oppressed by the sleep of wickedness.

The second watch extended from Noah to Moses. In it those who watched well deserved to enjoy converse with God, while those burdened by the sleep of negligence [fol. 330v] were partly consumed by sulphur and fire and partly swallowed up by the Red Sea.

The third watch was from Moses to Christ. In it cocks gave their song, as it were, from midnight onward, [Col. 1080C] when Moses, the Law, the prophets, and the writings awakened sleepers to the praise of God. Those watching in the commandments of the Lord took possession of the land flowing with milk and honey; those given over to the torpor of sloth perished in captivity and wars.

The fourth watch extends from Christ’s coming to the end of the world. In it Christ, the true Morning Star, appeared, through whom it became manifest that the rising of the eternal day was at hand. In it noble cocks awakened the slothful from sleep with wings and voices, when the apostles and their followers, by deeds and words, urged all nations to awake to the light of the true day. In it the vigilant will be made glad by the Bridegroom’s coming, but those enveloped in the sleep of error [Note: [Col. 1080D] Read: “of error.”] will be devoured by a torrent of fire. Three hours are assigned to each of these watches [Col. 1080D] because in each of these periods the righteous are known to have possessed faith in the Holy Trinity.

The guardians of these four watches, therefore, instructed us to watch by teaching us with words and examples the four principal virtues.

For the observers of the first watch instructed us in prudence; the watchmen of the second, in fortitude; the guardians of the third, in justice; and the warriors of the fourth watch, in temperance. And because the righteous in these four watches awaited Christ’s coming, four Sundays are accordingly appointed for the Advent of the Lord. And because the four elements of the world are to be purified at his second [Col. 1081A] coming, the Church, divided into four parts, customarily celebrates his coming with fourfold offices.

In the dark night of these times certain stars shone joyfully at diverse times and poured their light upon us; although they could not dispel the horror of the night, they nevertheless marked out beforehand the way for those journeying toward the true Sun.

In the first watch Abel shone like a star: he taught us to die for righteousness, when he himself, innocent, fell. After him others glimmered like stars in the night: Enos taught us through piety to call upon God; Enoch, through purity, to walk with God; and Lamech, through devout action, to hope for the rest to come.

[Col. 1081B] In the second watch others shone forth like the stars of heaven [fol. 332]: Noah showed us uprightness, Shem modesty, Heber steadfastness, Melchizedek devotion, Abraham faith, Lot hospitality, Isaac obedience, Jacob endurance, and Joseph chastity.

In the third watch varied clusters of stars painted the night with their rays: Moses taught us gentleness; Phinehas zeal; Joshua constancy; Job patience; Gideon trust; Samuel temperance; David humility; Solomon prudence; Hezekiah supplication; Josiah religion; Elijah abstinence; Elisha honorableness; Isaiah (as printed) holiness; and Jeremiah sincerity. The twelve prophets [Col. 1081C] likewise gleamed as the Pleiades (as printed), as they instructed us in concord; [Col. 1082A] and Ezekiel showed us kindness, Daniel faithfulness, the three youths praise, Tobias almsgiving, Esther honorableness, Judith modesty, and the Maccabees endurance, by their examples.

In the fourth watch Mary, virgin and star of the sea, gleamed with a splendid flame, showing by humility and chastity the way to the eternal Sun. In it also John the Baptist shone like a wandering star, first teaching sinners repentance. In this watch too Christ, the true Morning Star, the glory of the stars and light of angels, shone forth; he established the radiance of the eternal day by instructing us in charity. In it likewise shining stars scattered their flame-bearing radiance across the world: the apostles taught us love; the martyrs, fortitude; the confessors, sobriety; the hermits [Col. 1082B] mortification; the virgins, chastity; and the widows, continence. All these shone as stars in this night and offered us a path toward the eternal Sun.

But when this night has passed, the true Sun shall shine in his power, when the Son of God, the splendor of the Father, shall shine in his majesty for judgment. Then he shall illuminate with eternal brightness the moon—that is, the Church—freed from darkness, and shall transform all the stars into the glory of the sun. Then he shall reward the watchmen of these watches, when, passing on from judgment, he shall minister eternal sweetness to them at the wedding feast of the Lamb.

Therefore, dearest ones, in this Advent of the Lord let us live soberly, justly, and devoutly, so that at the second Advent we may joyfully receive him and reign with him eternally [Col. 1082C]: “Where eye has not . . .” (1 Cor. 2).

If a powerful man has died and is to be buried, the people are to be admonished in this manner.

[Col. 1081]

[Col. 1081C] [Fol. 332v] “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14). There are three deaths: one good and to be desired by all; another evil and to be avoided by all; a third miserable and to be endured by all. Whoever, leaving the world for God, crucifies himself to vices and desires, is dead to the world but lives to God; and because he dies to sin, his life is hidden with Christ in God. Blessed are those thus dead, who so die in the Lord, because they shall be made alive in Christ, who is eternal life. This is the precious death of the saints, through which the life of angels is acquired. Whoever dies this death shall never die eternally.

Moreover, the bodily death of the righteous is called sleep, through which eternal rest is granted, as it is written: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 126). But those who commit mortal sin die in soul, because they are abandoned by God, who is life. Those dead by this death bury the dead when they deceive their fellow sinners by flattery. “The death of sinners is very evil” (Ps. 33), because it leads to the company of demons. Let us all flee this death, but desire that one, so that we may live eternally. The bodily death of the wicked is called destruction, through which they are snatched away to eternal punishment.

The third death is that of the body, common to all, by which every human being dies because of Adam’s sin and is led by personal merit either to joy or to torment [Col. 1082C]. Hence Scripture says: “A heavy yoke is upon all the children of Adam, from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40). All people are called children of Adam because all are born from his seed. The heavy yoke is the labor by which a human being is oppressed here; the strap is the continual misery by which he is bound. This yoke is upon all people from the day when they are brought forth from their mothers until the day when they return to the earth, the mother of all. For as a bird is born for flight, so a human being is born for the torment of labor (Job 5).

Wishing to free us from this yoke, the Lord commanded us to take up his sweet yoke and light burden (Matt. 11); he commanded the weary and burdened to come to him, the living fountain, so that we might find rest [Col. 1082D] for our souls (ibid.). Therefore, while we have the light of life, let us run to this fountain of life by confessing and repenting of our sins, lest, suddenly overtaken by the darkness of death (John 12), we should wish to do so yet be wholly unable. For if a person delays, death does not delay.

And since we know neither the day nor the [fol. 334] hour of our death, let us all remain vigilant in good deeds, so that on the day of death we may joyfully meet the Lord, cease at last from labor, and be able to rest in joy. “The life of man upon earth is warfare, and his days are like those of a hired laborer” (Job 7). The hired laborer greatly longs for the day of his agreed term to arrive, so that, having received his wages, he may depart free from labor. [Col. 1083A] So the day of death is the day of release from labor, when one who has worked all day in the vineyard of the Lord—that is, has labored all his life in the law of the Lord—shall carry away the denarius of life (Matt. 20). But one who, like a barren fig tree, occupied the ground (Luke 13), and who, like a withering branch, did not bear fruit (John 15), shall be cut away from Christ the vine by the axe of death and cast into the fire of Gehenna (Matt. 7).

God has fixed for all people a limit of life which no one can pass beyond. Yet many do not reach the appointed limit because they lose the time of life through evil works. And therefore, because the wicked never think that they will die, they are all seized by sudden death; but because the righteous continually reflect that they must depart from here, they are never overtaken by sudden death. The Lord says: “If the householder knew [Col. 1083B] at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly watch and would not allow his house to be broken into” (Luke 12). The day of death shall come like a thief in the night. A thief coming at night and finding the householder asleep breaks into the house; after killing him, he plunders his goods. So, when unexpected death comes and finds the soul sluggish in good work, it breaks into the house of the body, extinguishes the soul, takes from it the pleasures of life, and drags it away to unforeseen punishments.

For the days of a human being decline like a shadow and fly past like a cloud driven by the wind. What indeed is a human being but rottenness? And what is the son of man but a worm? A human being, conceived from unclean seed, is born of a frail woman and lives here for a short time; he is moved like a reed by temptations and filled with many miseries (Job 14). Like a flower he comes forth in childhood; [Col. 1083C] in youth he is worn down by various pains; in old age, failing in strength, he passes away like a shadow; and in death, decaying, he is received again into the womb of the earth.

Every human being enters the world with pain and departs it again with pain. As soon as he is born, he cries out, thereby foretelling that labor and pain lie before him. Then, expending all his effort in superfluous toil like a spider [fol. 334v], he stores up wealth, not knowing for whom he gathers it (Ps. 38). After a little while he leaves his riches to others, and only the grave shall be his house forever (Ps. 48); and thus the human being shall inherit worms, beasts, and serpents. For the flesh is partly turned into worms, partly consumed by them, and partly reduced to decay and then to dust; [Col. 1083D] the marrow, however, is said to turn into serpents, and the brain into toads. And because a human being consented with the serpent in sinning, he dies and, after death, is therefore justly turned into serpents.

Scripture says: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7). At a feast people forget death and eternal life; in mourning for a dead person they remember their own death to come. If people reported to us that they die, perhaps we would not believe them; yet every day we see the dead before our eyes, and we think ourselves eternal. Behold him whose body you now see: he was the flower of the world, the glory of his country, the honor of the kingdom, the entire ornament of his race; he was honored by princes, revered by equals, feared by subjects, honored by all the people. Now, if you remove the cloak that covers him, [Col. 1084A] even you who were his closest friends shudder to look at him or approach him, and you judge even the poorest living person better than he. Moreover, if after a few days you saw him in the grave, you would certainly flee as far as possible from the stench of his decay; for the fatter anyone has been, the more intolerable his stench will be.

Today, dearest ones, pray for his soul; offer the saving sacrifice for him, so that God may forgive all his offenses and, as here he associated him with the faithful, so there may associate him in glory with the saints.

For this reason also the bodies of the dead are brought to church: that the prayer of the gathered people may aid them. And just as those dying to sins and to the world are buried through baptism in the death of Christ, in the womb of Mother Church, [Col. 1084B] so those dead in flesh are covered with earth in the bosom of the Church, so that when the faithful gather there, they may see their graves, pour out prayers for them, and keep in mind what is to come to themselves. It does no harm to the righteous if they are buried outside the cemetery of the Church; conversely, it profits the impious nothing if they are buried in a church. We perform their rites according to the rite of the Lord’s death because we believe that those dying [or: dead] in the Lord are participants in his death. We place them in graves [fol. 336] facing east because we know that they shall rise, just as we see the sun rise daily in the east.

On the first day we labor especially for them, so that we may help them while they stand before the Judge; for after death, that judgment is imposed upon each person by which [Col. 1084C] the whole human race will be judged at the end. But glory or punishment is then doubled when the body is reunited with the soul.

We observe the seventh day so that whatever they committed during the seven days of the week may be forgiven them. We observe the thirtieth so that what they sinned during the thirty days of the month may be remitted.

We commemorate the anniversary so that the sin they committed throughout the whole year may be wiped away.

Dearest ones, you ought to pray frequently for all the faithful departed, especially for your relatives. For just as one walking in heat and thirsting is refreshed by a fountain of cold water, so those set in punishments are refreshed by your prayers [Col. 1084D] or alms. When you pray for the good, it benefits them for honor and you for salvation; and your prayer shall return into your own bosom, because they pray that each person may be joined with them in glory. But when you pray for those who are in punishment, you also free yourselves, because one who prays for another frees himself. But one must not pray for the condemned—that is, pagans, Jews, heretics, and evil Catholics—lest your prayer become sin, because, as Scripture says, one who prays for an impious person blasphemes God.

The righteous, when dying, are received by angels as a bride and led with heavenly harmony into the joy of the Lord. But some, less fully corrected, will be purified by certain punishments, the least of which are said to surpass the greatest [Col. 1085A] punishments of this world. Some are tormented by excessive heat, some by the greatest cold, some by great stench, while others are punished by the horror of darkness. And just as here they are subject to different sins, so there they are afflicted with different punishments; the measure of punishment extends according to the measure of sin. All these will be freed by the prayers, vigils, fasts, and alms of the righteous and joined with the saints in joy. Yet these things will profit only those who, while living, did them for others.

The damned in hell will be tormented by diverse punishments according to their diverse deserts, one less and another more, but will never be freed. We would pray for the dead in vain if we did not hope that we ourselves shall rise. But all the dead shall rise at the age and stature [Col. 1085B] at which Christ rose [fol. 336v], namely thirty years of age: an infant of one night old as much as a person of nine hundred years (as printed). Then “the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13); and “as one is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, another the glory of the stars” (1 Cor. 15), so too there shall be diversity among the righteous. “Star differs from star in glory” (ibid.), and so too is the resurrection of the dead, because the learned, like the splendor of the firmament, instructing many unto righteousness, shine like stars in the glory of the righteous (Dan. 12).

All indeed shall shine like the sun, but some before others, as certain stars shine before other stars; others before these, as the moon gleams before the stars; and again others shine in glory before these, as the sun radiates before the moon. Thus, dearest ones, the blessed shall be made alive in glory who here die in the Lord to sins. [Col. 1085C] But those dead in soul who do not rise here through repentance shall perish eternally when dead in body. We read many things about souls often freed by the saving sacrifice or by alms, but we wish to relate a few to you.

A certain priest was bathing for his health in hot waters springing from the earth. In that very heat he found a man standing there, and the man rendered service to the priest as he entered and left the bath. One day the priest brought him bread out of charity, but [Col. 1086A] he refused to receive it. Sorrowful and anxious, he said that he had been a human being and had undergone that punishment after death for his sins; he asked that the priest offer that same bread to God for him, and said that if the priest returned and did not find him, he should know that he had been freed. Having said this, he vanished, and it became clear that he had been a spirit. The priest returned to the church and labored for him for a week with vigils, fasts, and prayers; he offered the saving sacrifice; then, going to the bath, he did not find the man, because he had now reached refreshment.

A certain soldier is captured in war, bound with chains, and shut up in prison. His wife, thinking him dead, offered the sacrifice for him daily. After thirty days he was delivered from his distress and returned home. To his rejoicing wife he related how, every day for thirty days, [Col. 1086B] some comfort (as printed) had come to him, and at last, when his chains were loosed and the prison opened, he himself had gone out free. From this it is clear that, if his soul had been in punishments, it would certainly have been freed just as his body was freed from prison.

Another soldier, wounded in battle, fell among the wounded; then, recovering his breath, he rose and went away. He was seized by enemies and bound in chains, but [fol. 338] the tightness of the chains was immediately loosened. When he was bound repeatedly and as often freed from his bonds, while all wondered and were astonished at the strange occurrence, someone said that he was skilled in an art by which he knew how to undo a knot. He denied that he had learned any such art, saying that he had a brother who was a priest, whom he thought had offered sacrifice to the Lord for him, and that in this way his bond had been loosed. And so it was. For, having been released by the enemy, [Col. 1086C] he returned to his own people and learned that his brother had celebrated Masses daily for him as though he were dead.

Behold how great is the power of the prayer of the righteous, devoutly offered for the spirits of the dead: by it even the captive bodies of the living are redeemed. Therefore, dearest ones, let us pray diligently for the departed, and prayer will one day be offered for us when we are dead. But if we neglect this, we too shall be neglected by the living. If we have lived well, certainly we shall not need prayer, but shall be with Christ in heavenly glory: “Which eye has not . . .” (1 Cor. 2).

## COMMENDATION OF THIS WORK

[Col. 1085]

[Col. 1085D] There are many sermons of the saints, diverse homilies upon the Gospels, passions of martyrs, and lives of saints, by all of which those who burn for heavenly things and desire to kindle others by the word may abundantly instruct the Christian people. But I ask those laboring in the Charybdis of secular philosophy not to despise this little scrap of divine law, knowing that it was written not for them but for the citizens of Jerusalem—that is, the humble—for whom alone the heavenly kingdom is promised as to sons. But the citizens of Babylon, namely the proud, are abundantly instructed by their own teachers. Let them rely on the teachings of those whose life they most earnestly imitate.

And therefore, those who embrace the trifles of worldly speculation should read Plato; those delighted by quibbling should study Aristotle; lovers of wars have Maro; those devoted to lust, Naso; Lucan and Statius spur on the contentious; Horace and Terence instruct the wanton. But because their names have been erased from the book of the living, I shall not remember their names upon my lips.

But I, the humble defender of humble Jesus Christ, instructed in humility, chastity, mercy, and concord, have taught those hastening toward life. Entering a great forest, I plucked diverse branches; from a broad field I gathered flowers of many colors; weaving a beautiful mitre, I placed it upon the head of Christ’s bride [Col. 1087A]. Sitting in Peter’s little boat [fol. 338v], I plaited a line to catch Gospel fish, by which I too desire with all my heart to be drawn out of the whirlpool of the world. For those hungering for righteousness and suffering the hunger of the word of God, I prepared a dish from sweet-smelling herbs, lest they fail on the way for want of bread. Drawing sweet drops from the great sea, I gathered them and, as it were, let them fall upon the lips of the thirsty.

But those accustomed to splendid [Col. 1088A] feasts should go to tables set with abundant dishes, which Augustine, Gregory, and their like—the stewards of highest wisdom—have prepared and with every good thing have filled their guests. Yet those entangled in various occupations should strive to do and teach these few things, and, with the Lord’s help, rejoice that they shall attain everlasting glory together with them. Through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## AT THE ASSEMBLY OF THE BRETHREN

[Col. 1087]

[Col. 1087A] “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118). We ought to consider, brothers, who we are and where we are, whence we have come, and what we shall be. Certainly we are citizens of Jerusalem, but alas! we are certainly placed in Babylon. We came from our homeland into exile; from life we shall pass into death. For the heavenly King established glorious soldiers in his most splendid palace and wished us to enjoy the beauty of his inestimable glory. But alas for us, most miserable people! We willingly fled our Lord and King; as deserters we followed a deceitful robber, a cruel brigand, an apostate thief. We abandoned our pleasant homeland, immeasurable glory, and abundance of every delight; deceived, we came into exile, into danger [as printed: *peraculum*], into labor and pain, distress and every misery.

But it did not suffice this most deceptive deceiver to strip us of glory and seduce us into this calamity; he also taught some to run after him by public paths and others by hidden tracks, [Col. 1087C] so that he might lead them from exile into eternal destruction. The public roads are murder, adultery, theft, perjury, idolatry, and lust, because almost everyone knows that those proceeding by these ways are heading toward ruin; and those who do such things go knowingly and with open eyes toward death. But the hidden tracks are heresies, sects, false righteousness, vain glory, pretenses, empty traditions, immoderate fasts, unsuitable vows or sacrifices in forbidden places, or assemblies in improper places. These ways seem righteous to human beings [fol. 340], but are evil before the Lord; and therefore their end leads to destruction. Those who walk by them are dragged to Tartarus [Col. 1088A] as blind and ignorant persons.

But our King, taking pity on his former soldiers as they fell through the precipices of vices toward destruction, sent his Son to lead them back to their lost warfare by the path of virtues. He taught us to avoid the ways of the impious, [Col. 1088B] to walk by the way of charity, and so return from this Babylon to the heavenly Jerusalem. This indeed is the way of the righteous, this the straight path of the upright, leading those who walk by it to the courts of the blessed. Blessed are the undefiled on this way, who walk in the law of the Lord. The law of the Lord is to love God and neighbor and, by this law and along this way, direct one’s steps toward the homeland of paradise.

As we return by this way, wisdom, our guiding leader, ought to lead us; the knowledge of sacred Scripture ought to shine before us like a lamp; heavenly joy ought to draw us; fear of Gehenna ought to impel us; and, lest we be allowed to turn from the royal road either right or left, counsel on one side and discernment on the other ought to mark out the straight path. But lest we fail upon this way, it is necessary that, when wearied, we frequently be refreshed with the bread [Col. 1088C] of reading and prayer. And lest, perhaps, our footing slip and we fall, Saint Benedict has stretched along the length of the way a rule like a measuring rod, by which we may be supported. If we take care to lean upon it with all our strength, we shall enter the royal city in triumph with uninjured foot.

Many and diverse paths lead into this way: the instruction and study of righteousness show these paths, and those who travel each one separately are led into the way of charity and through it into the heavenly homeland. These are the paths which tend on both sides toward charity:

> These are the many rules by which the saints govern conduct;  
> Those who proceed by them turn toward heavenly joys.

These, most beloved, are the paths of the righteous which, through the breadth of charity, lead to the banquets of the blessed. The patriarchs marked these out for us by their examples; the prophets showed them beforehand by their writings. Along these the apostles walked as forerunners; these the martyrs trod. The virgins made them level by their going; the widows wore them smooth. Eager boys ran upon them; by these all the righteous reached the heavenly kingdoms. But from this royal road very many byways turn aside, and those who walk by them proceed to destruction. These, then, are the paths that deviate from the way of charity:

(fo. 348v) These, most beloved, are the ways of the wicked, which lead to fellowship with demons. Whoever have walked by them shall burn eternally in the lake of fire and sulphur. Let us therefore shun them with all our effort; but let us walk with all desire along the paths of the righteous, so that we may deserve to reach those whom we rejoice have gone before us. Let us remember that we have left the world for the heavenly homeland, and that we have undertaken cloistered servitude for eternal freedom. For the observance of cloistered discipline is like the testing of a furnace, in which the rust of our sins ought to be purged and the image of God re-formed in our souls. But after we have been tested like gold in the fire of tribulation, [Col. 1092C] then, taken from the furnace, we shall be made equal to the angels in the palace of the heavenly King.

For we who are called monks are counted among the martyrs, if we match our profession by our deeds. The martyrs indeed suffered grievous but brief punishments; we, however, endure prolonged martyrdoms. For cloistered confinement, regular strictness, the lowliness of garments, continual silence, a rule imposed by another, frequent fasts, constant scourgings, unceasing vigils, the watches of the daily hours, moreover the shame of confession, the bitterness of penance, public rebuke before the brethren, bodily chastisement, persistence in prayers, watchfulness in readings—all these are torments of the flesh. [Col. 1092D] Therefore, by as much as the price of gold differs from silver, so much does the reward of our recompense differ from that of other righteous people. Other righteous people served God according to their own will and gave up what they chose; but we, subjected to the yoke of obedience and bound by the reins of regular precepts, do not follow ourselves but another who commands us, just as a beast follows one who threatens it [the text reads *sequitur*, “follows”]. For we are Christ’s beasts of burden, and therefore God has prepared pastures for us in sweetness.

Let us recognize that we are labourers in the Lord’s vineyard; let us bear the burden and heat of the day patiently and perseveringly, so that, when our work is complete, we may rest with Christ our rewarder. In the camp of the highest King, like soldiers ready for battle, we keep watch; night and day, standing in the battle-line, we labour by fighting against our enemies. [Col. 1093A] Therefore, most beloved, let us consider our habit in accordance with the form of the Lord’s cross; let us know that the world is crucified to us and we to the world. Bearing the banner of the cross through patience, let us hasten upon the way of charity; against the battle-lines of vices, [Col. 1094A] let us fight manfully with the weapons of virtues (fo. 348), so that, as victors, we may joyfully reach the King of glory and, triumphing in the heavenly court amid the multitude of angels, rejoice forever with Christ, crowned with laurels. Where the eye—

## To an Assembly of the People

[Col. 1093]

[Col. 1093A] Blessed are they who love you, Jerusalem, and who rejoice in your peace. For, most beloved, since today you, God’s animals, have gathered in greater numbers to the pastures of life, and have judged it best to relieve your hunger for hearing the word of God with the food of Scripture, new and old things from the Lord’s treasury ought to be served to you [Col. 1093B] according as the good shepherd has ordained that they be dispensed to sheep and goats.

For although one profession of the Christian religion gathers you all, as it were, into one flock, I greatly fear that in the end the judgment of the highest shepherd will not establish you all in one sheepfold. Diversity of conduct will indeed produce diversity of places. For many of you willingly hear the word of God and more willingly fulfil it in deed. These belong to Christ’s sheep, and these will stand at his right hand in judgment. Yet very many among you neglect to hear the word of God and scorn to fulfil it in deed. There are also many who are tormented by God’s words and, while we offer salutary admonitions in truth, [Col. 1093C] abhor Christ. These assuredly belong to the goats, and these will stand on the left. We must therefore set forth what is fitting for sheep and what is appropriate to goats.

But when the true shepherd comes, he will separate you from one another, as sheep from goats (Matt. 25); the sheep, indeed, he will place in a pasture where they will lack nothing (Ps. 22), but the goats he will consign to hell, where death shall feed upon them (Ps. 48).

Indeed, brethren, there are two cities: one is Jerusalem and the other is called Babylon. The king of the former is Christ, of the latter the devil. The citizens of both are mingled here and, as it were, enrolled in a single militia; yet they burn with great discord against one another, now secretly and now openly fiercely attacking each other. [Col. 1093D] This conflict will last as long as this world endures. But at last the citizens of Jerusalem shall triumph with their king in the heavenly court, while the citizens of Babylon shall be tormented with eternal punishments alongside their king in the prison of hell.

For almighty God, the supreme craftsman, founded in the heights that most splendid city, Jerusalem (fo. 348v), in which he established a most brilliant commonwealth in a most fitting order: he constituted the most excellent of the archangels as a kind of venerable senate, and arranged the remaining ranks of angels like the legions of an invincible army. In this commonwealth a certain prince seized tyranny, first bringing civil war upon his companions when Lucifer the archangel wished to be like the most high emperor. [Col. 1094A] When, therefore, Michael the archangel, prince of the army of the heavenly host, joined battle with him, he emerged victorious, expelled him and all his followers from the boundaries of the heavenly city, and compelled them to undergo the exile of this world.

And while in exile [Col. 1094B] he not only still rebelled but also shamelessly usurped a kingdom for himself, the eternal Emperor planted paradise, like a fortress in a most delightful place. There he placed the first man as a kind of prince to overthrow the tyrant; but the tyrant, having deceived him by guile, subjected him to his dominion and compelled him, taken captive, to depart with him into exile. In exile the man begot two human beings, one a citizen of the earthly city and the other of the heavenly. Civil discord immediately arose between them, Abel was killed by Cain, and another citizen of Jerusalem, namely Seth, was born in his place.

Cain, then, citizen of the earthly city, first founded a city, under whose dominion the army of King Devil [Col. 1094C] increased; it perished in the flood with all its people. But Seth, who possessed here no abiding city (Heb. 13), but acquired the future city, not made by hands but eternal in the heavens (2 Cor. 5), led forth Christ’s army, which sheltered from the storm of the flood in the ark as in a fortress. Then, from the ark—as previously from paradise—two armies emerged through two human beings, as from a city into the field of battle, when the elect came forth from Shem and the reprobate from Ham. Shem, citizen of heavenly Jerusalem, founded earthly Jerusalem as an image of that city above, in which the army of the elect mourned that it was in pilgrimage.

But Nimrod the giant, of the seed of Ham, founded Babylon, in which the army of the reprobate, under [Col. 1094D] the dominion of King Devil, gloried in reigning.

Meanwhile, the people of God, dwelling as strangers in Egypt, were grievously afflicted by Pharaoh, king of the unrighteous party; but they were wonderfully delivered by their own king through signs and portents. (fo. 350) They were led out across the Red Sea with dry feet; Pharaoh, pursuing with all his people, was submerged by the waves.

The king of the heavenly city gave his army guidance by a pillar of fire at night and a cloud by day. He fed them for forty years with angelic bread containing every delight of sweetness; refreshed them with honey-sweet water brought forth from the rock; and brought them into a land flowing with milk and honey. Having defeated their enemies on every side, he restored the city Jerusalem to Melchizedek, king of righteousness. There David the king, as a figure of Christ, [Col. 1095A] was the leader of this army; he taught the Lord’s army, here as pilgrims and strangers, to seek the homeland yet to come.

But Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon and leader of the unrighteous party, besieging Jerusalem, took the people of God captive and tormented them for seventy years with various injuries. Yet their king delivered them again and restored their lost camps. Therefore, when war was growing fiercer on both sides and no one came to the aid of those labouring, the King of glory descended from the hall of heaven, clothed himself with the breastplate of flesh, and brought prompt aid to his soldiers. For he immediately joined battle with the tyrant, prince of this world, with his own hand; having conquered him, he pursued him in flight after laying aside the breastplate of flesh, captured him together with Queen Death and bound him in the abyss, overthrew his kingdom, and from there freed his captives. [Col. 1095B]

He put on again the flesh he had laid aside, a garment fitted for battle; led the chosen cohort of apostles and legion of martyrs into the densely packed wedges of the enemy; and commanded that the citizens of Babylon be attacked on every side. Then, returning to heaven’s citadel, he sent the Holy Spirit and gave his people steadfastness of heart and hope of victory. Moreover, he directed numerous hosts of confessors, virgins, and other faithful persons into the battle line, and set before the victors the prizes of crowns. Thus, with such a selection by the highest Emperor, [the Church] fought manfully against the princes of darkness and spiritual wickedness with the armour of God; and, clad in the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of God’s word, [it] fought strenuously against its adversaries (Eph. 6).

[Note: [Col. 1095D] Something appears to be missing.]

When Antichrist comes to aid the enemies with all his forces, [Col. 1095C] he will spread all the legions of the wicked through Christ’s camps. But afterward the King will quickly assist his soldiers labouring in battle and will at last set an end to the war so long prolonged. For he will cast Babylon (fo. 350v), publicly rebellious, with her king and all her people into the lake of fire and sulphur; crowning with glory and honour and joining to himself his bride, long a pilgrim here—indeed, a captive. After victory, he will summon his soldiers, crowned with laurels, to the wedding feast; and attended by these in triumphant glory, while the court of angels rejoices, the King of glory will enter heavenly Jerusalem, to reign there eternally in peace.

Blessed, therefore, are those who love this Jerusalem and rejoice in her peace. They love her who believe the things said of her and of [Col. 1095D] her king Christ, and who fulfil his commandments in deed. They rejoice in her peace who subdue by virtues the vices of the flesh that fight against the spirit, and who, through love of heavenly peace, rest in the tranquillity of spiritual life apart from the tumults of the world and the noise of worldly business.

For the Church—that is, the people of the faithful—is called Jerusalem from the first Abel to the last elect person. Its name is interpreted “vision of peace,” because in heavenly Jerusalem it is to reign as a queen and enjoy the vision of eternal peace. This Jerusalem is built as a city from living stones, namely from all the elect; it is most fittingly ordered by laws and judgments. [Col. 1096A] The religion of this city is the worship of God; its law is love of neighbour; its pursuit is peace and concord among citizens. Its king, indeed, is the Prince of Peace. Its rulers were first the patriarchs, then the prophets, and thereafter the apostles, who established its civil laws; after them came bishops, who confirmed the decisions of their predecessors by their decrees.

The senators of this city are prelates and followers of the contemplative life. By their writings, words, or examples this commonwealth is governed, and the people of this city are fittingly ruled in conduct and discipline. The soldiers of this city are the martyrs, who fought unto death for the laws of their emperor. But the people of this city are all the faithful who live not according to man but [Col. 1096B] according to God. They are children of God and citizens of this city who live not according to themselves—that is, according to the desires of the flesh—but according to God’s will, by doing his commandments. Such are the chaste, modest, humble, merciful, kind, peaceful, and those flourishing in other virtues. This city is inhabited by such citizens, and Jerusalem is built as a city from such stones. In this city the gymnasia are exercises of virtue; the expenses for theatrical games are the performance of the divine office; the stadium in which one runs (fo. 352) is for the prize of eternal life; and the wrestling-school and contest are the struggles of the martyrs.

But the multitude of the wicked, from the first Cain to the last reprobate, is called Babylon, a name interpreted “confusion,” because it shall be clothed in eternal confusion [Col. 1096C] and, confounded, shall be removed far from the glory of heavenly Jerusalem. It is built by agreement in malice and wickedness, and formed by vices and crimes.

Its religion is idolatry; its law is the belly, gluttony, and luxury; its pursuit is civil discord. Its king, indeed, is he who always burns with envy and hatred, who was a murderer from the beginning.

The rulers of this city were first tyrants; after them, heretics, who divided it among themselves by various heresies.

Its senators were the founders of demonic worship and crimes; its soldiers, persecutors. Its people are all unbelievers and all who live not according to God—that is, according to God’s commandments—[Col. 1096D] but according to their own desires. All these are called children of the devil, since they wish to live according to themselves, subject not to God but to vices; and they are citizens of Babylon.

They are proud, insolent, malicious, unclean, rapacious, fornicators, adulterers, cruel, harsh, and enslaved to other vices. This city is gathered from such sheep, and glories in such children. But the citizens of the two cities burn against one another with grievous hatred and wage continual war on each other. For the citizens of Jerusalem attack the Babylonians with holy preaching and health-giving admonition, in order to draw them away from the devil’s snares and lead them into their own fellowship. [Col. 1097A] Conversely, Babylonian citizens attack Jerusalem’s citizens with secret hatred and open persecution, and do not cease to inflict harm not only upon them but also upon their possessions.

In this conflict Cain still deceitfully attacks his brother; Ham mocks his father; Ishmael afflicts Isaac; Esau hates Jacob; Joseph’s brothers sell him; the Egyptians oppress the Hebrews; David flees from Saul; Jezebel plots against Elijah, Herodias against John; Judas receives a price for the Lord; Simon offers a gift to Peter; and all the members of the Synagogue arm themselves against the members of the Church.

This Jerusalem is attacked outwardly by enemies and secretly assaulted inwardly by citizens. Pagans, Jews, and heretics, its enemies, attack it outwardly with a numerous army, with engines of persecution and the battering-rams [Col. 1097B] of perverse doctrines. But evil Catholics, citizens in name only but secretly enemies, attack it inwardly with depraved conduct. Yet, though it is struck by so many blows, no ruin moves it from its state of uprightness, since, founded upon Christ the firm rock, it is strengthened by him.

Often its citizens desert to the adversaries; entangled in many errors, they go mad while serving long in the tyrant’s camp. At last, grieving that they dwell with the inhabitants of Kedar, they flee through repentance to the camp of their emperor, put on the armour of righteousness, rise more fiercely against their enemies, and thus return as valiant soldiers to their king’s former favour. Conversely, citizens of Babylon often hide among Jerusalem’s citizens as false friends but true spies, feigning friendship; but when the weapons of virtue are offered them, terrified, they will flee back to their own people. [Col. 1097C]

The body of every faithful person is declared to be a fortress of this city, inhabited by the soul as prince and by the people of virtues; in it battle is waged against the army of vices. This fortress is besieged outwardly by a multitude of enemies and disturbed inwardly by a faction of citizens, when neighbours inflict outward harms upon it, while vices and desires of the flesh overwhelm its inward goods. But whoever guards this fortress by patiently enduring every adversity shall be crowned as a victor, triumphing in the palace of heavenly Jerusalem, with the laurel of highest blessedness by the King of glory.

But because the citizens of both cities are mingled here, they cannot easily be recognized, especially since they [Col. 1097D] come to church with us, receive Christ’s sacraments with us, fast with us, preach with us, and seem to perform the other works of holiness for which heavenly rewards are given to Christ’s soldiers. Yet the heavenly Emperor imposed a certain sign upon his own by which they might be known. This sign is love: “By this,” he says, “all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

At times two persons live under one monastic profession while pursuing different aims. One has wholly abandoned the world along with his habit, desires nothing earthly, flees human glory, afflicts his flesh with vigils and fasts, patiently endures every hardship, and longs with all his desires for [Col. 1098A] heavenly things. This one is indeed a citizen of Jerusalem; he serves in the army of King Christ. But the other changes his habit, not the world: he hungers after earthly things, gives himself to the desires of belly and flesh, is devoted to sluggishness and idleness, neglects God’s commandments, despises the greater admonitions, seeks human praise, and delights in every allurement. If he is perhaps corrected by another with a word of love, he immediately persecutes that person with the greatest hatred; by this he is recognized as a citizen of Babylon.

Likewise, two persons profess the canonical life, but have different practices. One lives chastely, constantly reads in rejection of the judgments of the world, devoutly performs the divine office, and instructs the people by word and example; he himself, as a guiding leader, leads them by good conduct to [Col. 1098B] the pastures of life. This one is certainly a citizen of Jerusalem. But the other, forgetful of God and his order, serves lust and luxury, pursues secular business, postpones the divine office, spends his time on games, spectacles, and hunting, neglects the salvation of the people—indeed, becomes their ruin—and by depraved conduct leads them onward to destruction. He attacks the life of the other with the greatest hatred, and by this openly shows himself to be a citizen of Babylon.

Likewise, two persons lead a lay life but live with different conduct. One, frequenting church, examines the Christian faith; turning aside from evil, he pursues good; he refreshes the poor, reconciles neighbours in peace and concord, loves his wife for the sake of offspring, and brings up his children in the fear of God. [Col. 1098C] This one, beyond doubt, is a citizen of Jerusalem. But the other devotes himself to thefts, robberies, and brigandage; he plunges himself into drunkenness, revelry, luxury, and uncleanness. He tears apart another’s life with the utmost hatred, and thus displays himself as a citizen of Babylon.

Therefore, when Babylon’s citizens hear through us the truth which they do not at all recognize in themselves, they immediately gnash their teeth against us and burn with the greatest hatred. And since they do not dare to lay cruel hands upon us, they stain our reputation by secret detraction. But when the king of the banquet enters and finds them without the wedding garment—that is, charity—he will command that, with hands and feet bound, they be cast into outer darkness; but he will make his own recline in joy and minister to them.

[Col. 1098D] Most beloved, because we useless servants scorn the life-giving commands of our emperor and, through desires of the flesh, follow the death-bringing counsels of the enemy, we are excluded not only from the palace of our king and the city of our fellow citizens—(fo. 355v) namely heavenly Jerusalem—but also here in exile we are crushed by many scourges along with our adversaries. For because of our sins there are justly brought upon us assaults of enemies or fellow citizens, the captivity of loved ones by pagans, pestilences, hunger, illnesses, the death of human beings and animals, unwholesomeness of the air, drought, rainstorms, thunder, lightning, the harmful harshness of cold, the violence of heat, wicked kings, very bad judges, blind priests, attacks by wild beasts, the loss of possessions, [Col. 1099A] and the like.

Moreover, laws are promulgated: they decree what is just and prescribe punishments, chains, tortures, scourgings, exiles, mutilations of limbs, loss of goods, various bodily torments, and deaths of diverse kinds. Crushed by so many punishments and so many evils, alas, grief upon grief, hardened, we go thence securely to outer darkness—as though beds adorned with curtains would be prepared for us there, feasts and delights arranged, servants attend us, gatherings of friends surround us, treasures be brought, and ornaments multiplied—without knowing, or rather pretending not to know, what is written: “There is neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom in hell, whither you hasten”; rather, it is “a land dark and covered with the gloom of death, where no order is and everlasting horror dwells,” [Col. 1099B] where there is a furnace of fire, in which are weeping and gnashing of teeth; unquenchable fire; a lake of fire and sulphur; lairs of dragons; dens of fiery serpents; the dreadful company of demons. Such places indeed are prepared for the enemies.

Most beloved, God created three living orders: angels, human beings, and animals. He created angels in heaven, that is, in the highest place; beasts in the lowest, that is, on earth; and placed human beings in the middle, that is, in paradise. Thus, as the human being stood lower than the angel, so he stood higher than the beast: if he kept his Creator’s commandment, he would be made equal to the angels above; but if he despised it, he would be made like the beasts below.

Therefore, when man was in the honour of paradise, he did not understand God, the giver of honour. Thus, cast [Col. 1099C] into this misery, he was compared to senseless beasts through pains and hardships, and through fleshly desires was made like them. Accordingly, even now infants are nourished with milk just as [Col. 1100A] the young of beasts are. Therefore the Son of God, equal to the Father, became mediator between God and human beings, so that man, created as the middle being between angels (fo. 356) and beasts, might return from likeness to beasts to equality with angels. He became the way in the lowest places while remaining life in the highest, so that, walking through his examples and commandments, we might joyfully attain the glory of the kingdom.

And because the human being, driven from glory into misery, is born in toil and nourished in pain, everything for which he labours he labours for two reasons: namely, to escape evil and obtain good. But what is worse than death, or better than life? Therefore, when a person ploughs, sows, reaps, gathers fruits, or undertakes any other labour, [Col. 1100B] he certainly does so in order to escape evil, namely death, and to possess good, namely life. Yet he strives in vain, since every person must at some time die, and thus the wretch is filled with many miseries: through labour he meets the death he laboured not to die.

Therefore, most beloved, since this miserable evil is unavoidable for all, let us labour with all our strength to escape the supreme evil, namely eternal death, and to possess the supreme good, namely eternal life without end. For when Christ our King comes with the winnowing fan, he will separate the chaff from the grain; by the last judgment he will burn the chaff—that is, the reprobate—in unquenchable fire, and gather the wheat—that is, the elect—into the heavenly granary. When he has made the boundaries of Jerusalem peace, [Col. 1100C] he will hand over the kingdom to God the Father, and God will be all in all. May he be blessed for ever. Amen.

## Sermon on the Dedication

[Col. 1099]

[Col. 1099C] “King Solomon made himself a litter of the wood of Lebanon; he made its columns of silver, its reclining-place of gold, its ascent of purple; he paved the midst with love for the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 3). King Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” is Christ, author of true peace, [Col. 1099D] in whom we shall have eternal peace when we shall no longer fear enemies of body or soul. He made a banqueting-house, and this from the wood of Lebanon.

Lebanon is the mountain from which the Jordan flows and on which cedars of incorruptible nature grow. By Mount Lebanon, whose name means “whitening,” is understood the exaltation of Jesus Christ. From him arises the Jordan, namely the font of baptism, in which the elect are cleansed white from the filth of vices and, growing upward in virtues like cedars, are called to the crown of unfading glory. From these our King made the house of refreshment—(fo. 356v) namely, the Church, made from the elect into a house of eternal contemplation. In such a house he made columns of silver. By silver columns are understood uprightness and firmness; by silver are signified brightness and resonance. [Col. 1100C] For the apostles and doctors were silver columns in this house: by the brightness of their lives and the resonance of their teaching they adorned the Church; upright in virtues and firm against vices, persecutors, and heretics, they sustained the structure of God’s house.

[Col. 1100D] “He made its reclining-place of gold, its ascent of purple.” Despisers of the world are called the golden reclining-place, because they are tested like gold in the furnace of tribulation; God in a manner reclines in their minds when he delights in their good deeds. But the martyrs were the purple ascent, since, dyed purple with their own blood, they ascended to heavenly things through Christ’s cross. “He paved the midst with love.” The midst, that is, the floors, were spread with marble slabs or carpets or cloths, upon which all things pertaining to charity were variously displayed in wondrous picture and weaving. By these is understood the remaining people, who are commanded to fulfil the law and the prophets in the two commandments of love.

And all this was for the daughters of Jerusalem: that is, so that [Col. 1101A] the souls of the faithful, who are daughters of Jerusalem, may imitate these things. By this court of Solomon is signified the refectory of the Church, namely this house whose annual feast we celebrate today, in which the fattened calf is daily sacrificed to God the Father for the banquet of the faithful, and the splendid cup of his blood, which brings intoxication, is drunk by the banqueters.

This festival, dearest brethren, is called the day of nuptials, because, just as a bride is joined to her bridegroom through a banquet and the crowded gathering of friends, so this building is consecrated today amid the acclamations of a great multitude, [Col. 1102A] in which the multitude of believers is joined to Christ as a bride through baptism and the body of Christ. For all who obey this church are called one Church and the bride of Christ, and they are commanded therefore to celebrate this their nuptial day with the highest joy. Therefore, dearest brethren, “appoint a solemn day in the dense throng even unto the horn of the altar” (Ps. 117), that you may deserve, “in the voice of exultation and confession, in the sound of one feasting” (Ps. 41), to pass from this life into the house of God, into “the place of the wondrous tabernacle” (ibid.). Scripture speaks to us elsewhere concerning this house.

If you wish, begin here:

[Col. 1101]

[Col. 1101A] (Fo. 358.) “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven pillars; she has set a table, sacrificed victims, mixed wine, and sent maidservants to invite people to the banquet” (Prov. 9). Wisdom, dearest brethren, which built itself a house, [Col. 1101B] is Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, who founded the Church from living and chosen stones as a dwelling-place for himself. To support this house he hewed out seven pillars, because he polished with every wisdom and knowledge the seven books called *agiographa*, that is, Sacred Scripture; by whose teaching the structure of the whole Church is so sustained toward heaven as some framework is held aloft in the air by pillars. The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit set these pillars beneath God’s building and strengthened and adorned God’s house by them.

The first pillar is the book of John, which the Spirit of wisdom raised up, for through it he brought the greatest wisdom into the Church.

The second is the Psalter, which the Spirit of understanding [Col. 1101C] supports, because in it he especially opens the mind of the Church to the understanding of spiritual things.

The third pillar is Proverbs, which the Spirit of counsel made firm, because in it he gave the Church very many counsels for life.

The fourth is Ecclesiastes, which the Spirit of fortitude fixed in place, because in it he abundantly girded the Church with strength against vices.

The fifth pillar is the Song of Songs, which the Spirit of knowledge strengthened, because in it he disclosed abundant knowledge to the Church.

The sixth is the book of Wisdom, which the Spirit of piety established, because in it he instructed the Church in the highest piety.

The seventh is the book of Ecclesiasticus, which the Spirit [Col. 1101D] of the fear of the Lord set beneath it, because in no book did he instruct the Church more fully in the fear of the Lord.

Later, distinguished painters expounded and depicted these seven pillars, set beneath the house of God by the sevenfold Spirit, and adorned God’s house with wonderful carving.

For the first, the outstanding painter Gregory, endowed with the Spirit of wisdom, decorated in a wondrous manner and graced the whole house of God with incomparable workmanship.

[Col. 1102A] Likewise, the noble painter Augustine, illustrious in the Spirit of understanding, encircled the second with varied ornament and, as it were, set the whole house all around with dazzling gems. Other men also, who loved the beauty of [Col. 1102B] the house of the Lord, made the other pillars illustrious by expounding them, as though with outstanding painting.

In such a house Wisdom set a table when she everywhere taught the faithful the sacred Scripture (fo. 358v). This table is supported by four feet, because sacred Scripture is understood in four ways.

The first foot is history, when it is received as the letter narrates it. The second is allegory, when one thing is said and another is understood. The third is morality, when conduct is shaped by what is read. The fourth is anagogy, that is, the higher sense, when heavenly and eternal things are taught.

Upon this table different persons served different dishes and satisfied the guests with varied sayings, as with varied courses. Thus Moses, when he recounted the creation of the world, the ordering of Paradise, the inundation of the Flood, Abraham’s obedience, Joseph’s chastity, the deliverance of the children of Israel, their journey through the Red Sea and the wilderness, and how manna rained upon them from heaven and water flowed from the rock, set before the feasters, as it were, sweet dishes of diverse kinds. But David and the other prophets, when they sweetly told of the sweetness of the heavenly homeland, offered sweet cups, as it were, to those at the feast. In this house Wisdom sacrificed victims when Christ offered his body to God the Father for the human race. She mixed wine when he shed his blood for our redemption. In certain places [Note: [Col. 1101D] Here the parchment is mutilated.] they mix *v[lacuna]dinem* with water; therefore they say, [Col. 1102D] “she mixed wine,” because water mingled with blood flowed from Christ’s side. To invite people to these banquets she sent not servants but maidservants, because she sent not noblemen but apostles—that is, rustic men, for example fishermen—to invite the peoples to the heavenly banquet.

This church, in which an altar is set in place of the table, bears the figure of that house. To it the people gather for a spiritual banquet; washed in the water of baptism and fed by the body and blood of Christ, while they hear diverse sayings from [Col. 1103A] the Scriptures, they draw, as it were, varied draughts of eternal sweetness. Therefore, dearest brethren, visit this holy temple of the Lord often; learn to behold the will of the Lord in it; diligently [Col. 1104A] ask one thing of the Lord, seek it often through good works: that you may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of your life (Ps. 22). Scripture speaks elsewhere concerning the construction of this building.

If you wish, begin here.

[Col. 1103]

[Col. 1103] “Behold, I send into the foundations of Zion a precious chosen cornerstone. Whoever stumbles upon it shall be broken; but he upon whom it falls shall be crushed” (Isa. 28).

Zion was the citadel of Jerusalem; its name means “watchtower,” and it is the Church, which [lacuna]

[NOTE.]

[Col. 1103] Here ends the Rhenau manuscript codex, whose gap we have no means of supplying. The Cologne edition presents here two sermons “On the Dedication of a Church,” but both differ from ours. We thought it worthwhile to append them here from the sole copy of the first edition now extant; the distinguished Count de L’Escalopier most kindly shared it with us.

TWO SERMONS FOR THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH. (*Speculum Ecclesiae, or Several Gospel Sermons Both for the Seasons and for Saints, of the holy priest Honorius of Autun, who flourished four hundred years ago and is counted among the illustrious writers of the Church.*—First edition.—Cologne, from the press of Quintel, 1531.)

[Col. 1103]

FIRST SERMON.

[Col. 1103B] Beloved brethren, we must consider the construction of this house of prayer, whose festal dedication we celebrate today. This building that you see here, whose dedication we celebrate, is called, according to the custom of the Church, a church; and “Church” means an assembly, because in it the people assemble to worship and adore God. It is joined together from four walls, because it is made firm from the four Gospels.

It has a sanctuary, in which the clergy are, and a forepart of the house, in which the people stand. So too the Church has the contemplative life, in which spiritual persons dwell, and the active life, in which secular persons are placed. The contemplative life is to abandon all earthly things for the love of God, to seek heavenly things alone, to pray continually, to read often, and ceaselessly [Col. 1104B] to praise God with hymns and songs. The active life, however, is to lead a chaste life with one’s spouse, bring up children in the fear of God, refresh the poor with food and drink, visit the sick and widows, and, for love of one’s neighbour, offer assistance according to one’s means to all who suffer need.

In the sanctuary is the altar, on which are the relics of the saints. This signifies Christ in the Church: in contemplation of him the minds of the blessed rest, and in whose presence “the righteous rejoice and feast, and delight in gladness” (Ps. 67:4).

The windows by which this basilica is illumined are the teachers through whom heavenly light enters the Church. The ceiling-painting of this *kyrica*, that is, “the Lord’s adornment,” likewise signifies the lives and examples of the saints, which every devout person imitates in the Church. [Col. 1105A] The banquet, the light by which it is illuminated, is the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which the Church is continually irradiated. The cross of Christ is fixed here and adored, and Christ’s Passion is venerated by all Christians. We follow the cross that is borne, because we must follow Christ’s footsteps if we wish to come to the heavenly temple.

The towers are the prelates of the Church; the bells are their preaching. This building signifies the temple at Jerusalem, from which the Lord drove out those buying and selling doves (Matt. 21:12). The doves are spiritual gifts. Therefore all who buy or sell churches, religious orders, or any spiritual gift are separated from this temple—that is, from the holy Church—together with Simon [Col. 1105B] Magus, and are cast into eternal fire.

All these things, dearest brethren, concern us. All these things were made for our example. We are God’s temple, dedicated as God’s dwelling-place, as it is written: “You are the temple of the living God” (2 Cor. 6:16). And again: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). “I will dwell in them,” says the Lord, “and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God. I shall also be their father, and they shall be my sons and daughters” (2 Cor. 6:18).

O how blessed is the person in whom God dwells! For just as [Col. 1105C] this house is constructed from four walls, so the temple of our body consists of four elements. And just as this building is first sprinkled with blessed water at its dedication and then consecrated with chrism, so our body is first washed in the water of baptism [Col. 1106A] and then hallowed with holy chrism.

Some basilicas are built in the shape of a cross; the body is fashioned in the shape of a cross. The sanctuary of this temple is our mind, which thinks spiritual things; the forepart of the house is the soul, which dispenses the necessities of life through the senses of the body; the altar upon which sacrifices are offered is our heart, in which pure thoughts and clean prayers are offered to God; the tower is our head; the bell is our tongue, by which we ought to call our neighbours to heavenly things. In this house the windows are our eyes, while the paintings are good works. The light of the lamp is the light of knowledge. Therefore, just as a person commits sacrilege who violates this temple, so whoever violates God’s temple [Col. 1106B] by any uncleanness or criminal sin, God will destroy and condemn that person.

At this festival this building is swept with brooms, washed with water, and richly adorned with flowers and hangings. Thus, dearest brethren, today we ought to cleanse ourselves, the temple of the Holy Spirit, with the brooms of confession, remove the dung of sins, wash ourselves with tears of repentance, and adorn ourselves with flowers of good works and the hangings of virtues. And just as Zacchaeus climbed a tree so that he might see Jesus (Luke 19:4), so let us climb the tree of charity, that we may deserve to behold Christ in the heavenly homeland. And just as Zacchaeus received him into his house and made him a banquet (ibid., v. 6), so let us receive him in the lodging of our heart and [Col. 1106C] make him a banquet through holy works, that he may deign to dwell in us and call us to the marriage-feast of the Lamb, and after the labour of this misery lead us into the temple of the eternal King in gladness and exultation. “What eye has not seen,” etc. (1 Cor. 2:9).

SECOND SERMON.

[Col. 1105]

[Col. 1105D] “Everyone who hears my words and does them is like a man building a house upon a rock” (Luke 6:48), against which rivers and winds beat; but because it is founded upon the rock, they cannot move it (ibid.). He builds a house unto heaven who places chastity upon humility, obedience upon patience, and works of mercy upon charity. He lays this house’s foundations upon Christ the rock who does everything for faith in Christ and solely for eternal reward. The rivers are human assaults, and the winds are devilish temptations. These will not prevail in undermining this house, because it is established upon Christ’s foundation; through it, one who thus builds may ascend to the summit of heaven. Blessed is the person whom the Lord chooses and receives as thus building, for he shall dwell in his courts (Ps. 64:5).

[Col. 1106D] Your charity ought to know whence the dedication of a church first arose. When Jacob had once received blessing from his father and, fleeing his brother’s rage, had fallen asleep in a field with a stone placed beneath him, he saw a ladder raised from earth to heaven, the Lord leaning upon the ladder, and angels of God descending by it and ascending into heaven. Terrified, he arose, raised the stone as an altar, consecrated it by pouring oil over it, called the place Bethel, that is, “house of God,” and, having returned from his journeying, offered sacrifice there to the Lord. It is handed down that Solomon later founded the Lord’s temple in the same place. Jacob and Esau were sons of Isaac, who was the son of Abraham. Abraham signifies God the Father; Isaac, whose name means “joy,” signifies the Son, through whom eternal joy is bestowed upon believers; and Jacob [Col. 1107A] and Esau signify the faithful and unbelieving peoples. Of these, the faithful people, like Jacob from Isaac, shall be blessed by Christ when at the final judgment it is told: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34). But the faithless people, like Esau, are deprived of the Father’s blessing when punished with the final curse: “Depart from me,” he says, “you cursed, into eternal fire” (ibid., v. 41).

Now Jacob, fleeing his brother, sleeps in a field and places a stone beneath his head, because the faithful humbly avoid the rage of unbelievers and, transferring themselves to the contemplative life, withdraw from the vices and desires of the world in a holy purpose, as though asleep. They place a stone beneath their head because they resolve to endure every hardship under Christ. They see heaven opened and behold angels ascending by the ladder, [Col. 1108A] because heavenly things are opened to such persons, and they themselves, climbing by the ladder of charity, are led into the heavenly palace. Having returned from their pilgrimage, they offer sacrifice to the Lord, because, returning from the exile of this life to the homeland of Paradise, they themselves shall be God’s sacrifice and become the temple of Christ, the true Solomon. Hence today the Church has the custom of singing Jacob’s very words at a dedication, because “this house is the court of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28:12).
