It is rightly called the court of God, because when the body of Christ, who is God of all, is made here, the host of angels is believed to stand here in attendance upon its King. It is also rightly called the gate of heaven, because when original sins are remitted here through baptism and actual sins through confession, heaven is undoubtedly opened here to believers.

[Col. 1107] The end of the Ecclesiastical Mirror of the holy Honorius, most necessary to all students of Sacred Scripture.

THE FOURTH PART OF THE WORKS OF HONORIUS OF AUTUN: DOGMATIC AND ASCETICAL.

[Col. 1109]

ELUCIDARIUM, OR A DIALOGUE ON THE SUM OF THE WHOLE OF CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY. [Note: [Col. 1109B] I have carefully collated the text of the *Elucidarium*, or *Dialogue*, which appears among the works of Anselm, with manuscript codex Paris, Royal Library, 5134. This thirteenth-century codex, badly written and showing signs of a scribe in excessive haste [Col. 1110B], nevertheless contains much that was useful to me in correcting the text. A. denotes the Paris edition of Anselm; P., the Paris manuscript codex. GILES.]

(*Works of B. Lanfranc*, ed. J. A. Giles, LL.D., priest of the Church of England, Oxford, 1844, octavo, vol. II, p. 280.—It is also found in the appendix to the *Works of St Anselm of Canterbury*, Paris edition, 1721, edited by D. Gerberon.)

PREFACE.

[Col. 1109A] Having often been asked by fellow students to resolve certain small questions, I could not resist their importunity by refusing, especially as I feared incurring that rebuke if I preferred silently to hide in the earth the talent entrusted to me. For Job says: “God shall draw out of his belly the riches which he has devoured” (Job 20:15), riches which he has concealed from one suffering hunger for the word of God. And so that my labour may benefit not only the present age, I have taken care to transmit these discussions to posterity in writing, asking that whoever undertakes to apply himself to reading them may strive to pour out prayers to God for me. Let the title *Elucidarium*, then, be placed before the work, if you please, because in it the obscurity [Col. 1110A] of diverse matters is elucidated. I wished my name, however, to be covered by silence, lest wasting envy command that a useful work be neglected out of contempt; yet the reader should ask that it be written in heaven and never erased from the book of the living. Therefore let the foundation of this little work be laid upon the rock, that is, Christ, and let the whole structure be supported by four firm pillars. Let prophetic authority raise the first pillar; apostolic dignity establish the second; the acuteness of interpreters strengthen the third; and the resourceful loftiness of teachers fix the fourth.

BOOK ONE.

[Col. 1109]

1. What God is, and how he is one and three, demonstrated by comparison with the sun.

[Col. 1109B]

DISCIPLE. Glorious master, I ask that you not be reluctant to answer my questions, for the honour of God and the benefit of the Church.—MASTER. Indeed I shall do so, insofar as

He himself grants me strength; nor shall this labour burden me.

D. It is said that no one knows what God is, and it seems very absurd to worship what we do not know. Let us therefore begin with him, and first tell me: what is God?—M. So far as a human being may know, God is a spiritual substance of such immeasurable beauty and such ineffable sweetness that the angels, who surpass the sun sevenfold in their own beauty, continually desire to gaze upon him insatiably.

D. How is the Trinity understood to be one God?—M. Look at the sun, in which are three things: namely, fiery substance, brightness, and heat. They are so inseparable [Col. 1111A] that, if you wish to separate brightness from it, you deprive the world of the sun; and if, again, you attempt to separate heat, you lack the sun. In the fiery substance, therefore, understand the Father; in the brightness, the Son; in the heat, the Holy Spirit.

2. On the names of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

D. Why is he called Father?—M. Because he is the source and origin from whom all things proceed, and whose wisdom is called the Son.

D. Why Son?—M. Because, as brightness is generated from the sun, so he is generated from the Father. The love of both is called the Holy Spirit.

D. Why Holy Spirit?—M. Because, proceeding eternally from both, he is, as it were, breathed forth by them. Thus that power of the Godhead which accomplishes all things by creating is called [Col. 1111B] the Father; that which holds all things together lest they dissolve into nothing is called the Son; and that which gives life to and adorns all things by inspiration is called the Holy Spirit. All things are from the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. The Father is understood as memory, the Son as understanding, the Holy Spirit as will.

D. Since omnipotence and supreme mercy are predicated of the Father, why is he not called Mother?—M. Because generation proceeds principally from the Father.

D. Since truth or wisdom is said of the Son, why is he not called Daughter?—M. Because the Son is more like the Father than a daughter is.

D. Why is the Holy Spirit not called the Son of both, so that one might be Father and the other Mother?—M. [Col. 1111C] Because he proceeds simultaneously and equally from both, and is himself the bond of the whole Godhead.

3. On God’s dwelling and place.

D. Where does God dwell?—M. Although he is potentially everywhere, he is substantially in the intellectual heaven.

D. What is this?—M. Three heavens are spoken of: one bodily, which we see; another spiritual, because spiritual substances—that is, angels—are believed to dwell in it; and a third intellectual, in which the holy Trinity is contemplated face to face by the blessed.

D. How is God said to be wholly in every place, simultaneously and always, and yet in no place?— [Col. 1111D] M. He is said to be wholly in every place because he is no less powerful in one place than in another; for he is as powerful in hell as in heaven. He is said to be simultaneous because, in the same instant in which he orders everything in the East, he orders everything in the West. He is proclaimed always in every place because he governs all things in every time. He is said to be in no place because place is bodily, whereas God is incorporeal and therefore without place. Consequently he is contained by no place, since he contains all things: “in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28). In this God differs from other spiritual creatures, which are bounded by the properties of their substance and held in a place; thus the angel who stood by the Apostle [Col. 1112A] praying in Asia could not at the same time be present elsewhere. For that is local which, when wholly somewhere, cannot simultaneously be elsewhere. But that is non-local which is wholly everywhere at once; and this belongs to God alone.

4. On God’s knowledge and speech.

D. Does God know all things?—M. So completely that he beholds all past, present, and future things as though set before him. Even before he created the world, he foreknew all the names, characters, wills, words, deeds, and thoughts of both angels and human beings, as though they were present before him. Hence in Greek he is called *Theos*, that is, “the one who sees all things.”

D. How does God speak to angels and human beings?—M. To angels through inward inspiration, but to human beings [Col. 1112B] through angels.

D. Since God existed without beginning, must we believe that before the world’s creation he led, as it were, a solitary life?—M. It is written: “What was made in him was life” (John 1:3–4). This makes clear that every creature was always visible in God’s predestination, though later it appeared visibly to the creature itself in creation. It is like a craftsman who wishes to build a house: he first considers how he wishes to arrange each part, and the structure that later rises in the building is the same as that [Note: [Col. 1111D] A. omits: “is the same as that.”] which first stood in his conception. Hence God is said not to be older than his creature in time, but in dignity.

5. Why and how the world was created, and to what extent all things perceive God.

[Col. 1112C]

D. What was the reason that the world was created?—M. God’s goodness, so that there might be beings to whom he could impart his grace.

D. How was it made?—M. “He spoke, and all things were made” (Ps. 32:9).

D. Did he speak with the sound of words?—M. God’s speaking is to create all things by the Word, that is, in the Son; hence it is said: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24).

D. Was there delay in creating?—M. In the blink of an eye: that is, as quickly as you can open your eye, or rather as quickly as the sight of an open eye can perceive light.

D. Did he create in parts?—M. He made all things together and at once, as it is said: “He who remains for ever created [Col. 1112D] all things together” (Ecclus. 18:1). Yet he distinguished all things in parts over six days: for three days the elements, and for three days the things below the elements. Thus on the first day he made the day of eternity, namely spiritual light and every spiritual creature. On the second day, heaven, which separates spiritual from bodily creation. On the third day, he created sea and land. In the other three days he made what is beneath them. On the first day he made the day of temporality, namely the sun, moon, and stars in the highest element, which is fire. On the second day, in the middle element, which is water, he made fish and birds. He left the fish in the denser part of the water, but raised birds into the thinner part of water, which is [Col. 1113A] air. On the third day he made beasts and human beings from the last element, that is, earth.

D. Do the elements perceive God?—M. God never made anything that is insensible to him. Things inanimate are indeed insensible and dead to us, but to God all things live, and all things perceive their Creator. Heaven indeed perceives him because, at his command, it revolves continually in unceasing motion; hence it is said: “He made the heavens in understanding” (Ps. 135:5). The sun, moon, and stars perceive him because they return unchangeably to the places of their course. The earth perceives him because it always produces fruits and shoots at a fixed season. Rivers perceive him because they always return to the places whence they flow. Sea and winds perceive him because, when he commands, they promptly obey by becoming still. [Col. 1113B] The dead perceive him because they rise at his command. Hell perceives him because, at his command, it gives back those whom it devours. All brute animals understand God because they continually keep the law implanted in them by him.

6. On the election and names of the angels.

D. What is meant by the words, “There was evening and there was morning” (Gen. 1:5, 8)?—M. Evening is the end of a work already completed—or rather ordered; morning is the beginning of a work, or rather of a work to be ordered.

D. Explain everything more plainly.—M. First, then, God, like a most mighty king, established for himself a splendid palace, which is called the kingdom of heaven; then this world, in which he established the destructive pit, that is, hell. For this palace he predestined [Col. 1113C] a fixed number of chosen soldiers, which could neither be exceeded nor fail to be filled. He willed this number to consist of angels and human beings. He fixed this number as ten: nine orders of angels, and the tenth of human beings.

D. Why nine orders of angels?—M. On account of the Trinity, for in the number nine, the number three is repeated three times.

D. Why one order of human beings?—M. On account of unity, so that unity in Trinity might be praised, worshipped, and adored by angels and human beings.

D. Why did he will the number of the elect to consist of angels and human beings?—M. Because God made two principal [Col. 1113D] creatures, one spiritual and the other bodily. He therefore willed to be praised by both: by angels from the spiritual creation and by human beings from the bodily.

D. When were angels made?—M. When it was said, “Let there be light” (Gen. 1:3).

D. Did God say these words?—M. No; rather, by these words their exalted nature is indicated to us, since they are called light.

D. What is the angelic nature?—M. Spiritual fire, as it is said: “He makes his angels a flame of fire” (Heb. 1:7).

D. Do angels have names?—M. There is such great knowledge in angels that they have no need of names.

[Col. 1114A] D. Are Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael not names?—M. They are rather by-names, because they were imposed upon them by human beings from an incidental circumstance; they do not possess them as proper names in heaven. Hence the first angel too received from an incidental circumstance the name Sathael, that is, “opposed to God.”

7. On the fall of the devil and his followers.

D. In what respect was he opposed to God?—M. Seeing that he surpassed all the orders of angels in glory and beauty, he despised all and wished to be equal to God—indeed, greater than God.

D. How greater or equal?—M. Against God’s will, he wished to seize a better state than God had given him and to rule others tyrannically.

D. What then?—M. He was driven from the palace and shut up in prison; and as he was formerly most beautiful, [Col. 1114B] so afterward he became blackest; formerly most splendid, afterward most dark; formerly praiseworthy in every honour, afterward detestable in every horror.

D. Did he foreknow his fall?—M. Not at all.

D. How long did he remain in heaven?—M. He did not stand in truth for a full hour [Note: [Col. 1113D] A.: “for he did not stand.”], because he fell as soon as he was created.

D. Why was he not there longer?—M. So that one who so promptly usurped such great majesty for himself might taste nothing of its inward sweetness.

D. What sin did the others commit?—M. They consented to him.

D. In what way?—M. His self-exaltation pleased them, and they thought that, if he prevailed against God, they themselves would be [Col. 1114C] preferred over others in power.

D. What happened to them?—M. Together with him, their leaders were cast into the destructive place, that is, hell; the others into this dark air, where nevertheless, as in hell, they endure a burning punishment.

D. Why were not all cast into hell?—M. So that the elect may be tested by them and receive greater crowns, but the reprobate may be deceived by them and, at the final judgment, be handed over with them to everlasting fire.

8. Why those who fell cannot rise again, and why they were neither redeemed nor made incapable of sin.

D. Why did they not return?—M. They could not.

D. Why?—M. Because, just as they fell with no one instigating them, so they ought to have risen with no one helping them [Note: [Col. 1114D] A.: “rise.”], which was impossible for them. Another thing also harmed them: because they freely chose evil, the will for every good was justly taken from them. Therefore they do not will it; and because they do not will, they can never return.

D. Why did Christ not redeem them as he redeemed human beings?—M. All angels were created at once, not born from one angel as human beings are born from one human being. Therefore, if Christ had taken angelic nature from one angel, he would have redeemed that angel alone; the others would have remained outside redemption. Nor could he redeem that one alone, since he could not die. For God willed nothing but death as satisfaction, whereas angels are immortal; therefore they remained beyond restoration.

[Col. 1115A] D. Why did God not create them so that they could not sin?—M. For the sake of justice: that there might be some merit in them which ought justly to be rewarded. For if they had been so created that they could not sin, they would have been as though bound, and would have had no merit, because [Note: [Col. 1115D] A.: “because.”] they did this as though compelled. God gave them free choice, that of their own will they might both wish and be able to choose the good; and if they voluntarily chose it, they might justly receive as their reward the inability ever to sin.

D. Since God foreknew that they would be such, why did he create them?—M. For the ornament of his work. As a painter lays down a black colour beneath so that white or red may be more precious, so the righteous become brighter by comparison with the wicked.

[Col. 1115B] D. Why did he not create other angels in their place?—M. Other angels ought not to have been restored or created in their place unless they were such as those fallen angels would have been had they remained, without having seen any punishment of sinners. That was impossible, for as soon as those angels sinned, they immediately rushed into punishments.

9. On the knowledge and power of demons; and the confirmation, form, and endowments of the good angels.

D. Do demons know everything?—M. By their angelic nature they possess very great knowledge, but they do not know everything. And the more subtle their nature is than human nature, the more skilful they are in every art than any human being. They do not know future things, except insofar as they infer them from things past or God [Col. 1115C] permits them to know them. Moreover, no one knows thoughts and wills except God and the person to whom he himself chooses to reveal them.

D. An evil thought is often called a completed deed. Is this unknown to them?—M. They see images of phantasms introduced by themselves being conceived by souls and formed in thoughts, because souls, which are light, are at once covered by certain darkness. But they do not see the forms of virtues introduced by God and conceived in the mind, because, just as our sight cannot endure the sun’s radiance, so they cannot bear the brilliance of righteousness. Nor would they tempt the righteous at all if they knew that they would be overcome by them.

D. Can they do everything they wish?—M. They neither will the good nor can do it at all. For evil they are very effective; yet they can do not as much as [Col. 1115D] they wish, but only as much as they are permitted by the good angels.

10. On the confirmation, form, knowledge, and power of the good angels.

D. What do you say about the good angels?—M. Immediately after the others’ fall [Note: [Col. 1115D] A. omits “immediately.”], they were so confirmed that they can never fall or sin.

D. What does “they cannot” mean?—M. They can never will to do so.

D. Why were they not similarly confirmed earlier?—M. They had not waited so long.

D. Was the fall of the others the cause of these angels’ confirmation?—M. Not at all, but their own merit. [Col. 1116A] For when they saw the others choosing evil through pride, they were indignant and clung firmly to the highest good. Therefore they immediately received confirmation as their reward, and those who had formerly been uncertain of their blessedness then became certain.

D. What form do angels have?—M. In some manner, the form of God. For just as the image of wax is impressed by a seal, so God’s likeness is impressed upon them.

D. What likeness?—M. In that they are light, are incorporeal, and are adorned with every beauty.

D. Do they know everything or can they do everything?—M. Nothing in the nature of things is hidden from them, since they behold all things in God. Certainly, whatever they wish to do, they can do without difficulty.

11. On the formation of the human being, and how he is a little world and in the image of God.

[Col. 1116B]

D. Did not the fall of the wicked lessen the number of the good?—M. Yes [Note: [Col. 1115D] A.: “no”; but the margin has “yes” or “indeed.”]; but so that the number of the elect might be completed, the human being was created as the tenth.

D. From what?—M. From spiritual and bodily substance.

D. From what is the bodily substance?—M. From the four elements; whence the human being is also called *microcosmus*, that is, “a lesser world.” For he has flesh from earth, blood from water, breath from air, and heat from fire. His head is round, after the manner of the heavenly sphere, and in it two eyes shine like two luminaries in heaven; it likewise has seven openings, as seven [Col. 1116D] harmonies adorn heaven [Note: [Col. 1116D] A.: “heavens.”]. His breast, in which breath and coughing [Col. 1116C] occur, resembles the air, in which winds and thunder are stirred up. His belly receives all liquids as the sea receives all rivers. His feet support the whole weight of the body, as the earth supports all things. He has sight from heavenly fire, hearing from the higher air, smell from the lower air, taste from water, and touch from earth. He shares the hardness of stones in his bones, the greenness of trees in his nails, the beauty of grasses in his hair, and sensation with animals. This is the bodily substance.

D. Of what is the spiritual substance?—M. From spiritual fire, as is believed, in which the image and likeness of God are expressed.

D. What image or likeness?—M. The image is understood in form; the likeness is considered in quality or [Note: [Col. 1116D] A., “is expressed in quality, or.”] quantity. Divinity consists in the Trinity; the soul bears its image, for it has memory, by which it remembers the past; it has understanding, by which it understands present and invisible things; it has will, by which it rejects evil and chooses good. All virtues subsist in God; the soul has his likeness, since it is capable of every virtue. And just as God cannot be comprehended by any creature, though he comprehends all things, so the soul cannot be comprehended by any visible creature, though it itself [Col. 1117A] comprehends all visible things: for heaven cannot prevent it from contemplating heavenly things, nor the abyss from thinking upon things below. This is the spiritual substance.

D. Did God form him with his hands?—M. By command alone. By these words his fragile nature is indicated to us.

D. Why did he create him from so base a material?—M. For the devil’s disgrace: so that he might be more [Note: [Col. 1117D] A., “for the devil’s disgrace and God’s vindication; so that, if perhaps he fell when tempted, the devil might not on this account insult God; but if he were not overcome, the devil might be more.”] confounded, when this frail being—mud and clay—should enter the glory from which he himself, glorious as he was, had fallen.

D. Whence did he receive his name?—M. Since he was the lesser world, he received his name from the four regions of the world, which in Greek are called *anatolē*, *dysis*, *arktos*, and *mesēmbria*—East, West, North, and South—because his race was to fill the four parts of the world [Col. 1117B]. In this too he possessed a likeness to God: as God presides over all things in heaven, so man should preside over all things on earth.

### 12. Of the animals created for the benefit of humankind

D. Why did God create animals, when man did not need them?—M. God foresaw that he would sin and would need all these things.

D. Why did God create flies and gnats, and other things harmful to man?—M. God showed as much care in forming flies, ants, and gnats as in forming other things.

D. For what purpose are such things?—M. All are for the praise of his glory. Flies, gnats, and similar creatures were created because of human pride, so that, when they [Col. 1117C] sting him, he may consider what he is, since he is unable to resist even tiny [Note: [Col. 1118D] A., “very small.”] little worms. Thus Pharaoh was not ravaged by bears or lions, but afflicted by gnats, flies, and *ciniphes*—small biting insects. Ants, spiders, and such creatures as persist in their work were created so that we might take from them examples of diligence and devout labor. Thus every creation of God is a great delight to one who considers it: in some there is beauty, as in flowers; in others medicine, as in herbs; in others nourishment, as in crops; in others signification, as in worms and birds. All things, therefore, are good and were created for humankind.

### 13. Of Paradise, in which man was placed by God, and of the woman’s formation; and why both were capable of sin

D. Where was Adam created?—M. In Hebron, where [Col. 1117D] he also later died and was buried; and he was placed in Paradise.

D. What is Paradise, or where is it?—M. A most pleasant place in the East, in which trees of diverse kinds had been planted against various deficiencies. For example: if a man ate from one at the proper time, he would never thereafter hunger; from another, at the proper time, he would never thereafter thirst; from yet another, he would never grow weary. Finally, if he made use of the tree of life, he would no longer grow old, become ill, or ever die.

[Col. 1118A]

D. Where was woman created?—M. In Paradise, from the side of the sleeping man.

D. Why from the man?—M. So that, as they were one in flesh, so through love she might be one with him in mind.

D. Why were not all the elect created at once, like the angels?—M. God wished Adam in this respect also to have his likeness: as all things are from God, so all human beings should be born from Adam; and thus Eve too was from him.

D. Why did God not create them such that they could not sin?—M. For the sake of greater merit. For if, when tempted, they had not consented, they would at once have been so strengthened that neither they nor their descendants could ever sin. Therefore God wished them freely to choose the good and to receive this as their reward.

### 14. Of generation in the state of innocence; further matters concerning that state; and the temptation and fall of the first parents

[Col. 1118B]

D. How would they have begotten children, had they remained in Paradise?—M. As hand joins to hand, so they would have joined without concupiscence; and just as the eye raises itself to see, so that bodily organ of sense would have performed its office without pleasure.

D. In what manner would woman have given birth?—M. Without defilement and without pain.

D. Would an infant have been so weak and unable to speak as now?—M. As soon as it was born, it would walk and speak perfectly; it would make use of the trees placed there against each particular deficiency; and, at the time appointed by God, it would eat [Col. 1118C] from the tree of life, and thereafter remain in one state.

D. How long ought they to have been in Paradise?—M. Until the number of the angels who fell should be fulfilled, and that number of the elect which would have been fulfilled had the angels not fallen.

D. How could Paradise contain them all?—M. Just as now one generation passes away through death and another comes by life, so then the parents would be taken up into a better state, while their children, at the fixed time—believed to have been about thirty years—after eating from the tree of life, would yield place to their descendants; and at last all alike would become equal to the angels in heaven.

[Col. 1118D]

D. Were they naked?—M. They were naked and were no more ashamed of those members than of their eyes.

D. What does it mean when it is said, “After sin they saw that they were naked” (Gen. 3:7), as though they had not seen this before?—M. Immediately after sin they burned toward one another through concupiscence; and shame arose in that member from which human offspring proceeds.

D. Why in that member more than in the others?—M. So that they might know that all their posterity was held liable under the same crime.

D. How [Note: [Col. 1118D] A omits “how.”] did they see God in Paradise?—M. [Col. 1119A] They saw him through an assumed form, as did Abraham and the other prophets.

D. Why did the devil deceive them?—M. Through envy: for he envied them lest they should attain that honor from which he himself, through pride, had fallen.

D. By what did he find an entrance for temptation?—M. Through pride; for man wished to remain in his own power, since he said: “In my abundance I shall never be moved” (Ps. 29:7).

D. Why did God permit man to be tempted, when he knew he would be overcome?—M. Because he foreknew how great the goods would be that he would make from his sin.

D. How did he deceive them?—M. Through the serpent.

D. Did the serpent speak?—M. No; rather [Note: [Col. 1119D] A omits “no, but.”] the devil spoke through the serpent, just as today he speaks [Col. 1119B] through a possessed person, and as an angel spoke through the ass; though neither the serpent nor the ass knew what those words sounded forth through them.

D. Why through a serpent rather than another animal?—M. Because the serpent is twisting and slippery, and the devil makes those whom he deceives twisting and slippery: twisting through deceit, slippery through lust.

D. Was knowledge of good and evil in that apple?—M. Not in the apple, but in the transgression. Before sin, man knew good and evil: good by experience, evil by knowledge; after sin, however, he knew evil by experience, good only by knowledge.

D. Would evil persons have been born in Paradise?—M. Only [Col. 1119C] the elect.

D. Why are evil persons born now?—M. For the sake of the elect, that they may be exercised through them.

### 15. Of their expulsion from Paradise, and the gravity of the sin for which they were expelled

D. How long were they in Paradise?—M. Seven hours.

D. Why not longer?—M. Because as soon as woman was created, she immediately transgressed. At the third hour the man, having been created, gave names to the animals; at the sixth hour the woman was formed and immediately presumed to take the forbidden apple, offering death to her husband, who ate because of his love for her; and then, at the ninth hour, God expelled them from Paradise.

[Col. 1119D]

D. What were the cherubim and the flaming sword?—M. The sword was a wall of fire by which Paradise was surrounded after sin; the cherubim were an angelic guard, so that the fire might burn bodies, while angelic spirits might keep them from the place of delight [Note: [Col. 1119D] A omits “keep them from the place of delight”; sentence truncated.].

D. Where did Adam then go?—M. He returned to Hebron, where he had also been created, and there begot children. Abel, slain by Cain, he mourned—as Jerome says [Note: [Col. 1119D] A omits “as Jerome says.”]—for a hundred years; and he refused any longer to unite with Eve. But because Christ did not wish to be born from Cain’s accursed seed, Adam, warned by an angel, was joined again to Eve, and Seth was begotten in place of Abel; from whose line [Col. 1120A] Christ was born. I also want you to know that from Adam’s time until Noah there was no rain, no rainbow, people did not eat flesh or drink wine, and the whole time was as it were a springlike temperateness, with an abundance of every kind of thing. All these were later changed because of human sins.

D. What sin did man commit that he was expelled from Paradise?—M. He desired to be like God, and therefore ate from the forbidden tree against God’s command.

D. What was so serious about eating an apple?—M. It was a crime so grave that it could not be redeemed by the whole world.

D. Prove this.—M. Does it seem just to you that a human being should obey the divine will?

D. Nothing is more just than that every rational creature [Col. 1120B] should set absolutely nothing [Note: [Col. 1120D] A omits “absolutely.”] before the will of the Creator.—M. Therefore God’s will is greater than the whole world.

D. Certainly.—M. If, then, you stood before God and someone said to you, “Look behind you, or the whole world will perish,” while God said, “I do not wish you to look behind, but to look upon me” [Note: [Col. 1120D] A, “look at me.”], ought you to despise God, who is Creator of all things and the joy of angels, in order to save the passing world?

D. By no means.—M. Adam did this: he stood before God and, while the devil shouted, looked backward, thereby committing a sin greater than the world.

D. How was it greater?—M. Because in this one crime he committed six capital offences, through which he involved the six [Col. 1120C] ages of his posterity in death.

D. What were they?—M. First was pride, when he wished to be equal to God; and therefore he who had been set over all was made lowest of all. Of this it is said: “Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God.” Second was disobedience, when he transgressed God’s command; and therefore all things formerly subject to him became disobedient to him. Of this it is said: “To be unwilling to obey is as the crime [Vulgate: ‘sin’] of divination” (1 Sam. 15:23). Third was greed, when he desired more than had been granted him; and therefore he justly lost all that had been granted. Of this the Apostle says: “Greed is the service of idols” (Gal. 5:20). Fourth was sacrilege, when he stole, by theft, what was forbidden in [Col. 1120D] a sacred place; and therefore he deserved to be excluded from the sanctuary. Of this it is said: “He who profanes holy things shall be driven out from holy things.” Fifth was spiritual fornication: for his soul was joined to God; but when, despising God, he admitted the devil, he committed adultery as it were with a stranger, and therefore lost the friendship of the true bridegroom. Of this it is said: “You destroy all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. 72:27). Sixth, he perpetrated homicide, by which he hurled himself and the whole human race into death. Of this Moses says: “Whoever kills shall die the death” (Lev. 24:47; Exod. 21:12)—namely, eternal death. [Col. 1121A] Thus he immediately died in the inward person and lay buried in the sepulchre of the body.

D. Was not that wretch deceived by a most wicked and lying spirit?—M. He was; but he was not thereby less liable [Note: [Col. 1121D] A, “harmful/guilty” (*noxius*).]. If someone assigned a task to his servant and showed him a pit, lest he fall into it and be unable to rise from it, but the servant, despising his master, willingly fell into the pit and the assigned task remained undone, would he not be guilty?

D. Indeed, he would be bound by a double guilt: one, because he despised his lord; the other, because he made himself unable to perform the task laid upon him.—M. So Adam acted: he despised God, abandoned the work of obedience, and fell into the pit of death.

### 16. Of the satisfaction to be offered to God for that injury

[Col. 1121B]

D. In what way ought he to return?—M. He ought to restore the honor which he took from God and make satisfaction for the sin he committed. For it is altogether just that one who has taken away another’s possessions should both restore what was taken and make satisfaction for the injury inflicted.

D. What did Adam take from God?—M. Everything that God had proposed to accomplish in his court concerning Adam’s generation.

D. How ought he to restore the honor taken away?—M. By conquering the devil in the same way that he himself was conquered by him, and by restoring himself and all predestined to life to such a state as they would have had if they had remained.

D. How, then, ought he to make satisfaction?—M. Since he committed a sin greater than the world, he ought to render to God something greater than the world. Neither of these things could he by any means [Col. 1121C] do. Therefore he remained in death.

D. And why did he not perish utterly?—M. God’s decree could not be changed: for he had proposed to complete the number of the elect from Adam’s race.

D. What then?—M. Since Adam did not render the honor owed to God, God took it from him against his will when he subjected him to punishments.

D. How is human punishment God’s honor?—M. Because the one whom he disdained to have as a sweet Father in glory, like a son, he experienced as his Lord in torments, like a rebellious servant.

D. When he wished to pay but could not, why did God, being merciful, not forgive him, or admit [Note: [Col. 1121D] A, “take up.”] such a one into glory?—M. If God remitted his honor to him because he could not possess it, God would be powerless; but if he received sinful man without punishment into glory, whereas he had cast out an angel for one thought, he would be unjust. Moreover, if sin remained unpunished, something in God’s kingdom would remain disordered; but nothing disordered is left in his kingdom. Therefore the sinner had to be punished. Who would place in his treasures an unpurified gem taken from mud?

D. To what end, then, ought he to have come?—M. Since a runaway servant had fled, with his master’s stolen property, to a most cruel tyrant, the king’s son was sent from the palace into prison after the exiled servant [Col. 1122A], to crush the tyrant and restore the fugitive servant, together with his master’s possessions, to the king’s favor.

D. Why could man return after his fall?—M. Because, just as he fell not by himself but was impelled by another, so it was fitting that, since he could not rise by himself though he wished to, he should rise with another’s help.

### 17. The necessity of the Incarnation of the Word for rendering that satisfaction

D. Why did he not send an angel to redeem him?—M. If an angel had redeemed man, man would then have been that angel’s servant; but man had to be restored in such a way as to be equal to the angels. Another obstacle also existed: an angel in his own nature was unable to redeem man; but if he became man, he would be less able.

D. Why did God not create another man from [Col. 1122B] earth, to send him for the lost one?—M. If God had created and sent a new man, redemption would not belong to Adam’s race; for he who made satisfaction for man had to be of man’s own race.

D. Why did God not send a patriarch or prophet?—M. Patriarchs and prophets were conceived and born in sins; therefore they could not redeem the human race.

D. Develop the rest.—M. Since, therefore, an angel ought not to redeem and man could not make satisfaction by himself, the Son of God, through whom all things were made, assumed complete humanity so that redemption too might be through him; and he became one person in two natures. In that nature in which he was God, he conquered the devil, just as the devil had conquered man; he opened heaven to all the predestined [Col. 1122C] and made them equal to the angels—something God alone could do. In that nature in which he was human, he rendered for the injury something greater than the world [Note: [Col. 1122D] A, “was, rendered for the injury something greater than the world.” P, “was born, rendered for the injury [something] world.”], when he underwent an undeserved death—something man alone ought to do.

### 18. Why the Word was incarnate, from a Virgin, and in the fullness of time

D. Blessed is the speech of your mouth, which has brought the Son of God down to me from heaven. But tell me why the Son was incarnate, and not the Father or the Holy Spirit.—M. If the Father or the Holy Spirit had been incarnate, two Sons would be counted in the Trinity: one, the Son of the Virgin, who would be incarnate; the other, the Son of God. There was another reason. The Son is the likeness of God; but angel [Col. 1122D] and man had assumed for themselves God’s likeness. Therefore the one to whom the injury had specially been done had to be incarnate, so that he might mercifully save man and justly condemn the angel. Another reason also is that, since all things are through the Son, redemption too is through him.

D. Why did he wish to be born of a virgin?—M. God makes human beings in four ways. In one manner, without father and mother, but from earth, as Adam; in a second manner, from man alone, as Eve; in a third, from man and woman, as all are born daily; in a fourth, from woman alone—a privilege reserved to Christ alone—so that, just as death entered [Col. 1123A] the world through a virgin woman, so life might enter through a virgin woman, life which excludes death.

D. Why did he not come immediately, before the flood or after it?—M. If he had come before the flood, people of that time would say that it had not been necessary for him to come, since they had learned every good thing from their parents, who had recently departed from Paradise and had been taught all things by God and his angels. But if he had come immediately after the flood, they would say that God had spoken to Noah and Abraham, and that they had learned from them all that should be done or avoided.

D. Why did he not come in the time of the law?—M. If he had then come, the Jews would say that they had been abundantly instructed by the law, and the Gentiles that they had been fully taught by philosophers.

D. Why did he not delay until about the end of the world?—[Col. 1123B] M. Then few would imitate him, and the number of the elect would not be fulfilled. It was therefore necessary for him to come when the fullness of time came.

D. What was that time?—M. That which God fixed before the ages of the world: namely, when the Jews groaned that they were more burdened than relieved by the law, and the Gentiles, abandoning natural use, lived shamefully against nature; and when neither priest nor Levite came to assistance. It was necessary that the true Samaritan should come, place the half-dead man upon the beast of his body, and bring him to the inn of the heavenly court.

### 19. Of the circumstances of Christ’s birth and the wonders wrought at it

D. How could he be born without sin from a sinful mass?—M. From the beginning God separated from others certain persons who worshipped him more intimately; from them the Virgin sprang forth as from a line. Just as the rod of old, dry and without moisture, produced [Note: [Col. 1123D] A omits “produced.”] a flower, so she brought the Savior into the world without concupiscence.

D. How did she bear him?—M. Without defilement and without pain. For through a closed gate he entered the bridal chamber of the womb, joined human nature to himself, and through the closed gate, as a true bridegroom, came forth from the bridal chamber.

D. Why was he enclosed in the womb for nine months?—M. So that he might lead human beings, enclosed in the miseries of this world or of hell, back to fellowship with the nine orders of angels.

D. At what hour was he born?—M. At midnight, as it is said: “While all things held the midst of silence, and night in its course had reached the middle of its way, your Word [Col. 1123D] came from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18:14–15).

D. Why at night?—M. First, because he came hidden; then, so that he might lead those who were in the night of error to the light of truth.

D. Did Christ as an infant know anything?—M. Everything indeed, as God, “in whom all treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden” (Col. 2:3).

D. Could he walk or speak as soon as he was born?—M. According to his power, he could do both; but he wished to imitate human nature in all things except sin.

[Col. 1124A]

D. Did anything wonderful occur at his birth?—M. Seven special miracles.

D. What were they?—M. A star of surpassing brightness appeared. A golden or purple circle shone around the sun. A fountain of oil burst forth from the earth. There was the greatest peace. The whole world was registered for a census. Thirty thousand persons who rejected the Lord were killed in one day; and a dumb animal spoke.

D. I should like to hear their mystical meaning.—M. Stars signify saints; therefore a splendid star shone because the Holy of Holies had come. A golden or purple circle gleamed around the sun, because the Sun of righteousness came to illuminate the Church with the gold of his divinity and crown it with the purple of his Passion. Oil signifies mercy. [Col. 1124B] A fountain of oil flowed from the earth because the fountain of mercy flowed forth from the Virgin. There was immense peace because true peace appeared on earth. The world was registered for a census because the human race was marked beforehand for the heavenly kingdom with chrism. Those who rejected the Lord were killed because those who said, “We will not have this man reign over us” (Luke 19:14), perished. The beast spoke because the people of the Gentiles were being converted to the praise of God. [Note: [Col. 1123D] After “were being converted,” A inserts: DISCIPLE. “I hear all that my heart desires to hear.”]

### 20. Of the Magi, Christ’s flight into Egypt, and the rest of his life until baptism

D. Why did he draw the three Magi with gifts?—M. Because he wished to draw to himself by faith and works the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe.

[Col. 1124C]

D. Why did he flee [Note: [Col. 1124D] A, “was.”] into Egypt rather than another land?—M. To show himself the true Moses: so that, just as Moses, liberating God’s people from Pharaoh and Egypt, led them into the promised land, so he, liberating the faithful people from the devil and hell, led them into the kingdom of blessedness. Hence after seven years he returned to the land of Israel, because through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit he led us back from the world to the heavenly Jerusalem.

D. Why did he neither teach nor work signs during thirty years?—M. He came into the world as an example; therefore he wished first to act and then to teach, as it is said: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1). By this example he warned that no one should presume to teach before the lawful age, or wish to teach before [Col. 1124D] learning.

D. Since in him was the fullness of divinity bodily and no grace could accrue to him, why was he baptized?—M. To sanctify for us the waters of baptism [Note: [Col. 1124D] A, “of baptisms.”].

D. Why was he baptized in water? [Note: [Col. 1124D] A, “is baptized in water.”]—M. Water is contrary to fire. What is sin but fire? As anger is in the soul, so concupiscence is in the flesh; hence it is punished by the fire of punishment. In order that this fire may be extinguished, one is baptized in water. There is another point: water washes away filth, quenches thirst, and restores an image; so [Col. 1125A] the grace of the Holy Spirit in baptism washes away the filth of sins, quenches the soul’s thirst with God’s word, and restores the image of God lost through guilt.

### 21. Of Christ’s beauty, passibility, and death

D. Since it is written of him, “Beautiful in form beyond the children of men” (Ps. 44:3), was he physically beautiful?—M. According to his nature, he was such as he appeared to his disciples on the mountain. But because human beings could not bear his radiance, he appeared under a veil, for his form was contemptible. Hence it is said: “We see him as having neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53:11).

D. Was he passible and mortal?—M. Passion and death are the penalty of sin; but he came without sin and lived without sin. Therefore, according to nature, [Col. 1125B] he was impassible and immortal; but according to power he chose to be both passible and mortal [Note: [Col. 1125D] A, “or immortal.”].

D. Why did he die?—M. For obedience, as it is said: “He became obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. 2:8).

D. Did the Father demand death from him?—M. By no means.

D. Why did the Jews kill him? This I wish to hear from you.—M. Because he steadfastly maintained justice by living and truth by teaching. Humanity owed this obedience to Divinity, and God requires it from every rational creature.

D. What father would permit his only and good son to be killed, if he were able to prevent it?—M. When God saw his Son willing to undertake such an outstanding work—namely [Col. 1125C] to overcome a savage tyrant and free a captive from him—he consented to this most praiseworthy work and permitted him to die [Note: [Col. 1125D] A, “by which.”].

D. How was it just before God that he gave the best one for the wicked?—M. Because the worst one had deceived a simple human being, it was just that the best should become a hostage for him, overthrow the worst, and restore the innocent person to his former liberty. And in this manner God showed his love to the world, as it is said: “To redeem a servant, you delivered up your Son.”

D. If the Father delivered up the Son, as it is said, “He did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all,” and if the Son delivered himself, as it is said, [Col. 1125D] “Who gave himself up for us” (Eph. 5:2), what sin did Judas commit, who also delivered him up?—M. The Father delivered the Son and the Son himself through love; Judas, however, through greed.

D. Why did he choose to die on wood?—M. So that he might overcome again the one who conquered through wood, and redeem the one who fell on wood.

D. Why on a cross?—M. To save the fourfold world.

D. Why did he permit five wounds to be inflicted upon him?—M. To redeem the five senses of the human race, held captive by the devil.

[Col. 1126A]

D. Was his death sufficient to exhaust the sins of all?—M. It surpassed them even infinitely.

D. Prove it.—M. If Christ stood before you, and you knew him to be the Lord of majesty, and someone said, “Kill him or the whole world will perish,” would you kill him to save the world?

D. By no means.—M. Why?

D. Because his life would seem [Note: [Col. 1125D] A, “seems.”] far worthier than infinite worlds, and I would seem [Note: [Col. 1126D] A, “would see.”] to commit such a crime as could not be expiated by innumerable worlds.—M. Therefore, just as Christ’s life is worthier than infinite worlds, so his death was far more precious than innumerable worlds, and thus it was sufficient for the redemption of all.

D. What did the Father give him for this merit?—M. What [Col. 1126B] could he give him, when all things were his own? As it is said: “Son, all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31).

D. Could he not himself give the reward of his death to whomever he wished?—M. He could; therefore he gave it to the human being for whom he endured all these things: for Passion, impassibility; for death, immortality; for exile, an eternal homeland.

### 22. What became of the parts of his humanity when their composition was dissolved

D. How many hours was he dead?—M. Forty.

D. Why?—M. To give life to the four parts of the world which were dead in the Decalogue of the law [Note: [Col. 1126D] A omits “of the law.”].

D. Who crucified him?—M. Since he wished to die for Jews and Gentiles, the Jews devised [Col. 1126C] his death, while the pagans crucified him.

D. Why did he lie in the tomb for two nights and one day?—M. The two nights signify our two deaths, one of the body and the other of the soul; the day signifies his death, which was the light of our deaths. Of these he took away one and left the other to the elect for their exercise; when he comes again, he will destroy it too.

D. Where did his soul go after death?—M. Into the heavenly Paradise, as he said to the thief: “Today you shall be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43).

D. When did he descend into hell?—M. At midnight of the resurrection, the hour at which the angel devastated Egypt. At that hour, that is, at midnight, Christ despoiled hell; returning from there in triumph, [Col. 1126D] he placed in Paradise those snatched from there, visited his body in the tomb, and raised it from the dead. Some think that from the hour of death until the hour of resurrection he was in hell with the elect, and that, departing from there with them, he rose.

### 23. Of the circumstances of the Lord’s resurrection

D. Why did he not rise immediately after death?—M. They would say that he had not been dead but had merely been stunned by torments. But if he had risen after much time, there would be doubt whether it was he.

D. Why, then, did he rise so quickly?—M. So that he might sooner [Col. 1127A] console his own, who grieved over his death.

D. Why on the first day of the week?—M. So that he might renew the world on the day on which he had created it.

D. Why on the third day of his Passion?—M. So that he might raise those who had been dead in sins in the three times before the law, under the law, and under grace; and so that we, who fall in deeds, words, and thoughts, might rise again through faith in the Holy Trinity.

D. Where did he remain during those forty days?—M. In the earthly Paradise, as is believed, with Elijah and Enoch and with those who had risen with him.

D. What form did he have after the resurrection?—M. Seven times brighter than the sun.

D. In what form did his own see him?—M. Such as [Col. 1127B] they had been accustomed to see him before.

### 24. Of Christ’s appearances after the resurrection

D. Did he appear clothed?—M. He had assumed garments from the air, which vanished into the air when he ascended.

D. How often did he appear?—M. Twelve times. Eight times on the first day: first, to Joseph of Arimathea in the prison where he had been placed because he buried him, as the writings of Nicodemus declare. Second, to his mother, as Sedulius makes plain. Third, to Mary Magdalene, as Mark asserts. Fourth, to the two women returning from the tomb, as Matthew relates. Fifth, to James, as Paul testifies, who had vowed on Good Friday not to eat until he saw Christ alive. Sixth, to Peter, as Luke narrates, who, because of his denial, [Col. 1127C] remained apart from the others in tears. Seventh, to two disciples on the road to Emmaus, as the same Luke relates. Eighth, to them all, with the doors shut, as John describes. Ninth, on the eighth day, when Thomas touched him. Tenth, at the Sea of Tiberias. Eleventh, on the mountain of Galilee. Twelfth, he appeared to the eleven disciples as they reclined at table.

D. Why does the Evangelist say, “He appeared first to Mary Magdalene” (Mark 16:9)?—M. The Gospels were issued with supreme authority; but the Evangelists were unwilling to write except those things known to everyone. Hence it is said: “Jesus did many other things which are not written in this book” (John 20:30), that is, in the Gospel. In other writings, however, some things—but not all—are found; for they did not wish to write things exceeding belief. [Col. 1127D] Thus, while John alone relates Lazarus’s resurrection, the other Evangelists are silent about it.

D. Did the Lord appear in Galilee on that very day?—M. A place on Mount Zion is commonly called Galilee, because those who had come from Galilee to Jerusalem used to lodge there. The Lord too lodged there when he dined in the great upper room; there he appeared with the doors shut; and there too he sent the Holy Spirit.

### 25. Of Christ’s ascension and sitting at the Father’s right hand, and how he prays for us there

D. Did he ascend alone?—M. Those who rose with him also ascended with him.

[Col. 1128A]

D. In what form did he ascend?—M. As far as the clouds, in the form he had before the Passion; but, received by the clouds, in that which he had on the mountain.

D. Why did he not ascend immediately after rising?—M. For three reasons. First, so that his own might learn by experience that he had truly risen, seeing him eat and drink. Second, he chose to ascend after forty days in order to show that those who fulfill the Decalogue of the law through the four Gospels can ascend to heaven. Third, because the Church, which is Christ’s body, is believed, after the Passion which it will suffer under Antichrist, thereafter to ascend to heaven after forty days.

D. What is Christ’s sitting at the Father’s right hand?—M. The humanity resting in the glory of Divinity.

[Col. 1128B]

D. How does he intercede with the Father for us?—M. By continually presenting his Passion.

### 26. Of the sending of the Holy Spirit, and of Christ’s joy

D. Why did he not send the Holy Spirit immediately, but after ten days?—M. For three reasons. First, so that the apostles might prepare themselves, through fasts and prayers, as fit for his coming. Second, that those should receive the Holy Spirit who fulfill the ten commandments. Third, because this occurred on the fiftieth day after the resurrection: so that, just as God’s people, after liberation from Egypt, received the law of fear on the fiftieth day, so the people of the faithful, after their liberation from the world, might receive the law of love on the fiftieth day. In the year of jubilee [Col. 1128C] also, that is, the fiftieth, the Christian people received [Note: [Col. 1127D] A omits “Christian.”] the lost freedom and the inheritance of Paradise [Note: [Col. 1128D] A omits “of Paradise.”]; so on this day the Christian people received the lost freedom and the inheritance of Paradise.

D. Does Christ now have full joy?—M. In one respect he has it, and in another he does not. With respect to his own person, it is most complete; with respect to his body, which is the Church, not at all. For not all things are yet subject under his feet. He is still blasphemed by Jews, mocked by Gentiles, torn apart by heretics, and attacked by evil Christians. He also suffers daily in his members. When he has gathered all these things to himself, then he will have full joy.

### 27. On the Mystical Body of Christ, That Is, the Church

[Col. 1128D]

**D.** How is the Church his body, and the elect his members?—**M.** As the body adheres to the head and is governed by it, so the Church is joined to Christ through the sacrament of Christ’s body; indeed, it is made one body with him. From him all the righteous, each in his own rank, are governed as members by the head. The eyes of this head are the prophets, who foresaw future things; and the apostles, who brought others back from the path of error to the light of righteousness. The ears are the obedient. The nostrils, those with discernment. The phlegm expelled through the nostrils are the heretics, who are blown out from the head of Christ by the judgment of the discerning. The mouth consists of the teachers. The teeth are the interpreters of Holy Scripture. [Col. 1129A] The hands are the defenders of the Church. The feet are the farmers who feed the Church. Further, the dung discharged from the belly for swine consists of the unclean and lustful ministers of the altar, and other criminals within the Church who burden the womb of Mother Church; through the discharge of death demons devour them as swine. This whole body is bound together into one by the structure of truth and charity.

### 28. On the Body of Christ in the Eucharist

**D.** Why is his body made from bread, and his blood from wine?—**M.** His body is from bread because he himself said, “I am the living bread” (John 6:41); and his blood is from wine because he himself said, “I am the true vine” (ibid. 15:1). And as the body is nourished by bread, so the soul is refreshed by Christ’s food. And as [Col. 1129B] bread is made from many grains, so Christ’s body is gathered from many elect persons. And as bread is baked by fire, so Christ is roasted in the furnace of the Passion. This bread is also called flesh, because, like a lamb, he is sacrificed for us. Wine likewise is strained from many grapes and pressed in the winepress; so Christ’s body is joined together from many righteous persons and is tortured in the press of the cross. This wine is changed into Christ’s blood, so that our soul, which is in the blood, may be made alive through it.

**D.** Since the appearance of bread and wine is seen, how is flesh and blood proclaimed?—**M.** Although it truly is that which Mary bore, which hung upon the cross, and which penetrated the heavens, the appearance of bread and wine remains, lest, if you saw pure blood—as it truly is—dripping from [Col. 1129C] his side, you should recoil from touching it with your lips; and so that your merit might be greater, since you believe not what is seen but what is understood.

**D.** What salvation is in this?—**M.** The highest. For as food is changed into the flesh of the one who eats it, so every believer, by eating this food, is changed into Christ’s body. Therefore, through faith we are crucified with Christ to the world, its vices, and its desires; and in baptism we are buried with Christ. Thus we are immersed three times. By the food of his body, however, we are incorporated into him; and therefore it is necessary that we be transferred to the place where Christ is.

**D.** Do those who receive more possess greater holiness?—**M.** As it is said concerning manna, “He who gathered more did not have more, nor did he who gathered less have less” (Exod. 16:18), so all receive equally; and each person eats the whole Lamb, while he nevertheless remains whole in heaven.

### 29. On Those Who Communicate or Offer Sacrifice Worthily or Unworthily

**D.** What reward will those have who handle this worthily?—**M.** They will be rewarded with a double prize: they will be crowned with one crown because they handle it reverently, and with another because they prepare themselves for it by worthy conduct.

**D.** What do you think of those who act unworthily in this matter and contrary to the decrees of the canons?—**M.** Those who live contrary to right and justice [Col. 1130A] in adultery, fornication, and other crimes; who sell or buy churches or ecclesiastical orders; who kill God’s people by their corrupt example; and who rashly defend all these things—such people are at once betrayers and crucifiers of the Lord.

**D.** For what reason ought priests to celebrate Mass?—**M.** For God alone, for their own salvation, and for that of the whole Church. But they themselves [Note: [Col. 1129] A: “D. For what reason,” etc. D: “Prove it.” M: “For what reason,” etc. D: “For God alone,” etc. M: “But they themselves,” etc.] celebrate for gain, namely in order to be honored by people and enriched with temporal possessions. Those, therefore, who sell the mystery of Christ’s Passion for human favor and temporal profit—what else do they do but betray the Lord? And when they presume to handle with filthy hands and a defiled conscience him in whose sight not even the heavens are clean, what else do they do but [Col. 1130B] crucify the Lord?

**D.** Can the people incur guilt through them?—**M.** When the sons of Eli defiled the Lord’s sacrifice, nearly the whole people perished with them, because they acted against the commandment of the Lord’s law. How much more, then, are those defiled who are called Christians and appear to be ministers of Christ, yet are subject to fornication and lust, take wives, and beget sons and daughters—which is unlawful, since the whole Church openly holds as binding what the Lord said first to the chief shepherd, blessed Peter, and then to his successors, namely apostolic men and archbishops: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). In all synods they are excommunicated [Col. 1130C] and are to be excommunicated; yet when admonished, they treat it lightly, and when excommunicated, they have no fear of God, but mock and say, “Let this anathema be upon us and upon our children.” Hence it is clear that all who, as blind people, follow these blind guides into the pit—or rather, accompany them by communicating with them—will share with them also in their punishments.

**D.** What if they have communicated with them unknowingly?—**M.** “He who touches pitch shall be defiled by it.” Therefore those who communicate with them, even unknowingly, are nevertheless contaminated by them.

**D.** What if they come to their senses?—**M.** Their error will not harm them.

### 30. That Evil Priests Truly Consecrate Christ’s Body, Though Their Prayer and Blessing Become Sin

[Col. 1130D]

**D.** Do such persons consecrate the Lord’s body?—**M.** Although they are most thoroughly condemned, nevertheless the Lord’s body comes to be through the words that they recite. For it is not they, but Christ, who consecrates; and through both friends and enemies he works salvation for his children. They receive it to destruction, while others receive it to salvation. Thus it is not made worse by the worst, nor better by the best; just as a ray of sunlight is not made filthy by the mud of a sewer, nor made more splendid by a sanctuary.

**D.** Since, then, what is consecrated through them is good, [Col. 1131A] and is given to those who receive it not by them but by Christ, why is a good thing changed into destruction for the one who receives it?—**M.** Not only does the good thing not benefit the recipient; it even harms him, if he receives it contrary to the prohibition from one from whom he ought not to receive it.

**D.** Prove it.—**M.** In paradise no fruit was evil, since God made all things very good; but man turned a good thing into evil for himself when he did not refuse to receive it from the serpent, indeed from the devil.

**D.** If someone is in danger of death, is he clean if he abstains from this viaticum?—**M.** If anyone, from zeal for righteousness, refuses to receive communion from them, yet does not hesitate to communicate daily through the mouths of priests in the unity of the Church, I believe that, if he dies, he is saved by this faith. But if someone, detesting their evil deeds and simply venerating Christ’s good, [Col. 1131B] receives communion from them, I believe that he too is saved by this faith, because Joseph asked for and received Jesus’ body from the unbelieving Pilate.

**D.** Can they propitiate God for the people?—**M.** Rather, they offend him all the more. By their entrance they contaminate sacred places; by their touch they defile sacred vestments and vessels dedicated to God. The assembly of angels abhors them; the Lord himself flees from them, as it is said: “His sons—or rather, not his sons—provoked him in uncleanness; therefore I will hide my face from them, says the Lord” (Deut. 32:19). He called them sons because of the priesthood; he added “not sons” because of their filth. The Lord does not receive their sacrifice but abominates it, as it is said: “My soul hates your sacrifice, says the Lord, because you have offered me polluted bread” (Mal. 1:7). And again: “Do not offer sacrifice in vain; your sacrifice is an abomination to me” (Isa. 1:13). Although the body of the Lord cannot be defiled, so far as it lies in them they defile it, when they receive it indiscriminately as though it were ordinary bread. Their prayer is not received, but becomes sin, because the Lord will not hear them. Their blessing is turned into a curse, as it is said: “I will turn your blessing into a curse, says the Lord” (2 Esdras 13:2). And elsewhere: “They did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from them; they chose cursing, and it shall come upon them” (Ps. 108:18).

**D.** Do these people receive the Lord’s body?—**M.** Only the children of God [Col. 1131D] receive Christ’s body: those who are to be incorporated into Christ and to see God. But those who do not abide in Christ, although they appear to stretch it toward their mouths, do not receive Christ’s body; rather, they eat and drink judgment upon themselves. Christ’s body is carried to heaven by the hands of angels, but a coal is cast into the mouth by a demon, as Cyprian testifies. Since they receive it carelessly as though it were other bread and other wine, it is changed for them into the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps.

**D.** Did not Judas receive the same thing as Peter?—**M.** By no means. Peter loved the Lord; therefore he received the sacrament received from the Lord together with its power. [Note: [Col. 1131] A: “having received the sacrament, he communicated with the Lord.”] Judas, however, because he hated the Lord, received indeed the appearance of bread, but the power of the sacrament remained in Christ. Therefore, immediately after the morsel, the devil entered into him. Yet he gave Judas not the body, but only a dipped morsel, not consecrated. Peter clung to the Lord [Col. 1132A] and obeyed his words. Judas walked bodily with the Lord, but in spirit and mind he was with the betrayers. Thus, while these men ought to render to the Lord the tribute of due service in nightly praises, they take delight in the embraces of seductive coupling. Likewise, while they ought by divine offices to propitiate God for themselves and for those entrusted to them, they play with their children and fondle them in their laps. They diligently attend to the uses of the belly; they seek out women, so that their children may sit or stand more carefully in the streets. By these and similar acts they provoke the Lord to anger, as it is said: “They provoked me by that which was not God, and I will provoke them,” etc.

### 31. How Evil Priests Are to Be Obeyed; Whether They Can Loose; and Whether They Are to Be Avoided

**D.** Must they be obeyed?—**M.** Where they command what is good, one must obey not them but the Lord; for “they say and do not do” (Matt. 23:3). Where they command evil, they must be disregarded, for “we must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

**D.** Can they loose or bind?—**M.** If they have not been separated from the Church by public judgment, then, although they themselves are firmly bound, they can do both; for [Col. 1132C] it is not they, but Christ through their office, who binds and looses. But if they have been excluded by the judgment of the Church, they must be despised as pagans. So long as Judas was with the apostles, he appeared as a friend; like the other apostles, he preached, baptized, and performed signs. After he left them, he was plainly revealed as a public enemy. So too these men: so long as they remain in communion with the Church, all sacraments performed through them are valid; if they are excluded, whatever they do will be invalid. Therefore, since they are wolves, Christ’s sheep must flee them, as it is said: “Come out from their midst, my people, lest you share in their punishments and torments” (Rev. 18:4).

**D.** Can a person leave what is his because of them?—**M.** This separation cannot, and should not, take place bodily; for if the good are separated from the evil, no one will thereafter be converted to the good through them. In certain respects, however, they must be avoided, especially at a meal and in the service of God, as it is said: “Not even to eat with such a person” (1 Cor. 5:11). They must be fled in mind and will, lest one consent to their works.

**D.** How does consent to their actions occur?—**M.** When their evil deeds are praised, or when they are assisted in committing crimes by counsel or money. Therefore not only those who commit such things, but also those who consent to those committing them, are worthy of death. Accordingly, although they are evil, so long as they have not been publicly separated from the Church, they are not to be avoided—unless all of them, both prelates and subjects, mutually consent to evil in such a way that none of them rebukes the wickedness of another. Then they must be fled in every way, because then they become the cause of the people’s ruin.

### 32. On the Guilt of Prelates Who Connive at Evil Priests, and on the Sons of Priests Not to Be Ordained

**D.** What of the pastors who consent to them?—**M.** We read of Eli that, because he consented to his sons who acted wickedly and rebuked them only lukewarmly for their transgression, he incurred bodily death. Here it is plainly shown that the death which he suffered in the body is suffered by these men in the soul. They encourage the sins of offenders so that they may receive temporal stipends from them; excluded from eternal blessedness, they will pay eternal punishments together with them. Some, when they assume the rights of a pastor, burn with desire to tear their subjects apart; they extort and plunder money from them, and prove altogether unfaithful to their sacred order, as it is said: “Your shepherds are unfaithful, companions of thieves; they pursue gifts, their hands are full of plunder” (Isa. 1:23).

**D.** Are the sons of priests to be ordained?—**M.** By no means. The decrees of the canons and the ordinances of the holy Fathers forbid them to enter sacred orders or to hold any ecclesiastical preeminence, because they are begotten through fornication and transgression. For the poison of poisoned fathers passes into their sons.

**D.** Prove it.—**M.** We read in Genesis that God commanded Adam not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. But he ate not from the tree itself, but from the fruit of the forbidden tree, and infected all posterity with the poison of transgression. Thus it is clear that the fruit of the poisoned tree was not free from the poison of disobedience, although he had not forbidden the eating of the fruit of the tree.

**D.** What is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? (Gen. 2:9.)—**M.** The knowledge of the divine Scriptures and the secrets of God’s mysteries, which was especially entrusted to them, as it is said:

> “To you it has been given to know the mystery of God” (Matt. 13:12).

**D.** What is the tree of evil?—**E.** Secular knowledge and rejection of God’s commandments, as it is said: “They know how to do evil; but good—never” (Matt. 23:2). Although these are inferior, they wish to appear superior. They seek honors; they desire to preside rather than to be subject. Such people must by no means be promoted to sacred orders. Among the rest they should always be regarded as shameful; repenting, they should cast off the poison by which they have been ensnared by their fathers, and by such shame the other priests should come to their senses. Unless they repent in proportion to their guilt, the tree together with its root will be destroyed without end, as it is said: “Therefore God will destroy you unto the end,” that is, forever, “and will pluck your root out of the land of the living” (Ps. 51:7).

### 33. The End of the Life of Evil Priests; and Whether They Must Be Admonished and Tolerated

[Col. 1134B]

**D.** Tell me, I pray: what will be the end or torment of these reprobate and unfaithful priests?—**M.** As it is written: “They have been corrupted and become abominable in their works”; therefore they will come to nothing like running water. Like sheep, so also the shepherds will be placed in hell; death will feed upon them, because God has rejected them (Ps. 13:1; 57:8; 48:15).

**D.** Should the words of God be spoken to evil people?—**M.** If they are known to be evil, they should not be spoken to them, because one is a betrayer who, when they are enemies, opens God’s secrets to them. Therefore it is commanded: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine, lest they trample them and mock” (Matt. 7:6). But where they are not known, God’s sayings must be brought forth to them for the sake of the elect hidden among them who are to be converted. Thus the Lord did not cease to minister words of salvation to Peter and [Col. 1134C] others who were to be saved, although he knew that Judas and the Pharisees would be tormented and scandalized by them.

**D.** Must evil people be tolerated, since Christ tolerated Judas?—**M.** Evil people in the Church must be tolerated, but not imitated, until he comes with the winnowing fan, who will shake the grain free from the chaff and, once the tares have been consigned to fire, store the wheat in his barns.

**D.** May God separate you from every evil and place you, good master, in the heavenly bosom. Amen.

## SECOND BOOK

[Col. 1133]

### 1. What Evil Is, and Whether It Is from God

[Col. 1133D]

**D.** My soul exults in the Lord, because, with the cloud of ignorance wiped away, I have been enlightened through you by so great a ray of knowledge. I ask you, therefore, ornament of the Church, that I may still be permitted to inquire into some matters.—**M.** Ask what you wish, and you will hear what you desire.

**D.** Evil is said to be nothing. If it is nothing, it seems very strange that God should damn human beings or angels when they do nothing. But if it is something, it seems to be from God, since all things are from him; and it follows that God is the author of evil and that those who do it are unjustly condemned.—**M.** Certainly all things are from God, and he made all things very good; and therefore evil is proved to be nothing in substance. All things which God [Col. 1134D] made subsist. Every substance is good; but evil has no substance. Therefore evil is nothing. What is called evil is nothing other than the place where good is absent, as blindness is where sight is absent, and darkness where light is absent, since blindness and darkness are not substances. Note these three things. A creature is placed in the category of substance. Substance is the reality of all things, considered in the being of its categories. Nature is called every thing in its own being, except those things which depart from their original constitution according to their proper dwelling-places. But a will or nature that departs from the Creator does not remain nature but becomes a perversion of nature, and such a thing is called sin. A made thing (*factura*) is a kind in dignity—that is, man among living creatures—who, having abandoned natural good, employs a perverse will. These three, according to divine teaching, are creature, nature, and made thing: creature, as the elements; nature, as the things born from them; made thing, as what a human being or angel does or suffers. Those who do evil suffer the penalties of sin. God does not make these, but permits them to occur, as it is said: “God did not make death” (Wis. 1:13). Sin, however, is nothing other than doing what one has been commanded not to do, or acting otherwise than one has been commanded; just as evil is nothing but lacking good, that is, joy. Even the term itself is from God only in this sense: it occurs through that substance which God made. God justly condemns—that is, does not grant joy to—those who do not do, or do otherwise than, what is commanded.

**D.** Who is the author of sin?—**M.** Man himself; the devil is its instigator.

### 2. The Gravity of Sin, and That It Ultimately Redounds to God’s Glory

**D.** Is it grave to sin?—**M.** The least sin knowingly committed is graver than the whole world. Yet whatever evil or sin is done is all turned to the praise of God; and therefore it is demonstrated that nothing evil exists or occurs in any creature of God.

**D.** What do you mean? Is homicide or adultery not sin?—**M.** Killing is often called good, as David’s killing of Goliath and Judith’s of Holofernes; it is called evil when committed by one’s own impulse. Marriage is believed to be good; but adultery is evil because it occurs otherwise than has been permitted. Yet these things are turned to the praise of God when they are justly punished by him. For as [Note: [Col. 1135D] A omits *enim* (“for”).] an emperor is praiseworthy when he rewards his soldiers, so he is also praiseworthy—indeed more praiseworthy—when he condemns brigands and robbers. Thus, just as God is glorified in the salvation of the righteous, so in every respect he is praised in the destruction of the wicked.

**D.** Since it is written, “You hate none of the things that you have made” (Wis. 11:25), how is God said to love the good and hate the evil?—**M.** God loves all that he has created, but he has not placed all things in one location. As a painter loves all colors but chooses some in preference to others and puts each in its fitting place, [Col. 1135D] so God disposes each person in the place suited to him. Thus he is said to love those whom he receives into the heavenly palace and to hate those whom he plunges into the infernal prison.

### 3. On Free Choice and Falling Back from Good

**D.** What is free choice?—**M.** Freedom to choose good or evil.
