In paradise man possessed this freedom; now, however, he possesses it captive, because he does not will the good unless God’s grace goes before him, nor can he act [Note: [Col. 1136D] A omits *agere* (“act”).] unless grace follows him.

**D.** What do you say about those who leave the world, take the habit of religion, and after some time [Col. 1136A] cast it off and become worse than they were before? And about some who begin certain good works, afterward abandon them, and return to wickedness?—**M.** Job says of them: “Hypocrites and crafty persons provoke God’s wrath” (Job 36:13). A servant often draws a wandering son back to his father and then himself returns to his work; so these people draw the elect to God and themselves return to evil pursuits. Thus too fear leads charity to the kingdom, though fear itself will not enter. For as the devil serves God, so his members serve the elect even in this way.

### 4. How the Devil Serves God, and Evil People Serve the Good

**D.** How does the devil serve God?—**M.** Because the glorious prince despised being in the palace, God made him a laboring smith in this world, so that he who did not wish to rest in enjoying God might be compelled to serve with all his strength, as it is said: “I will make him your everlasting servant” (Job 40:23). The forge of this smith is affliction and tribulation; the bellows are temptations and suggestions; the hammers and tongs are terrors and persecutors; the files or saws are the tongues of those who curse and slander. By such a forge and these instruments he purifies the golden vessels of the heavenly king: these are the elect, in whom he renews the image of God. But the reprobate, who act against the king, he scorches and punishes as enemies. In this way the devil serves God.

**D.** How do the devil’s members serve the elect?—**M.** When they draw them toward the kingdom through hypocrisy or drive them forward through adversity. They draw them through hypocrisy when they outwardly feign goods which inwardly [Col. 1136C] they do not love. Then the children of God, still placed in error, seize upon good things through their examples and love them with their whole heart. When the hypocrites abandon those good things which they did not love, these others persist more firmly in the good they have begun; just as, when the evil angels fell long ago, the good stood more firmly. They drive them forward through adversity when they take from them temporal things which they love more than is right and prevent them from being able to fulfill carnal desires. Hence the devil and evil people are shown to be useful—indeed necessary—since through them the elect, tested, are carried to heavenly things.

**D.** What do you say of priests who leave churches for the sake of profit and take others?—**M.** They are wolves, apostates, and thieves: deceivers, indeed betrayers, both of their own people and of those to whom they come.

### 5. Why the Way of the Wicked Prospers for Many Years, but Not Thus the Life of the Pious, Except Sometimes

**D.** Why do the wicked here abound in riches, flourish in power, and thrive in health, while the good waste away in poverty, are unjustly oppressed by the wicked, and wither through weakness?—**M.** These things overflow to the wicked for the sake of the elect, so that the good may despise things in which they see even the worst flourish. The wicked abound in riches, first so that, by God’s just judgment, they may be able through money to accomplish the evils which they desire; second, so that, if they do any good, they may be rewarded for it through these things. For everything they do, they do for earthly things, and thus they receive their reward. They shine in power: first for their own sake, so that they may powerfully fulfill the evils which they love; second, for the sake of the reprobate, so that they may defend them in evil; third, for the sake of the elect, so that they may chastise them and correct them from evil acts. They abound in health and do not feel afflictions with other people, so that afterward a more grievous pain may torment them. The good, however, are afflicted with hunger, oppression, and weakness lest they delight in evils; or, if they have committed sins against God, that these may be wiped away; if not, that they may be crowned for patience.

**D.** Why, on the contrary, do some good people here abound in riches, rise in power, and grow strong in health, while the wicked labor under want, illness, and oppression?—**M.** Riches are granted to certain elect persons so that they may accomplish by their resources the good which they love; and by these things they are also admonished that, if these temporal things seem sweet, how much more so do eternal things. They are raised in power, first for their own sake, so that they may powerfully perform the good they have conceived in mind. Second, for the elect, so that they may be their protection in good things [Note: [Col. 1137D] A: *bona*, “good things.”]. Third, for the reprobate, so that they may restrain them from doing as much harm as they wish. They are strengthened in health, lest the righteous be saddened by their sickness but rejoice in their well-being. Conversely, some evil people here groan under poverty, affliction, and bodily pain, so that through these they may learn how bitter are the things toward which they hasten in their corrupt conduct.

**D.** Why do some evil people live for a long time, while some good people die sooner; and conversely, why do some good people lead a long life while evil people die more quickly?—**M.** Evil people are permitted to live long so that the elect may be exercised through them and corrected from vices; afterward they themselves are tormented with greater punishments. But the good are taken away sooner, lest they be worn down here longer by adversities, but may be brought into enduring joys. Conversely, long life is given to the righteous so that their merit may increase, as more people are corrected through their example. Evil people, certainly, are swiftly carried off to torments so that fear may be instilled in elect persons who still err and they may thus be drawn back from error.

### 6. On the Good of Tribulation; and That No Good Befalls the Evil, but No Evil the Good

[Col. 1137D]

**D.** Are those happy who are untouched by adversity?—**M.** On the contrary, they are most unhappy: those who are allowed to live here agreeably in every respect and fulfill all their desires at will, but [Note: [Col. 1138D] A: *si*, “if.”] are untouched by adversity. For in this way they are nourished like dry wood for the fire. Conversely, those are most happy who here are restrained from their desires and exercised by many hardships, because in this way they are educated for the kingdom as children by scourges, as it is said: “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). I want you to know that the reprobate, although they possess a royal crown, are altogether powerless and will never be without punishment. But the elect, although captive and though placed in prison, are always powerful and will never lack reward.

**D.** For God’s love, make me see this more clearly.—**M.** The reprobate are powerless because, forestalled by God’s wrath, they do not will the good and therefore in no way can accomplish it. But evil they both will and can do. Yet evil has been proved to be nothing; therefore they are plainly able to do nothing. They are not without punishment because they are tormented by a savage conscience and continually troubled by fear that they may be captured, killed, or deprived of their possessions; hence it is said: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. 48:22). Conversely, the elect are exceedingly powerful because, forestalled by God’s grace, they both will and can do good, but reject evil. They do not lack reward because they remain without fear and rejoice, secure in hope of future freedom; hence it is said: “The righteous shall be without terror” (Prov. 28:1). I also wish to make clear to you in another way that no good befalls evil people and no evil happens to good people.

**D.** In God’s name, what are you saying? Do not the wicked here delight in banquets, rejoice in beauty, intercourse with women, and the embrace of children, glory in costly clothing, and exalt themselves by money and magnificent buildings? Conversely, are not the good here shut up in prisons, struck with blows, and afflicted by hunger, thirst, and other torments?—**M.** When favorable fortune smiles upon evil people and abundance from her horn fills them with the goods you have enumerated, they resemble the fish which bites the hook in delight, but is dragged from the water and killed by this merriment; or the person offered a cup of honey and afterward compelled to drink without end a bitter [Col. 1138C] sea. For in place of banquets they are filled, like that rich man, with the bitterness of wormwood; in place of love for women, with sulphurous stench; in place of the brightness of clothing, they will be clothed with shame; in place of money and buildings, they will inherit worms in infernal caverns. Hence it is said: “They spend their days in good things, and in a moment descend into hell” (Job 21:13). But the good, whom you say are afflicted with such hardships, are like those who first taste pepper or another bitter herb, so that wine drunk afterward may taste sweeter. Thus the righteous, in exchange for prison, will be received into eternal dwellings; in exchange for blows, will obtain joy and gladness; in exchange for hunger and thirst, “they shall hunger and thirst no more” (Isa. 49:10); in exchange for torments, pain and groaning will flee from [Col. 1138D] them (Isa. 35:10). From this it is proved that the righteous are always rich and blessed, while the ungodly are always poor and miserable.

### 7. Whence Dignities Come; That It Is Wrong to Sell or Buy Them; and What the Rule of Prelates Should Be

**D.** Whence do dignities come?—**M.** Certainly all dignities and powers, whether of evil or good people, are from God, as it is said: “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. 13:1). Why sometimes evil people and sometimes good people receive authority has already been said above.

**D.** What judgment do you pronounce upon those who sell [Col. 1139A] or buy them?—**M.** Those who buy them will undergo destruction with Simon; but those who sell them will incur leprosy of the soul with Gehazi. [Note: [Col. 1139D] P omits *animae*, “of the soul.”]

**D.** Do prelates have greater merit before God?—**M.** Rank of office or dignity of power contributes nothing to a person before God if merit is lacking. But those who preside in ecclesiastical matters, such as bishops, abbots, or [Note: [Col. 1139D] A omits *abbates seu*, “abbots or.”] priests, if they preside well in word and example, will have as many rewards beyond others as there are souls saved through them, as it is said: “He will set them over all his goods” (Matt. 24:47). But if [Note: [Col. 1139D] A omits *si autem*, “but if.”] they withhold the word of salvation from their subjects and lead them by corrupt examples into the pit of destruction, they will inherit as many punishments beyond others as there are souls who perish through their example, or as there are persons whom they neglect to save by preaching, [Col. 1139B] as it is said: “From him to whom more is entrusted, more will be required” (Luke 12:48). And again: “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6:7). Those who preside in secular matters, such as kings and judges, if they judge justly and treat their subjects mercifully, will obtain greater glory than others from God, the just judge, “because those who minister well acquire for themselves a good rank.” But if they oppress the people unjustly and cruelly, they will have more dreadful punishments than others, because “a most severe judgment will be made against those who preside” (Wis. 6:6), and: “Judgment without mercy is for the one who does not show mercy” (Jas. 2:13).

### 8. Why the Elect Suffer with the Reprobate; and on God’s Power and Providence

**D.** Since the elect are not of the world, why do they suffer the adversities of the world together with the reprobate?—**M.** Because they associate with evil people, they endure adversities with them; and because they are often ensnared by worldly things [Note: [Col. 1139D] A: *utuntur*, “make use [of them].”], they are afflicted by the misfortunes of the world.

**D.** Since God is almighty, as it is said, “He has done all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113:11); and again, “All power to do whatever you will is subject to you” (Wis. 12:8), why is it said of him that he cannot do certain things, such as lie or make what is past not [Col. 1139D] past?—**M.** When this is said of God, it is not his powerlessness but his supreme omnipotence [Note: [Col. 1140D] A omits *ejus*, “his.”] that is proclaimed: namely, that no creature is able to bend him to will a change in what he has established.

**D.** What is God’s providence?—**M.** That knowledge [Col. 1139D] by which he foreknew all future things—indeed, saw them as present.

**D.** If God foreknew all future things, foretold through the prophets that they would come in this manner, cannot be mistaken in his providence, and heaven and earth would sooner pass away than God’s words could be changed, it seems that all things which ever occurred or are still to come happened by necessity.—**M.** There are two necessities. One is natural, as the sun’s rising in the east or day following night. The other is voluntary, as someone’s walking or sitting. What God wills to happen—such as heaven and earth—cannot fail to occur, but must in every respect happen thus. But what he merely permits to happen, such as human beings through free choice doing good or evil, need not occur. Therefore God foreknew as future all things that human beings were going to do and foretold through the prophets that they would come to pass. Yet his foreknowledge imposed no necessity upon them that they should occur; rather, they themselves imposed necessity [Note: [Col. 1140D] A: *vim necessitati*, “force upon necessity.”] when they fulfilled their own will.

**D.** Does anything happen by chance?—**M.** Nothing whatever; rather, everything occurs by God’s ordering.

D. How then are certain churches of God, or even buildings [Col. 1140B] belonging to good people, when a fire happens to break out, burned as though by chance?—M. There is no such thing as chance. For it is written: “Nothing happens on earth without a cause” (Job 5:6). Hence it is clear that no church, nor any house anywhere in the world, is burned or destroyed unless it has first been adjudged by God. This happens for three reasons: first, if the churches’ [Note: [Col. 1140D] A., *the same*.] buildings have been constructed from unjustly acquired property; second, if their inhabitants defile them by impurities; third, if people love them more than eternal things [Note: [Col. 1140D] A., *eternal*.]. But not even the smallest beast dies or falls ill for a human being unless this is determined by God’s will.

D. Since death and illness are penalties for sin, why do beasts suffer these things, when they do not know how to sin by discernment?—M. A human being is punished through them, when he is tormented in mind by their suffering [Col. 1140C] or death.

D. This may apply to domestic animals; what do you say about wild ones?—M. That they are afflicted by illness happens to them through corrupt air, or through other things which, because of human sin, are changed into their opposites.

### 9. On predestination and the permission of sin among the elect

D. What is God’s predestination?—M. It is the ordering by which, before the creation of the world, he preordained some for his kingdom, of whom none can perish and all must be saved; and others for punishment, whom he foreknew to be guilty of sin, of whom none will be saved.

D. If no one can be saved except the predestined, why were the others created, or in what are they guilty, that they should perish? [Col. 1140D]—M. Whatever the predestined do, they cannot perish, because all things work together for their good, even sins themselves. For after more serious sins they will be humbler, and will offer praise to God for their salvation. But the reprobate were created for the sake of the elect, so that the elect may be exercised in virtues through them, corrected from vices, and appear more glorious by comparison with them; and so that, when they see them in torments, they may rejoice more greatly in their own escape. The reprobate also perish justly for their own sake [Col. 1141A], since of their own accord they choose and love evil, and wish to live without end so that they may sin without end.

D. Why does God permit the elect to sin?—M. So that he may reveal in them the riches of his mercy.

D. Are the predestined saved if they do not labor?—M. Predestination has been so instituted that it is attained through prayers or labors, as it is said: “Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21). Thus, for little children predestination is given through the bitterness of death; but for those advanced in age, through the exercise of labors. Since it is written, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14:2), each person will obtain a dwelling-place according to his own labor: thus, the more one has labored, [Col. 1141B] the worthier a place he will possess; but one who has labored less will possess an inferior one. Yet no one can labor more unless divine grace assists him. Nor will anyone inhabit another dwelling-place than that to which he was preordained before the beginning of the world, because “it depends not on the one willing or running, but on God who has mercy” (Rom. 9:16). So no reprobate can accomplish anything beyond what divine judgment permits him [Note: [Col. 1141D] A omits “him”.]; nor will he have a punishment other than that which divine judgment foreknew, before the beginning of the world, that he would have according to his merit; thus God, before they had done good or evil, said: “Esau I hated, but Jacob I loved” (Mal. 1:3).

D. How can they be recognized?—M. Whoever has persevered in good deeds until the end, or whoever [Col. 1141C], while doing evil, abandons it and hastens to repentance and perseveres in this until the end, will be among the predestined. But whoever persists in evils, or, though doing good, abandons these things, commits evil, and continues in it until the end, belongs to the reprobate. Just as those who have heard much about God and refused to obey are called guilty, so those who have never heard anything about God and for that reason have not acted are regarded as innocent. Human beings were created so as naturally to serve the Creator through love of neighbor, according to [Note: [Col. 1141D] A., *through*.] the saying: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tobit 4:16). No one wishes to suffer theft, adultery, or murder; let him do these things to no one. When people disregard this in their neighbor, they contradict God, who is love. Yet there is no corner of the world [Col. 1141D] where God is not known, since people travel together to various lands where God is worshiped, whether for trade or some other reason, and report at home what they have heard there about God; and therefore they are without excuse.

### 10. On ignorance of God

D. Can those who are ignorant of God and of good, and therefore do evil, be excused?—M. “He who is ignorant shall be ignored.” For the person who, like the Gentiles, is ignorant of God in faith and deed, God condemns as his enemy. But those who have known God through faith, yet in simplicity are ignorant of his will, like rustics, if they are condemned, are not condemned severely, as it is said: “The servant who does not know [Col. 1142A] his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with few stripes” [Note: [Col. 1142D] A omits “stripes”.] (Luke 12:48). But those who are able to know through intelligence, yet through malice pretend not to know, such as clerics and monks, will be punished more harshly, as it is said: “He who knows and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes” (ibid., v. 47). Those, however, who refuse to hear good things and scorn to learn what they ought to do will be subject to a double punishment: first, for stubbornness, because they knowingly sin; second, for contempt, because they refuse to learn what is good. Thus it is said: “The heavens shall reveal their iniquity, and the earth shall rise up against them” (Job 20:27), on the day of the Lord’s wrath, they who said to the Lord God: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” (ibid. 21:14).

### 11. What original sin is

[Col. 1142B]

D. What is original sin?—M. Injustice.

D. Explain more plainly.—M. God made the first human being just. It was just that he should preserve this justice and leave it to his descendants; for every human being ought to have been born with such justice as Adam possessed when he was created. But because Adam voluntarily abandoned it, every human being begins life in injustice. This injustice is called original sin, on account of which every human being is condemned unless it is forgiven in baptism.

D. Since every sin is committed by will alone, I do not see how sin is justly imputed to an infant newly endowed with a soul or newly born, especially since it has no will to sin and has no power either to perform or understand [Col. 1142C] justice.—M. An infant newly endowed with a soul or newly born is guilty for three reasons. First, because it does not possess the natural justice which God bestowed upon the first human being. Second, because it is liable to make satisfaction for the rashness of that abandonment. Third, because, by incurring miseries, it has rendered itself useless to its Lord. Every human being ought to have been born just and destined to be made equal to the angels, as God established. But because Adam abandoned that justice, God requires it from all his posterity.

D. Since it is written, “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18:20), and likewise, “Each shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6:5), how is what a parent has sinned justly demanded from an infant? [Col. 1142D]—M. No one’s sin is demanded from another, nor is anyone punished for another’s injustice, but for his own. God requires from every human being the justice which he first gave; but every human being is Adam in nature and Adam’s son in person. And because every human being is born without this justice, he is punished not because Adam abandoned it, but because he himself does not have it. Therefore, because natural justice is not found in the infant, it is justly excluded from the justice of God, and most justly subjected by God to punishment with the unjust; God also justly avenges sins unto the third and fourth generation.

D. I desire to hear nothing more.

### 12. How God punishes sins unto the fourth generation

[Col. 1143A]

M. God repaid sins in the first generation when he destroyed sinners by the Flood for despising the natural law. In the second generation he punished them when he overwhelmed offenders in the Red Sea for idolatry. In the third generation he punished sinners when he exterminated them in war for transgressing the written law. In the fourth generation he will avenge sins when the final fire devours the despiser for rejecting the Gospel. Although children are often justly abandoned in their own injustice because of their parents’ sins, so that they may be punished both here and there. There are likewise four kinds of sinning: thought, speech, action, and perseverance in evils. Therefore, in the third and fourth generation God repays sin when he punishes those who persist in evils for their deeds.

D. Since only flesh is derived from Adam, while the soul is bestowed by God, it is surprising how the soul is justly held accountable for what is contracted through the flesh.—M. I do not think you are so foolish as to suppose that flesh without a soul is a human being; for the soul is given in order that the flesh may be enlivened. Therefore nothing is demanded from the flesh before it receives the soul, nor is anything required from the soul before its union with flesh—especially since it is proved that there is no guilt in the seed of human conception, just as there is none in blood or spittle, and that the innocent soul is created by God. Yet a human being is said to consist of soul and body; therefore Adam’s debt is justly exacted, and because he is conceived in iniquities [Col. 1143C] and born in injustice, he is set before the just Judge as guilty.

D. How is one conceived in iniquity?—M. In concupiscence. For every human being ought to have generated without concupiscence, just as one hand is joined to another without pleasure. But because the first human being departed from natural justice and desired what was forbidden, concupiscence immediately made him its slave and compelled him and all his descendants to generate in concupiscence. Therefore everyone conceived in concupiscence is shown to be born unjust; and so, if he dies without baptism, which is the death of Christ, he is not taken into heaven to be made equal to the angels. For no one will be made equal to the angels unless no injustice rules over him, as it rules over none of them. But no one is clean [Col. 1143D] from defilement, not even an infant of one night upon earth.

### 13. What concupiscence is

D. A scruple still holds my mind and clings to it firmly.—M. What is it?

D. Since flesh is insensible and cannot do anything by itself, I see no way in which it is said to desire against the spirit and asserted to draw the spirit into consenting to it.—M. David’s key will quickly open what is shut. For it is agreed that a human being has flesh from Adam and soul from God; but no one is ignorant that he has concupiscence neither from Adam nor from God. When, however, the soul is joined to flesh [Col. 1144A], it draws concupiscence from it. No one doubts that the soul has two powers: one by which it gives life to the body, and another by which it contemplates invisible things. The one by which the body is enlivened is called animality, carnality, or sensuality. But that which contemplates invisible things is called spirit, mind, or understanding. Thus the lower part of the soul, called animality, is weighed down by the corruptible body and, immersed in the senses of the flesh, overwhelmed by them; it forgets spiritual things and delights only in earthly matters. Therefore it is called “flesh” and is said to desire against the spirit. But the higher power of the soul, called spirit or the inner human being, searches spiritual and heavenly things, rejects transient things, and delights in contemplation of invisible things [Col. 1144B]; it is therefore said to oppose the flesh. It is said to “desire” just as the ear is said to “hear.”

D. How can the spirit be overcome by the soul?—M. As Adam was overcome by Eve. For the soul is written to be the wife of the spirit; the flesh is said to be the servant of both. Therefore let the spirit rule its wife by reason; let the soul obey its husband through love; let the servant, the flesh, perform service through action. But if the wife, enticed by the servant, inclines her husband to consent to evil, and he with her commits sin through the servant, then—as the serpent persuading, the woman desiring, and the man consenting are subjected to punishments—so flesh enticing, soul desiring, and spirit consenting are justly excluded together from joy.

D. What, then, should they do?—M. Let Sarah—that is, the soul [Col. 1144C] cleaving to Abraham, that is, to the spirit—reject carnal things and desire spiritual things. Let her constrain Hagar the servant, that is, her flesh, to good works through vigils and fasts. Thus Isaac, that is, true joy, will be born to them; and they will rejoice together in it, not discordantly but united in everlasting peace.

D. Does the soul grow?—M. Not in quantity, but in reason.

D. How are some born foolish, since souls are rational?—M. When a denser humor is conceived in the sticky womb of the mother, the soul is in some way impeded in this little body, just as even adults are deprived of understanding by some illness.

### 14. On the origin of souls, and what they are like in infants

[Col. 1144D]

D. Were souls created at the beginning, or are they created every day?—M. God made all things together and at once in matter, as it is said: “Who made the things that were to be”; afterward he distinguished all things according to their form. Souls, therefore, were created at the beginning in invisible matter, but are daily formed according to their proper form and sent into the likeness of bodies, as it is said: “My Father works even now, and I work” (John 5:17) [Note: [Col. 1143D] A omits “and I work.”]; and elsewhere: “He who formed their hearts individually” (Ps. 32:15), that is, their souls.

D. Since God, supremely good and supremely holy, creates only good and holy souls, and the souls themselves enter bodies in obedience to him, it is beyond all admiration and astonishment why they should go to hell if that little body dies at once.—M. God, from whom comes every goodness and every holiness, creates only good and holy souls; and they naturally desire to enter a body, just as we naturally desire to live. Nevertheless, when they enter that unclean and polluted little vessel, they embrace it with such eagerness that they love it more than God. It is therefore just that, since they prefer the filthy vessel—or rather, the prison—in which they are enclosed to the love of God, God should exclude them from his fellowship.

D. Do souls know anything while in the bodies of infants?—M. It is read of blessed John the Baptist that [Col. 1145B] his soul, still in his mother, perceived that Christ was present. Hence it is clear that the souls of little children do not lack knowledge, but are unable, owing to the weakness of the body [Note: [Col. 1145D] A., *little body*.], to perform God’s work. Yet it is said that no soul knows more by itself than the body does, unless it receives this from the life-giving Spirit.

### 15. How sin is transmitted even from baptized parents

D. Why do you call unclean a body born from a Christian person?—M. Because it is conceived from unclean seed, as it is said: “Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed?” (Job 14:4); and elsewhere: “I was conceived in iniquities” (Ps. 50:7).

D. Since a human being is wholly cleansed in baptism, and marriage is proclaimed good, how is his seed called [Col. 1145C] unclean?—M. In baptism a human being is sanctified inwardly and outwardly; but his seed is again defiled through the concupiscence of the flesh.

D. Since that intercourse cannot occur without carnal pleasure, and the infant, still unformed as it were, cannot resist its parents, how is it itself unclean or liable either to guilt or punishment?—M. The parents are freed from the guilt of this pollution because of the faithfulness of marriage; but because of the injustice of the first transgression, it is transmitted, as if by hereditary right, in the generation of offspring. Therefore they are held liable to Adam’s guilt, in whom all sinned and in whom all died.

D. If all died in Adam, how are they born [Col. 1145D] alive?—M. Just as if someone shows himself at a window and immediately turns back, so a person being born, as it were, shows himself in the world and immediately returns to death.

D. If sins are forgiven in baptism, why are those born of baptized persons baptized?—M. If some dough has been corrupted with poison, every loaf made from it is deadly. So in Adam the mass was corrupted, and therefore all born from him were corrupted by sin and thus deserving of death, unless they are given life in the death of the Redeemer through baptism. Therefore, just as parents are cleansed for themselves in baptism, so their children must be renewed for themselves through Christ’s death in baptism [Col. 1146A], as it is said: “All who die in Adam shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:22).

D. If a pregnant woman is baptized, does that baptism benefit the infant if it dies within her?—M. Not at all. For it has not yet been born as Adam was; therefore it is not judged to have been reborn in Christ.

D. Why does God not allow some people to be born in order that they may be baptized, or take those already born away in death before they are regenerated?—M. God’s judgments are a great abyss and therefore hidden, although the reason is evident in these cases [Note: [Col. 1145D] A omits “in these cases”.], since it is known that this occurs for the sake of the elect: namely, so that, when they see these persons so undeserving and almost without sin in punishment, and themselves, after many crimes, so undeservedly in glory, they may with more abundant rejoicing give thanks to God, by whose grace they escaped such deserved punishments.

[Col. 1146B]

D. What punishment do little children who die without baptism have?—M. Darkness only.

D. Does it harm infants that they are born from an unlawful marriage—that is, from adultery, from relatives, from canons, monks, nuns, or other incestuous unions [Note: [Col. 1146D] A omits “or other incestuous unions”.]?—M. Not at all, if they have received baptism; just as it does not harm wheat if it has been sown by a thief after being stolen.

D. Do the sins of parents harm children, or the sins of children harm parents?—M. It is written: “The father shall not bear the iniquity of the son, nor the son bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18:20). If children have not consented to their parents in evils, or if parents have been unable to prevent their children from such things, the sins [Col. 1146C] of either will not harm the other; just as it did not harm Joshua that he had a wicked father, nor, conversely, did it harm him that he fathered a worthless son. But if parents give consent to children, or children to parents, in sins, they are evil together with them and will then be condemned not for the others’ evils but for their own.

### 16. On marriage with a blood-relative, a co-mother, or a goddaughter, and on polygamy

D. Is it a grave sin to marry a kinswoman?—M. According to nature, none; but according to the ordinance of the Church, a great one.

D. How do you prove this?—M. It was not a sin to eat the fruit; but to eat it against God’s command was a most serious sin.

D. Why did the holy fathers of old marry their blood-relatives? [Col. 1146D]—M. Among them love did not extend further than friends, as it is said: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5:43). Therefore they had to take the daughters of relatives, upon whom they could bestow their affection. Among us, however, love extends even to enemies, as it is said: “Love your enemies” (ibid., v. 44). Therefore, because blood itself compels us to love our relatives, the Church has decreed through the Holy Spirit that men should marry the daughters of strangers, so that a wife may be a bond of love between ourselves and strangers, through which charity may spread throughout the whole human race.

[Col. 1147A]

D. How do you prove that marrying a kinswoman is not a sin?—M. Is it permitted for two brothers to marry two sisters?

D. It is permitted.—M. My wife’s sister becomes my kinswoman through her blood. Again, through my blood my brother becomes a kinsman of my wife. If, then, it is a sin according to nature, why does my brother marry one who is both my kinswoman and his? Therefore, according to nature there is no sin, but according to prohibition it is a grave offense.

D. I cannot understand how it is unlawful to marry co-mothers or goddaughters.—M. This too, as I said above, is not a sin according to nature but according to sacrament. Just as your wife is the mother of your son in physical generation, so she who receives him from the font becomes his mother in spiritual regeneration; thus she becomes your *commater*, a co-mother, the sister of your wife, and a goddaughter becomes the sister of your daughter. Likewise, if you have lifted another’s daughter from the font, you will be her *compater*, that is, the brother of her father; and it is not permitted for a man to take two sisters or for a woman to take two brothers. Therefore, through the sacrament, such a marriage is wholly unlawful.

D. On account of what sacrament?—M. The sacrament of Christ and the Church is signified by carnal marriage. For just as a man joined to a woman becomes one with her, so the Church, through participation in Christ’s body, becomes one with him; and he, through assumption of human nature, becomes one with her, as it is said: “The two shall be one flesh; but I speak [Col. 1147C] of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:31–32). Therefore, just as human nature was alien to Christ when he joined it to himself, so the woman whom a man marries ought to be from an unrelated family.

D. What about co-mothers and goddaughters?—M. Co-mothers and goddaughters are forbidden to us in marriage because they are known to be spiritually joined to us in the sacrament; and it is judged unworthy to descend from the spiritual to the carnal.

D. Is it permitted to marry more than one wife?—M. Just as Christ is united only to the one Catholic Church, so by divine law a man is rightfully joined to only one woman; hence the first fathers are not said to have contracted marriage repeatedly. But among Christians, when one wife has died, another is taken not by divine command but by apostolic permission, as a remedy for incontinence, lest they fall into the abyss of fornication. Moreover, contracting marriage a third time is counted as fornication.

### 17. On ministers of the Church and monks

D. My soul, rejoice, for you have obtained to hear everything that you desired. Come now, noble teacher: abundantly pour forth for converts the cups of the Holy Spirit lavishly poured into you; and, since you have now spoken about prelates, explain what you think concerning the remaining ministers of the Church.—M. First, priests, if they live well, are by example the light of the world; if they teach rightly, they are by word [Col. 1148A] the salt of the earth. The remaining ministers of the Church are windows in the Lord’s house, through whom the light of knowledge shines upon those who are in the darkness of ignorance. If they live well but do not teach, they are coals of fire, which burn but do not give light. If they teach well but live badly, they are a burning candle which gives light to others while it fails itself as its wax melts, or a bell from which a sweet sound is produced for others while it is worn away by continual striking. But if they neither live well nor teach, they are smoke which obscures fire and strikes back the sight of the eyes. Of these it is said: “The stars did not shine” (Job 25:5); therefore they fell from heaven.

D. What do you say about despisers of the world, namely monks or others in religious dress?—M. If they fulfill their undertaking by living religiously, they will be judges with the Lord; but if not, they are more miserable than all people, because they possess neither the world nor God. Of them it is said: “Let them go down alive into hell” (Num. 16:30), because they know.

### 18. On the various conditions of laypeople

D. What do you think of soldiers?—M. Few are good. For they live by plunder, clothe themselves with robbery, buy possessions from it, and purchase benefices from it. Of them it is said: “Their days failed in vanity, and their years in haste” [Note: [Col. 1147D] A omits “and their years in haste”.]; therefore God’s wrath rose against them (Ps. 77:33, 30).

D. What hope do merchants have?—M. Little; for by frauds, perjuries, and profits they acquire almost everything that they possess.

D. Do they not often visit holy places, willingly [Col. 1148C] offer sacrifice to God, and give many alms?—M. They do all these things so that God may increase their goods and preserve what they have; and through these things they receive their reward. Of them it is said: “Those who trust in the abundance of their riches” (Judith 9:9), “shall be laid in hell like sheep, and death shall feed upon them.”

D. What do you think of various craftspeople?—M. Almost all perish; for whatever they do, they conduct it with the greatest fraud. Of them it is said: “There is no darkness and no shadow of death where those who work iniquity may hide themselves” (Job 34:22).

D. Do entertainers have hope?—M. None at all. For in their whole purpose they are servants of Satan. Of them it is said: “They have not known God; therefore God rejected [Col. 1148D] them, and the Lord shall mock them” (Ps. 2:4), because mockers are mocked.

D. What do you say about those publicly doing penance?—M. Do not call them penitents, but people mocking God. For they mock God and deceive themselves who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst deeds: when they have killed people, they sing; when they have committed adultery, they exult; when they commit perjury or sacrilege, they laugh aloud. While placed under penance, they seek varied dishes, eagerly desire to be made drunk by various drinks, and indulge in every luxury more than others. Of them it is said: “The Lord shall give worms and unquenchable fire into their flesh” (Judith 16:21).

[Col. 1149A]

D. What do you say about fools?—M. They are counted among children; for they do not know how to do better, and therefore they are saved.

D. What do you say about farmers?—M. For the most part they are saved, because they live simply and feed God’s people by their sweat, as it is said: “Blessed are those who eat the labors of their hands” (Ps. 127:2).

D. What about little children?—M. All who cannot speak—such as three-year-olds—provided only that they have received baptism, are saved, as it is said: “For of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:14). But among those five years old and above, some perish and some are saved.

### 19. On the small number of those to be saved, and how Christ died for all

[Col. 1149B]

D. It seems that few are saved.—M. Narrow is the way that leads to life, and few walk upon it. Yet, just as a dove chooses pure grains, so Christ gathers his hidden elect from all these classes; he even takes some from the class of thieves. For he knows who are his, those for whom he also shed his blood.

D. Since it is written, “Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:6), and that “by the grace of God he tasted death for all” (Heb. 2:9), did his death benefit the ungodly?—M. Christ died only for the elect, who will then be ungodly because they are placed in unbelief. But when he says “for all,” he means from all nations and all languages, not only of that time [Col. 1149C], but for all who were to come, and for those who were in the prisons of hell, as it is said: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). The house of Israel is the kingdom of heaven, the kingdom of those who see God. The lost sheep are the elect, whom Christ came to redeem by his death, as it is said: “I lay down my life for my sheep” (John 10:15). He said “my sheep,” not those concerning whom he said: “You are not of my sheep” (ibid., v. 26). Hence you have: “I pray for them, not for the world” (ibid. 17:9); and again: “You loved them before the foundation of the world” (ibid., v. 24). Of these it is said: “This is the blood which shall be shed for you and for many” (Mark 14:24). He does not say “for all.” For Christ’s death conferred nothing upon the reprobate except just [Col. 1149D] condemnation, and in this sense he also died for them. For all the wicked from the beginning of the world consented to Christ’s death; hence it is said: “All these things shall come upon this generation” (Matt. 23:36), namely, the generation of the wicked.

D. Since Christ is mercy itself, and “his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144:9), and he came not to call the just but sinners to repentance, why did he not have mercy on them?—M. Christ is merciful toward those who recognize themselves as miserable; but the ungodly think themselves just, and therefore the Lord does not call them, as it is said: “Do not have mercy on all who work iniquity” (Ps. 58:6). And [Col. 1150A] since he is justice itself, if mercy were bent over the members of the devil, he would be unjust. Therefore mercy belongs to the just, but justice to the ungodly. Moreover, “his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144:9), because he makes his sun rise upon good and evil alike (Matt. 5:45), sends rain upon them, and feeds them.

### 20. On distinguishing good people from bad, and the manifold remission of sins

D. Can good and bad people be distinguished by any signs?—M. They can. The just, conscious of being well disposed and certain of their future hope, are cheerful in expression; their eyes sparkle with a certain grace; they are modest in bearing; and, from the abundance of the heart, sweet in speech. But the wicked, because of their perverse conscience and bitterness of heart, are clouded in expression and unstable in word and deed; [Col. 1150B] excessive in laughter, biting in sadness, unrestrained in their gait—now slow, now hurried. The poison they carry in their heart they pour forth now in bitter, now in impure utterances.

D. If sins have been forgiven in Christ’s death, why are we baptized?—M. Sins are forgiven through Christ’s death if people are baptized in faith in Christ’s death.

D. In how many ways are sins forgiven?—M. Seven.

D. Which?—M. First, through baptism; second, through martyrdom; third, through confession and penance, as it is said: “I shall confess my injustice to the Lord, and you forgave my iniquity” (Ps. 31:5); fourth, through tears, as it is said: [Col. 1150C] “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5); fifth, through almsgiving, as it is said: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3:33); sixth, through forgiving those who sin against us, as it is said: “If you forgive people, my Father also will forgive you” (Matt. 6:14); seventh, through works of charity, as it is said: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

D. What is the value of confession?—M. As much as baptism. For just as original sins are forgiven in baptism, so actual sins are forgiven in confession.

D. And does judgment also have value?—M. There are two judgments of God: one here through confession; the other on the last day through examination. In the latter, God himself will be judge, the devil accuser, and the human being defendant. In the former, the priest, Christ’s vicar, is judge; the human being is both accuser and defendant; penance is the sentence. Whoever is judged here is not accused there, as it is said: “God does not judge twice in the same matter” (Nah. 1:9, according to the Septuagint); and elsewhere: “If we judged ourselves, we surely would not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31).

D. Does almsgiving or penance avail if sins are not abandoned?—M. Just as [Note: [Col. 1149D] A., *if*.] every medicine is useless for healing a wound so long as the iron remains embedded unless the iron is drawn out, so all good works will not profit unless sin is abandoned, as it is said: “Whoever commits sin is the slave [Col. 1151A] of sin” (John 8:34); and no one can make another’s slave free.

D. Will good works benefit the wicked?—M. For every good thing that people have done, they will receive recompense, either in this life or in the life to come. In this life, as is said to the rich man: “You received your good things in your life” (Luke 16:25). In the life to come, as it is said: “You shall receive a hundredfold” (Matt. 19:29). Conversely, for every evil a person has done, he will be punished either in this age or in the age to come, as it is said:

> Before God’s face nothing ever passes unpunished.

Therefore either the person himself punishes himself by repenting, or God exacts vengeance by punishing.

### 21. Why legal sacrifices were instituted, and on the origin of idolatry

[Col. 1151B]

D. Why did God permit the Jews legal sacrifices, since they did not take away sins?—M. So that they would not sacrifice to idols, a rite which they had learned while dwelling in Egypt. For this reason also he led them about through the wilderness for so long, that they might forget this custom. There was another reason: just as the Jewish people was a figure—indeed, a shadow—of the Christian people, so in the same people there had to precede a shadow of the true sacrifice, as in the paschal lamb, the red heifer, or the goat. But after Christ, the truth, came to give blessing—he who had given the law—he put an end to shadowy victims and, offering himself, instituted the unique sacrifice that takes away sins.

D. Since people worshiped only one God at the beginning, whence did the superstition of idol worship begin? [Col. 1151C]—M. At Babel, the tower of the giants is said to have risen, and is reported to have been sixty-four stadia high. In it Nemrod, the first king of this world, and afterward Ninus ruled. Ninus made an image of his father Belus and commanded all whom he had subdued to worship it. Later others imitated him, making idols for their dear ones or for mighty kings after they had died, and compelling the common people to worship them: thus the Cretans did for their king Jupiter, the Athenians for Cecrops, the Latins for Janus, and the Romans for Romulus. Hence it is said:

> Fear first made gods in the world.

(Petronius, *Fragments*.) But demons entered the images and, deceiving the people by oracles, made sport of them.

D. Where was Babel?—M. In the place where great Babylon now stands [Col. 1151D], which Queen Semiramis built of brick and bitumen, so that the bricks might resist fire and the bitumen water. She is said to have extended its length and breadth for sixty miles, and is reported to have constructed walls fifty cubits broad and two hundred cubits high. Idolatry is said to have begun in this city. The Antichrist too is said to be destined to be born there, as it is said: “From Babylon shall come forth a serpent, which will devour the whole world.”

### 22. Whether altars should be adorned with gold or gems, and in what ways God is propitiated
D. Should altars be furnished with gold or gems?—M. Altars are not to be consecrated with gold and gems in honour of God. Whether you bestow these upon one who has them because you claim to be his superior, or upon one who is your equal, whichever you do is an insult; for whoever invites heavenly things with prices gives offence.

D. By what is God most especially propitiated toward us?—M. By the Word: that alone which he has in common with humankind delights him exceedingly by its likeness to himself. For the Word is God; by it he created the world, by it he rules and sustains all things. This Word we venerate; this we love; from this we draw breath. Since God is spirit, he is to be pleased not by earthly riches or lavish generosity, but by devout works and thanksgiving.

### 23. Whether sacred pilgrimages are to be approved

D. Is it beneficial to seek Jerusalem, or to visit other holy places?—M. It is better to spend on the poor the money with which they intend to go. [Note: Col. 1151D: A., “extend.”] But if any, fired by love of Christ, or after confessing their own sins, go with money acquired from their own inheritance or by their own labour, commend themselves on the journey to the prayers of congregations of saints, and distribute some of their goods to those congregations themselves or to other poor persons, they are to be praised; for Helena and Eudoxia, who did these things, are praised. But those who run about to holy places for curiosity’s sake or for human praise receive this as their reward: that they have seen pleasant places or beautiful buildings, or heard the praise which they desired. But if any go with money amassed through profit-making, fraud, robbery, or oppression, they will be as acceptable to God or the saints as one who sacrifices his son before his father and then comes to him with bloodstained hands.

### 24. On frequent need for food and the term of life

D. Why did God not grant humanity the ability, after taking food, to go without it for at least a week?—M. Hunger is one of the penalties of sin. Man was created so that, if he wished, he might live blessedly without labour. But after he fell, he could return only through labour. If he did not endure hunger, cold, or other hardships, he would not wish to labour; and thus he would always remain excluded from the kingdom. Therefore God implanted hunger in him, so that compelled by this necessity he might labour, and might also have occasion to return. Understand this only of the elect; for for the reprobate all things conduce to punishment.

D. Is a term of life appointed for a human being, and can one exceed it by living, or anticipate it by dying?—M. It is appointed by God for each person how long he ought to live in this age; beyond that limit a person cannot live even one moment, as it is said: “You have set his bounds, which cannot be passed” (Job 14:5). Yet one may anticipate it in many ways: by rushing into arms or among wild beasts; by violently taking life with poison or a noose; or by throwing oneself into flames or waters. So too a hired servant, through bad conduct, may bring it about that he is not merely deprived of his wages, but even expelled before the appointed time.

D. Prove it.—M. God brought the children of Israel out of Egypt in order to give them the land of promise; but because of their sins they did not obtain it, and before reaching it they were struck down in the wilderness.

### 25. On the just execution of criminals and their salvation; on the instruction of children; on the ark and the prophets

D. Does a judge sin if he punishes criminals?—M. On the contrary, he sins if he does not punish them; for he is the avenger of God’s wrath, appointed for this very purpose.

D. Do officers sin when, commanded by judges, they inflict the penalty of death on the condemned?—M. Not at all; rather, they wash their hands in the blood of the sinner.

D. If persons have been caught in crimes, condemned by judges to the rack or some other punishment, and repent at the very point of death, is there any hope for them?—M. Great hope. Some are purified by that punishment and, like the thief on the cross, are saved; others are released from punishments through the prayers of saints.

D. Why is it that children can learn everything better than old people?—M. Because the soul is still new in them and curious about everything. In old people, however, the faculty of perception is blunted by daily use, sight, and hearing, and weakened through many thoughts.

D. Where did the Ark of the Covenant go?—M. When the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians was imminent, Jeremiah, by the Lord’s command, hid it in the tomb of Moses together with the other prophets. At the last time it will be brought forth by Elijah and Enoch, when the Lord reveals it.

### 26. Why signs are not now performed

D. Why cannot righteous persons perform signs in this age as they did formerly?—M. No saint has ever performed any sign; rather, God did it through them, he who presided over their mind, as it is said: “You are God, who alone do wonders” (Ps. 71:18). Formerly, because of unbelievers, he performed visible signs through the righteous when he healed sick bodies; now he accomplishes greater, namely spiritual, works through them, when he heals souls sick in various ways. Yet sometimes, when necessary, he performs outward signs through his own people, and sometimes even through the reprobate; nevertheless, he works marvels for the sake of the elect. Thus God is said to have withdrawn from certain fallen persons, although repentant, because he does not work signs through them. At the end of time, however, signs will be wholly withdrawn from the Church, so that the righteous, more thoroughly tested by temptations, may be more abundantly rewarded.

### 27. On the prophets and Holy Scripture

D. Did the prophets understand what they wrote?—M. They understood.

D. Why then did they publish their writings so obscurely and not plainly?—M. They ought not [to have done so]. For it belongs to masons to build, but to painters to paint. Thus the patriarchs, as it were, dug out in figures the marked site of the Church; the prophets laid its foundations by their writings; the apostles built its walls by preaching; and their followers painted it by expositions. [Note: Col. 1153D: A. omits *autem*, “however.”] But Holy Scripture was written only for the children of God, for whom Mother Church opens all closed things with the key of David. Those who are not children see only what is outside and do not understand, because they neither love nor believe.

D. Since the Seventy were Hebrews, why did they translate differently from what the prophets wrote?—M. Holy Scripture is understood in two ways, historically and allegorically. The prophets therefore composed the historical sense; but the seventy men, themselves also prophets, translated the allegorical sense.

### 28. On guardian angels

D. Do human beings have angels as guardians?—M. Angels preside over every nation and every city, dispensing and ordering rights, laws, and customs justly. Each soul also, when sent into a body, is entrusted to an angel, who may always urge it toward good and report all its works to God and the angels in heaven.

D. Since God knows all things and the holy angels behold all things in him, what can be reported to them that they do not know?—M. That angels tell God and the angels our actions means nothing else than that they rejoice together in God over our progress, as it is said: “There will be joy among the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:10). Conversely, their being saddened means their indignation over our evil deeds.

D. Are angels continually on earth with those whom they guard?—M. Whenever necessary, they come to help, especially when invited by prayers. For there is no delay in their coming, since in a moment they can descend from heaven to earth and return again to heaven. When they descend to us, they are not deprived of their inward glory, because wherever they are sent they always see the face of the Father.

D. In what manner do angels appear to human beings?—M. In human form. Since a human being is bodily, he cannot see spirits; therefore angels assume from the air a body which a human can see and hear. That visible body is more visible than tangible; nor is it visible to everyone, but only to those to whom they wish to show themselves.

### 29. On demons lying in wait and besieging

D. Are there demons lying in wait for human beings?—M. Demons preside over each vice, and each has innumerable demons beneath it, who continually entice souls to vices and report human evils to their prince with loud laughter. Yet if one of them is defeated in combat by one of the righteous, he is immediately thrust back into the abyss by that person’s guardian angel, nor is he thereafter permitted to encounter any of the righteous, although another may be substituted for him by the prince of demons. For just as a human being, defeated by the devil, was immediately cast out of paradise, so when any demon is overcome by the saints, he is at once put to shame and condemned to Tartarus. These often assume a tangible body from dense air, so that they may deceive more effectively.

D. Can demons besiege whom they wish?—M. They could not enter a herd of swine unless permitted; much less, then, human beings. Sometimes they besiege the body of a holy man: for that person’s crown, but for their own punishment. They always besiege the souls of the wicked, and sometimes torment their bodies as well. But in baptism the human body, as a temple, is consecrated to the Holy Spirit with oil and chrism, as it is said: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). Therefore this temple is always inhabited either by the Holy Spirit or by an unclean spirit.

### 30. On anointing, repentance at the end, and death

D. What benefit does the anointing of oil give to the sick?—M. Sins that have been confessed and not repeated, or daily sins, are forgiven through this anointing, as it is said: “And if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him” (James 5:15). If he has not repented of his sins, this anointing not only benefits him not at all, but harms him greatly.

D. Does repentance at the end of life benefit one?—M. Those who delay repenting of their sins until death do not themselves abandon their sins; rather, their sins abandon them, because they no longer wish to keep them as servants. Yet those who repent from the heart find mercy even in death itself, like the thief at the very departure of death, as it is said: “At whatever hour you groan, you shall be saved” (Ezek. 33:12).

D. From where is *mors* (“death”) named?—M. From bitterness, or from the bite of the forbidden fruit, from which death arose. There are three deaths: untimely, as in infants; harsh, as in the young; and natural, as in the old.

D. Since sins are forgiven in baptism, and since death is the penalty of sin, why is death permitted to rule even over the elect after baptism?—M. So that they may suffer for Christ and be more richly crowned. There is another reason. If bodily immortality were given in baptism, all would hasten to baptism not for God but for that immortality; and thus no one would return to the kingdom. Therefore God forgave sin in baptism, but did not remove the penalties of sin, so that the righteous may walk by faith and exercise themselves in works until death is swallowed up by life.

### 31. On the return of sins and the unforgivable sin

D. Are sins forgiven to the reprobate in baptism?—M. They are forgiven; but when they afterwards relapse into the same sins, the sins that had been forgiven relapse upon them also and return, as it is said: “I forgave you all that debt” (Matt. 18:32), and immediately afterwards: “He handed him over to the torturers until he should pay the whole debt” (ibid., 34). [Note: Col. 1155D: A. omits *rel.* [probably *relabuntur*] and *et*.]

D. Why does God permit them to approach baptism or the other sacraments, when he knows they will fall away from them?—M. For the sake of the elect, as has been said, so that they may draw them by example.

D. What is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which will be forgiven neither in this age nor in the future?—M. No forgiveness of sins is granted to impenitence and distrust regarding the Holy Spirit. Whoever therefore distrusts the grace of the Holy Spirit and does not repent blasphemes against the Holy Spirit; and this is the unforgivable sin.

### 32. On the death and burial of good and evil persons

D. Does it harm good persons if they are killed or carried off by sudden death?—M. Not at all. Those who always think that they will die do not die a sudden death. Whether they are sacrificed by the sword, torn apart by beasts, plunged into flames or waters, hanged, broken on the wheel, or die through any misfortune, “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.” As it is said: “By whatever death a righteous person dies, his righteousness shall not be taken from him.” Such a death does not harm them; indeed, it benefits them greatly, because any sin they have contracted through human frailty is forgiven through the bitterness of death.

D. Does it benefit the wicked if they lie long in beds before dying?—M. Not at all. Whatever death they die, they die an evil and sudden death: those who do not die in the Lord, and who never thought that they would die. Therefore the death of sinners is always most grievous.

D. Are the righteous harmed at all if they are not buried in the Church’s cemetery?—M. Not in the least. For the whole world is the temple of God, consecrated by Christ’s blood. Whether they are buried or cast out in a field, forest, swamp, or any place whatsoever, or devoured by beasts or wild animals, they are always cherished in the bosom of the Church, which is spread across the breadth of the earth.

D. Does it contribute anything to the righteous that they are buried in consecrated places?—M. Through certain righteous persons, the places in which they are buried are consecrated. Those who are in punishments benefit when their bodies are buried in holy places because they are aided by the prayers of those with whom burial associates them. It also benefits them because, when their friends gather there, reminded by the tombs, they pour out prayers to the Lord for them.

D. Does it benefit the wicked if they are buried in a holy place?—M. On the contrary, it harms them greatly if burial joins them to those from whom their merit has separated them far away. Thus many are said often to have been dug up by demons and cast a long way from sacred places.

D. May God, good Teacher, keep you far from the wicked, and may Christ join you in the stars with the citizens of heaven. Amen.

# BOOK THREE

## 1. On the leading of the righteous into paradise, and what paradise is

D. Now that the innumerable heads of the hydra have been cut off, while others and still others spring up in their place—come then, light of the Church, seize the sword of your noble tongue and cut down the forest of questions in which I wander, so that through you I, wandering, may be able to emerge into the plain of knowledge. Explain, then, what takes place concerning those who are dying.—M. Just as a bridegroom comes with a multitude of soldiers to receive his bride and joyfully leads her away with singing, so, when a righteous person is at the end, his guardian angel comes with a multitude of angels, takes his soul—the bride of Christ—from the prison of the body, and conveys it, with the sweetest melody, immense light, and most delightful fragrance, to the heavenly palace, into spiritual paradise.

D. Is this paradise a bodily place, or where is it?—M. It is not a bodily place, because spirits do not dwell in bodily places [Note: Col. 1157D: A. omits *corporalibus*, “bodily”]; rather, it is the spiritual dwelling-place of the blessed, which eternal Wisdom perfected from the beginning. It is in the intellectual heaven, where they behold the Godhead itself, as it is, face to face.

## 2. On the perfect and righteous who are led into heaven, and those to be purified

D. Are all souls of the righteous led there?—M. The souls of the perfect, when removed from the body, are immediately admitted there.

D. Who are the perfect?—M. Those for whom commandments do not suffice, but who do more than is commanded: martyrs, monks, and virgins. For martyrdom, virginity, and renunciation of the world are not commandments but divine counsels. Therefore those who do these things will possess the kingdom of heaven as if by hereditary right, as it is said: “You shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29). And elsewhere: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 126:3). But the righteous are still deferred in certain dwelling-places [Note: Col. 1157D: P. reads *differuntur*, “are deferred,” for *differunt*, “defer”], as is said of them: “May it avail them for honour, but us for salvation.”

D. Who are these?—M. Those who fulfil the Lord’s commandments without complaint, when stripped of their bodies, are led by angels into an earthly paradise, or rather into some spiritual joy, since spirits are not believed to dwell in bodily places. There is a certain order of righteous persons called imperfect, who nevertheless are all written in the book of God: namely, married persons, who, after death, will be received according to their merits into most pleasant dwellings. Many of these, before the day of judgment, will be raised to greater glory through the prayers of saints and the alms of the living, so that after judgment all may be joined with angels. There are some of the elect who fall far short of perfection and postpone repenting of their sins. As a sinful son is handed over to a servant to be beaten, so they are permitted by holy angels to demons for purification. Yet the demons cannot harm them more than they themselves have deserved or than the holy angels permit.

D. Do you know by what means these are released?—M. Masses, alms, prayers, and other pious labours benefit them, especially if while alive they did such things for others. Some of them are released on the seventh day, others on the thirtieth, others on the anniversary; some only after a long time. Nevertheless, after judgment all, as has been said, will be made equal to angels.

D. Why are these days observed especially?—M. Three and four make seven: by three is understood faith in the Trinity; by four, humankind, which consists of four elements. The soul also has three powers: rational, irascible, and concupiscible; and all time runs its course in seven-day weeks. Thus the seventh day is observed so that whatever the soul has sinned, in its three powers, through the four qualities of the body, during the seven days of this time, against the sevenfold Spirit received in baptism, may be forgiven in faith in the Trinity. Thirty arises from three and ten: by three is understood the new law because of faith in the Trinity; by ten, the old law because of the Decalogue. Moreover, every month passes in thirty days. Thus the thirtieth day is observed so that whatever a person has transgressed in months under the new or old law may be wiped away. The year is Christ, as it is said: “A year acceptable to the Lord” (Isa. 58:5). The months are the twelve apostles, as it is said: “You shall bless the crown of the year of your goodness” (Ps. 64:12). The sun’s course is through the year, the moon’s return after a month. Thus the anniversary day is observed so that whatever a person has done against Christ, the sun of righteousness, his Church, the moon, and the teaching of the apostles, who are the months of the good year, may be forgiven.

## 3. On Purgatory

D. What benefit is the purgatorial fire?—M. For some, purification in this life consists in bodily torments which the wicked sometimes inflict on them; for others, bodily afflictions which they impose on themselves by fasts, vigils, and other labours; for others, loss of loved ones or possessions; for others, pains or illness; for some, lack of food or clothing; for others, the bitterness of death itself. [Note: Col. 1158D: A. reads *est*, “is,” for *prodest*, “benefits.”] After death, however, purification will be excessive heat of fire, intense cold, or some other kind of punishment, the least of which is greater than the greatest that can be imagined in this life. While they are placed there, angels or other saints sometimes appear to them—saints in whose honour they did something in this life—and grant them a breath of air, a sweet fragrance, or some consolation, until, set free, they enter that hall which receives no stain.

D. In what form are they placed there?—M. In the form of the bodies which they bore here. It is also said of demons that bodies of air are given to them in which they are tormented.

D. Since the body is insensible and can do nothing by itself except what the soul works through it as through an instrument, on what grounds is it condemned?—M. When people besiege their enemy, they first destroy or burn his buildings; afterwards they kill him under torture, so that he may grieve in mind over the loss of his possessions and over the wounds inflicted in the destruction of his body. The body is the soul’s clothing or dwelling. Because the soul loved it while despising its Creator, it is destroyed and burned with the soul, so that the soul may be tormented by the burning of its own dwelling or garment. The body is also the soul’s instrument, not as a trumpet is the instrument of a trumpeter or an axe of a carpenter, but so united to it that whatever the soul does, the body too is said to have done. It is therefore justly condemned with it. [Note: Col. 1159D: A. reads *concepto*, “conceived,” for *contempto*, “despised.”]

D. How many souls will reach heaven?—M. As many as the angels who remained there; each soul will be associated with each order of angels, according as God distinguishes them by their merits.

## 4. On the leading of the wicked to hell and the punishments they endure there

D. You have sufficiently satisfied me concerning these. Now tell me how matters proceed at the departure of the wicked.—M. When the wicked are at the end, demons gather and come with the greatest clamour, horrible in appearance and terrifying in their gestures. They wrench the soul from the body with extremely severe torment and cruelly drag it to the gates of hell.

D. What is hell, and where is it?—M. There are two hells: an upper and a lower. The upper is the lowest part of this world, full of punishments; for there overflow excessive heat, great cold, hunger, thirst, diverse bodily pains, and mental lashes such as fear and shame. Of this it is said: “Bring my soul out of prison,” that is, out of hell—namely, my life (Ps. 141:8). The lower is a spiritual place, where there is unquenchable fire, of which it is said: “You have delivered my soul from the lowest hell” (Ps. 85:13). It is said to be beneath the earth so that, just as the bodies of sinners are covered with earth, the souls of sinners may be buried beneath the earth in hell; as is said of the rich man: “He was buried in hell” (Luke 16:22). Nine kinds of punishment are said to exist there.

D. What are they?—M. First, fire, which has been kindled in such a way that, if the whole sea were to flow into it, it would not be extinguished. Its heat surpasses this material fire as this fire surpasses painted fire; it burns and gives no light. The second punishment is intolerable cold, of which it is said: if a fiery mountain were cast into it, it would turn to ice. Of these two it is said: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 24:51), because smoke provokes tears in the eyes and cold gnashing of teeth. Third are immortal worms, or serpents and dragons terrible in sight and hissing, which live in flame as fish live in water. Fourth is intolerable stench. Fifth are the lashes of those striking, like hammers beating iron. Sixth is palpable darkness, as it is said: “A land of darkness, where there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells” (Job 10:22). Seventh is the shame of sinners, because all sins are open there to everyone and they cannot hide themselves. Eighth are the horrible sight of demons and dragons, whom they see amid sparkling fire, and the miserable cries of those weeping and mocking. Ninth are fiery chains, by which they are bound in every individual limb.

D. Why do they suffer so many miseries?—M. Because they neglected the fellowship of the nine orders of angels, they will justly mourn while subjected to nine torments. Because they burned here in the fire of lusts, they will justly burn there in fire. Because they stiffened here in the cold of malice, they will justly gnash there in punishing cold. They are said to glow outwardly in fire like iron in a furnace, and inwardly to freeze like ice in winter, as it is said: “They shall pass from snowy waters to excessive heat” (Job 24:19). Since envy and hatred gnawed at them here like worms, worms will deservedly bite them there. Those who here delighted sweetly in the stench of lust will there be cruelly tormented by putrid stench. Because here they would not receive discipline and did not deserve to be scourged with humankind, they are therefore beaten there without ceasing by straps, as it is said: “Judgments are prepared for blasphemers, and beating hammers for the bodies of fools.” Because they loved here the darkness of vices and would not come to Christ, the light, they will therefore be darkened there by dreadful darkness, as it is said: “They shall never see light.” Because they scorned here to confess the sins which they were not ashamed to commit, they will there forever be ashamed before all, naked and exposed. Because they disdained here to see and hear good things, they will justly be filled there with terrible sights and miserable sounds. Because here they were dissolved through every vice, they will justly be bound there with chains in every limb. They will desire to die, and death will flee from them.

D. How are they positioned there?—M. Their heads are plunged downward, their backs turned toward one another, their feet raised upward, and they are stretched out on every side for punishments.

D. Alas! Why was a human being ever born, to be punished by such a penalty?—M. Why do you weep? Why flow with tears? Only the devil and his members will suffer these things.

D. Who are the devil’s members?—M. The proud, envious, deceitful, faithless, gluttonous, drunken, lustful, murderers, thieves, cruel persons, plunderers, brigands, impure persons, avaricious persons, adulterers, fornicators, liars, perjurers, blasphemers, evildoers, slanderers, and contentious persons. Those found in these will go into the aforesaid punishments, never to return.

## 5. How the blessed regard the damned

D. Alas! Will the righteous see them?—M. The righteous will see the wicked in punishments, so that they may rejoice more that they have escaped these punishments. Before judgment the wicked will also see the good in glory, so that they may grieve more that they neglected it. After judgment, however, the good will always see the wicked in punishments, but the wicked will never again see the good.

D. Will the righteous not grieve when they see them so tormented?—M. No. Even if a father sees a son, or a son his father, in punishment; a daughter sees her mother, or a mother her daughter; a husband sees his wife, or a wife her husband: not only do they not grieve, but it is as delightful to them to see this as it is to us when we see fish playing in a whirlpool, as it is said: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees the vengeance of sinners” (Ps. 57:11).

D. Do the righteous not pray for them?—M. They would think against God if they prayed for the damned. For they are so united to God that God’s judgments please them in every respect; and therefore they will rejoice in them.

## 6. Which hell received the souls of the righteous before Christ’s coming

D. In which hell were the righteous before Christ’s coming?—M. In the upper hell, in a certain place adjoining the lower, where they could see one another. Those who were there, although free from punishment, considered themselves in some sense to be in hell, since they were separated from the kingdom. But to those in the lower hell it seemed that those in that hell adjoining the lower one were in the refreshment of paradise. Hence the rich man asked Lazarus to let a drop fall upon him.

D. What punishment did they have there?—M. Only a certain darkness, whence it is said: “For those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has risen” (Isa. 9:2). Some of them were in certain punishments. Therefore the Lord came to the upper hell in being born, to free those oppressed by the devil; he descended into the lower hell in dying, to redeem captives from the tyrant, as it is said: “Say to those who are bound, ‘Come out,’ and to those who are in darkness, ‘Be revealed’” (Isa. 49:9).
