He calls “bound” those who were in punishments, and the others those in darkness; all of them he absolved and led into glory—the King of glory.

## 7. How the blessed know one another and intercede for us

D. Do the righteous and good know one another in glory?—M. The souls of the righteous know all the righteous by name and lineage, and know their merits, as though they had always been with them. They also know all the wicked so fully that they know for what merit each person is there. The wicked too know the wicked, and the good whom they see, so well that they know even their names, as the rich man knew the names of Abraham and Lazarus. [Notes: Col. 1161D: A. omits *nomina*, “names”; Col. 1162D: A. omits *cognovit*, “knew.”]

D. Do souls pray for those dear to them?—M. The righteous pray for those whom they loved in the Lord, or for those who invoke them, that they may be preserved from evil and liberated from the temptations of the world; and, if they are in error, that they may be corrected and joined to them more swiftly.

D. How do they pray to God?—M. Their desire is their prayer. For whatever they desire they receive without delay. Their praying also consists in presenting to God the bodily sufferings they endured or the good deeds they performed for Christ. Yet they pray for nothing except what God himself has arranged to do; otherwise they would pray in vain.

## 8. On the joy, dwelling-places, knowledge, and appearances of the blessed; likewise on apparitions presented by the damned

D. Do the saints have full joy?—M. By no means. Just as those invited to a banquet are glad at their invitation and welcome, yet concerned about absent friends until all assemble together, so the souls of the righteous now rejoice indeed in their own glory but are concerned at our absence. When they have received their bodies and all have gathered into one, then they will have full joy.

D. What are the Father’s house and the many dwelling-places?—M. The Father’s house is the vision of almighty God, in which the righteous glory as they do in the Lord. The different dwelling-places are rewards according to merits.

D. Do souls know what is done here?—M. The souls of the righteous know all that is done here. Those who are in punishments do not know, except what angels or saints report to them. Those in hell know no more of what is done here than the living know of what is done there. Yet just as prophets of old knew some things which others did not know, though not everything, so some souls among the wicked know certain things which others do not, though not everything. Thus everything they know is either divinely revealed to them or reported to them by those dying and coming there.

D. Can souls appear when they wish and to whom they wish?—M. The souls of saints appear when they wish and to whom they wish, whether to those awake or asleep. Those in punishments do not appear unless permitted by angels, either that people may pray for their release or that, once released, they may announce their joy to their friends. Those in hell can appear to no one. But if they are sometimes seen to appear, whether in dreams or to waking people, they are not those souls but demons in their likeness, who even transform themselves into angels of light in order to deceive. If it ever truly happens, it does so because of the merit of some saint—as when the soul of a robber appeared to St Martin where he destroyed an altar—or as a warning, as when the soul of Pope Benedict appeared in a monastery. Its head and tail were those of an ass, its middle that of a bear; it declared that day and night it was dragged through rough and fiery places and, after judgment, would be swallowed by the cauldron of Gehenna.

D. In what form do they appear?—M. In a human body assumed from the air.

## 9. The source of dreams

D. Where do dreams come from?—M. Sometimes from God, when something future is revealed, as to Joseph through the stars and sheaves, that he would be preferred to his brothers; or when some necessary matter is advised, as to the other Joseph, that he should flee into Egypt. Sometimes from the devil, when he tries to tempt someone or hinder some good, as is related in the Passion of the Lord concerning Pilate’s wife. Sometimes they come from the person himself, when what he has seen, heard, or thought is imagined in sleep; in fear he is deluded by sad things, and in hope by joyful things.

## 10. On Antichrist and the coming of Enoch and Elijah

D. Blessed be God’s Word, which unlocks so many secrets for me through your mouth. Now, if I dared to ask, I would gladly hear about Antichrist.—M. Antichrist will be born in great Babylon from a prostitute of the tribe of Dan. In his mother’s womb he will be filled by the devil, and at Chorazin he will be nurtured by sorcerers. He will rule over the whole world and subject the whole human race to himself in four ways. First, he will enlist nobles by riches, which will flow to him in abundance, because all hidden money will be manifest to him. Second, he will subdue the common people by terror, because he will rage with the utmost cruelty against worshippers of God. Third, he will win over the clergy by wisdom and incredible eloquence, because he will know every art and all Scripture by heart. Fourth, he will deceive those who despise the world, such as monks, by signs and wonders. For he will perform such astonishing miracles that he will command fire to descend from heaven and consume his opponents before him, and will make the dead rise and bear witness to him.

D. Will he truly raise the dead?—M. By no means. Rather, through his sorceries the devil will enter someone’s body, bring it forward, and speak within it, so that it may appear alive, as it is said: “In every sign and lying wonder” (2 Thess. 2:9). He will rebuild ancient Jerusalem, in which he will command that he be worshipped as God. Jews coming from the whole world will receive him with the utmost desire; but through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch they will return to the Christian religion, and almost all will undergo dreadful martyrdom.

D. At what age will those two come?—M. At the age at which they were taken up. They too will be killed by Antichrist, who is called *Antemos*, that is, “the contrary one”; or *Arneomai*, that is, “I deny”; or *Titan*, that is, “sun” or “giant.” He will hold the monarchy for three and a half years; then he will spread his tent on the Mount of Olives to attack the righteous. There he will be found suddenly dead, slain by the breath of the Lord—that is, killed by God’s command—as it is said: “The Lord will cast down the illustrious one of the whole earth upon the holy mountain.”

D. Since it is said, “Those days will be shortened for the sake of the elect” (Matt. 24:22), will the days then be shorter than they are now?—M. The days will then be as long as they are now, as it is said: “By thy ordinance the day endures” (Ps. 118:91). But the days are said to be shortened because he will reign for a short time, that is, three and a half years. Moreover, human bodies are believed to be destined to be smaller [Col. 1164A] than ours, just as ours are also smaller than those of the ancients.

D. What will happen afterwards?—M. Forty days will be left for those who have fallen through his error or deceit, so that they may repent; after this, on what day the judgment will take place, no human being knows.

### 11. On the Last Trumpet and the Resurrection

D. What is the last trumpet?—M. When the Lord gave the Law on the mountain, the sound of a trumpet was heard. So angels appointed for this purpose, taking bodies and trumpets from the air, will thunder forth God’s terrible judgment with the sound of a trumpet; as it is said: “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise” (1 Cor. 15:52). And again: “Their memory has perished with a sound” (Ps. 9:7); and with a very loud voice they will cry to the dead, “Arise!” as it is said: “At midnight [Col. 1164B] a cry arose” (Matt. 25:6). At that voice all the dead, good and evil alike, will rise in the twinkling of an eye—that is, as quickly as you can open your eye, indeed, as quickly as, once the eye is opened, you can see light.

D. What is the first resurrection?—M. As there are two deaths, so there are two resurrections: one of souls, the other of bodies. When a person sins, the soul dies, because it is forsaken by God, who is life, and is buried, as it were, in the body as in a tomb. But when through repentance it returns to God, who is life, it rises, as it were, from death. The other resurrection will be that of bodies.

D. On what day?—M. On the day of Easter, at the hour when Christ rose.

D. Will anyone then be in the world?—M. The world will then be as full of people as it is today, who will be doing then as they do today. Some will be ploughing, some sailing, some building, some doing one thing and another.

D. What will happen to them?—M. When the righteous rise, they will immediately be caught up by angels into the air to meet Christ; and the elect who are alive will be caught up with them, and in that very catching-up will die and come to life again. This occurred beforehand in Mary, the mother of the Lord, and John the Evangelist: Mary, who, after death, having received her body, was assumed into glory; and John, who was indeed caught up bodily and is believed, in that very catching-up, to have died and come to life again. The reprobate will die from terror itself and immediately come to life again; and this is “to judge the living and the dead.”

D. Will those who died in their mothers’ wombs rise? [Col. 1164D]—M. All who received the breath of life will rise.

D. At what age or stature?—M. At the age they were, if they had been thirty years old, or would have been if they had not died beforehand.

D. Sometimes a wolf devours a human being, and the human flesh is turned into the wolf’s flesh; then a bear devours the wolf, and a lion the bear. How will the human being rise from these?—M. What was human flesh will rise; what was the beasts’ will remain. For he who knew how to create all things from nothing knows well how to distinguish these things. Therefore, whether they are devoured limb by limb by beasts, fishes, or birds, all will be restored at the resurrection, so completely that not even a hair of them will perish.

D. If cut hair and nails return to their place, [Col. 1165A] will they not be misshapen?—M. It must not be understood that they are to be restored to their former place. Rather, as if a potter were to break a newly made vessel and make another from the same clay, without attending to what had formerly been its handle or its base, so God forms from the same material another body, very unlike this one, from which every deformity and infirmity is absent and to which every wholeness and beauty is present—although God can fittingly restore every member to its own place.

D. Will those who here had two heads, additional limbs, or lacked some limbs, or who were fat or thin, rise in such a state?—M. Those who here had two heads: from them two bodies will rise, and each soul will have its own body, to which nothing unbecoming or deformed clings, but which has all its limbs sound, whole, and full of every beauty.

D. What do you think concerning miscarried children?—M. Insofar as it is the father’s seed, it will rise in the father; insofar as it is the mother’s blood, it will rise in the mother.

D. What sort of bodies will the righteous have?—M. Immortal and incorruptible, and transparent like shining glass. The reprobate likewise will have immortal bodies, since they will suffer continually in death without end; and incorruptible bodies in this sense, that although afflicted with every punishment, they will not be consumed—but they will be dark.

### 12. On the Judgment and Its Circumstances

D. At what hour will the judgment take place?—M. At midnight: the hour at which the angel devastated Egypt and the Lord [Col. 1165C] despoiled hell; at that hour he will free his elect from this world.

D. How will the Lord come to judgment?—M. Just as, when an emperor is about to enter a city, his crown and other insignia are carried before him, through which his coming is recognized, so Christ will come to judgment in the form in which he ascended, with all the orders of angels. Angels carrying his cross will go before him; with trumpet and voice they will summon the dead to meet him; all the elements will be troubled, while a storm of fire and cold rages everywhere in mingled fashion. As it is said: “Fire goes before him, and a mighty tempest is round about him” (Ps. 49:3); and elsewhere: “The whole world will fight for him against the senseless” (Wis. [Col. 1165D] 5:21).

D. Will the judgment be in the valley of Jehoshaphat?—M. The valley of Jehoshaphat is called the valley of judgment. A valley is always beside a mountain. The valley is this world; the mountain is heaven. Therefore judgment takes place in the valley—that is, in this world, namely in the air—where the righteous will be placed at Christ’s right hand, like sheep, while the ungodly will be set at the left, like goats.

D. How at the right hand or the left?—M. At the right hand, namely above in glory; at the left, below upon the earth. For the righteous will be raised on high by the twin wings of charity, as it is said: “The saints will take wings like eagles” (Isa. 40:31). But the ungodly, [Col. 1166A] weighed down by sins like lead, will be pressed downward toward earthly things, to which they had clung with their whole heart.

### 13. On the Judge and His Assessors

D. In what form will the Lord appear there?—M. To the elect, in the form in which he appeared on the mountain; but to the reprobate, in that in which he hung upon the cross.

D. Will the cross be there—the wood, that is, upon which the Lord suffered?—M. By no means; rather, there will be a light in the shape of a cross, brighter than the sun.

D. Why will the Son conduct the judgment?—M. The Son is the likeness of God; but angel and human being had arrogated to themselves the likeness of God. It is therefore just that he to whom injury was done should render judgment in vengeance, although the Father and the Holy Spirit cooperate with him.

D. Will there be a throne on which he sits, as it is said: “He will sit [Col. 1166B] upon the throne of majesty” (Matt. 25:31)?—M. Christ is now said to stand and fight for his bride; then, his enemies conquered and his bride received to himself, he will sit in majesty. That is, his humanity will rest in divinity. He will also sit upon his throne because he will cease from every labor in the Church. Yet, because he will appear as a human being there, he is believed to sit as judge upon a throne taken from the air.

D. Will the apostles have thrones, as it is said: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28)?—M. Their consciences are their thrones, in which, having conquered the world and its vices, they will rest triumphantly as though upon a throne. Yet they themselves will also be seen sitting upon thrones taken from the air, as it is said: “They will sit upon thrones in judgment.”

[Col. 1166C] D. How will the judgment take place?—M. Now good and evil are mixed together; many appear good who are evil, and many are thought evil who are good. Then, by angels, the good will be separated from the evil as grain from chaff, and divided into four orders. One order is that of the perfect, judging with God. Another is that of the righteous, who are saved through judgment. A third is that of the ungodly, who perish without judgment. A fourth is that of the wicked, who are condemned through judgment.

D. Who are those who judge?—M. Apostles, martyrs, confessors, monks, and virgins.

D. How will they judge the righteous?—M. They will show that these have imitated their teaching and their examples, and are therefore worthy of the kingdom of heaven.  
[Note: [Col. 1165D] A. *om.* “of heaven.”]

### 14. On Those Judged and Those Who Perish without Judgment; on God’s Wrath and the Opening of the Books

[Col. 1166D]

D. Who are those who will be judged?—M. Those who performed works of mercy within lawful marriage, or who redeemed their sins by repentance and almsgiving. To them it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father; for I was hungry and you gave me to eat,” etc. (Matt. 25:34–35).

D. Will these words be spoken aloud?—M. Since Christ will appear there as a human being and they themselves will stand there in bodies, it is possible that these words will be uttered audibly. Yet, since it will be manifest to all there by what merit each person is saved or condemned, [Col. 1167A] these words indicate to us rather the merits by which people are saved.

D. How will they be judged?—M. Those who have done these things will be deemed worthy of the heavenly palace.

D. Who are those who will perish without judgment?—M. Those who sinned without the Law, namely pagans, and those Jews who lived after Christ’s Passion. For after his Passion, observance of the Law is reckoned a superstitious form of idolatry.

D. Will they see Christ?—M. They will see him, but to their own destruction, as it is said: “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (John 19:37); for all the ungodly consented to the Lord’s death.

D. Why is it said of them: “The ungodly will not rise in judgment” (Ps. 1:5)?—M. It will not be granted them [Col. 1167B] to judge there, as they did here. Of these it is said: “You will make them like a fiery furnace at the time of your countenance” (Ps. 20:10).

D. Who are those who will be judged and perish?—M. Jews who sinned under the Law before Christ’s coming, and evil Christians who denied God by evil deeds. To these it will be said: “Depart from me, you cursed; for I was hungry and you did not give me to eat,” etc. (Matt. 25:42). These words indicate that they are condemned because they disdained to redeem their crimes by almsgiving. And you should note that he does not say, “Come, I bless you,” nor does he say, “Depart, I curse you”; but, “Because you are blessed, come,” and, “Because you are cursed, depart.”

D. Who blessed these, or who cursed those? [Col. 1167C]—M. Every day the Holy Spirit blesses the elect through the mouths of friends and enemies, as it is said: “You are blessed by the Lord” (Ps. 113:15). And again: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you” (Ps. 128:8). But through the mouths of all he curses the reprobate, as it is said: “Cursed are those who turn aside from thy commandments” (ibid., 21).

D. How will the saints judge them?—M. By their merits they will show that these followed neither their deeds nor their words, and are therefore worthy of every punishment. God will trouble them in his wrath, and fire will devour them.

D. Does the Lord have fury or anger?—M. There are no such passions in the Lord, who, as it is said, “judges all things with tranquility” (Wis. 12:8). But when the sentence of just condemnation is pronounced upon the guilty, he appears to be angry with those who suffer these things.

D. Will the righteous have defenders, or the wicked accusers?—M. They will have their own consciences. For all will be so illuminated by the splendor of the cross that, just as the sun is now seen by all, so then the consciences of all people will be openly visible to all.

D. What does it mean when it is said, “The books were opened; and the book of life; and the dead were judged from the things written in the books” (Rev. 20:12)?—M. The books are the prophets, the apostles, and other perfect persons. These books will be opened because their teaching and examples will be evident to all; in them, as in books, all will see what they ought to have done and what they ought to have avoided. But the book of life is the life of Jesus, in which all will read as in a book what, concerning his commandments, they have done [Col. 1168A] or neglected. The book of life is also the divine power in which all will see their consciences as though written down.

### 15. On What Will Follow the Universal Judgment, the Conflagration of the World, and Its Renewal

D. What follows?—M. When judgment has been completed, the devil with his whole body—that is, with all the ungodly—will be cast into prison, that is, into the lake of fire and sulphur. But Christ with his bride—that is, with all the elect—will return with triumphant glory to the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of his Father.

D. What does this mean: “Passing by, he will minister to them” (Luke 12:37)?—M. It means that, laying aside the form of a servant, he will show himself to the elect as he is in the Father’s glory, as it is said: “I will manifest myself to them” (John 14:21).

[Col. 1168B] D. What does this mean: “He will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Cor. 15:24), and “God will be all in all” (Col. 3:11)?—M. That is, Christ’s humanity and the whole Church will reign in divinity; and God will be the joy of all and the joy of each. For each will have a particular joy, and all together will rejoice in the vision of God.

D. What will then become of the world?—M. It will be consumed by fire. For just as in former times the flood-water prevailed over the world and rose fifteen cubits above all the mountains, so then the prevailing fire will burn fifteen cubits higher than all the mountains.

D. Will the world utterly perish?—M. The mutability of things and the punishment of sin—namely cold, heat, hail, storms, lightning, thunder, and other inconveniences—will utterly perish. But the elements, purified, will remain, as it is said: “Thou shalt change them, and they shall be changed” (Ps. 101:27). For just as the present form of our bodies will pass away and receive another form, utterly unlike and incomparable with this, so the present form of the world will wholly pass away, and there will be another form of incomparable glory, as it is said: “The Lord will make a new heaven and a new earth” (Isa. 65:17). Finally, heaven, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the waters, which now hasten with unretarded motion as though desiring to be changed into a better state, will then remain fixed, stable, and at rest, transformed by a wondrous glorification. For heaven will put on the glory of the sun; the sun will shine sevenfold more than it now does, as it is said: “The sun will have the light [Col. 1168D] of seven days.” The moon and stars will be clothed with ineffable splendor. Water, which deserved to touch Christ’s body and washed the saints in baptism, will surpass every beauty of crystal. The earth, which cherished the Lord’s body in its bosom, will be wholly like paradise. And because it has been watered with the blood of saints, it will forever be adorned, unfadingly, with fragrant flowers, lilies, roses, and violets. This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High: the earth, which was cursed and given over to thorns, will then be blessed forever by the Lord, and labor and pain will be no more.

### 16. On the Bodies of the Blessed and Their Endowments

D. You have filled me with the good things of the Lord’s house. Tell me: what sort of bodies will the saints have?—M. Seven times brighter than the sun, and more swift than thought.

[Col. 1169A] D. At what age or what stature will they be?—M. As Christ was when he rose. Yet, since here it is delightful to see boys mixed with old men, women with men, and short persons joined with tall ones, it is believable that there will be much greater delight there in seeing persons of every age and stature, of both sexes, men and women—just as here it is delightful to hear different sounds in organs or stringed instruments. Hence it is more to be believed that all will rise and appear there at the age and stature at which they happened to depart from here.

D. Will they be clothed or naked?—M. They will be naked, but shine with every beauty; and they will be no more ashamed of their other members than we are now of beautiful eyes. Yet the salvation and joy of the righteous will be their garments; [Col. 1169B] for the Lord will clothe their bodies with a garment of salvation and their souls with a covering of joy. And just as here there are different kinds of flowers—whiteness in lilies, redness in roses—so there is believed to be a diverse grace of colors in the bodies of the saints: martyrs will have one color, virgins another; and these will be counted as garments.

### 17. On the Activity and Joy of the Blessed

D. Can they gladly do what they wish?—M. They desire nothing but what is good; therefore, whatever they wish, they do freely, and wherever they wish to be, they are there without delay.

D. What do they do?—M. They are at leisure and behold God, and praise him forever and ever.

[Col. 1169C] D. What is the praise of the saints?—M. For the saints there, to praise God is simply to rejoice in the vision of God.

D. Do they remember the evils they suffered in the body?—M. They remember all things.

D. Do they not feel pain from this?—M. Indeed, they will have greater joy because they conquered all these things, just as someone who long ago escaped the danger of war tells the story of it afterwards with joy to friends.

D. Your golden tongue has lifted me above the height of earth. Now come, tell me of their joys.—M. The joys of the saints will therefore be those “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

D. What are these?—M. Eternal life, everlasting blessedness, and an abundance of every good without any want.

[Col. 1169D] D. Explain this more plainly.—M. They will have seven special glories of the body and seven of the soul. In the body: beauty, swiftness, strength, freedom, pleasure, health, and immortality. In the soul: wisdom, friendship, concord, power, honor, security, and joy.

### 18. On the Gifts of the Bodies of the Blessed

D. You have raised me above myself. These are the things my soul longed to hear. I ask you: express them in some way.—M. Would it please you if you were as beautiful as Absalom, in whose body there was no [Col. 1170A] blemish, and whose hair, when cut, was weighed at a great price?

D. O glory!—M. What if, together with this beauty, you were as swift as Asahel, who in running outstripped gazelles?

D. O grace!—M. What if, together with these two things, you were as strong as Samson, who struck down a thousand armed men with one jawbone?

D. O immense splendor!—M. What if, together with these three things, you were as free as Augustus, whom the whole world served?

D. O radiance!—M. What if, together with these four things, you abounded in pleasure like Solomon, who never denied his heart anything it desired?

D. O sweetness!—M. What if, together with these five things, [Col. 1170B] you were as healthy as Moses, whose tooth was never loosened and whose eye never grew dim?

D. O health!—M. What if, possessing all these things, you were destined to become as long-lived as Methuselah, who lived almost a thousand years?

D. O magnificence! It seems to me that, if anyone were given the choice of selecting one of these things, he would rightly choose each one in preference to a kingdom; but if anyone possessed them all, he would deservedly be preferred to the whole world.—M. You should sometimes be silent while you hear things still more excellent. What if, together with all the foregoing things, you were as wise as Solomon, to whom all things hidden and secret were manifest?

D. O excellence—or wisdom!—M. What if, in addition to this, all people were your friends, as Jonathan was David’s, whom he loved as his own soul?

[Col. 1170C] D. O blessedness!—M. What if, moreover, all were as harmonious with you as Laelius with Scipio, of whom neither willed anything except what the other willed?

D. O ineffability!—M. What if, in addition to all this, you were as powerful as Alexander the Great, who mightily subjected Asia, Africa, and Europe to himself?

D. O sublimity!—M. What if, moreover, you were honored by all as Joseph was by the Egyptians, who worshipped him as lord?

D. O loftiness!—M. What if, amid all these things, you were as secure as Elijah and Enoch?

D. O greatness!—M. What if, possessing all these things, you had such joy as one has who, [Col. 1170D] when being led to the rack, is suddenly snatched away on the road to a kingdom?

D. O majesty!—M. What if you had a friend whom you loved as yourself, and he likewise abounded, as you did, in all these goods? Would you not have double joy?

D. O immeasurable delight!—M. What if you had many friends, and they nonetheless abounded in these goods? Would you not have so many joys?

D. O unutterableness! So I delight in your words as in all riches. It seems to me that if anyone had some of these things—I do not say all—he would be worthier than the whole world. But if anyone were full of all these things, he would rightly seem to be God.—M. You judge rightly, for they themselves—that is, the saints—abound far more excellently in all these goods. [Col. 1171A] Absalom’s beauty would there be ugliness. But their comeliness will be like the brightness of the sun, as it is said: “The righteous will shine like the sun” (Matt. 13:43), which will then shine sevenfold more than it does now. And this is promised them: “He will reform the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:21). No one doubts that Christ’s body is brighter than the sun, since it is the body of the Creator rather than the body of a creature; moreover, human beings are called temples of God, while the sun is not so called. If, therefore, the bodies of the saints are conformed to Christ’s glorious body, which is brighter than the sun, and God dwells in them as in temples, it necessarily follows that God’s temples are more radiant than the sun. Behold the beauty of the saints.

[Col. 1171B] Asahel’s swiftness would there be sluggish slowness. Certainly they themselves are so swift that, as quickly as the rising sun touches the west with its ray, they can come from east to west; and as quickly as an eye, lifting itself, directs its sight toward heaven, so quickly they can pass down from heaven to earth and back from earth to heaven. For angels can do this, and they will be equal to them, as it is said: “They will be equal to the angels of God” (Luke 20:36). Behold their swiftness. Samson’s strength would there be weakness. For their power will be such that, if they wished to overturn mountains and the entire mass of the earth with their foot, they could do so powerfully, and as easily as we now see. For no one doubts that angels can do this, and the saints are said to be equal to them. Behold the strength of the righteous.

[Col. 1171C] The freedom of Emperor Augustus would there be captivity, for he could be captured, bound, and imprisoned. But their freedom is such that they can penetrate all obstacles, and no creature can hold them back; just as the tomb could not hold the Lord’s body from rising, and he entered when the doors were shut. They will be conformed to him. Behold their freedom.

### 19. On the Pleasure of the Blessed

D. Solomon’s delights would be miseries to them. O what is the pleasure of those for whom God himself, the fountain of all goods, is an inexhaustible fullness that satisfies without satiety!—M. There are two blessednesses: a lesser one of paradise and a greater one of the heavenly kingdom. Since we have experienced neither, we do not know how to provide a comparison for them. There are also two miseries: a lesser misery of this world and a greater misery of hell. Since we experience one of these daily, we know how to make a comparison from what we have experienced. Thus, if a heated iron were fixed in someone’s head and, glowing, passed through all the limbs, then, as that person would have pain inwardly and outwardly, so, by the contrary mode, they have pleasure inwardly and outwardly in all their members. Here, that is, in this world, it is pleasurable to see a multitude of handsome men and women, to wear precious garments, to behold splendid buildings, to hear sweet song, polished speech, organs, lyres, citharas, and such things; to smell incense and other kinds of diverse spices; to delight in varied feasts; to touch soft and gentle things; [Col. 1172A] to possess much money and diverse household goods. All these things overflow upon them infinitely. O what pleasure their sight will have, who will see with eyes closed as well as open! Whose individual members will be like the sun’s eye, and who will behold the King of glory in his beauty; they will see all angels and all saints inwardly and outwardly. They will see the glory of God, the glory of angels, the glory of patriarchs, the glory of prophets, the glory of apostles, the glory of martyrs, the glory of confessors, the glory of virgins, and the glory of all saints. They will behold their own eyes, their own faces, all their members inwardly and outwardly, and each person’s thoughts. They will contemplate all things that are in the new heaven and new earth. They will continually see in hell their enemies who formerly afflicted them, [Col. 1172B] and will rejoice ineffably in all these things.

O what will be the pleasure of their hearing, for whom the harmonies of heaven, the concert of angels, and the sweet-sounding instruments of all the saints will sound without ceasing! What will be their sense of smell, where they will draw the sweetest fragrance from God himself, the source of sweetness, and perceive the fragrance of angels and all saints! Come, what will be the pleasure of taste, where “they will feast and rejoice in the presence of God” (Ps. 67:4), and, when God’s glory appears, they will be satisfied and “made drunk with the abundance of his house” (Ps. 35:9)! What will be the pleasure of touch, where all rough and hard things will be absent, and all gentle and sweet things will smile upon them! O how great an abundance of sweet riches, where, in the Lord’s joy, they will be set over all his goods. Behold such are the delights of the saints.

Moses’ health would there be infirmity. But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord. If you tried to attack them with a sword, you could no more injure them than you can now cut a ray of sunlight; such is the health of the righteous. Methuselah’s long life would be the painful burden of protracted death to those from whom death and pain flee, because they live forever. Behold the duration of life they will have, who will happily inherit the eternity of unfailing life. And these are only the goods of the body.

### 20. The Gifts of Souls in the Blessed; That They Will Not Be Ashamed of Sins Properly Expunged; and the Fullness of Everyone’s Joy

D. As a sweet spring refreshes a thirsty farmer, so a delightful honeycomb dripping from your mouth refreshes [Col. 1172D] my soul. But O incomparably blessed people, who are predestined for such ineffable goods!—M. Truly blessed are those who dwell in the Lord’s house, because in all these things they will live for ever and ever. To them Solomon’s wisdom would be great foolishness. For all wisdom flows into them: they draw all knowledge from the very fountain of wisdom. Indeed, they know perfectly all things past, present, and whatever things are future. They know the names, families, and good or evil works ever performed by absolutely all human beings, whether in heaven or in hell; and nothing is hidden from them, since together they see all things in the sun of righteousness.

D. Alas, how many tears my misery now compels me to shed through the fountain of your eloquence! Will all the saints know what I have done? [Col. 1173A]—M. Certainly; they will know indelibly not only what you have done, but whatever you have ever thought or said, or any human being has done, whether good or evil.

D. What then is the value of confession and repentance for sins, if they are not erased, and if they must themselves know our shameful and foul crimes, which we shudder even to think about?—M. What do you shrink from? What do you fear? Are you afraid that there you will be ashamed of your deeds? You will be no more ashamed of your most foul and shameful acts, once confessed and washed by repentance, than if someone now told you what you did long ago in the cradle; nor will you blush any more than if you had been perfectly healed from wounds received in battle. To forgive or erase sins means nothing other than not to punish them. They are forgiven through repentance and confession; but they will never be erased from the knowledge of God and the saints.

D. I should like this proved to me by an example.—M. Do you not know that David committed homicide and adultery?

D. I know.—M. Do you know that Mary was a sinner, that Peter denied Christ with an oath, and that Paul cruelly persecuted the Church?

D. I know.—M. Do you believe that they are in heaven?

D. I believe.—M. If therefore you, still corruptible and frail, know these things, how much more do they know them, who will be free from all corruption and frailty? Yet they are not now ashamed because of them, but rather glory in the Lord over their salvation.

[Col. 1173C] D. Do angels or saints who have scarcely sinned at all not shrink from such persons? Will they not regard them more poorly?—M. By no means. Rather, just as friends rejoice together with those who escape shipwreck or some grave danger, so angels and saints rejoice together over the escape of those for whom all things, even sins themselves, work together for good. And just as a physician is praised more highly if he heals someone gravely and hopelessly ill, so God is more abundantly glorified by their salvation.

D. O immeasurable joy!—M. The friendship of David and Jonathan would be enmity to them. O how sweet is the friendship that joins those whom God loves as his sons, who themselves love God more than themselves, and whom all angels and all saints love as themselves. The harmony of Laelius and Scipio would be discord to them. Indeed, their harmony is like that of the eyes: where one looks, the other immediately turns itself there. Whatever any one of them wills, God wills, the angels will, and all [Col. 1173D] the saints will.

D. Come then: if God and all the saints will what I will, then I would wish to be like Peter?—M. Certainly: if you wish this, you will immediately be so. I do not say that you will be Peter, but like Peter. For if you wished to be Peter, you would wish not to remain. For if you put off your own essence, you would be nothing. Yet no one there desires more than he has deserved, just as a foot does not desire to be an eye, a hand an ear, or a man a woman. For if they desired anything more, they would not have full joy; but all will have full joy. Therefore they will desire nothing more than they have, and nothing can be added [Col. 1174A] to their joy. For what each does not have in himself, he will have in another: for example, Peter will have in John the glory of virginity, and John in Peter the glory of suffering. Thus each one’s glory will be that of all, and the glory of all will be that of each one. Tell me, then, what more they can desire, who will be equal to angels and will possess all these things I have mentioned, and more besides.

Alexander’s vast power would be a narrow confinement to them. For their power will be so effective that, if they wished to make another heaven, they could do so mightily. For they are sons of God and co-heirs with Christ, and therefore gods, as it is said: “I said, you are gods” (Ps. 81:6). And because they are gods, they can do everything they will.

D. If they can, why do they not make another heaven? [Col. 1174B]—M. God left nothing imperfect, because he completed all things perfectly in measure, number, and weight. And if they made another heaven, it would be superfluous; but they desire nothing unbecoming or superfluous. For we too can do many things which we nevertheless do not do, such as dance or run.

D. All these things may be believed concerning the apostles and the highest saints; it will go well with us if we are permitted to live in their service.—M. It has been said of all the righteous without exception: “They will be equal to the angels of God” (Luke 20:36). For just as that is perfectly hot from which all cold has been removed, and that perfectly cold from which all heat has been removed, although one thing may nonetheless be hotter or colder than another, so, although all the saints are equal in always seeing the face [Col. 1174C] of the Father, they differ in glory as the brightness of the stars, or the lights of sun and moon. Thus, if a king, passing by a sick man whom he saw lying in the mud, ordered him to be lifted up, bathed, clothed in his own garments, given his own name, adopted as his son, and granted the kingdom as an inheritance, so God, seeing us in the mud of sins, lifted us from it through faith, washed us in baptism, placed upon us the name of his Divinity, and enrolled us as heirs in his kingdom, as it is said: “To as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12). Therefore, although one receives glory more excellently than another and another more eminently than another according to merits, all will receive one house of the Father, though with different dwelling places, and one denarius from [Col. 1174D] the vision of God and fellowship with the angels.

Joseph’s honor would be dishonor to them. O what honor they will have, whom God will honor as sons, angels will honor as princes, and all saints will venerate as gods! For God is their debtor, because they prepared themselves with all their effort in order that what he had determined to do concerning them might come to pass. All saints are their debtors, because the double garment—or rather, the hundredfold reward—which they received, they will have in large part from them. Angels are their debtors, because they did what was in their power to bring their number to completion. Heaven, earth, and every creature are their debtors, because they hastened by their merits the time when these would be so excellently transformed.

The security of Elijah and Enoch would be anxious fear to them, because they are so secure that they will fear neither death [Col. 1175A] nor any misfortune, nor dread ever losing all these things. For God does not take them away, since they are his dearest children; and they themselves will never wish to lose them. Therefore they will never lose them. But, delivered from the rack and snatched into the kingdom, they will enjoy joy instead of sorrow. O what joy and exultation they will have, who enter into the joy of the Lord! O God, what joy they will have, who will always see face to face, as he is, the Father in the Son, the Word in the Father, and the charity of the Holy Spirit in both! They will have joy from fellowship with angels, joy from companionship with all the saints. They will therefore rejoice in the Lord’s goods inwardly and outwardly, above themselves and beneath themselves, around them and on every side. To these things I urge all my friends; [Col. 1175B] if they heed me, they will rejoice to abound and overflow with these delights in the company of those who are many thousands. Behold: this is full joy, and this is an abundance of every good without any want.

### 21. Antitheses of the Blessed and the Damned
D. You have so filled my heart with joy that I almost saw the face of the Lord, caught up in a cloud into heaven’s embrace. Therefore I rejoice over your words as one who finds abundant spoil.

—M. Therefore, just as these friends of God will glory in the Lord, happy for ever, so, conversely, his enemies, utterly wretched and unhappy, will be continually tormented. Behold: as the former will be illumined with the greatest beauty, so the latter will be disfigured with the utmost horror. As the former [Col. 1175C] will be raised with the highest agility, so the latter will be weighed down with the deepest sluggishness. As the former will be strengthened with exceptional vigor, so the latter will be weakened with exceptional infirmity. As the former will enjoy unfettered freedom, so the latter will be oppressed by anxious slavery. As the former will delight in boundless pleasure, so the latter will be embittered by boundless misery. As the former will flourish in excellent health, so the latter will fail through endless sickness. As the former, triumphant in blessed immortality, will rejoice, so the latter will lament their grievous continuance. As the former will be polished by the splendor of wisdom, so the latter will be darkened by the horror of folly. For whatever they know, they will know to increase their pain. As sweet friendship will unite the former, so bitter enmity will torment the latter. As the former, being at harmony with every creature, [Col. 1175D] will be glorified by every creature, so the latter, being at discord with every creature, will be cursed by every creature. As the former will be exalted by supreme power, so the latter will be constrained by utter powerlessness. As the former [Col. 1176A] will be endowed with the greatest honor, so the latter will be consigned to the greatest disgrace. As the former will dance in splendid security, so the latter will tremble in extreme fear. As the former will exult in ineffable joy, so the latter will wail endlessly in miserable sorrow.

For they will hate God, because, so far as lay in their power, they opposed him, lest his city should ever be built. They will hate the angels, because, so far as they could, they brought it about that their number should never be filled. They will hate all the saints, because, so far as lay in their power, they will never possess full joy. They will hate the new heaven, the new earth, and every creature, because, so far as lay in their power, they hindered them from ever being transformed. O marvelous opposition! As the joys of the former will be beyond thought [Col. 1176B] and beyond utterance, so the punishments of the latter will be incomparable and ineffable. Therefore they are called the lost, because they have fallen away from the worship of God.

D. I do not understand this.

—M. When God was building a palace for himself, a wall fell when the angels fell. Wishing to rebuild it, God sent his Son to gather living stones for this building. Mounting his chariot, he carried many along; he left those who fell from it behind, as it is said: “You will ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3:8). God’s chariots are the four Evangelists. The horses are the apostles, who by their preaching drew Christ in this chariot through the world and gathered many into God’s building. Those fallen from the chariot are heretics and schismatics, [Col. 1176C] as it is said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). But those who are brought in are placed in the heavenly building by the supreme craftsman as squared stones. These are the elect, polished by four virtues—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—by whom the walls of Jerusalem will be repaired, as it is said: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. 121:3).

But certain rough, unpolished stones are rejected by the craftsman, cast into the fire, and turned into lime; and the walls are strengthened with these as though with cement and adorned. These are the impious, rejected from the heavenly building and cast into the furnace of Gehenna. Through their destruction the righteous, by the bond of charity as though by cement, will be more firmly joined together as a wall; adorned by comparison with them in their glory, they will delight without end in the Lord God.

[Col. 1176D]

D. May the Lord God Almighty fill you, excellent master, with delight and exultation in the glorification of the saints; and may you see the King of glory in his beauty, and see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life.

[Col. 1175]

# ON THE KNOWLEDGE OF TRUE LIFE

(It appears in the Appendix to volume VI of the Works of St Augustine, *Patrologia*, vol. XL, col. 1003.)

[Col. 1177]

# BOOK OF TWELVE QUESTIONS

In which there is chiefly asked whether the holy archangel Michael precedes the blessed apostle Peter, or Peter Michael.

(Extracted from a manuscript codex of the illustrious Charterhouse of Gaming in Austria by the venerable Fr. Leopold Wydemann; edited by Fr. Bernhard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part I, col. 199.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1177A]

To Thomas, radiant with the splendor of wisdom, Honorius wishes the joyful sight of the Lord’s face. I thought it best to send for examination by your judgment a question, desirable, I think, to many, which I have recently resolved as best I could.

Two men happened to meet on the road, one of whom was a canon and the other a monk. As they began their journey, each asked the other who he was and where he was from. The canon said that he belonged to blessed Peter; the monk, that he belonged to the holy archangel Michael. The canon said that his lord was worthier, being the prince of the Church and the gatekeeper of heaven. The monk, on the contrary, maintained that his lord was loftier, being an angel and the ruler of paradise. When each had supported his own side with such reasoning or authority, certain persons [Col. 1177B] asked us to which of them the palm ought to be awarded. At the time I replied briefly, orally, as circumstances permitted; but at their request I set forth the entire question in writing.

## SUMMARY OF THE TWELVE QUESTIONS

In this evangelical question twelve questions are resolved.

I. That God the Father made all things simultaneously in the Son, and that this sensible world is the shadow of that archetype.

II. That the universe is arranged after the manner of a lyre, in which the different kinds of things harmonize like strings.

III. That, as no kind was created for another but for itself, so humanity was created not for the apostate angel but for itself; and thus, even if no angel had fallen, humanity would nevertheless have had its own place in the universe.

IV. That the elect human beings are taken up into heaven not in place of apostate angels but for themselves; while the reprobate, whether angels or humans, are placed as discordant strings in a fitting place so as to contribute to harmony.

V. That some fell from each of the angelic orders; and that elect human beings are to be joined, according to their merits, to the angels who remained standing, while likewise the reprobate are to be added, according to their merits, to the several orders of those who fell.

VI. That the choir of apostles is to be joined to the seraphim; and consequently Peter is above Michael in heaven, since Christ, God and man, [Col. 1178A] made Peter prince of the Church and Rome, the head of the world, granted him primacy.

VII. That a human being is worthier than an angel, but an angel happier than a human being, because angels worship the human God, whereas humans do not worship an angel-God.

VIII. That there are nine orders of the righteous in the Church corresponding to the nine orders of angels.

IX. That God, angels, and souls have no bodies, like justice and wisdom, and are seen by the mind alone.

X. That bodily things are discerned by bodily sight, images by spirit, and wills by intellect; and that in this manner they are discerned through the mind of angels.

XI. That angels have ethereal bodies, demons aerial bodies, and human beings earthly bodies; and that, just as we can change clothing, demons can transform their bodies into various shapes, and angels can alter theirs as they please.

XII. That the form of the body adheres to souls stripped of the body; and that after his resurrection the Lord manifested his body as he willed.

## CHAPTER I. First Question: That God the Father made all things simultaneously in the Son, and that this sensible world is the shadow of that archetype

Many suppose that humanity was created for this sole reason: to restore the fall of the angels. If this were so, it necessarily follows that humanity would never have been created had the multitude of angels remained in heaven. And if humanity had not been created, neither would this world have been created, of which humanity is made lord [Col. 1178C] and which is believed to have been established for humanity’s sake. If this world had not been made, then consequently there would be no hell, which certainly has been placed in this world and into which the devil was cast as soon as he was driven from heaven; nor would there be this air, which is part of the world and in which he is still said to be kept until the day of judgment.

If this were true, then the Evangelist’s saying would be false: “What was made in him was life” (John 1). Life in God is God, as the Son says to God: “I am the life and the truth” (John 14). If, therefore, everything made is life and truth in Christ, and life and truth are God, then this whole creation is the shadow of life and truth; and as life and truth have always existed, so their shadow has always existed.

For example: a composition made by me but not yet written down in some manner lives in me; I look to it as to an exemplar while I write it on tablets. What appears written outwardly is the shadow of the unwritten thing hidden within. The outward thing can indeed be reduced to nothing, but the inward remains incorruptible. Within, it is simple and uniform; without, it is manifold and varied—in letters, words, syllables, cases, tenses, schemes, and figures. So the whole creation, conceived in the divine mind, is simple, unchangeable, and eternal; but in itself it is manifold, changeable, and transitory, namely in genera, species, and individuals. Yet he who “created all things simultaneously” remains for ever; as though Scripture said: God the Father eternally begot from himself the Son—that is, his wisdom—in whom [Col. 1179B] he made all things simultaneously.

## CHAPTER II. Second Question: That the universe is arranged after the manner of a lyre, in which the different kinds of things harmonize like strings

Moreover, before the creation of the angels it is written: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). For what purpose did he make heaven? That it might be the dwelling-place of angels. For what purpose the earth? That it might be the dwelling-place of human beings.

The supreme craftsman made the universe like a great lyre, setting in it, as it were, diverse strings to produce manifold sounds, when he divided his entire work into two things—or into two things opposed to one another. Spirit and body, like a male and a boys’ choir, yield low and high sound: they differ in nature but agree in the goodness of their essence. The very orders of spirits produce distinctions of voices: archangels surpass angels in glory; the Virtues surpass the archangels in honor; the Powers exceed the Virtues in dignity; and the Principalities are above the Powers. Dominions surpass the glory of these; nor do they equal Thrones in brightness; and Cherubim eclipse the Thrones in knowledge, Seraphim in wisdom. All of these harmonize in sweet concord because, in united agreement, they praise their maker by loving him; each is satisfied with its own glory, and no one covets another’s gift.

Likewise bodily things imitate distinctions of voices, since they are divided into diverse genera, species, individuals, forms, and numbers. All these sound together harmoniously when they keep, like ringing measures, the law implanted in them. Spirit and body, angel and devil, heaven and hell, fire and water, air and earth, sweet and bitter, soft and hard, and the rest in this fashion, yield answering sounds.

## CHAPTER III. Third Question: That, as no kind was created for another but for itself, so humanity was created not for the apostate angel but for itself; and thus, even if no angel had fallen, humanity would nevertheless have had its own place in the universe

It should be noted that each thing is founded in its own place and that nothing is placed for another. Among genera, a bird does not arise in place of a fish, nor a fish in place of a beast; a stone does not arise in place of a tree, nor does a tree succeed in place of a stone. Likewise among species, an eagle does not arise in place of a stork, a palm in place of an olive, or a topaz in place of a chrysolite. Thus also humanity has its own proper place in the universe, as an angel has its own proper place.

Humanity, therefore, was created not for the angel but for itself. Otherwise a worm, having a proper place, would be of greater dignity than humanity, which would lack a place of its own and occupy another’s place; and thus discord would arise in the universe. God too would be unprovident if he placed something in another’s place. Since this conflicts with truth, sound reason proves that, if all angels had remained in heaven, humanity would fully have had its own place in heaven. After certain angels fell, as many human beings are taken up into the fellowship of those who remained as would have been taken up if all had remained, and, in addition, as many as fell from there. Yet they will not occupy the angels’ place, but will fill their own proper place.

## CHAPTER IV. Fourth Question: That elect humans are taken up into heaven not in place of apostate angels but for themselves; while reprobate angels and humans are placed as discordant strings in a fitting place so as to contribute to harmony

Some maintain that neither other angels nor human beings are substituted for apostate angels, just as neither other human beings nor angels are given back in the Church for condemned human beings. Rather, the angels who stood, strengthened in charity, remain in their own number; and righteous human beings fill their own proper place in their multiplication.

For God, who created all things that they might exist, and permits none of his creatures to be reduced to nothingness, since it is better to exist than not to exist, took angels and humans who, by free choice, turned from the highest good toward a lesser good—like strings sounding out of tune in a great lyre—from the place of the exalted and placed them among the low. There they cause no discord but sing fittingly in harmony with the universe.

Others think that half the angels fell, and therefore that as many human beings will ascend to heaven as angels remained there. And because it is written, “The dragon with his tail drew a third part of the stars and cast them to the earth” (Rev. 12), some think that a third part of the angels fell and that this number must be restored through elect human beings.

## CHAPTER V. Fifth Question: That some fell from each of the angelic orders; that elect humans are to be joined, according to their merits, to the angels who remained standing; and that likewise the reprobate are to be added, according to their merits, to the several orders of those who fell

Again, others suppose that there were ten orders of angels and that the entire tenth fell, led by the Gospel parable which recounts that a woman had ten drachmas and lost the tenth. Hence it is still commonly said that the tenth choir of angels fell. But we say, on the authority of Sacred Scripture, that there were and are nine orders of angels, and that some fell from each order.

That some angels fell is attested by John in the Apocalypse: “That great dragon, who is called the devil and Satan, was cast down to earth, and his angels were sent with him” (ibid.). Likewise the Lord says in the Gospel: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). This is likewise to be understood of archangels: those who preside over wicked angels in wickedness were among the archangels. The Psalm says of princes: “You shall fall like one of the princes” (Ps. 81). Likewise the Apostle says concerning principalities and powers: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6). Likewise the Apostle says: “He stripped principalities and powers, triumphing over them in himself” (Col. 2). The Apostle says of other orders: “When he has abolished every principality and power and virtue and dominion” (1 Cor. 15).

The Psalmist says concerning Thrones: “Can the seat of iniquity adhere to you?” (Ps. 93). Thrones are seats; those who fell from the Thrones are called seats of iniquity. It is written in Ezekiel concerning Cherubim: “You, the outspread and protecting Cherub, were in the delights of paradise; you fell from heaven” (the reference printed is Ps. 93). Concerning Seraphim, Job says: “He is the beginning of the ways of God, and he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 40). This is he who said: “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14).

Lost human beings will be joined, according to their merits, to these same orders; elect human beings, however, will be joined, according to their merits, to the orders of holy angels, as the Lord says: “The righteous shall be equal to angels.” Generally, however, all the orders of spirits are called angels.

But it should be observed that this argument seems contrary to Jerome—if indeed we have understood his words correctly. Jerome says in a sermon, in a certain passage, addressing Paula concerning the Assumption of the Virgin: “Thus the holy Church of God confidently sings everywhere that it is lawful to say and believe of no other saint that she has surpassed even the merits of angels or archangels.” He truly says that she surpasses them; and Gregory also seems to agree with him. For he asserts that every elect person is to be joined, according to the difference of merits, to the orders of angels.

## CHAPTER VI. Sixth Question: That the choir of apostles is to be joined to the Seraphim, and consequently Peter is above Michael in heaven, since Christ, God and man, made him prince of the Church and Rome, the head of the world, granted him primacy

Therefore, just as nine orders of angels are read of, so in the Gospel the Lord establishes nine orders of the elect. Of these, the poor in spirit are joined to angels; the meek to archangels; those who mourn to Virtues; those who hunger for justice are equated with Powers; the merciful are joined to Principalities; the pure in heart to Dominions; peacemakers are added to Thrones; those who suffer persecution for justice’s sake are compared in glory to Cherubim; and those who endure curses, reproaches, and lies for the Son of Man’s sake are compared to Seraphim.

But the apostles, whom the supreme Lord chose from among human beings and placed over his bride, the Church, will enter the highest choir of angels, namely the Seraphim, because, having been scourged and having suffered insult for Jesus’ name, they rejoiced. Therefore, by as much as the order of Seraphim exceeds the order of Archangels in dignity, [Col. 1182A] by so much does Peter, prince of the apostles, exceed Michael, one of the order of archangels. Hence Rome, the head of the world, granted the primacy of government to the apostle Peter, not to the archangel Michael; and the whole Church throughout the world bestowed the episcopal see upon Peter not only in private places but also in its principal cities.

## CHAPTER VII. Seventh Question: That a human being is worthier than an angel, but an angel happier than a human being, because angels worship the human God, whereas humans do not worship an angel-God

Since humanity has been exalted through a human being to such great glory, the question is raised: which is worthier, a human being or an angel?

**Reply.** Without doubt, a human being is worthier, although an angel is happier. For the human being in Christ is God, which the angel is not; and angels worship above themselves the human God, whereas human beings do not worship an angel-God. The angel is happier because it has always remained in blessedness; but the human being is worthier because, placed in misery and fighting against vices and demons, it has merited blessedness by virtue, whereas the angel did not lose it through God’s grace.

Angels are called ministering spirits because through them is administered the eternal salvation to be bestowed upon human beings through Christ. Thus the Law is handed down in writing through the ministry of angels, and the oracles of the prophets are believed to have been administered through them. They ministered not only to Christ the human being, but also to the apostles, when they freed them from chains or prison. Therefore, through Christ humanity surpasses the angel in dignity; but through God the angel surpasses humanity in happiness.

## CHAPTER VIII. Eighth Question: That there are nine orders of the righteous in the Church corresponding to the nine orders of angels

[Col. 1182C]

Since equality with angels is promised to blessed human beings, the Church has distinguished the orders of believers according to their orders: namely, patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, monks, virgins, widows, and married persons. Likewise it has distinguished their offices into nine: laypersons, doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, priests, and bishops.

## CHAPTER IX. Ninth Question: That God, souls, and angels have no bodies, like justice and wisdom, and are seen by the mind alone

But some ask in what form angels ought to be believed to exist, since they are often read to have appeared to human beings. We answer them: everything that exists is either spirit or body. A body has three dimensions—length, breadth, and height—and these three give form to every body. But spirit has neither length, breadth, nor height. Therefore God and angels have no form, as the Gospel attests: “God is spirit” (John 4). Therefore God does not have form; when the Apostle says, “Being in the form of God” (Phil. 2), he uses *form* for essence.

Angels too are spirits, as the Psalmist says: “He makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 103); therefore they likewise lack form. The souls of the righteous are also spirits, as Scripture cries out and says: “Spirits and souls of the righteous, bless the Lord” (Dan. 3). Souls pertain to life and sensation, spirits to reason and understanding; therefore they too have no form. This should be understood of spirits as of virtues, namely justice, wisdom, and so forth.

## CHAPTER X. Tenth Question: That bodily things are discerned by bodily sight, images by spirit, and wills by intellect, etc.

But someone may say: “How are spirits understood personally, if they are bounded by no form?” One should know that we see in three ways: bodies by bodily sight, images by spirit, and our thoughts or wills by mind. In this third way we see God and spirits. And just as by bodily sight we distinguish a human body from a horse’s body; just as by spirit we separate the image of a man from the image of a woman; and just as by mind we distinguish knowledge of grammar from knowledge of dialectic: so we discern the persons of spirits by intellect.

## CHAPTER XI. Eleventh Question: That angels have ethereal bodies, demons aerial bodies, and humans earthly bodies, etc.

Angels also have ethereal bodies, demons aerial bodies, and human beings earthly ones. As human beings can alter the color of their bodies—whitening them, blackening them, or covering them with some garment—so demons can transform their bodies into various shapes, displaying themselves either as brilliant in order to deceive or as hideous in order to terrify. The Apostle says: “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11).

And as we clothe ourselves at will in garments made from the fleeces of these or those animals, so demons now put on the forms of one beast or another, such as a lion, dragon, or another creature. Hence it is written: “Do not deliver to the beasts the souls that confess you” (Ps. 73).

The bodies of angels are simple, being made from pure ether. Ether is fire, namely the fourth element, bright not by heat but by perpetual light. Hence it is written concerning the creation of angels: “Let there be light” (Gen. 1). They appear to us in these bodies and alter them in accordance with the matters they are about to administer. Thus Michael appeared armed to Joshua when he came to aid the people of God. Gabriel also appeared to Daniel in the form of chrysolite when he foretold Christ’s kingdom. Raphael appeared girded to Tobias when he delivered Sarah from a demon and his father from blindness. At the Lord’s birth they appeared with light; at his resurrection or ascension they shone in white garments. The angel appeared to Mary as a young man, but to Cecilia with shining wings.

## CHAPTER XII. Twelfth Question: That the form of the body adheres to souls stripped of the body, and that after his resurrection the Lord manifested his body as he willed. Objections against the foregoing are resolved

The form of the body also adheres to souls stripped of their bodies, in which form they are accustomed to be seen. And this should be noted: after his resurrection the Lord transformed his own body as he willed; hence he could not be recognized by the disciples and at times suddenly vanished from them. Let this suffice concerning spirits.

It was said above that humanity is not substituted for an apostate angel but is taken up into heaven—that is, into blessedness—for itself. But because this seems too harshly stated to some, although all Scripture cries out that the number of angels must be restored through elect human beings, let the matter be explained more fully under the guidance of reason.

If everyone in the world looked at this sun simultaneously, each would see the whole sun, and no one would see less of its light because every person looked upon it wholly. But if one person shut their eyes or lost them by some mishap, that person would deprive themselves of the sight of the sun; the others would see neither more nor less than if that person saw it. If, moreover, another person, seeing, were born from that person or from another, that person would be placed in the universe not for the former but for themselves; and would see the light of the sun not for the blind person but for themselves, which they would nonetheless do if that person had not been blind.

But if that blind person were removed from the universe so as to be reduced to nothingness, and a new person, not from the human race, were created in their place, that person might perhaps rightly be said to have been placed in the blind person’s place. But since the blind person possesses their own place in the universe, just as the seeing person possesses theirs, it is evident that the seeing person does not hold a place for the blind one, but the blind person belongs to the place—that is, the number—of those who do not see.

The same may be said of life. All human beings equally enjoy life, and no one lives for another, even though one may be healthier than another. The person who dies is deprived of life; but the one who is born enjoys life not for the dead person but for themselves. For the dead person is not removed from the universe, but is not placed among—or in the number of—the living.

This is how one should think concerning God and angels. For Scripture testifies: “God is light, and in him there is no darkness” (1 John 1). And again it is written that he is “the sun of righteousness” (Mal. 4), into whom angels desire to look. He is the joy of angels, as this light is the joy of the eyes. All angels beheld one such God, and each saw him wholly according to its measure. But some shut the eyes of their mind when they turned themselves away from the light of truth and deprived themselves of that light. To deprive themselves of that joy was to fall from the fellowship of angels, for the vision of God is the joy of the blessed.

The elect human beings who will receive this joy—that is, who will see that light of which the others deprived themselves—will see it not in place of apostate angels but for themselves, just as the merciful will see God, whom they would nevertheless have seen if those others had not been deprived of the vision of God. Angels are not wholly removed from the universe in respect of their being, but they are judged not to see in the place of the rejoicing—or in heaven, that is, to see God, the eternal light. Elect human beings are therefore said to be substituted for them because they enjoy that joy or light of which the others are deprived.

For this reason the Lord said to humanity: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25), because the joy of the Lord—that is, of Christ—is the vision of God the Father. In this all the blessed will rejoice, when they obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and groaning flee away.

But someone may say: “When a king is removed from his kingdom or dies, another is appointed in his place; so, when an angel falls, a human being is appointed in that angel’s place.” This is mistaken. In bodily things, what one person possesses cannot be possessed by another. The gold which one person has another does not have; when it is taken away from the former and given to the latter, the latter has it and the former does not. A living king alone possesses the kingdom; when dead, he is wholly removed from human affairs. Likewise, the one appointed in his place alone is invested with the scepter.

But it is not so in spiritual things, because many can possess the same virtue equally, and many can have the same knowledge of grammar. Thus angels and human beings can equally possess God, who is light, life, and joy; only those will not possess him who turn their mind’s sight away from him. Therefore humans are not restored in place of angels, but enjoy God for themselves: eternal light, eternal life, and eternal joy.

[Col. 1185]

# LITTLE BOOK OF EIGHT QUESTIONS CONCERNING ANGELS AND HUMANITY

(Extracted from a manuscript codex of the illustrious Charterhouse of Gaming by the venerable Fr. Leopold Wydemann, librarian of that place; edited by Fr. Bernhard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part I, col. 213.)

## CHAPTER I. Whether humanity would have been created if the angel had remained in heaven

[Col. 1185B]

**DISCIPLE.** I should like to be shown by certain authority and proved by sound reason whether humanity would have been created if the angel had remained in heaven. For since the authority of a great man says that the human being was created as a tenth order in order that the number of the elect might be completed, it seems that the multiplication of human beings occurred for this reason alone: to fill up the diminished number of angels. Thus the fall of the angel was consequently the cause of humanity’s creation.

**MASTER.** Authority is nothing other than truth proved by reason; and what authority teaches ought to be believed, reason proves ought to be maintained. The manifest authority of Scripture declares, and clear reason proves, that if all angels had remained in heaven, humanity with all its descendants would nevertheless have been created.

For this world was made for humanity; and the world is heaven and earth and all things contained within their compass. It seems highly absurd to believe that, while angels stood, the being for whose sake the universe is said to have been created would not be created. To remove this error, Sacred Scripture, foreknowing future things, begins before the creation of angel and human being, saying: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). Why heaven? Certainly that it might be the dwelling-place of angels. Why earth? Namely, that it might be the dwelling-place of human beings.

Nor does the authority of that great man, Gregory, oppose this opinion; rather, it supports it. For the number of the elect did not consist in angels alone but in angels together with human beings; and because the number of elect in the nine orders of angels was not complete, humanity was created as the tenth order to complete this number. That humanity was created together with the angel is attested by God the creator himself when he speaks to Job: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you” (Job 40). This means: “When I made humanity, I also made the angel.”

There is a twofold creation of humanity: one in eternity through predestination, the other under temporality through formation. Concerning the creation by predestination it is written: “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness. And God made humankind in his image and likeness” (Gen. 1). Concerning formation it is written: “God formed humankind from the slime of the earth and breathed into its face the breath of life, and it became a living soul” (Gen. 2).

“He who remains for ever,” Scripture says, “created all things simultaneously” (Ecclus. 18). He created all things simultaneously by their matter, but distinguished them over six days by genera, species, forms, and numbers. Those six days, however, should not be understood as changeable days like these, but as fixed in eternity, after whose exemplar these were made. Since the number six is perfect, God is said to have made all things in six days, so that the perfection of God’s operation might be signified. This operation is divided into six parts: three elements and three things created from them.

The elements are fire, water, and earth. From fire were created angels, luminaries, and stars; from earth, human beings, trees, plants, and animals; and from waters, fish and birds. Water has a twofold nature: one thick, always clinging to the earth, which is called sea, from which fish are said to have been produced; the other thin, suspended above the earth, which is called air, from which birds are known to have been created.

That the angel is the beginning of God’s ways is written in Job; but humanity is read to be God’s last creation. Thus, through the angel the beginning, but through humanity the completion, of God’s works is signified; and every remaining creature is subjected to humanity. Therefore, just as angels are not created for lost human beings, so human beings are not believed to have been created for fallen angels, but to possess their own place of glory and fill the tenth order of the elect. They are said to have been made for lost angels because they are to be taken up into the glory from which those angels fell; yet this would likewise occur if none of the angels had fallen.

And behold, no human being worships an angel, whereas a multitude of angels worship above themselves the human God, who restored all things in heaven and on earth: by freeing humanity on earth from the power of the devil and associating it in heaven with angels.

## CHAPTER II. Whether Christ would have been incarnate if humanity had remained in paradise

**DISCIPLE.** Since it has been reasonably proved that the angel’s fall was not the cause of humanity’s creation, and that humanity was created not for the angel but for itself, I should likewise like to be taught, by the same authority accompanied by reason, whether Christ would have been incarnate if humanity had remained in paradise. For since all Scripture declares that Christ came in the flesh for humanity’s redemption, it is thought that he would never have come in the flesh if humanity, whom he might redeem, had not sinned. Thus humanity’s sin seems to have been the cause of Christ’s incarnation. If this is so, that sin was not evil but indeed a great good, through which God became human and consequently humanity became God.
