The Master. The whole world, with its many miseries, cries out that human sin was not a good but the greatest evil. For whence does death reign in the world with so many disasters, except from human sin? Therefore the sin of the first human being was not the cause of Christ’s incarnation, but rather the cause of death and condemnation. [Col. 1187C] The cause of Christ’s incarnation, however, was the predestination of humanity’s deification. For from eternity it had been predestined by God that humanity should be deified, as the Lord says: “Father, you loved them before the foundation of the world” (John 17)—understand: those to be deified through me.

But as God is immutable, so too is his predestination immutable. Therefore he had to become incarnate, so that humanity might be deified. And therefore it does not follow that sin was the cause of his incarnation; rather, it follows that sin could not alter God’s purpose concerning humanity’s deification. Indeed, the authority of Sacred Scripture and manifest reason declare that God assumed humanity even if humanity had never sinned.

[Col. 1187D] Finally, provident Scripture promises Christ before human sin, saying: “A man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh” (Matt. 19). The Apostle expounds this as follows: “This is a great mystery; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5). Behold: no sin has yet been committed by humanity, and the union of Christ and the Church in one flesh is proclaimed. Hence the same Apostle says: “God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1). Christ is God and man, in whom God chose before the foundation of the world those predestined to life, because in Christ he ordained that we should be deified. For when God put on human nature, all humanity—in the elect alone—then passes into God. [Col. 1188A] Moreover, the first angel, who arrogated to himself the likeness of God which the Son alone possessed, when he was driven out and fell from heaven, found Christ as Judge upon earth. For he through whom the Father created the earth was still hidden in the substance of the earth: he would plunge beneath the earth the angel fleeing from heaven, and raise above heaven the humble human being from the earth.

As for the fact that Christ, who is the life of all, died: there are three states of humanity. One is before sin, in which a person could die and could not die; another is after sin, in which he necessarily had to die; the third was to have been his had he not sinned when tempted, and is still hoped for after the resurrection, in which he could not die.

Therefore, if Christ had come in the first state, neither he nor humanity would ever have died; but humanity, already deified, would have been joined to the angels when the full number of the tenth order had been completed. This certainly would have happened had humanity, when tempted, not sinned. But Christ, foreknowing that humanity would sin and thereby die, therefore chose to come and die in the second state, in order to redeem humanity from death and restore it to the state of life. Thus he is said to have come for human redemption, because unless he had destroyed our death by dying, humanity could never after guilt recover the state of life. Therefore Christ’s incarnation was the deification of human nature; his death, the destruction of our death; his resurrection, the restoration of our life. And thus, according to the Apostle: “As all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. [Col. 1188C] 15).

## Chapter III. How angels were created from fire

The Disciple. This solution seems probable to me, where authority supports reason and reason authority. But since spirit is better than body, I wonder why you have said that angels were created from fire. For fire is a body, whereas angels are spirits; and I do not see how what is better can be said to be created from what is inferior unless this is proved by true assertions.

The Master. To say that spirit is created from body is madness; but to say that body is created from bodies or elements is an assertion of truth. Angelic spirits, human souls, and the unformed matter of the world were created from nothing; but from unformed matter the distinct elements were made, as Scripture says: “[God] made the world from unformed matter.” [Col. 1188D] But all bodies were formed from the four elements; that is, each body is especially assigned to that element which is more abundant in it. Hence some bodies are called celestial or fiery, others earthly, others watery, others airy.

The bodies of souls are earthly, as Scripture says: “God formed man from the slime of the earth” (Gen. 2), that is, the human body. But concerning the soul it adds: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life” (ibid.). Of the soul’s creation it had previously said: “God made man in his image and likeness” (Gen. 1), that is, the human soul. God is incorporeal; likewise, the soul, in which the image of God is found, is incorporeal. Of animal bodies [Col. 1189A] Scripture says: “Let the earth bring forth cattle and beasts according to their kind” (Gen. 1), that is, the bodies of cattle and beasts. Concerning fish and birds it likewise says: “Let the waters bring forth fish and birds according to their kind” (ibid.); understand, the bodies of fish and birds. It says “waters” because of the twofold nature of waters: dense, as in the sea; and thin, as in the air.

But the bodies of angelic spirits are fiery, as Scripture says: “Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire” (Heb. 1). That is to say: God made angelic spirits from nothing, but created their bodies from fire. Concerning their creation Scripture says: “God said, ‘Let there be light’” (Gen. 1), as though to say: let the luminous bodies of angels be made from fire.

[Col. 1189B] For just as a rational soul clothed with a body is called a human being, so an intellectual spirit clothed with a body is called an angel. Angels formerly appeared to people not in borrowed bodies but in their own: they spoke with them, walked with them, and ate with them. All these things occurred historically, not figuratively. Yet, for the administration of their office, they could transform these bodies into diverse forms; hence they were sometimes seen shining with faces like lightning, sometimes in white garments. And in many holy Scriptures demons are said to run through the air. For spirits without bodies do not run, since they are not located in space. It should be noted that Genesis says nothing about the creation of spirits, because it does not customarily narrate the creation of invisible nature, [Col. 1189C] but that of visible bodies. Yet the Apostle cries out: “Whether visible or invisible, in heaven and on earth, all things were made through him” (Col. 1). The invisible things are spirits; the visible things are their bodies.

## Chapter IV. Why God the Creator took the body not from fire but from earth

The Disciple. In this answer reason agrees well with authority. But since earth is the lowest element and the dregs of all the elements, while fire is the highest and purest element, what reason is there for God the Creator to have taken the body not from fire but from earth?

The Master. The center is more worthy than the circle: the center is fixed and immovable, while the circle turns in motion. Earth is the fixed and stable center of the elements; fire is like a circle, unstable in motion. And although all the elements are equal in the dignity of their creation, in their figures the center has primacy according to nature. Earth is the center of the world and the nourisher of all living creatures; fire, however, is their destroyer—although certain animals are unharmed in fire, as is reported of the salamander.

[Col. 1189D] Moreover, earth is the first of God’s works, as Scripture says: “In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth” (Ps. 101). God embodied two rational creatures from the first and highest element: humanity from earth, to be deified in himself; the angel from fire, to be glorified in heaven. Hence these two elements will be changed into the glory of the children of God, as Scripture says: “The Lord will make a new heaven and a new earth” (Isa. 62). In that new earth the bodies of the elect alone, now deified, will shine like the sun and be equal to angelic bodies; those human bodies will shine brightly like the sun—which indeed is fire—when Christ refashions the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory. He appeared on the mountain as the sun when he showed his disciples the glory of the future state.

Furthermore, it must be especially noted that human beings were killed by the first element, namely water; while angels, created from the highest element, namely fire, when they sinned were cast down into the second element, [Col. 1190B] namely air. Both will still be damned in fire, while earth, in Christ and in the elect, will be deified and exalted above the heavens.

## Chapter V. Whether the angel’s fall was irreparable because he was immortal, whereas humanity’s was reparable

The Disciple. The assertion of certain persons does not seem probable to me: they say that the angel’s fall was irreparable because he was immortal, whereas humanity’s was recoverable because humanity could die, although God wished nothing but death for the reconciliation of both.

The Master. This is proved neither by authority nor supported by reason, especially since authority cries out: “God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the dying” [Col. 1190C] (Wis. 1). And again through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner” (Ezek. 33). Reason does not allow any contrary thing to be joined to its opposite. Light is opposed to darkness: it does not receive darkness but drives it away. Life is contrary to death: it does not choose death but rather extinguishes it. Death, indeed, is the punishment of sin, which humanity would never have undergone. Therefore God, who is life, demands death neither from angel nor from human being, but removes it as contrary to himself and to nature.

Now the nature of things requires that things discordant within the universe be made harmonious through what is contrary or similar to them. For example, low sounds are contrary to high ones and are therefore discordant; but through the same harmonies they become alike and consonant.

[Col. 1190D] Humanity, disobedient to God, became obedient to the devil unto injustice, and for that injustice incurred the death due to it. Thus humanity introduced discord into the universe, because though created for life, it failed in death. But Christ by the contrary, from one like humanity, produced harmony: becoming obedient to God unto righteousness, for which righteousness he endured an undeserved death; and thus, destroying death, redeemed humanity from death.

For justice requires that, just as a human being created without sin offended by sinning and therefore underwent the punishment of death, so someone from that person’s race, existing without sin, should please God by living justly, should undergo death for that cause, and through it reconcile his companions to God. And because Christ did this, it is said that he willed nothing but death for satisfaction. But he did not require this of the angel, because the angel could not die.

It was just, however, that as that angel exalted himself above all things when he wished to be like the Most High and therefore fell below all things, so someone from that number, existing without fault, should humble himself below all things without seeing the punishment of those who had fallen, praising God’s justice in his judgments, accusing his own injustice, and by this confession of praise raising his companions. But he who fell from the truth, in which he did not stand, still persists in the lie of which he is the father (John 8), saying: “The rivers are mine, and I made them. I made myself. I am God and not man.” Since this utterance is incorrigible, his fall is irrecoverable.

## Chapter VI. How we all die when death is proclaimed destroyed through Christ

[Col. 1191B]

The Disciple. I am greatly troubled that we all die, though death is proclaimed to have been destroyed through Christ.

The Master. There are two deaths: one of the body, the other of the soul. Bodily death is the separation of soul from body; the soul’s death is the separation of soul from God. Therefore, just as bodily death takes away the joys of the world, so the soul’s death takes away the joys of heaven. Christ destroyed this death when he brought souls freed from punishments into the joys of heaven. He will yet destroy death when he clothes souls with their bodies, which no death thereafter will dissolve.

## Chapter VII. Why the resurrection of the dead will occur

The Disciple. I believed that the resurrection would occur at the last day even if Christ had never become incarnate, since, for example, it was foretold by the prophets.

The Master. The resurrection will not occur because it was foretold by the prophets; rather, it was foretold because it was going to occur. For the prophetic voice compels nothing to happen. But the Holy Spirit, to whom all past and future things are present, announced his own purposes beforehand to his own people—what he himself had once resolved to do, or what human beings were going to do—so that [Col. 1192A] they might know him as the observer of all things.

Now the resurrection takes place so that the good may receive complete joy and the evil complete punishment; neither can exist except in body and soul. But the just, reconciled through Christ, are received into life; and if they had not been reconciled, they would never be received there. Therefore, if Christ had not come in the flesh and destroyed our death by his death, and restored life to us by his resurrection, no one would ever rise to life; rather, all alike would remain in death.

## Chapter VIII. Why God does not transfer all people to blessed life after the resurrection, especially infants who die without guilt

[Col. 1192B]

The Disciple. Since the human race was created for life and has wholly been restored to life through Christ, I greatly wonder why he does not transfer all people after the resurrection to blessed life, especially infants, who were entirely without fault.

The Master. Christ, who is resurrection and life, will raise all people to life; and because he is justice, he will glorify only the just in blessed life and leave the unjust in misery. And because his hidden judgment surpasses every understanding, he receives into glory, when he wills, certain guilty persons purified by purgatorial fire; and, when he wills, leaves certain innocent persons in misery—namely, infants whom the water of baptism did not regenerate. For it is better to be saved by mercy than ever to be condemned by the sentence of the Judge.

[Col. 1192C] But why he does this, we can no more investigate than we can inquire why he did not make angels archangels, or those angels thrones; why he did not make women men, or beasts birds; or why he gave the peacock such beauty of feathers beyond other birds, and many things like these. “Whatever he willed, he has done and does” (Ps. 113).

[Col. 1191]

# *The Inevitable*, or a Dialogue on Predestination and Free Choice

(First extracted from the library of the Premonstratensian monastery of St. Mary at Tongerlo, through the work of the Reverend Father John Conen, licentiate in sacred theology and prior there; published in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons edition, vol. 20, col. 1129.)

## Preface to the Reader

Honorius, who first composed this dialogue, is said in the opening of his books to have required three things: author, subject matter, and intention. [Note: [Col. 1191] Honorius, prologue to the *Commentary on the Song of Songs*.] The author, certainly, so that the reader may know the name of the writer: whether he was a pagan or a believer, Catholic or heretic.

[Col. 1193] Therefore, kindly Reader, since I have ascribed this *Inevitable* to its author, I shall first show you briefly who and what sort of man he was. If you read the rest, you will understand.

Abbot John Trithemius [Note: [Col. 1193] *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*.], and more recent writers whom I have been able to consult, have handed down few but great things in his praise. I shall attempt to report them concisely.

Around the year 1087 from the passing of Christ the Savior from this world to the Father, under Pope Paschal and Henry the Younger—as is stated in the *Life of Our Most Holy Father Norbert* [Note: [Col. 1193] *Patrologia*, vol. 166.]—or, as the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius calculated, under the fourth, or according to others the fifth, Emperor Augustus of that name: in the duchy of Burgundy, a certain priest Honorius, deservedly to be crowned with glory and honor, shone in the clergy like a star in heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1193] Trithemius, cited above.] For he was most devoted to the Scriptures and very learned, nobly instructed in secular sciences, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech. Therefore at Autun—note that the city is vernacularly called *Austun*—the ancient metropolis and seat of the Aedui, having been made scholasticus, he conducted himself as a true teacher or illuminator of the Church. That is—as he himself described their dignity and office—[Note: [Col. 1193] *Commentary on the Song of Songs*; *Jewel of the Soul*, bk. 1, ch. 11; and Rodericus, bk. 2 of the *Mirror*, ch. 17.] by word and example he poured upon believers the light of doctrine like stars for everlasting ages, until they themselves began to invoke the Lord in their conduct and came to know Christ, the true light, as enlightening every soul. He followed the custom of the ancients—of holy Father Augustine, that is, and of the other ancient Fathers—writing books and teaching the unlearned. In this he represented St. Anselm so closely that his books *On the Image of the World* were attributed to Anselm.

He resigned these public duties and at a suitable time withdrew into solitude, the desert, or a monastery, in order to observe what he had read was once said to the apostles when they reported to their Master what, having been sent by him, they had done and taught: that they should “come apart into a desert place” (Mark 6:3) and rest a little. Having until then expended himself in teaching others, he wished to live for God alone during the remainder of his life and become a spiritual man. Thus he is found called by some “the Scholastic” and “the Solitary,” by others “the Recluse,” and sometimes even “the Anchorite.”

Both there and elsewhere he wrote many distinguished little works. In his own catalogue of illustrious men, entitled *On the Luminaries of the Church*, he listed *The Inevitable*, or the *Dialogue on Free Choice*, hitherto unprinted among his works.

Thus for roughly five hundred years this work of his appears to have lain hidden. Now, however, through my efforts it comes before the public from our library, in accordance with the manuscript preserved there, on the occasion of a certain *Dialogue on Predestination and Free Choice* issued under his name seventy years ago by George Cassander at Cologne, in the year 155 [sic; the printed date is materially uncertain], by Lambert Silvius.

It bears the title *The Inevitable* because this title was given it by its author. In restoring it whole, I have changed or enlarged no part of the text, on the advice of many equally learned and weighty men; I have only distinguished and corrected obvious errors of orthography with such punctuation and divisions as were necessary, and have somewhat furnished it with marginal notes.

No one, then, should suspect that I have altered anything here to suit any opinion or twisted it in a direction other than that in which it was written; or that I have spun anything in it out of myself, like a spider. I assure you with confidence and certainty that, apart from the labor of faithfully transcribing it, there is nothing of my own in the whole little book.

What pains me is that, just as in our regions we scarcely have wine except diluted, so we receive the writings of certain ancient authors only altered—or should I say corrupted. Who does not know how greatly Erasmus alone defiled the monuments of many holy Fathers with his dross, that is, his scholia?

How much more readily may this be thought of Cassander, whom the irrefragable judgment of the most holy Roman See condemned to the first class of prohibited writers? [Note: [Col. 1193] See the *Index of Prohibited Books*, first issued by the authority of Pius IV, later enlarged by Sixtus V, [Col. 1194] and finally revised and published by command of Clement VII, under “Cassander.”] Whether this was done rashly, no one but a rash man may ask. Nevertheless, if you please, listen, so that you may know no less certainly what kind of person he was than one recognizes a lion from its claws, and may not deny that he was an impostor.

Cassander is a patronymic, like Taxander or Tessander and ten other similar names derived from the soil of one’s homeland. George Cassander therefore took his name from the village of Cadsand, or Catsant, or, for euphony, Cassant—whence the island situated between Sluis and the German Sea was called Cassandria—as from the place of his birth.

To magnify that dwelling-place, he seems to have found the more celebrated city of Bruges a suitable homeland. I mean the city in which, around the time when Honorius, author of this *Inevitable*, underwent the death inevitable to all, Charles surnamed the Good, margrave of Flanders—others called him the first of that name, and a pious count—died as a martyr among the Flemings with no less glory than his parent Canute, king of the Ottomans [probably an OCR corruption; “Danes” is suggested by the context], among his Danes; and he left the remains of his body at St. Donatian’s, in the vestry of sacred garments. [Note: [Col. 1194] Peter Montanus, in the description accompanying Keer’s geographical maps. Jacques Marchant assigns 2 March 1126.]

This Cassander, well educated in the household of the Witts, taught both Greek and Latin letters for a salary from the public treasury and wrote works reported by Gesner and Marchant. By this he achieved the reputation at Rome, among the leaders of the universal Church, of being from Bruges. But, corrupted in faith among the people of Cleves and the Germans, he could not remain there long; he departed and afterward lived at Cologne for a long time, perhaps twenty years.

There he published various books, among them the aforementioned *Dialogue*, to which was added a *Consultation on Religion*, printed at Cologne after his death in 1577. The most learned Molanus [Note: [Col. 1194] In the *Index of Prohibited Books*.] cites it and, censuring its author, shows that he exceeded the bounds of Christian modesty. While outside God’s Church, he wrote that only traces of common and canonical life remain in buildings and names. He then added that deserters from the Rule are called by the monstrous name “secular canons,” that is, regulars who are irregular. Thus he had no small justification for calling Albert Crantz, a secular canon, a monster without example, a regular without rule, and a canon without canon.

Do you hear, friendly Reader, this man’s name, constancy, zeal, and spirit? Though uncalled, he presumed to come to a council, pronounce judgment on the adoption of religion, judge and reform colleges of canons—indeed the entire clergy, the Roman Church itself, and therefore the supreme and Catholic Church. Do you think that he spared the Scholastic Honorius, and did not reform this offspring of his by licking it with that slanderous tongue?

But I seem to hear someone objecting that he was once called to counsel, indeed to devise a form of religion. I admit it. But by whom, with what authority, and when?

[Col. 1195] Michael of Isselt, called Amorfortius, a highly received historian, states [Note: [Col. 1195] *History of His Own Time*, under the year 1564.] that when, in the year 1564, certain ambitious men eager for innovations demanded that the entire form of the civil government of Belgium and the Empire be changed, and deliberations in the tribunals began to be thrown into confusion, plans for innovations multiplied daily. They asserted that the Council of Trent could not be promulgated without injury to the king, certain privileges, and the commonwealth at great risk. They held that all so-called secular jurisdiction should be removed from the provost of St. Donatian’s at Bruges and from all other clergy, and that royal confiscations ought either to be abolished or reduced.

Meanwhile Louis of Nassau, brother of Prince William of Orange, who was then at Brussels—though a foreigner and holding no public office—was devising a form of religion which the Belgians might profess. For this counsel he summoned George Cassander and others who declared themselves unable to endure either the severity of the inquisitors and theologians or the excessively vehement temper of the Calvinists. But the affair did not succeed, and the moderators immediately returned whence they had come. Thus far Isselt.

What, I ask, follows from this, except that Cassander at one time went into the counsel of the impious, stood in the way of sinners, and sat in the chair of pestilence as a moderator in order to forge a new form of religion? Indeed, to speak with Blessed Gregory, [Note: [Col. 1195] On Job, ch. 41, ch. 10.] to show himself to be the devil’s hammerer; or, if you prefer—as Honorius says in this little book [Note: [Col. 1195] Below in this Dialogue.]—to offer himself as a hammer fit for the infernal craftsman, for beating the Church and shaping religion—or rather, heresy?

Such being the case, kindly Reader, will you think that Cassander imposed such restraint upon himself that, at the greatest opportunity—which is evident to anyone examining this little book—he would not bring the work of Honorius the priest back to the anvil, file it down, and make it his own; and would not fraudulently publish it under a specious but false name, as is characteristic of such people?

I do not think so. Rather—peace be with you, George, and assuredly it will be with you if, by repentance, you return from the state into which you have fallen—I think, as some suppose, that while people slept, an enemy acted through a fox feigning death to make prey of souls.

But come now, good man: again I address you, George, who, having once learned with the fox, learned nothing but fox-like behavior. Hear the truth and confess it. The man whom you judged dead because of prolonged silence or sleep, and therefore put on as a disguise in order to deceive, is not dead but asleep; indeed, if you wish me to say so, he lives. You thought that *The Inevitable* of Honorius, priest of Autun—an ancient, most learned, and excellent man, and thus a man of considerable authority in the Church—would remain dead and buried forever because of silence for more than four centuries, if you corrupted and removed the two copies, one at Brunwiler and the other at St. Pantaleon’s, the former worm-eaten and the latter faulty—or rather, to refresh your memory with your own words, [Note: [Col. 1195] In the dedicatory letter prefixed to this Dialogue.] “having certain gaps which it was necessary in several places to supply from this headless, rather carelessly and inelegantly written text”—and thereby deceived people under the appearance of something long dead.

But by God’s kindness it was provided that there should be a third copy, wholly sound: this one, which none but persons sound in faith would approve; wholly chaste and genuine, not adulterated, which none but a true son of holy Mother Church would receive into a willing bosom; wholly learned and seasoned with marvelous grace and sweetness of language, which would breathe only the fragrance of life unto life upon the humble and well-disposed. It had apparently been copied, preserved, and reserved for a suitable time deliberately, studiously, diligently, and carefully by our elders, or predecessors in religion, so that it might someday present its author as if alive, restore him to life, convict you of having been an impostor, and yet, if amended, free and deliver you from a more grievous punishment than you may perhaps have deserved through prolonged deception.

For who would not spit out as flat wine these words of yours, Cassander: “Just as fire necessarily is hot and ice cold, so all predestined to the kingdom of God will necessarily be saved”? And these: “Those who are plunged into the lake of sulphur and fire are thrust there more according to God’s judgments than their own merits.” How this flat wine stinks! Truly its odor is an odor of death; whoever has received it in such a way as to persevere in it to the end is surely destined by it for eternal death. So too it smells when it is maintained that God’s kingdom is given not according to grace, as this Cassandrian Dialogue seems to assert.

For where Honorius had proposed through the Disciple’s question: “If God works in us, etc., what reward is attributed to a human being?”, Cassander affirms through the Master’s answer: “What does a human being deserve except evil? Or for what merit does anyone expect a reward from God? Whatever good the elect do, God does in them,” and what follows there. Many similar things are scattered throughout that book over several pages; no trace of them is found in this copy. Conversely, in the whole extent of Cassander’s book, scarcely three or four complete and conforming periods of the doctrine taught here can be shown.

Therefore, in conclusion, against the Dialogue committed to print by Cassander, I would advise that, rejecting it, you embrace this one, which accords with sound doctrine and has faithfully been transcribed from the Tongerlo manuscript, as the true and genuine *Inevitable* written by Honorius, priest of Autun; and that you assign it no low place among the monuments of your ancient writers.

In this matter you should not be moved by the question commonly asked from St. Augustine: [Note: [Col. 1195] *On the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 14.] “What need is there for us to examine the works of those who, before this heresy arose, had no necessity to concern themselves with this difficult question requiring resolution?” For that most holy Father Augustine himself did not hesitate to establish his doctrine of God’s election from similar writers. [Note: [Col. 1196] In the chapter cited, and more fully in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, ch. 19.]

And certainly no Catholic has ever despised, failed to value, or failed to honor the venerable antiquity of such Fathers, except to his own confusion. Whatever orthodox opinion you ultimately follow, you embrace St. Ambrose honorably—if indeed the commentary is his—where he speaks as follows: [Note: [Col. 1196] Ambrose, on Romans 8, at the verse “For by hope we are saved.”] “They are called according to purpose, whom God foreknew would believe and be suitable for himself,” etc. Likewise: [Note: [Col. 1196] On chapter 9.] “Those whom he foreknew would be devoted to himself, he chose,” etc. And elsewhere: “He chose the Apostle Paul while persecuting, foreknowing, of course, that he would become good,” etc. You likewise maintain, defend in following or anticipating, explain, excuse, and revere others—such as Jerome, Chrysostom, Epiphanius, Cyril, and Hilary—who spoke in the same or a similar manner; you do not reject or condemn them.

I likewise urge you, Reader, to perform this office of Christian humanity toward Honorius, a most learned man and one praised throughout the whole Church. Do not judge before you read and understand. And if something of his does not satisfy you in any place, read again, and read the whole; for what may have been said only partially and incidentally in one place and may not please your mind will satisfy it when elsewhere it is presented completely, intentionally, and more clearly.

## To His Reverence the Prior, Defender of Honorius: Brother Willibrord Bosscharts, Canon of Tongerlo

[Col. 1197A]

While Cassander boasts that he prolongs illustrious Honorius’s life,  
he destroys it—alas, how ill-faithful a hand!

A spirit of heretics, under the flattering image of life,  
he casts into the abyss and harms in a thousand ways.

But you, Conen, more learned in Apollinean art,  
having pitied Honorius’s deadly ruin,

[Col. 1198A] tend what was wounded and restore the wounds,  
restoring his ancient life: O well-faithful hand!

After destruction, you grant him a long life; and he in return  
will extend your name into posterity.

After darkness you provide light, renown, and honor;  
from this will light, renown, and honor arise for you.

The virtue of both is increased with a twofold adornment:  
each has light from the other’s light.

Thus gold born with a gem shines more brightly;  
thus a gem set in gold gleams more brightly.

# *The Inevitable*, or a Dialogue on Predestination and Free Choice between Master and Disciple

[Col. 1197B]

The Disciple. The brothers walking in God’s house in concord are earnestly praying for your welfare; they offer prayers for your diligence, but to Christ, the Key of David, they render thanksgivings. For through the merits of his Mother, he has disclosed to them through you so many mysteries concerning her in the *Songs*. [Note: [Col. 1197C] Understand the author’s *Commentary on the Song of Songs*, especially *The Seal of the Blessed Mary, Virgin Mother of God*.] For this reason, and for other matters in which you have made them debtors by elucidating things unknown to many in her praise, they are indebted to you.

I now act as their envoy, therefore, and with the greatest devotion they ask you to untie for them the inextricable knot of free choice. If only the predestined, as some say, are saved whatever they do, free choice is thought wholly abolished; and those who are damned are thought to be punished not merely without guilt but unjustly.

[Col. 1197C] I therefore ask you to discuss this matter more fully and leave no slightest scruple behind for anyone dull or blind.

The Master. Since the greatest teachers have published many small works on this subject, what more do you ask of me, who am tongue-tied in comparison with them?

The Disciple. They indeed have argued excellently, but, holding different views as it seems to us, they have made us more uncertain. You, however—to speak the truth—make for us in brief something almost tangible which they, in long treatises, did not make even visible.

The Master. I do not refuse what you ask, because I seek not my own interests but those of charity. I scorn verbal ornaments while I provide for the brothers’ simplicity; I also despise the envious teeth of the jealous, [Col. 1198B] because my help is from the Lord.

The Disciple. I ask you to bear with me as truly foolish [Note: [Col. 1198C] 2 Cor. 11:19: “You gladly bear with fools.”] and to correct, by the word of truth, the ignorance of those who inquire through me.

The Master. Truth will free those who seek it from the darkness of error and illuminate them with the light of its brightness. For if charity’s cause makes you foolish, wisdom will meet you with the light of truth.

The Disciple. Three knots, in an excessively tangled bond, intertwine with one another; scarcely anyone passes through them without becoming entangled in them.

The first is the assertion that only the predestined are saved.

The second is the assertion that people attain salvation through grace alone.

The third is the claim that free choice alone works salvation.

First, then, cut through the knot of Predestination, which with a certain violence binds together the hinge of the whole question. For some think that Predestination pertains only to the elect, whereas the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined, them he also called, justified, and glorified.”

Therefore I beg you first to say what Predestination is.

**MASTER.** Predestination is nothing other than God’s eternal preparation, according to the merits of each person, either for glory or for punishment.

[Col. 1199A] There is, moreover, a twofold Predestination: one of the good to glory, the other of the evil to punishment.

But since some also murmur about Providence and Foreknowledge, as though these imposed necessity upon everyone, it must be understood that neither does Providence compel anyone to pursue the good, nor does Predestination forcibly draw anyone to life’s reward. Likewise, Foreknowledge compels no one to sin, and Predestination drives no one by necessity to punishment.

Accordingly, those foreseen as destined to persevere in good are predestined to glory; but those foreknown as destined to end their life in evil are surely preordained to punishment.

Therefore, those whom God foreknew would believe in his Son [Col. 1199B] and would voluntarily keep his commandments, he predestined before the ages; these he called to faith in their own time; these he justified through Baptism; these he exalted through virtues; these vessels of mercy he glorified. But those whom he foreknew would do none of these things, he rejected from the kingdom of glory, and predestined as vessels of wrath and dishonour, fitted for punishment.

**DISCIPLE.** Since it is written, “Father, you loved them before the foundation of the world,” those who were loved before the world’s beginning appear to be saved by necessity.

**MASTER.** To God nothing is future; rather, all things are present to him, both those that already are and those that will be. Therefore all who were to exist have always been in God’s presence, and for that reason they were loved before the foundation of the world; but in their own time they were chosen to glory according to their merits.

[Col. 1199C] Thus, those whom God chose by predestining them before the foundation of the world were drawn to glory not by necessity, but by their own merit. To them he himself will say at the end of the world: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

And that this kingdom is given to them according to their merits is shown by the divine voice, which immediately proceeds to rehearse their good deeds.

**DISCIPLE.** Since the barrier of Predestination has therefore been removed, come now, enter the forest of the discussion for which we have waited.

Explain what free choice is;

how Predestination or [Col. 1199D] Foreknowledge does not conflict with it;

and how it agrees with Grace; and cut away with the sword of reason whatever further heads arise from these matters.

**MASTER.** Tell me yourself what free choice is, and what you judge it to be.

**DISCIPLE.** It seems to me that free choice is called the liberty of choosing good or evil.

**MASTER.** Although this definition pleases many, I fear that penetrating reason may reject it.

For choice is spoken of only in relation to two or more [Col. 1200A] things, where the option of choosing among many is set before one.

But to angel or human being, to whom alone free choice was given, only righteousness was set before them; if they preserved it, they would enjoy eternal blessedness. Therefore the definition does not seem suitable to free choice.

**DISCIPLE.** What if one says that death and life were set before the human being, and that he chose death?

**MASTER.** This is not true. He did not choose death, but, deceived, desired a higher knowledge.

**DISCIPLE.** What if one says that good is proposed by God, whereas evil is urged by the devil, and that it lies within human free choice what he wishes to choose?

[Col. 1200B] **MASTER.** Both may be said of the human being, but not of the angel, since there was no one who persuaded him of anything evil. Moreover, between good and evil there is no middle term. But if a human being appeared to be situated in some middle position, then perhaps one could rightly say that he possessed liberty to choose good or evil. Yet he is established only in good; and choosing evil is nothing other than a certain failure of the mind while in good—namely, when it abandons the righteousness which it ought to preserve and turns toward the unrighteousness which it knows must be avoided.

**DISCIPLE.** But I eagerly await its definition.

**MASTER.** [Note: [Col. 1199D] St Anselm speaks in the same way in *On the Harmony of Foreknowledge, etc., and Predestination*, near the end of chapter 1, fol. 154, col. 2. He speaks in the same way in *On Grace and Free Choice*, fol. 226, col. 1; or, according to the more recent edition, [Col. 1200D] fol. 1580.] Choice is the judgment of one’s own will as to what it wills and what it does not will. It is called free [Col. 1200C] because it is not necessary: wherever reason is present, there is also liberty of willing and not willing.

And because free choice is given solely for preserving righteousness—in which the salvation of the soul consists—its fitting definition is judged to be this:

The liberty of choice is the power to preserve the rectitude of the will for the sake of that rectitude itself. For a right will is to will what God wills. God wills that a rational creature should be subject to him not under compulsion but voluntarily, so that it may be well with that creature; when it also wills this, then its will is right.

[Note: [Col. 1200D] See St Anselm above in various chapters.] It is free to preserve this rectitude, constrained by no necessity; and the rectitude of the will is righteousness. Therefore, if for no purpose other than righteousness itself it loves God—who is righteousness and supreme blessedness—it will have its reward. Thus the most fitting definition of free choice is: the power to preserve the rectitude of the will for the sake of rectitude itself, through which it rightfully possesses eternal blessedness.

**DISCIPLE.** But how does a person now have free choice for preserving righteousness when he does not possess righteousness?

**MASTER.** Just as someone has sight for seeing the sun even when the sun itself is absent—though he can certainly see it if it is present—so a human being naturally has free choice [Col. 1201A] for preserving righteousness, even when righteousness itself is absent, though he can preserve it if it is present.

But he cannot acquire for himself righteousness which he does not have, because no one, except God, possesses what he has not received. [Note: [Col. 1201D] I Cor. IV, 7: “What do you have that you did not receive?” etc.; John XX, 5.] If it is given to him, it is the grace of him who says: “Without me you can do nothing.” But not abandoning righteousness once received belongs to free choice. Preserving it, however, is merit.

[Note: [Col. 1201D] Rom. IX, 16. These same matters, though arranged in somewhat different words, occur in St Anselm’s treatise *On the Harmony of Foreknowledge and Predestination*, fol. 159, col. 2, near the end.] Therefore it is not of one who wills—understand, who wills—nor of one who runs—understand, who runs—but of God who shows mercy. With no preceding merits, but freely, he anticipates the person by grace, giving him righteousness; and he follows him, so that he may run in the course of righteousness and thus receive, or obtain, the prize of life.

Just as, if a needy naked person is clothed by a rich man, [Col. 1201B] it is not his own doing that he is clothed, but the doing of the one who gives the garment. Yet it lies within his choice whether he wears the garment or puts it off. So it is with prevenient grace, accompanied by free choice.

**MASTER.** Since the Apostle says: “Before they knew either good or evil, it was said: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated,’” [Note: [Col. 1201D] Rom. IX, 11, 12, 13. “For when they had not yet been born, nor had done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to [Col. 1202D] election might remain, not from works but from him who calls, it was said to her: ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’ as it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.’”] some appear to be saved or condemned not according to merits but according to God’s purpose; or God appears to punish the deeds of certain persons before they are committed. For by what merit did Jacob deserve to be loved, when he did not yet know how to do good? And for what guilt was Esau hated, when he had not yet done anything evil?

**DISCIPLE.** As was said above, nothing is future to God. Sacred Scripture testifies that Jacob was simple and Esau profane. What they were to become in their own time through free choice, they already were, before their birth, in the sight of the Lord.

Therefore, because Jacob was simple in the Lord’s sight, the Lord loved him; but because Esau was profane, he hated him.

“Loved” is put in the past tense on account of eternity: for just as the past is always past, so everything which eternity foresees as to be done is immutable.

Moreover, because there is no injustice in God, [Note: [Col. 1202D] Rom. IX, 14: “Is there injustice with God?”] he punishes no one without preceding injustice, though he mercifully forgives many sins after they have been committed.

[Col. 1201D] Therefore, although it is necessary that everything occur which God has purposed, foreknown, and predestined to occur, nevertheless purpose, foreknowledge, and predestination impose no force of necessity upon anyone, so as to prevent each person from doing by free choice what he wills.

Those who through free choice turn away from evil and do good are his people and the sheep of his pasture (Ps. LXXVIII, 13); for them he prepared the pastures of life, [Col. 1202A] and them he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world (Eph. I, 4).

[Note: [Col. 1202D] See St Anselm in various places in that book.] But those who fall away from freedom and, with no necessity compelling them, voluntarily subject themselves to slavery, becoming servants of sin (John VIII, 34) and continually serving demons who preside over vices—these are Pharaoh’s people. They are not among the Lord’s sheep, but are sheep to be set in hell, whom death shall feed upon (Ps. XLVIII, 15). Such persons, after hearing so many teachings, seeing so many signs, and suffering so many plagues, remain incorrigible; and the Lord rejects them when he justly leaves them in their unrighteousness.

Thus God’s Predestination and Foreknowledge remain immutable and fixed, because all that God foreknows and predestines to be done will happen unfailingly. [Col. 1202B] But grace and free choice effect human salvation in a harmonious covenant; the human being, however, failing from freedom by will alone, inclines toward sin.

**DISCIPLE.** Since you have elegantly untied the knot of free choice with the help of grace, I ask you to explain whether the devil was created for blessedness.

**MASTER.** It is agreed that a rational creature was created for blessedness. But the devil is a rational creature; therefore he was created for blessedness. For it is written of him: “Full of wisdom and perfect in beauty, you were in the delights of God’s paradise” (Ezek. XXVIII, 12–13).

**DISCIPLE.** And what is meant by the Lord’s saying of him [Col. 1202C] that “he did not stand in the truth” (John VIII, 44)?

**MASTER.** That is, he did not remain in the rectitude of his will. He voluntarily abandoned righteousness, and thus justly lost blessedness.

**DISCIPLE.** What is Blessedness?

**MASTER.** Sufficiency of every good, without any want.

**DISCIPLE.** Why did God not make him such that he could not lose it?

**MASTER.** Had he made him so, he would then have been subject to necessity like a beast. But he made him righteous, blessed, and free: righteous, so that he might will what God willed; blessed, so that he might always enjoy God; free, so that he might voluntarily will righteousness and thus, by merit, rightfully remain blessed forever.

[Col. 1202D] **DISCIPLE.** And why did the devil fall from this glory?

**MASTER.** Because he sought what he ought not to seek and what God did not will, and wished to be like the Most High (Isa. XIV, 14).

**DISCIPLE.** Like him in what way?

**MASTER.** He wished to be called God, and to be worshipped as God by the angels.

[Col. 1203A] **DISCIPLE.** Since an angel is non-spatial, that is, incorporeal, whence and how did he fall?

**MASTER.** Just as someone standing in sunlight, if he suddenly lost his sight, would be said to have fallen into darkness although he had not changed place—especially since he had been in no place at all.

**DISCIPLE.** Since God was blessed in every respect and always sufficient to himself, what cause was there for his wishing to create anything?

**MASTER.** He created all things because of his goodness, so that there might be beings into whom he could pour the abundance of his goodness. [Note: [Col. 1203D] Prov. XVI, 4: “The Lord has made all things for himself, even the wicked for the evil day.”]

For every creature in some way enjoys the goodness of God its creator: some because they exist; some because they live; some because they feel; some [Col. 1203B] because they understand. Thus each thing is good; and all things taken together are very good. [Note: [Col. 1204D] Ecclus. XXXIX, 21: “All the works of the Lord are very good.”]

He created angelic and human nature to see him; and so that they might have some merit of their own before him which he ought to reward, he gave them righteousness. And so that they might have full joy, he added free choice, by which, not compelled but free, they might preserve the righteousness given them and thus reign happily with him forever.

**DISCIPLE.** And if they were created for blessedness, why do so many perish?

**MASTER.** Because through free choice they fall away from good and subject themselves to sin; they are justly deprived of the glory of blessedness and handed over to punishments.

**DISCIPLE.** And how is it true that God wills [Col. 1203C] all to be saved? (I Tim. II, 4.)

**MASTER.** God created rational creatures for glory. But angels and human beings are rational creatures; therefore all were created for glory.

But he created them for glory either willingly or unwillingly.

**DISCIPLE.** He could not have done so unwillingly.

**MASTER.** Therefore he did it willingly.

**DISCIPLE.** That follows.

**MASTER.** But what God wills once, he wills always, for his will is immutable. Therefore he always wills all to be saved.

**DISCIPLE.** And if he wills it, why are not all saved? For who resists his will? (Rom. IX, 19.)

[Col. 1203D] **MASTER.** The perdition of those who perish does not proceed from God’s will, because he does not will the sinner’s death (Ezek. XVIII, 32), and he who did not make death does not delight in the destruction of the dying. [Note: [Col. 1204D] Wisdom I, 13: “Nor does he delight in the destruction of the living.”] Rather, it proceeds from free choice, by which they voluntarily abandon righteousness, which is the covenant of blessedness; having abandoned it, they lose blessedness and thus will be miserable forever.

**DISCIPLE.** How does this proceed from free choice?

**MASTER.** The angel, drawn by no predestination and no necessity, but by free will alone, abandoned righteousness when he wished to be like God (Isa. XIV, 14).

And because by his own will he broke the bond of blessedness, [Col. 1204A] which was righteousness, he justly fell, having lost blessedness, into misery—from which, as righteousness decreed, he never deserved to be delivered.

The principle of justice required this: for one who fell with no one impelling him ought justly to be raised by no one.

**DISCIPLE.** What of the human being?

**MASTER.** Likewise, the human being abandoned righteousness under no compulsion or force of necessity, but by free will, and subjected himself to unrighteousness when he desired to be like God.

**DISCIPLE.** Why did this fallen being deserve to be raised again?

**MASTER.** His restoration was grace; but the principle of justice also required it. For one who fell through another’s prompting ought justly to be raised by another.

**DISCIPLE.** It seems to me that it was not fitting for God to give them free choice, [Col. 1204B] through which he foreknew they would sin.

**MASTER.** This is as though you said: He ought not to have given them knowledge, which he foreknew they would misuse. If he had not given them knowledge, how would they differ from brute animals? If he had not given them free choice, they would be subject in every respect to necessity, like beasts, and would have no merit before God.

Therefore he ought to give them knowledge, by which they might recognize their Creator. Free choice also had to be added, by which they might freely preserve righteousness, through which they would always be blessed.

**DISCIPLE.** If God foreknows all things, he surely foreknew that they would act wickedly and would therefore suffer eternal punishment. Why then did he wish to create those who were going to commit so many [Col. 1204C] and such great crimes and wrongs, and bear eternal penalties for them?

**MASTER.** God foreknew all things, and this accords with his eternity, for he knows nothing future as though it were yet to be done, nor anything past as though it had passed away; rather, with immutable vision he beholds as present all things to be done and all things done.

That he created angel and human being, though he foreknew that each would act wickedly, was required by the principle of justice and of power.

By power, because he foreknew that their wickedness could do him no harm whatever, and how great were the goods that he had determined to make in the whole universe out of their evils.

By justice, because it was just that God should do everything that would be useful in some respect within the universe. [Col. 1204D] And wise persons do not fail to know how useful and necessary demons and wicked human beings are in God’s commonwealth.

Thus he gave righteousness to creatures whom he foreknew would not preserve it; indeed, he created them righteous, because it accords with his goodness that he should make nothing except what is righteous and right.

He also gave them free choice—that is, made them masters of their own will—because it accords with his perfection that he should bring nothing into being except what is perfect. For they would not be perfect if they were not free; and if they were not free, they would be subject to necessity like beasts. Therefore [Col. 1205A] he did everything as he willed and as he ought to have done.

**DISCIPLE.** Why did God not keep them from evil when he could? If he willed to do so but could not, why was he powerless? But if he could and would not, why did he will that they sin and consequently suffer punishments? And in permitting them to sin, he surely consented to their sins. For if a ruler foreknows that one of his subjects wishes to kill him, and does not prevent it although he can, he surely consents to the killer by allowing it to happen. But if he willingly permits it, he shows himself powerless.

**MASTER.** The principle of immutability forbade God to prevent them from evil.

For God created them for full joy; but they would not have full joy if they were not free.

[Col. 1205B] Therefore, in order that they might have full joy, he gave them free choice; indeed, he created them free, that is, masters of their own will, so that they might freely delight in joy and might enjoy joy not compelled by necessity or driven by force.

But God, being immutable, ought not, and indeed could not, take away the freedom which he had once given them. For if he had taken it away, he would then not will them to will righteousness—which is impossible, for he willed them to will righteousness. For sinning is nothing other than not willing righteousness. Therefore evil or sin has no substance, just as unrighteousness has no substance. Unrighteousness is nothing other than the absence of righteousness, just as silence is where there is no voice and darkness where there is no light. Thus to do evil is nothing other than [Col. 1205C] to fall away from a righteous will. In a certain sense God would have taken freedom away from them if, restrained by him, they could not sin. And if they preserved righteousness under compulsion, they would possess no merit for righteousness.

**DISCIPLE.** What then? Cannot the good angels sin?

**MASTER.** This does not arise from a necessity of weakness, but from the will that proceeds from great power. For it is great power always to will what one ought and what is fitting—for example, always to be sound and wise.

But it is the greatest weakness—indeed, madness—to will what one ought not and what is unfitting, as to will to kill oneself. For when the other angels turned toward unrighteousness, the good angels preserved righteousness by free will; and for this merit they were immediately so [Col. 1205D] confirmed in this will that they no longer will evil. Hence it is said that they cannot.

**DISCIPLE.** Yet, as has been said, God appears to have consented to the sin of those whom he permitted to sin; or rather, to have created for punishments those whom he did not prevent from sinning.

**MASTER.** Truth, when consulted, shows something quite different.

Although the Lord’s ways are as far removed from human ways as the heavens are exalted above the earth, [Note: [Col. 1205D] Isa. LV, 8: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, says the Lord.” [Col. 1206D] “For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so my ways are exalted above your ways,” etc.] this matter does not differ greatly from our own thoughts, as evident reason thus makes clear to us.

It does not always follow that one who permits something to happen [Col. 1206A] consents to its happening, even if he can prevent it. For when someone allows thorns to grow in his field, though he could prevent it, he nevertheless does not consent to their growth, nor allow them to grow as a hedge’s defence or as fuel for fires, though they are suited to both purposes. So God, although he permitted them to sin, did not consent to sin, nor create them for punishments. Yet after their sins he consigned them to punishments; while those who freely adhere to him, who is supreme blessedness, he crowned with glory and honour (Ps. VIII, 6); and those who nonetheless freely depart from him, who is eternal righteousness, he punished with fitting penalties. By their harshness, as with thorns, he strengthens the hedge of the former’s glory, and by their burning he illumines his whole work.

**DISCIPLE.** Why did God create those whom he foreknew would not preserve righteousness [Col. 1206B] and would therefore lose glory, instead of creating only those whom he foreknew would persevere in glory by preserving righteousness?

**MASTER.** This is as though you complained that God permitted night to exist because it is dark, as if bright day were useless and unnecessary, whereas night itself is the rest of those who labour and the renewal of their strength. Thus good is commended through evil. For the righteous, compared with the unrighteous, appear more glorious, just as day, compared with night, shines more pleasingly. Therefore the principle of good required God to permit evil to exist, so that through reciprocal measures and their oppositions, all things might harmonize. Although evil has no substance and therefore introduces no discord into God’s eternal ordering, yet [Col. 1206C] by its very existence it causes all substances to appear good and makes known how good it is to cleave to the highest Good.

**DISCIPLE.** God’s goodness seems very strange, in that he wished to create something subject to eternal pains and eternal torments, when it would seem much better that something not exist at all than exist miserably, or that it be an insensible stone rather than endure eternal pains.

**MASTER.** To the wise God it seemed better that both should exist than that nothing should exist at all. Therefore he made what is to exist.

That he did not make all things equal but diverse reveals both the ineffable wisdom of the craftsman and the inestimable, ordered fullness of his work. [Col. 1206D] And although God made punishments, he nevertheless created nothing for punishments; otherwise an insensible creature would be superior to a sensible one, since the latter feels the pain of punishment without end.

When a rational creature voluntarily cast away the righteousness it possessed, it then lost the glory set before it and thus fell into misery. Misery is grief for what it has lost, inability to possess what it desires, affliction by the conditions in which it finds itself, and inability to cast them off. To be tormented by punishments is nothing other than to suffer, against one’s will, something contrary to oneself.

For the beauty of the universe, God created two things [Col. 1207A] and two [Note: [Col. 1207D] Ecclus. XXXIV, 15: “Good is set against evil, and life against death; so also the sinner is set against the just. Thus behold all the works of the Most High: two and two, one against one.”] opposed to one another, such as water against fire and earth against air; and creatures formed from these opposites suffer pain from their contraries, just as things formed in waters or on earth are tormented by fire. For the salamander lives in flame and dies in water; but a fish, nourished in water, dies in fire.

For rational nature, therefore, to feel the bitterness of pains is not to possess the sweetness of blessedness. The principle of justice demands that those who voluntarily stripped themselves of the blessedness of glory should remain forever in the bitterness of misery. The reason that this is without end is that they were created immortal.

**DISCIPLE.** Since it had been ordained by God from eternity that his Son should be incarnate, the human being appears necessarily to have sinned, so that God’s purpose might be fulfilled. [Col. 1207B] For if he had not sinned, the Son of God would not have been incarnate, and God’s decree would thus have been frustrated. Therefore both seem to depend on necessity: that the former sinned and that the latter was incarnate.

**MASTER.** God foreknew from eternity the human being’s fall, and therefore from eternity determined that his Son should be incarnate for his redemption.

But the human being sinned by no necessity, but by free will alone; therefore the Lord imputed sin to him. If he had sinned necessarily, he would not have been guilty, since he would have done what he could not avoid.

But because the Lord warned him beforehand about sin, set before him the punishment of death, and he himself despised the divine warnings, he therefore became guilty.

That the Son of God was incarnate or [Col. 1207C] sacrificed for humankind was, as far as he himself was concerned, a matter of will alone; as far as the human being was concerned, it was an absolute necessity. For unless this one had been incarnate, that one would never have been saved.

It was therefore necessary for the human being that he should will to be incarnate.

**DISCIPLE.** Why was neither an angel nor a human being sent to redeem humankind, but the Son of God?

**MASTER.** The principle of justice required this. An angel ought not to have been sent for humanity, because human nature had nothing to do with angelic nature. But a human being ought not to have been sent because every human being was a sinner, and a sinner could not redeem a sinner. Therefore it was necessary to send him who alone, being without sin, could reconcile humankind to God. [Note: [Col. 1207D] Rom. III, 10: “For there is none righteous,” [Col. 1208D] etc.; and Rom. V, 12: “As through one human being sin entered into this world, and death through sin, so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned.”]

**DISCIPLE.** Why was neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit incarnate, but [Col. 1207D] the Son alone?

**MASTER.** Justice required it. For he is, as it were, God in the second place after the Father—not in dignity, but in order. He is equal to God the Father, that is, one with him. Hence he is called the likeness of God. But the devil arrogated this privilege to himself when he desired to be like the Most High—namely, to be called God and worshipped as God by angels. And because he did not obtain this in heaven from angels, he taught human beings in the world to worship and honour him as God. Therefore it was necessary that [Col. 1208A] the one against whom the injury had been committed should come, and show himself to be the true God and the devil to be false.

**DISCIPLE.** And why did he come as a human being?

**MASTER.** So that he, an innocent human being, might make satisfaction to God the Father for guilty humankind (Hebr. I, 33 [citation as printed]), restrain the tyrant through a human being, and rescue the human being deceived by him.

**DISCIPLE.** By what did the devil lose the human being whom he had once possessed?

**MASTER.** By God’s justice and power. He grievously offended against God’s power, like a blind man stumbling; for he not only made himself equal to God but exalted himself above God (Isa. XIV, 14), when in the temptation he commanded himself to be worshipped by the Son of God, who is equal to the Father. He grievously incurred offence against God’s justice in the Passion, when [Col. 1208B] he killed the righteous and innocent human being.

Thus through justice he experienced power. For when a righteous human being is unjustly killed, the unjust tyrant is justly crushed; and the deceived human being, unjustly oppressed, is redeemed through justice and established in power over the angel whom he had worshipped as God. Hence favourable circumstances are still called *secundae res* (“second affairs”), because through justice one comes to eternal power.

**DISCIPLE.** Is there free choice in infants?

**MASTER.** Free choice is naturally present in them, but, like fire concealed in flint, it does nothing in them.

**DISCIPLE.** Why are not all children saved through redemption, in whom free choice still does nothing [Col. 1208C] at all?

**MASTER.** This proceeds from the principle of justice, because nothing except punishment is owed to humanity.

**DISCIPLE.** And why are very many saved, in whom free choice equally does nothing?

**MASTER.** This descends from grace, which bestows its gifts even upon the undeserving.

If the people of some city offended their king, he might justly punish some and mercifully absolve others. So, when the whole world had offended God, he exacted punishment from some through justice, but forgave others through mercy.

**DISCIPLE.** Why is it that many people now capable of free choice are saved, while very many are not saved?

**MASTER.** The cause is the same as has been stated. Those who are saved are saved through grace and free choice, through God’s gift and not through their own merit.

For it is from God’s grace that, anticipated by God, they will the good; it is from free choice that they do not abandon the good. Perseverance in this good is ascribed both to God’s gift and to human merit, and for it the person will be rewarded with life’s prize. “For whoever perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. XXIV, 13).

[Col. 1209A] **DISCIPLE.** Why is it that some who have grown old in evils are finally saved?

**MASTER.** Through grace and free choice. Through prevenient grace, good will is freely inspired by God; through free choice, they cooperate with what is offered; and for this merit they are saved.

These two are together like soul and body. For through grace free choice is enlivened, as the body is enlivened through the soul; and free choice cooperates with grace, as the body cooperates with the soul. Grace without free choice is of itself able to save; free choice without grace is unable to perform good.

Thus through grace free choice accomplishes much, and its perseverance is crowned first. It is grace that, after they have pursued wickedness insatiably for many years, from childhood [Col. 1209B] to decrepitude, they are snatched at life’s very end through repentance from the jaws of the devil himself and led to enjoy the pleasantness of paradise.

**DISCIPLE.** And why are others not saved?

**MASTER.** This is known to arise from justice and free choice.

From justice: because they are not softened by grace toward good but are permitted to be hardened, although the fountain of grace frequently flows over them and grants them repentance for a time; they immediately reject it and return like dogs to their vomit (Prov. XXVI, 11; II Pet. 22).

From free choice: because they are unwilling to receive the righteousness offered and choose unrighteousness instead.

For those mentioned above, God’s word is the cause of salvation and the way to life; [Col. 1209C] but for these it is a cause of death and testimony leading to destruction. The former are vessels of mercy, prepared for honour; the latter are vessels of wrath (Rom. IX, 22), prepared for dishonour. None of the former can perish; none of the latter will be saved. For the former a kingdom has been prepared from the foundation of the world; for the latter, a furnace of fire with the devil and his angels. [Note: [Col. 1209D] Matt. XXV, 34. Monks and hermits.]

From this diversity it happens that many spend their lives in monasteries under severe discipline, and very many, dwelling in the wilderness, lead a solitary life with the highest abstinence, yet in the end descend to the lowest abyss.

**DISCIPLE.** This is astonishing beyond all measure.

**MASTER.** Learn the causes in each case. Those who perish in monasteries trust in their own prudence, despise the counsels of their superiors, and die in disobedience. Those who perish in the wilderness live without discernment, when they choose for themselves to follow examples of saints while scorning and rejecting their father’s commands. Of them it is written: “There are ways which seem right to human beings, whose end leads to destruction.” [Note: [Col. 1209D] Prov. XIV, 12 and XV, 25: “There is a way which seems right to a human being, but its final paths lead to death.”]

**DISCIPLE.** Why, when equal in the same fault, are some saved and some rejected?

**MASTER.** Here God’s incomprehensible judgments are proclaimed, [Note: [Col. 1210D] Rom. XI, 33: “O the depth of riches.”] he who is declared terrible in his counsels over the children of human beings (Ps. LXV, 5), who chooses in mercy whom he wills [Col. 1210A] and rejects in justice whom he wills; and no one can say to him, “Why do you act thus?” All his ways are mercy and truth (Ps. XXIV, 10).

**DISCIPLE.** Is salvation more ascribed to grace or to free choice?

**MASTER.** The whole of salvation is attributed to God’s grace, to which merits themselves are also ascribed; for no one can come to the Son, who is eternal life, unless the Father draws him through grace—that is, through the Holy Spirit (John VI, 44). For without him we can do nothing (John XV, 5). God indeed works in us both willing and being able, for good will. [Note: [Col. 1210D] Phil. II, 13: “He works willing and accomplishing,” etc.]

**DISCIPLE.** If God works, what reward is credited to a human being?

[Col. 1210B] **MASTER.** God works, and the elect cooperate. God works in his elect by his grace, preceding their willing and following with their ability. They cooperate by free choice, consenting with good will. This good will is rewarded in them, as it is written: “We have received grace for grace” (John I, 16). We receive grace when God anticipates us, so that we may will, and follows us, so that we may be able. For this grace he will give that grace when he rewards us in glory.

**DISCIPLE.** Some are accustomed to say that the predestined are necessarily saved. If this is so, why do they labour at all? Or why is the Gospel preached to the Gentiles so that they may be converted? Or why is the word of exhortation daily administered by priests to the people, so that they may advance in the service [Col. 1210C] appointed by God?

**MASTER.** God’s Predestination indeed saves or damns no one by force. Those long ago predestined to the kingdom according to their merits are then necessarily saved when, by justice, the glory proposed is repaid to their merits. But because no one presumes that he is predestined—since not even Paul, the vessel of election, presumed this of himself—it is necessary to apply oneself to labour with all effort, so that one may attain predestination.

For predestination to life is acquired through labour, as sacred authority says: “Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts XIII, 21). Thus Predestination is given to infants through the bitterness of death; to young persons [Col. 1210D] through the exercise of works; and to those repenting at the end of life through the testing of the torments of purgatory.

To the Gentiles, therefore, preaching is made because the predestined, who stand idle outside in the marketplace, are summoned into the Lord’s vineyard to labor (Matt. 10:6). A denarius is also set before them as their wage, because predestined glory will be given to those who labor unto the end.

Often, too, certain persons among the reprobate enter the vineyard with them; but at the beginning of the work they fall away from their labor, and either leave the vineyard blaspheming, or, remaining in it, hinder those who work. Of these it is said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” [Note: [Col. 1211D] 1 John 2:19. “They went forth from us.”] And again: “They were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39:6)—that is, beyond the number predestined for life. Many indeed have clung through faith to Peter’s net (Matt. 13:47); but because they were not foreknown among the number of the elect, they sprang back into the waves of vices when the net was broken.

The people of the faithful, wearied in the labor of a devout work, are strengthened by the word of admonition, lest they fail,

just as a sick man going to church, but becoming exhausted on the road, is supported by someone so that he may complete the journey.

For the word of God is the true seed (Luke 8:11), while the field is human hearts. When this seed is scattered by God’s cultivators, the seed is God’s grace. [Col. 1211B] But if it is received by the cultivation, it is free choice; and, when received through faith, if it puts forth the shoot of good works, its harvest will be in predestined glory.

**DISCIPLE.** Since clear reason brings all these things forth from the light of truth, they ought to be exceedingly pleasing in every respect to all earnest students.

Yet I am greatly troubled that angelic nature could fall, if it was created for blessedness. For it seems that some force impelled it, so that it fell thus irrecoverably. Indeed, I am deeply troubled by the human fall: how could humanity descend from such great glory into such great misery, if no necessity impelled it?

[Col. 1211C] Therefore I ask you to pour out your heart and utter the secret of truth.

**MASTER.** I shall briefly disclose God’s hidden things to you; listen attentively to the secrets of the heart that have been disclosed.

Before God created the world, he foreknew both the fall of the angel and that of humankind. He permitted it to occur because he judged that good is made more manifest by evil.

He also foreknew who and how many would remain with him, who and how many would depart, and who and how many would return to him. For if he had not known this, he would not be foreknowing of future things. And if there were not a fixed number of the elect, then the kingdom of God would rest not upon ordered arrangement but upon chance, into which a multitude of uncertain number would flock. But since with God the number even of hairs is fixed [Note: [Col. 1211D] Matt. 10:30 and Luke 22:7. “All the hairs of your head are numbered.”], much [Col. 1211D] more is the number of the elect fixed with God beforehand.

All who are prescribed by God within this number were chosen for blessedness before the foundation of the world. None of them will perish; rather, each will hasten with all effort toward predestined glory. But those who are multiplied beyond this number are not reckoned among Christ’s sheep.

And because this number was diminished by the angels who fell, it was restored by human beings who are born. Therefore, just as we begin counting from one, so the number began from one [Col. 1212A] human being. And, as the number grows toward completion, so the human offspring has succeeded one another until the elect are completed.

This sacred number, known to God alone and fixed by him with eternal certainty, is like the circuit of a certain city, within which all must necessarily be contained who have been foreknown from eternity as citizens of this city. The law of this city is inviolable justice, established by the most just king; those who observe it are called righteous, and these alone are counted among its citizens. The privilege of this sacred city is freedom; its kingdom is blessedness. Therefore all the inhabitants of this city are righteous. Those who were free did not wish to observe the law of this city. Therefore they could not be numbered among its citizens. Yet they aspired to its lordship, [Col. 1212B] since each desired to be God within it.

Thus no force and no necessity expelled them from this city; rather, the law of justice forbade violators of the law to be citizens in it.

**DISCIPLE.** O, to what lofty watchtower you have led me, in which I behold very many things! But because some things are still closed, I ask that they be opened to me.

If man falls through free choice, why does he not rise again through free choice?

**MASTER.** A man can cast himself from a high mountain into a deep precipice, but cannot return unless helped by another. So by free choice one may abandon righteousness; yet one can receive it again not through oneself, but through grace alone. For “the one by whom a person is overcome, of that one he also becomes the slave.” [Note: [Col. 1211D] 2 Pet. 2:19. “The one by whom someone has been overcome, of that one he is also the slave.” [Col. 1212D]] For one who voluntarily gives himself over to lust, or to any vice that rules him, is no longer able by free choice to shake himself free from the yoke of its domination, to whose rule he freely chose to submit himself—unless God’s grace goes before him, so that he may desire the good he despised, and follows after, so that he may be able to fulfill it.

**DISCIPLE.** Since the human will was made free, why is it so inclined toward evil and so sluggish toward good?

**MASTER.** Every rational will naturally desires the highest good; but, deceived by error, it falls into what is false, which is evil. Everyone wishes to be blessed, and therefore each person desires most intensely that in which he hopes to be blessed. But since the highest good, or blessedness, exists only in God alone, whoever desires anything placed below God as the highest good is mistaken.

The cause of this error is as follows.
