God created human beings righteous and blessed, without any lack, in sufficiency of every good thing [Note: [Col. 1212D] Eccl. 7:30. “I found that God made man upright, but he himself entangled himself in countless questions.”], and gave them a free will of righteousness and blessedness: by the will of righteousness, they were to rule the body subject to them; by the will of blessedness, they were to obey God. Thus they possessed righteousness for God’s honor, and blessedness for their own [Col. 1213A] benefit. Had they honored God by preserving righteousness, they would have attained the highest blessedness of the angels. But because they abandoned righteousness, they lost blessedness. Yet they retained the will for blessedness. Therefore, burning with desire for benefits but unable to possess the benefits proper to rational nature which they had lost, they turn themselves toward false benefits and the brutish advantages and bestial appetites. And because they became like senseless beasts [Note: [Col. 1213D] Ps. 48:13. “Man, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.”], they therefore mate through concupiscence like beasts; give birth in pain; nourish infants with milk, like beasts their young; and desire bodily benefits alone.

**DISCIPLE.** Why are beasts not condemned for these things?

**MASTER.** Appetites in brute animals are not sin, but natural; in human beings, however, they are irrational. For other living creatures are borne along by necessity, whereas man is governed by freedom. Hence it is written: “Whoever does what a human being ought not to do, let him be removed from among human beings.”

**DISCIPLE.** Why is it that some strive with immense effort to live rightly, yet make no progress? Or why do they fall away from their resolution after great progress? Does not some hidden force draw them back, so that they cannot complete the work they began?

**MASTER.** No necessity draws them back; their will alone turns them aside, while they prefer what temptation suggests to what reason persuades.

Some also presume more upon their own choice than upon grace, and ascribe everything to their own merits. Therefore, when grace abandons them, they justly lose their labor.

**DISCIPLE.** Why does God make human choice so changeable?

**MASTER.** For its great advantage: what can turn toward evil can also turn again toward good. If a person, once fallen, were not changeable, that person could never be converted to good.

**DISCIPLE.** Why did God not make him unchangeable in good?

**MASTER.** Then he would be equal to God; for this belongs to God alone.

**DISCIPLE.** If everyone acts by free choice, how does God work all things in all?

**MASTER.** All good things that are done, whether in heaven, [Col. 1213D] on earth, or in every creature, are wrought by God alone, who alone is good, through the elect—whether angels or human beings—while they cooperate by consenting through free choice.

God works through the elect, as when he converts the Gentiles through the apostles: he himself inspires inwardly and gives growth; they cooperate through their outward ministry, planting and watering.

But if the elect do anything contrary—as David did in the case of Uriah [Col. 1214A] (2 Kings 11:1)—God justly permits this to be done, yet turns it to his own praise, since after their fall they become more humble and give him more abundant thanks; indeed, even their sins work together for their good [Note: [Col. 1213D] Rom. 8:28. “All things work together for good to those who love God.”]. Therefore all things are from him and through him (Rom. 11:36).

God also works through the reprobate when he executes his judgment through them, as when he destroyed Jerusalem through the Chaldeans (Jer. 52:24). Behold: God and the Chaldeans performed one and the same act in different ways; yet he is praised for it, and they are condemned. What he did through justice, they did through cruelty.

Likewise, through Judas God delivered up his Son (Matt. 26:48) and redeemed the world from death. Behold [Col. 1214B] God and Judas performed one act with different intentions. Yet the whole world venerates God for it and detests Judas, because what God did out of love for the human race, Judas did out of avarice. I say boldly that God works even through the devil what he decrees shall be exercised through him in the reprobate by justice. But what God does through most just equity, the devil does through most wicked cruelty. Yet he cannot rage against them more than he is permitted. Hence God is gloriously magnified, whereas the devil is damnably rejected for the same act.

Whatever the reprobate commit by free choice against the ordinances is indeed permitted by God [Col. 1214C] to happen and turned to his praise, when they are justly subjected by him to punishments. Thus God works all things either by aiding or by permitting.

And because—as is read in the book of Wisdom—“good things and evil things” are from God [Note: [Col. 1213D] Sirach 11:14. “Good and evil, life and death, poverty and honor are from God.”], all things are good; and nothing is evil except that what is bitter to those who suffer something harsh is called evil. Therefore all things are for the praise and glory of God, who “has mercy on whom he wills” [Note: [Col. 1214D] Rom. 9:18. “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens.”], by bestowing grace, and hardens whom he wills by leaving him in wickedness.

**DISCIPLE.** Have these things never been heard in the world?

**MASTER.** On the contrary, they are heard daily in the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 1214D] Matt. 18:18. “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” And v. 19: “For if two of you agree on earth concerning whatever thing they ask, it shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.” And Matt. 28:19: “Go, teach all nations.”]; but they are not attended to by the idle and negligent, and therefore are not understood. But when they hear these matters from learned persons in disputation, they are astonished as though awakened from sleep. [Col. 1214D] They doubt that they are true because they think they are written nowhere. But the diligent read, hear, attend to, examine, understand, and recall them to memory.

For Christ the Bridegroom, departing, left to his bride the Church the keys of knowledge; to her children who knock daily, he opens by understanding the secrets of God, unlocking them. But he keeps the pearls shut away from dogs and swine, lest they be defiled.

[Col. 1215A] **DISCIPLE.** You establish all that you set forth with such strong testimonies and conclude it by inference, that one would show oneself more mistaken than a blind man if one presumed stubbornly to attack these things.

But, I ask, explain whether prosperity and adversity occur through free choice.

**MASTER.** Rather, through God’s grace and justice. God’s grace supplies prosperity, while justice dispenses adversity. The righteous are summoned through prosperity to everlasting goods; but the unrighteous, through prosperity, are rewarded as was that rich man [Note: [Col. 1215D] Luke 16:25: “Son, you received your good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, while you are tormented.”]. Adversity, however, touches the elect for three reasons. First, that some may be corrected from sins through adversity, as David; second, that some, when tested, may be more highly crowned, as Job; third, that some may be drawn back from the delight of sin, [Col. 1215B] as Paul.

It strikes the reprobate for two reasons. First, that the elect may be corrected through their punishments, as we read in the destruction of Korah; second, that they themselves may be restrained from wickedness, lest they harm as greatly as they wish, as is written concerning Antiochus and Herod.

**DISCIPLE.** You have dug through the wall, and behold, a door appears.

Since Scripture says that Pharaoh was hardened by God [Note: [Col. 1215D] Exod. 9:16. “For this reason I have set you up: that I may show my strength in you and that my name may be proclaimed throughout all the earth.” And Rom. 9:17: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.”]—indeed, that he was appointed for this very purpose, that God’s name might be proclaimed through him throughout all the earth—who does not see that he afflicted the people under compelling necessity, since he was appointed for this very purpose and was drowned as though drawn along by a certain fate?

**MASTER.** Note three things: the people afflicted; Pharaoh afflicting them; and God delivering them.

God tests the elect through the reprobate, as golden vessels in the furnace of tribulation; but the reprobate themselves do not intend that their oppression may contribute to the salvation of those whom the malice of cruelty alone torments.

Furthermore, he permitted the devil, who freely abandoned righteousness, to be hardened in unrighteousness like an anvil for hammerers, and appointed him as a smith for purifying the vessels of mercy. This smith made all the impious his instruments, one of whom was Pharaoh. When Pharaoh was unwilling through free choice to serve God, God hardened him by not freeing him from wickedness and hardness.

[Col. 1215D] And when the people of God were to be tested by affliction and proved by adversity, God appointed Pharaoh for this very purpose, to test the people, since Pharaoh himself, through free choice—like one of the devil’s hammers, so to speak—offered himself to beat God’s vessels. Thus Pharaoh, unknowingly, served the righteous as a servant [Col. 1216A] serves children, when, separating them from the vessels of wrath, he trained them by scourges.

The devil and the impious indeed will evil in themselves, but cannot do as much as they wish; they can do only as much as they are permitted. And when they are permitted by God to prevail against the elect, they are said to have been appointed for this very purpose. [Note: [Col. 1215D] On this subject and manner of speaking, Gregory the Great’s *Moral Exposition*, book XIII on Job 17, chapter 12, should properly be consulted; and book XXXIV on Job 41, chapter 10.]

God’s name, however, became known to all through Pharaoh, when he himself, with all his people, justly perished; and God delivered those oppressed by him through signs and wonders, as vessels already tested by fire in a furnace.

**DISCIPLE.** It is also written concerning Judas: “That the Scripture may be fulfilled: ‘He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me.’” [Note: [Col. 1216D] John 16:18: “He who eats my bread,” etc.] And again: “None of those whom you gave me perished, except the son of perdition, [Col. 1216B] that the Scripture might be fulfilled.” [Note: [Col. 1216D] John 17:12: “Those whom you gave me I have kept, and none of them perished except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.”]

And since Scripture must be fulfilled, as the Lord himself testifies, who but one blind in every respect would fail to see that Judas, impelled by some force of necessity, betrayed the Lord—especially since the Lord had come to suffer and it was necessary that he be handed over by someone?

**MASTER.** As regards himself, the Lord willed to suffer not by necessity but by most free will, because the divine nature was incapable of suffering; and this was greatly necessary for us, whom the necessity of death had driven toward destruction.

No necessity, but a malicious will, incited Judas to betrayal, because he preferred to hate the Lord with the Jews rather than to love him with the apostles.

Likewise, the Jews were compelled by no necessity, but driven by a most wicked will to kill him, since they hated without cause him whose power they were grieved to see established by signs and miracles.

But because the Holy Spirit, to whom all future things are present, foreknew that they would will and do such things, he foretold them in Scripture through the prophets just as everything subsequently occurred [Note: [Col. 1216D] Ps. 108:8. “May his days be few, and may another receive his episcopal office.”]. Yet that Scripture imposed upon them no necessity of willing or acting, just as, if I foreknew a war and foretold that it would happen, my words would not make the war necessary.

**DISCIPLE.** What then can one infer from this except that it was necessary for Christ to be crucified by the Jews, since he came to be killed by them—which he surely would not have done if he ought not [Col. 1216D] to have done it?

**MASTER.** And do you believe that the Jews alone killed Christ? All the wicked, from the beginning to the end of the world, consented to Christ’s death [Note: [Col. 1216D] Ps. 86:5. “Those who hate me without cause are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.”]. For all who hate righteousness and truth persecute the righteous for righteousness and truth—which he is—and all are found guilty of the Lord’s death. [Col. 1217A] For, if they could, they would wish to destroy all the righteous so that they might safely fulfill their desires without opposition. Therefore, if those men had not done it, men like them would have accomplished it.

**DISCIPLE.** Led by you into the interior, I consider many splendid things; but I grieve that I cannot see many things that are sealed. Therefore I ask that, since the key of knowledge has been entrusted to you, you open these closed matters to me and, unfolding those that are wrapped up, enable me to behold them.

**MASTER.** To one who knocks so diligently, the Lord will give a favorable answer through me and open to you the mysteries of secrets.

**DISCIPLE.** What cause, then, do we say there is for God’s permitting those whom he predestined to reign with him forever to wander for a long time?

**MASTER.** By this he displays the abundance of his patience and forbearance, in that he endures them even longer in error, as Paul (Rom. 2:4); and when he suddenly recalls them to repentance, as that same Paul and Mary (Luke 8), he makes known the riches of his mercy. For them he came into the world; for them he also underwent death.

And although he died for sinners, his death did not benefit Annas and Caiaphas, Herod and Pilate, but harmed them greatly—not only because they conspired in the Lord’s death, but because they hated the good without cause (John 15:25) and neglected to repent.

Moreover, many of the elect had consented, though ignorantly, to Christ’s death, [Col. 1217C] and for them he prayed even on the cross, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” [Note: [Col. 1217D] Note the efficacy of the prayer of Christ the Savior upon the cross. Luke 23:34. See these words in St. Gregory’s *Moral Exposition*, book XIII on Job 17, chapter 11, or according to the more recent edition.] They afterward drank in faith the blood which they had first shed in fury.

**DISCIPLE.** Since human evil deeds do God no harm and their good deeds confer nothing upon him, why does he separate them after death and not place all alike and equally together in one place?

**MASTER.** It conflicts with the rationale of justice for the righteous to occupy a place with the unrighteous, and conversely, [lacuna] and, by manifold variation, distinguishes the whole picture.

Therefore, just as a painter varies his work with colors, so God gloriously adorns his kingdom with distinct orders. What beauty would there be in a painting if one color covered the entire ceiling? Nor could it even be called a painting. Now the painter places different colors in different places and thus makes his work pleasing to the eye. Likewise, a setter of stones places various gems in different settings and thus makes his work more precious.

**DISCIPLE.** Why does the last judgment still remain?

**MASTER.** Justice requires that judgment be held: so that those who now conceal themselves under hypocrisy may be shown to be wicked; those who now publicly glory in shameful acts may then justly be subjected to fitting punishments; and those who despise laws, disdain justice, oppress the poor and the righteous, and, secure through power, flourish by plunder, rejoice in the loss of others, insult the righteous, [Col. 1218A] trample God’s words, are praised for such things and the like, and are honored by people through fear—these, I say, may then be separated from the righteous whom they here oppress, and from joy, and joined with the unrighteous in punishment. But the righteous, now unjustly oppressed, may be raised up; those who acted rightly while living well may be rewarded; and those who suffered reproach for righteousness may be honored.

**DISCIPLE.** Now tell me why humanity was placed in paradise when it was not to remain there.

**MASTER.** The first-created human, made for blessedness, was placed in paradise, that is, in a place of delight. But because he was unwilling to keep the Lord’s command, he rightly suffered exile as one who had despised it. Had he tasted none of paradise’s delights but violated the command received, perhaps he would never have repented and thus would always have remained an exile. But after he recalled to mind the sweetness of paradise which he had experienced and swiftly lost, he imposed upon himself a grievous penance. Therefore he returned, and therefore deserved return. From whose womb [the referent is uncertain in the text] there immediately came forth, as from a certain fortress, a twofold army: namely, the elect and the reprobate; and when this had occurred, they began a contest of implacable conflict.

In this great battle the struggle is waged on both sides. The victorious, crowned with laurel and triumphing, seek the stars; but the defeated, put to shame, descend to the depths of the abyss.

Pause here also, and consider the zeal of each side.

[Col. 1218C] **Concerning the humble citizens of Jerusalem.**

One person proceeds from childhood along the way of humility and, even to old age, always advances toward what is better. He considers all other people superior to himself and judges himself inferior to all. He praises everyone’s actions and condemns his own.

**Concerning the chaste citizen of Jerusalem.**

Another takes up the path of chastity, guards his senses with great vigilance, and yet reckons all others holy and judges himself unclean, as it were.

**Concerning the patient person.**

Another treads the path of patience, enduring patiently for Christ every hardship and bitterness; he considers others gentle and thinks himself lacking in meekness.

[Col. 1218D] **Concerning the abstinent person.**

Another walks the path of abstinence and mortifies his flesh by rigorous discipline; yet, honoring and considering others stricter in abstinence, he condemns himself as a glutton.

**Concerning one who possesses charity.**

Another, walking in the broad way of charity, loves not only friends in God but even enemies for God’s sake. When he has received an insult, he not only forgives injury to one who asks pardon, but himself hastens to be reconciled.

These and such like are the paths of Jerusalem’s citizens [Col. 1219A] by which they hasten from exile to the eternal dwellings.

**Concerning the citizens of Babylon and the reprobate.**

Turn toward the citizens of Babylon and see what they are like, and by what streets they go.

**Concerning the lustful person.**

One begins from early life with sexual lust and continues in it insatiably into decrepit old age, never reflecting on what he has already done, but only on what he can still do.

**Concerning the glutton.**

Another subjects himself from childhood to gluttony and drunkenness and persists in these until the last stage of old age.

**Concerning the rapacious and cruel.**

One hastens with all effort to plunder; another is intent upon thefts; [Col. 1219B] another feeds upon cruelty; another is not satisfied by gain. This one wastes away with envy; that one is defiled by impurity. This one, exalted by pride, despises all; that one, full of hatred, assails all with lies and slanders. Such and such are the streets of the reprobate, by which they hasten irrevocably toward the depths of hell.

**Concerning the different manner in which Jerusalem’s citizens fight against Babylon’s citizens, and conversely.**

Now observe also the battle lines arrayed differently for combat.

The reprobate abominate the words and deeds of the righteous, detest their company, and reject all their counsel. They often cunningly entrap them; more often they deceitfully, or even violently, [Col. 1219C] seize their goods; most often they afflict them with beatings or even tortures, or kill them through mutilation of limbs or various punishments.

Conversely, the righteous bear the conduct of the reprobate as a heavy burden; they groan over their miserable manner of life; they avoid their contagion as far as they can; they desire to be freed as soon as possible from their companionship; they pray to God for their salvation; and they supply them, so far as they can, with necessities.

**Concerning the good concord of Jerusalem’s citizens and the evil concord of Babylon’s citizens.**

Consider something else still.

All the elect agree in good and love in others the good which they themselves are unable to accomplish.

[Col. 1219D] But the reprobate are all united in evil and always discordant in good. If perhaps a word of rebuke or admonition is offered to any one of them by one of the righteous, they all resist, they all object together. Even those who do not do the evil act are troubled because they hate in others the good which they do not wish to do themselves. Therefore they all call him worthy of hatred, even one whom they do not know; they slander him with lies and provoke him with insults.

Contemplate carefully, and you will see throughout this entire conflict Cain always standing ready in battle against Abel; Ishmael armed against Isaac; Esau fighting Jacob; Saul resisting David; Judas attacking the Lord; and Simon Magus attacking Peter.

[Col. 1220A] See also in this contest how the reprobate often resolve to run alongside the elect, and sometimes run for a long time; then, wearied on the way, they fail and shamefully return like dogs to their vomit (Prov. 16:11; 2 Pet. 2:22).

**Concerning Babylon’s citizens in particular, and first those who are rulers and judges over others.**

Come here to the brow of the mountain, from which you may behold all the buildings of the condemned city.

Look at the rulers and judges. Behold, the beast’s seat has been placed in them. At all times they are intent upon evil, always insatiably occupied in enterprises of iniquity. They not only commit crimes but teach others to commit them; they sell sacred things, buy crimes, and labor with all their strength lest they alone come to Tartarus.

[Col. 1220B] **Concerning Babylon’s clerics and priests.**

Turn toward the clergy, and you will see the beast’s tent in them. They neglect God’s service; they devote themselves to earthly gains; they pollute the priesthood by uncleanness; they deceive the people by pretense; they deny God through evil works; they reject all Scriptures pertaining to salvation; in every way they offer themselves to the people as a snare and ruin, while, blind themselves, they lead the blind before them to destruction.

**Concerning Babylon’s monks.**

Contemplate also the assemblies of monks, and you will see the beast’s tabernacles in them.

By a feigned profession they mock God and provoke his wrath; in their conduct and life they trample his rule; by their habit they deceive the world. [Col. 1220C] Deceived themselves, they deceive many. They are entangled in secular affairs—that is, they are sluggish in God’s service. Very many of them are given to gluttony and sensual enticements; some rot in the filth of impurity.

**Concerning Babylon’s nuns.**

Look also upon the dwellings of nuns, and you will see the beast’s bedchamber prepared in them. From tender age these women learn unchastity; they gather very many accomplices to increase their damnation; they hasten to cover themselves with a veil so that they may more freely loosen the reins of lust with all fornicators; they are filled with the dung of impurity. They ensnare young men’s minds and rejoice if they deceive more people. And she [Col. 1220D] wishes to possess the palm of victory who is stronger than others in wickedness.

**Concerning the common people of the city of Babylon.**

Turn toward the remaining populace, and you will find the beast’s image.

They despise priests; they scorn to hear anything concerning God; they spend their whole lifetime in vanity and boasting, and are reprobate for every work. The unlearned crowd also possesses the beast’s idol. They do not know the true God; with their whole intention they serve the god of the belly; they are dissolved in various desires of the flesh and in every respect lead a beastly life.

**Concerning Babylon’s women.**

Come here to the slopes of this valley, and you will see [Col. 1221A] gatherings of the monstrous woman. In them the beast has placed all its pageantry and monstrosities, and has appointed these women to bear its weapons. You see how young men are ensnared through lust. One kills many by poison; another destroys a man’s life for gold; another kills her children; another provokes lawsuits; another incites wars. One alienates human minds by sorceries; another is satisfied by neither money nor lust; one deceives many by her appearance, another seduces most by weeping. These are the defenses of this city, and these are the beast’s missiles.

**DISCIPLE.** O God, how many monstrous things I behold!

**MASTER.** You have seen the walls of the city of Babylon; behold also its destruction. Now the Babylonian citizens, though greater in number, always wage war against the citizens of Jerusalem [Col. 1221B] who live among them in exile. But afterward God, the heavenly king of Jerusalem, coming with the army of angels, will utterly overthrow this ruined city and, freeing his elect from it, will bring them with him into the heavenly palace, to whom he now provides such a spectacle. This Babylon that you see—that is, the glory of this world—he will suddenly plunge into the lake of fire and sulfur with its prince the devil and all the citizens of this city, namely, the lovers of this world; and then he will change all things into a better state.

**DISCIPLE.** You have offered a great spectacle to all who read these things; may God grant you a place in that spectacle. And for what reason will the righteous be in glory?

[Col. 1221C] **MASTER.** Because, if they lived without end, they would wish always to be righteous. Justice therefore requires that those who have always embraced righteousness should always be blessed.

**DISCIPLE.** But what is the reason that the unrighteous will always be in punishment?

**MASTER.** Because they would wish to live without end in order that they might be able to do evil without end. Justice therefore demands that those who never wished for righteousness should never be without punishment.

**DISCIPLE.** Why can the righteous not sin after the resurrection?

**MASTER.** Because their free choice has been so confirmed that they wish no evil; since they will be equal to the angels, they will therefore be blessed forever.

[Col. 1221D] **DISCIPLE.** Why will the unrighteous not be able to turn toward good?

**MASTER.** Because they always hate the good, and therefore they will be miserable forever.

[Col. 1222A] **Conclusion, or recapitulation, of this book.**

Therefore, that I may conclude the doctrine of our disputation in a brief epilogue:

**God’s purpose:** to complete the number of the elect from angels and human beings.

**Predestination:** that the righteous should always glory in blessedness, and the unrighteous should always be tormented in misery.

**Foreknowledge or providence:** God’s ever-present beholding of future things.

**Necessity:** that a human being should die after sins.

**Justice:** willing what is right.

**Choice:** the judgment of willing upright justice.

**Freedom:** the power to preserve justice, or the judgment of choosing either not to will or to will.

**Grace:** the inspiration of good or deliverance from evil.

[Col. 1222B] **Merit:** perseverance in justice.

**The highest reward:** blessedness.

**Punishment:** eternal misery.

And because it is inevitable that certain infants, being baptized, are not condemned solely by their own justice; and that certain persons of mature age, who despise God’s justice through free choice, do not escape their deserved punishment—as justice itself decrees—the name is given to this little book on that account:

**The Inevitable.**

I offer these things concerning predestination, foreknowledge, and free choice to the children of the Church, because the children of Babylon will despise them. But whoever despises or [Col. 1222C] attacks this will show that he is not of the number of the predestined. Whoever thereafter raises a question about free choice stumbles, blind in broad daylight, into death.

**DISCIPLE.** Blessed be God, who inspired the brothers to wish to direct me to you, so that I might deserve to receive these marvels from your honey-flowing mouth. And indeed, know that the flocks of the reprobate will abominate you with great hatred for this venerable work, and will detest you especially because you have proved that they, who are children of vices—indeed, of demons—are such through free choice. But the glorious assembly predestined for life will render you great thanks because you have brought forth so marvelous a work in their praise. And, as I heard you say, because it is predestined by God that whatever the elect justly ask shall be granted them, they beseech God’s mercy with great prayers that your last day may find you in their fellowship. Amen.

**APPROVAL.**

[Col. 1221]

This Dialogue on predestination and free choice, formerly written by the Reverend Lord Honorius of Autun, and now brought forth to confound George Cassander by the Reverend Father, prior of the monastery of St. Mary of Tongerlo, Licentiate in Sacred Theology, has been read by many and found sound and free from every error. Thus the devout reader may safely read it, disregarding and consigning to Vulcan the work which George Cassander impiously procured to be printed under the name of this Honorius of Autun. This is my judgment.

December 1620.

Egbert Spitholdius, Licentiate in Sacred Theology, canon and parish priest of Antwerp, censor of books.

[Col. 1223]

# LITTLE BOOK ON FREE CHOICE

(Transcribed from a manuscript codex of the illustrious Carthusian house of Gaming in Austria by the venerable Father Leopold Wydemann, librarian of that Carthusian house; published by the Reverend Father Bernhard Pez in *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part I, col. 235.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1223A]

To Godescalc, who labours in faith and works within a holy purpose, and who has been set over Christ’s flock by word and example: Honorius wishes that, when the Prince of shepherds appears, he may see the God of gods in Zion. I have judged it best to unravel, in the service of an unlearned style, the question concerning free choice which lately arose between us. Believing that it would not be unwelcome to the brethren, I have sent it for examination by your judgment.

## Chapter I. The occasion of this little work was the ancient error of those who asserted that everything happens to a human being by a certain necessity.

Anyone who labours to solve a question must first recognize the root from which it arises, so that he may more easily disentangle what is involved, as it were, among the branches of a leafy tree. The root of this question, then, is the following error. There were once certain empty-talking people, ignorant of all truth, who, attributing their evils to the author of all goodness while excusing themselves, said that whatever happened in the world, or whatever anyone did, could not happen otherwise, because it had been so ordained by God. In this they plainly imitated Adam, who, rebuked by God for eating what had been forbidden, turned his fault back upon God, saying: “The woman whom you gave me gave to me, and I ate” (Gen. III). It was as though he said: “It was not I who sinned, but you, who gave me this companion, at whose prompting I could not avoid what was forbidden.”

Some deceived persons strengthened this error still further by writings, introducing constellations and asserting that everything is subject to immutable fate and unavoidable necessity: that those born under a good star must necessarily become good. For example, if someone were born under the star of Mars, he would become a murderer; if under the star of Venus, an adulterer; and if under the star of Jupiter, he would necessarily become gentle and good. Thus, ascribing all their deeds to fate and all human merits to necessity, they blasphemed God the Creator.

## Chapter II. The reported error is refuted, and it is proved that a rational creature naturally possesses free choice.

As this error spread its branches everywhere throughout the human race, certain men of keen intelligence, called philosophers because of their love of wisdom, investigated the natures of things more carefully and discovered that, under this error, prayers were offered in vain; that no place was left for justice in judges; that rewards for good deeds were taken away from the righteous; and that punishments for evil deeds were unjustly inflicted upon the unrighteous. Indeed, it would be the height of injustice for the righteous to be rewarded and the unrighteous punished, if they acted through necessity, fate dictating what they could in no way avoid. Likewise, everyone would pray in vain, if, because fate stood in the way, one hoped to obtain nothing by praying.

Considering this, the philosophers proved by strong arguments that a rational creature naturally has free choice: that is, the judgment of the mind in willing and not willing. For an *arbiter* is called a judge, and from this *arbitrium* means judgment, when someone judges in the mind what ought to be done or avoided. And this choice is free, that is, neither necessary nor compelled, because each person does what he wills, not forced by a star or by fate, but by his own free will. Once this is accepted, the ravings of astrologers are rendered void and the writings of philosophers stand firm: namely, that God is appeased by prayers, rewards are justly given to the good, and punishments are justly imposed on the wicked.

## Chapter III. An explanation of wherein freedom of choice consists.

Moreover, ecclesiastical men, enlightened by the Spirit, recognizing that freedom and power of choice are genera and dividing them into various species, found one power of walking or standing, another of eating or drinking, and so forth—none of which concerns the salvation of the soul. They understood that freedom of choice consists solely in the salvation of the soul, and they defined it thus: “Freedom of choice is the power of preserving justice for the sake of justice itself.”

For, according to Augustine’s definition, a person is not free who either avoids evil from fear of punishment or does good in hope of reward. Such a person serves, compelled by fear or enticed by hope; and since fear and hope rule him, he is rightly shown not to be free. Only the one who performs good solely from delight in justice is judged free. Thus free choice is shown to have been given only for preserving justice. Therefore the righteous alone are free; they are called sons, and to them the inheritance of the Lord is promised. But the unrighteous are called slaves, because “everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII); and these are children of wrath and perdition. They too have free choice, but misuse freedom unto slavery, as someone misuses for his own destruction a sword with which he ought to defend himself.

## Chapter IV. What freedom of choice belongs to God, angels, righteous human beings, the impious, and demons.

Because God and the angels cannot commit sin, some think that they do not have free choice. But if they do not have it, they are not free; and if they are not free, they are like beasts—which is most absurd to say of God or angels.

God alone, of himself, is supremely free, possessing in himself the freest power of choice to do whatever he wills. For “he did all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. CXIII), and what he did not will, he did not do. He himself is supreme freedom, to whom belongs the power to do everything that he wills. From him everything that flourishes in reason and understanding receives freedom.

The angels likewise have the freest choice, by which they refuse evil and will justice alone—the very justice for whose preservation alone they received free choice. Righteous human beings also possess free choice, but one weak without grace: just as a strong man who has been long ill may indeed be said to possess strength, but very feeble strength, because he cannot use it unless supported by a staff. For after the transgression of the first human being, free choice in humanity was so weakened by the frailty of the human condition that without assisting grace it is ineffectual for every good thing. Grace precedes it, so that it may will good; grace follows it, so that it may be able to do good. The person himself, through free choice, receives the offered grace by willing it; and, supporting himself upon it as upon a staff, performs good. His merit, therefore, is to receive the staff of grace and not reject it once received.

Evil human beings and demons likewise have free choice, which they either refuse when it is offered or reject when it has been received. Therefore they are like a sick person without his staff, or like one possessed of sight but placed without light in a dark house.

## Chapter V. How free choice falls away from good to evil, and how freedom becomes slavery.

It must briefly be said how free choice falls away from good to evil, and how freedom becomes slavery. God created the human being for blessedness and gave him a will by which he might will to be blessed. He also gave him justice, by preserving which he would always be blessed; and he gave him the will to be just, so that by this merit he might always be blessed. To preserve the will of justice, he gave him free choice, so that he might preserve it not under compulsion but freely, and in reward might never lose blessedness.

Justice is the highest good: that is, to love God and cleave to him in obedience. Injustice is the lowest good: that is, to love this world and to cleave to transitory things through desire. This is to sin; this is to fall away from freedom.

## Chapter VI. What is the will of blessedness, and what the will of justice—the latter of which humanity lost by sinning, while retaining the former.

Human beings therefore have two wills: one of blessedness, the other of justice. The will of blessedness is called nature, and the will of justice is called grace. The former is called a thing given; the latter, a gift. For existence is given to a human being, but well-being is bestowed. From these two wills proceed all human merits. Through the will of nature we follow the lusts and desires of the flesh; through the will of grace we carry out vigils, fasts, and other works of justice.

But by freedom of choice humanity abandoned the will of justice, and immediately lost blessedness, while retaining the will of blessedness. For every human being naturally wills to be blessed, just as each naturally wills to live. Yet no one wills to be righteous unless first moved by God’s grace, nor can anyone be righteous unless aided by God’s grace. Because a person wills to be blessed without justice, and because no one can attain true blessedness except through justice, he anxiously seeks false blessedness in frail and transient things; and, finding it nowhere, never rests.

But those who, through gratuitous grace, preserve by free will until the end the justice they had lost and that has been restored to them, rest without end in true blessedness.

Honorius published another little work on free choice, distinct from this one, which he entitled *The Inevitable*. Since it is found printed in the fifteenth volume of the Cologne edition of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, I refrain here from transcribing it. Honorius himself seems to have collected, for elucidation of his little work, the sayings of the Fathers concerning free choice and grace, which I append word for word among Honorius’s minor works.

Leopold Wydemann

**ISIDORE.**—Choice is the will of free power, which can of itself and spontaneously desire either good or evil. Grace, however, is the gratuitous gift of divine mercy, through which we merit both the beginning of a good will and the effective accomplishment of a work. For divine grace precedes a human being so that he may become good. Nor does human choice precede God’s grace; rather, the very grace of God precedes the unwilling person so that he may even will well.

For the human being is so carried by his own weight that he is quick to sin and slow to repent. From himself he has the means of falling, but he does not possess the means of rising, unless the grace of the Creator extends a hand to raise the fallen one. Finally, by God’s grace free choice is restored to humanity, which the first human being had lost. For he had free choice for beginning good, though it was to be completed with God’s help. We, however, receive from God’s grace both the beginning of free choice and its completion, because we have from him both the beginning and completion of good—from him through whom the gift of grace was given and free choice restored in us.

Therefore the good that we do belongs to God, because of grace preceding and following us; but it belongs to us because of the complying will of free choice. For if it is not God’s, why do we give thanks to him? And if it is not ours, why do we expect the recompense of good works? Thus, in that we are preceded by grace, it belongs to God; but in that we follow the preceding grace in working well, it belongs to us.

No one precedes the grace of the Lord by merits so as to be able to hold him, as it were, as a debtor. But in a marvellous manner the Creator, just toward all, has chosen some by predestining them, while by a just judgment he leaves others in their perverse habits. Hence it is most true that the gift of grace is attained not by human capacity or by the merit of choice, but is bestowed by the goodness of divine mercy alone. Some are saved through the preceding gift of his gratuitous mercy, having become vessels of mercy; others, however, rejected and predestined to punishment, are damned, having become vessels of wrath.

This is understood from the example of Esau and Jacob, not yet born. Though they had been begotten in one conception or birth and were equally bound by the tie of original sin, nevertheless the divine goodness, preceding one of them through gratuitous grace, drew him to itself in mercy; but the other, held in hatred by a certain severity of justice, was left and condemned in the mass of perdition. Thus the same Lord speaks through the prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I).

It follows that grace is bestowed with no preceding merits, but by divine calling alone; and that no one is saved or damned, chosen or rejected, except according to the purpose of the predestining God, who is just in those rejected and merciful in those chosen, as is said through the Psalmist: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV).

But every gift of grace is not given in its fullness to everyone; rather, distinct gifts are distributed to individuals, so that, like members of a body, each may have its own offices and one may need another—not that one person should possess what another has, or that all things should therefore become common to everyone, but because the members are necessary to one another.

**THE SAME [ISIDORE].**—Let defenders of free choice know that it can accomplish nothing good by its own strength unless it is sustained by the help of divine grace. Therefore the Lord says through the prophet: “Your destruction is from yourself, Israel; your help is only in me” (Hos. XIII). It is as though he said: “That you perish is by your own merit; that you are saved is by my help.” For what did that thief deserve from himself, who ascended from the jaws of hell to the cross and went from the cross to paradise? He came indeed stained with the blood of his brother, a criminal; but he was changed by divine grace.

Free choice is the will of the rational soul, moved without anyone’s prohibition toward whatever it wills, whether to good or to evil, and thus granted by the Creator. Again: free choice is the self-governing movement of the intellectual soul; while preference is the deliberate desire for things that lie within us, or desirable counsel. For what has been judged beforehand, we hold by choosing through counsel. Counsel, however, is an intention that carefully investigates what we must do.

**ISIDORE.**—Predestination is twofold: that of the elect unto rest, and that of the reprobate unto death. Both are carried out by divine judgment, so that it makes the elect always follow things above and inward, while it permits the reprobate, by abandonment, always to pursue things lowest and outward.

Although the conduct of the righteous in this life may be commendable, it is nevertheless uncertain to human beings toward what end they are predestined; all is reserved for the future judgment. It is a marvellous ordering of the heavenly dispensation by which here one righteous person is made more righteous and one impious person more defiled; at times an evil person is converted to good, and at times a good person is turned away from it. One wishes to be good and cannot; another wishes to be evil and is not permitted to perish. To one who wishes to be good, it is granted; another neither wills it nor is it granted to him that he should be good. One is born in error and dies in it; another perseveres to the end in the good in which he began. One stands only until he falls; another, having long lived wickedly, is saved at the end and is converted after having been despised. A righteous person wishes to benefit others in good and cannot prevail; an evil person wishes to harm and cannot. One wishes to devote himself to God and is hindered by the world; another desires to become entangled in business but makes no progress. An evil person rules; a good person is condemned in place of an impious one; an impious person is honoured in place of a righteous one. And amid such great obscurity, a human being cannot investigate God’s dispensation or comprehend the hidden order of predestination.

**PETER.**—The power of free choice is a faculty of the soul possessing the capacity by which it can incline itself toward whatever actions it wills.

**FULGENTIUS.**—God’s predestination is nothing other than the eternal preparation of his future works. For just as foreknowledge compels no one to sin—although God has surely foreknown before eternal ages the sins of each person—so likewise his predestination compels no one to punishment, although, before anyone is born, he may be predestined either to remain in justice for a crown or in iniquity for punishment.

**AMBROSE.**—No one goes to punishment because this had previously been in God’s predestination. Rather, because he was foreknown to persist in sins, he was also on that account assigned to punishment.

**ISIDORE.**—God predestined some to glory and some to punishment; but those whom he predestined to glory, he predestined to justice, whereas those whom he predestined to punishment, he did not predestine to fault. Thus in the saints God crowns the justice which he himself freely bestowed upon them, freely preserved, and freely brought to completion. But he will condemn the wicked for the iniquity or injustice which he himself did not make. In the former he glorifies his own works; in the latter he condemns their works.

**AUGUSTINE.**—By the name of predestination no coercive necessity of the human will is expressed; rather, the merciful and just everlasting disposition of the divine work is proclaimed. For by God’s predestination either the merciful remission of sins has been prepared, or the just punishment of sins. God predestined the good to the kingdom, but the wicked to eternal fire. For he will say to the good: “Come, blessed ones” (Matt. XXV), etc., etc.; but to the wicked he will say: “Go, cursed ones” (ibid.), etc., etc. The Lord predestined the iniquitous and impious to just punishment, not to any unjust deed; to penalty, not to fault.

**The same [Augustine].**—Free choice is to choose or abandon by free decision the paths of God’s commandments; once we have undertaken them, upheld by help, we follow them in continual devotion, and at the end he will crown the obedience made subject within us. But the free choice which we have from him flows into wickedness through a headlong fall; and, since it can do nothing toward the character of virtue when God’s help abandons it, it fails into every kind of sin and cannot stand unless supported by strength.

**The same [Augustine].**—The first human being had free choice and could by nature love virtues and avoid vices, for he had no warfare of vices within himself. But after he sinned willingly, he lost free choice in relation to good, so that he can now neither will, much less do, anything good by himself without God’s grace; and so that he sins not only willingly but even unwillingly. Thus evil indeed comes from ourselves, but good from God alone.

**JEROME.**—Through God’s grace, a human being has free choice to do whatever he wills. For if anyone did good unwillingly, he could gain no reward from it; and if anyone did evil compelled by God, he would suffer no punishment for it. Yet God sometimes mercifully compels an unwilling person to act well, provided nevertheless that afterward the person’s good will follows.

**AUGUSTINE.**—A person is not free who avoids evil from fear of punishment and does good in hope of reward; for he serves, compelled by fear and enticed by hope of reward, while fear and hope rule him. That person is free who is righteous neither through fear of punishment nor hope of reward, but solely through delight in justice. For this purpose he possesses free choice.

**GREGORY.**—Evil deeds alone are done by free choice. For after the first human being sinned voluntarily, he lost free choice with respect to good, but retained it with respect to evil. Therefore, unless divine inspiration comes first, no one can do anything good.

**JOHN CHRYSOSTOM.**—God granted free choice to rational nature; indeed, he made it such as to possess free choice. Therefore he does not take from nature what he gave it, and he himself is altogether incapable of error. Rational nature, then, has free choice from the beginning of its creation; but because of itself it voluntarily abandoned good, it no longer possesses that choice in relation to good, though it still possesses it in relation to evil. It is no longer sufficient, but wholly deficient, unless God’s grace precedes, assists, and follows it.

**ANSELM.**—Freedom of choice is the power of preserving rectitude of will for the sake of that rectitude itself.

[Col. 1229]

# The Greater Ladder of Heaven, or Dialogue on the Order of Knowing God in Created Things

Drawn from a manuscript codex of the distinguished Gemnic Carthusian monastery in Austria by the venerable Dom Leopold Wydemann, librarian there; edited by the Reverend Father Pezius, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part I, col. 155.

## Prologue

[Col. 1229C]

I often turn over in my mind, in frequent meditations, how very many strive with the utmost effort toward difficult heights, but, as though by some rebuff, fall away from the course they have undertaken. Searching more carefully for the hidden cause, I could discover nothing but ignorance, darkening their minds with its mist. Seeking out the hiding places of this deadly shame, I pressed it more vigorously into the light and, piercing it with the darts of arguments, reduced it to nothing.

For many strive to climb to spiritual things; but, ignorant of the order of the steps, they cast themselves down over precipices. Since they do not climb gradually but rush headlong and rashly downward, they find neither this nor that support of rectitude by which to steady their step; hanging by their weight and oppressed in their sight, they abandon the useless path and wander back into the opinions of profound falsehood and the darkness of ignorance.

Moved with pious compassion by the poverty of their minds, I have furnished for them a ship abundantly supplied for the journey from exile to their homeland, and have raised a ladder, arranged in suitable ordered steps, from the mud to heaven. If they strive to climb it rightly, they will see the King of glory in his beauty. Therefore, if it seems fitting, let this little book be called *The Ladder of Heaven*.

## Chapter I

**DISCIPLE.** In the instructions of your diligent disputation I frequently hear you introduce either a ship of life or the Ladder of Heaven. Tell me what those terms mean.

**MASTER.** We are separated from the homeland of paradise as though by the boundary of a certain sea, and we live as strangers in this world as though upon an island. This age is the sea, troubled by many bitter things; the ship is the Christian religion; the sail is faith; the mast is the cross; the ropes are works; the rudder is discernment; the wind is the Holy Spirit; and the harbour is eternal rest. By such a ship one crosses the ocean of this present age and returns to the homeland of eternal life.

## Chapter II

[Col. 1230D]

**DISCIPLE.** And what is the Ladder of Heaven?

**MASTER.** We are placed in the valley of tears—indeed, in the pit of misery—from which we are to ascend to the high mountain of the heavenly homeland by a certain ladder. This ladder is charity, joined together by the authority of the holy Scriptures. Its steps are knowledge and wisdom: knowledge, which instructs us in the active life of the present; wisdom, which teaches contemplation of eternal life. Knowledge instructs us from the Scriptures in the mystery of Christ’s humanity; wisdom teaches the majesty of his divinity.

This ladder is raised on either side by the twofold love of God and neighbour, to which the whole sequence of Scripture, Old and New Testament, is referred. Scripture is written through wisdom and expounded through knowledge. Since this ladder reaches to the third heaven, to which it will lead those who climb rightly, it rises joined together by three orders of steps: bodily, spiritual, and intellectual.

## Chapter III

**DISCIPLE.** I do not know what you mean by the third heaven.

**MASTER.** There are three visions: bodily, spiritual, and intellectual. Bodily vision is that by which this heaven and earth and all bodily things are seen through the body; it is called the first heaven. Spiritual vision is that by which the likeness of bodily things is formed in our spirit; it is called the second heaven. Intellectual vision is that by which neither bodily things nor likenesses of bodily things, but the very essence of divine truth, or the nature of angels or souls as it is, is contemplated; and this is called the third heaven.

## Chapter IV

**DISCIPLE.** I greatly desire to learn the order of the steps. What is the order of bodily vision?

**MASTER.** First we behold, to the praise of God, the elements—earth, water, air, and fire—from which all things consist. To these we add an equal number, when we view for the praise of the Creator: things which merely exist, such as stones; things which in some fashion live, such as plants and trees; things which live and sense, such as animals; and things which live, sense, and understand, such as human beings.

To these we attach another equal number, when we behold for the praise of God the four kinds of living creatures in the world: those that walk, crawl, creep, fly, and swim. To these we add as many more, when by sight we distinguish all beautiful things from ugly ones; by hearing, all sounding things from discordant ones; by smell, all fragrant things from fetid ones; by taste, all sweet things from bitter ones; and by touch, all smooth things from rough ones.

Then we interweave manifold steps, when upon the earth we distinguish in wonder: diverse kinds of stones, marbles, and gems; diverse kinds of trees, leaves, and fruits; diverse kinds of herbs, leaves, and vegetables; diverse kinds of roots, fruits, and seeds; diverse kinds of beasts, creeping things, and serpents; the many kinds of human faces and customs; the many colours and fashions of clothing; the lofty walls of cities, buildings of houses, paintings, sculptures, and various weavings; diverse crafts, exercises in games or arts; the ranks of those who serve, and the dignities of those who rule.

Next we arrange steps from water, when, praising God, we consider various kinds of birds, various kinds of fish, ice and different storms, and some waters sweet and others bitter. After this, climbing through the air, we set down steps in astonishment when we behold clouds, winds, lightning, thunder, rain, snow, hail, frost, and dew. From there we strive through steps of ethereal fire, when we gaze for the Creator’s praise upon the globe of the moon, now waxing and now waning; the tresses of the morning star; the flames of the sun; and the radiance of the other wandering stars. Finally, we are lifted through steps of this bodily heaven when, venerating God, we contemplate the firmament set in the midst of the waters and the stars shining brightly within it.

These are the steps of a beautiful ascent arranged according to the order of bodily vision. Nearly all animals share this vision with us, and some, such as ibexes and eagles, possess it more fully than we do.

## Chapter V

**DISCIPLE.** What is the order of spiritual vision?

**MASTER.** You know that the soul has several powers. That power which gives life to the body and senses bodily things through the body is properly called *anima*, “soul”; that in which images of bodily things are formed is called *spiritus*, “spirit”; and that which understands things inward and outward is called *mens*, “mind.” Spiritual vision, then, occurs when things not bodily but like bodily things are seen in the spirit. Twelve steps are attached to this ladder.

The first step occurs when the likeness of some body, perceived through the senses of the body, is formed in our spirit and laid up in memory—for example, the likeness of girls. The second occurs when we think of known bodies that are absent and form their images in our spirit—for example, cities. The third occurs when we behold in the spirit the likenesses, not as they are, of bodies which we do not know but do not doubt exist—for example, unicorns or griffins. The fourth occurs when we imagine at will things that do not exist, or whose existence is not known—for example, the chimera, a beast.

The fifth occurs when, without our willing it, diverse forms of things move about in the mind, as images of people fighting or building during prayer. The sixth occurs when, in planning something we are to do, we first form all things in the spirit by thought—for example, the construction of a house. The seventh occurs when, while speaking or doing something, we inwardly anticipate it in the spirit by similar movements. The eighth occurs when dreams are formed in the spirit of sleepers, though they signify either nothing or something—for example, Pharaoh’s seven ears of grain, foreshadowing seven years.

The ninth occurs when, with the senses disturbed through bodily illness, various phantasms are imagined, as commonly happens to persons with frenzy. The tenth occurs when, as bodily pain grows severe, the spirit is absent and marvels at images of bodily things presenting joys or punishments, as often happens to those not wholly dead. The eleventh occurs when the spirit of someone is taken from a sound body by some spirit to see likenesses of bodily things, as happens to persons placed in ecstasy. The twelfth occurs when the spirit is wholly turned away from bodily senses and enjoys, in spiritual vision, only likenesses of bodily things, as happened formerly in the prophets.

This spiritual vision is common to the good and the reprobate and is called the second heaven. It is opened to the learned through discernment and shut fast to the unlearned through presumption. In this heaven Moses saw the likeness of the tabernacle which he made in the wilderness. In this heaven Isaiah beheld the Lord upon a high throne, and seraphim with six wings crying, “Holy, holy, holy.” This heaven was opened to Ezekiel when he saw a wheel within a wheel and four living creatures full of eyes. From this heaven Peter saw a vessel full of animals let down and taken back again into it. John saw this heaven opened, and in it he beheld everything that he wrote in the Apocalypse.

## Chapter VI

**DISCIPLE.** Is there anything among existing things such as John or the other prophets saw, or such as certain persons, taken away from their bodies and restored again to life, reported that they saw?

**MASTER.** Everything that subsists in a form exists in this world. But nowhere does one read that in any land a beast with ten horns is found, such as is read of in the Apocalypse and Daniel; nor anywhere a stone with seven eyes, as is read in Zechariah; nor among any peoples a woman clothed with the sun or a dragon with seven heads. If such things had then existed substantially, they would likewise exist now. But since such things exist nowhere, neither in heaven nor on earth, it is clear that they did not exist then either.

Therefore they are not drawn from existing things. Rather, such things are formed in the human spirit by angels, through which certain future things are prefigured. Hence they are expounded by the learned, by whom they are also understood.

## Chapter VII

**DISCIPLE.** When someone sees such things, does he behold them through bodily eyes, or in the spirit alone?

**MASTER.** Bodily things cannot be seen except through the body, and spiritual things cannot be seen outside the body. Nor can spirit without a body travel to bodily places, nor can a body be taken up to spiritual things. Everything which is not a body and yet is something is spirit. Therefore such things are seen not through the body but in the spirit. For an incorporeal nature cannot be seen through the body; and if bodily things can be seen without the body, then they are seen in a far different and wonderful manner than they are now.

## Chapter VIII

**DISCIPLE.** Does the soul see these things within itself or outside itself?

**MASTER.** Just as all bodily things are seen within the body, so all spiritual things are seen within the spirit. And just as this bodily world contains within itself heaven, earth, and all bodily things, so the soul contains within itself a certain vast world, a spiritual heaven and earth, in which it sees all spiritual things resembling bodies. Therefore, when it contemplates the sun, moon, stars of heaven, cities, regions, islands of the sea, and other similar things, it wanders by imagination not outside itself but within itself.

Thus John and the other prophets saw not outside themselves but all things formed in their spirit by angels and signifying future events. Hence they were called “Seers.” Thus John says: “Immediately I was in the Spirit” (Apoc. I); and another prophet: “I saw in the spirit” (Dan. VIII). Likewise, those who were removed from the body and restored again to the living, and who saw or heard joys and punishments, bright light and dreadful darkness, or any other things, beheld them within themselves as though in a certain region.

## Chapter IX

**DISCIPLE.** Are punishments seen in the spirit true punishments or false ones? Likewise, are joys seen in the spirit true joys or false ones?

**MASTER.** Whatever it is by which the soul is afflicted with grief is a true punishment. Again, whatever it is by which the spirit rejoices is true joy.

There are certain degrees of the soul’s punishments. The first is when the soul is saddened because it is separated from familiar places, bodies, parents, or known people. The second is when it is troubled over the loss of outward possessions or friends. The third is when it is tortured by bodily pain. The fourth is when it is violently driven from the body. The fifth is when, as though in dreams, it is afflicted by dreadful visions. The sixth is when, taken into ecstasy, it is tormented by troublesome forms. The seventh is when, removed from the body, it is tortured by foul spirits in places of punishment. The eighth is when, the body being wholly dead, it is confined not by a bodily but by a spiritual and punitive substance. The ninth is when, after receiving the body again, it is handed over to eternal fire and joined to demons. The higher each degree is than another in order, the more terrible it is in torment.

Likewise, certain degrees of the soul’s joys are recognized. The first is when the soul rejoices in the company of people it loves. The second is when it delights in attaining desired things. The third is when it rejoices at escape from the loss of some thing or from bodily pain. The fourth is when it exults after overcoming adversaries. The fifth is when it rejoices at escaping the danger of death. The sixth is when joyful visions in dreams cheer it. The seventh is when it exults, taken into ecstasy. The eighth is when, removed from the body, it delights in marvellous light in spiritual places. The ninth is when, the body being wholly dead, it rejoices not in bodily but in spiritual delight, the very joy of truth. The tenth is when, having received the body again and been made equal to angels, it glories ineffably in the vision of God. The higher each degree is than another in order, the more eminent it is also in rank.

## Chapter X

**DISCIPLE.** From what are spiritual visions formed?

**MASTER.** From souls, demons, and angels. They are formed from souls when someone in darkness, while awake, imagines things which he saw or could have seen through the body; or, while asleep, contemplates things which happened or could have happened to the body. These are sometimes true and sometimes false.

They are formed from demons when an evil spirit transforms itself into various shapes and presents itself to the soul of one asleep or awake. These are called phantasms or illusions. Sometimes, besieging a body and mingling itself with the soul, it predicts certain true things and makes some persons possessed, others false prophets.

But those taken up in ecstasy or estranged from the senses of the body behold through angels certain marvellous things that signify something. At times the angels themselves explain these to them, as Gabriel did to Daniel and the angel to John; and these are called manifestations or revelations.

## Chapter XI
DISCIPLE. Is it a sin to imagine shameful things when someone is defiled by a nocturnal illusion? MASTER. When someone, while awake, takes pleasure in imagining shameful things and, while asleep, is defiled through the same images, this is imputed to him as sin. But if, against his will, he is mocked and defiled by demons, he is not judged guilty in this respect. If, however, he is defiled without consenting delight, he is thus free from sin; just as, while awake, when speaking of intercourse, we think of the same things.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 1235B]

DISCIPLE. Do demons see the imaginings in souls? MASTER. They do indeed see evil ones; they do not see good ones. For it is entirely certain that they know evil thoughts when these are reported by them; but if they knew good thoughts, they would not tempt the saints, by whom they would not wish to be overcome.

## CHAPTER XIII

DISCIPLE. How is it that they announce things done far away? MASTER. Because they possess a sharpness for perceiving bodily things: for their incorporeal nature is superior to ours and far subtler than ours.

## CHAPTER XIV

DISCIPLE. How is it that, sometimes, madmen foretell the future, or even some who are healthy, such as Caiaphas, who prophesied? MASTER. Some spirit mingles itself with their spirit and foretells the future. In such matters the soul ascends degrees in spiritual things; but it is sometimes deceived, when it takes one thing for another, and supposes that what is spiritual is bodily, or what is bodily is spiritual. Thus Peter supposed that the sheet let down from the spiritual heaven was a bodily thing. But this error of false opinion does not bind the soul with sins.

## CHAPTER XV

DISCIPLE. What is the order of the degrees of intellectual vision? MASTER. In these words, “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. XIX), three things are broadly [or: on the side, *latere*] considered: things that are seen bodily; the neighbour, who, when absent, is perceived in spirit; and love, which is understood by the mind. Intellectual vision, therefore, exists when neither bodily things nor things resembling bodily things are perceived, but when the true substances themselves of souls or angels, or virtues, or the supreme Truth itself, are understood by the mind as they are.

And this is called the third heaven, to which we ascend by three degrees. First, when we consider virtues in the soul; second, when we distinguish the orders of angels; third, when we understand all things in God. Moreover, the faithful soul disposes manifold ascents in its heart when it goes from virtue to virtue; and thus it enters the place of the wonderful tabernacle, as though a most spacious region of intellectual realities, when it contemplates what the mind itself, or every good affection of the soul—whose opposites are vices—may be: namely chastity, self-restraint, gentleness, faith, goodness, kindness, long-suffering, peace, joy, and charity.

[Col. 1236A] Having passed beyond these and such things, and having been joined to the holy spirits, it ascends through angelic ministries by nine degrees, contemplating in eternal glory angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. Thus ascending rightly, it comes to the house of God and the throne of majesty, where it shall see the King of glory in his beauty. There is secure rest and the ineffable vision of truth. There the one whole virtue is to love what one sees, and the highest happiness is to possess what one loves. There blessed life is drunk from its source; there, in the true light, the brightness of God will be seen—not by bodily vision, as it was seen on Mount Sinai; nor by spiritual vision, as Isaiah or John saw it in the Apocalypse; nor through enigmas, as the saints saw it in this life; but directly, as it is, face to face.

To attain this, we now undergo labours, assist the needy, refrain from pleasures, and endure adversities. To see this, we cleanse our hearts, because “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” In this third heaven is the paradise of paradises; in it is the rest of the saints; in it the glory of the blessed. But although spirit is superior to body, the spiritual heaven is superior to this bodily heaven neither by position in place nor by dignity; the intellectual heaven, however, is higher than the spiritual heaven.

## CHAPTER XVI

Bodily vision is divided into two kinds, lower and higher. The lower is when we behold the earth and [Col. 1236C] the things in it; the higher, when we observe heaven and the heavenly bodies, namely the sun, moon, and stars. Similarly, spiritual vision is divided into two kinds, lower and higher. The lower is like earth, when the mind imagines likenesses of things; the higher is like heaven, when images formed through angels are displayed. No less is intellectual vision divided into lower and higher kinds. The lower is like a kind of earth, while virtues are generated in the soul; the higher is like the highest heaven, when all things are understood in God.

## CHAPTER XVII

DISCIPLE. When the soul has departed from the body, is it borne to bodily places, or to incorporeal places resembling bodily ones, or to something else more excellent? MASTER. It is not borne to bodily places except with some body; nor can it be borne locally except bodily. But a soul stripped of its body has no body; therefore it is not borne to bodily places. It is, however, borne according to its merits to spiritual places resembling bodily ones, there to experience either joys or punishments. For just as, when it is withdrawn from the body, it is known to possess an image of its body, so after it has been stripped of the body it can possess a likeness of its body, in which it may either be affected by sorrow or enjoy gladness.

## CHAPTER XVIII

DISCIPLE. If the soul is not borne to places, it follows that hell is not bodily; and I am uncertain what ought to be thought in this matter. MASTER. If hell is a place of torments in which the soul is tortured either with the body or without it, then seven particular hells are found.

The first hell is the corruptible body, which weighs down the soul and tortures it with many pains. For in it the soul suffers hunger, thirst, toil, weariness, illnesses, pains, and various infirmities; because of its dwelling in it, it is afflicted by anger, envy, hatred, and sorrow, and harassed by avarice, carnal desire, and vainglory. In this hell the faithful soul groans that it is tortured, and asks to be delivered from it with tearful prayer, saying: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name, O Lord” (Ps. CXLI).

The second hell is this world, in which the soul is tortured together with the body as it laments its exile from the homeland of paradise. In it it suffers cold, heat, storms, pestilences, wars, plundering, fires, losses, and varied misfortunes. In its mind it is afflicted by the loss of children, parents, friends, or possessions; by insults, injuries, curses, and varied adversities. Delivered from this hell, the soul sings in thanksgiving: “He brought me out of the pit of misery and from the mire of dregs” (Ps. XXXIX).

The third hell is the cohabitation of those who hate one another. Thus either the righteous are tormented by dwelling with the wicked, as Lot was in Sodom, or the wicked are tormented by the conduct of the good when they are restrained from their ruinous habits. In this hell they suffer from one another beatings, chains, fasts, vigils, prisons, beasts, fires, and various sufferings. In their minds they are consumed by fear, grief, anxiety, faint-heartedness, distress, and sorrow. He grieves to be afflicted by the punishments of this hell who cries out in testimony: “The pains of hell surrounded me; the snares of death came before me” (Ps. XVII).

The fourth hell is a place situated in the middle of the earth, full of fire and sulphur. This, by customary usage, is called hell, or the lake of fire and sulphur. To it belong all burning places, whether in the earth or above the earth.

The fifth hell is when the soul, withdrawn from the body, is led to spiritual and punitive places resembling bodies, there to be tortured.

The sixth hell is when the body is wholly dead and the soul suffers not bodily things, but spiritual things resembling bodily things; and it is afflicted by pain, grief, and sorrow. Because this is lower and more depressed than the bodily realm, it is called the lower hell. Of it it is written: “You have delivered my soul from the lowest hell” (Ps. LXXXV).

The seventh hell is the eternal fire, into which the soul, having received its body again, is cast on the day of judgment to be tortured forever with the demons. Whether this hell will be in this world or outside the world is unknown.

## CHAPTER XIX

DISCIPLE. If hells are not bodily places, why are they said or believed to be beneath the earth? Or why are they called “lower regions” (*inferi*) if they are not beneath the earth? MASTER. Hells are said or believed to be beneath the earth because, fittingly, likenesses of those things are thus displayed in the spirit: just as dead flesh is buried beneath the earth, so a sinful soul released from flesh appears to be plunged beneath the earth into the lower regions. They are called *inferi*, moreover, because just as, among all bodily things that maintain the order of their weight, the heavier are lower, so among spiritual things the sadder are lower.

Hence some are so afflicted by sorrow that the frail body cannot contain it; consequently they take their life by hanging, by a fall, or by some violent means. After the soul is shaken free from the body, it is not thrust into some place, but plunged into an immeasurable abyss of sorrow and pain. For every place has length, breadth, and height; but since the soul lacks all these, it cannot be enclosed in any place.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 1238B]

DISCIPLE. Was not that rich man in a place of torments, and is it not written of him, “I am tormented in this flame”? MASTER. I think that rich man was in the sixth hell of which I spoke; but that the Lord spoke of the fourth—that is, of bodily punishment. Yet because they could not grasp what was truly the case, he recounted it to them as though it were a bodily torment. Nevertheless, how that flame of hell, that bosom of Abraham, that tongue of the rich man, that finger of the poor man, that thirst of torment, and that drop of refreshment are to be understood will perhaps scarcely be discovered by those who inquire gently, but never by those who investigate contentiously.

## CHAPTER XXI

DISCIPLE. By God’s illumination through you, I now see what should be thought about the lower regions; but I am wholly uncertain what should be believed about the kingdom of heaven. MASTER. The kingdom of heaven is not a bodily place but a spiritual one, resembling a bodily place, in which are peace, joy, and ineffable gladness amid every kind of glory; in which the substance of God—the Word also God, through whom all things were made—is seen as he is in the love of the Holy Spirit, and is possessed in blessed enjoyment without end.

This is the third heaven, in which paradise is and into which the Apostle was caught up. This is the heaven into which Christ was taken up. In this heaven are the hosts of angels and the souls of the blessed, distinguished not by local position but by the mercy of the disposer, according to their merits, in glory. Here are many dwellings in the one house of the Father, in which the righteous are arranged according to righteousness, in accordance with the merits of righteousness. Here is the expectation of our hope; here is the recompense of labour.

## CHAPTER XXII

DISCIPLE. And what need is there for bodies to be received again by souls to which that supreme blessedness itself can be granted without a body? MASTER. Souls possess a certain natural desire to govern the body; by that desire they are in some way delayed from proceeding with their whole intention toward that highest heaven so long as the body is absent, by whose governance that desire may be satisfied.
