Therefore it is necessary that they receive their own bodies, so that, now made equal to the angels by the special glory they have merited, they may rejoice forever in the vision of the highest heaven and in the freest contemplation of truth.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 1239A]

Then the three visions also will not be lacking. For through the body they will clearly see the new heaven, the new earth, and all things in them as new, when they shine like the sun. They will imagine the same things spiritually; [Col. 1240A] they will contemplate intellectual things in their integral nature and perfect blessedness, as they truly are. Therefore, whoever can ascend this ladder in due order through its degrees will rejoice that he has reached the third heaven into which the Apostle was caught up. Amen.

[Col. 1239]

# A SHORT WORK, “THE LESSER LADDER OF HEAVEN,” OR “ON THE DEGREES OF CHARITY”

(Brought to light from a manuscript codex of the illustrious Charterhouse of Gaming in Austria by the venerable Father Leopold Wydemann; edited by the Reverend Father Bernhard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part I, col. 171.)

## CHAPTER I. Charity is the ladder of heaven; its rungs are the various virtues.

[Col. 1239B]

Today a ladder is raised for us by which eternal glory may be reached, and by which the faithful attain the summit of heaven. For this ladder is charity, by which the humility of the Church tends toward the heights of heaven. The sides of this ladder are the commandments of the twofold love, namely of God and neighbour; but the rungs set between these sides are the various virtues by which the commandments of charity are fulfilled. Whoever ascends by them rightly will joyfully behold the face of the Lord, who is charity.

Fifteen rungs are woven together because heavenly things are sought through fifteen branches of charity. Thus, too, fifteen steps led up to the sanctuary in the Lord’s temple, because the one ascending this ladder is raised to the sanctuary of the heavenly [Col. 1239C] temple, namely Christ. Accordingly, fifteen degrees are first set forth, which are formed by these virtues through which the blessed ascend to the heavens. Fifteen, moreover, is three times five: through faith in the Holy Trinity we ought to fulfil works of charity by our five senses.

## CHAPTER II. The first three rungs of this ladder: patience, kindness, and piety.

The first rung of this ladder is patience, in which the eternal wisdom of God teaches souls to be possessed. We set our foot firmly upon this rung if we patiently endure injuries and insults for Christ’s love; for he endured reproaches, insults, scourges, and death itself for us, and grants the rewards of abiding glory to those who imitate him.

The second rung is kindness, through which the dignity of angelic fellowship is acquired. We place our foot upon this rung if, in return for evils, we repay not evil but good, and kindly bestow upon our neighbours necessary things according to our ability. For Christ also repaid good for evil to those who crucified him, namely eternal life through his passion; and he grants this likewise to his imitators.

The third rung is piety, through which the sweet fellowship of the citizens above is obtained. The pious mind, ascending this rung, is raised up, yet does not begrudge another’s happiness. “Through the devil’s envy death entered into the world; and those who are on his side imitate him,” etc.

## CHAPTER III. Other rungs: simplicity, humility, contempt of the world, and voluntary poverty.

The fourth rung is simplicity, through which one enters the abundance of heavenly joy. We place our foot upon this rung if we do not act wrongly, deceitfully, or perversely; if we withhold nothing from God’s service and perform good works not for popular favour, but solely for God’s sake.

The fifth rung is humility, through which angelic exaltation is attained. The ascending mind is made firm upon this rung if it is not puffed up by knowledge received, remembering that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.

The sixth rung is contempt of the world, through which the harmony of the heavenly kingdom is acquired. The soul exults gloriously upon it if it is not ambitious but courageously endures torments. For if it wishes to hear the Lord saying, “Friend, go up higher,” it does not refuse to undertake the Lord’s light burden, and benefits the brethren by word and example.

The seventh rung is voluntary poverty, through which freedom in glory and riches in the house of the Lord is received. He plants his footsteps upon this rung who seeks not only what is his own, but what is useful to all and pertains to the praise of Christ. Such a person ascends more joyfully, because “God has fed the poor in his sweetness.”

## CHAPTER IV. The higher rungs: peace, goodness, spiritual joy, and endurance.

The eighth rung is peace, which is the torch of eternal light. The mind is strengthened upon this rung if it is injured by no one either in word or deed; if the body is subjected to the soul in God’s service; and if the soul, in harmony with the spirit, continually serves the Lord God. Those placed upon this rung are called blessed, “for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. V).

The ninth rung is called goodness, through which one enters the delight of heavenly life. A person ascends this rung if he not only does not do evil, but does not even think it.

The tenth rung is spiritual joy, through which one reaches the fellowship of the saints. A person should rejoice to have ascended this rung if he does not rejoice at iniquity, at an enemy’s ruin, or at evils that happen to another; but rejoices with the truth [Col. 1241B] and with all deeds done for the honour of Christ, who is truth, the reward of life, and the fullness of every joy.

The eleventh rung is endurance, through which the height of heavenly glory is gained. The ascending spirit will attain this rung if it endures all the adversities of the world for Christ. Those established on this rung are written blessed if they suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake (ibid.).

## CHAPTER V. The final rungs of this ladder: faith, hope, long-suffering, and perseverance.

The twelfth rung is said to be faith, which makes human beings fellow citizens with angels. A person presses this rung with his step if he faithfully believes all things said or written devoutly about God and eternal life; for without faith it is impossible to please God.

The thirteenth rung is hope, which does not put to shame those awaiting spiritual things. The holy mind lifts its feet to this rung if it hopes for every good thing from the life to come.

The fourteenth rung follows: long-suffering, through which equality with angels is obtained. Whoever ascends will grasp this [Col. 1242A] rung if he endures all God’s promises with evenness of mind; if he bears God’s burden until the Lord himself comes, shakes the yoke from his neck, causes him to cease from labour, and makes him recline in rest.

The fifteenth and final rung is set down as perseverance, through which the verdant meadows of paradisal loveliness are attained. The mind seeking to have reached this rung should rejoice if it never falls away by despairing of God’s mercy: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. XIII).

## CHAPTER VI. This ladder is raised through fear, by which charity, brought to its summit, is itself introduced into the Lord’s inheritance.

Whoever ascends rightly through all these degrees, God—charity itself—will introduce into the storehouses of eternal sweetness. This ladder of the Lord is raised through fear; charity, brought by it to its summit, is introduced as a son into the Lord’s inheritance, while fear, as a servant, is cast out. But a twofold fear is distinguished: one is called servile, the other filial. A servant fears his master lest, if he sinned, the master should condemn him; a son fears his father lest he disinherit him. An adulterous woman fears that her husband may come; a chaste wife fears that he may depart.

Through servile fear we avoid sins lest we incur the punishment of dreadful torment; through filial fear we lament sins already committed lest we be deprived of our Father’s grace and eternal joys. Once charity has possessed the mind, it casts out servile fear. But the holy fear of the Lord, namely filial fear, remains for everlasting ages. For one will no longer fear Gehenna as a servant of sin, because one seeks to commit no sin; but as a son one will cleave to God through love in virtues. Therefore, through these fears let us love God and eternal life, and through charity accomplish every good thing, so that we may possess the sanctuary as God’s inheritance. May he who reigns forever accomplish all these things in us. Amen.

[Col. 1241]

# ON THE SOUL’S EXILE AND HOMELAND, OTHERWISE “ON THE ARTS”

(Brought to light from a manuscript codex of the illustrious Charterhouse of Gaming in Austria by the venerable Father Leopold Widemann; edited by the Reverend Father Bernhard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part I, col. 225.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1241D]

To Thomas, who has received the grace of an apostolic name and is distinguished by many gifts of Sophia, Honorius wishes him to behold in the glory of the Father him whom doubting Thomas deserved to touch on earth. Because with wakeful eye you perceive that very many people greatly desire their homeland, but, being ignorant of the way, hasten by devious paths, you urge me, best of men, as one experienced in the regions, to show them the route and to mark the nearer places in writing. Thus perhaps those who wander too far from the royal road may not be delayed in a byway and be carried farther from their homeland; as once those who departed Egypt and set out for their homeland wandered for a long time in the wilderness, not only in body but in heart, and by no means reached the homeland they desired.

But I shall not undertake the journey while consumed by envy [the transmitted syntax is uncertain]; nonetheless, I shall endeavour diligently to carry out your pious command. I shall lead diligent persons through unknown places to the homeland that is known; but the envious, spiteful, sick at heart, and unworthy of their homeland I shall leave in the darkness of error. You also, flourishing in zeal, go before the idle, rouse the negligent, compel the unwilling; draw by a delightful route to the joyful homeland those who are willing but unable; drive away the children—indeed, the slaves—of envy, even when they strive to follow; and take the holy thing from dogs and pearls from swine.

## CHAPTER I. Human exile is ignorance; the homeland is wisdom, which is reached through the liberal arts as through an equal number of cities.

Just as Babylon was exile for the people of God, while Jerusalem was their homeland, so ignorance is exile for the inward person, and wisdom is the homeland. For those situated in ignorance dwell, as it were, in a dark region, and are therefore called “children of darkness” (1 Thess. V). But those established in wisdom live, as it were, in a bright region, and are therefore called “children of light” (ibid.).

Knowledge is the way from this exile to the homeland: knowledge concerns physical things, while wisdom is considered in divine things. This way must be travelled not by the body’s steps but by the heart’s affections. It leads those tending toward their homeland through ten arts and books joined to them, as through an equal number of cities and dependent villages. This number is wrapped in many mysteries. For the divine law is contained in ten commandments, and secular wisdom within ten categories. The whole Church too is compared to ten virgins, because this number is set as the limit of all composite numbers. Hence a denarius is promised to those labouring in the vineyard.

## CHAPTER II. On the first city, grammar.

[Col. 1243C]

The first city is grammar, through which the homeland must be sought. Its gate is the fourfold voice, through which the way is the threefold letter; this, through vowels, semivowels, and mutes, leads to the dwellings of sentences. Moreover, the long and short syllables of words are like certain doorways of houses. This city is divided into eight parts, as into an equal number of regions—a number that comprises both human speech and the beatitudes of souls.

In it noun and verb rule as two consuls; pronoun claims for itself the place of proconsul, and adverb that of prefect. The other parts are fitted to other dignities, while genders and cases, tenses and other forms serve them like a subject populace. In this city Donatus and Priscian teach a new language to travellers and, by fixed rules, lead those walking along the way to the homeland. The villages subject to it are the books of poets, divided into four kinds: tragedies, comedies, satires, and lyric poems. Tragedies are those which treat wars, such as Lucan; comedies, those which sing of marriages, such as Terence; satires, those which write reproof, such as Persius; lyric poems, those which resound in a hymn-gathering voice with odes—that is, praises of gods or kings—such as Horace.

## CHAPTER III. On rhetoric, the second city.

The second city is rhetoric, through which the homeland must be approached. Its gate is public concern, and its way is the threefold class of concerns: namely demonstrative, deliberative, and judicial. In one part of this city the prelates of the Church compose Decrees; in another kings and judges issue edicts. From one side synodal ordinances are promulgated; on the other forensic laws are treated.

In this city Tully teaches travellers to speak ornamentally and orders their morals by the four virtues—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. Histories, fables, and books written in the oratorical and ethical manner are subject to this city; through them the mind’s steps must be directed toward the homeland.

## CHAPTER IV. Dialectic, the third city.

The third city is dialectic, fortified by many strongholds of questions, through which the way leads to the courts of the homeland. It receives those arriving through five gates: genus, species, difference, property, and accident. Hence they are called introductions (*isagogae*), because through them those returning to the homeland are introduced. The citadel of this city is substance; its nine surrounding towers are the accidents.

In it there are two champions, who settle disputes by sure reasoning. They arm travellers with the categorical and hypothetical syllogism as with splendid weapons. Aristotle receives these in the *Topics*, instructs them with arguments, and in the *Perihermeneias* brings them out into the broad field of syllogisms. In this city travellers are taught to resist heretics and other enemies with the weapons of reason—enemies who, like Amalek of old against the people of God, endeavour to obstruct them on this way.

## CHAPTER V. Arithmetic, the fourth city.

The fourth city is arithmetic, through which the homeland is sought. In it, under Boethius’ instruction, even and odd number intertwine in many ways. The sieve tests prime numbers by means of composite numbers. The abacus, proceeding through fingers and joints, multiplies; returning, it divides; by fractions it reduces the unit into a thousand parts. In it *rithmomachia* sets even and odd numbers to battle; the game of chess arranges its contest by fixed number; the board game gathers cast dice by the sixfold lot. In the school of this city the traveller learns that God has disposed all things in measure, number, and weight.

## CHAPTER VI. Music, the fifth city of those proceeding toward wisdom.

The fifth city is music, through which there is passage to the songs of the homeland. In this city, by Boethius’ teaching, a choir on one side sings to God with the low voices of men, on the other with the high voices of boys. Organs sound with pipes, lyres with strings, and cymbals ring with their beating. Seven distinct voices produce the consonant harmony. The threefold modulation made by wind, touch, and striking sings of the dignity of the number six, embracing the whole, through seven consonances, while it yields sweet melody by intervals and proportions of tones. In this city travellers are taught, through the harmony of moral character, to pass onward to the concord of the heavens.

## CHAPTER VII. Geometry, the sixth city.

The sixth city is geometry, through which the homeland is sought. In it Aratus spreads out a map of the world, showing Asia, Africa, and Europe; he enumerates the mountains, cities, and rivers of the whole world through which, he recounts, travellers pass.

## CHAPTER VIII. On astronomy, the seventh city.

[Col. 1245A]

The seventh city is astronomy, which leads to the dwelling places of the homeland. In it Hyginus, by means of the astrolabe, displays the waxing and waning of the moon, its circuits, the courses and returns of the sun and planets; he unfolds the sphere, in which he depicts the signs of the zodiac and the other marvels of heaven by scattered stars. In it Julius expounds the computus, by which he enumerates the years of the world through the succession of kings. In it the heavenly orbs sweetly leap in their collision, and urge travellers to praise the Creator.

## CHAPTER IX. Physics, the eighth city.

The eighth city is physics, through which the homeland is sought. In it Hippocrates teaches travellers the powers and natures of herbs, trees, stones, and animals, and by healing bodies leads them to the healing of souls.

## CHAPTER X. On mechanics, the ninth city.

The ninth city is mechanics, through which the homeland must be entered. It teaches travellers every craft involving metals, wood, and marble, as well as painting, sculpture, and all arts made by the hands. It raised Nimrod’s tower; it constructed Solomon’s temple. It devised Noah’s ark and all the walls of the whole world, and taught the various weavings of garments.

## CHAPTER XI. Household management, the tenth city.

The tenth city is household management (*oeconomica*), through which one arrives at the courts of the homeland. It arranges kingdoms and dignities; it distinguishes offices and ranks. It teaches those hastening to the homeland that people are joined to the orders of angels according to the order of their merits.

## CHAPTER XII. Having traversed the liberal arts, one reaches the homeland, or true wisdom, shining forth in the divine Scriptures and perfected in the vision of God.

Having passed through these arts as through cities, one reaches sacred Scripture as though the true homeland, in which manifold wisdom reigns. This Scripture builds herself a house, strengthened by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit as by seven columns (Prov. IX), and joined by a fourfold understanding in four walls: the historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical.

History is an event that occurred, as: Jerusalem was a city of the Jews in which was the temple of the Lord. Allegory is when one thing is said and another understood, as: Jerusalem is the Church; we ourselves are the temple of the Lord (2 Cor. VI). Tropology is moral interpretation, as: Jerusalem is every faithful soul, in which the temple is a clean heart and its inhabitant the Holy Spirit. Anagoge is the higher sense leading to God and to the age to come, as: Jerusalem is the heavenly city, in which the saints, joined to the angels, will have God present before them (Rev. XXI).

In this house Wisdom prepares a feast for those who come to her, satisfying them with varied and delicious dishes. At last she will introduce them into the heavenly Jerusalem, in which the King of glory will be seen in his beauty, whose loveliness sun and moon admire. In this place the nine orders of angels do not cease to praise the King of kings, upon whom they unceasingly desire to look. In this homeland the patriarchs prefigure Christ by types; the prophets announce him beforehand in writings; the apostles preach him to the world by signs and powers; the martyrs offer him their blood; and virgins, offering chastity, adore him.

In this homeland, too, the zealous ascend the mountain of contemplation, on which they behold Christ between Moses and Elijah, radiant like the sun in a snowy garment. For through sacred Scripture and visible creation, which are his garments, they understand him as judge of the living and the dead and equal to the Father.

## CHAPTER XIII. God will be seen by the saints according to each person’s virtues.

[Col. 1246B]

To meditate on such things now is to contemplate heavenly things; but, when stripped of flesh, to see them face to face is to rejoice in the heavenly kingdom. In it are many dwellings—that is, manifold manifestations of God—in which the saints will see the God of gods in Zion, that is, in divine contemplation, when they go from virtue to virtue. For example: the good will see God insofar as he is called goodness; the just, insofar as he is justice; the wise, insofar as he is wisdom; the peacemakers, insofar as he is peace (Matt. V); and others will see him through other virtues without end.

## CHAPTER XIV. God can be comprehended by no one except himself. The vision of God will eternally refresh the blessed; remembrance of crimes committed will torment the wicked without end.

[Col. 1246C]

But insofar as he surpasses every understanding, no one has ever seen God, nor will ever see him: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father alone” (Matt. XI). Whatever has been shown to the Fathers concerning God is called God; as concerning Jacob: “I saw the Lord face to face” (Gen. XXXII). And again concerning Moses: “Moses spoke with the Lord face to face, as a friend with a friend” (Exod. XXXIII). And likewise the prophet: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne,” etc. (Isa. VI).

But the pure in heart will see God in the future in Zion—that is, in divine contemplation—according as he appears to each one, when he manifests himself to those who love him. For each person will see God in himself and in every creature according to his measure, when God is all things in all. Those who reach this homeland will thus see the King of glory in his beauty, and he will be their joy as light is to the eyes.

But those who, delighted by transient things, remain in exile will undergo outer darkness, just as diseased eyes forever shun eternal light. Yet varied and manifold phantasms of vices, like savage beasts, confront them. They always wish to escape these but cannot get away, because one after another continually presses upon them and plunges them into an immeasurable abyss of sorrow and despair. Exercise yourself in these things; teach them to others, so that you may escape those things and reach these. Amen.

[Col. 1247]

# ON THE CLOISTERED LIFE

(Extracted from a codex of the Charterhouse of Gaming by the venerable Father Leopold Wydemann; edited by the Reverend Father Bernhard Pez, in the work cited above, col. 363.)

[Col. 1247A] The cloistered life was instituted by the Lord himself. Spiritually, it is compared to ten things, just as the whole Church is compared to ten virgins. First, it is like the shore of the sea: it receives those coming from the danger of the sea and restores them to the safety of a firm homeland. For this whole age is like a stormy sea, since it is disturbed by wars as the sea is by storms. Therefore those who boil with fear amid the snares of enemies are like people tossed by waves in a sea-storm; while those who dwell amid wars and seditions are like those sailing amid storms and winds. Those who live in peace are like people guiding a ship on a calm sea; yet it is uncertain whether they will reach shore unharmed. For many, when they have reached the shore, are heedlessly submerged by waves close to shore.

But those who reach the shore with their burden are those who come to the cloister; there they arrive safely and return to the homeland of heaven. Of this shore it is read in the Gospel that a net, cast out and full of fish, was drawn to shore; the good fish were selected into vessels, but the bad were thrown out (Matt. 13). For many people are drawn out of the salt sea of the world by the net of Scripture and brought into the cloistered life. The obedient are received by angels into paradise; the disobedient are cast out into punishment. Good fish also are those who persevere in their spiritual profession to the end; bad fish are those who abandon the cloister and return to the world.

Second, the cloister is like a shady shelter, which shades travellers [Col. 1247C] and cools them from the heat. For all whom care troubles and anxiety weighs down in the affairs of the world are like people making a difficult journey in great heat and seeking a shaded place in which to refresh themselves. When they hasten to God’s cloister, they turn aside, as it were, into a shelter, where they find true refreshment and, as the prophet says, security from storm and rain, or from enemies and wars (Isa. 4).

Third, it is like a bed in which those who labour rest. Those who are under harsh dominion and serve earthly wealth are in great toil. When they come to the cloister, they rest as though in a bed after labour. Of this bed the Lord says in the Gospel: “Two shall be in one bed; the one shall be taken, and the other left” (Luke 17). He signifies two kinds of people dwelling in the cloister: one that loves only bodily rest, and another that always seeks spiritual rest.

Fourth, it is an asylum, or house of refuge. For just as under the Law there was a city of fugitives, to which the accused fled and were saved from their enemies, so the cloister is the sole refuge of the guilty, in which those fleeing the world are saved from demons.

Fifth, it is a school for children, in which little ones in Christ are shaped by the Master’s rule toward the virtues.

Sixth, it is a gymnasium built in Jerusalem [Col. 1248B], or a place of exercise established in the Church, where Christ’s recruits train themselves for the various battles against vices.

Seventh, it is like a prison, in which criminals coming from the broad way are confined, so that they may deserve to enter the broad hall of heaven.

Eighth, it is a furnace of temptation, in which vessels of glory are tested, [while vessels of dishonour are rejected.

Ninth, it is like hell, in which penitents are purified, while the malicious and hard-hearted are tormented by punishments.

Finally, and tenth, it is compared to paradise, in which are the delights of the Scriptures, the varied exercises of the righteous, and diverse fruit-bearing trees.

[Col. 1248C] Therefore the cloister is all things to all people. To princes fleeing the storms of war, it is a harbour of salvation; to merchants avoiding the heat of cares, a refreshing shade; to servants or those under constraint, ceasing from excessive labour, a bed of rest; to soldiers fleeing their enemies, a sure asylum, like a strong fortress; to the unlearned, a school of virtues; to those unpractised, an exercise in various arts; to wanderers or criminals, a prison—indeed, a lodging; to the inexperienced, a furnace of testing; to penitents, a purifying hell; to rebels, a tormenting hell; to the wise and those fervent in charity, a paradise abounding in delights and filling them with eternal riches. Amen.

[Col. 1249]

# EUCHARISTION, OR THE BOOK ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD

Extracted from a manuscript codex of the exempt monastery of Melk by the venerable Lord Father Sebastian Treger, priest of the illustrious Charterhouse of Gaming; edited by the Reverend Father Pezius, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part I, col. 347.

## PROLOGUE

[Note: [Col. 1249C] The codex is preceded by the title: “Here begins *Eucharistion*, which means ‘good grace’: a treatise of Honorius.”]

[Col. 1249A]

May you, who toil fervently in the Lord’s abundant harvest, enjoy rest as the recompense of completed labour. You, beloved brother, have entered the garden of the Bride through the Holy Spirit. Seeking among the lilies in beds of spices, you are not delighted merely, as some are accustomed to be, by one beautiful sight or the sweet fragrance of fruits; but you also desire to be satisfied by the very taste of diverse fruits. And although with an easy hand you can bend down the top of any tree, you nevertheless ask me to bend toward you the branches of the desirable tree of life, so that you may, without effort, reach with your hand the fruit that bestows immortality, and may offer as a healing antidote to those languishing from the deadly food of death.

For among those who range through the fields of Scripture it is customary [Col. 1249B] for one person’s study to commend another person’s work. Thus those who love one another mutually, gathering diverse flowers from the meadows, are accustomed to take for themselves garlands woven by others and to place upon others garlands woven by themselves. Since, then, you ask this fraternally, I shall explain as briefly as possible, for the benefit of others, what I think concerning the Lord’s body.

## THE CHAPTERS FOLLOW

**Chapter I.** That the Lord’s body is understood in three ways.  
**Chapter II.** Why God was incarnate, and how his body cannot be diminished.  
**Chapter III.** Whether what Mary bore is truly eaten.  
**Chapter IV.** That through this food a human being is incorporated into Christ.  
**Chapter V.** That nothing other than Christ’s subsistent body is received.  
[Col. 1249C] **Chapter VI.** That both evil and good priests consecrate Christ’s body, but only the righteous receive it.  
**Chapter VII.** That the wicked receive not Christ’s body but judgment, and what it is to receive judgment.  
**Chapter VIII.** That the wicked receive the species, not the power, of the sacrament; why it is called a sacrament; and whether it is to be believed as reality or figure.  
**Chapter IX.** Whether the Lord’s body is one thing in the mouth of the good and another in the mouth of the wicked.  
**Chapter X.** What is to be thought if age or any animal consumes it.  
**Chapter XI.** Whether the Jews who ate manna ate the Lord’s body.  
**Chapter XII.** Why it is made from bread, wine, and water.

## CHAPTER I. That the Lord’s body is understood in three ways

[Col. 1250A]

Thus the Lord’s body is spoken of in three ways. First, it is that body which was incarnate from the Virgin, offered for us upon the altar of the cross, raised to heaven after conquering death, and placed at the right hand of God. Second, the Lord’s body is called that which, as a pledge of the Church, is handed over through the consecration of the Holy Spirit: daily it is made from the substance of bread and wine through the mystery performed by priests, and through the working of the Godhead it is transferred into the aforesaid body. Although eaten by all the people, it is nevertheless said to remain whole according to the Catholic faith. Third, the whole Church is proclaimed the Lord’s body, being joined together into one from all the elect as from many members.

The eyes of this body are the wise, leading others to the way of truth; its ears are the obedient; [Col. 1250B] its nostrils, those who discern between good and evil; its mouth, those speaking the word of God; its teeth, those expounding the sacred Scriptures; its hands, those doing good works; its feet, those carrying others in need. This third body is joined to the first through the middle one, just as the number three is formed from two and one. Hence not three but one body is rightly affirmed, united by the Holy Spirit, just as one soul gives life to a body in all its members.

And because one body is believed, it is made from one offering; but because, as we have said, it is received in three ways, the consecrated offering is therefore divided into three. The part cast into the chalice is that body of the Lord which is received in glory; the part received by the priest is that which is left as a pledge of the Church; and the part stored in a pyx [Col. 1250C] for viaticum is that which still bends down to this world, as though to a prison, for labour.

## CHAPTER II. Why God was incarnate, and how his body cannot be diminished

To a careful inquirer it will be evident why, or in what manner, the first body determined to incorporate the third into itself through the middle body and to make them one in the Spirit. God created the first human being for eternity and intended to grant him immortality through eating from the tree of life. But at the devil’s persuasion, the human being ate from the fruit of the forbidden tree and through this eating incurred death. It was therefore just in the justice of God that one who, through food, had lost life and was held subject to death should through food overcome death and be restored to life.

But because neither in heaven nor on earth could such food be found as might repair so great a fall, Life itself put on flesh and gave itself as food to mortals; when eaten, it repelled death, since it transferred mortals into itself as life. The body of this Life was like a grain of wheat, from which living bread might be made for our food. Since it seemed too small to distribute among all the people, by God’s will it was increased from that same kind of earth, so that the grain itself might remain ever whole for seed, while through its increase the people to be incorporated into it might eat daily without detriment. So the widow daily took from the jar of flour and the vessel of oil [Col. 1251B], yet did not diminish their fullness; and so the light of the sun is drunk in by the eyes of all, yet suffers no loss by diminution.

For the Word, sown from the heart of the supreme Father into the field of the world like a grain of wheat, was received by the clean earth of the virginal womb and, made flesh, brought forth as food for the people. This flesh is so united with the Word that flesh and Word are the one person of Jesus Christ. Therefore, just as the Godhead cannot in any respect be increased, so the food of this flesh can in no way be diminished.

## CHAPTER III. Whether what Mary bore is eaten

Perhaps someone here asks whether what Mary bore is eaten. The truth of this matter will become clearer to the reader if he takes care to consider the beginning of this institution. For Christ, eternal Life, returning to supper, after the eating of the Paschal lamb fulfilled the old law and initiated the new law by the eating of his body in this rite: he lifted up the bread set before him on the table, changed it by his blessing into the substance of his flesh, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “This”—understand, “what I hold in my hands”—“is my body, which shall be given for you” (Matt. 26).

Behold: he held in his hands the body born of the Virgin, and a body transformed from the substance of bread by the Word through which he made the ages. Then, lifting up the wine placed before him, he blessed it and changed it by the blessing into his blood. [Col. 1251D] He handed it to his disciples, saying: “This is the chalice of my blood” (*ibid.*), that is: the wine which is in this chalice is my blood, which shall be poured out for you. Behold: he held in his hands the body born of the Virgin, still wounded by no injury, and blood changed from the substance of wine.

It was as if he plainly said: “I have indeed been sent to you as food against the danger of death. But because you shrink from grinding me with your teeth to eat me, I change the substance of bread and wine for you into the food of my body, so that, just as you sustain the life of the body by bodily food, so by this spiritual food you may live in me, who am Life, in your soul.” Therefore, after the apostles had eaten Christ’s body—that body consecrated from bread and handed down by Christ’s body—when they had consumed it by eating and drinking, the body taken from the Virgin rose from the table whole; it went forth unharmed and met the raging Jews. Seized by them, it was crucified on the next day; afterwards it was received into heaven and set over all the hosts of angels.

You see, then, that when instituting this sacrament he gave them no part cut from his body—not even from finger, hand, or foot—but distributed to them the substance of consecrated bread and wine, while he transferred himself whole to the right hand of the Father. Therefore the body begotten of the Virgin, dwelling in heaven, rules over the whole creation; while the body consecrated from bread and wine through the Holy Spirit and transferred into the substance of the former body is truly eaten by the people of the faithful. Through this body, moreover, the third body, which is the Church, is incorporated into Christ.

## CHAPTER IV. That through this food a human being is incorporated into Christ

[Col. 1252B]

Indeed, Christ’s body eats Christ’s body. By this means Christ too becomes Christ’s body. For just as bodily food is changed into the substance of our body, so the Church through this food is changed into Christ’s body and becomes one flesh with him, as it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Matt. 19; Mark 10). And just as the Father abides naturally and substantially in the Son, and the Son in the Father, according to the Godhead, so Christ truly abides naturally in the Church according to his humanity, and the Church in Christ through eating this food. Therefore he is also called the mediator of God and human beings.

The Church is believed to be his body, joined in one person and one substance by charity. In it he still suffers in his members; he is fed by alms, and there he is despised. Therefore, when every necessity follows, where the head is, the whole body is gathered there. Yet no one is so transferred into Christ’s essence as to be called, in the manner of the Virgin, a son, or the Son of God by right. Rather, by faith and love he is united to Christ’s Godhead, and by communion in this food to his humanity, so that as his member he necessarily enjoys the glory of the Son of God as a co-heir.

## CHAPTER V. That nothing other than Christ’s subsistent body is received

[Col. 1252D]

Here the question is raised whether Christ handed down to the apostles something other than his own proper, subsistent body; whether the Church today receives something different from what it received then; whether individual priests make individual bodies, or rather whether all make one body; and whether it is eaten in parts by the people or wholly by each individual. Christ was the Word of the Father, through whom he made all things. That same Word changed the nature of bread and wine into the substance of his flesh and blood, just as he changed water into wine; and he gave his followers to eat nothing other than his own subsistent body, born of the Virgin, which he offered to God the Father on the altar of the cross on the following day for the life of the world.

The Church today likewise makes through the hands of priests the same thing, and not something else, that Mary bore. The people of the faithful today receive, likewise, the same thing and not something else—though made from different bread—that Christ handed down with his own hands. And although individual priests offer individual hosts, they do not make separate bodies; all make one body, though at different times. And although they divide the offerings into very many pieces, they do not thereby make parts: each receives the whole. Otherwise, if Christ, once divided, were eaten by the people, there would be nothing to give again to one who was hungry; or there would be as many bodies of Christ as there are sacrifices of priests. But now the one body of Christ is eaten wholly by all the people and wholly by each person; yet it is most truly believed to remain whole and entire at the right hand of the Father. What human reason cannot prove, Catholic faith permits no one to doubt. Whoever does not believe will have no share in this body, because he has proved worse than an unbeliever.

## CHAPTER VI. That both evil and good priests consecrate Christ’s body, but only the righteous receive it

It is also customary to ask whether unworthy priests consecrate Christ’s body, or whether the wicked eat this food. Christ, the true priest according to the order of Melchizedek, who formed his body in the Virgin’s womb, alone consecrates this same body through any Catholic priest; and he alone receives it in his members, and he alone presents it to his own, he who ascended to heaven made complete in all the elect. Therefore, since no priest is shown to make Christ’s body except Christ himself through the ministry of priests, this body is made no less through the ministry of the most wicked persons, provided that they remain within the Catholic Church, than through the ministry of the holiest persons. Yet it is received by no one except Christ alone in his own members.

Outside the Church—that is, among heretics, Jews, and pagans—this sacrament is neither performed nor is the offering received. Simonists, however, though reckoned among heretics, are nevertheless joined to Catholics by a most uncorrupted faith; by faith in the Trinity they make Christ’s body, but because of their reprobate life they do not become its participants. For only the children of God feed upon this food, and only they are known to be destined to see God, as Christ himself bears witness when he says: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6).

And what is Christ? Life. Who abides in life? One who lives in the soul. Who lives in the soul? One who commits no mortal sin and accomplishes in the work of love what he believes. Thus faith in Christ is the life of the soul, as it is written: “The righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1). But the life of faith is action, as it is again written: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2). The life of action is love, as it is said: “Whoever does not love abides in death. For God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him” (1 John 4). This love is fulfilled by seeking God and helping one’s neighbour in need. In such a person God abides by enlightening him through knowledge and supplying him with both the will and the power to do good; and that person abides in God, hoping in him by faith, turning away from evils, and doing good through love. Therefore only those receive Christ’s body who in this way live to Christ through charity in life.

## CHAPTER VII. That the wicked receive not Christ’s body but judgment, and what it is to receive judgment

But those who are dead in sins do not abide in Christ, who is Life; rather, they are far from him. Therefore they do not receive Christ’s body, but eat and drink judgment upon themselves. A person receives judgment in this sacrament when, entangled in a criminal offence, he presumes before confession and penance to eat this food of angels. For just as a guilty person brought before a judge and deprived by him of life is sentenced to death, so one who with polluted mind and conscience rashly thrusts himself, unworthy, upon the life-giving sacraments incurs the offence of Christ the Judge, is cast out from life as guilty, and, like Judas, is handed over to the devil’s power. Thus, through the devil’s agitation, every good thing may become hateful to him; and through a just judgment, with hardened and unrepentant heart, he may add evil upon evil, like a madman who kindles more and more the fire of a furnace in order to burn himself.

Accordingly, when the Lord said to such persons, “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6), they thought that he would cut portions from his flesh and give them to eat, and answered: “This saying is hard” (*ibid.*). Since, hardened by wickedness, they were dead in sins and could not bear the words of Life, they at once departed even bodily from Life. But to those remaining with him as though sound members abiding in life, he said: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (*ibid.*). That is, as though he said: “The Spirit received in this spiritual food gives life to souls; but flesh cut up, or eaten carnally as you suppose, profits nothing for the soul’s life.” Therefore those who do not believe, or live wickedly, do not receive the Lord’s body.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the wicked receive the species, not the power, of the sacrament; why it is called a sacrament; and whether it is believed as reality or figure

We must consider what they receive in fact, why this is called a sacrament, and whether reality or figure is to be believed in it. Two substances are proclaimed in Christ: visible humanity and invisible divinity. So too two things are considered in this sacrament. Because the appearance and taste of bread and wine are perceived outwardly, while the body and blood of Christ are understood inwardly, it is called a sacrament. Every sacrament shows one thing outwardly and indicates another to be understood inwardly, just as letters have visible shapes and characters, while their powers and meanings are understood inwardly. Therefore, although Christ’s flesh and blood are believed to be truly present, it is not inappropriate for it to be called a sacrament or a figure. Thus the outward species of this sacrament are received by the reprobate, but its inward and life-giving power is wholly withheld from them, just as Christ’s humanity was crucified by the Jews while his divinity was touched by no injury.

## CHAPTER IX. Whether the Lord’s body is one thing in the mouth of the good and another in the mouth of the wicked

Since this bread is substantially changed into Christ’s body after consecration, the question is asked whether it is changed into another nature in the mouth of those receiving unworthily. Just as Christ, risen from death, “dies no more” (Rom. 6), so his flesh made from bread will not be transformed into any other nature. For it is the same in the mouth of the most wicked as in the mouth of the most devout, just as the same body was in the hands of those cruelly crucifying him as in the hands of those devoutly burying him.

But just as the sun, while remaining the same in heat and splendour, nevertheless works different effects in the two—by its heat scorching the earth, by its brilliance giving light—so Christ’s flesh, remaining the same, works differently in different people: incorporating the righteous into itself, but cutting the unrighteous off from itself and from life. And just as daily bread strengthens the vigorous but chokes infants, so the same reality is to the worthy a cause of glory and to the unworthy a cause of punishment.

## CHAPTER X. What is to be thought if age or any animal consumes it

The Lord’s body is sometimes consumed by age, sometimes lost by accident, sometimes gnawed by mice or devoured by dogs. What is to be thought of this is asked. When the impious tore Christ with scourges and pierced him with nails upon the cross, drops of blood fell to the ground; yet they did not diminish the substance of the risen one. For it is not read that he resumed them after his resurrection; rather, blood flowing from his side is believed to have been received by the faithful and, as tradition relates, reverently kept even to this day in certain places.

But whether it is still really restored to that body which, risen whole and now incorruptible, is proclaimed to sit at God’s right hand, or whether it is dissolved into the matter of the earth from which it was taken, is uncertain. Nevertheless, since he himself says that not a hair of our head will perish but will return to the place of the body in the resurrection, some devoutly suppose that the blood shed for us will in a marvellous manner pass into Christ’s body. Likewise, whatever of the Lord’s body has wasted away with age, or fallen to the ground by accident and decayed, diminishes nothing of the substance of Christ’s body; but whether, reduced into earthly matter, it remains thus is uncertain. Yet teachers hold that it is transferred into Christ’s substance in an ineffable manner.

Animals, however, which lack understanding are neither benefited by eating this food nor harmed by it; rather, it greatly harms those through whose negligence what is holy is given to dogs. For just as flesh does not move itself without the Spirit, so this flesh, received without the life-giving Spirit, profits nothing, as he himself says: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6). Moreover, Christ’s flesh eaten by such creatures is believed to be transferred into Christ’s substance, just as there is no doubt that, when received by unbelievers or unworthy Catholics, it is changed into Christ’s essence.

## CHAPTER XI. Whether the Jews who ate manna ate the Lord’s body

[Col. 1256A]

It is asked whether the faithful under the Law ate Christ’s body, concerning whom it is read: “They ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink” (1 Cor. 10), and of whom it is written: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77). What does “the same” mean if not that which we too eat—namely, Christ’s body? Did that people eat Christ’s flesh when Christ had not yet at all been incarnate, but only took flesh more than two thousand years later? Their manna, their food, was materially bread, transformed by God’s command from the dew of heaven and possessing every delight. But in figure it was Christ’s body, filling the souls of believers with every sweetness.

Likewise their drink was water flowing from a material rock, at one time giving the flavour of oil, at another of honey; but in figure it was Christ’s blood, quenching the thirst of souls. Hence the rock from which it flowed is called Christ, just as he is written to be the true vine, though in substance he was God and man, while in figure he was a rock and a vine. Therefore that people is said to have eaten manna in substance but Christ’s body in figure. Hence they are said to have eaten the bread of angels, because angels feed not on bodily food but are unceasingly refreshed by Christ, the living bread.

## CHAPTER XII. Why this sacrament is made from bread, wine, and water

[Col. 1256C]

We must now consider why this sacrament is made rather from bread than from flesh, rather from wine than from milk, and why it is mixed with water rather than another liquid. It is made from bread because, just as bread is made from many grains, so Christ’s body, the Church, is gathered into one from many elect and is daily refreshed by this bread. And just as *pan*—Greek πᾶν—means “all,” so every grace is received in this living bread.

And just as bread is ground by two stones, moistened with water, kneaded by hands, and baked by fire, so Christ, the living bread, was ground in his Passion by two peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles; sprinkled with blood, kneaded by blows and slaps, and baked in the fire of suffering. This bread is formed in the shape of a denarius because Christ, the living bread, was sold for the price of denarii; and he himself is the true denarius, who will be given as a reward to those labouring in the vineyard of the Church through the Decalogue of the Law.

His blood is made from wine because, just as wine flows together from many grapes, so the Church is gathered from many righteous people into one structure, and the human being drinks this draught. And just as wine is pressed in the winepress, so Christ, the cluster of Cyprus from the vineyard of Sorek, borne upon the beam of the cross by two persons—namely, prophets and apostles—to the children of Israel, that is, believers who see God, is twisted in the press of the cross. Water is mixed in so that the people, signified by the water and reborn through the water of baptism, may be incorporated into Christ. For just as after consecration not two things but one thing, namely Christ’s blood, is understood, so every faithful person after communion in this sacrament is truly believed to be one member in Christ’s body.

Therefore the Church, Christ’s body, feeds upon this food because it too is baked in the furnace of tribulation like bread and pressed in the winepress of distress like wine. Those who press and afflict her do not partake of this food, but will be stubble for the fire on the day of the Lord’s wrath, when the righteous, refreshed by this food, will shine like the sun.

Thus through Christ’s flesh our flesh is made immortally alive; through his blood our soul—which is read to reside in blood, though it is known to be in the blood of sins—is raised to life. Learned persons recognize two parts of the soul: the higher part, which contemplates invisible things and what each thing is in the proper character of its substance; and the lower part, which gives life to the whole body and differentiates the senses by a reciprocal division. The higher is called spirit; the lower is called soul. Therefore body is offered for our flesh, blood for our spirit, and water for our soul; and thus the whole human being is redeemed and made one with Christ, the living bread.

Therefore let those redeemed by the Lord come gladly to the table prepared by Wisdom and to the wine which she has mixed. Eating and drinking from the Lord’s good things, let them rejoice over grain, wine, and oil; for one day they shall be intoxicated from the abundance of the Lord’s house, and, when the Lord’s glory appears, shall be satisfied from the torrent of his delight. If you delight in these things, brother, you will without doubt be a guest at the marriage feast of the Lamb.

Here ends *Eucharistion*, which means “good grace.”

[Col. 1257]

# SUMMA GLORIA: A BOOK ON THE APOSTOLIC AND IMPERIAL OFFICE, OR ON THE PRE-EMINENCE OF PRIESTHOOD OVER KINGSHIP

Extracted from a manuscript codex of the illustrious Charterhouse of Gaming by the venerable Lord Father Leopold Wydemann; edited by the Reverend Father Bernard Pezius, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part I, col. 179.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1257B]

To the leader of Christ’s little flock, who goes before it by word and example to the pastures of life, may HONORIUS rejoice forever with the sheep in the place of pasture where nothing shall be lacking, under the good Shepherd.

Because the governance of all human rule appears to rest upon two persons—namely, the royal and the priestly—as though the structure of the whole universe were supported by two columns, you, ever-watchful leader of Christ’s fold, command me, unskilled in speech and knowledge, to set forth in writing whether these persons are equal in the dignity of the supremacy granted to them, or whether one should be held greater. For just as it is great madness to wish to support this heavy burden on weak shoulders, so it seems to be the crime of idolatry not to obey you, who command in Christ’s stead.

Yet I judge it more tolerable, out of zeal for goodwill, to be oppressed by the judgment of the unskilled or envious [Col. 1257C] than, through the sluggishness of disobedience, to be overthrown by the censure of the learned or Christ’s devoted servants. Therefore, since many arrogate to themselves the name of learning while not knowing what they say or affirm, and puff themselves up with unskilled learning before the uneducated ears of the common people, boasting that they are supporters of secular powers, this little book is published to the honour of Jesus Christ, the true King and Priest, in order to restrain their shamelessness. Since its subject is his kingship and priesthood, let its name be *Summa Gloria*.

## CHAPTER I. The question is set forth: whether priesthood precedes kingship, or kingship priesthood, in right and dignity. It is shown from the figure of Abel and Cain and their descendants that priesthood surpasses kingship.

Since the whole body of believers is divided into clergy and people, and the clergy are assigned to the contemplative life while the people are assigned to the active life; since the former is often called spiritual and the latter secular; and since the former is governed by the priestly staff, the latter by the royal staff: many commonly ask whether priesthood should by right be preferred to kingship in dignity, or kingship to priesthood.

I could briefly answer that, just as the spiritual is preferred to the secular, or as the clergy surpass the people in rank, so priesthood surpasses kingship in dignity. But to the unskilled, blinded only by secular learning, nothing seems established unless it is supported by very many testimonies of Scripture. Therefore, that this question may be examined more fully, let the root for untying this knot be considered more carefully from the origin of the world.

The first Adam, created from clean earth, bore the form of the second, heavenly Adam, who took flesh from the pure Virgin. Adam begot two sons from his wife, because Christ purposed to beget clergy and people from his Bride, the Church. Each son also set forth each order by his office. Abel, who was a shepherd of sheep, represented the priesthood, in which pastoral care keeps watch in order to guard Christ’s sheep from the ravening wolves of heretical perversity. He sacrificed a lamb because he prefigured the Word of the Father, the Lamb taking away the sins of the world. His sacrifice is read to have been acceptable to God because the priesthood exercised by him is believed to have been imposed by the Father. He is not recorded to have begotten children because the Church’s priesthood is excluded from carnal marriage. He is killed by his brother because priesthood is often oppressed by kingship.

Cain, however, who cultivated the field and founded a city in which he also reigned, bore the type of kingship. [Col. 1259B] It is read that the Lord did not regard his offerings because he is said to have arrogated to himself his brother’s office, which was not his due. Therefore the Lord declares most clearly how greatly priesthood excels kingship: he praises Abel the priest and approves his sacrifice, but rebukes Cain the king and rejects his offerings.

Nor should it disturb you that Cain is written to have been older in age, because not the spiritual but the carnal is proclaimed first. Even here, while existing in the flesh, the spiritual is oppressed by those who are carnal; afterwards, in spiritual rest, it is clothed with special glory.

Here any malicious critic, seizing the opportunity, with the swelling flesh of pride lifted up, assails me as though I were unarmed; and, vomiting forth the poison of envy with a venomous tongue, cries out insultingly: “Did you not undertake to dispute concerning priesthood and kingship [Col. 1259C]? Why now do you turn aside evasively to byways concerning the character of persons? A person does not commend a dignity; rather, dignity exalts the person. Abel was praised not because of priesthood but because of the merit of his life. Likewise Cain was rejected by God not because of the honor of kingship but because of the horror of his cruel life. Therefore Abel’s righteousness did not enlarge the authority of priesthood, nor did Cain’s wickedness diminish the majesty of kingship.”

These exceedingly sharp horns of ignorance are blunted by the horns of the cross and cut down by the sword of the Word, so that, by this stoppage, the mouths of those speaking iniquity may be closed: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21); “for you are the ruin of the people,” says the Lord. But let the humble, who desire to understand the words of truth, patiently hear what is said by God’s inspiration [Col. 1259D].

It is the custom of Holy Scripture sometimes to commend an office through a person, and sometimes to condemn an office through a person. An office is commended through a person, as the Apostle praises the priesthood from the person of Christ: “For such a High Priest was fitting for us—holy, innocent, undefiled” (Heb. 7), etc. A person is commended through an office, as the Lord addresses David through the prophet, saying: “Go, and say to David, leader of my people: I have appointed you leader over my people” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 7), etc. Again, an office is condemned through a person, as the priesthood is declared polluted by the sons of Eli. A person likewise is condemned through an office, as the Lord says to Saul: “Because you have not kept my words, I have rejected you, that you may not be king” [Col. 1260A] (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 15). The loftiness of priesthood is read in Abel; priesthood is commended, yet rule is not thereby condemned in Cain. But lest anyone suppose that holiness is conferred by priesthood upon those who live wickedly, Eli the priest is rejected; and lest anyone think that the glory of kingship harms those who live well, David the king is praised.

By what prerogative priesthood shines above kingship, Holy Scripture declares in what follows: “The sons of God went in to the daughters of men” (Gen. 6). Behold: the descendants of Seth, who succeeded Abel in the priesthood, are called sons of God; the descendants of Cain, who succeeded him in kingship, are called sons of men. For priests in sacred discourse are customarily called now sons of God, now gods, now anointed ones of the Lord, now angels [Col. 1260B]. Sons of God, as in Deuteronomy: “His sons provoked God” (Deut. 32). And in Job: “One day, when the sons of God had come to stand before the Lord” (Job 1). Gods, as in Exodus: “You shall not speak evil of the gods” (Exod. 22); and again: “Offer sacrifice to the gods” (ibid.). Anointed ones of the Lord, as in David: “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Ps. 104 [105]). Angels, as in the prophet: “The lips of the priest shall preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2). But those who glory in an earthly kingdom are called sons of men. Therefore, by as much as these titles—sons of God, gods, anointed ones of the Lord, angels—differ from sons of men, by so much, by divine authority, do priests surpass kings in dignity.

## Chapter II. The same is proved from the sons of Noah and Abraham; and it is inferred that the king is subject to the supreme pontiff in divine matters, and the pontiff to the king in secular matters.

[Col. 1260C]

But it must be noted that even those who are called sons of God are drowned in the Flood, because priesthood certainly does not save those whom a reprobate life condemns. Noah too, who guided upon the waters an ark full of diverse living creatures, bore the type of Christ, who governs the Church, filled with diverse kinds of people, amid the waves of the world. His two sons, Shem and Japheth, most evidently bear the figure of priesthood and kingship, and represent clergy and people. For Shem is handed down by very learned men to have been Melchizedek, who is written to have been priest of the Most High; he is also read to have been king of Salem, because at that time the ruler of any city was called king. He is likewise written as the firstborn, because true priesthood is said to have begun from him [Col. 1260D]. From Japheth, however, the Roman Empire is found to have proceeded. The third son, moreover, who is assigned to the service of the two brothers, is understood as the people subject to priesthood and kingship; and the Jewish people, serving both, is intended. This son also mocks his father’s shameful parts, because the Jewish people reproach Christ’s humanity, or the frailty of prelates among the common people.

With what great distinction in dignity priesthood differs from kingship, the divine voice makes known through Noah: “May God enlarge Japheth; may he dwell in the tents of Shem” (Gen. 9). For the Roman kingdom, descended from Japheth, although extended over the whole world, nevertheless dwells in the tents of Shem—that is, in the churches of priests; of these Canaan is the servant [Col. 1261A], because the Jewish people, now deprived of both priesthood and kingdom, are subject to Christians willingly or unwillingly.

Nor should it be passed over in silence that from the seed of Ham descended the giant Nimrod, who built the tower of Babel against God, in which he first seized tyranny in the world; he first taught the worship of idols. From his stock proceeded Ninus, who first usurped for himself the sceptres of monarchy and subdued by force the peoples of both Shem and Japheth. Tyrants still imitate him when they seize unlawfully the rights of kingship and cruelly oppress clergy and people. And because the rule of this Ninus and of his successors is not supported by divine authority, it is attributed not to kingship but to tyranny. Therefore Abraham and his kindred [Col. 1261B] were not subject to him; rather, by divine command they fled his dominion. In the land to be given to his descendants, he instructed the chosen people of God as a priest; and there they are read not to have served kings, but rather to have had kings frequently entreat them.

Because from Abraham the kingship and priesthood of the faithful people took their beginning, he had two sons as figures: Isaac represented priesthood when, like a pontiff, he blessed his son; Ishmael, however, set forth kingship, since he devoted himself to hunting. Therefore, the same difference that existed between Isaac, who is written as his father’s heir, and Ishmael, who is read to have been cast out, is recognized by divine authority to exist between priesthood and kingship. Hence, as Ishmael then persecuted Isaac, so kingship still persecutes priesthood.

[Col. 1261C] Isaac too, offered by his father, bore the form of Christ, who was sacrificed for us by his Father. His two sons represented not only priesthood and kingship by figures, but also enacted them in their very deeds. For when Jacob offered sacrifice upon a stone, he most plainly exercised priesthood; Esau, however, set forth kingship when he produced twelve leaders from his line. But how greatly Jacob’s office surpasses Esau’s office, the divine voice declares in their father’s blessing: “Let peoples serve you,” says the father to Jacob, “and tribes worship you; be lord of your brothers, and let the sons of your mother bow before you” (Gen. 27). Likewise to Esau: “I have made him your lord and subjected all his brothers to his service. You shall live,” he says, “by the sword, and you shall serve your brother” (ibid.) [Col. 1261D]. And while they were still carried in their mother’s womb, the Lord said: “The greater shall serve the lesser” (Gen. 25).

What more do we seek? What could be said more plainly? Who, being sane, would oppose divine authority? See with how great a voice the multitude of laypeople is commanded to serve the devotion of clerics. Therefore, if a peasant rightly serves a deacon, then a soldier rightly serves a presbyter; and if a soldier serves a presbyter, then a prince serves a bishop; and if a prince serves a bishop, then most justly a king—who is certainly among the number of laypeople—will be subject to the Apostolic See. But perhaps the talkative contend with swollen arrogance that a king is not among the number of laypeople because he is anointed with the oil of priests. Clear reason mocks these senseless persons, and manifest truth will make the ignorance of imprudent people fall silent [Col. 1262A]. For is a king a layman or a cleric? If he is not a layman, he is a cleric; and if he is a cleric, then he is either a doorkeeper, reader, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, presbyter, or bishop. If he belongs to none of these ranks, then he is not a cleric. But if he is neither layman nor cleric, then he is a monk; but his wife and sword excuse him from being a monk. For he does not bear the sword without cause: “he is the avenger of God’s wrath, appointed for this very purpose” (Rom. 13). Yet neither a monk nor even a cleric may bear arms.

Therefore, since clear reasoning shows that he is a layman, and since a priest by sacerdotal office is set over all laypeople, it is necessary that in all things divine he be subject to the supreme priest, as to the head of the Church; and conversely, the supreme priest, with all the clergy, is subject in secular matters to the king himself as the superior [Col. 1262B]. Thus these two rulers of the people, outdoing one another in honor and firmly cleaving to Christ, the true King and Priest, shall reign with him forever.

## Chapter III. How great was the honor of priesthood among the Israelites, their kings, and even the Gentiles

But now let Moses come forth with the light of the law, and thoroughly shake from our minds the darkness of ignorance. Leading God’s people out of Egypt, he established law and ordinances for them, and appointed for their governance not a king but a priest. From his brother Aaron, moreover, the legal priesthood took its beginning.

[Col. 1262C]

From the time of Moses to the time of Samuel, therefore, God’s people were governed not by kings but by priests; and the judges, who seemed to preside over the people in secular matters, were in every respect governed by the decrees of priests. But when the people refused to endure priestly gentleness and resolved to try royal greatness, Samuel, prophet and priest, by divine command anointed a king for them and immediately wrote out the law of kingship. That king obeyed Samuel in all things that accorded with the divine law; likewise Samuel obeyed the king in all matters belonging to the law of kingship. For prophets were considered priests, since they are frequently narrated to have offered sacrifices. But after that same king claimed for himself the priestly office by offering sacrifice [Col. 1262D], the divine judgment immediately rejected him from the kingdom.

For David, the good king, and the whole succeeding line of kings over Judah or Israel were chosen and anointed for kingship by prophets or priests—nearly the same thing. Yet almost all are recorded as subject to them in divine matters; while the priests, conversely, reverently submitted to them in secular matters. Thus King David obeyed Nathan and the prophets when they commanded; when rebuked by them, he listened humbly. Solomon, wisest of prophets and mightiest of kings, with remarkable splendor both exalted priesthood wonderfully, honored it with the greatest reverence, and enriched it with the greatest benefits. Other kings too are found both to have revered the prophets and priests of the Lord and to have been subject to them in spiritual affairs [Col. 1263A]: Hezekiah revered Isaiah; Ahab, though most wicked and idolatrous, held Elijah in the highest honor, though severely rebuked by him. Joash is read to have been subject to Elisha, and Josiah to Jeremiah. And so long as kings honored priests—their own consecrators—and listened to prophets as their teachers, they remained in glory. But after they despised priests and killed prophets, they were immediately driven from the kingdom and dispersed among the nations in disgrace.

From the time of the Babylonian exile, priests alone governed the people of God, because kingship had wholly failed, until he came in the flesh from the tribe of Judah, for whom both the sceptre of kingship and priesthood had been reserved. Thus kingship was frequently changed [Col. 1263B], while priesthood always remained unshaken, although at times disturbed.

Why do I mention that kings honored the priests of divine worship, when sacred writings relate that even the Gentiles held their own priests in the highest honor? For, as Moses testifies, when the Egyptians, compelled by famine, sold their land and reduced themselves also to Joseph’s servitude, the priests alone were not compelled to sell their own property, because public allowances were provided for them from the king’s granary. Moreover, all histories of the Gentiles report that kings honored their priesthood, so that some consuls or emperors are read to have exercised that office as well. Let this suffice concerning the ancients; now let us consider the times of the Christian religion.

## Chapter IV. As the soul is more worthy than the body, so priesthood is more worthy than kingship, by which it is rightfully ordained

[Col. 1263C]

Our Lord Jesus Christ, true King and Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, established laws and ordinances for his Bride; and for her governance he appointed not kingship but priesthood. In it he set over her the Apostle Peter, to whom he also said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church,” etc., as far as: “it is loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16). Peter received this power of priesthood from the Lord and left it to his successors. Therefore, just as priests presided over the people of God from Moses until Samuel, so from Christ until Sylvester the priests of God alone governed the Church [Col. 1263D]. Under them, established most excellently by excellent morals and laws, she was notably trained for the eternal homeland. But kings attacked her on every side, striving in every way to turn her from the worship of truth and to convert—indeed, compel—her to the worship of demons.

But after the stone cut from the mountain without hands—rejected indeed by the builders of the wall of iniquity, but chosen by God and raised as the head of the corner—grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth with its greatness, it immediately changed times and transferred kingdoms. The height of kingship began to bow before Christ’s feet, and the summit of empire to bend in the assembly of the Church. That is, the God of peace, the great priest, changed the time of persecution into a time of peace; and the great king above all gods transferred the rebellious empire [Col. 1264A] of the pagans into the kingdom of Christians.

Accordingly Constantine, ruler of rulers of the kingdom, was converted to faith in Christ by Sylvester, prince of priests of the Church, and the whole world was clothed in the new rite of the Christian religion. Constantine placed the crown of kingship upon the Roman pontiff and decreed by imperial authority that henceforth no one should assume the Roman Empire without the consent of the Apostolic See. Sylvester received this privilege from Constantine and left it to his successors. And since the care of priesthood and the supreme direction of kingship rested upon Sylvester’s judgment, this man full of God, understanding that those rebellious against priests could not be restrained by the sword of God’s Word but by the material sword, took Constantine himself as his helper in the tillage of God [Col. 1264B], and as defender of the Church against pagans, Jews, and heretics. To him he also granted the sword for the punishment of evildoers and placed upon him the crown of kingship for the praise of the good.

From that point the Church began to have kings or judges for secular judgments: that they might sharply repel pagans attacking the Church or other enemies assaulting her; while within, by fear of punishments, they might subdue to the Church those rebellious against the divine laws. Secular judgments alone, therefore, belong to kings. Hence, when certain bishops brought their fellow bishops before the Emperor Constantine in a legal cause, he, knowing that it did not belong to his jurisdiction, replied: “Go, because you are anointed ones, and yourselves consider this matter among yourselves; I shall not be your judge.”

[Col. 1264C] Therefore, as the soul is more worthy than the body, which it gives life to, and as the spiritual is more worthy than the secular, which it gives life to, so priesthood is more worthy than kingship, which it appoints and orders. Hence the question arises: by whom ought these persons to be elected or appointed?

The Apostolic bishop is to be elected by the Roman cardinals, with the consent of the bishops and of the whole city—clergy and people—and is to be established by acclamation as head of the Church. By divine authority, the care of the universal Church—that is, of all people and clergy—belongs to his oversight. By apostolic authority belongs the solicitude for all Churches; but by imperial authority, the election and appointment of the Roman kingdom. To his jurisdiction also belongs the canonical ordering of all bishoprics and patriarchates and the correction, under the divine laws, of all clergy and people [Col. 1264D].

The bishop of each city, however, ought to be elected by the clergy of that city or province, and established as shepherd of Christ’s flock by the acclamation of the people. He must be invested with ring and staff by the Apostolic bishop; if an archbishop, he must be consecrated by twelve bishops, or at the least by three. His office is to govern the clergy subject to him canonically, summon the people to the ordinances of divine law, excommunicate those who resist, and absolve penitents.

The Roman emperor ought to be elected by the Apostolic bishop, with the consent of the princes and acclamation of the people; established as head of the people; consecrated and crowned by the pope. To his administration belongs the ordering, according to civil justice or the laws of the land, of prefectures, advocacies, presidencies, duchies, and counties; and the establishment for peoples, according to the circumstances of the time, of taxes, markets, and laws [Col. 1265A]. Kings and judges of provinces or regions are to be appointed by him; princes are to be set over cities by him.

But here perhaps contentious persons, unskilled in speech and knowledge, will burst forth and maintain that the emperor is to be elected not by the Apostolic bishop but by the princes. I ask them whether a king is to be appointed by subjects or by prelates. “By prelates,” they say. By whom? “By dukes and counts.” But dukes and counts are subject to bishops, their lords, because from them they hold benefices and the estates of churches. Therefore the king must be appointed by Christ’s priests, who are the true princes of the Church; although the consent of laypeople is to be sought. Thus, because priesthood rightly appoints kingship, kingship will rightly be subject to priesthood.

## Chapter V. Christ himself preferred priesthood to kingship, although he also taught, both in person and through his apostles, that honor ought to be shown to kings in secular affairs

How greatly the Lord himself preferred priesthood to kingship is clear from this: when men were about to come to seize him and make him king, he fled. But he devoutly performed the priestly office when, among the other marks of priestly office—namely preaching and performing miracles—he also blessed the sacraments of his body and handed down this rite for his followers to celebrate [Col. 1265C]. Indeed any priest, even of the lowest rank in the sacred order, is more worthy than any king. Hence it is read that the blessed Martin, bishop, was invited to a banquet by the Emperor Maximus. When, during the meal, the cupbearer presented the cup to the king, the king ordered it given to the bishop, so that he himself might receive it from the bishop’s right hand. But after Martin had drunk, he gave the cup to his presbyter, judging him more worthy than the king because he could consecrate Christ’s sacraments and bind the king when sinning or absolve him when penitent. Similarly, the Emperor Theodosius was excluded by Bishop Ambrose from the threshold of the Church when he was held guilty and liable on a charge of homicide; and he was bound with the bonds of penance, from which, after making satisfaction, he was absolved by that same bishop.
