[Col. 1265D] Although priesthood therefore far surpasses kingship, nevertheless, for the bond of peace and concord, evangelical and apostolic authority teaches that honor must be shown to kings, but only in secular affairs. When certain persons asked the Lord whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, he said: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22). Therefore, in matters belonging to the law of kingship, people must obey kings; but in matters pertaining to the law of God, they must seek to please God. Thus the most blessed Sebastian, a true worshipper of God, proved faithful in secular matters to Diocletian and Maximian, though pagan emperors; in spiritual matters he strove to please God alone, the Creator of all. So too the illustrious Maurice, with his army, supplied assistance against the enemies of the kingdom to the same emperors. But when they compelled him to act against the Christian religion, he refused, because he had learned what is written: “One must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5).

The blessed Apostle Peter likewise exhorts people to render honor to kings: “Fear God,” he says, “honor the king” (1 Pet. 2). And again: “Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake, whether to the king as superior, or to governors sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and for the praise of the good” (ibid.) [Col. 1266A]. In these words it must be considered that kings and judges are appointed solely for the punishment of evildoers, while they are said to bring praise to the good. For just kings and judges punish only the impious and unjust, but raise up the just and good with praises. The blessed Paul too exhorts to submission to rulers, saying: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers” (Rom. 13). And lest you think that powers are established by men by chance, he adds: “For there is no power except from God” (ibid.). Yet because at times bad judges are appointed because of the sins of the people, as is read in Job—“He makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people” (Job 34)—while at other times just rulers are placed over them because of the merits of some, he adds: “Those that exist have been ordained by God” (Rom. 13).

And lest you should suppose that the good are indeed to be obeyed but the bad resisted, he continues: “Therefore whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God; and those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves” (ibid.). And because judges are set over people only to restrain, indeed punish, the wicked, he plainly adds: “Rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do good, and you shall have praise from it” (ibid.) [Col. 1266C]. Peter said the same.

Paul further explains the office of king or judge, saying: “He is God’s minister to you for good. But if you do evil, fear; for he does not bear the sword without cause” (ibid.); that is, as is to be understood, in order that he may punish evildoers. “He is also God’s minister, an avenger for wrath upon one who does evil” (ibid.). What could be said more openly? The king is the Church’s minister, that he may restrain the rebellious; he is the avenger of God’s wrath, that he may punish the impious. For God did not set the first human being over human beings, but over beasts and brute animals [Col. 1266D], because judges are set only over those who live irrationally and brutishly, in order that they may recall them by fear to the proper measure of the innate gentleness of humanity. Hence the same God, through Noah, set Shem and Japheth over the descendants of their sinning brother, because he certainly subjected sinners to priesthood and kingship.

Hence too, when the disciples said to the Lord in the Gospel, “Behold, here are two swords” (Luke 22), he confirmed these words by his authority, because he showed beforehand that two swords are necessary for the governance of the Church in the present life: one spiritual, namely the Word of God, which priesthood uses to enlighten sinners; the other material, which kingship uses to punish those persisting in evil. For it is necessary that royal power subdue with the material sword those who, being rebellious against God’s law, cannot be corrected by the priestly stole [Col. 1267A].

## Chapter VI. Kings who do not obey the Roman See are indeed to be endured patiently, but their communion is to be avoided. They do not have authority to confer ecclesiastical dignities, but only secular ones

The question arises whether one must obey in all matters, or whether one must at times resist. Answer: while rulers command things belonging to the law of kingship, they must certainly be obeyed; but if they command things harmful to the Christian religion, they must be resisted. It is indeed read that Christians soldiers of old fought under pagan kings against the enemies of the kingdom, and yet did not abandon the worship of Christ. If they were called away from that worship, they immediately bore witness, even by death itself, that God must be obeyed rather than men [Col. 1267B]. For John and Paul, by command of Constantine, a most Christian emperor, set out with the still-pagan patrician Gallicanus against the enemies of the Roman Empire; but they entirely withdrew from the court of Julian the Apostate.

Therefore, if the king is obedient to the Roman Church, the head and mother of all Churches—as a son crowned by her, a minister of God and avenger of God’s wrath—and if, binding the Christian people to observe the divine laws, he defends them from pagans, Jews, and heretics, then he must in all things be obeyed by everyone. But if he is rebellious against the Roman and Apostolic See, which the King of kings and Lord of lords willed to be the head of the Church, and which itself established him as head of the nations; or if, turning aside into some heresy, like Constantius and Valens [Col. 1267C], he afflicts the Church; or if, apostatizing from the faith, like Julian, he persecutes her; or if, by schism, like Philippicus, he divides her into parties—such a one, I say, is indeed to be endured patiently, but communion with him is altogether to be avoided, because he is not an emperor but a tyrant. Martin rejected service under such an empire, saying: “I am Christ’s soldier; it is not lawful for me to fight.”

But there are certain men, who call themselves wise but have become fools, who dare to assert that kings may confer bishoprics, abbeys, or other dignities. For they say: “The king is anointed with sacred oil and set over clergy and people; therefore he is proved to have the right to confer the dignities of both.” Their wholly false affirmative assertion is overthrown by a wholly true negative; and their denial is established by truth’s affirmation. I therefore ask them: are bishoprics, abbeys, and provostships spiritual dignities or secular ones? “Spiritual,” they will answer, unless they are insane. But I ask: is kingship a spiritual dignity or a secular one? “Secular,” they say. Therefore spiritual dignity does not at all pertain to a secular person [Col. 1267D].

I ask them further: may a king celebrate Mass or not? “By no means,” they answer. Why? “Because he is not a priest,” they say. And I reply: if for this reason he may not celebrate Mass, because he is not a priest, then neither may he confer the church in which Mass is celebrated, because he is a layman. Therefore, because a king is a layman and secular, bears the sword for the punishment of evildoers, is appointed by priestly office as the avenger of God’s wrath, and is set over the people only in secular matters, against every opposing consideration he neither ought nor can confer bishoprics, abbeys, or provostships, which are spiritual dignities [Col. 1268A]. Yet he both ought and can confer secular dignities, such as duchies, presidencies, and counties; but the Church alone ought to entrust spiritual things to spiritual persons. Hence the sacred canons command that anyone who obtains a canonical dignity through secular power be deposed.

For the priest Jehoiada is read to have established King Joash; never is a king found to have established a priest. If it is objected that Jonathan received the priesthood from Alexander, a pagan king, and Simon his brother from Demetrius, likewise a pagan, it must be understood that they were priests and descended from a priestly line; but had been deprived of their office through bloodless wars, and from these kings they received authority to exercise their own office in the customary manner. Therefore this was permission, not conferment.

Moreover, if it is objected that the Tripartite History relates that the Emperor Valentinian said to Ambrose: “I entrust bodies to you; God, however, souls,” it must be understood that Ambrose had first been a provincial judge; but after canonically receiving the bishopric, the king additionally delegated to him the care of the province. We know that this practice is still observed in certain churches: namely, that a bishop holds the care of both bishopric and duchy [Col. 1268C]. Yet we know that this is by no means fitting for priests of Christ, because “no one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2).

And if it is further recalled that the Life of St. Gregory relates that the Emperor Maurice ordered him to be consecrated, it must be understood that Gregory had been canonically elected by clergy and people; but because, for the sake of peace and concord, the emperor’s consent was customarily required, he ordered him to be consecrated and gave assent to his ordination.

## Chapter VII. How did the corrupt custom arise by which ecclesiastical dignities were conferred by princes?

Whence this perverse custom arose—that bishoprics are bestowed by royal power—I shall relate as I received it in a truthful account. Pope Leo, of blessed memory, having been blinded by the Romans [Col. 1268D] and driven from the Apostolic See by a tumultuous people, came to Charles, king of the Franks, who received him honorably. Charles gathered an army and hastened to Rome; punishing the seditious with due retribution, he restored the expelled pope to the papal see. The one who performs wonderful deeds especially gave him sight. And because at that time the Roman Empire lacked a ruler—because, as is handed down, the Emperor Constantine V had been blinded by the hands of wicked men—the venerable Pope Leo, with the counsel of the princes and consent of clergy and people, handed the sceptres of the Roman Empire to King Charles; and, consecrating him Augustus, placed the crown of kingship upon him.

And because that king had raised the Roman Church to the highest honor, enriched it with many gifts and offerings, and further endowed it with very great freehold estates [Col. 1269A]; because in every respect he was Catholic and most worthy of God and of kingship by excellence of wisdom and conduct, subject to the Apostolic See and devoted to all the clergy: Pope Leo III, rejoicing in such a great helper, granted to him alone this privilege—that on this side of the Alps, in the regions of Gaul and Germany, he might establish bishoprics in his stead according to ecclesiastical custom. The successors of that king likewise obtained this privilege from the Apostolic See, because they too were in every respect devoted to the Roman Church. Yet they chose persons wise, approved in life, and suitable for the divine office, and placed worthy shepherds over churches without any payment.

But after men ignorant of God and abhorring the Church’s honor had violently seized the kingdom without Roman election [Col. 1269B], and stained the empire with criminal and depraved conduct, such men, casting aside royal gentleness after Nero’s manner and violently—indeed cruelly—extending tyrannical dominion over clergy and people, began to disturb the peace of the Church and concord of the people and to violate apostolic decrees and the edicts of earlier kings. Hating justice and equity, loving civil war, discord between clergy and people, and every iniquity, they chose persons suited to their own conduct and ignorant of justice and God’s law. To these they sold bishoprics, abbeys, provostships, and other dignities, contrary to law and right, for the highest price, in the manner of Gehazi.

But the Church, seeing the impious misuse her gifts and the gifts bestowed on her by Christ profaned by profane persons, would no longer give her honor to outsiders; instead she herself began to administer it to her own children as was fitting and expedient [Col. 1269C]. Priesthood may indeed be oppressed by kingship, but it cannot be overwhelmed; priests may be killed by kingship, but their office cannot be destroyed. Indeed, the Lord, Prince of priests, frequently exacts vengeance for the presumption of kings.

Saul, the first of kings, unjustly killed the priests of the Lord; therefore he himself, justly slain, fell in battle. King Ahab drove some prophets of the Lord from their homeland and put others to death; therefore he too, wounded, succumbed to death. King Joash overwhelmed the priest Zechariah with stones; hence he too fell, killed by his own servants. King Azariah usurped priesthood; therefore leprosy immediately seized him [Col. 1269D]. King Herod sold priesthood; therefore he killed himself with his own hand. The Emperor Nero crucified Peter, the first pope; therefore, driven from the kingdom, he became prey for wolves. The Emperor Decius caused Pope Sixtus to be killed; hence he too perished possessed by a demon. The Emperor Valens expelled Bishop Athanasius from his see; therefore he perished by fire at the hands of the Goths. The Emperor Julian persecuted Christ’s priests; hence he too was killed by enemies. King Theodoric killed Pope John; therefore he underwent eternal punishment by a sudden death. And what more? All who persecuted the priests of the Church were destroyed by a most wretched death.

## Chapter VIII. An answer to the objection drawn from the anointing of kings; it is concluded that in both the Old and New Testaments priesthood has always preceded kingship

[Col. 1270A]

If anyone should maintain that these two persons appear equal in honour and dignity because they alone are commanded in the Law to be anointed with holy oil, he should know that the king was anointed only with oil, whereas the priest was anointed with chrism; and in every respect the priest’s consecration was preferred to the king’s anointing. They differed also in this: just as the priest was consecrated by a priest, so the king was consecrated not by a king but by a priest. All this occurred figuratively, but represented Jesus Christ, the true King and Priest, whom the Father anointed with chrism and with the oil of gladness—that is, with the Holy Spirit—and [Col. 1270B] established as head of the nations; indeed, He set Him as Lord over angels and human beings. This King and Priest commanded that everyone enrolled in His service be anointed with oil and chrism; He made them a royal and priestly race and heirs of His kingdom. Hence we anoint those to be baptized with oil and chrism: by the oil we join them to Christ’s kingship, and by the chrism to His priesthood. By the mitre which we place upon their head we signify the crown of kingship; by the white garment with which we clothe them we indicate priestly dignity. Again, by the mitre we denote the pontifical headdress; by the white garment we display the royal robe. Therefore, both in the Old and in the New Testament, the priesthood was always preferred to royal power, since royal power itself was moreover established through the priesthood.

[Col. 1270C] Let us now inquire closely into those for whose sake we undertook this little nocturnal work: those who, from love of money, desire for favour, and hope of receiving from princes the honour of some dignity, preach to the unlearned—while themselves especially unlearned—that every dignity everywhere depends upon the will of kings. Those who say this are either laymen, monks, or clerics. If they are laymen, then they are to be laughed at as foolish, or rather corrected by the wise as ignorant. If they are monks, then they are out of their senses: whether they err through ignorance of the truth, or, knowing the truth, deliberately pretend not to know it through avarice. If they are clerics, they are madmen, robbing the ecclesiastical order of the right bestowed on it by the Lord Himself and transferring it to [Col. 1270D] lay power; indeed, they strip themselves of their own liberty and, together with Cain, subject themselves to the servile dominion of laymen.

Therefore the foolish assertions of all such persons must be refuted by sensible people—indeed, rejected by all who use reason—since the kingdom is by right subject to the priesthood, the people to the clergy; and since, as the sun surpasses the moon, spirit the soul, and the contemplative life the active life, so the priesthood surpasses royal power. But now let us draw in our pen from the praise of the priesthood, and strive to please it by worthy conduct, so that we may be able to enter its court, in which priests and kings alone shall be. Amen.

ANNO DOMINI 1136. STEPHEN OF BALGIAC, BISHOP OF AUTUN

[Col. 1271]

HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana*, IV, 389)

[Col. 1271A] Stephen of Balgiac (Baugé), son of Gauceran, lord of Balgiac, uncle of Humbert, bishop of Autun and archbishop of Lyons, had already ascended the episcopal throne in 1112, as is evident from a charter of Guy of Montfaucon, by which he relinquishes the customary right of hospitality owed to the church of Autun into the hands of Seguin the dean. For the charter ends thus: “In the year 1112: under Stephen, bishop of the Aedui; Louis, king of the Franks; Hugh, duke of the Burgundians; indiction V, epact I, concurrent I, a leap year.”

In the cartulary of Flavigny this charter is found: “In the year of the Lord 1113, in the presence of Lord Stephen, Hugh of Merlenniac claimed from the monks of Flavigny the fief which they had received from his father. They replied that the fief had indeed been granted, but on this condition: [Col. 1271B] that, after the death of Theobald, father of Hugh, it should return in full to the brothers’ table.” After hearing the parties, the bishop determined that Hugh should allow the monks to enjoy the fief and that they should pay him a certain sum. “Witnesses: Lord Stephen the bishop, Anseric, provost of Autun,” etc.

In the same year he induced Hugh, duke of Burgundy, to relinquish to St Nazarius and the Church of Autun the evil customs imposed in the town of Canavis, etc., as the instrument drawn up on this matter shows; its witnesses are “Sevinus the dean, Anseric, provost of Autun,” etc. A charter of his is found in the cartulary of Uchon, following the foundation of that monastery and bearing no date, in which he forbids that monks “be drawn into [Col. 1271C] secular lawsuits,” and orders that “if anyone should raise any accusation against them, he shall come before his court, so that a complaint arisen in the Church may be settled in the Church by judgment in his presence.”

In another charter, reported in the Chronicle of Bèze, he, together with Josceran, archbishop of Lyons, and Walter, bishop of Chalon, confirms by his subscription a gift made to the monastery of Bèze by the lords of Mont-Salions. In a third, reported by Dom Mabillon, vol. V, appendix, no. 72, he writes to Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, that he is greatly delighted by the sweet fragrance of that religious order, and grants the church of Combusy its freedom, etc. He attended the synod of Tournus in 1115. There survives a letter to him from Pope Paschal II, by which the pope receives the Church of Autun under his protection [Col. 1272A] and confirms all its possessions. It was issued at the Lateran, on the second Ides of March, in the year 1116 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

“In the year 1125 Herbert was made abbot [of St Stephen’s, Dijon],” in the presence and with the approval of Hubaud, archbishop of Lyons, Stephen of Autun, and Gauceran of Langres. Pérard reports his charter by which, as a judge delegated by the supreme pontiff, he adjudicates to the abbot of St Benignus of Dijon the village of Dianetum, which “Count Guy Salicus was laying claim to.” King Louis wrote to him, commanding him, by order of the lord pope, “to invest the church of Charity with the church of Ulmus.” He was present at the consecration of Philip, son of King Louis VI, in 1129. In that same year he subscribed the ordinance of that king for the restoration of the monastery of Argenteuil to the abbey of St Denis. In 1134 he grants and confirms to Herbert, abbot of St-Seine, seven churches which he enumerates, possessed by that monastery in his own time “and in that of his predecessor, Bishop Norigaud of holy memory.” After him subscribe William the dean, Gerard the archdeacon, etc. He is mentioned in charters of the monastery of Uchon in 1134 and 1135. In 1136 he approves a donation made to Constantine, abbot of that monastery, by Gaudin of Bruyères.

Among extracts from the first charter of Fontenay I read this: “I, Stephen, bishop of Autun, and the community of our Church, have given to Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, the place commonly called Fontenay, in order that an abbey may be built [Col. 1272C] there,” etc. There is also another charter of his in favour of the same monastery:

“Stephen, bishop of Autun, to Brother William, abbot of Fontenay . . . assenting to your requests, we receive that monastery . . . under the guardianship and protection of the holy Church of Autun and of our dignity . . . decreeing that whatever possessions . . . the monastery now holds . . . and whatever it may acquire in the future, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors, etc. I, Stephen the bishop, have subscribed; I, William the dean; Walter the precentor, etc. This was done at Autun in the year 1136 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction XIV.”

In his time—and, it seems, through the zeal and labour of the clerics of St Symphorian near [Col. 1273A] Autun—“they embraced the regular life not only in habit, but followed it also in heart.” He therefore left them many tokens of his goodwill. First, he gave them the churches of Dracy, Bencey, and Anlezy, as appears from a charter preserved among us. He settled a serious dispute which had arisen between them and the knights Hugh of Gissey and his namesake of Saffres, and preserved the canons’ rights. Finally, he went with them to the bishop of Geneva and by his entreaties obtained for them six churches with their appurtenances. We possess a charter ending as follows:

“This charter was made in the city of Geneva, by command of Lord V . . . . . . . . . bishop of the same city, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the nineteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II. Sign of W., bishop,” etc.

An error has crept into the figures of the year of Christ; it can readily be corrected from the years of the pope. Innocent II wrote to him, ordering him to consecrate, in the pope’s place, A., subprior of Cluny, whom he had given to the monks of Vézelay as abbot.

At length Stephen, wearied of worldly affairs, resigned his bishopric, embraced the religious life in the monastery of Cluny, and afterwards yielded his soul to God in the hands of [Col. 1274A] Peter the Venerable. This event is attested by the devout abbot in Letter 6 of Book V, in these words:

“Lord Stephen, bishop of Autun, venerable and worthy to be named with honour . . . having despised parents, nobility, pomp, riches, and even the episcopal mitre itself, followed poor Christ as a poor man; persevering in holy devotion with all the affection of his mind, he gave up his spirit to God in my hands. With the reverence fitting so great a priest, he was buried at Cluny, behind the choir on the side of the greater prior, both by me and by the brethren.”

There he has a tomb marked no. 22, and an epitaph painted upon the wall, recorded in Samuel Guichenon’s *History of Bresse and Bugey*, in which he is called “the peace of the Church and the fitting father of the poor.” These are the words of William Guirin [Col. 1274B], chief key-bearer of Cluny, in his manuscript *History of the Great Priors*. This Stephen seems to be meant by what one of our number testifies that he read in the old Martyrology of the Church of Autun:

“On the seventh day before the Ides of January died Lord Stephen, bishop of venerable memory, who, among the innumerable benefits which he bestowed upon the Church of Autun, also gave the church of Colomella to the brothers’ table.””

[NOTE.]

Peter, abbot of Cluny, writes the following concerning Stephen, first bishop of Autun, in Letter 6 of Book V, to Humbert of Balgiac, archdeacon of Autun:

“May that venerable Stephen, bishop of Autun, worthy to be named with honour—your uncle, I hear—add spurs to urge you to come to the camp of religious life. Having despised parents, nobility, pomp, riches, and, casting aside even the episcopal mitre, he followed poor Christ as a poor man; persevering in holy devotion with all the affection of his mind, he gave up his last breath to God in my hands, and was buried at Cluny, with reverence fitting so great a priest, both by me and by the brethren.”

[Col. 1273]

NOTE BY P. LABBE.

Nearly everyone I have seen attributes to this first Stephen that treatise *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, first published in 1517 by John Montolovius, cantor of Autun, and dedicated to Jacques Hurault, bishop of the same city; but I have not yet seen anyone who has attempted to establish this attribution by any argument.

[Col. 1273]

TREATISE OF STEPHEN OF BALGIAC, BISHOP OF AUTUN, ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE ALTAR.

(*Bibliotheca Patrum Lugdunensis*, vol. XX, p. 1872.) (G)*

PROLOGUE.

[Col. 1273C]

The wisdom of God, ordering all things, “reaching mightily from end to end and disposing all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8)—namely, the Son of God—clothing Himself with flesh in a wondrous and ineffable manner, clothed us with the robe of immortality and clothed our corruptible nature with the garment of incorruption. Having fulfilled the dispensation entrusted to Him by the Father, and wishing to leave us everything necessary for salvation, He instituted invisible sacraments through visible matter and commanded them to be performed. For how could a human being understand spiritual gifts unless he were moved by some visible thing to receive them? The power of the sacraments produces an invisible effect. [Col. 1274C] This will become clear from illustrative examples.

The sacrament of baptism is administered in waters of regeneration, because just as external stains are washed away by water, so interior defilements are cleansed by spiritual grace given in the laver of regeneration. Likewise, in the union of male and female called marriage is understood the unity of head and members, that is, of Christ and the Church. Likewise, by anointing with oil is symbolized the working of divine mercy. Oil heals, refreshes, and floats above; God’s mercy heals the broken-hearted, binds up their wounds, refreshes and satisfies the hungry with unfailing bread, and triumphs over judgment.

In this manner, in the ecclesiastical sacraments [Col. 1275A] established with the Holy Spirit cooperating, sevenfold grace works invisibly. Although the Spirit is one and the same, working in each person as He wills, nevertheless a division of graces is assigned according to the variety of distributions. For gifts are distributed according to the capacity of those receiving them. Thus there is no diversity in the Spirit, but identity without any change. He distributes to whom He wills and as much as He wills, yet is not divided; He contains all things and is in all things. He who gives is Himself the gift. Though the gifts are divided, He remains one and undivided; the giver is one, who, given in Himself, gives many things. And though He is that which is given, He Himself is diverse gifts. Everything bestowed is referred to one end: as when someone distributes gold to one person, silver to another, and an abundance of jewels to another, he distributes many things but intends to produce one thing—namely, reciprocal service and friendship accompanied by thanksgiving. So the Holy Spirit distributes many gifts and effects one thing.

But that one temple of God, of which the Apostle says, “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3), the Holy Spirit waters by His infusion, as by a life-giving rain, and preserves from every ruin and corruption. This is the voluntary rain by which sevenfold grace sprinkles the human being. The first guards the door of the heart and does not permit vices to enter. The second reads in the examination of the mind what is to be done and deliberates in order to instruct itself and others. The third cleanses the filth of vices and drives demons from possessed bodies. The fourth, having expelled darkness, introduces works of light. The fifth consists in works of mercy: visiting the poor, receiving pilgrims, washing feet, burying the dead. By the sixth, a person is released from slavery to sin in order freely to serve God. The seventh crucifies a person upon the altar of the cross with vices and desires.

Thus a person performs in himself the office of doorkeeper, reader, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, and priest. By these virtues the inner person is adorned. To signify this, the Church is adorned by the ministry of the aforesaid grades. But those intending to be promoted to these grades first receive the royal sign, marked upon the crown of the head and called a *corona* from its circular shape. The cutting and shaving of the hair show that the vices which spring up and grow must be cut away; the circular form of the tonsure indicates the spiritual kingdom by which they surpass others. “These are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession” (1 Pet. 2). Marked with the aforesaid sign, they are called clerics, because the Lord takes them as His lot (*sors*), and they take the Lord as theirs. Those who at the tonsure say in their person, “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Psalm 15), signify that they belong to the Lord’s portion. Likewise: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob” (Psalm 23). And in another psalm: “The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me” (Psalm 15).

To the glory of this splendid inheritance come Christ’s soldiers who renounce the world, serve God, seek from their labours the necessities of life, cast away superfluities, and despise the world. Therefore they are rightly marked with the royal sign, since they profess themselves heirs of God, destined to reign in a royal and splendid inheritance. The tonsure of the hair appears to have originated among the Nazarenes, who, after completing their vow while preserving their hair, shaved their heads. Hence the apostles instituted that those devoted to divine worship should be consecrated to the Lord with this sign. Having set these matters forth beforehand, let us proceed through the order of the aforesaid grades.

## CHAPTER I. The office of doorkeepers

First are the doorkeepers, whose prudent responsibility is to guard the church door, faithfully protect what has been deposited in the church, close the door against the unworthy, and open it to the worthy: admitting those whom they recognize as fit to be received and excluding those who ought to be repelled. Hence the keys of the church are given to them, the bishop saying: “So act as though you must render an account of the things opened by these keys.” But in order to discern who are [Col. 1276B] worthy or unworthy, the vigilance of the doorkeeper’s ministry requires the help of spiritual grace. For the primitive Church admitted catechumens until the Gospel. After the Gospel, they were commanded to leave, since, not yet called, they were unworthy to share in the sacraments. Pagans also were excluded, since they were altogether alien from the faith. Likewise, the excommunicated are to be excluded from entrance into the church and from participation in the sacraments.

## CHAPTER II. The office and ordination of readers

Second are the readers, who ought to read the canonical Scriptures and pronounce distinctly what they have read, and to understand devoutly and faithfully what they have pronounced. Those who read and pronounce distinctly prepare understanding for their hearers; those who do so confusedly disturb their hearers’ understanding. A reader ought to be endowed with knowledge and equipped with eloquence, so that he knows how to distinguish colons and commas, major and minor divisions, varieties of accent, and what must be pronounced according to *systole* or *diastole*, or enclitically. But unless there is One within who teaches, the tongue of the teacher labours in vain. He must be adorned with good conduct and proved in an honourable life, lest he repel from himself the Spirit who teaches.

They are given to hold in their hands the book of the divine Scriptures, while the bishop commands and exhorts them to exercise their ministry fittingly in these words: “Receive this, and become proclaimers of the word of God. If you fulfil your office faithfully and profitably, you shall have a share with those who have ministered the word of God well.”

## CHAPTER III. The office and ordination of exorcists

[Col. 1276D]

The third order is adorned by exorcists, so called from the power of adjuring, because in faith in the Holy Trinity they expel demons from the bodies of the possessed. They must shine before God and men with purity of life, their filthy vices expelled by the cleansing grace of the Holy Spirit. Those who have authority over unclean spirits must themselves possess a clean spirit. And those who, by the power committed to them, cast malignant spirits out of possessed bodies must, by the spirit of kindness and by clean works, drive vices and impurities from their own hearts, and know how to heal themselves with the medicine which profits others. A physician is not approved who heals another person while unable to cure the disease from which he himself suffers—especially when he and the person whom he heals suffer from the same illness.

Because they have their name from the thing itself, the bishop gives them the book of exorcisms, saying: “Receive it, and have authority to lay hands upon the possessed and catechumens.”

## CHAPTER IV. The office and ordination of acolytes

The office of acolytes, who hold the fourth grade, is to carry a lighted candle with its candlestick before the deacon as far as the lectern; they must hold them while the Gospel is read and while the most holy mystery of the Mass is celebrated. This signifies that, just as they carry visible light in their hands, so they should possess in mind, faith, and action the splendid light that is Christ. By the example of their life and the word of doctrine they are bound to expel darkness from their own hearts and those of others, and to enlighten others by the ray of their own light.

[Col. 1277B] Therefore, because they are candle-bearers in both name and fact, they receive a candlestick with a candle, so that they may know themselves devoted to lighting the lamps. They also receive a cruet, by which authority is given them to pour water into the Lord’s chalice. They are told: “Receive the candlestick with the candle, that you may know yourselves devoted to lighting the lamps of the Church. Receive the cruet, by which you may pour water into the Lord’s chalice.”

## CHAPTER V. The office, ordination, and continence of subdeacons

Subdeacons excel in the fifth grade, not by numerical rank but by the privilege of dignity. Their ministry is to read the Epistle, serve the Levites, prepare the altars, wash the altar-cloths, coverings, and corporals, pour the water of ablutions into the baptistery, [Col. 1277C] and place upon the altar as much of the offerings as may suffice for the people. They approach the ministry of the altar because they carry the vessels in which the Lord’s body and blood are consecrated. Hence the prophetic saying is directed to them: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52).

For this reason, the law of continence, which prepares and preserves purity, is prescribed for them; its observance belongs not to nature but to grace. “What is born of flesh is flesh; what is born of Spirit is spirit” (John 3). They are called subdeacons, as though ordained beneath the Levites in order to serve them. Because they are permitted to approach the altar’s ministry more closely than the other orders mentioned above, they are numbered among the sacred orders.

To signify their office, the bishop gives them the paten and chalice; the archdeacon gives them a water-jug and a hand-towel, with which the priest and Levite, when about to handle the Lord’s sacraments, may wash and cleanse the defilements of their hands. The bishop gives them the maniple, saying: “Receive the maniple; fulfil your ministry. For the Lord is able to increase grace in you.” When clothing him in the tunic, the bishop says: “May the Lord clothe you with the garment of salvation and always encompass you with the clothing of righteousness.”

## CHAPTER VI. That Christ assumed ecclesiastical ministries

Our Lord Himself assumed in His own person the aforesaid ministries, in order to show by His example that they should be assumed with devout devotion and amendment of life. For He who is the unbounded Spirit, the Holy of holies, God made man, bounded within [Col. 1278A] the Virgin’s womb, willed, from His fullness, to apportion to us the anointing of the Holy Spirit by which we are anointed in each order. Therefore whoever approaches to receive orders should carefully guard, by living well, against losing the effect of the spiritual anointing. For the Holy Trinity is driven away wherever foulness of life enters.

Those who pursue profits wickedly acquired by usury, simony, false witness, perjury, and other illicit means drive the anointing from themselves and become filthy with sordid dust. The Lord exercised the office of doorkeeper when, having made a whip from cords, He drove sellers and buyers from the Temple and overturned the seats of the money-changers. This is done spiritually in the Church when Gehazites, Simoniacs, and others who seek shameful profit from God’s freely given gifts are expelled from the fellowship of the faithful. Hence He Himself says: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will enter and go out and find pasture” (John 10). With Him working and leading, he will enter in the present life unto righteousness; and, having faithfully completed the stewardship entrusted to him, he will go out in the future life unto glory.

He was a reader when, in the midst of the elders, He read in the book of Isaiah: “The sweet Spirit of the Lord is upon me; He sent me to preach good news to the poor” (Isa. 61; Luke 3). He showed Himself an exorcist in the casting out of demons and in opening the ears of the deaf and mute, saying, “Ephphatha,” that is, “to open” (John 8). In this He left exorcists the sign that, through their ministry, mouths are opened for confession and hearts for believing and acting well. This occurs when, after the darkness of demonic works has been expelled, they receive the true light, Jesus Christ, into their hearts.

[Col. 1278C] He displayed the office of acolyte in Himself when He said: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness but will have the light of life” (John 8). He displayed that of subdeacon when He poured water into a basin, girded Himself with a linen cloth, and washed the disciples’ feet. In this we are taught that those wash their own feet and those of others who, driving away the dust of earthly desire, wash feet stained by vices with the irrigation of charity which makes glad the city of God, and expel fleshly desires.

## CHAPTER VII. The order or office of deacons

The order of deacons is commended by the authority of the New and Old Testaments, and by the humility of our Lord Jesus Christ in assuming this mystery in Himself. The sixth grade is assigned to it, so that its dignity may be shown through the perfection of the number six. In the Old Testament, after the ordination of Aaron and his sons, instituted by Moses at the Lord’s command, Moses was commanded to appoint the tribe of Levi as an aid to the divine mystery. They were charged with serving before Aaron and his sons in the tabernacle of the covenant. They carried the ark, vessels, and utensils, and, encamping around it, set up the tents. Since a man’s strength increases from the age of twenty and upward, they were commanded at this age to serve in all the aforesaid tasks of transporting, taking down, and setting up again.

Following the example of this institution, the apostles, in the time of grace, chose seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit, and, after prayer, ordained them by laying hands upon them. They were called deacons, as persons devoted to the service of the altar. They are instructed to fold the chasuble upon the same shoulder. For when they are ordained, they must receive the Lord’s yoke, by which they press down and despise everything belonging to the left—that is, temporal life—until, their labours ended, they rest on the right, that is, in eternal and blessed life.

It has been established concerning them by canonical and apostolic ordinance that, when the vicar of Christ enters the Holy of holies, seven standing in the more exalted grade should serve the altar-table, and, marked with sevenfold grace, should have the Holy Spirit as their helper. These are the seven angels sounding trumpets, the seven lampstands, the seven thunders. They ought to be wise, declaring sublime mysteries aloud, as it is written: “Lift up your voice like a trumpet, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift it up; do not fear” (Isa. 58). And again: “Cry out; do not cease” (ibid.).

[Col. 1279B] Their works must be bright, lest, after preaching to others, they themselves be rejected because of shameful life (1 Cor. 9). Their speech should be severe in correcting others, so that in threatening and rebuking (Titus 2) they may seem, in a manner, to send forth thunder. Thus the Lord frightened people by threats, saying: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 8; Luke 3). And blessed Luke: “Brood of vipers, who taught you to flee from the wrath to come?” (Luke 3).

Their office is to summon people to prayer, prompt the bending of knees, and read the Gospel. It also belongs to them to distribute the sacraments of the Lord’s body and to adorn God’s table. [Col. 1279C] The priest, moreover, must receive the Lord’s chalice from the hand of the deacon, in order to avoid presumption. While the priests celebrate, they should assist at the altar clothed in white and possess inwardly the whiteness which they show outwardly, signifying purity of mind, so that those humbly clothed in an outward habit may be spiritually clothed with virtues.

In certain matters they perform the office of priest: in administering baptism, communicating the faithful, and mercifully receiving the confessed sins of penitents. Woe to those who do not devoutly and justly fulfil the ministry committed to them, for they shall perish by a dreadful death. Let them hear what Moses decreed concerning bodily death for the Levites. Under the Law it was forbidden that they should presume to touch the uncovered vessels unless they had first been wrapped by the priest. They feared bodily death; the eternal death of the soul is more to be feared. Therefore, as the Apostle says, “Deacons must be irreproachable,” that is, without crime, continent, not double-tongued, not pursuing shameful gain. “Let each person test himself, and so minister” (1 Tim. 3).

## CHAPTER VIII. When Christ assumed the office of the Levites

The Lord assumed the ministry of Levites when, after supper, He dispensed the sacrament of His body and handed it to His disciples. When He stirred the sleeping apostles to prayer, He showed Himself a Levite. For He said: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation.”

[Col. 1280A] When a deacon is ordained—which ought to occur at the age of twenty-one or above—the bishop alone lays hands upon him, because they are ordained not to the priesthood but to ministry. He also places the stole over the left shoulder, by which they are warned to bear the Lord’s yoke with equanimity and to despise in heart and speech what belongs to the left. The book of the Gospel is given to them, through which they receive authority to read the Gospel and to preach.

> [Note: [Col. 1279] See St Cyprian, Book III, Letter 17; Bellarmine, Book I, *On the Sacrament of Orders*, chapter 6.]

## CHAPTER IX. The order of the priesthood

The order of presbyters, first and highest, is ordained last in the perfection of the number seven. In their figure Aaron and his sons served in the tabernacle of the covenant, as it is written: “Moses and Aaron were among His priests.” In the Law, those who are now called presbyters were called priests; and those then called chief priests are now called pontiffs or bishops. These successors of the apostles ordain others to the ministry of their order.

Presbyters are ordained to be fellow-workers of bishops in governing and instructing the Lord’s flock. Thus Moses chose seventy prudent men, by whose counsel he governed the countless multitude of the people. Hence they take the place of the seven disciples in the ministry entrusted to them. For just as those disciples were sent by the Lord into every city and place where He Himself was about to come, in order to prepare His way by preaching and working miracles and to turn unbelieving hearts to faith, so our presbyters, as fellow-workers, ought to supply our place by baptizing, instructing [Col. 1280C] unlearned peoples, communicating them, and administering the remaining sacraments.

Excepted are those acts in which episcopal dignity shines and takes precedence by a particular prerogative—five in number: dedication of basilicas, anointing with chrism, laying on of hands, ordination of clerics, and blessing over the people. This authority is attributed to bishops alone, lest, if claimed by all, it should generate insolence through the loosening of the bond of obedience.

Both are vicars of the supreme pontiff, who was first offended by original sin and is daily offended by actual sin. To remove the former, He died once upon the cross; to blot out the latter, He willed to be sacrificed through the ministry of priests in repeated immolation. Hence a certain versifier says:

> He died once, though He dies no more;  
> [Col. 1280D] yet the same is daily sacrificed without a wound.

He himself is both sacrificer and sacrifice, victim and priest, because he is God and man. His vicar, because he is only man, is only sacrificer and priest. That Mediator of God and human beings reconciled human beings to God; this one renders the people acceptable to God. That one intercedes at the Father’s right hand for us; this one prays for the flock entrusted to him. That one forgives sins; this one binds and looses. That one offered himself to the Father on the altar of the cross as a holy victim pleasing to God; this one offers that same one upon the table of the altar. But for us, who fall daily, it was necessary to have this author of our salvation present, so that we may be raised up through his intercession. [Col. 1281A]

Therefore merciful God willed, through the repeated immolation, to make himself present to us, though not visibly; so that, with the supreme and true Priest present, the hearts of the faithful might be more deeply contrite without any terror, and devotion of faith might increase. Thus we recall his Passion, resurrection, and glorious ascension. We must recall this in such a way that, mindful of his benefits, we ourselves may be conformed by dying with him, so that through him and with him we may be able to rise again in the glory of the Father. No means was more fitting for stirring sinners to repentance than recalling Christ’s deeds to memory. In his endurance of sufferings he appeared to perform repentance, though he neither repented nor needed the aid of repentance, as it is written: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Col. 1281B] (Isa. 53). Therefore repentance was not in him, but he gave us a model for repentance.

And although Christ’s cross represents all these things, the reality itself is more effective than the figure. And when the giver of pardon is present, the devout sinner has greater confidence of being heard. It is a wondrous power, not human but angelic, which the Lord, taking it upon himself, commended, and showed us to be undertaken with a contrite and humble heart. While at supper, giving his body and blood to his disciples, he said: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22); and he himself undertook it when he patiently and willingly endured the torment of the cross. For he was offered because he willed it. By his example he taught that it should be celebrated by us with the utmost devotion. Hence the Apostle: “Whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup [Col. 1281C] of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11).

Those, therefore, who are about to undertake the charge of the priesthood should shine before the supreme and true Priest in purity of conscience and cleanness of life. When these men are ordained, they are blessed by the bishop holding his hand over their heads. All the presbyters standing by raise their hands with the bishop and invoke the Holy Spirit. When the invocation has been made, a stole is placed over both shoulders, so that they may be armed through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left. A chalice with wine and a paten with a host are given to them; in this is conveyed to them the power of offering victims pleasing to God. For this reason their hands are anointed with holy oil: thereby is signified both the grace of the Holy Spirit offered to them and that they should abound [Col. 1281D] in works of mercy.

Moreover, in this the priest’s hands, marked with holy oil in the form of a cross, are conformed to Christ’s hands; and that notable and saving miracle which is believed to occur between the priest’s hands is effected by these hands of Christ, who said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). Hence the whole sacrifice is performed with him, through him, and in him. Bishops are anointed on the head because they are ordained as vicars of him who was anointed in fullness with the oil of gladness. In the visible anointing, which is the sacrament of spiritual anointing, the power of binding and loosing is given. Clothed with amice, alb, girdle, and stole, they are overvested with a chasuble, by which the pre-eminence of charity is understood.

## CHAPTER X. On the significance of priestly vestments

[Col. 1282A]

Since many have treated of the garments of the old priesthood and their meanings, we shall pass these over in silence and briefly undertake to explain, so far as concerns the present matter, the vestments of the new priesthood and their significations. It should be known that the priest who is about to celebrate the most holy mystery, surpassing every sacrament, takes upon himself the office of his head, namely Christ, whose member he is. His head is covered with the amice, in which the divinity veiled by humanity is figured. Hence in the Apocalypse an angel is said to have descended from heaven clothed with a cloud. The alb signifies the glory of the Lord’s resurrection, when the announcing angels appeared in white garments. [Col. 1282B] Therefore he is clothed in a white garment, so that the new priesthood may be shown to require adornment by the brightness of virtues.

The girdle, by which the alb is drawn tight and fitted about the loins, directs us to that Gospel saying in which the Lord exhorts us to gird our loins (Luke 12). The maniple, with which drops from the eyes are customarily dried, urges us to watchfulness. Hence the Lord says to the disciples: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Mark 14). And elsewhere: “Watch, because you do not know when the Lord will come” (Matt. 13). The stole placed around the neck and descending inward signifies the obedience of the Son of God and the yoke of servitude which he bore for humankind’s salvation. He obeyed the Father unto death on the cross (Phil. 2), and subjected himself to servitude. For what servitude was greater than that in which he endured reproaches, mockery, [Col. 1282C] and scourging? Therefore let one who lays the stole upon his shoulders know that the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden light, which he promised he would bear.

The chasuble, whole on every side, signifies the unity of faith. This is that garment of Aaron upon whose beard the ointment flowed down from his head, and upon the hem of his garment (Ps. 133). By this, moreover, is signified the spiritual anointing by which Christ was anointed above his companions (Ps. 45). This flowed forth upon the apostles and upon all ministers of the Church. The extension of the priest’s hands beyond the chasuble represents Christ’s outstretched hands on the cross. It seems, as it were, to be divided before and behind: this signifies that the two discordant walls are joined in one cornerstone. The amice, for adornment, is folded back over the chasuble, [Col. 1282D] because the whole Church is adorned by the humanity of the Son of God.

## CHAPTER XI. On episcopal ornaments

In addition, bishops use one tunic—or, according to some, two tunics—as well as a ring, pallium, mitre, and sandals. Aaron used a hyacinth-blue tunic, with which the Wisdom of God clothed himself and clothed the apostles, saying: “Everything whatsoever I heard from my Father I have made known to you.” This is that seamless tunic which could not be torn without harm. The other tunic, of silk and deriving its origin from worms, is Christ’s flesh, conceived from the Holy Spirit; he says of himself: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21).

The ring on the finger joins the Church, of which he is minister, as bride to Christ; and by its brilliance it displays the shining gifts [Col. 1283A] of the Holy Spirit. The pallium woven from sheep’s wool is an ornament of humility: for the higher anyone is, the humbler that person ought to be. It is given only to those bishops who are sent from the Apostolic See. The sandals signify that the Divinity came to us shod, as it is written: “Into Idumea I shall extend my shoe” (Ps. 60). The horned mitre represents the crown of thorns, through which the two Testaments came together in one faith: the former piercing sharply, ours gently caressing. The former is bitter; ours is full of sweetness. Woe to those who do not wear it with a repentant heart, for the correction of themselves and others. Woe to those who come down from the cross and portray the mystery of the cross in themselves.

## CHAPTER XII. On the observances in the celebration of Mass

[Col. 1283B]

Adorned fittingly in such vestments, the priest comes to the altar and confesses himself unworthy to celebrate so exalted a mystery, because in the sight of him whose immolation is represented no one is justified except through his grace. In confession, striking his breast, he groans for his sins and asks the Lord, through the prayer of the brethren, to pardon him, saying, “Through my fault”; he promises that he will do penance for those things in which his conscience accuses him. He kisses the Gospel and the altar, signifying him who, by the kiss of his incarnation, made both one through the conversion of Jews and Gentiles. He takes the right-hand side of the altar, because Christ, promised in the Law, preached first to the Jews rather than to the Gentiles. Then the Gentiles held the left side, because they were strangers to divine worship on account of [Col. 1283C] their worship of idols.

Meanwhile the choir sings praises to God from prophetic or apostolic writings; and, sustaining the final vocalization in *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—it begs him to have mercy on them. The thrice-repeated threefold phrase signifies the Trinity of angels, who, in threefold form, ceaselessly chant praises to the supreme Trinity. When the melisma is ended and the choir is silent, the priest turns westward and greets clergy and people, saying, “The Lord be with you,” as though saying: Since he deigned to dwell among you in visible presence, may he remain in you by his indwelling grace; and may he turn your hearts from the approach of unbelief toward the east of the true light. Bishops give this greeting by saying, “Peace be with you.” In this they are shown to be especially Christ’s vicars, for he greeted the apostles in this manner.

[Col. 1283D] On feast days the *Gloria in excelsis*—“Glory in the highest”—is customarily sung. This indicates that we should rejoice in the merits of the saints, who are holy companions of the angels through the grace of him whose birth was announced by angels to shepherds. Then the assembled body of all the clergy raises this praise with a cry, praising God as the multitude of the heavenly host. Afterward, looking eastward—that is, spiritually toward him of whom it is written, “His name is the East” (Zech. 6)—he cries, “Let us pray,” urging himself and others to pray, because the Lord prayed and stirred his disciples to prayer.

When the lesson or epistle has been pronounced, the responsory and *Alleluia* follow. The lesson represents the admonitions and exhortations of the holy Fathers; the epistle, the preaching of those who came after them. The responsory represents the faith of the hearers who [Col. 1284A] gave assent to their preaching; hence it is called a responsory, because a response is assent or agreement according to the wish of those asking. Or it is called a gradual, because one arrives at this through the steps of virtues. For the grace of God must precede those who receive the rudiments of faith; and, that they may remain steadfast, it must follow them. Hence the melody of the Alleluia chant follows, expressing the praises offered to God by the faithful and devout thanksgivings to God, through which they sigh for eternal joys. The word is short, but it is prolonged in a long melisma. Nor is it surprising if the human voice fails in speaking where the mind is not sufficient even for thought; for what voice, what tongue can recount what the Lord has prepared for those who love him? (1 Cor. 2).

The tract, which is sung at certain times while the Alleluia is omitted, [Col. 1284B] signifies the groans and sighs of penitents in the valley of tears. They groan and sigh, and rejoice with the joy of the citizens above, so that the lower stream flowing upward may be mingled with the higher stream. With this groaning sighed he who said: “My soul has melted away” (Song 5). Afterward the Gospel is moved by the deacon, or by the priest, from the right horn of the altar to the left: the right is assigned to the Jews because of their reverence for the Law; the left to the Gentiles because of their detestable idolatry. The Gospel teaching, entrusted to the former, was first rejected by the Jews. Therefore the Gospel is to be read on the left side and toward the north, so that the followers of him who wished to place his throne in the north may be converted from unbelief by Gospel preaching.

Sometimes, as [Col. 1284C] on feast days, it is proclaimed from the ambo, because he who evangelizes Zion is commanded to ascend, and the saints have set ascents in their hearts in the valley of tears; by these ascents, those whose glory is in heaven deserved remembrance on earth. Therefore their victory is proclaimed aloud from on high and in public, so that they may become more eager in battle. Thereupon the priest begins the creed, adding testimony to the words of the Gospel. The choir sings it through to the end, showing that it remains in the unity of the same faith. When it is finished, the priest, having first given the greeting, exhorts them to pray so that they may remain steadfast in the faith which they have professed in word.

Immediately the choir sings the offertory, as though saying: What I have confessed with my mouth I hold in my heart and shall fulfil in deed. First I offer myself, so that our sacrifice [Col. 1284D] may be humility and contrition of heart. Then the priest offers the gifts or offerings with incense: that is, the bread and wine to be consecrated; the people offer their gifts. By incense is signified a sweetness burning with the fire of charity: this is the ointment with which the house was filled, surpassing every aromatic. What I speak of is the Eucharist, namely the sacrament of bread and wine; from it comes every good fragrance and all the sacraments of our faith. Hence it is pre-eminently called *eucharistia*, that is, “good grace,” because in this sacrament he is received from whom every grace is given. For from him alone is every good gift; in him is the fullness of every grace (James 1). Incense in the fire is prayer kindled by charity. The Son of God lit this fire in the censer of assumed [Col. 1285A] humanity, so that, running in the fragrance of his ointments, we may offer him the fragrance of good works.

The gifts to be consecrated, namely bread and wine, reach the altar after being offered in this order. The deacon receives them from the subdeacon and presents them into the priest’s hands; or sometimes, for more diligent care, the priest arranges them on the right side of the altar. The mystery of this is that the Law, signified by the subdeacon, prefigured in its sacrifices the sacrifice of our salvation; Gospel teaching, whose minister is the deacon, revealed it and instituted its solemn celebration. Water is mixed with wine so that the regenerating water may be understood as joined to Christ’s blood. Since no one attains salvation through one without the other, this also signifies the union of Christ and the Church. Both flowed from Christ’s side [Col. 1285B]; this was not without a mysterious purpose.

Bread and wine are prepared for the making of the sacrament, so that things which provide bodily refreshment may become food and saving drink for the soul. For as they sustain the human body and gladden the spirit, so the reality of the sacrament, Christ our Lord, the Son of God, is the joy of human beings and angels, reconciling angels and human beings to himself. Therefore he who is received in the sacrament says: “My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink” (John 6). That bread ought to be wheaten, because the Lord compared himself to a grain of wheat, saying: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone” (John 12). He was one grain and alone before the resurrection; afterward he bore fruit and was multiplied through the propagation [Col. 1285C] of faith. As many faithful people as there are, so many grains are united to that divine grain; from these is made one body, which is Christ and the Church. It is unleavened, so that, according to the Apostle: “Not in the old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5).

When these things have been arranged and the choir is silent, the priest begins to pray silently, signifying that time when our Lord no longer walked openly among the Jews, when they were plotting to kill him, but went away into the region near the wilderness, to the city called Ephraim, and remained there with his disciples. And, bowing before the middle of the altar, he begs God the Father to grant him a spirit of humility, so that in commemoration of the Lord he may be able to offer God [Col. 1285D] a sacrifice of compunction. For humility is a virtue without which no prayer, meditation, or work is acceptable to God, who, instructing us, says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11). For the virginity of blessed Mary was pleasing because of humility, as she herself testifies: “He has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 2).

There follows the invocation of the Trinity, which should be made at the beginning of every speech or work. For he says: “Receive, O holy Trinity,” without faith in whom it is impossible for anything to please God. Then he prays to be helped by the prayers of all who stand by. Turning to the people, he says: “Pray.” And the choir prays for him, saying: “May the Lord send you help from the sanctuary, and defend you from Zion.” It should be known that in the celebration of Mass the priest turns five times toward [Col. 1286A] the people, to recall that the Lord appeared five times on the day of resurrection, consoling those desolated by grief for his Passion.

Having received the spirit of humility, the priest, not presuming upon himself but seeking the gift of prayers from clergy and people so that, interceding with God for himself and for them, he may be heard, says the prayers called “secrets,” because they are uttered secretly and in a humble voice. In this silence is the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, which is customarily celebrated in the week before Easter with hymns and praises discontinued. The Lord also, when his Passion was imminent, prayed secretly before the suspension upon the cross, saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26). While the priest prays silently over the offering, a certain preparation for the holy sacrifice takes place. This represents how, [Col. 1286B] when the Lord hid himself and did not walk openly among the Jews, he was preparing by a hidden dispensation for us the saving mystery of his Passion.

After the miracle of his beloved one raised from death, when he had been walking openly, the priest breaks the silence, crying: “For ever and ever”; and he asks the Lord to be with them, while the choir prays that the Lord may be united to his spirit. He also exhorts them to have their hearts lifted up to the Lord through the assistance of his grace, so that their minds may be on heavenly and eternal things, not earthly and transitory ones. Hearing the choir’s response that their minds are raised to the Lord, he confesses that it is worthy and just to give thanks to him who raises earthly things to heavenly ones and makes what is heavy and weighty flow upward. One rightly gives thanks to God who makes oneself acceptable to him through good works.

[Col. 1286C] In order that praises may worthily be returned by us to God, we must by right living be made like the powers of heaven, so that in rendering thanks there may be one voice of human beings and angels. They praise him unceasingly in glory; let us praise him as much as we can for the mercy shown to us. The Father must be entreated to grant us righteousness and, through the Son’s intercession and the assistance of angels’ prayers, to enable us to attain their glory, through him by whom we give thanks to God Almighty, believing in our hearts and confessing with our mouths; through Jesus Christ, his Son, eternally begotten and born in time, God is praised, adored, and reverently honoured by every human and angelic creature. For through him he creates, gives life to, and preserves all visible and invisible things.

[Col. 1286D] Blessed John declared this plainly, saying: “In the beginning was the Word. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1). Angels in their ministry praise the Father’s majesty through the Son. Dominions adore, bowing beneath the dominion of his footstool. Powers reverence him, because he can do all things and every power is from him. All the heavenly spirits likewise celebrate his praises with unutterable exultation, singing an endless hymn. Therefore the priest prays that human voices may be joined to the praises of the angels through Jesus Christ our Lord, who makes both share in eternal joys.

Then the choir, as though going to meet him with palm branches as he comes from Bethany to Jerusalem, [Col. 1287A] sings the angelic hymn: “Holy, holy, holy,” etc. The threefold repetition of *holy* is a confession of the holy Trinity. Because the Lord is spoken of once, the unity of substance in the persons is signified. Of whose glory heaven and earth are full: that is, angelic and human creation. Therefore, by “Hosanna in the highest,” we seem to beseech that, having attained salvation, we may glory with the angels; because blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, Jesus Christ your Son, through whom you save and bless us.

## CHAPTER XIII. Explanation of the Canon

“Therefore you, etc.” From what has been set forth, it is understood that God the Father is praised and glorified through his Son by every heavenly creature. Then follows the benefit of the glory given and its confirmation. From this understanding [Col. 1287B] the beginning of the Canon is connected with what precedes in this manner: “Since, most merciful Father, through Jesus Christ your Son you are praised together by the angels and heavenly powers, with whom we pray that our voices may be admitted to your praise, therefore through that same your Son we ask and beseech you that what we offer may be pleasing and acceptable to you.”

We ask humbly; we petition confidently. We ask you for the fallen, you who raised up the world lying low in the humility of your Son. We seek from you the saving gift, trusting in your mercy; for you willed to save us not because of works which we ourselves performed, but according to your mercy. We offer bodily food so that from it we may receive spiritual things; we offer bread and wine so that thence we may receive the Word made flesh. The petition is explained [Col. 1287C] by what follows: “That you may receive and bless these gifts, these offerings, these holy sacrifices.” A *donum* is what is given by a superior; a *munus*, what is given by an inferior. Thus bread and wine are gifts given to us by God, and offerings presented by us to God; for we customarily give gifts to those from whom we wish to obtain something. The same things are holy sacrifices, that is, dedicated to God and prepared for the holy sacrifice. They are undefiled: spoiled neither by bodily taste nor by any breaking, but whole and untouched. Thus whole bread must be set forth, and offerings are customarily made from bread and wine.

We pray that you may receive these things, so that through the offering of gifts pleasing to you our devotion may increase, and that, offended by our sins, you may be made favourable to us through their offering; and that you may bless them, so that by your blessing you may make them become that body of your Son which hung on the cross, which was glorified in the resurrection, which was deified in the ascension. They are marked by a threefold cross, showing that the whole mystery is accomplished through the cooperation of the holy Trinity. You should know that from the beginning of the Canon to its end the ordeal of the Lord’s Passion is recalled, especially what was done in the week before Easter.

There follows: “First of all, we offer these things to you for your holy catholic Church, which may you deign to pacify, guard, unite, and govern throughout the whole world, together with your servant our pope, our king, and our bishop, and all orthodox adherents of the catholic and apostolic faith.” [Col. 1288A] Prayer without charity is fruitless: it is a flower without fruit, an ear without grain, a voice striking the air without a hearer. Hence the Prophet: “If I have regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me” (Ps. 65). Charity consists in three things: love of God, of oneself, and of one’s neighbour. Therefore the priest ought to exclude no believer from prayer, which is made more pleasing to God through mutual charity.

Thus the priest first prays generally for the whole catholic Church, that the Lord may deign to pacify it from the assault of visible and invisible enemies, preserve it in tranquillity, and unite it—that is, preserve it in unity of faith—lest it be divided by the errors of heretics or schismatics; but that the unity of head and members may be preserved in faith in the sacraments; and govern it, so that all things [Col. 1288B] within it may be done and ordered by the direction of justice. Then, with a certain distinction, he enumerates the parts of the Church, saying: “Together with your servant our pope,” etc. For just as administrations are diverse, so prayers must vary. One concern must be given to public affairs, another to private matters, another to secular business, and another to ecclesiastical matters.

In another way ecclesiastical persons—such as the lord pope, archbishops, and bishops—require prayer for themselves; in another, the king and each of the faithful. Since unbelievers are not in the Church, they are not of the body of the Church, whose head is Christ; one alien to the faith has no share in it. And although prayers vary according to the differing persons, their intention is nevertheless brought to one end. For prayer should thus be made for all the faithful, [Col. 1288C] that they may be withdrawn from harmful things and directed toward saving ones: “Remember, O Lord, thy servants and handmaids.”

In the preceding chapter prayer is made generally for the Church; then, distinguishing the parts of the Church, we pray for the pope and the bishop, for the king, for all the orthodox—that is, for those whose glory is the rightness of Christian faith, their conscience bearing witness to holy meditation and honorable conduct—and also for those who cultivate the faith with the ploughshare of preaching and the seed of good work. But in this following chapter we pray for those close to us, absent and present; for those standing by, namely all who are present at the mystery of the altar. “Communicating, whose faith is known to God [Col. 1288D] and whose devotion is recognized.” For God alone searches hearts and reins: to him every heart lies open and every will speaks. Or: those whose faith God approves; for to know, in his case, is to approve.

For all those mentioned above we offer the sacrifice of praise, and they themselves offer it to God, rendering thanksgivings to him who willed to be praised, blessed, and glorified by us through his Son. We offer in deed; they offer in faith and devotion. We offer by celebrating the sacraments; they offer by fulfilling vows: they sacrifice a sacrifice of praise and render their vows to the Most High. Helped by the power of the sacrament, they restrain vices and sins, building up virtues and good works and vowing them to God. We offer wine, and they offer the oblation of a holy and devout mind. Thus we offer for ourselves [Col. 1289A] and for them; they for themselves and for us. Hence above we asked to be helped by their prayers, saying, “Pray for us.”

It must also be known that where we prayed for the whole Church, we prayed for these persons too. Yet we make particular remembrance of absent and present intimates, and of others standing by, so that the affection of our devotion toward them may be increased. Hence we are accustomed to name here those whom we hold dearer. The general prayer may also be repeated thus: “Remember, O Lord, thy servants and handmaids,” namely all faithful persons bodily absent and those standing by here. For prayers ought to be repeated, because by persistence in prayer God is often appeased and becomes favorable to our petitions.

Likewise, it should be known that, if only one person is present, or none [Col. 1289B] is present, as in solitary Masses, the prayers that are customarily made in the plural are not for that reason altered. At first, Masses were not customarily celebrated without a gathered multitude of the faithful. Later the practice developed of celebrating solitary Masses, as monks do; this was granted them by dispensation. From this secular clergy too became accustomed to sing private Masses. Then the salutations are made to all the faithful who stand by, as though present in faith and sharing in the sacraments through charity. For all who belong to Christ’s body, which is the Church, are greeted; and the intercessory help of those is sought whose faith, through God’s grace, aids in the performance of such great mysteries.

Nor is there any one of the faithful who does not share in the sacraments. Those who have been cut off from the body—which is the true vine—who are branches and putrid members, [Col. 1289C] are alien to this sacrament. For from the head into the members of the whole body, and from the vine into the branches, saving moisture is poured forth through the grace of God that gives life to the whole body. Thus, with one person present, the priest addresses and greets many, because the whole Church stands present. For the individual members adhere to one another, and to the head and body, so long as they are enlivened by the Spirit of God.

Hence it is that not only priests and clergy, who according to the ordering of ministries are occupied with diverse offices or offer this sacrifice with divine praises, cooperate; those also who receive the kiss of peace among the hearers cooperate, and all the faithful wherever they may be are included. None are separated except those who are cut off from Christ’s body. For all the members of this body, so long as they hold together [Col. 1289D] by the bond of charity, are as it were one person. Those divided from this unity and expelled from communion in the sacraments are strangers to Christ’s kingdom and to the Church.

The reason for the offering is added when it is said, “for themselves and all theirs.” They were offering for the salvation of their own souls and for all theirs; that is, for their friends and possessions and those of their friends: for their peace, for the return of travelers, for the health of the sick, for the conversion of those in error, for the fruits of the earth, for clear weather, for the acquisition or preservation of other benefits, and for the attainment of favorable success. For in him we have consolation for the present life and the future one: “for the redemption of our souls, for the hope of our salvation and [Col. 1290A] well-being.”

Our redemption was accomplished when Christ suffered once upon the cross. For through Christ’s passion we were redeemed and delivered from the hand of hell. As our sins demand, we fall daily; from this fall we rise and are renewed by the repeated immolation which takes place on the altar. The immolation is repeated; Christ is not killed, but, he being present, his passion is represented. Through overflowing mercy, the price was greater than our offense: for God became man and died, so that man might be made divine and might not die. He who gave himself could not give more. But if God could not give a greater price, what shall we render to him? We offer him the cup of the saving sacrifice, by which we are redeemed, delivered, and also saved, having the blessed hope of rising again with the salvation of our souls [Col. 1290B] and the incorruption of our bodies.
