Those mentioned above offer and render their vows to you—not to idols, not to demons, but to you, the living and true God. “Communicating and venerating the memory.” Otherwise, they could not fittingly offer to God or render vows unless they communicated worthily; for outside communion with the faithful and veneration of the saints there is no place for offering the true sacrifice. The prayers of the faithful and the intercessions of the saints assist, so that offerings and vows may become acceptable to God. Seeking their intercession, we venerate them, and Christ in them, who bestowed so much upon his saints that we may be helped by their merits and prayers. “He who honors the Son honors also the Father who sent him.”

In the remembrance and veneration of the saints, this order should be observed: [Col. 1290C] first the blessed Virgin, lady and queen of human beings and angels, is remembered; secondly the powers of heaven; thirdly remembrance is made of patriarchs and prophets; fourthly of apostles; fifthly of martyrs; sixthly of confessors; seventhly of virgins. These follow the Lamb wherever he goes. As the gift of graces is sevenfold, so this sevenfold division was made by the ordering of the Holy Spirit.

Before the consecration, remembrance is made of many martyrs who washed their robes white in the blood of the Lamb and, crowned with him, know God not with veiled face but by manifest vision. Venerating these in remembrance, we pray that the intercession of the blessed Virgin, who surpasses all saints, and of them may be a saving propitiation for us. We do not attend to the number—why there are more or fewer—because the one who arranged the canon established, as the Holy Spirit prompted him, whom he pleased to remember.

Therefore, because we offer this oblation in the unity of the holy Church with veneration of the saints, aided by their intercession, we ask concerning this oblation of our service—that is, of our humility, which is ready to serve you, fulfill vows, and offer you a sacrifice of praise. He significantly added “of service,” with reference to what was said above: “May we be received by thee, O Lord, in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart.” This offering is not the priest’s alone, but that of the whole household, that is, clergy and people—not merely the household standing by, but the whole Church. “This, we beseech thee, graciously receive.” Though you may be angered with us because of our sins, [Col. 1291A] we ask that you may be made gracious through the prayers of the faithful and the intercession, merits, and prayers of the saints.

From him, when gracious, we ask three things: that our days be kept in peace, that we be delivered from eternal damnation, and that we be numbered among the elect. There is no middle state between hell, where damnation is, and heaven, where blessedness and salvation are. For all who are not damned are without doubt saved. Thus there appears to be a redundancy of words when it is said, “to be delivered from damnation” and “to be numbered among the elect.” But this must be understood with regard to the present: make us now worthy not to be damned, so that in the future we may be saved through God’s grace.

It should be noted that there is a twofold peace of the world. One is that for which the Church prays: that the disturbances of the malicious and hostile attacks may cease. [Col. 1291B] The other is destructive and altogether to be avoided, since it allows people, without opposition, freely to indulge the desires of the flesh and their pleasures. The first is peace, but transitory; the second is not peace, but hateful disorder and iniquity.

Likewise, the peace of God, which is to be desired in every way, is twofold. One is tranquility of mind and the repose of holy meditation, of which it is written: “My soul chose hanging.” The other is that which surpasses every understanding, in which there is no unrest, no alternation of disturbances, but eternal blessedness (John 14). The Lord promised and gave both to his disciples, saying: “My peace I give to you; peace I leave to you” (Phil. 4). He leaves peace to those who are in conflict; he gives his own peace to those who come to him. Since both kinds of peace are from God, [Col. 1291C] his own peace is properly called peace beyond peace, surpassing all comprehension of the senses.

Having remembered those for whom we offer and whom we intend to reconcile to God the Father through the mediating and interceding victim, we ask that the oblation may have the effectiveness and power to confer what we seek; we ask that it be advanced to the better and inscribed in eternity, and be made ratified—that is, firm and immovable. We pray that the food of human beings may become the food of angels: namely, that the offering of bread and wine may be transubstantiated into the body and blood of Jesus Christ, who is the blessed offering, that is, full of the blessing of every grace, from whose fullness we have all received. For the Father does not give to the Son by measure, but the fullness of all graces has been given to him. He is he upon [Col. 1291D] whom rests the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord (John 3).

From his anointing ointment descends upon the beard of the high priest and flows down to the hem of his garment. He is the living fountain, the well of living waters, from which all streams of mercy, piety, and justice are derived. To him belong every kind of blessing and sanctification, by his inscription in the eternity of the Father and his equality with the Father’s majesty. The Son of God is called the “inscribed offering,” designated in the Scriptures of the holy Fathers and not liable to be erased by any oblivion; and therefore “ratified,” that is, firm and immovable—made firm in the state of immortality and incorruption, abiding forever and sufficient [Col. 1292A] to grant salvation and forgiveness of sins.

The Son is also in some manner called inscribed in relation to the Father, because Scripture, speaking of the Son, reveals the Father and, as it were, represents him. For he is the brightness of the Father’s glory and the figure of his substance. Hence he says to the Father: “Father, I have made thy name known to human beings.” He is the book of life, in which and through which the Father, disposing all things, writes and brings them into being. Hence it is written: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” The Father is the scribe writing swiftly; the Son is the writing containing all things. In him the Father engraved the forms of all things, and through him creates, governs, and orders all things. Hence the Prophet says: “Thou hast made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 10).

He is likewise the rational offering, [Col. 1292B] not a particular one. For although the blood of bulls and cattle sufficed for cleansing the flesh, it was not effective for cleansing the spirit or redeeming us from sins. Hence, for the redemption of humankind, a rational victim had to be offered: namely, the man assumed by the Word, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh. This alone suffices for the redemption of humankind, and none other could suffice: neither a human being nor an angel, but only the God-man. This alone is the propitiation acceptable to God for the offenses of all.

We may, however, refer the three preceding terms to the oblation and the two following terms to the offerer. For one who offers rationally divides rightly; therefore that person’s offering is acceptable. Thus, because Abel offered rightly and divided rightly, the Lord looked upon [Col. 1292C] his gifts. But upon Cain and his gifts he did not look, because, though Cain offered rightly, he did not divide rightly: he kept for himself an unrepentant heart. That person divides badly who does not give to God what most pleases him, namely a contrite and humbled heart. Such a person gives and offers external things to God but keeps himself for himself. Therefore, if anyone offers rightly and divides rightly, the victim is rational and acceptable; otherwise it is fruitless. Hence the Prophet: “If I looked upon iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear” (Ps. 65).

Thus it is for some unto resurrection, for others unto ruin: for those who divide rightly, salvation and eternal life; for those who do so badly, death and perpetual misery.

What the priest prays—that the oblation of bread and wine may become the body of the Lord and the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—was first accomplished while the disciples were at supper, through these words uttered by Christ: “This is my body. This is the cup of my blood of the new and eternal covenant.” But before the priest utters these words, he joins what follows to what precedes, saying: “Who, on the day before he suffered, took bread into his holy and venerable hands; and, lifting his eyes to heaven, to thee, his almighty God and Father, giving thee thanks,” etc. While he speaks these words, he takes the bread from the altar and, having raised it, blesses it by making the sign of the cross; afterward, having uttered and represented the aforesaid words of the Lord, he places it upon the corporal. Then he lifts the chalice and, making the sign, represents the Lord’s words, saying: “He blessed it, gave it to his disciples, saying: [Col. 1293A] Take and drink of this, all of you. This is the cup of my blood,” etc.

O outstanding miracle! O wonderful and most divine sacrament! What mind does not tremble? What understanding does not fail? Every sense is blunted; every reasoning vanishes. Let the investigation of dialecticians be wholly absent: faith alone proves and recognizes this, because the food of human beings becomes the food of angels. What the priest raises, he does not set down. What is raised and what is set down seem the same in appearance, color, and taste; nevertheless, one thing appears openly and another lies hidden within. Common bread is raised from the altar; the immortal flesh of Christ is set down. What was animal food has become spiritual food. What was the momentary refreshment of human beings has become the eternal and unfailing fullness [Col. 1293B] of angels.

## Chapter XIV. Question concerning Christ’s blessing of the bread at supper

Since the Lord blessed the bread at supper, the question is raised whether by his blessing he made his body out of the bread. This seems to be so because, after the blessing, he broke it and gave it to his disciples, saying: “This is my body.” Unless it became his body through his blessing, he would have broken and given his disciples nothing other than common bread.

Likewise, if by his blessing he converted the bread into his body in these words, “This is my body,” he did not leave us the power of the sacrament; for before he said these words, he blessed, broke, and, while giving it to his disciples, uttered the aforesaid words, thereby giving them the power of the sacrament, [Col. 1293C] as though he were saying: “The bread which I took, I transubstantiated into my body, and I give that to you.” Therefore we teach and believe that, when he blessed, he made his body, and that in the words “This is my body. This is the cup of my blood,” etc., the power of the sacrament was given. For “he spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 148).

Therefore it must be understood that the words uttered by the Lord were first said and then repeated. For it should be read thus: “He blessed, saying: ‘This is my body.’” Then he broke it and gave it to his disciples, again saying: “This is my body.” Or it may be that, after making the blessing, while handing his body to the disciples, he uttered the aforesaid words, thereby giving them the power of the sacrament.

## Chapter XV. What should be believed concerning the sacramental words

[Col. 1293D]

Therefore this is our faith, and it must truly be believed, that when the priest utters these words, “This is my body,” it is no longer earthly bread but that bread which came down from heaven, Jesus Christ, mediator of God and human beings. Likewise, through the power of these words, “This is the cup of my blood,” etc., wine is converted into his blood. Under each species, and under each individual particle of either species, the whole Jesus Christ is present and received: he remains in heaven, seated at the right hand of the Father; he himself is truly in this sacrament, is ground by teeth, and remains whole. He is eaten and is not corrupted; he is immolated and does not die. As he offered himself to the disciples for eating, so he offers himself [Col. 1294A] to us for communion; and he who, after the resurrection, though incorruptible and impalpable, presented himself palpable to the disciples, could, while mortal, give himself immortal to those same disciples.

## Chapter XVI. Question concerning the words, “Take and eat”

Likewise, since the Lord said to his disciples, “Take and eat,” the question is raised whether they took it and ministered it to themselves. To this we say that, because he came to minister and not to be ministered to, and because he who consecrated also ministered, he himself served it. Nor should it be understood that they took it in their own hands and ministered it to themselves; rather, the Lord ministered it from his own hand and commanded them to eat.

The Lord does not appear to have taken this chalice at supper, since perhaps the one taken by the Lord was earthenware or wooden, while this one is silver or [Col. 1294B] gold, or of another metal. Therefore it must be known that this statement is to be referred to likeness, not identity. For just as the Lord, while at supper, took wine in a chalice and, blessing it, made it his blood, so in this chalice the priest takes wine, and by the power of the words uttered by the Lord at supper it becomes his blood. Thus there is likeness in the taking of wine, identity in the truth of the sacrament. For every day the consecration takes place of that same blood which the Lord administered at supper.

Accordingly, the chalice is called splendid, not because wine is contained in it, but because what is consecrated from the wine is in it. The brilliance of the chalice is not attributed to its shine, but to the dignity of the sacrament. Nevertheless, if we consider [Col. 1294C] the unity of faith before and after consecration, it is one chalice, just as faith is one and the Church is one—one dove, one beloved, as in the Song of Songs. Of this chalice it is written: “My inebriating cup—how splendid it is!” (Ps. 22).

The phrase “this is the chalice of my blood” should be read with the container understood for the content, thus: “This is my blood of the new and eternal covenant,” with “confirming” understood. For in his passion the Lord abolished the shadow of the law and confirmed an inheritance for his heirs. A testament is ratified by the death of the testator. It is called a mystery, that is, a secret of faith, because what is hidden from our senses is revealed to faith. Human reason asks, saying: *manhu?*—“What is this?” [Col. 1294D] “How is it?” It does not comprehend the “how”; it does not ascend to this secret. Faith alone believes and recognizes.

To the senses, bread and wine appear in taste and color; faith contemplates under each species its Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To the senses appears what is not; to faith, what is. The senses judge what they see to be inanimate, and it appears to the senses of all living beings as bodily food; to faith it is the living bread which descended from heaven, indeed bread of angels, the living fountain of water springing up to eternal life. Faith believes and loves him through whom it hopes for sins to be forgiven, pardon to be given, and itself to be refreshed and satisfied in his glory. Hence the Apostle: “Faith is the substance of invisible things, the proof of things not appearing” (Heb. 11).

From faith [Col. 1295A] our hope is firm and has substance, charity is strengthened, and the things to be hoped for are proved. The Lord’s blood was shed for many, namely those called to faith, not for Jews, pagans, heretics, and those persisting in unbelief. Yet, according to that manner of speaking in which it is said, “The Lord came to save all,” and “he enlightens every human being coming into this world,” it may be said to have been shed for all. He offered the cup of salvation to all: some received it, while others refused to receive it—just as a physician comes to cure a sick person but does not cure one who, through negligence, does not keep his instructions.

Whenever we celebrate these sacraments, we ought to keep the Lord’s passion in memory and give thanks to Christ in heart and deed for his death: he who, through the tasting of humanity he assumed, invites us to a taste—that is, to love and knowledge—of his divinity. Therefore, in order to renew the remembrance of his passion, the Lord says with tearful affection to those about to approach this sacrament: “As often as you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me” (Luke 22). [Col. 1295B] For he knew that the memorials of writings were not sufficient for this, and that the souls of those following him would not be moved by the Scriptures to love him with as great a devotion as they would be moved by his presence itself.

For who can represent this immolation without sorrowful compunction? Who, holding in their hands their Lord crucified and dead for them, can, like a wicked servant forgetful of benefits, despise the testament which he wrote with his death? Here the justice of faith grows warm in the furnace of charity, [Col. 1295C] where the fire does not burn but illumines, does not consume but builds up. Hence, when the Lord, speaking to his disciples, said, “Where I go, you cannot come” (John 8), he commended his remembrance to them, so that, in remembrance of him, they might strive to follow him by celebrating these sacraments. When Peter asked, “Lord, where are you going?” the Lord answered: “Where I go, you cannot follow me now; but you shall follow afterward” (John 13).

## Chapter XVII. A threefold question concerning the matter of the sacrament of the altar
This point, however, must not be passed over: why bread and wine are offered for the making of this sacrament; whether the body and blood of the Lord are consecrated under both species or under one only; and why the offering [Col. 1295D] is made with unleavened bread rather than leavened. Three things in this sacrament challenge faith and urge the mind that thinks rightly and understands faithfully to believe: one is the species of bread and wine; another, the body and blood of the Lord; and again, the union of the members and the head. The first appears to the senses; the second is disclosed to faith; the third is effected by the power of the sacrament. The first is apprehended by sense; the second is beheld and believed by faith; the third is saving grace, through which Christ and the Church are two in one flesh. The second is the reality of the first; the third, the effect of the second. For the species of bread and wine is only a sacrament—that is, a visible sign of a sacred and invisible reality. What is seen is a sign of what is not seen.

[Col. 1296A] Earthly bread is seen, by which the flesh is refreshed, and wine, by which it is gladdened; yet it is not this, but the heavenly bread—the living bread that came down from heaven—by which the soul is filled, or rather by which fullness of joy is given, and thirst is quenched in unending gladness: he who drinks of it shall never thirst. Of this bread the Lord says: “My flesh is truly food”; and of this wine: “My blood is truly drink”; and again he says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6). The body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ are called the reality of the sacrament, hidden under the aforesaid species; and they are the sacrament of the reality, namely, of that grace and love which are bestowed. Thus the first is sacrament only; the second is both the reality of the sacrament and a sacrament; [Col. 1296B] the third is reality only, and not a sacrament.

It must be known that there is a twofold reception of the body and blood of the Lord: sacramental and spiritual. Both good and evil persons partake sacramentally; only the good partake spiritually. Of sacramental participation the Apostle says: “He who eats the flesh and drinks the blood of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11). Of spiritual participation the Lord says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6); and blessed Augustine says: “Believe, and you have eaten.” This must be understood where there has not been contempt for religion but an occasion of necessity.

Thus Christ’s flesh is twofold: that which was born of the Virgin and is received in the sacrament; and that which is eaten by believing faithfully, [Col. 1296C] without which the sacramental reception is of no benefit. For God has declared, saying: “The flesh profits nothing; it is the spirit that gives life” (ibid.); as though he said: To receive my flesh and drink my blood profits nothing unless it is received through faith and love. For although the Lord said, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3), nevertheless many have entered the kingdom of God baptized in their own blood. So to eat Christ’s flesh is to receive it in spirit and truth. This reception is unto salvation for all, but unto condemnation for none. Hence the Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6). Sacramental [Col. 1296D] reception is life to some and ruin to others. In such persons the effect of faith and love alone is rewarded.

This sacrament is made from bread and wine to signify that, as bread strengthens the human heart and wine gladdens it, so this sacrament is strength and salvation, and the perfect joy of bodies and souls. It is made from wheaten bread, because this is truly that grain of which the Lord said: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone” (John 12). Christ alone descended and died; he did not ascend alone, because in his Passion he germinated, grew, and bore fruit into an innumerable harvest. The holy Roman Church offers with unleavened bread, that, the old leaven having been purged out, we may be refreshed with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

[Col. 1297A] The Greeks, however, offer with leaven, to signify the swollen womb of the Virgin made pregnant by the Holy Spirit. This does not accord with the teaching of the holy Fathers, because in sacred speech leaven is never found to be taken in a good sense. When, in our customary way of speaking, it is said that the body and blood are received, do not understand them as received separately, since Christ himself is received whole and entire: whole under each species of bread and wine, and whole under every particle of either species. Hence bread and wine do not pass into the divine nature, but into the human substance. For we believe that in Christ there were two natures, divine and human, and three substances: divinity, flesh, and soul, as Athanasius [Col. 1297B] attests when he says: “As rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ.” He is the one who is eaten and received in the sacrament—not as another food is incorporated into the one who eats it, but rather the one who eats must be incorporated into him through faith and love.

He is not received in his proper form, lest the human mind recoil, and so that faith may be proved. In preparing the bread and wine, water is mixed with wine, so that it may be recalled that both flowed from the Lord’s side; and this also signifies that we are saved through water and blood. By water I mean baptism; by blood, that of Jesus Christ. Neither benefits if the other is lacking. Whenever we perform this rite, we proclaim or represent the Lord’s death. Therefore, lest the memory of the Lord’s Passion slip from our hearts, but so that, crucifying [Col. 1297C] ourselves with our vices and desires, dead to sin and alive to God, we may rise to life through the intercession of that same Son, we offer these most sacred things. This is what follows: “Wherefore, remembering,” etc.

All offer who stand in the unity of the Church through faith and works. Although the Lord performed many wonderful and unheard-of things in the ministry of our redemption, commemoration is made of three of them—his Passion, resurrection, and ascension—through which our salvation was brought to completion. The Lord’s body and blood are gifts and things given: for gifts are, or are called, those things which remain in the giver’s power; things given are in the recipient’s hand. Thus these gifts are eternal and were given to us in time. He who is offered is himself the pure, [Col. 1297D] holy, and spotless victim: the Lamb without blemish, “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). He was a pure victim in the Passion, holy and immortal in the resurrection, glorious and radiant in the ascension.

He is bread of life: not the bread which is seen, but that by which human beings and angels are nourished. Human beings use it as medicine; angels, in the glory of delight. This bread gives in the present life the glory of justification and, in the future, ineffable joy with the angels. Since the reality of the sacrament is one and the same, and the body is not without the blood nor the blood without the body, nevertheless we speak separately and in the plural, not because the realities are distinct, but because the forms of the species differ. And when blood is named in the chalice, and body outside the chalice, let both God and man be believed to be present both in the chalice and outside the chalice.

[Col. 1298A] Someone may say or ponder: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John 6). Let him attend to the one who works, consider the Almighty, and he will cease to wonder, because “whatever he willed, he did” (Ps. 113). We make the sign of the cross five times, not in order to sanctify him from whom all sanctification comes, but so that we may sorrowfully and devoutly recall the wounds of him hanging on the cross: two in the hands, two in the feet, and the fifth in the side. This continues until the corporal is lifted from over the chalice.

After the consecration we ask the Father to look upon the aforesaid gifts and hold them acceptable. But since nothing is more acceptable to the Father than the Son, whom, with gracious and serene countenance, he always beholds as God equal to himself, what else do we ask but that, through the Son’s mediation and intercession, God may become merciful and propitious to us, and that through him who pleases God we too may please him? Thus we ask that through these sacrifices he may become mercifully propitious to us, just as he had mercy on the fathers by being propitiated through their sacrifices.

[Col. 1298B] This comparison, therefore, must be understood as likeness alone, not as equality of quantity; nor must it be referred to the sacrifices, but to the vows of those who offer. The reality is greater than the figure. The Eucharist surpasses every sacrifice; yet the likeness is such that, by offering rightly, we may resemble our fathers who offered rightly and divided rightly. Three of them are named because in their sacrifices the victim was prefigured by whom hell was shattered.

Abel offered God a contrite and humbled heart; committing himself wholly to God, he did not keep himself for himself. He offered rightly and divided rightly; therefore the Lord looked upon his offerings. [Col. 1298C] Cain, however, sinned because, although in rendering to God the offerings he owed he offered rightly, he divided wrongly, because he kept himself for himself. He looked upon iniquity in his heart, and therefore God did not hear him. Abraham offered himself wholly to God; God tested him by commanding him to sacrifice his son (Gen. 22). Melchizedek set his heart on high, and therefore deserved to know beforehand and, in the figure of sacrifice, to offer bread and wine.

Thus, if we wish—as we pray—to be made like our fathers, let us not offer our heart to God through iniquity, but place our heart upon the high altar, that is, in the sight of the divine majesty. By living soberly, piously, and justly, we shall find him merciful and propitious to us. This is what we pray in what follows, saying: “Command [Col. 1298D] these things to be borne by the hands of your holy angel”; not that Christ, who stands before the Father’s face interceding for us, may always ascend to the Father by change of place, but that our devotion may be carried through the hands of the holy angel—that is, through your Son, who is your right hand, by whom you accomplish all things, and the Angel of Great Counsel, through whom you minister, order, create, sanctify, and bless all things. He himself is the Father’s presence, that is, the wisdom through which the Father makes and orders all things. Therefore through him, in him, and before him we pray that our petitions may be borne.

For who can bear them except he who says to the Father: “Father, you always hear me” (John 11), and in whom the Father created heaven and earth and established all things? What is received at the altar does not profit without spiritual grace. Therefore we pray [Col. 1299A] that, while visibly receiving the body and blood from the altar, we may invisibly be nourished at the invisible altar with the invisible flesh of Christ, from which blessing and grace are given to all who receive; and that from him who is bodily present on the visible altar every grace of blessing may be given. He who sits at the Father’s right hand is at the altar, mighty in heaven and on earth; he is everywhere, ascending into heaven and descending into hell: you will always find him.

We often repeat the signs of the cross; whenever we make them, we proclaim the Lord’s Passion and death. When we say, “To us also, sinners,” we raise the voice a little, so that from the groaning of the heart in silence may proceed the groaning confession of the mouth. Before the consecration and here also, we recount the names of the saints, asking for their intercessions and looking not to their number but to their assisting aid. [Col. 1299B] There commemoration is made of the blessed Virgin, who surpasses all the saints, and of the apostles and martyrs who have been made white in the blood of the Lamb, so that through the help of their intervention this ministry may avail for our salvation. Here we commemorate the saints so that they may have compassion on us sinners.

For God customarily becomes propitious to us out of reverence for his saints, granting forgiveness of sins. The Lord has shown this by manifest proofs, signs, and miracles, bestowing healing on the sick and consolation on the desolate to their praise and glory—which is his own. For one who honors the members also honors Christ, who is the head; and one who honors the Son also honors the Father who sent him (John 5), through whom the Father creates, sanctifies, gives life, and blesses these goods.

[Col. 1299C] Thus, as we have said, there is one single reality in the sacrament: Christ, God and man. Hence, in the figures and names by which the same reality is described, plurality appears; and where there is only one thing in substance, multiplicity is seen in figure. We speak of the Lord’s body sometimes as it is and sometimes as it appears. Thus, in our customary speech, we say: “We distribute many hosts in communicating; we reserved so many,” and we therefore call them several hosts, although we believe there to be one.

Nor is it surprising if the propriety of words fails where an ineffable sacrament is dispensed. The Father created nature through his Word and through the same Word gave grace; and although the creation of the universe belongs to the whole Trinity, the repair of our ruin belongs to the Son alone. [Col. 1299D] In making three signs of the cross, we portray them in honor of the saving cross, through which our redemption was accomplished: Life died upon the wood, and from the streams of blood and water flowing from it came forth all sanctification, life, and blessing. Hence such great grace is given to a human being that one who performs the rite worthily is sanctified, given life, and filled with every blessing.

The sacrament itself is sanctified and blessed through the power of the cross as the priest ministers, when the inanimate body passes into a life-giving one. These gifts are granted us daily when the body and blood are received at the altar. Therefore, because the Father works all things through the Son, he sanctifies and blesses through the Son himself, because the Son made the Father known to human beings; and with him, who is equal [Col. 1300A] and coeternal with the Father; and in him, who is “the brightness and image of his substance” (Heb. 1), and in whom the Father is wholly present and he himself wholly in the Father. To God the almighty Father be all honor and glory.

Here we make three signs, as though: through him who was crucified; and with him who died on the cross; and in him who is life, to God the Father be all honor and glory. For through the Son the Father is glorified, and in the Son he is honored. Hence it is written: “He who honors the Son honors him who sent him” (John 5). Here again we customarily make two signs of the cross, recalling the water and blood which flowed from the Son’s side. For he came through water and blood, that through faith in his Passion and the water of regeneration he might cleanse and sanctify us.

How the agony of the Lord’s Passion is represented in the order of the Canon, and [Col. 1300B] how truth was veiled beneath the ancient figures (Exod. 12), we have judged it worthy to explain, as it were by recapitulation, for the consideration of more diligent instruction. Matters treated in summary and in the order in which they occurred appear more clearly than if each were noted in its own place.

It must therefore be known that from the beginning of the Canon, namely, *Te igitur*, to the end, the events performed in the week following Palm Sunday are recalled. For as the paschal lamb was taken from the flock on the tenth day of the moon in the homes of the Jews and was sacrificed in the evening on the fourteenth, so our Lamb, Christ Jesus, saving and giving us life, came into Jerusalem on the fourteenth day to celebrate the paschal lamb, while the Hebrew people acclaimed him with praises: “Hosanna to the Son of David; [Col. 1300C] blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Luke 12). This is signified by the choir’s response, singing together: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth.”

The silence that follows that chant signifies the certain recollection of the approaching Passion and the words written: “Jesus no longer walked openly because of fear of the Jews.” That the mystery of the Passion begins with *Te igitur* is indicated by the signs of the cross placed immediately afterward. On the day called Palm Sunday, he begins to give himself up into the hands of the Jews. On Wednesday he is betrayed by Judas, in token of which a threefold sign of the cross is made. But on Monday and Tuesday they did not dare lay hands on him for fear of the Jews; on those days, however, he taught in the Temple, fearing nothing of the fury of those who plotted against him.

[Col. 1300D] The legal high priest entered the Holy of Holies once a year with blood, prefiguring him who entered heaven with his own blood (Heb. 9). The priest approaching this mystery with blood represents this: namely, that with tearful devotion he keeps in mind the memory of the Lord’s Passion. On Thursday—of which it is said, “the day before he suffered”—he celebrated the old Passover; and, bringing it to an end, delivered his body and blood to his disciples. During the following night he is bound, seized, and mocked with many insults. On Friday he is crucified. On Saturday he was in the tomb. On the third day he rose, announcing to his disciples peace for the whole world.

When “To us sinners” is said, the silence is customarily broken by uttering it in a slightly subdued voice, so that the confession of the thief and the Lord’s mercy in saying from the cross, “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23), may come to mind. When the words are reached, “Through whom [Col. 1301A] you create all these things,” the Lord’s word, “It is finished” (John 19), is recalled, as also that, crying with a loud voice, he gave up the spirit, and the veil of the Temple was torn. One corporal cloth is lifted from over the chalice. When the corporal is removed and “Through him” is said, it expresses the confession of the centurion, who, seeing the earthquake, confessed the Word of God.

Then the priest and deacon lift the chalice a little from the altar and set it down again, because Joseph, the centurion, and Nicodemus, having received permission from Pilate, took the body down from the cross and buried it. Hence the chalice is covered again with the corporal. And because a great outcry was made at the Lord’s death, both from the lamentation of the women and from the voice of the centurion and the other mourners, the priest breaks the silence by singing aloud: “For ever and ever.” There follows a brief silence, signifying the time of the Sabbath during which he rested in the tomb.

[Col. 1301B] Again, when the priest says aloud, “The peace of the Lord,” he looks to what the Lord, standing in the midst of his disciples, said to them: “Peace be with you” (Luke 24). Afterwards *Agnus Dei* is sung and the kiss of peace is mutually given, because God the Father raised the Son in order to grant the remission of sins and exalted him in his resurrection, giving him the name that is above every name and all authority in heaven and on earth, by which he reconciled us to God the Father and to the angels (Phil. 2).

After the saving food has been received follows communion, which is thanksgiving. For we customarily give thanks to God for bodily refreshment, and much more for that food of which those who taste shall neither hunger nor thirst. Because prayers are said at the end, this signifies that Christ, having risen, intercedes for us.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Another explanation of the Canon

From the chapter *In primis* to *Communicantes*: Aaron prayed within the Holy of Holies, and Christ, before he suffered, prayed for himself and his disciples, giving an example of prayer. The minister of the Gospel, following both, prays for the whole Church. From *Communicantes* to *Hanc igitur*, our minister commemorates the names of the saints, to whose life and conduct he ought to conform, so that in him may be kindled the censer [Col. 1301D] burning with the fire of love and the fragrance of virtues. This was prefigured in the legal high priest’s carrying a censer into the Holy of Holies and the names of the fathers written upon his breast.

Christ, however, full of the perfume of every virtue, ascended into heaven, knowing consciences and the names of his own. While the legal high priest prayed, he was overshadowed by the smoke of incense, lest he be seen while praying and burning incense. This was a figure of Christ interceding for us, which exceeds every sight and understanding. For no one is granted to know how Christ, seated at the Father’s right hand, intercedes for us; it cannot even be conceived. For it is hidden from human beings and angels how great a power lies in words and in the mystical signs of the cross.

From *Supplices te rogamus* to *Praeceptis salutaribus*, [Col. 1302A] according to the Law, the sacrament was outwardly sprinkled with blood. Christ, however, sprinkles when he sanctifies us by the shedding of his blood. The priest sprinkles when he propitiates God through this sacrifice, and the grace of pardon is given. In naming the “high altar,” he recalls the Holy of Holies of the Law and that Holy of Holies into which Christ entered once for all, and through his own blood.

The names of the saints are recounted twice in the Canon, to show figuratively the bearing of the breastpiece and ephod upon which the names of the fathers were written. When the legal sacrifice had been completed, the high priest returned to the people, washing his garments, and he was unclean until evening. He prefigured Christ, who daily comes to us in mercy, cleanses his faithful, and does not abandon them until the consummation of the age. [Col. 1302B] Our priest washes the people by praying, and yet remains unclean until evening, because no one is so clean that there is not in him, until death, something that must be washed.

As has been said, all honor and glory belong to the Father through the Son, who came to acquire a kingdom for himself and the Father, and who instructed and taught his disciples to pray. He instructed them by saying: “Watch and pray” (Matt. 26). He taught them when he composed the prayer and established in it a pattern for praying. For when the disciples asked him to teach them to pray, he formed them for prayer by this prayer. Therefore, when the priest is about to pray, he urges the others to pray with him, saying: “Let us pray: instructed by saving precepts,” namely evangelical ones, “and formed by the institution of this prayer from the Lord, we dare to say” with the confidence of him who instituted it, who is present and intercedes for us in obtaining pardon, [Col. 1302C] crying with heart and voice: “Our Father.”

Although the prayer which he composed is customarily said here, blessed Gregory considered it better that the prayer by which he formed the disciples for prayer should be said, saying: “Our Father,” etc. Having received this from the Greeks, he nevertheless wished it to be sung by the priest alone, though among the Greeks it was said by all the people. From the clergy’s response, sung together—“But deliver us”—the priest takes up again the beginning of prayer. He asks that he and others may be delivered from evils through the intervention of the blessed Virgin, the apostles, and the other saints, and that peace may be made in our days. The choir prays that, with the peace-making King present, its spirit may be in peace and free from every disturbance.

When, however, “The peace of the Lord” is said, a threefold sign of the cross is made within the chalice, in praise [Col. 1302D] and honor of the Holy Trinity, which sent the Lamb who through the cross saved the world and made peace between human beings and angels. The threefold cross is made within the circumference of the chalice to signify that blameless and hidden joy which shall consist in enjoying the vision of the Trinity, through which are given us the peace of pardon, the peace of righteousness, and the peace of glory.

Then follows the voice of the Church, beseeching the Lamb, giver of peace and mercy. It is sung three times with the same beginning and ends in two different conclusions. Thus it prays: “Have mercy on us,” by granting pardon; “Have mercy,” by preserving righteousness; “Grant us peace,” which surpasses every sense and understanding. Have mercy on captives; have mercy on pilgrims; grant us the end of labor. Have mercy on sinners; have mercy on exiles; grant rest to those who labor. Grant the remission of sins; lead us to the secure dwelling of our homeland; after labor, grant peace and rest.

[Col. 1303A] In the breaking of the bread, the minister of the Law is represented, who offered fine flour particle by particle; and the Lord, who broke bread at supper and whom the disciples going to Emmaus recognized in the breaking of bread (Luke 24). The host is broken and divided into three parts, dedicated to the Holy Trinity. One of them, cast into the chalice, is immersed in the blood for that part of the Church which, tossed about in the shipwreck of this world, is shaken by many disturbances of sufferings. The other two are outside the chalice: one for those who are tested by fire, namely the faithful; the other for the saints, who reign with Christ eternally.

Then, in devout remembrance of Christ, present and seated at the Father’s right hand [Col. 1303B] and interceding for us, thanks are returned for the glorified; for the living, that they may deserve to be numbered among them; and for the faithful departed, that they may more quickly be released from punishments. The deacon brings the Mass to its close, chanting: “Let us bless the Lord,” or, on feast days, “Go, the dismissal is made,” or, as at funeral rites, “May they rest in peace.” This is done so that we may always and without interruption give thanks to our Redeemer for benefits received; honor his saints, by whose merits and intercessions we are helped; and pray for all the faithful departed, that they may attain the desired rest.

By this farewell those standing by are warned to depart, because the victim to whom belong all praise and honor, blessing and glory, has been sent; to that victim we must hasten to pass from this exile by swift course and holy withdrawal of mind. For a mission sufficient for our reconciliation is sent. Therefore this most holy ministry is called the *missa*, “dismissal.”

## CHAPTER XIX. Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer

We find the exposition of the Lord’s Prayer fully and lucidly set forth by our fathers. Yet we have taken care to explain it briefly according to our capacity, not in a spirit of arrogance, but lest the reader find it burdensome, whenever he reads it, to turn over the books of others in search of it. This saying of the Lord is a brief and abridged word: poor in words, rich in meanings. For under a small number of words the Lord taught how to pray, refuting the superstition of the pagans who glory in a multitude of words. Hence the Lord says: “When praying, do not speak much” (Matt. 6).

[Col. 1303D] It is divided into seven petitions, corresponding to the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, so that, liberated from seven vices and fittingly adorned with an equal number of virtues, we may deserve to receive the sevenfold fruit of eternal blessedness. Thus there are seven petitions, seven gifts, seven virtues, seven vices, and seven beatitudes. Three of the things requested are the sanctification of the name, the coming of God’s kingdom, and the fulfillment of the divine will; these belong to the future state. Four concern temporal aid: these are daily and spiritual bread—which, though eternal, is suited to this temporal state because it is received daily—the forgiveness of sins, not being moved by the temptation of evils, and not being assailed by the affliction of tribulations.

Those placed first are prior in dignity; those placed later are prior in time. For through things done temporally one arrives at eternal things. There are seven divisions of graces: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord. [Col. 1304A] This does not mean that the Spirit is multiple according to the difference of these names, but that he is always simple and one, the same source and origin of all virtues and goods. For it is the same Spirit by whom people become mature in wisdom, provident in understanding, cautious in counsel, free in fortitude, discerning in knowledge, gentle in piety, and humble in fear.

There are seven vices: pride, envy, wrathfulness, *acedia*—that is, weariness of mind accompanied by sadness—avarice, *gastrimargia* (gluttony), and lust; from these are derived the defilements of all sins. [Col. 1304B] There are seven virtues: humility, piety, compunction, justice, mercy, purity, and peace or tranquility. Humility tramples pride; piety extinguishes envy; compunction mitigates wrathfulness; justice cheers the mind, driving away all sadness; mercy condemns avarice; purity restrains gluttony; peace eliminates lust.

Seven are the beatitudes: the kingdom of heaven, the land of the living, consolation without disturbance, satisfaction without hunger, mercy without judgment, the vision of God, sonship of God or likeness to God. Although there is a distinction in their names and properties, the beatitude is nevertheless one and the same. In meriting and attaining these, the sevenfold grace which Isaiah describes is necessary; without it no merit reaches salvation. [Col. 1304C] Observe that Isaiah begins from the highest, while the Lord in his discourse begins from the lowest. For there the Lord is taught as about to descend to the lowest things; here man as about to ascend to the likeness of God. Thus he assigns fitting rewards to each merit: to the poor, the kingdom of heaven, because the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Ps. CX); to the meek, the inheritance of the Father, who says of himself: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI); to those who mourn, consolation through knowledge; to those who hunger and thirst, as labouring in fortitude, refreshment; mercy to the merciful through the aid of counsel; to the pure in heart, the vision of God, with the eye of the mind cleansed by understanding; that is, to the peacemakers is granted likeness to God, as to his sons, in whom the flesh obeys the spirit, [Col. 1304D] sense serves reason, through the moderation and maturity of wisdom.

We have touched upon these matters beforehand, that the reader’s mind may be more readily prepared to understand what we intend. It must be known that everything which is salvation and life is sought in the Lord’s Prayer, because he himself, interceding for us, taught the form of prayer: namely, that we be cleansed from the dregs of vices, adorned with the brightness of virtues through illuminating spiritual grace, and brought to the reward of the promises.

First, therefore, we ask that the name of the Lord be hallowed in us: that, pride being trampled beneath the foot of humility, we may humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God, and fear and reverence him, the holy one by whom we are sanctified, with a chaste fear enduring for ever and ever. The sanctification which is bestowed on us by God begins from his humble coming, as the Apostle says: [Col. 1305A] “Neither fornicators nor those who lie with males shall possess the kingdom” (I Cor. VI). “Such indeed were you; but you were sanctified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, in the Spirit of our God.” Hence we do not pray that the Holy of Holies, from whom comes all holiness, be sanctified, but that we may persevere in the sanctification given us by him. And we, who had withdrawn from him through the vanity of pride, may return to him through humility, be joined to him in sanctification, and deserve to attain the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom, concerning which the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

The second petition is: “May thy kingdom come.” In the ascending order of gifts, the Spirit of piety is placed second. The kingdom of God is the common salvation of all, which will come when, at the end of the age, his kingdom is revealed. Piety, or kindness, consists in sympathizing with neighbours, rejoicing with those who prosper, and grieving with those who suffer adversity. Hence it belongs to piety to will and desire the common salvation of all, and thus to banish all envy. For one who faithfully wishes for others what he asks for himself wholly excludes envy. But since God has reigned from eternity and his kingdom shall rule over all, we ask that his kingdom come—that is, the promised salvation obtained by the passion of his Son—so that, stripped of this body of death or servitude, we may reign with Christ, as he promised: “Receive the kingdom of God, which has been prepared for you from the origin of the world” (Matt. XXXIV). Therefore, with envy rejected and kindness or gentleness attained through the Spirit of piety, may we possess the land of the living, which is the beginning and [Col. 1305C] stable foundation, according to the saying: “Blessed are the meek” (Matt. V), etc.

The third petition is: “May thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.” The will of God is the keeping of his commandments, in the performance of which there is great reward. We pray that the will of God may be done in heaven and on earth—that is, in body and soul—so that we may serve him with a chaste body and please him with a pure heart. For since we have a body from earth and a spirit from heaven, we ask that the will of God may be done in both parts of us, who are heaven and earth. This we carry out when the Spirit of knowledge is given, through whom we know how to obey the divine will; and by him we are enabled to moderate anger, indignation, and wicked unlawful impulses. “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. I). [Col. 1305D] For the flesh inclines itself toward earthly things, while the spirit raises itself toward heavenly things. Therefore divine aid must be implored, that it may send the Spirit of knowledge, through whose help we discern what is pleasing to the divine will, and may contritely reject worldly joys; so that amid a multitude of sorrows and compunctions, with the Spirit of knowledge gladdening our spirit, we may obtain the everlasting consolation of inestimable knowledge, according to the saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V). Then the will of God will be perfectly fulfilled in us through the attainment of his consolation.

The fourth petition is: “Give us this day our daily bread.” When the mind, languishing from the weariness of acedia, is drawn away from the love of inward goods, the soul lies torpid, as though sick, upon the bed of sloth; it must be refreshed by spiritual bread, that is, by the body of Christ. Therefore, by the Spirit of fortitude, let it desire that the soul be aroused from torpor and strive after works of justice, lest, through the intervention of some grave sin, we abstain from that bread of which the Apostle says: “Let each person test himself, and so let him eat of that bread” (I Cor. XI). Hence we pray that our daily bread be given us, so that, living in Christ by works of justice, we may not depart from his body, but that it may be our daily food, by which the righteous person shall be fully satisfied when his glory appears. Hence the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. V). Having received the strength of this spiritual food, forgiveness of sin is immediately and rightly sought. Thus follows: “And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.”

[Col. 1306B] Our sins are called our debts, because a human being becomes debtor to the lender—that is, the devil. Whenever one sins, one takes on a debt. Those who were debtors to God through righteousness, by sinning become debtors to the devil through unrighteousness. The devil advances the malice of sins to offenders at usury, so that they may thereby incur eternal death. The devil lent this debt to the first man, who did not wish to remain debtor to the Lord for the benefit received. If the merciful are blessed, it is sound counsel to show mercy to others and not to burn with the torches of avarice, but to distribute good things. This counsel is given through the Spirit of God: that we forgive hatreds and injuries, so that the Lord may forgive our sins and bestow mercy on the merciful. Hence he himself says: “When you stand [Col. 1306C] to pray, forgive, if anyone has a complaint against another, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you” (Mark XI). According to this, on the day of judgment you will be judged so as to suffer what you have done.

If those pure in heart are blessed, let us be cleansed in mind and body. Gluttonous excess in food and the provocations of appetite must be avoided; inward refreshment through the Spirit of understanding must be sought. For when the soul is inwardly refreshed, it suffers outward hunger less painfully. Hence the Lord answered the tempter: “Man does not live by bread alone” (Matt. IV). We must therefore pray that temptation may not cast us down, but that, with the clear eye of the mind, one may resist temptations; so that, never ceasing to behold God in contemplation, one may see God in the future as he is.

The final petition comprises everything necessary: namely, to be delivered from evil. [Col. 1306D] For nothing remains to be sought beyond this, since it is the perfection of all religion. One who has been delivered from evil rests within oneself, producing a spirit of peace and tranquillity. There is nothing inwardly or outwardly to resist, because neither flesh through lust, nor the world through avarice, nor the devil through malice can cast one down from tranquillity. This is effected by the Spirit of wisdom, which orders all movements of the senses and subjects them to reason. Of such persons the Lord says: “I said: You are gods,” etc. Hence: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. V).

The things said by Isaiah concerning the Spirit of the Lord, and the discourse which he spoke to the disciples on the mountain, appear fittingly assigned to the Lord’s Prayer. For he who uttered the prophecy and he who addressed the disciples upon the mountain is the same one who composed this prayer. The discourse before it and the prayer, like streams flowing from a spring, issue from that Isaian sevenfold gift, in which is the fullness of all goods.

## CHAPTER XX. On Additions to the Office of the Mass by Supreme Pontiffs

Observe that, as the master had taught, the apostles began, by communicating themselves and others, to perform the consecration of the body and blood of the Lord; and, by preaching, they established that it should be performed throughout all the churches. At first the mystery of the canon was performed without any fixed order; afterward the epistle and Gospel were read with the canon. Then certain Roman pontiffs, adding things for the adornment and decoration of the Church, adopted various observances to be celebrated.

Pope Celestine instituted the singing of the 150 psalms with antiphons. By this institution the custom grew up that, from among those psalms, the introit, [Col. 1308A] gradual, offertory, and communions should be selected. Gregory adopted from the Greeks the *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—and ordered it to be sung in resonant melody by the clergy alone; he also decreed that the Lord’s Prayer be said. Symmachus added *Gloria in excelsis Deo*—“Glory to God in the highest”—on festal days. Pope Telesphorus wished Masses to be sung at night only on the Nativity of the Lord, and prescribed the words of the angels which follow. Gelasius composed the prefaces. Innocent added the kiss of peace. Damasus instituted the singing after the Gospel of *Credo in unum Deum*—“I believe in one God”—by decree of the Council of Constantinople. Alexander ordered water to be mixed with wine, so that neither wine without water nor water without wine should be offered, to represent that both flowed from the Lord’s side. Sixtus set the threefold *Sanctus*—“Holy”—to music. Sergius sang *Agnus Dei*—“Lamb of God”—in a threefold refrain during Communion.

[Col. 1307]

# CHARTERS OF STEPHEN OF BALGIAC

## I. Settlement with Hugh of Gissey by Stephen, Bishop of Autun

(*Gallia Christiana*, IV, Documents, 86.)

[Col. 1307B]

Let the faithful of the holy Church, both present and future, know in what manner the controversy which had existed for some time between the canons of St. Symphorian and Hugh of Gissey and Hugh of Saphra was finally brought to an end through the counsel of Lord Stephen, bishop of the Church of Autun.

It was therefore decreed by the aforesaid bishop, whose authority intervened to settle this dispute, that in the land of St. Symphorian over which the controversy had arisen, the aforesaid knights should receive from the peasant cultivators and inhabitants of the land fifteen sextaries of grain, one half to be rendered in wheat and the rest [Col. 1307C] in oats. In the inhabited holdings they should likewise receive, in the same manner, a bundle consisting of hay and straw; moreover, the lord of Gissey should have corvée labour from the oxen of the peasants, excepting, however, the canons’ own possessions. In return for this, both the canons and their men should have, in the land of the aforesaid Hugh of Gissey, the use of pastures, waters, and woods for the equipment of wagons, ploughs, and harrows. Beyond the matters written above, the aforesaid knights are to have absolutely nothing in the persons or lands of the canons.

These acts were done at Sedelocum, in the presence of Lord Stephen, venerable bishop of the people of Autun.

The witnesses of this matter are Stephen the bishop; Ranulf, Zacharias, and Hugh, canons; Constantine the elder; [Col. 1307D] Agerius, Esperimus, Arbert, and Ulduin of Illyriacum; Gislebert of Tiliis; Raynald of Dorna; Jurannus Belet; and many others.

## II. Charter of Stephen, Bishop of Autun, no. XXVIII, in Favour of Ungy

[Note: [Col. 1307] This decree follows the foundation of Ungy in the Ungy cartulary.]

(*Gallia Christiana*, ibid., p. 87.)

[Col. 1308B]

STEPHEN, by the grace of God bishop of Autun, to his beloved sons, the clergy and laity of his diocese: greeting and paternal blessing.

Let your affection know that it pertains to our office to protect ecclesiastical rights and preserve the benefits bestowed, especially those granted to the poor of Christ, who have left all things behind and have resolved that they cannot possess villages, men, or other revenues, so that they may avoid lawsuits and not be dragged into legal proceedings. If anyone, therefore, raises any claim against them, we do not wish them to be brought into secular courts, but that recourse be had to our hearing, [Col. 1308C] so that, in our presence and by the judgment of the Church, a complaint arisen against the Church may be quieted within the Church. For how shall those who belong to our advocacy, and who cannot receive or possess anything without our assent, proceed without us to the hearing of laymen and submit to an alien judgment?

We therefore command and establish by episcopal authority that no one dare trouble them in any manner. But if anyone has a claim against them, let it be brought before us, who must speak and answer for them on earth, and whom we hope will speak and pray for us on the day of judgment. If anyone rashly opposes this our decree, we separate him from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord, and likewise from the threshold and all communion of the holy Church, until he duly repents and [Col. 1308D] makes satisfaction to us for transgressing our command. We also inflict upon such persons the sword of anathema, and, by the power received from God, hand over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh those who presume, not from regard for truth but at the prompting of greed, to harass them either before our tribunal or another’s. But upon those who maintain peace with them and defend what has been bestowed upon them, may there be an abundance of every good and eternal blessedness.

## III. Charter of Stephen, Bishop of Autun, for the Monastery of St. Benignus of Dijon

(PÉRARD, *Collection of Documents*, etc., p. 254.)

I, STEPHEN, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Autun, make known to those present and those to come that the lord pope delegated to me the case pending between John, abbot of St. Benignus of Dijon, and Guy, count of Saulx, concerning the village called Dianetum with its appurtenances. I, having taken counsel with discerning persons, [Col. 1309B] adjudged the aforesaid village and its appurtenances to the abbot of Dijon, and by judicial decision invested him with those matters concerning which the dispute between them had arisen. If, however, the count or anyone acting for him presumes to act against this, let him know that by the apostolic authority which we exercise in this matter, he is subject to excommunication. Engilbert, bishop of Chalon, by whose seal this charter is confirmed, and the abbot of St. Martin of Autun were present at this investiture.

## IV. Privilege for the Cistercians

(MABILLON, *Annals*, vol. VI, p. 677.)

STEPHEN, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Autun, to his beloved brother in Christ STEPHEN, abbot of Cîteaux, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Greatly delighted by the good fragrance of the Cistercian order, and assenting to the requests of you and your brethren, we have granted the church of Combusii free, while reserving episcopal right to the canons of the castle of Vergy. The canons themselves, at our request, renounced in our hand, for the Church of Cîteaux to retain in perpetuity, the rent which they had customarily received annually from you in the territory of Gergulium for your grange.

The witnesses of this gift and renunciation of rent were: Bertrannus, archdeacon of Beaune; Humbert, archpriest of Beaune; Walo, priest of Gilly; and Paganus Rabustel of Vergy.

## V. Notice concerning the Evil Customs Which Duke Hugh of Burgundy Remitted to Bishop Stephen in the Village of Canavis, etc.

[Col. 1309D]

Since, by the fault of the first parent, human life and memory—which would have endured eternally had man not sinned—were made mortal and quickly slip away and vanish, human reason has arranged that gifts, grants, and agreements which people make among themselves should be recorded in writing, lest they perish through forgetfulness. Approving this salutary counsel of the fathers of old, we have judged it worthwhile to record and make known, by the testimony of this charter to future as well as present persons, the free remission and complete liberty from the evil customs which Hugh, duke [Col. 1310A] of Burgundy, son of Duke Odo, had unjustly been accustomed to exact in the village of Canavis and Gratematium and their appurtenances. Thus may the rashness and audacity of evildoers wholly fear to transgress and violate what, by divine grace, is rightly done by cultivators of justice and the faithful.

Stephen, by divine grace bishop of Autun, after his election, diligently met Duke Hugh and William, count of Nevers, concerning the establishment and maintenance of peace; and, so that peace might be established and maintained throughout his whole bishopric, he fixed with them a day for confirming the peace. On the appointed day the bishop, duke, count, and very many other lovers of [Col. 1310B] justice assembled at Autun. They confirmed by oaths the peace which the monk-duke had previously established, and determined that, whenever it was broken, they should assemble at Autun every year on the feast of St. Nazarius to restore peace.

[Note: [Col. 1309D] The monk-duke mentioned here was Hugh I, duke of Burgundy. Having no children, he abdicated the principality in favour of his brother Odo and professed as a monk at Cluny in 1097. André Duchesne.]

At the following feast of St. Nazarius, the bishop and the community of clergy of the Church of Autun, grievously complaining to the duke of the evil and unjust customs which he tyrannically exercised in the villages of Canavis and Gratematium, and concerning Theobald of Cambosium and his sons, whom he claimed and held as his own dependants, raised an outcry against the wrongs which he inflicted upon them. The duke therefore appointed a day at the castle of Dijon on which to make satisfaction to the bishop and canons for their complaints, as justice required: namely, the feast-day of the revelation of Stephen the protomartyr. On the appointed day [Col. 1310C] and at the appointed place, the bishop and canons, the duke and his men, assembled in the house of Dominic the merchant in order to settle the aforesaid complaints. There, in the presence of the duke and his court, the bishop and canons again presented their complaint and accusation concerning the said villages, proving by sound arguments and authentic writings that the duke had absolutely no right in them.

Moreover, they recalled from memory that whatever the duke of Burgundy had held, justly or unjustly, in the aforesaid villages and their appurtenances and in Theobald and his sons, his father Duke Odo had entirely remitted to blessed Nazarius, to the Church of Autun, and to the canons on the final day of the council held at Autun by Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See. They also produced [Col. 1310D] the charter concerning the remission of evil customs and the complete freedom of Canavis and Gratematium, which his father had placed upon the altar of St. Nazarius in order that it might be firmly observed; and they stated, as the charter testified, that one of the sons of the Church had there been kissed by the duke in confirmation of the matter. Yet the duke did not then yield to their truthful arguments and writings; rather, claiming his long possession, he at last granted that his court should withdraw apart to render judgment upon the bishop’s and canons’ statements.

Accordingly, the following withdrew apart to render judgment: Anseric, canon and provost of St. [Col. 1311A] Nazarius; Abbot Walo and his brother Werric; Adimar of Maso; William of Fulventio; Hugh, the duke’s seneschal; Teccelinus Sorus; and Theobald Damac. Judgment was rendered, and Theobald Damac reported it in these words: “We judge that the Church of Autun ought, by right and by Duke Odo’s remission, to possess the aforesaid villages with their appurtenances and their present and future inhabitants, in complete freedom and undisturbed peace.”

When the judgment had thus been reported, Duke Hugh, who was present there, took the charter by which his father had rendered the named villages free and discharged from every evil custom and exaction; and he surrendered and relinquished to God, blessed Nazarius, and the canons everything that he had taken and held, justly or unjustly, in Gratematium, Canavis, and their appurtenances. Then, placing the charter [Col. 1311B] in the bishop’s hand, he declared in these words:

“I, Hugh, duke of Burgundy, give, deliver, grant, and wholly relinquish to God and blessed Nazarius, and to you, Bishop Stephen, and to the Church of Autun, all evil customs and exactions, and everything which, justly or unjustly, I have hitherto held or been accustomed to hold in Gratematium, in Canavis, and in their appurtenances, and in those living or who shall live there. If anyone presumes to violate this, let him be struck by the anathema of St. Leodegarius, bishop and martyr.”

The following were present as witnesses to this gift and liberty. On the duke’s side: William of Fulventio; Hugh the seneschal; Hugh of Besara, provost of Dijon; Teccelinus Sorus; Adimar of Maso; Abbot Walo; his brother Werric; Theobald Damac; and Odo Martinus. On the bishop’s side: Sevinus, dean; Anseric, provost; Sevinus, archdeacon; Raginald; Engelbert; Andrew; Peter Adjutus; and Warnerius, priest.

Laymen: Mainus the elder; Humbert, cellarer; Peter [Col. 1312D] of Ulgus; Theobald Cambosium and his sons, Paganus and Dominic; and Mainus Palmarius.

Done in the sixth indiction, the first epact, during the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, while Stephen held the bishopric of Autun. Amen.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1136, GERARD, BISHOP OF ANGOULÊME

[Col. 1311]

# NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. II, col. 995.)

[Col. 1311C] Gerard of Blaye was a man highly celebrated in his time, beyond measure either praised or defamed. Nothing could be more disgraceful than what Arnulf—first archdeacon of Sées and afterward bishop of Lisieux—and Ernald, abbot of Bonneval in the diocese of Chartres, relate about him. Conversely, nothing could be more exalted or glorious than the things written in his praise by the author of the *History of the Bishops and Counts of Angoulême*, chapter 32. A candid historian, as is fitting, should equally avoid both extremes. We shall therefore take the middle course. We shall weigh in a critical examination every assertion made about him and, laying aside every prejudice, affirm whatever seems truer, or at least more probable.

He was by birth a Neustrian, of the diocese of Bayeux; his father was Giraud, a man of moderate fortune, indeed almost none at all. Thus in youth he was compelled to change his place of residence and live in want of almost every necessity. Yet he repaired all this through industry, labour, and talent. First he devoted his mind to humane studies; when older, he embraced the clerical way of life and [Col. 1311D] gave himself wholly to sacred letters, theology, and [Col. 1312C] canon law. He made such progress in every kind of learning that he was fully prepared to offer others what he had absorbed.

“Thus it came about that he held the governance of schools in the city of Angoulême and at Périgueux, and in certain neighbouring castles.”

[Note: [Col. 1311D] Labbe, vol. II, p. 238.]

He did so with such wisdom, such talent, and such happy results that pupils flocked to his teaching from every direction, and those leaving his school appeared qualified for higher dignities in the Church. The canons of Périgueux themselves admitted him as a sharer in their honour, as we learn from the document recording a gift made to Uzerche by William, bishop of Périgueux.

[Note: [Col. 1311D] See Baluze’s *History of Tulle*, appendix, col. 877. “In the presence of Lord Gerald, bishop of Angoulême, [Col. 1312D] and a canon of our church,” says William, bishop of Périgueux, in a charter of 1104.]

Finally, he was appointed bishop of Angoulême in 1101, succeeding the deceased Ademar. Arnulf wrote as follows concerning this election:

[Note: [Col. 1312D] *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 339.]

> “While the divided multitude of electors rose against one another, and the alternating support demanded different persons, the votes of all turned fortune toward him; not because they believed that the Church had been sufficiently and fittingly provided for in him, but because, in order that the tumult might have some outcome whatever, each party knowingly preferred to accept him as unworthy rather than appear to have allowed the other party to prevail.”

We judge this statement presumptuous and remote from the truth. We do not deny that the matter was at first conducted, as often happens, by factions and solicitations; but we believe that the electors, having eventually come to a better mind, designated Gerard by unanimous agreement at the people’s request, as the *History of the Bishops of Angoulême* expressly testifies.

[Note: [Col. 1313D] Labbe, vol. II, p. 259; *Spicilegium*, ibid., p. 343.]

> “On account of his remarkable learning and honourable life he was promoted to the bishopric of Angoulême, at the people’s request, by election of the clergy and with the assent of the leading men.”

And he was certainly worthy of election, since, according to Arnulf’s testimony, he possessed “a recognized discretion in conducting affairs, strengthened indeed by very extensive knowledge of letters and adorned by eloquence in both kinds of speech.” He was a man “discreet in answering, outstanding in preaching, gracious in address, and witty in proverbs,” says the *History of the Bishops of Angoulême*.

Not long afterward he obtained a legation. But, if Arnulf is believed, it was procured and surreptitiously obtained. Let us grant that it was sought: but who could persuade himself that it was surreptitiously obtained? For the *History of the Bishops of Angoulême* says:

> “When he had attached himself to the lord Pope Paschal, who had come into the regions of Gaul, Paschal, recognizing his uprightness and outstanding wisdom, entrusted his own authority to him first in Brittany and afterward in the provinces of Tours, Bordeaux, Bourges, and Auch.”

Orderic Vitalis likewise writes, book XIII, under the year 1136, p. 908: “A most learned man, who was of great name and influence in the Roman senate in the time of Pope Paschal, Gelasius, Calixtus, and Honorius.” Finally, who could persuade himself that those four supreme pontiffs were so negligent or so wicked as either not to know Gerard to be openly unworthy, or, though knowing it, nevertheless to honour him with so great a dignity?

It is astonishing how many crimes Arnulf says were committed by him both in the episcopate and in the legation. “From that day,” he says, “truth and mercy departed from the Church of Angoulême, and deceit and impiety succeeded them; the condition of affairs changed for the worse, and the Church’s dignity and worship were diminished. You began to indulge the insolence which poverty had formerly checked; by the license which you could not exercise as a private person, to persecute whatever good men you wished and to drain the province by plunder and exactions, etc. But once the legation was obtained, your greed, poured out over wider spaces, rejoiced that abundant material for your rapacity was not lacking. Why should I enlarge upon your manifest exactions?” etc.

We see no way to deny that Gerard acted on some occasions from ambition and for gain, since Geoffrey of Vendôme, writing to Gerard himself, records certain matters to this effect. He begins as follows:

[Note: [Col. 1313D] Letters, book I, epistle 21.]

> “Since the holy Roman Church has so exalted your humility, not indeed by your merits but by grace alone, that your little finger seems thicker than your father’s back—as the lofty words which you frequently utter with much glory testify—you ought to obey it all the more faithfully . . . If you act otherwise, your eminence, which . . . the pope by his kindness created sufficiently from a lowly station, returns evil to him for good.”

Then, coming to the matter, he says:

> “What we have heard—and what is worse, the common people have composed a song about it, since the matter is public—we can neither conceal from you nor ought to conceal. First, we have heard, and grieve, that Andrew of Vitré sold you marriage with his daughter, and that the son of the viscount of Maloleone likewise purchased it from you. One of these paid you five hundred solidi as the price of the marriage, the other fifteen marks of silver. The bishop of Poitiers, his archdeacon William, and certain others who were present will not deny this, unless they wish to bury the truth. Secondly, you caused the abbot of Carroffe, not regularly elected but, as is said, violently intruded, to be consecrated [Col. 1314A] for one thousand solidi of barbarin coins, by authority excessively barbarous . . . although his consecrator was unwilling and his clergy protested by every means in their power; and a certain neighbouring abbot of yours, who saw it and took part in it, bore witness, and many say his testimony is true. Thirdly, Fulk, abbot of Biennais, sought your letters to obtain justice for himself; your prudence denied them to him so long that he bought them for one hundred solidi. But he lost his money and could not obtain justice through you. He himself declares this, complaining that he lost both together,” etc.

And after much else:

> “Some assert that you, like another Balaam, were corrupted by the money of the king of England and therefore pronounced an unjust sentence of excommunication against the count of Anjou.
