And although your excommunication could not have force even for one day, it nevertheless brought shame upon the friends of the Roman Church and gave its enemies matter for detraction . . . You promised, it is said, the abbot of Angeriac that, if he gave you three hundred Poitevin solidi ‘masculi,’ you would depose Rainard Chesnelli; and you sent him copied chapters by which he might accuse that man. The abbot himself acknowledges this and calls God as witness upon his soul that he speaks the truth. We have testified to these few matters out of many, these slight matters out of great ones, for the sake of affection: so that, if what is circulated against your cunning is true, the transgression of the past may become for you a safeguard for the future.”

He adds that Gerard, in his presence, preached even before laymen that he possessed the power to depose bishops—a claim which he calls a new kind of presumption.

Gerard may have exercised these things against outsiders; certainly nothing similar is recorded of his having committed them against his own Church of Angoulême. On the contrary, he heaped benefits upon that church and even upon the province insofar as he could. He worked for the reconciliation of princes and for the protection of the oppressed; he adorned his see, injured no one, and did good to all. He “helped [Col. 1314C] Vulgrin, count of Angoulême, with counsel and assistance,”

[Note: [Col. 1314D] Labbe, vol. II, p. 259.]

so that he might recover lands taken from him by force and fraud. He “calmed by his intervention the dissensions stirred up between him and Ademar of Rochefoucauld. He built the Church of Angoulême from its first stone . . . at his own expense he built a dormitory, refectory, cellar, presbytery, iron doors, and granted to the said church lands or churches at Julhac, Renenhorville, and Touzac. He also gave from his own resources so that twenty-four poor persons might always be fed in the said Church of Angoulême in every Lent, and he acquired twelve solidi in the church of Touzac for the poor persons’ tunics. He also gave the Church of Angoulême pontifical ornaments, which he bought from Bozo, bishop of Saintes, for a thousand solidi. He built a hall for the bishops; he gave the church gold textiles . . . gilded censers, and a silver cross,”

[Note: [Col. 1314D] Labbe, vol. II, p. 260.]

etc. After much else, the author adds:

> “He gave our church and the episcopal table one hundred volumes or more, nearly all works of the holy Fathers . . . and innumerable goods. He also established from his own resources that thirteen poor persons should always be fed at the table of the bishop of Angoulême . . . He built a hall for the bishops, a chapel, and a chamber at Poitiers, and gave the Church of Angoulême a gold-work ring set with precious stones.”

He adds: “Through his aid the church of La Couronne, and the churches of Grosbois, Aulaville, and Bornet began to be built . . . He built a church and houses for lepers.”

Now the deeds performed by the legate must be related. In 1107, together with Richard of Albano and Albert, bishop of Avignon, he was appointed by Paschal II as delegated judge in the case between the monks of La Chaise-Dieu and Aniane concerning the cell of Gordanica; having rendered judgment, he awarded the cell to Aniane. In the year of the Incarnation 1109, indiction II, in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, son of King Philip, he concluded an agreement [Col. 1315A] with Aimeric of La Mothe-Rochefoucauld concerning the exclusion of the mills of Castelar. He held eight councils, of which few have come to our knowledge. There survives, in Labbe’s edition of the councils, the Council of Loudun, held by him concerning the state of the Church:

> “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1109, epact XXVIII, indiction II, with Lord Pope Paschal presiding at Rome and Louis reigning in France.”

At it the church of St. Peter was vindicated for the monks of Trénor against the bishop and canons of Nantes. Present were the archbishop of Bordeaux; the bishops of Poitiers, Saintes, Agen, Périgueux, Angers, Le Mans, Rennes, Nantes, Dol, and Vannes; likewise several abbots. Nothing was more notable than what he did at the Lateran Council in 1112. The emperor Henry V had extorted from the captive Paschal II a privilege concerning the granting of investitures to priestly offices, adding the pope’s oath “that henceforth he would neither trouble him concerning investitures [Col. 1315B] nor impose an anathema upon the king personally.” No one in the whole council could see how all this might at last be revoked.

“Then Bishop Gerard, when at length consulted, gave this advice: that the investitures could be revoked without violation of the oath, provided that the emperor who granted investitures was not excommunicated. The whole synod praised this counsel and said: ‘It is not you who have spoken, but the Holy Spirit in your mouth.’” [Note: [Col. 1315D] Labbe, vol. II, p. 259.]

Paschal ordered him to put into writing the condemnation of investitures; this he did together with certain others appointed by the council. Then, when the document of condemnation had been read by Gerard himself, all the fathers cried out: “Amen, amen. Let it be done, let it be done.” Moreover,

> “It pleased the pope and the entire council that Bishop Gerard, through whom God had disclosed such counsel to His Church, should be sent with a certain cardinal to the emperor, to ascertain the emperor’s will, so that he might restore investitures to the Roman Church,” [Note: [Col. 1315D] Labbe, ibid.]

otherwise the council that had been held should be made known. We have seen the man’s wisdom; now let us admire the unconquered strength of his spirit. It was indeed a dangerous mission: he had to announce this to a proud prince prone to anger, and no one doubted that it would be exceedingly unwelcome. Yet the fearless bishop undertook it. “And when he had spoken with marvelous eloquence in the emperor’s presence, and the chancellor of the emperor, who was his interpreter, had explained each point, a violent tumult arose in the court. So great was it that the archbishop of Cologne, who had solemnly received him in his own lodging—for in Gaul he had been Gerard’s pupil—doubting for his life, said: ‘Master, you have caused a great scandal in our court.’ Gerard, indignant, replied: ‘Let it be a scandal to you; to me it is the Gospel.’ But Almighty God, who holds the king’s heart in His hands and inclines it wherever He wills, turned the emperor’s mind in another direction.” The emperor, marveling alike at the man’s constancy and wisdom, not only inflicted no violence upon him, but even gave him many gifts.

In October 1117 he attended [Col. 1315D] the Roman council presided over by Paschal II, where Orderic Vitalis, in book XII of his History, calls him a “leader in speech,” together with Atto of Viviers, Geoffrey of Chartres, and William of Châlons. In 1118 he held a council at Angoulême, of which nothing survives except what the Chronicle of Maillezais records: “There the archbishop of Tours and two other bishops were confirmed. One of them was Audebert of Agen.” In 1122 he obtained from Peter, bishop of Saintes, restitution of the estate of Ledeville, which had anciently belonged to the mother church of Angoulême and to its treasurer, who was then Gerard’s nephew. In the same year the monks of St. Macharius obtained from him by deception the pastoral staff, [Col. 1316A] by which their monastery was made an abbey and exempted from subjection to Holy Cross of Bordeaux. On the Kalends of March 1128, he was present at the translation of St. Albinus, bishop of Angers. In the same year, as legate, he presided over a council in the monastery of St. Gildas of Dol, according to the Chronicle of Quimperlé in volume I of Baluze’s Miscellanies. About the same time he held a council at Bordeaux, at which William, bishop of Dax, surrendered to the church of La Sauve-Majeure the church of St. Vincent of Dax.

We must now turn to the schism occasioned by the election of the two Roman pontiffs, Innocent and Anacletus. If Gerard had embraced Anacletus’s cause against Innocent II from the beginning, he would have had some ground of excuse; for at first there was some room for doubt. Each had been elected on the same day; and, if priority in time favored Innocent, the greater number of votes favored Anacletus. For the latter had been elected by twenty-seven, according to Onuphrius—or at least by twenty-two, according to others—while the former was elected by only seventeen cardinals [Col. 1316B]. Anacletus was further aided by the fact that those who had designated Innocent had acted contrary to their agreement, outside the appointed place, without not merely summoning the others but even notifying them. Thus, in those earliest times, the matter was ambiguous and difficult. [Note: [Col. 1315D] Suger, *Life of Louis the Fat*; William of Malmesbury, *New History*, vol. I, under the thirtieth year of King Henry of England; Arnald of Bonneval, book II of the *Life of St. Bernard*.]

For this reason St. Bernard came to the assembly at Étampes, where the dispute was to be decided, “not a little fearful and trembling.” For this reason, when the whole affair had been laid upon him, he used fasting and continual prayer, so that he might deserve the necessary light from the supreme divine power. For this reason the most devout abbot “scarcely persuaded Henry, king of England, to receive Innocent, although the bishops of England had altogether dissuaded him.” [Note: [Col. 1316D] Suger, ibid.] Nor could Henry be induced except by these words of Bernard: “You fear that you will incur sin if you obey Innocent. Consider that you must answer God for other sins; leave this one to me—let this sin be mine.”

In these circumstances, if Gerard had wavered, if he had stood for Anacletus, he might have had some excuse on the ground of ignorance of the facts. But the case was not so. Rather, if Arnulf is to be trusted, when he could not attend the Council of Étampes, he sent by messenger letters sealed with his seal, in which he testified:

> “That he knew both persons and had more fully investigated the order of the election; that beyond doubt justice was on the side of Pope Innocent, because he was plainly a man of exceptional uprightness, and because his election was first in time and had been celebrated by the principal persons of the Roman Church. But Peter had rather usurped the chair by a wealthy hand, being a man so discredited in life and in name that, even if some form of election defended him, the quality and infamy of his life could in no way allow his promotion.” [Note: [Col. 1316D] *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 355.]

When all had agreed upon Pope Innocent, Gerard immediately wrote to him “first, or among the first,” requesting “to be honored by a rescript from him, and that the office of legate which he had held be confirmed.” [Note: [Col. 1316D] Bernard, letter 126.] Indeed, he also wrote back to the chancellor, humbly pleading that he was “all the more unworthy to be burdened with the office of legate and honored with its title [Col. 1316D] the more humbly” he made the request. [Note: [Col. 1316D] *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 356.] Rebuffed, he became indignant, withdrew from Innocent, and went over to Anacletus. He recognized him as pope; he was appointed legate by him; and, as he boasts, all France and Burgundy were added to his former legation. Thereafter Gerard lapsed into open schism and attempted to set up altar against altar. [Note: [Col. 1316D] Bernard, letter 24.] He attacked Innocent with a venomous tongue and tore him apart with his slanders. By his speeches he endeavored to draw peoples away from Innocent to himself and the antipope; he acted with such force, zeal, and craft that he infected very many with his schism, shook Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, though he did not overthrow him, and so bound William, duke of Aquitaine, to himself and his own opinion that the prince depended wholly upon him [Col. 1317A]. Relying upon this authority, “he confounds right and wrong, strives to place abbots over abbots and bishops over bishops, to remove Catholics, and to promote schismatics.” He drove the bishops of Poitiers and Limoges from their sees and installed others; and because the bishops of the province refused to consecrate these unworthy men appointed by him, he so inflamed the prince’s anger against them that William, bishop of Saintes, and his canons were compelled to depart from their see, city, and church, “leaving behind their houses and possessions.” [Note: [Col. 1317B] Letter of William, bishop of Saintes, to Vulgrin, archbishop of Bourges. Labbe, vol. II, p. 85.]

Yet, if he harassed others, he also suffered much himself. At the Council of Rheims, presided over by Innocent, he was condemned for schism, excommunicated, and deprived of every ecclesiastical dignity. When he wished to exercise the office of his new legation in the diocese of Saintes, he was captured by the valiant knight Aimar of Archiac and held in prison for several months; he escaped free only after paying a great price. Again [Col. 1317B] he was struck with anathema by Vulgrin, archbishop of Bourges; the peoples and bishops of Aquitaine were forbidden to obey him in any matter or show him any honor. [Note: [Col. 1317B] William of Saintes, ibid.] Hence, when he was elected archbishop of Bordeaux through the count’s violence, without the assent of the bishops of the province—indeed, with the bishop of Agen opposing it [Note: [Col. 1318B] Arnulf, p. 363.]—the whole body, or at least the greater part, resisted; it could not be induced to communicate with him [Col. 1318A], and in the Church of Angoulême very many separated from him.

Finally, after Count William had been brought back to Catholic unity through Bernard, and thus “peace had been restored to the whole Church of Aquitaine, Gerard alone persisted in evil. But not long afterward . . . unrepentant and suddenly dead without confession and viaticum, he rendered up, as he departed from the body, his spirit to him whose minister he had remained to the end. His body, found by his nephews . . . lifeless in his bed and monstrously swollen, was buried in a certain basilica; but afterward it was removed from there by Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres and legate of the Apostolic See, and cast elsewhere.” [Note: [Col. 1318B] Ernald, book II of the *Life of St. Bernard*, ch. 39.]

The *History of the Bishops of Angoulême*, chapter 35, nevertheless speaks quite differently of his death:

> “On the day before his death, we learned that in his confession he had said to the priests: ‘If, in ignorance, I have supported the party of Peter Leonis against the will of God, I confess it and repent.’ . . . But on Saturday, celebrating Mass with the greatest devotion and outpouring of tears, he departed from this world on the following Sunday, in the year 1136 from the Incarnation of the Lord. He sat in the episcopate for thirty-three years, . . . months, . . . days. At his end he gave each chaplain of his bishopric one mina and one obol. And that splendid star, which by its brightness had illuminated the western regions, alas, lies outside the church which he built, beneath a humble stone. The bishopric was vacant until the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.”

[Col. 1317]

## COUNCIL OF LOUDUN CONCERNING THE STATE OF THE CHURCH, HELD BY Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the Apostolic See, in the year of the Lord 1109

(Labbe, *Councils*, vol. X, col. 762.—Nothing concerning the matters discussed at this council has reached us except the two decrees set out below.)

### I. The Church of St. Peter is vindicated for the monks of Trénor against the bishop and canons of Nantes

[Col. 1317C]

GERARD, by the grace of God bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Apostolic See.

When, at the Council of Loudun, which we held in the basilica of the Blessed Mother of God, with that same God as author and governor, I had dealt with very many matters concerning the state of the holy Church, the complaint of the monks of Trénor was brought before the council against the bishop of Nantes and his canons concerning the church of St. Vitalis. On the following day, meeting in the refectory of the same church with our brethren and fellow bishops—namely, the archbishop of Bordeaux, the bishops of Poitiers, Angers, Le Mans, and Rennes [Col. 1317D], the abbot of Saint-Cybard, and the abbot of Saint-Eparchius, together with many others—we heard the two lawful representatives of the said monks in this case and adjudged an oath to both parties. When this had been canonically taken, on the following day, [Col. 1318C] before the whole assembly, in the presence and at the command of the bishop of Nantes himself, I received from the hand of his archdeacon, by means of the charter which he held in his hand, the investiture of the aforesaid church; and, by the judgment and assent of the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and the entire assembly, I solemnly transferred that investiture by the same charter to the prior of Cunault and the aforesaid monks, saving nevertheless the canonical right of the Church of Nantes, if any such right existed. And in order that this matter may remain firm and unshaken, we caused it to be marked with the seal of our authority and took care to subscribe it with our own hand.

This was done in the castle of Loudun, in the presence of the aforesaid archbishops, bishops, and abbots, and many other religious and noble men.

[Col. 1318D] Mark of the bishop of Bordeaux. Mark of the bishop of Poitiers. Mark of the bishop of Saintes. Mark of the bishop of Agen. Mark of the bishop of Périgueux. [Col. 1319A] Mark of the bishop of Angers. Mark of the bishop of Le Mans. Mark of the bishop of Rennes. Mark of the bishop of Nantes. Mark of the archbishop of Dol. Mark of the bishop of Vannes. Mark of the abbot of Vendôme. Mark of the abbot of Maillezais. Mark of the abbot of Marmoutier. Mark of the abbot of Saint-Florent.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1109, epact XXVIII, indiction II, with Lord Pope Paschal presiding at Rome and King Louis ruling in France.

I, Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

### II. The Chapel of St. Stephen is adjudged to the monks of Marmoutier against the canons of Chemillé

[Col. 1319B]

I, GERARD, by the grace of God bishop of Angoulême, legate of the Roman Church, and the other brethren who were with us at Angers, in the monastery of St. Albinus, in the novices’ cell of the same monastery, assembled to hear and determine a certain case between the abbot of St. Martin of Marmoutier and the canons of Chemillé concerning the chapel of the aforesaid castle. Both the monks and the canons were present. Each side presented its case in order. Having heard the arguments of both, we began to deliberate upon judgment. Since we were not all of one mind, judgment was deferred until the present council to be held at Loudun. And when the council had been concluded in the customary manner, we summoned together the venerable brethren and fellow bishops who had attended it, and carefully deliberated with them concerning the judgment in the aforesaid case. It was decided and confirmed with common consent that the chapel of St. Stephen should adhere and be united to the parish church founded in honor of the Blessed Apostle Peter, so that the monks should possess both mother and daughter. The judges with us in this decision were Ernald, archbishop of Bordeaux; Peter, bishop of Saintes; Peter of Poitiers; Marbod of Rennes; and Hildebert of Le Mans.

[Col. 1320B]

After judgment had been solemnly pronounced, we restored his chapel to our venerable brother, Abbot William of Marmoutier, and to his monastery. That this decision might remain firmer, we ordered it sealed with our seal and subscribed it with our hand.

This decision was made in the church of Blessed Mary at Loudun, where the synod had sat, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1109, indiction III, while Paschal II ruled the Roman Church, King Louis held the kingdom of the Franks, and Fulk the Younger presided over the people of Angers.

I, Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, subscribed to this decision.

[Col. 1319]

## LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS IN THE CASE OF BELLE-ÎLE

(Dom Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, vol. VI, appendix, p. 631.)

### NOTICE

(*Benedictine Annals*, book LXXIII, no. 20.)

[Col. 1319] At this time (1117) a great controversy arose between the monks of Redon and Quimperlé concerning Belle-Île. Leo IX and Gregory VII had formerly awarded it to the men of Redon, against the donation made to the monastery of Quimperlé from its very foundation by Alan, count of Cornouaille. Notwithstanding the authority of these pontiffs, the monks of Quimperlé had possessed the island peacefully until this time, when Hervé, abbot of Redon, supported by the protection of Count Conan, occupied it. Gurhand, abbot of Quimperlé, brought complaints on this matter to Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the Apostolic See.

He first wrote to Count Conan about the affair and urged him to protect the abbot of Quimperlé and that monastery, which his predecessors had founded in honor of the Holy Cross. He says that he wonders that Conan forbids persons in his land to seek the justice of the holy Roman Church—something neither kings nor other princes dare to do. Still less ought a count to do it, since he holds his principality from the vicar of St. Peter, that is, from the supreme pontiff. If he persists in doing so, the sword of blessed Peter hangs over him and his principality.

After this, Bishop Gerard summoned the parties. Having granted one and then another adjournment to the abbot of Redon, and since Hervé, abbot of Redon, disregarding ecclesiastical censure, had invaded Belle-Île by the armed violence of Count Conan and seized it by force, Gerard pronounced sentence against him together with Peter, bishop-elect of Saintes; Hugh, abbot of Saint-Eparchius; Iterius, master of the schools at Saintes; and others, and decreed that the island be restored to the monks of Quimperlé. He notified Briccius of Nantes, Marbod of Rennes, Morvan of Vannes, Rivallon of Aleth, and the other bishops of Brittany of this judgment by letter. He also wrote other letters to Morvan, bishop of Vannes, in whose diocese the monastery of Redon was situated. In them he informed him that he had determined to hold a council in the second week of the coming Lent and ordered Bishop Morvan to attend with the abbot of Redon; otherwise, if the abbot did not appear, a sentence of canonical coercion would be pronounced against him.

When the abbot nevertheless did not desist from what he had begun, Gerard wrote to Countess Ermengard, mother of Count Conan, that she should restore peace and concord between the monks. Ermengard replied that she would gladly do so if only the sentence of interdict and excommunication against the monks of Redon were relaxed. Her son Conan complained that an injury had been done him in this matter, since he had done nothing without the command of the pope and of the legate himself. Yet he was ready to make amends if he had erred in any respect. Finally, she advised the legate to grant the count and the monks a truce until his council. Gislebert, archbishop of Tours, likewise sent Count Conan a letter about the same affair. The count replied that, if he had erred, he had erred at the pope’s command, and that he was ready to make amends if he had committed any wrong. At last, because the abbot of Redon had been absent from the council, the sentence of interdict and excommunication was confirmed against him and his monastery. Jocerannus, bishop of Lyon, approved it, and Pope Paschal confirmed it. All the documents of this affair are set out here, together with its history, composed by Gurhedenus, a monk of Quimperlé.

### I. Letter of Gerard, legate and bishop of Angoulême, to Count Conan concerning Belle-Île

[Col. 1321A]

GERARD, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, to CONAN, valiant count and illustrious prince of Brittany: greeting and blessing.

Because we have heard that you love peace and justice, we rejoice; for by acting thus good princes obtain the favor of the supreme King. We hope concerning you that, from good beginnings, you may always strive toward progress in what is better, just as, conversely, from evil beginnings one proceeds to an increase of evils. We therefore impart to you the blessing of the holy apostles and exhort you to show honor to the holy Church of God, so that God himself may deign to preserve your principality [Col. 1321B]. Moreover, we earnestly commend to your protection the abbot of Quimperlé and that monastery which your predecessors founded, out of regard for religion, in honor of the Holy Cross. But we have heard that you forbid persons of your land to seek the justice of the holy Roman Church. We greatly wonder at this, since neither kings nor other princes presume to do it, especially as it is clear, from the records, that your predecessors held their principality from the vicar of blessed Peter, namely the lord pope. If you should wish to do this on the wicked counsel of anyone, know for certain that the sentence of the holy Roman Church and the sword of blessed Peter hang over you and your principality.

### II. Letter of Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, to the bishop of Cornouaille

[Col. 1321C]

GERARD, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, to ROBERT, venerable bishop of Cornouaille: greeting and blessing.

We command your affection that, if Count Conan of your land should presume to lay hands upon the property of the abbot of Quimperlé, you are to place him under interdict and deprive all his land within your bishopric of divine offices. But if, God forbid, you should tolerate such sacrilege without justice, know that a canonical sentence hangs over you for your consent.

### III. Judgment rendered and determined by Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, in the dispute concerning Belle-Île between the abbots of Redon and Quimperlé

[Col. 1322A]

I, GERARD, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, wish it to be known to present and future persons that our brethren Hervé, abbot of Redon, with Briccius, bishop of Nantes, and certain of his monks, and Gurhand, abbot of Quimperlé, with Robert, bishop of Cornouaille, and certain monks, came to our court concerning the controversy between them over the land called Belle-Île. When each side had set out its arguments and we intended to render a judicial sentence upon their arguments, [Col. 1322B] the aforesaid abbot of Redon, perceiving that he was insufficiently prepared for the case, requested an adjournment from us. By the advice of our court, acceding to his request, we granted the adjournment he sought. When the date had been appointed, the aforesaid abbot of Quimperlé again came prepared to our court to pursue his case; but the abbot of Redon did not come. Through his messenger, however, he put forward his excuses and requested another adjournment. As the aforesaid abbot of Quimperlé insisted more earnestly that we bring his case to an end, we again took counsel with our court and allowed the abbot of Redon an adjournment.

Meanwhile, before the date fixed by us for their case had elapsed, the above-named abbot of Redon, employing perverse counsel, [Col. 1322C] setting aside ecclesiastical censure in favor of secular tyranny, entered by the violence of Conan, count of Brittany, upon the land called Belle-Île, concerning which the controversy existed; by armed force he expelled from it the men of the monastery of Quimperlé and occupied it without lawful cause. Since, therefore, a cry concerning so great an injury reached us, we warned the abbot of Redon by our letters and messengers that, on a date appointed, he should come prepared to answer for so great and enormous an invasion. On that date both he and the abbot of Quimperlé were present before us. When he was admonished by us to answer concerning the aforesaid invasion, he began to offer excuses and said that he would by no means answer at that time concerning the invasion. We, therefore, hearing him evade the matter and offer no canonical [Col. 1323A] excuses, together with our brethren Peter, bishop-elect of Saintes; Hugh, abbot of Saint-Eparchius; Iterius, master of the schools at Saintes; and Hugh, canon of Le Mans, adjudged full investiture of the aforesaid island to Gurhand, abbot of Quimperlé. Insofar as pertained to us, saving the right of the monastery of Redon, we invested him; and we commanded the abbot of Redon, who was present, to recall his men from there and permit the abbot of Quimperlé quietly to hold his investiture.

Present at this judgment were the aforesaid brethren who judged with us, also Renald, prior of Vertou; Tiso and Vitalis, clerics of the bishop of Nantes; William, Guardrard, William, Gerald, and Renald [Col. 1323B], clerics of Saintes; Richard, Jubanus, Raymond, Aldradus, and Teduinus, canons of Angoulême; and many other clerics and laymen.

And in order that this our judgment may remain firmer and more certain, we subscribed it with our own hand and caused it to be strengthened by the seal of our authority.

Done at Angoulême in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1117, indiction X, in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, son of King Philip.

### IV. Another letter of the same legate to Morvan, bishop of Vannes

GERARD, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, to MORVAN, bishop of Vannes: greeting and blessing.

[Col. 1323C] When our brethren Hervé, abbot of Redon, and Gurhand, abbot of Quimperlé, were present in our court concerning the case of Belle-Île, we judged that the abbot of Redon should invest the abbot of Quimperlé with Belle-Île, because he had despoiled him of it by lay force without hearing and judgment. For completing this investiture in full we established a period of less than a month; and, unless he made the investiture within that period, we ourselves orally forbade the abbot of Redon both the office of priest and that of abbot, and deprived the entire abbey of divine offices. We therefore command your brotherhood and, by the authority of the Apostolic See, order you to ensure that this our interdict, both upon the abbot and upon the abbey, is firmly and unshakably maintained by your authority together with ours [Col. 1323D].

### V. Another letter of the same to all the bishops of Brittany

GERARD, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, to the venerable brethren BRICCIUS of Nantes, MARBOD of Rennes, MORVAN of Vannes, RIVALLON of Aleth, and the other bishops of Brittany: greeting and blessing.

We wish your affection to know that we summoned the abbot of Redon before us because of the invasion he had made upon the monastery of Quimperlé, by taking from it its best possession. We corrected him for such presumption [Col. 1324A] and, by the counsel of wise men, decreed that he should completely reinvest the brethren of Quimperlé with everything taken from them. We set him an appropriate period within which he was to perform this; if he failed to do so, we forbade him the offices of priest and abbot and prohibited him and his monks from entering the church. But the abbot of Redon did not restore their property to the brethren of Quimperlé; rather, he broke our interdict—indeed, that of the holy Roman Church—and still presumes to break it. Therefore we command your brotherhood to publish this in your churches and assemblies, to regard him as a schismatic and excommunicate, and to announce to your parishioners that they are not to visit the monastery of Redon or entrust themselves to burial there. In their dependencies [Col. 1324B] and cells which they possess in your bishoprics, also forbid the performance of the divine office. Furthermore, on our behalf, diligently approach Count Conan, that within thirty days he may correct without delay so great and presumptuous an invasion; if he does not, we shall terribly unsheathe against him and all his land the sword of the Holy Spirit.

### VI. Another letter of the same to Hervé, abbot of Redon, concerning the invasion of Belle-Île and disobedience

GERARD, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, to HERVÉ, abbot of Redon.

[Col. 1324C] At the beginning of this letter I would greet you, were it not that you despise our interdict and knowingly participate with your monks, who have become schismatics. Therefore, by the authority of the Apostolic See, we summon you to attend, putting aside every excuse, the council which we are to hold at Angoulême in the second week of the coming Lent, there to accept whatever justice may prescribe concerning the invasion of Belle-Île and your disobedience.

### VII. To Morvan, bishop of Vannes

GERARD, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, to MORVAN, venerable bishop of Vannes: greeting and blessing.

[Col. 1324D] Against the growing vices and enormities arising in the Church and the people of God, by command of our lord pope we have resolved to hold a council at Angoulême in the second week of the coming Lent. We invite your brotherhood to it and, by the authority of the Apostolic See, command you, on our behalf and your own, to summon Hervé, abbot of Redon, to attend the same council with every excuse removed. If he withdraws himself from so great an assembly, he shall without doubt receive the sentence of canonical coercion.

### VIII. Letter of Countess Ermengard to Gerard, legate of Angoulême

To the venerable lord and pious father GERARD, bishop of Angoulême [Col. 1325A] and legate of the holy Roman Church, ERMENGARD, countess, humble servant of your humility: greeting.

I give thanks to your benevolence because you deign to honor my lowliness with your greeting and blessing—indeed, even with your prayer. As to your charging me to strive to restore concord and peace among the monks, I gladly accept this at your command. One thing troubles me: that you hold the monks of Redon both under interdict and excommunicated. If it pleased your discretion, this ought temporarily to be relaxed, especially since my son complains that in this matter he is very seriously burdened and that an injury is done to the monks. For he maintains that whatever he did here he did at the command of the lord pope and of you; and if he erred in anything, he is ready to make amends before the judgment of his bishops [Col. 1325B]. He also says that, in your presence, if you come to a suitable place, he will answer for everything and do what justice requires. You would therefore do well to grant a truce to both the count and the monks until your council. I also ask you meanwhile to send the men of Quimperlé to us, so that, God granting it, we may negotiate concord. And through you we ask the lord bishop of Cornouaille to return, in order that he may receive from my son, according to the counsel of the bishops, full justice or attain concord. But if none of these things commends itself to your prudence, my son will arrange to answer you at your council through his bishops and abbots in whatever manner reason shall show him.

### IX. Letter of Count Conan to Gislebert, archbishop of Tours

[Col. 1325C]

To GISLEBERT, by the grace of God archbishop of Tours, his beloved and most dear lord, CONAN, duke of the Bretons: greeting and service.

I offer you no small thanks for the good which you have deigned to communicate to me. But concerning what you have written to me about the bishop of Cornouaille and his abbot, I reply to you that, if there has been error, I erred at the command of the lord pope; and I shall most willingly correct my wrongdoing according to your counsel and that of the bishops of Brittany, or, if they prefer, shall render justice before you and the bishops of Brittany. Therefore I inform and earnestly beg you, for our sake, to urge them toward one of these alternatives.

### X. Letter of Gislebert, archbishop of Tours, to Count Conan

[Col. 1325D]

GISLEBERT, humble minister of Tours by the grace of God, to his beloved son CONAN, illustrious duke of Brittany: greeting and blessing.

In the first place, we render you the thanks due to you, because, as we have learned from his own words, you received our messenger honorably; and it was even more gratifying to us that you replied more favorably to the embassy of our entreaty and petition, if you carry it out. Yet concerning your statement that, if there was error, you erred by the counsel of the lord pope, know for certain that we have seen certain letters of his addressed to you concerning the complaint of the bishop of Cornouaille and the abbot of Quimperlé [Col. 1326A], and others addressed to the lord legate on the same business. In them, saving your favour, I say that the counsel of the pope which you allege is by no means in agreement with this. But that you promise to make amends for it, and to pursue this matter according to our counsel or judgment and that of our brother bishops of Brittany, pleases us greatly, and for this we thank you. Therefore our counsel is to send these our brethren—the bishop of Cornouaille, namely, and the abbot of Quimperlé—to the kindness of your affection, and faithfully to entreat and exhort you as a most beloved son that, in this matter, you should in no way strive to oppose the admonitions or even commands of the lord pope Paschal, or the injunctions of his predecessor pontiffs [Col. 1326B], whose privileges concerning this possession of the monastery of Quimperlé we have seen. Rather, in accordance with the counsel of the lord pope Paschal and of the legate of Angoulême, we praise, entreat, and admonish you fully to invest the abbot of Quimperlé with the revenues adjudged to him; and, if, with the counsel of our brother bishops of Brittany, you can bring this complaint to peace, God helping, we desire and permit it. But if—God forbid—it is not now to receive a peaceful end, we shall, by God's grace, at a suitable time and place, as you request and as is our duty, not fail the justice of either party.

### XI. The archbishops of the Churches of Lyons and Besançon to the bishop of Angoulême

[Col. 1326C]

To the distinguished brother Gerard, venerable bishop of Angoulême and vicar of the Apostolic See, Joceran, servant of the Church of Lyons, and Anserinus, archbishop of Besançon: greeting, and honour to your priesthood.

The lord pope, having heard the judgment by which your discernment settled the dispute between Gurhand, abbot of Holy Cross at Quimperlé, and Hervé, abbot of Redon, confirmed by the authority of his letters whatever you should do in the matter. We therefore, placing the fullest confidence in your justice and rectitude, earnestly entreat your dignity to ensure that the aforesaid judgment, confirmed by the lord pope, is held and observed for ever, and to secure for the abbot of Holy Cross the justice which is due and lawful, until he possesses the right of his Church in peace. Know certainly that we would do far greater things for you, should you need our assistance in any affair. We wish that you may always prosper and act valiantly in all things.

### XII. Copy of Pope Paschal’s letter to the legate of Angoulême.—He consoles the afflicted man. He confirms the interdict imposed upon the abbot of Redon

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“To your brotherhood,” etc.

See Paschal, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, no. 502.

### XIII. Letter of the same pope to Count Conan.—He urges him to compel the monks of Redon to restore Belle-Île to the monks of Quimperlé

[Col. 1327A]

“Paschal, bishop,” etc.

“You ought to know,” etc.

See above, no. 503.

### XIV. Copy of Count Conan’s charter concerning the restoration and confirmation of Belle-Île

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Conan, humble duke of Brittany, together with my sister Hadeuguis and my mother Ermenjart, give and grant, for the salvation of my soul and those of my parents, to the monastery built at Quimperlé in honour of the Holy [Col. 1327B] Cross, the land called Belle-Île with all its revenues, as my father Alan did, and my grandfather Hoel, and my great-grandfather Alan. For we know that the claim of the men of Redon, which in our time arose through greed and envy concerning this land, and on account of which Lord Robert, bishop of Cornouaille, with the clergy of Cornwall, and Gurguandus, abbot of Quimperlé, with his monks, persevered for a year and almost a half, has been proved false and entirely quashed by apostolic authority and judgment. To that judgment we sent Hervé, abbot of Redon, and Gurchand, abbot of Quimperlé, concerning the dispute which they had over this land.

Therefore I now restore in perpetuity to the monastery of Quimperlé and to all the monks dwelling there, into the hands of Gurchand, abbot of that Church, the aforesaid island, with all its appurtenances [variant: *suis*, “its own”], which Hervé [Col. 1327C], abbot of Redon, had seized by force of my authority; for this seizure he, with his entire abbey, had justly been placed under interdict and excommunicated by apostolic authority for more than a year. I restore it without any further disturbance by me or my successors. I also caused the monk whom the abbot of Redon had taken with him from the often-mentioned island to be restored from the cloister of Redon to his own place. Whoever hereafter troubles the monastery of Quimperlé over this matter shall be struck by apostolic authority and shattered by our comital severity.

[Col. 1327D] This was done at Redon in the year 1118 of the Incarnate Word, in the presence of Lord Robert, bishop of Cornouaille; Marbod, bishop of Rennes; Briccius, bishop of Nantes; and Morvan, bishop of Vannes.

The witnesses of this matter are these: [lacuna].

### XV. Account or record of the aforesaid dispute, made by Gurheden, monk of Quimperlé

Let all know that no abbot of Redon ever anywhere brought any claim against our monastery; rather, the abbots and convents of both monasteries lived unanimously in concordant brotherhood, until one of them, Abbot Hervé, supported by the aid of the count, attacked us. By the true reasoning of equity, with the grace of the Holy Spirit cooperating, we destroyed the injury he inflicted. But first let us see how many abbots there were on each side, and how concordantly they lived.

Thus Saint Gurloesius, first abbot of the Church of Holy Cross, governed it for twenty-five years in good quiet and peace. Through him God displayed many miracles during his life, and even now in death very many are manifested through daily experience. Saint John succeeded him in the government of the same Church and lived nineteen years without force or claim. Many good works of his are recounted by clergy and laity alike. After him Abbot Vitalis, troubled by no one, flourished commendably in the same seat for nine years; his bones restore many sick persons to health. The fourth, Vingomarus [variant: Jungomarius; Col. 1328B], obtained the same seat, which he ruled peacefully for three years. His body, giving forth a most sweet fragrance, is seen wholly intact when the tomb is opened in the Church of the Mother of God at Quimper Saint-Corentin. After these, Benedict, a man of very good reputation, flourished in the same government for fifty-two years. Yet this sixth abbot, against whom a claim is falsely lodged, was summoned neither personally nor through the bishop of the province before an outcry was wrongfully raised, as they say, before the Apostolic See and the legate, without our knowledge. Moreover, the abbot of Redon also complained to tyrannical and secular power—namely, the ruler of the land—about the aforesaid island, giving and promising money to overthrow another Church, while we nowhere fled from truth [Col. 1328C].

This our abbey was placed by its founders, Alan and his son Hoel, counts, and by the aforesaid abbots, under the protection and patronage of the holy Roman Church in perpetual defence. Two gold denarii were agreed and given as an annual payment and upon accession; privileges were received from holy apostolic men, preserved in the archive of our monastery, and copies are contained in this little book. It should also be known, on the other side, that Catwallon, abbot of Saint Saviour, was a co-worker in founding the Church of Holy Cross. He sent his prior Gurloesius to the count to become abbot; he also received our brotherhood from the abbot and brethren, in life and in death, and also bestowed it upon them—a compact which is preserved in writing between the two parties to this day [Col. 1328D]. His successor Abbot Hugunnanus held this same agreement with the firmest stability and never violated it. After him Perrenesius received the brethren of Quimperlé with the same tenor and the greatest charity. Then his successor Almodus observed the same under the bond of brotherhood. An abbot named Bili [variant: Vili] likewise maintained the same peace of the earlier predecessors. After these Robert retained, without any dissension, the mutual devotion of the two places within the aforesaid brotherhood. Justinus too, worn out by old age, preserved in the same way the inviolable fellowship of both parties. Gualterus, moreover, held valid in the same bond of friendship, as long as he lived, what his predecessors [Col. 1329A] had confirmed. All these existed in the aforesaid brotherhood and fellowship without any claim.

Lest the suit of Hervé, abbot of Redon, and Gurhand, abbot of the monastery of Quimperlé, somewhat debated in the court of Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, should be consigned to oblivion, we have decreed that a record be made. First, Hervé, abbot of Redon, complained that Belle-Île had been unjustly taken from his monastery by Count Alan; that thereafter his monks had been expelled with the killing of one hundred and twenty men; and that he had often raised an outcry in councils over this wrong but had never found justice. Abbot Gurhand [Col. 1329B], on the contrary, replied that Belle-Île had been given to his monastery without any claim by Count Alan, who possessed it by hereditary right; that his predecessors—namely, five abbots—had possessed it in peace; and finally asserted that the aforesaid island had been possessed by his predecessors for at least thirty years.

When he was asked how many years there were from the foundation of the Church to the time of Abbot Benedict, his predecessor, and in what year of the Lord’s Incarnation his Church had been founded, he replied that his Church was founded in the year 1008 of the Incarnate Word, and that from the foundation of the Church to the time of Benedict there were fifty-six years. To show also that the claim of the men of Redon was false, he stated that the first abbot of his monastery [Col. 1330A], Saint Gurloesius, had been sought and elected by Count Alan from the monastery of Saint Saviour with the agreement of his brethren. To this the abbot of Redon replied that his predecessors had allowed Saint Gurloesius to be abbot because the same island had not been taken from them during Saint Gurloesius’s lifetime.

But when the abbot of Redon was asked where, when, and before whom he had made his claim, he replied that Huguimarius, abbot of his monastery, had complained at Vercelli before Pope Leo concerning Saint Gurloesius, abbot of Quimperlé, where he was found to be opposed to reason. For above he had said that, in the time of the aforesaid saint, the same island belonged to his own right. Moreover, he added that his monks had made complaint in this matter at Saintes, Rennes, and Suldun. Again, when asked whether he had a written document given by the hand of any cardinal, or witnesses whom he could produce, he said that he had no witnesses, but that an unsealed written document had remained at home. Again he was asked which abbot of Quimperlé had taken the aforesaid island from him and his people. He replied that Abbot Benedict and Count Hoel, his brother, had taken the said island from him and his people—where he plainly lied, since at the beginning of his argument he had reported that Count Alan had taken the island from him. Having investigated the case thus far, the legate and his associates adjourned until mid-Lent.

[Col. 1330]

## Charter of Gerard, settling the dispute that arose between Bernard, viscount of Comborn, and the abbot of Uzerche concerning the place called Amanzenas. (Year 1116)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Lucae edition, vol. III, p. 66.]

[Col. 1329]

[Col. 1329C] I, Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, wish it to be known to present and future persons that Bernard, viscount of Comborn, and the abbot of Uzerche, with certain persons of his monastery, came into our court on account of a dispute which they had concerning a certain land that Bernard himself had given to the monks of Cluny for the salvation of his soul.

The abbot of Uzerche employed the following arguments against Bernard and against the gift he had made. He said that the land which Bernard had given to the aforesaid monks for building was part of the freehold of Saint Peter of Uzerche, which Count Odo of La Marche had given to Saint Peter of Uzerche. He further advanced another argument, saying that the Church of Trainiac, in whose parish that building was being erected, belonged by right to Saint Peter of Uzerche. A certain priest had given it to the monastery of Saint Peter of Uzerche, and after some time Umbaud, bishop of the see of Limoges, with the counsel of Gausbert, archdeacon, and Boso, archpriest, gave it to the same monastery. To establish the bishop’s gift, they produced a written charter recording the grant itself.

To this the aforesaid Viscount Bernard replied that the land called Amanzenas was not part of the freehold of the count of La Marche, but, he maintained, was his own inherited freehold from his grandfathers and great-grandfathers; he had given it into the hand of our brother Eustorchius, bishop of Limoges, to the monks of Cluny for building. He said that he was entirely unaware that Umbaud, bishop of Limoges, had made them a gift of the Church of Trainiac. Having heard these arguments of both parties, we, together with our venerable brethren and fellow bishops of Limoges [Col. 1331A], Périgueux, and Agen, judged by canonical authority that, if the count of La Marche should sue him within forty days from the day when judgment was rendered concerning the freehold which the monks of Uzerche claimed to possess through the count of La Marche’s gift, the aforesaid Viscount Bernard should answer him as justice required.

And because the charter which they had produced concerning Bishop Umbaud’s gift of the Church of Trainiac did not possess canonical validity, we judged with the aforesaid bishops that within the same forty days they should produce two lawful witnesses who could reasonably prove that they had seen and heard that the aforesaid bishop, with the counsel of the aforesaid Gausbert, archdeacon, and Boso, archpriest, had given the Church of Trainiac to the monks [Col. 1331B] of Uzerche. In the meantime, the monks of Cluny were to hold and build upon in peace the land which Viscount Bernard had given them.

The aforesaid brother bishops were present at and assented to this our judgment [Col. 1332A]: Ildebert and Gerald, archdeacons of Limoges; Arnaldus Guillelmi and William of Nanclars, archdeacons of Périgueux; Geoffrey, archdeacon of Agen; Peter, precentor of Angoulême; Esdradus, Julianus, and Raymond, canons of Angoulême; Helias of Gimel and Rennulfus of Garait, archpriests of Limoges; and many other venerable clerics.

And that this our judgment may be held and maintained more firmly and certainly, we have subscribed it with our own hand and caused it to be fortified with our seal.

I, Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

This judgment was rendered in the diocese of Périgueux [Col. 1332B], at the castle called Exidolium, in the year 1116 of the Incarnate Word, in the eighth indiction, in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks.

## In the Year of the Lord 1136: Lord Odo, Abbot of Saint Remigius of Rheims

[Col. 1331]

### Letter to Count Thomas concerning a certain miracle of Saint Thomas the Apostle

[Note: [Col. 1331D] This letter of Odo, abbot of Saint Remigius at Rheims, was written about the year 1135. For in the following year, upon his return from Italy, he granted land for the construction of the Carthusian monastery of Mont-Dieu. Thomas the count to whom the letter is addressed appears to be Thomas of Marle, lord of the castle of Coucy.]

[Col. 1331C] It is salutary for all worshippers of the Christian name always to seek and hear something edifying, and through the report of the faithful to learn how wondrous the Lord is in his saints. Since I have found you eager for this, in accordance with the prompting of your request I have wished to inform you in writing of what I saw and heard at the Roman court. This present year, on the Friday after the solemnity of the Lord’s Ascension, I was before the lord pope, intending to speak concerning our own affairs, when suddenly someone appeared to announce that the envoys of the emperor of Byzantium—that is, Constantinople—were at the doors. Delighted at envoys of so great a name, the lord pope sent from his side a bishop to introduce them honourably and present them to him. They came, and, having greeted [Col. 1331D] the universal pope and many members of the court, gave a sufficiently courteous report, as they had been questioned, concerning the emperor’s health and the condition of his affairs.

The cause of their mission was this. With them was an archbishop of India, a man of quite dignified appearance and, according to the competence of his own language, most eloquent. Deprived of the companionable assistance of his deceased ruler, he had come the day before to the aforesaid emperor to seek counsel. When the emperor heard his request, he gave him one of his own household, a prince; and, as though the matter had been accomplished, the archbishop prepared to return home. But as he journeyed, death intervened and he lost the new prince. Having buried him, he returned to the emperor to tell him the cause of his grief. The emperor consoled him, admonished him not to grieve, and, through imperial generosity, gave him another prince. Then the archbishop, his grief somewhat softened, set out, but did not complete his journey. For the sudden death of the second prince violently disturbed him with a grief now doubled. He did not know what to do, uncertain whether he ought to return to the emperor or complete the journey he had begun while his affair remained unfinished. At last the vigour [Col. 1332D] of a manly resolution overcame the loss arising from the imminent danger; encouraged by his followers and admonished not to despair, he retraced his route and presented himself before the eyes of the merciful emperor as bearer of his dreadful misfortune.

When the emperor learned the outcome of this unforeseen event, he was astonished and, saying that he had satisfied the archbishop’s petition, refused to send a third prince. Yet the humble [Col. 1333A] archbishop scarcely obtained, with many tears, permission to visit the Roman court for counsel and to take with him the emperor’s envoys bearing letters of supplication. When he was at the court, he reported that he presided over certain palatine churches, among which was the Church in which, it was said, the body of the blessed apostle Thomas rested. Among the other things he related concerning the situation of the Church, the abundance of its treasures, and the variety of its ornaments, he expounded one thing which the ears of listeners cannot receive without amazement.

The Church of the aforesaid apostle, of great height, is enclosed on every side by a river. When its waters have withdrawn, owing to excessive dryness it makes itself passable, even to a child of seven years, for eight days before the apostle’s feast and as many days after the feast. On the solemn day itself [Col. 1333B], when the nobles of the entire province, together with all the clergy and people, have assembled in one place, after many tears and deep sighs the archbishop with companions of his order approaches the shrine of the blessed apostle. He reverently raises the body from it and fittingly places it in the episcopal chair. Then, first to throw himself at the feet of so great an advocate, he honours the apostle with the gift of his offering. The blessed apostle raises his arm, opens his hand, and gladly receives whatever is offered to him by all worshippers of our faith. But if any heretic, mingled among the people, endeavours under the appearance of devotion to place something in the apostle’s hand, the saint closes his hand and refuses to receive the impious offerings.

When such things had been reported by certain persons in the ears of the lord pope, he ordered the bishop to appear and wished, under anathema, to forbid him to sow falsehood further in the palace. For what he had made public about the apostle appeared contrary to truth. But before all persons the bishop affirmed that nothing was truer, and, with the assent of the lord pope, proved by an oath upon the most holy Gospel [Col. 1334B] that it was so. At last the lord pope believed, and the whole court believed; and they cried out that the apostle was able to obtain still greater things from divine omnipotence.

[Col. 1333]

## Charter of Lord Odo, Abbot of Saint Remigius, concerning the foundation of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu in the diocese of Rheims

[Note: [Col. 1333D] As religious congregations—the Molesmes, Cistercians, and Premonstratensians, whose founder, Saint Norbert, died in 1134—were spreading through parts of the diocese of Rheims, one community of the holy Carthusian order was lacking. It appeared to have taken root only in the kingdom of Burgundy or Provence, as it was then called. At last it extended its branches into these regions, first through the agency of the venerable Odo, abbot of Saint Remigius. The following account is handed down of how this came about. Odo once travelled to Rome and, on his return home, happened to turn aside to the Grande Chartreuse. Having examined the admirable way of life of those pious solitaries, he resolved, on the counsel of Blessed Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and with the assent of the venerable Guigo, prior of the Carthusians, to build a house of the same institute in the diocese of Rheims. Guigo granted Odo the first propagators of that sacred institution. Odo accordingly formed this plan before the death of Saint Hugh, the bishop, which occurred on 1 April 1132; but it was scarcely put into effect before 1134, when Abbot Odo returned from the Council of Pisa. A tract of his monastery’s land was assigned for the building of the new house, in the territory of Rheims, two leagues from the city of Mouzon, beside the river Bar. It was then called Mont-Boson, and later Mont-Dieu.]

(Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, VI, appendix, p. 664.)

[Col. 1333C] It is fitting that we should be kindly disposed towards all who serve the Lord, who is supreme holiness, and persevere in the sacred profession of religion, especially those who, having cast aside the burdens of secular affairs, already taste beforehand in the tranquillity of life how sweet the Lord is. We ought not only to provide some relief for their necessities, but also to take careful care that whatever the devotion of the faithful may bestow upon them remains unimpaired for their use.

Therefore we wish it to be fixed in the memory of all, present and future, that I, Odo, humble minister of the Church of Blessed Remigius, and the entire chapter of the same monastery—sharing the work with me, and offering their ready will and devout devotion with gracious assent—have established [Col. 1333D] a monastery in which brethren of honourable conduct, Carthusians, may keep and observe the usages and sacred customs [Col. 1334C] of the Carthusian order. It is built upon land of our Church, namely in the place now called Mont-Dieu, formerly called Mont-Boson, in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary and Saint John the Baptist.

All this was done by the counsel of Lord Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and with the assent of the reverend Guigo, prior of the poor Carthusians. He sent us the first masters of this sacred institution and commanded and decreed that the place be called Mont-Dieu. The venerable Raynald, second archbishop of Rheims, was also an energetic collaborator in this work; at his desire and counsel the Carthusian brethren were summoned and the place established [Col. 1334D].

[Col. 1335A] Accordingly, to the brethren serving God there in the Carthusian order and living according to the sacred institutions of that order, given by their holy predecessors, we have willingly granted, with the common assent of our entire chapter, the aforesaid monastery and whatever our Church possessed in the district of the same monastery within the boundaries written below, free from every rent and exaction. We have also granted that, if the aforesaid brethren can acquire by gift or purchase the lands which peasants possessed within the same boundaries, they may hold them freely and for ever, without any rent. Likewise, Richard, abbot of Mouzon, with his brethren, and Lord Ursio, abbot of Saint-Denis, and his community, have offered and given with ready devotion a free donation, discharged from every claim, of all that they held there [Col. 1335B]. William of Sathon, Nicholas of Bourg, and Guy of Altrey likewise gave, in equal freedom and for the remedy of their souls, whatever they held there and whatever was judged useful and necessary for the needs of Christ’s poor.

These are the boundaries enclosing the aforesaid places: from the eastern side toward the south, from Asia as far as the stream flowing into Amosias; from Amosias to the royal road; along the royal road as it runs to Forest; from Forest by the summit of Mount Rouel as it slopes to Chermel; from Chermel to the Buten stream; and from Buten, as it flows, to the river Bar. Likewise, from Asia toward the north [Col. 1335C] as far as the stream called Altrepa, where that same stream flows into the Bar.

That this our benefaction may have force in perpetuity, be kept whole and unshaken for all time, and endure, we have caused it to be fortified by the authority of the privilege of Pope Innocent II. We also strengthen and confirm it with the impression of the seal of Blessed Remigius and the subscriptions of honourable persons and witnesses [Col. 1336A]; and whoever attempts to violate it we strike with the sentence of anathema.

The mark of Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons. The mark of Alvisus, bishop of Arras. The mark of Odo, abbot of Saint Remigius. The mark of Ingulrannus, abbot of Hautvillers. The mark of Richard, abbot of Mouzon. The mark of Hellinus, abbot of Saint Thierry. The mark of Jorannus, abbot of Saint Nicaise. The mark of Alberic, abbot of Saint Basolus. The mark of Urso, abbot of Saint-Denis. The mark of Fulk, abbot of Épernay. The mark of William, abbot of Mont-Maur. The mark of Alberic and Hugh, archdeacons. The mark of Leo, dean. [Col. 1336B] The mark of Gervasius, cantor. The mark of Henry, Gregory, and Roger, priests. The mark of Boso, Rainer, and Bernard, deacons.

The witnesses of this matter are also: Joscelin, then prior; Hugh, subprior; Rainald, provost; Sigibert; Macharius; Hugh, chaplain; Gauterus of Altrey; Arnulf, provost; Christian, cantor; Haydericus, cellarer; Otho; Gervasius; Benedict; Lambert; another Lambert; Baldwin; and indeed the entire convent.

The witnesses of this decree and establishment are also: among the clerics, Drogo, dean of Saint Timothy; Lethardus; Thomas; Constantius; Nicholas.

Among the knights, Peter and his brother Thomas. Among the laymen, Thomas the reeve; Simon the dean; Walter; [Col. 1336C] Lambert; Guy, alderman; and many others.

Done at Rheims in the year 1137 of the Incarnate Word, in the thirteenth indiction [Note: [Col. 1335C] The fifteenth indiction should be restored.], in the thirtieth year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, in the twelfth year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Raynald, and in the eighteenth year of our ordination.

[Col. 1335]

### Letter of Lord Odo, Abbot of Saint Remigius, to Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot

(See under Wibald, below.)

## In the Year of the Lord 1136: Adalbert, Archbishop of Mainz

[Col. 1335]

### Notice

(Dom Martène, preface to vol. I of the *Amplissima Collectio*, p. XXXIII)

[Col. 1335] Rothard was succeeded in the see of Mainz by Adalbert, heir no less to his sincerity of devotion toward the Apostolic See than to his dignity. Adalbert had been chancellor of King Henry, “his most intimate counsellor, first among the foremost,” [Col. 1337A] as Otto of Freising says in book VII, chapter 14, and, as Abbot of Ursperg relates, “had always been second to the king in all things.” Entirely devoted to the emperor, he had once advised him to commit Pope Paschal, who retained the investitures for himself, to custody. But after the Lateran council, when the privilege had been condemned, he repented of his evil counsel and deed, joined in opposition to the erring prince, and was himself committed to custody for four years. Released through popular favour, he was consecrated bishop at Cologne by Otto, the most holy bishop of Bamberg; he declared war against the schismatic emperor and did not cease until he was reconciled with Pope Calixtus.

How greatly he laboured for this reconciliation is shown by his letter to Pope Calixtus beginning, “In many and great persecutions,” etc. Its words establish that Adalbert was, above all others, the mediator of the peace concluded between Pope Calixtus and Emperor Henry, and that he strove not so much to avenge the wrongs inflicted upon him by the prince as to repay them with benefits; for he loosed from the bonds of censures the man by whom he himself had been cast into chains.

He showed the same care toward his suffragans. Henry, bishop of Paderborn, had been reconciled to the Church at the Council of Northeim by Archbishop Rothard, his metropolitan, but on the condition that he abstain from episcopal office. Pope Paschal permitted him in 1107 to perform the duties of his order, as Gobelinus writes. Yet, as Emperor Henry V declined, he too seems to have lapsed; this is clearly proved by the letter of Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz, to the bishop and canons of Paderborn.

It is unnecessary to discuss at length how much Adalbert laboured to bring Cuno of Strasbourg back to the bosom of the Church, since his own letter to Pope Calixtus II plainly declares it. Cuno, Adalbert says, had hitherto been “constant in the king’s service” and “was counted among the emperor’s chief friends.” He was present at the diet at Speyer in 1108 and at the funeral there of Henry the Elder in 1111; in 1113 he celebrated holy Easter with him at Worms, as may be inferred from a diploma granted to the monks of Saint Maximin. Finally, as the emperor’s inseparable companion, he left nothing undone to win the emperor’s favour, being not ashamed to follow him even while he erred and was attached to schism.

What then did Adalbert do? “We often admonished him,” he says, “to obey the Church of God; and, that we might make greater progress by this means, we wrote many times to the canons, urging them to withdraw from his error and return to the unity of Christ’s peace.” Nor indeed did those frequent admonitions of that excellent bishop prove fruitless. He adds: “Our brother Cuno, bishop of Strasbourg, immediately after the Council of Rheims sought mercy and received absolution from a cardinal of the holy Roman Church. [lacuna] After the bishop was absolved, he withdrew himself from the emperor in heart and body, and continued in the service and fidelity of the Church, though unjust and a sinner, yet a faithful and useful defender of truth.”

Since Henry persecuted him with grievous hatred on this account and drove him, stripped of everything, from the city, Adalbert wrote to Pope Calixtus in his favour, “not, however,” he says, “because we endeavour to defend or approve the bishop’s injustice.” These words indicate plainly enough that Cuno was marked by more than one charge of schism. Indeed, not long afterward, that is, in 1123, he is recorded in the Saxon Chronicle as deprived of office because of the killing of Duke Berthold, to which he had assented: “Cuno, bishop of Strasbourg only in name, is deposed from the episcopate because he consents to the killing of Duke Berthold.” Therefore certain writers who assign his death to this year must be corrected, unless it is established from elsewhere that he died in this very year.

[Col. 1337]
