### V. To the clergy of the Church of Halberstadt.—He grieves over the death of their bishop Raynard, because, without consulting him, they proceeded to an election and took a pastor for themselves from another Church

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, p. 680, from the manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.)

[Col. 1337B]

Adalbert, humble [Col. 1338A] minister of the holy Church of Mainz and legate of the Apostolic See, to the brethren in Christ of the Church of Halberstadt—abbots, provosts, and all the rest, both greater and lesser: the spirit to think what is right.

Of the death of our most dear and venerable brother, your father Bishop Reinbard, how greatly we have grieved and kept silence, almighty God knows; and he who is truth himself is our witness to the heavy sorrow with which we were afflicted because he was so suddenly taken from us. Since he and our persons and churches formed one body and one soul, we had long awaited some messenger from you concerning so great a desolation among you, who might both inform us more certainly of your wishes and not disregard the assent of our brotherhood concerning the ordering of your Church. For only a small distance separated us, and the established order of canonical institution required that this be done.

But you, forgetful of your ancient discretion and prudence, and—without speaking of what was due to our person—giving little attention to what you owed your mother Church of Mainz, have proceeded in your entire affair outside the custom of ecclesiastical practice. You chose a person from another Church [Note: Odo, provost of St. Sebastian at Magdeburg; concerning him see more fully in the cited Chronicle of Halberstadt.] and, by a novel usurpation, did not shrink from investing him, as it were, with ring and staff. Yet we cannot sufficiently wonder that this should have occurred in a Church hitherto so well instructed and worn down by so many labours and persecutions for the obtaining of canonical investiture. For it belongs to the consecrator alone to give ring and staff.

But, setting all these matters aside for the present, we write only this to your brotherhood: we are going to our brethren at Mainz, and, having taken counsel with them and with such others as we can consult, we shall willingly give you a fuller reply concerning whatever we can do for the honour of God and his justice. Farewell.

> [Note: Reinhard died on 6 March 1122, in the fifteenth year of his consecration, as is recorded in the Chronicle of Halberstadt. The Chronicle of Stederburg, where his death is assigned to 1124, must therefore be corrected. He was the son of Count Poppo of Bankenburg, and had two brothers, Conrad and Sigifred; from one or the other of them was born Poppo II, Count of Blankenburg, a cruel man and most hostile to New Corvey.]

## VI. Letter of Adalbert, Archbishop of Mainz, to Bishop H. and the Canons of Paderborn

*(Martène, Amplissima Collectio, preface to vol. I, p. XXXIV.)*

Adalbert, by the mercy of God archbishop of the Church of Mainz and legate of the Apostolic See, to his brother and fellow bishop in Christ, H. of the Church of Paderborn, ...

Recognizing your repentance ... and, by the mercy of God, [we exhort you] henceforth faithfully to persevere in obedience to holy mother Church, striving through his grace steadfastly to preserve and bring to completion the good work which he has begun in you: by the counsel and dispensation of our brethren, in whose presence we deliberated concerning your case, we have decided that indulgence ought to be granted to your infirmity. In view of the necessity of the time and the salvation of Christ’s faithful people to be advanced in your Church, we grant you the administration of the episcopal office.

Following in this the authority of our lord Pope Paschal, of blessed memory, pontiff of the universal Church, and establishing nothing new in the Church of God as proceeding from ourselves, we hold valid the measures which he took in your case and the matters in which he restored you; and we command, under the testimony of our brethren the bishops of Cologne and Bamberg and the abbot of Corvey, that these measures remain in force for you, free from the injurious slander of ill-wishers and detractors.

And to all of you, our most dear lords and brethren in Christ and for Christ, we command by exhorting and exhort by commanding, that henceforth you be of one mind with your bishop, and he with you; that you may love one another, so that on that day of harvest you may be able to carry sheaves of righteousness to the Lord’s threshing-floor. To you, brother, whom we embrace in the bowels of Christ, we give counsel in the affection of brotherly love; and by the authority of God, blessed Peter, and ourselves we enjoin you to nourish, embrace, and cherish your brethren with fatherly compassion. If any are weak or more infirm, condescend to them with the compassion due to them; and strive thus to provide for the sheep committed to you, that on the Lord’s day you may joyfully deserve to hear that “Well done” addressed to faithful servants. We wish all of you health in the Lord and faithful perseverance in the unity of holy mother Church.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1137: RAINALD II, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

## NOTICE

*(Gallia Christiana, new edition, vol. IX, col. 82)*

Rainald II (of Martigny, or des Prés), son of Brientius, of the family of Meduana in the province of Anjou, was transferred from the bishopric of Angers to the archbishopric of Reims in 1124, through the favour of King Louis VI; in that same year he attended the council of Clermont. In the following year, the first of his episcopate, he restored to the Cluniac monks the altar of Tours-sur-Marne, which had been seized by nobles; moreover, he granted three altars to the monks of Saint-Nicaise. He also subscribed the royal diploma by which the advowson and provostship of Laon, which had been granted in benefice to laymen, were restored by King Louis to that church at the request of Bishop Bartholomew.

In 1126 he built the monastery of Igny from its foundations and endowed it most generously. In 1127, while he had envoys at Rome, perhaps to obtain the pallium, he absolved Count Witer of Rethel, who had been excommunicated for the exactions he had imposed upon the villages of Saint-Remi, after the count repented. [Note: St Bernard, Letters 19 and 20.] In the same year he entered into an agreement with Albero, bishop of Liège, concerning the fief of Bouillon. We have taken care to print among the documents of this church a complete copy of this agreement from Marlot, rather than the defective and mutilated version published by the Sammarthani. Although the copyist erred in assigning the regnal year of King Louis, it is nevertheless clear that the agreement was made in 1127, not, as we formerly wrote, in 1137. [Note: *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 871.] Hence one may conclude that Rainald dealt not with Albero II but with Albero I.

In 1128 Rainald attended the assembly of bishops convened by Matthew, bishop of Albano; and, after expelling the secular clerics, established regular canons in the monastery of Saint Martin at Épernay. In 1129, on holy Easter Day, he consecrated at Reims Philip, eldest son of Louis VI, as king; Philip died two years later, and Henry I, king of England, was present. In the same year he subscribed the ordinance of King Louis restoring the monastery of Argenteuil to the royal abbey of Saint-Denis in France. Also in that year he established, or confirmed as established, regular canons at Cuisy; confirmed the possessions of the monastery of Hénin; and granted the church of Val-Dieu to Walter, abbot of Saint Martin of Laon. He also wrote to Robert, archdeacon of Tournai, [Note: *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 445.] concerning the placing of monks of Saint-Theodoric in the church of Petinghem, but the year is uncertain.

In October 1131 he attended the Council of Reims held by Pope Innocent II, who, at that same assembly and at the request of King Louis VI, consecrated Louis VII. In 1133 he attended the Council of Jouy, at which the murderers of Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor at Paris, were excommunicated. In 1134 he made certain grants both to the abbey of Igny—which in that same year gave birth to the abbey of Signy—and to the monks of Marmoutier living at Saint-Theobald near Igny; then, after dedicating the basilica of Ursicamp with seven other bishops, he went to the Council of Pisa. In 1135, having returned to his diocese, he confirmed the possessions of the abbey of Saint-Nicaise. In 1136 he likewise confirmed the goods of the monastery of Sept-Fontaines. In 1137, with this prelate’s cooperation, the Carthusian house of Mont-Dieu was founded by the monks of Saint-Remi.

Finally, having reached a great old age, he died in 1138 according to the Roman reckoning. This is inferred from a charter bearing Rainald’s name and executed at Saint-Theodoric in that year. His body was transferred to Igny and buried beside the altar on the south side, with this epitaph, added to his tomb in a later hand, I believe:

> I, RAINALD DES PRÉS, formerly archbishop of Reims and priest, believe that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and in my flesh I shall see God my Saviour. He died in 1137, on 14 December.

But the following inscription seems more certainly to record the day and year of his death:

> In the year one thousand, one hundred, and thirty-eight together,  
> When the Ides of January are named,  
> Rainald, bishop of Reims, memorable [for his deeds], died.

The necrology of Reims likewise has the following concerning him for the Ides of January: “Lord Rainald died, first bishop of Angers and afterwards archbishop of Reims; he rests within, and he bought for us the land of Hundilicourt, etc., for his anniversary.” Moreover, this most worthy prelate cannot be sufficiently praised because he adhered with the utmost constancy, unto death, to the legitimate pontiff against the antipope Anacletus. Indeed, the pseudopontiff’s reproaches and taunts, poured out against the archbishop of Reims before one of the bishops of that province, proclaim both Rainald’s fidelity and his hatred of the schismatics, in these words: [Note: Baronius, under the year 1131.]

> “Let no grief or sorrow affect you because that illiterate man of Reims, a useless block, is known to have acted wickedly and shamelessly against you and your church—especially since, against us and the Roman Church, to which he bound himself by oath, he has, like a drunken man heated with wine, insolently spewed out much in the manner of actors, setting his mouth in heaven so that his tongue passes over the earth. Like another Dioscorus, he has presumed to judge the Apostolic See,” etc.

# LETTERS OF RAINALD II, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

## I. To Robert, Archdeacon of Tournai—That he should install monks in the church of Petinghem. (1130)

*(Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, vol. II, p. 206.)*

Rainald, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, to his most dear Robert, venerable archdeacon of the Church of Tournai, greeting.

It has been reported to us that Lord Ingelbert, standard-bearer of the count of Flanders, obtained from Rabodo, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, of good memory, that the church of Petinghem should be endowed with freedom and that monks should be placed in it; and he is said to have had, and still to have, a privilege from that bishop. Later, however, at the exhortation and request of his mother, he placed priests and clerics in that church. Since they were placed there contrary to the former and better institution, they were unable to benefit either themselves or the church, and indeed almost failed entirely.

Therefore we exhort, request, and admonish your devoted affection that, for the salvation of your soul, you strive by every means to bring it about that monks of Saint-Theodoric, who live according to rule and serve God in holy religion, be placed in that church. For we understand that it is greatly necessary to them and that, through the prevenient mercy of God and with your assistance, it may through them be regularly ordered to the honour of God.

## II. To the Clergy of Arras—Concerning the Election of a Bishop. (1130)

*(Acts, etc., ibid., p. 206.)*

Rainald, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, to the clergy, knights, and entire people of Arras, greeting.

We believe that the merciful God, according to the multitude of his mercies, has looked upon your Church and city and has set over you as shepherd and bishop a wise and religious person, suited to the sacred canons. We therefore exhort your whole community and admonish you by these present letters to honour him with the reverence due to him, comply with his wholesome exhortations and admonitions, and obey him in all things as good children obey a good father.

Since, moreover, you have for a long time suffered grievous losses through the ravages of wars, we enjoin upon you, for the remission of your sins, to establish peace by his counsel, so that you may please the Author and Lover of peace and receive from God abundant fruit both in spiritual and temporal matters. Farewell.

# DIPLOMAS OF RAINALD II, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

## I. Confirmation of the Foundation of Saint-Josse of the Wood. (1125)

*(Gallia Christiana, vol. X, col. 303, Documents.)*

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen. Rainald, by the favouring mercy of God archbishop of Reims, to his beloved son Milo, provost of the church of the Holy Virgin Mary and Saint Josse of the Wood, and to his brethren who have professed the regular life in that church, and to their successors who shall remain for ever in the same observance.

It is fitting to grant a ready consent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a prompt result. Therefore, since you, most dear sons in Christ, prompted by prevenient divine grace, have resolved to restrain your lives under the regular discipline of blessed Augustine and to serve almighty God in common according to the ordinances of the holy Fathers, we rejoice with fatherly affection in your vows. Accordingly, at your request and in accordance with the petition of our fellow brother Ingerannus, venerable bishop of the Church of Amiens, we grant our due assent. By the authority of this present privilege we confirm the order of canonical life which you have professed, and we secure you and all that belongs to you under the protection of metropolitan authority.

We also confirm for ever, both to you and to your successors, all things lawfully belonging to your church: namely, the land which Ingerannus of Montreuil gave, upon part of which the church was founded; the four capons which Ermenfrid of Cuvilly and his brother Ingerannus granted to that church; the land and wood granted by Rorgo of Tortosonte; the church of Bury and the land belonging to it, and the wood granted by Hugh of Pont and Wiard of Arguvieu; the tithes and land conveyed by Drogo of Sélincourt; and also the tithes and land donated by Baldwin of Cayeux in the Boulonnais. Furthermore, whatever that church now justly possesses, and whatever it may lawfully acquire in the future, shall remain firm and unshaken to you and your successors, saving in all things the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Amiens.

We also decree that, when its abbot has died, the brethren there serving God shall have a free and canonical election, provided they steadfastly preserve the religious observance they have undertaken according to the Rule of blessed Augustine. Therefore, by God’s authority and our own, we decree and prohibit under anathema that no one whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions or other goods, or harass it with reckless vexations.

Done at Reims in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1125, indiction 3, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Louis, most glorious king of the Franks, and in the first year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Rainald.

Fulcrad, chancellor, examined, wrote, and subscribed.

The witnesses are Nicholas and Hugh, archdeacons of Reims; Bartholomew, bishop of Laon; Lisiard, bishop of Soissons; Robert, bishop of Arras; Ebalus, bishop of Châlons; Ursio, abbot of Saint-Denis; and Nicholas, abbot of Saint-Nicholas.

## II. Charter of the Foundation of the Monastery of Igny. (1126)

*(Gallia Christiana, vol. X, col. 37, Documents.)*

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. I, Rainald, though an unworthy minister of the Church of Reims, [wish] to all who know themselves to be sons of holy Church the reward of the heavenly inheritance.

When divine providence first called us to govern the Church of Reims, we made it our concern to choose the fellowship of honourable men and to delight in their company. It therefore seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to invite monks from Clairvaux and to labour with all our strength that an abbey of their order might be built in our diocese. For this purpose we freely granted them the entire land of Montaon with its valley; the whole slope by which one ascends toward Curvaville; and, as far as the wood toward Longueville, that wood itself, together with water, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands.

We also granted them all that we held at Igny, with the surrounding woods—namely Forest and Beleis—all our rights in the common wood, and all that we bought from Pontius of Arcis. We granted the aforesaid things without any reservation, for remembrance of our sins, under seals and the testimony of reputable persons.

Sign of the entire chapter of the Church of Reims, by whose seal this charter is authenticated. Sign of Odo, abbot of Saint-Remi. Sign of Jorannus, abbot of Saint-Nicaise. Sign of William, abbot of Saint-Theodoric. Sign of Ursio, abbot of Saint-Denis. Also the sign of Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis at Paris. Sign of Nicholas, archdeacon. Sign of Hugh, archdeacon. Sign of Joffrid, dean. Sign of Leo, cantor. Sign of Adam; sign of Albert; sign of Odo, priests. Sign of Boso; sign of Gervase; sign of Drogo, deacons.

Done at Reims in the year of the Incarnate Word 1126, indiction 5, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and the third year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Rainald.

Fulcrad, chancellor, examined, wrote, and subscribed.

## III. Agreement between Rainald II, Archbishop of Reims, and Albero I, Bishop of Liège, concerning the Fief of Bouillon. (1127)

*(Gallia Christiana, ibid., col. 38.)*

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Let all present persons know, and let those whose posterity is yet to come learn from this present document, what we have established, and in what manner, with Albero, venerable bishop of Liège, concerning the benefice of the Church of Reims which belongs to the castle called Bouillon.

I, Rainald, though an unworthy minister of the Church of Reims, have granted to Albero, bishop of Liège, and through him to his successors, subject to the following condition, the benefice which is known from ancient times to belong to the Church of Reims and which no one doubts pertains to Bouillon. If need arises for the Church of Reims through the attack of any persons, the lord bishop of Liège shall lead to me or to any successor of mine a mounted force of three hundred knights every year, if he has been warned forty days beforehand. If, having been so warned, he shows that he has a lawful or canonical impediment, he shall be excused from the said expedition, provided that, once he is free, he fulfils the stipulated agreement when again summoned within the same term.

The lord bishop of Liège shall lead this mounted force under his own command and at his own expense as far as Mouzon. Once it has arrived there, the archbishop of Reims shall provide all of them with necessities of food, on their advance, during their stay, and on their return as far as Mouzon. In whatever direction he wishes to lead this force in the environs of the city of Reims, for up to ten leagues, or to retain it with him for the securing of the Church’s advantage, he shall keep them for fifteen days at his own expense, so that within this period he returns them as far as Mouzon.

If they lose anything of their own on the journey there or back, the archbishop shall make no compensation to them for any of these losses. Whatever they gain, whether horses or other things, except captured knights, shall be theirs by right. If violence or attack is inflicted upon the bishop of Liège in respect of the said benefice, the archbishop of Reims shall assist him with counsel and aid. If any dispute arises, or any complaint worthy of a hearing, he shall appoint no day for the hearing except at Mouzon, and shall help him retain it by law and judicial sentence. Likewise, there and nowhere else, the bishop of Liège shall appear before the archbishop of Reims solely to answer concerning neglect of this service or breach of the agreement.

Because the bishop of Liège could not render us homage in the manner of other enfeoffed men, he presented to us eight of his men, from whom we received homage: four from the castleries of Bouillon—Walter of Bouillon, Ingo of Mirenvalt, Manasses of Herge, and Ingo son of Lambert—and four from his other fiefs—Cinger the advocate, Walter castellan of Huy, Rainald of Jupille, and Lambert of Tiembeche. Furthermore, he confirmed in our hand the tenor of this agreement and the maintenance of friendship. He also established that his successors must observe it in the same manner toward the archbishop of Reims.

Finally, should both bishops—the bishop of Reims and the bishop of Liège—be removed from the scene, the entire agreement, as stated above, shall be observed for ever by the successors of both churches under irrevocable law. Likewise, when the bishop of Liège comes to Mouzon, friendship having been confirmed, the agreement renewed, and the homages of the above-named barons rendered—if they survive, or by heirs succeeding them—he shall freely receive from the archbishop of Reims, without any contradiction, the established benefice. But if, through any eventuality, the Church of Liège should at some time lack possession of the said castle in such a manner that it cannot lawfully claim it, then the entire foregoing agreement between the bishop of Reims and the bishop of Liège shall remain void and annulled.

Therefore, since, as it is written, one generation passes and another comes, and time destroys alike our words and deeds, lest what has been done should be erased by the passage of time or altered by ambiguity, we have committed this agreement of ours to writing, confirmed it by the testimony of reputable persons, and moreover ordered it to be authenticated with the addition of our seal.

Sign of Odo, abbot of Saint-Remi. Sign of Jorannus, abbot of Saint-Nicaise. Sign of Ursio, abbot of Saint-Denis. Sign of Nicholas, archdeacon. Sign of Hugh, archdeacon. Sign of Joffrid, dean. Sign of Leo, cantor, etc. Of the laity: sign of Henry of Châtillon; sign of Blihars of Hercreio; sign of Nicholas of Bourg; sign of Ralph of Ralph’s Court; sign of Haimo, castellan of Hautmont; sign of Baldwin, dapifer, etc. Of the men of Liège: sign of Alexander, archdeacon; sign of Dodo, archdeacon; sign of Arnulf, provost; sign of William, provost, etc. Of the laity: sign of Count Lambert, etc.

Done at Reims in the year of the Incarnate Word 1127, indiction 5, in the fifth year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and the third year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Rainald.

Fulcrad, chancellor, examined, wrote, and subscribed.

## IV. Letter of Rainald, Archbishop of Reims, concerning the Excommunication and Absolution of Count Witer of Rethel. (1127)

*(Martène, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, vol. I, col. 367, from the cartulary of Saint-Remi.)*

I, Rainald, though an unworthy minister of the Church of Reims, have thought it fitting to set forth in this present document, for the memory of posterity, the course of the cause of the excommunication and absolution of Count Witer of Rethel.

We had excommunicated the aforesaid count because of the unjust exactions by which he oppressed the villages, lands, and people of Saint-Remi, and we had bound by the bond of anathema all the land subject to his jurisdiction. Compelled by this necessity, Odo, abbot of Saint-Remi, went to Rome and laid before Pope Honorius the intolerable evils which that count inflicted upon the Church of Saint-Remi. Moved by the bitterness of these evils, the lord pope confirmed the excommunication imposed upon the named count and commanded, by letters directed to them, all the suffragan bishops of the Church of Reims to pronounce it against the count.

Unable to endure the disgrace of this dishonour, the count came into our presence and begged us with quite tearful prayers to establish peace between him and the abbot. Having summoned the aforesaid abbot, together with other abbots and certain clerics of our Church, we debated the count’s case at length and finally settled it as follows.

The oft-mentioned count renounced and abjured, in our presence and that of the whole court, that neither he nor his officers would henceforth impose upon the villages of Saint-Remi any exaction—except from his own capitecensian men—which is commonly called *talliae* (“tallages”). He likewise renounced and abjured the protection-payment (*salvamentum*) which he demanded from four villages of Saint-Remi: Saulx-Saint-Remi, Roizy, Basilicourt, and Isle. He renounced and abjured the *lethum*, blood-fines, and redemption-payment imposed upon the men of Saint-Remi who do not receive their shares.

This count used to give men of Saint-Remi, who were under his advocacy, to his own men. They oppressed them with unjust customs as though they were their own; and he abjured that he would do this no longer, nor would he act as defender in respect of them for anyone, except insofar as pertains to his advocacy. The above-named count renounced and abjured all these matters in our presence and that of the whole court, unless perhaps the provost of Saint-Remi should make a complaint to him. Then he shall have a third part of the justice which he administers.

He further swore that, on account of all that he has surrendered, he will not take any opportunity for wrongdoing against the villages and people of Saint-Remi. If he violates any of the foregoing matters which he has sworn, then, having been warned, unless he makes amends within fifteen days, he shall be subject to excommunication without recall. Moreover, concerning the excessive lodgings which this count had been accustomed to exact too frequently in the villages of Saint-Remi, and concerning the works and cart-services by which he burdened the church’s people: if a complaint comes to the abbot and, having been summoned before the abbot’s court, he neglects to submit to justice within fifteen days, he shall without delay be subject to the same excommunication to which he is now subject.

Wishing this document of our authority to remain valid, we have caused it to be strengthened by the impression of our seal and by the subscriptions of suitable witnesses.

Sign of Odo, abbot of Saint-Remi. Sign of Engubran, abbot of Hautvillers. Sign of Jorrannus, abbot of Saint-Nicaise. Sign of Ursio, abbot of Saint-Denis. Sign of Hugh, archdeacon. Sign of Joffrid, dean. Sign of Leo, cantor. Sign of Adam; sign of Albert; sign of Odo, priests. Sign of Gervase; sign of Odo; sign of Drogo; sign of Boso; sign of John, deacons. Sign of Master Alberic. Sign of Master Graphio of Angers. Of the laity: sign of Hilary of Mont-Gai; sign of Pagan of Calmisiac; sign of Otrannus.

Done at Reims in the year of the Incarnate Word 1127, indiction 5, in the twenty-second year of the reign of the venerable Louis, king of the Franks, and the third year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Rainald.

Fulcrad, chancellor, examined, wrote, and subscribed.

## V. Regular Canons Established in the Abbey of Saint Martin of Épernay. (1128)

*(Gallia Christiana, X, 39, Documents.)*

Rainald, by divine mercy archbishop of Reims, makes known that the illustrious Count Theobald, pierced by divine inspiration, granted the church of Épernay, for the remedy of his own soul and those of his predecessors—namely, Stephen his father and his grandfather Count Theobald, who was buried in that church—freedom of this kind into his own hand.

Since the aforesaid Count Theobald held the said church, left to him by his forefathers as if by hereditary right, and had given the abbacy of that church to Galeran, son of his lord dapifer Andrew, that same church was, by the unchangeable will of God, who changes all things when he wills, transformed to a better condition. For the aforesaid Galeran, divinely inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit and strengthened by the prudent counsel of Lord Bernard of Clairvaux, approached the said count and announced that he would renounce the world and become a monk at Clairvaux. He requested that the count permit the church of Épernay to be transferred, through the hand of the said archbishop, to the order and rule of blessed Augustine.

The aforesaid count willingly assented to this very reasonable petition and surrendered the said church, free, to God and the aforesaid archbishop, to remain for ever under the Rule of Saint Augustine, etc. ...

Done at Reims in the year of the Incarnate Word 1128, etc. ...

## VI. Charter of Rainald, Archbishop of Reims, Granting the Monastery of Saint-Nicaise Exemption from Gists and Procurations. (1129)

*(Varin, Administrative Archives of Reims, I, p. 282.)*

Rainald, archbishop of Reims.

The pastoral care which, by God’s ordering, we have undertaken continually admonishes us to assist the oppressed and to extend the hand of compassion to those worn down by any anxieties. I therefore, Rainald, unworthy priest of the Church of Reims, considering that the brethren dwelling in the monastery of blessed Nicaise ... are pressed by very many necessities ..., granted for their use, for the remission of my sins, the altars noted below ... namely, the altar of Saint-Remi of Celto and that of Saint-Helen of Buxolio ...

Moreover, I consider it fitting to make known to all the faithful that, when I had challenged the abbot and brethren of the church of Saint-Nicaise concerning certain things which I believed belonged to my right—namely gists and procurations, both in the said church and in its dependencies—the aforesaid brethren declared that they had never rendered such a thing to any of my predecessors. Furthermore, they brought to me a privilege of our reverend father Pope Alexander II concerning such freedom and immunity; writings of our venerable predecessor Gervase, archbishop of Reims, who had built the said church; and letters of Lord Philip, illustrious king of the Franks, concerning the same freedom.

But I, having inspected the tenor of the aforesaid writings and noted from their information the liberty of the said church, by the counsel of wise men wholly remitted the claim which I had against the above-named brethren and decreed them free and exempt from the aforesaid complaints. And lest I leave any room for my successors to act maliciously, I considered it fitting to insert this in the present document.

Sign of Hugh, archdeacon. Sign of Frederick, provost. Sign of Hugh, treasurer. Sign of Leo, cantor. Sign of Adam; sign of Ermenric; sign of Albert; sign of Odo; sign of Henry, priests. Sign of Gervase; sign of Gerard; sign of Rainer; sign of Guy; sign of Boso; sign of John, deacons. Sign of Alberic; sign of Amalric; sign of Peter; sign of Gerard; sign of Guy, subdeacons.

Done at Reims in the year of the Incarnate Word 1129, indiction 6, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and the third year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Rainald.

## VII. The Foundation of the Monastery of Igny Confirmed. (1130)

*(Gallia Christiana, vol. X, col. 39, Documents.)*

Rainald, by divine dispensation humble minister of the Church of Reims, to his beloved sons in Christ, Robert, venerable abbot of the monastery of Igny, and his brethren who have professed the monastic life in that monastery of blessed Mary, and to their successors who shall remain for ever in the same observance.

Because we believe that the things known to pertain to the cultivation of religion bring eternal salvation to souls, when divine providence first called us to govern the Church of Reims, it was our chief care and endeavour to choose the fellowship of honourable and religious men and to delight in their company. It therefore seemed fitting to the Holy Spirit and to us to invite men from the monastery of Clairvaux and to exert ourselves that an abbey of your order should be built in our diocese. For this reason we granted to blessed Mary, mother of mercy, free and exempt from every exaction, all that we possessed at Igny, together with the surrounding woods—namely Forest and Beleis—as far as the mountain summits where the division was made, and with boundary-markers, ditch, and roads. Beyond the boundary-markers we granted you whatever would be necessary for the use of you and your successors.

We also gave to blessed Mary and to you, freely, the entire land of Mont-Taonis, with its valley and water. In our land beyond the water we grant what is necessary for your use, namely in woods and pastures. Henry, lord of Châtillon, renounced and restored the tithe which he held at Mont-Taonis and all that he possessed there; his wife Ermengard and their son Gualcher likewise did so. And we conveyed all of it to blessed Mary and to you.

By the authority of this present privilege, therefore, we confirm for you and for your successors both the things stated above and those which have already been bestowed upon you by other faithful persons and are to be bestowed in the future. Ponzard of Arcey and Albert of Jarcey, with the consent and approval of his son, gave to Blessed Mary and to you whatever they held as their own at Igny—namely lands, meadows, and pastures. Of the surrounding woods they gave you as much as an arrow can be shot once from a bow; and in the remaining parts of their woods, for you and your successors, whatever shall be necessary for your use and theirs. For the lands which the peasants held from them, we gave Ponzard money, and he restored other lands to those cultivators. Guarin Malus-privignus, from whose fief Ponzard and Albert held those lands, consented to and approved all this.

Moreover, Lord Andrew of Baldiment and his wife Agnes, and their sons William and Guy, bestowed upon your monastery as alms Resson, a certain small holding in the jurisdiction of Cheherey, together with the land adjoining it, from the valley of the meadow to the little valleys, including the valley-bottoms and, on both sides, the slopes up to the mountain-tops, as bounded. This land extends from the road of Cheherey and the road leading to Mount Saint Martin, to the boundaries of Villa Savoie, to the boundaries of Mont-Taonis, and to the boundaries of Avelerey. Whatever lies within these boundaries—whether arable land, meadows, pastures, or waters—is recognized as having been bestowed upon you in perpetuity. Furthermore, all the meadows and other lands which the same Andrew possessed around Perreium, and which are customarily within the jurisdiction of Avelerey, he freely gave to Blessed Mary and to you, with the consent of his wife and sons. He also bestowed upon you a certain small wood within the jurisdiction of Avelerey on the condition that neither he nor his descendants may give, sell, or exchange any part of it in any manner. In all his woods he likewise generously granted that you and your successors might have, without any opposition, whatever your need and their own needs should require.

The lord knight of Arcey, his wife Hildeburgis, and their sons Nicholas, Ado, and the others, gave to Blessed Mary and to you, from the arable land of Avelerey adjoining and contiguous with the land of Mont-Taonis, as much as will fully and abundantly suffice for two plough-teams throughout all seasons of the year in which land is ploughed and cultivated. Moreover, the brothers Giles and Elias, sons of Gerard, provost of Châtillon, bestowed upon Blessed Mary and upon you the land which they possessed at Mont-Taonis.

We indeed saw these gifts offered upon the altar of Blessed Mary on the day of the dedication of your monastery, and approved them; and by the authority of this privilege we confirmed them, forbidding under anathema that any secular or ecclesiastical person should ever presume to disturb you or your successors concerning the aforesaid gifts, etc.

Sign of Joscelin, bishop of Soissons. Sign of Ursio, bishop-elect of Verdun. Sign of the venerable Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. Sign of the Church of Reims, with whose seal this document is sealed. Sign of Odo, abbot of Saint-Remi. Sign of Ingelram, abbot of Hautvillers. [Col. 1352C] Sign of William, abbot of Saint-Theodoric. Sign of Jorannus, abbot of Saint-Nicaise. Done at Reims in the year 1130 of the Incarnate Word, in the eighth indiction, in the twenty-fourth year of the reign of Louis, most glorious king of the Franks, and in the fifth year of the archiepiscopate of Rainald II.

## VIII. Charter of Rainald, Archbishop of Reims, concerning the confirmation of Saint-Wulmar. (1132.)

[Gall. Christ., vol. X, col. 400.]

[Col. 1352D]

I, RAINALD, by God’s forbearance Archbishop of Reims, to my beloved sons in Christ, the venerable PETER, abbot of the church of Saint-Wulmar, and the other brothers professing the canonical life in the same place, and to their successors in perpetuity.

Since we owe watchful care to all who are contained within the bounds of the diocese entrusted to us, our efforts have been directed especially to restoring to peace and tranquillity churches and possessions of holy places which lay ambition had seized; and, having liberated them from unlawful encroachment by secular persons, to subject them more freely to the lovers of Christ.

I therefore, Rainald, have sought to bring to the knowledge of all, present and future, that Count Eustace, setting before his eyes fear of the Last Judgment, together with his religious mother Ida and his most noble wife Mary, in the presence of John, bishop of Thérouanne of blessed memory, freely and absolutely granted to the Lord Jesus Christ every right which he had in the church of Saint-Wulmar situated in the city of Boulogne, on the express condition that canons living regularly according to the Rule of Saint Augustine should be established there.

The count’s successor Stephen, together with his wife Matilda, confirmed this same gift in the presence of Lord Milo, John’s successor; he also restored the distribution of prebends and every right which he had unjustly appropriated in the aforesaid church after the said gift, and granted them there to brothers who were thereafter to live religiously under the Rule of Blessed Augustine. Therefore, dearest brothers and sons in the Lord, by metropolitan authority we confirm to you and to your successors, who will serve God under the Rule of Blessed Augustine, the aforesaid church and its possessions—those which it presently possesses and those which it shall possess and acquire in the future. Indeed, that provision concerning religious life, etc. And in order that the contents of this document may remain valid and unshaken in future times, we have caused it to be fortified by the subscriptions of reputable persons and the impression of our seal.

[Col. 1353C] Sign of Joscelin, bishop of Soissons. Sign of Milo, bishop of Thérouanne. Sign of Ursio, abbot of Saint-Denis. Sign of Hugh, abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi. Sign of Baldum, abbot of Saint-Vincent of Senlis. Sign of John, abbot of Blessed Mary of Boulogne. Sign of Adam, abbot of Saint-Josse-in-the-Wood.

Done at Reims in 1132, in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks [Note: [Col. 1353C] Read the twenty-fourth or twenty-fifth year.] and in the ninth year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Rainald.

## IX. Rainald, Archbishop of Reims, confirms all the possessions of the monastery of Selincourt. (1135.)

[Gall. Christ., vol. X, col. 305.]

[Col. 1354A]

RAINALD, by divine favour Archbishop of Reims, to all sons of the holy Church in perpetuity.

Since we ought to form the minds of those subject to us toward good works and be an example of life, if, because our sins demand it, we are by no means able to fulfil the office of shepherd, let us at least endeavour to rejoice in their good works and to share in them in some way. Therefore, granting with fatherly affection, as is fitting, the just requests of our venerable fellow-bishop Guarin, bishop of Amiens, we confirm by the authority of this present privilege the place established in the parish of Selincourt to Abbot Walter and his successors to be canonically appointed, and to the brothers professing in the same place the canonical observance of Blessed Augustine and their successors. We confirm likewise all that the faithful have presently bestowed upon the said place, all that the aforesaid church will reasonably possess in the future, and also the things which we shall set down below.

These are the things which we confirm: namely, the land around the church, etc., almost as in the charter of Bishop Guarin.

[Note: [Col. 1353D] It continues thus: “Around the church; two parts of the tithe of Selincourt; and three parts of the same tithe held by John of Boiasvile, Ralph Haleus, and Aluric of Poiz; and one third of the tithe of Worluis. All these Drogo and his son freely granted to the church. Also one third of the tithe of Tenceneul-Maisnil, given by Roger of Selincourt; likewise the tithes of all the animals and gardens of the same place, granted by Lord Frumald, prior, and the whole chapter of the church of Blessed Martin of Amiens to the brothers serving God there; and the tithe of the whole land of Ernold the priest and his brother Clarus; and the third part of the tithe belonging to the altar of d’Estruisuiz; and the tithe of the land of Walter Wastel and his son Ralph.

“Also the land of Teneulmaisnil, which Roger Claboldus, Eustace, and Walter Bonard gave to the same church, with the consent of Drogo of Selincourt, from whom they held it; and the tithe which Bernard le Wales gave; likewise the land of the court of Gislebert-Maisnil, extending from the road leading to Vilers to the road running toward Broecort, and the meadow beside that same road. All these William Bisete and his men—namely Ingerannus of Belnay and Renold of Gislebert-Maisnil—granted to the same church whatever they possessed in them; and also the third part of the tithe of that same land, which Ralph of Gislebert-Maisnil and his sons gave.

“The third part of the tithe of the altar and the free court, which Lord Bishop Guarin and Lord Simon the archdeacon granted to the same church; and the field which the aforesaid Renold gave, while retaining for himself its land-rent and tithe; and also the share in the mill which had belonged to William, lay brother of the church of Saint-Josse, which the abbot and the entire convent of Saint-Josse granted to the same church.”]

In order that the text of this decree may remain valid and unshaken in the future, we have caused it to be fortified by the impression of our image and by the naming of reputable persons.

Sign of Ingulram, abbot of Hautvillers. Sign of Jorannus, abbot of Saint-Nicaise. Sign of Ursio, abbot of Saint-Denis. Sign of Hugh, abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi.
