## X. Privilege of Rainald, Archbishop of Reims, concerning the water of the Vidula, the marsh, grazing rights, and jurisdiction of Saint-Theodoric as far as Haymon’s Cross. (1137.)

[VARIN, *Archives administratives de Reims*, I, p. 290.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1355B]

I, RAINALD II, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, wish all present and future persons to know in what order and on what grounds we settled that old and renewed controversy in the time of Abbot Hellin: the controversy unjustly stirred up so often against the church of Saint-Theodoric by Gerard of Rozoy and his predecessors, concerning the water of the Vidula near the village called Châlons, the adjoining marsh or swamp, all fishing, the soil of that land itself, grazing rights, the ban, and jurisdiction—and justly brought to rest by us.

In the first year, in the fourth month, of the abbacy of the aforesaid abbot, Gerard came to the Vidula and, by threats and intimidation, drove off the fishermen of the church, who were setting their fish-traps in the marsh, namely in certain ditches commonly called *Raheria*, into which water, together with fish, is diverted from the mother-channel. Having driven them off, he compelled them to cease fishing. He also forbade the abbot to quarry stones in the hills without his permission, though the church of Saint-Theodoric held and holds, possessed and possesses, by hereditary right and lawful possession, the entire ban and jurisdiction over those hills, and for the greater part the soil itself. In imposing this prohibition, he supported it solely with the claim that those hills were said to lie within his viscountship.

Concerning these injuries, our dearest fellow-bishop Bartholomew, venerable bishop of Laon, at the abbot’s request summoned Gerard, his parishioner, in our presence. Since Gerard would by no means agree to peace, he accepted a day on which a more careful negotiation for restoring peace between them should be conducted. Treating lightly the obligation to come, he accepted a day again and a third time; but neither the second nor the third time did he take care to appear. Therefore, as neither he ceased from injury nor the abbot from complaint, we ordered the bishop to appoint a suitable place and time at which, when both parties had come together before us, the dispute might receive its due judicial conclusion.

This was done, and a great multitude of both parties came together at the cross called Haymon’s Cross. With our permission, the abbot produced a certain privilege fortified with two seals, namely ours and the bishop’s. When Master Bernard openly read and carefully explained it to Gerard and to all present, we heard and recognized that this dispute had formerly been settled in the time of the venerable Abbot William, under the testimony of many persons. For, when we were sitting on the hill near Châlons, seven lawful men of Saint-Theodoric established by oath that all the water and marsh, from the mill called Mascele upstream to the place called Vidua, together with the soil, fishing, grazing rights, the ban, and jurisdiction, belonged to Saint-Theodoric. The grazing and pasturage, both in the marsh and on the hill as far as Haymon’s Cross, were common to the men of Saint-Theodoric and Gerard’s men. The fishing, however, in all the water was the exclusive and unrestricted property of Saint-Theodoric, from the aforesaid mill to the dividing structure by which that water is divided toward the mills of Machot and Puisun, and as far as the ditch or fishpond called Raherium; above that point it was common. The ban and jurisdiction everywhere within these bounds—namely from the water to the aforesaid cross—belonged solely to the church of Saint-Theodoric.

When we had recognized the course and settlement of this affair from the wording of the privilege, Gerard at first did not sufficiently submit to its authority. The abbot declared orally that he would prove and confirm it, as judgment required, through lawful persons who were present there and who had likewise been present at that settlement. At last, overcome by the force of this reasoning and assenting to the truth, Gerard accepted the privilege. Moreover, he acknowledged that he had unjustly forbidden the quarrying of stone on the hill. Witnesses to this are: Jorannus, abbot of Saint-Nicaise; Luke, abbot of Cuisy; clerics of Reims—Peter of Curvavilla, Boso, Master Amalric, Master Bernard, Master Fulk, and Letbert the dean; clerics of Laon—Dei Amicus, Ansellus, Herbert the subdecan, Adzo of Rozoy, and Ralph.

Laymen:

Hugh Coxardus, Otrannus, Thomas of Rohas, his nephew Walter, Ertaldus of Rozoy, and Elias.

Done at Reims in the year 1137 of the Incarnate Word, in the fifteenth indiction, in the thirtieth year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and in the twelfth year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Rainald II.

Drogo, chancellor, authenticated, wrote, and subscribed.

## XI. Charter of Rainald, Archbishop of Reims, concerning the peace settlement made between the church of Saint-Theodoric on one side and Gerard of Rozoy and Aldric Malet on the other. (1138.)

[VARIN, *Archives*, etc., I, p. 293.]

RAINALD II, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, to present and future persons, in perpetuity.

We wish to make known to you the terms of the peace which, at one time in the days of Abbot Hellin, was restored between the church of Blessed Theodoric and Gerard of Rozoy, in our presence and with our efforts to the extent that the Lord granted. But the sequence of the matter seems to require that we first unfold the cause of the dispute and then the peace.

Gerard seized a man of Saint-Theodoric called Aldric Malet and, after long harassing him by confinement in prison, finally compelled him to ransom himself for ten pounds. The abbot, both in person and through the bishop of Laon and through us, justly demanded his man; but Gerard was unwilling either to return or to restore him to the abbot, the bishop, or us. Hence the bishop, whose parishioner Gerard was, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him and his entire household, and we confirmed it.

The church also possesses certain land at Melphi, namely that which belonged to the pagan Hastamorsel and Odard Cervus. Gerard alleged that it was of his fief and therefore maintained that it was either his own or ought to be held from him. For two years he violently exacted *guionagium* from wine merchants on the church’s land and from that land. From a certain vineyard at Chocheriis which had belonged to Hebert, he said that half a muid of wine was owed to him every year. At Châlons he newly established, contrary to local custom, aldermen to render judgments in his courts. From ancient times the church had held, securely and peacefully, one or more wine-presses at its pleasure in its own land in the same village; yet he forbade anyone to go there for the purpose of pressing.

For some time, therefore, contention concerning these things persisted between the abbot and Gerard, while the abbot sought a hearing which Gerard refused to attend. At length, with the Lord’s help and through the cooperation of our efforts, both parties came by mutual consent to our court for the sake of peace. There, through the mouth of Lord Hugh Cossiart, the following settlement was openly determined before all, approved by both sides, and duly put into effect.

Of the ten pounds mentioned above, the abbot remitted one hundred shillings, but retained one hundred on this condition: if Gerard should ever in any respect break the peace against the church, then, after formal warning, unless he makes satisfaction and restores the damage within fifteen days, he and his entire household shall immediately, without objection or appeal, be subject to the same sentence of excommunication to which he is now subject, until he has restored both the new damage and these hundred shillings.

He renounced the land which had belonged to the pagan Astamorsel and Odard Cervus, and promised that henceforth he would guarantee it for the church against all persons. He will no longer collect the said *guionagium*, and for what he had received he repaid twelve pence. He will demand no wine from the aforesaid vineyard. He removed the aldermen. With respect to the wine-presses whose operation he had compelled to cease, he acknowledged his error, fully acknowledging that he had no right in the land of Saint-Theodoric at Châlons; and, having obtained forgiveness for the past, he devoutly promised that henceforth he would impose no opposition or obstacle whatsoever upon those going to the aforesaid presses.

This settlement, as we have said, was determined at Reims in our presence before the witnesses listed below; afterward it was recited in the chapter-house of Saint-Theodoric, in Gerard’s presence and as he humbly sought absolution, before witnesses who are also separately listed below.

Odo, abbot of Saint-Remi; Gervase, cantor; Boso; Guy; Roger of Châtillon; Hugh Cossiars; Thomas of Rohaiz; Hugh of Manso; Elias.

Witnesses from the chapter:

Guiric, dean; Elias; Obertus; Hugh of Manso; Theobald Linotet; Odard Hairicus; Theobald Guichardus; Robert; Enaldus of Melphi; Pontius of Tilia; Nicholas.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1137. SAINT OLLEGARIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF TARRAGONA

[Col. 1357]

## NOTICE

(Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana vetus*, vol. II, p. 20)

[Col. 1357]

Blessed Ollegarius, a native of Barcelona, born in 1060, was bishop of his native city and at the same time for several years Archbishop of Tarragona. Finally renowned for holiness and miracles, he died on the sixth day of March 1136, in the seventy-sixth year of his life.

[Note: [Col. 1357D] The Life of Ollegarius was published in 1760 by the distinguished Matthew Aymerich, formerly our friend, at Barcelona, by Joan Nadal, in *Nominibus et Actis episcoporum Barcinonensium*, from p. 318. He is to be excused at the beginning of p. 325, where, through insufficient attention, he mistakenly wrote the name of Callixtus II—who had died seven years earlier—instead of Innocent II, as he ought to have written. The distinguished Flórez also published two other Lives, the latter of which had hitherto remained unpublished, in his posthumous vol. XXIX, pp. 472 and 492. See Cardinal Aguirre, vol. III of the *Councils of Spain*, p. 342 of the old edition. In Martène, vol. I of the *Ancient Writers and Monuments*, col. 717, there is: “A charter of Ollegarius of Tarragona, by which he gives beds and cloths of deceased clerics to the poor, 7 Kalends of April, in the twenty-fifth year of King Louis [A.D. 1132].”]

His life and deeds were described by Antonio Juan Garsia Caralps, penitentiary canon in the Church of Barcelona.

[Note: [Col. 1359A] Published at Barcelona in 1617, octavo.]

But before him an anonymous canon of the Church of Gerona is praised as the author of the same Life, as Francis Diago in his *History of the Counts of Barcelona* and James Rebullosa—who likewise gave us, after others, a Life of this most holy man—have noted; so Henschenius and Papebrochius stated under 6 March in the *Acts of the Saints*. This anonymous Life was found in the archives of the Church of Barcelona, where the saint’s body is held in great veneration, according to the testimony of Antonio Domenico, book II of the *History of the Saints of Catalonia*, p. 75.

[We have published two letters of this most holy bishop in vol. II of the *Great Collection of the Councils of Spain*: one to Raymond, bishop of Ausona—

[Note: [Col. 1359A] Raymond consulted Ollegarius about a young man who, while himself a boy, knocked down another boy at play; the latter was wounded by the fall, but, after he had recovered from the wound, relapsed after not many days into an illness and died. Was the first to be judged irregular? He replies: “Since the counsels of Blessed Augustine and other doctors teach us that such uncertainties should be interpreted in the more favourable sense, we, trusting in God, whose mercy is better than lives, commend this young man of good disposition as able to be promoted in the Church of God to minor orders; and thereafter to sacred orders, if his praiseworthy life and honourable moral conduct, advancing with age, shall recommend him as acceptable at the canonical time.” In these few words he shows himself no ordinary master of Scripture and the Fathers, and of both laws as well. Compare a doubt not unlike it in the jurist Paulus, book XXX, §4, *Digest*, on the Aquilian law.]

—and another addressed to Pope Innocent II. We first brought the latter to light. In it he consults Innocent concerning the consecration of the bishop of Barbastro, elected by the canons. CARDINAL DE AGUIRRE.]

[Col. 1359]

## LETTER OF SAINT OLLEGARIUS TO POPE INNOCENT II

(See among the letters of various persons to Innocent, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX.)

[Col. 1359]

## LETTER OF SAINT OLLEGARIUS TO RAYMOND, BISHOP OF AUSONA, HIS SUFFRAGAN. (About A.D. 1125.)

He answers an inquiry about a boy at play who knocked another down so that his head was broken, etc., and whether he is to be regarded as irregular.

[Cardinal d’Aguirre, *Concilia Hispanica*, III, 340.]

[Col. 1359B]

OLLEGARIUS, by the grace of God Archbishop of Tarragona, to his venerable brother RAYMOND, bishop of Ausona: greeting.

Concerning the young man about whom you consulted me so that I might advise you: when he was a boy, while playing, he knocked down another boy at play, causing him to fall and break his head. This seems to us to be the answer that should be given. Since, as you report, the wounded boy afterward recovered, and many days later, having relapsed into illness, died, we cannot determine a doubtful matter by a definite judgment. For it seems uncertain whether the illness that overtook him upon relapse arose from the occasion of the wound, from neglect, or from some accident, as is customary.

[Col. 1360B]

But since the counsels of Blessed Augustine and other doctors teach us that such uncertainties should always be interpreted in the more favourable sense, we, trusting in God, whose mercy is better than lives, commend this young man of good disposition as able to be promoted in the Church of God to minor orders. If, however, a praiseworthy life and honourable conduct, progressing with age, commend him as acceptable at the canonical time, he may nevertheless attain sacred orders through the grace of God.

I, Ollegarius, Archbishop, have subscribed.

Raymond, by the grace of God Bishop of Ausona.

[Col. 1361]

## CHARTER OF OLLEGARIUS, by which he gives beds and cloths of deceased clerics to the poor. (1132.)

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, col. 717.)

[Col. 1361A]

Let it be known to the faithful that I, OLLEGARIUS—

[Note: [Col. 1361A] In 1114 he was made bishop of Barcelona from being abbot of Saint-Ruf near Avignon, and afterward became Archbishop of Tarragona. He died in 1137, on the sixth day of March, with a great reputation for sanctity.]

—by the grace of God Archbishop of Tarragona and Bishop of Barcelona, together with the entire convent of that see, give to God and to the hospital for the poor adjoining the see all beds with the cloths of deceased clerics, whoever they may be, excepting any silk cloths that may be there, on this condition: henceforth neither I nor any person may dare in any way to reclaim this. If anyone attempts to violate this gift of our generosity, let him be excommunicated as a murderer of the poor.

Done on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the twenty-fifth year of King Louis.

## A.D. 1137–1148. GEOFFREY GROSSUS, MONK OF TIRON

[Col. 1361]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON GEOFFREY

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XII, p. 163)

[Col. 1361]

Geoffrey, surnamed “the Fat,” had the advantage of being trained in the religious life by Blessed Bernard, founder of the abbey and congregation of Tiron, and of making his profession in Bernard’s hands. He was probably one of Bernard’s last disciples. Gratitude, respect, and admiration later led him to write the Life of his master. The year in which this work was composed is uncertain. M. Baillet [Note: [Col. 1361] *Table critique*, 14 April.] dates it to the thirteenth or fourteenth year after the saint’s death, which occurred in 1117. The date appears to be somewhat later, since the author mentions King Louis the Younger as reigning alone; this did not begin until 1137. But it cannot be later than 1148, because the work is dedicated to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, who died on 14 January of that year. This is all that can be positively asserted on the subject.

Geoffrey says that he divided his history into three parts or books. Instead of retaining this division, copyists agreed in dividing it into seventy chapters, at the head of each of which they placed a hexameter verse containing a summary—indeed, a very imperfect one. Souchet, canon of Chartres, followed this arrangement in the edition he published at Paris with Billaine in 1649. When the Bollandists reproduced Geoffrey’s work in their great collection under 14 April, they judged it more suitable to distribute it into fourteen chapters.

The history of Blessed Bernard’s Life is among the best written and most reliable works of the twelfth century. The author professes that he advances nothing except what he saw himself or received from witnesses beyond suspicion. He reports very few miracles and takes pains in the preface to show that the merit of saints should not depend on this kind of proof. He would have done well to be equally sparing with revelations. Among those which he attributes to the saint, there are some that seem somewhat dependent on imagination. He may also be criticized for making the devil too often a party to setbacks which can readily be explained naturally. Apart from this, his reflections are pious and sound, drawn from the heart of the subject and suitably placed. His narrative is continuous; his style polished, ample, and elevated. From time to time he intermingles with his prose verses of his own composition, which rank among the best of his age. In short, Geoffrey the Fat is good evidence that the founder of Tiron regarded study as a means proper to preserve and enhance his establishment, far from believing it incompatible with the spirit and duties of the monastic state.

In chapter 52 of Souchet’s edition there is a passage which greatly perplexed that critic and which the Bollandists vainly tried to clarify by emending it.

[Note: [Col. 1363] Liron, *Singularités historiques*, vol. I, pp. 45–46.]

Speaking of his hero’s renown, the author says: “Thus it came about that his fame not only filled the neighbouring regions of Gaul, but also passed through the farthest bounds of the Burgundians, Alans, and Aquitanians.” Souchet, in a note on the word *Alanorum* (“of the Alans”), discusses it at great length without explaining anything. The Bollandists, admitting that Souchet’s reading agrees with all manuscripts, maintain that *Catalanorum* (“Catalans”) or *Alamannorum* (“Alemanni”) ought to be substituted for *Alanorum*, on the supposition that the Alans are no longer mentioned in Gaul after they crossed into Spain and thence into Africa—that is, around the beginning of the fifth century. But the Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre by Constantius and the Chronicle of Prosper prove that, after this people’s migration, a colony of them remained in the southern part of Gaul; and nothing proves that they had merged with the Franks before the twelfth century.

[Col. 1363]

## LIFE OF BLESSED BERNARD, FOUNDER OF THE CONGREGATION OF TIRON IN GAUL, BY GEOFFREY GROSSUS

(*Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, April, vol. II, 14 April, p. 220, from several manuscripts and Souchet’s edition.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

### § I. Tiron, head of the ninth congregation in the Benedictine Order. Life of Blessed Bernard written.

[Col. 1363]

1. The monastic state, which has always flourished above the rest in the Church of God through outstanding religious devotion and holiness, acknowledges as its chief founder and restorer in our West the most holy patriarch Benedict, whose Acts we illustrated on 21 March, the day on which he departed this life in 542. For after he had written the Rule for monks, praised by Saint Gregory the Great as outstanding for its discretion and clear in expression, it was not only propagated throughout all the provinces of Europe, through innumerable monasteries founded in the course of a few centuries by his disciples and successors; it was also gradually adopted in all monasteries of an observance different from Benedict’s.

There subsequently sprang up, as if from a most fruitful root, various congregations of this institution, professing observance of the common Rule under particular ordinances framed by each for restoring or maintaining the vigour of discipline. The oldest of these, and the most fortunate in its yield of holy men, was Cluny, begun in Gaul around 910 by Blessed Berno, as we have related in his Life under 13 January. A similar congregation may be reckoned that of Cava in Italy, founded toward the end of the tenth century by Saint Alferius, whose life we illustrated on 12 April; he died in 1050. Three hundred and thirty monasteries in Italy and Sicily are counted as subject to it.

At the same time Saint Gerald in Aquitaine, near Bordeaux, founded the monastery of La Sauve-Majeure, with such success that the little church which he found ruined by age became fruitful in offspring: “so that filial devotion, raised up from it, reveres it as its mother in Spain and in many regions of Gaul,” as Christian, monk of La Sauve-Majeure, writes in the Life which we gave second under 5 April, composed near the end of the twelfth century, §15. A catalogue of all such daughter houses and of the monasteries joined to them is still preserved in the archives of that monastery; it was courteously promised that it would be sent to us, but the new prior restrained the ready hands of his religious, unaware that such things were desired only for the greater praise of his monastery. We can therefore say only that even today more than thirty priories retain their ancient subjection.

Not unlike this was the new congregation begun by Blessed Bernard of Tiron in the diocese of Chartres at the beginning of the eleventh century. In the Life below, §52, one hundred cells are said to have been subject to it, whether these were abbeys or provostries; and this is said although his Acts were written some years after his death. John Iperius, in chapter 40 of part III of the *Chronicle of Saint-Bertin*, treats of the foundation of several religious communities under a new rite and habit, and among them lists that of Tiron under the Rule of Saint Benedict. Its habit is reported in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 704, in the account of Furness Abbey, to have been grey in colour. We discuss the location of the monastery of Tiron in the county of Perche in the Life of Blessed Bernard himself, especially chapter 12.

2. It was written by Geoffrey Grossus, who had lived as a monk at Tiron under Bernard himself. In the prologue he declares that he committed to writing and transmitted to posterity, in a truthful style, what he had seen or learned from the report of trustworthy persons. Thus, in no. 88, when Blessed Bernard was at Chartres and learned that the monk Gervasius, tormented by an evil spirit, was being kept bound in the infirmary, he adds that Bernard explained to us, who had assembled there, why he had returned so swiftly. Likewise, in no. 94 he testifies that he saw what he relates; but above all, concerning what he writes in chapters 12 and 13 about Bernard’s illness, exhortations to his brethren, reception of the last sacraments, pious death, and funeral rites, he professes himself an eyewitness. Moreover, he appears to have learned from Blessed Bernard himself very many things which he had formerly done here. Thus, in no. 27, when describing his solitary life on the island of Causeum, he adds: “But when we asked him by what food he sustained his life, he refused to tell us, being a skilful concealer of his own virtues.” Meanwhile, he could have learned much from the monk Christian, who brought him back from the said island together with Peter of the Stars; in no. 36 he says that, when he was writing this Life, Christian was still alive, a man of remarkable simplicity [Col. 1365] and innocence. Finally, in no. 110 the author declares his sincerity thus:

> I call Jesus to witness, whom he served and whom I too desire to serve, that I invent nothing in either direction, but, as a Christian speaking of a Christian, set forth what is true.

And near the end of the following section he says:

> I call Truth itself and His holy angels to witness, and also that angel who was the guardian and wondrous companion of this admirable man: I say nothing to please him in the manner of flatterers; but whatever I shall say, I say as testimony, and it falls short of the merits of him whom the whole world praises.

3. We obtained two manuscript copies of this Life. One was sent to us from Rouen by Guillaume Thiersault; the other from Dijon by Pierre-François Chifflet, both priests of our Society, and well deserving concerning this work because of the various Acts of Saints they supplied. Chifflet noted that his copy had been transcribed from an old parchment manuscript of the Most Holy Trinity of Tiron.

Jean-Baptiste Souchet, doctor of sacred theology and canon of Chartres, published the same Life in Paris and illustrated it with his own observations. He was delighted by the author’s elegant style, sufficiently polished and lucid for the age’s depravity—or rather barbarism—as he writes in his dedication to Henri de Bourbon, bishop of Metz and abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and of the Most Holy Trinity of Tiron. He adds more in his preface to the reader:

> As for the author of the Life, he needs no recommendation; he is sufficient unto himself. I read the Life, read it through—not merely willingly but eagerly—with such pleasure that I was immediately captivated by the elegance of its writing and had it copied lest I be deprived of it. It truly grieved me that its author, polished by learning beyond what might be expected from that age’s ignorance and not to be despised—for he had woven his work in prose and verse with such abundance of talent, interspersed it with the proofs of pointed maxims, and adorned it with historical descriptions—should remain obscure and perish in neglect.

Jacques Dinet, an outstanding preacher of the Society of Jesus, supplied Souchet with a copy of this Life while Dinet was delivering Lenten sermons in the principal church of Chartres. He was also rector of the Collège de Clermont in Paris and provincial of France, and sought to serve our studies by sending various Acts of Saints. André Duchesne did likewise, granting Souchet another copy of this Life, transcribed from the manuscript of Papire Masson. Souchet found a third parchment manuscript at Tiron, loosened by age at the binding and scarcely holding together. This, evidently, was the source of the copy sent to us by Chifflet, in which some passages are missing here and there. Finally, he received a fourth copy from Guillaume Laisné, prior of Mondaville.

4. Souchet does not doubt that this last copy, above all the others, is Geoffrey’s genuine offspring. This is chiefly because he judges that the other copies were taken from the original exemplar, transcribed with the diligence and care of John of Chartres, abbot of Tiron; and he thinks this is evident from the end of the book.

At the end also of our copy sent by Thiersault occur these words:

> These things were written by me, Philip Bernyer, priest of the church of Saint-Albin in Champ-Rond, in the Perche, in the Jubilee year 1600, in which year I also offered my first Mass. The prior of Huis and superior of the house of the Most Holy Trinity of Tiron gave me the exemplar of this volume, written on old parchment; at the end of it the following was written in red letters:

> J[ohn], of Chartres, Father of the Church of Tiron.  
> He caused me to be written; glory and praise to him. John Pignore of Valleca wrote me.

This John of Chartres was the fifteenth abbot, elected in 1290 and dead in 1297, as Souchet relates in his catalogue of the abbots of Tiron published with the Life of Blessed Bernard.

After that catalogue Souchet appends the regular and secular benefices dependent upon the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity of Tiron: eleven or twelve abbeys, forty-seven or forty-eight priories, and thirty-two parish churches. After number or chapter 42 he lists fifty-eight abbeys or priories dependent on Savigny Abbey and made subject to Tiron Abbey by Blessed Vitalis. Souchet describes the name and location of each. In the said preface he writes that, to aid the reader’s memory, he added numbers and chapters without prejudice to reader or book. We have divided the chapters differently, according to our custom, and appended our own notes under each, omitting Souchet’s longer observations, to which we refer the reader as highly learned and well composed. For clarity we have also added the marginal synopsis customary with us, which he neglected.

## § II. The time of Blessed Bernard’s life and death; inscription of his name in the calendars; the titles Saint and Blessed bestowed on him

5. Blessed Bernard is said, when he died, to have had a broken, aged, and weakened little body, with limbs shattered by old age. We therefore judge that he completed seventy years of life. He was consequently born about the year 1046. Having embraced scholarly studies until nearly his twentieth year, he began to aspire to a holier life; and, setting out for Aquitaine, he became a monk in the monastery of Saint-Cyprian about 1066.

After he had lived for ten or more years in the cloister of Saint-Cyprian, he became prior at the monastery of Saint-Savin, remaining so until 1096. When its abbot died in the Holy Land, Bernard fled into the wilderness lest he be elected abbot. Three years later he went thence to the island of Causeum. Brought back from it first to the wilderness and then to Saint-Cyprian’s monastery, he was made abbot in 1100. Later, in 1110, he attended the Council of Poitiers, then went twice to Rome. Leaving his abbey, he withdrew; and after various wanderings he built the monastery of Tiron, having obtained the bull of donation on the third day before the Nones of February, 1113. But since among the French years then began at Easter, it must, on that reckoning alone, be counted as the year 1112.

6. At that time Ivo, bishop of Chartres, flourished; we shall speak below of the year of his death. When Geoffrey had been enthroned in his place and a dispute was occurring between the clergy and the count, Abbot Bernard came, worthy of the memory of all good men, whose praise endures to this day throughout all the churches of Gaul. So we read on 25 February in the second Life of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, no. 15.

Concerning the deaths of Robert and Bernard, the Chronicle of Saint-Maxentius, commonly called the Malleacensis Chronicle, contains these words in Philip Labbe:

> In the year 1116, Robert of Arbrissel, founder of the Fountain of Evrand, died on the sixth day before the Kalends of March. In the same year Bernard, founder of Tiron Abbey, which is in the Perche, died on the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

But below, chapter 3, letter A, we show that the author of that Chronicle was not sufficiently accurate in calculating years, and we note that he erred not merely by five years, but perhaps by eight or nine. Thus it would not be surprising if an error of one or two years had entered at this point. First, in the Life of Robert of Arbrissel, under 15 February, we show that Robert died not on the sixth day before the Kalends of March but on the fifth, and that this occurred in 1117. Yet, because the French then customarily began the year at Easter, that year could be called 1116. Why, then, should the death of Blessed Bernard not likewise be assigned to 1117, when the very manner of speech used by the chronicler seems to indicate that he departed this life within the same year after Blessed Robert?

7. We took great pains here to obtain some light from the death of Ivo, bishop of Chartres; but we found fresh darkness which must be illuminated from elsewhere. First, the continuation of Sigebert’s Chronicle, published by Laurent de la Barre in the *Christian History of the Ancient Fathers* under the name of Robert of Torigni, places Ivo’s death and Geoffrey’s succession to the see of Chartres in 1114 [Col. 1367]. On the other hand, in the genuine continuation of the said Robert of Torigni, published by Luc d’Achery with the works of Guibert, abbot of Blessed Mary of Nogent, there is an excellent epitome of Ivo’s Life, and he is said to have died in 1117. Matthew Paris, in his account of Henry I, king of England, likewise reports that Ivo ended his days in that year.

Other writers choose one of the intervening years, namely 1115 or 1116. The former occurs in the martyrology and calendar of the churches of Chartres; the latter is produced from an ancient calendar of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais, where Ivo had been abbot before his episcopate and where, at his death, he bequeathed various gifts. He died on 23 December; thus both Robert and Bernard could subsequently have been present for the accession of his successor Geoffrey, and yet each could have died in 1117.

8. In that year Easter was celebrated on 25 March, with the lunar cycle XVI, solar cycle VI, and Sunday letter H. Since below, in the Life, no. 105, Blessed Bernard is said to have fallen into his final illness on the eleventh day after Christ’s Resurrection, this would have occurred on 5 April. In no. 112 he is said to have been fortified by the last sacraments on the fifth day of his illness, namely 10 April of that month.

Then, as no. 117 relates, two days before he went to the heavenly dwellings, he summoned to him from the tower of the castle of Nogent a certain matron with her daughter, appearing to the latter among monks clothed in white. On the following day both women came. On the next night, as stated in no. 119, he commanded the brethren who attended him to refresh their wearied limbs by sleeping, when he himself was visited there by holy dead monks. On the following and final day, having instructed and kissed all who had been summoned to him with pious counsels, he closed his eyes amid pains and rendered his spirit to God, as is read in no. 60 and the following section. This may have been 14 April, namely the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May; through an easy error, the seventh day before the Kalends of May was printed instead in the above-mentioned and frequently erroneous Chronicle of Saint-Maxentius.

Yet the manuscript calendar of the Church of Tiron agrees with the latter date, for under 25 April it has this note in red letters:

> Death of our venerable Father Bernard, first abbot of Tiron.

But he is commemorated on 14 April in the Benedictine Martyrology of Hugh Menard in these words:

> At the monastery of Tiron, Blessed Bernard, first abbot of that place, a man of great holiness.

And in Book II of the *Observations* an abridgment of the Life, drawn from Geoffrey his disciple, is given; there again he is honored with the title Blessed.

9. On the same day André Saussaye, in the Gallican Martyrology, gives this encomium:

> At the monastery of Tiron, the passing of Blessed Bernard, first abbot of that place, glorious in eminent virtues, in the spirit of prophecy, and in the gift of miracles.

Bucelinus also celebrates him in the Benedictine Menology with a long encomium, drawn chiefly from Menard’s observations. In volume IV of the *Gallia Christiana*, p. 865, the Sainte-Marthe brothers, citing the Malleacensis Chronicle, assert that he died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May and quote these words from an old necrology of Chartres:

> Bernard, abbot of Tiron, died. He built the church of that place from its foundations and gathered there many monks under the rule of holiness and religious observance.

Other encomia occur below in our notes to the Life. Geoffrey Grossus repeatedly uses the title “Saint Bernard” in the Life, as may be seen in all manuscripts and in the edition published by Souchet, nos. 78, 79, and 94. He also frequently calls him “confessor” and “confessor of Christ,” and in the prologue implies that Bernard’s heavenly birthday was celebrated and that the Life had been written by him to be read on that occasion. This was done after 1131, when Louis the Younger was crowned king of the French, a fact mentioned in no. 97.

# THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 1367]

# PROLOGUE

[Col. 1367A]

To the most reverend father, Lord Geoffrey, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Chartres and legate of the Apostolic See, Geoffrey, least of all monks, sends greeting.

1. Your wisdom, most blessed Father, knows far better and more clearly than I that we are sufficiently and plainly instructed, through Raphael the archangel, bearer of healing, that the deeds of holy persons ought to be recorded and, gathered in written characters for usefulness, transmitted to the knowledge of posterity. For Raphael says to Tobias: “It is good to conceal a king’s secret, but honorable to reveal and confess the works of God” (Tobit 12:7).

The lamp of the world, Jerome, also urges us to this by his example [Col. 1367B]. After faithfully translating the Old and New Testaments in lucid language, and carefully expounding the prophecies and [Col. 1368A] the Gospel, he portrayed in a most flourishing style the lives of the anchorites Malchus, Paul, and Hilarion.

> **Note:** [Col. 1367B] We have annotated the Life of Saint Paul, the first hermit, on 10 January; the Lives of Saints Malchus and Hilarion will be given on 21 October.

Likewise, the springs of eloquence flowing from the lofty mountains of God’s incomprehensible wisdom and watering with philosophy’s heavenly dew the whole dry surface of earthly hearts—namely Athanasius, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, and many other most illustrious doctors of Christ’s Church, whose names we refrain from inserting on our pages because it would take too long—invite us to a like zeal for labor.

> **Note:** [Col. 1367B] From the Acts of Saints published by these Fathers, we have given: the Life of Saint Antony the Great by Saint Athanasius, 17 January; the Lives of Saint Sebastian and Saint Agnes, virgin and martyr, [Col. 1368B] by Saint Ambrose, 20 and 21 January; the Life of Saint Marcellinus, martyr at Carthage, and of the Massylitan martyrs, by Saint Augustine, 6 and 9 April; and the Life of Saint Benedict, abbot of Monte Cassino, 21 March, together with very many others, by Pope Saint Gregory.

After innumerable volumes of books in which they expounded with fullest and most brilliant eloquence the deepest reasons and interpretations of sacred Scripture—bringing captive by reasoned arguments drawn from invincible proofs every understanding of the Christian faith that raises itself [Col. 1368B] against Catholic doctrine—they published not only the victorious contests of martyrs, flourishing with flowers of rosy hue [Col. 1369A], but also the flower-bearing deeds and habits of confessors and virgins, holding the lilies of chastity and breathing the sweetest fragrances, in blooming narratives.

2. The body and sequence of canonical Scripture, and the order of the Old Testament, also endeavored, through signs, figures, narratives of shadowed things, the obscurity of enigmas, and the wonderful and intricate descriptions of material works, to signify the life, character, actions, manner of life, labors, sweats of contests, constancy in struggles, triumphs of victory, and triumphant palms of reward of all the saints of the New Testament collectively—whose life had not yet been made manifest.

For God commanded Moses to complete with such care, after the pattern he had seen on the mountain, all the works of the testimony, prefiguring in them the pattern of the saints’ manner of life, that he should make also bowls, cups, the rim of the table, the branches of the lampstand, goblets, little spheres, and the spreading forms of lilies, the snuffers of the lamps, and every other thing which Scripture indeed enumerates one by one [Col. 1369B].

Likewise, the Temple of Solomon, with all its measurements, sets forth with such carefulness not only its buildings but all the carved adornments of the buildings that it omits neither the architraves of the columns nor their capitals, the latticework of the capitals, nor the axles, spokes, rims, and hubs of the wheels. The building of the city lying southward, seen in the spirit by Ezekiel, is also described so minutely that it omits not even carvings of palm trees, nor passes by so much as the threshold of a gate without measuring it [Col. 1369C]. All these things, as the Apostle testifies, were shadows of things to come (Hebrews 10:1).

3. Therefore, if the providence of divine wisdom, distinguishing the periods of shadows and realities, willed and commanded that figures and signs be described with such zeal through persons of that age whom it had rendered fit for this by its inspirations, what sound-minded person does not understand that it both wills and intimates that the deeds of saints, foreshadowed and signified by them, should be preserved and made known with how great a diligence in written accounts for the knowledge of future believers?

And since knowledge of the divine will is a complete and manifest command of admonition, if we, sluggish in the torpor of idleness and snoring in the sleep of inertia, neglect to set down in writing the acts of the saints of our own time that are known to us [Col. 1369D], and to direct them to the benefit of future posterity, do we not incur the guilt of offense and fall into damage to our salvation?

Let us therefore, diligently seeking the increase of our salvation, mark out in writing the merciful works of saints; and in marking them out, let us proclaim the magnificence of Christ, who is wondrous in his saints. For when we recount the praises of Christ’s soldiers, we exalt in sublime fashion the splendid triumphs of their King; since whatever virtue is discovered in their minds must without doubt be attributed to divine power and strength [Col. 1370A].

The disseminators of such writings, moreover, by drawing the minds of their hearers back from committing wickedness through the example of the righteous purpose, convert the sinner from the error of his way, save his soul, and cover a multitude of their own sins.

4. Moreover, when we see memorials of mortal things erected in waxen [images]—

> **Note:** [Col. 1369D] In both our manuscripts, “bronze images.” Souchet has “waxen,” and discusses these at length from ancient writers.

—and the pompous badges of various boasts of praise inscribed in letters gleaming with gold, set before successors for imitation: who among us, observing these things, will not blush to cover the victories of Christ’s athletes with silence? Who will not, for the praise of their Emperor, commit at least to cheap pages how they fought [Col. 1370B] and conquered against the aerial powers and the rulers of the darkness of this world, and explain it more carefully to encourage the spirits of those who fight?

And who does not see more clearly than daylight that when we recite such writings on the heavenly birthdays of saints, we offer the worship of praise due to God, cultivate the saints’ memory, imbue the minds of believers with the benefits of edification, and render to the saints the fitting honor of veneration? From this the minds of unbelievers are cast down with grief; the incredulous waste away with envy; the undisciplined are constrained by anxieties. While all the saints rejoice in gladness, the devil alone groans, seeing the fruit of all his temptations and combats brought to this end: that he sees himself cast beneath the feet of the saints, bound in the chains of their virtue, wasting away in the gall of pain [Col. 1370C]; and, compelled by the torment of his vexation, he recognizes their magnificence whether he will or no.

For when, driven from possessed bodies as from the kingdom of his tyranny, he utters a bellow through lunatics and demoniacs, he confesses and bewails the torment of his own burning, and thereby most plainly demonstrates that those through whom he suffers this live happily with God and are mighty in power. Indeed, when life is restored to the dead and healing to the sick through them, it is most certainly made known to Christian peoples how firmly they cleave to true life and power.

5. Thus far, most blessed Father, I have in some detail and however inadequately explained the causes and reasons why the deeds of saints ought to be written. In obedience to your exhortations—which I judge it absurd not to obey—I have described the Life of our father [Col. 1370D] Bernard and compressed it into the division of three volumes.

> **Note:** [Col. 1369D] This division is nowhere indicated. Souchet judges the first volume to comprise the first seven chapters [Col. 1370D], according to the division of chapters made by us; the second to contain the remainder of the Life together with the death; and the third to be the collected materials which we present in the final chapter.

It is cast, to be sure, in a lowly form of words, yet in a brief one, so that a reader who recoils from the unpolished face of the style may at least be refreshed by the brevity of the reading. For, knowing that nothing is more excellent than truth, I have transmitted to posterity, in a truthful rather than polished style, holding to the low ground of humility, what I saw or learned from the report of trustworthy people [Col. 1371A]. I diminished rather than displayed the dignity of the work, supplying only material for better writers. I did not wish to veil the truth of the matter in the adornments of language, lest a reader intent upon verbal pomp and trappings should receive the holy man’s virtues less attentively.

But if anyone, in the manner of Jewish unbelief, demands signs and measures any saint by the number of miracles, what will he think of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, of whom the Gospel narrative, though relating many other things about her, does not say that she worked miracles? And what will he think of John, Christ’s forerunner, of whom the Evangelist most plainly affirms that he worked no miracle, saying: “John performed no sign”?

It is therefore more soundly determined that, when many who performed signs have been rejected on the Day of Judgment, only those who pursued works of righteousness will be gathered unto salvation. Therefore we commend not our father Bernard by his performance of miracles—although these will by no means be altogether lacking—but show that he imitated Christ, being meek and humble of heart. But lest the time be spent in preliminaries, let us now begin to speak more fully of him of whom we have spoken at length beforehand.

> **Note:** [Col. 1371A] The Life follows, divided into many chapters, and an argument expressed in hexameter verse is prefixed to each chapter [Col. 1371B]. This division is so defective that we do not doubt that a number of chapters three or four times greater was intended by the person who first made it. But because verses were not written in many places, which the poet, whose vein was not always equally ready, may later have wished to add, we judge that many things were joined in the copies which were read as separately written in the parchment manuscript. Since we judged that a new division should be made, we removed these verses from the context, lest the sequence of the narrative be interrupted again and again by their intrusion; but, lest the curious reader complain that any kind of summary of the Life, expressed in them, had been omitted, we present them here collected together, with numbers noted alongside, to which each pertains. We do this all the more freely because we suspect that the verses are neither complete nor composed by Geoffrey, but were added by John Pignore [Col. 1371C] of Valleia, the copyist of this Life. They are in the same style as the verses mentioned above as added at the end; and they differ greatly from the style in which the other verses were written—the verses which, in no. 13 and elsewhere, Geoffrey himself appears to have incorporated into the context.

## METRICAL SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTERS

9. How he withdrew from acquaintances, seeking heavenly things in his desires.

[Col. 1371D] 18. How the gracious Mother of God appeared to him.  
19. How, unwilling to preside, he fled and wished to be subject.  
20. This concealer of his name was also a cultivator of the wilderness.

[Col. 1372A] 51. The priest dissolved the marriages of many.  
[Col. 1372B] 55. Why, riding an ass, he first set out for Rome.

59. How great were the privileges entrusted to the man by the pope’s care.

[Col. 1372C] 79. By prayer, Rotrou, you are delivered from your fierce enemy.

# CHAPTER I. Blessed Bernard’s upbringing and monastic life in the monastery of Saint-Cyprian

[Col. 1373A]

6. Bernard, then, was by birth from Ponthieu—

> **Note:** [Col. 1373D] Ponthieu, or Ponticum, is a district between the rivers Somme and Vimeuse; its chief town is considered to be Abbeville. More is said of it in the Life of Saint Richard, abbot of Centula, 26 April.

—in the territory of Abbeville, born of honorable and devout parents. They cultivated hospitality and kindness and, as their means allowed, diligently ministered to Christ in his needy members. They devoted him to literary studies, and the grace of heavenly condescension received him into the bosom of its favor, so that he readily mastered all the subjects in which he was instructed. Thus he became proficient in grammatical and dialectical reasoning and in certain other branches of literary learning.

Living among young students, he did not enter upon the broad ways of this world [Col. 1373B], but shunned licentiousness as studiously as he would have fled the serpent’s venom and a deadly plague. While his fellow adolescents, as is customary at that age, pursued the spectacles of vain things, he withdrew into the inner rooms of his lodging, writing, reading, or meditating upon something useful. He wished to turn away his eyes lest they behold vanity, because he thirsted ardently to be quickened in the way of God.

7. Already at that time his spirit was inflamed with such devotion to religious life that he clothed himself in a regular garment in the manner of a canon. In accordance with the fashion and tenor of this dress, he observed such sobriety in life and such modesty in conduct that many of his fellow students mockingly [Col. 1373C] called him a monk. Yet the young man of good disposition preferred to endure their derisive attacks rather than abandon the purity and purpose of a good life or mingle himself with the deadly actions of corrupt men.

For the inspiration of divine love was already drawing him; it strengthened his mind to endure the annoyance of mockery and, separating him from the mass of the lost, adorned him with gifts of holiness. Thus, until nearly his twentieth year, having embraced the disciplines of scholarly education, he acquired no slight vigor and keenness of understanding in the knowledge of the Scriptures.

8. But his desire for a holy way of life burned more and more fiercely each day [Col. 1373D], because that fire which the Son of God came to cast upon the earth, desiring that it should burn, had kindled his mind from early youth. Growing daily, revealing itself by sparkling through signs of holiness, it could not be concealed. For who can hide a fire? But now it had taken on such strength of growth that it wished to break forth in the blaze of a greater flame; and, breaking forth and inflaming his mind more vehemently, it drew him to cast aside wholly the pursuit of temporal things and join himself to the followers of monastic profession.

For divine goodness worked this: that the shoot of a good plant, which it had already cut away from love of perishable things, might be grafted into the tree of good stock. It did not wish him to remain longer in the company of scholarly men, lest the example of their wickedness and depravity turn his mind away from his good purpose.

9. The young man therefore, yielding to holy inspirations, did not delay to do what he was drawn to do. Leaving his native Ponthieu [Col. 1374B], he entered the regions of Aquitaine, accompanied by three companions of the same age, aflame with the same purpose as himself. As they traveled eagerly on their way toward their goal, they encountered the king of the French.

> **Note:** [Col. 1373D] This was Philip I, who reigned from 1060 to 1109.

Warned by this omen, Bernard is said at once to have spoken to his companions:

> Come, companions, let us go forward with cheerful spirits and confidence. We shall find the King of Heaven whom we seek, since on our journey we have found the king of earth, whom we were not seeking at all.

With the Lord as their guide, they reached Poitiers and remained there for some time. They carefully sought to discover which monks in Aquitaine observed the stricter discipline of regular life. For they wished to join themselves to better men and entrust the direction of their lives to holier ones.

Not far from that city stands the monastery of Saint-Cyprian [Col. 1374C].

> **Note:** [Col. 1373D] The Chronicle of Saint-Maxentius, commonly called the Malleacensis Chronicle, reports that Saint-Cyprian’s monastery was built in sight of the city of Poitiers by Pippin, king of Aquitaine, son of Louis the Pious. Below, no. 58, it is said to have flourished before Cluny began to exist, about the year 910, as was stated on 13 January in the Life of Blessed Berno, first abbot of Cluny.

At that time the monastery was governed by an abbot named Raynaud—

> **Note:** [Col. 1374D] Raynaud II, the seventeenth abbot, of whom more is related below.

—a man exceptionally learned, endowed with such wisdom that at public councils he was a most eloquent pleader of cases. For this reason he was well known and esteemed even in the Roman curia, and was held in the highest repute in Aquitaine. He had also been a disciple of Saint Robert—

> **Note:** [Col. 1374D] The Life of Saint Robert, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, is elucidated on 24 April.

—the founder of the monastery called La Chaise-Dieu. Bernard had heard this by report, and the report had made him intensely eager to hear Raynaud’s teaching.

10. The aforesaid monastery at that time [Col. 1374D] had many monks, noble by birth, but far nobler in holiness of life and uprightness of conduct. One of these was Hildebert, who afterwards became abbot of the monastery of Dol [Note: [Col. 1374D] The monastery of Dol, or Burgidol, commonly Bourgh de Deolz, lies on the river Andria, commonly the Indre, in the duchy and diocese of Bourges. We treated of it on 13 January, in the Life of the said Blessed Berno, no. 28.], and then archbishop of Bourges [Note: [Col. 1374D] Archbishop of Bourges, he held office from the years [Col. 1375D] 1093 to 1098, and is frequently called Aldebert. Consult the patriarchate of Bourges in Labbe’s *Aquitanica*, p. 81.]. The blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, is said to have appeared to him [Col. 1375A] in a certain tribulation and brought him consolation. There was also Gervasius, afterwards abbot of the monastery of Saint-Savin [Note: [Col. 1375D] The monastery and town of Saint-Savin lie ten leagues east of the city of Poitiers, on the river [Col. 1376D] Gartempe. Saint Savin or Sabinus, an anchorite, lived in the district of Poitiers and is entered in the Roman Martyrology on 11 June.], a man of the utmost abstinence and renowned for the adornment of every virtue. There was likewise Garnerius, who had been lord of the castle called Mont-Maurillon [Note: [Col. 1376D] Mont-Maurillon, a town on the river Gartempe, above the town of Saint-Savin.]. He, a lover of poverty and solitude, abandoned the fellowship of cenobitic monks and pursued the calling of the anchoritic life. One day, while walking through the wilderness of the desert, he saw a man possessed by a demon. Moved with pity for his misery, he invoked in prayer the power of Jesus Christ, expelled the demon by which the man was held, and sent him away unharmed.

Divine providence, wishing to unite its servant Bernard with these and many other such men—by whose number the monastery of Saint-Cyprian was then [Col. 1375B] ennobled—brought him by a favourable journey into the presence of the aforesaid Father Raynaud, so that, when this most valiant man had been joined to stronger soldiers, the whole army might be rendered bolder and more vigorous against its enemies. After first carefully strengthening him with adequate instruction and exhortation, the abbot gave him the habit of holy religious life and, having marked him as a monk by the tonsure, joined him to the body of the community.

11. Received into the monastery and trained by the holy brothers whom we have mentioned in the institutions and customs of monastic life, he immediately ascended to such a height of perfection that he was regarded as admirable by all. For who can [Col. 1375C] express in words the humility in which he governed his life, or the submission with which he subjected himself? He served all, ministered to everyone, was the servant of all; he regarded everyone as his superior, revered them as elders, and showed them reverence as his masters and teachers. Obedient to all, contradicting none, loving all without pretence, he embraced everyone with the inward affection of piety and mercy. He sympathized with all, cared for their advantage, and set aside his own. He envied no one and spoke ill of no one; never murmuring, never whispering, judging no life and condemning no person. His words always resounded with Christ, peace, and mercy. Who ever knew him angry, [Col. 1375D] who turbulent? Always serene in mind, gentle in address, polished in speech, cheerful in manner, outstanding in discernment, an assailant of injustice and defender of justice: confident in faith, strong in hope, overflowing in charity, and, to conclude briefly, distinguished by every excellence of conduct. Who ever subdued his body more sternly by the torments of abstinence, cold, and vigils?

12. He applied himself especially to reading and meditating upon the Scriptures [Col. 1376A], so that for the greater part of the nights he kept watch over the reading of sacred volumes and spent long hours awake in contemplation of divine truths. One night, while engaged in this study, he was overcome by sleep; and the large candle which he had prepared for this work slipped from his sleeping hand onto the book. He slept; it burned as it lay upon the page until it was wholly consumed, yet the codex was not burned.

For ten years or more, then, he lived in the cloister of Saint-Cyprian with such strictness of abstinence and shone with the radiance of such great virtues that he illuminated the whole congregation with the rays of his holiness. He stirred it to better things not so much by words as by deeds; and he taught by his actions those teachers who had formerly instructed him—not by force of argument [Col. 1376B] or elegance of speech, but by the power of his works. Thus it came about that he began to preside over the whole congregation, not by rank of office, but by excellence of holiness and the authority of good works.

## CHAPTER II. His administration of the priory of the monastery of Saint-Savin, restoration of discipline, and other notable deeds

13. At that time a certain monk from the monastery of Saint-Cyprian—namely Gervasius, whom we mentioned above—was urgently requested by the prayers of the entire community to undertake the governance of the church of Saint-Savin. But he could by no means be induced to do so, neither by an ordering bishop nor by his own abbot claiming obedience from him, [Col. 1376C] unless they gave Saint Bernard to him as an assistant. When this was at last granted him, Gervasius was appointed abbot and Bernard was established as prior in the community.

This was done by the merciful counsel of God, so that these two great lights might be sent to dispel the darkness of that church. Through the negligence of the preceding abbot, the community of that place had abandoned the path of regular life and exchanged the rigor of discipline for the softness and laxity of life. Gervasius had previously perceived this clearly; and, by sound and good counsel divinely inspired, he refused to assume their care alone, lest, while he laboured outwardly in administering temporal matters, there should be no one inwardly to sustain spiritual matters. But with the two joined together and helping one another—one providing outwardly, the other [Col. 1376D] overseeing inwardly—by the grace of the Lord the monastery was restored within a short time to such integrity of holy life that what had been marked by infamy because of laxity was afterwards renowned for religious observance.

14. At the same time, on account of a certain church, a considerable dispute arose between the oft-mentioned Gervasius and the venerable Bernard, while the monks of the same monastery took opposing sides. For Gervasius, eager to acquire the aforementioned church in order to enlarge and enrich the cenobium, pressed hard for it; but Bernard would by no means consent, perceiving that the pestilence of simony was entering by a side way. Consequently, after Gervasius saw that he had not prevailed and that the then abbot of Saint-Cyprian had obtained the aforesaid church for which he had sighed so eagerly, he was violently angered against the man of God Bernard. Disdaining the care entrusted to him, he abandoned it, and out of the revenues of Saint-Savin built himself a residence at Saint-Cyprian, [Col. 1377A] in which he subsequently lived for a very long time.

We have related these matters not in order to offer to any simple-minded persons a pretext for dissension, but so that, as will be shown below, we may make known to succeeding generations the fearful judgments of God and the mighty works that must be proclaimed. For many read far more eagerly that “there arose a contention among them” (Luke 22:24)—among those who, according to the Gospel’s testimony, visibly adhered to heavenly teaching—than what is reported in their Acts: “the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). But since we do not now wish to satisfy those who judge the divine Scriptures with a crooked gaze and devise by inexplicable evasions to distort them, let us return to the interrupted subject from which we have digressed a little.

15. Bernard meanwhile, deprived of the support [Col. 1377C] of the aforesaid Gervasius but not bereft of divine help, acted as a prudent steward. With watchful care he attended now to the outward and now to the inward welfare of the entire monastery of Saint-Savin; and he worked all the more diligently as the greater burden of care lay upon him. Therefore, lest anything less honourable should result from his negligence, he repeatedly reviewed matters in his mind.

But since there cannot be an Abel whom Cain’s malice does not persecute, nor is a rose seen to bloom except among thorns, he is said to have suffered very many vexations and been provoked by most frequent assaults from certain opponents of canonical institutions, who dwelt in that cenobium only in body. One of them, known to be more obstinate than the rest and bolder in causing every kind of trouble, one day rashly rose against him in a repeated verbal attack. Bernard, indeed, committing vengeance to him who reserves it to himself, admonished the man by way of example, saying: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Rom. 12:19), [Col. 1377D] and bore the insults inflicted upon him with equanimity. But divine vengeance immediately and publicly punished his assailant with a manifest and very celebrated judgment. For that most unhappy man, sitting healthy and cheerful with the others in the cloister, suddenly and unexpectedly expired in death, being made an example to others for the increase of his own condemnation. And because, in the oracle of the Wise Man, “When the pestilent man is scourged, the wise man becomes wiser” [Note: [Col. 1377D] The common version has: “When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser”; or, as Vatablus has it, “he will become more cautious”; or, as the Septuagint has it, “he will consider understanding”; or, as Saint Bernard has it, following the words of this author in his book *On the Solitary Life, to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu*: “When the pestilent man is scourged, the wise man will become wiser.”] (Prov. 19:25), the rest, terrified by so strict a punishment, immediately and manfully devoted themselves to more elevated exercises of monastic rigor.

Finally, after suitable stewards had been assigned to the management of external affairs, Bernard, the servant of God, given with unyielding persistence to prayer and silence, attained such purity of mind that he knew by prophetic inspiration very many things which human knowledge had not yet learned.

16. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096 [Note: [Col. 1377D] Others say that he took the habit in 1095, on 17 November; hence the events that follow concerning those who departed for the Holy Land occurred in 1096, as this author intends.], Pope Urban [Note: [Col. 1378D] Urban II held office from 1088 to 1099.] admonished the Christian people to go to Jerusalem, free the city from the hands of the heathen, and cleanse the Lord’s Temple and sepulchre from their defilements. The Christian people received the pope’s exhortation with such eager feeling and desire that certain abbots, monks, and hermits abandoned their monasteries [Note: [Col. 1378D] Baldric, bishop of Dol, confirms this in book I of his *History of Jerusalem*: “Many hermits, recluses, and monks, not wisely enough abandoning their homes, set out on the road. Some, having received permission from their abbots for the sake of prayer, departed; most withdrew by flight.”] and went to Jerusalem. With them the aforesaid Gervasius set out for Jerusalem, without making satisfaction for the injury he had inflicted upon the man of God Bernard; but, since “a man’s way is not his own,” he would neither arrive there nor return again.

Setting out on his journey, and with prosperous outcomes succeeding for both himself and his company, he had already reached the desired shore; he had already, as it seemed, attained all his wishes and arrived at the plains of Jerusalem, when, by the permission of Him whose judgments, though sometimes hidden, are never unjust, a most savage lion sprang from its lair and tore him limb from limb together with the ass on which he rode, killing him. Having accomplished this dreadful spectacle, it hurried back with swift steps to mountain caves and its familiar dens, leaving the others untouched, though utterly terrified by so prodigious a calamity. While these things were happening in the territory of Jerusalem, Bernard, being in Aquitaine not far from his monastery, knew of them by the Spirit on that same [Col. 1378C] day. Moved by an affection of pious remembrance, he summoned a monk of that church whose care, as we have often said, he then held, and informed him: “Go,” he said, “and tell William Samuel that Gervasius the abbot, his uncle, and his ass have been killed by a lion in the province of Judaea; and see that he announces his death to the brothers and has the bells rung, so that the funeral rites may be performed with due reverence.” [Col. 1378D]

The monks accordingly carried out their customary duty, though they did not know how he himself had learned this. But in the same year they learned from those who had returned from Jerusalem that Gervasius had died with his little ass on the very day on which Bernard announced his death. Thus it was beyond doubt that he had known it by the spirit of prophecy.

17. While Bernard wisely and regularly governed the aforesaid monastery entrusted to him, through whom its religious observance had especially been restored, such a revelation was divinely disclosed to him. It was his custom to remain in the oratory after Compline and spend a long time awake in prayer through the night. One night, [Col. 1379B] as he was going from the oratory to the dormitory after prayer, he saw a multitude of monks sitting in the chapter-house, white as snow. Stirred by the novelty of this vision, he is said to have entered the chapter-house and, after humbly requesting and receiving their blessing, to have sat with them for a while, that he might learn the matter more carefully.

Then one of those seated there, who seemed more worthy than the others both in age and rank, disclosed to the others Bernard’s office and title as prior—as he had been charged by that same Bernard to do, while Bernard alone heard—and said to him: “Dearest one, we were monks of this monastery, and we have permission to visit these holy places in which we once lived while working out our salvation. We render you fitting thanks, [Col. 1379C] because, with divine grace leading the way, through your work the congregation of this cenobium has returned to the state of religious observance and holiness, though it once wandered far from the rule of righteousness. We also command you to announce this to the brothers tomorrow: within a short time nineteen of them will depart this life.”

When the vision had ended, he declared that he had seen this to a certain monk and warned the brothers to cleanse their consciences by confession and prepare themselves to receive life’s end. One of those who were to die, however, asserted that Bernard was delirious and uttering the words of a dream. But he immediately heard this answer from Bernard: “So that you may learn by experience that I am not recounting the uncertainties of dreams, you will be the first of all [Col. 1379D] the brothers to die, and you will not pass beyond the appointed term.” Thus, beginning with that man, he showed each one by name the time of his sickness and specified also the day of his death. The deaths of the brothers followed in the same order in which he had foretold them, and it was thus proved that he had seen them with certainty.

18. In the oratory of this monastery, one night [Col. 1380A], after Compline as usual, while Bernard was earnestly weeping and praying,

> Bright in appearance, and white likewise in snowy raiment,  
> The Mother of God appeared, the renewer of the world, and spoke thus:  
> “After first enduring many distresses and labours,  
> You shall joyfully attain the heavenly throne. But, dearest Bernard, do not be angry at the hardship of labours and distresses foretold to you. Rather, gladly submit to the reasons of God’s judgments and rejoice thankfully; and again I say, rejoice, because he who has purposed that you be afflicted for a time on earth holds you eternally enrolled among the number of his saints in the indissoluble records of his predestination.”

After saying this, she disappeared. And he, rejoicing with inexpressible joy at the happiness of his lot made known to him, afterwards revealed what he had heard to a certain elder, through whom knowledge of this event reached us.

## CHAPTER III. The eremitic life in the solitude of Maine

19. But so that what the Mother of God had foretold to the holy man might be proved true in fact, a cause of suffering immediately arose for him. For, learning of the monks’ intention to make him their abbot, he secretly departed from them, intending to seek what he had desired for many years: namely, the pursuit of the anchoritic life and the acquisition of his food by the labour of his hands.

Not far from the monastery of Saint-Savin there lived a venerable and religious hermit named Peter of the Stars, who later became founder of the monastery [Col. 1380C] called Font-Cambaud [Note: [Col. 1379D] The Chronicle of Saint-Maxentius contains the following: “In the year 1091 the cenobium of Saint Mary called Font-Gombaud was begun, on the border of the cities of Poitiers and Bourges, by the Blessed Abbot Peter surnamed Stella.” And later: “In the year 1114 Peter, first abbot of Font-Gombaud, died of the disease *arpeta*, that is, an inextinguishable fire consuming him; William succeeded him, and after William, Airaud.” But since the preceding account establishes that Gervasius did not perish in the Holy Land before 1096, after which Blessed Bernard, about to be chosen abbot, fled to this Peter while he was still a hermit, it appears that he founded the monastery only near the end of that century.]. Bernard turned aside to him, since he was already known to him and a friend, and revealed the reason for his coming. Peter received him with great eagerness of heart; but because monks were nearby who were striving to make Bernard their abbot against his will, Peter could not keep him with himself long, though he greatly desired to do so.

Bernard, burning both with desire for the poverty and solitude he had long sought and with intense fear that, unless he departed swiftly, he might be forced by his abbot or bishop to become abbot and be entangled in the anxieties of pastoral care, urgently begged Peter to remove him quickly and secretly from there and lead him to unknown solitudes in a most remote region [Col. 1380D]. Peter therefore yielded to the petitioner’s entreaties and, becoming his guide, accomplished what he requested.

20. On the border of the regions of Maine and Brittany were vast solitudes which at that time flourished like another Egypt with a multitude of hermits living in separate cells—holy men renowned for the excellence of their religious life. [Col. 1381A] Among them were the leaders and teachers Robert of Arbrissel [Note: [Col. 1381D] We treated extensively of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, founder of the Order of Fontevraud, on 25 February.], Vitalis of Mortain [Note: [Col. 1381D] Blessed Vitalis was later abbot of Savigny in the territory of Avranches; we published certain Acts concerning him, gathered by us, on 8 January.], and Raoul of La Futaie [Note: [Col. 1381D] Raoul afterwards became director of the nuns [Col. 1382D] in the monastery of Saint-Sulpice, founded in Brittany and the diocese of Rennes in 1112, where he is said to have died on 16 August 1129.]. They later became founders of many great congregations. Divine providence took care, through Peter, who had known them before, to add this fourth man to those three, so that, with a fourth joined to the three, a firm quadrangular structure might be formed, destined later to support great and broad buildings.

After completing a journey of many days, Peter of the Stars arrived at the holy Vitalis, one of the aforesaid men whom we have said were leaders and teachers of hermits. First, by the assistance of eloquent speech, he made Bernard sufficiently commended and praised to him, and asked that he allow Bernard to live with him. He entirely concealed Bernard’s name [Col. 1381B] and the office of prior which he had held, calling him not Bernard but William, as Bernard himself had earlier instructed him, so that henceforth he might everywhere be considered insignificant and remain unknown.

21. Peter, having commended him, returned to Aquitaine. Lord Vitalis then summoned the hermits together in the manner of a council and laid William’s desire before them. When the hermits learned the man’s wish, they consented out of charitable affection, welcomed him into their fellowship, and eagerly offered him their cells. But the ardour of charity moved Vitalis, and resolving the dispute to his satisfaction, he decreed by authority of the synod that William should travel through the woods, inspect the dwellings of all the Fathers, and choose for habitation whichever one pleased him [Col. 1381C].

Accordingly, with the company of hermits going before him, as had been decreed in the council, he inspected every cell. Proceeding into the farther wilderness, he came to the last landmark; there he found the dwelling of a brother named Peter. This man knew neither how to cultivate fields nor how to dig gardens, but provided his daily table only from the fruits of shrubs and with the aid of the turner’s craft. He had also made for himself a small hut of tree-bark amid the ruins of a certain church of Saint Medard [Note: [Col. 1382D] Saint Medard, bishop of Noyon, is commemorated on 8 June.]; the violence of the winds had torn away its better part. But lest the fury of raging winds should again prevail, he had fastened the remaining portion of the hut, with a stronger framework of some protective construction, to oak branches hanging over it, using wicker ropes [Col. 1381D].

William thus beheld on every side the household equipment of such chastened possession, such profound poverty, and poverty carried to the utmost point, as he had desired; and finding the contempt for the world which he sought so exalted and complete, he immediately told the brothers with whom he had come that he would remain there and declared that he would not depart from it.

22. [Col. 1382A] Peter, seeing the riches of his fortune preferred above those of the others, rejoiced exceedingly, as though he had won a triumph of victory by the lot of election. He exulted, danced for joy, and taunted his companions. He favoured William’s judgment, praised his mind, and approved his will, which loved poverty and scorned the help of greater resources. He promised to instruct him in the art of turning and to make him heir to the tools of that craft, should William happen to outlive him after his death; for such were the treasures that he stored up for his successors.

When these things had been done, Peter, greatly exhilarated with joy, invited them to dinner. But having searched his storerooms, he found his provisions so scant that, even if all were set out, they would not suffice for one person. This was neither new nor unfamiliar to him, since the condition of his household resources continually pressed him with such difficulties. Yet, reflecting that a table unable to feed one would not satisfy many, and not knowing how to feed those whom he had invited, he quickly seized his baskets and entered the forest surrounding his dwelling on every side. He energetically gathered thorns and brambles, stripped hazels and other wild trees of their fruit; and while piling different kinds of fruit into his baskets, he found in the hollow of a trunk a swarm of bees with such an abundance of wax and honey that one might have believed such plenty flowed from the horn of abundance itself.

Astonished at such favourable fortune, he attributed to the merits of the foreign monk whom he had just admitted to fellowship the fact that God had bestowed such a supply of light and food [Col. 1382C]. Returning home, he loaded the table with food: he set out immense dripping honeycombs, wild fruits of diverse trees, and brought a dish made from leaves of trees. It would have been a sumptuous banquet, had bread not been lacking—the worthier part of the feast. When the celebration of brotherly joy had passed, each returned to his cell.
