23. Peter then taught William, who remained with him, the discipline of turning, as he had promised; and William, having an apt mind, soon surpassed his master. Peter was pleased by the ready capacity of William’s intelligence, for zeal and envy were far removed from the secret recesses of his heart. Peter, an old inhabitant of the wilderness and accustomed to such things, sought his food from the fruitful bounty of wild trees [Col. 1382D] and by practicing the said craft. William, however, always remained at home as an obedient disciple, fulfilling the offices of an inexpensive kitchen: he made country herbs into a dish, seasoning them with salt on feast days so that they might become softer and sweeter.

After Vespers, when they ate once a day, Peter reclined and William served. For he had learned from a good teacher: [Col. 1383A] “I came not to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 20:28). Having embraced the purpose of the anchoritic life, he immediately surpassed all others in the rigor of abstinence, sustaining life on tree leaves and herbs, subduing his body by hunger, thirst, vigils, cold, and harsh bodily labours.

24. He persevered also in prayer and contemplation with such tirelessness that, while dwelling in the body, he seemed to live beyond bodily affections. The sacrifice of a contrite heart was not absent from the secret place of his conscience; groaning was not absent, compunction was not absent; contemplation of divine things was not absent from the mind’s gaze; nor was the abundant and unceasing outpouring of tears absent from his eyes.

> Setting earthly things aside, in spirit he surveys the heavenly;  
> Dwelling bodily in caves of the wilderness, in mind he inhabits heaven.  
> An inhabitant of forests, through the trackless haunts of wild beasts,  
> Humble and unknown, he hides alone, without a name;  
> Yet joined to the citizens of heaven by the light of his heart,  
> Known, exalted, great, renowned, and venerable,  
> He enters the spacious palaces of the starry kingdom,  
> And already the whole court of the Thunderer favours his entrance.  
> Set above the stars by inward vision,  
> He ranges about the flowering fields of the world above,  
> Plucking flowers and tasting health-giving fruits,  
> Whose flavour puts languor and pains to flight,  
> Removes distress, and with their fragrance also removes labours;  
> And he already tastes beforehand the sweet joys of the highest Good.  
> Amazed as he beholds the miracles of bright heaven,  
> He marvels at the mystical volumes of great mysteries.

25. During the three years in which William lay hidden with Peter near [Col. 1383C] Saint Medard, monks of Saint-Savin sent out searchers who ranged through the hidden places of forests throughout all Gaul, through the depths of the earth, and over mountain precipices, seeking Bernard wherever they might find him. At last, having learned where he was, they returned and reported where and with whom he was hidden. The monks heard the confirmation of this matter joyfully and immediately sought with diligence sealed mandates from their bishop and abbot, allowing them to bring Bernard out of the wilderness and establish him as their pastor, as their common agreement had requested.

Having obtained these, while they prepared the necessities for the journey, one of their monks, named Hugh, secretly left the monastery. Coming to Bernard, he burst out with these words: “You are struck with anathema if you remain here any longer, unless you undertake the governance of our monastery, as your bishop and abbot require.” [Col. 1383D] Having said this, he related in order the whole course of events: that they had sought him for the entire three years, and that they had received mandates from the bishop and abbot to bring him back and make him abbot.

When Bernard heard this, he groaned and resolved to flee to the islands of the sea, so that at least the ocean might hide one whom the land could not conceal. Departing, then, after bidding farewell to the brothers, all of whom wept for sorrow, he went away.

## CHAPTER IV. The solitary life on the island of Chausey; pirates reformed

26. One of the hermits, taking pity on Bernard’s poverty, gave eighteen coins to one of his companions, charitably providing that they might have a small amount of money from which to purchase provisions for the journey, at least for a few days. When the man of God learned of this, he was greatly indignant that his companion carried silver with him, and said: “Either you shall not be my companion, or you shall cease to carry these coins. Do you think that you will find Christ poor in those regions to which we are hastening, when we know him to be rich everywhere? Do not fear poverty when Christ is rich. For Christ will sufficiently provide what you need, if first you faithfully seek the kingdom of God.”

After these words, a poor peasant met them, and Bernard ordered the coins to be given to him at once. The poor man rejoiced on receiving the silver because he had acquired coins so easily; Bernard rejoiced still more because he had entirely rid himself of coins. Thus each was gladdened in a different way: the one hurried home with money, while the other, without money and without anywhere at the first stopping-place to lay his head, did not know where to go. Yet trusting in the bounty of God’s goodness and hastening to complete the journey he had undertaken, he reached the Breton sea. There he learned that less than ten miles out at sea was an island offering a solitude suitable for hermits, called by the ancients Causeum [Note: [Col. 1383D] Causeum, still called Chausey, is more properly reckoned among tidal islets than islands. It lies between the English island of Jersey and the town of [Col. 1384D] Saint-Malo in Armorican Brittany.]. He boarded a ship [Col. 1384C], reached it, and lived there for many years.

27. Set in so hidden a retreat, separated from the noise and disturbance of people and removed from all hearing of human intercourse, he was wholly absorbed in heavenly contemplation. Persevering day and night in prayer, contrition of heart, and the outpouring of tears, he thought upon the days of old and kept eternal years in mind. Contemplation of the highest Good nourished him; nor did he any longer burn with much desire for earthly food, since the sweetness of divine contemplation continually satisfied him.

He remained many days in that place without bread, without a fire, and without a companion. When we asked him by what food he sustained his life while these things were lacking, he refused to tell us—an artful concealer of his own virtues, as any perverse person is a cunning hider of his sins. But in truth, as was afterwards discovered by certain of his companions, he used the raw roots of herbs. Nor did the demon’s temptation fail to visit him while he dwelt there, seeking to frighten him and expel him from those places. By its phantasmal arts it presented terrifying forms, which the soldier of Christ, armed with the sign of the cross, overcame bravely and confidently.

28. In those days pirate raiders from Armorican Brittany [Col. 1385A] set out in three armed boats. In the English sea they found two ships laden with diverse merchandise. Their owners, preparing to defend themselves boldly, engaged them in naval battle. The fighting was fierce on both sides: fiercely by the pirates, in order to plunder what belonged to others; manfully by the merchants, in order to defend their own goods. At length the raging multitude of pirates prevailed. The wretched merchants were overcome, wounded, and bound half-dead to the rowing-benches. The rapacity of the raging men, having attained its desire, immediately turned toward Brittany; but, through the action of heavenly mercy, contrary winds drove their vessel to the island of Causeum.

Bernard, a lover of piety and practitioner of mercy, whose whole being overflowed with compassionate feeling, saw the captive men lying near death in the bilge-water, their hands bound behind their backs, robbed of their money, crying out in lamentable complaints, and covered in their own blood. He also saw the robbers exulting and dancing with joy. Moved by pity for the misery of both, he drew sighs from the depths of his heart and immediately shed tears. He wept for those who destroyed their souls through cruel rapacity; he exhorted to patience those whom such harsh misfortunes grievously afflicted. He reproved, frightened, rebuked, and beseeched the raiders to cease resembling the demons whom they imitated through cruelty; to restore to their brothers the losses they had inflicted; and to make satisfaction for their injuries by humble supplication and a request for pardon. He urged the wounded merchants, in imitation of Christ, to ask God’s pardon for their persecutors and, retaining the virtue of wisdom in their minds, to love those who had inflicted such great evils upon them [Col. 1385C]. But the wretched merchants, who possessed the higher understanding, lamented the evils they endured; while the most cruel raiders, who rejoiced in wicked deeds, mocked the words they heard.

29. Then, about the twilight of day and night, the winds blowing according to the pirates’ wish, they departed, making nothing of the holy man’s warnings; and with the plunder they had taken, they hastened to reach their native harbors. Bernard, however, whose mind was stirred by brotherly compassion, gave himself to prayer; and, spending the whole night sleepless, he invoked in devout entreaties the Mother of God, who had been accustomed to aid him, and won the other saints of God to his aid by the price of tears and groans [Col. 1385D]: that divine goodness might turn the minds of the pirates toward good, and might restore to their families, free and unencumbered, those whom they had captured, their money having been recovered.

But the devil, author and instigator of all cruelty, by no means sleeping, inflamed his followers, under the pretext of gain, to deeds of cruelty, so as afterward to drag them down to hell. For among them he stirred up a quarrel over the division of the spoil: some of them claimed the larger share for themselves; while others maintained that in this division the rules of justice and equity ought to be observed [Col. 1386A]—rules which, however, they had by no means observed in acquiring it. And because quarrels are always found among the wicked, being utterly at variance with one another in this matter, and with the devil inciting and urging them, they began, with swords drawn, to strike one another in turn. There would have been a great slaughter of the wretches, had not the merit of the holy man praying for them intervened.

Thus throughout that whole night Bernard and Satan stood as two great champions in the field of combat, fiercely assailing one another in mutual and unceasing encounters. Satan strove to destroy, Bernard to deliver; each fought for his own side and labored to gain the victory.

30. But at last our champion, rising more forcefully, redoubled the blows of prayer, slew the enemy, and allowed him no rest [Col. 1386B]; he compelled him to retreat, pursued him as he gave way, and finally drove him from the field of combat. By prayer he disturbed the elements, in order to bring back to himself the wretched merchants, together with the ships and the savage pirates.

Meanwhile the aforesaid pirates had already reached the harbor they desired; they had already begun to seize the rocks of the shore with the iron teeth of their anchors; they were already hastening to put out gangplanks from the ships, fasten mooring-pickets, and hold the vessels in place by the retaining ropes of the *prosnesium*.

> [Note: Col. 1385D. *Prosnesium*: a rope by which a ship is tied from the shore to a post.]

But behold: a violent wind, contrary to them and stirred by Bernard’s prayers, rose up; it gathered the air into clouds, heaped up dark masses of cloud, and from their collision thunder was soon produced, frightening them with a dreadful sound. Terrifying flashes of lightning burst forth, and the gleam of flashing flames, striking their eyes [Col. 1386C], went before them. The whole upper surface of the sea appeared everywhere to them burning and belching flame. At the command of the wind, the fleet was carried back into the open sea against their will. The thickness of the clouds, because the air could bear it no longer, dissolved into storm-rain; and such an inundation of rain arose that one might think the sluices of heaven had again been opened to make a flood, and that the ancient times of Noah had returned. So great a turmoil of the elements arose that anyone standing there would immediately think that the whole fabric of the shaken world was being reduced again to its ancient chaos. By the furious blasts of battling winds, immense masses of waves rose like mountains; on their crests the ships’ hulls were lifted to the stars, and then, as the waters opened, they plunged with greater speed than flying arrows down to the lowest depths of the abyss [Col. 1386D].

31. The rowers, overcome by the stench of lightning striking close by, fell stretched out upon the benches like dead men; and, as the *stranipes* broke and the oars struck the waves, they were dragged out from the rowing-benches.

> [Note: Col. 1385D–1386D. For *stranipis*, Souchet preferred the reading *struppis*, and maintained that Vitruvius calls them *strophae* and Cicero *scalmi*. What if one should read *strangis*, so that the word is ancient French, derived from the German *strange, strenge*, “a coil of ropes” or “a nautical rope”?]

The yards also, their lashings loosened, fell down together with their supporting gear. The fabric of the sails, torn into pieces by the violence of the winds, was scattered here and there through the empty air. The rigging and other working ropes fell when the masthead pulley-blocks were shattered. Immediately [Col. 1387A] the masts, deprived of the necessary support of the ropes, were driven here and there by the shaking of the wind; their swaying almost overturned the ships’ hulls, and finally, unable to endure the fury of the winds, torn out from their very socket-hollows and with their braces shattered on every side, they fell by their own weight into the waves, almost sinking the ships.

At last, through the open seams between the planks, water was found to have entered as far as the deck-boards, so that it seemed not so much that the ships were among the waves as that the waves were now within the ships. In the final violence of the storm, the rudders were torn from their nail-fastened joints. Thus the vessels, without steering, turned their sterns into prows and were whirled about like a vortex. Then the helmsman himself turned pale; then the wretches, despairing of life, released the bound merchants from their bonds [Col. 1387B], humbly begged forgiveness for the injuries they had inflicted, restored their money—which, as they supposed, would henceforth benefit neither themselves nor the merchants—and asked them not to conceal whatever counsel they knew in this common danger:

> But what counsel, what purpose could then be theirs,  
> When the whole world was already crushing the wretches on every side?

32. Yet they jointly employed every contrivance by which the skill of nautical practice is accustomed to preserve life from the furious gulf of raging waves. But when they saw that their efforts had no power against the frenzy of the sea, all hope of life utterly removed, the transgressors came to their senses. Affliction giving understanding to hearing, they then confessed that they had sinned and that they were guilty [Col. 1387C]; they tore their garments, beat their breasts, and bound themselves by vows of various pilgrimages. Some vowed that they would become pilgrims to Jerusalem; others that they would journey as far as the city of Romulus, Rome, in order to deserve its intercessions. Very many of them solemnly declared, pledging promises, that they would seek the renowned memorial of the Apostle James at the furthest limits of Galicia.

But after these vows, while the storm nevertheless continued in its violence, driven by the intensity of fear, they began to reveal publicly, by confessing in the hearing of all, the sins they had shamefully committed—more shamefully still. Usurping for themselves the priestly office, they gave and received penances in turn.

> [Note: Col. 1387D–1388D. Even in this age we have sometimes heard of persons so ignorant regarding the usurpation of sacraments that, in such a crisis, they believe the lack of a confessor can be supplied in this way.]

Then they bestowed upon one another the kiss of peace, so that death might find them, as it were, united in peace—those whom the devil, the author of discord, had long since joined together to wage war against Christ’s faithful. Clasping hands, they held themselves fast together, because it seemed to them an act of piety if they should perish together beneath the waves—those whom the cruelty that breathes slaughter and rapacity had formerly united [Col. 1387D].

33. While the pirates thus prepared themselves to receive death, one of them, considering within himself not how he might receive it but how he might find escape from it, spoke thus: “Comrades, why are we perishing? Do what I say, and without doubt we shall live. Do you not remember that yesterday on the island of Causey you saw [Col. 1388A] the holy hermit whose warnings we despised, whose words we mocked? Let us make a vow, lifting up our hands; and let us firmly resolve within ourselves that, if the Lord brings us back to him, we shall do whatever he commands us. By his merits we shall be drawn away from the jaws of this death, which is now swallowing us.”

All unanimously received these words as though they were an oracle sent from heaven; and, as a testimony of this profession, they raised their hands as their leader had directed. Immediately, having received a certain confidence, they burst out in these words:

“O power of the Most High,” they said, “whom we have now learned by the most certain proofs of experience to be most mighty, allow us to live! Grant us a time for amendment; give a place for pardon—which, as it seems to us, you cannot justly refuse—for we are no longer piratical robbers [Col. 1388B], but professed followers of the hermit. From now on we do not keep merchants captive; rather, we help them, as our brothers whose burdens we ought to bear, fulfilling Christ’s law. Struggling against the fury of the sea lest they be swallowed by its abyss, we assist them as best we can. We had coveted their money as greedy robbers; but now, laboring for their protection as servants of the holy hermit, we keep it in order to restore it.”

34. But almighty God, who had wonderfully terrified their minds, even more wonderfully preserved their lives through the merit of his servant Bernard, to whom they cried with special devotion. For while those wretches, driven by fear of death, cried out these and similar words, the terrible blast of lightning-filled air drove their ships toward the shores of the island of Causey [Col. 1388C], and with the violence of its swiftest force carried them up onto the dry land of the shore. Four of the ships suffered shipwreck, but the fifth, with its equipment, was preserved unharmed.

When pirates and merchants found themselves and their money upon solid ground amid fragments of ships, seeing that they had escaped the abyss of death, they are said to have wept for joy. Then they sought the holy man, to whose sanctity they did not doubt that this had been granted; then they proclaimed aloud his merits as miracles of divine power. When found, he was worshipped by them as though he were a heavenly divinity, although he himself forbade it. Then the robbers begged him with tears to receive the merchants, together with their goods, as free persons [Col. 1388D]—those whom, on the preceding day, he had been unable to free despite repeated and earnest entreaties.

Then the pirates, prostrate at his feet, asked him to prescribe for them a measure of penance for their former offenses. They set forth the vows of pilgrimage they had made, and some of them received his command to fulfill those vows; while others remained with him in order to imitate the innocence of his life. The merchants too urged the holy man to build himself a house from the timbers of the shipwreck, and offered money to hire craftsmen for the work. For Bernard, though he had remained on the island for many years, had not yet possessed a house [Col. 1389A], but had hidden in caves among the rocks, or in poor huts like a vineyard-keeper or a keeper of cucumber-beds.

35. This is the provident ordering of your condescension, O Christ; this is your power; this is the gracious transformation wrought by your strong right hand. For you willed the elements to be disturbed for the merits of your servant, in order to convert the minds of rapacious men; to draw captives away from prison bonds; to build for your anchorite a dwelling in which to hide amid your cold rocks; and to reveal his life to the world.

Finally, after they had remained for several days on the island with the holy man, when provisions had entirely failed, they could not imitate him by living on raw roots of herbs in order to sustain themselves. Compelled by hunger, they greatly wished to depart; but frightened by the fury of the preceding disturbance at sea [Col. 1389B], they did not know what to choose. For ravenous hunger, consuming their limbs, commanded them to leave; but fear of the sea’s fury, shaking their hearts with terror, compelled them to remain. They were therefore hemmed in by difficulties. Yet it was necessary to choose one of two things: either to perish from lack of food, or to repeat the navigation which they had found so dangerous.

Unable to endure any longer the tyranny of the tormenting hunger they presently felt, they strove to find some assurance by which they might sail safely. They approached Bernard, for, taught by their earlier experiences, they did not doubt that he could command both winds and sea. They asked him to undertake responsibility for the motions of the elements on the security of his faith, to stand surety for them before God, so that [Col. 1389C] the sea-waves might remain calm until they reached their desired harbors with a favorable voyage.

The holy man, to whom divine grace had granted great faith, seeing men laboring under the danger of death, recalled Christ’s saying: “If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move” (Matt. 17:19). He accomplished what they had requested and sent them back to their own country by a peaceful voyage.

## CHAPTER V. The return of Blessed Bernard to the former hermits, and then to the first monastery of Saint Cyprian

36. Meanwhile the monks of Saint-Savin, unable anywhere to find Bernard, to whom they had intended with all their effort to entrust the governance of their church, appointed another shepherd for themselves [Col. 1389D]. Peter de Stellis, who lived in their neighborhood, learned this at once. He hurried immediately to the aforesaid wilderness of the hermits and, coming to Lord Vitalis, asked where the man was whom he had commended. Vitalis replied that he was hiding on a very remote island in the sea.

Peter, now judging it useless any longer to conceal what he had previously kept silent about Bernard, related to the brothers in a common hearing his name, learning, holiness of character and life, and refusal of prelacy. He proclaimed concerning him in Neustria the kind of reputation he had known for many years in Aquitaine. He urged them to draw him back from the islands of the sea, even against his will, if they loved the teaching of Catholic preaching, counsel for life, and the example of holy conduct [Col. 1390A].

The multitude of brothers received his opinion in their hearts, recognizing from the man’s former manner of life among them that what Peter reported was true. By common decree they immediately decided to send to him such envoys as they did not doubt could, by their concern and industry, bring him back. Accordingly, they sent to him Peter de Stellis himself, through whose authority and affection he could be brought back, joining to him as guide for the journey a man still living, named Christian, of remarkable simplicity and innocence. When they had completed the toil of the journey and the danger of the voyage, they at last reached him.

37. But Bernard, the man of God, seeing Peter—who had long been most familiar to him and the most faithful promoter of his flight—wondered that he had undertaken the labor of so distant a journey. Shedding tears for joy and exchanging embraces, he kissed him repeatedly, revered him as a father, and received him as a guest, bestowing as far as he could every service of usefulness, humanity, and charity [Col. 1390B].

After sweet conversation about eternal life, by which they refreshed one another, Bernard said: “Dearest Father, tell me about the condition of the Aquitanian region: whether in those parts the churches of Christ now have peace, and whether the monasteries preserve the rigor of discipline and religious life.”

Peter replied that, by God’s grace, all Christians were joyful and tranquil in festive peace; and at last he added that the monks of Saint-Savin had already set an abbot over themselves. Hearing this, Bernard was made glad, and the fear which had previously troubled his mind—that he might be compelled to become their abbot—departed [Col. 1390C].

Peter, therefore, desiring to fulfill the business of his embassy, said: “I have visited our brothers, the hermits, and have brought you their commands: that you return to them and do not entirely abandon their fellowship. With what affection of mind and longing of heart they await this, I cannot express in words.”

Bernard, indeed, being wholly overflowing with the affections of brotherly charity, is reported immediately to have given this answer: “I will do what they ask, lest I seem to despise the authority of the envoy and of those who request it, although I should not wish to leave the solitude of this remote island.”

When this embassy had been completed, Peter returned to Aquitaine.

38. At this time the Spirit of prophecy touched the mind of the man of God, enlightening it to behold certain absent things as though they were present before him [Col. 1390D]. There were two among the number of hermits who had received him and had long lived harmoniously together in the woods. One of them, named Albert, was already an old man and tirelessly devoted himself to abstinence and prayer; the other, younger, was called Adelinus and was notably endowed with the virtues of gentleness and obedience. He was so pleasant in the mildness of his manner that all who had shared his company regarded him as lovable.

By privilege of his long life Albert presided as master; the other, as subordinate, obeyed his commands. Desiring intensely to be formed by the example and instructed by the teaching of Bernard, the man of God, Adelinus left the aforesaid master and set out for Bernard’s island [Col. 1391A]. The elder, deprived of the consolation of his beloved disciple, fell into so deep an abyss of temptation that, overwhelmed by excessive and irrational grief, he would have hanged himself, had not the vigilant guard of certain brothers, who had foreseen this, kept him from such danger of death.

Meanwhile, through the Spirit, the man of God knew that the disciple was coming to him and that the master was preparing himself for a dreadful death by hanging. The younger man reached the shores of the island as he had desired. The holy man received him gladly and said these things to him: “You have come to us, dearest one, and you will remain with us for a few days; indeed, you will return to the place from which you fled, and will never afterward come back here.”

But because he had firmly resolved never to leave the one to whom he had gone, the young man did not believe Bernard’s words and did not understand that he spoke by the prophetic Spirit. He remained with him for several days among the high rocks of the island; but burdened by the violence of the cold, he returned to the woods, intending to take up the garments he had left there and come back again [Col. 1391B].

Coming to the aforesaid Albert, he found him wasting away with grief and nearly failing, surrounded by guards lest he take his own life with a noose. Compassionating his distress and striving to ease his pain, Adelinus fell at his feet, begged pardon, and promised that he would never again leave him. He also received from the leaders of the wilderness, mentioned above, a sentence of excommunication should he ever again depart from Albert. Held by this necessity, he could not return, as the man of God had foretold [Col. 1391C]. Thus it became clear that Bernard possessed the spirit of prophecy.

39. Then, not long afterward, Bernard returned, accompanied by his companions and carrying his modest belongings, as he had promised, to the woods of the hermits. Received with joy, and aided by them, he built himself a cell at a place called the Fountain of Syhard; there he lived for some time with several of his disciples.

> [Note: Col. 1391D. In our manuscripts it is called the Fountain of Gyard; Souchet reads the Fountain of Goyard, as in the forests of Le Mans.]

When he had remained there for a long time, because a lamp could not lie hidden under a bushel, he ministered the word of life to all who came and strengthened them by the example of his conduct. For not only a great multitude of nearby hermits came to him, but also crowds of ordinary people [Col. 1391D]. Thus he was hidden and yet not hidden; and the more he humbled himself, the more Christ raised him up. By fleeing glory, he deserved glory—the glory which sometimes abandons those who seek it and seeks those who despise it.

Men of the world admire those who possess such privileges. We praise those who have despised these things for the Savior’s sake; and, strangely enough, we make little of those who possess them, but extol them if they have refused to possess them. Therefore, while he preached to all, instructed every person according to his manner of life and rank of order, and taught each according to the capacity of his mind, he became so renowned everywhere [Col. 1392A] that his fame reached the ears of the often-mentioned Abbot Reginald of Saint Cyprian. Bernard’s holiness of life and the grace of his preaching were spread far and wide.

40. The aforesaid abbot, having learned the place where Bernard lived through scouts sent ahead, was greatly rejoiced. For many years he had desired to bring him back to his monastery, so that after his own death there might be someone to uphold the discipline of the regular path. He knew Bernard to be a man of remarkable simplicity and endowed with much wisdom; but he saw himself already as a *silicernius*—an old man bent by sickness and age—and therefore felt without doubt that the end of his life was near.

> [Note: Col. 1392D. *Silicernia* means old men, because, bent over and leaning on a staff, they look at stones.]

Taking precautions, therefore, lest Bernard’s distinguished merits should cause him to be drawn away to govern some church unless he brought him back quickly [Col. 1392B], Reginald himself promptly came unexpectedly to the place where Bernard lived and brought him back to his monastery by a rather praiseworthy deception, in the following manner.

After lavishly performing the offices of hospitality appropriate to the place and time, Reginald addressed Bernard thus:

“Dearest one, a certain most necessary business of our church has brought me to these regions. But hearing of the renown of your kindness, for which I congratulate you with the paternal affection due to you, I would not pass through without seeing and greeting you and commending myself to your prayers, which are most desirable to me. Moreover, I am carrying with me no small and irrecoverable sum of money, which, by the favor of heavenly mercy, I have acquired in this province; and I fear [Col. 1392C] that in these forest-wastes it may be taken from me by unknown robbers through some violent fraud. Therefore, may it please your fraternity not to hesitate to weary yourself by accompanying me in person—your presence being exceedingly renowned and loved in these regions—until we have passed beyond any hidden snares that may threaten us.”

41. Bernard, being most kind and unaware of any deceit, assented to these veiled roundabout words. Having acted as companion and guide for the journey, he led the aforementioned father safely through the wilderness to a secure place. When Bernard wished to return with a companion whom he had taken for this purpose, Reginald detained him and said:

“My own weakness did not compel me to enter these remote regions through any necessity [Col. 1392D] except love for you, my son; nor did any worldly ambition impose such labor on my old age. You alone, dearest one, I sought to acquire. I feared no robbers except your hermits and disciples. But by God’s grace we have now escaped their hands, and we no longer fear that they will forcibly take you away from us. I now securely possess so great a treasure: I desire greatly to enrich our monastery with the treasure of your holiness and wisdom. You, once lost and now divinely recovered, I would exchange for no price whatever.

“Yet, sweetest son, from now on I ask you to regard yourself as having been entreated: do not take it badly, do not be angry with me, your father, because I have brought you back, as it were, deceitfully into our fellowship. For I do this from excessive love, knowing certainly that unless I somehow deceived you, I could never draw you away from the solitude so dearly loved by you” [Col. 1393A].

42. The servant of the Lord, seeing that he could neither escape from Reginald nor return any longer to his disciples, and recalling at the same time that such things could happen to him only by the always just judgment of him who, in order to benefit many, went forth from the very bosom of the Father into our public world, answered with sound judgment. Both because of the compassion due to the old man who begged him and because of the authority of one commanding, he said:

“I know, Father, I know that refusing to comply with you is as the sin of idolatry; but it is dangerous and hard for me to leave altogether, desolate and as though orphaned, the disciples whom I have gathered. Therefore, let your provident judgment henceforth provide what ought to be done concerning them” [Col. 1393B].

To this Reginald replied: “Let this companion of yours, who is here present, return to them as my envoy and explain what has happened concerning you. Let him truthfully tell them that whoever among them wishes to follow you to the monastery, I shall most willingly, for your sake, provide sufficiently for them the support of both kinds of life.”

When all this had been accomplished, they completed a long journey and reached the monastery of Saint Cyprian. The monks joyfully and gratefully received Bernard, whom they had not seen for many years. They were astonished at a man hairy and bearded, clothed in poor and shaggy garments according to the custom of hermit life [Col. 1393C]. Detesting such a habit, they promptly stripped it off, shaved his beard, clothed him in their own garments, and, after a few days, made him prior, though he resisted. Thus, though they stripped him outwardly and took away his garb of poverty, they could not draw his mind away from love of the wilderness.

43. But as great as was the joy in that church at his return, so great was the sorrow that suddenly arose in the aforesaid solitude at his departure. Those rejoiced who had found him as though lost; those grieved who had lost him by his removal. The former clung tightly to their old companion; the latter earnestly begged that their new teacher be returned to them. The former confessed that they were adorned by his presence [Col. 1393D]; the latter that they languished in his absence.

While these things took place, the venerable Bishop Peter governed the bishopric of the city of Poitiers.

> [Note: Col. 1393D. Peter II, made bishop in 1087, governed peacefully until 1112.]

He afterward endured exile for justice’s sake until his death.

> [Note: Col. 1393D. He was driven into exile by William VIII, Duke of Aquitaine, because Peter had rebuked him for living in adultery after repudiating his lawful wife, as we said on 10 February in the Life of Saint William the Hermit. William VIII and his son William were commonly treated as one and the same person in this matter.]

> [Note: Col. 1393D–1394D. Peter died at the castle of Calvinia in his diocese on 4 April 1115; we discussed him among the omitted saints for that day.]

The holiness of his life was wonderful, as the testimony of miracles made clear after his death [Col. 1394A].

> [Note: Col. 1394D. “Frequent miracles at his tomb speak and proclaim his holiness,” as is read in the Chronicle of Richard of Poitiers, in the Samarthani, who add that “his body and holy ashes rest in the church of the abbey of Fontevraud, built by him.”]

The oft-mentioned Reginald sought an audience with Peter and carefully explained how he had brought back from the wilderness a praiseworthy fugitive. He earnestly represented how useful Bernard would be for governing the monastery after Reginald’s own death, which was now almost at the door. He further warned and fortified the bishop’s resolve by adding that Bernard must not learn of this, lest he secretly withdraw himself by flight, as he had once secretly withdrawn from the monastery of Saint-Savin for the same reason. The bishop willingly assented to all this, as the outcome later proved.

## CHAPTER VI. He is made abbot of Saint Cyprian; because of persecution he turns to preaching. The morals of the clergy reformed

[Col. 1394B]

44. It happened that, after four months had passed, Reginald was seized by a grave illness and took to his bed. As the day of his death drew near, the brethren assembled before him and with earnest prayers asked him, since the Holy Spirit revealed it to him, to show who ought to be his successor. For he was a man highly learned and adorned with the privileges of supreme holiness, innocence, and wisdom.

He answered them: “Although it does not belong to me to decide so great and important a matter, nevertheless, because I fear your desolation, if you are willing to trust me, appoint Bernard, the religious man whom God has only recently restored to you for this purpose, as a worthy steward over the house. For, to speak according to my conscience, I know no one holier than he, God being my witness” [Col. 1394C].

They unanimously accepted the counsel of so great a father. After he had paid the debt of human nature, they hastened to place in the abbot’s office the man whom he had named, and, as is customary, to drag him unwilling and resistant to consecration.

> [Note: Col. 1394D. Chronicle of Saint-Maixent: “In the year 1100 Raynald, abbot of Saint Cyprian, died. Bernard succeeded him; he left the abbacy,” as will be related below.]

45. Therefore, when he had undertaken the office of pastoral care, he sought to administer it more worthily precisely because he remembered that it had been laid upon him not by the impulse of his own will but solely by the decision of the divine will. He did not seek merely to appear a teacher; but as he surpassed others in rank, so he strove to surpass them in holy conduct. In every respect he labored to conduct himself so that not even slanderous rumor would dare invent anything against him [Col. 1394D].

By a simple life he removed occasions from detractors; by sound teaching he resisted opponents. For he was not of the number or kind of those who impose the heavy burdens of a stricter life upon disciples, though they themselves are unwilling to touch them even with the smallest finger [Col. 1395A]. Rather, whatever he preached in words, he adorned in conduct and established by examples.

He had not come untrained to govern such a burden. What he had learned from early age, not by sudden or rash excitement but by constant practice, he proposed for others to carry out. He did not exult in the abundance of overflowing possessions, nor delight in praise of himself. He did not lift up his heart toward honor, nor in secret inward meditation feed upon the subjection of others. He grieved over his own honor and hastened to avoid and flee the mouths of those who praised him.

Many are accustomed to give certain gifts to their trumpeters and, lavish toward a few, to withdraw their hand from the rest. He was wholly free from this fault; for he distributed to each person according to what he knew each required.

46. Now let the virtue which was especially his own be described more fully. In setting it forth, I profess before God, witness and judge, that I add nothing and magnify nothing beyond measure, as panegyrists do. For as the most precious jewel glitters among many gems, and the radiance of the sun overwhelms and obscures the small sparks of the stars, so by his humility—humility, the first virtue of Christians—he surpassed the virtues and power of all others. He was the least among all, that he might be greater than all.

He so humbled himself that anyone who saw him, even if he had wished to see him because of the renown of his name, would believe him to be not Bernard himself but the last of his disciples. Even when surrounded by frequent choirs of monks, he was least of all in clothing and voice, habit and gait [Col. 1395B]. He was slow to speak and swift to hear (Jas. 1:19), mindful of the command: “Hear, O Israel” (Deut. 6:14), “and be silent.”

He devoted himself so fully to works of hospitality and mercy that every day he welcomed sixty, a hundred, or even more clergy to his table, serving them with a generous hand, besides his munificent distributions to pilgrims and other poor persons who arrived. What shall I say of his most merciful disposition and kindness toward all, extending even to those whom he had never seen? Since he thought chiefly not of his own gain but of that of others, remembering that he was set over vices, not over people,

> A fatherly rod for the devout,  
> And a saving staff for the sick,  
> He lived without anyone’s complaint.

47. He was so outstanding in this virtue that he publicly preached to all that the divine commandments consisted in it alone [Col. 1395D]. For he was pure in thought, eminent in action, discreet in silence, useful in speech, near to every person in compassion, lifted above all in contemplation, strong in the vigor of abstinence, refreshed by the feast of learning, most humble in the long-suffering of patience, raised upright by the authority of fortitude, kind through the grace of piety, and strict in justice.

And what among worldly people was regarded as slight or as nothing, he said was a most serious offense in monasteries. Recalling especially the divine oracle, “Let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22:17), he began, as one overflowing with charity, to bring everyone within and to draw the poor and lowly to God [Col. 1396A]. But the monks, lukewarm and cold, more anxious for the present life than the future, repeatedly began to oppose him out of envy, saying that the monastery lacked possessions sufficient to receive so many people.

48. At the same time two cardinals, John and Benedict, acting as legates of the Apostolic See, summoned a council at the city of Poitiers.

> [Note: Col. 1395D] The same Chronicle, under the said year 1100: “On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October] there was a council, held by the two cardinals John and Benedict . . . and in that council they excommunicated King Philip.” The reader should consult what is contained concerning this controversy, previously unpublished, in the new Councils edited by our Labbe [Col. 1396D].

At it there were present one hundred and forty assembled Fathers, who struck Philip, king of the French, with the punishment of anathema because of the wife of Fulk, count of the Angevins, whom he kept in adultery. [Col. 1396B] When this excommunication became known, Duke William of Aquitaine, who was present, an enemy of all chastity and holiness, fearing that he might suffer a like punishment for similar offences, was inflamed with excessive rage and ordered them all to be plundered, scourged, and killed. When his servants began to do this, bishops and abbots fled in every direction and strove to find safe hiding-places in order to preserve their temporal lives. But Bernard and Robert of Arbrissel, who were attending the council, most valiant champions of justice and assailants of every iniquity and injustice, remained so unmoved and steadfast while the others fled shamefully that they did not desist from the excommunication they had begun, but considered it most glorious to suffer death or reproach for Christ. [Col. 1396C] And although their persecutors did not inflict death upon them, they nevertheless endured martyrdom, insofar as it lay within themselves.

49. Bernard had appointed stewards for the management of external affairs; he himself gave heed to contemplation, prayer, silence, and the observance of the religious life. In great purity of life he governed wisely and according to rule the monastery committed to him. Yet the ordering of divine mercy did not wish him to remain there longer, because it purposed to do something else through him and by means of him. Therefore it permitted such a persecution to arise against him that, compelled by it, he abandoned that monastery. The Cluniac monks, asserting that the church of St Cyprian ought to be subject to their jurisdiction, [Col. 1396D] approached Pope Paschal, then governing the summit of the Roman Church.

> [Note: Col. 1396D] Paschal II sat from the year 1099 until 1118. Souchet, in his notes, has Paschal’s bull in favour of the Cluniacs, confirming the subjection of the monastery of St Cyprian to them, made by Gregory VII.

They compelled him to forbid Bernard the office of abbot unless he subjected himself and the church to their laws. When Bernard heard this prohibition, framed as an alternative, he gladly accepted one part of the alternative—namely, relinquishing the office and honour of abbot. But he refused the other, fearing to subject to servitude a church which he had received free; and also greatly fearing, on the other hand, to hinder the rights of the Cluniacs, who maintained that they had a just cause. [Col. 1397A] What he judged safer for himself, he did not delay to do. Burning with love of poverty and solitude, he returned to the secret place of the wilderness from which deceitful violence had drawn him away, and found there the mind which he had left behind. There he joined Lord Robert of Arbrissel and Vitalis of Mortain, of whom we have already made mention.

50. These men travelled barefoot through the regions of Gaul. In villages, castles, and cities they preached the word of God. Rescuing people from the errors of their lives, like powerful and most sturdy rams, aided by the strength of divine power, they struck and shattered the walls of unbelief and vices. They tore the hearts [Col. 1397B] of men away from love of perishable things; they destroyed their evil conversations, which corrupt good morals; they scattered the wickedness of evil deeds; they dispersed the accumulated heap of every iniquity; and, planting virtues in their hearts by God’s agency, they built them up by confirming what had been planted with their example. Though they were not raisers of dead bodies, they did something greater: they gave life to souls dead in sins and, once restored to life, united them to God, the true life.

Performing such signs, sometimes together and sometimes individually, they travelled through various provinces, where, through the devil’s contrivance, tribulations did not fail them. Thus, while Bernard was preaching through the maritime districts of Normandy and sowing the word of God, [Col. 1397C] he spared no one and, from love or fear of no person, concealed the truth.

51. Now throughout all Normandy the custom at that time was for priests publicly to take wives,

> [Note: Col. 1397D] Orderic Vitalis, Book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, describes at length these dissolute customs of the clergy in Normandy [Col. 1398D]; and in Book XII he says that wives were forbidden to the priests themselves.

to celebrate marriages, and to beget sons and daughters, to whom, after their death, they would leave churches by hereditary right. When giving their daughters in marriage, they often gave a church as dowry if another property were lacking. But when they took wives, before joining themselves to them, they swore in the presence of their parents that they would never abandon them. By doing this, they bound themselves by an oath never to cease being fornicators, never to approach Christ’s body and blood except as guilty and unworthy persons, and, by approaching unworthily, [Col. 1397D] to eat and drink judgment upon themselves.

Against this deadly custom Bernard, servant of God, disputed earnestly in assemblies of priests and laboured greatly to make them abandon it. He drew some away; yet he could not draw the greater part of them from the abyss of this death. Hence the priests’ wives, fearing separation from them, sought to kill him with their helpers; the priests also prepared ambushes, hoping by intimidation to recall him from preaching.

[Col. 1398A] 52. One day, when he was publicly preaching to the people at Coutances, a maritime city of Normandy, a certain archdeacon who had a wife and children arrived with a great company of priests and clerics, and asked why he, a monk and dead to the world, preached to those who were alive. Surrounded by them, Bernard replied thus in the presence of all the people:

“Have you not read, dearest brother, in the Scripture of God, that Samson, that most mighty man, slew his enemies with the jawbone of a dead ass? (Judges 15:15.)”

Taking this opportunity, and with the people listening, he expounded this passage of Scripture in his defence. “Samson,” he said, “whose name means ‘sun,’ signifies Christ, the sun of righteousness; his enemies are demons and sinful people, who cling to him through malice and attack Christ and his law. The dead ass signifies the simple, obedient people, bearing Christ’s easy yoke and light burden, following the paths of humility, dead to the world—that is, mortified as to sins and vices—as Scripture says: ‘For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God’ (Colossians 3:3). [Col. 1398B]

53. “The jawbone, possessing the strength of bones and being harder than the softness of flesh, the instrument of biting and chewing in an ass’s head, signifies a preacher of the Church. He must possess the strength of bones, because he must resist sins and vices manfully and bravely endure adversities in defence of justice and holiness. A preacher must be harder than the softness of flesh, because he must cut away from his life and conduct the carnal pleasure of delight through the labour of more rigorous abstinence; he must not lie weakly subject to vices that soften the mind. A preacher is an instrument of chewing if he understands subtly the word of God—which is food for our soul, as the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God’ [Matthew 4:4]—and, having understood it, fulfils by works what he says. For if he teaches well but lives badly, he does not instruct the people but corrupts them. While he lives badly, his preaching is despised and not received; by his example the people are not built up but destroyed.

“He must therefore live well and, by chewing and grinding the Scripture, the food of souls, examine it subtly: that is, he must distinguish the historical sense from the allegorical, [Col. 1398D] separate the allegorical from the tropological, and set the tropological apart from the anagogical. Then he must first swallow the food of God’s word, chewed and crushed into small pieces, testing through right action the power of its savour; afterward he must convey it to the body of the dead ass—that is, to the intellectual capacity of the simple people who mortify themselves—in order to guide them, through all the aforesaid modes of interpretation, toward attaining eternal life. Thus, by the teaching of continual preaching, wisely and judiciously arranged, he may advance their conduct and way of life [Col. 1399A] to better things.

“Nor should he forget that he himself is an instrument of biting: by the bite of correction and rebukes, he must cut sinners off from the body of the devil and restore them, justified by the tears of repentance, to the body of Christ, which is the Church. And just as he is situated in the more eminent part of the ass, namely in its head, through the dignity of prelacy, so he must surpass the people, who are understood through the ass, by the virtue of his deeds and the holiness of his life.

54. “You see, then, dearest brother, according to the authority of Holy Scripture, that if the Christian people, signified by the dead ass, ought to be dead to the world, much more must their preacher, signified by the jawbone, be crucified with Christ [Col. 1399B] (Galatians 2:19) and dead to the world. So that true preacher, crucified with Christ, spoke of himself as dead to the world, in order that by the authority of his own mortification he might chastise those still living in sins and vices and make the chastised conform to himself, who was dead; so that what the Apostle says might be fulfilled: ‘Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ’ (1 Corinthians 11:1).

“Therefore, since a preacher of the Church ought to be dead to the world, and the people despise the preaching of one whose life is not yet believed to have been mortified with respect to vices and sins, on what ground can you forbid me to preach because I am a monk and dead to the world? By the example of my mortified life I can benefit peoples and, by the word of doctrine, advance them to better things. And since it is established that blessed Gregory and Martin, [Col. 1399C] and many other holy monks, by the merit of their mortification received pastoral government in churches and, along with the honour of prelacy, the office of preaching, it follows that through the virtue of mortification one comes to licence to preach. Thus, because I am a monk and dead to the world, the right to preach is not taken away from me but is bestowed upon me all the more fittingly.”

While the man of God continued these and other such statements, and the people shouted agreement with him, by God’s nod the aforesaid archdeacon for a time laid aside the fierceness and arrogance of his spirit and restrained the priests and their wives from harming him. So great a multitude of both had assembled for the feast of Pentecost, in order, according to the custom of the country, to render the prescribed processions to the principal church, that the place could scarcely contain them. [Col. 1399D] Bernard, Christ’s soldier, as has been said, preached to the people; therefore he patiently endured conflicts without and fears within.

## Chapter VII. Twice undertaking a journey to Rome in defence of his abbey; after leaving it, he gathers disciples elsewhere.

55. Meanwhile, for almost four years the monks of St Cyprian, spending much labour and expense in their efforts to free their church from the claim of the Cluniacs, were unable to do so. Compelled by this necessity, they went into the wilderness with letters from the bishop of Poitiers, found their abbot, and begged him to help their struggling church. Touched by pity and compelled by his bishop’s command, he [Col. 1400A] returned to St Cyprian and stayed there for several days. Thereafter, at the urging of the bishop and monks, he took with him a few brothers from the wilderness; seated upon an ass and clothed in the garments of his poverty—that is, hermit’s garments—he set out for Rome with this very humble company.

After reaching it through many hardships, he approached Pope Paschal and asked why he had deprived him of the office of abbot. The pope, having heard much concerning Bernard’s holiness, received him kindly through his cardinals John and Benedict, who had previously known him in Aquitaine and had seen his constancy at the council when excommunicating the king. Taking his hand, the pope led him into a private chapel, and alone with him alone held conversation for a great [Col. 1400B] part of the day. He then brought him back to the palace and, in a public audience, graciously restored the office which he had forbidden him to exercise. Bernard then received his blessing, returned to Poitiers, and held his monastery peacefully for several years.

56. But the monks, compelled by his instruction to change the lukewarmness of their lives into strict discipline and the laxity of their conduct into a more exact observance of the rule, found that they were no longer permitted to do what was unlawful and—because they did not wish—to abandon their accustomed ways. They tried by some means to drive him from the monastery. They secretly carried off and hid the greater part of the wheat and wine from his dwelling, so that, having nothing with which to feed those subject to him and the poor, in whose refreshment he especially delighted, he might grow weary from obtaining provisions and return to the secluded wilderness. But “there is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel against the Lord.” While they strove to press him with straitened household resources, they made him richer in more abundant wealth. For a certain canon, who knew him as a most compassionate provider for the poor, gave him at that time so much grain and wine as he believed sufficient to sustain him for a year. [Col. 1400C] In that same year divine providence also restored to him the grain and wine which the monks had concealed; but first it miserably afflicted them with the punishments of a vengeful death.

Their accomplices, who had died under punishment, were not terrified even by their deaths. Unable to expel the holy man in this way, they sought another method. They fled to the Cluniac monks, pledging their aid in subjecting the monastery of St Cyprian to Cluniac laws; for if this were done, they did not doubt that Bernard would leave. Encouraged by this proposal and exhortation, the Cluniacs again approached the pope and once more compelled him to suspend Bernard from the office of abbot unless he subjected the monastery to them. [Col. 1400D]

57. Bernard therefore resumed his labour in full, lest he should succumb to the blows of a harsher fortune. Fearing that he would sin if, through his own sloth and negligence, the monastery of St Cyprian lost its freedom, he came again to Rome and asked the aforesaid pope [Col. 1401A] to examine attentively the causes of both sides and render a just judgment. The pope evaded doing this and commanded him either to subject the church to the Cluniacs or never again to exercise office in that abbey.

When the man of God certainly knew that he could achieve nothing in the Roman court and could not bend the pope from his decree, he was compelled to appeal to the hearing of a higher court.

> [Note: Col. 1401D] Orderic Vitalis, Book VIII, contains the same account, in nearly the same words, taken from this source.

Although this court cannot be found in the tribunals of mortals, Bernard did not fail to know from where it ought to be invoked. Inflamed with zeal for justice, then, and following Solomon’s saying, “The righteous shall be confident as a lion without terror,” he firmly summoned the pope and all his accomplices in this affair—not with presumptuous audacity but with free magnanimity—to answer before the judgment of the Last Day, before a tribunal [Col. 1401B] that cannot be deceived by any darkness of ignorance or corrupted by any gifts.

On hearing such freedom of speech, the pope angrily ordered the man of God to leave his presence. He then asked his counsellors what ought to be done in the matter. They unanimously replied that it would not be safe to dispute this controversy with so holy a man before the Judge of all, nor would they in any way agree to participate in a dispute against him. Rather, by a common decree, they declared it just that his dignity be restored to him and that pardon be sought from him for the labour and injury inflicted upon him. John and Benedict, the two cardinals present, made known before the pope the splendid praises of Bernard’s virtues which they had learned in Aquitaine; they described him to the Romans as the very man whom they themselves had seen at the council of Poitiers, ready to suffer martyrdom for justice. [Col. 1401C]

58. When the pope learned of such perfection in the man, he restrained his anger and ordered him to return to the council. When Bernard entered, he allowed him to speak for himself and imposed silence so that he might be heard more freely by all. The man of God began as follows:

“Most reverend Pope, I entreat the exalted excellence of your sublimity to bear patiently for a little while with my saying a few words that do not depart from the truth. Your fatherhood and very many men present in this sacred assembly—men most worthy of honour by reason of their lives and wisdom—are not unaware that, for the course of many years, the church of St Cyprian, entrusted to the governance of my insignificance, enjoying its own freedom, flourished again in great religious observance before the monastery of Cluny had even come into being. [Col. 1401D]

“Now, however, the abbot of Cluny, in accordance with Isaiah’s prophecy, does not cease to neigh after my wife,

> [Note: Col. 1401D] Rather, it is Jeremiah, chapter 5, whose words these are, censuring the lust and intemperance of the Jews: [Col. 1402D] “They became lustful and roaming stallions,” he says. “Every one neighed after his neighbour’s wife.”

and, though I am merely some sort of abbot, he nevertheless desires to lord it over me like an archabbot in proud tyranny. He strives to bring it about that our church should serve him as a handmaid while his own church reigns and rules. This kind of ambition is new and unheard of. It takes its beginning from that vice which, unless cut off root and branch at its source, will put forth much offspring of poisonous growth and, if permitted to arise, will sprout into a seedbed of boundless corruption. This truly detestable evil, which I do not doubt will rightly be cut off by the greatness of your judicial authority, I call new and unprecedented.

“For in the divinely given writings we read of archbishops, archpriests, and archdeacons; but we have not yet found the title of archabbot in them. The Rule of St Benedict—of which I, who am accused, am a professed adherent, and so is he who accuses me—ordains that an abbot alone has the right to order all things in his own monastery; concerning an archabbot it is wholly silent, because it believed that no seeker after this proud [Col. 1402B] vanity had existed or would exist in the world.

“To demonstrate the falsity of this accusation, if I am granted room for defence, and to establish the freedom of our monastery, I have come, most excellent of Fathers. I have approached the presence of the Roman court all the more confidently because I know more certainly that, under the examination of your judgment, prejudice and injustice can by no means prevail there. Therefore the community of our place, for whose embassy I act, and the lowliness of my insignificance ask that the pre-eminent sublimity of your majesty—which is placed in the higher part of Christ’s body, the Church—may, after the manner of a head, provide governance to the other, lower members; preserve in peace the unity of the whole body by the rules of justice, rendering to each what is his own; suffer with the suffering member; examine attentively the cause of both parties; and render a just judgment, considering no profit of any passing advantage, [Col. 1402C] but the endless fruit of eternal recompense.”

59. Having spoken these things clearly, the holy man was silent. The pope ordered the advocates of the Cluniac monks’ cause to speak. But, since they could find no arguments of truth, without corners or evasions, by which they might prove that the church of St Cyprian ought to be subject to their laws, they began through veiled detours, full of ambition and circumlocutions, to invent certain fictions. When the assembly present understood that these utterly disagreed with the rules of justice, it declared the monastery of St Cyprian free from them. The pope confirmed this judgment, [Col. 1402D] restored to the holy man the office of abbot which he had forbidden, and with many entreaties sought to obtain from him that he should accept the dignity of cardinal-priest and remain at Rome with him, handling ecclesiastical cases.

But Bernard, desiring to be satisfied in the solitude of the wilderness by continual contemplation, feared to undertake the entanglement of external cares and did not agree to the request. Rather, he asked permission to leave the monastery which he governed and return to solitude. Only with many supplications did he at last obtain this permission. [Col. 1403A] Since the pope could not retain with himself a man of such steadfastness and holiness, who desired nothing in the world and sought nothing but God alone, he imposed upon him the following office: that he should preach to the people, hear confessions, impose penances, baptize, travel through regions, and diligently carry out all things which a public preacher must do.

After entrusting him with an apostolic commission, and not wishing one sent to preach without money, as a vicar of the apostles, to lack food, he instructed him to receive bodily food from those whom he refreshed by the word of salvation. Wishing to begin with himself, he invited Bernard to dinner; and because Bernard remained long in Rome, he made him a daily participant at his table.

[Col. 1403B] 60. Bernard departed with the pope’s blessing. He returned to Poitiers; and after a few days, leaving the monastery and desiring with great ardour of spirit to pursue the anchoritic life, he entered with a few disciples the island of Causeum, because it was remote from everyone. He wished to remain there longer but was unable. For a pirate band of robbers landed on the shores of that island. They plundered for themselves the vessels and vestments of its little altar-church and handled them disgracefully in his presence. Seeing sacred objects basely dishonoured, he was so moved and indignant in spirit, and grieved that this profanation had been committed, that before long he left the island on account of it, never thereafter to return, and went back to the woods, where he lived. [Col. 1403C]

The Lord wished this plundering to be done by pirates in order to draw Bernard out from the enclosure of that island and bring him back to inland places,

> [Note: Col. 1403D] It is certain that the places indicated here lay among the Normans in the diocese of Avranches, not far from Armorican Brittany, from the monastery of Savigny, only ten [Col. 1404D] or eight miles distant, of whose beginnings discussion will shortly be made. See what was said on 8 January in the *Acts of Blessed Vitalis*.

where he would benefit not himself alone but very many others. The monks of St Cyprian, seeing that they would no longer have him, appointed another abbot for themselves with his counsel and goodwill.

After several days had passed, the sea-robbers mentioned a little above, who had dishonoured the man of God and the objects of his altar, were unhappily swallowed by the sea-waves, by the command of their leader, named Heobold, almost the most cruel of all pirates, while pursuing ships which they wished to plunder. Nor is it surprising that those who had caused countless faithful persons to perish by this same manner of death should themselves perish by death through drowning. [Col. 1403D] At their death innumerable armies of demons, gathering in the form of ravens, filled the spaces of the air with earthly darkness; sounding trumpets with a horrible noise, under bodily appearance they grievously terrified the minds of those sailing nearby. Because priests were lacking, they came together to celebrate their funeral rites. They received their most wretched souls, not to carry them to the joys of paradise but to drag them with fiery cords into the depths of the abyss. Thus the end of their lives had such attendants to commend their souls as one did not deserve who had not had the ministers of Christ’s Church. [Col. 1404A]

61. In those days Bernard had not yet gathered any congregation or begun to establish any monastery. Thirsting ardently to pursue the anchoritic life, he lay hidden with a few disciples in a place called the Learned Oak (*Quercus docta*). But when report spread that he would no longer return to St Cyprian, nor go back to dwell on the island—unloved by all because access and departure were difficult—many began to flock to him, wishing to be instructed by his teaching and strengthened by the examples of his life.

Since they had no means of living unless they acquired it by the labour of their hands, necessity itself compelled them to work; and the lengthy multiplicity [Col. 1404B] of the customary psalms which they then recited kept them from the work of labour for a great part of the day. Therefore the brothers approached the holy man and asked what he decreed concerning this matter. He replied:

“As for the psalms customarily sung in almost all monasteries, unless the Lord reveals something, I fear to omit them. Yet necessity itself commands you to labour more diligently. This, however, seems fitting: let us meanwhile endeavour to pray more attentively to God, that he may somehow indicate to us what we ought to do in this matter.”

62. After eight days, when the prayer had been completed, such heavy sleep overwhelmed everyone on the following night—even Bernard, the man of God, who had always been accustomed to rise before the others in the depth of night—that no one could emerge from sleep until the bright light of day filled their eyes. Rising, they nevertheless began the office in the regular manner, which they scarcely completed after almost half the day had passed. [Col. 1404C] This oppression of sleep was truly a revelation sent by God that they should leave off the aforesaid psalms, especially because it was a winter night, and scarcely any of them had been accustomed to sleep even until its midpoint.

From that time Lord Bernard ceased reciting these psalms and commanded his disciples thereafter to rest from them. He said that he knew with certainty that God preferred them to acquire their livelihood by working rather than to devote themselves to such multiplied psalmody. Now a certain nobleman, namely Ralph of Fougères, to whom belonged the forest in which they lived, could not endure the fear that it would be destroyed by their cultivation. It lay near his castle of Fougères, and because he loved it greatly and wished to preserve game there for his hunts, he had enclosed it with a fence. [Col. 1404D] He therefore gave them another forest, namely Savigny, much better: its soil was fertile, it was pleasant with streams, but it was six miles farther from his castle. There they made and built for themselves a suitable dwelling; leaving a few brothers in the former place, they lived there for several years, gaining their livelihood by the labour of their hands. Lord Vitalis, of whom we have spoken, had built a cell for himself in the same forest, almost two stadia away from them, and later built a monastery there. But since divine providence did not wish two such great lights to dwell together, it caused one to remain there and sent the other to explore other regions. [Col. 1405A]

## Chapter VIII. A monastery built in the county of Perche; benefits received and bestowed upon others.

63. The providential nod of God moved the mind of his servant Bernard and of all his disciples to migrate into other regions and seek distant solitudes. Therefore he sent one of his younger disciples to look for some wilderness [Col. 1405B] in which they might build a dwelling large enough to contain them all together, so that none of them might be compelled to live apart from him, for this was most painful for them to bear. They found such consolation in his words and presence that they preferred to endure with him the burden of the most severe poverty rather than abound in riches without him.

When they found no such place and returned to him without any fruit from their labour, this message was given them from heaven:

> That they should return swiftly and seek places  
> Fit for Bernard, who would one day be granted heaven.

For one of them saw such a vision in a dream, shown by angelic ministry. A young man, splendid in appearance and beautiful in snow-white clothing, seemed to place his hand upon his [Col. 1405C] head and speak these words: “Rise swiftly from sleep and direct your journey to Count Rotrou of Perche,

> [Note: Col. 1405D] Rotrou, son of Geoffrey II, count of Mortain and viscount of Châteaudun, who died about the year 1100, won notable victories over the Saracens in Spain and in the Holy Land, and lived until 1143. See Orderic Vitalis, Book XIII; Matthew Paris under the year 1096; William of Tyre, Book I of the *History of Jerusalem*, chapter 17, and Book VI, chapter 17; and others. He will be discussed again below.

who will give you what you seek.”

> [Note: Col. 1405D] Perche—also called *Perticus*, *Perticum*, or *Particum*—whose count is likewise called Rotrou, is a region between the territories of Chartres, Le Mans, Vendôme, and Évreux.

Immediately awakening, he recounted to his companions what he had seen. They, however, made little of the vision and returned to their master, reporting that they had found no habitation sufficiently suited to them. Later, two of his disciples, after much searching without finding a dwelling, remembered the vision related by their companion and at last came to the aforesaid count. They explained what they were seeking, and he most graciously assented to their request, promising to give what they asked.

64. This venerable prince possessed a territory [Col. 1405D] called Arcisses, one mile distant from his castle of Nogent,

> [Note: Col. 1406D] Nogent of Rotrou, so called from its spacious county. Henry of Bourbon, prince of Condé, is said to have disliked this name and called it French Enghien; but the ancient designation prevailed. Orderic, Book XIII, calls it Nogent in Perche. It is still the capital of Lower Perche.

Its soil was fertile, woods bordered it on every side, it was watered by springs and streams, distinguished by the pleasantness of its meadows, suitable for the cultivation of vines and the building of houses, [Col. 1406A] and convenient for every need. His predecessors had built an oratory there, made a pond, and planted shrubs. Without delay he led the two monks there to show it to them and granted it to the holy man of God Bernard and his monks for perpetual possession. The disciples received it joyfully, gave due thanks to the Giver of all good things and to the prince himself, and, assured by so favourable and swift an outcome that the vision received from their companion had been true, did not doubt it in the least.

Ordered by the count to return, they went away and, as he had commanded, brought their master. The count strove to honour him with due diligence. But deceived by the advice of certain persons and obeying his mother’s commands, he withdrew the gift which he had made. [Col. 1406B] Nevertheless, he earnestly invited the aforesaid servant of God to accept another territory.

For his mother Beatrice,

> [Note: Col. 1406D] Beatrice, Rotrou’s mother, was the daughter of the count of Rochefort according to Orderic, Book XIII; according to some, she was the daughter of Hilduin, count of Ramerupt.

was making every effort in those days to remove the holy man from the vicinity of Nogent, because she feared that his connection with it might bring about certain inconveniences for the Cluniac monks, many of whom she had gathered in the aforesaid town. Bernard, however, who remained unmoved against every blow of fortune and could not be disturbed by any adversity of events, was likewise in no way moved by this matter. Serene in mind and cheerful in countenance as always, he did not refuse what the count now repeatedly offered; rather, on the next day he sent two disciples to inspect it. Led by a guide, they came to a place [Col. 1406C] called Tiron.

> [Note: Col. 1406D] According to others, it is called the wilderness of Tiron. Both places were in the parish of Brunelles.

After carefully examining it, they returned to their master that same day and reported what they thought of the place shown them. “We have seen,” they said, “a place in which almost everything necessary for human use is lacking.” Seeing that they had laboured in vain, they were disheartened and resolved to return on the next day to the place from which they had come.

65. On the following night, over the territory which he was to receive from the count,

> A hanging lamp, inflaming the neighbouring lands with light,  
> Was shown to Bernard from heaven in a clear sky.

It flashed with such a blaze of rays that the whole province glittered round about with its fire-bearing light. This revelation, indeed, for you—
[Col. 1406D] He admonishes—indeed commands—that the count’s gifts not be refused. And when morning came and the disciples were preparing to return home, he said that he himself would first see the place before they departed. Coming to the forest called Tiron, he took care to survey it more closely; and its situation and appearance [Col. 1407A] so pleased him that thereafter his mind could not be torn away from it. Yet it was not the pleasantness of the region, the extent of the property, the agreeable beauty of its meadows or streams, the abundance of its vineyards, or the fruitful richness of its fertile soil, that so bound his heart to it; rather, it was the necessity laid upon him by the divine ordering, through the revelation previously shown. Having therefore received this small holding from the count, Bernard, the man of God, returned to his disciples who had remained in the regions of Normandy and Brittany, in order to gather them to himself and, once gathered, to bring them with him more swiftly to the place he had received.

66. While he was travelling from Nogent toward Mortagne [Note: [Col. 1407D] Mauritania, commonly Mortagne-au-Perche, belongs to the diocese of Séez. It is a royal seat and castle, where the governor of Perche has his residence.], a knight named Pagan of Tilley [Note: [Col. 1407D] Tilley, commonly Le Teil, six stadia west of Nogent.] [Col. 1407B] was taking the same road and overtook him as he sat on a little donkey, along with two of his disciples walking beside him on foot. Seeing them clothed in patched hermits’ garments, he judged from their very appearance of humility and poverty that they were men of good conscience and despisers of the world.
