Moved at the same time by compassion for their labor, he asked where they were going. Bernard, the man of God, replied that they intended, if able, to go as far as Mortagne that day. Hearing this, the man declared himself an inhabitant of that town and earnestly begged them, with devout entreaty, to consent to lodge with him. The man of God did not refuse the hospitality offered by charity, but accepted it with due thanksgiving. Thereafter, along the length of the road, he sought to refresh his host with the bread of God’s word [Col. 1407C] and to instruct him with the counsels of saving doctrine. Thus, when Pagan reached Mortagne, he led the man of God to his house and wished, with the greatest eagerness and care, to render him every office of hospitality, so that in return he might feed the one from whom he had received on the journey the nourishment of heavenly wisdom.

67. But the enemy of humankind and rival of every good, envying the charity of the one and the refreshment of the other, and wishing to disturb the joy of host and received guest, so infected the squire of Pagan with the poison of his malice that at nightfall he stole away his lord’s charger [Note: [Col. 1407D] A *dextrarius* is understood by authors as a spirited horse fit for riding. Thus, on 22 January, in the Life of Blessed Walter of Birbeke, no. 9, a very beautiful horse is called one “having the appearance of an excellent *dextrarius*.” Souchet here and Vossius, *On the Vices of Language*, p. 407, give other examples. It would now be called a saddle-horse, from the riding-saddle, to distinguish it from horses intended to draw carts or carry loads, which are called draught-horses and pack-horses. [Col. 1408D]] by theft. When Pagan learned this, he became sad, for he loved the horse greatly [Col. 1407D] and knew it to be especially necessary for the protection of his person. At that time there was no small war between the men of Bellême [Note: [Col. 1408D] Bellême, an ancient county in the territory of Perche; its town is equally distant from Nogent and Mortagne, lying somewhat to the west. Orderic, book XIII, under the year 1100, says: “A great conflict arose between Rotrou and Robert of Bellême, cousins, over certain claims which these lords advanced concerning the boundaries of their lands; consequently they waged a savage war against one another in their territories.” Pagan, together with the men of Mortagne, supported the party of Rotrou.] and those of Mortagne. Yet, lest he darken the joy of the festive hospitality by the shadows of his grief [Col. 1408A], he displayed a cheerful face outwardly and, concealing his sorrow, warmly urged his guests to dine.

But the loss and the sorrow of his host could not be hidden from the man of God. He endeavored to gladden his heart with words of consolation and reasonably showed him that he ought not to grieve greatly over a transient thing. Yet the gracious condescension of divine goodness wished to make known what merit belonged to the guest whom Pagan had received into his house:

> While the thief leads away the horse, so great a stupor overwhelms him  
> that he does not know how thereafter to return—or to restore the stolen goods.

For God allowed the thief’s senses and understanding to be so blinded that he did not recognize at all the places, roads, and villages in which he had been brought up from his very [Col. 1408B] childhood. Rather, he thought Mortagne was Bellême, and in turn imagined Bellême to be Mortagne. Thus it happened that throughout that night he avoided Bellême as though it were hostile territory of the men of Mortagne, and fled to the town of Mortagne as though to a safe hiding-place in Bellême.

68. Deceived by this blinding, he returned to Mortagne and, standing before the door of Pagan’s house, believed himself to be in the place to which he had intended to flee with the horse. When he was seized and asked why he had returned in this way, he did not conceal the truth, but answered that divine power had compelled him to return that same night:

> Thus Bernard works by prayers; thus he restores what has been taken away.

[Col. 1408C] These are your mighty works, Christ; these are your powers, Christ. For your friend’s merit you offer the world this exceedingly beautiful spectacle: you make the thief so intoxicated and maddened by his own wickedness that he returns, as if to the receivers of his stolen goods, to those from whom he had stolen the horse; and he hastens as if toward trusted defenders of his life to those whom the guilt of his crime warned him to avoid at the peril of his head. Reflecting on this in his heart, Pagan thereafter strove to admire and love the man of God—not as much as he wished, but as much as he could—and later bestowed much money upon his monastery.

69. Bernard, having completed the journey he had begun, gathered his disciples and brought them with him to Tiron [Col. 1408D], where thereafter he lived with them. Therefore, in the year 1109 of the Incarnate Word, when his disciples had been assembled and he had received the blessing of Lord Ivo of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 1408D] Ivo himself says in letter 229: “Rotrou, the noble and valiant count of Mortagne, came into the presence of our humility, asking us to consecrate the cemetery of a certain monastery on the river called Tiron, for the use of certain religious monks,” etc.], then bishop of the Church of Chartres [Col. 1409A], he celebrated the first Mass on holy Easter Day in the already-built wooden monastery, on the property which the aforesaid prince Rotrou had given him.

In this solitude, much beloved by him because it had been divinely foretold, the man of God acted steadfastly and manfully. He diligently encouraged the brothers in building the place and carefully shaped them by the disciplines and instructions of heavenly life, saying:

> Behold, dearest brothers, now we have a wilderness, a place sufficiently fitting for us: sufficiently open, suited to silence and quiet, and fitting for divine meditations and prayers. Here Christ’s cross must be borne; here the crown of unfading life must be earned—the crown your devotion has long sought and which the gracious condescension [Col. 1409B] of divine generosity has afterwards deigned to confer upon you. But if you dislike the fact that its condition is not suitable for human conveniences, then let this please you: its opportunity for solitude is fitting only for religious men and those seeking the solitary life. Moreover, the harshness of this place will grant you this: false brothers, corrupting good morals by evil conversations and perverse examples, will not be able to maintain among you a feigned fellowship for long, because of the very scarcity of things.

70. At that time, because of a flood of rains that had preceded in earlier years, the ground could not yield crops, and so great a famine prevailed that many thousands of people died under the compulsion of want of bread [Note: [Col. 1409D] Letter 204 to Pope Paschal states that “the poor were afflicted by famine because of the barrenness of the land.” Meyer, under the year 1110: “The barrenness of this land,” he says, “was severe, with prolonged frost and snow.” Matthew Paris, under the year 1111: “There was then a very great mortality among animals and a severe famine in Normandy.” The Chronicle of Saint-Maixent, under the year 1110: “There was great mortality and famine, and salt was exceedingly dear.”]. The multitude of monks who were with Bernard entirely lacked provisions, and also money [Col. 1409C] with which provisions might be bought. Yet, obedient to the Gospel oracle, they sought the kingdom of God more intently and did not fear that the other things would be denied them.

Since they did not distrust divine generosity but persevered constantly in prayer and labor, he who had taken pity on his servant Daniel and sent a meal from Judaea to Babylon by Habakkuk likewise stirred the heart of William [Note: [Col. 1409D] In the Second Life of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, 25 February, no. 17, “William, the religious count of Nevers, by the merits of his life, was dear to both”—namely, to Blessed Robert and Blessed Bernard. He lived to nearly extreme old age; and, according to the monk of Auxerre, “in the year 1147, leaving secular rule and trampling underfoot every honor, he sought the Charterhouse. There, living worthily before God in the humblest poverty, he happily completed the course of his life within a year of his conversion.”], then count of Nevers, to send from Burgundy to Bernard, the man of God, who lay hidden in the most remote wildernesses of Perche and whom he knew as yet only by reputation, a great golden vessel [Note: [Col. 1410D] All note that Nevers, or the Nivernais, was formerly part of the duchy or kingdom of Burgundy. It is now subject to the Parlement of Paris and forms a separate province. The city lies at the confluence of the Loire and Nièvre rivers.]. When it was sold, provisions could be bought sufficient for the monks then living with him and also for beggars. Thus animated by such a divinely given token [Col. 1409D], and strengthened by the frequent exhortations of the man of God, they set themselves to build the place and persevered in labor, [Col. 1410A] without, however, putting aside their devotion to prayer, silence, and religious observance.

71. They burned with zeal for holiness and were ready to endure every burden of poverty. They were entirely unknown to the inhabitants of that country. They wore the habit of monks, but it was mean, unkempt, shaggy, very unlike the habit of other monks, and very like the sheep from which it had been taken. For poverty’s command compelled them to possess garments obtainable at the least cost; nor did this differ at all from the Rule of Saint Benedict, which they professed. The rude and brutish people dwelling in those regions, not having known such clothing before, shrank from it. They thought them not monks but Saracens, who had come through underground [Col. 1410B] caverns to spy upon their fellow citizens. Moved by this rumor, the neighboring natives sent scouts. These immediately approached and observed men unwarlike and unarmed, plotting no evil, weaving small cells rather than erecting camps or towers—men who did not roar out war but murmured psalms and hymns.

72. They returned with better news and, beating their guilty breasts, reported to their people that not Saracens but new prophets sent by God had settled in the wilderness. When this was spread abroad, people rushed there, rich and poor alike, desirous of seeing them. Seeing so great a multitude coming, the holy man came out publicly, addressed the people, and taught them whom they ought to fear and whom they ought to serve. He urged them to set heavenly things before earthly, [Col. 1410C] and to exchange transitory things for eternal. As he thus instructed those flocking to him, declaring how glorious and marvelous it is for a human being to be made divine by participation in the highest good, showing how wretched and fleeting is the happiness of this life, and proving how dreadful and enduring are the torments awaiting sinners in hell after death, many, frightened and pierced with remorse, renounced the world, assumed the monastic habit, and submitted themselves to his direction.

73. Our account too should not, as if despising certain very small matters, neglect to tell the things by which supreme Providence carefully wished to make known the holiness of its warrior. When the man of God was newly an inhabitant of the wilderness of Tiron, it happened that [Col. 1410D] the keeper of his calves, acting rather negligently one day by chance, left a calf in the forest. When he realized [Col. 1411A] that he had abandoned it, he most diligently searched the forest, but did not find it.

Two days later, the man of God was sitting with several brothers outside the door of his little cell, beneath the shade of a tree. He saw a wolf emerge from the darkness of the forest, slowly leading the calf. To prevent it from straying from a certain path that ran from the forest across a stretch of open fields to the cell of the man of God, the wolf gently threatened it with the lash of its tail. O wondrous thing!

> The biting wolf becomes the calf’s guardian and guide home,  
> restraining its hungry and ravenous teeth.

When it drew nearer by the straight path, the monks with the servant of God recognized the calf as their own, the one their herdsman had lost. They were astonished beyond belief, amazed that the greedy maw of wolfish [Col. 1411B] rage had not merely spared it, but had guarded and brought it back. The wolf, unafraid at the presence and sight of the monks, did not fear to come almost to the feet of the man of God. Looking at him with a gentle expression, it paused a little while; then, lowering its head to him as if entrusting its calf to him, it returned to the woods. O mighty innocence of most holy Bernard! O humility most commanding, which so binds beastly ferocity that it cannot harm you, indeed is compelled to benefit you.

74. Bernard, the man of God, overflowing with the tender depths of divine charity, trusting in the abundance of God’s goodness, and strengthened by the example of him who said, “The one who comes to me I will not cast out,” wished to exclude no one. Rather, he strove by word and example to make all conformed to Christ. Many monks also—holy and religious men—from diverse monasteries hastened to him, moved by the fame of his holiness, that they might see a new Antony dwelling in the wilderness and follow in the footsteps of his poverty. Very many nobles likewise assembled from every side and, applying themselves to the service of almighty God, sought to live with him. Some also offered their sons and relatives to the Lord, to be trained through his instruction. By the example and teaching of God’s servant, many of these attained the summit of great perfection and were afterwards [Col. 1411D] appointed to govern churches, becoming abbots of different monasteries.

75. One day, while Bernard, the man of God, was blessing the monks, a monk named Ligier, a religious man and priest, was present. He saw roses descending from high in the air upon

> the monks whom Bernard joins to himself  
> and marks with the habit.

For the Lord wished through the sign of an outward miracle to show either the merit of his confessor or that he renewed human consciences unto the flower-bearing [Col. 1412A] life of holiness. Then, after the course of one year had passed, a monk named Antiquillus, a man of great simplicity and innocence, who was present, saw this:

> As the elder Bernard, never slow in good deeds,  
> offers them to those above and utters words of prayer,  
> snow and dew fall alike upon them; and plainly,  
> from on high, flowers and fragrances arrive together.

By such a prodigy it pleased the divine will to make known the privilege of its warrior, or the purity and celibacy of monastic life.

76. One day, while Bernard, the man of the Lord, was intent upon contemplation in the oratory and the brothers were working above, a fire in springtime invaded the dry forest. Driven violently by gusts of wind, [Col. 1412B] it reached the densest thicket of briars which surrounded their cell on every side. When that thicket was seized by flames, almost all their workshops were being burned. The brothers struggled long and hard to extinguish the attack of the fire, but could not do so. Therefore, despairing, they entered the cell and carried all their belongings out onto the level fields, leaving in tears their whole dwelling, which they thought would soon be consumed by fire.

But hearing their commotion, the servant of God came out of the oratory, and at once:

> Seeing the immense wind and taking pity even on the fire,  
> he sprinkled holy water against the flames  
> that were already almost invading the workshops; and so,

[Col. 1412C]

> restraining the heat of the flames and the fury of the blasts,  
> he made them turn back by prayers, lest they rush within.

For the fire did not dare pass the limits of that sprinkling. Turned back against the force of the wind and broken back upon itself, it subsided to nothing. O man of great merit, at whose will even the elements themselves are restrained!

## CHAPTER IX. The monastery built on the River Tiron. Benefits bestowed upon Count Rotrou.

77. At the same time, lest Bernard, Christ’s warrior, lack the struggle of labor and tribulation, the monks [Note: [Col. 1411D] The Cluniac monks living at Nogent, at Saint-Denis.] already mentioned claimed that the tithes and dead bodies of the land which the aforesaid count had given him were under their jurisdiction [Note: [Col. 1411D] The parish of Brunelles, in which the monastery had been built, belonged to the said monks, who there performed the duties of parish priests.]. Compelled by this legal claim, he abandoned the buildings which his disciples had made with the greatest labor [Col. 1412D] and intended to seek another piece of ground on which he might be permitted to live.

He therefore went to the venerable bishop and canons then serving the most renowned Church of Chartres, dedicated in honor of Saint Mary, ever Virgin: that is, the aforesaid Ivo [Note: [Col. 1412D] Sebastian Rouillard treats the Church of Chartres, the worship of the Mother of God—whose garment is believed to be preserved there—and various miracles in a separate book printed at Paris in 1609.]. He asked them to give him some small portion of the estate adjoining his own small holding which they possessed, for founding his monastery. There was [Col. 1413A] a small village belonging to the aforesaid canons, adjoining the little tract that the count had given the man of God, named Sarzay. They received God’s servant with due reverence, heard him with gracious goodness, and, in accordance with the magnificence of their nobility and the generosity of their liberality, granted more land than he had asked for.

The donation having been made, they drew up a charter [Note: [Col. 1413C] Souchet published the charter of donation from the Chartres archives. It was made “on the third Nones of February in the year 1113” [1114 in modern reckoning], and grants “to Lord Bernard, venerable abbot, with the flock entrusted to him, one ploughland of land on the stream called Tiron, within the parish of Gardais, for building a monastery and cloister,” together with the other things necessary for the brothers’ use.]. They then sent Lord Geoffrey, a canon of that church and provost of the territory [Note: [Col. 1413C] He was called provost of Fontenay, perhaps because the springs of the Loir and of many rivers were in that provostship. There were three other provosts under the bishop of Chartres: of Belsia, of Nogent-le-Roi, and of Amilly; they administered all the chapter’s revenues. A charter published by Souchet shows that they were removed from office or replaced in 1193.], with certain persons to show the land. After they had arrived at the aforesaid estate [Note: [Col. 1413D] Orderic, book VIII, says concerning Blessed Bernard: “After many wanderings, he turned aside to the venerable bishop Ivo; being kindly received by him, he settled with some brothers on an estate of the Church of Chartres, and in a wooded place called Tiron built a monastery in honor of the Holy Savior.”], in accordance with the chapter’s decree, they granted him, beside the stream called Tiron [Note: [Col. 1413D] This stream, the Tiron, flows into the Loir near Illiers.], the land he had requested for constructing the buildings of his monastery, as free [Note: [Col. 1413D] The charter of the cited donation: “We give the land free and exempt from synod and *circada*, from every parochial customary due and every exaction, saving the obedience justly owed to the bishop.”] as they themselves had held it.

[Col. 1413B] 78. Meanwhile, a certain noblewoman [Note: [Col. 1413D] Adela, daughter of William the Conqueror, king of England, then widow of Stephen-Henry, count of Blois and Chartres. She governed the counties for her children and later, from about 1128, lived at Marcigny, a Cluniac nunnery in the Lyonnais.], namely Adela, countess of Blois, born of royal stock, was at that time offering Saint Bernard broader tracts of land and much more useful places for building his monastery. He nevertheless refused them, preferring to establish the seat of his monastery under the protection of Blessed Mary, ever Virgin, rather than under the advocacy of any secular person whatever.

The aforesaid canons greatly rejoiced that so eminent a guest had been received on the estate of their church. Throughout his life they loved him with extraordinary affection of devotion, bestowed upon him many benefits and ecclesiastical ornaments, diligently took care to extend the patronage of their protection over the affairs of his monastery, and shrewdly set the shield of their defense against certain hostile persons [Col. 1413C]. Bernard, having founded his dwelling on the property of the blessed Mother of God, thereafter strove to honor her with such great devotion that he ordained a special Mass in her honor [Col. 1414A] to be celebrated daily in perpetuity for the salvation of all who conferred benefits upon his monastery, and especially for the aforesaid canons. It is solemnly celebrated to this day.

79. Meanwhile it happened that the oft-mentioned Count Rotrou—whom Bernard, the holy man of God, loved more than any mortal—was forcibly taken from the custody of a certain man who held him bound, by Fulk, count of Anjou and later king of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1414C] Fulk, having married the only daughter of Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, succeeded him as son-in-law and heir in 1131; he died in 1142.], [Note: [Col. 1414C] Rotrou seems to have been captured in 1113 or the following year, in the war between the said Fulk and Henry I, king of England, whose army Rotrou commanded. Victory remained with Fulk, who had him captured and bound by one of his men. See Souchet, who treats this war at length.]. Fulk did this not intending to free him, but in order to extort a great sum for him from Robert of Bellême, a beast of the most savage cruelty [Note: [Col. 1414D] William of Jumièges, *History of the Normans*, book VIII, chapter 35; Orderic, book VIII; and others exaggerate the cruelty of Robert of Bellême.].

Robert bought the count from the said Fulk for a huge price, not wishing to receive any ransom from him [Col. 1414B], but intending to make him perish under various tortures in his prisons. He hated him so greatly—for Rotrou had publicly defeated and put him to flight in war with his army [Note: [Col. 1414D] Orderic, book VIII, says of Robert: “He entered into many battles against his bordering neighbors. Geoffrey, count of Mortagne, and his son Rotrou experienced this to their advantage.” We have indicated some conflicts above.]—that he wished for himself not so much a prosperous life as for Rotrou a miserable death. At the tyrant’s command, therefore, it was devised and arranged that the noble feet of the prince should be fastened in a wooden torture-frame. His shins were wrapped in many rings and fetters; his hands and arms were condemned to iron gloves; immense weights of iron and diverse chains were hung from his neck. Then he was thrust, bent over, into a very short and constricting enclosure, cunningly made for this purpose, never again to be removed from the prison. And, lest he die too soon, Robert further ordered that he be sustained somehow only twice a week [Col. 1414C].

80. When this became known to the count, he sent word through a messenger to his mother and the nobles subject to his authority [Note: [Col. 1414D] Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, writes in letter 39: “Count Rotrou was held in chains in the tower of Le Mans. Summoned to him as he trembled in fear of death, I came. Then, after making confession to me, he arranged his household, made his testament, and made distributions to the churches. To ensure that it remained intact, he earnestly obtained from me that I myself should go to his mother and bear witness to the testament … The count’s mother received me with a kiss, approved the testament, and gave thanks that I had gone to the count.”], asking them, since they should now regard him as virtually dead, to appoint another lord for themselves [Col. 1415A]. He also asked that Bernard, the man of God, be informed through his own mother, so that he might intercede for the salvation of his soul and no longer trouble himself over the rescue of his body, which could now no longer be accomplished.

When the man of God heard this, he was immediately bathed in tears. Then, filled with a prophetic spirit, he instructed the messengers to trust in God’s mercy and not at all despair of Rotrou’s deliverance. He added that this very adversity would be changed into prosperity for Rotrou, but into the greatest adversity for Robert. And so it happened. For, by the provident ordering of him who knows how to catch the wise in their own craftiness, after a quite short course of days, as the man of God had foretold, the count was restored free and unharmed to his country [Col. 1415B], while Robert [Note: [Col. 1415D] Orderic, book XII; William of Malmesbury, book V of *The Deeds of Henry I*; John of Worcester; and others discuss Robert’s imprisonment and removal to England.], in the very chains we have described, was conveyed to England by King Henry’s command and bound in perpetual imprisonment until the day of his death. O man worthy of the highest praise! By whose tears the very fountain of mercy is moved; by whose counsels a country bereft is strengthened; at whose prophecy the captive is freed, while the tyrant, caught in the very snares he had spread, is consigned to exile.

81. Therefore Count Rotrou, restored to his country and his former prosperity, immediately gained possession of the castle of Bellême [Note: [Col. 1415D] William of Jumièges, book VIII, chapter 35: “Robert having been put in chains, in which he also died, King Henry took the most noble town of Bellême and gave it to Rotrou, count of Perche, his son-in-law.”] and the territories adjoining it, and subjected them to be possessed thereafter by himself and his heirs. As soon as he could, he came to Bernard, the man of God, by whose merits and prayers he had been freed. He rendered the thanks he owed, not so much in words [Col. 1415C] as in tears and subsequent proofs. Thereafter he loved him with such affection that he obeyed him in many things, restrained himself from robbery and cruelty in accordance with his teachings, reformed his life for the better, and, lest he seem ungrateful for so great a benefit, bestowed many gifts upon him—gifts which we refrain from listing, lest we cause weariness to devout readers.

For should we wish to recount individually what he gave our monastery in varied ornaments for the church, in gems, in gold and silver vessels, in the pleasant properties of lands, estates, and woods, in lordships of ponds, vineyards, and mills, and in revenues of diverse tithes [Note: [Col. 1415D] See Souchet, who lists some gifts from ancient charters.], we would be shown [Col. 1416A] to be weaving some extensive history rather than describing the deeds of the holy man. He also restored the territory which, as we said above, deceived by the counsel of certain persons, he had taken from the blessed man [Note: [Col. 1415D] In the above-mentioned Arcisses, under the parish of Brunelles, a priory was then built for the monks of Tiron. In 1225 it was elevated to an abbey by William, bishop of Châlons. The Sainte-Marthe brothers print the charter of donation in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 75; later, by a papal charter, it was ceded to nuns.]. There he enlarged the establishment by constructing suitable dwellings for many of Bernard’s monks and assigning many revenues to them.

The aforementioned Beatrice, having learned of his holiness, left the residence of her castles and, after buildings had been erected at Tiron, lived there for the rest of her life. There she built a great basilica at great financial expense. At her death, her daughter Juliana [Note: [Col. 1415D] Orderic, book VIII, mentions this “Juliana, wife of Gilbert of L’Aigle,” who governed the county of Perche while her brother Rotrou was staying in Spain.] succeeded her as heir to her mother’s virtue. Juliana later expended considerable sums and most diligently completed no small part of our buildings.

[Col. 1416B] 82. While Bernard was building his monastery in Francia, Robert of Arbrissel [Note: [Col. 1416D] These matters have already often been discussed. Aquitaine, beyond the Loire, is distinguished from Francia properly so called. The Aquitanians lived under the laws of the Emperor Theodosius and were considered Romans; the Franks lived under Salic law. The Bretons, Normans, and Burgundians were also distinct from these, since they lived under their own dukes or kings.] had built his in Aquitaine, namely Fontevraud; Ralph of Fougères had built his in Brittany; and Vitalis of Mortain was building his in Normandy, namely Savigny in the diocese of Avranches. Savigny later passed to Lord Bernard with the monasteries [Note: [Col. 1416D] Souchet counts in all fifty-eight monasteries, in both France and English dominions, subject to Savigny. We stated on 17 March, in the prolegomena to the Acts of Saint Patrick, no. 21, how under its fourth abbot, Serlo, Savigny with all its daughter-houses passed to the Cistercian Order and was handed over to Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. Souchet likewise counts sixty-three monasteries subject to the monastery and order of Fontevraud.] dependent upon it [Note: [Col. 1416D] The words “concerning Vitalis afterwards” were added in the copies and seem to have crept from the margin into the text.].

The heavenly Judge willed that these men, far removed from one another and separated into different regions, should remain so; for each built so many and such great monasteries that one region could not contain them, nor one province suffice for the congregations assembled by them. But Christ’s warrior Bernard, after he had established the seat of his monastery on the estate which the Mother of God herself had given him through the hand of her [Col. 1416C] canons, was driven away by no legal claim, nor could any adversity of stormy weather move him from there; for he had clung to Christ, who is the firm solidity of immovable stability.

## CHAPTER X. A second revelation concerning the monks’ eternal salvation. Other miracles.

83. One night, while the brothers in the oratory were singing the psalmody of the nocturnal office, it happened that one brother came to his end. For this reason, the board was struck according to custom, and the brothers assembled. As they wished quickly to complete the rites for the brother now dead and return to the oratory [Col. 1417A] in order to render the remainder of the interrupted psalmody, something happened other than they had intended: a delay intervened and held them there longer because circumstances required it.

For the infirmarian, having no water with which to wash the lifeless limbs of the dead brother, could not bury him, since he was unable to find the key to a certain door through which there was an exit to the fountain. Greatly distressed, he seized an axe to break down the door. But Saint Bernard gently checked his agitated disturbance and restored to him the key which the devil had taken away, which he had long sought and had not found. Thus, when the funeral rites had finally been completed, they returned to the church and finished the office of divine service which they had not yet completed.

The next day, as the brothers discussed this delay among themselves, Bernard, Christ’s warrior, declared that a certain brother had been present at the funeral rites, who had seen so great a multitude of demons come to accuse the dead brother’s soul that they filled the whole valley in which the monastery stands [Col. 1417B]. But because they had been unable to take salvation from him, as they had tried to do, they brought about this obstruction and delay to his burial. Yet because we knew for certain that he had spoken falsely—namely, that no one had been present at the service except the one who had seen what he reported—we did not doubt that he had spoken of himself.

84. At the same time, while they were preparing to commit to monastic burial the body of a certain brother who had led a very devout life, and were discharging the prescribed office of psalmody [Col. 1417C], Bernard, the man of God, withdrew to the oratory to pray more privately. There he long commended to God in prayer the soul of the deceased brother. Heavenly mercy graciously heard him, as will be shown below, and immediately chose kindly to assure him, lest he harbor any doubt concerning the man’s salvation. For the brother whose body lay in the bier appeared to him—while, as we have said, he was intent upon prayer—clothed in white garments, with a maniple in his hand, and exceedingly radiant. Asking Bernard’s blessing, he entered into conversation with him, and earnestly begged him to greet the brethren on his behalf and to tell them that he had now attained rest.

[Col. 1417D] 85. In the vicinity of our monastery there lived a certain knight named Robert of Moteja.

> [Note: Robert of Moteja occurs among the witnesses in donations made to the monasteries of Tiron and Saint-Denis of Nogent. His lordship was at the place called Monteja, commonly *les Moteis*, in the parish of Culdreia, commonly Coudray, not far south of Nogent. Consult Souchet.]

At that time he was not yet overflowing with the abundance of wealth which, as we later learned, he came to possess. For he was burdened by prolonged poverty, to the astonishment of his neighbors, although he appeared enriched by the revenues of very many villages and estates [Col. 1418A]. He himself wondered more than others at the misfortunes of his poverty, especially because everyone said that he administered his affairs with diligent industry and prudent foresight. Therefore, coming in good faith to the man of God, whose friendship he had already obtained, he earnestly begged him in devout prayers to honor his house with his presence, and ventured to add the request that he would deign to lodge with him for a single night. Bernard, being most gracious, willingly accepted his pious request, came to the house, and received its hospitality. Why say more?

> Full of riches—but of wealth that does not perish—  
> the new guest enters the dwelling of the needy knight;  
> hence he puts the man’s poverty to flight,  
> and, by the gift of him who fills all things, supplies everything.

For from that time, as later became publicly clear, such abundance entered the house of the aforesaid knight that he rejoiced that he had received in his lodging not merely God’s servant, but the very lord of all generosity and goodness [Col. 1418B]. Later, remembering that he had acquired such outward prosperity at Bernard’s entrance, he was by no means ungrateful. From then on, as far as he could, he served him continually; after Bernard’s death he bestowed upon us certain benefits and increased our monastery with very many revenues from tithes.

86. At Saint Leobinus of Five Springs—

> [Note: Commonly Saint-Lubin de Chassant, not far from Tiron. Robert of Moteja and his son Geoffrey relinquished this parish to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, who gave it to the monks of Tiron. Saint Leobinus, bishop of Chartres, is commemorated on 15 September [Col. 1418D].]

—there was a little boy whose entire eye had been covered from the day of his birth [Col. 1418C] by a fleshy growth that had formed over it. His mother heard that Bernard, the man of God, would be passing through that village. As quickly as she could, she presented herself and her child before him, and with tears contrived to obtain from him the laying-on of his hand upon her only son. Then, moved by the mother’s cries and consenting to satisfy the people standing about,

> That Christ’s praise and the blind man’s healing might appear,  
> the holy man drives from the eye the disease which he saw had deprived it;  
> with prayer he fittingly applies the worthy sign of the cross.

He restored the child to health so swiftly that the whole disease vanished with the sign of the cross.

87. Thus from every direction so great a multitude of people flowed to God’s servant, wishing to renounce the world and desiring to submit themselves to his instruction [Col. 1418D], that within three years he became father of five hundred monks.

> [Note: William of Malmesbury, Book I of *The Life of Henry I, King of England*, after treating of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, adds this concerning Bernard: “Another famous lover of poverty, leaving a monastery of very great riches, withdrew with a few men to a wooded and desert place. There, because a lamp could not remain hidden under a bushel, many flocked to him from all sides, and he founded a monastery more distinguished by the religious devotion and number of its monks than by the splendor and accumulation of money.”]

O wondrous man, born not for himself alone but for all! See that he labored not for himself alone, but for all who sought the truth. In this alone did the Holy Spirit take pleasure [Col. 1419A]: the harmony of brethren and love of neighbors, things which, Solomon testifies, are approved before God and men (Ecclus. 25:2). Three hundred of these he retained with him; the other two hundred he ordered to live twelve at a time in cells in different parts of the world. When they were oppressed by extreme poverty, the generous providence of divine mercy—which never ceases to feed the birds of heaven—most kindly cared for them and, because of the holy man’s faith, supplied them with food.

Yet for many days bread was so lacking that a pound of bread had to be divided between two men, and sometimes between four. At times they lacked bread altogether, sustaining life only on herbs and legumes. As for wine, I think it better to be silent than to say anything. They had no wine; nor at that time did they desire to have wine [Col. 1419B]. Moreover, in the very harshest winter many were without fur garments and even more without cowls, at a time when the frail bodies of mortals could scarcely endure life even when sufficiently clothed because of the excessive severity of the cold. Though oppressed by so great a lack of temporal things, they rejoiced no little to bear for Christ the burden of immense poverty.

For them, abundant in divine consolation, the presence of their most holy father Bernard was a sufficient abundance of temporal goods. While he sat among them and refreshed their minds with the heavenly words of his teaching, so great a love of the Godhead filled the disciples that they rejoiced more in devotion to such teaching than they would have rejoiced, in his absence, in abundance of passing goods. Indeed [Col. 1419C], when bread entirely failed them and they were refreshed, as we have said, only with herbs or legumes, they were so strengthened by the consolation and presence of the man of God that they gave thanks to God more cheerfully than usual and believed that they had been visited and consoled by him. Their abstinence in food, drink, and clothing was greater than the Rule of Saint Benedict, father and founder of monks, commands, or than the ordinances of any other writing require.

88. At the same time Bernard, the man of God, restored to his former health a certain brother named Odo who was possessed by a demonic spirit. He set the sign of the cross against him and ordered him released from the bonds in which he had been bound for that reason. Once released, he immediately became so calm and peaceful [Col. 1419D] as though he had previously suffered no madness.

Let us add another miracle, by which we may show that Bernard, Christ’s soldier, shone with a prophetic spirit. On account of some business he went one day to Chartres.

> [Note: In the aforementioned *Life of Blessed Robert*, no. 13, it is indicated that there was a serious dispute between Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and Bernard or Bernerius, abbot of Bonneval, on account of which “Robert, having consecrated the religious Bernard as abbot for himself, hurried to Chartres.” Whether this or some other occasion is meant here, we cannot determine [Col. 1420D].]

But before he had begun to deal with the matter, to the surprise of his companions who had gone with him, he suddenly returned to the monastery. When he asked the brothers whether any misfortune had occurred after he had left them, they reported [Col. 1420A] that a certain brother named Gervasius, tormented by an evil spirit, was being held bound in the infirmary. The man of God told us who had gathered there that while he was at Chartres he had immediately known this, and that this was why he had returned so quickly. He ordered that the brother be released from his bonds and brought to him. When he was brought, the servant of God made the sign of the cross upon him, and he at once sat down peacefully, after divine goodness had freed him from madness for the sake of its confessor’s merit.

89. In summer, while the brethren were working to gather hay and carrying it on carts and other vehicles to store it within the enclosure of the monastery, there occurred one day—by the permission of him without whose nod not even a leaf falls from a tree—an accident which nevertheless disturbed their minds [Col. 1420B]. A small boy named Amelinus hastened to approach a cart, apparently so laden with hay that it could scarcely be drawn by ten—

> [Note: Souchet adds “oxen,” a word absent from our manuscripts, so that the cart seems to have been drawn by ten men [Col. 1420D].]

—or more. As he hurried to assist it, he came too close without sufficient caution, fell backward, and was immediately overtaken at the side by the heavy rolling motion of the approaching wheels. He lay beneath them on his back while they passed completely over him. Those standing around thought him nearly dead and judged that only his burial now needed consideration. With tears, they gathered his crushed limbs onto a shovel, commonly called a winnowing-fan, and carried him, half-dead and barely breathing, to the infirmary.

When Bernard, who was as usual in the oratory, learned of this, he hurried at once, heedless in his steps, to the bed [Col. 1420C] on which the pitiable little boy lay. First, remembering the Lord’s oracle, he did not fail to greet the aforesaid room with words of peace and the sign of the blessed cross. A marvelous thing! The boy thought to be lifeless was awakened by his voice and opened his eyes at Bernard’s entrance. Then, as soon as the same servant of God laid his hand upon him, he recovered so completely that he who had been carried there in others’ hands, as though for burial, rose on his own feet and—while we watched and magnified the Lord for this—returned unharmed to the company of the others.

90. Accordingly, as long as the man of God breathed mortal air, none of his disciples was idle. Rather, unless prevented by some impediment, each worked with his own hands at the appointed hours [Col. 1420D]. There were among them many craftsmen, who practiced their respective trades in silence. Overseers of discipline were always set over them, so that, by the Father’s command, they might diligently maintain the strictness of regular observance. If unavoidable necessity compelled anyone to speak, he avoided much speaking and idle talk, since their rule did not leave such things unpunished.

Indeed, although the venerable Father had appointed, as we have said, overseers of discipline [Col. 1421A] over each group, he himself went about among all of them. Remembering the apostolic saying, “Whoever does not work shall not eat” (John 6), he allowed no one to be idle. Through the example of the man of God, such humility had grown in their hearts that they eagerly performed even the meanest tasks with their own hands, carried wood from the forest on their shoulders, took turns preparing the kitchen without the aid of servants, and were wholly ignorant of rebellion, disobedience, or insulting speech. The example of the man of God had also raised their minds to such heights of charity that they loved one another without pretense, strove to anticipate one another in honor, relinquished their own wills in serving those of others, deferred their own advantage to fulfill that of others, and shared in every way in their brothers’ miseries [Col. 1421B].

## Chapter XI. Hospitality. Prophetic spirit. Renown for holiness.

91. One of the man’s disciples, newly professed as a monk, began, in great astonishment, to wonder within himself

> Why such proclamations of fame followed him,  
> when he did not see him raise the dead, cleanse lepers, or give sight to the blind.

He paid too little attention to the fact that the performance of miracles does not bestow holiness of life, but the practice of light and righteousness does. Since for a long period he did not cease from this thought, but became a diligent observer of Bernard’s life, one night [Col. 1421C] he saw

> A great lantern, filled with radiant light,  
> borne by no one and carried back by no one,  
> leading Bernard’s steps, whether going out or returning.

For it was Bernard’s custom never to have a lamp carried before him, either by himself or by anyone else.

> [Note: Our manuscripts sometimes have *nonnunquam* (“sometimes”), and others in Souchet have the same; it appears that *non unquam* (“never”) should be read, or simply *nunquam* (“never”).]

When we asked why he permitted himself to lack light at night, he replied that, like us, he knew all the entrances and doorways of the house. Therefore this investigator

> marveled in wonder at such, or so great, a lantern.

The next day, as soon as he could, he told the man of God what he had seen and did not blush to confess how he had judged his life until then. Saint Bernard replied that his eyes might have deceived him and, with a threat, forbade him to be deceived further in this matter [Col. 1421D]. Clearly, the Lord wished by the lantern, bearer of light to travelers, to signify the shining abundance of the works of his confessor, which went before all who followed him.

92. Bernard, the man of God, extended hospitality so diligently to all arrivals that he excluded no one from lodging and taught his monks to receive everyone: rich and poor, lame and infirm, little children, women, lepers, and people afflicted with every disease. He excluded neither sex nor age [Col. 1422A], but gathering every sort of person into the guesthouse, he met all their needs as far as he could. The poorer they were, the more willingly he served them. Cheerfully, as a giver, he prepared food and bedding for them insofar as his resources allowed. Often, perhaps, because he had no other bread, he took from the tables the bread that had been set before the brethren in the refectory and gladly placed it before his guests. He made all that was his common property for all; he even sometimes took off his own shoes in order to shoe the horses of guests. In the bitterest winter he frequently deprived himself of clothing that was not superfluous and mercifully clothed the naked limbs of the poor with it.

No needy person ever returned empty-handed from him. He stripped his own people in order to clothe strangers [Col. 1422B] and aid everyone. How often he chose to be in debt, or how often he himself remained naked, covered only by a cowl, for this reason—he alone knows, from whom nothing is hidden. No one gave more to the poor than he who left nothing for himself. There are three kinds of martyrdom without shedding blood: chastity in youth, abstinence amid abundance, and generosity amid poverty. Since he had already triumphed over the first two in Aquitaine, in order also to obtain the palm of the third, he was a martyr daily in France. For though afflicted by extreme poverty, he withheld from himself and his own whatever he could possess and distributed it among the poor and those who came to him.

Hence the custom established and instituted by him remains in our monastery to this day:

> [Note: Souchet adds: “to his own times,” that is, to the year 1649, the same thing being done in the said monastery.]

All persons whatsoever are received into the guesthouse [Col. 1422C], and necessities of food and beds are supplied to them insofar as resources permit.

93. By God’s witness, no mortal in our times shone more brightly than he in the virtue of charity and generosity; no one practiced hospitality and humility more diligently; no one more completely neglected care for his own flesh. He afflicted himself with such strict abstinence that he never treated his body with the aid of medicines, with bloodletting, or with frequent baths. Nor, after professing as a monk, did he sit by a fire even to warm his limbs. While still young, though severely seized by the force of fevers, he did not leave the convent even for the space of a single day. Later, when already old, he suffered a broken rib through an accident, but he used no remedy to relieve this misfortune and told no one that he was suffering such injury until he had recovered [Col. 1422D].

Through the negligence of the refectory servants, it often happened that water was not placed at his table—for that was the drink he used—and so he ate for three or four days without drinking, yet gave no indication to anyone that he lacked a cup. He rejoiced that he had found a greater torment of abstinence and affliction with which to afflict himself; and when the servants blamed themselves for this, he forbade them to speak of such things thereafter [Col. 1423A]. If the self-denial of those who abstain only from things capable of causing intoxication is proposed to all as admirable, what worthy comparison can be made with Bernard, who abstained even from water? Give me someone who refrains from more sumptuous foods and is content with barley bread; I shall give you Bernard, who often sustained himself, however scantily, on raw roots of herbs, and was exceedingly sparing even in those.

He always ate in the community and with the brethren; and as he surpassed the disciples in rank, so he surpassed them in the virtue of abstinence. He never permitted any enticement of taste to be served to him which was not generally shared by all; indeed, he abstained even from some things that others ate.

94. We demonstrate clearly that divine grace bestowed the spirit of prophecy upon its confessor Bernard if, out of the many things which he knew by the prophetic spirit, we recount even a few. There was in his monastery a monk named Vitalis, a priest by order, who had committed theft from the brethren’s goods and had resolved in his heart to return to the vomit of secular life which he had abandoned. One night, while standing in choir with those chanting the psalms, he suddenly fell. The next day, when the brethren asked why he had fallen so disgracefully, he replied that sleep had overtaken and thrown him down. Saint Bernard, however, replied: “Brother, it is not as you claim; rather, in truth, this night I saw a demon rise up frightfully against you and inflict this fall upon you. Unless you strive promptly to cleanse your conscience from the crime you have committed by confession [Col. 1423C], and repent of the purpose of evil will in which you are still entangled, it will drive you into a worse fall.”

> O man to be marveled at and especially revered,  
> whose mind conceals nothing which his tongue does not reveal;  
> he sees both the monk’s inclinations and his meditations,  
> making known deeds already done and violent passions.

To him are revealed the phantom forms of demons; he knows human sins; the secrets of hearts are not hidden from him. And indeed, as he had predicted, not long afterward, as we ourselves saw, this happened to Vitalis: abandoning the monastic habit, he returned to his former wickedness and again clung for five years to the concubine with whom, before professing himself a monk, he had had intercourse [Col. 1423D].

95. The fame of the holy man thus grew more and more every day, carrying the marks of his virtues through the world with the swiftness of its wings. It portrayed him to hearers in such a way as to describe the measure of his stature and the features of his unadorned face, in which goodness of character, the piety of innocence, and gentleness of spirit appeared as in a seal [Col. 1424A]. It described the rigor of his abstinence, the holiness of his life, his great age, and the whiteness of his hair; and so, portraying him, it set him before their eyes while absent as though present, and made him known and beloved by all.

Thus it happened that he filled not only the neighboring parts of the French region, but also reached the furthest boundaries of Burgundy, of the Alans, and of Aquitaine—

> [Note: So the manuscripts. With Souchet, we would prefer to read “Catalans,” who were nearest Aquitaine beyond the Pyrenees at the entrance into Spain; or “Alemanni,” whom the French call Germans and who were neighbors of the Burgundians. For the Alans, who had formerly invaded Gaul and then passed into Spain, inhabited no region there at that time, nor did their name survive anywhere except, as we have said, transformed into the name Gottalania or Catalonia.]

—and reached the territories of the Britons, Normans, and English, even as far as the Scotland of the Scots, as later became clear from the effects themselves. From the borders of all these regions many hurried to him, that they might see in the flesh the presence of the man whom fame had already made known to them, receive from his mouth the counsels of saving doctrine [Col. 1424B], and learn his outstanding virtues for themselves. Some of these took care to bestow many benefits in movable wealth upon his monastery. Others, unable to have him bodily present with them in their own territories, took twelve of his monks and built monasteries for them in their lands.

96. One of these was Henry, king of the English and duke of the Normans. He sent two most eminent princes—

> [Note: They are called princes because Theobald was nephew of King Henry, through Henry’s sister Adela, who was discussed in no. 91; and Rotrou was his son-in-law, having married Henry’s daughter Matilda. Henry reigned from 1101 to 1135.]

—namely Theobald, count of Blois, and Rotrou, count of the Perche. With earnest entreaties he begged that this same servant of the Lord would come as far as Normandy [Col. 1424C] and grant him his bodily presence, excusing himself on the ground that the unforeseen occurrence of various events prevented him from daring to leave the boundaries of his lands. Bernard consented. As soon as the king saw him, he stretched both hands toward heaven and gave immense thanks to Christ, Bernard’s indwelling inhabitant. They embraced one another, and the king received him with due honor.

After hearing his fitting teaching, the king offered him very many gifts. In addition, he gave his monastery fifteen marks of silver, to be possessed every year in perpetuity. Because of the exceeding sweetness of love which he thereafter bore toward Christ’s confessor, he loved Bernard’s monks so greatly for the rest of his life that, every year, besides the revenue already mentioned, he sent them sixty or fifty marks of silver [Col. 1424D], or more or less. He carefully urged them not to depart from the religious observance of Bernard’s institution. He also undertook to build the structure of our dormitory, which royal magnificence completed at great expense.

97. Likewise Louis, king of the Franks—

> [Note: Louis VI, called the Fat, reigned from 1108 to 1137.]

—kindled by the same desire as the king just mentioned, after he had conversed with Bernard, granted as a gift the territory of Cintreiacum [Col. 1425A], which we possess to this day. He also showed the greatest reverence to Bernard’s successors after Bernard’s death, to such a degree that he wished his sons—Philip and Louis, later kings—to be received by them from the sacred font. In our monastery he bestowed innumerable benefits until the day of his death.

> [Note: Philip was crowned king during his father’s lifetime in 1129; he died in 1131 after falling from a horse.]

> [Note: Louis the Younger, after his brother’s death, was crowned king in 1131 at ten years of age; after his father’s death, he reigned until 1180.]

Theobald, whom we mentioned above, besides the two cells which he built for us during his lifetime, bestowed upon our church after his death so many and such great ornaments and other gifts that it would be tedious to enumerate them because of their multitude. He also had a sufficiently suitable infirmary residence built at his own expense.

[Col. 1425B] 98. If we wished individually to mention the others who came from different kingdoms and regions to see Bernard, bestowed on him very many gifts and territories, built cells, and conferred benefits known to God alone—for example, William, duke of Aquitaine; Fulk, count of Anjou and thereafter king of Jerusalem; Robert, count of Gloucester; Henry, count of Nevers; Guy the Younger, count of Rochefort; William, count of Warwick; Robert son of Martin; Guichard of Beaujeu; Geoffrey, viscount of Châteaudun; Giraud Berlay; Brice of Chillo; and many others—we could not be released from the complexity of this work by a brief account.

> [Note: Souchet should be read concerning these persons; William of Aquitaine and Fulk have been discussed above. Robert of Gloucester was the natural son of Henry, king of England. “Guy of Rochefort, called Rufus, being about to undertake the journey to Jerusalem in 1110, says: ‘Commending myself to the prayers of the most compassionate Father Bernard, abbot of Tiron, and of his community, I gave them one mill,’” etc. [Col. 1425D].]

> [Note: Souchet maintains that an error has arisen here and that Henry should be called count of Warwick, or Warwickshire, in England, while the William immediately following should have been count of Nevers, of whom no. 36 has spoken.]

> [Note: Guichard of Beaujeu, otherwise commonly *Bello-joco*, married Luciana, daughter of Guy Rufus of Rochefort, who had been betrothed to King Louis the Fat, according to Orderic, Book VIII under the year 1108. Peter of Cluny, Book I of *Miracles*, ch. 27, indicates that Beaujeu was a castle in the diocese of Mâcon, where Guichard founded the monastery of Joug-Dieu near Villefranche on the Rhône; it is discussed below at no. 125 [Col. 1426C].]

> [Note: Souchet records charters of donations made by Geoffrey, Giraud, and Brice of Chillo.]

Some of these, after the death of the man of God, enlarged the cells that they had formerly built, out of reverence for him, with more extensive estates, revenues, and territorial possessions. Yielding to their requests, we installed abbots there, on the condition, however, that both they and their successors should obey our commands in all things, depart in no respect from our customs [Col. 1426A], and remain entirely subject to the laws and institutions of our jurisdiction under the same rule by which their predecessors had formerly governed the cells.

99. At the same time a certain Robert—

> [Note: Souchet proves from a charter of King Henry, confirming to the monks of Tiron the donation which Robert son of Martin granted in Wales, that this was Robert son of Martin, previously mentioned.]

—of very noble birth, came to the holy man from the regions of the Ocean. Taking thirteen of Bernard’s disciples with him, he crossed Norman and English territories and reached the furthest borders of the Welsh regions.

> [Note: “Galensian” is said for the Welsh, or the region of Wales, where the Teifi River mentioned here separates the county of Cardigan from Pembroke and then flows into the Irish Sea. Among the dependent abbeys, Souchet records one of Saint Mary of Carmarthen, in Wales and in the diocese of Menevia, or Saint David’s.]

There, on the shore of the Irish Sea beside the Teifi River, he first established a cell, and later, after obtaining an equal number of monks together with an abbot, he made it into a monastery furnished with all customary necessities, under the agreement already described.

At the same time David—

> [Note: David, son of Malcolm III, king of Scots, and Queen Saint Margaret—of whom there will be discussion on 10 June—during the reign of his brother King Alexander I married Matilda. Through her, if John Lesley and other Scots are to be believed, he became heir of Northumbria and Huntingdon. After his brother Alexander died, he was made king in 1121 and lived until 1151.]

—first ruler of the Lothians and Northamptons, and later king [Col. 1426B] of the Scots, heard through report of the notable merits of the most blessed Father, who was still alive among us. Through most capable envoys he brought to himself a substantial community of Bernard’s disciples. In Lothian—bordering the Scotland of the Scots on one side and adjoining the boundaries of Northumbria on the other—he built for them a monastery in a suitable location beside the River Tweed, and sufficiently endowed it with extensive possessions and revenues.

> [Note: The Twida or Tweed is the boundary of modern England and Scotland. Thus Lothian then comprised present-day Lothian and the Marches, Scottish provinces on the German Sea.]

After doing this, he ardently desired to see the man of God. He set out from the shores of Artois and, having passed through the boundaries of many intervening regions, crossed the expanse of the British Sea and traversed the provinces of Normandy, until he reached Tiron. But because the holy Father had already departed to heaven [Col. 1426C], he could not see him as he had hoped. Yet, lest he appear empty-handed or ungrateful toward so great a man’s household, setting aside the hauteur of royal dignity, he bent his knees and presented himself with due reverence at Bernard’s tomb. He enlarged the monastery which he had already founded with more extensive estates and territories. Taking with him twelve monks, obtained with an abbot [Col. 1427A] under the aforesaid order and rule, in addition to those whom he already had, he at length reached the provinces of his kingdom after completing the labors of a very long journey.

100. We have recorded the names of certain kings, dukes, counts, and nobles who took care to see Bernard, the man of God, and to increase his monastery with their possessions; but, because of their multitude, we have briefly touched upon a few out of many. Indeed, if we wished to weave into this work all those who in different kingdoms enlarged our monastery by building cells for him, this little book would exceed its proper measure; and I do not say merely that it would be wearisome, but that even the most diligent reader would be overcome by weariness. For who could name individually the foundations of the hundred cells—

> [Note: These cells or monasteries seem to include those said in no. 82 to have been founded by Blessed Vitalis and later subjected to Blessed Bernard. Among the proper daughters of Savigny was the third abbey of Furness in England, which the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 704, says was “of the Savigniac order, that is, Tironian under the Rule of Saint Benedict”; it is discussed at greater length on 17 March before the *Acts of Saint Patrick*, no. 21.]

—which our church possessed before this little book was composed [Col. 1427B]? Who could designate, by naming terms unknown to our people, the locations of so many places or territories in which we possess them? Who would turn through volumes of such great length by reading them, if such matters, which the sequence of narrative would nevertheless demand, were written down?

101. The aforesaid servant of God was so full of the bowels of compassion that, if anyone confessed to him a grave crime—for very many came to him for such a cause—he was affected as though he himself had committed the crime, so that by his tears he moved the guilty person to tears. The grace of the Holy Spirit had bestowed upon him, by an infusion of its sweetness [Col. 1427C], such steadiness in contemplation and prayer that he spent the greater part of day and night in their continual practice. Such an abundance of tears flowed in them that anyone wishing to look upon his face would see, as it were, two streams issuing from his eyes.

For the sweet-flowing taste of divine sweetness had sprinkled him with the dripping of the torrent of God’s delight, had made the soil of his heart fruitful by the upper watering, and had thus lifted him toward the desire for divine blessedness. Because even for a moment he was absent from God’s presence, he tormented himself with lamentations through excessive grief. Thus he wept even for light sins as though you would think him guilty of the gravest crimes. His mind, too, distressed by the weariness of present life, deeply lamented the prolongation of his earthly sojourn [Col. 1427D]. And because he saw the reprobate, in frenzied fashion, rejoicing when they did evil and exulting in the worst things, he mourned their destruction with brotherly compassion.

102. Since the overflowing of grace had joined his mind to the divine mind with such affection and constancy that, as the Apostle says, “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6), his face, taking on the form of such union, displayed in itself the likeness of an angelic appearance. Those who looked upon him seemed to see [Col. 1428A] an angelic countenance in him, and his face shone with the sweetness of a certain radiance. This was especially so when he celebrated the most holy solemnities of the Mass: then such an abundant flood of tears poured forth, moved by the bodily presence of his Creator, that his priestly vestments became thoroughly wet with the rain of his tears. If he blessed the monks, performed the office for deceased brethren, or sent one of his disciples to distant regions, he was so filled with the bowels of brotherly compassion that he could not refrain from weeping and stirring others to tears by his own weeping.

103. Nor is it surprising that so abundant an outpouring of tears was in him, to whom the grace of the Holy Spirit had bestowed every increase of virtues. [Col. 1428B] For such prudence flourished in him that whatever he thought and whatever he did, he directed wholly according to the rule of reason; he willed and did nothing other than what was right, and ordered human actions as though by divine judgments. By contemplation of divine things he despised this world and everything in the world; and he directed every thought of his soul toward divine things alone—not as though he were advancing in self-exaltation, but as though he knew these alone and beheld them in his mind as though no others existed, and by a kind of flight from human things attached himself to divine things alone. From this virtue there arose in him reason, understanding, circumspection, foresight, teachableness, and caution. Fortitude also strengthened him so greatly that it raised his spirit above every fear of misfortune, [Col. 1428C] so that he feared nothing but disgraceful things; he bore adversity and prosperity alike with courage; nor did he at all shrink from the dissolution of body and soul. And now the virtue of fortitude desired not to overcome vices but to be ignorant of them, so that he no longer knew how to be angry and desired nothing. Fortitude moreover afforded him magnificence, greatness of soul, confidence, security, endurance, firmness, and constancy.

104. Temperance likewise so regulated him that he sought nothing to be regretted and exceeded the law of moderation in nothing. Everything required for bodily use he reduced beneath the yoke of reason; insofar as nature permitted, he set all such things behind reason. Nor did he now merely restrain earthly desires, but, as if through a certain [Col. 1428D] forgetfulness, erased them utterly from himself. Hence arose in him modesty, reserve, abstinence, chastity, honourableness, moderation, purity, frugality, and sobriety. Justice too bound him to itself to such an extent that he rendered to each person what was his due; and he directed the service of every virtue toward this single path of his purpose. Thus he joined the intention of his mind in fellowship with the divine mind, that by imitating it he might enter with it into an everlasting covenant. From this virtue, indeed, came to him innocence, friendship, [Col. 1429A] concord, piety, religion, affection, and humility.

## Chapter XII. Final illness: a twofold exhortation to his own people. Reception of the last sacraments.

105. Bernard, therefore, like fragrant nard—which, not by chance but, I think, by the providence of the supreme Disposer, is found expressed in the letters of his very name—by the fragrance of such great virtues breathed forth a most sweet odour amid the sickly corruptions of worldly wickedness. He was like a little column of smoke ascending through the wilderness of this life from spices of myrrh and incense, or like a gathered abundance of every kind of perfumer’s powder. But when the end drew near, at which the Creator and Redeemer of humankind, the generous rewarder of His warriors, [Col. 1429B] wished to put an end to his many and great labours and summon him to inestimable rewards, he was visited by bodily illness on the eleventh day of this Resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 1429] On 5 April in the year 1117, as we have demonstrated above.]

What more need be said? Nevertheless trusting in the divine mercy—for he was made confident by a mind conscious of complete purity—after the dismissal of the Lord’s service, at which he had been present with the disciples in the night-time, he left the church alone. Having entered the gate of the cloister, and calling for no assistance, alas, compelled by illness, he collapsed and fell into a most severe infirmity—or rather found what he desired: that he might henceforth leave us. Some of us, however, alarmed because he had not returned to the choir of those chanting, since he had never previously been accustomed to do such a thing, sought him here and there and found him lying in the aforesaid [Col. 1429C] place. For no secular matter, nor any person however powerful—although he had very frequently been disturbed by such persons while he lived—ever deprived him of the canonical hours of either day or night; nor did any bodily illness make him slower, except this alone, by which the blessed man completed his blessed course. He was always especially eager to be present at them, first or among the first, until they were finished; and so, more by example than by fear, he summoned the others with due fatherly care to imitate him. Drawing deep sighs from their hearts, they led him into the little chamber situated opposite, pondering what was afterwards to happen.

106. At last, when the psalmody had been performed as usual, the company of monks, about to be deprived in the near future of the presence of so great a protector, wandered around him hither and thither with tearful and unconsidered steps, seeking him; and, because they could not find him as they wished, they wept inconsolably. O congregation to be afflicted with incomparable desolation at his death—already shaken, as you perceive, by grievous sorrow at his momentary, so to speak, absence! What have you perceived, miserable flock? Why do you weep for one whom you have not yet lost? What grief has struck you? Who has made you privy to God’s secrets? The shepherd has not yet been struck, and you seek where to flee. Now indeed, because he is absent for an hour, you lament; but when the certainty of the matter becomes known, I think you will be utterly desolate. [Col. 1430A] Consider that your shepherd is mortal and cannot in any way escape the laws of mortality.

Therefore, when the most holy Father’s bodily strength had somewhat failed, he was first, by his own order, carried by the hands of others into the chapter-house. Addressing his sons, who were weeping inconsolably, with such strength as he could, he attempted to moderate their tears by eloquent and reasonable arguments. He showed them that, because of grief over his approaching dissolution, they were resisting the divine disposition; but the force of their love and sorrow could not be restrained by the laws of reason.

107. Yet, when the mournful groans had somehow been checked, the most holy Father began in these words:

> “Do not fear, little flock, for your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom. If, mindful of my most humble [Col. 1430B] poverty, you are willing to follow the examples which I have shown you and the rules which I have handed down, rejecting sects contrary to these, you will not, after my death, be burdened by such a lack of resources as has hitherto, by the Lord’s permission, continually pressed upon you. Let the rules which you have found suffice for you, therefore, most beloved; do not seek higher things, nor search out greater things; and do not presume to nullify the Catholic institutions of him to whose teaching you freely submitted yourselves for Christ’s sake.
>
> “For I chose you; you did not choose me. Do not overlook that I entered not into your labours, but that you entered into mine. Believe me as one who has experienced all that you have so far received only by hearsay; give ear to me; as you ought, comply without hesitation with the very depths of my heart. For I do not offer you a stone instead of bread, nor a scorpion instead of an egg, nor, God is witness, do I set a serpent before you instead of a fish. [Col. 1430C] And although I do not doubt that in very many respects you will decline from your stock, nevertheless I discharge what is mine to do. I say this not to put you to shame, but I labour to make my dearest sons forearmed.
>
> “Therefore do not wholly reject the trembling admonition of your aged Father—unless, perhaps, you shrink from being imitators of Christ Himself, poor and crucified for you, and of His priest. For if you disdain to obey Him who cries, ‘Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart’ [Matt. 11], you greatly err, since the servant is not greater than his lord. Being absent, I shall be able to help your necessities more than while present here in the exile of this most wretched pilgrimage. [Col. 1430D] And know that I am powerful in the court of heaven by this sign: if, after my departure, so great a scarcity of temporal things does not afflict you. For the more familiarly a servant has been admitted to the secrets of his master, the more effectively he can assist his fellow-servants before him.”

108. Thereafter the desirable treasure that rested in his mouth was set forth publicly: he declared what heavenly joys are, how great and of what kind they are, and for whom they are prepared; he did not pass over in silence whom the torments of hell await; he made clear by evident reasoning that eternal blessedness is promised to those who begin well, but is to be given only to those who persevere; he urged that the many mercies [Col. 1431A] of the Lord are not to be despaired of; he revealed the crafty devices of the ancient and most cunning enemy; and, to gather very many things briefly together, he brought forth things new and old—not to the full extent that the mind of this most eloquent speaker could do so, but insofar as he knew the capacity of the grieving flock could bear it.

“At last,” he said, “brothers, looking to the salvation of your souls, I have perhaps proved troublesome and difficult among you. Therefore I beg you that whoever is hurt by anything may forgive me; and if our severity has perhaps exceeded the due measure in any matter, pray that the Lord may not charge it against me as sin.”

When, as the blessed man uttered these things with tearful sobs, they all likewise fell upon their knees and unanimously cried out that he had always been good, always judicious, always gracious, and had watched over the salvation of all as was fitting, he bade the brothers a tearful farewell and was led back. He who had hitherto been accustomed, with apostolic authority, to rejoice with those who rejoiced, now wept with those who wept in brotherly compassion. [Col. 1431B]

109. Indeed, contrary to everyone’s expectation, guided by the help of God’s prevenient mercy, he drew greater strength of spirit from bodily weakness. The weaker he became, the more abstinent he was; he continually reflected upon everlasting salvation, while committing bodily health to the Lord’s judgment. Thus, while his little body, which he had wasted by incredible abstinence and excessive fasts, was tormented, he sustained himself only with those things in taking which certain persons considered themselves exceedingly abstinent—though, once they had also gorged their belly with them, they imagined that they had thereby obtained complete chastity. Although he provided all things liberally for other sick persons and denied nothing necessary from his small means, he now reckoned as harshness toward others what he regarded as leniency toward himself. No young man, sound and vigorous in body, had given himself to as great self-restraint as this man did with his worn, aged, and weakened little body. When many most honourable persons who flocked to him from all sides urged him to restore himself with richer food, he said: “We know that life is usually preserved by meals, not that health can be bestowed by them. For if, in order that illness may be cured, the appetite of the throat must be satisfied, why do those also fall ill who are daily fattened with more lavish banquets?” [Col. 1431C]

110. When physicians urged him to use baths, he said: “Can baths prevent a mortal man from dying once the term of his life has been completed? If death is truly near, not even the fomentations of hot waters can repel it. Why, I ask you, do you persuade me to relax at the end the rigour of a profession long maintained?”

I confess that in this matter he was rather obstinate: he did not spare himself even in old age, nor yield to anyone who warned him. Let the prudent reader say that I write blame in place of praise. I call Jesus to witness, whom he served and whom I too desire to serve, that I invent nothing in either direction, but as a Christian speak true things concerning a Christian: his vices are the virtues of others. I call them vices according to the judgment and desire of all of us who loved him and seek him now that he is absent. We do not mourn that we have lost such a man; rather, we give thanks that we had such a man—indeed, that we have him. For he completed his course and kept the faith, and now enjoys the crown of righteousness. He follows the Lamb wherever He goes; he is satisfied because he hungered, and joyfully sings: “As we have heard, so have we seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God” [Ps. 47:3]. [Col. 1432A] O blessed exchange of conditions! He wept in order always to laugh; he thirsted in order to find the Lord as a fountain.
