Whether pain afflicted him, fever burned him, or exhaustion dissolved him, amid so many most acute sufferings of bodily infirmity, clothed in the roughest garments, he did not at all use better clothing or changes of clothing, so that he might now use white garments and say: “You have torn my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness” [Ps. 29]. [Col. 1432B]

111. Thus he bore his illness patiently and practised abstinence with sufficient humility. Thinking all that he had done to be little, he desired to become better from day to day. Amid the stings of pain, which he endured with wonderful patience, forgetting his age and bodily frailty, he did not permit even soft bedding to be placed beneath him. Poor in spirit, he followed the poor Lord unto death, rendering back to Him what he had received, having become poor for His sake. We know that very many have given alms, but have given nothing from their own body; they have stretched out a hand to the needy but [Col. 1432C] been overcome by the pleasure of the flesh; they have whitened what was outside while within they were full of dead men’s bones. But Bernard was not such a man. At the very point of death he practised such continence that he nearly exceeded the measure, weakening his body by excessive fasting and the rigour of his lying down. The compassionate and merciful Lord, supporting this purpose of his heart with the aid of heavenly help, bestowed on him such constancy that not even a fiery sting could force a groan from him. Yet he himself, pierced by repeated stabbing pains, gave thanks with tears, to crown his virtue.

But what am I doing? I abandon the order of narration; while I linger over individual matters, I seem to write of many things but fail to preserve the rules of discourse. Envy always follows virtues, and lightning strikes lofty mountains. Nor is it surprising if I say this of human beings, since the Lord too was crucified through the jealousy of the Pharisees, and all saints have had rivals; even in Paradise there was a serpent, through whose envy death entered into the world. [Col. 1432D] I call Truth itself and His holy angels to witness, and also that angel who was guardian and companion of the admirable man, that I say nothing in his favour in the manner of panegyrists; whatever I shall say, I say as testimony—and it is less than his merits, whom the whole world proclaims.

112. Therefore, on the fifth day of his illness—

[Note: [Col. 1431D] On 10 April.]

—while the most holy sick man lay upon the very bed on which he had collapsed, he was again carried into the chapter-house. Before the venerable countenance of the Crucified One the blessed bearer of the Cross was set down. Then, addressing the assembled novices, who lamented inconsolably and listened with raised ears, thirsting for their advocate’s final admonition, the veteran began. Since “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks,” he placed first among the chief virtues—which charity holds—and which most especially summons each person to the battle-array of faith, the need to preserve charity wisely above all else. Since no disciple is above his master, and since Christ, when about to return to the Father, made known to His followers at His farewell on the day before He suffered that this was especially to be retained, the blessed servant of Christ, lest he should seem to depart in anything from Him whose office he fulfilled, made the same point, with due paternal care, to those to whom it should be made and in the manner appropriate, as he was departing from the world. [Col. 1433A] By authoritative proofs he taught that every virtue apart from this one is to be emptied and utterly destroyed; [Col. 1433B] and by very many testimonies he asserted that charity covers a multitude of sins, that it is the surest sign of those who serve God, and that in it consists the sum of the divine commandments. Supported by the utterance of Truth itself and confirming his point by such arguments as he could, he eloquently declared that by charity alone the disciples of Christ are to be distinguished from the companions of Antichrist.

113. “In this alone,” he said, “will people know that you are Christ’s disciples: not if you prove observers of superstitious traditions, but if you have love for one another. Such observances produce not so much edification as transgression. For this reason, beloved, I knowingly passed them over in silence among you, because I knew that they would do more harm than good; for I myself had been subject to them for no short time, and for a number of years had insistently imposed their observance upon others. And although I did not doubt that some of you eagerly yearned for them, judging it healthier that the strong should desire something than that the weak should flee from it, I repeatedly refused to consent. I avoided useless [Col. 1433C] inventions by which I might make you transgressors, and sought those things by which, like a father, I might lead you as sons toward things most necessary. For where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

114. Having carefully instructed them, with such voice as he could command, by these and similar teachings, he added:

> “About to enter, by the Lord’s permission, upon the path of all flesh, now deprived of my own strength and sustained by that of others, as you yourselves see, I have come, little children, to bid you farewell. I have sought your presence, so greatly desired by me, because I am already being poured out and the time of my dissolution is at hand. But, beloved, do not let the absence of our little body make you sorrowful. Allow me to leave this arena gladly and attain the starry possessions full of delights. I ask that your tears be turned into joy. You ought not to mourn as though I were to perish, when you believe that I shall reign with Christ.
>
> “Yet because no one is clean from defilement—not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day—I ask forgiveness from the broad and immeasurable bosom of mercy, and from you, for all the offences which I have committed in word, heart, and deed. And I humbly beg you to render me that which is due to all servants of Christ.” [Col. 1434A]

Sighs followed this utterance, unwelcome to those present and never credible to those absent. [Col. 1434B]

115. Thereupon he was anointed with the sacred unction according to custom and fortified by receiving the Lord’s body and blood. When, in our presence, he had obtained what he requested, after a tearful farewell and after commending his flock to the supreme Shepherd not so much with words as with tears, the pious shepherd was carried back to the cell from which he had been brought. The weeping and wailing multitude of disciples followed him. Tearful voices, accompanied by mournful sighs, were lifted high; proclaiming themselves wretched and orphaned, they lamented beyond remedy:

> “Alas,” they said, “you depart, most holy Father, by whose even course we were able to stand, by whose strength we remained upright; when you fall, we slip; when you fail, we are cast down. Why do you abandon us while we are only beginning? Why do you scatter us before we have yet been gathered? What limit will there be to our desolation? What end to our dispersal? What boundary to our destruction? In whom will there now be counsel for life, in whom hope, in whom salvation, in whom refreshment? Under whose protection shall we find refuge? Who, once the shepherd has been taken away, will restrain the savage rage of wolves from tearing the sheep? Who henceforth will be the comforter of misery, the provider of what is useful?” [Col. 1434B]

## Chapter XIII. The remaining preparation for death. Revelations, death, burial.

116. While some among them shouted these and similar things, and others lay upon the ground as though dying from a seizure that had come over them, the man who practised compassion was forced into uncertainty as to what he preferred. He neither wished to abandon the desolate flock nor to remain longer absent from the presence of the highest Good. O man entangled alike by excessive compassion and hope of heavenly things! Therefore, lifting his hands and his eyes upward, he said:

> “O God, most beautiful Maker of all beauty, before whom is all my desire and from whom my groaning is not hidden: You know with what ardour of longing my mind thirsts to see You, and how, wearied by this exile through love of You, it languishes. Yet if You command me still to remain in the contest of struggle for the protection of Your own, I do not refuse; I shall endure hard sweats so long as it pleases You.”

Thus committing all things to the judgment of the divine will, he continually longed for the joys of the happiness that was at hand. [Col. 1434D]

117. Now two days before the man of God entered the heavenly dwelling-places, a certain matron named Mary—who, because of the works of piety to which she devoted herself, had been most intimate with him—according to custom lit a candle in honour before many holy relics then kept in the tower of the castle of Nogent, and lay prostrate before them in prayer. She had a virgin daughter, whom the servant of God had requested from her mother so that she might be consecrated to Christ. While she was praying, as we have said, the aforesaid relics made a great noise in the chest in which they were kept, and greatly terrified her. Then she seemed to see a multitude of white-clad monks extending from our monastery to the same tower, which stood no less than three stadia away, proceeding in the manner of a procession and preceding the man of God, who was arrayed in priestly vestments. [Col. 1435A] As she trembled while awaiting the outcome of the strange vision, the same tower suddenly shone within as though the very rays of the sun were enclosed in it. As the brightness gradually increased, Bernard, the Lord’s confessor, appeared to the terrified matron, removed all fear by his presence, and said to her: [Col. 1435B]

> “Tomorrow, bring your daughter with you and hasten to me, for I shall soon depart from this world. Know certainly, dearest one, that unless you hasten, you will not see me again.”

Having said this, he vanished, accompanied by the brightness with which he had come.

118. She returned home and, not without the greatest astonishment of her neighbours, remained almost mute for the space of two hours. At last, when they asked what misfortune had happened to her, she related the entire vision in order. On the following day, therefore, obeying the holy man’s command and accompanied by her daughter, she hastened to him as quickly as possible. In the presence of those who were there, she said to him: “Obeying your commands, my Father, I have come; I have brought with me the daughter whom you ordered.” “Good,” replied the elder, “for, dearest one, if you had delayed even a little, you would certainly have returned without bidding farewell. Therefore I wish you not to delay any longer in giving me your daughter, which you have hitherto put off.” [Col. 1435C]

Then the mother answered: “Most willingly. Whatever pleases your fatherhood, I grant.” After he had received her in his hands, to the amazement of all who stood by, he blessed them and sent them home. But she, not many days afterward, doubtless to be joined to the virgin choirs, died unstained and exchanged the light of this world for everlasting light, through the merits of the holy man nonetheless. O glory of death, held better than life, because what it snatched away from earth it sent to heaven! Truly, as I judge, it was greater to die thus than to be raised again. For it is assured salvation not to be defiled by sins. How many would wish, if they could perhaps find a merchant, to purchase such a passage by surrendering their possessions along with their life! [Col. 1435D]

119. Therefore, as his limbs failed and the moment of death approached, the holy man ordered the brothers who ministered to him to relieve their wearied bodies with sleep, because they had kept watch too long at his bedside. They placed themselves on the ground as best they could and began to doze; but awakened by his voice, they perceived that he was speaking with certain persons. For a multitude of monks came with such glory that Bernard, as he died, was immediately filled with joy. Drawing near with attentive ears, they tried to extract from him what he had seen. He said:

> “O how immeasurable are the depths of outstanding compassion! How gracious is His mercy! I had indeed heard, Lord, that one who humbles himself for You for a time on earth is exalted by You in heaven; but now by Your grace You have willed to assure me eternally how great is the joy bestowed upon those who have submitted themselves to our lowliness. Pleasant is the service that so great a reward follows! Truly, to serve You is to reign.”

120. As the most holy Father rejoiced over these and similar things concerning the vision shown to him from heaven, he at last added with tearful prayers:

> “Know most certainly, beloved, that all who have professed in this church and have been delivered from this mortality are now endowed with ineffable glory, entirely certain of their own salvation and most greatly concerned for yours. For they appeared to me just now, white-clad and joyful, and, soon to be gathered to them, invited me to the Lord’s supper, where I shall reign eternally with Christ. But, as you now draw near here, they departed after bidding you farewell. Their radiant splendour reflects the rays of the sun; their fragrance surpasses balsam; their beauty outdoes lilies and roses.” [Col. 1436A]

Again, as tears arose, he said: “How blessed are the mothers who bore them! How blessed the knees that supported them! How happy the breasts that they sucked!” [Col. 1436B]

Those present, remembering a certain monk whose salvation they doubted, asked whether he had been seen with the others. He denied it, saying: “Rather, he is in torments.” When they likewise asked whether any end would be imposed upon his misery, he said: “He will be worn down by most grievous punishments.” When they again inquired more explicitly whether he would ever obtain any pardon, they could extract nothing else except that he would be afflicted by many torments. Since we have mentioned him, we judge it fitting briefly to relate how he lived and died. [Col. 1436C]

121. This man, entangled in many crimes and, moreover, having held no rank in any sacred order—something astonishing even to state—had for many years usurped the exercise of priestly office. Coming thence to the man of God, he assumed the monastic habit, yet disclosed to no one that he had committed such acts. Thus, when six months had elapsed and he came to his end, what he had hitherto concealed became known. He received, together with the viaticum, the blessing of the tonsure, which he had not yet received, and died. At his departure, when the serenity of the air had changed, terrible thunder suddenly followed; fearful lightning came; there was an immense flooding rain and, at the same time, a flashing of dreadful flames. So great was the disturbance of the elements that the whole air seemed about to collapse at once. Yet this agitation of the air was neither seen nor heard by anyone except those present in our dwellings. [Col. 1436D]

On the following day, when we had gathered in the chapter-house according to custom, the man of God said: “How intolerable is the tribulation that awaits sinners in hell, since such a disturbance of the elements came upon us because of one wretch! The greatness of the storm did not conceal how great that man’s misery was. Truly, on this night I saw demons dragging the wretch out through a window, and I also saw among them a most fierce struggle for his soul; but what the outcome of the dispute was, I entirely did not know.” [Col. 1437A] Such an end did the pitiable man suffer, who did not deserve to be seen glorified with the rest.

122. Now the man of God, assured by the vision already recounted and gladdened by the joy due to it, if compelled to speak of anything else, immediately returned to these words; and he could scarcely say anything but what he had seen and heard. Hence some who stood by, goaded by heartfelt grief at his approaching departure, broke out in these words: “This account does not turn out prosperously for us. For, now abhorring our company, he longs instead for the fellowship of those whom he saw.”

At last he ordered the disciples to come to him together; according to the particular strictness of their orders, he repeatedly instructed them as best he could. He admonished the priests and the other ministers of God to serve the altar in such a way that they themselves might become a living sacrifice. He exhorted the youths whom he had received and raised with fatherly affection to guard their virginity as an irrecoverable treasure and to devote themselves wisely to keeping it inviolate. Finally he admonished the unlettered, that, like the skins and goat-hair cloths of the tabernacle of the Lord, they should protect purple, fine linen, and hyacinth-blue cloth from rainy storms; and that, by serving in outward matters, they should render their own service in the divine office which they were unable to perform. [Col. 1437B]

123. Then, in turn, giving the kiss of peace with tears, he said: “May He Himself henceforth provide you with a suitable shepherd—He who is the most gracious comforter of all who mourn.” [Col. 1437C]

His inward parts were tormented and struggled with pain as though being torn away from his own limbs. And in this he was more wonderful than all others: that he overcame great suffering by charity.

[Note: [Col. 1437D] The manuscripts read: “In this he was more wonderful than all others, because he overcame great charity,” words which yield no sound sense; we have explained them by conjecture.]

Among the hands of enemies, amid the dreadful bitterness of death and the harsh necessity of captivity, nothing is more cruel than separation from one’s children. We mourned our own course and seemed rather to envy his glory. He, with his eyes closed, as though already despising human things, did not open them again until the expiration of his soul.

What are you doing, page? Why do you fear to come to his death? We writers who compile these things have long been consumed; and the book has long been drawn out, while we fear to reach its end, as though, if we remained silent and busied ourselves with his praises, his death could be deferred. Until now we have sailed under favourable winds, and the gliding keel has furrowed the crisp surface of the sea. Now the narrative strikes upon rocks, and amid the swelling mountains of waves the imminent shipwreck of countless persons is threatened, so that we are compelled to say: “Master, save us; we are perishing” [Matt. 3]; and: “Awake, why do you sleep, O Lord?” [Ps. 34]. [Col. 1437D] For who could recount Bernard dying with dry eyes?

124. Not many days had passed, when behold, the good lord required his faithful servant. He who called him to glory hastened his passage, and he who was weary from labours was invited to rewards. Therefore, when the hour of blessed recompense came—desired with innumerable sighs—at which that husbandman, about to receive the fruit of pious labour from the generous master of the household, should ascend from the snares of this present life to eternal kingdoms, he bequeathed to the Church of Tiron, by hereditary right, limbs broken by happy old age and utterly mortified by incredible frugality, because the poor man of Christ had nothing dearer. He returned to heaven the spirit entrusted to him from heaven; and with such an end he completed the course of his pilgrimage. [Col. 1438A]

> O happy course whose prize is Paradise!
>
> O happy end, followed by everlasting life!

[Col. 1438B]

> The life of the blessed bears witness and is the reward of labours. O pious confessor of Christ, what a good contest you have fought, what a happy course you have completed, what unshaken faith you have kept!
>
> Resplendent with so many titles, you have departed—not died,
>
> Joined forever to the citizens of the ever-flourishing homeland,
>
> And heir of the everlasting kingdom and co-heir with Christ,
>
> Whom Zion, the most tranquil city of peace, full of rest,
>
> Now cherishes and nourishes, and also opens her joys to him.

O how faithful was He to whom you entrusted your labours and sweats, and from whom you have now received them back with such great increase; from whom you deserved to hear that desirable, distinguished, incomparable word, “Well done.” For on this day, in the most welcome voice of His mercy, it was said to you: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” [Matt. 25]. [Col. 1438C]

> O you now happily joined to the starry choirs, the course of your pleasant voyage has now reached the borders of the heavenly Jerusalem. The anchor of your ship, guided by a favourable helmsman, has laid hold upon the harbour of eternity through hope of forgiveness:
>
> Now it has escaped the waves of the sea and the chains of death;
>
> Now it holds the hoped-for harbour and homeland.

125. Thereupon the deceased shepherd, carefully arrayed in sacred vestments as his distinction required, and laid most becomingly upon a bier draped with a pall—

[Note: [Col. 1437D] In certain manuscripts, *bacapulo*.]

—was carried on priestly shoulders into the church which he himself had founded. Before being committed to burial, he remained there for three days and as many [Col. 1438D] nights. Some of his disciples residing by the river Rhône in the territory of Beaulieu learned of his death by a sign on the following day.

[Note: [Col. 1438D] We have discussed the territory of Beaulieu above, chapter 11, note 90, and said that this monastery was called the Yoke of God (*Jugum-Dei*). The Sanmarthani also discuss it.]

For while he was still alive, they had taken some of his beard as relics. They reverently placed it in a small box and sometimes washed it for the healing of the sick; after receiving this washing, the sick returned whole. But at the very hour when God’s servant departed this life, so great a fragrance of marvellous odour issued from the aforesaid box, as though kinds of diverse spices had been heaped up in it. Attracted by this sweetness, the brothers recognized the truth of the matter as it was and, in brotherly compassion, grieved for us, who had been deprived of so great a light. [Col. 1439A] At the same hour a certain monk in Gaul, while dwelling in Brittany, also saw his triumphant funeral rites being celebrated.

126. Meanwhile, as the report flew everywhere with swiftest wings that the comforter of this country had departed from this world, priests and clerics, abbots and monks, consuls and nobles, deeply grieving, flocked in crowds from the surrounding cities, and an innumerable multitude of people from every quarter of the region, all earnestly striving to attend his memorable obsequies—which they believed to be a triumph rather than a funeral. What monk, concealed in his cell in the wilderness, remained there? What inner chambers of matrons concealed them? Whoever had not rendered the last office to such a man considered it sacrilege. No delay held anyone back: neither public business, nor the weakness of sex, nor feminine modesty, nor domestic necessity; finally, no dignity of office, however exalted, could keep anyone from hastening there in rivalry with all the rest, to add grief to grief, sighs to sighs, laments to laments, tears to tears. For they hurried not to some ridiculous spectacle accompanied by laughter.

> [Note: Col. 1439D. Here Souchet inserted a sermon in which he is compared with the patriarchs, apostles, and martyrs. This sermon is absent from both our copies; yet in them, before no. 128, this heading is written: “Sermon.” It is also absent from Souchet’s other manuscripts; he supplied it from the Papirian codex, where it may be read. It seems, however, to have been an introduction, to which the following Analecta concerning Bernard’s virtues were consequently appended.]

## CHAPTER XIV. Selections concerning various deeds in his life

[Col. 1439C] 127. If anyone wishes to hear how intolerably he bore having something better than the others served to him in the refectory, let him hear what he often did. One day, entering the kitchen, he saw a small vessel cooking at the fire together with the others; asking whose it was, he learned that it was his own. Greatly offended, he seized it and poured its contents in among the others. After this he sharply rebuked the brother who had done this without orders.

Likewise, at mealtime, entering the refectory in order to ring the bell, he approached the serving-table. Seeing there bread set out that was whiter than the rest, he quickly and secretly snatched it away and hid it before a certain elder, taking that elder’s bread for himself.

> [Note: Col. 1439D. That is, in the place where the elder was going to sit; [Col. 1440D] for in monasteries each person has his own place according to the age of his profession.]

The brother serving in the refectory, having forgotten to put water in his cup, often threw himself at his feet, confessed his fault, and begged forgiveness with tears. The gentlest man of God raised him up and kindly comforted him, saying: “Do not be distressed over this, son. It did not happen through your fault, as you thought, but by the will of God, who orders all things. Since he knows that I have no need, he judged it superfluous to urge you to provide it for me.”

> [Note: Col. 1440D. The same incident is treated more fully in no. 93. From this and similarly related events above, we are more strongly confirmed in believing that this chapter does not contain a supplement to the history, but part of an encomiastic sermon. Nevertheless, its conclusion as well as its beginning—since it contributes no more to the history—is absent from these same manuscripts.]

No one also took such care to escape the snares of gluttony or vanity. Lest he be struck by the weapon of empty glory, he tasted beforehand whatever was placed before him; and lest gluttony flatter him, he more quickly rejected from himself what he had tasted.

128. He diligently cared for the sick and weak, but watched especially to relieve the diseases of souls. That he was by no means a respecter of persons was clear from his welcome and continual association with the poor: he devoted himself wholly to their company, which was sweetest to him. He did not neglect diligently to investigate everyone’s character, life, and disposition; for he understood himself to have been sent by God as a physician more for the infirmities of souls than of bodies. [Col. 1440B] Bodily infirmities, therefore, he treated as of little account and passed over; but he carefully investigated the ailments of souls and strove altogether to heal them, because he rejoiced above all in the salvation of souls, not in the pinnacle of prelacy, like many who make light of their own souls, much less those of others.

What more need be said? This heavenly light, which the merciful Creator of brightness had kindled for the illumination of the world, wished to lie hidden in the darkness of this wilderness; but almighty God, whose counsel endures for ever and changes the plans of men, since he had ordained otherwise, had already diffused its rays far and wide and illuminated the world with the splendor of so great a light.

129. Thus, stirred by the widespread renown of so illustrious a man, innumerable peoples of diverse nations [Col. 1440C] hastened to him as to a light set up by God for them on the lampstand of holy Church. The admirable servant of God, inwardly refreshing them with the grace of the divine word, warned them to avoid the vanities of this fleeting life and worldly follies. He said that the person who hesitated to exchange the least things for the greatest, cheap things for precious, and transitory things for eternal, was not of sound mind.

For he said that the joys of a brief, passing life vanish like dreams, and that the last day lies in wait for a person like an enemy: it will plunge sinners and unbelievers into the abyss, where they will burn eternally with the devil and his angels; but it will transfer the holy person from this life’s exile into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. As the man of God spoke these and similar things, [Col. 1440D] so many already adhered to him, having abandoned the vanity of the world, that it might deservedly be said of those who had changed so well: “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Isa. 58).

What wonder? For, as is read in Isaiah, he was like a watered garden and like a spring of waters whose waters do not fail. In him the ancient wastes were built up, and he raised up the foundations of generation after generation. [Col. 1441A] Rightly, therefore, he is called a builder of hedges, turning paths into rest. Thus there already dwelt in the wilderness, as it were, a great heavenly army, keeping watch until their king should come with hymns and praises.

130. Let anyone who can say whether he has ever read or heard that so unprecedented an abundance of charity overflowed in the breast of any human being. For I cannot sufficiently marvel, much less express it in words. He repelled no one who came to him and rejected no one who wished to live with him: not the blind, not the lame, not the bandy-legged, not the hunchbacked, not the maimed. Rather, with the bosom of mercy enlarged, he gathered all alike. He did not hesitate to receive men together with women carrying their nursing infants upon their shoulders. No weak person, no despised person, no one however poor departed rejected.

When fatherless children and orphans heard this, seeking their food by begging or tending other people’s livestock in the fields, they encouraged one another, saying: “Let us also go to the harbor that receives everyone.” And when he sat among them—not let me, brothers, be ashamed to say, nor you to hear, what that most merciful man of God was not ashamed to do; for he considered nothing shameful except sin—let us say, then: when he sat among them and saw some bandy-legged, others lame or half-human, or blind or scrofulous, or maimed or deformed, reflecting silently within himself, he said in his heart: “Perhaps these are those vile things by which the Lord [Col. 1441C] breaks the strong; and the kingdom of heaven is said to belong to such people. For God chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong.”

131. Comforting them, he urged them to endure patiently for a little while the hardships of this brief life, saying: “My little children, bear them for a little while without failing, and be strengthened by hoping in the Lord, who never abandons those who hope in him. For the Lord sets free those in bonds; the Lord gives light to the blind; the Lord raises up those cast down; the Lord loves the righteous. The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and he lifts up. He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dung-heap, that he may sit with princes and possess a throne of glory. The Lord alone is the refuge of the poor, [Col. 1441D] a helper in due season, in tribulation.

“Fear the Lord, beloved ones, for those who fear him lack nothing. Know that a little belonging to a righteous person is better than the many riches of sinners, who store up and do not know for whom they gather them. Therefore sing to the Lord in your hearts, saying: ‘Lord, all our desire is before you, and our groaning is not hidden from you. Hear our prayers, and bring us out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth.’ And God will wipe away every tear from your eyes; your sorrow shall be turned into joy, and you shall be satisfied when his glory appears.”

132. With such bread, O Christ, this your faithful and prudent servant fed your fatherless children, whom you had set over your household to give them their measure [Col. 1442A] of wheat in due season. Thus he often relieved the need caused by poverty with spiritual food—a poverty which, as stated above, sometimes oppressed them severely. For it was often announced that bread was lacking, that his children had no food, and that crowds of arrivals were present, whom it was necessary not to send away fasting since they had come from afar.

What then? Do you suppose, reader, that this most faithful servant of God, though bread was lacking and there was a people to feed, hesitated even briefly in anxiety about what he should do? He did not doubt; he did not hesitate. For his remarkable faith had become accustomed to trust in God’s generosity. Therefore, without concern, he promised what he did not possess, because, trusting in the goodness of the Almighty, he truly believed that he would have it.

For if he ever, anxious in heart over the crowds thronging about him, asked the Lord what the apostles are reported to have asked when crowds hurried to the Lord and they had nothing with which to feed them, saying: “Lord, dismiss the crowds, that they may go into the towns and villages to buy food for themselves, because we are here in a desert place”; to whom the Lord said: “You give them something to eat” (Matt. 14)—if, I say, similarly moved with compassion for the multitude streaming in from every side, he ever asked the Lord with contrite heart, saying: “Lord, dismiss them, that they may go to richer places where they can obtain necessities, because we are here in a desert and arid place,” immediately he understood that the Lord was suggesting to him by divine inspiration what he said to the apostles: “You give them something to eat.”

133. Therefore he confidently invited everyone to the meal, [Col. 1442C] having the Creator of heaven and earth as steward. O thrice-blessed soul, temple of God the Father, seat of Wisdom, resting-place of the Holy Spirit, dwelling of the most holy Trinity! It is right to believe that the divine grace dwelling in you revealed to you, before they occurred, those things which it was to accomplish through you. For with what mind would you, having no bread, invite arrivals so often to a meal, unless, through the Lord’s provision, you swiftly beheld with spiritual eyes that which was to come?

Therefore, he who gives their food to beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him—do you suppose he would not give wages to his soldier and to his fellow-soldiers? Indeed he gave them, and so abundantly that all marveled, especially the unbelieving and unfaithful. For it happened very often what happened once in the time of Elisha. As is read in the Book of Kings, Samaria was held shut up under siege, but was in still greater peril through grievous famine. Thus the king, pitying his citizens who were failing from want, came to Elisha. Elisha, not ignorant of the reason for his coming, immediately said to him: “Hear the word of the Lord: Tomorrow, at this time, at the gate of Samaria, a measure of fine flour for one stater, and two measures of barley for one stater” (4 Kings 7). One of the captains, upon whose hand the king leaned, incredulously answered his word: “Even if the Lord made floodgates in heaven, could what you say be possible?” The man of God said: “You shall see it with your eyes, but you shall not eat of it.”

In no different manner, some people, driven by curiosity to see, came to the man of God, rebuking him under the guise of advice because he received so many and such people when he had no means of feeding them. To these he answered in a faithful and most steadfast voice that the Lord, not he, was their provider. “Do you think,” he said, “that he who feeds the beasts of the earth and the birds of heaven can forget human beings formed in his own image and likeness?” But they, being as persons of little faith, despaired that what the man of God promised could happen, even if the Lord made floodgates in heaven.

134. Do not be indignant, dearest brothers, that I so often return to his humility and his delight in poverty. Believe me: many and splendid miracles he performed by divine power. Although he endeavored to conceal them more carefully than a criminal conceals his wicked deeds, he could not conceal them all, because divine goodness did not wish many things useful to posterity to remain hidden. Yet I, dearest brothers, whatever others may think, admire more the humble association of this most glorious man with Christ’s poor than the power divinely given to him, however radiant with miracles. For the latter has cast many down from the height of angelic life; the former has raised every humble person to higher things. The man of God knew this: therefore he loved and cultivated the latter, while, so far as he could, he avoided and declined to exercise the former. But what could compassion for the sick and suffering fail to draw from the depths of his charity?

135. Therefore, to speak first, as is fitting, of spiritual [Col. 1443C] maladies: what proud or exalted person came to him and did not immediately return cast down and humbled? What adulterer or fornicator? What miser or covetous person? What envious or malicious person, upon hearing him, did not at once turn and change? Robbers ceased to rob; cruel persons laid aside their cruelty; tyrants ceased from tyranny; the wicked abandoned their crimes. The rich, making light of their riches, recognized them to be a burden rather than an aid; the powerful understood that the summit of eminence was not security but a precipice for them; lovers of the world discovered that they had been enslaved to vanity.

What more? He opened the eyes of the blind, filled with the dust of worldly filth, that they might see the true sun; [Col. 1443D] he unlocked with heavenly song ears which the Lord laments are shut in humankind; he directed the steps of the lame into the way of peace and righteousness. If anyone had received the poison of a deadly draught from serpentine suggestion, he healed him with the antidote of the divine oracle; as a spiritual physician, he cured those sick in faith, hope, and charity. Who can tell how many persons afflicted by demons he delivered by mighty power? How many did he draw from the jaws of the ancient serpent and restore as a faithful servant to God? Finally, he recalled the dead to life—not only those dead for two or three days, but even those dead for four days. For when he found people dead through the pernicious delight of lethal thoughts, though these were still enclosed within the dwelling of the breast; or when he found those raised up through the deadly commission of a pestilent act; [Col. 1444A] or those bound by the most miserable habit of sinning, or buried under a stinking reputation like earth, divine power of heavenly grace was not lacking to him to raise all such persons from this tomb of the dead.

136. These, therefore, are the divine miracles which the almighty Creator worked through him, rightly to be admired all the more because they are more salutary. For these deliver soul and body from everlasting death and quicken them with eternal life. This, then, is that world-saving power which the Gospel declares that the Savior bestowed upon the apostles and apostolic men. He taught it; he commanded it to be exercised for the sick world, saying to his disciples: “Go, heal the sick, cleanse lepers, give light to the blind, [Col. 1444B] raise the dead, cast out demons.”

Therefore, if we think rightly concerning the Lord, we clearly understand that he preferred his disciples to exercise these things in souls rather than in bodies. For, as the Gospel indicates elsewhere, when on a certain day they returned to him joyfully because demons were subject to them, seeing them brought low by the exaltation of vainglory, he said to them as though indignant: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). To those also who boast of curing diseases and casting out demons he will say at the end: “I do not know you” (Luke 13).

137. Therefore this most blessed worshipper of God took care not to please a human being, lest he displease the sinner; and he made little of exercising the grace of such miracles, which he understood to be shared with the reprobate. [Col. 1444C] Indeed, as harmful to many, he avoided it, as has been said, unless compassion for the miserable afflictions of the tormented and suffering utterly forced and compelled him. For he was not among those who strive to walk in great matters and in wonders above themselves.

Why do we hesitate? Let us at last disclose what he concealed; let us reveal what he wished to be hidden, since “what profit is there in hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure?” Let us say, then: whose head or other limb hurt, and who did not immediately feel relief at the touch of his holy hand? How very many have I heard testify that they experienced this for themselves! Who, disturbed by diabolical assaults, fled to him and confessed [Col. 1444D] by what goads of temptations he was being pressed, and did not at once find rest upon receiving a remedy?

138. A certain brother—whose name I suppress because he is still alive—harassed by assaults of unbelief through evil angels, fled in distress to the man of God. Confessing the intolerable labor of his mind, he begged that assistance be given him through the man’s most holy prayers. The most merciful servant of God, sympathizing with his anxious affliction, said: “Be of good courage, son. For this temptation has happened to you, by the Lord’s permission, not for destruction, as you fear, but for testing. The most merciful Creator is accustomed to test his soldiers with temptations. Stand, therefore, in the contest as a vigorous athlete, never doubting God’s assistance; for no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully.”

When the brother [Col. 1445A] declared with tears that, as it seemed to him, he was tempted beyond his strength, the most blessed man said to him: “If, then, you wish to be rid of this trouble, go, trusting that the Lord will send you help from his sanctuary.” From that hour onward—as the brother himself used to tell me—the assault ceased so completely that it was as though he had never been tempted at all.

139. It happened also at one time that he was journeying with his brothers through a village. In the middle of it they met a woman elegantly and carefully dressed. The servant of God, as a shepherd solicitous for his sheep, noticed that some of them had fixed their eyes upon her too heedlessly. When they had passed by, he said to them: “That woman whom we met would be beautiful, if she were not one-eyed.” They, [Col. 1445B] not knowing why he said this, replied that she was not one-eyed, but saw clearly with both eyes. To them he said: “Believe me, dearest brothers, I took no great care to discover whether she had one eye or two.” Hearing this, they at last understood that they had been outwitted by the most shrewd stratagem of the man of God, and they blushed.

140. If anyone again wishes to hear how skillfully he tested human minds and corrected them through testing, let him hear what follows. When, fleeing worldly tumult, he lived on that island which, surrounded by the sea and adjoining no land, he had long desired with great longing, freely devoting himself to prayer and reading, and tirelessly nourishing his whole mind in heavenly contemplation with divine visions, he nevertheless had disciples who [Col. 1445C] procured bodily support for him by the labor of their hands. After prayer, contemplation, and meditation upon reading, he went out to visit them as they worked.

One of these was mild in spirit, but the other impatient. They worked separately rather than together. Thus the wise man tested and examined their spirits by this device. Coming to the first, he would say, “Give a blessing.” Then, as though wishing to work, he would take the tool from the brother’s hands and sometimes tell him to rest. As he dug and threw clods this way and that, taking no care about where or in what order they should be placed, he asked the brother whether he was doing well. Because the brother was very well pleased with him, he answered that whatever the holy man did, he did exceedingly well.

[Col. 1445D] Then, going to the other and acting in the same manner, that impatient man, when he threw down the clods carelessly, tried to instruct him how he ought to arrange them.

141. Seeing, therefore, that he could do nothing according to that brother’s wish, the most blessed man withdrew from him [Col. 1446A] and returned to the other, teaching him something from the Scriptures amid the work of labor. Seeing this, the other was envious and groaned that the man was preferred to himself. At last he approached the venerable man of God and complained with tears that he despised him and preferred another: he comforted the other, taught the other, instructed the other with divine words, loved the other more and himself less.

The wise man answered him with rebuke: “But why, brother, do you complain that I do not come to you, when everything I can do displeases you? Your impatience shows that I harm you rather than help you. But the gentleness of the other—who finds good in what I know how to do—testifies that I do him no harm but give him help. It is therefore not without reason that I leave you, whom I harm, and go to him whom, [Col. 1446B] as he himself testifies with rejoicing, I believe I help.”

Pierced by these remedies of the skilled physician, the brother threw himself at his feet, begged forgiveness, and confessed his fault. Having obtained forgiveness without difficulty, he was afterward corrected. See how shrewdly the outstanding shepherd knew how to snatch straying or lost sheep from the jaws of wolves.

142. Let us also add to this account what we have judged should by no means be passed over in silence. A servant was employed in the service of the man of God and of the brothers, who, in order to eat, stole provisions, as often happens with such persons. When the brothers discovered this, they placed the food under lock and key. But since the lock could not restrain the servant’s grasping hands, the brothers reported the matter [Col. 1446C] to the most holy Father.

Greatly angered at them, the man of God said: “What have you done, not brothers but fratricides? Why have you, merciless murderers, driven into this pit of ruin a man whom you ought to have loved as yourselves? You—yes, you—have done this. You forced a hungry brother to steal, when you locked up bread under a bolt lest he take it—he to whom Christ, the bread of life, never denied himself. You are guilty and answerable for this harm, unless you quickly repent.”

Hearing this, the brothers, fearful and terrified, prostrated themselves upon the ground, asked forgiveness, and begged the holy man to tell them what they should do. After first pouring out prayers to the Lord for them, he said: “Go, remove all the locks, and freely allow the brother to take food for himself. Persuade him to take as much as he wishes. [Col. 1446D] With charity coming to aid, I see this as the sole remedy for both your evil and his.” O wisdom not human but divine; not earthly but heavenly; not from man but from God; not from the world but from heaven.

> [Note: Col. 1445D. There followed a Prayer to Blessed Bernard, composed in the manner of a rhythm or sequence, such as used to be recited in sacred worship. Since it is printed by Souchet, it is omitted here for the sake of brevity.]

## Little Book of Twelve Questions

Prologue. 1177  
Summary of the twelve questions. 1177  
Chapter I.—First question: That God the Father made all things at once in the Son, and that this sensible world is a shadow of that archetype. 1178  
Chapter II.—Second question: That the universe is arranged in the manner of a cithara, in which diverse kinds of things harmonize like strings. 1179  
Chapter III.—Third question: That, just as no kind was created for another but for itself, so man was created not for an apostate angel but for himself; and therefore, if no angel had fallen, man would nevertheless have had his place in the universe. 1179  
Chapter IV.—Fourth question: That elect human beings are taken up into heaven not in place of apostate angels but for their own sake; while reprobate angels or human beings, as discordant strings, are assigned a fitting place within the harmony. 1180  
Chapter V.—Fifth question: That some from each order of angels fell; that elect persons are to be joined to the angels who remained standing according to their merits; and likewise that the reprobate are to be added, according to their merits, to each order of the fallen. 1180  
Chapter VI.—Sixth question: That the choir of apostles is to be associated with the seraphim, and therefore Peter is superior in heaven to Michael, whom Christ, God and man, made prince of the Church, and to whom Rome, the head of the world, granted primacy. 1181  
Chapter VII.—Seventh question: That man is worthier than an angel, but an angel happier than man, because angels worship the God-man, not human beings an angel. 1182  
Chapter VIII.—Eighth question: That there are nine orders of the righteous in the Church according to the nine orders of angels. 1182  
Chapter IX.—Ninth question: That God, souls, and angels have no bodies, like justice and wisdom, and are seen only by the mind. 1182  
Chapter X.—Tenth question: That bodily things are discerned by bodily sight, images by spirit, and acts of will by understanding. 1183  
Chapter XI.—Eleventh question: That angels have ethereal bodies, demons aerial bodies, and humans earthly bodies. 1183  
Chapter XII.—Twelfth question: That the form of the body adheres to souls stripped of the body, and that after his resurrection the Lord displayed his own body as he wished. Objections against the foregoing statements are to be resolved. 1183

## The Supreme Glory Concerning the Apostle and the Emperor

Prologue. 1257

CHAPTER I.—The state of the question is set forth: whether the priesthood precedes kingship, or kingship the priesthood, in right and dignity. From the figure of Abel and Cain, and of their descendants, it is shown that the priesthood excels kingship. 1258

CHAPTER II.—The same is proved from the sons of Noah and from Abraham; and it is inferred that the king is subject to the supreme pontiff in divine matters, and the pontiff to the king in secular matters. 1260

CHAPTER III.—How great was the honor accorded to the priesthood among the Israelites, their kings, and even the Gentiles. 1262

[Col. 1469]

CHAPTER IV.—As the soul is more worthy than the body, so the priesthood is more worthy than kingship, which is rightly ordered by it. 1263

CHAPTER V.—Christ Himself preferred the priesthood to kingship, although both in His own person and through His apostles He taught that honor ought to be rendered to kings in secular affairs. 1265

CHAPTER VI.—Kings who do not obey the Roman See are indeed to be tolerated patiently, but their communion must be avoided; nor does it belong to them to confer ecclesiastical dignities, but secular ones. 1267

CHAPTER VII.—Whence has the evil custom arisen that ecclesiastical dignities are conferred by princes? 1268

CHAPTER VIII.—An answer is made to the objection drawn from the anointing of kings, and it is concluded that, both in the Old and in the New Testament, the priesthood has always preceded kingship. 1270
